en: Now begins the section on vowel sandhi (a-sandhi).
(41) *iko yaṇ aci* | Pāṇini 6.1.77. When a vowel follows, the *ik* vowels (*i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*) are replaced by their corresponding *yaṇ* semivowels (*y*, *v*, *r*, *l*).

*iko yaṇ aci*. In the case of references to *pratyāhāras*, there is a conventional (*nirūḍha*) secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) directed toward that which is denoted by the *pratyāhāra*; this is established by the indications in the rules *ṭhyūstryākhyau* and *vādibhyaḥ*. Therefore, by the word *ik*, sixty-six [sounds] are included, and by the word *yaṇ*, four; as is the case with an *aṇ* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*).

Because [the substitute] does not include its own homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). And thus, in this case, when there is a *yaṇ* [substitution], one should not even suspect a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for that which is denoted by it;

for since a *aṇ* that is being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its own homogeneous counterparts, there is an absence of those things denoted by the *yakāra* and so forth which are themselves denoted by the *yaṇ*. Therefore, there is no correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṅkhya*). Not so.
Nor should it be argued that, by taking the knowledge of the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) which precedes the comprehension of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*),

the correspondence [of the vowels] with the consonants may be established according to their respective order; for even so, since the third and fourth vowels, *ṛ* and *ḷ*, would each bring about the presentation of thirty [consonants], [the desired result would not follow].
Because there would arise the undesirable consequence of substituting *r* for the vowels *ṛ* and *ḷ*, and substituting *l* for the vowels *a* and *ā*.

Therefore, he will state immediately below that the desired result is achieved here by the rule "the most similar [substitute] in place" (*sthāne ’ntaratamaḥ*) alone: "due to proximity in terms of place of articulation" (*sthānata āntaryāt*). Regarding the word *aci*: "[when] a vowel (*ac*) follows this."
In response to this inquiry, the phrase "such as meaning" (*arthādika*) is connected [to the rule]. Regarding the term "subject matter" (*viṣaya*) in the *saṃhitā* [context]:

the sense is that the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs only when an excessive proximity (*atiśayita-saṃnidhi*) between the element undergoing the operation (*kāryin*) and its cause (*nimitta*) is intended, as in the case of "adhyatre" and so forth.

(42) *anaci ca* | Pāṇini 8.4.47. Regarding *anaci ca*: the phrase *yaro dve vā* [from 8.4.46] is understood here; from the rule *yaro ’nunāsike*, *yaraḥ* and *ve* are carried over (*anuvartate*). From the rule *aco rahābhyām*, *ayaḥ* and *dve* are also carried over. Thus he says: *acaḥ*.

"Of another," and so forth. The point is that since the desired result is established here by the continued application of the option (*vā*) alone, the three rules—"in *ri* and so forth, according to Śākaṭāyana," "in all cases, according to Śākalya," and "after a long vowel, according to the Teachers"—need not have been formulated. [This applies] to the vowel (*ac*).

Why? [So that] there would not be the doubling of *m* in examples such as *ādātmyam*. If the rule *ṭh-a-na-c-i* were a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), then, according to the maxim "that which is joined with a negation refers to something other than that, and the meaning is understood in a similar way," the meaning would be "in a consonant (*hal*) other than a vowel (*ac*)," namely, in a consonant dissimilar to a vowel. Consequently...

One should say "balī" [instead of "bali"] for the sake of brevity; therefore, he states that this is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) by saying "but not in the case of *ac*" (*na tvacīti*).
And thus, even at the end of a word, doubling occurs: *vāk*, *vāk*.
(43) A substitute (*ādeśa*) is like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), except in the case of an operation concerning a phoneme (*al-vidhi*). Pāṇini 1.1.56.

*sthānivadādeśaḥ*: When a substitute (*ādeśa*) has been applied, because its form differs from that of the original (*sthānin*), the operations conditioned by the original would not otherwise take place; therefore, this rule of extension (*atideśa*) is commenced. [For example: *ṭhasterbhūḥ*. When an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is intended to follow, a substitute for a verbal root (*dhātu*) is treated like the original root. By this [rule],...

The suffixes for verbal roots, such as *ṭhak* and *ya*, have become applicable. [By the rule] *imaḥ kaḥ*, the substitute (*ādeśa*) is treated like the original base (*aṅga*). Therefore, the properties of lengthening, shortening, and so forth apply to the substitutes of *in*. [Examples: *kena*, *kābhyām*, *kaiḥ*. Why is the mention of "substitute" (*ādeśa-grahaṇa*) necessary? Is it not sufficient simply to say "as if it were the original" (*sthānivat*)?

If it is argued that this [meaning] is obtained through the power of correlative terms—just as when it is said, "he studies like an *itara*," it is understood that he is an *uttra*—to this they reply: an *ādeśa* (substitute) is of two kinds, namely, direct (*pratyakṣa*) and inferential (*ānumānika*). The rule "for *sthā*, *bhū*" and so forth is direct; [the rule] "*astuḥ*" [is inferential].

The phrase "ityādi" (and so forth) refers to inference (*ānumānika*). For in the rule *theruḥ*, by means of the vowel *i* [in the term *thiri*], a substitute (*sthānin*) ending in *ī* is inferred, and by means of the vowel *u* [in the term *uru*], a substitute (*ādeśa*) ending in *ū* is inferred. Thus, the resulting meaning is "let there be *ū*. In that context, if the mention of the substitute (*ādeśagrahaṇa*) were not present, only the perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) would be grasped.

It might be argued that this applies only to what is inferential (anumānika). However, by the force of the inclusion of the term "ādeśa" (substitute), both [the original and the substitute] are encompassed;

thus, the designation *pada* is established for forms such as *pacatu*, because they are *tiṅ*-endings. Now, one might object: let rules such as *ṭheryuḥ* remain exactly as they are heard in the text; since that which is modified in one part is not different from the original, the status of being a *pada* will still obtain.

If it is argued that this is not so, we reply: no, because the application of "in place of" (*sthāne*) and so forth rests solely upon that which possesses meaning, and it is precisely such [meaningful] entities that are subject to the present discussion. For it has been stated: "The genitive case [is used] in connection with 'in place of' (*sthāne*).

And "place" (*sthāna*) is the occasion for application (*prasaṅga*). And that [occasion] belongs only to that which possesses meaning, since a word is employed for the purpose of conveying meaning. Even if...

This [substitution] is impossible in the case of *cli* followed by *sij* and so on; nevertheless, it is precisely by this mention of "substitute" (*ādeśa*) that it is signaled: when a possibility exists, the application must be understood as being driven solely by the meaning. And it has been said:
"For Pāṇini, the son of Dākṣī, all substitutes are substitutes for entire words; for when there is a modification of only one part, there is no permanence [of the original form]."

The word *nopapadyate* (“is not possible”) is meaningful here, based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that it is “that by which one proceeds” (*padyate ’nena*). Although the impossibility of permanence is even more extreme in the case of every modification (*vikāra*), the intended meaning here is simply that no modification exists at all. This is clear in the *Śabdakaustubha*. [This applies] in the rule *analvidhau*.

What [is meant]? Let it not apply where there is a rule concerning an *al* (vowel), a rule concerning an *al* that belongs to another, a rule concerning an *al*, or a rule concerning an *ali* (consonant). Among these, as an example for a rule concerning an *al*: *vyūḍhoraskena*.

Here, by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) of the *s*, one might assume it possesses the property of being an *aṭ* (vowel), and thus [apply] the rule *ṭhaḍvyavāye*.
The state of being *al* has been established. An example for [an operation] following what is *al*: *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*.

Here, the elision (*lopa*) by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* does not apply. An example for an operation prescribed with reference to what is *al*: *dyaukāmaḥ*. The elision by the rule *lopo vyor vali* does not occur. Nor can it be argued that the elision does not take place due to the force of the prescription of the substitution of *u*.
This is to be doubted; for that [rule] has its scope in cases such as *yauyānam*. Regarding the rule for the suffix *ali*:

the suffix *kta* is applied after the root *yaj*, resulting in *iṣṭaḥ*. By the rule *haśi ca*, the substitution of *u* (utvam) does not occur. Nor is there [an objection] here on the grounds that even if the substitution of *u* were to occur by virtue of the principle of "acting like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), and subsequently the *guṇa* substitution (*ādguṇa*) and the *av* replacement (*avādeśa*) were performed, [the form would still be valid] in the presence of a consonant (*hali*).

It should not be argued that the form *aiṣṭa* is established by the constant elision of *sarveṣām* [in Pāṇini 8.3.12], because this would entail the impossibility of establishing the alternative form *ayiṣṭa*. According to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however,
since the elision of *ya* is optional by the rule *hobhagoaghoapūrvasya*, both *aiṣṭa* and *ayiṣṭa* are established.
Thus, two forms are accepted. Here, however, it is sufficient that only the constituent part of the substituend (*sthānin*) is taken;
by this, the lengthening [of the vowel] in *āmāya* and so forth is established by the rule *upi ca*.

For in the formulation of that rule, the status of being preceded by *yañ* and so forth is relied upon, and *yañ* is a constituent part of the substitute (*ādeśa*), not a constituent part of the substituend. Likewise...

In examples such as *aruditām*, the augment *iṭ*—characterized by the rule *rudādibhyaḥ*—is also established; this is what is meant by the statement that [the operation] does not depend on the original *al* (the substitute). Here, "dependence" (*āśrayaṇa*) means in whatever manner possible, and there is no insistence that it must be through predominance alone. Therefore, in the case of *rapaṭhiṭe*, the augment *iṭ* characterized by the rule *valādi* does not apply.
(44) *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* | 1.1.57 | Regarding *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau*: what is the purpose of *acaḥ*? [Example: *āgatya*.

In this case, when *tuk* is to be applied, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*)—by the rule *vā lyapi*—is not *sthānivadbhūta* with respect to the subsequent element. This is because [the elision] occurs in relation to a subsequent element.

What [is the example]? *ādīdhye*. Because it is eternal (*nitya*), the augment *iṭ* is applied, and the substitution of *e* for *i* occurs; furthermore, that substitution is not caused by what follows. Therefore, when the elision of *y* and *v* (by P. 6.1.66, *ṭhyīvarṇayorlopaḥ*) is to be performed, that [substitution] is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Why [is the condition] "in the case of a rule concerning what precedes" (*pūrvavidhau*) stated? [Consider] *naidheyaḥ*. From the root *dhā* preceded by *ni*, [the suffix] *ki* is applied by [P. 3.3.92,] *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*.

The suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rules “*ṭhāto lopaḥ*,” “*vyacaḥ*,” and “*itaścāniñaḥ*. However, if the status of the *ākāra* were treated as *sthānivadbhāva*, then its designation as having three vowels (*tryactva*) would sublate its designation as having two vowels (*dvyactva*), because the two are contradictory.
For one who has three sons does not receive the designation of being a man with two sons. [Objection: Even so, what is the purpose of including the word “*vidhi*” (prescription) in the rule?

If it is argued that [the mention of] *vidhi* is redundant because the meaning—that "in place of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*)—can be understood as "when an operation (*kārya*) is to be performed"—we say no; for the term *vidhi* is included in order to obtain two possible compounds: *pūrvasya vidhiḥ* (an operation of the preceding) and *pūrvasmād vidhiḥ* (an operation from the preceding). Even though the alternative of a fifth-case compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*) is mentioned here in the root text...

Although it was not explicitly stated, nevertheless, under the view that "there is the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva) even for what precedes a rule," the substitution of *ṇ* in this instance occurs by the rule "ṭhaḍvyavāye" alone; this has been accepted in the section beginning with "addan. This [present sūtra] is for the purpose of a rule concerning vowels (*alvidhi*). Consequently, in the rule "vavraśca," there is no vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the *v*.

Because the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uradatva*) is treated as a *saṃprasāraṇa* by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, it is prohibited by the rule "there is no [substitution] when a *saṃprasāraṇa* follows" (*na saṃprasāraṇe*). Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* does not have a subsequent element as its cause; for that substitution is prescribed when a suffix—implied by the term "stem" (*aṅga*)—follows. The expression "a rule prior to another" (*pūrvavidhiḥ*) means a rule preceding [the one under consideration].

However, the purpose of the *pañcamī-samāsa* (genitive compound) alternative is as follows: [in the forms] *tanvanti* and *tanvate*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur because of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the *yaṇ*-substitution. For here, it is established that "the *aṅga* is non-eternal," and that [non-eternality] occurs prior to the original element (*sthānin*), which is the vowel *u*. Now, one might object: this is not a valid purpose.

Since the *yaṇ* substitution is *asiddha* (non-existent) from the perspective of the external operation, the augment *iṭ* does not apply here. Nor does the prohibition "not when there is immediate sequence of vowels" (*nājānantarye*) apply; for according to the view of Haradatta and others—that the prohibition operates even when there is immediate sequence of vowels whether in an internal or external context—the subsequent operation [is what is affected].
In Kaiyaṭa’s opinion, where immediate contiguity (*ānantarya*) is relied upon, there is no assumption of externality (*bahiṣṭva*);

therefore, that [assumption] is absent here. Nor does this preclude *apīpacan* from being a valid example; for in this case, after the single-substitute *pararūpa* (the form *i*) has been applied to the *a* of *anta* and the *caṅ*-affix *a* by the rule "guṇa is substituted for the final vowel and the following semi-vowel" (*ato guṇe*), and of that...

Since the suffix *jhi* is included by the mention of *jhi* due to its status as being like the following element (*parādivadbhāva*), the substitution *jus* would apply according to the rule "ij-abhyasta-".

It must be stated that this does not occur because of the status of the substitute as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) in the case of either the elision of the *ṇi*-affix or the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). For indeed, in the case of the root *vī*, the suffix *jhi* can only occur immediately after it in the *laṭ* (present tense).

Because of its association with that [laṅ], even though it has been practiced [in other contexts], only the *laṅ* is intended here, since the substitution of *jus* for *jhi* is prescribed [specifically for it]. Nor should one suspect that, due to association with *sic*, only the *luṅ* should be understood; for, according to the rule "in case of conflict, the subsequent [rule prevails]," association with the subsequent [term] is stronger. And this being so...

It should not be argued that the *pañcamī-samāsa* (genitive compound) alternative is necessary in order to prevent the substitution of *ad* for *at* [by P. 7.3.101], because once the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) operation has been applied by P. 6.1.97 (*ato guṇe*)—due to the *caṅ* prefix and the vowel *a* of *antaḥ*—the substitute *ad* would not apply due to the absence of *jha*. However, in this case, [the issue concerns] the single-substitute operation.
Due to the status of being "like the latter" (*parādivadbhāva*), there is no inclusion [of the sound *jha*] by the mention of *jh*;

for in a rule concerning phonemes (*alvidhi*), the status of being "like the end or the beginning" (*antādivadbhāva*) does not apply. Otherwise, in cases such as *ṭhayaje indram*, the long vowel resulting from homogeneous merger (*savarṇadīrgha*) would indeed be unavoidable. Or, even if the status of being "like the latter" were to apply, nevertheless, regarding the sound *jha*:

If it is argued that when the substitution *at* for *ad* is to be applied, the substitution of the final letter (*antādeśa*) is not *sthānivadbhūta* because it is not a rule concerning vowels (*alvidhi*), and therefore the view of the genitive compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*) is indeed purposeless— on this point they say: [it serves as] an illustration for the rule *arītaścann*, by way of being the purpose of the genitive compound.

For the Blessed One (Pāṇini), however, co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) is not accepted here as a restrictive factor. This is because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *vitricatur-*, where the mention of the sense of frequency (*kṛtvo'rtha*) shows that co-occurrence is not to be relied upon in all cases. And thus, in the case of *bhū* with the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*), since the suffix *jus* applies by virtue of its dependence on the reduplicated form (*abhyasta*), we have "abhobhūvuḥ."

The form *rūpam* is established because Mādhava and others have explained that the rule *ṭhātaḥ* applies specifically to cases where the *jus* is obtained by relying on the suffix *sic* following [the root] *sthā*. For this very reason, it is stated in the root-text (*mūla*) that "the *jus* is based on the reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*); because it is obligatory (*nitya*), there is *buk*: *abobhūvuḥ*."

It is stated in the *Yaṅluṅnta* [section] that, likewise, for the sake of establishing forms such as *apīpacan*, one must resort to the alternative of a genitive compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*). However, others say: since the examples *ebhiditāḥ* and *āthitikaḥ* are also cited in the *Bhāṣya* as the purpose for the genitive compound alternative, that [alternative] is not [the intended one].
One should not entertain the suspicion of futility; for even though, without the application of *sthānivadbhāva* to the elision of the vowel *a* in the *yaṅ* suffix,
the prohibition of *iṭ* would not apply because of the adoption of the "prescribed" (*vihita*) as a qualifier in the rule *ekāca upadeśe ’nudātāt*.
Although the form *bhebiditṛ*— derived from the causative (*yaṅnta*) of the root *bhid* with the suffix *tṛc*— is easily established,

that alternative must nevertheless be accepted for the sake of deriving forms such as *āthitika*. Furthermore, in the case of *māthitika*, meaning "one whose merchandise is *mathita*," the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *adasya paṇyam*, and the substitution of *ik* occurs.

Since the elision [of the *i*] occurs by the rule "kṛte ṭhyasyeti ca," the substitution of *ya* for the *ik* vowel— which would otherwise apply by the rule "ṭhisusuktāntāt"— is easily resolved even without the status of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original).
This is because, in the rule "hasyekaḥ," the vowel *a* in both the original (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is merely for the sake of pronunciation.

If this is accepted, since the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) would not apply because the rule is not prescribed by an *al*-affix, the substitution of *ik* in place of *th* would not occur; consequently, the substitution of *kā* would not even arise, and the form *māthitika* would be established [without further effort]. Therefore, one might ask: what is the purpose of resorting to this position of the compound with the fifth case (*pañcamī-samāsa*)? [The answer is: consider the derivation of *mathitayati* followed by *kvip*.

Because of the elision of *ṭi*, the elision of *ani*, and the elision of the *apṛkta* *v*— as in *mathit*, and consequently in *māthitika* (one who travels by means of that)— the position [of the elided *v*] is necessary to establish the single-substitute (*ikādeśa*) for the suffix *ṭhak* in the sense of "he travels" (*caratīti*).
For in this case, even without the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is no substitution of *ka* as an exception to the substitution of *ik*.
It is easily refuted; nor should it be suspected that there is a lack of evidence for such a conceptualization, because the example from the Bhāṣya, "āthitika," itself serves as the proof.
It might be argued: since priority (pūrvatva) requires a limit, it is appropriate that the limit be something proximate.

And here three factors are present: the original element (*sthānin*), the substitute (*ādeśa*), and the cause (*nimitta*). Among these, first of all, the original element is not the limit (*avadhi*), because it is superseded by the substitute. Nor is it the cause of the substitute; for otherwise, in the case of *vaiyākaraṇa*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *ay* for the vowel *e*. Anticipating this objection, he says: *acaḥ* (P. 1.1.57).
Regarding the phrase "of that which was seen as prior": the sense is that "prior-ness" (pūrvatva) is a secondary characteristic (upalakṣaṇa), not a defining qualifier (viśeṣaṇa).

(45) [The term *sthānin*] does not denote that which is replaced in the rules concerning: the end of a word (*padānta*), doubling (*dvirvacana*), the suffix *vareya*, elision (*lopa*), vowels (*svara*), homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), the nasal *anusvāra*, lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the substitution of *jaś* and *car* sounds.
Pāṇini 1.1.58.

"Not at the end of a word" (*na padānta*). This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "end of a word" (*padānta*) and so forth, up to "semivowels" (*caranta*). This is then compounded with the word *vidhi* in a genitive relationship, as in "the rule for [those ending in] *ṭh*" (*ṭhvidhi*). The word *vidhi* is derived in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*), meaning "the act of prescribing" (*vidhānam vidhiḥ*). Because it is heard at the end of the *dvandva*, it is connected to each member individually. [This applies to] the word "word" (*pada*).

Regarding the term *caramāvayava* (the final element): one who knows a tree is *vṛkṣavīḥ*; one who blows upon a tree is *vṛkṣavāḥ*. To cause him to speak [thus] is *vṛkṣavayati*. From this, the suffix *vic* is applied, resulting in *vṛkṣav*.

Here, the elision of *v* by the rule *opo vyor vali* does not occur, because of the status of the original position (*sthānivadbhāva*) of either the elision of the *ṭi* suffix or the elision of the *ṇi* suffix.

Nor should one suspect that, according to the view of Haradatta and others—based on the rule *ub-antāṇ-ṇ-iC*—the prohibition *na padānte* would apply because the word-status (*padatva*) arises from the *sup* suffix contained within; for the elision (*lopa*) which is the prescribed operation is not a constituent part of the word.
However, if the rule is explained as "in a substitution for what ends in *a*, [the *ṇatva*] does not occur," then the prohibition *na padānte* [would indeed apply].

It is established in the *Manoramā* that because the status of being "as if occupying the original place" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited, the elision of the semivowel (*yalopa*) must indeed occur, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "and in the case of reduplication, etc.": the word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to the elision of *ya* (*yalopa*) and other such operations. However, the rule "in the case of *vare*" (*vare*) should be interpreted to mean: "that substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśa*) which occurs in the context of *vare* is not like the original. This remains so even in the absence of a desire to express [the two elements] together (*sahavivakṣā*).
This is a *dvandva* compound by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), with the elision of the locative case ending (*saptamī-aluk*).

Now, the examples: at the end of a word, *kāni santi* (what are they? and *kau staḥ* (who are they?). Here, when the *yaṇ* and *av* substitutions are to be applied, the elision of the *a* of *śna* and *as* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Nor is this the case for the substitution of the phonemes *i* and *u*.

It should not be argued that the elision of *al* (allopa) is not "as if having its original position" (*na sthānivat*) simply because it lacks the status of being prior to the vowel that serves as the original locus (*sthānin*); rather, the example to be cited is [the elision of *y*] in the word *vākya*. For in this case, the vowel *o* is indeed seen as preceding the vowel *u*, which is the original locus (*sthānin*).

In the case of reduplication, [the form] *śuddhyupāsyaḥ* [is derived]. Because of the prohibition "when there is immediate succession with a vowel" (*ājānantarye*), the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* does not apply here;
this is also due to the force of the prohibition regarding the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Thus, it should be inferred in other cases as well.
*vare-yāyāvaraḥ*: From the root *yā* with the intensive (*yaṅ*) suffix, [the suffix] *varac* is applied by the rule *yaśca yaṅ*. By the rule *ato lopaḥ*, the final *a* is elided.
And that [elision of *a*] is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* when the elision of *ā* is to be performed by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*.
Regarding the elision of *y*: from the root *yā* with the intensive suffix, [the suffix] *ktic* is added; then there is the elision of *a* (*ato lopaḥ*), followed by the elision of *y* (*yalopaḥ*).

Due to the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) of the elision (*allopasya*), there is the elision of the long vowel *ā* (*āto lopaḥ*). Then follows the elision of *y* (*yalopaḥ*). Furthermore, one should not suspect a recurrence of the elision of *ā*, because the elision of *ā* is as good as non-existent (*asiddhatva*) according to the maxim regarding the *ciṇ* suffix in the *luṅ* tense, and because of the *sthānivadbhāva*. [Objection: But if, with respect to the rule for the elision of *y*...
If that is so, how is the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* [to be applied] in the case of *vāyvoh*? It is said:

because the *yaṇ* [substitution] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is non-existent," there is no elision of the *y*. Nor does the prohibition "when there is immediate succession of vowels (*ājānantarye*)" apply here, because that prohibition is accepted only in cases where there is immediate succession of a vowel (*ac*) within an internal operation (*antaraṅgakārya*).

Furthermore, there is a Vārttika on this point which states: "In the case of *vṛddhi*, lengthening, and the elision of *y*, that which is a substitute for an elided element (*lopājādeśa*) alone is not treated as *sthānivat*. By this rule, any other [substitute] is indeed treated as *sthānivat*, so there is no fault.

Regarding accent (*svara*): in the word *cikīrṣakaḥ*, when the acute accent (*udātta*) is to be applied to the vowel *ī* by the rule "the *i* of *san* [is acute]," [the substitution of *at* for *an* of *san* is not *sthānivat*].

The elision (*lopa*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Nor can it be argued that the rule beginning with "iti" (P. 1.1.56) is purposeless, for it finds its scope of application in forms such as *āraka*. Regarding the elision of *a* in the case of *śna* and *as* before *śi* and *ḍhi*:
*śiṇḍḍhi*. This elision of *a* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Even though the anusvāra is not [substituted] for the original vowel (*sthānin*), [the rule still applies].

Regarding the word *pūrva*, they say that although there is no possibility of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) of the elision of *al* (*al-lopa`) when a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) is to be applied, nevertheless, since an anusvāra is also seen [to occur] by way of *sthānivadbhāva*, the possibility of that [application] certainly exists. Now, one might object: "Is it not possible to imply the anusvāra as well merely by the mention of 'homogeneous sound' (*savarṇa*)?"

What is the purpose of this separate mention of *anusvāra*? True. In the absence of a separate mention, one might suspect that [the rule applies] only where there is a possibility of *parasavarṇa*. Consequently, in cases such as *iṣantī*, where there is no occasion for *parasavarṇa*, the mention of *anusvāra* is intended to prohibit the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original substitute).

Thus, it should be understood that in cases such as *yāti*, where there is no possibility for the substitution of *aja* (a vowel) before a *var* (vowel), the separate mention of *yalopa* (the elision of *ya*)—distinct from the mention of *var*—is made in order to prohibit the application of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element) when *ya* is elided. Regarding the long vowel: *pratidīvna*, *pratidīvne*. [This is governed by] the rule *hali ca*.

When a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is to be applied, the elision (*allopa*) is not *sthānivat*; however, the substitution of *yaṇ* remains *sthānivat*. This is because it has been stated that "only the elision of *a* (*akāralopa*) is not *sthānivat*. Consequently, since the rule for lengthening (*dīrgha*)—namely, *hali ca* and *upadhāyāṃ ca*—does not apply, we have *kiryau* and *giryau*.
The forms beginning with *vivyatuḥ* are established. Regarding *jaśi-sagdhiśca me*: *gdhi* means eating (*adana*).

In that context, from the root *ad-* with the suffix *ktin*, there is the substitution of *ghas* by the rule “*bahulam chandasi*” (variously in Vedic). Then, by the rule “*hasibhasor hali ca*,” there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*).
By the rule “*halo jhali*,” there is the elision of the *s*. [And finally,] by the rule “*haṣastathoḥ*... [the substitution of *dha* occurs].

The status of being a *dhātu* (verbal root). When the *jaś*-substitution [of *dha*] is to be applied by the rule "halāṃ jaśjhaśī," the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) is not *sthānivadbhūta*. By the rule "amānasya chandasyamūrdhaprabhṛtyudarkaṣu," the *sa*-substitution occurs.
Thus, *samānā gdhiḥ* becomes *sagdhiḥ*. Nor does the rule "pūrvasmād api" apply here when the elision of *sa* and the *dhātva* are to be performed.
One should not suspect that the form *sagdhiḥ* would be impossible due to the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element);

for the rule regarding the compound with the fifth case (*pañcamī-samāsa*) is non-mandatory (*anitya*). This is indicated by the evidence in the rule *iṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi*. To explain: in that context, the word *seṭi* does not [apply].

This is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *aniṭ* (the absence of the *iṭ* augment) in the case of the causative (*ṇijanta*), because such an absence is impossible there. If it is argued: "In the example 'aṃjñāpitaḥ paśuḥ' (the animal was signaled), since the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule 'yasya vibhāṣā' applies, the status of being *aniṭ* is indeed possible, because the *iṭ* is optional according to the rule 'anīvantardha...'";
we say no. This is because in the rule 'yasya vibhāṣā',...
This is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ṭhekācaḥ*. Otherwise, in the case of *aridriti*, the augment *iṭ* would not occur;
for in that instance, by the Vārttika "after *ani*, *pat*, and *daridrā*", the *iṭ* is optional (*vikalpita*) for the suffix *san*.

Therefore, the mention of *seṭ* (the root with *iṭ*) is for the purpose of determining the time [of the operation]. Once *iṭ* has been applied, there is the elision of the *ṇi* suffix, but not otherwise.

Regarding the phrase "tataḥ prāk" (before that): otherwise, in cases such as *ārita*, once the *ṇi*-suffix has been elided, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "ekāca upadeśe" would apply. However, if there were *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) with respect to a preceding operation, then the prohibition would not apply because of the intervention of the *ṇic* suffix. Therefore—
In the word *aṭayat*, because it possesses the status of a *pada* by virtue of the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*), the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stops) would apply.

This is not so; for by the designation *bha* in the rule *tiṣṭhava* (Pāṇini 1.4.17), the designation *pada* is sublated, and thus the application of *jaś*-substitution does not occur. [Examples: *car-i-atus*, *car-i-us* (from the root *car*); *jakṣ-atuḥ*, *jakṣ-uḥ* (from the root *ghas* in the perfect tense, with the suffixes *atus* and *us*).

And: in *amahanat*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). According to the rule *hari ca*, this [elision] is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* with respect to the substitution of *c* for *t*. However, in the Bhāṣya, relying on the principle that "when a preceding operation is *asiddha*, the subsequent is not *sthānivadbhūta*," the rules concerning reduplication, homogeneous vowels, *anusvāra*, long vowels, and the substitution of *c* for *t* have been rejected. According to that method, however:
It should be understood that when the substitution of *dha* for *tha* is to be applied, there is no possibility at all of regarding it as *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original).
(46) *adarśanaṃ lopaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.1.60: Non-appearance is termed *lopa* (elision).

"Non-perception (*adarśana*) means elision (*lopa*). Here, the root *dṛś* denotes cognition in general; "perception" (*darśana*) is cognition. In this context, because the subject under discussion is the instruction of grammar, it results in perception pertaining to words, which is to say, hearing. That [hearing] is the activity of the listener; its negation is non-hearing. Now, if this is so, [the rule] "elision... [applies].

In rules such as *vyorvali*, if it were said that the sounds *v* and *y* are not to be heard, then only the activity of the listener would be prohibited, while the activity of the speaker—the act of utterance—would remain unprohibited. Regarding this, they say:
since utterance would be purposeless in the absence of hearing, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), the prohibition applies to hearing.
The utterance that serves as the cause for that [substitution] is also prohibited. Regarding the phrase "of that which is applicable" (*prasaktasya*):

here, because the word "in place of" (*sthāne*) is understood by context, this meaning is obtained. Why is it said "of that which is applicable"? [So that] in examples such as *dadhi* and *madhu*, the augment *tuk* does not occur; for in those cases, there is indeed the non-appearance (*adarśana*) of the suffix *kvip*.

And since that [suffix] is characterized by elision (*lopa*), in the absence of the qualifier "that which is about to occur," the *tuk* augment would indeed apply by virtue of the rule for suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); this is the general direction. (47) *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.2.23. "There is elision of a word-final conjunct."

The phrase "of that which ends in a conjunct" (saṃyogāntasya) means "of that which has it [the conjunct] at its end" (tadantasya), according to the technical rule (paribhāṣā) "of the final [element]" (alo’ntyasya).

Although it would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as "of a conjunct" (saṃyogasya) since the extension to "ending in that" (tadantavidhi) is obtained through the qualifying term, nevertheless, this is done in view of the position that "each individual [consonant] constitutes the designation 'conjunct'."

In the *Manoramā*, it is established that the inclusion of the word *anta* (end) in the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.7] is for the purpose of obtaining a compound with a dual ending— namely, "that which has a *saṃyoga* at its end"— in order to prevent the elision [of the penultimate vowel] in examples such as *ṛṣṭatkaroṭi*.
Furthermore, by virtue of the employment of the technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*) "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), a single [consonant] does not receive the designation of *saṃyoga*.

The apprehension of an extreme view—that [the rule] will apply—can be abandoned here. The phrase "a prohibition regarding *yaṇ*" is based on an explicit statement (*vācanika*). Alternatively, it must be explained through interpretation (*vācya-vyākhyeya*).
And that interpretation is twofold: by carrying forward (*apakṛṣya*) the mention of *jhal* from the rule *halo jhali*, [it applies] only to a *jhal*.
Either it is because elision (*lopa*) is prescribed [as a subsequent operation], such that when the internal *lopa* is to be applied,

the external *yaṇ*-substitution is considered non-existent (*asiddha*); or else, one should not say that the Paribhāṣā of the sixth book does not perceive the internal *lopa* belonging to the third book (*traipādika*).

Because the position that [grammatical operations apply] at the time the effect is to be produced (*kāryakālapakṣa*) is accepted. Nor is there a prohibition by the rule *ājānantarye*, because when the elision (*lopa*) applies at a later time, there is no immediate sequence (*ājānantarya*) with the vowel *a*.
As it has been said: "There is a prohibition of the elision of the final consonant of a *saṃyoga* [cluster] when it follows a *yaṇ*," or "Or rather, [it applies] after a *jhal*..."
"Because of elision, or because it is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*).

Regarding the four forms: here, when the doubling of the letter *dh* has been performed and the substitution of the *jaś*-sound [j] has also been applied, since the rule "that which is previously established is not subject to the rules for doubling" does not apply to the *jaś*-substitution, [the form is derived accordingly].
Furthermore, due to the distinction in the target of the rule (*lakṣya-bheda*), when doubling occurs for the letter *d*, there is an increase in the number of forms.

Regarding this, some say: "When doubling has already occurred for a *yara* following the *ṭhuk* [the *ṭhakāra*], doubling does not occur again for a *yara* following the *ukāra*, because the causal condition (*nimitta*) no longer exists. It is with this intention that this was stated.

However, regarding those [roots], the explanatory passage in the root text (*mūla*) under the rule *vavraśca*—which states that because of the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uratvam*), there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* by virtue of the principle *acaḥ parasmin* [P. 1.1.57], and thus the *utva* of *v* does not occur]—would be contradicted, since there is no difference in the *liṭ* (perfect tense) that causes it. This is the general direction [of the argument].

Others, however, maintain that once the substitution of the *jaś* sound (*j*) for the letter *dh* has been made, the doubling (*dvitva*) of the *d* occurs again because the *jaś* substitution is not considered "asiddha" (non-existent) with respect to doubling— according to the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham advitve*— since the individual phonetic instances (*vyakti*) are distinct. For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya cited examples such as *sayyantā* where doubling occurs after the substitution of the homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*).

Regarding the form *aṭṭassanta*, it has been stated even in the *Manoramā* that "the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham advitve*" [is applicable] in order to establish the doubling of the letter *s*. Likewise, there is no defect in the recurrence of doubling even for the letter *y*, because the doubling prescribed by the eighth book (*Aṣṭādhyāyī*) takes the place of [the original].

Because it consists of reduplication, and because there is a distinction between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*). As for what was stated in the *Manoramā*—namely, that "a single grammatical rule applies only once to a single individual instance"—this is because it was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ. How then...

Furthermore, the claim that "the application [of the rule] occurs repeatedly, otherwise there would be the consequence of an infinite regress of dualities," and so forth, is based on a lack of careful attention; for in that regard, by means of the scriptural example of *ādhāna* and other rites,

it has been established as a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the scriptural injunction regarding qualities and the like applies even in subsequent performances, rather than the scriptural injunction applying only once.

Furthermore, the consequence of infinity (*ānantyāpatti*) is not a fault in the present context. For that [consequence] would be a fault because the performance accompanied by infinite operations would be impossible, and because, due to the absence of any completed performance that could be the duty of the scripture, it would follow that the scripture itself fails to prompt action.

In the present case, however, this does not apply; for since duality is optional, the rule achieves its purpose through that very [duality] which is established as being accompanied by the employment of duality as long as the capacity exists. As for the duality [prescribed] by the rule "iṭi dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.8), however—

Because [the application] would otherwise result in infinity due to its constancy, and because when one must postulate a point of rest somewhere, it is simpler to postulate that rest at the very first occurrence; thus, the inclusion of the term "non-repeated" (*anabhyāsa*) has been rejected. For this very reason, the rule *sarvasya dve* (Pāṇini 8.1.1) does not apply repeatedly either.

They say it is *pravṛti*. Now, if it is argued that here there may be another form according to the opinion of Śākalya by the rule *ṭhiko’savarṇe*, we say: not so; for that [option] is prohibited in a compound. Nor should it be said that the prohibition applies only to obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*); for [the rule] states: "In the case of *in* and obligatory compounds..."
This is because the inclusion of the term *nitya* in the Vārttika "śākalapratiṣedhaḥ" was rejected in the Bhāṣya.

However, in the *Manoramā*, it is stated that there are eight forms by doubling the *s* (after the *d* has been changed to *j* by the rule *jaśtvam*), and sixteen forms by doubling the *visarga*. This is based on the intention that there is no doubling of the *d* once it has been changed to *j*.

Regarding the term *dvidham*: although there is no pair of *dh* sounds because the *jash* substitution of *dh* results in *d*, this statement is nevertheless made by relying on its former state (*bhūtapūrvagati*). In the example *sudhyupāsya*, there is a compound with the third case ending according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*. Now, one might object that even the *yaṇ* substitution is difficult to obtain here.

If it is argued that because the word *udhī* is derived from the root *dhyai* through *saṃprasāraṇa*, the rule "after a *saṃprasāraṇa*" (*aṃprasāraṇācca*) would cause the substitution of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*), we say: not so;
for the Vārttika states, "When there is a preceding *saṃprasāraṇa*, the term 'identical stem' (*samānāṅga*) must be understood [as a condition]. It is not [the case].

And even so, one should not suspect the prohibition of *yaṇ* by the rule *na bhūsudhiyoḥ*; for that prohibition operates only when a suffix (*pratyaya*) follows as an *aṅga*. Furthermore, by carrying over the word *supi*, the prohibition of *yaṇ* applies only when a *sup* suffix follows. As for *dhātraṃśaḥ*: here there is no doubling of the *repha*, because [the doubling] occurs within the section on doubling.

In the case of *ahābhyām*, because the status of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) is explicitly heard [in the rule], it subverts the status of the letter *r* as that which undergoes the operation (*kāryitva*). However, in cases such as *udhyupāsya*, the status of the vowel *i* as a cause is not subverted by its status as a substitute (*sthānitva*), according to the principle: "That which follows from this [is affected]."

This is because of the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) found in such rules as *ṭhvāyvṛtupitruṣasaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.29). However, the doubling of the letter *t* certainly occurs; and due to that [doubling], there are two forms.
(48) *nādinyākrośe putrasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.48).

By means of the *nādini* [affix]. Since verbal abuse generally occurs toward women, he cites a feminine form as an example: *putrādinī*. Here, the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule "also after a non-jāti [word]. And regarding the phrase *tatpare ca*: even when followed by that [word], namely the word *putra* which follows *ādin*, there is no [shortening] of the word *putra*.
The meaning is that there are two [forms]. Regarding "or *hata*": some say that if the doubling were optional, this *vārttika* need not have been composed;
others, however, maintain that the doubling occurs specifically for the word *putra* when followed by *hata* or *jagdha*, according to the rule *ṭhanaci ca*.
They say that this [rule] must indeed be commenced for the sake of establishing restrictions such as "not for others," and so forth.
Regarding *putrahatī*: she by whom a son (*putra*) has been killed (*hata*). The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *ṭhasvāṅgapūrvapadād vā*.
Similarly, she by whom a son has been eaten (*jagdha*) is *putrajagdhī*.

(49) *aco rahābhyāṃ dve* | 8|4|46| [The rule] "after a vowel, following *r* or *h*, there is doubling. Why "after a vowel" (*acaḥ*)? [To ensure that] in examples such as *ṭhhlute*, the doubling does not occur for the letter *n*.
(50) *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ* | 8|4|64| [The rule] "there is elision of *yama*s (semivowels and nasals) when followed by a *yama* after a consonant."

*Halo yamāṃ yami*: [The doubling of a consonant occurs] before the *yam* sounds (*ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, *ha*). Why say *halo*? [Consider] *nyāyyam*. Here, examples for the *yam* sounds beginning with *y* followed by another sound beginning with *y* are stated as far as possible: *sudhyupāsyaḥ*; *madhvariḥ*. In these cases, after the doubling of the *y* or *v* following *mayaḥ* (as per the rule *ṭhyaṇo mayaḥ*), [the subsequent application of the rule follows].

By this [rule], there is elision (*lopa*). As in *durlabhaḥ*, *durñurve*, and *kurmaḥ*. However, in the case of *pratyaṅṅātmā*, *sugaṇṇīśaḥ*, and *sannacyutaḥ*, after doubling (*dvitva*) the *l*, *ñ*, and *m* respectively according to the rule "after *ṭh* and *ca*, following *r* and *h*" (*ṭhaco rahābhyām*), elision occurs by this [present rule] when there is doubling of the *ṅ* according to the rule "and in the case of a non-vowel" (*anaci ca*).

There is the elision of the *ṅ*, the *k*, and the *ara*. It may be elided, or it may not; the intention is that the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is understood from the rule *hayo hṛḥ*. The result of instituting this elision is seen in the form *ādityo devatā*. This occurs when the suffix *ṇya* is applied to the word *āditya* by the rule *ityadityādityapatyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ*.

The point is that by the elision of the *a* in *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148) and by this [rule] for the elision of *ya*, the form *ādityam*— containing a single *y*— is established, and not otherwise. Nor can it be argued that the form containing a single *y* is established by the elision of *ya* through the rule *āpatyasya ca taddhite ’nāti* (Pāṇini 6.4.151).
It must be stated [as an exception]: because that [rule] does not apply when there is the intention to express such things as "born in Aditi" (*āditya*);

and because of the understanding of the correspondence [of elements] according to their order; and because, in the examples already mentioned, there is no result for undertaking the rule, and because there is no example of a *ra* occurring after another *ra*.

The *yathāsaṅkhyasūtra* has not been cited here because [the intended] greatness [of the rule] would be lost; the meaning here is that there is no elision of the *m*. However, the rule "when a *hal* follows, there is elision of a *yar* before a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) [consonant]" was not formulated as a *sūtra*, because [if it were], there would be the undesirable consequence of eliding the letter following the *r* in words such as *ūrdhvaḥ* and *ārṅga*.
(51) *eco'yavāyāvaḥ* |6|1|78|. [The word] *ecaḥ* [is understood as] "in order. Now, one might object: it would be more appropriate to state the rule for correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*) right here.
For even when accepting that, in the case of the mention of *pratyāhāras*, there exists a conventional indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) regarding that which is expressed and that which expresses.

This is because the correspondence between the number of elements (yathāsaṅkhyatva) must necessarily be stated by taking into account the knowledge of the primary meanings (*śakyārtha*) that precedes the understanding of the secondary meanings (*lakṣyārtha*). Otherwise, the sequence *ay*, *āv*, and *āv* for the vowels *e*, *o*, and *ai* would not be established. Do not say so; for that [correspondence] is established even by way of being the closest (*antaratamatva*). To explain: the diphthongs (*ec*) are the *sandhyakṣaras*. And therefore—
The *e* sound, which has a closed articulation and is palatal, has [the phoneme] *a* with a closed articulation and palatal place of articulation;
the *o* sound, which has a closed articulation and labial place of articulation, likewise has [the phoneme] *a*.

And because the latter components (*i* and *u*) predominate in the diphthongs *ai* and *au*, the *i* sound constitutes one and a half morae (*mātrā*) in *ai*, while the *a* sound constitutes exactly half a mora.

Likewise, in the syllable *o*, the *u* is one and a half measures (*adhyardhamātra*) and the *a* is half a measure (*ardhamātra*). And thus, for the palatal *ai*, which has an open *a* and is palatal, there is *āy*; for the labial *au*, which has an open *a* and is labial, there is *āv*.
(52) *vānto yi pratyaye* |6|1|79|.
When a suffix beginning with *y* follows, the final element of the *va* and *ānta* groups [is replaced by *au*]. Why does it say "when *y*" (*yīti*)? [To exclude forms like] *gobhyām*, *naubhyām*.
Why does it say "in a suffix" (*pratyaye*)? [To exclude forms like] *goyānam*. It means "beginning with the letter *y*. This is according to the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya*.

This meaning is obtained through the Vārttika *yasminvidhistadādāvalgrahaṇe*, which serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule; namely, that when a term is mentioned [in a rule], it includes itself and what precedes it. Regarding the phrase *odautoḥ*:
[the principle is] "between that which is present and that which is not present, the present is stronger"; in the preceding rule, it is precisely those two [vowels, *o* and *au*,] that are intended.

The sense is that [the substitute] *vānt* has been determined to be the substituendum (*sthānin*). As for the word *advai*: this is for the sake of the commentary (*bhāṣya*). The meaning is that even in common usage (*loka*), the substitution of *vānt* would apply to the word *go* if the measure of a road (*adhvan*) is understood by means of the whole [compound]. [The example is] *avyūtiḥ*.
"Strī-krośa-yugam" is according to Amara. Regarding the statement "it is declined [as such]," the meaning is that it ends in the suffix *ktin*.

Now, one might object: although there is no elision of *v* in "avya" and "āvya" because they are treated as *bha*-pratyayas and thus are not *pada*s, in the case of "avyūtiḥ," there would be elision either by the rule "hali sarveṣām" or by "lopaḥ śākalyasya."

Since there would otherwise be elision [of the *v*], he says: "In this case, in the rule *vānto yi pratyaye*," meaning that the letter *v* is not elided. And thus, even though *vyoḥ* is carried over from the rule *hali sarveṣām*, it becomes consistent with the forthcoming explanation that "there is elision of that which has [the *y*]," by setting aside the letter *v*. And this [is explained] right there.
It will be made clear:
(53) *dhātostannimittasyaiva* |6|1|80|.
[The rule] *dhātostannimittasyaiva*—since this was already established by the preceding [rule], this is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). In this case...

The preceding sūtra is carried over, as is the word "eca". By the pronoun "tat", the suffix beginning with *y* (the *yaṅ* and others) is referred to due to its suitability, and not the immediately preceding verbal root; for a sound (*ec*) that is part of one's own [suffix] cannot be the cause for oneself.

The particle *eva*, however, serves the purpose of restriction according to our desired meaning. Otherwise, a reversed restriction might be suspected, namely: "if a vowel *iC* occurs that is caused by something other than a verbal root, then it must be caused by a verbal root alone. Consequently, [the suffix] would not apply in the case of *ābhravya*; whereas it would apply even to a verbal root when the cause is not that [specific condition], as in *oyate*.

In such cases as these, having intended all of this, he says: "When the suffix *ya* follows, if the *ec* vowel of the root is to be replaced by *va* or *au*, and so forth. Regarding *lavyam*: from the root *lū*, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *aco yat*;
the *guṇa* substitution occurs by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*. Regarding *avaśyalāvyam*: [the same process applies].

The suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *ṭhori avaśyake*. The compound is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. The elision of the letter *m* occurs by the rule *umped avaśyamaḥ kṛtye*. This is a restrictive rule (*niyamasūtra*), since the form *avaśyam* and so forth would already have been established by the preceding rule alone.

He objects that it is useless, asking: "Why [is it said] 'of that very cause'? Even though only a portion [of the sūtra] is being objected to, this objection ultimately results in an objection to the sūtra itself. Regarding the form *oyate*: it is the present tense (*laṭ*) in the passive voice derived from the root *veñ* preceded by the prefix *ā*; there is the *yag* substitution for the passive marker and the *ātmanepada* ending, and due to its belonging to the *yajādi* class, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), followed by the formation of the single substitute *pūrvarūpa*.

The vowel is lengthened by the rule *ṭhaki* (Pāṇini 6.3.120). The point is that although the root *dā* becomes subject to the substitution of *ec* (i.e., *ai*) by the rule *ādguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87), this substitution is treated as if it were part of the subsequent element (*parādivadbhāva*), and thus the condition of being caused by an affix beginning with *ya* does not apply. Regarding *oyate*: this is the *laṅ* (imperfect) in the passive voice from the root *veñ*; the *yaṅ* and other suffixes are applied as before. The augment *āṭ* is added by the rule *āḍajādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.4.72).
There is *vṛddhi* by the rule "ṭhāṭaśca" (Pāṇini 7.2.116).

(54) *kṣayya-* and *jayya-* [occur] in the sense of "possible" (*śakyārtha*). By the rule "akṛtsarvidhau ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5), *yat* is applied. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), the *kṛtya* suffixes [are also included]. Thus, *kṣeyam*. [The suffix] *yat* is applied in the sense of "deserving" (*arha*).
Regarding the rule *kṛtyatṛcaś ca*: (55) *krayyas tadarthe* (Pāṇini 6.1.82).
[The word] *prakṛtyarthāya* [is used here]; the meaning of *prakṛti* is the exchange of goods (*dravyavinimaya*).

(56) *lopaḥ śākalyasya* | Pāṇini 8.3.19. There is elision [of *y*] according to Śākalya. [Question: Why is it said "preceded by *a*-vowels"? [Example: *dadhy atra*, *madhv atra*. [Question: Why is it said "when *aś* follows"? This [condition] is carried over from the rule *ha-bhago-*. [Question: What is the purpose of saying "when *aś* follows"? [Counter-example: *tad yunakti*.

One forms *vṛkṣavyakaroti*. Here, let there not be elision (*lopa*). Nor can this be resolved here by treating the elision of *ṭi* as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element), because it is accepted that "what is *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to what precedes it does not undergo *sthānivadbhāva*. And even so, [one might argue] that by the rule *ṭhali sarveṣām*, [the substitution] would be obligatory.

One should not suspect that there would be elision (*lopa*) [of the *y*]; for in that context, by carrying forward (*anuvartana*) the term *aśi* from the rule *ṭhaśi*, the vowels (*aś*) serve as qualifiers for the consonants (*hal*). Furthermore, elision according to the rule *opo vyorvali* is certainly not to be suspected;
this is because the rule *apadānte* [in the *paribhāṣā*] states that there is no substitution of a *sthānivadbhāva* [for the elided *y* or *v*] when they are followed by a *val*.
Because it has been stated thus: "Hara ehi" (O Hara, come). Here, the rule *ṭhomaṅeśca* would have resulted in a single substitute (pararūpa) [of 'e' for 'ehi'];

however, that is prohibited. Nor can it be argued that even if the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* is prohibited, the substitutions of *yaṇ* and *āv* still occur because the elision (*al-lopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule *asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*.
This must be stated, because those two [substitutions] are themselves *bahiraṅga* on account of depending upon two words (*pada*),
and because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] "when there is immediate succession with *ā*" (*ājānantarye*).
(57) *uraṇ raparaḥ* | 1.1.51 | [A substitute for *ṛ* or *ḷ* is followed by *r* as its *apṛkta* suffix.]

"Uraṇ raparaḥ. Even though the technical rule (paribhāṣā) "the genitive [case ending] is used in the sense of 'in place of'" (*aṣṭhī sthāneyogā*) is not present here as a restatement (*anuvāda*), the author says "that *aṇ* which is in its place" (*tatsthāneyo’ṇ*) with the intention that the term "in place of" (*sthāne*) is carried over from that [rule]. This is also because of [the rule] "in place of [something], the most similar [element]" (*sthāne’ntaratamaḥ*).

The term *sthāne* (in place of) is understood here by way of anuvṛtti. Therefore, it is only in the state of *prasaṅga* (the occasion for substitution) that the *aṇ* is followed by *rapara*. This is what [the author] explains: "being *rapara*, it operates. Why [is the condition] *uḥ*?
[Consider] *ṭhīdyati*—[the forms] *geyam* and *deyam*. Why [is the condition] *aṇ*? [To prevent] the *rapara* status of *rīṅ* and the other [substitutions].

It has occurred: *mātrīyati* [from *mātrī*] and *kriyate* [from *kṛ*]. "Due to proximity" (*āntaratamyāt*) means that there is a similarity of place (*sthāna-sāmya*) between the sound *ṛ*, which has the letter *r* as its head, and the vowel *a*, by way of the letter *r*.
"In the alternative case, there is doubling" refers to the fact that [the rule] *añceḥ dhaśca* applies.

(58) *Jharo jhari savarṇe* [Pāṇini 8.4.65]. Regarding *jharo jhari*: the term *hal* is understood from the previous rule *halo yamām*. Therefore, he says: "following a *hal*. Why "following a *hal*"? Consider *pratam*. Why "a *jhara*"? Consider *śārṅgam*.

Why [is it] "jharīti"? [Consider] *tṛptā*. Due to the force of the inclusion of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*), there is no correspondence by order (*yathāsaṅkhya*) here. Therefore, in the case of *iṇḍī*, the optional elision (*lopa*) of *ḍ* is established; such is the direction [of the argument]. Regarding "lopoveti": because the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is understood from the rule *hayo haḥ*. In its absence...

Regarding the term *lopa* (elision): it is to be understood as following from the phrase “in the absence of doubling” (*dvitva-abhāve*). Thus, the meaning is: when both doubling and elision are absent. Regarding *tridhami*: since there is another rule, *ṭhyaṇo mayaḥ*, which causes doubling once again, one should understand that the form becomes *caturdham*.
The doubling occurs only of *l* or only of *k*, not of both;
the wise should understand these four forms in cases such as *tavalkāra*.

(59) *vṛddhir eci* | P. 6.1.88. The term *vṛddhi* is [the subject]; from the preceding sūtra, the word *āt* is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "when followed by *ec*" (*ādeci*).
The word *ṛṣṇe* is a separate word used in the vocative; likewise, *eve* is also [a separate word]. And thus, in this case—
Having accepted that this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), one might raise the objection regarding the prohibition by the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*.

However, it should be understood that the explanation offered by some— namely, that "the prohibition by *uṇ* is not absolute" based on the citation of rules such as *ajñāpramāṇatvāt*— is not strictly necessary.

(60) *etyedhatyūṭhasu* | Pāṇini 6.1.89. Regarding *etyedhatyūṭhasu*: here, the word *aci* is understood from the previous rule [P. 6.1.78]. That (*aci*) qualifies *eti* and *edhati*, but not *ūṭh*, because [the latter] is impossible [in that context]. From the rule *ādguṇaḥ* [P. 6.1.87], the word *āt* is indeed understood to carry over.

He explains: "after a vowel other than *a*, before [a suffix] beginning with *j* or *ñ*" (*avarṇād ejādyoḥ*). Regarding *praṣṭhauhaḥ*: [the word] *praṣṭhavāṭ* means "one who carries the leader" (*praṣṭham vahati*). By the rule *vahśca*, the suffix *ṇvi* is applied. Then, in the nominative plural (*śas*), by the rule *vāha ūṭh*, *ūṭh* is substituted. By this [rule], *vṛddhi* is applied as an exception to *guṇa*. Regarding *predidhat*: it is derived from the root *edh* preceded by *pra*, with the suffix *ṇic*.
*luṅ* is *rūpi*. Because of the rule *“a māṅyoge”* (Pāṇini 6.4.74), there is an absence of the augment *āṭ*. Regarding the word *purastāt*:

the meaning is that this follows the maxim, “An exception [apavāda] situated before [a general rule] subverts the immediately following rules, not those situated further away. Regarding *akṣāt*: the words *ṭha* and *aci* are understood from the context; therefore—

This occurs only between the preceding and following vowels; the same should be inferred for other cases as well. There is an additional rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) regarding *akṣa* before *ūhinī*: the form is *akṣauhiṇī*. *Ūha* means a collection (*samūha*);
that which possesses such a collection is *ūhinī*. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "the collection (*ūhinī*) of dice (*akṣāṇām*)."

An *akṣauhiṇī* is an army distinguished by a specific measure. The substitution of *ṇ* [for *k*] occurs according to the rule “*ūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*” (Pāṇini 8.4.3). When the word *akṣaṇām* is compounded with the word *ṭhūha*, and the suffix *in* is subsequently added, the form becomes *akṣauhiṇī*; however, there is no *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) in that case, because the internal *guṇa* (vowel substitution) takes precedence.

Because of sublation (*bādhāt*). For even the augment *vṛddhi*, which serves as an exception (*apavāda*), has its purpose fulfilled by being compounded with the word *ūhinī*. As it was stated previously: "If an exception has its purpose fulfilled elsewhere, then it is sublated by another rule that is further or more internal (*antaraṅga*)."
[The rule applies] to *svādu* and *īrin*. The reading *īreriṇyoḥ* is an occasional corruption;

for if it were *vairi*, which ends in the suffix *ṇini*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of *vṛddhi* in the feminine. He states the purpose of including the term *īrin*: "to be moved by one's own [nature]. However, when [the word is] *īraṇa* or *īra*...

When the word *sva* is compounded with a form ending in the suffix *ghañ*, such as in *avādīraḥ* (where the *vṛddhi* vowel has been applied), the possessive suffix *ini* is added; or, when the word *sva* is compounded with the word *īrin* which itself ends in the possessive suffix *ini*, then too the constituent element *īra-* certainly exists within it— thus, there is a separate mention of *īrin*.
The sense is that [the effort] would be in vain. Regarding *svairī*: the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *supyajātau*;
this is an *upapada* compound. Regarding *svairiṇī*: the *vṛddhi* strengthening occurs by taking the word *īrin*, which precedes the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
Some say that here the *vṛddhi* occurs by the *paribhāṣā* concerning words qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭa*), but that is fruitless.

The meaning [of the rule] is as follows: since it is impossible to abandon an already present meaning when it is possible for that meaning to serve as a qualifier for the word, [the term "meaningless" (*anarthaka*) must refer to something else]. Regarding the word *praiṣya*: because of its association with *eṣa*, *eṣya* also refers to that which is not an indeclinable (*anavyaya*).

It is understood; therefore, when *iṣ* is followed by a causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the suffixes *ktvā* and *lyap*, there is only the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), and not *vṛddhi*.

Thus, *preṣya gataḥ*. Anticipating the objection regarding the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel, he says: "Because those two have a long penultimate vowel. Regarding *pravatsatara*: here some insert the words *vatsa* and *vatsara*.
This should be disregarded, as it is not seen in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) and other such works. Regarding the form *vatsatarārṇam*:

there are four forms due to the optional doubling of the letters *t* and *m*. However, when doubling occurs for the letter following the *repha* (the *ṇ*), according to the rule *“ṭhaco rahābhyām”* and by another statement, *“ṭhyaṇo mayaḥ”*...

Furthermore, with the doubling of the *ṇa*, there are twelve forms: *ekaṇam*, *dviṇam*, and *triṇam*. With the doubling of the *sa* in *hayaḥ śaraḥ*, there are twenty-four (24). Nor should one suspect a prohibition of doubling here by the rule *aro'ci*; for that [rule] applies only to doubling occurring within the context of the Sūtra itself. Precisely for this reason, it is said: *hayaḥ śaraḥ*.

The Vārttika provides the examples *ṭhvatssaraḥ* and *ṭhapssarāḥ* in the Bhāṣya. Nor should one raise the objection that, when the suffix *sara* follows the root *vad*, once the change of *d* to *t* (*cartva*) has occurred, the *s* would not be followed by a *khaya* sound (as required for the substitution of *ṣ*) because that *t* is considered "not established" (*asiddha*). This is because it is stated: "That which is 'not established' regarding what precedes does not apply in the case of doubling. For this very reason...

In the *Manoramā*, regarding the rule "aṭ santaḥ," it is accepted that there is doubling of the *s* following the letter *ṭ*; this is the general direction [of the analysis]. (61) Pāṇini 6.1.91: "After a prefix (*upasarga*), [the augment *ṭi* is inserted] before a verbal root beginning with *ṛ*."

*Upasargād ṛti*: Why "after a prefix" (*upasargāt*)? [Observe: *khaṭvarcchati*. Why "before *ṛ*" (*ṛti*)? [Observe: *upetaḥ*. The inclusion of the short *ṛ* (*tapara*) is for the sake of the subsequent rule; for here, since a verbal root (*dhātu*) beginning with a long *ṛ* is impossible, there would be no instance to exclude. Why "in a verbal root" (*dhātau*)? [Observe: *uparkāraḥ*. But surely, in this case...

The prefix *upa* is not [merely] the word *ṭhupa*; for a prefixhood exists only through connection with a verbal action (*kriyāyoga*). Even when analyzing the compound as "the vowel *ṛ* has approached" (*upagata ṛkāraḥ*) to establish its connection with an action, it remains a non-prefix (*anupasarga*) with respect to the vowel *ṛ*, according to the rule: "Prepositions such as *pra* and others, when connected with an action, receive the designations 'gati' or 'prefix' only with respect to that [action]."

And if it is argued that even without the mention of "dhātu" (root), the *vṛddhi* substitution will occur only for roots beginning with the vowel *ṛ* because the root is implied by the term "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*), and not in other cases—this is true;
for this very reason, he will state immediately after that [the rule] is intended "for the sake of re-enjoining by means of a *yogavibhāga*. Therefore, [the objection does not hold].
There is no inconsistency whatsoever.

(62) *Antādivacca* [Pāṇini 6.1.85]. *Antādivacca*: here, the rule "ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ" (one [element] replaces both the preceding and the following) is understood to carry over; according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*).

Intending to say that [the previous rule] is also resorted to, he says: "The end of the preceding [is like the original]. This is already established by the *sthānivad-ādeśaḥ* sūtra itself. Nor should one suspect that this [sūtra] exists for the purpose of an operation concerning an *al* (phoneme);
for even this is undesirable in the case of an *al*-vidhi. Otherwise, in the case of [the derivation of] *ṭhayaje indram*, [undesirable results would follow].
Because [otherwise] there would be the occurrence of *savarṇadīrgha* [vowel lengthening].
(63) *kharavasānayor visarjanīyaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.15. "There is no *visarga*"—this should also be understood to apply in cases such as *ukhārta*.
(64) *vā supyāpiśaleḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.92. Regarding the term *subdhātāv*: it means "in that which has a *subanta* as its constituent part.
This is because a *dhātu* consisting of a *subanta* is impossible. Although words such as *ṛja* ("to go") possess the status of a *dhātu* when followed by the suffix *kvip*, [the rule still applies].

Although the status of being a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is possible [in such cases], nevertheless, it is not well-known that such forms are excluded by the rule regarding *tapara* (the vowel *a* with a following *t*).
Since this possibility occurs only in the case of nominal stems (*nāman*) and verbal roots (*dhātu*), it is understood that only those are intended here.
Regarding the form *prārṣabhīyati*: there is a prohibition of reduplication (*dvitva*) by the rule to be stated later, *aro'ci*.

(65) *eṅ* becomes a single substitute for two vowels (*pirarūpa*). [Pāṇini 6.1.94] Since the substitution of *eṅ* for *ai* and *au* is already established by the rule "when *ai* or *au* follows," the inclusion of the term "*ara*" is for the sake of subsequent rules.

The inclusion of the term "*ūpa*" (meaning "single substitute"), however, is for the sake of clarity; for even without it, the result would be established by the rule "in the case of *ami*, *eṅ* is the single substitute for the preceding [vowel] as before."
Regarding *prejata*: the root *ṭhejṛ* means "to shine. However, when it has the sense of "trembling," it is conjugated in the *parasmaipada* (active voice), as in *prejati*.
Furthermore, the particle *eva* is used except in the sense of *aniyoga*. *Niyoga* means "ascertainment" (*avadhāraṇa*), which is to say "determination" (*nirdhāraṇa*).
As it has been said: "When *eva* is observed in the sense of *anavaklṛpti* (impossibility or non-admission), it is the domain of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*)."
"When this [particle *eva*] occurs in the sense of restriction (*niyama*), it is the domain (*viṣaya*) of *vṛddhi*.

This is the meaning: when the particle *eva* is seen in the sense of "impossibility" (*anavaklṛpti*) or "uncertainty" (*aniścaya*), it is the domain of the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form); however, when it is seen in the sense of "restriction" (*niyama*) or "determination" (*nirdhāraṇa*), it is the domain of *vṛddhi*.

However, those who explain that "niyoga" means "application" (vyāpāra)—interpreting it as "the application of two yojanas"—in order to conform to the counter-example found in the earlier text stating, "But if there is no union, you must go this very day," for them [the following applies]: "At the very moment when the body [is cast] into the fire... "This very... [and so forth].

Otherwise, common usages such as *janmāntarapātakānām* (“of sins from other births”) would not be established, nor would Vedic sutra usages such as *apastapaḥkarmakasyaiva* (“only for that which has *tapas* as its object”) and *aṅḥ śākaṭāyanasyaiva* (“only according to Śākaṭāyana”).
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the verse cited in the commentary (*vṛtti*). This is so for those who explain [the rule] as *ṭhavadhāraṇam* (“ṭha denotes restriction”).
But there is the attainment of all desired success. (66) *aco’ntyādi ṭi* | Pāṇini 1.1.64.

*aco’ntyādi ṭi*. The genitive case in *aco’ntya-* is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). The singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jātāvekavacanam*); thus he says, "among the vowels."
"In the case of *śakandhu* and others, a subsequent form (*pararūpa*) should be stated. Regarding the phrase "in the case of *śakandhu* and others":
the meaning is that, with respect to the category beginning with *śakandhu*, a subsequent form should be stated in accordance with the establishment of those forms.

For this very reason, he says: "And that [subsequent form] is of the final phoneme (*ṭeḥ*). However, if it were intended that this applies only to the vowel *a* because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of "*ṭhāḥ*," [the rule would not apply here].

In that case, the derivation of "Manīṣā" as "Patañjali" would not be established. Some, however, claim that by applying the *pṛṣodarādi* rule to the words *manas* and *patat*, with the elision of the final syllables and the substitution of the single form of the vowel *a*, [the name is formed]. An *andhu* is a well belonging to the Śakas, a specific region; likewise, it is a well belonging to the Karkas, a specific class of kings.

*Karkandhu* is *aṭati*, hence *aṭā*. With the suffix *ac* (from the *pacādi* group) and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, we have *kula-aṭā* = *kulaṭā*. However, if the analysis were *kulam aṭati* (she wanders through the family), then with the suffix *aṇ* after an object (*karman*) and the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, it would become *kulāṭī*. [The roots] *ṭhīṣa* in the sense of "gleaning" and *ṭhīṣa* in the sense of "going," etc.—from these two, by the rule *uraśca halaḥ*, the suffix *ap* is applied.

*Īṣā*: *manasa īṣā* is *manīṣā* (the impulse of the mind); *halasya īṣā* is *halīṣā* (the shaft of a plough). *Īṣā* refers to the pole of a plough. *Patañjali*: he is so called because "hands joined in reverence (*añjali*) fall (*patant-*)" upon him due to his being worthy of homage. Regarding *mārtaṇḍa*:
by this [rule of] *pararūpa*, since *ṛtaṇḍa* is established, the *vṛddhi* [vowel] is applied from that point via the suffix *aṇ* and so forth. "The spokes... [etc.]

In cases such as "mārtāṇḍamāsyat" and "mārtāṇḍamābharat," the intention is that the long vowel is Vedic (chāndasa). Some, however, maintain that this is simply a case of the lengthening of similar vowels (savarṇadīrgha); the aforementioned Vedic usages support their view.

Regarding "otvoṣṭhayoḥ": this rule applies when the vowel *a* and the sounds *o* or *uṣṭha* coexist within a single compound. Therefore, it does not apply here: *ṭhvṛṣalasutauṣṭhavraṇaste*. (67) *omāṅeśca* | Pāṇini 6.1.95.

"Come, O Śivā! [The opponent asks: "But surely, in the case of *iva ā ihi*, once the long vowel by position (*savarṇadīrgha*) has been applied and subsequently the *guṇa* substitution by *ādguṇaḥ*, the desired form is established; so what is the purpose of including the mention of *āṅ*? [The author replies: "True.
However, according to the view that 'the verbal root is joined with the prefix first,' in the case of the sequence of root and prefix—"

Because the operation is "internal" (*antaraṅga*), the *guṇa* substitution would have occurred first, and subsequently the *vṛddhi* would have applied; the mention of *at* [in the rule] is intended so that this does not happen.

[The rule] "for the imitation of an indistinct sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*), when *at* is followed by *iti*" [is stated]. Although the word *ataḥ* is understood from the preceding rule "for *at*, when followed by a *guṇa*,"...

Thus, by following [the previous rule], the mention of *ataḥ* here could have been dispensed with; nevertheless, because the term *ataḥ* in the preceding sūtra contains the *tapara* marker (Ṭ), it refers to the short vowel *a*, whereas here, by resorting to the view that the word *at* functions as a technical heading (*adhikāra*), it refers to the word-form *at*. Such an interpretation involves unnecessary complexity.
The word "syāt" (it may be) is used here again for this reason. He explains the term "avyakta" (unmanifest): "of the sound" (*dhvaneḥ*). "Of the imitation" (*anukaraṇasya*); the meaning is:
of that which possesses clearly manifest phonemes such as *a*, *kāra*, and so forth. And its status as an imitation (*anukaraṇatva*)—
This should be understood through partial similarity. Although this *pararūpa* [substitution] is eternal, it does not occur when *saṃhitā* is not intended; therefore, he says: "paṭat-iti" etc.
(68) *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.101.

"Neither *a* nor *ahal*" (*nājjhalau*), etc. The intention is this: since a difference in the objects to be prescribed (*vidheya*) results in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), and since syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is impossible when such a split occurs, [the rule] "those produced by the same place and effort" (*tulyāsyaprayatnam*) and "neither *a* nor *ahal*" (*ājjhalau*) must be understood as forming a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*).

The meaning of "distinct from *ṭh* and *jhal*" (*ṭhajjhalbhinna*) is accepted as follows: in the expression "distinct from *ṭh* and *jhal*," what is intended is the state of being different from both *jhal* sounds that possess an internal effort (*āsyaprayatna*) characterized by mutual similarity. Thus, a sound that consists of either short or long [vowels]— [...is distinct from *ṭh* and *jhal*.]
"By whatever phonetic quality (*varṇa*) two [sounds] have an identical articulatory effort (*tulyāsyaprayatna*), those two are mutually *savarṇa* (homogeneous)";
likewise, "by whatever consonant (*hal*) a consonant has an identical articulatory effort, those two would be mutually *savarṇa*";
and "by whatever consonant a sound consisting of a long (*dīrgha*) or protracted (*pluta*) vowel [has an identical articulatory effort]..."
The resulting meaning is that both [sounds] produced with equal effort in the same location are mutually *savarṇa* (homogeneous).

Consequently, once the designation *savarṇa* has been established by these two rules, the rule "ṭh-ṇ-u-d-it [denotes] its homogeneous" (*aṇuditsavarṇasya*)—which functions as a "grāhaka" (specifying) rule—comes into operation, and not prior to that. Therefore...

By the rule *ājjhalau*, the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) of only those vowels and consonants included in the traditional alphabet (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) is excluded, but not that of all [sounds].
