Therefore, since homogeneity between the long vowel *ā* and the letter *ś* does indeed exist here, it is appropriate to carry forward the term *aci* from the rule *ṭhakaḥ savarṇe* in order to prevent that [undesired application]. When...
Having postulated that the *uṣman* sounds possess a slight degree of openness (*īṣadvidhṛtatva*), the rule *ājjhalau* is rejected;
consequently, the term *aci* need not be supplied here from the *savarṇa* rule.
Thus, in cases such as *he piṣāso*, once the protracted vowel (*pluta*) of the syllable following a heavy syllable (*guru*)—by the rule *guroranṛtaḥ*—has been applied, then...

One might raise the objection that, because a long vowel followed by *h* is not considered homogeneous (*sāvarṇya*) with *h*— despite the fact that in the rule *ājjhalau* the letter *ā* is elided [to include the long vowels]— the protracted (*pluta*) vowel *ā* would still be an *iṇ* vowel (by virtue of being homogeneous with *h*), and thus the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* should occur when it follows another *iṇ* vowel. Anticipating this doubt:

To avoid that [undesired consequence], one might propose a strained interpretation—forming a *dvandva* compound of *āś-ca āś-ca* and applying the rule for long vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) so that even the *pluta* vowel following a long vowel is included; however, such an interpretation should not be resorted to. Furthermore, in cases such as *viśvapābhiḥ*, there would be no application of the substitution of *ḍha* and other such rules either.

This path is easy to understand because there is no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the vowels and the sibilants due to the difference in their effort (*prayatna*). [The phrase] "only *ako’kī*" means "only [the rule] *ako’ki dīrghaḥ*.
It is easily stated [that this is sufficient] by virtue of the connection through respective order (*yathāsaṅkhya*).

Since there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *adhyatre*, and since it has been stated that the term *ṛ* is the designation for thirty sounds, there is indeed the condition of an *ṛ*-sound being followed by an *ṛ*-sound in the case of *hotṛ-lṛkāra*; thus, there is no possibility of [the rule's application] failing, given the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the vowel *ī* and the letter *ś*.
The sense is that even though the term *aci* follows [from the previous rule], the forms are established without it, because the desired form is already accomplished.
He recites the Vārttika— "when *ṛ* there is *ṛ*, or when *lṛ* there is *lṛ*"— by connecting it with the word *savarṇa* found in the sūtra.

Regarding the passage beginning with *ṛti savarṇa*: [the opponent objects]—"In that case, since the word *savarṇa* is not included in the rule *ṭhakaḥ savarṇe*, the mention of *savarṇa* must be made in the two Vārttikas; however, in the Sūtra itself, one should instead say *ṭhako’kī*.
Thus, because the opposite would involve greater complexity (*gaurava*), how can it be that [the Sūtra] says simply *ṭhako’kī*?"

If it is argued that it has been stated [in the Mahābhāṣya] that "it is easy to pronounce" (*suvacam*), to this they reply: because the author of the Bhāṣya rejects these two Vārttikas, there is indeed no prolixity (*gaurava*). As for the justification for this rejection, it will be examined in the discussion concerning words ending in the vowel *ḷ*.

"The two phonemes [lṛ and ḷ] have two morae. By this, it is implied that the ancient explanation—"when length is applicable, the short *lṛ* is prescribed"—is contrary to the authoritative source (*ākaraviruddha*). (69) *eṅaḥ padāntād ati* 6.1.109.

*eṅḥ padāntādati* (Pāṇini 6.1.109). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rules] *aya-v-ayoḥ*. Since the rule *siṅsośca* (6.1.110) has already begun, it was established in the *Manoramā* that although the domain of this [rule] is already understood to be "after a word-final [eṅ]," the phrase "after a word-final" (*padāntāt*) is placed here specifically for the sake of clarity regarding the subsequent rule. However, some [hold a different view].
The condition *adāntāt* (provided it does not end in /d/) is also necessary here; otherwise, [the substitution] would apply even after what does not end in /d/.

However, the rule *siṅsośca* would then serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) meaning: "If the single-substitute form (*pūrvarūpa*) occurs when *ati* follows an element related to a case-ending (*up*), then it must occur only when *ṅsi* or *ṅs* follow. The result of this [restriction] is...

They say that in examples such as *harayaḥ*, *guravaḥ*, and *iḥ smṛto yaiste smṛtayaḥ*, the rule for *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitution of the preceding vowel) does not apply. Why [is the condition] *eṅaḥ* (after *e* or *o*) stated? [Example: *dadhyatra*. Why [is the condition] *padāntāt* (from the end of a word) stated? [Examples: *cayanam*, *lavaṇam*, *acinavam*. Why [is the condition] *aci* (before a vowel) stated? [Counter-examples: *harayiha*, *viṣṇaviha*.
Why [is it] "followed by *t*"? [Consider: *vāyavāyāhi*. (70) *sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ* | 6.1.122.
"Everywhere, optionally. Although the word "in Vedic" (*chandasi*) is not explicitly mentioned here, nevertheless—
Because of the introductory context beginning with "In the Yajurveda, [the substitution of] *u* for *ū*," one might suspect that this applies only to Vedic usage;
therefore, it is stated, "everywhere. He explains this as "in both worldly [usage] and the Veda.
Here, having carried forward the rule "eṅ" (Pāṇini 1.1.4), it should be explained as "of that which ends in eṅ, [there is] *goḥ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.79). By this, here—

No—[the form] *citragvagram*. Regarding the term "original form" (*prakṛtibhāva*): this is obtained by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "original form" from the sūtra *prakṛtyāntaḥpādam*. However, if the reading were *āntaḥpādam*, then by the sūtra *sarvatra vibhāṣā*, the optional formation of the single substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) would simply be prohibited.

This is to be noted. It is established in the *Manoramā* that, with the intention that the alternative of a prohibition results in the alternative of a prescription, it is the original form (*pūrvarūpa*) itself that is subject to optionality;
thus [it says]: "The *avaṅ* [substitution] for Sphoṭāyana," 6.1.123.

*avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya*. He whose *ayana* (goal) or ultimate resort is *sphoṭa* is a grammarian devoted to the exposition of *sphoṭa*; [the term] *sphoṭāyanasya* refers to that [grammarian]. Here too, it should be explained as *ṭheṅntasyāgo’ri* (after a word ending in ṭh or eṅ, before a non-guṇa vowel). It would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as *ṭha’g*.
The mention of Sphoṭāyana is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*), because [the rule] follows from the *Vibhāṣā* [of Pāṇini 6.1.123]. The word *ati* has ceased to apply;
otherwise, forms such as *aveśaḥ* and *avoddhaḥ* would not be established—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "when *ac* follows":
here, *aṭ* and *aci* are understood to carry over [from previous rules], whereas *ati* has ceased to apply; this is precisely the explanation given here.

"Refuge. Regarding "gavākṣa": the analysis of the compound is "the eye (akṣi) of rays (gavām) of light. The suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-ending by the rule "akṣṇo'darśanāt. This word is conventionally established in the sense of a window (*vātāyana*). Its masculine gender is derived from common usage.

(72) *indre ca* |6|1|124|. Also before *indra*. By virtue of its very formulation, this [substitution] is compulsory. Some say that this sūtra could even be dispensed with; for the desired result is achieved simply by resorting to the principle of *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (restricted optionality), which has been adopted for other purposes as well.

Regarding the phrase “plutapragṛhyāḥ,” the reading “atha prakṛtibhāvaḥ” (now, the preservation of the original form) is generally seen in the root manuscripts immediately preceding that sūtra; however, that is indeed a corrupt reading. Some maintain this because the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) has already been commenced by the rule “arvatra vibhāṣā goḥ” (optionally everywhere for the word *go*). Others [hold a different view].

However, although the two rules "tuṭ" and "avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya indre ca" are recited in the section concerning *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form), it must necessarily be stated that they fall outside that scope, because those two rules do not prescribe that [specific] *prakṛtibhāva*.
Nor is there [any need for such an objection] regarding the rule for "avaṅ."

It must be stated that because it serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the state of original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), and thus possesses the nature of an exception to a general rule (*utsargāpavāda*), its inclusion in this section is easily established; furthermore, this applies even to the rule "ṭhindre ca" which is recited immediately after, for the purpose of the continued application of the substitution *avaṅ*, since the rule for *avaṅ* is also an exception to the rule for the single-substitute *pūrvarūpa*.
Because it is easy to understand; for the reading of this section has already served its purpose by ensuring the continued application of the word *go*.
And thus, those two sūtras have been written outside the section on the *prakṛtibhāva* of *sva-lekhya*.

They say that because it is favorable to that [rule], the application of the sūtra "arvadviṣāṣa" (Pāṇini 6.1.34) should be understood as occurring in that very same context for that which is established there.
Now begins the section on the *ad*-class [roots] in the *Tattvabodhinī*.

(223) *ṛterīyaṅ* | Pāṇini 3.1.29. Regarding *ṛterīyaṅ*: this verbal root ends in *t*, and it is indicated by the vowel *ṛ* (ṛkārānta), not by the vowel *i* (ikārānta), as is evident from the rule "vañciluñcyṛtaśca. Some, however, [interpret] *īyaṅ*...
It is understood from its long pronunciation that this [suffix] ends in *-i*. For if it ended in *-id*, it would have been established by the *savarṇa-dīrgha* rule alone;

thus, they say that [the author] would have simply used *iyaṅ*, but that is not correct. For if it ended in *-id*, the *savarṇa-dīrgha* would be superseded by *yaṇ* according to the rule "ṭheranekācaḥ. Nor is there any [justification] for the application of *yaṇ* in the rule prescribing *yaṅ* after *ṛti* by the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ... [which applies to short vowels].
It must be stated that the prescription of *īyaṅ* for the root *dīrgha* (to feel pity) serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for its having a nasal stop (*ta*) at the end;
otherwise, in the rule prescribing *yaṅ*, the form *anyaṅ* would result due to reduplication. Regarding the phrase "and in the sense of pity":
[as stated in the lexicon] "the words *artanā*, *ṛtīyā*, and *hriṇīyā* have the meaning of *ghṛṇā* (disgust/compassion)," and "disgust, compassion, and *ghṛṇā* [are synonyms]."
And [the author] says *amaraḥ*.
(224) Pāṇini 6.4.101: *hujhalbhyo herdhiḥ* ("For *hi* following *hu*, *jha*, or *hal*, there is *dhi*").
[In the example] *juhudhi*, having carried over the word *halī* from the rule *hasibhasorhalī*, [it means] "when preceded by a *hal*."

They say that by virtue of the explanatory statement (*vyākhyāna*), there is no substitution of *dh* for the root *hi* in cases such as *rudihi* and *svapihi* (due to the presence of *iṭ*, etc.); however, in the case of *ṭhatā*, because *dhi*-ness is subsequent, once *tātaṅ* has been applied, *dhi*-ness would again apply by way of the status of being "as if in the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), yet it does not apply due to the maxim "that which is not a verbal root (*akṛt*) is not [governed by] *gati*. Others, however—

They say that in the word *herdhi*, the vowel *i* in both the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is for the sake of pronunciation; thus, the substitution of *dh* for *h* occurs, so that there is no need to maintain the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *hal* [from Pāṇini 6.4.103], nor is there any risk of the *tātaṅ* substitute being subject to the designation *dh*.
Consequently, one need not even resort to the maxim of "that which has occurred once" (*sakṛdgatinyāya*).
(225) *adaḥ sarveṣām* | 7|3|100|. From the rule *adaḥ sarveṣām*, the term *aṭ* is understood as being carried over from the previous rule *aṅgārgyagālavayoḥ*.
This is done to prevent the suspicion that the term *gārgyagālavayoḥ* might also be carried over.
The inclusion of all [roots].
(226) *luṅ-sanoḥ ghaslṛ* (Pāṇini 2.4.37). *jighatsati*. *praṇihanti*. The substitution of *ṇa* occurs by the rule *eṛ-adeḥ*.
(227) *anudātopadeśavanatitanotyādīnāmanunāsikalopo jhali kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.37). Regarding the term *anudātopadeśa*: if it were explained here as "the elision of the nasal [of] these," [then...]

In that case, there would be the elision of the *nam*, *nah*, *muh*, *majj*, and so forth, even when they are not at the end of a word; consequently, forms such as *mataḥ*, *nataḥ*, *naddhaḥ*, *mīḍhaḥ*, *muktaḥ*, and *magnaḥ* would not be established. Therefore, he says: "with the sixth case [marker] elided. [This refers to the rule] "of the others, *van*" and so on.

The sense is that the qualifier is redundant because there is no deviation from the suffix *van*. [Regarding] *vati*: since the suffix *ktin* is present here, by the rule “*eḍvaśi kṛti*” (*Pāṇ. 6.1.45*), the prohibition of *iṇ* applies; thus, when a *jhal* consonant follows a *kṅit* suffix, there is no elision. [The phrase] “there would be elision” means that, according to the rule “*alo’ntyasya*” (*Pāṇ. 1.1.52*), the elision would apply to the final [letter].

He shows those taught with an *anudātta* accent that end in a nasal (*anunāsika*)—namely, *yama*, *rami*, and so on. He also shows those beginning with *tanu* that end in a nasal—namely, *tanu*, *kṣaṇu*, *kṣiṇu*, and so on.
Among those beginning with *tanu*, there are nine excluding *kṛ*; among them is *sanu*.
The substitution of *ā* in the case of the roots *ana*, *sana*, and *khana* will be stated [later], so they are not included here. Therefore, examples such as *kṣataḥ* and *kṣitaḥ* follow.

Because the roots beginning with *tan* are marked with the indicatory letter *u*, there is an option regarding the augment *iṭ* after the suffix *ktvā*; however, there is no *iṭ* after the *niṣṭhā* suffixes. This applies to those ending in a nasal (*anunāsika*).

What [is the meaning of the conditions]? *śaktaḥ* (capable), *ruddhaḥ* (obstructed). Why say "when a *jhal* [consonant] follows"? [Consider: *gamyate* (it is gone), *namyate* (it is bent). Why say "when *k* or *ṅ* followed by *t* [i.e., *ktvā*, *kta*, etc. follows"? [Consider: *gantā* (one who goes), *mantā* (one who thinks). (228) *vamor vā* | Pāṇini 8.4.23. [The substitution of *iṭ* is optional before suffixes ending in *va* or *ma*.]

"He killed" (*jaghāna*), "they two killed" (*jaghnatuḥ*). Although here the rule *abhyāsācca* also applies, nevertheless, because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*), the rule *ho hanteḥ* is presented first. (229) *hanter jaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.36].

Regarding the phrase "because it is ābhīya": some maintain that even by means of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*, one could say that *lṛṅ* does not replace *hi*. That is weak; for the modern scholars (*navyāḥ*) hold that due to the force of the introduction of the rule "*ato heḥ*" (P. 6.4.105), that paribhāṣā does not apply here.
(230) What is the authority?

[Pāṇini 2.4.43] states that *vadh* is a substitute ending in *a*. Therefore, because it is taught as a substitute with more than one vowel (*anekāc*), the prohibition of *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.10] "of a monosyllabic [root]" (*ekācaḥ*) does not apply in forms such as *avadhīt*; thus, by [Pāṇini 7.2.7] "after *at*, [there is *iṭ*] before *sic* when beginning with a consonant" (*ato halādeḥ*), [the augment *iṭ* is applied].
The sense is that the *vṛddhi* substitution does not apply because of the status of the elision (*allopa*) as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*).
(231) *dviṣaśca* |3|4|112|. The root *duh* means "to fill" (*prapūraṇa*), and "filling" here implies "causing to give up" (*tyājana*). It is also like the *laṅ* [tense]; thus: *adugdha*.

*adugdhāḥ*, *adhugdhvam*, *aduhvahi*. [The root] *diha* means accumulation or growth (*upacaya-vṛddhiḥ*). In *praṇidegdhi*, there is the substitution of *ṇa* by the rule *eṛade*. In *alikṣata*, the suffix *ksa* is applied by the rule *ala igupadhe*. [Examples: *alikṣātām*, *alikṣanta*. In *alīḍhe*, there is optionally the elision (*luk*) by the rule *ugvā duheḥ*.

*alīḍhāḥ* (licked). *alīḍhavat* (having licked). Regarding *cakṣiṅ*: "even in the sense of seeing. The intention is that in the passage "he beholds all forms with his powers" (*viśvā rūpā abhicaṣṭe śacībhiḥ*), it has been explained as having the meaning of seeing. Regarding "for the sake of the suffix *yuc*": [the suffix] *yuc* is applied according to the rule *anudātetaśca halādeḥ*. Regarding "ending in *it*": [this refers to the rule] *iditaḥ*.

The intention is that in the rule for the insertion of *num*, the word "at the end" (*anta*) is understood to carry over from the previous rule, "of *oḥ* at the end of a *pāda*" (*oḥ pādānte*). And thus, since the suspicion regarding the addition of the augment *num* does not arise, it is appropriate to employ the vowel *a* itself in place of the *i* of the root *cakṣiṅ*; for the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are already established by its being marked with the *anudātta* accent.

Anticipating the objection that the syllable *ṅ* is redundant, he says: "The syllable *ṅ*, however... Regarding the word *sphāyan*: [it is derived from] the root *sphāyī* meaning "to grow," which is anudāteta; thus, the present participle suffix *laṭ* is replaced by *śatṛ*. Regarding *caṣṭe*: there is the elision of *k* according to the rule "the *k* [of *cakṣ*] is elided," followed by the change to *ṣṭu*.

(232) *cakṣiṅḥ khśāñ* [Pāṇini 2.4.54]. Regarding the term *khśādi*: it has already been stated in the first half [of this work] that, because of this [substitution], there is no substitution of *r* by the rule *umaḥ khayyampare* in the case of *uṃkhyānam*, and so forth.

(233) *vā liṭi* |2|4|55|. In the section on what is "not established" (*asiddhakāṇḍa*), the phrase "immediately after the section on *ṇatva*" is to be understood as the remainder [of the commentary]. Consequently, in the word *paryākhyānam*, because of the intervention of the letter *śa*, the *ṇatva* substitution [of *kha* for *k*] does not occur by virtue of the rule *ṛtyacaḥ*.
Similarly, that which is produced from *suprakhyā* is *sauprakhya*; one who belongs there is *sauprakhyīya*.

It should be understood that because this [suffix] is not established [by the rule for *vuñ*], the suffix *vuñ*—as in the rule "after *han*, *an*, and a word with *u* as a penultimate letter"—does not apply, but rather only the suffix *cha*. [In the form] *acaṣṭe*: the elision of *k* occurs by the rule "after *ka*" (*kor iti*), and then the substitution of *ṣṭu* [for *ṣṭ*].

In the rule *ṭhasyativaktikhyātī*, the substitution of *yat* is not considered *asiddha* due to the force of the injunction itself; for it will be stated later that the independent root *khyā* has as its domain only the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. Furthermore, since the root *as* belongs to the *puṣādi* group, the *aṅ* affix is already established; thus, the inclusion [of *as*] is for the sake of the *tarap* suffix, and so forth, as he will explain among the *puṣādi* roots.
(234) *asyativaktikhyātibhyo’ṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.52).
Regarding the word *vakti*: both [roots] are included—namely, *ruvo vaciḥ* and *vaca paribhāṣaṇe*. [From the root *īr*: *īritā*, *īriṣyate*.
[In the *laṅ* (imperfect): *airat*, *airātām*, *airata*; *airi*, *airvahi*.
Let us worship.
(235) *īśaḥ se* | 7|2|77|. Regarding *īśaḥ se*: according to the literal formulation of the rule, when the word *dhve* follows *īś*, [the substitution of *īśe* for *īś* occurs], as in *īśidhve*.
The form *īśidhvam* is not established; therefore, he says:
(236) *īḍajanordhve ca* |7|2|78|. [The rule] *īśīḍjanām* is for the sake of variety; there is a back-reference (*apakarṣa*) of the word *hve* to the preceding rule.
The meaning is that the word ‘e’ is carried forward into the subsequent rule for the sake of producing a specific understanding.

Here, in the *Kāśikā* and other works, an example is given from the root *jan*. Specifically, from the root *jan* in the sense of “manifestation” (*prādurbhāve*), there is the Vedic *śyan* suffix and the elision (*luk*) of the *śyan*, as well as the absence of the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*). Thus: *janiṣe*, *janidhve*.

*janiṣva* (be born), *janidhvam* (be born); from the root *jan* meaning "to be born," with the elision of the *ślu*-affix and the elision of the penultimate vowel, we have *vyatijajñiṣe* (you have mutually begotten) and *vyatijajñidhve* (you have mutually begotten). The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are used here because of the rule “*kartari karmavyatihāre*” (the ātmanepada is used when there is a reciprocal action). (251) P. 1.2.1: *gāṅkuṭādibhyo’ñṇiti ṅit*. From *gāṅ* and the *kuṭādi* group. Here, the root *gāṅ* meaning "to go" (*gati*) is not included, because it belongs to the *tarṅ* class.

Because the *taṅ* (the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes marked with *ṅ*) has its purpose fulfilled there [in the context of the *kuṭādi* group], whereas the *ṅ* in the substitute (*ādeśa*) has not yet fulfilled its purpose;
since the *taṅ* would already be established by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, he says: "due to the substitute *gāṅ*.
The *kuṭādi* is a sub-group within the *tudādi*. Some, however, hold that the *kuṭādi* are those for which *kuṭ* is the first.

They say that by relying on two types of compounds— namely, *kuṭa-ādiḥ* (the beginning of *kuṭa*) and *kuṭādiśca kuṭādayaśca* (both *kuṭādi* and *kuṭādayaḥ*)— the inclusion of the root *likh* preceded by *kuṭa* is also understood, thereby establishing the usage *kuṭalikhanam*. And that [is supported] by the word *vā* found in the rule *ṭhralo vyupadhād dhalādeḥ saṃśca*.

This contradicts both the commentary (*vṛtti*) which states, "having written (*likhitvā*), having painted (*lakhitvā*), he wishes to write (*likhiṣati*), he wishes to paint (*lekh-iṣati*)," and the Vedic usage found in the sūtra, "in the sense of painting (*ālekhane*), [the root *kṛ* becomes *kṛṇoti*] when not followed by *ku*. Why is it said "not followed by *aṇ*"?
Consider: with the suffix *ghañ*, we have *koṭaḥ* ("a wall") and *poṭaḥ* ("a child"); with the suffix *ṇal*, we have *cukoṭa* ("he cut") and *pupoṭa* ("he split").

(252) *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali* [Pāṇini 6.4.66]. From the rule *īṅe yuḍaci*, the term *kṅti* is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*). The term *ārddhadhātuke* is likewise still in force (*adhikriyate*). What is the purpose of the condition *kṅti*? [Example: *dātā*, *dhātā*. What is the purpose of the condition that the suffix begins with a consonant (*hal-ādau*)? [Example: [The suffix must not be a vowel-initial one.]

[The forms] *dadatuḥ* and *daduḥ* [are derived from the root *dā*]. Otherwise, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the substitution of *ī* (by P. 7.1.100) would occur instead of the elision of the long *ā*. Why [specify] "in an *ārddhadhātuka* affix"? [Observe] *mātaḥ*, *māthaḥ*. [In the form] *adhyagīṣṭa*, the substitution of *ī* occurs because the *sic* affix has the marker *ṅ*. [The root] *ik* means "to remember. Here, the letter *k* is for the purpose of specification, according to the rule "the *ik* is like *ṭhiṇ*" (*ṭhiṇvadikaḥ*). If, however, [the rule] were stated as "after *i*" (*er*), then...

They say that in the case of *ṭhiṭa kiṭa kaṭī*, there would also be the inclusion of the root *ī* (the prashliṣṭa form) because it is included [in the rule]. [The solution is: "It should be stated that [the substitute] is like *iṇ*. Regarding the phrase "some, however": since the rules taught within the jurisdiction of the *ārddhadhātuka* section are present due to the reading of the Vārttika in that jurisdiction, the extension (*atideśa*) applies only to those operations.

This is the intended meaning. Regarding "adhīyan": it means "remembering. Regarding "rāghavayoḥ": here, the genitive case is used according to the rule "the object of verbs meaning 'to study,' 'to remember,' 'to pity,' and 'to rule' takes the genitive. Regarding "vī" (in the sense of motion):
in "aviyan," the substitution *iyaṅ* occurs because it is subsequent to the augment *aṭ*. This is so when the augment *aṭ* is present.

The intention is that [the substitution] is *nitya* (obligatory) merely because it applies whether [the augment] *aṭ* has been applied or not. For this very reason, out of dissatisfaction [with the previous explanation], some have stated [the view] with the following intention: "By the rule *asiddhavadatrābhāt*, since *aṭ* is treated as non-existent when the *yaṇ*-substitution—which shares the same locus—is to be performed, the form *iyāre* is appropriate. Thus it was said, "some [hold this view]."
However, it should be understood that according to the view that "the augment *aṭ* occurs only in this specific state," there is simply *yaṇ*-sandhi.
As for the mention of the vowel *ī*, they indeed employ it—as in: "For the sun rises, its movement dependent upon the quarters. And this has been explained in the *Manoramā*: [text omitted].

"In the case of *vyatihāra* (reciprocity of action), the *ātmanepada* suffix is used; nor should one fear the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.3.15], 'not after roots meaning motion or injury,' because the root preceded by *ut-* here has the sense of manifestation. Regarding this, they say: "To conceive of reciprocity of action without the word *vyati-* is laborious; and as for the action belonging to another..."
In the case of a reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*), mutual dependence is required, and that is present here; however, mutual acting is simply not possible.
Therefore, in the word *codite*, the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) should be understood as denoting the abstract state (*bhāve*).
Thus, the meaning is easily understood as: "at the time of the rising [of the sun], the sun does not have its movement dependent on another direction."

(253) According to Śākaṭāyana alone, [the substitution of *ṇ* occurs] for the root *laṅ*. In *praṇidāti*, there is an optional substitution of *ṇ* by the rule *eṣe vibhāṣā*. In *adāsīt*, because it does not end in a vowel (*aghu*), there is no elision of the *sij* suffix. In *namaḥ khyātre*, if this [root *khyā*] were also employed in the *ārddhadhātuka* domain, then...

The sense is that, because the rule "visarjanīya is substituted [for *r*] when followed by a non-*r*-vowel (*apare*) in the presence of a suffix ending in *tṛ*" would not apply here, the substitution of the *jihvāmūlīya* (the *k*-like spirant) by the rule "after *u*, *p*, or *v*" would be unavoidable; thus, the statement of the Vārttikakāra and others— that "the absence of *at* is the purpose for the inclusion of *khśādi*"— would be contradicted.

Regarding "saṃpūrvasya" and so forth: there is no such usage as *saṅkhyāti* and so on. However, the intention of the author of the Nyāsa is that the form *aṅkhye* arises from the substitution of *khyāñ*. [The root] *mā* means measuring (*māne*). Regarding "not of this": because of the reading *hu-prakṛti-māṅ*, the inclusion there is of the form ending in *ṅ*; and thus, in the case of *eṣe*...

With the intention that "vibhāṣā" (the rule of optionality) implies that only the alternative form (*vikalpa*) proceeds, he says: *praṇimāti*, etc. [The root] *vac* is used in the sense of speaking. [Examples: *uvāca* (he spoke), *vaktā* (speaker), *vakṣyati* (he will speak), *vaktu* (infinitive), *vaktāt* (imperative), *avak* (aorist), *avaktām* (aorist).
This [root] takes the suffix *anti*. And likewise: *vacanti* (they speak), *vakṣyanti* (they will speak), *vacantu* (let them speak), *avacan* (they spoke).

The forms *avocan* and *avakṣyan* are incorrect. [The rule applies] when followed by a plural ending. According to this view, in the present tense (*laṭ*), the second person plural is *vaktha*, while the first person plural is *vacmaḥ*. In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), the third person plural is *ūcuḥ*, the second person plural is *ūca*, and the first person plural is *ūcima*. In the periphrastic future (*luṭ*), it is *vaktāraḥ*. In the benedictive (*liṅ*), it is *ucyāsuḥ*.

*vacyāsuḥ* and other such forms are also incorrect. Regarding the rule *jhiparaḥ*: according to this alternative view (*pakṣa*), *vaktha*, *vacmaḥ*, *ūca*, *ūcima*, and so forth are correct; this is the general direction (*dig*). (254) *vido laṭo vā* |3|4|83|.

The suffix *laṭ* [is intended] after the root *vid*, or it is the fifth case (ablative), not the sixth (genitive). Therefore, because there is no *laṭ* immediately following the roots *vid* (in the sense of "to know") and *vindati* (in the sense of "to find"), these substitutions do not apply.
Thus he says: "of *veti*."

(255) *vidāṅkurvantu* optionally [is used]. Regarding the rule *loṭo luk*: for those who explain the rule *āmaḥ* by carrying forward *leḥ* from the preceding rule *anne ghasaḥ*, [the meaning is] that there is elision (*luk*) of the *liṅ* suffix following *ām*.

This has been stated according to one opinion; however, it should be understood that, in the final analysis, there is elision (*luk*) by that very [rule]. Regarding the phrase "in the person and number" (*puruṣavacane*): the meaning is the first person (*prathamapuruṣa*) and the plural number (*bahuvacana*).
According to the view of some, even the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is not intended to be expressed in the case of reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*).
Let it be understood that *vyatividāṅkurutām*, *vyatividāṅkurvātām*, and so forth, are to be known [as examples].
(256) *tanādikṛñbhya uḥ* | Pāṇini 3.1.79. [The suffix *u* is added after the roots beginning with *tan* and after *kṛñ*.]
The meaning is that by this [rule], the absence of *śap*-elision in the form *viśvaset* is established.
If it is asked, "Even so, how is there an absence of *iṭ* in *aviśvastam*?", understand that it is because the rule concerning augments (*āgama-śāstra*) is not invariably obligatory (*anitya*).

(257) *ata utsārvadhātuke* 6.4.110. What is the purpose of the condition *kṅiti*? [Consider: *karoti*, *karoṣi*. Because the elision (*luk*) is considered as if it had not taken place (*asiddhatva*), the mention of *sārvadhātuka* is necessary only for the sake of what follows; it is not required here. In this case, it is by way of referring to what previously existed (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*).

It should be understood that, according to the view of the *Vṛtti*, there is not even a trace of utility in describing [the substitution] as "not yet established" (*asiddha*), because it relies on the condition of being followed by an affix of the *sārvadhātuka* class. (258) *daśca* | 7|2|75|
The words *api*, *dhātoḥ*, *ruḥ*, and *ve* carry over [from previous rules], as do *padasya* and *anta* from the rule *halāṃ jaśo 'nte*. Thus he says:
"of the *da* of a root," and so forth. Why [specify] *sipi*?
[Because] in *avet* (with *tip*), the desired result would be established by the rule "ru occurs for the *da* of a root ending in *d* before *sip*" alone.

Some say that the recurrence of the term *padānta* (end of a word) [in this rule] serves little purpose; however, that is questionable, because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *vetsi*, since [the *s* there] is a dental due to the *ca*-substitution being treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). (259) *śnasorallopaḥ* | 6.4.111 | [The *a* of the roots *śī* and *as* is elided.]

Regarding *śnasorallopaḥ*: they say that by carrying forward the word *ataḥ* from the rule *ata ut*, the mention of *ad* can be dispensed with. Regarding *śnasoḥ*: he says that the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) is due to the *śakandhvādi* group—namely, *śnaḥ* and *asteḥ*. An example of *śna* is *rundhaḥ*, *rundhanti*, and so forth, when followed by a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*.

What [is it that] obstructs? It exists. Let there be the inclusion of the *ta* (the long vowel marker); for in the case of *āstām* and *āsan*, once the augment *āṬ* has been applied, this is done so that its elision (*lopa*) does not occur. However, the detailed explanation will become clear in the following section.

(260) *ghvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca* | P. 6.4.119. Regarding *ghvasoreddhā*: the substitution of *e* applies to the final letter [of the root], while the elision (*lopa*) applies to the whole [of the reduplicated syllable] because it is marked with the *śi*-pratyaya; this is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and other sources. Thus: *dehi*, *dhehi*. [Objection: But if [the augment] *āṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to this rule, then—[the following objection arises].

If it is argued that the inclusion of *ta* (the long vowel marker) in the rule for *adas* is redundant because the elision (*lopa*) would not occur for the form *an-as*, [the commentators] say here: the inclusion of *ta* is intended to indicate the non-universality (*anityatā*) of the grammatical system (*śāstra*).
By this, forms such as *ebhatu* are established. This might be so; however, some here [object] to the mention of *ad*.

If [the vowel *u*] were fruitless, the fact that the addition of the *tapara* marker (*t*) serves a purpose as an indicator (*jñāpanārthatva*) would not be established. Nor should it be argued that the *tapara* marker in the rule *ata ut* itself must serve as the indicator; for when one says "of this" (*asya*), there is greater complexity (*gaurava*), whereas it can be easily stated that the *tapara* marker is used there [in *ata ut*] for the sake of the brevity of half a mora (*ardhamātrālāghava*).
Therefore, they say that the inclusion of the word *ad* is necessary for the purpose of making the aforementioned point known.
(261) *upasargaprādurbhyāmastiryacparaḥ* |8|3|87|. [The sūtra consists of] *upasargaprādurbhyām*. *prāduḥ* is an indeclinable ending in *s*. In the reading *rāduṣaśca*, [the same applies].

The reading *prādurbhyām* [ending in *m*] is incorrect; therefore, the reading ending in *ṣ* (*prādurbhyaḥ*) found among the ancients is erroneous. Regarding the word *parasya*: this is a qualifier of the *s* of the root *as*, not of the root *as* itself. Consequently, in the case of *prādurasti*, there is no substitution of *ṣ*. Why [is the condition] "after a prefix" (*upasargāt*) stated? [Consider: *dadhi syāt*.

Why [is the condition] "of the root *ās*" stated? [Consider: *parimārṣṭi*. The root *mṛj* means "to clean. This [root] is not marked with the indicatory letter *ṣ*, because of the force of its inclusion in the *bhidādi* group.
(Pāṇini 7.2.114) *vṛddhi* [occurs] for *mṛj*.

"Vṛddhi [is substituted] for the root *mṛj*. This is an exception to [the rule regarding] *guṇa*. He states that "when a grammatical element (*pratyaya*) following a verbal root (*dhātu*) is used to denote the root's own form, the operation is understood to apply to that [element]."—What is the example for "in a verbal root-element"? [Answer: *kaṃsaparimṛḍbhyām*.
"[The substitution occurs] before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*, and before one beginning with a vowel (*ijādi*). And this is the opinion of other grammarians—that [the term] *ika-*...
This was accepted by the author of the Bhāṣya in the sūtra "guṇavṛddhī. [The form] *mṛḍḍhi* is derived as follows:
*herdhiḥ* by the rule "hujhalbhyaḥ raḥ"; then the substitution of *ṣatva*, *ṣṭutva*, and *jaśtva*.
(263) [The rule] "rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke" (Pāṇini 7.2.76).

"Of a sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with *val*. Why "beginning with *val*"? [Consider: *rudanti*. Why "sārvadhātuka"? [Consider: *svaptā*. [Why is there no substitution of *dhi*? Because of the maxim "that which has already occurred once does not recur," or because of the previously mentioned resolution that in the rule *her dhiḥ*, the vowel *i* in both the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
The suffix *bhāva* [is applied].
(264) *rudaśca pañcabhyaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.8: "And after the root *rud*, and after five [roots]. Why say "after five"? [Consider] the *laṅ* of *jāgarti*: *ajajāgar*.

(265) *aṅgārgyagālavayoḥ* |7|3|99|. Regarding the rule beginning with *prakṛtipratyaya* etc.: because they depend upon a suffix beginning with a consonant (*halādi*) that has an indicatory *p* (*pit*), as well as upon a *sārvadhātuka* suffix that is not a single phoneme (*apṛkta*), the augment *aṭ* and the augment *iṭ* are considered *bahiraṅga*. Thus, [we have] *arudit* (with *aṭ*), and *arodīt* (with *iṭ*, by the rule *ṭhīrito vā*).

The augment *īṭ* is applied by the rule "ṭhastisicaḥ. It is not, however, applied by the rule "rudaśca," because the root *rud-* and its class-mates (*rudādi*) are not followed immediately [by the suffix], being separated by *sic*. Regarding *suṣupatuḥ*:
there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "vacisvapi-," followed by reduplication.
(266) *su-vinir-dur-bhyaḥ supi-sūti-samāḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.88. Regarding the rule *supi-sūti-samāḥ*: *ūti* ends in the suffix *ktin*; *ama* ends in the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*).
Examples: *suṣuptiḥ*, *suṣūtiḥ*, *suṣamā*, *viṣamaḥ*. [The rule applies] provided there is no reduplication (*advirvacane*). By that [rule]...
There is doubling of the [consonant] accompanied by the *ṣ* [of *ṣatva*], because there is an absence of the form of a *sup* [suffix]. However,
the principle "that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]" does not apply here,
because it is supplementary to the *sthānivat* rule, and because *ṣatva* belongs to the third section [of Pāṇini’s grammar], and thus [the rule] does not operate with respect to that operation.

They say that this is because there is an absence of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original). However, in reality, it has been stated that the Tripādī is established (*siddha*) with respect to the rule "an ādeśa is like its original" (*sthānivadādeśa*). Therefore, others maintain that another solution must be sought here. (267) *aniteḥ* | Pāṇini 8.4.19.

Regarding *aniteḥ*: from the rule "upasargādasamāse’pi" (*Pāṇini 8.4.14*), the term "upasargāt" (from a prefix) is understood; and from the rule "aṣābhyām" (*Pāṇini 8.4.1*), the phrase "o ṇaḥ" (for *o*, there is *ṇ*) is also understood. Thus he says: "standing after a prefix," and so forth. (268) *adabhyastāt* |7|1|4| [The suffix *at* is substituted for the final vowel of the root *an* when it follows a prefix and is part of a reduplicated stem.]

Regarding the term *antāpavāda*: it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *ad* for [the final consonant] in the word *anta*. However, it should be understood that *jus* is an exception to this. As in *babhrāma*, because the status of being a *jaśādi* (belonging to the *jaś* class) in the *Upaniṣad* passage “*akṣan krīḍan ramamāṇaḥ*” is beyond dispute, [the rule] “*ābhyastāc chatuḥ*” provides a prohibition.

Regarding the form *akṣann*, although the *num* augment is Vedic (*chāndasa*), it is improper to assume that it possesses the status of being a *jaśādi* (belonging to the *jhal* class) for the sake of such an application; furthermore, because [the root] is listed as a *jaśādi* in the *Dhātuvṛtti* and other works. (269) *Jāgro ’viciṇṇalṅitsu* 7.3.85.

Regarding the rule *jāgro ’viciṇṇalṅidbhyo ’nyismin*: [the suffix] *vi* occurs after the root *jāgṛ*. By the word "or" (*vā*), the suffix *in* is also included. According to the opinion of those who state that "the letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation," it does not occur even with the suffix *kvasu*. Examples: *jajāgṛviḥ*; *jajāgṛvān*; *jajāgṛvāṃsau*. With the suffix *ciṇ*: *ajāgāri*.

From the root *jāgṛ* (to wake): In the *ṇal* suffix: *jajāgāra*. In the *ṅti* suffix: *jāgṛtiḥ*. In the *thas* suffix: *jāgṛthaḥ*. Regarding the scope of *vṛddhi*: In the *ṇvul* suffix: *jāgarakaḥ*. In the *ghañ* suffix: *jāgaraḥ*. In the *ṇic* suffix: *jāgarayati*. And it should not be argued that even after *guṇa* has been applied in these cases, *vṛddhi* would still occur by the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116).
Because it would otherwise result in the rule for the prescription of *guṇa* and the prohibition of *ciṇṇal* becoming purposeless.
(270) *jusi ca* | 7.3.83 | Regarding *jusi ca*: the particle *ca* is for the sake of clear comprehension.
He says that from the rule "after *as* and *ac*" (*sasyācī*), the term "*ac*" is understood to carry over; thus he says "before an *aj*-beginning [suffix].

In forms such as *jāgṛyuḥ*, and likewise in *śṛṇuyuḥ*, *cinuyuḥ*, and so forth, it should be understood that there is no *guṇa* substitution. Because the *yāsuṭ* augment has the marker *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* in *śṛṇuyuḥ* and similar forms.

The statement of the *Prācīna* [commentator] has been refuted in the *Manoramā*, on the grounds that [the rule] "usi ca" is an exception (*apavāda*) to the prohibition of *guṇa*. However, some say that there is no such fault because, in the rule "jusi ca," the word "us" is repeated and explained as "in the case of *jus* having the form of *us*. [This refers to the rule] "ajādau jusi."

The resolution, however, is established in the Bhāṣya. He demonstrates the sequence of the application of *yaṇ* and so forth when *iṭ* is added to the root *jāgṛ*—in the phrase "here, *jāgṛ-is*"—and regarding the words "that being done":
there is an annulment (*bādha*) of the *vṛddhi* prescribed for roots ending in a consonant by the *guṇa* of *jāgṛ*; therefore...

This is because the status of having a final consonant (*halantatva*) is established by means of the *guṇa* substitution. The sense is that when *guṇa* is about to take effect, it is the *vṛddhi* that is sublated, and nothing else. Examples include *ajāgariṣṭām*, *ajāgariṣuḥ*, *ajāgarīt*, and so forth. [Now for the root] *daridrā*.
(271) *iddaridrasya* |6|4|114|. It would be more appropriate to state *iddaridra*. (272) *śnābhyastayorātaḥ* |6|4|112|.

[The forms] *śnabhyasta-krīṇanti*, *krīṇate*, *punanti*, *punate*, *dadhati*, and *dadhate* [are examples]. Why [is the condition] "before a suffix marked with K or Ṅ" (*kṅiti*) specified? [Because otherwise one would get] *krīṇāti*, *punāti*, and *dadhāti*. Why [is the condition] "of a long vowel *ā*" (*ātaḥ*) specified? [Because otherwise one would get] *bibhrati*. [Objection: Since the result is already established by the rule for *o* (P. 6.4.120), [the mention of *ā* is redundant]. [Response: The point is that there is no evidence for abandoning the first [condition, i.e., *ātaḥ*]. [Objection: It is entirely baseless [to claim such evidence exists].

As for what is argued by the commentators— that in the absence of *ām*, once the *ā* is elided, the substitution of *au* (for the final vowel and following consonant) does not apply because the condition of ending in *ā* is no longer met— that is incorrect. For in the rule *āta au ṇalaḥ*,
although the substitution of *o* should have been prescribed first, the prescription of *au* ensures that it applies even when there is elision of the *ā* of the root *daridrāti*.

This is because it contradicts the works of Haradatta, Mādhava, and others, who state that the *liṅga* (the grammatical gender) exists for the sake of hearing [the sound] when there is a constant presence,

as well as contradicting his own treatise. As for the argument that the substitution of *au* does not apply because the two measures (*mātrā*) of the vowels *o* and *au* are indistinguishable, and thus the rule for *au* is prescribed— this too [is incorrect].
It would be more appropriate [to read it as a locative]. For in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the elision of *ām* could not be prevented.
It should be stated that when an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix is intended to follow, the elision of the *ā* of the root *daridrāti* occurs. Regarding the word "intended" (*vivakṣite*):
by this, in the case of *daridrāti*, the form *daridra-* is derived only by means of the *pacādyac* suffix. However, if it were a locative in the sense of "following" (*parasaptamī*), then...

The sense is that by the rule *yādvyadhi*, etc., there would be the suffix *ṇa* characterized by a final vowel; if that were present, then by the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*, the augment *yuk* would apply, resulting in *daridrāya*. Regarding the phrase *sani ṇvuli*: the meaning is that in these cases (the suffixes *san* and *ṇvul*), there is no elision of the penultimate vowel (*ālopa*). Thus: *didaridrāsati* and *daridrāyakaḥ*.

Regarding *daridrāṇām* and *adaridruḥ*: the substitution of *jus* for *jhi* occurs by the rule *ij-abhyastāt*. The optional substitution [of *śn*] characterized by a final vowel, which would apply according to *aṅ-śākaṭāyanasyaiva*, does not take place here; because it is superseded by the subsequent rule *na-abhyastayoḥ*, which causes the elision (*lopa*) of the *ā* of the reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*), there is no longer any form ending in *ā* remaining. *Ī*...

In the case of *haly-agh-oḥ*, the substitution of *ī* for *ā* should not even be suspected here; the point is that because the suffix *jus* follows a consonant (*hal*), it lacks the status of being followed by a vowel (*at*). Now, one might object: when *daridrā-jhi* is present, since the rule for *ī*-substitution is both subsequent and an exception (*apavāda*) to the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*), would it not apply before *jus*? Not so.

Because the prohibition regarding *akṛtavyūha* is active; for the status of beginning with a consonant (*halāditva*) is the cause for the substitution of *ī*, and that [status] is on the verge of being destroyed, since the *jus* is about to occur. [The rule] "for *jha*, *at*" [is applied] by the rule "after a reduplicated stem" (*adabhyastāt*). [The rule] "except for *asti*" applies to *tip*. Why "of a word-final"? [Consider] *cakāsti*. [The rule] "of *s*"...
What [is the example]? *avaṭ*—this is from the root *vaś* with the suffix *laṅ* and the suffix *tip*. What for *tip*? *cakāḥ*—this is with the suffix *kvip*.
What for *anasteḥ* (not being *as*)? *sarvam*, *idam*. The form *āḥ* is the form of *as* with *laṅ* and *tip*; by the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*,” the augment *īṭ* does not occur.

(273) *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.34. The substitution of *i* for the root *śās* occurs before the affixes *aṅ* and those marked with *k* or *ṅ*. Before *aṅ*: *aśiṣat*. Before *kṅit* affixes: *śiṣṭaḥ*, *śiṣṭavān*, *śiṣyāt*, *śiṣyāstām*. Due to its association (*sāhacarya*) with *aṅ*, this substitution of *i* occurs only before Parasmaipada endings; it does not occur here [in the following cases].

He expresses this hope: others, however, having explained that the substitution of *i* occurs only for that [root] from which the suffix *aṅ* arises, accept the substitution of *i* even in the *ātmanepada* forms *vyatiśiṣṭe* and *vyatiśiḍhve*.

(274) *śā hau* | 6|4|35|. Regarding *śā hau*: [the rule] states that there is the substitution of *śā*. Although the form *śādhi* is established by the elision of *s* (*salopa*) through the rule *hi ca*, the elision of *s* (*salopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of subsequent rules; consequently, the substitution of *i* (*itvam*) would apply by the rule *āsaḥ*. To prevent this, [the rule *śā hau* is stated].
They say this is the rule for the prescription [of the augment].

(275) *yīvarṇayordīdhīvevyoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.53. Regarding *yīvarṇayoḥ*: although it would have been sufficient to state *yvoḥ*, the expression "of the letters *ya* and *i*" (*yakārekārayoḥ*) is used [for clarity].

The mention of the letter *y* (in the rule) was made so that there would be clear comprehension. Regarding the phrase "the two sounds *y* and *i*": here, the letter *i* is for the purpose of pronunciation and is not intended to be significant;
thus he says: "in [the presence of] the letter *y* and the sound *i*. This refers to the expression "of the two sounds *y* and *i*."
The reading "bādhitvā" (having set aside) is appropriate. As for the elision of *r* (*ralopa*), the examples are:
*ādīdhya gataḥ*, *āvevya gataḥ*; *dīdhitā*, *dīdhiṣyate*; *vevitā*, *veviṣyate*.
Why [is it said] "of *y* and *ivarṇa*"? [Consider: *ādīdhyanaṃ*, *āvevyanaṃ*. [The root] *ṣas*: *asaditi*.
In *asipyanaste*, the substitution of *d* occurs [by Pāṇini 8.2.36]. Regarding *asaḥ*: by [Pāṇini 8.2.41] *ipi dhātoḥ*, there is optionally *r*;

in the alternative case, *d*. Regarding *santi*: because it is marked with the *it* indicatory letter *t*, *num* is inserted; thus, when we have *sansanti*, the *s* is dropped by [Pāṇini 8.2.23] *skoḥ*.
Then, by [Pāṇini 8.4.65] *haro jhari savarṇe*, the *t* is optionally elided. Thus: *saṃsti*, *saṃsta*.

Thus [it is said]. Here too, as before, the elision (*lopa*) of the *v* should be understood. The root *vaś* means "to desire. Its usage is also seen in the common language (*bhāṣā*), as in: "Bhāguri effects the elision of the *al* [suffix]" (*vaṣṭi bhāgurirallopam*) and "the gods desire Senānī" (*ayāya senānyamuśanti devāḥ*). (Ga) *carkarītaṃ ca*: this is a *gaṇa*-sūtra; *carkarīta* refers to...

The term *yaṅluganta* is a designation used by the ancient masters (*pūrvācāryas*). It should be understood as belonging to the *adādi* class. By this, the meaning is that in the case of *yaṅluganta* forms, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap* according to the rule "after roots beginning with *ṭhadi*.
However, the Easterners (*prācām*) have stated that *arkarītam* is a *parasmaipada* form ending in *yaṅluk*.
That [topic] has been set aside here because it is not relevant to the present context.
Thus ends the section on the *ad*-class roots in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
Now begins the section on masculine nouns ending in vowels (*ajanta-puṃliṅga-prakaraṇam*).

(146) *arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam* | 1.2.45. Now begins the section on masculine stems ending in vowels (*ajanta-puṃliṅga-prakaraṇam*). Regarding the rule *arthavad adhātu*: the sense is that both [the terms *pratyaya* and *pratyayānta*] are intended in the sūtra by means of *tantra* and other methods; thus it says *arthavat*.
In accordance with the neuter designation [of the compound], he supplies a qualifying term—namely, "the nature of the word" (*śabdasvarūpam*).

They say that the masculine designation in the rule *adhātur apratyayaḥ* is to be understood as having the gender of the final member of the compound, according to the principle: "The gender of a *dvandva* or *tatpuruṣa* is like that of its last member. If...

However, if it is explained that a "non-suffix" (adhātu) is a suffix applied [to a base] while abandoning its original meaning, then it should be understood that there is no possibility of the neuter gender arising at all. Why [is the term] "meaningful" (arthavat) specified? [So that] in cases such as *hanaṃ* and *ṭhvana*, the designation [of "suffix"] does not apply to every individual phoneme.

And when that [suffix] exists, there would be [the application of] *svādi* suffixes. If it is argued that this will not occur because of the absence of number, object, and so forth, we say no; for according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "the singular number shall be applied by way of default (*utsarga*)," the suffix *su* would be unavoidable, just as it is after words such as *huṃ* and *phaṭ*. Not so.

It should not be argued that [the rule] would not apply to a meaningless element due to the *paribhāṣā* regarding the mention of meaningful items, because that *paribhāṣā* pertains only to cases where a specific form is explicitly mentioned. In the case of *rādūhoḍha*, however, the specific form *ūḍha* is mentioned; therefore, there is the inclusion of the word *uḍha*—which is a part of the suffix *ktavat* and is itself meaningless.

It has been said "no," for here there is no such inclusion of a specific form. Although meaningfulness is obtained through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of "that which is not a verbal root" and so forth, nevertheless, the mention of "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is placed right here for the sake of clarity in understanding, even though it is required for the subsequent rule. It is not...

One might object that, according to the principle of singular and dual forms, the designation would apply only to the whole and not to its parts; thus, the inclusion of the term *arthavat* (meaningful) here would be redundant. However, this is not a valid concern, because when a whole is repeated, its parts are also repeated—just as a tree, when it moves, moves together with its branches.

This is according to the maxim "that which moves [is considered to move its parts]"; however, here there is a disparity because the designation of *prātipadika* (nominal stem), which applies to the whole, does not result in that same grammatical operation for the individual parts. For this very reason, it is stated: "Where many consonants (*hal*) are joined together, the designation of *saṃyoga* (conjunction) applies without distinction to any two or to many."

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is thus consistent. Otherwise, according to the logic you have presented, the designation "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) would apply only to the aggregate as a whole. Regarding this, some [object]: even though the designation [of "consonant"] applies to each individual letter in words such as *dhanaṃ* and *vanaṃ*, there is no harm [to the grammatical operation], even when the case-endings beginning with *sva-* (i.e., *su*, *au*, *jas*) are present.

[The final *s*] is elided by the rule *ṭh-ḷ-ṅy-āp* etc. Nor should one fear that the *n*-elision and the *jaś*-substitution (of *dh* to *d*) would apply; for they say that such [operations] do not take effect due to the force of the specific pronunciation of *hana* and *vana* in the Dhātupāṭha. That is incorrect.

Because *ru* is applied when the suffix *su* arises from *kārāt*. Although *ru* would not apply because the suffix *sup* is elided (*luk*) as part of the entire nominal stem (*prātipadika*), nevertheless,
in cases such as *cikīrṣati* and *vidma*, since the letter *r* and the letter *d* are at the end of a word (*padānta*), [the rule applies].

The point is that there would be the contingency of the *visarga* [being replaced] by the rule *“haravasānayoḥ”* and the contingency of the *anunāsika* [substitution] by the rule *“ṭhyaro ’nunāsike”*. Why [is it specified] “not a verbal root” (*adhātuḥ*)? [Consider the example] *ahan*.

If a verbal root were to receive the designation of *prātipadika*, then because the *tiṅ*-suffixes would be an exception (*apavāda*) to the *svādi* suffixes, [the form] *ahan* [would not be established as it should].

Even when *sip* is applied [after *han*], since the designation of the base (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) established previously has not been removed—despite the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule *ṭi-lopa* and the elision of the consonant by the rule *hal-ṅy-ādi-lopa*—the elision of *n* by the rule *alopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* would occur; let this not happen. Thus, the substitution of *r* by the rule *ahan* [is applied].

Furthermore, the substitution of *ratva* for *o* in the word *oḥ supi* need not be suspected here, because it is merely a technical (*lākṣaṇika*) rule. Nor should it be argued that, under the view that the application of rules occurs at the time of the formation of the word (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the designation of *prātipadika* would be absent due to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of items ending in an affix, and thus the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not take place; for, by the principle of "as if the affix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the aforementioned exclusion does not apply.

This is because it has been made known by the prohibition [of *na-lopa*] in the rule "a ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ. Otherwise, how could there be the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) in forms such as *rājā*? Even though, according to the theory of etymological derivation (*vyutpattipakṣa*), the word *rājan* ends in the suffix *kanin*, and thus in forms like *rājā* the designation of base (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) applies by the rule "ṛtaddhite," [the elision would still not occur].
There would be the elision of the *n* (nalopa), and thus the prohibition "a ṅsibanadhdyoḥ" would not serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Consequently, under the view that rules apply at the time of their operation (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the inclusion of the term "non-root" (*adhātu*) [in Pāṇini 6.4.13] would be redundant. Nevertheless, since it does indeed serve as an indicator under the view that words are not derivationally formed (*avyutpattipakṣa*), it must be accepted as such even under the *kāryakāla* view; nor does [the rule] "upo dhātvoḥ" [apply here].
It should be stated that this designation does not apply to a verbal root (*dhātu*) because the term "verbal root" is mentioned separately from "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) in the *sūtra*;

for otherwise, the mention of "verbal root" would be purposeful in cases such as *utrīyati*, where it occurs at the end of an affix. Why [is it specified] "not an affix"? [Consider] *hariṣu* and *karoṣi*. Here, [the designation] must not apply to the *sup* and *sip* affixes.

Why is it not [considered] ending in a suffix? [The answer is: so that [the designation *prātipadika*] does not apply to those very forms when they are qualified by case-endings (*vibhakti*). Nor should it be argued that, by virtue of the rule of "behaving like the end" (*antavadbhāva*), the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) would indeed apply to forms such as *āṇḍe* and *uḍaḷe*;
for if that were the case, the shortening prescribed by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake* would apply, and the suffix *su* would consequently arise.

The direction is that, by the mention in rules such as *aptamyadhikaraṇe ca*, it is not accepted that a single substitute for case-endings (*vibhaktyekādeśa*) possesses the status of being "like the final" (*antavadbhāva*). Now, one might object:
the exclusion of suffixes (*pratyayaparyudāsa*) need not be formulated, since its purpose is already served by the exclusion of words ending in suffixes (*pratyayāntaparyudāsa*).

If it is argued that this [suffix] also ends in a suffix by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it is not so; for when a suffix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed, and a solitary [element] is not of such a nature. Otherwise, even *su*, *tiṅ*, and *ṅ* would possess the status of a word (*pada*) because they too would end in a suffix.

And likewise, in cases such as *hariṣu* and *aroṣī*, the substitution of *ṣ* would not occur, because of the prohibition [stated in the rule] "after a word ending in *āpta*, *pada*, etc. Nor is the rule for the substitution of *ṣ* without scope, since it finds its application in forms such as *arpiṣe* and *eṣa*. However, others [hold that...]

They explain: for in the rule *kṛttaddhita* (Pāṇini 1.2.46), the extension of the rule to include that which ends with those [suffixes] (*tadantavidhi*) will be stated. Thus, by relying on the restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatā*) of the mention of *taddhita*—namely, that the technical designation applies only to those ending in *taddhita* suffixes and not to those ending in other suffixes—the exclusion of suffixes (*pratyayāntaparyudāsa*) need not be made here. Or else:

Since it is established by the inclusion of the word *sāti* in the rule *ātpadādyoḥ* that a suffix (*pratyaya*) is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the explicit mention of "suffix" (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) there must, by implication, refer to that which ends in a suffix (*tadanta*). As for the mention of "secondary suffix" (*taddhita*) in the subsequent rule, let it be taken as serving merely the purpose of a formal injunction (*vidhi*). Alternatively, since the inclusion of *sāti* establishes that a suffix lacks the status of a nominal stem, [the subsequent mention of *taddhita* is required].

Furthermore, if the mention of *taddhita* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) according to the aforementioned method, then it would be more appropriately stated that "a meaningful element that is not a root is a *prātipadika*"; in that case, the rule *iko yaṇaci* would be redundant. [The phrase] *asmādityuttarasya*...
Because the desired result is established by the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of such rules as *ṭhvāyvṛtupitruṣasaḥ*,
even the root text of the *Mūlagrantha*— namely, *ājjhalau*, where *aj* is defined as a vowel accompanied by the letter *ā*—
would be contradicted; for the absence of *ḍha*-substitution is established precisely by the indicative power of examples such as *ālasamaya-velāsu*.

If it is argued that rejection by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is improper, and if it is further asserted that the very mark for that [rejection] lies in the elision of the vowel *ā* (*ākārapraśleṣa*), such that the desired result is established by the very words of the sūtra itself— then, having accepted the suffix *ṭha*, the mention of *āti* would be the mark for the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of suffixes.

If, however, the purpose is to exclude suffixes ending in other suffixes, then let the term *taddhita* be mentioned [in the rule], and let the term *apratyaya* itself be repeated and explained; what is the use of this convoluted construction? This is the general direction. Since the form would be established by the rule *na dhātu-pratyayau*, the employment of two negative particles (*nañ*) is for the sake of facilitating the repetition of the term *apratyaya*.
The formation of these great designations is in accordance with traditional scripture (*śruti*). Thus it is recited in the *Atharvaṇa*:

"What is the root (*dhātu*), what is the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and what is the suffix (*pratyaya*)? In this context, words such as *ḍittha* and so forth serve as examples; for this very [point] is the basis for the theory of non-etymological derivation (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*).

The ancients [hold that this rule] is merely indicative (*jñāpaka*). In reality, however, the moderns maintain that the rule is intended for cases such as *ahupaṭavaḥ* (those who are not very skillful) under the view that words are derived through etymological analysis (*vyutpattipakṣe*). Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the rule should simply have been formulated as *ahucpūrvaḥ prātipadikam*;
for [in that case], there would be no basis for the elision of the *taddhita* suffix in forms such as *ūlakenopadaṃśam*.

Because there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) due to the fact that [words] ending in *kṛt* suffixes are included; for even those preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* are *kṛdanta*. Nor can one find a solution by claiming that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because without the formulation of the *arthavat*-sūtra, it is impossible for the mention of "compound" to function as a restrictive rule.

(147) *Kṛt*, *taddhita*, and *samāsa* [are meaningful]. 1.2.46. *Kṛt*, *taddhita*, and *samāsa* [are meaningful]. The term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is understood from the previous rule; by virtue of that, the rule applies to that which ends in these [suffixes]. Now, if "meaningful" is intended in an ultimate sense, that [quality] belongs only to a word (*pada*) or a sentence (*vākya*).
But this does not apply to that which ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix; however, if what is postulated during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) is intended,

then since such [postulation] exists for *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes as well, how can there be a reference to those ending in them by means of the continued application of the rule "that which has meaning" (*arthavat*)?

If they say to this: "For this very reason, the capacity of the term *arthavat* (meaningful) has been stated. For here, that meaning which is perceived through a suffixal element that has attained a unified meaning (*ekārthībhūta*) is what is grasped; because it is more closely related to the worldly meaning, and because the possessive suffix *matup* refers to excellence (*prāśastya*), it is that [suffixal meaning] alone which is grasped. And for this very reason:

The inclusion of that [term] is purposeful; for, since the previous sūtra [Pāṇini 6.4.170] states "after a root ending in ṛ," and because an exclusion (paryudāsa) would apply in cases such as "artā" (from the root *ṛ*) and "āṬpagava" (ending in the suffix *ap*), the present rule "ṛtaddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.151) is commenced.
It is for the sake of restriction (niyamārtha). Nor is it the case that an exclusion based on being "ending in a suffix" would apply here.
It should not be suspected that [the rule] is intended for the sake of an injunction (*vidhi*); for the word [in question] does not end in a suffix (*apratyayāntatvāt*).

When there is the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇe*), only that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed is understood. Nor, even so, does this apply to a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) that is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*).

It might be argued that, because there is no restriction regarding the initial [element] of that [suffix], the rule should apply for the sake of a prescriptive injunction (*vidhi*) in cases such as *rājakumārī*, which ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. However, this is not so; for, according to the principle that "an external operation (*bahiraṅga*) subverts even internal operations (*antaraṅga*)," the elision (*lop*) prescribed by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68) does not take effect when the suffix is subject to elision (*luk*). Consequently, the case-ending (*sup*) remains audible.

Because the formation of a compound occurs [only] when the word *kumārī* is in the state of ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). In that context, although the word *kumārī* ends in a case-suffix, the word *kumārī* joined with *rājan* does not; thus, since it does not end in an affix (*apratyayānta*), the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) [of "compound"] applies easily even after the elision of the case-suffix (*vibhaktiluk*) by the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). For this very reason...

In cases such as *omatpriya*, the augment *num* and others do not apply; however, they would indeed apply if the internal (*antaraṅga*) elision of the case-endings *has* and *ṅi* occurred prior to the elision (*luk*). This is the general direction. He states the body of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) as: "wherein there is a cluster [of sounds]. And here, the restriction is with respect to its own class (*sajātīyāpekṣa*).

Thus he says: "The prior member is the *pada*. Since the status of being a *pada* for the prior member is never absent across all six types of compounds, this [prior member] is a homogeneous instance. The phrase "the prior member" is an illustration; it should also be understood that "the subsequent member, however, is not a suffix (*pratyaya*). Otherwise, [the definition would fail].

In cases such as *anmavān*, the designation [of "word"] would not apply because the preceding portion is a word by virtue of the rule *vādiṣu*. Nor should it be argued that it must indeed apply there due to the force of the mention of *taddhita* [in Pāṇini 1.4.14], for the mention of *taddhita* has its purpose fulfilled in examples such as *hānava*, where the preceding portion [is indeed a word]. For in that case, [the preceding portion]...

It is *bhatva* (the status of being a *bha*), and not *padatva* (the status of being a word). Nor should it be argued that, in this way, a collection such as *ayamiyān* would necessarily possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*), because even if the preceding portion were a word (*pada*), the subsequent portion would still be a suffix (*pratyaya*), and thus it could not be excluded by this restrictive rule.

In the rule *ṭhuto ra pratyayo na*, the explanation is that "the suffix not prescribed as *advihita* is *na*. Why [is it said] "the preceding portion is a *pada*"? So that the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) may apply to that which is qualified by the suffix *bahuc*. By this, in the example *atipaṭavaḥ*, the acute accent on the penultimate syllable (*upottama*) is established.

In the case of the elision (*luk*) of *jas* after the first [suffix], once the *cit*-accent has been applied by the rule "this [accent applies] to the entire base along with its suffix for the sake of the plural marker *ajakar*" (*bahvakajartham*), *jas* arises again; if, however, the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) were not present, the acute accent would belong to *jas* itself. Or rather, if it applies to a composite whole that has not yet entered into the relationship of base and suffix, then...
The mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of restriction, meaning that [the rule applies] only to a compound.
Consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *gavity ayam āha* ("He says 'cow'"). This is the general direction. He states the result of the restriction:
"Therefore, not for a sentence. The meaning is that it does not apply to a sentence such as *ām abhyāja śuklām*.

For if the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) were present, there would be elision of the case-ending (*subluk*). Now, one might argue that even so, the designation for a sentence such as *‘ūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte’* (he eats with a side-dish of *ūlaka*) would be unavoidable, because "when *ṛt* is mentioned [in a rule], that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is also included. But this is not so.

Because it is superseded by the restriction resulting from the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*), [the *kṛt* rule] is barred due to its being subsequent. And thus, in the rule *ṛtaddhite*, the maxim regarding the mention of *kṛt* (*kṛdgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) does not apply, as it would be rendered fruitless. The scope of that maxim, however, is found in examples such as *vyāvakrośī* and *vyāvahāsī*; for in those cases, [the *kṛt* suffixes are indeed added after a compound].

Regarding the rule *‘armavyatihāre ṇac striyām’*, when the suffix *ṇac* is applied to the root, because it is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) and ends in *ṇac*, the suffix *añ* is added by the rule *‘ṇacaḥ striyām’*. Consequently, the initial *vṛddhi* and accentuation apply to the vowel of the prefix. When a *kṛt* suffix is included [in the definition of a compound], this serves as an example even for a case where a *kāraka* (case-relation) precedes: *avatapte*.

The passage beginning with "nakulasthitam" and so forth will become clear later. The particle *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by this, the Vārttika—"the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) should be stated for a meaningless particle"—becomes redundant. This [rule] is intended for those cases where there is no meaning even to be indicated (*dyotya*), such as in the word *avadyati*.

In the case of imitative sounds (*anukaraṇa*), however, when there is an intention to express non-difference from the original sound (*anukārya*) that they imitate, they lack the status of being meaningful (*arthavattva*) and therefore do not possess the status of nominal stems (*prātipadika*). This is as in the case of *hū* [in the rule] "hū satāyām. But when there is an intention to express difference, they would certainly be nominal stems, as in the case of *bhuvaḥ* [in the rule] "bhuvo vuk."
(148) *pratyayaḥ* | 3|1|1| This is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*). The meaning is that the word *pratyaya* is introduced as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*). (149) *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* | 4|1|1|

"From a nominal stem ending in *ṅī* or *ā*" (*ṅyāpprātipadikāt*). The singular number is used for a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*). The term "ī" is a general reference to the suffixes *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn*. Likewise, "ā" refers to *ṭāp*, *ḍāp*, and *cāp*. This continues until the completion of the fifth book (*āpañcamaparisamāpteḥ*). Now, one might object: [is this not covered by] the rule "in the case of words denoting time and *tana*-suffixes"? (*hakālataneṣu*)...

If it is asked, "Since it is accepted that the production of taddhita suffixes occurs from a word ending in a case-suffix (subanta) by virtue of an indicator (jñāpaka), what is the purpose of the governing rule (adhikāra) regarding nominal stems (prātipadika) in the section on taddhitas?", they reply as follows: If this governing rule did not exist, then in the rule *ata iñ* ("*iñ* after [a stem] ending in short *a*"), the phrase *ataḥ* would qualify only a word ending in a case-suffix; and consequently...

In the case of *dakṣasyāpatyam*, the suffix *iñ* should apply here alone, but not in cases such as *dakṣayoḥ* or *dakṣāṇām*. Furthermore, in the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*, let the term *vṛddha* not be a qualifier of the inflected word (*subanta*). Otherwise, in the derivation of *jñānām ayam*: [from] *jñānti* [they know] = *jñāḥ* (where *ka* is applied by the rule *ig-upadha-kaḥ*), [if *vṛddha* qualified the inflected form], then in *jñānām ayam*, [the suffix *cha* would not apply].

Due to its being a *vṛddha* (polysyllabic) word, the suffix *cha* does not apply; rather, it is *aṇ* that applies. However, if this governing rule (*adhikāra*) did not exist in the *Śabdakaustubha*, suffixes such as *kap* could arise even after a sentence (*vākya*).
Consequently, since the qualified member (*viśeṣya*) would possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the elision of all case-endings (*sup*) would result in a clearly undesirable outcome.

[The word] "sthitam" [is used]. "[Of that which is qualified by a gender-marker]" means: even of that which is qualified by a suffix that indicates gender. The purpose of this paribhāṣā is as follows: *śvaśrūḥ*. Although it is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) because it ends in a suffix, here the case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) do apply.

Nor should it be argued that the formation of *sva* is established solely by the mention [in the sūtra] of *śvaśuraḥ śvaśrūḥ*; for that mention refers to the word-form itself, just as in the cases of *vipārābhyāṃ jeḥ* and *ReĀryaḥ*. Furthermore, in the derivation of *kumārayati* from *kumārīm ācaṣṭe*, there is the elision of the suffix *ṭilopa* according to the rule *ṇāviṣṭhava*. Thus...

In the example *ahāni rātrīyantīva* ("the days act like nights"), the suffix *kvip* also serves as a result [of the rule]; this is because of the statement "before the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp*" (*ṅyābbhyāṃ prāk*). By that [rule], forms such as *thenikā* and *āryakā* are established. For instance, the suffix *ka*, which will be taught as being purely pleonastic (*atyantasvārthika*) by the rule "not when expressing a part" (*na sāmivacane*), [is applied here].

The suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* would be superseded by these two [suffixes] *ṭha* and *ika*; consequently, the forms would have been only *ṭhetikā* and *ṭhāryikā*. However, by virtue of the inclusion of *ṅī* and *āp*, the form *ṭhenikā* is also established from a word ending in *ṅīp* when followed by the suffix *kan*, because the rule *varṇādanudātād* is optional. Furthermore, [the form *ṭhenikā*] is also established from a word ending in *āp* when followed by *kan*.

However, because of the optional substitution of *i* by the rule "tuṣṭhūdīcām ātaḥ sthāne," the two forms *āryaka* and *āryikā* are established. In reality, however, the mention of the suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* need not be included;
for, by the force of the rule prescribing non-elision (*aluk*) in the expression "hakālataneṣu," the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) arises from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).
This is the essential point. Thus, the suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* operate even before the case endings (*sup*).

This should be noted because it is accepted that the operations triggered by the meanings of the base—namely, its own meaning (*svārtha*), substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and grammatical relation (*kāraka*)—occur in a sequential order.

(150) *sv-au-jas-am-auṭ-śas-ṭā-bhyām-bhis-ṅe-bhyām-bhyas-ṅasi-bhyām-bhyas-ṅas-os-ām-ṅi-os-sup* || 4.1.2 || The term *sv-au-jas-am-auṭ* is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). [The sequence] *su-ṅ-sy-auḥ* [is formed]; the letter *u* in *su* is for the sake of pronunciation (*ukāraḥ*).

In the rule *ṭhasya ṭhaḥ*, the letter *ṭha* serves as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). For if only *ṭha* were stated, the substitution would apply to the letter *ṭha* following an *a*-vowel; consequently, forms such as *vājam arvatsu* would not be established.
The letter *i* in *ṅsi* is for the purpose of [including] the rules *āṅsiṅsośca* and *ṅsiṅyoḥ smātsminau*.

The *ja*- and *śa*-sounds in the forms *jaśśasoḥ* and *jakāraśakārau* are for the purpose of distinguishing the respective domains of the rules *asaḥ śī* and *tasmāc chaso naḥ*. [If it is argued: "Let one of these two [the *j* and *ś*] simply be without an *anubandha*," [we reply: No; for in the absence of the *ja*-sound, the rule *āṬ* [would apply].

If *āv* were [the substitute], then the suffix would be possible as ending in *v*; likewise, in the absence of the *ś* of *śas*, the status of *āṬ* as having the marker *ṅ* (indicating that it causes the elision of the penultimate vowel) would be possible, and consequently, there would be elision of the *ṭi* in forms such as *ejasi*. Alternatively, in cases such as *ihā*, by virtue of the power of the marker *ṅ*, even that which is not a *bha* [would undergo elision].
The elision of the *ṭ* might be suspected. The *ṭ* in *āṬ* is for the purpose of forming the pratyāhāra *uḍ*.

However, the *ṭ* in *ṭā* is for the purpose of distinguishing it in the rules "āṅsiṅsām" and "dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ. By this, that which was stated by the author of the Kāśikā regarding the sūtra "ādirantyena"—namely, [the inclusion of the first letter] with the last—is [addressed].

Why [is this said]? [Because] it was rejected [by others] with the thought, "Let it not be [the case that the substitute occurs] by means of the single element *u*, which is the third person singular ending. This is because the inclusion of the letter *ṭ* serves another purpose, and because [the substitution] is possible through that very [element], due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). For this very reason, in the *Śabdakaustubha*, something else is stated there.

The purpose has been stated: "By means of the term 'with the last' (*antya*), it is grasped so that the first vowel (*ādi*), when accompanied by the middle vowel (*madhyama*), might not also be a grasper for those that follow; and by means of the term 'with the first' (*ādi*), it is grasped so that the middle vowel, when accompanied by the last vowel, might not also [be a grasper] for those that precede. Keeping this very meaning in mind...
