Having set aside [the previous point]—it was stated previously that "by means of the initial and final constituent parts, the whole aggregate is implied"—we now follow the present subject: the letter *ṅ* in *ReĀ* and so forth is for the purpose of specification, as in the rules "ṅti" (*herṅiti*) and "ReĀrām. However, the letter *p* in *sup*...
The purpose is for the sake of exclusion (*pratyāhāra*).
(151) *vibhaktiśca* | 1.4.104 | "And [the term] *vibhakti*. From the rule "iṅstrīṇi trīṇi—" [1.4.103], the mention of *tiṅ* is understood even though it is separated [by intervening rules].

It continues by the force of its *svarita* accent; and intending that "upaḥ" is also proximate, they say: "sup-tiṅ-av". The purpose of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *tiṅ* as a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is [stated in the rule] "a-vibhaktau tu-smāḥ". For *sup*, however, there are also purposes such as the substitution of *yat* for pronouns beginning with *tyad*.

The particle *ca* (and) serves the purpose of ensuring the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the two designations, "person" (*puruṣa*) and "number" (*vacana*). Otherwise, because of the governing rule of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), there would be an option (*paryāya*) between the two designations due to the authority of both sets of rules, such as those for the singular number (*ekavacana*) and so forth.
Consequently, in forms such as *rāmebhyaḥ* and *amāma*, in the case where the designation "plural" (*bahuvacana*) applies...

Because it lacks the status of being a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the letter *s* would receive the designation *it*. "In this case too" means even in this system [of grammar], in rules such as *Pāṇini 2.3.46*: *arātipadikārthaliṅgaparimāṇavacanamātre prathamā*.

Regarding *supaḥ*: here he explains that from the sūtra *iṅstrīṇi trīṇi*, the phrase *trīṇi trīṇi* and the sūtra *ānyekavacane* continue [into subsequent rules] with the exception of the word *āni*. This is stated by the words *supastrīṇi trīṇi* and so forth. The term *ekaśaḥ* means "one by one" (*ekaikam*).
By the rule *saṅkhyaikavacanācca*, the suffix *śas* is applied after a word ending in the nominative case when expressing repetition (*vīpsā*).
(153) *dvayekayordvivacanaikavacane* 1.4.22: [The dual and singular endings are used] for two and one. Here, the words *dvi* and *eka*— [End of fragment]

Intending to refer to those that transcend number (*saṅkhyāparau*), he says: "of duality and unity. The implication is that if they were intended as the objects of numbering (*saṅkhyeyaparatve*), the plural form would have been used.
(Pāṇini 1.4.21): "The plural is used for many."

Regarding the word *bahuṣu* (in many): he says that this too refers specifically to number—namely, "in plurality" (*bahutve*). As for the plural ending, it is employed by superimposing the plurality residing in the substratum substances onto the property [of number] itself. Its purpose, however, is merely to indicate that the term "many" (*bahu*) as used here does not include the sense of "vastness" found in expressions such as *bahuḥ parvataḥ* ("a large mountain"). In reality...
That [objection] is futile, because the singular number is possible due to its being *para* (subsequent); this is established in the *Śabdakaustubha* and other works.

Regarding the statement "the *ru*-sound and the visarga": [an objection is raised]—"But surely, since the *ru*-substitution is *asiddha*, the *it*-designation and elision of the vowel *u* do not occur; therefore, by the rule 'a substitute is like the original' (*sthānivad ādeśaḥ*), [the *ru* should behave as the *u*]."

If it is argued that, because this [rule] also does not apply within the Tripādī, the designation *pada*—defined as "ending in a suffix marked by ṅ or k" (P. 1.4.14)—is absent for a word ending in *r*, and thus the visarga is difficult to obtain here; and that the rule for the visarga has already fulfilled its purpose in cases such as *unnaḥ* (P. 8.2.63), we say: not so, because of the rule *a mu ne* (P. 8.2.3).
Having analyzed the *yoga* [of the rule] as "e" and explained it as "ṭhasiddhaṃ na," because it was stated that "the desired result is established" (*iṣṭasiddhiḥ*), [we have the form] "rāma.

In the view that this is a conventional name (*saṃjñāśabda*) which is not etymologically derived (*avyutpanna*), the designation of a nominal base (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) is obtained by the rule "artha-vat" (Pāṇini 1.2.45).

The distinction is as follows: under the governing rule (adhikāra) "araṇādhikaraṇayośca," the suffix *ghañ*—which is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the general rule for *ghañ*]—is applied by the rule "halaśca" to derive the form *āram* in the sense of "that in which they delight. However, it is derived by the rule "ṛtaddhite" [in the case of the word *āraṇya*].
On this point, some clarify: "The gandharva, the śarabha, the rāma, the sṛmara, the gavaya, and the śaśa..."

According to the statement of Amara, "The species of animals such as lions, elephants, cows, and so forth," if the word *rāma* is employed for a specific animal, then this word *rāma* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) and is thus a technical name (*saṃjñā*) by virtue of the rule *arthavat-sūtra*. However, when it is employed for the Blessed Lord Rāmacandra, they [the wise] delight (*ramante*) [in him].
By relying on the etymological derivation "that which belongs to this [yogin]," the term is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) according to the rule *kṛd-dhita-*.
There is a single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) of identical forms. The meaning of the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is the remaining [of one] preceded by the exclusion of the others.
Nor does the absence of a single-remainder formation among dissimilar forms lead to the undesirable consequence of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) such as "gold-pot" (*ahaṭakalaśau*).

This is to be suspected, because the *vārttika* "of those having different forms" (*ṭhvurūpāṇām*) will be stated later. In reality, however, the meaning of the *vārttika* is obtained from the very syllables of the sūtra itself. That which is formed or understood is "form" (*rūpa*), meaning "object"; those whose form is the same are "having the same form" (*sarūpāḥ*). [The compound is formed] by [the rule] *jyotirjanapada-* etc. (*Pāṇini 2.1.44*).

The state of being "samāna" (identical) is *sabhāva*. Likewise, those whose form (*rūpa*) or essential nature (*svarūpa*) is identical are *sarūpa*. By means of the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a class), the term is explained as "those who are both *sarūpa* and *sarūpa*. Nor should it be argued that there is an impossibility of an operation upon itself according to the maxim of the non-completion of a sentence (*vākyāparisamāpti*).

Because an operation applies even to itself when it is pervaded by the form that constitutes the delimiting condition (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) of its own scope; otherwise, the rule for long vowels with homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*) would not apply in cases such as *ulyāsyaprayatnam*.
Similarly, the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would not apply to the words contained within the *arthavat* sūtra, nor in the cases of *pratyayaḥ* and *paraśca*.

There would be a total collapse of all grammatical rules: the *sup* suffix, the substitution of *ru* by the rule "asajuṣo'ruḥ," and the *visarga* by the sūtra "haravasānayoḥ" would not occur. Just as the injunction "the Veda is to be studied" and the scriptural passage beginning with "iha nānā" apply even to themselves, so too [would these grammatical operations apply].

If it is argued that [the fault] applies equally to *dīrgha* and so on even in the case of *ekaśeṣa*, by this [argument] the objection—"Why is there no sandhi operation such as *ṭhādguṇaḥ* in cases like *ṭhaiuṇ*?"—is refuted. For the resolution offered by some—that "sandhi does not occur because the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *aj* have not yet been established at the time of the instruction of the phonemes (*varṇopadeśa*)"—is rejected; because once the instruction of phonemes, the designation *it*, and the pratyāhāra *at* have been completed, the operations such as *guṇa* which then apply must necessarily function even in the instruction of phonemes and so forth, provided they fall within the scope of the defining property of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), just as they do in a bystander's name like *Upendra*.

It might be argued: "Let the rule simply be 'sarūpāṇām eka ekavibhaktau'; what is the purpose of including the word 'eṣa'? To this they reply: If that were the case, the meaning would be that "in place of [words] having the same form (sarūpa), a single substitute occurs which is the most similar (antaratama). Consequently, in the case of *aśvaś ca aśvaś ca*, there would result a substitute possessing two acute accents (*udātta*) in place of the two [syllables] possessing two acute accents, and likewise a substitute possessing two grave accents (*anudātta*) in place of those possessing two grave accents. [The phrase] "those which [occur] in a single case-ending" [is used to avoid this].

The mention of "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) when there is similarity of form, but it is not the cause (*nimitta*) for the single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*). Thus, because it is not dependent on a specific cause, this *ekaśeṣa* operates even prior to the production of case-endings. If it were not commenced, then a case-ending would apply to each [word] individually and the *dvandva* compound would also apply. However, once the *ekaśeṣa* has been commenced, since there is an absence of multiple *subanta* (inflected nominal) words, the *dvandva* simply does not obtain; such is the intended meaning.

[Objection: But surely, if the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) operation were to apply prior to the arising of the case-ending (*sup*), then the remaining stem would express only a single meaning; consequently, since dual endings and so forth would not arise, forms such as *rāmau* and *rāmāḥ* would not be established. [Response: This is not a fault, because that which remains expresses the meaning of what has been elided. For this very reason, *ekaśeṣa* is enumerated among the types of *vṛtti* (compound-like operations) in the rule "in the case of primary derivatives, secondary derivatives, compounds, and *ekaśeṣa*" (*ṛtaddhitasamāsaikaśeṣe*). Indeed, *vṛtti* consists in the expression of another's meaning. And for this very reason, even when the suffix is elided—as in *liṅ* and *dhuk*—the agent is still understood. Such is the direction of the argument.
(155) *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau* |1|2|64|.
"Only those that are similar" (*sarūpāṇy eva*). This is understood because the particle *eva*, which occurs in the subsequent rule, is drawn back (*anukarṣaṇa*) here.
And in this context, it means that even when followed by a single case-ending (*vibhakti*), forms that are dissimilar (*virūpa*) have not been observed.

The meaning is concluded: therefore, there is no *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) between the two words "mātṛ"—one denoting a biological mother and the other denoting a measurer—because, although they are identical in form in cases such as *mātṛbhyām* and *mātṛbhiḥ*, they differ in form in the *ṅi*, *osi*, and other case endings. But if this is so...

If it is argued that an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would indeed occur in cases such as ‘ayaḥ payo nayati’ (‘He brings iron and milk’) or ‘evadeva’ (‘Just this god’), it is replied: the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member) occurs only when there is a desire to express [the members] together;
that is to say, it is the domain of the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) *dvandva*. For where there is a plurality of referents—
The connection of one with another when they are combined is the object [of the grammatical operation] in that manner;

this is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *ṭhito num dhātoḥ* and also from reasoning. For instance, once it is established by the principle "that which remains expresses the meaning of what is elided," that which is presented by the single word being heard—

Everything ought to be connected in a uniform manner without distinction. Alternatively, one should interpret the rule by carrying forward the word "in a dvandva compound" from the sūtra *iṣya-punarvasv-au* as "when a dvandva compound is about to be formed," rather than "when a dvandva compound has already been formed. [Thus,] *anthānau* and *anthāna*.

In such cases as *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ*, there would be the occurrence of a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) [by Pāṇini 5.4.74]; and in cases such as *arauṣṭrakāḥ*, there would be the occurrence of singular collective status (*ekavadbhāva*) [by Pāṇini 2.4.2]. This is the general direction. He states that in the Sūtra the word *eṣa* is derived in the sense of an object (*karmasādhana*), meaning "only one remains."

If the mention of "one" (*eka*) were not there, the elision (*śeṣa*) might apply even to two or many; therefore, the mention of "one" is made. Nor should it be suspected that the mention of "one" in the rule *ekavibhaktau* is redundant even with this [present rule], for its purpose is to secure the meaning: "even when following a single case-ending, those that are dissimilar in form are not observed [to coexist]."

Because that [principle] is necessary. Furthermore, in cases such as *vasā ca svasārau ca* ("the fat and the two sisters"), since a dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) is observed between the preceding members when followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) in the form *svasārau* would not occur there.
Likewise, in the case of *vasari ca svasrośca*, because a dissimilarity is observed, the form *svasṛṣu* would not occur.

However, [this fault] would indeed apply in cases such as *amalau* and *amala*. But once the mention of "single" (*eka*) is made, this fault does not arise; for when a single case-ending (*ekavibhakti*) follows, no dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) is observed in what precedes it. When, however, singularity is intended in the rule regarding the case-ending (*vibhaktau*), let there be no [fault] here.

If it is said that the term "single" (*eka*) is used [in the rule], then some suggest that it should simply be for the sake of clear understanding. Others, however, say: the inclusion of the word "single" is for the purpose of obtaining the meaning "in each individual case-ending. And thus, by obtaining the meaning "in all case-endings," the desired result is established even without having to extract the particle *eva*.
Direction (*dik*).

In cases such as "one and one" (*ekaśca ekaśca*) or "two and two" (*dvau ca dvau ca*), a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) does not occur because it is not so expressed (*anabhidhānāt*). A copulative compound (*dvandva*) is also to be excluded here for the very same reason of non-expression; this is the general rule (*utsargataḥ*).

The same applies to numeral words as well. However, it should be understood that in the case of *viṃśati* and so forth, the formation by means of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one of identical forms) is indeed desired.
(156) *cuṭū* | 1.3.7 | *cuṭū*. [The word] *ṭhādiḥ* is supplied from the rule *ṭhādir ñiṭuaḍavaḥ*, and [the word] *aḥ* is supplied from the rule *aḥ pratyayasya*.
The phrase "at the beginning of an affix" (*pratyayādau*) also carries over; thus he says, "at the beginning of an affix (*pratyayādau*).
What is the purpose of saying "at the beginning of an affix"? [Consider the example: *vācāṭaḥ*.
Regarding the rule *ena-vitaścuñcup-caṇapau*, the letter *y* is indicated as elided at the beginning of the affix; therefore, he will state that *c* does not receive the designation *it*.

(157) *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* | 1|3|4| "Not in a case-ending (*vibhakti*). This is an initiation of a prohibition regarding the application of the technical designation *it*, which would otherwise have been obtained by the rule *ṭh-alo-'ntyam*. The example for the letter *u* is *rāmāt* and *paceyuḥ*. For the letter *m*, however, the examples are *rāmam* and *adrākṣam*.

What is the purpose of specifying "in a suffix" (*vibhaktau*)? [It is so that] in rules such as *aco yat*, *ūrṇāyāṃ yus*, and *rudhādibhyaḥ śnam*, the final letter of these affixes may receive the designation *it*. Furthermore, it is understood from the addition of the indicatory vowel *u* in the rule *idamasthamuḥ*—which serves to protect the *m*—that this [designation of the final letter as *it*] is not universal.

Otherwise, since the suffix *tham* would be a case-ending (*vibhakti*) according to the rule "the case-endings beginning with *rāc* [are *vibhakti*]," the prohibition of *it* would be established by this very sūtra— just as it is for the *m* of *dānīm*— so what would be the purpose of that [separate rule]? By that [rule],
the form *kvā* in *imo't kvā* is established.
(158) *Ekavacanaṃ saṃbuddhiḥ* | 2|3|49|.

[The term] *ekavacanaṃ* [is understood]. It would be more appropriately stated as: “*uḥ saṃbuddhiḥ*” (the letter *u* is the vocative). Nor is there the risk of over-extension to the locative plural, precisely because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) “in the sense of addressing, the first case.”

"Because that [condition] is absent," say the moderns (*navyāḥ*). Regarding this, they have explained: although it would have been sufficient to state "suḥ is the vocative" (*saṃbuddhiḥ*), the inclusion of the term "singular" (*ekavacana*) is for the purpose of designating as such only that affix by which a single object is expressed.

Otherwise, since the preceding rule "the vocative" (*āmantrita*) had established the designation of the vocative for the entire word ending in that affix, [the mention of "singular" would be redundant].
To avoid breaking the continuity of the context, this designation (*saṃjñā*) should also apply only to that which ends in such [an element].

[The rule] *eṅhrasvātsaṃbuddheḥ* [is interpreted as]: if, in this case, one does not carry over the term *hal* from the preceding rule *ṭhhalṅyābbhyaḥ*, but rather [interprets it as] "there is elision of the *a* of a vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) following a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *eṅ* or short vowels."

If it were explained [as follows]: "even when *haL* is understood to follow, either as 'that which follows an *aṅga*' or as 'the *haL* which belongs to that vocative'," then in both cases, the form *he jñāne* would not be established.

This is because, after the elision (*lopa*) [of the *su* suffix], the *am* suffix would apply to the stem ending in *ā*; and since this *am* is subsequent and obligatory (*nitya*), it would take precedence over the substitution of *e* for *ā*. Consequently, by the rule of *pūrva-para-bhāva* (the single substitution of the preceding vowel), the form would become *he jñānam*.

Since, once the single-substitute (ekādeśa) has been formed, [the rule] would apply as if it were the beginning of the subsequent element (*parādivadbhāva*), there would be no occurrence of what follows a short vowel;

and since, if it applied as if it were the end of the preceding element (*pūrvāntavadbhāva*), the suffix *am* itself would not exist; and because of the prohibition "neither as the end nor as the beginning" (*nāntādivat*) when relying on both simultaneously—he explains this with the passage ending in "if [it were considered] as having *eṅ* as its final, etc. (*eṅntāditvādinā cet*).

(159) *eṅhrasvātsaṃbuddheḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.69]. Regarding the phrase "of that which is implied by the vocative" (*saṃbuddhyākṣiptasya*): it should be understood that if one were to accept the designation [of *eṅ* and *hrasva*] as applying only to that which ends in them, then the stem (*aṅga*) could not be implied by the vocative. [The condition is] "being after a short vowel" (*hrasvātparatvam*).

"It does not exist. Thus, the sense is that the inclusion of *eṅ* in the sūtra is necessary. Furthermore, in the usage by Śrīharṣa—"ṭhimāṃ kimācāmayase na cakṣuṣī" (Why do you wash these two eyes?), the word *e* is a separate word;
it means "O Alakṣmī (O unfortunate one), O Damayantī," according to the sūtra *igaraṇacalanārthebhyaśca*.

This has been explained in the *Manoramā*. Consequently, even there, the mention of *eṅ* is indeed necessary for the purpose of eliding the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhi*). It might be argued that since the mention of *eṅ* finds its scope in the case of ‘*e*’, the elision of the vocative suffix would not occur in examples such as ‘*he hare*’.

It might be argued that [the rule *ambārthanadyor hrasvaḥ*] would apply because the mention of "short" (*hrasva*) has its scope in cases such as *he rāme*, whereas in cases like *he gaurī*, since the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* (by *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt su ti kṣu*) is subsequent, it would override the shortening, and once the short vowel is applied by *ambārthanadyor hrasvaḥ*, [the elision would not occur]. However, this is not so, because it would contradict the technical rule regarding the simultaneous occurrence of operations (*saṃnipātaparibhāṣā*).

Furthermore, since the mention of "short" also finds its scope in *he rāme*, in *he gaurī* and similar forms, the shortening by *ambārthanadyor hrasvaḥ* would indeed take effect by virtue of being subsequent [to the elision rule]. Thus, [the objection does not hold].

The elision of the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhi-lopa*) would not occur. Furthermore, since even the elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* suffixes does not apply to the word *lakṣmī*, the elision of the vocative suffix would all the more not occur in the form *he lakṣmi*. True; however, it should have been stated as "after [a stem ending in] *uṇ*, [there is elision] of the vocative suffix."
The direction is this: by virtue of the mention of *eṅ* and *hrasva*, the elision of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi-lopa*) proceeds even after setting aside the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*.
(160) *am-pūrvaḥ* | 6.1.107 | [When the case-ending *am* follows, the preceding vowel and the following *m* coalesce into the single substitute of the first vowel.]
[The rule] begins with *ami*. This is commenced because [the previous rule] *pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ* would otherwise apply to forms such as *rathamayaḥ*.
From the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, the term *aci* is understood to carry over; thus he says: *amyaci*. That is, when there is an *ac* [vowel] within *ami*.
In other words, it refers to the *ac* that is a constituent part (*avayava*) of *am*. Consequently, [the substitution applies] to that which includes the letter *m*.
It is established in the *Manoramā* that this is not the *pūrvarūpa* (vocalic coalescence).
Similarly, in cases such as *ṭhakṣādūhinyām*, it should be understood that [the rule] applies as *ṭhūhinyāṃ yo’ctasmin*.
Furthermore, the indications (*liṅga*) found in the grammatical references such as *adāsvairibāhye* support this interpretation.

[This is] established. If it is asked: "How is it then that in the *Kāśikā* and other works it is stated simply as 'after *am*' (*ami paraḥ*), and not as 'after *am* and a vowel' (*amyaci*)?", they say in response: Since it has been determined by the rules "that which is [stated] after 'from that' (*tasmāt*)," "of the subsequent," and "of the beginning" (*ādeḥ parasya*) that the substitute (*ādeśa*) refers only to the beginning [of the subsequent element], the substitute prescribed by the rule "one [element] for the preceding and the following" (*ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*) applies only to the two phonemes (the preceding and the following).
It was not stated [in the previous rule] with the intention that it would occur here.
(161) *laśakvataddhite* | 1.3.8 | *la-śa-k-v-at-taddhite*. From the rule *ṭhādir ñiṭuaḍavaḥ*, the word *ādi-* is carried over (*anuvartate*), as is *aḥ*.

Regarding the phrase "of the suffix" (*pratyayasya*) [repeated] from the previous rule, he says—"[the letters] beginning with *la* of the suffix"—because it is obtained through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) expressed by the rule *ataddhite*. In the compound *la-śa-ta-ku*, it is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), and thus, according to the rule *aśakvi*, it takes the neuter gender. That [neuter form] is then [treated] as an itaretara-yoga copulative compound.
He explains: "the letters *l*, *ś*, and the *ka*-group. [The suffix] *lac* is used when it is not a *taddhita* suffix;
for example, *cūḍālaḥ* (from *cūḍā* with the suffix *lac*). [The suffix] *śa* is used after words beginning with *oman*; for example, *lomaśaḥ*.

Regarding this, the modern scholars (*navyāḥ*) maintain that since there is no purpose [for the application of the rule] here, the designation *it* does not apply, and thus this is not a valid counter-example.

In the word *arṇalalāṭā*, the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of "existence" (*bhavārtha*). It is *karṇikā*. If there were a technical name (*saṃjñā*) [for the suffix], then by the rule "iti ca," there would be *vṛddhi* [of the vowel]. Why say "beginning with a suffix"? Consider *alpabhikṣā*, where *ṣākan* is added after the root *vṛḍ*. It is *varākaḥ*. Here, by the rule "ṅiti ca," *guṇa* would not occur.

(162) *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* | Pāṇini 6.1.103. Regarding *tasmāc chaso*: by the word *at*, the preceding homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) which is in immediate proximity is referred to. If there were a reference to the long vowel in general, however, the substitution of *na* would undesirably apply even in a case such as *etān gāḥ paśya*.

The term *asaḥ* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), and that part is qualified by its position as being subsequent—namely, "of the *śas* which follows the long vowel resulting from the homogeneous substitution (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*).
This is what [the author] expresses by saying, "that *sakāra* of *śas* which is subsequent. It is not the case that he says, "that *śas* which is subsequent."
This has been explained. Once the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) has been applied, it is impossible for *śas* to follow thereafter. (163) *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi* 8.4.2.
[The rule] *aṭkupvāṅ*: since the rule *ṭhraṣābhyām* specifies the ablative case (*pañcamī*), there would be no application [of the suffix *ṣ*] when an intervening element exists.

This is the statement. In that regard, it is impossible for there to be an intervention by all [the letters]. Nor does it mean "an intervention by each one individually," because of the force of the inclusion of *kṣu* in the list of *kṣubhnādi* words.

Intending to state that this is also because of the mention [in the sūtra] beginning with "of the vowels" (*arūpāṇām*), he says: "by those [consonants] individually or as combined as possible," and so forth. [Objection: But if this were so, then in cases such as *ṛtsnam* and *ārtsyam*, even though there is no *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) due to the absence of an intervention by *aṭ* and other augments, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases like *ādarśena*, because of the intervention of *aṭ*. Nor is there a restrictive rule that the intervention must be by *aṭ* and others alone, since it has been stated that "this is a rule [applying] where [the substitution] has not otherwise obtained. [Response: True. A split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) should be understood here. One yoga, "even when there is an intervention" (*vyavāye ’pi*), serves the purpose of a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

The rule *ṭhaṭkupvāṅnum* is another restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). The elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *bhisaḥ* is Vedic. Regarding this, the modern grammarians (*navya*) maintain that the explanation can be easily accomplished even without a formal division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*). To explain: in the sūtra *aṭkupvāṅ*, the word *ṭhraṣābhyām* is understood from a previous rule. By virtue of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "from this [ablative], the subsequent [element]" applies. Even though that rule applies, it does not operate when there is an intervention by *aṭ* (vowels), *ku* (gutturals), *pu* (labials), *āṅ*, or *num*, due to the authority of the specific statement. However, it certainly does operate when there is an intervention by anything other than those.

Therefore, as will be stated in the sūtra *ugantalaghūpadhasya*, "that by which there is no intervention [is the one considered], and thus, even when there is intervention, on the authority of the statement, the *guṇa* substitution occurs for an *ik* vowel separated by exactly one consonant, but not for an *ik* vowel separated by multiple consonants in cases such as *bhinatti*"—so too, in cases like *rāmeṇa* where the intervention is caused by *āṭ* and the like, the substitution of *ṇa* certainly takes place.

In this context, [the rule] regarding "intervention by something other than *t* and so forth," as seen in examples such as *ādarśena*, does not apply there, because the *paribhāṣā* "from this" (*asmāt*) remains active. [The phrase] "in order to set aside the prohibition" means that by this, the *ṇatva* (nasalization) in *aryaṇaddham*—by the rule "also after a prefix, even in a non-compound"—is established; this is the intended meaning. [The term] "for the sake of indication" (*upalakṣaṇārtham*) means that the mention of *num* is for the purpose of indicating any *anusvāra* whatsoever, whether it is in the place of *num* or is inherent (*svābhāvika*). Therefore, in the case of the root *ṛhi* (meaning "to grow"), *num* is applied because it is marked with the *it* letter *i*.

Its anusvāra [is as follows]: *ṛṃhū* "in the sense of injury. Here, the anusvāra is inherent (*svābhāvika*). [Thus we have] *bṛṃhaṇam* and *tṛṃhaṇam*; in both cases, the substitution of *ṇ* is established. Regarding the term *ayogavāhānām*: those whose connection (*yoga*)—that is, their inclusion within the pratyāhāra [lists]—does not exist are *ayogāḥ*. Because they are not taught [as independent phonemes] and because they are not grasped by the taught [phonemes], the meaning is that they are devoid of connection with the pratyāhāras. They are called *vāhāḥ* because they carry forth (*vāhayanti*) or bring to completion the linguistic usage (*prayoga*). Being both *ayogāḥ* and *vāhāḥ*, they are *ayogavāhāḥ*.

The meaning is: "while being heard [in the text], yet not taught [by grammatical rules] and not grasped by those [rules] that have been taught. Regarding the term *aṭsu*: the essential point is that [the rule applies] when [the letter ṣ] follows the vowel *a*. Consequently, in forms such as *payassu*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* by the rule *iṇaḥ parasya* does not occur. For this very reason, it was stated previously: "after the vowel *a*, [the following letters] anusvāra, visarga, jihvāmūlīya, upadhmānīya, and the *yamas* [are included].
(164) *padāntasya* | 8|4|37|. The meaning is that the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* shall not occur. From the rule *a-bhā-bhū-pū-kami-gami-*, the word *e* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).
The state [of being an *aṅga*].
(165) "That from which a suffix is prescribed, beginning with that, is the *aṅga* before a suffix" (Pāṇini 1.4.13).
"From which" (*yasmāt*). "Beginning with that" (*tadādi*): this refers to a word-form whose beginning consists of that which constitutes its original base (*prakṛti*).

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Now, one might object: "Let it simply be 'that from which a suffix is prescribed is its *aṅga*' (P. 1.4.13); what is the purpose of including the word 'beginning' (*ādi*)?

To this, he says: "In the case of *bhavāmi*, etc. However, by the principle of "treating that which lacks a designation as if it possessed it" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), [the term applies] to the base alone.
The meaning is that because [the suffix] begins with that [vowel], it possesses the status of being an *aṅga* (stem); by virtue of this, forms such as *artā* and *āraka* are also established.

The phrase "for the sake of the designation *aṅga*" implies that otherwise, the rule "a long vowel replaces the final short *a* before a suffix beginning with *yaṇ*" (*ato dīrgho yañi*) would not apply to produce the long vowel. Nor should it be argued that the long vowel would occur simply by the force of the rule's formulation itself.

Because [the rules] *aya gatau* and *vaya gatau* have already fulfilled their purpose in forms such as *pāpāmi*, *pāpāvaḥ*, *vāvāmi*, and *vāvāvaḥ* through the elision (*yaṅluk*) of the *yaṅ* suffix, [the rule for *strīyati* applies]. Thus, *strīyati*: from *idam* with the suffix *vatup* in the sense of measure; by the rule *imidabhyāṃ vo gha*, there is the suffix *gha*; its substitution is *iy*.

[The form] *strī* is derived as follows: from *striyām*, by [Pāṇini 6.4.148] *ṭhidaṃkimaḥ*, the substitution of *ī* occurs; then by [Pāṇini 6.4.149] *yasyeti ca*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *ī* of *īś*; and by [Pāṇini 4.1.6] *ugitaśca*, the suffix *ṅīp* is added. If this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) were already established, then by [Pāṇini 6.4.149] *yasyeti ca*, the elision of the *ī* of the word *strī* would occur. However, because the elision of the *ī* of *īś* is considered "not yet established" (*asiddha*) in this context by [Pāṇini 6.4.22] *asiddhavadatrābhāt*, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Thus it should be stated; for the commentators explain that [the objection] is based on the acceptance of the position that "it is unestablished due to the absence of *rūpabheda*" (difference in form), or else because of its non-eternality (*anityatva*). However, the moderns (*navya*) maintain that in the example "he sees a woman" (*strīm apaśyati*), the substitution *iyaṅ* would apply to the word *strī* by the rule *striyāḥ*. This is because when the case-ending *am* is applied after the vowel *a*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule "the preceding [vowel] takes the place of both before *am*" would apply.

Because it is a suffix by virtue of being treated as if it were *para* (the subsequent element) and so forth; and because when the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *at* and the *ṭi*-portion is elided, the letter *a* is itself a suffix. However, if the term "vidhi" (prescription) is included [in the rule], this fault does not arise, because the suffix *am* and the suffix *ḍa* derived from the vowel *a* [are excluded].
Even though [the suffix] *cātat* is prescribed, it is not prescribed after the word *strī*. It might be argued:

"Even if *vatup* and the suffix *am* are not prescribed after the word *strī*, the prescription of *su* certainly exists; therefore, that same fault remains as before. This is not so; for by the force of proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), [the rule applies] "from which [stem], whichever... [is intended].

This is because of the explanation: "That which is prescribed before a suffix is called its *aṅga* (base). [The question] "What is meant by 'before a suffix'? arises from the expectation, "Of what kind is the form beginning with *ad*? Since the suffix is explicitly mentioned in the rule "that before which a suffix is prescribed," one might think that the *aṅga* will extend only up to the suffix; it is with this thought that the question is asked. [Regarding] the suffix...
Even if it is heard as a suffix (*pratyaya*), it might be something qualified by that suffix, or even more than that, or perhaps an unlimited limb (*aṅga*);

with the intention that the hearing of the suffix is exhausted in determining the meaning of the word beginning with "tat" (*tad-ādi*), he explains [the text] with the words "of that which is qualified by a suffix," and so forth.
What is meant by "qualified by a suffix"?

And [the case of] *vavraśca*: here, since the designation of the specific [reduplicated stem] as an *aṅga* does not provide for the cause of the substitute *ṛ* (by the rule *ṭhuraḥ*), the rule *acaḥ parasmin* does not apply; consequently, because the prohibition by the rule *na saṃprasāraṇe* is absent, there is once again *saṃprasāraṇa* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

[The rule] would apply. Likewise, in the case of *bhrvartham* (meaning "for the sake of *bhrū*"), the substitutions *iy*, *u*, and *uvaṅ* would occur by the rule *śnudhātubhruvām* [Pāṇini 6.4.77], because according to the aforementioned method, this [rule] does not yield the result that [the substitution applies] when there is a suffix beginning with a vowel (*ac*) by the rule *aci* [Pāṇini 6.4.77]. Consequently, if the technical designation *aṅga* (base) were applied to anything more than that, then [the form] would be *evadata*.

In the case of *odanam apākṣīt*, the augment *aṭ* would have to be inserted before the word *devadatta*, because the entire preceding unit [i.e., *apākṣīt*] would constitute the *aṅga* (base) for the suffix *suṭ* prescribed after the word *devadatta*. However, this does not occur when the second mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is made.

No fault whatsoever follows [from this]. Others, however, say that because the rule for the *luṅ* and other suffixes applies by proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the augment *aṭ* would belong to that very base (*aṅga*) alone; therefore, the statement "even more than that" was said without firm conviction.
Rather, they maintain that the very same fault which applies when this [augmented form] is considered a base (*aṅga*) qualified by the suffix remains.

(166) *ṭāṅsiṅsāminātsyāḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.12. *ṭā*, *ṅsi*, and *ṅs*. Because of the coreferential (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) qualification by the word *ataḥ*—which is carried over from the rule *ṭhato bhisa ais* (7.1.9)—the governing term *aṅgasya* (of the stem), although in the genitive case, is also [understood as qualifying] these [suffixes].

The fifth case [ablative] is changed [to the genitive]; by means of the qualifier, there is an application of the rule to that which ends in it. Thus he says: "from a stem (*aṅga*) ending in the vowel *a*. (167) *supi ca* | 7|3|102|.

And [the rule applies] when a *sup* suffix follows. The term *ṭhyañi* is understood from the previous context. Because of the mention of the letter *a*, it is stated that this is a rule concerning the beginning of a form (*tadādividhi*); thus, it says "when a *sup* suffix beginning with *yañ* follows. Why "beginning with *yañ*"? [Consider] *rāmaḥ*. Why "after *at*" (a vowel)? [Consider] *agnibhyām*.

(168) *ato bhisa ais* [Pāṇini 7.1.9]. Regarding *ato bhisa ais*: one might ask, "Why not simply say *ṭheḥ*? It is not the case that the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) by the rule *ato guṇe* would apply here; for if it did, the explicit pronunciation of the vowel *e* would be rendered purposeless. Otherwise, [the rule] would result in *ais* alone.

If it is argued that [the rule] should be formulated thus, that is true; however, since there is no distinction between *e* and *ai* regarding their having two morae (*dvimātra*), there would be no increase in complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, in the case of the usage cited in the *Kāśikā* under the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*—namely, *nadyai*—it cannot be accounted for without the employment of *ai*.
Some have explained that the substitution of *ai* for *e* in *nirjarasair* is intended for the purpose of hearing the vowel *ai*;

however, this is questionable. For, by the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*, the substitution of *jaras* would not apply, as it has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the Bhāṣya that the form is simply *nirjaraiḥ*.

(169) *ReĀryaḥ* |7|1|13|. The term *ReĀ* refers to the dative singular (*caturthī-ekavacana*), not the locative singular (*saptamī-ekavacana*), according to the traditional interpretation (*vyākhyāna*). For this very reason, it is not included in the rule *ReĀrām* [Pāṇini 7.3.101].

And because of such indications as "in the case of a feminine [suffix] not in grammatical apposition with the word denoting the object of comparison" (*amānādhikaraṇe’ṭhstriyām*). Regarding the phrase "by virtue of being like the original form" (*sthānivadbhāvena*):

the meaning is that there is no prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* in a rule that depends on the substitute (*ādeśa*). Regarding the lengthening by the rule "and before a *sup*" (*supi ca*): it is not [the case that this is superseded] by the rule "before a suffix marked with Ṭ or K, and before a sārvadhātuka suffix" (*aṅgasya kṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*), because the latter is subsequent [in the order of the rules].

One might suspect that there should be lengthening [of the vowel], but in this case, because the term "ṅti" is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*) from the sūtra *ṭhayaṅyi kṅiti*, otherwise there would also be lengthening in the case of *uruyā*.
The substitution of *yā* for the word *ā* following the word *uru* occurs by the rule *upāṃ suluk*. And this...

This is clear in the *Kāśikā*. Although the substitute *ReĀrya* possesses the marker *ṅ*, because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "a lyapi," it is accepted that there is *sthānivadbhāva* even in operations concerning markers (*anubandha-kārya*), provided they are not operations dependent on the letter itself (*analvidhi*); nevertheless, by the evidence of the marker *ś* in *śānac*, in certain operations concerning markers—
This [argument] is stated on the assumption that the designation *ṅt* does not apply to the substitute because the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is not accepted;
or else, it is stated with disregard for the fact that, since there is no contradiction, the priority [of the rule] here is irrelevant,
as the form *jyāyān* is established by the lengthening [prescribed] in the rule *ṭhakkṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*.

It is established in the Bhāṣya that [the rule] would now be contradicted; however, if *kṅti* were to carry over [from the previous rule], then in the case of *yāyāt*, the lengthening prescribed by the rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātuka-* would not apply. Thus, in the sūtra *ṭhakṛt-*, *kṅti* should not be carried over, as in the examples *uruyā* and *dhṛṣṇuyā*.

If it is argued that the absence of the long vowel [in *āyate* and *ānāti*] must simply be accepted as a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*), the [commentators] say here: "The inclusion of the letter *ā* in the rule *ñā-jan-or-jā* (Pāṇini 6.4.32) is an indicator (*liṅga*) of the aforementioned technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). Otherwise, [the sūtra] would have prescribed only *ja*. Furthermore, the long vowel is established in forms such as *āyate* and *ānāti* by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi* (Pāṇini 7.3.101)."

This is established in the Bhāṣya, and that serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) even when *kṅti* is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*) in the rule *ṭhakṛt*. This being the case, let the mention of the vowel *ā* in the rule *yādāt* be considered merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhavāda*) in the Bhāṣya.
"The rule characterized by conjunction (*saṃnipāta*) is the cause (*nimitta*) for its own destruction. Regarding "conjunction":
conjunction (*saṃnipāta*) means close contact (*saṃśleṣa*); that which has this as its characteristic or cause is "characterized by conjunction" (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*).

That which destroys that conjunction is "its destruction" (*tadvighāta*). [The suffix] *aṇ* is added in the sense of an object (karmaṇi), with the substitution of *ku* for *k* and the change of *t* to *d*.

The meaning is that a rule providing for the derivation of a form (*upajīvaka-vidhi*) does not become the cause for the subversion of the very form upon which it depends (*svopajīvya-vighātaka-vidhi*).

(170) *bahuvacane jhalyet* (Pāṇini 7.3.103): [In the case of] *rāmaḥ* and *rāmasya*. Although in the case of *rāmasya*, the substitution of *e* could have occurred even by means of the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* (the technical rule regarding the non-disturbance of a grammatical occasion),...

Although it is easily avoided, nevertheless, with the intention that the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* does not apply in the prescription of *etva* because of the rule "ṭhataḥ sarveṣām," it was stated [in that way]; thus, the underlying logic of what has been established must be supported.

(171) *vāvasāne* 8|4|56. Regarding the rule *jaśtvaṃ vāvasāne*, they say here: one should not think that after *jaśtva* has been applied, *cartva* applies in the case of the pause (*avasāna*); rather, by the maxim *yenanāprāpti*, *cartva* [applies] in the pause.

Because it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *jaśtva*, one should apply the rule that *jaśtva* occurs in the alternative case where *cartva* does not take place. Regarding "in the case of doubling" (*dvitve*), this is by the rule *ṭh-anaci ca*. It has already been stated previously that in the expression *anaci*, there is a prohibitive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). However, if one were to accept an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*), then doubling would not occur here. [This concerns] the substitution of *ta*.

Regarding the statement "it begins": in forms such as *vatsyati*, the substitution of *t* for *c* is not obtained; therefore, by the rule *aḥ syārddhadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.3.99), the letter *t* is prescribed in place of the letter *s*.
(172) *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* (Pāṇini 7.1.54).

The phrase "of the *aṅga*" from [Pāṇini 7.1.70] *hrasvanadyāpo ṅDīp* continues to apply. That [term], being in grammatical apposition with the ablative [in *hrasvāt*], is transformed into "from the *aṅga*" (*aṅgāt*) and is then qualified by "short vowels" (*hrasva*) and the others;
with the intention that the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies due to this qualification, he says: "from that which ends in a short vowel" (*hrasvāntāt*). By this...

It is indicated that in the rule *ṭhhrasvanadyāpaḥ*, the ablative case is used and not the genitive; the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this is the word *ām*. For if it were an augment (*āgama*) to the base (*prakṛti*), a name (*nāma*) based on the designation of the stem (*aṅga*) would not be possible.
And thus, by this ablative case, which has no other purpose, [the principle] "after this, the subsequent [element]" is established.

By virtue of the presence of the paribhāṣā [P. 1.1.66], the word *ām*—which is understood from the rule *ṭhāmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.52)—is transformed from its locative case ending into a genitive case ending, just as in the rule *aḥ si dhuṭ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.48). This is because the locative form *ṭhāmi* has already served its purpose in the rule *restrayaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.69). With this intention, he says: *āmaḥ*.

"An augment *nuṭ* should occur. Regarding this, the modern grammarians (*navyāḥ*) analyze the rule by splitting the *yoga* as "ṭhnuṭ," thereby establishing the general rule (*utsarga-vidhi*) that "the augment *nuṭ* occurs after the case ending *ām* following a stem (*aṅga*).

Then, by means of the portion "adyāpaḥ," they establish a restrictive rule (*niyama-vidhi*) stating: "If the augment *nuṭ* occurs after *ām* following a long vowel, then it occurs only after stems ending in *nadī* or *āp*."

Having explained [the rule], the inclusion of the term *hrasva* (short vowel) may be rejected. Nor should it be argued that this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *ihām* and *uhām*; for we accept the restriction that "if [the substitution] occurs after a word ending in *ṭh* or *hal*, then it occurs only after the words *ṣaṣ* and *catuḥ*. [This applies to] *hrasva* and *anaḍuh*.
This is because of such indications as *atipipataścarāṃ*, *yajikruñcā*, and *halām*.

Therefore, they say that there is no fault whatsoever in rejecting the mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*). Here, however, they argue: if the rule were split into separate sūtras, *nuṭ* and *iṭ*, then once *ReĀrām* has been applied, the subsequent *āṭ* would also [apply].

Because it is antaranga (internal), the augment *nuṭ* would supersede [the *āṭ*]; and thus there would be a contradiction with the forthcoming passage stating "the *āṭ* supersedes the *nuṭ* because it is subsequent," as well as with the Bhāṣya passage stating "once the *āṭ* has been applied, the *nuṭ* does not occur due to the maxim of 'that which has once taken effect' (*sakṛdgati*)."
Even though, according to the view that "the operation of these rules proceeds by way of injunction (*vidhimukhena*)," once *ReĀrām* has been applied,

the augment *nuṭ* would indeed be applicable to it by the rule *adyāpaḥ*; yet, since that [application] is sublated by the rule *āṇnadyāḥ*, the passage beginning with "because it is not *at*, *āṭ* sublates *nuṭ*" is consistent.

Nevertheless, under the view that "this [rule] operates by way of prohibition for those not governed by the sūtra," the augment *nuṭ* would certainly occur due to its being *antaraṅga*, even overriding the subsequent *āṬ*. Furthermore, in the case of *adyāpaḥ*, the meaning would be: "only *nuṭ* should occur after *apaḥ* when followed by *ām*, and nothing else. And thus...

The rule "of all [suffixes] in all [feminine bases]" would not apply to *gauryām* and *ramāyām*. However, for the augment *suṭ* in the masculine, and for the augments *āṭ*, *yāṭ*, and *syāṭ*, their purpose is already fulfilled by intervening *ṅ*-sounds and *d*-sounds.
Furthermore, in cases such as *gauryām*, once the suffix *ReĀp* is applied, the augment *āṭ* would apply, overriding the augment *nuṭ*.

The mention of *nadī* is for the purpose of setting aside [the application of] *yāṭ*. Similarly, in cases such as *ramāyām*, *sarvāsām*, and *sarvasyām*, the mention of *āp* is for the purpose of setting aside the application of *yāṭ*, *suṭ*, and *syāṭ*. Thus, the rule *adyāpaḥ* would serve solely as an injunction (*vidhi*) and not as a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Consequently, in the case of *viśvapām*...

In cases such as *vātapramyām*, the insertion of the augment *nuṭ* is indeed unavoidable; for one must rely on the indications found in [Pāṇini’s] rules— such as “*matup* after *adya*,” “*[the suffix *kan* is used] in the vernacular after *sad*, *vas*,

and *śru*,” “the observation of *sarvasām* is generally seen,” and “a weapon [is denoted] after *adas*”— to establish that these rules serve as injunctions (*vidhi*) rather than mere restatements (*anuvāda*), and thus conclude that *nuṭ* must indeed be applied.

Furthermore, regarding the previously mentioned restriction—that "if [the suffix] occurs after a word ending in /ā/, /ī/, or /ū/, then it must be *nadī* or *āp*"—this would also apply in cases such as *viśvapām*, *vātapramyām*, and *khalapvām*. Consequently, there would be an excessive burden on the learner (*pratipatti-gaurava*) due to the need to exclude such instances from the aforementioned rule.
Moreover, since that very restriction would also be applicable here, [the formation of those forms would be impossible].

Even in the absence of the augment *nuṭ*, *nuṭ* would occur in forms such as *gavām*. Nor should it be argued that because of the rule *oḥ pādānte* (Pāṇini 6.1.115) which begins with reference to the Vedic language (*chandas*), *nuṭ* would not occur after the word *go* followed by *ām* in the common language (*loka*). For [the counter-argument is]: "If *nuṭ* occurs after the word *go* followed by *ām* at the beginning or end [of a word], that applies only in the Vedic language."

For if [the rule] were mandatory, even though the usage *āmnām* does not occur at the end of a word in the world, it would follow that it could not be avoided when it is not at the end of a word; furthermore, it would be difficult to prevent its occurrence in forms such as *rāyām*, *glāvām*, and *nāvām*. However, if [the rule applies] to an *ām* following a long vowel...

If there were a restrictive rule (niyama) such as "nuṭ [is applied] after [a word ending in] /a/, etc.," then the sūtra "oḥ pādānte" would be for the purpose of an injunction (vidhi). However, if there were a restrictive rule such as "nuṭ [is applied] after [words ending in] /akāra/ and so on, and after [the word] ām," then it would be for the purpose of a restriction. In that case, between an injunction and a restriction, the injunction alone is superior.

Even if it is argued that, by not pursuing the logical consistency [of the system], the very rule— "there is *nuṭ* after *ām* following a stem ending in a long vowel," and so forth— is accepted, even then there remains the same burden of repeated comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*),
as one must still accept the rule: "there is *nuṭ* after *ām* following a stem ending in a long vowel," and so forth.
Even if that were said, there would still be a need for the weightiness of a counter-argument;
therefore, since the rejection of the inclusion of the short vowel would require excessive effort, it is more appropriate to accept the matter exactly as it was heard in the tradition.
(173) *nāmi* | P. 6.4.3. The term *dīrgha* ("long") is understood from the rule *hrasvlope* [P. 6.1.69].
By virtue of this mention of "long," the term *acaḥ* ("of a vowel") is understood and serves as the qualifier for *aṅgasya* ("of the stem").

The rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension of a grammatical operation to that which ends with the specified element) does not apply because of the qualification [of the term]. This is what is stated in the passage beginning with "of a stem (*aṅga*) ending in a vowel" (*ajanta*).
By the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of meaningful elements (*arthavadgrahaṇa*), the suffix *ām* is understood here as being accompanied by the augment *nuṭ* (i.e., *āmī*).
Consequently, it does not occur in forms such as *pāmanām* and *aṅganām*, for in those cases, the suffix *ām* is prescribed by the rule concerning the *pāman*-class of stems.

When the suffix *ṭāp* is applied after *napratyaya* and the singular accusative case ending (*am*) is also applied, although each of these three suffixes is individually meaningful, the aggregate "ām" is itself devoid of meaning. Even though the long vowel in "āmanām" is easily resolved by this rule— since the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of this operation— [the objection remains].

Nevertheless, it should be understood that [the substitution] would indeed occur by virtue of the rule *opadhāyāḥ*. However, it was not formulated as a sūtra simply as *uṭi*. This was so that [the substitution] might not apply to the word *bhṛṅga*, which ends in the Uṇādi suffix *gan* according to the rule *hṛñaḥ kinnuṭ ca*. This may be so.

Since the augment *nuṭ* is a part of the *ām*, the letter *m* in the term *ām* will also include the *ām* with the nasal *n*; therefore, let the rule simply be "before *ām*" (*āmi*). Furthermore, because the long vowel in *āmī* is obligatory—being applicable both before and after the application of other rules—it would override even the subsequent *nuṭ*.

Regarding the rule *agnīnām indūnām*, it should not be argued that once the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is applied, the augment *nuṭ*—which depends on a short vowel (*hrasva*)—would no longer occur; for by the force of the specific statement *nuṭ* [is added] after those ending in a short vowel, the augment applies even when the long vowel has been substituted, by resorting to the consideration of its prior state (*bhūtapūrvagati*). Nor does the prohibition *na tisṛcatasṛ* apply here.

It must be stated that there is a purpose for the rule *nuṭ* after a short vowel in the case of the forms *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*; however, in the form *catasṛṇām*, the *nuṭ* is already established by the rule *aṭcaturbhyaśca*. This is because in the sūtra *hrasvanadyāpaḥ*, [the word] *tisṛbhyo* has been taken from the rule *restrayaḥ*.

By carrying forward the word *ṛt* and interpreting it as "the augment *nuṭ* is added after the case-ending *ām* following a word ending in the sound *ṛ*," the form *tisṛṇām* is also established. Although there is a need for the rule in the case of *nṛṇām*, nevertheless, a single example does not justify the formulation of a rule; otherwise, [the rule would be unnecessary].
If it is argued that one should simply say *ṛnadyāpaḥ*, and therefore there is no obstacle to saying *ādam*— thus making the inclusion of the letter *n* in *san* redundant—
it is replied here: the inclusion of the letter *n* in *san* must be made for the sake of what follows, so that the rule *opadhāyāḥ* may apply the lengthening [of the vowel].

"Nuṭ would not occur. [This is because of the rule: "By virtue of a specific statement, it does not occur where that [condition] is absent, nor after a penultimate vowel of words meaning 'armor' (varman). Regarding this, they say: "The application of that [rule] by resorting to the state of having previously existed on account of a specific statement is to be considered; for in the case of secondary (gauṇa) usage, [the rule] 'aṭcaturbhyaśca' [applies]."

This is incorrect, because the statement regarding the short vowel (*hrasva*) in the rule *ari ca catasṛṇām* has already fulfilled its purpose by providing scope for the insertion of the augment *nuṭ* through the non-application [of the long vowel];

thus, its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) is exhausted. For in that context, it is intended that *nuṭ* should apply by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to the substitution of *r* prescribed by the rule *um-a-ci-ra-*. That is improper, because of the rule *ṛ-n-nady-āpaḥ*.
Thus, even though it is stated in the Sūtra [in this way], the augment *nuṭ* is indeed established after a stem ending in short *ṛ*;

therefore, the force of the mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*) is not exhausted [by that alone]. This is the general direction. Regarding the phrase "due to conflict with the Paribhāṣā": because [the rule] applies both when the condition is already present and when it is yet to be produced, [it is governed by] the rule *āmi*.

Because even that which is long is impermanent. Regarding the phrase "by virtue of its capacity for initiation" (*ārambhasāmarthyāt*): the meaning is that the [rule] *upi ca* lacks such capacity, because it finds scope in forms such as *rāmābhyām*. Now, one might object: in the case of *atinām*, since the rule *aṭcaturbhyaśca* applies by virtue of being subsequent (*paratvāt*), the augment *nuṭ* would apply, and thus [the form would be] *āmi*.

Since the long vowel [of the genitive plural ending] operates even without subverting the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*, the force of its original formulation is exhausted; thus, the rule "āmi" (Pāṇini 7.1.54) also does not apply to the form "hrāmāṇām" due to the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. And so, in the case of "ācāryāṇām"...

If it is argued that, by relying on the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the previously stated technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) as indicated [by the author], the long vowel substitution prescribed by "upi ca" should indeed prevail because it is subsequent,
some here offer this resolution: [the substitution occurs] only after a consonant-ending stem that possesses the designation "ṣaṭ," due to its association with the mention of the word "catur."
The augment *nuṭ* occurs after the genitive plural suffix *ām* when it follows a word that possesses the designation "ṣaṭ" (the number six), but not after the word *kati*.

Thus, in the form *atīnām*, the *nuṭ* is based solely on the short vowel; therefore, the force of the rule's formulation is not exhausted by this single instance. Others do not accept this [interpretation]. Just as the letter *r* is designated as a *hal* (consonant), so too...

Since that which is designated as *aṃ* (the nominative-accusative dual ending) also exists [as part of the base], the augment *nuṭ* occurs based on the designation of "six" (*ṣat-saṃjñā*) for the following *ām* only when it follows a base designated as "six" (*ṣaṭ-saṃjñaka*), and not in cases such as *priyapañcām* or *priyaṣaṣām*.
According to this established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the *nuṭ* augment is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) with respect to the designation of "six. Likewise...

Because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*), in the case of the word *katīnām*, the augment *nuṭ* applies specifically on the basis of the short vowel; thus, the lengthening by the rule *āmi* (Pāṇini 7.1.54) proceeds precisely by overriding the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*.
Consequently, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the passage from the root-text stating, "by virtue of the capacity of *āp* and *bha*."
[They] established [the rule]. But others [hold that] the meaning of "by the force of the commencement [of the prohibition]" (*ārambha-sāmarthyāt*) is:

"by the force of the commencement of the prohibition [stated in the sūtra] *na tisṛ-catasṛ*. For if, in the case of *tisṛṇām*, the augment *nuṭ*—which is conditioned by a short vowel at the end of the stem—had been applied, and then the long vowel [substitution] prescribed by "*āmi*" had taken effect, [the prohibition] *na tisṛ-* [would have been unnecessary].

Thus, the prohibition is commenced. But if, by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (the metarule regarding the destruction of a cause), the long vowel were not to apply, what would be the purpose of this prohibition? Therefore, it is understood that the long vowel [prescribed] by the rule *āmi* subverts the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. By those, however, who [interpret] the rule *hrasvanadyāpaḥ*...
The mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*) is rejected; for them, in the case of the long vowel [in the rule] "āmi," the necessity of the initial formulation need not be relied upon at all.
(174) *apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ* | 8|3|55| [A retroflex substitute occurs for a non-final *n* when followed by a sibilant.]

*Apadāntasya*. Since the rule would have been established by the mention of *a* alone, the explicit mention of the cerebral (*mūrdhanya*) is for the purpose of applying the substitution of *ḍha* in the rule *ṭhiṇaḥ ṣīdhvam*. Examples: *cakṛḍhve*, *akṛḍhvam*. (175) *iṇkoḥ* 8.3.57.
*Inkuḥ*. In a collective dvandva compound, the masculine gender is used by Vedic (sūtra-based) authority. Why "of *ku*"? [Consider] *gavākṣu*, *gavāṅṣu*.
(176) *Ādeśapratyayayoḥ* 8.3.59. [The substitution of *ṣ* occurs for the sibilant of an affix or a substitute.]

Regarding the rule *ādeśapratyayoḥ*: the word *pratyaya* is used here figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean a portion of an affix (*pratyayāvayava*). This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the rule *hali sarveṣām*, as well as the inclusion of the term *sāti* in the rule *ātpadādyoḥ*. With this intention, he explains: "an substitute (*ādeśa*) and a portion of an affix (*pratyayāvayava*). However, if...
If it were taken as a part of the substitute (*ādeśāvayava*), then there would be a fault in forms such as *isṛṇām*. Even though,
by virtue of the explicit utterance of the letter *s*, the substitution of *ṣ* would not occur there, nevertheless,
in cases such as *bisam-bisam* and *musalam-musalam*, the substitution of *ṣ* would be unavoidable.

This is because the genitive dual ending in *āṣṭamika* functions as a substitute (*ādeśa*). If, however, one were to understand [the rule] as "that *sakāra* which is a suffix," then [the substitution] would not apply in cases such as *rāmeṣu* and *ariṣyati*, but would instead apply only in cases such as *indro mā vakṣat*. In this regard, even a single genitive case is mentioned in the *Manoramā*.

Having stated that [the compound] is divided due to a difference in scope (*viṣayabheda*), it was said that it is a *dvandva* because it is found in the Sūtra even in the absence of a desire to express [the members] together; this should be understood as having been stated with the literal sense (*yathāśruta*) in mind, without accepting a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *pratyaya*. [The phrase] "of one whose harshness has been removed" (*vivṛtāghoṣasya*).

When it is stated that "the [place of articulation] of an open [consonant] is the same as that of the vowel," there is the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of this rule to the vowel *ṛ*; to prevent this, the term "unvoiced" (*aghoṣa*) is added.
If only the term "unvoiced" were stated...

In the case of the letter *ṭha*, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); to prevent that, both [conditions] are prescribed. "Of such a kind alone is *ṣa*" means that only such a *ṣa* becomes the substitute, and no other. Nor is it necessary to prevent the substitution of *ṣ* in compounds such as *adhisecau* and *adhiseca* prior to the production of case-endings (*sup*).

If it is argued that the *bhāṣya* states that "the beginning of a word" (*padādi*) is a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*)—namely, "the beginning [relative] to a word"—and therefore here too the prohibition in the rule *ātpadādyoḥ* would apply (as in *ariṣyati*), because the prescription for *ṣatva* would otherwise find its scope; we reply: not so, for the technical designation "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*) applies to those [elements] beginning with *va*.
Because it has been indicated by the inclusion of the word *ati* that the aforementioned prohibition does not apply when that [augment] is present.

Regarding the form *rāmasya*: although one could have simply stated “*āṅ siṅs āmin ātsyāḥ*,” the fact that the letter *s* is explicitly uttered implies that *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) does not occur; this is because in the *naḍādi* group, the rule states “*ṭhamuṣya*” [which prevents such substitution].

If it is argued that, due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*) and the mention in the Vārttika— "after *phak* etc., [the suffix] *ṭhak* [is applied] in the sense of *āmuṣyāyaṇa*"— the substitution of *ṣ* should occur in the form *āmuṣye*, then in that case, examples such as *viśvapāsu* must be cited as counter-examples. Furthermore, in that instance as well, one should have said "after *u*" (*ubiti*), rather than "after *ū*" (*ūbiti*).
One should not suspect that [the doubling] would not occur simply by the power of the pronunciation of the letter *s*;

for in the rules *liṭtsu* and *raśāntsu*, the pronunciation of *s* must necessarily be accepted in order to apply the augment *dhuṭ* via the rules *aḥ si dhaṭ* and *aśca*. This is the general direction.

(177) *sarvādīni sarvanāmāni* | 1.1.27. Regarding the term *sarvādīni*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (where the qualities of the members are understood). The evidence for this is the rule *tasmāt sarveṣām*. Here, the word *ādi* denotes a constituent part. [The list begins with] *sarva*.

The analysis of the compound is: "those whose first members are the initial [sounds]. Since a collection (*samudāya*) in which the distinction between its constituent parts is manifest is the meaning of a compound, the plural number is used. Because that collection cannot be applied simultaneously to the object of grammatical description (*lakṣya*), the maxim "when [a rule] is purposeless with respect to the whole, it applies to its parts" (*anarthakyāt tadaṅgeṣu*) is invoked.

Since the designation *sarvanāman* (pronoun), which applies to its constituent parts, applies to the word *sarva* as well due to the absence of distinction, it is logical that it possesses the quality of *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*. This means that the qualities (*guṇa*) of that external referent (*anyapadārtha*)— namely, the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) consisting of the meanings of the constituent words— are understood (*saṃvijñāna*) as being included in the operation (*kāryānvayitayā*).

The literal meaning of the term *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (retaining the quality) is that [the compound] refers to that [subordinate member] as possessing its own quality. This occurs in both common usage (*loka*) and the Veda (*veda*) whenever there is a relationship of either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*),
as in examples such as "the priests go about wearing turbans" (*ohitoṣṇīṣā ṛtvijaś caranti*) and "bring the long-eared one" (*lambakarṇam ānaya*).

In this case, it is indeed a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* [bahuvrīhi]. However, in the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), as in the example "bring the man with a brindled cow" (*itragumānaya*) and so forth, it is an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*. Now, one might ask:
why does the substitution of *ṇ* not occur in the word *arvanāmāni* according to the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*?
If it is argued that [the *ṇatva* substitution] does not apply because it is based on a sūtra, and that this would result in the ungrammaticality of the word *sarvanāma* in common usage—

and consequently lead to the ungrammaticality of the subsequent text stating "they shall be called *sarvanāman*"— this is not so; for the *ṇatva* is [established] by way of an irregularity (*nipātana*).

Since the desired result is established by resorting to the explanation given in the Bhāṣya, the position adopted here— following the Bhāṣya— is that nipātanas (irregular forms) function only as exceptions (*bādhaka*). However, the alternative position— that nipātanas can also function as optional alternatives (*vibhāṣā*)— is supported by the mention of the word *śravaṇā* in the rule *vibhāṣā phālgunī*.

Even though [the suffix] has been elided, the usage *rāvaṇī* is indeed correct; it is for this purpose that [the rule] will be resorted to. He supplies the substantive (*viśeṣya*) in accordance with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)—namely, "the forms of words" (*śabdasvarūpāṇi*). And regarding the phrase "and in a copulative compound" (*dvandve ca*): for that is a prohibition.

He will state that [the designation applies] to the whole alone and not to its parts; the sense is that, without the rule for "that which ends in this" (*tadantavidhi*), there would be no possibility of the technical name applying to the whole. An objection is raised: in cases such as *aramasarvasmai*, where the augment *āṭ* is added to the base ending in *a*, the designation occurs even without the *tadantavidhi*.

To the question, "What is the result of the designation [of a suffix] ending in that [suffix], given that [suffixes such as] *smāy* and others have already been established?", he says: "By that" (*tena*). Nor should it be argued that here too, because the term *prātipadika* is understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over), and since the pronoun [in the rule] functions as a qualifier of that [prātipadika], the designation of what ends in that [suffix] will necessarily follow; for there is a prohibition regarding the application of suffixes after a compound or a secondary derivative (*amāsa-pratyaya-vidhau pratiṣedhaḥ*).
The sense is that this has been stated [in the rule]. By the word *ca* in *akac ca*, the suffix *tasil* is applied in the case of *paramasarvataḥ*.
(178) *jasaḥ śī* | 7.1.17 | *jasaḥ śī*. The lengthening of the vowel is for the sake of subsequent rules—as in *vāriṇī*, *madhunī*.
The meaning is: "because it consists of more than one letter," and not "because it is marked with the *ś* indicatory letter" (*śit*).

This is because the designation *it* simply does not exist [in that case]. In the rule for *ṛ*, the *ṛ*-vowel receives the *it* designation at the very time of its instruction (*upadeśa*); however, in the case of the substitution of *śī*, since it is a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*), it subsequently acquires the status of an affix (*pratyaya*) by virtue of being treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*).

The point is that there is a discrepancy between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*): by the rule *aśakvataddhite*, the *ś* at the beginning of an affix is designated as *it*.
(179) *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ* 7.1.52.

"Avarṇāntāt" means "from a suffix following a base ending in the vowel *a*. By this, there is no lack of application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "ṭhyeṣām" and "eṣām. Regarding the phrase "of that which is prescribed after a pronoun," it is not stated as "after a pronoun" (*sarvanāmnaḥ parasya*), because [if it were so], [the rule would fail to apply] in the case of "varṇāśrametarāṇām."

Because of the undesirable consequence that [the term] *suṭ* would [be included]; for even though the prohibition of the designation *sarvanāman* for a whole compound is established by the rule "in a dvandva," there is no prohibition for its constituent parts.
Furthermore, the authority for adopting [the view that the word] "prescribed" (*vihita*) is a qualifier [of the whole] is the rule: "akṣiṇī-uttara-pūrvāṇām."

This is indeed the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya: *āma*. The sense is that because the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the rule *arvanāmnaḥ* has no other scope [for application], it is understood as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) modifying the locative case (*saptamī*) in *ṭhāmī*, which has already fulfilled its purpose in the subsequent rule *restrayaḥ*. Regarding *pañcatriṃśat*: it is five and...

"Thirty-three" (*triṃśat-trayaḥ*) is either a *dvandva* compound, or it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "thirty plus five. Nor should it be argued that the suffix *ḍac* would apply to this compound by virtue of the upcoming *vārttika*, "In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* following a numeral," because that very *vārttika* specifies: "Except in cases other than those where there is elision of *adhika*."

Because it has been stated thus: [“The term *sarvanāman* applies to all pronouns”]. Now, an objection may be raised: since the designation *sarvanāman* is etymological (based on its meaning), only *sarva*, *viśva*, and so forth will be the things designated (*saṃjñin*), and no others; therefore, what is the purpose of this enumeration of thirty-five, or of the rule *arvādīni*? Do not say so.

Because, in the absence of such an enumeration, there would be the over-extension [of the designation] to words like *kṛtsna*, *sakala*, and *samasta*. And thus, for the sake of the restrictive rule that "only those beginning with *sarva* which are thirty-one in number are designated as *sarvanāman*, and no others," the sūtra *arvādīni* is necessary; it is not [necessary merely for the purpose of listing them].
It should be understood that this rule is of little utility, much like the technical definition of the term *anunāsika*.

Regarding *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*: when used in the sense of relative position (*vyavasthā*) and not as a proper name (*asaṃjñā*), the words *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *apara*, and *adhara* are included in the *sarvādi* group.

The meaning is "not others. The designation *sarvanāman* (pronominal) is established by the rule itself: “*arvādīni sarvanāmāni*” (Pāṇini 1.1.27). This should be understood in the same way for the two subsequent sūtras as well. The words *yad* and *ad* refer back to what has been previously mentioned. Regarding this, the first [form] is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

The statement of the author of the *Gaṇaratna* is not to be respected; for otherwise, the inclusion of the term "in Vedic" (*cchandas*) in the rule *asya cchandasi bahulam* would result in redundancy. Regarding the word *eka*: "The word *eka* is employed in the senses of 'other,' 'principal,' 'first,' 'alone,' 'common,' 'equal,' 'small,' and 'number. Therefore...

"Thus [it is said]. The sense is that the dual number alone is appropriate for the two [words]. "Always ending in the dual" means at all times; that is, it ends in the dual suffix. And it is not as if one were to ask: "What is the point of the rule *ubhādudāto nityam* (Pāṇini 5.2.44), since *ubhaya* is already a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)?"

It should not be suspected that this contradicts the usage of the author of the *Sūtras* and the author of the *Bhāṣya*, for it is accepted that the state of always ending in the dual number applies only when the word is used in its sense (*arthapara*), and not when it is used as a phonetic imitation of its own form (*svarūpānukaraṇapara*).

Furthermore, the inclusion of the word *ubha* among the *sarvādi* (the list beginning with *sarva*) would otherwise be useless, since the pronominal operations such as *smāy* and so forth [would not apply].

Because [the dual form] does not exist in the dual number. Nor should it be argued that the result of the rule *arvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca*—namely, the establishment of the genitive and instrumental cases for both causes as in *ubhābhyāṃ hetubhyām* and *ubhayor hetvoḥ*—is intended to apply here.
For there is the rule: *nimitta-kāraṇa-hetuṣu sarvāsāṃ prāyadarśanam*.
This is because the matter has already been established by the Vārttika itself. Nor should it be argued that, since the author of the Vṛtti read [the rule] "arvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca" (P.

2.3.27) under the heading of the sūtra [concerning] pronouns, this Vārttika also applies only to pronouns and provides all case-endings for them alone and not for anything else; for [this is refuted] in the Bhāṣya under the sūtra "hetau" (P. 2.3.23).

Since that *vārttika* has been cited [elsewhere], it must be stated that this *vārttika* also causes the application of all case endings (*sarva-vibhakti*) for the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) alone and not for anything else; for that *vārttika* was cited in the *Bhāṣya* under the rule "in the sense of cause" (*hetau*). For this very reason, [examples such as] "he dwells because of food" (*annena kāraṇena vasati*) and "of food" (*annasya*)...
Anticipating the objection that this has already been cited by Haradatta as an example of the suffix *kāraṇa*, [the author] says: "But its reading here is...

Now, one might ask: since the desired result is achieved even with the suffix *ka*, what is the purpose of this reading for the sake of the suffix *akac*? Nor should it be argued that there is no difference between *kā* and *akac* regarding accent, because [in the case of *kā*], the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) would prevail over the accent of the *cit* designation (*citsvara*).
Anticipating the objection that there would be no difference in the case of an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*), he says: "And not...

The suffix *akac* does not destroy the fact that the word *ubha* is intended for the dual number, because it arises before the final phoneme (*ṭi*); this is due to the principle that what falls within a certain domain is included by the mention of that domain. However, the suffix *kap* does indeed destroy it.
Anticipating the objection that [the suffix] arises after the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), he says: "because of the absence of being followed by a dual ending.
Regarding the phrase "due to the contingency of *ayac*": just as the suffix *ayac* occurs in its own sense (*svārtha*) after the word *ubhaya* when followed by the suffixes *tratas*.

The sense is that it would be so when the suffix *kap* is present. Although even in the example of *ayaj*, [the suffix] is difficult to obtain in its own sense (*svārthe*), nevertheless, it is indeed easily obtained through the analysis (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule “*ityam*” from the sūtra “*ṭhubhādudātaḥ*. To explain: [the sūtra reads] “*ṭhubhādudātaḥ*,” and then “*vitribhyām*” [is added].
The word *vā* (or) from the preceding sūtra does not carry over, because it is not marked with the svarita accent.

From the word *ubha*, which denotes a number and functions as a part (*avayava-vṛtti*), the suffix *ayac* shall be applied in the sense of a whole (*avayavin*). Examples: *ubhayo maṇiḥ* (a gem consisting of both parts), *ubhayaḥ pāśaḥ* (a noose consisting of both parts). From that [suffix], the form *ittham*. From the word *ubha*, within its scope of application (*vṛtti-viṣaye*)...

The suffix *ayaC* would necessarily apply in its own sense (*svārthe*). By that, forms such as *ubhayataḥ*, *ubhayatra*, and *ubhayapakṣavinītānidrāḥ* are established.
