[Objection: But even if *akac* is applied, this *ayaC* would still be unavoidable, because of the rule: "In the domain of a compound (*vṛtti*), *ayaC* necessarily applies in its own sense."

If it is argued that this is because [the rule] was stated by you yourself, then, since the division of the *yoga* (sūtra) is for the sake of achieving the desired result and because of the mention in the form "ubhau sābhyāsasya," this [rule] is explained as applying only where the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is not heard, and not within the scope of a compound formation (*vṛtti*); thus, there is no fault.
Regarding the phrase "tad uktam" (it has been said): the word "by the author of the Vārttika" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Regarding the phrase "ubhayo 'nyatra": the meaning is that the form *ubhaya*, which is a primary derivative (*svārthika*) lacking the suffix *-yañ*, is employed elsewhere [than in the dual], but not when followed by a dual case-ending. Furthermore, in examples such as *ubhau*, there is no occurrence of being followed by a dual case-ending.

It should not be argued that [the application of *ayac*] is difficult to justify because the status of being "like the beginning" (*ādivadbhāva*) or "like the end" (*antādivadbhāva*) is absent when there is a dual ending based on both [elements];
for it is stated in the *Manoramā*: "The intended meaning is that *ayac* applies elsewhere than where the dual ending produced from the word *ubha* has been elided by *luk*. And thus:
It is established that the inclusion of the word *ubha* in the list beginning with *sarva* (the *sarvādi* group) is for the sake of the suffix *akac*.

However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the inclusion of the word *ubha* in the *sarvādi* list is rejected on the grounds that since the suffix *kap* denotes its own meaning (*svārthika*), the word *ubha* is capable of expressing its own referent; thus, it is assumed that the condition of being followed by a dual ending (*dvivacana*) exists after the word *ubha*.

In the Manoramā commentary, however, it is established that the rejection [of the rule] is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), because it is appropriate to accept here only that *dvivacana* which has been produced by a verbal root; otherwise, there would be over-extension (*atiprasakti*) to suffixes such as *atra* and *tasil*, and so forth.

Regarding the word *ubhaya*: that which has two parts (*ubhau avayavau yasya*) is *ubhaya*. By the rule "after *ubha*, *ayac* is always substituted for *tayap*," the suffix *ayac* is applied. The sense is that [the neuter singular form] does not exist because it is not so designated by usage. Thus, since the word *ubhaya* does not produce a dual number, it would follow that it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) because it does not take all case-endings.

In the sūtra *addhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ*, Kaiyaṭa introduces the Bhāṣya statement: "The mention of taddhita suffixes [ending in] *ṛt* occurs in the recitation [of the sūtra]. This means that since the purpose of the recitation is exhausted by the exclusion of forms such as *acati*, its absence serves as the authority for non-usage (*anabhidhāna*).
The sense is that [the suffix] does not exist. "Therefore" means from the word *ubhaya*.

"By virtue of ending in the suffix *tayap*"—the remainder of the sentence is "of the word *ubhaya*. The essential point is that if the suffix *ayac* occurs after the word *ubhaya*, it is independent, and not a substitute for *tayap*.

Even if that were accepted, it should be understood that there is still no possibility of the optional application [of the suffix] in the case of *rathamacaramatayā*. As for the statement "it is eternal," however, the form *ubhayā amitrāḥ* should be understood as being Vedic (*chāndasa*). Regarding the suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama*:

The suffixes *ḍatarac* and *ḍatamac* are prescribed by the rules "Of two [things], one is designated by *ḍatarac* when there is a restriction" (*iyatador-nirdhāraṇe dvayor-ekasya ḍatarac*) and "Or *ḍatamac* [is used] among many when there is an inquiry regarding a genus," as well as "Also after a word ending in *eka*, according to the Eastern grammarians.
These two [suffixes] are unanalyzed (avyutpanna). This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *Paspaśā* section. The phrase "some say" (*eke*) refers to this.
The authors of the *Kāśikā* [state] that this is because we observe the anudātta [vowel] in "ṭhetaṃ tvaṃ manye" and also the anudātta in "ṭhuta tvaḥ paśyan. The word "eka" means "first.
Even though the fact that it ends in "-t" is not clear in the *saṃhitā* reading, the word "vaḥ" must be understood as ending in "-t."

Otherwise, one should recite it all at once with a single tone (*ekaśruti*). Nor should there be any disagreement regarding the final *t* sound, because of the Phiṭ-sūtra rule: "The sounds *va*, *tva*, *sa*, *ma*, *si*, and *me* are not pronounced [with high pitch]. Thus says a Rigvedic mantra: "From you it becomes barren, from you it is brought forth. Jayadeva also [says]:

He employed [the word] as "drinking the honey-sweet nectar from the lower lip of someone other than you. The analysis is "the lower lip of another than you" (*tvad-anyasyā adharaḥ*), and not "your lower lip" (*tavādharaḥ*), because that would result in a lack of syntactic connection with the preceding sentence: "he kisses you in secret in every direction. Thus it is equal. And so:

It is heard [in the Veda]: "mā no vṛkāya vṛkye samasmai" (Pāṇini 1.4.25), "uta samasmin" (Ṛgveda 10.87.16), and so forth. Regarding the statement "the word *sam* may be used in the sense of 'entirety' (*kṛtsna*) and 'capability' (*śakta*), as well as when bound by a limit (*maryādā*)," this refers to a *gaṇasūtra*.
Although there is a *vārttika* in the Bhāṣya stating that for the sūtras contained in the Aṣṭādhyāyī, one should say "except for a city (*apurī*)"...

Although this has been recited, it is nevertheless a supplement (*śeṣa*) to that very *gaṇasūtra* alone, and not to the rule prescribing the optional (*vibhāṣā*) application before the suffix *jas*. This is because, under the governing heading (*adhikṛtya*) of "after *ṭha*," the substitution of *śī* for *jas* is prescribed;
therefore, since there is no possibility of its application after a stem ending in long *ā*, [the rule] states "in the case of *antarāyām*."
The meaning is: "either outside the enclosure wall or situated within it.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the status of being a *sarvanāman* (pronominal) is obtained because, by the technical rule regarding gender-distinctive elements (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included as part of the preceding element. Having thus explained the group of words beginning with *sarva*, now—
He explains the *trisūtrī* contained within the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, which has the same form as that [other] *trisūtrī*:
(180) *pūrvaparāvaradakṣiṇottarāparādharāṇi vyavasthāyām asaṃjñāyām* | 1|1|34|.
By the passage beginning with "pūrva-parāvara," etc. [it is meant]. "Svābhidheya" means:
the restriction of the limit (*avadhi*) which is required by the denotation (*abhidheya*) of its own word, such as "east" (*pūrva*).
"Apekṣa" means that which is depended upon (*apekṣyate*); the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*). How then [is it explained] in the case of: "Be a co-wife of Īśa"?

Regarding the phrase "of the south" (*dakṣiṇasyāḥ*), they say: even here there is indeed a fixed rule; however, because it is well-known, a word denoting a limit is not employed. Nor is there a prohibition based on its being a technical name (*saṃjñā*). For a technical name is a recent convention, and such a convention does not exist regarding the directions. "Ikṣu... [The text continues].

In the case of [the statement], "The term is ancient; make it a modern convention," the word of the commentator alone is the authority. By this, the expression "of all the gods" (viśveṣāṃ devānām) is explained; for since the word *viśva* is well-known in the Veda as referring to a specific class of deities, there is no modern convention [attaching to it].
“Dakṣiṇā-gāthakāḥ” means “southern singers. The suffix *thakan* is applied here in the sense of a craftsman (*śilpin*).
The point is that although there may be a possibility of specifying a particular limit or lineage by saying “they are skilled in such-and-such a place,” there is no such restrictive rule.
Likewise, one may say, “he is skilled in the lower [register],” “in the betel-stain [of the throat],” or “in the upper and further-upper [registers].”

One should provide a counter-example: "the Northern Kurus. They say that while there is a fixed convention here—since the word "northern" (uttara) is applied to the Kurus in relation to Sumeru as a limit—this is nonetheless a modern convention.

(181) *svam ajñāti-dhana-ākhyāyām* | 1|1|36 | *Svam ajñāti*: The word *sva* denotes self (*ātman*), what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), kinsmen (*jñāti*), and wealth (*dhana*). Since [the rule] excludes kinsmen and wealth, the intention is that "self" and "what belongs to the self" remain; with this in mind, he explains: "belonging to oneself" (*ātmīyā*).

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "or *ātmanaḥ*": as for what some say—that the word *sva* is neuter when referring to the self (*ātman*), and thus the examples *te ve* and *vā* are incorrect in that context—that is due to haste. For [the lexicon states]: "The form *vaḥ* means 'kinsman' or 'self'; *svam* in three genders means 'one's own'; *svaḥ* in the masculine (not feminine) means 'wealth'."

This is because, according to the statement of Amarasimha, the word *sva* possesses masculine gender even when referring to the self (*ātman*). Nor should it be argued that, since in the Amarakośa— where it says “*vau jñātau*” (the two *v* sounds mean known)— the word *ātmani* is construed with the subsequent word *va*, the word *sva* denoting the self must be neuter.

This is because it is appropriate to explain that, contrary to the contradiction with the *Medinīkośa*— which states, "The word *sva* means one's own sons, oneself, a kinsman (in the masculine), and in the three genders [it means] one's own property (in the neuter)"— the term *ātmani* connects with the preceding [word] and not with the subsequent one. Furthermore, in the section beginning with the rule *vibhāṣā jasī*...

Since the author of the Sūtra, by employing a heavy grammatical designation (*gurunirdeśa*) when he could have simply said ‘*vam ātmīye*’, provides proof that the word *sva* denoting the self is masculine; therefore,
it is established that the gloss ‘*ve*’ or ‘*vā*’ = ‘*ātmānaḥ*’ (the selves) is indeed correct.

Regarding the phrase "but [those] denoting kinsmen and wealth": by means of the suffix *ṇini* which expresses habit (*tācchīlya*), he indicates that even for words denoting kinsmen and wealth, the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) certainly exists when they function by prioritizing the sense of "belonging to oneself" (*ātmīyatva*). Indeed, it is precisely for this purpose that the term *ākhyā* ("designation") was included in the rule.

Although one should have stated “*vam* [is used] in the sense of *ātman* and *ātmīya*,” the recourse to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *jñāti* and *dhana* is for the sake of brevity (*mātrālāghava*). Nor should it be argued that if it were stated as “*vam* [is used] in the sense of *ātman* and *ātmīya*,” the mention of *ākhyā* (designation) would not be required; for in reality, even *ātmīya* is included under *jñāti*.
Since it is necessary [to specify] that when there is an intention to express [the word *antara*] as wealth (*dhana*), it should not be treated as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), [the rule is stated].

(182) *antaram* [is used] in the senses of being outside (*bahir-yoga*) and being worn next to the body (*upasaṃvyāna*). 1.1.36. *Antaram* [is used] in the senses of being outside (*bahir-yoga*) and being worn next to the body (*upasaṃvyāna*). "Outside" (*abahiḥ*) refers to an uncovered place; "external" (*bāhyam*)...

It is said: taking the first meaning there, he says—"the external" means [external]. In the second case, however, the meaning "the internal" is to be understood. For indeed, there is a connection of the internal with the external.
Both meanings are established in the original source (*ākara*). Keeping these two meanings in mind, [he speaks of] "in the interval" (*antarāyām*).

Regarding the word *purī* (city), it has been explained as referring either to that which is outside the ramparts or to that which lies within them. Furthermore, the word *upasaṃvyāna* (undergarment) refers to the upper garment when derived from the instrumental sense (*karaṇa*), but refers to the inner garment when derived from the accusative sense (*karman*).

(183) *pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā* Pāṇini 7.1.16. Regarding the word *eka*, eight meanings have been stated; therein he states a specific rule: "in the sense of number. However, in the other seven senses, there may indeed be another form as well, such as *eke* and *ekoṣām*.
The sense is "just as.
(184) *Na bahuvrīhau* |1|1|29|.
Regarding *na bahuvrīhau*: once a *bahuvrīhi* compound has been formed, the prohibition [of the rule] would be redundant.
Because it will be stated later that "those [words] beginning with *sarva* are not [included] when they have become subordinate (*upasarjanībhūta*)," he says:

"when intended to be formed" (*cikīrṣite*). This meaning is obtained by resorting to a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*) in the rule *abahuvrīhau*. Regarding the form *tvakam*: the suffix *akac* is applied according to the rule *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ* when [the word] is either unknown (*ajñāta*) or contemptible (*kutsita*).

The same applies here in the case of *evamahakam*. Regarding the phrase "in the analytical sentence" (*prakriyāvākye*), the meaning is "in the non-orthodox analytical sentence" (*alaukikavigrahavākye*).
And that [sentence] takes such forms as *yuṣmad su pitṛ su* and so forth. Now, one might ask:
"Even if *akac* were to apply there, what would be the fault? To this, he says: "And that... and so on. Nor...

It should not be argued that because the *nimitta* (the cause) of non-subordination (*anupasarjanatva*) is on the verge of destruction, the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) will not apply even prior to the formation of the compound due to the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*; for that paribhāṣā is non-eternal (*anitya*), as it is precisely this very sūtra (*Pāṇini 1.1.29*) that serves as its indicator (*jñāpaka*). [Thus we have] *atibhavakān*.

The intention is that this very [rule] serves as the result of the indication (*jñāpanaphala*). The compound *pratyācakhyau* is a *prādi*-compound according to the rule *tyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā*. Regarding the form *pratyācakhyau*: the inclusion of the augment *tuṅ* in the rule *hravoḥ śūḍ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2), or the statement concerning the restoration of the original form (*prakṛtipratyāpatti*), serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the non-universality (*anityatva*) [of grammatical rules], and it is also due to compliance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*).

The meaning is that there is a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*). Regarding the phrase "according to the subsequent [rule]": the sense is that, at present, the established rule is precisely as stated by the author of the Bhāṣya.

Regarding the phrase "due to the arrangement of the *gaṇa*": by this it is implied that the inclusion of the term "in the designation *ṭha*" within the *gaṇa*-sūtra "ūry-ādi-gatādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.4.61) serves little purpose.

Because there is no inclusion [of the terms] "pūrva" and so forth within the group (gaṇa) of "saṃjñā," it can likewise be stated that the designation *ṭha* does not apply even in the rule "pūrvapara... located in the Aṣṭādhyāyī; and in the absence of that [designation], when *jas* follows...

It should be stated that in the case of *saṃjñāyām ṭhutarāḥ kuravaḥ*, there would be an option regarding what has not been previously established; however, since the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāmasaṃjñā*) is based on its etymological meaning (*anvartha*), an injunction for what has not been previously established is impossible in the case of a proper name. Therefore, by the preceding rule, the designation [of pronoun] applies only when it is not a proper name, in the case of the suffix *jasi*.
For it would be appropriate to say "or it might be. Regarding the phrase "the operation of a technical name" (*saṃjñākāryam*):

the meaning is that [operations] such as *smāy-* and so forth, which are occasioned by the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*). Regarding the phrase "an operation belonging to a sub-group" (*antargaṇakāryam*):
this refers to [rules such as] *ṭhadḍḍatarādibhyaḥ*, *ṭhtyādādīnāmaḥ*, and *‘adoḥ saḥ sau’*.

The meaning is "and so forth. Regarding the term *atikatarām*: here, the substitute *āḍ* does not apply. However, in the case of *ati-ta*, the intention is that there is neither the substitution of *at* for the *tyad*-class stems (*tyadādyatva*) nor the substitution of *s* for *adas* in the nominative singular (*ado’sau*).

(185) *Tṛtīyā-samāse* |1|1|30|. Regarding the rule *tṛtīyā-samāse*: although the term *samāsa* is understood here by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from the preceding rule *vibhāṣā dik-samāse*, the explicit mention of *samāsa* again is intended to include even the secondary (*gauṇa*) sense of a compound.

Intending to include [this case] for the sake of summary, he says: "having the sense of a third-case compound. Here, the compound prescribed by the rule *ūrvasadṛśe* is understood, because it is taught as a specific rule (*pratipadokta*). However, the compound [prescribed] by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe* is not; therefore, there is no prohibition in the case of *tvayakā kṛtam*.
It occurs. Since it will be established that [the suffix *aC*] applies when a *sup* beginning with *ṭh*, *k*, *r*, *s*, or *bh* follows, here *aC* (*akac*) is applied before the *sup* suffix.
(186) And in a *dvandva* compound. 1.1.31.

And in the case of a *dvandva* [compound], [the rule applies] to the whole [compound]. This is because the word *dvandva* has its primary application (*mukhyatva*) precisely there. Nor can there be a connection [of the rule] with the words "those which are *sarvādi* in a *dvandva*," because grammatical factors (*kāraka*) must connect only with a verb. Nor can there be a connection with the words "those which exist in a *dvandva*," because that would require the implicit supply (*adhyāhāra*) of the verb "to exist" (*vidyate*).

The sense is that, due to respect [for the rule], it is only logical for the connection to be with the verb *bhavati* itself, as it is that which is primarily to be negated. Regarding the phrase "the contingency of *suṭ*": this is not so, because of the force of the prohibition in the rule *dvandve ca*.

It should not be said that [the prohibition] does not apply in cases such as *ṭhvarṇāśrametarāṇām*, because the capacity of the rule [to exclude] *tratasil* and so on— which are not part of the *aṅga*— is already exhausted by that very exclusion.
(187) *vibhāṣā jasi* 1.1.32.

Regarding the phrase *jasādhāram*: although the *ja* has been removed by the substitution of *śī*, its status as a locus (*ādhāra*) here should be understood in a figurative sense. Alternatively, *jasiḥ* means "in *jas*" (i.e., *ir* [the substitute] for *jas*); he explains this by the meaning of the rule, stating *jasādhāram*, based on the elision of the locative case ending (*saptamyā luk*) as prescribed in the Sūtras. Otherwise, if *akac* were present, the rule *asaḥ śī* would apply.

The sense is that the form *varṇāśrametarake* would also be possible. When one forms the compound *varṇāśca āśramāśca itarakaśca* (the castes, the stages of life, and the "other"), by first applying the suffix *akac* to form *itaraka*—meaning either "unknown" or "despised"—then indeed two forms would result. However, [in the case of the intended meaning...]

When the word *itara* is compounded with [the preceding members] to form a *dvandva*, and then joined with the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth— as in the expression *ajñātavarṇāśrametarāḥ*— then it should be understood that the single form *varṇāśrametarakāḥ* alone is grammatically correct.

But surely, the suffix *akac* would also be unavoidable for the word *itara*, which is a member of the *dvandva* compound, since its status as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is not lost. If it is argued that by the rule "in a *dvandva*" (*dvandve ca*), the prohibition applies to the whole compound and not to its members; to this they reply: according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), [the term] "retaining its own meaning" (*ajahatsvārthā*)...

The position that [the term *vṛtti*] refers to the compound (*samāsa*) is the primary one; however, under that view, since the constituent parts (*avayava*) are devoid of meaning, they lack connection with meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*), and thus there is no possibility at all for the suffix *akac* to apply.
For those [who hold the view], however, by the particle *ca* in the rule *dvandve ca*, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prohibited even for the constituent parts.
Thus it is said; even if one accepts the view that these words do not abandon their own primary meanings (*ajahatsvārtha*), there is no fault.

(188) *Prathama-carama-taya-alpārdha-katipaya-nemāś-ca* | Pāṇini 1.1.33. This rule is formulated because the suffix *tasi* is already established for the words *prathama*, *carama*, and *nema*, while it is not yet established for the others.

The suffix *taya* [in the word *dvitīya*, etc. is prescribed by the rule “*aṅkhyāyā avayave tayaP*” [Pāṇini 5.2.42]. Regarding the term *tīyasya*: it refers to that which is prescribed by the rules “*vestīyaḥ*” [Pāṇini 5.2.54] and “*reḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca*” [Pāṇini 5.2.55].
(189) *jarāyā jaras anyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 7.2.101]: “In place of *jarā*, *jaras* may optionally [be substituted].”
From the rule *jarāyā jara*, [the word] *vibhaktau* is carried over from the rule *ṭhaṣṭana ā vibhaktau*.
Then, from the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ*, the term *aci* which is carried over qualifies [the word *vibhaktau*].

Here, by means of this qualifier, there is the application of "that which begins with it" (*tadādividhi*), according to the principle: "In a rule where a specific element is mentioned, the operation applies to that which begins with it."

With the intention that this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the inclusion of the final element (*tadanta-vidhi*), he says: "in a case-ending beginning with a vowel (*ajādau vibhaktau*). Why "beginning with a vowel"? [Consider: *jarābhyām*, *jarābhiḥ*. Why "in a case-ending"? [Consider: *jarāyā idam* [meaning] *jāram*. Nor should it be argued that [the suffix] *asun* could apply after the word *jarā* by means of the rule *ReĀvā*; for [the suffix *asun* applies] after the word *jarā-*...
From the root *kṛ* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, by the rule "after *ṇi*, as if it were *iṣṭha*," there is the elision of the *ṭi*-portion;

then, after the addition of the *kvip* suffix and the elision of the *ṇi*, because the modified part (*a*) is not different from the original, the word *jarā* applies to this *a*. Consequently, by the rule "asuṅ in the case of *siti* and *cit*," the final vowel undergoes the *asuṅ* substitution, resulting in the form *asau*.

Because it falls under the category of *rūpa*. However, even here, forms such as *arasau* and *arasaḥ* are accepted. Nor should it be argued that because of the status of the elided *ṇi* as *sthānivadbhāva*, the absence of a following case-ending (*vibhaktiparatva*) would prevent the derivation of forms like *arasau*;
for there is a prohibition stating, "that which is elided before *vā* is not *sthānivat*. Even though [the rule] says "before *vā*"...

The rule *na sthānivat* is only occasional (*kvācitka*); nevertheless, it should be noted that here, the very fact that the heavy substitute (*gurūpadeśa*) is applied in the case of *araḥ* serves as the proof for resorting to that [principle].
Regarding the phrase *padāṅgādhikāre*: this is a *paribhāṣā* (technical metarule) which is an elaboration of the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya*.

Therefore, it is stated in the *Manoramā* that "the member (*pada*) is the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and by means of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is the rule of extension to what ends with it (*tadantavidhi*). However, it should be understood that the term "qualified" (*viśeṣya*) is used generally.
Consequently, in the rule *allopo’naḥ*, [the word *an*] refers to that which is an *an* that is a constituent part of a member (*aṅgāvayava*).
The text to be explained hereafter follows its own natural sequence. Regarding this, the modern scholars (*navyāḥ*) state:

"Indeed, in the *ākāra* [of the sūtra], the reading 'asya tad-uttarapadasya ca' is the most prevalent. However, if the reading were 'adantasya ca,' then with the intention that [the rule] would not apply to forms preceded by *bahuc*, they [the commentators] have focused on stating the resultant meaning."

Regarding the statement, “And [the rule] *adutarapadasya ca* has been recited, but this is not a new injunction,” he says *nirdiśya* (having specified) in order to preclude the possibility that the substitute *jaras* might apply in place of every [form of the stem] when accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*). Now, one might object: even by means of the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*), [the substitution would apply] only to that base (*aṅga*) which ends with the word *jarā*.
When the word *jarā* is being specified, the substitution of *jaras* must apply [only] there and not elsewhere; therefore, he says:

"of that which is modified in one part" (*ekadeśavikṛtasya*). Even though the context concerns words (*pada*), the example for the rule of extension to what ends with such a word (*tadantavidhi*) is as follows: when the substitution of *ru* and *ra* applies even to that which ends in it, we have *dīrghāhā nidāgha*.

Thus he will say. The governing rule *utarapade* (in the case of a subsequent member), as found in *ṭhalugutarapade*, is also included by the mention of the governing rule *pade*. The result of this will be made clear in that very place.
"In the alternative" (*pakṣe*) means in the absence of the substitution of *jaras*.
"By those who follow that [view]" means by those who explain [the rule] as "irjarasine," and so forth;

that is, by those who follow that opinion. "Only *nirjarasya*" means that once the substitution of *sy* has occurred by means of the prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the substitution of *jaras* does not apply.

Their intention is that there is only one single form (*rūpa*). For this very reason, considering the usage by the poet Bhāravi—*“the supreme, pure state of Brahman, free from birth and old age”*—to be inconsistent, they have stated that it should be read as *“free from birth and dust (or passion)”* (*vītajanmarajasaḥ*). And this...

For the author of the Bhāṣya, having rejected the suffixes *in* and *āt* in the rule *āṅsī*, and having prescribed the substitutes *nā* and *adā*, established [the form] by dividing the rule *ṭhāṅ ca* into two parts so that the substitution of *et* occurs when *nā* follows; thus, for example, *nirjarasinaḥ*.

It is quite clear that [the claim] "by *nirjarasā*" contradicts the Bhāṣya. Nor should it be suspected that, once the substitute (*ādeśa*) is applied, the elision (*lopa*) would apply before a consonant (*hal*), thereby failing to account for the form *ṭhanenā*; for a specific rule ordaining the non-substitution (*anādeśa*) is provided when the word *naśabda* follows. To explain: [the form] *ṭhanāpyakaḥ* [is established thus].
In this context, the word division is *ṭhan-nāpi*. Due to its neuter gender, there is elision (*luk*) of the nominative suffix *su*, resulting in the elision of the nasal *n*.

The term *āpi* is the singular locative case of a collective dvandva compound. Nor should one suspect that the substitution of *at* for the genitive ending *ṅsi* would result in a single substitute form (*pararūpa*).

Because of the capacity for pronouncing the vowel *a* [in *atijara-*], a long vowel is possible; likewise, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on this very sūtra, *arāyā jarasanyatarasyām*, that "the form *atijaraiḥ* should occur by virtue of the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*. Consequently, *irjarasaiḥ* is also [valid].

This is indeed contrary to the Bāṣya. By this, it is clearly evident that the explanation offered by some— namely, that in the rule *ṭhato bhisa ais*, instead of saying *ṭheḥ*, the use of *ais* is for the sake of the form *irjarasaiḥ*— is merely based on negligence (*prāmādika*).

(190) *paddannomāshṛnniśasanyūṣandoṣanyakañcchakannudannāsañcchasprabhṛtiṣu* || 6.1.63 || *paddanno* || "In the case of the [suffixes] beginning with *śas*, it is optional. (*anudātasya*) || 6.1.59 || [This rule applies to the substitution of *an* for the final vowel of a word ending in *m* when followed by a suffix beginning with *śas* and having an unaccented initial vowel.]

The intention is that the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is understood to carry over from the rule *cardupadhasya*. Here, the suffixes beginning with *śas* are presented as the cause [of the substitution], and they imply specific bases corresponding to the substitutes such as *pada* and so on; thus he says: *pādadanta-*.

Even though the term "in Vedic" (*chandas*) continues from the rule *yadyasi īrṣaṃśchandasī*, nevertheless, forms such as *padāt* occur even in the common language (*bhāṣā*). As he will state, this is due to the force of the inclusion of the word "Vedic" in the Vārttika *āsaścchandasī*. [The objection that it is] "due to negligence" (*prāmādikam*) is as follows: for instance, in the case of *āsnaḥ*...

In the mantra "the quail of the wolf," the meaning is "from the mouth," because of the context; and also because of the corroboration from another mantra: "even the quail from within the mouth of the wolf. Likewise, in the mantra "offering oblations in the mouth," the meaning is "in the mouth. Similarly, [it is said] "they spoke to the breath in the mouth" (*āsanyaṃ prāṇamūcuḥ*).
This should also be understood in such cases as the following:
(191) *suḍanapuṃsakasya* | Pāṇini 1.1.43. Regarding the rule *suḍanapuṃsakasya*: although it could have been stated as *uṭ strīpuṃsayoḥ*, [the author] says *anapuṃsakasya*.

Kaiyaṭa states that the statement [of Pāṇini] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is a *nañ*-compound even when there is a prohibition of the suffix *ra-sajya*. By this, forms such as *asūryampaśyāni mukhāni* ("faces not seeing the sun") are established.
(192) *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne* 1.4.17.

Regarding *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne*: one should not suspect that *u* here refers to the locative plural; rather, because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule *asarvanāmasthāne*, it must be the nominative singular.
With the intention that the inclusion of the word *ādi* (beginning) serves to encompass more than what would be established by the form *upi* alone, he says:

"—up to the limit of the *kap* suffix. Now, one might object: in this case, the elision of the *n* in *rājñi* would not occur, because by the rule of "indicatory power" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), there is no status as a word (*padatva*) due to the following of a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix.
This is not a fault; for although the status of a word is impossible by the rule "in the case of *su*, etc.," when *su* follows, [the elision still takes place].

When the technical designation *pada* is applied to that which is preceded by a suffix (*sub*) or followed by a verbal ending (*tiṅ*)—according to the rule "that which ends in *sup* or *tiṅ* is a *pada*"—the *su* suffix is elided by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*.

By the principle of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), the word remains a *pada* because it ends in the letter *n*. However, if one were to argue that a preceding element becomes a *pada* when *svādi* suffixes follow, based on the rule *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne*, [then the following would apply].

Having prescribed the designation *pada* for the preceding element, in the rule *ṭhyaci bham*, the term *ṭhyaci* is split [as *ṭhi* and *yaci*]; thus, it is prohibited that the preceding element is a *pada* when followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* beginning with *yak* (the suffixes *au*, *jas*, etc.).
However, in the case of the nominative singular (*su*), since the status of being a *pada* is possible when that suffix follows, [the prohibition does not apply].
In cases such as *āje* and others, when the elision (*lopa*) of *n* is to be applied, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
(193) *yaci bham* | 1.4.18 | *yaci bham*. By the inclusion of the term *yac* [in the rule], the letter *a* is understood.

Because of the mention of the seventh case (locative), the rule applies to that which begins with [the element mentioned]; thus he says, "in those beginning with *yakāra*," and so forth. What is the purpose of saying "in those beginning with *yakāra*"? [Consider] *gārgyaḥ* and *vātsyaḥ*. This is so that the elision of the vowel *a* may occur by the rule *yasyeti ca* following the suffix *yañ* after bases such as *garga*. Why say "except in the case of sarvanāmasthāna endings"? [Consider] *supādau*.
[The term *supāda* is used] so that rules such as *ādaḥ pat*, *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, and *vāha ūṭh* do not apply in cases like *vidvāṃsau*, *vidvāṃsaḥ*, *dityavāhau*, and *dityavāhaḥ*.

(194) *Ā kaḍārādekā saṃjñā* | 1.4.1 | "Up to *kaḍāra*" (*ā kaḍārāt*). Here, [the rule] *rākaḍārāt samāsaḥ* does not serve as the limit (*avadhi*), because of the principle of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*) and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *tatpuruṣo dviguśca*.
For the purpose of introducing two designations simultaneously, the particle *ca* is used there. Thus he says: "from the rule *kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye*.

Regarding the principle that "one thing has only one designation," when both [designations] have their own scope (*sāvakāśatva*), the subsequent one is adopted according to the rule *vipratiṣedhe param*; however, when [one] lacks its own scope (*niravakāśatva*), that very [designation] is adopted. In that case, of the subsequent...

The example is: *dhanuṣā vidhyati* ("he pierces with a bow"). Here, while the bow is indeed the point of departure (*apādāna*) relative to the departure of the arrows, it is the instrument (*sādhaka*) relative to the act of piercing. Since both [designations] would thus apply, the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa-saṃjñā*), being subsequent [in the rules], subverts the designation of "point of departure" (*apādāna-saṃjñā*). This is because the latter would otherwise be left without scope.

The illustration for the former [rule] is *bhavadīya* (your), derived from *bhavat-tas*. For here, by the rule *iti ca*, the designation *pada* supersedes even the subsequent designation *bha*, because it is without scope (*niravakāśatva*).
Consequently, the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) occurs for the letter *t*. However, in the present case, the subsequent *bha*-designation is without scope.

With the intention that [the rule] subverts the designation *pada*, it is appropriate to understand that very same [designation] when an *ac* vowel follows the suffixes beginning with *śas*; thus he says, "yā para" and so forth. Regarding "the elision of *y*" (*yalopa*), this is by the rule "hali sarveṣām. However, the rule "opo vyor vali" does not apply.
Because that [rule] is not established for this [case]:
(195) *allopo'naḥ* | P. 6.4.134. In the rule *allopo'naḥ*, a specific suffix is implied by the word *hasi*, as well as the *aṅga*.

Intending that the qualifier "dvayan" (consisting of two) refers to the vowel *a*, he explains [the rule] with the words "aṅgāvayava ik... and so forth. According to the explanation of the ancients—that there is elision of the *a* of an *aṅga* ending in *an* which is a *bha*—there would be elision even of the *a* of the *t* in forms such as "akṣṇe."

There would be elision (*lopa*). However, if one were to explain [the rule] as "of the *an* of a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *h*," then it would apply in cases such as *ṭhanasā* and *anase*. Even if one were to explain it there—by means of repetition (*āvṛtti*) and so forth—as "of the *an* belonging to a *bha*-stem (*bhasya*) which is a stem ending in *an*," [the fault remains].

The point is that there is indeed over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in examples such as *ṭhanastakṣṇe* and so forth. Some maintain that the inclusion of the marker *t* (*taparakaraṇa*) in the rule was intended to prevent the misconception that it is a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*). Now, one might object: from *prāṇ* (derived from *pra-an*), when suffixes such as *śas* follow, as in *prāṇaḥ* and so on, [the rule] *ṭhaniteḥ* would apply.

If it is argued that the inclusion of *ta* (the long vowel marker) is intended precisely to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—since the substitution of *ṇ* would otherwise be subject to the rule of being "unestablished" (*asiddha*)—we say: not so. For once the *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel lengthening of homogeneous vowels) has taken place, the [original] *a* no longer exists there. Nor can it be claimed that, by the principle "an operation affecting a letter is stronger than one affecting a suffix," the *savarṇadīrgha* should occur first.

It must be stated that elision (*lopa*) indeed occurs [even] when there is no *ayū* [substitution], because if that were the case, the purpose of employing the *tapara* marker would remain futile due to the absence of anything to be excluded. In reality, the paribhāṣā concerning vowels (*vārṇaparibhāṣā*) does not apply here; for the principle "the internal (*āṅga*) [operation] prevails over the phonetic (*vārṇa*)" applies only when both rules operate simultaneously.

Because [the rule] is stronger; for when the *kvip* suffix is applied, due to the lengthening by the rule "ṭhūlope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.111), there is no *an* even prior to the application of the *savarṇadīrgha* [substitution], and thus [the *an* is absent]. Therefore, their intention is that the inclusion of the *tapara* (the *ṛ*) is solely for the purpose of dispelling error, and not for the purpose of preventing the elision of the vowel *a* in forms such as *rāṇa*.

In reality, however, by the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would indeed occur there; therefore, the modern grammarians (*navyāḥ*) maintain that the inclusion of *ta* (in *tapara*) is absolutely necessary here. (196) *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade* | Pāṇini 8.4.1: After *ra* and *ṣa*, *na* becomes *ṇa* when within the same word (*samānapada*).

Regarding *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ*: here, having carried forward the phrase "for a non-final *ṭh*, there is the cerebral [substitute]," the mention of *ṇa* and the sūtra "for a non-final" (*adāntasya*) have been rejected in the Bhāṣya. As for "in the same word" (*samānapade*):
since it is impossible for the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*) not to reside within a word, the term "in a word" (*pade*) alone would suffice.

Since the status of being a single word is already established by implication, the inclusion of the term *samāna* (identical) is for the purpose that the rule should apply only where there is a single identical word—

meaning, where there is no occurrence of the cause [of doubling] in a word different from the word containing the cause. Therefore, in compounds such as *rāmanāma* and *andhargāna*, [the doubling occurs].

It does not occur; for in that case, although the letter *n* resides in a single word, it resides in a word distinct from the word containing the cause [of the change]. Indeed, in forms such as *uṣṇa*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs because the letter *n* resides in a word that is not distinct from the word containing the cause. In the form *ātṛbhogīṇa*, however, it does not occur.

In such cases as well, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* certainly occurs; for even though [the *n*] resides in a suffix (*pratyaya*), it lacks the quality of being situated in a word different from the word containing the cause (*nimittavat*). By this, having explained that the mention of "samāna" (identical) is for the purpose of obtaining the status of an indivisible word (*akhaṇḍapada*),...

Even though the over-extension (*prasaṅga*) in cases such as *āmanām* has been prevented, some have argued that under-application (*avyāpti*) would still occur in cases such as *ātṛbhogīṇa*; however, this statement is refuted because, according to the method already explained, the suspicion of under-application has been eliminated. Regarding *yūṣṇaḥ*: *yūṣa* means broth (*maṇḍa*).
For it is seen [in the medical texts] that "the broth of *udra* and *āmalaka* is a laxative, digestive-stimulant, and a digestive.

Regarding the rule "that which is not established in the preceding [portion of grammar] does not behave like its original" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*), this is established by logic; for since the final three chapters (*tripādī*) are considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule "when followed by something else" (*ṭhacaḥ parasmin*) does not apply to an operation to be performed therein. As for the word "of that" (*tasya*).

Regarding the rule "na padānta-di-sī-dvi-rvacana-vare-yalopa-svara-savarṇa-anuṣṭhāna-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avāya-avā

Regarding *latva*: in *nigālyate*, the substitution of *la* for *na* occurs because the elision (*lopa*) of *ṇi* is treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original element) by the rule *aci vibhāṣā*.

Regarding *ṇatva*: in *māṣavapanī*, the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* does not occur here because, due to the elision of *ya* by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the elided portion is treated as *sthānivadbhūta*; consequently, the *nakāra* is no longer at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus the condition for *ṇatva* is absent. Now, one might object:

Just as there is no occurrence of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) in the case of *argabhaginī*, so too there is no occurrence of *ṇatva* in the case of *āṣavapanī*, because it will be stated later that [the rule applies] "to the end of that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which constitutes the second member (*uttarapada*)".

Regarding this, they say: when a compound is formed with a word ending in *lyuṭ* according to the rule *sādhanaṃ kṛti*, and subsequently the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, [the elision occurs] by the rule *yasyeti*.
Once this elision (*alopa*) has been applied, since the *n* is now at the end of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the application of the rule for changing it to *ṇ* certainly remains valid.

It might be argued that in forms such as *yūṣṇa*, the rule *raṣābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.1) serves no purpose, because the desired form is established by the rule *ṣṭuan* (Pāṇini 8.4.40) alone. For this very reason, it is stated in the authoritative commentary (*ākara*) that "the mention of *ra* is for the sake of what follows."
If it is argued that [the mention of *ṣ*] is for the sake of establishing stability, then the inclusion of *ṣ* here remains established for that very purpose;

consequently, in forms such as *uṣṇaḥ* and *uṣṇāti*, by what could the application of the rule *raṣābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.1) regarding the substitution of *ṇ* be prevented? If it is argued that this is prevented by the status of *ṣṭua* (as taught in Pāṇini 8.4.39), no, because that [rule] is not yet established (*asiddha*). Nor...

It might be suspected that [the rule] is established by the authority of the verbal testimony [of the sūtra], because it has already served its purpose in cases such as *ṛṣṭaḥ*, *uṣṭiḥ*, and *aṣṭhaḥ*. If it is argued that the portion [of the rule] stating "when there is a conjunction with *ṣ* (asya ṣayoge ṇa)" has not yet served its purpose, we say no;
for that [portion] was not stated separately. Furthermore, the statement here that "[the change occurs] after what follows *ṣ*" (*ṣātparasya*) has likewise not yet served its purpose.
And because [the author] himself is satisfied [with this]. If it is argued that even so, the mention of *ṣ* in the original source (*ākara*) contradicts the purpose of the subsequent rule, we say no;
for what is intended in the source is merely that without the mention of *ṣ*, there is no failure to establish the target forms such as *puṣṇāti*, and not that...
In examples such as *uṣṇāti*, the rule *ṭhraṣābhyām* does not apply.
(197) *na lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* | 8|2|7|. [The sūtra] *na lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*: the genitive case ending is elided because it is a Vedic (sautra) usage; however, it is not...

These are genitive *tatpuruṣa* compounds; the sense is that a compound is impossible because the first member is dependent [on another word], and because a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) serves as a qualifier of a word (*pada*). Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in this":
this is a genitive *tatpuruṣa*. "Of that" refers to the word bearing the technical designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and "that which is at the end" refers to...

The meaning is that the negative particle *na* belongs to it (the suffix). However, it is established in the *Manoramā* that if the word (*pada*) were also qualified by the rule "before a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *iṭ*," then the mention of the word "end" (*anta*) in the sūtra could have been omitted, since the rule for "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) would apply through the qualifier. Why [is there] the mention of "nominal stem"? [Example: *akārīṣṭām* (third person dual, imperfect, middle voice of √kṛ). [Why is this not a counter-example? Because the augment *iṭ* is added after the verbal root (*dhātu*), and the prohibition applies only when the augment follows a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Therefore, since the augment here does not follow a nominal stem, the prohibition does not apply. Thus, the form *akārīṣṭām* is valid. [Another example: *ajāgaruḥ* (third person plural, perfect, active voice of √jāgṛ). [Why is this not a counter-example? Because the augment *iṭ* is added after the verbal root, and the prohibition applies only when the augment follows a nominal stem. Therefore, since the augment here does not follow a nominal stem, the prohibition does not apply. Thus, the form *ajāgaruḥ* is valid.
I shall explain. What is the purpose of the word *padam*? [Consider: *rājānau*, *rājānaḥ*.
(198) *vibhāṣā iṅśyoḥ* | 6.4.136. Regarding *vibhāṣā iṅśyoḥ*: the term *ī* refers to that which is prescribed by the rule *napuṃsakācca* (7.1.19), and not [to the *ī* of *iṅ*].

But [the rule] "aśśasoḥ śiḥ" applies because [the suffix] is not *am*. This is because, by the rule "hasya," there is an implication that only a suffix beginning with *y* (such as *jas*) that is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* is intended. This is what he states: "not being a *sarvanāmasthāna*" and so forth. [The example is] *kakuddoṣaṇī*.

The analysis is *kakut-doṣaṇī*. If it were treated as a single word (*ekapada*), the inconsistency will be explained immediately below. Regarding *āsanyam*: because of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ*, the *ṭilopa* (elision of the final vowel) prescribed by *astaddhite* does not occur. For this very reason, [the form] is *akuk- doṣaṇī*.

The meaning is "precisely from the application [of the rule]. Although one might argue that the compound *kakuddoḥ* is formed by the collective combination (*samāhāra*) of *kakud* and *doḥ*, and that once *kakud-doṣaṇī* is formed, the Bhāṣya is easily reconciled—
thereby serving as evidence for the neuter gender of the word *doḥ*— nevertheless, [this is not the case].

The view that *aku* is indeed a separate word is more logical; otherwise, although the duality of the arms would be established, the singularity of the hump (*kakuda*) would not be obtained—this is the sense. As in Raghuvamśa: "The night-stalker rushed forward, raising his right arm (*dakṣiṇaṃ doriṃ*)," where he raised his right arm.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "He rushed toward him. Regarding the phrase "his fault" (*doṣaṃ tasya*): this is a usage by Śrī Harṣa;

the connection is with the bow (*cāpasya*), which both incurs a fault (*doṣam*) and possesses the quality of being a defect (*dūṣaṇam*). Regarding the expression "occurring in two days": it is a compound formed according to the rule for the meaning of a secondary suffix (*taddhitārthe*). By the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied, and by the rule *ahno'hna-*, [the substitution of *ahna-* occurs].

From these [words], there is the substitution of *ahna* [for *aha*]; then, by the rule *kālāṭ ṭhañ*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is introduced, which is subsequently elided by the rule *avigaurādibhyaḥ lug anapatye*. (199) *saṅkhyā-visāya-pūrvasyāhnasyāhan anyatarasyāṃ ṅī* 6.3.110: For the word *ahna* preceded by a numeral, *vi*, or *sāya*, the substitution of *ahan* optionally takes place before the feminine suffix *ṅī*.
Regarding *ahnaḥ sāya*: the word *sāya* denotes the conclusion [of time] when derived from the root *si* with the suffix *ghañ*;
it forms a partitive compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*) by virtue of the indicative rule (*jñāpaka*) "saṅkhyā-visāye. Thus end those [words] ending in short *a*. Regarding *viśvapā*:
in the analysis (*vigraha*) "he protects (*pāti*) or guards (*rakṣati*) the universe (*viśvam*)," [the word is derived] from the root *ā* in the sense of protecting.

The commentators explain that in the rule *ṭhāto ’nupasarge* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), the suffix *ka* is set aside by the rule *ṭhāto maninkvanibvanipaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.74), because of the particle *ca*. Here, however, in Vedic usage (*chandas*), the suffix *vic* applies according to *ṭhāto manin-*, whereas in common worldly usage (*loka*), it applies by the rule *ṭhanyebhyo ’pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.75); such is the distinction.

(200) *dīrghāj jasi ca* | Pāṇini 6.1.105. The word *jasi* follows from the previous rule, and by the force of the particle *ca*, the word *ici* is drawn in [from the preceding rule], while the word *na* is understood to carry over as well.
Therefore, he says: "after a long vowel, before *jasi* and *ici*. If the particle *ca* were absent from the sūtra, [the substitution] would apply only before *ici* after a short *a*.

The sense is that, because of the form *dīrghāt* [in Pāṇini 7.3.101], one might suspect that a restrictive rule (*vyavasthā*) applies to the case ending *jas*. Regarding the phrase "for such purposes as these":

[an objection is raised]—but surely, based on the indications in the rules *ṅy-āp-stryākhyau* (P. 1.4.3) and *vādibhyaḥ* (P. 6.1.155), the conventional technical designation (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) applies only to the pratyāhāra *ik* and the pratyāhāra *ac*?

"Let it be explained: since a long vowel (*dīrgha*) lacks the status of being an *ac* (vowel), the rule for the homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) would not apply in cases such as *gaurī-au*; therefore, what is the purpose of this prohibitive sūtra?
If you say this, it is not so; for from this very prohibition, it is understood that the term *pratyāhāra* includes even those [vowels] other than *ig*.

Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted [in these cases]. Otherwise, in forms such as *aurī* (from *auras-ī*), the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ*) would not occur when the suffix *śas* follows. Furthermore, in forms such as *upārchatī*, the substitution of *ṛ* for *ṭha* by the rule "ṭhuraṇ raparaḥ" would not apply;
nor would there be the substitution of *ka* for *ṭha* in forms such as *aiṣādakarṣukaḥ* by the rule "isusuk-tāntāt kaḥ."

In examples such as *ṭhamīṣām*, the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* following *iṇ* is not established; this is the general direction [of the argument]. Following the sūtra *“rathamayoḥ”* (Pāṇini 6.1.220), it would be more appropriately stated as *“īrghāccchasī”*.

Its meaning would be that a long vowel (*dīrgha*) followed by *śas* undergoes the substitution of a homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). And in this way, the letter *ca* [in the original rule] is unnecessary.

Some maintain that [the rule] should not be applied, and that one should not follow it with "not" (na), as this would result in excessive brevity (*mahallāghavam*). Others argue that if one were to rely on the indications *ṛnne* and *ānāmreḍite* in order to prevent the erroneous restriction "only after a long vowel" (*asidīrghādeva*), there would be a burden of comprehension (*pratipatigauravam*); therefore, the original formulation (*yathānyāsa*) itself is better.
Thus say others.
(201) *āto dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.140). In the case of *hāhān*, this is an unanalyzed nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a specific type of Gandharva.

"Ṭhāhā, hūhū, and others such as these are the Gandharvas," according to Amara. Some, however, explain that *sāḥ* means "those who exist together with *saḥ*, namely Vāsudeva (whose initial letter is *a*)," and they cite this as a counter-example for the suffix *sān*.

Regarding *ktva* and *śna*: although it is stated that "the suffix *lyap* replaces *ktvā*" and "the suffix *śānac* replaces *śnaḥ* when followed by *jhi*," and also that "the suffix *ram* is added after *ktvā*," [the following applies].

Thus, although the elision of *āt* (ā-lopa) is established by this rule (*nirdeśa*) within these sūtras, this has been stated in order to dispel any suspicion of incorrectness regarding the explanatory statements (*vyākhyāna-vākya*), such as "the suffix *lyap* occurs for *ktvā*" and "the suffix *śānac* occurs for *naḥ*. Thus end those [roots] ending in long *ā*.

(202) *Śeṣo ghy asakhi* [Pāṇini 1.4.7]. He states the purpose of the word *śeṣa* in the sūtra: "not being designated as *nadī*. From the rule *yū stryākhyau*, the term *yū* is carried over (*anuvartate*), and from the rule *iti hrasvaśca*, the term *hrasva* is carried over.

Thus he says: "as long as they are short," and so forth. Regarding the form *matyai*: even under the view that [the stem] has the designation *nadī*, if it also possesses the designation *ghi*, then after the addition of the augment *āṬ* by the rule *āṇ nadyāḥ*, and after the *guṇa* substitution by the rule *her ṅtī*, and finally the substitution of *ay* for *e*, the form would have to be *matayai*; such is the intended meaning.

(203) *āṅe nā ’striyām* | P. 7.3.120. [The substitute] *nā* [is applied] after *āṅ*, provided it is not feminine. However, it was not stated as *uṃsi* [instead of *nā*], so that [the form] might occur in the case of *ṭhamunā kulena*. Nor is the desired form established by *num*, because *mutva* is considered *asiddha* with respect to *iko ’ci* [P. 6.1.77].

The prohibition [of *asiddha* status] applies because of the non-occurrence of *num*; however, there is no lack of *asiddha* status in the case of *ādeśa* (substitution), because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] "a mune. Nor should it be argued that the prohibition "a mu ne" might apply only to *num*, on the grounds that the vowel 'a' in "na" is not intended to be significant;
for [the form] "amunā" [would otherwise be incorrect].

Because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of non-establishment in examples such as *ghaṭena*, and because of the unwanted application of the augment *num* in cases such as *amuṣmai kulāya*.

Nor should it be argued that the augment *num* does not apply once the substitution of *smāi* has occurred there; for the augment *num* applies by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), thereby subverting the substitution of *smāi*. The term "of the Easterners" (*prācām*) refers to "the teachers" (*ācāryāṇām*).
The remainder [of the rule].

(204) *ṅsiṅsośca* | Pāṇini 6.1.110. Regarding *ṅsi* and *ṅs*: here there are two instances of *ṅsi* and *ṅs*, and there are also two instances of *eṅ*; these correspond respectively (*yathāsaṅkhyam*).

No, because it lacks the svarita accent; because there is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the shorter vowel is not placed first [in the rule *alpāctaram*]; and because of the specific grammatical indications in the rules *acca gheḥ* and *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*. (205) *acca gheḥ* | 7|3|119|

Regarding the rule *acca gheḥ*: with the intention that the three words *idudbhyām*, *ṭhāṬ* (from *ṭhāṬ dīrghāt*), and *ReĀ* (from *erā*) are carried over [as governing conditions], he explains: "After *i* and *u* ending in *ghī*, there shall be *ReĀ*. The ancient explanation, namely *herutarasya*, is not mentioned here.

Because in the sūtra *heḥ* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), and because there is no authority for [applying] *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, and so forth; and because it is improper to abandon the established relationship in the preceding sūtra *ṭho’d*—namely, that "ReĀ" follows "ṭhi" and "udbhi"—as stated in the rule *ṭho’d uttarasya ReĀḥ*. As for what they [the commentators] have explained—that the *tapara* (the *t* following *a*) in *ṭha’d*...

Regarding the statement that [the rule] "after *uddhā*, etc. is intended so that the suffix *ṭāp* might not occur when the substitution of *atva* has been applied in the feminine—this is questionable. For, due to the inclusion of the marker *t* (in *tapara*), let there be no long vowel with *ṭāp*; however, *ṭāp* itself would certainly still apply, as there is no evidence to justify the subversion of two grammatical rules simultaneously. Precisely for this reason, in the sūtra "ṛnmajanta" (Pāṇini 6.4.11)...

In the *Bhāṣya* and other works, it is stated that in the rule "addhatāu," the suffix *ṭāp* is not applied due to the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* (the metarule regarding the destruction of a grammatical cause), for if there were an intervention by *ṭāp*, the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) would be violated. However, since the letter *t* is present in the suffix *ṭāp*, the absence of *ṭap* would contradict the application of the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* mentioned therein. Furthermore, as for [the argument]...

They have explained that "the letter *t* [in *ReĀT*] is *svarita* for the sake of pronunciation," but that too is not correct; for in examples such as "tīrṇe barhiṣi samidhāne agnau" (*Rigveda* 10.70.1), the *svarita* quality is not observed. Furthermore, in the rule "na vibhaktau" (Pāṇini 1.3.4), he himself stated that the *t* in *ReĀT* is merely for the purpose of pronunciation and does not bear the technical designation *it*.

"And because it has already been stated [that the *tapara* rule does not apply here], it is established in the *Manoramā* that in both cases the inclusion of the *tapara* marker (*ṛt*) is solely for the purpose of pronunciation. (206) *anaṅ sau* 7.1.93.

*Anaṅ* [is substituted] for *su*. The letter *a* in *na* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule "in the vocative singular" (*ṭhasambuddhau*), *sāu* is understood as the nominative singular, and not the locative plural.
Although the form would have been established by the rule "*aurḍā*" alone, this is stated to indicate that *anaṅ* should also apply after feminine bases ending in long *ī* and *ū*.

Therefore, the ancients maintain that the *ṅīp* suffix does not apply in the case of *uśanas* when it is in a state of non-awakening (i.e., not in the vocative singular). Although one might argue that even if the rule "ṛduśana—
" were stated as "orḍe," the *ṅīp* would still apply by the subsequent rule, and consequently, in the form *uśane*,
there would be a lengthening of the vowel according to the rule "arvanāmasthāne cāsaṃbuddhau," whereas in the form *purudaṃse* [the same would apply].

Their intention is that although there would be a long vowel [in the form] "āntamahataḥ," this can nevertheless be resolved— either because a rule based on a technical designation (saṃjñāpūrvaka) is not invariably valid, or by means of the maxim regarding the occurrence within a stem (aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā).

(207) *alo'ntyāt pūrva upadhā* | P. 1.1.65. "Preceding the final *al*"—the word "final" (*anta*) qualifies the word "consonant" (*al*), which is in the ablative case; thus he says, "the consonant preceding the final [consonant]. Why "consonant" (*al*)? [Consider the examples: *iṣṭāḥ*, *iṣṭavān*.

Let it not be that the *ś* preceding the final cluster [of consonants] in words such as *nitya* is [treated as the *upadhā*]. For if that designation were present, then by the rule *āsa idaṅhaloḥ*, the substitution of *i* for the *ś* would occur.
Now, even so, if the cluster preceding the final *al* (consonant) were designated as the *upadhā*, [the fault remains].

If it is argued that in cases such as *iṣṭa*, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) fault remains unavoidable— since the vowel *a* qualified by the letter *ś* would undergo the substitution of *i*— it is replied: just as in common worldly usage,
when it is said, "Among these Brahmins, let the one who is the penultimate (*antyāt pūrvaḥ*) be brought," [the penultimate is understood].

Just as that which is of the same nature as the final [element] is brought forward from before the final, so too here, since the final consists of the letter *a*, that which precedes it is also understood as being simply *a*. This is what he says: "the preceding phoneme. Here, just as in the rule "from the end of a *ṭac*-ending word, etc., there is *ṭī*," so too [is the case with] "*ala*."

Some say that it is also easy to explain this as a genitive used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe ṣaṣṭhī*), since an interpretation such as "among the *ṭha*-letters, the one which is the last, the letter preceding it shall be designated as the *upadhā*" is also logically possible.

(208) *sarvanāmasthāne cāsaṃbuddhau* 6.4.8. With the intention that the rule *opadhāyāḥ* and the mention of *dīrgha* from the rule *hrasvālope* are both understood to carry over [into this rule], he says: "of that which ends in -n," and so forth.

(209) *apṛkta* is a suffix consisting of a single phoneme (*ekāl*). Here, the word *eka* means "unaccompanied" (*asahāya*), or it may mean "one" (*saṅkhyā*) in the sense of number. If it were taken in the sense of number, [the rule would apply] to the suffix following a consonant-ending base in forms such as *abhaitsīt*.

It should not be argued that there would be elision (*lopa*) because the *sic* suffix is uncombined (*apṛkta*); for it is explained that, by association with the case-endings (*vibhakti*), the elision applies only to case-endings. Why [specify] "consisting of a single phoneme" (*ekāl*)? Consider *jāgṛviḥ*: here, the elision [of the *sic*] does not occur by the rule "elision of an uncombined [suffix] after a vowel" (*varepṛktasya*). Since singularity is already obtained by the term "a" (*al*) in the rule "elision of the augment *a*" (*allope*), this mention of "single" (*eka*) serves to indicate the inclusion of a phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*).

Regarding the statement "it makes known": in the form *dhīpsati* (desiring to deceive), derived from the root *dambh* with the suffix *san*, there is *kitva* (the status of being a *kit*) by the rule *halantācca*. In that context, if the mention of *hal* were intended to refer to individual phonemes (*vyaktiparatva*), then the *san* suffix would not follow the single *hal* phoneme *n* which is adjacent [to the root-final], nor would that [root-final *b*] from which the *san* follows be the first [consonant].

In that case, the *kit* designation would not apply; consequently, the elision of the *n* would not occur. Having accepted this, we stated that it would be possible to omit the mention of *ekāj* in the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ* (Pāṇini 1.1.14).

(210) *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68): [A consonant] following a long vowel from [a stem ending in] a consonant (*hal*), a feminine suffix (*ī*, *ū*, or *ā*), or the suffix *ap*, is elided when followed by the nominative singular suffix *su*, the vocative singular suffix *ti*, or an *apṛkta* [consonant].

In the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt*, the term *dīrghāt* (from a long vowel) is a qualifier only for *ṅī* and *āp*, and not for *hal*, because [a long vowel] is impossible in the case of *hal*. Thus he says, "those two which are long. However, this [interpretation] is not correct, because it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *ṭhyaḥ* and *saḥ*, and under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *kartā* and *sakhe*. Even though...

When it is accepted that in the rule prescribing the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and so on, the term "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) functions as a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), then the aforementioned fault does not arise in rules such as *yā ā e*. This is because it is possible for a case-ending (*suvibhakti*) to be prescribed after a stem ending in long *ā*.
Similarly, in the rule prescribing *anaṅ*, if the term *sau* is taken as a locative of scope...

There is no fault even in cases such as *artāṭhsakhe*, because the suffix *su* can follow a word ending in a consonant (*hal*); nevertheless, the intention is that there would be the undesirable consequence of non-application (*avyāpti*) in the case of *ahuśreyasaḥ*. Regarding the term *hal*:
its form as *sutisī* should be understood through the maxim of "modification by a single substitute" (*ekādeśavikṛtanyāya*). It is elided...

Thus [it is said]. Although here the word *lopa* (elision) is understood from the rule *opo vyor vali*, and although in that [original] context it is a noun derived from the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*), nevertheless here it is a noun derived from the sense of an object (*karmasādhana*), because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *hal*, which ends in the nominative case; this is the intended meaning. [Examples: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* and *atikhaṭvaḥ*.

In a *prādi*-compound, there is shortening by the rule "in the case of what is not a feminine" (*oḥ striyāḥ*). Now, one might object: "But here the entire compound does not end in a feminine suffix (*ṅy-anta*); nor can it be said that the restriction regarding the initial element (*tadādiniyama*) does not apply to feminine suffixes," for while that is true when the suffix is not an *upasarjana*, here, because it is an *upasarjana*, the restriction regarding the initial element certainly does apply. Otherwise—

In the case of *ṭhātikārīṣagandhyāputra*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *saṃprasāraṇa* [of the *i* of *kārīṣagandhī-*, which ends in *ṅīp*] due to the rule governing a prior member ending in *ṣyaṅ*. True;
nevertheless, because the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) ends in *ṅīp*, that [substitution] follows from it.

Because the status of being "other" (paratva) does not disappear and because there is no mention of the term "long" (dīrgha), the elision of *su* would indeed occur even in the absence of the mention of *ṅy-āp*.
For it has just been stated that this mention of *ṅy-āp* is not a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*). This might be so:
one who desires the Gaṅgā for oneself is called *gaṅgī*; then, after the suffix *kvip* is applied and the elision of *al* occurs, we have *aṅgīḥ*.
In this case, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because the *ī* [of *strī*] would, by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), possess the status of *āp* and be long.

Nor should it be argued that, due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision of *al*, the suffix *su* is not subsequent to *āp*; for that objection is invalid, as there is a prohibition stating "that which is elided before *kvip* is not a substitute. This is not so, however, because [the rule applies to] *ṅī-ī* and *ā-āp*.

Since the mention of the long vowel (*dīrghagrahaṇa*) has been rejected in the *Paśliṣya* commentary, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the present case, as the form of *āp* consisting of the vowel *ā* is absent. However, in the case of *niṣkauśāmbīya* with the suffix *kvip*, the form *niṣkauśāmvī* indeed occurs; because it ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīp* with the vowel *ī*, the elision of the case-ending *su* takes place.

"What does the *apṛkta* support? This example is also to be considered, because [the *apṛkta*] is not a consonant (*ahal*). For it is improper to state an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by providing a strained interpretation of the rule "of *u*, *ti*, and *sī*, when followed by a consonant" (*utisīnāṃ haḷ iti*). As for that which...
They have explained [the matter as follows]: "One who presses *surā* is a *surā-sut*; one who causes him to do so is *surāsayati*.
From that, by applying *kvip*, we get *surāḥ*. [The forms are] *surāḥ*, *surāsau*, *surāsaḥ*.
Here, the mention of *apṛkta* is intended to prevent the elision of the *s* which is a part of the root *su*. That too is questionable.

Because, by virtue of mutual association (*parasparasāhacarya*), there is the apprehension of only those suffixes that possess case-endings; otherwise, as has been stated, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the elision (*lopa*) of the *sic* suffix. Furthermore, between a suffix and a non-suffix, it is the suffix alone that is apprehended. As for what was stated by Kaiyaṭa in the rule *itsvaritam*: "Nowhere is this... [the ellipsis continues].

[The claim that] "this is a technical rule (paribhāṣā) resorted to by the authors of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika" is due to haste; for it is recited in the Bhāṣya and other works on the sūtra "aṅgasya," and he himself has explained it there as well. [The objection] "because the elision of a final consonant in a conjunct (saṃyogāntalopa) is treated as non-existent (asiddha)"—but surely...

The elision of a consonant at the end of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is not considered non-established (*asiddha*), because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *a ṅsiṃbujdyoḥ*, which includes the mention of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*). Nor does it follow that the elision of *n* would likewise apply in cases such as *omāṃ* and so on, because the indicator applies specifically to its particular scope. For where—
The immediate sequence of the letter *na* and the case-ending occurs only in that specific instance, as established by the [traditional] commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
As for what some have said—"The form *he brahmānn* is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*) because it refers to a neuter object"—that is incorrect;

for when [the case-ending] is elided by *luk*, there is no application of the rule regarding the "characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). [This is because of the rule: "Or, in the vocative, [the substitution of *n* applies] to neuter nouns."

Furthermore, because the mention of "samabuddhi" (equal intellect) cannot possibly refer to a neuter object, the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*) remains firmly established. Therefore, if it is argued that the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is not the purpose [of the rule], then in this case, the substitution of *u* for *ru* (*rorutvam*) would not occur in the example "abhino'tra."

In the case of *sipi ‘aśce’ti*, when the *r*-substitution (*rutva*) occurs and the *s* of the case-ending is elided by the rule for the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), that [elision] is treated as non-existent (*asiddhatva*). Likewise, in forms such as *abibharbhavān* and *ajāgarbhavān*, the elision of the *t* would not occur, because of the restrictive rule *rātsasya*. As it has been said: "In the elision of the final of a conjunct..."

For otherwise, the elision of *n* (nalopa) and so forth would not be established; since there would be no elision by the rule "of a consonant" (*hal*), it is therefore prescribed [by the rule] "of a consonant. Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "elision of *n* and so forth," the substitution of *ū* (*utva*) is included.
In this regard, it should be noted that the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is a qualifier only of the suffix *su*, and not of anything else.

Because of the [specific] explanation, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *mālevācarat* from *amālā*, or *agaṅgād* from *gaṅgevācarat*. Thus, a single-consonant (*apṛkta*) suffix consisting of *su*, *ti*, or *si* following a word ending in a consonant (*halanta*) is elided; likewise, [the suffix is elided] following a word ending in the long vowels *ṅī* or *ap*.
The meaning of the rule established here is that the single-consonant (*apṛkta*) *u* is elided when followed by a consonant (*haL*).

As for what they [the commentators] have explained—that there is simply no possibility of *ti* or *si* following a feminine suffix ending in *ṅī* or *āp*—it is true that there is no possibility of them following a stem ending in *yan*. However, regarding a stem ending in *āp*:

The suffixes *laṅ*, *tiṣ* (*tip*), and *sip* indeed exist as endings of the *ācārakki* [suffix]. This is just like [the forms] *ṭhagaṅgāt* and *ṭhagaṅgā*. Nor is there an intervention by the *śap* [augment], because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included as having the final boundary (*pūrvānta*) of the preceding element.
Nor does the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) apply, because this is not a rule concerning something previously established (*apūrvavidhi*). Others [say]:

They say: "What was stated—that the mention of *ṅi* and *āp* cannot be a qualifier of *ti* and *si* precisely because of impossibility—is indeed correct. Nor should it be argued that there is no such impossibility in cases like *agaṅgādagaṅgā*, for in that instance, [the rule applies to] the *śap* which is the substituendum (*sthānin*)."

Since the elision of *ti* and *si* must occur based on the preceding cause (the *nimitta*), the elision of *si* would not apply due to the intervention of the *śap* by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*. Nor should it be argued that the *pañcamī-samāsa* (ablative compound) alternative is not accepted because it lacks utility; for [there is indeed a purpose].

"Because its purpose has already been demonstrated. Regarding the word *sakha*: it is called *sakhā* because it is "known together" (*samānaṃ khyāyate*) by people. While the rule *cci ṭhyalopaḥ* is being followed, [the rule] *samāne khyaḥ sa codāttaḥ* applies; thus, from the root *khyā*, the suffix *iṇ* is added, the word *samāna* becomes *sa*, and it is accented acute (*udātta*). It is not [otherwise].

In this case, one should not suspect that because the *anaṅ* replacement for the word *sakhi* is applied through the application of a specific case-ending (*suvibhakti-saṃniyoga*), the elision of the suffix *su*— as prescribed by the rule *ṭh-ḷ-ṅy-āb-bhyo dīrghāt sutisy apṛktaṃ hal*— would be blocked by the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*;
for this is shown by the citation of forms such as *vatantraḥ kartā*, which relies on the *n*-sound of *anaṅ*.
Because that paribhāṣā does not apply when a *sulopa* (elision of the nominative suffix *su*) is to be performed. (211) *sakhyurasaṃbuddhau* 7.1.92. Regarding *sakhyurasaṃbuddhau*: here...
From the rule "ṭhitaḥ sarvanāmasthāne," the term "sarvanāmasthāne" is carried forward (anuvartate);
it is then qualified by the word "asaṃbuddhau. From the rule "oto ṇit," the term "ṇit" is carried forward;
by virtue of its grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), the locative case is interpreted as a nominative.

Thus he says: "All [stems] except for those ending in -sa- and -as- are called *sarvanāmasthāna* except in the vocative singular. It is established in the *Manoramā* that it would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as "the [stems] -a-, -i-, and -u- are [called *sarvanāmasthāna*] except in the vocative singular. Now, an objection is raised: in the case of the form *sakhe* (vocative singular of *sakhi*), since the rule "of the penultimate vowel" (*upadhāyāḥ*) applies later than the rule for lengthening the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*), wouldn't it subvert the latter?

If it is argued that there must be *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) because [the suffix] is followed by a vowel (*u*), they say in response: since permanence (*nityatva*) is accepted even on the mere basis of its application whether [the condition] has been performed or not (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitva*),
