and because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*), [the rule for] *vṛddhi* is sublated in the case of "akhe" by [the rule for] *ar* in place of the *an* ending.

In the case of *asaṃbuddhau*, there must indeed be lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*), because the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*— which operates here by depending on the status of being treated as having a *ṇit* suffix (*ṇidvadbhāva*) according to *akhyurasaṃbuddhau*— is extrinsically conditioned (*bahiraṅga*).
(212) *aco ñṇiti* | Pāṇini 7.2.115.

Regarding *aco ñṇiti*: from the rule *ṛjervṛddhiḥ*, the term *vṛddhiḥ* is carried over (*anuvartate*), as is the term *aṅgasya*. This [latter] is further qualified by the term *acaḥ*; thus, it is specified by the qualifier.
With the intention that this is a rule concerning what follows the end of that (*tadanta-vidhi*), he explains: "of a stem ending in *ac*. (213) *khyatyāt parasya* | 6.1.112.
Regarding *khyatyāt*: since it is a designation in the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*), the phrase "following [what ends in]" is obtained; thus, it means "following what ends in *kh* or *ti*."
"One [element] takes the place of both the preceding and the following" (Pāṇini 1.1.53) is not applicable here;

however, it is employed in this context for the sake of *dhvanana* (suggestive indication). In the compound *khyatyaṃ*, formed as a collective *dvandva* from *khyaśca tyaśca*, the term *khya* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the words *khi* and *khī* after they have undergone the substitution of *yaṇ*. Thus...

Regarding the words *tit* and *tya*: in both cases, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), and this is not an imitation of a portion of primary words such as *apatya*. [This is evident from the rules:
“*ya*” after a numeral,” “*na*” after *pati*,” “of a numeral and of that which consists of a number of years,” and “of *apatya*.”

Intending to state that this is because of the specific mention [of the forms] beginning with *cet*, he says: "by means of the two words *khi* and *ti*," and so forth. And thus, the substitution of *utva* occurs only where the application of *yaṇ* takes place, but not in cases such as *atisakheḥ*. Nor, even if this were so, would there be a grasping only of those ending in short vowels (*hrasva*)—due to the aforementioned purpose of the mention by means of *yaṇ*—and not otherwise.

The doubt that [the term] "of the two long vowels" (*dīrghantayoḥ*) should be understood is refuted; the sense is that since the grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*) is common to both short and long vowels, and since it is improper to restrict a rule when its application could be broad, the scope of the teaching should not be narrowed. (214) *āṬt* 7.3.118.
Furthermore, this sūtra is superseded by the preceding rule, *ṭh-id-ud-bhyām*, with respect to those [stems] designated as *nadī*;
and it is superseded by the subsequent rule, *acca gheḥ*, with respect to those designated as *ghi*.
Therefore, its scope consists of those [stems] devoid of both designations (*saṃjñā*). And since there is no such vowel *u* [that is devoid of both], therefore—

He says: "The vowel *u* is carried over. However, the Easterners (Prācāḥ) have stated: "After *id* and *ud*, provided they are not [the words] designated as *hin* and *dī*, [the suffix *ṭac* is applied]. That is incorrect; for instance, in *tādṛk* and *tādṛśaḥ*, the vowel *u* of that kind is not established [as being followed by *ṭac*].
In *susakhā*, in a *prādi*-compound, [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] by the rule "after *rājan*, *ahan*, and *sakhi* [the suffix *ṭac* is applied]. The *ṭac* [is elided].

The prohibition [of the *hi* designation] is by the rule "pūjanāt. In the case of "eṣo dhyasakhī," the term "asakhī" is not a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), because that would result in faults such as an ungrammatical compound (*asamarthasamāsa*); rather, it is indeed an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*).
Thus, since "asakhī" means "different from the word *sakhi*," the technical name *hi* would certainly apply. Nor is there...
One might object: "Even though the aggregate [of letters] is distinct from the word *sakhi*, it is not distinct from that which ends with the word *sakhi*;

therefore, how can the prohibition by the rule *asakhī* apply? This doubt is to be resolved by the principle: "In the absence of a specific qualificand (*viśeṣya*), [the term refers to] that by which... [in the case of *asakhī*].

Because the rule *vidhis tadantasya* (a grammatical operation applies to that which ends with the specified element) does not apply here, he says "of the whole aggregate," etc., implying this very point. In the same way, one should understand the prohibition of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) and so forth in the case of *atisakhi* as well. [The phrase] "even when it is secondary" (*gauṇatve’pi*)...

The meaning is that in examples such as *sthātṛdaṇḍe*, it is like the substitution of *anaṅ* for the final vowel of *asthi* and so on. And thus, regarding the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya*, Kaiyaṭa states that in the example *paramasakhāyau*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; for if it were a *tatpuruṣa*, the suffix *ṭac* would have to occur [by Pāṇini 5.4.91]. Similarly, in the rule *dvitīyā śrite*, the form *omamasakhe* [is cited].
He himself states that because it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound formed by taking the initial portion (*pratīka*), there is no addition of the suffix *samāsānta*.

Thus, usages such as "ṭhanudyaukṣovaruṇa indrasakhā" (RV 2.38.9), "ṭhagne yāhi marutsakhā" (RV 10.141.3), and "īvraṃ somaṃ pibati gosakhāyaṃ" (RV 10.105.6) are likewise accounted for. In that case, [the augment] *tuṭ*...

Because the initial accentuation of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) is observed in the application of *bahuvrīhi* compounds, [the term *sakhi*] is secondary (*gauṇa*). By this, Haradatta, Nyāsakāra, and others who follow them—citing "one whose friend is excellent" (*susakhi*) as an example under the rule for the designation *ghisaṃjñā*—are to be disregarded. This is because [the rule] is non-universal (*anityatva*).
The inclusion of the words *ghaṭa* and *ghaṭī* in the *vārttika* "aktilāṅgalāṅkuśe" is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this [rule].

(215) *patiḥ samāsa eva* | 1.4.8. The word *patiḥ* [is a governing term] only when it occurs in a compound (*samāsa*). The particle *eva* is used for the purpose of restrictive emphasis according to the intended meaning; otherwise, [it would apply] even in a non-compound (*asamāsa*).
A restriction (*niyama*) might be assumed that [the substitution] applies only to the *pati* (husband), and consequently,

the usage of forms such as *ahākavine* would not be established. However, if one were to follow the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) found in rules such as *ṭhanalvidhau* and *hātvādeḥ*, there would be excessive complexity (*pratipattigaurava*) in the understanding of the system.
[This is] the state [of the term]. Regarding the passage beginning with "patyā" and so forth: one might object, "In that case, let it simply be stated as 'eṣo dhy-asakhipatī';
what is the use of this rule 'atiḥ samāsa eva'? If you say this, we reply: no;
for if the entire compound were not considered to have the form of "pati," then even the word "pati" preceded by the prefix "bahuc" would incur the designation *ghisamjñā*.

Furthermore, [if that were the case], forms such as *bahupatinā* would result— just as in the case of *usakhinā* and so on— whereas *bahupatye* and the like are what is intended. Nor should it be suspected that the rule should instead have been formulated as *akhipatī samāsa eva* ("the words *akhi* and *pati* occur only in a compound").

Otherwise, as in the case of *bahusakhyā* and so forth, one would expect forms such as *bahuahupatya*, whereas *bahuahusakhin* and so forth are what is desired. Now, how is it that [the form] *ītāyāḥ pataye namaḥ* occurs? [It is formed] by the addition of the Uṇādi suffix *ipratyaya* according to the rule *aṣṭe mṛte pravrajite klībe iḥ*, and by the elision of the *ṇi* [augment] according to the rule *ṇeraniṭi*.

This word *pati* as a completed form (*niṣpanna*) is not included in the rule "the suffix *ati* occurs only in a compound," because it is derived through a secondary derivation (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*). By this, the *Mahābhārata* passage "Juna is the friend of Kṛṣṇa" and the *Rāmāyaṇa* passage "by the lord of monkeys, Añjanā’s son" are explained. [The question] "How many words? refers to *kā*.

Those whose number [is such] are called *kati*. By the rule “*imaḥ saṅkhyāparimāṇe ḍati ca*,” the suffix *ḍati* is applied; because it is marked with the *ḍi*-indicator, there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*).
(Pāṇini 1.1.23) "The words *bahu*, *gaṇa*, *vat*, and *ḍati* are numerals (*saṅkhyā*)."

The terms *bahu*, *gaṇa*, and *vatu* are understood here as denoting numerals that express a specific count, and not as words for a mere collection or magnitude; this is because the technical designation is understood according to its etymological meaning, namely, "that by which things are counted" (*saṅkhyāyate anayā*). For this very reason, the suffix *ḍati* also [is included], as in the case of *im*.

Only the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) prescribed by the rule *saṅkhyāparimāṇe ḍati ca* is understood here, because of its association with *vatu*; it is not, however, the *ḍati* prescribed by *āterḍatiḥ*. Although in the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñāvidhi*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of that which ends in it (*tadantagrahaṇa*), nevertheless, in this case, the mention of *vatu* and *ḍati* alone [is sufficient].

Since there would be no purpose for a technical name (*saṃjñā*) [if it applied to the whole], and by virtue of its being etymologically meaningful (*anvarthatā*), the name applies only to those two [suffixes] that end in them. They say, however, that the mention of the suffix with its *anubandha* (e.g., *kta*) is intended to dispel the suspicion of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "he lives like a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇavad vasati*). It is not [the case that the *anubandha* is necessary].

Furthermore, it must be stated that in the case of the functions of number, such as those expressed by suffixes like *kṛtvasuc*, only the technical (kṛtrima) number would be understood and not the non-technical (akṛtrima) one;
consequently, forms such as *pañcakṛtvaḥ* would not be established, because when there is a choice between a technical and a non-technical term,
the application of the grammatical operation is restricted to the technical one.

In the rule *aṅkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan*, by the force of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of those ending in *ati* and *śat*, the maxim regarding artificial (*kṛtrima*) and non-artificial (*akṛtrima*) [technical] terms does not apply to the operations concerning numbers. [Objection: But if this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix *kṛtvasuc* being applied after the word *bhūri*.

If they say here: "If the operation of number were to apply to words expressing indefinite numbers, then there would be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because the understanding of number as the result of such a restriction is limited to *bahu* and *gaṇa* alone," [the author replies:
"Also [the suffix] *ḍati*. 1.1.25.

And [the suffix] *ḍati*. From the rule "ṣaṭ is [the name for numerals] ending in *ṇ*," the term "*aṭ*" is carried over. Since "number" (*saṅkhyā*) is the subject under discussion, it is qualified by the word "*ati*"; thus he says: "a number ending in *ḍati*.
Why "number"? [Consider] *patayaḥ* (lords).

(218) *luk-ślū-lup* [are the names] for the elision of an affix. 1.1.61. The term *adarśana* (non-appearance), which is carried over from the rule "Non-appearance is *lopa*," is understood here as having these specific technical names (*saṃjñā*) by virtue of the fact that multiple names are assigned to it; this is based on the principle of *tantra* (the application of one thing to many). Therefore, there is no confusion of technical names (*saṃjñā-saṅkara*) in this context. This is what the author expresses with the words "by the terms *luk*, *ślū*, and *lup*, etc. If there were indeed a confusion of technical names, then in the word *hanti* (he kills), where *śap* is elided by *luk*, the doubling [of the root] prescribed by the rule *lau* would apply. Furthermore, in the word *luhet* (he might choose), where *ślu* is present, the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) prescribed by the rule *uto vṛddhir luki hali* would apply.

Nor should it be argued that because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "not" (*na*) in that context, there will be no *vṛddhi*—as in the case of *yoyoti*, *nonoti*, and so on—because, under the view that there is a confusion of technical names (*saṃjñā-saṅkara*), such a recurrence is impossible; otherwise, the rule would become devoid of scope (*nirviṣaya*). Nor can forms like *yauti* be considered its scope, because even in those cases, the occurrence of doubling (*dvitva*) would be unavoidable under the theory of the confusion of names. In the application of rules such as "there is *luk* after *hal*," "there is *ślu* after *hu* etc.," and "there is *lup* in the sense of a country (*janapada*"), there is no circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*), because the technical name is understood as being prospective (*bhāvin*), like the example of the cloth mentioned in the *sūtra-śāṭaka* [maxim]. (219) *paṅbhyo luk* 7.1.22. [There is *luk* (elision) of the case-ending after the word *pañcan* in the plural.]

*Pañcabhyo luk*: Although one could have simply stated "luk after *pañca*"—just as one says "*arvanāmnaḥ smai*"—the use of the plural form here is intended to indicate that the meaning [of the word] is primary. This is because, by the maxim of the artificial and the non-artificial (*kṛtrimākṛtrimanyāya*), the exclusion of the word-form itself is already established. Therefore, [the elision applies] only when [the case endings] express the number inherent in the meaning of the word *aṣ*.
Since the meaning [of the rule] culminates in "there is elision (*luk*) of *jas* and *śas*," there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *priyapañcan*.
Because [the word] *āt* is understood to carry over from the rule "for *as* and *śas*, *śi*" (*aśśasoḥ śi*), he says: "there shall be elision (*luk*) of *jas* and *śas*.
(220) When a suffix is elided, the operations conditioned by that suffix still take place. (Pāṇini 1.1.62).

The meaning is that even when a suffix is elided (*pratyayalopa*), the specific technical designations such as *luk* and so forth do not sublate the designation *lopa*; for the principle is that, except under the heading of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), a relationship of sublation and sublated is not admitted between technical designations. [This is stated] because the result is already established by the rule regarding what is "as if the original" (*sthānivat*).

This sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*): "When the cause of an operation is the unique form of the suffix itself, that operation alone takes place upon the elision of the suffix, but not [an operation] caused by what is unique to both the suffix and non-suffix. By this, in the case of *yasya śobhanā dṛṣadaḥ*...

In the case of *sudṛṣatprāsāda*, the rule *ormanasī alomoṣasī* (Pāṇini 6.2.117) prescribes that the first syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is udātta, thereby overriding the final-udātta status prescribed by *añsubhyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.172); furthermore, the lengthening of the vowel by *tvasantasya ca yat-haḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14) does not occur. Alternatively, this occurs where the suffix (*pratyaya*) is relied upon as the primary factor.

In that regard, even in the case of a rule concerning a vowel (*al-vidhi*), the purpose of the rule is established. By this, in the rule *tṛṇeḍaḍ*, although the augment *im* prescribed before a *pitt* sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) is elided, it still takes effect. However, the statement "there is no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of a suffix-based operation) when the primary factor is a phoneme (*varṇa*)" concerns cases where the phoneme is predominant; therefore, [the rule applies] in *gave hitam*.

In the word *‘ohita’*, there is no substitution of *ava* for *o*. Although both these views are established in the authoritative grammatical treatises (*ākaras*), nevertheless, the view supporting the restrictive rule (*niyamapakṣa*) alone is stronger; this is the position maintained in the *Manoramā* regarding forms ending in *yaṅ-luk*. It might be argued that even if this sūtra were necessary, [the desired form] would follow simply from the rule *‘pratyayalope tallakṣaṇam’*.
"Let it be formulated as such; what is the purpose of this second mention of *pratyaya*?
To this they reply: "The second mention of *pratyaya* is for the sake of obtaining [the definition] beginning with 'where the unique form of the suffix [is found]'."

(220) *na lumatāṅgasya* | 1|1|63|. "Not [an operation prescribed for] a stem (*aṅga*) when [a suffix] marked with *lu* is elided. What is the purpose of the word *lumatā*? [Consider: *kāryate*, *hāryate*.

Here, even though the *ṇi* is elided by the rule *ṇer aniṭi*, the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] still occurs in the alternative where *ṇic* is present. [The word *lumatā* is used] because of the mention of "the stem" (*aṅgasya*).

What [is the purpose]? So that, in cases such as *añcaṭhsaptaṭhkatī*, the operation pertaining to suffixes (*pratyayāntakārya*)—namely, the technical designation of a "word" (*pada*) by the rule *uptiṅntam*—may take effect. Regarding *asmad*: the Easterners (Prācāḥ) have read it as *avyayāsmad*; however, the term *avyaya* has been disregarded there, because [the word] is not seen in the three genders.

Regarding the phrase "in genders": this is because the term refers to the absence of the three genders and so forth, since indeclinables (avyaya) lack gender; furthermore, although an avyayībhāva compound is neuter by rule, it lacks any other gender. Regarding the word *tri*: [it is derived from] *ara-teṅgriḥ*.
Due to the status of being *ḍit*, there is elision of the suffix *ṭi*.
(221) *trestrayaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.53.
In the rule *trestrayaḥ*, the word *treḥ* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and not the ablative (*pañcamī*). The word *trayaḥ* ends in the vowel *a* and does not end in the consonant *s*.
Intending to show that this is because of the specific mention [in Pāṇini’s rule] “of the three roots beginning with *nij*,” he says: “there is the substitution of *traya* for the word *tri*.
If it is argued: “Since the substitution of *traya* is already established by the very irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the rule ‘*anu nijāṃ trayāṇām*’ (Pāṇ.
7.4.75), what is the purpose of this present sūtra?”—it is not so. For irregular formations (*nipātanas*) do not necessarily act as exceptions (*abādhaka*) to other rules.

Because this is indicated by the statement "they become," the form *urātanam* is established. Otherwise, it would be sublated by the rule for irregular forms (*nipātana*), namely "in the case of those taught by Uraṇa. The form *rerayati* is not stated as a separate sūtra;
rather, it is derived from the sense "he does that" or "he describes that" by means of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) according to the rule "that which he does... and so forth.

Then, with the suffix *kvip*, because of the rule "rakṛtyaikāj" (Pāṇini 6.4.149), there is no elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant); subsequently, by the rule "hrasvasya pitī tuk" (Pāṇini 6.1.71), the augment *tuk* is added, resulting in the form *rit*. Then, when the plural sense is intended and the case-ending *ām* is applied, the form "rayāṇām" would not be established due to the rule "trerayaṅ" (Pāṇini 7.1.53). Nor can it be argued that the *tuk* [augment] prevails over [the substitution of *ayaṅ*] on the basis of the principle "a grammatical operation affecting a phoneme (*vārṇa*) is stronger than one affecting a word-base (*āṅga*)".

It should not be suspected that this [substitution] would occur even earlier, because the *āṅga* (the substitute) possesses greater force precisely when both [rules] apply simultaneously. Regarding the phrase "some [say]": their intention is that, based on the understanding that [the rule applies] "to the *ī* belonging to *reḥ*," the substitution of *trai* does not occur even in the case of a secondary (*gauṇa*) form.

The phrase "in reality" (vastutastu) means that although [the word *traya*] is subordinate, the substitution of *traya-* is logical because there is no plural number (*bahuvacana*) to indicate the predominance of the meaning; the sense is that it is like the substitution of *anaṅ* for *asthi-* in forms such as *priyāsthn-*.
(222) *tyadādināmaḥ* | 7|2|102|.

Regarding *tyadādināmaḥ*: since the phrase "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) is understood from the previous rule "*aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*," [the author] asks: what is the purpose of specifying "in a case-ending"? [Consider the forms] *tat* and *yat*; because the *su*-suffix has been elided by *luk*, there is no application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the rule that treats an elided suffix as present).

(223) The rule is intended only for those ending in *dvi*. Why [is it] "only for those ending in *dvi*"? Even in the absence of the desired [application of the rule] to the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, there is no fault, because the general rule for *atva* is superseded by the specifically prescribed [rules] for *ātva*, *yatva*, and elision (*lopa*). Likewise...

There is no fault even with the word *kim*, because a specific substitution of *kā* for *kimaḥ* is prescribed; such is the question. [The form] *bhavān*: when *bhavat-su* is situated, after the substitution of *at* in place of the letter *t*, the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule "ato guṇe" applies; then, when the *num* augment [is added] by the rule "ugidacām...", [the form *bhavant-su* arises].

The intention is that when the long vowel [ā] is applied by the rule *arvan-nāma-sthāne*, and after the elision of *su* and the elision of *n*, the form would be *havā*. Regarding *bhavantau*: the intention is that as before, when the substitution of *at* occurs for the *t*, followed by the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*), the insertion of *num*, and the lengthening of the vowel, the form would be *havānau*. [The phrase] *uḍūnīva lomāni* means "like hairs like stars."
The offspring of such a person is Auḍulomi.
(224) Regarding the suffix *akāra* [applied] to the word *loman* when denoting many descendants:
this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *iñ*. Thus, in the sense of plurality, this word *auḍuloma* ends in the vowel *a*; it—

It should be understood that [the word] *āṬḍulomi* is indeed different [from the others], and its derivation ending in the vowel *i* is incidental. Thus end those [words] ending in *i*. Regarding *kid*:
by this, there is the elision of the long *ā* according to the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*; such is the intention. As for *vātapramī*, it is formed from the root *māṅ*.

When the doubt arises that the substitution of *ī* (ītvam) is prohibited by the rule "the substitution of *ī* does not occur after *kkip* when followed by [a suffix] beginning with *ṭha* or *ava*," it should be understood that the root *mīnāti* alone is intended here for the formation of *kkip*. Alternatively, it should be understood that *kkip* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) to the word *vātapramī*, which ends in the suffix *ī* and is itself derived from a verbal base ending in *ācārakvip*. [This refers to the form] *śreyasī*.

Thus: in the word *bahuśreyaḥ*, there is the substitution of *śrā* for *praśasya* before the suffix *iyasun*. By the rule *ugitaśca*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. In the form *bahuśreyasī*, there is the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) according to the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*. Furthermore, by the rule *īyasaśca*, the suffix *kap* is not added.
Nor is there shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasva*), because of the prohibition: *īyaso bahuvrīher na*.
(225) *yū stryākhyau nadī* | 1.4.3. *yū stryākhyau*: *yū* refers to *ī* and *ū*. Due to the explanatory context (*vyākhyāna*), only the long vowels are understood here.

Some maintain that this is an indeclinable (*avibhaktika*) designation. [This is because] there is an option (*vā*) regarding the prohibition [of *eḍsvād*] by the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.105).

Others say that because [the application of] *cchandasi* is optional, the long vowel occurs by the rule "the single substitute for two vowels of the same quality (*pūrvasavarṇa*) is long" (*Pāṇini 6.1.102*), and thus the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "only the suffix *ṭh* is understood here" does not apply;
this is indicated by the prohibition "those which have *neyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* as their substitutes, provided they are not feminine. Therefore...

In forms such as *radhyai* and *pradhya*, the grammatical operations pertaining to the feminine (*nadī*) would indeed apply. The term *stryākhyau* (the two called "feminine") refers to those words that denote a female;
the suffix *ka* is applied here because the word belongs to the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*. By the rule *akṣiḍaḥ khyāñ*, the root *khyā* is substituted for *akṣi*;

then, by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*, there is elision of the long *ā*. Regarding the phrase *īdudantam*: here, it should also be understood that the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies only to the phonemes *ī* and *u*.

There is this position, based on the natural force (*svarasa*) of the rule *ṭhācchīnadyoḥ*: the designation "feminine" (*stryākhyatva*) for those two [the suffixes *ṭhā* and *śī*] is inherent in the case of *ṅī* and so forth;
however, in cases such as *tantrīḥ* and *lakṣmīḥ*, it arises because they enter into the collection of phonemes that denote a female by virtue of being constituent parts thereof. Therefore...

The conventional usage regarding "ending in a river name" (*nadyanta*) and so forth is not contradicted. Likewise, it should be understood that in the case of the rule *eṣo dhyasakhī*, there is also the view that the designation *ghisamjñā* applies only to those [words] ending in the vowels *i* and *u*. By this, the conventional usage—"of those ending in *hi* (ghit) or beginning with a vowel (*ajādya*), the one ending in *ghi* is subsequent"—becomes consistent.

In the view that *varṇasaṃjñā* (the designation of a phoneme) applies, the meaning of the rule *ṭhasakhī* is "that which is different from *sakhi*," and not "excluding that which is a constituent part of the word *sakhi*. Therefore,
it should be noted that since the whole [compound] is distinct from the word *sakhi*, forms such as *atisakhin* are unobjectionable.

Since it would have been sufficient to say simply “*striyām*” (in the feminine), the inclusion of the term “*ākhyau*” (called) is intended to secure the sense of being "perpetually feminine"; with this intention, he says: “*nityastrīliṅgau*” (those which are perpetually feminine). What is the purpose of [specifying] *yū* (the dual ending *au*)?
[Consider: *mātre*. Why [specify] “*stryākhyau*” (called feminine)? [Consider: *grāmaṇyeṣa pūrvam* (this leader was previously...). This is from the *vṛtti*.

The meaning is "previously. This [rule] is established by logic (*nyāya*) under the *yathoddeśa* interpretation of technical names (*saṃjñā*), whereas they say it is merely a matter of statement (*vācanika*) under the *kāryakāla* interpretation.
(226) *ambārthanadyor hrasvaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.2.48. "The short vowel is substituted for [the final of] words meaning 'mother' (*ambā*) and for feminine stems ending in *nadi*."

Relying on the alternative view that [the term] *varṇa* denotes a phoneme, he says: "of those ending in a feminine suffix (*nadī*)". In the example *he bahuśreyasi*, the guṇa substitution does not take effect by virtue of the incapacity of the short vowel to trigger it;

otherwise, he would have simply said, "guṇa occurs for [stems ending in] *am*, a word denoting a female (*strī*), and a feminine suffix (*nadī*)". Nor should one suspect a lack of parsimony (in the formulation).

Because by employing the term "short" (*hrasva*), there would be an increase in syllables, and because it is even more concise to omit the mention of "guṇa" in the subsequent rule, *ṭhhrasvasya guṇaḥ*, [one might argue that the term *hrasva* is unnecessary]. Others, however, maintain that even if the term *hrasva* were used, if a *guṇa* were intended there, then after stating *ṭhambārthānāṃ hrasvaḥ*, [the rule would proceed as follows].

They say that one should simply state, "There is guṇa for [the vowels] other than long and short. Although there is no economy of words (padalāghava) in this case, there is economy of procedure (prakriyālāghava); however, it should be understood that there is difficulty in the case of "asi ca" because the single-word mention of "hrasvasya" must be continued [from a previous rule].

(227) *āṇ nadyāḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.112. The rule *āṇ nadyāḥ* could have been stated more simply as *āṇ nadyāḥ*. By virtue of the specific formulation [of the rule], the application of *ato guṇe* is precluded, so that through either *vṛddhi* or *savarṇadīrgha*, we obtain *ahuśreyasyai*.

This is because the formation of forms such as *ahuśreyasyā* is established [by this rule]. Now, one might object that the *sāmarthya* (the functional force) of the rule is exhausted, since— upon considering the subsequent text stating "the augment *nuṭ* is superseded by *āṬ* due to the presence of *ar*"— the prescription of *aṭ* is necessary to prevent the arrival of the *nuṭ* augment once *ReĀrām* has been applied.

If that is so, then let the rule be formulated as *ReĀrne* immediately after *ṭhhrasvanadyāpaḥ*, since by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of *āmī*, the meaning *ṭhReĀrāmo nuṇne* would be obtained. Therefore, by the force of the injunction *ṭhaṇnādyāḥ*, the rule *ṭhato guṇe* does not apply.
Dik | (228) *āṭaśca* | 6.1.90 | *āṭaśca*. Although here [the form] would be established by the rule *vṛddhireci* even when the suffix *ṅī* follows, [this is stated] for the sake of *ReĀ*.

One might argue that [the form] *siṅsoḥ* is established by the rule for lengthening homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), and thus the sūtra should not be introduced here; nevertheless, it is presented because it is appropriate even in this context for the sake of forms such as *aindidaditi*.

This is according to the opinion of the Vārttikakāra, who maintains that the sūtra "āḍajādīnām" (P. 6.4.72) need not exist, since [forms like] *āṭiṣṭhat* and so on are already established by the augment *āṭ* applied to roots beginning with vowels other than those starting with *a*.
It should be understood that the rule is simply *ṭhaṭ ca*.
(229) *ReĀrāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ* |7|3|116|. [The term] *ReĀrām*: the form *ReĀ* is taken as the locative singular (*saptamyekavacana*), [referring to the word] *amānādhikaraṇe*.

Because of the specific mention [in the sūtra] beginning with "triyām," the augment *āṭ* supersedes the *nuṭ* augment; however, once *āṭ* has been applied, it does not apply again. This is because one relies on the maxim "that which has already occurred does not recur" (*akṛt-gati*). As for the phrase "there is no elision of *su*": the word *lakṣmī* ends in the feminine suffix *ī* belonging to the *aiṇādika* group, derived from the root *lakṣ* with the addition of *muṭ*.
Thus, it should be understood that even the shortening of a *upasarjana* does not apply here. Regarding the word *kumārī*:

although shortening would have applied because the form ending in *ṅī* is a *upasarjana* with respect to the meaning of the *kvip* suffix, nevertheless, in the rule “*ostriyoḥ*,” the technical (*kṛtrima*) status of being a *upasarjana* is intended, and not the sense of being a subordinate element (*aprādhānya*).

The short vowel does not apply here; for this very reason, in the case of *harītakyaḥ* (the fruits of the *harītakī*), the short vowel also does not occur. However, in the rule *uktaddhitalukī*, only that which is a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) by virtue of its secondary status is understood, and not the technical *upasarjana*, because the latter is impossible in this context—as we shall explain.

(230) *aci śrudhātubhruvāṃ yvoriyaṅuvaṅau* | Pāṇini 6.4.77. Regarding *aci śru*: because the word *bhrū* ends in the suffix *ḍū* [by the rule] *bhrameśca ḍūḥ*, it is mentioned separately from "roots" (*dhātu*). Others, however, say that in the rule *gamaḥ kkau*, there is also *ūṅ*.

The word *bhrū* is formed by applying the rule from the Vārttika stating that "it should be stated [that the substitution applies] to *gam* and others," whereby the nasal is elided and *ūṅ* is substituted. Thus, since the desired form would be established by the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone, the specific mention of *bhrū* is redundant. Furthermore, while one could have simply said "after *ṭhiṇ*," the use of the cumbersome designation "*yvoḥ*" indicates the inclusion of the *ṭhiṇ* pratyāhāra.

The purpose [of the marker] is to indicate that it is grasped by the subsequent letter *ṇ* alone. Here, the intention is that in the rule "hyvoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.78), the term refers specifically to the verbal root (*dhātu*), and not to the suffixes *śru* and *bhru*, because those do not deviate from being roots; with this in mind, he says: "of a verbal root ending in an *i*-vowel."

If it is argued that in the commentary [on Pāṇini 7.2.89], *‘rudhādibhruvām ivarṇovarṇayor āt’*, the rule *‘iyaRuvoḥ ṅtviṃ’* would be redundant because the possibility of it being a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśatva*) could arise through the distinction of the grammatical operation (*vaidhikaraṇya*), [we reply: no;

for since *bhrū* and *abhru* would also be indicated [as operands], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of them becoming substitutes for the whole. *ṭhi u* (This appears to be a scribal or marginal notation).
Since it has been stated that there are eighteen *saṃjñās*, the rule of "correspondence by order" (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) does not apply here;

thus he says: "due to proximity" (*āntaratamyāt*). The intended meaning is "by position" (*sthānataḥ*). [Examples for] "after *yv*" (*yveḥ*): *cakratuḥ*, *cakruḥ*. [Example for] "in *aci*" (*aci*): *āptuyāt*, *juhuyāt*.

(231) eranekācaḥ asaṃyogapūrvasya | Pāṇini 6.4.82. *eranekācaḥ*: From the rule *iṇo yaṇ*, the term *yaṇ* continues to apply here. From the rule *aci śnudhātu-*, only the word *dhātu* (root) is carried forward here, and not the words *śru* and *bhru*.

Because [the condition] "between two vowels" (ivarṇa) is impossible in those two cases, he explains that the mention of "root" (dhātu) qualifies both by repetition—as "of the conjunction" and "of the stem" (aṅga)—in the words "conjunction that is a part of a root," and so forth. Therein, because the conjunction is qualified by the root, there is *yaṇ*-substitution here: *unnyauḥ*, *unnyaḥ*.

In rules such as *ṭhharī’ṭhharī* (Pāṇini 6.1.7), the base (*aṅga*) is qualified by the verbal root (*dhātu*) for the sake of establishing the correct form. Otherwise, as in the case of *radhyaṃ* and *pradhya*, the *yaṇ* substitution would occur, overriding both the *pūrvarūpa* and the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* [rules],
because [the vowel] is not preceded by a consonant cluster that is part of the verbal root.

Because the *aṅga* (stem) ends in the vowel *i*, [the rule applies]. The word *pradhīḥ* is derived as follows: from the root *dhyai* (to meditate), with the suffix *kvip*, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) and the formation of the *pūrvarūpa* (single substitute);
then, by the rule *halaḥ*, a long vowel is substituted. However, when it is analyzed as *yasya prakṛṣṭā dhīrbuddhiḥ* ("one whose intellect or understanding is excellent"), then...

Since the word *dhī* is eternally feminine, by the Vārttika "The first gender and the mention of *liṅga*," there is an extension of the eternal feminine gender; thus, the grammatical operations (*nadī-kārya*) applicable to a *nadī* should be understood as far as possible.
Regarding the Vārttika "The first gender and the mention of *liṅga*," the first gender refers to [suffixes] ending in *ṭh* and *yū*.

By the rule *stryākhyau*, it follows by implication that the status of being a river name (*nadītva*) must be stated; for some say that since this falls within the scope of the *yaṇ* substitution prescribed by *eranekācaḥ*, the prohibition in *neyaṅuvaṅ-sthānāv astrī* does not apply.
Others, however, say: "In that case, if the rules operate according to their location (*yathoddeśa*), this is established by logic."

Otherwise, works such as the *Manoramā* would be contradicted; for even according to the view that the rule is merely illustrative (*yathoddeśa*), the statement [of the feminine suffix] is necessary because it constitutes the meaning of the word *pradhī*.

For in the root text it is stated: "Even though it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), its status as a river-name (*nadītva*) must be asserted," but it does not say "its status as an invariably feminine (*nityastrītvam*) [must be asserted]. Therefore...

By the phrase "the first apprehension of the gender," that status as a *nadī* (feminine noun) which was previously present in the base (*vṛti*) due to its gender is extended (*atidiśyate*) here. However, in the case of the word *dhī*, because the status as a *nadī* is absent due to the prohibition by the rule "eyaṅuvaṅ—" [Pāṇini 6.4.77], there is no extension of the *nadī* status at all in the word *pradhī*. Thus.

Furthermore, the optional application of the designation *nadī* (feminine noun) by the rule *hrasvaśca* is not extended here. According to the principle established by the statement *rathamaliṅge*, which follows the *yathoddeśa* (definition-first) interpretation of the *paribhāṣās*,
the designation *nadī* applies only to that which already exists as such, even when it is regarded as a constituent part (*avayava*) in the state prior to the formation of the compound.

Because [the designation] is accepted with respect to the aggregate (samudāya). Furthermore, in examples such as *pradhye* or *pradhya*, where the word *dhī* ending in the nominative case occurs before a suffix beginning with *ṅ*, the designation *nadī* does not apply; this is the general direction [of the argument]. Regarding *unnī*: the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *tatsūdviṣa-* etc. Regarding *ReĀrām*: [this refers to the vowels *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*].
The sense is that because it is an *aṅga* (suffix), the suffix *ReĀr* occurs even after a word ending in *nī*. Regarding *grāmaṇīḥ*:

one who leads a village (*grāmaṃ nayati*) is a *grāmaṇīḥ*; the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "after *agra* and *grāma*, the *ṇ* is substituted for the *n* of *nayati*. Regarding *nīḥ*: one who leads (*nayati*) is a *nīḥ*; this is formed with the *kvip* suffix.

(232) A *yaṇ* [substitution] is not desired for a preceding member that is neither a *gati* nor a *kāraka*. Regarding the phrase "neither a *gati* nor a *kāraka*": it was not stated as "a *yaṇ* is desired only when preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*," because in cases such as *kumārī* (a Brāhmaṇa desiring a young girl), *kumāryau*, and *kumāryaḥ*—[if the rule were restricted to those two categories, the *yaṇ* would not apply here].

Because of the consequence that [the rule for] *yaṇ* would not apply. Regarding the term *śuddhadhiyau*: when the analysis is made as *śuddhaṃ brahma dhyāyati* ("he meditates on pure Brahman"), then *yaṇ* indeed occurs: *śuddhadhyau*, *śuddhadhyaḥ*. The same applies in the following cases as well. [Objection: "How then [is it explained]? [Response: Since here there is no preceding word other than a motion (*gati*) or an agent (*kāraka*), it must necessarily be by means of *yaṇ*.

The question: Regarding the term *ūrdhviya*, with the intention that the elision of the second member (*uttarapadalopa*) is to be understood by means of the Vārttika "after words beginning with *ra*, there is elision of a suffix derived from a verbal root," he says: "those whose intellect (*dhī*) is ill-situated.
Regarding the word *vṛścika*: for the author of the Bhāṣya, indeed, relies upon a path imagined by the intellect (*buddhiparikalpita*).

The rule *hītrārthānām* has been rejected. Consequently, when there is a desire to express mere relationship (*sambandhamātra*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone is used; thus, the sense is that here there is no precedence of a grammatical factor (*kāraka*).
He says this because the term *supi* is carried over (*anuvartana*) from the rule *oḥ supi*.
(233) *na bhūsudhiyoḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.85. [The rule] *aci supi* [is understood]. What is the purpose of *supi*? [Consider: *sudhyupāsyaḥ*.
In reality, however, there is no harm even if *supi* is not carried over [from the previous rule], because of the principle *anantarasya* ("the [operation] applies to what is immediately preceding").

For it is accepted that the *yaṇ*-substitution, which is obtained by the two rules "ṭheranekācaḥ" and "ṭhoḥ supi," is precisely what is prohibited by the rule "na bhūsudhiyoḥ. As for the statement "the *yaṇ* is obtained through *sthānivadbhāva*," this refers to the rule "ṭheranekācaḥ. Nor [can one argue] by relying on the case-ending (*vibhakti*) contained within [the compound].

It should not be argued that because the word *sakhi* is a *pada*, the elision of the final vowel (*allopa*) is not subject to the rule "not at the end of a word" (*na padānte*), since by the restriction "naḥ kye," a word ending in *n* is a *pada* only when followed by a *kyac* suffix.

"Whatever is elided before *kvip* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Regarding the phrase "elided before *kvip*": the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) in the neuter gender;

thus, the meaning is "an elision occurring before *kvip*. All of this should also be understood to apply in the case of *kimārī*, derived from *kumārīm icchan*. The reading "elided before *v*" is merely occasional (*kvācitka*), for [the rule] "with respect to an operation (*vidhi*) concerning *v*" does not apply.

This is because the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* (as if occupying the place of the original) is accepted [only when a substitute is followed by an operation that would apply to the original]. Otherwise, the rule to be stated later under the section on neuter stems ending in consonants—namely, in the example "ebhir brāhmaṇakulāni"—would not be consistent. For in the case of the verb *bebhidya-te*, after the addition of *kvip*, with the elision of *al* and the elision of *y*, the elision of *al* would lack the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* since it has been elided in the presence of *kvip*.

Because of the undesired consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the augment *num* being triggered by the condition of ending in a *jhal* consonant. However, an example of the rule "in the case of *kvip*, a substitute is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* regarding an operation prescribed for [a suffix] beginning with *v*" is *lauḥ*, derived from *lāvayati* (causative of *lū*) followed by *kvip*.

Here, there is the elision of *ya* due to the *ṇic* suffix, and the elision of *ṇi* due to *kvip*; both of these [elisions] would cause the substitution of *ū* for the *v* by the rule "for *hv* and *y*, there is *ū*" (*hvoḥ śūḍ*).
When *ūṭh* is to be applied as a substitute, it is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Thus, by the rule *ṭhetyedatyūṭhasu*, the *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs.

Here, this should be noted: regarding the rule *na padānte*, there is the supplementary statement (*upasaṅkhyānam*) that it applies to the cases of elision (*luk*), the status of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhātva*), the *aṅ* suffix, the subsequent reduction (*paranirhrāsa*), and the substitution for *ku*.

This is a partial restatement (anuvāda) of that Vārttika, namely "vau luptam" and so forth. Examples for rules such as "ukā lupte na sthānivat" are also stated here: *pañcapaṭuḥ* ("bought for five clever [pieces]"). Here, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule "ṭharhāt," and of that [suffix], [the elision occurs] by the rule "adhyardhapūrva-".

*Luk*: By the rule *uktaddhitalukī*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṅīṣ*. Since that [suffix] has been elided by *luk*, it lacks the status of being "as if present" (*sthānivadbhāva*); therefore, the substitution of *yaṇ* does not occur here. Nor should one raise the objection that the elision of *ṅīṣ* cannot be considered *sthānivadbhūta* because it is not caused by something subsequent (*paranimittaka*), for [the elision of] *ṅīṣ*...

This is because the elision of the *taddhita* suffix is accepted as being subsequent (*paratva*) by way of its position relative to the *luk* [elision of the feminine suffix]. Alternatively, since a sequence of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) conceived through the intellect exists even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), there is no inconsistency here. Nor does the prohibition mentioned above apply, on the grounds that when an *ataddhita* suffix is intended, the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would occur according to the rule "of this [word] ending in a short vowel before an *ataddhita* suffix."
Nor should it be suspected that the desired result is achieved even without [the application of the rule], for Kaiyaṭa has stated:

"The substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs only where there is the status of being a nominal stem (*bhatva*); however, here, since the status of being a nominal stem is absent due to *luk*, how could there be a substitution of the masculine form? Similarly, in the case of *pañcendraḥ*, meaning "he whose deities are five Indrāṇīs," [the rule applies]. "Of this..."

By the rule *devatā-at-yañ*, the suffix *yañ* is elided by *vigor-lug-anapatye*. Then, when the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is elided, because that [elision] lacks the status of being *sthānivadbhāva*, the *ānaṅ* substitution—which is prescribed in conjunction with *ṅīṣ*—is heard [in the form].
Furthermore, there is not even a suspicion here of *puṃvadbhāva*, because [the word refers to] Indra.
Because the basis for the application (*pravṛtinimitta*) differs— namely, "Indra-hood" in *indrāṇī* and "being Indra’s wife" in *indra-strī*—

the status of being a word that has been spoken with masculine reference (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) is not admitted [in the latter case]. However, for those who apply a *praśleṣa* (insertion) of the vowel *ī* as "vare-ī" in the rule *a padānte*, the mention of *luk* (elision) is not required here.
The operation [is as follows]: when the status of having *ṭh* as an *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) is to be applied, it is not *sthānivadbhūta*.

Consequently, when the suffix *aṇ* is added to the word *parikhā* according to the rule for the four meanings (*cāturarthika*), and then the suffix *cha* is added to the word *pārikha* by the rule "after a word ending in *vṛddhi*, beginning with *aka* or *ekā*, etc.," the form *pārikhīyaḥ* is established. Otherwise, [it would not be so].

Since the designation *upadhā* (penultimate) is a rule dependent on what precedes it (*pūrvavidhi*), when that designation is to be applied, the elision of *ā* (*ālopa*) would be treated as *sthānivat* (as if it were still present). If it is objected that, in this case, there would be *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) in forms such as *aṭayati*, we say no; for this prohibition applies only where the suffix upon which the designation *upadhā* depends is itself prescribed [by a rule].

Because it is established in the Bhāṣya; and in that context, the very mention of *caṅ*, *para-nih*, and *hrasva* serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*)—namely, "In that [context], *caṅ*, *para-nih*, and *hrasva* are not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. For example: *avīvadvīṇāṃ parivādakena* ("he caused the lute-player to play the lute"). Here, regarding the elision (*lopa*) of the first *ṇi*:

Because [the substitute] is treated as the original (sthānivadbhāva), the vowel *ā* is not considered a penultimate (*upadhā*); thus, the shortening of the penultimate vowel prescribed by the rule *ṭhṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ* does not apply.

If it is argued that this is established because the term *ṇi* refers to the general category of the causative suffix, then another example must be cited: *avīvarat* from the root *vṛ* with the prefix *ā*. Nor should one suspect a prohibition based on the rule *aglopi*, for that rule is superseded by the rule for *vṛddhi* (which applies later).

Because it is accepted that there is elision of the suffix *ṭi*, there is an absence of the status of being *aglopi* (having an elided penultimate vowel). For this very reason, the substitution of *halaka* and *kalaka* for *halika* and *kalika*—ending in a vowel—in the rule "uṇḍamiśra" is meaningful. [The principle] "it is not as if it were the original form (*na sthānivat*) when an *ṛt* vowel is the cause" applies: from the root *arc*, we derive *arka*. The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule "after roots ending in *ṛt*, and after *ādhāra*, *arca*, and *kali*."

From the root *pāc* (causative of *pac*), we have *pākti*. Here, although the substitution of *k* for *ṭ* and *ṭh* by the rule "u" [Pāṇini 7.3.52] applies, the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. In this Vārttika, the inclusion of the terms *kvip*, *caṅ*, *paranirhrāsa*, and *upadhā* is necessary. [The elision of the affix] is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* because of the insertion of the vowel *ī* after the elided suffix (*luk*).
It should be noted that this is because the meaning has already been conveyed, and because the substitution of *k* (kutva) is considered asiddha with respect to what precedes it.
Regarding the rule *ajo’ruṇ*, an example for the application of *kutva* must be sought elsewhere. As for *sakhaḥ*:
in the *bahuvrīhi* compound [formed] by the rule *tena saheti*, the substitution of *s* for *sa* occurs by the rule *vopasarjanasya*. The forms *sakhīḥ* and so forth follow accordingly.

By the rules *upa-ātmanaḥ kyac* and *yaci ca*, there is the substitution of *i* for the final vowel. Regarding the phrase "even though it is long": the intention is that the substitution of *yaṇ* was made for this very purpose. If it is argued that the mention of *yaṇ* is intended to exclude the scope of *guṇa* in the case of *atisakher bhūpateḥ*, let it be so; nevertheless, the rule still applies to the long vowel.
By what could it be prevented? For there is no authority for the claim that a *yaṇ* substitution must not occur in short vowels nor in long vowels.
Since the mention of the modified form (*vikṛtinirdeśa*) in the Sūtra serves to exclude both under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*), it gains its essential strength thereby.

This is likewise due to propriety and because it is established in the Bhāṣya. Regarding *lūnam*: by the rule *vādibhyaḥ*, the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is replaced by *n*. Regarding *kṣāmam*: by the rule *ṣayo maḥ*, [the *t*] is replaced by *m*; and by the rule *tyaprapūrvasya*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). Regarding *śuṣkī*: by the rule *uṣaḥ kaḥ*, the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is replaced by *k*.

Regarding *pakvī*: by the rule *aco ñṇiti*, the suffix *vaḥ* is applied; the term *iyaṅ* is used because, due to the preceding conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), the *yaṇ* substitution does not apply to the vowel *i*. These are the words ending in *ī*. Regarding *harivat*: the meaning is that it is to be formed in the same manner. (234) *tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.95.
*tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.95). The root *kruś* means "to call" and "to cry.

From this root, by the rule *tsitanigamimasisacyavidhāñkruśibhyas tun*, the suffix *tun* is applied to form the word *kroṣṭṛ*. With the suffix *tṛc*, however, the word is *kroṣṭṛ*. Both words denote a jackal.
In that regard, since the application of both [suffixes] would occur without distinction, the suffix *tun* in *arvaṣṭuḥ* is derived from a word ending in the nominative case,
while the suffix *vati* in *ṛjavaḥ* is derived from a word ending in the instrumental case.

Although extension (*atideśa*) is of many kinds—having as its objects cause (*nimitta*), designation (*vyapadeśa*), identity (*tādātmya*), grammatical operation (*śāstrakārya*), and form (*rūpa*)—here, for the sake of prominence, only the form is extended. Thus he says: "the form like that of a word ending in *tṛc*. And this does not apply to just any word ending in *pac*, but rather to *kruś* alone, because it is proximate and because of semantic proximity; with this in mind, he states the result: "in place of the word *kroṣṭṛ*, the word *kroṣṭṛ* [is substituted]. An example of extension of cause is: *cikīrṣati*, *cikīrṣate*.

In this context, by the rule *ūrvavatsanaḥ*, the status of having the marker *ñ* is extended (*atideśa*) to the causative (*sannanta*), whereby the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is established when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent. Now, one might object: "Is this not already covered even by the extension of the grammatical operation (*kāryātideśa*)? To this they reply: "Because that [extension of the operation] is preceded by the recognition of the cause, the extension of the cause (*nimittātideśa*) is stated separately."

Regarding the extension of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*): for example, by the rule *ādyantavadekasmin*, the designation of being "initial" (*āditva-vyapadeśa*), which has the result of making the initial syllable of a suffix acute (*pratyayādyaudātatva*) and finds its scope of application in forms such as *kartavyam*, is extended to forms like *aupagava*. Regarding the extension of identity (*tādātmyātideśa*): for example, by the rule *subāmantrite parāṅgavatsvare*, when the word *śubha* in the phrase *savatpāṇī śubhaspatī* functions as the "subordinate member" (*parāṅga*) of the vocative, the acute accent on the vowel *u* following the *ś* is established by the rule *āmantritasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.198).

An extension of a rule (*śāstrātideśa*) is as follows: by the rule *kālebhyo bhavavat*, whatever rule is prescribed under the governing heading *atra bhavaḥ* for words denoting time is extended to the meaning *asya devatā*. Consequently, in the cases of *āsikam* and *prāvṛṣeṇyam*, the forms are established through the application of the rules *āl̥aṭṭhañ* and *prāvṛṣ eṇyaḥ* respectively, exactly as they are ordained. However, in the case of an extension of an operation (*kāryātideśa*), there would be a confusion of base (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and so forth. Regarding the extension of an operation, [we have] *oto ṇit*: *gauḥ*, *gāvau*, *gāvaḥ*.

In this context, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) of *vṛddhi* is extended because it is the primary element. Some, however, cite *oto ṇiḥ* as an example of the extension of a cause (*nimitta-atideśa*); according to their view, examples for the extension of an operation (*kārya-atideśa*) should be cited such as *armavat karmaṇā* and *sthānivadādeśaḥ*. An example of the extension of form (*rūpa-atideśa*) is: *vataṇḍī cāsau vṛndīrikā ca* = *vātaṇḍyavṛndarikā*. Here, by the rule *pumvat karmadhāraye*, the form of the masculine word *vātaṇḍya* is extended to the word *vataṇḍī*.

In this *Manoramā*, six types of extended application (*atideśa*) have been stated. Others, however, say there are seven types, as it is said: "The seven extended applications are declared to be those termed: effect (*kārya*), form (*rūpa*), cause (*nimitta*), meaning (*artha*), treatise (*śāstra*), identity (*tādātmya*), and designation (*vyapadeśa*). An example of extended application by meaning (*arthātideśa*) is: *gargī ca gargyāyaṇau ca gargāḥ* ("Gargī and the two Gargyāyaṇas are [collectively called] the Gargas").

In this context, by the rule *'trī puṃvat'* [Pāṇini 6.3.34], when a feminine word ending in a *gotra* suffix functions as a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) under the rule *'vṛddho yūnā'* [Pāṇini 1.2.65], the masculine meaning is extended to the feminine meaning. Consequently, when there is a plurality caused by offspring (*apatya*), the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* is established by the rule *'yañañośca'* [Pāṇini 2.4.64].

(235) *ṛto ṅsirvanāmasthānayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.110]: "After an *ṛt* vowel, [the substitution of *guṇa* occurs] before the case-endings beginning with *ṅ* and before *sarvanāmasthāna* endings. This refers to the phonemes *ṛ* and *ṝ*; the mention of these two is for the purpose of preventing *guṇa* in words ending in the vowel *ṛ*.
It should be understood that the inclusion of *ta* [in the sūtra] is for the purpose of including the long vowel.

(236) *aptṛntṛcsvasṛnaptṛneṣṭṛtvaṣṭṛkṣattṛhotṛpotṛpraśāstṛṇām* | 6.4.11 || [The long vowel is substituted for the final vowel of the stems] *ap*, *tṛn*, *tṛc*, *svasṛ*, *naptṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *kṣattṛ*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, and *praśāstṛ* [before the nominative singular ending *su*].

Regarding *aptṛn*: although [the forms] would have been established by the rule *uriṣṭhemeyassu* through the inclusion of *vṛtṛ*, the separate mention of *tṛn* and *tṛc* is for the purpose of indicating that "even when a general term is used, sometimes only a specific [sub-type] is intended. Consequently, even though a general term is used in the rule *a-kā-padhāyāḥ*, [it is understood as referring specifically to *tṛn*].

Some say that only those [suffixes] ending in *taddhita* or *vuñ* are taken here, and not *ka* alone; therefore, what he will state later—"in the prohibition regarding *upadhā*, there is the inclusion of *taddhita* and *vuñ*"—becomes logically consistent. Others, however, say that since it should have been stated simply as "aptṛ," the mention of "ṛn" and "ṛk" is for the sake of brevity.

The separate mention of *arvan* is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] the three [rules]. Although the exclusion of that [application] is established by the *arthavat-paribhāṣā*, nevertheless, their separate mention is for the sake of making known the non-universality (*anityatva*) of that *paribhāṣā*. By means of this, [it follows that] the mentions of *ṭhan*, *ini*, *as*, and *man* apply only to meaningful elements (*arthavatā*).
And since it is established that [the rule] does not apply when there is no meaningful purpose, they employ the rule regarding what ends with that [suffix].

On the view that words are derived through etymological analysis (*vyutpattipakṣa*), since [the forms] would be established as ending in *tṛn* or *tṛc*, the mention of *naptṛ* and so on would be redundant; therefore, he says: "for the sake of restriction" (*niyamārtham*). [This applies] to others, such as those belonging to the *uṇādi* group.

The meaning is that this is for the purpose of preventing [the application of the rule] to words that are technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*). However, since the word *dhātṛ* is derived from an *uṇādi* suffix and is not a technical name, the long vowel occurs there as well: *dhātārau*, *dhātāraḥ*. But according to the view that [words like *dhātṛ*] are not etymologically derived (*avyutpattipakṣa*), the inclusion of *naptr* and the others in the rule is for the sake of a mandatory injunction (*vidhyartha*).
It should be understood that for words such as *pitṛ* (father) and *bhrātṛ* (brother), there is no long vowel [substitution] at all.
By the word "tena" (by that), the meaning is that there is no long vowel in forms such as *pitarau*, *pitaraḥ*, *bhrātarau*, and *bhrātaraḥ*.
Regarding *kroṣṭṛ*: [the substitution of] *anaṅ* [occurs]; because it is subsequent to the elision of the *ṅī* and other suffixes, the penultimate vowel becomes long, and that [long vowel]...

Although [the substitution] could be obtained by the rule *arvan-nāma-sthāne ca*, nevertheless, because it is subsequent, the rule *ṛt-ṛn* is more appropriate. For even when *anaṅ* has been applied, since the modified portion is not different from the original, it still possesses the nature of being a *tṛc* suffix. Otherwise, even if the guṇa substitution were made, there would be no long vowel in forms such as *roṣṭārāu*.
The sense is "it might be so.

(237) *Vibhāṣā tṛtīyādiṣv aci* (Pāṇini 7.1.97). Regarding *vibhāṣā tṛ*: [the rule] "in a rule where a specific element is mentioned, the operation applies to that which begins with it" (*yasmin vidhis tadādau*).
He states that this is a rule concerning the initial element [of a following suffix], saying "in the case of *aja* and so forth.
(238) *ṛta ut* 6.1.111. Regarding *ṛta ut*: when there is a single-substitute replacement for both the vowel *ṛ* and the vowel *u*, it shall be the short *u* alone, and not [the long one].

By the use of *tapara* (the long *ā*) in [Pāṇini 1.1.70], which has the same meaning as "long" (*dīrgha*), it is indicated that an *aṇ* being taught [as a substitute] sometimes includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). Consequently, when *y*, *v*,
or *l* follow *ha*, the *y*, *v*, and *l* prescribed for *ma* become nasalized (*anunāsika*).

(239) *rātsasya* | 8|2|24| Regarding *rātsasya*: since this [result] is already established by the rule *ayogāntasya lopaḥ*, he states that this [present rule] is for the sake of restriction—namely, *of the *s* alone*. It does not apply to anything else. [As in the example: *ṭhurk*.

In examples such as *parimārṣṭi*, the meaning is that there is no elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) after the letter *r*. Here, the reverse restriction—that "the elision occurs only after *r*" (*rādeva sasya*)—does not apply, because we observe forms like *umān* (from *umā + an*), where the elision of the final consonant cluster has already taken place despite the presence of *u*. [The reason for this is] "because it is subsequent" (*paratvāt*). It is not...

The sense is that it should be stated that *nuṭ* is obligatory; for once the substitution of *tṛjvat* has been applied, *nuṭ* becomes difficult to obtain due to the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* (the technical rule regarding the destruction of a cause).
[Therefore, it is said: "By prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), *nuṭ* takes precedence over *num*, the nasalization (*anunāsika*), and the *tṛjvat* substitution."

The examples for *numaci* [Pāṇini 6.1.173] are, respectively, *ṭhvārīṇām*, *tisṛṇām*, and *roṣṭuanām*. Now, it may be argued that everything applicable within its own scope must be set aside by this [rule], because one resorts to a general consideration regarding what is to be set aside; for this very reason, it is said that [this rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules concerning *uṇ*, lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the substitution of *ūṭh*.

He will say [later]: "And thus, because there is no distinction, *nuṭ* is also sublated by this [rule]; so how can there be a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) here, since that is impossible between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*)? To this they reply:
for this very reason, having refuted the conflict regarding that portion [of the rule], [the author] says "there is *nuṭ*" on the basis of the *jñāpaka* [sūtra] "atisṛcatasṛ".

The author of the Bhāṣya has stated: "In this way, it is more appropriately expressed as ‘um-tṛj-vadbhāvābhyām’. Thus end the words ending in /u/. Regarding *hu-hu*: this is an unanalyzed nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a specific type of Gandharva. Regarding *hū-huv-i*: [the rule] ‘īrghajjasi ca’ applies.

Since the substitution of the long vowel identical with the preceding one (pūrvasavarṇadīrgha) is prohibited, the *yaṇ* [substitution] applies according to the rule *ikaḥ*. Regarding the word *aticamū*, however, it is because of the statement: "The mention of gender (*liṅga*) is for the sake of meaning. Thus, the sense is that the statement made by the ancients—that "in this way, *aticamū* and others [are formed]"—is not to be respected. Regarding *khalūpa*: [it means] "one who purifies the threshing floor" (*khalaṃ punāti*). [This is derived from] the root *pūñ*.
The *kvip* suffix: (240) *oḥ supi* 6.4.83.
Regarding *oḥ supi*, [the rule] *yaṇ* is supplied from *ṭhiṇo yaṇ* [6.1.77], and the sūtra *theranekācaḥ* [6.4.64] is also [to be supplied].

Everything follows [the previous rule], with the exception of the vowel *i*, because the vowel *u* is specified as the subject of the operation by the rule *ṭhor*. With the intention that the word "root" (*dhātu*) from the sūtra *aci śnudhātvi* is connected here just as it was in the rule *ṭeranekācaḥ*, he explains: "in a conjunction that is a part of a root," and so forth.

(241) *varṣābhvaśca* |6|4|84|. In the forms *varṣābhvau* and *varṣābhvaḥ*, the rule *iko yaṇ aci* [Pāṇini 6.1.77] is superseded by the rule *rām-nathoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.108], which would result in the substitution of the homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). However, that [result] is further superseded by the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.105].
Furthermore, when a prohibition [of the *yaṇ* substitute] occurs, the *yaṇ* substitute would again apply by the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām*.

That being set aside, the *yaṇ* substitute applies by the rule *āṬḥ supi*; when that is prohibited by the rule *abhūsudhiyoḥ*, the *avaṅ* substitute would again apply, but it should be understood that the *yaṇ* substitute applies instead by the rule *varṣābhvaśca*.

In this manner, other general rules (*utsarga*) and exceptions (*apavāda*), as well as specific injunctions (*vidhi*), are to be inferred elsewhere. Regarding the term *dardūra*, Amara states: "The words *maṇḍūka*, *varṣābhū*, *śālūra*, and *dardūra* are synonyms for a frog. Yādava states: "The word *varṣābhū* is feminine when referring to the plant *punarnavā*, but masculine when referring to a frog (*dardūra*). [The root] *hambh* [is used] in the sense of lowing.
The root *ṭhhambh* belongs to the *tudādi* class. *Hambhūḥ* means "an author" (*granthakartā*); others say it means "a narrator" (*kathaka*).
Regarding the form *vyacutpādit*, the meaning is that the suffix *ū* and the augment *num* are here irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*).
However, in the *Daśapādī-vṛtti*, it says: "*Arbhaṇam* [is] *hambhūḥ*; the augment *num* and the *anusvāra* [are applied]."
It has been stated that [the vowel] is elided. Since this *u* is not part of the verbal root (*dhātu*), the substitution *uvaṅ* does not apply;

rather, by the rule "ṭhiko yaṇaci," *yaṇ* occurs, and with the intention that this is subsequently sublated by the rule "ṭhami pūrvaḥ," he says: *hambhūm*. This is the opinion of Śrīpati. However, Mādhava...

It is stated that by the rule beginning with *ṭhandūhambhū*, when the word *haḍha* is used as an upapada, the suffix *kū* is applied to the root *bhū*, and the substitution of *han* for the upapada is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). It should be stated that when preceded by *han*, *kar*, or *punar*, the *yaṇ* [substitution] applies to *bhū*. Thus, *hambhū* is formed. [An example is] *taruḥ*.

Some say it is a specific species of snake; others say it is a monkey. It should be stated [as such], because the particle *ca* in the rule *varṣābhvaśca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned. And thus, when the *yaṇ* substitution obtained by the rule *oḥ supi* is prohibited by the rule *na bhūsudhiyoḥ*, [the form] *varṣāhan* [is established]. *karapunaḥ*...

It is established that the mention of *pūrvasya* (of the preceding) in the rule *bhuvo bhuv-iti* is for the purpose of restriction (*vidhy-artha*). Regarding this, the moderns (*navyāḥ*) argue: "Having accepted that *varṣā-hankare* serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatā*), it could have been said that the inclusion of *bhū-* in the rule *a-bhū-sudhiyoḥ* is superfluous. This is not correct, because [the rule] *hankara-punaḥ-pūrvasya*...

Otherwise, there would arise an inverted rule (*viparīta-niyama*) such that [the substitution] would apply even where it should not; consequently, forms such as *unarbhvau* and so forth would not be established. "The long reading" means the reading *han-kāre*.
Thus, in the short reading, the substitution *uvaṅ* applies only to that preceded by *kāra*, whereas in the long reading, *uvaṅ* applies to that preceded by *kara*.

Commentary: Regarding the word *punarbhū*, since it is stated in the *Amarakośa* that "the term *punarbhū* refers to a woman who has been remarried (*dvidhūr̤hā*"), the word *punarbhū* is invariably feminine. Thus, one might raise the objection that it is appropriate to mention it only in the section on feminine nouns and not here;
in response to this doubt, he says: "It is etymologically masculine. [This is because] she is one who becomes [a wife] again (*punarbhavati*).

The meaning is that the verbal root *punarbhū* exists even in the masculine gender. Regarding the phrase "like *svayambhū*": the older grammarians have cited the words *haṃbhū* and *kārāmbhū* as examples, like *varṣābhū*, but that should be disregarded; such is the intention. Thus end those ending in *ū*. Regarding *dhātā*: he who sustains (*dadhāti*) is *dhātā*, the lotus-born [Brahmā].

From the root *ḍudhāñ* (to place), the suffixes *tṛc* or *tṛn* are applied. [The resulting forms are] *dhātṛ* and *dhātṛ*. There is the substitution of *anaṅ*, lengthening of the vowel, elision of the *su* (nominative case ending), and elision of the nasal (*n*).

It should be stated that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the *n* following a vowel of the *ṛ*-class. This refers to the view that words are derived etymologically (*vyutpattipakṣa*). In the view that words are not etymologically derived (*avyutpattipakṣa*), there is no possibility of applying the rule for lengthening at all, because [the word *dhātṛ*] is not listed among the *ab-ādi* group; this is the intended meaning. "Not so" [refutes the objection].
In the rule *ayater ḍicca*, the word *ṛ* ending in the suffix *ṛt* [is intended]. *Anaṅ* and so forth are as before.
(242) *nṛ ca* | 6.4.6 | *nṛ ca*. Here, from the rule *chandasy ubhayathā*, the term *ubhayathā* (in both ways) is understood to carry over.

Intending this, he says: "or it may be long. Some, however, here also carry forward the term "in Vedic usage" (*chandasi*); for them, [the examples] such as "Alas, what peace can there be for men whose minds are shattered by anxiety? and "The one among men... [are justified].

Otherwise, constructions such as *gamyas tvam asi* would not be consistent. Furthermore, since the form *ṛṇām* is already established by the preceding rule *chandasy ubhayathā*, the rule *ṛ ca* would be redundant. Moreover, regarding what was stated in the previous rule...

They maintain that the term "isṛcatasṛ" is to be supplied [from a previous rule], but that too is incorrect; for we observe the option [between short and long vowels] without distinction. Thus, for example, in the mantra "dhātā dhātṛṇām," the Taittirīyas pronounce a short vowel, whereas the Bahvṛcas pronounce a long one—this is the general direction.

Thus end those [words] ending in *ṛ*. Thus end those ending in *ṛ*. [The principle of] "an imitation (anukaraṇa) is like its original form (prakṛti)" and so forth is the indicator here; for in that [sūtra], there is the indication "from *yat*, *etad*, and *tad* regarding measure," which serves as evidence because the application of the *tyadādi* substitution (*yatva*) occurs there, and because the original form is maintained while the absence of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one of identical forms) is observed.

"Optionality" means: [the rule] "itve raparatvam" (in the case of *it*, there is substitution by *ra*). When *it* applies according to the rule "ṛta id dhātoḥ" (for *ṛ* of a root, *it* is substituted), then *raparatvam* applies according to the rule "uraṇ raparaḥ" (for *u*, *ṛ*, or *l*, *aṇ* is substituted, followed by *ra*). "Kīḥ" means the root *kṛ*. Similarly—"tīḥ"—means the root *tṛ*. "And so forth" refers to the rule "ṛta uḥ" (for *ṛ*, *u* is substituted).

Because of the inclusion of *ra* (in the term *rapara*), the substitution of *at* does not occur in the case of *ṅsi* and *ṅs*—e.g., *kroḥ*. Because it ends in a long vowel, *nuṭ* is not applied to *ām*—e.g., *krām*. But in the case of *ṅi*, there is the substitution of *rī*, and so forth. Thus end those ending in *ṛ*. Thus end those ending in *ṛ*. [The rule] *anaṅ ṛto’ṅitaḥ* applies because of the phonetic identity (*sāvarṇya*) between the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ*.
This is because of the application of the rule *ṛduśanas-*. This refers to the domain of *guṇa* [substitution].

In the domain of *guṇa*, by the rule *ṛto ṅī*, [the form] becomes *gamṛn*. Since there is no long vowel for the *ḷ*-vowel, the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* [substitution] prescribed by the rule *ratnamayaḥ* results in the vowel *Añ* (the long *ḷ*) in place of both the *ḷ*-vowel and the vowel *a*.

It occurs. If it is argued, "In this case, let the long *lṛ*—which contains two *l*-sounds—be [the substitute]," they say here: regarding the rule *pūrva-parayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*, when there is a vowel (*ac*) following either the first or second [vowel] of the *ak*-group, that long vowel which is homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with the preceding one takes the place of both the preceding and the following.

By the statement that [the sounds] *bh* and *v* exist [in place of *ṛ* and *ḷ*], there is a state of phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*) between *ṛ* and *ḷ*; therefore, it is *ṛ* alone that occurs in place of *ḷ* and *ṛ*, and not a long vowel containing two *ḷ*s.

This is because, due to the difference in articulatory effort—specifically, because [the latter] has the effort of being slightly contacted (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*)—it lacks phonetic similarity with *ḷ*. Thus...

It should be understood that in forms such as *caṣṭhohotrī*, where there is a double *ṛ* (repha) within the word, a long vowel does not occur in place of both the *ṛ*-vowel and the *a*-vowel. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*): [the forms] *gamlṛbhyām*, *gamlṛbhiḥ*, and *gamlṛbhyaḥ*. However, some maintain that before the suffix *ām*, the form is *gamṛṇām*; but in reality, [it is otherwise].

In place of *lṛ*, there ought to be a long vowel with two *l*s in its interior, because proximity (*āntarya*) based on place of articulation is stronger [than proximity based on effort]. However, in the case of *ṭhhotṛṇām*, only *ā* occurs, because there is equality in both place and effort. This might be argued: [what about] that which is joined with two *r*s?
Since the two *l*-sounds (*lakāra*) possess a slightly contacted articulation (*ceṣatspṛṣṭaprayatna*), they differ from the *ṛ* and *ḷ* sounds in their mode of articulation (*prayatna-bheda*).

Consequently, because they lack homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) with *ṛ* and *ḷ*, they do not qualify as vowels (*ac*) under the rule *ū-kālo ’j...*. Thus, how could there be a designation of "long" (*dīrgha-saṃjñā*) for them by that rule? Therefore, [the forms] containing the two *l*-sounds must be derived from the rules *ṛti ṛ vā* and *ḷti*.
Otherwise, how could the Vārttika *lṛti* be consistent?

For by the rule *ṭhakaḥ savarṇe*, the desired forms would not be established. On this point, they say: to ensure that both [the vowels *ṛ* and *lṛ*] possess the status of being vowels (*actva*), the phonetic series (*varṇasamāmnāya*) must be recited after the sūtra *ṛlṛk*; by means of that—

All desired results are established. Nor should it be suspected that, even when length is established, because of the similarity in the effort of openness (*vivṛta-prayatna*), in the case of *ṭhhotṛ-lṛkāra*, the long *ṛ*-vowel alone would occur rather than a long vowel consisting of two *r*s; for there is a parity between the two instances of *ṛ* and the [substitution] of two *r*s in their place.

Regarding the occasional substitution [of *ṛ* for *ḷ*] even in the case of a single *parvan*: in the example "hotṛlṛkāra," due to similarity (*āntarya*) with *ḷ*, it sometimes becomes [the *ṛ*] joined with two *ḷ*s, and sometimes, due to similarity with *ṛ*, it becomes [the *ṛ*] joined with two *r*s.
However, according to the view of the Vārttika, in "hotṛlṛkāra," it does not contain two *r*s.
There is a discrepancy, for while [the substitution] occurs [in some cases], it only occasionally occurs under the view that [the rule] is rejected;

in this regard, one must either accept the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*) or admit that the rejection of the rule is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*). On this point, it should be understood from the *bhāṣya* on the sūtra *akaḥ savarṇe*.

The statement "ṛti ṝvā" and "ṛti lṛve" has not been rejected; for even if it were rejected in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ulyāsye," that would be untenable due to the difference in results [it produces]. However, if that [sūtra] is accepted, then it can simply be stated as "ako'ki"; thus, the [opponent's] argument is indeed inconsistent.

If, however, the Vārttika *ṭhṛ-u-ṛve* were read as *ṭhū-aÑ-i-ṭhṛ-ve*, then, by not relying on the recurrence of the word *savarṇa* from the two Vārttikas, it would simply state its own [rule]. Let us return to the subject at hand: in the case of the suffix *ṅai*, by the rule *ṛto ṅi* there is *guṇa* substitution, with the *l* following after the vowel. Thus: *gamali*.

*gamlṛḥ*, *gamlṛṣu*. In the same way, this should be inferred for the word *śaklṛ* as well. Thus end those ending in *ḷ*. Thus end those ending in *ḷ*. Regarding the rule *ser* [Pāṇini 7.3.104]: *asyāpatyam iḥ kāmaḥ* ("the offspring of this one is desire"), *asya strī īr lakṣmīḥ* ("the female of this one is Lakṣmī"). In the analysis (*vigraha*) "existing together with him" or "with her," [the rule applies] by the rule *tena saheti tulyayoge* [Pāṇini 2.2.28].
In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule "ṭhvopasarjanasya," there is the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-*, and then by "ādguṇaḥ," [the form] *saya-* is obtained.

Now, one might object: since the single vowel *e* (in *say-e*) would, by virtue of being treated as the final element (*antavadbhāva*), be considered a word-final (*padānta*), it would block the *ayādeśa* and—because *jas* follows—result in the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the *pūrvarūpa* according to the rule "eḥ padāntāddhrasva ūṭh"; and thus, [the form would be different].

If it is argued that the form should be *e* alone and not *aya*, some here reply: "In that case, let it be an imitative word (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) for the word *se* as prescribed by the rule *hāsaḥ se īśaḥ seṭ*; for in that instance, the substitution of *ay* before the suffix *jas* is beyond dispute. [The word] *smṛteḥ* [means]: *iḥ* is desire (*kāma*).
The analysis of the compound is either "he by whom [Lakṣmī] is remembered" (*smṛtaḥ yena saḥ*) or "she by whom he is remembered" (*lakṣmīḥ smṛtā yena*).

In the form *iṣṭhā*, there is the prior placement of the word *smṛta* [according to the rule for the superlative suffix]. Regarding the form *smṛtayaḥ*: one might object that here, according to the previously stated method, there ought to be a single substitution of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) by the rule *ṭheṅḥ padāntādati*, and not the substitution of *ay*. No.
