If it is argued that the assumption of this being an imitative word (*anukaraṇaśabda*) here gains its propriety, the moderns (*navya*) reply as follows: because of the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule by the statement "there is a prohibition when the following member is a word, provided the operation concerns what is not at the beginning of a word," the rule "a vowel preceded by *e* or *o* at the end of a word [is elided before a vowel]" does not apply. Furthermore:

In the rule *vādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne ’ṭhyaci bha*, the author of the Bhāṣya has explained that "in the case of suffixes beginning with *v* (vādi), the preceding element receives the designation *pada*. Consequently, by this [rule], both designations—the one from *suptiṅanta* and the one from *vādiṣu*—are negated; thus, [the status of] being preceded by a suffix (*pūrvantatva*) is established.

Since the status of being at the end of a word (*padāntatā*) is difficult to establish here, the form *amṛtaya* is indeed free from objection. Likewise, there is no inconsistency even under the alternative of deriving it as *aya* together with *ṭhinā* and so forth. Nor can it be argued that because the substitute for *ekāra* (the *ayādeśa*) is treated as if it were the preceding element, it would be an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and thus the case-suffix (*sup*) would be elided.
This is to be suspected: since the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) is based on its etymological meaning (*anvartha*), that designation does not apply to a subordinate (*upasarjana*) element.

Nor, even so, should one object that once the form *aharga-i* is established, the substitution of *sā-* for the word *saha* would not occur because the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of *guṇa* would have already taken effect;
for when the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as if it were subsequent (*paravad-bhāva*), the substitution of *sa-* for the word *saha* does indeed take place.

Nevertheless, one should not suspect that the form would be *a* ending in *a* (adanta) rather than *ai* ending in *e* (edanta); for, by the prohibition of vṛddhi in the final member in the rule "indrasya parasya," it is established that "the operation pertaining to the first [member] occurs first, and only then does the single-substitute (ekādeśa) take place."
They say [the suffix is used] because it makes known the general rule.

(243) *oto ṇit* | Pāṇini 7.1.90. [The word] *gotaḥ* [is formed from *go* with the suffix *ṇit*. The locative form [of *gotaḥ*] is understood as being carried over (*anuvṛtta*) from the rule *ṭhito't sarvasmādbhasthāne*.

The term *sarvanāmasthāna* is transformed into the nominative case [to mean "that which is a *sarvanāmasthāna*"], because it stands in apposition with the word *ṇit*. Thus he says: "*sarvanāmasthānam*" [meaning] "that which performs the operation of a *ṇit*.
The meaning is: when a *ṇit* follows, it effects whatever operation is prescribed for a preceding element when a *ṇit* follows.

(244) *āṬtaḥ am-śasoḥ* |6|1|93|. [The substitution of] *āṬ* occurs for the final vowel of words such as *gauḥ* before the case-endings *am* and *śas*. However, it does not occur in the case of *itigauḥ*, because, as will be stated later, the rule *otaḥ* applies; that is, a *śas* that follows a taddhita suffix does not follow a word ending in *o*.
With the intention that [the suffix] *śas* occurs, he says: "by association with *sā*.
It is also stated in the *Kāśikā* that this is because of the continued application (*anuvartana*) of the term "*upī*. Kaiyaṭa, however, asks:
"Since *śas* occurs even after an *ad-dhita* suffix, how can *amraḥ* be [understood here] through association?"

Anticipating the objection that [the form] might be *asuptvām*, he says *acinavam*— on the basis of the governing rule *aci* (Pāṇini 7.2.70)— since only a suffix beginning with *ś* (such as *śas*) is possible after the root *ac*, and not a *taddhita* suffix; thus, from the root *ci* (to gather), in the *laṅ* tense, for the first person singular ending *mip*, the substitution *am* is applied by the rule *asthasthāmipām...* (Pāṇini 7.1.5).

It should be stated that "after *o*, [the suffix] is marked as having the *ṇit* designation. The meaning of "it should be stated that 'after *o*', [the suffix] is marked as having the *ṇit* designation" is that one should say "after *o*" (*ota*) instead of "after *ā*" (*ota*). And thus, there is no room for the objection that in the case of "ām," the *vṛddhi* substitution would apply because it is subsequent; for by the absence of such an occasion, the *āt* [substitution] prevails.
Because it is precisely the [substitution of] *vṛddhi* that is barred. Thus end those words ending in *-ī*.
(245) *rāyo hali* | Pāṇini 7.2.85. Regarding *rāyo hali*: from the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (7.1.21), the word *ā* is understood, as well as the word *vibhaktau*.

It occurs. Thus he says: "The form [rai] is a substitute for the final [element]," and so forth. Amara states: "Artha, ra, and vibhava are synonyms. As for the statement in the Bhāṣya that "the word *rāya* is Vedic," Kaiyaṭa on the rule *vanto yī* explains that this refers to the Vedic nature of the word *rai* when it ends in the *kyac* suffix, and not to the word *rai* in general. He himself...
He states another alternative view, that [the form] *kevala* is also Vedic (*cchāndasa*). Thus end those words ending in *ai* and *au*. Regarding *glauḥ*:
Amara says, “*glauḥ* is the moon, the storehouse of digits. Similarly, one who protects people is an *anauḥ*.
By the rule *varatvara-*, there is the substitution *ūṭh*; then by the rule *ety-ed-at-ūṭha-su*, there is *vṛddhi*.
The substitution of *acyau* [for *aci*] applies in cases such as *janāvau* and *janāvaḥ*. It does not apply;

thus, one should also understand that in *he glauḥ*, the elision of the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhi-lopa*) does not occur, and in *glāvaḥ*, the single-substitute form (*pūrvarūpa*) prescribed by the rule *siṅsośca* does not occur. This is because [the rule] indicates a disregard for homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*). However, if...

Since there would be a single designation for the twenty-four sounds of the *sāvarṇya* group, the rule *vṛddhir ādaic* could have been read as *vṛddhir ādeṅ*; thus, the fact that the rule *ai-au-jit* exists as a separate sūtra indicates the absence of *sāvarṇya*. For this very reason, there is no [confusion] between *e* and *o*, nor between *ai* and *au*.

The meaning is that mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) has already been stated in the very sūtra *aṇuditsavarṇasya ca pratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), by virtue of the necessity for formulating the sūtra *aiāṬc* (Pāṇini 1.1.1).
Now, one might object: if the sūtra *aiāṬc* did not exist, then in the sūtra *a yvābhyām* (Pāṇini 7.2.11)...

If it were stated as *ābhyām ai*, this pratyāhāra would not be established; however, when it is stated as *pūrvau tu tābhyām eṅ*, because that which is being prescribed [as *eṅ*] does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*),
in cases such as *vaiyākaraṇaḥ* and *sauvaśvaḥ*, only *ai* and *au* are the augments, and not *ai* and *au*.

Furthermore, one might argue that the formulation of the rule *ai au* is for the sake of avoiding redundancy (*vaiyarthyābhāvāt*), and thus does not indicate the absence of *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) between *ai* and *au*. But this is not so; for even by reading the rule as *ūrau tu tābhyām ai au*, the desired result is achieved, and the redundancy of the original rule remains as it was. This being established...
This is merely an indication of the direction;

in reality, however, when it is stated that [the rule] is due to the force of the commencement of the sūtra "ṭhe o’ṅ," there is indeed no inconsistency in the rule "ābhyām aiC. Nor would there be any problem in the absence of the sūtra "ṭhe o’ṅ."
It might be asked: "How can the pratyāhāra eṅ be established in rules such as 'ṭhadeṅ guṇaḥ', 'ṭheṅi pararūpam', and 'eṅaḥ padāntādati'?
However, if there were *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) [between *ai* and *au*], one could have read the rules as 'ṭhadej guṇaḥ', 'ṭheci pararūpam', and 'ṭhecaḥ padāntādati'.
Because it is possible [to achieve the desired result]; for even if the term *aj* were not included, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would be equal [in both cases].

Nor should it be argued that, even so, both sūtras—*aiAu caturṇām* and *thaiĀṬ j*—are necessary for the purpose of establishing the respective substitutes *āy* and so forth for the four sounds *e*, *o*, *ai*, and *au*; for by the rule *sthāne ’ntaratamaḥ* alone, the [correct] substitutes for the *ec* sounds...
For we have already established previously that the *ayādi* vowels are established in their sequence; for when it is accepted—
on the basis of the aforementioned *Śikṣā* statement beginning with “of the *varṇas* and the *ṛṣmas*”—
that *eṅ* are open (*vivṛta*) and *ai-au* are more open (*vivṛtatara*), [then the subsequent ones are progressively more open].

It should be understood that since there is no possibility of mutual *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) between *e* and *ai*, or between *o* and *au*, at the time [of their production], the rule would not have been stated as *ṭhaiāṬ’j*, *ṭheo’j*, or *ṭhaio’ṅ*; thus, it is not the indicator (*jñāpaka*) mentioned above. Some, however, [hold that] although *eṅ* is not the most open (*vivṛtatama*), it is more open than other vowels.

They say that since openness (*vivṛtatva*) exists in its highest degree in *vivṛtatara*, by taking that [degree] as the basis, both the *eṅ* vowels and the *ai-au* diphthongs possess equal effort (*tulyaprayatnatva*); thus, when the possibility of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) arises, it is entirely correct to rely on the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*). Others, however, do not accept this. For if that were the case, [the rule] "iko... [would apply].
For otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with the passage from the *Śabdakaustubha* on the rule *guṇavṛddhī*,
which states that, in accordance with the *Śikṣā* beginning with "of vowels and of sibilants (*ūṣman*)...", guna would not apply in cases such as *cetā* and *netā*.
One should not suspect that there is a distinction in the nature of being more or less open (*vivṛtatara*),

because [if that were so] the rule would be rendered devoid of its object (*nirviṣayatva*); for this is established by the indications in rules such as *ayaḥ karaṇam* and *dhānyānāṃ bhavane*, which allow us to infer the substitution of *guṇa* in the case of *i*-sounds and others.

This has been settled by another method. According to the reasoning stated there, if [the consonants] possessed equal effort (*prayatna*), then the apprehension that *guṇa* substitution would not apply in cases such as *etaḥ* and *aneṭha* would be groundless.
Therefore, [the consonants] differ from the vowels slightly by being more open (*vivṛta*), just like the sibilants (*ūṣman*).

The absence of phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*) here can easily be stated by means of the distinction between "more open" (*vivṛtatarā*) and "most open" (*vivṛtatama*); this is the direction [of the argument].
Thus end the masculine stems ending in vowels.
(246) *āṬṅ āpaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.18.

Now follow the feminine bases ending in vowels. *Ramā*: she delights, thus *ramā*. From the root *ram* (to sport) with the suffix *ac* (by Pāṇini 3.1.134) and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, [the form is derived]. According to the rule regarding words qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭapara*), this [suffix] is included here.
The elision [of the *ṭāp*] occurs by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.68). And it is not the case that [this elision] occurs here solely because of the ending in *ā*.

It might be argued that let there be the production of the *svādi* suffixes [from the base ending in *ṅī*], even though the form ending in a *pratyaya* is not a *prātipadika*, because of the separate mention of *ṅī* and *ūp*. However, this must be rejected, because it has already been stated that the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* serves another purpose, and because that mention has been refuted; thus, the rule would apply to the form ending in *śas*. "Of *as*... [Pāṇini 6.1.172].
The meaning is that the word *īt* follows from [the previous rule] *śī-t-yaḥ*. (247) *saṃbuddhau ca* | 7|3|106|.

Regarding *saṃbuddhau ca*: [the word] *et* is supplied from "in the plural, when a *jhal* [consonant] follows, *e* [is substituted for *ā*]" (*ahuvacane jhalyet*), and [the word] *āp* is supplied from "also after *āṅ* and *api*" (*āṅ cāpiḥ*). Thus, *et* and *āp* [are supplied].

And since it follows [the previous rule], he says: "it would be *āpa*. Regarding the rule *eṅhrasvāt*: one should not suspect that here the elision of *su* (*sulopa*) might instead occur by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, because by the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treating the suffix as present), the application of the substitution of *i* (*etva*) by the rule *eta iddhāvādibhyaḥ* is also possible.

Because the substitution of *e* (by P. 6.1.90) applies both due to its being subsequent and its being taught as a specific rule (*pratipadokta*), the elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* suffixes (by P. 6.1.68) does not apply once that substitution has been made;

furthermore, even if the status of the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*) were to apply, there would still be no occurrence of the actual form *ā*. This is because the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) in the rule was rejected by interpreting *ā* and *āḥ* as a single long vowel *ā*. Consequently, only the elision prescribed by P. 6.1.69 (*eṅhrasvāt*) applies.
The sense is that [the rule] is logical because it applies to something else (*paratvena nyāyyatvāt*). (248) *Āṅ* and *apiḥ* [are karmapravacanīyas]. 7.3.105.
Regarding *āṅ*, he says "and when *os*" (*osi ca*), because by the mention of the letter *ci*, the previously established [rule] *osi ce* is referred back.

Regarding the words *paraḥ* and *ramābhiḥ*: [an objection is raised]—"But here, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatva*), the rule *ato bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9) would require the substitution of *ais* for *bhisa*. Nor should it be argued that this does not happen due to the force of the indicatory letter *t* in *ataḥ*; for that [indicatory letter] has already served its purpose in cases such as *viśvapābhiḥ*, where the single-substitute has not yet been applied. If this is said, it is not so.
Because the rule *anta-ādivacca* does not apply in the case of an *al*-vidhi.
(249) *yāḍāpaḥ* | P. 7.3.113. Regarding *yāḍāpaḥ*: the word *iti*, which is understood from the rule *heṅtīti* (P. 6.1.69), is a locative case ending (*saptamyanta*) and refers to *āp*.
He says—"of the dual"—because the word ending in the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhyanta) is modified in accordance with the fifth case (pañcamī).

Here, because the word "upi" is carried over from the rule "upi ca," the augment *yāṭ* applies only to a *sup* [ending]. Consequently, even though the *sarvadhātuka* suffix beginning with *ap* is marked as having the *ṅ* designation, [the augment does not apply] in cases such as *mālāta*, which means "one who acts like a garland."

Therefore, [the substitution] does not occur. And this was stated by accepting the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* interpretation—that "a rule concerning what precedes" (*pūrvavidhiḥ*) means "a rule with respect to what precedes" (*parasmin*)—in the context of the rule *ṭhacaḥ parasmim*.
However, if one accepts the *pañcamī-samāsa* interpretation, there would be an intervention caused by the status of *śap* as *sthānivadbhāva*.

They say that in cases such as *ālā* [in the feminine], there is no possibility at all for the application of the augment *yāṭ*. Although it would have been sufficient to state simply *ṭhyaṅ*, the long vowel is pronounced for the sake of clear understanding. Nor does the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97) result in the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) for the preceding and following sounds; for that is precluded by the very force of the pronunciation of the letter *a*.

Regarding the rule *vṛddhireci*: the statement presented by the Easterners (*prācām*) as *ṭhāṭaśca* has been disregarded here, because since the letter *ṭ* in *yāṭ* and *syāṭ* functions as a marker for the entire suffix (*samudāyānubandha*), there is no occurrence of *āṭ* in this context. (250) *sarvanāmnaḥ syāḍhrasvaśca* 7.3.114.

The suffix *syāṭ* is applied after a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). The long vowel in the pronunciation is for the sake of clear understanding, as before. Anticipating the objection that a word ending in *āp* (the feminine suffix) cannot be a pronoun because it is not listed in the *sarvādi* group, he says: "by virtue of being the prior portion (*pūrvānta*) of the substitute for *ekāj-īś*."

(251) *Bibhāṣā diksamāse bahuvrīhau* |1|1|28|. This option (*vibhāṣā*) applies when there is a compound of directions (*diksamāsa*). One should not be mistaken into thinking that this option is introduced because the rule was not otherwise applicable due to being secondary (*gauṇatva*), nor that it is introduced despite the prohibition by the rule *na bahuvrīhau*. Rather, since the general rule [of substitution] is already applicable, this option is stated.

Because that [rule] pertains to all items beginning with *sarva* occurring within sentences involving non-worldly (alaukika) derivation, whereas this [present rule] pertains to compounds (*samāsa*). The phrase "for the sake of clarity" refers to the rule *iṅmānī* which prescribes a specific compound (*pratipadoktasamāsa*), [derived] from the [previous rule] *eṣo bahuvrīhiḥ*.

The intended meaning is that this is because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in the sense of an *ahuvrīhi*. (252) Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā dvitīyatṛtīyābhyām* [Pāṇini 7.3.115], it is possible to say that [the suffix] *am* is not applied to the words *dvitīya* and so on when they end in *a*.
It should not be suspected that the rule *vibhāṣā dvitīyā* is necessary because the word ending in the suffix *tīya* is absent;

for, since the substitute [ekādeśa] is treated as the end of the preceding element, the word "dvitīya" and so forth do not end in the suffix *tīya*, and thus the rule *vibhāṣā dvitīyā* is indeed necessary.

This is to be suspected; for, because the single-substitute (ekādeśa) is included as part of the preceding element, even that which ends in *ā* is considered to end in the suffix *tīya*. As for the rule "of *tīya*": since this very [rule] must necessarily be stated for the sake of the masculine and neuter genders, the rule "optionally in the case of *dvitīya*" (*vibhāṣā dvitīye*) need not be formulated.
The term *bhāvaḥ* [refers to the following rule]:

"In the case of words meaning 'mother' (*ambā*) and those ending in *nadi*, there is shortening. Here, because of the statement that "the word meaning 'mother' must consist of two syllables," the intention is that shortening occurs only for a word meaning 'mother' that has two syllables, and not for others.
He states the result:
"The short vowel is not [substituted] for those that possess the unaspirated *ḍa* and *la* sounds. This refers to the phrase beginning with "those that are unaspirated *ḍa* and *la*," etc.
Regarding *jarā*: from the root *ṛṣ* in the sense of "loss of vitality" (*vayohāni*), [the suffix] *ap* is applied according to the rule *ṣidbhidādibhyo'ṅ*.

When the *guṇa* substitution is applied by the rule "ṭhṛd-daś-āṅ-e," the suffix *ṭāp* is added. Because it is subsequent to the rule for *śī*-bhāva, the form *jaras-* etc. [is obtained]. As for the forms *ārāyāḥ*, although this might be the case because the rule "āṅ-āpaḥ" and the rule "hrasva-nady-āpo nuṭ" are superseded by the subsequent rule "arāyāḥ," nevertheless, the rules "āhi ca āpaḥ," "yāḍ-āpaḥ," and "ReĀrām" [must still apply].
If it is argued that the substitution *jaras* would occur by virtue of its being subsequent (paratva), thereby overriding [the rule for] *āḍ* and *āp*, the following is said in response:

even when the single-substitute *ai* has been applied by the rule "āṬ ca āpaḥ," the substitution *jaras* would still apply to the form *arāyāḥ* according to the maxim of "modification of a part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*).
Consequently, because it is obligatory (*nitya*), the substitution *jaras* itself overrides the single-substitute *ai*.
It occurs. Nor can it be argued that the single-substitute (ekārādeśa) is also invariably permanent, such that even when the *jaras* substitute has been applied,

the feminine suffix *āp* would still be present by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule, thereby triggering the application of the *ṣatva* rule (*aṅcāpi*)— for, as will be explained immediately below, the term *āp* is everywhere understood to refer exclusively to the form consisting of the letter *ā*.

Because it will be stated later that [the substitution] does not apply there; however, the augment *yāṭ* (prescribed by the rule *yāḍ-āpaḥ*) is superseded by the substitute *jaras* because the latter is *antaraṅga*. This is because *yāṭ*, which is prescribed for the case-ending *ṅti* following an *āp* consisting of the vowel *ā*, is *bahiraṅga* due to its dependence on many factors. The same applies to *rām*.

The substitution of *jaras* prevails because it is obligatory (*nitya*). Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *jaras* is not obligatory because, once the suffix *ReĀ* (the genitive plural ending *-ām*) has been applied after a stem ending in the feminine suffixes *āP* or *āN*, the substitution of *jaras* would not apply due to the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the non-disturbance of the cause of a grammatical operation); for this is stated in the *Rūpamālā*.

Because it has been stated that "it is not *ara*," there is no obstacle to accepting the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the aforementioned paribhāṣā in accordance with the desired conclusion. "Dependent on its own substratum" (*svāśrayam*) means dependent on the *sub*-suffixes such as *yañ* and others; the meaning is "caused by them. [This refers to] the *sub*-suffixes such as *yañ* themselves.

By the very word "āt" [in the sūtra], that [substitute] is referred to by its own term through the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule. Nor should it be argued: "In this case, since [the substitute] is defined by a technical rule (*lakṣaṇika*), how could *yāṭ* apply here? For, regarding the scope of an extended application (*atideśa*), the paribhāṣā concerning "that which is taught by a technical rule versus that which is expressly mentioned" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*) does not operate.
Because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of futility, he therefore explains: "that stem which ends in *ā*.

By the rule—"When a suffix is prescribed after something, that which begins with it and ends with it is understood"—the stem *atikhaṭvā*, for instance, does not end in *ā*; whereas that which does end in *ā*...

The meaning is that because [the condition] "after *haṭ*" does not constitute a grammatical stem (*aṅga*) in that context, the application of the augment *aṭ* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.71) is not triggered here.

Regarding this, the modern scholars (*navyāḥ*) maintain: when there is a mention of an affix (*pratyaya*), there is an inclusion of that which ends with it; thus, by the mention of *ab*, that which ends in *ab* is understood.
Since [the term *ab*] qualifies the stem (*aṅga*) as ending in *ab*—

If it is argued that the aforementioned defect remains unavoidable because of the inclusion of the suffix *tvā* (as in *atikhaṭvāyai*), then let the term *ābanta* be qualified by the word *aṅga*—that is, "an *ābanta* which is an *aṅga*. In this way, they say, not even a trace of the suspicion of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) mentioned before arises. Regarding feminine suffixes, there is the rule of initial application (*tadādiniyama*).

Anticipating the objection that this is not so, he says: "as an upasarjana. The underlying intention is this: by the rule *strīpratyaye cānupasarjane na*, a prohibition of the restriction regarding the initial element (*tadādiniyama*) will be stated for a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) when it is not an *upasarjana*, but not for one that is an *upasarjana*. For this very reason, [in the case of] *paramakārīṣagandhaputra* (the son of one who is supremely fragrant like kārīṣa), there is [the form] *atikārīṣagandhyāputra* (the son of one who is excessively fragrant like kārīṣa).

In this case, the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution does not occur by the rule "there is *saṃprasāraṇa* for *putra* and *pati* in a *tatpuruṣa* after [a stem ending in] *yaṅ*," because in *atikārīṣagandhya*, the final element (*ṣyaṅ*) does not end in a vowel (*ak*). Nor is it the case that, as in the example *ahuśreyasī*, where the subsequent member *reyasī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*...

One might suspect that the elision of the *hal* and following [suffixes] would apply there as well, and consequently, because the latter portion ends in *ṣyaṅ*, there would necessarily be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). However, this is not the case; for according to the rule "there is vocalization of the *ṣyaṅ*-ending prior member when *putra* or *pati* follow as the subsequent members," [the vocalization applies only in those specific instances]. *ṣyaṅḥ...* [etc. (Pāṇini 6.1.13).
Because it will be stated right here [in this very section] under the rule *saṃprasāraṇam*.

(253) *vraścabhrasjasṛjamṛjayajarājabhrajaccchaśāṃ ṣaḥ* | P. 8.2.36. "In place of *ṭa* and *ta*, there is not *ṭha* and *tha*"—thus, in the absence of *dhuṭ*, *ṭa* does not become *ṭha*; but in the case where *dhuṭ* is present, *ta* becomes *tha*.

The analysis is "not so. That is to say, it does not occur. Because [the condition] has not yet become a *ja*-sound (*jaś*), the substitution of *k* for *ṣ* (known as *kutva*) does not take place before the *s*.
(254) *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (Pāṇini 8.2.41).

"Some," namely the author of the *Pariśiṣṭa* and others, [hold this view]. Regarding "nicśu": here, it should be understood that the substitution of *ccha* occurs according to the rule "aśchāeṭa" in certain grammatical systems.
In the case of the words *māṃsa*, *pṛtanā*, and *sānu*, the forms *mām̐s*, *pr̥t*, and *snau* should be stated as optional substitutes before suffixes beginning with *śas*.

In the word *māṃsapṛtanā*, *pṛtanā* means "army. The sense is that [the feminine suffix] *ṭāp* is not applied here because of the exclusion [of such words] by the rule *na striyām*. (255) *ṅiti hrasvaś ca* | Pāṇini 1.4.6.
In the rule *ṅiti hrasvaśca*, the word *vā* is understood from the previous sūtra *ṭhvāmī*. This is an option where there was no prior application;

for while it would not have applied to the two short vowels (*hrasva*), it would have been barred by the prohibition *neyaRu-vāṅ-sthānau* in the case of the other two [long vowels]. Since this rule is initiated, it provides the necessary scope.

The three terms—*iṭhiya*, *ruvaṅsthānau*, and *aṭstrīśabdabhinnau*—are qualifiers of *ī* and *ū*; however, for the short vowels (*hrasvayoḥ*), the qualifier is simply *striyām* (in the feminine), and not extending as far as *nityastrītvam* (being exclusively feminine). Otherwise, [the rule would apply] to words like *iṣu* and *aśani*, which are of both genders.
Even though words such as *paṭu* (clever) and *mṛdu* (soft), which possess all genders, may be feminine, they would not attain the designation of *nadī* (feminine declensional class).

For according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, these lack "constant femininity" (*nityastrītva*), and because the inclusion of the term "constant" (*nitya*) in the rule regarding short vowels serves no purpose, its exclusion cannot be established. Therefore, [the author] has omitted the mention of the word *ākhyā* (designation).
The word "feminine" (*strī*) alone is extracted and connected [to the following]; this is what is stated: "The short vowels *i* and *u* [denote] the feminine. (256) *idudbhyām* | Pāṇini 7.3.117.

Regarding the phrase "when *au* is obtained": the intention is that this [rule] takes precedence due to its posteriority over the rule *ReĀrām*. However, the ancient commentators (*prācaḥ*), having taken the meaning obtainable from the force of the two preceding and following rules—namely *idudbhyām* and *acca gheḥ*—from the sūtra *āṬt* [sic], state: "from those [stems] excluding the technical designations *hi* and *nadī*."
This has been explained. Furthermore, it is inconsistent that the sūtra *ṭhidyubhyām* was not cited here. (257) *tricaturor striyāṃ tisṛcatasṛ* 7.2.99.
Regarding *tricaturor*: since the word *vibhaktau* is understood by being carried over from the preceding rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, he says—*in a case-ending*.

Regarding the phrase "from another [word]": some ask, "What is the purpose of the condition 'in a case-ending'? They cite examples such as *priyabhāryaḥ* and *caturbhārya*. That is weak, because the desired result is established even by the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) according to the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*.
However, since the masculine form does not apply when [the feminine stem] occurs within the group beginning with *priyā*, examples such as *tripriya* should be cited.
The new [rules]: (258) *aci ra ṛtaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.100.
Regarding the phrase "of the substitutes for *guṇa*, *dīrgha*, and *utva*": in the example *tistraḥ tiṣṭhanti*, there is the substitution of *guṇa* by the rule *ṛto ṅī*.

The rule *ratvam* is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the substitution of] *is*. However, in the case of *tisraḥ paśya*, the rule *rathamayaḥ* is an exception to the long vowel resulting from the homogeneous preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). The distinction is that in *priyatisra āgataḥ* and *priyatisraḥ svam*, the rule *ṛta ud* (Pāṇini 6.1.107) applies. Although, according to the principle of "an intermediate exception" (*madhye ’pavādanyāya*), [the latter would apply first].
The substitution of *rat* (the *ṛ*-vowel) for *dīrgha* and *utva* would indeed be an exception (*apavāda*), but not to the *guṇa* [substitution] prescribed by the rule "ṭhṛto ṅī" (Pāṇini 4.1.38).

Nevertheless, the underlying principle is that when one adopts the perspective of considering exceptions as a general class (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*), everything that applies within its own scope is indeed set aside.

(259) *na tisṛcatasṛ* [Pāṇini 6.4.4]. The meaning is that because *tri* and *catur* are mentioned as specific qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), the term *striyām* ("in the feminine") qualifies *tricatur* itself as it is directly heard in the rule, and not the *aṅga* (the nominal stem). For example: *priyāstisraḥ*.

When *priyā jas tri jas* is established, the rule "the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) subverts even internal rules" applies; thus, the elision of the case-ending occurs before the substitution of *tisṛ* has taken place. Once the elision is effected, the subsequent case-ending belonging to the compound is present, and it is in relation to that ending that the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs. Furthermore, by the rule "for *tri*, the masculine form," the word *priyā* [becomes *priya*].

There is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). By the rule *ṛduśanaspurudaṃso’nehasām anaṅ*, the suffix *anaṅ* is applied. Although, under the view that a compound abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārthavṛttipakṣa*), it is difficult for the word *tri-* to denote a female because it is then devoid of meaning, nevertheless, its application to a female should be understood by way of its former state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*).

This is because the established doctrinal maxim, "the *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the subsequent member as its predominant factor," must be interpreted in this very way. Furthermore, according to the view that "the compound functions without abandoning its own meaning" (*ajahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*), the intended sense is expressed by the rule "of *tri* and *catur*, which convey the number residing in three [objects]"; therefore—

In the case of *priyatri* (meaning "one who has three beloveds"), although the word *priyatri* functions as a feminine, there is no occasion for the substitution of *tisṛ* [for *tri*]. The textual passage from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *pratyayottarapadayośca* serves as the authority for the aforementioned explanation. Regarding [the rule being] "non-eternal" (*anityatvāt*), the inclusion of the term *aj* in the sūtra *iko’ci* is the indicative mark (*liṅga*). For instance, in forms such as *bhyām* and *bhis*, even though the augment *num* occurs, the elision of *n* by the rule *allopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* is possible; thus, the mention of *aci* would be redundant.

Nor should it be argued that because of the prohibition "na ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ," elision is impossible in the vocative case, and therefore the condition "acī" (before a vowel) is necessary to prevent an undesired result; for since the vocative case ending is elided by *luk*, the occurrence of *num* (the augment) is impossible there anyway, as the rule "na lumatāṅgasya" prohibits the application of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the influence of an elided suffix) except when that rule's non-eternality (*anityatā*) is invoked. Nor can it be said that the term is intended for subsequent purposes, because if it were needed only later, its inclusion here before "acī" would be redundant.

Regarding the statement "a lumate" (Pāṇini 1.1.63), if the prohibition [of the augment *num*] were considered non-eternal (*anitya*), then the mention of the vowel *a* (*aj-grahaṇa*) would indeed serve as an indicator (*liṅga*) to block the application of *num*—which would otherwise be required by the rule concerning the presence of a case-ending (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*)—in the vocative singular. Furthermore, one should not insist that this non-eternality applies solely to the domain of the vocative singular; for there is no contradiction in accepting it in other instances as well, provided it conforms to the observed forms (*lakṣya*). For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa accepts both forms, *priyatisṛc* and *priyatris*. [The form *priyatisṛc* arises] by applying *num* through a prior exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to the substitution of *ra*. As for the phrase "from the substitution of *ra*": therein...
The commentary (*bhāṣya*) provides the authority for the form *riyatisṛṇī*, stating "riyatisṛṇī, riyatisṛṇī. Regarding such cases as these:

*priyatistre*, *priyātisṛṇe*, *priyatisraḥ*, *priyatisṛṇaḥ*. In the case of the genitive plural suffix *ām*, *num* is applied by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), thereby overriding the substitution of *rā*; and that *num* is further overridden [by the subsequent rule].

By the rule of prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the augment *nuṭ* [is applied]. In *priyatisṛṇām*, since there is no substitution of *at* for *dvi*, the suffix *āP* applies. Furthermore, even though the substitution of *at* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad-* (i.e., *tad-*) is caused by its conjunction with a case-ending (*vibhakti-saṃnipāta-kṛtam*), it nonetheless serves as the cause for the suffix *ṭāP*; this is because the irregular form *ayāsīyauḥ* indicates that the *paribhāṣā* concerning the destruction of a cause (*saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*) is not absolute (*anityatvāt*).
The state [of being feminine].

Regarding the rule "there is no inclusion of the gender-distinct form when a case-ending follows," [it means] because it does not end in an *aṅga* [suffix]. Some here desire the optional *ṅīṣ* by the rule "after a root ending in *ṛ* or *ik*" (*ṛdikārāt*); in their view, however, there is optionally the elision of the *su* [case-ending].

This must indeed be so; for this very reason, Rakṣita maintains that in the case of the forms *vātapramī*, *śrī*, and *lakṣmī*, they are well-formed as words ending in a *ṅī* suffix (*ṅyantāḥ*). Furthermore, the *Dvirūpakośa* states: "The two forms *akṣmī* and *lakṣmī* [denote] the beloved of Hari. (Pāṇini 4.1.3) *striyāḥ* | 6.4.79 | [Translation of the Sūtra: [The substitution of *hrasva* occurs] in place of the long vowel of the word *strī*. (Pāṇini 6.4.79)

Regarding the word *strī*: it is derived from the root *syai* with the suffix *ḍraṭ*, as in "that in which semen and blood coalesce" (*asyāṃ śukra-śoṇite*). By the rule *ope vyoh*, there is the elision of *y*. Because it has the marker *ṭ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. Due to its ending in *ṅī*, the case-ending *su* is elided. (261) *Vāmśasoḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.80. [This sūtra provides for the optional substitution of *am* for the nominative singular *su* and the accusative plural *śas* after words ending in *ṅīp*.]

"Because it is subsequent": this refers to [the rule] *striyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.79). The substitution *iy* occurs before a vowel (*aci*) and not elsewhere. That substitution *iy* which is prescribed for the word *strī* when it is in the masculine gender as an upasarjana, applies only before the four case-endings beginning with *os*, and not elsewhere, because of [the intervention of] *guṇa*, *nābhāva*, and so forth.

The meaning is: "because it is sublated by what was stated previously. Regarding the phrase "those which have *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* as their substitutes": since the term "feminine" (*stryākhyā*) from the rule *yū stryākhyau* is understood to carry over, the expression "those which have *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* as their substitutes" serves as a qualifier for *ī* and *ū*.

Consequently, only those *ī* and *ū* vowels that have *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* as their substitutes are excluded when they do not denote a feminine; however, [other instances of *ī* and *ū*] are not [excluded].
The meaning is "short" (*hrasvau*). Regarding *śrī*: by the rule “*vibvacipracchī-*” etc., there is the suffix *kvip* and lengthening of the vowel;
because it lacks the status of being a stem ending in *ṅī*, there is no elision of the nominative suffix *su*. (Pāṇini 1.4.4) *neyaṅuvaṅsthānāvastrī*.
"Ne-yaṅ-vaṅ-sthānau" means "those two which stand in the place of *i*, *yaṅ*, and *vaṅ*. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*).
Thus, "ne-yaṅ-vaṅ-sthānau" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) meaning "those two which are the locus of *i*, *yaṅ*, and *vaṅ*.
Accordingly, he states the resulting meaning: "those two in which there is the standing (*sthiti*) of *i*, *yaṅ*, and *vaṅ*. Why is the word "locus" (*sthāna*) included?

*Prakṛṣṭā dhīḥ* = *pradhīḥ*. O *pradhi*! Here, because the *yaṇ* [substitution] by the rule *ṭheranekācaḥ* overrides the *iyaṅ*, the prohibition [of the *nadī* designation] by the rule *neyaṅuvaṅsthānau* does not apply. The prohibition of the *nadī* designation applies only where *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are actually produced; however, where it is overridden by an exception (*apavāda*), there [the prohibition does not apply].

The mention of the word "sthāne" (in place of) was indeed made for the purpose of this prohibition; otherwise, one would have simply said "eyRuvaṅ". For from that, the meaning would be obtained as: "the vowels *ī* and *ū*, which are the causes for the substitution of *ey* and *uvaṅ*, are not designated as *nadī*. Why [is it specified] "not when [the word] is not feminine"? [Consider: "he strī" (O woman).

(263) *vāmi* |1|4|5|. Regarding *vāmi*: since the phrases *ṭhyū stryākhyau nadī* and *eyahuvaṅsthānāvastrī* are being carried over [as governing rules], he says "those that stand in the place of *iy* and *uvaṅ*" and so forth. Although the prohibition (*niṣedha*) which was previously established by the word *na* is here made optional (*vikalpita*) by this rule, nevertheless, when a prohibition is made optional, the result is effectively an option regarding the positive injunction (*vidhi*). With the intention that this alone is the appropriate meaning of the sūtra, he says: "they optionally have the designation *nadī*. This is exactly the same in the case of the sūtra *iti hrasvaśca*. As for the word *pradhī*, however...

Because the substitution *iyaṅ* (and *uvaṅ*) subverts the rule for the *ṭhēraneKāCa* suffixes, the prohibition [contained in Pāṇini 1.4.4]—"those having *eyAṅ*, *uVaṅ*, and *sthāna*"—does not apply here. However, with the intention that the prohibition does not apply where the exception (*apavāda*) consisting of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* subverts [the general rule], he explains: "the form is like *lakṣmī*. He will state immediately below the specific distinction regarding the cases *ami* and *śas*. "The form is like the masculine" refers to this difference of opinion, which should be understood as applying when the analysis is either *yasyāḥ prakarṣitā dhīḥ* ("she whose intellect is preeminent") or *prakarṣeṇa dhyāyati* ("she who meditates intensely"). "Like *lakṣmī*" [is the other view].

The phrase "even in the absence of that" (*atadvaye’pi*) is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). Regarding the analysis *suṣṭhu dhīryasyāḥ* (she whose intellect is excellent): one might object that, even if Kaiyaṭa’s view holds that the word *sudhī* lacks inherent femininity, the word *dhī* does possess inherent femininity. Consequently, by the rule *prathamaliṅgagrahaṇaṃ ca*, the word *sudhī* should behave like *śrī* (which retains its feminine form) and not like a masculine. To this they reply: because the technical designation *nadī* is prohibited for the word *dhī* by the rule *neyaRuvaṅsthānāvastrī*, the rule *prathamaliṅgagrahaṇaṃ ca* does not apply to the word *sudhī*; thus it is so.

The phrase "according to Vṛttimat" is consistent with the natural sense [of the text]. "In another opinion" means according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, namely that "it does not denote a different gender. "Just like *śrī*" means that since the word *dhī*, which denotes the intellect (*buddhi*), is eternally feminine, it is "just like *śrī*" in both opinions. (264) *striyāṃ ca* | 7|1|96|. "And in the feminine. This rule is commenced for the sake of meanings other than those ending in *asarvanāmasthāna*. The term "*ṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ*" (P. 7.1.95) carries over. Just as there, so here too, there is an extension of form (*rūpātideśa*). The word "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is taken as a reference to the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*).

Therefore he says: "The word *kroṣṭu* denotes a female," and so forth. And in this way, the substitution of the *tṛj-vat* form is established even in cases such as *pañcakroṣṭrabhiḥ rathaiḥ* ("chariots purchased for five female jackals"). As for those who explain *striyām* as "in the case of a feminine suffix" (*strī-pratyaya*), [they do so] for the sake of the *ṅīṣ* suffix.
The word *kroṣṭu* is recited among the *gaura-ādi* group; for those who hold this view, the feminine suffix *tṛc* would not be established here.

This is because the suffix *ṭhak* in the sense of "bought with that" (*tena krītam*) is elided by the rule *adhyardhapūrva-*, and when a *taddhita* suffix is elided, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is also elided by the rule *luktaddhitaluki*; consequently, since the condition of being followed by a feminine suffix is absent, the application of *tṛc* would fail.
(265) *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* | Pāṇini 4.1.5. *ṛnnebhyo*: *ṛt* means the vowel *ṛ*; *n* means the letter *n*. The plural number is used with reference to usage.
Because it qualifies the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the rule of "ending-in" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. The governing term (*adhikāra*) "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is also carried over.

Regarding this, he says: "from those ending in *tṛ*, etc. As for *kroṣṭrī*: because of the rule "and in the feminine" (*striyāṃ ca*), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied; since the suffix is drawn in by its *aṅga* (stem), the substitution of *tṛjvat* occurs only when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows, and from that, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is understood. As for *bhrūḥ*: [it is derived] as "she wanders," thus *bhrūḥ*.

In the word *subhrūḥ*, the suffix *rūp* is applied to the root *bhram* (to wander). Because it is marked with the indicatory letter *ḍ*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*). Thus we have *he subhrūḥ*. Since the suffix *rūp* is not a feminine suffix (*astrīpratyaya*), the rule *go-striyoḥ* does not apply, and therefore the shortening [of the final vowel] does not occur. Furthermore, because the designation *nadī* is prohibited by the rule *ey-ruvaṅ-sthānau*, the shortening in the vocative case also does not take place.
The sense is "no. He raises an objection, [asking] "How then?"—namely, that the short vowel here is untenable.
It should be understood that even the usage by Kālidāsa in the verse, "O fair-browed one, whence this disrespect in the father's house? is likewise untenable. [He says] "many."

Keçutu—[they] resolved [the difficulty] by carrying over the word "vā" from the rule "vāmī" and by assuming a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) in the rule *kecutu-aṅi*. That is incorrect; for if that were the case, the mention of "a" here and the subsequent rule *vāmī* would both be redundant.
For it would have been possible simply to say "ṭhveyaRuvaṅsthānau. Others, however, somehow justify this by saying that "the neuter is used for the general category" (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*).
(266) *ekājutarapade ṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.4.12. [When the second member of a compound consists of a single vowel, the substitute *ṇa* takes the place of the final *i* or *ī* of the first member.]

"Ekāc" means that which has one vowel (ekam ac). That which has such [a root] is "ekāc. The term "ekāj-uttarapada" is a *bahuvrīhi* containing within it another *bahuvrīhi*: that whose subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is a word consisting of a single vowel. The word "uttarapada" is a conventional term for a constituent member of a compound; by this [word], the compound itself is implied and thus qualified.

Thus he says: "In that month. Although the word "ṇa" is understood from the rule "ṛṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ," he states "by the force of the initial formulation" (ārambhasāmarthyāt), anticipating the objection that the explicit mention of "ṇa" here is necessary for the sake of making the rule obligatory.

The meaning is that, because the substitution of *ṇ* is established by the option [provided] in the rule "and in the case of *ratipadika*, *anta*, *nu*, and *vibhakti*," the force of this present rule's commencement [is such]. As for "svayaṃbhūḥ" being treated like a masculine:
since the designation *nadī* is absent in both systems, rules such as "before a *ṅit* suffix, there is a short vowel" do not apply.
This is the intended meaning.
(267) *na ṣaṭsvastrādibhyaḥ* |4|1|10|. "That which was prescribed for the feminine does not apply [to these].
*na ṣaṭsvastrādibhyaḥ*. "That which was stated regarding the feminine does not occur."

With the intention that, following the previous explanation, not only the suffix *ṅīp* but also the separated suffix *ṭāp* is prohibited, he says: “*ṅīṣ-ṭāp-au na*” (neither *ṅīṣ* nor *ṭāp*). For the words beginning with *svasṛ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applicable;

for those designated as *ṣaṭ* (the numerals six and so on), both are applicable. [The examples are] *svasā* and *tisraḥ*; [in the latter case], by the rule “*na tisṛcatasṛ*” [before the *nām* ending].

In the *Ṛnmejantaḥ* sūtra, Kaiyaṭa states that since the absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is already established by the very indicator (*jñāpaka*) that prohibits lengthening, the inclusion of the words *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* in the *svasrādi* group need not have been made. Regarding *svasā*: [it is derived] from the root *avas* with the suffix *ṛn*. By the rule *ṛduśanaspurudaṃso’nehasām ca*, *anaṅ* is applied. [The feminine form] *svasā* is thus formed. However, *anāndā* is indeed *svasā*.
"Women belonging to the group of brothers should be [mutually] non-seizable by one another.

Regarding the word *dyauḥ*: it is derived from the root *div* with the suffix *ḍoḥ*; due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), it is also formed from *dyut*. Because the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*).
Due to the status of being treated as having the augment *ṇi* (by the rule "ṭhoto ṇiḥ"), there is vṛddhi [of the vowel]. Regarding the word *rāḥ*: although it is masculine...
This word is exclusively masculine, because Amarasimha states that "rāḥ" means wealth, property, or power (*artharaivibhava*).
This is because he has established the rule that there is no *dvandva* compound of words with different genders;
nevertheless, Kṣīrasvāmin [mentions] its feminine gender in the passage: "Some say it is feminine: 'ātyenaṃ rāḥ'."
This was stated even by way of concession, namely, "like *nau* and *glau*. [The suffix] *ṅai* is applied after the roots *lā* and *nud* by the rule *lānudibhyāṃ ṅaiḥ*.
Due to the *ḍi*-marker, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion. Amarasimha states: "In the feminine, *nauḥ*, *taraṇiḥ*, and *tarī*.
From this [root], [the suffix] *am* is applied by Pāṇini 7.1.24 (*ato'm*).

Now follow the neuter stems ending in vowels. Regarding the rule *ato'm*: the term *ataḥ* is a qualifier of the *aṅga* (stem) under discussion, and the phrase *napuṃsakāt* from the previous rule (*vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*) is understood to carry over;
with this intention, he says "from an *aṅga* ending in *at*" and so forth. The meaning is: "from an *aṅga* ending in the letter *a*."

Regarding *svamoḥ*: the prescription of *am* is for the purpose of subverting the elision (*luk*) that would otherwise apply by the rule *vamor napuṃsakāt*. Regarding *amsyāt*: although one might analyze [the rule] as *ām* followed by *it*, once *ām* has been applied, the rule *upi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.102) would not apply due to the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* (the technical principle that a grammatical operation caused by a specific configuration does not apply when that configuration is destroyed), and thus the form would be *añānam*.

The form *rūpam* is established as follows: in the second case singular (*dvitīyaikavacana*), when the letter *a* of the suffix is replaced by *m* according to the rule *ṭhādeḥ parasya*, the final *m* is elided by the rule *saṃyogāntalopaḥ*; thus the desired form is achieved. Nevertheless, this has been explained with the intention that the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopaḥ*) applies only to a *jhal* (consonant) sound.
As for what they say— that if one does not divide the word as *ṭha-am*, the form *ṭhatijirasam* would not be established—

that is due to haste; for when *su* is replaced by *am*, the substitution of *jaras* does not apply by virtue of the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*, and thus it is precisely the form *ṭhatijara* that is desired.

In the second singular case, however, the rule *ato ’m* (Pāṇini 7.1.24) is superseded by *jaras* (Pāṇini 7.2.101) because it is subsequent; since the *liṅgaviśeṣa-paribhāṣā* (the technical rule regarding the non-application of a grammatical operation when its cause is destroyed) prevents the application of the *luk*-elision, the form *atijarasam* is established. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Regarding *jñānam*: *jñaptiḥ* is *jñānam*; the suffix *lyuṭ* [is applied].
By the rule *ṭhyuvoranākau*, [the suffixes] *na* and *aka* are substituted for *yu* and *vu*; then, because it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the case endings beginning with *su* arise.

Regarding *halmātra*: when the form *he jñāna su* is established, since the substitution of *am* (for *su*) takes effect later than the elision of the vocative marker (*saṃbuddhi-lopa*), and after that *am* has been applied, by the principle of "treating the preceding as the end" (*antavadbhāva*), the base (*aṅga*) comes to have a short vowel at its end.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is elision of the letter *m* connected with the perfective suffix (*saṃbuddhi*).

(269) *napuṃsakācca* | Pāṇini 7.1.19. [The word] "from the neuter" (*napuṃsakāt*) [is understood]. From the rule *'asaḥ śī'*, *'ṭāṅasiṅasām'*, and *'āṅi cāpaḥ'*, [the words] *'ī'*, *'ṭā'*, and *'ṅasi'*, *'ṅas'* [are understood].
Intending to show that [the rule] also follows, he says "of what comes after a klība," and so forth.
(270) *yasyeti ca* | Pāṇini 6.4.148. Regarding *yasya*: *ya* consists of *i* and *a*; [the word is] *yasya*. He explains this as "of the vowels *i* and *a*" (*ivarṇāvarṇayoḥ*).

Regarding the phrase “*ṭhīti ce*” (if it is said “after *ṭh*”), the word *taddhita* is drawn forward by the particle *ca* from the rule “*āsta ddhite*” (P. 7.3.44). Thus he says: “and after *ī*, when a *taddhita* [suffix follows]. The feminine gender in the expression “*āṬṅḥ śyām*” is used in view of the case endings (*vibhakti*). This statement need not have been made; for [the desired forms are obtained] by the rule “*vibhāṣā*... (P. 7.3.44).
From the rule *ṅśyo’i*, the word *yām* is understood from the context; from the rule *asaṃyogāt*, the word *e* is also understood.

In that case as well, only the connection [of these words] must be made: "there is elision (*lopa*) of that [vowel] which occurs before an affix containing *ī* (īkāra) or a *taddhita* affix, but not before a feminine suffix (*śyām*)," according to the grammatical tradition (*ākara*).

(271) *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.20. Regarding *jaśśasoḥ*: because of its association (*sāhacarya*) with *jas*, only the *śas* that belongs to the nominal suffixes (*sub*) is understood here. Therefore, it does not apply here: *kuṇḍaśo dadāti* ("he gives by the pot").
(272) *śi* is a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix]. The use of this great technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is for the sake of following the tradition of the ancient teachers.
(273) [The substitution of] *Num* occurs after a neuter stem ending in a consonant (*jhal*) or a vowel (*ac*).

Regarding the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*: the term *num* is understood from the previous rule *ṭhidito num dhātoḥ*; the term *arvanāmasthāne* is understood from the rule *ugidacām*; and the governing heading *aṅgasya* (of the stem) is also understood. Thus, the neuter stem is qualified by both *jhal* and *ac*.
And because a rule applies to that which ends with [the element specified by] a qualifier, he says "of that which ends in *jhal*" (*jhalantasya*), etc.

(274) *adḍ ḍatarādibhyaḥ pañcabhyaḥ* |7|1|25|. [The sūtra states: "The suffix *adḍ* [is applied] after the five beginning with *itarāt*. Why "after the five"? [Consider: *nemaṃ tiṣṭhati* ("he stands here"), *nemaṃ paśya* ("look here").
The words beginning with *itará-* are listed among the *sarvanāman* (pronominals) in the rule "atara-ḍatama-etara-anyatara.
[In this context,] there should be the substitution of *adḍ*. The retroflexion (*ṣṭutva*) has not been applied here for the purpose of indicating the actual form of the desired substitute.

(275) *ṭeḥ* | 6|4|43|. From the rule *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvaṃ-lṅkṣvanyatarasyām* [P. 8.3.78], the term *ṅti* is understood as anuvṛtti, and *hasya* is also governed by context. Thus it says: "when a ṅit suffix follows, of the bha-stem. Why say "of the bha-stem"? Consider *pañcamaḥ*. Here...

When *ḍaṭ* is applied, because the augment *maṭ* occurs, the status of being a *bha* is absent; therefore, the elision of *ṭi* does not take place. Instead, due to the status of being a *pada*, there is only the elision of *n*. He states the purpose of making *adḍ* a *ḍit* suffix with the words "because *ṭi* has been elided," and so forth. [He asks: But surely, this is for the sake of preventing the long vowel by homogeneous substitution (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*)?

Anticipating the objection that "let only the substitution of *dā* be made; what is the use of [the word] *aj-ādi* (beginning with a vowel)? he says: "eṅ hrasvāt," etc. The intention is that if the substitution of *dā* were applied, [the form] would be "he katare. As for the word *anyatama*, however... and thus.

The sense is that usages such as *āmānyādiṣvanyatamatamaḥ* are merely due to negligence (*prāmādikā*). A prohibition [of the suffix] after *ekātara-* must be stated. Regarding *ajaram*: that of which aging (*jarā*) does not exist.
By the rule *ostriyoḥ*, there is shortening of the feminine stem in the upasarjana, and then *ataḥ am*. [The objection] "because it is subsequent" refers to [the application of] *ajara-*.

When *śī* is established, although the augment *num*— characterized by having a stem ending in a vowel (*ajanta*) according to the rule "for neuter stems ending in a consonant or a vowel" (*apuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*)— would indeed apply even before the substitution of *jaras*, that *num* is part of the stem (*aṅgabhakta*) and thus would not obstruct the stem itself; however, it certainly acts as an obstruction for the constituent element *jarā*.

An injunction being prescribed for that which is being pointed out does not apply; nevertheless, according to one's own view, by accepting the principle that "the *it* (*it*) following the final vowel shall be a constituent part of that very [vowel]"—
wherein a constituent of a constituent is also a constituent of the whole— [the rule holds].

The point is that even if, by some means, the substitution of *jaras* occurs, the long vowel [of the genitive ending] prescribed by the rule "āṇ nady-āḥ" would not apply because the word would lack a final *ān*; therefore, the rule "āṇ mahataḥ saṃyogasya" [is required]. (276) [The rule: "After a word ending in *ān*, and after *mahat*, the genitive ending is *āṇ* when followed by a consonant cluster. 6.4.10.
Regarding the rule *sānta-mahataḥ*: here, the phrases *upadhāyāḥ* and *sarvanāmasthāne cāsaṃbuddhau* are understood to carry over. In the word *ante*, the genitive case ending is elided;
it stands in apposition with [the word *yaṇ*] from the rule *saṃyogāntasya*.

He explains [the rule] beginning with "of that which has a final consonant cluster" (sāntasaṃyogasya), etc. "Of its penultimate vowel" (tasyopadhāyāḥ) means "of that which precedes it. "In the case of *am*, this is an exception to elision" (ami luko’pavādaḥ), etc.
By this, the statement of the ancients—"only after the substitution of *am* for the dual endings *vas* and *as*, optionally *jara*"—is refuted.

*Māṃspacanyām* means "in that which meat is cooked"; *pacanī* [is derived from] the root *pac* with the suffix *lyuṭ* according to the rule *araṇādhikaraṇayośca*. Because it has the marker *ṭ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied, resulting in *māṃsasya pacanī = māṃspacanī*. Here, since the genitive case ending (*ṅsi*) is elided by *luk*, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix) does not apply; therefore, without the inclusion of the word *prabhṛti* (beginning with) in the rule, the suffix would have to be treated as having the sense of "type" (*prakāra*).

The intention is that the substitution of *āṃs* for the word *māṃsa* would not be established. Now, one might object: since it will be stated in the *pṛṣodarādi* rule that "for *āṃsa*, [the substitute is applied] before *pac*, *yu*, and *ghan*," this form is also established through the elision of the final syllable (*antyalopa*). To this, [the author replies:]...

On this point, they say: since the rule "pṛṣṭhodarādīni yathopadiṣṭam" (Pāṇini 6.1.105) falls under the governing heading of "the subsequent member of the compound" (uttarapadādhikāra), the elision of the final vowel would apply only where the subsequent member ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*, as in examples such as "āṃspacanam. For in this case—
The subsequent member [of the compound] ends in *rūp* (the suffix *-ru*), but not in *lyuṭ*; therefore, there is no elision of the final vowel here.

Regarding the rule *māsaś chandasi*: the meaning of the Vārttika is that "the letter *t* shall replace the word *mās* before an affix beginning with *bh*, in the Vedic language. An example is: *ādbhiḥ śaradbhir durodaraṃ tava*.

(277) *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* | 1|2|47|. "Short vowel in the neuter. Here, by virtue of the mention of "short" (*hrasva*), the term "vowel" (*ac*) which is present [in the mind] serves as a qualifier for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); thus, by the rule of "having that as its final member" (*tadantavidhi*), he says: "of that which ends in a vowel" (*ajantasya*).

If, however, one were to explain *prātipadikasya* as being in a different grammatical relation (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) with *acaḥ*, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *uvāg brāhmaṇakulam*. This point has been clarified by us in the very rule *ṭhacaś ca*. Why [is it said] "of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikasya*)? [Consider: *kāṇḍe*.
In *kuṇḍale*, *jñānavati*, *śrīpāṇi*, and so forth, the specific distinction is the application of the rule for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) by the rule *ekājuttarapade*.

In *śrīpeṇa*, after the substitution of *īn* has occurred and the *guṇa* replacement (*e*) is applied, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the end of the preceding element; consequently, according to the rule *acaḥ parasmin*, a grammatical operation from the preceding element applies.

Regarding "the previous rule": by resorting to the analysis of the compound as a *pañcamī* (ablative) tatpuruṣa, or because of the status of being *sthānivadbhāva*, since there exists a single-vowel (*ekāj*) following member (*uttarapada*), the substitution of *ṇa* would indeed occur. Regarding "the principle of *saṃnipāta*":

how could the substitution of *ya* (for *yavakrīta*), which was effected by depending upon the vowel *a*, serve as the cause for the elision of that very vowel *a*? Nor does [the rule] "upi ca" apply.

It must be stated that the acceptance of the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the technical rule regarding the combination of vowels (*saṃnipātaparibhāṣā*) for the sake of lengthening is indeed necessary;

for although its non-eternality is accepted in the case of the prescription of lengthening—as evidenced by the citation "aṣṭāya"—it is not accepted when the elision of the vowel *a* (*avarṇalopa*) is to be effected. Even if [the rule were applied],...
The direction is this: because the universal *atva* does not disappear even when the manifestation of shortness (*hrasvatva*) disappears in the case of the long vowel.
By this, the explanation of some who claim that the word *rīp* [is formed] from the root *rī* with the suffix *ṅyi* to denote beauty (*śrītye*) is refuted.
(278) *svamornapuṃsakāt* | Pāṇini 7.1.23.

The suffix *su* and the case-ending *am* following a neuter noun undergo elision (*luk*) by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), thereby setting aside both the substitution of *at* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad-* and the substitution of *ka-* for *kim*. For if, due to its higher status (*paratva*), the substitution of *at* for *tyad-* were applied first, and the *su* were replaced by *am* according to the rule "of *adas* and *su*" (*adoḥ su-...*), the form would result in *aṃ kulam*; however, what is desired is *tat kulam*.

(279) *iko’ci vibhaktau* |7|1|73|. [The rule] "iko’ci": what is meant by "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*)? [Consider: *madhu* means wine; its derivative is *mādhava*. Here, if the augment *num* were applied, there would be elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*).
The *num* augment occurs by way of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) against the rules for *vṛddhi*, *au*-vocalization, the treatment as *tṛj-vat*, and *guṇa*.

Regarding "vṛddhy-autva": in the case of *sakhinī* (from *sakhi*), *vṛddhi* would have been required by the rule *akhyurasambuddhau*; however, in the case of *vāriṇī*, *au*-vocalization would have been required by the rule *acca gher*.

In examples such as *riyakroṣṭūn*, the substitution of the form of the suffix *tṛc* (*tṛjvadbhāva*) would otherwise apply. Now, one might ask: what is the difference between the augment *num* and the augment *ruṭ*? To this he says: "By [the rule] *nāmī*, there is lengthening. The meaning is that because *num* is a part of the stem (*aṅgabhakta*), when it is present, lengthening would not occur.

(280) *Tṛtīyādiṣu bhāṣitapuṃskaṃ puvad gālavasya* [Pāṇini 7.1.74]. Regarding the phrase "in the case of the third case endings and those following": if it were understood here that a word is *bhāṣitapuṃska* (having a masculine counterpart) simply because a masculine form has been uttered for it by that word, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *īlune*. Therefore...

He explains: "when the cause of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is identical. This is the intended meaning: that which has been spoken as masculine in a certain sense is the "masculine-mentioned" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) cause of application; because it possesses that [cause], the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for the *arśa-ādi* group.
Thus, when there is identity in the cause of application, [the word] is one that has been spoken as masculine.

"That which is the nature of the word [ending] in *ś* is elided. Because the term *aci* is carried over from the rule "iko ’ci vibhaktau," he says: "before a case-ending beginning with *t* when followed by a vowel (*aci*). What if it ends in an *ik*? *somapena kulena*.
What if it is not a vowel (*aci*)? *grāmaṇibhyāṃ kulābhyām*. What if it does not begin with a *t*?

"Beginningless" (*anādinī*); "beginningless" (*anādīni*). "Its fruit" (*tatphalam*): the fruit of the *pīlu* tree is a *pīlu*. [The suffix] *orañ* is elided by the rule "the elision of *orañ* after *hal*" (*hale luk*). "Because of the difference in the grounds for application" (*pravṛtinimittabhedāt*): for indeed, the ground for the application of the word *pīlu* is the genus (*jāti*) subsumed under "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) when referring to the tree, whereas in the case of the fruit...

The meaning is that, whether it be a genus not coextensive with its fruit (*phalatvāvyāpyajāti*) or the state of originating from a specific type of tree, in either case there is no single basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) common to both the masculine and neuter genders. (281) *asthidadhisakthyakṣṇām anaṅ udāttaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.75.
In the case of *asthi* and *dadhi*, when the augment *num* would otherwise apply by the rule *ṭhiko’ci*, this [present] rule is prescribed.

The letter *a* after the *n* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). The letter *ṅ*, however, is for the sake of substituting it for the final letter (*antādeśārtha*). By the *phiṭ-sūtra* "abviṣayasyānisantasya," these words beginning with *asthi* have their first syllable acute (*ādyaudātāḥ*). In that context, there is the low-pitched (*anudāta*) vowel *i* at the end.

Since the *anaṅ* substitute being prescribed would be unaccented according to the rule "that which is not the nearest [substitute] is unaccented," it is stated that it is accented. This accentuation is evident in cases such as *masthani* and *dadhani* under the view that there is no elision (*allopābhāva*); however, in cases such as *adhnā* and *dadhne*, where the vowel *i* of *anaṅ* is elided, the rule "and of the unaccented [vowel]" applies.

It should be understood that where there is elision of an udātta vowel, the purpose [of this rule] is to provide for the udātta accent of the case-ending by means of the *anudātta-nivṛtti-svara* (the accent replacing an anudātta). The words "in the third cases" (*tṛtīyāsu*) and "before a vowel" (*aci*) are carried over [from previous rules];

thus he says: "before a case-ending beginning with /ṭ/ and before a vowel. What is the purpose of "before a case-ending beginning with /ṭ/"? [Consider the forms] *dadhinī*, *dadhīni*. What is the purpose of "before a vowel"? [Consider the form] *dadhibhiḥ*.
*dadhibhyām*. [The rule] applies even to that which ends in it; the intention is that this is because it is part of a *prakṛti* (stem). *Atidadhna*:
the meaning is "by one who has surpassed the curd. Even in the feminine form, it remains *atidadhnā* alone, by virtue of both the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* and the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*.

Because the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply. However, the Eastern grammarians have stated: "by a Brāhmaṇa who has *priya-dadhi*. Furthermore, some have even stated that in the feminine, forms such as *priyadadhnyā* and *priyadadhnyai* occur. That is incorrect;
because the word *dadhi* is listed among the *uraḥ-prabhṛti* group, the suffix *kap* necessarily applies in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, resulting in *anaṅ*.

Because there is no possibility of application; for, by the two previously mentioned *paribhāṣās*, the occurrence of the suffix *ṅīp* is rendered impossible. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Regarding *sudhinī*: by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), the *iyaṅ* substitution is superseded by the *num* augment. Regarding *sudhiyā*:
the state of possessing excellent knowledge (*śobhanajñānavattva*) is the sole basis for the application (*pravṛtinimitta*) in both the masculine and neuter genders.

Because it is a word that has already expressed the masculine gender (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), when the option of treating it as masculine applies by the rule *ṛtīyādiṣu*, there is an absence of the augment *num*; furthermore, because the prohibition of *yaṇ* by the rule *na bhūsudhiyoḥ* applies, the substitution *iy-aṅ* occurs. Thus, we have *pradhyeti*. Here too, the state of possessing excellent knowledge is one and the same for both the masculine and the neuter.

Because it is a word that has already expressed the masculine gender (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), it follows the rule *tṛtīyādiṣv* [Pāṇini 7.1.94] and takes the masculine form (*puṃvat*) in the third case and onwards; however, it should be understood that in the neuter form, the augment *num* is applied. In the example "the family which has many *śreyasī*s" (*bahuśreyasī kulam*), the neuter short vowel does not apply, because of the specific prohibition: "there is no shortening for the suffix *īyasun* in a *bahuvrīhi* compound."

Some say [the prohibition applies] because of the general prohibition. Others, however, maintain that only the shortening of the *upasarjana* (secondary member) is prohibited, whereas the neuter shortening (*napuṃsakahrasvatvam*) would indeed still occur; thus they cite "ahuśreyasi" and "bahuśreyasini. Regarding "madhu": "madhu" refers to intoxicating drink and flower-nectar; "madhu" also refers to the spring season and the month of Caitra. Here [in this context].
In the case of masculine and neuter [nouns], there is no single basis for their application;

rather, [the bases] such as *madyatva* (liquor-ness) and *vasantatva* (spring-ness) are each distinct. Consequently, because they lack the quality of having been previously expressed as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃskatva*), the forms are simply *madhune*, *madhunaḥ*, and *madhunaḥ*.
But it is not [the case] in forms such as *adhave* or *iṣmadhaḥ*; this is the general direction. Regarding the phrase *snur veti*:

the intention is that this is based on the statement in the Vārttika, *āṃsapṛtanāsānūnām*. The word *sānu* has both genders, as seen in the statement *truḥ prasthaḥ sānur astriyām*; when it is neuter...
He states the forms for the neuter: *snūni* and *sānūni*. In the masculine, however, they are *snūn* and *sānūn*, and so forth.

Regarding *sulvā*: since the quality of being an excellent cutter (*lavana*) is identical for both the masculine and the neuter, it is considered a word that has been "spoken as masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*).
Consequently, in the alternative where the masculine form is applied, there is an absence of the *num* augment; thus, by the rule *ṭhoḥ supi*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs.

Regarding *suluneti*: because it is subsequent (*paratvāt*), *num* replaces [the final vowel] by overriding *yaṇ*. Regarding *dhātrī*: since the capacity to sustain and nourish is one and the same for both the masculine and the neuter, *yaṇ* occurs in the case where the masculine form is applied.

(282) *eca igghrasvādeśe* | Pāṇini 1.1.48. [This sūtra states: When a short vowel (*hrasva*) is substituted for an *ec* vowel, that short vowel is treated as being of the same class (*ik*) as the original *ec*.

*Ecaḥ*: that which is enjoined (*ādiśyate*) is an *ādeśa* (substitute); being both short (*hrasva*) and an *ādeśa*, it is a "short substitute" (*hrasvādeśa*). The locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdharaṇe*), and the singular number is used generically; thus, he explains: "among the short vowels that are being enjoined.
The first part of the *ec* sounds resembles the vowel *a*, while the latter part resembles the *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels.

In that case, since there is no short vowel among the two internal [substitutes], both the letter *a* and the letters *i* and *u* would occur by way of alternation. Therefore, with the intention that this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) serves as a restrictive injunction so that the letter *a* never occurs, he says: "it must be only an *iK*."
Due to proximity (*āntaratamya*), *i* is substituted for *a* and *u*, while *u* is substituted for *o* and *au*.

An example of the exclusive case (*ekānta*) is: "he by whom [the Lord] is remembered is 'smṛtaḥ'"; "that which has a beautiful memory is 'susmṛtiḥ'," and so forth. However, this technical rule (*paribhāṣāsūtra*) is meaningless.

And so it has been stated by the author of the Vārttika: "The [substitution of] *eṅ* is established because of being a common place of articulation (*sasthānatva*), and that of *aic* because of the greater number of subsequent [elements]. The meaning of this is as follows: by the rule of "the later [prohibition] regarding words" (*śabdapara-vipratiṣedha*), it is established that, due to proximity (*āntaratamya*), only the *i*- and *u*-sounds [are substituted for *ai* and *au* respectively]. In the phrase "and of *aic*" (*aicoca*), the particle *ca*...

The sequence [of the words] is inverted; one should understand that the reason for this is "because of the greater number of subsequent parts. [For example: the *ardhamātrā* (half-mora) belongs to the vowel *a*, while the *adhyardhamātrā* (one and a half moras) belongs to the vowels *i* and *u*; thus, due to the excess of the subsequent part, it is like the village of Mallas being [called] after the majority.

The [short] *i* and *u* vowels will also occur by way of designation (*vyapadeśena*). As in the example *pradyumnā*. Now, since the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—such as "possessing an excellent heaven" (*prakṛṣṭasvargavattva*)—is the same for both the masculine and the neuter, there is optionally the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) here because it has been spoken with a masculine gender (*bhāṣitapuṃska*).

Anticipating the objection that this might indeed be the case, he says: "if it ends in -i. This has been clarified by Mādhava under the root *rā* (in the sense of "giving") in the context of the passage beginning with "here, a family of Brāhmaṇas. How then is it that the Easterners have cited *radyavā*, *prarāyā*, and *sunāve* as examples?

If they say here: because the basis for the application [of the word] is the same—namely, the state of having *prakarṣa* (excellence) and so forth—the word *sudyu* is one whose masculine form has been mentioned (*bhāṣitapuṃska*); that very same word is now an *iganta* (ending in an *ik* vowel). And likewise, the word *pradyu* is also indeed *bhāṣitapuṃska*, because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]; therefore, there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).

It becomes [thus]. And in this way, it should be understood that according to Mādhava’s opinion, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur for neuter words ending in *ej* (e, ai, o), whereas according to other opinions, it does occur. Regarding *prarī*: that whose excellent *rā* (splendor) it possesses is "rari"; that whose beautiful *nau* (boat) it possesses is "sunu"—so it is stated in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
Neuter stems ending in vowels.

(815) *alug uttarapade* [Pāṇini 6.3.1]: "The non-elision (*aluK*) [of the case-ending] occurs when there is a following word. This is a prohibitive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). It refers to that which was previously applicable by the rule *supo dhātv...* [Pāṇini 2.4.71].
The meaning is that it becomes a *luṅga* (neuter).
(816) *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ* |6|3|2|. [Examples: *stokānmuktaḥ*. The purpose of forming a compound is the formation of a single word (*ekapadya*) and a single accent (*eka-svaratva*).

Furthermore, there is the absence of the application of specific [suffixes]. Moreover, another purpose is the derivation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) from a collective compound, as in: "the offspring of one who is slightly liberated" (*stokānmuktasyāpatyam*), "slight liberation" (*stokānmuktiḥ*), or "the wife of one who is slightly liberated" (*stokānmukteyaḥ*). Nor [is this purpose achieved] by the prohibition of the elision (*luk*) of the initial case-ending in a compound.

One might suspect that because its purpose has been fulfilled, the elision (*luk*) caused by that secondary suffix (*taddhita*) would be unavoidable; however, this is not so, because since the rule *supo dhātu* is a single rule, it is accepted that the elision of both types [of suffixes] is prohibited without distinction. In this context, only those [words] read in the rules for compound formation (*samāsa-śāstra*), such as *stoka* and *antika*, [are intended].

The words *stoka* and so forth are understood here, and not those mentioned in the rule *karaṇe ca stokālpakṛcchre*; for when the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) would otherwise have occurred in a compound, the rule prescribing non-elision (*aluk*) brings to mind those words listed in the rules for compounds without delay, and this is due to the maxim of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*).

For in the rule *stokāntika*, because the term "meaning" (*artha*) is employed, many other instances are also included. Keeping this in mind, he says: "In this way. However, a compound of words ending in the dual or plural numbers is not desired, due to the absence of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*). Therefore, in cases such as *stokābhyāṃ muktaḥ* ("released by two small [amounts]"), there is only a sentence (*vākya*).
The term *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* must be added [to the list]. Regarding the word *śastrāṇi* (recitations):

according to the ritualists (*yājñika*), a *stotra* is a praise consisting of the expression of qualities residing in a substratum, accomplished by means of chanted mantras; whereas a *śastra* is the expression of qualities residing in a substratum, accomplished by means of unchanted mantras.
Usage: (817) *ojaḥ-saho-ambhas-tamasa-stṛtīyāyāḥ* | P. 2.1.30.

[The words] *ojas*, *sahas*, [and *ambhas* and *tamas*] [form a compound with a word ending in] the third case-ending. *Ojasā kṛtam* ("done by force"). This is a compound formed by the rule *kartṛ-karaṇe kṛtā bahulam* (P. 2.1.32). How [is this so]?...
"In that case, how is one to explain Bhāravi’s statement: 'tarhi satatanaiśatamovṛtamanyataḥ'? To this they reply:

from the root *vṛt* in the sense of "turning" (*vartane*), by the rule "the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of *ghañ*" (*ghañ-arthe ka-vidhānam*), the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).

Since a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) is then formed with that [derivative noun] ending in *ka*, there is no fault. As for the fact that [the rule] occurs only under the heading of "simple words" (*kevala-pada-adhikāra*)...

The rule regarding substitution at the end of a word (*tadanta-vidhi*) does not apply within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*).
