Thus, it is stated in the *Durghaṭavṛtti* that in the case of *naitaśatamasā*, the elision (*aluk*) of the third-case ending does not occur. That is not correct; for in the context of the headings concerning "words" (*pada*) and "bases" (*aṅga*), [we find examples such as] *iṣṭakacitam* and *pakveṣṭakacitam*.

Because of the examples cited in the Bhāṣya, the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with a specified element) applies even when there is an adhikāra (governing heading) regarding a subsequent member (*uttarapada*).
This is seen in the cases *puṃsānujaḥ* ("younger brother by a male") and *januṣāndhaḥ* ("blind from birth"). Regarding *januṣā*:
Amara states that *janu*, *janana*, and *janman* are synonyms for "birth."

(818) *ātmanaśca* |5|3|6|. [The compound] *ātmanāpañcamaḥ* [is formed]. The compound is possible through the splitting (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule for the third case. Some say that here, by virtue of being included in the group beginning with *prakṛti*, the third case is used in the sense of the first case; thus, it means "he who is the fifth by himself. *Ātmanā kṛtaḥ pañcamaḥ*.
Others hold that it [the suffix] depends on the action of "making" (karoti-kriyā).

It should be stated as "pūraṇa" (a filler/numeral); it should be understood as a *bahuvrīhi*. The sense is that even in the case of a single entity, one must intend to express both its status as the meaning of the constituent member (*vartipadārthatva*) and its status as the meaning of the whole compound (*anyapadārthatva*), by postulating a distinction based on limiting conditions (*aupādhika-bheda*).

(819) *vaiyākaraṇākhyāyāṃ caturthyāḥ* |6|3|7|. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after a word ending in the fourth case (*caturthī*), provided that it is a name for a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇākhyā*). [Example: *vaiyākaraṇī*. [Derivation: "That which exists in grammar" (*vyākaraṇe bhavā*) is *vaiyākaraṇī*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *aṇṛgayanādibhyaḥ*. This is a *karmadhāraya* compound: "that which is both this [suffix *aṇ*] and a name. [The rule applies] only when [the word] refers to "oneself" (*ātmanaḥ*). Here, [the example is] *ātmanaḥ*.

They say that if one does not follow this [interpretation] and instead explains the rule as "there is no *aluk* in the designation *vaiyākaraṇa* when it is in the dative case," then the subsequent sūtra, *parasya ca*, could have been omitted. Regarding the term *ātmanebhāṣā*:
although this designation does not exist in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, the intention is that it exists in the *Dhātupāṭha*.

Anticipating the objection that there should be no compound—just as one does not say "the pot for cooking" (*randhanāya sthālī*) because of the absence of the relationship between material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*)—he says: "Because of the division of the rule" (*yogavibhāgāt*).
Here, the compound is easily justified even by the force of the rule prescribing the non-elision of the case-ending (*aluk-vidhi*).
(820) And also [the word] *para*. 6|3|8. And also [the word] *para*: the fourth case ending of the word *para* shall not be elided when it forms part of a name for a grammarian.

(821) *gaviyudhibhyāṃ sthiraḥ* | 8|3|95|. Regarding *gaviyudhi*: this word *sthira* is derived from the root *sthā* with the *kirac* suffix belonging to the *ajira-śiśira-* group of Uṇādi derivatives. Since the prohibition [of doubling] by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* would otherwise apply, [the following sūtra is stated].

This is the commencement of the statement: "By the word *gavi* itself. Nor should it be argued that, by overriding *luk*, the substitution of *ā* (for *i*) occurs because it is subsequent (*aparatva*) and internal (*antaraṅga*), and thus the non-elision (*aluk*) is established by the rule *haladantāt saptamyāḥ*;
for [the rule] *antaragān api vidhīn*...
The meaning is that elision (*luk*) is stronger because it subverts what is external (*bahir-aṅga*).
[The rule] *hṛddyubhyāṃ ca* [is illustrated by] *hṛdispṛk*, *divispṛk*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which touches the heart (*hṛdayam*) and the sky (*divam*)" [respectively].
Due to the force of the rule prescribing non-elision (*aluk*), the locative case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Or, it may be due to the intention to express the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) of the action.
(822) *Kāranāmni ca prācāṃ halādau* [Pāṇini 6.3.10]: "In the case of the names of tools used by the Easterners, when beginning with a consonant.
*Avikaṭoraṇaḥ*: "A sheep-pen"; this ends in the suffix *kaṭac*, derived from the root *kaṭ* in the sense of "a collection" (*saṅghāte*). *Uraṇaḥ* means "a ram."

(823) *bandhe ca vibhāṣā* | 6|3|13 | And [the suffix *ṭac*] is optional (*vibhāṣā*) after the word *bandha*. The word *bandha* here ends in the suffix *ghañ*. In the example *hastebandhaḥ*, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. However, in the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it would be governed by the rule to be stated later: *nañ-siddha-bandhāt-iṣu ca*.

They say that this is indeed a prohibition. Regarding the form *apsavya*: by adding the suffix *yat* due to its inclusion in the *dig-ādi* group, the *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *o* results in the *vānta* replacement (*au*). However, the author of the *Prācīna* commentary, having read *jaṃ* in place of *yat*, has cited *apsujaḥ* as an example;
that contradicts the original source.
The two *ājyabhāga* mantras are "In the waters, in the wombs of the mothers" (*apo yoniṣu matuṣu*) and "Possessing the waters" (*apsumantau*).

In the *Kārīrī* sacrifice, there are the two *ājyabhāga* mantras: "O Agni, you have your seat in the waters" (*apsv agne sadhiṣṭhava*) and "Soma has told me [so] in the waters" (*apsu me somo abravīt*).
For since the word "waters" (*ap-*) occurs therein, by that means the two *ājyabhāgas* also possess the quality of being "possessing the waters" (*apsumat*). However, according to the Easterners...
Having read "matiṣu," the form *apsumatiḥ* is cited as an example. Regarding this, some ask:

is the word *apsu* here an imitative (anukaraṇa) term ending in the locative case, or not? In the first case, since there is no nominative suffix following a locative ending, the suffix *matup* itself would be difficult to justify. In the latter case, however, [the difficulty is avoided] by the elision (*luk*) [of the case-ending].

The attainment [of the suffix] does not exist at all, because of the absence of the locative case. Thus, the reading "matiṣu" stated by the ancient [author] is indeed correct. Nor should it be argued that this reading is not seen in the Bhāṣya and other works;
for the reading "matiṣu" and the example "apsumatiḥ" are found in manuscripts of the Bhāṣya, the Vṛtti, and other such texts.
They say that since the reading *matuṣu* is never observed anywhere in the sense of being visible (*dṛśyamānatvena*), and because [the alternative] would be redundant;

for in cases such as *asyavāmīyam* or *kathāśubhīyam*, where elision (*luk*) is to be applied, the desired result is established precisely by the non-application of the rule "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*).

(824) *nen-siddha-bandh-atiṣu ca* | Pāṇini 6.3.19. Regarding *nen-siddha-bandha*: as in *cakra-bandha*. Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule for *tatpuruṣa* compounds, this prohibition applies only to *tatpuruṣa* compounds. However, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*) according to the rule *bandhe ca vibhāṣā*.

The suffix *ka* is applied after the words *vāk*, *dik*, and *paśyat*, when combined with the words *yukti*, *daṇḍa*, and *hara* respectively. Thus, *paśyatohara* means "one who steals while being watched";

the sense is that he steals while disregarding the person who is looking on. The genitive case is used here according to the rule *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare* ("the genitive is also used in the sense of disregard"). Furthermore, the term *devānāmpriya* refers to a fool; for fools indeed [bring] pleasure (*priyam*) to the gods. Thus, "of the gods" (*devānām*). Fools, it is said, are dear to the gods.
"They produce [the gods] because of their status as cattle for the gods," says Manoramā. The meaning is this:
worldly beings are fools because they lack knowledge of Brahman;
yet, while performing rituals such as sacrifices, they [act] by means of offering the *puroḍāśa* and other oblations.

They produce joy for the gods; however, those who possess knowledge of Brahman do not [produce such joy], because they lack the performance of sacrifices and other rites. Therefore, because they occupy the position of cattle and the like, only fools are "god-cattle."

Regarding the words *śepa*, *pucca*, and *lāṅgūleṣu* [in the compound] *śunaḥśepa*: [the term] *śepapuccha* [is explained as follows]. *Śunaḥśepaḥ* means "one whose tail (*śepa*) is like that of a dog (*śvan*). Although the word *śepas* ends in the letter *s*, according to Amara’s lexicon (*Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*) which states, "The word *śepas* [denotes] a bull, a sexual organ, or a mark," nevertheless, by virtue of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), the suffix *pap* is applied to the root *śīṅ*.

It indeed exists ending in the vowel *a*; for instance, in the mantra: *yasyākamuśantaḥ praharāma śepam*. However, it should be understood that if the reading were *cihnaśephasoḥ*, there would be no suspicion at all of the word *śepha* ending in *s*. This is also the case in examples such as *śunaḥ puccha*.

*Bahuvrīhi*. These three are also names of specific sages. In the rule *mātuḥ piturbhyām*, the word "in a compound" (*samāse*) is understood from the preceding rule *aṅguleḥ saṅgaḥ*; he demonstrates the result of this by saying "but in the absence of a compound" (*asamāse tu*). [This refers to] the sentence (*vākya*).
The meaning is that even the optional substitution of *ṣ* does not occur;
thus ends the section on *aluk* compounds in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
(881) *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā* (Pāṇini 4.1.82).

Desiring to explain the secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) by way of their connection through exception (*apavāda*), he states the governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*) for them: "of those that are semantically connected" (*samarthānām*).
This is because of the continuation of the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*), as will be stated in the root text: "there is also a compound."

It has been indicated that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules on compound formation (*samāsa*). Because no element to be prescribed (*vidheya*) is specified, and because there is a requirement for a specific base (*prakṛti*) in what follows, he states "it is governed" (*adhikriyate*) to show that this is not an independent rule (*svatantra-vidhi*). By the term "the three [words] beginning with *ad-*," each [word]—

The declaration of the *svarita* accent has been indicated. Its purpose, however, is that even when one [element] is withdrawn, another may not be withdrawn; thus, in the rule *rāgdiśaḥ*, while *asamarthānāṃ prathamā* is withdrawn, *vā* continues to apply.
The root text to be explained hereafter is consistent [with this]. (882) *prāgdīvyato ’ṇ* 4.1.83.
Regarding the phrase *prāgdiśa iti*: because the suffixes that follow it are *svārthika* (having their own meaning), they are [included] under the category of *anarthaka* (meaningless/tautological).
The sense is that the purpose of the word *ratham* is not for the sake of the two words [of the compound]. Now, one might object:

since the meaning is already established by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "a rule concerning words applies to those that have a single meaning" (*asamarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), the expression "of those that have a single meaning" (*asamarthānām*) is redundant. Nor should it be suspected that this is not a rule concerning words (*padavidhitva*).

Because the rule for the formation of *ali* (nominal stems) in the case of "hakālataneṣu" establishes the accepted doctrine that "the addition of *taddhita* suffixes occurs after a stem ending in *u*," and because this is universally agreed upon, he says: "capacity" (*sāmarthyam*).
This means "having undergone the operation of sandhi. The result of this, however, is explained in the very root-text under the rule "asyāpatyam" (Pāṇini 4.1.92).
This will become clear later. In this context, it would have been more appropriate to state, "after a word ending in the sense of 'not' (nañ), the first [suffix] is optionally [used].
He states the general rules with the words beginning with *prāgdīvyataḥ*. In the sūtra, the single portion *īvyat* has been included as a limit (*avadhi*), even though it is itself devoid of meaning.

Some say it is like *rāgrīśvarāt* and *aditeḥ*. Others, however, say that *dīvya-* is a form ending in the present participle suffix *-śat*; therefore, the meaning is simply "one who plays at dice," and this is the limit [of the application]. (883) *aśvapatyādibhyaśca* 4.1.84.

Regarding the term *prāgdīvyatīyeṣu*: "prior to *dīvyati*" is *prāgdīvyat*. The ancient commentators (*prāñcaḥ*) hold that this is an avyayībhāva compound formed by the rule *ṭhapaparihahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā*. However, some maintain that *prāgdīvyataḥ* is more appropriate, because the suffix *ṭac* applies [only] after words ending in *hay*. That is not correct; for the suffix *ṭac* [is indeed applied] after *hay*.

Because it is only optional (*pākṣikatvāt*). Otherwise, the root example (*mūlodāharaṇa*) found in that very sūtra—"upasamidham upasamidhi"—would result in being inconsistent. Nor is it the case that, in the absence of the *ṭac* suffix, the form "rāgdīvyatīya" would not arise due to the elision of the *ṭi* portion by the rule "avyayānāṃ bhamātre."

This is to be doubted. For the purpose of making the *avyayībhāva* compound an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is established by its inclusion in the list [of indeclinables] as "the application of the accent of *ūḍhamukha*. That which exists prior to the suffix *dīvyat* is *prāgdīvyatīya*. This is derived by the rule "after a base ending in a *vṛddhi* vowel, the suffix *cha* [is applied]. Furthermore, the suffix *tyap* is certainly not to be suspected here.

Because of the enumeration [in the rule] "only from *ṭham*, *ekavata*, and *sitra*," and because it is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*) due to the enumeration [of indeclinables] beginning with "the *luṅ* augment, *bhukha*, and *svara*. Regarding the phrase "of that which is to be stated": it refers to that which is to be stated [in the rule] "after *ati* as a prior member, the suffix *ṇya* is added."

(884) *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.117. Regarding this, with the intention that "among the vowels (*acām*), the first vowel (*ādiḥ*) is [the one affected]"—and based on the fact that the word *acaḥ* from the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115) is understood to carry over here—he explains: "of the vowels" (*acaḥ*). "There shall be *vṛddhi*" means...
The intention is that [the word] "vṛddhi" from the rule "ṛjer vṛddhiḥ" is carried over [by anuvṛtti].
(885) *Kiti ca* | Pāṇini 7.2.118. This [rule] also applies for the sake of forms such as *vāhīkaḥ*, which ends in a *kit* suffix.

This has been presented here for the sake of easy explanation. With the intention that the *ik-paribhāṣā* does not apply here because [the rule] "ṭhacāmādeḥ" specifies a particular locus, he provides the example beginning with *āśvapatim*. [The phrase] "only a mistake" (*prāmādikameva*) refers to this.
This is established in the *Haradattagrantha*:

"If, however, it is explained that [the suffix] *ṣyañ* is applied after a word ending in *aṇ* which has the sense of a deity—since words such as *cāturvarṇya* belong to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class—then this usage is entirely faultless. [Examples include: *Aśvapati*, *Gaṇapati*.

*Rāṣṭrapati*, *kulapati*, *gṛhapati*, *paśupati*, *kṣetrapati*, *aśvapati*, and so forth. (886) Pāṇini 4.1.85: *dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṇya* is applied after [stems ending in] *diti*, *aditi*, *āditya*, or when the word *pati* is the final member (*uttarapada*) of a compound. [This is explained by] forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the word *pati* and the term *uttarapada*.

The compound should be made as a *dvandva* last; it is not that a *bahuvrīhi* follows the *dvandva*. Thus he says: "and after a word ending in *pati*. The mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) was made so that [the suffix] might apply even when a polysyllabic word precedes, provided that the meaning "absolute lordship" is expressed. Regarding the example *daitya*: but surely...

The suffix *ṇya* [in the rule *dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ*] has its scope of application in cases such as [derivatives from] *ditis*, while the suffix *ḍhak* [in the rule *itaścāniñaḥ*] has its scope of application in cases such as *dauleyaḥ* for the sense of "offspring. Thus, in the case of *diter apatyam* ("the offspring of Diti"), where both would apply, the *luk* (elision) would occur by virtue of its being the subsequent rule. This is not so.

Regarding the rule for *ṭhañ* and other suffixes, the *Bhāṣya* states that they apply "by prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*)" to the exception to *aṇ* based on specific meanings. Why does it say "in the case of specific meanings"? Consider the word *auṣṭrapatam*. A leaf named *uṣṭrapati* [is meant here]. Here, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rules "this belongs to this" (*asyedam*) and "after *adhvaryu* and *pariṣad*" (*atrādhvaryuparipadaśca*). In this instance...

By the rule of prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the suffix *ṇya* does not occur in the sense of "this belongs to this" (*asyedam*), because the word *idam* has a general meaning. How then is the form *aiteyaḥ* derived?
To this they say: from the feminine form ending in *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*. However, *ṇya* is not used here.
It occurs because the technical rule regarding gender-distinction (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) is not universally valid.

Nor should one be misled into thinking that the suffix *ṇya* must necessarily apply by virtue of the preceding element being treated as the end of the word (*pūrvāntavadbhāva*), according to the rule "as if it were the end of the preceding [word]"; for when the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added to the word *diti*, there is elision by the rule "of that which is preceded by *y*" (*yasyeti ca*).

"Because there is no long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha*. When the suffix *ṇya* is added to the word *āditya*, after the elision of *y* by the rule *yasya*, there is optionally the elision of *y* by the rule *halo yamām*. Nor can the elision of *a* (the penultimate *a*) be treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were still present), because that is prohibited by the rule *na pādante*; furthermore, [the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*] does not apply here.
And because of the statement [in the Mahābhāṣya], "as if it were the original element" (sthānivadbhāva). The phrase "in the Kāśikā" implies that this is not seen in the Bhāṣya.

The usage with the suffix *ṣyañ* in its own sense (*svārthika*) after a stem ending in *aṇ* is easily established. The feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur, because the *ṅīṣ* of *ṣit* suffixes is not obligatory.
The suffixes *ñā* and *ña* are applied after the word *pṛthivī*. He provides an example in the feminine gender to demonstrate the difference in their respective results: *pārthivāḥ* and *pārthivī*.

Regarding the rule "after *bahiṣ*, there is elision of the sixth case-ending and the suffix *yañ*": the mention of the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel) is for the sake of [excluding] indeclinables.
This is to indicate the non-eternality (*anityatā*) of the rule *bhamātre*. By this, the form *ārātīya* is established.

[The substitution of] the vowel *a* occurs in place of the final syllable of *sthāman*. From the example given in the Bhāṣya, *aśvatthāma*, it follows that there is an application of the rule to the end of the word (*tadantavidhi*). And not...

It should not be argued that, because the word *sthāman* denoting "strength" cannot logically be connected with a descendant (*apatya*), the rule must be interpreted as applying to words ending in *sthāman* by virtue of the force of the grammatical formulation;

for that force is exhausted by the possibility of such a connection when the sense is "born from" (*jāta*) and so forth— as in the case of "one whose strength is like that of a horse" (*aśvasyeva sthāma yasya*).
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Regarding the rule "after *loman*, when there are many descendants": *uḍuloma*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "one whose body hairs (*lomāni*) are like the stars (*uḍūni*), that is, the constellations (*nakṣatrāṇi*). [The suffix is applied] to the word *loman* alone in relation to the descendant.
Due to the absence of *yoga*, the rule of "final elision" (*tadanta-vidhi*) applies; consequently, the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *ṭi-lopa*.

[The rule] *sarvatra ṭ-gor ajādiprasaṅge yat* [applies]. Regarding the word *go*: it should be understood that this suffix is not used only in the sense of "offspring," but rather in all senses belonging to the group beginning with *prāgdīvyatīya*. Thus, *gavyam* means "belonging to the cow" (*gavi*).

The meaning is "the Lord," "the deity of this," "this belongs to the cow" (gavi), and so forth. Some, however, say that because of the inclusion of the word "all" (sarva) in the Bhāṣya, this suffix *yat* applies even to meanings other than those falling under the category of *prāgdīvyatīya*; thus, forms such as *gavya* (one who moves with a cow) also occur. Examples include *goḥ uṣṭram* (the camel of the cow), and so on.
From the words *hetu* and *manuṣya*, the suffixes *rūpya* and *mayaṭ* optionally occur [to form derivatives meaning "made by"]; thus, *rūpya* and *mayaṭ*.
(887) From the group beginning with *utsa*, the suffix *añ* [is applied]. This is an exception to the suffix *aṇ* and to the suffixes such as *iñ* which are exceptions to that. Here...
The *gaṇasūtra* states: “*aṣkayāse*. [This applies] when *ase* is not in a compound; this is a technical term (*saṃjñā*) of the ancient teachers.

The offspring and so forth of *baṣkaya* is *bāṣkayaḥ*. Why say “not in a compound” (*ase*)? [Consider: *gaubaṣkayiḥ*. Because of the prohibition [stated by the word] “*ase*,” it is indicated that here there is an application of the rule to that which ends in [the word] (*tadantavidhi*); therefore, the word *dhenu* is included here.

From the recitation [of the rule], it is established that a collection of *adhenus* is called *ādhenava*. Now, one might object: "In this case, would not the suffix *añ* apply in the words *dhainukam* and *gaudhenukam*? For although *dhainukam* is established by the rule 'ṭhañ after *cit*, *hasti*, and *dhenu*', *gaudhenukam* would not be established."
If it is argued that this is not so, we say no; for there exists a specific statement in the Bhāṣya:
"The suffix *ik* produces [the suffix] *ṭhak*. Here, "*ika*" means *ṭhak*.
Regarding the rule "The suffix *ḍhak* should be stated after the words *agni* and *kali*": the meaning is as follows—"*sā'sya*... [and so forth].

Under the governing rule *devatā* (Pāṇini 4.1.24), the sūtra *agnerḍhak* should be removed; and under the governing rule *dṛṣṭaṃ sāme* (Pāṇini 4.2.7), the vārttika *alerḍhak* should also be removed. Instead, this very [sūtra *agnerḍhak*] should be read as applicable to all suffixes belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group. By means of it, one forms: *agnerapatyam* (the offspring of Agni), *agninā dṛṣṭaṃ sāma* (a Sāman seen by Agni), *agniridam* (this belongs to Agni), and *agnau bhavam* (occurring in Agni).

The form *āgneya* is established as meaning "that which has come from Agni. Likewise, in the sense of "the offspring of Kali," the form *kāleya* is also established. By this, since the suffix *ḍhak* is seen even in other meanings in the Śruti passage—"That which he caused to move (*akālayat*) is the reason for the Kāleyas' being called Kāleyas"—it follows that [the rule] is "from *kali*, the suffix *ḍhak*."

The Mīmāṃsaka assertion that the Sūtra is meaningless is thereby refuted. Furthermore, the mention of "Sūtra-hood" in the Vārttika is intended merely to deceive those Mīmāṃsakas who are not experts in grammar; such is the general direction of the argument.
Thus end the suffixes common to the meanings beginning with "offspring" (apatya) and ending with "modification" (vikāra).

(888) *strīpuṃsābhyāṃ nañ-snañau bhavanāt* | P. 4.1.87. [The rule begins with] *strīpuṃsābhyām*. The word *prāk* (before) is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "in the sense of 'before' (*prāgartheṣu*)". Regarding *pauṃsna*: here, because it is a *pada* by virtue of being among the words beginning with *va* (P. 1.4.14), there is elision of the final *s* of *puṃsaḥ* due to the rule on the elision of a consonant at the end of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*).

Even in the case of *nivṛta*, the suffixal *sakāra* is indeed heard. For this very reason, the negative particle *nañ* alone is not prescribed after both [prefixes], because it would otherwise result in the failure to establish the form *pāésna*.
It might be argued: let there be the suffix *añ* itself, as introduced by context, after both [prefixes], and by its association with that...

One might argue: "Let only *nu* be prescribed by the rule *trīpuṃsayor nuk ceṭi*. Nor should it be claimed that this would lead to the undesired elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* in forms such as *traiṇāḥ* and *pāésnāḥ* (by the rule *yañañoś ca*), nor that it would lead to the application of the suffix *aṇ* in cases such as *sraiṇānāṃ saṅghaḥ* (by the rule *aṅghāhkalakṣaṇeṣu*)."
In both cases, the term *gotra* is understood by virtue of its recurrence [from a previous rule]. For in that context, *gotra* refers specifically to what is established in the *Pravarādhyāya*.

Otherwise, in forms such as *autrāḥ* and *dauhitrāḥ*, there would also have to be elision (*luk*) of the suffix *añ*. And thus, in the Vārttika "after *añ*, *snañ*, *īkak*, *khya*, and *un*," the mention of *nañ* and *snañ* would be unnecessary, since [the elision] would follow simply from the fact of ending in *añ*.

If it is argued that another [form] is also favorable because *ṅīp* would be established, they say here: in this case, by the rule "when a *taddhita* suffix does not follow," there would be elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) due to the presence of *nuk*. Nor is *nuk* thus rendered meaningless, for its purposefulness is secured precisely by the application of the elision of the *ṭi*. Even though its purposefulness exists in the word *strī*, [it would still apply here].
Although the elision of the vowel *i* could also occur by the rule "nāsti, ṭhyasyeti ca," nevertheless,

in the case of "rīrdeavatā’sya śrāyaṃ haviḥ," the vṛddhi [substitution] would take effect because it is subsequent to the elision; however, since the *ṭilopa* (elision of the final syllable) applies when there is *nuk*, let the *nuk* be purposeful even in the word *strī*.
Therefore, one must accept the rule *nañ-snañ-au* exactly as it is stated. Others, however, suggest:
let there be the rule *trī-puṃsayor nuk ca*; in this view, the vowel *a* is intended in the augment (*āgama*).

Even when the elision (*lopa*) of that [augment] occurs by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) does not take place because of the status of being "as if it were the original form" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

It will be so. And thus, since the feminine suffix *ḍīp* is established by the rule *iḍḍhāṇañ* itself, they say there is great economy [of effort] in not having to provide a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for *nañ* and *snan*. Regarding the sense of *vat* (likeness): "The suffixes *nañ* and *snan* do not apply after *strī* and *pums* in the sense of *vat*."
The sense is that the indicator (jñāpaka) depends upon the general rule. For this very reason, he provides an example: "like *strī*.

He will state later that the *ca* in the rule *ā ca tvāt* is for the purpose of including both *tva* and *tal* after the suffixes *nañ* and *snan*. By this, the forms *strītva*, *strītā*, *puṃstva*, and *puṃstā* are established.
(889) *dvigor lug anapatye* | 4.1.88.

Regarding the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*: the term *dvigoḥ* is in the genitive case, and its meaning is "for the sake of that" (*tadartha*), which implies causality; and this causality is applicable even to something that is yet to come into being (*bhāvin*).
With the intention that [the suffix] arises from the determination based on friendship (*buddhy-adhyavasāya*), he says: "The cause of a *dvigu*. Regarding "beginning with *aja*":

this is obtained by carrying over the word "in *ac*" (*aci*) from the subsequent sūtra, or alternatively, by applying the option (*vā-grahaṇa*) and resorting to a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). Why say "pertaining to what comes before *dīvya-tīya*"? [Consider: *pañcamyaḥ*.
That which is beneficial for skulls is *pañcakapālīya*.

(890) *gotre’lugaci* |4|1|89|. [The rule] "in the case of a *gotra* [suffix], there is no elision (*aluk*) before a vowel-initial [suffix]. Why "in the case of a *gotra*"? [To ensure that] the non-elision applies only to a suffix having the sense of *gotra*, as follows:
It may be so; however, it is not the case here—namely, *kauvalam* (this belongs to the *kuvala*) and *bādaram* (this belongs to the *badara*).

For the words *kuvalī* and *badarī* end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the *gaurādi* group; from these, when denoting a product (*vikāra*) in the form of a fruit, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *anudātādeśca*.
That [suffix] is elided by the rule *halastaddhitasya*. Then, in the sense of "belonging to this" (*idamarthe*), [the suffix *aṇ* is applied].

The meaning is that when a suffix beginning with *aja-* and falling under the category *prāgdīvyatīya* is intended, the *aluk* (non-elision) does not occur by this rule; consequently, because the condition for *vṛddhi* is absent, *cha* is not applied. Regarding the phrase "when intended": the locative case in *aci* is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
If it were a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*), then since the stem would not be *vṛddha*, *cha* would not apply, and thus only *aṇ* would occur—this is the underlying point.

(891) *Āpatyasya ca taddhite ’nāti* [Pāṇini 6.4.151]. Regarding the form *gargāṇām*: when there is a desire to express plurality of descendants (*apatya*), the suffix is elided by the rule *ṭhyañañośca*. However, that elision is prohibited by the present sūtra when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) is intended to be applied; thus, when the suffix *cha* is added to the word *gārgya*, [the result is *gārgīya*].

The substitution of *īya* occurs for that [suffix]. Regarding the rule *āpatyasya ca*, he states it for the purpose of eliding the *y* after the elision of the *a* by the rule *yasyeti ca*. From the rule *he lopo ’kadr̥vāḥ*, the word *lopa* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*), and from the rule *ūryatiṣyetyayebhyaḥ*, the word *ya* is understood.
And [the word] "hala" is taken from the rule *ṭhhalastaddhitasya*. Thus he says: "of what follows after a consonant," and so forth.

Even though it belongs to the *ābhīya* group, the elision of *at* (*allopa*) is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*), because of the force of its specific formulation. For this very reason, he explains that the term "of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*) does not carry over [from the previous rule], by saying "of the letter *ya*. Why [is the condition] "of a descendant" (*āpatyasya*) stated?

*Saṅkāśyakaḥ*, *Kāmpilyakaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṇya* is applied according to the rule *aṃkāśādibhyo ṇyaḥ*. From that, [the suffix] *vuñ* is applied according to the rule *hanvayopadhāt*. Why specify "in a secondary derivative" (*taddhite*)? [Consider: *Gargyaḥ*, *Gārgyayoḥ*. Why specify "not ending in ā" (*anāt*)? [Consider: *Gargyāyaṇaḥ*. [And consider: *Gargīyam*. [This is for] *asmai*.
The substitution of *ch* for *hit* occurs [in the sense of "beneficial"].

(892) *yūni luk* |4|1|90|. There is elision (*luk*) when a descendant in the younger generation (*yuvan*) is to be expressed. The term *prāgdīvyatīya* ("belonging to the period prior to Pāṇini 4.1.83") is understood here, as are *aci* ("before a vowel") and the governing heading *pratyaya* ("suffix").

The term "affix" (pratyaya) is understood [from the context]. This is what is stated: "an affix beginning with a vowel in the sense of 'prāgdīvyatīya'. Since the designation "affix" (pratyaya) is obtained from the rule "there is elision of the affix" (pratyayasya luk), that affix which has been thus acquired is qualified by the word "yūni" (in the sense of a younger generation). Thus, the meaning is "the elision of that affix which occurs in the sense of a younger generation," and this is what he states.

(893) *pailādibhyaśca* |2|4|59|. [The phrase] "of the secondary suffix (*yuvan-pratyaya*)" refers to what will be stated hereafter. [The phrase] "to be stated" refers to what will be stated in the rule: *rācām avṛddhāt phin bahulam*. Why [is it specified] "before a suffix beginning with a vowel"? [Consider: *glaucukāyanarūpyam*. [This falls under] the section *prāgdīvyato 'ṇ*.

What is this? It is *glaucukāyanīya*. [The suffix] *ccha* is applied according to the rule "that which is beneficial for this" (*asmai hitam*). In this context, the sūtra should have been formulated as: “There is elision (*luk*) of *yañ* and *yaṅ* in the absence of a patronymic (*apatya*), provided the following vowel is not a *pratyaya*; however, in the case of a *gotra* [term], it does not apply to a younger descendant. Thus, it is established in the *Manoramā* that “the mention of the elision of *yañ* and *yaṅ* could have been omitted. In that regard—

The sense is that, in the rule *hikphiñaḥ*, one must resort to the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) for the term *yūni*; thus, this difficulty must be endured for the sake of brevity. [Regarding] *pailādibhyaśca*:
from the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣe* [the word] *yūni luk* is understood to carry over. Thus he says:

(894) *na taulvalibhyaḥ* |2|4|61|. This refers to the elision (*luk*) of the secondary suffix (*yuvan-pratyaya*). Regarding "of *pīlā* optionally," and so forth: when the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed for a descendant, it is indeed *aṇ* even for a lineage-descendant (*gotrāpatya*), because it will be stated later that "there is only one [suffix] in the lineage" (*eko gotre*).

Therefore, although the suffix *phaiñ* is prescribed after the word *paila*—which is derived from *aṇ*—to denote a descendant, it ultimately applies to a young descendant (*yuvāpatya*). The meaning of this rule is that there is elision (*luk*) of that *phiñ* by the present [sūtra]. In this way, the word *paila* is used without variation to denote the offspring of Pīlā, whether as a lineage-descendant (*gotrāpatya*) or as a young descendant (*yuvāpatya*).

Thus he says: "Paila, the father, and the son. Regarding Paila and others—those ending in *iñ* such as Śālaṅki, Sātyaki, Audameghi, Paiṅgali, and so forth—it should be understood that their inclusion [in the list] is for the sake of those who are not easterners (*aprācām*), since the elision (*luk*) is already established by the rule "after an *iñ* suffix denoting a person from the East" (*ṭhiñaḥ prācām*). Furthermore, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after a *tadrāja* [suffix].

This is a collective rule (*gaṇasūtra*). Its meaning is that there is elision (*luk*) of the *yuvan* suffix following a word that bears the designation *tadrāja*, provided that it is a *gotra* name belonging to the Easterners (*prācām*). Here, the mention of "Easterners" (*prācām*) is a qualifier for *gotra*; it does not serve to introduce an option (*vikalpa*), as is the case in rules such as "for the Easterners, [the suffix is elided] after a non-*vṛddha* [word]" and so forth. This is the sense.

The commentary provides the refuge [for understanding]: "Dākṣi is the father," and so forth. A male descendant of Dakṣa, whether a lineage-descendant (*gotrāpatya*) or a descendant generally, is called *dākṣi*.
However, the intention is that a young descendant (*yuvāpatya*) is called *dākṣāyaṇa* (or *dākṣāyaṇa*). [This applies] except for those belonging to the Tolvalis.

Intending to show that the meaning of "and others" (*ādi*) is understood from the use of the plural number and the force of the list in the *gaṇapāṭha*, he says: "from *taulvali* and so forth. *Devamitra*, *devayajñi*, *śvāphalki*, *āsuri*, *naimeṣi*, *pauṣkarasādi*, *vaikarṇi*, etc., constitute the *taulvalyādi* group. (895) *Phak-phiñoḥ anyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 4.1.91]. Regarding *kātyāyanasya*: *kātyaḥ* is the lineage descendant (*gotrāpatya*) of *kata*. By virtue of belonging to the *gargādi* group, the suffix *yañ* is applied. From that...
The suffix *phak* is applied by the rule "yūni ṭhyañiñośca" [Pāṇini 4.1.79]; thus we have *Kātyāyanī*. By the rule "ṭhāpatyasya ca" [Pāṇini 6.4.151], there is elision (*yalopa*) of the *y*.
(896) *tasyāpatyam* [Pāṇini 4.1.92]: "his offspring. In this rule, the word "asya" (of him) does not denote its own form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*), but rather—

With the intention that the genitive ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is merely illustrative, he says "from the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhyantāt*). The meaning of the ablative case is to be supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). Alternatively, there is the elision (*luk*) of the ablative after an imitation word (*anukaraṇa*), as prescribed by Pāṇini’s rules. Regarding the phrase "have been stated":
*aṇ*, *ṇya*, and so forth have been stated. Regarding "will be stated": *iñ* and so forth. Now, [one might object]: "In the case of *upagu-a*..."
When [the suffix] *u* is present, because it is subsequent to the *guṇa* substitution, the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule "ṭhaco’ñṇiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.115) ought to apply.

However, the substitution of *ghuṇ* has its scope in cases such as *picavya*. Furthermore, once the *guṇa* and the *av* substitute have been applied, the *vṛddhi* prescribed by "ṭhata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116) ought to apply; therefore, he says: "the initial *vṛddhi*," because it is subsequent.
This is the state of affairs. The scope for the final and penultimate *vṛddhi* (P. 7.2.117) is, for example, *gauḥ* and *pācakaḥ*.

However, the scope for initial *vṛddhi* (P. 7.2.118) is, for example, *suśrut*, *sauśrut*, and *sauśrutaḥ*. In cases such as *vāṣṭraḥ* and *āgataḥ*, where both rules would apply, initial *vṛddhi* alone occurs because it is subsequent in the order of the rules (*paratvāt*).

In this case, the principle of *sakṛdgati* (the rule that a word undergoes modification only once) is adopted in accordance with the requirements of the specific grammatical object (*lakṣya*). For the inclusion of the words *puṣkara* and *sada* in the *anuśatikādi* group serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this. Otherwise, since forms such as *pauṣkarasādi* would already be established through the initial *vṛddhi* and the subsequent *guṇa*, their inclusion in those lists would be purposeless. Nor can it be argued that [the form] *uṣkarasadā*...

It should not be argued that for the sake of deriving the form *auṣkarasādika*—meaning "one who acts as an auṣkarasa"—the inclusion of this word in the *anuśatikādi* group is necessary [to trigger the *vṛddhi* substitute for the penultimate vowel before the suffix *ṭhak*]; for it must be stated that the substitution of *vṛddhi* for the penultimate vowel is accepted only before suffixes marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, and not before those marked with *k*.
This is because Kaiyaṭa has established the resolution that the suffix *ṭhak* does not apply here due to non-usage (*anabhidhāna*).

By this, the objection that the relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) is not tenable when the objects are different is refuted; for, by the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*), it must necessarily be accepted that "sublation occurs even when [the objects] are distinct. Now, even so—

If it is argued: "Let the *upadhā*-vṛddhi (vowel strengthening of the penultimate) be set aside in cases such as *āgata*; however, in the case of *āṬpagava*, since the *upadhā*-vṛddhi has not yet occurred at the time the initial *vṛddhi* (strengthening of the first vowel) is about to take effect, how could there be any sublation?
To this they reply: Once it has been determined that the *upadhā*-vṛddhi is to be sublated in cases such as *jāgata*, [the same principle applies here].
In some cases, even though that [vṛddhi] would apply at a later time, it is appropriate that it be sublated.

This might be asked: why does the vṛddhi characterized by the final and penultimate vowels not occur where the initial vṛddhi has not taken place? For example, *vaiyasavam* (the state of being distressed), derived from *vyasum* with the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *igantācca*. In the case of *vyāpad*, [the same applies].

*Bhava-vaiyāpradam*. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule *atra bhavaḥ*. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa says: "In this case as well, since [the diphthongs] *ai* and *au* are subsequent, they sublate that [suffix], and thus all desired results are established. [The author] objects, disregarding the fact that there is indeed a difference in the resulting verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).
The phrase "tasyedam ity apatye 'pi" (even in the case of offspring, [the rule] "this belongs to that") would have been formulated for the purpose of setting aside [other rules].

Regarding "tasyedam ity apatye 'pi": since the meanings of "this belongs to that" include offspring, collections, modifications, and so forth, the suffix *aṇ* applies even in the sense of offspring by the rule "asyedam" (this belongs to that).

The meaning is: "What is the purpose of this rule *asyāpatyam* [Pāṇini 4.1.92] for the sake of [the derivation of forms] such as *pravartate*? Although the rule *asyāpatyam* must indeed be stated for the sake of rules such as *ata iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95], the objection here should be understood as asking: "For what purpose is this division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*)? He provides the solution: "For the purpose of sublation (*bādhanārtham*)," namely, [to sublate] the application of the rule *asyedam* [Pāṇini 4.3.120].

The meaning is that a separate rule would have had to be formulated for the purpose of overriding the suffix *cha* prescribed by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*. Now, one might object: since the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "belonging to this" (*asyedam*) is excluded from this context, and since both this *aṇ* and the *cha* prescribed after bases with a *vṛddhi* vowel are *śaiṣika* (secondary) suffixes, there is no possibility at all for them to apply in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*).

Since it is not accepted that "the *śeṣa* (remainder) is any meaning other than those beginning with *apatya* and ending with the four meanings," he says: "This [meaning] is indeed the general rule (*utsarga*) for the *śeṣa*. This refers to the meaning of *apatya*.
The underlying intention is this: if there were no division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), [the definition of *śeṣa* would be too narrow].

Since the meaning of "offspring" (*apatya*) connected specifically to bases such as *adanta* (ending in -a) is already accounted for by its utility [in other rules], the meaning of "offspring" connected to bases such as *upagu* would remain as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*). Consequently, the suffix *cha* would apply after bases like *bhānu* when they are *vṛddha*, thereby subverting the application of *aṇ*. However, once the *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) is made, since the meaning of "offspring" connected to the general category of bases is also utilized, it no longer constitutes a "remainder"; thus, there is no possibility at all for the application of *cha*.

[Objection: But since Upagu and others are not *vṛddha*, there is no possibility for the application of the suffix *cha*; therefore, the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is fruitless. To this, he says: "The *vṛddha* [bases]. The word "nominal bases" (*pratipadikāni*) is to be supplied as the remainder. [Question: "Why [specify] 'after a [base] whose internal sandhi has been performed'? [Answer: Since sandhi is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the suffix will apply immediately after that [sandhi] has taken place; thus, the question is: what is the purpose of including the term "samartha" (semantically connected) in the governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*)? [Response: "Without having performed... [etc.]

Haradatta and others maintain that this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is indicated by the inclusion of the term *samartha* (having the same meaning); others hold that it is established from common usage. [The purpose is] so that this [undesirable] arising [of the suffix] may not occur. Since the rule "after what ends in *ṭha*" (*ṭhakṛte*) serves as an exception to the rule regarding internal operations (*antaraṅga-paribhāṣā*), the suffix would apply only when no sandhi has yet taken place. The sense is that the mention of *samartha* in the governing rule (*adhikaraṇa-sūtra*) is necessary in order to prevent that.

Although it is stated there without qualification that "completion" (*pariniṣṭhitatvam*) means "capacity for usage," nevertheless, it must be understood that completion belongs only to the *ṅy-āp-prātipadika* and not to that which is qualified by a *sup*-suffix. By this, forms such as *aupagavaḥ* and *daṇḍimān* are established; otherwise, one would have *aupagaḥ* and *daṇḍīmān*. Furthermore, the mention of *aśvimān-aṇi* and so forth serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in this regard.

However, they say that if it is accepted—on the basis of the inclusion of the term *akṛtasandhi* in the rule *pāmādibhyaḥ ṣṭhan ṭhañ ca viṣvagityuttarapadalopaśca*—that the production of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) occurs when the words are not yet joined by sandhi (*asamartha*), then the mention of *samartha* (semantically connected) would indeed be redundant. Regarding the question "Why [specify] 'from the first' (*prathamāt*)?": In the phrase "the offspring of this" (*asyāpatyam*), between the two words mentioned, only the first is the provider of the base (*prakṛti*), whereas "offspring" (*apatyam*) is not. Thus, since that very [first word] will be understood when there is a requirement for a base, what is the purpose of this [specification] "from the first"?
(897) 4.1.162: *apatyaṃ pautraprabhṛti gotram* ("Offspring beginning with the grandson is called a *gotra*").

Regarding the phrase "from that which denotes offspring": there might arise the suspicion that, just as a suffix prescribed by rules such as *asyāpatyam* ("this one's offspring") is accepted after words like *upagu* ending in the genitive case, so too should a suffix occur after words like *devadatta* which denote an offspring.
The point is that, in order to prevent that [undesired application], the mention of "the first" (*prathamāt*) is necessary. Now, one might object:

even though in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) "the offspring of Upagu" (*upagor apatyam*), the word denoting the offspring does not stand first, it would still occur in the sentence "Upagu is the offspring" (*apatyam upaguḥ*), because there it stands first; thus, the suffix would indeed be applied from the word denoting the offspring.

If you say this, it is not so. Here, primacy is based on the technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) because it is fixed; it is not based on the etymological analysis (*vigraha*), which is variable. Otherwise, the term "rathamādi" would be meaningless.
[The phrase] "let there not be [the application of the suffix] in the sense of the genitive" means this: just as in the case of "Indra is the deity of this oblation" (*indro devatā asya haviṣaḥ*).

The suffix occurs after a word ending in the nominative case, as in *aindraṃ haviḥ* ("the oblation for Indra"). Likewise, [in the case of] "Upagu is the progenitor of this Devadatta," we have *aupagavaḥ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta is the descendant of Upagu"); and [in the case of] "Devadatta is the progeny of this Upagu," we have *devadato 'patyam asyopagoḥ*. [This rule is necessary] so that we do not end up with *devadato 'patyam asyopagoḥ* or *devadato upaguḥ*. This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary.
But surely, because it is an exception (*apavāda*), the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would necessarily supersede the compound;

nor should it be argued that since the secondary derivative is optional, the compound will also occur in its alternative form, for where both a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) are made optional by the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*), once the subject is released by the exception, the general rule does not apply.

Anticipating the objection that [the suffix] occurs because it has been indicated by the inclusion of the word *vā* (or) in the rule *āremadhye*, he says: "because of the recurrence of the mention of *aṅ* for either one. [He adds:
"because of its being a genus (*jāti*)," with the words "and *otra* along with the *caraṇas*" being understood as the remainder. But according to the Easterners (*prāc*),...

It has been stated that [the suffix] *ṅīp* occurs because [the word] ends in *ṭhan*. And its commentators have stated that it occurs by the rule *iḍḍhāṇañ*. However, both of these [views] are in accordance with the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *otrādyaūnyastriyām*, which states: “And *otra*...”

It should be understood that they say this [verse] was composed with the intention that in the rule *caraṇebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.120), only an artificial lineage (*kṛtrima-gotra*) is intended, and not merely offspring (*apatya*) in general.
He provides examples of the general rules found in the Sūtras in their proper order, beginning with *āśvapata*. *Āutsa*.
According to Amara: *ṭhutsaḥ prasravaṇaṃ vāri pravāho nirjharo jharaḥ* (a spring, water, a stream, a waterfall, a cascade).
Its connection with the suffix *ṭac* [denoting] offspring is like [the case of] "Bhīṣma is the son of Aṅga" (*aṅgeyo bhīṣmaḥ*). "Offspring" here means a grandson.
Now, one might object that the mention of "offspring" is redundant, since there is no deviation from the fact that a grandson and so forth are indeed offspring; therefore—

He says: "It is intended [to be understood] as offspring. What is meant by "intended"? They say: so that it does not apply when, in reality, the grandson and those following him are intended to be expressed as a subordinate element (*śeṣatvena*) in the sense of "this belongs to this person" (*asyedam*). Others, however, [hold that it applies] when there is an intention to express the grandson and others as being such [as the primary object] in reality.
That [technical term *gotra*] is for the purpose that it may apply only when there is the intention (*vivakṣā*) to denote [the descendant] as an offspring (*apatya*).

By means of this, even in cases such as *aupagavaḥ*, the designation *gotra* is established for the meaning of the suffix *aṇ*. For the property of being a grandson (*pautratva*) and so forth is not the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of *aṇ*; rather, it is simply the state of being an offspring (*apatyatva*). Otherwise, [the rule would fail].
The objection is raised: "In this context, the designation *gotra* should apply only to that which falls under the heading of *gotra*, namely [the primary] progeny (*apatya*).

One might argue: "Since the technical designations *gotra* and *yuvan* are established under the heading of *apatya*, the term 'progeny' is already understood by implication; therefore, since the intended purpose is accomplished by that very fact, what is the use of including the word 'progeny' (*apatya*) here?"
Regarding this, they say: in the rule *te tadrājāḥ*, by the word *tat* (that),

only those suffixes such as *añ* and others prescribed by rules such as *anapadaśabdāt kṣatriyād añ* are understood, and not the suffixes preceding them, because [the latter] have been separated by the section dealing with the technical designations of *gotra* and *yuvan*.

This will be explained [later]. Furthermore, since the capacity [of the suffix] to function as taught in the section on *apatya* (descendants) has already been exhausted, the term *apatya* is mentioned here once again to dispel the doubt that there might be no connection with the descendant. Why say "starting from the grandson" (*pautraprabhṛti*)? So that it does not apply to the immediate descendant—for example, *kauñji* or *gārgiḥ*. Nor should it be argued that even so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of Garga’s immediate grandson who is the grandson of Aṅgiras, because it is accepted that "the designation *gotra* applies only in relation to one for whom there is a grandson or later descendant."

And thus, O Gārgī, even when there is an intention to express [the relationship] as that of an immediate descendant, the status of being a *gotra* with respect to Garga remains unimpeded; therefore, the suffix *yañ* after *Garga* and so on would indeed apply—this is the general direction.

(898) *jīvati tu vaṃśye yuvā* | 4.1.163. But when a member of the lineage is living, [the suffix denotes] a *yuvan*. "Lineage" (*vaṃśa*) refers to the continuous succession of progenitors, such as the father, grandfather, and so forth. That which exists therein...

*Vaṃśyaḥ*. The suffix *yat* is applied because [the word] belongs to the group beginning with *diś* (Pāṇini 4.3.54). He says "of the grandson and so forth" (*pautrādeḥ*), because the term "from the grandson onwards" (*autraprabhṛti*) is understood from the previous rule and is transformed into the genitive case through interpretation, and also because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule "for the feminine, after *otra*, *yaūn*, and *ya*. The word *tu* indicates a change in word order.
The word *yuvā* should be understood as following after *asmāt*. He explains that it has the sense of the particle *eva* (only).

(Pāṇini 4.1.165): "When another sapinda who is older is living, [the younger one] receives the designation *yuvan* only. By this, even though they fall outside the scope of the governing rule on "single designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*),...

The intended meaning is that there is no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the two designations, *gotra* and *yuvan*. If it is asked, "Let there be co-occurrence of the two designations; what is the harm?"—do not say so. For it would result in the non-establishment of forms such as *śālaṅkāḥ* and *pailīyāḥ*. To explain: the offspring of Śalaṅku is Śālaṅki.
In the case of *paila* and others, there is the suffix *iñ*; for *śalaṅka* and others, there is the substitution of *śalaṅka*. The descendant of *śalaṅka* is *śālaṅki*.

The young descendant (*yuvāpatya*) of *śālaṅki* takes the suffix *phak* by the rule "after *iñ* and *yañ*. There is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix] by the rule "also after *paila* and others. Then, when one intends to express the meaning "the pupils (*chattrāḥ*) of the young descendant of *śālaṅki*," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "after *iñ*."

The form ‘ālaṅka’ arises [in this way]. Similarly, from *pīlā*, the offspring or descendant of *pīlā*—by adding the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *pīlāyā vā*—we get *pailaḥ*. His youthful descendant (*yuvan*) is formed by adding *phiñ* according to the rule *amo dvyacaḥ*. Then, by the rule *ailādibhyaśca*, there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. Thus, [the form] *pailasya* [arises].

The students who are youths are called *pailīyāḥ*. In that case, if there were a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of both the *gotra* and the youth, then by the rule "in the presence of a vowel, there is elision [of the suffix] after a *gotra*," the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *-phak* and *-phiñ* would result. Nor can it be argued that the desired result is established because the elision of the youth-suffix will occur due to its higher status (*paratva*), for [the elision of the *gotra*-suffix] is even higher than that.

Because of the contingency of an option [arising] from the rule "hakphiño'nyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.91). Nor should an option be suspected even in the established doctrine (siddhānta), for the rule "hakphiñaḥ" is an exception specifically to the elision (luk) in the sense of a *yuvan* descendant, and not to the rule "ailādibhyaśca," according to the maxim "of that which is immediately preceding. Even though [the suffix] is in the sense of a *yuvan*...

It might be argued that even the elision (*luk*) by the rule *‘elādibhyaśca’* would supersede the optional alternative *‘hakphiñoḥ’* due to its being a subsequent rule; nevertheless, they say that because an internal factor (*antaraṅga*) is stronger than even a subsequent one, the elision by *‘elādibhyaśca’* is indeed obligatory. [The rule] *‘bhrātari ca’* [also applies].

The purpose [of this rule] is for those who are not lineage-members (*avaṃśya*). A brother, however, is not a lineage-member, because it is accepted that "lineage (*vaṃśa*) is the continuous succession of progenitors. Having carried over [the word] *apatyam* from the rule *pautraprabhṛti apatyam*, and having modified *pautraprabhṛteḥ* into the genitive case, [the meaning is established].

He states the result of the explanation: "the fourth and so forth. Here is the meaning: even when the elder brothers among the Gargas and others have died, the younger brother is designated as *yuvan* (younger) provided the elder is living.

Regarding the word *vā* ("or"), he explains that the word *jīvati* ("is living") here is a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), and not a locative case ending (*saptamyanta*)—thus: "only while [the elder] is living."

The meaning is that he who lives is designated as "young," whereas one who is dead—even if still living—is merely "Gārgya" among those even more aged, and not "Gārgyāyaṇa. Regarding the word "one" (*ekam*), it means "pertaining to this world" (*ihatyam*). Regarding the word "second" (*dvitīyam*), it means "the following [word] ending in the locative case. As for what was stated regarding "both," [it refers to the two cases mentioned].
He explains that very point with the words: "by station and by age," and "or to the maternal grandfather’s brother.
Some say that because of proximity, the word "brother" (bhrātari) means specifically "the maternal grandfather’s brother" (mātāmahabhrātari).
Others say it means "the son of the paternal uncle" (pitṛvyaputre). However, in the Vṛtti, it says: "to the paternal uncle" (pitṛvye), meaning "the maternal grandfather’s brother" (pitāmahabhrātari).

The reading is *ve* (or). [Question: Why is there the word *jīvati* (if he is living)? [Question: What is the purpose of the two occurrences of *jīvati*? For this very reason, the phrase *“ṛte mato vā”* (or, if he is dead) is appropriately connected. [Question: What about the other case? [Answer: So that the option (*vikalpa*) regarding one who is living does not apply when the brother is alive; however, the previous rule applies when the brother...
The statement "for the sake of designating the younger as 'yuvan' while the elder is still living" is not without its scope;

it should be stated that [the designation applies] for the purpose of honoring the elder. Thus, the rule "vṛddhasya ca" (Pāṇini 1.2.65) is merely illustrative (*vārkatika*). Likewise, the subsequent rule "yūnaśca" (Pāṇini 1.2.66) is also [merely illustrative].

(900) *eko gotre* |4|1|93|. "In the case of a *gotra*, [the suffix] is one. The word "*gotre*" is in the singular number with reference to the genus (*jāti*). The word "one" (*eka*) denotes a number. When a *gotra* is intended to be expressed, only a single suffix denoting descent (*apatya*) is employed.
When it is stated that [the suffix] *syāt*, only the very first word [denoting the lineage] receives the suffix for the offspring of a lineage (*gotrāpatya*), and no other.

For if a suffix were applied even after a word already ending in a suffix denoting immediate offspring (*anantarāpatya*), then only a single suffix would not have been prescribed for the offspring of a lineage. And thus:

With the intention that the meaning of the Vārttika—"A prohibition must be stated for [a word] ending in a suffix denoting offspring"—is also subsumed by this, he explains: "only in the case of the *gotra* (lineage)," and "a suffix denoting offspring. This [latter point] is obtained from the governing context (*adhikāra*). Others, however, hold that the word *eka* is a synonym for *prathama* (first).

And the first [meaning] is devoid of the sense of offspring (*apatya*). Thus, they explain the meaning of the sūtra as: “the first base (*prakṛti*) receives the suffix of offspring in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*). That is strained; for when it is said, “bring one from this row,” the meaning of “first” is not understood from the word *rathamām*.

In reality, however, having explained that "the patronymic suffix is added to the very first nominal stem within the *gotra* [lineage] due to the governing rule concerning the Sun (*āditya*)," they say that the mention of the word "one" (*eka*) can be dispensed with here. For example, in the form *aupagavaḥ*, the word *upagu* itself receives the suffix, and not...

Regarding the word *tvaupagavaḥ*: even though it denotes a descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*), the suffix *aṇ* alone is applied as if it were a descendant of the immediate generation (*anantarāpatya*), and not the suffix *iñ*.

Regarding *gargyaḥ*: because the suffix *yañ* is specifically prescribed for descendants in the lineage by the rule "from *garga* and others, *yañ*" (*gargādibhyo yañ*), the suffix *iñ*—which applies as if it were an immediate descendant—is not used here; rather, only *yañ* is applied. And that [suffix]...

It occurs even in the case of a descendant of Gārgya, but here [the suffix] *phak* does not follow from a stem ending in *yañ*, because of the restriction "there is only one [suffix] in the *gotra*. Regarding *nāḍāyaṇa*: since the rule "after stems beginning with *aḍ*, there is *pha*" prescribes it for a *gotra* descendant, here too *iñ* (from the rule *ata iñ*) does not apply; rather, it is *pha* itself, and that—

[The suffix] *iñ* occurs even for the descendant of Nāḍāyana, but not [the suffix] *iñ* from a stem ending in *phak*, because of the stated restriction. Now, one might object that this sūtra is useless, since it is impossible for multiple affixes to apply simultaneously to a single gotra;
anticipating this, he establishes the purpose of the sūtra’s formulation according to different opinions—starting with "in the gotra."

The phrase *svaikonā* means: "one less than itself. With respect to that [number], the sequence would entail one for those numbering one less in the third generation, two in the fourth, three in the fifth, four in the sixth, and so forth. To illustrate: in the third generation from Upagu...
The succession of *aṇ*, *iñ*, and so forth; however, in the fourth [case], there is the succession of *aṇ*, *phiñ*, and *iñ*.

Although the expression "the succession of *aṇ*, *iñ*, and so forth" is not strictly consistent here—because by the elision rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*, the elements beginning with *aṇ* no longer exist, and thus the succession of *aṇ*, *iñ*, etc., cannot be maintained—nevertheless, *iñ* is produced from that which ends in *aṇ*.
It should be understood that the mention of a succession of suffixes (*pratyaya-paramparā*) is intended merely to indicate the final form ending in *iñ*.

Regarding the phrase "from those whose number is two less than itself" (*svadvyūnasaṅkhyebhyaḥ*): "itself" (*svam*) refers to the *gotra* [the original base]; from nominal bases (*prātipadika*) whose number is two less than that, there arises an undesirable result in the third generation.

The meaning is that [the suffix] is applied from two [stems] in the fourth case, from three in the fifth, and so forth. Regarding "the offspring belongs only to the father," Amara states: "Ātmaja, tanaya, sūnu, suta, and putra—these are used for a son;
however, they all say *duhitṛ* for a daughter; *apatya*, *toka*, and *tayoḥ same*" (meaning both son and daughter).

He states the primary view: "Then [the offering] reaches those who are prior," etc. This means: "those who are prior in relation to the father," namely the grandfather, great-grandfather, and so forth. Herein lies the intention: the word *apatya* (offspring) is based on a specific etymological derivation (*apayantyanena iti apatyam*—"that by which they do not fall away"), and is not a mere synonym for "one's own son" (*ātmaja*).

Since the author of the Bhāṣya has demonstrated this derivation in the sūtra *aṅktiviśatī*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the instrument by virtue of the rule of multiplicity (*bāhulaka*). The resulting meaning is: "that from which there is no falling away is its offspring. And thus, [the term] *autra* and so forth also [are derived accordingly].

Because they are the cause of the non-falling [into hell] of the grandfather and others, they possess the status of being offspring (*apatyatva*). And it is well known from the legends of Jaratkāru and others that even one who is separated by generations is the deliverer of the grandfather and others. Furthermore, the sūtra "offspring begins with the grandson" (*apatyaṃ pautraprabhṛti*) is also consistent with this view. For, in the first position...

One would have to resort to a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) such as "offspring-like offspring" (*apatyam ivāpatyam*). However, the *Amara-kośa* is to be disregarded because it contradicts the *Sūtras*, the *Bhāṣya*, and other authorities. Regarding the phrase *taddhānyai*: in the first view, it is for the purpose of preventing a series of suffixes (*pratyayamālā*);
others, however, hold it is for the purpose of preventing the occurrence of undesirable forms from bases with two or fewer syllables.

This is the meaning: [the objection] that there would be the suffix *iñ* in *aupagavi* is based on the intention that the third [generation], in relation to Upagu, is not a descendant (*anapatya*). And thus, in the absence of this rule, under this view, the undesirable form *aupagavi* would result, while the desired form *aupagava* would not be established.

"Bodhyam" (it should be understood). Regarding "ajo'bjyeṣṭhe": the sense is that when the designation *yuvan* (younger descendant) applies to one whose elder brother is living or whose grandson is living, the designation *gotra* does not apply. Regarding "even though [the desired result] is established":
in this view, the offspring of an *aupagava* is also the offspring of that [original] *upagu*.

The meaning is as follows: although when the suffix *ya* is applied [to *upagu*], the desired form ‘aupagavaḥ’ is indeed established, nevertheless the undesired form ‘aupagaviḥ’ would result. The word “tataḥ” means “from that which ends in *iñ*”. The phrase “phagiñoḥ” means: from that which ends in *pha*, there is *iñ*; and from that which ends in *iñ*, there is *phak*.

The meaning is that even when there is a succession beginning with *iñ* and so forth following that [suffix]. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of restriction": one might object—under the first view—the suffix would arise from the word denoting the father himself, and not from the original [stem], because *aṇ* and the other suffixes, having already fulfilled their purpose in the case of an immediate descendant where the relationship is primary, would not apply even when the relationship is secondary.

Because such an application would be improper; and thus, since there is no primary relationship between Upagu and the offspring denoted by "aupagava," this sūtra serves solely to enjoin [the suffix] where it was not otherwise obtained, rather than being for the purpose of restriction. Consequently, the application of the suffix from the word "aupagava" itself would be unavoidable.

Regarding this, they say: if the meaning of the sūtra is taken to be that when a lineage (*gotra*) is to be expressed and there is the contingency of multiple suffixes occurring in succession, only one apatya-suffix shall apply, then—
since the word *aupagava* already ends in an apatya-suffix— a further apatya-suffix would not be applicable thereafter.

Thus, since there is no other way, by accepting a successive relationship (*paramparā-sambandha*), it is established that the desired result—that the production [of the suffix] occurs from *aupagava* itself and not from the word *aupagava*—is achieved. Regarding this, some explain: "In the first alternative, when a succession of suffixes would otherwise result, only one suffix is applied by the rule 'ekaḥ gotre' (P. 4.1.93)."

It is thus prescribed; and since the term "one" (eka) results in the meaning "of the same class" (ekajātīya), when the secondary suffix *aṇ* and others—which denote lineage (*apatya*)—are to convey a *gotra*, they must be of that same class as the primary suffix *aṇ* and so forth belonging to the root-principle (*mūlaprakṛti*). Therefore, from a word denoting the father [of that person], the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word ending in *ṭhañ*.

[The rule] "from that which ends in *iñ*, [the suffix] *iñ*; from that which ends in *yañ*, [the suffix] *yañ*" applies. And it should not be argued that, even though such a mutual exclusion (*nivṛtti*) of *aṇ* and *iñ* has occurred, there would still be a succession of *aṇ* suffixes in the case of *aupagavaḥ*, or a succession of *yañ* and so forth in cases like *gargyaḥ*, even though [the original suffixes have been excluded]. For [the rule] remains true.

"Because there is no undesirable consequence for that [view]"—this is to be considered. For if the suffix *phak* were applied after a word ending in *pha*, an undesirable result would follow in cases such as *āḍāyana*. This is the general direction. Regarding the phrase "it should be inferred":
according to the view that "the offspring belongs only to the father," when a youth who is a fourth-generation descendant is intended to be expressed, [the rule] *gotrād ya-ūni* applies.

In the case of the restrictive rule (*niyama-sūtra*), whether it exists or not, the suffix denoting the *yuvan* (descendant) is applied only after a suffix denoting the *gotra* (lineage); thus there is a sequence of two. And because this is desired, it is not excluded by the restriction. However, in the fifth [generation], since there is no restriction regarding the *yuvan*, a sequence of three would result. But in the sixth...

Regarding the passage beginning with "of four," etc.: under the second alternative, namely "also for those prior to this [generation]," an undesirable application would arise for the fourth generation descendant (yuvan) from Garga, [as a suffix] would apply immediately after both the original base (mūlaprakṛti) and its immediate predecessor. However, in the fifth generation, it would apply after the original base, its immediate predecessor, and the *yuvan* [descendant]. The same applies to the fourth *yuvan* descendant from Naḍa.

As before, there is the arising of an undesirable form from two [suffixes] in the case of *pūrvavat*; from three in the fifth; and in the case of expressing *upagu* in the fourth, the undesirable arises from the primary base (*mūlaprakṛti*) alone, but not from the immediately preceding suffix that expresses *patya*. Therefore, even when *iñ* is produced from this, there is no undesirable form, and so forth.
The meaning is that this should be inferred there according to the possibility [of the case]. (901) *gotrād yaūni striyām* | Pāṇini 4.1.94.
Regarding *gotrād yaūni*: in the absence of this sūtra, according to the primary view (*mukhyamate*), when a descendant in the fifth generation or beyond (*yuvan*) is intended to be expressed...

Although it is established that when the *yuvan* suffix is desired to arise after a *gotra* suffix, it occurs [after that], there is the possibility of an undesired result—that it might also occur after the *mūlaprakṛti* (the original base), the *anantara* (the immediate descendant), or the *yuvan* itself.
With the intention of providing a restrictive rule (*niyama*) to prevent this, he says: "only after what ends in a *gotra* suffix. It is not, however...

The meaning is "from those immediately following the root *prakṛti*. In the *Manoramā*, however, it is also established that in the first alternative, the meaning is "from that which ends in the suffix *yu*.
Regarding this, they say: when a youth (the fifth generation and so on) is intended, his *yuvan* [suffix] is the third.

Since [the suffix] would not apply because of the absence of a descendant (*anapatyatva*), this rule would serve merely as an injunction (*vidhi*) and not as a restrictive rule (*niyama*); consequently, the application of the suffix from a word ending in a *yuvan*-suffix would be unavoidable. Therefore, in this context, the position that "the descendant is [denoted] by the suffix *it* alone" should not be adopted. Others, however, say: in the first position...
By repeating the phrase "gotrād yaūni," the first [part] establishes a suffix where none was previously obtained, and the second part restricts it, stating:

"in the case of a *yaūna*, [the suffix] must come from the *gotra* [stem] alone. In this way, there is uniformity between this rule and the alternative view expressed as "ataḥ prācām api" (also for those who are prior to that). [The restriction is: "if from a *gotra*, then only in the case of a *yaūna*."

However, a contrary restriction has not been made here, because there is nothing to be excluded [by such a rule]. Nor should it be said that the secondary (*śaiṣika*) suffixes beginning with *cha* are what must be excluded, for this is indicated by the evidence of the rule "there is no elision (*aluk*) of the suffix when the feminine marker *ī* follows, provided it is not followed by a vowel. As for the phrase "but in the feminine": if this were to form a single syntactic unit with the word "not in the feminine" (*astryām*), [then the following would apply].

If the meaning is established as "in the case of a youth who is distinct from three [categories], such as the *gotra*," then, because there is no prohibition of the designation *yuvan* (youth) for women, a succession of suffixes would result for women belonging to the *yuvan* category.
Nor can this be resolved by the rule "one [suffix] in the *gotra*," because the designation *gotra* [is superseded] by the designation *yuvan*.

Because it would be contradicted. Now, if the meaning "the suffix *yuvan* is not [used] in the feminine" is established by means of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), then a young woman (*yuvatī*) would not be denoted by a *gotra* suffix. Consequently, the female descendant of Gārgya would not be called Gārgī; rather, there would only be a syntactical phrase. Therefore...

With the intention that this [sūtra] is solely for the purpose of prohibiting the designation *yus*, he explains: "not the designation *yu*. Here, the underlying intention is as follows: the rule "astriyām" (in the non-feminine) is divided; the word-form "yūnī" is carried over [from the previous sūtra]; and this is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule): wherever there is an injunction for the designation *yuvan*, [this applies].

Regarding the statement, "He worships with the mantra *ṭhastriyām*," this is the established interpretation. However, it would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as: "When a descendant in the paternal line is alive, the suffix *yuvan* [is used] except when feminine.

Therefore, regarding the suffix *iñ*: even if one accepts—on the basis of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *hakālataneṣu*—that secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) arise only from words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), the mention of the "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) under discussion is not redundant; rather, it serves a specific purpose. This is what [the author] intends to suggest by stating: "that nominal stem which ends in the vowel *a*."

The point is that if *ṭha* were a qualifier of a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), then in the intended meaning "the offspring of the two Dakṣas" and so forth, forms such as *dākṣi* would not be established. Why is it specified as *tapara* (followed by *t*)? [Consider: the offspring of *viśvapū-* is *vaiśvapaḥ*. However, in the expression "let it be given to the son of Daśaratha" (*dāśarathāya*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *asyedam* ("this belongs to him").
But when the intention is to express the state of being an offspring (*apatyatva*), the suffix *iñ* alone is used.
(903) Pāṇini 4.1.96: *bāhvādibhyaśca*. From the root *ādhṛ* in the sense of "shaking" (*loḍane*), [the suffix *iñ* is applied] to *eḍaka*.

Suggesting that Mādhava’s statement— “*saubāhaviḥ*, because the application of the suffix *apatya* (denoting offspring) to *bāhu* is impossible, [the rule] applies by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) to include what ends with it"— is to be considered doubtful, he says: "*bāhaviri*" [as in] "Ānanti, Bāhavi, Gārgya, Gautama."

The point is that the word *bāhu* exists as a proper name (*saṃjñārūpa*), based on the application of the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra* and examples from the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vṛtti*, and other sources. Regarding the form *ĀṬḍulomi*: although in the [Gaṇapāṭha] list—beginning with *bāhu*, *kṛṣṇa*, *yudhiṣṭhira*, *arjuna*, *pradyumna*, and so forth—the word *loman* appears alone.

Although [the suffix] is thus prescribed, by implication there is the inclusion of that which ends in it. According to the statement of Amara, "ārakāpyuḍu vā striyām," the word *uḍu* denotes a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). The offspring of one whose body hairs (*loman*) are like stars (*uḍu*) is *auḍulomi*. The offspring of one whose body hairs are like arrows (*śara*) is... [śāralomi].

[The suffix] *śāri* [is applied]. However, regarding the plural number, the rule for the suffix *a* (ākāra), which is an exception (*apavāda*) to *iñ*, has already been stated for bases ending in vowels. Examples:

*uḍulomāḥ*, *śaralomāḥ*. Here, in these rules prescribing specific forms (*pratipadavidhāna*), only those words that are established as technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*) from antiquity are understood, because they are more readily available in the mind (*śīghropasthitikatvāt*). Therefore, one who is contemporary...

In the case of *bāhu*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to form its offspring-name as *bāhavaḥ*, and not *iñ*. And it has been stated by Hari: "The meaning of the treatise should be applied to those words whose referents are clearly manifested, which are independent, and well-known in the world; [the rule] does not apply to their derivatives. [Thus, the suffix is] meaningless [in that context].
That which has an ambiguous meaning and that which is not in common usage are, respectively, excluded by the three qualifiers.

"In their utterances" means "in those similar to them. For this very reason, in the case of *śvāśuriḥ*—meaning the offspring of the father-in-law (*śvaśura*)—the rule *rājāśvaśurād* does not apply [to form the patronymic suffix]. [The word] *mātā* [is derived from the root] *mā*, meaning "she measures. Her sister...
