Regarding *prāgvateṣṭhañ*: although it would have been sufficient to state simply *hañ*, the specific mention of *prāgvateḥ* is intended to indicate that any exception (*apavāda*) such as *agada* occurring in the intervening section [between 5.1.1 and 5.1.18] is superseded by this rule.

The rule “*arvabhūmipṛthivībhyāmaṇañau*ṭhśīrṣaccedādyacce” and so forth [is stated]; by this, even when there is a separation [of the suffixes], it is for the purpose that in cases such as “*ārāyaṇa-turāyaṇa*,” the suffix *ṭhañ* itself should apply. And it is not the case that this [should be done] only in the sūtra concerning *pārāyaṇa* and so on.

It should be stated that *ṭhañ* is being prescribed here; for in the subsequent sūtra, there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of words such as *gopuccha*, and without this present sūtra, *ṭhañ* would not be obtained from them. Thus, in examples such as *gaupucchikaḥ* and *sāptatikaḥ*, this sūtra is required in this context to provide the meaning of *ṭhañ*.
It should be understood that [the suffix] has been introduced.
(1280) *Ārhād agopucchasaṅkhyāparimāṇāt ṭhak* (Pāṇini 5.1.19). From the word *ārhāt*, excluding *gopuccha*. [The sense of the sūtra is: "that which deserves it. Here, [the word] *adarham* [is used].

The intention is that what is imitated within the sūtra is not a word ending in the suffix *ac*, but rather only that which ends in a verbal root (*śabanta*), being a portion of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), as established by the commentary. Regarding the term "pervading" (*abhivyāpya*): the meaning is that in the example *vaitacchatrika*, the suffix *ṭhak* occurs in the sense of fitness (*arhatya*). Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: ...nanu... (But surely...)

If it is argued that the separate mention of number (*saṅkhyā*) is redundant because it is already included under dimension (*parimāṇa*)—since dimension is that by which something is measured or delimited, and since a thing is also delimited by number, therefore number too is simply dimension—then there is this verse from the *Ślokavārttika*: "Unmeasured (*unmāna*) is indeed measurement by height; but dimension (*parimāṇa*)..."
"Length shall be the measure on all sides, but the number is external on all sides.

The meaning of this is: having placed [the object] on a scale or similar device, the weight of gold and so forth is measured by means of a stone or other substance denoted by terms such as *pala*, which possesses a specific gravity determined by another substance.
That is unmāna (measurement). Āroha is height; pariṇāha is width.

That object made of wood or other materials by which rice and the like are measured through those two—height and width—belonging to itself, is parimāṇa, such as a prastha and so forth. The prefix *pari-* signifies "on all sides."

Length is extension; that by which it is measured is the measure (*pramāṇa*). And this occurs in some cases with respect to an object situated horizontally—as, for example, a cubit and so forth in the case of cloth and the like;
and in other cases with respect to an object situated in the vertical direction—as, for example, water in an elephant-trough.

"Water contained in both thighs. As for number (*saṅkhyā*), it is distinct from the three—weight (*unmāna*), capacity (*parimāṇa*), and linear measure (*pramāṇa*)—namely, from the *pala* and so forth, the *prastha* and so forth, and the *hasta* and so forth;
it consists of unity, duality, and so on. Although only number and dimension are under discussion here, there is a distinction made between weight and linear measure as well.
It should be understood that this was stated as an incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*).
(1281) *Asamāse niṣkadibhyaḥ* |5|1|20|.
[The suffix *śas* is applied] after the words *niṣka* and others when they do not form a compound (*asamāsa*). [The group begins with: *niṣka*, *paṇa*, *pāda*, *māṣa*, *vāha*, *droṇa*, *ṣaṣṭi*.
There are seven [items], beginning with *niṣka*. Among them, the word *droṇa* denotes a measure (*parimāṇa*), while the word *ṣaṣṭi* denotes a number (*saṅkhyā*);

since the suffix *ṭhañ* would have applied by those two rules, this specific statement is made. As for the other five, however, because they denote measures of weight (*unmāna*), the suffix *ṭhak* is already established by the preceding rule alone.

Some say that this statement is for the purpose of prohibiting compound formation. Others, however, say: in the previous sūtra, the word *parimāṇa* includes any measure distinct from number (*saṅkhyā*), whether it be a mere delimiting factor or not. Therefore, since *ṭhañ* would apply to all such cases, this statement is intended to prescribe *ṭhak*. And thus, [the rule] "but *arimāṇaṃ*... [is established].
It should not be said that the detailed exposition by means of the distinction "in all cases" (sarvataḥ) is useless;
for this [distinction] is useful in such instances as "when there is doubt regarding number, as well as length and breadth," according to both positions in the *Padamañjarī*.
This is clear.

(1282) *parimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ* | P. 7.3.17. [The suffix ṭhaÑ is applied after a word ending in a measure-word (*parimāṇa*), provided it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñā*) and does not end in *śāṇa*. Now, for what purpose is the condition "in a non-compound" (*asamāse*) stated here, given that we are dealing with the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)?

Since the desired result is established simply by the absence of the inclusion of that member [of the compound], he says: "the inclusion of the non-compound. Regarding *sugavyam*: [it is derived] by the rule *ugavādibhyo yat*. Regarding *yavāpūpyam*:

[it is derived] by the rule *vibhāṣā havirapūpādibhyaḥ*, which prescribes *yat*. Since it would have been established by the fact of being a modification of food (*annavikāra*) alone, [the mention of] *apūpa* and so forth...

The sense is that the statement in the *Nyāsa* commentary—that the rule of "inclusion of what follows" (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply by virtue of the power of the explicit recitation of the words—should be disregarded, because it contradicts the *Vṛtti* and other such texts. For this very reason, we stated regarding that sūtra: "The recitation of certain items such as *apūpa* and others is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). [The phrase] "from here onwards" [is used] because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
Even though the rule regarding the final element (*tadanta-vidhi*) has already been established, this [sūtra] is stated for the purpose of providing a specific restriction.
Why [is it said] "of those whose prior member is a numeral"? So that it does not apply here: *paramapārāyaṇaṃ vartayati* ("he performs the supreme recitation of the Veda").
It is accepted that for compounds preceded by a numeral, the inclusion of those ending in such a numeral applies before the suffix *vati*, provided there is no elision (*aluk*).

Thus, in the case of *dviśūrpa* ("two winnowing-baskets"), it is a *dvigu* compound formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Since this base does not end in an elided suffix, the rule "after a numeral-prefixed word, the suffix *añ* is optionally applied after *śūrpa*" applies.
For the suffix *añ* (or *aṇ*) that has been obtained, there is optionally elision (*luk*) by the rule "after *adhyardha* and before a word beginning with *t*. Thus, we have *dviśaurpika*.

By the rule "when the final member ends in a measure-word," there is vṛddhi of the final vowel of the second member. Since the suffix *ṭhañ* is not the cause for the formation of the *dvigu* compound, there is no elision [of the *ṭhañ*]. Even though in the sūtra "after *adhyardha*" [the term] *dvigu*...

Although it will be explained in the root text that *luk* (elision) applies specifically to the subsequent *arhīya* suffix, it must nevertheless be interpreted as applying to that which is caused by a *dvigu* compound; otherwise, elision would occur here [in the case of *dvimodaka*] for the suffix *ṭhañ* itself. This point will be made clear under the rule *adhyardhapūrva-dvigor luk*. [Question: Why [is the term] *taparaḥ* (followed by *t*) used?

The question is that even when an increase in length has been effected, there is no distinction in the form [itself], and thus the prohibition [of the long vowel] would not apply. Therefore, the sense is that the use of *tapara* (the long vowel marker) is necessary in order to avoid the absence of such a prohibition. And this...

The prevention of the absence of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) is effected for the first member (*pūrvapada*) in the alternative where *vṛddhi* does not occur. However, when *vṛddhi* does optionally occur for the first member, then,
because the *taddhita* suffix is a cause of *vṛddhi* that benefits the result, the vowel *a* of the second member (*uttarapada*) [is affected].
It should be understood that even when the addition of the suffix *vṛddhi* is prohibited, the prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) still applies.
(1283) *śatācca ṭhanyatāvaśate* | Pāṇini 5.1.21. [Sūtra:
*śatāt ca*. When "not one hundred" (*aśate*) is to be expressed, the suffixes *ṭhan* and *ṭa* occur in the sense of the *ārhīya* (relating to price). This is by the subsequent rule.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *kan*. The particle *ca* serves to carry forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the rule "in a non-compound (*a-samāse*)" from the rule for *ṭhak*.

Regarding the example *dviśatakam*: "two and a hundred" (*dvau ca śataṃ ca*) form *dviśatam* by means of collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). From that, the suffix *kan* is applied by the desired rule: "In the case of words preceded by a numeral, there is inclusion of the final member when the elision of *ṭi* does not occur."
The sense is that since [the suffix] is obtained even from a compound, it is appropriate to bring forward the rule "ṭha-samāse" (Pāṇini 5.1.20).

(1284) *saṅkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan* (Pāṇini 5.1.22). Regarding the expression "ending in 'ti' or 'śat'": this is a compound with elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*), meaning "that which ends in 'ti' together with that which ends in 'śat'. Then...

"Pañcaka" is an example of a worldly number. "Bahuka" is an example of a technical (paribhāṣikī) number. "Sāptatika" [is formed] with the suffix *ṭhan*; because it has the marker *ñ*, there is vṛddhi of the first vowel.
When the single-substitute *ik* replaces the *ṭha*, the letter *i* is elided by the rule "of that which has *ṭh*" (*ṭhyasyeti ca*). [This applies] to the meaningful word "ti."

The exclusion of the word *ti* as a constituent part [of the suffix *kat*] does not apply to the suffix *ka*. Thus we have *katikaḥ* and *cātvāriṃśatkaḥ*, according to the rule "after a word ending in *t*, *s*, *u*, or *k*, the suffix *ka* is added" (Pāṇini 5.1.128). [Now, regarding the suffix *vat*:
] 5.1.23. *vator iḍ vā* ("After the suffix *vat*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied").

Regarding the rule *vator iḍ vā*: the term *vataḥ* is the genitive case of *vat*, and since it is understood as *aṇ* (by the rule *aṇ*), it is interpreted as the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) of the first case (*prathamā*).

Thus he says: "after a word ending in *vat*, the suffix *kan* [is added]. In the form *tāvatikaḥ*, the suffix *vatup* is applied by the rule *yatadetebhyaḥ*, and the substitution of *āt* occurs by the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ*.

(1286) *viṃśatitriṃśadbhyāṃ ḍvun asaṃjñāyām* |5|1|24|. It should be stated [that the suffix is applied] after *viṃśati* and *triṃśat*. Otherwise, because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of stems ending in *ti* and *śat*, it would be difficult to obtain the suffix *kan* after *viṃśati* and *triṃśat*; this is the intended meaning. In the form *viṃśakaḥ*, [the *ti* is replaced by *i*] by the rule *i viṃśater ḍiti*.

There is elision [of the suffix]. It should be stated that this applies even after the word *ardha*. Thus, [the form] *ārdhika* [is derived]. Since the word *ardha* here refers to half of a *kārṣāpaṇa*, it cannot be said that there is a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) with respect to the "portion," as is the case when it refers to a mere part; for [the meaning] is determined by the context and other such factors.

It should be understood that once the specific nature of the entity (*bhāva*) is known, there is no lack of capacity [for the suffix]. By this, the assertion of certain [grammarians]— that because the word *ardha* is dependent, the suffix *ṭiṭhan* applies only after a compound ending in it, as in *droṇārdhikaḥ* and *prasthārdhikaḥ*— is refuted.

(1287) *śūrpādañ anyatarasyām* |5|1|26|. The suffix *añ* [is applied] after the word *śūrpa*. Since the word *śūrpa* denotes a measure (*parimāṇa*), the suffix *ṭhañ* would have been required; however, *añ* is prescribed as an optional exception (*apavāda*) to that.

(1288) *Śatamāna-viṃśatika-sahasra-vasanād aṇ* [Pāṇini 5.1.27]. Regarding the phrase "of *ṭhañ*, *ṭhak*, and *ka*": since *śatamāna* is a measure (*parimāṇa*), the suffix *ṭhañ* would have been applicable [by 5.1.19]. *Viṃśatika* means "bought for twenty"; this is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*). For if it were not a technical term, [the suffix] *ṭhan* would apply after *viṃśati*.

The suffix *ḍvun* should be applied after the word *triṃśat*. If it refers to a name (*saṃjñā*) of a measure (*parimāṇa*), then the suffix *ṭhañ* is obtained; if it refers to something else, then the suffix *ṭhak* is obtained. However, from the word *vasana*, only *ṭhak* is applicable. Since the word *sahasra* denotes a number, [the rule] "after a number ending in *ati* or *śat*" applies.
The distinction is that [the suffix] *kan* is applied when [the number] has been reached.

(1289) *adhyardhapūrvadvigor lug asaṃjñāyām* |5|1|28|. [The rule begins with] *adhyardhapūrva*. That in which a half is added (*adhyārūḍham ardhaṃ yasmin*) is *adhyardha*. [From the rule] *rādibhyaḥ*...

In the term *dhātujasya*, there is an elision of the final member [of the compound]. Having formed a *bahuvrīhi* containing another *bahuvrīhi*—namely, that in which the word *adhyardha* precedes—the compound *adhyardhapūrvadviguḥ* is formed by means of a *dvandva* according to the rule *adhyardhapūrvaśca dviguśca*.
The masculine gender is Vedic (or based on the *sūtra*). The intention is that the word *dvigoḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), and not in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
He explains [the rule] beginning with *adhyardhapūrvāt* and so forth; this has been explained according to the method of the Vṛttikāra. Here, the Vārttika states: *vigorluki tannimitagrahaṇam*.

It should be stated that when there is elision (*luk*) of a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) that is the cause of a *dvigu* compound, [the feminine suffix] is also elided. For example, from two *śūrpa*s...
"Purchased for two *śūrpa*s" is *dviśūrpam*; "purchased with two *śūrpa*s" is *dviśaurpikam*.

However, in the previously cited example, this is so that the suffix *ṭhañ* does not elide. Now, one might object: if the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which is purchased by *dviśūrpī*—where *dviśūrpī* is the collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) of two *śūrpa*s"—then the form would not be *dviśūrpam*.
It might be argued: "In this case, since the *dvigu* compound is not the cause for the secondary suffix (*taddhita*), the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *adhyardha-* would not apply;
however, if one explains the rule as 'after a *dvigu*,' then our desired result is established.
This is not so, because of another statement: "When a specific meaning is not understood, [the suffix is applied] even from that which is not its cause."

This is because it has been stated by the author of the Vārttika himself: "Where the meaning of the *taddhita* suffix does not differ from that of the *dvigu* compound, one must state that the elision (*luk*) of the suffix following a *dvigu* occurs even from that [base] which is not the cause for the application of that *taddhita*. Such being the case, [the form] is *dviśūrpa*.

Since the meaning of "purchased with two winnowing-baskets" (*dviśūrpyā krītam*) does not differ from that of a *taddhita* derivative formed with a *dvigu* compound, the *luk* (elision) of the *taddhita* suffix following a collective *dvigu* indeed occurs; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. In fact, however, one should rely on the genitive case (*dvigoḥ*) in the sūtra.

Having explained that "the taddhita suffix is applied to that which is the cause of vigour," it is possible to reject the first Vārttika. However, assuming that in the analytical statement (vigraha) "bought for two winnowing baskets" (*dviśūrpyā krītam*),
the suffix is applied only to *dviśūrpa* and not to the word *dviśūrpī*, on the basis of the principle regarding parts (*avayavinyāya*).

The second [objection] can also be refuted. Is it not the case that the word *adhyardha* denotes a number, and thus it is counted in common usage as "one and a half" (*eko ’dhyardhaḥ*, *dvau*)? For this very reason, we have the suffix *kan* in *adhyardhaka*, the *dvigu* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in *adhyardhakasaṃsa*, and so on in cases such as *adhyardhasaṃvatsarika*.

If it is argued that the rule "there is vṛddhi of the final syllable of a numeral and of a word denoting a number of years" already applies [to *adhyardha*], then what is the purpose of including the mention of "preceded by *adhyardha*" (*adhyardhapūrvagrahaṇa*)? To this they reply: this is for the sake of making known that "this [term *adhyardha*] does not undergo any operation pertaining to numerals. By this, [it is understood that...].

This occurs except in the case of *kandvi-gu*, compounds with a subsequent member (*otarapada*), and words characterized by *vṛddhi*. For example: *adhyardhaṃ karoti* ("he performs [the action] one and a half times"). Here, the suffixes *ku*, *tṛ*, and *vasuc* do not apply. One who, having once completed an action ending in its fruit, then repeats that very same action but desists in the middle, is described in this way.

Regarding *pāñcakalāyikam*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "that of which the measure is five *kalāya* beans," the compound is formed by the rule *adhyardhapūrvād dvigor lug* (Pāṇini 5.1.28) [with the application of *adhyardha* as a qualifier]. Then, by the rule *tadasya parimāṇam* (Pāṇini 5.1.57), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied. In the same way, *pāñcalohitikam* should also be understood; it refers to five red *guñjā* seeds.

In the analysis *parimāṇam asya* ("of which this is the measure"), the compound and the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) are formed as before. Due to the rule *hasyāḍhea taddhite* ("the [feminine] suffix *ā* is elided when a *taddhita* beginning with *aḍha* follows"), there is the absence of the vowel *i* and the nasal *n* in the word *lohinī*, resulting in the masculine form. These two [suffixes] are applied to denote the name of a specific measure. The exclusion of the term *asaṃjñā* (non-name) applies to that which ends in a secondary derivative suffix.
This is a qualification [of the word *samāhāra*], but not of the *dvigu* compound. And this has been explained by the author of the *Vṛtti* in accordance with the intention of the *Sūtra*;

thus it has been stated here as well. However, in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*, the mention of the term *asaṃjñā* (non-technical name) is rejected. For instance, the mention of *asaṃjñā* is a qualification of the *dvigu*.
The two compounds *pañcakalāpa* and *pañcalohita* are technical names (*saṃjñā*) that are formed as *dvigu* compounds with the elision of the *taddhita* suffix; however,
the suffix *ṭhañ* which arises from them is indeed heard [in pronunciation], because there is no elision of it since the *dvigu* is not the cause for such elision.

(1290) *vibhāṣā kārṣāpaṇasahasrābhyām* || 5.1.29 || The word *vibhāṣā* [is understood here]. [This refers to] the rule *ṭiṭhanor luk*. It should be understood that in the alternative case (*pratyādeśapakṣe*) where the suffix is replaced by its substitute, the elision (*luk*) does not occur, because the substitute is prescribed as being conditioned by the presence of the suffix itself.

Regarding the term *adhyardhasahasram*: there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule “*ata-māna-viṃśatike*” [Pāṇini 5.1.27]. However, in the alternative case where that elision does not occur, there is vṛddhi of the final vowel of the second member according to the rule “*saṅkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsara-saṅkhyasya ca*” [Pāṇini 7.3.15]. This is because it was stated just now that the word *adhyardha* denotes a number. [The rule continues: “After [compounds] preceded by *dvi*, *tri*, etc. [Pāṇini 5.1.28].

The mention of *adhyardha* (one and a half), although it recurs from a previous rule, is not connected here; however, the term *vigau* (in the case of two or three) is indeed connected in order to exclude the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In this matter, the commentary alone is the authority. Furthermore, since the formation [of the word *dviniṣka*] would already be established by the rule *vitribhyāṃ niṣkāt*, the inclusion of the word *pūrva* (preceded by) is for a specific purpose.
Haradatta says that the purpose [of the suffix] is to be considered. Regarding the term *dvinaiṣkika*, [the suffix] *iṣṭhan* is applied according to the rule *rāgvateṣṭhañ*.

However, in another opinion, it is stated in the *Manoramā* that the suffix *ṭhak* is used; for even in that other opinion, since there is no *ṭhak* after words such as *niṣka* when they are part of a compound, only *ṭhañ* is taken as the measure of the portion.

In that view, since weight (*unmāna*) is also a type of measure (*parimāṇa*), the suffix *ṭhak* would be excluded by the rule "ṭhagopucche" and so forth; thus, in the absence of *ṭhak*, the suffix *ṭhañ* would apply after words such as *niṣka*. For even though *ṭhak* is prescribed when there is no compound, *ṭhañ* alone would apply when there is a compound—so say others.
In the case of *arimāṇāntasya*, there is vṛddhi of the final syllable of the second member. Because of the connection with the rule *vigauḥ*, there is no elision (*luk*) here.
For example, two niṣkas make a *dviniṣka*; what is purchased with that is *dvinaiṣkika*.
Since the rule *adhyardhapūrva-* does not apply here, there is likewise no elision in the case of *adhyardhanaiṣkika*.

[The suffix *kan*] occurs after *bista*. (5.1.31) [The rule] "and after *bista*": by the word *ca* ("and"), the term *pūrvāt* ("after a word preceded by *vi-* or *tri-*") from the previous rule (*vitripūrvāt*) is drawn forward.
The result of that is that it is not "drawn along" (*anukṛṣṭa*) to what follows; thus, there is an absence of its recurrence in subsequent rules.

(1292) *viṃśatikātkhaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.1.32: "After *viṃśatika*, [the suffix] *kha* [is applied]. Since the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise be applicable by the rule *atamap-aviṃśatike*, and since that [suffix *aṇ*] is elided (*luk*), [the suffix *kha* is introduced].
In this case, *īkan* is prescribed [after the word *khārī*].

(1293) *khāryā īkan* | Pāṇini 5.1.33. After *khārī*: when the suffix *ṭhañ* would otherwise apply by the rule "the measure of this" (*adasya parimāṇam*), and when the elision (*luk*) of that suffix would also apply, [the suffix *īkan* is ordained instead].

The suffix *ikan* is prescribed; however, in the rule for *kan*, the short vowel [of the penultimate] would apply by the rule "eṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.72). Furthermore, even in the prescription of *ikan*, the desired form is not established because of the elision [of the final phoneme] by the rule "yasyeti ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.148); this is the intended meaning.
(1294) Pāṇini 5.1.34: *paṇapādamāṣaśatādyat*. The suffix *yat* is applied after the words *paṇa*, *pāda*, *māṣa*, and *śata* [to denote a price].
"Only that which has the meaning of a limb of a living being. This is the intended meaning:

in the rule "pādasya padājyātigopahateṣu," only the word *pāda* signifying a limb of a living being is understood, because only such a *pāda* can logically have a connection with words like *ājāti*, which denote movement. And so it is.

In examples such as *adyati*, that same [term] continues to apply; however, here, due to association (*sāhacarya*) with *paṇa* and *māṣa*, only those words denoting measure are understood. (1295) *śāṇādvā* || 5.1.35 || [The suffix *kan* is optionally applied after the word *śāṇa*].

Regarding the suffix *ṭhañ* in the sense of "in a portion": although *śāṇa* is a measure (*unmāna*), nevertheless, according to the view of those who maintain that in the rule *ṭhārhāt* (Pāṇini 5.1.19), the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is understood through its etymological derivation (*yogavṛtti*) as "that by which something is measured or delimited"— therefore signifying any delimiting factor at all— this [suffix] applies here as well.
The sense is that [the suffix] *ṭhañ* occurs when there is an absence of the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*). However, according to the primary view, it should be understood as *ṭhak* itself.

Regarding the rule *śāṇād vā*, it should have been stated as *ataśca*; since [the suffix] was already obligatorily obtained by the preceding rule, this is for the purpose of providing an option. And thus, instead of employing the mention of *śata* in the previous rule, [one could simply say] *śata-śāṇābhyām*.
They say it is proper to say "vetyeva" (or simply "eva"). [Examples: *adhyardhaśatyam* / *adhyardhaśatam*;

*pañcaśatyam* / *pañcaśatam*. In the absence of that [suffix], there is elision (*luk*) of the *kan* suffix which has the characteristic of a numeral. However, the rule "after a word ending in *ata*, the suffixes *ṭhan* and *ṭi* [are applied]" does not apply here.
In that regard, because the mention of "non-compound" (*asamāsa*) is carried over [from the previous rule],
[the rule] *dvitripūrvādaṇ ca* [is applied]. This is a Vārttika inserted by the author of the Vṛtti into the Sūtras.

With the intention that the inclusion of the word "śata" (hundred) is not connected here because of the authority of the Bhāṣya and other sources, he says: "only from *śāṇa*. However, the author of the Nyāsa, mistaking a Vārttika prescribing the suffix *aṇ* for a Sūtra, explained it thus: "The Sūtra should have been formulated as 'śata-śāṇābhyāṃ vā'."
Regarding the mention of "a hundred" (*śata*) in the preceding rule *aṇvādeḥ*, this is its purpose:

although the word "hundred" (*śata*) is carried over by virtue of being *svarita*-accented, it is connected only with the rule *āṇādvā*; however, it is not connected with the subsequent rule *vitripūrvādaṇ ca*.

Therefore, [the suffix] *aṇ* does not apply after the word *śata*. This description of the functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) is consistent if it were a rule (*sūtra*) prescribing *aṇ*, but not otherwise; let this matter rest for now. Regarding "the three forms" (*trairūpya*), he demonstrates this with the words beginning "dvaiśāṇam": one form is by means of *aṇ*, and the second is when there is elision (*luk*) of *ṭhan*.

"Yat is the third; there are thirteen beginning with ṭhañ. Now, an objection: only eleven suffixes have been introduced as the subject matter, since the suffix *yat* is prescribed by two separate rules; if it were counted twice, there would be twelve, and thus the statement "thirteen" is indeed difficult to justify. Nor...

It should not be argued that the number thirteen is easily established by taking the suffix *thañ* obtained from the rule "ūrdhvādañanyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 5.1.118); for, by the same logic, there would be the undesirable consequence of obtaining fifteen, since one could likewise take the suffixes *yañ* and *thañ* obtained from the rule "āṇo dve" (Pāṇini 7.3.52). Nor...

The derivation is accomplished by counting the *aṇ* suffix mentioned in the Vārttika "after words preceded by dvi or tri, [the suffix] aṇ [is applied]" along with the twelve [suffixes] included in the Sūtra. According to the method stated above, in the rule "ṭiṭhan after kaṃsa," it should be stated that "after ardha, [the suffix] ṭhañ [is applied]."

The suffix *ṭiṭhan* found in the very sūtra "ārṣāpaṇāṭṭiṭhan" is not distinct [from the one mentioned elsewhere], as it is referred to by the words *adhyardha* and *kārṣāpaṇa*. However, the suffix *aṇ* found in the vārttika "vitripūrvādaṇ ca" is indeed distinct, because of the [restriction] "atamānaviṃśatike" regarding that *aṇ*.
Because it is impossible to refer to [something] as being situated at a distance.
(1297) *tena krītam* (5.1.37). Regarding *tena krītam*: after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*), suffixes are applied according to the rules prescribed for the sense of "bought with that."

[The suffixes] would be *ṭhañ*. [This is because] in the rule *ṭhārhāt* (Pāṇini 5.1.19), since *ṭhak* is excluded by the exception (*paryudāsa*) beginning with *gopuccha*, the meaning is that *ṭhañ* occurs after the words *gopuccha*, *saptati*, and *prastha* in the absence of *ṭhak*. Now, [one might object]: "Purchased by Devadatta..."

If it is argued that this leads to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), as in cases such as "bought with the hand" (*pāṇinā krītam*) or "bought with contentment" (*saṃtoṣeṇa krītam*), the reply is as follows: here, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) alone is the capable case-ending (*samarthavibhakti*); moreover, it must be produced from a word that presents the substance serving as the price (*mūlyadravya*), and not from any other word. However, in other instances, it does not apply because there is no such expression.

[This is] a suffix (*pratyaya*). And this is understood from the formation of the technical term "taddhita" [in Pāṇini 4.1.76], because of the explanation that "those which are beneficial (*hita*) for those applications (*prayoga*) are taddhitas.
(1298) *id goṇyāḥ* | 1.2.50 | [The substitution of *it* occurs in place of the final vowel of the word *goṇī*.]
"An exception to the elision [of the feminine suffix]" means that this is an exception to the elision of the feminine suffix which would otherwise apply by the rule "uktāddhitaluki.

(1299) *goyacyo'saṅkhyāparimāṇāśvāder yat* |5|1|39|. This prescribes the suffix *yat* after words ending in *go* or having two vowels (*dvyac*), provided they do not denote a number, a measure, or the word *aśva*.

Regarding *pañcaka*: the suffix *kan* is applied by virtue of the characteristics of number (*saṃkhyā*). Regarding *āśmika*: the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "made from stone" (*aśmanaḥ nimittam*); there is elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*) by the rule "astaddhite" [Pāṇini 6.4.149].
(1300) *putrāc cha ca* [Pāṇini 5.1.40]: the suffix *cha* is also applied after the word *putra*.

And regarding the word *putrīya*: since the suffix *cha* (forming *īya*) is invariably prescribed by the rule *ovadyacaḥ*, this statement [in the Vārttika] is necessary. If it is asked, "How can there be a sacrifice called *putrīya*? For a sacrifice (*kratu*) is neither a *saṃyoga* (conjunction) nor an *utpāta* (calamity)," Haradatta replies to this: through the etymological derivation "that by which one is joined" (*saṃyujyate ’nena*), the sacrifice (*kratu*) is indeed a *saṃyoga*.

For it is by means of performing a sacrifice that a person is joined with the fruit; therefore, the sacrifice and so forth are also "conjunctions" (*saṃyoga*), and there is no insistence that they are merely "relations" (*saṃbandha*).
(1301) [The suffixes] *āṇ* and *añ* are applied after the words *sarvabhūmi* and *pṛthivī*. Pāṇini 5.1.41.

The suffixes *mañ* and *añ* occur after [the word] *sarva-bhūmi*, according to their respective order. (1302) *tasyeśvaraḥ* | 5.1.42. Regarding *tasyeśvaraḥ*: although the rule would have been established by the recurrence of the word *asya* from the previous rule *asya nimittam*, the word *asya* is stated again for the sake of clarity.

The mention [of *nirdeśa*] is for the purpose of excluding the meaning of "that which is indicated by a form" (*nimittarūpapratyayārtha*). Otherwise, even Īśvara might be considered a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix, as in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and origin (*utpāda*).
(1303) Regarding that, [the rule] is: *vaditi iti ca* 5.1.43.

In this context, the rule *vadi* is also [to be understood] as a separate *yogavibhāga* for the sake of subsequent rules and to prevent the application of the rule according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*).
Regarding *tasya vāpaḥ*, he states "of the *prastha*" because the genitive case is used in relation to the act of sowing (*vāpa*), as indicated by the word "of this" (*asya*).
The sense is that the genitive case would indeed occur in the agentive sense, as in examples such as "devadattasya vāpaḥ kṣetram" ("the field is the sowing of Devadatta").
Regarding the word *khārīkam*:
[it is formed by the rule] "tadasmin vṛddhyāyalābhaśulkopadā dīyate" (Pāṇini 5.1.47).

Therefore, in this context, after a word having the first case-meaning, a suffix is applied as prescribed when the sense of the locative case (asmin) is intended. The explicit mention of *śulka* is for the sake of elaboration, because it too is a specific kind of income (*āya*).
Thus, according to the rule "after *haga*, *āya*, and *sthāna*, [the suffix] *ṭhak* occurs," Haradatta says: *śaulkaśālikaḥ*. [The suffix] *upadā-*...

Regarding the word *dīyate*: after the *s* of *jas*, there is *ru*-tva (the substitution of *r*), followed by *yatva* (the substitution of *ya*), and then the elision of *y*. Regarding *sāhasra*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule beginning with "atamāne" (Pāṇini 5.1.27). Regarding *rakṣānirveśa*: *nirveśa* means wages (*bhṛti*).
A wage that has protection as its cause is a *rakṣānirveśa*; this is a compound formed with a genitive of relation (*saṃbandha-ṣaṣṭhī*).

"Equal," and so forth. The sense is that since the desired result is achieved by expressing the recipient (*sampradāna*) itself as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) need not be observed. (1306) *pūraṇārdhāṭ ṭhan* | 5.1.48 | [The suffix *ṭhan* is added after ordinal numbers and the word *ardha* to form feminine nouns denoting a part].

*Pūraṇa-ardhāt ṭhan*: The suffix *ṭhan* shall be applied after a word expressing a "filler" (*pūraṇa*)—meaning that by which something is filled—as well as after the word *ardha*. For example, *ardhika*. [Objection: Since it is stated that "it should be mentioned that [the suffix] *ṭiṭhan* applies after *ardha*," the suffix *ṭiṭhan* would be expected; and if that were present, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would occur. However, this is not desired.
The suffix *ṭāp* [is applied].
(1307) *bhāgād yañ ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.49).
Regarding the word *rupakasya*: *rūpaka* means a *kārṣāpaṇa*. It is a conventional term (*rūḍha*). And thus...
The intended meaning is that, because it depends upon a substance belonging to the Lord (*bhāgavat*), its lack of capacity (*asāmarthya*) should not be raised as an objection here.

(1308) *taddharati vahatyāvahati bhārād vaṃśādibhyaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.1.50. [This rule means: after words such as *vaṃśa* when they signify a load (*bhāra*), the suffix *ṭhan* is added. Now, one might ask: how can words such as *vaṃśa* [be so used]?

Because they have become a burden, he says "to those who have become a burden" (*bhārabhūtān*). The intention is that the word "burden" (*bhāra*) qualifies the bamboo poles and so forth by way of their function (*artha*). Although one might expect the form "from the burdens" (*bhārebhyaḥ*), the term "from the [individual] burden" (*hārāt*) is used in the Sūtra because it intends to express the connection with each individual member.
(1309) *vasnadravyābhyāṃ ṭhankanau* || 5.1.51 || [The suffixes] *ṭhan* and *kan* are added after the words *vasna* and *dravya*. *Vasnika* means "one who deals in goods"; *vasna* means "price.
(1310) *saṃbhavatyavaharati pacati* || 5.1.52 || [The suffix *ṭhan* is added after a word denoting a measure when it means] "is capable of containing," "deals in," or "cooks."

It contains and carries away. The meaning of the root *sambhū* (to contain) is "the non-excess of the measure of the contained over the measure of the container," which constitutes a subordinate act of holding (*dhāraṇa*). Because it is thus transitive, the subsequent application of the accusative case in the word *tat* (it) is not contradictory. This is what he says: "a *prastha* within itself."
Regarding *prāsthikī*: the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied because it ends in the suffix *ṭhañ*.
He explains "he brings" (*avaharati*) as "he collects" (*upasaṃharati*).

Regarding "he cooks that" (*tatpacati*), there is the suffix *aṇ* after the word *droṇa*. In this *vārttika*, the mention of the root *pac* (to cook) [is for the sake of including other similar roots].

The phrase "it arises from" (*saṃbhavati*) is used for the purpose of excluding [the application of the suffix] to that which merely carries [the measure]. In the case of rice and other grains measured by a *droṇa*, the word *droṇa* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*). The intention is that the suffix *ṭhak* does not apply because, according to one view, the suffix *ṭhañ* applies to measures such as the *āḍhaka* and others due to their being units of measurement.

(1311) *dvigoḥ ṣṭhṃaśca* | Pāṇini 5.1.54. The analysis of the sūtra is *dvigoḥ* and *ṣṭhan*. He explains this by saying "because it has the indicatory letter *ṣ*" (*ṣitvāt*). Regarding the form *dvyāḍhakikī*, one should not suspect the addition of the augment *aij* (as prescribed by *ayvābhyām*), because that augment is applied in conjunction with the prohibition of *vṛddhi*.
Because there is no possibility of its application due to that specific rule and because of the increase [of the suffix]. Regarding the word *aparimāṇa*:
the sense is that although a heap (*ācita*) is a measure (*parimāṇa*), it is not specifically mentioned in that sūtra.
(1312) *kulijālluk khau ca* | 5.1.55 | [The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *kulija*, and there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of the suffix, as well as the suffix *kha*.]

Regarding *dvaikulijikī*: it is said that even the word *kulija* is intended in the rule *ṭha-saṃjñā-śāṇayoḥ*, and therefore there is no vṛddhi of the subsequent member. (1313) *tad asya parimāṇam* (5.1.57).

That is its measure (*parimāṇa*). Here, by the word "measure," any delimiting factor whatsoever is understood, and not only measurement on all sides, because in the subsequent sūtra, number is qualified by "measure. [The example is:
"Sixty is the measure of his life" → *ṣāṣṭika* ("lasting sixty years"). [This is derived from] the rule *o'sya*.

Furthermore, because the term *adasya* ("belonging to this") is included in the present rule, in examples such as *dviṣāṣṭikaḥ* ("having sixty-two as its measure of life") and *triṣāṣṭikaḥ*, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *adhyardhapūrvād dvigor lug* does not occur.
This is clear from the *Kāśikā* and other commentaries. Regarding the "previous rule" (*pūrvasūtra*), by that [rule], [the word] *pañca gāvaḥ* ("five cows") [is formed].

In such cases as "a herd of five cows" (*pañcako go-saṅghaḥ*), the formation is established because the number serves to delimit the measure (*parimāṇa*) of the object. However, when the number serves to delimit the meaning of the base itself— as in "five cows belong to this herd" (*pañca gāvo 'sya saṅghasya*)— then the suffix does not occur, because the measure is not the meaning intended by the suffix.
And this is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *sūtra* "ṭhaḷ-arhād-agopuccha" (Pāṇini 5.1.19).

It should be stated that when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is intended, a suffix is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Thus, [we have] "pañcaiva" (exactly five). Regarding the rule "ḍavidhiḥ stome" (Pāṇini 5.1.58), the addition of the marker *ḍ* is for the purpose of eliding the *ti* in "ekaviṃśati," and also for the purpose of eliding the *ti* in "trayastriṃśat" and so forth.

The rule regarding the *stoma* is as follows: "There are fifteen mantras. For the scripture states: "One should praise with the *āma*," and "A single *sāman* is performed upon three verses (*tryṛca*). In that case, by repeating the three-verse hymn five times, there are fifteen mantras. In the seventeen-fold *stoma*, the final verse is repeated seven times.

Regarding the repetition (*āvṛti*): for the first and middle [stomas], it is exactly five times; however, it should be understood that for the twenty-one-fold stoma (*ekaviṃśa-stoma*), there is a sevenfold repetition of the triplet of verses (*tryṛca*). "The meters and the cow" (*cchandogauḥ*) means by the Sāma singers (*sāmaga*).
The words *paṅkti*, *vaṃśati*, *triṃśat*, *catvāriṃśat*, *pañcāśat*, *ṣaṣṭi*, *saptati*, *aśīti*, *navati*, and *śata* [are used as feminine]. 5.1.59.
*Paṅkti-viṃśati*. The phrase "the measure of this" (*adasya parimāṇam*) is understood [from the previous rule].

There is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of the word *pañcan*, the suffix *ti* is added, and by the rule "of *u* there is *ku*" (*oḥ ku*), there is the substitution of *k* for *n*.
According to the *Kāśikā*: "That which has five feet as its measure is the *paṅkti* metre. Here, the word *pada* is a synonym for *pāda* (foot/line).
Thus says Haradatta. Regarding the term "conventional words" (*rūḍhiśabda*): accordingly, one should not insist upon the meaning of the individual parts [of the compound] here.

For the word *paṅkti* has multiple meanings. It occurs in the sense of a sequential arrangement—as in *brāhmaṇapaṅkti* (a row of Brahmins) and *pipīlikāpaṅkti* (a row of ants). And it occurs in the sense of the number ten—as in *paṅktiratha* (a chariot with ten horses).

The meaning is "Daśaratha. For there is a specific meter [defined as]—"that which has five feet, each consisting of five syllables. Thus, it should be understood that this particular meaning applies only to this specific meter and not elsewhere.
They do not read [the rule] as "the substitution of *vi* for two *daśan*s, the suffix *śati*, and the status of not being a word (*apadatvam*)."

There is the substitution of *tri* for three tens (*daśat*), and the suffix *śat* is added. According to another opinion, however, there is the substitution of *triṃ*. That which has three tens as its measure is *triṃśat*. Similarly, for four [tens], *catvāriṃ*; for five [tens], *pañcāśat*. From these two as well, the suffix *śat* is added. For six tens, *ṣaṣ* is substituted, and *ti* is added.
The suffix *ti* is applied, and there is the absence of the *pada* designation. "Six tens" (*ṣaḍ daśataḥ*) constitute its measure; thus it is *ṣaṣṭiḥ*.

After those three [words] as well, only the suffix *ti* is applied. Seven tens are *sapta*, eight tens are *aśīti*, nine tens are *navati*, and for ten tens there is the change to *śat*; and that [suffix *ti*].
The suffix *pratyaya*. That which has ten tens as its measure is a hundred (*śatam*).
(1315) *Pañca-daśatau varge vā* |5|1|60|.
*Pañca* and *daśa*: these two, ending in the suffix *ḍati*, are irregularly formed (*nipātyete*) when a group (*varga*) is to be expressed. "Of this... (*adasya*)...
The term "parimāṇam" (measure) continues to apply here. Regarding "daśa": it means that ten is its measure. Regarding "pakṣe" (optionally):
the intention is that because of the inclusion of the word "vā" (or), the suffix *kan* also occurs by virtue of the rule "aṅkhyāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 5.1.58).
(1316) Pāṇini 5.1.62: The suffix *ḍaṇ* is applied after "triṃśat" and "catvāriṃśat" when forming a proper name (*saṃjñā*) denoting a Brāhmaṇa.

Regarding the forms *triṃśat* and *catvāriṃśat*: the genitive dual ending is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*) in the sense of the ablative. However, in the reading *‘atvāriṃśato brāhmaṇe’*, the ablative singular is derived from a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*).
In this context, it would have been more appropriate to indicate [the rule] with a genitive compound as *‘brāhmaṇasaṃjñāyām’*. For instance:

If [the rule] "sati ‘rāhmaṇasya cetsaṃjñā’" (when there is the designation ‘Brāhmaṇa’) is stated, the meaning becomes clear. Otherwise, if it were [stated as] "yasya kasyacitsaṃjñāyāṃ brāhmaṇasthe ca prayoge," an unintended meaning might be possible;
consequently, the suffix *ḍaṇ* would not be established in either the Vedic mantras or the common language (*bhāṣā*), yet that is desired.

Therefore, it should be explained that the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī-artha*) in accordance with the intended meaning. However, in the *Kāśikā*, it is explained as "when the Brāhmaṇa is the object to be denoted. Regarding the suffixes beginning with *ṭhañ*: an example of *ṭhañ* is *prāsthikaḥ* (worth a *prastha*), *drauṇikaḥ* (worth a *droṇa*), and so forth; these should be inferred accordingly.
He provides an example for the suffix *ṭhak*, which is included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*):
(1317) *tadarhati* (Pāṇini 5.1.63). Thus: *śvaitacchatrikaḥ* ("one who deserves a white umbrella"), as well as *khārīkaḥ*, *śatyaḥ*, *śatikaḥ*, and *sāhasraḥ*.
Examples such as these should be cited.

(1318) *chedādibhyo nityam* (Pāṇini 5.1.64). Regarding the mention of *nityam* (always) here, it is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *ṭhak*, just as it was in the rule *ityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.10).

This is not for the purpose of excluding a statement that would otherwise be obtained through the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, because its exclusion is already established by the very force of the rule's formulation; rather, it emphasizes that it is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix—namely, "that which deserves cutting eternally. In the *Bhāṣya*, however, the inclusion of the term "eternally" (*nitya*) has been rejected.
The *Manoramā* states that the intention [of the author] was that the rule itself should not exist; the underlying thought is as follows:

here, the mention of "eternal" (*nitya*) is not an attribute of the meaning of the suffix, because the sense of "that which deserves cutting eternally" is impossible. For its [cutting] occurs only at another time.

Because it functions as a restrictive rule (*chedapravartanāt*). Nor should one suspect that the rejection of this rule is improper on the grounds that, even if the term "eternal" (*nitya*) were omitted, the rule would still be necessary to prevent the application of the analytical compound *chedamarhati* and so forth.

This is the direction [of the argument], because the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is accepted in the *Bhāṣya* and other works. The terms "cutting" (*cheda*), "dividing" (*bheda*), "hostility" (*droha*), and "fault" (*doṣa*) are examples of such words beginning with "cutting. He states the *gaṇasūtra*: "After *virāga*, etc.
(1319). Pāṇini 5.1.66: *daṇḍādibhyo yat* ("The suffix *yat* is applied after *daṇḍa* and others").

Regarding the rule *daṇḍādibhyaḥ*: he asks what follows from the previous sūtra, and answers, "that which would be [the suffix] *yat*. Some, however, read it as *aṇḍādibhyo yaḥ*, but they say that this is indeed a corrupt reading because it contradicts the Bhāṣya and other authorities. For instance, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *aco yat*, it says:
It has been stated: "Or, [the suffix] *ghan* [is applied], as in *vadha-deśa*"; *vadhya* means "one who is to be killed" (*ghātya*). Or, [it is derived] from the root *addhita*.

[In this case], one who deserves killing is called *vadhya*. And this is only appropriate here if that which is prescribed [as the suffix] is indeed *ghan*, because in both alternative views, [the word] would otherwise have an acute accent (*udātta*) by the rule "after *yat*, except for *āvaḥ*" (*yato ’nāvaḥ*). However, if *ara* were what is prescribed...
In that case, the accent would be different. However, in the *Manoramā*, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*:

"In the rule for the suffix *yat*, there is optionally *vadh* for the root *han*, or [the suffix] *taddhita*. This is only appropriate if what is being prescribed here is indeed *yat*; for otherwise, the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātatva*) would apply both to the *kyac* and to the *yat* that is a *taddhita*.
It is established that the initial vowel in "ṭhyato ’nāvaḥ" and so forth is udātta, and so on.
(1320) *Kaḍaṅkaradakṣiṇāc cha ca* | 5.1.69.
[The suffix] *cha* is added after *kaḍaṅkara* and *dakṣiṇā*. As for the reading "aḍaṅgara," it is to be disregarded.
It makes *kaḍaṃ*—that is, it produces *kaḍa*. [The root] *aḍ* means "to intoxicate. That which *kaḍati* (produces intoxication) is *kaḍaḥ*.

This refers to the husks of beans, mudga-beans, and so forth. And Amara says: “*Aḍaṅkara* (husk) is neuter. Regarding the word *gaura*, Raghuvamśa says: “With the *kaḍaṅkara* of wild rice (*īvāra*) and other grains.”

(1321) *sthālībilāt* |5|1|70|. From *sthālībila*, the suffixes *cha* and *yat* are understood [to follow]. These two suffixes, *cha* and *yat*, occur after this word. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhak*. [The resulting forms mean] "fit for cooking," that is to say, "having been husked three times."

(1322) *yajñartvigbhyāṃ dhakhañau* || 5.1.71 || [The suffixes] *dhak* and *khañ* are applied after the words *yajña* and *ṛtvij* [to form the word for one who] "deserves" (*arhati*) the sacrifice or the officiating priest. What is the meaning of "one who deserves"? It means "one who is not excluded by the scriptures. Since a region (*deśa*) is not of such a nature, this [usage] has been added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*).

The addition [to the rule] is: "The suffix *khañ* is applied after the words *yajña* and *ṛtvij* in the sense of 'one who is worthy of that action'. For example, *yajñiya* means "a place fit for the performance of sacrifice," i.e., suitable for the execution of sacrificial rites. Regarding *ṛtvij*, since the suffix *khañ* would not otherwise be applicable by the rule [Pāṇini 5.1.71], this addition is made to ensure its application in the sense: "one who is worthy of the duties of an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)," rather than "an officiating priest" itself.
The limit for the twelve affixes beginning with *ṭhak* belonging to the *ārhīya* group has been reached.
Thus ends the section on *ārhīya* and related affixes in the *Tattvabodhinī*. Now begins the formation of the *ātmanepada* endings within the section on verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*).

(431) *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* |1|3|13|. Regarding "in the sense of the action [of being] and the object": the meaning is that when the *l*-suffixes occur in the sense of the action of being (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), they take the *ātmanepada* endings. (432) *kartari karmavyatihāre* |1|3|14|. [The *ātmanepada* endings are used] in the sense of the agent when there is a reciprocal exchange of actions.
"By another" means that a Brāhmaṇa performs for a Śūdra the work appropriate for him, such as the cutting of crops and so forth.

"Mutual action" (*karmavyatihāra*) also [falls under this category]; for example: *saṃpraharante rājānaḥ* ("the kings strike at one another"). Although this is established by the very commencement of a separate rule, the mention of the term *kartṛ* (agent) is for the sake of what follows.
Regarding *vyatiṣṭe*: because there is an absence of *para-tva* (the status of being subsequent), the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. Regarding *vyatiṣe*:

here, the substitution of *ṣ* does not take place by the rule *upasargaprādurbhyām*, because the *s* lacks the status of being a constituent part (*avayavatva*). However, the substitution of *ṣ* [would apply] by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*.

It was prohibited by the rule *ātpadādyoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.39], because by the principle of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), the suffix alone possesses the status of being a word (*padatva*).
(433) *na gatihiṃsārthebhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.4.15].

"Not after [roots] meaning motion or injury. The word *artha* (meaning) is connected with each [of the two]. This is a prohibition of that ātmanepada which occurs in the sense of reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*). By the force of the inclusion of the word *artha*, only those roots are understood here that denote motion or injury without depending on another word [such as a prefix]. However, the root *hṛ* (to take away) denotes injury only by virtue of a prefix.

They say that the Vārttika, "The [suffix] *kta* is not prohibited after the root *hṛ* when used with the word *pravartate*," is indeed obtainable through the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*artha*). (434) *Itaretara-anyaonya-upapadācca* 1.3.16.

Regarding *itaretara*: [An objection is raised]—"Since the reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*) is already indicated by words such as *itaretara* itself, the ātmanepada ending that indicates it would not apply; therefore, what is the purpose of this prohibition? To this, they say: "In worldly usage, because there is no regard for brevity (*lāghava*), the ātmanepada [is used]."
This prohibition is undertaken because [otherwise] an undesirable consequence would follow; for this very reason, in forms such as *vyatilunīte*,
both the prefix *vyati-* and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) are employed together to indicate the reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*).
(435) *ner viśaḥ* |1|3|17|. [The rule] "after *ni*, [the root] *viś*" [is applied]. Why [specify] "after *ni*"? [Consider: *praviśati* ("he enters").

By means of the two paribhāṣās—the rule regarding the inclusion of meaningful elements (*arthavadgrahaṇa*) and the rule regarding the specifically prescribed form (*pratipadokta*)—there is the inclusion of *ni* as a prefix (*upasarga*).

Therefore, it is not the case here that [the reading] "aṅgāni viśanti" (the bees enter the limbs) is used; for after stating, "The bees now enter the [lotus] stalks," [the text says], "Having said this, Maithilī, out of fear, settled upon her husband's lap.
However, in the reading "aṅke ni viśati" (she enters upon the lap), there is no fault even under the theory of word-formation (*padasaṃskāra*).

This must be said: otherwise, by your own reasoning, even such usages as *tvaṃ karoti* (you do) and *bhavān karoṣi* (you do) would result in being grammatically correct; furthermore, [the rule] *ṭhvā lipsāyām* and so forth would become redundant.
It might be argued: "In the case of *‘avāmbudaśyāmatanur nyavikṣata’*, the ātmanepada [suffix] is not..."

It might be argued: "Because of the intervention by *aṭ*; and it should not be said that one's own member (*svāṅga*) does not constitute an intervention, for although *aṭ*—being a portion of the *aṅga* and thus a part of that which is qualified by the *vikaraṇa*—is indeed a constituent of the *aṅga*, it is not a constituent of the verbal root (*dhātu*). To this they reply: "The augment *aṭ* occurs in the state [of the root] as an *aṅga*."

According to the view of the Bhāṣya, there is no fault whatsoever. However, in other systems of thought, there exists the Vārttika: "In the rule regarding prefixes (*upasarga*), there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the case of intervention by *ṭha* and *ḍha*" [this is the direction].
(436) *Āṅe do’nāsyaviharaṇe* | 1.3.20 | [The substitution of *d* occurs for the root *do* after the prefix *āṅ*, except when it signifies the opening of the mouth.]

The two [roots] beginning with *āṅ* are included. This is for the purpose of expressing that the result of the action does not benefit the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). Consequently, the usage "the lord of birds opened his own mouth" (*vyādadau vihagapatirmukhaṃ svakīyam*) is established even in the case of opening the mouth, because there is an intention to express that the fruit of the action belongs to the agent.
(437) *krīḍo ’nusaṃparibhyaśca* | 1.3.21.

Regarding the rule *śikṣer jijñāsāyām*: the root *ikṣa* meaning "to acquire knowledge" (*ikṣa vidyopādāne*) is not intended here, because the ātmanepada is already established for it by its being anudāteta; rather, it refers to the desiderative form of the root *śak* (*śikṣ*).
He explains by means of the passage beginning with "in the domain of the bow" (*dhanurviṣaye*). Regarding the phrase "for the sake of restriction" (*niyamārtham*):

the intention is that the fact that the root *nāth* is marked as *anudāteta* (having an indicatory vowel *a*) is for the purpose of establishing the form *nāthana* through the suffix *yuc*, according to the rule *anudātetashca halādeḥ*. As for the expression "he imitates his mother" (*māturanuharati*), here there is merely a similarity.
What is intended is the habitual nature [of the action], not merely the manner [of performing it].
(438) *apāccatuṣpācchakuniṣvālekhanē* |6|1|142|. In the example *gaur apakirati*, although there is joy (*harṣa*), there is an absence of scratching (*ālekhanābhāva*).
The non-occurrence of *suṭ*.

In the sense of "cursing" (*upālambha*), [the rule] *śapa upālambhe* applies, as in *kṛṣṇāya śapate*. By the rule *lāghahnu ṅiti*, the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) is applied. But when the hand is placed by the beloved upon the head of the friend... [sakhyaḥ!].

Regarding the rule *upānmantrakaraṇe*: where a mantra is the instrument (*karaṇa*), that is "mantra-instrument" (i.e., praise); in that case, the Ātmanepada suffix shall occur after the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *upa*. As in the example *āgneyyā*:

Even though the mantra has no direct utility in that [act of approaching], its status as an instrument for the act of attendance (*upasthāna*) is not destroyed, because it is useful for the praise (*stuti*), which is the effect of that act. As for the accusative case in "āgnīdhram," it connects with the implied word "in order to praise" (*stotum*), since that implication is necessary to account for the accusative denoting the object. This means that after the prefix *sam*, the suffix *lyap* is optionally used before the roots *gam* and *ṛcchi*. Thus, from *saṃgam* we derive either *saṃgatya* (using *lyap*) or *saṃgamya* (using *ktvā*). Similarly, from *saṃṛcch* we derive either *saṃṛtya* (using *lyap*) or *saṃṛcchya* (using *ktvā*). However, this rule does not apply when the root *gam* is preceded by the prefix *pra*. In such a case, the suffix *ktvā* alone is used, as in *pragatya*. This is because the rule *samogamyṛcchibhyām* is superseded by the subsequent rule *na lyapi* (6.4.69), which prohibits the substitution of *sam* with *saṃj* before the suffix *lyap*. Since the prohibition applies specifically to the context of *lyap*, it does not affect forms like *pragatya*, where *lyap* is not present. Therefore, the form *pragatya* is established. Furthermore, the rule *samogamyṛcchibhyām* is not applicable when the root *gam* is preceded by the prefix *pari*. In that case, the suffix *ktvā* is used, resulting in *parigatya*. This is because the rule *parinivibhyaḥ sevasitasayasivusahasuṭstusvañjām* (8.3.70) prescribes the substitution of *sa* for *saṃ* before these specific roots, including *gam*, when preceded by *pari*, *ni*, or *vi*. Consequently, since the condition for the application of *samogamyṛcchibhyām* is absent, the form remains *parigatya*. Thus, the rule *samogamyṛcchibhyām* is restricted to cases where the prefix *sam* is directly followed by the roots *gam* or *ṛcchi*, and it is not extended to instances where other prefixes intervene. This explains why forms such as *pragatya* and *parigatya* are correctly derived without the optional application of *lyap*. In summary, the rule *samogamyṛcchibhyām* governs the optional use of *lyap* after *sam* before *gam* and *ṛcchi*, provided no other prefix intervenes. When *pra* or *pari* precedes *gam*, the rule is set aside by subsequent provisions, resulting in the mandatory use of *ktvā* instead. This ensures the correct formation of verbal participles in Sanskrit grammar.

Because of the rule *ṭhhrasvādaṅgāt*, the elision of the *sic* suffix would not apply, and thus the form would have to be *samārṣṭa*. Nor should it be argued that the desired result is achieved by interpreting the rule as "of that which is prescribed after a short vowel," for there is no evidence for such a qualification of "prescribed. On this point, some maintain: "By the rule *ij-lopa ekādeśe siddho vācyaḥ*, the elision of *s* (the *sic* suffix) occurs first, and subsequently the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] takes place, because the locative case in *ekādeśe* is understood as a locative of occasion (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Nor does this fail to account for forms such as *adhyaiṣṭa*; for there too, according to the aforementioned method, the elision of *s* occurs first."

It should not be argued that the form *adhyaita* would result because the rule for *vṛddhi* is present; for, according to the principle "an operation concerning a vowel (*vārṇa*) is stronger than one concerning a suffix (*āṅga*)," the *guṇa* substitution occurs first, and once it has taken effect, the elision of the *sic* suffix does not apply.
Thus, when the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule "āṭaśca" has been applied, the form *adhyaiṣṭa* is established without any obstacle.

Regarding the form *samārta*, however, they say there is a discrepancy: because the suffix is *kit* by the rule *ṭuśca*, the *guṇa* substitution does not apply; thus, the *sij*-elision occurs first, and subsequently, by the rule *āṭaśca*, the *vṛddhi* substitution takes place. Others, however, maintain that the elision of *sic* is established only in those cases where a partial replacement (*ekadeśa*) would otherwise apply immediately after the elision of *sic*.

As in the case of *agrahīt*. However, such a subject does not exist here. Furthermore, as for what was stated—that because "a rule concerning vowels (*vārṇa*) is stronger than a rule concerning a suffix (*āṅga*)" (Pāṇini 1.4.2), the *guṇa* substitution occurs first and so forth—that is incorrect.
For a rule concerning a suffix is stronger than one concerning a vowel only when they have the same locus (*samānāśraya*). Otherwise, [one could derive] *dyaurivācarati*.

In the case of *dyavatī*, the *yaṇ* substitution would not occur; rather, by the rule "before a vowel-ending [affix] following a stem ending in *u*," (*ugitaśca*), only *guṇa* would apply. Thus, they say that while one ought to have said *samārṣṭi*, the form *samārtti* is merely a scribal error.

This is the analysis of the compound. The word *daka* also signifies water; thus, the meaning here does not differ. And it has been stated by Halāyudha: "The wise have called the world *bhuvana*, *amṛta*, *jīvanīya*, and *daka*.

"Taking as one's own" (*svakaraṇa*) means "acceptance" (*svīkāra*). Regarding the term *svakaraṇa*, the suffix *cv-* does not occur because of the optional rule: "after words that do not denote a substance, [the suffixes] may optionally [be added] after the first [member of the compound]. The author of the *Vṛtti* maintains that by the word *svakaraṇa*, the acceptance of a wife is understood. However, Bhaṭṭi employed it even in the sense of mere acceptance, as in the verse: *upāyaṃsta*.
"Regarding the rule *mahā’strāṇi* (Pāṇini 2.4.84): [the term] *vibhāṣopayamane* (Pāṇini 1.3.56) [is understood];
[and it applies] when [the action] is subordinate to *gandhana* (hinting). Furthermore, a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *aveṣṭi vibhāṣā*."

It has been stated: "The *kit* status [of the suffix] is constant. This means by the preceding rule, "In the sense of threatening (*gandhana*), after the root *yam*. (461) *jñā-śru-smṛ-dṛśāṃ sanaḥ* | 1.3.57.

[The rule begins with] *jñā-śru-smṛ*. [The suffix *san* is applied] after the roots *jñā* etc., by the rule "After *jñā* in the sense of denying (*apahnava*)... and so forth, and by the rule "Also after *ṛ*, *śru*, and *dṛś*."

It should be understood that although [the form] is established by the rule "ūrvavatsanaḥ" in the case of the roots *śru* and *dṛś* when the ātmanepada is applied, this [present rule] prescribes [the substitution] from the causative (saṇ-anta) stem in other contexts.
(462) *pūrvavatsanaḥ* | 1.3.62 | [The causative suffix saṇ behaves like the original root in respect to the application of parasmaipada and ātmanepada.]

Regarding the form *nivivikṣate*: because the rule “*erviśaḥ*” prescribes the Ātmanepada, the Ātmanepada ending occurs even after the desiderative (*sannanta*) stem. The phrase “the *na* [of *na lokāvyaya...*] is understood to follow” refers to the two rules “*ānorjñaḥ*” and “*ūrvavatsanaḥ*. This is the ellipsis to be supplied.

(463) *samaḥ kṣṇuvaḥ* | 1|3|65|. Regarding *samaḥ kṣṇuvaḥ*: although one might have read [the rule] as *amo gamyṛcchikṣṇubhyaḥ*, its separate recitation here indicates that it applies even to the transitive (*sakarmaka*) verb; thus, he provides an example to illustrate this.
"He sharpens the weapon.
"Avana" means protection. Although it should have been stated as "adane" (in eating), the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is expressed as "anavane" (not in protecting).

There are two purposes: first, because disjunction, like conjunction, serves as a cause for determining a specific [meaning], there is the inclusion of only the root *bhuj* belonging to the *raudhādika* class; second, it is so that the *ātmanepada* occurs even when "eating" is not the meaning, but rather other senses such as "enjoying."

Thus he says: "The protector of the earth enjoyed [it]. Regarding the word *iha* (here): the term "enjoyment" (*upabhoga*) is illustrative, including also the act of making something one's own (*ātmasātkaraṇa*). He "enjoyed the earth" means he brought it under his own control. This is because the root *bhuja*, in the sense of "protecting" and "eating," belongs to the *rudhādi* class.

Regarding the term *grahaṇa*: from the root *bhuja* meaning "to bend" (*kauṭilya*), which belongs to the *tudādi* class, only the *parasmaipada* endings are used. For example: *pāṇiṃ vibhujati* ("he bends his hand"), *mūlāni vibhujati* ("he bends the roots").

(465) Pāṇini 1.3.67: *ṇeraṇau yatkarma ṇau cetsa kartā’nādhyāne*. [When a root ending in the causative suffix *ṇic* has a *karmakartṛ* (an object that becomes the agent), the *ātmanepada* ending is used provided that the same object is the agent in the non-causative form, except in the case of the sense of "remembering with longing" (*ādhyāna*).]

"Whatever is the object of the causative (*ṇi*) [becomes the agent of the non-causative] when the ātmanepada is applied. Here, four subordinate sentences are understood. "The ātmanepada [is used] after the causative (*ṇi*)" is one sentence;
that has been explained up to the word *syāt*. "Whatever is the object of the causative (*ṇi*), if it is also [the object] of the non-causative (*aṇi*)" is the second [sentence].

The word *karman* here refers to "action," as in the rule *artari karmavyatihāre*. Thus, the meaning is: "if that very action which exists in the non-causative (*aṇ*) form is expressed in the causative (*ṇyanta*) form. This being established, he states the resulting conclusion: "and if that same [action] is expressed by the causative" (*saiva ceṇṇyantenocyeta*). The third sentence is "that [agent]" (*sa kartā*). [This applies to the portion beginning with] *aṇau* and so forth.

The word *ceṭ* ending in the suffix *śatṛ* is understood here. Furthermore, the word *karman* (object) in this context refers specifically to a particular *kāraka*, because it relies on the governing topic of "words" (*śabdādhikāra*). He explains this with the passage beginning with "that which [is the object] in the sense of *aṇ*" and ending with "it would be. He explains the separate rule "not in the sense of remembering" (*anādhyāne*) with the words "but not... (*na tu*).

*Ādhyāna* is recollection preceded by longing (*utkaṇṭhā*). In reality, however, a *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation) should be adopted for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*). On this view, since the meaning is "other than *ādhyāna*," the phrase *'na tvādhyāne'* is established as the result. Thus, it should be understood that there are only three sentences here. [The word] *vikalpa*...
Thus: the connection is with the subsequent phrase, “because [the agent] is already obtained [as the object]. Regarding the term *pūrvavipratiṣedhena* (by prior exclusion):
the scope of *vibhāṣopapadena* is, for example, *svaṃ yajñaṃ yajati* or *svaṃ yajñaṃ yajate*, and so forth; whereas the scope of *ṇeraṇau* is, for example, *darśayate rājā*, and so forth. Likewise...

The scope of the rule *ṇer akarmakāt* is exemplified by: "Kṛṣṇa lies down; the cowherd girl makes him lie down" (*śete kṛṣṇas taṃ gopī śāyayati*). However, the scope of the rule *ṇer aṇau* is exemplified by: "The field reaps itself" (*lāvayate kedāraḥ svayam eva*). For in that case, in the second stage—namely, "the field is reaped" (*lūyate kedāraḥ*)—it is intransitive (*akarmaka*) because the *aṇ* suffix is absent; such is the intended meaning. Nor... [is there any contradiction].
One should not be deluded into thinking that, just as in the case of *aśyati bhava*, in the second stage the usage would be *lunāti kedāra*;

for since the act of cutting (*lavana*) is an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*), the application of the *yaṅ* affix and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*. However, the moderns [hold] that [the root] is intransitive (*akarmaka*) when preceded by *pra*.

The usage in the Bhāṣya, "darśayate rājā" (the king shows himself), is the authority for the sublation of that [general rule]. For in that case, under the view where the instigation has ceased (*nivṛttapreṣaṇapakṣa*), since the root *dṛś* is non-transitive (*akarmaka*) and its agent possesses consciousness (*cetana*), the active voice (*parasmaipada*) would otherwise apply; however, this is not so because the option provided by the rule "vibhāṣopapadena" (Pāṇini 1.3.77) sublates it.

What proof is there? Furthermore, even if the rule *ṭhaṇāvakarmakāḥ* were to be set aside, there is no evidence at all [for its invalidation], because the previously cited Bhāṣya has its purpose fulfilled in cases where the fruit of the action accrues to another.
Thus, when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, the rule *ṭhaṇāvakarmakāḥ* prevails due to its superior status.

They say that since there is no obstacle to its application [in the case of *lāvayate kedāraḥ*], the statement "this alone is desired by way of the subsequent prohibition" (*paravipratiṣedha*) should be reconsidered; for in reality,
the rule *ṇeraṇau* has its scope even when the agent is non-sentient (*acetana*), as seen in examples such as *lāvayate kedāraḥ*.

By the rule *ṭhaṇāvakarmakāḥ*, since the fruit of the action accrues to another (*paragāmini kriyāphale*), the *parasmaipada* would have been obtained by virtue of its later position; however, on the strength of the usage in the Bhāṣya, *darśayate rājā*, it is accepted that the earlier rule (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) applies, namely *ṇeraṇau*.

Thus, even when the ātmanepada affix is applicable, in cases such as *ātmārthaṃ darśayate* ("he shows for his own sake") and *vārthaṃ darśayate* ("he shows for the sake of a bird"), there is no obstacle to the application of the rule *vibhāṣopapadena* (Pāṇini 1.3.77), because it is subsequent [to the previous rules]. Furthermore, because it is even more subsequent than that, the rule *aṇāvakarmakāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.88) applies.

If it is argued that since the *parasmaipada* alone would [otherwise] apply, and thus a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior contradiction) has been accepted to override that, then by implication a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* must also have occurred to override the rule "vibhāṣopapadena" (*Pāṇini 1.3.77*); if so, then how do you account for the usage in the Bhāṣya, "arśayate rājā," where [the *ātmanepada*] occurs even in the absence of an *upapada*?

Because its purpose has already been served, he dispels the suspicion that the meaning [of the rule] is already established by the phrase "ṭhaṇ after intransitives" when used with a prefix, by stating: "those whose action resides in the agent.
An action (bhāva) is the meaning of a verbal root that is accomplished by means of instruments that do not involve physical motion. 6.1.193.

But action (*kriyā*) is that which is to be accomplished by means of an instrument (*sādhana*) accompanied by vibration (*saparispandana*). An instrument is indeed a causal factor (*kāraka*), because the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is to be accomplished by it. Now, one might object: in the expression “he sees the object existing at the very moment [of seeing],” the verb *dṛś* (to see) would not have its state (*bhāva*) residing in the agent; rather, it would only have its action (*kriyā*) residing in the agent. And this is not [the case].

If it is argued that by the word "sādhana" (instrument) one intends the *kāraka* (participant in action) denoted by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*), [then we reply] that this objection remains as forceful as before in cases such as "the dancing Bhava sees. To this, they say: just as Devadatta and others, while actually possessing motion, serve as the instrument in acts like climbing, so too [is it] not the case in acts like seeing and hearing.
It occurs, however, that even when devoid of motion, the aforementioned fault does not arise.
He provides an example of a verb where the state (bhāva) resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*)—namely, "they see" (*paśyanti*). Regarding the phrase "the element of instigation" (*preraṇāṃśa*):
the sense is that it is intended to express ease (*saukarya*). As for the word "thence" (*tataḥ*): the meaning is "from the verbal root from which the element of instigation has been discarded."

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of that which has the sense of *ṇi*" and so forth: one should not argue that if this were the case, the *ṇic* suffix would also apply [to the root], and thus forms such as *arśayate bhavaḥ* would not be established; for Kaiyaṭa has stated that even when the means (*upāya*) ceases, the goal (*upeya*) does not necessarily cease. In that context, it is said "for the third case" (*tṛtīyāya*), whereas for the first and second cases...

The point is that because the suffix *ṇic* is absent, there is no possibility of the application of the suffix *taṅ*. "Even when the action is the same" means together with the first stage (*kakṣyā*). "Taking the second [stage]" refers to the rule: "If the action which exists in the non-causative (*aṇ*) is the very same as in the causative (*ṇic*)."
This was stated on the assumption that the purpose is to exclude both deficiency and excess.

However, when it is accepted that the purpose is solely to exclude excess, then that [exclusion] becomes possible by taking the first [alternative]. Now, he provides an example of an action residing in the agent (kartṛsthakriyā), beginning with the words "In this way," and so forth.
"He makes the elephant mount" (*ārohati hastī*); this is an example when the aspect of instigation (*preṣaṇāṃśa*) is abandoned. Then [the text says] "from that, *ṇic*" (*tato ṇijaiti*).
This means that from a verbal root in which the aspect of instigation has ceased, when there is a desire to express the aspect of instigation, the suffix *ṇic* is applied.
Furthermore, he provides an example for the case where the meaning of *ṇic* itself is not intended to be expressed: "he causes himself to mount" (*ārohayate*). Thus...

Having established the position in which the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is withdrawn, he now states the position in which the instigation is superimposed (*adhyāropita*), beginning with "Or else" (*yadvā*).

Regarding "due to the superimposition of causality" (*hetutvāropāt*): the meaning is "due to the superimposition of the status of an instigating agent" (*prayojakakartṛtva*). Here too, the sole motive is the desire to express ease (*saukarya*). Regarding "of those who see" (*paśyataḥ*): [it means] of the devotees who see, and of those who ascend.

The meaning [of the word] *hastipakān* is to be understood according to the sequence. Regarding the phrase "because of excess" (*ādhikyāt*): in this view, by the rule *ṇau cetsā kriyā*, only excess is excluded, and not deficiency as well. Otherwise, even in the third case, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) affix would not occur, because the *preṣaṇa* (impulsion) inherent in the root would have been abandoned.
The sense is that [the rule would apply] because of the existence of deficiency (nyūnatā). Why [is the word] *ṇeḥ* [stated]?

[To exclude cases such as] *paśyati*, *ārohati*, etc., which have become *ātmanepada* due to the cessation of instigation (*nivṛta-preṣaṇa*). Nor should it be argued that, because of the explicit mention of *ṇau* [in the rule], the substitution would occur only after a causative stem (*ṇyanta*); for the term *aṇau* is also explicitly mentioned [in the same rule].

This is for the sake of clarifying that which must necessarily be performed for the purpose of the subsequent application (*agrimayoga*), and because it is appropriate to perform it right here; [it asks: "Is that very action which exists in the *aṇ* (the non-causal base) also present in the *ṇic* (the causal suffix)? [The answer is: In the case of *darśayati bhavaḥ* ("Bhava causes himself to be seen") and *ārohayati hastī* ("the elephant causes itself to be mounted"), according to the view that superimposes the instigation (*preṣa*), in the second stage (*dvitīyakakṣā*)...

Let it not be so. How then are the usage of Māgha, “*areṇurārohayate niṣādinaṃ*,” and the usage of Bhāravi, “*asantataṃ darśayate gatasmayaḥ kṛtādhipatyāmiva sā du bandhutām*,” to be reconciled? To this, they say: [The answer follows:]... [as per the original Sanskrit commentary].

By the rule "ṭhṇicaśca," the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffixes are applied when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, but not by the present sūtra. Why [is it said] that "if that which is the *kāraka* object (*karman*) in the *aṇ* [denominative base] becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *ṇi* [causative]"? Consider the example *darśayanti bhavam* ("they cause the Lord to see [himself]"); this belongs to the fourth stage in the view where the prompting (*preṣaṇa*) has ceased.

However, in the case of superimposed causation (*adhyāropitapakṣa*), it should be understood that this constitutes the third stage. Some, moreover, observe in the Bhāṣya on this sūtra the example "he causes the servant to go" (*darśayate bhṛtyāyājā*) and the counter-example "the thicket of forest makes him remember" (*smarayatyenaṃ vanagulmaḥ*). Consequently, in the view where the instigation is superimposed (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇapakṣa*), [the following applies].
It is understood that by this [rule], the ātmanepada occurs only in the second stage (kakṣā) and not in the third stage;
and thus, having repeated the word "object" (karman) and accepted its status as denoting an action,
it is held that the very same action which exists in the non-causative base (aṇ) is expressed by the causative suffix (ṇic).

Even if another sentence were admitted, it is understood from this very Bhāṣya that the particle *eva* does not exclude excess, but rather excludes deficiency alone. And thus, [examples such as] "bhavaḥ ārohayate" (Bhava causes himself to be mounted) and "hastī ārohayate" (the elephant causes itself to be mounted), which are devoid of the mention of an object, [are established].
