They say that the example from the root text (*mūlagrantha*) and the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), "he causes [the deer] to remember the thicket" (*smarayati vanagulmam*), are indeed contrary to the Bhāṣya. Others, however, have maintained that the sequence is not intended here, and thus they have supported the Bhāṣya text without contradicting the root text. Their intention is as follows:

In the expression "the cowherd settlement on the deep river" (*gabhīrāyāṃ nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), after there has arisen the cognition of identity between the referents of the words "deep" (*gabhīra*) and "river" (*nadī*)— namely, that it is a river non-different from being deep— there follows the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the bank.
This is because the bank itself lacks depth, and even though the river possesses depth, it is impossible for [the property of] depth to be construed with only a part [of its referent].

Just as the word *gabhīrāyām* (in the deep), though seemingly meaningless, becomes meaningful by taking its primary sense, so too here, in the view that the causal suffix (*ṇic*) expresses the instigation (*preṣaṇa*), [the verb] is connected to the object in the second stage; subsequently, upon the abandonment of both the meaning of the *ṇic* and the object, [the same applies] to the *ṇic* suffix and the word for the object.

There is meaningfulness by taking the initial cognition as the basis, because it is accepted that the "definition" (*lakṣaṇā*) consists in the relation to its own object of cognition. And since the qualified sentence-meaning is what is to be cognized here, the relation to that—consisting in the state of being the producer of the cognition—is present in the sentence. This very [principle] applies to the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*s).

The recourse is to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) based on excellence (*prāśastya*). Otherwise, regarding the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the injunctive sentence "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu"—namely, "Vāyu is the swiftest deity;
he approaches Vāyu with his own portion; he indeed leads him to prosperity"—[the meaning would be inexplicable].

In this regard, [if one were to follow the literal reading], there would be the futility of employing different case-endings for forms such as "vāyumeva svena bhāgadheyena" and "eva enaṃ," as seen in the passage beginning with "ityādi.
Now, one might object that both the example and the counter-example for this sūtra are according to the literal interpretation of the Bhāṣya.
If it is argued, "Let [the root] simply be transitive; what is the use of this laborious effort to establish that the existing object is not intended to be expressed?", do not say so.
For [this is necessary] in the view where the instigation has ceased (*nivṛtapraiṣapakṣa*), regarding the example *darśayate bhavaḥ* and its counter-example.

Since that which is devoid of an object must be accepted as having a uniform nature even in this view, it is appropriate to explain the non-specification of the object (*karma*) for the sake of establishing both the example and the counter-example of the *akarmaka* (intransitive) roots; furthermore, [this follows] from the rule: "Like the transitive [root], when there is an object... (*karmavat karmaṇā*).

Since this is already established by that very [rule], the aphorism is intended for the sake of actions whose state (bhāva) resides in the agent; thus, according to the natural sense of the passage in the Bhāṣya, only intransitive examples are appropriate for both the illustration and the counter-example.
Nor can it be argued that, even by the word "equal" (*tulya*) in the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*, [the action] is restricted to those residing in the object.

It should not be argued that if one accepts that only deficiency (*nyūnatā*) is excluded and not excess (*ādhikya*), there is no violation of the natural sense of the Bhāṣya text; for if that were the case,
even when it is stated that "the action resides in the object as in the agent" (*armavatkarmasthakriya*), [it would follow that] the agent is simply that agent whose action resides in the object.

Because the meaning [of the sūtra] is obtained as "like the object" (*karmavat*), if the desired result were established thereby, the rule *karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* would become redundant. In the second stage (*kakṣā*), there exists both an instigation toward the production of the state of being an object with respect to the elephant, and an instigation toward the act of subordination (*nyagbhavana*).

Because there exists an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*), which consists in the attainment of the status of being an object and in the state of subservience (*nyagbhavana*), even when [the agent] is a sentient being (*sattva*). However, if it is argued that the word "equal" (*tulya*) in the rule *'karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ'* serves to exclude both deficiency and excess in order to ensure the meaningfulness of that rule, then:
Since the rule *arma-vat karmaṇā* does not apply in the second stage [of the analysis],

there would indeed be a violation of the natural consistency (*svārasya*) of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "it is established by *arma-vat karmaṇā* alone. Consequently, in the view that attributes the instigation (*adhyāropita-preṣaṇa-pakṣa*),...

It must be accepted that the example applies only to the third stage (*kakṣā*) and not to the second stage; by this, it is established that in the view where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed,
the rule *ṇau cetsā kriyā* excludes only excess and not deficiency.

Since there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamanā’bhāva*) [to prefer one over the other], if one accepts the exclusion of deficiency alone, then in the second stage that [exclusion] would be unavoidable; therefore, those who argue that the exclusion of both deficiency and excess must be accepted—and thus that the position of four stages is superior—are refuted. As in the example: "The king causes his servants to see [himself]."
This is the general direction: by the force of the examples given in the Bhāṣya, the side [of the argument] that involves superimposition (*adhyāropita*) alone is more powerful.
The roots *gṛdh* and *vañc* are used in the sense of "deceiving. This rule is commenced for the purpose of including cases where the result does not benefit the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*).
(466) Pāṇini 1.3.71: *mithyopapadāt kṛño ’bhyāse* ("After the root *kṛ*, when preceded by the word *mithyā*, [the Ātmanepada affix is used] in the sense of repetition").
[The suffix *ṇamul* is applied] after the root *kṛ* following the prefix *mithyā*, when there is repetition. Here, the root *kṛ* is intransitive because it has the sense of "uttering.
Uttering is [equivalent to] emitting. However, the causative (*ṇic*) form, which functions in the sense of uttering, is transitive;
for example, *uccārayati* means "he causes to emit" (i.e., he utters). But when there is repeated utterance, the verbal root itself possesses a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The *ātmanepada* ending, however, is merely indicative; since it has already been indicated by that very ending, there is no reduplication [of the verb] according to the rule "in cases other than repetition" (*avīpsayoḥ*). As for the statement "the priests sacrifice," the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth are not the fruit of the sacrifice, because [the injunction] such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" prescribes heaven and the like as the objective.
The sense is that because of the injunctions for sacrifices and the like, heaven and so forth are indeed the fruit.
(467) *Samudāṅbhyo yamo’granthe* (Pāṇini 1.3.75).

Regarding *samudāṅbhyo*: since [the desired form] would have been established by the rule *āṅe yamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.28), the specific mention of *āṅ-pūrvaka* is for the sake of [restricting the application to cases where the object is not a book].
Intimating that the purpose is to include [roots] with objects (*sakarmaka*), he provides the example: *vastram āyacchate* ("he stretches out the cloth").

(468) *anupasargāj jñaḥ* | 1.3.76. Regarding *anupasargāj jñaḥ*: since this would already be established by the rule "and from an intransitive [root]" (*akarmakācca*), the present rule is commenced for the sake of including [roots] with objects.
(469) *vibhāṣopapadena pratīyamāne* |1|3|77|.

Regarding *vibhāṣopapadena*: when the fact that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent is indicated by an accompanying word (*upapada*), this is an option (*vibhāṣā*) for that which was not previously established. [For otherwise,] when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, the *taṅ* suffixes would apply invariably.

Others say that when [the condition] is met, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding what has been attained. Regarding the phrase "his own sacrifice" (*svaṃ yajñam*): the word "his own" (*svam*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
One should also understand examples such as "he performs a sacrifice for the sake of others" (*vārthaṃ yajñaṃ yajati*) and "he performs a sacrifice for his own sake" (*ātmārthaṃ yajñaṃ yajati*).
Thus ends the section on the middle voice (*ātmanepada-prakriyā*) in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
(398) *svarādinipātamavyayam* | 1.1.37.

"The [words] beginning with *svara* and the particles (*nipāta*) are indeclinables. This is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) consisting of "those beginning with *svara*" and "particles.
Now, one might object: why not simply list the *svara*-beginners among the "and-so-forth" (*ādi*) particles and then discard this present sūtra?

If it is argued that the four sūtras beginning with “*addhitaś-cāsarve*” should be placed after the rule “*ādayo’satve*,” and that they should henceforth be designated by the term *nipāta* alone in the sections dealing with indeclinables (*avyaya*),
we say no; for [otherwise] there would be no basis for forms such as “*vāsti vācayati*,” “*svaḥ paśyati*,” and “*svaḥ*.”

In examples such as *patati* ("he falls"), because these words denote a substance (*satva*) through their connection with grammatical factors (*kāraka*) such as the object (*karman*), they would not incur the designation of "particle" (*nipāta*). For the designation of particle applies only to words like *ca* ("and") which do not denote a substance, and not to those that do. However, in the case of words beginning with *svar*, it applies both to those denoting a substance and to those not denoting a substance.

Furthermore, there would be no established rule for the designation of "indeclinable" (avyaya). Now, one might suggest that the rules should be formulated as *rāgrīśvarānnipātāḥ*, *svarādīni*, and *cādayo’satve*;
for if this were done, the designation "particle" (nipāta) would be established even for those words beginning with *svara* that denote substances (satva).

If it is argued that this is not so, [we reply: for if that were the case, the designation *pragṛhya*—by the rule "an indeclinable consisting of a single vowel (*ekāc*) is *pragṛhya* before a suffix beginning with *aṅ*"—would undesirably apply even to monosyllabic items such as those in the *svarādi* group.
For among the *svarādi* items, there are indeed monosyllabic *taddhita* suffixes, such as in "imo't" and "dakṣiṇadāc. Furthermore, the suffixes beginning with *ken* are also monosyllabic.

And there are also *kṛt* suffixes [included here], because these two *gaṇa*-sūtras— "beginning with *asi* and ending with *edhāc*, which are *taddhita* suffixes"— and "ending in *ṛ*, *m*, or a diphthong"— are recited in the *svarādi* group. Although these two *gaṇa*-sūtras are not recited in this root-text (*mūla*) among the *svarādi* words, nevertheless, according to the ancient [authorities]...
That it exists in the recitation (*pāṭha*) will be clarified immediately below.
He provides examples of *svara* and the others with the words beginning "svar": *svaḥ* means in heaven or in the next world;
*antar* means in the middle; *prātar* means at dawn; *punar* means again, for the sake of another, or as a distinction.

The word *sanutiḥ* means disappearance. The five words beginning with *svaḥ* and ending with *repha* [are included]. Therefore, in cases such as *svaryāti* and *prātaratra*, the substitution of *u* does not occur. For if they were to end in *-s*, this very fault would indeed arise. *Uccais* means "greatly"; *nīcais* means "slightly"; *śanais* means "in the slowness of action."
*Ṛdhak*—also in the sense of "truth"; others say it means separation, haste, proximity, and lightness.
*Ṛte*—in the sense of exclusion. *Yugapat*—at one time. *Ārāt*—in the sense of distance and proximity.
*Pṛthak*—different. *Hyas*—on the past day. *Śvas*—on the future day. *Divā*—during the day.

*rātrau* means at night; *sāyam* means at the beginning of night; *ciram* means for a long time; *manāk* and *īṣat*—these two mean "slightly"; *joṣam* means in happiness or in silence; *tūṣṇīm* means in silence;
*bahiḥ* and *avaḥ*—these two mean "outside"; *samayā* means near or in the middle; *nikaṣā* means in the vicinity.

*svayam* means "by oneself" (*ātmanā*); *vṛthā* means "in vain" (*vyarthe*); *naktam* means "at night" (*rātrau*); *nañ* is used for negation; *hetau* means "on account of" (*nimite*); *iddhā* is used for what is illuminated (*prakāśye*); *addhā* is used for clarity and certainty (*sphuṭāvadhāraṇayoḥ*), though others say it denotes reality and excellence (*tatvātiśayau*).

[The suffix] *vat* [is used] in the senses of similarity (*sāmīpya*) and contempt (*jugupsita*). The suffix *vat* prescribed by rules such as "that which is equal to that" (*tena tulyam*) is what is understood here. Thus it says: *brāhmaṇavat* (like a Brāhmaṇa), *kṣatriyavat* (like a Kṣatriya).
Since there is no purpose for a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of the suffix alone, examples are given using words ending in that suffix.
However, that [suffix] which is prescribed by the rule *upasargāc chandasi dhātvarthe* is not included here;

for in the example *yad udvato nivato yāsīt*, we observe the application of the properties of a nominal stem (*satvadharmasya*), namely its connection with gender and number. Regarding this, they say: in the rule *taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ*, [the word] "asivatī" [is cited].

The suffix *vat* is also included [in the list], but that should not be done, because its purpose is already served by its inclusion in the *svarādi* group. Alternatively, the word *vat* need not be recited among the *svarādi* words. Thus: *sanā*, *sanat*, *sanāt*—these are indeclinables (*nitya*). *Upadha* is used in the sense of "difference. *Tiras* is used in the sense of "disappearance" (*antardhi*) and "across" (*tiryag-artha*).
*Paribhāve* (in contempt); *antareti* means "in the middle" and also "without"; *antareṇeti* means "excluding";
*jyogiti* is used for the abundance of time, for inquiry, for speed, and for the sense of "now"; *kamiti* is used for water, the head, censure, and happiness; *śamiti* is used for happiness.

*Sahasā* signifies "suddenly" and "without reflection. *Vinā* signifies "exclusion" (*varjana*). *Nānā* signifies "many" and "without" (*vinā*). *Svasti* signifies "auspiciousness" (*maṅgala*). *Svadhā* is used for offerings to the ancestors (*pitṛdāna*). *Alam* is used in the senses of "adornment," "sufficiency," "ability," "prevention," and "prohibition. *Vaṣaṭ* and *śrauṣaṭ*.
*vauṣaṭ*—these [are used] in the offering of oblations; *anya* means "other"; *asti* is used in the sense of existence (*satā*);
*upāṃśu* refers to that which is uttered inaudibly or as a secret; *kṣaṇa* is used in the sense of patience (*kṣānti*);
*vihāyas* is used in the sense of the sky (*viyat*); *doṣā* means "night"; and *mṛṣā* and *mithyā* mean "false."
In the *vithatha*, *mudha*, and *vyartha* [groups], from this point onward,

the three *gaṇa*-sūtras— namely, “*tvātoḥ sun kasun*,” “*kṛn makāra-sandhyakṣarāntaḥ*,” and “*avyayībhāvaś ca*” — which have the same meaning as the three sūtras found in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, have not been recited here.
It should be understood that even though this is found in the ancient Gaṇapāṭha, its redundancy will be refuted later. *Pura* means "without ceasing," "long past," or "imminent.

*Mithaḥ* and *mithas*—these two [forms] are used in the sense of "in secret" (*rahaḥ*) and "together" (*saha*), primarily (*prāyas*) in the majority of cases (*bāhulye*). *Muhus*—[is used in the sense of "repeatedly"].

Furthermore: *prabāhukam* means "at the same time" and "upwards. *Pravāhikā* is an alternative reading. *Āryahalam* means "by force. Śākaṭāyana, however, says: *ārya* means "obstruction," and *halam* means "prohibition" and "dispute. *Abhīkṣṇam* means "repeatedly."
The words *punar* and *sākam* are used in the sense of "together with" (*sārdham*). *Namaḥ* signifies "bowing" (*natī*). *Hiruk* signifies "exclusion" (*varjane*).

*Dhik* signifies "censure" (*nindā*) and "reproach" (*bhartsanayoḥ*). From this point onward, the taddhita suffixes beginning with *asi* and ending with *edhāc*—namely, *śastasī*, *kṛtvasuc*, *suc*, *āsthālau*, and those having the sense of *cvi*—are to be understood.
It should be understood that this is found in the *Prācīna-gaṇapāṭha*.

The meaning of the phrase "beginning with *tasil*" (*tasilādi*) is as follows: the *tasi* in *pañcamyās tasiḥ*, the *tasi* in *tenaikadik*, and also this *tasi* [in *tasiśca*]. [The suffix *tasi* is used] in the sense of repetition of action (*kriyābhyāvṛtti*).

The suffix *āsi*, prescribed by the *Uṇādi* sūtra "kṛtvasuc-avitricaturbhyaḥ suc-ṭhiṇa āsiḥ"; the suffix *athal* in the sense of "preceded by *ratna* and *viśva*" in the Vedic language (*chandasi*) according to "ratnapūrvaviśvemātthalcchandasi"; the suffix *cvi* in the sense of "becoming something else" (*ampadyakartari*) according to "ampadyakartari cviḥ";

and those ending in *sāti* and *trā* in the sense of "totality" (*kārtsnye*) and "what is to be given" (*deye*) respectively, according to "vibhāṣā sāti kārtsnye deye trā ca"—these [suffixes] as well [are used].

Regarding the term *grāhyau* ("to be understood"): *am* is used in the sense of "in speed" (*śaidhye*) and "in smallness" (*alpe*); *ām* is used in the sense of "acceptance" (*aṅgīkāre*). Some maintain that although *am* and *ām* are prescribed by rules such as *ṭhamu ca cchandasi* (Pāṇini 5.4.11), *kimetiṅavyaya-*, and *āspratyayāt-* (Pāṇini 6.4.52–54), they are still to be understood here [as substitutes for case endings]. Examples include: *prataṃ naya prataram* and *yayācatarām*.

He caused [it] to be made. *Pratām*—in the sense of exhaustion (*glāni*). *Praśān*—in the sense of tranquility (*samāna*). *Pratān*—in the sense of expansion (*vistāra*). *Mā*, *māṅ*—these two are used for prohibition (*niṣedha*) and apprehension (*āśaṅkā*). "It is an *ākṛtigaṇa*" means that others should also be understood [as included]. For example: *kāmam*—in the sense of one's own will (*svācchandyena*).

*Prakāmam* means "excessively"; *bhūyas* means "again" (*punar*); *sāmpratam* means "properly" (*nyāyye*); *param* means "but" (*kiṃtu*); *sākṣāt* means "before the eyes" (*pratyakṣe*); *sāci* means "obliquely" (*tiryag-arthe*); *satyam* means "partial acceptance" (*ardhāṅgīkāre*); *maṅkṣu* and *āśu*—both mean "speedily"; *saṃvat* means "in the year."

*Avaśyam* signifies certainty. *Uṣā* means at night. *Om* is used for assent and for Brahman. *Bhūḥ* refers to the earth. *Bhuvaḥ* refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). *Jhaṭiti*, *jhagiti*, and *tarasā*—these denote speed. *Suṣṭhu* is used in the sense of praise. *Duṣṭhu* denotes the inferior. *Su* is used in the sense of honor. *Ku*... [is used in the sense of reproach].

Thus, *kutsita* (contemptible) and *īṣadartha* (a little) [are the meanings of *ku*]. *Añjasā* [is used] in the senses of reality (*tattva*) and speed (*śīghra*). *Mithu* means "two. *Astam* means destruction (*vināśa*). *Sthāne* means appropriate (*yukta*). *Varam* means slight excellence (*īṣadutkarṣa*). *Sudi* refers to the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), and *vadi* to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), and so forth.
He illustrates the words beginning with *ca* and so forth:
*ca* is used in the senses of conjunction (*samuccaya*), disjunctive addition (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*), and collective aggregate (*samāhāra*).

*Vā* may be used in the senses of option (*vikalpa*), comparison (*upamā*), the sense of *iva*, and also conjunction (*samuccaya*). *Ha* is used in the sense of renown (*prasiddhi*). *Aha*... [is used in the sense of]... (Note: The provided fragment ends mid-sentence regarding *aha*. The full definition for *aha* is typically "in the sense of calling out" or "renown," depending on the specific lexicon.)
*pūjāyām* (in the sense of honor); *eva* is used for restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*); *evam* is used for referring back to what has been said (*uktaparāmarśa*);
*nūnam* is used for certainty (*niścaya*) and conjecture (*tarka*); *śaśvat* is used for repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) and the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*);
*yugapat* means at the same time (*ekakāla*); *bhūyas* is used for the sense of "again" (*punarartha*) and excess (*ādhikya*); *kūpat* is used in questioning (*praśna*).

And [it is used] in the sense of praise. *Kuvit* is used in the sense of abundance and in praise. *Ned* is used in the sense of apprehension, as well as in prohibition, deliberation, and conjunction. *Cet* is used in the sense of "if. *Caṇ*—this has the sense of *cet*; the marker *ṇ* is for the purpose of specification, according to the rule: "The particles *yat*, *yadi*, *hanta*, *kuvit*, *cet*, and *caṇ*..."

In *samuccaya* (conjunction) and other such cases, however, it is without an indicatory letter (*anubandhaka*). In the sense of an inquiry regarding something desired, there is *kaccit*. In the senses of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*), intolerance (*amarṣa*), censure (*garhā*), and wonder (*āścarya*), there is *yatra*—as in: "I do not consider it possible, I cannot tolerate it, or [expressing] censure or wonder: 'that you, sir, should cause a low-born man (*vṛṣala*) to sacrifice. In the sense of a counter-undertaking (*pratyārambha*), there is *na hi*.

*Hanta* is used in the sense of joy, dejection, compassion, or the commencement of a sentence. *Mākiḥ*, *mākim*, and *nakir*—these three are all used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). *Mām* and *nañ* are mentioned among the *svarādi* (vowels and so forth) [in the list of indeclinables]. However, their inclusion here is for the sake of their being *nipātas* (particles); thus, some maintain that the result is the attainment of the initial acute accent (*ādy-udātta*). That is incorrect.

Since the desired result is achieved even by means of the *phiṭ-svara* accent, others, however, say: "The inclusion [of these words] in the list beginning with *svar* is for the purpose of assigning the designation of indeclinable (*avyaya*) even to those expressing existence (*sattva*). That too is incorrect, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence that the word *mā*, which denotes the goddess Lakṣmī, would also be an indeclinable. Therefore, in both cases...

The purpose of this reading is to be considered. Insofar as these two [words, *yāvat* and *tāvat*], are used in the senses of totality (*sākalya*), limit (*avadhi*), measure (*māna*), and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*):
In the sense of totality: "As much work as there was, so much has been done. In the sense of limit: "Stay for as long as there is to be traveled.
In the sense of measure: "As much as was given, so much was eaten. In the sense of restriction: "Only as much as is in the vessel."

In these cases, *tāvat* is used to address Brahmins; *tvai* is used for "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) and "deliberation" (*vitarka*); *dvai* is used for "deliberation" (*vitarka*); and *nvai*—this is another reading—is used for "indeed" (*iti*). *Rai* is used in the sense of "giving" (*dāna*) and "disregard" (*anādara*); *rai karoti* means "he gives. [For example: "What will you do? *Śrauṣaṭ* and *voṣaṭ*—these two [are sacrificial interjections].
*Havirdāne* (in the giving of the oblation); *svāhā* (hail) is used for the offering to the deities; *svadhā* is used for the ancestors.

The multiple-syllable forms such as *śrauṣaṭ* and others are recited in both places for the purpose of distinguishing their accents. *Tum* refers to the sound *tuṃ*; as in "having made a wide *tuṃ*-sound" or "having made a *huṃ*-sound. Likewise, *tathāhi* is used as an illustration. *Khalu*...
Thus, *iti* is used in prohibition, ornamentation, and ascertainment; *kila* in report and falsehood;
and *atho*, *atha*, and *iti* in auspiciousness, immediate succession, commencement, inquiry, totality, authorization, promise, and conjunction.

This [term] applies even at the beginning of a word (*svarādi*). Consequently, although it denotes the auspiciousness (*satva*) inherent in the word *maṅgala*, its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is established.
For this very reason, Śrīharṣa says:
"Having cast aside the golden jars upon the altar-like belly of the city, which possessed the beautiful luster of a fourfold courtyard..."
"Then, according to family custom, a group of matrons bathed the daughter of the lord of the earth"—
in this passage, the meaning of "atha snapayāmbabhūva" is "he performed an auspicious bath. For the particle *atha*, by its very nature, is auspicious, like the sound of a drum.
*Suṣṭhu* means "excellent. *Sma* is used for the past tense and as a particle for filling the meter (*pādapūraṇa*).

*Ādaha* is used in the senses of beginning, injury, and reproach. However, in the phrase *ādaha svadhāman*, the authors of the *pada-pāṭha* read *ā* as a separate word. Regarding *avadatam*: here, because *ava* is not a prefix (*upasarga*), [the rule does not apply].

The rule *upasargādaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.29) does not apply here. The word *aham* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that resembles a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), used in the sense of ego (*ahaṅkāra*). Similarly, in the phrase *eye kena vinītau vām*, the word *vām* is an indeclinable resembling a form ending in a case-suffix; it means "you two" (*yuvām*). However, the word *asti* is an indeclinable resembling a form ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). Thus...
In the expression *vāmasmi vāgmī*, the word *asmi* is a particle resembling a verbal form used in the sense of the stem *aham* (I).
*Āha* means "said" (*uvāca*). *Āsa* means "was" (*babhūva*). Such examples should be understood in this way.
Regarding *ahaṃyuḥ*: [it is derived] by the rule *ahaṃśubhamoryus*. However, if one follows the rule *vāhau sau*...

If the suffix *yas* were applied to the word *aham*— which is derived after the substitution of *ah* for the portion ending in *m* and the elision of the remainder (*śeṣalopa*)— then, with the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*), the form would be *asmad-yau*. At this stage, since the substitution of *mā* for the portion ending in *m* (maparyanta) would apply as in the case of *madīya*, the result would be *mayau*.

The meaning is: [the word] *asti-kṣīrā* [is used]. However, the intention is that if [the first member] were a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), this *bahuvrīhi* compound would not be possible. The particle *a* is used for addressing, for reproach, and for prohibition.

The particle *ā* is used for introducing a sentence and for recollection. The particle *i* is used for addressing, for loathing, and for wonder. [The particles] *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *āṬ* [are likewise used].

*Saṃ* is used in addressing; *paśu* in the sense of "correctly"; *aśu* in the sense of "thinking" (*manyamānāḥ*); *śukam* in the sense of "quickness" (*śaidhye*); *yathākathāca* in the sense of "disregard"; the seven particles beginning with *pāṭ* are used in addressing; *dyā* in the senses of "injury," "desire," and "filling a verse-line" (*pādapūraṇe*); *viṣu* in the sense of "variety" (*nānārthe*).

*Ekapade*—in the sense of "suddenly" (*akasmāt*). *Yut*—in the sense of "contempt" (*kutsā*). *Ātaḥ*—in the sense of "even from this" (*ito’pi*). It is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of particles). For example: *yat* and *tat* in the sense of "because" (*hetau*); *āho-svit* in the sense of "optionally" (*vikalpe*); *sīma* in the sense of "on all sides" (*sarvatobhāve*); *śukam* in the sense of "excessively" (*atiśaye*); *anukaṃ*.

*vitarke* (in deliberation); *śambaṭ* (in the internal organ and in the sense of being face-to-face); *va* (for the purpose of completing a verse and in the sense of *iva*); *diṣṭyā* (in the sense of joy); *caṭua* or *cāṭua* (in the sense of a pleasing word); *hum* (in the sense of reproach); *iva* (in the sense of similarity); *adyatve* (in the sense of "now" or "at this time")—and so forth. Here [is the list].

Although there is no distinction between the *svarādi* and *cādi* groups in that they both belong to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class, those for which an enclitic accent (*nipātasvara*) is desired are placed among the *cādi* group, while others are placed among the *svarādi* group; however, those that possess both accents should be understood as belonging to both. (398) A primary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) that does not take all case-endings [is called an indeclinable]. 1.1.38.

"A taddhita [suffix] is also [called] *asarvavibhakti* (not all case-endings). Regarding "all": the meaning is that which consists of the three numbers. "It is not produced": the sense is that only the singular number is produced. Why "taddhita"? [Consider: *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *trayaḥ*. Why "not all" and so forth? [Consider: *aupagavaḥ*. [Objection: But [in the case of] *pañcālāḥ*, *gadau*, *varaṇā*...

In such cases, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor can it be argued that there is no over-extension because the author, by stating "due to the non-observation of usage" (*prayogāprakhyānāt*) in the rule for *taci*, has not admitted that these are formed with secondary suffixes (*taddhita*); for even so, [the fault remains].

Anticipating the objection that over-extension (*ativyāpti*) would be unavoidable in cases such as *acatikalpam* and *ṭhpacatirūpam*, he says: "A specific enumeration must be made. Regarding the phrase "beginning with *tasil*": this means those suffixes beginning with *tasil*—which is prescribed by the rule *pañcamyāstasil*—and ending with the suffix *pāśa* prescribed by the rule *vyāpye pāśa*. Regarding "beginning with *śas*": this means those beginning with *śas*—which is prescribed by the rule *bahvalpārthāt*—and ending with the rule *samāsāntāḥ*. Regarding "those having the sense of *kṛtvas*": [the same applies].

The three suffixes beginning with *kṛtvasuc*—namely *kṛtvasuc*, *dhā*, and *śas*—are prescribed by the rule *aṅkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛtigaṇane kṛtvasuC*. Regarding the phrase “*tasivatī*”: one should not argue that the specific enumeration of *tasi* is redundant because the suffix *tasi* is already obtained through its inclusion in the group beginning with *śas* (by the rule *ṣaṣṭhyā rūpya-ca-tas-pratyayāḥ*), since it is necessary for the sake of the rules *tenaikadik* and *asiśca*. The suffix *vati* is prescribed by the rule *tena tulyam*. Regarding *nānāñau*: these two are prescribed by the rule *vinabhyāṃ nānāñau na sahe*. As for *pacatikalpam*:
the point is that if the designation of an indeclinable (*avyayasaṃjñā*) were applied here, there would be elision (*luk*) of the nominal suffix (*sup*).

(399) *kṛnmejantaḥ* | 1|1|39|. Regarding this rule, because the term *ejanta* is explicitly heard [in the sūtra], it qualifies *kṛt* itself, and not the unexpressed *kṛdanta*. Otherwise, [the forms] *ratām* and *ratāmaḥ*—derived from the causative (*ṇau*) of the root *ram* meaning "he causes to rest"—would not be included.

The sense is that even here [in *smāraṃ smāram*], the application of the rule for *auḥ* would follow—namely, the elision of the *ṇi* suffix after the *kvip* suffix, the substitution of *uṭh*, and the *vṛddhi* strengthening.

For this [form] is indeed a *kṛdanta* by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix), and it is heard as ending in *ej* (the vowel *e*). Therefore, he says: "a *kṛt* suffix which ends in *m* or *ej*. [The example is] *smāraṃ smāram*.

From the root *smṛ*, with the suffix *ṇamul* expressing frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*), there is *vṛddhi* [of the vowel], substitution of *ra* for *ṇ*, and doubling [of the root] by the rule "for repetition" (*āvṛtti*). Regarding *jīvase*:

the suffix *ase* is applied by the rule "in the sense of the infinitive (*um-arthē*), [the suffixes] *se* and *ase*. Regarding *pibadhyai*: [this is formed] by that very same rule, "in the sense of the infinitive (*um-arthe*)."

The suffix is *adhyai*. In the word *āghra*, there is the substitution of *piba*. Although the rule "that by which an operation is prescribed applies to that which ends with it" (*yena vidhis tadantasya*) would have already established this, the inclusion of the term *anta* (end) in the sūtra is for the purpose of ensuring the application of the original form (*aupadeśika*). Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *ādhaye*.

Regarding the form *cikīrṣave*: it is established in the *Manoramā* that this [rule] is intended to indicate the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the two [paribhāṣās], namely the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā* and the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā*, since [the desired forms] would already be established by those two. And this [point] is made in the commentary on *Pāṇini 2.4.82* (*avyayād āpsupaḥ*), where it is stated that there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) following an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

This was stated with reference to the explanation according to the literal recitation (*yathāśruta-vyākhyāna*). However, in the explanation of [Pāṇini 1.1.38] *avyayād vṛtivṛṣivyadhirucisahitaniṣu kviṣ* (which includes *vihikasya*), one must infer another undesirable consequence regarding the designation of *avyaya* (indeclinable) in forms such as *ādhaye*. (400) *ktvātosunkasunaḥ* | 1.1.40 | [The items ending in] *ktvā*, *tosun*, and *kasun* are called indeclinables (*avyaya*).

Regarding *ktvātosunkasunaḥ*: [the form] *kṛtvā* is derived by means of the suffix *ktvā* according to the rule beginning with *samānakartṛkayoḥ*. Regarding *udetoḥ*: [the form] *etos* is derived from the root *iṇ* preceded by *ut*, by means of the suffix *tosun* according to the rule beginning with *ahāvalakṣaṇe sthe’ṇ*.
Regarding *visṛpa*: [the form] *visṛpa* is derived by means of the suffix *kasun* according to the rule beginning with *ṛpitṛdoḥ kasun*.

(401) *Avyayībhāvaśca* | 1.1.41. An *avyayībhāva* compound shall also be designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*). In this context, a restrictive enumeration (*parigaṇana*) must be made, stating: "In the case of *uk*, [the rules for] the accent of the initial syllable (*mukhasvara*) and the substitution of *upacāra* are suspended."
An example for the elision (*luk*) [of the case-ending]: *upāgni*. By the rule "after an indeclinable, the case-endings are elided" (*avyayād vibhakti-luk*), there is elision of the *sup* suffix.

An example for the prevention of the acute accent on the first syllable (*mukhasvara-nivṛtau*) is: *upāgnimukhaḥ*, *pratyagnimukhaḥ*. Although the rule "the word *mukha* [when denoting] a body part" would have resulted in the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada-antodātta-tve*), it is overridden by the rule "after an indeclinable or a directional word," etc. (*āvyaya-dikśabdety-ādinā*).

This is a prohibition. Thus, by the rule "in an *ahuvrīhi*, [the accent is] that of the base," the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the word *pūrva* alone remains, and the first member (*pūrvapada*) is accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*) by the general accentuation of the compound. The letter *s* in place of the *visarga* is designated as *upacāra* according to the terminology of the Eastern grammarians.

An example for its exclusion is: *upapayaḥkāraḥ* (one who makes milk) and *upapayaḥkāmaḥ* (one who desires milk). Here, the substitution of *s* [for *k*] which would have been required by the rule *ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa...* is excluded by the rule *anavyayasya*. Why is there an enumeration [of specific cases]? Consider: *upāgandhīyāna*. Here, by the rule *vāmantrite parāṅgavat*, it behaves as if it were part of the preceding word.

In the case of *yāne* and so forth, let it not be [the case that the rule applies]. Likewise, in *ṭhupāgnikaḥ* and so forth, there is no application of *akac* by the rule *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ*. [The example] *upakumbhamanyaḥ* is given while the phrase *hityanavyayasya* is in force; this is a prohibition of the *muṭ* suffix prescribed by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya mum*.
No; [the rule] *upakumbhībhūtaḥ* does not apply here. In the rule *ṭhasya cvau*, the substitution of *i* (itvam) is not prohibited for the suffix *ṭha*.

For the prohibition of *i*-substitution is stated specifically regarding the *cvī* suffix in the rule *avyayasya cvau*—namely, so that it does not occur in cases such as *doṣābhūtam ahar* ("the day became evening") or *divābhūtā rātriḥ* ("the night became day").

It might be argued as follows: since [the forms] are already established by virtue of being included in the *svarādi* group, the four-sūtra sequence beginning with "and after an *addhita*" is redundant. For in that context, by the passage starting with "an *āsi* suffix beginning with *as* and ending with *edāc* is an *addhita*" and concluding with "and it is meaningless," [the author] excludes the *āsi* suffix derived from the *uṇādi* class.
The meaning of the rule *addhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ* is summarized [by the term *avyayam*].

The meaning of the rule *ṛnmejantaḥ* is summarized by the expression *ṛnmakārasandhyakṣarāntaḥ*. However, the two rules *kṛtvo'rthaprayoge kāle'dhikaraṇe*, *tosunkasunau*, and *avyayībhāvaśca* are included by their very form alone.

Regarding the word *paṭala*: on this point they say—the repetition is for the purpose of indicating that [the rule] is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). By means of that, the previously mentioned enumeration, “*uṅ-mukha-svara-upacārāḥ*,” is obtained. [Examples are: “*urā sūryasyodetoḥ ādheyaḥ*” and “*urā krūrasya visṛpaḥ*.”

In the rule *aloṇtyasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], it will be stated that "when there is a prohibition regarding indeclinables (*avyaya*), there is no prohibition for the suffixes *tosun* and *kasun*"; this too is obtained by this very [present rule].
(402) *avyayād āpsupaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.82].

He states that "elision" (luk) is understood here from the rule *ṭhṇyakṣatriyārṣe’ti*, saying "there shall be elision. The designation "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) is made as a technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*) for the purpose of establishing a definition based on its etymological meaning: it does not change (*na vyeti*), that is, it does not undergo various modifications.

It does not go; that is to say, it does not take on the properties of *satva* (such as gender and number). By this, forms such as *atyuccaisau* and *atyuccaisaḥ* are established. Because there is no designation of indeclinable (*avyaya*) here—due to the absence of the assumption of the properties of *satva*, since [the suffix] has transcended its primary status.
But even so, since the status of the word *uccais* as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) remains unchanged, the elision of the case-ending (*supo luk*) is unavoidable;

therefore, he says: "because of the qualification of what is prescribed" (*vihitaviśeṣaṇāt*). [The example is] *atyuccaisau*. Now, [one might object: "indeed, words such as *ati* are compounded with a word ending in the second case when they have the sense of 'surpassing' (*krānta*), etc."

Since *uccaiḥśabda* primarily denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) possessing the capacity [for action], it cannot function as the object (*karman*), and thus it does not take the second case ending (*dvitīyā*). True; although some indeclinables (*avyaya*) primarily denote capacities, they occasionally become primary denoters of the locus possessing the capacity within the scope of a compound (*vṛtti*). For example: *doṣāmanyamahaḥ*.

"Day is one thing, night another. And thus, in the state of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*), it is possible for the word *uccaiḥ* to end in the accusative case; such is the direction of the argument. Now, if it is objected: "Since the word *uccaiḥ* is listed among the *svarādi* group [of indeclinables], how can there be any possibility of its being a compound ending in that word?"—the answer is no, because of the very nature of this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) as being based on its etymological meaning (*anvartha*).

This is because it also indicates that the rule applies to the final element [of a compound]. Otherwise, since there would be no possibility of its application to a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), the descriptive technical term (*anvartha-saṃjñā*) intended to exclude such cases would be rendered useless. Consequently, in examples such as *aramasvaḥ* and *paramoccaih*, the status of being an indeclinable (*avyayatva*) is established due to the non-inclusion of the property of *satva*.

Success! This is what he says: "In the definition of the technical term *avyaya* (indeclinable), although... and so forth. Keeping in mind the Vārttika—"The statement that there is no need to prescribe the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *āp* after an indeclinable is redundant because of the absence of gender"—he says:
"The mention of *ap* is useless. However, the possibility of stating the rule [as it is] arises from the word "feminine" (*striyām*).

It should be understood that this adopts the position [of the Vārttikakāra] that [the suffix *ṅīp* applies] after a word in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with a feminine. However, that position is not established, because it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as "this Brāhmaṇī woman has been summoned" (*hūtamiyaṃ brāhmaṇī*). But if, immediately after the sūtra *ṭhāmoḥ*, the sūtra *upo dhātuprātipadikayor upabhyayāt* were formulated, then...
The modern scholars [the Navīnas] maintain that even the inclusion of the prefix *upa* is redundant, because its recurrence [from the previous rule] is possible.

Anticipating the objection that if it lacks gender (*aliṅgatva*), it would contradict the scriptural statement found in the *Atharvaṇa-praṇava-vidyā*, he says: "similar" (*sadṛśam*). Regarding these...

The construction is: that which does not depart, but rather remains similar and of one kind, is "indeclinable" (*avyaya*). Alternatively: because it does not depart, therefore it is indeclinable. Regarding the phrase "gender and case": the intention is that the words *vibhakti* (case) and *vacana* (number) refer to grammatical relation (*kāraka*) and number (*saṅkhyā*), respectively. Even though [this applies] to the *avyayībhāva* compound...
Although there is connection with gender, number, and case, it nonetheless possesses the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by virtue of its being specifically mentioned.

Regarding a particular type of indeclinable, he states another grammatical operation: "vaṣṭi," etc. Bhādurī is the teacher. "And also *āp*"—the word "vaṣṭi" is to be supplied here as well. For example, "vācā. Some maintain that this is an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*).

Others, however, say that this is merely an illustrative example. Regarding the word *vagāha*, the sense is that by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), only the initial vowel *a* is elided, not the final one. Thus ends the section on indeclinables (*avyaya*) in the *Tattvabodhinī*.

(566) *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* | A rule concerning words applies when they are semantically related (*samartha*). This semantic relation (*sāmarthya*) is of two kinds: that characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) and that characterized by unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). Among these—

The mutual relationship among words, which terminate in their own respective meanings, that arises by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors, is *vyapekṣā*. This very [relationship] exists in a sentence such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). When that *vyapekṣā* is present, a relationship is accepted with whatever is proximate and compatible. For example:

For example: *rājñaḥ puruḥo’śvaśca* ("the king's man and the horse") and *rājño devadattasya ca puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man and Devadatta's man"). However, the state of "becoming a single meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) occurs only in a compound (*vṛtti*), such as *rājapuruṣaḥ*. This [single-meaningness] consists in the attainment of a specific unified meaning by that which was previously grasped as having separate meanings during the stage of grammatical analysis (*prākriyā*). For this very reason, in the case of *rājapuruṣaḥ*, [the relation] resides in the king...

The qualifier "of the wealthy one" (*ṛddhasya*) does not connect [with the meaning of the compound], because it is a part of the referent of a single word (*padārthaikadeśatvāt*). Nor should it be argued that this would result in a lack of connection in cases such as "Devadatta’s teacher’s house" (*devadattasya gurukulam*), since even there the meaning of the genitive case following Devadatta connects with the teacher (*guruṇā*). [This is not so,] because of Devadatta’s...
The connection [of the genitive] is mediated solely by the teacher who is present as the primary member of the family group;

it is the meaning of the sixth case (genitive), and not any other. And it has been said: "Those whose connection is with a whole, such as a teacher or a family, are joined with that which possesses those parts once the parts have been touched."
Alternatively—even when it constitutes a part of a relational entity (*saṃbandhikapadārtha*), the connection with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) certainly occurs.

And it has been said: "Every word denoting a relative is always compounded while being dependent; for that mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), which exists in the sentence, is not lost even in the compound. Now, [one might object] that in this way, the king’s...
"Even though [the word *rājñaḥ*] is always dependent [on another], its connection with the qualifier *ṛddhasya* (of the prosperous) is possible because it is a location.

This is not so; for although the king (*rājñaḥ*), as the ruler, has an expectancy toward the subject ruled (*īśitavya*), he has no expectancy toward the prosperous (*ṛddham*). Now, [one might argue that] since the sentence is established through the very power of its constituent parts...

"Let there not be a separate power (*śaktyantara*) whose object is a qualified meaning. True—[as stated: "If the properties of many [words] were established by means of [separate] utterances alone, there would be excessive prolixity; therefore, the state of having a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is resorted to."

"Furthermore, you must perform the prohibition of [the use of] 'ca' and so forth, as well as the dismantling of many grammatical derivations; however, it is established that for us, this is already established by logic. For instance, in the case of 'dhava-khadirau', the word 'ca' is not employed because its purpose has already been fulfilled by the compound itself; likewise, in cases such as 'citragu', the word 'yat' [is not used]."
But you must provide an answer: the conventional (nirūḍha) secondary function (lakṣaṇā) does not differ significantly from the primary power (śakti).

Furthermore, in the case of the compound *prāptodako grāmaḥ* ("the village to which water has come"), since the word "water" (*udaka*) is correctly used as an adjective when the members are analyzed (*vyasta*), it follows that the use of the adjective "water" applies even in the compound (*samasta*). [This is like the case of the compound "water-jar."]

The [undesired] application of [the suffix] *ṭ* to words would follow; that must be prevented by the very statement, "there is no connection with a qualifier for what has already occurred" (*vṛttasya viśeṣaṇayogo na*). Furthermore, there would be an abandonment of the established grammatical principles (*vyutpatti*) that "non-case-inflected items (*ām*) are construed as non-different (*abheda-anvaya*)" and "the meaning of the affix is the primary element. This applies in cases such as *prāptodaka*.

This is because it is accepted that [the compound] has the sense of "an action of reaching whose agent is water" (*udaka-kartṛka-prāpti-karma*). However, there is brevity (*lāghava*) when there is a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*); such is the direction [of the argument]. Why is the word *pada* mentioned? So that the paribhāṣā concerning semantic competency (*samartha-paribhāṣā*) does not apply in the case of a rule for phonemes (*varṇavidhi*). [Otherwise, in the example] *tiṣṭhatu dadhy ānaya takram*, the substitution of *yaṇ* would indeed occur here. But as for the mention of the word *vidhi* (rule)...

The mention of *pada*—as in "the rule for a *pada*," "the rule for two *padas*," or "the rule for many *padas*"—is intended to ensure that compounds consisting of multiple inflected words are included. They say that if only *pada* were mentioned, this [term] would apply only in cases such as *upapadamatiṅ* (P. 2.2.19) and so forth. This is stated in the Sūtra.

Indicating that the word *samartha* (capable/competent) is used here in a technical sense (*lākṣaṇika*), he says: "based on what is capable" (*samarthāśrita*). Why [is it qualified by] "capable"? [So that] in examples such as *paśyati kṛṣṇam* ("he sees Kṛṣṇa") or *śrito devadattam* ("resorted to Devadatta"), a compound like *kṛṣṇaśrita* should not occur. This is just as in the case of *vastram upagoḥ apatyam caitrasya* ("the cloth of Upagu's son, Caitra's").

The rule "asyāpatyam" (the offspring of this) is stated so that the suffix *aṇ* might not arise from the word *upagu*. However, in certain cases, even when there is dependence on another word, a compound (*vṛtti*) is admitted based on the authority of the Bhāṣya. For example: "kimodanaḥ śālīnām" (of which rice is the meal?), meaning "of which *śāli* grains is the meal? and "saktvāḍhakam āpaṇīyānām" (a measure of groats belonging to those who sell).

The meaning is "an *āḍhaka* measure of marketable barley-flour (*saktu*). In the example, “*ṛto bhavān pāṭaliputrakaḥ*,” there are two Pāṭaliputras; the meaning is: "From which of the two Pāṭaliputras have you come?
The suffix *vuñ* is applied according to the rule "after a place-name ending in *oṣadhi*, [the suffix is added] for those in the east."

(567) *prākkaḍārātsamāsaḥ* |2|1|3|. "Up to *kaḍāra*, it is a compound. The term *prāk* ("before") is repeated; by this, it is understood that first the designation of "compound" (*samāsa*) applies, and thereafter other designations as well. Consequently, there is co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the designations of *avyayībhāva* and so forth.
It is established. Otherwise, there would be a mere synonym. *Samāsa* means "compression" (*samasana*); the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

Some say the meaning is "the becoming of many words into a single word. However, in reality—the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) according to the rule "also when [denoting] an agent other than the karty" (*akartari ca kārake*)—otherwise, the subsequent text, "a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is compounded," would be contradicted.

It would not apply. Anticipating the objection that—since the designation "compound" (*samāsa*) is based on its literal meaning (*anvartha*), there is no possibility of [the designation] applying to *pratīta*, the mention of *saha* is redundant—he says:

"The yoga is being analyzed. From the rule "ubhāmantrito—" (Pāṇini 2.1.2), the term *sub* is understood by anuvṛtti; thus he says, "ending in a *sup* [suffix]. "Is compounded" (*samasyate*): this is the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending of the root *as* preceded by *sa-* with the suffix *ṇic*.

"By the Teacher" (*ācāryeṇa*) is the ellipsis. However, in the phrase "with a capable word" (*samarthena*), the third case is used in the sense of association (*sahayoga*). [This refers to] the act of compounding.

The object is that which ends in a *sub*-suffix, and not the agent (*kartṛ*). Although the ātmanepada ending is obtained in the form *samasyate* even when the status of being an agent is attributed to the word ending in a *sub*-suffix— by virtue of the Vārttika "after a prefix, [the roots] *as* and *ūh* take the ātmanepada"— nevertheless, this is explained in the commentary on the rule concerning compound formation (*samāsa*).

The suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) is difficult to obtain; however, since the principle of "diversity" (*bāhulaka*) is a resort for those with no other way out, it is better simply to accept that [the object] functions as the agent. As for the phrase "and that," this too is obtained precisely because the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is intended to establish the desired result. [Regarding the statement] "only in the Veda": if...
In the world as well, in cases such as *yat prakurute*, there would arise the production of the nominative case-ending (*su*);

and even after assuming the neuter gender for the universal gender (*sarvanāman*) and applying the elision (*luk*) by the rule *vamornapuṃsakāt*, the shortening [of the final vowel] by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake—* would still occur; such are the objections.
We have pointed this out in our commentary on the Sūtra: "He goes after him with an arrow" (*anuvyacalat*).
Since the singular number is intended for the *su* suffix, it should be understood that the compound is formed by alternation (*paryāyeṇa*).

Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the Sūtra "u-gati... (Pāṇini 6.2.49), states that when there is the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final member of the compound, the remaining members are unaccented (*śeṣanighāta*).

(569) *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* | Pāṇini 2.4.71. The term *sup* refers to the pratyāhāra (comprehensive designation) of all case-endings. This is known from the rule prescribing the elision (*luk*) of case-endings in compounds such as *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ* (P. 2.1.39), which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). [The word] "from the mention" (*nirdeśāt*) is used; for otherwise—

The sense is that although there is no distinction in terms of being "first-mentioned" (*prathamānirdiṣṭa*), because the technical designation *upasarjana* is based on its meaning (*anvartha*), it is precisely the word *pūrva* that should undergo prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*). [The rule] "with *iva*" (*ivena*) prescribes a compound and the non-elision of the case-ending; this too is a compound.

As before, this [application] is merely occasional. Therefore, in cases such as *jīmūtasyeva*, the Taittirīyas read it as separate words (*pṛthakpada*). Furthermore, it is established in the *Manoramā* that the analysis of the compound in examples such as *udbāhuriva vāmanaḥ* is thus rendered consistent. [The rule] *vibhaktyalopaśca* (and there is no elision of the case-ending) [is now addressed].

It should be understood that although the elision (*lopa*) of the case-ending (*sup*) is prescribed for the members of a compound, the elision (*luk*) of the *s* (nominative singular) produced after the compound still occurs by the rule *avyayād apṛktam hal*; for even when it is a member ending in such a suffix, it remains an indeclinable (*avyaya*) provided it is not a subordinate element (*anupasarjana*).

(570) An indeclinable [compound] is formed with words expressing case-meaning (*vibhakti*), proximity (*samīpa*), prosperity (*samṛddhi*), decline (*vyṛddhi*), absence (*abhāva*), "with" (*saha*), "not yet" (*asamprati*), speed (*śabda-prāṭ*), state (*bhāva*), "after" (*paścāt*), sequence (*yathā-anupūrvya*), simultaneity (*yaugapadya*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), attainment (*sampatti*), totality (*sākalya*), and limit (*anta*).

[Pāṇini 2.1.6] "Indeclinable" (*avyaya*) [refers to the first member]. Here, "case-meaning" (*vibhakti*) refers to the power of the grammatical factor (*kāraka-śakti*). It is by means of this that [the meaning] is divided.

This is because of the etymological derivation [of *avyaya*] as "that which has the meaning of a nominal stem" (*prātipadikārtha*). For this very reason, he will state later: "An indeclinable (*avyaya*) is that which exists within the meanings of case-endings (*vibhaktyartha*), etc.
(571). That which is designated by the nominative case in a compound is the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). (Pāṇini 1.2.43)

"First-mentioned" (prathamānirdiṣṭam). Here, the compound-word (*samāsapada*) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) with reference to that which prescribes the compound; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of interpreting it as "that which ends in the nominative case when a compound is intended to be formed," which would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to words such as *śrita* in examples like *kṛṣṇaśrita*. With this intention, he says: "in the rule for compounds" (*samāsaśāstre*). [This refers to] the analysis (*vigraha*).

Thus, the sense is that by the mention of "compound" (samāsa) which follows [in the previous rule], it is indicated as applying to the analytical statement (vigraha). However, it is not the case that "of that" (tasya); for, according to the maxim "that which is nearest [is affected]," the status of being a prior member (pūrvanipāta) prescribed by the preceding rule is not prohibited. Therefore, there is no fault in examples such as *kumārīśritaḥ*.

(572) *gostriyor upasarjanasya* |1|2|48|. [The word] *gostrīyoḥ* [is the subject]; *upasarjanasya* is a qualifier of *gostrīyoḥ*. The singular number, however, is used with reference to each [of the two] individually. By the words *go* and *strī*, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is qualified.

With the intention that the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension of a grammatical operation to a form ending with the specified element) applies by virtue of the qualification, he says: "of that which is an *upasarjana*.

Here, *upasarjana* is understood in its technical (*śāstriya*) sense, and not in the sense of being non-primary (*apradhāna*). Therefore, there is no fault in the case of a Brāhmaṇa who behaves like a young girl (*kumārī*), where the word *kumārī* [is used]. Thus it has been stated.
"Ending in a feminine suffix" means ending in *ṭāp* and other such suffixes taught in the section on feminine stems (*strī-adhikāra*).
By this, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *atilakṣmīḥ*. If it is objected that even so, there would still be an over-extension in cases such as *ajakumārīputraḥ*:

On this point, they say: since a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is necessarily correlative, there is no fault, because it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya* and other works that shortening occurs only when the two words "go" and "strī," which constitute the second member (*uttarapada*), are subordinate with respect to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) for which the shortening is prescribed. This is also the case in the *Bhāṣya* and elsewhere.
It should be understood that the sense "of two words which have become the latter members" is obtained because the word *samāsa* (compound) is carried over from the rule *ṛtaddhite*.

(573) *nāvyayībhāvādato’m tvapañcamyāḥ* | Pāṇini 2.4.83. [This sūtra states: "In the case of an avyayībhāva compound ending in /a/, the suffix *am* is substituted [for the case endings], except for the fifth case."

Not in the case of an indeclinable (*avyayībhāva*). Here, by the rule "not after the fifth [case-ending]," the prohibition applies only to *am* because it is the immediately preceding element, and not to *aluk* even though it is separated. To illustrate this very point, the word *u* is used in the sūtra.
This means: "except for the fifth case-ending. Thus, when something other than the fifth case-ending follows an indeclinable *avyayībhāva* ending in *a*, [the elision of *su* does not take place].

It is established that in the case of the *luṅ* elision (of the locative), neither the elision (*luk*) nor the substitution (*am*) occurs for the fifth case (*pañcamī*). What follows from this? [The forms] *adhihari* and *diśayoḥ*. Even when there is an analysis (*vigraha*) with a consonant-ending word as *diśoḥ*, the form remains exactly the same. This is because the word *diś* is listed among the *śaradādi* group, which takes the suffix *ṭac*.

(574) *Tṛtīyāsaptamyor bahulam* [Pāṇini 2.4.84]. The example *apadiśam* is an illustration for case-endings other than the ablative (*pañcamī*). For the ablative, however, one should cite *apadiśāt*. The word *tāvat* in the phrase *vibhaktau tāvat*... [is used] as a particle.

This is the meaning of the sequence. He demonstrates the non-technical (alaukika) analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) as "in Hari" (*harau*). However, the analysis provided by the ancients as "having made Hari the subject" (*harim adhikṛtya*) is incorrect; for in the form *adhihari*, the sense of "having made [something] the subject" is not perceived. [The derivation proceeds as] *hari* + *ṅ*. In the non-technical stage, it is indeed the word *ṅ* that is used.

The entry [of the rule] is appropriate according to the maxim: "Even internal [elements are superseded by external ones]. Otherwise, if *ReĀrautva* were applied first, the vowel *e* in the word *hari* would become unavailable within the compound *adhihari*. This is the intended meaning. Here, the statement of the ancients—namely, that the form *harāvadhī* arises when the word is in the state *harau adhī*—has been disregarded, because in obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*), [the application of the rule must occur before the formation of the compound].
Because it is appropriate only for that which lacks its own constituent analysis (asvapadavigraha). "Even when [the locative] is expressed" means even when it is indicated.

"By the force of the statement" means the sense is that, by the force of prescribing a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix while carrying over the term "upa," the locative case would indeed occur.

If it is objected that, since the locus (adhikaraṇa) is already expressed [by the verb], the nominative alone should apply by the rule "when only the meaning of the nominal stem remains," and not the seventh case (saptamī), they reply: since the compound with the word *aci* must necessarily be with a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it is precisely the case-suffix expressing the sense of the locus— which is indicated by the word *adhi*— that is intended here.

This is because it is appropriate to accept [the rule]. As for what the author of the *Prasāda* has explained— namely, that "because of the enumeration [in the rule] 'by means of verbal suffixes, kṛt-derivatives, taddhita-derivatives, and compounds,' the locative case would indeed occur even when [the sense of location] is already expressed by the prefix *adhi*"— that is not correct, because such an enumeration has been rejected in the original treatise (*ākara*).

For this is stated by the author himself in the rule *‘armaṇi dvitīyā’* (Pāṇini 2.3.2), and because it would contradict the usage in the verse: *‘ramādamuṃ nārada ity abodhi saḥ’*. Regarding this, they explain: “The mention of the word *vacana* (number) is connected with each [of the categories] beginning with case-ending (*vibhakti*) individually.”

Since it would have been sufficient to say simply "in the vicinity of words" (*ākalyanteṣu*), the inclusion of the term *vacana* (word) implies that, by its force, only indeclinables (*avyaya*) functioning solely in the sense of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) are intended here. Consequently, in examples such as *vṛkṣasyopari* (above the tree) and *vṛkṣasya puraḥ* (before the tree), no compound occurs; for [words like] *upari* and so forth— [The remainder of the sentence is not provided in the source text.]

[The suffixes] occur with respect to direction, place, and time as well, and not merely for the sake of expressing a case-relation (*vibhakty-artha*). For this very reason, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "He addressed him as 'Nārada' out of affection" (*ramādamuṃ nārada ityūbodhi saḥ*), because the word *iti*—like a pronoun—refers back to the subject at hand and therefore does not denote mere accusative status (*karmatva*). Thus...

And he employed the word "vibhakti. Others, however, argue that since it would have been simpler to say "simīpasamṛddhau," the inclusion of the term "vibhakti" indicates that the word does not terminate in the locative case; consequently, in the sense of merely indicating the object (karmatva), we have the example "itihāradaḥ."
They say that it indeed becomes a compound;
(575) "and it is an *avyayībhāva*" [Pāṇini 2.4.18], meaning it shall be neuter. And this is obtained from the rule "that [compound] is neuter" [Pāṇini 2.4.17]. Proximity...

Thus, because the technical name *avyayībhāva* is based on its etymological meaning (*anvartha-saṃjñā*), this compound occurs only when the sense of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) ending in the locative case is predominant. However, when the proximity (*samīpa*) is predominant, he will later state that a *bahuvrīhi* is formed by the rule "a number or an indeclinable with *āsanna*"—as in the example *upa-daśāḥ*. [The opponent asks: "But [how can you say this]? regarding the phrase "by the force of the rule" (*vidhāna-sāmarthyāt*). Indeed...
In cases such as *‘amayā grāmam’*,
let there be no *avyayībhāva* compound due to the force of the rule prescribing the second case (*dvitīyā*); however, in *‘ārād vanāt’*,
it would certainly occur, because the prescription of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) by the rule *‘anyārāt...’* applies when used in conjunction with the word *ārāt* in the sense of distance.

If it is argued that [the genitive] is applicable because there is scope for it, some here speculate: "Since both the genitive and the ablative would be applicable by the rule *dūrāntikārthaiḥ ṣaṣṭhyanyatarasyām*, the ablative alone is prescribed by that [rule] as an exception to them. And thus, in connection with the word *ārāt*, which has the sense of 'near'..."

The prescription of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) as an exception (*apavāda*) to the sixth case-ending is indeed without scope; therefore, the statement that "there is no *dvandva* compound" by virtue of that [prescription] is entirely correct. However, others do not accept this, because there is no specific rule prescribing the fifth case-ending in connection with the words *antikāt* and *ārāt*.
"Furthermore, because the rule *ṭhaṇy-ārāt* has its purpose fulfilled elsewhere,
the avyayībhāva compound *ārād vanaṃ* (near the forest) would be unavoidable. For those who explain it in this way,

since there is no downward extension (*apakarṣa*) of the word *padasya*, this *yaṅ* suffix has scope for application in the sense of intensity (*bhṛśārtha*), whereas [it is restricted] to repetition (*paunaḥpunye*).
The point is that [the rule] would be sublated by a subsequent doubling; thus, the *Manoramā* commentary on the sūtra "ity-avīpsayoḥ" is favorable [to this view]. Regarding *sumadram*:
if the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule "ugati" (Pāṇini 6.2.192)—meaning the Madras are prosperous.

[The examples] "sumadrāḥ" and "duryavanaḥ. Nor is there establishment [of the compound] here through the absence of meaning, because a compound is accepted only when there is an absence of the specific meaning belonging to that which is being compounded. And here there is not an absence of Yavanas, such that the compound would occur due to the absence of meaning; rather, it is the absence of their prosperity.

Regarding the term *nirmakṣika* ("free from flies"): this compound denotes an absolute absence (*saṃsargābhāva*), and not even a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*). This is because, by the force of the inclusion of the word "object" (*artha*), only that absence which is the opposite of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the cognition produced by the compounded words is grasped. However, as for mutual absence...

Because there is contradiction precisely with the delimitator of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*), and because that [delimitator], even when it functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*), is not the substantive (*viśeṣya*). As for those who say: "Even in the case of 'the cloth seen is not [there],' the meaning is simply the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of cloth-ness (*paṭatva*), according to the principle of the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* regarding the universal (*jāti*)," [they are mistaken].

Regarding the phrase "because it is a word-meaning" (*padārthatvāt*): even in their view, since the substratum (*dharmin*) is already implied by the very capacity of the term "object" (*artha*), this compound refers to the absence of the object itself and not the absence of its attributes (*dharma*);
thus there is no fault. The term *atyaya* is for the sake of clarity. [The phrase] "by the absence of the object" (*arthābhāvena*).

Because the meaning has already been conveyed. What is intended is the absence of relation due to the absence of the object, and not mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "a pot is not a cloth"—this is the conclusion.
Regarding the word *saṃprati*: the indeclinable *saṃprati* means "now" (*idānīm*). [The commentary says: "Now" (*etarhi*).
According to the statement of Amarasimha, "saṃprati" means "now.

Since this [term] primarily possesses the power of the locus (adhikaraṇa-śakti), it is fit for connection only with a verbal root (kriyāpada). A negation, moreover, is appropriate only for an action. This is what he says: "it is joined," namely, with "asaṃprati."
However, it should be understood that in the usage of the sūtra, there is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) through the inclusion of the action of "joining" (*yuj*).

As for what was stated by the author of the *Prasāda*: "‘Not now’ (*asaṃprati*); the meaning is ‘the absence of being present. By this, the current time of a useful object is negated. That is not correct.

Because it is improper for that which primarily possesses the power of being a locus (*adhikaraṇa*)— and which is fit for connection only with an action— to be construed as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) in relation to a negation; for no one accepts that by the statement "there is no jar on the ground" the ground itself is negated, such that [the objection] would apply here.

The negation of the present time would be logical. "Iti harīti": there is a compound of the word *iti*, meaning "thus," with the word *hari* ending in the genitive case, which refers to its own form (*svarūpa*). Then, "afterwards" (*paścāt*): if this is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*), the indeclinable *paścāt* is placed first.

The intended meaning is "it may be so. Regarding the phrase "from the usage in the Bhāṣya": it should also be understood that this is because of the usage in the Bhāṣya on the rule *anekam anyapadārthe*, namely the example *pūrvāparāt*. Regarding the word *pratyartham*:
since the distributive sense (*vīpsā*) is already included within the compound formation (*vṛtti*), there is no reduplication. Regarding the word *prati*: [it is used here as a preposition].

As for what they say—"In the case of *grāmasya vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati*, because there is a lack of compounding due to the presence of a dependent relation (*sāpekṣatva*), the prescription of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) has its scope"—that is not correct. For in the case of obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*), the rule "there is no formation [of a compound] for those that are not qualifiers" (*aviśeṣaṇānāṃ vṛtir na*) does not apply. [The word] *ānupūrvyeṇa* [is used].

The state of being successive is *ānupūrvyam*; [the suffix] *ṣyañ* is applied because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class [of words]. (Pāṇini 5.1.124) Regarding the rule *avyayībhāve cā’kāle* (Pāṇini 6.3.81), as in the example "simultaneously with the wheel" (*yugapaccakram*), some maintain that this is expressed by the compound alone.
It must be so, because the word *yugapat* is also an indeclinable (*avyaya*);
however, they say that it is more appropriate to analyze [the compound] as "at the same time as the wheel" (*cakreṇa ekakālam*), and so forth. Regarding the example *saha pūrvāhṇam*:

this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of totality (*sākalya*). Regarding the phrase "even though it is subordinate" (*guṇabhūte api*): if it were not stated that [the *saha* compound] occurs in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*), [then the rule would fail].

The point is this: it would apply only where similarity (*sādṛśya*) is understood as the predominant factor, because in an *avyayībhāva* compound, the predominance of the indeclinable’s meaning is the general rule. Regarding the word "end" (*anta*):
it refers to that extent of the textual portion [of a work] such that one thinks, "Now, this much section is to be studied."

"Acceptance" (parigraha) refers to the completion [of study] in relation to that; this is what is intended here by the word "end" (anta). And since that [completion] occurs even when the study is incomplete, it is mentioned separately from "completeness" (sākalya). Regarding the phrase "one who maintains the sacred fires" (sāgnī):
the word "fire" (agni) refers to the text that explains those fires; that [word], ending in the third case, is used invariably [with the suffix -mat].

It is compounded. Nor should it be said that such a usage as "together with fire" (agninā saha) is difficult to obtain; for its employment is justified when one intends to express mere association (sāhityamātra). However, when the intention is to express the state of being the limit (antatva), the compound is obligatory; thus, the analysis using non-co-occurrent words (asvapadavigraha)—namely, "up to the section on fire" (agnigranthaparyantam)—has been shown. As for that which...
Some say that the analysis [of the compound] is either "fire is its end" (*agniḥ anto ’sya*) using the nominative case, or "the end of fire" (*agneḥ antaḥ*) using the genitive case;

they further claim that the compound itself may likewise be formed with either the nominative or the genitive. That is not correct, because the word *saha* does not denote "end," and because "being an end" (*antatva*) is even more certainly not obtained [as the meaning of *saha*].

Furthermore, because the use of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) with a word joined in association (*sahayukta*) is logically correct; and because, just as in the case of *atṛṇamati* (‘not even grass’), where completeness (*sākalya*) is indicated by the association, so too in *sāgni* (‘together with fire’), the state of being final (*antatva*) is indicated by the association—it is therefore without any basis to abandon that [rule] here after having accepted a compound with a word ending in the third case. In this regard:

Regarding the term *bodhyam*: since the suffix denoting one who studies (*adhyetṛ*) is optional according to the rule *tad adhīte*, the suffix *aṇ* is not mentioned in the case of *sāgni*. Even if the suffix *aṇ* were applied, the form would still be *sāgni* alone, because it will be stated later that "the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* must be prescribed after words beginning with *sarva* and those beginning with *sa*."

(577) *Yathā’sādṛśye* |2|1|7|. Regarding *yathā’sā*: To ensure there is no doubt, since one could have simply said "in the sense of non-similarity (*asādṛśye*) when [the word] *yathā* [is used]," the reversed pronunciation is for the purpose of obtaining the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the negative particle (*nañ*). Thus, Vāmana explains it as "in the sense of non-similarity" (*asādṛśya*).

"Yāvantaḥ" means "those whose measure is such. The suffix *vatup* is applied according to the rule "yat-tad-etebhyaḥ... (Pāṇini 5.2.39). (578) Pāṇini 2.1.8 states: "yāvat in the sense of limitation. In the expression "yāvac-chlokam," the indeclinable "yāvat" is compounded; however, the analytical statement (*vigraha*) is as follows:

The analysis of the compound as ending in a *taddhita* suffix indeed constitutes a non-syntactic (*asvapada*) analysis. What is the purpose of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*)? [In the example] "as much was given as was eaten" (*yāvad dattaṃ tāvad bhuktam*), the meaning is that one does not ascertain exactly how much was given or how much was eaten.
(579) *suppratinā mātrārthe* | Pāṇini 2.1.9. [When *prati* is used with a word ending in a case-ending (*sup*) in the sense of "measure" (*mātrārtha*), it forms an indeclinable compound.]
While the term *sub* is already understood from the preceding context, the repetition of *sub* here is intended to exclude indeclinables (*avyaya*);
making this clear, he provides the example: *śākaprati*. [Objection: But surely, by the very force of its formulation, it must refer only to that which is distinct from an indeclinable.

If it is argued that [the term *sub*] should be compounded with a case-ending (*sup*), they say in response: in the absence of the repeated mention of *sub*, there would be the fault that compounds such as *doṣāmanyam ahar* ("a day other than the evening") and *divāmanyā rātriḥ* ("a night other than the day")— which, within the scope of the *vṛtti* (derivative formation), are seen to have substantives as their primary meaning— would not be compounded with *prati* in the sense of "measure" (*mātrā*), since only indeclinables of that specific type [those primarily denoting action] would be so compounded.

And likewise, it might be possible to conceive of [the meaning] as "a portion of the day" (*divasasya leśaḥ*) being the "recipient" (*āharaṇatva*) of the non-perception during the day (*divā-prati*) and the perception at night (*doṣā-prati*), and so forth. Regarding the example *vṛkṣaṃ prati*: [one might object] that, by the force of the rule prescribing the designation of *karmapravacanīya* for *prati* when used in the sense of a marker (*lakṣaṇa*) and so on, there would necessarily be a sentence containing the accusative case (*dvitīyā*).

If it is argued that this is not a compound, because the term *samāsa* has scope only in the sense of "a small portion" (leśa), we say: not so. For, in examples such as *vṛkṣaṃ prati siñcati* ("he waters toward the tree"), the prescription of the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* serves the purpose of preventing the application of the rule for *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*); thus, if the inclusion of the word *mātra* were absent, the designation would be rendered useless.

Because by this [rule], there would also follow the application of a compound even in the case of *lakṣaṇa* (marking). However, since in an *avyayībhāva* expressing distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), words such as *prati* are prescribed to be placed first, in cases like "she sprinkles for the sake of pleasure" (*aratyarthaṃ siñcati*), the rule for *karmapravacanīya* would otherwise serve no purpose due to the non-application of the rule for *ṣatva*. Therefore, by the force of that [prescription], the [compound] contains a second case ending.
