The author of the root-text (Patañjali) has stated that a word [ending in the accusative] may also form a compound, as in the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti*. Regarding this, the moderns (*navya*) maintain: in the avyayībhāva compound *pratyartham*, the indeclinable existing as a marker (*dyotaka*) of repetition (*vīpsā*) is compounded. This is provided that there is a rule for designating the marker of repetition as a *karmapravacanīya*.

Even if that were accepted, the designation of *prati* and so on as *karmapravacanīya* is indeed purposeful for the sake of preventing the substitution of *ṣ* in expressions such as *pratistavanaṃ* and *pratisthānam*. In reality, however, the designation of *karmapravacanīya* applies to *prati* and the others when distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is the governing factor, and not otherwise.

[The suffix *prati*] is used only as an indicator of repetition (*vīpsā*). Otherwise, in the example "he waters tree after tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati siñcati*), the repetition is indicated by the doubling [of the word *vṛkṣa*] alone; the word *prati*, however, is connected with the action. The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is applied because it is an object (*karman*). Since the technical designation of *karmapravacanīya* overrides the designation of *upasarga*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur.

Otherwise, one would have to offer a libation of water to the *Akṣeṭthaṃbhūta* rule contained in the beautiful treatise beginning with *ne’ti*, and consequently, since the force of the rule for prescribing technical names (*saṃjñā*) would be exhausted,
even a sentence containing an accusative case— such as the usage in the Bhāṣya, "pratītyārtham artham"— would [be untenable].
They say it should be explained as "it happens. To indicate defeat, he says: "the choice was made in reverse.
This means that it was not chosen in the same manner as when victory was previously attained. "One reversed" means that one [element] was chosen in reverse; likewise for "two reversed," and so on.
He explains by dividing the rule *vibhāṣā 'pa-pari-bahis* into two parts:
Regarding *vibhāṣā*: for the compounds preceding this [sūtra], just as in the case of technical designations such as *ṭi*, *ghu*, and *bha*, [the subsequent rules apply].

Since there is no mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*), its permanence is established by logic alone; and he confirms that very point through an indicative mark (*liṅga*) with the words "this [is]... Now, one might object: in this case, the rule *'upsupā'* would also be permanent. If this is accepted as the desired conclusion, then [the example] *'ūrvaṃ bhūto bhūtapūrvaḥ'*—wherein the compound is formed by *'sup supā'*—[would follow].

Otherwise, the *Vṛtti* text would be contradicted. Likewise, regarding the *Śākala-sūtra*, "The prohibition of the *Śākala* [substitution] applies to *it* and *nitya* compounds," the *Bhāṣya* states: "'*Itya*' need not be mentioned; by this [omission], the following is also established:
*vāpyāmaśvo vāpyaśvaḥ* (a horse in a pond). Kaiyaṭa has explained this as: "*vāpyaśva*..."

Regarding the phrase "iti supsupeti samāsasaḥ," [the author] says "supsupeti tu" in response to the following doubt: "But since the prohibition [of the genitive case] is established by the fact that the locative compound (saptamīsamāsa) under the rule 'aṃjñāyām' is compulsory, even that textual passage would be contradicted. Now, what is the point here?

To provide the justification for this, he says: "the word 'indeclinable' (avyaya), etc. The meaning is that although the compound is already established by the rule *sup-supā* alone, the fact that compounds are prescribed again by rules such as *avyayam* indicates that the application of those specific rules is only occasional (*kvācitka*). And thus, since the compounding with *iva* is also only occasional, [the desired form is obtained].

The form *udbāhur iva vāmanaḥ* and so forth is established. Regarding the Vārttika *ivena*, although it is recited under the rule *ugati* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), Kaiyaṭa maintains that it is actually recalled here under the rule *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19) within the context of the compulsory (*nitya*) section. This being the case, [the example] *udbāhur iva*...

Those who postulate that the compound with *iva*—for the sake of establishing the usage in common speech such as *vāmanaḥ* and so forth—is restricted to the domain of Vedic meter (*chandas*), have been refuted; for even in the Veda, it is not admitted that such a compound is mandatory.
For instance, in the case of *mūtasyeva*, although the followers of the Ṛgveda admit the compound, [it is not considered obligatory].
Because it is recited as being split [into separate words] by the Taittirīyas; and this point is established in the *Manoramā*.

(581) *Apa-pari-bahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.12). Regarding *apa*, *pari*, and *bahis*: in connection with *apa* and *pari*, [the rule] "with *apa*, *pari*, and *añc*, the fifth case" (*apa-pary-āṅ-paribhiḥ*) [applies].

That which is prescribed by the rule for the fifth case (*pañcamī*) remains prescribed even when joined with a word ending in *añc* or *utarapada*, by virtue of the rule beginning with *ṭhanyārāu*. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "fifth case" (*pañcamyāḥ*) here is for the purpose of indicating that "the fifth case occurs in connection with the word *ahi*. Since "that which is established by an indicatory mark (*jñāpaka*) does not apply everywhere," [we see] in the example *arasya karabhaḥ*...
The form *bahiḥ* is also established [as a separate word].
(582) Pāṇini 2.1.13: *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ*. For example, *ā bālam* ("from childhood"), and *ā paramāṇor ā ca bhūgolakaṃ* ("from the smallest atom up to the entire earth").

The application [of the rule] in the *Kiraṇāvalī* is erroneous, because the use of the word *ca* in the middle of a compound is impossible; rather, the reading "ṭhā ca bhūgolakāt" is appropriate. (583) Pāṇini 2.1.14: "When *abhi* and *prati* denote direction toward (*ābhimukhya*), they form a compound with a word denoting a mark (*lakṣaṇa*)."

By "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*): Amara states that *ihna*, *lakṣma*, and *lakṣaṇa* are synonyms; thus he says, "by that which denotes a mark. It follows that here [the prepositions] *abhi* and *prati* express both the relationship between the indicator and the indicated (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*) and the sense of direction (*ābhimukhya*). Thus: *agnim abhi* and *agniṃ prati*. [This is according to Pāṇini’s rule: *abhir abhāge*.
In the expression *akṣaṇetthaṃbhūte*, the accusative case is used because *abhi* and *prati* function as *karmapravacanīya*s (prepositions governing a noun).

Why [is the rule] "by means of a characteristic" (*lakṣaṇena*) stated? Consider: *srugdhnaṃ pratigataḥ*. This means he has returned from Srughna; that is, he has turned back toward Srughna itself. For in this instance, Srughna is the object (*karman*), not the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

What is the meaning of *abhipratī*? [It is] "he has gone by way of where the fire is. Since there is the cognition that he has gone by the same path as the fire, fire is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) of the act of going; furthermore, since there is also the sense of "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*), there would be a compound with the word *agni* using the words *yena* and *tena*. What is the purpose of [specifying] "facing toward"?

*Abhyaṅkā gāvaḥ* (cows with marks on their sides) and *pratyaṅkāḥ* (cows with marks facing them). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those whose mark (*aṅka*) is new (*abhinava*) or facing (*pratinava*). For in this context, the "mark" refers to a characteristic of the cows; it does not mean "facing toward.
But surely, since an *avyayībhāva* compound is accepted when the sense of an indeclinable is predominant by general rule, how can there be any occasion for this [compound] here?

On this point, they say: in this section, this [sūtra] is intended to indicate that even when the context concerns a *bahuvrīhi* compound, an *avyayībhāva* may occur. By means of this, forms such as “*dvimuni vyākaraṇam*” (the grammar [taught by] two sages) are established under the rule “*saṃkhyā vaṃśyena*.”

(584) *anu* [is used] with *yat* and *samayā* | Pāṇini 2.1.15. The word *anu* [is used] with *yat*; by using *yadi*, it indicates that the second case is employed when joined with *samayā*—namely, "that object" (*yaṃ padārtham*).
The meaning is "the vicinity of which object. The term *lakṣaṇena* (by way of a characteristic mark) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

Thus he says: "by that which serves as a characteristic. This means by that which expresses a mark. Since [the formation] is already established by the rule "avyaya-vibhakti" (Pāṇini 2.4.82), this sūtra is for the purpose of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*). Therefore, it is established in the *Manoramā* that in the alternative case, "vanasyānu" should be cited as an example. Regarding this, some say: "The genitive case here in 'vanasya' is difficult to justify."
Since the use of the second case (*dvitīyā*) would otherwise be unavoidable when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*,
and since this [rule] serves as an injunction (*vidhi*) to prevent the resulting sublation of compounding (*samāsa)— as in the case of *samayā laṅkām*—
one should not argue that this particle *anu* merely indicates proximity (*sāmīpya*) and does not indicate the relationship between the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*).

Because the inclusion of the word "lakṣaṇena" (by way of indication) would otherwise be redundant. Nor should it be argued that even with this [addition], there is no indication of mere indication (*lakṣaṇamātra*); for in the rule *akṣaṇettham*, the word "mātra" is absent. Furthermore, this would contradict the examples and counter-examples found in the preceding sūtra, such as *agnim abhi* and *agniṃ prati*.

Therefore, in this view, the example to be cited is *anu vanaṃ*. However, the explanatory statement found in the root text, "gone near the forest" (*vana-sya samīpaṃ gataḥ*), should be interpreted as "gone near the forest which has become [an object of] sight" (*akṣaṇa-bhūtasya vana-sya samīpaṃ gataḥ*). Why [is the word] *anu* used? [Example: *grāmaṃ samayā*. Why [is the phrase] *yat-samayā* used?
The lightning flashes along the tree. Why [is it] by way of a characteristic? *anu-vacaṭnam*.
Here, as in the case of *upa-kṛṣṇam*, there is always an avyayībhāva compound. (585) *yasya cāyāmaḥ* || 2.1.16 ||

And with regard to this [sūtra], having carried over the word *anu* from the previous rule and having repeated it, he explains it by transforming one instance into the third case, saying: "by *anu*. [He says] "as a characteristic" (*lakṣaṇabhūtena*);
the sense is that the word *lakṣaṇena* is carried over. [The example is] *anugaṅgam*.

Here, the status of "length" (*āyāma*) as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) is illuminated by the suffix *an*, whereas the indicated object (*lakṣya*) is the meaning of the compound. For this very reason, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Vārāṇasī.
This being the case, he states the resulting conclusion: "the length of the Gaṅgā," etc., and "Vārāṇasī. [The etymology is: it is both excellent (*vara*) and eternal (*anaś*).

*Varāṇasī*: "Varāṇa" means excellent water; "ṭhana" [is a suffix] applied to *klība* (eunuch), water, sorrow, a mother, and a chariot—so state Rudra and Rabhasa. That which exists not far from that [place] is [denoted by] *adūrabhava*. By the rule "adūrabhavaśca," the suffix *aṇ* is applied. There is vṛddhi of the first vowel. By the rule "ūrvapadātsaṃjñāyām," there is the substitution of *ṇa*.

Regarding "gaṅgāyā anviti": they say that in the alternative where a compound (*samāsa*) is not formed, one should cite *gaṅgām anv* according to the method previously stated. (586) *tiṣṭhadguprabhṛtīni ca* || 2.1.17 || And [the group] beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu* [are indeclinable compounds]. 2.1.17.

And the words beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu* [are indeclinable]. The particle *ca* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*. Therefore, there is no other grammatical derivation (*vṛttyantara*) for these;
the meaning is that forms such as *paramatiṣṭhadgu* do not occur. Regarding *tiṣṭhadgu*: the short vowel is applied by the rule *ostriyoḥ*. It is in apposition with the nominative case.

Since the substitution of *śatṛ* is impossible [in these cases], he says: "here, the substitution of *śatṛ*. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should include: *khaleyavaḥ*, *khalebuṣam* (with non-elision of the locative case), *lūnayavaḥ*, *lūyamānayavaḥ*, and so on.
(587) *pāre madhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā* |2|1|18|.

[The words] *pāre* and *madhye* [are used as indeclinables]. This is stated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). The purpose of this irregular formation ending in *-e* is for cases where the sense of the locative case is not possible. However, when the sense of the locative is possible, [the compound is formed] according to the rule for the *tatpuruṣa*.

Regarding the phrase "kṛti bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.3.109), since the desired form is established even without the elision [of the case-ending] due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various cases), the author provides an example ending in the ablative case—namely, *pāregaṅgāt* and so forth—in order to indicate the absence of the locative sense here. [He says: "by means of the *mahāvibhāṣā*."

But surely, when the *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of an exception (*apavāda*) is optionally excluded by the *mahāvibhāṣā*, the general rule (*utsarga*), namely the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*, applies; and since that too falls under the jurisdiction of the *vibhāṣā* rule and is thus optional,
the analytical sentence (*vākya*) is also established in its turn— so why is the word "or" (*vā*) mentioned in the sūtra?

If it is argued that [the rule] is indeed useless, here they say: since the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is optional according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, when that single integrated meaning is intended, an *avyayībhāva* compound would necessarily apply, thereby superseding the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*.
Therefore, in this case, [the rule is stated] for the purpose of allowing the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* to optionally coexist.

The mention of "or" (*vā*) [is used]. However, under the view that "some hold that semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) consists in mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*)," since even in a compound (*vṛtti*) the competency is defined solely by mutual expectancy, it follows that the compound would be permanently superseded by the sentence (*vākya*).
To prevent this, the formation of the compound is made optional. Thus, when the *avyayībhāva* compound is optionally formed, according to the previously mentioned method, in one alternative case—

Since that *tatpuruṣa* compound is also optional, the sentence form is indeed established; nevertheless, this [rule] is intended to provide the following indication: "Where both a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) are made optional by the *mahāvibhāṣā*, once the form has been released by the exception, the general rule does not apply again. Therefore, previously...
When the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is precluded by the part-whole compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*) in the case of *kāyasya*, the [genitive] compound does not occur;
and when the suffix *iñ* is precluded by *ata iñ* in the case of *dakṣasyāpatyaṃ dākṣiḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* does not occur— rather, in both instances,
there is only the analytical sentence (*vākya*).

(588) *saṃkhyā vaṃśyena* | 2|1|19| A numeral [is compounded] with a word denoting a member of a lineage (*vaṃśya*). A lineage (*vaṃśa*) is a continuous succession; that which occurs therein is "of the lineage" (*vaṃśya*). The suffix *yat* is applied because it belongs to the class beginning with *diś*. "Two Munis" refers to Pāṇini and Kātyāyana. "Three Munis" refers to those two plus [Patañjali].
Patañjali—these three are the lineage-holders (*vaṃśya*). The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used here in connection with "of grammar" (*vyākaraṇasya*).

This compound is formed when the primary significance lies in the meaning of its own members (*svapadārtha-prādhānya*). However, when there is an intention to express the predominance of the external referent (*anyapadārtha-prādhānya*)—namely, "the three sages who are the lineage-holders of whom [grammar is the property]"—then...
They say that it is indeed a *bahuvrīhi* compound, as in the expression "the grammar of the three Munis" (*trimunivyākaraṇam*).

Although this is also logically possible as a *bahuvrīhi*, the intention is that there is nevertheless a difference in form even when other case-endings are applied. In reality, however, regarding the rule "with *abhi* and *prati* [used with] *akṣaṇa*... (Pāṇini 2.1.14):

We have already stated that because of the inclusion of the term *ābhimukhya* (facing toward), the *avyayībhāva* compound occurs even in cases where a *bahuvrīhi* would otherwise be expected; thus, forms such as *dvimuni vyākaraṇam* ("the grammar [studied by] two Munis") are established. He provides an example with respect to birth (*janman*): *ekaviṃśatibhāradvājam*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is:
"twenty-one Bhāradvājas belonging to the same lineage. Now, [an objection is raised]:...

The elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule "after *bharadvāja*, there is elision of *vidat* and *yañ*, as well as of *ṭhyañ* and *añ*" would apply; nor can it be argued that there is no elision because the constituent members (*vartipada*) undergo a transition to another meaning qualified by singularity subordinate to their own referent.

The statement of Kaiyaṭa is to be respected; for otherwise, since the *luk* elision—which is *antaraṅga* because it applies even before the entry of the *vṛtti*—would be unavoidable, the form *gargakulam* (the family of the Gargas) would not even exist. Regarding this, they say: the absence of *luk* in this case is to be understood precisely from the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya.
And this is clear from the *Śabdakaustubha* on the rule "ṛtīyāsaptamyoh" (Pāṇini 6.3.9).
(589) *nadībhiśca* (Pāṇini 2.1.20):
"And with [words denoting] rivers. Here, neither the word-form itself nor its technical name (*saṃjñā*) is intended to be included, because of the use of the plural number in the citation.
Rather, it refers to the meaning; and since a compound of that [meaning] is not possible, this compound belongs to those words which express that meaning.

And these are not only particular terms, but general terms as well. By this, *pañcanadam* (the land of five rivers) and *saptagodāvaraṃ* (the region of seven Godāvarīs) are established, according to the rule: "And [the compound is formed] with the word *godāvarī* and the word *nadī*."

He says "number" (*saṃkhyā*), explaining that the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule to be stated hereafter, and by the letter *ca*, the word "number" is drawn forward [from a previous rule]. This might be the case: by the principle of "prior exceptions," this [rule] would only be a sublater of the rule "pūrvakālaika-".

Furthermore, in the case of *evanadī* (formed as an *avyayībhāva*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffix *ṭac* prescribed by the rule *adīpaurṇamāsya-*; however, if it were a *samāhāra-dvigu*, the *dvigu* itself would apply because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Therefore, he says:
"And this is desired in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*). In the phrase "and this," the vowel *a* has the sense of the particle *eva*.
Thus, it follows that the *avyayībhāva* compound is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *dvigu* compound.

(590) *anyapadārthe ca saṃjñāyām* | 2.1.21. [The sūtra states: "And when the meaning is that of another word, provided it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). The term "number" (*saṅkhyā*) is understood from the previous rule. The mention of "river" (*nadī*) is also carried over (*anuvartate*).

Thus he says: "A word ending in a case-suffix [is compounded] with words denoting rivers. Why does it say "when it refers to another object" (anyapadārthe)? [Consider the example: *kṛṣṇaveṇī*. [The answer is: because it is not understood as a name (*saṃjñā*). A *saṃjñā* is that which is correctly known (*samyak jñāyate*). By the rule "after [a root ending in] ā, when preceded by a prefix, the suffix aṅ is used in the sense of the object," the form *saṃjñā* is derived. The meaning is: because the specific region that serves as the bearer of the name (*saṃjñin*) is not understood.
However, it was not stated that [the compound] is impossible because the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is not understood;

for the meaning of another word is indeed perceived through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with other words such as "of whom" (*yasya*). This is precisely why a *bahuvrīhi* is not considered an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). What is the purpose of the restriction "when it is a technical name" (*saṃjñāyām*)? [Consider: *śīghragaṅgaḥ*.

[The word] *deśaḥ* [is the example]. Now, regarding the *avyayībhāva* compound, he states the uncommon suffixes for the compound: *avyayī*. Although it could have been stated as "after words beginning with *apara*," the inclusion of the term *prabhṛti* was made because consideration for brevity (*lāghava*) is not observed among synonyms. [Thus,] the suffix *ṭac* shall be applied.
The intention is that [the suffix] *ṭac* follows from the rule "ājahaḥ sakhibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.91).
(591) *samāsāntāḥ* (5.4.68): Regarding the term *samāsānta*, it refers to the final member (*caramāvayava*) of a compound, or of the final word which constitutes the meaning of the compound.

This is the meaning. By this [rule], the suffix *am* is established in the case of *upaśaradam* because the *avyayībhāva* compound ends in *a*; however, in cases such as *dvipurī*, the suffix *ap*—prescribed by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ*—is an integral part (*avayava*) of the final member (*uttarapada*), and thus it ends in the letter *ṛ*.
It should be understood that because the word *dvigu* is feminine according to the rule *pado dviguḥ striyām*, the suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed by the rule *avigor iti*.
(592) *avyayībhāve śaratprabhṛtibhyaḥ* 5.4.107.

Regarding *prativipāśam*: the compound is formed according to the rule *akṣaṇenābhipratī-*. Amara states: "The river Vipāśā is called *vipāṭ* in the feminine. He recites the list [of words] beginning with *śarat*. Here, for those words ending in a *jhay* consonant, since the option of *hayaḥ* would otherwise apply, this reading is for the sake of making it compulsory (*nitya*). In this case...

The two *gaṇasūtras* are “*arāyā jaras*” and “*ratipara*. Regarding the form *upajarasam*, the meaning is “near to old age” (*jarāyāḥ samīpam*). Regarding the rule *yasyetica*: the intention is that because the suffix *ṭac* is a *taddhita* suffix, there is elision of the vowel *i* when this [suffix] follows. Regarding *pratyakṣam*: it is a compound formed with the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) by virtue of its literal correspondence (*yathārthatvena*).

The compound is formed either by the rule *akṣṇābhipratī-* (Pāṇini 2.1.14) in the sense of "facing the eye," or as *akṣṇaḥ param* ("beyond the eye"), meaning "not within the range [of vision]. In the context of its derivative function (*vṛtti*), the word *akṣi* refers merely to the sense organ. How can this be an *avyayībhāva* compound, given that it is not a compound formed with an indeclinable (*avyaya*)?
Anticipating the objection that there is no sūtra prescribing this, he says: "By the force of the injunction" (vidhānasāmarthyāt).
Regarding the term *samakṣam*: it means "suitable for the eyes" (*akṣṇo yogyam*). Regarding the term *anvakṣam*: it is an avyayībhāva compound in the sense of "behind the eyes" (*akṣṇaḥ paścāt*).

(593) *nāstaddhite* | 6|4|144|. The term "a" (*a*) qualifies the governing heading "of a *bha*" (*bhasya*); because it is a qualifier, the rule of "extension to that which ends with it" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, and thus he says: "of a *bha* ending in *na*. The mention of "in a taddhita suffix" is redundant, because the desired form is established simply by the elision of the *ṭi* portion via the rule "for indeclinables, [the elision occurs] before any *bha*-affix. Nor should it be argued that the status of being an indeclinable is not sufficient for the [elision] when the suffix is specifically *ṭac*,
because the designation of *avyayībhāva* must be presupposed for the application of *ṭac*.
Because the indeclinability of the first member is not lost either. On this point, they say:

there is no fault, because the designation "indeclinable" (avyaya-saṃjñā) for an *avyayībhāva* compound is prescribed in the Bhāṣya only for three specific operations—namely, the formation of the *luṅ* aorist, accentuation (*svara*), and usage (*upacāra*). And this is logical; otherwise, [the objection would hold].

In examples such as *upaśaradam*, the elision of the *ṭi* suffix would result. Although it was indicated by the long-vowel pronunciation in the rule *aḍ-uta-masya pi ca* that there is no priority (*paurvaparya*) with respect to its own constituent part, even when *ṭhaṅ* is stated, by the principle of "including what begins with that" (*tad-ādi-grahaṇa*), that which is qualified by it possesses the status of an *aṅga*; therefore, the long vowel [is applied] from *ataḥ*.

Although the long vowel [ā] in *yañ* is established by rule, it should nevertheless be understood that, on account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *ahnaṣṭakhoreva*, that [long vowel] is not relied upon when forming compound suffixes (*samāsānta*). In *ādhyātmyam*, the term *adhyātma* means "with respect to the self" (*ātmani*);
this is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) in the sense of a case ending.

(594) *napuṃsakād anyatarasyām* |5|4|109|. The mention of "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) is a qualifier for that which ends in the suffix *-an*, not for the *avyayībhāva* compound, because the latter does not deviate from being neuter; thus he says: "that which is neuter and ends in *-an*. By virtue of ending in *-an*...

He states that because it is a qualifier of an *avyayībhāva* compound, there is an extension of the rule (*tadantavidhi*) to include those ending in such a term—hence he says "from that which ends in [the suffix] *tat*.

Regarding *upacarmam*: when the suffix *ṭac* is applied, there is elision of the *ṭi*-portion; and because the stem ends in *a*, the substitution of *am* for *ap* occurs. (595) Pāṇini 5.4.110: *nadīpaurṇamāsyāgrahāyaṇībhyaḥ*. [The suffix *ṭac* is applied after feminine stems denoting rivers, as well as *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī*, to form adverbs.]

In the case of *nadīpaurṇamāsī*, only the word-form (*svarūpa*) is intended to be grasped, not the technical name (*saṃjñā*), because *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī* are mentioned separately [in the rule]. Regarding *upanadī*: in the absence of the suffix *ṭac*, the short vowel occurs by virtue of the neuter gender. On this point, they explain: "This statement of an option follows the text of the commentary (*vṛtti*)."

In the ultimate sense, however, the phrase "in either one" (*anyatarasyām*) does not apply here, because that would contradict the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ahnaḥ khaḥ kratau*. For in that [Bhāṣya], having raised the objection that the word *nadī* might include specific rivers such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā among those beginning with *śarad*, [it is stated]:
The objection that [the suffix] does not apply because of the mention of the word *vipāṭ* has been settled.

Furthermore, this commentary does not fit with the view that the suffix *ṭac* is optional in the rule "adīpaurṇamāsī," since the reading of that rule is justified as having the sense of being obligatory (*nitya*). For this very reason, the mention of Senaka later on is purposeful. Kaiyaṭa, however...
He has somehow justified the commentary (*vṛtti*) by relying on the *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (the rule of restricted option).

Regarding [Pāṇini 5.4.112]: *gireśca senakasya*, the sense is that the option is established through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally), which serves as an honorific (*pūjārtha*).
Thus ends the section on *avyayībhāva* compounds in the *Iti-tattva-bodhinī*.

(718) *śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ* |2|2|23|. "The remainder is the *bahuvrīhi*. [The word] *śeṣa* [is derived from] the root *iṣ* in the sense of "not being used for everything," with the suffix *ghañ* in the objective case (*karman*). Regarding this, the author of the *Vṛtti* says: "That for which no other compound has been stated is the 'remainder' (*śeṣa*). Of those...

Haradatta has explained that the meaning is: "that sense for which a compound designated as *avyayībhāva* and so forth has not been prescribed among words is the *śeṣa* (remainder). And this should be understood with reference to the reading: "That which follows [the section] up to *kaḍāra* is the operation (*kārya*). However, in this view, if the mention of *śeṣa* were absent...

In the case of *unmattagaṅgam*, because the *bahuvrīhi* would apply due to its higher status and because the *avyayībhāva* would have no scope [otherwise], the undesirable result such as *unmattagaṅga* would follow in that alternative view.
This is so under the view that accepts the reading "from *ā* up to *kaḍāra*" (*ā kaḍārādekaike*).
However, since forms such as *avyatigangam* are established by the governing rule of "single designation" (*eka-saṃjñā-adhikāra*), the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa-grahaṇa*) would be redundant;

for the designation of *avyayībhāva*, being without scope elsewhere, would sublate the designation of *bahuvrīhi*. Therefore, he states the purpose even in that case: "by [the rule] *dvitīyā-śrita-* etc."

It should be understood that the mention of *śeṣa* (remainder) is also necessary for the purpose of securing the application of the suffix *kap* by the rule *eṣādvibhāṣā* only to a *bahuvrīhi* situated within the scope of *śeṣa*, and not to any other *bahuvrīhi*.
Regarding the phrase "of which triad": although the rule *rādayo gatādyarthe* [states that] "words beginning with *ra-* are used in the sense of 'gone' and so forth..."

Although it was stated [in the Vārttika] that "by the first case ending," the meaning is that it was not stated by the author of the Sūtra that "the first case ending is compounded with something," as is the case with the rule "the second case ending is compounded with words such as *śrita*. Alternatively, although the author of the Vārttika stated "by the first case ending," it was not stated by the author of the Sūtra. [The term] "ending in the first case" means...

The intention is that the bahuvrīhi compound such as *aṇḍhekāla* is to be established by means of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). "The meaning of another word" means the meaning of a word other than the words being compounded. For by a [single] word, the meaning of the suffix—such as the object (*karman*) or the agent (*kartṛ*)—subordinated to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), is expressed.

In the case of a word ending in the nominative case, however, there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Even though, according to the view that the triplet [of meanings] is denoted, number is the meaning of the suffix, nevertheless, because that number is a qualifier with respect to the meaning of the base, the meaning of the suffix does not have the meaning of the base as its subordinate element (*upasarjana*) in a word ending in the nominative. And thus:
The result is: "after a word ending in the second case [accusative], in the sense of 'and so forth'.

(719) *anekam anyapadārthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.24). "In the sense of meanings other than the first case-ending" means "in the sense of the remaining [case-endings]. And this is obtained from the mention of the word *śeṣa*. *Anekaṃ*...
What [is the purpose]? So that it may apply even to many [roots]. And this will become clear at the very root [of the discussion].

Having taken the mention of the word *kevala* (alone) in the rule for the suffix *niC* as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), they say that the mention of the word *aneka* (many) here is easily dispensable. What is the purpose of the mention of the word *anya* (other)?

The distinction between the respective domains of the *bahuvrīhi* and the *tatpuruṣa* [compounds] is understood as follows: since the *tatpuruṣa* has scope within its own constituent members (*svapadārtha*), the *bahuvrīhi*—by virtue of its priority—supersedes it when it applies to a meaning external to those members (*anyapadārtha*). However, if the term "external" (*anya*) were not included [in the rule], then in cases such as *aṇḍekāla*, where there are words with different grammatical referents (*vyadhikaraṇapada*), the *bahuvrīhi* would apply to a collection of many [members].

Furthermore, [if the word *pada* were not used], a *tatpuruṣa* compound with coreferential members (*samānādhikaraṇa*)—such as "a blue lotus pond" (*nīlotpalaṃ saraḥ*)—would subvert the *bahuvrīhi* even when the meaning of another word is involved, just as it does in its own word-meaning (*svapadārtha*). Why is the word *pada* mentioned?

So that it does not apply to the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). For example, in the case of "The river has crocodiles" (*grāhavatī nadī*), let there be no such [compound] here, because this is the meaning of a sentence.

It is understood. Why is the word "meaning" (artha) included? Since a word cannot function [to denote] another word simply because such a function is impossible, it will naturally refer to the meaning of the word. To this they reply:
so that there may be the expression of the meaning of the suffix as qualified by the meaning of the base; otherwise, [it would not be so].

Because of its predominance, only the meaning of the suffix would be grasped. If that were accepted, however, the expression "citragu" (owner of brindled cows) would refer solely to the relationship denoted by the genitive case; and consequently, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with [proper names] such as Devadatta.

In this regard, the following should be noted: the word *sup* does not carry over [from the previous rule]. Consequently, the established meaning here is that multiple words ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*) are mutually compounded. Thus, the two-word *bahuvrīhi* remains entirely unimpeded. However, those who, carrying over the term *sup-supā*, interpret it as "multiple words ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) together with a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*)"—

They explain [the compound as follows], but for them, a *dvipada-bahuvrīhi* (a bahuvrīhi with two members) is indeed difficult to establish. He provides examples according to the sequence of the meanings of the second case (*dvitīyā*) and subsequent cases, beginning with "prāptam" and so forth.

In the analysis (*vigraha*), the meaning is "water which is the agent of the action of reaching, having the village as its object"; [alternatively,] it is "the object of the action of reaching, having water as its agent."

This is the summarized meaning (*samāsārtha*). However, when the term *saḥ* (he/it) is used in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), its meaning is also exactly this: a chariot which is the object of the act of carrying whose agent is an ox; whereas the agent of the act of carrying whose object is a chariot is the meaning of the compound. A sacrificial animal (*paśu*) which is the object of the act of offering whose recipient is Rudra.

The meaning of the compound, however, is the bringing [of the fire] as an instrument for the act of cooking the animal. In the case of *sthālyadhikoddharaṇakarma odanaḥ* ("the rice which is the object of the act of taking out more than [what is in] the pot"), the meaning of the compound is the pot (*sthālī*) as the limit of the act of taking out the rice as its object, and so forth. Here, because the object (*karman*) and other factors are expressed by the compound itself, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used. But [one might object]: in a sentence, with respect to the meaning of the verbal root...

If it is argued that since the agent or the object— being the referent of the *kta* suffix— is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the same should be appropriate in the case of a compound (*vṛtti*) as well; and thus, in examples such as *prāptodaka* ("to whom water has come") or *ūḍharatha* ("by whom a chariot has been carried"), the analysis as "the arrival having water as its agent" and so forth is not tenable.

It is said: since a distinct power (*śaktyantara*) directed toward a qualified meaning is accepted for the complex formation (*vṛtti*) on account of the unification of meanings (*ekārthībhāva*) and so forth, and not the power of the individual components, there is no inconsistency.
However, by those who maintain the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvādin*), a separate grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) must necessarily be accepted. Furthermore:

If "attainment" (*prāpti*) qualified by the agent were the meaning of the word, then since that alone would be the referent of the nominal stem (*nāmartha*), it would have to be stated that water is non-different from it;
however, that is contradicted, for it is not possible to say that "water is attainment qualified by the agent. For this very reason, [it is said that] among the many properties of a compound...

We have already stated in the commentary on the *samartha-sūtra* that, because of the argument beginning with "there would be great difficulty in establishing [the compound] by means of words alone," the view of *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning) is indeed the stronger one; however, this does not apply to the sense of the first case (*prathamārtha*). This is because the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is avoided either by the word *śeṣa* or by the phrase *anyapadārtha*.

The sense is that the statement "in the sense of the first case-ending" need not be formulated. Regarding the phrase "of those with different substrata," etc.: here, since the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the Vārttika is already prevented by the word "śeṣa" (remainder) itself, the sense is that the rule "Bahuvrīhi of those with non-co-referential [members]" also need not be formulated.
However, according to the opinion of the authors of the Vṛtti and others— that "the remainder [of compounds] consists of those for which no other compound has been stated"—
it must be understood that this statement is indeed necessary, because the rule "the bahuvrīhi applies only to words ending in the nominative case" would otherwise not be obtained.

"Regarding the rule *prādibhyo dhātujasya vācyo vā cottarapadalopaḥ*: [the commentary explains] *prādibhyaḥ*. This is a restatement of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the Sūtra: that when a word derived from a root (*dhātujam*) follows *pra* and other such prefixes (*prādibhyaḥ*), a Bahuvrīhi compound should be explained as being formed with another word [as its final member]. [The commentary continues with] *vā ca*. However, this..."

This is a statement based on explicit scriptural authority (*vācanika*). The meaning is that the elision (*lopa*) of the verbal root portion (*dhātujā*) contained within the second member (*uttarapada*) of a compound must be stated. And this is easily established by relying on the fact that prefixes such as *pra* and others possess specific meanings when they function within a compound.

"Of words expressing the sense of 'is' (astyartha), when following the negative particle *nañ*, either the meaning is expressed or there is elision of the subsequent word. Regarding "of words expressing the sense of 'is'":
the analysis as a *bahuvrīhi* compound is to be understood for words expressing the sense of "is" that follow *nañ*, with another word;
however, the meaning is that there is elision (*lopa*) of those words expressing the sense of "is. Why "of words expressing the sense of 'is'"? [Example follows: *na brāhmaṇaḥ* ("not a Brāhmaṇa").

"Anupanītaputraḥ" (one whose son has not been initiated). Why [is the negative particle] *nañ* mentioned? [Consider] "nirvidyamānaputraḥ" (one whose son is becoming despondent). Now, one might object: even if "upa" is understood by way of recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), the term "sup" (a nominal ending) also recurs; thus, the usage "astikṣīrā" (having milk) would be difficult to justify.
Anticipating this objection, he establishes [the validity of such usage] by stating: "it is a word that is a mere semblance of a case-ending."

(720) *striyāḥ puṃvad bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ samānādhikaraṇe striyāmapūraṇīpriyādiṣu* || 6.3.34 || "The feminine [stem] is treated like the masculine" (*striyāḥ puṃvat*). This is due to a formal rule of derivation (*nipātana*). And this [principle] should also be applied to what precedes; otherwise—

A *bahuvrīhi* compound of words with different grammatical bases (*vyadhikaraṇa*) would not be established by its own inherent force [without this rule]. [The word] *lugati* [is explained as follows]: *anūṅ* is in the nominative case; Haradatta says that the nominative is used in the sense of the genitive. Thus, the reading of the Sūtra found in some manuscripts as *anūṅḥ samānādhikaraṇe* (with the genitive ending) is not traditional.

This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "when [the genders] are equal" and so forth: this meaning is obtained through the explanation beginning with "that in which the masculine has been expressed," as established in the rule *ṛtīyādiṣu bhāṣitapuṃskam*.
If, in this context, [the word] "by which the masculine has been expressed" (*bhāṣitaḥ pumān yena*)...

If it were stated that "it [the feminine] has a corresponding masculine form" (*tadbhāṣitapuṃskam*), then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *kuṭībhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a hut") and *droṇībhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a trough"). For indeed, the word *kuṭa* is masculine when meaning a jar, but feminine when meaning a house; and the word *droṇa* is masculine when meaning a specific measure of capacity.

"But in the case of *gavādanī*, it is feminine. This means that it is where there is an absence of the suffix *ūṅ*. For if the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) were "that which is other than *ūṅ*," then only those ending in *ṭāp* and so forth would be included. If you ask what follows from this, consider: the offspring of a Darada is a *Dārada*. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule "after *vṛddha* [names], after *Magadha*... and so on; of that—

[In the case of the word] *darat*, there would be elision (*luk*) by the rule "striyām ṭhaṇaśca. Consequently, forms such as *dāradavṛndārikā* (the daughter of a Darada woman) would not be established. The point is that here, unlike in cases such as *darśanīyabhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is beautiful"), there is no feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) present. [Objection: But surely... [text continues]

If it is argued that the rule should simply be formulated as *kopadhāyā ūṅ ca* (and *ūṅ* [is applied] after a word ending in *ka*), this is not so; for by the rule *uṃvat karmadhāraye*, which serves to prevent the sublation of a sublation, there would arise the contingency of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) in a *karmadhāraya* compound such as *vāmorūbhāryā*. However, in the final established view (*siddhānta*), there is no such fault, owing to the force of the separate prohibition.

He prevents the suffix *tariyā* from being followed by a feminine suffix by stating "of that which denotes a female. For if it were said, "the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) for a feminine suffix," the meaning would result in nothing more than the elision of the feminine suffix; consequently, forms such as *dāradavṛndārikā* would not be established. Furthermore:

In the case of *aṭuabhāryā*, because the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is conditioned by the subsequent member (*uttarapada*)—is elided, the substitution *yaṇ* would occur due to the status of being "as if in its original place" (*sthānivadbhāva*), according to the rule *paraśca*. Furthermore, [in the case of] *vataṇḍī*, meaning a female descendant of Vataṇḍa: the suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule *vataṇḍācca*, and that suffix is elided by the rule *luk striyām*.

From the *śārṅgarava* group of stems, the suffix *ṅīn* is applied. Thus, *vataṇḍī* and *vṛndārikā* together form *vātaṇḍayavṛndārikā*. Here, although the suffix *ṅīn* is removed by the rule of masculine equivalence (*puṃvadbhāva*), because the femininity inherent in the meaning has not been removed, the suffix *yañ* is elided by the rule "when [the feminine suffix] *uk* [is followed by a masculine stem]."

The sense is that [the fault] would follow. Regarding the word *hrasva* (short vowel): the sense is that because of the rule *anekam*, the word *go* is treated as an *upasarjana* (secondary member) since it is designated in the nominative case by the rule *prathamānirdiṣṭam*, or else because of the rule *ekavibhakti ca*.
[The example is] *citrā gāvo yasya asau*.

By the maxim "even internal [rules] do not apply," the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) does not operate here. Otherwise, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would be treated as belonging to the subsequent part (*parādittvena*), the *luk* elision of the case-ending (*sup*) would occur, and consequently, the vowel *a* would not be obtained in the form *citrāgūḥ*; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "not here": in this very rule, [the example is] *asya citrāgavaḥ*, where *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive) and *mṛdvī* (feminine) are his wives.

The point is that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing a *dvandva*, [the rule applies] because of the example "aṭvīmṛdubhārya" cited in the *Bhāṣya*. Regarding "ānaṅ": likewise, in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "anartha" (Pāṇini 6.3.25), in the case of the *dvandva* of the four—hotṛ, potṛ, neṣṭṛ, and udgātṛ—the third member [neṣṭṛ] takes the substitute "ānaṅ."

This has been stated. However, if there were an attraction (*ākṣepa*) for a preceding member (*pūrvapada*), that [formation] would not be established; for in this case, *na* is not intended as a preceding member, because *hotṛ* alone is the preceding member—this is the sense. "For this very reason" means:
precisely because there is no attraction of a preceding member. "Citrā-jarat" [is an example].

Even though the word *jarat* is the final member (*uttarapada*) within the compound *dvandva*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is not elided because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Nor can it be argued that, despite this, the elision of *ṭāp* would be unavoidable due to the masculine-like transformation (*puṃvadbhāva*), since the first member, being a *dvandva*, is followed by a final member that is coreferential with it.

It must be stated [as an exception]: although the two words *citrā* and *jaratī*, which are included within the *dvandva* compound, are each bases for feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*) that have undergone masculine speech (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), the *pūrvapada* consisting of the *dvandva* as a whole is not such [a base].
[The phrase] "of both" means that even in the case of the first [word], it depends upon the subsequent word (*uttarapada*) contained within the *pūrvapada*.
The intention is that there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). In the example *jaraccitra*, the compound is formed by the rule *pūrvakālaika-* (Pāṇini 2.1.49).

By means of the maxim regarding the inclusion of gender-distinct forms (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), the term *jarat* includes the word *jaratī* as well. Thus, in *citrajaradgavīka*, *jaradgavī* is analyzed as "a cow (*gauḥ*) that is old (*jaratī*)."

In the case of *orataddhite*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied; because it is marked with the indicator *ṭ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* follows. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *citrā jaradgavī asya*, the suffix *kap* is applied by the rule *adyaﬁtaśca*, which will be stated later. In *vāmorūbhāryaḥ*, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied by the rule *aṃhitaśaphalakṣaṇavāmādeśca*. The word *pradhānam* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ* denoting an abstract state (*bhāva*).
It is always neuter. Regarding the word *pañcamī*: the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied by the rule *asya pūraṇe*;
the augment *maṭ* is added to *ḍaṭ* by the rule *āntād asaṅkhyādeḥ*; and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *iḍḍhea*.
(721) [The rule] *appūraṇīpramāṇyoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.116).

Regarding the term *pramāṇī*: the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). Since that which ends in this suffix functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. If it is asked, "How then is the Śābara-bhāṣya [to be explained] when it says, 'when there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāyām*) consisting of Smṛti'?"—on this point, the Bhaṭṭas [state]: "Because it attains (*ayate*) or reaches (*yāti*) the Veda (*śruti*), which is its source (*mūlabhūtā*). Thus, it is called *pramāṇā*. Alternatively, it may be derived from the root *mā* with the suffix *anaṭ*, meaning "that by which one measures" (*mīyate'nena*). Or, it may be understood as a Bahuvrīhi compound: "that which has a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇam asyā asti*). In all these cases, the feminine form is established through the addition of the suffix *ṅīṣ*. Furthermore, since the word *smṛti* is feminine, the feminine gender of the compound is justified. Alternatively, the word *pramāṇa* itself may be taken as a Bahuvrīhi, and the feminine form derived from it is simply *pramāṇā*. This is the view of some. Or again, the word *pramāṇa* may be derived from the root *mā* with the suffix *anaṭ* in the sense of "that which is measured," and the feminine form is derived from that. In this way, the reading *pramāṇāyām* is also consistent. However, the Bhaṭṭas maintain that the reading *pramāṇāyām* is indeed correct. They argue: "Because it attains or reaches the Veda, which is its source, it is therefore called *pramāṇā*. That is to say, because it proceeds toward the Veda, it is designated as such. Alternatively, the suffix *anaṭ* is applied to the root *mā* in the sense of "that by which one measures," and the feminine form is derived from that. Or, it may be a Bahuvrīhi: "that which has a means of valid cognition. In all these instances, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added. Moreover, since the word *smṛti* is feminine, the feminine gender of the compound is appropriate. Or, the word *pramāṇa* itself may be a Bahuvrīhi, and the feminine form derived from it is simply *pramāṇā*. This is the opinion of some. Or again, the word *pramāṇa* may be derived from the root *mā* with the suffix *anaṭ* in the sense of "that which is measured," and the feminine form is derived from that. In this way, the reading *pramāṇāyām* is also consistent. However, the Bhaṭṭas maintain that the reading *pramāṇāyām* is indeed correct. They argue: "Because it attains or reaches the Veda, which is its source, it is therefore called *pramāṇā*. That is to say, because it proceeds toward the Veda, it is designated as such. Alternatively, the suffix *anaṭ* is applied to the root *mā* in the sense of "that by which one measures," and the feminine form is derived from that. Or, it may be a Bahuvrīhi: "that which has a means of valid cognition. In all these instances, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added. Furthermore, because the suffix *rūpya* is also prescribed there, the meaning is that these [suffixes] are enumerated in order to exclude it. He provides examples of the enumerated suffixes, such as *tratas*, in their proper sequence, beginning with "in many" (*bahvīṣu*).
Although forms such as *bahutra* are established even in the absence of the optional *ṅīṣ* suffix when applied to words like *bahu*, etc., [the enumeration is necessary for other reasons].

The sense is that what was cited as being "more skillful" (*paṭutara*) is merely due to negligence (*prāmādika*). Regarding *paṭucarī*: [it is formed] by the suffix *caraṭ* after a word meaning "formerly called. Regarding *paṭujātīya*: [it is formed] by the suffix *jātīyar* when expressing a quality similar to that denoted by the base word ending in *ra*.

Regarding *darśanīyarūpā* and so forth: the suffix *rūpap* is used in the sense of praise. The suffix *pāśap* is used in the sense of frequency. Regarding *bahudhā*: [it is formed] by the suffix *dhā*.
In the statement regarding the suffix *thāl*, the governing rule “*isarvanāmabahubhyaḥ*” (Pāṇini 5.3.2) is indeed in force there.
Regarding *vṛkatī*: the suffix *til* is applied by the rule “*vṛkajyeṣṭhābhyāṃ tiltātilau ca cchandasī*” (Pāṇini 4.1.108).
Regarding *ajathyā*: the suffix *thyam* is applied by the rule “*ajāvibhyāṃ thyam*” (Pāṇini 4.1.109).

Regarding the suffix *śas*, the application of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like behavior) must be stated for words meaning "much" (*bahu*) or "few" (*alpa*). The term "*śasi*" [in the rule] refers to that *śas* which follows the rule "after words meaning 'much' or 'few'" (*bahvalpārthāt*); the meaning is that it should be understood as belonging to the group beginning with *tasil*.
In other words, it must be included in the enumeration of the *tratasādi* suffixes.

Regarding the rule *tvatalorguṇavacanasya*: although it would have been sufficient to say *guṇasya* (of a quality), the inclusion of the word *vacana* (denoting) is for the purpose of including only those qualities that are well-known as such. Therefore, he cites examples accordingly: *śuklatvam* and *śuklatā*. Now, here...

That which was stated by the ancients— that a *guṇa* (quality) is merely a property distinct from the notion of genus (*jāti*)— must be accepted; otherwise, in cases such as "he considered the autumns to have achieved their purpose" (*īkṣya mene śaradaḥ kṛtārthatām*) and "she abandoned her habit of suffering for love" (*ā mumoca ratiduḥkhaśīlatām*), the rule for masculine-like substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not apply.

Lest there be a long vowel [ending], he says: "The neuter gender is used for the general class. And thus, the usage such as *eṣṭaṃ puro dvāravatītvam āsīt* ("the state of being Dvāravatī was desired in the city") is unobjectionable; this is the intended meaning.
[In the rule] *bhasyāḍhe taddhite*, [the example] *hāstikam* ("an elephant-herd") is formed with the suffix *ṭhak* by the rule *ṭhājādāvūrdhvam dvitīyād acaḥ*. It is not [formed by *ṭhañ*].

Furthermore, there can be no resolution here by means of the elision of *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), because that [elision] is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*) in this context by the rule *ṭhasiddhavadatre* (Pāṇini 6.4.22),

and because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) by the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), which would prevent the elision of the *ṭi* portion by the rule *nastaddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144). Nor can it be resolved by the rule *hakcchasośca* (Pāṇini 6.1.163) alone in this case.
The application of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) rule might be suspected [of being inapplicable] because of the association with *cha* and *sa*,

since in the rule *“havataṣṭhakcchasau”* it is specifically the suffix *ṭhak* that is intended there. Nor should the prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva* by the rule *“āteśca”* be suspected, precisely because of this very example from the Bhāṣya.
This is because it is made known that "the prohibition applies only to [the suffix] *cha*, and not to that which is added as a secondary rule (*aupasaṅkhyānika*).

Regarding the form *rauhiṇeya*: from the word *rohita*, the feminine suffixes *ṅīn* and *ṅīp* are applied by the rule "from a color-word beginning with an unaccented vowel" (*varṇādanudātādi*). However, if the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) were to occur, those two suffixes would be removed, and the form would instead be *rauhiteya*.
The meaning is: "it is grasped. The word "by way of explanation" (*vyākhyānāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. Regarding *agnāyī*:
from the word *agni*, by the rule *vṛṣākapyagnī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the substitution of *aikāra* (*ai*) [for the final vowel] are applied. Regarding *āgneya*:
the intention is that if there were no absence of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), it would instead be *āgnāyeya*.
"From the synonym for enemy (*śatru-paryāyāt*). In this context, the grammatical indication (*liṅga*) is the rule *vyan sapatne*.
Amarasimha states: "The words *ripu*, *vairin*, *sapatna*, *ari*, *dviṣan*, *dveṣaṇa*, and *durhad* [are synonyms for enemy].

"Based on marriage" (*vivāha-nibandhana*): the meaning is that it is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) with respect to that which is characterized by a specific refinement (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*) produced by such [marriage].
Regarding the word *sāpatna*: because it does not have a corresponding masculine form (*abhāṣitapuṃska*), the second member does not undergo the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).

If the masculine substitution were to apply, there would be no replacement of the letter *n*, and the form would be *sāpata*. However, in the case of the first [member], even if the masculine substitution applies, the form remains *sāpatna*—this is the intended meaning. [The rule applies] only to words that are conventional (*rūḍha*).

The first word [in *amāvasyā*] is based on conventional usage (*rūḍha*), while the second is based on both etymological derivation and conventional usage (*yogarūḍha*). Therefore, the analysis (*vigraha*) as "she whose lord is not present" (*amānaḥ patir yasyāḥ*) is not contradicted; this is the general direction. Regarding the rule *ṭhak-chasoś ca*: this is commenced for the purpose of excluding the designation *abha*. As in *bhāvatkāḥ*, [the suffixes] *ṭhak* and *chas* are added by the rule *havataṣṭhak-chasau*. This occurs precisely at the stage of the suffix *ṭha*.

When the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) has been applied, the substitution of *ka*—characterized by the presence of the suffix *-ta*—occurs, overriding the substitution of *i* according to the rule "for *ha*, *ika*" (*hasyekaḥ*). Now, one might object: since the status of a nominal stem (*bhatva*) exists during the substitution of *i*, and once the masculine treatment has taken effect via the rule "for *ha*, when followed by a non-ṅī-affix" (*hasyāṅye*), the desired form can be established through the application of the *ka*-substitution; so what is the purpose of including the mention of the suffix *ṭhak* here? Do not say so. [This is necessary for the sake of forms such as] *mathitam*.

In this case, just as in the example *māthitikaḥ*, the substitution of *kā* (for *ka*) is difficult to establish— either because it is not subject to the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* due to being an *al-vidhi*, or by virtue of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. Therefore, the mention of *ṭhak* in the rule *hak-chasoh* [is necessary].

It must indeed be done. Because of the addition of the *s* in *cchasaḥ*, the designation *pada* applies by the rule "iti ca. Consequently, *jaś*-substitution occurs here. And thus, because the *pada*-designation subverts the *bha*-designation, the rule "hatyāḍhea" does not apply; for this reason, the mention of *ccha* was made in the Vārttika.

"By the phrase 'as desired by the author of the Bhāṣya,' it is implied that there is the possibility of such a statement being made in both the Sūtra and the Vārttika; for, having seen what follows, the preceding [rule] does not apply. However, he says—'because its purpose has already been served'—that in the final analysis, [the rule] would be entirely redundant. He provides examples of what is desired: *sarvamaya*..."

By [the words] beginning with “ityādinā,” the sense is that the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by the rule “*ayaṭ ca*” in the meaning of “come from this” (*ata āgataḥ*). The point is that this [form] would not be established because *mayaṭ* and others are not included in the list of suffixes beginning with *tasil*. As for the example “*sarvakabhāryaḥ*,” its purpose is not already served by the rule “*striyāḥ puṃvat*. [The reason is that] “*a*”...

This is because of the prohibition [stated in the rule] "kopadhāyāḥ. Nor should it be suspected that this [desired form] is also prohibited by that rule, for that prohibition applies only to what is taught within the specific section beginning with "striyāḥ puṃvat," whereas this desired form is not included in that section. Furthermore, it does not apply to that which is contained within a *vṛtti*.
It should not be argued that because it lacks the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), the masculine-like substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not occur;

for by the force of the commencement of this specific rule, or by the inclusion of the term "mother" (*mātr*), it is accepted that the masculine-like substitution applies even when those [words] which were previously observed to function as pronouns no longer possess that designation at the present time.

For this very reason, in the case of *uttarapūrvāyai*, there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) even though it is not a technical name (*saṃjñā*). However, in the case of *sarvāputra*— meaning "the son of a certain woman named Sarvā"—

there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because the word *sarvā* functions as a member of the *sarvādi* group when it is a primary term (*vṛtti*) that has become a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) within a compound.

Even previously, because it was not a *sarvanāman* (pronoun), [the rule applied]. Regarding the example *sarvapriyaḥ*: the intention is that the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of words beginning with *priya* in the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* is utilized in cases such as *rūpavatīpriyaḥ*.
As for *taditarā*:

Anticipating the objection that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) in examples such as *tadanya*, he says: "of the preceding one alone" (*pūrvasyaiva*).
This means: "of that which is preceding in relation to something [else] among the multiple constituent parts (*bhāga*) forming the compound.
He says "on account of the indicative mark" (*liṅgāt*); for otherwise, in cases such as *eṣā dvā etayoḥ*, [the rule would apply to] the vowel preceding the *k* [in *etayoḥ*].

The sense is that if [the feminine suffix] were prescribed [by the rule *anaṅ ṛto dvandve ca*], it would be without a scope (nirviṣaya). It should be understood that the example from the Bhāṣya, “*akṣiṇapūrvā dik*,” is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this point. As for what the Easterners have stated—that in a compound, the preceding [member] of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) undergoes *puṃvadbhāva*—and...
They have explained: "He restates the meaning of the Vārttika with the words *sarvanāmnaḥ* etc. That is based on mere negligence, because the reading *vṛtāmātre* alone is established in the Bhāṣya;
furthermore, it would result in the failure of the examples already stated, namely *sarvamayaḥ* and *sarvakāmyati*.
The statement beginning with "ṭhvārtikārthaṃ" (for the sake of the Vārtika) and so forth is merely due to negligence, because this is not found in the Vārtika text itself.

Nor should one suspect that the rule "arvanāmno vṛtimātre" (in all compound formations involving pronouns) is merely a Vārtika and not the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra; for [this would contradict] the Vārtika "ṭhakcchaso ’rit."

Because it would result in the [cognition] being without an objective basis (*nirālambana*). As for the view favored by the author of the *Bhāṣya*, the possibility of such a statement in the *Vārttika* has already been mentioned previously. (724) [The rule] *kyaṅbhāninośca* 6.3.36.
Furthermore, regarding *eta-yate* and so forth: [the rule] *artuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* applies.
When the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) has been applied to *eta* and *eti*, the lengthening occurs by the rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātuke*.

The inclusion of the term *mānin* is intended for the purpose of [applying the rule] when there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) and for the purpose of excluding the feminine gender (*astrī*). This is the underlying intention.

He illustrates them in order with the words beginning "svābhinnām" (considering herself as non-different from him). Regarding the term "darśanīyamāninī": the suffix *ṇini* is applied after the root *man*, and because it ends in *n*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. As for one who considers herself beautiful (*darśanīyā*), that is already established by the rule "striyāḥ puṃvat" (the feminine form is like the masculine). This applies even to a single woman.

The sense is that although there is a distinction between the states of being an object (*karman*) and an agent (*kartṛ*) due to the difference in intention— namely, whether one intends [the action] as the most desired goal (*īpsitatama*) or as the locus of the operation (*vyāpārāśraya*)— there is no disruption of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because they are not different in reality. Regarding "pācikābhārya": she who cooks is a *pācikā*. [The suffix] *ṇvul* [is applied]; after the substitution of *a* for *ṭhi* and *yu* by the rule *ṭhyuvoḥ*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, and by the rule *pratyayasthāt*, the final vowel is changed to *ī*. Regarding "rasikābhārya": she in whom there is taste (*rasa*) is a *rasikā*. [The suffix] *ṭhan* is applied by the rule *ata iniṭhanau*. Regarding "madrikāyata": [this is derived from *madrikā*].
The rule "yaṅbhāninośca" results in the application of the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva). [For example: *madrikā*, meaning "one born among the Madras.
[This is derived from] "adravṛjyoḥ kan. The point is that if the masculine form were applied, the short *i* (*itva*) would not be heard.

thus, the meaning is that both the mention of *taddhita* and the mention of *vu* [apply]. In the example *pākā bhāryā*, this word ending in the suffix *kap*—as in the rule "the suffix *kap* is applied to *vayas* in the sense of *ṛbha*, *pṛthu*, and *pāka*"—is prescribed among the *uṇādi* derivatives. And this [suffix] is not a *taddhita*.

"Tāvatī" means "that which has that much as its measure. The intention is that when the suffix *vatup* is applied by the rule "tat etebhyaḥ," the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel by the rule "ā sarvanāmnaḥ" is not a *vṛddhi* vowel as prescribed by the term *vṛddhi*. Regarding "kāṣāyī": in the sense of "colored with *kaṣāya*," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "tena raktaṃ rāgāt," and then the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. Regarding "haimī": it is a derivative (*vikāra*) of gold (*heman*).

In this sense, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *ṭhanudātadeśce*t. Regarding the term *phalopadhāna*: the word *mimata* refers to that which is accompanied by the result (*phalopahita*). The point is that if it were taken to mean "capable by its own nature" (*svarūpayogya*), then the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not be established in the case of *vaiyākaraṇabhārya*. Or else, [the compound] means "one who studies grammar" (*vyākaraṇam adhīte*).
*Vaiyākaraṇī*: [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule "after that, [the suffix] *aṇ* [is used for the feminine]. *Sauvaśvī*: the female descendant of *svaśva*;

[the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule "the descendant of this. In both cases, the initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) which would have been obtained because the suffix is marked with *Ṇ*, is prohibited by the rule "a [vowel] after *y* or *v* [is not strengthened]. Thus, this [suffix] does not result in *vṛddhi* as its actual fruit; rather—

But it is inherently capable [of being the cause]. Although this taddhita suffix is indeed "phalopahita" (endowed with the result) with respect to *vṛddhi* because it is the cause for the substitution of *aij*, nevertheless, the point is that it does not become so with respect to the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the word *vṛddhi* itself. On this point, they explain: in the sūtra, the word *nimitta* refers to that which is endowed with the result.

Otherwise, the mention of the "cause" (*nimitta*) would be purposeless; for even if it were stated that "the *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs when there is a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*)," the relationship would still be understood as being that of a cause, thereby yielding the meaning "that secondary derivative suffix which has *vṛddhi* as its cause.
By this, the sense of "the *vṛddhi*" is obtained. Otherwise, one would obtain the sense of "having the suffix as the ultimate goal" (*phalopahitaparatva*).

[The suffix] would be fruitless, because the aforementioned fault remains as it was; therefore, one should say "amāninī" (not proud). [In the case of] "sukeśī," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "vāṅgāccopasarjanāt.
[In the case of] "akeśā," there is an absence of *ṅīṣ* due to the prohibition "na nañ-vidyamāne."
(728) And [the prohibition applies] after a genus-word (*jāti*). 6|3|41.

Regarding the phrase "and after a genus-word": if this were explained here as "only that which is prescribed by the rule *ātiḥ*," then in the example *hāstikam*, the prohibition would not apply because it is an addition (*āgama*) to the suffix *ṭhaÑ*.
Otherwise, the statement in the Bhāṣya would be inconsistent. From the word *hastin*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is not prescribed by the rule *ātaḥ*;
rather, because it does not end in the vowel *ā*, the suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*.
Consequently, since there is no possibility of the prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) applying here, he says: "after [a word denoting] a genus (*jāti*). And thus:
The intention is that the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] is established even in cases such as *hastinī-bhāryaḥ*.

(729) *saṅkhyāyā avyayāsannādūrādhikasaṅkhyāḥ saṅkhyeye* [Pāṇini 2.2.25]. Regarding the phrase "the feminine suffix": this refers to *ṭāp* and the others. However, the practice of the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*) was to apply only *ṅīṣ*; that is incorrect.

He provides an illustration while explaining [the rule]: *śūdrābhārya* (one whose wife is a Śūdra woman) and *brāhmaṇī* (a Brāhmaṇa woman). [The suffix] *ṅīn* is applied according to the *śārṅgarava*-class. However, the Easterners (*prāc*), having explained [the rule] as “*īṣ* is not [subject to] *puṃvat*,” have cited *brāhmaṇībhārya* as an example; that is due to haste. [The phrase] “of the sūtra itself” is because of the [authoritative] commentary.

This is the state of affairs. The prohibition [stated] in the rule *a kopadhāyāḥ* applies even to that which was obtained by the rule *hasyāḍhea*. By this, the form *vailepikam*—meaning "that which pertains to *vilepikā*"—is established. If the *aṇ* suffix were applied according to the rule *ṭhaṇpahiṣyādibhyaḥ*, then there would be *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine stem substitution), and in that case, the vowel *ī* would not be heard here.
And this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "a-kopadhāyāḥ. Having concluded this incidental discussion, he returns to the subject at hand with the words "by number" (saṅkhyayā).

Since there is an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and an absence of the function [of the compound] as a word denoting something other than its own members (anyapadārtha-vṛtti), the previous [rule] does not apply.

Regarding the word *daśānām*: [the compound] *upagatā daśa yeṣām* ("those to whom ten have approached") is not analyzed separately, because it is already established by the preceding rule. As for *upadaśāḥ*: the prefix *upa-* is used in the sense of "near" (*samīpe*) and "nearby" (*samīpini*). The distinction is that in the first case it is an *avyayībhāva* compound, while in the second it is a *bahuvrīhi*. Nine.
The meaning is "or eleven. The intention is that a relationship mediated by number is more immediate (antaraṅga).
Consequently, expressions such as *upadaśāḥ*—referring to cows and the like that exist near ten trees and so forth—are not employed. This is because [the word] *iti* is present in the sūtra.
With the intention that the sixth case ending has been elided, he says:
(730) *ti-viṃśater-ṅiti* [Pāṇini 6.4.142].
Regarding the word *tiśabdasya*: "āsannaviṃśāḥ" (those who are nearly twenty). Here, after the elision of the suffix *ti*, [the rule] *ato guṇe* [applies].

It is only the single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), and not the elision of the *ṭi* suffix; for the elision of the *ṭi* is considered "as if not having taken effect" (*asiddha*) by virtue of its being an *ābhīya* operation.
Nor should it be suspected that even the *pararūpa* would not occur here because of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position) of the elided *ṭi*;
for since the elision of the *ṭi* is a substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*) and not a substitute for a consonant (*hal-ādeśa*), the rule *acaḥ parasmin* does not apply.

However, the rule *sthānivadādeśaḥ* does not apply at all; for the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that its application occurs when a grammatical operation (*kārya*) prescribed by a rule is to be performed, but not for the purpose of the original formulation itself. Regarding *viṃśateḥ*: here too, the analysis is not made as *āsannā viṃśatir yeṣām*, due to the reasoning already stated. Regarding *adūra-* and so forth...
The analyses (*vigraha*) should be understood as "not far from thirty" and "more than forty. Regarding the term *dvitrāḥ*:

this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound used in the sense of "or" (*vā*). Furthermore, this sense of "or" does not mean "optionality" (*vikalpa*), because that would entail the possibility of the dual number as well; rather, it means "doubt" (*saṃśaya*). And that doubt refers to an indefinite number.
In that case, since all three are always manifest, the plural number is used precisely with reference to them.
However, they say that the connection with actions such as "bringing" is indefinite, pertaining either to two or to three.
The phrase "repeated twice" means a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of the suffix *-su*. But in the commentary (*vṛtti*), however—

Because the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is based precisely on the inclusion of the sense of "well" (*su*), the suffix *suc* is not employed. Why [is it said] "a numeral" (*saṅkhyā*)? [Example: *catvāro brāhmaṇāḥ* ("four Brahmins"). Why [is it said] "an indeclinable," etc.? [Example: *brāhmaṇāḥ pañca* ("five Brahmins").
Why [is it said] "with respect to that which is to be numbered" (*saṅkhyeye*)? [Example: *adhikā viṃśatir gavām* ("more than twenty cows"). This [word *adhika*] has the meaning of a numeral.

The term *saṅkhyā* does not include compounds. Numbers up to ten function as *saṅkhyā* [numerals] when they denote the act of counting (*saṅkhyeya*), but not when they denote a number itself (*saṅkhyā*). However, numbers such as twenty (*viṃśati*) and so forth function as both *saṅkhyā* and *saṅkhyeya*.
When the word *viṃśati* denotes the object being counted (*saṅkhyeya*), then a compound indeed occurs—as in *adhikaviṃśāḥ* ("more than twenty").
Thus [it is said].
(731) *tatra tenedam iti sarūpe* (Pāṇini 2.2.27). Regarding the rule *tatra tenedaṃ*, "grahaṇaviṣaye" means that which is grasped by this is the "grahaṇa," such as hair (*keśa*) and so forth.

Those two whose denoted objects are similar to that [object] are "sarūpa" (of identical form). A "praharaṇa" (weapon) is that by which one strikes, such as a staff and the like; those two whose denoted objects are similar to that are to be understood as before.
"Karmavyatihāra" (reciprocal action) consists of mutual seizing and mutual striking. Now, [an objection]:

To the question, "How is this specific restriction of scope—namely, that [the words] ending in the seventh case are compounded when referring to a receptacle (*rahaṇa*), and those ending in the third case when referring to a weapon (*praharaṇa*)—to be understood from the literal words of the Sūtra? he says: "From the word *iti*. For that word indicates the worldly intention (*vivakṣā*). In common usage...
The meaning is that in expressions such as *keśākeśi* ("hair-to-hair"), a *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs to convey whatever meaning is understood from it.
(732) *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.3.137).

It is also seen in other [grammatical systems]. Regarding this, the ancient [commentators] have stated: "In a *bahuvrīhi* compound involving reciprocal action, due to the mention of the root *ṛś*, there is lengthening of the final vowel of the preceding member, or alternatively, the substitution of *ā* [for *ṛ*], except before a vowel. Among these, the alternative "or the substitution of *ā*" is un-Pāṇinian. For this very reason...
The example "muṣṭāmuṣṭi" is likewise entirely without authoritative basis; this is made clear in the *Manoramā*. (733) *orguṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.146.

The *orguṇa* [substitution applies]. Why [is it specified] "in a *taddhita* suffix"? [Consider the examples: *paṭhavī* (earth) and *vāyvoḥ* (of the two winds). Regarding the mention of "guṇa": although the rule could have been formulated simply as *oro'd*, there is indeed the status of being preceded by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) in the form *hasya taddhite*. Nevertheless...

The meaning is: where a word that serves as a designator (saṃjñārūpa) presents that which is to be enjoined (vidheya), that alone is what is meant by "an injunction preceded by a name" (saṃjñāpūrvako vidhiḥ).

Although, according to the rule *ṭho’d*, a *tapara* [vowel] is indeed a name for its own duration, nevertheless, in this context the letter *t* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), because there would be no result in it being a *tapara*. Or rather, let it simply be *ṣṭhoro’*. "Vaṃ... [and so on].
The sense is that the view that "form (rūpa) belongs to sound (śabda)" has been rejected.

This might be argued: since the rule *taparas tatkālasya* (P. 1.1.70) establishes that a vowel followed by *t* denotes its own duration, the prohibition of the protracted (*pluta*) vowel in the rule *uroranṛtaḥ* (P. 6.4.107) is also considered non-eternal (*anitya*) because it is preceded by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*). Therefore, in the case of *klṛ3ptaśikha*, [the protraction would not apply].
For the sake of establishing the *pluta* vowel, the separate teaching of the vowel *ḷ* in the rule *ṭhṛlṛk* (Pāṇini 1.1.50) after the vowel *ṛ* would be useless;

for even if there were phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*), since the *pluta* status of the vowel *ḷ* is established by the aforementioned method, there would be no point in knowing it to be non-eternal (*anityatva*). Nor is this the case...

It must be stated that the declaration of their non-eternality (anityatva) is necessary in order to prevent the application of the rules regarding *ṛdit* and *amlṛdit*, as well as those regarding *amlṛdit* and *amṛdit*;
this is because of the functional force of providing separate indicatory marks (*anubandha*) for the roots *rājṛ*, *bhrājṛ*, *gmlṛ*, and *śaklṛ*.
