If it is argued that the non-confusion of those operations is established by the force of the separate mention [of the rules] "āglopiśāsvṛditām" and "ṛditaḥ parasmaipadeṣu," [we reply: regarding this, they say that by the rule "guroranṛtaḥ," [the term *anṛta* refers to] a heavy syllable (*guru*) other than one containing the vowel *ṛ*.
Because of the rule for *pluta* [protraction],

the phrase "other than *ṭh* and *ṛ*" (*ṭhanṛtaḥ*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) by way of qualifying the heavy syllable (*guru*) which is being referred to; it is not a word that provides a technical name (*saṃjñā*) for that which is to be enjoined.

Because the prohibition of *pluta* [protracted vowel] for an *ṛ*-based position is not established as being non-eternal (*anitya*), the *pluta* in "aklṛ3ptaśikha" would not be established; therefore, both must be taught in order to establish that [the *pluta*], and for the sake of that establishment, the aforementioned indication (*jñāpana*) is necessary. Others, however, maintain that the *lṛ* sound must indeed be taught separately from the *ṛ* sound.

Because the *ḷ* vowel is not obtained through the instruction of the *ṛ* vowel; nor should it be suspected that it is obtained by the statement "there is mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the *ṛ* and *ḷ* phonemes," for they say that the author of the Sūtras did not act upon having seen the Vārttika.

(734) *tena saha* [is used] when there is equality of connection (*tulyayoga*). Regarding *tena saha*: what is meant by "when there is equality of connection"? Consider: “Just today, the she-ass carries the load with ten sons. Here, the word *saha* does not express equality of connection, because it refers to the action of carrying which has the load as its object.

Because there is no connection with the sons [in the sense of accompaniment], the word [saha] here has the meaning of "existing"; that is to say, it means "while ten sons are existing. This was stated in order to show that the word *saha* can indeed have the sense of "existing. However, the actual form of the counter-example is simply "aha putraiḥ" (I [went] with the sons).
The word *bodhya* [is formed] by the rule "ahayukte" itself.
(735) *vopasarjanasya* | 6|3|82 | Regarding *vopasarjanasya*: the term *upasarjanasya* is not a qualifier for *saha*, because there is no deviation [in its application].
Rather, it refers to the compound brought to mind by the subsequent word, and that [application] occurs through its constituent parts;
the meaning is "of a compound whose every constituent part is a subordinate member" (*upasarjana*).
He states the result of this as follows: "in a *bahuvrīhi*. Therefore, it does not apply here in the cases of *sahayudhvā* (one who has fought together) and *sahakṛtvā* (one who has acted together).

In the words *rājani* and *yudhi*, these two are compounds with an *upapada* formed by the suffix *kvanip* [after the root *kṛ*] according to the rule *ahe ca*. He says "the substitute *sa-* shall take the place of *saha-*" because of the continued application (*anuvartana*) from the rule *ahasya saḥ saṃjñāyām*.
The term "generally" (*prāyika*) is used because it is indicated by such rules as *vibhāṣā sapūrvasya*.
"Transitive" (*sakarmaka*) means having an existing object (*vidyamānakarmaka*).

(Pāṇini 6.3.83) "In the case of a benediction, [the suffix *ka* is applied] by the base form (*prakṛtyā*). How then [is it explained] in the case of: "For the sacrificer, together with his sons, together with his brothers"?

If it is argued that such applications as "May there be an increase in the lifespan, health, and sovereignty of [the person] together with their retinue" are thus consistent, it is replied: "The statement 'May there be an increase in sovereignty;
may you grant your favor' is a sentence of petition, not a benediction."
As for the benedictory expression "athāstu" (so may it be), in that case, [the addition of] "saputraka" and so forth is simply not employed;
thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

(737) *Bahu-vrīhau saṅkhyeye ḍaj-aba-hu-gaṇāt* | Pāṇini 5.4.73. [In a Bahuvrīhi compound, when a numeral is the object to be qualified, the suffix ḍac is applied, except after the words bahu and gaṇa.]

Regarding the rule "in a bahuvrīhi denoting a number": he says that there is a transposition of the case ending, so that the locative is used in the sense of the ablative—meaning "from that which is a bahuvrīhi. Since there is no difference in form between the presence and absence of the suffix *ḍac* in the word *upagaṇa*, he says: "there is a difference in accent. When *ḍac* is present, [the word becomes] *itaḥ*.
The meaning is that there would otherwise be an acute accent on the final syllable; however, when [the suffix] is absent, the original accent of the first member (pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara) applies.
Nor should one suspect that even when the suffix *ḍac* is present, the original accent of the first member would still prevail by virtue of its being subsequent;
for the accent of "itaḥ" is *satiśiṣṭa* (remaining after others have been applied), whereas the *ḍac* is marked with the *cit* indicatory letter.
And because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of futility.

Regarding the phrase "of a number" (*saṅkhyāyāḥ*): the meaning is that the suffix *ḍac* should be stated as the final member of a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in a numeral. However, in cases such as "twenty-one" (*ekaviṃśati*), etc.,...
It does not occur, because of the statement by the author of the Vārttika: "Except in the case of the elision of the suffix *adhika*.

(738) Regarding the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ svāṅgāt ṣac* (Pāṇini 5.4.113): the genitive case is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). This is merely an illustration; the locative case is also used by way of transposition.

He says this: "denoting its own limb," and so forth. By "its own limb" (*svāṅga*), that which is characterized by the definition beginning with "non-fluid and possessing form" (*adravaṃ mūrtimat*) is understood. Therefore, they say that usages such as *śobhanākṣī pratimā* ("a beautiful-eyed image") are entirely free from objection. Regarding the statement "there should be *ṣat*": *ṣa* is for the purpose of [triggering] *ṅīṣ*; however, *ca* is for the purpose of [triggering] *ṅīp* after a stem ending in *it*.
This means that the final syllable is udātta. Consequently, the *prakṛtisvara* (original accent) of the first member does not apply here.

Regarding *sthūlākṣī*: she is one whose eyes (*akṣīṇi*)—meaning the joints and sprouts—are large. However, the Easterners have cited *sthūlākṣir ikṣuḥ* (a sugarcane with thick nodes) as a counter-example; that is incorrect, because [the rule] "of *akṣan*, when there is no perception [of the whole]" applies to vowels (*ac*).

Because it is difficult to prevent [the application of the suffix]. As for the explanation offered by some that the suffix was not applied because the rule for compound-final suffixes (*samāsāntavidhi*) is non-mandatory (*anitya*), that is without substance; for if that were the case, the suffix *ṣac* would likewise not apply in the same manner, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of the counter-example being incoherent.

(739) *aṅgulerdāruṇi* |5|4|114|. Regarding *aṅguli*: [the suffix] *mātrac* is elided by the rule *avigornityam*. *neturnakṣatre’bvaktavyaḥ*. Regarding *netṛ*: *netṛ* means a leader (*nāyaka*). In the case of a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), [the suffix] *ap* is to be stated [after *netṛ*]. *Netṛ*... [is the leader]. That which is in the lunar mansion...
The meaning is that the word *netṛ* [triggers the suffix] when it occurs at the end of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Regarding the example *mṛganetrāḥ*:

*mṛga* refers to the lunar mansion *Mṛgaśīrṣa*. In the expression *candranetā mṛgaḥ* ("the deer whose leader is the moon"), however, the suffix does not apply; for here, although it is a *bahuvrīhi*, the word *netṛ* does not stand at the end of the compound when referring to a lunar mansion.
[The suffix] *na* is applied after the words *khura* and *khara*, [forming] *khuraṇas* and *akharaṇas*. The word "of the nose" (*āsikāyāḥ*) is understood [from the previous rule].

The explicit mention of the substitute alone is for the purpose of excluding the suffix. Thus, *khuraṇāḥ*. [The lengthening of the vowel is] by the rule "of a word ending in *ṭh* or *as*" (*ṭhatvasantasya*).

The word *dīrghaḥ* [is used]. (740) *upasargācca* | Pāṇini 5.4.119. From an *upasarga* as well; the mention of *upasarga* is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the group beginning with *pra*.

Because the word *nāsikā* is not denotative of an action (*akriyārtha*), it cannot function as a prefix (*upasarga*) with respect to it. Nor should it be suspected that it might still be a prefix even in the absence of connection with an action; for [if it were], in the avyayībhāva compound *sāvakam* (from *sa-avaka*), the rule "after a prefix, [the *s* of] the root *su*" would apply to the *s*.
Because it would lead to the undesirable consequence [of the substitution of *ṇ*] for all [nasals]. He says this with the words "of *pra*, etc.
(Pāṇini 8.4.14). [The rule: *upasargādbahulam* (8.4.28). [The rule:
*upasargādanotparaḥ* (8.4.29). [Question: Why does it say "not followed by *anu*" (*anotparaḥ*)? [Answer: So that in the example *pra no muñcatam*, the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*) shall not occur.

"Having broken that"—the meaning is: having removed [the restriction] "when followed by *ṭ* or *th*" and having applied the term *bahulam* (variously). Otherwise, there would be under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *praṇonayati*, and over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *pra naḥ pūṣā*; this is the intended sense. *Praṇasāyi*: "one whose nose has gone forth."
[The opponent asks: "What is the analysis [of the compound]? How then?"—this is the question, implying that one of the two [members] must be a word ending in a case-suffix.

[The author replies: "By means of the nose" (*nāsikayā*). Thus, *vinasā* does not end in the nominative case; rather, the sense is that it ends in the instrumental case, with the substitution of *nas* for *nāsikā* according to the rule *addannapūṣārthamāṣartuṣu...* (Pāṇini 6.1.63).

(742) *suprāta-suśva-sudiva-śāri-kukṣi-caturaśra-eṇīpad-ājapada-proṣṭhapadāḥ* | 5|4|120 | [The forms] *suprāta*, *suśva*, *sudiva*, *śāri*, *kukṣi*, *caturaśra*, *eṇīpad*, *ājapada*, and *proṣṭhapada* [are derived by adding the suffix *aṇ*]. [Example:
*śobhanaṃ prātar asya* ("whose morning is beautiful"). [This applies to] a word whose primary force is that of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Some say that because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible, the word *prātaḥ* indicates the morning ritual (*prātastanaṃ karma*). Others maintain that, as in the case of the term *rātaḥkalpa*, the word *prātaḥ* in its derivative sense refers to that which possesses the capacity [for the action], and thus coreferentiality is not untenable; this applies to words such as *eṇīpada*.
The substitution of *pad* occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
(743) Pāṇini 5.4.121: *nañ-duḥ-subhyo halisakthyor anyatarasyām*. [Objection: But here, the mention of *hali* is redundant; for one could form *ahala* by taking the word *hala*.

Because the formation [of the compound] is possible. Nor should it be argued that *ahaliḥ* is not *madadhaliḥ*, and therefore the inclusion of *ahal-* there is for the purpose of allowing the usage *ahalaḥ* in that same sense; for one might suspect that in the form *ahalaḥ*, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) would result.
Because the rule "aṃśubhyām" prescribes that [the word] ends with an udātta accent. On this point, they say:
that [mention of the word] is for the purpose of excluding the secondary suffix *kap*, and for the purpose of ensuring the final udātta accent in the rule "urhaḷaḥ.
Regarding the phrase "of the two powers": some students were taught by the Teacher [Pāṇini] to read the sūtra as "haliśaktyoḥ."
The suffix *bhāva* [is applied].
(744) *nityamasic prajāmedhayoḥ* | Pāṇini 5.4.122. Regarding *nityamasic*: the pronunciation of the vowel *a* is for the purpose of establishing its status as a *bha*-stem; thus, they...
In examples such as *nasuprajāsau*, the elision of the vowel *a* is established by the rule *yasyeti ca*.

Since the word *anyatarasyām* does not recur [from the previous rule] because it is not marked with a svarita accent, the inclusion of the term *nityam* (always) serves to ordain the operation elsewhere; by this means, forms such as *alpamedhas* are established.
The authors of the *Vṛtti* and others [state]: (745) *dharmād anic kevalāt* | Pāṇini 5.4.124.
[The rule] *dharmād anic* [is stated]; some say that the vowel *a* in *anic* has no purpose to be considered; others, however, [say it serves to indicate] *dharma*.
It performs or teaches [it]; thus, from the causative form *karoti* with the suffix *kvip*, we have *dharma*. One whose supreme (*parama*) dharma is this is a *paramadharma*.
Because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original], the word *dharma* here includes the vowel *a*; hence the pronunciation of the vowel *a* in this context.
They say that [the rule] indeed has a specific purpose. He will state immediately below that, in this case, the prior member is implied by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

And he says that this [prior member] is qualified by the word "only" (*eva*), stating: "from the prior member alone. However, according to the older commentators, the subsequent member is also qualified.

It has been explained that [the phrase] "even that produced by faith" is a qualification of both the word *dharma* and the preceding word [of the compound], solely because of the word *kevalāt* (from alone); however, both of these points are to be reconsidered. This is because there is no evidence for such a repetition (*āvṛtti*), and because there is no purpose in qualifying the word *dharma*. Nor does it end with the word *dharma*.
Where it must be stated that the result is the exclusion of that [other meaning] from the latter member of the compound,

there is no fault, because such a thing is simply impossible in the case of the word *dharma* following a prior member that constitutes part of a *bahuvrīhi*. As for the phrase "because of being intermediate," it is not the case that...

One might suspect that, according to the rule *arvānāmasaṅkhyayoḥ*, the word *sva* should be placed first [in the compound]; however, this has been resolved by Haradatta and others on the grounds that [the rule] belongs to the class of *āhitāgny-ādi* (a class of compounds defined by usage).
Regarding the term "relative" (*āpekṣika*): [an objection is raised]—"In that case, the mention of the word 'only' (*kevala*) is redundant, because [the meaning of] the word *pūrva*..."

If it is argued that the exclusion of the middle term is possible precisely because [the compound] is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as having its first member as its constituent part, they reply here: "Because the word alone is meaningful as a factor that captures the intended sense (*tātparya*) when there is an implication of the preceding member. Regarding the phrase "the preceding member of a *karmadhāraya*": now, one might object that here the suffix *anic* is difficult to obtain.
If it is argued that this is because the word *kevala* in the rule *kevalād iti* functions as a qualifier for a compound (*samāsa*), we say: not so.
There is no evidence that the mention of *kevala* refers to a preceding member (*pūrvapada*) that is not a compound;
furthermore, this would contradict usage such as *nivṛttidharmā hi sthānī bhavati*.

The meaning we have stated is clear from the root *hṛ* in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇe*) according to Mādhava’s treatise. By this, the analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which has a property to be proved" (*sādhyadharman*) is one whose property is yet to be established; and that which is both "doubtful" (*saṃdigdha*) and "having a property to be proved" (*sādhyadharman*) is the [subject]. Furthermore, that doubt ultimately results in being mediated solely by the property to be proved (*sādhyadharma*).

The explanation offered by some has been refuted; for when the probandum is directly understood as being doubtful through the very manner of the statement itself, any effort to establish that [doubt] is futile. "It is indeed correct" (*sādhveva*):
this is when the compound is analyzed as *paramasvaḥ* (the supreme self) and then [the possessive compound] *yasya paramasvo dharmaḥ* (of whom the supreme self is the duty).
The meaning is "therefore.

(746) *dakṣiṇermā lubdhayoge* |5|4|126|. *dakṣiṇermā*. *Lubdha* means a hunter (*vyādha*). The irregular formation (*nipātana*) of *ermaniṣ* occurs specifically due to its connection with that [hunter].

The meaning is that nothing else [is required]; this is what he states with the words "by the hunter. As for the usage, "The one who wears a garland of golden lotuses, a treasury of virtues, was made right-handed by the arrow," it must be interpreted in some way as being figurative (*aupacārika*).

(747) *ic* [is added] when there is a reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*). In the example *keśakeśī*, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed by the rule *tenedam* [Pāṇini 2.2.28] to express reciprocal action. Because the suffix *ic* is listed among the *tiṣṭhadgu*-type words, it possesses the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) when it functions as an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*).

[Objection: But in this way, the inclusion of the word *aci* [in the rule] is useless; for since the designation of *avyayībhāva* would subvert the designation of *bahuvrīhi*, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) would be established by the accent of the compound itself. [Response: On this point, they say: it is indeed necessary for the sake of distinction. For if only the vowel *i* were recited in the list beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*, etc., [the following problem would arise].

Because there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *sugandhi*. Furthermore, in this case, the designation of *avyayībhāva* does not sublate the designation of *bahuvrīhi*; rather, there is simply a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of both, since it is improper to violate that upon which one depends (*upajīvyavirodha*). And thus, the *cit* suffixation is also for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*).
"It must indeed be done.
(748) *Dvidaṇḍy-ādibhyaś-ca* [Pāṇini 5.4.128].
Regarding *dvidaṇḍī*: this is due to the technical designation (*nipātana*) of the entire compound as a whole.
Because it serves the purpose of denoting a specific object (*viṣayaviśeṣa*), the suffix *ij* does not occur in the case of *dvidaṇḍā śālā*.
[Examples include] *ubhāhasti* and so forth. Here, the optionality of the suffix *āyac* arises precisely from this irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
(749) *prasaṃbhyāṃ jānunorjñuḥ* | Pāṇini 5.4.129. [When preceded by *pra* or *sam*, the word *jānu* is replaced by *jñu*.]

Regarding the rule *prasaṃbhyām*: although the word *jānu* is singular, the dual form *jānunoḥ* is employed by resorting to a duality based on the two parts [of the knee] (*upapaja*). The purpose of this, however, is to clarify that it is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). For if it were stated as *jānunaḥ*, one might wonder whether this is a fifth case (ablative).

Because this is the section concerning suffixes (*pratyaya*), there might be the doubt that *jña* is itself a suffix; intending to clarify this, he says: "In the words *jānu* and *jñu*, there is the substitution of *jñu*.
(Pāṇini 5.4.133) *Vā saṃjñāyām*. 5.4.133.

Regarding the term *śārṅgadhanvā*: if it is asked how the usage by Puṣpadanta, "He quickly treated as a blade of grass the one who had taken up his bow out of hope for the slaughter of Bala and Arṇa," is possible, they say here that there is no inconsistency because the rule regarding the suffix at the end of a compound is not mandatory (*anitya*). As for its non-mandatory nature—
O King, the authority for [the word] *aśvādi* being included in the *gaṇa* is its recitation in the list of words;

for that [recitation] is intended to establish the final acute accent (*antodātta*) by the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa*, [words] beginning with *aśva* and others [are antodātta] after *rati*. However, if the suffix *ṭac* were obligatory by the rule "The suffix *ṭac* is applied after *rājan*, *ahan*, and *sakhi*," then what would be the purpose of that [recitation]?

(751) *lopo vyor vali* | P. 6.1.66. Regarding the rule *lopo vyor vali*: although it could have been stated simply as *vyor lopaḥ*, the mention of the operation first—namely, that the elision of *v* and *y* occurs by prior application (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) over the elision of the single-consonant suffix (*apṛktalopa*) after *veḥ*—is intended to indicate [this specific priority]. By this, [the following is established:]...

The form *sukhī* is established from the root *sukhīyati* by means of the *kvip* suffix. Regarding [Pāṇini 5.4.135], *gandhasyedutpūtisusurabhibhyaḥ*: with the intention that the letter *t* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), he says—“the letter *i* is the substitute for the final [element].”

The rule *ṭhādeḥ parasya* does not apply here, because of the governing heading *am-ās-antāḥ*. On this point, some say: "Even if the vowel *i* were a suffix (*pratyaya*), there would be no harm; for forms such as *udgandhiḥ* are established by the elision [of the suffix] according to the rule *yasyeti ca*. And it is not...
One should not suspect that the designation *itsvarita* would result in the final syllable being svarita,

because it is accepted that the letter *t* serves merely for the purpose of pronunciation. Nor should it be argued that, because of its mention in the genitive case, it is an *ādeśa* (substitute) rather than a *pratyaya* (suffix).
"Because the genitive case is observed even in rules prescribing suffixes such as *āpoṣṭak* and others.

Regarding the substitution of *it* for *gandha*, there is the inclusion of the term *tadekānta*. By the phrase 'without distinction,' the resulting meaning is that only those denoting qualities (*guṇavācin*) are to be understood, and not those denoting substances (*dravyavācin*). And [the word] *dravyāṇi* exists..."

The word *gandha* denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*), as seen in such usage as "this [stone] carries water and grinds scents" (*vahati jalam iyaṃ pinaṣṭi gandhān*). Furthermore, it is stated in the lexicon (*kośa*) that: "The word *gandha* refers to fragrance, dance, sulphur, pride, and a small portion; it is recorded as denoting a substance in the plural and in the masculine."

Some, however, say that in the Vārttika "gandhasyetve," the term *tadekānta* intends to express inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*); therefore, [the suffix] does not apply to that which is adventitious (*āgantuka*). Thus says Bhaṭṭi: "The fragrant wind, having smelled... And it has been explained [as follows]:

In the *Jayamaṅgalā*: "By the rule *gandhasya* etc., the compound-ending suffix *ic* does not apply, because of the statement: 'When [the word] *gandha* undergoes the substitution of *it*, that refers exclusively to [the specific sense of] fragrance. For example, as in *sugandha āpaṇikaḥ* ('a perfumer'). For this very reason, forms such as *hagnabālasahakārasugandhau* are considered erroneous."
The author of the *Durghaṭavṛtti* has stated:

When there is a designation of "small" (*alpākhyā*), for a word denoting "fragrance" (*gandha*) that expresses smallness, there shall be the substitution of a final vowel ending in *i* in a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

"the fragrance of the soup" (*sūpasya gandhaḥ*). For this very reason, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with non-co-referential members (*vyadhikaraṇapada*) as indicated by this [grammatical] authority. Alternatively, this is a statement of the resultant meaning; the analysis (*vigraha*) is simply "that in which the soup has fragrance.
Even though the word *gandha* is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), its placement at the end [of the compound] occurs precisely because of this same authority.

(754) *pādasya lopo’hastyādibhyaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.4.138. Regarding the word *pāda*: if this elision (*lopa*) were not a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), then by the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, it would apply to the beginning [of the following member]. Consequently, the suffix *ka* prescribed for the remaining cases (*śaiṣika*) would also undesirably apply, as in the case of the optional rule *eṣadvibhāṣā*.

Because the "remainder" (śeṣa) is resorted to as depending on the compound-final suffix (samāsānta), he says: "as a compound-final suffix. But how can a non-entity (abhāva) be a constituent part (avayava) of an entity? To this he replies: "by way of its substituendum" (sthānidvāreṇa).
The meaning is that, by the force of the statement, a figurative (aupacārika) status as a constituent part is understood.

(755) *kumbhapadīṣu ca* | 5|4|139|. Regarding the rule *kumbhapadīṣu ca*: since the plural number is used and because of the force of its inclusion in the list (*gaṇapāṭha*), one understands that it refers to the group as a whole; with this intention, he says "in *kumbhapadī* and so forth. In this list, the items *kumbhapadī*, *ekapadī*, and *jānapadī* are read as complete compounds; and the purpose of this is to include specific objects [of application]. With this in mind, he says "in the feminine."

Furthermore, regarding those forms where the suffix is read preceded by a comparison or preceded by a numeral, since its elision is already established, this statement is made for the sake of ensuring the compulsory application of *ṅīp*; therefore, the optional rule "āto ’nyatarasyām" does not apply.

(Pāṇini 5.4.141) *vayasi dantasya datṛ*: [The substitute] *datṛ* takes the place of *danta* when expressing age. For example, *dvidadan* ("two-toothed") means that two teeth have been produced in him; however, the state of infancy is understood here.

In *ṣaṇṇām*, the augment *num* is applied by the rule *ṣṇāntāṣaṭ*. Because the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered as if it had not occurred (*asiddha*), the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) does not take place.

In *ṣoḍan*, the substitution of *u* for *a* and the substitution of *ṭh* for *ḍ* are applied by the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*; however, here [in the nominative singular], the *u* and *ṭh* substitutions are applied by the rule *aṣa utvaṃ datṛdaśadhe*. In *sudatī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṣṇāntāṣaṭ*.

(757) *striyāṃ saṃjñāyām* ||5|4|143|| [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after the word *samada* when it denotes a feminine name. Example: *samadantī*. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] by the rule beginning with *āsikadīrā-* etc. (758) *bibhāṣā śyāvārokābhyām* ||5|4|144|| [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is optionally applied after the words *śyāva* and *aroka*.]
*Śyāvadant* means "one with black teeth. According to Amarasimha, *śyāvaḥ syāt kapiśaḥ*, meaning "śyāva" refers to a brownish-black color.
*Arokadant* means "one whose teeth are without gaps (*arokāḥ* = *acchidrāḥ*).
[The rule governing these formations is: *agrānta-śuddha-śubhra-vṛṣa-varāhebhyaś ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.145).
The particle *ca* here has the sense of including what has not been mentioned; therefore, they say that [the suffix] *ṭhan* applies [to form] *mūṣikadanna*.
(760) *kakudasyāvasthāyāṃ lopaḥ* | 5.4.146. [In this rule, there is the elision of *kakuda* when expressing a state.]
"Ajāta" [is derived as follows]: the analysis of the compound is "that which has an unborn (*ajāta*) hump (*kakuda*). Here, indeed, the state of childhood is understood.

(761) *Uraḥprabhṛtibhyaḥ kap* (Pāṇini 5.4.151): after words beginning with *uraḥ*, the suffix *kap* is applied. That is to say, the suffix *kap* is added to a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in words such as *uraḥ*.

However, according to the view that "the suffixes *samāsānta* (compound-final suffixes) apply to compounds ending in the word *artha*," one must explain that the suffix *kap* is added after the final members of a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *uraḥ* and others.
Because it is a *taddhita* suffix, there is no substitution of *it* for the *ka* of *kap*. Thus, we have *vyūḍhoraskaḥ*, meaning "one whose chest (*uraḥ*) is broad (*vyūḍhaṃ viśālaṃ*)".

In *saḥ*, the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *s* according to the rule *o-padādau*. In *priyasarpiṣkaḥ*, the *visarjanīya* is changed to *ṣ* according to the rule *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*. Regarding the mention of the word ending in the singular number (*ekavacanānta*): although this is already established by the rule *ady-ataś-ca*, the inclusion of the word *lakṣmī* here is intended to apply specifically to a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose constituent member is the word *lakṣmī* ending in the singular.
The suffix *kap* is compulsory, whereas elsewhere there is only an option regarding the form *eṣāt*; this is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).
By this, the usage of Bhāravi—“*akṛśamakṛśalakṣmīścetasā śaṃsitaṃ saḥ*” (he was praised in his mind as one whose fortunes were not meager)—is established.
The analysis (*vigraha*) is: “one whose fortunes (*lakṣmyaḥ*) are not meager (*akṛśāḥ*)”; as for what was stated by the ancients, namely, “*uṭhnadyaﬁtaśca*,” [that is incorrect].

[The example] "kap, bahulakṣmīkaḥ" is incorrect; for the word *bahu*, when expressing a number, lacks the singular ending, and thus it is excluded by the present rule. [This is so] because in the analysis (*vigraha*) "one whose prosperity (*lakṣmī*) is much (*bahvī*) or excessive," the word *bahu* expresses abundance (*vaipulya*).

Even though the possibility of a singular ending exists, because the rule prescribing the qualifier (*viśeṣana-vidhi*) is stronger, it is more appropriate to state simply: "The suffix *kaP* [is applied] after words such as *uras*. However, when it is maintained that "this [work] proceeds by way of prohibition for those who do not follow the formal grammatical treatises," then even what was stated by the Easterners (*Prāc*) is entirely correct.

This is to be understood. Regarding the statement "after a word meaning 'object' (artha), the negative particle (nañ) [is not applied]," this is a *gaṇasūtra*. As for the phrase "even by one that is meaningless," how is it then that the form *upathī nagarī* is mentioned among the words ending in consonants (*halanta*), given that the suffix *kap* would be unavoidable here? Nor can it be argued that by the rule *a pūjanāt*, there is a prohibition of the *kap* suffix belonging specifically to the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ*.
This is not to be doubted; for it will be stated that this prohibition applies only to those [words] ending in *ṣac* that are archaic (*prācīna*).
Since the suffix *kap* follows after *ṣac*, [the objection does not hold]. True;
however, the matter is to be resolved by noting that the rule governing the addition of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), and thus [the form] is correct.
It has been stated [in the commentary] that this is because of the rule *ṭhyuvoranākau* and because of the example *supathī* in the Bhāṣya.
(762) *inaḥ striyām* || 5.4.152 || [The suffix *ka* is applied after a stem ending in *in* when forming a feminine word. Example: *bahuvāggmikā*. [This is derived from] *vāco gminiḥ*.

(763) *śeṣad vibhāṣā* |5|4|154|. Regarding *śeṣadvi*: if "remainder" (*śeṣa*) here were intended with reference only to those [compounds] previously mentioned, then it would also apply to cases such as *vyāghrapāt* and *sugandhi*; therefore, in this context, "remainder" is intended with reference to the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*).
He says, "it is understood," namely: "from that which does not have a prescribed compound-ending (*samāsānta*). Regarding *vyāghrapāt*:

it has been stated that even the elision (*lopa*) [of the final *t*] by way of the substituend depends upon the compound-ending. Regarding *sugandhi*: the compound-ending *it* is applied by the rule beginning with "after *gandha*" (*andhasya*). Regarding *priyapatha*.

In *ṭhṛkpūḥ*, the suffix *up* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*). In *upabahavaḥ*, the compound is formed by the rule beginning with “*aṃkhyāvyaye*” (Pāṇini 2.2.25). In *utara-pūrva*, the compound is formed by the rule beginning with “*iṅnāmni*” (Pāṇini 2.1.50). In *suputraḥ*, the compound is formed by the rule beginning with “*tena saha*” (Pāṇini 2.1.30). This...

The meaning is as follows: from the rule "śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ," the word *śeṣa* (remainder) is carried forward (*anuvartate*) only into that very sūtra, "anekam anyapadārthe," but it is excluded (*nivartate*) from rules such as "saṃkhyāvyayāsannādūrā... and so forth. And thus...

Because there is an absence of the status of being under the governing rule of *śeṣa* (P. 2.3.50), the suffix *kap* does not apply in cases such as *upabahavaḥ*. Thus, the separate formulation of rules such as *saṅkhyāvyayāsannadūrādhikaṃ saṅkhyeye ḍaḥ* (P. 2.2.25) after the rule *anekam anyapadārthe* (P. 2.2.24) is also necessary for the purpose of preventing the application of *kap*.

[The word *śeṣa*] stands [as the subject]. Now, one might ask: how can the word *śeṣa*, uttered only once, have both the sense of "that which has not been assigned a specific compound-ending" and the sense of "that which falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *śeṣa*"? To this he says: "by means of *tantra* and so forth. There are two views: first, that "the word *śeṣa* differs according to the difference in meaning"; and second, that "even when there is a difference in meaning, the word remains non-different. In the former case...

The distinction is that "obstruction" (*āvṛtti*) applies to the second [case], while "the rule" (*tantra*) applies to the first. As for what they say—"The compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) prescribed by specific rules act as exceptions (*bādhaka*) within their own scope; therefore, what is the use of the term *śeṣa* (remainder), which is intended to refer to those compounds for which no suffix has been specifically stated?"—that is not correct. For in the case of compounds such as *ṛkpūḥ* and so forth, [the suffixes apply] even in other types of compounds.
Because its purpose has already been fulfilled, there would otherwise be an obstruction by the subsequent *kap* suffix in cases such as "ariyapatha" (the noble path).
(764) *īyasaśca* | 5|4|156 | [The rule] "and after [a stem ending in] *īyas*" [prohibits the suffix]. All instances of *kap*, whether mandatory (*nitya*) or optional (*vaikalpika*), are prohibited.

"Bahuśreyān" means "exceedingly praiseworthy"—that is, *śreyān* (better). [The suffix] *īyasun* is applied according to the rule "vibhajanavibhajyopeta-". [In this formation], *śra-* is substituted for *praśasya-* by the rule "praśasyasya śraḥ". The suffix *kap* is optionally applicable here by the rule "eṣadvibhāṣā".
It should be stated that the suffix *ka* is not added after a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *īyas*. Thus, in the case of *bahuśreyasī*,

although the suffix *kap* would have applied invariably by the rule *adyantaśca*, it is prohibited by the rule *īyasaśca* on the basis of the technical principle regarding the qualification of a stem (*laṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*).
(765) *nāḍītantryoḥ svāṅge* |5|4|159|. [The example] *bahunāḍiḥ* [shows that] there is shortening of the *upasarjana* because it does not end in a feminine suffix;
for [the suffix] *i* is applied by the rule *avitṛstṛtantribhyaḥ*.
The sense is that [the suffix] is not prescribed under the governing rule *triyām*.
(766) *saptamī-viśeṣaṇe bahuvrīhau* |2|2|35|. When it is known that "something is in the throat," that which qualifies it (*viśeṣaṇa*) [is placed first].

The word *kāle* means "in the case of time"; therefore, this mention of the locative case (*saptamī*) is for that purpose. On other occasions, however, it is established even without it, simply by virtue of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Regarding the example *citraguḥ*: one should not say that this is already established by the rule "the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) comes first," because when it is stated in the rule "the locative [member] in a Bahuvrīhi," [it implies] *takra*...

Since, by the principle of Koṇḍinya, there would arise the undesirable consequence of the prior status of the subordinate member being sublated, the term "viśeṣaṇa" (qualifier) was included [in the rule].
There is an extension of the application to pronouns and numerals. Regarding the word "sarvanāma" (pronoun): how then [is it explained] in the case of *aḥ paraḥ*?
Since it is said that "it is superior to the good" (*sataparaḥ*), how can it be that "there is a function [of the compound] while abandoning its own meaning" (*jahatsvārthe vṛttiḥ*)?
For here, *jahatsva* is a term where the word *sva* is abandoned; that which has such a [term] as its object is a *bahuvrīhi* containing within it another *bahuvrīhi*.
And thus, because the words *spa* and *para* are pronouns (*sarvanāman*), they would require prior placement [in the compound].

If it is argued that [the compound] must be formed thus, they say here: "The word *sva* does not take the prior position in the compound with *para* because of its usage in the Sūtras and Bhāṣya; or rather, its establishment is due to its inclusion in the *rājadantādi* group. As for the example *dviśukla*:
although the prior positioning of the word *dvi* is established simply by its being a numeral (sarvanāman), nevertheless...
The term "saṅkhyā" (numeral) is included in the Vārttika for the sake of establishing forms such as "dviśukla. Now, one might object:
since "saṅkhyā" has fewer syllables than "sarvanāman," it would have been more appropriate to state the rule as "saṅkhyā-sarvanāmnoḥ";
therefore, the reversed formulation seems improper. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the compound of these two, the numeral comes first. Regarding "of these two":
the intention is that the very reversal of the order of utterance here serves as the indicator [of this rule].
"Of the smaller numeral" (*saṅkhyāyā alpīyasyāḥ*): "of the smaller" means "of that which expresses a smaller number."
The seventh case [suffix] following *gaḍu* and so forth [is elided]. Regarding the phrase "of *gaḍu* and so forth": the word *ādi* (and so forth) expresses a class (*prakāra*).
By this, one obtains forms such as *padmanābhaḥ*—meaning "one whose navel has a lotus" (*padmaṃ nābhau yasya*)—and *ūrṇanābhaḥ*—meaning "one whose navel has wool" (*ūrṇā nābhau yasya*).
They say that the shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "yāpoḥ—" [Pāṇini 6.4.157], whereby *ūrṇanābhaḥ* is established.

The suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle) should be stated as coming after [words denoting] genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), happiness (*sukha*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "genus, time":
the intention is that this is indicated by the rule *atikālasukhādibhyo ’nācchādanāt*.
As for *sāraṅgajagdhī*: it is that by which a *sāraṅga* [deer] has been eaten (*jagdha*).

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṭhasvāṅgapūrvapadād vā*. How then is [the form] *cārusmitaḥ*, *cāruhasitaḥ*, and so forth explained? Regarding this, they say: by the rule *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*, the suffix *kta* does not undergo prior placement (as a compound), because here only that which is prescribed by the term *niṣṭhā* is understood.

The suffixes *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) and the locative case (*saptamī*) follow words denoting weapons [when they are the first members of a compound], but not in certain instances. The intention is that this is because of the assumption of the status of being "headed by *āhitāgni*" (*āhitāgny-ādi*) or due to non-expression (*anabhidhāna*).
Thus ends the section on *bahuvrīhi* compounds in the commentary *Tattvabodhinī*.
Now begins the section on the *bhāva* (intransitive/abstract action) and *karman* (passive) voices.
(476) *sārvadhātuke yak* | 3|1|67|.

[The suffix] *yak* [is applied] after a verbal root when a *sārvadhātuka* affix follows. From the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ* [3.1.22], the word *dhātoḥ* ("after a verbal root") is understood; from *iṇ...*, [the word *ārdhadhātuke* is understood].

From the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ," the phrase "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" is carried over [as an anuvṛtti]. "Bhāva" means "bhāvanā" (the efficient force). The word "bhāvaḥ" is derived from the root *bhū* in the sense of "origination" (*utpatti*), with the suffix *ṇic*, followed by the suffix *ac* according to the rule *erac*.
However, Kaiyaṭa on that very sūtra states that the reading "*ṇeraniṭi*" is not the word of the Ṛṣi (i.e., it is not original).
He demonstrates that the root *bhū* has the sense of "origination" (*utpatti*) and that the causative form *bhāvayati* has the same meaning as the simple root *kṛ* ("to do")—

namely, "the action of producing" (*utpādanā kriyā*). Just as in expressions such as "he makes a jar" (*karoti ghaṭam*), the activity conducive to origination resides in the potter, so too does it reside in the agent of *bhāvayati*.

This applies even in cases such as "the pot" (*ghaṭam*). Even in the case of "the pot comes into being" (*bhavati ghaṭaḥ*), there certainly exists an operation conducive to arising that resides in the pot; however, the distinction is this: that [operation] is co-located with the result (*phala-samānādhikaraṇa*), whereas the operation residing in the potter is located in a different locus from the result (*phala-vyadhikaraṇa*). For this very reason, regarding the result and the operation...

They say that because of their coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), roots such as *bhū* are intransitive (*akarmaka*), whereas because of their non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), roots such as *kṛ* are transitive (*sakarmaka*). By this, [the question is raised] regarding the phrase "what is meant by 'expressing action' (*kriyāvācin*) in the rule *hūvādayo dhātavaḥ*? with reference to the passage beginning with "the *hāva* is the *bhāvanā*."

The suffix *liṅ* (optative) should not apply to the word *vā* when used in the sense of "option" (*vikalpa*). Otherwise, since the word *vā* alone is listed in the *bhvādi* class, even the particle *vā*—which does not denote an action—would be a verbal root (*dhātu*). Consequently, because of the rule stating that "the meaning of a root alone, in its pure form, is called *bhāva* (action/state)," the particle *vā* would also incur the status of being a *bhāva*.

The explanation of certain scholars—that the *liṭ* suffix must necessarily occur after the word *vāś*, which denotes that [action]—is refuted, because the *liṭ* in the impersonal (*bhāva*) sense is accepted only after a word denoting *bhāvanā*. This is because an option (*vikalpa*), however, is distinct from *bhāvanā*. Otherwise, even if the qualifier "denoting movement" (*gatyarthavācin*) were provided, [the objection would remain].

Because that same defect remains as it was. Furthermore, one should not even suspect that *laṭ* and the other suffixes would occur after a word expressing a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) even in the absence of the *liṅ* suffix, since the rule for *laṭ* and the others prescribes them only when they denote present action and so forth.
Why, then, do all [grammarians] state there that "the roots beginning with *bhū* denote action"?

Is it not explained? If you argue that even in the case of *yāḥ paśyasi*, because the word *yāḥ* cannot be a verbal root (*dhātu*) according to the paribhāṣā regarding "that which is taught by its technical definition" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*), the elision of *ā* by the rule *āto dhātoḥ* does not apply there—on this point they say: "The time of the Ārya..."

If it is argued that, according to the view that "technical definitions and paribhāṣās [apply] simultaneously," the elision of *ā* (prescribed by *āto dhātoḥ*) would not apply there because the word *sthā* cannot be a verbal root (*dhātu*),
the following is said:
"Under the view that 'definitions and paribhāṣās [apply] at the time of the operation,' [the rule] *āto dhātoḥ* applies at the locus where the operation is to take place."

The rule *bhvādayo dhātavaḥ* ("*bhu-* and so forth are verbal roots") applies [by proximity]. Since the word *yā-* is read among the *bhu*-class roots, even the word *yā-* denoting a substance (*dravya*) applies there; for when a mere phoneme (*varṇa*) is being referred to, the paribhāṣā regarding "that which is indicated by a technical definition versus that which is explicitly stated" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā*) does not operate. [Thus,] from *ātaḥ*...

In the rule "dhātoḥ," however, because of the mention of the phoneme *ā* (in *āt*), the term "verbal root" (*dhātu*) would not apply to the word *yāśabda*, which consists of two syllables; therefore, the qualification "expressing action" (*kriyāvācin*) must certainly be stated so that this does not happen. By the phrase "action is production" (*utpādanā kriyā*), it is [defined as] that which expresses action.

The objection raised by some—that here the mutual dependence between the root-meaning (*dhātu*), the meaning of the root, and the action (*kriyā*) is difficult to avoid—is refuted, because the action is the operation conducive to production (*utpatti*). As it has been said: "The operation is *bhāvanā*; that itself is production, and that itself is the action."

Regarding the phrase "as the state of being a verbal root" (*dhātutvena*): whether the state of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) across all roots is a universal (*jāti*) or an impartible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) is another matter; however, that [state] is the delimitor of denotative capacity (*vācakatāvacchedaka*).

The point is that while the state of being an action (*kriyātva*) is the delimitor of denotedness (*vācyatāvacchedaka*), the state of being a verbal root is the delimitor of denotative capacity. As for the phrase "denoted by a verbal root": [an objection follows: But if this were so...

In cases such as *pacati*, there would be no cognition having the action as its qualificandum— namely, "the act of cooking occurring in the present with a single agent"— because it has been established in instances such as *aupagava* that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) functions as a qualifier relative to the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). And thus, [it would follow] that "the *tiṅ*-suffix is expressive of the locus of the sacrifice."

If it is argued that the Mīmāṃsaka view alone is the most pleasing, they reply here: "The meaning of the suffix is primary"—this is a general rule (utsarga), and it is abandoned here because of the traditional teaching that "the verb has action as its primary meaning.
Furthermore, regarding femininity, which the Mīmāṃsakas accept as the meaning of [suffixes] such as *ṭāp* in words like *pācikā*, [it is not so].
Furthermore, because it is not admitted that [the suffix] functions as a qualifier, the rule that "the meaning of the suffix is primary" has been abandoned.

Moreover, in expressions such as *bhoktavyam* ("it is to be eaten"), the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is understood even without the suffix *tiṅ*, and a requirement for a factor of action (*kāraka*) is observed. And there is indeed grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb *karoti*. Furthermore—

In expressions such as "it is to be eaten" (*bhoktavyam*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is understood even without the suffix *tiṅ* (the verbal ending), and a requirement for a factor of action (*kāraka*) is observed. Furthermore, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb "to do" (*karoti*): "What is to be done?"—"It is to be eaten"; "What has been done?"—"It has been eaten. Nor is this [coreferentiality] found even in the case of [suffixes] ending in *kṛt*.
It should not be suspected that suffixes such as *tavyat* denote the productive operation (*bhāvanā*),

because even opponents accept that suffixes like *tavyat* apply to the object (*karman*) and so forth— on the grounds of the requirement for non-differentiation (*abheda-anvaya*) between the meaning of a noun and its referent. Otherwise, [expressions such as] "Devadatta is a cook" (*pācako devadattaḥ*) would be untenable.

In the expression "the rice is to be cooked" (*paktavya odanaḥ*), there would be no cognition of identity [between the agent and the action]. Thus, the view that *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is denoted by the verbal root itself is indeed more elegant. This is stated with the intention that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the personal suffix (*lakāra*) is possible only for those suffixes that denote the agent or the object, and not for those that denote the abstract action (*bhāva*).

He explains: "Because of the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Nor should it be argued that, in this case, since the words other than *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are coreferential, the first person should occur—as in "devadattaḥ pati" and similar examples—and thus the first person would not even appear here.

Regarding the phrase "this is the first," it is explained that "the first [case-ending] should occur when the middle and last [cases] are not applicable. As for the statement "denoted by a *tiṅ* suffix," while it is indeed accepted that what is denoted by *ghañ* and other such suffixes possesses the nature of a substance (*sattva*), this allows for the application of the second case and others as appropriate in examples such as *pākam* and *pākena*.

They function [in this way]. For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "An action denoted by a verbal root (*ṛt*) manifests like a substance (*dravyavat*). The meaning is that it assumes the properties of a substance, such as gender, number, and case-role (*kāraka*). The statement "it is only in the singular" is a general observation (*prāyovāda*). Otherwise...

In the *Mahābhāṣya*, regarding the indication of the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) with the suffix *ṇvul*— in the examples "seats are being sat upon" (*ṭhuṣṭrāsikā āsyante*) and "beds are being slept upon" (*ṭhhataśāyikāḥ śayyante*)— although the plural number is established for the words *āsikāḥ* and *śāyikāḥ* because "a state expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix appears like a substance" (*kṛdabhihito bhāvo dravyavat prakāśate*), [the same applies] in the cases of *āsyante* and *śayyante*.

That [interpretation] would not be established. Nor should it be suspected that the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) here refers to the object (*karman*) itself, because that is impossible given that both roots are intransitive (*akarmaka*), and because it would result in a semantic inconsistency. For in that context, such as "the seats of camels were like this" and "the beds of those who were slain were like this," [the meaning would be lost].

The meaning is that there are various acts of sitting and so forth, having Devadatta and others as their agents. Because similarity is perceived here, even though the "being" (bhāva) expressed by the verbal suffix is a single entity, it appears as distinct; hence the use of the plural number. Nor should it be argued that if it were thus connected with number, it would lose its non-substantial (asattva) nature.

Because it has been stated among the *kārakas* that the status of being a non-substance (*asattvarūpatva*) is established merely by the absence of connection with gender, action, and a substratum; some here, having accepted a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the words *uṣṭrāsikā* and *hataśāyikā* in the sense of things similar to them, [explain] by means of [the analysis] "they sit," and so forth.

They state that there is non-differentiation in the coreferential relation (*abhedānvaya*). However, in the *Manoramā*, it is stated that forms such as *āsikāḥ* and *śāyikāḥ* are in the second case plural; this is because, by virtue of being adverbs, they possess the status of an object (*karman*).
Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, they would necessarily be neuter and end in the singular number; for [the rule] states: "In the feminine..."

It has been stated that because of the governing rule *kta-annitya*, the determination of femininity precludes the application of the rule *napuṃsakam anyatarasyām*; and because of the determination of plurality, the singular number does not apply.

(477) Pāṇini 6.4.62: *syasicsīyuṭtāsiṣu bhāvakarmaṇor upadeśe ’j-jhan-agrahadṛśāṃ vā ciṇvad iṭ ca*. [In the rules for] *sya*, *sic*, *sīyuṭ*, and *tās*, when the sense is that of the impersonal (*bhāva*) or passive (*karman*), there is optionally the substitution of *ciṇ* (as in the *ciṇ* augment), and the *iṭ* augment is also applied after roots beginning with a vowel (*aj*), those ending in *han*, *grah*, and *dṛś*, as they appear in the original grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*). Although the roots beginning with vowels (*aj-ādayaḥ*) are listed as a *dvandva* compound...

Nevertheless, since [the term] "upadeśa" (in the original instruction) has been specified, this qualification applies only to the vowels (*ac*) and not to *han* and the others, because there is no deviation [of those in the upadeśa]. Thus he says: "the vowel (*aj*) which is in the upadeśa. It is not explained as "of those ending in a vowel (*ajanta*) in the upadeśa," for if that were the case, it would not apply to a form ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*.

Because there is no direct instruction for that [root]. For "instruction" (upadeśa) refers to direct pronunciation, and such does not exist for a root ending in the causative suffix (*ṇic*). The term *ciṇvat* is a *vati*-derivative from a locative form (*ciṇi*);
this is because, in the rule "in the presence of *yaṅ*, *sīyuṭ*, and *tās*" (*yasic sīyuṭ tāsiṣu*), the locative case is used to indicate the point of comparison (*pratiyogin*). Therefore...

He explains: "as in *ciṇ*" (*ciṇīva*). But surely, if there were an extension (*atideśa*) of every grammatical operation seen in the *ciṇ* suffix—such as *vṛddhi* and so forth—then in forms such as *ghāniṣyate*, *āyiṣyate*, and *adhyāyiṣyate*, the substitution of *avadha* for *han*, the substitution of *gā* for *iṇ*, and the substitution of *gāṅ* for *iṅ* would also occur.

If you say this, it is not so; for by the force of the governing rule regarding *aṅga*, only an operation pertaining to the *aṅga* itself is extended. Furthermore, these substitutes (*han*, *ṇiṅ*, etc. are not operations pertaining to the *aṅga*; thus he says: "Or it would be an operation of the *aṅga*. Regarding "sīyuṭ": likewise, by the word *sīyuṭ*, that which is qualified by it is indicated.

This is the intended meaning. By the term "ārddhadhātuka," that which is excluded is the *vidhiliṅ* (the optative suffix of injunction). Therefore, in the case of *bhūyeta*, [the substitution] does not occur. Nor should it be argued that here, because of the elision of *s* by the rule "iṅḥ salopaḥ," there is no status as beginning with a consonant (*valāditva*); for that [rule] is not required in this context. As they say:

"Vṛddhi as in *iṇ*, the augment *yuk*, the substitution of *gh* for *han*, and the lengthening [of the vowel] which is said to optionally apply to the roots of the *mit* class after the suffix *ciṇ*; furthermore, the augment *iṭ* is non-existent (*asiddha*). Therefore, my *ṇi* suffix is elided; and this *ṇi* is constant and destructive because it is conditioned by a *val* sound. This is the meaning of that [verse]: the *vṛddhi* and other operations resulting from the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "as in *iṇ*" [are affected].
The purpose [of this rule] is as follows: in forms such as *hāvitā* and *hāviṣyate*, there is *vṛddhi*;

in forms such as *āyitā* and *āyiṣīṣṭe*, there is *yuk*; in forms such as *hānitā* and *ghāniṣyate*, there is the substitution of *gha*; and when the *l*-suffix occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*) after a causative (*hetu-ṇic*) form, as in *āmitā*.

In forms such as *amita*, *āmiṣyate*, and *amiṣyate*, the rule *ciṇṇamuloḥ* applies, whereby there is optionally a lengthening of the penultimate vowel of roots ending in *m* (*mitām upadhāyā vā dīrghaḥ*). In this very context, in forms such as *śamitā*, the augment *iṭ* added by the rule *yasic-sīyuṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) because it is *ābhīya*.

Therefore, since the prohibition "when there is no *iṭ*" does not apply, the elision of *ṇi* takes place. In forms such as *hāviṣyate*, when the stage *bhū-sya* has been reached, the *iṭ* characterized by the *valādi* rule is superseded even though it occurs later, and only the *iṭ* of the *ciṇvad* type applies; for this [latter] is obligatory (*nitya*). Thus, from *vilinamita* comes *vighātī*.

This [augment] is not permanent; when that [ciṇvadbhāva] is applied in the seventh case (the *sāptamika*), this [augment] becomes like *ciṇ* (*ciṇvad-iṭ*); but when this [augment] is applied, that [ciṇvadbhāva] does not occur, because it is prescribed as being conditioned by [roots] beginning with *val*. And thus, due to its permanence, this very augment occurs even for those [roots] that have the *iṭ* augment. However, in the alternative where this [augment] is absent—
It should be understood that the augment *iṭ* occurs after [roots] beginning with *val* following the suffix *liṭ*.
(478) *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* |3|1|66|.
Regarding *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*: [the rule] *leḥ sijabhyastavidibhyaḥ* [is applied], and [the rule] *iṇ te padaḥ* [is also applied].

The phrase "from that" (ityataḥ) and "those" (te) also carry over [from the previous rule]. However, because the mention of *ciṇ* there was obscured by the prohibition "not after *ru*" (*a ruvaḥ*), the mention of *ciṇ* is repeated here. What is the purpose of [specifying] the word *taśabda*? [Consider: *abhāviṣām*. [This refers to] the *iṭ* augment as if it were *ciṇ* (*ciṇvad-iṭ*), [which applies] to the causative (*ṇyanta*) form.

The sense is that even though there is no explicit mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) in the rule, the *ciṇvad-iṭ* (the augment *iṭ* as if it were *ciṇ*) does indeed apply here, based on the explanatory gloss (*vyākhyāna*) that "that which is *aj*" [is the base] when there is an *upadeśa*. Regarding the phrase "on account of being subsequent" (*paratvāt*), this refers to its priority over the *ciṇvad-iṭ*. Regarding the phrase "on account of being obligatory" (*nityatvāt*), one might object that the obligatoriness of the *guṇa* substitution is not established because the *ciṇvad-iṭ* would have already applied first; however, once the *ciṇvad-iṭ* has been applied, the *vṛddhi* substitution takes effect, thereby establishing the obligatoriness of the *guṇa*.

This objection is not valid; for, having set aside the *vṛddhi* [prescribed] by the rule "aco ñṇiti," the *guṇa* [substitution] applies because it is subsequent, followed by the replacement of *r* (*raparatva*), and subsequently the *vṛddhi* prescribed by "ṭhata upadhāyāḥ" takes effect, so that the *guṇa* remains constant and cannot be removed. [The phrase] "because of the mention of *upadeśa*" means: by the force of that [mention], in the *upadeśa*...

The point is this: by applying the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), one takes the vowel *a* that exists at the end of the root *mṛ*, and based on that, the *ciṇ-vat* augment *iṭ* is applied even after the causative (*ṇic*) in forms such as *smārita*. [Objection:
But if this were so, forms such as *smārita* would not be established, because the vowel *a* in the word *smā* is not the vowel *a* that occurs in the original enunciation (*upadeśa*).

If it is argued that [the rule] does not apply because the suffix lacks that as its final element, and that according to the interpretation "for those ending in *ac* (vowels) in the original instruction (*upadeśa*)," it would not apply to a form ending in *ṇi*, [we reply: True. For this very reason, out of dissatisfaction, it is stated in the *Manoramā*: "Or let it be that which ends in *ac* in the original instruction..."
The word "tasya" (of that) is an explanation [of the term *aṅga*]. The genitive case in "aṅgasya" (of the stem) is a non-co-referential (*vyadhikaraṇa*) genitive;

its meaning is "of that which has an *a*-vowel as the final element of a stem-part. And thus, even in the case of a causative form (*ṇijanta*), such as *śāmita*, the *ciṇvad-iṭ* augment is established, because by the principle of "acting like the original" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it is treated as if it were the causative suffix itself.

Because it is accepted that the *aṅga* consists of the causative (*ṇijanta*) form, including its constituent parts, such as *śāmīya*, [the forms] *āritā* and *smāritā* etc. are also established. This is because the verbal roots *ṛ* and *smṛ* are vowel-ending (*ajanta*) in their original instruction (*upadeśa*), and thus the *aṅga* consisting of those parts becomes *ār* and *smār*.
Regarding the phrase "due to the continued application of the mention of 'nitya'," this is from the rule *ityaṃ chandasi*.

However, in the *Kāśikā*, it is stated that because the augment *suṭ*—which is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*)—is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), or because the root does not begin with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) when the augment is not part of the stem (*abhakta*), the condition for the stem (*aṅga*) does not exist; therefore, the *guṇa* substitution does not apply here.
The suffix *ka* prescribed by the rule "before *utka*" is a part of the primary word (*prātipadika-bhakta*), not a part of a subordinate element (*aṅga-bhakta*);

therefore, because it is not a part of a subordinate element, the intention of the rule "because of the absence of connection" (*asaṃyogāt*) is that [the suffix] is indeed a subordinate element (*aṅga*).
(Pāṇini 6.4.44: *tanoter yaki*).

Regarding the suffix *yaK*: from the sūtra "ṭhviḍvanoḥ" [Pāṇini 3.1.63], the word "āt" [from 3.1.62] is understood, and from "ye vibhāṣā" [3.1.64], the word "vibhāṣā" is also understood. What is the purpose of [specifying] *yaK*? [Consider: *taṃtanyate*. (480) [The rule] "tapo’nutāpe ca" [Pāṇini 3.1.65].

By the word *tapaḥ* [in the rule], the phrase *karmakartari* ("when the object is the agent") is drawn over from the rule *ṭhacaḥ karmakartari*. He indicates that this is an example for the object (*karman*) by stating, "the meaning is 'struck'. He further states that this is also an example for the abstract state (*bhāva*), saying "by sin" (*pāpena*).

Regarding the word *puṃsā*: the meaning is that having performed an action without reflection, he later repented. However, regarding the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*), he will provide an example in its specific grammatical derivation.
(Pāṇini 7.3.33): *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*.
The term "ñṇiti" is understood from the rule "āto yuk-ṭhaco ñṇiti.

This qualifies the *kṛt* suffix, not the *ciṇ* suffix, because the *ciṇ* suffix is never anything other than *ṇit*. What is the purpose of specifying both *ciṇ* and *kṛt*? [Consider] *cauḍiḥ* and *bālākiḥ*; here, the suffix *iñ* is applied because they belong to the *bāhv-ādi* group. [Consider also] *dadau*. Why specify "ñṇiti"? [To exclude cases where the suffix is not *ṇit*.]

In *pānīyam*, *dānīyam*, and *adāyiṣātām*, because the *ciṇvad-iṭ* (the augment *iṭ* as if it were *ciṇ*) applies by virtue of being subsequent [to the rule], it subverts the rule *“thādhvor ic ca”*; consequently, the substitution of *ī* by the rule *“hmuṇāstheḥ”* does not occur, because [the stem] begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). The rule *“thādhvor ic ca”* also...

"It occurs again, because it begins with a non-jhal letter," so they say. Their intention is as follows: from the rule *iko jhaL* (Pāṇini 1.2.9), the term *jhaL* is understood by anuvṛtti. Thus, only a *sic* that begins with a *jhaL* letter is *kit*, but this *sic* does not begin with an *it* vowel. And in this way, since [the *it* property] is taught as being conditioned by that [being *kit*], the *it* designation does not apply here either.
It occurs as *bhavati*. In reality, however, even if that [suffix] were present, there would be no harm here;

for even though the suffix *sic* is *kit*, the prohibition does not apply to [vṛddhi] characterized by *niṅ*, since the form is established by the vṛddhi prescribed by the rule "aco ñṇiti. It is in the *āśīr-liṅ* (optative), and not in the *luṅ* (aorist), because in the latter case there would be the application of *ciṇ-vat* behavior.

The sense is that because the substitution *vadh* [for *han*] is also optional by the rule "in the *ātmanepada*, *anyatarasyām*," the principle of *yena nāprāpta* (where a rule applies even when another would have applied) does not hold. [This refers to the discussion regarding] "the *sīyuṭ* augment in the *ārddhadhātuka*," etc.;
for although in the rule "for *han*, *vadha* in the *liṅ*" (*hano vadha liṅi*), there is also the governing heading of *ārddhadhātuka*, [it is still considered an *ārddhadhātuka* context].

The form *liṅi* is also common [to both], yet the meaning is that while the word *liṅi* applies to both [types of *liṅ*], the augment *sīyuṭ* is prescribed specifically for the *ātmanepada* alone. Regarding *ahasātām*:

in the absence of the *ciṇvad-iṭ*, because of the rule *hanaḥ sic* (Pāṇini 1.2.14), the suffix is marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*), and by the rule *anudātopadeśa-* (Pāṇini 6.4.37) [the nasal is dropped].

There is the elision of the nasal (anunāsika-lopa). Fearing that, because the substitution of *vadh* is seen in the case of *ciṇ*, it might apply by virtue of the *ciṇvad-bhāva* rule to the suffixes beginning with *sya*, he refutes this with the words "not so" (*na ca*) and so forth. Regarding *adarśiṣātām*: since the suffix *ksa* is prohibited by the rule "a dṛśaḥ," here the augment *iṭ* applies to the *sic* suffix as if it were *ciṇ*.

“Because *sic* has the *kit* designation” refers to the rule *iṅgicāvātmanepadeṣu*. “The substitution of *l* for *r*” refers to the rule *aci vibhāṣā*. When the *r* of *girati* is replaced by *l*, there are six forms. “The substitution of *ḍh* for *ṣ*” refers to the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ*.
When *ḍh* is substituted for the six [forms], there are twelve. “And the three instances of doubling” refers to the rule *anaci ca*.

Among the twelve [consonants], there are six instances of doubling for *ḍha* and six for *dha*, making twenty-four (24). In the alternative view where the fifth case (*aya*) and the sixth case (*ṭhyaṇ*) are applied, there are forty-eight (48) instances of doubling for *va*. When the doubling of *ma* occurs according to the rule *anaci ca*, there are ninety-six (96).

Regarding the word *ḍhavamāna*: when there is doubling by the rule *ṭhaco rahābhyām*, there are two (2). When there is doubling of the *v* in both instances by the rule *yaṇo mayaḥ*, there are four (4). When there is doubling of the *m* in all four instances by the rule *anaci ca*, there are eight (8).

(482) After the causative suffix *ṇic* and after a root ending in *muc*, a long vowel may optionally be substituted [for the penultimate short vowel] before the suffixes having the marker *k*. 6.4.93.

In the case of *ciṇṇamuloḥ*, in forms such as *śāmita*, although a short vowel would necessarily replace the penultimate (*upadhā*) by virtue of its being designated as *mit* (by the rule *ani-jṛ-ṣityādinā*), this [rule] provides an option for a long vowel. Regarding the phrase "after a causative suffix (*ṇi*) in the context of *ṇic*": the intention is that there is an intervention caused by the status of the elision of the *ṇi* as *sthānivadbhāva*.
The long vowel is established; the meaning is that this is because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini 8.2.39] stating "not at the end of a word. Now, one might object:

since the absence of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) when a long vowel situated in the third quarter [of the Aṣṭādhyāyī] is to be applied is already established by the rule "that which is not yet established is as if non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), there would be no utility for the explicit mention of "long" (*dīrgha*). Nevertheless, in the case of a causative suffix (*ṇic*) following a root ending in a *ṇi*-suffix...

Regarding the statement "‘iṇṇamula’—the mention of ‘dīrgha’ (long vowel) is necessary to prevent the application of *sthānivadbhāva* when a long vowel ought to be applied," he says: "The reference is to the genus (*jāti*). The intention is that this [genus-based reference] need not be; for the desired result is established even by means of the optional short vowel (*hrasva-vikalpa*). However, in reality...
In the rule *ciṇṇamuloḥ*, the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) must indeed be made. For instance:

the root *heḍ* (meaning "disrespect") belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group. When the shortening prescribed for roots marked with the indicator *mit* is to be applied, *eC* is replaced by *iK*. Thus, *heḍayati*.
Here, if the shortening were optionally applied even when *ciṇ* and *namul* suffixes follow, the forms would have to be *ahiḍi* and *aheḍi*.
But when there is lengthening, it becomes *ahiḍi* or *ahīḍī*; this is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on this very sūtra.

Regarding *śaṃśāmita* and so forth: in the case of *ciṇ*, [we have] *aśaṃśami*; in the case of *aś*, *aśaṃśāmi*. In the case of *ṇamul*, one should observe forms such as *śaṃśamaṃ–śaṃśamaṃ* and *śaṃśāmaṃ–śaṃśāmam*, and so on. [The statement] "there is no lengthening" refers to the elision (*al-lopa*) of the *yaṅ* suffix.

The sense is that, because [the root] is treated as if it were in its original state (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is an absence of the condition of being followed by *ṇic*; consequently, neither the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*) nor the strengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāvṛddhi*) applies.
Thus, since there would be a difference in the resulting form (*phalabheda*), the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) of the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is not tenable. [For example: *śamyate*.

Regarding "muninā": because the root is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the *la*-suffix occurs in the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*). (Pāṇini 7.3.34): "Not for a root taught with an udātta vowel that ends in *m*, except for *ācam*. [The rule applies] when a *kṛt*-suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ* follows: *śamaḥ* (from *śam*), *damaḥ* (from *dam*). [This refers to the suffixes] *ghañ* and *ṇi*.

*Śamakaḥ*, *damakaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṇvul*. Why is it said "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*)? [Consider] *śamī*, *damī*. Here, if the suffix *ghinuṇ* were applied, because there would be no acute accent (*udāttatva*) due to the excluded accent (*varjyamānasvara*), the prohibition [of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*] would not apply. If one asks, "How then is the usage of Śrīharṣa, 'When Hari’s foot alone ascended the sky' (*hareryadakrāmi padaikakena kham*) to be explained?"—on this point they say:

When the causative suffix (ṇic) is elided after a root whose causative function has ceased, the *ciṇ* suffix should be understood as applying to the original (prākṛta) meaning. Consequently, because the *ṇic* has not been applied, there is no prohibition against the *vṛddhi* vowel substitution. Furthermore, the shortening prescribed by the rule "after [a root] marked with *it*" does not occur here; this is because the word "optionally" (*vā*) is carried over from the rule "optionally in the sense of becoming discolored" (*vā citavirāge*), and one must rely on the principle of restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

Because it has already been stated regarding [the word] *ghaṭa* and others; furthermore, there is no harm even if [the vowel] is short, because of the optional lengthening prescribed by the rule *iṇṇamuloḥ*. How then is the usage *aḍa udyame* and *yama uparame* possible? It should be understood that there is an absence of *vṛddhi* because a rule based on a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). Alternatively—

The words *udyama* and *uparama* are to be understood as being formed by the suffix *ka* in the sense of the affix *ghañ*. The same applies to forms derived from the causative (*ṇiC*) and the denominative (*ṇiṄ*). The point is that whether the form is derived from a denominative ending in *ṇiṄ* or from a causative ending in *ṇiC*, the resulting form is identical once the *ṇi* is elided by the rule *ṇer aniṭi*.

(484) *vibhāṣā ciṇṇamuloḥ* |7|1|69|. The term *vibhāṣā* [is understood]. From the rule *abheśca*, the word *labheḥ* continues [to apply here]. Regarding the suffix *ṇamul*: *labhaṃlabham* or *lābhaṃlābham*. But for prefixes such as *pra-* etc., it is only *pralambhaṃpralambham*. Now, those who...

Regarding those [verbs] that take two objects (*dvikarmaka*), there arises a doubt as to whether the affixes *la*, *kṛt*, *kt*, and those having the sense of *khal* apply to the primary object (*mukhya-karman*), or to the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*), or to both. To establish the rule, he says: "But of those that take two objects... and "of *duh* etc."—these are the twelve [roots] mentioned in the first half of the verse beginning with *duh-āc-pac*.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "the *l*-suffixes and others are considered to occur after roots such as *duh* (to milk) when the object is secondary (*gauṇa*). That which receives the designation of "object" (*karma-saṃjñā*) by the rule *a-kathitaṃ ca* is the secondary [object]. Regarding those transitive roots (*dvikarmaka*) that are mentioned in the rule *ati-buddhi-pūjārtha-śabdakarma-akarmakāṇām aṇi kartā sa ṇau*, he states the restriction: "that [object] is secondary. He says "prayojya" (the one to be impelled) with reference to the non-causative state (*aṇi*).
That whose agent (*kartṛ*) is designated as the *karman* [by rule P. 1.4.52] is the *prayojyakarman* (the indirect object). Regarding the phrase "of others":

this refers to roots meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*), intransitive roots (*akarmaka*), and the roots *hṛ* and *kṛ*. Regarding the phrase "beginning with *la*" (*lādayaḥ*): by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the *kṛtya*, *kta*, *ktavatu*, and *khal-artha* suffixes are to be understood. In the example "The cow is milked," [the agent is indicated] by the word "Devadatta."

The remainder [is as follows]: with respect to the kṛtya suffixes and others, examples include: *gaur dogdhavyā* (the cow is to be milked), *payaḥ dohanīyā* (milk is to be milked); *gauḥ sudohā* (the cow is easy to milk) or *durdohā* (difficult to milk) regarding the milk; *ajā grāmaṃ netavyā* (the goat is to be led to the village), *nayanīyā*, *haratvayā*, *haraṇīyā*; *ajā grāmaṃ neyā*—such examples are to be cited. Also: *grāmaṃ gamyate* (it is gone to the village).
The word "by Yajñadatta" is to be supplied as an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). "Māṇavaka" (the boy) is the prompted agent (*prayojya-kartṛ*).
"By Devadatta" is the prompter (*prayojaka*), which must likewise be supplied.
Thus ends the section on the formation of verbal nouns and passive voices (*bhāvakarmaprakriyā*) in the *Tattvabodhinī*.

(1351) *tena tulyaṃ kriyā ced batiḥ* | 5|1|115 | "Equal to that" (*tena tulyam*), if the action is the same, the suffix *bati* is used. The word "equal" (*tulyam*) is neuter in its general sense. After a word ending in the third case, the suffix *bati* occurs in the sense of "equal to that," provided that what is equal is the action. [Example: *brāhmaṇena*.

Regarding the term "equal": if it is objected that the meaning of the sentence here—"the study performed by a kṣatriya and others proceeds in the same manner as that performed by a brāhmaṇa"—is incoherent, they reply:
the word *brāhmaṇa* functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote the study performed by [any] agent.
There is no fault whatsoever in [interpreting] the sentence-meaning as "a study similar to that performed by a Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding the phrase "similar to a quality" (guṇatulye), this is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa); its meaning is "similar to a non-action" (akriyātulya).
And thus, in the sense of "the Kṣatriya is similar to the Brāhmaṇa," one says "the Kṣatriya is like the Brāhmaṇa" (brāhmaṇavat kṣatriyaḥ).
This usage is indeed incorrect. For this very reason,

regarding the sentence "The mountain possesses fire like a kitchen," since the suffix *vat* is considered incorrect when it means "the mountain is similar to a kitchen," one says "The mountain ought to possess fire like a kitchen" (*arvato vahnimān bhavitumarhati*) and so forth, in order to preserve the correctness of that *vat* suffix.
The elders employ the term *kriyāpada* [in this context]. (1352) *tatra tasyeva* 5.1.116.
*tatra tasyeva*: A suffix is applied in the sense of "like" (*iva*) after a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*) or the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). [The word] *kriyā*...
Since the word *cet* does not recur here, the suffix *vat* occurs in the sense of similarity with respect to substance (*dravya*) and so forth. For example:
*mathurāvat srughne*. This means that the wall in Srughna is similar to the wall in Mathurā; that is, it is like the wall found in Mathurā.

(1353) *tadarham* |5|1|117|. *Tadarham* means "deserving that. [The suffix] *ah* is added in the sense of "he deserves" (*arhati*), by the rule *pacādyac*. Although one might expect the genitive case in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix, some maintain that here there is a Vedic-style transposition of cases (*vibhaktivyatyaya*) as prescribed by Pāṇini’s sūtras.

This [sūtra] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the non-obligatory nature of the genitive case prescribed by the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). Consequently, the usage by Bhāravi, *hāyairāmodamuttamam*, is justified;

this we have explained in our commentary on the *Kārakaprakaraṇa*. To clarify that the suffix is added only after a word ending in the accusative case, [the author] uses a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*).

He grasps [the meaning]: "it deserves the injunction. If it is asked, "How then [is this so] in the case of *ato yathāvadvihitādhvarāya*, since there is an impossibility of the status of object (*karmatva*) for that which has no referent in reality (*asatvārthaka*), and thus there is an absence of the second case ending?"—to this they say: in the domain of *vṛtti* (compound formation), the word *yathā*...
It serves the purpose of sentient beings (*satvārthaka*), because suffixes such as *tva* and *tal* are observed in expressions like *athātva* and *yathātva*;
otherwise, since even the genitive case would not exist [in that context], the suffixes *tva* and *tal* would not occur.
Thus, from the word *yaśas*, ending in the accusative case, the suffix *vati* is applied in the sense of "deserving" (*arha*), meaning "one who deserves fitness."
The phrase "vidhānam" implies that the connection with purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is also easily established.
(1354) *Tasya bhāvas tvatalau* (Pāṇini 5.1.119):

"The suffixes *tva* and *tal* [are used] to denote the state (*bhāva*) of that. Regarding the word "prakṛti": it does not refer to just any property (*dharma*), as in the case of *ghaṭatvam* ("the nature of a jar").

Because [categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and earthness (*pṛthivītva*) do not appear [in cognition].
