Regarding the expression "the state of a cow" (*go-bhāva*), there are two alternatives: here, the word "cow" (*go*) either refers to the object (*artha*) or it refers to the phonetic form of the word itself (*śabda-svarūpa*). When it refers to the object, the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya-artha*) is a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*), and that [property] appears precisely as a property (*dharmatvena*). As for the statement beginning with "produced from the base" (*prakṛti-janya*), etc., [it follows accordingly].

The adjunct (*upādhi*) is the application (*prayoga*). However, when [the word] refers to the verbal form (*śabda*), then the mode of the cognition produced by it is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*); and that is indeed a specific property (*dharma*).
In the case of "denotative-ness" (*vācakatva*), however, the mode is the relation consisting of agency (*kartṛtva*). In the case of "being denoted" (*vācyamānatva*), however...

The relation [expressed] is that of the nature of an object (*karmatva*). Similarly, in the case of *aupagavatvam*, the relation is that of being produced (*janyatva*), which serves as the qualifier (*prakāra*). In the case of *rājapuruṣatvam*, however, it is a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*); such cases are to be understood accordingly. This being the case, as for what was stated in the commentary of Hari: "The expression of the relation [occurs] after primary derivatives (*taddhita*) and compounds (*samāsa*)."

Regarding the phrase "by means of an abstract suffix" (*bhāvapratyayena*): in that case, no new, distinct power (*śakti*) need be postulated, because it is established there as well by the very method already stated; this is the summary. (1355) *Ā ca tvāt* | Pāṇini 5.1.120.

"With the exceptions" means by rules such as *ṛtvādibhya imanij vā*. "The word 'ca' (and)" is used because otherwise the suffixes *tva* and *tal* would not apply after the words *strī* and *puṃs*; the sense is that those two [suffixes] would have no scope elsewhere. In the examples *pausnam* and *puṃstvam*, there is the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*).

By the rule "umaḥ khayi," *r* is substituted [for *m*]. Optionally, either the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) or the *anusvāra* occurs. When the *visarga* has been applied, *s* is substituted [by the following rule].

[The suffix *tva* is applied] after a Tatpuruṣa compound beginning with the negative particle *nañ*, except for those ending in *catura*, *saṅgata*, *lavaṇa*, *vaṭa*, *yudha*, *katara*, *sala*, and *seba*.

[Example: *apatitvam* ("the state of not having fallen"). Here, the suffix *ya* does not occur because of the rule "after *ati* and others. [Another example: *apaṭutvam* ("the state of not being clever"). But here...

The suffix *aṇ* does not apply after words ending in *ṭhik* when preceded by a light vowel; thus, one says *ācāturyaṃ* and so forth. [In this case], the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because the word belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class.
(1357) *pṛthvādibhya imanij vā* || 5.1.122 || [The suffix] *imanij* is optionally applied after words beginning with *pṛthu*.

Regarding "from *pṛthu* and so forth": it should be understood that in the case of words such as *pṛthu*, *mṛdu*, and others ending in short vowels (*iganta*) where the preceding vowel is light (*laghu*), there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the suffix *aṇ*. In the case of quality-expressing words (*guṇavacana*) such as *caṇḍa* and *khaṇḍa*, there is the suffix *ṣyañ*. In the case of words denoting age (*vayovacana*) such as *bāla* and *stava*, there is the suffix *añ* characterized by that category. However, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are indeed included by the previous rule alone.
In the case of attainment:

(1358) *ra ṛto halāder laghoḥ* | 6|4|161|. [The substitution of] *ra* for *ṛ* occurs when it is preceded by a consonant and is light. Why "preceded by a consonant"? Consider *ṛjiṣṭhaḥ* and *ṛjīyān*. Why "light"? Consider...
*kṛṣṇimā*. However, if one includes *ṛthu*, *mṛdu*, and *bhṛśa* in the list [of words ending in short vowels], then the rule *ṭhhalāder laghoḥ* could be dispensed with.
(1359) *varṇadṛḍhādibhyaḥ ṣyañ ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.123).

[The rule applies] after words denoting color and after *dṛḍha* etc. Although [the suffix] is already established by the fact that these are adjectives (*guṇavacana*), this statement is for the sake of [introducing] the suffix *iman*.
Because of the enumeration [of specific cases] in the rule "after *ṛju*, *mṛdu*, and *bhṛśa*," the substitution of *ra* does not occur here:
one who describes what has been done is called *kṛtayati*. In the case of the denominative suffix *ṇic*, there is the treatment as if it were *iṣṭhan* (the superlative suffix). Thus: *āṬcitīti*.

The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because *brāhmaṇa* and others belong to the *ākṛtigaṇa* (class of words defined by their form). By the rule *ṭhhalasataddhitasya*, there is the elision of *y*. In this way, we have *yāthākāmī*. [Likewise] *dṛḍha*, *vṛḍha*, *parivṛḍha*; *bhṛśa*, *kṛśa*, and so forth. In this regard, there are two *gaṇa*-sūtras: "After the word *vi*, [the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied] to *īrya*, *tala*, *ābha*, *mati*, *manas*, and *śārada*. This means that when the word *vi* precedes these, [the suffix is applied].

The meaning is that the suffix *ṣyañ* occurs immediately after compounds ending in the five [suffixes] beginning with *yāt*. For example: *viyātatvam*, *viyātatā*, *viyātimā*, *vaiyātyam*; *vilābhimā*, *vailābhyam*; *vimatimā*, *vaimatyam*. Because they end in a short vowel (*iganta*), the suffix *aṇ* also applies—thus: *vaimatam*.

*vimanitā* (the state of being dejected), *vaimanasyam* (dejection); *viśāraditā* (the state of being confident), *vaiśāradyam* (confidence). Through the co-occurrence of the suffixes *-tva* and *-tal*, [we have] *vilābhatvam* (the state of non-acquisition). Forms such as *vilābhatā* and others should also be inferred accordingly. [The rule] *amo matimanasoḥ*: when *mati* or *manas* follows immediately after *sama*, [the suffix *a* is applied] to those ending in them.

The meaning is that the suffix *ṣyañ* occurs after the two [words] *sammati* and *sammana*. Thus: *saṃmatitva*, *saṃmatitā*, *saṃmatimā*, and *sāṃmātya*. Because it ends in an *ik* vowel, with the suffix *aṇ*—[we have] *sāṃmatam*.
Likewise: *saṃmanastva*, *saṃmanastā*, *saṃmanimā*, and *sāṃmanasya*.

(1360) Pāṇini 5.1.124: *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ karmaṇi ca*. The suffix *ṣyañ* is understood [from the previous rule]. *Karma* means action (*kriyā*) and duty (*kārya*). Actions such as ritual purity (*śauca*) and the like are accomplished merely by physical effort; sacrifices (*yāga*) and the like are prescribed by the scriptures.
They say that there is a distinction between these two, namely that [the suffix] *kārya* applies.

Regarding the rule *arhato num ca*: Kaiyaṭa states that the word *arhat*, ending in the *śatṛ* suffix by the rule *arhaḥ praśaṃsāyām*, denotes the sense of "worthy of worship. [The list] is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.

For some, however, the reading is for the sake of another purpose. For instance, the reading [of *anyabhāva*] is for the sake of the *num* augment in the rule "ṭharhato num ca. The readings of *ekabhāva*, *tribhāva*, and *anyabhāva* are intended to establish these as their own respective meanings (*svārthe*).
Accordingly, there is the use of a Vārttika in the *Pratyāhārāhnika*: "ānyabhāvyaṃ..."
"But because of the exclusion by the word *kāla*. *Ānyabhāvya* means simply *anyabhāva*;
that is to say, "otherness. As for what was stated by Bhaṭṭapāda in the section on grammar (*vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa*)—namely, "incorrect usage is *ānyabhāvya*"—that refers to the non-grammarian.
It should be noted that this is for the satisfaction of the Mīmāṃsakas. Regarding the term *sarvaveda*: it is a compound formed by the rule “*pūrvakālaika-” (Pāṇini 2.1.49).

Regarding *caturveda*: there is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) of the application of the suffixes to words such as *caturvarṇa* in their own primary sense (*svārtha*). It is used in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

The *dvigu* compound [is formed]. In the case of *caturvidya*, the suffix *aṇ* is elided by the rule "after *vi*, *go*, *su*, and *gana*, when not meaning 'offspring'" (*vigorsuganapatye*). In the case of *caturvidya*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule "after words ending in *vidyā*, *lakṣaṇa*, and *sūtra*" (*vidyālakṣaṇasūtrāntāt*), and that suffix is elided. (1361) *Stenād yan nalopaś ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.125). [This sūtra prescribes] the suffix *yan* after the word *stena*, and there is also the elision of the final *n*.

Regarding the phrase "the mention of a composite whole" (*saṅghātagrahaṇam*): the point is that if there were a mention of individual phonemes (*varṇagrahaṇa*), then when the *akāra* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the desired form would not be established; for, due to the status of the elision as a *sthānivat* by the rule *acaḥ parasmin*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the substitution of *ay*. Now, [one might object]:...

If it is argued that even when a composite (saṅghāta) is intended to be grasped, by the rule *ṭhalo’ntyasya*, only the letter *a* would be elided and not the composite itself—this is not so. For that [result] is established either by the force of the original formulation [of the rule] or by the prohibition: "When [an operation] is meaningless, the rule applies to the final [element]."

(1362) *kapi-jñātyor ḍhak* | 5|1|127|. Regarding *kapi* and *jñāti*: here, although there are two [words], *kapi* and *jñāti*, and there are also two meanings, namely *bhāva* (state/abstract quality) and *karman* (action/object), the application of the suffixes does not follow their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*), because it is declared that they are not *svarita*. Thus...
This should also be understood in the case of the rules "atyantapurohitādibhyaṣṭha" and "vanditamanojñādibhyaḥ.

Regarding the phrase "because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇādi* group": although the word *rājan* is listed in the *brāhmaṇādi* group as a standalone item, this very prohibition [by the rule] "ṭhas-e" indicates that there is indeed a suffix *ṭhak* in this section.

"By the word *rājan*, the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) applies. Thus, since the inclusion of *brāhmaṇa* and so forth in the list [of *brāhmaṇādi*] finds its purpose in compounds, in non-compounds only the suffix *yañ* prescribed as a specific rule occurs. Others, however, maintain that because the *brāhmaṇādi* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the suffix *ṣyañ* is already established after a compound ending in those words.

The inclusion of the word *rājan* there is for the purpose of its co-occurrence with the suffix *yak*. Accordingly, it is stated in the Śābara-bhāṣya on the section concerning the *Āveṣṭi* sacrifice: "The duty (*karma*) of a king (*rājan*) is *rājya*;
[the suffix] *ṣyañ* is applied because it belongs to the class beginning with *brāhmaṇa*. [Examples include: *purohita*, *saṅgrāmika*, *pathika*.

"Sārathika" and so forth refer to the family of priests such as the *purohita*. (1363) Pāṇini 5.1.129: *prāṇabhṛjjātī-vayo-va-canod-gātrādibhyo ’ñ*. "Prāṇabhṛt" means a living being. *Prāṇa* is the air moving through the mouth and nose. [The suffix applies] after words denoting a class of living beings (*jāti*), age (*vayas*), voice (*vacana*), and *udgātṛ*, etc. [The suffix *añ* is applied] specifically after words ending in *prāṇin*.

[The word] *suvaca* [is an example]. Why [mention] *prāṇabhṛt*? [Consider] *tṛṇatva*, *tṛṇatā*. Why [mention] *jāti*? [Consider] *devadattatva*. Regarding *audgātra*: since the suffix *cha* would apply by the rule "after the words for officiating priests, including *udgātṛ*, the suffix *cha* is used," the suffix *añ* is here prescribed.

Regarding *suṣṭhu* and *duṣṭhu*: when the suffix *ṣyañ* is applicable by virtue of the two [words] being characterized as *guṇavacana* (expressing a quality), the suffix *aṇ* is applicable by virtue of the word *vadhū* ending in a vowel, and the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are applicable to the remaining words. However, here it is stated that "in the context of a mantra, [the form] *subhagaṃ* is used. This word-form *subhagam* occurs in the domain of mantras.

The meaning is that one produces [the suffix] *añ* in application. Regarding the phrase “for unimpaired good fortune” (*ahate saubhagāya*): because all rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandas*), the rule "after *hṛd*, *bhaga*, and *sindhu*, there is vṛddhi of the final syllable of the second member" does not apply here.
For this very reason, even in mantras, the suffix *añ* is sometimes absent. [Thus: “her good fortune” (*aubhāgyam asyai*).
Having given [the suffix] *ṣyañ* here;
(1364) *hāyanāntayuvādibhyo’ṇ* | Pāṇini 5.1.130. Regarding words ending in *hāyana*, since *tva* and *tal* would otherwise apply, the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed. From the words *yuvan* and *sthavira*—

When the suffix *añ* is applicable by virtue of the characteristic of expressing age—as in *yauvanam*—the stem remains unchanged (*prakṛtibhāva*) because of the rule *ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 6.4.153) following an *aṇ*. Furthermore, because *manojña* and others are included in the list [of words taking *vañ*], the suffix *vañ* also applies, resulting in *yauvanakam*. In the case of the suffix *aka*, the stem remains unchanged according to the rule: “In the case of *aka*, the forms *rājanya*, *manuṣya*, and *yuvan* remain as they are. (Pāṇini 6.4.175).

Regarding the rule *śrotriyasya yalopaśca*: as for the term *śrotriyasya*, when it is explained according to the Vedic derivation in the rule *śrotriyaṃśchando’dhīte*—where *śrotra* becomes *śrotriya* and the suffix *ghañ* is added—then here [in our present rule] the elision of the *y* is taken exactly as heard (*yathāśrutam*). However, when one follows the principle that "a word may express the meaning of a sentence," [it is understood differently].
In that case, by the word *gha*, the form *iya* is indicated. In some places, however, the reading is *ṭhyalopaśca*;

there, it should be explained as a reference to the cluster *ye*. For if it were a reference to a single phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), the substitution of a semi-vowel (*yaṇādeśa*) would apply to the vowel *i*, and not the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*. This is because [otherwise] the elision of the vowel *a* would not occur.

Because, by virtue of being treated as the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*), that which ends in *i* lacks the status of a *bha*-stem; this is clear in Haradatta’s commentary. In the root manuscripts, the primary reading is generally seen as "elision of *y*" (*yalopaḥ*), rather than the reading "elision of *h*" (*halopa*).

(1365) *Igantāccalaghupūrvāt* |5|1|131|. [The suffix *ka* is applied] after a nominal stem ending in an *ik* vowel, provided that the preceding constituent is light (*laghu*). The term "preceding" (*pūrva*) is a qualifier of the nominal stem, referring to that which precedes the final *ik* vowel. This "precedence" is determined solely by immediate proximity. Consequently, the suffix does not apply to the word *atipāṇḍu*.

It would be more appropriately stated as *laghupūrvekaḥ*. This refers to that which has a light vowel (*laghu*) preceding it and is also an *iK* (a short vowel); thus, "having a light vowel preceding it" is *laghupūrveka*. According to the modern grammarians (*navyāḥ*), because this qualifies the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the suffix [tva/tal] is understood to follow such a stem. Why [is the condition] "ending in an *iK*" specified? Consider *ghaṭatvam* (the state of being a jar). Why [is the condition] "having a light vowel preceding it" specified? Consider *pāṇḍutvam* (whiteness). How then is the word *kāvyam* (poetry) formed?
Although the form [kāva] is established by the rule *kudhātoṣṭhorāvaśyake*, the question arises as to whether *kāvam* would be the correct form in the sense of "the work of a poet" (*kaveḥ karma*).

(1366) *yopadhādgurūpotamādvuñ* || 5.1.132 || [The suffix] *vuñ* is applied after a word ending in *ya*, having a heavy penultimate syllable (*gurūpotama*), [provided it denotes a genus]. || 5.1.132 ||
"From that which has *y* as its penultimate letter": this means from that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) whose penultimate (*upotama*) [letter] is heavy (*guru*).
Why "from that which has *y* as its penultimate letter"? [Consider] *vimānatvam*. Why "from that whose penultimate is heavy"?
[Consider] *kṣatriyatvam*. [The example] *ābhidhānīyakam*: here, the base is *abhyaḥ*.
The root *dadhāti* ends in the suffix *anīyar*. The meaning is "the state or the action of one who is to be approached.
Or, [it means] "from an associate. Regarding the phrase "or from an associate": although [the suffix] is obligatory by rule, this statement is for the purpose of making it optional.
[The suffix applies] after *dvandva* and *manojñādi* groups. *Manojña*, *priyarūpa*, *bahula*, *avaśya*.

The [group] beginning with *manojña* and so forth is as follows: (1367) *gotracaraṇācchalāghātyākāratadaveteṣu* |5|1|134|. From *gotra* and *caraṇa*: the suffix *vuñ* is added after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) denoting lineage (*gotra*) and school (*caraṇa*), when expressing praise (*ślāghā*), censure (*atyākāra*), or being one who has mastered that [subject] (*tadavedin*). From a nominal stem denoting lineage or a school... [the suffix *vuñ*].
It may occur in the sense of the agent or the object. Since the section on offspring (*apatya*) has concluded, "lineage" (*gotra*) here refers to the worldly lineage;

thus, the meaning is "from those ending in suffixes denoting offspring. Others say it refers to those recited in the *Pravarādhyāya*. Because of the rule "a lineage (*gotra*) together with the Vedic schools (*caraṇas*"), it possesses the nature of a genus (*jāti*).

This statement is made because [the suffix] *añ* would otherwise apply by the rule beginning with *rājabhr̥j-jātī*. Regarding *rślāghādi*: the meaning is "when *ślāgh* and the others function as the objects. Regarding "it is obtained": this is because the root *iṇ* has the sense of "obtaining" (*prāpti*).
Since the root *iṇ* preceded by *ava-* is well-known in the sense of "knowing," he says: "or he understood."

Regarding the term *gārgadikayā*: there is the elision of *ya* by the rule *apatyasya ca taddhite ’lāti* (Pāṇini 6.4.151). An example for the suffix *vuñ* after a *caraṇa* [Vedic school name] should be understood as *aṭhikayā ślāghate*, and so forth. Why is it said “in connection with *ślāghā* and the like”?
[Consider] *gārgyatvam* and *kaṭhatvam*.
(1368) *hotrābhyaś chaḥ* |5|1|135|. The word *hotrā* [is derived from] the root *hu-* with the suffix *tran*.

Regarding the phrase "it should not be said [that the suffix *cha* is used]": since the suffix *cha* has been prohibited, the suffix *tva* is established by the rule "the suffixes *tva* and *tal* express the state of being (*asya bhāvaḥ*"); furthermore, there is economy of expression (*lāghava*) because the case-ending need not be uttered—this is the intended meaning.
He demonstrates the result of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "from [words denoting] *hotṛ*s" with the words "from a synonym of *brāhmaṇa*."
Thus end the meanings of the *bhāva* (action) and *karman* (object) [affixes] in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
[This concludes] the *Siddhāntakaumudī*, combined with the *Tattvabodhinī*, the *Bālamanoramā*, and the *Śekhara*.
The latter half of that [work] is now presented as *Tattvabodhinī*: "atha tiṅante bhvādayaḥ" (Now, the roots beginning with *bhū* in the section on verbal suffixes).
Though praised by great sages who possess the qualities of Vedic learning, Arhatship, and discernment, the Lord—
who is himself devoid of such attributes— triumphs all the more.
I take refuge in Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who is skilled in destroying ignorance, consecrated in the protection of devotees, the three-eyed one who dwells at the foot of the banyan tree. 1.

He composes the benediction performed at the beginning of the work for the purpose of destroying obstacles, in order to instruct his disciples, starting with the words "Śrautra" and so forth. The state of being a *śrotriya* is *śrautra*.
This is according to the rule: "The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after words ending in *hāyana*, *yuvan*, etc., and there is the elision of the *ya* of *śrotriya*."

When the suffix *aṇ* is applied without the elision of the initial vowel (*vārtika*), there is the elision of the final *i* by the rule *yasyeti ca*. The state of being worthy (*arhat*) is *ārhantī*; according to the rule *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ*, since it is stated that *arhat* takes the augment *num*, both the suffixes *ṣyañ* and *ṅīṣ* are applied. Because of the marker *ṣ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added, and the *y* is elided by the rule *halastaddhitasya*.

"By those two, *vitaiḥ*—meaning by those skilled (*caṇaiḥ*) in the Vedic and Ārhantī [traditions]. By that, *vitaḥ* is formed with the suffix *caṇ*. The meaning is: 'renowned for both Vedic learning (*śrotriya*) and capability. Furthermore, *guṇyaiḥ* means 'possessing qualities' (*guṇavadbhiḥ*).
That is to say, 'endowed with praiseworthy qualities. This is according to the rule: *rūpād āhata-praśaṃsayoḥ*."

Regarding the suffix *iṭ* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), since it is stated that "it is seen after other [roots] as well" (*ṭhanyebhyo ’pi dṛśyate*) and because the example "the *uṇyā* Brāhmaṇas" (*uṇyā brāhmaṇāḥ*) is cited in the *Bhāṣya* and other works; [we have] "every day" (*ahardivam*). This means "day by day" (*ahanyahani*), i.e., "daily.
It is grammatically correct due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) prescribed by the rule beginning with "not in *catur*" (*ṭhacature*). [The word] "being praised" (*toṣṭūyamānaḥ*).

The suffix *śānac* occurs after the root *stu* when followed by the causative marker *ṇic*, in the sense of the object (*karman*). By the rule “*ārdhadhātuke yak*,” the suffix *yak* is added to the verbal root.
By the rule “*āne muk*,” the augment *muk* is inserted. The word *api* indicates an apparent contradiction;
however, in reality, there is no contradiction.

Although the infinite auspicious qualities that serve as the basis for praise are established by the Śruti and Smṛti, they are merely phenomenal (vyāvahārika), like the ether and other elements; therefore, their absence is the ultimate reality (pāramārthika).
This is indeed clear in the Uttara-mīmāṃsā. The Supreme Lord is all-pervading and omnipresent.
"He conquers exceedingly" means "he triumphs completely";

this is the resultant meaning. This is because [the rule] *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ* does not apply here, as [the form *vijayate*] is neither a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*) nor a finite verb (*atiṅanta*). Nor can it be argued that [the suffix *ātmanepada*] applies here by the rule *sahayukte ’pradhāne*, since [the word *saha*] is not present.

It should not be argued that by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule), the word *vi-* would indeed possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when compounded with an *atiṅanta* (non-finite) word; for this would contradict the text of that very [sūtra], which states, "and [the suffix] *a* occurs only in the Vedic language. Furthermore, if the status of a nominal stem were admitted, the case-ending *su* would have to arise.

By accepting that the *liṅga* (gender) is a universal (*sarvanāman*), because it is neuter, even when the *su*-suffix is elided, the shortening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule "the vowel is shortened in the neuter" (*hrasvo napuṃsake*) would be unavoidable. Furthermore, although the constituent part "ayate" within the whole is a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), because it is semantically dependent [on another word], there is no syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*); therefore, [the rule] could not apply from that [part] either.

If it is argued that [the suffix *tarap*] is not applicable because "a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*) applies only when there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*)," they reply as follows: The suffix *tarap* arises precisely from the root *ji* (to conquer) which is contained within the compound. Since this [root] has a mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) with the word *vi*, its lack of semantic competency should not be suspected. This is because the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is the primary element.

Because there is no fault even in the case of mutual expectancy, and since a prefix functions as a mere indicator (dyotaka), it has no independent meaning at all; thus, it is impossible to assert that there is any state of expectancy.
The suffixes occurring in the fourth and fifth chapters have been explained in the first half [of this work]; now, those pertaining to the third chapter are being explained. (2)

Having first provided an account [of what has passed], he states what is about to follow with the words "in the first half" (*pūrvārddhe*). The intention is that the derivation of *kvip* and other suffixes—such as in the rules "after the root *pṛś* when not meaning water, *kvip* is added," "for *ṛtvij*, *dadhṛk*, etc.," and "in the case of *yat* and so forth"—is merely incidental (*prāsaṅgika*) to the discussion of roots ending in consonants. The word *turyaḥ* means "the fourth."

Because it has been stated that [the suffix] *turaśchayatāv* involves the elision of the first vowel; as for the word "atha" (now): here too, the derivations such as "ṇacaḥ striyāmañ" and "aṇinuṇaḥ" should be understood as incidental (*prāsaṅgika*), whereas primarily those belonging to the third chapter are what are being discussed here.
This is the intended meaning. Relying on the distinction based on the difference in their grammatical suffixes (anubandha), he says: "the ten *lakāras*.

Regarding the phrase "they are shown": although the forms of the fifth *lakāra* are not being derived now, nevertheless the *lakāra* itself is shown by its own form [in the rule]: "The suffix *aḥ* is used after transitive verbs in the sense of the object and the passive, and after intransitive verbs."
The intention is to demonstrate that [the suffix] is the object of the rule beginning with "asya" (Pāṇini 3.4.79). Regarding the term "fifth":

it means the *leṭ* suffix. It should be understood that the *leṭ* is the fifth in consideration of the sequence stated by the author himself (*laṭ*, *liṭ*, etc.), and not according to the order mentioned in the Sūtra.

(1) *vartamāne laṭ* | 3|2|123|. Regarding *vartamāne laṭ*: he states that "the present" (*vartamāna*) is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), saying: "of a root denoting a present action. The word "root" (*dhātu*) [is mentioned] because of the rule [Pāṇini 3.1.91].

The meaning is that [the discussion] is being introduced up to the end of the third chapter. As for the statement "the present tense (laṭ) should occur," its status as a denoted meaning will become clear immediately below. However, the present time is not denoted by it;
rather, it is merely indicated (dyotya). Likewise, in the case of the imperfect (laṅ) and other tenses, past time and so forth are indicated according to their respective cases.

This is how it should be understood. In reality, however, the acceptance of its being directly denotable (vācyatva) is also easily established, as we shall explain in the sūtra concerning injunctions (vidhi) and so forth. Regarding the statement "aṭ and āv are indicatory letters" (itau), it was not stated that "the letter ṭ is for the sake of pronunciation," because it must necessarily be stated in order to bring about a distinction from [suffixes] such as liṅ.

(2) *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* |3|4|69|. *L:* [The suffixes] *la* [are used] in the sense of the object (*karman*) and [the agent (*kartṛ*)]; by the word "and" (*ca*), the term "agent" (*kartari*) is drawn over from the preceding rule *kartari ka*. This [rule] concerns the domain of transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*). In the case of intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*), the portion [of the rule] stating "in the sense of the object" is set aside.
And because a specific rule is provided there by the subsequent statement, "and in the sense of the abstract state" (*bhāve ca*). He states this very point:

"from transitive roots" (*sakarmakebhyaḥ*) and "in the sense of the abstract state" (*bhāve ca*). By the word "and" (*ca*), only the agent (*kartṛ*) is drawn forward [from the previous sūtra], but not the object (*karman*), because that is impossible. Thus he says: "in the sense of the abstract state and in the sense of the agent" (*bhāve kartari ca*). But surely...

Since the *ātmanepada* endings are prescribed for the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), and since the *parasmaipada* endings are prescribed by the rule "after [roots ending in] *eṣ*, the agent" (*eṣātkartari*), the meanings of the *lakāra*s—the action, the object, and the agent—can be inferred; so what is the purpose of this sūtra? Do not say so. For if this sūtra did not exist...

Since *lakāra*s would also arise in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) even from transitive verbs—just as they do with suffixes such as *ghañ*—an undesirable usage such as "the killing is performed by Devadatta" (*haṭṃa kriyate devadattena*) would result; it is for the sake of preventing this that the present sūtra is necessary. And it is not the case that...

It might be argued that the rule should simply be formulated as *ṭhakarmakebhyo bhāve laḥ* (“after intransitive roots, the suffix *la* occurs in the sense of the abstract action”), and that this is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) meaning “the suffix *la* occurs in the sense of the abstract action only after intransitive roots. However, this would result in the undesirable consequence of a reversed restriction (*viparīta-niyama*), namely that “the suffix *la* occurs in the sense of the abstract action only after intransitive roots,” which would then preclude the occurrence of the *l*-suffixes in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) after those very roots.
Otherwise, the suffix *lakāra* would not apply. Therefore, the word *ca* (and) in the rule *bhāve ca* is necessary.

Nor should it be argued that one could simply say *bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (and in the sense of the abstract state [bhāva], after intransitive roots), because if that were the case, a restriction (*niyama*) would follow—namely, that just as in the sense of the abstract state, so too in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), the suffixes would apply only after intransitive roots—and consequently, [the suffixes] would not apply after transitive roots in the sense of the abstract state.

Furthermore, [if that were the case], the *lakāra* affixes would not even apply in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Now, one might argue: "Even so, let it simply be 'aśca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ' (and *a* occurs after intransitive roots in the sense of the object and the agent); by the force of the particle *ca*, the word 'agent' (*kartari*) is drawn over from the previous rule, and thus the meaning results in: 'the *lakāra* affixes occur after transitive roots in the sense of the agent, and after intransitive roots in the sense of the object and the agent.'"

If it is argued that since [the suffixes] will occur in the sense of the object (*karman*) by virtue of the previously stated indicator (*jñāpaka*), what is the purpose of this [rule] "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*), we say: not so. For in the subsequent sūtra, the mention of "of the two" (*ayoḥ*) is necessary for the sake of referring back to the object as well; therefore, the labor of following the indicator is redundant.
Therefore, the original formulation alone is preferable. On this point, the Naiyāyikas argue:

"The expressive power (*śakti*) of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) resides in the action (*kṛti*) alone due to parsimony (*lāghava*), and not in the agent (*kartṛ*); for there is complexity (*gaurava*) in assigning power to that which possesses the action as its agency. Furthermore, the agent is obtained through the nominative case-ending word, such as 'Devadatta'. [They continue: "Devadatta..."

"For in the case of 'pacati' (he cooks), Devadatta is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), effort (*yatna*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) is the relation (*saṃsarga*). And thus, the verbal cognition—namely, 'Devadatta is the substratum of an effort conducive to cooking' and so forth—is also easily established. This is not correct; for when "pacati" is uttered...

There would arise the expectancy: "In what [locus] does the agent of cooking [act]? or "Of what [object]? Nor should it be suspected that even if one accepts the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) as "the act of cooking has a single agent," the expectancy "Who? remains untenable; for when there is a cognition of the agent in general, the question "Who? [arises].

Because there is no sublation [of the meaning] when there is an expectancy for a specific agent; nor should it be suspected that even when it is stated that "the act of cooking has Devadatta as its agent," an irrepressible expectancy remains as to "in what [substratum] does it exist? or "to whom [does it belong]?";
for the act of cooking is precisely the operation conducive to the softening [of the rice], and [the agent is simply] the locus of that [operation].

Because Devadatta is the agent, once it is determined that he is the substratum of the action, there is no further occurrence of expectancy such as "in what [does he act]? Furthermore, in cases such as "Look at Devadatta eating," "Give to Devadatta who is eating," and "The food of Devadatta who is eating," [the agent is clearly perceived].

Since suffixes such as *śatṛ* and *śānac* are also substitutes for *l* (the *l*-class suffixes), just like *tiP* and others, there would be no distinction between them, and consequently, they too would result in the cognition of mere effort (*kṛti*). Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion, because it has been stated that "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*) is the relation [between the effort and the agent], and thus one would have to accept meanings such as "see Devadatta, who is the substratum of the effort conducive to cooking."

It should not be said that this is due to the absence of defects, because the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between a noun and its meaning through difference contradicts both our own and others' established tenets (*siddhānta*). Nor,

in accordance with the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) regarding the relation of non-difference (*abheda-saṃsarga*) between a noun and its meaning, [is it possible] for the suffixes *śatṛ*, *śānac*, and *ājñī*.

It should not be argued that a disparity is accepted—namely, that the suffixes *ti* and so on denote the agent (*kartṛ*), whereas [the suffix] *kṛt* denotes only the action (*bhāva*)—because "philosophical weightiness" (*prāmāṇika-gaurava*) is not a fault;

for this would entail the abandonment of your own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta*), which states: "The substitute (*ādeśa*) is not the denoter due to its complexity (*gaurava*), but rather the original form (*sthānin*) is the denoter due to its simplicity (*lāghava*)."

Furthermore, this would lead to an inconsistency in your own linguistic practice, such as when you state that in cases like *āmaḥ*, *ñānam*, and *ataraḥ*, once the *s* of the nominative case-ending has been replaced by *visarga*, or by *am*, or by *adaḍ*, the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in the general property of being a *su*-ending (*sutva*) for the sake of brevity, and not in each specific form. And thus:
It is established that the *śatṛ* suffixes and others serve as substitutes for the *lipi* (the written sign), acting merely as reminders, whereas the letter *l* itself is the actual indicator.

Now, if it is accepted that this [letter *l*] denotes the agent (*kartṛ*) when it occurs at the end of a *śatṛ* suffix, how could it convey the sense of "action" (*kṛti*) when occurring at the end of a *tiṅ* suffix? For it is an established principle that "it is unjust for a single word to have multiple meanings."

By logical necessity; however, if one follows the tradition of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) and accepts that in all cases only the substitutes (*ādeśa*) are expressive, then— according to the maxim "all [substitutes] are substitutes for entire words"— there would follow the word-sphoṭa and the sentence-sphoṭa in instances such as *ghaṭam*, *ghaṭena*, *hare’va*, and *viṣṇo’va*.

That it should be established [as such] would be a great undesirable consequence for you. Furthermore, since the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) in the rule *artari kṛt* is itself drawn over (*anukṛṣyate*) by the particle *ca* in the sūtra *aḥ karmaṇi*, how could there be a difference in capacity between the *ṇvul* suffixes and the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*)? Nor is it the case that...

It should be stated that the very acceptance of the relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) and the relation of connection (*saṃsarga*) between the word and its meaning is the reason why the agent is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) in suffixes such as *ṇvul*; for, in accordance with examples such as "Devadatta is one who cooks somewhat like [the act of] cooking" (*pacatirūpaṃ pacatikalpaṃ devadattaḥ*), it is appropriate that even in the case of *tiṅ* suffixes, the agent alone is the expressed meaning. Now, [one might object]: "But [if the agent were the meaning], how would you account for the collective..."

If it is argued that although it is a noun, the *tiṅ* suffix is not a noun, then it is equally true that in the word "pācaka," the element "aka" is not a noun. If it is argued that a noun is that which ends in a letter of the *ak* group, then it is equally true that a noun is that which ends in a *rūpa* (consonant) or a letter of the *ac* group. Consequently, in this case, Devadatta is the agent of the excellent act of cooking.

Since such non-differentiation (abheda-anvaya) must be accepted by you, you must likewise admit that the agent (*kartṛ*) is denoted even in the case of finite verb endings (*tiṅ*). Furthermore, if the denotation of the agent were not admitted,

[the rules] "the middle [person] occurs when co-referential with the second person (*yuṣmad*)" and "the highest [person] occurs when co-referential with the first person (*asmad*)" would be untenable.

How can the grammatical rules regarding person (*puruṣa*) based on grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as well as the rule "when the agent is expressed by a verbal suffix, the third person is used" (*abhihite kartari prathamā*), etc., be consistent with your own position? As for the description of the term *anabhihite* as meaning "that whose number is not expressed," [in the case of] "Devadatta..."

It has been stated that in cases such as "he cooks rice" (*pacaty odanam*) and "rice is cooked by Devadatta" (*odanaḥ pacyate devadattena*), the application of the nominative, accusative, and other case endings is established; however, that is not correct, because the expression of number (*saṅkhyābhidhāna*) is not established in the case of *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compound (*samāsa*) formations. Consequently, [in examples like] "a grain of rice smeared with oil" (*aktaḥ kaṭukaḥ taṇḍulaḥ*) and "an excellent horse" (*atyaḥ*...), [the rules would fail].

In cases such as "a hundred-year-old horse" (*śatiko ’śvaḥ*) or "a village with abundant water" (*prāptodako grāmaḥ*), if the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā* were to apply, the nominative case would not occur. Nor should it be argued that here too there is a prescription of number by supplying the word "is" (*asti*), for [if one were to supply] "is standing" (*sthita*) or similar verbs...

Because of the absence of that [action], in cases such as "This Devadatta is a grammarian (ābdika), not a Naiyāyika," there is no necessity for supplying a verb— as there is in the case of "This is blue, not red"— and thus [the meaning is conveyed] by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). [Regarding the word] *ābdadarduram*...

Alternatively, because the agent number (*kartṛ-saṅkhyā*) is not expressed by the suffix *ṭhak* in the word "karoti," there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the third case ending would arise for the agent Devadatta. Therefore, one must accept the explanation that [the rule applies] when the agent has not been expressed (*anabhihite kartari*), and so forth. Furthermore, the agent is the substratum of the activity (*vyāpāra*) conveyed by the verbal root (*dhātu*).

In that case, the meaning of the *l*-suffixes (*lakāra*) is merely the substratum (*āśrayamātra*), and not the operation (*vyāpāra*) as well, because that [operation] is already obtained by the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself. For this very reason, there is no lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) between the meanings of the base and the suffix in expressions such as "the agent" (*kartā*) or "the factor" (*kāraka*); for if the meaning of the suffix were the substratum of the operation, [such a connection would be impossible].
In that case, the connection of the verbal root (*dhātu*) with its meaning through its own inherent function (*vyāpāra*) would be problematic. However, one might argue:
"The meaning of the verbal root is 'action' (*kṛti*); the suffix (*kṛt-pratyaya*) also has its power (*śakti*) in action alone, and not in the agent (*kartṛ*).
For in the rule *'kartari kṛt'* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), the mention of 'agent' (*kartari*) is an indication where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant."

"Agency" (*kartṛtva*) is the state of possessing an action (*kṛtimattva*). And that [state] is simply the action itself; however, in cases where there is a co-occurrence with words such as "Devadatta," [the term refers to] the one possessing the action through a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in suffixes such as *-tṛ*.
According to this view, there is all the more a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) in the previously mentioned examples such as "the agent" (*kartā*).
In the sūtra "armavatkarmaṇe," the root *kṛ* has the sense of "production" (*utpādana*), and production resides in the object (*karmastha*).

However, if [the root] had the sense of "exertion" (*yatna*), the aforementioned refutation—that expressions such as "the jar will be produced" (*ariṣyate ghaṭaḥ*) would not be established—would be difficult to avoid. But if the meaning of the suffix were merely the locus (*āśrayamātra*), then [in the case of] "the chariot... [the fault remains].

In the case of the statement "the chariot goes," there is no inconsistency whatsoever, because even though the chariot is insentient and lacks effort (*yatna*), it serves as the substratum for activities such as the rotation of its wheels, which are conducive to its motion. This being the case,
the claim that "there is potency (*śakti*) in the action" (*kṛti*) is simply not possible, since [potency] would also have to reside in the action itself.
Because, for the most part, [the meaning] is obtained from the verbal root itself by virtue of being a specific operation (*vyāpāra*).

Furthermore, you yourself must admit that in cases such as *jānāti* ("he knows"), the meaning of the suffix is the locus (*āśrayatva*), since it cannot be said that knowledge does not arise without effort (*yatna*). For indeed, it is not the case that knowledge fails to arise in the absence of effort.

Someone accepts [this]. Therefore, since it is difficult to establish a distinction between the kṛt suffixes and the verbal endings (tiṅ), one must accept that [the suffix] has the agent as its meaning. By this, having refuted the expressibility of the agent by the verbal ending in the *Kartradhikaraṇa*, [the author] [establishes it] in the *Jañjabhyamānādhikaraṇa* regarding the form "jañjabhyamāna," which is derived from a reduplicated base (*yaṅanta*).

Even the Mīmāṃsakas, who accept that the *kṛt* suffixes denote the agent, have been cited [as authority]. As for what they have stated—that the grammatical rule "after a root ending in *āna*, the suffix *kṛt* is used in the sense of the agent" (*ānajaṃśeṭhkartari kṛd*) is the means of apprehending the expressive power (*śaktigrāhaka*)—that is not correct. For this is merely a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the rule concerning *kṛt* suffixes, intended to supply the missing meaning in cases where the meaning is not explicitly specified.
[The suffix] *ṇvul* and others alone are applicable [by the rule], because of the maxim: "An operation that fulfills an expectancy is superior";

however, it does not apply to *śatṛ* and the like, because those [suffixes] have their expectancy satisfied by the very meaning of the base (*sthānin*) and the sense of the letter *l*. Otherwise, the suffix *śānac* would become difficult to obtain in the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*).

Furthermore, in that case, constructions such as "this person has gone while [he] was being eaten" (*aryamāṇe*) or "while [he] was being seated" (*āsya-māne*) would not be possible in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*);
nor would constructions such as "being carried" (*riyamāṇa*) be possible in the sense of the object (*karman*).
As for what the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda said: "When there is singularity in the agent, then *tip* [is used]; [it is used] in the agent..."

The claim that "because of the explanation through the syntactic unity of *aḥ karmaṇi* and *vyekayoḥ* by means of the sequence beginning with *yad dvitvaṃ tatra tas iti*, the expression of the agent does not follow from the sūtra" is to be considered. [For it is stated: "*ānyekavacanadvivacane*"...

For the technical designations (saṃjñā) such as "dual" and so forth are established as culminating in the substitutes (ādeśa) beginning with *tiP*. Consequently, let there be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the rule for the designation of the dual and so forth and the rule prescribing *tiP* and the others, namely *aveyakayoḥ*. Moreover, in the rule prescribing *tiP* and the others, the term *kartari* ("in the sense of the agent") is present.

How could it be led [to apply] in some way as a qualifier such as duality, singularity, and so forth? Now, one might object: in the rule *aḥ karmaṇi*, the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) which is carried over from the rule *kartari kṛt* certainly exists in the prescription of the *tiṅ* suffixes and others.
If it is argued that even the rule for *la* and the rules for *tiP* and so forth are accepted as forming a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*), that is true;

however, this is indeed a case of "sentence-level unity" (*vākyaikavākyatā*) and not "word-level unity" (*padaikavākyatā*), because the rule prescribing the substitutes *tiP* and so forth proceeds by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the *lakāra* prescribed in the rule "ṭh laḥ karmaṇi". And thus:

In the rule for the suffixes (lavidhi), how can the mention of the "agent" (kartṛ) qualify "number" (saṅkhyā)? For wherever there is a mention of the agent, there is no element present that brings number to mind, because the L-affix is devoid of designations such as "dual" (dvivacana) and so forth. Consequently, [the phrase] "when there is singularity in the agent" [is problematic].

An explanation is not possible in any way whatsoever. It might be argued as follows: in the rule *aḥ karmaṇi*, the term *a* does not constitute a general reference (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*) to the *laṅ* and *laṭ* moods which have the phonetic marker *a* as their anubandha;
rather, it is beyond dispute that it constitutes a general reference to all *lakāra*s from which the anubandhas have been dropped.

In that context, let it not be the case that *a* is in the nominative plural (*jas*), but rather let it be in the genitive singular (*ṅs*), as in the rule "the [suffix] *aḥ* is for the *parasmaipada*. This genitive case is in relation to a substitute (*ādeśa*)—as in "that which is the substitute for *la* is used when there is an object," and so forth. Nor is it possible to refer back (*anuvāda*) to a *la* that has not been previously prescribed.

It must be stated that since the suffix *la* is prescribed by rules such as "the *la*-suffixes occur in the present tense" (*vartamāne laṭ*), this [use of *la*] is an *ādeśa* (substitute) in place of *la*. Thus, it is easily understood that when *la* is replaced by this [suffix], if the root is transitive (*sakarmaka*), it occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*), whereas if it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), it occurs in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). This is the meaning of the rule beginning with "when there is singularity."

If it is argued that the *ujjanikā* (reconciliation) proposed by Bhaṭṭapāda is indeed unassailable, the following is said in response: If the word *laḥ* were taken as being in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), then the meaning expressed would belong only to the substitutes (*ādeśas*), such as *tiP* and the rest, and not to *śaP* and the others, because the latter lack the designations (*saṃjñās*) of dual and so forth.

For you have stated that this [rule] forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the rule beginning with *vyekayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.79). Nor can it be maintained according to your own method by means of the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), because it has already been stated that the suffix *śānac* would then be impossible in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Nor [can it be maintained] by the prescription of *śānac*...

The desired result is achieved through the syntactic unity of this rule with those rules that establish the application of the *ātmanepada* endings, by means of the [Pāṇinian sūtra] "ahāvakarmaṇoḥ. Furthermore, since the *śānac* suffix occurs even after a transitive verb in the impersonal (*bhāva*) sense, and moreover, because of its form ending in the nominative plural (*jas*), it connects directly with what is heard [in the sūtra]; whereas if it were in the genitive case, it would have to be a substitute (*ādeśa*).

Thus, by supplying the word [“respect” (*gaurava*)] from the preceding context, we have “respect,” and so forth. Here, this should be understood: by the inclusion of the term *akarmaka* (intransitive) in the rule *hāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*, those roots whose object is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitakarman*) are also included.

For this very reason, in the rule *ṇeraṇau*, the suffix *lakāra* (verbal ending) is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) in the examples *neha pacyate* (“it is not cooked here”) and *neha bhajyate* (“it is not eaten here”).

Thus says Haradatta. According to him, there is the inclusion of only those [roots] for which the object (*karman*) is entirely non-existent; however, in cases such as *ehi, pacyate*, the *lakāra* suffix occurs precisely in the sense of the object (*karmani*). There is another opinion that the object is not explicitly employed because it is merely implied (*gamyamānatvāt*). This is clearly stated in Haradatta’s commentary on the sūtra beginning with *atibuddhi*.

As for what has been said by some— "The statement made by the author of the *Prasāda* that 'in this [system], the *lakāra* occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) for roots whose object is not intended to be expressed' is incorrect because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya* and other works"— that is to be reconsidered,
since both positions are established in the texts of the *Bhāṣya*, Kaiyaṭa, Nāgeśa, and others.

On the contrary, the position that even those roots whose objects are not intended to be expressed are *akarmaka* (intransitive) is indeed the stronger one. For instance, in the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyām kriyārthāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.10), Haradatta, wishing to explain the form *icchati kriyate*, stated that the suffix *laṭ* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*).
Similarly, in the rule *ṇeradhyayane vṛttaṃ* (Pāṇini 6.2.87), Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others have likewise maintained this view.

It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) only after intransitive roots; for in the rule "only after those ending in *ya* or *ra*, the *kṛtya* and *kta* [suffixes]," there is a mention of *kṛt* suffixes in general, and because in that context the phrase "in the sense of an abstract state and after intransitives" is understood to carry over, otherwise [if it were not so], such forms as *ghaṭaṃ kṛtam* ("the pot was made") would result. This being the case:

If, in this sūtra, those roots whose objects are not intended to be expressed were not included by the mention of "intransitive" (akarmaka) roots, then [the rule] that will be stated by the author himself later in the section on *niṣṭhā* suffixes— namely, under the sūtra "The *kta* suffix is used in the sense of the commencement of an action" (*ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ*)— as well as the rule "In the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), the suffix *kta* ending in *adarśa-ādyac* is applied," as seen in examples such as "the cows have been milked" (*pītā gāvaḥ*) and "the Brahmins have eaten" (*bhuktā brāhmaṇāḥ*), would be untenable.

How could Haradatta’s forthcoming statement, as well as the explanation by Kaiyaṭa and others that in the word *kṛtapūrvī* the suffix *kta* denotes the abstract state (*bhāve*), be consistent? And how could usages such as ‘*ataṃ tiraścīnam*’ and so forth be consistent? [This is addressed] in the rule *atibuddhī*.

By the inclusion of the term "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) [in the definition], those verbs whose objects are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitakarmaka*) are also not included in that rule; for by that rule, the suffix *kta* is prescribed even when the agent (*kartṛ*) is to be expressed, which would lead to such forms as *dataḥ* and *pakvaḥ* being used in the sense of "one who has given" (*datavān*) and "one who has cooked" (*pakvavān*). However, in this present rule, there is no such issue, because [the term] is understood as "intransitive" by virtue of the object not being intended to be expressed.
Let it be that there is no fault whatsoever.

(3) Regarding the rule *laśakvataddhite* (Pāṇini 1.3.8): when a letter (*varṇa*) is mentioned [in a rule], the two paribhāṣās—the rule concerning the mention of suffixes (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) and the rule concerning the mention of meaningful elements (*arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*)—do not apply.

If it is asked: "Why does the substitution of *tiP* and other affixes not occur in cases such as *pravartate*, *lunāti*, and *cūḍāla*?"—to this they reply: "Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the meanings 'agent' (*kartṛ*) and so forth, which were specified in the rule *aḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), there is the selection of the *lakāra* prescribed for the sense of the agent and others."

For this reason as well, the hypothesis that the rule prescribes the meaning of the agent and so forth by restating *ti* and other substitutes is refuted; for it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), since the prescription of *ti* and other substitutes for the place of *L* would presuppose that *L* has already been prescribed for the meaning of the agent and so forth. Furthermore, [the alternative]—dvā... [is untenable].

Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*), only that *la* which is prescribed after a verbal root is understood here; thus, the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) does not occur. Furthermore, the designation *it* is not applied to *la*, because there would be no purpose for it. Nor is the accentuation of the *liṭ* affixes the result, since the absence of such an accent is indicated by the fact that the *ṇal* suffix itself is marked with the *liṭ* designation. Nor is the mere non-hearing [of the suffix] the result.

[Otherwise] the fruit [of the rule] would follow, which would result in the utterance of that [substitute] being purposeless, and because the hearing of the original form would be obtained through the injunction of the substitute itself. However, if one accepts that *laṭ* and so on are the substituends (*sthānin*) for *tiP* and the rest, then statements such as "the *aṭ* augment follows a parasmaipada ending" become naturally consistent; this is the general direction of the argument.

(4) *tiptasjhisipthasthamibvasmastātāṃjhathāsāthāṃdhvam-iḍvahi-mahiṅ* || 3.4.78 || This is a collective *dvandva* compound. The letter *ṭ* in *iṭ* is not an indicator (*liṅga*) of an augment (*āgama*).

[The mention of *ṭi*] is because of its co-occurrence with seventeen [suffixes] that are designated as such; however, it is for the purpose of qualifying [the suffix] by means of *ṭi*. If it were stated simply as *ṭeraḥ*, it would apply even in cases such as *edhevahi* and *edhemahi*, because when a letter (*varṇa*) is being referred to, the two paribhāṣās—the rule regarding the reference to suffixes (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) and the rule regarding meaningful items (*arthavadgrahaṇa*)—do not operate.

However, some [maintain]: since *liṅ* is understood to carry over from the rule for *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere*, if one explains the rule as being in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—namely, "of the *ivarṇa* that is a substitute for *liṅ*"—then there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) at all in cases such as *edhevahi* and *edhemahi*. For in those instances, [the condition is not met].

The substitute is merely the letter *i*. Therefore, they say that in the rule *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭer e* (Pāṇini 3.4.79), the letter *ṭ* is intended solely for the sake of clear comprehension. This, however, is questionable; for by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original), *vahi* and *mahī* would also possess the status of being *liṅ* (optative). Furthermore, the letter *ṅ* in *mahiṅ* [is required] because it is part of *taṅ* (the set of endings for the middle voice).

There is no prohibition [of the substitution]. Thus, in the case of the roots *vṛścati* and *pṛcchati* used in the sense of the object (*karman*) with the suffix *ral* (the *liṭ* aorist), there is no vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "rahijy... in forms such as *vavraścimahe* and *papracchimahe*. (5) *taṅ-anau ātmanepadam* | 1.4.100 | The term *ātmanepada* consists of the suffixes *taṅ* and *anu*.
With the intention that, due to the recurrence of the word *lasya*, only the substitute *la* (the L-affixes) is understood as referring to *āna*, he says:

"and [the affixes] *śānac* and *kānac*. By this, even after roots that take the *parasmaipada* endings, the affix *cānaś* occurs by virtue of the rule "when expressing habit or age" (*ācchīlyavayovacane*), as in: "those who are here constantly striking" (*atīha nighnānāḥ*).
(6) *anudātaṅti ātmanepadam* |1|3|12|. *Anudāta* and *ṅ* [form] *anudātaṅ*; that which has these two as its *it* (indicatory letters) is called *anudātaiṅ*.
The word *it*, heard at the end of the *dvandva* compound, is connected with each member individually. Among those, regarding the portion *anudāta*:

With the intention that there is no purpose for the rule of "specifying the end" (*tadantavidhi*) [in this context], and that the mention of "ending in that" (*tadantagrahaṇa*) applies only to the other portion [of the word], he says: "anudātetah," etc.
Furthermore, the term *upadeśa*, which is carried over from the rule "upadeśe'janunāsikaḥ" (P. 1.3.2), also applies specifically to the *ṅit* portion.
It is connected [only] here and not elsewhere, because of its non-deviation; thus he says: "that which is marked with Ṅ in the Upadeśa.
Since a *tadanta-vidhi* (a rule concerning that which ends in something) is difficult to obtain here without a qualified term (*viśeṣya*), he says: "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*).

Regarding "of the *la*" (*lasya*): [an objection is raised] that here, due to the absence of recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), both [the connection to the root and to the *la*] would be difficult to obtain, as in the case of "the roots beginning with *hu*."

If it is argued that, although the word *dhātoḥ* is somehow obtained from the sūtra by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*)—where the word *dhātavaḥ* from a previous rule is understood and its case-ending is changed—it is still not possible to obtain the word *laḥ*, then they say: [the word *laḥ* is obtained] from the sūtra *iko jhal* (P. 1.2.9), where *sanā*...
In this case, just as with the verbal root (*dhātu*), the relationship of mutual dependence between the *lakāra* (the marker) and the root should be understood through the *ātmanepada* designation;
for the *tiṅ* suffixes are substitutes for *la*, and *la* is prescribed after a root. Why is the term "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*) used?
[Consider] *cukuṭiṣati*. Here, the *ṅ*-ness of the *san* suffix is derived by extended application (*atideśa*) from the rule "after roots beginning with *kuṭ*."
Why [is the condition] "from a verbal root" (dhātoḥ) specified? To prevent [the application of the rule] after the suffixes *caṅ* and *ṇamul*; as in *adudruvat* and *avocat*. Now, one might object:

even if the restriction regarding the forms of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and the active voice (*parasmaipada*) does not apply because of the intervention [of the suffix], since the suffix *syapratyaya* is added to roots such as *vṛt* etc. by the rule *yatāsī* etc. precisely at the stage of the *lā* suffix; [The answer follows: ... [text continues] ... [The text provided ends abruptly here].
Since *la* is internal (*antaraṅga*) by virtue of being the general substratum for both [the *syas* affix and the *tiṅ* affixes], when the *tiṅ* affixes such as *tip* etc.

are present, *parasmaipada* is established in one alternative and *ātmanepada* in the other alternative even before the *syapratyaya*. Thus, the mention of *syapratyaya* in the rule *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ* is redundant; [it was included] for that very reason.

By the inclusion of the term *sy* (the future suffix), it is indicated that a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is stronger than the *ṭh*-class verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*). Consequently, although the Ātmanepada would necessarily apply due to the low-pitched (*anudātta*) nature of the root according to the rule "from [roots] ending in *ṛ*, the suffix *syasan* [takes Parasmaipada]," the Parasmaipada also optionally occurs by the rule "after roots beginning with *vṛt*, the suffixes *sya* and *san* [take Parasmaipada]. And thus, regarding the verbal suffixes...

Furthermore, because the restrictive rule (*niyama*) is stronger, the fault regarding *caṅ* and *ṇiṅ* would certainly remain. This position is clear in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the sūtra "adeḥ śitaḥ.

Moreover, the mention of *dhātu-* (root) is also necessary for the purpose of obtaining the rule of extension to what ends with that (*tadantavidhi*). [As in] "from a root having one vowel... (*dhātor ekāca-*)...

By such rules as these, the *yaṅ* [intensive suffix] is applied: *bobhūyate*. By the rule "ṛterīyaṅ," [the suffix *īyaṅ* is applied]: *ṛtīyate*. However, in cases such as *śete* and *hnute*, the status of having a final *ṅ* is established through the principle of "designation by analogy" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). If one asks how it is that *citrīyate* is formed with the *kyac* suffix by the rule "amovarivaścitraṅ," the answer is as follows: Regarding this, they say: [The word *citra* is treated as ending in *a*]. Thus, *citrīyate*.
The letter *ṅ*, which has no function within its own constituent part, serves as a qualifier for that which ends in *kyac*. Thus,

although the letter *ṅ* is an augment (*anubandha*) of the entire complex, its status as ending in *ṅ* (i.e., being *ṅt*) should be understood through the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).

(7) *svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* |1|3|72|. The word *it* is connected with each [term] as before. "Aiming at the agent" (*kartrabhiprāya*) means that which goes toward the agent. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*. "Of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) means "of the *la*-portion of the root."
The implication of the letters *la* and *dhātu* is to be understood as before.

(8) *tiṅstrīṇi trīṇi prathamamadhyamottamāḥ* | 1|4|101|. There are six *tiṅ* [suffixes] consisting of three groups of three; however, since there are only three technical names (*saṃjñā*), a one-to-one correspondence is impossible, and therefore [the names apply] to each individual [group].

Regarding the phrase "of the triad" (*trikasya*) in the context of the three designations (*saṃjñāsu*), the terms *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* are understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). Therefore, the meaning is that since there are three triads for each of the two sets of verbal endings, these designations apply according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*). Now, [one might object]: "The first and the first are 'the two firsts' (*prathamau*)."

When the single-remainder (ekaśeṣa) formation "madhyamau" is made from "madhyamaśca madhyamaśca," and when a copulative compound (dvandva) is accepted as "prathamau ca madhyamau ca uttamau ca = prathamamadhyamottamāḥ," then for the two triads [of persons], there is a correspondence according to their respective order.
If [the suffixes] were designated as *prathama*, *madhyama*, and *uttama* collectively, rather than individually, the rule "ṭhṇal uttamasya vā" would be contradicted,

because the designation *uttama* would not be obtained for the suffix *ṇal*. Consequently, in the expression "prathamamadhyamottamāḥ," where *prathama*, *madhyama*, and *uttama* form a *dvandva* compound, [the designation would not apply].

If it is argued that one should resort to *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one out of several identical terms) such that "the first, the last, and the middle" [are understood], and that this being so, the technical names (*saṃjñā*) would also be six, thereby achieving the desired result without the trouble of continuing the application of the mention of *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada*— do not say so; for if one resorts to a partial [interpretation]...

Out of respect for the tradition and to avoid redundancy, you too must certainly follow the inclusion of the terms *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada*. Otherwise, the designation *parasmaipada*, which has its own scope of application regarding the suffixes *śatṛ* and *kvasu*, would be sublated by the designations *prathama* and so forth. Consequently, [the form] *krāmyati* [would not be established].

If you argue that the designation *parasmaipada* is not sublated by the designations *prathama* and so forth— on the basis of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "for the *ṇal* prescribed for roots ending in vowels, there is an option regarding *ṇit*-ness via the rule 'ṭh-ṇal-utamo vā'"— then the difficulty of comprehension is all the greater.
(9) *tāny ekavacanadvivacanabahuvacanāny ekaśaḥ* | 1.4.102. The explanation of the term *āni* is "labdha" and so forth.

Otherwise, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding "one technical designation" (*eka-saṃjñā*), there would be a conflict between the designations of the first case (*prathamā*) and so on, and the designations of the singular (*ekavacana*) and so on.

It would be a synonym (*paryāya*). However, if [the desired result] were accepted, then by applying the rule *aṭer loṭo ‘erniḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.35), when singularity is intended, the designation *udātta* would be absent; consequently, since the rule *āḍ udāttaś ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.71) would not apply, forms such as *annī* and so forth would also be grammatically correct—this is the sense. Regarding the word *pratyekam*: as for that which...

It has been stated that [the suffix] *ṭha* occurs in the sense of "one by one" (*ekaikaśas*), but that is incorrect. Since the distributive sense (*vīpsā*) is already expressed by the suffix *śas*, the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is inappropriate; for the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that, according to the maxim "that which was not previously applicable [is now set aside]," the suffix *śas* is an exception (*apavāda*) to reduplication. Likewise, in the rule *upa-saraḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.81), the form *ekaikaśaḥ* is also used.

What was stated previously is indeed incorrect; this has been said in accordance with the *Manoramā* text. Others, however, maintain that *ekaikaśaḥ* consists of the word *ekaika* alone with the suffix *śas* added in its own sense (*svārthe*), and not here for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). Nor should it be argued that a *śas* used in its own sense is not understood from the foundational grammatical treatises (*ākaragrantha*), for [it is seen in the usage]: "one brown cow each" (*ekāṃ kapilāmekaikaśaḥ*).

Because of the statement in the Bhāṣya, "having given a thousand times," and because Kaiyaṭa explains that the suffix *śas* ending in the word refers to each individual item— thereby making it clear that the suffix *śas* can also have a distributive sense (*svārthika*)—
they say that what was previously stated by the ancients, namely that the form *ekaikaśaḥ* is incorrect, is itself incorrect.
(10) When *yuṣmad* is present as a co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) term, even if it is merely implied (*sthānin*), the second person [ending] is used. 1.4.105.

Regarding *yuṣmadi*: the explanation of "co-referential" is "expressing the same grammatical participant (*kāraka*) that is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Of those [words] whose grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) are distinct...

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the occurrence of words in reference to a single object. The explanation of the term *sthānin* is "not being employed" (*aprayujyamāna*). What is the purpose of the condition "in co-referentiality"? [Consider: *tvaṃ paśyasi*, *tvayā kriyate*, *tubhyaṃ dadāti*.

(11) *prahāse ca manyopapade manyateruttama ekavacca* 1.4.106. This sūtra consists of two sentences. The first sentence is: *prahāse ca manyopapade*. The term *madhyama* (the middle person) is understood here from the previous rule. [The compound means] that for which the verbal root *man*, with the *śyan* suffix (*manyate*), is the subordinate word (*upapada*).

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. By the force of hearing the word "manyamāna" (being thought), the term "in the verbal root" (*dhātau*) is obtained as the qualified object (*viśeṣya*). Thus he says: "the verbal root *man*" and so forth. "When that [root] is the base form" (*prakṛtibhūte*) means: "in place of the *la* suffix of that verbal root. "The middle [person] should be used" implies the rule "when *asmat* is the attendant word" (*asmadyupapade*). [The suffix] *madhyama*...

This is because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of that [rule] from the subsequent sūtra. And thus, this rule for the middle person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*). The second sentence is: "After the root *man*, the first person (*uttama*) is used, and it is treated as singular. He explains that: "After the root *man*, the first person shall be used"—the remainder being "when *yuṣmad* is the attendant word (*upapada*)."
This is because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of that [term] from the preceding sūtra. Regarding "sa ca" (and he): "he" refers to the first person of the root *man* (to think);

the meaning is that it receives the singular ending even when there is duality or plurality. This is for the purpose of reversing the order of the middle and first persons. All of this is illustrated by the very examples of the following words.
It will become clear [later].

(12) *asmadyuttamaḥ* | 1|4|107|. Regarding the phrase *tathābhūte*: when [a word] expressing a case-role (*kāraka*) denoted by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is employed—or even when it is not employed—[the first person endings are used for the speaker].
This is the meaning.

(13) *tiṅśitsārvadhātukam* |3|4|113|. To what does [the term] "stated after a verbal root" (*dhātvadikāroktā*) refer? [It refers to] *harīn*. Because of the rule *sārvadhātukam api* [P. 1.2.4], there would be the designation *ṅit*, and consequently, by the rule *her ṅtī* [P. 6.4.75], there would be *guṇa* [substitution] in forms such as *lihaḥ* and *śriyaḥ*, which end in *śas*.

By the rule *ārdhadhātuke yaK*, there would be the suffix *yaK*. However, some say that in the case of *vāriṇī*, even after the addition of *num*, the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would still occur. That is not correct; because of the prohibition by the rule *kṅti*, if *num*—which is conditioned by the fact that the stem ends in an *ik* vowel—were to cause *guṇa*, [it would contradict the prohibition].
And because it would contradict the prohibition against the combination [of suffixes] (*sannipātaparibhāṣā*). (13) *kartari śap* | Pāṇini 3.1.68.
From the rule *sārvadhātuke yaṅ* [3.1.67], the term *sārvadhātuke* is understood to carry over [as an adhikāra].
From the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.120], the word *dhātoḥ* is understood; thus he says: "for the sake of the agent," and so forth.
(14) *jho’ntaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.3].
The vowel *a* after the letter *t* is for the sake of pronunciation. [This refers to the rule] *āyaneyīnīyaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.2].

The term *pratyaya* (suffix) is carried over from the preceding *sūtra*, but not the term *ādi* (beginning), because it is declared to be *svarita* (accented) only in one part [of the compound]. If that [term *ādi*] were also carried over, however, the form *ayāntai* would not be established. [This is because] for the root *śīṅ*, there are the augment *iṭ* and the augments *araṭ* and *aṭ*.

Thus, because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the augment *āṭ* is applied before the substitution of the final letter (*antādeśa*); consequently, since the letter *jh* no longer stands at the beginning [of the suffix], [the rule does not apply]. This is what he states: "of that which is a part of the suffix. The statement by the ancients—that it applies to the *jh* that begins the suffix—has been refuted by this. In this regard, it is stated in the *Manoramā* that the mention of "beginning" (*ādi*) has been removed.
That is only superficial, because it is impossible for the term *ādi* (beginning), which does not apply elsewhere, to be excluded [from the rule].
Or else, the phrase "it is excluded" (*nivṛtam*) must somehow be explained as meaning "it does not recur" (*ananuvṛtam*).
As for those who explain [the rule] in order to justify the text *pratyayādeḥ*—namely, that once the augment *āṭ* has been applied...

"Granted that a suffix may indeed be accompanied by that [augment], yet there is no restrictive rule that it must be accompanied by that alone. This is not so; for it is impossible for something to be a whole (avayavin) while being divested of its parts (avayava).
Otherwise, in forms such as *bhūyāstām*, the augment *iṭ* would undesirably apply to *tām* and other such elements.
If it is argued that the augment *iṭ* belongs to a suffix following a stem (*aṅga*), whereas a form ending in *yāsuṭ* is not a stem, [we reply]:
according to the view of those who maintain that a suffixhood exists even for a suffix when divested of its augments,

[the rule applies] in cases such as *bhavāmi* and *bhaviṣyāmi*, by virtue of the inclusion of the initial element of the suffix, just as it does for the entire form ending in a verbal affix (*vikaraṇa*).

Because the status of being a *aṅga* (stem) would be unavoidable even for that which ends in *yāsuṭ*. Furthermore, in the case of *laviṣīya*, once *sīyuṭ* has been applied by virtue of its specific prescription, *iṭ* is added in place of the *liṅ*;
since the initial status [of the suffix] is destroyed by that augment, the acute accent on the beginning of the suffix (*pratyayādy-udāttatva*) does not apply.

Anticipating the objection that [the augment] would be included when the accent of the suffix is to be applied, the extension (atideśa) that "augments are as if non-existent" is accepted in the Bhāṣya and other works on the sūtra *dyudāttaśca*.
And this is not tenable even if the suffix were to stand alone; nor is it so according to that [opponent's] view.

It should not be argued that there is no contradiction with the original treatises (ākaragrantha), because even for the vowel *i* which is part of an augment (*āgama*), it would have to be acute (*udātta*) since it is part of a suffix (*pratyaya*); therefore, the passage beginning with "when the accent of a suffix is to be applied" must indeed be accepted to prevent that. [This is incorrect] because of the rule: "augments are unaccented (*anudātta*)."

The direction is as follows: since the specific statement has also rendered the *āgama* unaccented (*anudātta*), the initial acute accent (*ādy-udātta*) does not apply there. Regarding [the rule] *jhasya*: the vowel *a* after the letter *jha* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

Regarding [the rule] *ato guṇe*: however, the rule *ato dīrgho yañi* does not apply, because it is a prescription of a substitute (*ādeśa*) for a phoneme (*al*) that is the original locus (*sthānin*).
The meaning is that [the substitution] is prohibited by the rule regarding *sthānivadbhāva* (treating a substitute as the original).
(15) *ato dīrgho yañi* (Pāṇini 7.3.101): from the sūtra *uru-stu-śamyamaḥ*, the term *sārvadhātuke* (in a *sārvadhātuka* affix) is understood to carry over. In a *sārvadhātuka* [affix]...

What [is the purpose]? [The example is: "Keśava, woman! (keśava aṅganā). Since it could have been stated simply as "after *a*" (*ata ā*), the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is for the sake of ensuring that the *pluta* occurs only after a long vowel. Otherwise, in an instance such as "Devadatta, did you cook the rice? (*apākṣīrodanaṃ devadatta*) or "Indeed, I am cooking" (*nanu pacāmi bhoḥ*), the *pluta* would occur even for a non-final syllable, according to the rule "in questions and narrations" (*praśnākhyānayoḥ*).

However, some say: "The rule *ata āt* is easy to state; by the force of the inclusion of *t* (taparakaraṇa), there would be an exclusion of the *vikāra* (modification), so that the protracted (*pluta*) vowel does not apply.
Thus, in place of an acute (*udātta*), an acute *ā* is substituted, and in place of an unaccented (*anudātta*), an unaccented *ā*, and so forth."

This is already established by the rule *sthāne ’ntaratamaḥ*. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Manoramā* and other works that in the sūtra *vṛṣākapyagni*, the word *vṛṣākapi*—being udātta on the middle syllable—is the sole cause for the application of the udātta accent; however, in the case of *agni* and others, the result is established solely by the rule *sthāne ’ntaratamaḥ*. And thus:
Since there is no purpose [for it], the addition of *ta* (the *tapara* marker) for the sake of the rule (*vidhi*) need not even be questioned.
However, if— as in the case of *ā-āb* in the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ*— a *praśleṣa* (splitting of the vowel) were made as *ā-ā* in the rule *ata ā* as well, then the addition of *ta* would be necessary.
They say that even without [the particle *iti*], the desired result is achieved. He provides an example for the rule *rahasye ca*:
*ehi manye*. The meaning is: "I think you will eat rice. Regarding *etam eta vā*, [the examples are]:
