*etam manye odanaṃ bhokṣyethe* ("I think you two will eat this rice") and *eta manye odanaṃ bhokṣyadhve* ("I think you all will eat this rice").
This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). The meaning is respectively: "you two think 'we two shall eat'," and "you [plural] think 'we [plural] shall eat'."

(16) *liṭ* [is used] for what is beyond the senses (*parokṣe*) [3.2.115]. Although every action consisting of operations such as placing [the pot] on the fire is indeed entirely beyond the senses—as it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "This thing called 'action' is absolutely imperceptible; since its constituent parts exist in a temporal sequence [of before and after], it cannot [be perceived directly]."...

"Though it is said that [the object] is presented as a unified whole, nevertheless, what is intended here for examination is the instruments (*sādhana*) which possess the capacity conducive to that [action] and are engaged in its operation.
Therefore, even when there is perception of mere instruments not yet entered into the action, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) indeed occurs: 'He cooked' (*ayaṃ papāca*); 'You...'"

[Objection: Is it not the case that, although the upward and downward movements denoted by verbal roots—such as *āśrayaṇa* (ascending) and *avaśrayaṇa* (descending)—are objects of simultaneous perception, they are nonetheless objects of sequential perception? However, where there is no sequential perception either, there indeed is the transcendence (*pārokṣya*) of the action.
And if it is argued that, consequently, the third person singular of the optative (*liṅ*) is difficult to obtain, they reply here:

even when one’s own activity is not personally recognized due to distraction and so forth during its state of occurrence, it certainly exists when it is inferred from its effect, as in the case of [the thought] "I spoke."
Regarding the statement "it is indeed considered that he said thus" (*purastāt tasya matā kilaivam ity āheti*), [the rule] *liṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.115) applies;
[this suffix] is designated as *ārddhadhātuka* only. [This is also the case for the rule] *aṅḥ śākaṭāyanasya*.
The intention is that the particle *eva* is carried over from the preceding sūtra.
(18) *parasmaipadānāṃ ṇalatususthalathusaṇalvamāḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.82.
Here, since the vowel *a* is prescribed for the term *tha*, it would follow that it applies to the final letter [of the suffix]. It does not.

Nor should it be said that the letter *a* (in the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*) is redundant in the prescription of the letter *ā*, because its purpose is fulfilled by establishing a correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*). On this point, they say:

since the governing term "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is in force, the substitution of *ā* applies to the entire initial consonant cluster according to the rule "of what follows [the first element]" (*ādeḥ parasya*).

In the case of two [vowels], by the rule *dvayoḥ ṭhato guṇe*, there is a substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). Alternatively, the mention of the two *a*-sounds in the sūtra is by way of the subsequent form; thus, because it consists of more than one *al* (phoneme), it is established as a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*), which achieves the desired result. Now, an objection: since the compound (*dvandva*) consists only of nominal endings (*subanta*), if one were to assume two *a*-sounds there, there would simply be a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrgha*).

If it be argued that this is so, it is not thus; because substitutes possess meaning only through the meaning of their original bases (*sthānin*), the two *a*-sounds being prescribed for the word *tha* do not individually possess meaning. Consequently, as a whole it functions as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and by the rule "guṇa after *at*" (*ato guṇe*), only the single substitute form (the *para-rūpa*) is applied.

(19) *bhuvo vug luṅ-liṭoḥ* |6|4|88|. From the sūtra *aci śnu-dhātu-bhruvām y-v-oriyaṅ-uvaṅau*, the word *aci* is understood [as anuvṛtti]. Thus he says: "in the case of *luṅ* and *liṭ* when an *ac* follows. Why does it say "when an *ac* follows"? [Consider: *abhūt*, *abhūḥ*. When *vuk* is present, [the rule] *opo...* [applies].
[Objection: By the rule *vyoḥ*, the elision [of *y*] would be superseded by the elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* group because it is subsequent. [Reply:

But surely, because the elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* group is *antaraṅga*, the elision by *opo vyoḥ* alone will occur. And thus, from the root *mavyati* in the *laṅ* with *luṅ* elided, after the *laṅ*, *it*, and *sip*, there is *am* for *am*.

In the case of *amāma*, Mādhava and others have accepted only the elision (*lopa*) of the *v* and *y*. Thus, the inclusion of the term *ac*—which follows for the sake of subsequent rules such as *ṭhūdupadhāyāḥ*—has been applied here by the Vṛttikāra and others merely as a secondary indicator (*uparañjakatayā*), and not as an essential requirement; this alone is the appropriate conclusion.

Regarding this, they say: Since the substitution *vuk* (in *juhuvatuḥ*) is dependent on the verbal root *hu*, it is as "external" (*bahiraṅga*) as the elision of the suffix by Pāṇini 6.1.68 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...*).
Consequently, because *vuk* is considered non-existent due to its being external, the elision of *val* (the *u* of *hu*) never even arises;
therefore, it is more logical to maintain that the mention of *ac* here is indeed for the sake of the present rule.
This section containing the doubt and its resolution is found in the *Manoramā*.

Here, the moderns [hold that] there is no such thing as a *ṇamul* suffix with the elision of the *avyaya* (i.e., *avyayībhāva*) compounds; forms such as *ṇamāmat* and so forth are rejected from afar, because for words ending in *yakāra* and *vakāra* which do not undergo the substitution of *ūṭh*, [the rule does not apply].

That there is no *yaṅluk* [elision of the *yaṅ* suffix] is indicated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ahvoḥ śūḍ* and clarified by Kaiyaṭa. Furthermore, this [prohibition] pertains to those cases where *ūṭh* occurs after *ch* and *hv*; however, for the roots *sṛ* and *vī*, which undergo *ūṭh* according to the rule *vṛto vā*, the *yaṅluk* certainly exists.

This is logical and is also accepted by Mādhava and others; for it will be stated in the root-text that the root *avya* in the sense of "binding" ends in *yaṅ* and undergoes the substitution of *ūṭh*. Thus, they say that the present passage in the *Manoramā* contradicts that work. However, if...

If it is read in the *Manoramā* that [the rule applies] "from the yaṅ-luk form of *mavati*," then there is no contradiction between the preceding and following sections of that work; such is the direction [of the argument]. (20) *ajāder dvitīyasya* | Pāṇini 6.1.2.

If the genitive case [in Pāṇini’s rule] were derived from a *bahuvrīhi* compound, then in forms such as *indrīyati* (he desires Indra for himself), *indrīyitum icchati* (he desires to desire Indra), and *indidrīyiṣati*, there would be a prohibition of doubling for the letter *d* by the rule *andrāhra*. However, [the correct analysis is that] it is both *añ* and *ādi*, hence it is *ajādi* (beginning with a vowel). Thus, [the prohibition does not apply].
This fifth case ending [is used] after a *karmadhāraya* compound.
(21) Regarding the rule *liṭi dhātoranabhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.8), he says: "But [the doubling occurs] of that which follows the initial vowel. As in *bhūvbhūviti*. Although here...

The status of being a constituent part of a verbal root (*dhātu*) and the quality of being "first" (*prāthamya*) are not logically consistent; nevertheless, this should be understood through the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as if it were what it is designated). Now, in this case, there are four monosyllabic roots, and among them three are constituents, namely: *bhū*, *ū*, and *ūv*. [The first is] *bhū*.
The fourth [view] is that it is the whole (samudāya). If that were so, then by way of non-restriction, doubling (*dvitva*) would apply to whatever [element] one might choose.

This is not correct; for it is logical that doubling applies only to a single vowel (*ekāc*) as a whole, because when that [whole] is doubled, the constituent parts are necessarily doubled as well, just as when a tree moves, its branches move too.
Like the movement of all the limbs.
(22) *pūrvobhyāsaḥ* |6|1|4| [This occurs] in the section beginning with *ṭhekāco dve*. (23) *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* |7|4|60|
The mention of "of the reduplication" (*abhyāsasya*) refers to the class [of sounds] (*jāti*); by this,

the exclusion of the letter *t* and others in forms such as *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ* is established, because it is prescribed that after a consonant at the beginning of a reduplicated syllable, there is sometimes the substitution of *s*, while in all other cases, there is the elision of everything except the initial [consonant].
(24) *bhavetaraḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.73.

Here, the word *abhyāsa* (reduplication) is understood from the preceding sūtra, *atra lopo ’bhyāsasya*. Regarding this, the Easterners (*prāc*) have stated: "Because the root *bhū* is specified by its agent (*kartṛ*), the substitution of *āt* does not occur in the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) or the passive (*karman*). And this has been explained [by them].

Regarding the statement by his grandson (Kaiyaṭa): "The meaning is that [the forms] *śtip* and *śap* are specified because they denote the meanings of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*)," that is not correct.

For *śtip* is prescribed merely for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*), and *śap*, being a suffix (*vikaraṇa*), is devoid of meaning; thus, even though that *śtip* is prescribed when a following element denotes the agent, [it does not signify the agent].
Because the operation [of the rule] occurs here precisely by the force of the presence of the letter *ś*, otherwise— according to the method you have stated—
the rule "after a prefix, in the case of *su* and *nu*" (*upasargāt sunotisuvati*) and so forth would also fail to apply in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*),
resulting in a total collapse of the system; furthermore, this would clearly constitute a contradiction of your own established tenets for those who have examined the original treatises (*ākara*).

Poets also employ the suffix *kāra* even with non-action (intransitive) roots— as in "he bore [the king's] parasol" (*asyātapatraṃ bibharāṃbabhūve*) and "the nights bore [the moon]" (*vibhāvarībhirvibharāṃbabhūvire*), and so forth.
This refutation of the *Prakriyāprasāda* is established in the *Manoramā*.
Regarding this, the moderns [object]: "As for what was stated—that the application of *śap* here occurs solely by virtue of the *śitva* (the *ś* marker) of *tip*—that is not so;

for in cases such as *apibati* and *glāyati*, the purpose of *śitva* is already fulfilled by the application of the substitutes *piba-* and others, and by the removal of the *ātmanepada* marker (*āt*). And thus, [the rule] "after a prefix, [the substitution of *sunoti* and *su-vati* applies]"...

One must explain that the *śap* and other affixes occur even when a suffix does not denote the agent, based on such indications as ‘*havateraḥ*’ and ‘*hyāyateḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca*’. Otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with the author’s own forthcoming statement in the commentary on the rule ‘*ikśtipau*’. Some, however, [hold that] because of its *śit*-ness, the *tip*...

They explained that the status of being a *śit* suffix (having *ś* as its marker) serves a purpose by preventing the addition of the augment *iṭ*— via the rule *ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*— in cases such as *bhavati* due to its being a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, while simultaneously effecting the application of the augment *iṭ* in *ravīti* via the rule *ruva īḍi*.

That is to be considered: because of the prohibition of *āṭ* by the rule "itutre," there is no harm even though [the suffix] is an *ārddhadhātuka*; for in the commentary on the rule "ruva īḍ," only this much was explained in the root-text—that "there is the augment *īṭ* after 'ru' before a following *hal*-beginning *pit* [suffix]"—and not that it must be a *sārvadhātuka*.
There is no harm even in the absence of a qualifier. Nor should it be argued that,

in the absence of the qualifier "ārddhadhātukasya" for a *pit* affix beginning with a consonant (*hal*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *uvaktha*— derived from *brū* with *liṭ*, the substitution of *vac* for *brū*, and the *sip* affix *thal*— because here [the *thal*]...

Because [the suffix] *pit* is absent; nor can *pit*-ness be attributed through the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), because the *śit*-ness of *śnaḥ* (the substitute for *śānac*) serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) that, even in certain operations involving an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), the prohibition "not when [the operation] depends on a letter" (*analvidhi*) applies.
Therefore, according to the previously stated method, by virtue of the *śit*-ness of *śtip*, the *śap* [suffix] occurs even when not denoting an agent.

They say that the rule *pravṛtiḥ* must be rejected; however, others do not tolerate this. For if the affix *thal* lacked the designation *pit*, then because it would be *kit* by the rule *ṭha-saṃyogād liṭ kit*, the forms *uvacitha* and *uvaktha*—which result from the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) prescribed by *vacisvapi-*—would not be established; rather, [the form] would be *ūcitha*.

It should be *ūktvā*. Therefore, since the status of *thal* as having a *pit* marker is accepted by virtue of its being *sthānivadbhāva*, the rule "the augment *iṭ* is added to a *sārvadhātuka* beginning with *it*" has indeed been explained [in this context] in order to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *uvaktha*. And thus, in the case of *bravīti*, the presence of the *śit* marker [is justified] through the application of the augment *iṭ*.
That which has been stated by some, namely that "the purpose has been accomplished," is also entirely correct.

(25) *asiddhavat* *ā bhāt* | Pāṇini 6.4.22. The inclusion of the suffix *-vat* is for the sake of brevity in comprehension; otherwise, if one were to employ the expression *asiddhe asiddhaḥ*, it would be logically untenable, and one would have to infer by implication that it means *asiddhavat*.

Just as when the domestic priest (*purohita*) is distinct from the king, one might somehow conceive of the usage "this is the king" (*rājāyam*) by means of the expression "like the king" (*rājavat*), whereas when it is said, "this priest is like the king" (*rājavadayaṃ purohitaḥ*),
there is a swift comprehension; so too, by necessity, [the rule] "that which is not established in the *at* and *tu* positions is unestablished" (*atvatukorasiddhaḥ*).

In this context, it should be understood that the phrase "as if unestablished" (*asiddhavat*) is supplied [from a previous rule]. Furthermore, in the rule *asaṃyogallikṭi*, it should be known that the word "as if having the *kit* designation" (*kidvat*) is likewise supplied out of necessity. Regarding the expression *ā bhāt*: the particle *āṅ* here denotes inclusion (*abhividhi*). The meaning is "extending up to the section on *bh-*. And this is an *adhikāra* (governing heading). The mention of the word "here" (*atra*) [is for the purpose of...]

The mention of *āb* is for the purpose of indicating the object (*viṣaya*). As for the determination of the limit (*avadhi*) for the governing rule (*adhikāra*), it is established through interpretation alone, as in the cases of *ṭhaṅgasya*, *pratyayaḥ*, and *araśca*.
Thus, when this [rule] is present in the application of the rule *anudāttopadeśe*...
The meaning is this: "There should be elision of the nasal [ṇ] of these [roots] when followed by a *jhal*-beginning *kṅit* suffix;

and that [elision] is considered *asiddha*. In this case, while that which is to be performed depends precisely upon the *jhal*-beginning *kṅit* suffix, when that [suffix] is to be applied... [Thus we have] *jaṅgahi*, *jaṅghahi*. [This is governed by] the rule *ato heḥ*.

Thus, there is no elision (*luk*), because the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its dependence on the word *hi*. Now, if this were a governing rule (*adhikāra*), then wherever it applies, the status of being non-existent would apply only to that which is to be performed within its own scope, but not to what precedes it. Consequently—

If it is argued that the substitution of *e* in the word *hrasvaḥ* should not be considered *asiddha* even when the preceding *dhitva* (the substitution of *dh* for *t*) is to be applied—this objection would hold true if the governing principle were based on the form of the words (*śabdādhikāra*). However, this is a governing principle based on meaning (*arthādhikāra*).
Consequently, in this context, the limit established by the rule *nānna lopaḥ* remains in force and applies to every subsequent sūtra.

Intending all this, he says: "thus, upwards. Here too, the fact that [the substitution] is not established by the rule (*śāstre'siddhatvam*) remains as it stands in the original treatise (*ākara*). Therefore, in the case of *edhi* and *śādhi*, because the perception of the substituend (*sthānin*) as ending in a *jhal* consonant has not been removed, the rule "let there be *dhi* for *hi* after a *hal* or *jhal*" applies.

The desired result is established. However, it is not established under the view that what was previously stated is *asiddha* (non-existent), because of the maxim: "When the killer of Devadatta has been killed, Devadatta does not return to life. Thus, even if the cognition of *etva* (the substitution of *e*) is subsequently removed once the cognition of *jhal* (the *jhal*-pratyāhāra) has been removed by the rule for *etva*, [the result is not achieved].

They say [the rule applies] because the operation of *dhitva* does not take place. Why [is it specified] "having a common locus" (*samānāśraye*)? Consider: *papuṣaḥ*, *cicyuṣaḥ*, *luluvuṣaḥ*. Here, the *saṃprasāraṇa* that occurs for the suffix *vas* following the roots *pā*, *ci*, and *lū* results in the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "there is elision of *ā* before *iṭ*" (*āto lopa iṭi ca*).

In the case of the rule *ṭheranekācaḥ*, when the substitution of *yaṇ* or *uvaṅ* is to be applied, [the preceding operations] are not treated as *asiddha*. For the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) and so forth occur in the context of the *kvasu* suffix, whereas the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs in the context of a case-ending; thus, because they depend on different bases (*vyāśrayatvāt*), one cannot argue that [the *saṃprasāraṇa*] is *asiddha* by virtue of being *bahiraṅga*, according to the principle of *ājānantarya* (non-proximity).

Because of the prohibition [of the *ūṭh* substitute], and because the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* found in the rule *vāha ūṭh* is also *ābhīya*, it is consequently treated as *asiddha* when the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) and other such operations are to be performed. Nor should it be doubted that the aforementioned *paribhāṣā* and the elisions of *ā* (*āllopa*), etc., do not share a common basis (*samānāśrayatva*).
When the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) has taken place in *vasu*, the elision of *a* (*allopa*) and other operations proceed by virtue of being dependent on [the suffixes] beginning with *aj*.
Since the *saṃprasāraṇa* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) when those operations are to be applied, the *paribhāṣā* concerning "that which is external" (*bahiraṅga*) also applies to that domain;
thus, because they exist for them, such is the direction [of the argument]. The mention of *ābhāt* is for the purpose of securing the scope [of the rule].
Why? For the purpose that an operation prescribed for a specific case (ābhīya) should be unestablished (*asiddha*) only with respect to that same specific case, and not with respect to anything else.

By means of this [principle], when the *na*-elision is applied in the words *abhāji* and *rāga*—by the rules "after *hañ* before *ciṇ*" (*hañjaśca ciṇi*), "after *añj*" (*añjeśca*), and "after *hañ* in the sense of the abstract action or the instrument" (*hañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ*)—[the elision remains unestablished only for the purposes of those specific rules].
They say that because there is no lack of established proof for that [rule], the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs by the rule "atha upadhāyāḥ.

It might be argued: in the forms *debhatuḥ* and *debuḥ*, even though the *liṭ* affix is *kit* according to the rule to be stated later—"ranthi-granthi-dambhi"—the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication would not occur due to the elision of *na*.

Because the elision of *nal* is considered asiddha (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent operations). On this point, they say: "By the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the inclusion of the long vowel *ā* in the rule *naś-oral-lopaḥ*, it is established that the *ābhīya-asiddhatva* (the non-validity of an operation within the same governing rule) is not absolute; thus, there is no fault here. For the purpose of the inclusion of the long vowel *ā* [in the rule] is so that the augment *āṭ* might not be elided in forms such as *āstām*."

If the augment āḍ were non-existent (asiddha) with respect to the elision of the *śn* and *as* due to its being an ābhīya operation, then what would be the purpose of that *tapara* (long vowel marker)? In this way, the rule "ambheśca" which is about to be stated is not a new Vārttika,
but is rather obtainable by virtue of the principle of optionality (*anityatva*).

The suffixes *vuK* and *yuṬ* should be stated as established [even when the root ends in a consonant]. *VuK* is for the sake of the grammatical rule (*śāstra*). The same applies hereafter. An example of *yuṬ* is "itīye" (in the sense of "thus") and "babhūve" (he became). Regarding this, the ancient commentators, having explained the rule "indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca" as being intended to make the *liṭ* affix *kit* even after roots ending in *i*, [proceed as follows]...

It was stated that when the rule *ṭhaco’ñṇiti* would have required vṛddhi, the prohibition *ṅiti ca* applies; however, that has been disregarded. This is because the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) holds that the prohibition applies only to those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* operations characterized by the marker *ṅ*. Otherwise, if the prohibition applied to all [substitutions] having *ik* as their substituend, then even in the case of *aigavāyana*, [the rule would be overextended].

There would be no *vṛddhi*. Nor can it be argued here that, by the force of the *kit* designation, the rule applies even to that which is not characterized by *it*; for there is a Vārttika stating: "Since the root *indh* pertains to the Vedic domain (*chandas*) and since the *vuk* augment after *bhū* is obligatory, the prescription of the *kit* designation for the *liṭ* [affix] is redundant. Even if, in this case, the *vuk* augment were to apply due to the occurrence of a different word-form...

Although there is no absolute permanence, the position that permanence is accepted in some cases merely on the grounds of the contingency of "what has been done" versus "what has not been done" (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitva*) is understood from this very *Vārttika*;
therefore, when the causative suffix *ṇic* follows the root *radh*, [the substitution of *iṭ*] prevails by virtue of its permanence, overriding even the subsequent *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel.
When the augment *num* is applied by the rule *‘adhijabhoracī’*, the form *randhayati* is established. [Objection:

Even so, the portion *‘indheśca’* is still required for the sake of making the *liṭ* affix following a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) *kit*; otherwise, in the example *‘amīdhe dasyu hantamaṃ’*, there would be no elision of the nasal of the root *indh*. [Reply: Not so.

For, by the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, both the designation *sārvadhātuka* and the designation *ārddhadhātuka* are prescribed; thus, according to the intention of the Vārttika— namely, that because of this [rule], even though the *laṭ* [present tense] has the designation *sārvadhātuka*, there would still be elision of the *n* [in forms like *bhavanti*]— the moderns [hold that] in the case of *abhūva*...
Because of the prohibition of the substitution of *aci* by the rule "virvacane'ci," the suffix *vuk* operates even before guṇa and vṛddhi; thus,

the citation of the reason "on account of its being *nitya*" in the Vārttika "huvo vuko nityatvāt" is purposeless, since the *nityatva* of *vuk* [is established] through the acquisition of a different form (*śabdāntaraprāpti*).

Fearing that [the rule] might not apply, they raised an objection—arguing that even the mere fact of being subject to the dilemma of whether an action has been performed or not performed leads some to accept permanence—and thus rendering even such a resolution as the aforementioned one futile;

however, they themselves provided the following solution: for at the end of the section on the duality of the sixth [case], the author of the Vārttika established a "prior counter-exception" (pūrvavipratiṣedha).

It is recited [in the Mahābhāṣya]: “The reduplication [is not applied] due to the substitution of *yaṇ*, *ay*, *āv*, *ā*, elision (*lopa*), elision of the penultimate (*upadhālopa*), and the substitution of *u* for *ki* and *kin*.
Thus, with the intention that the rule “before a reduplicated suffix beginning with a vowel” (*dvirvacane’ci*) need not be commenced, [the author says] “because it is obligatory” (*nityatvāt*).
Regarding the phrase "the cause has been set forth":

according to the view that the rule *virvacane'ci* prescribes the status of a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for that which is not a substitute for *ra*, since the substitution of *vṛddhi* and so on would have already been accepted prior to the doubling, the suffix *vuk* [would apply] even after the substitution.
The passage beginning with "There is the occurrence [of the substitution] because *bhu* is followed by *vuK*, since it is permanent" is entirely correct. Even so, one might ask:

how can the following passage be consistent: "In the case of nominal roots, as in *tvāpayati* and *māpayati*, because it is permanent, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the long vowel) before the application of the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*)"? This is because the rule for the elision of the *ṭi* is indeed permanent.

It must be stated that the rule *prakṛtyaikāj* was rejected in the Bhāṣya; it is with this intention that its application [in the present case] occurs. For this very reason, it was stated therein that *tvādayati* and *mādayati* alone are correct; such is the direction.

(26) *ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* |7|2|35|. While the word *iṭ* is already understood from the previous rule *eḍvaśi kṛtī*, the explicit mention of *iṭ* here again is for the purpose of excluding that *iṭ* which is connected with prohibitions (*niṣedha*). In reality, however, [the rule applies] to those [roots] that are not meaningful [on their own].

In the midst of the three words following from *prathamādvē*, after *arāddiś* and before *am-arthānām prathamā*, [the word] *veti* is explained as having ceased its application (*nivṛtam*), while *iḍ* continues to apply (*anuvartate*).
This is just as one would explain that [the word] *eti* has ceased its application, while *iḍ* continues to apply.

It has been stated that the mention of *iṭ* is unnecessary because it is possible [to derive the forms otherwise]; nevertheless, it should be understood that it is accepted for the sake of clear comprehension.
What is the purpose of the rule "of the *ārddhadhātuka*"? [Consider: *āste*, *śete*.

What is the purpose of "of that which begins with a consonant (*valādi*)"? [Consider: *edhanīyam*. But surely [the form *edhanīyam*] is obtained by the rule "after roots beginning with *rud*, [there is *iṭ*] before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix"?

If it were the case that the augment *iṭ* occurs only for a sārvadhātuka suffix, then by the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "only after roots such as *rud*," the augment *iṭ* would not occur in forms like *āste* and *śete*; thus, the mention of "ārddhadhātukasya" [in Pāṇini 7.2.35] would be redundant. Nor can there be a reverse restriction—namely, that *iṭ* occurs only for a sārvadhātuka after roots such as *rud*—because [if that were so], it would not occur in *arodīt*.

It might be argued that in cases such as *syāt*, *āste*, and *śete*, one should instead expect *syāt* [to apply]. However, this is not the case; for in the formation of the suffix *ktvā* according to the rule *ud-avi-damuṣa-grahi-svap-pracchaḥ saṃśca*, the original *kit*-designation (*āṬpadeśika-kitva*) remains firmly established. Furthermore, by the rule *halantaśca*, the suffix *san* begins with a *jhal* sound.
And because of this [logical] necessity, since an opposite restriction is impossible, the mention of *ardhadhātuka* is indeed redundant.
[Objection: But if that mention were absent, then in the rule *valādeḥ*, the term *aṅgasya* (of the stem), which is the governing topic (*adhikṛta*), would become the qualified element (*viśeṣya*).
Consequently, the augment *iṭ*—just like the augments *aṭ* and *āṭ*—would remain in its current state [applying to the stem].

Even if that [restriction] were not adopted, the desired result is achieved by explaining it as: "the *iṭ* augment belongs to that *val*-initial [suffix] which is the cause for the *aṅga*. Therefore, since either of these two explanations must be accepted, the abandonment of the rule "ārddhadhātukasya" alone is preferable. But if this is so, [how do you explain] "eśavaḥ"?

In the case of *ṭhaṅganā* and *ṭhvṛkṣatvam*, the augment *iṭ* would occur. Even though a solution might seem possible—by relying on the word "root" (*dhātu*) which is carried over from the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* so that the augment does not apply to what follows a non-root—the introduction of the augment *iṭ* remains unavoidable in forms such as *lūbhyām* and *pūbhyām*. This [undesirable result] persists even if one attempts to provide a solution by treating the term [in the rule] as a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*).

It cannot be prevented; for since verbal roots ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as roots, in forms such as *lūbhyām* and *lūbhiḥ*, the suffixes *byām* and so forth are prescribed after a root, and this status remains unimpaired. Furthermore, in cases such as *jugupsate*, the augment *iṭ* would be unavoidable for the *san* suffix, which is prescribed after a root by the rule *uptijkidbhyaḥ*.

It might be argued: "In this context, for the sake of obtaining the interpretation that [the substitution applies] to a suffix beginning with *va* or *la* prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), a fifth-case form of *dhātuḥ* is required; however, that is difficult to find, because in the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, the word *dhātuḥ* is in the genitive case. And so it is.
It should not be argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the augment *iṭ* even in cases such as *vṛkṣatvam*;

for, according to the view that [the rule] pertains to words (*śabdādhikāra-pakṣa*), a word similar to that [which follows] is inferred by virtue of its being marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*), thereby obtaining the sense of the ablative case. Alternatively, let it be the genitive case; for by explaining the meaning of the genitive as "being prescribed" (*vihitatva*), the desired result is established.

Therefore, the mention of *ārddhadhātuka* is for the purpose of preventing over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *jugupsate*. Some, however, argue that if it were explained as "the augment *iṭ* belongs to that suffix which is prescribed after [mentioning] the verbal root (*dhātuḥ*)," then [the rule would apply to] *lūbhyām* and *jugupsate*.

Thus, they say that because there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in this case, the rule *ārddhadhātukasya* is redundant. Regarding the form *babhūviva*: one should not suspect that if the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *ṛśyukaḥ kitī* were to apply here, the augment *vuk* would also not occur; for the *iṭ* is applied by virtue of the restriction (*niyama*) of the *krādi* group.

(27) *luṭ* [is used] for the non-today (*anadyatana*) [time]. Pāṇini 3.3.15. It has been established in the rule *ālopasarjane ca tulyam* that "the day together with the latter half of the past night and the former half of the coming night is called 'today' (*adyatana*)."

(28) *Ārdhadhātukaṃ śeṣaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.114. This is obtained because, while the word *dhātoḥ* (“of a verbal root”) is already understood from the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ* [3.1.22], this new introductory rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*) beginning with *dhātoḥ* again is established for that very purpose. And this [is explained] right there.
This is clear in the *Manoramā*. Why [is it specified] "prescribed after a root"? Consider: *lūbhyām* (from the roots *lū* and *bhī*) and *jugupsate* (he feels disgust).

(29) *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.86]. The meaning is that the phrase "separated by many [intervening elements]" qualifies the *ik* vowels such as those of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes and so forth, and not the *aṅga* (the verbal base).

(30) *tāsastyorlopaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.50. From the rule *aḥ syārdhadhātuke*, the term *si* is carried over (*anuvartate*). Since the suffix implied by the term "stem" (*aṅga*) is qualified by this *si*, the rule of "beginning with that" (*tadādividhi*) applies according to the principle *yasmin vidhis tadādau*.
This is what he says: "at the beginning" (*sādau*). In the same way, this should also be inferred for "at the beginning of *r*" (*rādau*).
(31) *ri ca* | Pāṇini 7.4.51. "As before" means that there is elision (*lopa*) of the root *tās*. However, the root *as* is not connected here; therefore...
Because the cognition of "ra" and so forth is impossible.

(32) *lṛṭ śeṣe ca* |3|3|13|. It was previously stated that "the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* [are used] when one action is for the sake of another action. He says "in the remainder" (*śeṣe*) to refer to cases other than that—namely, when [the action] is not [for the sake of another]. Haradatta, however, says: "Precisely because [the word *śeṣe*] is not marked with the svarita accent..."

The phrase "in [the case of] an action whose purpose is another action" does not carry over [from the previous rule]. And thus, [the objection that] "eṣa eṣa" is easily abandoned is to be considered. For in examples such as "sthīyate ayiṣyate" (it is stayed in order to go), there would result the sublation of the future suffix *lṛṭ* by the suffix *tumun*, because [the rules for] *ktalyuṭtumun* apply in the sense of the *khala* suffixes.

This is because there is no rule regarding the non-application of the *vāsarūpa* principle. Furthermore, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*); for he will state later in the section on *kṛt* suffixes that the rule "the *kṛtya* suffixes are also used in the senses of permission (*atisarga*), invitation (*prāptakāla*), and so forth" is prescribed again so that they may not be superseded by the *loṭ* suffix. That this too is an indicator is another matter. As for what was stated by the ancients—
The example "he goes thinking 'it will be an oblation'" (*haviṣyatīti vrajati*) was cited merely for the sake of appearance;

it is of no utility for establishing that "the *lṛṭ* [future tense] occurs even in the domain of the *tumun* [infinitive suffix], and the *lṛṭ* is not sublated by the *tumun*," because in the word "will be" (*bhaviṣyati*), the *tumun* does not occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

The attainment [of the result] exists, for that [attainment] occurs when there is existence [of the action]; moreover, it will be stated that [the suffixes apply] only when the agents are the same. Even if the sūtra were composed merely as "lṛṭ" (without the "anadyatane" portion), the form "haviṣyatīti vrajati" would indeed be established; let this matter rest for now.
The phrase "in the sense of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*)," and so forth, is understood [from the preceding rule]. Therefore, he says: "in the sense of injunction and so forth."

(34) *Āśiṣi liṅ-loṭau* | 3|3|173| If it is asked: "Why should not [the terms] 'inquiry' (*saṃpraśna*), 'request' (*prārthanā*), and 'benediction' (*āśis*) have been stated directly in the rule for injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth, instead of this separate formulation of a sūtra?"—to this they say: For here, [in the previous rule], *tiṅ* and *kṛt*...
The term *āśiṣi* (in the sense of benediction) is certainly necessary here, as per the subsequent sūtra. Furthermore, the *liṅ* and *loṭ* suffixes should also be prescribed in this very context;

for if *āśiṣi* were included in the rule concerning injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth, then by the rule *me loṭ*, etc., these suffixes would subvert [the present rule] in their own domain due to their higher status. In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, this rule prevails due to its higher status.
"‘This is a great distinction, because [the cognition] ‘this is a jar’ and so forth possesses a sublater."

(35) *tuhyostātaṅṅaśiṣy anyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 7.1.35. Although it could have been stated as *ihyostātaṅ*, nevertheless, because there would be no economy of expression (*lāghava*) and to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the imperative (*loṭ*) is resorted to by relying on the association with the word *hi*.
While this [rule] continues to apply, the term *tuhyaer* is stated because of its greater weight.

(36) *loṭo laṅvat* (Pāṇini 3.4.85). Since the word *loṭaḥ* is seen in the genitive case as the object of comparison (*upameya*), [the genitive suffix] must also be applied to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Thus, [the rule means] "like the *laṅ* [after a root ending in the genitive]."

The suffix *vat* [is meant]; thus he says "by that" (*tena*). However, the augment *aṭ* and the others are not extended [to the substitute], for those two are not produced from the *laṅ*; rather, the meaning is that they belong to the characteristic (*liṅga*) of the *laṅ*. Now, even so, in forms such as *yāntu* and *vāntu*, the *jus* [substitution] does not occur because the mention of "optionally" (*vā*) from the rule for *aṅ* is carried over here, and a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) is resorted to.

Alternatively, in the rule *aṅḥ śākaṭāyanasya*, since the desired result is established simply by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *ti* from the preceding rule *ityaṃ ṅtiḥra*, the mention of *laṅ* is considered redundant; for [the substitution of] *luṅ* is separated by *isic*,
and *lṛṅ* is separated by the suffix *syapratyaya*, whereas *liṅ* is separated by the *jus* [substitution] according to the rule *herju*.

And because [the suffix] is prescribed, the term "iti" results only in the *laṅ* [suffix]; therefore, the mention of *laṅ* is analyzed separately. This restriction means: "Only for that which is *laṅ*, the *jus* replaces *jhi*, but not for that which becomes *laṅ* by way of substitution (*laṅvadbhāva*). Thus, it is argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply. That, however, is to be considered.

In the case of *āduḥ*, because the rule *ijabhyaste* would invariably require the substitution of *jus*, the alternative provided by *śākaṭāyanasya* would apply by virtue of its superior status (paratva), thereby resulting in an undesirable optionality. Therefore, the mention of the *laṭ* [present tense] must indeed be included in Śākaṭāyana’s sūtra; it is not redundant. Nor does [the rule] *ātaḥ* [apply here].

Regarding the rule *sūtreṇā’duḥ*, the modern grammarians (*navyāḥ*) maintain that it should be stated that *jus* occurs invariably [after an ārdhadhātuka affix beginning with *j* following a root ending in long *ā*]; for that rule serves as a restrictive injunction (*niyamārtha*) and cannot function as a prescriptive injunction (*vidhyartha*). Otherwise, in the case of *abhūvan*, the application of *jus* by the rule *ijabhyastavidibhyaśca* would be unavoidable. However, if one were to apply the rule *ātaḥ* here again by repeating it—

If both the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*) and the sense of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) were explained, then— since the aforementioned defects would be absent— the resolution beginning with "or else" (*yadvā*) would indeed be correct, because for Śākaṭāyana the *jus* suffix is optional. Furthermore, in the alternative where it is absent, since the *jus* is accepted by the rule "after *ij*, in the case of reduplicated forms" (*ijabhyasta*), the principle of re-application (*punar-prasaṅga*) is recognized.

This is indeed perfectly correct; however, regarding the forms *juhvatu* and *vindatu*, one must certainly resort to the principle of *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted optionality) in order to prevent the application of *jus*. This is the general direction of the argument. (37) *Nityaṃ ṅtiḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.99.
Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in /s/": the ancient explanation, "of that which has /l/ as its final [consonant] before /s/", is incorrect;
the intention is that this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *bhūyāsam*.
The phrase "of that which has /ṅ/ as its penultimate" means "of that which has /l/ as its final [consonant] before /ṅ/. By this, [the rule applies] in cases such as *bhavāva* and *bhavāma*.
There is no over-extension [of the definition].
(38) *serhyapicca* |3|4|87|.

[The rule] *so'picca* [is understood]. And thus, although the substitute *hi* for *sip* in the place of an unaccented (*anudātta*) *si* would [otherwise] be unaccented by the principle "the most similar [substitute takes the place of the original]," it does not become unaccented; [as in] *ahārṣīt śatrūn*.
"Have you heard this?"

(39) *ato heḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.105). [The example is] *bhavatāt*. The sense is that because *heḥ* is subsequent with respect to *luk*, it undergoes *tātaṅ*; thus, *heḥ* subverts the *luk* which is itself *antaraṅga*, rather than being subverted by it.
(40) *āḍ-uta-masya pi ca* |3|4|92|.
They say that by the word "a" [in this rule], that very element to which the augment *āṭ* has been applied is referred to.

(41) And from this [sūtra]: *itaśca* |3|4|100|. Following the rule *itaśca lopaḥ*, the term *parasmaipadeṣu* (in the parasmaipada endings), which has been carried over, is transformed into the genitive singular (*parasmaipadasya*) and is qualified by the word *itaḥ* (of the *it*). Thus he says:

The form *yatasya* ends in the letter *i* and belongs to the *parasmaipada*. However, the statement by the ancient [commentators] that "there is elision of the *i* in *parasmaipada*s" is incorrect, because it would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *bhavet*. Now, one might argue: let there be the long vowel *ī* in the rule *ato yeyaḥ*; thus, there would be no over-extension in the case of *itaśca*.
If it is argued that because of the inclusion of the long vowel *ā* (taparakaraṇa), there is no fault even in cases such as *abobhavīt*, we say:
not so. For it is established in the *Manoramā* that a fault remains inevitable in cases such as *karoter laṅ* and *iruditām*.

(41) "The *liṅ* [optative] is used in the senses of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), permission (*āmantraṇa*), entreaty (*adhīṣṭa*), inquiry (*saṃpraśna*), and urging (*prārthana*)—whether these are indicated (*dyotya*) or expressed (*vācya*). This is because both positions are established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*). Regarding this, the justification for the first position is as follows: it is inappropriate for injunction and the others to be the meaning of the suffix itself.

For if that were the case, since meanings such as the agent (kartṛ) are already fulfilled by other *lakāra*s, [meanings like] injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth would become sublaters of those meanings; consequently, the optative (*liṅ*) would not be a designator of the agent and so on,
and thus the dual and plural endings would not occur, nor would the *śap* augment and other such affixes.

Furthermore, there would be no established status for the *puruṣas* (persons), and the absence of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth—conditioned by the fact that [the agent] has already been expressed—would not be established. In the second view, however, the justification is as follows: the agent and other factors are not sublated by the injunctive suffixes (*vidhi*) and so forth, because there is no mutual contradiction between them. And thus, in the rule "aḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.2.124), the term "aḥ" [is used].

Thus, by the use of the plural designation, since all verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) are included, the meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth would also belong to the optative (*liṅ*) and other suffixes. Furthermore, the meanings such as the agent would have no scope [elsewhere], nor would the *laṭ* and other suffixes serve as their scope; this is because the same logical principle applies.

Because, just as in the case of the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and others, the present tense (*vartamānatva*), the past tense (*bhūtatva*), and so forth, are also denoted by their respective verbal suffixes (*lākara*). Nor does it follow that, in cases such as *pacati*, the present tense and so forth—being the meaning of the suffix—would become the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the root-meaning; for if that were so, [the sentence would mean] "a single agent who is present..."
It should not be argued that the description of verbal cognition as "pacikriyā" (the act of cooking) and so forth would be improper;

for the principle that [the meaning of] the suffix is the primary element and [the meaning of] the base is the qualifier applies equally even to the agent (*kartṛ*) and other such factors. Now, it might be objected that in the case of a verb (*ākhyāta*), it is a general rule that the meaning of the suffix is the principal and the meaning of the base is the qualifier.

If it is argued that this is because of the established tenet (siddhānta) that "the verb is primarily characterized by the manifestation of effort" (bhāva-pradhāna), then for that very reason the aforementioned fault does not arise; such is the direction [of the argument]. Regarding the phrase "in instigation" (pravartanāyām): the meaning is that the property of being an instigation (pravartanātva) is common to all four, beginning with the injunction (vidhi). On this point, they say: "activity... (pravṛttiḥ).

And instigation (*pravartanā*) is both [the result and the operation]; it is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because it is accepted that both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are denoted by the verbal root. However, the locus of that [result] is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*lakāra*).
Even though instigation is the meaning of the verbal root by virtue of being an operation, as for instigation in its specific nature as instigation (*pravartanātvena*), it is [denoted by the suffix].

There are two positions: that the meaning expressed by the *lakāra* suffixes, such as the optative (*liṅ*), is [the *bhāvanā*] itself, or that it is merely indicated (*dyotya*). That which resides in the person (*puruṣaniṣṭhā*) and has activity (*pravṛtti*) as its object is called "efficient force" (*arthī bhāvanā*). However, the injunction (*vidhi*) is the act of impelling (*pravartanā*); because one experiences "it impels me," that which resides in the optative suffixes and so forth is called "verbal efficient force" (*śābdī bhāvanā*). [This applies to] the Veda.

Some maintain that this [efficient force] resides in the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, because of the absence of a speaker; however, in common worldly usage, it resides in the person. For this instigation (*pravartanā*), the person's activity itself is the goal to be accomplished (*bhāvya*).
As for the person's activity, however, acts such as sacrifice and giving are superior. This is because the verbal suffix (*lakāra*)—in its form as the optative (*liṅ*) and so on—[denotes it].

Because it is cumbersome to postulate a separate power (*śakti*) within the act of setting something in motion (*pravartanā*), the same applies to the causative suffix (*ṇic*). However, there is this distinction: in all views, the instigation (*preraṇā*) manifested by the *ṇic* suffix resides in the person (*puruṣa*) and so forth, and not in the *ṇic* itself; whereas that manifested by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) depends on the difference between philosophical positions.
Is it based on the verbal suffix (*liṅ*) or based on the person (*puruṣa*)? It might be argued:

according to the view that "in the world, the instigation (*pravartanā*) manifested by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) resides in the person," there would be the usage "Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to eat rice" (*ācayaty odanaṃ devadattena yajñadattaḥ*), just as one says "Devadatta eats rice by means of Yajñadatta" (*acayati odanaṃ devadattena yajñadattaḥ*).

It might be so. To this they reply: In the view that [the meaning] resides in the person (*puruṣa*), the *pravartanā* (incitement) is expressed solely by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the like, and not by the verbal root (*dhātu*).

And thus, since the person who is the locus of the operation to be performed by the suffix lacks the status of being the agent (*kartṛ*), the aforementioned fault does not apply. This is as in examples such as "Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook."

However, because a root ending in *ṇic* is itself a verbal root (*dhātu*), both the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*) possess the status of agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of being the substratum of the activity denoted by the root; since the instigated agent is not expressed by the *l*-suffixes, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) applies to it—this constitutes the asymmetry. In the *Kaustubha* and other works, however, [it is stated]: "In the sense of the causal agent (*hetumat*)."

In this *sūtra*, the view that the causal agent’s activity (*prayojakavyāpāra*) alone is expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is established as the primary one. However, if both activities were to be the meaning of the base of the causative suffix (*ṇicprakṛtyartha*), then—when the word *abhi* has the activity denoted by the causative suffix as its qualificand—it would be *abhisāvayati*; but when it has the activity of the base itself as its qualificand, [it would be *abhisavayati*].

For [otherwise], there would be a violation of the natural consistency of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) regarding the rule *ṣṭhansunoti*, which prescribes the substitution of *ṣ* in forms such as *abhiṣāvayati*. Likewise, in the rule *atibuddhi*, the qualification "the agent of the non-causal [action]" (*aṇikartā*) would be non-excludent (*avyāvartaka*), because in your view, the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) is also [included].

Since the meaning of the causative base (*ṇic-prakṛti*) includes the agent of the non-causative (*aṇau*), the instigator (*prayojaka*) is also the agent; this is the general direction [of the argument].
*Prārthanam* means begging (*yācñā*).

(42) *yāsuṭ* is acute (*udātta*) when followed by a *ṅit* affix in the *parasmaipada*. The term *hal* does not apply [here], because in the Bhāṣya it is explained that "the augment *it* occurs before a suffix marked with *ṅ*, and *ṅ* is also marked with *p*"; thus, since the *pit* designation is superseded by the specific rule for *ṅtv*, the *ṅtv* of *yāsuṭ* (which will be discussed under the section beginning with *ad-ādau*) cannot be taken as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Due to this lack of complete satisfaction, he says: *śnaḥ*.

The *s* of *yāsuṭ* is elided because it belongs to the beginning of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) that follows a *jhal* sound. Thus, the form with a single *s* is identical [to the one without *suṭ*]. In the absence of *suṭ*, when the doubling of the *s* of *yāsuṭ* has been performed, and then *suṭ* is added, the *s* of *suṭ* itself undergoes doubling after the elision of the *s* by the rule "koḥ" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 8.2.30).

Since a form with two *s* sounds (*sakāraka*) is exactly the same [as one with one], the prescription of *suṭ* would be useless; therefore, out of dissatisfaction [with that view], he says: "But more clearly," meaning in cases such as *edhiṣīṣṭa*.

(45) "Therefore, by the rule *yeyaḥ* 7.2.80, according to the principle of 'an intermediate exception' (*madhye’pavādanyāya*). The sense is that this principle applies because the term *sārvadhātuka* does not continue [from the previous rule] after the sūtra *rudādibhyaḥ*.

therefore, this is not the case, because even though multiple things are relied upon, the base (*prakṛti*) is not relied upon, as it relies only upon the suffix (*pratyaya*).

(47) *liṅaśiṣi* |3|4|116|. Regarding the designation *ārdhadhātuka*: the particle *eva* from the rule *“aṅḥ śākaṭāyanasyaiva”* must be understood as carrying over [to this rule]. (48) *kidāśiṣi* (Pāṇini 3.4.104). Since the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is already established by the rule *ṅti*, the explicit mention of *kit* is for the purpose of [prohibiting them] in cases such as *ijyāt*.

considering that to be incoherent, they state here the definitive conclusion: in the forms *bhūyāstām*, *bhūyāstam*, and *bhūyāsta*, there is the elision of the *s* of *yāsuṭ* because it is the initial element of a *saṃyoga* following a *jh* sound.

In the case of *bhūyāt*, however, the elision of the *s* of *yāsuṭ* occurs precisely because it is the initial member of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) at the end of a word, just as in the case of *suṭ*. Otherwise,

since the elision of a *jhaṣ* (voiced stop) following a *ra* (repha) would be considered *asiddha*, there would instead be the elision of the final member of the *saṃyoga* by the rule of *saṃyogāntalopa*.

In examples such as *bhṛṣṭa*, the elision of the *jhaL* [consonant] following a *saṃyoga* [cluster], which has its own scope of application, does not subvert the elision of the final member of a *saṃyoga*. (49) *kṅiti ca* 1.1.5.

Regarding the phrase *ṅinnimitte*: it has not been explained as "when followed by a *ṅit* suffix, there is no *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* for an *ik*" [Pāṇini 1.1.5], because that would result in the non-prohibition of the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) in forms such as *cchinnaṃ* and *bhinnam*. The sense is that [the rule] has already achieved its purpose. Others, however, argue that because of the mention of the suffix *kṅti* in the rule *kṅti*, the term *aṅga* (stem) is brought to mind by that suffix;
thus, by interpreting it as "when *kṅt* follows," forms such as *chinnaṃ* and *bhinnam* are indeed established. And it is not the case that [the desired forms] do not occur.

With the intention that [the suffix] might be attached [to the root], it was stated: "before a *kit* or *ṅit* suffix. Why mention *git*? Consider: "the suffix *gsnu* is added after *lā*, *ji*, and *stha*" (*lājisthaśca gsnu*), as in *jiṣṇuḥ*.

If this were a *kit* suffix, however, then in the case of *sthāsnuri* (from *stha* + *snus*), the substitution of *ī* for *a* by the rule "humāsthe" would undesirably apply. Nor is there a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* for *gsnu* when it is *git*, as in *bhūṣṇuḥ* (from *bhū* + *snus*).

It should not be argued that [the substitution of *gsnu* for *bhū*] would not occur because of the acceptance that *gsnu* also applies to *bhū* due to the particle *ca* in the rule *lājisthaśca*; for even in the rule *ṛt-śyukaḥ kiti*, one must explain that by including the letter *ga* through *cartva* (the substitution of *c* for *ṭ*), the suffix *gi* does not apply when a *kit* follows. Nor is this the case.

It should not be argued that because the *cartva* (retroflexion) is not established, the visarga cannot be obtained in the rule *rṭhśyukaḥ*, and thus only the substitution of *u* by *haśi ca* would apply; for [the desired result] is achieved through the sūtra-status [of the rule] and because, in the rule *a mu ne*, the word *na* is separated as a distinct *yogavibhāga*, thereby removing the status of being "not established" (*asiddhatva*).
Vāmana, however, [argues] that because of the *praśleṣa* (splitting) of "ā" from "sthā" in the rule *glājisthaśca*,
there will be no substitution of *i* for *sthā* in the word *sthāsnuḥ* by the rule *humāsthe*; thus,
due to the absence of the *praśleṣa* of the letter *g*, [the rule] *śyukaḥ kitī* does not apply here.

He states that there is no difficulty in establishing the absence of the condition of being a non-existent *ca* suffix by saying, "characterized by an *iK*" (*iglakṣaṇe*). This means when [a suffix] is prescribed as having the designation *ika*. Why "characterized by an *iK*"? [Consider] *laigavāyanaḥ*.
Here, *phaK* is applied because *liṅga* belongs to the *naḍādi* group. In this case, although in reality there is both the initial *vṛddhi* and the *guṇa* of the *o*, [the rule applies].

Even though [the substitute] has the same place of articulation (*iksthānikatva*), there is no prohibition. Nor should one suspect that, even though "ika" is mentioned, a prohibition would not apply here by virtue of the introduction of the rule "iti ca," because that [rule] finds its scope of application in cases such as *nāḍāyana*. [The example] is *bhūyāt*; here, [the rule] "koḥ" applies.

Because the elision (*lopa*) [of the *t*] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the elision of the final consonant of a cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) applicable to the letter *t* is superseded by the elision of the first member of a cluster at the end of a word (*padāntasaṃyogādilopa*), which has no other scope for application. But even so, since the elision of the first member of a cluster is non-existent by the rule "that which precedes is non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), would there not then be the elision of the consonant by the rule "after *hal*, *ī*, etc. (*halṅyādilopa*)?

If it is argued that [the rule for elision] would apply at the end of a word because it finds scope in cases such as *bhṛṭ* and *bhṛḍ* due to the elision of the initial of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*), here they say: since *suṭ* and *asuṭ* are present, that which is qualified by them is itself a suffix (*pratyaya*) and thus lacks the status of being "unaccompanied" (*apṛkta*); therefore, for a stem ending in a consonant (*halanta*), [the rule does not apply].
And because there is an absence of "otherness" (*paratva*), there is no suspicion whatsoever of the aforementioned fault.
