Because the substitution of *bhū* for *ṣṭhā* exists by virtue of being *sthānivadbhāva*, the augment *īṭ* after an unreduplicated (*apṛkta*) consonant would be unavoidable there as well. Likewise, even when there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic* after the roots *gāti*,
*sthā*, *ghu*, *pā*, and *bhū*, by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*, [the properties of *sic* would persist].
Furthermore, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *partavān*, *apāyāt*, *agāt*, *asthāt*, and *abhūt*.

Indicating this, he explains: "si and ca. He states that this is the *bha*-status prescribed by the sūtra; the implication is that because of this, the substitutions of *kutva* and *jaśtva* do not occur here. [He says] "from what exists" (*vidyamānāt*).

The meaning is that [the augment *it*] does not apply to the *sic* that has been elided by the qualifier "existing" (*vidyamāna*), nor to the root *as* after it has undergone the change to *bhū*. However, the authors of the Bhāṣya say: "In the rule *astisico'pṛkte*, this is a reference containing two *s*-sounds. Regarding this, Mādhava says: *as s iti*.

"Since the entire complex [of suffixes] is not a verbal root (*dhātu*), the *śtip* affix would not apply by the rule 'ṭhik-śtipau dhātunirdeśe'. To this, they reply: "The statement that *śtip* would not apply when there is a mention of two *s* sounds is merely a hasty remark. For such is the intention of the Bhāṣya regarding *sic*:"

Immediately after this [word *asti*], the letter *s* is elided (*praśliṣyate*), but not before the *śtip* affix; for this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya that "this citation [of *asti*] contains two *s*s, according to the rule *ico ’pṛkte*. Otherwise, he would have simply said, "the citation *astīti* contains two *s*s"; and thus, from the root *as-* ending in *s*, [the form *asti* is derived].

The meaning of the rule *sāntātsicaḥ* is indeed unimpeded. Furthermore, the second *sakāra* is elided because of the interpretation of the rule *saṃyogāntasya padāntasya*, since the second *sakāra* is considered a "word-final" (*padānta*) by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Nor can it be argued that this is invalid due to the fact that the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*).

It should be stated that the substitution of *u* for *r* (by the rule *ṭhato roḥ*) is difficult to obtain here, because the Vārttika "the elision of the final member of a conjunct [consonant] is not considered *asiddha* when *r* undergoes the *utva* substitution" prohibits its being treated as *asiddha*. However, if one explains [the rule *ṭhato roḥ*] as "that which is the end of a word (*padam*) following a conjunct," then there is no elision of the final member of the conjunct here; rather, [it is the elision of the *visarga*].
Even when *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) is applied to both instances of the syllable *sa*, there will be only a single *u* by virtue of the rule *ṭhato roḥ*;

for the singularity that qualifies the element to be prescribed (*vidheya*) is intended to be significant, just as in the case of the singularity of the animal in the injunction regarding the sacrificial animal (*paśvekatva*). Nor is there any harm even if two *u*s were to exist due to the difference in their original locations (*sthānin*), [as the grammatical operation applies to the single substitute].
It should not be argued that the desired form is established by first applying *savarṇadīrgha* (the lengthening of similar vowels) and then *ādguṇa* (the guṇa substitution for *a* + *u*),

because since *ādguṇa* is *antaraṅga* (internal) as it depends on a single word, the substitution of *av* would apply subsequently, resulting in the failure to obtain the form *ahastisico ’pṛkte*. Therefore, according to the reasoning stated, there is only one *ukāra*.

Thus it must be accepted. For this very reason, because the singular number inherent in the element to be prescribed (*vidheya*) is intended to be significant, the mention of the word "one" (*eka*) in the rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* was rejected in the Bhāṣya and other works. Now, one might object: the *ru* that occurs when *ati* follows is not "after" (*para*) the *at*, nor is that which is "after" (*para*) the *at* preceded by *ati*.

How could there be the substitution of *u* for *r* in the place of *ru*? It is not so; for since the rule *ṛto ṅsirvanāmasthānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.110) is stated by referring to the genus (*jāti*), both the status of being subsequent (*paratva*) and preceding (*pūrvatva*) are possible.
Nor should it be argued that even so, because of its subsequent position, the *u* would apply only to the first *r* by the rule *haśi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.114).

Because the substitution of *ru* is considered *asiddha*, there is an absence of a following *haś* sound. Nor should it be argued that this constitutes an "unestablished basis" (*āśrayāsiddhatva*), for even if such were the case regarding the element to be replaced (*sthānin*), it cannot apply to the *haś* sound which serves as the cause (*nimitta*). Although, given the unity of the class *sat*, only a single *ru* would occur for both [the *s* and the *r*], according to this interpretation, this [objection] does not hold.

Nevertheless, they say that although the rule for *ru* (the substitution of *u*) applies, because the term *pada* is understood to carry over from the preceding sūtra, the condition of being "at the end of a single word" (*ekapadāntatva*) cannot be fulfilled;
this is because the second *s* constitutes a separate word. Regarding the rule *apṛktasya halaḥ*:
the statement by the ancients, *apṛktasārvadhātukasya*, has been rejected.
Because there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) in cases such as *aidhiṣi*, and because no instances to be excluded by the mention of *sārvadhātuka* could be found.
(56) *ātaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.110.
The term *sic* is understood from the previous rule, as is *jher jus*. After *sic* and after [a verbal root ending in] *ā*, *jus* is substituted for *jhi*.

In that case, the position of being subsequent (*paratva*) to *sic* is established by means of the technical designation of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), whereas its position subsequent to *ā* is established by direct hearing (*śruti*). Thus...

Regarding the established point, he states the result: "by *sijlukī*. This means by the rule *ātistheṭ*. Since the substitution of *jus* for *jhi* is already established even after a root ending in long *ā* by the preceding rule *ijyabhyaste*, he says—regarding this established point—that the present rule is for the purpose of restriction: "only after a root ending in long *ā*."

(57) *Liṅ* is used when there is a cause (*liṅ-nimitta*) and there is a failure of the action (*kriyātipatti*). Regarding the phrase "from the relation of cause and effect, etc.," some explain that by the word "etc. (*ādi*), "words expressing hope" (*āśaṃsā-vacana*) are included; thus, even in the case of *liṅ* used with words expressing hope, when there is a cause for it...

In the case of the non-occurrence of an action (kriyātipatti), the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is used; for example, they cite such instances as: "If the teacher had come, I would have studied," and so forth. Others, however, maintain that starting from the rule "in the future tense" (*bhaviṣyati*) and "in the sense of a limit" (*maryādā*), the conditional suffix *liṅ* is prescribed only when those specific conditions are present.

They say that the *lṛṅ* suffix occurs when there is a non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*), and not otherwise. Regarding the phrase "when there is a cause for the *liṅ*": this will become clear in the section on the derivation of verbal suffixes (*lakārārtha-prakriyā*) under rules such as *hetuhetumator liṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.156) and *icchārtheṣu liṅloṭau* (Pāṇini 3.3.157). The term "non-accomplishment" (*aniṣpatti*) refers to this.
"If there had been rain, then there would have been plenty"— he will cite this very example later [at 3.3.139]. (58) *te prāgdhātoḥ* | 1.4.80.

The meaning is that [the augment] does not occur after another word, nor when separated [by intervening elements]. For this very reason, it is prescribed in the sūtras: "In the Vedic language, even when [the suffix] follows," and "even when separated. (59) *āni loṭ* | 8|4|16|

Although it would have been sufficient to say simply "after *loṭ*," the inclusion of the term *āṅ* is intended to indicate that the rules concerning augments (*āgama-śāstra*) are not universally obligatory (*anitya*). By this, forms such as *āgaṃ tartukāmasya* and *aptvā stotram* are established.
The mention of *loṭ* is for the sake of clear understanding. [The objection] "and [the word *prāśu* does not apply to] those whose *vapā* (omentum) is excellent... is not valid.
Regarding the form *tāni pravapāni māṃsāni*, one might argue that the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* should always occur here by this very rule;

however, it does not apply because of the mention of "upasarga" (preverb) and the mention of "meaningful [elements]" (*arthavat*). On the other hand, the optional substitution of *ṇ* according to the rule "at the end of a nominal stem" (*prātipadikānte*) occurs precisely because of this [mention of the preverb].

Regarding the rule *duraḥ ṣatvaṇatvayoḥ upasargatvapratiṣedho vaktavyaḥ* ("It must be stated that *dus-* is not an upasarga for the purposes of the rules concerning the substitution of *ṣ* and *ṇ*"): as for the statement by the Easterners (*prācām*) that "there is no *ṇatva* for what follows *dus-*," that is incorrect. For if that were so, *ṇatva* would occur according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), and that would contradict the presence of the vowel *ā*. This is the intended meaning.

The status of *antaḥ* as a preposition (*upasarga*) must be stated in rules concerning the suffix *aṅ*, the suffix *ki*, and the substitution of *ṇ*. Thus, in *antarddhā*, [the suffix] *aṅ* is applied by the rule *ātaścopasarge*; then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. In *antardhiḥ*, [the suffix] *ki* is applied by the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*.
Furthermore, the status of the word *śrac* as a preposition is added as a supplementary statement (*upasaṅkhyāna*) in the rule for the application of *aṅ*.

It has been disregarded because it is not useful for the present context, and because its meaning is already established either by its inclusion in the *bhidādi* group or by the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*) "rañja-śraddha.
(60) *Śeṣe vibhāṣā akakhādāvaṣānta upadeśe* [Pāṇini 8.4.18].

Regarding the phrase "other than *gadanada*," he says that this is a remainder (*śeṣa*) with respect to what was stated in the Sūtra: "in something other than *gada*, *nada*, etc. Why [is it specified] "in the Upadeśa"? [So that] the prohibition may also apply in cases such as *pranicakāra* and *pranicakhāda*. Why [is it specified] "not ending in *ṣ* or *h*"?

It crushes (*praṇipiṇaṣṭi*). Because of the inclusion of the term "instruction" (*upadeśagrahaṇāt*), it will be crushed (*praṇipekṣyate*). [In the rule] *akṣiṅḥ kśāñ*, there is also a prohibition regarding *praṇicakśe*. The mention of the word "remainder" (*śeṣagrahaṇa*) is for the sake of clarity. Since the rule for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) has the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "in *saṃhitā*," when *saṃhitā* is not intended, there is no *ṇatva*.

One should not entertain the doubt: "Since the substitution of *ṇ* is already established as an option by the rule regarding *saṃhitā*, what is the purpose of this mention of *vibhāṣā*? To this he says: "In this case, of the prefixes," and so forth.

Although the result is already established by the phrase "in a single word" (*ekapade*) alone, the inclusion of the term "compound" (*samāsa*) is according to the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*).

"Bodhyam" (it should be understood). Regarding "vākye tu" (but in a sentence): the meaning is that this *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) is dependent upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), and is not obligatory (*nitya*) here. Regarding "upalakṣaṇam": this is also the consensus of Bhīmasena, who provided the definition of the meanings of *sat* and so forth, as seen in the passage: "urda khurda gurda guda... [and so on].

The particle *eva* in the phrase "only in the sense of play" (*krīḍāyām eva*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Furthermore, in the rule "of the root *edh* in the sense of going" (*edhater gatau*), the mention of "in the sense of going" (*gatāv*) is appropriate only if it is intended as an illustration for the full range of meanings such as "to rise" (*idha gatyām*), and not otherwise. This is the general direction [of the argument]. [The phrase] "from meanings such as 'it arises'" (*utpadyata ity-ādy-arthāt*) is used; and thus, the prefix (*upasarga*)...

The point is that even in cases such as *udbhavati* ("arises"), where the meaning of arising is understood even without [the prefix], the prefix employed is merely indicative (*dyotaka*) and not expressive (*vācaka*). This is expressed by the rule "the meaning of the root is [modified] by the prefix. For this very reason, it was also stated by Amara: "Conversation is talk; idle chatter is meaningless speech."
"Anulāpa is speaking repeatedly; vilāpa is lamentation;
vipralāpa is contradictory speech; saṃlāpa is conversation between two; supralāpa is eloquent speech; and apalāpa is concealment."

(61) *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere* (Pāṇini 7.1.5). Now, one might object: since the suffix *śānac* is also an *ātmanepada* that takes the place of a *la*-suffix, shouldn't *ṭer* (the substitution of *e*) apply in forms such as *pacamānaḥ* and *yajamānaḥ*? To this, they say:

There is no fault, because the *tib* and other affixes are qualifiers of the *ātmanepada* affixes. However, it would be more appropriate to state the rule simply as: "In place of the *ṭi* of *taṅ*, [there is *e*].
(62) *thāsaḥ se* | 3.4.80 | [In place of *thās*, there is *se*.]

The pronunciation of the letter *e* is for the purpose of making it known; this will become clear in the rule *iṭastajhayoḥ*. Therefore, regarding the phrase *ato guṇe*: once the substitution of *e* for *iṭ* has been made, although *vṛddhi* would have applied by overriding *ādguṇaḥ*, the present rule prescribes the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) instead.

(63) *ijādeśca gurumato ’nṛcchaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.1.36. He explains that the term *dhātu* ("root") is carried over from the rule *hātorekācaḥ*, while *ām* and *liṭi* are carried over from the rule *āspratyayāt*. Thus he says: "A root beginning with *ij* which is heavy," and so forth. "Heavy" (*gurumān*)...
What? He desired; he honored you who were worthy of honor.

(64) *āmaḥ* |2|4|81|. By the maxim "that which is explicitly stated [in the rule] (*pratipadokta*)" and the maxim "when a suffix is mentioned (*pratyayagrahaṇa*)," it is not [the case here that] *ām*, *āmatuḥ*, etc., [are meant]. [The rule applies to the genitive ending] *ām* [of the second person plural], because of the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*parasay luk*). [This is understood] from the rule *antre ghase*.

Carrying over [the word] *sūtrāt* from the previous rule, it is explained in the *Kāśikā* and other works that there is elision (*luk*) of the affix; however, that is disregarded here because there is nothing to be excluded [by such an interpretation].
Since this [elision] is an exception to the *tiṅ* and other affixes, this very elision occurs in the state of the *lā* suffix. Therefore—

Because the suffix *ām* is not a finite verb (*tiṅ*), even when it follows words such as *devadatta*, there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) by the rule "iṅṅtiṅḥ. The meaning [of the rule] is that the *nighāta* applies to a finite verb (*tiṅ*) that follows *ām*. Nor does it follow that, because it is not a finite verb, it lacks the status of a word (*pada*), and thus the *nighāta* of what follows *ām* cannot be established.

It might be suspected [of this fault]: because the *liṭ* suffix is marked with *k*, by the rule of "suffixal indication" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), it is a *kṛdanta*; thus, being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the case ending *su* arises.
Then, although the *su* is elided because the suffix *ām* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), by the rule of "suffixal indication," it remains a word (*pada*) because it is a "suffix-ending" (*subanta*).

(65) *kṛñ* is employed after [a verbal root] when the *liṭ* suffix follows. How then [is it explained] in such cases as: “He first caused himself to fall (*pātayām āsa*), then he fell (*papāta*)”? And:
“He who caused Nahuṣa to fall (*aṃśayām cakāra*)”? This is simply an error. It is not [correct].

It should not be argued that because the *sūtra* intends merely to exclude erroneous application, a subsequent application does not incur fault even if it is separated [by other rules], for this would contradict the *vārttika*: "For the purpose of excluding inversion and for the purpose of excluding what is separated. [Regarding the phrase] "of another as well": if here...

The point is that if only the single root *kṛ* were understood by the word *kṛñ*, then because no other root would be applicable, the qualification "of *kṛ*" in the rule *ṭhām-pratyayavat* (Pāṇini 3.1.40)— which prescribes the subsequent application [of the suffix]—
would be redundant. Nor is it the case here that [the rule applies to] "the root *kṛ*."

It might be suspected that by the word "eva" (only) it is understood that the suffix *anuprayoga* (subsequent application) belongs to another [verb] as well; however, this is not the case, because the rule is exhausted by providing the sense that "the suffix *ām* shall be added to the verbal root, and *kṛñ* shall be subsequently applied when followed by *liṭ*. [Furthermore,] there is a relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*).

The point is that the non-differentiation and co-referentiality (*abhedānvaya*) between the general and the particular is established by worldly convention. And thus, in cases such as *edhāñcake* and *edhāmbabhūve*, the cognition is identical: [it is] an action non-different from growth, performed by a single agent, in the past, not of today, and beyond direct perception. Now, one might object: "But the root *kṛ* is transitive (*sakarmaka*)."

If it is asked, "Since *bhavati* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), how can there be equality here?", they say in response: When the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is used independently in the sense of production—such as "he made a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ cakre*) or "he ruled a kingdom" (*rājyaṃ cakāra*)—then it is necessarily transitive (*sakarmaka*). But when...

The verb *karoti* (to do) is employed as having the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*) as another action—such as in "he performed the oblation" (*juhavāñcakāra*) and so forth; in that case, by virtue of whether that [other action] with which *karoti* shares its locus is transitive or intransitive, it itself likewise assumes that same character. Thus...
It should be understood that even the roots *bhū* and *as* can occasionally be transitive when they share the same locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the base form of the *ām*-affix.
For this very reason, because the root *bhū* used in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) is transitive, the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) occurs in the objective sense (*karmani*).
Thus says Māgha: “He bore the parasol” (*asyātapatraṃ bibharāṃbabhūve*), and so too Śrīharṣa.
"...even apart from [the usual] offerings, masses of fat were borne throughout the nights.

Here, this should be noted: in expressions such as *juhāva*, *juhavāṃcakāra*, and *juhavāṃbabhūva*, only the act of offering (*homa*) is understood; however, in the other case (the verse cited), the understanding is that of an action consisting of the act of offering. Regarding the result (*phala*):

However, there is no distinction [between them], just as in the case of "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*) versus "bring the substance-jar" (*dravya-ghaṭam ānaya*). And thus, the result of the auxiliary verb (*anuprayoga*) is the manifestation of distinctions such as the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), the state of becoming (*gati*), the kāraka, and the number. Regarding the term *ananvita*: there is no syntactic connection (*abhedānvaya*) between the meaning of the suffix *ām* and the meaning of the verbal root to which it is attached.
The meaning is that it is possible, because both possess the nature of being specific forms.
(66) Regarding *āmpratyayavat kṛño ’nuprayogasya* 1.3.63:
[the sūtra says] *āmpratyayavat*. Since there is no ātmanepada for a form ending in the suffix *ām*, he says "not possessing that quality" (*atadguṇa*).
"From that which is employed as equivalent to the root by its very nature"—this means that *vati* follows a word ending in the third case.

The sense is that in the term *anuprayogasya*, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Because the word from *anudātetaḥ* is understood to follow [from the previous rule], he says: "the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) shall occur. Thus, [it concerns] that which was not previously obtained.
Since it is not possible to prohibit what has already been established even by this very sūtra through its formulation, he says:

"by means of a split in the sentence" (*vākyabhedena*). And the authority for this is the very statement "like the *ām* affix" (*āmpratyayavat*). Otherwise, by the mere continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of "as before" (*pūrvavat*), the subsequent employment of the root *kṛ* after the *ām* affix would be [governed] by the preceding rule.
Since the desired result is achieved by obtaining the meaning "equal" (*tulyam*), what is the use of that [rule] which states "the suffix *tha* becomes *ām*"? (Pāṇini 7.1.37).
Regarding the rule *liṭas tajhayoḥ eś irec* (Pāṇini 3.4.81):
the inclusion of the letter *ś* in *eś* is for the purpose of ensuring that the *t* sound, characterized by the letters *e* and *ś*, functions as a substitute.

(68) *asaṃyogāl liṭ kit* (Pāṇini 1.2.5): Why does the rule specify "not after a conjunct consonant"? [Consider: *mamanthe*. Here, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) does not occur. (69) *dvirvacane 'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59).

In this regard, a secondary metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted for the word *dvirvacana* with respect to its cause, in order to achieve grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Alternatively—*vacana* means "that which is spoken"; that vowel (*ac*) in which there is a twofold speaking (*dviḥ-vacana*) is called *dvirvacana*. Or else, it is derived from the *arśa-ādi* group, meaning "that in which there is a twofold speaking. This is what he states:

Regarding the phrase "dvitvanimitte’ci": here, from the rule *ṭhacaḥ parasmin* (P. 1.1.57), the word *aci* is understood; from *sthānivadādeśaḥ* (P. 1.1.56), the word *ādeśaḥ* is understood; and from *na padānte* (P. 8.2.23), the word *na* is understood. Thus he says: "there would be no substitute for the vowel (*ac*). Although in the *Vṛtti* and other such works—

The view that there is an extension of form (*rūpātideśa*)—namely, "the substitute for *ṭh* and so on shall be as the original"—has been accepted, and the result is the same in both cases; nevertheless, since the view that prohibits the substitute (*ādeśapratiṣedha*) is also established in the Bhāṣya, that very one is accepted here.
Furthermore, rather than accepting the substitute and then resorting again to the form of the original, [this latter view is preferred].

An interpretation focused on prohibition alone is indeed simpler, according to the maxim: "It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off. Furthermore, since this is the case, the fact that [the rule] is recited immediately after the prohibition "not at the end of a word" (a padānte) is also supported; thus, this position is superior.

Repeating the phrase "dvirvacane" (in the case of reduplication) according to the desired interpretation, he explains it as being intended to determine the time [of the application of the rule]: "when reduplication is to be performed. The sense is that once the reduplication has been performed, the substitution (ādeśa) shall indeed take place accordingly. What is the purpose of specifying the cause for reduplication? [Consider] the example *dudyaūṣati*.

Because of the priority of doubling (*dvitva*) over *ūṭh*, if doubling were to occur before *yaṇ* substitution, then the undesired form *didyaūṣati* would result. To prevent this, it is stated that [the rule applies] "when there is a cause for doubling. Indeed, *ūṭh* is not the cause of doubling. Why [is the condition] "before a vowel" (*aci*) specified? [Consider: *jeghrīyate*, *dedhmīyate*.

The ancient grammarians [hold that] the rule *śāśayyate*—whereby the substitution of *ī* by the rule *ṭhī ghrāghmoḥ* and the substitution of *iy* by the rule *ṭhayaṅ yi kṅti* would otherwise be prohibited—is stated so that those substitutions do not occur. Others, however, say:
the mention of *aci* is redundant; for [the forms] *ghrīy*, *dhmīy*, and *śayy* [are established].

The second [reason] is that, because the single vowel (*ekāc*) following the limit of the *aj* (vowels) is the subject of the operation, it lacks the status of being the cause for the doubling of the *yaṅ*. Why [specify] "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*)? Consider *asūṣupat*. Here, when the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) prescribed by the rule "vā caṅi" is prohibited, the *u*-vowel does not [occur] in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

It would be heard [as such]. And even when the doubling has occurred, as in the case of *ṭhyūna*, there is a prohibition of the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the preceding *yaṇ* by the rule *na saṃprasāraṇe*. This might be argued: in *cakratuḥ*, since the prohibition does not apply to the substitute for a vowel (*ac*), the *yaṇ* would indeed occur. [This is so] because of the suffix *atus*.

Even though *a* is the cause for doubling (*dvitva*), it does not possess that status [of being the cause] here. Nor is the rule *virvacane’ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59) redundant, because it finds its scope of application in forms such as *cakre*. Thus, since there is an absence of "being a single syllable" (*ekāctva*), doubling would not occur here by the rule *iṭi dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.1). If this is argued, do not say so; for here—

Because, in accordance with the requirements of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*), everything that serves as the cause for doubling—whether directly by the word "dvitvanimitta" or by being a constituent of the aggregate—is included;
this is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra *hasyekaḥ*. Thus, in the case of the root *ūrṇu* followed by the suffix *san*:

In the alternative where the suffix is not treated as *ṅit*—by the rule *vibhāṣorṇoḥ*—the form *ūrṇunaviṣati* is established. Even though reduplication (*dvitva*) is prescribed for the desiderative (*sannanta*), since the *san* suffix is the cause of reduplication, when it follows, the operations of guṇa and the substitution of *av* (for *o*) would apply; however, [these are superseded] by reduplication.

Because there is a prohibition regarding what ought to be done. For this very reason, they say: "In this context, the status of being a cause [for doubling] exists merely by the fact of not being sublated by the augment *ad*. And thus it is established that, as part of the cause for doubling, both the augment *iṭ* of the suffix *san* and the vowel *a* of the root *at* are causes for doubling. But if this is so, then in the case of a root ending in *ṛ* with *san*...

If the augment *iṭ* were applied by the rule "sanīṭ ca" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.49) after roots ending in *m*, *p*, *ṛ*, *u*, *ṝ*, *añj*, and *vaś*, then— given that the guna substitution caused by the sound *is* would be prohibited by the rule "virvacane'ci" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.59)—

the reduplication of the second syllable would apply to the whole under the rule "ajāderdvitīyasya" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.2), and thus the form *aririṣati* would not be established. [This is because] the [reduplication] caused by the sound *ris*...

If it is argued that although [the substitution of] *ṛ* for *ri* is established here, nevertheless the word *ri* itself remains difficult to obtain when there is a negation of the *guṇa* vowel, they say in response:

"When *ra* is substituted for the *guṇa*, it is relied upon as a cause [for the subsequent operation], because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *‘śaṇḍilācchayitari vrata’*. Otherwise, [the rule] *‘śīṅo ṅtvaḥ’*..."

Because of the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule "ṅiti ca," the form *śayitṛ* would result in being unestablished. Nor should it be argued that the explanation "when *ṅit* follows, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* do not occur" does not serve as a *jñāpaka* (indicative proof) for the stated meaning in the case of *śayitṛ*; for if that were the explanation, [the forms] *chinnaṃ* and *bhinnam* [would be unaccounted for].

This is because the fault—that there would be no negation of the *guṇa* substitution and so forth—has already been demonstrated in the very sūtra "aṅiti ca. Nor, in this way, by not resorting to the status of the cause (*nimitta*) for that which undergoes the operation (*kāryin*), [does the rule fail], since the desiderative stem (*sannanta*) is the subject undergoing the operation; therefore, after that *san*, [the rule applies].

It should not be argued that *ūrṇunaviṣati* would also be impossible because there is no prohibition against the occurrence of *guṇa* and *ādeśa* once they have been attained; for by means of the possessive suffix *-in*, only that which actually undergoes an operation can be considered the "subject" (*kāryin*) of that operation.
In the case of the root *ūrṇ*, it is the element *nu* itself that undergoes the operation of reduplication, and not the suffix *san*.
But in the case of *aririṣati*, the word *ris* is the part that undergoes the grammatical operation; thus there is a disparity.

(70) *ekāca upadeśe'nudātāt* [Pāṇini 7.2.10]: it is connected to both. Because it is read in the middle, by the maxim of the "lamp on the threshold" (*dehalī-dīpa-nyāya*), it applies to both the preceding and the following rules.

The meaning is that it is connected [to the preceding]. In that context, the result of its connection with what follows is the prohibition of the *iṇ* augment in forms such as *kartum* and *gantum*, because [the suffix] is currently acute by virtue of the *nit*-accent. However, the prohibition of the *iṇ* augment in forms such as *pipakṣati* and *bibhatsati* is the result of its connection with what precedes, provided there is doubling (*dvitva*).

Because [the root] has multiple vowels (*anekāctvāt*) when the suffix is applied. Now, one might object: "Since it is stated 'of a monosyllabic root' (*ekācaḥ*), a connection with the word 'in the original enunciation' (*upadeśa*) must also be accepted; therefore, let that [word 'enunciation'] not be used at all, for the desired result is achieved by the rule 'anudātta in the original enunciation' (*upadeśe'nudāttāt*) alone.

To this, he raises the objection: "Why [specify] 'of a monosyllabic root'? [The answer is: even in the case of *yaṅ*-luṅ, as in *pipakṣati* and so forth, there would be a prohibition of the augment *iṇ*.

Anticipating this very doubt, he says: "There is no *ṇatva*. For example, as in *bhara*. Consequently, in the case of *bibhariṣati* from the root *bhṛ* with the suffix *san*, the optional *iṭ* prescribed by the rule "anītvaṃtarde" does not apply;
rather, *iṭ* is obligatory. This is because the prohibition "ekāca" (for monosyllabic roots) does not apply here. [The mention is] by means of an indicatory letter (*anubandha*).

It is twofold: by way of its own form (*svarūpa*) and by way of being designated as an *it* (an indicatory letter). An example by way of its own form is: “There is *guṇa* substitution for *īṅ* before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix,” and “*yuṭ* is added after *īṅ* before a vowel. The forms *śeśitaḥ* and *dedyitaḥ* are examples in sequence for the suffixes *tasi* and *kta*. An example by way of being designated as an *it* is as follows:

[Regarding the rule] "ṭhanudātahitaḥ": because of this, the ātmanepada [suffixes] do not apply after roots such as *spardh* or *śīṅ*, according to the rule "ṭhanudātaṅtiḥ". Thus: *pāspardhīti*; *śeśayīti*. As for the examples from the [dhātu-]gaṇa: *bebhidīti*.
[Here] *śnam* is applied by the rule "udhādibhyaḥ". The mention of "ekāc" (single-vowel) is in the present sūtra; therefore, [the form] *bebheditā* [is derived].
In forms such as *cecchidita*, there is no prohibition of the augment *iṇ*. Regarding the phrase "and this":

one should not suspect how this can be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) with respect to the portion consisting of *śtip* or *śap*, because it has been observed in rules such as *upapadam atiṅ* that an indication applies everywhere by means of the admission of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). For this very reason, in that [rule]...

It has been stated that the rule regarding the formation of compounds between words ending in *kṛt* suffixes and words beginning with *ati*, *kāra*, or *upa*—occurring prior to the addition of case endings—is established. This is because such a rule can be inferred from the very forms of *syati*, *hanti*, *bhareti*, and so forth, which are taught with the *śtip* and other markers and serve no other purpose. This is also evident in the rule *aparasparāḥ*.

We have already stated in that very place that by the inclusion of the term *sātatyam* (continuity), the verse of the ancient masters beginning with *ekadeśānumatyā ‘umped avaśyamaḥ kṛtye’* is indicated; however,
in the *Manoramā*, [it is argued] that through the principle of assenting to a partial statement (*ekadeśānumati*), [the rule] refers to the *paribhāṣā* recited by the ancient masters.
It has been stated that the purpose [of the rule] is to provide an indication (*jñāpana*), because such a usage is observed in rules like *atikārakopapadānām* and so forth;

however, the moderns (*navya*) maintain that this is incorrect. For the rule *atikārakopapadānām* and its like is indeed a technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācāryas*). And it is not logical to claim that the indication of that maxim is observed in that very same rule.

Regarding the phrase "to speak": [the word] "tadvataḥ" (possessing that). Nor is there a lack of evidence for the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), because the very fact that words such as *vasati* are recited with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*) serves as proof in this regard.
Furthermore, the unaccented recitation has not been lost even now, as it is maintained by modern scholars.

It should not be suspected that the reading *vasati-śalaki*, etc., lacks authority because it is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*); for those very roots marked as *anudātta* (unaccented) by Pāṇini were subsequently compiled by the successive tradition of modern commentators. Otherwise, [the rule] "that which has one vowel" (*eko’c yasya*)...

Even though the mention of "single" (eka) was made for the sake of obtaining a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because the reading of the *anudātta* accent has been lost, there would be no determination that "roots such as *vasati* and *śaklā* are *anudātta*, but not roots such as *bhū* and *edh*" [if the rule were otherwise]. Regarding the mention of "single" (*ekagrahaṇa*): [an objection is raised] "But surely it is the mention of 'single-vowel' (*ekāj*)..."

If it is argued that after stating "for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ [formation]," one would then face a mutual contradiction by saying "by the force of the mention of the word 'one' (*eka*) again," they reply here:
It is not the case that the mention of the term "one-vowel" (*ekāc*) by means of the word "one" is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ; rather—

The apprehension of "one" (ekāj) occurs precisely because of the vast scope [of the term]; and since that apprehension of "one" is obtained even without [explicitly stating] "that," there is no fault.

Regarding the word *vadheḥ*: as for the exclusion of roots ending in 'a' (*adanta-paryudāsa*) mentioned by Vyāghrabhūti in the *aniṭ-kārikās* in order to exclude that [case], that very point was followed by the ancients.

"Roots ending in vowels that consist of a single syllable, excluding those ending in *ṭha*, *dṛ*, *dṛ*, *anta*, *ru*, *sruk*, *ṣṇu*, *śī*, *yu*, *nu*, *kṣu*, *śvi*, *ḍīṅ*, *śri*, *vṛ*, and *vṛñ*, are aniṭ (do not take the augment *i*). This exclusion of roots ending in *ā* has been disregarded here because it is inconsistent with the rules of the grammatical sūtras. For instance, it is stated: "All substitutes for words [in the place of a word] are [treated as] the whole word (*sarva-pada-ādeśāḥ*)."
According to this principle, just as the substitution of *ka-* for *ṛ-* and so forth— having been grasped according to the original instruction (*sthānyupadeśa*)—

triggers the application of the prohibition in forms such as *kartā* and *hartā*, who could possibly prevent that same prohibition from applying even in the case of the substitute *vadh-*? If it is argued that this is due to the force of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of stems ending in *a*, we say no.
The sense is that [the root] has not been excluded by the author of the Sūtras.
(71) *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvaṃluṅliṭāṃ dho’ṅgāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.78).

Although there is the governing rule *iṇkoḥ* (8.3.57), the mention of *iṇ* again [in this sūtra] is for the sake of [indicating that the substitution applies to] a *dh* following a *ka*-class consonant.
This is for the purpose that [the rule] should not apply here. Therefore, one does not say *likṣīdhvam*. [The phrase] "of those following an *aṅga*" is used;

for if it were stated as "of those prescribed [after an *aṅga*]," there would be non-application (*avyāpti*) in the case of *dāña* in *luṅ* (e.g., *adāt*), where the augment *iṭ* is added in *iddhavam*.
However, in the case of *lih*, *duh*, and *nah*, when *ḍhatva*, *ghatva*, and *dhatva* are applied, [the forms] *likṣīdhvam* and *dhukṣīdhvam* [would result].
It should be understood that there would also be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of *natsīdhvam*. Why [is it said] "from the *aṅga*"?
[Consider] *veviṣīdhvam*. Although, because of the inclusion of *ṣīdhvam* as having a meaningful [suffix], [the rule] would apply only to cases like *kṛṣīdhvam* and not here.

Nevertheless, this was stated in order to indicate that a non-technical term (*aparibhāṣā*) which possesses a specific meaning does not apply everywhere. By this, the rule "the mention of *ṭhan*, *ini*, and *asman*" is established.
This applies to forms such as *edhām-babhūva* and others, according to the sūtra "before the suffix *ām*."

Because of the inclusion of the root *kṛ*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings do not apply in other instances of subsequent application (*anuprayoga*); thus, by the rule "after *eṣa* when the agent is expressed," only the *parasmaipada* occurs.

However, in the case of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), it would indeed occur—as in *tedhāṃbabhūve* and *īkṣāṃbabhūve*. But regarding the root *as*, once the *taṅ* has been applied for the abstract action and the object, there is a disagreement concerning the forms when *eiś* and *iṭ* are added.

For instance: in both cases, when the substitution of *ha* for *eti* has been applied, some say that [the forms] are *edhāmahe* and *īkṣāmahe*. Others hold that, by association with *tāsi*, the substitution of *ha* applies only to the augment *iṭ* and not to *eś*.
Precisely because of that association, the substitution of *ha* for *eti* occurs only in the case of a sārvadhātuka suffix. And thus:

In the case of the reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*), the suffix *taṅ* (the *ātmanepada*) occurs only in the rule *vyatīhāre taṅ*, and not in the two cases mentioned above. Therefore, others maintain that the forms are simply *edhāmāse* and *īkṣāmāse*. Regarding the expression *kṛbhvi-iti*:
although there would be brevity (*lāghava*) if one had simply said *kṛñ*, nevertheless, [the term *kṛbhvi*] is used for the sake of obtaining both roots.
The sense is that there would be difficulty in resorting to *pratyāhāra*.
(72) Regarding the rule *ata ādeḥ* 6.4.70, the term "exception" (*apavāda*) refers to this very word "exception."
This contradicts one's own work situated within the *Nāmadhātuprakriyā*; for therein it is stated: "He acts like 'a'—*ati*.

Having brought forward the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*), it is called a *nāman* because of the rule "after *kāsi*, that which has more than one vowel" (*kāsyanekāc*). [The forms] *āṬ*, *atuḥ*, and *uḥ* [are derived];
there is reduplication, and by the rules "*ata upadhāyāḥ*" (P. 7.2.116) and "*ata ādeḥ*" (P. 7.2.115), there is lengthening; [finally], *āṬ* is the substitute for *ṇal*.

Because it has been stated that [the rule] "vṛddhi" applies; and since the substitution of the long vowel by "ata ādeḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.102) occurs earlier than the application of "halādiḥ śeṣaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.60) due to its higher status in the order of rules, there is not even a suspicion of *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form) in that case— thus, the modern grammarians (*navyāḥ*) consider this passage to be worthy of reflection.

(73) *āḍajādīnām* |6|4|72|. This rule has been rejected by the author of the Vārttika on the grounds that it is already accomplished by the augment *aṭ* for roots beginning with vowels. [Objection: Granted that forms such as *aidhata* are established by the rule *vṛddhireci* even when *aṭ* is applied, [forms] such as *aindat* would not be.
[Otherwise,] it would not be established. Furthermore, by the application of the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule in *ato guṇe*, forms such as *aidhata* would also not be established.
If, however, the sūtra *āṭaśca* were made *aṭaśca*, then in *asvapaḥ* and *ahasat*, there would be *vṛddhi*. [And regarding] *rudaśca pañcabhyaḥ*...

If it is argued that [the substitution of *u* for *ru*] does not occur because the augment *aṭ* applies by the rule "ṭhaṅgārgyagālavayoḥ," and because *ru* becomes *u* by the rule "ato ror aplutāt" due to being followed by a vowel (*ac*), we say no; for, having extracted the word "dhātau" from the rule "upasargād ṛti dhātau," the explanation is that [the substitution occurs] when the root begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). Nor is this the case...

It should not be argued that in forms such as *asvapaḥ*, the aforementioned defect remains unavoidable because the vowel *o* (in *asvapaḥ*) is treated as the final element (*antavadbhāva*), thereby becoming an *aṭ*, and because a root beginning with *ā* follows; for this is refuted by interpreting the rule as "there is *vṛddhi* after an *aṭ* consisting of the letter *a* when followed by an *ac*," by carrying forward the word *āt* from the previous sūtra. By this same reasoning, the objection that if one were to state simply *aṭaśca*, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *aṭanam*—derived from the root *ṭhaṭ* (meaning "to go") with the suffix *lyuṭ*—is also dispelled. Nor does it follow that forms such as *ātat* and *ātīt* would remain unestablished even under this interpretation.

It should not be argued that, because the rule *ṭhaṭaśca* has its scope in cases such as *aiṇḍadi* (from *aiṇḍada*), it prevails here by virtue of being subsequent to the rule *ṭhato guṇe*; for we accept that the *ca* in this [rule *ṭhaṭaśca*] is intended to re-enjoin the *vṛddhi*. Alternatively, due to its being *antaraṅga*, it is precisely the rule *ṭhaṭaśca* that applies. One might object: "In the absence of the sūtra *āḍajādīnām*, how would *āstām* and *āsan* be formed? For, by the elision of *ā* via the rule *anasoḥ*, the rule *ṭhaṭaśca* would not apply there to effect the *vṛddhi*. This is not so.

Because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the augment *āṬ* is applied first, and once the vṛddhi has been effected, the elision of the *a* of *śna* and *as* does not subsequently apply. Nor should one suspect that, according to the maxim "that which pertains to a vowel is stronger than that which pertains to an operation" (*vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ*), the elision itself would occur prior to the vṛddhi; for this is precluded because the two operations depend on different bases (*vyāśrayatvāt*), or because the paribhāṣā "that which pertains to a vowel is stronger than that which pertains to an operation" is not universal (*anitya*). In that regard, the very use of the long vowel marker *ta* (in *śnasoḥ*) in the rule "elision of the *a* of *śna* and *as*" (*śnasorallopaḥ*) is the proof: if the elision were to occur prior to the vṛddhi, what would be the purpose of that *ta*-marker?

Although, in the Vedic procedure, one might argue that the rule for the augment *āṭ* must be formulated because the augment *āṭ* will be prescribed later by the rule "it is also seen in the Veda" (*chandasyāpi dṛśyate*) in cases such as *ānaṭ* and *āva*, they state the solution for this established position: even without *āṭ*, it can somehow be explained there either through the transposition (*vyatyaya*) of *āṭ* or by treating it as preceded by *āṅ*.

(74) Regarding *liṅaḥ sīyuṭ* 3.4.102, [the phrase] "elision of *s*" refers to the rule "there is elision of the non-final *s* of *iṅ*" (*iṅaḥ salopo’nantyasya*). [The example] *edheyātām* [is formed accordingly].

When *sīyuṭ* is elided by the rule *salopaḥ*, *ādguṇaḥ* applies [to form *edhiṣīdhvam*]. Regarding the rule *iṭo’t* (Pāṇini 3.4.106), although there is the presence of *iṇ*, because it does not follow immediately after an *aṅga* ending in *iṇ*, the [substitution] of *ṣ* for *dh* does not occur.
In *ṣīdhvam*, the substitution of *ḍha* does not occur.

(76) *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.5. [The suffix *jha*] is replaced by *āt* when it follows an *ātmanepada* ending that does not contain the vowel *a*. [This is derived from] *ho'ntaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.3), which provides *ha*, and from *ṭhabhyastāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.4), which provides *at*.
And it follows [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "In place of *jha*, there shall be *at*. Why [specify] "in the *ātmanepada*s"?

[Consider: *adanti*, *sunvanti*. Why [specify] "not ending in *an*"? [Consider: *edhante*, *plavante*. [The term] *iṇ* refers only to that which is distinct from *iṭ*; for, by the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the specific mention of *iṭ* in the rule "optionally after *iṭ*" (*vibhāṣeṭaḥ*) serves to exclude it.
The intention is that by some [grammarians], the root *iḍ* itself is understood here as being included. "By those ending in *ū*, *ṛ*, or *ṝ*" means: excluding those ending in *ū*, *ṛ*, or *ṝ*;

excluding *yu* and the others; and excluding *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*. Other roots that are monosyllabic and end in a vowel (*ajanta*) are "struck down" (*nihata*). This means they are unaccented (*anudātta*). For example: *dātā*, *dhātā*.

The suffix *iṇ* does not occur after roots such as *cet* and *stu*. Roots ending in long *ū*, such as *bhū* and *lū*, [take *iṇ*]. Roots ending in long *ṝ*, such as *kṛ* and *tṛ*, [take *iṇ*]. Regarding the root *ṭhyu* in the sense of "mixing" and so forth, and the root *ru* in the sense of "sound," both are included by virtue of the paribhāṣā concerning the absence of an *anubandha*. As for *ruṅ* in the senses of "motion" and "seeking," both are likewise included.
And this is also due to the *paribhāṣā* rule: "Between a root with a *vikaraṇa* suffix and one without a *vikaraṇa* suffix, the latter is understood.

Nor should it be suspected that, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), only the root with a *luk*-elided *vikaraṇa* is intended, because that [association] is not universal. [The roots are: *ṣṇu* in the sense of sharpening; *īṅ* in the sense of sleeping; and *ṇu* in the sense of trickling.
The roots are: *ṭhṇu* in the sense of praise; *ukṣu* in the sense of sound; *uaośvi* in the senses of motion and growth;
*īṅ* in the sense of moving through the air; *riñ* in the sense of service; *vṛṅ* in the sense of sharing;
*vṛñ* in the sense of choosing. Now, if these distinct roots were all merely single-vowel (*ekāc*) roots with anudātta accent, [the form] *ūrṇutaḥ* would [not be accounted for].
If it is argued that forms such as *ūrṇutavān* would not be established, do not say so;
for the desired result is achieved by the forthcoming Vārttika: "The substitution of *ṇu* for *ūrṇoti* should be stated.
Consequently, in the case of *ūrṇonūyate*, the suffix *yaṅ* applies by the rule "after a root consisting of a single vowel (*ekāc*)."
In the case of *ūrṇunāva*, because it consists of more than one vowel (*anekāctva*), the absence of *ām*—which would otherwise be required—is established.
And it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The substitution of *ūrṇu* for *ūrṇu* should be stated;

its purpose is the establishment of the *yaṅ* [intensive] and the prohibition of *ām*, provided that [the root] is monosyllabic (*ekāc*) when it undergoes reduplication. [And regarding the rule: *vibhāṣā*...
In the rule *guṇe’striyām*, this is a fifth case (*pañcamī*) used in the sense of cause (*hetu*). Here, "cause" means the result (*phala*).

This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. "Upagraha" means prohibition; the meaning is that it is for the purpose of prohibiting *iṭ*. And thus, by virtue of being treated as having one vowel (*ekāctva*) through the substitution of *ṇu*, [the suffix] is not subject to the rule *ṛt-śyukaḥ kitī*.

The application of the prohibition [of *iṭ*] in forms such as *ūrṇutaḥ* and so forth is established; however, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "a root with a single vowel (*ekāc*) in its original enunciation (*upadeśe*)" does not apply here, because although there is the status of being a single-vowel root through the substitution of *ṇu*, it lacks the quality of being unaccented (*anudātta*).

Because the roots *ūrṇu* and *ṇud* have an udātta accent on the radical vowel, forms such as *ūrṇavitā*, *ā-ūrṇavīt*, and so forth, are also established. Disregarding the reading of the ancient grammarians which states "after *vasati*, *śaklṛ*, and *ghaslṛ*," he provides the list for roots ending in consonants according to the order beginning with *ka*—starting with *śaklṛ*. Thus ends the section on roots ending in *ka*.
One [root]; and at the end [of the list], six roots beginning with *pac*, *muc*, *ric*, and *sic*: namely, ‘*upa-caṣ* in the sense of cooking’;
‘*ac* in the sense of making manifest’—both of these are included by the term ‘*ac*’;
‘*uclṛ* in the sense of releasing’; and by the term ‘*ric*’, both ‘*ṛc* in the sense of evacuation’ and ‘*ric*’ [are included].

In the phrase "viyojana-saṃparcanayoḥ raḥ," both [roots] belonging to the *yaujādika* (the sixth class) are included. By the mention of "vaci," however, both "bruvo vaciḥ" (*vac* in the sense of speaking) and the *yaujādika* *vac* are included.

"Vicir pṛthagbhāve" (*vic* in the sense of separation); "ic kṣaraṇe" (*ic* in the sense of flowing). Among those ending in *ch*, *praccha* is one; among those ending in *j*, [the following are included].

There are fifteen [roots]: *tyaj*, *nij*, *bhaj*, *bhañj*, *bhuj*, *bhrasj*, *masj*, *yaj*, *yuj*, *ruj*, *rañj*, *vij*, *svañj*, *sañj*, and *sṛj*. By the mention of *bhuj* here, both ‘*huja* (pālanābhyavahārayoḥ)’ and ‘*hujo* (kauṭilye)’ are included. By the mention of *yuj*, both ‘*yujir* (yoge)’ and ‘*yuj* (samādhau)’ are included. Some, however, say that in the verse of Vyāghrabhūti and in the Bhāṣya, this *yuj* is a partial citation of ‘*yujir* (yoge)’, and according to their view, ‘*yuj* (samādhau)’ is *seṭ* (taking the *iṭ* augment).

By the root *sṛj* (in the rule *sṛji*), both the *divādi* and *tudādi* classes are included, as per the rule *ṛja visarge*. Among those ending in *d*, there are fifteen: *ad*, *kṣud*, *khid*, *chid*, *tud*, *nud*, *pady*, *bhid*, *vid* (the piercing), *vinad*, *śad*, *śad*, *svid*, *skand*, and *had*. By the root *khid* (in the rule *khidi*), the roots *khidyati*, *khindati*, and *khinati*—meaning "to feel dejection"—are included. Regarding *vidyati*: it refers to *ṭhvida sattāyām* ("to exist"). Regarding *vinad*: it refers to *ṭhvida vicāraṇe* ("to deliberate"). Among those ending in *dh*, there are eleven: *krudh*, *kṣudh*, *budh*, *bandh*, *yudh*, *rudh*, *rādh*, *vyadh*, *śudh*, *sādh*, and *sidhyati*.

By *rudhityena*, both the root *rudhir* in the sense of "obstructing" (*āvaraṇe*) and the root *rudh* in the sense of "desire" (*kāme*), belonging to the *divādi* class, are included. Among those ending in *n*, there are two: *man* and *han*. *Ana* in the sense of "knowing" belongs to the *divādi* class. Among those ending in *p*, there are thirteen: *āp*, *kṣip*, *chup*, *tup*, *tip*, *tṛp*, *dṛp*, *lip*, *lup*, *vap*, *śap*, *svap*, *sṛp*. By the mention of *kṣip*, both *kṣipyati* (from *ṣipa* in the sense of "impelling") and *kṣipati* are included. *Hup* is in the sense of "touching. By the mention of *tap*, both *tap* in the sense of "heat" (*saṃtāpe*) and *tap* in the sense of "sovereignty" (*aiśvarye*) from the *divādi* class are included; *tap* in the sense of "burning" (*dāhe*) is also included in the alternative view where the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is absent.

The root *ip* is used in the sense of "flowing. Although the roots *tṛp* and *dṛp* are included [in the list], this reading here is for the purpose of [the rule] "anudātasya cardupadhasya" (Pāṇini 7.1.58). Among those ending in *bh*, there are three: *yabh*, *rabh*, and *labh*. Among those ending in *m*, there are four: *gam*, *nam*, *yam*, and *ram*. Among those ending in *ś*, there are ten: *kruś*, *daṃś*, *diś*, *dṛś*, *mṛś*, *riś*, *śru*, *śliṣ*, *viś*, and *spṛś*. Regarding *riś* and *ruś*, they mean "to injure. By the mention of *riś*, both the root *riś* meaning "to diminish" belonging to the Divādi class and the root *riś* meaning "to go" belonging to the Tudādi class are included. Among those ending in *ṣ*, there are eleven: *kṛṣ*, *tviṣ*, *tuṣ*, *dviṣ*, *duṣ*, *puṣ*, *ypiṣ*, *viṣ*, *śiṣ*, *śuṣ*, and *śliṣ*.

Regarding *kṛṣi*, both the root belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa* and that belonging to the *tudādigaṇa* are included. By the mention of *viṣi*, both the root *viṣlṛ* (meaning "to pervade") and the root located in the *jiṣviṣmiṣitidaṇḍaka* list are included. However, by the mention of *śiṣi*, both the root *iṣlṛ* (meaning "to distinguish") and the root located in the *kaṣa khaṣa viṣa* list are included. Regarding *viṣi*, only the root *viṣlṛ* from the *jauhotyādigaṇa* is included, not the one from the *daṇḍaka* list. Similarly, regarding *śiṣi*, only the root *iṣlṛ* from the *raudhādigaṇa* is included, not the one from the *daṇḍaka* list; so say Bopadeva and others.

Among those ending in *s*, there are two: *ghaslṛ* and *vasati*. Regarding *ghaslṛ*, as in the root ‘*haslṛ* (to eat)’, its formation is established even by the fact that the substitute *ghaslṛ*—prescribed by the rule ‘*uh sanorghaslṛ*’—is itself anudātta (unaccented). Among those ending in *h*, there are eight: *dah*, *diha*, *duh*, *miha*, *naha*, *ruha*, *lih*, and *vah*. Regarding *duhi*, the ancient grammarians maintain that the root belonging to the Bhūvādigaṇa is not intended here; rather, it is specifically the root ‘*uha* (to fill)’ from the Adādigaṇa. In this regard, a summary verse (*saṅgrahaśloka*) is stated in the *Manoramā*: “*ac*, *cch*, *j*, *ā*, *da*, *dha*, *na*, *p*, *bha*, *ma*, *ś*, *ā*, *ṣ*, *sa*, and *ha*, in their respective order.”

The meaning is as follows: "The roots ending in the fourteen letters mentioned in the first half [of the verse] should be understood to be equal in number to the letters appearing in the sequence beginning with the second half. For this very reason, it is explained that there is one root ending in *ka*, six ending in *ca*, one ending in *cha*, fifteen ending in *ja*, and so forth. This is because it is accepted that *ka* is the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for one, *ca* for six, *ṇa* for fifteen, and so on. Among those ending in *pa*, two have *śyan*.

He states the result of this explanation: "In the *tud*-class," etc. The roots *tṛp* and *dṛp* are situated in the *tud*-class according to one opinion; however, *tṛpi* is situated in the *cur*-class according to all opinions. As for *dṛpi*, it is [in the *cur*-class] according to the opinion of some alone—this is the distinction. For this very reason, he will say: "ṛpa, tṛmpha, in the sense of satiation. Others hold that both [roots] end in the second vowel (*ṛ*). [Furthermore,] "ṛpa, dṛmpha, in the sense of agitation": the first ends in the first vowel, the second ends in the second vowel. Some hold that the first ends in the second vowel—thus it is stated in the *tud*-class.

In the *curādi* (tenth) class, however, some say: "ṛpa in the sense of satisfaction" (*tṛptau*) and "tṛpa and dṛpa in the sense of kindling" (*saṃdīpane*). [The phrase] "for the sake of excluding others" means that those which ought to be excluded are: *ñiṣvidā* in the sense of "moistening and releasing"; *pada* in the sense of "stability"; *ṣidha* in the sense of "motion"; *ṣidhū* in the sense of "scripture" and "auspiciousness"; *budhi* in the sense of "awakening"—this belongs to the *bhūvādi* (first) class; *anu* in the sense of "understanding"—this belongs to the *tanādi* (eighth) class; *uṣa* in the sense of "nourishment"—this belongs to both the *bhūvādi* and *krayādi* (ninth) classes; *liṣa* in the sense of "burning"—this belongs to the *bhūvādi* class; and *vasa* in the sense of "covering"—this belongs to the *adādi* (second) class.

These [roots] are *seṭ* (having an indicatory *i*) because they lack the grave accent (*anudātta*). The root *yuñ* in the sense of "binding" belongs to the *kryādi* class; since it is grave-accented, it is *aniṭ*. By means of the mention of the *śyan* suffix, the following should be included: *ṇiṣvidā* in the sense of "oozing from the body," *ada* in the sense of "eating," *ṣidhū* in the sense of "accomplishment," *udha* in the sense of "understanding," *mana* in the sense of "knowing," *puṣa* in the sense of "nourishing," *liṣa* in the sense of "embracing," and *vasa* in the sense of "dwelling. These are *aniṭ*. The root *yu* in the sense of "mixing and not mixing" is *seṭ*. "These [others] are likewise": *ṇiji* in the sense of "purification" and *ovijī* in the sense of "fear and trembling."

The meaning is that these roots with their respective *anubandhas*—namely *aka*, *marṣaṇe* (from the *adādi* class), *aka* (from the *tudādi* class), and *marṣaṇe* (from the *divādi* class)—are specified in order to exclude [the application of rules] to those belonging to the *adādi*, *tudādi*, and *divādi* classes respectively. Regarding *vindati*: [it is derived from] the root *vidlṛ* in the sense of "acquisition" (*lābhe*). "Desired" (*iṣṭa*) means "because it is *aniṭ*" (*aniṭtvena*); this is the remainder [of the explanation]. Regarding "not mentioned in the Bhāṣya": they were not mentioned by the author of the Bhāṣya, but they were not rejected either; thus, there is no contradiction here.

Therefore, the intention is that the *Bhāṣya* should be understood as merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), in accordance with the works of Vyāghrabhūti and others, as well as due to Vedic usages such as *uṣkadhṛṣṭau* and *tena nañviśiṣṭenānañ*, and common worldly usage such as *atum* and *pratipatum*. Regarding the term *akarmaka* (intransitive): here some maintain that the meaning of the verbal root is the desire to overcome; thus, a root signifying rivalry is seen to be transitive, as in the verse: "He challenged Amarāvatī to Meru."

And he himself will state this under the rule *āṅaḥ spardhāyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.31): "He challenges Aṇūra, being a Ṛṣi; the meaning is that he competes. Śrīharṣa also employed it thus: "The Tretā age is capable of competing with the age of the two Aśvins. Therefore, they say that its transitivity is logical. (77) *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.4.61). [Regarding] *śarpūrvāḥ*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualifying property is not included in the reference (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). Consequently, the sibilants (*śar*) are not what remains.
However, it occurs only in the case of *khaya*. It should be understood that in this instance, in the word *spardha*, the doubling of the *repha* (the letter *r*) also takes place;

for the prohibition "not after *an"* (*andrāḥ*) applies specifically to the *repha* belonging to the second *ekāc* (monosyllabic) element. [The root] *gādhṛ*: the vowel *ṛ* is for the purpose of the prohibition in the rule "after a monosyllable ending in *ā*, or after a root that elides its penultimate vowel, or after one marked with *ṛ*" (*āglopiśāsvṛditām*).

He explained: *āspada* means a place, a station, or a firm footing; it refers either to being established in one place or to a composition (*saṃdarbha*) or a book (*grantha*). Regarding the roots *nāthṛ* and *nādhṛ*, [the term] *upatāpa* means disease. Since the desired form is already established by the fact that these roots are *anudātta*, he states that the *vārttika* is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).
In the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), the word *nātha* should be stated; [and] only in the sense of a benediction. Regarding the rule *ata ekahalmadhye*:
here the word *eka* signifies "without a companion. The meaning is "between two single consonants" (*hal*).
He explains this by saying "not joined" (*asaṃyukta*). In accordance with what is desired, the word *liṭi* is repeated.
He says that this *etva* (the substitution of *e*) is qualified by the condition of being an *ādeśa* (substitute), and that it is also subject to *namana* (lengthening):

(78) *ata ekahalmadhye’nādeśāderliṭi* |6|4|120|. This refers to [the conditions] "caused by the *liṭ*" (*liṇnimitta*) and "in the case of a *kit* *liṭ*" (*kiti liṭi*). Although in the sūtra *ahamane*... [the rule applies].

The term *kṅti* continues [from the previous rule]; nevertheless, the intention is that *ṅti* does not continue here because it serves no purpose. What is an example of *kit*? *nanāda*. Why "in the *liṭ* [perfect]? Consider *pāpacyāt*.
(79) *thali ca seṭi* | Pāṇini 6.4.121.

Regarding the form *cakaṇatuḥ*: one should not argue that even in this case, in the formation of *babhaṇatuḥ*, the substitution of *e* for *ab* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) still occur because the rule *abhyāse carcā* is considered established (*siddha*) with respect to it;
for by the inclusion of the terms *phala* and *bhaja*, it is made known that the aforementioned rule is established only with respect to the prescription of *e*. Thus...
Furthermore, it must necessarily be explained that in this context, only a substitute (*ādeśa*) that brings about a change in form (*vairūpya*) is intended; such is the direction [of the argument].
(80) *idito num dhātoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.58.
*madi* means praise; *modaḥ* means contentment; *madaḥ* means pride; *svapnaḥ* means laziness.

(81) [The rule] *na śasadadavādiguṇānām* [Pāṇini 6.4.126] applies. Regarding *na śasadada*: the root *asu* in the sense of "injury" ends in a dental (*d*). In the sūtra, there is a relationship of part and whole [between the listed items].
This is the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*). Thus, although the syntactical connection "the *akāra* which belongs to the roots *śas*, *sad*, *vad*, etc.

is possible, one might object that because the *akāra* is of the nature of a *guṇa* (a phonetic modification), a genitive based on a distinction [between the original and the modified] is not possible.
Anticipating this objection, he explains it in order to resolve it: "of that which has been brought about by the word *guṇa*. And as for this state of being "brought about" (*bhāvitatva*):

This applies to both direct and indirect [substitution]. Thus, in forms such as *śaśaratuḥ* and *paparatuḥ*, it refers to the vowel *a* which is a constituent part of that [element] being produced by the term "guṇa. However, in forms such as *lulavitha*, it refers to that which is being produced by the term "guṇa"...

The meaning is that the vowel *a* is a constituent part of the *av*-substitute which takes the place of *o*; therefore, there is no inconsistency here. In forms such as *dadade*, *śaśasatuḥ*, *śaśasuḥ*, *vavamatuḥ*, and *vavamuh*, the prohibition should likewise be understood to apply. [The roots] *ṣvada* and *svarda*. "This" refers to...

They say that this was stated with a specific intention: "sakarmaka" (transitive) means "svadasva havyāni" (taste the sacrificial offerings), which has the sense of "experience. "Akarmaka" (intransitive) is illustrated by Śrī Harṣa: "For one already satiated by water, even a cool, sweet, and fragrant stream of water does not *svadate*," meaning it does not please or does not appeal.
This is the meaning.

(82) *dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ* | P. 6.1.64. What is the purpose of including the term "root" (*dhātu*)? [Consider: *ṣaṭ*, *ṣaḍ*. What is the purpose of including the term "initial" (*ādi*)? [Consider: *laṣati*.

(83) *upadhāyāṃ ca* | Pāṇini 8.2.78. From the rule *ipi dhātoḥ*, the word *dhātoḥ* is understood to carry over; from *ṛt-ur-ṛt-upadhāyāḥ*, the phrase *ṛ-vor-i-kaḥ* is understood; and from *hali ca*, the word *halī* is understood. Thus he says: "of the root," and so forth.

Why [is the word] *dhātoḥ* [stated]? [Consider the rule] *ṭhūR-utaḥ*. [In the forms] *kurūḥ*, *kurvau*, and *kurvaḥ*, let there not be lengthening of the single vowel (*ekaḥ*). Nor can it be argued that, although the *repha* here is the penultimate (*upadhā*) of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the lengthening would still not occur simply because it is not the penultimate of the word (*pada*).

It should be stated that the recurrence of the word *dhātoḥ* here is not necessary; however, if *padasya* were to recur, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-formation of forms such as *kūrdate* and *gūrdate*. In reality, however, because it is accepted that "what is not established in the preceding [rule] does not behave like the original" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*), the status of being a substitute (*sthānivattva*) by the rule *ṭhacaḥ parasmin* [does not apply].

Even if the prohibition [of the *guṇa* substitute] is accepted, according to the view that the operation takes place at the time the effect arises (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the paribhāṣā "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as if non-existent" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam*) would apply;

consequently, because the *yaṇ*-substitution is external and thus considered non-existent, the rule "upadhāyāṃ ca" (Pāṇini 7.1.101) would not cause the lengthening of the vowel in forms such as *kurvau* and *kurvaḥ*. Therefore, there is the necessity of continuing the reference to the term "dhātu" (root).

It is not absolutely necessary [to include the word "pada"]; they say that by not carrying over the term "pada," the long vowel is indeed established in forms such as *kūrdate*. What is the purpose of [specifying] the letters *repha* (r) and *vakāra* (v)? [Consider] *puṣpyati* from the root *uṣp* meaning "to blossom. What is the purpose of [specifying] "followed by a consonant" (*halpara*)? [Consider] *ciraṇoti* and *jiriṇoti*. Why [is it said] "of *ik*" (*ikaḥ*)?

Regarding the objection that the rule *arvate nardati* is redundant—since the form *kūrdate*, *gūrdate*, and others are already established by the interpretation of *hali ca* as "there should be a long vowel for *i* and *u* when followed by *r* or *v* which are themselves followed by a consonant"—the following is said in response: [The answer is: Here they say...

In the rule *ṭhali ca*, the term *dhātu* (root) must indeed be understood as carrying over [from previous rules]. Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *divyati* (he desires heaven), where one intends [the suffix] after *div*. Furthermore, in the absence of the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca*, the lengthening [of the vowel] would not occur before the semivowels *r* and *v* when they function as *upadhā* (penultimate). Why?

Since this rule [Pāṇini 8.3.79, *ṣṭuanunāsike ca*] applies only to roots ending in the letter *t* or *th*, the present sūtra is indeed necessary. As for *sūdate*, it means "it flows. Now, one might object: why not simply read the roots as *svarda* and *sūda* with dental *d*s, just like *svardati*?

[Objection: "One should read the *ṣopadeśa* words [as having an initial *ṣ*] because of the weight of the rule for *satva* (the substitution of *s*). [Reply: Not so. For if that were the case, then in forms such as *ṇyant-caṅ* [causative with reduplication] *isiṣvidata* and *asūṣudat*, and in the *liṭ* [perfect tense] forms *suṣūde* and *siṣedha*, the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.41) would not occur, because [in those cases] the *ṣ* would not follow immediately after an *iṇ* vowel.
If the rule for changing *s* to *ṣ* were applied to every instance of the letter *s*, then it would also occur in forms such as *supisau* and *supisaḥ*.

Therefore, just as Pāṇini read certain roots with palatal or dental *s* in his Dhātupāṭha, he also read those designated as *ṣopadeśa* (roots beginning with *ṣ*) according to a specific systematic arrangement;
however, that original reading has now been lost. This applies to roots such as *sādh* and others.

Since only the reading beginning with "sādi" is observed, he establishes those [consonants] by means of their defining characteristics—namely, "sa e," and so forth. "Dantyādau" means at the beginning of the dentals (dantya) and the *a*-sounds (*añ*); that which has these two as its final elements (*antau*) immediately following it is "dantyājanta. And that which is both "dantyājanta" and "sa" [is the subject].

Those roots which end in a dental consonant (dantyānta) or the letter *s* (sakārānta), as well as those which begin with such letters (dantyādisādayaḥ) or end in the vowel *a* (ajantasādayaḥ), and which consist of a single syllable (ekācaḥ), should be understood as being taught with the letter *ṣ* (ṣopadeśāḥ). Accordingly, the *s* currently seen in the root *sādh* and others does not exist in its original teaching (*upadeśe*).

Thus ends the section on the inferable *dant* suffixes. To prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the definition already stated, he says: "sig-iti. [The roots are: *akṛ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*);

*ṛplṛ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*); *tṛñ* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*); *ṛja* in the sense of "emission" (*visarge*); *stṛñ* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*); and *tyai* in the senses of "sound" and "collection" (*śabda-saṅghātayoḥ*). These are other than those [previously mentioned]. By the preceding [rule]...
Because some [roots] have not been included, he says: *vaṣka*, etc. The connection is as follows: *vaṣka* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*);

*ñiṣvidā* in the sense of "oozing from the body" (*gātraprakṣaraṇe*); *vada* in the sense of "tasting" (*āsvādane*); *vañja* in the sense of "embracing" (*pariṣvaṅge*); *ñiṣvap* in the sense of "sleeping" (*śaye*); and *miṅ* in the sense of "slight laughter" (*īṣaddhasane*). These are the roots taught with the prefix *ṣ*. [The root] *vāda*...
Anticipating the objection that there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) in cases such as *āsvādane*, he says: "dental" (*dantyaḥ*) means "purely dental.
Thus, the intention is that in forms such as *asisvadat*, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. [The root] *hlādī* is used in the sense of pleasure;

by the word *ca* ("and"), it is also used in the sense of indistinct sound. The long vowel *ī* is for the purpose of prohibiting the application of the suffix *iṇ* according to the rule "vīdito niṣṭhāyām."
*prahlannaḥ* means "one who has become refreshed. Here, by the rule *ṭh hlādo niṣṭhāyām*, there is shortening of the penultimate vowel.
Regarding the word *ślāghā*: it is the making known of a connection with qualities that do not actually exist—this is *ślāghā*. Regarding *ātatuḥ*:
because the [root vowel] is not situated between consonants (*hal*), the substitution of *e* does not occur.

(84) *iṭa īṭi* | 8|2|28| The word "lopa" (elision) is understood from the rule "*aṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*" [8.2.23], and the word "saḥ" (of *s*) is understood from the rule "*ṭhrātsasya*" [8.2.29]. Therefore, it says: "there shall be elision. Why [specify] *iṭ*? [Consider: *ahārṣīt*. [This applies] when *īṭ* follows.
What [is the purpose]? [The forms] *ātiṣṭām* and *ātiṣu*.
It must be stated that the elision of *sij* is established (*siddha*) when there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). Regarding the phrase "elision of *sij*," they say here:
although it should have been stated as "elision of *s-*" (*salopa*), the mention of *sij* indicates that the three rules beginning with *halo jhali* pertain specifically to the domain of *sij*.

This is for the purpose of making it known. Therefore, here *somastut* is the agent of praise (*stotṛ*). [The forms] *dviṣarkaṭarām* and *dviṣṭamām* [are derived from the root *dviṣ*]. However, in the rule *hi ca*, according to the opinion of Vāmana there is the elision (*lopa*) of *sic*, whereas according to the opinion of the Bhāṣya there is the elision of *s*; this distinction is to be understood.

(85) *vadavrajahalantasyācaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.3. In the case of the roots *vad*, *vraj*, and those ending in a consonant (*halanta*), [the vowel of the root] undergoes compulsory *vṛddhi* [before the suffix *sic*]. Examples: *avādīt* (he spoke), *avrājīt* (he walked). This rule sets aside the optional application prescribed by the rule *ato halāderlaghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.7); thus, *vṛddhi* occurs invariably here.
