*ayatiṣṭa*, *ayatiṣātām*. In the case of *acakāsīt*, if—by the maxim *yena nāvayavavyavadhānam* ("that by which there is no intervention of a part")—only an intervention of a single phoneme were accepted in order to prevent the *vṛddhi* of the vowel *a* after the letter *c*, then...

They say that even in the case of *tvarakṣīt*, since there is no possibility [of the application of the rule], the word *laghoḥ* could have been omitted. The inclusion of *taḥ* (the *tapara*) is for the sake of clarity. Regarding the phrase "beginning with a labial" (*pavargīyādi*): if it were not [specifically] dental-labial (*dantyoṣṭhya*), then because of the prohibition of *etva* and elision of the reduplication in the case of *asadat*, forms such as *bedatuḥ* and *beditha* would not be possible.
The sense is that it would be accomplished.
(102) *nergadanadapatapadaghumāsyatihantiyātivātidrātipsātivapativahatiśāmyaticinotidegdhiṣu ca* | Pāṇini 8.4.17.

The mention of the four roots beginning with *gad* by means of the suffix *śap*, and the mention of the eleven roots beginning with *syati* by means of the suffix *śtip*, is for the purpose of excluding the forms of the *yaṅ*-lopa (intensive without the *yaṅ* suffix). Consequently, in examples such as *raṇijāgadīti*, *pratinānadīti*, *pranisāseti*, and *pranijaṅghanīti*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not occur.

By the word *ghu*, the six roots beginning with *āḍ* (to eat) that bear the designation *ghu* are understood. By the word *mā*, only the roots *meṅ* (to exchange) and *bhāṅ* (to shine) are included, because in the *Mahābhāṣya* and other works, they have explained it by reading [the rule] as *hu-prakṛti-māṅ*.

(103) *ṇo naḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.65. Regarding *ṇo naḥ*: [the rule applies] to the beginning of a verbal root (*dhātu*). Because the phrase "of the beginning of a verbal root" (*dhātvādeḥ*) is carried over from the previous rule, "The *ṣ* at the beginning of a verbal root becomes *s*" (*dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ*), it refers specifically to the beginning of a verbal root. It does not apply here: *aṇati*.
He states the roots with the prefix *ṇ* by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), saying: "The roots with the prefix *ṇ* are... [as follows]: *arda* in the sense of "sound";

*aṭa* in the sense of "flowing" (curādi class). However, the root *naṭa* in the sense of "dancing," which belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group, is not included here, because of the mention of the long vowel in the form *nāṭī*. *āthṛ* and *nāthṛ* in the sense of "begging" and so forth; *uanadi*...

The meaning is that [the letters] are distinct from these eight: *samṛddhau* (in the sense of prosperity), *akka nāśane* (in the sense of destruction), *ṛÃ naye* (in the sense of leading), and *ṛtī gātravikṣepe* (in the sense of the movement of limbs). Regarding the phrase "in the *tavarga*": according to their view, however, the *ṇa*s are taught as being distinct from five [of those].

(104) *upasargādasamāse’pi ṇopadeśasya* Pāṇini 8.4.14. Regarding the word *upasargāt*: because the phrase *aṅguleḥ saṅgaḥ* from [Pāṇini 6.1.62] is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartana*), it would apply only in a compound; therefore, the inclusion of the term *asamāse* ("even when not in a compound") is made. However, once that term is included, it would follow that the rule applies only when there is no compound; therefore, the inclusion of the particle *api* ("also/even") is made.
It has been done. Regarding the form *praṇinadati*: the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *ṇer aṇau* [Pāṇini 6.1.83].

However, the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the verbal root does not occur by the rule *upasargādasamāse* [Pāṇini 8.4.14], because there is an intervention by an element other than the *aṭ* augment and so forth.
(105) Therefore, [the augment] *nuṭ* is applied after a reduplicated root having two consonants [as its penultimate part]: *tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.71].

Therefore, he says "from that which has become long" (*dīrghībhūtāt*), meaning that by the word *tat* (that), the form with the lengthened vowel is referred to. Regarding *kharda*, since it denotes a "biting serpent" (*daṇḍaśūka*)— and because it is a serpent,
its status as a verbal root (*dhātu*) would not be appropriate if it were merely a noun— he says "in the action of a biting serpent" (*daṇḍaśūka-kriyāyām*).

The meaning is: "in that which has *daṇḍaśūka* as its agent. Regarding *ānanta*: because it is marked with the *it*-augment, *num* is added; from that, *nuṭ* is added by the rule *tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ*. Regarding "a part of the face": the meaning is "in the action thereof.
(106) *ādir ñiṭuaḍavaḥ* | 1.3.5 | [The augment *āṭ* is placed at the beginning of the root before the affixes *ñ*, *iṭ*, *tu*, and *aḍ*.]

Because [the condition] "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśe*) does not carry over from the rule "a nasalized vowel in the original enunciation" (*ṭhupadeśe’janunāsikaḥ*), he says: "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśe*). What is the purpose of specifying "in the original enunciation"? Consider *ñikārīyati* (derived from the root *ñiṣvap*); here, by the rule "after a root ending in *ñī*, the suffix *kta* is applied," we have *suptaḥ*. Furthermore, by the rule "after a root ending in *vit*, the suffix *athuc* is applied," we have *nandathuḥ*. And by the rule "after a root ending in *vit*, the suffix *kriḥ* is applied," we have *kṛtrimam*. [Also consider the root] *klid*.
Regarding *parivedana*: its inclusion here among the roots marked with an anudātta (low-pitched) accent is for the purpose of deriving the *parasmaipada* (active voice).
Although the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartṛ*), it was not included among the roots marked with a svarita (circumflex) accent for the sake of the *parasmaipada*.
*Śundha* means "to purify"; this root belongs to the *yujādi* class in the sense of the act of cleansing and is auspicious.
The root *edhati* was mentioned ending in a *tavargīya* (dental) letter; in accordance with that, several roots ending in *tavargīya* letters were recited.
Now, he speaks according to the order of the well-known worldly recitation beginning with *ka*, starting with "atha" and so on. Regarding *cukuke*:
because it is *nitya* (eternally applicable), the *kitva* (the status of being a *k*-suffix) applies by the rule *ṭhasaṃyogā’d*, overriding even the subsequent *guṇa*.
A prohibition of the suffix *sat* must be stated for the verbal roots *sub*, *dhātu*, *ṣṭhivu*, *ṣvaṣk*, and *tī*. [The rule begins with] "for *sub*, *dhātu*, etc.

Examples of roots beginning with *su* (i.e., *sub*): one who has six teeth is called *ṣoḍan*. To express that [one causes someone] to indicate him, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied, and there is elision of the *ṭi* portion (*ṣoḍayati*). Similarly, one who makes or indicates a group (*ṣaṇḍa*) is expressed as *ṣaṇḍayati*.

In the case of *ṣaṇḍīyati*, however, it should be understood that the substitution of *ī* occurs after the word *ṣaṇḍa* when the suffix *kyac* is applied. Furthermore, this Vārttika has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. For instance, in the rule *hātvādeḥ*, the term *upadeśe* (in the original form) continues to apply. Now, there is no original enunciation (*upadeśa*) for words formed with the *sub*-suffixes; moreover, the roots *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣvaṣk* begin with *yakāra*. [The rule regarding] *opa-*...

In *vyoḥ*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of *y*. In *praṇikakhati*, the intention is that because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of roots beginning with *k* or *kh* in the rule *eṣe vibhāṣā*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not occur. (107) *abhyāsasyā’savarṇe* 6.4.78.

What is the purpose of the condition "not being of the same class" (*asavarṇe*)? [Consider: *ūkhatur*. What is the purpose of the condition "before a vowel" (*aci*)? [Consider: *iyāja*, *uvāya*, and *uvokha*. In the case of *uvokha*, because of the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule "before a vowel during reduplication" (*virvacane'ci*), reduplication occurs first; subsequently, when the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) has been applied, the *uvaṅ* replacement occurs for the reduplicated syllable. Similarly, in *iyeṣa*, the *iyaṅ* replacement occurs.

It should be understood that by virtue of the inclusion of the term *asavarṇa* (non-homogeneous vowel), the *guṇa* substitution does not take effect here when *iyaṅ* and so forth are to be applied, and thus [the rule] is not *sthānivadbhūta*. Regarding the phrase "by the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā*": the intention is that if the suffix *ām* were present, the condition of being followed by *liṭ* would not be established for the verbal root. Others, however, [interpret] the word *gurumān* in the rule *ijādeḥ*... as follows:

The suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of constant connection (*nityayoga*). Consequently, forms such as *gurumān* (possessing a guru) and *ṭedha* (in the sense of increase) would apply only in that specific context; thus, they say there is no possibility for the application of *ām* here. Regarding *ūkhatur*:

because the suffix is *kit*, there is an absence of *guṇa*, and consequently, by the rule "for the reduplicated [root] before a vowel not homogeneous with itself," *uvaṅ* does not occur. Now, [an objection]:...

If it is argued that even in the case of *iyeṣa* and *uvokha*, since the long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) applies first due to its being an internal rule (*antaraṅga*), the conditions for the application of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*—namely, the presence of a following *ac* vowel—are absent; thus, the desired forms would not be established, so what is the purpose of including the term "non-homogeneous" (*asavarṇa*)? To this, they reply: "An operation pertaining to an *aṅga* (suffix) is stronger than one pertaining to a phoneme (*vārṇa*)."

The mention of *asavarṇa* (non-homogeneous) was made precisely for the purpose of conveying this technical instruction (*paribhāṣā*). Consequently, in the case of *bhavati*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs, overriding even the *yaṇ* substitution which is internally conditioned (*antaraṅga*).
Similarly, in the case of *ghañ* after the root *kṛ*, in the form *āra*, the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs, overriding the *yaṇ*. And it is not thus...

In the case of *sivi*, [the substitution of *u* for *i*] occurs because of the suffix *nap* prescribed by the *Uṇādi* rules; however, in this present instance, there is a difference of locus (*vyāśrayatva*) due to the difference in the cause (*nimitta*). Regarding the phrase "by the mention of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsagrahaṇena*), the meaning is: "by virtue of the preceding [portion] being treated as if it were the whole.
The principle is "like Parjanya" (*parjanyavallakṣaṇā*); that is, a grammatical rule operates regardless of whether its application is useful or useless.

The meaning is that the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) applies the short vowel even in the place of a short vowel; thus, the sense is that a rule applies only once to a single object of application (*lakṣya*), and there is no further application of it. [Regarding the statement] "the subsequent (*āṅga*) is stronger": but here—

If it is asked: "Since there is an absence of having a common locus (*samānāśrayatva*) due to the difference in the causes for the short and long *savarṇa* vowels, how can the internal (*āṅga*) rule be stronger?"—it is true; however, in accordance with the desired results (*iṣṭānurodha*), it is accepted that they have a common locus by taking the original element (*sthānin*) into account. For this very reason, from the root *uṅ* (meaning 'to weave'), in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), we have *ūve*.

The desired form *ūvāte* and others are established. [Otherwise], if the *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel-lengthening) were to apply before the substitution of *uvaṅ*, that would not be established; such is the direction [of the argument]. As for the phrase "because of its being subsequent" (*paratvāt*), this is a reason based on a superficial appearance, because the short vowel (*hrasva*) is *bahiraṅga* (extrinsic) due to its being a constituent part (*aṅga*), and thus [the *uvaṅ*] is *antaraṅga* (intrinsic) with respect to the *savarṇadīrgha*.
Because it is improper to introduce [the suffix] *paratva* (the state of being subsequent). Regarding *uṅkhati*: because it is marked with *idit*, the augment *num* is applied.

In the *liṭ* [perfect tense], it becomes *uṅkhāñcakāra*. In the benedictive (*āśis*), it is *uṅkhyāt*. Regarding *vavakhatuḥ*: because it belongs to the *vādi* group, there is no substitution of *e* for the root vowel nor elision of the reduplication. *ekhati*. *iṅkhati*. *iṅkhāñcakāra*.
*īkṣati*, *īkṣāñcakāra*; *iṅgati*, *iṅgāñcakāra*. Regarding *tvagi kampane* (the root *tvag* in the sense of trembling):

this is read in order to indicate a specific type of motion for that which is listed in the *daṇḍaka* group under *ukha-ukhi* as "motion. For this very reason, because it serves no further purpose, it is not found in many manuscripts.

It is read [in the Dhātupāṭha] as *sev*. And regarding the rule "and in the sense of serving" (*sevane ca*), in passages such as "the Pūrus attend upon the slayer of Vṛtra" (*tyam pūravo vṛtrahaṇaṃ sacante*), the learned have explained that it means "they serve. Among the roots marked with a svarita accent, it will be stated that *ac* is used in the sense of "coming together. Regarding *locṛ*: because it is marked with an *ṛt* (indicating the *ṛdit* class), the prohibition of shortening by the rule "āglopi" applies. Thus, *alulocat*.
The root *añc* is used in the sense of "making manifest" (*vyaktīkaraṇe*) and "speaking extensively" (*vistāravacane*), according to the *curādi* (tenth) class. The root *ṛj* means "to go.

"Acquisition" (*arjanam*) is primary, whereas "earning" (*upārjanam*) is incidental. Regarding the rule for the insertion of the augment *nuṭ*, etc.: "But in the case of the prescription of *uṭ*, substitutes, and elisions..."

The sense is that, because of the statement "one should understand [the rule] as applying to the whole," a portion of a phoneme (*varṇaikadeśa*) is treated as a full phoneme (*varṇatva*) in rules such as those concerning the augment *nuṭ*. Alternatively, the mention of "two consonants" (*dvihal*) is rejected in the *Bhāṣya* and other works.

Furthermore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *āṭaḥ* and *āṭatuḥ*, because by the rule "and after the root *aś*," it is understood that [the condition applies] only to that which has *a* as its penultimate vowel (*avarṇopadha*).

If it occurs, then by the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "only from the root *asnoti*," the desired form is established; this is explained in detail elsewhere. Regarding the roots *ṛji* and *bhṛjī*: *bharjana* is a specific kind of heating of rice and other grains without water. Because the root is marked with the indicatory letter *ī* (*īdit*), the augment *iṭ* is not applied by the rule "after a root ending in *ī*, there is no *iṭ* before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes. Thus: *bhṛktaḥ* (past passive participle), *bhṛktavān* (past active participle). Regarding *ejṛ*...

Regarding *bhejṛ* and *bhrājṛ*: the addition of the marker *ṛt* to the root *bhrāj* has the sole purpose of making it *anudātta*. This is because, by the rule “*hrājabhāse*” etc., the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is optional when followed by a *ṇi*-causative that is itself followed by *caṅ* (the reduplication of the aorist).
Thus, we have *abibrajat* and *ababhrājat*. These are called *parasmaipadins* because they end in a dental consonant (*cavargīya*).

[The roots] ending in *parasmaipada*. Regarding the phrase "but in the sense of worship": the meaning is that this is because of the prohibition [of *ātmanepada*] by the rule "āñceḥ pūjāyām" (Pāṇini 1.3.46).
(108) Pāṇini 1.3.58: *jṛstanbhumrucumlucugrucuglucugluñcuśvibhyaśca*.

The roots *jṛ* (to grow old), *stanbhu* (a Vedic root meaning "to support"), *aś* (to pervade), and *śvi* (to swell) take the *caṅ* suffix optionally by the rule *vibhāṣā dheṭśvyo’r*. Examples: *ajarat*, *ajārīt*; *astabhat*, *astambhīt*; *aśvat*, *aśvatām*, *aśvan*;
*aśvayīt*; and with *caṅ*: *iśiśviyat*. The root *arc* (in the sense of worship) is included here among the *yuj*-class roots as having a svarita accent.
The reading, however, is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukha*), even though the fruit [of the action] resides in the agent; this is because there is no long vowel (*dīrgha*).
The meaning is: because there is no long vowel in place of an inherent short vowel (*svābhāvikahrasva*).
[The word] "even after" refers to that which follows a long *ā* in place of a short vowel that has been substituted.

The intended meaning is that the substitution of *nuṭ* indeed occurs. [Regarding the root] *yucch* in the sense of "to err": from *yucchati*, because the *tuk* augment applies by virtue of being *antaraṅga* (internal), there is no *guṇa* substitution due to the absence of a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*). Nor should it be argued that "an operation concerning a phoneme (*vārṇa*) is stronger than one concerning a suffix (*āṅga*)," for such a rule applies only when the *āṅga* and *vārṇa* operations apply simultaneously.

Because it is more powerful. Nor should one object, "Since [the rule] *yuci* mentions both the letter *c* and the letter *ch*, what is the purpose of this rule prescribing the *tuṅ* augment? For there would be the disadvantage of having to pronounce both *c* and *ch* in many verbal forms; thus, [the form] *he ce* [would result].
And because it is necessary in cases such as *śivacchāyā* and others:
(109) *ajervyaghañapoḥ* | Pāṇini 2.4.56. The analysis is *ajeḥ vy* and *vī*. By this, forms such as *saṃvītaḥ* and *saṃvītiḥ* are established.

The phrase "in the domain of an ārdhadhātuka" means that by this [rule], forms such as *vevīyate*—where the substitution of *vī* for *yaj* occurs prior to the addition of *yaṅ*—are established. The point is that if the locative were interpreted as "after" (*parasaptamī*), then because the root would not begin with a consonant (*halāditva*), *yaṅ* would not apply.
However, *yaṅ-luk* does not occur after this [root], because when *yaṅ* is elided by *luk*, [the conditions for its application are no longer met].

Because there is an absence of the domain of an *ārdhadhātuka* [affix], there is no manifestation of an *ārdhadhātuka*; thus, the substitution of *vī* [for *bhū*] is simply not applicable. This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *a lumatā*.
Why [is it said] "except for *ghan* and *ap*"? [Consider: *samājaḥ*. [In this case,] *ap* is applied by the rule *amudorajaḥ paśuṣu*. [Resulting in: *samajaḥ*.

*Udajaḥ*. [In the form] *vivyatuḥ*, the substitution of *yaṇ* applies by the rule "ṭheranekācaḥ". As for the statement that a substitute is indeed a zero-substitution (*lopa*) when it begins with a vowel (*ajādeśa*), this has already been demonstrated by us in the very rule "na padānte". Regarding the phrase "of a monosyllabic root" (*ekācaḥ*): although the root *aj* is udātta, its substitute *vī* is anudātta; furthermore, monosyllabic roots ending in a vowel (*ajanta*) are distinct from those ending in *ū*, *ṛ*, and *ṝ*.
Because it is accepted that all [these roots] are anudātta (unaccented). (110) *kṛ-sṛ-bhṛ-vṛ-stu-dru-sru-śruvo liṭi* | Pāṇini 7.2.13.
*kṛ-sṛ-bhṛ*: ‘*kṛñ* in the sense of making (*karaṇe*)’; ‘*ṛñ* in the sense of harming (*hiṃsāyām*)’. Here...
Because of the mention of "without an indicatory letter" (*niranubandha*), there is the inclusion of both those that have one indicatory letter and those that have two.

Similarly, further on, there is the inclusion of both *hṛñ* in the sense of "supporting" and *ubhṛñ* in the senses of "supporting" and "nourishing. [Also included are] *ṛ* in the sense of "motion" and *vṛṅ*.

Regarding the roots *saṃbhaj* (from *bhaj* with the prefix *sam*) and *vṛ* (from *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing"): here, because of the mention of the root-forms without an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), both forms—even those with different indicatory letters—are included. Since the roots *kṛ*, *sṛ*, and *bhṛ* are *anudātta* (unaccented), the prohibition [of *iṭ*] based on the *prakṛti* (the verbal base) applies by the rule "*ekāca upadeśe*" (Pāṇini 7.2.10). Thus, the prohibition having been established, [the following applies].

Since the roots *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* are udātta, the prohibition [of iṭ] based on the rule "rṭhśyukaḥ kitī" would apply; therefore, he states that this is a restrictive rule (niyama) by saying "of the four beginning with *krī*. Here, regarding the inclusion of the four beginning with *stu*, there is also the prohibition of *iṭ* as prompted by the Bhāradvāja-niyama.

It was not stated that "the mention of eight [vowels] is for the purpose of making known the *prayojana* (purpose)," because the prohibition of *iṇ* applies only to the absence of *iṇ* brought about by the negative particle (*nañ*) following the introduction of the rule *eḍvaśī*; it does not apply even to that which is obtained through the force of the option (*vibhāṣā*). Furthermore, according to the maxim *anantarasya* ("of what is proximate"), it applies only to that which is immediately contiguous.

The restriction is appropriate. By that [restriction], both forms—*siṣedhitha*, *siṣeddha*, *siṣidhiva*, *siṣidhva*, and so on—are obtained; but not from others. By this, forms such as *peciva* and *babhūviva* are established. Nor, in this way, does the rule for the *krādi* group alone [apply] to the form *eḍvaśi kṛti*.
One might object: "If the prohibition [of *iṭ*] does not apply, then forms such as *sedivān* and *jakṣivān* would be established anyway;

therefore, what is the purpose of prescribing *iṭ* by the rule *vasvekājādghasām*? This doubt should be raised, for that rule will be explained as having a restrictive (*niyamārtha*) function. Otherwise, the augment *iṭ* would also apply in a form such as *babhūvān*.

It might be argued: "But here, why could there not be a reversed restriction (viparīta-niyama), such that 'if *iṭ* does not occur after roots beginning with *ṛ*, then it occurs only after the *liṭ* [affix]'? And in that case, would there not be the *iṭ* augment in forms such as *kartā* and *akārṣīt*?
Do not say so. For there are the exceptions: "except when referring to a book" (*ṛte granthe*) and "one who is hired, not commissioned" (*amadhīṣṭo bhṛtaḥ*).
Otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with such indications as "the chariot is surrounded" (*parivṛto rathaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "in *vam* and so forth":

by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *sedhve*, *vahe*, and *mahe* is intended; for example: *tuṣṭudhve*, *tuṣṭuvahe*, *tuṣṭumahe*, and so on. This might be argued: let there be a restriction regarding the prohibition based on the root (*prakṛti*).

But it is not possible for [the prohibition] to apply to that which depends on the affix (*pratyayāśraya*), because in the case of *vavartha* from the root *vṛ*, it would result in the application of a prohibition where none was previously applicable. For here, a prohibition depending on the affix does not apply, because the affix *thal* is not marked with *k*. Nor does it depend on the base (*prakṛtyāśraya*), because the root *vṛ* is udātta. Not...

And it should not be argued that "let there be the status of being for the purpose of restriction (niyamārthatva) even in this case," because [the specific form] is not apprehended as such. Even though there is no specific apprehension of *vṛñ* [as opposed to *vṛ*],

nevertheless, since its result would be the attainment of what was previously unattained and the prohibition of what was not [otherwise] prohibited, the inclusion of *vṛ* would necessarily result in the inclusion of *vṛñ* alone.

According to the maxim that "between a prohibition and a restrictive rule, the restrictive rule alone is superior," if one objects that in forms such as *babhūviva*, the prohibition of *ṅ* by the rule *ṛt-śyukaḥ kiti* would be unavoidable,
they reply: [this is not so] because of the rule *abhūthātatanthajagṛbhmavavartheti nigame*.
Because of the Vedic nipātana (irregular formation) *vavartha*, in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*) the augment *iṭ* must be accepted for the root *vṛñ* in the suffix *thal*;

therefore, it is impossible for the mention of *vṛ* to refer to the scope of *thal*. Furthermore, since the roots beginning with *vam* are marked as *kit*, the restrictive rule remains firmly established.

(111) *acaḥ tāsvat thaly aniṭo nityam* | Pāṇini 7.2.61. The phrase *acaḥ tāsvat* [is formed]. From the subsequent sūtra, the word *upadeśe* ("in the original enunciation") is drawn back (*apakṛṣyate*) by attraction; and since that qualifies a root ending in a vowel (*ajanta*), he says: "ending in a vowel in the original enunciation. By implication, the word "root" (*dhātu*) is understood. Not... [the rest of the sentence is not provided in the source].

This occurs from the root *sthā*. The mention of "always" (*nitya*) is a qualifier for the roots that do not take the augment *iṭ*. When the question arises as to where it is always without *iṭ*, it is understood—due to proximity—to refer to that very [root] itself; or rather, the immediately preceding rule, "also after *klṛp*," is carried over. [The prohibition applies] "not after the roots beginning with *vṛt*."

From this [context], the word "not" (na) is understood to carry over; thus he says: "that [root] which is always aniṭ, after which... and so forth. The suffix *vati* is added to a locative ending (*tāsu*), as in *tāsvat*, meaning "like in the case of *tās*" (the third person plural aorist). The sense is: "just as [the substitution of *iṭ*] does not occur in *tās*, so it is also in *thal*. Why [is the condition] "after a vowel" (*acaḥ*) stated? [Consider: *bibheditha*, *rurodhitha*.

What is the purpose of the condition "in the original form" (*upadeśe*)? Consider *jahartha*. Here, because the substitution of *guṇa* and the subsequent substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* take effect—due to their being subsequent rules and obligatory rules—the verbal root no longer ends in an *a*-vowel. Consequently, since this [rule] would not apply, the augment *iṭ* would undesirably follow; therefore, "in the original form" is stated. What is the purpose of the condition "after [the suffix] *thāl*"? Consider *papiva* and *papima*. Why is it specified as "of that which is invariably without *iṭ*" (*nityamaniṭaḥ*)?

*Sasvaritha* and *sasvartha*: this [root] *svar* is not invariably *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment) in the *tās* (the suffix of the periphrastic future), because the *iṭ* is optional according to the rule *varati-sūti*. Some maintain that since the desired result is achieved here simply by carrying forward (*anuvṛtti*) both "in the *tās*" and "not" from the previous rules, the mention of *tāsvat* is not particularly useful.

Others, however, say that this [sūtra] is intended to secure the prohibition of *iṭ* for another [root] in the *thala* suffix only when that [other root] possesses the state of being present (*vidyamānatva*); thus, there is no prohibition in cases such as *uvayitha* and *jaghasitha*. (112) *upadeśe'tvataḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.62.

[The substitution of *i* for *th* occurs] after a root that contains the vowel *a* in its original form (*upadeśa*). Examples: *papaktha*, *iyaṣṭha*. Why "in its original form"? [Consider: *karṣṭhā*, *cakarṣitha*. Why "containing the vowel *a*"? [Consider: *bhetā*, *bibheditha*. What is the purpose of the marker *t* (the *tapara* designation)? [Consider: *rāddhā*, *rarādhitha*. Why "in the *tās-* [affix]"? [Consider: *jighṛkṣati*, *jagrahitha*. [The rule applies] when there is no *ni*...
Regarding the root *kram* (to step): it is always *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment) when followed by the suffix *san* (desiderative), as in *cikraṃsati*.

It is marked with *ū* (*ūdita*), and because it optionally takes *iṭ* before the suffix *ktvā*, there is no *iṭ* before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*. Thus, it is both invariably and optionally *aniṭ*. Furthermore, by the rule *anukramoranātmanepadanimite*, it takes the *parasmaipada* (active voice) endings when not caused by a condition for the *ātmanepada* (middle voice).
Because it is a *seṭ* [root].

(113) *ṛto bhāradvājasya* | Pāṇini 7.2.63. Regarding *ṛto bhāradvājasya*: because of the inclusion of *ta* as a marker (*taparakaraṇa*), this [rule] does not apply to roots such as *kṛ*, *gṛ*, etc., which end in long vowels.

The prohibition applies. In the case of roots such as *hṛ* and *dhṛ*, which end in short vowels, the formation is already established by the rule "ṭhac after those [roots] ending in *tāsi*" (*tāsvat*).

As for *vṛñ* and *vṛṅ*, although they are *seṭ* (taking the *iṭ* augment), nevertheless there is no occasion for the suffix *thac* after *vṛṅ* because it is an *ātmanepada* root; however, in the case of *vṛñ*, the form *vavartha* occurs due to the Vedic irregularity (*nipātana*) "vavartha" [prescribed] in the sense of the root *vṛ*.
In the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), [the suffix] *iṭ* should be applied. He states that this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*)—namely, "only after a root ending in *ṛ*"—by saying:

*jahartha*, *dadhartha*. It would indeed apply to others as well; thus, according to the view of Bhāradvāja it would apply, while according to other views it would not—this results in an option (*vikalpa*). Examples: *papitha*, *papātha*, *pecitha*, *papaktha*.
*Iyajitha* and *iyaṣṭha*: [the latter] is one possessing the vowel *a*. This means it possesses a short *a*. "Such as this" (*īdṛk*):
the meaning is that whatever root is *aniṭ* in the *tās* (the conditional suffix) remains invariably *aniṭ* in *thali* when it ends in *ṛ*. [Objection:
But would not *iṭ* also be inserted in *thali* for the roots *stu*, *dru*, *sru*, and *śru* by virtue of Bhāradvāja’s rule? [Reply: It is not so.
It should not be argued that their inclusion in the *krādi* list [of roots] is purposeless;

for that inclusion is fruitful, as it serves to exclude the augment *iṭ* in the case of *vam* and others. Otherwise, by the rule of the *krādi* group, the addition of *iṭ* would be unavoidable there. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And not," and "by two rules."

The sense is that [the rule] does not cause the reversal of that which has been obtained through the application of *krādi-yoga*. To the inquiry "Why so?", he says: "Of the immediately preceding. Nor should it be argued that in this way there would be a sublation of the rule "upadeśe 'tvataḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.72), because [the sublation applies only] among those verbal roots (*dhātu*) that possess the vowel *a*.

If the prohibition of *iṇ* in the case of *tāsi* were based on the non-observation of roots ending in *ṛ*, then it would be impossible to restrict it to roots ending specifically in *ṛ*. [Objection: In that case, let there simply be a sublation (*bādha*) of the rule *ṭhacastāsvat*;

Even if the sūtra were formulated simply as "ṭhupadeśe’castāsvat," since the word "upadeśa" could still be understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over) from that rule— just as it is in the case of words such as "tāsvatthalī"—
it would follow that the word "upadeśa" would apply to the sūtra "atvataḥ," while the word "aca" from the preceding sūtra would apply to words such as "tāsvatthalī."

From this formulation, it is understood that both [rules] share the same status regarding their application and avoidance. It should be understood that if this [interpretation] is accepted here, there is not even a trace of doubt. Others, however, explain:

"The rule *ṛto bhāradvājasya* should be recited immediately after the rule *acaḥ tāsvat thaly aniṭaḥ*. Since this [rule, *ṛto bhāradvājasya*] begins after both [preceding rules], it follows that here [in the present context] the rule *tāsvat thaly aniṭo nityam* applies.

Carrying forward the word "was" (āsīt), let this prohibition of *iṭ* in the case of *thala* after a root that is invariably without *iṭ* serve as the sublater; for this is due to the force of the commencement of the section on prohibitions earlier [in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*].
Just as mere *iṭ*, without relying on any specific rule, is [sublated] by the prohibition taught independently [of any particular context], so too...
For that undertaking has the purpose of [stating] "it should exclude"; having taken this very meaning as established, [the author of the Vārttika says]:

The mention of *asphūrjan* (in the rule *asphūrjan*) serves both to prohibit the augment *iṭ* in the case of the suffix *niṣṭhā* by the rule *niṣṭhāyām aṇyadarthe*, and to provide an option for the same by the rule *vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ*, as in the forms *asphūrjitam* (by him) and so forth.
Furthermore, the explicit teaching of the long vowel here is intended to indicate that the lengthening prescribed by the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca* is not universal; therefore—

Some say that there are also forms such as *hurcchati* and *mūrcchati*. The root *kṣi* [is used] in the sense of destruction; its inclusion among roots ending in vowels (*ajanta*) is appropriate. The root *ṣi*, meaning "to dwell" and "to go," belongs to the *tudādi* class. (115) *akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.25.

By the inclusion of the term "long" (dīrgha), the *paribhāṣā* "ṭhacaśca" [P. 1.3.9] is brought to bear; hence he says, "ending in a vowel" (*ajanta*). Regarding the phrase "an affix beginning with *ya*" (*yādau pratyaye*): having carried forward the word "in *yi*" (*yī*) from the rule "ayaṅ yi kṅtī" [P.
7.2.80], the affix implied by the term "stem" (*aṅga*) is qualified by it; and by that qualification, the rule of "extension to what begins with it" (*tadādividhi*) applies.

The intention is that the *paribhāṣā* "yasmin vidhis tadādau" (a rule applies to that which begins with the element in which it is prescribed) is brought into play. However, [this is not the case] in the case of *kṛd-yakāra*—for example, in *prakṛtya*, *prahṛtya*, and *uccaiḥ kṛtya*. Because it is subsequent (*aparatvāt*), the long vowel (*dīrgha*) would supersede the *tuk* augment. But the rule for *tuk* finds its scope of application (*caritārtha*) in cases such as *agnicit* and *somasut*.
They say that even the substitution of *pi* for *lyap* is purposeful, as it serves the purpose of making [the affix] *anudātta*.

However, regarding the *yak* of the *sārvadhātuka*—as in *cinuyāt*, *sunuyāt*, and *kṛñīta*—the intention is that since the meaning is identical, it is appropriate to read [the rule] in one place. *laj* and *lañj*: *lajyāt*, *lañjyāt*.

The root *laj* means "to reveal" in the sense of storytelling and the like; it also means "to reproach," and by the word "and" (*ca*), it also means "to parch. *Tuj* means "to protect. This [root] has the meaning of "speaking" in the *yuj*-class. *Gaja* and *gaji*: "a *gañjā* is a house for liquor. *Gaja* also means "intoxication"; intoxication is passion—a transformation of the mind. *Vaja* and *vraja*.
There is no elision due to *abhyāsa* (reduplication) after [the roots] *vad* and *vaj*. Thus: *vavajatuḥ*, *vavrajatuḥ*. Regarding the phrase "ending in *śāḍ*":

this means those ending in the root *ślāgh* (from *āṅ ślāghāyām*). This [root] has *d* as its penultimate letter; and thus, because the rule for *ṣṭu* substitution is considered *asiddha*, by the prohibition of doubling in the rule *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*, the *d* [is not doubled].

The sense is that if the letter *ṭ* is the penultimate (upadhā), then by doubling the syllable containing *ṭ* and subsequently applying the *ṣṭun* rule to the *d*, forms such as *aṭṭiṭiṣate* and *āṭṭiṭat* are established; however, if *ṭ* were the penultimate, the forms would be *aṭiṭṭiṣate* and *āṭiṭṭat*. As for the phrase "with *t* as the penultimate" (*topadha*), in this alternative view—

Forms such as *atiṭiṣate* and *ātiṭiṭat* are to be understood [in this manner]. According to the modern grammarians (*navyāḥ*), when the *ṭ* is removed by the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, the *ṣṭu*-ness (the substitution of *ṣṭu*) which was caused by that *ṭ* is also removed.
However, in the *Manoramā*, it is stated: "The rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* does not apply regarding reduplication (*advirvacane*)."

It has been stated that because the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭh* is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*), when the doubling occurs for the form accompanied by two *ṭ* sounds, and after the application of *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, forms such as *aṭiṭṭiṣate* and *āṭiṭṭat* are established. However, his intention is that the principle "when the cause [of a grammatical operation] is removed, that which was caused by it is also removed" is not universal. [Thus we have] *ānaṭṭe*.

In this context, there is no prohibition [of the augment] for *na*, *da*, and *ra* by the rule "not for *na*, *da*, and *ra*" (*na ndrāḥ*), because that rule—due to the continued application of the phrase "of the second" (*dvitīyasya*)—prohibits [the doubling] only of those single-vowel (*ekāc*) roots among *na*, *da*, and *ra* that are second [in their respective classes]. *jeṭatuḥ*. *jajhaṭatuḥ*. In these cases, however, because they begin with a substitute (*ādeśa*), the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication do not occur. The root *haṭ* means "to shine. *Hāṭaka* means gold; the suffix *ṇvul* is applied by the rule *aṃjñāyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.109), and by virtue of its irregularity (*bāhulaka*), it occurs even when not denoting a feminine. Regarding the form *iyāya*: when reduplication has occurred and *vṛddhi* has been applied in the *ṇal* suffix, the substitution of *āy* takes place.

In *īyatuḥ*, the substitution *iyaṅ* applies by the rule "ṭhabhyāsasyā’savarṇe" (P. 6.1.77). When reduplication has occurred, the rule "ṭheranekāca" (P. 6.4.82) for *yaṇ* is set aside because the homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) is more internal (*antaraṅga*). Subsequently, *iyaṅ* is applied by the rule "ṭhaci śnudhātu-" (P. 6.4.77). Because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as if it were part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntavat*), it is included within the scope of the term "abhyāsa" (reduplicated syllable).

Some say [the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs] by virtue of the inclusion [of the term *abhyāsa*] in the rule "ṭhabhyāsasyā’savarṇe" (Pāṇini 6.4.78). Others, however, maintain that *yaṇ* applies because "that which pertains to the vowel (*vārṇa*) is stronger than that which pertains to the suffix (*āṅga*)," thus overriding the long vowel (*dīrgha*). Nor should it be argued that there is no common locus (*samānāśrayatva*) here, for [it applies] to the *ik* following the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

Because they share the same basis (*samānāśrayatva*) with respect to the substitution of *savarṇadīrgha* and *yaṇ*, [the rule] applies. For this very reason, in the case of *īyatuḥ*, the *yaṇ* substitution is applied by the rule *iṇo yaṇ*, and subsequently, the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is prescribed by the rule *dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti*. Otherwise, this sūtra would be rendered purposeless.

They say it is because of the absence of repetition (*abhyāsa*). This might be argued: "In the case of *ṇal* and *thal*, the substitution *iyaṅ* for the reduplicated syllable would be difficult to obtain; for when that [substitution] is to be applied, by the rule 'before a subsequent element' (*thacaḥ parasmin*), the status of the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*) would apply to the *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* [augmentations], and thus the prohibition 'when not of the same vowel class' (*asavaṇe*) would block it. To this they reply: "No."

A single example necessitates the commencement of the yoga; otherwise, one would have stated "in the case of practice" (*abhyāsasyārtau*). Thus, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), once the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of homogeneous quality) has been applied, and subsequently the *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* substitutions have occurred, there would be *āya* in the case of *ṇal* and *etha* in the case of *thal*. However, there is also the concern that in the alternative where *iṭ* is present, the form would be *ayitha*.
It need not be [included], because that would result in the rule *ṭhabyāsasyā’savarṇe* becoming redundant. [Examples: *etā*, *eṣyati*.

By the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ dīrghaḥ*, there is lengthening: *īyāt*, *aiṣīt*. The root *kuḍi* means "deficiency" or "distinction. *tuḍṭ* means "crushing," "splitting," and "injuring. *roḍṭ* and *loḍṭ*.

And consequently, by the rule *udāttādanudātasya*, a svarita accent occurs. If the rule were explained as "when there is a *ṇi* that has a light syllable," the [desired form] would not occur; however, if it is explained as "when there is a *ṇi* followed by an *aṅ* which is part of the *aṅga* (stem)," then it would occur. Thus, the meaning is that there are two forms—*acacakāsat* and *acīcakāsat*—due to this difference in interpretation. Now, as for the statement "when there is a *ṇi* followed by an *aṅ*..."

In the commentary on the rule *yallaghvi*, by the maxim "that which does not allow for intervention," both [the operations] apply only in cases such as *apīpacat* and the like, but not when there is an intervention of multiple elements,
as in *acacakāsat*; likewise, by the same logic, the rule *agho yoy abhyāsaḥ* [is restricted].

If it is argued that since even here a single [consonant] must be accepted as an intervention, then in forms such as *acikṣaṇat*, the substitution of *i* (by the rule *sanvallaghuni*) would not occur; to this they reply: by the mention of *at* in the rule *atsmṛdṛtvare*, which refers to a homogeneous class [of consonants], there is an exclusion of the *saṃyoga*.

Since it has been established that shortening (*itva*) occurs even when there is an intervention, the aforementioned fault does not apply. For this very reason, the term "of the light syllable" (*laghoḥ*) in the rule *dīrgho laghoḥ* is meaningful. Mādhava also states exactly this regarding the root *jāgṛ*. By speaking thus, he adhered precisely to the *yathoddeśa* (definition-first) view. And so, in the case of the root *ūrṇu*:

Regarding what was stated by the venerable teacher (*yateḥ*) concerning the form *aurṇunavat*: "In the rule *dīrgho laghoḥ*, the long vowel does not apply to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), because the meaning of the sūtra is that the long vowel occurs for that which is the *aṅga* when followed by *caṅ* and *ṇi*;
however, in this case, the reduplication belongs to a part of the *aṅga*, not to the *aṅga* itself," and so forth; therein—

It is understood that even he has no such insistence; for this very reason, he cited "cakāsta" and "acicīkapat. Thus, the contradiction between the preceding and following passages is to be resolved by considering them as representing different viewpoints. (From the *Kātantra-Parिशिष्ट*)

The example *ajījāgarat* cited for both the short and long vowels is to be disregarded, as it is impossible even under that [opponent’s] view. He explains the very restriction with the words *ṇeḥ*. The term “proximate” (*annihitam*) is an attributive containing a reason, while “*aghunī*” is the headword (*viśeṣya*) qualified by that *ṇi*.
"It exists" means "because it is present. Regarding the phrase "only when it is an *aṅga*":

the sense is that although there is no expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for the portion consisting of the substitute (*ādeśa*) in the rule *caṅpare*, there is indeed an expectancy for the portion consisting of the affix (*pratyaya*) in the word *ṇau*; thus, the reason is quite clear. [The phrase] "by Kaiyaṭa himself" [is used].

Thus, the sense is that those who explain [the rule] by distinguishing between the views of Haradatta and Kaiyaṭa as two separate positions are to be disregarded. Having repeated the word "caṅpare" (in a context where *caṅ* follows), it is also applied as a qualifier for "aglopi" (a stem that loses a vowel); he states its result with the words "ṇeḥ" (of the suffix *ṇi*).

It should be understood that because [the rules] such as *śridrusruṣu* apply even when there is no elision (*aglopitva*), here too the condition "when followed by *caṅ*" (*caṅpare*) alone suffices to obtain the meaning "when followed by *ṇi*. Regarding the phrase *agitām api*:
this means "of roots such as *pac*, *kam*, *śak*, and so forth. For there is no elision of those [roots] designated with the marker *it* when followed by *ṇic*.

The sense is that "he awaits. Regarding "the result of teaching with *ṇ*": the meaning is the insertion of the *anusvāra*. In the case of *daṃdhranti*, the augment *nuk* is applied to the reduplication by the rule "of a root ending in a nasal, when preceded by *u*. (132) *ye vibhāṣā* 6.4.43.

"In *gatyādiṣu*": the meaning is "in the case of [roots] beginning with *gam*, such as those involving motion, sound, and contact. Regarding *mīmṛ*: the purpose of its being marked with the *ṛt* indicatory letter (*ṛdit*) is for the prohibition [of lengthening] by the rule *āglopi*. Thus, *amimīmat*. (133) Pāṇini 7.3.75: *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti*. [The augment *iṭ* is not applied after the roots *ṣṭhivu*, *klam*, and *cam* when followed by an affix marked with the *śit* indicatory letter.]
Regarding *ṣṭhivu* and *klam*: [the roots] *ṣṭhīvati* and *klāmati*. Regarding *āṅ cim*:
the sense is that the reading cited by the author of the *Vṛtti*, namely *ṭhivuklamvācamām*, is incorrect. Regarding "some [read] *jimi*": thus they employ *jemanam* in the sense of eating.

(134) *vā bhrāśa-bhlāśa-bhramu-kramu-klamu-vasi-vuṭi-laṣaḥ* | 3|1|70| This is an optional rule (*ubhayatra-vibhāṣā*). *Bhramiḥ* in the sense of "unsteadiness" (*anavasthā*), as well as *klam* and *tras*, belong to the *divādi* class; for these, the suffix is already obligatory (*nitya*) by virtue of that class. For the others, however, the suffix has not yet been established, and since this rule is formulated for them, it is optional. [The roots *hrāśṛ* and *bhlāśṛ*...]

These two [roots] are used in the sense of "shining" and so forth. *Hramu* (in the sense of "moving") belongs to the *bhvādi* class and the *jvalādi* class; it is also read as belonging to the *haṇādi* class in the *Manoramā*, though the modern grammarians consider that to be due to an oversight. *Hramu* (in the sense of "lack of stability") belongs to the *divādi* class, the *puṣādi* class, and the *śamādi* class. Among these, from the *bhvādi* class: *bhramyati*.
It conjugates as *bhramati*. However, when the suffix *śyan* follows *śam* and others, there is lengthening, resulting in the three forms: *bhrāmyati*, etc.
[The roots] *lamu* in the sense of exhaustion, *rasī* in the sense of agitation, *ruṭa* in the sense of cutting, and *aṣa* in the sense of desire [are treated similarly].
(135) *kramaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* 7.3.76. [In these cases, the substitution of *i* for the final vowel occurs before the Parasmaipada endings.]

The sequence [of rules] follows from the recurrence of the phrase "after the roots *ṣṭhivu*, *kramu*, and *cam*" [from Pāṇini 7.3.75]; therefore, he says: "in the *parasmaipada* [voice], when followed by the suffix *śatṛ*.
Why "in the *parasmaipada*"? [Consider: *upakramate*, *parākramate*.
(136) *snukramoranātmanepadanimite* [Pāṇini 7.2.36].

*snukramoḥ*: "in the absence of a cause for the middle voice" (*ātmanepada-nimitta*); that is to say, when there is no occasion for the middle voice. Others, however, say that the singular number is used by way of substitution (*vyatyaya*) in place of the dual, meaning "in the absence of two causes for the middle voice. This applies to both [interpretations].

It should be understood that the conditions for the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are "state" (*bhāva*), "object" (*karman*), and "reciprocity" (*karmavyatihāra*); however, in the case of the sequence [of roots], "existence" (*vṛtti*), "creation" (*sarga*), and so forth are also included. Since the augment *iṭ* is already established for the roots *snū*, *kam*, and *mṛ* because they are udātta, he states "only here is there *iṭ*" (*atreveṭ*) as a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Why does he say "not in the non-ātmanepada" (*anātmanepade*)? [To exclude cases where the ātmanepada does not apply].

[The suffixes] *ṭhuka* [are applied] after the roots *snau*, *kram*, and *ā-kram* when followed by water (*jalena*). For example: *sthopakramsyate* (he will begin to flow with water), *sthopakrāṃsyate* (he will begin to flow with water), *sthākrāṃsyate* (he will begin to flow with water). Why is it said "when indicated" (*nimita*)? Consider: from the root *snau* we have *snavitā* (he will flow); then, by applying *ky-aṅ* to form a denominative, we get *snavitrīyate* (he acts like one who flows).
Here, they say that although *ky-aṅ* is the cause for the *ātmanepada* voice, the root *snau* itself is not the cause.
(137) *vibhāṣeṭaḥ* |8|3|79|. [This rule applies] to the *dh* of the *luṅ*, *liṭ*, and *lṛṭ* [tenses]. In the *liṭ* [perfect], [the forms are] *lilihidhve* or *lilihidhve*.
(138) *upasargasyāyatau* |8|2|19|. [The long vowel substitution occurs] for the [final *a* of a] preposition before the root *yat*.
Now, as to how [this is so]: the intention of the objector is that it ought to be formed with the suffix *śānac*. The root *knūyī* means "to sound";
*unda* means "moistening.
(139) *liṅyaṅeśca* 6.1.29.
Furthermore, it is caused to drink (*pepīyate*).

(140) *dīpa-jana-budha-pūri-tāyi-pyāyibhyaḥ anyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 3.1.61. [The roots] *dīpa*, *jana*, *budha*, *pūri*, *tāyi*, and *pyāyi*: [the suffix *kyac* is optionally applied after these]. ‘*īpī* means “to shine,” ‘*janī* means “to appear,” and ‘*budha* means “to understand.”’
The root *ūrī* is used in the sense of "satisfying. These [roots] belong to the *divādi* class.
(141) *ciṇo luk* | Pāṇini 6.4.104: "There is elision (*luk*) of the *ciṇ*. This means that there should be elision of what follows. Some read the rule as "of the word *at*" (*adaśabdasya*).

That is the statement of the meaning of the word *tat*. When the suffix *ciṇ* is prescribed after that word *tat*, the elision (*luk*) that occurs for what follows *ciṇ* belongs to the word *tat* itself, because it is clear from the rule "the elision (*luk*), *ślu*, and *lup* apply to the affix" [that the elision applies to the affix]. "This" refers to the root *ṣevṛ*.

"Contrary to the Bhāṣya": if this [root] were a *ṣopadeśa* (one whose initial consonant is marked with *ṣ*), then like the root *styā*, it too would have been excluded by the definition of *ṣopadeśa*; since that was not done, the implication is that it is not a *ṣopadeśa*.
Regarding "in the sense of moving by leaping": some say that *plava* is a separate verbal root (*dhātu*). That indeed...
In the *Manoramā*, it is criticized: "If *lav* were a separate root, then the optional prescription of the suffix *ghañ* for *plu* in the rule *vibhāṣā iṅru-p-luvoḥ* would be redundant;
for the word *āplāva* would already be established by adding *ghañ* to *lpev*. Likewise...

Furthermore, the prescription of *it* (the substitution of *i*) for the vowel *u* of the root *plu* in the case of reduplication by the rule *‘ravatiśraṇoti’* would also be redundant; for that rule is indeed made for the sake of establishing the form *apiplavat* as an alternative, yet that form is already established from the root *plu* by the rule *‘anyataḥ’*, so what is the purpose of including it?

The elision [of the *y*] does not occur by the rule "yasya halaḥ," because it has been established as a settled principle that the term "yasya" refers to a cluster [of sounds]. However, when referring to a single phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of meaningful units (*arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) does not apply; consequently, elision occurs even in forms such as *putrakāmyā*.

This is the general direction. In the *luṭ* (future) [suffix], it is *mavyitā*. In the benedictive (*āśis*), it is *mavyāt*; here, by the rule "the *yam* following a consonant is elided before *am*," there is optionally the elision of the *yakāra* of the root. Thus, *sūrkṣya* and *īrkṣya*. In the *ṇal* [perfect suffix], it is *suṣūrkṣya*.
[In the periphrastic perfect: *īrṣyācakāra* or *īrṣyācakāra*. From these, with the *kvip* suffix, there is elision...

In *vyoṭaḥ*, following the elision of *y* by the rule *koḥ*, there is the elision of *k* by the rule *koḥ*, and after the application of *jaśtva* and *cartva*, the form is simply *sūrṭ*. The root *haya* means "to go. [The forms] *jahāya* and *hayyāt* [are derived from it].
Regarding "loosening" (*śithilīkaraṇa*), this is because it is observed in such passages as "*omam abhiṣuṇoti*" (he presses the *oma*). [This refers to] *surā* (liquor).

Thus [it is said]. In that context, because of the statement by Amarasimha, "The pressing (*abhiṣava*) would be for the blind," [the rule applies] to that which ends in *l*. 7|2|2. "To that which ends in *l*": if, by means of the word *anta* ("end") used in the sense of a constituent part, a *bahuvrīhi* compound [is formed] with respect to the *aṅga* (base).

Furthermore, in that view, since the rule of *tadantavidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with the specified element) is established by means of the qualifier itself, the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) is redundant. Moreover,
there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *aśvallīt*, because the word "end" (*anta*) denotes proximity.

In the case of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) is redundant, since the rule of extension to that which ends with [the specified element] (*tadantavidhi*) is already established by means of the qualifier. Furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of *aśvallīt*.
This is because, in the case of a genitive compound, the word "end" (*anta*) denotes proximity.

There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as *rapiraṇiśvallaprabhṛti*, because the *aṅga* is in proximity to the *at* [augment] following *lṛ*. Furthermore, in the case of a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *anta*—meaning "that which ends in *ar*"—the word *anta* would have to be placed first due to its status as a qualifier. Therefore:
He says: "The genitive case ending is elided. Intending that the word *anta* signifies "proximity," he says:

"Those which are near to this. [This means] "vṛddhi shall occur from this. In this context, one must accept that the term *ataḥ* functions through *tantra*, repetition (*āvṛtti*), or other such grammatical devices; otherwise, [the rule would not hold].

The sense is that, even if the *akṣarapari-bhāṣā* (the rule concerning the non-application of a paribhāṣā due to lack of purpose) does not apply here, the substitution would still occur for the final letter by virtue of the *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā* (the rule that an operation applies to the final letter). Although it might be argued that even if the rule were stated as *ato larsyeṭ*,
the meaning could be understood as "vṛddhi occurs for the final *at* of an *aṅga* ending in *lṛ* when followed by *sic*," [this is not the case].

Consequently, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *aśvallīt*; to prevent this, the word "end" (*anta*) was included in the sūtra. It should be understood that, in accordance with that [sūtra], the word "end" is taken to mean "proximity," and the repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the word "hence" (*ataḥ*) is accepted. Therefore, [the question arises: from what proximity?

*akhorīt*, *amīlīt*. Why [is it said] "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*)? [Consider: *śval* in the sense of "going quickly. *aśvallīt*. That *l* which is near the vowel *a* is not the end of the stem; whereas that which is the end of the stem, the *r*, is not near the vowel *a*. But surely, regarding this term *lare*:

If it is argued that even without assuming the elision of the genitive case, one may accept that the word *anta* denotes a "part," and thus explain the rule as meaning: "the *vṛddhi* substitute occurs for the *at* which is at the end (*anta*) of the *aṅga*, or for the *at* immediately preceding that [final *at*]," then there would be no need to repeat the word *ataḥ*. To this, they reply: [The objection continues: If the genitive were elided, then by the principle of *ekadeśisamāsa* (a compound denoting a part), the word *anta* would refer to the final syllable of the *aṅga*; consequently, the rule would apply to the *at* of the *aṅga* itself, and not to the *at* of the affix *laṭ*. Furthermore, if the genitive were not elided, then since the word *anta* would denote proximity (*sāmīpya*), the rule would apply to the *at* of the affix *laṭ* rather than to the *at* of the *aṅga*. Therefore, in order to ensure that the *vṛddhi* applies specifically to the *at* of the *aṅga*, the repetition of the word *ataḥ* is necessary. This is the established view.

In the *Manoramā* commentary on the sūtra *ṭhhalantyam*, the view that "proximity (*āmīpya*) is the meaning of the genitive case" has been refuted; following that [line of reasoning], an elision (*āvṛtti*) of the word *ataḥ* is resorted to here. Regarding this, some say: in the rule *ato larantasya*, the word *lare* contains a dropped locative case ending (*luptasaptamīkam*). Alternatively, *ataḥ*...

It would have been possible to formulate the rule as *larante* alone. In that case, since the interpretation could be "there is vṛddhi of the *a* immediately preceding a *lṛ* which is at the end of an *aṅga*," there would be no difficulty of resorting to *tantra* (simultaneous application) or *āvṛtti* (repetition). Nor is it the case that the *aṅga* can only be construed as the qualified member (*viśeṣya*).

It cannot be argued that [the term *padasya*] is logically connected as a qualifier, because the intention of the *paribhāṣā*— "In the context of operations concerning a *pada* or an *aṅga*, [the rule applies] to that and to what ends with it"— is described as making both the *pada* and the *aṅga* the qualificands; for [this would contradict the application of] *allopo ’naḥ*.

In this sūtra, because the authors of the Bhāṣya and others have explained that "aṅga-avayava" (a portion of the *aṅga*) is qualified by the phrase "not being in the place of a pronoun" (*asarvanāmasthāne*), they say that even when the *aṅga* functions as a qualifier in certain instances, there is no harm [to the application of the rule]. This refers to [the prohibition] such as "not before *iṭ*" (*neṭi*). Although, according to the maxim of the "prior exception" (*purastādapavāda-nyāya*), [the subsequent rule would otherwise take precedence].
The sense is this: the rule *eṭī* is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the general rule], but not an exception even to an optional alternative (*vikalpa*).
Nevertheless, when considering the general category of what is to be sublated (*bādhyasāmānya*), everything that has been obtained within its own scope is sublated;
thus, the maxim of the "exception first" (*purastādapavādanyāya*) does not apply here. [The root] *mīla* means "contraction."
The usage of *til* in the sense of "closing the eyes" is very common. *Til* is listed in the *curādi* group in the sense of "smearing.

*Dal* means "to split"; splitting is the separation of constituent parts. From the root *dhaurṛ*, we have *dhoritaka*, which is a specific mode of galloping for horses. The suffix *kan* is added after a word ending in *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix) when it functions as a proper name; thus, *tsaraḥ*.

*Chadmagatiḥ* means movement by means of deception or fraud (*cchadmanā kapaṭena*). [The root] *kmar* is used in the sense of "bending" (*hūrchane*); bending is crookedness (*kauṭilyam*). [The root] *ṣṭhivu* is used in the sense of "spitting out" (*nirasane*); with the suffix *lyuṭ*, it becomes *ṣṭhevanam*. This is as in the passage: "One should not cast spittle (*ṭhīvana*), blood, feces, urine, or semen into water."
They say that in the alternative view based on the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the long vowel *ī* is substituted [for the short *i*].
(143) *saṃlliṭorjeḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.57. [The rule] *saṃlliṭorjeḥ*. [The phrase] "conditioned by *san* and *liṭ*" means: if, however, *san* or *liṭ* follows...

If one were to respect the explanation of the predecessors that "it is repetition" (*abhyāsa*), then, according to the maxim "that by which there is no intervention," the intervention of the root (*prakṛti*) would indeed have to be tolerated;

however, in the case of *jejayiṣati*—formed with the desiderative suffix (*san*) from the reduplicated base (*yaṅluganta*)—the substitution of *k* for *j* (*kutva*) would result, and that is not accepted in the works of Mādhava. This is the intended meaning.
(144) *dhinvikṛṣvyora ca* | Pāṇini 3.1.80. Regarding *dhinvikṛṣvyora ca*: by the rule *ṭhalo’ntyasya*, the vowel *a* is substituted for the letter *v*.
By the inclusion of the letter *ca*, the suffix *u* is drawn forward [from the previous rule]. However, Bopadeva considers these two roots to belong to the *tanādi* class.
It is accepted. In his view, however, the suffix *up* is obtained even without the particle *ca*. Therefore, there is elision (*lopa*).
Although the state of having a final *a* does not exist in the original instruction (*upadeśa*), it nevertheless exists in the instruction for the *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes.
This is because, as stated in the rule *“hinvikṛṇvyora ca,”* once the substitution of the vowel *a* has been made, [the suffix *up*] is drawn forward (*anukṛṣṭa*)...
The meaning is: "because it arises subsequently.
(145) *lopaścānyatarasyāṃ mvoḥ* |6|4|107|. [The sūtra begins: *lopaśca*. [The commentary states: "the *u*-phoneme which is a suffix," meaning "a suffix that is not preceded by a conjunct consonant."

However, the qualification "pratyaya" (affix) was not applied [in the rule], because even though there is no undesirable result in forms such as *akṣṇuvaḥ* and *akṣṇumaḥ*, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *aśnuvahe*. Similarly, in the rule *utaśca*, although there is no fault in the case of *akṣṇuhi*, [the same logic applies].

They say that the restriction "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogapūrva*) was added as a qualification of the suffix because otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *aśnuhi*. Although the form *aśnuhi* in the Parasmaipada is rare in common usage, its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) should nevertheless be understood with reference to the Veda. [The example given is] *āpnuhi*.
The reading is *utiḥ*. (146) *utaśca pratyayād asaṃyogapūrvāt* [Pāṇini 6.4.106].
*kṛvi*. This means "he performs" (*kṛṇoti*) and so forth; for it belongs to the *svādi* class.

The root *kṛvi* is not recited [in the Dhātupāṭha]; rather, it is *kṛñ* in the sense of "injuring. The resulting meaning is that its forms, such as *kṛṇoti* and so forth, are identical when used in the *parasmaipada* for *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. *Av* means "protection. There are nineteen meanings. *Kāntiḥ*—beauty.
They say that *dīpti* (radiance) is *tejas* (splendor). *Tṛpti* (contentment) is the cessation of desire. *Svāmyartha* (the meaning of sovereignty) is lordship (*svāmitva*).

*Hiṃsā* (violence) is killing. *Ādāna* (taking) is grasping. Nor should it be argued that in this context the meaning [of the root] must be "giving" alone; for the meanings have been specified as "leaving," "growth," "grasping," and "killing."
Because it has been enumerated by Bopadeva. Regarding the root *bhikṣ* (to beg): there are three meanings—begging, obtaining, and not obtaining.

However, the author of the *Svāmī* (Svāmī Dīkṣita), having read [the root] as ‘*liś* in the sense of indistinct speech,’ considers these two also to be meanings of the root *bhikṣ*. [The root] ‘*liś* in the sense of affliction’ belongs to the *divādi* class; [the root] ‘*liśū*... [belongs to the *tudādi* class].

In the *Rigveda* and other texts, [the root] *vibādh* occurs; *dīkṣ* has five meanings. *Īṣ* means "to go. By the rule *urośca halaḥ*, the suffix *ap* is applied, and with the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, we have *īṣā*. The "reins" (*īṣā*) of the mind (*manas*) is *manīṣā*. It belongs to the *śakandhvādi* group.
That which is fixed upon by the *manīṣā* is *manīṣita*. [The suffix *kta* is added] after a nominal stem in the sense of verbal action.

In the rule *bahulam iṣṭhavat ca*, the suffix *kta* is applied after a root ending in *ṇic*. However, the root *iṣ* meaning "to glean" (*uñcha*) belongs to the *parasmaipada* conjugation. There are three [roots] beginning with a short vowel: *iṣ* meaning "to go" (*gati*) belongs to the *divādi* class; *iṣ* meaning "desire" (*icchā*) belongs to the *tudādi* class;
and *iṣ* meaning "repetition" (*ābhīkṣṇya*) belongs to the *juhotyādi* (or *rkyādi*) class.

Regarding the form *kāsāñcakre*: the suffix *ām* is applied by the rule *āspratyaye*. The root *bhāsṛ* means "to shine. Its status as having a *ṛt* vowel (like *bhrāj*) results solely in the application of the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings. This is because, by the rule *hrājabhāse*, the shortening of the penultimate vowel is optional. The root *ṇas* means "crookedness" (*kauṭilya*).

Because it lacks the characteristics of being marked with *liṭ* or having an indicatory letter (*ādi*), the substitution of *e* does not apply. [The forms] *nesa* and *āṅḥ śasi* [are derived from other roots].
However, the root *aṃs* meaning "to praise" will be discussed among the *parasmaipada* roots. Regarding the roots *grasu* and *glasu*:

by the rule *udito vā*, there is optional *iṭ* before the suffix *ktvā*. Thus, we have *grasitvā* or *grastvā*. By the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, there is no *iṭ* [before the suffix *kta*]. Thus, *grastaḥ*.

Regarding *vehat*, *jehat*, and *vāhat*: the word *vehat* is established as a *nipāta* (irregular form) with the suffix *ati* added to the root *vi-hṛ*, as indicated in the rule *oṭāyuvatī*. The meaning is "a cow that miscarries," as in the expression *vehad-garbhopaghātinī*. Regarding the final [example], it concerns the word *bāhu*, a synonym for *bhuja*, according to the rule *ṣubdhasvāntadhvānte*.

The sense is that the word *bāḍham* is established as being without dispute. Regarding the phrase "the dentals and labials," it is connected with the words "both [of them]. The ātmanepada resulting from the [designation] *anudāteta* is not mandatory; by this, the form "vavāha raktaṃ puruṣāstato jātāḥ sahasraśaḥ" is established. Not [otherwise].

And they say that there is no inconsistency here with the meaning, because since verbal roots have multiple meanings, there is no obstacle to its having the sense of "flowing forth" (prasravaṇa). [Objection: How then is it that the statement "the wise person infers even what has not been stated" (anuktam apy ūhati paṇḍito janaḥ) is possible? [Response: To this they say—there is no fault, because the *taṅ* (the Ātmanepada suffixes) characterized by the anudātta accent is not mandatory (*anitya*).

Thus: *gāh*. Because it ends in *ū*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied. In the absence of *iṭ*, there is the substitution of *ḍh* for *gh*. By the rule "ekācaḥ," there is the substitution of *bhaṣ* (the voiced unaspirate *gh*). By the rule "aḍho kaḥ si," there is the substitution of *k* for *gh*. There is the substitution of *ṣ* for the letter following *k*—thus: *jaghākṣe*. Optionally, by the rule "vibhāṣeṭaḥ," the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) substitute may apply—thus: *jagāhiḍhve* or *jagāhidhve*. However, in the absence of *iṭ*, the *bhaṣ* substitution applies [to the *dh*].

‘*ḍhea lopaḥ*’—as in *jaghāḍhave*. Why [specify] *ḍhe*? [Consider] *ūḍhaḥ*. In this case, let there not be the elision of *ḍh* first. However, when the mention of *ḍhe* is made, the desired result is established by relying on the rule ‘*ṭuanā ṣṭua*’; thus they say the intended goal is achieved.

(147) *ḍho ḍhea lopaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.13. [In the example] *agāḍhata*: there is the elision of *s* by the rule *halo jhali*. Then follow the substitution of *ḍha*, the substitution of *dha*, the substitution of *ṣṭu*, and the elision of *ḍha*. However, the *bhaṣ*-substitution does not occur prior to the elision of the *sic*-affix, because it is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) [at that stage]. As for the *bhaṣ*-substitution...

Even after the elision of *s* (*sijlopānantaram*), [the substitution] does not take place, because there is an absence of a *sakāra* following [the *jhal*]. Nor should it be suspected that even when the elision of *s* has occurred, the substitution of *bhaṣ* would be unavoidable due to the status of being followed by *sic* by means of the principle of "treatment as a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); for there is no "treatment as a suffix" when the operation depends on a phoneme (*varṇāśraye*). Otherwise, [in the case of] *gave hitam*...
In the word *go-hitam*, there would be the substitution of *av* [for the final vowel]; this is the general direction. Regarding *jagṛhe*:

although the rule *ug-antānām* (Pāṇini 1.1.9) would require *guṇa* due to the suffix being *kit*, there is an absence of *guṇa* because of the *vārttika* "from roots with *ṛ* as the penultimate letter" (*ṛd-upadhābhyaḥ*).
Thus, by virtue of the *kit* designation, *guṇa* does not occur.

(148) *śala igupadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.1.45. The term *śala* [refers to roots] having *ig* as their penultimate (*upadhā*). Because the word *ala* is a qualifier of the verbal root (*dhātu*), it is understood that [the root] must end in *la*. Why say *śala*? [Consider: *atipta* (from √tip). Why say *ig*? [Consider: *agāḍha* (from √gāh). Why say *aniṭaḥ*? [Consider: *āuṣiṣṭa* (from √uṣ). [The suffix *ksa* is replaced by *iṭ*] before a vowel (*aci*) following *ksa*.

Regarding the phrase *ajādau*: here, the suffix (*pratyaya*) implied by the term *aṅga* is the qualificand. Some say that the addition of the word *aṅi* is an interpolation, as it is not mentioned in the *Kāśikā* and other such works. Others, however, maintain that because the word *ātmanepade* is drawn back (retrojected) from the rule *ugvā duheḥ*, the condition *aṅi* is thereby obtained; thus, [the rule applies] to *ṛśe-*...
They say that the elision of the *ksa* suffix mentioned in the Vārttika does not occur in cases such as *sadṛkṣaḥ* and *anyādṛkṣaḥ*. (149) *ksasyā’ci* | Pāṇini 7.3.72.

The root *ghuṣ* is used in the sense of "making manifest" (*kāntikaraṇe*). In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense: *ighuṃṣiṣṭa*, *aghuṃṣiṣātām*. However, if it is read with a short *u* as the penultimate vowel (*adupadhā*), then: *aghaṣiṣṭa*, *aghaṣiṣātām*. (150) The root *takṣ* is used in the sense of "making thin" (*tanūkaraṇe*). [Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.76]

Regarding *atakṣīt*: by the rule *eṭi*, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies. In the absence of *iṭ*, however, it is *atākṣīt*. Regarding *praṇikṣati*: by the rule *upasargādasamāse’pi*, there is obligatory *ṇatva*. The rule *vā niṃsanikṣanindām*, however, pertains to *kṛt*-affixes. [In the case of the affixes] *ṇvul* and *tṛc*: *praṇikṣikaḥ*.

*praṇikṣakaḥ*, *praṇikṣitā*, *pranikṣitā*. Regarding "disregard" (*avajñā*) and so forth: according to the meaning of the *Amarakośa*, *sūrkṣaṇa* means respect (*ādara*), and that which is other than this is *asūrkṣaṇa*. However, if *sūrkṣaṇa* were said to mean disregard (*anādara*), then *asūrkṣaṇa* would not be a synonym for disregard (*avajñā*).

The state [of being]. *Kākṣi*. *Kāṅkṣā*—desire. *Drākṣi*, *dhrākṣi*, *dhvākṣi*. *Ghoravāsitaṃ*—a terrible sound. From the root *vāsṛ* in the sense of "sound," it is that which cries out (*dhvāṅkṣati*), hence *dhvāṅkṣa*—a crow. *Drākṣi*. From the root [with the suffix] *uraḥ* and *hal* according to the rule *urośca halaḥ*, there is the suffix *ṭha*; thus, *drākṣā*. In the *yavādi* group...

The elision of *n* occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). [The form] *drākṣāmān* [is derived from *drākṣāmat*]; here, the substitution of *v* for *m* in the suffix *mat* does not occur, because of the rule stating "after words ending in *ṭha*, *ya*, etc. [the suffix *mat* becomes *van*]. The root *tūṣ* means "to be satisfied"; however, in the *divādi* class, it has a short vowel as its penultimate. The root *mūṣ* means "to steal.
When the suffix *kvun* is applied to form a name, [it becomes] *ūṣakaḥ*; however, in the *kryādi* class, this [root] has a short vowel as its penultimate.

The root *bhūṣ* is used in the sense of adorning; it also belongs to the *curādi* (tenth) class. The root *īṣ* is used in the sense of ploughing; by the rule "uruśca halaḥ," the suffix *ap* is applied, resulting in *īṣā*, meaning the shaft of a plough. The roots *kaṣ* and *khaṣ* end in *ṣ*.
This root *iṣ* is also not restricted to the *tudādi* class, but rather belongs to the *rudhādi* class as well, in the sense of contraction.
Intending to show that there is an absence of [any other] authority (*māna*), he provides an example: *śeṣṭā*, *aśikṣat*, and so forth.
(151) *tīṣasahalubharuṣariṣaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.48. *tīṣasaha*: *iṣa* (in the sense of desiring), *ṣaha* (in the sense of enduring), *lubha* (in the sense of greed), *ruṣa*, *riṣa*.

In the sense of injury: *eṣitā*, *eṣṭā*; *sahitā*, *soḍhā*; *lobhitā*, *lobdhā*. (152) Pāṇini 3.1.38: "After the roots *uṣ* (to burn), *vid* (to know), and *jāgṛ* (to wake), [the suffix *ktvā*] optionally [takes the augment *iṭ*]. Regarding *uvoṣa*: the substitution of *guṇa* occurs by the rule "after a root ending in *u*"; then *uvaṅ* is substituted by the rule "in place of *abhyāsa* before a non-homogeneous vowel. *ghṛṣu*.
In the word *saṃgharṣe*: with the suffix *lyuṭ*, [we get] *gharṣaṇam*. [The root] *ghaslṛ* means "to eat. Regarding the phrase "this [root]":

the sense is that if this were universal (*sārvatrika*), it would also be employed in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]; consequently, the rule prescribing the optional substitution [of *ghas* for *ad*] by the sūtra "iṭo 'nyatarasyām" would be rendered useless. "In this very [section]" refers to the reading in this very context.
The meaning is that its recitation is in the *bhvādi* class in the *parasmaipada*. Regarding "in the case of *kmarac*": this refers to the rule *ṛghasyadaḥ kmaraḥ* (3.2.161).
(153) *saḥ syārddhadhātuke* (7.4.49).

The word *saḥ* is to be split as *sa-iti*. Why [is the condition] "beginning with *s*" (*sādau*) specified? [Consider] *ghasmarah*. Why [is the condition] "in an *ārddhadhātuka* affix" (*ārddhadhātuke*) specified? [Consider] *vasse*. Regarding the term *āśiṣi*: it means "in the *āśīr-liṅ* (the precative mood). And this has been stated with reference to the agent (*kartari*). However, in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*), there is no application [of this rule] where *yaK* is the scope.
The object of cognition (*bodhyam*).

(154) *puṣādidyautādyalṛditaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* | Pāṇini 1.3.91. [The root] *puṣ* etc., [the root] *dyut* etc., and those roots ending in short *ṛ* take the *parasmaipada* endings. The root *puṣ* occurs in the *bhvādi*, *divādi*, *kryādi*, and *curādi* [gaṇas].

It is recited [in that manner]. However, if the *puṣādi* group were taken as beginning with the root *uṣa puṣṭau* from the *bhūvādika* class, then the mention of the *dyutādi* group would be redundant, because the *dyutādi* roots are recited later after the root *puṣ*. Nor is it a sub-group (*antargaṇa*) within the *krādya* group, for in that case, the root *uṣa* follows immediately after the root *puṣ*.

Only four [roots] are recited: *stai* (in the sense of stealing), *bhū* (in the sense of manifestation of a being), *hiṭha* (in the sense of taking away), and *raha* (in the sense of seizing). If these alone were intended to be included, then for the sake of brevity, they would have been formed with the marker *ḷ*. Even though *grah* is marked as *svarita*, it too was [intended to be] by means of the *ḷ* marker alone.
Because there is no possibility of that [curādigaṇa] being applied, there is also no concern regarding the excessive burden of attaching numerous suffixes (*anubandhas*).

Nor is it the *curādi* class, because due to the intervention of the *ṇic* suffix, the occurrence of *cler* (the *liṭ* suffix) after it would be impossible in either case. Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), only the *divādi* class is understood; thus he says: "of the *puṣādi* roots which take the *śyan* conjugational sign."
Some, however, say that only the root *puṣ* and others belonging to the *divādi* class are included here, on the basis of the traditional explanation (*vyākhyāna*).

Their intention is that, according to the view that the suffix *ṇic* is optional for all roots of the *curādi* class, the *cli* suffix can also follow *puṣ* and other roots of the *caurādi* class. This is similar to the rule "from *andi*, *grah*, *pac*, etc. (*andigrahipacādibhyaḥ*).

It would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule as *‘uṣadyautādyalṛditaḥ’*. If it is asked, "Why were the *puṣādi* and *dyautādi* groups not made *lṛdit* [ending in the marker *ḷ*]?", they say in response:
because if the letter *ḷ* were recited for each individual root—both those without markers (*niranubandha*) and those with markers (*sānubandha*)—the opposite [undesired result] would follow.

There would be prolixity (gaurava). Nor should it be suspected that there is no fault of prolixity due to the attachment of multiple indicatory letters (anubandha), on the grounds that the purpose for which the *ātmanepada* is prescribed for other indicatory letters is also accomplished by the addition of the *ḷit* marker; for among those [roots], there are those marked with *ādi*, *īdi*, and *ūdi*.

Because the accomplishment of various tasks through the syllable *satvāt* is impossible due to the difficulty of warding off the weight of attachment to numerous entanglements; [this applies] to *jarja*, *carca*, and *jharjha*, along with their associated reprimands and so forth.

They say that there is no [application of] numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*), because of the [specific] explanation. *Paribhāṣaṇa* is a reproachful censure. It is appropriate to read all three [roots] with endings ending in the *ca*-class consonants, but not here with endings ending in sibilants (*ūṣman*). *Ṇiśa* means "concentration" (*samādhi*); concentration is the restraint of the internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*).

Regarding *praṇeśati*: the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *upasargādasamāse ’pi*. Regarding *roṣakṛte ca*: the word *ca* (and) implies *samādau* (in *samādi*). The root *śaś* means "to leap. Intending that the form ending in *s* (*sānta*) is what is included in the prohibitive rule *aśasadade*, he explains it as *śeśatuḥ*. However, according to the Easterners (*prācām*)...

The sense is that what was stated—namely, "he should not cause to cut" (*aśaśatu*)—is incorrect. [In the form] *acaḍhīt*, there is no *vṛddhi* because of the rule "before *hayanta*" (Pāṇini 7.2.5). The root *raha* means "to abandon. This [root] also belongs to the *kathādi* group. Furthermore, it is recited in the section on *mit* roots according to the opinion of certain authorities by the rule "*ñapa micca*" (Pāṇini 1.3.5). [The author] says "they do not accept this."
The commentary itself is the authority here: *mā bhavān uhat*. By the rule *a māṅ-yoge*, there is the absence of the augment *āṬ*;
by the rule *ṭhiritovā*, the suffix *aṅ* is optionally applied; hence it belongs to the *dyautādi* group. The root *dyaut* means "to shine.
(155) *dyauti-svāpyoḥ saṃprasāraṇam* || 7.4.67 || [In the formation of the causative, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the semivowel in the roots *dyaut* and *svāpi*.]
