Regarding *dyauti-svāpyoḥ*: the term *vāpi* refers to the causative (*ṇijanta*) form. In *didyaute*, once the semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) has been applied, the single-substitute *pūrvarūpa* is applied by the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca*. Therefore, it does not apply here:
from *svāpi* with the suffix *ṇvul* we have *svāpakaḥ*; one who desires that is expressed as *svāpakīyati*; from that, the desiderative (*san*) suffix is added.
*sisvāpakīyiṣati*.

(156) *dyaudbhyo luṅ* [Pāṇini 1.3.91]: after roots beginning with *dyu* and *au*, the *luṅ* suffix is used. Because of the mention of the plural number (*bahuvacana*), there is an inclusion of those that begin with them, just as in the case of *śāṭṛṇḍṬar* [in Pāṇini 1.3.89].

Regarding this, he says: "after *dyauta* and the others. The roots beginning with *dyauta* are limited by the rule "√haṭa in the sense of movement. Intending that the locative case in the rule "aḥ sī" (Pāṇini 3.1.56) functions as a genitive, he says: "the parasmaipada of the luṅ [aorist]. [The root] √ñimidā.

(157) *mider guṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.82. Regarding *mider guṇaḥ*: from the rule *ṭhivuklamucamām*, the term *śit* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). Therein, because it is a *karmadhāraya* compound—namely, that which is both *ś* and *it*—the locative case is used. As for the suffix, it is implied by the word "stem" (*aṅga*).

[The word *yasmin*] is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Therefore, by the rule "in which [element] there is an injunction" (*yasmin vidhiḥ*), the rule for the initial element (*tadādividhi*) applies. Thus he says: "when preceded by a *ś* that bears the technical name *it*. Regarding the phrase "because of the absence of being an *ādiśit*": however, in forms such as *medyati* and *medyate*, the guṇa substitution certainly does occur because the suffix *śyan* (the marker of the present middle) is an *ādiśit*. [As in: *mimide*.

Thus [it is said]. In the case of the *bahuvrīhi* compound *iti*, the *guṇa* substitution would indeed occur here. Likewise, in forms such as *pape* and *tasthe*, the roots *pā-* and others would also [be subject to this rule]; such is the intended meaning. Regarding *ñiṣvidā*: because the root *svid* is indicated by the suffix *śyan* in the list of roots that do not take the augment *iṭ* (*aniṭkārikā*), this root takes the augment *iṭ*. [Examples: *sveditā*, *svediṣyate*.

"And *ñikṣvidā*. It should be understood that this [root] has the same two meanings as those previously mentioned. Regarding *haraye*: the dative case is used because of the designation "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) according to the rule *ṭhrucyarthānām*. *Ghuṭ*: turning—wandering here and there. *Jughuṭe*.

Due to the rule "ṭhasaṃyogā’d," there is an absence of guṇa because of the *kit* designation. *Kṣubha*: agitation—meaning a reversal of the natural state and churning. [The forms] *kṣobhate*, *kṣubhyati* (belonging to the *divādi* class), and *kṣubhnāti* (belonging to the *rukyādi* class) are used. As for "nāsrasat," "nāsraṃsat" is simply a corrupt reading. It is not [the correct form].
The meaning is that this [root] *lah* is *rūpa*, because in that context the *parasmaipada* endings are impossible.
(158) *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ* | Pāṇini 1.3.92. The five beginning with *vṛt* are meant.

(159) *na vṛdbhyaś caturbhyaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.59. "Not after the roots beginning with *vṛ* [and] the four. Because this is an operation dependent on a specific class (*gaṇakāryatva*), it does not apply when there is *yaṅ*-elision (*yaṅluk*). Examples: *varvartiṣyati*, *varvartiṣati*. However, the purpose of mentioning the "four" will become clear in the root-text itself.
From the rule *eṣicīḥ*, the word *se* is carried over (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "of that which begins with *s*.

Regarding the phrase "there shall not be *iṭ*": since for the root *syand* there is an option due to its being marked with *udit*, and for others [the option] is already established, and for others *iṭ* is established as obligatory, this is a prohibition. [The phrase] "in the case of *taṅ* and *na*" refers to the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada* endings.

In forms such as *jigamiṣitā* and *jigamiṣitārau*, it is accepted that for the sake of establishing the augment *iṭ* after the suffix *san* when followed by the suffix *tṛc*, the mention of *parasmaipada* (active voice) in the rule *ameḥ ṭ* indicates the absence of *taṅ* (middle voice). That [indication] applies here in exactly the same way.

This is because of the reliance on the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the meaning. Therefore, even in the absence of the *parasmaipada* designation, the prohibition of *iṭ* after the suffix *san* is established both in the case of *vivṛtsitār-au*—where the *luk* elision of *hi* occurs by the rule "ato heḥ"—and in the case of *vaṃ vivṛtse*. This is the intended meaning here.

It is established in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika* that, because the augment *iṭ* is prescribed for roots such as *vṛt* when they occur within the same word with the *ātmanepada* endings, there is a prohibition of *iṭ* elsewhere. Consequently, *iṭ* occurs in forms such as *vivartiṣate* and *vivardhiṣate*. [However, it does not occur] in *vivṛtsatevācarati*.

In the case of *vivṛtsitryate*, however, because this prohibition— which is internal (*antaraṅga*)— applies prior to the arising of the ātmanepada suffix due to the absence of being situated in the same word (*samānapadastha*),
it does not cease even after the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffix has been applied, owing to the force of the mention of the word "four" (*caturgrahaṇa*). In this regard:

They explained: "It would be more appropriate to say 'pañcabhyaḥ'. And thus, the rule should simply be formulated as 'āsi ce'. Nor is there over-extension (ativyāpti) to roots such as *vṛt* and others, because *taṅ* and *an* are present there.
Regarding the word *atyanteti*: here, the elision (*lopa*) does not occur by the rule "aniditām".
Because the elision of *si* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), [the letter preceding the suffix] is not a penultimate vowel.
(160) Pāṇini 8.3.72: *anu-vi-pary-abhi-nibhyaḥ syandateḥ aprāṇiṣu*.
Regarding *anu-vi-pary-abhi-nibhyaḥ*: the meaning is "from these five. The change to *ṣ* certainly occurs.
The intention is that even for an action performed by both sentient and non-sentient agents, the status of being "performed by a non-sentient agent" is not lost.

With the thought that a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) is not intended in the Sūtra—due to the faults of resulting in an *asamartha-samāsa* (irregular compound) and a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*)—he says: "if it were stated as 'not among sentient beings' (*prāṇiṣu na*). [The root] *kṛpū*.
Regarding the capacity [of the rule], he states the explanation of the commentators: *kṛpa u iti*.
He indicates that the modern reading *kṛpo ro laḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.18)—as opposed to *ṛpo ro laḥ*—is not to be respected.

By the rule *kṛper ṛkārasya* and so forth, since a portion of a phoneme (*varṇaikadeśa*) is included by the mention of the whole phoneme, he says "resembling the letter *r*. Thus, in this context, a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the word *kṛpa-* must necessarily be accepted; and so [the rule] is *uṭi ca klṛpaḥ*.
The meaning is that such scriptural indications as those in the Sūtra are also logically consistent.

(162) *tāsi ca klṛpaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.60. Regarding *tāsi ca klṛpaḥ*: by the word "ca" (and), the ārdhadhātuka suffix beginning with *sa* (i.e., *sādi*) is included. Thus, [the form] *klṛpsīṣṭa* [is derived].

Because of the *kit* designation [of the suffix] by the rule "iṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu," there is no *guṇa* [substitution]. (Ga. *vṛt*: *vṛd*. From the root *vṛtu* (to turn/revolve), the suffix *kvip* is applied. Following the rule "ñitvarā saṃbhrame," it is stated that "the roots beginning with *haṭ* are marked with *ṣ*"; therefore, only the last thirteen [roots], ending with *tvar*, are marked with *ṣ*, but not [the others].
It is established that all [roots] end in a *phaṇ* (a nasal). Nevertheless, for the sake of clear understanding, he says:

"and after a root ending in *ṣit*" (*ṣitaśca*). The purpose, however, is that by the rule "after roots ending in *ṣit*, *bhidā*, etc., [the suffix] *aṅ* [is applied]," the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added;
thus, forms such as *ghiṭā* and *vyathā* are established. Those roots which have been studied elsewhere [in other sections] are [to be understood] here...

The recitation [of the root] is for the purpose of restricting its meaning. However, it is established in the *Dhātuvṛtti* and other works that for those roots which are recited here [in this list], the status of being a *mit* vowel remains even when their meaning is shifted toward another sense by means of prefixes (*upasarga*) and so forth. Making this very point clear, he provides an example: "he causes to open" (*vighaṭayati*).

(162) *vyatho liṭi* | Pāṇini 7.4.68. "In the case of *vyath* before the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix. The meaning is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.60), because it is introduced as a continuation of the discussion on *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*. And thus, according to the principle "an exception [applies] to the same portion as the general rule," the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) occurs only for the subsequent [vowel].

According to the reasoning of Kaiyaṭa and others, namely that "it occurs [only] for what follows, not for what precedes," the prohibition "when there is no *saṃprasāraṇa*" (*asaṃprasāraṇe*) is not required here. However, some, considering that even if the *yakāra* is removed by *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, the *vakāra* remains and thus this sūtra still has its scope (is *sāvakāśa*), maintain that it cannot function as an exception (*apavāda*).

By the rule "vocalization (saṃprasāraṇa) and the operation dependent upon it are stronger," the substitution of the remaining consonant (halādiśeṣa) is set aside; thus, when the subsequent [consonant] undergoes vocalization, there is a prohibition of the preceding one. However, in the absence of the rule "vocalization and that which depends upon it," there would be vocalization by the rule "of *vyath* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*)."

They say that because it depends on many factors— namely, its being based on a specific phoneme (dhātu) and a specific suffix (pratyaya), as well as its being based on two specific technical designations (saṃjñā), namely *ṭh* and *gyaṇ*— the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution is considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*).
Consequently, it is set aside by the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, and once that has occurred, the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the letter *v* would take place.

Regarding the word *tasya*: the intention is that this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of the semivowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*) for the *yakāra* included within the reduplicated syllable, but not to the substitution for the *thakāra*. Why is *liṭi* (in the perfect tense) specified? [Consider: *vivyathiṣate*.
Here, by the rule *anyataḥ*, there is the substitution of *it*. [Examples: *vāvyathyate*, *vāvyathīti*. [The root] *krapa* means "to pity" and "to go."
They say that even in the absence of the letter *ca*, it should be understood that there are two meanings here. [The roots] *kadi* and *kradi*:

*krandayati*, *krandayati*; *akrandi*, *akrāndi*; *krandaṃkrandam*, *krāndaṃkrāndam*. Regarding *ñitvarā*: the status of being *ādi* (having an indicatory *ā*) is useless here, since the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is established even by the pronunciation of a short vowel.
Nor should one suspect that [the mention of *tvar*] is for the purpose of prohibiting the *it*-augment by the rule "na ca niṣṭhāyām ṭhāditaśca";
for by the rule "uṣyamatvare," the *it*-augment is optional (*vikalpita*) in the case of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Thus: *tūrṇaḥ* and *tvaritaḥ*.
The root *jvar* means "to be feverish" or "to afflict with disease. In the causative (*ṇau*): *jvarayati*. Aorist: *ajvari*, *ajvāri*. Repetition: *jvaraṃ jvaram*.
*jvāraṃjvāram*. The root *gaḍ* means "to sprinkle. With the causative suffix *ṇic*, it becomes *gaḍayati*. [In the imperfect: *agaḍi* or *agāḍi*.

[The intensive forms are] *gaḍaṃgaḍām* and *gāḍaṃgāḍam*. In other cases as well, this should be inferred accordingly. The root *heḍ* means "to surround. Since its indicatory marker (*anubandha*) has been dropped, there is no concern regarding the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule "āglopi" (Pāṇini 1.1.4) in the sense of surrounding.

The meaning is that [the vowel] does not exist. "Only when taught with the letter *ṇ*" refers to forms such as *praṇaṭati* and *praṇaṭayati*. However, for the root *āṭ*, it is *pranāṭayati*. The meaning is that by this [rule], the substitution of a short vowel for those ending in *i* (*itāṃ hrasva*) does not apply, because [the long vowel] is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). "Because of the priority of the irregularity" means that it pertains to the domain of irregular prescription (*nipātana*).

Because it follows the rule "itāṃ hrasvaḥ," that very rule is set aside by this nipātana (irregular formation), but not the subsequent rule "iṇṇamuloḥ. This is the meaning. Regarding *vana*: since it is listed in the sense of "gathering" (*saṃbhakti*), this is a restatement for the purpose of assigning it the designation *mit*. [Examples: *vanati*; in the causative (*ṇau*)—

*vanayati*, *avani*, *avāni*, *vanaṃvanam*, *vānaṃvānam*. Regarding the phrase "of that which begins with *tān*" (*tānādikasya*), the meaning is "of the root *vanu* [meaning] 'to beg'. Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the force of the context" (*sāmarthyāt*), [the point is that] in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), since the quality of having been uttered (*uditva*) was established there [in the rule for the suffix *ktvā*], there would otherwise result the optional application of *iṭ* for the suffix *ktvā* and the prohibition of *iṭ* for the suffix *niṣṭhā*.
The purpose of making [the root] *idit* again for the sake of *siddhi* (establishment) is that it might serve as a marker (*it*). Regarding "in *vanati*" and so forth:

with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), one has *vanayati*; but for the root belonging to the *tanādi* class, one has *vanute* or *vānayati*. The optionality of the *mit* designation is due to the *gaṇa*-sūtra: “*lāsnāvanuvamāṃ ca*. It is for the sake of the *ṇapratyaya* suffix.

The rule "jvalitikasantebhyo ṇaḥ" is intended to provide the suffix *ṇa* for roots beginning with *jval*. The root *dṛ* signifies fear; because roots possess multiple meanings, it also carries the sense of "fear. Thus, one forms *dṛṇāti* and *darayati*. Regarding the phrase "tanneti," this is Mādhava’s intention: the reading with the long vowel (*dīrghānta*) alone is universally accepted in the Sūtra.

Even in the case of *ghaṭa* and other such words, it is read by all authorities with a long vowel at the end. If this [root *dṛ*] were to have a short vowel at the end, then the mention of *dṛ* in the rule "ṛdṛprāṃ hrasvo vā" (Pāṇini 7.4.12)—which prescribes an optional shortening—would be purposeless;
for the two forms *dadratuḥ* and *dadaratuḥ* would already be established by two distinct verbal roots (*dadṛ* and *dadar*). Nor is it the case that [the root is] *ṛ*...

It must be stated that the inclusion of the term *dṛ* (to see) is necessary for the sake of obtaining two forms of the root *vidṛ* (to tear), since the desired result is achieved because roots have multiple meanings. *Nṛ* means "to lead": *nṛṇāti*, *narayati*;
*anari*, *anāri*; *naraṃnaram*, *nāraṃnāram*. Regarding *śrai*: this indeed...
The root [sū] to be mentioned belongs to the *bhūvādi* class. Regarding the phrase "lug-vikaraṇa," they explain here as follows:

although the term *ūṅ* is recited in the rule *svarati-sūti-*, the separate mention of both *sūti* and *sūyati*—even though the inclusion of both would have been established by that alone—is purposeless, and thus [it serves to indicate this].

This indicates a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). One might object: "Why should the opposite not hold—that the suffix lacking the *aluk* augment (*alugvikaraṇa*) is stronger? This doubt is to be set aside because it would contradict the desired result. Furthermore, if the term *ūṅ* were recited [in the rule], then by association with *svarati*, only that which lacks the *aluk* augment would be understood, and not both; thus, this objection is also invalid.

This is to be suspected, because concomitance (*sāhacarya*) is not invariable. Therefore, the separate mention [of the term] is useless and serves merely as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Regarding the phrase "by the two *paribhāṣās*": although the desired result is established even if the two stated *paribhāṣās* do not apply due to mutual contradiction, nevertheless, because there is no distinction between the two...

The sense is that activity (pravṛtti) is indeed appropriate here as well. Regarding the term *iśāmana*, since it is derived from the root *śam* meaning "to perceive" (*ālocana*), he says: "visual cognition. Regarding the phrase "in these senses": *paśuṃ saṃjñapayati* means "he kills the animal"; *viṣṇuṃ vijñapayati* [means "he informs Viṣṇu"].

The meaning is "he satisfies. *Saṃjñapayati rūpam* means, according to Mādhava’s view, "he shows his form"; however, in another opinion, it means "he makes himself known. *Pra-jñapayati śaram* means "he sharpens the arrow. This might be argued: "Niśāmana is merely making known (*jñāpana-mātram*)."

In the opinion of those who maintain [the view], the *vṛtti* commentary on the sūtra "ślāghahnusthe" (Pāṇini 1.4.34)—which states that "the one intended to be informed (*añīpsyamānaḥ*) is meant to be made aware"—is indeed consistent. However, in the opinion of Mādhava, what is the status of that passage? To this he says: "jñap micca" (Dhātupāṭha 10.259). [The term] "jñāpanam" (making known) [is used]. Thus...

The sense is that the commentary (*vṛtti*) is consistent even with the view of Mādhava. As for the phrase "and killing, etc.": this was stated with reference to another school of thought (*matāntara*), because it will be stated later under the *cur*-class (the tenth class) that "the root *ñap* is *mit*, and it occurs in the senses of knowing and making known. [The questioner asks: "How so?"

The intention is that because of the *mit* designation for the roots *jñā* and *jñapa*, there ought to be shortening [of the penultimate vowel] when followed by the causative suffix *ṇi*. Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of the *mit* designation": in this way, one should understand that according to Mādhava’s opinion, there are two forms—*jñāpayati* for the root *jñā* in the sense of making known, and *jñapayati* for the root *jñapa*. [The rule] *cchadirurjane* [is stated]; [the root] *ūrja*...

Regarding *balaprāṇanayoḥ*: here, the root *chad* belongs to the *yaujādika* group within the *curādi* sub-class. The absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is for the sake of the root's own meaning (*svārthe*), because the suffix is optional according to the rule *ādhṛṣādve*. [The forms] *laḍayati* and *jihvām* mean "he makes the tongue known" (*jihvāṃ jñāpayati*). [The form] *jihvayā* means "by means of the tongue."
The meaning is that it makes known another object. He provides an example regarding the function of the tongue:

"he torments the enemy" (*laḍayati śatrum*). This means that with reference to the enemy, he performs such acts as reviling (*gālidānādika*) or [as the variant reading suggests] squeezing out (*gālanādika*). "He churns the curd" (*laḍayati dadhi*); this means he agitates or stirs it.

Some, however, apply [the roots] in reverse: *laḍayati dadhi* (he stirs yogurt) refers to the activity of the tongue, whereas *laḍayati śatrum* (he torments the enemy) refers to agitation; and *lāḍayati putram* (he fondles the son) means he gratifies him by giving sugar and other such things. Thus, the two roots *laḍ* and *laḍ* have been illustrated.

The sound *dhvani* is cited without any intervening element, whereas *raṇi* is [cited] as *asvāni*, *asvani*, *asvāni*, *svanaṃsvanam*, and *svānaṃsvānam*. (Ga) Regarding *ghaṭādayo mitaḥ*: this means they have the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *mit*. Others, however, explain them as having the marker *m* as their *anubandha*. [This refers to the root] *haṭam* in the sense of "movement" (*ceṣṭā*).

The intention is that, because it would be cumbersome to assign the designation *mit* to each individual [root] in the recitation (*pāṭha*), this sūtra either prescribes the designation *mit* for all [roots] in one place, or rather prescribes the property of having *m* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) for them.
(Ga) *janījṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca*. [The roots] *janī*, *jṛṣ*, *knasu*, and *rañj*, as well as those ending in *am*. *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāve*). *jṛṣ*...

In the sense of "loss of vigor" (vayohāni); *knasu* in the senses of "bending" (*hvaraṇa*) and "shining" (*dīpti*). All three [roots] belong to the *divādi* class. *Rañj* in the sense of "coloring" (*rāga*); it belongs both to the *devādi* and the *bhūvādi* classes. Those ending in *-am*: *kram*, *gam*, and so forth. [Examples: *janayati*, *jarayati*, *knasayati*, *rañjayati*. [He colors] deer; he colors birds.

*kramayati*, *gamayati*, *ramayati*. (ga) Regarding *jvala-hvala-nam-ā-man-upasargāt vā*: [The rule states] *jvala-hvala* [and so on]. The designation *mit* applies to these. Here, because the term *it* (from a previous rule) is understood, its status is that of a primary quality (*bhāva-pradhānatā*).
However, the phrase *anupasargāt* must be explained with difficulty as a fifth case (*pañcamī*) used in the sense of a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
The meaning is as follows: there is an alternative reading, *amo ’nupasargād vā*, and in that case, there is no difficulty whatsoever.

[The term] "optional by virtue of being already established" (*prāptavibhāṣā*) refers to the fact that the three roots *jvala* (to blaze), *hvala*, and *hmala* (both meaning to move) have been previously mentioned [in the rule for obligatory application], whereas *nam* ends in the letter *m*. [The question] "How is it *saṃkrāmayati*? [is raised].

Because of the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "of that which is taught with an udātta accent" (*odātopadeśasya*) when the suffix *ghañ* is applied, the form becomes simply "ma," and not "rāma. Since the previously mentioned solution is inapplicable here, a separate question is raised. Regarding the phrase "vyavasthitavibhāṣā" (restricted option) and so forth: in some cases, the shortening of the *mit* roots does not take effect in the causative (*ṇic*).

This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). Regarding the phrase "the author of the *vṛtti*": some accept the word *krāma* as being derived from the root *kram* with the suffix *ghañ*, and then, by adding the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule for words beginning with *prajñā*, they form *krāma*.
From that, by applying the causative suffix *ṇic* according to the rule "he causes to do" (*atkaroti*), they derive *saṅkrāmayati*.
This is their resolution (*samādadhate*). Regarding the phrase "when the other two [suffixes] are applicable": prior to the root *van*.
The intention is that this is because of the reading [of the root] and because it ends in *m*. [Examples: *glāpayati*, *glapayati*; *snāpayati*, *snapayati*;
*vānayati*, *vanayati*; *vāmayati*, *vamayati*. "Like *śāmyati*":
just as the root *śam* is used in the sense of seeing in such expressions as *niśāmayati*, so too is the *cur*-class [root].

The meaning is that the root *śam* will also apply in the sense of "hearing. (Ga) Regarding *yama* in the sense of "other than serving food": as for the statement "the root *yam*," this root *yam*, meaning "to cease," applies elsewhere than in the context of eating.
The word "eating" (*bhojana*) should be understood as being formed with the suffix *yuñ* according to the rule *ṇyāsa-śrantho yuñ*. Here, "serving food" (*pariveṣaṇa*) refers to...

The activity conducive to eating is [the subject]; thus, there is a prohibition regarding any other purpose. Regarding the term "niyamayan": it should be understood that from the word *niyama* with the suffix *ṇic*, followed by the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *vin* and *matup*, and then the addition of the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śap*, and the application of *guṇa*. As for the phrase "the reversal has borne fruit": according to the author’s own view, however, it refers to the non-servicing [of food].
It means "he causes to eat. But in the sense of serving food—*yamayati brāhmaṇān* ("he causes the Brahmins to eat"). Regarding the root *skhad*, preceded by *ava* or *pari* (as per the *gaṇa*-sūtra):

from *skhad*, *avaskhadayati* and *pariskhadayati*. However, when preceded by *pra*, one should know that there is a reversal [of the vowel length], as in *praskhādayati*. It should be disregarded. 'a... [text breaks off]'.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the rule *pādimyāṅ* (Pāṇini 6.1.49), after citing the example *ṭhāyām ayate*, it is stated:
"By the rule *yamo’pariveṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.50), the status of being a *mit* [causing vṛddhi] is prohibited. In the *Nyāsa* as well, it is said:

"In this case, the word 'not' (*na*) is understood from the preceding rule *na kamyamī* (Pāṇini 6.1.52). For it is thus that, immediately following the prohibition, [the status of being a *mit* is denied].
The reading is appropriate; the intention is that otherwise he would have recited the three sūtras immediately before "akamī" (Pāṇini 6.4.110).
(163) "And [the substitution of] 'pha' for the seven [nasals]. (Pāṇini 6.4.125)

The root *phaṇ* means "to go. It is conjugated as *phaṇati*. In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense: *iphāṇīt*, *aphaṇīt*. However, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is added, there is optionally a lengthening of the vowel by the rule "iṇṇamuloḥ" (*Pāṇini* 6.4.24): *aphaṇi*, *aphāṇi*. [In the frequentative: *phaṇamphaṇam*, *phāṇamphāṇam*. [The phrase] "because of impossibility" [is used]; for here, since a prohibition is impossible without the prior application of the status of being *mit*, [the rule applies].

This does not connect with that [rule], but rather it is the designation *mit* itself. He states this as follows: "phaṇayati" (he causes to expand). (Ga. *vṛt*. *vṛt*. "By virtue of the force" means by virtue of the force of its inclusion among the *phaṇ*-class roots. "For there" means for in the rule prescribing the substitution of *ṣ* (the *ṣatva-vidhi*). And thus: *vibhrāṭ*, *vibhrāḍbhyām*. Previously...

The intention is that for the root *paṭh*, forms such as *vibhrāk* and *vibhrāgbhyām* are established. Regarding *asyamīt*: because it ends in *m*, there is no *vṛddhi*. Now, regarding the *jvalādi* group: *ajvālīt*; here, by the rule "vṛddhi occurs before *la* when it has an *a* [as penultimate]," *vṛddhi* applies. Regarding *vaiklavya*: *vaiklavyaṃ*— The meaning is that for the root *paṭh*, forms such as *vibhrāk* and *vibhrāgbhyām* are established. Regarding *asyamīt*: because it ends in *m*, there is no *vṛddhi*. Now, regarding the *jvalādi* group: *ajvālīt*;
here, by the rule "vṛddhi occurs before *la* when it has an *a* [as penultimate]," *vṛddhi* applies. Regarding *vaiklavya*: *vaiklavyaṃ*—

"Agitation produced by fear and so forth. "Its operation" means an operation favorable to kinsmen. (164) *pataḥ pum* [Pāṇini 7.4.19]. By virtue of being designated as *mit*, it follows after the final vowel. Regarding *akvathīt*: because it ends in *eṭ*, there is no *vṛddhi*.
Likewise in *apathīt* and *amathīt*. Regarding *ṭu-avam*, some, having read it as *udit*, cite *vāntvā* and *vamitvā*; however, that contradicts Vāmana.
For he, relying on the fact that the particle *ca* in the rule *āditaś ca* has the sense of an inclusive "and" (*anuktasamuccayārthatva*), [accepts] *vānta*.

In this context, the absence of the augment *iṭ* has been established. However, if [the root] were marked with the *u*-diacritic (*udit*), then by the rule "for that which is optionally [marked with *u*]" (*yasya vibhāṣā*), the form would already be established by the rule "ending in *va*" (*vānta*); thus, that [previous argument] would be inconsistent. And so, in the case of the *ktvā* suffix, only *vamitvā* is correct. Regarding the statement "due to irregularity" (*nipātanāt*): otherwise, if *guṇa* were applied, the form would be *udgaraṇa*. Even though...

It should be understood that although the explanation of the meaning is modern, the intended sense lies precisely in the fact that [the word] belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. It has been cited as such for this reason. Some say it was cited in that way in accordance with usages such as "and some [call it] *rudhira*" (*vemuśca kecid rudhiram*). But [one might object]: "Since it is a derivative [formed from a verbal root],..."

If it is asked, "How can the elision of *et*, *ātv*, and reduplication occur here due to the prohibition? they say in response: even though the rule were formulated as "a-śasa-dada-vādi-guṇānām," [the desired result would follow].

By including the group ending in *v* (the *vakārānta-saṅghāta*), the desired result is achieved; however, the inclusion of the word *ādi* ("beginning with") is for the purpose of understanding those [roots] taught as such in the original instruction (*aupadeśika*). Furthermore, it is accepted that "those ending in *ṭ* are *anubandhas*. Thus, this root is not *vādi*, but rather *ṭvādi*. Others, however, say that in the beginning of the root *vam*, the letter *y* is elided by the rule *opo vyoḥ*, and is then inserted (*praśliṣyate*) [back into the root]. Consequently, because it does not end in *v* at the time of its original instruction (*upadeśe*), the prohibition [against the substitution of *samprasāraṇa*] does not apply. The root *bhramu* means "to move. Its meaning is specifically movement in the form of a circular motion (*maṇḍalākāreṇa*), and not merely movement in general.

The meaning of the verbal root is a cognition that has as its qualificandum something which lacks that [property] and as its qualifier that [property]. This is because of the usage: “He sees the statement and is deluded, thinking it is silver. Regarding the suffix *ktvā* in the rule *“udito vā”* (Pāṇini 7.2.56), there is optionally the augment *iṭ*: *bhramitvā* or *bhrāntvā*. Regarding the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the rule *“yasya vibhāṣā”* (Pāṇini 7.2.15), there is no *iṭ*: *bhrāntaḥ*. Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of including this root in the *jvalādi* group?

If it is argued that the reading here is intended solely for the sake of the suffix *ṇa*, and that the form *abhrama* can be established by the suffix *ac* as well—since the *pacādi* group is an open class (*ākṛtigaṇa*)—and that because of the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "of that which is taught with an udātta vowel," the form is identical whether the suffix *ṇa* or *ac* is applied; to this they reply: if the suffix *ac* were applied on the basis of its belonging to the *pacādi* group, then in the word *abhrama*, the final syllable would be udātta according to the rule "in *ṭhak* and *ka*, when there is incapacity" (*ṭhakāv-avaśaktau*), because of the following negative particle (*nañ*).
However, when the suffix *ṇa* is applied, the word becomes udātta on the first syllable by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when the sense is 'equal to' (*tulyārtha*)" and so forth.
(Pāṇini 6.4.124) *vā jṛbhramutrasām*.

*vājṛ*, *abhramu*, and *trasām*. This is an optional rule (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*). Regarding *abhramīt*: because it ends in a nasal (*māntatva*), there is no *vṛddhi* [of the penultimate vowel]. Regarding *akṣārīt*: although the *vṛddhi* conditioned by a root ending in a consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇā*) is prohibited by the rule *eṭi*, the *vṛddhi* [is still applied] by the rule *ato lāntasya*. *Ṣaha*: the non-manifestation of anger even when an offense has occurred.
*Marṣaṇam*.
(166) *sahivahor odavarṇasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.112). Since the elision of the letter *r* is impossible here, [the word *halopa*] is supplied from the rule *halope pūrvasya*.

It follows accordingly. Thus he says: "In the case of the elision of *ḍh*. What is the purpose of [specifying] "in the case of the elision of *ḍh*"? [Consider: *sahate*, *vahate*. (167) *soḍhaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.115.
The meaning is that the rule for *ṣatva* does not apply; the word "not" (*na*) is understood from the preceding sūtra, *a raparaḥ*.
(168) Pāṇini 8.3.71: *sivādīnāṃ vā ’ḍvyavāye ’pi*. [The rule applies] to the roots beginning with *siv*.
*Siv*, *sah*, *suṭ*, *stu*, and *svañj* are the roots beginning with *siv*. Examples: *paryaṣīvyat* / *paryasīvyat*; *paryaṣkarot*; *nyaṣṭaut* / *nyastaut*; *vyaṣvajat*.
He released her. Regarding the word *ram*, some have cited it as *amumuditaṃ matvā* (having considered him delighted) and *rantvā ramitvā* (having sported, having caused to sport);

however, Mādhava and others do not accept this. Thus, in the case of the suffix *ktvā*, only *rantvā* is correct. In the form *remiṣe*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule governing roots beginning with *krī*. [In the feminine form] *ramā*, the suffix *ṭāp* is added after the root ending in *pacādi*.

With the suffix *ghañ*, however, it becomes *rāmaḥ*. Because it ends in *am*, it is designated as *mit*; thus, with the suffix *ṇic*, there is the substitution of *hr* for *ram*: *ramayati*. The root *sadlṛ* means the dissolution or separation of parts; *avasādanam* means destruction. (169) [The following rule applies to] the roots *pā*, *ghrā*, *dhmā*, *sthā*, *mnā*, *dāṇ*, *dṛśi*, *ṛ*, *sṛ*, *śad*, and *sad*.

*Piba, jighra, dhamati, tiṣṭha, manaya, ccha, paśya, rccha, dhau, śīya, sīda* || 7.3.78 || The roots *pā*, *ghrā*, and *dhmā* [are affected]. *Pā* in the sense of "drinking" (*pāne*) is intended; however, the root *pā* in the sense of "protecting" (*rakṣaṇe*) is not included here, because it belongs to the *lug-vikaraṇa* class.
Regarding the reading *ṛṣṭri* found in some texts, the augment *am* is applied by the rule *ṛjidṛśo ’m*. In forms such as *arti* and so forth, [the same applies].

It should be understood that, just as there is an absence of the substitute *ṛccha* due to its being a *sautra* (technical) term, so too there is an absence of the substitute *paśya*. However, the reading *ṛśyarti* is indeed faultless. Regarding the phrase *pādīnām*: the meaning is that for these eleven [roots], there shall be eleven substitutes beginning with *piba*, respectively, according to their order.

From the rule "ṣṭhivuklamucamām," the term "śit" is understood to carry over. Intending that this is a *karmadhāraya* compound, he says: "in a word beginning with a śakāra having the technical designation 'it'. Why say "beginning with a śakāra"? [Consider: *pape*, *jighre*, *dadhme*. However, if one were to accept that "śit" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, then in these cases...
The substitutes *piba* and so forth shall indeed occur.

(170) Regarding *sadeḥ parasya liṭi* [Pāṇini 7.2.118]: in forms such as *seditha*, although the augment *iṭ* is prohibited by the rule *upadeśe'tvataḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.62] which restricts the application of *iṭ* according to the *krādiniyama*, [the substitute still applies].

The rule *bhāradvājaniyamāt* is prescribed. [In the rule] *sadeḥ parasya*, the word *sadeḥ* is in the genitive case. He states the result [of this analysis]: "after the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsāt*). This is the application [of the rule] from [the sūtra] *thādiṣvabhyāsena ca*. Why [is the condition] *liṭi* (in the perfect tense) stated? [Consider the example: *niṣiṣitsati*; although the reading is established in the commentary as *adisvañjyoḥ*.
This has been overlooked here because it is not consistent with the Bhāṣya. Regarding the form *niṣasāda*:

since the word *aprati* is used as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) in the rule *adi-raprateḥ*, it should be understood that in *pratisasāda*, the substitution of *ṣ* does not apply even to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

Anticipating the objection that the statement "in the sense of tearing apart" (*ātane*) is inconsistent when one ought to have said "in the sense of being shattered" (*viśīrṇatāyām*), he provides a partial resolution: "But *śātana*," etc.

For indeed, from the root *śad* itself with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), by applying the rule "the substitution of *t* for *d* occurs except in the sense of motion" (*aderagatau*) and then adding the suffix *lyuṭ*, the form *śātana* is derived.

The term *rūpa* [is used here]; and the intention is that this form of the root *dā* itself is well-known, which is why that designation was made—just as in cases such as ‘*amlṛ* in the sense of going’ or ‘*upacaṣ* in the sense of cooking. This is the meaning.

(171) *śadeḥ śitaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.3.60. The root *kuc* [is used] in the sense of "rubbing together" (*saṃparcana*) and so forth. As for the root *uc*, which is listed among those ending in the *ra*-class (the *cu*-group) in the sense of "loud sound," its repetition here is due to its inclusion in the *jvalādi* group, [which applies it] specifically to the sense of "rubbing together" and so forth.

It is established in the *Manoramā* and other works that the suffix *ṇa* [is used] so that [the form] may occur. Regarding this, the moderns (*navya*) say: "By this very passage, it is inferred that Pāṇini himself provided a statement of meaning (arthanirdeśa) in certain instances;
otherwise, the natural consistency (*svārasya*) of the text at this point would be violated. [The word] *bodhitā* means "taught."
The sense is that this [root *budh*] is *seṭ* (possessing the augment *iṭ*), because it is recited among the roots ending in *aniṭ* in the *Kārikās*.

Regarding *akāsīt*: although the *vṛddhi* prescribed for a root ending in a consonant is prohibited by the rule "before *eṭ*" (*eṭi*), the optional *vṛddhi* is still applied by the rule "after *at*, before a consonant-initial suffix" (*ato halādeḥ*). Regarding *vṛt*: here the moderns (*navyāḥ*) say—
From the mention of *valitikasantebhyaḥ*, it is inferred that the formation of the *vṛt* group here is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*);
otherwise, they say, one would have simply formulated the rule as *valādibhyo ṇaḥ*. [The root] *añcu* means "to go.

By the rule *ṭhaniditām*, there is elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*). Thus: *acyāt*. However, according to the opinion of some, because [the root] is marked with the *idit* designation, [the nasal is not elided].

—*añcyāt*. And *medhṛ* [is used] in the sense of "meeting. Regarding the previously mentioned meaning in the phrase “*rajāyai gṛhamedhinām*,” the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "those who meet (*medhante*), that is, come together (*saṅgacchante*), with their households (*gṛhaiḥ*), that is, with their wives (*dāraiḥ*). The suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule "*supyajātau*. [The roots] *śṛdhu* and *mṛdhu* mean "moistening," that is, the state of becoming wet (*ārdrībhāva*).

This is the meaning. After [the roots] *ud* and *vit*, there is optionally the augment *iṭ*. From *śṛdh*: *śardhitvā* or *śr̥ddhvā*. From *ubundir*: *bunditvā* or *butvā*. In the case of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*): *bunnam*. "Observation" (*niśāmanam*) refers to visual cognition. From *veṇṛ*: the five meanings beginning with "motion. It means the taking up of a musical instrument for the purpose of playing it.
The term *vāditra* is derived from this same root. Forms such as *veṇi*, *veṇī*, and *veṇu* belong to this very root.

As for the statement "it also ends in *n*," the intention is that the form ending in *n* is observed in the passage: *uta mātā mahiṣam anv avenat*. From the root *khanu*: the gerund forms are *khanitvā* and *khātvā*; in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), it is *khātaḥ*.

(172) *gamahana-jana-khana-ghasāṃ lopaḥ kṅtyinaiṅ* [Pāṇini 6.4.98]. From the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām*, the word *aci* is understood to carry over here. Furthermore, from the rule *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ*, the term *upadhā* is also understood. Therefore, he says: "of these, of the penultimate [vowel]," and so forth.

*jagmatuḥ* (they two went), *jagmuḥ* (they went); *jaghnatuḥ* (they two struck), *jaghuḥ* (they struck); *jajñe* (he was born), *jajñāte* (they two were born); *jakṣatuḥ* (they two ate), *jakṣuḥ* (they ate). Why [is it said] "not when there is *anaṅ*"? [Example: *agamat* (he went). *cīvṛ*: *cīvaraṃ*—a garment; this is a word established as a *nipātita* (irregularly formed) term in the *uṇādi* list by the rule "īvara-pīvara-mīvare. *vyaya* (in the sense of going).

The *Manoramā* states that [the root] *vit* is always *ātmanepada* when used with the sense of "abandoning" (*tyāga*). However, that view is merely a matter for reflection, as it is not established anywhere that it is so. Regarding the form *avyayīt*: because it ends in *y*, there is no *vṛddhi*. The root *spaś* means "to afflict" and "to touch. By the rule *ṭhṇiśrī* etc., the suffix *cli* becomes *caṅ*, resulting in *apaspāśat*.
By the rule *ṭhatsmṛdṛtvaraprathe* etc., the substitution of *at* for the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) is an exception to the *san-vat* treatment.

[The form] *paspaśā* is derived as follows: after the *yaṅ*-affix, when an *ac*-beginning suffix follows, there is elision (*luk*) by the rule *yaṅe’ci ca*. Then, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added by the rule *ajādyataḥ*. However, the lengthening of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) by the rule *dīrgho’kitaḥ* does not occur here.

They say that this is because a grammatical rule conditioned by a specific technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). In the rule *apajabhadahadaśabhañjapasāṃ ca*, the term *pasa* refers to a Vedic root (*sautra-dhātu*). Thus, one finds forms such as *pasati*. However, in the case of the *yaṅ*-intensive and its elision (*yaṅ-luk*), the augment *nuk* is applied to the reduplicated syllable by the very rule *apajabha*. For example, in the *yaṅ*-intensive, one has *piṃpasyate*; in the elided form (*luk*), [the same applies].
—*paṃpasīti*. *Paṃpas* belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* group. [Thus] *paṃpasyati*. (173) *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ* |6|4|9|.
[The sūtra reads: *ūdupadhāyāḥ*. [This refers to] "when there is a cause for *guṇa*. And this [is understood] from the word *goha*.
This is understood from the specific formulation [of the rule].

By the word *aci*, which is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) from the rule *ṭhaci śnudhātubhruvām yvoḥ* (P. 6.4.77), the suffix implied by the term *aṅga* is qualified. Through this qualification, the rule of "application to what begins with that" (*tadādividhi*) applies. Thus he says: "when beginning with a vowel" (*ajādau*).

(174) *lug vā duhadihalihaguhām ātmanepade dantye* || 7.3.73 || The word "in a dental" (*dantye*) means "when the *taṅ* [terminations] begin with a dental. Examples include: *adugdha*, *adhukṣata*; *adigdha*, *adhikṣata*; *alīḍha*, *alikṣata*, and so forth.

(175) *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu* |7|4|28|. In the rule *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu*, the term *yī*—which is carried over from the previous rule *ṭhayaṅ yi kṅtī*—is a qualifier of *liṅ* alone, because it is impossible [for it] to apply to anything else; as for *yak*, however, it would be redundant. Thus...

Intending that the phrase "of the *ṭhakṛt* [suffixes] and the *sārvadhātuka* [suffixes]," though it is a recurring rule (*anuvṛtta*), serves as a qualifier for the *liṅ* [optative] alone, he says: "beginning with *ya*" and so forth. In *śe*—as in *mriyate*—the suffix *śa* is applied by the rule "after roots beginning with *ud*. In *yaki*—as in *kriyate* and *mriyate*.

(176) *uś ca* | 1|2|12| The word *uḥ* [is the subject]. From the rule *ṭhiko jhal* [1.2.9], the mention of *jhal* is carried over (*anuvartate*), as is the preceding rule *iṅsicau*. Thus he says: "from an *ṛ*-vowel," and so forth. Regarding *abhārṣīt*: [in the context of] *ici*...
The word "vṛddhi" [in the rule] means *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution].

(177) *hrasvādaṅgāt* | Pāṇini 6.1.105: "After a short vowel, there is elision of the suffix. Since it is intended there as well that this applies only to a suffix, the elision occurs only for *sic*. Therefore, it does not apply here in *astaṃ*.

"Most hostile. Some say that if the mention of the term *aṅga* (stem) were absent here, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) even in cases such as *ayāviṣṭām* and *alāviṣṭām*. Others do not accept this, because a solution is possible even through the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the non-disturbance of a grammatical occasion). Why [is it said] "when *jhal* follows"?

*abhṛṣātām*, *abhṛṣata*. The root *hṛñ* is used in the sense of "taking. Here there are four meanings: 1. *bhāraṃ harati*: He carries a burden; the meaning is that he brings it to a destination. 2. *aṃśaṃ harati*: He takes a share; the meaning is that he accepts it as his own. 3. *svarṇaṃ harati*: He steals gold; [the meaning is] he robs. 4. *pāpaṃ harati*: He removes sin; [the meaning is] he destroys it. The root *dhṛñ*: *dadhāra*, *dadhratuḥ*, *dadhārtha*.
*dadhre*, *dadhrāte*, *dhartā*, *dhriyāt*. Regarding *ṇīñ*: *ninayitha*; here there is an option for the substitution of *iṅ* according to the rule of Bhāradvāja.
(178) *ādeca upadeśe’śiti* 6.1.45.

In the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti*, the term *ec* is qualified by the phrase *iṭi dhātoḥ* which is understood from the previous context. Thus it says: "of a verbal root ending in *ec*. Why specify "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśe*)? [Consider] *cetā* and *stotā*.
If it is argued that this will not apply here simply because the forms are derivative (*lākṣaṇikatva*), they say: in the case of the mention of a specific phoneme...

The inclusion of the term *upadeśa* is for the purpose of indicating that the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which is taught by its specific technical name [is understood]" is not being relied upon.

Consequently, in forms such as *krāpayati*, where the substitution of *ā* has already occurred according to the rule “*rīṅjīnāṃ ṇau*,” the augment *puk* is successfully established; this is the view of the author of the *Manoramā*. Why is the word *dhātoḥ* (of a root) used? [Consider] *gobhyām*, *naubhyām*; for here too, [the condition of being a root] exists.

In the instruction “*amer ḍoḥ*” and “*lānudibhyāṃ ḍau*,” the *ec* vowels [are taught]. He says “but not when followed by a *śit* [suffix],” because this is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (a prohibition that applies to the general rule). For if it were a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), then in forms such as *jagle* and *magle*, the substitution of *ā* would not occur due to the prohibition “*na dvirvacane’ci*,” and the vowel *i* would remain in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

It would be so heard. Furthermore, in *ugla*, there would be the suffix *ka* by the rule *ātaścopasarge*; in *ugle*, there would be the feminine suffix *aṅ* by the rule *ātaścopasarge*; and in *uglāna*, there would be the suffix *yuc* by the rule *āto yuci*. For the substitution of *ā* is caused by the suffix, and the suffixes are applied to a stem ending in *ā*.

Thus, there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). However, in the case of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), no fault arises. Furthermore, the re-enactment of the rule for *aṇ* in the sūtra "hvāvāmaśca" (Pāṇini 6.4.123) in order to override the suffix *kap* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the view that it is a simple negation. As they say: "The substitution of *āt* is not conditional; however, there is a prohibition when a *śit* affix follows."

If it is argued that even so, forms such as *eṣaḥ* (this) and *śitvākāle mamle* (he withered at the time of cold) would not be established, they reply: If *śiti* were a bahuvrīhi compound, then this fault would indeed occur here.
However, this is a karmadhāraya compound. Thus, in the case of *aśiti*, when a suffix beginning with a letter having the technical designation *it* follows, [the rule applies].

The meaning is "not others. Because the suffix, which is implied by the mention of the verbal root (dhātu), is qualified by the term *śit* through a *karmadhāraya* compound, there is no harm even if this is understood as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), since the locative case would then signify the domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*), resulting in the meaning: "the substitution of *ā* occurs in the domain of suffixes other than those beginning with the *it*-marked letter *ś*."

(179) *āta āṬ ṇalaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.34. "After [a verbal root] ending in long *ā*, *āṬ* is substituted for *ṇal*. Here, the term *aṅgasya* ("of the stem") is understood from the preceding context; the mention of *dhātoḥ* ("of the verbal root") is merely a statement of the resultant meaning. Thus, the sense is: "after a stem (*aṅga*) that ends in long *ā*."

(180) *āto lopa iṭi ca* | Pāṇini 6.4.64. The term *ārddhadhātuke* is understood from the preceding rule. From the rule *īṅe yuḍ aci kṅtī*, the terms *aci* and *kṅtī* are also understood. He states the resulting conclusion as follows: "in the case of *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes beginning with a vowel or having the augment *iṭ*."
Why [is it said] "not after *aja* and others"? [Consider: *glāyate*. With *yak*: *jāglāyate*. With *yaṅ*: *dāsīya*.
[In *dāsīya*,] the suffix *liṅ* (optative) is in the third person singular, and *iṭ* is added. Why [is it said] "before *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes"?
[Consider: *yānti*, *vānti*, *vyatire*. [The rule applies] when there is reciprocal action; *rā* is used in the sense of giving.
The suffix *laṭ* has the augment *iṭ* in the third person singular; thus, from *vyati + rai*, we have *vyatirai*. And since *laṭ* takes *iṭ*, there is *dadhiva* and *dadhimā* etc.

In this way, although the elision of the vowel (*āto lopa*) is established for forms such as *dadhiva* and *dadhimā* because the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a vowel is treated as *kit*, the mention of "in the case of *iṭ*" in this rule is for the sake of establishing forms such as *dadhitha* and *papitha*.

It should be understood that the inclusion [of the augment] is necessary. However, if only the augment *iṭ* is taken here based on the explanation, then in the rule *aci kṅti* (Pāṇini 1.2.5), it would qualify only the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, and not both.

(181) *dādhā ghu adāp* | 1.1.20 | *dādhā ghu adāp*. Here, there are four roots of the form *dā*: *ḍudāñ* (to give), *dāṇ* (to give), *do* (to cut), and *deṅ* (to protect). There are two roots of the form *dhā*: *ḍudhāñ*...

The roots *dhṛ* and *pṛ* mean "to hold" or "to nourish"; *dheṭ* means "to drink. Because the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) are not invariably fixed, the rule *ādaica upadeśe* (Pāṇini 1.1.20) applies the substitution of *āT* [for the final vowel of the root]; thus, in the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of *eṅ* and *dheṭ*, there occurs the form *dā*. Consequently, *dā* (from *dai*), *dā* (from *do*), and *dā* (from *dheṭ*) are grouped as *dāḥ*; likewise, *dhā* (from *dadhāti*) and *dhā* (from *dheṭ*) are *dhau*; and finally, *dāḥ* and *dhau* together are *dādhāḥ*.

[The sūtra] *vigrahaḥ* [is explained as follows]: *dāp-dai-pau vineti*. [The roots] *dāp* (in the sense of cutting) and *daip* (in the sense of purifying)—the meaning is "excluding these. Here, the fact that *daip* is marked with the *ṅit* indicatory letter (*pi*) is for the purpose of prohibition, and not for the purpose of making it *anudātta*, because [by the rule] *anudātau sup-pitau*, the *anudātta* status applies only to the suffix.

[The root *dāp* is not included] because it has the marker *p*. Nor should one suspect that this prohibition does not apply to *daip* because it is "derived" (*lākṣaṇika*), for that would result in the marker *p* being rendered purposeless.

And they say that this very fact of *daip* having the marker *p* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the paribhāṣā rule: "In rules involving the mention of *ām* and so forth, there is no distinction [between the primary and derived forms]."
What is the purpose of [the restriction] "not after *adā*"? Consider *dātaṃ barhiḥ*. The meaning is "cut. Here, the substitution of *dad* [for *dā*] by the rule "o daddhoḥ" does not occur.
Consider *avadātaṃ mukham*. The meaning is "pure. Here, however, the substitution of *t* [for *d*] by the rule "aca upasargāt" does not occur.

(182) *erliṅ* |6|4|67|. *erliṅ*. [The rule applies] "to *mā*, *sthā*, etc."—that is to say, to *mā*, *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, and *jahāti*. Although there is no distinction among the roots *mā* (in the sense of measuring), *māṅ* (prohibition), and *meṅ* (exchange) when they are included under the general term *mā* in rules such as *gāmādāgrahaṇeṣu*, neither *māṅ* nor *meṅ* is taken here; rather, it is *mā* (prohibition) that is intended, because of the context of the *liṅ* (optative) suffix.

Because of the impossibility of having an *ik*-affix (*ikitva*). [The roots] √ṣṭhā (to stop), √gai (to sing), and √gāṅ (to go) are not included here, precisely because of the impossibility of having an *ik*-affix. [The roots] √pā (to drink), √ohāk (to abandon), √ṣo (to destroy), √dā (to give), √dhā (to place), √mā (to measure), √sthā (to stand), and √gai (to sing): [the forms] *deyāt*, *dheyāt*, *meyāt*, *stheyāt*, *geyāt*.
*peyāt*, *heyāt*, *avasaṃyāt*. Why [is it specified] "in an ārdhadhātuka suffix"?
[Consider: *māyāt*, *māyātām*, *māyuḥ*. Why [is it specified] "when followed by a *k* or *ṅ*"? [Consider: *dāsīṣṭa*.
Here, although the term "*kṅtī*" is understood from the previous rule "īṅe yuḍacī," it is [re-stated] for the sake of the present context.
The word *kit* itself is continued [from the previous rule].
(183) *vibhāṣā dheṭ-śvyoḥ* | Pāṇini 3.1.49. Regarding *vibhāṣā dheṭ*: the words *li luṅi* are continued from the previous rule, and *kartari* is continued from the rule *ṇi-śri-* [3.1.48].

Thus he says: "The affix *caṅ* optionally [replaces *liṭ*]," and so forth. Regarding the form *adadhat*: the *caṅ* affix is applied, and there is elision of the final vowel (*ā*) by rule Pāṇini 6.4.64.
An example of the root *śvi* is *aśiśviyat*. (184) Pāṇini 2.4.78: "The substitution of *caṅ* for *liṭ* is optional after the roots *ghrā*, *dheṭ*, *śā*, *chā*, and *sā*."

[The rule] *vibhāṣā ghrā* [is stated]. Here, the elision (*luk*) is carried over from the rule *ṭhṇyakṣatriyārṣe*, and [the condition] *parasmaipadeṣu* is carried over from the rule *ātistheḥ*. Therefore, he says: "the elision of *sic* optionally," and so forth. Regarding *adhur*: by the rule *ātaḥ*, the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *jus*. Why "in the parasmaipada"? [Consider: *vyatyaghrāsta*.

(185) *yamaramanamātāṃ sak ca* || 7.2.73 || [The rule] *yamaramanamātām* [is explained as follows]: Here, from the rule *ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*, the word *it* (the augment *iṭ*) is understood to carry over.
From the rule *aṅgasya sicī* [sic], the mention of *sic* [is carried over], and from the rule *tusudhūñbhyaḥ*... [the mention of *sak*].

And there is the mention of the *parasmaipada* (active voice). Thus he says: "After these [roots], the suffix *sic* takes the augment *iṭ*, etc. Examples: *ayaṃsīt*, *ayaṃsiṣṭām*; *vyaraṃsīt*, *vyaraṃsiṣṭām*; *anaṃsīt*, *anaṃsiṣṭām*. Why [specify] "in the *parasmaipada*s"? [Observe: *udāyaṃsta bhāram* (he lifted the burden); *araṃsta*, *araṃsātām*.

(186) *vā'nyasya saṃyogādeḥ* |6|4|68|. [The rule] *vā'nyasya*. What is meant by "of another" (*anyasya*)? [Answer: *stheyāt*. [In the root] *dyai* in the sense of "humbling," [we have] *dyāyati*, *dadyau*, *adyāsīt*. Because of the explanation [in the rule] *ghumāsthā...* (*Pāṇini 6.4.66*), [the substitution of *ī* for *e* occurs] here; according to other systems of grammar (*tantrāntara*), it is said that this applies to the roots *jahāti* and *syati*.

The intention is that it is because of the indication by the form *śyan*. [In the rule] *vibhāṣā ghrā*, the intention is that it refers to the roots *śā* and *chā* due to their association with the *kaśyan* suffixes.

Likewise, it should be understood that even in the prescription of the *yuk* augment in [the rule] *śācchāsāhvāvyāvepāṃ yuk ca*, only *syati* and its relatives are intended to be included. Therefore, for this root, there is only the *puṅ* augment according to [the rule] *arti-hrī-*.

It means "he causes to dry," "it dries," "it causes to drink," or "it blows"; the sense is "it withers. By the rule *ṭhoditaśca*, there is the substitution of *ṇatva* for the final consonant in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*): *vānam*. As Amara states: "The word *vāna* [meaning 'dry'] occurs in all three genders. Regarding the phrase "because it ends in *a*": some, however, maintain that the absence of *guṇa* is established even by the *aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding operations within a stem).
They justify [this]. *Ghrā* [is used] in the sense of grasping odor; "grasping odor" means the apprehension of odor.

If it is objected that, in this way, because the object is subsumed within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the verb would be intransitive (*akarmaka*), and thus usages such as *jighrati kusumam* ("he smells the flower") would not be established—here they say: that which [is grasped] by the meaning of the verbal root...

The inclusion of an object that resides within the agent (kartṛniṣṭha) is what constitutes the intransitivity (akarmakatva) of that very root, and not of any other. For instance, roots such as *bhū*, *jīv*, and *nṛt* are indeed intransitive, because their objects are included within the meaning of the action and reside in the agent. However, the root *ghrā* is not intransitive because its object does not possess that quality [of residing in the agent]. [This applies to] *dhmā*.
Regarding "sound" (śabda) and "contact with fire" (agnisaṃyoga): by the word "sound," the air conducive to it is understood here.
Therefore, they say that just as one says "he blows the conch," one does not use the expression "he blows the drum.
Regarding "contact with fire"—as in "he smelts gold"; the meaning is "he joins [it] with fire. "It should remain steady," etc.

In *ṭherlaṅī*, there is always this shortening (*etva*). Regarding *luṅ*: *isthāt*. The root *mnā* means "to study" or "to practice. In *manati*, it means "he studies the science"; that is, he practices it. [The forms] *mamnau* and *amnāsīt* follow. Because it belongs to the second class (adādi), there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic* by the rule *ātistheḥ*.

(187) *ṛtaśca saṃyogāder guṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.10. [The rule states: "And after a root ending in *ṛ*, there is *guṇa* [substitution] for the *liṭ* suffixes. Why say "after a root ending in *ṛ*" and "beginning with a conjunct consonant"? [Consider the counter-examples: *cakratuḥ*, *cakruḥ*. The inclusion of the long vowel marker *ṝ* (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of clarity, as in cases such as *tastaratuḥ* from the root *stṛñ* and others when followed by *liṭ*.

Because the *guṇa* [substitution] arises in the case of the root *ṛ* (as in *ṛcchatyṛtām*), the particle *ca* is of little utility. He says "there would be *guṇa* in the *liṭ*" because it is understood from the rule "after *ayati*, when *digī* follows in the *liṭ*.
However, the ancient explanation—"in the *liṭ* which is not the cause of *vṛddhi*"—is not to be respected. Nor...

It should be stated that this statement is intended to express the resultant meaning—that "increase" (*vṛddhi*) is the sublater within its own domain; however, the underlying intention is that, by virtue of being subsequent in the order of rules, "guṇa" substitution alone is more appropriate.
(188) *Guṇo’rtisaṃyogādyoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.10.
The term *ṛti* includes both the *bhū* and *hvā* classes [of roots], as indicated by the elision (*luk*) [of the suffix].

Although *ṛ* should have been mentioned [directly], the mention using the *śtip* affix is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa (the intensive with elided *yaṅ*). From the rule *rīṅ ṛtaḥ*, the word *ṛtaḥ* is understood [as a governing element], and it is further qualified by being the beginning of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*). Thus he says:

Regarding the phrase "saṃyogādeḥ": although the vowel *a* is prescribed by the rule "arti-saṃyogādyoḥ," the mention of "guṇa" (vowel strengthening) is of questionable utility. From the preceding sūtra "ayaṅ yi kṅti," the term *ayaṅ* is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*).
That [term] serves as a qualifier for the *liṅ* (optative suffix). Furthermore, from the sūtra "riṅ śayagliṅkṣu," the mention of *yag* [is also understood].
Intending to show that the mention of the *liṅ* (optative) continues [from the previous rule], he says: "in *yaki*, *yādi*, etc.
This is understood by considering the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ārddhadhātuke* from the rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayordīrgho‘nyatarasyām*.

This should be understood as "the statement of the meaning of the *phala* (result). Why [is it said] "of *saṃyoga*, etc."? [Consider] *kriyāt*. Why [is it said] "beginning with *ya*" (*yādi*)? [Consider] *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*. Why [is it said] "in an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix"? [Consider] *iyṛyāt*. [The root] *svṛ*.
"Affliction" (*upatāpa*) means disease (*roga*).

(189) *ṛśyukaḥ kiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.11]. Regarding *ṛśyukaḥ kiti*: from the rule *ekāca upadeśe* [7.2.10], the term *ekāc* is understood to carry over. He states that this qualifies *uk*, namely: "from a one-syllable root ending in *u*. Examples: *śritaḥ*, *śritavān*.

Examples of [the suffix] *gi* are: *śritvā*, *bhūtaḥ*, *bhūtvā*, *bhūtiḥ*, and *bhūṣṇuḥ*. In the case of *bhūṣṇuḥ*, the suffix *gsnu* is applied by the rule *lājisthaśca*; and that [suffix] is *gid*, not *kit*. In the case of *sthāsnur*, if it were *kit*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of shortening the vowel [to *i*] by the rule *hrasvāsthi-*. Why is it specified that it must be a single-vowel root (*ekāc*)? Consider the example *jāgaritaḥ*.

He has awakened (*jāgaritavān*). Regarding the root *ūrṇu*, when the suffix *nu* is applied—*ūrṇutaḥ*; "he has covered" (*ūrṇutavān*)—thus it is established. Why [specify] "ending in *u*" (*ugantāt*)? [Consider: "he has lain down" (*śayitaḥ*), "he has lain down" (*śayitavān*). "Earlier," etc.: before the prescriptive section beginning with "the augment *iṭ* is added to an *ardhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant" (*ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*), [the rule] "before *ej* and *aś*" (*ej-aśi*)...

The meaning is: "by virtue of the commencement of the section [of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*] that prohibits [the substitution of *iṭ*] in cases such as *kṛtī*. Regarding the phrase "when a prohibition has been established," the intention is that it is just as in examples such as *svṛtaḥ*, *sūtaḥ*, and *dhūtaḥ*. [The root] *sṛ* means "to go": *sarati*, *sariṣyati*.

(190) *sartiśāstyartibhyaśca* | Pāṇini 3.1.56. Regarding *sarti-śāsti-arti-*: the phrase "in the parasmaipada [endings]" (*parasmaipadeṣu*) is not connected here, because this rule is separated from the *puṣādi* group. Furthermore, there is no inclusion here of the root *śās* meaning "to desire" (from *āṅḥ śāsu icchāyām*), but rather—

Some say that because of its association with *sarti* and *arti*, [the substitution applies] only to the root *śās* when it is parasmaipada; thus: *asarat*, *aśiṣat*, *ārat*. (191) *ṛcchatyṛtām* 7.4.11.

"As before" means that although the *guṇa* substitution was initiated [by P. 7.3.84], it is replaced by *ṇal* due to its higher priority; then the substitution of *r* for the final vowel occurs (*raparatva*), and subsequently the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel takes place. (P.
7.2.66) *iḍatyartivyayatīnām*. The suffix *iṭ* is added after the roots *at*, *ṛ*, and *vyay*.

The sense is that [the suffix] *iṭ* must always be applied; thus, the option (*vibhāṣā*) from the rule "optionally for the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś*" does not carry over. The root *dhvṛ* means "to bend" (*hūrchanam*), where "bending" refers to crookedness (*kauṭilyam*). The root *sṛ* means "motion" (*gati*); although motion is stated in a general sense, here it refers specifically to the motion of a liquid substance.
It should be understood that *ghṛta* flows.
(193) *stusudhūñbhyaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* [Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.72]. Regarding *stusudhūñbhyaḥ*: why "in the *parasmaipada* endings"? [Observe: *atoṣṭa*, *adhoṣṭa*.

(194) *śruvaḥ śṛ ca* |3|1|74|. Regarding *śruvaḥ śṛ ca*: they say that if this root *śru* were recited in the *svādi* group, then the letter *ca* would not need to be employed, which would result in brevity (*lāghava*).

(195) *huśnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke* |6|4|87| [The substitution of *ū* for the vowel of the roots] *hu* and *śnu* occurs before an affix beginning with a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. Examples: *juhvati*, *sunvati*. Why "of *hu* and *śnu*"? [Consider: *yoyuvati*, *nonuvati*. Why "before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix"? [Consider: *juhuvatuḥ*, *juhuvuḥ*.

What is the purpose of the phrase "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogapūrva*)? [Consider the example: *akṣṇuvanti*. This qualification applies to the roots *ghu* and *mā*, not to the suffix *śnu*.

Therefore, even in the case of *āpnuvanti*, the prohibition of *yaṇ* (the substitution of *i* for *u*) is established. However, if it were a qualification of the suffix, [the rule would not apply here].

The intention is that the prohibition would apply only in cases such as *akṣṇuvanti*. It might be argued: since the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*) is Vedic, in forms such as *yoyuvatī*, the substitution of *yaṇ* would not occur because one may resort to the status of being "half-a-syllable" (*arddhahrasvatva*) for the suffix by the rule "in the Veda, [a suffix] is optionally both ways" (*chandasyubhayathā*).

"What is the use of including *hu*? Nor should it be argued that its inclusion is for the purpose of preventing over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *yuvaṃti* and *nuvaṃti*, because the aforementioned fault does not arise since the term 'anekācaḥ' is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. To this, they say:
Because of the Vedic irregularity (*nipātana*) in the rule *ādhartidardhartidardharṣibobhūtu*,
the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *hūsuvoḥ* does not apply in the case of forms such as *bobhavīti* when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided in the common language (*bhāṣā*).
This is because it will be stated later that the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*) is established even in the common language.
The mention of *hu* and *śnu* must indeed be made in order to prevent over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *yoyuvati*.

Based on the *jñāpaka* provided by the mention of *hu* and *śnu*, the authors of the Bhāṣya maintain that the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*) occurs even in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*) in certain instances. And thus...

Regarding the doubt as to why the term *anekāc* ("having more than one vowel") is continued [from a previous rule] here—given that there is no deviation from the condition of "having more than one vowel" in the case of the *huṬ* and *śnu* suffixes when followed by *sārvadhātuka* affixes—that doubt is entirely without foundation;
for if that term were not continued, it would be impossible for the mention of *hu* and *śnu* to serve as an *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence). This is the general direction of the argument.

Regarding *dudāvitha*: by the rule of Bhāradvāja, the augment *iṭ* is applied; thus, *dudrotha*, *dudruve*. Because it belongs to the *krād-i* group, there is no *iṭ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). Regarding the root *gāṅ* (in the sense of "going"): [the forms] *gāte*, *gāte*, *gāte*. When the long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) has been formed with the preceding *śap* [augment], the rule "āto ṅtiḥ" does not apply.
However, the rule "ṭhātmanepadeṣvanataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.5) applies; thus, the meaning is that the forms are identical in the cases of *ātām* and *jha*.
[The forms are: *gai*, *gāvahe*, *gāmahe*; *jage*, *jagāte*, *jagire*;
*gātām*, *gātām*, *gātām*; *gāsva*; and in the first person—*gai*, *gāvahai*, *gāmahai*; *agāt*.

[The two roots] *agātām* [and *agāt*] do not, however, [take the *taṅ* substitutes]. This is because, in forms such as *gāte*, the *taṅ* substitutes have already been applied, and thus the *ṅ* [in the root *gā*] has already served its purpose. The *ṅ* in the substitute [root *gā*], on the other hand, has not yet served its purpose; the point is that the *taṅ* substitutes are established by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) based on the *ṅ* [of the substitute]. [The author notes: "This [root *gā*] belongs to the first class (*adādika*). And thus, [we have] *gāte*.

The sense is that in examples such as *gāte* and *gāthe*, there is no possibility at all for the application of the rule "ṭhāto ṅtiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.84). Furthermore, there is no difference in the result;
for even if a long vowel by class-similarity (*savarṇadīrgha*) is applied to *gāte* and *gāthe* along with the suffix *śap*, when a rule applies to what follows an earlier element...

One might suspect that because [the substitute] is *sthānivadbhūt*, the substitution of *iy* for the *ā* of *ṅtām* would occur due to its being followed by an *at*-ending [suffix]; however, the intention is that this is not so, because the view that the *pañcamī-samāsa* (genitive compound) is applicable here is accepted as being non-universal (*anitya*). Regarding *ñuṅ-uve*: the *ñ* replaces the *ṅ* by the rule *uṅeścu*. Regarding *cyuṅ*: from this root, the suffix *ac* is added according to the *pacādi* group.
*Viklavaḥ*: others say *viklaba* because of the non-distinction between *v* and *b*. Regarding *meṅ*, [the form] is *praṇimayate*. Now, one might object:

how can there be *ṇatva* here by the rule "ergade"? For in the domain of *śit* suffixes, due to the absence of *ātvam*, the form *mā* does not exist; and even if *ātvam* has occurred outside the domain of *śit* suffixes, *ṇatva* would still be difficult to obtain in this case.
Since it is appropriate to understand the root *mā* as that which is explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*) and not this one which is derivative (*lākṣaṇika*),

if one were to accept the principle that "there is no distinction in the case of the mention of *ām*, *ā*, or *āP*," then an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would occur in forms such as *pranimātā* and *pranimāsyati*, where the substitution of *ā* for the roots *mīnāti* and *minoti* has already taken place. Therefore, he says:

Regarding the phrase "therein" and "because it is desired": this is the intended meaning—the commentators on the *ghu* designation rule established this as their final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in order to justify the application of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) in forms such as *praṇidayate* and *praṇidhayati*:
that in the rule prescribing *ṇatva*, namely *ergadanada*, the term *hum* should be replaced by *huprakṛtimāṅ*.
It should be read as follows: *ghu*, *prakṛti*, and *māṅ* form a *dvandva* compound.

When there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to whose *prakṛti* [is meant], it refers only to the immediately preceding and following [elements] due to proximity (*saṃnidhāna*). Consequently, there is no non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) anywhere, nor even in the case of the rule *ā māne*.
Furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the roots *mīnāti* and *minoti*, because [the rule] prescribes the form *māṅ* specifically as that which has the indicatory letter *ṅ*.
(196) *dayater digi liṭi* | Pāṇini 7.4.9.

Regarding the phrase "by the substitution of *digī*": when the suffix *liṭ* follows the root *day*, both reduplication and the substitution of *digī* are applicable. In that case, the rule for reduplication is superseded by the substitution of *digī*, which is specifically prescribed for this instance. However, it is not the case that the same would apply to the forms *pī* and *khyāñ*—as in *yāyaḥ pī* and *akṣiṅḥ khyāñ*—because these two are also specifically prescribed.

It should not be argued that there would be a sublation of the dual number, because the substitution of *liṭ* occurs precisely before the application of those two [rules], by resorting to the locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*). However, in the rule prescribing the substitute *digy-* (for *dvig-*),
the locative *liṭi* is indeed a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*) and not a locative of scope, in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*).

This indicates the following: "it is desired. It has not been stated that "when *dvitva* (reduplication) is applicable after the root *ay*, the substitution of *digy* takes its place by virtue of being subsequent (*para*), thereby overriding it"; for a subsequent rule is stronger only when both rules have found their respective scope. This is because, even though *dvitva* would otherwise find its scope without the substitution of *digy*, [the latter prevails].

The direction [of the rule] is that without duality there is no substitution for *diś* and so forth, because of its absence; this is the general principle (*dig*). (197) *sthā-dhvo-ric-ca* | 1.2.17 | Regarding *sthā-dhvo-ric-ca*: here, from the sūtra *iṅ-sic-au*, [the word] *ātmanepadeṣu* [is understood].

It was not followed [by Patañjali], because in the *parasmaipada* forms there is no possibility of excluding the application of the elision (*luk*) in the case of *ātisthe*. [Examples are: *asthita*, *asthiṣātām*. They say that this very use of the *tapara* marker (*t*) is also an indication for the rule: "A vowel being substituted by a single phoneme (*aṇ*) sometimes includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)."

Regarding this, they say: even though that which is being prescribed would include its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), the inclusion of *ta* (the *tapara* marker) here is redundant. Nor should it be argued that a long vowel (*dīrgha*) might occur here; for that is already established by the rule "humāsthe" itself, and thus the prescription would be rendered useless. Nor should it be argued that even so, a protracted vowel (*pluta*) might occur; [for that too is excluded].
This is because of the established grammatical rule (siddhānta): "The suffix 'lut' is applied in the sense of jumping, and 'alut' is prescribed when referring to the object.

[The root] *ḍīṅ* [is used here]. "By means of the sky" (*vihāyasā*) means by means of the atmosphere (*ākāśena*). They say that the reading "by means of the sky" (*vihāyasām*) is not found in the authoritative sources (*anākara*).

(198) *ṛta iddhātoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.100. The vowel *ṛ* of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is replaced by *i*. Examples: *kirati*, *girati*; *kīrṇaḥ*, *gīrṇaḥ*; *stīrṇaḥ*. Why "of a verbal root"? [Consider: *mātṛṇām*.
“By the rule *itvotvābhyām*, guna and vṛddhi [substitutions] take precedence through conflict. Regarding the phrase *itvotvābhyām*:
although it should have been stated that “guna and vṛddhi occur because they are antaranga,” one might ask, “Is this a vārttika?
To this they say: since an antaranga operation is stronger even than a subsequent one, the substitution of *it* would have applied first.
This *vārttika* has been commenced:
(199) *vṛto vā* | Pāṇini 7.2.38. Regarding *vṛto vā*: here, from the rule *ārddhadhātukasyeḍ vaḥ*, the word *iṭ* is understood as being carried over (*anuvartate*). [The word] *rahaḥ*...
From the rule *liṭi* and from *liṭi dīrghaḥ*, it is said: "The long vowel for *iṭ* optionally," and so forth. (200) *sici ca parasmaipadeṣu* |7|2|40|.
Regarding *sici ca*: since *na* is understood from the previous rule *na liṅi*, it is said: "There is no long vowel for *iṭ*."

(201) *mān-badha-dān-śān-bhyo dīrghaśca ābhyāsasya* | Pāṇini 7.4.54. The analysis of the sūtra is: *mān-badha-dān-śān-bhyaḥ* and *dīrghaḥ ca ābhyāsasya*. "Modification of the reduplication" (*ābhyāsa*) refers to the term *ābhyāsa*.

In this context, by the rule *anyataḥ*, it is specifically the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the reduplication. If, however, [the word] *hrasvaḥ* ("short") were understood [instead of *dīrghaḥ*], then there would be a reference to a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

It would be useless. This is what he says: "of the root *kṛ* with the prefix *abhi*. He shows the meanings established by the author of the Vṛtti and others, starting with "of *gup* in the sense of censure," and so forth. (202) *sanyaṅeḥ* 6.1.9.

Regarding the rule *sanyaṅeḥ*: if one were to explain it as "when *san* or *yaṅ* follows," then forms such as *ratīṣiṣati* and *ṭhaṭāṭaḷte* would not be established, because the doubling would apply only to the radical portion (*prakṛtibhāga*) of the stem. Therefore, he says: "of that which ends in *san*" (*sannantasya*). Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: ...nanu...
Even according to the seventh alternative (the view that the suffixes are included), reduplication would apply only to *san* and *yaṅ*, and not to the radical portion;

for forms such as *jugupsate* and *titikṣate* are established by the vowel *a* of the *śap* suffix itself, and thus the purpose of pronouncing the vowel *a* in those two [suffixes] is to trigger the rule "of the second syllable beginning with a consonant" (*ajāder dvitīyasya*).

Because it has the meaning of "duality. Although, if the cause (nimitta) were accepted as the subject of the operation (kāryin), then in cases such as *āṭatuḥ* and so on—where *liṭ* follows—the doubling of only the preceding portion would not be established;
nevertheless, by the force of the utterance of the vowel *a*, one must accept that the suffixes *san* and *yaṅ* are the subjects of the operation.
If you argue that this is possible, it is not so; for there are many instances where the vowel *a* is the result [of the suffix]. To illustrate:

in the words *ditsyam* and *dhitsyam*, when the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *aco yati*, the desired acute accent (*ādyudātta*) is established by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*. However, in the absence of the vowel *a*, the desired accent would not be established by the suffix *ṇyat* according to the rule *ṛhaloḥ*.

Furthermore, in the case of *ipathiṣi brāhmaṇakulāni*, because the elision (*al-lopa*) is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the augment *num*—which is conditioned by a stem ending in a consonant (*jhal*)—does not occur; however, in the absence of that *a*-elision, *num* would indeed occur.
Moreover, in forms such as *āpacaka*, because of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision of *a*, [the suffix] *ṭhak*...

Because of the rule *upadhāyāḥ*, the *vṛddhi* substitution does not apply. Furthermore, it is universally accepted that in the rule *yasya halaḥ*, the mention of the compound *yasya* is for the purpose of excluding the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) in forms such as *aharyīt*.
Thus, in cases like *apāpaciṣṭa*, the elision of *y* is also a result of the vowel *a*; therefore, [the rule applies] to *anyaṅe*.

Thus, the genitive alone is appropriate. For in this way, when the *yaṅ* affix is elided (*yaṅluk*), reduplication is established by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the rule that an operation dependent on an affix applies even when it is elided), because the form still possesses the character of being *yaṅ*-ended.

However, if the locative were used [in the rule], then since reduplication would be an operation pertaining to the *aṅga* (stem), the prohibition "when there is elision marked by *lu*, [an operation] does not apply" (*a lumate*) would take effect. This is the general direction of the argument.
"And *dāna* and *jñāna*": the sense is that they mean "straightness" (*ārjava*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*). "But in another meaning" means:
