in a meaning such as "concealing," which is included in the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*). "Those without indicatory marks" (*ananubandhakāḥ*):
for if they possessed indicatory marks (*sānubandhakatva*), the mark would serve no purpose in its isolated form.
The intention is that, just as with roots ending in *san*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings should also occur after a root ending in *ṇic* when the fruit of the action does not accrue to the agent.

Thus, it follows that even though there is a mere similarity in their sequential order, the *bhū*-class roots (*bhvādayaḥ*) are indeed distinct from the *cur*-class roots (*curādayaḥ*). Regarding "there is no *iṭ* or *guṇa*": although [the suffix] *san* could also be *kit* by the rule "after a [root] ending in a consonant" (*halantācca*), [the *iṭ* augment and *guṇa* substitution do not apply].

The absence of [the suffix] *guṇa* is easily established; therefore, for the sake of avoiding that defect, the very reason already stated must be relied upon—what is the point of resorting to another reason? This is the sense. Some, however, maintain that by the paribhāṣā "the mention of a meaningful element," the term is included only in the case of the desiderative (*san*) under the rule *halantācca*, and thus it does not apply to this *san* in its own sense (*svārtha*).

They say: *kitva* (the suffix *kit*). The root *rabh* is used in the sense of "impetuosity" (*rābhasyam*), which means "undertaking" (*upakrama*). In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), [the forms are] *rebhe*, *rebhāte*.

In the aorist (*luṅ*), [the forms are] *irabdha*, *arapsātām*. The root *ḍulabhaṣ* [is used in the sense of obtaining]. By the rule "from a root ending in *vit*, the suffix *kri*" [is applied], we get *labdhri* (one who obtains). By the rule "after roots beginning with *bhid*, the suffix *aṅ*," we get *labhā* (acquisition). In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), [the form is] *lebhe*.
*luṅ*—not obtained.

(203) *veḥ skander aniṣṭhāyām* |8|3|73|. After the prefix *vi*, [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] occurs in the case of the root *skand*, provided it is not followed by an *niṣṭhā* suffix. The phrase “*it* of *ivādīnām* and *ṭhve*” is understood to carry over.

Since this [suffix] would not otherwise apply because it is not taught as an upadeśa, this is an optional rule (vibhāṣā). He says "this is only for the sake of a kṛtya suffix" in accordance with the views of Mādhava and others. As for the example "vikandati" cited by the Easterners (Prāc), its source must be sought; such is the sense.

(204) "And [the rule] *pareśca* [Pāṇini 8.3.74] does not apply here. For this very reason, he provides an example of the substitution of *ṣ* even for a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), namely *pariṣkandati*. The root *ṣkand* means "to stoop" (*prahvatve*). Some read this root as marked with the *u* indicatory letter (*uditam*).
They say that this is due to negligence (*prāmādika*).
[The rule] *iṣugamiyamāṃ chaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.77) applies.
Regarding *jagmatuḥ*, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) by the rule *amaṅṇe*.

(206) *anudātasya ca ṛdupadhasyānyatarasyām* || 6.1.59 || Regarding *anudātasya*: the term *upadeśe* (in the original instruction) is understood from the rule *ādeca upadeśe ’śitī* [6.1.45]. Why "in the original instruction"? Consider *sraptum*; here the suffix *tumun* is acute (*udātta*). Why "having *ṛ* as its penultimate"? Consider: [the example *sraṣṭum*].

The agent [is expressed]. Why [is it said] "after a consonant" (*jhalīti*)? [Consider] *sasarpa*. Why [is it said] "not after a kit" (*akitīti*)? [Consider] *sṛptaḥ* and *asṛpat*; because it is marked with the indicator *ḷ*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied. Regarding the addition of *sṛp* to the optional rule for the *sic* suffix stated as "pṛśamṛśa," some cite *ṭhasrāpsīt* and *asārpsīt* as examples; however, they say that this is based on a mere error.
Regarding the word *ayaṃsīt*: the suffixes *iṭ* and *sak* follow the root *yam*.
(207) [Pāṇini 8.3.102] states: *nisastapatāvanāsevane*. While the term *ūrdhanya* is understood to carry over, he states the result: "there shall be *ṣ*."
But in the case of *āsevana*—it means "it refines" (*niṣṭapati*), that is, "it heats repeatedly.

(208) *vibhāṣā sṛjidṛśoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.65. Since [the suffix *ktvā*] would have been obligatory by the rule governing roots beginning with *kṛ* (*krādi-niyama*), this is stated as an option (*vibhāṣā*).

(209) *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti* | Pāṇini 6.1.58. Why [is it said] "before a consonant (*jhal*)"? [Consider: *sasarja*, *dadarśa*. Why [is it said] "not before a kit-affix (*akiti*)"? [Consider: *sṛṣṭaḥ*, *sṛṣṭavān*;
*dṛṣṭaḥ*, *dṛṣṭavān*.

(210) *ṛdṛśo’ṅ guṇiḥ* |7|4|16|. [In the case of the root] *dṛś*, the augment *aṅ* is applied when a suffix marked with *guṇa* follows. Thus: *adāṅkṣīt*. By the rule *vadavraje* [Pāṇini 7.2.3], there is *vṛddhi*. [The forms are: *adāṃṣṭām*, *adāṅkṣuḥ*. (211) *na dṛśaḥ* |3|1|47|. [The *liṭ* affixes are not replaced by *kvasu* after the root] *dṛś*.

*Kraṣṭā* and *karṣṭā*: by the rule *ṭhanudātasya ca*, the substitution is optional. It should be stated that for the roots *spṛś*, *mṛś*, *kṛṣ*, *tṛp*, and *dṛp*, the *sij* affix is optionally substituted for the *cli* affix. In *dhakṣyati*, there is the substitution of *gh*, *ṣatva*, and *bhaṣbhāva*. In *adhākṣīt*, the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule *astisicaḥ*; then there is *vṛddhi*, followed by the substitutions of *gh*, etc.

As before. The root *miha* means "to sprinkle. Here, "sprinkling" is intended in the sense of "mixing," and not merely the act of sprinkling. Amara states: "The words *eḍhra* and *mehana* mean the penis. The root *kit* means "to dwell.
It has been stated that the desiderative (*san*) suffix is applied to *kit* only in the sense of counteracting a disease and so forth. He provides an example of this:

"Cikitsati" means "he removes a disease. "He cikitsati an enemy" means "he subdues him. "He cikitsati weeds in a field" means "he removes them or destroys them. It has been stated that [the root] belongs to the *curādi* (cur-class) in other meanings; he illustrates this with "ketayati."
The root *ṣac* means "to join" (*samavāya*). *Samavāya* here means "connection" (*sambandha*). Regarding *bhājiṣyate*:
by the rule *ṛt-phala-bhaja-*, there is the substitution of *e*. Regarding *bhakṣyati*: there is the change to *k* (kutva) and the change to *ṣ* (ṣatva). Regarding *tviṣ* in the sense of "shining":
regarding *atvikṣat*, the suffix *ksa* is applied by the rule *al-ig-upadhāt*; then there is the change to *t* (katva) and the change to *ṣ* (ṣatva). Regarding *atvikṣātām*.

In the word *sasyācī*, there is elision [of the final consonant]. In this context, sacrifice (*yāja*) to the gods is the renunciation of a substance, enjoined by an injunction with reference to a deity. (212) *liṭaḷbhyāsasyobhayeṣām* 6.1.17.

Regarding the rule *liṭ-abhyāsasya*: the roots beginning with *vac* are *vac*, *svap*, *yaj*, and so forth; whereas the roots beginning with *grah* are *grah*, *jyā*, *vayi*, and so forth. Although there is no difference whether the semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the reduplication is performed or not for the roots *grah*, *pṛcch*, and *bhṛjj*, nevertheless, the grammatical rule [applies] like a rain-cloud (*parjanya-vat*).
[The suffix] *pravartate* [is applied]; [the root] *jagrāha*; [the root] *papraccha*; [the root] *babhrajj*. However, there is a distinction regarding the root *vṛśc*:

if the semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) were not performed, then in the form *vavraśca*, the vocalization of the letter *va* would occur; but when the vocalization has been performed, the prohibition "not when there is vocalization" (*na saṃprasāraṇe*) becomes applicable. [This refers to the rule concerning] the present tense (*laṭ*).

What [examples]? *vivakṣati* (he wishes to speak), *pipakṣati* (he wishes to cook). [The rule applies to] the roots *vac*, *svap*, and so on, up to the end of the *gaṇa*. "The nine beginning with *yaj* are: *yajir*, *vapir*, *vahir*, *vasir*, *veñ*, *vyeñ*, *hveñ*, *vī*, and *śvayati*. Why [specify] "before a *kit* suffix"? [Consider: *iyaṣṭha*.
*ḍuvap*, *ṭuṣiv*, *ṭvitaḥ kriḥ*, *uptrimam*.
(213) *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca* | 8|3|60 | This rule applies to the root-final *s* where it would otherwise not have been obtained. Now, one might object: [why is this necessary?]

If it is argued that the rule "ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.41) may be discarded by accepting it as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)— namely, that "this [ṣatva] applies only to the *s* of a verbal root if it follows these very [sounds]"— in order to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *supisau* and *supisaḥ*, then the reply is: here they say that [the rule is necessary] to prevent the application of *ṣatva* to a portion of a substitute (*ādeśa*).

The portion "of the substitute" (ādeśasya) is indeed necessary. Once that [term] has been included, the mention of "affix" (pratyaya) must also certainly be made, in order to prevent the contingency of a restrictive rule (niyama) such as: "if [the substitution] occurs for an 's' distinct from a verbal root, it occurs only when it is of the form of a substitute."
Regarding *avātsīt*: by the rule *vadavraje* (Pāṇini 7.2.3), there is vṛddhi; by *aḥ si* (Pāṇini 7.3.96), *ta* is substituted for *ti*;

and by *astisicaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.96), *iṭ* is added. As for the statement "for the purpose of pronunciation": the intention is that if it were marked with the *it* designation, then by *iditaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.58), the augment *num* would occur.
Regarding *uvāya*: because of the inclusion of *vayi* in the rule *rahijye* (Pāṇini 6.1.19), the prohibition [of vṛddhi] concerning *veñ* does not apply here.
They say [the rule] "it proceeds" applies.

(214) *grahi-jyā-va-vi-vyadhi-vaṣṭi-vicati-vṛścati-pṛcchati-bhṛjjatīnāṃ ṅiti ca* | Pāṇini 6.1.16. [The semivowel *y* is substituted for the vowel *i* of these roots when followed by an affix beginning with a *ṅit* consonant.]
Regarding the roots *grah*, *jyā*, and *ve*: [from *grah*] we have *gṛhṇāti*, *gṛhṇītaḥ*; [from *ji*] *jināti*, *jinītaḥ*, *jīnaḥ*.

There is no example for *ve* with an affix beginning in *ṅ*. However, with an affix beginning in *k*, it is established by the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), because *veñ* is included among the *yajādi* roots. For this very reason, the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the reduplication is also established.

However, the prohibition of *saṃprasāraṇa* in the case of the root *ṭhveñ* does not apply, because that prohibition begins with the rule "iṭi vayo ya" (Pāṇini 6.1.38). Therefore, it should be understood that the inclusion of *vayi* among the roots beginning with *grahi* and *jyā* is for the sake of clarity alone.

(215) *vaścāsyānyatarasyāṃ kiti* |6|1|39|. By the rule *vaścāsyāṭhasya*, the [term] *vayo yaḥ* is referred to. Thus he says: "that whose [substitute] is *ya* for *vayas*. It would have been more easily expressed as *vo vā kiti*; however, [the rule] *liṭi vayo yaḥ* [is stated].

Because it is the subject under discussion. Having raised the objection regarding the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 7.2.61] as "in the case of a verbal root ending in short /a/ taught [in the Dhātupāṭha]," he says: "because there is no such [short /a/] in the suffix tāsi. Now, one might object: since the original element (sthānin) does exist in the suffix tāsi, its existence [therein] is easily established through the principle of "behaving like the original" (sthānivadbhāva). To this, they say:

For the status of being "as if the original" (sthānivadbhāva) applies to grammatical operations, but not to worldly matters. Although the prohibition [contained in Pāṇini 4.1.70] beginning with "ṭhacaḥ tāsi" is itself a grammatical rule, it is not extended here; this is because the mention of "ṭhac" constitutes a rule concerning vowels (alvidhi).

(216) *veñaḥ* |6|1|40|. [The substitution of *ū* for the root *veñ* occurs] before the suffix *liṭ*. Why [is it said] "before *liṭ*"? [Consider: *utam*, *utavān*. (217) *na vyo liṭi* |6|1|46|. [The substitution of *ū* for the root *vyo* does not occur] before the suffix *liṭ*.
Why [is it] "in the case of the periphrastic perfect" (*liṭ*)? [Examples: *vyātā*, *vyāsyati*.
(218) *abhyastasya ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.33]. Regarding *abhyastasya ca*: the preceding rule, however, applies in the domain of *ṇi*, *saṅ*, and *caṅ*.
*juhāvayiṣati*; *ajūhavat*. Regarding the rule *abhyastībhaviṣyataḥ hveñaḥ*:

the established meaning is that when a suffix conditioned by reduplication (*abhyasta*) follows, the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution for the root *hveñ* occurs even before the doubling of the syllable. That which possesses reduplication is "reduplicated" (*abhyasta*); this refers to the class beginning with *san*, and of that [class], the *hveñ*...

This is because the explanation beginning with "tatprakṛtibhūtastasya" (it is the nature of that) has been accepted. Consequently, in the form *jihvāyakīṣati*—derived from the desire for one's own tongue (*jihvā*)—there is no vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the root *hveñ*, because the suffix *ṇvul* is not the cause of reduplication. For this very reason, [the rule applies] to the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
To prevent [the application of] the cause for doubling, the rule *ṭhhvaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* is divided into separate *yoga*s;
this is clear in the original treatise (*ākara*). (219) *lipisici hvaśca* 3.1.53.
*lipi-sici*: *lip* means "to smear" (*upadehe*), and *ṣic* means "to pour" (*kṣaraṇe*). [Examples: *alipat*, *asicat*. (220) *padeṣv anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.4.74):
"He speaks towards" (*acccha vadati*). Because of the rule *ṭh acche* (Pāṇini 1.4.69), since *accha* functions as a *gati* when joined with *vad*, it is placed before the verbal root.

(221) *vibhāṣā śveḥ* |6|1|30|. Regarding *vibhāṣā śveḥ*: [the phrase] "in the *liṭ* and *yaṅ*" [is understood], and the meaning is that the preceding rule, *iḍaḷṅeśca*, is carried over (*anuvartate*) here. This is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both respects; in the case of the *liṭ* portion, it is an option regarding the augment *iṭ*.

Since [the substitution] is obligatory before suffixes beginning with *atus* and so on, it is non-obligatory (*aprāpta*) before suffixes beginning with *ṇal* and so on; however, regarding the *yaṅ* affix, it is an optional rule where it was previously non-obligatory (*aprāptavibhāṣā*).
Thus, one forms *śośūyate* and *śeśvīyate*. The reason for stating "there is no *saṃprasāraṇa*" is that otherwise, forms such as *śuśvāya* would result.

(222) *śvayateraḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.18. Regarding *śvayateraḥ*, he states—by means of the maxim that "an operation applies to the final [element]" (*alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*)—"of the letter *i*. He says "the single-substitute form of the subsequent" (*pararūpam*). However, the elision of the *a* (*ato lopaḥ*) does not occur, because of the rule: "that which ends in *a* in the original enunciation of an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix..."

Because it has already been explained. [The rule] "iyaṅ" [applies]. The sense is that it is *antaraṅga* (internal) with respect to the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*). Regarding the form *aśvayīt*: one might object, "In this case, since the *guṇa* and the *ayādeśa* would have already taken effect due to their being *antaraṅga*, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* would occur simply because the root ends in *yā*; so what is the purpose of this [rule]?"

If it is argued that [the inclusion of *ṇi* and *śvi*] is for this purpose, here they say: the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* is for the sake of indicating that "in the case of *sic*, there is no internal operation (*antaraṅga*).
By this, [the rule applies] to the forms of *ciriṇoti* and *jiriṇoti* when followed by the *yaṅ*-luṅ suffix, as well as to *cinī* and others when followed by *sic*.

The external *vṛddhi* alone takes place: *acirāyīt*, *ajirāyīt*, *acecāyīt*, and *anenāyīt*. [And] by that [it is meant]. And it has been stated by the author of the Vārttika: “The mention of *anekāc* [in the rule for the substitution of *āṬ*] is for the sake of [roots] such as *culump*. Thus, *culumpati* means “he swallows” (*lumpati*), since *culumpa* is used in the sense of “swallowing” (*lopa*).
Thus it is stated in the *Kavikalpadruma*. Thus ends the section on the *bhvādi* [roots] in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
(1264) *prāk krītāc chaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.1.1. Regarding *prāk krītāc chaḥ*: the word "before" (*prāk*) is understood here as a limit (*avadhi*), and not as a point of departure (*nirdeśa*).

[The term] *pratyaya* [here] means either "condition" (*prakṛti*) or "suffix. Therefore, since the possessor of the limit (*avadhimān*) is indeed the referent (*artha*), this [suffix] presents itself before those referents such as *hita* and so on that follow the word *kṛt*. For the possessor of a limit is of the same category as the limit itself.
Just as in the expression "later than this" (*asmāt paraḥ*), time (*kāla*) is understood; and in "prior to Rāma" (*rāmāt pūrvaḥ*), place (*deśa*) is understood.

[The suffix] *cha* [is applied] only by the rule "before the final letter" (*ṭhalaḥ pūrvam antyaḥ*). And thus, when the meaning is the same, the suffix *yat* and others, which arise from a specific base (*prakṛti*), sublate the suffix *cha*—which has scope in other bases—by the maxim of the curd for Kauṇḍinya (*takrakauṇḍinyanyāya*). Otherwise, there would be a conflict between *cha* and *yat*.
Since there is no distinction in proximity, there would be an alternation (paryāya) as if between the suffixes *tavya*, *anīya*, and *ya*.

Therefore, in this context, the meaning is taken as the limit (*avadhi*). Now, it may be argued that the suffix *cha* will not apply to words beginning with *yad* and so on, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule “*vibhāṣā havirapūpādibhyaḥ*,” which contains the mention of the word *vibhāṣā*. And thus...

If it is argued that there is no harm even if the suffix *pratyaya* or the base *prakṛti* is accepted as the limit (*avadhi*), since the over-extension of the suffix *cha* after words such as *ugavādi* is prevented by the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*), [the critics] say here:
"In that case, let the governing rule (*adhikāra*) simply be 'chaḥ'; there is no need for the mention of a limit."

However, this [term *prāk*] has no governing force (*adhikāra*) in the section beginning with "before *vat*, *iṣṭhan*, *añ*, etc.," because it is supported by another governing rule. If it is argued that the mention of the limit (*avadhi*) is for the sake of clear understanding—otherwise there would be complexity in comprehension—then [the answer is: in that case, [the rule] "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*)...

If one were to rely on the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) such as the word *havis*, it would result in excessive complexity (*pratipatti-gaurava*) in understanding; therefore, it is more appropriate to indicate the actual meaning itself as the limit.

Thus, the meaning of [Pāṇini’s rule] *ugavādibhyaḥ* is not "the suffix *yat* shall occur after words beginning with *u* and after words beginning with *go* or *vaḥ*," because [the suffix *yat*] is already included in the list of the *gavādi* group.

He states the *gaṇasūtra* beginning with *go*: "and *nābhi* becomes *nabha*. This means that the word *nābhi* receives the suffix *yat* and undergoes the substitution of *nabha*. In the example "the axle is for the nave" (*nabhyo 'kṣaḥ*), the *nābhi* is the hollowed-out center of the chariot wheel;
the specific piece of wood inserted into it is the *akṣa* (axle). And because it is suitable for that [nave], it is beneficial to it.

“Anjanam” refers to ointment for the eyes; because it is oily (snehanatvāt), it is not beneficial for the navel. The rule applies specifically to the navel [of a chariot]. However, when referring to a part of the body, the form is simply “nābhyam,” because this [application of the suffix -ya] is superseded by the subsequent rule: “after a word denoting a part of the body, [the suffix -ya is added] with the meaning ‘good for’” (*śarīrāvayavād yaḥ*). Thus is the intention. [The example is] *śunaḥsaṃ*.

It is *śūnyamita*. Because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*), the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) does not occur by the rule *astaddhite*. However, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ* is difficult to obtain; for once the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the subsequent single-substitute replacement (*pararūpa*) have been applied, the form *ayūp* no longer exists [to trigger that rule]. But in the alternative where the long vowel is retained...

The absence of *ṭilopa* is also easily established by the force of that very rule (*tadvidhāna-sāmarthyāt*). Regarding *naṅ ca*: the particle *ca* (and) brings in [the suffix] *yat*. The *Manoramā* states that it is better to say "after *aś*" (*aś-ca*). Others, however, say:
from the word *ūdhanya*, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule "he does that" (*tat karoti*) or "he describes that" (*tad ācaṣṭe*), [the form *audanika* arises].
In the case of *ṭhṇāviṣṭhava*, after the elision of the *ṭi* suffix (*ṭilopa*), the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied; then, from that *ṇij*-stem, the agentive *kvip* suffix is added.

Once the elision of *ṇic* and the elision of *ya* have been performed, the rule *ṭhanunāsikasya kvau* applies to lengthen the vowel. Subsequently, from that *kvib*-stem, another *kvip* is added in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra-kvip*). Finally, the suffix *naṅ* is added for the sake of the Ātmanepada endings in forms such as *ūdhānate*.
The addition of the suffix *ṅ* is necessary. Regarding the form *audhanya*: there is the preservation of the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule "and [after a word ending in] *ya*" (*ye ca*).
(1265) *kambalācca saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.1.3): after the word *kambala*, the suffix *yat* shall be applied in the sense of the *prākkrītīya* categories when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
This is an exception to [the previous rule].
(1266) *vibhāṣā havirapūpādibhyaḥ* | 5|1|4|. Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā havirapūpādibhyaḥ*: because the word *havis* is listed among the *gavādi* group, it is optional here.

The term "specifics of the oblation" (*havirviśeṣaṇa*) is employed. Nor should it be asked: "Why could the specifics of the oblation not be applied only to cows and the like? For in those cases, it is logical to grasp the essential nature (*svarūpa*) because no contradiction has yet arisen. Regarding the word *apūpyam*: it means flour that is beneficial for cakes (*apūpa*). *Apūpa*—
*Rice*, *separate*, *pestle*, *ear-rings*, and so forth are recited in the group beginning with *apūpa* (cakes) and others, as well as among the *annavikāra*s (food-modifications).

The meaning of "from those food-modifications" (*annavikārebhyaḥ*) is "from those varieties of food, specific kinds of eatables," or alternatively, it means "whatever may be. [The word] *ādanya* refers to that which is edible.

Rice grains are *odanīya* (fit for boiled rice). Thus, since [the meaning] is already established by this very *gaṇasūtra*, the inclusion of certain items such as *apūpa* (cakes) in the list is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*).
(1267) *tasmai hitam* (5.1.5): [The suffix *cha* is added after a word in the fifth case to form a word meaning] "beneficial for that."
Regarding the rule *havir-apūpādibhyo vibhāṣāyā ugavādibhyo yat pūrva-vipratiṣedhena*:

"saktavyā dhānāḥ" (the parched grains are to be eaten), "caṣvyāstaṇḍulāḥ" (the rice grains are to be chewed). According to the Kāśikā, *caru* is a type of sacrificial oblation (*havis*). The word *caru*, which primarily denotes a cooking vessel, is applied through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) to the oblation contained therein.
Kaiyaṭa and others [state]: (1268) *śarīrāvayavād yat* (Pāṇini 5.1.6).

Regarding the word *nasyam*: it means "beneficial for the nose" (*nāsikāyai hitam*). However, if the analysis (*vigraha*) were "existing in the nose" (*nāsikāyāṃ bhavam*), [the suffix would be different].

Regarding the suffix *yat* [prescribed] by the rule *arīraivayavācce*: *nasyam*. An example of this is *nastaḥ*, where the suffix *tasi* is applied by the rule *apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ*. Regarding *kṣudra*, however: *nāsikāyāḥ kṣudraḥ* becomes *naḥkṣudraḥ*; this is a compound formed by the rule *upapadamanipātena*. Regarding *nābhyam*: it is derived by the rule *ābhi nabhaṃ ca*.

The meaning is that the designation *nabha* occurs only in the sense of "hub of a chariot wheel" (*rathanābhi*), because its application is taught as being restricted by its association with [the word] *go* and so forth.
(Pāṇini 6.1.61): *ye ca taddhite*.
And because the word *chandasi* (in the Veda) follows from the rule "ye ca chandasī" [Pāṇini 6.1.121], he says: "the substitute *śīrṣan*.

[The form] *śīrṣaṇyaḥ* [is derived with the suffix *-yat*] optionally when referring to hair; here, by the rule "ye cābhāve" [Pāṇini 6.4.168], there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). In the case of *śirasyati*, due to the restriction "a kye" [Pāṇini 1.4.15], there is an absence of *padatva* (word-status), and consequently, an absence of the substitution of *ru*.

(1270) *khalayavamāṣatilavṛṣabrahmaṇaśca* |5|1|7|. [The suffix *cha* is applied after these words in the sense of "belonging to" (*tasyedam*). *khalayava-*: here, the word *vṛṣa* is understood as ending in the vowel *a*, and not as ending in the consonant *n*. Otherwise, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, he would have indicated it without eliding the *n*, as in the case of the rule *ātmanviśvajane*.
That which is beneficial for a bull (*vṛṣan*) is called *vṛṣyam*. However, it would not be *vṛṣaṇyam* because of the rule *nāntādyati* [Pāṇini 6.4.135].

As for *brahmaṇyam*, the word *brahman* is a synonym for *brāhmaṇa*. The preservation of the original stem form (*prakṛtibhāva*) occurs here as before by the rule *ye ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.159]. In this case, there was no possibility at all for the suffix *yat* to apply after either the word *vṛṣan* or the word *brahman*.

The source [of this rule] states "no," because it is not explicitly mentioned. Therefore, compounds such as *vṛṣṇe hitam* (beneficial for the bull) or *brāhmaṇebhyo hitam* (beneficial for the Brahmins) remain merely syntactical phrases (*vākya*). Furthermore, [the suffix] would not be applied; the word *ratha* is not listed among the words beginning with *go*.
Thus, the form *rathyā* would occur only in the sense of "beneficial" (*hitārtha*), and not in other senses.

(1271) *ajāvibhyāṃ thyan* |5|1|8|. From the words *aja* and *avi*. Here, the word *aja* is understood in the masculine gender; for this very reason, by the rule *ajādyadantam*, the word *aja* is placed first, overriding the rule *dvandve ghi* which would otherwise have caused the word *avi* to be placed first.

The prior placement [of the word] has been made. According to the rule "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included," the suffix *thyan* occurs even from the feminine form. Because *thyan* is enumerated among the suffixes beginning with *tasil*, the form is identical when the masculine-like state (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies. Regarding *ajathyā*: the analysis of the compound is "that which is beneficial for goats (*aja*)" or "born from goats (*ajāṅya*)."
(1272) *ātman* and *adhvan* [take the suffix *kha*] after [the word *khe*].
The sense is that this applies only when [the compound] is a *karmadhāraya*, according to the explanation. Regarding *viśvajanīyam*:
*viśvasya janaḥ* refers to those common to all, such as prostitutes and the like; it also applies in a *bahuvrīhi* where "one whose people are universal" is meant.
That very thing is the meaning of the external member [of the compound]. The analysis [of the compound] is: "beneficial for that" (*tasmai hitam*).

There is an addition to the rule regarding *pañcajana*: [the form] *pañcajanīna*. The four castes with the chariot-maker as the fifth are the *pañcajanāḥ*; [the suffix -īna- denotes] what is beneficial for them. The compound is formed by the rule: “*ika* [is applied] after a numeral when it is a name” (*iksaṅkhye saṃjñāyām*).
The three *vārttikas* beginning with "añcajanād" refer exclusively to *karmadhāraya* compounds.
Consequently, after a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* or a *bahuvrīhi*, only the suffix *cha* is applied. Thus we have *pañcajanīyaḥ* and *sarvajanīnaḥ*.
[In *sarvajanaḥ*], "all people" (*sarvo janaḥ*) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule "ūrvakālaika-". [The suffix *kha* is added] by the rule "tasmai hitam" (beneficial for that).

The word *vigraṅ* [is used]. However, for the sense of "proper" (*sādhvartha*), the words *sārvajanīna* and *vaiśvajanīna* are derived by adding the suffix *khañ* according to the rule "after *rati*, *jana*, and so forth, the suffix *khañ*.
The word *mātṛbhogīṇa* is formed by adding *ṭhañ* after *mahājana*. Here, even though there is an absence of indivisible wordhood (*akhaṇḍapadatva*), [the rule still applies].
It has already been established previously that *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) occurs by the rule *ṭhaṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye ’pi*.

The analysis of the compound is: "beneficial (*hita*) to the mother’s body (*bhogaḥ = śarīram*). Although Amara states, "The word *bhoga* refers to pleasure, the maintenance of women and so forth, and the body of a serpent (*ahi*)," nevertheless—

That [rule] intends a multiplicity of applications; however, the source [of the tradition] states that the capacity [to form the derivative] resides only in the body [of the word]. By the words *mātṛ* and *pitṛ*, the suffix *cha* is indeed the general rule: *mātrīyaḥ*, *pitrīyaḥ*.
But by the words *rājan* and *ācārya*, etc., even the general suffix *cha* does not occur, because of the absence of such usage (*anabhidhānāt*). Why?
The source [of the rule] is the statement: "beneficial to the king" (*rājñe hitam*) or "beneficial to the teacher" (*ācāryāya hitam*).
(1273) *sarvapuruṣābhyāṃ ṇaḍhañau* |5|1|10|. From the two words *sarva* and *puruṣa*, the suffixes *ṇa* and *ḍhañ* respectively occur [to denote] "beneficial to that."
The meaning of the sūtra is that [the suffix] *cha* is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *krīta* when the sense is "beneficial" (*hita*).
It should be stated that [the suffix applies] optionally after *sarva*. Thus, [we have] *sarvād*.
Because it is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*), there is an absence of the grammatical operations (*kārya*) pertaining to pronouns (*sarvanāman*).

In the case of *puruṣādvadhavikārasamūhatena kṛteṣu*: regarding the phrase *puruṣādvadha-vikāra*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is understood here as the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*) by virtue of its semantic fitness; whereas in the expression *tena kṛte*, the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*) is explicitly stated. Thus he says: "the killing of a man" (*puruṣasya vadhaḥ*). Regarding the suffix *aṇ* [applied] to the word *samūha* as well: [The rule is: *puruṣād vadhe vikāre samūhe ca*. [The commentary explains: In the case of *puruṣādvadhavikārasamūhatena kṛteṣu*, the genitive is obtained through its functional capacity (*yogyatābalāt*) as the governing case for the words *vadha* and *vikāra*; however, in the phrase *tena kṛte*, the instrumental is already present. Therefore, he states: "the killing of a man. Furthermore, the suffix *aṇ* is also applied to form the word *samūha*.

By the rule "asya samūhaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.37), [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule "granthe 'ṇ" (Pāṇini 4.3.116). By the phrase "ṛte granthe" (Pāṇini 4.3.116), it is understood that [this rule applies] where [the suffix] has not already been obtained. The intention is that in examples such as "auruṣeyaḥ prāsādaḥ" (a palace built by men), this suffix *ḍhañ* is not an exception (*apavāda*) for anything.

(1274) *māṇavacarakābhyāṃ khañ* [Pāṇini 5.1.11]. The addition of the marker *ñ* to the suffix *khañ* after the words *māṇava* and *caraka* is for the purpose of causing *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) and for the sake of the accent (*svara*). Although *vṛddhi* is already established by itself in the case of *māṇava*, it is nevertheless required in forms such as *āṇavina-ābhārya* by the rule *vṛddhinimittasya ca*.

It should be understood that this is for the purpose of prohibiting the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva). Regarding the word *māṇavāya*: a contemptible descendant of Manu is a *māṇava*. According to the rule, "In the sense of a contemptible descendant, or a fool, the suffix *aṇ* is traditionally prescribed after *manu*, and the nasal *n* [of *manu*] is changed to a retroflex [ṇ]; by this, the form is established."

The form *māṇavaḥ* contains the suffix *ṇa*, according to the Vārttika under the heading of offspring (*apatya*). They say that this Vārttika is intended to explain the meaning established by the usage found in this very sūtra. Regarding *cārakīṇam*:
one who moves is a *caraḥ*; [the suffix] *ac* is added according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*). There is reduplication according to Pāṇini 6.1.12 (*aricalipativadīnām*).
Because it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpita*), it does not exist here. Therefore, by the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ kan*, [the suffix] *kan* is applied, resulting in *caraka*.
(1275) *tadarthaṃ vikṛteḥ prakṛtau* |5|1|12|.
Regarding *tadarthaṃ vikṛteḥ*: from the rule "beneficial for this" (*asmai hitam*), the word *tasmai* ("for that") is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*).
Thus he says: "from that which ends in the fourth case. The term *tad-artha* is used in the neuter gender in a general sense (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*).
With the intention that the nominative stands in place of the locative by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), he says:
"in [the sense of] *tad-arthā*," meaning "in the sense of a modification (*vikṛti*). For by the pronoun *tat*, it is indeed the modification that is denoted.

It is examined as follows: since the modification (*vikṛti*) itself is thus indicated first, the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "the nominative case for words not connected with another" (*asamarthānām prathamā*) is also unimpeded here. Regarding the word *śaṅkavyam*: it is derived by the suffix *yat* [according to the rule] *ugavādibhyaḥ*.

(1276) *cchadir-upadhi-bal-er ḍhañ* | Pāṇini 5.1.13. In the compound *cchadir-upadhi*, the masculine gender is used according to the Vedic rule (*sautra-puṃstvam*). This [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *cha*. An example is *chādiṣeyāṇi*. That by which something is covered is called *cchadiḥ*.

The suffix *isi* is applied after the roots *ṭharc*, *śuci*, *husṛp*, *chād*, and *chard*, according to the rule *ṭharc-śuci-husṛp-cchādi-cchardibhya isiḥ*. Furthermore, shortening of the vowel occurs by the rule *is-man-tran-kviṣu ca*. However, when *chadiḥ* denotes a derivative of leather (*carma-vikāra*), then, because it is subsequent in the order of rules, the suffix *añ* would apply by the rule *carmaṇo ’ñ*. Nevertheless, by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrva-vipratiṣedha*), only the suffix *ḍhañ* is desired in this case.
This leather is for covering. And it says: “The rule for *yañ*, *īya*, and *avañ* is a prior exception to [the rule] ‘*han* and *ce*’.

Therefore, the example is *stāsanaṅgyam*: leather for the purpose of a leather product (*stāsanaṅgu*) made from a bull’s hide; [this is formed] by the suffix *yat* according to the rule “*ugavādibhyaḥ*.”
An example of this is *aupānahyam*, which he will explain immediately below. Regarding *bāleyāḥ*:
Amara states, "The word *bali* is masculine when it means an offering (*arpaṇa*) or a tax (*kar*), and feminine when it refers to a creature born from a limb [of another].
The suffix *cha* (yielding *-īya*) is desired after the word *upadhi* in its own sense; thus we have *upadhiḥ*. This is derived by the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*.

The suffix *ki* is applied after the root *dhāñ*. Regarding the elision [of the final vowel], it is said that "the elision of the *ā* of *sthā*" (*thāto lopaḥ*) occurs by way of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict of rules). This means it is by the *vārttika* beginning with "after *yañ*, *ñya*, and *añ*. Now, one might object: since *chadiḥ* is specifically mentioned in the rule for *ḍhañ*, and *upānah* is specifically mentioned in the rule for *ñya*, [these] are "expressly stated" (*pratipadokta*).
Since it is already established that [a rule] is stronger [by virtue of being a pratipadavidhi], what is the purpose of this *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior prohibition)?

On this point, they say: "It is inferred from the sage’s statement that 'being a pratipadavidhi is the cause of strength only when there is no other scope [for its application],' and not when there is scope."
Therefore, "vampi taḍākāni" alone is correct, because the *num* augment applies later [and thus supersedes the other].
The opinion that "vāmpi taḍākāni" is correct by relying on the long vowel due to its being explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*) is weak;
for the long vowel in "ṭhaptṛn" [is taught] as in "āpastiṣṭhanti."
In this example, because the rule [for the suffix *cha*] has an opportunity for application (*sāvakāśatva*), the status of being explicitly stated (*pratipadoktatva*) is weaker.

(1277) *carmaṇo’ñ* | Pāṇini 5.1.15. Regarding *carmaṇo’ñ*: after the word *carman*, the suffix *añ* shall apply in the sense of "made from that" (*tad-artha*), etc., as previously mentioned. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *cha*.

In the word *ārmaṇaḥ*, it is the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and not the ablative (*pañcamī*). For if it were the ablative, the suffix would apply to the base word *carman* in the sense of "for the sake of leather," as in examples such as *ārmaṇe dvīpī*; however, the form *ārmaṇo dvīpī* is not desired. Therefore, he says: "of the leather... (*carmaṇo yā*).

Regarding the word *vikṛtiḥ*: [the form] *vārdhryai* is derived as follows. From the roots *vṛdh* and *vap*, by the rule *vṛdhivapibhyām*, the suffix *ran* is applied; thus the word *vardhra*, meaning "hide," is udātta on its first syllable. By the rule *asya vikāraḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is added. Then, by the rule *iḍḍhea*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Thus *vārdhrī* means "a leather thong," and [the form] is for it (*tasyai*). However, when the Uṇādi suffix *ṣṭran* is applied to the root *vadhi*, the form is *vadhrī*.
[The suffix *matup*] occurs [in the sense of "it exists in this"]. From that, however, *vadhra* becomes *vadhrī*. Amara states: "The word *varatrā* may be *adhrī*, *vadhrī*, or *varatrā*.
The Bhāṣya says: "Look at the oxen (*añcaḥ*), look at the female oxen (*vadhrikāḥ*).
(Pāṇini 5.1.16): "That which may belong to him, or may be in it..."

Therefore, from this first [word] which is a meaningful nominal stem (*prātipadika*), an affix occurs as prescribed in the sense of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and the seventh case (*saptamī*). "It may be" (*syāt*): here the potential mood (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvana*), according to the rule beginning with *saṃbhāvane ’lam iti cet*. Because of the great number of bricks, there is a wall of them.

"This might be" (syāt) is what is being considered. For, by virtue of the quality of the location, it is considered possible that "there might be a rampart on this [spot]. Here, neither the relationship of material cause and modification (prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva) nor the state of being for that purpose (tādarthya) is intended;
rather, only mere suitability (yogyatā-mātra) is meant. Therefore, this is not the subject matter of the preceding [rule]. The word *tat* is mentioned twice.
This is for the sake of clear understanding;
for the desired result could have been achieved by using the word *tat* alone, as in the expression "this belongs to that" (*asyedam asti*) or "I am this" (*asminn asmi*).
Thus ends the section on *cha* and *ya* in the *Tattvabodhinī*.

(1023) *tadasminnastīti deśe tannāmni* |4|2|67|. From a word ending in the nominative case, provided it has "it exists in this" as its qualifier, a suffix shall be applied as prescribed when the sense is locative (*asmin*), if the resulting form with the suffix is the name of a region (*deśa*). That [region] shall end in that suffix.
The term *nāma* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has a name. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *matup*.

The word *ṭhi* is used so that [the designation] applies to a place well-known to all the world, and not even to a modern convention; this is the purpose [of the rule]. In the two subsequent sūtras as well, [the word *deśe* is understood].
The phrase "bearing that name" (*tannāmni*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
(1024) *tena nirvṛtam* (IV.2.68): "produced by that. The suffix *kta* is applied to the root *vṛt* with the sense of the causative (*ṇic*) included within it, in the sense of the object (*karman*).

(1025) *adūrabhavaśca* |4|2|70|. *Adūra* means "not far" (*adūram antikam*). That which exists there is *adūrabhava*. This is a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*) by virtue of a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*). It belongs to the fourfold set of meanings (*cāturarthika*), that is, to the four meanings [of the suffix -aṇ]. "Of the four meanings" means...
The compound *caturarthī* is a collective (*samāhāra*). Those suffixes occurring in those four senses are called *cāturarthika*. Regarding the rule *adhyātmāditas ṭhañ*:

since they occur in four senses, they are *taddhita* suffixes. However, if there were a *dvigu* compound [of the word *catur*], then by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*, there would be elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhañ*.

(1026) *matoś ca bahvacaḥ* |4|2|72|. [The commentary asks: Why is it stated as *matoś ca*? Could it not simply be *ator bahvacaḥ*? For by explaining it through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*)—namely, "from that which ends in the suffix *matup* prescribed after a polysyllabic base"—the desired result would be established.
Anticipating the objection, "What is the purpose of including the term 'aṅga'?", he refutes it with the words "the inclusion of the term 'aṅga'. [He explains:

"It is a qualifier of that which ends in the suffix -mat. This is because, when grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, it is improper to assume a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*); therefore, in the absence of the inclusion of the term 'aṅga', it would be a qualifier of that which ends in the suffix -mat.
It would indeed be so; consequently, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *ahimatam*, which is the intended meaning.
(1027) *roṇī* | 4|2|78|. The word *roṇī* [is a base] that produces a suffix; this is the meaning. And thus...
He states the result: "from the word *roṇī*. Others say that the ablative case ending is elided by a Vedic (sautra) rule.
Regarding the phrase "from that which ends in [the suffix]," this is because of a specific statement found in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *yena vidhis tadantasya*;

and because, having adopted the principle that there is freedom of choice between the qualifier and the qualified, it is stated: "In the formulation of rules for compounds (*samāsa*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*)."
The meaning is that because the prohibition [of the suffix *cha*] has been rejected, the rule *tadanta-vi-dhiḥ* (the application of a suffix to a word ending in another word) applies here.

(1028) Pāṇini 4.2.80: *vuñ-chaṇ-kaṭhañ-ilas-eni-ra-ḍhañ-ṇya-y-aphak-phiñ-iñ-ñya-kak-ṭhaka-arīhaṇa-kṛśāśva-ṛśya-kumuda-kāśa-tṛṇa-prekṣā-aśma-sakhi-saṃkāśa-bala-pakṣa-karṇa-sutaṃgama-pragadin-varāha-kumudādibhyaḥ*. [The suffixes] *vuñ*, *chaṇ*, *kaṭhañ*, *ila*, *en*, *i*, *ra*, *ḍhañ*, *ṇya*, *ya*, *aphak*, *phiñ*, *iñ*, *ñya*, *kak*, and *ṭhaka* are added respectively after the following groups: *arīhaṇa*, *kṛśāśva*, *ṛśya*, *kumuda*, *kāśa*, *tṛṇa*, *prekṣā*, *aśman*, *sakhi*, *saṃkāśa*, *bala*, *pakṣa*, *karṇa*, *sutaṃgama*, *pragadin*, *varāha*, and the *kumuda*-group.
The suffix *vuñchaṇ* ending in *haka* constitutes one compound word. The other group begins with *arīhaṇa*.

In that regard, first a *dvandva* compound should be formed of the four words ending with *kumuda*, and then a second *dvandva* should be understood by joining that with the second *dvandva* beginning with *kāśa* and ending with *kumuda*. By this—

Even though the word *kumuda* is recited twice, there is no single-remainder (*ekaseṣa*) formation. He states that the word *ādi* is connected with each [member] by saying "from *arīhaṇa* and the rest. He states the internal-group rule (*gaṇasūtra*) contained within the section on *pakṣa*, etc., by saying "of *pathin*.
(1029) 4.2.81: *janapade lup*. [In the sense of a country, the suffix is elided.]

The suffix *lup* is applied [to the name of a village] when it is the name of a country (*janapada*). Only when it is the name of that [country]. Not here: *audumbaraḥ janapadaḥ* ("the country of Udumbara"), because in this case the name ending in *lup* is not the actual designation. Since a country is a single entity, the singular number would have been expected; therefore, he states an extended application (*atideśa*) resulting in the plural number and so forth.

(1030) *lupi yuktavadvyaktivacane* |1|2|51|. Regarding the rule "when there is *lup*, it is like that which is joined": what is the purpose of specifying "gender and number"? [Example: A village not far from *śirīṣa* trees is called *śirīṣāḥ*.
Here, by the rule "*vāraṇādibhyaśca*" (*Pāṇini 4.2.82*), there is *lup* [of the suffix]. Its forest is *śirīṣavanam*. In this case...

The status of being a *vanaspati* (tree) would be extended [by analogy]. Consequently, by the rule "optionally after herbs and *vanaspatis*," the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would occur. If it is objected: "But why is the genitive plural *śirīṣāṇām* not extended here?"—to this they say: "In this context, *vacana* means 'number,' and not the singular, dual, and so forth. Not so.
Nor should it be argued that the genitive case-ending itself, as heard in the text, should be accepted here because it expresses number;
for since the meaning of the genitive is already included within the function of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the use of the nominative alone is more appropriate for the stated sense.
As in the example "pañcalāḥ" and so forth: although the desired result is achieved even though [the word] possesses the gender of its denoted object, nevertheless...

The intention is that there is an extension of the gender of the base (*prakṛtiliṅgātideśa*) for the sake of establishing forms such as *kaṭuabadarī*, which refers to a village located near *kaṭuabadarī*. He now explains the rule (*sūtra*) which was formulated in accordance with the ancient teachers.

(1031) *Tadaśiṣyaṃ saṃjñāpramāṇatvāt* | 1.2.53. Regarding the rule *tadaśiṣyam*: [words such as] *pañcālāḥ*, *aṅgāḥ*, *vaṅgāḥ*, *kaliṅgāḥ*, and so forth, are names (*saṃjñā*) for regions that are by their very nature plural in form; no special effort is required in this regard.

The gender and number [of the word] are to be established, as in the cases of *ṭhāpaḥ* and *ārāḥ*, etc. The point is that in those instances, the gender and number are not established by the grammatical rule (*śāstra*). Having rejected the dependent (*upajīvaka*), he rejects the basis upon which it depends (*upajīvya*).
(1032) *Lup* [is applied] because the connection is not perceived; 1.2.54.

Regarding "the *lup* of the connection": the two sūtras beginning with "there is *lup* when there is no word" (*anapade lup*) and "also after *varaṇa* and so forth" (*varaṇādibhyaśca*) are intended by the term "*upa*" here. The phrase "it is not to be taught" (*aśiṣyam*) is indeed connected [to this].

He says this with the words "even [the suffix] *lup*. With the intention that the connection between the meanings of the base and the suffix is "yoga" (connection), he states the resulting conclusion:
"of the meaning of the constituent parts. He explains "due to non-appearance" as "due to non-comprehension. Just as the words "Pañcāla" and so forth [are applied] to Kṣatriyas...

The meaning is: since [names] are already established as denoting a country (*janapada*) by the rules "his residence" (*asya nivāsaḥ*) and "not far from it" (*adūrabhavaśca*), the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) would not arise at all; what, then, is the purpose of this prescription of elision (*lup*)? [The objection continues: "It would not be seen," meaning that words such as *Pañcāla* are used to denote countries even without a connection to the Kṣatriyas.

The meaning is that there is no purpose for the rule in the Sūtra. In passing, he refutes another technical convention established by the ancient teachers with the words beginning "pradhāna" (P. 1.2.52):
*viśeṣaṇānāṃ cājāteḥ* (1.2.52).

Regarding the qualifiers: although this sūtra should have been explained in that very place—since it is read immediately after the sūtra "upayuktaḷ" in the recension of the sūtras, and because the word "adaśiṣyam" [is used there] as a negation—it nevertheless concerns only the prohibition of [the suffix] *jāti*. It does not, however...
They say that it was not stated there with the intention of applying the status of the possessor (*yuktavadbhāva*); for example, "The Pañcālas are beautiful.

If one asks, "How then is the usage 'The country of Pañcāla is well-supplied with food and abundant in water' possible?", understand that it is because [the quality] serves as an adjective qualifying the country (*janapada*).

But if it is accepted that [the word *pañcālāḥ*] is a qualifier of the country (*janapada*), then its gender and number are indeed established—as in: "The country of the Pañcālas is well-supplied with food and abundant in water.
In the case of *harītakī* and so forth, there is singular number, as in *harītakyaḥ*; this is because of the rule *harītakyādibhyaśca*, which prescribes the suffix *aṇ*.
*Lup*: For in that context, *lub* is understood from the rule "up ce" (Pāṇini 5.3.50).

Regarding the mention of *khalatikādi* [in the rule]: *khalatikam*. Here, *lup* applies by the rule "varaṇādibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 4.2.82). There is a prohibition of *lup* when it refers to a human being. Regarding *cañcā*: here, *kan* is applied by the rule "añjñāyām" (Pāṇini 5.3.75).
In the case of *umanuṣya*, there is elision (*lup*). [The example is: *añcā tṛṇamayaḥ pumān* (“a man made of grass”).

(1034) *varaṇādibhyaśca* | Pāṇini 4.2.82. [The word] *varaṇādi* [is a compound]. The particle *ca* (and) serves to include those not explicitly mentioned; by this, it is established that this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).

Regarding "varaṇā": examples such as *kaṭubadarī*, *śirīṣāḥ*, *godau*, and *khalatikam* should likewise be cited. With the intention that since the substitution of *v* (for *m*) is not established (*asiddha*), the elision of the *ṭi* suffix (*ṭilopa*) should not behave as if it were in its original place (*na sthānivat*) when that [substitution] is to be applied, he says: "after a consonant other than a semi-vowel" (*jhayaḥ*). This also applies to *naḍvān*.
The point is that because it is subsequent, the substitution of *v* occurs by the rule "hayaḥ" alone, and not by the rule "ādupadhāyāḥ.
Nor should it be argued that, due to the status of being "asiddha," the rule "ādupadhāyāḥ" alone would be more appropriate there; for it is said:
"In the case of a section (*prakaraṇa*), the preceding section is asiddha, but not so in the case of individual rules (*yoga*)."

This is because it has been settled in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṭhupasargādasamāse’pi*. Now, one might object: in the word *vetasvān*, since the word *vetasa* is a *pada* by virtue of being a *subanta*, the *ṅ* in the suffix *matup*—by the force of its being marked with *ḍ*—causes the elision of the final vowel; and then, by the principle of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), the resulting form remains a *pada*, whereby the *s* should undergo *rutva* (change to *r*).

It might be argued that the desired result is achieved through the status of being *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element), and that this is because [the rule] is prohibited by the principle "that which is not established in what precedes" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe*).

But do not say so; for with respect to the internal *r*-substitution (*rutva*), the external *ṭi*-elision (*ṭilopa*) is considered unestablished (*asiddha*). Nor does the sixth-lesson paribhāṣā on external elements apply to what belongs to the three final chapters (*traipādika*).

It cannot be said that [the word] does not know [this], because the position of the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that grammatical operations apply at the time the operation is required) is accepted. Now, even so, since the word *vādiṣu* ends in a sibilant (*s*), it is a *pada*;

therefore, because the substitution of *ru* (r) based on that [sibilant] lacks the status of being *antaraṅga* (internal), the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning external operations) does not apply.

Thus, the substitution of *ru* is indeed unavoidable. Nor should one suspect that the status of *bha* applies here by the rule "asau matvarthe," on the grounds that the suffix *matup* in "nadyāṃ matup" (Pāṇini 4.2.85) is prescribed for the fourfold sense (*cāturarthika*) and is therefore a *matvarthīya*; for the *ṭilopa* (elision of the *ṭi*) remains as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*). Nor...

If it is argued that the same applies even when [the word] is a *pada*, because by the rule for *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) and the principle of "simultaneity of operation" (*kāryakālatā*), the prohibition "in what precedes, that which is not yet established is as if non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na*) would apply, then they say: in the case of the designation *pada*, one must resort to the view that the technical names apply according to their original enunciation (*yathoddeśapakṣa*), and thus the prohibition "in what precedes, that which is not yet established is as if non-existent" does not apply.

Because the prohibition does not apply, the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) takes effect; consequently, since that which ends in *s* is not a *pada*, [the desired result follows]. By this, the following doubts are also refuted: namely, that in the case of *ghaṭī-āmalakī*, because it would be a *pada* by the rule "in the presence of *vā* etc.," there would be the substitution of *jaś*; whereas in the case of *āṬtsīt*, there would be the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. Now, [one might object]: [The objection: But surely...

For the sake of brevity in the grammatical process (*prakriyālāghava*), let only *ḍvatup* be prescribed; or rather, let the *ḍit*-ness of the suffix *matup*, which is currently under discussion in the rule "after *uma*, *udanaḍa*, and *vetasa*, [the suffix] *ḍi*," be extended [to this case].
What is the use of this prescription of *ṅmatup*? True. [But it serves] for other purposes...
That is for the purpose of providing a rule. The Vārttika states "and from mahiṣa" (mahiṣāt ca), which is intended to explain the establishment of that [form]. (1035) *Śikhāyā valac* 4.2.89.
This is for the purpose of superseding the suffix *yaṇ* when [the word] *śikhā* denotes a place where [something] has originated (*nirvṛta*) or similar meanings, and serves as its name.

The rule "from *antaśikhā* in the sense of a name" (*antaśikhātsaṃjñāyām*), which will be stated in the fifth [chapter], is for the purpose of establishing the form *piṭhśikhābala* even in your own school. (1036) *Naḍādīnāṃ kuk ca* | Pāṇini 4.2.91.

Regarding *naḍādi*: *naḍa*, *plakṣa*, *bilva*, *veṇu*, *vetra*, *vetasa*, and so forth, are the members of the *naḍādi* group. He states the internal sub-list (*gaṇasūtra*) for the *naḍādi* group: "after *kruñca*" and likewise "after *takṣan*. In both cases, there is the elision (*luk*) of the genitive case ending by Pāṇinian convention (*sautra*). This occurs while the word "elision" (*lopa*) is being carried over from the rule "elision of *he*."

Anticipating the objection that the mention of *lug* (elision) is redundant, he says: "For the sake of eliding everything. Regarding the phrase "of the whole [suffix]": one should not argue that by the rule *ādeḥ parasya* ("the substitute takes the place of the first letter of what follows"), it would be the vowel *i* that must undergo the change; for the word *lopaḥ* ("elision") is understood here as following from the rule *ūryatiṣyagatisthākulāyasamāsattināṭakāni*, which specifically refers to the elision of the suffix *yat* in connection with the letter *y*.
This concludes the section on the four types of suffixes (*cāturarthika*) in the *Tattvabodhinī*,
followed by the section on the *cur*-class verbs under the heading of verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*).
(340) *satyāpapāśarūpavīṇātūlaślokasenālomatvacavamavaṇacūrṇacurādibhyo ṇic* 3.1.25. Regarding *satyāpa-pāśa*: examples of these will become clear later in the section on nominal verbs (*nāmadhātu*).
These [forms] are not derived by us. The word *tvac* ends in the vowel *a*. The phrase "for the sake of elaboration" (*prapañcārtham*) is used;
however, it should be understood that the mention of *atyāpa* is for the purpose of including the augment *āPuk*. Others, however, say:
these are included even from dependent [bases] for the sake of the causative suffix *ṇic*; otherwise, [in the case of] *ramaṇīyaṃ ghaṭam*...
Just as in examples such as *karoti*, the suffix *ṇic* would also apply in cases like *ramaṇīyaṃ rūpayati*.
(Pāṇini 1.3.74) Regarding *acūcurat*, the ancient commentator [Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita] explains that the status of being like the *san*-affix (*sanvadbhāva*) applies by the rule *anvallaghuni*.

This was stated because of haste; for the long vowel that arises in the domain of *sanvadbhāva* does not depend upon *sanvadbhāva*. "With reference to the general" means that this refers to the fact that all roots beginning with *cur* optionally take the suffix *ṇic*. And it is not thus...
It should not be said that [the rule] *ṭhārdhaṣādve* is redundant, because that which is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is not universally applicable.

Thus, in this view, the optional alternative (*vikalpa*) regarding the roots belonging to the *ādhṛṣīya* group is at will, whereas for others it is fixed according to the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭaprayoga*). Examples are *jagāṇa*, *jagaṇatuḥ*; and in the *Vṛtti*: *akāṇa*.

The reading *cakaṇatuḥ* is more common; however, with that reading, the intended meaning is not established at all. Some, on the other hand, argue that even in the absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—and thus in the absence of forms such as *gaṇayāmāsa*—the form *gaṇāmāsa* must occur because the root *gaṇ* ends in the vowel *a*.

They say that the reading beginning with *jagāṇa* is to be considered doubtful. As for the phrase "not [the charge of] uselessness": the sense is that this very position—that there is not even a suspicion of uselessness—is the correct one. In that regard, if the previously mentioned position were weak, how could there be the usage in the *Vṛtti*: *jagāṇa*, *jagaṇatuḥ*?

It should not be suspected that [the root] *saṅgacchati* is [unattested], because it is established as such from a root belonging to the *bhvādi* class, which is an open-ended group (*ākṛtigaṇa*). As for the statement "that is to be considered," the vowel *i* in roots such as *yat*, *tat*, and *mat* is indeed redundant and not intended as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), since those [roots]...

Because of the rule regarding "ending in a conjunct" (*saṃyogānta*), even though the letter *n* is recited in the forms *yantra*, *tantra*, and *mantra*, the elision [of the final *n*] is not obtained by the rule *na ṅiditām*, because the *n* is not in the penultimate position (*anupadhā*). However, in the case of *cintyāt*,
if there were a reading with the *n* in the penultimate position according to the rule *hinu smṛtyām*, the elision of the *n* would indeed occur.

The intention is that the inclusion of the vowel *i* (in the root *laḍ*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the purpose of preventing that [undesired application]. *Laḍ*: service preceded by affection is "upasevā. One "lāḍayati" a son; because there is no distinction between *laḍ* and *laḍ*, one also says "lālayati. Regarding the statement "some say the vowel *o* is *it*": the designation as *odit* is for the sake of [the application of] the rule "of a root ending in an *odit* vowel," which applies immediately after the root.

Some hold that because the *niṣṭhā* suffix *-ta* has the purpose of causing the substitution of *na*, by virtue of that, the augment *iṭ* does not occur; thus [the form] is *laṇḍanaḥ*. Others hold that even when there is an intervention by *iṭ* due to the force of the rule regarding roots ending in *o* or *i*, the substitution of *na* still occurs; thus [the form] is *laṇḍinaḥ*. Regarding the root *pīṭ* (in the sense of "immersing"), in the view where the vowel is short according to the rule *hrājabhāsa-*, because it falls under the scope of the *sanvadbhāva* rule, [there is] "long [vowel]..."

The rule "laghoḥ" [Pāṇini 7.4.94] prescribes lengthening for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). However, he states that there is no lengthening in the alternative case where the syllable is short—namely, in forms such as *apīpiḍat* and so on.

(342) Pāṇini 7.4.3: *bhrājabhāsabhāṣadīpajīvamīlapīḍāmanyatarasyām* || [In the case of the roots *bhrāj*, *bhās*, *bhāṣ*, *dīp*, *jīv*, *mīl*, and *pīḍ*, the penultimate vowel may optionally be lengthened.]

The root *pṛ* is used in the sense of "filling. Regarding the statement "the long vowel is pronounced," etc.: the meaning is that the long vowel is pronounced so that forms such as *pārayati* and others—which would also be established by pronouncing a short vowel—are correctly formed; thus it is for the sake of [forms like] *parati*.
On this point, they say: it was specifically marked with an acute accent (*udātta*) by Pāṇini, the author of the Dhātupāṭha.

Furthermore, they are recited as having the anudātta accent; for it has been stated by him [the author of the Paribhāṣā] that "roots ending in ṛ are not seṭ," by which his intention in this matter might be inferred. However, in the *Kavikalpadruma*, it is stated that this root is invariably accompanied by the causative marker (ṇic). Thus, on this view, the pronunciation of the long vowel would be purposeless.

The result [of this analysis] is established. Others, however, maintain that the long vowel in *parīt* and *parītya*, etc., is for the purpose of allowing an optional lengthening of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *vṛto vā*; and consequently, since the optional application of the causative suffix *ṇic* is already established, they state that forms such as *parāti* are possible. [The root] *ūrj*: *ūrjayati*—he becomes strong; he lives.
The meaning is "or.
(343) *ur ṛt* | Pāṇini 7.4.7. Regarding *ur ṛt*: the word "or" (*vā*) from the rule "after the root *ghrā*, optionally" (*ghrāter vā*) is understood here. [The substitutes] *ir*, *ar*, *ār*, and *ā*.

However, when there is an *ṛ*-vowel as the penultimate (*upadhā*), the substitution of *ir* is obtained by the rule "ṭhupadhāyāśca" (Pāṇini 7.1.102) in cases such as *acīkṛtat*; the substitution of *ār* is obtained by the rule "mṛjer vṛddhiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.114) in the case of *amīmṛjat*; and for other roots with an *ṛ*-vowel as the penultimate, the substitution of *ar* occurs by the rule of *guṇa*, as in *apīpṛthat* and so forth—this is the distinction. Now, one might object: "In this context, since *ur* is being referred back [as an anuvāda]..."
If it is argued that [the rule] *ṛt* prescribes the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*), yet it does not include them when enjoined, and thus in the case of *acīklṛpat*,
since there is an *ṛ*-vowel by the rule *ṛt*, the form *acīkṛpat* would result— this is not so; for because the substitution of *l* (*latva*) is considered unestablished (*asiddha*), first...

Since the desired result is achieved by the subsequent application of the rule *ṛpo ro laḥ*— which prescribes the substitution of a portion of the letter *lṛ* for a portion of the letter *ṛ*— within the operation of the rule *ṭhurṛ’dit*,
the rule *ṛpo ro laḥ* is not required for the sake of the substitution of *l* in forms such as *calīklṛpyate*, where the augment *rīg* and others would otherwise apply.
It might be argued that even if this [separate root] were necessary, one should simply read *kṛpū dātau* as *kṛpū sāmarthye*;

for in this way, simplicity of procedure (*prakriyālāghava*) would be gained, and the interpretive difficulty of explaining a portion of the vowel *ṛ* as being a portion of the vowel *ḷ* would also not arise. To this it must be said:

In the case of *acīklṛpat*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the application of the rule *ṭhuṛ* (Pāṇini 7.1.102). However, if one were to accept that the single element *ṛ* in the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.18) refers to a portion of the *lṛ* vowel, then the aforementioned difficulty of providing such an explanation would remain inevitable. (And this has been stated according to Kaiyaṭa’s view; however, this is not...)

[The root] *kṣud* is capable of being reduced [by *guṇa*]. Since the form is established by the inclusion of the *ḷ*-vowel through the rule "ṛta ut" (Pāṇini 6.4.110), which uses a long vowel (*tapara*) to include the *ḷ*-vowel, it is clear that this [root] has a dental *ṭ*.
The point is that if it had a labial *ṭ*, the form would be *āṭiṭṭat*. [The roots] *śaṭha* and *śvaṭha*: [they] cause to deceive (*śāṭhayati*). One who is unrefined...

The meaning is "it comes into being" or "it goes. Regarding *smāyayati*: the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) does not occur here because, by the rule "ityaṃ smayate," that [substitution] is prescribed only for the root *miṅ* belonging to the Bhūvādigaṇa (*miṅ īṣaddhasane*) when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*. *Śraṇa* means "giving"; *viśrāṇanam*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

*Vitaraṇa* means crossing over. From the root *cuda* with the sense of "inciting" (*saṃcodane*), the suffix *yuc* is applied according to the rule *ṭhṇyāsaśranthaḥ*, resulting in *codanā*. *Vaja* means "path. One *vājayati*; one *mārgayati*. Some, however, explain that *mārga* is not a separate root, but rather that the single root *vaja* signifies both the preparation of a path and motion. *Jñapa* is marked as having an indicatory *m*.
Some say that by the force of the word *ca* [in the rule], the root *jñā* optionally receives the *ṇic* affix; others say it receives the designation *mit*.

Thus, it signifies both "knowing" (*jñāna*) and "making known" (*jñāpana*), as in the verse: "Delight, understanding, and consciousness. In the rule *pracccha jñīpsāyām*, it means "knowing," while in the sūtra *lāghahnuṅ*, it is explained as "one who is being made to know" (*ñīpsyamāna*), meaning one who is desired to be informed.
The sense is that [the rule applies] because we observe its usage in the sense of "explanation" (*vyākhyā*) and "making known" (*jñāpana*).
(344) *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.92. Regarding the word *veṣṭana*: Amarasimha states, "The enclosure (*paridhi*) is called *ariveṣṭa*. As for the phrase "but not," etc., this...

The meaning is as follows: regarding the root *yam* in the sense of "not serving" (*apariveṣaṇe*) as listed [in the Dhātupāṭha], the form *pariveṣaṇa* there is indeed the form of the causative (*ṇic*) suffix.
For the meaning of the causative suffix is either "feeding" or "encircling. Thus, by the term *apariveṣaṇa*, [it refers to] from feeding...

Even though elsewhere, in the context of the prohibition of the *mit* designation, it is explained that for those two meanings [of the suffixes], the *mit* status is established simply because they end in *am*,
despite the absence of the *ṭhyañ* affix— since in cases such as *ghaṭa*, the rule "the *ṭhyañ* affix occurs after words other than those meaning 'food'" (*bhojana*) has been explained—
nevertheless, in accordance with the text at hand, this should be understood as an illustrative extension (*upalakṣaṇa*).

They say that this must be explained. Here, this should be understood: in the case of *ghaṭādi* (the group beginning with *ghaṭa*), the form in the rule *yamo’pariveṣaṇe* is derived from the root *viṣ* preceded by *pari* and followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), with the suffix *lyuṭ*;
however, in the rule *yama ca pariveṣaṇe*, the form is derived from the simple root alone with the suffix *lyuṭ*, and not from the causative form. Likewise...

And since the act of wrapping food is also included within the meaning of the word *pariveṣaṇa* (serving), the substitution of *i* for *m* (mitva) is established in both cases precisely because they end in *am*.
However, in the case of wrapping (*veṣṭana*), although the substitution of *i* for *m* occasioned by ending in *am* is prohibited by the rule *na pariveṣaṇe*, [the desired form is still obtained].
The status of *mit* for the root *ṭhiv* is established by the rule "ṭhiv ca pariveṣaṇe"; this is the general direction.
(345) *cisphurorṇau* | 6.1.54. Regarding *cisphurorṇau*: from the previous rule "ādeca upadeśe," the word *āt* is understood to carry over, as is *vibhāṣā*.
And from that [sūtra], the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) is also [understood]. Thus he says: "There may be the substitution of *ā*. (Pāṇini 7.3.36):

*arti-hrī-vlī-rī-krnūyī-kṣmāyy-ātām puṅ ṇau*. In the case of *arti*, *hrī*, etc., because it is both subsequent and internal (*antaraṅga*), the augment *puK* is applied first, and afterwards the *guṇa* substitution. Thus: *arpayati*.

He causes to tremble (hraepayati), he causes to cover (vlepayati), he causes to pay (repayati). There is the elision of the letter *y* [in the following]: he causes to moisten (knopayati), he causes to rest (kṣmapayati), he causes to stand (sthāpayati), and he causes to move (capayati). When a specific phoneme is mentioned, the paribhāṣā "the rule as it is explicitly stated takes precedence" does not apply, because [the mention of the root] is for the purpose of precluding the suffix *ka* prescribed by the rule *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*.
The intention is that [the rule] begins with "ṭhhvāvāmaśca" and so forth. Regarding "jñapādibhyaḥ": according to the primary opinion, there are five roots beginning with *jñap*;
however, in another opinion, some say there are seven, while others say there are eight.
In such cases, it is impossible to determine the purity of the reading; for this very reason—

Kṣīrasvāmin has said: "Due to the loss of tradition in the reading and in the meaning, even the great are deluded; we do not know what we should abandon here and what we should adopt. In words such as *pūla* and *pūrṇa*, there is a corruption in the reading. Is the meaning of the root *paj* the preparation of a path, or...?

In the sense of "only a conditioned formation" (*saṃskāra*), there is a lapse [in the tradition]. This lapse arises from the loss of scripture—that is, from the loss of the treatise (*śāstra*). Regarding the root *cūrṇ*, it means "to contract. As for its recitation again after having been previously taught, this is intended to indicate a difference in meaning. Regarding the inclusion of *marca*: even though it is not seen in some recensions of the Dhātupāṭha, one should not consider this to be unauthoritative.
This is because Kaiyaṭa has cited it under the rule *idaco ’ntyāt paraḥ*,
and because the usage *arto martaṃ marcayati dvayena* is observed. (347) *upadhāyāś ca* | Pāṇini 7.1.101.
"And [the vowel] of the penultimate (upadhā). The phrase "of a root ending in ṛ" (*ṛta id dhātoḥ*) is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "of the penultimate of a root. If it is objected:

"In the rule *Añta id dhātoḥ*, the desired result is established by explaining 'of a root ending in ṛ' (*dhātoḥ ṛtaḥ*) as being in a different grammatical relation (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*); so what is the purpose of this present rule?"—it is not so. For instance:

In the case of *sati* and *añkārīyati*, there would also be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of shortening (*itva*). Regarding the statement "some say [the root is] *ardana*," they argue here as follows:
the roots *lub* and *tub* are recited in the *bhvādi* class for the sense of "piercing" (*ardana*);

their inclusion there would be redundant, because forms such as *lumbati* and *tumbati* are already established simply by virtue of their being marked with the *idit* designation. [This applies] to the sense of "disappearance."

Because there is a difference in meaning when used in its own sense (*svarthe*), the inclusion [of this root] in the *bhvādi* class is meaningful; however, since the state of having "ardana" (distressing) as its meaning is inappropriate for the two roots belonging to the *curādi* class, the word "one" (*eka*) was stated out of dissatisfaction with that view. *mrakṣa* means to smear (*mlecchane*).
This [root] also applies to the act of smearing (*mrakṣaṇe*), which is anointing with oil and the like. [Examples: *mrakṣayati*, *amamrakṣat*. *gurda*...
In the sense of "dwelling in a former residence," one says *gurdayati* or *pūrvayati*. Some, however, read it as *ūrvaniketane* and explain that the root *gur* signifies "dwelling in a former place.

[The root] *jasu* is used in the sense of "injury"; the addition of the marker *udit* is for the purpose of making the augment *iṭ* optional after the suffix *ktvā*, and by the force of that [marker], this [root *jasu*]...

The suffix *ṇic* is compulsory. [Examples: *jāsayati*, *jasati*; [gerunds] *jasitvā*, *jastvā*; [past participle] *jastaḥ*. Regarding the root *cit* in the sense of "perception" (*saṃcetane*)—perception being the knowledge that occurs subsequent to the cessation of states such as fainting—the form *daṃśati* is given. Here, having raised the doubt regarding the elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule “*aṃśasañja-*,” he says:

"Because of its association with *sañj*" [is the rule applied]. Regarding *spaś*: from the root *spāś*, the form *apaspaśat* occurs; by the rule "atsmṛdṛtvar... etc., the substitution of *a* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *i*. Regarding *tarja* and *bhartsa*, both meaning "to threaten": *tarjayate* and *bhartsayate*. As in: "He seemed to threaten with his banners. (*tarjayan iva ketubhiḥ*).

The application [of the suffix] should be understood as being from this root with the causative marker *ṇic*, or from the root *atarj* belonging to the *bhūvādi* class with the causative *ṇic*. *Bhrūṇa*: *bhrūṇayate*. Amara states: "The word *bhrūṇa* refers to a child and to an embryo in a woman. *Gūra* means "to exert" or "to raise"; this has a long vowel in its penultimate syllable (*dīrghopadha*). One says *gūrayate*. However, that which has a short vowel in its penultimate syllable (*hrasvopadha*) belongs to the *divādi* class.

[The root] is situated in the *manoramā*. Although in the *tudādi* class there is the reading "urī udyamane" (urī in the sense of exertion), which implies a short vowel in the penultimate syllable (*hrasvopadha*), nevertheless, in the *divādi* class there is the reading "dhūrī gūrī hiṃsāgatyoḥ" (dhūrī and gūrī in the senses of injury and motion), and thus, according to the modern scholars (*navyāḥ*), there is no short vowel in the penultimate syllable. [The root] *śama* means to mark (*lakṣa*). Now, [regarding the form] *śāmaya*: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

Regarding the form *śāmaya* in the phrase *tadutpattiṃ śāmaya*, some raise the objection that since this is derived from the root *śamu* (meaning "to pacify") with the causative suffix *ṇic*, it ought to have a short vowel due to the presence of the *mit* designation; they then ask how the form is established by this rule. [The answer is: because it belongs to the *ākusmīya* group, the form is *ini śāmaya sveti*.

If it is argued that this is because [the word] is accepted by all, they reply here: from the root *śam* (in its causative form with the suffix *ṇic*) used in the sense of one's own purpose (*svārtha*), the form *niśāmaya* is derived by adding the causal suffix *ṇic*. Nor is there an inconsistency in the meaning, according to the established principle (*siddhānta*) that "the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed for a verbal root when the original sense [of the root] is already expressed" (*nivṛtapreṣaṇāddhātoḥ prākṛte'rthe ṇijucyate*). The root *kuts* is used in the sense of reviling (*avakṣepaṇe*).

The suffix *aṅ* is applied [to the root *ṭhyūn*] because of the grammatical rule stating "and after *ṭhyūn*, in the sense of contempt" (*ṭhyūnaśca kutsāyām*); thus, *kutsā*. The suffix *yuc* is applied by the rule "*ṇyāsaśrantho yuc*" (Pāṇini 3.3.107), resulting in *kutsanā*. They say that *bhala* means "mockery" (*ābhaṇḍanam*) or "investigation" (*nirūpaṇam*). The root *vañcu* is used in the sense of "deceiving" (*pralambhane*); with the suffix *lyuṭ*, it becomes *vañcanam*. Since the addition of the marker *udit* is for the purpose of making the suffix *ktvā* optional regarding the augment *iṭ*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied invariably.

[The forms] *vañcayati*, *vañcati*, *vañcitvā*, *vañcitvā*, and *vaktvā* [are derived as follows]: because of the optional *kit*-status of the *ktvā*-suffix when it is followed by the augment *iṭ*—according to the rule "ṭhvañci-luñcy-ṛtaś-ca"—the elision of the nasal (*n*) is optional; however, in the absence of *iṭ*, the elision is obligatory. But in the case of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), [the form is] *vaktam*. [This applies to] that which...
The prohibition [of the suffix] applies to the past tense (*atīta*). He explains the word *vā* in the rule *“āmno vā”* with the words *“atha vā”*.

Regarding the term *“prātipadika”*: since it will be stated later in the rule *“anyeṣv api dṛśyate”* that the suffix is seen after “others as well,” when the suffix *ḍa* is added to the root *smi* preceded by *ku*, and the *ṭi*-portion is elided, the compound is formed by the rule *“gati-kāraka-pūrvasya”*.

And the meaning is that it is established. Although forms such as *kusmayate* are established for the root *smi* preceded by *ku* in the *laṅ* and other moods, nevertheless, forms such as *prakusmayate* would not be established because of the impossibility of an upasarga being separated from the verbal root. Furthermore, the form *kusmeti* is also [stated] for the sake of forms such as *usmayāṃ cakre*.

The reading is meaningful. Thus ends the section on the *ākusmīya* roots. Now, regarding *carca*: although all roots beginning with *cura* take the *ṇic* suffix optionally, in the alternative case [when the suffix is not applied], the suffix *ap* is added by the rule "after a root ending in a consonant preceded by *u* or *ū*" (*urośca halaḥ*). Hence, *carcā*. Regarding *kaṇa* (in the sense of closing): this word refers specifically to the closing of one eye, due to its inherent nature. Hence, *kāṇaḥ*. This is according to the rule for words such as *kāṇya*, etc. (*kāṇyādīnām*).

These will be explained among the causative (*hetumaṇṇic*) and denominative (*yaṅanta*) formations.
