And [the roots] having the meaning of "to kill" (*han*): therefore, *ghātayati* and *hanti* have the same meaning. *Arj*: "effort" (*pratiyatna*) means the imparting of a quality; thus, *arjayati* means "he gathers" (*saṅgṛhṇāti*). *Ghuṣi*: "non-proclamation" means "promising" (*pratijñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "from the indicative mark of the prohibition": by the rule *ghuṣir aviśabdane*, the suffix *iṭ* is prohibited for the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) when the meaning is not "making a sound. Since this root [ghuṣ] has the sense of "making a sound," there can be no past participle immediately following it at all, because of the intervention of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Therefore, the rule *ghuṣir aviśabdane* [applies].

Since the prohibition of *iṇ* in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix would apply only to the root belonging to the *bhūvādika* class, what is the purpose of the prohibition of *viśabdana*? Therefore, the underlying intention is that by this very prohibition of *viśabdana*, it is indicated that the *ṇic* affix for this root is not invariably obligatory (*anitya*).
Some maintain that the optionality of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is established even from the sense of "making to move" (*irita-karaṇāt*). Regarding "application of craft" (*śilpa-yoga*):

craft (*śilpa*) is skill in action. [The root *yat* is used] in the senses of "disparagement" (*nikāra*) and "improvement" (*upaskāra*). Disparagement (*nikāra*) is either effort or a command. There is an alternative reading: *irākāropaskārayoḥ*.
It has been stated: "The prefix *ni* [is used] in the sense of effort (*yatna*), command (*praiṣa*), lack of form (*nirākāra*), a tree (*pādapa*), and also in the sense of preparation (*upaskṛti*);

this *ni* [is used] in the sense of the giving back (*pratidāna*) of grain (*dhānya*) and wealth (*dhana*). The meaning of this is as follows: one should employ the verbal root *yat* in the four senses beginning with effort, provided that the prefix *ni* is employed.

Then this [root] occurs in the sense of returning grain or wealth; it means "he pays back a debt" (*ṛṇaṃ niryātayati*), that is, "he gives back. Furthermore, there is the sense of "distinguishing" (*viśeṣaṇa*). Distinguishing is exclusion (*vyāvartana*).

Regarding the statement "the root *hu* is used in the sense of mixing" (*avakalkane*), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to the root *bhū*; thus, "he causes to be" (*bhāvayati*) means "he mixes."

The meaning is "he thinks" (cintayati). And [the rule] *kṛpeśca*: the affix *ṇic* is applied to the root *kṛp* in the sense of "mixing" (*avakalkana*). Regarding "up to *svad*" (*ā svadaḥ*): since it is universally accepted that the prefix *āṅ* has the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*)—as in the previous rule *ā kusmāt* and in the subsequent rule *ā dhṛṣād āvargāt*—it must be understood as such here as well, as it falls within that interval.

The sense is that it is appropriate to explain it as *vka-yā-khyāna*. Others, however, have explained it as derived from the root *svad* preceded by the prefix *ā*, with the suffix *ṇic* added because it is transitive. All roots beginning with *ā-svad* are transitive.
As for [the form] *ghaṭayati*: this root is already included in the *curādi* class in the sense of "assembling" (*saṅghāta*); its repetition here, however, is...
Because of the difference in meaning.
(348) *nāglopiśāsvṛditām* 7.4.2;
"some say *āsvāda*"—according to this view, even in the preceding [sūtra], *āsvāda* [is understood] as being transitive.

[The reading is] *pāṭhaḷm*. Now, one might object that the long-vowel reading (*dīrghapāṭha*) is redundant, because even with the short-vowel reading (*hrasvapāṭha*), the forms such as *svādayati* would be identical due to the *upadhā*-vṛddhi; therefore, he says: "But of the long [vowel]," etc. By the rule *aḥ svidisvadisahīnāṃ ca*, the *s* following the *ṣ* of the reduplicated syllable does not become *s*.

Since it will be stated that "there is *ṣatva*," the forms such as *sisvādayiṣati* and so on are exactly the same even in the case of the desiderative (*sannanta*). With this in mind, he says: *asisvadat*. Thus end the derivatives of *ā-svad*. "Up to *ā-dhṛṣ*"—either by way of explanation or by the force of suitability, the term *ṇic* is connected [to the list]. *Ayaukṣīt*.

The sense is that this [root] is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) in its causative (*ṇij*) form. Regarding the root *lī* in the sense of "liquefying," the author of the *Bhāṣya* states: "In the case of *ināti* and *līyati*, the mention is by means of *yak*. By this statement, he indicates that the substitution of *āt* (long *ā*) prescribed by the rule "vibhāṣā līyateḥ" does not apply here; hence he says *letā*. [He also gives the form] *varītā*.

Alternatively, there is a long vowel due to the rule *vṛto vā*. In the *liṅ* (optative) mood: *vṛṣīta* (active); but in the *ātmanepada*, *vṛṣīṣṭa* or *variṣīṣṭa*. According to the rule *iṅsicorātmanepadeṣu*, there is optionally *iṭ*. By the rule *a liṅī*, the lengthening of *iṭ* is prohibited. In the alternative where *iṭ* is absent, there is no *guṇa* substitution because of the *kit* designation by the rule *uśca*.

*luṅ* (aorist): *avārīt*, *avāriṣṭām*, *avāriṣuḥ*. By the rule "ici ca parasmaipadeṣu," there is a prohibition of the lengthening [of the vowel]. But in the *ātmanepada*, it is *avarīṣṭa* or *avarīṣṭa*; when there is no *iṭ* augment, there is the elision of *sic*. *avṛta*. Regarding *ric*: he says that this [root] is *aniṭ* in the absence of *ṇic*—namely, *rekte*. *aśikṣat*.

The suffix *k* is applied [to the root *tṛp*] by the rule *ala igupadhāt* (Pāṇini 3.1.135). Regarding *tṛp*: because it is listed among the roots that do not take the augment *iṭ* (*aniṭ*) in the *śyan* form, he indicates that this root does take *iṭ*—as seen in the form *tarpitā*. Regarding *chṛd*: because it is marked with the indicatory letter *ī*, there is no *iṭ* augment in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). By the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* after a vowel ending in *ṛ*, we have *chṛṇṇaḥ* and *chṛṇṇavān*.

The augment *nuk* should be stated after the roots *dhūñ* and *prīñ*, and [the vowel] is short. *Dhūñ* means "to shake. Regarding *avākṣīt*: because of the mention [of the root] with a *luk*-elision in the rule *asyativaktikhyātibhyo’ṅ*, there is no *aṅ* suffix; this is the sense. There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti*. [The optative form is] *ucyāt*. *Dhṛṣ* means "to dare" or "to overcome."

Some, however, say that [the root] is *dhṛṣ* (with a short *u*), while in their opinion it is *dhṛṣṭa*; but according to the primary opinion, it is *dhṛṣita*. Now, one might object: "In this case, by the rule *iṣṭhā śīṅ* etc., the suffix *niṣṭhā* is prohibited from being *kit*, and therefore *guṇa* substitution ought to occur. To this they reply: By virtue of the association with roots beginning with *ā* (*āditsāhacaryāt*), it must be one of those beginning with *ā*—namely, *ñidhṛṣ*.

In that regard, [the suffix] is included because of its mention there. Nor should one suspect that the augment *iṭ* is difficult to obtain for the *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) suffix from the very beginning;

for its possibility is established by the rule "vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ" (optionally applied in the sense of the abstract action or the reflexive/impersonal). Thus end the roots beginning with *yuj* belonging to the *ādhṛṣīya* class. Now, regarding those ending in short *a*: in the roots to be mentioned hereafter, the final constituent is the vowel *a*.

But it does not mean for the purpose of pronunciation; the meaning is that there is no *vṛddhi* because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), according to the rule "when a subsequent [element] follows an *ac*" (*acaḥ parasmin*). Nor is it the case that only that operation which occurs when the original element (*sthānin*) is present is extended by this [rule], while that which is occasioned by the substitute (*ādeśa*) is excluded; otherwise, [the form] *nāyaka*...

It should not be argued that [the rule] *pāvaka* and so forth would not be established, and thus an increase (*vṛddhi*) here is unavoidable; for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the rule *ṭhacaḥ parasmin*, by carrying over the term *sthānivat* and relying on the perspective of the governing topic of words (*śabdādhikārapakṣa*), both presence and absence are extended. This applies to the original element (*sthānin*).

This is because even when there is a substitute for *vṛddhi*, [the result] does not occur; for the principle that "what does not occur when there is the original element (*sthānin*) does not occur even when there is its substitute" is supported by the inclusion of the term "elision" (*lopa*) and so forth in the rule *a padānte* (Pāṇini 8.2.39).
This is the general direction of the argument.

(349) *ī ca gaṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.97. The rule *ī ca gaṇaḥ* means that the vowel *ī* is also included in the *gaṇa*. In the rule *atsmṛdṛtvarapratheṣṭadastṝspaśām*, the letter *at* is conjoined by the particle *ca*; thus, the *ī* is added to it. [The roots] *stan* and *gad* are included. In the term *adī* [within the rule], the short *i* is used for the purpose of indicating the elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel of the root *ad*.

Because it is taught as having multiple vowels (*anekāctva*), the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur; thus, *tistanayiṣati*. In the case of *tani*, *hṛṣi*, and *puṣi*, when the suffix *ṇi* is followed by *iṣṇuc*, there is the substitution of *ay* for the final vowel in the penultimate position according to the rule "in the penultimate [of a word ending in] *ṭha*. Thus, *tanayitnuḥ* means "a rain-cloud" (*balāhaka*). Alternatively, the root *pat* means "to go"; this is a *gaṇasūtra*. [The form] *kṛpayati* is derived from the same principle.

The rule *ṛpo ro laḥ* does not apply here, because in that context the root *kṛpū* (meaning "to be capable") is intended, whereas the causative (*ṇij*) form derived from *kṛp* is a different verbal root altogether. *Spṛhā* means the desire to obtain (*īpsā*). Regarding the form *ābhāmād*: due to the status of the elision (*allopasya*) as *sthānivadbhāva*, [the rule] applies in the presence of the suffix *ṇau*.
In the case of *caṅ*, there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*). Regarding *sūca*: *piśuna* means a wicked person; his action is *paiśunya* (malicious talebearing).

[The objection is raised] that because it is not taught as having *aṣ* [in its upadeśa], [the rule does not apply]. The implication is that it has more than two vowels (*anekāctvāt*). As for the statement "of the past [root] *sāma* in the sense of conciliation" (*sāntvane*), this root does not appear anywhere in the original manuscript prior to this point.

It has been observed; it should be sought in other manuscript copies. Some, however, maintain that although the root *āma* in the sense of "consoling" (*sāntvane*) is not found anywhere, *āntva* in the sense of "employing conciliation" (*sāmaprayoge*) was indeed previously recorded.
In that case, two roots, *āntva* and *āma*, function in the same usage (*prayoge*). And as for this usage:

He is intent on the application of conciliation (*sāntva*). Having thus described the intention of the author—that this [application] is indeed conciliation itself—the possible interpretations for one who remains [in that state] are supported. *Gaveṣa* means seeking—searching.

The root *ūn* is used in the sense of diminution (*parihāṇi*). From this, with the suffix *ṇic* and the *caṅ* substitute, because it is subsequent and because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), [the reduplication occurs].

If, by the rule "allopena ṭhajāderdvitīyasya," there were doubling [of the consonant] along with the causative suffix (ṇic), the undesirable form *āṬninad* would result; however, the desired form is *āṬnanad*. It must be stated that this is achieved through the doubling of the element *na*, because the causative suffix (ṇic) is not the cause of the doubling; therefore, he says: *oḥ*.

Regarding the phrase *pūyañjītyādi*: in order to dispel the misconception held by some that a complete *sūtra* constitutes a *liṅga*, he says *payayoḥ*. The intended meaning is as follows: by the two *sūtras* "after *pūṅ*, *ñi*, and *vṛś*, [the suffix] *san*" and "after *anīṅ*, [the suffix *san* is used] except for *ṛddhi*," the *san* following *pūṅ* and *yauti* [is prescribed].

If the augment *iṭ* were applied, then because of the status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to the rule "in reduplication, [the substitute] is like the original when followed by a vowel" (*avirvacane'ci*), or due to the prohibition of substitution, there would be reduplication of only that which ends in *u*. Consequently, undesirable forms such as *pupaviṣate* and *yuyaviṣati* would result. Therefore, for the sake of the *it* (short *i*) of the vowel in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), the requirement of the rule *payayoḥ* is necessary.
Otherwise, forms such as *pipaviṣate* and *yiyaviṣati* would not be established. Regarding the phrase "varga-pratyāhāra":
the purpose of including the first letter of each varga in the rule *uyaṇjī* is [to account for] *abībhavat*, *amīmavat*, *arīravat*, *alīlavat*, *ajījavat*, *bibhāvayiṣati*, and *mimāvayiṣati*.

It should be stated that the formation of such forms as *rirāvayiṣati* and *lilāvayiṣati* is well-established; both are easily explained. Since the operations of *vṛddhi* and so forth take precedence due to their being subsequent (*paratva*) and internal (*antaraṅga*), once reduplication has occurred, the vowel *u* is no longer available in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Consequently, by the rule "anyataḥ," the vowel *a* is replaced by *i*.

And because the form [cukṣāvayiṣati] is established [by this rule], the inclusion of the group beginning with *v* (i.e., *vargād*) is redundant; the sense is that this redundancy serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned meaning.
The result of this indication should be understood to apply where the rule *ṭhoḥ puyaṇjī* does not otherwise apply.
For example: *cukṣāvayiṣati*; in the *caṅ* [reduplication], it becomes *icukṣavat*. Furthermore, *tu* is a verbal root (*dhātu*) from the Sūtra collection (*sautra*). From that...

After the causative suffix *ṇic*, there is *san* [desiderative]. *tutāvayiṣati*. In the case of *caṅ* [reduplication], it is like *it* and *tavat*. *nunāvayiṣati*. *anūnavat*. *pusphārayiṣati*. *apuspharat*. According to the rule "there is optionally *ā*-vṛddhi for *sphur* after *ṇic*," there is optionally *ā*-vṛddhi. In forms such as *apuspharat*, the vowel *u* is heard in the reduplicated syllable due to a specific technical indication (*jñāpana*); otherwise, [the form would be different].
[Otherwise] forms such as *cikṣāvayiṣati* would result [as unintended consequences]. Having all this in mind, the author of the Vārttika stated:

"The statement [of the rule] *ṭhoḥ puyaṇjiṣu* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) in the case of the causative suffix *ṇi*. The term *sthānivadbhāva* here is also an indication for the prohibition [of the substitution of *vṛddhi*].

"In this case, the substitute would not occur"—this was stated with the intention that the position of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) is primary. Alternatively, it should be understood that "prohibition" is also an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Now, an objection: if this were so, in the case of the root *kṛ* in the form *saṃśabdane*, when the *caṅ* affix follows the causative (*ṇi*), before the substitution of *ir* occurs, [the question arises regarding] the form *kṛta*.
Since the forms would be *acakīrtat* due to the doubling and the substitution of *ur*, rather than *acikīrtat*, he says:

"where there is doubling" (*yatra dviruktau*). "The first vowel" (*ādyaḥ aj*)—this was stated by accepting that the subsequent portion (*uttara-khaṇḍa*) is accompanied by the suffix *caṅ*. Others, however, [hold that] the mention of "the first" (*ādyagrahaṇaṃ*)...

They say that this is for the sake of clear understanding, because when a single-vowel (*ekāc*) root is reduplicated (*ditva*), it is impossible for two vowels (*aj-dvaya*) to exist in the subsequent portion (*abhyāsottara-khaṇḍa*). [The author] says "in the process of derivation" (*prakriyāyām*) because, in completed forms such as *āu jaḍhat* and *āu nanat*, the vowel *a* (*avarṇa*) is not obtained. [This applies] in cases such as *cukṣāvayiṣati*.
He says, "or in the final form," because the vowel *a* is not found in the process of derivation (*prakriyā*).

The word "or" (*vā*) indicates a lack of insistence; the sense is that in some cases being followed by the vowel *a* is intended, but there is no dogmatic restriction that it must be only in such-and-such a place. This is because [the rule] depends upon its own kind (*sajātīya*).

In the subsequent section [of the commentary] on the word *uyañji*, vowels ending in *a* (*avarṇa*) occur; therefore, the meaning is that this is the very indicator (*jñāpaka*) for that [rule]. For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya stated in examples such as *acikīrtat* that "the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* occurs only when followed by an *a*-vowel, even when there is another consonant (*hal*) following the initial *a*-vowel."

It has been established as the settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Now, one might object: since the word "in *ṇic*" (*ṇici*) does not occur in the sūtra *ṭhoḥ puyaṇjī*, how could this [mention of *ṇic*] serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the purpose of ensuring that a substitute for a vowel (*ac-ādeśa*) does not occur when *ṇic* follows? Nor can it be argued that, in general, when a doubling (*dvitva*) is to be applied, a substitute for a vowel does not occur.

If it is argued that one should simply state "let it be known as *syāt*," because in forms such as *didavanīyiṣati* and *ninayiṣati*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of hearing the vowel *u* in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), [the author] says here: "By the rule *yena nāvyavadhānaṃ tena vyavahite 'pi syāt* (whereby there is no intervention, [the operation applies] even when there is an intervention by a single suffix), [the reduplication occurs] after the suffix which is the cause of the doubling."
An intervention is required, and since that is possible only with the suffix *ṇi*, this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) specifically concerning the domain of *ṇi*.

However, in the case of *didavanīyiṣati*, because there is an intervention by both the suffix *lyuṭ* and the suffix *kyac*, there is a multiple intervention; therefore, it is not an indicator concerning that [domain]. According to our view:

From the word *div* ending in the *kvip* suffix, when followed by the desiderative (*san*), the form would be *dudavaniṣati*; however, this is not desired, because of the statement in the Vārttika: "The [rule] regarding the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) is an indicator [of its application] in the case of the causative suffix (*ṇi*).

By virtue of that *sthānivadbhāva*, or rather by the prohibition [of doubling], there must be an *u*-vowel in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) precisely in the case of the causative suffix (*ṇi*).

Therefore, based on the very statement of the Vārttikakāra, one must accept that [the substitute] is *sthānivadbhūta* when the causative suffix *ṇic* follows. And thus, there is no fault in the previously cited examples; such is the direction [of the argument]. He states the result: "But in the present case... and "āṬnanat. Regarding "he causes to sound" (*onayati*) and "he causes to resound" (*dhvanayati*), the prohibition of *caṅ* does not apply here. In that regard—

Because of the continued application of the rule *cchandasī* (Vedic usage), that [substitution] is prohibited specifically in the Veda, as seen in examples such as *ā tvāyato jarituḥ kāmam ūnayīḥ*. Even so, for those such as Bopadeva who maintain that— on the grounds that the status of being followed by an *avarṇa* applies only to the established form (*pariniṣṭhita*)— the substitute for the letter *u* alone should be treated as the original (*sthānivat*), and no other [substitute], [the following applies].

It should have been stated simply as "mate āṬ na it" (in *mate*, *āṬ* does not [apply]); for if the substitute of the vowel *a* were treated as *sthānivadbhūta*, the condition of being followed by a vowel (*avarṇa*) would not be met in the final form. Nevertheless, in cases such as *acikīrtat*, there is a suspicion of *sthānivadbhāva* because the vowel *a* is absent in the subsequent portion.

Upon examining the refutation stated by the author of the Bhāṣya, there is no restrictive rule that only the substitute for *u* (i.e., *ū*) is *sthānivadbhūta*; thus, the form *aunanat* is entirely unobjectionable. Otherwise, the statement in the Vṛtti—that because of the elision (*lopa*) of the *upadhā* vowel in *caṅ*, the substitute is *sthānivadbhūta*, and consequently the word *pā* undergoes reduplication—would be contradicted. Moreover:

Furthermore, the usage *oṭaḍhat* in the Vārttika of Vaiyāghrapadya—namely, “*uṣkikā*, *śuṣkajaṅghā*, *kṣāmimānau*, and *oṭaḍhat*”—would also be contradicted; for this is a Vārttika intended to state the purpose of the rule "that which is [already] established in the preceding [section is treated as not existing for the following]. For example, in the case of *uṣkikā*, [the rule] "*udīcām ātaḥ*" applies.

Thus, there is no substitution of *it* (the short *i*), because since the substitution of *k* in "uṣaḥ kaḥ" is considered *asiddha* (not yet established), the condition of being preceded by *ya* or *ka* is absent. In the case of "uṣkarajaṅghā," precisely because the substitution of *k* is *asiddha*, the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule "a kopadhāyāḥ" does not apply. However, in the case of "kṣāmimān,"...
The substitution of *v* [for *s*] by the rule *ādupadhāyāḥ* does not apply here, because the substitution of *m* [for *s*] by the rule *ṣāyo maḥ* is considered asiddha (unestablished).
In the case of the root *vah*, after the suffix *kta*, followed by *ṇic* and *caṅ*, and before the *āṬ* augment, the substitution of *ḍh* [for *h*] by the rule *āṬjiḍhad* is asiddha;

furthermore, due to the status of *sthānivadbhāva* regarding the *ṭi*-elision effected by *ṇi*, there is reduplication of the syllable *hta*. Then, by the rule *uhoścuḥ*, [the *c* is substituted for the *h*].

One should reflect upon this practice: however, the status of being like *san* (sanvadbhāva) does not occur here because of the prohibition "not when there is elision of [the penultimate] *an*" (*anaglopi*).

Similarly, in the *Kāśikā*, under the rule "that which is earlier is unestablished" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), after citing *aujaḍhat* as an example, it is stated that *aujiḍhat*—meaning "he described the carrying away"—occurs from the word *ūḍhi* ending in *ktin*.

That too would be contradicted; for under the restrictive rule that "only a substitute of a vowel (*avarṇa*) is treated as *sthānivadbhūta*," there would be no *sthānivadbhāva* here for the *ṭilopa* (elision of the suffix) performed after the causative marker (*ṇi*), and consequently, neither the form *hata* nor *hti* could undergo reduplication. Thus, in the case of the root *aṅk*, when the causative marker is added and the elision of the vowel (*al-lopa*) occurs, [the same difficulty arises].

It should be understood that because the substitute *kā* is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the form *āñcakat* alone is universally accepted upon the doubling of the root, and not *āñcikad* as stated by Bopadeva. Now, one might object: "In forms such as *acicīrtat*, the Bhāṣyakāra, while raising the possibility of *sthānivadbhāva*, states that it does not apply because there is no *avarṇa* (short 'a') in the subsequent portion [of the reduplicated syllable]."

If it is argued that this is contrary to the work of Bopadeva, because it can be said that the Bhāṣyakāra stated it in that manner with the intention that, in its final form in the latter part [of the grammar], the substitution of *u* for *ava* is possible only when followed by *a*, and not for anything else— do not say so. For it is thus...

For if [the rule] were indeed [to apply], then even where the rule *ṭhoḥ puyaṇjī* does not apply, the substitute for the vowel *u* would still be treated as *sthānivadbhūta*; the author of the Bhāṣya would have stated this very point because an indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends upon its own class of similar cases.
This is so because it is improper to establish a matter that can be accomplished by a direct path through a circuitous one.

Regarding the direction: "The four roots here [beginning with *diś*]"; this refers to the alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*) ending with ‘*aṅkocane*’. By stating ‘*atistenad*’, he indicates that because the root has more than one vowel (*anekāctva*), it is not an *aṣopadeśa*, and therefore the substitution of *ṣ* does not apply. As for ‘*gṛhyate*’: due to the status of the elision (*allopasya sthānivattva*), [the rule does not apply].

The suffix *guṇa*. In the *luṅ* [aorist], *ijagṛhata*: because there is elision (*alopa*) of the penultimate vowel, there is no application of the *sanvadbhāva* rule. Regarding *mṛgayate*: this is from the root *mārga* meaning "to search," belonging to the *ādhṛṣīya* group. Regarding *arthayate*: because the elision of the vowel (*alopa*) is stronger than *vṛddhi*, the *vṛddhi* substitution does not take place.
Bopadeva, however, states that when *vṛddhi* has been applied and *puK* added, the form is *arthāpayate*;
this is due to his haste. Nor should it be argued that by the rule "of *artha*, *veda*, and *satya*" (*arthavedasatyānām*), the suffix *āPuk* would indeed occur here;
for in that rule, a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is what is being referred to. [The form *arthāpayati*] is justified by the force of its ending in the vowel *a*.

In cases such as *kathā* and others, the status of having an /a/ as the final vowel (*adantatva*) is meaningful because it excludes the strengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāvṛddhi*), lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the treatment as *saṃvadbhāva*.

In the case of words such as *sāra-bhāma*, etc., it serves to exclude the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāhrasva*), while in the case of *gṛha-mṛga*, etc., it excludes the guṇa-strengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāguṇa*). However, in the present instance, regarding the status of having an /a/ as the final vowel—
The sense is that, because the previously mentioned result would otherwise be absent, this [rule] makes known the optional nature of the *ṇic* affix.

Now, if it is argued that one should simply accept what was stated by the ancients—that "there is optionally elision" (*vā lopaḥ*)—in order to make the final *a* meaningful, they say in response: "The fact that the root *intyati* is marked with the *it* indicator..."
In the view that "the indicator depends on the general," the purpose of the final *a* here is indeed clear.

However, in the view that "the indicator depends on the specific," just as the markers (*anubandhas*)— namely *ā*, *ī*, *u*, and *ū*— are accepted as indicators in their respective places, so too is the state of ending in *a*.

Let it rather indicate the optionality of the *ṇic* suffix; for since the purpose is accomplished by the established optionality of *ṇic*, it is improper to postulate a new rule that would sublate the elision (*lopa*). For this being the case, the same result is obtained in both views. [Regarding the form] *asusūtrat*: because it contains more than two vowels (*anekāctvāt*), [the *ṇiṅ* suffix does not apply].

Regarding the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]: some hold that the phrase "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*) implies that if the suffix *ṇic* were added to a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), then in forms such as *srajayati*, the substitution of *k* [for *j*] (*kutva*) would occur; however, this is not correct.

Because, by virtue of the treatment as being like the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*), the word attains the status of a *bha*-stem, the application of *kutva* is precluded. In this context, *ṇic* is applied diversely (*bahulam*). It...
Because of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the rule "and [the suffix] *ṇic* becomes like *iṣṭhan*," he states that in some cases there is also a sentence (*vākya*), namely:
*paṭumācaṣṭe*. The intention is that by the term "meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvartha*), the expression of an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth is included.
Now, an objection: in the form *bhāvayati* from *bahūn ācaṣṭe*, the suffix *yiṭ* would also apply to the *ṇic* by the rule "for *iṣṭhan*, *yiṭ*."

It might be so. To this they say: in the rule *eḥ*, according to the Vārttika *ṇāviṣṭhavat prātipadikasya*, the mention of the word *prātipadika* is for the purpose that the operations pertaining to suffixes (*pratyaya*) should not be extended [to the base]. Therefore, in this case, the suffix *ṇic* also does not become *iṇ*; in its absence, [the desired result follows].
There is another opinion that it should not be understood as having the sense of "becoming" (*bhū-bhāva*), because [the suffix] is taught in conjunction [with the specific meaning];

rather, it should be understood simply as "he causes to grow" (*bahayati*). This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on that very sūtra. Others, however, say: for the suffix *vati* in the expression *iṣṭhavad* is derived from a word ending in the locative case.

Because the locative case is seen in the word *nau* (in the phrase *nauprabhṛtibhyaḥ*), what is intended is that when the suffix *iṣṭhan* follows, the grammatical operation applicable to the preceding element is extended [to it], but not the operation of the suffix *iṣṭhan* itself. Regarding the term *puṃvadbhāva*: in the example *paṭiṣṭhā*, meaning "most clever" (*atiśayena paṭvī*), there is the substitution of the masculine form by the rule *hrasvāḍhea taddhite*. [The example] *kraśiṣṭhaḥ* [is formed similarly].

In *draḍhiṣṭha*, the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* occurs by the rule *ṛto halādeḥ*. In *ādhiṣṭha* and similar forms, there is elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *ṭi*. In *srajiṣṭha*, meaning "one who possesses a garland to an extreme degree," the suffix *vin* is elided by the rule *vinmatorluk*. In *gaviṣṭha* and similar forms, meaning "one who possesses cows to an extreme degree," there is elision of the suffix *matup*. [The form] *sthaviṣṭha*...

In examples such as these, there is the elision of *yaṇ* and other sounds by [the rule] *sthūladūretyādi*. In examples such as *preṣṭha*, there is the substitution of *pra* and so on by [the rule] *riyasthiretyādi*. Regarding the phrase "those two vowels as well": an example of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) is *etayati*, derived from *enīm ācaṣṭe*; here, it occurs precisely through the elision of the *ṭi* suffix.

It should be understood that since the exclusion of the suffix *nak* is already established by the rule of *sanniyoga-śiṣṭa* (mutual dependence), the explicit mention of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) is for the sake of establishing forms such as *dāradayati* ("he describes one from Darada").

In forms like *draḍhayati*, there is the substitution of *ra*. In the case of *srajayati* ("he describes one who possesses a garland"), derived from *sragviṇam ācaṣṭe*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *vin*.

In the example *gavayati* (he describes as having cows), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *matup*. By the principle that "an operation affecting a constituent element does not apply to the whole" (*aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*), the *vṛddhi* substitution does not occur here. However, in cases such as *priyam ācaṣṭe prāpayati* (he describes as dear, i.e., he makes dear) and *sthiram ācaṣṭe sthāpayati* (he describes as firm, i.e., he makes firm), the *vṛddhi* substitution certainly does occur; this is because of the specific mention of the term *vayaḥ* [in the rule governing such cases].

The direction [of the argument] is that this indicates the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). Regarding the phrase "because it is subsequent, [the *vṛddhi* substitute applies]": the elision (*lopa*) is non-eternal because it results in the attainment of a different word-form; the *vṛddhi* is also non-eternal. Between these two non-eternal operations, the *vṛddhi* applies because it is subsequent. Once that has been performed, even before the substitution of *āv* for the diphthong *au*, [the subsequent rule would apply].

The meaning is that there is elision because a suffix (*āṅga*) is stronger than a substitute (*varṇa*). And thus, since it does not lose its *an* (the *a* of the root), the long vowel and the *sanvadbhāva* apply; this is why he says "apīpaṭat. Here, due to the intervention caused by the *sthānivadbhāva* of the *ṭilopa*, the long vowel and the *sanvadbhāva* do not occur.

One must consider [the rule] as applicable; for even if there were *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original), the condition of the *aṅga* (stem) being followed by *ṇic* would not be lost.

Even under the alternative view that "when *caṅ* follows *ṇi*, [the penultimate vowel] which is light," since the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) precedes the designated vowel (*ādiṣṭādacaḥ*), there is simply no *sthānivadbhāva* at all; thus, both the lengthening (*dīrgha*) and the *sanvadbhāva* (treatment like *san*) indeed occur. Some, however, [hold that] "the *aṅga*..."

In the alternative view that "when there is *ṇi*, [the penultimate vowel] is short" (*pare ṇau yallaghu*), once the *vṛddhi* of the vowel *u* in the word *paṭu* has been applied, a short vowel preceding the *ṇic* becomes impossible; thus, since the condition for *sanvadbhāva* is not met, the resulting form is simply *apapaṭat*.

This is based on the view that first the *ṭilopa* (elision of the suffix) occurs, and subsequently the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) of the stem takes place. Regarding the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*):

As for what was stated in the *Manoramā*—that there is no status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) at all because [the operation] precedes the enjoined vowel—that should not be accepted. This is because the prohibition—"there shall be no substitute for a vowel when a *ṇic*-affix follows, provided that reduplication is to be performed"—was stated previously as the primary position; thus, the *ṭilopa* (elision of the suffix) occurs first.

They say that this is difficult to establish; however, that is weak. For it is beyond dispute that in the form *apīpaṭat*, there is reduplication of the first constituent ending in the second vowel (*ac*). And thus, because the second vowel is made to undergo reduplication, the elision of the *ṭi* (the penultimate *a*) would indeed occur first. This is expressed by the rule "elision [occurs] in place of the *vṛddhi*."

In this view, the elision (*lopa*) is permanent (*nitya*) by the mere fact of its occurrence whether [the condition] has been fulfilled or not; however, the *vṛddhi* substitution is non-permanent (*anitya*), because when the *ṭi*-elision has taken place, it would act as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element) with respect to what must be done before it, and because there is no *sthānivadbhāva* of an element with respect to itself in its own rule. But in this alternative, regarding the rule "uṇḍamiśra... [the following applies].

The designation of *halika* and *kalika* as ending in *a* would indeed be useless, because once the *ṭilopa* occurs prior to the *vṛddhi*, the condition of being *aglopin* (having an elided penultimate vowel) becomes possible. Thus,
by the force of their being designated as ending in *a*, [the rule applies] prior to the *ṭilopa*.
It is understood that because there is no elision of the penultimate vowel (*anaglopitva*), the form *apīpaṭat* alone is correct, as it results from the rule for *vṛddhi*.
However, many hold that both forms are correct due to the authority of the two [conflicting] Bhāṣya passages. As for the meaning of the *laṭ* suffix:
since the expression "he performs" (*karoti*) or "he describes" (*ācaṣṭe*) refers to the agent, the *laṭ* is used in the singular.
The point is that when the sense of the *laṭ* (present tense) is not intended to be expressed,

a suffix indeed occurs after a causative (*ṇic*) stem to denote the state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), as well as the past and future times, and the dual and plural numbers. Although number such as singularity is not the meaning of the *laṭ*, nevertheless—
It should be understood that here even the sense of *tiṅ* (the verbal suffix) is taken as the sense of *laṭ* (the present tense marker), because it is a substitute for *laṭ*.

Therefore, [the derivation is] from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) "atikrāmati" which stands in the third case (*tṛtīyā*), the suffix *ṇic* is added. Others say that the suffix *ṇic* is added to the word ending in the third case. The same applies in the case of "tat karoti."

The suffix *ṇic* is applied after a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) that has become the base (*prakṛti*) for that second case; it is not applied to a word already ending in a *sup* (case) suffix. This is because, in cases such as *vācam ācaṣṭe* ("he tells [her] to speak") or *vācā atikrāmati* ("he oversteps with speech"), which result in *vācayati*, the designation *bha* must necessarily be extended [to the stem] in order to block the application of *kutva*—a phonological change that would otherwise apply to the word-form (*pada*) once the *vin* suffix has been elided.

And because it conforms to such grammatical indications as "atkaroti," they say that the view that the suffix *ṇic* follows a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is indeed superior. (350) *hanasta’ciṇṇaloḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.32.

Regarding the term *ṇicprakṛti*: the word *vadha* is a base (*prakṛti*) for the causative suffix (*ṇic*); however, in the present case, the meaning is that only the portion remaining after the *kṛt* suffix has been elided is the base. As for the phrase *ākhyānāt kṛtaḥ*:
although the word *vadha* ends in a *kṛt* suffix, it is not itself a narrative (*ākhyāna*); nevertheless, it denotes a narrative.

The word *kaṃsavadha* is indeed a derivative formed with a *kṛt* suffix, because when a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned, that which is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or a kāraka is also included. Regarding the phrase "elision of the *kṛt* suffix" (*kṛlluk*): it refers to the elision (*luk*) of the *ap*-suffix prescribed by the rule *hanaśca vadhaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "restoration of the original form" (*prakṛtipratyāpatti*): [it refers to the restoration of the original base].
The meaning is that it is the remaining in its own form by means of the abandonment of modification.
Having intended all of this, he says: "when *kaṃsaṃ han* is established.
[He explains] "of that which is qualified by *kaṃsa*"—the sense is that the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed precisely from that [root]. [He mentions] "the fault."
The meaning is that the augment *aṭ* would be inserted before the word *kaṃsa*, and thus there would be reduplication of *kaṃs*. As for the phrase "and what [more]":
the implication is that in this way, the desired form *kaṃsam ajīghatat* would not be established. Regarding the term *tatpratyaye*:
it means a suffix prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*). Consequently, in the case of *vārtraghnam*, the substitution of *t* by the rule *hanasta* does not occur.
It should be understood that [the rule] "it becomes" applies. He avoids the aforementioned faults by saying "it is true.
Regarding the statement "and like the base-form," he says "because of the word 'and' (ca), for the purpose of including what was not mentioned"—namely, the augment *aṭ* and reduplication.
Even though both *aṭ* and reduplication could be established by the rule of "substitution of one part" (*anyatarādideśena*), nevertheless...

According to Dhātuprasiddhi, there is no insistence on the condition "only when followed by ṇic" regarding the illustrative narratives (aupākhyāna) such as the slaying of Kaṃsa; rather, it applies to illustrative narratives in general. Consequently, forms such as *rājānam āgamayati* ("he causes the king to come") are established, because even though the king is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the base form of the *kṛt*-derivative, [the causative suffix] *ṇic* is applied to the root *gam* in the sense of instigation (*hetu*).

By the term *atibuddhi*, its status as an object (*karman*) is accepted through the force of the formal extension (*rūpātideśa*), such that it appears precisely in the accusative case. However, in the example *devadattapākam ācaṣṭe* (he describes Devadatta’s cooking) or *devadattena pācayati* (he causes Devadatta to cook), because Devadatta’s status as the agent (*kartṛ*) has not been lost, the instrumental case alone occurs. [In the same way, one says] *rukmiṇīharaṇam ācaṣṭe* (he describes the abduction of Rukmiṇī).

In such cases, because of the optionality provided by the rule *hṛkroranyatarasyām*, the usage appears as either *hārayati rukmiṇīm* or *hārayati rukmiṇyā*. Regarding the phrase *kartṛkaraṇāt*: if the mention of the *kartṛ* (agent) were absent, the suffix would apply only in instances such as *cakṣuṣā paśyati* → *cakṣayati*, but not in cases like *karibhir avabadhnāti*.

In examples such as *avakarayati*, since in common worldly usage it is well known that only the sense organs (*indriya*) function as instruments (*karaṇa*), the *Manoramā* maintains that the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is intended to include those [organs].
However, the moderns (*navya*) hold that what is intended to be expressed as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) is what is grasped by the term "instrument," and not otherwise.

The instrument (*karaṇa*) is precisely that which is well-known in common worldly usage. Otherwise, since there would be the undesirable consequence of including even the instrument as understood in common worldly usage in rules such as "the third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument" (*kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā*), forms such as *āṇena hata* ("killed by a knife") would not be established. Thus, even without the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*), the form *avakarayati* is established.

Having explained that there is some obstacle [to the rule], they considered the compound in *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* to be a collective dvandva (*samāhāradvandva*) and cited *devadattena pācayati* and *devadattayati* as examples. It would be easier to say: "because of being seen at one time" refers to "being seen at one time due to the instrument. [The inclusion of] the roots beginning with *ad* is due to the strength of their recitation in the list.
The meaning is that because there is no other result for [the suffix] *ada*, the rule for *vṛddhi* prevails, overriding the elision (*lopa*).

Regarding *saṅgrāma*: the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) *saṅgrāma*, which denotes battle, takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of "acting as" (*karoti*). Regarding the phrase *anudāttet*: this is mentioned in the rule *hṛśādibhyo bhuvī*.

Kaiyaṭa has stated: "Because of the elision (praśleṣa) of the letter *a*. By this, the elided (*praśliṣṭa*) [vowel] receives the designation *it*, while for the original (*prakṛti*) vowel *a*, there is elision of the *ṭi* by the rule "ṭeḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.153). Consequently, in the example *asasaṅgrāmatā* ("the state of not having fought"), there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel (*nopadhāhrasvaḥ*) due to the elision of the *a*. [The examples are] *sukha* and *duḥkha*. By the word *tat* (in the commentary)...

The meanings of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the verbal root (*dhātu*) are being referred to. Since the meaning of the root is already established by the rule "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*), the inclusion of these two [terms] is for the purpose of indicating that the suffix occurs after a root with a prefix (*sopasarga*); so say some. Furthermore, the purpose of this inclusion is so that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) should occur only in the sense of performing those actions denoted by *sukha* and *duḥkha*, and not in the sense of "explaining them" (*ācaṣṭe*).

Thus say others. "In the case of *puccha* and so forth" refers to the statement of Bhīmasena. "At the end of the book" means at the end of the Dhātupāṭha (the list of verbal roots) beginning with *bhū* in the sense of "existence. Thus ends the section on the *cur*-class verbs.
Now, the *div*-class verbs.

*Div* means "to play. The addition of the *udittva* (the property of having *u* as an *it*) is for the purpose of making the *iṭ* augment optional after the suffix *ktvā*, and for the purpose of making it absent in the *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) suffixes.
Examples: *devitvā* (having played), *dyūtvā* (having played), *dyūtam* (played). Regarding "play": *māṇavakā dīvyanti* ("the boys play").
Regarding "desire for victory": *śatruṃ dīvyati* ("he plays against the enemy"); the meaning is that he desires to conquer. *Kāntiḥ* means "desire."

Because of the separate mention of *dyauti*. In the case of *ṣivu*, as in *pariṣiṣeva*, the restriction that "the reduplication [occurs] only before affixes beginning with *th*" does not apply here, because the recurrence of the phrase "before *sita*" (*rāk sitāt*) is absent; and since this [root *ṣivu*] occurs prior to *sita*, the reduplication of the stem occurs. Thus, of the reduplication...

The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs precisely by the rule "after *ari*, *ni*, and *vi*. Thus we have *nyaṣavīt*. Regarding the root *nṛtī*, the inclusion of the marker *ī* is for the purpose of prohibiting the augment *iṭ* in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) by the rule "of roots marked with *ī* or *u*" (*vīdito niṣṭhāyām*). Even though the augment *iṭ* is optional after the root *sū* by the rule "after *sū*, *sici*," [the marker *ī* here serves its specific purpose].

Although the desired result is established by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā" alone, the addition of the marker *it* is nevertheless for the purpose of indicating that "yasya vibhāṣā" is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). By means of this,
forms such as "āvitam ibharājadhiyā" are established.

(290) *se'sici kṛt-chṛd-tṛd-nṛtaḥ* |7|2|57| In the presence of *sa* (the desiderative suffix), except when *sic* follows, [the augment *iṭ* is optionally added] after the roots *kṛt*, *chṛd*, *tṛd*, and *nṛt*. Examples: *nārtiṣyati* / *nartsyati* (he will dance); *ninartiṣati* / *ninṛtsati* (he desires to dance).
*kartiṣyati* / *kartsyati* (he will cut); *cikartiṣati* / *cikṛtsati* (he desires to cut). The same should be understood for other cases as well.

*anartīt*: Since it is stated that [the suffix] *ṭhasic* [is used], *iṭ* is here obligatory. *tresasuḥ*: By the rule *vā jṛbhramutrasām*, there is optionally the substitution of *et* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplication. *kutha*: the state of becoming putrid—i.e., becoming pure. *kuthyati bhūmiḥ*: the earth becomes putrid; the meaning is that it becomes purified. *puṣpa*...
In the sense of "blooming": in the rule *ālātsādhupuṣyatpacyamāneṣu*, the root *puṣ* ends in the suffix *śatṛ*.

With the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class), we have *puṣpa*. With the suffix *kan* when used as a name (*saṃjñā*), we have *puṣpaka*. Regarding *vrīḍ*: by the rule *ghuroraśca halaḥ*, the suffix *ap* is applied, and with the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, we have *vrīḍā*. If the suffix *ghañ* is applied instead, we have *vrīḍa*. For this very reason, it brings shame to me... [he says].
"Saṃprati" [is used] by Kālidāsa; and Māgha also says: "As if out of shame, it melted away through repeated practice.
Regarding the roots *ṣaha* and *ṣuha*: in the rule "arinivibhyaḥ," the vowel *a* in *saha* is for the sake of pronunciation, and thus the substitution of *ṣ* occurs here [in the presence of *pari*].
Thus we have *pariṣahyati*. However, the optional insertion of *iṭ* (as prescribed by the rule "īṣasahe") does not apply to this root.

It exists [as *ah*], because of the citation of the stem-form (*śabanta*) as ‘*ahe*’; however, Ātreya and others maintain that this [form] belongs specifically to the root ‘*ah marṣaṇe*’. Since the citation as ‘*saha*’ is identical in both cases, the citation with the suffix *śap* occurs in the rule ‘*īṣatsaha*’, but not in the rule ‘*ari-ni-vibhyaḥ*’—this is like the "half-old woman" fallacy (*ardhajarati*).
This alone is the truth; however, it must be determined by the great ones following the actual usage.

The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) in the neuter gender, as in *suhitaṃ tṛptiḥ*. For this very reason, in the rule *ūraṇa-rapara-guṇe*, it is explained that words meaning *suhita* have the sense of satisfaction (*tṛpti*). [The form] *jeratuḥ* [is derived as follows].

In the case of *jṛ*, when the *guṇa* [substitution] has been applied by the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām*, the subsequent application of *ata ekahalmadhye* is prohibited because the word *guṇa* in the rule *aśasadadeḥ* refers to that which has already undergone *guṇa*. Consequently, there arises an option for *etva* (the substitution of *e*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) by the rule *vā jṛbhramutrasām*. As for *sūṅ*, its meaning is procreation or birth.

The word "living being" (*prāṇin*) is used because there is no such usage as “a lump of clay produces a jar” (*ṛtpiṇḍo ghaṭaṃ sūyate*). Since it will be stated later that "the roots *va* and so forth are marked with *odit*," the rule "*oditaśca*" applies, resulting in the substitution of *na* for the *t* of the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*). Thus, [the forms] are *prasūnam* and *vikalpam*. The word "also" (*api*) is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. This occurs when a prohibition would otherwise have applied.
Thus [it is said]. The intention is that this follows from the force of the commencement of the section on prohibitions (*pratiṣedhakāṇḍa*) which precedes it.

(291) *dīṅo yuḍ aci kṅiti* | P. 6.4.63. Regarding *dīṅaḥ*: he explains by supplying the word "of the following" (*parasya*), taking it as an ablative case (*pañcamī*). Regarding *ajādeḥ*: [the rule is] *aṛ...* [etc.]... "not beginning with *a*" (*aja-ādi*).

Just as in the case of *sī* [Pāṇini 6.4.65], when both [the locative and ablative] are mentioned, the mention of the ablative is stronger; thus, the seventh case (*saptamī*) is interpreted as a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Why [is it said] "before a vowel" (*aci*)? [Consider: *dedīyate*. Why [is it said] "before *k* or *ṅ*" (*kṅti*)? [Consider: *upādānam*. Fearing that [the rule] might be considered non-existent due to being "unestablished" (*asiddha*) by virtue of being an *ābhīya* (an intermediate operation), he says: "The *vuk* and *yuṭ* [augmentations]."

It should be stated that *yuṭ* and *uvaṅ* are established [as being already present] before *ṇi*. For example, in *didīye*: although *yaṇ* occurs later, *yuṭ* applies first because it is obligatory (*nitya*). If *yaṇ* were applied first, the vowel *ī* would not be heard;
therefore, it is said that *yuṭ* is established.

(292) *mīnātiminotidīṅāṃ lyapi ca* | Pāṇini 6.1.50. [The substitution of ā for ī applies] to the roots *mīnāti*, *mīñ* (in the sense of injury), and *ḍu-mīñ* (in the sense of throwing), even when followed by the suffix *lyap*. Examples: *pramāya*, *upadāya*;
*pramātavyam*, *upadātavyam*. The locative case in the rule *ejñimita* is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Therefore...

First there is the substitution of *ā* (by *ātaścopasarge*), and afterwards the suffix *ghañ*. Then, by the rule *āto yuc*, the suffix *yuk* is added; thus, the form *upādāya* is established. Otherwise, if the suffix *ac* were applied first, and then the substitution of *ā*, the form would have been *upada*. Regarding *adāsta*: because of the prohibition for the root *īṅ* (*īṅḥ pratiṣedhaḥ*), the rule *thādhvoritveṭaḥ* does not apply, and thus the form *adita* does not occur due to the absence of the *ghu*-designation.
Some say it occurs. Others, however, maintain that the rule *thādhvoricca* does not apply here;

for since this is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the root *dīṅ*, the form *dā* is impossible, and thus it is not a *ghu* vowel. For this very reason, they say that in forms such as *pranidātā*, the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade* (Pāṇini 8.4.1) does not occur. This is the underlying point: "a..."

The status of being a *ghu* (the technical designation for certain roots) is possible for [the root] *dā* in the sense of "cutting" (*avakhaṇḍana*) and so forth, because the rule "ādeca upadeśe" (Pāṇini 6.1.45) is not conditional (*anaimitika*). However, in the case of the root *dīṅ*, the substitution of *ā* occurs only when a suffix marked with *eṅ* follows;
since such a suffix is absent in the case of the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the form *dā*, the status of being a *ghu* does not apply. And thus:
Since there is also no *ghu*-nature [in this case], the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not apply. Regarding the root *ḍīṅ*:

*ḍīnaḥ*, *ḍīnavān*. Because of its placement among the roots beginning with *svādi*, there is no *iṇ* augment in the *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle). For if *iṭ* were present, the *n* would be separated [from the suffix], and thus the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule "after a root ending in *ṭh* or *ud*" would not occur. [This applies] among the *svādi* roots.

One should not suspect that the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs even when there is an intervention by *ḍ*, on the strength of the traditional recitation (*pāṭha*), because [the rule] must conform to what is desired [by the grammarians]. As for the usage *ḍayati*, however, it belongs to the root *ḍī* of the Bhūvādigaṇa. Regarding the form *niṣṭhā* in the rule *iṣṭhā śīṅ*, they say that by splitting the yoga as *niṣṭhā*, the *guṇa* [substitution] applies when the suffix *aka* is added. The root *mīṅ* means "to injure."

*mīñ* belongs to the *kry-ādi* group. "Separation from life" (*prāṇaviyoga*) means: *mīyate*; the sense is that one is deprived of the vital breaths. *līṅ*: *lī* in the sense of "adhering" (*śleṣaṇa*) belongs to the *rky-ādi* group. (293) *vibhāṣā līyate* Pāṇini 6.1.51.
The term *yak* refers to that which is prescribed by the rule *ārdhadhātuke yak*; it does not refer to *śyan*. The intention is that otherwise, he would have simply said *īṅ*.
He states the purpose of the reference by means of *yak* in the phrase *līlīṅoḥ*:
*lyapi*—as in *vilāya* and *vilīya*. [The root] *vīṅ* has the meaning of covering (*vṛṇoti*).

The root *vṛ* [in the sense of] "choosing" (*varaṇa*), because it will be listed among the *svādi* roots as *vṛñ varaṇe*. Although one could have simply said "in choosing" (*varaṇe*), the expression "the meaning of *vṛṇoti*" (*vṛṇoty-artha*) is used for the sake of stylistic variety. The root *vrī* [in the sense of] "choosing" belongs to the *rkyādi* group. [The root] *māṅ*: [it means] "to measure" (*māyate*). It does not take the *it* augment by the rule *humāsthe*.
In this context, because of the governing rule *ardhadhātuke* [Pāṇini 3.4.114], [we have] *otaḥ śyani* [Pāṇini 7.3.71].
[The root] *ṣo* [ending in] *anta-* means "destruction. [Thus: "O Rāghava! [the destruction] by his fierce arrows..."

In the phrase "rāvaṇamāhave," *rāghava* is in the vocative case (*saṃbuddhyanta*). *Asya* is the second person singular present indicative middle (*loṇmadhyamaikavacana*). Regarding *abhiṣyati*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *upasargātsunoti*. Regarding *abhyaṣyat*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *rāksitādaḍvyavāye’pi*. Regarding *abhisasau*:
In the case of *sthādiṣu*, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur due to the restrictive rule. The root *do* means "to cut" (*avakhaṇḍane*).

The employment of the prefix *ava-* is for the sake of stylistic variety (*vaicitrya*), since the desired result is established even if only "cutting" (*khaṇḍane*) were stated. In *praṇidātā*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *ergade*.
"deyāt"—here, by the rule "ṭeret," the *etva* (substitution of *e*) occurs. "adāt"—here, by the rule "ātisthā," there is the elision (*luk*) of the *sic* suffix.

(296) *jñājanorjā* | Pāṇini 7.3.79: "In place of the roots *jñā* and *jan*, [the substitute] *jā* [is applied]. As in *jānāti*. Why "before a *śit* [suffix]"? Consider *jñātā*. [The substitute is] *ā*.

Even though a long vowel would be established by the rule *ṭhato dīrgho yañi* despite the short pronunciation [of the suffix], the explicit mention of *jā* is for the purpose of making known the *paribhāṣā* "that which is performed on the *aṅga* [does not recur]. By this, when the substitute *piba* is applied to the root *pā*, *guṇa* does not occur; this is because the substitute *piba* is based on its having an *a* as its final letter.
They say this is another means [of avoiding the substitution].

(297) *janivadhyośca* | Pāṇini 6.1.6. And for the roots *jan* and *vadh*, when followed by an affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*. Regarding "when followed by an affix marked with *ñ*," an example with the affix *ghañ* is *janaḥ*. When followed by an affix marked with *ṇ*: [example follows].

But as for the forms: *janakaḥ* [is derived from] *jan*, meaning "to produce. In the case of *janayati*, because the vowel is subject to *upadhā-vṛddhi*, the rule *an-ij-ṛt* applies, whereby the suffix is marked with *mit*;

consequently, by the rule *itāṃ hrasvaḥ*, the vowel is shortened. *Dīpī* means "to shine. Because it is marked with *īt*, there is no substitution of *iṇ* before the *niṣṭhā* suffix; thus, we have *dīptaḥ*. From the root *pūrī* (meaning "to fill") and others, because they are marked with *īt*, we have *pūrṇaḥ*, and so forth.
This is to be understood. Regarding the phrase "some, however": in their opinion, the usage is *aiśvarye tapyate* (he suffers in sovereignty) and not *tapatīti* (he heats).
Regarding *nyaviśata*: from the root *viś* preceded by *ni*, the suffix *ksa* is applied in the *luṅ* tense according to the rule *ila igupadha*;
the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is applied according to the rule *erviśaḥ*. The root *vāśṛ* means "to sound"; the suffix *urac* is applied according to the rule *andivāśī*.

The word *vāśurā* means "night. Regarding the term *titikṣā*, the suffix *san* is applied by the rule *uptijkidbhyaḥ*. For it is stated therein: *ije kṣamāyām* (the root *ij* takes *san* in the sense of endurance). *Śuci-* is derived from the root *ī*; because it is marked with *īt*, there is no augment *iṭ*. Thus, *śuktam* means "moistened. In the form *nanaddha*, the substitution of *dh* for *h* occurs by the rule *aho dhaḥ*.

(298) *ciṇ te padaḥ* | 3|1|60|. Regarding *ciṇ te padaḥ*: the word *ta* refers—by virtue of its semantic fitness—to the third person singular of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Why [is it specified] as the word *ta*? [To exclude other forms.]

*apatthāḥ*. [The form] *praṇyapādīt* [is derived as follows]: by the rule *iṇo luṅ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ta*; by the rule *eṛṇadeḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṇa*. *abodhīt*: by the rule *īpajanabudheḥ*, there is the suffix *ciṇ*. Regarding *ano rudha kāme*: the root *rudh* following the prefix *anu* means "desire" or "wish," because of its inclusion among the roots beginning with *div* (the fourth class).

By the rule *udhādibhyaḥ*, the suffix *śyan* supersedes *śnam*; thus we have *nāpyam*. This is because the rule *ṛjidṛśorjhalyamakitī* prescribes the suffix *am* only when a non-*kit* affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant follows. Regarding *liś*:
the state of becoming small (*alpa-bhāva*) from what was not small due to heat and so forth is "becoming small" (*alpībhāva*). Thus: *likṣīṣṭa*.
In *alikṣata*, there is no *guṇa* substitution because the suffix is *kit* by the rule *iṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu*.

In *alikṣata*, the suffix *ksa* is applied by the rule *ala igupadhaḥ*. Regarding the rule *rādho ’karmakāt*, he shows that the word order is different—namely, that it means "only from an intransitive [verb] *rādh*"—by explaining that the suffix *śyan* is applied to *rādh* only in the sense of "increase" (*vṛddhi*) when it is intransitive.
The qualification would be redundant because this [root] is intransitive (*akarmaka*) in the sense of "growing" (*vṛddhi*). What is the purpose of the term "intransitive"?

[Consider: *śatrum aparādhnoti*. The meaning is "he injures. The root *rādh* is listed in the *svādi* group in the sense of "attainment" (*saṃsiddhi*). Because of the restatement [of the rule] "√*rādh* in the sense of injury" (*ādho hiṃsāyām*), this [root] also applies in the sense of injury. He states an example.

The sense is: "of any meaning whatsoever that serves as the cause for [the verb] being intransitive. He shows the usage of the form ending in *śyan* when it is intransitive with the words beginning with "yan mahyam" (that which [is given] to me). "Kṛṣṇāya": the dative case is used according to the rule "rādhīkṣyor yasya vipraśnaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.4.39). "Apuṣat": there is an absence of guṇa due to the suffix *ṅti*. [The root is] *śuṣ*.
*śoṣṭa*, *śokṣyati*. He explains the rule *śliṣa āliṅgane* by means of a division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*)—namely, *śliṣaḥ*. (299) *śliṣaḥ* | 3|1|46|.

"Ksa is substituted for the *cli* affix of a root that does not take the augment *iṭ*. The intention is that this [rule] follows from the rules "the *sic* is substituted for *li*" and "for a root ending in a consonant with a penultimate *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*, the *k* is added. Why specify "of a root that does not take *iṭ*"? So that it does not apply to the root *liṣ* (meaning 'to burn') belonging to the Bhūvādigaṇa, which takes *iṭ*; as in *aśleṣīt*. [Objection: This is already established by the rule "for a root ending in a consonant with a penultimate *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*... [Response: True, but [the present rule is stated] for the sake of brevity (*laghava*).
Again, he states the result regarding the rule for *kṣa*: "puṣādyaṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.55).
Regarding "āliṅgane" (3.1.46):
[the phrase] "by virtue of the sense" (*sāmarthyāt*) is used because if *kṣa* were restricted as being applicable only when it has already been obtained by the root *liṣ*, then...
The sense is that the *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) would be rendered useless.

This applies to the rule *śala igupadhāt* as well; consequently, in cases such as *karmaṇy ātaḥ* and so forth, when there is no embracing (*anāliṅgane*), only *sij* occurs and not *ksa*. As in the example: *amāśliṣata jatūni kāṣṭham*.

The intention is that if the suffix *ksa* were applied, the form would be *samāśliṣanta*. Regarding the phrase "in the case of proximity" (*pratyāsattau*), the meaning is that embracing is performed by sentient beings, not by inanimate objects such as wood.
He demonstrates the result of the explanation: "the suffix *ksa* is applied after the root *liṣ* only in the sense of embracing."

By the words "karmaṇi" and so forth: although there is no difference between the suffixes *ksa* and *sic* in forms such as *aślikṣātām* because of the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "sasyāci," nevertheless, there is indeed a difference in cases such as *thās* and others; indicating this, he provides the examples—*aśliṣṭhaḥ* and *aśliḍḍhvam*. The phrase "the Nyāsakāra and others" refers to [the authors of grammatical commentaries].

And thus, according to that view, when the rule "the suffix *kta* follows a root ending in *ṭh* or *ñī*" is in force, the suffix *kta* occurs. Because the root begins with *ā*, there is no *iṭ* augment in the *niṣṭhā* (past participle) suffix: *svinnaḥ*. By the rule "optionally [there is no *iṭ*] in the case of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*)," forms such as *svinnam* and *sveditam* are established. Regarding the root *ṣidhu*: its meaning is "accomplishment" (*saṃrāddhi*) or "completion" (*niṣpatti*). [It is marked with] *udit*.

In the word *ve*, there is an option regarding the augment *iṭ* after the suffix *ktvā*. In the case where *iṭ* is applied, the suffix may optionally be treated as *kit* by the rule *ṭhralo vyupadhāt*. Thus, we have *sidhitvā*, *sedhitvā*, and *siddhvā*. As for the statement "it is an error": the meaning is that the inclusion of *sidhyati* among the *ūdita* (roots marked with *ū*) roots in the list of *anudāteta* (unaccented) roots would otherwise be redundant.

(301) *radhādibhyaśca* | Pāṇini 7.2.45. From the roots beginning with *radh*, the suffix *iṭ* is optionally applied before the *liṭ* affixes. The word "optionally" (*vā*) is understood from the previous rule, *varatisūti*. The division of the sūtra into two separate rules is for the sake of variety. Because the root is specified by its inclusion in the list (*gaṇa*), when there is elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅ-luk*), the form is only *rāradhita* and not *rāraddha*.

(302) *neṭi liṭi radheḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.62. "Except before the augment *iṭ* in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]. Why say "except before *iṭ*"? [Observe: *randhakaḥ*. Why say "except in the *liṭ*"? [Observe: *rarandhiva*. Once the *num* augment has been applied, because it follows a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), the base is no longer considered *akita*; therefore, the elision of the *n* does not take place.

(303) *masjinaśor jhali* [Pāṇini 7.1.60]. Regarding *naṣṭa*: one should not suspect the application of the *kutva* substitution here by the rule *aśervā*, because that rule is prescribed only for word-final positions. Otherwise, forms such as *naṣṭam* and *naṣṭiḥ* would not be established. As for *praṇaśyati*: [the *ṇatva* substitution applies].
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "ṭhupasargādasamāse’pi" (Pāṇini 8.4.14).
Regarding the rule "naśeḥ ṣāntasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.36):
from the rule "na bābhūpūkamiganī" (Pāṇini 8.4.35), the word "na" is understood to carry over. Therefore, he says: there is no substitution of *ṇ*.

It might be so. Even though "of this" (*asya*) is stated, since the word "of a word" (*padasya*) is understood as a qualifier for "ending in *ṣ*," the inclusion of the term "final" (*anta*) would be redundant; therefore, he says—"having previously been so"—to indicate that it serves as a technical indicator (*jñāpaka*).
As for "kāṣṭhānām": the genitive case is used because the instrument (*karaṇa*) is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*). In that context, [the rule applies] to *tatra-pṛthā*.

The augment *am* is optionally applied by the rule "ṭhanudātasya cardupadhasya. The term "radhādayaḥ" means the roots beginning with *radh*, namely: *radh*, *naś*, *tṛp*, *dṛp*, *druh*, *muha*, *ṣṇuh*, and *ṣṇih*. Because it is marked with the indicatory letter *u*, there is optional *iṭ*: *śamitvā* or *śāntvā*. By the rule "yasya vibhāṣā," it is *aniṭ* in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*): *śāntaḥ*.

(305) *śamāmaṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ śyani* 7.3.74. *bhramu* means "to wander" or "lack of stability. Regarding the word *śeṣam* ("the rest"): it means that which is other than what has been stated as the specific rule regarding the lengthening [of the vowel] before the suffix *śyan* and the substitution of *iṅ* for *luṅ*. In the case of *cakṣaṇva*, once the substitution of *na* for *ma* has been made by the rule *vośca*... [the form is derived].

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs. Regarding the mention of the group beginning with *śam*: [the rule] is “*ghinuṇ* after the eight beginning with *śam*. Regarding the group beginning with *śam*: it means *śam*, *tam*, *dam*, *śram*, *bhram*, *kṣam*, *klam*, and *mad*. (306) Pāṇini 3.1.71: *yaso ’nupasargāt* (“[The suffix *ghinuṇ* is added] after the root *yas*, provided it is not preceded by a prefix”).
Regarding *yaso'nupa*—here they say: let it simply be *yasaḥ*. Then [the word] *amaḥ* follows.

This is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning: "If there is *yasa-* with a prefix (*sopasarga*), it occurs only when preceded by *sam-.*" And thus, the mention of *anupasargāt* in the preceding sūtra and the mention of *yasaḥ* in the subsequent one may be dispensed with.

Regarding "śakya": "it is recited in the [section on] burning" means that *vyuṣ* (to burn) is recited in this very same class [of roots]. Regarding "arṅtham": for that which is recited in the [section on] burning, however, there is only the *sij* [augment]. "avyoṣīt"—thus ends the section on the *divādi* [roots] in the *Tattvabodhinī*.

(767) *cārthe dvandvaḥ* | 2|2|29|. A *dvandva* compound occurs in the sense of *ca* ("and"). From the rule *anekam anyapadārthe*, the word *anekam* ("more than one") is understood to carry over; from *vāmantrite...* (*ubhe amantrite...*), the term *sub* ("ending in case-suffixes") is understood; and from the preceding rules, the terms *samāsaḥ* ("compound") and *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") are also understood.
And indeed, [the word] is further qualified. Thus he says: "several words ending in *su*-affixes," and so forth.

"The meanings of *ca*" means those things manifested by the word *ca*. "In one" means in an action such as worship and the like. "Worship the Lord and the teacher"—this is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of two substances within a single action. Likewise, [in the case of] the king...

"An elephant and a horse"—this is a conjunction (samuccaya) of two substances (*dravya*) with a substance. "A cloth that is white and red"—this is a conjunction of two qualities (*guṇa*) with a substance. One should infer accordingly: "A red cloth and an earring"—this is a conjunction of two substances with a quality.
[And: "Go for alms and bring the cow. For here, because it is not seen, even one who does not bring the cow [is understood].

He indeed goes for alms; however, one who does not go for alms does not bring the cow. Likewise, even when going, he brings the cow without having specifically sought it out. Therefore, the primary purpose is the wandering for alms, while the bringing of the cow is merely incidental. "Due to incapacity" means due to the absence of the formation of a single integrated meaning (ekārthībhāva).

For instance, just as the formation of a *bahuvrīhi* compound necessarily requires the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) through the inclusion of objects (*karman*, etc. within its constituent members, so too must the formation of a *dvandva* compound require the inclusion of a collective sense (*cārtha*) within its members;

this is because of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "a grammatical operation concerning words [occurs] when there is no meaning [to be expressed separately]" (*asamarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), and because of the statement "a *dvandva* occurs in the sense of 'and' (*ca*)". Not so.

If, in the case of mutual connection (*itaretarānvaya*), a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) were possible among elements that are mutually independent— by virtue of which conjunction (*samuccaya*) and sequential mention (*anvācaya*) would be included within unification— then,
because of the existence of mutual association in both "conjunction with another" (*itarayoga*) and "aggregation" (*samāhāra*), a compound would occur; but it does not.
In the case of *samuccaya* (conjunction) and *anvācaya* (sequential addition), however, it should be distinguished that in *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction),

the collective association (*sāhitya*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the substance (*dravya*) is the qualified (*viśeṣya*), whereas in *samāhāra* (aggregation), the collective association is the primary element and the substance is the qualifier. Now, [one might object] regarding examples such as "blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*).

Because the analysis (vigraha) shows the inclusion of the word *ca* ("and") and because there is a state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), the formation of a *dvandva* compound would be unavoidable.

This is not so; for, since the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" prescribes a *tatpuruṣa* compound when there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), that *tatpuruṣa* designation sublates the *dvandva* designation.
However, that [rule] has its scope when there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*).

But when one intends to express the absence of coreferentiality, then even in the case of *nīlotpala* (blue lotus) and the like, just as in the case of *pramāṇaprameya* (means of knowledge and object of knowledge) and so forth, the desired result is simply attained in a copulative compound (*dvandva*). As for *hotṛpotṛ* (the Hotṛ and Potṛ priests): [this is explained as follows].
Because these two [words] do not have another word following them as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the *ānaṅ* substitution does not occur.

(Pāṇini 2.2.31) "In the case of *rājadanta* and similar compounds, the subsequent [member is placed first]. Although these are listed here among both *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds, for the sake of the meaning...
This [word] is presented in a *dvandva* compound with the intention of beginning with "dharma" and so forth.
In a *dvandva* compound, [the case-ending of] the *ghi*-ending [member] [is elided]. [The word] "aneka" [applies] to all of them.

Since there would be no fixed rule due to the lack of distinction in their status as secondary members (*upasarjana*) because both are designated as the first [member] by the rule, this [sūtra] is commenced.
However, where there are multiple words ending in the suffix *dhi*, a restriction regarding the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of both would follow; therefore, he says:

"When there is the possibility of multiple [applications], there is a restriction to one; there is no restriction regarding the remainder. Regarding "when there is the possibility of multiple," the commentators have explained: when the word-meaning is a class (*ākṛti*), the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) applies once to the collection [of instances], not by repeating it for each individual instance. In that case, when one [term] is placed first, the rule applies to the genus (*jāti*).

"Since it has already occurred, it does not occur again. Here, the view that [the rule applies to] individual instances (*vyaktipakṣa*) is not adopted, because one must follow the actual usage of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*). Regarding the example "Hari-hara-guravaḥ," the sense is that the restriction [of the elision of *na*] does not apply to the words *hara* and *guru*.

(770) *ajādyadantam* | 2|2|33|. [The rule] "feminine stems beginning with *aja-* and ending in short *a*" is not universally applicable (*anitya*), as indicated by such rules as *amudrābhrāddaḥ* and *akṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*. Therefore, [the form] *asauṣṭha-*...
The usage by the poet Bhāravi, "vaidūryaviśeṣaśālinī," is thus consistent.

[The compound is formed with] that which has fewer syllables. Precisely for this reason, the suffix *tarap* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) by means of a formal rule (*nipātana*), and there is an absence of the changes to *kutva* and *cutva*.

If, however, the suffix *tarap* were used in the sense of excellence (*prakarṣa*), then the restriction would apply only to two [things], because the rule for *tarap* is prescribed specifically for cases where the accompanying word (*upapada*) ends in the dual number. Consequently, in instances such as "the *hari*, *vadira*, and *palāśa* trees," the restriction would not apply to a plurality.

Regarding the phrase "of the seasons and the lunar mansions" (*ṛtukṣatrāṇām*): the sequence of the seasons is determined by their manifestation, whereas that of the lunar mansions is determined by their rising. Furthermore, it is [a matter of] relative honor (*abhyarhitam*). And [it is a matter of] relative honor. [As stated in the rule: "The suffix *vuñ* is applied after *vāsudeva* and *arjuna*."

The commentary on the fourth [chapter] states that this is made known by the *nirdeśa* (explicit statement). Since the rule "that which has fewer syllables" (*alpāctaram*) and the rule "that which begins with a vowel and ends in 'a'" (*ajādyadantam*) would have required *arjuna* to be placed first, the fact that he was not so placed makes it known that "in that very same rule (*ajādyadantam*), it will be stated: 'that which is more important (*abhyahita*) comes first.'"
Regarding "the elder brother":

the intention is that even though Arjuna possesses a superior status— due to being the son of Indra, an incarnation of Viṣṇu, or being a Śūra— this does not establish a fixed rule [regarding precedence] by means of him alone.
(772) *Dvandva* [compounds] consisting of parts of living beings, musical instruments, and armies [are singular].

2.4.2. The rule *dvandvaścaprāṇi* [is explained as follows]: "parts of living beings, musical instruments, and armies" (*prāṇitūryasenānām aṅgāni*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with the word *aṅga* in the plural. Furthermore, the word *aṅga*...

It follows each individual member. Therefore, a *dvandva* compound consisting of parts of living beings [with other] parts of living beings, musical instruments with musical instruments, or military units with military units becomes singular, but not when there is a difference [in category]. Thus, in this case, it is not so: *mārdaṅgika-aśvārohau* (the drummers and the horsemen). Here...

The term *aṅga* refers to a limb or constituent part of living beings (*prāṇin*) and armies (*senā*). However, in the case of musical instruments (*tūrya*), *aṅga* should be understood as a contributing component. The phrase "the dvandva of these" means: a dvandva compound of limbs of living beings, a dvandva compound of components of musical instruments, and a dvandva compound of components of armies. This follows from the rule "a dvigu takes the singular number."

The singular number is employed. Therein, thinking that by the etymological derivation "that which speaks one [thing]," it should denote an object in the form of a collective (samāhāra) qualified by oneness, he states the resulting conclusion: "it should be treated as a singular. As in the case of *pāṇipādam* ("hand and foot"), although here—

The rule is already established by the phrase "after words denoting non-living beings" (*ātiraprāṇinām*); nevertheless, some say that the mention of "living beings" (*prāṇi*) is for the purpose of ensuring the suffix occurs even when the substance (the object) is predominant. Others say the statement is for the sake of restriction, so that it does not apply in cases of confusion such as *prāṇipaṇau*. Regarding *mārdaṅgika*: it means one who plays the mṛdaṅga drum.

In the sense of "this is his craft," the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *adasya śilpam*. In the same way, one also forms *āṇavika*. Regarding the term *rathikāśvāroham*: those who move about by means of a chariot (*ratha*) are *rathikās*;

[this is derived] with the suffix *ṣṭhan* according to the rule *ṛgṛdibhyaḥ ṣṭhan*. These [charioteers] and the horse-riders (*aśvārohāḥ*) together constitute their collective compound (*samāhāra*). [Objection: But surely, in the sense of...?
