Anticipating the objection—"By the rule *dvandvaḥ*, the collective *dvandva* (samāhāra-dvandva) is established, and since it is singular, the use of the singular number is also established; so what is the purpose of this [present rule]?"—he says: "For the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*). That is to say, "only in the case of a collective. Here, the reverse restriction—that "it applies only to parts of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*) and so forth when forming a collective"—does not occur.

This is because of the inclusion of the plural number in the sūtra “iṣyapunarvasvau. Indeed, that [plural] was employed so that, in the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), a singular form might not become a dual; otherwise, it would not have been “iṣyapunarvasvau. And thus, by the rule “dvandvaśca prāṇitūryasenāṅgānām,” [the dual is established].
Even for those words that have become numerous due to their specific context, a collective copulative compound (samāhāra-dvandva) certainly occurs; therefore,
it should be understood that the reading "a copulative compound of many [members] optionally becomes a singular" is not an unprecedented statement.

(773) *anuvāde caraṇānām* |2|4|3|. Regarding the word *caraṇānām*: it means "of those denoting Vedic schools (*śākhādhyetṛ*). It should be stated that [the prohibition applies] after the roots *sthā* and *iṇ*. Regarding *sthā* and *iṇ*: *sthā* is in the sense of "cessation of motion" (*gatinivṛtau*), and *iṇ*...

The meaning is: when the words *gata* (gone), *sthita* (stood), or those having *eṇ* as their suffix (i.e., *utpanna*, etc. are present as the *upapada*. Why [specify] *stheṇoḥ*? [Consider: *abhūvan kaṭhakālāpāḥ* ("the Kaṭhas and Kālāpas have come into being"). Why [specify] *luṅi*? [Consider: *tiṣṭhantu kaṭhakālāpāḥ* ("let the Kaṭhas and Kālāpas stand") and *udagāt* ("it has risen"). Here, when the Kaṭhas and Kālāpas have become established and have arisen...
Having made an agreement that "the two of us must go there," and having forgotten that agreement, he says this to one who is sitting [there]: "The Kaṭhas are those who study what was taught by Kaṭha.
The suffix *ṇini* is applied because he is a pupil of Vaiśampāyana; its elision is according to the rule "aṭhacarakā-".

As for the study [of it], there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "after *ru*, *lu* is elided. Regarding "one who recites" (*ālāpin*), there is elision of the suffix *aṇ* by the supplementary rule (*aupasaṅkhyāna*) beginning with "not a religious student" (*abrahmacārī*). As for "the *yajus*": the meaning is that in the sūtra, the word *adhvaryu* indicates the *Yajurveda*.

(774) *adhyayanato’viprakṛṣṭākhyānām* || 2.4.5 || [The suffix *vuñ* is added after words denoting names of persons who are not remote from one another in terms of study. Regarding the example *padaka*: one who studies the *pada-pāṭha* is called a *padaka*. [This is formed by adding] *vun* [to *pada*] according to the rule *ramādibhyo vun*. Similarly, there is also *kramaka*. Since the *krama-pāṭha* is to be studied immediately after one has studied the *pada-pāṭha*, the proximity [of the two] is clear. Why [is it specified] "from study" (*adhyayanataḥ*)? [To exclude cases where the relationship is based on other factors.]
"Father and son. Why [is it specified] "not separated by distance"? [Consider: "the ritualist and the logician. (775) *Jātir aprāṇinām* | 2|4|6|.
A genus (*jāti*). Even a dvandva compound whose constituent members denote a genus is metaphorically designated as a "genus."

With this intention, he says: "of those denoting a genus" (*jātivācinām*). Regarding the example "Viṭ-Śūdrāḥ," even though the genus is predominant, the plural number is justified by the rule: "in the case of a name for a genus, [the singular is used] when there is one.
Therefore, the meaning is that here there is no deficiency of two members [of the compound].

"Of those belonging to the class of substances (*dravyajātīyānām*) alone. The meaning is that because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not [of] non-living things" (*aprāṇinām*), by the maxim of "that which is connected with *naÑ*," there is a single-remainder formation (*ekavadbhāva*) for those belonging to the class of substances, but not for those belonging to the classes of qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*kriyā*). What is the purpose of the word "class" (*jāti*)? [Example: "The Nandaka and the Pāñcajanya [conchs]. (In this case, although they are substances, they are not treated as a single remainder because they do not belong to the same class.)
These two—*saṃjñā* (name) and *śabda* (word)—refer exclusively to that in which the genus (*jāti*) is predominant. And this is obtained from the mention of "genus" (*jāti*).

Otherwise, since it would be possible to include even those words denoting a substance where the genus is subordinate by means of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) itself, what would be the purpose of that [mention]? This is the sense. [Regarding the phrase] "a particular substance": but if this is so...
If it is argued that the usage by Bhāravi, "‘Are the various trees and mountains now anointed?
is indeed consistent [with the rule], and therefore why was it explained in the *Manoramā* as "mountains accompanied by trees"?
To this they say: what is intended there is the anointing of all the trees and mountains collectively, and not...

Regarding the phrase "of certain particular snowy mountains," it was stated in that way because one might suspect a singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) due to the predominance of the genus (*jāti*);

thus, [the author] says "badarāmalakān" (jujubes and emblic myrobalans). [The suffix] is elided by the rule "hale lūg" (Pāṇini 5.4.106), and [the feminine suffix] is elided by the rule "uktaddhitalukī" (Pāṇini 1.2.49).

Even when the feminine suffix is elided (*luk*), these two words denote a substance (*dravya*) where the genus (*jāti*) is subordinate to the fruit-ness; as will be stated under the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛga*—"badarāṇi cāmalakāni ca" [forms] "badarāmalakam"—by means of the rule *atiraprāṇinām*, which prescribes the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*). However, that point is not established by this particular passage.

It is objected: "The rule stated in the Vārttika *hal-senā-vana-spatī*, which accepts the restriction that 'only a dvandva compound of words denoting the genus *hal* (consonants) ending in the plural becomes singular, but not a dvandva ending in the singular,' applies here."

(776) *viśiṣṭaliṅgo nadīdeśo’grāmāḥ* | 2|4|7|. With the intention that in this sūtra all four words denote a *dvandva* compound as a whole by means of the property belonging to its parts, he says "grāma" and so forth. Here, there is a *dvandva* of words denoting rivers.

The rule “*eśavācināṃ dvandvaḥ*” (there is a *dvandva* compound of words denoting regions) should be explained as a separate syntactical unit (*vākyabheda*). Consequently, it does not apply in cases such as “*aṅgākurukṣetre*”. Here, by the word “region” (*deśa*), only a well-known inhabited territory (*janapada*) is understood, because rivers are mentioned separately [from regions]. Therefore, it does not apply to mountains, as in “*kailāsaśca*.”

[The examples] "Gandhamādanaṃ ca kailāsagandhamādane" and "nadīdeśa" [are given]. Why [is this rule stated]? [To exclude cases such as] "kukkuṭamayūryau" (a cock and a peahen). He states the meaning of the word *viśiṣṭa*: "of those with different genders. For the root *śiṣ* preceded by *vi-* has the sense of "differentiation. Therefore, in the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified," it means that which differentiates.

The term "by way of division" has already been explained. It was stated that a *dvandva* compound would be a collective (*samāhāra*) with the intention of extracting the essential meaning. However, it should be understood that according to the literal sense of the text, it is explained in certain sūtras as "a *dvandva* shall be treated as a singular."

Regarding the phrase "Uddhyerāvatī": Uddhya is a river; because it is a specific type of river, it is included under the term "river" (*nadī*). The same applies to the Śoṇa. Regarding the rule for "villages" (*grāma*), it must be stated that there is an exclusion for cities (*nagara*).
Consequently, in the case of "Mathurā-Pāṭaliputra," the prohibition does not apply, as both are [cities].
Because it is a city.
(777) *Kṣudrajantavaḥ* | 2|4|8|.
"Small" (*kṣudra*): smallness consists in having a diminished dimension. And that [smallness], being relative, is not fixed.

And as it is recorded: "A small creature may be one that has no bones, or it may simply be small; those whose weight is a hundred [in a handful] when measured by a handful (*prasṛti*), or even down to a mongoose. Regarding this, he provides an example that applies to all these positions: "lice and nits," and so on, up to "down to a mongoose."
The meaning is "ending with Nakula.

(778) *yeṣāṃ ca virodhaḥ śāśvatikaḥ* |2|4|9|. "And of those whose enmity is perpetual. Here, "enmity" (*virodha*) means hostility (*vaira*), not the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*). Therefore, in this case—

No—[the terms] "shadow" (chāyā) and "sunlight" (ātapa) [are not intended here]. The indeclinable (avyaya) "aśva" occurs in the sense of the three times (traikālya); that which exists therein is "eternal" (śāśvatika). [The suffix] -ṭhañ [is applied] by the rule "ālāṭhaṭhañ. Precisely because of this irregular derivation (nipātana), there is no substitution of *ka* for the final letter according to the rule "ti-susuktāntāt," nor is there elision of the *ṭi* (the first vowel) by the rule "avyayānāṃ bhamātre. Thus, it is "śāśvatikaḥ."

What [is the example]? The gods and asuras churned the ocean for the sake of the nectar (*amṛta*). For their opposition, occasioned by the nectar and so forth, is occasional (*kādācitka*) and not eternal (*nitya*), because it is absent at the time of engaging in the churning.

Regarding the term "on account of being subsequent" (*paratvāt*): the scope of the *dvandva* compound of animals and birds is, for instance, *gomahiṣam* (cow and buffalo) or *gomahiṣāḥ* (cows and buffaloes).

In "haṃsacakravākam" and "haṃsacakravākāḥ," the scope for the rule "yeṣāṃ ca... (Pāṇini 6.3.137) should be understood to apply in cases such as "mārjāramūṣakam" and "śramaṇabrāhmaṇam. It is said that [the former rule] is set aside by the word "ca"; the sense is that the word "ca" functions as a restatement (punarvidhāyaka).
(779) [The suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *śūdra* when it refers to those who are not excluded [from the community], provided they are Śūdras who are not outcastes.

Regarding the phrase "of the Śūdras": the word *śūdra* here refers to humans other than those belonging to the three higher castes (*raivarṇika*), and does not refer to the specific caste-essence (*jāti*) of being a Śūdra; this is because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] "not for those who are excluded" (*aniravasitānām*). [The rule continues with the condition] "starting from a vessel" (*pātrāt*).

The meaning is: for those [people] by whom even a vessel is not purified by the purificatory rite prescribed in the Smṛti, such as "a bell-metal vessel is purified by being smeared with the ashes of those who have eaten from it.
(780) *gavāśvaprabhṛtīni ca* || 2.4.11 || [And the words beginning with "cow" and "horse"].

"According as they are recited"—the meaning is that they are correct (sādhūni) exactly as they were taught by Pāṇini in the Gaṇapāṭha. Consequently, since the substitution *avaṅ* is optional, when *avaṅ* does not occur, there is no optionality provided by the subsequent rule. Thus, we have *goaśvam*. [The Vārttika states: "Others are indeed not cattle."

In *go-aśvebhyaḥ*, [the term] *paśavaḥ* refers to cattle such as cows and horses; thus, *gavāśvam*. Here, in a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of animals, the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) is applicable. In *daśī-dāsam*, the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) stated as "when followed by a feminine" (*pumān striyā*) is set aside. (781) *Vibhāṣā*.

Pāṇini 2.4.12: *vṛkṣamṛgatṛṇadhānyavyañjanapaśuśakunyaśvavaḍavapūrvāparādharottarāṇām* | *bibhāṣā* | *viśeṣaṇānām eveti* | This is the meaning: each word beginning with *vṛkṣa* (tree) is qualified by the term "dvandva" individually; it is not the case that the single word *vṛkṣa* is the dvandva, nor is there a dvandva consisting of two [words] together.

The application [of the rule] is not to the case of synonyms, because of the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) rule for "those that are not forms" (*arūpāṇām*). Nor is it to the case of synonyms that have different forms, because of the *ekaśeṣa* rule for "even those with different forms that have the same meaning" (*virūpāṇām api samānārthānām*). Nor is it to the case of a general term and a specific term, such as "tree" and "dhava," because there is no expression [of such a combination] in that regard.
He states a restrictive rule as a supplement to the entire section, [based on] the fact that there is simply no occurrence of a *dvandva* [compound] in these cases:

"It should be stated that for fruits, armies, trees, wild animals, birds, small creatures, grains, and grasses, only a *dvandva* consisting of many members is singular. [This begins with] "fruits, armies," and so forth.

The meaning is that when a *dvandva* compound such as *phalasenā* and so forth becomes a singular entity (*ekavadbhāva*)—either by the rule "optionally in the case of trees and wild animals" (*vṛkṣamṛga*) or by another grammatical characteristic—it becomes singular only when it has many constituent bases (*prakṛti*). That is to say, its cause (*prakṛti*) consists of many constituent words (*vartipada*), or rather, many items ending in the plural number. This is the sense. "Many" refers to the constituent word-meanings, or those ending in the plural; this is its "base" (*prakṛti*), meaning its cause.

It has many constituent members: "jujubes and emblic myrobalans. According to the rule "in a collective name consisting of a single [member]," the plural number is optional; thus, one may say *badarāmalakāni*. Even when the genus (*jāti*) is predominant, there is no formation of a singular compound (*ekavadbhāva*) because the *dvandva* ends in the singular.
The term *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. Regarding the mention of *paśu* (animals), it is understood that the phrase "for the sake of option" (*vikalpārtham*) is to be supplied.

Having raised the objection that the mention of *mṛga* (wild animals) and *śakuni* (birds) is redundant—since [the formation] is already established by the rule "a copulative compound [expressing] a single meaning" (*ārthe dvandvaḥ*)—he says: "of wild animals, only with wild animals," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the neuter gender": this is the intended meaning—since the status of being a *paśu* (animal) is already established for the compound, the specific mention of *aśvavaḍava* is for the purpose of prescribing the form by its own rule (*pratipadavidhi*).
Therefore, in the case where the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) applies, such as *aśvavaḍavam*, [the rule] *ūrvavadaśvavaḍavau* is set aside.

The term ‘napuṃsaka’ (neuter) itself [is applied here]. For, by referring with the word ‘a’ to that which possesses the state of being treated as a single unit (ekavadbhāva), the neuter gender prescribed [by the rule] becomes just like the state of being treated as a single unit, as it is directly enjoined (pratipadavihita). And thus:
The neuter gender is established because that which is expressed by the first rule [P. 2.4.12] possesses greater force.

(782) *vipratiṣiddhaṃ cānadhikaraṇavāci* (P. 2.4.13). "Mutually contradictory" (*vipratiṣiddham*). Here, "substratum" (*adhikaraṇa*) refers to a substance (*dravya*). The particle *ca* is for the purpose of drawing back the option (*vibhāṣā*) from the preceding rule.

He explains this with the words "of contradictory objects," and so forth. The examples, however, are: cold and heat, cold and warm, pleasure and pain, pleasure and painful, and so on. Here, contradiction is characterized by non-coexistence. [The phrase] "it indeed occurs" [is used]; for if the term "contradictory" (*vipratiṣiddha*) were not included, that [non-coexistence] would not [be established].
The intention is that this would be so because of the restriction "only for those denoting non-substances.

Why [is it said] "not denoting a locus"? [Consider: *śītoṣṇe udake staḥ* ("cold and hot [qualities] exist in the water"). In this case, there might also be an optional collective dvandva compound; such is the direction [of the argument].

(783) Not [the dual forms] *dadhi* and *payaḥ*, etc. || 2.4.14 || Not [the dual forms] *dadhi* and *payaḥ*. For example: *dadhipayasī* ("curds and milk"). Because these are considered *vyañjana* (condiments/sides), the optional application [of the rule for vowel-initial endings] was obtained. The same should be understood for *madhusarpiṣī* ("honey and ghee") and *sarpirmadhunī* ("ghee and honey"). Here, [in the case of] *brahmaprajāpatī* ("Brahmā and Prajāpati"), [the rule does not apply].
In examples such as *‘ivavaiśravaṇau’*, this [sūtra] establishes an *itaretara-yoga* (copulative) compound by way of prohibiting a *samāhāra-dvanda* (collective).
By association with that, the same applies in cases such as *‘dadhipayasī’*. Therefore, in those instances—

One should not suspect that even though the alternative involving the nature of a *vyañjana* (consonant) has been refuted, there might still be a permanent state of singular concord (*ekavadbhāva*) characterized by *jāti* (genus). Furthermore, there is no insistence here on a specific definition; rather, the point is merely that "these [sounds] would not be singular."

Because of the prohibition; for example, in the rule *a ṣaṭsvasrādibhyaḥ*, in order to establish the prohibition of both *ṅīp* and *ṭāp*, it is prohibited in a general sense by stating, "That which is prescribed for the feminine does not apply here.
This is the direction [of the argument]. Regarding the expression *ṛksāme vāṅmanase*: here, [the suffix] is applied by the rule *ṭhacatura-*, etc.
The suffix *ac* is introduced as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) at the end of a compound. Regarding the term *adhikaraṇa*:

the substratum (*āśraya*) of the meaning of the compound is the *adhikaraṇa*, which is the meaning of the prior member (*upapada*). Its "extent" (*etāvatva*) is the restriction regarding its enumeration. He explains [the phrase] "when that is being understood"—namely, when the number of substances (*dravya-saṅkhyā*) is apprehended.
Thus [it is said].

(784) And in the case of "the measure of the substratum" (adhikaraṇaitāvatva), there would be no restriction; nor does the rule "only as one" (ekavad eva) apply here, because it is already established by virtue of being a part of a living being (prāṇyaṅga).
It should not be argued that even when the rule [of the restrictive compound] is prohibited, a collective dvandva (samāhāra-dvandva) would still occur by the rule "dvandva in the sense of *ārtha*";

for, since it is accepted that "there is no formation of a compound for those lacking qualifiers," there is no possibility for a collective dvandva to arise. Nor can it be said that, by the aforementioned logic, even the *itaretara-yoga* dvandva (copulative compound) would not occur.

It must be stated that [the rule] applies because of the indicator (liṅga) in the sūtra “āṅmayo ’prayoge,” since it is accepted that even a primary element may be dependent [on another]. For it is said in the Bhāṣya: “Indeed, there occurs the formation of a compound even for a primary element that is dependent.
This might be so—[but only if] there were no possibility here of a collective dvandva (samāhāra-dvandva). As for [the rule] “dvandvaśca... [it applies otherwise].

If it is argued that this sūtra is redundant because the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) *dvandva* is unimpeded due to the non-application of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "in the case of living beings and musical instruments," they say in reply: according to the view that "restrictive rules function by way of prohibition," the sūtra "and *dvandva* [is singular] in the case of living beings and musical instruments" [is necessary].

This [sūtra] is solely intended to negate the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) type of *dvandva* compound. Thus, by means of negating the mutual conjunction, this [sūtra] serves to establish the *dvandva* compound in its alternative form (*samāhāra*). And so it is.
This is the conclusion for the purpose of making known the position that [the rule] functions by way of negation; such is the direction [of the argument].
(785) *vibhāṣā samīpe* | 2|4|16|. Regarding *vibhāṣā samīpe*: although here, even if one were to explain it as "only in the case of an *amāhāra* dvandva," there is no...
Nevertheless, since the prohibition of restriction was stated in the preceding sūtra, he says "or there may be a restriction" in accordance with that. Regarding the example *upadaśaṃ dantoṣṭham*:
in the case where there is singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*), only the avyayībhāva compound is employed as the subsequent member; however, if it is a bahuvrīhi, then...
The genitive case would apply in the sense of "of the teeth and lips" (*dantoṣṭhasya*) in the phrase *upadaśasya dantoṣṭhasya*;

however, the grammatical tradition (*ākara*) intends only *upadaśaṃ dantoṣṭhasya*. Thus, even though the genitive case is employed with the intention of expressing "ten of the teeth and lips," the genitive is not desired with the word *upadaśa*. Therefore...
The intention [of the author] is that there is no subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) for a *bahuvrīhi*, but rather only for an *avyayībhāva*.
(786) *ānaṅ ṛto dvandve* |6|3|25|. [The substitute] *ānaṅ* [is applied]. In the expression *ṛtaḥ*, the genitive ending is used in the sense of a class (*jātāvekavacana*). Of those ending in *ṛ*.

The phrase "from those denoting relations of learning or birth" (vidyāyonisaṃbandhebhyaḥ) is understood [from a previous rule] and is here modified to the genitive case; thus he says: "of those denoting relations of learning or birth. Now, one might ask:
since the result is already established by the continued application of the word "ṛtaḥ," what is the purpose of this explicit mention of "ṛtaḥ"?

On this point, they say: the word *ṛtaḥ* is heard as a qualifier of the *dvandva* compound. However, when it recurs [from a previous rule] before a subsequent member of a compound, it is a qualifier of that which precedes it; for instance, when *ānaṅ* is prescribed before the word *putra*, it is for the purpose of specifying the element undergoing the grammatical operation (*kāryinirdeśārtha*). Otherwise, [the substitution] would also apply in cases such as *tātāputrau*.

Regarding the term *uttarapade* (in the following word): this is obtained from the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "ṭhaluguttarapade" (P. 6.4.130). The meaning is that when a following word (*uttarapada*) occurs, the substitute *ānaṅ* takes the place of the final vowel *ṛ* of the preceding [word]. In the example *hotāpotārāu*, because the substitute *ānaṅ* contains the marker *ṅ*, it replaces the final *ṛ* of the preceding [word], and subsequently, there is the elision of the *n*. It is not [the case that the *n* is elided immediately].

Nor should it be argued that only the *ākāra* (the vowel 'ā') is prescribed [by the rule], for that would result in the application of the *rapara* (the letter *r* followed by *a*) as in the rule "uraṇ raparaḥ. Now, one might object: "In this case, the preceding word is not implied by the word 'hotṛ'; otherwise, in the compound 'hotṛ-potṛ-neṣṭod-gātāraḥ,' the substitution of *ānaṅ* would not occur for the middle member."

Furthermore, since the substitute must occur in the very place where the qualified element (viśeṣya) is absent, it should apply to the place of the [entire] word ending in /ṛ/, and not specifically to the place of the [final syllable] ending in /ṛ/. So what is the purpose of adding the marker /ṅ/ to *anaṅ*? True.

In the absence of the marker /ṅ/, in cases such as *mitrāvaruṇau*, where the rule "in a dvandva of deities" (*devatādvandve ca*) applies to the final member (*uttarapada*), [the substitution would not take place].
Since there is no restrictive rule [stating] that this substitute being prescribed must belong either to the preceding syllable or word,

or specifically to the preceding vowel (*alaḥ*), it follows from the statement that "ṛtaḥ" is for the purpose of indicating the element undergoing the operation (*kāryinirdeaśārtham*) that the substitute applies only to the ṛ-vowel that is being pointed out.

The suspicion that the addition of the suffix *ṅt* would be redundant is also refuted by the example *neṣṭodgātārau*. For in this case, *neṣṭā* is not the prior member (*pūrvapada*), because only the first constituent [of the compound] is considered the prior member.

As for *mātāpitarau*: in the procreation of a son, there is between these two a relationship based on the womb (*yoni*); whereas in the previous case [the relationship was] based on the Veda (*śruti*).
The distinction is that the relationship established by the knowledge of the forms of the *hotṛ* priest and others is of the nature of officiating (*ārtvijya*) at a single sacrifice.

Regarding the phrase "by leaping over like a *maṇḍūka*": the intention is that [the word *sambandha*] is not connected with the rule "optionally [before a taddhita suffix] after *svasṛ* and *pati*" (*vibhāṣā svasṛpatyoḥ*). As for "father and son": in these two cases as well, [the relationship] is established by birth (*yonikṛta*).
The relationship [between the two members] is characterized by that of producer and produced.

(787) *Devatādvandve ca* |6|3|26|. [The term] *devatā* [is used here]. This statement is for the purpose of including those not ending in the vowel *ṛ*, and for the purpose of including relationships other than those of teacher and student (*vidyā-yoni*) or blood relation (*ayoni*).
(788) *īdagneḥ somavaruṇayoḥ* |6|3|27|.

*īdagneḥ*: This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ānaṅ*. It applies specifically when [the compound] is a *devatā-dvandva* (a copulative compound of deities), as established in the commentary on the *Vṛtti*. Furthermore, the substitution of *īt* occurs for *agni* even in compounds that are not *devatā-dvandva*, provided they end in *jyotis* or *latā*.

The ritual application of Āśvalāyana, namely "agnīṣomau praṇeṣyāmi," is correct because it originates from a seer (ārṣa). Alternatively, let there be no adherence to that [rule]; in the case of "agnīsomau māṇavakau" (the two boys Agni and Soma), there is no fault according to the maxim: "Those whose word-meanings are manifest, who are independent, and renowned in the world [are to be treated as such]."

(789) *agneḥ stutstomasomāḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.82. [The word] *agneḥ*: This rule is commenced because it is an exception to the prohibition [contained in 8.3.101], *ātpadādyoḥ*. Examples include *agniṣṭut*. That particular sacrifice (*kratuviseṣa*) in which Agni is praised is [called] *agniṣṭut*. The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*), as it belongs to the group beginning with *sampad* (Pāṇini 3.3.94).

Regarding the term *agniṣṭoma*: it is the *stoma* (laudatory hymn) of the fires (*agnīnām stomah*). This refers to the first of the *saṃsthās* (concluding forms) of the Soma sacrifice. (790) *id-vṛddhau* | Pāṇini 6.3.28.

In the rule for the *vṛddhi* [increment], the letter *t* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). The prescription of *ik* for the vowel *i*, however, is for the purpose of subverting a sublater (*bādhakabādhanārtha*). Here, by the word *vṛddhi*, that which possesses *vṛddhi* is understood, because it is impossible for the subsequent member of the compound (*uttarapada*) to be merely the increment itself. Therefore...

He explains: "when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) contains a *vṛddhi* vowel. Regarding the phrase "having set aside *ānaṅ* and *ītvam*": although *ānaṅ* and *ītvam* would indeed apply first because they are *antaranga* (internal) relative to *vṛddhi*, nevertheless, according to the maxim "a general rule does not apply until it has bypassed the scope of an exception," *ānaṅ* and *ītvam* [must be considered].
The sense is that [the *it* augment] does not occur here. Regarding the term *āgnāvaiṣṇavam*: because the *it* augment is absent, the form remains as *ānaṅ*.

(791) [The rule] *divasaśca pṛthivyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.30) is stated so that the substitution of *ru* may not take place; when the vowel *a* is present, the *s* sound is heard, and thus it appears in actual usage.
The meaning is that the absence of modification is inferred.

In the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is conformity with what is observed. Regarding the word *visargam*: likewise, one must infer that "in some cases the letter *v* does not occur," because of the necessity of following the actual usage of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*). This is the intended sense.
[The forms] *uṣāsāsūryam* and *mātarapitarau*. [In the first case: *uṣāsā* and *sūryaḥ*; the compound is their collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). [In the second case: *mātā* and *pitā*;
for the word *mātṛ*, the substitution of *araṅ* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).

(793) *dvandvāccudaṣahāntātsamāhāre* 5.4.106. [The suffix *ṭac* is added] after a *dvandva* compound ending in *cu*, *ṣ*, or *ha*, when it denotes a collective (*samāhāra*). The mention of "end" (*anta*) is for the sake of clarity. The purpose of including *cu* as a designation for the entire class of consonants is indicated by the example *tvaksrajam*. However, in a *dvandva* of many members, one says *vāktvaksrajam*.
In a *dvandva* compound that contains another *dvandva*, [the first member] is optionally [retained]; for example, *vāktvacasrajam*.
Thus ends the section on *dvandva* in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
(1588) *sarvasya dve* 8.1.1. [The entire word is repeated twice.]
Regarding the rule *sarvasya dve*: one should not suspect that this is an injunction (*vidhi*) stating that two forms of the word *sarva* occur;

rather, because rules such as *ityavīpsāyām* are expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) due to the non-specification of both the operation to be enjoined and its subject, and because it is marked with a svarita accent, this is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). Thus he says: "having taken this as the governing heading."

The meaning is: "with reference to this form of the object. However, there is no apprehension of the word's own form (*svarūpa*), because of the indicative mark (linga) in the rule: "But [the substitution applies] optionally to the final [letter] of the *āmreḍita*. For if there were apprehension of the word's own form, then only the entire word repeated twice would be the subsequent *āmreḍita*, and not [the individual parts].

How can the prohibition of the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule and the optional rule for the final *t* in the case of the word "param" following a reduplicated (*dvirukta*) sound that imitates an indistinct noise (*avyaktānukaraṇa*)—specifically in the rule *āmreḍitasya*—be consistent? [Objection:
Is it not the case that in rules such as *ityavīpsayoḥ*, the term *adasaḥ* which is to be stated later is drawn back (*apakṛṣya*) [to apply here]?

If it is argued, "Since the doubling (*dvitva*) is prescribed for the *pada* itself, what is the purpose of this mention of 'of the whole' (*sarvasya*)?", they say in response: By adopting the technical term *pada* through the rule "in *svādiṣu*," there would be doubling of only the original base portion (*prakṛtibhāga*) in forms such as *vṛkṣābhyām*; however, when the mention of "of the whole" is made, [the doubling applies to the entire form].

Since the word *arva* functions in the sense of both a part and the whole, the desired conclusion is established by the implication that "there is a doubling of that which is endowed with its parts, and yet no part whatsoever is excluded. Here,
when the expectation for a number to be counted (*saṅkhyeya*) arises for the word *ave*, the two forms of the word itself are taken as the objects.

This is because the context is the instruction on grammar (*śabdānuśāsana*). The term "of all" (*sarvasya*) is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, this is the position that there is doubling in place of [the original]. However, if the number were to be applied to the act of utterance (*uccāraṇa*), then the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) would not be possible; for the original element is characterized by cessation, whereas the substitute comes into being.

If everything were already ceased, for whom would there be utterance? Therefore, in relation to the word "utterance" (uccāraṇa) which has been brought forward [as the object], the genitive case in "of all" (sarvasya) is used in the sense of the object according to the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti*. The resulting meaning is: "one should utter 'all' twice. This is it.

The position is that "doubling" (*dvirvacana*) consists in separation (*viprayoga*). But [an objection may be raised]: in the first alternative, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the status of being a word (*padatva*) would belong only to the entire aggregate and not to the two constituent parts; consequently, the grammatical operations (*padakārya*) pertaining to words would not apply.
Nor is this a desirable consequence, for [otherwise] *ṅmuṭ* would not occur in *apacannapacan*, nor [would it occur] in *vṛkṣān*.

In the case of *vṛkṣān nity atra*, the prohibition of the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule *adāntasya* would not be established; and in the case of *agre agre ity atra*, the formation of the single substitute by the rule *eṅaḥ padāntād ati* would not be established. Furthermore, grammatical operations conditioned by non-finality (*apadāntatva*) would apply. For example, in the case of *ayaḥ payaḥ ity atra*: The word *ayaḥ* (iron) ends in a visarga (*visarjanīya*), which is substituted by *s*. This *s* is then subject to the rules of sandhi (*saṃhitāyām*). If the preceding vowel were considered part of the same *pada*, then the following *p* of *payaḥ* would be treated as *paśu* (by the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ*), resulting in the undesirable form *ayor payaḥ*. However, because the preceding vowel is not part of the same *pada*, the *s* remains unchanged, and the correct form *ayaḥ payaḥ* is obtained. Thus, the designation of *pada* is essential for the proper application of grammatical rules.
In the case of *‘o’padādau’*, there would be the substitution of *s*; in *‘apīḥ papīḥ’*, there would be the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *‘ṭhiṇaḥ ṣaḥ’*.

Even if one were to somehow avoid the substitutions of *s* and *ṣ* by relying on the commentary (*vṛtti*) stating *‘āśakalpakakāmyeṣu’*, [the problem remains] in the case of *‘aśītāśnīte’* by the rule *‘ato guṇe’*.

If it is argued that there would be the form of another (pararūpa), they say in response: if the substitute were merely the aggregate in which the distinction between its parts has vanished, then the dual ending "ve" would be untenable;
therefore, by virtue of the statement "ve," two words together take the place of one word.

It is prescribed as being taught simultaneously; in that case, by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original), the word-status (*padatva*) belongs to the whole aggregate, and it indeed belongs to the two constituent parts as well, so there is no fault whatsoever.
This might be argued: even though the designation "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*) is established for each [part] under the view of double employment (*dviḥprayoga-pakṣa*),...
If it is argued that [the accentuation] is not established for the aggregate, and consequently, in cases such as *devadattaḥ pacati-pacati*,
the rule *iṅtiṅḥ* would fail to establish the *nighāta* (elision of accent) for the entire word—
on this point they say: in *pacati-pacati* and the like, indeed that same root and suffix are repeated twice.
It is recited thus:

"Therefore, since the designation *pada* is prescribed for that which begins with the element after which a suffix is enjoined and ends with that suffix, it applies to the entire aggregate as well; by this, the *avagraha* and other such markers are established."

(1589) *nitvavīpsayoḥ* |8|1|4|. Regarding the rule *nitvavīpsayoḥ*: he explains that here "constant" (*nityam*) means "repetition" (*paunaḥpunyam*), as indicated by the term "frequency" (*ābhīkṣṇye*). It should be understood that the compound *apuṃsakamanupuṃsakena* is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), and its singular form (*ekavadbhāvaḥ*) is to be understood.

Regarding the term *padasya*: by this, the reduplication prescribed for the state of obligatoriness (*nityatā*) does not apply to the entire verbal root (*dhātu*). Furthermore, since the *yaṅ* affix prescribed for the verbal root in the sense of frequent repetition (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas the reduplication stated for the word (*pada*) is external (*bahiraṅga*), the latter does not subvert the former.

For otherwise, since *kriyā-samabhihāra* (intensive repetition) consists of both frequency (*paunaḥpunya*) and intensity (*bhṛśārtha*), this suffix *ṭyaṅ*, which finds its scope in the sense of intensity, would be superseded by the subsequent reduplication (*dvirvacana*) when applied to frequency. Furthermore, if one accepts the reduplication of the entire word (*pada*), then in the case of *prapacati* [where *pra-* is a prefix], the rule for reduplication would not apply to the word together with its prefix.
It should not be argued that there would be no reduplication for forms such as *prapaṭhati* and the like;

for that [reduplication] is established by the statement of the Vārttikakāra. On this point, they say: when a root preceded by a prefix undergoes reduplication, there is no single-word status (*aikapadya*) at all, because since the original base (*sthānin*) lacks the status of being a word (*padatva*), that status is likewise difficult to obtain for its substitute (*ādeśa*).
In the view that there is a double application (*dvirprayoga*), however, with the exception of the first occurrence, the status of being a word (*padatva*) is obtained for the remainder;

even when that [status] exists, there is no harm. In reality, however, the view of doubling in place (*sthāne dvirvacana*) alone is primary here, because since the original element (*sthānin*) is a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), the substitute (*ādeśa*) is also a word ending in a case-suffix, and [the rule] *subantāt taddhitaḥ* applies.

Thus, under this view, since the suffixes *ṣyañ* and *ṭhañ* can occur from a collective compound, the forms *paunaḥpunyam* and *paunaḥpunikaḥ* are established. Even if one accepts the alternative view that "the taddhita suffix follows a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt taddhitaḥ*), it applies only to that which ends in an actually heard suffix.

Because the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) is prohibited [for the second member], the word *punar* itself remains a nominal stem; since the substitute *naṭ* is also a nominal stem, forms such as *paunaḥpunyam* are indeed established. However, according to the view that there is a double application [of the suffix], the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) occurs after the indeclinable due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), and subsequently reduplication (*dvitva*) takes place.

Thus, because the aggregate (samudāya) lacks the status of being a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) and lacks the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the suffixes *ṣyañ* and *ñañ* do not apply. Nor does the aggregate become a *subanta* through the production of the nominative suffix *su* and its subsequent elision (*luk*) by virtue of the rule "that which is meaningful, other than a root... (*arthavad adhātuḥ...*) and so forth, which would grant it the status of a nominal stem.

And it cannot be argued that the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) is indeed possible; for by the restrictive rule—"wherein a compound has a preceding member that is a word (*pada*), if [that member] is [itself] a nominal stem, [then the whole] is only a compound"—the status of being a nominal stem is impossible, and consequently, the status of being a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is also impossible. Nor can it be said...

Regarding the view that there is a double application (*dvir-prayoga*), one might object: "Since it has just been stated that the entire aggregate also receives the designation *pada* because the same root and suffix are recited twice, the aggregate 'punaḥ-punaḥ' indeed possesses the status of being a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). This objection should be raised, but it is refuted by the fact that the elision (*luk*) of the case-suffix occurs due to its being an *antaraṅga* (internal) operation.

Because when there is reduplication of the *prakṛti* portion, it is difficult to obtain the designation of a "word" (*pada*) for the entire aggregate— since that designation is prescribed by the rule stating that "that which begins with the element after which a suffix is ordained and ends with [the suffix] is a word"— and consequently, in the absence of a single word, [the expression] "the ancient one being born again and again" [would not apply].

In such cases, even the *avagraha* (word division) would not be established. Regarding the term *ābhīkṣṇya* (repetition): for that is a property residing in the action (*kriyā*). Therefore, in order to indicate that [property], reduplication is logically appropriate only for those [words] where the action is predominant. And the predominance of the action exists in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), as well as in certain *kṛt* formations, such as the indeclinable *kṛt* suffixes.

The meaning is that this will be stated later with the words "bhave" (in the sense of becoming). Some, however, maintain that doubling occurs only for those [verbal roots] where the action is predominant;

since an action whose means (*sādhana*) has already been grasped is alone useful for linguistic usage, and because the root alone does not express that [means], doubling does not occur for the mere verbal root.

However, they say that there would be no harm even if the word "of the word" (*padasya*) were not elided, because [the rule] would apply only to a word that denotes such an action. This is to be considered;
for, according to the aforementioned reasoning, it would follow that even a sentence capable of expressing an action qualified by various *kārakas* would incur duality.
Furthermore, according to the method you have stated, there would be no duality for those [words] ending in verbal suffixes that denote an action (*bhāvārtha*) or for indeclinables (*avyaya*).

Now, one might argue: "In those cases, after the understanding of permanence [of the action], the requirement for a means (*sādhana*) is fulfilled by other words; therefore, duality should indeed occur for words such as *bhūyate* and *paktvā*."

If [you say this], then who could prevent the doubling of the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone in that very case? Furthermore, in the same way, even in instances where the suffixes denote the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*), the doubling of the verbal root alone would be unavoidable; thus, the extraction of the word "of the word" (*padasya*) is indeed necessary. This is the direction [of the argument]. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of distributive repetition" (*vīpsāyām*).

*Vīpsā* (repetition) is the desire to pervade; that is to say, the wish to convey pervasion. And this is a property of the speaker, like *ābādha* (affliction). Just as when one says "he has gone," it is understood that the speaker utters the sentence because he is afflicted by the long absence of his beloved, so too [in the case of] "tree after tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam*).

Even in cases such as "he sprinkles" (siñcati), since it is understood that this sentence is intended by the speaker to convey pervasion (vyāpti), the object of the verbal cognition is indeed pervasion itself. Thus, it would have been possible to formulate the rule simply as "ity-avyāptyoḥ. Here, pervasion means entirety (kārtsnya), and that [entirety] pertains to the qualified subject (adhikārika).

Just as in cases such as “All Brāhmaṇas have been invited,” although a restriction is accepted there— on the grounds that it is impossible for everyone existing on the surface of the earth to be invited by anyone— the term refers specifically to the Brāhmaṇas of one’s own village and own caste.

In that case, here too, since no human being possesses the capacity to water all trees, it must be accepted that in expressions such as "he waters tree after tree," the term "tree" is understood to denote in its entirety only those trees situated within the specific garden or area for which he has the authority to water them.
However, where there is no reason for restriction, non-restriction is indeed intended,

as in the case of "That which is born from 'āt' reaches its end [in 'an']" (*ātoj jāto nidhanam upaiti*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of using the plural in expressions such as *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam*, even though many trees are being perceived.

This is because plurality (*bahutva*) is not manifested there; rather, it is established in the *Manoramā* that only singularity residing in each individual is manifested there. Furthermore, since the aggregate in the expression "vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam" lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is no possibility for the plural number to apply at all. Nor...

It might be suspected that the status of being a *prātipadika* applies here by virtue of the rule "that which has meaning is a *dhātu*," because of the restriction: "In a composite (*saṅghāta*) where the prior portion is a word (*pada*), if [the whole] is a *prātipadika*, then it must be a *samāsa*. Furthermore, since the doubling prescribed in the eighth [chapter] is of the nature of a substitute (*ādeśa*), the composite is not [a *prātipadika*].

It might be suspected that [the rule] applies as well, but this is not so; for it has been stated previously that by the expression "ve" (or), two combined words are simultaneously prescribed as a single substitute in place of one word.
However, even if this were the case, [it would still apply] in instances such as *aritsarit* and *yoṣāyoṣe*.

If it is argued that the occurrence of the plural number is indeed unavoidable—because when the base *ari* is possible as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then its substitute, such as *sarit* or *sari*, is also possible as a nominal stem by virtue of the rule of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*)—then [we reply]: [The answer follows: This is not so. For the application of the designation "nominal stem" depends upon the presence of a case-ending (*vibhakti*). Since the substitutes *sarit* and *sari* do not possess a case-ending, they cannot be considered nominal stems; consequently, the plural number does not arise. Furthermore, the designation "nominal stem" applies only to a sequence of sounds ending in a case-ending, and since the substitutes in question lack a case-ending, the designation does not apply to them. Thus, there is no room for the objection regarding the plural number.

On this point, they say: [The word] is already occupied by its own internal singular number; its meaning has been expressed by reduplication, and it is therefore devoid of expectancy for any other number. For it cannot be claimed that a verbal cognition of plurality must necessarily arise merely because plurality exists in reality; otherwise, such a cognition would undesirably follow even in the case of words denoting non-substances (asatvārthaka). Indeed, not...

With the intention of expressing multiplicity regarding the act of lying down, someone might employ the form *śayyante* (they lie down) in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) with the word *devadattaiḥ*. If it is argued that this is inappropriate in that case, it is equally so in the present instance.
And here, the proof is the grammatical indication (*liṅga*) found in the rule: *ekaikasya prācām* ("for each one, according to the Easterners").

(1590) *paryapābahir* [Pāṇini 2.1.12]—the word *pari* is used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "In the sense of exclusion, *pari* [is compounded] when not in a compound. An example here is: *paritrigartaṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("It rained all around Trigarta"). It should also be stated that [this applies] optionally (*vā*); thus, for instance, *apa...* [etc.]
The example for the *kāraka*s is "saṃsāraḥ hareḥ pari hareḥ" (the cycle of worldly existence [is] around Hari, [and] from Hari).
Regarding the word *pari*, there is an optional rule (*vā-vacana*) for its use in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). Thus, one says "pari pari vaṅgebhyaḥ" (away from the Vaṅgas).
Because of the designation of *karmapravacanīya* by the rule "aṅ-parī varjane," the ablative case is applied by the rule "pañcamy apāṅ-paribhiḥ."
The fifth [section]. (1591) *upary-adhy-adhasaḥ sāmīpye* |8|1|7|.
Regarding *upari*, *adhi*, and *adhas*: "proximity" (*sāmīpyam*) means closeness; and that may be produced either by time or by space. *adhyadhi*.
"Happy. This is an example of [proximity] produced by time. Why [is the term] "sāmīpya" (proximity) mentioned?

[Consider: "The moon is above that. However, in the case of "He holds an umbrella above his head," although proximity exists in reality, it is not intended to be expressed; rather, only the state of being higher is intended.

The reduplication does not occur when there is a desire to express [the action]. For the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is the primary cause for the derivation of words. In this regard, they say that the use of the desiderative form in the rule "ṭhupajñopakramaṃ tadādyacikhyāsāyām" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

(1592) *vākyāder āmantritasyāsūyāsaṃmatikopakutsanabhartsaneṣu* | 8|1|8| [The first word] of a sentence that is an address (*āmantrita*) [takes the acute accent on its first syllable] when expressing envy, approval, anger, censure, or threatening. Example: *sundara-sundara* (O handsome one! and so forth.

Regarding the rule *‘varitamāmreḍite’sūyāsaṃmatikopakutsaneṣu’* and the rule *‘āmreḍitaṃ bhartsane’*, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) that would otherwise have been required according to these sūtras is not applied here because it is optional. For it was stated previously: “Every protracted vowel is optional. Now, [one might object]: “But here...”
The separate mention of reviling and threatening apart from anger and envy is redundant;
for one does not revile without envy, nor does one threaten without being angry.
To this they reply: "Indeed, teachers, because of their desire to correct [their students], may issue threats even when they are not angry."
The author of the Sūtra has made a separate mention [of *asūyā*] because they produce contempt even without *asūyā*.
As it is said: "Teachers strike with hands that are like nectar, not with those sprinkled with poison;
faults reside in indulgence, while virtues reside in discipline."

(1593) *ekaṃ bahuvrīhivat* |8|1|9|. "The single [word] is treated like a *bahuvrīhi*. The word "two" (*dve*) is understood [from the previous rule]. And that [word "two"] serves to provide the subject for the statement;
thus he says: "when reduplicated" (*dvirukte*). Regarding the phrase "by that": although these two [words] are not specifically distinguished within a *bahuvrīhi* compound...
The meaning is that even though [the two] have been prescribed there, they are extended [here] by the mere fact of being observed there.

Regarding "the elision of *su* and the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*)," it should be understood that the original accent of the prior member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) also applies. As for "the *su* from the whole," that is indeed the singular number alone, being restricted by the internal (inherent) singularity.
The meaning has already been stated previously: that the sense of repetition is independent when there is a different number.

Regarding the phrase "in the prior portion": it does not apply to the latter portion as well. For instance, here the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs in two ways: either by the rule "in all compounds involving pronouns" (*arvanāmno vṛtimātre*), or by the rule "the feminine becomes like the masculine" (*striyāḥ puṃvat*). Of these, the first [applies].

It has been stated that [the substitution] applies only to the first member, on the basis of the *jñāpaka* rule "hastraiṣa-". However, the second [substitution] is prescribed when a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) follows; and the point is that the latter member cannot have a word in apposition following it. This refers to the specific case regarding the *avagraha*.

The meaning of "ekaikayā" is "ekaikayā" [occurring] as it is; that is, "ekaikasyai. Now, one might object: since the elision of case-endings (*sub-lopa*), the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), and even the absence of the technical designation "sarvanāman" (pronominal) are observed in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, this [absence of pronominality] should also be extended by way of the treatment of a *bahuvrīhi*; and thus, the substitution of *smāy* would apply here.

If it is argued that [the designation *sarvanāman*] is difficult to establish, they reply: unlike the elision of the suffix *su* or the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), the absence of the technical designation *sarvanāman* is not observed by the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). Rather, because a *bahuvrīhi* compound is secondary (*gauṇa*), its capacity to denote "all" is impossible; thus, its absence is observed.

This is not extended [to the formation of the compound]. For the rule "a bahuvrīhau" is a prohibitor with respect to the *alaukika-vākya* (pre-compositional phrase), and not because it was stated [as a prohibition] specifically for the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself.
(1594) And [the substitution of *nañ* by *a* occurs] when there is affliction (*ābādha*). Pāṇini 6.2.10.

And in the case of *ābādha*, [the term] *iha* [is used]; the phrase “as in an *ahuvrīhi*” (*ahuvrīhivad-bhāvāt*) is supplied [from the previous rule]. Thus, the rule “*striyāḥ puṃvat*” (P. 6.3.34) continues to apply. Nor should it be argued that for a reduplicated form, there is no subsequent member (*uttarapada*), because by the force of the extension (*atideśa*) “as in an *ahuvrīhi*,” the status of being a subsequent member (*uttarapadatva*) is also established.

[This is] due to the acquisition [of the status of being a final member]. Now, one might ask: since the status of being a final member (*uttarapadatva*) is obtained through the application of the *bahuvrīhivadbhāva* rule, why does the rule "the elision of the *nañ*" (*alopo nañaḥ*) not apply here in the word *ane*?

It is said in reply: in the rule "the elision of the *nañ*" (*na lopo nañaḥ*), the term "in a final member" (*uttarapade*) is understood to carry over [from a previous rule], and the mention of "*nañ*" (*nañaḥ*) indicates that which undergoes the grammatical operation (*kāryin*). In that context...

The status of the negative particle (*nañ*) as a cause [of doubling] is set aside by its being directly subject to the operation of the *śiṣṭa* (the remaining element), as in the case of *madrahradaḥ* becoming *bhadrahradaḥ*. Regarding this, when the doubling of the letter *r* would otherwise occur according to the rule *ṭhaco rahābhyām*, it is stated in the *Ākara*: "These two *r*s are the subjects of the operation, but they are merely the cause for the doubling."
If it is argued that even so, in cases such as *hūrdhūḥ* and *anthāḥpanthāḥ*, the suffix prescribed by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ* would still apply to the compound, [the answer is:
since the word *samāsāt* ("from a compound") is understood from the rule *samāsācca tadviṣayāt*,
the repeated mention of "compound" (*samāsagrahaṇa*) in the rule *samāsāntāḥ* is indeed for the purpose of [restricting the application].

This is for the purpose of including that compound which is prescribed under the heading of "compound" (*samāsa*). Therefore, the rule regarding compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) does not apply to a compound formed by extension (*atideśika*); such is the direction. (1595) *karmadhārayavad uttareṣu* |8|1|11|.

"In the subsequent [rules], it is like a *karmadhāraya* compound. The commentary (*vṛtti*) states: although this is already established by the governing rule itself, the explicit mention "in the subsequent [rules]" is for the sake of clarity.
(1596) *prakāre guṇavacanasya* | Pāṇini 8.1.12. [In the sense of manner, a word denoting a quality takes the suffix *ām*.]

[The rule] "of a word expressing a quality, when [used] in the sense of *prakāra*. Although the word *prakāra* occurs in both the senses of "distinction" (*bheda*) and "similarity" (*sādṛśya*), as is understood from such examples as "he eats in many *prakāras*" (meaning "in many distinctions" or "in many specific ways"), and also from "this boy is a *brāhmaṇa-prakāra*" (meaning "similar to a *brāhmaṇa*"); nevertheless, in this [present] context...

He states what is intended: "in the case of similarity" (*sādṛśye*). Here, the commentary itself is the refuge [for understanding]. Regarding the term "masculine form" (*puṃvadbhāva*), it follows from the rule *pumvat karmadhāraye*. And that [rule] also applies in cases such as *kālakakālikā* and others within the *koradhādi* group. Therefore, while the application of the masculine form in a *bahuvrīhi* compound is currently under discussion...

It should be understood that the objection—that the statement regarding the treatment as a *karmadhāraya* is redundant—is without foundation. Regarding the example *paṭupaṭu*, it is not accepted here that the suffix *jātiya* is barred by [the application of] doubling; Vāmana states, "one who belongs to the class of *paṭu*" (*paṭujātīya*). Otherwise, in cases such as *brāhmaṇajātīya*, even though it is not a word denoting a quality (*aguṇavacana*), [the suffix would apply].

The meaning is that the suffix *jātiya*, which finds scope when the referent is a distinct entity (*bhedarūpa*), would be sublated by the subsequent suffix *dvit* (forming *dvitīya*) in the case of quality-words (*guṇavacana*) when used in the sense of similarity. Why specify "of a quality-word"? [Consider: *agnirmāṇavakaḥ* ("The boy is fire") and *siṃho māṇavakaḥ* ("The boy is a lion"). Even though here the words "fire" and "lion" function metaphorically (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*),...

Although qualities such as sharpness and cruelty are understood [in the case of words like *tīkṣṇa*], nevertheless, because of the force of the term *guṇavacana* (denoting a quality) when it occurs in the sense of "existing in a manner" (*prakāre vartamānasya*), duality applies only to those words that primarily refer to qualities, and not to others; this is the established tradition (*ākara*). As in the example: *avaṃnavaṃ prītiraho karoto*.

The doubling [of a word] occurs in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). However, by this rule, when there is doubling, the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) would occur. In the example "avanavā vanavāyubhir ādade," the doubling occurs by this very rule, and not by way of distributive repetition; thus, the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) applies. How then is the form "hītabhīta iva śītamayūkhaḥ" explained?
Bhāravi: Since similarity is already expressed by the word *iva*, a double application (*dvitva*) here in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*) is inappropriate.

True; however, it must somehow be explained as "terrified among the terrified. By this, the result is "extremely terrified. According to the Vārttika rule, "in cases of excess, two [words] are to be expressed," as in *bhītabhīta* and so forth.

The solution proposed by Durghaṭa and others—that there is a doubling [of the consonant]—is not to be respected, because such a Vārttika is unknown. Now, how is it that [the verse reads]: "Worn out and exhausted, having set foot upon the mountain peaks, you shall go where, being ever more diminished, you may drink the very light water of the streams"?

*The Cloud Messenger*. If it is argued that this is because there is no possibility of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) due to the absence of difference between the objects [of the action], they say in response: even in the case of a single entity, distributive repetition is to be understood by postulating a distinction between its states of increase and its states of decrease. Now, how is it that "the favorable breeze pushes gently, gently"?

Regarding the phrase *yatā tvām amitaḥ* from the *Meghadūta*: if it is argued that since a distributive sense (*vīpsā*) is impossible here, a double application of the word would result in a case-suffix elision (*subluk*)—as in the example *mandaṃ mandaṃ uditaḥ prayayau kham*—that is true.
However, [the meaning is] "the wind is gently pushing you, who are yourself slow-moving, along gently. How [could there be a distributive sense]?
This must be explained as *civdi*. Since the movement of that which is already established (*siddha*) is to be considered, [the example] "white-white" (*śukla-śuklam*) is given;
this indicates that it is an illustration of a word expressing a quality alone—namely, "form" (*rūpa*).

Regarding the rule for "sequence" (*ānupūrvye*), two [words] are to be expressed. As for the term "sequence": this new formulation is undertaken because the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) does not apply here.

Regarding "at every root" (*mūle-mūle*): one should also cite "subtle at every tip" (*agre-agre sūkṣma*). For a single object, such as a bamboo staff, there is only one primary root and one primary tip; the designations "tip" and "root" for the other parts are merely relative. Furthermore, thickness and subtlety are not uniform.
Rather, thickness is accumulated according to the root, and fineness according to the tip;

since the other parts do not possess these qualities [in that same way], a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is impossible here. However, in the expression “*ūlemūle pathi viṭapanām*” (branches at every step along the path), the doubling occurs due to distributive repetition. This is stated in the work of Haradatta.
This is clear.
When acting out of haste, the usage of multiple forms as desired is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*). Regarding "established by logic":
it means that however many words are required for the person being addressed to understand the intended meaning, that many [should be used].
The intention is that [the suffix] is to be employed.

Regarding *kriyāsamabhihāre*: "in the sense of repetition" (*paunaḥpunye*). The suffix is applied to the word *punaḥ*—which denotes that which occurs repeatedly—to express the abstract state (*bhāve*) of "again and again. This [suffix] is used together with the imperative (*loṭ*).
Regarding the word *samuccitya* (having combined): [the opponent objects]— "But just as here there is reduplication by combining with the imperative (*loṭ*),

so too in the case of frequent action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), there would be reduplication by combining with the intensive suffixes *yaṅ* and *yiṅ*— as in *pāpacyate-pāpacyate* or *bobhūyate-bobhūyate*."

On this point, they say: the *loṭ* suffix deviates from [indicating] the intensification of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), because it also occurs in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Consequently, it is logical that the two *loṭ* suffixes themselves indicate that [intensification], and not each one individually; thus, reduplication applies to the form ending in *loṭ*. As for the *yaṅ* suffix...
