*ekāco baśo bhaṣ jhaṣantasya sdhvoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.37).
[The portion] "ekāco baśo" [is explained as follows]: the word "jhal" has been removed [from the context]. This is seen in forms such as *hugbhyām* and *hukṣu*.

The intention is that the substitution of *bhaṣ* is established by the rule itself through the word "adānte" (not at the end). However, the explanation given by the ancients— that it applies "to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) before a *jhal* consonant or at the end of a word"— is merely an error, because it would result in the impossibility of forms such as *adhok* and *adhog*.

Furthermore, because the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has not been introduced as the subject. Now, one might object: if there were an oblique construction (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) such that [the rule] means "an augment *gh* occurs after a portion of a verbal root," then even though the root *duh* ending in *kvip* would have the *jhaṣ* designation due to the substitution of *gh* for *ādi* by the rule *ādeśca*, the change to *bhaṣ* would not occur; for [in that case], the *u* in the word *ughi* refers to the entire complex...

The portion *u* is not a single-vowel (*ekāc*) initial member of the whole [root] *ughi*, because it lacks the property of ending in a *jhaṣ* consonant; nor is the subsequent member *ugh* a *baś* sound. Therefore, he says: "by virtue of being treated as if it were the designated entity itself" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvena*). And it is not the case that a part of a verbal root is itself a verbal root.

It should be stated that [the term] should be designated [as such], so that "ardha" would be established; for the designation as if possessing meaning (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) applies only to those things that possess meaning, and since a mere part does not possess meaning, it is impossible to designate it as a verbal root (*dhātu*). Regarding the term *bhaṣbhāva*: [it refers to] that which occurs prior to the application of the suffix *kvip*.

The intention is that because the designation *dhātu* remains uncontradicted, once the substitution of *gh* has been applied by the rule *āder dhātoḥ*, the word ends in a *jhaṣ* sound. Thus, [the form] is *dhuk*. [The root] *duh* is used in the sense of "filling"; [it takes] *kvip*.
(Pāṇini 8.2.33) *vā druhamuhaṣṇuhaṣṇihām*.

The roots *druh* (in the sense of malice), *ruh* (in the sense of desire to kill), *uh* (in the sense of perplexity), *ṇuh* (in the sense of vomiting), and *ṇih* (in the sense of affection) [are under discussion]. Since *druh* belongs to the *adādi* class, the suffix is already obligatorily required; for the others, it was not previously required. Therefore, this is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. Now, one might object: "But *druh* and the others are recited in the *divādi* class in this very same order; in that case..."
Let it be simply "ṭhā druha-ādīnām" (the ṭha augment occurs after *druh* and the others). [Objection: *puṣ* etc. belong to the sub-group within the *div* group, and *radh* etc.

belong to a sub-group within that; *druh* etc. belong to a sub-group within that [sub-group]. Since the marker *vṛt* has been placed immediately after the root *snih* to mark the end of the *radh* group, there is a concern regarding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Because there would be no scope [for the rule]. Do not say so; for if that were the case, forms such as *dodhruḍ* in the *yaṅluk* [derivation] would not be established, due to the prohibition: "That which is prescribed by a *guṇa* [rule] is [also prohibited].
(Pāṇini 1.1.45): *igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* ("The substitution of *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, or *ḷ* for *y*, *v*, *r*, or *l* is called *saṃprasāraṇa*").

"igyaṇaḥ" means "in place of yaṇ. In the context of rule-enunciations (*vidhipradeśa*), because future technical designations (*bhāvisaṃjñā*) are adopted—like a cloth already cut and folded into a garment—there is no mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). [Objection: But if *ik* were the designation for that which stands in the place of *yaṇ*, then in the case of "ṭhaduhitacarām" (from the root *duh* with the suffix *laṅ*), [the rule would apply].

If it is argued that, in place of the *lakāra*, there is the third person singular (*uttama-puruṣa-ekavacana*) with the augment *iṭ*; and since this [augment] is a substitute for a semivowel (*yaṇ-sthānika*), it receives the designation *saṃprasāraṇa*, whereby a long vowel would occur by the rule "ṭhhalaḥ" because the element ending in *laṅ* is a stem (*aṅga*) in relation to the suffix *tarap*. To this, [the reply is: here...
Kaiyaṭa says: "Due to the connection according to order (*yathāsaṅkhya*), the technical designation *samprasāraṇa* does not apply here.
[Objection: But since technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) do not apply in the context of a restatement (*anuvāda*), how is the attainment of "according to order" achieved here?
Nor should it be argued that, in this way, even the connection with the "place of substitution" (*sthāna*) would not be obtained; for [the rule] "the genitive case... [is available].

In the commentary on the rule *sthāneyoga*, this sūtra is understood to apply because it is obtained there [by implication]. Regarding this, they say: by resorting to methods such as *tantra* (simultaneous application) and *āvṛtti* (repetition), since the term "that which has undergone the change" (*tadbhāvita*) is understood in the sūtra *aṅgasya*, the augment *iṭ* belonging to the *laṅ* ending *hal* in the form *aduhikarām* [is included].

The long vowel does not occur for a *saṃprasāraṇa*, because the *iṭ* augment in place of the *laṅ* suffix is not designated by the term *saṃprasāraṇa*. [Objection: Even so, in forms such as *akṣadyauvau* and *akṣadyauva*, since the *ūṭh* would receive the designation *saṃprasāraṇa*, there would be a substitution of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) according to the rule "after a *saṃprasāraṇa*" (*aṃprasāraṇācca*).

If it is argued that [the substitution] should occur, we say no; for the author of the Vārttika has stated, "When there is the priority of Samprasāraṇa, the mention of 'having the same base' (samānāṅga) must be made," or else, because an internal rule (āṅga) is stronger than one concerning phonemes (vārṇa), only *uvār* would result.
On this point, the moderns [hold that] in the very places where rules such as "for *ṣyaṅ*, Samprasāraṇa" are applied, [the term] *hyas* refers to *ig*.
Having recited the sūtra defining the technical term *saṃprasāraṇa*, they say that it could have been omitted.
[The rule] *vāha ūṭh*: the letter *ṭh* is for the purpose of distinguishing it [from other *ṭh*s] in the rule *ṭhetyedhatyūṭsu*.

By the rule *ṭh-ḷ-antyam*, [the final letter] receives the technical designation *it*. Here, the rule *abhasyeṭ* is the governing heading (*adhikāra*), and the term *saṃprasāraṇa*, which is carried over from the rule *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, serves as a qualifier for *ūṭh*.
Consequently, the rule *alo’ntyasya* does not apply here; this is what he expresses by saying "of the *bha*-stem *vāh*," and so forth. However, according to the ancients...

It has been stated that there should be *saṃprasāraṇa* of the vowel *v* of the word *vāh*; however, they say that this must somehow be interpreted as being intended merely to state the resulting meaning.
(289) *Saṃprasāraṇācca* | Pāṇini 6.1.108.

From the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca*, the word *pūrva* (from the rule *ṭhami pūrvaḥ*) is understood to carry over as *pūrvaḥ*; from the rule *iko yaṇaci*, the word *aci* is understood; and the governing rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* applies. This is what he states with the words beginning with *saṃprasāraṇādacī*. As for the statement "the suffix *ṇvi* occurs only in the Veda," it refers to the rule *vahaśca*.

The intention [of the author] is that the suffix *ṇvi* is understood from the rule "ahajo ṇviḥ" and the term "in the Veda" (*chandasi*) is understood from the rule "sahaś chandasi"; thus, the suffix *ṇvi* applies in the Vedic language. It might be argued: let the rule simply be "vāhaḥ," and let only the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) be prescribed here; once that has been applied, the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel would then take effect.
The forms such as *viśvauhaḥ* and so forth are established by the rule "ṭhṛddhireci" (Pāṇini 6.1.88), which prescribes *vṛddhi*; what then is the purpose of including the mention of *ūṭh*?

True. Even though this is the case, the inclusion of the mention of *ūṭh* serves to indicate the *paribhāṣā* concerning external elements (*bahiraṅga*). For when that *paribhāṣā* is present, [it prevents the application of a rule] for that which has arisen as an external element.

It is established in the Bhāṣya that because the *saṃprasāraṇa* is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*), the internal (*antaraṅga*) *guṇa* substitution would not occur. Now, one might object: "But there would be a difference in form depending on whether the word following [the root] ends in a vowel other than *a*, or whether it is a prefix ending in *a*; so how can the mention of *aṛṭha* (in Pāṇini 6.1.128) be taken as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? To this, they say:

Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that, by the very force of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) stated by the author of the Bhāṣya, the absence of the *ṇvi* suffix in such instances is inferred. By this, the usage of forms such as *bhūvāṭ* (from *bhuvaṃ vahati*),
*bhūhaḥ*, *bhūhā*, *prauhaḥ*, and *prauha* are refuted.
(290) *caturanaḍuhorāmudāttaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.98. Regarding *caturaḍuhoḥ*:
since the phrase "in the case of a sarvanāmasthāna ending marked with Ṭ or Ṅ" (*ṭhitotsarvanāmasthāne*) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), he says "in the case of a sarvanāmasthāna."
(291) *sāvanaḍuhaḥ* | 7|1|82 | Regarding *sāvanaḍuhaḥ*: taking the word *num* as a governing term (*anuvartamāna*) from the rule *ṭācchīnadyoḥ*, he says "there shall be *num*.
Just as the general *sīyut* is superseded by the specific *yāsut*, so too [is it superseded] by *num*.
He dispels the apprehension that [the rule] might be sublated by stating "this [suffix] follows a vowel" (*avarṇāt paro’yam*), and so forth.
The sense is that there is no relationship of sublation and sublated because there is no contradiction between the dependent (*upajīvya*) and the dependent-upon (*upajīvaka*).
(Pāṇini 7.1.99: *am saṃbuddhau*).

"And *ām*. The phrase "even by that which is specifically prescribed" (*viśeṣavihitena*) is to be supplied [from the previous rule]. Some read: "And *num* is not superseded even by *ām*. The meaning of this is as follows: in the case of the rule *bahvanaṅvāṃ hrasvaḥ*, once *ām* has been applied because it is subsequent, the rule *apuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* applies again due to the principle of "re-occurrence" (*punaḥprasaṅga*).

It indeed exists, but it is not sublated; having raised the doubt regarding the substitution of *d* for *n* in *num*, he says: "By the force of the rule for *num*" and so forth. The sense is that, by the force of its prescription, *num* must occur everywhere in its unmodified form.

If it is objected that, in this way, in the example *anaṅvāstatra*, the substitution of *ru* by the rule *aśchavoḥ* would also not occur, the authors of the Bhāṣya say in response: "That rule for which the grammatical description (*upadeśa*) is rendered purposeless with respect to a particular operation is sublated; however, that rule whose very cause [for application] remains intact is not sublated."

For the rule for *num* is indeed purposeless with respect to the state of being a *dat* (the substitution of *d* for *t*), whereas it serves as a cause with respect to the state of being *rut* (the substitution of *r* for *n*). Regarding the term *anaṅvān*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "one who carries a cart" (*anaḥ śakaṭaṃ vahati*), the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *vah* after the word *anas*. [The rule] *ano ḍaśca* applies; due to its inclusion in the *yajādi* group, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). Thus, *anaḍuh-* [is formed].
This being the case, when the elision of *am* and *su* has been performed, the letter *ha* is elided by the rule for the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*).
(293) *vasusraṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ* | Pāṇini 8.2.72.

The term *vasusraṃsu* [is explained as follows]: *vasu* is a suffix (*pratyaya*), by which that which ends in it is to be understood. From the rule *asajuṣoḥ*, the word *sa* is carried over (*anuvartate*); and that qualifies *vasu* alone, not *sras* or *dhvas*, because there is no deviation [in the application]. Nor does it qualify *aduh*.
Intending to show that [the suffix] is impossible, he says:

"of *sāḍvasvantasya*. (294) *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.56. [The rule states: "In place of *saḍ*, [the substitute *ṣ* is applied] after *sah*. What is the purpose of specifying *sah*? [Consider: *saḍaḥ*, which means "that which exists together with *ḍa*" (*saha ḍena vartate*). Of that...

The letter *a* exists in a name that is not a word; for example, *ṛḍa*. [From *ṣaḍa*, "descendant of Ṣaḍa" is *sāḍiḥ*. Thus end those ending in *h*. (295) *diva āṬt*: [In the place of the final phoneme of the stem *div*, there is the substitute *āṬ*. 7.1.84.

*diva āṬt*: the *takāra* (t) is for the sake of pronunciation. Regarding the term "of the nominal stem" (*pratipadikasya*): it refers either to an un-derived stem or to one derived by the rule *iver ḍivi* as supplied in the *Nyāsa*, but not to the verbal root *ivu* [meaning] "play," etc., because "when there is a reference to a suffix marked with *it*, [the rule does not apply to the root]."

This is by the *paribhāṣā* "sānubandhakasya" (that which possesses an *anubandha* [is not affected by a rule]). Therefore, it does not occur in cases such as *akṣadyūḥ*. Nor should it be argued that, because it is *antaraṅga*, only *ūṭh* would apply there and not the possibility of *āṬtvam*;
for even when *ūṭh* has been applied, by the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), the rule "iva āṬ" remains applicable.
The phrase "because of the possibility of application" indicates the general direction [of the argument].

(296) *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131). Regarding *diva ut*: the inclusion of the long vowel marker (*t* in *tapara*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the *u* in forms such as *dyubhyām* is treated as a *saṃprasāraṇa*.

They say that this [rule] is stated to prevent the application of the long vowel [substitution] prescribed by the rule *halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2). Thus end the forms ending in *vānta*. Regarding the four [forms]:
the word *catur* ends in the suffix *uran* according to the rule *ateruran*; thereafter, in the *jas* case-ending, the suffix *ām* is applied by the rule *caturanaduhorām*.

(297) *ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca* | Pāṇini 7.1.55. Regarding the rule *ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca*: because the plural number is used in the citation, it is intended that the meaning (*artha*) is the predominant factor. Furthermore, the status of being "after" the word *ām* is mediated through the meaning; therefore, even though there is the application of the rule for "that which ends in [the cited form]" (*tadantavidhi*), [the suffix is applied] after the meaning.
The [doubling] occurs only in cases such as *aramacaturṇām* and the like, but not in a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
This he will state with the words: "But when [the word] is secondary (*gauṇa*), doubling is not desired," and so forth.
As for "doubling" (*dvitvam*), it is by means of the rule *aco rahābhyām*.

(298) *roḥ supi* | Pāṇini 8.3.16. Regarding *roḥ supi*: the term *supi* here is not a pratyāhāra (a technical abbreviation for a class of suffixes), because the word *hari* is understood from the previous rule. Consequently, this rule does not apply to forms such as *arābhyām*; rather, it applies only by virtue of the rule *haravasānayoḥ*.
He states that this undertaking is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*)— namely, "only after *r*" (*roreva*).

However, a contrary restriction— such as "the *visarjanīya* occurs only after *r* when followed by a *sup* [suffix]"— does not apply here, because of the technical designation in rules such as "a cluster (*saṃyoga*) consists of consonants that are contiguous" (*halo’nantarāḥ saṃyogaḥ*).

(299) *śaro’ci* | 8|4|49|. Regarding *śaro’ci*: since the word *ave* is understood from the rule *ṭhaco rahāmbhā’m* and the word *e* is understood from the rule *ādinyākrośe*, he says: "there are not two [instances]. Now, let there be doubling of one [instance].
[Objection: "The desired result is established by the elision [of the *visarga*] according to the rule *haro hali savarṇe*. [Reply: Not so;

because that elision is optional, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing both [the *visarga* and the *s*] in one alternative case. For example, one who has four dear ones—whether four [males] or four [neutrals]—is called *priyacatvāḥ*. This is because the suffix applies even to that which ends in such a form, since it is part of the *aṅga*."
In the case of *āturanaḍuhaḥ*, the suffix *ām* is applied by the rule *āturanaḍuhoḥ*. However, in the case of *he priyacatva*, the suffix *ām* is applied by the rule *aṃsabuddhau*.
Thus end the words ending in *r*. Regarding *kamala*: Amara states, "Kamalā is Śrī, the beloved of Hari. Regarding the form *kamalam*:

by the rule *tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added; then, due to the application of the *iṣṭhavadbhāva* (the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix *iṣṭha*), there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*).

When the suffix *kvip* is added to a root ending in *ṇic*, the *ṇi* is elided by the rule "ṇer aniṭi. In this way, one who speaks of *salila* [is called] *salil*—forms such as *salilau* and *alila* should be understood accordingly. Now, if this is so, then those speaking of *toya* would also easily form *tay*, *toyau*, and *toya* with a final *y*; and yet, it is not so.

If it is argued that the elision of *y* (yalopa) should be suspected here by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to the rule "the elision of a single consonant [occurring] after a semivowel" (*ṭhverapṛktalopādvali lopaḥ*),

because when the elision of *v* and *y* (*opo vyorvali*) is to be applied, the elision of the *ṇi*-affix or the *ṭi*-portion would, through the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), prevent the *y* from being followed by a *val* sound— this is not so. "A..."

Because the elision of *y* by the rule "at the end of a word" (*padānte*) precludes the application of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the elision of *y* and *v* by the rule "the elision of *y* and *v* when followed by a consonant" (*lopo vyor vali*) would indeed occur; therefore, roots ending in *y* have not been mentioned [here]. Thus end the roots ending in *l*.
Regarding the phrase "at the end of a word": although the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*) have stated that it also applies "before a consonant" (*hali*), that should be disregarded as it is fruitless.

(300) *mo no dhātoḥ* |8|2|64| [The substitute *na* takes the place of *m* at the end of a verbal root. Thus, *praśān*. [Derivation: From the root *am* in the sense of "pacification," with the suffix *kvip*; the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *anunāsikasya kvau*. (301) *kimaḥ kaḥ* |7|2|103| [The substitute *ka* takes the place of *kim* when followed by a case-ending.]

*kimaḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.103). The word *kiṃ* is derived from the suffix *ḍimi* by the rule *ādy-ator ḍimiḥ*. Regarding the phrase "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*): the meaning is that this [condition] is understood as being carried over (*anuvartate*) from the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.1.21). Now, one might object: why not simply formulate the rule as *timaḥ*? By doing so, [the rule would apply to] *tim*, *ṣṭhim*, and so forth...

In order to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding words ending in *kvip*, one should carry forward (*anuvartayitvā*) the term "of *tyad* etc. and explain [the rule] as: "for *yad* etc., *ima-* shall be replaced by *a-*. The word *kim* should be placed before the word *dvi*. [This applies] according to the rule "when not meaningful" (*ānarthake*).

Since there is a prohibition and because of the force of the commencement [of the rule], the operation concerning the final letter (al-antyavidhiḥ) will not apply; so why would there be a substitution of *ka*?
To this he says: "even when accompanied by *akac*. The intention is that in the rule prescribing the vowel *a*, the form of that which has *akac* would be "aka. But if this were so...
[Objection: It might occur even when [the pronoun] is subordinate (*upasarjana*), because it lacks the status of being the subject of a collective operation (*gaṇakāryatva*). [Reply: Not so;
for, by carrying over the word "of *tyad* and so forth" (*tyadādīnām*) from the previous rule, the commentary explains it as "of *tyad* and so forth, [including] *kim*.
(302) *idamo maḥ* | 7.2.108 | [The substitute *ma* takes the place of the final phoneme of *idam* in the nominative singular.]

*idamaḥ* [replaces *idam*] in the nominative singular. By the rule *ṭeḥ kaṃ khyatyāt parasya nalopaśca*, [the suffix *ka* is added and the final *ṭi* is elided]. From the rule *idaṃ* [which follows], and because of the continued application (*anuvartana*) from the rule *adoḥ saḥ sau*, he says: "when *su* follows. (303) *ido'y puṃsi* 7.2.111. [The substitute *ay* replaces *idam* in the nominative singular when it is masculine.]

Why does [the rule] specify "in the masculine" (*puṃsi*)? [Consider: *iyaṃ strī* ("this woman"). There is no vocative for words beginning with *tyad-* and so on; the reason for this is simply that such usage is not observed in common practice. (304) *daśca* 7.2.109.

Regarding the term *utsarga* (general rule): by this, the meaning is that there is no contradiction with the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *adoḥ saḥ sā*, which asks "why [is it said] 'of the two non-final [sounds]'?"—namely, the example *he saḥ*; nor is there contradiction with practical usages such as *ho acyuta* and *bhavann acyuta*. This is the intended sense.
(305) *anāpyakaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.112.

Regarding *anāpyakaḥ*: the term *ā* refers to a *pratyāhāra* (a grammatical abbreviation) and not specifically to the suffix *ṭāp*, because of the qualification "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*). Therefore, he explains: [the *ā*] beginning from *ṭā* up to the *p* of *sup*.

(306) *Hali lopaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.113. [Objection: According to the principle *nānarthake’lontyavidhiḥ* ("the rule regarding the final letter does not apply when [an operation] is meaningless"), one might argue that in forms such as *bibharti* and *piparti*, by the rules *hṛñām it* and *artipipartyoś ca*, the substitution of *it* would apply to the entire reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

Anticipating the objection that while a single [element] may be meaningful in the absence of duality, it is only the aggregate that possesses meaning when duality exists, he says: "The modification of non-repetition" (Pāṇini 1.1.59).
Then: "In a single [element], as if it were the beginning and the end" (Pāṇini 1.1.21).
"Having a beginning and an end": it is well known in the world that "that which has nothing before it is a beginning," and "that which has nothing after it is an end.
Since both of these cannot exist in a single, solitary entity, those [qualities] designated as beginning and end [are applied to it].

Since this grammatical operation must be performed, this extended application (*atideśa*) is commenced. Nor should it be suspected that—because of the subsequent status [of the rule]—once the lengthening by *upadhā* (P. 6.4.7) has occurred and subsequently the elision of *hal* (P. 6.1.68) takes place, forms such as *ābhyām* will be established; for what is the purpose here of citing the sūtra *ādyantavad ekasmin*? This is because the elision of *hal* is obligatory (*nitya*).

Because this [suffix] applies even before the long vowel [is substituted], and because the locative case is seen in the rule "in one [word] when the object of comparison is present," he says—intending that the suffix *vat* occurs only in the sense of the locative—"as at the beginning" and "as at the end.
What is the purpose of [specifying] "as at the beginning"? [The example is] *ĀṬpagavaḥ*. Here, it is so that the first syllable of the suffix *aṇ* may be acute-accented (*udātta*).
In the Bhāṣya, however, having removed the rule *ādya-vidi*, the sūtra *vyapadeśivadekasmin* has been inferred. A "designation" (*vyapadeśa*) is a specific designation—the primary usage.
That which possesses such [a designation] is "possessing a designation" (*vyapadeśin*), meaning "primary. By that [rule]:

The meaning is that the same effect would apply even when [the vowel] occurs within a single *asagāya* (non-composite) word. By this, the doubling (*dvitva*) established by the rule *ekācaḥ* is successfully achieved in cases such as *ṭhiyāya* and *ṭhāre*. Otherwise, because [the vowel] is designated as being at the beginning or end [of a word], the doubling would not occur; such is the direction of the argument.

(308) *nedamadasorakoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.11. [The rule] *nedamadasoḥ* [is stated]. However, in the Bhāṣya it says: *idamadasoḥ kāt*. This [rule] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). It is established that [the substitution of] *ais* for *bhis* occurs only after *kā* (i.e., the form *kim*) of *idam* and *adas*, and not from anything else.

The moderns [Navīnas], however, argue: if the rule were formulated as *idamadasoḥ kāt*, then a reversed restriction (*viparīta-niyama*)—namely, that *ais* occurs only after *idam* and *adas* followed by *adbhis*—might also be possible. In that case, forms such as *ābhiśca* would not be established. Rather, [the correct formulation is] *idamadasoḥ kāt adbhis*.
They say that it would be easier to state two separate rules: "ais" and "thataḥ.

Anticipating the objection that the substitution of "an" might occur instead of "smai" because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules], he says: "Because it is obligatory, 'smai' takes the place of 'he'."

(309) *idamo’nvādeśe’śanudātastṛtīyādau* | 2|4|32|. [The rule] "In the case of a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), the substitute *aś* takes the place of *idam*, and it is unaccented, when the third case-ending and those following it occur. [Objection: Now, even if the substitution of the unaccented *aś* for *idam* were prescribed by the rule beginning with *ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.102), the desired forms such as *ābhyām* would still be established through elision (*lopa*) before a consonant (*hal*). However, in the case of *enayoh*, [this would not be possible].
Since a specific rule has been prescribed [for the substitution of *sarva*], one might ask: "What is the purpose of this mention of *śit*?

To this he replies: "It is for the sake of including the element *kaC*. Although the inclusion of the marker *ś* here is redundant—since the substitution of *sarva* for the whole word is established by the very force of prescribing the replacement of *a* with *ā*—[the *ś* is necessary].

Nevertheless, one might suspect that the prescription of the vowel *a* is solely for the sake of making it unaccented (*anudātta*); to prevent this, they say that the *śit*-marker (the *ś* in *śi*) is employed. However, the *Kāśikā* states that if the term were taught by compounding *ṭha* and *a* as *ṭha-a*, then because it would consist of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would necessarily be a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*), and thus the inclusion of the word *sid* could have been omitted.

(310) *dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.24. Regarding *dvitīyāṭaussu*: from the rule *idamo’nvādeśe*, the term *idam* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*), as is the term *anvādeśe*. From the rule *etadastratasoḥ*, the term *etad* is also understood to carry over.
Regarding this, he says: "The substitution of *enā* for *idam* and *etad*, etc.

Since the term "anudātta" (unaccented) is understood to follow from the previous rule, it should be known that the substitute *enā* is unaccented. "To prescribe an operation" means to cause something not previously established to be understood. [This applies] when used in the sense of "slightness" (*īṣadartha*) or in connection with a verb (*kriyāyoga*).

And in the rule for the substitution of *na* in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*) and a prohibition (*niṣedha*), as in the example "one should know this [person] to be an Ātreya," the meanings such as "slight" (*īṣadartha*) and so forth are not being prescribed, but rather are being restated (*anūdyate*); therefore, the substitution of *enā* does not occur there. By this same principle, [the verse] "This man is afraid; you yourself, O Rādhe, must lead him home" is also explained.
This has been explained; for cowardice (*bhīrutva*) is intended as that which is to be restated (*anuvādya*). Thus end those [words] ending in *m*.

Regarding *sudān*: [the suffix] *kvip* is applied. Nor should one suspect that, when the rule "of a nasal before *kvip*" (*anunāsikasya kvī*) requires the lengthening of the vowel, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) would apply to the elision of the *a* (*allopa*) and the elision of the *ṇi*, because this is a rule prescribing lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*).
Because of its prohibition; and because of the prohibition regarding a rule [applying] to *kvip*. Thus end those ending in *ṇ*.
(311) *na ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ* | Pāṇini 8.2.81. "By the force of the prohibition" refers to when, in the rule *a ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ*, [the word *a* is used].

They say that if one explains [the rule] by relying on the state of being in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyantatām*), such that it means "of a word ending in *ya* and of a word ending in the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhyanta*)", then the application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the rule regarding the treatment of a suffix as present) is easily obtained; therefore, one need not undergo the trouble of following the force of the prohibition for that purpose. This is also [the case] from the preceding [rule].
Fearing that the rule regarding *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element) might apply here, he says: "Not so. [He refers to] the Paribhāṣā of the sixth [Adhyāya].
The sense is that, because it is established as a *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) in the rule *vāha ūṭh*, it resides in that same location.

(312) *nalopaḥ supsvarasaṃjñātugvidhiṣu kṛti* | Pāṇini 8.2.2. [The elision of *n* does not take effect in the operations concerning case-endings (*sup*), accent (*svara*), technical names (*saṃjñā*), and the *tuka*-augment, when a *kṛt* suffix follows.]

The elision of *n* (*nalopaḥ*) [is considered as not having taken effect] in the context of *sup*-suffixes and accents. He states—"not elsewhere," etc.—to show that this rule is commenced for the purpose of restriction by means of the very principle "that which is taught earlier is as if not established" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*). Therefore, the meaning is that in cases such as *rājāśva*, when the long vowel of homogeneous quality (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*) is to be applied, the elision of *n* is not treated as non-existent.

He illustrates this secondary rule (*subvidhi*) with the words beginning with "ātvam" and so forth. A rule dependent on a *sup* (case-ending) is a *subvidhi*. However, in the rule for accent (*svaravidhi*), there is the example "añcārmam. In the compound [formed by] "iksaṅkhaye saṃjñāyām," once the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) has occurred, the preceding member becomes one ending in an *a*-vowel.

In the case of *dharme cā’varṇam*, the rule *dyactryajiti* would have resulted in the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the prior member; however, this does not occur because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as if it had not taken place (*asiddha*). Furthermore, regarding the formation of feminine suffixes, he will explain under the rule *añceḥ* with the words "even when the elision of *n* has been performed," and so forth.
Others, however, cite "daṇḍiguptau" and "guptadaṇḍinau" as examples.

They say that because the elision of *n* (nalopa) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) here, the designation *hi* does not apply; consequently, the rule for mandatory prior placement—"in a *dvandva*, [the word ending in] *hi* [comes first]"—does not take effect. Why is it stated "in the rule prescribing *tuṅ* before a *kṛt*-suffix"?
The word *vṛtrahat* [becomes] *vṛtrahacchattram*. Here, the augment *tuk* would indeed apply by the rule *he ca*.

Although in the case of *vṛtrahabhyām*, the non-application of the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) is established by the very principle that "what is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as good as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what is internal (*antaraṅga*)," nevertheless, regarding this maxim...
The inclusion of the term *tug* is for the purpose of making known [the rule's] impermanence (*anityatva*); by this, forms such as *aṭhyā* and *aṭhaḥ* are established.

Otherwise, because the substitution of *at* (for *as*) which depends on a case-ending would be considered *asiddha* due to its being *bahiraṅga*, the suffix *ṭāp* would not occur. And this is stated in the context of the principle: "In the absence of immediate succession with a vowel (*aj-ānantarya*), there is the application of the status of being *bahiraṅga*."

Regarding this, some have stated, following the opinion of Haradatta and others, that "there is no immediate sequence of vowels (*aca-anantarya*) whether the operation is internal (*antaraṅga*) or external (*bahiraṅga*). However, according to the view of Kaiyaṭa—that "the immediate sequence of vowels [is required] for a subsequent operation"—the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* does not apply here. This is because in the rule *yāṭ-se*, the suffix *ṭāp* [is present].

It should be understood that this is established by the very rule *ayāsyoḥ* alone, even setting aside the prohibitions regarding the *saṃnipāta* (phonetic combination) condition. Regarding *pratidiv*: the suffix *kanin* is applied according to the rule *anin yuvṛṣitakṣirājidhanvidyaupratidivaḥ*.

(313) *hali ca* | Pāṇini 6.4.2. The phrase *hali ca* [is stated]. From the rule *ṛt-ṣṭhvor upadhāyā dīrgha ikaḥ*, the word *dīrghaḥ* (long vowel) is understood by anuvṛtti; and from the rule *ipi dhātoḥ*, the word *dhātoḥ* (of a verbal root) is also understood. Furthermore, that mention of "verbal root" (*dhātu*) is connected with the word *ṛt-ṣṭhvoḥ*.

It is qualified by the qualifier; thus, he states the rule for that which ends in [the specified element]—namely, "of a root ending in *r*," and so forth. Examples of roots ending in *r* are *īryati*, *paryati*, *gīrṇam*, *pūrṇam*, and others. Why "of a root"? [To exclude cases such as *kṣīram*].

Let it not apply to a word ending in *repha* (the sound *r*), as in *agniḥ karoti* and *vāyuḥ karoti*. Now, one might argue that although there is a recurrence (*anuvartana*) of the term "dhātu" (root), the root is not qualified by the rule *ṛt-ṣṭhivoḥ*; rather, [it is qualified] as "a root ending in *repha*. But why?

It is thus specified: "When a root ending in *repha* (r) has a long vowel before the suffix *au*, provided that *repha* and *va* follow [the vowel] within the root. Here, the word *anta* signifies "proximity. Consequently, the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca* could be dispensed with, as forms such as *mūrchatih* and *hūrchatu* would be established by this very rule.

If you say this is not so, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *urukarīyati*. Therefore, by the rule *rṭhvoḥ*, the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone is the thing to be qualified. This is clear in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*). As for what has been proposed by some regarding the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca*, that is incorrect.

Because the *v* of *div-* is not a penultimate letter (*anupadha*). "By the aforementioned reasoning" means that, according to the view that [the rules] are applied in their stated order (*yathoddeśapakṣa*), the long vowel is *asiddha* with respect to the sixth case-locative technical rule (*paribhāṣā*).
In the form *pratidivnaḥ*, the prohibition applies only to a *bha*-stem ending in *r*, because the word *raṭhaḥ* is understood as a governing term (*anuvartana*) in the rule *na bhakurchurām*.

Thus, the prohibition of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) should not be suspected here, because the final portion (*nānta*) is a *bha*-stem in this context. (314) *Na saṃyogād vamantāt* 6.4.37. [The example] is *yajvā*. One who has performed a sacrifice is a *yajvā*; [the suffix] *ṅvanip* is applied after the roots *yaji* and *uñji*. [The example] is *brahmaṇā*.

Having begun with the rule “*manin*” after roots ending in *ṛ*, the substitution of *at* for *na* is prescribed by the rule “*ṛn-ṛtoḥ sya ca*”; thus, this word *brahman* is derived from the suffix *ṭhan*.
(315) [Pāṇini 6.4.12] states: “In the case of *in*, *han*, *pūṣan*, and *aryaman*, [the nasal is dropped] before the nominative plural ending *śas*.”

Since this [result] is already established by the rule *inhanpūṣāryamṇāṃ śau cāsaṃbuddhau*, this [present rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Thus he says: "only before [the suffixes] *śi* and *au* [is there lengthening] of the penultimate vowel.
This restriction applies only to the lengthening of the penultimate vowel; therefore, in the form *vṛtrahāyate*, the lengthening [of the *a*] occurs by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*.

It indeed occurs. In the case of *vṛtrahaṇī*, the lengthening prescribed by the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ* is also excluded by this restriction. This is because the understanding of the restriction is based solely on the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), as established in the *Manoramā*. [The restriction applies] only before the suffix *śa*.
Since [the substitution] would not apply to the long vowel by rule, he says:
Regarding *sau ca*: although it could have been stated as *isvaḥ*, the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. *vṛtrahā*.
"He slew Vṛtra. [The suffix] *kvip* is applied by the rule "brahmabhrūṇa-".

(317) *ho hanter ñṇinneṣu* | Pāṇini 7.3.54. [This means] "the *h* of the root *han* [is replaced by *gh*] before suffixes marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*". Here, the terms "*ñiti*" and "*ṇiti*" qualify the root *han*, while the term "*akāre*" [qualifies the suffix].

However, it should be understood that "tu" (the substitution of *ṭh*) occurs as far as possible. Alternatively, all [affixes] beginning with *ñ* and *ṇ* are qualifiers of "hrasva" (short vowel) itself. Regarding the portions "in a *ñ*-marked affix" and "in a *ṇ*-marked affix," the principle of "non-intervention by anything else" (*yena nāvyavadhāna-nyāya*) allows for an intervention of two [sounds]. Thus, in the examples "ahātaḥ" and "ghātakaḥ," the substitution of *k* (*kutva*) takes place. But here—
It does not occur; one who desires his own killing is called *hananīyati*.
From the root *hananīyati*, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied, resulting in the form *hananīyaka*. This is clear from the *Mahābhāṣya*, Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, and other sources. (318) *Hanteḥ* | 8.4.22.

He explains the sūtra *ṭhano 't pūrvasya* by means of a division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*), stating *hanteḥ*. In connection with this, he provides an example: *prahaṇyāt*. He then states the portion relevant to the present subject:
(319) *at pūrvasya* 8.4.22.

Regarding the rule *atpūrvasya* and the phrase *ekājuttare*: one should not argue that once the elision (*al-lopa*) has taken place, the condition of being "a single vowel" (*ekāctva*) no longer exists;

for even in a rule concerning what precedes, the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) is maintained. Nor should it be argued that "the status of the original element does not apply when what precedes is treated as non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*), because this is an exception (*doṣa*).

This is because it is stated [in the grammatical tradition]: "In the case of *saṃyoga*, elision (*lopa*), *latva*, and *ṇatva*. As for the phrase "it is set aside," it should be understood that the *ṇatva* prescribed by the rule "also when *um* follows" (*umati ca*) is likewise set aside. However, in the Bhāṣya it is said: "A prohibition must be stated regarding the substitution of *ha* when there is an intervention by *ku*. What is the purpose? [Examples: *vṛtraghnaḥ*, *srugghnaḥ*."

It was stated that [in the rule] *prāghāni*, the mention of *atpūrva* in the rule *ṭhhanteratpūrvasya* need not be made; however, this is merely a description of the intention (*āśaya*) of the Vārttika, and not the actual state of affairs (*vastusthiti*), because [the Vārttikakāra],
rather than rejecting a portion of the Sūtra via a Vārttika, has resorted to a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*).
The *Manoramā* maintains that it is indeed logical to summarize the meaning of the *Vārttika* [as follows]:

"But surely, in the rule *at-pūrvasya*, is the *tapara* (the final *t*) intended or not? If it is intended, then forms such as *bahuvṛtrahāṇī* would not be established. If it is not intended, then [forms such as] *rāghānī* [would not be established]."

Even in the case of the *ciṇ* [affix], there would be *ṇatva*; consequently, one would have to accept the statement: "There is a prohibition when there is an intervention by *u* and when there are substitutes for *ha*. What, then, is the purpose of this division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? On this point, they say: here, [the suffix] followed by *tu* is indeed intended. Nor [does this apply] in the case of *ahuvṛtrahāṇī*.

The substitution of *ṇ* is not established as non-existent (*asiddhi*), because since the substitution of *ṇ* is internal (*antaraṅga*), the long vowel is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that operation. Nor should it be argued that the *ṣaṣṭhī-paribhāṣā* does not apply to an internal rule belonging to the third section of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, for we accept the *kāryakāla-pakṣa* (the view that rules become operative at the time they are required). And thus, [it remains] internal.

It should not be argued that the rule for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) would apply even in the case of *arāghāni*, because on the view that "a verbal root is joined with its suffixal element (*sādhana*) first," the *ṇatva* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). This is because, in accordance with established usage, the alternative view that "the verbal root is joined with the prefix (*upasarga*) first" is not accepted. Others [hold this view].

However, because the word "upasargāt" is understood to carry over into the rule "hanteratpūrvasya," even though there is no application of the rule "ekājuttare" (Pāṇini 8.4.12) to form *hrūṇapraghna* due to the significance of the separation by *ud*, [the rule still applies] in cases such as *vṛtraghnaḥ* and *srugghna*.
In the case of the form *dvāram*, the Vārttika "uvyavāye" must indeed be accepted;

for even by setting aside the maxim "the rule applies only to what immediately precedes" (*anantarasya*) through the analysis of the yoga-rule (*yogavibhāga*), that [Vārttika] achieves its purpose, whereas there is no capacity [in it] to set aside the connection with a prefix (*upasarga*). Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that when the *kvip* suffix is prescribed with *brahma* and other words as upapadas, it would apply only to the bare root and not to the root preceded by a prefix— such that forms like *brahmaprahā* and *bhrūṇaprahā* would be impossible; for in the rule *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*, the term *anupasarge* [is intended to mean]...
Because the suffix *kvip* is possible after the root *han* when preceded by a prefix, on the basis of the general indicator (*jñāpaka*) [implied by the rule],
and because the mention of "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) serves as a general indicator,
the aforementioned *vārttika* itself is the authority. Therefore, there is a formal separation (*yogavibhāga*) here of the rule "after *han*."
They say that [the suffix] is indeed meaningless.
(320) Regarding *maghavā bahulam* 6.4.128, it was stated by Mādhava; for such is the text of his work: "In the case of the designation *bha*, when there is elision of *al*..."

Since the final member (*uttarapada*) lacks a vowel (*anacka*), the status of being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply because this is not a rule concerning vowels (*alvidhi*).

Consequently, due to the absence of the condition of having a single syllable as the final member (*ekāj-uttarapadatva*), the optional application prescribed by the rule *rātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca* occurs—resulting in the forms *vṛtraghnau* and *vṛtraghnaḥ*. Furthermore, regarding that [statement in the] Bhāṣya...

The statement "because it is a rule conditioned by a *ṭha*-suffix" (*ṭhalvidhitvāt*) is inconsistent; for the rule *acaḥ parasmin* was indeed commenced for the very purpose of preventing such [substitution]. Since that [rule] does not apply, another justification must be stated. Furthermore, even though the rule *ekājuttareṭ* does not apply, there is the rule *kumati ca*.

Because it is impossible to prevent, the optionality of the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is indeed inconsistent. Nor can it be argued that even within the "tripadī" (the final three rules of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*),

since a subsequent rule is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to a preceding one, the rules "ṭhEkājuttarapade ṇaḥ" and "Um iti ca" would not apply, and thus the substitution of *ṇ* in "rātipadikānte" would necessarily be optional.

It must be stated that [the rule] applies; for it is clear from the Bhāṣya and other sources that "a connection is not established, but rather a context [is required] within a context. This is the general direction. Regarding the phrase "the mentions of *an*, *in*, *as*, and *am*":
*an* refers to the meaningful [element] in *rājñe* and the meaningless [element] in *āmnā*; *in* refers to the meaningful [element] in *daṇḍī*.
In the word *vāggmī*, [the suffix] is meaningless; in *supayāḥ*, it is meaningful. Here, in *trurūbhyām*, the augment *tuṭ* is added to the suffix *asu*; in *man*, it is meaningful as in *suśarma*;
in *uprathimā*, it is meaningless. And this is according to the rule *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam*.
The point is established by the fact that the mention of "stem" (*aṅga*) in the Sūtra indicates that the paribhāṣā "that which possesses meaning [is understood]" is not universally applicable.

For indeed, the mention of "stem" was made there [in P. 8.3.78] so that the term *ṣīdhvam* would not be included in the rule *veviṣīdhvam*. Yet that mention is redundant, precisely because [the term *ṣīdhvam*] is meaningless [as a whole].
Because the inclusion of that [word] would otherwise be unestablished, it is therefore known that the paribhāṣā "that which has a meaning" (arthavadgrahaṇa) is not universally obligatory (anitya).

In the rule *maghavā bahulam*, the word *tṛ* is understood from the preceding rule *arvaṇastṛsāvanaḥ*; and since that [word *tṛ*] is in the genitive sense (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), the word *maghave* is in the nominative case. Thus he says:

(321) *ugidacāṃ sarvanāmasthāne'dhātoḥ* | P. 7.1.70. Regarding the word *maghavat*: [the mention of] *adhātoḥ* is for the purpose of including that which was previously not a verbal root (*adhātubhūtapūrva*).
Indeed, the inclusion of *añc-* is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning: "If [the suffix] occurs after a verbal root ending in *ugit*, it occurs only after *añc-*."

In that case, [the rule] applies only to *añcati*. And thus, in examples such as *gomān ivācarati* (he acts like one possessing cows), even though it is a verbal root (*dhātu*) at present, the mention of "non-root" (*adhātu*) is for the sake of the prescriptive rule. This will become clear in the root text itself.
Now, if the mention of *añcati* implies that the operation of an *ugit* suffix applies only to a root that is taught as such (*aupadeśika*), then [the rule] applies only to *añcati*.

If it is argued that the mention of "non-element" (*adhātu*) should be abandoned after the explanation, the moderns (*navya*) say here: this restriction does not apply solely to the domain of *un* suffixes; rather, it is restricted such that if the operation of an *ugit* applies to a verbal root, it applies only to the root *añc*. Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *ukhāsrat*, according to the rule *ugitaśca*.

Because it will be stated in the Sūtra [Pāṇini 6.3.43]. Consequently, if it were explained that "the operation of *ugit* applies to a root that is *aupadeśika* (original/primary)," then in the previously mentioned examples such as *gomān*, the suffix *ṅīp* would undesirably follow for the feminine according to the rule "*ugitaśca*" [Pāṇini 4.1.6], since a root ending in *kvip* used in the sense of habitual action (*ācārakvibanta*) lacks the status of being *aupadeśika*. It is not [so].

Regarding the *ceṣṭāpati* (the undesirable consequence): since the author of the Sūtra has specifically excluded the verbal root (*dhātu*) [from the scope of the rule], one can infer that the suffix *ṅīp* is not intended there;

such is the direction of the argument. Now, an objection might be raised: the augment *num* should apply only to the root *añc-* which loses its *n*, and not to the root *añc-* with its *n* used in the sense of "worship"; for this very purpose, the mention of *acām* [in the rule] was made.

If it is asked how this [rule] can have the purpose of establishing a general restriction (*sāmānyaniyama*) given its meaningfulness, it is replied: in the rule *acām*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is not intended to be significant. Thus, the aforementioned status as a general restriction, as stated by the Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa, and others, is indeed consistent.

Even in the case of *añc* in the word *pūjārtha* followed by *num*, the desired form is established by the rule *aś-cāpadāntasya*, which— adopting the view that the rule refers to the class (*jāti*)— prescribes *ṇatva* for the entire class and thereby ordains the *anusvāra*.
However, under the view that the rule refers to individual instances (*vyakti*), since *anusvāra* is recited among the *śar* consonants, when another *anusvāra* follows...

When there is an *anusvāra*, a form as if containing two *anusvāras* is desired; for even in your view, that form cannot be avoided due to doubling (*dvitva*) by the rule "ṭh-anaci ca. Nor should it be feared that, according to your position, there would be three *anusvāras* due to doubling, because [the second one] is elided by the rule "haro jhari."

Because it is possible to prevent [the application of the rule]. If it is argued that, in the absence of elision (*lopābhāva*), there would be the hearing of all three [sounds], we reply that there is no obstacle to accepting that [elision] in accordance with the rules stated by the Bhāṣyakāra, Kaiyaṭa, and others. Following what is desired, one must resort here to the *jāti*-theory (the theory of classes) alone; otherwise, the augment *num* would occur.
The intention is that the term *num* is understood to follow from the rule "ṭhito num dhātoḥ. Now, one might object:

"In cases such as *urvann*, since the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered *asiddha*, the word would not end in *n*, and thus the lengthening [of the vowel] should not occur. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this case, when the lengthening is to be performed..."
Thus [it is said]: "Because of the inclusion of the term *bahula*. This means that in some instances, the meaning is indeed something else.

[The word] *bahulam* is derived from the sense of "taking (*lāti*) many meanings (*arthān*). The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *āto ’nupasarge* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), with the object (*karman*) serving as the upapada. [The forms] *śvan* and *ukṣan* [are examples].

The meaning is that [the word *maghavan*] is derived by the *uṇādi* sūtra "van-ukṣan-paṣan-plīhan-kledan-snehan-mūrdhan-majjan-aryaman-viśvapsan-parijman-mātariśvan-maghavan" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.157). Regarding the phrase "by means of irregular derivation" (*nipātanāt*), the meaning is that it is due to the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of these three elements: the substitution of the letter *gh* for the letter *h* in the root *maha*, the addition of the augment *av*, and the suffix *kan*. The phrase "rejected in the original source" (*pratyākhyātam ākare*) refers to this.

Thus, since there is no possibility of rejecting the substitution (*ādeśa*) due to the difference in results, it has been stated that even in the view of substitution, the long vowel is indeed sanctioned by the Bhāṣya and other authorities; therefore, by virtue of the mention of *bahulam* (diversely), the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is not treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). As for what some say—that even in the view of the suffix *matup*, the long vowel does not occur because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*), and this is the intention of the Bhāṣya—that is incorrect, because there is no evidence for the Vedic nature of the form ending in *matup*, and because it contradicts the usage of Bhartṛhari cited as an example. This is the direction [of the argument]. [The rule] *cchandasīvanipau* [is also mentioned].

The meaning of the Vārttika is: "In the Vedic language, the suffixes *ini* and *nip* occur when they are in accordance with the sense (*anvarthe*). He will provide examples such as "umaṅgalīriyaṃ vadhūḥ" and "maghavānamīmahe" in the section on Vedic grammar. [He says] "it has the udātta accent on the final syllable."

Although the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātatva*) is obtained for these words by examining the *Ujjvaladatta* commentary and other texts—which state that they end in the suffix *kanin*—nevertheless, since the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) of words such as *ukṣan* mentioned in that very sūtra is beyond dispute in instances like "the ocean is *ukṣā*, *aruṇaḥ*, *suparṇaḥ*," "may *pūṣā* lead you from here," and "Agni is the head of heaven" (*agnirmūrdhā divaḥ*), the suffix *kan* alone is appropriate; this is the intended meaning.
(322) *śvayuvamaghonāmataddhite* [Pāṇini 6.4.133].
Regarding *śvayuvamaghonām*: having drawn down the word "na" from the rule "allopo'naḥ" [6.4.134], he explains [the sūtra].

Regarding the phrase *annantānām iti*: [the question is] "Of what [words ending in *an*]? [The answer is] "Of those ending in *maghavan*. Even though, despite the substitution of *na* for *n*, the word still possesses the status of ending in *an* because a modification of a single part does not alter the identity of the whole, nevertheless—by virtue of the force of the qualifier—the samprasāraṇa occurs only for that which actually has a manifest *n* at its end.

Regarding this, they say: "In this case [the rule applies]. However, the author of the Vārttika stated: "The mention of words ending in *n* in the rule for *saṃprasāraṇa* is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of the rule] to those not ending in *n*. Now, one might object:
"Even so, the elision of *a* by the rule *allopo’naḥ* would still be unavoidable"; but do not say so, for the author of the Bhāṣya...

Following the previously mentioned *vārttika* here, [it is understood that] the elision of the *an* [in *anaḥ*] applies only to that which ends in *nakāra* (the letter *n*), because it has been over-explained in that manner; this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṛlṛk*. By this, there is likewise an absence of the elision of *akāra* in the forms *bahudhīvarī* and *rājakīya*.

[The form] *siddhaḥ* [is established]. Because, after the substitution [of *ka*] by the rule *vano ra ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.7) and *rājñaḥ ka ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.137), the word no longer ends in *c*, [the suffix *ṭāp* does not apply]. Regarding the feminine form *maghavatī*: *maghavatī*, *maghavatyau*, *maghavatyaḥ*.
In this case, the augment *num* is not applied by the rule *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70), because of the maxim *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the rule applies to the word qualified by its gender).
It might be suspected [that the rule applies], but they say: "In the case of a case-ending, there is no inclusion of that which is qualified by gender.
(323) *Na saṃprasāraṇena saṃprasāraṇam* (P. 6.1.37). [The word] *na* [is understood]; from the rule *hvaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (P. 6.1.32), [the word *saṃprasāraṇam* is carried over].

Even though the term *saṃprasāraṇa* is understood from the preceding context, because the word *saṃprasāraṇa* is mentioned again here, the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution prescribed in another rule—namely, *vayuvamaghonām*—is also prohibited.
Thus he says: "Thus, there is no *it* [vowel-shortening] for the letter *y*. As for the form *yūnaḥ*: [one might object] that by the vowel *ū*...
How can there be a prohibition here due to intervention?
For the prohibition has its purpose fulfilled even in cases like *vivyādha* and *vivyathe*, where there is no intervention.
Nor should it be said that intervention follows solely from the mention of *samprasāraṇa*, as in [the rule] *acaḥ*.

[The objection is raised: "Because of the rule *sthānivat*, [the substitution] applies to the subsequent [element]. To this they reply: Since the mention of *samprasāraṇa* is repeated for the purpose of prohibiting [the operation] when the [substitute] is situated in another place (*videśastha*), the prohibition will indeed apply here even when there is an intervention; thus there is no fault.
Nor is it the case that, after the *samprasāraṇa* of the letter *y* has been effected by the rule *vyatho liṭi* (P. 7.4.68), which operates in another place, [the prohibition would fail].

One might suspect that, in order to prevent that [substitution], the rule *a-samprasāraṇe* could be applied, and thus the re-mention of *samprasāraṇa* would become purposeful; consequently, the prohibition would not apply when there is an intervention. However, this is not so, because in the authoritative treatise (*ākara*) it is stated that the rule *vyatho liṭi* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*.

Because it is clear; and because Kaiyaṭa has explained that "the exception resides in the same location as the general rule" (*utsargasadeśaścāpavādaḥ*), so that the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs only for the subsequent [vowel] and not for the preceding one.
(324) *arvaṇastrasāvanañaḥ* | 6.4.127 | [The substitution of *tṛ* for the final vowel of *arvan* occurs before the case-ending *asi*, provided it is not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*.]

The [rule] "arvaṇas tṛ" continues [from the previous sūtra], and that [term *arvan*] is qualified by both "arvaṇā" and "nañaḥ. Therefore, he says: "of that which is devoid of the negative particle (*nañ*)," and so forth. If it were a prasajya-pratiṣedha (a simple negation), it would apply only when a case-ending follows; consequently, it would not apply in forms such as *arvatī*.
With this intention, he says: "But not that [suffix]," etc. Nor is there an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *arvapriya*, because here the suffix is elided by *luk*;

since the suffix is thus lost, the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply here, as the suffix is implied by its own cause only through the *aṅga* (the stem). By this, [the rule] "it was destroyed by the vāhas" is explained.

The usage of Śrī Harṣa in the phrase “sahasragarvagarvaḥ” has been explained. Now, if this is so, then regarding the rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ*, it would follow that "substitutes for verbal roots, verbal bases, kṛt-affixes, taddhita-affixes, indeclinables, case-endings, and finite verbs should be treated like their original bases (*sthānin*)."

Having cited the preceding text and raised the alternative—"Is this merely an illustrative example?"—the *Manoramā* states: "The latter [alternative] is not tenable, because it would be redundant to mention 'avyaya' separately from both 'aṅga' and 'pada'.
How could that statement be consistent?

This is because, according to the stated principle regarding indeclinables (*avyaya*), [the suffix] is not an *aṅga*. Nor should it be argued that even if the operation of an *aṅga* is prohibited by the rule "a lumate" (P. 1.1.63), there is no such fault because the designation (*saṃjñā*) of an *aṅga* itself is not prohibited; for [the prohibition applies] to what precedes an affix (*pratyaya*).
By examining the *Manoramā* commentary on the sūtra *ṭhyaṅe’cu ca*, it is understood that all operations—whether they pertain to the *aṅga* (the stem) or not—are prohibited by the rule *a lumate*;
for when a suffix is elided by a term containing the word *lumat*, the designation (*saṃjñā*) of the *aṅga* must also be rejected. This applies to that [designation] as well.

Because the operation applies to the preceding element when a suffix follows. However, if it is accepted that the status of being a *aṅga* (base) persists even when [the suffix] is elided by *luk*, then this passage [in the commentary on] "ṭhyaci bham" and "vṛṣaṇvasvaśvayoḥ" would refer to:
"one whose *vasu* (wealth) is *vṛṣan* (rain-giving), i.e., *vṛṣaṇvasu*; one whose horse (*aśva*) is *vṛṣan*."

The statement that "in the case of *vṛṣaṇaśva*, as it has been cited, there is no elision of *n* here because [the condition] does not apply, but there is elision of *a* because it is not part of the *aṅga*" contradicts the text to be stated later in the section on Vedic grammar (*vaidikaprakriyā*) which says "there is no *it*" because it is not part of the *aṅga*. Nor...

One should not be deluded into thinking that the resolution—that because the *alopa* (elision of *a*) does not apply there due to it not being part of an *aṅga*—is redundant, based on the interpretation of *Pāṇini 6.4.134* (*ṭhallopo’naḥ*) as: "the *an* which is a constituent of an *aṅga*, which is not final in a word (*asarvamānastha*), and which is followed by a suffix beginning with *ya* or *ja*, etc., or by a *s*-class suffix. This is because [the elision] occurs precisely through the designation *bha*.

If it is argued that—since the rule *yajādi-svādi-paro yaḥ ‘n* (P. 6.1.15) provides an interpretation for the *an* following roots beginning with *yaj* and those beginning with *svap*, by analogy one may also obtain an interpretation for the *an* following *vasu* and *aśva*; and since one could simply have said "separate from that word" (*tasmāt padāt pṛthak*), the inclusion of the term *aṅga* in the expression "from the *aṅga* and the word" (*aṅga-padābhyām*) is merely due to haste—on this point they say: "No."

When it is explained in the *Lumat* rule that "when a *lumat* [marker] has been elided, no operation pertaining to that which is designated as an *aṅga* (stem) caused by that [elision] shall take place," then,
even though the operations of the *aṅga* such as *ṭharaṇas tṛ* are suspended, the designation as an *aṅga* [remains].

Because it is free from contradiction, the mention of "aṅga" (stem) found therein is entirely correct. However, upon careful consideration of the natural sense (*svārasya*) of the *Manoramā* passage beginning with "whether it is a stem or not a stem," as well as the root text stating "because of its being a non-stem" (*anaṅgatvāt*), and because there is no purpose in treating an indeclinable as a stem due to parsimony (*lāghava*) when a suffix follows, [the term refers to the suffix].

When the operation of what precedes is negated by what follows, then, because the designation *aṅga* (base) would also be negated without distinction, the mention of *aṅga* there [in the rule] is merely due to haste. Nor [can it be argued that] by the rule "a lumate" (P. 1.1.63), when the *aṅga* designation is negated, [the forms] *yuvan* and *uran* [would not apply].

It should not be argued that there would be a contradiction with the *Sūtra*, the *Bhāṣya*, and Kaiyaṭa, for those two works proceed there by way of a *prauḍhavāda* (an argument made for the sake of the system). Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is "a lumatā tasmin" (P. 1.1.63), and the *Manoramā* text states: "An operation of what precedes is prohibited when a suffix follows."

"It occurs by its own inherent force (*svarasataḥ*). [Objection: But surely the form *ṛtaḥ* is derived from the root *ṛdh* with the suffix *viC*, followed by *guṇa* substitution, and then the suffix *ṭha*;

from that, the forms *arvantau* and so on will be established by adding the possessive suffix *matup*. Furthermore, by the rule "in the Veda, the suffix *vanip* [is used] after [roots ending in] *ṛ*," the form *arva* will be established in the Veda. [Response: Only for the root *ṛdh* does the rule "after *am*, *adi*, *pad*, *ṛ*, etc. apply.

However, even in common worldly usage, the word *arvan* is established as meaning "horse," for this is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) according to the Amarakośa: "vājī, vāhaḥ, arvaḥ, gandharvaḥ, hayaḥ, saindhavaḥ, and saptiḥ.
Consequently, since the meaning does not differ [from that of *aśva*], what is the purpose of this sūtra?
If they say here: "Since the application of both forms ending in *n* and *t* would otherwise apply everywhere,

this [sūtra] is for the purpose of establishing a restriction— that when *su* follows and the preceding member is preceded by *nañ*, the form ending in *n* is used, whereas the form ending in *t* is not— just like the three sūtras beginning with ‘ṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ’."

As for what some have said—that even the words *arvan* and *maghavan* are indeed ungrammatical (*asādhutva*) in the common language (*bhāṣā*)—on the basis of the Vārttika: "The forms *arvaṇas-tṛ* and *maghonas-tṛ* are not to be taught [for the common language], for they are Vedic (*dhāndasa*); moreover, because of the rule for the suffixes *matup* and *vani*, both [forms] are seen in the Veda."
That is merely apparent, because the *Vārttika* intends [the suffix] *vanip* to be *madhyodātta* (accented on the middle syllable); for *vanip* is prescribed only in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

Thus, Śrī Harṣa employed it in the phrase: "The pride of the pride of the thousand horses was destroyed by the horses" (*vāhairalupyata sahasradurgarvagarvaḥ*). [Examples of the dual and plural are: *arvantau*, *arvantaḥ*.

By virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the word ends in *arvan*, and thus the substitution of *ar* [for *an*] occurs. Nor should it be argued that the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" does not apply to what is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*),
because that principle is restricted to the domain of rules for the introduction of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*).

(325) *pathimathyṛbhukṣām āt* 7.1.85. Regarding *pathimathi*: the word *mathin* is derived by the rule *anthaḥ*, while the suffix *ṭhin* is carried over from *amer iniḥ* and the vowel *i* is carried over from *aramaki*. From that [suffix], [the form *mathin* is produced]. *atastha*...

[The words] *cañcā* etc., *pathin*, and *ṛbhukṣaḥ* [are used] in the sense of "heaven" (*svarga*) and "thunderbolt" (*vajra*). From that, it should be understood that *ṛbhukṣin* is formed by the possessive suffix *ini*. Now, one might object: since the desired form is established even by the *anaṅ* substitution prescribed in the rule *asthidadhi...* where it is read as having an acute accent (*udātta*), why is the mention of "acute" (*udāta*) in the rule *anuR udātaḥ* necessary? [This is for the sake of the *uṇādi*...]

It is indisputable that [the sūtra] indicates the position that [the vowels] are non-distinct (abhedaka). And so, according to that position, even when an anunāsika vowel is uttered in the sūtra, an anunāsika *ā* would result due to the principle of closest similarity (*āntaratamya*); therefore, he says "ā-āt".

(326) *ito't sarvanāmasthāne* | Pāṇini 7.1.86. When the rule *ito't sarvanāmasthāne* is applied, while the term *at* from the previous rule (*ṭā-ḍasi-ṅasām-in-ḍyo-yāt* etc. is still in force, for what purpose is the word *at* repeated? Even if the word *at* were not repeated, the long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha* would have to occur in the case of *an-thā*, whereas in other cases [the substitution] would apply to the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).

If it is argued that [the lengthening] is by virtue of the rule *dīrgha* (Pāṇini 6.3.134), it is not so; for in the case of *ṛbhukṣaṇam*, since there is an option for lengthening according to *vā ṣapūrvasya nigame* (Pāṇini 6.1.130), the singular mention of *ad* is necessary to ensure that the short vowel is heard in one alternative. (327) *tho nthaḥ* | 7.1.87 | [The substitute] *ntha* is applied in place of *tha*. 7.1.87.

The final letter (*th*) and the substitute (*n*)—both are vowelless (*anacka*). Since the result would have been established by the rule "herthaḥ" alone, the mention of "ṭhito'tsarvanāmasthāne" is for the sake of *ṛbhukṣin*. With the intention that [the condition] "not being in a *sarvanāmasthāna*" does not apply to the *ṛbhukṣas* (those ending in *ṛbhukṣin*), even though the three [conditions] do not recur [in this specific case], he says:

(328) *Bhasya ṭerlopaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.143]. Regarding the rule *pathimathoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.85], he states "in the feminine" (*striyām*) by way of incidental discussion. As for the phrase "characterized by having *n* as its final letter" (*nāntalakṣaṇa*), the meaning is that because of the prohibition [by the rule] *a pūjanāt* [Pāṇini 5.4.69], the suffix *ap* [prescribed by the rule] *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.74] does not apply here.

Regarding *supathī*: the suffix *kap* was not applied [after *pathin*] by the rule "ṭhinaḥ striyām," because the application of suffixes at the end of a compound (*samāsāntavidhi*) is not invariably obligatory. This is also supported by the *bhāṣya* on the sūtra "yuvoranākau," which uses the form *supathī*. Furthermore, this is not an instance of the prohibition stated in "na pūjanāt."

The scope [of this rule] applies only to the preceding [rules], as will be stated later. Regarding the forms *pathimathi*, the substitution of *ā* and the change of *th* to *nth* would have applied by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim that a grammatical operation prescribed for a word applies also to its feminine form), but it does not occur here because of the prohibition against including a word with its feminine suffix (*liṅgaviśiṣṭāgrahaṇa*) when a case-ending follows. Here, this should be understood: [in the case of] *panthānam ātmanaḥ*...

It desires; it goes along [the path]. From that [root], the suffix *kvip* is applied. There is elision of *a* and elision of *ya*. Because a form that has undergone a partial modification is not considered different from the original, the substitution of *ā* occurs by the rule *athimathī*. By the rule *hoḥ nthaḥ*, [the *h* becomes *nth*], resulting in *panthāḥ*. The substitution of *a* does not occur by the rule *ṭhito’tsarvanāmasthāne*, because [the condition] *ṭhit* [is not met]. "Ṭhit" means...

Because of the inclusion of *ṭha* [in the rule], the substitution *yaṇ* (prescribed by *ṭheranekācaḥ*) is superseded—both because it is subsequent and because it is obligatory—by the rule *tho nthaḥ*. Due to being preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), there is no *yaṇ* substitution.
Thus: *panthiyau*, *panthiyaḥ*, *panthiyam*, *panthiyau*. By the rule *hasya ṭeklopaḥ*, [the final *i* is elided]: *pathaḥ*.
*pathā*, *pathībhyām*, *pathībhiḥ*, and so forth. Similarly, from the root *math* with the suffix *kvip*:

*manthāḥ*, *manthiyau*, *manthiyaḥ*; *ṛbhukṣāḥ*, *ṛbhukṣiyau*, *ṛbhukṣiyaḥ*, and so forth. By this [analysis], the purpose of the *tapara* (long vowel marker) in the rule *ṭhito't sarvanāmasthāne* applies both to the original form (*sthānin*) and to its substitute (*ādeśa*).
The commentary of Haradatta is employed for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukhārtham*).

Although the addition of the *t* marker (*taparakaraṇa*) in the substitute (*ādeśa*) is not strictly necessary, it is essential in the case of the original element (*sthānin*) in order to establish forms such as *anthiyau*. [Objection: But surely, because of the rule that the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddhatva*), [the *t* marker is unnecessary]?
If it is argued that in the case of *athimathyṛbhukṣām*, because of the substitution of *āt* for *na*, the forms must be *panthyāḥ*, *manthyāḥ*, and *ṛbhukṣyāḥ*,

and not *anthāḥ* and so forth— on this point they say: the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is internally conditioned (*antarvartin*), whereas the substitution of *āt* is externally conditioned (*bahirvartin*).

For here, by virtue of immediate proximity (*pratyāsatti*), there is only one *su*-affix that serves as the cause; it is precisely with respect to that [cause] that the elision of the *n* (in *rājā*) is considered non-existent for the purposes of the rule "elision of *n* before a *su*-affix and in svarita-accented syllables" (*alopaḥ supsvare*), and not with respect to anything else.
Thus, in this case, the substitution of *ā* does not apply to the *n*, but rather to the vowel *ī*.

(329) *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ* | 1.1.24 | "Words ending in ṣ or n are called *ṣaṭ*. The mention of the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*) is intended to specify the number; by virtue of that, the term "number" (*saṅkhyā*), which in the preceding rule was intended as a technical name (*saṃjñā*), is here understood as referring to the thing named (*saṃjñin*).

He says "it is accomplished" with the intention that it is not [otherwise]; thus he says "number" (*saṅkhyā*). However, what was stated by the elder [teacher] at the time of instruction—that it ends in *ṣ* and ends in *n*—is contradicted by his own forthcoming text, beginning with "even when the *n*-elision has been performed in the case of 'añc'. This is because, even if it does not end in *n* at present, it [did so] during the instruction.
The point is that [the argument] "there was no end" cannot be used as a reason for its being unestablished; this is the direction of the argument. Regarding the term *saṃnipāta*:
the sense is that the interpretation "at the time of the original instruction (*upadeśa*)" is likewise fruitless.
As for what they say—that because the paribhāṣā is non-eternal (*anitya*), the suffix *lak* would occur—that is mere recklessness.

For even if it were applied to the desired place, the Paribhāṣā would become useless, as it would have no effect. As for what they say— having raised the objection, "From where has the mention of 'upadeśa' (original enunciation) come here?", [they reply] that "the status of being original is obtained through the force of the inclusion of the word 'anta' (end) in the rule 'ṇānta'"— that too is not correct.
Because the capacity [of the rule] is exhausted by the attraction of the word *aṅkye* and by establishing its status as referring to a technical term (*saṃjñā*),
[the rule] *nopadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.7) does not apply.

Regarding *nopadhāyāḥ*: the word *e* is a term with its genitive case ending elided, serving as a qualifier for *aṅgasya*. Since the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered *asiddha*, the rule for lengthening [the vowel] before *ām* would not otherwise apply; thus, this sūtra is commenced.

As for the phrase “but when [the suffix] is secondary” (*gauṇatve tu*): the intention is that the use of the plural number in the reference [of the suffix] is intended to signify the predominance of the meaning [rather than the formal suffix itself].
Regarding *priyapañca*: there is a *cakāra* (*ca*) between the two *ña*s. (331) *aṣṭana vibhaktau* 7.2.84:
*aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*. Because this is a sūtra-formulation (*sautratvāt*), the elision of *a* (*allopa*) has not been applied here.
From the rule *ani nyuṣitakṣi*, with *ani* continuing as a governing term (*anuvartamāna*),

the words *saptan* and *aṣṭan* are formed by the rule *aspyaśūbhyāṃ tuṭ ca iṭ*. Intending that the word *halī* is extracted from the subsequent rule *rāyo hali* and serves as a qualifier for the case-ending (*vibhakteḥ*), [the following is stated].

He explains: "In the case of [stems] beginning with a consonant. If the word *hal* were not extracted [from the previous rule], then forms such as *aṣṭānām* would not be established. This is because, due to its higher status and its obligatory nature (*nityatva*), the augment *nuṭ* would apply first; once *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan*) had been applied, the stem would no longer end in *an*, and thus, due to the absence of the designation *ṣaṭ*, the *nuṭ* augment would not occur. Nor...

It might be argued that, since the six technical names (*ṣaṭsaṃjñā*) were already applied under the view that the rule applies according to its enunciation (*yathoddeśapakṣa*), they remain easily available even after the substitution of *kṛt* by *at* on the basis of the maxim of partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). However, this maxim is not applicable in a rule concerning the substitution of an *al* (a phoneme). Furthermore, [consider] the forms *priyāṣṭānau*, *priyaṣṭānaḥ*, and *priyaṣṭnaḥ*.

It should be understood that even forms such as *aṣṭānām* would not be established, because, according to the reasoning already stated, the substitution of *āt* would apply there as well. (332) *aṣṭābhya auś* | Pāṇini 7.1.21.

The suffix *āṬ* is substituted for the eight [cases]. Because it is marked with *ś*, it is a substitute for the whole (sarvādeśa). Now, one might object: in the rule *anekāl-śit sarvasya*, the mention of *śit* could be dispensed with, as it can be stated that it is a substitute for the whole simply because it has more than one phoneme (*anekāltva*).
Nor should it be argued that once *ś* is assigned the technical designation *it*, it no longer possesses the status of having more than one phoneme.

Because of the capacity for the explicit mention of the letter *ś*, one must here resort to the principle of referring to what previously existed (*bhūtapūrvagati*). Nor should it be argued that, by this logic, the substitute *trā* in the rule *ṭharaśrasrāsāv* would also become a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*), for in that case, the purpose of the letter *ṛ* is exhausted by its role in producing the effect of the marker *ugit*. Not so.
Furthermore, one should not suspect that in cases such as *aśīti*, the letter *ś* is intended solely for the purpose of pronunciation;

for, by the mention of *ṭhaihalaukika* in the *anuśatikādi* group, it is accepted that the letter *ś* bears the technical designation *it*. [The phrase] "from that which has taken the form *ā*" [is used]. Now, an objection: ...
