It was stated that *ṭhali* is elided; how then is the form *kṛtākāratā* (the state of having the vowel *ā*) established? To this he says: "from *aṣṭabhyaḥ*. This is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the form *aṣṭābhyaḥ*, which already possesses the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*), and not an *ātva* produced by the force of a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*). For if it were so [produced by a rule], then by the subsequent indicator (*jñāpaka*) to be mentioned, its...

The intention is that, for the sake of brevity, one might simply say "from the eight [suffixes] beginning with au" (aṣṭabhya āṬśi) or "from the eight [suffixes] beginning with a" (aṣṭabhya āśi), since they are optional. "This" (idam) means both what is directly heard and what is inferred.
Regarding the rule "after *aṣṭan* when it ends in a long vowel": a case-ending other than a sarvanāmasthāna suffix following *aṣṭan* ending in a long vowel is acute (udātta).

It could be [accented] by eight [syllables]. Why [is it] "from a long vowel"? [Consider] *aṣṭábhiḥ*. This word has the middle syllable as its udātta (acute accent). This is because the rule *halyupotamam* takes effect, overriding the rule *aṭatricaturbhyo halādiḥ*. [The latter rule states that] when a case ending beginning with a consonant follows the words *aṣṭan*, *tri*, or *catur*, [the penultimate syllable is acute]. In a word ending in such a case ending...

The meaning of that [sūtra] is that [the word] should be udātta when it is *upotama* (penultimate). Now, one might object: "In rules such as *ri-aṣṭnaḥ*, the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is necessary here in order to prevent the udātta accent of the case-ending; how then can this [mention of the long vowel] be understood as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the optional substitution of *āt*? To this they say: [it is because of the rule] *aṣṭano dīrghāt*.

By interpreting [the rule] as "after *aṣṭan*, when it is oxytone, and when followed by a case-ending beginning with a vowel," the acute accent on the case-ending in forms such as *aṣṭabhiḥ* is established;
this is because *aṣṭan* is oxytone by virtue of belonging to the *ghṛtādi* group. This applies in bahuvrīhi compounds such as *priyāṣṭnaḥ*.

However, since the acute accent on the final syllable of *aṣṭan-* would not apply due to the acceptance of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [of the compound], the acute accent on the case-ending (*vibhakti*) does not take effect; thus, the inclusion of the long-vowel marker (*dīrghagrahaṇa*)—being otherwise redundant—is indeed an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned point. Regarding the form *aṣṭānām*: it is established in the *Manoramā* that the substitution of *ā* occurs only after the insertion of *uṭ*, because the rule regarding the non-eternality of the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* applies, and not prior to it.

On this point, the moderns (*navyāḥ*) argue: even in the absence of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for *au*) due to the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* (the rule that an operation which causes the destruction of a condition that brought about another operation does not take effect), there is no defect here. For the desired forms such as *pañcānām* and *saptānām* are established by the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] according to the rule *nopadhāyāḥ* and the subsequent elision of *n*. Nor should it be argued that the purpose of the rule prescribing *ātva* is to ensure the acute accent (*udātta*) on the case-ending according to the rule *ṣaṣṭhno dīrghād iti*, because that [accentuation] is already established by the rule *aṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ*. [The phrase] "even from what precedes" (*pūrvasmād api*)...

Nor should one suspect here the prohibition "when a subsequent operation is not established, [the substitute] is not as if it were the original" (*na sthānivat*), because it has been stated: "this is a fault in the case of the elision of the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*), the substitution of *l* (*latva*), and the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*). This is the general direction. Regarding the phrase "only when [the suffix] is primary": for the substitution of *auṭ* occurs only when [the suffix] is primary, just like the augment *luṅnuṭ*, and not when it is secondary (*gauṇatva*), because of the mention of the plural number in the rule "after eight [stems]" (*aṣṭābhya auś*). Otherwise, even if there were an imitation of the form where *ātvam* has already been applied, he would have mentioned it in the singular alone—as "auś after aṣṭan" (*aṣṭa auś*) or simply "auś after aṣṭa."

And this is clear from the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the sūtra *nāntāḥ ṣaṭ*. Thus, the intention is that in the rule for the substitution of *auś* for the nominative plural, the substitution of *āt* (for *an*)—which is inferred by the force of the mention of the form with *āt* applied (*kṛtātvanirdeśa*)—is appropriate only when [the word] is predominant. *Priyaṣṭā* is the nominative singular. He summarizes the stated meaning: "Like a king, [the word] *priyāṣṭan*. Thus end the words ending in *n*. *bhud* [is formed as follows]: *kvip* is added to the root *budh*. Thus end the words ending in *dh*.
(333) *ṛtvigdadhṛksragdiguṣṇigañcuyujikruñcāṃ ca* |3|2|51|. *ṛtvig-dadhṛk*. Regarding "something": when *ṛtu* is the upapada, *kvin* is added to the root *yaj*.

From the root *dhṛṣ* (to dare), there is reduplication and the acute accent on the final syllable (*udātta*). From the root *sṛj* (to emit), the suffix *kvin* occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*), along with the augment *am*.

From the root *diś* (to point), the suffix *kvin* occurs in the sense of the object. From the root *snih* preceded by the prefix *ut*, the suffix *kvin* occurs, with the elision of the final vowel of the prefix and the change of *s* to *ṣ*.
The meaning is that the suffix *kvin* occurs after the root *añc* (to bend) when a noun (*sup*) is present as an upapada. After the root *yuji* (to join), it occurs without an upapada.

The same applies to *kruñc*; however, the absence of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is an additional feature. As for the statement "the suffixes *kan* and *avi* are added," the intention is that the vowel *i* is merely for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
Regarding the term *saṃnihita* ("proximate"): the statement made by the elder [grammarian], namely that "in the third [section], there is the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of 'dhātu'," is incorrect;
for in the rule prescribing the suffix *san*—namely, *hātoḥ karmaṇaḥ*—"the mention of *dhātu*" does not recur in subsequent rules, and thus there is no triple governing heading.
(335) *yujerasamāse* |7|1|71|. From the rule *yujerasamāse*, the phrase *arvanāmasthāne* is understood from the preceding rule *ugidacāṃ sarvanāmasthāne*.
With the intention that the word *num* is understood from the rule *idito num dhātoḥ*, he says: "in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix]."
It might be argued: (336) *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ* | Pāṇini 8.2.62.
Regarding the rule *kvinpratyayasya*: even though it was stated as *kvinaḥ kuḥ*, the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) is included [in the sūtra].

Since the inclusion of that which ends in *kvip* would already be established by the mention of the final element (*tadantagrahaṇāt*), he explains [the rule] with the intention that the mention of the suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇam*) is for the purpose of understanding it as a *bahuvrīhi*: "that from which the suffix *kvip* [occurs]. However, the result of resorting to this *bahuvrīhi* is [the formation of forms] such as *pṛk*.
It will become clear.

"No," [the author] says; for the meaning is not manifold. However, the *kvin* suffix would indeed occur, because of the mention of the vowel *i* in the word "yuj" in the sūtra beginning with "ṛtvig... [Pāṇini 3.2.59]. Regarding "khaj": one who limps is a *khan*.
[The root] *haj* means "to have a deficiency in movement. Similarly, regarding *vibhrāj*: this belongs to the *phaṇādi* group. In a specific sense...

"He shines" (bhrājate) thus he is *vibhrāṭ*. "He worships the gods" (*devān yajati*) thus he is *deveṭ*; [the form *deveṭ* is derived] from the root *yaj* with the suffix *kvip*, where, due to the rule for *yaj*-class roots, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), and then the formation of the single substitute vowel (*ādguṇaḥ*). "He creates the universe" (*viśvaṃ sṛjati*) thus he is *viśvasṛṭ*, ending in *kvip*. Anticipating the objection that [the form] would be *bhavati*, he says: "No; it will be stated that [the substitution occurs] for the neuter," because of the usage of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) in the form *rajju-sṛgbhyām*. Alternatively, the meaning is that it will be stated in the rule *vraśca-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36) that "for the roots *sṛj* and *yaj*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* at the end of a word, which is an exception to the substitution of *k*. Thus, *parimārṣṭi* becomes *parimṛṭ*.

The two [suffixes] *vraj* follow. From the previous sūtra of the *Uṇādi* class, "vibvacipracchiśrisrudruprujvāṃ dīrgho’saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca," the suffix *kvip* and the rule for lengthening (*dīrgha*) are carried over here;
thus he says: "there should be *kvip* and lengthening."
(338) *viśvasya vasurāṭoḥ* |6|3|128|. Because [the word] *hrasve* is understood from the previous rule (*hrasve*), he says: "there shall be lengthening of the word *viśva*."

(339) *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* | P. 8.2.29. The term *skoḥ* [is used]. The word *adas* is understood from the previous rule (*P. 8.2.27*), and the word *hali* is understood from *P. 8.2.26*. The term *saṃyoga*, which has its genitive case-ending elided, qualifies the two [consonants] ending in *jhal*.
This is what he says: "when followed by a *jhal* consonant at the end of a word. Why say "when followed by a *jhal*"? [Consider] *bhraṣṭā*.
From the root *bhṛjj* (to fry), we derive *bhṛṭ* with the suffix *kvip*. There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "rahi-jyā," and the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "vraśca.
[The example] *ūrg* is from the root *ūrj* (meaning 'strength' and 'vitality'); from this, after adding the causative marker *ṇic*, [the form is derived] by the rule beginning with "hrasva-bhāse."

In the case of the *kvip* suffix, there is the elision of the *ṇi* augment; and this [elision] is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original element) when the change of *cu* to *ku* occurs, because it is a rule concerning the end of a word (*padāntavidhi*) and because it is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it. Here, among those ending in *j*, we have: *avayāḥ*, *avayājau*. The form *avayājaḥ* is not cited [as an example], because [the rule] "after *anta*, *śveta-vah*, and *uktha*" having been stated, [the rule] "the substitution of *ava* for *yaja*" applies.

Since the suffix *ṇvin* is prescribed [by Pāṇini 3.2.75], and its exception (*apavāda*) *ṅs* is appropriate to be mentioned only within the Vedic grammatical system due to its being Vedic (*chāndasa*) at the end of a word; thus ends the section on words ending in *j*.

(340) *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ* | 7|2|106| [The substitute *sa-* is applied for the final phoneme of *tad-* and *doṣ-* before the nominative singular suffix *su*, provided they are not final in a compound.]

Regarding the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ*: because the phrase *yadādīnām aḥ* is understood as a governing element (*anuvṛtti*) from that [previous rule], he says—“of *tyad* and so forth. Why say “of *tyad* and so forth”? [Counter-example: *ātapaḥ* (heat), *tārakaḥ* (star). Why say “of *tad* and *doḥ*”? [Counter-example: *yaḥ* (who). Why say “of the non-final [two]”? [Counter-example: *he sa* (O, he!). Here [the substitution does not apply].

Since the status of being a *parasmaipada* ending and the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* would set aside [the application of] *da*, and when *da* is replaced by *sa*, the elision of *su* by *hal-ḍy-āb-bhyo dīrghāt sutisy apṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68) would occur, resulting in *rutva* and *visarga*; thus, the form would become *ṭhhe saḥ*. Furthermore, in the feminine, the form would not be *sā*. However, if *sa* were produced for the final [element], even then...

If it is accepted that the substitution of *sa* for *yat* and so forth occurs again by virtue of the recurrence [of the rule], then nothing undesirable follows; thus, the phrase "of the two non-final" (*anantyayoḥ*) cannot be abandoned. However, if, immediately after the rule "for *adaḥ*, *saḥ* and *sā*" (*adoḥ saḥ sā*), one were to split the rule "for *adas*, *auṭ* and elision of *su*" (*adasa āṭ sulopaśca*) into a separate rule "for *adas*" (*adasaḥ*)...
If a restriction is accepted— that the substitution of *s* occurs for the *d* of *adas* alone and not for any other *d*—

then, by the maxim "not occurring in a verbal root" (*akṛdgatā*), the phrase "of the two non-final [sounds]" (*anantyayoḥ*) could also be dispensed with. Nor would it follow that from the form *dvau ātmānau icchati*, one would derive *dvīyati* (with the elision of *au*) and subsequently the *kvip* suffix.

It should not be said that the form would be *va* instead of *vā*, because the restrictive rule (*niyamapakṣa*) is untenable due to the difference in result; for it has been stated in the *Manoramā* that since both the substitution of *at* (short *a*) and *as* (long *ā*) are impossible in the case of the secondary (*gauṇa*) [suffix], the form *vī* alone is logically correct. [This applies] after the suffix *su*.
What [is the result]? *tau te taṃ tau tān*. If it is argued: "Let the rule simply be *oḥ saḥ sau*;

what is the use of this separate mention of *ado*?", do not say so, because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the substitution of *s* for the letter *n* in *aneṣa*. [The rule *alopa...*]...

By the rule *nañaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.73], which prescribes the augment *nuṭ* for a word beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) that follows the negative particle *nañ*, the form *natārasya* arises because it belongs to the *tyad-ādi* group and ends in the *tavarga*. Nor should it be argued that the prescription of *nuṭ* is redundant once the substitution of *satva* has occurred; for it finds its scope of application in forms such as *anaśvaḥ*. Thus, the rule should simply be *adau* (instead of *ad-antāt*).

This is correct. Now, one might argue: "In the rule *asmān nuḍ aci*, let the word *tasmāt* be omitted and let it simply be stated as *ug aci*; thus, when a vowel-initial suffix follows, the augment *nuṭ* would apply only to the negative particle *nañ*, and so the aforementioned fault would not arise in the case of *aneṣaḥ*. If this is said, [we reply]: if that were the case, then [the rule] *alopaḥ*...

In the rule *prātipadikāntasya*, the ablative ending (*pañcamyantam*) is indeed necessary, as is the indicatory letter *ṭ* (in *ṭid-anubandha*). In the rule *adoḥ*, it is impossible to state [the condition] as *toḥ*.
This is because of the fault mentioned in the rule *ane*. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa says: even if one were to state *toḥ*, in the case of *aneṣaḥ*...

The *satva* [substitution] would not occur because the augment *nuṭ*, being dependent on two words (*padadvayāśritatvena*), is *bahiraṅga*; therefore, by the principle that what is *asiddha* due to its being *antaraṅga* is not applied.
This is because the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* does not apply to operations falling under the jurisdiction of the term "uttarapada," as stated in the rule *ṭhica*.

Because this was stated in the Bhāṣya under the rule *ekāco'm-*, Kaiyaṭa’s [interpretation] is to be considered doubtful. [The reason given is] "because it has its purpose fulfilled in the case of the secondary (gauṇa). For in the case of the secondary, since it is an operation belonging to the internal group (*antargaṇakārya*), the substitution of *s* does not take effect. However, if it were stated as *vāhau sāu*, the form would result in *atisvām*. This is the intended meaning.
"Not in the case of *at* and *asatve*"—the meaning is that these two are subject to operations belonging to the group beginning with *sarva* and ending with *anta*.
"Atityad"—that which has transcended *tyad* is *atityad*. (Pāṇini 7.1.28):
*ReĀ prathamayoram*.

In the rule *ReĀ prathamayoram*, the phrase *yuṣmadasmadbhyām* is understood from the preceding rule *ṭhyuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅso’s*. The term *ReĀ* is a separate word with its genitive case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīkam*).
By virtue of the dual number in *prathamayoḥ*, the word *prathamā* signifies both the nominative and the accusative cases.

With this intention, he explains [the rule] with the words: "of the suffix *reĀ* that follows *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, etc. It would be easier to say: "of *reĀ* and *suṭ*" (*reĀ-suṭoḥ*). (342) *tvāhau sau* | 7|2|94|.

*tvāhau sau*: Although the substitution of *tvā* for *yuṣmad* is already established by the rule "the forms *tvam* and *aham* occur in the singular," this [present rule] is nevertheless stated for the sake of providing the substitution of *ah* for *asmad*. Furthermore, by the rule "the forms *tvam* and *aham* occur in the singular," a form such as *atitvam*—meaning "one who has surpassed you two" or "one who has surpassed you all"—would not be established.
The meaning is that [the substitution] does not apply because there is no expression of a single referent (*ekārthavācitva*). Regarding the rule *yuṣmadasmadoḥ*:
this is obtained from the rule *yuṣmadasmador anādeśe*. Regarding *śeṣe*: "remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to something other than what has been stated;
since the substitution of *ātva* and *yatva* was previously mentioned, the case endings here refer to those other than the scope of those two.
He explains the meaning of the word *śeṣa* (remainder) as follows:

(343) *śoṣe lopaḥ* | P. 7.2.90. [The rule] "other than that which is the cause of the substitution of *āt* or *yat*" [is understood]. [The phrase] "of the final" [is understood] by virtue of the paribhāṣā *alontya* (P. 1.1.52); this is the intended meaning.
Therefore, it is called a *guṇa*. Regarding the statement "vāhau sā," some say:

"Let the final vowel *ā* in the substitutes *tvā* and *āha* simply serve the purpose of pronunciation; what is the use of this effort to apply the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule? [Examples: *tvam*, *aham*. Now, one who has surpassed you (*yuṣmān atikrāntaḥ*)...
In examples such as *tvat* and so forth, there is scope for the rule *vāhau sau*;
in examples such as *atitvayā* (meaning "by one who has surpassed you"), there is scope for the rule *tvamāv ekavacane*.
However, in the case of *tvam* and *aham*, where both rules would apply simultaneously, it is by the rule *tvamāv ekavacane* [that the forms are determined].

"It must be [considered] subsequent. This is not a fault, because it will be stated later: "They also supersede the *tvam* and *mā* forms by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Regarding the phrase "with the intention of expressing the locus" (*adhikaraṇatvavivakṣayā*):
if, however, *eṣe* were a qualifier of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), then that [specification] would be entirely redundant.
Since the substitution of *āt* and *yat*, being specifically prescribed (*viśeṣavihita*), can indeed sublate the elision (*lopa*) within their own scope,

one need not object that the statement "the elision of the final [letter] of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*" would be untenable, as it would render the alternative view— that there is elision of the final letter— without support.

The intention is that because the rule *āma ākam* is stated with the augment *suṭ*, that alternative [of applying the augment first] has also been indicated. Therefore, it operates once the *guṇa* substitution has taken place.

However, the principle *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (an internal operation is stronger than one based on external phonetic elements) applies only when the two operations have the same locus (*samānāśraya*), not when they have different loci (*vyāśraya*).

The point here is that in this case, the cause for the elision of the *śeṣa* (the remaining vowel) is the case-ending (*vibhakti*), whereas the cause for the *pararūpa* (substitution by the subsequent form) is the letter *a*; thus, there is a difference in their substrata (*vyāśrayatva*). An example where they share the same substratum (*samānāśraya*) should be understood as ‘āraka’ and so forth;
for in that instance, when both *yaṇ* (semivowel substitution) and *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) are applicable, only *vṛddhi* takes place.
He states that because it is an *aṅga* (a grammatical base), the rule *tadanta-vidhiḥ* (application of a rule to what ends with that) applies, beginning with the words "paramatvam" and so forth.
(344) *yuvāvau dvivacane* | 7|2|92|. *Yuvāvau dvivacane*. *Uktiḥ* means expression; *dvivacanam* is the expression of two.

This is what he says: "when two are mentioned. Nor should one suspect here a contradiction with the principle of the artificial versus the non-artificial (*kṛtrimākṛtrima-nyāya*), because that [principle] is set aside by the very force of the inclusion of the word *vacana* ("mention"). Otherwise, he would have simply said "in the case of duality" (*dvitve*). Since the term "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) is understood from the rule "of *aṣṭan*, [the substitute *ā* occurs] before a case-ending" (*aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*), when there is duality...
Because the interpretation "the case-ending follows it" is possible.
(345) *Dvivacane bhāṣāyām* |7|2|88|.

[The forms] *yuvaṃ* and *vastrāṇi*. *Śeṣe lopaḥ* ("there is elision of the remainder"). [Question: Why does [the sūtra] say *maparyantasya* ("of that which ends in m")? [Answer: It is a governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*).

The question is: for what purpose? [The forms] *yuvakām* and *āvakām*. But surely, even though *yuva-* and *āva-* are not considered composite bases (*samudāyāśatva*), forms such as *yuvakām* and so on are established; for when a case-ending (*sup*) beginning with *o*, *s*, or *bh* follows, the suffix *aKac* is added before the final vowel of a pronominal stem, whereas otherwise...

Since it will be stated later that, for the sake of establishing the rules regarding *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the forms *tvayakā*, *mayakā*, and so forth are derived from the base ending in *su* before the suffix *aṭ*, one might feel dissatisfied with this [current] governing rule (*adhikāra*) "of that which does not end in *ap*" (aparyantasya); therefore, he says: "In the case of *tvayā* and *mayā*."

But surely, even if the two substitutes (*ādeśau*) were substitutes for the entire composite (*samudāyādeśatva*), it would still be possible to justify forms such as *āvayai*; for, by discarding the rule *hy acī* and adopting the rule *acy e*, when an initial-vowel case-ending (*aj-ādi-vibhakti*) follows, the final vowel *e* would be replaced by *ai*, thereby allowing the application of the substitute *ay*.
Furthermore, due to dissatisfaction [with the previous rule], he says:
(346) *yūyavayau jasi* |7|2|93|.

[The forms] *yuvakābhyām* and so forth [are derived]. Regarding the phrase "an operation pertaining to the *aṅga*" (*aṅgakārya*), by this [it is meant that] when an operation occurs within the *aṅga*...
The *paribhāṣā* "no rule applies again once it has applied" (*punarvṛtāvavidhiḥ*) is established by implication.

In the section concerning the constituent elements (*aṅgādhikāre*), that treatise which has its application (*vṛttaṃ vartanam*) upon a constituent element is called an "element-applying treatise" (*aṅgavṛtaṃ śāstram*); when such a treatise has already applied, there is no further application of another element-applying treatise.

The meaning of that technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is: "When [a grammatical operation] has already taken effect, there is no further application of the rule. And this *paribhāṣā* is made known by the rule "ñ-ṇ-ā-jan-oh ṅe" (P. 7.1.3). The justification for this should be understood from the *Manoramā*.
Nor does it follow that, in the case of "vābhyām," once the substitution of *ya* for the pronoun stem has occurred, the lengthening prescribed by "upi ca" (P. 7.1.96) would not apply.

It should be said that [the objection] may be so, because the indication in the rule “of one of us” (*vayorekasya*) and so forth makes known the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the aforementioned paribhāṣā; this is the direction [of the argument]. Furthermore, the phrase “another method” (*makārāntaram*) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication), for in the rule “*asaśśśī*” (*asaśśśī*), by compounding the letter *s* as “*asaḥ s*” (*asaḥ s*), [it refers to] the *jas* ending when it ends in *s*.

It should be understood that this is either because the word *ataḥ* is carried over from the sūtra *ato ’m* and the rule is explained as "only *am* [is substituted] after *at*," or because of such an explanation.
(347) *tvamāvekavacane* | 7|2|97|.

Regarding the term *avibhaktikam* (without case-endings): it was raised as an objection in the *Bhāṣya* that this [prohibition] is actually a prohibition of what would have been obtained by the preceding rule, *ṛṅe prathamayoḥ*. One might ask: why should it not be exactly so?

[For one could argue that after applying] the substitution of *ā* by *dvitīyāyāṃ ca*, the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of the same class as the preceding), and the substitution of *n* by *asmāc chasaḥ*, [the form would be established].
It should not be said that [the desired result] follows from the attainment [of the suffix],

because since the substitution of *na* does not apply to feminine and neuter stems, there would be the undesirable consequence of the forms *ṭhyuṣmānbrāhmaṇīḥ* and *ṭhyuṣmānkulāni* being unestablished. However, under the view that [the pronoun] lacks gender, [the form] *yuṣmām* [is established].
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-establishment of forms such as *brāhmaṇāt* and others.
(348) *yo’ci* | 7|2|89|. [The rule] *yo’ci*. Why "before a vowel" (*aci*)? [Consider] *yuvābhyām*. But if...
In the rule *yuṣmadasmador anādeśe* (Pāṇini 7.2.86), the term *halī* is understood by anuvṛtti from the preceding rule *rāyo halī*.
Therefore, the term *aci* need not be stated here, as the desired result is established by the principle of remainder (*pariśeṣāt*).
(349) *yuṣmadasmador anādeśe* 7.2.86.
[The rule applies] to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when there is no substitute (*ādeśa*). Why "when there is no substitute"? [Consider the example: *yuṣmabhyam*.

It should not be argued that, since in the view of those who do not accept the substitute, the [suffix] beginning with a consonant (*hal*) is not a substitute, the mention of "no substitute" (*anādeśa*) could be omitted;

for that [mention] is necessary for the purpose of carrying over (*anuvṛtti*) the condition "before a vowel" (*aci*) from the previous rule *yo'ci*. [The phrase means: "when followed by something beginning with a consonant."
This is established by elimination because of the mention of *ac* and *i*; or it is obtained through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule "rāyau halī" (Pāṇini 7.2.85).
(350) *bhyasaḥ abhyam* (Pāṇini 7.1.30): [The substitute *abhyam* takes the place of *bhyas*].

"It is correct in both alternatives. Now, one might object: "In the alternative where there is elision of the final [letter], shouldn't the long vowel by *savarṇa-dīrgha* (P. 6.1.101) apply, overriding the *pararūpa* (P. 6.1.97), on the strength of the explicit utterance of the letter 'a'? To this they reply:
the purpose of uttering the letter 'a' is for the sake of preventing the substitution of *ait* (P. 7.3.103) when the suffix begins with *jhal* and is in the plural.

Regarding the phrase *caritārthatvāt* ("because its purpose has been fulfilled"): although the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*) is easily accomplished by means of the *aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā* (the maxim that an operation dependent on the status of being an *aṅga* does not recur), nevertheless, the fact that this maxim is non-eternal (*anityatva*) is indicated by this very mention of the vowel *a*; such is the truth. (351) *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso’ś* | Pāṇini 7.1.27.

In place of the genitive suffix *ṅsi* following the bases *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, *aś* is substituted. The property of being *śit* (having *ś* as its indicatory letter) is for the purpose of making it a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). Otherwise, by the rule "of that which follows, beginning with *ṭha*," it would only replace the first sound. Nor is the prescription of an *a*-vowel for an *a*-vowel redundant;

for, by means of the technical designation of a "substitute" (*ādeśa*), it serves to prevent the application of *yatva* (the substitution of *ya* for *i*). Furthermore, even if the substitute were applied only to a part [of the base], [the desired result would follow].

It must be stated that the case-ending (vibhakti) indeed remains without substitution, because of the established principle (siddhānta) that "all [substitutes] are substitutes for entire words. It is precisely this status of being marked with *ś* (śitva) that indicates the principle: "all [substitutes] are substitutes for entire words. The meaning is that the application of the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) rests only upon that which possesses meaning. As for the suffixes *sic*, *caṅ*, and so forth—
It is established in the *Manoramā* that by the force of the wording [of the rule], the [substitution] occurs even for that which is meaningless.

(352) *sāma ākam* 7.1.33: [The substitution of] *ākam* [occurs] for *sāma*, as in *tava* and *mama*. Now, one might object: "In this case, if the alternative of eliding the final [vowel] were adopted, the *syādeśa* [the replacement by *si*] would apply to the *aś* [portion]."

Because the substitution of *sy* has its purpose fulfilled by the fact that it serves as a substitute for *iṭ*, and it should not be said that the substitution of *sy* is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the elision], since at the time the substitution of *sy* would take effect, the elision of the remainder (*śeṣe lopa*) does not yet exist, and thus the substitution of *sy* is not even applicable. On this point, they say: [this is explained] by the maxim regarding what occurs within a stem (*aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*).

It should be restricted to a specific location. However, if that operation belongs to the *aṅga* (the stem), then that *paribhāṣā* applies specifically to that [stem], and not with the stubborn insistence that it pertains to the entire *aṅgādhikāra* (the governing rule for stems).

Consequently, in the rule *aśiti*, by applying the *pararūpa* substitution according to "ato guṇe," another *a*-vowel is superposed; thus, the *aś* becomes precisely the form of the vowel *a*, and not otherwise.

It must be explained that [the word] *vikriyate* [is used here]. Now, one might object: since prior to the substitution of *ākām*, there is no substitute (*anādeśatvāt*), the rule *yoci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77) applies, as stated in the Bhāṣya; consequently, because the elision of the suffix (*śeṣe lopa*) does not occur, the [suffix] prescribed by the rule *avarṇāntāt* [would apply].
Since the augment *suṭ* would not otherwise apply [to the word *sām*], the mention of *sasuṭka* (accompanied by *suṭ*) in the rule for *sāman* would be purposeless; therefore, he says:
"of that which is about to be. For once the elision of the remainder (*śeṣalopa*) has been applied, *suṭ* would apply because of the ending in the vowel *a*;
however, by the force of the mention of the base as being accompanied by *suṭ*, that [application of *suṭ*] is prevented—this is the intended meaning. [In the case of] *eṣe*...

However, under the view that "the elision of *ṭi* is the elision [of the suffix]," the mention of *suṅ* would indeed be redundant. The long vowel in the pronunciation of *ākam* is for the sake of *savarṇadīrgha* (lengthening by homogeneity); otherwise, *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form) would apply.

Nor can the force of the vocalization of the letter *ā* be invoked [to justify it], because its purpose is already fulfilled by *abhyam* alone through the prevention of *etva* (the substitution of *e*).

In this context, it has been explained that in both of the two sūtras—"ṭhyuvāvau dvivacane" and "ṭhvamāvekavacane"—the terms *dvivacana* and *ekavacana* refer to the meanings [of duality and singularity], and not to the suffixes themselves.
He demonstrates the result of this [explanation] with the words beginning "samasyamāne," etc. [The phrase is] "expressive of duality and singularity."

This was stated with the intention of the position that "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of [gender, number, and] case. However, under this position, since number (*saṅkhyā*) is also part of the meaning of the nominal stem, the reading should be "denoting three things" (*tryekārthavācinī*) according to the *trika* (threefold) theory. This is so even though, according to the other view, number is the meaning of the case ending (*vibhakti*).
Because the status of being the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārthatva*) for the number (*saṅkhyā*) has not been lost. "If it is another number" means:
if it is possessed of a number other than the numbers residing in the meanings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. "They are" (*staḥ*):

precisely by virtue of resorting to the primacy of the meaning (*arthaparatva*), one also accepts the understanding of what was previously so (*bhūtapūrvagati*); thus, the dual (*yau*) and the plural (*āvau*) [are applied].
The sense is that [the forms] *tvam* and *āvām* would exist, but they would not exist when a suffix follows; thus there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*).
Similarly, in the fourth verse as well, by stating "the forms *yu* and *vā* do not become *tv* and *au* when a suffix follows," the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is implied. Thus...
Thus, it follows that the status of being "intended as the meaning" (*arthaparatva*) has been resorted to in order to avoid the faults of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "In this case, even when *su*, *jas*, *ReĀṅ*, and *su* [are present], if *yuṣmad* and *asmad* have multiple meanings (*bahvarthatva*), would *yuvau* and *āvau* not occur;
yet if they have a single meaning (*ekārthatva*), would *tvam* and *āvam* not occur? To address this doubt, he says: "In *su*, *jas*, *ReĀṅ*, and *su*..."

Regarding the phrase "from others" (*parataḥ*): in response to the question "What are those substitutes?", he says: "tvāhau, yūyavayau," and so forth. It may be granted that *tvā* and *āh* exclude *yuṣmad* and *asmad*; however, how can *tvam* and *au* be excluded by them, since they follow after those [substitutes]? To this he replies: "tvamāv api. This refers to the rule "in the case of a conflict, the latter prevails" (*vipratiṣedhe param*).
The intention is that the word *para* signifies "desired. Regarding *atitvām* and *atimām*: the analysis is "those who have surpassed you" (*tvām*) or "me" (*mām*).

Regarding *atiyūyam* and *ativayam*: the analysis is "those who have surpassed you" (*tvām*) or "me" (*mām*). The same should be inferred for what follows as well. Regarding *atitvākam* and *atimākam*: [the analysis is likewise].
In this case, regarding the alternative view of the elision of the final [augment], the augment *nuṭ* must be prevented by the *aṅgavṛtta-paribhāṣā*,
or else by the interpretation of the rule *hrasvanadyāpaḥ* as meaning "the *nuṭ* [is applied] after an *ām* prescribed following a stem ending in a short vowel.
Now, if this is so, then because they occupy different domains (*bhinnaviṣayatayā*), [there would be no conflict with] *suṭ*.

If it is argued that, because there is no absence of the *nuṭ* augment as an exception, the *nuṭ* alone would apply by virtue of its higher priority to the *ām* prescribed after pronouns ending in vowels other than *a*, and not the *suṭ* augment— since the latter has its scope in forms such as *yeṣām* and *teṣām*— to this they reply: since one ought to state "the *suṭ* [is added] to the *am* of *tyadādi*," [the rule is stated as] "to the *ām*."

By virtue of the inclusion of the term "sarva" in the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ*, and by the indicative evidence (*nirdeśa*) of forms such as *sarveṣām* and so forth, the augment *suṭ* alone is applied to the suffix *ām* after all pronouns ending in *a*, and not the augment *nuṭ*. Furthermore, in the expression "*asprabhṛtiṣu*", the locative case denotes the scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Therefore...

It should be understood that even in cases such as *paddanna*, the rule "āmi nuṭ" applies; thus, by the mention of *āma* together with the augment *suṭ*, the concern that the augment *nuṭ* would be unavoidable in forms like *yuṣmākam* and *asmākam*—despite the absence of *suṭ* before *ām*—is rendered groundless. As for what [was said]...

They say: although in the rule *sāma ākam*, the mention of *suṭ* is not a qualifier of the substituend because it would be redundant (*bādhāt*), nevertheless, it serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). That is to say, only that *ām* which is to be preceded by *suṭ* should be replaced by *ākam*; and this is not possible in the case of the substitution of *aut*. Therefore, *ākam* [is applied].
And thus, the form would be *atitvayām* and *atimayām*, but not *atitvākam* and *atimākam*.
That is incorrect; for when the *ām* has been superseded by *ākam*, there can be no connection with *suṭ*. If it is argued that *suṭ* occurs after *ākam*, then—

One should characterize that very [element]. If one characterizes the *sthānin* (the original element) through a mediated relationship by means of the *ādeśa* (the substitute), then in cases such as *yuṣmākam*, the suffix *suṭ* would be heard.
If it is argued that it is not heard because of the force of the technical designation *ām*, we say no; for the designation...
Because its purpose is fulfilled by the exclusion of the secondary sense, it lacks the capacity [to denote the primary]; this is explained in detail elsewhere.

Having stated examples for the case where *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, functioning as subordinate elements (*guṇabhūta*), have a single referent, he now provides examples for when they express two referents, beginning with "one who has surpassed you both" (*yuvāmāvāṃ vā atikrāntaḥ*) and so forth.

He gives an example for the two meanings [of the suffix *vat*]— namely, *yuṣmānasmānveti*— by means of the rule: "The substitute *ṭ* [is applied] in place of the final phoneme of a word" (Pāṇini 8.3.353),
and "A retroflex [substitute is applied] in place of a non-final phoneme of a word" (Pāṇini 8.3.55).

This is an overarching rule (*adhikāra*) stating that [an operation applies] to the preceding word because of its mention in opposition [to a subsequent one]. By this, in forms such as *rājā* and *rājabhyām*, the elision of the *n* by the rule "elision of the final phoneme of a nominal stem" (*alopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*) is established;
however, it does not apply in cases such as *rājānau* and *rājānaḥ*. Likewise, it applies in cases such as *omān* and *yavamān*.

The elision of a final conjunct (saṃyogāntalopa) occurs [only] there, but not in cases such as *omāntau* or *ṭhyavamantāu*. Likewise, the substitution of *na* for *n* according to the rule *o no dhātoḥ* occurs in *raśānbhyām* and so forth, but not in *raśamau* or *praśām*. Similarly, [the sandhi rules apply] in cases such as *hariṃ vande*.

The *anusvāra* occurs [in cases such as *mum*], but not in forms such as *amyate*. Nor should it be argued that, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "after a word" (*pade*) from the sūtra *uñi ca pade*, the *anusvāra* would apply to the *m* when followed by a word—as in *gam-yate*—and therefore what is the use of the governing rule "after a word" here? [This is because the governing rule applies only where a specific condition is met.]

Because it would otherwise follow that the form *uṃsvi* could not be established; therefore, in the rule *o'nusvāraḥ*, the term *adas* must indeed be carried over [from the previous rule]. We have already stated this under the rule *tuñica pade* that the term *ade* has no application even in the subsequent rule. Here, [the reading is] *adaso*.

The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expresses a general relationship; however, in the subsequent rules, it is restricted to specific types of relationships as appropriate. In some instances it denotes a locative relationship (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), while in others it denotes a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*).
This is evident in such rules as *aṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*, *ṭhmo no dhātoḥ*, and *o’nusvāraḥ*.

The term *padasya* is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). It is not, however, a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). In rules such as *ādupadhāyāḥ*, it is indeed a genitive of part. Otherwise, in the case of *vṛkṣvān*, the substitution of *v* for the *m* of *matup* would apply only there, and not in cases like *vṛkṣavantau* or *vṛkṣavantaḥ*.

And this will be demonstrated later. Although, by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "the genitive [case ending] is used in the sense of 'in place of' (*sthāne-yoga*)," the genitive in *adas-ya* is understood only as a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) and not as a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), nevertheless, a genitive of part is also obtained due to the indicative force (*jñāpaka*) of the inclusion of the word *anta-sya* in the rule for the elision of the suffix *san*. If...

If, however, [the genitive] were taken as a locative genitive (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning "in place of this," then since the elision of the final sound of a word ending in *n* would apply to the final sound (*alo'ntyasya*),
the mention of the word "final" (*anta*) would be redundant. But if it is accepted as a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), then the mention of "ending in *ṭ*" (*ṭhantasya*) becomes meaningful.
For example, in the *Nalopa-sūtra*, there is an indication of an uncompounded form in the rule *prātipadikāntasya*.

The meaning of the sūtra is that there is elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n* which is the final constituent part of a word (*pada*) designated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Now, one might object: "In this case, the inclusion of the term 'final' (*anta*) is for the purpose of indicating that it is a genitive of relation to a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*)."

Regarding the phrase *svīkṛtatvāt padasya*, how indeed can there be the attainment of a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), given that since the specific relation has been determined, the paribhāṣā concerning the genitive of location does not apply? On this point, they say: because the traditional grammatical memory (*vyākaraṇa-smṛti*) is rooted in actual usage, it must conform to the observed linguistic data (*lakṣya*).

Although a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) is also accepted, it is stated in the *Manoramā* on the rule for the elision of *n* (*nalopa-sūtra*) that a genitive of constituent (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*)—established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*)—is not accepted everywhere;
thus, it was said that the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) [in the sūtra] could have been omitted. However, in the *Bhāṣya* and other works...

The mention of *ant* is for the purpose of making it known that, regarding the word *adas* which is the subject under discussion, a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) is also accepted, and not exclusively a genitive of position (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). By this,
the substitution of *v* [for *d*] in the forms *vṛkṣavantau* and *vṛkṣavantaḥ* is established by the rule *ādupadhāyāḥ*.

Because the *matup* suffix is a constituent part (*padāvayava*) of the word. Otherwise, if "belonging to him" (*adasya*) were the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), then according to the rule for suffixes ending in that [suffix], the meaning would be: "The *m* of the *matup* suffix, which is a constituent part of a word ending in *at*, becomes *v* when it follows *ma* or a vowel. And thus:
It is established that [the substitution] would occur only in the case of *vṛkṣavān*, and not in the cases of *vṛkṣavantau* or *vṛkṣavantaḥ*. (354) *padāt* | 8|1|17|
From the word *padāt* [in Pāṇini 8.1.17] up to [the rule] *utsane ca supyagotrādau* (8.1.27), this is the governing heading (*adhikāra*). However,

if the term *padāt* were to carry over even into the rule *apatsane ca supi* (8.1.19), then the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) would apply only in cases such as *devadattaḥ pacati pūti*, and not in cases such as *pacati pūti*.

(355) *anudāttaṃ sarvam apādādau* 8.1.18. Everything [that follows] is unaccented (*anudātta*) except at the beginning of a verse-quarter (*apāda*). These three words are governed [as a heading] until the end of the chapter.

(356) *yuṣmadasmadoḥ ṣaṣṭhīcaturthīdvitīyāsthayor vānāvau* 8.1.20. [The rule begins: *ṣaṣṭhīcaturthīdi*. By the rule *alpa-actaram*, the word *ṣaṣṭhī* is placed first. [The meaning is] "of those characterized by the sixth, fourth, and second cases. Now, since it was stated [in the sūtra] that this applies to *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, it would follow that these two alone [are affected].

Even if there were no defect in forms such as *vas* and *nas* according to the aforementioned method, the occurrence of the substitutes *vān* and *āvān* for the simple forms *yuṣmad* and *asmad* would be unavoidable when followed by [suffixes] such as *bhyām*, because they would possess the status of being *pada*s. Consequently, the usage "ukhaṃ vāṃ nau dadātv īśaḥ" (May the Lord grant the vessel to you two/to us two) would not be consistent. Nor...

One should not say that by the force of the mention of *stha* in the rule "the two forms of *stha*" (*vitīyāsthayoḥ*), the substitutes would apply only when [the roots] are qualified by specific case-endings; for that force of the mention of *stha* is exhausted by what will be stated later, namely, "by the mention of *stha*, [the substitutes apply] only when they possess the case-ending currently being uttered. This is not so, because of the rule "everything is unaccented" (*anudātaṃ sarvam*).

Since it is clear in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that, by virtue of the governing rule for "all" (*sarva-grahaṇa*), substitutes apply to every [word] qualified by a case ending, some say that if the word "of all" (*sarvasya*) were to carry over from the rule *sarvasya dve*,
then the mention of "all" (*sarva-grahaṇa*) here could be dispensed with.
(357) *tvāmau dvitīyāyāḥ* |8|1|23|.
He provides examples for the aforementioned substitutes in the order they were stated, beginning with *śrīśa* and so forth.
Regarding *smī te me’pi*: since the rule *“vāmīśvarādhipatī”* prescribes [the substitutes] *vām* for both the genitive and locative cases, the genitive is used here.
He provides an example for the two dual forms with "pātu vām" and so forth;
for the two plural forms, however, he gives "so'vyād vo naḥ" and so on, as well as "sevyo'tra vaḥ sa naḥ.
[In the latter case,] the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule "arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca," and the genitive case is used by the rule "ṛtyānāṃ kartari vā."

Regarding the phrase "vedairaśeṣaiḥ": the older reading, "yuṣmān rakṣatu govindaḥ," has been disregarded because the rule [requiring the substitution of *vaḥ* for *yuṣmān*] does not apply, precisely because *yuṣmān* does not follow immediately after a word (*padāt*). However, in the case of *asmān*, even though it follows a word, [the rule applies].

Because there is an absence of being subsequent to a word situated within the same sentence. Now, one might object: let the rule be formulated as *yuṣmadasmadoḥ ṣaṣṭhīcaturthīdvitīyānām*; through the principle of "extension to that which ends in [the specified term]" (*tadantavidhi*) by means of this qualifier, it will result in the application to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they end in the sixth, fourth, or second case endings. And there would be no need for the mention of *stha*.

It should be stated that the meaning is "vām, nau, and āv" for the genitive, dative, and accusative cases belonging to *yuṣmad* and *asmad*; however, because the phrase "of every word" (*sarvasya padasya*) is understood from the previous rule, he explains [the meaning] by means of the mention of the root *sthā*.
Here, the root *sthā* signifies "non-abandonment" (*ahāni*). As in: "to Agni... [etc.]

"Stay, O Sugrīva!"—it is understood that this means "do not abandon the agreement. Therefore, the meaning is that the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occur only when [the words] do not abandon the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth. In the example *itiyuṣmatputraḥ*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is either "the son of you two" (*yuvayoḥ putraḥ*) or "the son of you all" (*yuṣmākaṃ putraḥ*).

But [the form] "tava putram" (your son) does not occur; for if that were the case, it would simply be "vatputra. The same should be inferred for "asmatputra" (our son). The word "iti" is used to ensure the status of being "after a word" (padāt paratvam). Now, in the analyses "rājñoḥ puruṣaḥ" or "rājñām puruṣaḥ," [the compound] "rājapuruṣaḥ" [is formed].

If it is argued that [the dual form] is not accepted because it contradicts the *Śuddhānta* (the section on word-formation), and thus a compound analysis such as "your son" (*yuṣmatputraḥ*) or "our son" (*asmatputraḥ*)—
where one would expect forms like *yuvayoḥ* or *yuṣmākam*— is impossible, they reply:
where there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) indicating a specific number within the formation of the compound, [the dual is indeed used].

In that very case, the number one is heard, as in the example "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*). For in the expression "the king's man," once the case-ending has ceased [to function], there is nothing whatsoever that conveys duality or other numbers regarding the referent of the word "king. However, where...
When there exist factors such as meaning or context that indicate a difference in number,

there occurs the application of the dual and plural endings as well; however, in the present case, since the analysis (vigraha) ends in the singular, [the suffix] applies to both the affix and the subsequent member (uttarapada).

By virtue of the connection with the Lord of Speech (Pāṇini), the formation will occur through the sense [of plurality], namely by means of words ending in the dual or plural; this is the meaning. "By the sense" (*arthāt*) means as follows: for example, *maudgika* ("purchased with mung beans"). For it is not possible that a purchase is made with only one mung bean or even with two mung beans.
"Because of the context and so forth, our words are intended to provide an opportunity for the speech of Your Majesty;
for that is the meaning there of the words 'bhavato rājñaḥ' (of Your Majesty). Regarding the rule 'in a single sentence' (*samānavākye*):
in the example 'Devadatta, here is this staff; Devadatta, take it with this,' the word 'staff' (*daṇḍa*) is situated in the preceding sentence."

Because there is an absence of being situated within the same sentence (*samānavākyasthatva*), the *āmantrita-nighāta* (the accentual suppression of a vocative) does not occur. Regarding the term *ekātiṅ*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is a single finite verb (*tiṅanta*). But surely, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in a case such as "The rice is to be cooked by you;
it shall be yours," since one could supply the word "is" (*asti*) [after *paktavyaḥ*].
Even if one were to support the view that these are separate sentences, observe that in cases such as "The deer runs," the conventional usage of them being a single sentence would not occur. True;
this was stated for the sake of relevance to the present topic. However, in cases such as "The deer [is] here," there is oneness [of sentence] because of the unity of meaning.
One [scholar] maintains that the statement "if, upon division, there remains an expectancy" is well-known from other treatises (*śāstra*).

Others, however, based on the observation of the Vārttikakāra’s statement, "A sentence is a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) accompanied by its qualifiers," hold that in the example "one who cooks" (*pacati*), it is the finite verb that constitutes the sentence.

It is intended that [the word] conveys the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); therefore, they say that even though there are two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) in the sentence "He sees the deer running" (*paśyati mṛgo dhāvati*), the fault mentioned does not arise because only the word *paśya* conveys the qualificand. The word *eka* (one) signifies identity (*samāna*) and does not denote number (*saṅkhyā*).

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; therefore, Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the *Samartha-sūtra*, states that in the example "rūhi brūhi devadate," the *cita*-accentuation of the *ām* affix is established because it constitutes a sentence (*vākya*). He then recites the *vārttika*—"optionally [the accent is applied] to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when not used in a subsequent reference (*ananvādeśa*)"—according to its meaning.

These words, *vām* and so forth, are [the examples]. Although this is recited under the rule "optionally for the first [feminine] case ending that has no preceding [word]," the intention is that this option is prescribed without distinction;
thus, with the view that the option applies even in the absence of a preceding word, he provides an example: *dhātā te bhakta*.
Thus [it is said]. However, in the case of an *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference), he cites it as necessarily occurring thus: "tasmai te namaḥ" (salutation to you).

Since the meaning of "joined with" (*yukta*) is already obtained through the mention of the third case—as in the rule beginning with "with words having the same meaning" (*tulyārthaiḥ*), etc., and by the rule "not with *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, *eva*" (*na ca vā hā haivaiḥ*)—the inclusion of the word "joined with" (*yukta*) would be redundant. To this, he says:

(358) *Na cāvāhāhaivaiḥ yukte* || 8.1.24 || [The rule] "because of the mention of *yukta*" [means]: where particles such as *ca* and others indicate conjunctions and so forth residing in the referents of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, then there is a direct connection (*sākṣādyoga*) between *yuṣmad* and *asmad* with the particles like *ca* by way of their meaning.

The meaning is that this prohibition applies only in that specific case. Regarding the example *haro hariśca*: here, the word *a* expresses the conjunction (*samuccaya*) residing in Hara and Hari. Since the connection of the pronoun *asmad* (‘I’) is with Hara and Hari individually, and not with the conjunction itself, there is no direct connection; rather, it is an indirect connection (*paramparā-yoga*). Therefore, the prohibition does not apply.

[The word *paśya* denotes] the state [of seeing]. By virtue of the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*), the suffix *śa* is applied in the sense of a state (bhāva) after roots meaning "to see" (*paśyārtha*) when not preceded by a prefix (*anāṅka*).

Thus, *darśanam* becomes *paśyaḥ*. And here, that [seeing] refers merely to cognition (*jñānamātra*), as in the rule "elision is non-perception" (*adarśanaṃ lopaḥ*), and not exclusively visual perception, because of the prohibition [in the rule] "not when it is not a direct observation" (*anālocane*).

(359) *paśyārthaiścā’nālocane* (Pāṇini 2.4.25). This is what he says: "with words meaning non-visual cognition. Regarding the phrase "even when there is no connection with another": this is made known elsewhere by the inclusion of the word *yukta* ("joined") in the preceding sūtra.
"Even in the case of an indirect connection, there is a prohibition.
(360) *sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyā vibhāṣā* |8|1|26|. Regarding *sapūrvāyāḥ*: here, the word *sa-* has the sense of "existing," just as in the word *aloma-ka*. By this...

Since it will be stated that the expression of equality (*tulya-yoga-vacana*) in the rule *saheti* is merely occasional (*prāyika*), there is a compound of *saha* even with a word denoting existence (*vidyamāna*). The substitution of *sa-* [for *saha-*, as in *sahita*] occurs by the rule *vopasarjanasya*.
And [the feminine form *sahitā* is derived] by the rule *prathamāyāḥ*.

Having stated that the rule of "that which ends with [the element]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies because of the mention of the condition (*pratyaya*), he says: "from what is preceded by an existing [element]," and so forth.

To dispel the doubt—"Since these substitutes, *va*, *āna*, *āv*, etc., are established by the very same option (*vibhāṣā*) mentioned without distinction, what is the purpose of this statement?"—he says: "even in the case of a subsequent reference" (*anvādeśe*).

Regarding the passage beginning with “You are a devotee,” it should be understood that for those who explain it as “You are a devotee of Hari, and for that very reason, I am also [His devotee],” there is the difficulty of having to supply the word *yat* (which). In this context, the word *ene* exists previously; after that is *hariḥ* in the nominative case; and then follows the subsequent [word].
The word *yuṣmad* undergoes substitution [with *tvad*]. Likewise, in the form *rāyate*, the word ending in the nominative case *it* follows;
after that, the word *asmad* undergoes substitution [with *mad*]. (361) *sāmantritam* || 2.3.48 || [That which is used in address is called *āmantrita*.]
It is addressed (*sāmantritam*). From the rule "and in address" (*ambodhane ca*), the term "in address" (*ambodhane*) is carried over (*anuvartate*).
By the word "e," the nominative case is indicated.
Due to the force of employing a technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*), in the formulation of this designation, there is no inclusion of that which ends with it (*tadantagrahaṇam*).

The term *āmantrita* refers to that which is addressed (*āmantraṇa*). By metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), it denotes that which effects such addressing. With the intention that one is addressed by means of a word ending in a case-suffix, and not by the case-suffix alone, he says: "ending in that" (*tadantam iti*).
(362) *āmantritaṃ pūrvam avidyamānavat* (P. 8.1.72): An *āmantrita* [word] standing before another is as if non-existent.
Regarding the word *iha*: in the phrase *agne tava evāsmān*, there is no substitution [of the enclitic forms] for the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*;

in *agne naya*, there is no low-pitched accent (*nighāta*) on the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) because of the rule *iḍḍatiṅaḥ*; however, in *agna indra varuṇa*, there is no low-pitched accent on the vocative by the rule *āmantritasya ca*. This is the distinction.

"The elision (nighāta) applies to all [vowels]. Furthermore, this elision is observed at the time of the *padapāṭha*, but not at the time of the *saṃhitāpāṭha*; for in the *saṃhitā*, the rule "of non-acute vowels following an acute vowel" prescribes a single uniform tone (*ekaśruti*).

(363) *vibhāṣitaṃ viśeṣavacane* |8|1|74|. [In the example] *agne tejasvin*, because the word *tejasvin* follows a word (*padāt*) [within the same sentence], it undergoes the eighth-lecture (*aṣṭamika*) *nighāta* (elision of accent) by the rule *āmantritasya ca*, resulting in all syllables being unaccented (*sarvānudāta*).
(364) *vibhāṣitaṃ viśeṣavacane* | 8|1|74|.
Regarding the example *supāt*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose feet are beautiful.
There is elision of the final vowel of the first member when preceded by a numeral or the word *su*.

(365) *pādaḥ pat* 6.4.103. [The substitute] *pat* [is applied] in place of *pāda*. [This applies] to that which is a constituent part of it. This is obtained through the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating, "Substitutes take the place of that which is being indicated. And this technical rule is established by the rule *aṣṭhīsthāneyoga*.
It has been made known [that this is so], for instance, in rules such as *ṭhasterbhūḥ* and *ṭhiko yaṇaci*,

even when there is the possibility of relations such as proximity (*sāmīpya*) and so forth, [the substitution is established] because of the interpretation [of the rule] in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*), because it is an integral part of the grammatical system (*aṅga*), and because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) provided by the rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ*.

Even though the status of being a "substitute" (*sthāne-yoga*) is already established, by the commencement of the rule *aṣṭhī-sthāneyogā*, it is understood that only a genitive case-form (*ṣaṣṭhī*) which is actually uttered is connected with the "place" (*sthāna*), and not one that is merely implied. Thus, the principle follows: "Substitutes apply to that which is being pointed out (*irdiśyamāna*)."

Success! The two rules—"of the final [element]" (*alo’ntyasya*) and "of that which follows what begins with *ṭha*" (*ṭhādeḥ parasya*)—are exceptions to the *nirdiśyamāna-paribhāṣā* (the rule concerning the specifically mentioned element) by virtue of their very formulation; therefore, there is no fault in cases such as "umaḥ khayyampare" and "udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ. This is the direction of the argument. Thus.

*dāntāḥ* (those ending in *t*). *agnimat*: this very form arises from the roots *mathati* and *manthati* with the suffix *kvip*. However, from the root *idita* (having an indicatory *i*), there is no elision of the nasal (*nalopa*), resulting in *agnimanthau* and *agnimanthaḥ*. Thus end those ending in *th*. (366) *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* [Pāṇini 6.4.24].
"Aniditām": those whose *it* designation consists of a short *i* are called *idit*;

those that are not *idit* are *anidit*. This [term] qualifies the *aṅga* (stem), as does the term "consonantal" (*hal*). Thus he says: "of those ending in consonants that are *anidit*. [The rule continues with] "of the *n* of the penultimate (*upadhā*)": "not [applied] to a nasal (*na*)."

The meaning is that from the rule "lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.109), the word with the sixth case ending elided is understood as an *anuvṛtti*, and it is further qualified by the mention of *upadhā*. Why [is the condition] "of roots whose penultimate vowel is not marked with *i* or *ī*" (*aniditām*) stated?
[Consider: *nandyate*. Why "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*)? [Consider: *nīyate*. Why "of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*)? [Consider: *hanyate*.

(367) *acaḥ* | 6|4|134| The word *acaḥ* [is used]. From the rule *allopo’naḥ*, the term *al-lopaḥ* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*), as is the word *hasya*. Therefore, he says: "There shall be elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *a* when it belongs to a *bha*-stem. In this context...

The Navyas [the modern grammarians] argue: if here the coreferential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of *añcateḥ* with *bhasya* is accepted, then forms such as *pratīcaḥ* and *pratīce* would not be established; for only that which is accompanied by a prefix (*upasarga*) possesses the status of a *bha*, whereas the simple root *añcati* lacks the status of a *bha*. [This is because the rule applies to] "that which has *añcati* as its constituent part."

If, however, there were a grammatical connection through different case-roles (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), then in forms such as *pratyagātmanā*, the elision of the letter *a* belonging to the root *añc* would occur. Furthermore, according to the interpretation that "the *a* of a *bha*-stem ending in *añc* is elided," the *a* of the words *rātraḥ* and *rātrīce* would also undergo elision.

Even if one explains [the rule] as "of the *bha* ending in *añc*, up to and including *añc*, when followed by *tan*, *āvṛti*, etc., and the letter *a* of the root *añc*," there would still be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *pratyak* (from *pratyakṣam añcati*) and *pratyakca* (in *śas*-stems and so on). Therefore—

Just as in the rule *ṭhallopo’naḥ*, here too it should be explained that there is elision of the vowel *a* belonging to the root *añc*, provided that this *añc* is a constituent of an *aṅga* (stem) followed by a suffix beginning with *sva* (the nominative case ending) that is not an *asarvanāmasthāna* and begins with a consonant other than *y*.
They say that the mention of *yauprāgapāgudakpratīcaḥ* here is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this interpretation.
Regarding [the rule] *cau* 6.3.108: because of the mention of *ajoḥ*, there is no inclusion of the *ca*-class (the palatal series).
He says, "when *ākāra* and *nakāra* are elided" (*luptākāranakāreñcatāv iti*).
Here, since the elision of *nakāra* is already implied by the elision of *ākāra*, stating it separately is indeed redundant;

rather, they say it would be better to simply say "when *ākāra* is elided in the case of *añcat*" (*luptākāre’ñcatāv iti*). [Regarding the rule] "when there is elision of a short vowel" (*hrasvalope*).
Because the [sūtras] *sūtrāt* and *aṇo dīrghaḥ* are carried over [as governing rules], he says: "There shall be a long vowel for *aṇ*.

[The examples are] *prācaḥ* and *prācā*. The intention is that, since the elision of *at* must necessarily be admitted for the sake of forms such as *pratīcaḥ*, this [rule] prescribes the lengthening [of the vowel] once that elision has been performed. [The example is] *prāgbhyām*; [this is governed by] *oḥ kuḥ*.
It is by [the rule] *kutvam*, and not by the rule *vinpratyayasya*, because that [latter rule] is unestablished (*asiddhatva*).
(369) *viṣvag-devayoś ca ṭer adry-añcatāv apratyaye* | 6|3|93|.
[The words] *viṣvak* and *deva*: by the word *ca* (and), [the rule] *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* is brought forward from that [preceding rule].
It is said that [the word] is derived from the pronominal base *arva* by the rule "of these two and of the pronominal base" (*anayoḥ sarvanāmnaśca*).
Regarding the phrase "in *añcat*, which ends in a non-suffix" (*apratyayānte’ñcatāviti*): a "non-suffix" (*apratyaya*) is one in which no suffix exists—such as *kvip*, *kvic*, and so forth.
However, if the reading were "in *añcat* with the suffix *vap*" (*vapratyaye’ñcatāviti*), then it would mean "in *añcat* ending in the suffix *vap*."
This is to be explained. As for the examples of *viṣvak* and *deva*: one who moves everywhere is *viṣvadyaṅ*;
one who moves toward the gods is *devadyaṅ*—this is how it should be understood. (370) *adaso'serdādu do maḥ* | Pāṇini 8.2.80.

Regarding the rule *adaso'seḥ*: in the rule *ṭhaseḥ*, the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation; thus he says: "of *adas* when it does not end in *as*. Why "when it does not end in *as*"? [Consider:
*adasyati*, meaning "he desires that (person) for himself. Why "after *d*"? [Consider: *amuyā*.

In the case of *ṭhamuyaḥ*, let it not be [the substitution] of the final *y*. [This is because of the rule] *hrasvavyañjanayoḥ*; for the meaning is that a short vowel is somewhat similar to a consonant, whereas a long vowel is dissimilar.

However, the earlier teachers (prāñcaḥ) do not form a collective dvandva compound of "short and long" (*hrasvadīrghayoḥ*), and thus maintain that even though *aṇ* is being prescribed [by the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*], [it does not include the long vowels].
Having applied the *sāvarṇya* rule by stating "it takes [the substitute] of the same class (*savarṇa*) in some cases," they explain that,
due to *āntaratamya* (closest similarity), a short vowel replaces both a short vowel and a consonant, while a long vowel replaces a long vowel.
Regarding the phrase "exclusion of the final" (*antyabādha*), the genitive in the sūtra *ṭhadasaḥ* is not a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), but rather...

The genitive case here denotes location; for in this way, the paribhāṣā "alo'ntyasya" (of the final letter) applies. Thus, their intention is that since the final letter of *adas-* does not follow the *d*, and that which follows the *d* is not the final letter of *adas-*, when the final letter is thus barred, the operation takes place on the letter immediately preceding the final one. This has been stated.

And so, the word "by the author of the Vārttika" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus, the sense is that the example given by some—"amandya" with the augment *aṅ*—should be disregarded because it is not mentioned in the Bhāṣya or other such works.
"Like the substitution of *l*" means: just as in the case of "kalīklṛpyate," both [rules] apply, namely "ṛpo ro laḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.18).

The meaning of *latvam* is "it becomes *la*. Now, one might object: even in the absence of the mention of the suffix *apratyaya*, since this falls under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of "the subsequent word" (*uttarapada*), the substitution of *ādy* would apply only when *viṣvañc*, *devañc*, or *tyañc* are the subsequent words, and not otherwise.
Regarding the rule *ṭhviṣvag-adañc-am*, he explains here that the mention of "not being a suffix" (*apratyayagrahaṇam*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpakam*).

He says "elsewhere," meaning in rules such as *ṭhataḥ kṛkami-* and so on. He says "by that," meaning otherwise, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "compound" (*samāsa*) from the rule *ityaṃ samāse*, the final member of the compound (*uttarapada*) would be implied; therefore...

The point is that when the root *kṛ* is mentioned [in a rule] as in *kṛ-kam-i*, the substitution of *s* would occur only in cases like *ayaskṛt*, where *kṛ* is the final member of the compound, and not in cases like *ayaskāra*, where the final member ends in the suffix *aṇ*.
(371) *uda īt* | 6.4.139. [This sūtra prescribes that the vowel *u* at the end of a word is replaced by *ī* before the particle *ud*.]

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *uda īt ṭhacaḥ*. Here, both *ṭhacaḥ* and *hasya* are understood to carry over. Thus he says: "of that which follows the word *udac*, when its *n* has been elided," and so forth. Why [specify] "of a *bha*-stem"? Consider:
*udañcau*, *udañcaḥ*, *udagbhyām*. Why [specify] "when its *m* has been elided"? [Consider: *udak*.
In the context of worship (*pūjā*), [the rule] is intended so that forms such as *udañcaḥ* and *udañce* may occur.
(372) *samaḥ sami* | 6.3.94 | Regarding *samaḥ sami*: the form *samī* is cited without a case ending. Similarly, *irasastiri* is also [cited without a case ending].

The term *samyaṅ* means "going together" (*saṅgatam añcati*). [In this formation], there is lengthening by the rule *au* [Pāṇini 6.1.93] when there is elision (*alopa*). [Alternatively, it means] "going along with" (*saha añcati*).
By the rule *sahasya sadhrir* 6.3.95, the substitute *sadhrir* is applied for *saha*.
In the domain of *sadhryañc*, there is elision of *al* and lengthening [of the vowel]. Thus, *sadhrīc-* and so forth.
(374) *tirasastiry- allope*: 6.3.94. Regarding *tiras*: the term *alopa* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which elision (*lopa*) does not exist."

The term *añcataḥ* is understood as continuing from the previous rule and functions as the object of another word (*anyapadārtha*). Intending to show that the elision (*lopa*) occurring in a part is figuratively attributed to the whole, he says: "whose form is not elided," and so forth. He did not say "when the letter *ṭ* is elided," because [the specific condition] is established through the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). Why [is the suffix] *apratyaya* mentioned at the end? To prevent [the application of the rule] in cases such as *iro'ñcanam*.
In the case of *bhūt-tiraścī*, because the vowel *a* has been elided, the substitution of *tiry* does not occur; consequently, the *s* is changed to *ś* by the rule for *ścutva*.

Nor should it be argued that *ścutva* would not apply because the elision of the vowel (*al-lopa*) is treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if the original element were still present); for *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply when a preceding operation is considered *asiddha* (non-existent), and furthermore, this is a rule concerning the end of a word (*padāntavidhi*).

(375) *nāñceḥ pūjāyām* |6|4|30|. The rule *nāñceḥ* is stated so that, although the form is already established by the *num* augment alone, the nasal *n* may be heard in forms such as *arāñcaḥ* and *prāñcaḥ*, even in the absence of *num*. Thus, *prāṅ* means "one who honors" (*prakarṣeṇa añcati pūjayati*).

From the root *añc* (to bend), the suffix *kvip* is applied for the purpose of forming nouns of worship (*pūjārtha*). Thus we have *praṅkṣi*. According to the rule *“ṇoḥ kuk ṭuk”* (Pāṇini 8.3.28), the augment *kuk* is optionally added;

furthermore, according to the rule *“ayo dvitīyāḥ”* (Pāṇini 8.4.48), it should be understood that when *kṣ* occurs, the letter *kh* may also appear. In this same manner, in the case of the *śas*-class endings and so forth: *pratyañcaḥ*, *pratyaṅbhyām*; *amumuyañcaḥ*, *amumuyaṅbhyām*.

*udañcaḥ*; *udaṅbhyām*, etc., should be understood accordingly. *Kruṅ*: from the root *kruñc* (to bend). Regarding "the elision of *s*" (*salopa*): because the substitution of *ś* (*ścutva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), first either the *dhuṭ* augment is applied by the rule *aḥ sī* [Pāṇini 8.3.34], and then the substitution of *c* (*cartva*). Thus end those ending in *c*. Regarding "they are treated as irregular forms" (*nipātyante*): [from the roots] *ṛṣu* (to sprinkle) and *ṛha* (to grow). Here...

There is an absence of the suffix *guṇa*. The suffix is added to the root *maha* in the sense of the object (*karman*). For this very reason, he explains that "the great one" (*mahān*) is so called because it is "honored" (*mahyate*) or worshipped. In the case of the root *gam*, however, there is the substitution of *jagat*. All four [words] thus end in the suffix *ati*.
This will be made clear in the *Uṇādi* section.

(376) *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.14. Regarding the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ*: because of the carry-over (*anuvṛtti*) from the previous sūtra *hrasvālope* [of the word *dīrghaḥ*] and from the word *apadhāyāḥ* [of the rule *apo dīrgho yajñakarmaṇi*], it is said: "there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*)."
It may be so. Here, the rule "adhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.149) is divided [into two separate rules];

by the force of that [division], the prohibition applies only to the immediately preceding suffix *as* and not to the suffix *at*, according to Kaiyaṭa and others. This very point he demonstrates with the words: "and of that which ends in *as* other than a verbal root."

The meaning is: "that which is distinct from the root (dhātu) and ends in as. By this, forms such as *ukhāstrat*, *parṇadhvat*, and so forth, are established. If one were to explain it as "that which is distinct from the root and is an *as*," then although there is no lengthening in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) for *trat* and *dhvat*, here [in the case of *ukhāstrat*, etc.]...

"Let it be so"—this is the direction [of the argument]. Here, from the rule *arvaṇas tṛ maghono noca* (Pāṇini 6.4.127), the term *asaṃbuddhau* ("except in the vocative singular") is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). From the rule *au ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.132), the term *au* is also understood. Therefore, he says: "when *su* follows, provided it is not the vocative singular. [The reason for this] is the absence of the suffix *at* at the end [of the stem].

The meaning is that because it is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the suffix *ṭha* which has *a* as its *anubandha*, the rule does not apply to a word ending in *cha*. The neuter gender in the term *ubhe* is used with reference to the form of the words themselves. [The phrase] "of the sixth case dual" is intended to convey the principle that "for a word ending in *ṭhan*, there is either an injunction or a prohibition."

(378) *ubhe abhyastam* |6|1|5|. Since the rule would have been established by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "both" (*ubhe*), he explains that the explicit mention of "both" is for the purpose of indicating a collective pair (*samudāya*), stating: "both [roots] taken together. Otherwise, [in a case like] *enijati*, etc.,...
In the case of reduplicated (*abhyasta*) stems, the initial acute accent (*ādy-udātta*) prescribed by rules such as *ādir ñiṭuḍavaḥ* would otherwise apply to each syllable in turn.

(379) *na abhyastāc chatuḥ* | 7.1.78 | "Not [the acute accent] after a reduplicated stem for the suffix *śatṛ*. Here, even though it is separated, it is specifically the *num* augment that is prohibited.

Intending to show that [the suffix] would not apply to others because they are not applicable, he says: "num na syāt" (there would be no *num*). Regarding "dadat": it means "one who gives" (*dadāti*), thus *dadat*. This is the substitution of *śatṛ* for the present tense marker (*laṭ*) of the root *dāñ*; there is *ślau* (elision) of the *śap* (present tense marker); there is doubling (*dvitva*) by the rule "in *lau*"; there is shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); and there is elision of the long *ā* by the rule "nābhyastayor ātaḥ". [The roots] beginning with *jakṣ* are included.

The word *ṣaṭ* (six) is a separate word. By the word *sthiti*, only *jakṣi* is referred to. [The phrase] "those of which *ādi* (beginning with) is the first" is an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound; this is what he expresses by saying "the other six roots. Thus end those ending in *t*. Regarding *gup*: it is derived from the root *gup* in the sense of "to protect" (*gopāyati*). When the suffix *kvip* is intended, there is an absence of the *āya* suffix here because the rule "āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā" (Pāṇini 3.1.31) makes it optional. In the alternative case where the *āya* suffix is applied, the form *gopā* should be understood as resulting from the elision of the *a* (by Pāṇini 6.4.64) and the elision of the *y* (by Pāṇini 6.1.66). Thus end those ending in *p*.

(380) *tyadādiṣu dṛśo’nālocane kañ ca* | 3|2|60| [The rule applies] when *tyad* and so forth [are the objects]. An example of that which ends in *kañ* is *ādṛśaḥ*, *yādṛśaḥ*, and so on; however, that has not been mentioned here because it is of no use among [words ending in] consonants (*halanta*). Why "not in the sense of seeing" (*anālocane*)? [Consider: *taṃ paśyati* ("he sees him").

*Taddarśaḥ* [is derived as follows]: *aṇ* is added after a verbal root when it denotes an object (*karman*). However, words such as *tādṛśa* and others are established by convention (*rūḍhaśabda*); therefore, they are etymologically explained even though their constituent meanings (*avayavārtha*) may not exist. For this very reason, the rule "after the root *dṛś* in the sense of 'not knowing'" is appropriate. In the Bhāṣya, however, the derivation is shown with respect to the reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*): "People see him as this; he is like this."

"He sees" means, by implication, that it becomes an object of knowledge (*jñāna*). However, the reading "for the sake of ignorance" (*ajñānārthāt*) is more appropriate; for in that case, although the root *dṛś* (to see) functions merely as the attainment of being an object of knowledge, it does not function as the act of making [something] an object (*viṣayīkaraṇa*).

(381) *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* |6|3|91|. [The word] "the final substitute is the vowel *ā*" means that when the substitute *a* is applied, [by the rule] *ato guṇe*, [the form] would become *ittha*. Nor should it be argued that by the force of the explicit utterance of the long vowel *ā*, the long [vowel] must necessarily occur.
Because, in the absence of a specific rule for the letter *a*, there would otherwise necessarily follow the pronunciation of a consonant (*hal*) [instead]. Regarding the term *viṭ*:
