it is derived from the root *viś* (meaning "to enter") with the suffix *kvip*, or alternatively from the root *naś*. Some explain this by carrying over the word *hali* from the previous rule and interpreting it as "when a consonant follows or at the end of a word," but that is not correct.
Because there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *aṣṭan* and so forth; or [it applies] to the root *naś*.
[The substitute] *nag* [is used]; the six *aṅgas* are as before.
(383) *spṛśo ’nudake kvin* (Pāṇini 3.2.58).

The suffix *kvin* is added after the root *spṛś* when it does not mean "water. The letter *k* is for the purpose of preventing *guṇa* substitution; the letter *n*, however, serves as a marker (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the rule *vin-pratyayasya kuḥ* [which prescribes the substitution of a guttural for the final consonant of a word ending in the suffix *vin*]. The actual purpose of the suffix *kvin* is... [to form nouns such as] *vastu*.

Since the verbal roots (*prakṛti*) consist of a single vowel, that [accentuation] is already established by the accent of the root itself. As for the word *adhṛk*, because it is an irregularly formed (*nipātana*) word with an udātta accent on the final syllable, an acute accent on the first syllable is not required at all; such is the direction of the argument. Here, the term *upa* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*), while the term *karmani* is understood to have ceased its application (*nivṛtam*); with this intention, he says: "provided it is not *udaka*."

Regarding the rule *supyupapade* ("when a *sup*-ending word is an upapada"): *ghṛtaspṛk* ("one who touches ghee"). The analysis (*vigraha*) is "he touches ghee" or "by means of ghee. Why [is it specified] "not when meaning water" (*anudake*)? [Consider: "he touches water," which results in *udakasparśaḥ*.
By the force of this prohibition, the suffix *kvip* also does not occur here; for if that were present, the suffix *kvin* would apply.

Because, by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the word *yasmāt*, the substitution of *k* for *t* (*kutva*) is unavoidable; thus, the prohibition [by Pāṇini 6.3.57], *ṭhanudake*, would be rendered fruitless. Some, however, offer *udākaspṛk* as a counter-example, their intention being that by the force of the prohibition, let there be no *kutva*, and let the suffix *kvip* simply apply. Thus [they argue].

[The words] are *śāntāḥ*. Regarding [the phrase] "but in the case of being secondary" (*gauṇatve tu*): (384) Pāṇini 8.2.76 states, "There is lengthening of an *ik* vowel when preceded by *ru* or *rv*, provided it is in the penultimate position. [Furthermore, the elision of the suffix is governed by] "there is elision after bases ending in *aṅ*" (*aṅbhayo luk*) and "also after *aṭ* and *catur*" (*aṭcaturbhyaśca*).
The intention is that because of the mention of the plural number, the suffixes *luṅ* and *nuṭ* occur only when the six meanings are predominant.

When the suffix *kvip* is elided after the desiderative root *pipaṭhiṣ*, and the case-endings (*svādi*) are produced due to its being a *kṛdanta* (a word ending in a primary suffix), we have the form *pipaṭhiṣ-su*.

Then, after the elision of *s* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, the *s* [of the nominative] becomes [subject to the following rule] because it is at the end of a word (*padānta*) by virtue of the definition of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

[The substitution of] *ru* occurs. Furthermore, one should not suspect that the elision of *al* (*al-lopa*) would be treated as *sthānivadbhāva* when the substitution of *ru* is to be applied, because that [treatment] is prohibited by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhe*. (385) Also when there is an intervention by *num*, *visarjanīya*, or *śar*. 8.3.58.

Regarding the rule *numvisarjanīyaṣṭhūṭhin koḥ*: this is a statement [providing] what would otherwise not apply because of the intervention [of sounds], due to the mention of the fifth case (*pañcamīnirdeśāt*).

As for the phrase *ṣṭuatvena pūrvasya*: when the *s* of *san* has undergone the substitution of *ru* and *visarga*, and these have subsequently been replaced by *ka* and *ta*, there is an option according to the rule *vā śari*. Consequently, in one alternative, the *s* remains; and thus, when there is an intervention by the sibilants (*śar*), the *s* of the locative suffix (*sup*) [is affected].

The state of being *ṣ* [is established]. The preceding [consonant] becomes *ṣṭu* (i.e., *ṣ*), but it does not become *ṣ* by the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*, because of the prohibition "not when there is a substitute beginning with *ṭ* or an affix" (*na tu ṭhādeśapratyayayoḥ*). This is the intended meaning. Others hold that this being the case, the mention of *ś* includes the *visarjanīya*. As for *niḥsva*: [it refers to] each of the initial *s* sounds.

Even when there is an intervention, because [the *s*] lacks the status of being a part of either a substitute (*ādeśa*) or an affix (*pratyaya*), the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. Nor should it be argued that, due to the absence of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "of the substitute and the affix" (*ādeśapratyayayoḥ*) here, the substitution of *ṣ* for the *k* of the verbal root would occur by the rule "before *u*, *m*, and *visarjanīya*" (*umisaṃjñānīye*); for that [rule] functions independently.

This is because its status as an injunction is not accepted; for, like the rules "ṭh-apa-dāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ" and "ṭhiṇ-koḥ," the rule "u-m-bi-sarjanīye" is also an *adhikāra-sūtra* (a governing rule).

Because the status of being a *vidhāyaka* (an original prescriptive rule) is not accepted; for, just like the rules "ṭhapadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ" and "iṇkoḥ," the rule "umiṇśarīyāḥ" is also an *adhikāra-sūtra* (a governing heading). From the root *kṛ*, one who desires to act is *cikīrṣati*; from *cikīrṣati*, the *kvip* suffix is applied—yielding *cikīḥ*. This is according to the rule "ekāca upadeśe."
Regarding the form *anigrahīṣuḥ*: by the rule *vāsaNeḷabhāve*, the suffix *san* is applied;

by *ṭhiko jhaL*, the *kit* designation is assigned, which results in the absence of *guṇa*; by *ṭhajjhanagamāṃ sanī*, the lengthening of the vowel occurs; by *ṛta iḍitītvam*, the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* takes place, followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*; then reduplication occurs; by *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, all but the first consonant of the reduplicated syllable are elided; and by *kuhoścuḥ*, the second *k* is replaced by *c*. Finally, there is the elision of the *a* (by *allopaḥ*).

Because of the elision of *sarvanāmasthāna* and other suffixes, [the word] ends in a *pada*; therefore, by the rule "a long vowel is substituted for the penultimate [vowel] before *ṛt*, *th*, or *v*," the lengthening occurs.

Regarding the form *doḥ*: it is called *doḥ* because it tames (*dāmyati*). As for the phrase "by the elision of the final consonant cluster" (*saṃyogāntalopa*), one should not suspect that the elision of the *a* (in *dām-*) is *asiddha* due to being *bahiraṅga* when this [elision of the cluster] is to be applied.

The direction [of the argument] is as follows: because the elision of the *saṃyoga* (the doubling) is indeed *bahiraṅga*, due to its dependence on the designation (*saṃjñā*) of the word-form which depends in turn upon an external cause (*nimitta*). Regarding *viviṭ*: this is the desiderative (*san*) of the root *viś*.
Since the prohibition of *iṭ* applies by the rule *ekācaḥ*, there is an absence of *guṇa* because the suffix is *kit* according to the rule *halantācca*.

Regarding the operations concerning doubling and repetition: in the word *taḍit*, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *akṣū* (or *tvakṣū*) in the sense of "making thin. [The form] *goraṭ* is derived from [the root *rakṣ*] with the object *go* as an upapada; by the rule "optionally when the [upapada] is similar," the suffix *kvip* is applied. The reason given is "because the substitution of *k* [for *kh*] is not established" (*kutvasyāsiddhatvāt*). The intention is that otherwise, by the rule *koḥ*, there would be the elision of the *k*.

*pipakṣati*: he wishes to cook; *pipak*. *vivakṣati*: he wishes to speak; *vivak*. By the rule "āder" (Pāṇini 7.2.16), there is the substitution of *gh* [for *k*]. By the rule "ṭhekāco baśo bhaṣ" (Pāṇini 8.2.37), there is the substitution of *bhaṣ* [for *k*]. *didhak*: he wishes to burn. Thus end those ending in *ṣ*. Regarding *sutū*: he satisfies well, thus *sutūḥ*. *vidvan*: he knows.
From the root *ṣṭhiv* (to spit), the suffix *śatṛ* becomes *vasu*. Due to its inclusion in the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment.

Because it is marked with the indicatory letter *ṅ* by the rule *ārdhadhātukam apit*, the guṇa substitution does not apply. Due to the presence of the indicatory letter *uk*, the augment *num* is added.

By the rule *ānmahataḥ*, the vowel is lengthened. Because the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) does not take place.

(386) *Vasoḥ sa-prasāraṇam* | Pāṇini 6.4.131. Regarding the word *vasoḥ*: since the rule involves the mention of an affix (*pratyaya-grahaṇe*), it implies the inclusion of that which ends with it; thus he says, "of that which ends in *vasu*. In the form *sedivān*, the affix *kvasu* is applied to the root *sad* by the rule *bhāṣāyāṃ sadavasaśruvaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.108], which prescribes *kvasu* for the perfect tense (*liṭ*) in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*). [The subsequent rule *iṭi*... applies when there is the augment *iṭ*.
The doubling [of the root] occurs by the rule *dhātv-ari*. The remaining [consonant] is the first after a *ṭh* or *hal* by *ṭhhalādiḥ śeṣaḥ*.

The substitution of *e* for the radical vowel and the elision of the reduplication occur by *ata ekahalmadhye*. The augment *iṭ* is added by *vasvekājādhasām*. Then comes the *num* augment. The lengthening occurs by *ān-te*. Thus we have *seduṣaḥ*. Now, an objection is raised: "In the case of a reference to a term containing an *anubandha*..."
By the paribhāṣā "nā'tadanubandhakasya," it would be more appropriate for the samprasāraṇa to apply only to the *vasu* of the rule "videḥ śaturvasuḥ" and not to that of *kvasu*. True;

however, the addition of the indicatory letter *u* (the *ukāra-anubandha*) to *vasu* is for the purpose of including *kvasu* as well through general reference (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*), because [otherwise] it would lack the status of being an *ugit*.

Since the formation is established even by the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule, the suffix *kvasu* has not been illustrated here after roots such as *gam*, because it belongs to the Vedic language (*chāndasa*). For this very reason,
in the section on Vedic grammar (*vaidikaprakriyā*), examples such as *tasthivān* and *jagmivān* should be cited.

They say that [such forms] do not exist here [in the classical language]. However, poets employ them—as in "śreyāṃsi sarvāṇyadhijagmuṣaste" (of him who has attained all blessings) and "aṃ tasthivāṃsaṃ nagaropakaṇṭhe" (who stood at the outskirts of the city), and so forth. Regarding this, they say: even some Vedic forms, like *paddat* and others, occasionally occur in the common language (*bhāṣā*).
This can somehow be resolved by relying on the fact that the rule *āsaścchandasī* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) with reference to general cases.

As for *suhin*: because the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*nopadhādīrghaḥ*) does not apply.

Regarding *suhintsviti*: by the rule *aśce*, the *s* optionally becomes a *dhut*. From the roots *dhvaṃsu* (in the sense of falling away) and *hraṃsu* (in the sense of going or begging), the suffix *kvip* is applied; the elision of the nasal is by the rule *aniditām*; and the substitution of *d* for *s* is by the rule *vasusraṃsudhvaṃsu*. Thus we have *dhvat* (from *dhvasate*) and *srat* (from *sraṃsate*). The root *srasu* means "falling away," while *hraṃsu* means "going" and "begging. The suffix *kvip* is added to these two, the nasal is dropped according to the rule *aniditām*, and the dental *d* is substituted [for the *s*] according to the rule *vasusraṃsudhvaṃsu*.

(387) *puṃso'suṅ* | 7|1|89|. Regarding *puṃso'suṅ*: since the term "in a *sarvanāmasthāna*" (*sarvanāmasthāne*) is understood from the previous rule *ṭhito'tsarvanāmasthāne*, he says "in a *sarvanāmasthāna*". [The word] "intended" (*vivakṣita*)...

In the case of *tenaṭ paramapumān*, because the suffix *asuṅ* is applied due to the word being "para" (subsequent), the udātta accentuation of the final syllable of the compound belongs specifically to the vowel of *asuṅ*. However, this would not be established if the locative case were interpreted as "para-saptamī" (in the subsequent word).
For if the udātta accent of the vowel *u* in the word *pum-* were applied even before the occurrence of the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix, [the desired result would not follow].

Because, in place of a *hal* (consonant) subject to elision (*sraṃsanadharman*), there arises the contingency of a substitute that is likewise subject to elision and is necessarily unaccented (*anudātta*). Nor can it be argued that even if an accent were assigned to the vowel *u*, it would be set aside because it is not final; for the suffix *asuṅ* will be applied precisely because it occupies the final position.

It must be stated that this is because, when an internal (antaraṅga) vowel operation is to be applied, the external (bahiraṅga) *asuṅ* substitute is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*). However, in reality, according to the *akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā*...

Because it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the internal rule (*antaraṅga-paribhāṣā*), the view that [the suffix] occurs in the locative case of the subsequent word (*parasaptamī*) is also easily established;

this is clear in the *Manoramā*. Regarding the root *pūñ*: although it will be stated in the *Uṇādisūtras* that "after *āp*, there is the suffix *ḍumsun*," nevertheless, one should understand that what is stated here follows an alternative reading. He...

Regarding "pumann": because it is stated that [the substitution applies] "to the vocative ending in ṭha," there is no lengthening by the rule "ānte. Regarding "puṃsu": when the final consonant is elided, the *anusvāra* is substituted for *o*.
This is not governed by the rule "num-bisarjanīya... because it is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) specifically for the *anusvāra* that stands in the place of *num*.

The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]. Regarding *uśanā*: [it is derived] from the root *vaś-* with the suffix *kanas*. By the rule *rahi-jyā-*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). Regarding "in its vocative": this is a *vārttika*. However, Haradatta and others say:
since it should have been stated that *su* becomes *ḍe*, the statement *anaṅ sau* indicates that in some cases the form *anaṅ* is heard [instead].
This is established because it has been made known. Although, once *su* has been replaced by *ḍe*, the form *anuṣṭar* would result—

due to the elision of the final vowel by virtue of the marker *ṭ* [in *ḍe*], followed by the lengthening according to the rule "in a non-vocative *an*-stem nominative-accusative case ending" (*arvan-nāma-sthāne cāsaṃbuddhau*)— nevertheless, by the *aṅga-vṛtta-paribhāṣā* (the maxim regarding operations within a stem), [the desired form is obtained].

Their intention is that, by considering [the rule] "dīrgho na" (P. 6.4.12) as an *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence), the application of the rule is consistent. For example: *anehā* and *vedhāḥ*. In the section on the suffix *asun*, because of the derivations "from the root *han* with the suffix *añ* and the augment *ehac*" and "from the root *vidhāñ* with the suffix *asun* and the change to *vedha*," these words end in *as*. Consequently, by virtue of being *asan*-stems, the vowel is lengthened. Thus, *anehā* means "time," and *vedhāḥ* means "the creator of the universe."

(388) *adasa āṬ sulopaśca* | Pāṇini 7.2.107. The word *adasaḥ* is in the genitive case. From the rule *adoḥ saḥ sau*, the term *sau* is understood here; thus he says: "When *su* follows, the substitution of *āṬ* shall take place for the final [portion] of *adas*."
[Objection: Let there simply be the ablative case ending *-as* in *adas-*; let the vowel *au* be prescribed for the *su* that follows it.
The form *asau* is established through the substitution of *at* for *tyad* and so on; what is the use of prescribing the elision of *su*?

Nor is there a difference in accent, because the single substitute *au* resulting from [the combination of] the acute-accented [suffix] and [the preceding vowel] is itself acute. [Reply: Do not say so.
In the case of *ṭhasakau strī*, because of the suffix *ṭāp*, there would be the undesirable consequence of shortening [the vowel] by the rule *atyayasthāt*. As for *asukaḥ*:
in the absence of the *āṬ* augment, when the substitution of *yat* for the *tyad*-class stems occurs, there is the substitution of *sāt*. In the feminine, however, it is *ṭhasukā* and *ṭhasukā*;
the forms *ṭhamukī* and *ṭhasukī* are indeed ungrammatical. The same applies to forms such as *amukaśarmā*.
Because [the reading] beginning with *ṭhadakaḥ śarmai* is alone logical;
(389) *eta īd bahuvacane* | 8|2|81|. Regarding *eta īd bahuvacane*: if the technical term (*paribhāṣika*) "plural" were taken [here], then [in the case of *amībhiḥ*...]

Even if [the forms] *rityādi* and so forth were established, the form *jasu ṭhamī* would not be established; for in this case, the vowel *e* (of *ete*) is not followed by a plural ending (*bahuvacana*). Therefore, he explains: "when expressing a plurality of objects.
[The phrase] "the operation of the case-ending first" refers to the seven chapters and a quarter beginning with the rule *yadādīnām aḥ*.

The point is that because the rule *ṭhadaso'sedhrī* (Pāṇini 7.1.12) is *asiddha* according to the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Pāṇini 8.2.1), the operations of *utva* and *matva* do not apply since the word still ends in *s* as long as the case-ending operation has not yet taken place. However,
if in the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* one were to accept that it is the *effect* (*kārya*) that is *asiddha*, then—

Otherwise, forms such as *ṭhamū* and *ṭhamu* would not be established. For, once the substitution of *ya* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad* has been applied, if the substitutions of *u* and *a* (for *au* and *as*) were performed even before the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*), then—because the operation of *mutva* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) at that stage—the rule *ato guṇe* would apply the single substitute, resulting in the undesired forms *ṭhamau* and so forth. Furthermore:

In *carma vaste* [the form] is *armavaḥ*, and in *suṣṭu vaste* it is *uvaḥ*. Here, because the rule *skoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.29] applies later, the elision (*lopa*) would occur; however, since that [elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the elision of *hal* and following [consonants] by [Pāṇini 6.1.68] would not apply, and thus the stated forms would not be established.

Therefore, the position that "the effect is non-existent" (*kāryāsiddhi-pakṣaḥ*) must indeed be rejected. Regarding this, they say: "That which is prescribed within the seven chapters and one quarter..."

Some maintain that, according to the view of non-application (*asiddhatva*) of an operation as stated in the *Prakriyā-grantha*—namely, "that which is prescribed for a subsequent operation is non-applicable"—forms such as *anorathaḥ* and *ṭhamum* would not be established.
That is not correct; for the statement in the *Prakriyā-grantha* regarding "with respect to an operation" means "in the context of an operation."
Regarding that which is to be performed, "asiddha" means it has not yet arisen at all; this is the meaning.

Even in the case of the *asiddha* status of a rule (*śāstra*), the resulting sense is exactly the same. As stated by Kaiyaṭa: "It is impossible for a rule (*śāstra*) that has been uttered [to be *asiddha*]."

"Because of the statement 'to make [it] unestablished' (kartum), an extension (atideśa) is resorted to. And thus, the property of being unestablished (*asiddha*), which consists in not causing an operation to take effect, being extended by way of *atideśa* according to the treatise, results precisely in the unestablished status of the operation itself. And so, in the case of *anoratha*, when the substitution of *u* (*utva*) is to be applied, [the elision of the *r* is unestablished].

Since the substitution of *rorutva* (the replacement of *ru* for *r*) would not be obstructed even before the application [of the subsequent rule], the fulfillment of the desired object (*manoratha*) is established without modification.
Likewise, the establishment of forms such as *ṭhamum* follows; thus, in the view that "a rule is not yet applied" (*kāryāsiddha-pakṣa*), there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

(390) *na mu ne* |8|2|3|. Regarding *na mu ne*, he states that the locative case [in *ne*] denotes the sphere of application (*viṣayasaptamī*), saying: "when *nā* is to be applied. The underlying intention is that otherwise, because the condition of being followed by a *ghi*-stem would be absent, the substitution of *nā* would not occur. But even if this were done...

If [the rule] were not present, the long vowel would occur even in the case of *na-abhāve*; since the substitution of *m* (mutva) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the lengthening, he says: "and when it has been performed. This is obtained by repeating the word *e*, because one instance is taken as a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*) and the other as a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*).

In reality, however, the explanation of the rule *ṛte ca* is redundant, because even by the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*, the lengthening [of the vowel] in the case of *api ca* must be established. If it is objected: "Why not simply say *amunā* as one says *adhunā*; what is the use of this prohibition regarding the status of being *asiddha*? [the answer follows].

On this point, they say: the statement "na mu ne" is for the purpose of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) with the word "a"; by means of this, forms such as "āmaḥ" and "rāmebhyaḥ" are established. Otherwise, since the substitution of *ru* would be considered *asiddha*, how could the designation *it* and its subsequent elision apply to the vowel *u*? It is not [the case that it would not].

Nor should it be argued that, by the force of the notation with the nasal (anunāsika), the substitution of *ru* is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of the technical designation (*itsaṃjñā*) and its subsequent elision;

for in rules such as *arumūlam* and *evaruhī*, the nasal alone is specified in the rule *ato roḥ* in order to exclude the application of *haśi ca*, and thus [the nasal notation] has already served its purpose in that very instance.
And thus, when the *sthānivad-ādeśa* rule also applies, the visarga is obtained because of the status of being a *pada*.

Furthermore, the indications such as the mention of *artyayaḥ* and *paraśca* serve as evidence (*liṅga*) in this matter; such is the direction [of the argument]. This concludes the section on masculine stems ending in consonants.

(391) *naho dhaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.2.34. Regarding *naho dhaḥ*: it was not stated simply as *naḥ*, because if that were the case, in the word *addhā*, there would be the substitution of *ṇ* by *adābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.2.39), and the rule *haṣastathoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.31) would not apply. *Nahaḥ*.

The sense is that, due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule *ṭhho ḍhaḥ* or by the rule *alo’ntyasya*, the substitute applies specifically to the letter *h*. The terms *jhal*, *pada*, *skau*, and *ayogādyor ante ca* recur from the preceding rules.

He says this: "when a *jh* sound follows," and so forth. The meaning is: when a *jh* sound follows, or when [the word] is at the end of a word (*padānte*). Regarding *upānat*: from the root *nah* preceded by the prefix *upa*, with the suffix *kvip* because it belongs to the *saṃpad-ādi* group, there is lengthening of the first syllable according to the rule "ahivṛti. After the elision of the case-ending *s* by the rule beginning with "haṅyādilopa," there is the substitution of *dh*. Then follow the substitutions of *jaś* and *cartva*.

In this regard, the following should be understood: in the bahuvrīhi compound *suṣṭhvanaṅvāhī* (one who has a well-yoked ox-cart), the form is *suṣṭhvanaṅvāh* by virtue of the rule for masculine forms (*puṃvat*). Thus: here, the suffix *ām* [prescribed] by the rule *atura-naḍuhoḥ* does not occur; for, since it is superseded by the subsequent [rule], once the substitution of *catasṛ* has been applied, that [suffix] does not apply again according to the maxim of "once occurred" (*sakṛdgatinyāya*).
[In the form] *catasṛṇām*, there is no lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *tun-sṛ-catasṛ*. [The phrase] "like *sarva*" means: by that...

In the word *tulyam*, the suffix *vati* is applied. The substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs by the rule "in all derivative formations (*vṛtti*), the neuter replaces the feminine of a pronoun. (Pāṇini 7.1.77).

Regarding the rule *yaḥ sau* (7.2.110): this substitution of *yat* for *idam* applies only to the feminine, because of the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*). This is established by the rule *ido'y puṃsi*.

[The form *vāk* is derived] because [the suffix] is not present in the masculine, and because [the suffix] is elided by *luk* in the neuter. "In this way" means: *sā*, *te*, *tāḥ*; *yāḥ*, *ye*, *yāḥ*;

*eṣā*, *ete*, *etāḥ*, and so forth. Regarding *vāk*: from the root *vac*, by the rule "in *vibvac* etc. (*vibvacītyādīnām*), there is the feminine suffix *kvip*, lengthening of the vowel, and non-conversion (*asaṃprasāraṇa*). Then, by the rule "of *u* becomes *ku*" (*oḥ kuḥ*), [the *k* is substituted for the *v*].

(393) *apo bhiṃ* | Pāṇini 7.4.48. In the word *ap*, [the substitution of] *at* occurs. [The form *ap* is derived from the root] *āp* with the suffix *kvip*; by the rule *āpnoterhrasvaśca*, there is shortening, and because of the word *ca* ("and"), the suffix *kvip* is also included. Since the phrase "after a prefix" (*aca upasargāt*) is understood as being carried over (*anuvartana*), he says: "there should be the letter *t*. [The word] *dig*.

The substitution of *k* [for *ṣ*] occurs because it is a feminine form (*strītvāt*). The six *aṅga*-operations are to be inferred as before. "In other cases as well" means even in the absence of a word beginning with *tyad-* as an upapada. Regarding *tviṭ*: the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *viṣ* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*); then the substitutions of *jaś* and *cartva* apply. Regarding *sajūḥ*: [from the root] *uṣ*.
From the root *prī* with the suffix *sevana*, the suffix *kvip* is applied. By the rule *asajuṣoḥ*, the *ṣ* is replaced by *r*.

By the rule *ṛtvoḥ*, a long vowel is substituted. Regarding *āśiṣau*: by the statement "for the root *āśas*, the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel should be stated," the penultimate vowel is changed to *i*;
then, by the rule *āsivasīṣu*, the *ṣ* is substituted. Regarding *asau*: [the same process applies].

The substitution of *ad-*, *tyad-* etc., and the suffix *ṭāp* [apply]. Because the single substitute is considered as belonging to the end of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatva*), [the rule] "for *adas*, *auṭ* and elision of *su*" applies; some say that by the rule "of *adaḥ*," there is the substitution of *s*. Others, however, say that because it is subsequent and a specific rule, the substitution of *au* occurs first; therefore, in this case, there is neither the substitution of *ā* nor the suffix *ṭāp*.
Thus ends the section on feminine nouns ending in consonants.

Regarding the rule "And when it is an *uttarapada*, there is a prohibition [of the application of rules] regarding what is not at the beginning of a word (*apadādau*). The term "uttara" refers to the *uttarapada*. When the *uttarapada* possesses the status of a "word" (*pada*), [the following applies].

The meaning is that the characteristic of being a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply when [the compound] is to be treated as a word (*pada*). By this, the objection—that in the forms *udhiyau* and *udhiya*, the status of being a word (*padatva*) due to the internal *sup*-suffix would result in the optional application of the Śākala rule—is refuted, because the characteristic of being a suffix is prohibited according to the method stated above. What is the purpose of the condition "when it is the second member of a compound" (*utarapadatve*)?

In examples such as *ājapuruṣa*, the elision of *n* (nalopa) occurs as required. Even in cases such as *aśyati dadhi*, although the word *dadhi* is a *pada*, the rule regarding the presence of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) still applies, because the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) is conventionally used for a member of a compound. Thus, in *dadhisecau*: *siñcataḥ* means "those two who sprinkle," [forming] *sec-au*. [This is derived] from the suffix *ṭhan* [added] after other roots as well.

The phrase *dadhnaḥ secāv iti* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). However, in an *upapada* compound, since the formation of the compound occurs prior to the addition of case-endings (*sup*), the word *sec* would not yet have the designation of a "word" (*pada*);

consequently, the *s* of *sec* would not be considered the beginning of a word (*padādittva*), and [the rule for] *ṣatva* would not apply. But if this is so, how is there *ṣatva* in an *upapada* compound?

If it is argued that [the rule] is difficult to maintain, Kaiyaṭa says on this point: "The substitution of *ṣ* does not occur after a word with an upapada because of non-mention (*anabhidhāna*), as there is no usage such as *dadhisecau*. In reality, however, under the view that "the beginning of a word [is *padādi*] when preceded by a word" (*padādādiḥ padādiḥ*), the substitution of *ṣ* is easily avoided even in the case of an upapada compound (*upapadasamāsa*).

In the case of a subsequent reference (anvādeśa) involving a neuter noun, *ena* should be prescribed. This applies to the subsequent reference; it is ordained here [for the accusative singular], but not for the *auṭ*, *śas*, and other cases, because there would be no result. Even though the *am* suffix is elided by the rule "elision of *am* after a neuter [stem]" (*vomornapuṃsakāt*), the designation of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) still operates here.

They say [this is so] by the force of the statement; however, in reality, *enad* should be prescribed in the very rule *dvitīyāṭaussu*. Forms such as *enam*, *enau*, and *enān* are established through the substitution of *tyadādyatva* (the replacement of pronouns with *a*).
Even though the suffix *am* in the neuter is elided by *luk*, the substitution of *enad* occurs due to the power of the pronunciation of the letter *t*.
Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *ena* even in the case of *śrita*, because when the compound *dvitīyā-śrita* is formed,

the *sup* suffix is elided by luk, and thus the condition of being followed by the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) no longer exists. Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *ena* occurs here by virtue of the expressive power (*sāmarthya*) of the pronunciation of the letter *t*.

It is established in the *Manoramā* that because [the elision of *su* and *am*] has its purpose fulfilled by the internal (*antaraṅga*) elision of *su* and *am* through their dependence on a single word, it does not apply to the external (*bahiraṅga*) elision occurring in a compound. Thus, in the case of *brahmaṇī*, the elision of *a* prescribed by "vibhāṣā ṅśyor" does not take place, because [the condition] "after a conjunct consonant ending in *m*" applies.

Because of the prohibition [in Pāṇini 8.2.67]. [The rule] *ro'supi* [applies in cases such as] *aharbhāti*. The point is that if the substitution of *ru* for *ahan* were applied, then by the subsequent application of *utva* (the substitution of *u*) according to *haśi ca*, the form would have to be *ahobhāti*. (394) *ahan* |8|2|68|.
It should be understood that by postulating the elision (*lopa*) of the *n* in *nalopa*, and by incorporating another *n* into the rule *ahan* (Pāṇini 8.2.68),
one can explain it as "the *ru* [substitute] of the word *ahan* ending in *n*"; thus, the status of the *n* as the locus for both the *ru*-substitution and the *ra*-substitution will be established.
"Of that ending as well"—the intention is that this is because it occurs within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning words (*pada*). One might object:

"In this case, by the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treating a word as if it ended in a suffix), one could rely on the case-ending contained within the end of the compound; thus, even for the word *ahan*, which is but a part of the compound, it would indeed be a *pada*, and the substitution of *ru* (for *n*) would necessarily occur. What is the purpose of this [sūtra]?"

One should not suspect that this depends on the application of the rule regarding "tadanta" (that which ends with such an element). For, by the prohibition "and when there is an *uttarapada*, [the rule] does not apply to what is prescribed for the beginning of a word," the *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa* (the treatment as if a suffix were present) does not operate. Regarding the rule "sṛji-dṛśoḥ...
(Pāṇini 6.1.58), this is merely an illustrative example (*lakṣaṇa*), because that same usage occurs even in the rule "mṛjer vṛddhiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.114).

Regarding the forms *rajju* and *sṛṅ*, [one might object]: "Since the suffix *ati* begins with a consonant (*jhal*) and is not *kit*, the augment *am* should apply by the rule *ṛjidṛśoḥ*. This is not so; for one should not suspect this, because the root is not presented in its own form [as the base]. Rather, an operation prescribed for a root applies to that which follows the suffix.

This is because of the refinement [of the rule] by the word *eva*. And thus, in cases such as *rasṛṅbhyām* and *rasṛṅbhiḥ*, this fault does not apply. This is clear in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ*. If it is argued: "But an operation prescribed for a verbal root (*dhātu*) should apply only to its suffixes (*pratyaya*)," [the answer follows].
In forms such as *hiyau* (from *hī*) and *huvau* (from *hū*), the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would not occur;

rather, they would occur only in cases such as *ikṣiyatuḥ* (from *ikṣ*) and *luluvatuḥ* (from *lū*). This is true. In reality, the operations such as *iyaṅ* and so forth are not applied directly to the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself.

However, because it is stated [in the rule] that this applies to a member of a compound (*aṅga*), there is an inequality; the sense is that this is an exception to the *kutva* [substitution], since in the sūtra on *ṣatva*, the term "ṛj-mṛja-yaja" is specifically mentioned.
As for the word *asṛk*, this is clear in the commentary of Kṣīrasvāmin; it should be understood as being formed with the suffix *ṛj*.

Thus [it is said]. Although in this view the accent (*svara*) differs, nevertheless, because accent is not strictly observed in common usage (*loka*), while in the Veda it is desired by way of general rule (*bāhulaka*), the intended accent is established; such is the sense. [The term] *bahūrji* is a prohibition regarding the suffix *ni*. [The form] *bahūrji*: this is based on a specific scriptural statement (*vācanika*) that "this [suffix] is final. And so:

The *vārttika* states: "There is a prohibition regarding *bahūrji*; some [hold that] the *num* augment occurs before the final letter. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the first *vārttika* is rejected on the basis of the assumption that the *num* augment belongs to that which ends in a *jhal* consonant following a vowel (*acaḥ paro yo jhal tadantasya num*).
Consequently, in the case of *bahūrji*, the *num* augment is difficult to obtain. Furthermore, in *urdamāne*...

It should be understood that, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, forms such as *kriḍāyām* and *arhaṃ garhāyām*, which end in the suffix *kvip*, cannot possibly undergo the insertion of *num*. This is because of the status of the elision (*allopasya*) as "as if it were still present" (*sthānivadbhāvāt*). However, the rule "that which is elided before *v* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*" is not relied upon here, because that rule applies only in specific instances (*kvācitkatvāt*).
The intention is that the rule "na sthānivat" (Pāṇini 1.1.56) applies universally in these cases.
Nine [forms] arise after the suffix *su*, and likewise nine after *am*;
when combined with *bhyām*, *bhis*, and *bhyas*, there are six in number; likewise, there are exactly nine in the *sup* [case-endings], three in *jas*, and similarly three in *śas*.
"O wise ones, for whom do these four other forms of words belong? Let them know that;

if they possess the creative intuition (*pratibhā*) to declare it, let there be a six-month deadline for this. Thus was a challenge posed by some ancient scholar in the assembly of the king, and [it was answered] by the ancient scholars themselves.

By some, the arrangement of the assembly was not stated by means of the two verses beginning with "of the word *avāk*" and ending with "*vibhāvaye*"; therefore, he states those same two verses because they are useful for the present subject: "the forms of the word *avāk*. In the root *añc-* meaning "to go," there is no elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*).
With the intention that this is not the case regarding worship (*pūjā*), he says: "due to the difference in the modes of worship" (*arcāgatibhedataḥ*).
The suffix *tasi* is used here because it belongs to the group beginning with *ādi*.
Due to the distinction between the meanings of "worship" (*pūjā*) and "going" (*gati*), there are one hundred and nine forms [of the verb], including those such as *asaṃdhi*, *vaṅk*, and so forth.

The meaning is "the bases of awakening" (*bodhyāni*). He states the aforementioned number: *svamsupsu*. The word "each" (*pratyekam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Similarly, it should be understood in the subsequent cases for *aṭ*, *trīṇi*, and *catvāri*.
Regarding "forms" (*rūpāṇi*): by summation, there are one hundred and nine forms. Here, *ayo*...

It should be understood that the statement "one hundred unobstructed forms" was made without relying on the Vārttika rule "dvitīyāḥ"; for if one were to rely on that [Vārttika], it would be stated immediately thereafter that "three forms increase.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," other examples are also to be understood by the word "ādi. For instance: *gavāgbhiḥ*.

In the *ṅi* case: *goagbhiḥ*, *gogbhiḥ*, *gavāṅbhiḥ*, *go’hbhiḥ*. In the *ṅsi* case: *gocaḥ*, *gavāñcaḥ*, *goañcaḥ*, *go’ñcaḥ*. In the *bhyām* case, it is as before (*prāgvat*). In the *bhyas* case: *gavāgbhyaḥ*, *goagbhyaḥ*, *gogbhyaḥ*, *gavāṅbhyaḥ*, *goaṅbhyaḥ*. In the *ṅsi* case: *gocaḥ*, *gavāñcaḥ*, *goañcaḥ*, *go’ñcaḥ*.

The forms *bhyām* and *bhyas* are as before. The suffix *ṅsi* is the singular of the fifth case (*pañcamī*). In *osi*: *gocoḥ*, *gavāñcoḥ*, *goañcoḥ*, *go’ñcoḥ*. In *āmi*: *gocām*, *gavāñcām*, *goañcām*, *go’ñcām*.
But in *ṅi*: *goti*, *gavāñci*, *goañci*, *go’ñci*.
The forms are as before. But in the locative plural (*sup*), they are: *gavāṅkṣu*, *gavāṅṣu*, *goaṅkṣu*, *goaṅṣu*, *go’ṅkṣu*, *go’ṅṣu*, *gavākṣu*, *goakṣu*, *gokṣu*.

Now, one might object that since the forms are identical in the three instances of the instrumental dual (*bhyām*), the two instances of the ablative-genitive plural (*bhyas*), and the two instances of the genitive-locative singular (*ṅsi* and *ṅsoḥ*), [there is no need for further distinction].

If it is asked, "How is it stated here that there are one hundred and nine [forms]? they reply: It was stated thus by relying on a difference in form based on a difference in meaning. One might suspect an excess of six; however, because the letter *kha* optionally occurs in place of the letter *ka* among the nine, there is no excess of six forms.
The meaning is "there is doubt. [Regarding the phrase] "they indeed increase": since it is thus possible for there to be an excess of three, there are twelve forms in the *sup* [case endings];

thus, by summation, the accepted number is one hundred and twelve, and not one hundred and nine—this is the sense. [Regarding the phrase] "becoming horses and eyes": [this refers to the number twenty-seven].

The meaning is five hundred and twenty-seven. Among those nine, when the final one is doubled, there are eighteen. Among the four *āṬ* vowels, for the three used in the sense of honor (*pūjā*), when *ñ* is doubled, there are seven.
As for the nasalization (*anunāsika*) [of the vowel] in the rule "ṭhaṇo’paragṛhye," it does not occur here because of the status of being *paragṛhya*. In the case of *jas*:
Because of the optionality of doubling and of the nasalization, there are twelve forms;

in total, this sums to thirty-seven (37). Thus, in the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) as well, there are thirty-seven. And so, in total, this sums to seventy-four (74). Among the four [forms] in the *ṭā* ending, those used for the purpose of worship—

When the three [consonants] are doubled, there are seven; and when those seven are doubled with the nasal, there are fourteen. By summation, there are eighty-eight (88). In the case of *bhyām*, when the six forms have doubling of the *bh* preceding them, there are twelve; and when those twelve also undergo doubling of the *y* according to the rule "ṭhyaṇo mayaḥ," [there are further variations].
There are twenty-four; when the *m* of these is doubled, there are forty-eight.

By summation, there are one hundred and thirty-six. In the case of *bhis*, there are twenty-four; because of the doubling of both the preceding *bh* and the *visarga*, by summation there are one hundred and sixty-six. In the case of *ṅi*, among the four...

For the three [forms] ending in *pūjārtha*, there are seven when *ñ* and *dvitva* (doubling) are applied; however, there is no nasalized form (*anunāsika*) because the vowel *e* is not included among the *aṇ* vowels. By summation, there are two hundred and sixty-seven.
For the four [forms] ending in *ṅsi*, there are seven when *ñ* and *dvitva* are applied; and for those seven, when *visarga-dvitva* (doubling of the visarga) is applied...

Fourteen. By summation, there are two hundred and seventy-seven. Among the four [consonants] in *ṅsau*, there are seven when *ñ* is doubled; and when the visarga is doubled for those seven, there are fourteen.
By summation, there are two hundred and seventy-seven.

In the case of *bhyām* and *bhyas*, as before, there are forty-eight forms for each; thus, by summation, there are three hundred and seventy-three. In the case of *ṅsi*, *ivaṅ*, *sosām*, and *ṅi-os*, there are likewise fourteen for each. Among the four forms [of the locative], when the *ñat* suffixes are doubled, there are seven [variants] for the final [element] of all [four].

Because of duality; but in the case of *ṅai*, since there is an optional substitution of an anusvāra for the final *ṭhaṇ* of all seven [suffixes] by the rule "of that which is not a *pragṛhya*," the total sum is four hundred and forty-three. In the case of *sup* with the sense of motion, there are six [forms] due to the doubling of the three *ka*s; and of those...

In the case of the word *‘hayaḥ śaraḥ’*, there are twelve forms when the *ṣat* (six) doubling occurs. When the nasalization (*anunāsika*) of the letter *u* occurs, there are twenty-four. By summation, this totals four hundred and sixty-seven. However, in the context of worship (*pūjā*), when the suffix *ku* is absent, there are twelve forms due to the doubling of the three instances of *ṅ* and the occurrence of nasalization; but in the alternative where *ku* is present—

When *dvitāya* is substituted for *ṣaṣ*, there are six forms. When both *ṅ* and *ṣ* are doubled before a nasal, there are forty-eight. The meaning is that by summation, there are five hundred and twenty-seven. In the case of *tiraścī*, because it has the status of a *bha*-stem, there is elision of *ac* according to the rule *acaḥ*; [this applies] by the rule *alope*.
Because of the statement, there is an absence of the designation [of the stem] as feminine.
(395) *vā napuṃsakasya* | Pāṇini 7.1.79. *dadat*—this is derived even as a masculine form. *śatṛ*—this is the suffix.
In the word *dhṛduśan*, the suffix *anaṅ* is applied; this means the *śatṛ* suffix [is present]. (396) *ācchīnadyornum* (Pāṇini 7.1.80).
Regarding *ācchīnadyoḥ*: the inclusion of the term *num* here is of questionable utility, as [the rule] *ābhyastāccchatuḥ* already provides for the optional [application of *num*].

In the rule *napuṃsakasya*, the requirement for the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule *ṭh-idito num dhātoḥ* is necessary; since there is no obstacle to that same continuation applying to the subsequent rules as well, [the analysis proceeds]. Regarding the phrase "having *śatṛ* as its constituent": because the *śa* of the *tud*-class roots is internal (*antaraṅga*), it undergoes a single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa*) with the vowel *a* of the substitute *śatṛ*.

The rule "of the *śatṛ* [suffix] when followed by a vowel other than *a*" is not possible here; the intention is that this is because it will be stated later that "when both sides are relied upon, [the preceding and following elements do not behave as] an end or a beginning. Regarding *bhāt*: [the root is] *bhā* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*). From the present tense (*laṭ*) with the suffix *śatṛ*, there is elision of *śap* due to its belonging to the *ad*-class. [This is governed by the rule] "nityam after *śap* and *śyan*."

Although permanence (*nityatva*) is established by the very force of the rule's commencement, the explicit mention of "permanently" (*nityam*) here is for the purpose of terminating the governing scope (*adhikāra*) of "in the place of *ṭh* and *v*" (*ṭhve*). Otherwise, one might suspect that by the force of the commencement, this [rule] applies permanently while the subsequent [rules] apply optionally.

(397) *śap-śyanor nityam* | 7|1|81| In *pacantī*, the *num* augment is obligatory after the *śap* [affix] when denoting the agent (*kartṛ*). In *dīvyantī*, the *num* augment is obligatory after the *śyan* [affix] following roots such as *div*. However, in the plural forms *pacanti* and *dīvyanti*, [the rule applies] to the neuter (*apuṃsakasya*).

The augment *num* should be understood [to apply] by the rule *jhalacaḥ*. Regarding *svab*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "a lake (*saras*) in which the waters (*āpaḥ*) are beautiful (*śobhanāḥ*). When the suffix *a* (as the final member of the compound) was about to be applied by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe*, there is a prohibition by the rule *na pūjanāt*.
Then, by the rule *adyantarupasargebhyaḥ*, the suffix *īn* occurs; therein, [the form] is *svāpī*.

This is because it will be stated later that [the word] is an imitation (anukaraṇa) of a form ending in a compound-suffix (samāsānta). The principle of being "taught as a specific term" (pratipadoktatva) constitutes its lack of occasion for application (niravakāśatva); this very position is stronger, as established in the *Manoramā* on the rule *chadir-upadhi-bal-er ḍhañ*. Regarding *dhaneḥ usi*: from the rule *janer arsiḥ*.

The meaning is that, while *ṭhu* is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartamāna*), [the suffix] *ni* is applied by the *uṇādi* rule "after the roots *ṛ*, *at*, *pṛ*, *vapi*, *yaj*, *tan*, *dhani*, and *tap*, [the suffix] *ni* [is added]. Regarding the form *dhanurbhyām*,
one should not suspect a lengthening of the vowel according to the rule beginning with "for *ṛ* and *v* when followed by a non-penultimate *i*" (*ṛtvoripadhāyāḥ*).

Because that which ends in *r* is not a verbal root (*adhātu*), it lacks the *cut* designation. Thus [it is said]: "The suffix *śi* [is applied] after the root *akṣ*, and because of the word *ca*, [the suffix] *usi* [is also applied]. From this, *cakṣuḥ* is formed.

By the rule beginning with "ṭharciśucihusṛpi," the suffix *isi* is applied to the root *hu*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), words such as *sarpi-* and *arci-* are to be understood. Regarding *supumāṃsī*: in the sūtra "uṃso'suṅ," [the substitution of *asuṅ* for *uṃsa* occurs].

In the opinion of the Easterners (*prācaḥ*), although the desired form is achieved for the nominative plural (*jas*) when explaining [the word] as *uṭī*, it would not be achieved for the accusative plural (*śas*). Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [applying] *āṬ* [by Pāṇini 7.1.18].
Having considered the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) from [Pāṇini 7.1.16] *ṭita āt sarvanāmasthāne*, [one understands that this applies] to a *sarvanāmasthāna*.

Thus, for those who speak according to what has been heard [in the scriptures], there is the accomplishment of all desired goals. Thus ends the section on Neuter Nouns ending in Consonants in the *Tattvabodhinī*. Now begins the section on Consonantal Sandhi (*halsandhiprakaraṇa*).
(91) *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* | Pāṇini 8.4.40. The term *stoḥ* is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). It is a Vedic [sautra] usage.
Masculinity. Similarly, it should be understood that *cuḥ* and *ṭuḥ* are also [masculine]. Regarding *ścunā*:
the third case ending is used because it will be stated later in the rule *aha yukte-* that "the third case is used even without connection to that.
Regarding *yoge*: this is to be supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). Here...

The correspondence between the substituend (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) follows their respective order; however, this does not apply to the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*kāryin*), as indicated by the rule *ād* (Pāṇini 1.1.50).

The sūtra on correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*) has not been cited here because the desired result is established even by the rule *sthāne ’ntaratamaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50), and thus it is not absolutely necessary. For example: *hariśśeta*. [Or] *vā*.
Regarding the term *śar*, because the *visarjanīya* is optional (*pākṣikatvāt*), when joined with *śa*, it becomes *śa*:

as in *āmaścinoti*. When joined with the *ca*-class (*cavarga*), it becomes *śa*: as in *acci’dityādi*. However, when the *ta*-class (*tavarga*) is joined with the *ca*-class, it will provide examples such as *tacśivaḥ*.
(92) *śāt* | Pāṇini 8.4.44. The word *śāt* [is used]; the words *e* and *o* are understood as being carried over [from previous rules]. Therefore, he says "of the *tavarga*," etc.
This is for the purpose of providing an instruction by the commentator that is free from doubt, such as in the expression "the state of becoming *ś*" (*aśtva*).

In the case of *ṭhvaśca*, neither the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) nor the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) was applied; likewise, the substitution of *ś* (*ścutvam*) was also not applied. Since such an avoidance is possible, he cites only the final letter of the class (*varga-antya*) as examples: *viśnaḥ* and *praśnaḥ*. [The roots are] *vicch* in the sense of "going" and *racch* in the sense of "desire to know. By the rule *yajayāca...* etc., the suffix *anaṅ* is added. [From the roots] *hu* and...

In *śūḍ*, the substitution of *ś* for *ch* occurs. In *naṅ*, due to its being marked with *ṅ*, there is an absence of *guṇa*. In *praccha*, however, there is an absence of *saṃprasāraṇa* because of the specific grammatical indication (*nirdeśa*) in the rule "in *raśna* and when not near. Now, one might object: since the letters *ña, ma, ṅ, ṇ, na* possess an additional nasal place of articulation (*nāsikāsthāna*), they lack a common place of articulation with the first four letters of each varga; therefore—

If it is argued that, because there is no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), the letter *n* is not included by the word *u* in the rule *toḥ ścunā*, but rather only the first four letters of its own class are intended—so that since the substitution of *ścu* does not apply in cases such as *viśna* and *praśna*, what is the purpose of this prohibition? To this they reply: [the prohibition is necessary] precisely because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) provided by the prohibition in the rule *śāt*.

In the rule *tulyāsyaprayatnam*, by the inclusion of the word *āsya* (mouth), the places of articulation such as the palate (*tālu*) and so forth—excluding the nose—are understood; since that place of articulation is indeed the same [for both sounds], the word *u* includes the fifth vowel (*ū*) as well. Consequently, since the occurrence of *ścutva* (the substitution of *ś* for *s*) would follow, this prohibition is necessary. And thus:
Because the letter *u* in the word ‘*orlī*’ also includes the letter *n*, forms such as *vidvāṃllikhati* are established;

and since it has been stated that this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rejection of the rule of one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*) between the cause and the effect, by that very [indication]...

Furthermore, it must be explained how [the rule] could serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the stated meaning if it were merely for the sake of meaningfulness; for once the inclusion of the letter *n* is established by the word "u," the cessation of the correspondence between the respective elements (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) is what must be indicated by this [rule], and thus there is no obstacle to its indicating both. Nor is there any issue in the case of the expression "ulyāsye."

If one intends to express the equality of place for whatever [sounds] may occur, then all five letters within each *varga* would be mutually *savarṇa*; thus, in the example already mentioned, since the substitution of *ścutva* would apply, one must state: "Why is it necessary to formulate the rule beginning with 'ā' (A 1.1.69), by resorting to that as a *jñāpaka*? For if that were the case...
Just as there is mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) among *ṅ*, *m*, *ṇ*, *n*, and *na*, so too in examples such as *nayasī* and others,

by the rule "the *anusvāra* becomes a homogeneous letter before *ya*-class consonants," the *ñ* and other letters might also [optionally] replace the *anusvāra* at the end of a word by the rule "optionally [before a semivowel or sibilant]. This would occur even in the absence of identity in the place of articulation (*sthāna*), such as the palate, because there is some commonality in the nasal cavity as their location.

Because they are equal. Furthermore, if one were to explain "equal" as meaning "neither less nor more," then there would be no mutual *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) among the *ña*-class sounds; for although they share the same nasal place of articulation, they lack identity in places such as the palate, and thus possess fewer [common] places of articulation. Consequently, [the rule] "vaṃ... [would not apply].

There is no over-extension [of the rule] in cases such as *nayasi* and so forth; however, there would indeed be homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between *ñ* and the others with their own respective groups and so on,
because even though they possess an additional nasal organ (*nāsikā*) as a place of articulation, they do not lack that [other] place of articulation.

It should not be argued that the desired result is established even without resorting to a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence), because for the first letters of the classes (*vargādyāḥ*), there is no deficiency in their place of articulation due to the absence of a nasal place (*nāsikāsthāna*), and thus, despite the lack of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) with the fifth letter of their respective class, there is no harm [to the rule]; for [the following] would be required: "O Gauri! (*he gauri*).

In cases such as *ehi*, there would be the undesirable consequence of applying the rule for long-vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*). Furthermore, the *śākala-prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) prescribed by the rule *iko’savarṇe* would not apply; this is because the vowel *e* shares the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) as the vowel *i*, since it possesses no fewer points of articulation than *i*. [The reason is that] "the organs of articulation for the semivowels and the spirants (*ūṣman*) are indeed wide open (*vivṛta*)."
It has been stated [in the *Śikṣā*]: "From those [vowels], ai and au are open; from those two, e and o are likewise.

Thus, even though the undesired consequence has been avoided by accepting the lack of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) due to a difference in effort (*prayatna-bheda*), [the rule] *or lī*—which prescribes the substitution of the following homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) for the vowel *u*—would apply to the letter *da* in the words *advastu* and *adastram*.

Because of the inclusion of *va* [in the rule for *la*]: although *va* shares the same place of articulation as the lips (*oṣṭha-sthāna*), it is not deficient in its place of articulation relative to *la*, since it possesses the commonality of the dental place (*danta-sthāna*). However, if one were to argue that because of the collective designation "dantoṣṭha" for *va*, the place of articulation "dantoṣṭha" is distinct from the lip place (*oṣṭha-sthāna*) [and thus *va* is not a substitute for *la*], [that would be incorrect].

If you argue that there is no over-extension [of the rule] in examples such as *tadvastu* because the letter *va* lacks homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) with the letter *la*, then, by the same logic, the substitution of *taṅ* (the middle voice endings) prescribed for dental [roots] by the rule *ugvā duhaḥ* would not apply in the case of *rakṣas tasya luk-ṭhaduhvahīḥ*, but would instead apply only in cases such as *ṭhadugdhe*.

Similarly, in cases such as *iṣūrtah* and *iṣūratī*, the substitution of *u* prescribed by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* would not apply in forms like *uṣūṣati*, because according to the aforementioned reasoning,
the *v* [in the root *viṣ*] lacks the quality of being labial (*auṣṭhya*). Nor can it be argued that [the *v*] possesses both the quality of being labial and the quality of being final.

One should not be misled by the thought that the separate mention of *svid* and others in the definition of roots taught with an initial *ṣ* (in the rule *‘ekṣṛp’*) would be redundant, since these too begin with a dental sound;
for this will be stated in the root text itself in such passages as: “The final [dental] is one produced solely by the teeth, and not even one produced by the teeth and lips.”

However, since Pāṇini’s Śikṣā states that the nose is the place of articulation for the *yama* sounds and the *anusvāra* alone, others maintain that the nose is not the articulatory place (*sthāna*) for other sounds;
rather, it is merely a quality (*guṇa*), namely *anunāsikatva* (nasality), consisting simply in being articulated through the operation of the nose.

Regarding the statement that the nose is the place of articulation (*sthāna*), some argue that since the vowels beginning with *a* are also articulated at the nose according to the aforementioned method, there is an omission in the description of the places of articulation for not mentioning them.
However, for them, the desired result is achieved even without resorting to the *jñāpaka* (indicative rule) mentioned here. Others, however, [hold that] for the vowels beginning with *a*...

The quality of being nasal (*anunāsikatva*) is a secondary property (*guṇa*) because it is not always articulated through the nose, as it is characterized by the definition: "that which enters [the object] and departs from it. However, for the letters *ñ, ṅ, ṇ, n,* and *m*, the quality of nasality does not depart, since they are always articulated with the nose; therefore, it is not a secondary property.

However, just as with *ya* and *anusvāra*, the place of articulation (*sthāna*) is indeed the nose; thus, in the determination of places of articulation, it is stated in the rule "ṭh-ñ-m-aṅ-ṇ-n-ān [have] the nose as well" (*ṭhñamaṅṇanānā nāsikā ca*) that these [consonants] have the nose as their place, but not that [the nose is the place] for *a*-sounds and so forth.
As for what was stated in the commentary on the rule regarding "having the same oral cavity" (*tulyāsyatvam*), namely "not having a lesser oral cavity," in the context of examples such as *tadvastu*:
Regarding the objection that in the word *orlī*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the letter *da* becoming *va*, they reply that this is merely a superficial appearance.

They maintain that since two instances of the letter *la* are specified in *orlī*, one can explain it by applying the rule of *parasavarṇa* (the substitution of a letter by its homogeneous counterpart) when a following *la* of the same form occurs; thus, they argue, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

(93) *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* | P. 8.4.41. Regarding *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ*: here too, there is no one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) between the substituends and the causes [of substitution], because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *oḥṣī*. As in *sarpiṣṭamam*; the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] is by the rule *hrasvātādau taddhite*. [The rule applies to] *yaro*...

What is the purpose of the phrase "at the end of a word" (*padāntasya*)? [Consider the examples: *vedmi* and *stabhrāti*. [The objection is that] the rule has its application fulfilled in the case of a stop (*sparśa*).

This was stated with the intention of referring to well-known usage. However, in cases such as *amalmurāriḥ* and *vṛkṣavnete*, when the nasalized (*anunāsika*) forms of the letters *l* and *v* occur...
Because there is no sublation [of the rule]. Or, one may interpret it in accordance with the older texts stating "it is desired for *sparśa* alone" as follows:

the rule for the nasal (*anunāsika*) does not apply to those sounds other than *sparśas*, because such usage is not attested (*anabhidhānāt*). As for the statement "it does not apply to *repha*": although, under the view that "the individual phoneme (*vyakti*) is the meaning of the word," there would be a difference in the target forms (*lakṣya*), [the rule still does not apply].

Because the definition [of the term] has not yet fulfilled its purpose with respect to this specific instance due to the difference in its characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*), its application would indeed be unavoidable even for the letter *repha*; nevertheless, this was stated by resorting to the theory of the universal (*jātipakṣa*) in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*). Regarding the phrase "due to the insertion of the sound *da*": [an objection is raised]—"But in the *yavādi* group..."

The word is read simply as *aku*, and not as *akudmanta* qualified by the possessive suffix *matup*. Consequently, the application of the rule *yaro ’nunāsikaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.45) is unavoidable. Furthermore, when the substitution of a nasal (*anunāsika*) for a *yar* occurs, the final element is no longer a *jhay*; thus, the rule *hayaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.31), which would otherwise apply to the *m* of *matup*, does not take effect.
It should not be argued that the reading "akuḍ" in the *yavādi* group would be meaningless;

for since the rule regarding the substitution of an *anunāsika* is considered *asiddha*, the status of the word as ending in a *jhay* consonant remains intact, and thus the inclusion of that reading in the list is purposeful.
To this, they reply: if the substitution of *n* for the *k* of *kakud* were intended here, then...

One should always read "gaṇe ’ku" and not "gaṇe ’kud. Even though the base word *kakut*—which serves as the stem for the possessive suffix *matup*—is prescribed as ending in *n*, the usage of forms ending in *d* elsewhere remains unimpeded. Therefore, the rule "yaro ’nunāsikaḥ" does not apply here.

[The rule] "it proceeds" [is applied]. Others, however, say: in the *saṃhitā* reading of the rule "a stem ending in *y* or *v* is called *bha*; *t* and *s* [are called *bha*] when a suffix with the sense of possession (*matvartha*) follows," one can also resolve this by eliding a *d* before the *t* in the word *asau*, thereby establishing its status as a *bha*. As for the mention of the dual form *asau*, it is a collective *dvandva* compound of *da* and *ta*.
Having formed a *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction) *dvandva* compound, [the form] "samupapadyate" is established.

(94) *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya* Pāṇini 8.4.61: "After *ud*, [there is *ru* for the initial consonant of *sthā* and *stambh*]. In the rule *anusvārasya yayi* (8.4.58), the entire mention of *savarṇa* (homogeneous sounds) applies here as well.
Having extracted [the word] and connected it—intending that this is because the status of being *svarita* is promised for one part—he says: "it shall be the same as the preceding vowel."

(95) *śāśchāe’ṭi* |8|4|63|. Regarding *śāśchāe’ṭi*: here, one should explain it by continuing [the word] *padāntāt* from the previous rule as *padāntād jhayaḥ*. Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of: *adhvaścotanty abhito virapśam*.
The suffix *śa* is added to the root *rap* preceded by the prefix *vi-* according to the *auṇādika* rules.
Regarding the change of *ccha* to *ch*, the meaning is that the rule *aśchāeṭi* should be read as *aśchāmī*. "By that verse" means...
Expressions such as ‘acchamaśruṇi’ and others should also be cited as examples.

(96) *mo ’nusvāraḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.23. The rule *mo ’nusvāraḥ* [is stated]. From the previous rule *ṅṇoḥ ku-ṭu-haśi* and *hali sarveṣām*, the term *hali* is understood to carry over, as is *adaso māt*. Therefore, he says "of that which ends in -m," and so forth. Why [specify] *hali*? [Consider: *tvam atra*.
What is the point here?

(97) *naścāpadāntasya jhali* (Pāṇini 8.4.24). [The rule states: "And [the substitution of *anusvāra* occurs] for a *n* that is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*) before a *jhal* [consonant]. Why specify "not at the end of a word"? Consider: *rājan pāhi* ("O King, protect! and *ākraṃsyate* ("he will step upon").
In *ṭhāṅ udgamane*, the suffix *taṅ* is applied; by the rule *na kramoḥ*, the augment *iṭ* is not added. (98) *Anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* |8|4|58|.
[The word] *anusvārasya* [is understood]. Here, the mention of *yayi* is for the sake of clarity, because there is no occurrence of *anusvāra* when a vowel (*ac*) follows.

However, since a *parasavarṇa* that is most similar to the *anusvāra* is not possible for a *śal*, the rule for *parasavarṇa* does not apply here either—in cases such as "aṃśanam"—just as it does not in "uṇḍaṃ rathena. On this point, they say:
according to the view of the Bhāṣya, "the spirants (*ūṣman*) are slightly opened (*īṣadvivṛta*), while the vowels (*svara*) are fully opened (*vivṛta*)."

The term *ṭhyayī* is meaningless [in this context]. According to the view of the author of the Sūtras (*sūtrakāra*), it is indeed necessary. Otherwise, in examples such as *aśanam*, the *parasavarṇa*—which is the closest homogeneous sound (*antaratama*) to the anusvāra—would become the nasalized vowel *ī*. This is because, according to his view, there exists phonetic identity (*sāvarṇya*) between the vowel *ī* and the consonant *ś*. Likewise, in *uṇḍam*...

In examples such as *śete*, the substitution [of *anusvāra*] would occur by the rule *vā padāntasya*. Regarding *aṅkita*: the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *aṅka*, which belongs to the *cur*-class (*curādi*) and is followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), meaning "to mark" or "to characterize"; the suffix *ṇi* is elided because it is marked with *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment) in the sense of the superlative (*iṣṭhā*).
The nasal *ṅ* becomes a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) with the following *t*. Alternatively, the suffix *kta* may be applied to the root *aṅka* itself, meaning "to mark."

In *numo’nusvāre*, [the *m*] becomes a nasal of the same class (*parasavarṇa*) as the following sound, resulting in *ṅ*. Thus, in *añcitaḥ*: the suffix *niṣṭhā* takes the augment *iṭ* by the rule *ṭhañceḥ pūjāyām*; the prohibition of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is by the rule *āceḥ*. In *kuṇṭhitaḥ*: from the root *kuṭhi* in the sense of "obstruction," the suffix *kta* is applied; then, by *numo’nusvāre*, [the *m*] becomes a nasal of the same class as the following sound.

Regarding *śānta*: [it is derived from] the root *am*, meaning "to pacify" (*upaśame*), with the suffix *kta*. The absence of the augment *iṭ* is due to the rule "optionally in *dānta* and *śānta*" (*vā dānta-śānta*). The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "the long vowel for a nasal before *kvip*" (*anunāsikasya kvau*). Then, the *m* becomes an *anusvāra*.

The letter *n* becomes a *parasavarṇa*. Regarding the word *gumphita*: it is derived from the root *umpha* in the sense of "binding" (*granth*), with the suffix *kta*. When the letter *m* undergoes *anusvāra*, it becomes *m* again by the rule of *parasavarṇa*.

(99) *mo rāji samaḥ kvau* | 8|3|25| [The final *m* of] *samaḥ* [is changed to *ṇ* before the root] *rāj* when followed by a *kvip* suffix. Why say "*rāj*"? [To exclude cases like] *saṃpat*. Why say "*samaḥ*"? [To exclude cases like] *idaṃ rāṭ*. Why say "*kvau*" (before a *kvip* suffix)? [To exclude cases like] *saṃrājituṃ*, *saṃrājitavyam*. [This rule concerns] the change of the letter *m*.
The mention of the letter *ma* is for the purpose of excluding the *anusvāra*; thus he says: "it should be *ma* itself. Regarding the word *samrāṭ*:
from the root *rājṛ* (meaning "to shine"), with the prefix *sam*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *atsūdviṣe* etc.;
then, by the rule *vraścādi*, the change to *ṣ* occurs, followed by the changes to *jaś* and *car*.

(100) *he mapare vā* | 8|3|26 | "In the presence of *ha* followed by *ma*, [the substitutes] *ya*, *va*, and *la* optionally [occur]. The term *mapara* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The meaning is: when *ha* is followed by one to which *ya*, *va*, or *la* are subsequent (*yavala-paras*), then in the presence of that *ha*, the substitutes *ya*, *va*, and *la* optionally take the place of *ma*.

(101) *Yathāsaṅkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām* | 1.3.10. "According to the number, there is a subsequent designation of equals. "Anudeśa" means that which is subsequently designated (*anudiśyate*); the meaning is that it is uttered later. The genitive case in "of equals" (*samānām*) is used in the sense of a relationship; thus he says: "belonging to the same [category]."

Regarding the term *vidhi*: it has not been stated that "a *vidhi* is an operation (*vidhāna*) that does not have an object (*akarmaka*)," because if that were the case, then only in instances where there is an equal number of objects (*uddeśin*) and equal numbers of operations— such as the substitution of *piba* and others for *pā* and others, or *prastha* and others for *priya*, *sthira*, and so on— would the application occur according to their respective order.

However, it is accepted that even between two things to be restated (*anuvādya*), there is correspondence according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyatva*), as in the rule: “*han*, *kṛñ*, and *grahaḥ* [are used] with *amūla*, *akṛta*, and *jīva*. Why say “of equal number” (*samānām*)?
Consider the rule: “*akṣṇā*, *itthaṃbhūte*,” where there are four meanings such as *lakṣaṇa* (marking), etc., but only three suffixes beginning with *prati*.
In that regard, so that the designation *karmapravacanīya* may apply to all [words] in all instances, [the sūtra states]:
[The term] *napare* is also a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The word *he* is understood as being carried over (*anuvartate*).
Thus he says: "not before the letter *ha*.

(103) *ṅṇoḥ kuk ṭuk śari* (Pāṇini 8.3.28). [The commentary continues: "After *ṅ* and *ṇ*, [the augment] *kuk* or *ṭuk* [is added]. This is according to the rule *cayo dvitīyāḥ* ("the second of the *caya* group [is substituted]"). And this is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *nādiny-ākrośe*.

This is established. Therefore, in the *Manoramā* on the rule *aḥ sī*, it is stated that if *uṭ* were prescribed [instead of *tuṭ*], then according to the alternative view that "the second consonants [of the *ṣaṭ* group] [are doubled]," the letter *th* would result. However, if [the doubling] were governed by the rule *ṇoḥ*, then it would be easier to simply say *uṭ*. This is because *tuṭ* is [regarded as] non-existent (*asiddha*) [for the purposes of the subsequent operation].
Because the rule "the second [consonant] is the augment" (Pāṇini 6.1.2) does not apply here. Regarding "Pauṣkarasādi":
one who sits at Puṣkara, a particular sacred site, is a *puṣkarasat*. His descendant is the teacher Pauṣkarasādi. The suffix *iñ* is applied according to the *bāhvādi* group.
There is vṛddhi of both members [of the compound] because it belongs to the *anuśatikādi* group.
(104) *ṅ-si-dhuṭ* | Pāṇini 8.3.29:
*ṅ-si-dhuṭ*. When there is an indication by two [case endings], the indication by the fifth [ablative case] is [to be understood].

Intending to show that [the rule] is stronger because it is subsequent, he says: "of *sa*. The use of the locative case (*sīti*) is for the sake of brevity. Regarding "six ending in *s*": the *t* arises from the *c*-substitution of the *ḍh* (the *dhuṭ* augment).

It does not become *th* by the rule "the second consonants after *ay*" (Pāṇini 8.4.43), because the *c*-substitution is considered asiddha (non-existent) for that purpose. For this very reason, in the absence of the *dhuṭ* augment...
In the word *aṭsanta*, the substitution of *ṭha* for *ṭ* does not occur. Now, one might object: "Even so, let the rule *ḥ si dhuṭ* be applied;

since it is possible to explain *dhuṭ* as occurring after the letter *ḍ* when followed by *s*, what is the purpose of this acceptance that *dhuṭ* is added at the end [of the preceding element]? Do not say so.

If, however, [the word] were considered as ending in *pūrva*, then because the prohibition *na padāntāṭ ṭoranām* would not apply, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the substitution of *ṣṭu* for the letter *dh*. For this very reason, the *tuk* augment that will be mentioned later has not been applied here. Furthermore, if *tuk* were added to *ḍa*, then since that [substitution] would be treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the rule *cayo dvitīyāḥ* would also undesirably apply. *Iga*...

When there are two forms due to the optional doubling of the *dh* sound, sixteen forms arise from the optional doubling of the *ṭ*, *n*, and *visarga*. When the *khayaḥ śaraḥ* rule applies doubling, there are thirty-two forms.
The prohibition by the rule *śaro’ci* does not apply here; for its—

For it has been stated that [the rule] has as its scope only the doubling of the sūtra. Nor should it be suspected that, because the substitution of *c* for *t* (*cartva*) is not established (*asiddha*), there is no occurrence of letters other than *khay* following [the doubled consonant]; this is because it is stated: "That which is not established is treated as non-existent except in the case of doubling."

(105) *śi tuk* | 8|3|31|. Regarding *śi tuk*: since the locative case (*īti*) has already served its purpose in the preceding rule, it indicates that the ablative case (*a iti*) is to be understood as a genitive; thus he says—“of the *n*” (*nasya*). “Elision of the *l*” (*calopa*) refers to the rule *haro jhari*.
The intention is that, by virtue of the inclusion of the term *savarṇa* (homogeneous), the rule of "correspondence according to order" (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) does not apply. Regarding *sañcchambhuḥ*:

here, one should not suspect the application of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) by the rule *aścchavī*, on the grounds that *ścutva* and *tuk* are considered asiddha (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding rule);
this is because *chatva* (the substitution of *ch*) is itself asiddha. Regarding *catuṣṭayam*: here, when *ścutva* applies to the *tuk*, [the rule] *ayo...* [is invoked].

In the alternative view that "the second letters [are optionally doubled]," since there is an option for the substitution of *ch* for *ś*, one should understand that two forms arise: *sañcchambhuḥ* and *śañchaśambhuḥ*. Nor should it be argued that when *ś* is substituted by *ch*, because the condition of being followed by a sibilant (*śarpara*) is absent, the rule "the second letters [are optionally doubled]" would not apply to the *c*.

It may be doubted [that this is so], because the substitution of *ch* for *ś* (the *chatva*) is considered unestablished (*asiddha*). However, they say: "There are four forms here—*ñachāṬ*, *ñacachā*, *ñacaśā*, and *ñaśā*—due to the optional application of the augment *tuk*, the substitution of *ch*, and the elision of *c*."
(106) *ṅmo hrasvād aci ṅmuṇ nityam* | 8|3|32|.

[The rule] "after a short vowel ending in a *ṅm*" [is explained as follows]: *ṅm* is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term). Since the status of being *ṭit* is applied to it by virtue of its being a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), it is connected by implication with the elements that possess those designations (*saṃjñin*). Therefore, the suffixes *Ruṭ*, *ṇuṭ*, and *nuṭ* are applied respectively.

[The operations] proceed [constantly]. The inclusion of the word *nitya* (constant) is for the sake of clarity, because constancy is already obtained simply by the fact that this rule is placed between the two optional rules: *ṭhhe mapare* and *aya uño vā*. Now, one might object: if the word *nitya* were absent here, would the mention of the word *vā* (or) in the rule *ṭhhe mapare vā* not apply to the subsequent rules as well?

If it is argued that there might still be a doubt as to whether [the rule] applies to all five cases or not, that is true; for this very reason it was stated "for the sake of clarity," and not because it is redundant. Therefore, [the rule is] *parasyācaḥ* ("of the following vowel"). Now, one might object:
by resorting to the genitive interpretation of *maḥ*, let the operation be prescribed for the preceding [vowel] alone when a vowel follows; what [is the point of the other formulation]?

If it is argued that this is a fault, it is not so; for if that were the case, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that the *ṅ* of a word ending in *ṅ* would become the initial member of a preceding element.

Even if one were to explain it through grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) as "of that which is the *ṅ* of this [word]," the substitution of *ṇ* would still undesirably apply in the case of *urvannāste*.
Because the prohibition "of that which is not bound" (*adāntasya*) does not apply. Although the desired result is established by the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*—

since the rule for the augment *ṅmuṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*)— nevertheless, under the *yathoddeśa* view, the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* does not apply to an *antaraṅga* operation within the three chapters (*traipādika*), and thus the undesired consequence remains.
The substitution of *ṇ* is correct according to the aforementioned explanation; this is the general direction. Regarding *sugaṇṇīśa*:

the *ṇya*-affix and elision (*allopa*) are not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*, because that prohibition applies when a preceding operation is *asiddha*.
