Now, one might object: in cases such as *aramadaṇḍinā*, since there is the status of a word (*padatva*) due to the intervening case-ending, the augment *nuṭ* would have to occur.

If you say this, it is not so; for there is a prohibition against treating a suffix as a marker (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) by the rule "and when there is a subsequent word, [the suffix is not considered] for the application of rules concerning the beginning of a word.

For this very reason, in cases such as *paramavācau*, *aramagauduhau*, and *aramalihāu*, the substitutions of *k* for *g*, *gh* for *d*, and *ṇ* for *n* do not occur. However, according to the older grammarians, [the rule] "in *uñ* and in a word" (*uñi ca pade*) is extended from that point to "in *ad*" (*ade*).

Having followed [the previous rule], it was stated that "ṅmuṭ" applies because of the interpretation "of a word beginning with ṭha, ja, etc."; that has been refuted by this [present argument]. For even he must follow the very same method already mentioned here in order to prevent the elision of the *n*.

(107) *samaḥ suṭi* | 8|3|5| [The word] *samaḥ* [is replaced by *sam*] before the augment *suṭ*. Although this is established by the substitution of *m* for the final vowel with *anusvāra*, this rule is nevertheless stated for the sake of establishing the three *sakāra*s in the case of the nasalized [forms].

(108) *atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā* 8.3.2. Regarding this, there are two positions: whether this [sūtra] is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) or an injunction (*vidhi*). In the first case, the mention of *atra* would be purposeless, since the context of the *ru*-pratyāhāra is already obtained through the governing rule itself. However, the word *u*— [The remainder of the sentence is omitted from the source text.]

In the view that this is a restrictive rule (*adhikāra-pakṣa*), the word "u" serves to highlight the distinction between the subsequent operation and the preceding one— namely, that "the substitution of *r* is obligatory for the subsequent [sound], but optional for the preceding [sound] as nasalization. In the view that it is an injunction (*vidhi-pakṣa*), the word "u" would be redundant, and the mention of "vā" (or) would be for the sake of clarity.
This is established by the very *jñāpaka* (indicative rule) "ṭhanunāsikātparaḥ," for without an option (*vikalpa*), the alternative case of the absence of the nasal (*anunāsika*)—

expressed as "leaving aside the nasal" (*anunāsikaṃ vihāya*)— would not be possible. It is precisely to indicate this that the *Vṛtti* does not mention the words "ūrdhva" and "iti," but rather [states] "the nasal of the preceding [element] of *ru*."
It has been stated: "of the *ru* which precedes. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes elision (*lopa*) as well.

Here, the extracted meaning is: "that which precedes whatever rule occurs within the section concerning *ru*. Similarly, for the rule "after the *u* which precedes," [the meaning is] "that which follows whatever rule occurs within the section concerning *ru*."
The meaning should be understood as "after the preceding [element].
(109) *Anunāsikātparo’nusvāraḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.4).
Regarding *anunāsikāt*, he says—taking it as a fifth case (*pañcamī*) with the elision of the suffix *lyap*—"leaving aside the nasalized [sound] (*anunāsikaṃ vihāya*)."

The meaning is: "in the case where there is no nasalization (*anunāsika*). Intending that the word *pūrvasya*, which is under discussion, is changed in its case-ending to become a fifth-case form (*pañcamyanta*), he says: "from what precedes the *r*.
Because separation, like conjunction, is a cause for the comprehension of a specific distinction, [the example] is "the calf-less cow" (*avatsā*).

Just as in the case of "dhenur ānīyatām" (let the cow be brought), because [the letter *u*] is present with the quality of nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) as a possibility, and because it is required by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣita*), it is connected as the limit (*avadhi*);
intending this, he says: "from what precedes the *r*"—this is introduced in the *Manoramā*.

They say that this was stated with the intention that the desired result is established by worldly logic alone, without depending on the continuation of the term *ūrvasthe* or the modification of the case ending.
Regarding the phrase "the addition of an *anusvāra*," the status of being an augment (*āgama*) is understood precisely through the word *para*. As in the example: *ūrvau*.
In the rule *tu tābhyām aij* (Pāṇini 1.1.48), the intention is that by the word "prior" (*pūrva*), the status of *ai* and *au* as augmentals (*āgama*) is indicated.
(110) *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.34).
[The word] *visarjanīyasya* [is understood]. [The word] *khari* [is understood]. And this [refers to] the rule *kharavasānayoḥ*.
From the sūtra, [the word] *saṃskartā* follows by means of a "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*). Regarding *saṃskartā*: the augment *suṭ* is applied to the root *kṛ* by the rule *aṃparibhyām*.
Now, one might object: since the anusvāra is not a vowel (*anac*), why does doubling not apply to the following [consonant]?

Anticipating the objection—“If this were so, how could there be a form with three *s* sounds in the case where the *anusvāra* is applied?”—he says: “*anusvāravisarga-* etc. [The phrase] ‘above the letter *a*’ means that if they were read above the letter *i*, then in forms such as ‘*ayaḥsu*’ and ‘*tyaśaḥsu*,’ [the rule] ‘*iṇaḥ*’ [would apply].”

The intention is that *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) would apply [to the visarga] because it is "of another" (*parasya*). As for the phrase "because it is a vowel" (*actvāt*): even so, there is no risk of the application of *yaṇ*-substitution and the like in cases such as *hariḥ kartā*, *hariṃ smaret*, or *rāmaḥ pāti*, because the visarga and other such elements are considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to their being situated within the "three chapters" (*tripādī*). This also applies to the doubling of the *anusvāra*.

Thus [it is said]. By the word *api* (also), the letter *k* is included. "By another statement" means that even when [the rule] *aco rahābhyām* has been applied, [the doubling] still occurs by virtue of *yaṇo mayaḥ*. (111) *pumaḥ khayyaṃmpare* 8.3.6.

*pumaḥ khayi*: this is an imitation of the remaining portion [of the word] after the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) of *puṃsaḥ*. The term *ampara* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. "Because it is an exclusion" (*paryudāsāt*): the intention is that this refers to the rule prescribing the substitution of *ṣ* (the *idudupadhasya* sūtra). "In the case of *khya*, there is no substitute *ñ*" refers to the root *akṣiṅ*.

In the word *khyān*, this substitute begins with *khś*. It will be stated later that in the section on what is "unestablished" (*asiddha*), the rule “*asya yo vā*” follows immediately after the rule for *ṇatva*. Thus, because the substitution of *y* is unestablished, there is no *amparatva* (the condition of being followed by *am*); consequently, the rule “*umaḥ khayi*” does not apply, and the substitution of *r* does not occur.

Regarding the term *puṃkhyānam*: the substitution of *khyāñ* for the root *cakṣiṅ* occurs when the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied by the rule *yuṭ ca*. Now, one might object that this substitution is difficult to justify here, because of the Vārttika stating, “there is a prohibition regarding the [suffix] *ṇa*, and also regarding *ṭha* and *asana*. This is true; however, [the substitution occurs] because of the rule *bahulam*...

This is to be resolved by the inclusion of the term *bahula* (in the sense of "diversely") in the Vārttika: *taṇyannavadhakagātravicakṣaṇājirātadyartham*. The detailed explanation should be sought in the *Manoramā*.
Regarding *trāyasva*: from the root *raiṅ* in the sense of "protecting," in the imperative (*loṭ*) with the suffix *śap*, there is the substitution of *āy*.

(112) *naścchavyapraśān* | Pāṇini 8.3.7. Regarding the word *praśān*: it is derived from the root *śam* with the prefix *pra*, followed by the suffix *kvip*. The lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *anunāsikasya kvi jhaloḥ kṅitīti*. Then, by the rule *o no dhātoḥ*, the *o* is replaced by *na*. Because that [substitution] is considered *asiddha* (not having taken effect), the elision of the *n* does not occur.

(113) *nṛn pe* | 8|3|10|. In the rule *nṛn pe*, the vowel *a* following the letter *p* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). By this, forms such as *ṛṇāṃ punāti* are established. Because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ubhayathā* from the preceding rule *ubhayatharkṣu*, there is an option (*vikalpa*).

With the intention of stating that [the rule] has already been applied, he says: "ruḥ syād vā" (ru may optionally occur). [In the example] *kupvoḥ kaḥ pau*, here, by the rule *upvoḥ*, the visarga replaces the *repha* (r), because the *jihvāmūlīya* is included within the *kha*-class (*khartvāt*). By the rule *harpare śari*, this visarga is elided, because the *jihvāmūlīya* is included within the *śa*-class (*śartvāt*). [And finally,] by the rule *ṭhvā śari*.
The substitute for *visarga* is *visarga* itself; the two substitutes, *k* and *p*, are for the sake of pronunciation. The word "and" (*ca*) implies "and *visarga*.

However, the Easterners (Prācāḥ) have stated that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the vowel *ā*; that is incorrect, because if *k* and *p* were absent, the rule for *satva* (substitution by *s*) would undesirably apply to the *visarjanīya*.

(114) *kānāmreḍite* | 8|3|12| Regarding *kānāmreḍite*: although one could have simply said *ān kān*, the inclusion of the term *āmreḍita* (reduplication) is so that [the substitution] occurs only where there is a doubling [of the word]. It should not apply here: *kān kān paśyasi*.

In this context, one *kim* is used for interrogation (*praśna*), while the second is used for censure (*kṣepa*). The meaning is: "Whom—whom do you look upon as contemptible? With the intention that the substitution of *s* (satva) is established even in the absence of the mention of *kān* in the Vārttika, he says "or rather" (*yadvā*). However, in the case of *saṃ* and *puṃs*, the substitution of *s* occurs only by virtue of the Vārttika.

In the *kaskādi* group, [the forms] *saṃskartā*, *saṃskariṣyati*, *puṃskokilaḥ*, *puṃskāmaḥ*, and so forth— because reading many such forms would result in excessive complexity— it is impossible to discard the entire Vārttika by simply reading "aṃpuṃkān" in the *kaskādi* list, since the *iṇ* [substitution] occurs in forms such as *puṃskokila*.

Because if it were treated as a *para* (subsequent element), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the visarga becoming *ṣ*. However, others maintain that, like the mention of *kān*, the mention of *sam* in the Vārttika can be dispensed with.
(115) *kaskādiṣu ca* 8.3.48.

And in the *kaskādi* group: here, the word *saḥ* from the rule *aupadādau* and the sutra *ṭhiṇaḥ ṣaḥ* are both understood; thus he says, "in these [words], after *iṇ*, the substitution of *utaka*," and so forth. Regarding *kautaskuta*:

although the suffix *tyap* would apply by the rule *avyayāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.104) in the sense of "come from where?", they say that because of the force of its inclusion in this specific list (*gaṇapāṭha*), the suffix *aṇ* is used instead.

The elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) here occurs by virtue of the rule that will be stated later: "In the case of indeclinables, [the elision occurs] when there is mere connection (*bhamātre*). Regarding the form *saśapakuṇṭika*:

although this would be established even by the rule "in a compound" (*ityaṃ samāse*), he will explain that the purpose of including this specific reading here is for the sake of the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) even in non-compounds where there is no mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*).

(116) *saṃhitāyām* | Pāṇini 6.1.72. Regarding the phrase "with reference to *saṃhitāyām*": although this should have been stated right at the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, it is mentioned here in accordance with the sequence of the Sūtras.

The letter *ca* [in the rule] is for the sake of pronunciation; this is because of the mention [of the root] as *vidi-bhid-i-c-chid-* [in Pāṇini 7.3.32]. By this, forms such as *vicchinna* are established. Regarding the phrase *hrasvasya*: and this...
The [term] *piti* from the rule *ṭhhrasvasya piti kṛti* follows here, as does *tuk*.
(118) *Dīrghāt* 6.1.75. As in *senāsureti*. For if there were *tuk* for *ch*, then, after the substitution of *c* for *ch*, [the following would occur].

The sense is that if there were doubling [of the *c*], then by the rule regarding "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*), the substitution of *t* for *c* would not apply; consequently, the letter *c* would be heard immediately after the letter *ch*. (119) *padāntādvā* | 6|1|76 | [This sūtra provides] an option when [the doubled consonant] follows a word-final [consonant]. 6|1|76 |

"Or [the augment *tuK* is optional] after the end of a word (*padāntāt*). Although the desired result is achieved by the inclusion of the term "end" (*anta*)—since the current rule regarding lengthening (*dīrgha*) qualifies the word (*pada*), thereby obtaining the designation "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*)—the explicit mention of "end" (*antagrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the *tuK* augment applies only to the end of a word and not to the word itself. Otherwise, [the rule would apply to the whole word].

Because it is a rule dependent on case-inflection (*padavidhi*), when the maxim regarding semantic competency (*samarthaparibhāṣā*) is invoked, [the rule] would apply only to cases such as *akṣṇecchāyā* where there is semantic competency; it would not apply in cases such as *iṣṭatu kumārī* or *chatraṃ hara devadatta*, because of a lack of semantic competency. The same applies to the rule *na padāntāṭṭoḥ*.

They say that although the rule could have been stated simply as *adāṭṭoḥ*, the inclusion of the term *anta* (end) is for the purpose of prohibiting the *ṣṭu* substitution even in cases such as *uṣṭāḥ ṣaṭ* and *antastrayaḥ*.
Thus ends the section on Consonant Sandhi (*halsandhi*) in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
Now, [the section on] the oblations and so forth.

Now, [the roots] beginning with *hu* [are discussed]. *Hu* means "giving. Although giving (*dāna*) consists precisely in the production of another's ownership preceded by the cessation of one's own ownership, nevertheless, following common usage, he explains it as "offering" (*prakṣepa*).
"Vaidhe" means in the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth. "Of the oblation" (*haviṣaḥ*).

The meaning is: "of the substance prescribed by the injunction. Regarding the phrase "by its own nature": if, while a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is to be cast into the Āhavanīya fire, a stone is cast in by mistake, anger, or desire—or if the cake itself falls into a pit or similar place—that casting is not a *homa* (an oblation).

It should be understood that [the suffix] belongs to the parasmaipada. Therefore, the usage *hoṣye* found in some texts is indeed incorrect. However, the usage in the *Ānandalaharī*, *marāgnau juhvānāḥ*, is perfectly correct, even though the *śānac* suffix does not apply there.
Because it is not characterized by the suffix *cānaś*.

(276) *bhī-hrī-bhṛ-hu-vām śluvac ca* |3|1|39|. [The augment] *āṭ* [is applied] by the rule *āḍ ajādīnām*. [The reason for its application is that it is] "later" (*paratvāt*) than [the rule] *hu-śnuvoḥ*.
The meaning is: "because it is subsequent with respect to [the preceding rule].
(277) *bhiyo’nyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 6.4.115. Regarding *bhiyo’nyatarasyām*: what is the purpose of the condition "in a sārvadhātuka [affix]"? [Consider: *bhīyate*, *bibhīye*.

What is the purpose of [specifying] "when beginning with a consonant" (*halādau*)? [Example: *bibhyati*. What is the purpose of [specifying] "before *k* or *ṅ*" (*kṅiti*)? [Example: *bibheti*. Some maintain that here the phrase "before *k* or *ṅ* when beginning with a consonant" (*halādau kṅti*) is not very useful, because the prescription of the short *i* (*itva*) has its application fulfilled in cases such as *bibhitah*, and because in cases such as *bibhyati* and *bibheti*, [the shortening would be blocked] by the substitution of *yaṇ*.
They say [the suffix *ya* is applied] because of the occurrence of the verbal roots *ar* and *piparti*.
(Pāṇini 7.4.77): *artipipartyośca*.
[The rule] "and of *arti* and *piparti*" (*artipipartyośca*). He will state the example for *arti* as *iyarti*. (279) *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* 7.1.102.

[In the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*,] why is it said "*aṅgāvayava-*" [meaning "belonging to a member of the verbal base"]? [Consider the case of] the root *ṛ* "to go," which belongs to the *kry-ādi* class; from that [root, the form *iyarti* arises].
When the *kta* suffix follows, because of the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "ṛt-ṣṭhiv-ūkaḥ kit-i," the form becomes *samīrṇa*; otherwise, however, it would be *amūrṇa*.
(280) *śṛ-dṛ-prāṃ hrasvo vā* || 7.4.12 || [The vowel of the roots *śṛ*, *dṛ*, and *pṝ* is optionally shortened before the *kta* suffix.]

Regarding *śṛḍṛprām*: *śṛ* means "to injure" and *dṛ* means "to tear"; these two belong to the *ky*-class. "Optionally there is *guṇa*" refers to the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām*. As for *papratuḥ*, in the case of the short vowel, *yaṇ* substitution occurs. Now, one might object: let the mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*) not be included here; let its optionality follow from the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *guṇa* itself. And so [it would be]: [The objection continues: "In that case..."

If it is argued that forms such as *papratuḥ* and *śaśratuḥ* are established by means of the substitution of *yaṇ*, while on the alternative view of *guṇa* (vṛddhi) forms such as *paparatuḥ* and *śaśaratuḥ* would also be established, this is not so; for in the case where *guṇa* is absent, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the substitution of *it* by the rule "ṛta id dhātoḥ. Nor can it be said that *yaṇ* alone would apply due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*).

It should be stated [that the substitution occurs], because a rule concerning a suffix (*aṅga*) is stronger than one concerning a phoneme (*varṇa*). From the root *ḍubhṛḍh* (to support/maintain), with the suffix *kri* by the rule *vitaḥ kriḥ*, we have *bhṛti*.
[In the formation of *bhṛtya* etc.,] there is the application of *bhṛñām it* 7.4.76.

Because of the continuation from the rule "bhṛñām, ṇijām trayāṇām" (Pāṇini 6.4.75), he says: "of these three. Some, however, say that the number "three" is obtained by the principle of the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa* (the rule regarding the quail). Why "of three"? [Consider] *jahāti*. Why "in the *lū* [affix]"? [Consider] *babhāra*.

(282) *ī halyaghoḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.113. The rule *ī halyaghoḥ* [is applied] by virtue of the rule *śnābhyastayoḥ*. Examples: *lunīte*, *punīte*. Why "before a suffix marked with K or Ṅ" (*kṅti*)? Observe: *lunati*. Why "not being a root ending in GH" (*aghoḥ*)? Observe: *dhataḥ*, *dataḥ*. [And] *mimīte*.
The substitution of *i* for *hu* and *mā* does not apply here, because the term *ārddhadhātuke* (before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in forms such as *mātaḥ*, *māthaḥ*, *gāte*, and *gāse*. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kāśikā*: "The governing rule (*adhikāra*) of *ārddhadhātuka* does not extend to the suffix *lyap*."

Regarding the word *yāvat*: (283) *jahāteś ca* |6|4|116|. [The rule applies] also after the root *jahāti*. Why [is it specified that the suffixes] must be *kṅit*? [Answer: [Because the rule does not apply in cases like] *jahāti*. Why [is it specified that they must be] *sārvadhātuka*? [Answer: [Because the rule does not apply in cases like *hīnaḥ*].
It is elided. (284) *ā ca hau* 6.4.117: [The substitution of *e* for *ā* occurs] before *ca* and *dītau*. For this very reason, Bhaṭṭi employed [the form]: *ahihi jahīhi jahāhi*.

"Rāmabhāryā" [is an example]. (285) *lopo yi* |6|4|118|. [The rule] "the elision [of the final vowel and consonant of a stem] before the suffix *yi*. Why [specify] "before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix"? [Consider the counter-examples: *heyāt* and *praṇidadāti*. [In these cases, the elision applies] by the rule *ergadeḥ*.

Regarding *ṇatvam* [the substitution of *ṇ*]: in *dadaḥ*, there is elision of *ā* by the rule *nābhyastayor ātaḥ*. Because it is stated that [the root] ends in *agh* [a consonant], the substitution of *ī* does not occur. In *adāt*, there is elision of *sic* by the rule *ātiṣṭha*. (286) *dadhastathośca* 8.2.38.

Regarding the rule *dadhastathośca*: he explains that by the statement "of *adha*," only the root *dhā* (to place) is understood after its reduplication and the application of the abhyāsa-kārya, and not the root *dadha* (to hold)—this is indicated by the phrase "of that which is reduplicated. Why [is it specified] "ending in a *jhaṣ* consonant"? [Consider:
*dadhāti*. But if this were so, would it not also fail to apply in cases such as *hate*, because of the elision (*āllopa*)?
Because [the root] would not end in *aj* or *ghu* by virtue of being treated as the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*), he says: "By the force of the explicit statement.
(287) *nijāṃ trayāṇāṃ guṇaḥ ślau* | 7|4|75|. Regarding *nijām*: what is the purpose of the condition *ślau*? [Consider: *nineja*.

(288) *nābhyastasyā’ci piti sārvadhātuke* [Pāṇini 7.3.87]. [The rule] *nābhyastasya* [means]: "of a reduplicated root. Why "of a reduplicated root"? [Consider the example: *dveṣāṇi*. Why "before a vowel" (*aci*)?
[Consider the example: *veveṣṭi*. The mention of *pit* is for the sake of the subsequent rule: *uto vṛddhir luki halī* [Pāṇini 7.3.89].

Why [is it] "sārva"? [As in] *nineja*. [This is] due to the substitution of *i* by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (optionally in the Veda). And this [rule] applies both to what precedes and what follows. [In] *iyarti*: there is *iyaṅ* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), but *guṇa* for that which follows the reduplicated syllable. [In] *iyati*: [the substitution of] *at* occurs by the rule "ad-abhyastāt". [In] *aryāt*: there is *guṇa* by the rule "uṇo 'rti".
Regarding *ārat*: by the rule *artiśāstrtyaṅ*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied; by the rule *ṛdṛśo’ṅīti*, there is *guṇa*. Regarding *babdha*:

by the rule *haṣastathoḥ*, the *t* of the suffix *tas* becomes *dh*. Regarding *tutūrta*: by the rule *hali ca*, there is lengthening (*dīrgha*). [The root] *dhana* means "in grain"; the meaning is "in the acquisition of grain. Regarding *dadhanta*: this is due to its being Vedic (*chāndasatvāt*).
They say that the long vowel [ā] does not apply here by the rule "ṭh-anu-nāsikasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.15).

(289) *janasana-khanāṃ sani jhali* (Pāṇini 6.4.42). [The sūtra states: *janasana-khanām*. Both [roots]—*jana* in the sense of "birth" (*janane*) and *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāve*)—are included.

The inclusion [of the root *jan*]. In the case of a suffix beginning with a *jhal* sound followed by *san*, we have *siṣāsati*. In *jajñati*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) according to the rule "not when meaning 'to kill'. In *jajāyāt*, the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) is optional according to the rule "optionally before *ya*.
The same applies to *jāyāt*. In *jigāti*, the substitution of *i* (itvam) occurs according to the rule "diversely in the Veda."
Thus ends the section on *juhoty-ādi* verbs in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
Now, the *kaṇḍv-ādi* verbs:
(430) *kaṇḍvādibhyo yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.27). [The suffix *yak* is added after the verbal roots listed in the *kaṇḍv-ādi* group.]

Regarding the rule *kaṇḍvādibhyo yak*: from the previous rule *dhātor ekācaḥ*, the word *dhātoḥ* (from a verbal root) is understood to carry over. The word *vā* (optionally) has ceased to apply; otherwise, forms such as *kaṇḍavatī* would result. Therefore, he says: "from the verbal root, [the suffix *yak*] is obligatory. Some, however, maintain that the word *nityam* (obligatorily) carries over from the rule *itthaṃbhūte kauṭilye gatau*.

Thus they say; but that is to be considered. For in that context, the inclusion of the word *nitya* (eternal) functions in the sense of the particle *eva* (only/exclusively), as was explained previously to indicate the non-universality (*anityatā*) of the *takrakauṇḍinya-nyāya* (the maxim of the curd for Kauṇḍinya). Furthermore, this also applies to the entry: "The root *itya* [is used] in the sense of crookedness and motion."
The word *veti* (in the rule) is understood as "or. Otherwise, the suffix *yaṅ* would apply invariably after roots meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*). Regarding the phrase "in its own sense" (*svārthe*):
the intention is that the statement by the Easterners (*prāc*)—that *yak* should be added after *kaṇḍvādi* roots in the sense of the root *kṛñ* (to do)—is incorrect.
As for the phrase "for it is twofold": it is understood from the fact that *yak* is marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*) that these are verbal roots (*dhātavaḥ*). Thus, [the form] *kaṇḍū-ya-ti*.

"By the long recension, even nominal stems [are included]. However, if these were indeed verbal roots, then even when they were read with a short vowel at the end, forms such as *kaṇḍūyati* would be established by the rule "ṭh-akṛt-sārvadhātuka-ārddhadhātuka" (Pāṇini 7.3.94), which prescribes lengthening before the suffix *yak*; so what would be the purpose of that long-vowel reading? But if there is this twofold nature [of being both roots and nominal stems], [then it is necessary].

In the case of the suffix *yaK* added after verbal roots (*dhātu*), the designation *kit* is meaningful because it prevents *guṇa*. Furthermore, the reading of the long vowel [in the root] is also meaningful, as it establishes forms such as *‘aṇḍūa’* which are not otherwise included [by other rules]. For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: “Because of the context of verbal roots, it is a root; and also because of the non-attachment of *ka*. He says:

"And I consider this [root] *kaṇḍū* to have been declared by the grammarian as long (dīrgha). By this, even the analysis (*vigraha*) stated by the Easterners (*prācya*)—namely, "he performs scratching" (*kaṇḍūaṃ karoti*) or "he scratches" (*kaṇḍūyati*)—is refuted, because it is not accepted that *kaṇḍū* and the others are merely nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Nor is there any issue even if a twofold nature is accepted.

It should be stated that *yak* should be applied directly from the root (*dhātu*) itself; for if it were otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of forms such as *kaṇḍavati* occurring after the *laṭ* and other suffixes following the root.

Furthermore, since elision (*alopa*) would be impossible for roots meaning the attainment of pleasure, pain, and so forth when *yak* is added, there would be the undesirable consequence of the failure to establish forms such as *sukhyati*. As for what some [grammarians] have said...

Regarding the statement that there is no obstacle to the ancient explanation— which asserts that by the rule *‘abdavairakalahe’* and by the recurrence of the term *karaṇe*, the suffix *ya* occurs in the sense of the root *kṛ*— that is to be reconsidered, because there is no authoritative evidence for such a recurrence. Otherwise, as in the case of causative (*ṇijanta*) forms, [the meaning would arise] from both the base and the suffix.
"Because two operations would result"—this is the general direction [of the argument]. "Prior existence" means the state of being prior. Regarding "leṭitā":

there is the elision of *y* by the rule "ṭhyasya halaḥ". Regarding "sukhyati": in the *curādi* group, however, it is cited as "ukha duḥkha tatkriyāyām" [meaning "to cause pleasure or pain"], as in "sukhayati" and so forth. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* follows a root ending in *yaṅ*.
The suffix *ṭāp* is applied in the sense of the *apratyaya* by the rule "pratyayāt 'urośca halaḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.6).

*Saparyā*, *arara*, and *ārā* mean a goad; an action performed with that [goad] is *ārākarma*. This word ends in *a*. In the case of *likh*, one says *lekhayati*; however, in the case of the root ending in *ā*, one says *lekhāyati*. The root *mahīṅ* [is used thus]: "Having gone to heaven, he is honored (*mahīyate*)."

Thus [ends] the Rāmāyaṇa. Regarding "prasṛtau": *prasṛti* is a specific measure. Regarding "prabhūtobhāve": the meaning is "in abundance. Amarasimha states: "prabhūtam, pracuram, prājyam, adabhram, bahulam, bahu" [all mean abundant]. Regarding "saṃbhūyasyati" and "asaṃbhūyasīt": the prefix *sam-* is not used here.

Regarding "separation" (*pṛthakkṛti*): they say that separation occurs only in those cases where a suffix that triggers the designation *dhātu* (verbal root) is prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). It is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); by this, forms such as *duvas* in the sense of "to kindle" are established. And it is employed [in the Veda] in such expressions as *‘amidhāgni duvasyati’*.
Thus ends the section on the *kaṇḍvādi* group in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
(471) *Pāṇini 2.3.46*: "The first case ending (*prathamā*) is used merely to express the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), gender, measure, or number.
By the rule beginning with "*vaujasamauṭ*" [Pāṇini 4.1.2], the suffixes beginning with *su* [i.e., the case endings] are introduced.

The [case-endings] derived from *ṅyāp*-prātipadikas have been shown. He now begins to demonstrate their specific distribution according to meaning, starting with the words "the meaning of the prātipadika" (*prātipadikārtha*) and so forth. Since the terms beginning with the nominative (*prathamā*) and ending with the locative (*saptamī*) are technical designations (*saṃjñā*) used by the Eastern grammarians (*Prācām*), they are employed here as well; thus [the rule] begins with "v-au-jas-am-auṭ... and so on.

The author of the *Mūla* states in the *Sūtra*: "However, in the *Kaustubha*, it is said that here the words 'first' (*prathamā*) and so forth refer to the triplets of *sup*-suffixes, according to the maxim: 'The [suffix] *am* should be [assumed] because it is not heard. Thus, since this is established by logical reasoning (*nyāya*), even though the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as 'first' and so forth are not explicitly formulated in this treatise, there is no fault."

This should be understood as a deficiency. For when it is accepted that "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of number," then the mention of gender and number would be redundant, since [the desired result] is already established by the phrase "in the meaning of the nominal stem" alone;
furthermore, because of the inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*), there would be no exclusion of the object (*karman*) and other such factors.

Because it is not distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), even in the view that [the meaning of a word] consists of a triad [of gender, number, and case], the mention of "gender" (*liṅga*) is indeed useless; having raised this doubt, he shows the distinction by stating, "that which has a fixed presentation. When a nominal stem is uttered...

The meaning is that the object which necessarily presents itself is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*); that is to say, it is the "denotable" (*śakya*) meaning. [Objection: But if this were so, the nominative case would not occur in examples such as *siṃho māṇavakaḥ* ("the boy is a lion").
[Response: To this they say: since the nominative case arises by taking the denotable meaning, subsequently—
Because there is no deficiency even when the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) is understood through the co-utterance with another word, [the author] uses the word "mātra" (only).

Here, the term "mātra" is analyzed as "avadhāraṇamātra" (mere restriction) by means of the particle "eva" (only), though this is not a *svapadavigraha* (analysis using its own constituent words). However, the compound is...

It should be understood [as a compound] because it belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. Regarding the word "each" (*pratyekam*): the intention is that [the case endings] are heard at the end of the *dvandva* compound. Now, an objection might be raised: in expressions such as *vūraḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the brave man"), since an additional relation of identity (*abheda-saṃsarga*) appears, the nominative case would not occur. Nor can it be argued...

It should not be argued that the rule prescribing the formation of compounds such as *ūrvāvīra* (in *ūrvāpare*) serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the initial arising [of the sentence-meaning], because that rule finds its fulfillment even in cases where words ending in the second case and other cases are involved, such as in "bring a heroic man" (*vīraṃ puruṣam ānaya*). This is not so; for the meaning of a sentence consists in the relation (*saṃsarga*) [between the word-meanings].
Because it is external, it is impossible for it to subvert a grammatical operation that has already taken effect;

for here, the view of word-level grammatical processing (*padasaṃskārapakṣa*) alone is accepted. By the word "only" (*mātra*), the nominative case would not occur when there is an addition of object (*karman*) and so forth;
nevertheless, because gender (*liṅga*) and measure (*parimāṇa*) are included, [the nominative occurs] even when there is an addition of gender or an addition of measure.
And he says, "in the case of an excess of gender alone, etc.," to show that this must indeed be so.

Although the literal meaning of the word *liṅgamātre* is simply "in the case of mere measure" (*parimāṇamātre*), nevertheless, because the cognition of gender and so forth is impossible without the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), it is stated as "in the case of an excess" (*ādhikye*).

Regarding the word *uccaiḥ*: because it is a nominal stem (*pada*), the substitution of *ru* and the subsequent *visarga* occur here. Furthermore, since this [word] ends in the nominative case, it is not a name; thus, in examples such as *uccais tava svam* and *uccais te svam*, the optional application of the substitutes *te* and *me* is established by the rule *apūrvāyāḥ*, which is also a result [of this designation].

Regarding the word *kṛṣṇa*: although this [term] has all three genders (*sarvaliṅga*) when referring to a dark substance, its meaning is that it has a fixed masculine gender (*niyatapuṃliṅga*) when referring to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva. Regarding the word *jñāna*: the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). As for the examples *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*: in the view that there are two [levels of] meaning, the fixed gender is not part of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*); however, in the view that there are three [levels of] meaning, it is.

Although it is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), nevertheless, because that particular gender is only optionally present, its purpose is not already covered by the rule "in the sense of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārthe*). Regarding the example *droṇaḥ*: one should not argue that the nominative case should apply here simply by the rule "only in the sense of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārthamātre*); for if that were the case, [the following would ensue].

Because it is impossible for the relationship between the object to be delimited and the delimiting factor to appear by way of a relation of inherence (*saṃsarga*), since the relation of non-difference (*abheda*) between the meaning of a noun and its stem is well-established in linguistic usage. As for the word *vrīhiḥ* (rice):

the singular number is used in reference to the genus (*jāti*). However, when there is an intention to refer to individual instances (*vyakti*), one says, "These rice grains are red" (*roṇo vrīhayaḥ*).

It is indeed so. Regarding the phrase "by non-difference" (*abhedeneti*): it should not be argued that the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the meanings of a base (*prakṛti*) and a suffix (*pratyaya*) through difference is difficult to find, because in all instances such as *acati*, *ācakaḥ*, and *aupagavaḥ*, only a connection through difference is observed; for in cases such as secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) denoting a deity, a connection through non-difference is observed.

The point is that since everyone accepts the understanding of the phrase "ṭhaindra haviḥ" (the oblation for Indra) as "an oblation having Indra as its deity," there is no room for doubt. Regarding the statement "number is the denotation": this is because the former teachers [treated it] in that very way by determining the non-difference between the signified and the signifier.
The sense is: "on account of common usage. Regarding the phrase "the statement [is made] when [otherwise] unobtained":
this means that the word *vacana* (statement) is included in the sūtra. In reality, however, the inclusion of the word *mātra* (only/merely) in the sūtra is redundant;

for [the application of the case endings] would be blocked by specific rules such as "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) and so forth, in the case of the object and other kārakas.

Because the nominative case does not apply [in those instances]. Under the view that the rules such as "the second case is used for the object" (*karmani dvitīyā*) constitute a restriction on the suffixes—meaning "only the second case is used for the object," and "only the third case is used for the agent and the instrument, and not elsewhere"—there remains the possibility that the nominative case could also apply to the object and other roles; therefore, the inclusion of the word *mātra* ("only") is indeed necessary.

It must be stated [that this is not so]. For, under the view that the rule is restricted to specific suffixes (*pratyayaniyamapakṣa*), since the meaning would conclude with "the nominative occurs only for the meaning of the nominal stem (*prakṛti*) and nowhere else," the nominative would not apply to the object (*karman*) and other cases;
thus, even the inclusion of the term "word" (*vacana*) [in the sūtra] would be redundant, precisely because of the prohibition: "A base (*prakṛti*) alone should not be employed."

Because the establishment of the primary [meaning] arises first. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be a lack of systematic order such that "the singular number [would result] from the words *viśabda* and *bahuśabda*, and the dual number from the word *ekaśabda*";
for the employment of an explanatory (anuvādaka) case-ending is preferable to the employment of a case-ending whose meaning is not syntactically connected (*ananvita*).

Because it is logical: just as in the case of the expression "aurvāhīka," the word *droṇa* is used metaphorically for that which is measured by a *droṇa*, so that in the phrase "a *droṇa* of rice" (*droṇo vrīhiḥ*), there is a relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*), since two nominal stems (*nāman*) are related through identity. However, according to the view that "the meaning of the suffix is measure" (*pratyayārthaḥ parimāṇam*), [the analysis would be] that which is the measure in the form of a *droṇa*.

The phrase "the rice-grain delimited by that [measure]" (*tat-paricchinno vrīhiḥ*) expresses a relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*); thus, there is a relation of non-difference between the meaning of the noun and the meaning of the nominal suffix. If it is asked, "In that case, how can there be a rejection [of the rule] when there is a difference in the resulting measure?"—to this they reply: here, disregarding the distinction necessitated by the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) has been rejected. Precisely for this reason...

The objection is: since the suffix *aṇ* is established for [words] such as *āṬpagava* by the rule "this belongs to that" (*asyedam*) alone, what is the purpose of the rule "this is the offspring of that" (*asyāpatyam*)? Furthermore, since [the meaning] is already established by the possessive suffix *in*, what is the purpose of prescribing the suffix *ini* in the rule "after *āṇḍuka* and *kambala*, the suffix *ini*" under the governing heading "a chariot belonging to an enemy" (*ari-vṛto rathaḥ*)?

The objection, "For what purpose? which is about to be stated, becomes consistent [only under this view]. However, if one were to accept that a distinction [in grammatical operation] is caused by verbal cognition (śābdabodha) in every single case, then the statement of the solution—"the suffix *in* is prescribed for the sake of subverting (*bādhanārtham*) the *aṇ* suffix"—would mean "it is for the sake of subverting the *aṇ*. Thus, the objection is logically connected.

"And because it would result in the futility of [the requirement for] concentration (*samādhāna*). Now, an objection is raised: "In some cases the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is fivefold; in some cases it is threefold; in some cases it is twofold," and so forth. Whose views are these positions, and how [are they established]?

If it is argued that their occurrence [in such cases] is possible, the commentators have explained this as follows: the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five factors—namely, its own referent (*svārtha*), substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and case-role (*kāraka*). This is evident even without a case-ending in examples such as *dhi*, *madhu*, and so forth, from the nominal stem alone.

The commentator [the Bhāṣyakāra] maintains that there is no loss of the status of being the meaning of the base (prakṛtyarthatva) merely because meanings such as duality, plurality, gender, and instrumentality are also perceived in instances like *vṛkṣau*, *vṛkṣāḥ*, *vṛkṣam*, and *vṛkṣeṇa*,
even when they are associated with case-endings;
for these are employed solely as indicators (*dyotaka*).

"From the beginning, there is a group of four," says Kaiyaṭa; for in the rule "here the upapada is that which stands in the locative case," he maintains—whether according to the view of four factors or the view of five—that the *kāraka* is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*).
The author of the Vṛtti, however, says, "From the beginning, there is a group of three," based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Because it is certain that number, case-role (*kāraka*), and so forth constitute the meaning of the nominal suffix (*vibhakti*). Although number and case-role are understood even without a suffix in cases such as *adhi* and *madhu*, the status of being the meaning of the suffix is not thereby lost in instances such as *vṛkṣau* and *vṛkṣāḥ*. For indeed, [the meaning is not lost] even in cases such as *argāḥ* where [the suffix is absent].

The notion that "the offspring of whom is understood" is also the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). Nor can it be argued that because an agent is understood even without a suffix in cases such as *āviḥ* and so on, it is therefore logical to say that the agent is also the meaning of the base in cases such as *bhettā*. Consequently, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists of exactly three factors.

However, some maintain that number, the object (karman), and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings (*vibhakti*), while gender is expressed by the feminine suffixes (*ṭāp*) and others; according to this view, there are only two [meanings] at the outset. In that context: the "own-meaning" (*svārtha*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*);
the "substance" (*dravya*) is the qualified (*viśeṣya*); "gender" (*liṅga*) is femininity and so on; and "number" (*saṅkhyā*) is singularity and so on.
*Kāraka*—namely, the object (*karman*) and so forth.

(472) *Sambodhane ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.47). Regarding the rule *sambodhane ca*: even in the view that rejects the mention of the word *mātra* [in Pāṇini 1.2.45], it applies only to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*).

Or rather, because of the restrictive rule [that the vocative occurs] only at the beginning, this [sūtra] is commenced since it would otherwise not apply when there is an excess of vocatives. Here, the vocative is the qualificand (viśeṣya) with respect to the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha), and it is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) with respect to the action (kriyā).

And thus, in cases such as "vrajāni devadatta" ("O Devadatta, let us go"), once its status as a sentence is established by the rule "ekatiṅ vākyam" ("a sentence consists of one finite verb"), [the present sūtra applies].

The *nighāta* (accentual suppression) occurs in the case of "ṭhāmantratasya ca" [Pāṇini 8.1.19], but this would not be established if [the word] were not an adverb with respect to the action, because it would constitute a separate sentence; for there is the Vārttika: "In a different sentence, the *nighāta*, as well as the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, must be stated. And so it has been said: "That which is a word of address..."
This is an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyā*). When that is the case, there is the *nighāta* (elision of accent) in the phrase "vrajāni devadatta" (I am going, O Devadatta).
And thus, the meaning of the sentence "Rāma, protect me" is protection performed by me, directed toward Rāma as the object of the vocative address. [The word] "vrajāni... [is explained as follows].

In the case of "devadatta," however, the meaning is the act of going performed by me, which has as its object the vocative directed toward Devadatta. Thus ends the discussion on the nominative case (prathamā).
(473) "The object is that which is most desired by the agent" (Pāṇini 1.4.49).
"The object most desired by the agent is the *karma*. The word "of the agent" (*kartuḥ*) is a genitive case used for the agent according to the rule *tasya ca vartamāne*.
[The suffix] *san* is added to the root *āp*; there is reduplication; by the rule *āpjñapyṛdhāmīt*, the vowel *ī* is substituted;
and by the rule *atra lopo ’bhyāsasya*, the reduplication is elided. [The suffix *san* is also applied] after roots meaning "to understand," "to honor," and so forth.

The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the present tense. In this context, "desire" (*mati*) means longing, not cognition, because the word "cognition" (*buddhi*) is mentioned again later. From that, by the rule "in the sense of excess, the suffixes *tamap* and *iṣṭhan*," the suffix *tamap* is applied to denote intensity. Thus, the meaning is: "the object (*karman*) which is most desired to be reached by the agent (*kartṛ*). And the agent is the substratum of the action expressed by the verbal root. He...

And since it is understood by implication that [the agent] desires to obtain [the object] through an operation (*vyāpāra*) which serves as a qualifier—namely, "by what [means] does he wish to obtain?"—he says: "by means of an action" (*kriyayā*). Furthermore, the present tense (*vartamānatva*) conveyed here by the suffix *kta* is not intended to be significant; therefore, forms such as *kaṭaṃ kṛtavān* ("he has made a mat") and *kariṣyati* ("he will make") are established. [The term used is] *kāraka*.

And this [term] is obtained by the governing force of the word "ārake" (in the sense of "at a distance"). For there, the locative case is used in the sense of the nominative by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). By splitting the sentence for each individual rule (*sūtra*), the technical designation *kāraka* is prescribed by this [treatise]. For example:
"That which is fixed (*dhruva*) in relation to a departure (*apāya*) shall have the designation *kāraka*. Then [it says]: "The *apādāna*. Thus it has been stated.

The *kāraka* would be the *apādāna*. Furthermore, by the force of the recurrence of the term *kāraka*, its coexistence with specific technical designations (*viśeṣasaṃjñā*) is established. Consequently, in the word *tamberama*, the locative case (*saptamī*) occurs because of its status as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

By the rule *kāraka-kvā-gati-kopa-padāt kṛt*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member ending in a *kṛt*-suffix is established. Otherwise, by the rule *atpuruṣe tulyārthe* and so forth, the original accent of the first member would result.
Nor should it be suspected that this is otherwise established by the accent of the *upapada*, for [the present case] is not one of those instances.
Because of the mention "in *tāmra-kaṇau*," although the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) serves as a subordinate word (*upapada*),
the form ending in the locative case does not; for even though the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) is established here by the rule for *thā-thādi* compounds,
nevertheless, due to the association with the suffix *ya*, only the suffix *ac* (as in *era-ac*) is taken there, and thus [the desired result] does not follow.
They say that its establishment [as a term] occurs through the accentuation *thā-thā* and so forth. Furthermore, this designation is etymologically meaningful:

it is called a *kāraka* because it "effects" (*karoti*) [an action]. Consequently, in the sentence "He asks the Brāhmaṇa's son the way," [the word *brāhmaṇasya*] does not fail to be connected with the action. For here, the Brāhmaṇa is a qualifier of the son, and not [directly connected to the action of asking].

Regarding the phrase "connected with the action" (*kriyānvayī*): as in the case of "with milk" (*payasā*). Although milk is an excellent instrument for the act of eating, it is the rice alone that is here the most desired object (*īpsitatama*); milk, however, being a means of refinement (*saṃskāra*), is the instrument (*karaṇa*). For he is not satisfied by drinking milk alone, but rather—

[The objecthood of milk] occurs with rice that has been prepared with it; however, when milk itself is what is most desired by the agent, then its status as an object certainly arises—as in "he drinks milk" (*payaḥ pibati*). This is because [the word] "object" (*karman*) is understood from the rule *adhiśīṅsthāsāṃ karma* ("the locus of *adhi*, *śī*, *sthā*, and *ās* is the object").

(474) *anabhihite* 2.3.1. Regarding the rule *anabhihite*: [the suffixes] *kalpa*, etc., do not apply when the meaning has already been expressed; for instance, in examples such as *ahupāṭavaḥ*, since the meaning has already been conveyed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound, just as *kalpa* and other suffixes do not apply, so too [should it be here].

In cases such as *‘riyate kaṭaḥ’*, the accusative case will not occur because the meaning [of the object] has already been expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and so forth. Furthermore, in examples such as *‘aṭṃa karoti’*, the accusative finds its scope; however, in cases like *‘ṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ’*, it will be superseded by the nominative, which is otherwise without scope. Nor is it the case that "the tree is the *plakṣa* tree" [a contradiction].

In such cases as these, there would be scope for the nominative case; however, even there, since the implied action of "being" (*asti*) is understood, the third case would result by virtue of [the subject] being its agent. Now, if it is argued that in expressions such as "this is blue, not red," where the intention is the exclusion of other qualifiers, [the action of] "being" is...

If it is argued that since the first case-ending (*prathamā*) has its own scope due to not being mandatory, then when both [the first case and the nominative-accusative rules] have their scope, the first case alone would apply by virtue of its higher status; and thus the governing rule *anabhihite* (P.
2.3.1) would be rendered useless—on this point they say: the formulation of the sūtra is intended for the view that "number is the meaning of the case-ending."

It is necessary. For instance, at the commencement of the sūtra, the meaning of "armaṇi dvitīyā" is: "when the object (karman) is not already expressed [by another means], then the singular case-ending of the second triplet applies to that singularity which belongs to the object. If the sūtra were not commenced, however, the sentence-meaning would instead be: "the singular case-ending of the second triplet applies to that singularity which belongs to the object. And thus...

In examples such as *sati kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat was made while [he] exists"), although the past passive participle (*kta*) expresses the mere object (*karman*), its singular number is not expressed; therefore, the accusative case ending (*am*) would be unavoidable. Nor can it be argued that the nominative (*prathamā*) alone would apply by virtue of its higher status (as per Pāṇini 2.3.46), because in cases like *aryavyaḥ kaṭaḥ*, the accusative would still prevail due to its being even higher than that.

Because there would be the undesirable consequence of applying the sixth case-ending characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix. However, under the view that "case-endings express the *kāraka*," since the *kāraka* has already been expressed by the *kta* suffix and so forth, the nominative case—having been applied to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—is capable of conveying singularity and so on; thus, the case-endings beginning with *am* do not apply.

The rule *ṭhanabhihite* has been rejected in the original treatise (*ākara*). However, according to the alternative view (*pakṣe*), since the kāraka is already expressed by the suffix *kta* and so forth, the nominative case—which applies to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*)—is capable of conveying singularity and so on; thus, when the case endings such as *am* do not apply, the meaning is that [the number] is "suggested" (*adyotye*).

And thus, the meaning of the sentence is that the accusative case is employed when the object (*karman*) is not already expressed by suffixes such as the *kta* affix. Furthermore, if one accepts the principle that once an element has been expressed by one indicator, another indicator does not apply, then the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*) would not be of much utility; this is the general direction of the argument.
(475) "The second case ending is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2).

In the example *hariṃ bhajati* ("he worships Hari"), because joy (*prīti*) arises toward Hari through the act of worship, Hari is the object (*karman*) by virtue of being pervaded by the action as qualified by that joy; alternatively, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is the act of worship as qualified by that [joy].

The explicit meaning is: "the present activity residing in Hari, etc., which is conducive to the pleasure residing in Hari, etc. This is exactly the same even in the case of *hariḥ sevyate* ("Hari is served"), according to the established tenet that "the verb has action as its primary meaning" (*kriyāpradhānam ākhyātam*). The action presented by the verbal root is the meaning of the suffix.

The meaning of that [sūtra] is that [the agent] is a qualifier with respect to the object to be qualified (viśeṣya), but not a qualifier with respect to the meaning of the kṛt-affix as it is [with respect to the verb]. For this very reason, "pacati vrajati" (he cooks while walking) does not constitute a single sentence, unlike "ācaṣṭe vrajati" (he speaks while walking). For the meaning of "ācaṣṭe vrajati" is "walking performed by one who is a speaker."

The act of cooking has a single agent, and the act of going has a single agent; thus, the meanings of the roots *pac* (to cook) and *vraj* (to go) are indeed distinct. Consequently, the objection raised by the Naiyāyikas—that the cognition must have a noun in the nominative case as its primary qualificand—should not be heeded by those who follow the Bhāṣya and other authoritative texts. For, according to their own view:
The meaning of the sentence "the cook goes" (*ācako vrajati*) is: "the cook possesses an activity conducive to going.

However, since the determination of the sentence-meaning occurs in such a form as "the activity conducive to cooking" for *pacati* and "going" for *vrajati*, this [interpretation] contradicts the texts of the *Bhāṣya* and other works. Furthermore, Hari...

It has been stated that in the cases of "Devadatta worships" (*bhajati devadattaḥ*) and "Hari is served by Devadatta" (*hariḥ sevyate devadattena*), the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is indeed of one and the same form. However, in the view of the Naiyāyikas, they differ:
[the former is understood as] "Devadatta is the locus of an effort conducive to pleasure residing in Hari."
Since in both cases the sentence-meaning culminates in a distinct [cognitive relation]— namely, "Hari is the locus of the pleasure produced by the action whose end is the giving"—
therefore, a cognition having the nominative case-ending as its primary qualificand (viśeṣya) must certainly not be accepted by those who follow the Bhāṣya and other authoritative sources.
Yāska also said: "A verb has action as its primary meaning; nouns have substance as their primary meaning.
In sentences such as "The deer runs," the running performed by the deer is indeed the object of the act of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*). And it has been said:
"Just as many inflected words (*subanta*) serve as qualifiers for a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅnta*)," so too...

"Even a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) can be a qualifier of another finite verb," it is said. Nor should it be thought that the qualification of a finite verb by another finite verb is rare in common usage;
for instance, in the verse of Māgha: "Leap upon the city! Reap the Nandana grove! (*urīm avaskanda lunīhi nandanam*).
The meaning is that "activity of ill-being" (asvāsthya-kriyā) consists of forms such as besieging a city, attacking, cutting down a forest, and so forth;
this will become clear in the root text under the rule *anuccaye 'nyatarasyām*.
And thus, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, the meaning of "he cooks—he exists" (*pacati—bhavati*) should be understood as "the act of cooking comes to be."

This is the general direction. Regarding the phrase "but when [the object] is already expressed" (*abhihite tu*): if it is objected that, in that case, the accusative case would not occur even in the sentence “he eats boiled rice with ghee” (*saktūn odanaṃ bhuṅkte*), do not say so. For here, two capacities for objecthood (*karmatva-śakti*) are determined by the verbs *pibati* (drinks) and *bhuṅkte* (eats); among these, [the accusative is used] for that which is not already expressed by the primary action of eating (*bhujikriyā*).

Taking the capacity from the second case-ending (dvitīyā), for this very reason the locative case in "āste āsane" (he sits on the seat) is justified; because although the status of being a locus (adhikaraṇatva) has been expressed by the suffix *lyuṭ*, the locus-hood relative to the action denoted by the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) has not yet been expressed. [The word] "śatya" [is explained as follows]:

Regarding the statement "from *ata* [comes] *-ṭhan* and *-yat*"—in the word *prāptānanda*, the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) according to the rule "after roots meaning 'excessive' or 'intransitive'. The meaning is: "one who has become the object of an attainment whose agent is bliss.
He states the result of what was mentioned as "by means of wealth" with the words "sometimes by a particle," namely: "the poison-tree."

It should be understood that in the phrase *aṃvardhya* and in the phrase *hetum*, the meanings "enemy" (*dviṣat*) and "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) are respectively implied. The meaning is "it is joined. By this, it is suggested that there is no fixed rule that particles (*nipāta*) function solely as indicators (*dyotaka*). Likewise, it is appropriate [to say] "so. When it is said "so," [the question arises: "In what way is it appropriate?"
In response to this inquiry, he says: (476) *tathā yuktam cānīpsitam* 1.4.50.
[The word] "as [in the case of] that which is most desired" (*īpsitatamavat*) [is understood from the previous rule]. And in the sūtra, the word *ca* functions in the sense of *api*.

He speaks with intonation, saying: "even that which is not desired" (*anīpsitam api*). This is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) meaning "that which is other than the desired"; by this, both that which is to be disregarded and that which is loathed are included here. With this intention, he first provides an example: "While going to the village, he touches grass. For instance:

The meaning is this: there is a connection with the action for that which is touched, such as a village, when it is intended [as a goal], because it is the locus of the result—such as conjunction—produced by that action; and the same applies even to unintended things like grass. For in this case, the touching of grass by one going to a village is an inseparable concomitant (nāntarīyaka).

Because grass is not intended as the desired object (*īpsita*). However, when even grass becomes the most desired object (*īpsitatama*), it is established by the previous rule itself. And that which is to be disregarded (*upekṣya*)—it is not the object of a cognition of disregard; for instance, in the case of "the riverbank is eroding," such [a cognition] is impossible in the case of an insentient thing. But rather...

What is intended here is that where there is an absence of desire and aversion, that is to be regarded with equanimity (*upekṣya*). Regarding the word "poison" (*viṣam*): although poison is something to be abandoned, it is an object (*karman*) because of its connection with the act of eating, just like rice. Now, as for that person who, being afflicted by disease and the like, considers death itself to be better—his...

If it is argued that poison is indeed desired, since even one who eats it by mistake has poison as something desired because it is determined by the intellect to be like molasses and so forth—otherwise, how could he proceed [to eat it]? Therefore, this example is indeed improper; to this they reply: when...
Even someone who is terrified of death may consume poison when being seized by an enemy;
this is the illustrative example [for that case]. The inclusion of the term *anīpsita* (not intended) is for the sake of clear understanding.
If it is argued that the two sūtras could have been stated as "atha yuktam" [instead], they say in response: "agnim māṇavakam... [etc.]

In the case of the word *vārayati* ("he wards off"), the status of the boy (*māṇavaka*) as the *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) is obtained by the rule *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ*; however, to set that aside, it must indeed be stated that "the object most desired by the agent" [is the *karman*]. And thus, for the sake of including both the hateful and the indifferent, [it is said: "Now..."
It is appropriate— [the rule] "it is also necessarily so" [is required].
(477) *Akathitaṃ ca* | 1.4.51 | And that which is not otherwise specified.
In response to the inquiry "By what is it called 'unspoken' (akathita)?", he says: "by specific [grammatical relations] such as the ablative (apādāna) and so forth.

This means by these specific relations: the ablative, the dative (sampradāna), the locative (adhikaraṇa), the object (karman), the instrument (karaṇa), the agent (kartṛ), and the cause (hetu). "Unintended" (avivakṣita) means not intended to be expressed.

However, when there is a desire to express specific distinctions such as the ablative (*apādāna*) and so forth— as in "He milks milk from the cow" (*gordogdhi payaḥ*), "He begs the earth from Bali" (*baleryācate vasudhām*), or "He shuts the cow in the pen" (*vraje’varuṇaddhi gām*)— the meaning is that the fifth case (*pañcamī*) and others indeed occur. By this, [it is explained] that in the case of "She milks with a ladle into a bronze vessel" (*āṇinā kāṃsyāpātryāṃ dogdhī*), [the respective cases are used].

There would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the technical designations of instrument (*karaṇa*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*). However, this objection—that examples such as "he acts with a staff" (*daṇḍena karoti*) or "he stands on a mat" (*kaṭe tiṣṭhati*) would lack scope because they are excluded from the enumeration of roots beginning with *duh*—is refuted, since it is the designations of instrument and locus that are intended here. But if...

If it were accepted that the word *akathita* in the Sūtra is a synonym for *apradhāna* (non-primary) and not a synonym for *anukta* (unexpressed), then this objection would indeed apply, but not otherwise. Regarding the term *kāraka*: consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of "he asks the Brahmin’s son" (*brāhmaṇasya putraṃ pṛcchati*). Regarding *duhyāj*: "the egg... [and so forth].
The root *daṇj* belongs to the *acurādi* group. Here, however, *daṇḍi* has the sense of "seizing" (*grahaṇa*), not the sense of "punishing" (*nigraha*).

The form *pracchī* is indicated by means of the adventitious vowel *ī*, and not by the vowel *i*, because [if it were *i*] there would be the undesirable consequence of *saṃprasāraṇa* according to the rule *rahijyā*. [Regarding the term] *karmayuk*: that which is joined with an object (*karman*) is *karmayuk*.

By the rule *‘atsūdviṣa-’* etc., the suffix *kvip* is applied. Regarding the phrase “if it is connected with an object” (*karmaṇā yadyaujyate*): the meaning is that a factor of action (*kāraka*), when connected with an action along with a primary object (*mukhyakarman*), receives the technical designation of "object" (*karman*) provided it is not already designated by specific categories such as the ablative (*apādāna*) and so forth. By this, the fact that roots such as *duh* (to milk) govern two objects is established.
[This has been] explained. Others, however, say: "In the expression *karmayuṅ*, the word *karman* denotes action (*kriyā*).

Therefore, the meaning is "that which is connected with action. [The term] "enumeration" (*parigaṇana*) is used so that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *aṭasya śṛṇoti gāthām*; for in this case, [the object] is the *gāthā*.

The sentence-meaning is the act of hearing related to the actor; therefore, because it is connected with the action, the actor indeed possesses the status of a *kāraka*. In the example "gāṃ dogdhi" (he milks the cow), the meaning is the act of milking related to the cow, having milk as its object. Here, the milk is the primary object (*mukhya-karman*) because it is that which is most desired by the agent; however, the cow...

Since milk is apprehended merely as the cause (*nimitta*) [of the separation], and not as a real entity serving as the limit (*avadhi*), the designation of *apādāna* does not apply; therefore, it receives the designation of *karman* by this [rule]. This has been stated by Haradatta: "Even though the cow functions as the limit..."

"Even so, when that [ablative sense] is not intended to be expressed, but rather only the cause (nimitta) is intended to be expressed, the example is justified. By this, it is clear that when the status of being a limit (avadhitva) is intended to be expressed, the ablative case alone is used, as in "gor" (from the cow). However, when this word "goḥ" [is connected] with milk (payasā)...

It should also be understood that when [the relationship] is thus connected, the genitive case alone occurs after the word *go* (cow). As for what was recited by the ancients—"The objects of the roots *duh*, *aci*, *rudhi*, *pracchi*, *ci*, *brū*, *śās*, and *ji*;
and the objects of *nī*, *hṛ*, *kṛṣ*, *manth*, *vah*, *daṇḍ*, *grah*, *muṣ*, *pac*, and *ci* [take the accusative]"—in that list, regarding the root *grah*:

The reading [of *duh* as having two objects] is unauthoritative. Although the status of others as *dvikarmaka* (having two objects) is indeed authoritative, there is nevertheless a corruption of the context. For instance, after listing roots such as *duh* and *ni* in two groups, at the end of the section on the *bhāva* and *karman* operations, it is stated: "Do [affixes] other than *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khalartha* [occur] in the primary sense from *dvikarmaka* roots?"

In response to the doubt as to whether [the suffixes] would apply to the object when it is secondary (*gauṇa*), he himself recited: "The roots *nī* and others, when followed by *ṇic* and having the sense of motion without an object, take the suffix in the primary object; *duh* and others do so in the secondary object, while others follow as they please. And thus, [the suffix] would also occur in the primary object for the roots *daṇḍi* and *manthi*. Not so.

[The word *ceṣṭāpati*] is the master of the action. This is because it contradicts the Bhāṣya statement: "A fine of one hundred [paṇas] for the Gargas. For here, the hundred is the primary element, not the Gargas, as indicated by the supplementary statement: "And kings become desirous of gold. It has been stated that in this context, the root *daṇḍ* (to punish) has the sense of "taking" (*grahaṇa*), not "restraining" (*nigraha*).

Therefore, in this case, the completion of the sentence occurs with the aggregate [of the two], because the primary element cannot function in accordance with the subordinate element. Likewise, the action of *manth* (churning) would also pertain to the primary element, yet it is intended to apply to the subordinate one.
And thus says Bhāravi: "By whom the abodes of the Nāgas were made manifest by the waters cast forth..."

"In the case of *devāsurair amṛtam ambunidhim amantheyuḥ* (the gods and asuras churned the ocean for nectar)," here *amṛtam* (nectar) is the primary [object] because it is the intended goal (*uddeśyatva*), whereas *ambunidhiḥ* (the ocean) is secondary. In the case of *balim yācate* (he begs Bali), here the primary object (*karma*) of the root *yāc* (to beg), which has the sense of requesting, is the earth (*vasudhā*); that by which [the subject] is connected is the primary.
In reality, although *bali* is a limitative point (*avadhi*), when that status is not intended to be expressed, it becomes the object (*karman*) by this rule.

Regarding the word *avinītam*: for the verb *yāci*, which has the sense of "entreaty," *avinīta* is the primary object; the meaning is "he entreats the ill-behaved person for the sake of discipline" (*vinayāya*). When the purposefulness of the discipline (*vinaya*) is not intended to be expressed...
The term *akathita* (unspoken) refers to the designation of the object (*karma-sañjñā*). Regarding the word *taṇḍulān* (rice grains):

for the root *pac* (to cook) in the sense of "producing," boiled rice (*odana*) is the primary object, meaning "he produces boiled rice. However, the rice grains (*taṇḍula*) are the unspoken object when their status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) is not intended to be expressed. Others, however, say that the root *pac* has two meanings.

Due to a failure to carefully examine the Bhāṣya, [some claim] that the meaning of "he cooks rice-gruel by means of rice" (*taṇḍulair odanaṃ pacati*) is "causing the rice to soften while bringing about the rice-gruel. However, the inclusion of *pac* among the roots beginning with *duh* (the *duhyādi* group) is without authority, as it is not mentioned in either the Bhāṣya or Kaiyaṭa. Regarding the word *gargān*:

In the case of *daṇḍi* (one who punishes), there is an object (*karman*) consisting of the hundred [coins] for the purpose of seizing; however, in the case of the *Gargas*, since the status of being an ablative (*apādāna*) is not intended to be expressed, they are an "unspoken" object (*akathitaṃ karma*). Regarding the word *vrajam* (the pen):

here, the cow is the primary object (*mukhyaṃ karma*), while the pen, because its status as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is not intended to be expressed, is an "unspoken" object according to the rule *akathitaṃ ca*.

The action occurs. The same should be inferred for what follows as well. Regarding the phrase "based on the meaning" (*artha-nibandhanā*): it does not depend on the [inherent] form of the word itself; for in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the *Pāṇini-sūtra* 6.1.94 (*adrāja-*)—which is a synonym for *pṛcchati*—it is observed that even the root *cud-* is transitive (takes two objects). This is the intended sense. For this very reason, [one says] "to stand in battle... (*raṇe sthātum*).

With a smiling face, he spoke these words of great significance to Mārīca; thus Bhaṭṭi employed [the term]. And in this way, many verbs such as *nāth* and others should be understood as having two objects (*dvikarmaka*).
It might be argued: "If this designation is based on meaning, then why is it not applied to either *nī* or *vah*?"

If it is argued that both should be recited because they have the same meaning, that is true; however, if a distinct difference in meaning is experienced in such cases as "he carries a burden" (*bhāraṃ vahati*) and "he leads a burden" (*bhāraṃ nayati*), then both should indeed be recited. But if no such difference is experienced, then only one of the two need be recited.

Because the object of definition (*lakṣya*) remains uncontradicted in both cases. Regarding this, they say: "The statement in the *Manoramā* that even the example ‘He seized Indra with a thunderbolt’ (*jagrāha dyūtaru śakram*) is incorrect is indeed to be questioned;
for a technical name (*sañjñā*) is based on its meaning, and the root *daṇḍi-* has the sense of seizing. [The example] is: “He begs Bali.”
The root *hikṣ* [is used] in the sense of "begging," whether there be lack of gain or gain. It means "he begs" or "he asks.

It should be stated that when used in conjunction with intransitive roots (*akarmakadhātu*), place (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), and the distance to be traversed (*gantavyādhvā*) are designated as the object (*karma*). Regarding "place": here, only [regions] such as Kuru and Pañcāla are understood.

Therefore, the rule *adhi-śīṅ-sthāsāṃ karma* (Pāṇini 1.4.46) is not rendered redundant; for even if one accepts that this rule serves as a restrictive injunction (*niyamārtha*)—to the effect that "only when preceded by *adhi* do these [roots] take the locus as their object"—one must still consider that an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would occur in cases such as *vaikuṇṭhe vartate*. This is the intended implication.

He illustrates this very point with the examples "the Kurus" and "the milking. Nor is there establishment [of the case ending] here on the basis of being time (*kālatva*), because in common usage the word "time" refers only to those things well-known as time, such as months and the like.
Therefore, expressions such as "he sits for a while" (*haṭam āste*) do not occur; rather, it is simply that which is produced (*janya*).

Time is an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*), because even objects such as a jar possess temporality. As for the statement by the ancients—having said, "When used in conjunction with intransitive roots (*akarmaka-dhātu*), the second case is applied to words denoting place, time, distance, and state"—and their citation of the example *adīmāsta* ("he stayed for a day"), that is inconsistent; for [in that context], the collection of Rāma-s and so forth is indeed the agent (*kartṛ*).

"A region (*deśa*) is understood, and not merely a portion of it; therefore, the expression 'he sleeps in the village' (*grāmaṃ svapiti*) does not occur," according to the *Ākara*. Furthermore, the term "path" (*adhvan*) is used in its full sense, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the expression 'he sleeps on the path' (*adhvānaṃ svapiti*). For this very reason, in the *Ākara*, the path is specified as that which is to be traversed (*gantavyatvena*). By way of being that which is to be traversed...
It has also been explained that [the distance] such as a *krośa* is well-known and possesses a fixed measure.

Furthermore, the mention of "the second [case]" is also inconsistent; because the designation of "object" (*karman*) would not apply, the suffixes *la* and others would not occur in the sense of an object, leading to the undesirable consequence that usages such as *āsyaṃte māsaḥ* ("a month is being sat through") would be impossible.
It has been explained in some way that the statement “*eci*” is intended to indicate the weakness of that [opposing] doctrine;
yet, even if the previously mentioned fault is thus avoided, one must reflect that the fault of inconsistency in the example “*nadīm āste*” remains exactly as it was.

(478) Pāṇini 1.4.52: "In the case of roots meaning motion (*gati*), cognition (*buddhi*), consumption (*pratyavasāna*), or those having sound as their object (*śabdakarman*), as well as intransitives (*akarmaka*), the agent (*kartṛ*) of these [roots] when used without a causal suffix (*ṇic*) becomes the object (*karman*) when they are used with a causal suffix. *ṇa* = motion; *buddhi* = cognition; *pratyavasāna* = consumption (eating); "those having sound as their object" means that sound is the object (*karman*).

The meaning is "of those for which there is a *kāraka*. For here the word *karman* refers to a *kāraka*, and not to an action (*kriyā*) as it does in the rule "in the sense of the agent when there is a reciprocal action" (*artari karmavyatihāre*), because grammatical operations apply to technical (*kṛtrima*) terms, and because of the force of the explicit mention of the word *karman*. Otherwise, indeed...

One should simply say: "Of those roots whose meanings involve excessive intellect (*ati-buddhi*), consumption (*praty-avasāna*), or sound (*śabda*), and which are intransitive (*akarmaka*). [The phrase] "that which is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *aṇ* [causative]" means: when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) has not yet been applied—that is, with respect to the action expressed by the root in its pure form—that which is the agent shall be designated as the object (*karman*) with respect to the action expressed by the root in its causative form (*ṇyantadhātu*).

The ancient scholars maintain that this sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*): "If [the status of] agent applies to one who is being caused to act by the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), then it applies only to the agents of roots meaning 'motion' (*gati*) and so forth. Consequently, in the example *pācayati devadatto yajñadattena* ("Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook"), the status of agent with respect to the root-meaning belongs only to the prompted agent (*prayojya*).

The third case ending is established because [the agent] is situated in a state free from objection. And it has been said: "Having attained the status of an object (*karman*) through the act of commanding due to independence in the performance of a subordinate action, it is expressed by its own grammatical property (*svadharma*) because of the restrictive rule regarding the technical designation of 'object'.
By "its own property," the meaning is "by the third case ending" (*tṛtīyā*). Now, an objection:

Having set aside agency with respect to the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), agency with respect to the meaning of the base root is established precisely because it is more remote (*para*) and because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*). For an action qualified by its own factors of action (*kāraka*) is connected with the meaning of the causative suffix, since the causative suffix is prescribed for that which possesses a motive (*hetumat*), and the one who prompts the agent is the motive.
