Therefore, even though it is sublated [by other rules], the designation of "agent" (kartṛ-sañjñā) remains applicable.

And thus: "Because it is subsequent, because it is internal (antaraṅga), and because it is that which is depended upon (upajīvya), let the status of agent belong to the one being employed (prayojya); this is appropriate according to the rule for motion (gati) and so forth. Even if this were the view of the injunction (vidhi-pakṣa), the objective (lakṣya) remains as follows:

[This objection is] indeed without basis; nevertheless, if it is argued that this contradicts the writings of the ancients who state that "this is a restrictive rule" (*niyama-sūtra*), they reply: "By prioritizing the verbal predominance of the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the technical designation 'object' (*karman*)—which follows the predominant factor—is more powerful, and thus there is no conflict at all."

The claim that "the status of being an agent is established because [the suffix] is subsequent" is not tenable. Even if [a rule] is internal (antaraṅga) or dependent (apajīvyatva), these two do not necessarily confer superiority with respect to the primary element. Consequently, the statement by the predecessors regarding its restrictive purpose (niyamārthatva) remains entirely unassailable. He provides examples for roots ending in the causative marker ṇic, such as *gam* (to go), in their respective order—beginning with "śatrūn... and so forth.

"The enemies went to heaven; Śrī Hari caused them to go to heaven"—in this case, the enemies were the agents (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative (*aṇyantā*) state, but they became the objects (*karman*) in the causative (*ṇyantā*) state. That movement which had the enemies as its locus and was performed by themselves [became the object].
The meaning of the sentence is: "That activity, established in which [the Lord] is favorable toward that [end], He, Śrī Hari, is my refuge.

This should be inferred in the same way for what follows. Regarding the phrase *vedārtham*: those who did not know their own Vedic meaning (*vedārtham*), to them Śrī Hari made known the Vedic meaning (*avedayat*). Likewise, the gods drank the nectar (*amṛtam āśran*); to them He caused it to be drunk (*āśayat*).

The Creator (Vidhi) studied the Veda; he taught—that is, caused Brahmā to study—the Veda. The earth was situated upon the water; that Hari who caused it to sit—that is, established it—is my refuge (gati).
This is the grammatical connection (anvaya). Now, if the enemies are made the object by this [verb], then regarding the object...
Heaven is that which is most desired to be attained (*īpsitatama*), but not by the agent;
thus, because heaven lacks the status of being "most desired by the agent," it would not possess the status of an object (*karman*).
On this point, some [object]—on account of the fact that the status of an object [derived from the rule] *gati-buddhi-* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*)—[conclude that... from that...

Since the status of heaven as the object (*karmatva*)—being prompted by the operation (*vyāpāra*) which is the meaning of the verbal root—is established even prior [to the application of the *kāraka* rules], there is no fault. Others, however, maintain that in the rule "that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamam*), the mention of "agent" (*kartṛ*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that which is independent (*svatantra*). For "agent" is designated [by convention] in relation to independence.

It should not be argued that the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word is untenable in that very context, because the simultaneous acceptance of both primary denotation (*śakti*) and metaphorical indication for a single word in reference to one and the same object is disapproved by the authors of the treatises;
for [the word] is conventionally established as independent when it is not overlaid by another technical designation (*saṃjñā*).

For there is no obstacle to accepting an independent secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) that is common to both that which is endowed with another designation and that which is not; therefore, the root *ji* has primary denotative power (*śakti*) in the sense of "victory," while it has secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "intense victory. According to the principle that "secondary function occurs when something is known under a form other than its own [primary] one," this applies in the case of the word *prajayati*.

The Naiyāyika statement—that the prefix *pra-* is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), whereas the meaning of "victory" (*prakṛṣṭajaya*) belongs to the verbal root *ji* itself—is consistent. Nor should it be doubted that there is a lack of evidence for the definition of the agent (*kartṛ*) as being "independent" (*svatantra*). [As stated: "In the case of verbs with two objects (*dvikarman*), they say that the *l*-affixes and so forth express the principal object; when the non-principal [object]..."

This is because the Bhāṣyakāra himself is the authority when he states, "after [roots] such as *duh*," and then says, "and after causative forms (*ṇijanta*), the agent [becomes the object]," for without this secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the status of having two objects (*dvikarmakatā*) cannot be obtained for causative forms, which would otherwise leave room for the rule "after [roots] ending in *ṇic*, the agent [is the object]."
They say: "It should be so.

Regarding *nīvahyena* and *nīvahyai*: although the meaning of these two roots is "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*) and not "going" (*gati*), nevertheless, since "going" also enters into the middle of "causing to reach" as a qualifying factor, [the rule] applies merely on that account.
Thinking thus, the prohibition was stated.
However, there is no prohibition for the root *vah* when it has a controller as its agent. Regarding the term "controller" (*niyantr*):
a controller is one who impels animals, and not merely a charioteer. By this, the form "he causes the oxen to carry the barley" (*vāhayati balīvardān yavān*) is established.

From this very example in the Bhāṣya, the maxim "convention sets aside etymological derivation" (*rūḍhir yogam apaharati*) is not accepted here. The meaning resulting from the statement "it should be stated that [the suffix] *yat* is applied in the sense of an object (*karman*)" is that there is no prohibition. By those, however, for whom "attainment" (*prāpaṇa*) is understood by the word "going" (*gati*), or for whom "heaven" (*dyu*) is not so understood—

This statement is necessary for both [schools]. However, it should be understood that the statement "īvahyaerne" is not necessary for those who take the word *gati* (motion) to include the sense of "reaching" (*prāpaṇa*). Regarding the word *sūta*: Amarasimha states, "The charioteer (*prājita*), the driver (*yantā*), the *sūta*, the *kṣattṛ*, and the *sārathi* [are synonyms]."
Since [the roots] have the sense of consuming (*pratyavasāna*), they would normally attain the status of an object (*karman*); therefore, he states an exception: "Not for *ad* and *khād*.

Regarding "not for *ad* and *khād*": *ad* is in the sense of eating (*bhakṣaṇe*), and *khād* is in the sense of eating (*bhakṣaṇe*). The reading *ādī-* found among the Easterners (*prācām*) should be understood as an imitation of the causative (*ṇyanta*) state. Thus: *ādayati*.

The restrictive rule for the *parasmaipada*—namely, "after the roots meaning 'to stand,' 'to swallow,' and 'to move' [the *ātmanepada* suffixes are used]"—does not apply here, because that rule is prohibited by the exception "there is a prohibition regarding the root *ad*. Therefore, when the fruit of the action does not benefit the agent (*akartṛbhiprāya*), the *parasmaipada* suffix is used according to the rule "after the root *eṣ* (in the sense of 'to go'), the *kartari* [suffixes are used]"; however, when it benefits the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*)...

It should be understood that the *ātmanepada* affix indeed occurs by the rule "ṭhṇicaśca. [This applies] to the root *bhakṣi* when it does not mean "to injure. Now, an objection is raised: by the rule "atibuddhi-," the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) of the non-causative (*aṇau*) verb, but not for the agent of the causative (*ṇau*).
If it is argued that this prohibition is redundant because the very possibility [of the application] does not exist, they say in response:

since the rule is in the causative form (hetu-ṇic), the prohibition "in the non-causative" (aṇau) also, by virtue of its proximity, refers specifically to the causative (hetu-ṇic); therefore, it applies even to the root *bhakṣ* when it takes the causative suffix of the *cur*-class (*curādi-ṇic*).

The prohibition [of the suffix *ṇic*] is stated because [the action] exists as an attainment (*prāpti*). Regarding the example "he causes [them] to eat": "the oxen eat the grain"; the meaning is "he causes them to eat. Indeed, injury (*hiṃsā*) is to be understood as occurring when the barley standing in the field is being eaten, because at that stage they possess sentience (*cetana*).

The addition of *jalpati* and others to the list [of roots for which the agent becomes the object in the causative] is prescribed. That is, for *jalpati*, *patati*, and so forth, the suffix *am* [is applied]. Regarding the root *apa-jalp* in the sense of "speaking clearly": in the sentence *putro dharmaṃ jalpati* ("the son speaks of dharma") and *taṃ devadatto jalpayati* ("Devadatta causes him to speak of that"), the son is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the state without the causative suffix (*aṇ*), but becomes the object (*karman*) in the state with the causative suffix (*ṇi*). Likewise...

The son speaks the Dharma, and Devadatta causes him to speak it. One should not fall into the error of thinking that this supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) is redundant, since the forms *jalpati* and *bhāṣate* are already established by the rule *atibuddhipūjārth...*, given that both involve the action of sound (*śabda-kriyatva*). This is because the phrase "having sound as its object" (*śabda-karmaṇām*) means that sound is the objective factor (*karmakāraka*).

"Of whom" means, by implication, of those [who are currently studying]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that examples such as "he causes the Creator to teach the Veda" would not be established. In the same way, one should also infer cases such as "the son laments something, and he causes him to lament."

And [the rule applies] after the root *dṛś* (to see). Regarding "it causes to remember": the intention is that the designation *mit* (which triggers the substitution of *i* for *a* in the penultimate vowel) applies only to the root *smṛ* in the sense of "meditating upon" (*ādhyāna*)—as per the rule "haṭādayo mitaḥ"—and not to the root *smṛ* in the sense of "thinking" (*cintā*).
Regarding [the prohibition] after the root *śabdāy*: [as in] "Devadatta causes him to sound. However, in the case of "the thicket of forest causes him to die," [the suffix is applied].
In the *bhāṣya* on the sūtra "ṭhṇeraṇau," the status of being an object (*karmatva*) should be understood precisely from that usage:

*śabdāyayati*. In the sense of "he makes a sound" (*śabdaṃ karoti*), the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by the rule "śabdavairakalahābhraroga... and so forth; from that, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added by the rule for "hetumaṇṇic. [The phrase] "because it is included within the meaning of the verbal root" refers to this: *śabdāyayati*.

Soldiers are defeated when they employ the action [of fighting] against enemies (*ripūn*), but not when the object is not intended to be expressed. Just as in the rule *aḥ karmaṇi ca*, where even those whose objects are not intended to be expressed are understood as "intransitive" (*akarmaka*), so too here, if...

If [the object] were to be included [in the definition], then when the action of cooking rice and so forth is not intended to be expressed, one would have to say *odanam ādayati devadattam* ("He causes Devadatta to eat rice"), and not *devadattena pācayati* ("He causes Devadatta to cook"). Similarly, in the rule *atyarthākarmaka-*, those whose objects are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitakarmāṇaḥ*) are not understood as "intransitive" (*akarmakāḥ*). [For example: *dattavān*.
Otherwise, in the sense of "one who has cooked," the form *pakva* would result from the root *pac*.

As for what was stated by the ancients—"there is no [application of the rule] after the roots *krand*, *śabda*, and *hvay*"—that is incorrect; for the prohibition regarding *yat* is baseless, since it is accepted there that the agent of the *aṇ* becomes the object of the *ṇic*. However, as for *krand* and *hvay*:
Even though sound is an action (*kriyā*), it is not a *karman* (object) *kāraka*;
this is because there is no possibility of its attainment (*prāpti*). Thus it is established in the *Manoramā*.
Although the status of being an object is stated for the roots *ruj*, *grah*, and *dṛś* by the rule "of *ruj*, *grah*, and *dṛś*," the inclusion of *dṛś* therein is indeed authoritative.
The fact that *śru* has two objects is established because it has sound as its object. As for *grah*, although there is the usage of Bhaṭṭi:

"That bow was produced by him who grasped [it]," and the usage of Kālidāsa: "Indeed, the Mountain was not able to give his daughter to the God of Gods who had come to ask for her," [the rule of its having two objects is still valid].

And although it is consistent [with grammar], it is still disapproved by many; for this very reason, they have justified the usage expressed as "he informed" (abodhayat), meaning "in order to cause her to grasp [the truth], he informed her that she was to be married. Nor is it the case that even without the sense of "informing," the word retains its meaning according to its literal form.

It should not be argued that the root *grah* (to seize) possesses two objects; for if that were the case, in the expression *āyāpratigrāhitagandhamālyām*, the past passive participle suffix (*kta*) would denote the cow as the prompted object (*prayojyakarman*), and not the perfumes and garlands which are the [direct] objects. This is because, in the case of a causative verb (*ṇyanta*), the suffix denotes both the agent and the prompted object.
Because it is stated that [the agent] is "of the action" (*karmaṇaḥ*), since the cow, impelled by its owner, accepts the perfume and garlands,

the cow indeed becomes the *prayojyakarman* (the object of the instigator). Consequently, one would have to say, "she was caused to accept the perfume and garlands by her [owner]," because the object, namely the perfume and garlands, is not expressed by the *kta* suffix.

Regarding the second application [of the rule]: according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the fragrance and garland which were caused to be accepted by the wife. Because the verb lacks two objects (*dvikarmaka*), it is the fragrance and garland alone that are expressed by the *kta* suffix. As for the third case ending in "by the wife" (*jāyayā*), it is used in relation to the sense of the causative (*ṇij-artha*).

Even though the wife is the agent [of the action], it is appropriate because the cow is the agent with respect to the acceptance (*pratigraha*), which is the meaning of the base of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Thus, the meaning of the word *vṛtti* here is: "that acceptance which has fragrance and garlands as its object and is the domain of an instigation residing in the wife. Although...

The meaning of the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "the perfumes and garlands which are the objects of that acceptance (*pratigrahaṇa*), wherein the acceptance has the cow as its agent, is the object of the wife's desire, and has the perfumes and garlands as its object.
Nevertheless, it exists precisely by virtue of being a distinct external referent (*anyapadārtha*).

The formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is postulated by reversing the relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*); thus, there is no inconsistency here—this is the general direction [of the argument]. (479) *hrasvāt anyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 1.4.53.

Regarding *hrakroḥ*: the analysis is that *hr* and *kr* are *hrkau*, [meaning] "of those two. Alternatively, it is *hu* and *ku* which are *hrkroḥ*. This is because of the established principle that the analysis of a compound is performed using a word ending in the nominative case, or with its inflection fully established. The term *atibuddhi* and so forth does not carry over here; therefore—

This is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. Since *harati* preceded by *abhi-ava-* has the sense of eating, and *karoti* in the sense of transformation is intransitive, the status of the agent in the *aṇi*-stage becoming the object in the *ṇi*-stage would apply by the rule "atibuddhi," etc.; however, this applies when these two roots have those specific meanings, whereas in other senses they do not.
Because [the rule] would not otherwise apply due to the verb being transitive, this [sūtra] is commenced.
He provides an example for the case where [the agent] has not [previously] been so designated: *hārayati*.

In the state without the causative suffix (*aṇ*), as in "the servant carries or makes the mat" (*harati* or *karoti kaṭaṃ bhṛtyaḥ*), the servant is the agent; that very same person becomes the object in the state with the causative suffix (*ṇi*).
As for the examples when [the suffix] *kha* is applied:

*tṛṇam abhyavahārayati saindhavān* (he causes the Saindhavas to eat grass), *tṛṇam abhyavahārayati saindhavaiḥ* (he causes the Saindhavas to eat grass by means of grass); likewise, *vikārayati saindhavān* (he causes the Saindhavas to undergo a change) and *vikārayati saindhavaiḥ* (he causes the Saindhavas to undergo a change by means of something) should be understood. Now, one might object: if the phrase beginning with *atibuddhi* were not to recur here...
If it is argued that this might be so, yet we do not see any authority for it in that very context, we say: "Do not say so.

For in the rule *a vā iti vibhāṣā*, the author of the Bhāṣya has included this very sūtra among those where the option applies in both ways (*ubhayatrabhāṣā*); thus, the aforementioned doubt does not arise.
It should be stated that for the roots *abhivadi* and *dṛś*, the Ātmanepada [ending] is optional. Regarding *abhivādi*:

the root *vad* in the sense of "speaking a message" belongs to the curādi class and is included among the *ādhṛṣīya* roots. Because it is preceded by the prefix *abhi*, it carries the meaning of "salutation.
This option applies because the Ātmanepada is not otherwise obtained for *abhivadati*, whereas it is already obtained for *dṛś*. [Example: *abhivadati devam*.
The devotee prompts him, [and thus] he salutes: *abhivādayate*. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here by the rule *ṇicaśca*.

But in the active voice (*parasmaipada*), it would be *abhivādayati devaṃ bhaktena* (the devotee causes the god to be saluted). Likewise: *paśyati devaṃ bhaktaḥ* (the devotee sees the god), *darśayate devaṃ bhaktam* (the god causes the devotee to see himself), and so forth.

(480) *abhiniviśaśca* | P. 1.4.47. Regarding *abhinivi*: since *ni* has fewer syllables (*alpāctara*), it ought to have been placed first [in the compound]; the fact that it is pronounced in the reverse order is for the purpose of intending the inclusion of the entire cluster (*saṅghāta*). Thus he says: "preceded by a cluster" (*saṅghātapūrvasya*). By this, the example "if the tip of a grain awn enters into the foot" (*niviśate yadi śūkaśikhā pade*) is included. As for the statement "sometimes not": the sense is that the usage in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*, namely "of those who are intent upon these objects" (*eṣvartheṣvabhiniviṣṭānām*), is the authority here.

(481) *upānvadhyāṅvasaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.4.48. Regarding the rule *upānvadhyāṅvasaḥ*: because of the principle that "a suffix with a non-elided *vikaraṇa* is stronger than one with an elided *vikaraṇa*," only the root *vas* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*, meaning "to dwell" (*vasa nivāse*), is understood here; it is not the root *vas* belonging to the *adādigaṇa*, meaning "to cover" (*vasa ācchādane*). This is the intended meaning.

He states the citation of the *śap* [suffix]: "of the root *vasati* preceded by *upa*, etc. He explains the meaning of the *vārttika*—"there is a prohibition for *vas* when it does not mean 'eating'"—as follows:
"not when it means eating; not when it means eating. In the *vārttika*, the word *artha* [means]...
It expresses cessation. The meaning is that for the root *vas*, which denotes the cessation of eating, the locus is not the object (*karman*).

As in the example: "He fasts in the forest" (*vane upavasati*). If it is asked: "How then does the example 'he has fasted for a day' (*haridinam upoṣitaḥ*) accord with the rule *arthā-karmaka* (Pāṇini 1.4.52)? [The answer follows:]...
Regarding this, they say: the meaning of *vas* here is "staying," while the cessation of eating is implied; thus, there is no fault.
He states the case-governed by the accompanying word (*upapada-vibhakti*) with the rule beginning "ubha-sarvatasoḥ" and so forth.

The term *ubha-sarvatasoḥ* refers to the forms *ubha-tas* and *sarva-tas*; the meaning is that when used in conjunction with those ending in these, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is to be applied. This is because the base form [of *ubha*] is doubled.

The mention of *tasi* here indicates the dual number. In this case, the suffix *ayac* is not applied after the word *ubha*, because as a word of imitation (*anukaraṇa-śabda*), it does not denote a numerical quantity. Thus, according to some, the word *ubha* indicates the word *ubhaya*, since *tasil* cannot occur after the simple form [of *ubha*]. However, in reality:

Even though the suffix *ayac* applies to the scope of the *vṛtti*, since that which is prescribed after the word *ubha* ending in *tas* still exists [therein], it is correct according to the literal reading; this is the position established in the *Manoramā*.
Regarding "dhig": the meaning is that the accusative case must be employed even when joined with the word *dhik*. In this regard—
The predecessors say: "The mention of *ghi* is without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*), just as in the expression *gavityayamāha*.

This is not correct; for if that were the case, then just as in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya* does not apply because it is not at the end of a word (*apadāntatayā*), so too in the instance under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*), the substitution of *jaś* would likewise fail to apply. Furthermore, this [term *ghi*] does not end in the letter *g*.
It should not be suspected that "let it be so," for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the example *haki* being inconsistent with the rule *asya ca daḥ*.
For by the rule *asya ca daḥ*, the substitution of *d* is prescribed for the indeclinable ending in *ka* in conjunction with the addition of *akac*; therefore, [the form] is *dhig*.

It consists precisely of that which ends in a case-ending; however, by the extended application (atideśa) of the rule "an imitation [of a word] is like the original form," it is treated as an indeclinable (avyaya), and thus there is elision (luk) of the case-suffix (sup). If, however, the ancient authors' text consisted only of the statement that *dhik* is indicated without a case-ending, then that would be entirely correct.
Since it is possible to state that the case-ending (*sup*) is elided due to the indeclinable nature (*avyayatva*) [of the word], the citation is made without a case-ending.

In the expression *ubhayataḥ kṛṣṇam*, the meaning is "on both sides of Kṛṣṇa. The suffix *tasi* is used here because [the word *ubhayatas*] belongs to the *ādyādi* group. The accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive. This should be understood in all instances where a case-ending is employed for a governing word (*upapada*).

Regarding this, they explain: in the rule *ubha-sarvatasoḥ*, because of the mutual association (*parasparasāhacarya*) between *ubha* and *sarva* within that group, only the suffix *tasil* [as derived from *tasi*] is understood, and not the *tasi* [from the *ādyādi* group]. Thus, in forms such as *ubhayataḥ*, one should understand that the substitution of *tasil* occurs by the rule *aseśca*; therefore, where...
In the case of *sañjñāyām*, there is no substitution of *tasi* by *sil*; therefore, the second case (*dvitīyā*) does not apply, but rather only the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

The absence of *tasi*, however, is due to the fact that in the rule *aseśca*, the phrase *iṃsarvanāmabahubhyaḥ* is understood as a governing element (*anuvartana*). [The example is] *dhik kṛṣṇābhaktam*. Of that...

The meaning is "he should be censured. The accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive; thus, the meaning is "he is censurable. Some maintain that the accusative is used in the sense of the nominative. [Objection: How is it that there is the form *dhik sūrkaḥ*? [Response: Since it has already been stated that a vocative word must be construed with a verb, the accusative does not apply here because of the absence of connection with the word *dhik*.
In the case of "ambhodhane ca," the nominative case alone occurs. A verbal action (kriyāpada) is sometimes explicitly heard and sometimes implied.

Thus, in this instance, it is to be inferred that "Fie, fool! This is the practice of forbidden acts. However, the meaning of the sentence is that the practice of forbidden acts by a fool who is being addressed is to be censured.

The meaning of the sentence spoken by those who say, "Alas, O charioteer! Alas, O second one! is that it is censurable and constitutes a prohibited act directed toward a fool. As for the statement, "The case-ending denoting a *kāraka* is more powerful than the case-ending of an *upapada*," [it implies that] the nominative (*prathamā*) alone occurs in the sense of address (*sambodhana*).
They say that this is because the vocative case expresses the agent (*kartṛ*) kāraka; however, that is questionable.

For if the vocative were the agent kāraka, there would be no possibility of such an utterance [as "O King, be gracious"]. Nor can it be argued that in cases such as "O King, be gracious," an utterance is indeed possible because, in reality, the King himself is the agent.

It must be stated that even if [the deity] possesses actual agency (*vāstavakartṛtva*), the status of being a *kāraka* case-ending is not obtained. Furthermore, in cases such as "I worship you thus" (*evaṃ tvāṃ bhaje*) or "devotees worship you" (*tvāṃ bhajanti bhaktāḥ*), the addressed deity lacks actual agency; let this matter rest for now. Regarding the expression "higher and higher" (*uparyupari*): how [is it used]?
"In that case, [what is the meaning of] *ṭhuparyuparibuddhīnāṃ carantīsvarabuddhyaḥ*?
To this they reply: the meaning is "moving above those whose intellects are elevated" (*uparibuddhīnām*) or "above those whose intellects are not elevated" (*anutānabuddhīnām*).
Therefore, because there is no repetition (*āmr̥ditatva*) here, the accusative case is not used. Or rather, [it refers to] that which is explicitly prescribed (*pratipadokta*).

Because the Vārttika includes the form where the doubling occurs according to the rule *ṭhuparyadhyadhasaḥ sāmīpye*, and because here there is a doubling for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), there is no possibility of the accusative case. This also applies in connection with *abhitaḥ*, *paritaḥ*, *samayā*, *nikaṣā*, *hā*, and *prati*. Regarding *abhitaḥ* and *paritaḥ*: [the rule is as follows].
And they have explained that this [rule] "and this is seen elsewhere as well" (*etacca ṭhanyatrāpi dṛśyate*) is an elaboration of what was stated previously. [For example:
"He will kill near Laṅkā" (*laṅkāṃ nikaṣā haniṣyati*), according to Māgha. The word "ha" expresses dejection;
thus he says: "his state of being pitiable. Regarding the word *bubhukṣitam*: it means "of one who is hungry" (*bubhukṣitasya*).
This word *prati* is a prefix (*upasarga*) because it qualifies the action (*kriyā*), and not a particle governing an object (*karmapravacanīya*).
Therefore, one should not suspect that its meaning is already covered by the rule "when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*" (*karmapravacanīyayukte*).
(482) [Pāṇini 2.3.4: "When joined with *antarā* or *antareṇa*."
The term *antarāntareṇa* refers specifically to the two particles [as taught by Pāṇini], and not to the feminine form ending in *ṭāp* (i.e.,
*antarā*) or the instrumental case (*antareṇa*), because of their being explicitly mentioned [in the rule] and due to their mutual association (*sāhacarya*).
For example, when "Guru and Bhārgava" are mentioned, only the two planets are understood, and not the teacher [Vasiṣṭha] and Paraśurāma.

Therefore, it is established that what is understood by means of the interval between these two? The meaning is: "What is known as the qualifier of these two? Regarding the example *antarā tvāṃ mām*, the meaning is "between you and me.
However, the accusative case does not arise after the word *hari* (in the phrase *antarā hariṃ*), because the nominative case alone arises due to its being an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation.
"Without Hari" (antareṇa hariṃ) means "excluding Hari. The word *antareṇa* also occurs in the sense of "in the middle of," as in:
"He stood between the two waving chowries, pure as a lotus fiber.
The meaning is: "he [stood] in the midst of the two waving chowries."

Because it is not used in conjunction [with a case-ending], there is no accusative here in the example: *antarā tvāṃ māṃ kṛṣṇasya mūrtiḥ* ("between you and me is the form of Kṛṣṇa"). In this instance, the word *kṛṣṇa* does not take the accusative, because even though the word *antarā* is employed, it lacks syntactic connection with *antareṇa*.
(483) [The term] *karmapravacanīya* [is defined by Pāṇini 1.4.83].

Regarding the heading "the *karmapravacanīyas*": it should be understood that this extends up to [Pāṇini 1.4.90], *itarābhyo 'pi dṛśyante*. The designation (*saṃjñā*) "heavy" (*guru*) is made for the sake of its etymological significance (*anvarthatva*). They are called *karmapravacanīyas* because they have expressed (*proktavantaḥ*) an action (*karman*, i.e., *kriyā*).

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *anīyar* is applied here with the sense of the past tense (*bhūte*) and the agent (*kartari*). Consequently, they do not indicate an action at present.
It is thus obtained. And so Hari says: "This [particle] is not an indicator of an action, nor is it an expresser of a relation;

nor does it imply a verbal root for action, but rather it is a specifier of a relation. For instance, in the expression *anu prāvarṣat* ("it rained after that"), the particle *anu* does not indicate a specific quality of the action.

It is not as in the case of "pleasure is experienced" (*sukham anubhūyate*) and so forth; nor is the relationship expressed by the genitive alone, because it has already been expressed by the accusative. Nor is it as in the case of "he draws the line around the altar" (*vedim ādeśaṃ viparilikhati*), where the word *vi-* implies another action, just as the action of measuring does in the phrase "having measured, he draws [the line]" (*vimāya parilikhati*).

This is because it would otherwise entail the application of a case-ending denoting a grammatical participant (*kāraka*). Rather, since the relationship understood through the accusative case—that "the raining is connected to the recitation"—is specifically recognized as being the relationship between the indicator and the indicated (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*), it is precisely that relationship which is established by the particle *anu* in its specific sense. In some instances, however, [the particle] also indicates a particularity inherent in the action.
This technical designation (*saṃjñā*) proceeds from explicit statement, as in the rules: "The particle *uḥ* is used in the sense of worship" and "*ati* is used in the sense of transgression.
The phrase "having the designation already mentioned" means having the designation *karmapravacanīya*.
(484) *anur lakṣaṇe* | 1.4.84 | [The particle *anu* has the designation *karmapravacanīya* when it denotes a characteristic mark.]

Regarding the statement "this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of 'motion' (*gati*) and 'prefix' (*upasarga*)," one might object: "In the example *apamanu prāvarṣat*, since the prefix *anu* has no connection with the act of raining, there is no connection with the action [itself]; therefore, these two designations do not apply at all. How, then, can this designation be an exception to them?"

On this point, they say: since there is an attainment (*prāpti*) of those two in relation to the action of perceiving (*niśamana*) that which is being traversed, the root [of the verb] remains uncontradicted by mere possibility (*saṃbhāvanāmātra*). Nor should it be argued: "If the accusative case is established simply because it is an object (*karman*), what is the use of this technical designation (*saṃjñā*)?"—for [this applies to] *japa*.
Since there is a desire to express the relationship known as "cause" (hetutva) through the act of perceiving (*niśamana*), and since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is absent—

thereby necessitating the third case (*tṛtīyā*)— this [use of the fifth case] is commenced. Nor can it be argued that, even so, because the meaning "the god rained after perceiving him" is understood, this [fifth case] is merely for the purpose of setting aside the fifth case prescribed for the elision of the suffix *lyap*.

It should be stated that [the word *japa*] receives the designation *saṃjñā*. For when there is elision (*lopa*) of a suffix ending in *lyap*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is employed for both the object (*karman*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); however, in the case of *japa*, there is no intention to express it as the object or by means of other such categories. Furthermore, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is prescribed for the cause (*hetu*), and so forth. This is the intended meaning: regarding the designation of *karmapravacanīya* in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The scope for [the use of] that which is not a cause is, for example, in the expression "lightning flashes following the tree" (*vṛkṣamanu vidyotate vidyut*).

The scope for the third case (instrumental) expressing a cause is, for example, "the family by means of him" (*anena kulam*). However, in the case of "it rained following him" (*apamanu prāvarṣat*), since it expresses a cause that is also a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the third case would apply by virtue of its higher priority [in the grammatical rules].

By the force of the re-enactment of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) in the rule "ṭhanurlakṣaṇe," the second case ending alone occurs, even though it would otherwise be sublated. Nor should one suspect that the purpose of this [present] rule is already served by the sūtra "ṛtīyārthe," for that [sūtra] is governed by the principle of the prior exception (*purastādapavādanyāya*).
Because it is a sublater of only that much—namely, [the meanings] "connected with" (*ahayukta*) and "secondary" (*apradhāna*). "By virtue of its capacity" (*sāmarthyāt*):
the sense is that for this very reason, even the status of being a cause (*hetutva*) is accepted as an object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).
"Along the river" (*nadīmanu*): the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is "relation" (*saṃbandha*).

This [usage] of the second case is due to it being an exception (*apavāda*) to the sixth case; and here, that relationship is expressed by the prefix *anu* as having the nature of accompaniment (*sāhitya*). (485) *Hīne* 1.4.86.

The second [prefix] *upa* is used only after a superior object, not after an inferior one, because of its inherent nature (*śaktisvabhāva*). With this intention, he provides an example: *anu hariṃ...* (after Hari). Regarding the rule *upo’dhike ca*:
by the word *ca* ("and"), the term *hīne* ("inferior") is drawn over from the previous rule; thus he says: "in the sense of 'superior' and 'inferior'. In the case of the superior...
He states that the prescription of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not for the sake of the second case (*dvitīyā*), saying, "the seventh case will be taught";

the intention is that this is by means of the rule *yasmād adhikam*. Even in that sūtra, because the phrase *karmapravacanīyayukte* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*), the technical name is prescribed for that which is "in excess" (*adhika*).
It should be understood that [the suffix] *avaśyam* is indeed required.
(486) *Upa* is used when there is an excess. 1.4.87. In the word *upaharim*, the second case ending is applied as before, but only when there is a sense of superiority (*utkarṣa*).

(487) *Pati*, *pari*, and *anu* [are used] in the senses of indication (*lakṣaṇa*), description of a state (*itthambhūta-ākhyāna*), division (*bhāga*), and distribution (*vīpsā*) [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.90]. Regarding "indication": *vṛkṣaṃ prati*. The meaning is the illumination of that which is related to the tree; and since the relation is that of the indicator (*lakṣya*) and the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), the words beginning with *prati* illuminate this. Regarding "description of a state": *bhakto viṣṇuṃ prati*.

The relationship between Viṣṇu and his devotee as that of the object and the subject is to be illustrated by the examples. The meaning is that the devotee has attained a certain state. "Lakṣmī towards Hari" means that there is a relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) between the portion consisting of Lakṣmī and Hari. "Tree after tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam*): here there is repetition (*vīpsā*).
The meaning is expressed by the repetition itself; however, the word *prati* and others are connected with the verb.

The second case ending occurs only when [the action] is directed toward an object (*karman*). Because the designation of *karmapravacanīya* subordinates the designation of *upasarga*, there is no substitution of *ṣ* (i.e., no *ṣatva*); it is for this very purpose that it was stated: "Words such as *akṣaṇā* are employed in the sense of the object."

This has been explained in the *Ākara*. However, the rule *pañcamyapāṅparibhiḥ* does not apply here, because of its association with the word *apa* in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). In the example *pariṣiñcati*, the meaning is "he sprinkles all around. The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *upasargātsunoti*.
(488) *amirabhāge* |1|4|91|. [The rule states: *mamābhiṣyāt*—"May it fall to my share. The meaning is: "May there be a portion for me.
However, the older commentators (*prāñcaḥ*) offer the counter-example *māmabhiṣyāt*, where the meaning is "may it reach me."

Because the root *ās* becomes transitive by virtue of the prefix (*upasarga*), the word *mām* takes the second case (*dvitīyā*). Furthermore, since the meaning here culminates in "my portion" (*mama bhāgaḥ*), the designation of *abhi* as a *karmapravacanīya*—which would have prohibited [the application of the rule] by the sūtra *abhāge*—is negated;
consequently, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *upasargaprādurbhyām*.
(489) *adhi* and *pari* are meaningless [as prefixes] when followed by *kṛt* suffixes. 1|4|93.

As in: *adhyāgacchati* ("he comes toward"). Here—in *prayāti*, *parābhavati*, and *vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate*—just as *pra* and others serve to indicate a specific sense (*viśeṣadyotaka*), so too do *adhi* and *pari* in these cases.

It should be understood that because it lacks the quality of indicating a specific distinction (*viśeṣadyotakatva*), there is no purpose for its inclusion; however, since it merely indicates the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), its status as a suffix (*pratyaya*) certainly exists. In the rule *gatir gatau*, the word *padāt* is understood as being supplied from the governing context (*adhikāra*);
thus, the word *uta* is stated in order to establish the condition of being "after a word" (*padaparatva*).

(490) *Atiratikramaṇe ca* |1|4|95|. [The sūtra means] "and also in the sense of exceeding. He explains that by the word *ca* ("and"), the term *pūjāyām* ("in the sense of honor") is drawn in from the previous rule—thus, "and also in the sense of honor. *Atikramaṇam* (exceeding) means the performance of more than what is prescribed.

In both meanings, they cite the same example: *ati devān kṛṣṇaḥ* ("Kṛṣṇa surpasses the gods"). Others, however, cite *atisiktam* and *atistutam*; the meaning is that it was sprinkled or praised excessively, or in a more excellent manner. In the sense of "excessive," there is a transgression (*atikrama*), while in the sense of "excellent," there is honor (*pūjā*).
Viveka:
(491) *api* [is used] in the senses of a word-meaning (*padārtha*), possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), permission (*anvavasarga*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*).
1.4.96. *apiḥ padārtha*. *Sarpiṣo’pi syāt*—the meaning is "there might even be a drop of clarified butter. [End of section on] *api*.
He states the result of its being a *karmapravacanīya*: "Because it is not an *upasarga*, there is no *ṣ*.

The meaning is that, due to the absence of the designation *upasarga*, the rule "after *upa* and *pradus*, [the verb] *as*" does not apply here. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of possibility" (*saṃbhāvanāyām*), the meaning is "only in the sense of possibility."

Regarding the passage beginning with "kartṛdaurlabhyāt" (due to the rarity of the agent): the meaning is that the word "api" (even/also), while indicating the rarity of the action of coming into being (*bhavana*) due to the rarity of the agent, is connected with the word "yā" (which denotes the action of coming into being). Regarding "avayavāvayavibhāva" (the relation between part and whole): clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) is the whole; a drop (*bindu*) is the part.
The phrase "this very [particle]" means that it serves precisely to indicate the difficulty of attainment caused by the scarcity of the *bindu*.

Regarding the term "the second": this refers to that which is prescribed by the rule "when joined with an *armapravacanīya*. As for the phrase "but not *api*": it is not the case that when there is a connection with the *bindu*, a connection with the word *api*—which also indicates that [scarcity]—has necessarily occurred.

It should not be suspected that the connection between words is accepted here by way of their meaning; for the word *api* does not indicate the *bindu*. If it is asked, "How then is the *bindu* understood?
listen: that very difficulty of becoming (*bhavana*) which is indicated by *api* implies the difficulty of the agent (*kartṛ*).

In this context, however, it is understood that the agent is the *bindu* alone; for this very reason, it is said "of that which is understood by the force of the word *api*" (*apiśabdabalena gamyamānasya*), and not "of that which is understood by *api*" (*apinā gamyamānasya*). The phrase "because it has been stated" (*uktatvāt*) means "because it has been stated as such. [This is] by means of the expression "the word *api* would be... (*apiśabdaḥ syāt*).
Because it is stated that "it is connected," the implication is that there is a connection with *syāt* (the verb) and not with *sarpiṣā* (the word for clarified butter);

this is the final sense of the meaning. Regarding the phrase *apaḥ stuyāt*: this is an additional statement meaning that one might even praise Viṣṇu, who is beyond the reach of speech and mind. In the case of praising such a being belonging to another—
The sense is: what more need be said regarding the fact that there is capacity?
Here, the word *api* indicates possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), whereas in the previous case it indicated the rarity of the object of that possibility; thus, there is a great difference.
The substitution of *ṣ* does not occur by the rule "ṭhupasargāt sumanoti," etc.,
because the designation of *karmapravacanīya* subordinates the designation of *upasarga*. This should be understood in subsequent cases as well,
such as "api siñca" and "api stuhi," which mean "sprinkle also" and "praise also."

(492) *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge* [Pāṇini 2.3.5]. Regarding *kāla* (time) and *adhvan* (distance): "beyond the end" (*atyanta*) means having transcended the limit (*anta*), which is the cessation (*virāma*); that which is both this and a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is "absolute conjunction" (*atyantasaṃyoga*). The meaning is uninterrupted proximity.
When there is an expectancy as to "by what?", it should be understood from contextual propriety that [the answer] is "by means of qualities (guṇa), actions (kriyā), or substances (dravya).

It is stated that "the second case ending (dvitīyā) shall occur. Because this is explicitly taught by the sūtra, it applies only to those expressing time (kāla) and distance (adhvan). However, the inclusion of the word *svarūpa* (its own form) does not apply here, because [the rule for *svarūpa*] is found in the rules prescribing compounds, namely: "in the case of *kālāḥ*" and "also in the case of continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*)."

By the use of the plural form in the word ‘ālāḥ’, it is indicated that in the rule prescribing the second case (dvitīyā), there is no prescription of the word's own form (svarūpavidhi). For this very reason, he will provide examples for the rule prescribing the second-case compound (dvitīyā-samāsa) such as ‘āsapramitaḥ’ and ‘muhūrtasukham’, as well as ‘māsaṃ kalyāṇī’ and so forth.

The point is that since the designation "object" (*karman*) is prescribed for place, time, and so forth only when they are connected with intransitive roots (*akarmaka-dhātu*), the accusative case (*dvitīyā*)—by the rule "the second [case] after an object"—does not apply here. Regarding the expression *māsasya dviḥ*, the ancient grammarians (*prāñcaḥ*) maintain that the genitive case is applied by the rule "when used with words meaning 'season' (*ṛtu*) or 'purpose' (*artha'), [the word denoting] time is in the locative case. That is not correct; for in that [rule],...

Because the result [of this rule] is precisely the prevention of compounding with a *kṛt*-derived form such as "avirahno bhojanam" through the continued application of the term "śeṣa," they say that here the genitive case is established by the rule "ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe" alone, owing to its being more immediate (*antaraṅga*). This is so even though [the genitive] was already commenced for another purpose.

Regarding the sūtra *ṛtvorthaprayoge*, some hold that there is no obstacle to its application in the case of *dvirahno bhuṅkte* because it is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*). This concludes the second [section]. (493) *svatantraḥ kartā* | 1.4.54 | [The independent agent is called the *kartṛ*].

The agent (*kartṛ*) is independent (*svatantra*). Independence consists in being the substratum of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) which is the primary factor. And it has been said: "An agent is always intended as such when the action is expressed by the verbal root. Although pots and the like lack independence in reality, [in expressions such as] "the pot cooks" or "the firewood cooks," [they are designated as agents].

He indicates that even such usages as "pacantī" (the cooking woman) are indeed correct by stating "the intended meaning. (494) *Sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam* | 1.4.42. [The most effective means is the instrument.]

The most effective means is the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding the word "preeminent" (*prakṛṣṭa*): that whose operation is immediately followed by the production of the result is preeminent. And it has been said: "When, in a particular case, the production of the result from an action is intended to be expressed as occurring immediately after a certain operation, that [operation] is then called the instrument."

It is recorded [in the *Vākyapadīya*]: "By the phrase 'it is intended to be expressed' (*vivakṣyate*), it is indicated that even things such as a cooking pot possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*). And it says: 'In reality, that [instrumentality] cannot be definitively assigned, for an entity is not fixed [in its function];
since we observe the intention to express it thus: "the food is cooked by means of a pot" (*sthālyā pacyate*). This..."

"Being"—that is, the state of being a *kāraka*—as well as that sixfold set beginning with agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth, is not fixed with respect to a particular entity in the same way that the relationship between qualifier and qualified is fixed; rather, it is relative to intention (*vaivakṣika*). For it is not the case that a qualifier is "an ox" in relation to everyone, while "not an ox" in relation to someone else, such that it would be [fixed] for everyone.

It can indeed be stated that [the agent] is merely a qualifier. Thus, when an object is presented by a particular verbal root (dhātu-vyakti), in response to the question "What is the agent and so forth?",
the agent is that which is intended as the substratum of the activity conveyed by that specific verbal root.

It is established that the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the substratum of the result which is non-co-referential with the operation; it is the substratum of either the operation or the result through a relationship mediated by the agent or the object. Furthermore, the operation denoted by the root *pac* (to cook) is manifold. And thus:

When the fire is intent upon such acts as placing [the vessel] on it, pouring in the rice, or adding fuel, then Devadatta, who is the substratum of those acts, is the agent; when it is intent upon flaming, the fuel is the agent;
when it is directed toward holding the rice and so forth, the cooking pot is the agent; and when it is directed toward the separation of parts and so forth—

The rice grains are the agents (*kartṛ*). In the expression “he cooks in a pot” (*sthālyā pacati*), although the pot is the locus of the operation denoted by the instrumental case, it is indeed the instrument (*karaṇa*) and not the agent; for that [operation] is expressed by the verbal root as being the operation of Devadatta and others. Likewise...

When the meaning conveyed by roots beginning with *ad* (to eat) and *khād* (to eat) involves a prompted agent (*prayojyakartṛ*), that agent is [designated as] the object (*karman*); when the same meaning is conveyed by the root *bhakṣ* (to eat), that prompted agent is the object. When the meaning conveyed by roots such as *śī* (to lie down) preceded by *adhi* involves a location, that location is the object; when conveyed by these roots alone, it is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). This should be understood accordingly. By this—

The assertion by some that there is a contradiction between the agent and the object (*kartṛ-karmavirodha*) regarding the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of cognition is refuted. When a person's independence (*svātantrya*) is intended to be expressed with respect to an action denoted by a verbal root, then that person is the agent (*kartṛ*) of that action; and when, with respect to the action performed by the agent, [something] is desired most intensely as the goal to be attained...
Whatever is intended to be expressed at that time is the *kāraka* and the object (*karman*) of that action;
for it is impossible to state in perception that agency and so forth are qualified by specific words, since [the grammatical relation] is not directly perceived.
Furthermore, some maintain that the nature of being an object (*karmatva*) consists in possessing a result produced by an action inherent in another.

In cases such as "the leaf falls from the tree," although there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the agent (*kartṛ*)— who possesses the result of disjunction produced by an action inherent in itself— there would nonetheless be over-extension to the ablative (*apādāna*). Therefore, one must accept that the definition of the object (*karman*) is simply "that which possesses a result delimited by the meaning of the verbal root."

And this being the case, even if one accepts that in transitive verbs such as "he goes to Rāma" (*rāmaṃ gacchati*), the delimitor of the verbal root-meaning is the conjunction produced by the act of going— this being done in accordance with the intended meaning— in intransitive verbs such as "he falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt patati*), [the same principle applies].

Because the status of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) is not postulated for the ground (*ajina*) and other such things in cases like "falling from the tree," there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the ablative (*apādāna*); nor is there any in cases such as "he goes to the village."

They say that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the agent (*kartṛ*), because the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) which produces a result such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is qualified by "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*); and since the word "another" (*para*) here intends that which is different from what is intended as the object (*karman*). That too is refuted by this [very point]: "Rāmam... [etc.]
In cases such as *gamayati devadattam* ("he causes Devadatta to go"), there would be no application [of the definition] to the agent (*gantṛ*),
because the activity of the prompted (*prayojya*)— namely, the act of going produced by the instigation (*preraṇā*) which is the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—
lacks the status of being delimited by the meaning of the verbal root. However, if that were accepted, then for Devadatta...
Because there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the instigating agent (*prayojyakartṛ*) in examples such as *pācayati*;

and because, without accepting the grammatical rules (*śāstra*) such as *atibuddhi*, it would be impossible to determine that in some cases the status of being an instigating agent (*prayojyakartṛ*) is equivalent to the sequence [of action], while in other cases it is simply the status of being an agent (*kartṛ*).

Furthermore, without the grammatical rule "ṭhhṛkroranyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 1.4.53), it would be difficult to justify the optional status of the object in such instances as "he causes the servant to carry the mat" (*hārayati* or *kārayati kaṭaṃ bhṛtyena bhṛtyam*). If you argue that even in such cases the resolution is achieved solely through the statement of the Grammarians, then [we reply]: [The argument continues: If this were so, then... [the text continues with the critique of the opponent's position].

Since it has been stated that "from among [conflicting] designations, only one prevails—namely, that which is subsequent and without scope"—the designation of *apādāna* (ablative), being without scope, overrides the designation of *karman* (object), which has scope; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) resulting from what was previously mentioned.
So what is the point of this laborious effort beginning with the phrase "in that which delimits the meaning of the verbal root" (*hātvarthatāvacchedaka*)?

This might be the case: how can such usages as "you know yourself by yourself" (*ātmānam ātmanā vetsi*) and "you create yourself for yourself" (*sṛjasy ātmānam ātmane*) be consistent, given that it is impossible for a single entity simultaneously to possess the status of agent and object as defined by a single action?

[Objection: This is not a fault, because the designation of the agent (*kartṛ-sañjñā*) by means of a superior [designation] sublates the designations of object (*karman*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and so forth.

For, relying on the distinction of the self (*ātman*) even when it is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), the usage in expressions such as "he kills himself by himself" (*ātmānam ātmanā hanti*) has been established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*). [Objection: But what is the sublater?

"Let it simply be 'karaṇa' (instrument); since the section on *kārakas* is current here, the term 'kāraka' is understood [by context]. For 'sādhaka' (that which accomplishes) and 'kāraka' are synonyms. Thus, with the inclusion of both terms, excellence is obtained"—with this intention, he asks: "What is the purpose of including the suffix -tamap? The other [the opponent], however, [responds] within the context of *kārakas*:

With the intention that the inclusion of the suffix *tamap* is for the purpose of making it known that the principle of primary and secondary (guṇa-mukhya-nyāya) does not apply elsewhere than in this very sūtra, he illustrates the result of that indication with the example: "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*).
However, if this indicated rule were not accepted, the designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa-sañjñā*) would not apply here in the case of "in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu*).
The sense is that [the definition] has its purpose fulfilled in a primary substratum, as in the cases of "oil in ghee" or "butter in curd.

Regarding this, they explained: when the property of being a substratum belonging to the bank is metaphorically attributed to the current due to proximity, then this [definition] serves as a purpose; however, when the word *gaṅgā* itself refers to the bank, [this definition does not apply].

But in that case, there is no purpose [for the locative], because the bank (*tīra*) is the primary substratum (*mukhyādhāra*). In the first alternative, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is figurative (*lākṣaṇikī*); in the second, however, the base (*prakṛti*) is figurative, and so forth. (495) "The third case-affix is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). (Pāṇini 2.3.18).

Regarding the phrase "by Rama": although those factors of action (kārakas) presented by case-endings are indeed qualifiers with respect to the action, nevertheless, those presented by a *kṛt* suffix are the qualificands, because of the statement: "Nouns have as their primary meaning the substance (*dravya*).
[This applies] to the result and the operation presented by the verbal root (*dhātu*). As for the object [of the action], it is... *han*... [is killed].

Thus, while there is no reversal of the qualifier-qualified relationship when co-occurring with an object-denoting finite verb (*ākhyāta*) such as "it" (in *ityādi*), there is indeed such a reversal when co-occurring with an object-denoting kṛt-affix (*karmakṛt*) such as "hata" (in *hata ityādi*). And so, [the relation] residing in Rāma...

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: Vālī is the substratum of the separation of life-breaths (prāṇaviyoga) which is to be accomplished by the operation of the arrow—such as piercing the body—which itself is the object of the operation [of the agent], such as the drawing of the bow.
However, in cases such as "he kills Vālī" (*vālinaṃ hanti*) or "Vālī is killed" (*vālī hanyate*), [the analysis differs].

The meaning to be understood is that the activity of Rāma, such as the drawing of the bow, has as its object the operation of the arrow— such as the piercing of the body— which is conducive to the separation of the life-force residing in Vālin.

In this regard, the following should be noted: "The verbal root (dhātu) is traditionally held [to denote] the result and the operation, while the personal ending (tiṅ) is held [to denote] the locus; the operation is primary with respect to the result, but it is a qualifier for that which is expressed by the personal ending. Here, the construction is "the verbal root is traditionally held... The word "as the denotator" (vācakatvena) is to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding the phrase "while the personal ending is held [to denote] the locus":

By changing the case ending, it is connected with the word "mṛtā" (dead). "As a denoter" is as explained previously. The mention of "tiṅ" (verbal suffixes) is illustrative, because some second, third, and other case endings also have "mere substratum" as their meaning. Now, if they thus have the substratum as their meaning—
There would be a confusion between the second, third, and seventh case endings. This is not so;

for there is a distinction based on the difference in what is being defined (*nirūpaka*). The locus as defined by the fruit (*phala*) is the meaning of the second case. However, that which is defined by the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the meaning of the third case. [Furthermore,] it is defined by the operation through its own substratum (*svāśraya*).

It is inferred through deliberation that the meaning of the locative case is both "determined by the fruit" (*phalanirūpita*) and "not determined by the fruit" (*aphalanirūpita*), as in the example: "The plough is the primary [instrument]. And this is merely the general rule; for it has been stated that when used in conjunction with a *kṛt* suffix denoting the object (*karmakṛt*), there is indeed a reversal. However, in cases such as "Devadatta worships Hari," etc., [the distinction holds].

The predominance of the operation (*vyāpāra*) is indeed established. Here, the relation is identity between the meanings of the base and the suffix—namely, the hare and its locus—and the hare and the locus denoted by the *tiṅ*-suffix (the agent). Thus, the sentence-meaning is: "the operation, which has Devadatta as its locus, is currently present and is conducive to that pleasure which has the hare as its locus. Nor should it be thought that the status of being a locus (*ādhāratā*) itself is what is denoted; for that would result in excessive complexity (*atigaurava*), as the property of being a locus residing in that [hare] would have to be the delimitor of the denotability (*vācyatāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, it would result in a violation of the natural intent of rules such as *Pāṇini 2.3.2*: *karmaṇi dvitīyā* ("the second case ending is used for the object").

For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya also says: "The meanings of the *sup*-suffixes include the objects (*karman*) and so forth, as well as number; and likewise for the *tiṅ*-suffixes. What is the purpose of the condition *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed")? [Consider: *hariḥ karoti* ("Hari does"). *pācakaḥ* ("cook")—here the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). *śābdikaḥ* ("grammarian")—[this is derived] from the rule *'abdadarduraṃ karoti' iti ṭhak*. *kṛtaviśvaḥ* ("one by whom the universe was made")—the meaning is "the substratum of the action of making whose object is the universe" (*viśvakarmakakṛtyāśraya*). *jīvanaḥ* ("one who lives by means of this")—here the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). There is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) [of the application of the rule] to words such as *prakṛti* ("nature") and others. Regarding the phrase "to *prakṛti* and others": this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).
By this, forms such as *āmnā sutīkṣṇaścaritena dāntaḥ* ("by his lineage he is sharp, by his conduct he is self-controlled") are established. [Also] *cāririti*.

The meaning is "handsome. Since no verbal action (*kriyā*) is explicitly heard and there is an absence of both agent (*kartṛ*) and instrument (*karaṇa*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would here be expected. However, this is established by the fact that the implied action of "doing" (*karoti*) functions as the instrument;
for it is intended that the base itself (*prakṛti*) serves as the instrument, in order to exclude any other instrument.

The meaning is that this person was made beautiful by his very nature, and not by ornaments and the like. "Generally a performer of sacrifices" (yājñika): this too is established as an instrument with respect to the implied action of knowing; for the meaning is that people know him to be a performer of sacrifices because of his abundance of ritual conduct and so forth.

"By Gautra, Gārgya": the meaning is that "Gārgya is his *gotra*. Here, the nominative case would have been expected. However, because the sense is "I am known as a Gārgya by my *gotra*," the instrumental case is established here as well.

Regarding "he goes along with [on] level ground" (*samena eti*), etc.: in the sense of "he goes on level ground" and so forth, the accusative case is used for the object after the words *sama* and *viṣama*.
The third [case ending] is established here as well, because it is accepted that even the *path* (*panthā*) functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act of going.
(496) "And [the word] *div* [takes the third case] as the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.43).
Regarding the example *dvidroṇena*: the aggregate of two *droṇas* is *dvidroṇa*.

Due to its inclusion in the *pātrādi* group, there is an absence of feminine gender. The meaning is "grain related to two *droṇas*. Here, the genitive case would have been expected; however, since the word *dvidroṇa* refers to a price consisting of grain measured at two *droṇas*, and that [price] functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the purchase, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is established here as well—this is the general direction. [The word] *ca* (and) [is used].

By the recurrence of the word *karaṇa* (instrument), or by the downward extension (*apakarṣaṇa*) of the term *anyatarasyām* from the subsequent rule, "In the act of purchasing, [the person] to whom [something] is given is optionally [called] *saṃpradāna*," the two technical terms are established as optional alternatives (*paryāya*). In this context, the inclusion of the particle *ca* (and) serves to indicate a conjunction (*samuccaya*). By means of that, [in the example] *anasā*...

In the word *anasadviva*, both [the suffix] *aṇ* in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the third case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) are simultaneously established by the rule *divyatīti*. Furthermore, the non-elision (*aluk*) [of the case-ending] occurs by the rule *anasaḥ saṃjñāyām*. Moreover, in the example *akṣairdevayate devadatto yajñadattena*, because the root is transitive (*sakarmaka*), when the suffix *ṇic* is applied, the agent (*kartṛ*) [becomes the object].

By the term *atibuddhi*, it does not possess the status of an object (*karman*); consequently, by the rule *ṭhaṇāvakarmakāḥ*, the *parasmaipada* (active voice) ending also does not occur. Now, one might object: since the co-occurrence of the designations "object" (*karman*) and "instrument" (*karaṇa*) was intended for the sake of the suffix *ka* in the rule *āna-sādeḥ*, in the example *akṣān dīvyati*, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) alone should apply due to its higher priority, and not the second case (*dvitīyā*).

If it is asked [why], they say here: because its application under the rule "the second case ending is used for the object" (*karmani dvitīyā*) occurs according to the view that grammatical operations take place at the time the word is produced (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the designation "second case" (*dvitīyā*) prevails due to its lack of any other occasion [for application].
This might be so—even though the object is already expressed in the example "the dice are being played with" (*dīvyante akṣāḥ*).

Since the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is not expressed [by the suffix], the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would be required. Similarly, in the example "evanā akṣāḥ" (dice for gambling), even though the status of being an instrument is expressed by the suffix *lyuṭ*, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would be required because the object (*karman*) is not expressed. This is not so;
for in this case, there is only one power (*śakti*) which is associated with two designations (*saṃjñā*). And thus, in that single [power]...

When one [participant] is expressed by the verbal suffix (*śakti*), because the other is also expressed, there is expression (*abhidhāna*) in both cases; it is not the case that [either] is unexpressed (*anabhihitatva*).
(497) *sahayukte ’pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19).

Regarding the rule *sahayukte* (Pāṇini 2.3.19): although it could have been stated simply as *sahenāpradhāne* ("with the word *saha* when [the agent] is not the primary factor"), he says *sahārthena* ("with a word having the sense of *saha*") in order to include the term *yukta*.
The meaning is: "with a word whose sense is 'together with' (*saha*), 'along with' (*sākam*), 'in company with' (*sārdham*), and so forth. The example given is *putreṇa*.

The connection with the action of coming belongs to the father directly through the word (*śābda*), whereas for the son it is only implied by the sense (*ārtha*); it is on this basis alone that his [the son's] non-primacy (*aprādhānya*) is stated. Indeed, the mention of "non-principal" could have been omitted. Nor does this result in the application of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) to the father as well; for in that case, [the father is used] merely in the sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*).

Because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), [the application of the rule] occurs first. Nor should it be argued that the mention of "non-principal" (*apradhāna*) is necessary to prevent the third case ending from applying even to the father in cases where the first case ending does not otherwise apply, such as in the example *utreṇa saha pitur āgamanam* ("the arrival of the father with the son-in-law"), since there the father would be the principal; for [in such cases], the third case ending would indeed apply to the father.

Because the case-ending denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) or object (*karman*) is more powerful, the genitive alone is applied there by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*; such is the direction [of the argument].
(498) *yenāṅgavikāraḥ* || 2.3.20 ||

Regarding the phrase "by which limb" (*yenāṅgena*): by the pronoun *yena*, it is precisely the limb—which constitutes the primary meaning—that is grasped, due to its proximity. And that [limb] is necessarily modified, for a modification of the whole body cannot occur through an unmodified limb; this is what he expresses by saying, "by which limb, when modified. [This refers to] the possessor of the limbs (*aṅgin*).
Thus, the intention is that in the Sūtra the word *aṅga* ends in the suffix *ac* (added after the class beginning with *arśas*).

(499) [Pāṇini 2.3.21] *itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe*. He establishes that matted hair (*jaṭā*) serves as a characteristic mark of such a state: "made known by matted hair" (*jaṭājñāpya*). That which is made known by means of matted hair—
The meaning is that he is distinguished by the state of being an ascetic (*yatāpasatva*).

(500) *saṃjño ’nyatarasyāṃ karmaṇi* |2|3|22|. Regarding *saṃjña*, only the root *ñā* in the sense of "perceiving" (*avabodhana*) is taken here, and not *anī* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāva*).

Because that [root] is intransitive, and because the initial portion of the suffix *ṅs*, namely *añ*, is considered *lākṣaṇika* (derived) due to having been produced by the elision of *an* according to the rule *allopo’naḥ*, he says— with this intention— "of the root *jñā*"— in the phrase "he recognizes" (*saṃjānīte*).

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is applied by the rule *aṃpratibhyāmanādhyāne*. When used with a *kṛt* suffix, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone is used according to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]; for example, "the father is known by the son" (*pitur sañjñātā*). However, in the sense of *ādhyāna* (intense longing), one says "he intensely longs for his father" (*pitaram vā sañjānāti*). Haradatta, however, says that in the sense of *ādhyāna*, the rule *adhīgartha-* applies because it is subsequent [to the rule *aṃpratibhyām-*].

The sixth [case]—as in "he perceives from his mother"—is not [applicable here]; for it is established in the *Manoramā* that this is because of the governing rule of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). (501) *Yenāṅgavikāraḥ* 2.3.20.

Regarding the phrase *yenāṅga*: by the pronoun *yena*, it is the very limb (*avayava*) which constitutes the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) that is grasped, because of its proximity. And that [limb] is indeed modified. For a modification of the whole body (*śarīra*) is not possible through an unmodified limb;
this is what he expresses by saying, "by whichever limb is modified. [This refers to] the possessor of the limbs (*aṅgin*).
Thus, the intention is that in the Sūtra, the word *aṅga* ends in the suffix *ac* added after the class beginning with *arśas*.
(502) Regarding the rule *itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.21):
he establishes that matted hair (*jaṭā*) functions as a characteristic mark of such a state by saying "made known by matted hair" (*jaṭājñāpya*). That which is made known by the matted hair—
The meaning is that he is distinguished by his asceticism (*yatāpasatva*).
(503) *saṃjño ’nyatarasyāṃ karmaṇi* |2|3|22|. Regarding *saṃjña*: only this root *ñā* in the sense of "understanding" (*avabodhane*) is taken here, and not [the root] *anī*.

Regarding the word "prādurbhāve" (in the sense of manifestation), it is because that [root] is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Furthermore, with the intention that the portion "ñ" preceding the "ṅs" has become *lākṣaṇika* (derived) due to the elision of "an" by the rule "ṭhallopo ’naḥ," he says: "of the root *jñā*"—namely, "saṃjānīte."

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is applied by the rule *aṃpratibhyāmanādhyāne*. Since it is subsequent [in the order of the Aṣṭādhyāyī], the genitive case alone is used by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*, as in "the father is recognized by the son" (*putreṇa pitā saṃjñātaḥ*). However, in the sense of *ādhyāna* (intense longing), one says "he intensely longs for his father" (*pitaram vā saṃjānāti*). Haradatta, however, says that in the sense of *ādhyāna*, the rule *adhīgartha-* applies because it is subsequent [to the rule *aṃpratibhyām-*].

As for the sixth [case], it is said that [the genitive] occurs because [the mother] recognizes [the child]; however, that is not so, for it is established in the *Manoramā* that in that instance [the genitive] falls under the heading of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). (504) [The rule] *hetau* (Pāṇini 2.3.23).

Regarding the word *hetau*: here, "cause" (*hetu*) is understood in its worldly sense as that which serves as a means to achieve a result, and not in its technical (grammatical) sense defined by the rule *'atpratyayojako hetuśca'*. Since the latter [technical] cause is assigned the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) by the particle *ca* [in that same rule], the third case ending would already be established for it simply by virtue of its being an agent; therefore, he says: "in the sense of a cause."
And so forth. Now, one might object: "Since even a worldly cause (laukika-hetu) is established as having the status of an instrument (karaṇa), what is the purpose of this [definition]?
Anticipating this doubt, he states the distinction between the state of being a cause (hetutva) and the state of being an instrument (karaṇatva) with the words "substance and so forth" (dravyādi).
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), qualities (guṇa) and actions (kriyā) are to be understood. [Thus, it refers to that which is] defined by substance, quality, and action.

The meaning is that being a cause (*hetutva*) consists in residing in both that which is devoid of operation and that which possesses operation. As for "being an instrument" (*karaṇatva*), the meaning is that it consists in residing in that which possesses operation and is defined solely by reference to an action (*kriyā*).
Thus, because there is a distinction between being a cause and being an instrument, one should not suspect that the one is superfluous (*anyathāsiddhi*) in relation to the other.

This is the state [of being]. And it has been said: "The cause (hetu) has substance and so forth as its object; the agent (kāraka) is that which possesses a restricted action; however, when no operation is observed, the instrumental cause (nimitta) is accepted as the cause. He illustrates the causality with respect to substance: "A jar by means of a staff. The meaning is: "A jar having the staff as its cause. In this case...

The point is that whether there is an operation (*vyāpāra*) or not, because it lacks connection with the act of direct perception (*sākṣātkriyā*), it does not possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*). He provides an example regarding the object of an action: "seen through merit" (*puṇyena dṛṣṭaḥ*).
Here, by the word "merit" (*puṇya*), the supreme *apūrva* is meant, and of that...

The point is that even though it is possible for the act of seeing turmeric (*haridrā-darśana*) to be connected with the action, it does not possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) because it lacks an intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*). However, when sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like are intended by the word "merit" (*puṇya*), then it certainly possesses an intermediate operation; thus, [the designation of instrument] occurs precisely by the rule *kartṛ-karaṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.18).
The third case is established. Regarding qualities (*guṇa*), however, examples such as "a white color by means of *uṇi*" (*uṇyena gauravarṇa*) should be cited.

But in cases such as "an ascetic by means of his matted hair" (*aṭābhis tāpasaḥ*), since there is an intention to express the relationship between the indicator and the indicated (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*), the cause (*hetu*) is not intended; therefore, the third case does not apply by this [rule].

They say that [the rule] beginning with *ṭhita-stambhū-talakṣaṇe* has been commenced. On this point, some speculate that since the status of being a cause (*hetutva*) is common to substances (*dravya*) and so forth, the usage in such expressions as *āṇena hataḥ* ("struck by the goad") would be established by the very rule *hetu* alone; therefore, the mention of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) in the sūtra *kartṛ-karaṇayoḥ* could be dispensed with.
It is possible [to accept this], yet the technical designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) is necessary for the sake of rules such as *araṇādhikaraṇayośca*.

Others, however, maintain that if something is the most effective means of accomplishing an action and is intended to be possessed of an operation (*vyāpāra*), it is an instrument; otherwise, it is a cause (*hetu*). As for things like a staff, which are the most effective means of accomplishing a substance, even though they possess an operation—

It is precisely the state of being a cause (*hetutva*). And thus, in cases such as "Rāma killed [him] with an arrow," when one intends to express merely that the arrow and so forth are the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) of the act of killing, then the third case ending is applied by the rule *hetau* alone. [The meaning is: "the substratum of the separation of life, which is to be accomplished by the operation of the arrow. Thus...

However, they say that when there is an intention to express [the agent] as being engaged in an operation (*vyāpārāviṣṭatva*), since the status of being a cause (*hetutva*) is not intended to be expressed, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is initiated for the instrument (*karaṇa*) by the rule "kartṛkaraṇayoḥ... (Pāṇini 2.3.18). The phrase "the result also" is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra "pratyayaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.1). Regarding the example "adhyayanena": *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The full context of the example "adhyayanena" typically refers to the attainment of a specific state through study, such as "he becomes a scholar by means of study" (adhyayanena paṇḍitaḥ).*
