Since the dative case also occurs when one intends to express "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*), this instrumental case is presented as an alternative to the dative. For example:
*adhyayanāya vasati* ("He dwells for the sake of study"). Regarding this, some refine the analysis as follows:
in the expression *adhyayanena vasati*, the dwelling has study as its cause (*adhyayanahetuka*), just as in the phrase *aṇḍahetu ko ghaṭaḥ* ("a jar caused by an egg").

Even if this meaning is accepted, there is this distinction: the relation between the study and the fruit is identity (*abheda*), whereas the relation with the state of being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*) is that of a qualifier (*nirūpakatā*). Consequently, [the activity] is conducive to residing in that which is the substratum of the state of being a benefactor as qualified by the study, which is non-different from the fruit.

The meaning is "operation. In the case of "the jar [is produced] by the staff," however, the meaning is that the jar is the locus of the state of being assisted (upakāryatva), as determined by the state of being an assistant (upakārakatva) residing in the staff.

For that which is to be assisted is precisely that which is to be accomplished (sādhya); and the fruit (phala) is also that very same thing. [This applies even when it is] "being understood" (gamyamāna).

By the word *ṭhapi*, the expressed action (*śrūyamāṇakriyā*) is included. The intended meaning is that it is not only the expressed action that serves as the motivator for the case-ending (*vibhakti*), but also the implied one. Regarding the term *sādhanā* (means/realization):
the meaning is that it refers to the sense of the verbal root (*dhātu*) which constitutes the base (*prakṛti*) in the form *ādhyam*.

Regarding the term *aśiṣṭa* (unrefined): it is established in the *Manoramā* that this is indicated by the rule *āṅaśca sā ceccaturthyarthe* ("and after *āṅ*, [there is *ṣatva*] if that [following word] has the sense of the dative"). Some here explain it as follows: the portion "unrefined usage" (*aśiṣṭavyavahāra*) is indeed based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*), while the other portion...

Regarding the phrase "established by an indicator" (*jñāpakasiddha*): in the example *dāsyā saṃyacchate*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffix occurs because of the rule *āṅaśca sā ceḥ*; and the substitution of *yaccha* for *yam* occurs because of the rule *āṅrdhmoḥ*. In the word *kāmuka*, the suffix *ukañ* is applied according to the rule *aṣapatapadetyādi* after the root *kam*. Thus ends the third [section].
(505) That which one aims at by means of an object is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

1.4.32. [The word] "by means of an object" (*karmaṇā*): the use of this great technical term is for the purpose of establishing a definition that accords with its etymological meaning. It is called *saṃpradāna* because it is "properly given to" (*samyak pradīyate*) it. For this very reason, he says: "of the act of giving" (*dānasya*).

The meaning is that the *kāraka* which the agent (*kartṛ*) intends to connect with, or desires to connect with, through the act of giving (*dānakriyākarmaṇā*), is designated as the recipient (*sampradāna*). By this [definition], there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "he leads the goats to the village" (*ajāṃ nayati grāmam*) or "he places his hand on the tree" (*hastaṃ nidadhāti vṛkṣe*). Giving...
Furthermore, [giving] consists in the production of another's ownership preceded by the cessation of one's own ownership, for the purpose of non-reacquisition.

For this very reason, it does not occur in cases such as "he gives the garment to the washerman," because in that instance the verb *dadāti* (to give) is used figuratively. And this is the view of the Vṛtti; however, according to the Bhāṣya, there is no insistence on [the term being] etymologically descriptive.
This is because of such usages as "The potter gives a slap to his pupil.

As for the usage "He gives to the goat," it will occur when there is an intention to express [the goat] as a *śeṣa* (a residual relation). Nor should one fear an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "He leads the goat to the village," because with respect to the goat...

Because the village lacks the status of being the residual beneficiary (*śeṣin*). For by the statement "he aims at whom," the status of being the residual beneficiary is obtained for that which is indicated by "whom" (*yam*), and the status of being a subordinate factor (*śeṣatva*) is obtained for the object (*karman*); however, since the Brahmin possesses the status of being the residual beneficiary with respect to the cow, it receives the designation of recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Here, *abhi*... [pra]...

The three words *eti*, *ityetad*, and *padatrayam* do not form a compound. Haradatta maintains that this is because the Vārttika—"A compound of a finite verb (*tiṅ*) with [words] meaning 'like' (*udāvat*) or 'possessing motion' (*gātimat*) should be stated"—is restricted to the domain of Vedic meter (*chandas*). However, if it were applicable to the common language (*bhāṣā*), then in examples such as *yat prakurute*, the suffix *su* would arise due to the presence of a compound.

It might be argued: having accepted the neuter gender for the universal gender-marker (liṅgasarvanāman), even when the elision (*luk*) is applied by the rule "vamornapuṃsakāt," the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] would still occur by the rule "hrasvo napuṃsake-"; however, in the case of the form *yatprakurvīran*, there would be the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). Therefore, [the necessity of] the aforementioned Vārttika...

It is indeed appropriate that [the recipient] is the object of desire (*cchandoviṣayatva*). Regarding the term *dānīya*: by virtue of the rule of abundance (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *anīyar* is applied in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of an action" (*kriyayā*): since an action cannot be a grammatical object (*karman*) in the technical sense, the designation [of "recipient"] would not apply to one intended [as such] through that action; therefore, this statement [is made]. And this [applies to] "that which has a verb-meaning as its subordinate word" (*kriyārthopapadasya*).

This is established by the rule *karmaṇi sthāninaḥ*. In cases such as *patye śete*, there is no contradiction in accepting meanings such as "she lies down in order to please her husband. However, according to the view of the author of the Bhāṣya, this is established by the very rule *karmaṇā yam abhipraiti*.

"Since even an action (*kriyā*) is acquired through [the factors of] non-perception, desire, and determination, it too is an artificial object (*karma*)," as they have stated. Nor should it be argued that, even so, because there is an absence of the status of being the object of the verb *dadāti* (to give), the rule "that which one intends by means of an action" must necessarily apply here.

Because the Bhāṣya accepts that the designation [of *saṃpradāna*] is based on its etymological meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*). But then, in cases such as "he makes this mat" (*enaṃ kaṭaṃ karoti*) or "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), there would follow the undesired consequence of [the object] being a *saṃpradāna*.
Thus, by the force of these two rules, since *karman* and *saṃpradāna* would be interchangeable, [one might ask]: "To whom for the sake of whom? (*aṭāya...*)

If it is argued that there would also be the undesirable application [of the term *karman*] in cases such as "he makes [her] do" (*karoti*), they say in response: in the case of "she lies down for her husband" (*patye śete*), which is a context where [the verb] is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the designation of *saṃpradāna* (recipient), which finds its scope there, is sublated by the designation of *karman* (object), which has no other scope; therefore, there is no possibility of the undesirable consequence. Nor is this so...

It should not be argued that the rule "the second and fourth [case endings] are used after a word denoting an object of excessive action" (*atyarthakarmaṇi dvitīyācaturthyau*) is absolutely necessary, and therefore its rejection found in the *Bhāṣya* is inconsistent; for the rejection in the *Bhāṣya* is merely a statement made in the spirit of boldness (*prauḍhivāda*). This is the direction [of the argument]. It might be [objected]: regarding the act of giving...

Since it is for the sake of that [recipient], the fourth case ending is already established by the rule for "being for the sake of" (tādarthya); what is the use of this technical designation "recipient" (saṃpradāna)?
Do not say so. For the recipient exists for the sake of the act of giving, but the act of giving does not exist for the sake of the recipient;
this is because grammatical factors (kārakas) exist for the sake of the action.

The designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) is applied to the "object" (*karman*), and the designation of "object" is applied to the "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*). Regarding the statement "the object is designated as the instrument," and so forth: this is a Vedic usage. For this very reason, the objection that [this rule] is established by means of a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*) is rejected.

(506) *rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ* |1|4|33|. [The word] *rucyarthānām*: those whose meaning is "to please" (*ruc*) are *rucyarthāḥ*; of these. [The word] *prīyamāṇaḥ*: from the root *prīñ* in the sense of "satisfying," the present passive participle (*liṭ*) is formed. For example: *haraye rocate* ("it pleases Hari"). [In this case, *hariṃ*...]

The meaning is "he pleases. This statement is made because the designation of the object (*karmasaṃjñā*) would otherwise apply. Although the root *ruc* is also listed in the sense of "shining," nevertheless, shining is not intended here;
thus he says: "desire whose agent is another. For this very reason, [the example] "the sun... [is given].

In the example *rocate dikṣu*, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) does not apply because the sense is that of "shining. [The commentary states: "because of the pleasure residing in Hari. By this, it is stated that here the agency of another refers to the fact that the substratum of the pleasure has another as its agent. [The example is: *modakaḥ pathi*.
The sense is that Devadatta alone possesses the state of being pleased (*prīyamāṇatva*), and not the path; therefore, the path does not have the status of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
However, in the absence of the word *prīyamāṇa* (being pleased), the path would also [be considered a recipient].

(507) AŚ 1.4.34: "In the case of the roots *ślāgh* (to praise), *hnuṅ* (to hide/shame), *sthā* (to stand), and *śap* (to curse), the one who is intended to be informed (*jñīpsyamāna*) [is the recipient]."

The roots *ślāgh* (in the sense of praising), *hnuṅ* (in the sense of taking away), *sthā* (in the sense of stopping from motion), and *śap* (in the sense of cursing). Regarding "he praises Kṛṣṇa": in this view, since the genitive case would otherwise apply by the rule for the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), this statement [of the sūtra] is made. Regarding "taking away" (*hnuti*): [as in] "he conceals Kṛṣṇa from his co-wives."

The meaning is that by hiding [his intention], he makes Kṛṣṇa understand that very matter; or rather, he makes anyone whatsoever understand it. Regarding "tiṣṭhati": by standing [in a certain posture], he makes Kṛṣṇa understand his own intention. The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is used here according to the rule "rakāśanastheyākhyayośca. Regarding "śapati" (he curses).
The meaning is that he makes Kṛṣṇa understand his own intention by means of a reproach. The suffix *taṅ* (ātmanepada) is applied according to the rule "apa upālambhe" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.79).
(508) "In the case of the root *dhṛ*, the creditor [is the agent]. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.35).
The creditor (*uttamarṇa*) [is the agent] of the root *dhṛ* (in the sense of "to owe"). The root *hṛṅ* means "to remain"; here it is used with the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

The creditor is the owner of the wealth. From the root *ṛ*, the suffix *kta* is applied, forming *ṛṇam* ("debt"). In the rule *ṛṇam ādhamarṇye*, the mention of *ādhamarṇya* ("the state of being a debtor") is intended as an illustration of a specific type of legal transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Due to this specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*), even when the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) is the object, the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle ending) appears [at the beginning]. From this very exception, it should be understood that in this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word ending in *niṣṭhā* is placed at the end. "To the devotee" (*bhaktāya*), etc. Here, the devotee is the creditor and Hari is the debtor. Since the root *dhṛ* is intransitive, the agent of the action of releasing (*mokṣa*) in the non-causative (*aṇi*) state becomes the object in the causative (*ṇau*).

[The word *grāma* would then have] the designation of object (*karmatva*). If it is argued that "because of its higher status [in the order of rules], the designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā*) will apply here," then Haradatta states that the designation of cause (*hetu-saṃjñā*) would likewise apply to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*).
Consequently, in the absence of the mention of the creditor, just as with the designation of cause, so too with the designation of locus...
The intention is that the mention of "the creditor" (*uttamarṇa*) is for the purpose of preventing this [undesired] exception. And thus,

even when the mention of "the creditor" has been made, since the technical designation "cause" (*hetu*) would apply by the rule "one who prompts another is a cause," this statement of the designation "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) is intended to set aside that [designation of cause].

They state the conclusion: however, it is established in the *Manoramā* that this rule applies when the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise have been obtained. (509) *spṛher īpsitaḥ* | 1.4.36 | [The object desired by one who longs is called *saṃpradāna*.]
"Regarding *spṛh*, the desired object [is designated as the *saṃpradāna* kāraka]. The root *spṛh* meaning "desire" belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in a long vowel (*-ā*).

Consequently, in the form *spṛhayati*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). [The rule applies] because of its priority; thus, in examples such as *paraspareṇa spṛhaṇīyaśobham* ("mutually possessing desirable beauty") and *spṛhaṇīyaguṇair mahātmabhiḥ* ("by great souls whose virtues are desirable"), [the desired object is indeed the *saṃpradāna*].

The suffix *anīyar* is established when [the object] is expressed as the direct object (*karman*). However, Haradatta and others maintain that when there is a desire to express the object as a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*), the genitive case is also established—as in the example, "Like the wives of a lover, they tremble and long for him.
Furthermore, in the *Vākyapadīya* and its commentary by Helārāja, regarding the construction with the verb *spṛhayati*, the technical designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) [is discussed].
It is established that this designation of "recipient" (saṃpradāna) supersedes the remaining [application of] the sixth case (genitive). And this is appropriate;

for if the desired result were already achieved by the rule "one whom one intends through the action" (*kriyayā yam abhipraiti*), then, according to the opinion of Haradatta and others, the sūtra "that which is desired in the act of *pṛ* [stealing]" (*pṛher īpsitaḥ*) would be rendered superfluous.

Therefore, in accordance with works such as the *Vākyapadīya*, in cases like "araspareṇa spṛhaṇīyaśobham," one should explain that the suffix *anīyar* is used for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) by way of general rule (*bāhulaka*), just as in the example "ānīyo vipraḥ. However, in the case of "umārya iva kāntasya," it is because [the word] has the sense of "trembling" (*trasyanti*).
Some maintain that the genitive form *kṛtārthasya* in the phrase *kṛtārthasya kāntasya* should be interpreted by changing the case-ending as *kāntāya spṛhayantī* ("longing for her beloved").

(510) *krudhadruherṣyāsūyārthānāṃ yaṃ prati kopaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.4.37. [The dative case is used for the object of verbs meaning "to be angry," "to hate," "to envy," and "to be malicious," provided it is the person toward whom the anger is directed.]
Regarding *krudhadruha-īrṣyāsūyārthānām*: *krudh* means "anger," *druh* means "desire to harm," and *īrṣy* means "envy.

*Asūyati* is a verb ending in *yaṅ* from the *kaṇḍvādi* group. The meaning is: those verbal roots whose meanings are similar to the meanings of these [four]. "Harm" (*droha*) means "injury" (*apakāra*), as in the rule *druha drohe*.
This was stated with the intention of the specific reading; or rather, it is a restatement of the meaning as "the desire to kill and malice.
"Intolerance" (akṣamā) means the inability to endure another's prosperity. Since *krudh* and *druh* are intransitive, the genitive case would be required when used with them;
however, since the other two [verbs] are transitive, the accusative case would be required. Now, one might object:

If it is asked: "Let it simply be 'of those things cited as objects' (citedoṣārthānām); what is the purpose of specifically mentioning 'anger and so forth' (krodhādīnām)?"—to this they reply: The specific mention is for the sake of preventing over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to cases such as hatred (dviṣ). By that [rule], [the prohibition applies] in the case of: "He who hates us, and whom we hate."

The fourth case [the accusative] does not occur there, for in that context the meaning of the root *dviṣ* (to hate) is "to take no pleasure in. For this very reason, it is not employed with insentient objects—as in the example, "Devadatta hates medicine. [The rule specifies that hatred] arises only from anger. How then is one to explain the expression, "Why are you angry at someone"? For anger is not itself produced by anger. In this regard—

They explain that *kup* here has the sense of "malice. They say that since the form would be established by the rule *riyayāyam*— just as in the case of *patye śete*— the inclusion of *krudh* and *druh* [in the rule] is of questionable utility.

(511) *rādhīkṣyor yasya vipraśnaḥ* |1|4|39|. [The rule] *rādhīkṣyoḥ*: the root *rādh* means ‘to accomplish,’ and *īkṣ* means ‘to see. Here, however, the meaning of these two roots is the deliberation upon what is auspicious or inauspicious; and with the intention that this [deliberation] is preceded by inquiry (*praśna*), [the genitive is used].

He explains this with the words "Garga, when questioned. Since the two actions, consisting of auspicious and inauspicious forms, are subsumed within the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), these two are intransitive (akarmaka). For this very reason, the suffix *śyan* is applied in the form *rādhyati*, according to the rule to be stated among the *divādi* roots: "after a root ending in *ā* that is intransitive, [the suffix *śyan* is used] only in the sense of increase (*vṛddhi*)."

Since that [suffix] is prescribed only after roots that are intransitive (*akarmaka*) according to the *Gaṇasūtra*, and since it is accepted that the meaning is "the auspicious or inauspicious [result] related to Kṛṣṇa," this statement [is made] when the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise have applied.
(512) *anu-prati-gṛṇaś-ca* | 1.4.41.

In *anuprati*, the genitive case is used after the imitative word *uṇa* (meaning "of the one who is weary"). Since the preceding sūtra uses a dual-number reference (*pratyāṅbhyām*), it is determined that the connection with the verbal root applies to each [prefix] individually;
by association with that, here too, it applies to each individually.

Indicating the connection with the verbal root *dhātu*, he says: "from these two, [the root] *gṛ*. Regarding the word *hotre*: this is a specific rule because the status of being the object (*karman*) would otherwise have applied.
(Pāṇini 1.4.44) "In the sense of 'willing' (*paṇi-kriyā*), that which is other than the agent is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*)."

"The fourth case ending (*caturthī*) should be prescribed in the sense of *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that). Regarding *tādarthya*: that which is for the purpose of a certain effect is *tadartha* (for the sake of that), meaning the cause; the state of being so is *tādarthya*. [The suffix] *ṣyañ* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class. According to the rule: 'The expression of a relationship [between a base and a suffix] following a primary derivative (*taddhita*) or a compound is effected by means of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*')."

According to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the relation is expressed by the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*). Furthermore, that relation is of many kinds and is not restricted solely to the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*); therefore, expressions such as "curd for the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāya dadhi*) are also established.

This is because, although the curd is not produced by the Brāhmaṇa, he is its recipient of refinement (*saṃskārya*). Nor does it follow from this that [the genitive] would also apply after the word "curd."

It might be suspected that the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) should occur; however, even though a relation resides in two relata, it is accepted in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that, like the sixth case, it arises from the qualifier alone. Similarly, in the expression "wood for a sacrificial post" (*yūpāya dāru*), the fourth case does not occur after the word *dāru*. Furthermore, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) by the rule "in the sense of cause" (*hetau*) also does not apply here.

Since [the genitive] occurs only in the domain of the sixth case (genitive), it does not apply here either; rather, only the nominative applies to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Furthermore, one should not mistakenly think that this *vārttika* is unnecessary because the rule "the fourth case [is used] for the recipient" (*caturthī saṃpradāne*) would then be redundant; for it is required for meanings such as "it pleases Hari" (*haraye rocate*).

Because that [the *tādarthya* sense] is also necessary; and because it has already been stated that even in the case of "a cow for a Brahmin" (*viprāya gām*), there is no application of the dative case in the sense of *tādarthya*. This is the general direction [of the argument].
Regarding the rule *klṛpi saṃpadyamāne ca*: as for *klṛpi*, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) due to its inclusion in the *saṃpad-ādi* group.

The seventh case [suffix] occurs after that which ends in such [a word]. Here, "becoming" (*saṃpatti*) means the manifestation of what was previously non-existent. When a verb having the sense of *klṛp* (to prepare/make) is employed, the fourth case is used for that which becomes [the object];
the meaning is that the fourth case is used for that which expresses the transformation (*vikāra*), for it is that which becomes, i.e., manifests.
He illustrates this with the phrase "devotion [becomes] knowledge. The meaning is that it transforms into the nature of knowledge.
When there is an intention to express a distinction between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*), the dative case is used for the word denoting the modification.
However, when non-distinction is intended, the nominative alone is used because of its higher status, as in: "devotion is conceived as knowledge" (*bhaktir jñānaṃ kalpate*). But when...

Even if one intends to express that devotion (*bhakti*) is the source (*apādāna*)—as in the phrase "of the non-agent" (*anikartuḥ*)—nevertheless, because knowledge (*jñāna*) has its agent already expressed, the nominative case alone is used, as in "knowledge is fashioned from devotion" (*bhakteḥ jñānaṃ kalpate*).
With the intention of including the meaning of the root *klṛp* (to be fit/attain), he says "it is accomplished" (*saṃpadyate*), and so forth. Although...
The use of the dative case in expressions such as *bhaktir jñānāya* ("devotion for the sake of knowledge") is established by the very rule for the dative denoting purpose (*tādarthye*);
nevertheless, they say that this statement [of Pāṇini] is intended to produce a cognition in which the relation of being a transformation (*pariṇāmatva*) is the mode (*prakāra*).
And [the rule applies] when something is indicated by a portent (*utpāta*). Regarding "by a portent": it is that which indicates the auspicious or inauspicious fortune of living beings.
An *utpāta* (portent) is a transformation of an existing entity; the meaning is that the fourth case (*caturthī*) should be prescribed when it denotes an object made known by such a portent.
For example, *vātāya*: the meaning is "that which makes the wind known. And [it is used] in connection with *hita* (beneficial). Regarding *hita*: [it refers to the word *hita*].

The sense is that this is understood from the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) of the rule prescribing the fourth case compound (*caturthī-samāsa*). In the same way, it should be understood that the fourth case is also employed when joined with "pleasure" (*sukha*). [Regarding the term] *kriyārthopapada*:
that whose purpose or motive is action is "action-purposed" (*kriyārthā*); that which has such an action-purposed action as its subordinate word (*upapada*) is [the compound].

Although it is not possible for an action (*kriyā*) to function as a subordinate word (*upapada*), nevertheless, in this context, that status is to be understood by means of a word that expresses it. The meaning is: "that which expresses an action whose fruit is another action.

Furthermore, although it is not possible for a verbal root (*dhātu*) expressing an action to function as an *upapada* in the form of a word uttered immediately after it, [the definition still applies].

Since only that which ends in a nominal suffix (*suP*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) possesses the status of a *pada*, nevertheless, the intended meaning here is "having a verbal root as its base" (*kriyāvācakaprakṛtika*).

The extracted meaning is: for that infinitive ending in *tumun* which has such a word as its *upapada*, the fourth case (*caturthī*) occurs in the sense of its object (*karman*). This is based on the rule: "The suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* [are used] when there is an action... (*umunṇvulau kriyāyām*).
With the intention that the greatness of the Sūtra results in the word *upapada*—when it signifies an action—expressing only the action itself, he says:

(514) *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ* | 2|3|14| The word *kriyārthā* means "that which has an action as its purpose. The phrase *sthāninaḥ* is explained by the meaning "of that which is not being employed" (*aprayujyamānasya*).

The term *tumun* is also an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the suffix *ṇvul*; for there is no obstacle to explaining "he goes for fruits" (*phalebhyo yāti*) as "one who brings fruits" (*phalāny āhārakaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*):
the intention is that this [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the second case ending (*dvitīyā*). As for what was stated by the author of the *Prasāda*:

The claim that "the sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (niyama), so that [the designation] may apply only to an unexpressed object (karman) and not to an expressed object" is incorrect; for a restriction cannot apply to what has not already been established. Furthermore, one should not suspect that there is any possibility of such an application here on the grounds of "usefulness" (ādarthya).

Because the act of going (*yāna*) does not have [the eating] as its result; for the act of going has the bringing [of the object] as its purpose. However, that the bringing has the fruit [of eating] as its object is another matter altogether. [Question: What is the meaning of *kriyārthopapada* (“having a word denoting an action as a subordinate element”)? [Example: *praviśa piṇḍim* (“enter to eat the ball of food”). Although the entering of the house is for the purpose of eating, nevertheless, with respect to the act of eating—

There is no status as an artificial adjunct (*kṛtrimopapada*). Nor should it be argued that this counter-example is inappropriate because, since the *tumun* suffix is prescribed for the object [of the action], there is no possibility at all for a dative case to occur with the object of "eating" (*bhakṣi*). For [the rule applies] when...

Regarding the phrase "of that which has a word denoting an action as its upapada," this rule applies specifically to the domain of the sūtra "umunṇvulau kriyāyām"; thus, the term "umunaḥ" is obtained [as the subject], and since there is no lack of relevance for the counter-example (pratyudāharaṇa) otherwise, [the objection] is untenable.

(515) And [the suffix *ṇvul*] is used after a word expressing an action that has the sense of *tumun* (infinitive). 2.3.15. Regarding the phrase "after a word having the sense of *tumun*": since it is established that the sense of that [suffix] expresses an action (*bhāva*)—because the *tumun* suffix is prescribed only for the expression of an action according to the rule “*avyayakṛto bhāve*” (P.
3.4.68)—the mention of “expressing an action” (*bhāvavacana*) once again is for the sake of... [restricting the application].

He says "and [the word] *bhāvavacana*" for the purpose of including specific types of sūtras. Nor should one suspect that the meaning is already established by the rule *ādarthye* alone; [this is said] so that [the designation *kṛt*] may apply only to words expressing an action (*bhāvavacana*), such as in *paktum vrajati*, and not to [words ending in] *ṇvul*, such as in *pācako vrajati*.

This sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). That is not correct, because since the suffix *ṇvul* denotes the agent, it lacks the sense of "for the sake of" (*tum-artha*), and thus it is impossible for it to serve as a restriction. Furthermore, because the agent is primary in relation to what ends in *ṇvul*, there is no sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) with respect to the agent.

Even though there is a possibility of [the suffix] having the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) with respect to the attainment (*prāpti*) as a subordinate element (*guṇībhūta*), [the suffix is still required] because the verbal root denoting the attainment is joined with a dative case.
Why [is it said] "after a word having the sense of *tumun*"? Example: *pacanaṃ vartate* ("cooking is taking place").

Why [is it said] "after a word expressing an action" (*bhāvavacana*)? Example: *pākaḥ* ("cooking"), *tyāgaḥ* ("giving up"). On this point, they say: "Of that which has another action as its object... (*kriyārthopapadasya*).

Thus, since there is no obstacle to explaining [the sūtra] by carrying forward [the word *bhāve*] from the previous rule and modifying it into the ablative case (*pañcamī*), it is possible to state "from that which expresses an action" (*bhāvavacanāt*). Nor should it be argued that, in this way, one ought simply to say "from that which has the sense of √as" (*umarthāt*). For [in our interpretation], the economy of syllables (*varṇalāghava*) is achieved.
"Because resorting to [the status of] respect (*gaurava*) is untenable.

The case ending denoting a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is stronger than the case ending of a secondary word (*upapada*). Regarding the phrase "namas to Hari" (*haraye namaḥ*), however, the connection between Hari and the mental attention (*manaskāra*) is mediated by the act of aiming; that is, [it is] one in which Hari is the object aimed at (*uddeśya*).

Regarding the term "namaskāra": some hold that since there is a delay in understanding the act of enjoining (*uddeśana*) in this way, the case-ending expressing the *kāraka* (the agentive/instrumental) possesses greater force. Others, however, maintain that through the nominal suffix (*upapada-vibhakti*), a general relationship is understood.

The understanding of its specific [meaning], however, depends upon the consideration of context, purpose, and so forth. But because the specific relation—such as being an object (*karmatva*) and the like—is understood immediately through the case-ending denoting a *kāraka*, they say that this [kāraka-usage] possesses greater force. Regarding the phrase "the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) also": one might object, "In connection with words such as *prabhu* (master), let there simply be the genitive."

Anticipating the objection that the word *alam* should be understood as having only the senses of "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*) and its opposite, he says: "it is sufficient for him" (*tasmai prabhavati*). [This refers to the examples] "not even a blade of grass for you" (*na tvāṃ tṛṇam*), and so forth. Now, one might argue that just as with words like *tṛṇa*, the dative case should optionally occur after the word *yuṣmad* as well. This is not so; for in the rule "when disregard is meant" (*anādare*), the term [denoting the object] functions as a qualifier of the action (*karma-viśeṣaṇa*).

Because it is explained that the dative case is used for an action that indicates disregard (*anādara*). For in this instance, it is the *tṛṇa* (grass) that indicates disregard, not the referent of the pronoun *yuṣmad*. One might object: "Let 'I consider you as grass' (*tvāṃ tṛṇaṃ manye*) or 'as grass' (*tṛṇāya*) be cited as examples; what is the use of employing the negative particle *nañ* here? To this they reply: "Having extracted [the essence]..."

There is a Vārttika stating, "The mention of 'contempt' (kutsita) must be made. By this, when the dative case is prescribed for that which expresses something, the dative occurs only if contempt is conveyed by way of its being inferior;
it does not occur when there is an intention to express equality. And such a perception of contempt arises from the negative particle (nañ).
It is stated that "a tvām" is used because [the action] occurs instantaneously in the performance (*prayoga*).
(516) *Manyakarmaṇyanādare vibhāṣā’prāṇiṣu* |2|3|17|. [The word *manya*] is indicated by means of the suffix *śyan*; one might ask: why could it not be indicated by the suffix *yak* instead?

It must be stated [that the rule applies] because of the governing heading *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed"). For when there is a connection with the suffix *yak*, an unexpressed object (*karma*) is not possible. Furthermore, the suffix *śyan* is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for roots belonging to the *divādi* class and others; it is not itself intended to be significant. Therefore, [in the verse]: "Thinking it to be a debt, even the joy of the Raghus [Rāma], with an arrow... [the object is expressed].
The usage *pradhānān nirāsthat* by Bhaṭṭi is thus justified.
It should be stated that [the rule applies] except in the case of *nau*, *kāka*, *anna*, *śuka*, and *śṛgāla*. Regarding the phrase *nau-kāka-anna*:
the sense is that this should be understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*).

(517) *gatyarthakarmaṇi dvitīyācaturthyau ceṣṭāyām anadhvani* 2.3.12. Regarding "the object of a verb meaning motion": why [specify] "meaning motion"? [Consider: *odanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"). Why [specify] "the object"? [Consider: *aśvena vrajati* ("he goes by horse"). In the rule "anadhvani," the term *adhvan* is not taken as a formal designation (*svarūpagrahaṇa*). For instance:

He would have simply said "sati ṭhanadhvanaḥ"; why, then, is there the inclusion of the word *artha*? Because of the indication by the locative case, and because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term *karmaṇi*. For it is only the *artha* (meaning) that can possess the status of being an object (*karman*), not the phonetic form of the word itself; therefore, there is a prohibition of all [suffixes] denoting distance (*adhvan*). And thus:

The Vārttika states: "The inclusion of the word *adhwani* (on the road) [is for the sake of] the meaning of 'object' (*artha*). The sense is that [the rule applies] only when [the road] is occupied by a traveler, based on the Vārttika: "'A prohibition must be stated regarding that which has already been reached' (*āsthitapratiṣedho vaktavyaḥ*).
Here, *āsthitaḥ* means "already arrived at. For in the example *panthānāṃ gacchati* ("he goes along the roads"), the roads have indeed already been reached.

The fourth case ending (*caturthī*) is used optionally. However, when there is an intention to express that [the action] has not yet been attained (*aprāptatva*), then it certainly occurs in that optional case. Here, having removed the restriction *anadhvani* ("not on a path"), the rule is completed as *ṭhasaṃprāpte* ("when not attained"). Therefore, in the example *striyaṃ gacchati* ("he goes to a woman"), since the woman is already attained, the fourth case does not apply. Regarding this, they explain: in the example *ajāṃ nayati grāmam* ("he leads the goat to the village")...

However, the fourth case (dative) does not apply at all here, because it does not have the sense of "going. For in this context, "going" is understood through implication (*ākṣepa*) and the like, but it is not the actual meaning of the root *nī*, since that root signifies "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*). Thus, although it should have been stated as "the fourth case is optionally used for the object of the root *ati*," the mention of the second case indicates that the second case also applies even in the domain of exceptions.

This is for the purpose that it may be so; therefore, the author of the Vṛtti has stated that in the example "rāmaṃ gantā" (one who will go to Rāma), the genitive case characterized by connection with a *kṛt* suffix does not occur. Thus ends the section on the fourth case.
(518) Pāṇini 1.4.24: "In separation, that which is fixed [is called] the *apādāna*."

*Dhruvamapāye*: From the root *dhru* in the sense of "motion" or "stability," with the suffix *ac* (by *pacādyac*), there is the substitution of *uvaṅ* due to its being a *kuṭādi* root. Some say it is from *dhruva* in the sense of "stability"; in that case, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ṭhigupadhāt kaḥ*. Thus, *dhruva* means "stable. He states what is intended by the word *apāya*: "separation" (*viśleṣa*). And so it is.

The resulting definition is: that which, while not being the locus of the action expressed by the verbal root in question, is the locus of the disjunction produced by that [action], is "fixed" (dhruva). And since this, by implication, is nothing other than a limit (avadhi), he says: "becoming a limit. Regarding the word "running":
here, even though the horse is qualified by the action of running, it relates to the action denoted by the root *pat* (to fall) in the context at hand.

The status of being an *apādāna* (ablative point) is not contradicted; however, in the case of the expression “two rams move away from each other” (*parasparasmān meṣāv apasarataḥ*), since the root *sṛ* denotes both movements, the other’s status as an *apādāna* with respect to the movement residing in one [of them] is likewise not contradicted. And it has been stated by Bhartṛhari: "In separation... (*apāye*)...

Whether it be stationary or moving, whether stable or unstable, that which remains fixed because it is not entered by the action is called the *apādāna* (ablative). For example, when someone falls from a horse, the horse is certainly fixed for him because he falls from it; yet, even for that horse, the wall or other such object against which it falls is considered fixed.
"The status of being a limit (avadhitva) with respect to the respective actions of two rams is distinct for each;
likewise, the status of being an agent (kartṛtva) with respect to their own respective actions is distinct for each.
In the case of "he falls from the mountain, [which itself] is falling from the horse," however, [the subject] is the locus of the falling that has the mountain as its limit.

The meaning [of the sentence] is the falling, residing in Devadatta and others, which has the horse as its limit (*avadhi*). In this construction, the referent of the base (*prakṛti*)—such as "Devadatta"—is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the limit, which is the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), through the relation of non-difference; whereas the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) resides in the action of falling.
Furthermore, that limit is a substantive (*dharmī*) characterized by the property of being a limit, and not merely the property (*dharma*) itself.

In the example "the pot from which rice has been taken out" (*uddhṛtaudana sthālī*), the pot is seen to be in grammatical apposition as the limit (*avadhi*) of the act of taking out whose object is the rice; this point is established in the *Manoramā*. Now, what is the purpose of including the term *dhruva* (fixed/immovable) here? Is it not so that [the rule would otherwise apply] in cases such as "he comes from Rāma by means of a cart"?

The term "that" (tat) must be stated in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a cart; for in that case, the technical designation of "instrument" (*karaṇasaṃjñā*) applies because it is subsequent [to the present rule]. Nor is the mention of "the fixed" (*dhruva*) intended to specify the named entity (*saṃjñin*);
since the governing heading is "participant in action" (*kāraka*), the word "participant" (*kāraka*) is already understood, and thus the mention of "the fixed" (*dhruva*) serves [another purpose].
If it is argued that the purpose is merely conceptual (*cintya*), the [authorities] here reply:

if there is an intention to express only the pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*) consisting in the nature of being an agent (*kārakatva*), then in a state where there is no intention to express [it] as the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*), the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) would undesirably apply, resulting in the cart (*śakaṭa*) being designated as the "ablative" (*apādāna*).
The term *dhruva* (constant) is included for the purpose that this [fault] should not occur.
There is a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding the roots meaning "aversion" (*jugupsā*), "cessation" (*virāma*), and "negligence" (*pramāda*). Regarding "aversion":
*jugupsā* means censure; *virama* means cessation; *pramāda* means lack of attention.
The meaning is that the *kāraka* of roots having this sense [of separation] should be designated as the *apādāna*.

Separation (*vibhāga*) is disjunction preceded by conjunction; however, such [physical] separation does not exist here. Furthermore, separation produced by the intellect is not accepted here because it is secondary (*gauṇatva*). Thus, since the rule [Pāṇini 1.4.24] would otherwise not apply, the Vārttika is commenced.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, maintains that this Vārttika is based on the assumption that *jugupsā* and the like denote the cessation [of an action] preceded by those [feelings], because it has been indicated by the inclusion of the suffix *-tamap* that the principle of "primary and secondary" (*gauṇa-mukhya-nyāya*) is not resorted to in the section on kārakas.
He also rejected the sūtras beginning with “hītrārthānām...”.

For, having first apprehended the departure [of an object] through the intellect, one subsequently desists from it upon seeing its defects; thus, there certainly exists here an intellectual departure.

(519) *Bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ* | Pāṇini 1.4.25. Regarding the rule for roots meaning "fear" (*bhī*) and "protection" (*trā*), the cause of fear [is the ablative]. In the *Rāmāyaṇa*, however, in the passage: "The gods themselves are afraid of him when he is provoked to anger in battle," the word "of him" (*asya*) is construed with "in battle" (*saṃyugena*); therefore, it does not function as the cause of fear.
The employment of the genitive case is indeed appropriate.

Nor should it be argued that this would result in "battle" (*saṃyuga*) being designated as the *apādāna* (ablative); for the designation of *apādāna* is superseded by the subsequent designation of *adhikaraṇa* (locative). However, when the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) is not intended to be expressed, the desired result [the genitive] follows.

What is the purpose of the phrase "bhītrārtha" (meaning 'to fear' and 'to protect')? [Consider: "He sees a tiger. Nor should it be suspected that this is barred by [the rule for] the accusative case (*karmatva*), for they say that if the status of being an object is not intended to be expressed, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) would apply by overriding the sixth case of the residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).
The inclusion of the term "cause of fear" (*bhaya-hetu*) has a purpose that requires further consideration; for instance, in the case of "he fears in the forest" (*araṇye bibheti*).
If it is argued that the designation of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) applies because [the word *corāt*] is a term denoting the "other" (*paratva*), the proponents here reply:
in the absence of the mention of the "cause of fear" (*bhayahetu*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) when one intends to express the word as a mere residual factor (*kārakaśeṣa*).
Consequently, the usage "he fears the thief in the forest" (*araṇyasya corādbibheti*) would not be possible.

(520) *parājer asoḍhaḥ* |1|4|26|. [The word] *parājeḥ* [is understood]. [The word] *adhyayanāt* [is understood]. The meaning is "fatigue related to study. This [sūtra] applies when the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise have been required by virtue of being a residual factor (*kārakaśeṣa*). [The example is] *parājayate*.

The suffix *taṅ* (i.e., *ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule "after the prefixes *parā* and *vi*, [the root] *ji* [takes *taṅ*]. In the rule "not having endured" (*asoḍha*), the past time denoted by the suffix *kta* is not intended to be significant. Consequently, forms such as *adhyayanāt parājeṣyate* ("he will be defeated in his studies") are established.

Now, one might object that the mention of "not having endured" (*asoḍha*) is redundant; for in the case of *śatrūn parājayate* ("he defeats the enemies"), the [application of *parasmaipada*] would prevail due to its higher status [in the rules].

This is because the designation "object" (*karman*) is established [by rule]. On this point, they also say: if the status of being an object were not intended to be expressed, the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) would occur, overriding the sixth case-ending for the remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*); therefore, so that this [undesired result] does not occur, the mention of *asoḍha* ("unable to endure") must indeed be made.

(521) *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ* |1|4|27|. [The word] "having the sense of warding off" (*vāraṇārthānām*). As in the example *yavebhyaḥ* ("from the barley"): since he wards off the cow even before it comes into contact with the barley, this rule is commenced because [the previous rule] *dhruvam apāye ’pādānam* would not have applied.

However, in the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra, who accepts that the removal (*apāya*) is merely imagined by the intellect, the futility of this [rule] is quite evident. In the example *gāṃ vārayati* ("he restrains the cow"), the term *vṛñ* belongs to the curādigaṇa in the sense of "restraining" (*varaṇe*).
In the word *ām*, the designation of *apādāna* based on being the most desired (*īpsitatva*) does not apply.

It occurs; for when there is a desire to express the state of being most desired (*īpsitatamatva*), the designation *karman* (object) applies by virtue of its higher status [in the *paribhāṣā*]. Now, one might object that the mention of *īpsita* (desired) itself would be redundant, since in the example "he wards off [him] from the field" (*kṣetre vārayati*), the designation *adhikaraṇa* (locus) would apply by virtue of its higher status. True; however, regarding the *adhikaraṇa*...

This is a counter-example when there is an intention to express the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣa*), because, according to the method previously stated, the purpose of the word [in the sūtra] can be inferred here as well. (522) *antarddhau yenādarśanam icchati* 1.4.28.

Regarding the term *antardhau*: the instrumental case in *yena* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Nor does there arise the contingency of the genitive case due to connection with a *kṛt* suffix, because of the restrictive rule: "When both [agent and object] are possible, [the genitive] is used only for the object. For here, since "of himself" (*ātmanaḥ*) is understood, there is indeed the possibility of both [being expressed]. As for *nilīyate*: the root *iṅ* means "to adhere" (*śleṣaṇe*).

[The root] *div* and so forth [belong to the fourth class]. Now, is the mention of "in the sense of disappearance" (*antardhau*) redundant? For in the example "the thief desires not to be seen" (*didṛkṣate cauraḥ*), the designation of the object (*karmasaṃjñā*) is established by the subsequent rule [P. 1.4.49]. To this they reply: the intended meaning here is "the thief does not desire to see himself," with the thought, "May the thieves not see me"; in that case, [the agent is indeed the object].

When there is an intention to express the status of being a "remainder" (śeṣa), this serves as a counter-example to the previous rule. However, in the *Śabdakaustubha*, it is established that the purpose of the rule "ṭhantardhau" is questionable. (523) Ākhyātopayoge 1.4.29.
The word *ākhyāta* [is used here] with the sense of "not preceded by anything else"; the intention is that the word *upayoga* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that very sense.

He states that *ākhyāta* ends in the suffix *tṛc* by saying "the speaker" (*vaktā*). Regarding "from the teacher" (*upādhyāyāt*): one is called an *upādhyāya* because one studies (*adhīyate*) from him after approaching (*upetya*); it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* by the rule "after the root *iṅ*. As for the study (*adhyayanam*), however...
"The utterance following the utterance of the teacher according to the prescribed rule" refers to the act of singing;

the meaning is that it is the hearing related to the actor (*naṭa*) which has the song as its object. However, if the word *naṭasya* were construed with "song" (*gāthā*), then because [the actor] would lack the status of a grammatical factor (*kāraka*), the [rule] would not apply; thus, the inclusion of the term "useful" (*upayoga*) would be justified.

(524) *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* | Pāṇini 1.4.30. *janikartuḥ*: "Janis" means birth or origination (*jananam janiḥ = utpattiḥ*). The suffix *iñ* is applied to the root *jan* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) by the rule *iñajādibhyaḥ*.
The prohibition of *vṛddhi* [strengthening] occurs by the rule *anivadhyośca*. The term "of its agent" (*tasyāḥ kartā*) is a genitive used in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).
This is a compound, and not a genitive of agency as in the rule "tṛtīyā-ṣaṣṭhyau kārake" (Pāṇini 2.3.27).

He states this very point with the words "of that which is being born" (*jāyamānasya*). By this, one should understand that the mention of the root *jan* here is by means of the suffix *ik*, according to the rule "ik-śtipau dhātu-nirdeśe" (Pāṇini 3.3.108), rather than [the form] *am-a-han-* [from Pāṇini 6.4.98].

The sense is that, having raised the objections regarding the elision of the *upadhā* vowel, the lack of semantic connection, and the impossibility of forming a compound, the aged Mīmāṃsakas reached a resolution in the section on grammar (*vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa*).
Here, the author of the *Vṛtti* holds the view that the mention of the "base" (*prakṛti*) refers merely to the cause, as in the example: "from the *utū* [comes] joy."
This is because of the example provided [in the commentary], "is born. However, the view of the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa is that [the term] refers only to the material cause (*upādāna*);

therefore, he provides an example common to both [the efficient and material causes]—namely, "of Brahmā. Brahmā is Hiraṇyagarbha; and he is indeed the efficient cause (*hetu*), not the material cause. Furthermore, Brahmā is consciousness conditioned by *māyā*; for that [consciousness]...
The Vedānta established doctrine is that [the Self] is the material cause of all effects.

(525) *Bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* |1|4|31|. [The word] *bhuvaḥ*: *bhuvanam* [is derived from] *bhū-*; the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) because it belongs to the *saṃpad-ādi* group. In the preceding sūtra...

He says "of the agent of the root bhū" because the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*), though stated in the compound, continues by virtue of being *svarita*. That from which something originates is its "source" (*prabhava*);
according to the governing rule "and [the suffix] ṭhaÑ is used for a kāraka other than the agent," the suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*).
Anticipating the objection that this [rule] is redundant since the desired result is already established by the rule *janikartuḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.30), he says:

"In that case, it is manifested" (*tatra prakāśate*). This means "it is first perceived. And this meaning is obtained because verbal roots have multiple meanings. Thus, *jani* (the act of being born) here signifies the manifestation of what was previously non-existent (*abhūtaprādurbhāva*).
The sense is that there is a difference in meaning: "origin" (*prabhava*) refers to the first perception of something already established elsewhere.

This group of seven sūtras, beginning with *hītrārthānām...*, has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. The justification for this is as follows: in the case of *caurebhyo bibheti*, the meaning is that one turns away from fear because of thieves.

"Protects" (trāyate) means he turns [the person] away from thieves by means of protection. "Is defeated" (parājayate) means he turns back due to exhaustion. "Wards off" (vārayati) means he turns [the person] away by obstructing their activity.
"Hides" (nilīyate) means he turns back by means of concealment. "Studies" (adhīte)—[referring to one] emerging from the presence of the teacher...

The meaning is that it utters sound. In the case of "the manifestation (prapañca) is born from Brahman," here too the meaning is that it departs from or issues forth from it. In the case of "it originates" (prabhavati), the meaning is likewise an emergence preceded by coming into being. And thus:
"In the sense of departure from a fixed point... (*Pāṇini 1.4.24*).
Thus, the desired form is established by this very [derivation]. However, in reality,

even if one were to somehow justify the usage of words spoken [in such a way] by relying on a function [of the root] whose own meaning is qualified by the meanings of other verbal roots (dhātus) such as "cessation" (nivṛtti) or "emergence" (nissaraṇa), [this would still be inferior] when compared to the presentation of the primary meaning.

The application of the genitive case is unavoidable—as in the expression "he hears the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*)—for indeed, no distinction can be stated between the teacher and the actor regarding their activity conducive to the action.
To offer a rejection by resorting to the "Brahma-weapon" of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*) is not particularly convincing. Thus...

The Vārttika beginning with “*ugupsāvirāma*” must also be commenced; thus, the system of the Sūtras and Vārttikas alone is authoritative here. Furthermore, the mention of the technical bases (*saṃjñin*) such as “*hravam*,” “*hayahetuḥ*,” and “*ṭhasoḍhaḥ*” becomes meaningful, even though those respective technical designations (*saṃjñā*) would otherwise apply by virtue of their being subsequent rules.

When there is an intention to express the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣatva*), as in examples such as *bhāṣāṇām aśrīyāt* ("one should eat from among the languages"), the genitive case is desired; therefore, the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) must be precluded in those instances. This is clearly stated in the *Śabdakaustubha*.

[The rule] *lyablope karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca* ("when there is elision of a word ending in *lyap*, [the sixth case is used] for the object and the locus")—the term *lyablope* means "in the case of the elision of a word ending in *lyap*."
The meaning is that there is no [actual] usage because the sense is already understood. Here, the mention of *lyap* refers to the meaning of *lyap*;
by this, the elision of *ktvā* is also established. For example: *āsane sthitvā prekṣate*, *āsanāt prekṣate*, or *āsanāt prekṣate*.
"And the fifth [case-ending] is used where there is the manifestation of a path or time. Regarding "where [it is manifested]":

the meaning is that the fifth case-ending is used from that which is resorted to as the limit (avadhi) for the manifestation—that is, the delimitation—of either a path or time. Thus, by means of the sense conveyed by the word ending in the fifth case, through its referent...
The first (*prathamā*) and seventh (*saptamī*) case endings occur after a word denoting a path that is being traversed by one who is joined [to it].

It should be stated that the seventh case ending also occurs after a word denoting time (*kāla*). Regarding the rule "after a word denoting time": here too, the phrase "by one who is joined to it" (*tadyauktāt*) is required [as a governing condition]. The example *āgrahāyaṇī* means "that which has the *hāyana* (winter solstice) at its beginning."

Because *prajñā* and so forth belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* (open-ended groups), the suffix *aṇ* is applied in its own sense (*svārthika*). The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule “*ūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*” [Pāṇini 8.4.3]. Regarding the mention of the word *artha*: the intention is that this is due to the traditional commentary (*vyākhyāna*). As for the phrase “for the sake of elaboration” (*prapañcārtham*): one might object that since Amara states, “*itara* is used in the sense of *anya* and *nīca*,” this [term] refers to the meaning of “low” (*nīca*).

It should be stated that there is indeed a [separate] mention [of the fifth case], because [the usage] is already established by the rule "pañcamī vibhaktau" (Pāṇini 2.3.42), just as in the example "asmāt tāro mandro vā.
(526) *anyārāditarartedikśabdāñcūtarapadājāhiyukte* (Pāṇini 2.3.29).

"Is it different, distinct, or otherwise? Nor should it be argued that there is an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of this principle to cases such as "the pot is not a cloth," because the negative particle (*nañ*) also possesses the power to denote difference;

for it is accepted that particles (*nipāta*) possess only the capacity to indicate meaning (*dyotakatva*), but not the capacity to denote it directly (*vācakatva*). [The example] "from afar from the forest": here, by the rule "with words meaning 'far' or 'near'..."

The genitive case ending is obtained by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī anyatarasyām*. As in the example *ṛte kṛṣṇāt*. If it is asked, "How then is the usage *ṛte puruṣārādhanam halati* (without the propitiation of man) employed?", Haradatta says that this is an error.
Others, however, [justify it] on the basis of the inclusion of the word *dṛśi* (is seen) in the rule *tato ’nyatrāpi dṛśyate*, which allows for such usage even elsewhere.

They say that, just as in the case of *yāvacchītam* and similar expressions, the accusative case is also valid when used with *ṛte*. In this interpretation, the Cāndra rule *ṛte dvitīyā ca* is favorable. Regarding the phrase "seen in the direction," the word *rudhyai* (for the purpose of obstructing) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Therefore, the directions such as *aindrī* (the eastern quarter) are not included here. But if this is so—
If it is argued that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of including words such as *kakub* [which are not directions], they say here:
"By virtue of association with one of the two [members of a pair] or by way of traditional commentary (*vyākhyāna*), that which is not observed in the sense of a direction is what is included here.
This is stated even though [the word *diś*] is a term for direction (*dik-śabda*). Even if... [text continues].

Although the word *dik* (direction) also occurs as a member of a compound where *añc* (the suffix for "bent toward") is the subsequent member—such as in *sadhryaṅ* and so on—nevertheless, due to its association with the term *dik*, only a directional word such as *prāk* (eastward) and the like is understood by the phrase "having *añc* as the subsequent member.
The intention is that, because of this, there is no over-extension [of the rule] to cases such as *sadhryaṅ devadatenā*. [The example is] *dakṣiṇā*.

Regarding the word *grānāt*: since [the rule] is already established by the fact that it is a directional word (*dikśabda*), they say that the inclusion of *ājāhi* has an uncertain purpose. Regarding the phrase *prabhṛtiyoge*: the meaning is "in connection with words having the sense of *prabhṛti*" (starting from).
Thus, while explaining the Bhāṣya passage "from the *ārtikya* onwards," Kaiyaṭa states: "Therefore..."

The meaning is "starting from" (*ārabhya*). The example used is *grāmād bahiḥ* ("outside the village"). [The principle that] "what is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*) does not apply everywhere" applies here; therefore, the form *arasya karabho bahiḥ* ("the camel is outside the desert") is established. (527) *apa-parī* [are used] in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). Pāṇini 1.4.88.
Regarding *apa* and *pari*: [the rule applies] when they signify exclusion (*varjana*). What is the example for when they do not signify exclusion? *pariṣiñcati*. The meaning here is "on all sides.

Because these function as prefixes (*upasarga*), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. As for the mention of the word "vacana" (statement): the distinction introduced here—namely, that "limit" (*maryādā*) means "without that" and "inclusive limit" (*abhividhi*) means "with that"—is a specific aspect of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) in this context.

It is not [the word] *āṅ* that is taken, because of the force of taking the word "vacana" (expression); rather, the meaning is that only the limit (*avadhi*) is intended to be expressed—this is the inclusion of two meanings. Alternatively, the word *maryādā-vacana* refers to that expression in which the word *maryādā* is uttered; for that is the rule (*sūtra*) "ṭhāṅbhāryādābhividhyoḥ," wherein the *āṅ* occurs.
The meaning is that he has been seen with the aforementioned designation.
(528) *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ* |2|3|10|. Regarding *parihareḥ*: the meaning is "excluding Hari. There is an optional statement [in the commentary] regarding *ari-* when used in the sense of exclusion.

According to this Vārttika, there is an absence of reduplication in certain cases. Regarding *pariratra*: the intention is that here, in the rule prescribing the ablative case (*pañcamī*), [the word *pari*] is associated with *apa*, which has the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). Regarding *ā mukteḥ*: the meaning is "having made liberation the limit" (*muktiṃ maryādīkṛtya*). Regarding *ā sakalāt*: the meaning is "pervading the whole" (*sakalamabhivyāpya*).
(529) And [the fifth case ending is used] after [words expressing] a substitute (*pratinidhi*) and an exchange (*pratidāna*).

[Pāṇini 2.3.11]. Regarding *pratinidhi* and *pratidāna*: by this very indication (*liṅga*), the fifth case ending is used in connection with these two. Since it is said that “what is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is not universally applicable,” there is also the usage: *kṛṣṇasya pratinidhiḥ*.

They say "siddham" (it is established). When the primary [item] is absent, that which is taken as similar to it is the *pratinidhi* (substitute). *Pratidāna* is the repayment of what was to be given. [The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied] when the agent is not expressed. The sense is that the word *hetubhūta* (become a cause) follows from the rule "in the sense of cause" (*hetau*).

(530) *Akartari ṛṇe pañcamī* |2|3|24|. The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall be used [in connection with a word denoting debt]. This is an exception to the third case (*tṛtīyā*). As in *śatena* ("by means of a hundred"): here, the hundred is a debt because it is to be held by the creditor; [this is so] according to the rule: "That which prompts [an action] is also called the cause (*hetu*)."

By the word "ca" (and), it is also designated as the *kartṛ* (agent). Regarding the form *bandhita*: since the prompter (*prayojaka*) who is the agent in a causative (*ṇyanta*) construction also possesses the designation of *hetu* (cause/motive), the ablative case would indeed apply here; therefore, the intention is that the term "non-agent" (*akartṛ*) was stated in this context. [The phrase] "due to the division of the rule" (*yogavibhāgāt*) refers to the rule beginning with *hetumanuṣyebhyaḥ*.
This is clear in the *Padamañjarī* (531):

"Optionally [the genitive is used] when expressing a quality (*guṇa*), provided it is not feminine" (Pāṇini 2.3.25). Regarding the phrase "if it is feminine," [it is said]: "The irregularity (*āhulaka*) is due to the limited observation of the original form."
The mention of the *vārttika* here also serves as an indicator [of this].
(532) *Pṛthag-vinā-nānābhis tṛtīyā ’nyatarasyām* | 2|3|32|. [The rule states:

"With *pṛthak*, *vinā*, and *nānā*, the third case is optionally [used]. Now, in the alternative where the third case is absent, the contextually relevant rule *ṭenapā dvitīyā* ("with *tena* and *apa*, the second case") applies.

It would necessarily be the second case (dvitīyā). However, if the second case were optional, then the fifth case (pañcamī) would also be possible; yet that [second case] is indeed obligatory. Therefore, since the coexistence of three case-endings is difficult to justify, he says: "The mention of *anyatarasyām* is for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*)."

The intention is that particles have multiple meanings (*anekārtha*). Regarding "the fifth": there, the fifth case is used by way of the *bhaṇḍūkapluti* (the skipping of intervening cases); the second case, however, is already present. Here, although it would have been sufficient to formulate the rule as *pṛthagarthaiḥ*, the employment of three synonyms is for the purpose of excluding other synonyms; therefore—
Regarding the example *hirug devadattasya*, they say that [the genitive case] does not apply.

It is easier to state: “The third case is optionally used with words meaning ‘separately,’ ‘variously,’ and with the suffix *añ*. By taking *nānāñ* as a reference to the suffix, the two words *vinā* and *nānā*—which end in that suffix—are included. Thus, it is said: *nānā*.

According to Amara, "ṭhhiruṅnānā ca varjane" [the word *nānā* is used in the sense of exclusion]. There is also the usage: "ānānāraĀ niṣphalā lokayātrā" [the worldly course of life is fruitless without *nānā*]. (533) And [the instrumental case is used] for *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, and *katipaya* when they denote a non-substance (*asatvavacana*) in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). Pāṇini 2.3.33.

And regarding the *karaṇa* (instrumental) case: the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") and *pañcamī* ("the fifth [case]") carry over from the previous rule. Therefore, while the third case (*tṛtīyā*) would normally apply in the sense of the instrument, the fifth case is prescribed as an alternative;
since the third case is established by the very fact of being the instrument when the fifth is not used, he says with this intention: "The third and fifth cases occur."
"By a little" (*stokena*) means "liberated without effort.

(534) *Pāṇini 2.3.35*: "The second case-ending is also used after words meaning 'far' or 'near. For example: *dūram*, *dūrāt*, or *dūreṇa*. Here, the seventh case-ending will also be mentioned. Furthermore:

Because the rule *‘ūrāntikārthebhyaḥ’* is also carried over into the subsequent rule *‘saptamyadhikaraṇe ca’*, it should be understood that these [words] take four case-endings even when expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus, one employs such usage as: *‘ūrād āvasathān mūtram’*.

"From afar, [the place for] washing the feet"—this means at a distance from the dwelling. Regarding the phrase "of that which does not denote a substance": here, "denoting a substance" means being a qualifier of a substance. And thus, by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), that which qualifies the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is excluded.

Thus he says: "The path is far. By this, the passage from the commentary of the ancients on the rule *araṇe ca stoke*—"What is the purpose of [specifying] the instrument? Let it not apply to an accusative that is a qualifier of the action, as in *stokaṃ pacati* ('he cooks slightly'), for an action is not a substance"—is also explained. Nor [does it apply] because the action is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
It should not be argued that this is not a valid counter-example because [the action] necessarily possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*);

for it is well-established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that the action denoted by a verbal root (*dhātu*) is of a non-substantial nature (*asatvarūpa*). Nor does its status as a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) entail such an inconsistency.

For its nature as non-existence (*asattva*) is established merely by its lack of connection with the gender and other case-role (*kāraka*) attributes belonging to the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*).

And it has been said: "Action is not joined with gender, action, or the substrates that are the case-roles; let this very nature of non-existence be determined for it. Action consists of both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*).

The distinction is that *karma* is the agent that brings about the result (*phala*), while the *kartṛ* is the agent that brings about the operation (*vyāpāra*). [Now follows] the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*).
(535) *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* | 2|3|50|. The sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the remaining relations (*śeṣa*).

"The sixth [case-ending] is used for the remainder (ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe). The 'remainder' is that which is other than what has been mentioned. Since the objects of action (karman) and so forth—ranging from nominal stems (prātipadika) up to their meanings—have already been mentioned, because the second case and others have been prescribed for those, the sixth case is therefore applied only to the subordinate element, due to its lack of predominance. In this context, however, the meaning of the suffix is a qualifier of the person."

When the intended meaning is "a person who possesses the relationship of being a servant appointed by the king," the genitive case is not used after the word *puruṣa*, which is the principal member [of the compound], because that would contradict the aforementioned rule and because there is no status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*).

For in expressions such as "an obedient person stands," the word *puruṣa*— [The sentence continues: ...is indeed [the subject]. (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly; this translation reflects the logical structure of the grammatical argument.)

[The genitive suffix] occurs when it denotes the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). However, in expressions such as *rājñaḥ puruṣeṇa kṛtam* ("done by the king's servant"), it has the sense of a grammatical participant (*kāraka*). But when there is the intention to convey the meaning "the king who possesses the relationship of being served as defined by the servant," then the genitive indeed occurs after the word *puruṣa* as well, as in *puruṣasya*.
Regarding the term "king": as for what has been stated by some that "that which is not the primary [meaning] is the *śeṣa* (remainder)," that is incorrect.

For if it were so, the genitive case would undesirably apply to the qualifier in instances such as "the white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*) or "the dark pot" (*śyāmo ghaṭaḥ*), since these consist merely of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Nor can it be argued that the nominative case sublates [the genitive], because the nominative applies to the primary [meaning].

"Because its purpose has been fulfilled. Regarding the phrase "of action and so forth": the sense is that this too is established by logic, just as one uses the term "possessing form" (*rūpavān*) when specific qualities are not intended to be expressed, but uses "blue," "yellow," and so on when specific qualities are intended to be expressed. "The way of the virtuous" (*satāṃ gatam*) means that which pertains to virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*).

The meaning is "going. However, in the case of the sentence *santo gacchanti* ("the virtuous go"), since the relationship with the agent (*kartṛtva-sambandha*) has already been expressed by the verb (*ākhyāta*), it is impossible to intend to express a mere relationship (*sambandha-mātra*).
Therefore, they say that the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not occur here; rather, only the nominative (*prathamā*) occurs because the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) alone is intended.
"He knows [the location] of the ghee" (*sarpiṣo jānīte*). In reality, when there is a desire to express merely the relationship of the instrument (*karaṇa*), the genitive case is used;

the meaning is "an activity related to the ghee. Alternatively, the ātmanepada affix *taṅ* is applied to the root *jñā* by the rules "after an intransitive verb" (*akarmakācca*) or "after *jñā* when not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargājjñaḥ*). Others, however, have explained it as [referring to] the object (*karman*).
The genitive case is used here because there is an intention to express a state of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*). The meaning is: "knowledge related to clarified butter" (*sarpiḥ-sambandhi jñānam*).

Regarding the term *edhodakasya*: *edha* (firewood) and *udaka* (water); their collective compound is *edhodakam*. The singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) is applied according to the rule "the genus [is singular] for non-living things. Alternatively, it may be analyzed as *ca* (and) *dakam* (water).

In the compound, there is the formation of a singular unit (*ekavadbhāva*) as in the previous case; or alternatively, in the analysis *edhāṃsi ca dakaṃ ca*, there is the formation of a singular unit as before. There is also a word *daka* which is a synonym for water (*udaka*).
Thus Halāyudha says: "The world (*bhuvana*), nectar (*amṛta*), that which gives life (*jīvanīya*), and *daka*. [He] "adorns" (*upaskurute*).

The *ātmanepada* [endings] are applied by the rule *gandhanādisūtreṇa*. The augment *suṭ* is added by the rule *ṭhupātpratiyatne*. Nor, in this way, would there be [the application of the following rules]:
*ño'vidarthasya karaṇe*, *adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi*, *ṛñaḥ pratiyatne*, *rujārthānāṃ bhāvavacanānāmajvareḥ*, and *āśiṣi nāthaḥ*.
It should not be argued that this set of eight sūtras— “*āsiṣi prahaṇana-āṭopa-viṣāṇāṃ hiṃsāyām*,” “*vyavahṛ-paṇoḥ samarthayoḥ*,” and “*ṛtv-arthaprayoge kāle ’dhikaraṇe*”—

which are intended to prescribe the genitive case for the remaining relations (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), would be fruitless [because the required meanings are already covered]; for [the sūtra] “*arpiso...*” [is necessary].
In examples such as *jñānam*, the purpose of that [rule] is to prevent the application of the compound-ending elision (*samāsaniṣṭhiti*). To explain:

in rules such as *ño 'vidarthasya* (Pāṇini 2.3.51), the term *eṣe* is understood to carry over; however, when the [root] is intended to be expressed as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is already established for the instrumental and other relations. Thus, the meaning here is this: only the sixth case is applied, and there is no elision (*luk*) of it.

And thus, because the *luṅ* [augment] has become the cause [of the prohibition], the compound itself does not even come into being. Nor should it be argued that the group of eight sūtras should have as their sole result the exclusion of the *luṅ* augment, while the compound itself is accepted;
for, in accordance with the desired conclusion, it is precisely the compound that does not occur.

This is because such an explanation is appropriate. Accordingly, the *Vārttika* states: "The genitive case prescribed for each specific word (*pratipadavidhānā*) is not compounded. And Hari says: "Furthermore, when a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is designated and the action is explicitly heard, the genitive prescribed for each specific word is stated for the purpose of precluding compounding. And so it is.

When the sense of "remainder" (śeṣatva) is intended, forms such as *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee") and *mātuḥ smaraṇam* ("the remembrance of the mother") are correct only when they remain uncompounded. However, forms such as *harismaraṇam* ("remembrance of Hari") are to be understood as compounds formed with the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) used in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix, provided that the sense of "remainder" is not intended. And in that case:

Because it is preceded by a *kāraka*, by the rule "atikāraka... (*Pāṇini 6.2.139*) and others, the word has a middle-pitched accent (*madhyodātta*) due to the natural accent of the base of the subsequent member of a *kṛt*-derivative compound. However, in a compound with a genitive of the "remainder" (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), there would be a final-pitched accent (*antodātta*), which is undesirable. Thus, these eight sūtras are for the sake of the accent.
The conclusion: furthermore, in examples such as *pitus smṛtam* ("remembered from the father"), the absence of compounding is also a result;
for in that case, the genitive of the *kāraka* (agentive/ablative) is not obtained, due to the prohibition by the rule *a loka-*. And it has been said:
"In the case of a past participle (*niṣṭhā*), the genitive relating to the object is prohibited; [only] the genitive characterized as 'the rest' (*śeṣa*) [is allowed]."
"Compound formation is not desired there"—this is established in the *Manoramā*.

(536) *ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge* |2|3|26|. [The word] *ṣaṣṭhī* [is used] when *hetu* is employed. Here, the word *hetau* is understood from the previous rule; thus he says: "when the cause (*hetu*) is to be indicated."

Regarding the word *annasya*: when the third case ending would have been required by the rule "in the sense of cause" (*hetau*), the sixth case is used here by this [sūtra]. What is the purpose of employing the word "cause"? [Example: *anne vasati* ("He dwells because of food"). Why is it stated "when the cause is expressed"? Some say it is so that the sixth case may occur after the word *anna*; for instance, in the expression *annasya hetostubhyaṃ namaḥ* ("Salutation to you, because of food"), [the sixth case occurs] after the word *anna*, but [it does not occur] after the word *yuṣmad*.
Others say it was *bhū*.
(537) *sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca* | 2|3|27|.
From a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) [is also used]. Here, in the word *sarvanāmnaḥ*, the genitive case is used in relation to its usage (*prayoga*).

However, with the intention that on the fifth [sūtra], because of the word *hetu*, the sixth and third case endings would not occur, he says: "and of the word *hetu* when it is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).
