When the expectation arises as to "from what does it arise?", it follows by implication that [the suffixes occur] after both a pronoun and a cause (*hetu*).

It is connected [to the preceding]. Here, they have explained: although the word *sarvanāmnaḥ* ends in the ablative case, there is no harm even if it is construed in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *hetu* as its qualifier; nevertheless, if it were the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), this...
It should be understood that [the rule] would not apply.

Regarding the phrase "in the usage of synonyms for *nimitta*," there is a general observation (*prāyadarśana*) regarding all [cases]. He states the purpose of including the term "synonym" (*paryāya*) with the words beginning with "thus" (*evam*). By this Vārttika, [the application of] the sixth case...

It should be understood that the two rules, "hetuprayoge" and "arvannāmnas tṛtīyā ca," have already been explained. (538) [Pāṇini 2.3.30] "With a word ending in the sixth case, when used with a suffix having the sense of 'tas'."

The meaning of the genitive case [is as follows]: the term *atasarthapratyaya* refers to that suffix whose meaning consists of direction, location, or time—namely, the sense of the rule *akṣiṇotarābhyāmatasuc*—as well as the suffixes beginning with *astāti*.
The meaning is that [the prohibition applies] when there is a connection with a word ending in such a suffix.

They say that although *acasu* immediately precedes *astāti*, the form *astātyarthe* was not stated out of consideration for brevity (*lāghava*). Regarding the phrase "an exception to the fifth case" (*pañcamyā apavādaḥ*): because of the usage in the Bhāṣya, "after this it will perish (*paścāt straṃsyate*) and be destroyed (*dhvaṃsyate*"), the fifth case is indeed employed when joined with the word *paścāt*.

It is correct. From this very usage in the Bhāṣya, it will be stated that an avyayībhāva compound does not occur with the word *paścāt*. Why is there the mention of "an affix" (*pratyaya*)? So that it may not apply here: *prāg grāmāt* (east of the village), *pratyag grāmāt* (west of the village). If it is argued: "Even if the mention of 'an affix' is made, why should it not apply to [words ending in] *kṛt* [affixes]? To this they say:

Kaiyaṭa and others [state]: "The mention of 'affix' (*pratyaya*) being added is understood for the purpose of referring to an affix that is actually heard; thus, when the affixes *astāti* and *ati* have been elided, there is no occurrence of the genitive case.
Furthermore, this same purpose has been stated in the rule *anyārāt...* with respect to a compound where *añc* is the final member."

In this regard, one or the other [of the two options] could not be stated as impossible, because they serve the same purpose; however, it is established in the *Manoramā* that the mention of the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is unnecessary. Regarding the word *pura*:
by the rule *īrvādharāvarāṇām*, the substitute *pur* is applied when the suffix *asi* follows.
Regarding "purastāt": the suffix *astāti* is applied by the rule "dikśabdebhyaḥ" etc., and by the rule "astāti ca," the word *pura* is substituted for the preceding [term].
(539) *Enapā dvitīyā* || 2.3.31 || [This sūtra prescribes] the second case ending after a word ending in *ena*.
[Objection: How then [should one explain] the phrase, "In this place, our house is to the north (uttareṇa) of the mansion of the Lord of Wealth"?

[Response: They say that this word *uttareṇa* is a third-case ending (*tṛtīyānta*) in grammatical apposition with *toraṇa*—as in the verse, "With a beautiful archway to the north (uttareṇa), like the rainbow of the Lord of the Gods"—and is not a form ending in the suffix *-enap*.

If some read "to the north of the houses of the slaughterers (*hanapatigṛhān uttareṇa*)," then that is indeed correct. Regarding "to the south" (*dakṣiṇena*): the suffix *enap* is applied in the sense of "not far from the south," according to the rule *ṭhenab anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.3.35).
(540) [The rule] *dūrāntikārthaiḥ ṣaṣṭhy anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.34) [states that the sixth case may optionally be used with words meaning "far" or "near"].
With words meaning "far" (dūra) or "near" (antika), when the sixth case (genitive) would otherwise apply, this rule prescribes the fifth case (ablative) as an alternative.

Here, the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") serves the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*); therefore, by virtue of the commentary (*vyākhyāna*), even the remote fifth case is conjoined, but not the second or third cases which are proximate.

This is what he says: "And the fifth [case-ending] as well. Regarding the example *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee"): the meaning is that it is an activity related to the ghee which is, in reality, functioning as the instrument (*karaṇa*). There is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the root *jñā* (to know) in the sense of an activity preceded by knowledge.

(541) *Adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi* |2|3|52|. [The mention of the word] *adhi* [in the rule] is for the purpose of indicating that the roots *iṅ* and *dhā* do not deviate from being accompanied by this prefix. Otherwise, one would have simply said *mṛtyarthadayeśām*; [one would not have specified] *adhīgarthe*.

Or [one might argue]: "If it is claimed that this is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*) with respect to the portion *iR*, then let the utterance of the word *adhi* in the rule ‘*ṭhṇeradhyayane vṛtam*’ be the indicator for that portion. Regarding this, they have explained: "What is the purpose of [specifying] *karman*? It is so that [the suffix] does not apply when the instrument (*karaṇa*) is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), as in: *māturgaṇasmaraṇam* (the mother’s recollection of the rosary). Here, the mother..."

In the case of *karma* (object) and *guṇa* (quality), however, they are the instruments (*karaṇa*). Even when there is an intention to express the residual relation (*śeṣatva*) in both instances, the genitive case is applied after the word *mātṛ* by this very rule, whereas it is applied after the word *guṇa* by the rule "the genitive in the sense of the residual" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*). Consequently, the compound *guṇasmaraṇam* is formed.

(542) *Rujārthānāṃ bhāvavacanānām ajvareḥ* | 2|3|54| *Rujārthānām*: [The word] *ruj* means "to break. By its inclusion in the *bhidādi* group, or by this very technical derivation (*nipātana*), the suffix *aiṅ* (i) and *ṭāp* (ā) are applied. Thus, *rujā* means "disease. Those roots whose meaning is "disease" are called *rujārthāḥ*. [The rule applies to] those verbal roots whose meaning is "disease."

Because it is never non-deviant from denoting an action (*bhāva*), the word *bhāva* here refers to an accomplished state (*siddharūpa*) expressed by the suffix *ghañ* and others. The term *vacanaḥ* means "that which speaks" (*vakti*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*); however, the primary meaning of the verbal root is not intended here, for an action cannot possibly be a speaker. Therefore, [the focus is] on the suffix.

It should be understood that the word *vacis* is used solely for the sake of establishing correctness (*sādhutva*). Thus, the meaning is: "of those verbal roots whose agent is the state of being (*bhāva*)," i.e., "of those [roots] denoting a state.
He explains this very point by saying "of those whose agent is the state" (*bhāvakartṛkāṇām*). [This applies to] the roots having the sense of *ruj* (to afflict).

It would be more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as *bhāvakartṛkāṇām* ("of those [roots] having a state as their agent"). Regarding *caurasya*: a thief (*caura*) is one whose nature (*śīla*) is stealing (*cura*). Here, the sixth case ending is applied by this rule because there is an intention to express the "remainder" (*śeṣatva*) regarding the object. It should be stated that the prohibition applies except for the roots *jvar* and *saṃtap*. Regarding *rogasya*: [the word *roga* is derived] with the suffix *ghañ* by the rule *adaruja-*.

The word *roga* (disease) is designated as a *bhāva* (state/abstract noun), and it is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the act of afflicting (*rujā*). By the rule “*artṛkarmaṇoḥ*,” the genitive case is applied after the word *roga*. [An example of] what [is meant by] "those whose agent is a *bhāva*"? *śleṣmaṇaścaurarujā* (the thief’s affliction caused by phlegm).
According to Amara, *āyus*, *pitta*, and *kapha* are synonyms for *śleṣman* (phlegm).

(543) *nātha* [is used] in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). Regarding the example *caurajvara* ("the fever of a thief"): here, since the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not apply after the word *caura* by the rule "of those meaning 'to suffer' (*rujārthānām*)," the sixth case is applied by the rule "the sixth case in the sense of the remainder (*aṣṭhī śeṣe*"); thus, there is a compound with the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
The sense is that it indeed occurs. Regarding "sarpiṣo nāthanam" (the praying for ghee): the meaning is the aspiration, "May ghee be mine. Regarding "māṇavaka-nāthanam" (the praying for a boy):
although when there is an intention to express the object, the genitive case is used by the rule "kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ," then [this form] applies even in the case of an aspiration.

A compound certainly exists here; nevertheless, in that case, by the rule *atikārakopapadāt kṛt*, the original accent of the final member ending in a *kṛt*-suffix applies. However, it is established in the Kaustubha that the rule regarding the final acute accent of a compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) applies only to words such as *yācñā* and the like, but not to words expressing a benediction (*āśis*).

(544) *jāsiniprahaṇanāṭakrāthapiṣāṃ hiṃsāyām* |2|3|56|. Regarding *jāsi*: this refers to the root *asu* belonging to the *curādi* group—meaning “to strike” (*tāḍane*) and “to injure” (*hiṃsāyām*)—and not to the *divādi* root *asu* meaning “to release” (*mokṣaṇe*). Thus, it is *jāsī*.
This is because of the specific mention [in the rule] and because of the statement "in the sense of harming" (*hiṃsāyām*). Regarding *niprahaṇanam*:

the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule "the substitute *ṇ* is applied to *han* when preceded by a vowel other than *a*" (*hanteratpūrvasya*). Regarding *praṇīti*: the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule "after a preposition ending in *e*, *o*, or *a*, the *n* of roots beginning with *ṇ* is replaced by *ṇ*" (*ergada-*) etc.
Regarding "it belongs to the *cur*-class": the intention is that the root *aṭ* meaning "to move" (*nṛtau*) is intended here, because of the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha-nirdeśāt*).

Regarding *krāthanam*: the root *kṛth* is listed in the *ghaṭādi* group [of roots] with the meaning "to injure. Although it possesses the *mit* designation, here there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) due to a specific irregularity (*nipātana*). As for the purpose of the *mit* designation, he will explain in the *ghaṭādi* section that it finds its application in the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *iṇṇamuloḥ*, which takes precedence over the irregularity. As for that which...

Haradatta stated: "The mention of *ghaṭa* and so forth [in the list] is for the purpose that, otherwise, the status of *ṣit* would not apply by extension (*atideśika*) to *haṭa* and so forth via the rule *haṭādayaḥ ṣitaḥ*. This is weak.
For the rule *haṭādayaḥ ṣitaḥ* is indeed sūtra-ed in the middle; therefore, it applies to those preceding it...

The status of having the marker *ṣ* belongs only to those roots ending in *tvar*, and not to others such as *jvara* and so on. For this very reason, he will state in the section on the *ghaṭādi* group: "Thirteen roots ending in *tvar* are *anudāteta* and possess the marker *ṣ*.
(545) *vyavahṛpaṇoḥ samarthayoḥ* || 2.3.57 || [When used with a word that has the same meaning.]
Regarding *paṇanam*: because it will be stated later that [the suffix] occurs "only when there is praise (*stu-tau*)," there is an absence of *āya*.
In *brāhmaṇapaṇanam*, there is an option for *āya* by the rule "āyādaya ārddhadhātuke vā" (P. 3.1.31). (546) *divastadarthasya* (P. 2.3.58).
In that [sūtra], the words *vyavahṛ* and *paṇ* are referred to by the word *tat*;

and with the intention that these two have the same meaning as in gambling (*dyūta*) and in the transaction of buying and selling (*krayavikraya*), and were already included in the previous sūtra, he says: "in gambling. Since *div* was indeed recited in the previous sūtra itself—

Regarding the phrase "tadarthasya" (of that which has that as its purpose), although it need not be stated—since there would be brevity—it is nevertheless separated [from the following rule] for the sake of what follows, namely the word "karmaṇi" (in the objective case). Here, the word "śeṣe" (in the remainder) is not connected, because of the force of the commencement of an option in the subsequent sūtra; otherwise, if the genitive were optionally applied, once it had been released by that [option], [the rule would fail].
The sense is that, since no other case-ending would apply in the "remainder" (śeṣe), the initiation of this optional rule (vikalpa) would be entirely redundant.

Others, however, say: because of parsimony (lāghava), since the word *divaḥ* could have been included in the previous rule itself, the fact that it is treated in a separate rule (pṛthagyoga) indicates by its force (*sāmarthyāt*) that the term "remainder" (*śeṣe*) is not connected here. Not so.

It should not be argued that because the rule is not a separate *yoga* (independent sūtra) but rather has a shared purpose (*cotarārthatva*), it cannot indicate the meaning already stated; for, since there is no evidence (*māna*) for such a restriction, both results can easily be maintained. Since the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is not connected here, he provides an example of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) from this group of three sūtras: "he plays for a hundred" (*śatasya dīvyati*).

(547) *preṣyabruvorhaviṣo devatāsaṃpradāne* | 2|3|61| In the case of the roots *pra-iṣ* and *brū*, [the genitive is used] for the oblation (*havis*) when it is the recipient of a deity. Regarding *preṣya* and *bruvaḥ*: *pra-iṣ* belongs to the *iṣu-gaty-ādau* class; its second-person singular imperative form is *preṣya*. By association with that, *bruvi* is also understood in the same way.

Thus it is understood. For this very reason, the mention of *śeṣa* (remainder) is not connected here, because a compound with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is impossible. What is the purpose of [mentioning] *preṣya* and *ābruvaḥ*? [Example: *agne ya cchāgasya haviṣo vapāṃ medo juhudhi*. Why [mention] *haviṣaḥ*? [Counter-example: *agnaye gomayāni*.
What is the purpose of the condition "when the deity is the recipient"? [Example: *māṇavakāya puroḍāśān preṣya* ("Send the sacrificial cakes to the boy").

It should be stated that there is a prohibition when the oblation (*havis*) is qualified by its being prepared (*prasthita*). [Example: *indrāgnibhyāṃ chāgasya havir vapāṃ medaḥ preṣya* ("Send the goat-oblation—the omentum and the fat—to Indra and Agni").
(548) *Kṛtvo'rthaprayoge kāle'dhikaraṇe* |2|3|64|. "Those whose meaning is like that of *kṛtvasuc* are called *kṛtvortha*.
Regarding the word "śeṣe" [in the sūtra]: here, although the group of six sūtras beginning with *iva-stadarthasya* is interrupted, [it is understood to apply].

The term "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) is understood [from the previous rule], because of the explanation. Regarding *pañcakṛtvaḥ*: the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is applied by the rule "after a numeral, [the suffixes *thām*, *kṛtvas*, and *suc* are used] when there is repetition of an action" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ kriyā-...*). Regarding *dvis*: the suffix *suc* is applied by the rule "after *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur*, [the suffix *suc* is used].
(549) [Now follows: "When a *kṛt* suffix [is used], the agent and the object [take the genitive case]" (Pāṇini 2.3.65).

Regarding the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*: the word *śeṣe* (in the remaining cases) has ceased to apply. Although it might be possible to carry forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the word *karmaṇi* from the sūtra *kartari ca kṛti*—since that word is carried forward by the particle *ca* through the sequence starting from *adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi* up to *caturthyarthe bahulaṃ chandasi*—it is nevertheless stated here again.

Because of the mention of "action" (karman), others hold that in this case, the explanation itself is the only refuge. What [is the purpose of specifying] "agent and object"? [Example: "The one who cuts with a weapon. Regarding the word *kṛti*: "the instrument is *kṛti*"; it is formed by the suffix *ktin* according to the rule *striyāṃ ktin*. Here, Kṛṣṇa is the agent. He gives an example for the object: "of the world. [This refers to] Kṛṣṇa's...

Because it has already been expressed by the triplet (*tṛc*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not occur after it. [The questioner asks: "Why [is the word] *kṛti* used? [The answer is: Surely, in this context, the action is implied by the agent and the object, and the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone is the expresser of that [action]. And there are two types of suffixes for a verbal root: *kṛt* and *tiṅ*. Among these, in the case of the employment of a *tiṅ*-suffix, as in "he makes a mat" (*kaṭaṃ karoti*), etc., [the rule would apply].

There must be a prohibition [of the genitive] by the word "lokā" (in the rule *kartṛ-karmanoḥ kṛti*). Consequently, by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*), the genitive will occur only in connection with a *kṛt*-affix; therefore, the question is: "What is the purpose of mentioning *kṛt*? [The answer is:
It is desired [to apply the genitive] to the subordinate object (*guṇakarman*). For example: *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*. Here—
The sense is that since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) belonging to the mat (*kaṭa*) remains unexpressed with respect to the action of making, the genitive case would indeed occur;
however, the mention of *kṛt* [in the rule] is for the purpose that this [genitive] should not occur when there is an addition of a *taddhita* suffix.
But [one might object]: in the analysis "the mat was made by him previously" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ pūrvamanena*), the *kta* suffix denotes the object.

If it is argued that since the action is already expressed by that very [instrumental] suffix *vidhānāt*, neither the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) nor its exception, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), would apply here as well—on account of the governing rule *anabhihite* (when not already expressed)—and furthermore, that because the word *kṛta* depends on *kaṭa*, a compound is impossible, and the same applies to the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix; [Response: This is not so. Just as in the case of *odana-pākaḥ* ("the cooking of rice"), where the action is expressed by the verbal root itself, yet the accusative case is employed for the object, so too here, although the action is expressed by the instrumental suffix, the accusative case is applied to express the object. Moreover, the rule *anabhihite* is intended to prevent the application of a case ending when it has already been expressed by another grammatical element (*pratyaya*), such as a primary suffix (*kṛt*) or a secondary suffix (*taddhita*). However, in this instance, the action is expressed by a suffix belonging to a different category (*vibhakti*), namely the instrumental; therefore, the application of the accusative is not barred. Furthermore, the dependence of the word *kṛta* upon *kaṭa* does not preclude the formation of a compound, because the relationship between the two words is one of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣya-bhāva*). Thus, the compound *kṛta-kaṭaḥ* is perfectly valid. The same logic applies to the secondary derivative. Therefore, the objection is untenable.

Regarding this, they say: in the analysis "pūrvaṃ kṛtam anena" (this was done by him previously), since the object is not intended to be expressed, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Consequently, because the word *kṛta* lacks dependence on [the object] "mat" (mat), both the compound and the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) occur. Thus, the form *ṛpūrvī* has the same meaning as "one who previously performed [an action]."

It is established that even when an action is subordinate, the relationship of the factors of action (*kāraka*) with it is observed—as in examples such as *kaṭaṃ kṛtavān* ("he made a mat")—and therefore here too, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) for the mat is accepted in relation to the action of "making. And that status of being an object has not been expressed by anything; for [the suffix] *-ta* occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*).

And because the suffix *ini* is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), if the term "kṛt" (verbal derivative) were not mentioned [in the rule], the genitive case would indeed occur. Thus, in the case of "odanasya pācakatamaḥ," where the genitive is considered ungrammatical, the only recourse is to accept that very result as intended. In the case of "ṛtapūrvī," both compound (*samāsa*) and secondary derivative (*taddhita*) formations occur.

Thus it has been stated. In that regard, the compound should be understood as formed by the rule *sup supā*. As for the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), however, the suffix *ini* is applied in the sense of the agent (kartṛ) according to the rules *ūrvādiniḥ* and *apūrvācca*;
for in the prescription of that suffix, the word *anena* is carried over from the sūtra *rāddham anena*. This might be the case—from the causative form (*ṇyantāt*) of the root *bhid*.

By the rule "aryāyārhaṇotpatiṣu," when the suffix *ṇvuc* is applied, in both examples— "hedikā devadatasya" and "yajñadatasya kāṣṭhānām"— the genitive case based on connection with a *kṛt*-suffix arises by this very rule; and in that situation, when both a primary and a non-primary [relation] are present, the operation applies only to the primary one.

It should occur only from that which expresses the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), because of the requirement for mutual understanding (*sampratyaya*). Otherwise, in a sentence such as *ācayaty odanaṃ devadattena yajñadattaḥ* ("Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to cook rice"), since both the prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*) would be expressed by the affix,
the nominative case (*prathamā*) would have to appear after both words expressing the agent.
Not so; for the genitive case arises through the distinction between the words denoting the prompted (prayojya) and the prompter (prayojaka), and it is not the case that there is only one [genitive].

Therefore, the principle of the primary and the secondary does not apply here. In that other case [the verbal suffix], however, because the suffix (lakāra) is a single entity, the aforementioned principle applies when one assumes that the agent is its expressed meaning.

Because of the irregularity [of the rule]. And thus, it should be understood that in examples such as *odanaḥ pācyate devadattena yajñadattena* ("The rice is being cooked by Devadatta and Yajñadatta"), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would indeed apply to both agents.
Regarding this, they explain: on account of the mention in the rule *tadarham*, [the word *arha*] is included within the scope of *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*.

This is impermanent; thus, the usage by Bhāravi, "tathā ca dhāryair āmodam uttamam," is consistent. (550) When both [the agent and the object] are eligible [for the designation of *kartṛ*], the designation applies to the object (*karman*). 2.3.66.

When both [agent and object] are applicable, the term *kṛti* (a kṛt-affix) is understood to carry over from the previous rule. Therefore, because it serves as the referent for another word, he states that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "that in which there is the applicability (*prāpti*) of both.
By the word *ubhaya* ("both"), the agent and the object are referred to. Consequently, when there is a single [kṛt-affix]...

Because the [simultaneous] application of the rules for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) is obtained, this [rule] is considered a marvel; thus, in the case of "the cooking of rice (*odanasya pākaḥ*)" and "the appearance of Brahmins (*brāhmaṇānāṃ prādurbhāvaḥ*"), this restriction does not operate. The intention is that, however, in the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would indeed occur. [This is so] because [the desired form] is already established by the preceding rule alone.

He indicates that this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction by stating "only with respect to the object" (*karmaṇyeva*). And thus, it is established that the result of this sūtra is the prohibition of the genitive case in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), and not the prescription of the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).

This restriction does not apply to the *akāra* and *ākāra* that are feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "of the two feminine suffixes," the meaning is: those prescribed under the governing rule (adhikāra) "ktin in the sense of the feminine" (*striyāṃ ktin*). Regarding the phrase "this is not a restriction," it refers to the restriction that when the *ṭhakāra* and *ākāra* suffixes are employed, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) must denote only the object (*karman*) and not the agent (*kartṛ*).

It has been stated that [the genitive] does not apply there, but rather the genitive applies even to the agent (*kartṛ*). This is the established conclusion. How then is the commentary on the rule *uṭtithoḥ*—"there is no sublation of *uṭ*, *ās*, or *īyuṭ*"—to be understood? On this point, they say: the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used here because the agent is intended to be expressed as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Regarding *bodhyā*: *bhedikā* means "that which divides" (*bhedanam bhedikā*). The suffix *ṇvuc* is applied according to the rule *aryāyārhaṇotpattiṣu*.

Some maintain that the suffix *ṇvul* is used here by the rule *hātvarthanirdeśe ṇvul vaktavyaḥ*. By the rule *yuvoranākau*, the suffixes *yu* and *vu* are replaced by *an* and *ak* respectively. In the feminine, the suffix *ṭāp* is added, and by the rule *pratyayasthāt—*, the vowel *i* is substituted for the final *a*.
*bibhitsā* means "the desire to split.

From the root *bhid* with the suffix *san*, there is an absence of *guṇa* because of the rule *halantācca* [Pāṇini 1.2.10], which makes the suffix *kit*. Then, by the rule *apratyayāt* [Pāṇini 3.3.102], the suffix *a* is added, followed by *ṭāp* to form the feminine.
Regarding the phrase *śeṣe vibhāṣā*: "in the remainder" (*śeṣe*) means in cases other than those beginning with *ktin* that follow after vowels other than *a* and *ā*.

Since the rule *ubhayaprāptau*— which results in the prohibition of the genitive case in the sense of the agent— and the statement *stripratyayayor akākārayoḥ*— which results in the introduction of the genitive case in the sense of the agent in those very instances—
have already been established, this supplementary statement (*śeṣavacana*) provides an option (*vibhāṣā*) specifically regarding the agent.

With the intention that [the suffix] is applied [after a verbal root] and not after a noun (*karman*), he provides an example: "The creation of the world is by Hari or by a lion" (*jagataḥ kṛtir hareḥ hariṇā vā*).

Regarding the phrase "without distinction": the meaning is "in all *kṛt* suffixes whatsoever, excluding those ending in *ak* and *āk*. Regarding the term "instruction" (*anuśāsanam*): they are instructed (*anuśiṣyante*) [to distinguish them] from incorrect words (*asādhu-śabda*).
The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*) in the phrase "by which [means] they are awakened after having been distinguished.

(551) Regarding the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.67), it refers to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). This too is an exception to the prohibition. As for the word *āsitam*, it means "it is sat" (*āsyate*).
"In this [place] they have always sat"—here, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) according to the rule *'to'dhikaraṇe ca'*.

"This belongs to them"—this is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). However, when the suffix *kta* follows transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*) in the sense of the locus, the genitive applies to both the agent and the object, since there is no distinction in their being unexpressed (*anabhihita*). "This belongs to them..."

In the case of *bhuktam odanasya*, the restrictive rule "when both [agent and object] are possible, [the genitive is used] for the object" (*ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*) does not apply here; for it is accepted that this [rule] prescribes the genitive specifically as the one immediately following [in the sequence] from "of the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*). This is clear in the *Kaustubha*.

(552) *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* | 2|3|69|. *Na lokā*: [The rule begins with *na*. Because there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of the form intended to be grasped (*jighṛkṣita-rūpa*), the substitution of *ṇ* has not been applied in the term *tṛnām*. The analysis of the compound is as follows: *u* and *uka* are *ūkau*; *la* and *ūkau* are *l-ūkau*. The term *la* refers to the *laṭ* (present tense) and other suffixes.

The mention of "general" (sāmānya) is for the purpose of including all of them. Since their direct application is not possible, he says "the substitutes for *l*" (*lādeśāḥ*) to indicate that their substitutes are taken; the word "are illustrated" (*udāhriyante*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. In the example *kaṭaṃ kārayāñcakāra*, although there is a connection with the end of a form ending in a *liṅ* suffix bearing the technical designation *kṛt*, [the rule applies] to *kaṭa*.

They say that the genitive case [denoted by] *ṣaṣṭhī* does not occur [after the words *kartṛ* and *karman*] when a *kṛt* suffix follows, because the substitution of *ām* (as in *pāpam*) is also a substitute for an *l*-suffix due to the rule "āmaḥ. But even so, in the example "abhrir vajram, papiḥ somam, dadir gāḥ," the genitive would still be unavoidable because the prohibition "na lokā—" does not apply; for indeed—
The two *lakāra*s [in *liṭ*] are not themselves [the substitutes for the roots], nor are they the substitutes for those [roots]. This is not a fault.

By the rule "the *liṭ* [is used] in place of *ik* and *kin*," an extension (*atideśa*) of the operations (*kārya*) of *liṭ* is effected, but not the designation (*sañjñā*) of *liṭ*. Thus, since when there is an extension of a specific property, the general property is also extended, there is no inconsistency.

Regarding the word *didṛkṣu*: by the rule *“anāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ”*, the suffix *u* is prescribed. With the intention that because of the qualification by the letter *u*, forms ending in that suffix are also included, he says *alaṅkariṣṇu*. The suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied by the rule *“alaṅkṛñ-nirākṛñ...”*. Regarding *ghātukāḥ*: the suffix *ukañ* is applied by the rule *“aṣapate...”*.

The prohibition regarding the [suffix] *kamaC* [is as follows]: "It is easy to perform" (*īṣatkaraḥ*). Here, the suffix *khal* is applied by the rule beginning with "in the presence of *īṣat*, *duḥ*, and *su*.

Because of the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*), one should also cite as an example: "the Soma becomes easily drunk" (*īṣatpānaḥ somaḥ*). To avoid the charge of under-extension (*avyāpti*), he says: "it is a pratyāhāra. Regarding "pavamānaḥ," [the suffix] *śānan* is applied by the rule "after a root ending in *ūṅ* or *yaj*, [comes] *śānan*."
Regarding the word *maṇḍayamāna*: [the root] *maḍi* is used in the sense of "adornment. Because it is marked with the *it* indicatory letter (*it*), the augment *num* is applied.

By the rule "ācchīlyavayovacana... (Pāṇini 3.2.129), the suffix *cānaś* is added. Regarding the word *adhīyan*: by the rule "ṭhiṅdhāryoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.130), the suffix *śatṛ* is applied. Since the term *aṭaḥ* does not recur in the rules for *śānan* and the others, the designation of these as substitutes for *la* (lādeśa) is not established.

The intention is that the term *tṛn* is understood as a pratyāhāra (a grammatical abbreviation). Regarding *tṛn*: this refers to the suffix *tṛn* prescribed by the rule *ṛn* for those [words] expressing habitual action (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Since a permanent prohibition would otherwise apply due to the inclusion of *tṛn* as a pratyāhāra, he states an option (*vikalpa*).

"Or [the genitive is prohibited] after the root *dviṣ* with the suffix *śatṛ*. Regarding "after *dviṣ*": the meaning is that the prohibition of the genitive applies when the suffix *śatṛ*—prescribed by the rule "the suffix *śatṛ* occurs after *dviṣ* in the sense of 'enemy'" (*dviṣo'mitre*)—is employed. "All this [is said]" refers to the principle that "an operation applies to what is immediately preceding" (*anantarasya*).

"Remainder" (*śeṣa*). Regarding the statement "the sixth case [is used] for the remainder": the sense is that there is a distinction in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Thus, it should be understood that in the sentence *āścaryo gavāṃ doho 'gopena* ("It is wonderful, the milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd"), when the status of being a "remainder" is intended, the sixth case occurs even for the agent.

(551) *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ* || 2.3.70 || Regarding *akenoḥ*: since *aka* cannot occur in the sense of debt (*ādhamarṇya*), he says "in the future sense for *aka*. Since *in* can occur in both senses, he says "and in connection with *in* having the meaning of the future and debt. [The application of the rule] is according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*).

But it does not apply here; rather, the suffix *ṭhak* will apply according to the *bhāṣya*, because the rule has been explained by dividing the *yoga* as “*ṭhin* [is used] in the sense of future time (*bhaviṣyad-*) and in the sense of habit (*ābhīkṣṇye*)”. Here, the word “future” (*bhaviṣyat*) is emphasized (by accentuation);
therefore, only the suffix *ṇvul* applies, as prescribed under the governing rule “*umun-ṇvulau*” within the section beginning with “*haviṣyati gamyādayaḥ*”.

With the intention that [the word] is understood [in this sense], he provides an example: *sataḥ pālakaḥ*. Here, *sataḥ* ends in the present participle suffix *-at*. However, there is no prohibition regarding the suffix *ṇvul* when it is prescribed in the sense of general time by the rule *ṇvultṛcau*; such is the meaning [of the objection]. For instance, [examples like] *odanasya pācakaḥ* ("one who cooks rice") and *utrapautrāṇāṃ darśakaḥ* ("one who sees grandsons and great-grandsons") would be valid. [The word] *vrajam*...

Regarding the word *gāmī*: the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of necessity according to the rule “*ṇiniḥ* [is used] after [roots] signifying what is necessary or a debt. Although this suffix is prescribed for general time, it nevertheless conveys a future meaning because of the statement: “*gamyādayaḥ* [denote] the future. Certain words such as *gamyādayaḥ* belong to the *uṇādi* group.

Haradatta says that some [rules] belong to the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*. Now, one might object: since the desired form is already established by the rule "the fourth case is also used for the sake of an excessive action" (*atyarthakarmaṇi caturthī ca*), the mention of the second case (*dvitīyā*) must be intended to ensure that the second case applies even in the domain of exceptions; thus, forms such as *vrajaṃ gaccha* would indeed be established. To this, they reply: in this very sūtra...

Based on the example given in the Bhāṣya, "grāmaṅgamī," that sūtra is not accepted. Consequently, in the case of "grāmasya gantā," the genitive alone is correct, and not the accusative as in "grāmaṃ gantā. As for "śatandāyī," the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of a duty (*dharmya*) according to the rule "āvaśyake" and so forth.

Because it has been stated that "there is a connection with the sense of fitness for the sacrificial offering (*haviṣyadā-dharman-ārtha*"), there is no prohibition here. *Avaśyaṅkārī* means "one who necessarily makes" [the mat] (*kaṭasya*). Since this [suffix] is not included among the *gamyādi* group, it occurs even in the present tense.
(Pāṇini 2.3.71) "The suffixes *kṛtya* may optionally have the sense of the agent."

Regarding *kṛtya* suffixes: although [the rule] "of the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*) would have applied obligatorily, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*). In the case of *sevya*, from the root *ṣevṛ* (in the sense of "service"), by the rule "after roots ending in *ṛ* or *hal*," this [suffix] is used for the sake of negating the [application of the] object [case-ending].
However, as for the statement "it is desired [to apply] optionally when there is no object," that refers to a situation where neither [the agent nor the object] is present.

The rule finds its application in examples such as *netā aśvasya* ("the leader of the horse"), and so forth; this is the general direction. Regarding words having the same meaning [as those denoting "agent" or "instrument"], when the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise have applied by way of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is optionally prescribed by this rule. When that [third case] is not employed, the genitive alone occurs; thus he says, "in the alternative, the genitive. Precisely because of the mention of the plural number, synonyms are included.

Regarding the rule *siddheṭhtulyārthaiḥ*, they say that the inclusion of the word "artha" (meaning) is for the purpose of including those words which have the same meaning independently of other words; therefore, [the suffix] does not apply in cases such as *gaur iva gavayaḥ*.
How then is one to explain Kālidāsa’s verse: *ulāṃ yadārohati dantavāsasā*?
And what of Māgha’s statement: “*phuṭopamaṃ bhūtisitena śambhunā*”?

It is said in reply: the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here according to the rule *sahayukte'pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19). Nor should it be doubted that there is no connection with the word *saha* (together) here, for it is accepted that the third case occurs even without such a connection. Or rather—

The mention of the word *anyatarasyām* in the present rule is for the purpose of carrying forward its own status by means of the particle *ca* in the subsequent rule; otherwise, only the third case (*tṛtīyā*) would be carried forward,
because it is the most proximate.

(553) *tulyārthair atulopamābhyāṃ tṛtīyā ’nyatarasyām* || 2.3.72 || The word *tulya* means "equalized by a scale" (*tulayā saṃmitas tulyaḥ*). The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *avayodharma-* etc. [Pāṇini 4.4.91]. The terms *tulā* and *upamā* mean "weighing. This very point is addressed in this same sūtra.
Mādhava states that [the form] is correct due to the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of *ṇiluk* and *gaṇ*. *Upamiti* means "comparison" (*upamā*).
[The suffix] *aṅ* is applied by the rule *ṭhātaścopasarge*.
(554) *Caturthī cāśiṣyāyuṣyamadrabhadrakuśalasukārthahitaiḥ* | Pāṇini 2.3.73.

Regarding the word *hitam*: the sense is that since the rule *hitayoge ca* has its application fulfilled in cases other than benediction (*anāśiṣi*), this option applies specifically in the case of benediction. Regarding the phrase *vyākhyānāt*: the sense is that in the sūtra, the word *artha* is also a separate cause [for the formation of the compound], and thus this is indeed a *dvandva* compound, not a *bahuvrīhi* with the word *artha*.
Thus ends the sixth [section]. (555) *Ādhāro’dhikaraṇam* | Pāṇini 1.4.45.
"The locus (*ādhāra*). That in which something is supported is called the locus (*ādhāra*). This is according to the rule *adhyāyanyāya-* [Pāṇini 2.4.3].

The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*) due to the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) "after the words *sthā*, *hṛ*, and *ādhāra*. When there arises the expectancy as to whose locus it is, it is understood—by virtue of the governing context of *kāraka* (participant)—that it is the locus of an action (*kriyā*).
Furthermore, this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not possible for the direct loci of an action, because of the supersession by the two other designations: *kartṛ* (agent) and *karman* (object).
Because [the previous view] is refuted, he therefore explains: "by means of a single word (*ekapada*) or a compound (*samāsa*).
And thus, in cases such as "there is a jar on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭa*), it should be understood that the verb "is" (*asti*) is to be supplied. "In three ways":
this is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *aṃhitāyām*. This is for the sake of examples such as "he was not [seen]" (*nadyamāsta*).

Some also accept a fourth type of locus, namely the proximate locus (*sāmīpika-adhikaraṇa*), as in "he sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste*). This is an example of the substratum of the action by way of the agent. An example of the substratum of the action by way of the object (*karman*) is "he cooks in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacati*). He illustrates the objective locus (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇa*) with "in liberation" (*mokṣe*).

"There is desire" (*icchāsti*). But for that which is pervasive (*abhivyāpaka*), [the locative is used] in the sense of "in all" (*sarvasmin*). They say that examples such as "oil in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu tailam*) are also instances of the pervasive. "Four" (*catasraḥ*);
the meaning is "in the mere sense of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārthamātre*). From words expressing distance and proximity...

Because this [rule] continues here, these [suffixes] should also be understood as being used in the locative case (*adhikaraṇa*). Regarding the statement "there is an addition [to the rule] for the object (*karman*) of a word ending in *kta* which has *inu* as its scope": the meaning of "having *inu* as its scope" is that it refers to a word ending in *kta* whose scope (*viṣaya*) consists of a word ending in the suffixes *inu* or *in*. Others, however, say: "of *inu*..."

The term *viṣaya* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Here, by the word *viṣaya*, the base (*prakṛti*) is intended, because that which ends in a *kta*-suffix serves as the base for the suffix *ina*. In the example *adhīti vyākaraṇe*, the suffix *kta* is first applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), and subsequently, the suffix *in* is added in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) according to the rule *iṣṭādibhyaśca*; thereafter, [the connection] is made with the action, which has become subordinate.

Since the object (*karman*) is not expressed when the verbal suffix is connected [to the noun], the accusative case would apply here, as in the example *kṛtapūrvi kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat"). However, in cases such as *ā samadhīti vyākaraṇe* ("he studied grammar until he mastered it"), there is a temporal object (*kāla-karman*) arising from the connection with intransitive roots (*akarmaka-dhātu*).

Because it is external (*bahir-aṅga*), there is no inclusion here, and thus the genitive case does not occur. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the accusative case would also not occur there; for, in order to conform to the observed forms (*lakṣya*), the rule for the accusative is established by resorting to the theory of individual instances (*vyakti-pakṣa*). And this is settled in the *Kostubha*.

"And in the usage of the correct and the incorrect. And "in the usage of the correct and the incorrect": where reverence (*arcā*) is not intended to be expressed, but rather merely the statement of a fact, even there the locative case ending is used according to this Vārttika; for example, "the servant is correct toward the king" (*sādhuḥ bhṛtyo rājñi*).

The distinction is this: in the rule *ādhunipuṇābhyām*, the inclusion of the word *sādhu* is for the purpose of preventing the seventh case (*saptamī*) from applying when the connection [of the action] with the object is intended, provided that respect (*arcā*) is not intended.
[In the rule] *nimitātkarmayoge*, "cause" (*nimitta*) here means "result" (*phala*). However, if it were said to mean "instrumental cause" (*kāraṇa*), [the following would apply].

The point is that, in that case, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in examples such as *āṅyena baddha* ("bound by a yoke"). Regarding *carmaṇi*: for [animals] such as the *carma-dvīpī* (leather-clad leopard), the relationship is one of inherence (*samavāya*).
Regarding "the third case [ending] for the cause": it should also be understood that the fourth case ending is used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*). *Sīmā* means the eggshell.

Thus says Medinīkāra: "The word *sīmā* [is used] in the feminine gender for a boundary, a field, and an eggshell. And: "Furthermore, *puṣkalaka* [is used] for a musk deer, a mendicant, and a boundary-pillar. Haradatta, however, states: "A *puṣkalaka* is a stake (*śaṅku*), driven into the ground to mark a boundary for the purpose of knowing the limits."
He says, "it is buried. But in this alternative view, there is a relationship of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between the boundary (*sīman*) and the abundance (*puṣkala*).

(556) *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* | 2|3|37|. And [the seventh case ending is used] for that whose action indicates another action; for an action whose time is well-known serves to indicate an action whose time is not well-known.

Because it delimits time, it is a *lakṣaṇa* (indicator). In this context, since the words "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth denote the agent or the object which are the substrata (*āśraya*) of well-known actions, the seventh case (*saptamī*) is employed here—taking the place of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) that would otherwise have been required—to express the relationship between the indicator and the indicated (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*). In this case, the action itself is directly the indicator, while its substratum is [the indicator] by extension.

It should be understood, however, that in the case of Brahmins and others, [the action occurs] by way of their activity (*kriyā*). "I went while the Brahmins were studying" is an example of the agent (*kartṛ*). Regarding the object (*karman*), he says: "while the cows... [and so on].
This applies when those who are worthy are the agents and those who are unworthy are not, or when the reverse is the case.
"Of the Arhats," and so forth. Those who are appropriate for a particular action are "fit" (arha).

When their status as the agent is intended to be expressed, the locative case should be prescribed there. Likewise, when those for whom agency in a particular action is inappropriate have their non-agency intended to be expressed, the locative case [is used].

The locative case is to be prescribed in two ways: first, when those for whom agency is appropriate are treated as non-agents; second, when those for whom it is not appropriate are treated as agents. This is the meaning. He provides the first example: "while the virtuous were crossing. For the virtuous are indeed fit for the action of crossing.
The author provides a second example of this [type of agent]: "while the wicked remain" (*asatsu tiṣṭhatsu*).
Here, by the word *tiṣṭhatsu* ("remaining"), it is indicated that the wicked are unfit for and incapable of the act of crossing.
He provides the first example of the opposite case: "while the virtuous remain" (*satsu tiṣṭhatsu*). For the virtuous...
Crossing is appropriate for them, and their agency is understood by the word "while they stand.

He gives a second example: "while the non-existent cross over. For crossing is inappropriate for non-existent things, and their agency is understood by the word "while they cross," even though this [agency] belongs to the suffix.

[The rule] is established by the word *bhāvena* alone; nevertheless, Kaiyaṭa and others hold that this [sūtra] is for the sake of the locative case-meaning (*saptamy-artha*) when there is no intention to express the relationship between the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). However, others maintain that it is indeed useless in reality. (557) *ṣaṣṭhī cā’nādare* (2.3.38). [In the sense of disregard, the sixth case-affix (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is also used. 2.3.38.

"And the sixth [case-ending] is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*). Regarding the term "disregard": the locative case here is by force of the rule *yasya ca bhāvena*. This means that when there is disregard, that which indicates a state (*bhāva*) [takes the sixth]. He states the resulting conclusion: "when there is an excess of disregard. When there is merely the indication of a state, only the seventh case is used; however, when there is an excess of disregard, [the sixth is used].
The essential point is that [the sixth and seventh cases] are used [with these words].
(558) *svāmīśvarādhipatidāyādasākṣipratibhūprasūtaiś ca* |2|3|39|.
Regarding *svāmīśvara*: although it should have been stated as "in the sense of ownership" (*vāmyarthe*), the inclusion of the triad beginning with *svāmin* is for the sake of clarity.

This is for the purpose of excluding other synonyms. Here, the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) rule—stated as "even for words that are dissimilar in form but have the same meaning"—does not apply; because [the words] refer to their own specific forms (*svarūpa*), they lack the quality of having the same meaning.
Regarding the term *dāyāda*: he is a *dāyāda* because he takes (*ādatte*) the inheritance (*dāya*). Even from a root ending in *-ā* preceded by a prefix, the suffix *a* is applied by this very rule.

The suffix *ka* is applied by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). In the expression “an heir (*dāyāda*) among cows,” although the word *gavām* functions as a qualifier for the entire compound, nevertheless—by the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) that "that which is given is a *dāya*" (inheritance)—it still touches upon the partial meaning (*avayavārtha*), namely the portion (*aṃśa*). And thus, in this case...
The result is that [the word] means "one who takes a portion consisting of a cow.

(559) *Pañcamī vibhakte* |2|3|42|. [The rule] *pañcamī vibhakte* [states]: "The fifth case-affix is used when there is a distinction (*vibhakta*). That is, only when there is a differentiation; it is not otherwise.
The intended meaning is that [the word] is pervaded by a generality conveyed by another word. In that case, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) would apply. But if one objects:
"In that case, the ablative would also apply here in the example *māthurāḥ* (the people of Mathurā)," we say: "Not so.
The previous rule (*pūrvasūtra*) is carried over (*anuvartate*) here; therefore, by implication, the meaning is "from that very thing out of which [the group] is being singled out."

Others maintain that because the ablative case (*pañcamī*) operates only when there is a basis for selection (*nirdhāraṇāvadhi*), and because of the governing rule regarding what has not already been expressed (*anabhihitādhikāra*), there is no over-extension of the rule in the example "the people of Mathurā" (*māthurāḥ*). For in this case,
there is no relationship between a basis of selection and a selected item, as there is in examples such as "among cows, the black one."
There exists a relationship of generality and particularity; however, there is indeed a contradiction between the two as presented by the words [of the rule].
Furthermore, this sūtra was rejected in the Bhāṣya on the section concerning the *apādāna* (ablative), based on the removal (*apāya*) as it is conceptually constructed by the intellect.

(560) *sādhunipuṇabhyāmarcāyāṃ saptamyaprateḥ* |2|3|43|. [The rule] "with *sādhu* and *nipuṇa*, when [the sense is] worship (*arcā*), [the seventh case ending is used, provided that *prati* does not follow]. Regarding *nipuṇa*: from the root *puṇa* meaning "to be auspicious" (*śubhe*) with the prefix *ni*, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule for roots having a light penultimate vowel (*igupadhalakṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*). Regarding *arca*: it means "worship" (*pūjāyām*).
From the root *arc* belonging to the *bhūvādi* class, the suffix *ap* is applied by the rule "urośca halaḥ," and then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, resulting in *arcā*.
However, from the root *arc* belonging to the *curādi* class, the suffix *yuc* is applied by the rule "ṇyāsaśranthayuc," and thus the form would be *arcanā*.
Regarding the phrase "skilled in [serving] the king": when employing the word *sādhu*, the locative case indeed occurs even without the word *arcā*.
[This is] from the Vārttika: "And [the rule applies] when used with words meaning 'proper' (sādhu) or 'improper' (asādhu).

It should be stated: "[The prohibition does not apply] when used with *prati* and so forth. Regarding "with *prati* and so forth": these are the words beginning with *prati* that are included in the rule "akṣaṇettham—" (Pāṇini 2.1.14).

(561) *Prasita* and *utsuka* [govern] the third case ending as well. [Pāṇini 2.3.44]. Regarding *prasita* and *utsuka*: Amara states, "One who is intent on another is *prasita*, [meaning] attached. Because of its association with *utsuka*, *prasita* here is understood only in the sense of being intent on something, and this is established by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Therefore—
In the sense of "excessively white" (*prākarṣeṇa sitaḥ* = *uśukla*), [the suffix] does not occur.

(562) *nakṣatre ca lupi* | 2|3|45|. Regarding the rule *nakṣatre ca lupi*, with the intention that the word *lup* here is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote a specific meaning, he says: "that which..."
"By means of the designation *lup*, etc. Regarding "in the locative":

the intention is that this [designation] is carried over by *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap) from the rule "the seventh case ending is used for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and [for the agent and object]. What is the purpose of specifying "in the locus"? [Examples:

*mūlaṃ pratīkṣate* (he waits for the root), *mūlāya spṛhayati* (he longs for the root). Regarding *mūlena*: [this refers to] the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed] by the rule "time joined with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)" [Pāṇini 4.2.3].

In the case of *ubaviśeṣe*, there is elision (*lup*). Why [is it said] "when referring to a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatre*)? [Consider: *pañcāleṣu tiṣṭhati* ("he stays among the Pañcālas"). Here, the elision occurs by the rule "elision when not denoting a location" (*anapade lup*).
(563) Pāṇini 2.3.7: "The locative and ablative cases [are used] to denote that which lies between two agents."

Regarding the seventh and fifth case endings: from the rule “*ālādhvano ratyantasaṃyoge*” (Pāṇini 2.3.5), the words *kāla* and *adhvanaḥ* are understood by way of anuvṛtti; these are then transformed into the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Thus he says: “from those two, namely time and distance. Here, [the rule applies] to time and distance.

The rule of correspondence by number (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) does not apply here because the markers (*anubandha*) are not marked with the *svarita* accent. For example: *adya bhuktvā’yam* ("Having eaten today, this person [will eat tomorrow]").

Now, one might object: "In this case, the agent (*kartṛ*) is only one; so how can there be time situated between two factors of action (*kāraka*)? This is true. However, in this context, it is not the substance (*dravya*) which is the substratum of capacity that is designated as the *kāraka*, but rather the capacity (*śakti*) itself. And that...
It is indeed distinguished by the difference in time. For one [action] is the means for eating today, while the other is for eating after two days have passed.
This he explains: "This time lies between the agent and the power. (564) *The locative case is used for that which is the point of reference and for that which expresses sovereignty.* 2.3.9.

Regarding the phrase *upa parārdham*: by the rule *upa adhike ca*, the term *upa* receives the designation *karmapravacanīya*. Furthermore, by the rule *yasya ceśvaravacanam*, two meanings are intended through the mechanism of *tantra* (simultaneous application). To explain: by the word *yasya*, one’s own property (*sva*) is indicated; [it refers to] "of which property..."

In the explanation that "the related one is called Īśvara," therefore [the word is used in] the seventh case (*saptamī*), one meaning is that the seventh case is used because it denotes its own substratum (*svāśraya*). In the alternative explanation where the word "Īśvara" is taken as emphasizing the state (*bhāvapradhāna*)— namely, that the seventh case is used from that which is said to possess the nature of being a lord (*īśvaratva*)— [the same result follows].
Another [teacher] says that the locative case occurs after a word denoting its own [object]. This being the case, he states the resulting conclusion: "by means of the self and the owner alternately.
Since the relationship residing in the other [participant] is already expressed by the locative case produced from either one of the two, there would not be a locative case simultaneously for both.
The state [of being]. Regarding "dependent on Rāma" (*rāmādhīna*): when used as an indeclinable expressing the sense of a case ending, it becomes *adhirāmam*.
(565) *vibhāṣā kṛñi* |1|4|98|. Regarding "he who here": he who will act toward me—that is, he who will employ me—his...
The meaning is that the lordship of my employer is understood. Regarding the rule *tiṅ codāte*:

the meaning of the sūtra is that when an accented *tiṅ* [ending] follows, the preceding verb (*gati*) is elided (or loses its accent). Here, the word *kariṣyati*, being a *tiṅ*-ending form, is accented;
however, the elision of the accent prescribed by the rule *tiṅṅtiṅḥ* is precluded by the rule *nipātairyadyadi*.

Because of the prohibition by such [rules] as "there is no *nighāta*," the sense is that the accusative case in *mām* is established by the rule "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) alone. This concludes the seventh case. Thus end the meanings of the case-endings.
Thus ends the section on *kārakas* in the *Tattvabodhinī* composed by the monk Jñānendra.

Now begins the section on the *karmakartṛ* (the object acting as the agent) among the verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*). Regarding the rule "of the object" (*karmaṇas tu*): the phrase "to indicate an excellence of ease" (*saukaryātiśayaṃ dyotayitum*) is to be supplied. Regarding the word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*): [this indicates that there are exceptions].

The meaning is that roots such as *bhid* (to split) and *chid* (to cut), which have only one object, are intransitive (*akarmaka*), whereas those that have two objects are transitive (*sakarmaka*). He states the result of being intransitive: "in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*)," because it has been stated that [the suffix *lyuṭ*] occurs after intransitive roots in the sense of the abstract state. Regarding transitive roots, [the suffix is used] for the object (*karman*).

An example when there is an intention to express agency (kartṛtva) is: “The ocean churns nectar” (*mathnāti sāgaro’mṛtam*) and “We, having been drawn by his virtues, milk the treasures from the earth, which is like a cow of plenty” (*vayaṃ pradugdhe’sya guṇairupasrutā vasūpamānasya vasūni medinī*).
In the case of *pradugdhe*, the rule *armavatkarmaṇe* would have applied, but [it is instead governed] by the rule *akarmakāṇām*.

Regarding the prohibition [of *yak*] by the rule "a-duha-snu-namām," which is an exception (*pratiprasūta*) to the rule "niṣedhe duhi-pacyoḥ": they say that, in accordance with the usage already mentioned, among intransitive verbs, one intends to express the agency of only the secondary (*gauṇa*) object, not the primary (*mukhya*) one. That, however, is questionable. [As in the example: *ajāṃ grāmaṃ...*

In the case of [the verb] *nayati* ("he leads"), we observe that the primary object (*mukhya-karman*) is intended to be expressed as the agent (*kartṛtva-vivakṣā*). Here, this must be noted: when the status of the pen (*vraja*) as the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) is not intended, the pen becomes the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*), and thus the form *ruṇaddhi vrajo gāṃ svayameva* ("the pen restrains the cow by itself") occurs. However, when the pen does not possess the status of an object (*karmatva*), then...

There is also a desire to express the agency (kartṛtva) even of the primary object (mukhyakarman). For example: "The cow itself is obstructed in the pen" (*rudhyate vraje gauḥ svayameva*). Likewise, when there is a desire to express the cow as the point of departure (apādānatva), one says: "The milk is being milked by the cow itself" (*gaurduhyate payaḥ svayameva*), and so forth.

(485) *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* |3|1|87|. [The rule] *karmavat karmaṇā*. For what purpose is the suffix *-vat* used? Just as when the word "Brahmadatta" is employed in place of "Abrahmadatta," it conveys the meaning "like Brahmadatta," so too, even if it were simply stated "like the object" (*karmavat*), [the same understanding would follow].

This is because the meaning [of the sūtra] is obtained as "like the object" (*karmavat*). True; if it were stated that "the agent whose action is similar to that of the object is called the object" (*karma*), the meaning would be that he receives the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "object.

If that were the case, since there would be no designation of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*), the *L* suffixes would not occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), but rather only in the sense of the object (*karman*).

It might be argued: "The rice is being cooked (*acyate odanaḥ*), the wood is being split (*bhidyate kāṣṭham*)". Although this usage is indeed accepted in the final system (*siddhānta*), it should nevertheless be understood that in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*), one would not have forms such as "the cooking is done by the rice" (*acyate odanena*) or "the splitting is done by the wood" (*bhidyate kāṣṭhena*). Here, by the word "object" (*karman*), the action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*) is indicated.

Thus he says: "situated in the object" (*karmasthayā*). This means "situated in the case-factor of the object" (*karmakārakasthā*). Having carried over the term *kartari* from the rule *kartari śa*, it is transformed into the nominative case. And since that [term] is the qualificand, he says: "having an equal action" (*tulyakriyaḥ*), [meaning] "the agent" (*kartā*). This is an extension of the grammatical operation (*kāryātideśa*). Even though there is also an extension of the technical designation (*saṃjñātideśa*) from the scripture...

Although the intended meaning (*lakṣya*) is established in that way, because the scripture (*śāstra*) is primary insofar as it serves a functional purpose (*kāryārthatayā*), recourse is taken specifically to the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*). Regarding the phrase "when the *l* affix denotes a state" (*bhāve lakāre*):
the sense is that in that case, the agent (*kartṛ*) is not expressed. Regarding the phrase "from that which has two *l*-affixes" (*dvilakārakāt*): [this refers to] the irregularity (*vyatyaya*).

In the *saṃhitā* reading of the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi liṭaḷlaṅlaṅkṣu* (Pāṇini 3.4.6), when the *anusvāra* is replaced by its *parasavarṇa*, the letter *l* arises; the meaning is that there are two *l*s above it.
By this, he states the result of the grammatical derivation: "The agent denoted by the letter *a* possesses the status of an object (*karmavatva*) in that very [context]. Thus...

The meaning is as follows: [the suffixes] do not occur. Since the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*) is already presented by the *lakāra* itself, there is no possibility for the application of *kṛtya*-suffixes and the like, because those whose meaning has already been expressed are not employed.

Furthermore, prior to the prescription of the *la*-suffixes, there is certainly no such possibility, because in the absence of an agent presented by a *lakāra*, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) cannot exist. This is the intended sense.

In this regard, the following should be understood: in the rule *ṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ*, the inclusion of the term *kta* (the suffix -ta) is appropriate even though it was [previously] excluded, because its application to the reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*) is desired—as in the example: "The granary opened itself" (*hinnaḥ kusūlaḥ svayameva*). And he himself will state this in the Vārttika: "Of the root *si* (to bind), when the object is the agent of the act of eating" (*sinotergrāsakarmakartṛkasya*), as in: "The morsel has been eaten" (*inaḥ grāsaḥ*).

"By oneself alone. [Objection: But surely, in the rule "atyarthākarmaka," those whose object is not intended (*avivakṣitakarman*) are not understood as "intransitive" (*akarmaka*), because that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of forms such as *dataḥ* and *pakvaḥ* being used in the sense of *datavān* and *pakvavān*. To this they reply: [The prohibition applies] to the *niṣṭhā*-suffix *ta* following the root *in*, when its agent is a dog (*śvā*).

By the force of the prescription of the letter *n*, even roots whose objects are not intended to be expressed are sometimes included; otherwise, the letter *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix would not be obtained there. Consequently, such forms as ‘*inaḥ grāsaḥ svayameva*’ (the morsel was swallowed by itself) and ‘*hinnaḥ kusūlaḥ svayameva*’ (the granary was split by itself) are justified. In this regard—

Some say that if the agent were indeed the object as expressed by the suffix *l* (i.e., if the agent were designated as the object), then the mention of the word *vat* in the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* would be redundant. Nor should it be argued that if the agent were given the technical designation of "object" (*karman*), then the *l*-suffix could not occur in the sense of the action (*bhāva*).
For when one intends to express the agency of what was previously the object, the verbal root becomes intransitive (*akarmaka*).

Thus, since the application of the *lakāra* suffix in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) is unimpeded—just as it is in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) for roots that do not take an object—even if the agent were designated by the technical term "object" (*karman*) when expressed by the *lakāra*, the status of being a mere agent would not be admitted; for the *lakāra* in the sense of the abstract state does not denote the agent. Nor, in the absence of the particle *vat*, would there be the designation of the agent as an "object."

It should not be argued that because there is an absence of designation as agent (*kartṛvyapadeśābhāva*), even though the suffix *yak* is prohibited by the rule "a duha-snu-namām" in the case of *na mate daṇḍaḥ*, the suffix *śanac* would still occur; for when the term *vat* is employed, the functions of the agent would also apply.
This is because, under the governing heading of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), the coexistence of two designations elsewhere results in the desired outcome being established.

"But not equal to that. For equality means similarity, and that is based on difference; however, in the present case, there is no difference, because when the agency of the object is intended to be expressed, the very action—which consists of the fruit residing in the object—becomes resident in the agent. Thus, the sense is that this sūtra is inconsistent.

He states that even though there is no real difference, there is a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*): "karmatva... etc. The meaning is: by resorting to a difference in action (*kriyābheda*) which is co-located with the difference in states caused by those [adjuncts], namely the difference between the states of being an object (*karmatva*) and being an agent (*kartṛtva*). Thus, because the action differs according to the difference in state, the sense is that the agent possesses an action equal to that of the action residing in the object. [This refers to the phrase] "by means of the instrument and the locus" (*karaṇādhikaraṇābhyām*).

If only "one who performs an independent action" (*svatantra-kāraka*) were stated, then in cases such as "he cuts with an axe" (*asinā chinatti*) or "he cooks in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacati*), the very operation that belongs to the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) would now—by the rules *asiś chinatti* or *sthālī pacati*—be considered to reside in the agent (*kartṛ-stha*). This would result in an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); the purpose [of the definition] is to ensure that this does not occur.

Nor should it be argued that there is no over-extension because, although the operation of the pot (*sthālī*) exists in reality even during its state as an instrument—just as its softening (*viklitti*) and so on exist during its state as an object—it is not expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*). This is because the action that serves as the counter-correlate for similarity is not specified as being "expressed by the verbal root. For in this sūtra, it is not stated that "one who has an action similar to the action expressed by the verbal root" [is the agent], such that an over-extension would be avoided.

Now, it might be argued that when it is stated, "An agent whose action is similar [to that of the object] becomes like the object" (*karmavat*), even though there is an expectancy as to "by what [is it similar]" and many *kārakas* present themselves, the word "object" (*karman*) is indeed obtained through proximity (*pratyāsatti*) by the phrase "like the object. To this, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). As for the second half of the verse beginning with "he attains" (*adhigacchati*), it is: "Salutation always to that Guru, by a mere fragment of whose compassion [this was achieved]. Now, both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and that alone is denoted by the word "action" (*kriyā*). In that context, the agent (*kartṛ*) is the locus of the operation, while the object (*karman*) is the locus of the result.

Now, since verbs such as *pac* (to cook) and *bhid* (to split), as well as *gam* (to go) and *ruh* (to ascend), are equally transitive and have results residing in the object (*karmaniṣṭha*), how is it to be known that *gam* and others belong to the class of "verbs whose state resides in the agent" (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*)? To this, he says: "Where [the action is] in the object... and "in the villages... It should be understood that even in cases such as "on elephants mounted or unmounted" or "among those who have mastered or not mastered the meaning of the scriptures," no difference is perceived. Regarding the form *kāriṣyate*: the augment *iṭ* of the *ciṇvadiṭ* type is optional by the rule *yasic-sīyuṭ*.

In the alternative [where the *ya*-affix is present], the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "ṭhṛddhanoḥ sye"; thus, *kariṣyate*. Likewise in the conditional (*lṛṅ*), *akariṣyata*. When there is the augment *iṭ* as if in the case of *ciṇ* after the suffix *sic*, we have *akāriṣṭa*; in the other alternative, *akṛta*. When there is the augment *iṭ* as if in the case of *ciṇ* after the suffix *sīyuṭ*, we have *kāriṣīṣṭa*; in the other alternative, *kṛṣīṣṭa*. But with the suffix *tās*, we have *kāritā* or *kartā*. However, in the cases of *yak* and *ciṇ*, forms such as *kriyate ghaṭaḥ svayameva* ("the pot is being made by itself") and *akāri* ("it was made") would not be established. This means that the status of being "like the object" (*karmavat*)—by the rule "as the object, so the agent"—would not be established.

By this [argument], the Naiyāyika claim that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has its power (*śakti*) in effort (*yatna*), because one intends to express "he cooks" as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), is refuted. For if the root *kṛ* had effort as its meaning, then like the verb *yat* ("to strive"), it would lack a direct object (*akarmaka*). By the phrase "by this," the meaning is: by the acceptance that cognition (*jñāna*) resides in the agent (*kartṛstha*). Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of *ya*" (*yagabhāvāt*): the sense is that if [the suffix] *ya* were present, there would be the form *anuvyavasīyamāna*. Regarding "elision of *o*" (*ollopa*): this is by the rule *otaḥ śyani*.

[Objection: But if there is an absence of being *sakarmaka* (having an object), how can there be the suffix *śānac* here? To this he says: "In the sense of habituality (*tācchīlya*) and so forth. [He adds: "But not..."—the meaning is that the suffix *śānac* does not occur. In the example "Devadatta and Yajñadatta touch each other," since both possess the status of object and agent, one might suspect the application of *karmavadbhāva* because an action residing in the object (*karmastha*) is here residing in the agent (*kartṛstha*). Anticipating this, he says: "Of those [roots] that are *sakarmaka*..."

Furthermore, in this case, one must necessarily not assume a difference in action such that "Devadatta touches Yajñadatta" and "Yajñadatta [touches] Devadatta. Thus, there is agency with respect to the action residing in oneself, but with respect to the other action, there is the status of being an object (*karman*). Otherwise, both would have the status of agent alone, as in the example "these two touch the Gaṅgā. And so, because the action residing in the object (*karmastha*) does not reside in the agent (*kartṛstha*), the application of the rule *karmavat* (treating the agent like the object) does not apply.

Nor should it be suspected that [the rule] applies here because conjunction resides in both [relata] and because the fruit residing in the action resides in the agent; for the conjunctions determined by each respective [action] are distinct. Otherwise, if the fruit and the operation had a single locus, the status of being transitive (*sakarmaka*) could not be established at all. Furthermore, since the actions of *ruh* (to climb) and *gam* (to go) reside in the agent, the status of being treated like a transitive verb (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply in cases such as "the elephant climbs" (*ārohate hastī*) or "he goes to the village" (*gacchati grāmaḥ"); this is the consensus of the Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa, and others.

And thus, since the result in the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is equal in all cases, it is difficult to establish a distinction between the roots *ruhi*, *gami*, and *spṛś*; consequently, there is no possibility here of [the verb] being "agent-located" (*karmavat*). Therefore, he provides another example: *ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati* ("He leads the goat to the village"). The point is that in the absence of this prohibition, the suffix *yak* would apply, and even though the fruit of the action does not accrue to the agent, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would occur. If it is argued: "Even here, no difference produced by the action is perceived in the object; therefore, it is difficult to establish that the action is 'object-located' (*karmastha*)," [the response follows].

On this point, they say: Just as the perception or non-perception of a specific change produced by the action [determines the classification], so too is the "intendedness" (*uddeśyatā*) a restrictive factor. Where the intendedness belongs to the aspect of the state [resulting from the action], that is an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*); but where it belongs to the aspect of the operation (*vyāpārāṃśa*), that is an action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyā*). For instance, in the cases of seeing and ascending, because no specific change is perceived in the object—which remains subordinate—the action resides in the agent. Furthermore, the intention conforms to the desire "May I see," and not "May this object come into being."

The general sense is "I shall go upward" and not "let there be a downward orientation of the hand. Going upward is a specific activity conducive to conjunction with an upper location; that alone is the meaning of the root *ruh*, and not merely downward orientation. For even when a person standing on the ground bends down a tree branch with both hands, one does not say of him, "he is ascending. It is for this very reason that the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *yaddhituparaṃ chandasi* states: "the root *ruh* has the sense of going (*gati*)."

For this very reason, in such usages as "the elephant-drivers mount the elephant" and "the mahout causes them to mount," the status of the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *aṇ* [causative] becoming the object (*karman*) in the *ṇic* [causative] is logically consistent. However, in the case of the roots *pac* and *bhid*, a specific change—namely, softening (*viklitti*) and splitting (*dvidhābhavana*) respectively—is observed in the object; since the activity of the factors of action (*kāraka*) is directed solely toward that [change], these are actions residing in the object (*karmasthakriya*). Consequently, in examples such as "the rice is being cooked" (*pacyate odanaḥ*) and "the wood is being split" (*bhidyate kāṣṭham*), the treatment of the object as the subject (*karmavadbhāva*) indeed occurs.

In the example *ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati* ("He leads the goat to the village"), the factor residing in the object (*karman*)—namely, the conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—is the intended goal (*uddeśyatā*), and not the factor of the operation (*vyāpārāṃśa*). Thus, since the status of being "like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) would apply here, this prohibition is necessary; such is the general direction. (486) *na duhasnunamāṃ yak-ciṇau* (Pāṇini 3.1.89). Regarding the rule *duhi-pacyoḥ*: because these two roots are *dvikarmaka* (having two objects), [the rule applies] to one of the two objects.

Since the root *duh* (to milk) is transitive when there is an intention to express the agent [of the action], a prohibition [of the ātmanepada ending] would otherwise apply; this rule is therefore commenced. In the example "The cow milks milk" (*gauḥ payo dugdhe*), the ātmanepada ending occurs invariably by virtue of the treatment as a reflexive-passive (*karmavadbhāva*). This is because it has been stated that "for roots such as *duh*, etc., [the ātmanepada occurs] when the primary object is intended as the agent. Thus, when the primary object [milk] is intended as the agent, [the ātmanepada is used].

They say that "gāṃ dugdhe" (he milks the cow) is not cited as an example. And thus, because it has been stated that "in the case of roots meaning 'to lead,' 'to carry,' and 'to draw,' [the object becomes the agent]," it follows by the same logic that for roots such as *nī* (to lead), there is an intention to express the agency of the primary object itself.
(487) *acaḥ karmakartari* |3|1|62|. From *acaḥ karma*, the words *ciṇ* and *te* are carried over from the rule *iṇ te padaḥ*; and the word *anyatarasyām* is carried over from the rule *dīpajana*.

Therefore he says: "ending in a vowel," and so forth. What is the purpose of [specifying] "after a vowel" (*acaḥ*)? Consider *abhedikāṣṭham* ("the wood that split itself"). Here, the substitution of *ciṇ* is obligatory. What is the purpose of [specifying] "in the sense of object-agent" (*karmakartari*)? Consider *akāri ghaṭaḥ kulālena* ("the pot was made by the potter"). Here too, it is likewise obligatory.
