And [the rule applies] after the root *duh* as well, provided it is in the sense of object-agent. However, in *adohi gaur gopena* ("the cow was milked by the cowherd"), it is obligatory.

"Udumbara is the fruit. When the sentence "The *āla* tree ripens the udumbara fruit" (*āla udumbaram phalaṃ pacati*) is established, there occurs here the treatment as an object (*karmavadbhāva*) because of the intention to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the secondary object (*gauṇakarma*), namely the udumbara. Now, for those who claim that the reading of the root *pac* among roots with two objects (*dvikarmaka*) is unauthoritative, this text [serves as a refutation].

If it is asked, "How are these two [rules] reconciled?"—on this point they say: In the case of the sentence *udumbaraḥ phalaṃ pacati* ("The udumbara tree ripens its fruit"), since the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* does not apply, the status of being treated like an object (*karmavadbhāvaḥ*) is prescribed extensively by the rule *duhipacyor bahulam*, just as in the case of the roots *sṛj* and *yuj*; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

The suffix *śyan* is prescribed for the roots *sṛj* and *yuj*; its *nit*-designation is for the purpose of making the first syllable acute. If, however, the suffix *yak* were used, then once the *lasārvadhātuka* accent has been rendered grave by the rule “*āsyanudāte*” and so forth, the acute accent of *yak* would be heard [instead]. As for the expression “one endowed with faith” (*śraddhopapanna*), when the agent is devoid of faith, only the suffix *yac* is used.
Regarding the phrase "bhūṣāmakarma" (the non-objective [use] of roots meaning adornment): he states that the word *karma* denotes action—namely, by saying "of those denoting adornment.

Regarding the phrase "elsewhere": the prohibition applies to anything other than the Ātmanepada; the meaning is that only the Ātmanepada occurs. He expresses this very point by saying "yak and ciṇ. [The example is] "avākīrṣṭa."

In the case of *ādriyate*, there is optionally the augment *iṭ* by the rule *iṅsicau*. Because it belongs to the *tudādi* class, the substitution of *ṛ* for *ri* occurs by the rule *ṭhriṅ śayagliṅkṣu*. In *ādṛtā*, the suffix is *kit* by the rule *uśca*;
consequently, the *sic* is elided by the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt*.

(488) *na rudhaḥ* | 3|1|64|. The word *ciṇ* is understood from the rule *iṇ niṣṭhāyām seṭi* [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.19], which itself follows from *iṇ gāpāsthāmnādadṛśyati...* [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.1]. It is understood as "only when the root ends in a vowel (*acaḥ*) in the case of the reflexive agent (*karmakartari*)."

(489) *tapas-tapah-karmakasyaiva* || 3.1.88 || [The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied after a verb meaning "to perform penance" (*tapas*) when it has *tapas* as its object. Regarding *atapta*: the phrase *tapas tāpasaḥ* is supplied from the preceding rule. [Regarding *na duha-snu*: But surely, since the root *sru* also has two objects by virtue of being synonymous with *duh*, the object consisting of the cow (*go*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the partial nature of the source.]

If it is argued that even when agency (*kartṛtva*) is intended to be expressed, since the object in the form of milk (*payas*) exists, there is no possibility at all for the *yak* and *ciṇ* affixes due to the prohibition against transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*), [the author] says here: the meaning of the root *snu* is a longing conducive to the flowing of milk through contact with the calf and so forth; and that...

*Goniṣṭhā*: Regarding *snu* in the sense of "flowing" (*prasravaṇa*), here too the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the instrumental sense (*karaṇe*). That which flows by means of this is a "flow" (*prasravaṇa*), and that is longing (*utkaṇṭhā*). In the usage, "We are milked (*upasnutāḥ*) by the virtues of him who is like a cow (*vasūpamānaḥ*) for wealth (*vasūni*)," the word *upasnutāḥ* [is used].
The meaning is "longing. A calf causes the cow to flow [milk];
here, the root *snau* has the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized. When the cow is intended as the agent, one says "the cow flows" (*prasnute gauḥ*).
In the form *prārasnāviṣṭa*, the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule for *ciṇvat*. Nor is it the case that [the augment] is prohibited in the *ciṇ* formation.

One might suspect that even the *iṭ* augment [of the *ciṇvad* type] would not occur; however, by the rule "as in *ciṇ*" (*ciṇvat*), it is the grammatical operation (*kārya*) itself that is extended (*atidiśyate*), just as in the case of *ciṇ*. Furthermore, that extension cannot be negated by the statement "not in *ciṇ*" (*ciṇna*), such that there would be a prohibition of the *ciṇvad-iṭ* augment. Thus, [the form] is *prāsroṣṭa*.

By the rule "‘nu’, ‘kam’, ‘ram’, and roots ending in ā take the ātmanepada," the augment *iṭ*—characterized by beginning with a consonant—is not applied [in the case of *nam*]. Thus we have *namate daṇḍaḥ* ("the staff bends").

Here, because a difference is observed between the bent (*namita*) and unbent states, and because it conforms to the intended meaning (*uddeśa*), the action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*). However, it is the aspect residing in the object that is the intended meaning (*uddeśyatā*), and not that which is conducive to it.

The meaning is that there is the possibility of the application of the *karmavadbhāva* (the treatment as an object) to the operation [of the causative]. In the form *acīkarata*, since the *ciṇ* affix is prohibited, the *caṅ* affix is applied by the rule *ṇiśri*.
There is an extension of the rule to include the roots *ṇi*, *śranth*, *granth*, *brū*, those that take the *ātmanepada* endings, and those that are intransitive (*akarmaka*).

Regarding *ṇiśranthīti*: he states the result of the general inclusion of the affix *ṇi*—namely, "he shakes his tail," and so forth. In the case of *ucchabhāṇḍe*, the affix is *ṇiṅ*. He provides an example of that which is intransitive for the purpose of prescribing the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)—namely, "the Saindhava horses exert themselves. [The rule applies to] the roots *kuṣ* and *rañj*.

From the rule "a duhasnunamām," the word "na" (not) carries over. Thus he says: "not *yac*. Rather, it is *śyan*. The sense is that this applies to that very same scope. In the passage, "One should not say 'girā gireti,' but having uttered 'airaṃ,' one should sing," the word *girā* is prohibited while the word *aira* is prescribed.

Just as in the case of *girāpada*, it occurs in the very place [of its original], so too here, having prohibited *yak*, the *śyan* that is prescribed occurs in the place of that very [suffix]; therefore he explains: "But in the domain of *yak*, this [parasmaipada] does not exist. Because the parasmaipada is taught in conjunction (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*) with *śyan*, it does not occur in the absence of *śyan*.

He provides examples of the ātmanepada [middle voice] as follows: *koṣiṣīṣṭa*, *koṣiṣyate*, *cukuṣe*, *akoṣi*, *akoṣiṣyata*. Similarly, one should understand the following: *rarañje*, *raṅkṣyate*, *arañji*, *araṅkṣyata*, and so forth. In the case of the *śyan* [suffix], as in *kuṣyantī*, it is always [the active voice].

However, in the *yak*-alternative (*yakpakṣe*), there is an optionality (*vikalpa*) according to the rule *ṭhācchīnadyoḥ*. There is indeed a difference in accent (*svara*) as well. In this context, the expression "the wood splits itself" (*ahidyate kāṣṭhaṃ svayam eva*) is employed in the *Vṛtti* and other works; therein, the word *svayam* should be understood as having the sense of an instrument (*karaṇārthaka*). [It means] "by itself" (*ātmanā*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of the instrument" (*karaṇena*): if [the agent] were intended as the agent (*kartṛ*), then the *la*-suffix would occur in the sense of the object (*karman*). This is clear in the works of Kaiyaṭa and others.
Thus ends the section on the "Agent-as-Object" (*karmakartṛprakriyā*) in the *Tattvabodhinī*.

Now begins the section on the kṛtya suffixes following the section on the past participles (*pūrvakṛt*). I pay homage to Pārvatī and Parameśvara, the lords of all the worlds, the bringers of joy to the world, and the progenitors of the universe. (1)

Since the rule *ṛdittviti* (Pāṇini 1.1.5) assigns the technical designation *kṛt* to suffixes other than *tiṅ*, and because the knowledge of *kṛt*s depends upon the knowledge of *tiṅ*s, it is appropriate to explain the *kṛt*s immediately after the explanation of *tiṅ*s; thus, having explained *tiṅ*, he speaks in order to explain the *kṛt*s:

(540) *dhātoḥ* |3|1|91|. [The word] *dhātoḥ*. Now, one might object: since the derivation of *kvin* and other suffixes was already established prior to the definition of verbal terminations (*tiṅ*)—by rules such as *pṛśo'nudake kvin* and *ṛtvig-daghṛg-*—how can this [rule *dhātoḥ*] be justified?
If it is argued that the consistency you have stated holds true, they reply here:

since the discussion of *kvin* and other suffixes was incidental (*prāsaṅgika*) there, whereas the primary [discussion] was conducted right here, there is no room for the aforementioned doubt. This is because [the rule] "from a root having a single vowel, beginning with a consonant... applies.

Although the word "dhātuḥ" (from the root) continues to apply from the preceding sūtra, the term "dhātuḥ" is mentioned again so that the designation *ārddhadhātuka* may be understood as depending on the operation of the verbal root (*śabda-vyāpāra*). Otherwise,
by the rule "the remainder is *ārddhadhātuka*," [the designation would apply] to everything other than *tiṅ* and *śit*.
If the designation *ārdhadhātuka* were applied to every suffix prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), then in forms such as *lūbhyām* and *pūbhyām*, the augment *iṭ* and *guṇa* would occur;

this is because *byām* and the other suffixes would be considered *ārdhadhātuka* by virtue of being prescribed after a root. However, once the term "root" (*dhātu*) is [repeatedly] mentioned [in the definition], [the rule applies only to those suffixes prescribed after a root that have not already been assigned another technical name], such as *tavyat* and *tavya*.

Since there is no such rule as "as if from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*), the status of being an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix does not apply to [suffixes] beginning with *abhyām*; this is the general direction [of the argument].
With the intention that the position stating "the governing rule for verbal roots (*dhātvadhikāra*) continues until the substitution of *rāg*" is incorrect, he says:
"until the end of the third [chapter]. This means up to the conclusion of the third *adhyāya*.

In the view that [the term] "rāglādeśāḥ" [is intended], however, because there is no governing rule (adhikāra) of the word "dhātoḥ" in the rule "iḍ-śit-sārvadhātukam," all *śit* suffixes would be *sārvadhātuka*. Consequently, since *śas* would also be *sārvadhātuka*, by the rule "ārdhadhātukam api," it would take the marker *ṅ*.
It should be understood that in forms such as *harīn*, there would be the substitution of *guṇa* by the rule *herṅtī*. This might be argued:

when a lakāra follows a verbal root, because it is obligatory (*nitya*), the suffix *syapratyaya* would apply first in cases such as *kariṣyati*, resulting in the non-occurrence of *tip* and other suffixes; however, where there is an occasion for *tip* and the like...

If it is argued that in forms such as *bhavati*, the suffixes *tiP* and so on would apply even when there is no intervention because the *vikaraṇa* (verbal affix) is present right there, this is not so. For it is accepted that "the restriction (*niyama*) is stronger than the *vikaraṇas*.
Alternatively, by resorting to the qualification of what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*), [the rule applies] to the *laṭ* prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*).

Because the desired result is established through the explanation [of the rule]. Now, one might object: "If one resorts to such a restrictive qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), then after the root *vidlṛ* in the sense of 'obtaining' (*lābhe*), the affixes *ṇal* and so forth would occur even when there is an intervention by the *śap* verbal class marker (*vikaraṇa*) in the present tense (*laṭ*), according to the rule *vido laṭo vā*. To this, Haradatta says: "In this case, by the word 'root' (*dhātu*)," [the intervention is excluded].
The prescribed [element] is qualified by the condition of being "immediately following" (*vidanā*) the root; thus, the meaning results as follows:

because it is accepted that the *ṇal* and other suffixes apply to the *laṭ* immediately following the root that is prescribed, the *ṇal* and others occur only after the *laṭ* prescribed for the root *vī*, and not otherwise.
The phrase "vidante laḍ iti dik" (the details are known from the *Laḍ* rule) indicates the direction.

He states, "This is an *adhikāra-sūtra*," because there is no mention of anything to be prescribed (*vidheya*) and because it is marked with a svarita accent. Regarding the rule "tatra upapadam" and so forth: by this, it is implied that a second *dhātu-adhikāra* (heading for verbal roots) is necessary for the sake of properly formulating the definitions of *kṛt*-suffixes and *upapada* (co-occurring word). This is the underlying point: if a second *dhātu-adhikāra* did not exist, then the designations of *kṛt* and *upapada* would apply even within the scope of the first *dhātu-adhikāra*.

If, however, the word *iṣṭa* were intended [to mean "desired"], then in rules such as *li luṅi*, since anything merely indicated by the seventh case (*saptamī*) would function as an *upapada*, the undesired meaning—that *cli* occurs when a suffix ending in *luṅ* is the *upapada*—would result.

Furthermore, since the technical designation *kṛt* applies to suffixes taught under the heading of "roots" excluding those marked with *tiṅ*, the suffix *syap* in forms like *kariṣyati* would be a *kṛt*; consequently, by the rule *ṛtaddhite*, it would possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus, being universally accepted that the default singular number applies, the suffix *sup* would necessarily follow. Therefore, this heading exists for the purpose of prescribing these two designations within specific governing scopes. (541) *vā’sarūpo’s-triyām* | 3|1|94 | [An affix] not of the same form [as another previously taught affix] may optionally [apply], except in the feminine gender.

Regarding the rule *vāsarūpa* [Pāṇini 3.1.94]: since there would otherwise be a constant sublation (*nityabādha*) by an exception (*apavāda*), this sūtra is intended to ensure that the general rule sometimes applies even in the presence of a prefix. For this very reason, forms such as *tavyat* and others also occur in cases that are the domain of exceptions, such as *aco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97) and *ṛhalorṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124).
[The suffixes] are employed [as follows]: *bhavyam*, *bhavitavyam*; *kāryam*, *kartavyam*, *karaṇīyam*;

*vācyam*, *vaktavyam*, and so forth. Regarding the term "paribhāṣā" (technical rule) and "adhikāra-sūtra" (governing rule): if the governing rule for feminine nouns (*stryadhikāra*) were accepted, then because of the interruption [caused by it], the rule *vāsarūpa* (P. 3.1.94) would not apply, and thus [the form] *āsitvā bhuṅkte* [would be incorrect].
Forms such as *ṭhāsyate bhoktum* ("he will sit in order to eat") and the like are not established; for here,

because the sitting has the purpose of eating, its priority in time is understood, and since the suffix *ktvā* occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) according to the rule governing the meaning of *tum*, the *l*-suffix (the future tense marker) likewise occurs in that same sense.

Because both [rules] have the same object, there would be a relationship of sublation and sublated between them. Furthermore, the general rule is that "after a vowel, [the suffix] 'ka' occurs," and this would be sublated by the rule "after *ṭh* and so on, [the suffix] 'pha' occurs. Nor is this an acceptable consequence, as it is said: "O Pārvatī, for me who am listening to names beginning with the letter 'a'..."

Because this would contradict such applications [of the rules] as *ityādi*. Keeping this very point in mind, Haradatta and others have stated that this is a *paribhāṣā* (a metarule). By this, since the rule *aki liṅ ca* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the provision for optional forms (*vā-sarūpa-vidhi*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), [the following applies] to those [rules] subsequent to the section on feminine endings (*stryadhikāra*).

The established conclusion (siddhānta) that the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply in the case of suffixes having the sense of *kṛtya*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, or *khalartha* is thus consistent; this is the general direction [of the argument]. In the rule *vāsarūpa*, the word division is *asarūpa*. Otherwise, since there would be no difference in brevity [between the two readings], one would have to say *arūpo vā* for the sake of avoiding ambiguity.

With the intention of stating this, he says: "asarūpa" (of dissimilar form). What is meant by "of dissimilar form"? The rule "aṇ after an object" (*karmaṇyaṇ*) is a general rule (*utsarga*); the rule "ka after a root ending in ā when no prefix is present" (*āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*) is an exception (*apavāda*). This [exception] must always override the general rule, as in *godah* ("cattle-giver") and *kambaladah* ("wool-cloth giver"). And even if the mention of "dissimilar form" were not made...

It should not be argued that the desired result is not established because the two *aṇ* suffixes are dissimilar (*asarūpa*), for the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that "dissimilarity caused by an *anubandha* [is disregarded]. In the rule *astriyām*, the word *strī* is marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*). With the intention that the scope of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) is understood through the circumflex accent, he says:

"Except as stated in the rule for *stry-ādi* (Pāṇini 3.3.94). By this, the exception (*apavāda*) "not when there is no suffix" (*apratyaya*) always overrides the general rule (*utsarga*) "the suffix *ktin* is used in the feminine" (*striyāṃ ktin*). [Examples: *cikīrṣā*, *jihīrṣā*.
Now, having declared that the word *strī* is marked with a svarita accent in the rule *na striyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.75).

If it is argued: "Setting aside the explanation that 'the understanding of a governing rule [occurs] by means of an accented vowel' (*svarita*), let it be explained instead that the *vāsarūpa* rule does not apply when the feminine gender is to be expressed, or that the *vāsarūpa* rule does not apply to that which is prescribed after the word *striyām* has been uttered. To this, they say:
In the view that [the word] *strī* (feminine) is to be expressed, in cases such as *lavyā* and *lavitavyā*,

the suffix *tavya* would not apply because both [forms] here denote the feminine. However, in the view where the word *striyām* itself is uttered [as the condition], in the case of reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*), as in *vyāvakrośī* and *vyāvakruṣṭiḥ*, [the suffix applies].

Furthermore, the suffix *ktin* should not occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*) when it denotes an object (*viṣaya*). This is because [the suffix] is prescribed by stating "after both [roots and nouns], when feminine" (*dvayor api striyām*).
Consequently, the interpretation that "except for what is stated within the section on the three [suffixes]" (*tryadhikāroktam vinā*) is indeed superior; such is the direction [of the argument].
(542) *kṛtyāḥ* | 3.1.95 | [The suffixes called] *kṛtya* [begin here]. 3.1.95.

Regarding the *kṛtya* suffixes: here, since the desired result is achieved by the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of *kṛtya*—just as in the case of *ratyaya* and so forth—the use of the plural number is for the purpose of including suffixes not explicitly mentioned;
thus, they say that *kelima* and others, which are established by implication (*jñāpaka*), need not be added as supplementary rules (*upasankhyeya*). [This concerns] the suffix *ṇvul*.

"Prior to" (prāk) means prior to the rule "ṇvultṛcau. It does not have "rogākhyāyāṃ ṇvul bahulam" as its limit, according to the principle of proximity (pratyāsatti). However, the specific indicator for this limit is precisely the separate mention of *tṛc* in the rule "arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca," [which distinguishes it] from the *kṛtya* suffixes. And it is not so...

Even if the *tṛc* suffix does not denote an action (*akṛtyatva*), the status of being an action (*kṛtyatva*) for the *ṇvul* suffix would be unavoidable; however, accepting this [undesirable consequence], he [the author] refuted it by stating that "only for those two" (*ayoreva*), meaning only for the meanings of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), does the *ṇvul* suffix apply.
(543) *Tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ* || 3.4.70 || [The *kṛtya*, *kta*, and suffixes having the sense of *khal* occur only for those two.]

"Of those two alone. By the word "tat" (that), the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) are referred to; the particle "eva" (alone/only), however, serves to exclude connection with the agent (*kartṛ*). Thus he says: "of the abstract action and the object alone.
Although this is indeed obtained by the maxim of the *kratu* and *kauṇḍinya*, nevertheless...

Some say that the particle *eva* is used for the sake of clarity regarding the meaning of the locative case (*pratītyarthe*). Others say it is for the purpose of indicating that this rule is not universally applicable (*anitya*).
(544) Regarding the suffixes *tavya*, *tavyat*, and *anīyar*:

they are [stated] for the sake of accent (*svarārthau*). The letter *t* is for the purpose of making the *it* accent (*svarita*) according to the rule "itsvaritam" (Pāṇini 6.1.185). As for the letter *r*, [it serves as an *it* marker].
The phrase "ṭhupottamaṃ ritī" has the sense of "acute on the middle syllable.
(545) *Kṛtyacaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.213. [The sūtra] *kṛtyacaḥ* follows from the previous rule; the words *upasargāt* and *raṣābhyām* also carry over. In that context:

He states that a word may denote something by virtue of being located therein, saying "from one situated in a prefix" (upasargasthāt). [The rule] "of the *n* situated in a *kṛt*-affix" (*kṛtsthasya nasya*)—the point is that if the phrase "following an *ac*" (*acaḥ parasya*) were a qualifier of the *kṛt*-affix, then [the rule would not apply] in cases such as *prayāpaṇam*.
In *pramagna*, from the root *masj* in the sense of "cleansing," there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the *niṣṭhā*-suffix by the rule "and after a root ending in an *udit* vowel" (*oditaśca*).
Because that [suffix] is unestablished, there is elision of *s* by the rule *koḥ*, and [the substitution of] *ku* by the rule *oḥ kuḥ*.

Regarding the mention of *nirviṇṇasya*: in the word *nirviṇṇa*, the substitution of *n* for the final *t* of the root *vid* followed by the suffix *kta* occurs by the rule *adābhyām*, as does the substitution of *n* for the preceding *d*.

(546) *ṇervibhāṣā* |8|4|30|. Regarding the form *prayāpaṇīyam*: the root *yā* means "to cause to reach. After the causative suffix (*ṇic*), by the rule *arti-hrī-*, the augment *puk* is added. Then, by the rule *ṇer aniṭi*, there is the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇi*). Regarding the form *prayāpyamāṇam*: after the root *yā*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is added, followed by the augment *puk*; this is the form of the stem ending in *ṇi*.
When the verbal root *vṛt* is used in the sense of an object (*karman*) in its state as an element (*dhātu*), the suffix *laṭ* is applied; for *laṭ*, the suffix *śānac* is substituted.
Because this [suffix] has the marker *ś*, it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* by the rule *iṅśīd...*. Consequently, by the rule *sārvadhātuke yak*, the suffix *yak* is added.
Then, by the rule *ṇer aniṭi*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the *ṇi*-augment. Following this, by the rule *āne mug*, the augment *muk* is inserted, and finally, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs.

The form *rūpyate* is established; however, when the specific condition (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not prescribed, the suffix *yak* is not established because it does not follow immediately after the causative (*ṇyantāt*) due to the intervention [of the augment]. Nor should it be argued that it will be established by the rule *aḍvyavāye ’pi*, because regarding the portion "after *ra* and *ṣa*," the paribhāṣā "from that which is indicated" (*tasmād iti nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) applies.

Since the rule "even when there is an intervention" (*vyavāye ’pi*)—applied by way of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule)—would otherwise sublate [the requirement for immediate proximity] in order to establish forms such as *rāmāṇām*, and since an over-extension would then follow in cases such as *ādarśena*, the portion beginning with *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye* serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). As for the inclusion of *āṅ*: [The text continues: ...is for the purpose of excluding [interventions] other than those consisting of *āṅ*. Otherwise, because the word *vyavāye* is present in the rule, the intervention of even a single consonant would suffice to trigger the application of the rule. However, since the intervention of a vowel is already established by the preceding rule, the mention of *āṅ* is intended to exclude all other intervening elements. Furthermore, the mention of *āṅ* is not merely for the sake of excluding others; rather, it is intended to indicate that the intervention must consist of *āṅ* alone. Otherwise, the intervention of *āṅ* would be understood as being optional, and consequently, the intervention of *āṅ* would not apply in cases such as *āṅ + ṛcchati = ārcchati*. Therefore, the mention of *āṅ* is made to ensure that the intervention of *āṅ* is mandatory. Moreover, this restriction is not limited solely to the intervention of *āṅ*; rather, it is intended to restrict the intervention of *aṭ* and the others as well. For if the intervention were unrestricted, the intervention of *aṭ* and so forth would also be permitted. It is established that [the mention of] *padavyavāye’pi* is intended to set aside the prohibition [of the rule *na bhābhūpūkamigami...*]. However, the intention is this: how could the requirement of non-intervention (*avyavadhāna*) between the causative suffix (*ṇi*) and the *kṛt*-suffix in the rule *ṇervibhāṣā* be precluded by the mention of *aṅ*?

(547) *halaścejupadhāt* | Pāṇini 6.4.24. Regarding *halaśca*: since a root ending in a consonant (*halanta*) cannot possibly have the vowel *i* as its penultimate (*ijupadha*), the term *halaḥ* indicates that the root begins with a consonant (*halādi*). Thus he says: "of one beginning with a consonant. [The example is] *prakopaṇīyam*. [The root is] *kup* in the sense of anger.

Regarding *prohaṇīyam*: the root *ūh* means "to deliberate. Here, the substitution of *ṇ* is obligatory by the rule *ṛtyacaḥ*. The same applies to *pravapaṇīyam*. [The root] *vap* (548) means "to sow seeds.
[The rule applies] by *ijādeḥ sanumaḥ* 8.4.32.
Regarding the rule *ijādeḥ sanumaḥ*: since the desired result is already established by the rule *ṛtyacaḥ*, this [present rule] is stated for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*).

Thus he says: "if it has *num*," and so forth. Here, the term *hal* which is carried over from the previous context refers to that which ends in a consonant (*halanta*), and not to that which begins with one (*halādi*), because it is impossible for a root beginning with *ij* to begin with a consonant. Therefore, he says: "from that which ends in a consonant."

Regarding the word *vihita*: if the qualifier *vihita* were not explained [as part of the compound], then its restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatā*) would not be obtained; for even in the case of a *kṛt*-suffix ending in *n* that is prescribed after a causative (*ṇijanta*), once the *ṇi*-affix has been elided, it would follow a consonant (*halanta*), and thus the rule *ṇervibhāṣā* would apply as an optional alternative, thereby subverting the intended restriction.

Because of the possibility [of the rule] applying to the suffix *vidhi*. If, however, [the desired result] were accepted [as it stands], then examples such as *preṅkhaṇīyam*, which ends in the suffix *anīyar* derived from a base that does not have the causative suffix *ṇic*, would not be possible; rather, the example would necessarily have to be one derived from a base that does have the causative suffix *ṇic*. What, then, is the purpose of this sūtra?
Since there would be no purpose for a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatva*), in the case of *praṅganīyam*, the substitution of *ṇ* would occur by the rule *ṛtyacaḥ*;

therefore, one must necessarily accept that the term [in the rule] qualifies what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*). This is the general direction. Now, even so, the status of being a restrictive rule is not tenable in the case of *prenvanam*.

Because the possibility of [the rule] having a prescriptive purpose (*vidhyarthatva*) is precluded by the intervention of the *num* augment, and because the rule "ṛtyacaḥ" does not apply here, he says: "The mention of *num*... Just as in the rule "aṭku-pv-āṅ," here too the *anusvāra* is indicated by *num*; thus, there is no prescriptive purpose in this case.

The sense is that it is to be suspected. Regarding *prombhaṇam*: the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) to the root *umbh*, meaning "to fill," following the rule *ṛtyacaḥ*. He states [the following], because the [preceding] rule continues to apply: (549) *vā niṃsanikṣanindām* Pāṇini 8.4.33.
Regarding the phrase "after a *kṛt* affix":

(550) *na bhābhūpūkamigamipyāyīvepām* Pāṇini 8.4.34. There is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for roots beginning with *bhā* when followed by a *ṇic* affix. Regarding the phrase "of those beginning with *bhā* when followed by a *ṇic*": [this refers to] that which ends in *ṇic*.

This statement is made because [the rule] would otherwise not apply due to the difference in base-form (*prakṛtyantaratva*). Some say that this is established by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not after *aṅ*" in the sūtra *heracaṅi*, which indicates the principle: "when a base-form is mentioned, that which has an additional suffix (*ṇi*) is also included. However, that is due to haste; for the indication [itself] is as follows: [The sūtra *heracaṅi*] prohibits the substitution of *ru* for the *hi* of the root *ah* when it is preceded by a verbal prefix (*upasarga*), provided it does not follow the augment *aṅ*. Now, if the base-form *ah* were not included here, then since the form *āha* (from *aṅ + ah*) is different from the base-form *ah* due to the addition of the augment, the prohibition would not apply, and *ru* would be substituted for the *hi* of *āha* even after a prefix. To prevent this, the mention of "not after *aṅ*" (*acaṅi*) is necessary. This very fact—that the mention of the base-form includes that which has an additional suffix—is what is indicated. Thus, the inclusion of the form *āha* is established by the exclusion "not after *aṅ*," and it is not by means of the principle "when a base-form is mentioned, that which has an additional suffix is also included. Therefore, the claim of some is incorrect. Furthermore, the principle "when a base-form is mentioned, that which has an additional suffix is also included" is actually indicated by the sūtra *na lyapi* (P. 6.1.41), which prohibits the shortening of the final vowel of a word ending in *lyap* when it follows a word with a long vowel. If the base-form *kṣība* were not included here, then since the form *kṣībīkṛtya* (from *kṣība + kṛt + lyap*) is different from the base-form *kṣība* due to the addition of the suffix *kṛt*, the prohibition of shortening would not apply, and the shortening would occur. To prevent this, the mention of the base-form *kṣība* is necessary. This very fact—that the mention of the base-form includes that which has an additional suffix—is what is indicated. Thus, the inclusion of the form *kṣībīkṛtya* is established by the mention of the base-form *kṣība*, and it is not by means of the principle "when a base-form is mentioned, that which has an additional suffix is also included. Consequently, the claim of some is incorrect. Moreover, the principle "when a base-form is mentioned, that which has an additional suffix is also included" is actually indicated by the sūtra *aninasmangrahaṇānyarthavatā cānarthakena ca tadantavidhiṃ prayojayanti* (Vārttika on P. 1.1.72), which states that mentions of *an*, *in*, *as*, and *man* cause the application of the rule regarding endings (*tadantavidhi*) both when they have meaning and when they are meaningless. If the base-form *an* were not included here, then since the form *rājānam* (from *rājan + am*) is different from the base-form *an* due to the addition of the suffix *an*, the mention of *an* would not include it, and the elision of the case-ending (*am*) would not occur. To prevent this, the mention of the base-form *an* is necessary. This very fact—that the mention of the base-form includes that which has an additional suffix—is what is indicated. Thus, the elision of the case-ending in *rājānam* is established by the mention of the base-form *an*, and it is not by means of the principle "when a base-form is mentioned, that which has an additional suffix is also included. Therefore, the claim of some is incorrect. Furthermore, the principle "when a base-form is mentioned, that which has an additional suffix is also included" is actually indicated by the sūtra *pratyayagrahaṇe yasmātsa vihitas tadādestadantasya grahaṇam* (Paribhāṣā 29), which states that when a suffix is mentioned, the mention includes that which begins with the element after which that suffix is prescribed and ends with it. If the base-form *pati* were not included here, then since the form *patyā* (from *pati + ā*) is different from the base-form *pati* due to the addition of the suffix *ā*, the mention of *pati* would not include it, and the substitution of *ya* for *pati* would not occur. To prevent this, the mention of the base-form *pati* is necessary. This very fact—that the mention of the base-form includes that which has an additional suffix—is what is indicated. Thus, the substitution of *ya* in *patyā* is established by the mention of the base-form *pati*, and it is not by means of the principle "when a base-form is mentioned, that which has an additional suffix is also included. Therefore, the claim of some is incorrect. Finally, the principle "when a base-form is mentioned, that which has an additional suffix is also included" is actually indicated by the sūtra *na lumatāṅgasya* (P. 1.1.63), which prohibits operations on the base-form (*aṅga*) when a suffix marked with *lu* follows. If the base-form *rājānam* were not included here, then since the form *rājani* (from *rājan + i*) is different from the base-form *rājānam* due to the addition of the suffix *i*, the mention of *rājānam* would not include it, and the substitution of *n* for the final *m* would not occur. To prevent this, the mention of the base-form *rājānam* is necessary. This very fact—that the mention of the base-form includes that which has an additional suffix—is what is indicated. Thus, the substitution of *n* in *rājani* is established by the mention of the base-form *rājānam*, and it is not by means of the principle "when a base-form is mentioned, that which has an additional suffix is also included. Therefore, the claim of some is incorrect. Consequently, the statement that this is established by the exclusion "not after *aṅ*" is due to haste. The indication [of the principle] is as explained above.
This is because it has been established as the settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the *Bhāṣya* and other works that [the rule] concerns only the substitution of *kutva*.

(551) *aco yat* |3|1|97|. The term *acaḥ* [is used]; *yat* [is the suffix]. The word "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood [from the previous rule]. And the mention of *ac* is a qualifier of the verbal root.

By means of the qualifier, there is an application of the rule to that which ends in such [an element]; thus he says: "from that which ends in a vowel" (*ajantāt*). Regarding the statement "it could have been omitted": here some hold that the mention of *ac* (vowel) is required so that the rule might apply even to that which was previously an *ac*-ending [though not so at the time of the suffix].
By this, in forms such as *ditsyam* and *dhitsyam*, when the suffix *yat* is applied, the acute accent (*udātta*) prescribed by the rule "*hyato ’nāvaḥ*" occurs.

If the suffix *ṇyat* were applied, the rule "itsvaritam" (Pāṇini 6.1.197) would result [in the circumflex accent]. Nor should it be argued that in forms such as *ditsyam* and *dhitsyam*, there is no possibility of the suffix *ṇyat* at all by virtue of the rule "ṛhaloḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.124); for once the elision of the vowel *a* has occurred due to the intended application of an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, the root becomes *halanta* (ending in a consonant), thereby making the suffix *ṇyat* applicable.

They say that this [occurrence] arises from that; however, this is only superficially so. For this [result] would indeed be possible if the elision were to occur when an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix was intended to be expressed. But the elision is properly applicable only when an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix follows.
Otherwise, in the absence of a subsequent cause, there would be an absence of "having a substitute" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

The meaning is that [if the suffix were applied to *gaṇ*], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of vṛddhi in the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) in forms such as *gaṇayati*. Regarding the phrase "because it is easy to read": the roots are of two kinds, ending in vowels (*ajanta*) and ending in consonants (*halanta*). Since he will explain the formation of the denominative (*ṇyanta*) for those ending in consonants later on, the implication is that by process of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*), the suffix *yat* will apply only to those ending in vowels. Regarding *takiśasī*: *taka*...
The root *has* is used in the sense of laughing; *śas* in the sense of injury; and *cat* in the sense of begging.

As for the fact that some read *śaṃs* with an anusvāra (*śaṃs*), that is to be disregarded, because one must accept only *śaṃs* with the suffix *ṇyat*, in accordance with the rule: "After the roots *īḍ*, *vand*, *vṛś*, *śaṃs*, and *duh*, [the suffix] *ṇyat* is applied."

(552) *īdyati* | Pāṇini 6.4.65. It should be stated that for the root *han*, there is optionally the suffix *yat* and the substitution of *vadha*. That is to say: for the root *han*, the suffix *yat* may optionally occur; however, the substitution of *vadha* for *han* occurs invariably in conjunction with the suffix *yat*. Even though the word *vadhya* is derived in the sense of "one who deserves killing" (*vadham arhati*), [the rule applies].

Even though [the form] could be established by the *taddhita* suffix *yat* according to the rule "aṇḍādibhyaḥ" while the word "yat" is understood from the preceding rule "īrṣyācchedādyace," nevertheless, a compound such as *asi-vadhyaḥ* (to be killed by a sword) or *musala-vadhyaḥ* (to be killed by a club) would not be established. However, when [the suffix] is a *kṛt* [suffix], it is established by the rule "kartṛ-karaṇe kṛtā. It is not [established otherwise].
It should not be argued that, in the analysis (*vigraha*) "one who deserves the killing of an *asivat*," the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) may be applied directly from the compound itself;

for the word *vadha* is listed alone among the items beginning with *daṇḍa*, and there is a prohibition against the extension of the designation [of the base] to a form ending in that [suffix] when a suffix is prescribed. Furthermore, there would be a difference in accent (*svara*). For if the suffix *yat* were applied to the word *asivadha*, [the accent would differ].

Otherwise, the *svarita* accent would apply [to the first syllable] by the rule "itsvarita. However, in a compound with a *kṛt*-derived word, the word *vadhya* is acutely accented on its first syllable (*ādyaudāta*) by the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derived compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*). For this very reason, one should not claim that there is a *sup-supā* compound with the word *vadhya* ending in a *taddhita* suffix.

The direction [of the argument] is that it would result in the vowel being *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable). Regarding the form *ghātya*: by the rule *hanasta’ciṇṇaloḥ*, there is the substitution of *t* for the *n* of the root *han*; by the rule *ho hanteḥ*, there is the substitution of *k* for the *h*.
(553) *poradupadhāt* 3.1.98.

What is the purpose of [the condition] *poḥ*? [Example: *pākyam*. What is the purpose of [the condition] *adupadhāt*? [Example: *kopyam*. What is the purpose of adding the marker *t* (i.e., *tapara*)? [Example:
from the root *āplṛ* in the sense of "pervasion," we have *āpyam*. [The rule states] "not when there is an *anubandha*.

Because *anubandhas* are not integral parts [of the word], the lack of similarity (*asārūpya*) caused by them is not taken into account. This remains true even under the view that [the *anubandha*] is entirely external (*ekāntatva*).
The mention of the word "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) in the rule *adādidhātyor vibhāṣā* indicates that the [distinction between] markers (*liṅga*) is not being relied upon.

Otherwise, since there would already be dissimilarity (*asārūpya*) caused by the markers, the suffix *ṇi* would apply in the domain of *śap* anyway; so what would be the purpose of that mention of "optionally"? Consequently, even in both alternative views, the suffix *ṇi* does not apply in forms such as *śapyam*.
That which comes into being is a *bhāva*. Furthermore, this [explanation] applies to both positions regarding the inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā* in the sūtra beginning with *dadāti*:

namely, that when the view is that the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) are non-exclusive (*anekānta*), the option (*vibhāṣā*) applies because the substitution of *ṇa* for *śa* would otherwise not occur; whereas when the view is that they are exclusive (*ekānta*), it is an option regarding what is already established. Thus, it is common to both positions.
The mention of *vibhāṣā* is cited as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the *Manoramā*, where it is presented only in support of the view that [the rule] is absolute (*ekāntatva*).

Following that, it has been stated here as well. However, according to the view that it is not absolute (*anekāntatva*), the mention of *māṅ* in the sūtra *udīcāṃ māṅaḥ* is the specific indicative mark. For even though *meṅ* exists [in the sense of "to exchange"], [the mention of *māṅ* would otherwise be redundant].

Since the suffix *ṇ* is attached, its status as ending in a vowel (*ejanta*) remains unimpeded because it possesses no constituent parts; thus, by accepting the substitution of *ā* according to the rule "ādeca upadeśe," [the form is established]. This is the general direction. Regarding the phrase "only with *ṇya*":
by that, when the circumflex accent (*svarita*) applies according to the rule "itsvaritam," there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound in the word *ālambhya*.

The intended result—that the word ends in a circumflex (svarita) accent—is established by setting aside [the rule for the first syllable] through the natural accent of the second member of the compound (*kṛdutarapadaprakṛtisvara*).
However, if the rule *ṭhyato ’nāvaḥ* were applied, the initial syllable of the second member would necessarily become acute (*udātta*), which is undesirable; such is the meaning.

(554) *upāt praśaṃsāyām* |7|1|66|. After the prefix *upa*, when a suffix beginning with *ya* is intended to be applied, the augment *num* is added to the root *labh* in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). And here, that [praise] is a qualifier by virtue of being implied; however, the meaning of the verbal root [remains as it is].
It is indeed attainment (*prāpti*). Therefore, that for which there is attainment, or from which attainment arises, serves as the cause for praise;

this is the illustrative example (*udāharaṇa*) here. Conversely, the opposite case is the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). Here too, when the suffix *ṇya* is intended to be applied, since the augment *num* has already been applied by virtue of the meaning, the circumflex accent (*svarita*) applies to the final syllable when *ṇya* is present.

[The suffix] *yat* occurs; however, if the initial syllable of the subsequent member were to have the udātta accent, [it would be incorrect]. But the Easterners (Prācāḥ), disregarding this specific accentual distinction, accepted only the rule "oradupadhāt" (Pāṇini 3.1.107) for *yat*, and explained that *num* is inserted when *yat* follows. This [explanation] should be rejected as it contradicts the established practice (ācāra). Thus they say.

(555) *gadamadacarayamaś cānupasarge* |3|1|100| The words *gada*, *mada*, *cara*, and *yama* [are mentioned] with a change of case; that is, the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative. After these roots, when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), the suffix *yat* shall be applied.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇyat*. Why "not preceded by a prefix"? Consider: *na eṣadhe kāryam idaṃ nigādya*. (In this case, the suffix is *ṇyat*.)

Thus says Śrī Harṣa. [The rule] "one should move away from" (*carer āṅ*) and "from *yami*" (*yameḥ*); the intention is that [the desired form] is already established by the rule "*or ad upadhāt*" alone. [The word] "proper in relation to restraint" (*niyame sādhur*) is formed by the rule "*yamaḥ samupaniviṣu ca*."
When the optional suffix *pratyaya* is applied, the meaning is that the *taddhita* suffix *yat* is used in the sense of "one who is skillful (*sādhu*) in this.

Although, under this view, the third case ending for the agent is difficult to obtain because the rule "optionally for those ending in *ṛt*" does not apply, nevertheless, the forms *tvayā* and *tena* are used by intending to express the instrument (*karaṇatva*).

The transition (*gati*) of one who stands in the third [case] is to be understood. Others hold that the word *kevala* is compounded with *yata* by means of the particle *ni*. Alternatively, relying on the opinion that "the root *yam* takes *mi* when not meaning 'to serve food' (*apariveṣaṇa*)," one may accept its status as having *mi* (i.e., *mit*), just as in examples such as "he restrains what has been concluded" (*aryavasitaṃ niyamayan*), and thus [the form] is to be understood as derived from the causative (*ṇyanta*). Or else—

Because a grammatical rule preceded by a technical name (saṃjñāpūrvaka) is not invariably valid, the *vṛddhi* substitution does not apply in the case of the suffix *ṇyat* alone; this is the general direction [of the argument]. Thus, the usage of the Vārttika is also established otherwise, and the sense is that one should not postulate the rule "after the prefix *ni*, [the root] *yaj*" on the strength of that [Vārttika].
(556) *Avadya*, *paṇya*, and *varya* [are formed with the suffix *kyap*] in the senses of "blameworthy," "to be sold," and "not to be obstructed" [respectively].
III.1.101. Regarding *anūdyam*: here, the suffix *kyap* alone is applied after the root *vad*. There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) because it belongs to the *yaj*-class [of roots].
[The rule] *alopo nañaḥ* [applies], and [the augment] *nuṭ* is added by [the rule] *asmānnuḍaci*. Regarding *vyavahartavya*: although... [the text continues].

Although the word *paṇitavya* is common to two meanings, nevertheless, because this technical designation (*nipātana*) is conventional (*rūḍhi*) here, it refers specifically to that which is to be employed [as a technical term]. And it has been said by Bhartṛhari: "For the purpose of obtaining the [technical] markers (*anubandha*), the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the tenses (*kāla*), and the restrictive rules (*niyama*), as well as for the modifications (*vikāra*)."

And the term *nipātana* (irregular formation) refers to that which has an established meaning (*rūḍhārtha*). The phrase "and for the purpose of obtaining a restriction regarding the modifications of the *anubandhas*" connects with what precedes it. Regarding the word *śatena*: the word *śata* here refers to an indefinite number.
The meaning is that there is no fixed rule regarding the suitors when choosing a bride. Regarding the word *varyā*: [it means a girl who is to be chosen].

The meaning is "to be shared" (*saṃbhaktavya*). This is a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) of the root *vṛñ*, which means "to share," because it is only in that sense that the meaning of "non-obstruction" is possible; this is the intended sense.

By using the word "functioning" (*vṛttyā*), he suggests that if the term "in non-obstructions" (*anirodeṣu*) were not stated, the root *vṛñ* might also be applicable [in its primary sense of "covering" or "obstructing"].

The suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *vṛ* by the rule *ṭheṣṭiśās* etc. In this sūtra, words such as *avadya* and others are presented as separate, uninflected items; among them, the word *varyā* is cited with the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. This is not an indication made by a *dvandva* compound ending in the nominative plural suffix *jas*; therefore, *varyā* is prescribed specifically for the feminine gender.

In the feminine, however, from the root *vṛ*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied according to the rule *ṭhṛ-halorṇyat*. Thus, [the word] is *vāryā*, as in "the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)". Although there is no restriction because even the officiating priests are to be chosen for the sacrifice in general, since they lack femininity, only the suffix *ṇyat* occurs. This is the opinion of the author of the *Vṛtti*. Nor should one suspect that the suffix *kyap* applies here by the rule *ṛt-vyeñ-śīṅ-bhū-sru-pū-dhṛ-kṣu-bhā-yā-hr-ñi-iṇ-vasi-genīḥ*.

In this context, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), only the root *vṛñ* (to choose) is to be understood, and not *vṛṅ* (to choose as a bride). However, Bhaṭṭi, considering this to be a compound followed by the nominative suffix *jas*, employed the masculine form *varya* [in the verse]:
"This Sugrīva is my *varya*."

(557) *vahyam* is [the word] *karaṇa*. (Pāṇini 3.1.102). That which is *vahyam* means that which is the object of carrying (*vahanakarma*). (558) *Upasaryā* [is used in the sense of] "fit for breeding" (*kālyā prajane*). (Pāṇini 3.1.104).
*Upasaryā*: The suffix *ya* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation) after the roots *sṛ* or *sṛt* preceded by *upa*. *Kālyā*: Her time has arrived;

[this is formed] with the suffix *yat* according to the rule *ālādyat*, while the governing context is "that which has reached its proper time" (*ādasya prāptam*). *Prajana* means procreation or the conception of an embryo; it is derived from the root *jan* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), according to the rule *anivadhyośca*.

The prohibition of the suffix *niṣ* [is as follows]: regarding the word *upasārya*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), while *yat* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

The point is that although the suffix would have been expected in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) by the rule "of these two alone," it is here prescribed as *yat* in the sense of the agent. (559) *ajaryam saṅgatam* (Pāṇini 3.1.105).

Regarding the phrase *saṃgataṃ cet*: the suffix *kta* is used here in the neuter sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Regarding the term *viśeṣya* (the substantive): one must not understand the meaning here to be that "the whole [compound] *ajaryam* has *saṃgataṃ* as its expressed meaning. This is because synonyms cannot be used simultaneously; otherwise, the usage *ajaryam-satāṃ saṃgatam* would result, which is ungrammatical.
And because the usage by Bhaṭṭi, “*ena saṅgatam*,” would otherwise be untenable.

(560) *Vadaḥ supi kyap ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.106). Regarding *vadaḥ*: since it is transitive, a *kṛtya* suffix in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) is difficult to obtain; [this is because of the rule] *aḥ karmaṇi*.

Just as in the case of the Sūtra "ayoreva," the established doctrine is that [the affix *lyuṭ*] occurs after transitive verbs in the sense of the object (*karman*), and only after intransitive verbs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). Therefore, he says: "The word 'bhāva' is drawn over [from the previous rule]. This is because in the rule "huvo bhāve," the term "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) is understood to carry over; thus, it applies only to the verb *hū* when it is without a prefix.
Since the root *bhū* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffixes known as *kṛtya* are established by the rule "only for these two [roots] in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*).

In response to the objection that the explicit mention of *bhāva* (the abstract state) in the rule is therefore redundant, it is settled in the *Bhāṣya* that the mention of *bhāva* is for the sake of subsequent rules. The author states the view of those who grasp the true intent of that *Bhāṣya*: "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*). [This applies] when there is no prefix (*anupasarga*).
Thus [it is said]. What is the purpose of [specifying] *supi*? [Consider: *ghātaḥ*, formed by *hanastaḥ aciṇṇaloḥ*. What is the purpose of [specifying] *anupasarge*? [Consider: *praghātaḥ*;
here *ghan* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*).
(561) *eti-stu-śāsvṛ-dṛ-juṣaḥ kyap* 3.1.109. [The suffix] *kyap* is applied after the roots *i*, *stu*, *śās*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, and *juṣ*.

The intention is that [the previous rules] "etistu" and "ebhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.89–90), as well as "supyanupasarge bhāve" (Pāṇini 3.3.94), have ceased to apply. The term "eti" refers specifically to the root *iṇ*, and not to the roots *iṅ* and *ik*; for if it referred only to *ti* and *yati* preceded by the prefix *adhi*, the mention of "eti" would be untenable. And thus it is said: "Grammar should be studied for the protection of the Vedas."

In the Bhāṣya, it is stated: "It should be said that 'like ṭhin' applies even to the ika suffixes. Having studied this, they cite *adhītya mātā* as an example. [Note: *adhītyā* is to be remembered as being derived from *smartavyā*. (562) *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk* (Pāṇini 6.1.71). [The rule: The augment *tuk* is added after a short vowel before a *kṛt* suffix beginning with a *pit* letter. [Commentary: Regarding the statement "it should be said that 'like ṭhin' applies even to the ika suffixes," the point is that by this rule, the suffixes belonging to the *ṭhin* class (such as *ktvā*) also function like the *ika* suffixes (such as *iṣṇu*). Having studied this principle, grammarians provide the example *adhītya mātā* ("having studied, [the mother]"). Here, the suffix *ktvā* is treated as an *ika* suffix, and thus the elision of the *y* in *adhyayana* occurs. [Note: *adhītyā* is to be understood as a form where the *y* has been elided, which is to be remembered as a derivative of *smartavyā* (to be remembered). (562) *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk*: The augment *tuk* is inserted after a short vowel when followed by a *kṛt* suffix that begins with a *pit* letter (a consonant other than *y*, *v*, *r*, *l*, or a nasal). For instance, in *adhi-itya*, the short vowel *i* of *adhi* is followed by the *pit* suffix *ktvā*, resulting in the form *adhītya*. Final Answer: The final answer is the translation provided above. I hope it is correct.
How, then, is the word *upeya* derived? It is formed from the root *īṅ*, belonging to the *divādi* class, with the suffix *yat*.

The form *vṛ* is intended as the inclusion of the root *vṛñ* (to choose), and not *vṛṅ* (to choose in marriage). This is indicated by the rule *īḍavanda-*. For in that rule, due to its association with *īḍ* and *vand*, only *vṛṅ*—which is conjugated in the ātmanepada—is understood.

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. Regarding the phrase "also for another": the scope of the suffix *ṇya*, as prescribed by the rule *ṭhorāvaśyake* (Pāṇini 3.1.125), is exemplified by *avaśyalāvyam*. When the necessity (*āvaśyakatā*) is not intended to be expressed, the scope of the suffix *kyap* is exemplified by *stutyaḥ* and so on. In cases such as *avaśyastutyaḥ*, where both [suffixes] would apply, [the rule] *vipratiṣedhe* [applies].
The intention is that since the suffix *ṇyat* would apply [by rule], the mention of *kyap* again is for the purpose of preventing that.

Regarding the statement "there is an extension [of the rule] for *añj* preceded by *āṅ* when it is a name": as for the phrase "for *añj* preceded by *āṅ*," one might ask: "Why is the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) not stated to occur precisely when *ṇyat* follows? If this is asked, the answer is no.

Because it would lead to the undesirable consequence [of the word] being *kutva* [i.e., changing the *j* to *g*], and because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of its being *titsva* [i.e., having the *t* as its final sound]. Therefore, the word *ājya* must indeed end in the suffix *kyap*. If it is objected: "In that case, however, the *avagraha* (the pause in the Pada-pāṭha) would follow; and this is not desired, since the makers of the Pada-text did not apply it in such instances as 'ājyaṃ kimāsīt'";
to this, the Bhāṣya states: "The makers of the Pada-text do not act according to a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*)."
The intention [of the author] is as follows: "The makers of the *pada*-text must follow [the tradition], and that which is followed is the *lakṣaṇa* (the grammatical rule).

Even when there is an intermediate word-division (*avāntarapadatva*), as in cases such as *ṛtvijam* and *ūrvebhiḥ*, the *avagraha* (word-separation) is not made in certain instances out of deference to established tradition; this is the underlying thought.

(563) Pāṇini 3.1.110: *ṛdupadhāccā’klṛpicṛteḥ*. [The rule states: "But not after *klṛp* and *cṛt*. [The roots are: *kṛpū* in the sense of capability (*sāmarthya*); *cṛtī* in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*) and tying (*granthana*).
[The example is] *kalpyam*. Because the substitution of *l* for *ṛ* in *kṛp* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), [the rule applies to] the vowels *ṛ* and *ḷ*.
And because of the prescription of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), the condition of having *ṛ* as a penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadhatva*) is established.

(564) *ī ca khanaḥ* |3|1|111|. "The short [vowel] is easier to recite. However, the intention of the author of the Sūtra, who reads [the rule] with a long [vowel], is this: the mention of the long [vowel]...

The *i-i* [in the sūtra] is for the purpose of *praśleṣa* (conjoining); there, the second *i*-kāra is for the purpose of subverting the *ātva* (substitution of *ā*) prescribed by the rule *ye vibhāṣā*. Otherwise, the scope (*avakāśa*) of *ye vibhāṣā* would be—*khāyate*, *khanyate*;
whereas the scope of the *itva* (substitution of *i*) would be that alternative in which *ātva* does not occur. However, in the case where *ātva* applies...

When both [rules] would apply simultaneously, *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) should take effect because it is subsequent (*paratva*) and because it is internal (*antaraṅgatva*). For in the rule *hye vibhāṣā*, the term *ye* is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). Thus, even when the suffix beginning with *y* is merely present in the mind, the application of *ātva* is internal; whereas the substitution of *i* is external (*bahiraṅga*), as it is prescribed together with the suffix *kyap*.

And thus, in order to override the internal *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*), the prescription of a second *ikāra* by means of *praśleṣa* (juxtaposition) is necessary; for this reason, the long vowel *ī* is explicitly pronounced in the rule *ī ca*. However, *ātva* is external (*bahiraṅga*), because it relies on the locative case in *ye* [as in Pāṇini 7.1.2]. And so, *ātva* is overridden by *itva*.

It is indeed logical that the long vowel should not be recited; since there is a saving of a *mātrā* in the short-vowel reading, it is also appropriate to rely on the locative case "in the following" (*pare*) as "ye," in accordance with that. It might be argued:
if the short substitute "i" is accepted, then by the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, that substitute would form a *guṇa* vowel with the preceding [vowel].

If it is argued that because that [substitution] is not established, the *tuk* augment would apply by the rule "a short vowel before a *pit* suffix" (*hrasvasya piti*), and since the rule "that which precedes *at* and *tuk* is unestablished" (*atvatukorasiddhaḥ*) requires both the *ṣatva* and the *tuk* to be applied while accepting the unestablished status (*asiddhatva*) of the rule for single-substitute substitution (*ekādeśaśāstra*), therefore only the long vowel (*dīrgha*) should be prescribed—do not say so. For [the rule states]: "A substitute for what ends in *a* or begins a word is unestablished... (*adāntapadādyorādeśo'siddhaḥ*).

However, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), no other [substitution] occurs either. Otherwise, in the case of *vaṅkṣe chatram*, since the substitution of *guṇa* would be considered non-established (*asiddha*) by the rule *na ṅi* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), the rule *che ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73) would necessitate the obligatory insertion of *tuk* based on the short vowel;
yet it is desired that the insertion be optional by the rule *dīrghācche ca padāntād vā* (Pāṇini 6.1.75). This is the general direction [of the argument].

Regarding the statement "‘hṛño’saṃjñāyām’—by the force of the inclusion of the term *asaṃjñā*, [the suffix] *kyap* will not apply even by another rule in the case of *bhāryā*," he says: "It has its purpose fulfilled in the masculine. This means, for example, in the phrase *bhāryā nāma kṣatriyāḥ*. Regarding the expression *tadanubandha*: [this refers to] the root *ḍubhṛñ*.
The sense is that because the root *bhṛ* has many prefixes (*anubandhas*), the suffix *kyap* does not apply [to it].

(565) *mṛjer vibhāṣā* | 3.1.113. Regarding *mṛjer vibhāṣā*: since the suffix *kyap* would have applied obligatorily to this root because it has *ṛ* as its penultimate letter (*ṛdupadha*), this rule is introduced.

(566) *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.52. Regarding *cajoḥ*: Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others have stated that a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) is not intended here, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *ena raktaṃ rāgāt*. Having considered that, he says: [the substitution applies] to *ca* and to *ja*.
And so forth. The distinction is that when the suffix *ghin* or *ṇyat* follows, there is the substitution of *k* for *c*, and when *ghin* or *ṇyat* follows, there is the substitution of *k* for *j*.
(567) *nyaṅkvādīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.53).
*nyaṅku*. According to Amarasimha: "The *ṛṣya*, *sāra*, *ruru*, *nyaṅku*, *raṅku*, *śambara*, and *rauhiṣa* [are types of deer].
(568) [The following is a rule from Pāṇini 3.1.114]: "In the words *rājasūya*, *sūrya*, *mṛṣodya*, *rucya*, *kupya*, *kṛṣṭapacya*, and *avyathya*..."

The meaning is that this is observed in such instances as "they purchase the King" (*rājānaṃ krīṇanti*) in the context of the *rājasūya* sacrifice. Since the root *ṣuñ* (meaning 'to press') ends in a short vowel, he says: "the lengthening occurs by way of an irregularity (*nipātana*). And this irregularity serves the purpose of establishing the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*). Therefore, in the first view, [it applies] in cases such as the *aśvamedha*, while in the second view...

And there is no over-extension [of the rule] to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such [rituals]. Regarding "utvam" (the substitution of *u*): the intention is that because of its being followed by *r* (*raparatva*), the long vowel is applied by the rule "hali ca. Regarding "nityaṃ kyap": the intention is that, by this [rule], the *yat* suffix prescribed by "vadaḥ supi kyap ca" does not apply.
(569) *bhidyodbhyau nade* |3|1|115|.

[The sūtra states: *bhidyodbhyau*. [The word] *kyap* [is understood]; [the word] *arteri* is the remainder [of the context]. Regarding *uddhya*: [as stated by] Ragh[u]: “The conduct of Uddhya was similar to that of the name [itself], as if the augment *oyat* had been applied.”

(570) *puṣyasiddhyau nakṣatre* |3|1|116|. [The words] *puṣya* and *siddhya* [are used as indeclinables] when referring to a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). Why "when referring to a lunar mansion"? [Consider: *poṣaṇam* (nourishing), *sedhanam* (accomplishing). [Here] the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*). Although *puṣya* and *siddhya* are synonyms, they appear as a copulative compound (*dvandva*) in the sūtra because the rule intends to refer to their specific forms.
Regarding the statement "‘uṣye tu sidhyatīṣyau’ [the forms *sidhya* and *iṣya* occur after the root *vas*]," this is from Amara.

(571) As for the rule *vipūyavinīyajityā muñjakalkahaliṣu* (Pāṇini 3.1.117), there is the expression "it is sin" (*pāpam iti vā*). This begins with the passage: "Water is not *kalka*; study is not *kalka*."

The sense is that this is because we see in the *Mahābhārata* the usage "the two eyes themselves, when afflicted, are a *kalka*," and because the lexicon (*kośa*) states: "The word *alkaḥ* [is used] for a wicked person, a sinner, a rogue, and also for excrement.
(572) [The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the roots] *prati*, *apa*, and *grah*. 3.1.118.
"It should be stated that [this applies] in Vedic usage (*chandasi*). Regarding the phrase "it should be stated": the author of the *Vṛtti*, however, has inserted this into the sūtra itself.

The example for the suffix *kyap* occurs only in Vedic usage: "It is not to be accepted by him; therefore, it is not to be grasped. As for the phrase "but in common usage (*loke*)," the intention is that only the suffix *ṇyat* is used.

(573) *padāsvairibāhyāpakṣyeṣu ca* |3|1|119| The suffix *kyap* is applied after the root *grah* when the meanings of "word" (*pada*), "not independent" (*asvairin*), "external" (*bāhya*), and "belonging to a faction" (*apakṣya*) are intended. *Avagṛhyam*: that word for which the separation (*avagraha*) is made is called *avagṛhya*. *Avagraha* means a pause or division.
To indicate the designation of an intermediate word (*avāntarapada*), it remains for a brief moment during recitation.

Regarding the term *pragṛhya*: that word is called *pragṛhya* which possesses *pragraha*. *Pragraha*, however, consists in the absence of *yaṇ*-substitution and so forth due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), resulting in the close proximity of vowels to one another. [This applies] to that for which the designation *pragṛhya* has been prescribed.

The commentary states: "That [term] is *pragṛhya*. Although the designation *pragṛhya* applies to the dual ending and so forth which are parts of a word (*padāvayava*) and not to the word itself, nevertheless, it should be understood that the property of a part is metaphorically attributed to the whole.
The terms *avagṛhya* and *pragṛhya* are well-established (*nirūḍha*) in the *Prātiśākhyas* and other texts as referring to specific types of words.

"Independent" (*asvairī*): one whose nature it is to move by himself is *svairī*, meaning independent; the vowel lengthening occurs according to the rule "vṛddhi in the case of *vā* and *īrin*. With the negative prefix *nañ*, it becomes *asvairī*. "Domestic" (*gṛhyakāḥ*):
the suffix *kan* is added according to the rule "in the sense of compassion," etc.; those clever birds that are attached to the house are *gṛhyakāḥ*. And they are... [the rest of the sentence].

Thus [ends the discussion on] *abhara*. Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā kṛ*: since the suffix *kyap* is not otherwise obtained after the root *kṛ*, and since it would have been obligatory after the root *vṛṣ* due to its having a short *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel, this new rule is commenced.
(574) *yugyaṃ ca patre* |3|1|121|. And the word *yugya* [is derived with the suffix *kyap*] when it means "a vehicle."

*Patram* means "a vehicle. In the sense of "that by which one goes," the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied according to the rule *ānīśas-*, etc., to form the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding *yugyo gauḥ* ("an ox for the yoke"): although this could be established even by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix *yat* according to the rule *advahati rathayugaprāsaṅgam*, this sūtra is nevertheless provided to exclude the suffix *ṇyat*.

Otherwise, it would have to be "yogyaḥ gauḥ" (a fit ox). However, others say: "yugyaḥ hastī" (a beast of burden elephant) is cited as an example in the *vṛtti*, but that is not established by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). For an elephant does not carry a yoke. It is, however, established by means of a primary derivative (*kṛt*); for it is joined to, or connected with, a rug and so forth.
Therefore, in this case, there is no suspicion of futility; such is the direction [of the argument].
(574) *amāvāsyāyā vā* Pāṇini 4.3.30. [The commentary states: "When there is vṛddhi. By that, the taddhita suffix prescribed by *amāvāsyāyā vā* [is applied].

It is established even in the case of the short vowel, because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]. However, if it were assumed that this is an optional (*pākṣika*) irregular derivation (*nipātana*) for that which ends in the suffix *yat*, then, in the absence of the suffix *yat*, the suffix *ṇya* would be difficult to obtain in the locative sense. Even if it were obtained through the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*), [the desired form would still not be secured].
Even so, the direction is this: a taddhita suffix prescribed after a word ending in *ṇyat* would not occur after a word ending in *yat*.
Regarding the rule *ṛhaloḥ*: the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative.

The term *ṛ* does not refer to the verbal root *ṛ*, but rather to the vowel *ṛ*, because of its association with *hal* (consonants), and because of the indication that "the subsequent operation [takes precedence]. This is seen in the rule *īḍvanda-* [where *īṭ* refers to the augment].

This is also evident from such indicative marks [liṅga] as these. The rule *ṛ-haloḥ* is a qualifier of the verbal root (*dhātu*) which is being carried over [from a previous sūtra]. By means of this qualifier, there is the application of the "rule of ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*). This is what he states: "ending in an ṛ-vowel.
Here, this should be noted: in all the original manuscripts, in the rule *vibhāṣā kṛvṛṣoḥ*, [the reading is as follows...]
In order to state that the suffix *ṇyat* occurs in this context, [the author] first cites the rule *ṛ-halor ṇyat*,

and subsequently cites *yugyaṃ ca patre* and *ām-ava-sya-d-anya-tara-syām*. However, in the *Manoramā*, following the sequence of the sūtra-pāṭha, it says *yugyaṃ ca patre* and then *ām-ava-sya-d-anya-tara-syām*.
Having explained the sūtra *ṣṭhivuklamvācamo yaṅi*, it has been explained here in the same manner. (575) *na kvādeḥ* 7.3.59.

Regarding the word *garjyam*: from the root *garj* (meaning "to roar"), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *ṛhalor ṇyat*. Since the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* would have required the substitution of *k* for the *j*, this [present rule] prohibits it. Thus, the substitution of *k* indeed occurs. Furthermore, because the suffix *ktvā* optionally takes the augment *iṭ* by the rule *udito vā*, and because the suffix *niṣṭhā* does not take *iṭ* by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, [the form *garjitvā* and *garjita* are established].

The meaning is as follows: "the opposite. According to the opinion of the author of the *Sūtras*, roots such as *gruc* and *gluñc* do not undergo the substitution of *k* (kutva) by the rule *a kvādeḥ*.

However, according to the opinion of the author of the *Vārttikas*, because these roots do not take the augment *iṭ* in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), the substitution of *k* (kutva) does occur by the rule *ajo ṇitaḥ*.

The meaning is that they are mutually contradictory. Regarding the phrase "yathottaram" (according to the latter): the intention is that, in accordance with the Vārttikakāra, the substitution of *k* (kutva) must be accepted. (576) *ajivrajyośca* | Pāṇini 7.3.60.

Regarding *samāja*: from the root *aja* in the sense of "going" or "throwing," when the suffix *ghañ* is applied, the rule *'ajo:'* would require the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *ja* becoming *ga*); this [rule] prohibits that. The same applies to *vraja*.
(577) *Bhuja-nyubjau yajñāṅge* | Pāṇini 7.3.62.

Regarding the word *nyubja*: the root *ubj* means "straightness. In the case of this root preceded by the prefix *ni*, the absence of *kutva* (the change of *j* to *g*) is applied, and the substitution of *b* for *d* is prescribed.
(Pāṇini 7.3.64) *oka ucaḥ ke*. [The suffix *ka* is added after the root *uc* when it is preceded by *ni*].

Regarding the phrase "since [the form] is established by means of *ghañ*": from the root *√huca* (meaning 'to assemble'), the form *oka* is established by adding the suffix *ghañ*, applying the rule *ajo’r* for the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *o*), and the *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel; however, the intention is that the initial udātta accent prescribed by the rule *ñnityādirnityam* would otherwise be undesirable.

(579) *ṇya* is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). [Pāṇini 5.1.118] Necessity is *avaśyambhāva*; [the suffix] *vuñ* is applied because it belongs to the *manojñādi* group. By the rule "there is elision of the *ṭi* of indeclinables when followed by any *bha*-affix," the *ṭi* is dropped. Thus we have *avaśyapācyam*.
The suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule "ṭhāvaśyakādhamarṇyayorṇiniḥ," and the suffix *ṇyat* by the rule "kṛtyāśca.
The word *āvaśyaka* is for the purpose of indicating the meaning and is not intended for actual usage.
Therefore, even when that [meaning] is understood through context, the sense, and so forth, the suffix *ṇyat* occurs and there is an absence of *kutva*.

As in the verse, "Thus you have grieved for those who should not be grieved for. Some, however, explain this in the *Bhagavadgītā* as follows: "those worthy of being grieved for" (*śocyāḥ*) are the "grievable ones" (*śocyāḥ*), while "not grievable" (*aśocyāḥ*) means those who are not worthy of being grieved for;

but that [explanation] is to be considered. For according to the rule "arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca," if the suffix *ṇyat* were applied, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *k* for *j* by the rule "ajoḥ".

The substitution of *ku* (the change to *j*) in the word *aja-* occurs by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.59]; however, according to the view of the Vārttika "in the case of the superlative suffix *iṣṭha*, [the substitute is applied] to that which does not take the augment *iṭ*," it is perfectly correct [that the form *ajāniṣṭha* arises].
This is the general direction.
(580) [Pāṇini 7.3.66: The roots *yaj*, *yāc*, *rucch*, *pravac*, and *arc* [take the augment *iṭ* before the suffix *ktvā*].

*Yaja* (yaj) is used in the sense of worshipping the gods and so forth; *ṭuyācṛ* (yāc) is in the sense of begging; *ruca* (ruc) is in the sense of shining; *vaca* preceded by *pra-* (prapūrva) is in the sense of speaking;

and *ṛca* (ṛc) is in the sense of praising. Regarding the phrase "a specific type of composition" (*granthaviśeṣa*), the point is that since this is a technical name (*saṃjñā*), the prohibition [of the substitution of *samprasāraṇa*] applies because the rule *vaco’śabdasaṃjñāyām* ("the word *vac* does not undergo *samprasāraṇa* except when it is a technical name") would otherwise have no scope to apply. Thus, this is a prohibition.

"Because of the indicator (jñāpaka)": the sense is that one should not suspect that the suffix *ṇyat* would apply here by virtue of the rule for optional application (*vāsarūpa*) due to the similarity of form. (581) *vaco’śabdasaṃjñāyām* | Pāṇini 7.3.67.

Regarding the term *vākya*: "A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of verbal and nominal stems. Here, "food" (*bhojya*) is intended to mean anything that is swallowed, and not specifically food that is eaten with a crisp texture.
Therefore, they say that the expression "gruel is food" (*bhojyā yavāgūḥ*) is also valid.

(582) *Bhojyam* [is used] in the sense of *bhakṣya*. /7/3/69/ The word *bhojya* here intends merely that which is to be swallowed (*abhyavahārya*), and not specifically that which is solid (*kharaviśada*). Therefore, they say that the expression *bhojyā yavāgūḥ* ("rice gruel to be eaten") is also valid.

"Bhogyam anyat" means that which is to be protected and that which is to be enjoyed. Regarding the statement "it should be stated after the roots *lap* and *dabh*": this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *yat* which would otherwise be obtained by the rule "oradupadhāt. Jayāditya, however, [cites] "āsuyuvapari-pī... [as the basis].

Having inserted *lap* into the sūtra and read it as "ṭh-rap-i-lap-i-trap-ī," he stated that *dabh* is included by means of the particle *ca*, which serves to aggregate what has not been explicitly mentioned; however, it should be understood that such an unequal explanation is groundless and clearly contradicts the Bhāṣya. Thus, [the reading] must be accepted.

The meaning is that, by the force of the *vārttika*—"The suffix *ām* should be prescribed after a root consisting of more than one vowel for the sake of words such as *culumpa*," just as *ām* is accepted after roots like *culump*, so it is here. And thus it is employed in such [Vedic] passages as "They perish not; the thief does not deceive them" (*atā naśanti na dabhāti taskaraḥ*) and "Viṣṇu is the protector, the undeceivable one" (*viṣṇurgopā adābhyaḥ*).

(583) *orāvaśyake* |3|1|125|. The sense is that if one were to explain [the sūtra] as "when *āvaśyaka* is the attendant word (*upapada*)," then forms such as *lāvyam* would not be established. However, in some cases, due to a disregard for brevity (*lāghava*), as in *vyatisa* and so forth...
The usage of even a word whose meaning has already been expressed by another word is observed, as in the case of the word *vyati*. For example: *avaśyalāvyam* ("that which must necessarily be cut").
Although a compound with an *upapada* is impossible here, the compound is formed because [the group] beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).

(Pāṇini 3.1.26: *āsuyuvapirapi[lapiṭtrapicamaśca*. (Note: The term *avaśyalāvyam* is derived from the root √lū with the prefix ava- and the suffix *ṇyat*, meaning "that which is to be cut down inevitably. The formation is justified by including it in the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group, which allows for such irregular compounds despite the absence of a standard *upapada-samāsa*.)

Regarding *āsu* and *suñ* in the sense of *āsāvya*: the root *uñ* meaning ‘to press’ (*abhiṣava*) is intended here, and not the root *u* meaning ‘procreation and sovereignty’ (*prasava-aiśvarya*). The intention is that this is due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) in the rule *ṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.
Regarding *yu* meaning ‘mixing’: the root *yuñ* meaning ‘binding’ (*bandhana*) is not intended here.
