The intended meaning is "because it possesses a continuous sequence. Here, one forms a *dvandva* compound of *yu* and the others first, and subsequently forms a *dvandva* with the word *āsu*. Consequently, one should not suspect that the word *yu* would undergo *pūrvanipāta* (prior placement) by virtue of the rule *alpa-actaram*. In this case, for the first two [words], [the shortening occurs] by the rule *aco ñṇiti*, whereas for *rapitrapicam*, [the shortening occurs]...

This [sūtra] is commenced because the suffix *yat* would otherwise apply by the rule “*oradupadhāt*. If its application were intended for all impermanent things (*anityamātra*), there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of applying it to objects such as a jar (*ghaṭa*); therefore, he says: “a particular kind of *dakṣiṇāgni*, etc.”
(585) *Ānāyyaḥ* [is used] for that which is not permanent; 3.1.127.

Regarding the phrase "from the house of a Vaiśya, etc.": for the source (*yoni*) of the *dakṣiṇāgni* is indeed optional, as it is stated: "Either from the house of a Vaiśya who possesses two fires, or from the *bhrāṣṭra* fire, or from the *gārhapatya* fire."

(586) *praṇāyyo’sammatāv* |3|1|128|. [The word *praṇāyya* is used] in the sense of "not approved" (*asaṃmati*). That is to say, the meaning is as follows: that which is not the object of the affection of people—such as a thief and the like—is called *asaṃmati*.
In reality, however, because it is more parsimonious than taking "consent" (saṃmati) to mean "becoming an object of affection," consent is simply affection itself.

That which lacks this [affection] in relation to thieves and the like is "non-consent" (asaṃmati). Alternatively, one who lacks consent—that is, affection—toward objects of affection is a detached person, meaning he is "non-consenting."
By means of the *tantra* method, both meanings are grasped.
(587) *Pāyya*, *sānnayya*, *nikāyya*, and *dhāyyā* [are formed] in the senses of measure, oblation, dwelling, and *sāmidhenī* verses respectively;
Pāṇini 3.1.129.

The four [derivatives] *pāyya*, *sānnāyya*, and the other two are prescribed as substitutes for four meanings. In the sense of "that by which one drinks," from the root √*pā* (to drink), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the instrumental sense (*karaṇe*); thus, *pāyya* means something else, specifically a particular oblation (*haviḥ*) prescribed [in the texts] as "sour milk for Indra on the new moon day" and "milk for Indra on the new moon day."

It has the specific form of curd and milk. [The term] "dhīyate anayā" (it is placed by means of this) refers here not to all *sāmidhenī* verses, but rather specifically to that verse beginning with "ṛtāṣāḍ ṛtajā amartyaḥ," which is inserted among the *samidhyamānavatī* and *samiddhavatī* verses in the *vikṛti* sacrifices. And this is the specific rule regarding the grammatical formation.

It is obtained because its meaning is conventional (*rūḍha*). If it is argued that, in this way, since the word [is established] by nipātana as denoting a specific *sāmidhenī*, the mention of *sāmidhenī* in the rule is redundant—here they say:
the mention of *sāmidhenī* in the sūtra is for the purpose of indicating a specific usage (*prayoga-viśeṣa*). And thus, it is seen even in what is not a *sāmidhenī*: [Example follows]
‘Hāyyā śaṃsati’—for indeed, the fuel is not thrown into the fire by means of the *śastra* hymn.
(588) *Kuṇḍapāyya* and *saṃcāyya* [are names of sacrifices] in the context of a ritual (*kratu*).
Regarding *kuṇḍapāyya*: when the word *kuṇḍa* ending in the third case is used as a subordinate word (*upapada*), it is derived from the root *pā* (to drink) in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

[Objection: Since the suffix *yat* and the augment *yuk* are prescribed [by rule], why not simply prescribe the suffix *ṇyat* here because it is the more fundamental form? In this way, since the form would be established by the rule "āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ," the form *dyauk* need not be prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*), and thus there would be economy of effort (*lāghava*). [Reply: Not so. For that would result in the accent falling on the final syllable (the *tit-svara*) due to the presence of the *t* marker.

However, it is accepted that [the suffix] *ṇyat* has an initial udātta accent according to the rule "ṭhyato ’nāvaḥ" and so forth, which is the original accent of the *kṛt*-suffix in the second member of a compound.

Thus it is employed in the forms "raṇāyyāt" and "kuṇḍapāyyaḥ. But for the root *ci* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the suffixes *ṇyat* and *āyī* are treated as irregular (nipātana). Why "in the context of a sacrifice" (*kratau*)? [Consider: "kuṇḍapānam" and "saṃceyam."

(589) *agnau paricāyyopacāyyasamūhyāḥ* |3|1|131|. Regarding the word *agni*: here it does not mean fire (*jvalana*), but rather the specific site constructed by piling bricks for the purpose of maintaining that fire; thus he says—“a particular place. These [words] are correct [in this sense].
The meaning is that when a specific type of place is to be expressed, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *ci* preceded by *pari*, with the substitution of *ā* for *i*;

however, in the case of the root *vah* preceded by *sam*, there is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) involving both *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) and lengthening. (590) *cityāgnicitye ca* | Pāṇini 3.1.132.

*cityo ’gniḥ* ("the fire-altar is called *citya*"). The suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *ci* (to pile) in the sense of the object (*karman*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule] beginning with *yataḥ*. In this sūtra, the word *agnau* is understood from the previous context; however, it qualifies only the word *citya*, not the second [word]. This is because the latter, having the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), cannot possibly denote "fire. [The application of the suffix occurs] other than in the case of fire.

It is simply "ceyam. However, in the *Śabdakaustubha* and other works, it is stated that in the case of *agnicityā*, the suffix *yak* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) along with the elision of the *t* (tuk), and not the suffix *kyap*. Consequently, the word has an udātta accent on the final syllable. If *kyap* were applied, then because *kyap* is marked as *pit*, it would be anudātta; thus, by the accent of the verbal root, the form would be *cityā*.

Thus it is established that [the suffix] should be udātta. Now, one might object: "By the rule of *vāsarūpa*, the kṛtya suffixes will also occur. To this, he says: "After the section on feminine gender," and so forth. Regarding *kta* and *lyuṭ*: "The laughing of the student" (*hasitaṃ hasanaṃ chātrasya*). This concerns the scope of the two rules: *apuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ* ("*kta* is used for the neuter gender in the sense of an action") and *yuṭ ca* ("and *yuṭ*").

In the case of *bhāve* (in the sense of an abstract action), the suffix *ghañ* is applied: *bhuktiḥ*. In *icchati bhoktum* (he wishes to eat), the suffix *tumun* is applied because of the rule: *icchārtheṣu liṅloṭau* (after verbs meaning "to wish," the optative and imperative suffixes are used). However, the optative (*liṅ*) also occurs here, according to the statement: *samānakartṛkeṣu tumun liṅ ca* (when the agents are the same, the suffixes *tumun* and *liṅ* are used). In *īṣatpānaḥ* (easy to drink), the suffix *yuc* is applied by the rule *ato yuc*. Here, [the prefix *īṣat-* is compounded] by the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu*.
The word *laṅ* does not [apply here]. The intention is that by means of the particle *ca*, *laṅ* is drawn over from the rule *iṅ yadi*.

(591) *Bhavya-geya-pravacanīya-upasthānīya-janya-āplāvya-āpātyā vā* || 3.4.68 || [The suffixes *kṛtya* and *ṇyat*] are optionally applied after the words *bhavya*, *geya*, *pravacanīya*, *upasthānīya*, *janya*, *āplāvya*, and *āpātya*.
Because of the restriction "only for those two [the *bhavya* and *arha*] when they denote the agent," this rule is stated to apply even when the agent is not expressed.

Regarding the word *sāmnām*: this is a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the phrase "and so forth": the teacher is *pravacanīya* (fit to teach) with respect to his own Vedic study;
the Vedic study is *pravacanīya* (fit to be taught) by the teacher; the student is *upasthānīya* (fit to attend upon) the teacher.

The teacher (*guru*) is one who is to be attended upon (*upasthānīya*) by the disciple. [The suffix] *jya* is applied: he is born (*jāyate*), or he is that by which one is born (*janya*). [The suffix] *ṇyat* is applied: he bathes (*āplavate*), or he is that by which one is bathed (*āplāvya*). [The suffix] *ṇyat* is applied: it is to be bathed (*āplāvyam*), or it is that by which one is bathed. Regarding the rule "after the root *śak*, the potential (*liṅ*) and [the suffix *tavya* may be used]," [we have] "it is to be carried" (*voḍhavya*). From the root *vah* in the sense of "carrying," the suffix *tavya* is applied. By the rule "the *h* becomes *ḍh*" (*haṣastathordho 'dhaḥ*), the *h* is changed to *ḍh*; then, by the rule "after *ha*, *ṣ*, and *t*, [the following *th* becomes *ṭh*]" (*haṣastathordho 'dhaḥ*), [the *th* becomes *ṭh*].

When *ṣṭu*-substitution [by P. 8.4.41] has applied according to the rule *dhatve ‘ṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ*, and when *ho ḍho lopaḥ* [P. 8.2.31] applies, the substitution of *au* for the vowel *a* occurs by the rule *ahivahoḥ*. Here, one should not suspect that the *ṣṭu*-substitution is invalid (*asiddha*) at the time the *ḍha*-elision is to be performed; for it is *asiddha* only with respect to its own basis (*āśrayāsiddhatvāt*). This is so that there may be no sublation [of the subsequent rule].

The word “of the kṛtya suffixes” (kṛtyānām) is to be supplied [as the object of the verb]. “The mention of kṛtya” means the mention of the particle *ca* which draws in the category of kṛtya suffixes. Thus ends the section on kṛtya suffixes in the Tattvabodhinī.
Now, regarding the *ṛk* class and others: (332) "After roots beginning with *ṛk*, the suffix *śnā* [is applied].
Likewise, there is the substitution of *at* for *jha* by the rule "In the *ātmanepada*, [the substitute] *an* [is applied] after [a root] not ending in *a*. They are called *sautra* [roots].

It should also be understood that [the root] has *na* as its penultimate letter. In the form *viṣṭabhnoti*, there is the elision of *n* according to the rule *ṭuniditam*. There is the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *stanbheḥ*.
(333) *veḥ skabhnāternityam* 8.3.77.

The term *nityam* (always) [is used] for the sake of clarifying that the word *veḥ* does not follow from the previous rule *veḥ ivādīnām vā*; thus, it is "always" [that the substitution occurs]. Regarding *viskabhnoti*:
in the rule *kabhnāteḥ*, the specific form containing the suffix *śnā* is not intended; rather, [the root itself is meant].

It is merely the *dhātu* (verbal root), for otherwise, even in cases such as *viṣkambhitā* and *viṣkambhitam*, the substitution of *ṣa* would not occur; nor is this a desired outcome, because it would contradict the works of Mādhava and others—this is the intended meaning. (334) *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau* | Pāṇini 3.1.83.

[The rule] *halaḥ śnaḥ* [is applied]. In the form *stabhāna*, because of the force of the introduction of the rule *ato heḥ*, the *paribhāṣā* concerning the loss of cause (*saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*) does not apply, and thus there is elision (*luk*). For this very reason, it is said that this *paribhāṣā* was not cited in the case of *ahī* for the purpose of preventing the elision of *hi*. As for what...

The interpretation by some that the substitution of *śnā* for *śnu* occurs after roots listed in the Dhātupāṭha but not after those mentioned in the Sūtras— and their citation of *stabhnīhi* as an example— is without authority and contradicts the works of Mādhava and others.

(335) *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ* | 7|3|80| The rule "there is shortening for *pvādi* [roots]"—he says [this] because the word *śiti* is understood from the previous rule *ṭhivuklamucamām*; that is, "when a *śit* affix follows. "Except in the case of the *liṅ* [optative]"—by this [sūtra], it is indicated that the long vowel of the *iṭ* augment added after *vṛt* does not occur in the *liṅ*.
This has been reminded [by the rule] *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*. Since the mention of *oṣṭhya* (labial) includes both the dental (*danta*) and the labial (*oṣṭhya*), he says:
"from *vṛ*" [meaning *vṛ* and *vṝ*]. Regarding *variṣīṣṭa*: by the rule *iṅsicorātmanepadeṣu*, there is optionally *iṭ*.
[In the alternative,] *vūrṣīṣṭa*. Regarding *avūrṣṭa*: because of the rule *ṭhuśca*, the *liṅ* and *sic* suffixes are *kit*, and thus, due to the absence of *guṇa*, [the form is established].
The state of being *sat* [is established].
From *halaḥ*: the phrase "of the *saṃprasāraṇa*" (*raṭhsaṃprasāraṇasya*) is understood to carry over. "Of the *aṅga*" (*aṅgasya*) is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). "After *hal*" (*halaḥ*).

Thus ends the fifth [section]. This is what he says: "from a member of the body" (*aṅgāvayavāt*). What is the purpose of "from a member of the body"? [Examples: *niruttam* ("uttered"), *duruttam* ("ill-spoken"). What is the purpose of [specifying] that it belongs to a member ending in that [suffix]? [Example: *vidhyati*. [The root] *kṣi* is used in the sense of "injury. Because it has the marker *ṣit*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied; thus, *kṣiyā*. [As stated in the rule: "after *ṣi*, in the sense of injury (*kṣiyā*)."

Regarding the passage beginning with *ṣiyāśīḥ*, the author will state that "ṣiyā" means the transgression of dharma and the deviation from established conduct (*ācārabheda*). As for the phrase "by the force of the long-vowel indication": one might object that it is established in the *Ākara* (the *Mahābhāṣya*) that the mention of the long vowel serves to indicate the *aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā* (the maxim that what is applied to a base does not apply to its substitute). Otherwise, [the author] would have prescribed *jaṃ* for the roots *jñā* and *jan*, rather than [using *jña*] after *ataḥ*.

If it is argued that since the lengthening is already established by the rule *dīrgho yañi*, and thus the force of the explicit mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is exhausted, how can the absence of the short vowel be established here?
To this they reply: it is precisely because the short vowel is absent that the mention of the long vowel serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned Paribhāṣā.

However, since the operation of the *aṅga* (stem) has already taken effect when a short vowel occurs, [the absence of the short vowel] is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Thus, there is no obstacle whatsoever to establishing the non-existence of the short vowel. Furthermore, the very body of the paribhāṣā is: "When an operation dependent on the *aṅga* has taken effect, there is no further application of an operation dependent on the *aṅga*."

And that [rule] is established by the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*). However, if the reading in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *hyasobhyaḥ* is indeed *pariniṣṭhitasya*, then this statement is an independent rule rather than an indicator; this position is also understood from the end of the *Manoramā* commentary on the words *yusmad* and *asmad*.
However, in that view, since the purpose of including the long vowel [in the rule] is not exhausted, this passage is indeed correct.

Some, however, say it should be explained that the short vowel does not occur because a rule conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is non-permanent (*anitya*). [The form] *badhnāti* [is derived such that] there is elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) according to the rule "of those ending in an *it*, etc. (*aniditām*).

"abhāntsīt": by the rule "vadavraje," there is vṛddhi; then the substitution of *bhaṣ* (the voiced unaspirated stop) occurs. "abānddhām": by the rule "haṣastathoḥ," the *t* is replaced by *dh*; or, by the rule "haro jhari," there is optionally its elision. The root *vṛṅ* means "to share in" (*saṃbhakti*); "sharing" (*bhakti*) means devotion or partaking. Regarding the root *śranth*: "in the case of the *kit* suffix."

Because it has been stated in another grammatical treatise that "the *liṭ* [perfect] affixes of the roots *rañj*, *granth*, *dambh*, and *svañj* are optionally *kit*," [the rule applies]. (337) *niraḥ kuṣaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.46.

The word *niraḥ* [is the cause of the substitution of *kuṣ* for *kṣubh*]. From the sūtra “*valādau vā*” (Pāṇini 7.2.35), the particle *vā* is understood to carry over. The governing rule (*adhikāra*) “*ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*” (Pāṇini 7.2.35) indeed remains in force. Thus he says: “of that which begins with a *val* letter,” and so forth. Why is *niraḥ* mentioned? [Consider: *koṣitā*, *koṣitum*. In the form *nirakukṣat*, there is the affix *ksa* due to the absence of *iṭ*.

Regarding the phrase "by association with *sah*": although there is also a root *sahi* belonging to the *divādi* class— since *ṣaha* and *ṣūha* mean "to be able"— nevertheless, because it is indicated by the suffix *śap*, they say that the association is only with the *bhauvādika* (first-class) *sah*.

Regarding the rule *iṣeḥ takāre śyan-pratyayāt pratiṣedhaḥ*: the term *śyan-pratyayāt* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The meaning of the Vārttika is that there is a prohibition of the optional *iṭ* augment when the root *iṣ* (belonging to the class of roots marked with *śyan*) is followed by the letter *t*. Thus, it follows that the optionality [of *iṭ*] does not apply to the root *iṣ* belonging to the *divādi* class. And so, in the case of *īṣasaha*, etc., [the rule applies].

It should be understood that *iṣṇāti* is also included [in this rule]. Regarding *poṣitā*: since *puṣyati* is cited among the roots that do not take the augment *iṭ* by using the suffix *śyan*, the intention is that this [root] takes *iṭ*.
(338) *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* | Pāṇini 6.4.19.

Regarding the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*: the term *cchvoḥ* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of [the sound] *cch* together with its *t* (the *t*-augment). He states that by the rule for *cutva*, the letter *ca* takes the place of the letter *ta*; thus he says "of that which is accompanied by *t*" (*satukkasya*). Consequently, it should be understood that in the sūtra, the letter *ca* precedes the letter *ccha*. Why "accompanied by *t*"? Consider the case of *vicchā-pracchā*.

When the letter *cha* is changed to *śa* by the internal rule (*naṅ-pratyaye*), it is so that the *tuk* augment may not be heard [in the resulting form]. However, the maxim regarding the non-application of rules when a grammatical operation has already taken place (*akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*) is not universal, precisely because of this very mention of *satuk* (with *tuk*). Therefore, they say that forms such as *atibhavakān*—meaning "one who has surpassed those possessing the suffix *-vant*"—are established. This is stated by the author of the Sūtra...
He states that by the word *ca* ("and"), the rule *kvijhaloḥ kṅtī* is drawn in, saying "in *kvip*, etc.

[The rule is: "In the *liṭ* [perfect], there is lengthening for the root *grah*. Why "having only one vowel" (*ekācaḥ*)? [To show] that it should not apply in cases such as *jāgrahitā* and *jāgrahiṣyati* where there is elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ* [intensive suffix]. Why "of that which is prescribed" (*vihitasya*)? [To show that it does not apply to] *grāhitam*. Nor is this [the case] here...

It should be stated that because of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position) of the elision (*ṇilopa*), the suffix *kan* follows after the root *grah*; however, this is not so, because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies specifically to the prescription of a long vowel (*dīrghavidhi*). If, on the other hand, one accepts that "the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies only to the prescription of a long vowel belonging to the *raipādika* (the first three quarters of the Pāṇinian grammar)," then there is a distinction regarding what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣa*).

They say that [the rule] is indeed useless; because the *iṭ* augment pertaining to the present context (*prakṛta*) is what is being grasped, there is no lengthening in forms such as *grāhitā* and *grāhiṣyate*, which involve the *ciṇvat-iṭ*. (339) *graho’liṭi dīrghaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.37. "In the case of the root *grah*, there is lengthening [of the vowel] except before the *liṭ* [perfect suffix]."

Regarding *grahiṣīṣṭa*: since the term *vṛtaḥ* is understood [from the previous rule], the prohibition of lengthening by the rule *na liṅi* does not apply. Regarding *agrahīṣātām*: this is the *luṅ* [suffix] in the second person dual of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Thus ends the section on the *ṛkārādi* roots in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
Now begins the section on the meaning of the *lakāras* within the *tiṅ*-inflections.

(490) *abhijñāvacane lṛṭ* | 3|2|112|. "In the case of a word expressing recognition (*abhijñā*). The term "in the past" (*bhūte*) is understood from the governing context. The term "not of today" (*anadyatana*) is understood from the rule *anadyatane laṭ* | 3|2|111|.
It occurs. *Abhijñā* means memory (*smṛti*); its etymological analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that by which one is awakened (*bodhyate*) [to the object].
Thus he says: "awakening through memory," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "we shall dwell" (*vatsyāmaḥ*), the meaning is "we have dwelt.
Just as in the sentence "the deer is running here," there is the act of running performed by the deer—which constitutes the meaning of the sentence—so too in the case of "you remember."
The sentence-meaning is the act of dwelling, performed by us, located in Gokula, during the recent past; this is the object [of the verb].
The vocative "O Kṛṣṇa" is an attribute of the act of remembering. Thus, the resulting meaning is: "the remembrance of the aforementioned dwelling, having Kṛṣṇa as its object of address."

(491) *na yadi* |3|2|113|. When *yadi* is present, the prohibition of the future tense (*lṛṭ*) applies; in its place, the general rule (*utsarga*) for the imperfect (*laṅ*) takes effect. (492) *vibhāṣā sākāṅkṣe* |3|2|114|. [The same substitution of *laṅ* for *lṛṭ*] is optional when there is a mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*).

"Vāsaḥ" (dwelling) is the *lakṣaṇa* (indicator); the meaning is that it is an indicator because it is well-known. "Cāraṇam" (tending) is the *lakṣya* (the indicated); it is not something to be made known because it does not immediately enter the intellect. "In the alternative, [the suffix] *laṅ*" [is used], as in: "We dwelt in the forest," "we tended the cows. "Even when there is connection with the word *yat*"—for this very reason, [the rule applies] prior to the connection with "a-yadi."
The intention is that [the rule] was not formulated as *vibhāṣā sākāṅkṣe*.
"In the case of absolute concealment (*atyantāpahnav*), the suffix *liṅ* should be prescribed. Regarding "absolute concealment": concealment means denial;
its absoluteness consists in this, namely, that even the motive for the action is denied by one who is questioned about it.

"‘I am not,’ and so forth. Kaliṅga is a prohibited region, for there is a traditional legal text (*smṛti*) stating: ‘Having gone to Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Saurāṣṭra, and Magadha, except for the purpose of a pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*), one deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again. Since you have gone to that country..."

When someone is told by another, "You have stayed for a long time," he replies, "I did not go to Kaliṅga. Here, not only is the staying itself denied, but rather the going which was its cause; thus, there occurs an absolute negation (*atyantāpahnavah*). But when...

When it is said, "I went to Kaliṅga," if one denies the very act of going—rather than merely denying the specific time—it results in *laṅ* (the imperfect tense), as in: "It is not that I went to Kaliṅga. (493) And [the imperfect tense is used] in a question concerning a recent past time: 3.2.117.
And [the suffix *liṭ* is used] in a question; however, they say that when it refers to a remote time in the past, non-remote (bhūtānadyatana) and non-evident (*parokṣa*), [the suffix *luṅ* is used].

Regarding "when being asked": the meaning is when the sense of the verbal root—which functions in the past, non-remote, and non-evident—is something that must be inquired about, and the time is proximate. Why "in a question"? [So that] in the past, non-remote, and non-evident, only *liṅ* [is used].
Caitra went.
(494) *laṭ sme* | Pāṇini 3.2.118: *laṭ sme*. The indeclinable *sme* indicates past time.

(495) *nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane* |3|2|120|. The analysis of the compound is: "in the case of a reply to what has been asked" (*pṛṣṭasya prativacanam*). If it were a collective dvandva compound, the rule would apply in both cases [the question and the answer], yet it is desired that the present tense (*laṭ*) be used only in the reply. Thus he says: "Indeed, I am doing it" (*nanu karomi*). And not... [the rest of the sentence].
It might be argued that the inclusion of the term "pṛṣṭa" (asked) is redundant, since a response necessarily follows a question;
however, Kaiyaṭa has established that the term must be included because even a contradictory statement can be a response, and even speech directed toward departing can be a response.

(496) *nanvor vibhāṣā* |3|2|121|. After the particles *na* and *nu*, [the suffixes prescribed by the previous rule apply] optionally. [The rule] "after *bhṛ*" remains in force. In one alternative, there is *luṅ*; but for what is not of today (*anadyatana*), there is *laṅ*. In the other alternative, it is as prescribed [by the general rules]. Thus, when there is no application of *luṅ* or *laṭ*, there is *laṅ*; however, in the case of something out of sight (*pārokṣya*), [there is *liṭ*].
The meaning is the optative (*liṅ*). "In the future" is according to the rule *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ*.

(497) *yāvat-purā-nipātayoḥ laṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.4): "After the particles *yāvat* and *purā*, the present tense (*laṭ*) [is used]. By the mention of the particle (*nipāta*), it is indicated that the paribhāṣā regarding "the specific form and the general form" (*lakṣya-pratipadokta-paribhāṣā*) is not universally obligatory (*anityā*).

It is made known [by the word] "yāvadbhuṅkte" (he eats as much as...). The meaning is that he will certainly eat. Regarding "yāvaddāsyati" (as much as he will give), however, in the case of the future not belonging to the current day, one should provide the counter-example: "yāvaddātā tāvadbhoktā" (as much as he will give, so much he will eat).

(498) *vibhāṣā kadākarhyoḥ* |3|3|5|. [The sūtra states: "Optionally. Now, one might object: since the suffix *rhil* is prescribed for *kim* when it does not refer to the current day by the rule *ṭhanadyatane rhilanyatarasyām*, there should necessarily be the periphrastic future (*luṭ*) in connection with *karhi*.

How is this illustrated? By the example: *karhi bhokṣyate* ("When will he eat?"). Regarding this, they say: in the sense of a general future, *bhokṣyate* takes the suffix *lṛṭ*; however, when joined with *karhi*, there is an understanding of the non-recent (*anadyatana*) future through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Or [one might say]: *bhoktā*. But surely, since this *laṭ* is prescribed for the general future, how can it coexist with *luṭ*?

If it is argued that [the application of different tenses] is due to a distinction in the objects [of the rules], they say in response: In the rule "luṅ for non-recent time" (*anadyatane luṅ*), certain subsequent sūtras such as "optionally for *kadā*" (*vibhāṣā kadā*) are carried over by virtue of what is desired; therefore, even in the domain of *luṅ*, *laṭ* occurs, and *laṭ* is not sublated by *luṭ* despite the condition of non-recent time.
Thus [it is said].
(499) *kiṃvṛte lipsāyām* |3|3|6|. Regarding *kiṃvṛte*: that which is surrounded by *kim* is *kiṃvṛtam*. Some, however, maintain that this also applies to *yad*, *kadā*, *kutra*, and so forth.

What is the meaning? Even so, that [suffix] is not employed there because it is not prescribed. Therefore, they say that in examples such as *kadā bhojayiṣyasi* ("When will you feed [me]?"), the suffix *laṭ* occurs in the sense of the future (*bhaviṣyati*).
(500) And [the suffix *laṭ* is used] when the accomplishment of what is desired to be obtained [is indicated]. 3.3.7.

Since desire (*lipsā*) exists when there is the attainment of what is desired to be obtained, this rule is established even by the preceding one; nevertheless, the author provides an example—*yo ’nnam*—"he who [gives] food"—to indicate that this rule is for the sake of excluding the sense of *kiṃvṛtta* (interrogative pronouns). (Pāṇini 3.3.156) *loḍarthalakṣaṇe ca*. 3.3.8. And [the suffix *liṅ* is used] when the meaning of the imperative (*loṭ*) is indicated. 3.3.8.

*Loḍartha-lakṣaṇa*: This is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the indicator of the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*). For example, "Kṛṣṇa’s eating" is the indicator of the imperative sense of "the command to graze the cows. The meaning is: "At the time of eating, you must perform the grazing of the cows. In the alternative case, [the word] *luṅ* [is used]: "If Kṛṣṇa is to eat..."
The meaning is: "If Kṛṣṇa will eat, you must tend the cows.

(502) *Liṅ* is also used for what occurs after a muhūrta [Pāṇini 3.3.9]. Regarding *liṅ cordhvam*: [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after *āla*. In the rule *addhitārthottarapade*, [the term] *iksaṅkhye* applies.
Anticipating the objection that a compound is difficult to obtain here because of this [preceding] rule's application, he says: "By virtue of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). (Pāṇini 3.3.131):
*vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavadvā*. "When there is proximity to the present time, the present tense may optionally be used."

Regarding the rule *vartamāna-svarthe ṣyañ*: since the suffix *ṣyañ* is already established here by the very mention of *sāmīpya* (proximity), they say that the Vārttika *cāturvarṇādibhyaḥ* is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañcārtha*). Nor should it be argued that, because of the prohibition *ūraṇaguṇe*, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) would not be possible here.

By this very explanation, the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of that prohibition is accepted; by that, forms such as *uddhamāndyam* are established. Regarding the phrase "by which condition" (*yenopādhinā*):
it refers to a condition such as a specific verbal root (*dhātuviśeṣa*). For instance, the suffix *śānan* is prescribed after the roots *pūṅ* and *lūñ*.

It occurs from those very two roots, and not from any other root. Furthermore, the suffixes beginning with *iṣṇuc* and ending with *hrājabhās*, which are taught starting from *ṭhalaṅkṛñ* up to *hrājabhās*, also occur after roots such as *kṛñ* only when that specific condition [of being characterized by that habit, etc. is present in the agent.

The interrogative sentence “Have you come? (*adā āgato’si*) employs the past tense; in the response “I am coming” (*āgacchāmi*), the word “this” (*ayam*) is used to manifest the past time, while the expression “I have just now arrived” (*idānīm evāgamam*) serves to indicate a past time proximate to the present.

For by that [word], that form which is invariably concomitant with coming—characterized by the girding of one's loins and so forth—is being indicated. Nor should it be suspected that there is an inconsistency because time is not mentioned in the two subsequent sentences in response to the question "Is it not so? (na ca ade).

Because in the subsequent [sūtra], the time is understood through the words "now" (*idānīm*) by means of these two terms "this" (*ayam*) and "that" (*eṣa*). What is the purpose of [the rule concerning] proximity (*sāmīpye*)?
Example: "When did you arrive? "I arrived in the month prior to this month.
Furthermore, this sūtra has been rejected (*pratyākhyāta*) in the original source (*ākara*). Example: [The word *gaṅgā* used for] the vicinity of the Gaṅgā.
Because, just as there is the superimposition of being the Gaṅgā [upon the river Yamunā], it is possible to superimpose the state of being present upon that which is near to the present.

(504) *Āśāsāyāṃ bhūtavacca* (Pāṇini 3.3.132). Regarding "in the sense of hope" (*āśāsāyām*): hope (*āśāsā*) is the act of hoping; it is the desire to obtain what has not yet been obtained. In the case of hope...

Even though the object [of the desire], such as the rainy season, is present, it is stated as "it will be" because of its connection with a future time. What is the purpose of using [the term] *āśaṃsā* (expectation)? [Example:
*gamiṣyati* ("he will go").

(505) *kṣipravacane lṛṭ* |3|3|133|. Regarding the term *kṣipravacane*: the inclusion of the word *vacana* is for the purpose of excluding the [literal] form [of the word itself]. Thus he says: "a synonym for 'quickly' (*kṣipra*)". Regarding the phrase "in the previous scope": this means "in the case of expectation" (*āśaṃsā*). By that...
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the previously mentioned verbal suffixes.

(506) *āśaṃsāvacane liṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.134). Regarding the expression of hope (*āśaṃsāvacana*): this is an exception to the suffixes [prescribed for] the past and the present. It is not as if it were the past. Not so.

It should also be understood that [the suffix] is used as if referring to the present. One might say, "I hope I shall study" (*āśaṃse ’dhīyīya*). Similarly, one should understand such expressions as "I pray I may study" (*prārthaye ’dhīyīya*) and "we desire that we may study" (*icchāmo vayam adhīyīmahi*). Regarding the word "quickly" (*kṣipram*):
the intention is that even when used with "quickly," the *liṅ* (optative) suffix applies because it is taught later [in the rules].

(507) *Nānadyatanavat-kriyāprabandha-sāmīpyayoḥ* |3|3|135|. The suffix *laṅ* is prescribed for the past non-remote (*bhūtānadyatana*) tense, while *luṭ* is prescribed for the future non-remote (*bhaviṣyat-anadyatana*). These two are prohibited in these two specific senses. Thus it is said: "The *laṅ* and *luṭ* do not [apply]. And so it is.

With the intention that the *luṅ* suffix is used for the past (*bhūte*) and the *lṛṭ* suffix for the future (*bhaviṣyati*), he provides examples such as *annamadāt* ("he ate food") and *dāsyati* ("he will give"). Regarding *agnīn*, it refers to the *āhavanīya* and other sacrificial fires.
(508) *bhaviṣyati maryādāvacane’varasmin* (Pāṇini 3.3.136).

A boundary (maryādā) will be established. This statement is for the purpose of preventing the application [of the rule] and for the purpose of excluding immediate proximity (asāmīpya). He says: "The term *anadyatana* follows. The meaning is that *luṅ* does not apply here. In this sūtra, the boundary is defined by space; in the subsequent one, it is defined by time. In that regard—
He will state the distinction: "that which is posterior to it. This means that portion of the road extending from Kauśāmbī up to Pāṭaliputra as its limit;
that is to say, the part prior to Kauśāmbī. What will happen? [It will be designated] by that path which has been traversed up to Pāṭaliputra.

"We shall drink barley-meal at that point which is nearer to Kauśāmbī. Why does the rule specify "in the sense of a limit" (*maryādā-vacane*)? [Because otherwise it would apply to] "the path that is to be traveled without end; we shall drink barley-meal at that point which is nearer to Kauśāmbī. Why does the rule specify "at the nearer point" (*avarasmin*)? [Because otherwise it would apply to] "the path that is to be traveled..."
From Pāṭaliputra, wherever it may be beyond Kauśāmbī, there we shall eat barley-meal (*saktu*).

(509) *Kālavibhāge cā’nahorātrāṇām* |3|3|137|. "Division of time" (*kālavibhāga*) means a specific portion of time. In the phrase "of non-day-and-night periods" (*anahorātrāṇām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of a relationship (*saṃbandha-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Regarding the phrase "the preceding sūtra": this is its meaning—when a limit (*maryādā*) is expressed, that which is subsequent to a particular time [is treated] like the future non-immediate (*anadyatana*), provided that this temporal division is connected with a day-and-night (*ahorātra*); if it is not so connected, it is not. Here, in the case of a temporal division...

Regarding the statement "in *satyavara* [the suffix] is like that of the non-present (*anadyatana*), except for *na*" (Pāṇini 3.2.112), some say that when the question "from what? arises, it is understood by implication to mean "from a specific time.

Others, however, say that the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe saptamī*), meaning "from a division of time" (*kālavibhāgāt*). This is for the sake of the subsequent rule.
In the sūtra "arasmim vighāṣe," it is intended that only the limitative sense (maryādā) should apply.

Why [specify] "in the future" (bhaviṣyati)? [Consider: "We drank milk during that period which is prior to the month within the year that has passed. Why [specify] "in the limitative sense" (maryādāyām)? [Consider: "The time which is without a fixed limit (niravadhi)."
"From that point on, we shall drink milk there for fifteen nights. Now, one might object:

"In this case, according to the rule *aṅkhyāpūrvaṃ rātraṃ*, the word should be neuter. Nor should it be argued that the masculine gender is established by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that fortnight (*pakṣa*) in which there are fifteen nights," because [the rule applies to] *ahaḥ*...

If it is argued that this would result in the absence of the suffix *it* in the sense of "one part of all" (*sarvaikadeśe*), that is true; for precisely because of such usage in the Bhāṣya, they say that the neuter gender does not apply here.
(510) *parasmin vibhāṣā* || 3.3.138 || [The suffix *it* is optional when another [suffix] follows.]

In the case of *parasmin*, it is optionally prohibited by the rule "haviṣyati-anadyatana-vartamāne. Regarding *varjyam*: from the causative (*ṇijanta*) root, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the object by the rule "ṭhaco yat. Regarding *varjam*: in that reading, however, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied by the rule "dvitīyāyāṃ ca. It refers specifically to that which is not a day-and-night (*an-ahorātra*). This [term] refers to the year (*vatsara*).
"I shall drink milk there, which is beyond fifteen nights from now," and so forth.
[This is an example of] "when there is a cause for the conditional mood" (*liṅ-nimite*). "Failure to accomplish" (*atipatti*) means non-accomplishment (*aniṣpatti*).
(511) And [the conditional mood is used] when referring to the past (*bhūte*). 3.3.140.
And regarding the past: when the conditional (*liṅ*) is the cause, the periphrastic future (*lṛṅ*) shall be used for both the past and the future upon the failure of the action.
Here, "general past" (*bhūtasāmānya*) should be understood as that which is common to both the recent (*adyatana*) and non-recent (*anadyatana*).
Its examples begin with the rule: "The conditional (*liṅ*) is used after *uta* and *api* when they are semantically connected... and so forth.
In the seven sūtras following "tumun" in the section on verbs with different agents, [the suffixes] are to be understood;
for in the rules preceding that, an option is stated by the rule "votāpyoḥ.
"Or *lṛṅ*. This option applies only when the past tense (*bhūta*) is the condition for the use of the conditional mood (*liṅ*); however, in the future (*bhaviṣyat*), *lṛṅ* is mandatory.
(513) "The present tense (*laṭ*) is used after the particles *api* and *jātu* when expressing censure (*garhā*). (Pāṇini 3.3.142)

In the sense of censure (*garhā*). Here, the rule *votāpyoḥ* does not apply. Since the *laṭ* (present tense) prescribed for the present time would otherwise not be applicable here, this is an original injunction (*vidhi*). "In all three times" means that no specific time has been mentioned; such is the intention. "On account of its being subsequent" (*paratvāt*).
It should also be understood that this is because [the rule] leaves no room for other applications. Regarding the phrase "even his wife" (*api jāyām*):

even in cases such as *tyakṣyasi* (future) or *atyākṣīḥ* (past), the present tense suffix *laṭ* alone—found in the verse, "He who abandons even his wife and takes up a courtesan"—must be employed as an exception to the verbal suffixes denoting the three times.

Because the condition for the *liṅ* (the conditional mood) is absent here, the *lṛṅ* (the conditional) does not occur when there is a failure of action (*kriyātipatti*). Regarding the statement "the *lakāras* [tense markers] apply to the three times": for the remote past (*parokṣa-anadyatana-bhūta*), the *liṭ* (perfect)—how did you abandon dharma? For the recent past (*bhūtānadyatana*), the *laṅ* (imperfect)—how did you abandon dharma? For general past time (*bhūtasāmānya*), the *luṅ* (aorist)—you abandoned it.

In the future not remote from the present, *luṭ* is used—as in "you will be abandoned. In the general future, *lṛṭ* is used—as in "how will you abandon dharma? and so forth. Regarding the word "here" (*atra*), it should be understood as referring to the occurrence of the "non-occurrence of action" (*kriyātipatti*). (514) When accompanied by an interrogative particle (*kiṃvṛta*), the optative (*liṅ*) and the future (*lṛṭ*) are used. 3.3.144.

Regarding *kiṃvṛte*: the potential (*liṅ*) and the periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*) occur in all three tenses. It does not carry over [from the previous rule]. Thus, in this context, the meaning is that they are used invariably for the past, or optionally. (515) Pāṇini 3.3.145: "In the sense of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*) and intolerance (*amarṣa*), [the potential and periphrastic future occur] even when *kiṃvṛta* is absent."

In the sense of "impossibility" (*anavaklṛpti*) and "impatience" (*amarṣa*), the suffixes *liṅ* and *lṛṭ* are understood to recur; since these two occur in all three times, they serve as exceptions to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). Since the term "that which contains an interrogative pronoun" (*kiṃvṛta*) is not under discussion here, both [suffixes] will apply without distinction even in the absence of such a pronoun; therefore, it is stated "even when there is no *kiṃvṛta*."

It should not be applied. The placement of the word with fewer syllables at the end—despite its eligibility for prior placement—is intended to prevent the application of *yathāsaṅkhya* (correspondence by order). Regarding the rule "the conditional suffix (*lṛṅ*) is as before": the meaning is that it is optional when referring to the past, but obligatory when referring to the future.
[Example: "I do not believe that Caitra will sacrifice to Hari."
One should cite examples such as *nindiṣyat* (he would have censured).

(516) *Kiṅkila-astyartheṣu luṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.146): "In the presence of *kiṅkila* and words expressing existence (*astyartha*), [the conditional *luṅ* is used]. Since both the optative (*liṅ*) and the conditional (*luṅ*) were applicable here, the explicit mention of *luṅ* excludes the optative.

With the intention of saying "let it cease," he says: "the conditional (liṅ) is an exception. "It exists" (*asti*) means "there is [the act of] approaching a Śūdra woman with you as the agent," and so forth. "The conditional (lṛṅ) does not [apply]" because, since the conditional (liṅ) has been set aside, there is an absence of the conditions that would trigger it.

(517) *jātuyador liṅ* | Pāṇini 3.3.147. The term *anavaklṛptyamarṣayoḥ* ("in the sense of impossibility and intolerance") carries over [from the previous rule]. Thus, since the suffixes *liṅ* and *luṭ* would otherwise apply by virtue of the rule *tathā caṭhanavaklṛptyamarṣayoḥ*, this present rule is stated.

The suffix *lṛṭ* is for the purpose of superseding [other rules]. Thus it is said: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *lṛṭ*. This [suffix] applies to all three times. Regarding the statement "*lṛṅ* as before": the meaning is that it is used optionally when there is a failure of action (*kriyātipatti*) in the past, but it is obligatory in the future. Examples such as "May you not have censured Hari" (*mā bhavān hariṃ nindiṣyat*) should be cited. This is intended to exclude cases involving censure (*agarhā*).

The *laṭ* [present tense] is prescribed when *jātu* is used in the sense of reproach. (518) *Yaccayatrau* | 3.3.148 | Regarding *yaccayatrau*: the phrase "when there is no possibility or when there is indignation" (*anavaklṛptyamarṣayoḥ*) is understood here. There is a correspondence of order (*yathāsaṅkhya*) in this case.

This is not accepted; it is also an exception to the *liṅ* and *lṛṭ* [affixes]. The division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), however, is for the purpose that the terms *yat* and *yatra* alone may carry over into the following two sūtras. When there is a failure of action (*kriyātipatti*), the *lṛṅ* [affix] is used as before: "If you had done so, I would not have believed it" or "I would not have tolerated it," and so forth.

(519) And [the suffix *liṅ* is used] in the sense of censure (*garhā*). 3.3.149. "And in the sense of censure. This applies to all three times (*kālatraya*), and thus it is an exception (*apavāda*) to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). It should be understood that only *liṅ* occurs. Since the rule "optionally when *katham* is used" (3.3.143) would otherwise allow for the present tense (*laṭ*) in the sense of censure, the word "except in the case of *iva*" (*ivṛte*) is supplied right there [from the previous rule].

Thus, the *lṛṭ* (future tense) is obtained; however, the sense is that this *liṅ* (potential mood), which is prescribed when used in conjunction with *yat* or *yatra*, serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to those two. The *lṛṅ* (conditional mood) is as before. For example: "If you had caused a Śūdra to sacrifice, that would have been improper," and so forth.

(520) *citrikaraṇe ca* |3|3|150|. Also when there is a sense of wonder (*citrikaraṇa*). This [suffix] also applies to all three times. The conditional (*lṛṅ*) is used as before. "That you would have caused a Śūdra to sacrifice, or that you would have done so—this is a marvel!"*

(521) *śeṣe lṛḍayadau* |3|3|151|. In the "remainder" (*śeṣe*), the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is used when *yat* or *yadi* do not follow; this is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*sarvalakārāpavādaḥ*). For example: *so ’dhīyīta* ("he would study"). Because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) regarding *yat* and *yadi*, the optative suffix *liṅ* is applied by the rule *ātuyadoḥ*. Since the specific conditions for *liṅ* are absent here, the conditional *lṛṅ* does not apply.

(522) *utāpyoḥ samarthayor liṅ* || 3.3.152 || [The suffix] *liṅ* occurs after a verbal root when used with *uta* or *api*, provided they are semantically equivalent. It applies to all three times; even in the past, it is obligatory.
Since the mention of the word *vā* ("optionally") has been withdrawn from this rule, the conditional *lṛṅ* will necessarily occur in the past tense just as it does in the future.
It is understood that "the king might have killed the robber," "he did not kill him," and "he will not kill him.

(523) *Kāmapravedane ’kacciti* (Pāṇini 3.3.153). [The sūtra states: "In the expression of one's own desire (*kāmapravedana*), the potential suffix (*liṅ*) should be used. This applies to all three times and is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*).
"Is he living? To this, "Yes, indeed" (*āmo me*) is to be supplied. The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here according to the rule *vartamāna-sāmīpye*.

(524) The suffix *ala* is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvana*). "Proficiency" (*prauḍhi*) means "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*). [The locative case] is used with the nominative and the locative.
And so it is said. Now, one might ask: "Since [the word *asambhāvanā*] has been transformed into the nominative case (*prathamā*), how can the sense of the locative (*saptamī*) be obtained here?

To this they reply: by repeating the rule "*asambhāvane'lam*" and transforming only the second instance [of the word], all that is desired is established. *Sambhāvanam* (possibility) refers to actions.

The determination of fitness (*yogyatā*) is [the meaning of] "enough" (*alam*). As for the phrase "if it is so": the meaning is that if that possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) occurs such that [the action] is capable, then the conditional suffix (*liṅ*) would be used. Regarding the word "established" (*siddha*): it refers to that in which there is no usage of the word when "enough" is present; that is, where the word *alam* is not employed, its meaning is nevertheless understood.

In that context, this is the established meaning. However, in the *Manoramā*, it is stated that it would be more appropriate to formulate the rule as: "alam iti saṃbhāvane siddhāprayogaśca" (The particle *alam* is used in the sense of possibility when there is non-employment of what is established).
In that formulation, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "siddhasya aprayogaḥ" (non-employment of the established); [the question arises: of what is there non-employment?
In response to this inquiry, it should be understood that [the agent] is implied by the word *alam* (sufficient). Regarding the phrase *api girim*:
the particle *api* indicates possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). Here, the sense of possibility is understood as "he is capable of carrying away even a mountain.
This *liṅ* (optative) is used for general time; the *lṛṅ* (conditional) is used as before. Even a mountain...
"He will break it with his head. If you say, "Enough," what then? He will likely go.
(525) *Vibhāṣā dhātau saṃbhāvanavacane ’yadi* | 3|3|155|. "Optionally before a verbal root": that by which possibility (*saṃbhāvana*) is expressed is called *saṃbhāvanavacana*.

"In that *dhātu*": the meaning is "in a verbal root (*dhātu*) having the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). [The example is] *bhuñjīthāstvaṃ* ("you might eat"). Here, by the preceding rule, the *liṅ* (optative) is mandatory. Why "in a *dhātu*"? So that there might not be a literal apprehension of the word-form (*svarūpa-grahaṇa*) when it means possibility. But since the expression "meaning possibility" is used, there is no application here of the verbal root itself which expresses that [possibility].
There is no optionality (*vibhāṣā*). One should eat (*bhuñjīta*). Here, the *liṅ* [optative] is compulsory by virtue of the preceding rule.
(526) *Hetuhetumator liṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.156). Regarding *hetuhetu*: since the term *vibhāṣā* is understood to carry over, he says "it may optionally (*vā*) occur."

Regarding "nameccet": bowing to Kṛṣṇa is the cause for attaining happiness; it is intended [to occur] in the future, as in "it will surely come to pass. While the suffix *liṅ* was already understood from the preceding rule, the repetition of the word *liṅ* here is for the purpose of indicating a specific time (the future). As for "hanti" and so forth...

Objection: Should not the suffix *śatṛ* be applied to the root *han* in the expression “akṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ,” since the act of killing is the cause for fleeing? Reply: Not so. For it is said: “In the case of *eva*, *trātaḥ*, *galaḥ*, *grāhaḥ*, and in connection with *iti*, the rule for *sat* [the present participle] applies; however, these are not optionally combined with one another, as in the examples *gavākṣaḥ* and *saṃśitavrataḥ*.”
This is because it was established in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ācchāyanyatarasyām*;

and Kaiyaṭa explained it under that very same rule: "The term is *evatrāt*. In that case, by the rule *udavidondatrāghrāhrībhyo 'nyatarasyām*, the substitution of *ṇa* does not occur—[as in] *devatrāṇa*."

Thus [it is said]. However, it is *devatrāta* itself. By the rule *ro yaṅ*, and by the rule *vibhāṣā*, there is obligatory substitution of *la* for *ra* when referring to a part of a living being; thus *galaḥ*. It does not occur in the word *ara* when it denotes poison.
By the rule *vibhāṣā grahaḥ*, the suffix *ṇa* occurs when referring to an aquatic creature—thus *grāhaḥ*. It does not occur when referring to a celestial body (*jyotis*).

—this is the point. In the rule *akṣaṇahetvoḥ*, by carrying forward the word *vibhāṣā* from the preceding rule *anvorvibhāṣā* and resorting to a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the application of the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* is prohibited when joined with the word *iti*. For example: "He flees because he kills" (*hantīti palāyate*). In the case of a window: *avākṣaḥ*.

But elsewhere, *avaṅ* does not occur—as in *go’kṣaḥ*. In the compound *saṃśitavrataḥ*, which is a *bahuvrīhi*, the optional substitution of *itva* (the change to *ī*) as prescribed by the rule *ācchāyeryanyatarasyām* does not apply, so we have *saṃśāta-*; otherwise, however, we have *śātaḥ* or *śitaḥ*. These aforementioned rules, such as the substitution of *natva* and others, [apply] mutually, that is, one after another.

They are not optionally applied when the subject matter is the same; the meaning is that this is because one must resort to the *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (restricted option) established in the respective prescriptive rules (*vidhāyaka-sūtra*). However, in the case of the conditional mood (*kriyātipatti*), the *lṛṅ* suffix is obligatory for both the past and the future: "If it had rained, the crops would have grown."

(527) *icchārtheṣu liṅloṭau* || 3.3.157 || Regarding words expressing desire, the suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* [are used]. When these [words] are present as governing terms (*upapada*), these two [suffixes] occur after a verbal root. This is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). By the rule *iṅ ca*, the suffix *liṅ* is used when the agent of the action of desiring is the same as the agent of the action of hearing.

It should be understood that here, the suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* occur after a verb when the actions have different agents (*asamānakartṛka*). It should be stated [in the rule] "when making known a desire" (*kāmapravedane*); for example, "he acts while desiring. In this case, because there is no conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*), the suffix *tumun* does not apply even though the agents are different. Now, one might object: [why is this so?]

If it is argued that the mention of *liṅ* here is unnecessary—since the sense is already established by the rule "āmapravedane kaccitī" (Pāṇini 3.3.152), which prescribes *liṅ* for expressing a wish—and that *loṭ* alone should be prescribed, we say no; for the mention of *liṅ* is essential here so that *loṭ* does not subvert *liṅ*. Otherwise, one would have to state simply "icchārtheṣu loṭ ca."

It should be stated that "let it be formulated as a sūtra. For if the optative suffix (*liṅ*) were attracted by the particle *ca*, there would be the possibility of attracting the term *vibhāṣā* which is connected to it, and thus [the rule] would apply even to other verbal suffixes (*lakārānta*).
Nor can it be argued that this is already established by this very rule through the supplementary statement (*upasaṅkhyāna*) "in the case of informing others" (*āmapravedane*).
It should not be said that the rule *āmaḥ pravedane ’kaccitye* is unnecessary;

for it was formulated for the sake of those cases where the expression of desire (*kāmapravedana*) is understood through the context or the sense of the matter, and no governing word (*upapada*) with the meaning of "desire" is present.

(528) *Liṅ ca* | Pāṇini 3.3.159. Regarding the rule *liṅ ca*: since the application of *liṅ* and *loṭ* prescribed by the rule *icchārtheṣu liṅloṭau* would be superseded by the rule *samānakartṛkeṣu tumun*, this sūtra is intended as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to restore the use of *liṅ*.
Nor should it be suspected here that, by the rule of *vāsarūpa*, there is no constant supersession of the *liṅ* and *loṭ* moods;

for that rule does not apply to the suffixes *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and those having the sense of *khala*. Even if the *vāsarūpa* rule were to apply, the rule must still be commenced for the purpose that, in such cases, only the *liṅ* occurs and the *loṭ* does not.
In the case of the non-occurrence of an action, the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is used as previously prescribed.
(529) After verbs expressing desire, the conditional suffix is optionally used in the present tense. Why "after verbs expressing desire"? [Observe: *pacati gacchati* ("he cooks, he goes").

(530) P. 3.3.163: *kṛtyāś ca* [are used] in the senses of command (*praiṣa*), permission (*atisarga*), and the arrival of the proper time (*prāptakāla*). Regarding "command and permission": they say that although one could have simply used the term *vidhi* (injunction), the use of the term *praiṣa* (command) is for the sake of clarifying the student's understanding. [The word *loṭ*] is carried over [from the previous rule] by the phrase "*loṭ ca*" (P. 3.3.162).

This alone is the purpose of the *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules). For if there were a single rule (*ekayoga*), there would have to be a carrying forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the suffix *liṅ* as well.

The meaning is that [the separation is made] for the sake of expressing the sense of "proper time" (*prāptakāla*), because the senses of "command" (*praiṣa*) and "permission" (*atisarga*) are already established by the preceding rule.

(531) *liṅ* is used for that which occurs after a muhūrta [Pāṇini 3.3.164]. The word *cordhvam* [in the rule] is for the purpose of prescribing *liṅ* where it was not previously obtained, specifically regarding a particular time that has arrived. However, in the case of command (*praiṣa*) and permission (*atisarga*), *liṅ* is already obtained by the preceding rule.
The word *ca* is used [in the sūtra] so that the *liṅ* may not occur in this specific time-period for those [verbs] whose endings are *loṭ*.
(532) *sme loṭ* 3.3.165. This refers to the scope of the preceding sūtra; thus, *praiṣa* and so forth, as well as *ūrdhvamauhūrtike*, are understood to carry over.
This is the intended meaning. (533) *athīṣṭe ca* | 3|3|166|.
Also when there is a request (*adhīṣṭa*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule for] the optative (*liṅ*). There is a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*).
The purpose [of the sūtra] is to exclude that which lasts longer than a muhūrta.
*liṅ yadi*; and *kāla-samaya-velāsu ceti*. [This is stated] because of the rule *upapadeṣu*.
It is connected by a modification of the wording. It is an exception to the suffix *tumun*. As in "yad bhuñjīta" (that he might eat).
However, it does not apply in "yatkālaḥ pacati" (at which time he cooks), because [the conditions of] "preṣa" and so forth do not recur there.
(535) *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca* |3|3|169| [The kṛtya suffixes and the suffix *tṛc* are used after a root when it denotes fitness.]

When the agent (*kartṛ*) is understood as being "fit" (*arha*) or "suitable" (*yogya*), the *kṛtya* suffixes and the *tṛc* suffix occur. For example: *tvayā kanyā voḍhavyā*, *vahanīyā* ("the girl is to be carried by you"); *tvaṃ kanyāṃ voḍhā* ("you are the one who will carry the girl").

[In the phrase] *kanyāṃ vaha*, the meaning is that "you are fit for carrying the girl. Now, for what purpose are the *kṛtya* suffixes and the *tṛc* suffix used when [the sense of] "fitness" (*arha*) is intended?

If it is argued that [the suffixes] are prescribed by virtue of being generally enjoined, and will therefore apply even where [the agent] is not fit [to perform the action], here they say: the *liṅ* is enjoined when fitness (*arhatā*) is to be expressed and [that fitness] has not yet been attained;
however, the prescription of the *kṛtya* and *tṛc* suffixes is so that there may be no sublation (*bādhā*) of the *liṅ*. Nor is this...
The desired result is achieved by the rule *vāsarūpa* (Pāṇini 3.1.94), because that rule does not apply after the section on feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*).

(536) *Dhātusaṃbandhe pratyayāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.1): "When there is a connection with a verbal root. Here, a relationship such as qualifier-qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) between two verbal roots is untenable.

Because [the word] is exhausted by reminding one of its own referent (*svārtha*), and because it is accepted that the sentence-meaning is either the relation between word-referents (*padārthasaṃsarga*) or an action qualified by its factors (*kāraka*), the word itself also appears in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), based on the principle that "there is no verbal cognition apart from the following of words."
Even if this is accepted, the word functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*) only with respect to its own meaning, and not with respect to another word.
Consequently, the connection between verbal roots (*dhātu*) is not understood through the sentence;

thus, since it is impossible for that [connection] to be the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), the verbal root-word (*dhātu-śabda*) indicates the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Now, [one might object]: "From the rule *dhātoḥ*..."

If it is argued that— just as in the rule for the suffix *san* (Pāṇini 3.1.7), where "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛka*) and "the object" (*karman*) are accepted as qualifiers of the verbal root by way of their meanings, so too here there may be a connection between two verbal roots by way of their meanings— this is not so. For if that were the case:
If suffixes were to occur only upon the employment of multiple verbal roots that express mutually related meanings,

then forms such as *gomān āsīt* (the owner of cows was) and *gomān bhavitā* (the owner of cows will be) would not be established; for in these cases, there is no present tense *as-* (to be), just as there is no present tense *vas-* (to dwell) in the phrase *vasan dadarśa* (while dwelling, he saw).

[The suffix] is applied; and for that which is not being applied, there can be no connection with another verbal root. If a connection between two meanings is admitted, then even in the absence of two roots, because the two meanings of the roots exist, there is no inconsistency in cases such as *gomān āsīt* ("the owner of cows existed"). With this in mind, he says:
Regarding the phrase "of the meanings of roots" (*dhātvarthānām*): the plural number is used with reference to the multiplicity of objects (*viṣaya*).
However, when referring to each individual object, it should be understood as "of two root-meanings" (*dhātvarthayoḥ*).
This has been explained according to the *Manoramā*. Some, however—

If one accepts that there is a relationship between two bases mediated by meaning, then the forms *omāna*, *āsīt*, and *bhavitā* would not be established; thus, what is stated in the *Manoramā* is indeed to be considered.
Just as in the rule "it performs that" (*tat karoti*) and "it describes that" (*tad ācaṣṭe*), [the same applies] to "it belongs to him" (*at asya asti*) and "I am that" (*at asmi*).

They say that here too, because both singularity and present time are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*), that [result] is established independently of the present sūtra; for in this rule prescribing the suffix *matup*, there is no inclusion of a specific time, as there is in rules such as "the suffix *laṭ* is used for the present" (*vartamāne laṭ*). However, that is inconsistent with the Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa, and others. Thus...

For in the Bhāṣya, having raised the objection— "Since the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is already understood from the previous context, what is the purpose of mentioning *pratyaya* again here?"— it is resolved that this is so that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of compounds involving even non-verbal suffixes may be established, as in the examples "gomān āsīt" (the cow-possessor was) or "bhavitā" (will be). However, Kaiyaṭa [explains it differently]:

It has been stated: "The suffix *matup* [in the form] ‘this belongs to that’ or ‘it exists in this’ is prescribed as being connected with the meaning of the base qualified by present existence (*vartamānasattā*). And thus, in the rule prescribing *matup*, although singularity is not intended to be expressed in the word ‘exists’ (*asti*), presentness [is indeed intended].

That this is the intended meaning is understood from the force of that very text. Furthermore, when it is said, "Bring the man with the staff" (*daṇḍinam ānaya*), only one who possesses a staff characterized by its existence at the present time is brought, and no other. Likewise, in accordance with the verbal forms *āsīt* ("was") and *abhūt* ("became"), in the expression *omān*, [it is understood that] "cows were his."

The suffix *matup* in the expression "gāvo 'sya bhavitāraḥ" (cows will belong to him), which is connected to a base meaning qualified by a past or future existent, is enjoined by this very sūtra and is not obtainable by the method stated therein; such is the direction [of the argument]. Now, one might object: "Are not the suffixes already established in their respective domains by those various specific injunctions?"

To the question, "What is the purpose of this sūtra?", he says: "In this [sūtra], 'time' (kāla). The sense is that, beginning with the rule *vartamānasāmīpye*, the alteration of time (*kālānyatvam*) is generally taught, and it is precisely that which is intended here.
This is evident in examples such as *vanāni paśyan yayau* ("he went along seeing the forests").

In response to the inquiry, "Among the suffixes denoting present, past, and other times, which one is displaced from its own time? he says: "expressed by a *tiṅ*-ending [verb]. The sense is that it is appropriate for a subordinate element (*guṇa*) to be guided according to the principal element (*pradhāna*), but not the reverse. [He uses] the word "suffixes" (*pratyayāḥ*).
The meaning is that they exist as persisting through a period of time. Regarding "bhūte laṭ" (the present tense suffix occurs when there is past time):
thus, having stayed, he saw—this is the sense. Regarding "atīta": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that seeing whose agent was one who performed a stay in the past.
Regarding "somayājī": the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the future sense according to the rule "araṇe yajaḥ. Therefore...

Thus he says: "one who is about to sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yakṣyamāṇa*). And likewise, in the phrase "he went having seen" (*dṛṣṭvā yayau*), the present tense suffix *laṭ* is used for the past sense of the root *dṛś*; the meaning is "having seen, he went. But in the phrase "his mind did not waver [even] when he was about to inform," the future tense suffix *lṛṭ* is used for the past sense of the root *vid*; according to the rule "for *lṛṭ*, there is optionally *sat* (the suffix *liṭ*)."

The suffix -śatṛ [is used here]. The meaning is "one who has performed the offering," and so forth; this should be inferred accordingly. It might be argued that in the phrase "hāvi kṛtyam āsīt" (the oblation was to be made), according to the method of the Sūtra, if the word "hāvi" is accepted as being in the past tense, then the sense is "the becoming [of the oblation] was past"; consequently, the word "āsīt" (was) would also have a single agent and refer to the past.

Because the meaning of "was" (āsīt) is already contained within the sense of "will be" (bhāvi), the simultaneous use of both words would be redundant, as the meaning of the word "will be" is already obtained through the word "was. Consequently, the meaning here must necessarily be accepted as: "That which was treated as being 'to be' for all this time, that now *was*."

If this [the view that the suffix denotes the present] is accepted, then even in the case of "omānāsīt," let the meaning be that he was an object of the linguistic usage "gomān" (possessor of cows). In examples such as "vasan dadarśa" (while dwelling, he saw), the *laṭ* and other suffixes should be accepted as denoting the past through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), according to the specific requirements of each case. However, in the case of "omayājī," the *ṇini* suffix denotes the past alone.

If it is argued: "Even when [the action] has occurred, one might say 'he will be' (*bhavitā*); and since this occurs in co-utterance with a form ending in *luṭ* (future), one could supply the word 'one who will be called a Soma-sacrificer' (*somayājīti vyavahariṣyamāṇaḥ*), and thus the usage would occur either by means of the suffix *ṇini* or by indicating the future sense. So what is the purpose of this sūtra?"—to this they reply: [The answer follows: ... [as per the original commentary].
The commencement of the Sūtra is for the purpose of providing a general solution without the exertion involved in supplying ellipses (*adhyāhāra*) or resorting to indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

For it is not appropriate to accept such [supplementation] everywhere simply because, in instances such as "there was something to be done" (*hāvi kṛtyam āsīt*), the supply of ellipses and so forth occurs out of necessity.

(537) Pāṇini 3.4.2: "In the sense of intensification of action (kriyāsamabhihāra), there is the imperative (loṭ); for the imperative, hi and sv are substituted; and optionally, so also for ta and dhvam.
Regarding "in the sense of intensification of action": it is that which is to be expressed. Intensification of action is indeed the meaning of the verbal root itself.
The sense is that the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is merely indicative (*dyotaka*); and for that [imperative], *hi* and *sva* are prescribed. Now, one might object:

by means of the rule *oḍ*, having indicated the *tiṅ* suffixes, *hi* and *sva* should be prescribed as substitutes for those very *tiṅ* suffixes. This being so, since they would possess the status of a word (*padatva*) due to being *tiṅ*-ending forms, there would also be the benefit of [avoiding] *guṇa* substitution.

Furthermore, the supplementary statement "and [the substitutes] ṭhva and tadhvam" also accords with the natural sense [of the rule]. Otherwise, by the maxim *yena nāprāpte*, it would not be logical for the *tiṅ* designation to apply to *hi* and *sva*,
because the initial part [of the rule] is stronger due to its lack of conflict at the time of its arising, and because of the reliance on the locative case [in the rule].

And because the remainder of the sentence is thus established. Furthermore, if [the substitute] were a substitute for a *tiṅ* (verbal suffix), then since *hi* is prescribed in place of *ti*, *sip*, and *mi*, it would—by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitute behaving like its original)—be *pit* (having a *p* marker) and lack *ṅtva* (the *ṅ* marker);

consequently, in the case of *unīhi*, the substitution of *ī* by the rule "ī halyaghoḥ" would not occur. Likewise, in the case of *rūhi*, [the substitution of *ū* by the rule] "rū... [would not occur].

If the augment *iṭ* were applied [to the root], there would be the form *aravīt*; however, in the case of *ṛṇḍhi*, if the augment *im* were applied [to the root] as in *ṛṇaha i*, there would be the form *tṛṇeḍhi*. Furthermore, the technical designations *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* apply only to the substitutes for *l* (the verbal suffixes), and not to the substitutes for *tiṅ* (the personal endings) among those substitutes for *l*; thus, [the designation applies] to all of them.

Both *hi* and *sva* would apply alternately to *tiṅ* (verbal suffixes) generally, but not specifically to *hi* for *tib* and so on, nor *sva* for *tiṅ*, according to the established rule of word-order (*padavyavasthā*). Consequently, *hi* and *sva* would become substitutes for the *lakāra* itself;
therefore, he says "and those two" (*tau ca*). This is the intended meaning: in the sentence "after *oṭ*, [there are] *hi* and *sva*,"...

By the rule *riyāsamabhihāre loḍ*, the term *loṭ* is understood to carry over; and since that [term *loṭ*] qualifies *hi-sv-au*, it follows by implication that the suffixes *hi* and *sva* possess the properties of the *loṭ* [imperative]. In that case as well—
The extension (*atideśa*) of the property of being a suffix (*pratyayatva*), which belongs to the primary *loṭ*, would be purposeless,

since that is already established by the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* alone. Rather, it refers to those *tiṅ*-forms which, having acquired the designation *loṭ* through *sthānivadbhāva*, are [actually] *hi* and *sva*.

The properties of those two [the imperative and the optative] alone are extended here. Some, however, argue that immediately after the rule "līṅ for the repetition of an action" (*kriyāsamabhihāre loṭ*), one should have simply stated "hisvau tasya" (the suffixes *hi* and *sva* take the place of that) for the sake of brevity;
rather, by the force of the explicit mention of *loṭ*, it follows that *hi* and *sva* possess the properties of the imperative (*loṭ*) and occur in the place of *loṭ*.

This is the meaning that results. And thus, according to the method previously stated, it is established that what is desired is achieved: here, the properties of only those *hi* and *sva* which have become *tiṅ*-suffixes are extended. Furthermore, in the rule "oṭo hisvau," the mention of the *loṭ* [mood] is carried over from the preceding rule.

They say that [the suffixes] should not be treated as *anuvartanīya* (to be carried over). And because they are designated as *tiṅ*, they possess the status of a *pada*, and the rule *iṅṅtiṅḥ* applies. Regarding the prescription of *hi* and *sva*:
if these two were also designated as *puruṣa* (person) and *vacana* (number), then [the rules for] *yuṣmad*-coreferentiality and singularity would apply.
The sense is that since the [suffixes] *hi* and *sva* must necessarily occur [in these cases], the rule prescribing *hi* and *sva* would be redundant there.

For *hi* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), while *sva* denotes the action (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*). As Kaiyaṭa has also stated: "The agent is the meaning of the word *hi*, whereas the action, the object, and the agent are the meanings of the word *sva*. On this point, the moderns say: "In the case of 'alpe'..."

In examples such as *ṭhṛṣva*, this imperative (*loṭ*) suffix, like the suffix *kap*, is purely expressive of the frequent repetition of an action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*). One should not, however, assume for this imperative meanings such as "the agent" or "the object," as there is no purpose for doing so. If, on the other hand, the meaning of the word *hi* were the agent, [it would refer to] going again and again or with intensity.
Otherwise, the upcoming section of the text stating "the meaning of *hyanta*" would not accord with its natural sense.

In cases such as *yāhi yāhi*, however, the cognition of the agent and so forth is easily obtained through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with forms such as *yāti*. This is just as in the case of *edhāñcakre*, where [the operation] applies even before the substitution of *taṅ* for the suffix following *ām*.

Even though number and existence are absent in the case of *ler-luk* (the elision of the *l* suffix), a number is nevertheless understood as being present because of the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the verb *cakre*, which indicates that the action consisting of "increase" has a single agent; in exactly the same way, even at the end of *hi-sva* forms, there is a cognition of time, grammatical relation (*kāraka*), and number by virtue of the subsequent application of verbs such as *yāti*.

They say: "This might be so—let there be the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre hisvau loḍ vā ca tadhvamoḥ*. And thus, since *hi* and *sva* are not the *loṭ* [mood] itself, but rather possess the properties (*dharma*) of the *loṭ*, all that is desired would be established according to the method previously stated."
If it is asked, "What is the purpose of using the genitive case ending in *loṭaḥ*?"— on this point they say:

if the status of being a substitute for *loṭ* were not accepted for *hi* and *sva*, then, because those two would not undergo the same operations as substitutes for *loṭ*, rules such as *ī haly aghoḥ* would fail to apply.

Even if forms such as *lunīhi* were established [by P. 6.4.75], the status of being an imperative (*loḍanta*) would not be established for those ending in *hi* and *sva*. Consequently, the optional substitution of the anudātta accent prescribed by P. 8.1.34 (*hanta ce*) would not apply in cases such as: *hanta pralunīhi pralunīhīty ayam lunāti*. Therefore, in order to obtain the status of being an imperative, [the rule] "of *oṭ*"...
The substitution of *hi* and *sva* is prescribed [by the rule *loṭo laṅvat*]. If, however, you argue that even if it were stated as *hi-svau loṭ*,

the operation of the *loṭ* ending— namely, the optional accentuation by the rule *hanta ca*— would be established by resorting to the status of being like a *loṭ* ending, then [we reply that] those two [substitutes] possess the properties of the *loṭ* obtained through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*.

Because the meaning of *hi* and *sva* would not be adopted [as substitutes for the *loṭ* suffixes], the grammatical operations pertaining to the substitutes of *loṭ*—namely, the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *parasmaipada*, *ātmanepada*, and *tiṅ*—would not be established. Consequently, the aforementioned defect would remain as it was. However, if it were stated that "the *oṭ* augment is applied to *loṭ*, and *hi* and *sva* [are its substitutes]," [then the desired results follow].

By virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element), because *hi* and *sva* possess the nature of the imperative (*loṭ*), the optional accentuation resulting from the operations applicable to the imperative is established; for it has already been explained that, by carrying forward the term *loṭ* from the rule "the imperative is used in the sense of frequent repetition" (*riyāsamabhihāre loṭ*), *hi* and *sva* are treated as imperatives, and thus, through their status as substitutes for the imperative, they undergo elision and other such operations.
The designations *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada*, and so forth, are also established.

(Pāṇini 3.4.3) *samuccaye’nyatarasyām*: in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). From the root *ci* (to collect), the suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of abstract action (*bhāva*) by the rule *ṭerac*. "As previously stated" refers to the *loṭ* (imperative) mood of the verbal root.
The meaning is that *hi* and *sva* are optionally used in place of *ta* and *dhvam* respectively within the scope of the imperative (*loṭ*). Regarding "according to the rule" (*yathāvidhi*):
(539) *pūrvasmin* 3.4.4.
In the preceding [rule], within the scope of the intensive repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), here [the application of] number, grammatical case, and so forth [is determined].
Since there is no comprehension from the root *hi* alone, the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of a verb is obtained by logical necessity for the purpose of making that meaning understood;

this is then restricted by the rule "according to the specific form" (*yathāvidhi*). Consequently, because it is a restriction of what might otherwise optionally occur, forms such as *yāhi yāhi gacchati* do not arise. Even though [this is so] elsewhere...
In rules such as *ṭhAn-bhi-s-ai-s-ā-dy-ai-s-ā-n-ām ś-au* (Pāṇini 7.1.9), the term "restriction" (*niyama*) is used to denote "exclusive specification" (*parisaṅkhyā*),
