Some, however, say that the word *varti* is a form derived from the root *vṛt* with the suffix *ik* according to the rule "ṭhik-śtipau," and that the desired meaning is obtained through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

(425) *śabdavairakalahābhrakaṇvameghebhyaḥ karaṇe* || 3.1.17 || He says that [the word] *karmaṇaḥ* (from an object) is understood [to follow] from these: "from these as objects. (426) *sukhādibhyaḥ kartṛvedanāyām* || 3.1.18 ||

Regarding the phrase "sukhādibhyaḥ": the word "kartu" (of the agent) is a separate term with its genitive case ending elided. Furthermore, since the root *vid* belongs to the curādigaṇa in the sense of "cognition," "narration," and "dwelling," the word "vedanā" here signifies "knowledge. Agency is understood precisely in relation to that [knowledge], and the agent is construed with "pleasure" (*sukha*) and the other [feelings].

This is what he says: "of the very agent of sensation" and "another's pleasure. Here, the sentence itself means that the agent of sensation is distinct from that in which the pleasure resides. "Pleasure and so forth" refers to pleasure, pain, joy, sorrow, and the like.

(427) *namas-varivas-citraṅaḥ kyac* [Pāṇini 3.1.19]. The addition of the suffix *kyac* after the verbal roots *namas*, *varivas*, and *citraṅ* is for the purpose of causing the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel; the inclusion of the marker *ṅ* is for the sake of causing Vṛddhi. Others say that [the root *citri*] means "to cause wonder. Thus Bhaṭṭi [writes]:—

‘And thus, being made a spectacle by him’— the meaning is that this illusory deer (*māyāmṛga*), being made a spectacle (*citrīyamāṇaḥ*), was producing astonishment. (428) *puccchabhāṇḍacīvarāṇṇiṅ* | Pāṇini 3.1.20.

Regarding *puccabhāṇḍa*: because the term *karaṇe* (in the sense of "instrument") is understood as a carry-over here as well, the suffix *ṇiṅ* denotes a specific type of action. He demonstrates that very specific action with the words beginning with *puccāt*.
Here, the letter *ṅ* serves both to include the suffixes *ṇiṅ* and *ṇic* generally under the rule *ṇer aniṭi*, and for the purpose of ensuring the compulsory use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
He caused [them] to be produced.

(429) *Muṇḍamiśraślakṣṇalavaṇavratavasrahalakalakṛtatūstebhyo ṇic* || 3.1.21 || [The suffix] *ṇic* is added after these words when used in the sense of the root *kṛ* "to do. This refers sometimes to action in general, but more commonly to a specific action.

Regarding "vratādīti": *payo vratayati* means "he eats milk"; *śūdrānnaṃ vratayati* means "he avoids the food of a Śūdra. Regarding *vasrāditi*: the meaning is that the suffix *ṇic* is applied after the word *vasra* when it signifies "covering," in the sense of "doing" (*karoti*). Thus, *saṃvasrayati* means "the covering with cloth."

The meaning is "he performs. Regarding the state of having a final *a* (adantatvam): this very irregularity (*nipāta*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rule "when there is no *vṛddhi*, there is elision of the *ṭi*. If the elision were to occur first, then since the effect of an elided stem (*aglopakārya*) would already be established, what would be the purpose of this irregularity? And thus:
The derivation of *apapaṭat* as being established, and so forth, has already been explained specifically within the *curādigaṇa*.

Regarding *kṛtayati*, the meaning is "he accepts assistance. Regarding "it is proper to read [them separately]," the intention is that there is brevity (*lāghava*) in composing them as a single sūtra. Regarding "even from [roots] that are dependent," etc.

The intended meaning is "by virtue of its capacity to convey understanding. However, in other cases, the *vṛtti* states only "he speaks articulately and pleasantly" (*ramaṇīyaṃ paṭum ācaṣṭe*), and not "he causes to speak articulately" (*paṭayati*). He demonstrates this very state of dependence by means of the words beginning with "the boy" (*māṇavakam*). The underlying idea is that the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed after a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyāntāt*).

Because it is a rule based on word-formation (*padavidhi*), the operation would not occur when there is mutual dependence; rather, the formation of the derivative (*vṛtti*) as *muṇḍayati* would only take place when it is understood through context and the like that [the object] belongs to the boy (*māṇavaka*), and not upon the actual employment of the word *māṇavaka*. This is because a causative form ending in *ṇic* is a verbal derivative (*sanādyanta*), and thus, according to the rule "of those with qualifiers," [the operation applies only when the qualifier is part of the same complex].
"And because of the absence of [the feminine] suffix" (vṛttyabhāvāt). "Gha" refers to [Pāṇini 4.1.72]: *puṃsi saṃjñāyām*.

"Puṃvadbhāva and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the elision of the penultimate vowel (*rabhāva*) and the elision of the suffix *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) are included. Since forms such as *etayati* are established by the elision of *ṭi* alone, the mention of *puṃvadbhāva* [is for the sake of other cases].
We have stated in the *curādigaṇa* itself that [the suffix *ṇic*] is added for the sake of establishing the form *dāradayati*.

The offspring of Darada is *dāradaḥ*, by the rule "dvyañ-magadha... which prescribes the suffix *aṇ*. When this [suffix] is elided in the feminine by the rule "ataśca," one says *darat*; to cause her to act thus is *dāradayati*. In this case, there is an absence of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution).

When there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant), one would have *darayati* and *prathayati*. In the case of *prathayati*, the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* occurs by the rule *ra ṛto halādeḥ*. In the form *apiprathat*, once the *vṛddhi* has taken place, because the root is not *aglopi* (having lost its penultimate vowel) due to the elision of the *ṭi*, the condition for *sanvadbhāva* applies; consequently, by the rule *sanyataḥ*, the substitution of *i* (itvam) occurs. [This is] from the *vṛddhi*.

But if the *ṭi*-elision occurred first, [the forms would be] *apraprathat* and *ājaḍhat*. Since, if the *ṭi*-elision were to take place here, the vowel *a* in the reduplicated syllable would be difficult to obtain after the doubling of the entire root along with the *ṇic* suffix, he says: "for *o* before *pu*, *yaṇ*, and *ji*, etc. [This refers to Pāṇini 7.4.80]. As for the forms *tvamau*, they are derived by the rule "and when a suffix or a subsequent member follows" (*pratyayottarapadayośca*).

Regarding the phrase "because of being internal" (*antaraṅgatvāt*): one should not argue that, by the rule *vārṇādāṅgam*, the elision of the suffix *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) alone ought to take effect; for that would involve a conflict of dependencies (*vyāśrayatva*). As for the statement "of the Bhāṣya":
the authors of the Vṛtti have indeed cited examples such as *preyān* and *preṣṭhaḥ* under the rule *prakṛtyaikāj*. And these...
Either by virtue of the status of being "as if unestablished" (*asiddhavat*)— according to the rule *ṭhasiddhavadatrābhāt*— for the grammatical instruction (*śāstra*) beginning with *priyasthiram*,

which prescribes the substitution [of *pra*] for *prastha* and so forth; or else, by the force of the pronunciation of the letter *s* in *prastha* and other such forms, as stated in the Bhāṣya, even without the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).

[The forms] are established. Even in cases such as *sragvān* and *srajiṣṭha*, the elision of the *ṭi* [suffix] will not occur, because the *luk* elision of the *vin* and *matup* suffixes—which is an exception (*apavāda*) to that [elision of *ṭi*]—is applied there. This is precisely the principle to be followed in cases such as *payasvān*, *payasiṣṭhaḥ*, and *campakasrajiṣṭhaḥ*; and it is not by this much alone [that the rule is undermined].
It should be understood that the rule *akṛtyaikāj* has been rejected; the intention is that it is necessary in cases such as *svāpayati*. As for *yuvām* and *āvām*:

even when the analysis (*vigraha*) is *yuṣmān* and *asmān*, the forms remain *yuṣmayati* and *asmayati* respectively. Nor is it the case that *yuvau* and *āvau* apply only when two [persons] are expressed.

In the form *bhavataḥ*, a specific [grammatical operation] might be suspected, but it cannot apply because there is no following case-ending (*vibhakti*). Nor can it be argued that the rule for suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) applies, because the suffix has been elided by *luk*. Furthermore, one should not say that the substitution (*ādeśa*) should occur even earlier; for it is a principle that "the elision (*luk*), being an external operation (*bahiraṅga*), overrides even internal rules (*antaraṅga*)."

This is because of the logical principle (*nyāya*) and because the maxim regarding the non-application of a rule when its requirements have already been met (*akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā*) remains active. Regarding the phrase *yena nāprāpti*:

wherever the rule *prakṛtyaikāc* (P. 6.4.163) applies, there the rule *ṭeḥ* (P. 6.4.155) applies, but not the rule *ataddhite* (P. 6.4.149); the point is that the latter does not apply in cases such as *srajiṣṭha*.
Others say it is according to the maxim: "A rule or a prohibition applies to that which is immediately preceding.

Regarding the term *saṃprasāraṇa*: one should not raise the objection that since the *ṭilopa* (elision of the suffix *ṭi*) occurs, the word no longer ends in *an*, and therefore the *saṃprasāraṇa* cannot take place by the rule *vayuvamaghonām*.

Because of the status of being "as if that which precedes" (*sthānivadbhāva*), or because of the rule "this [operation] is as if unestablished" (*asiddhavadatrā*), even when the *ṭi*-portion is elided, the quality of ending in *ann* is obtained.

For in that context, the phrase "not a *taddhita*" (*ataddhite*) is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), not a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). Consequently, there is neither a prescription nor a prohibition regarding a *taddhita*; rather, the prescription applies when something other than a *taddhita* follows. This "being other than a *taddhita*" (*taddhitabhinnatva*), however—

Since the suffix *ṇic* is indeed present, there is no obstruction to the *saṃprasāraṇa*. Nor should it be argued that because the *guṇa* substitution is observed for the vowel *i* before the suffix *aṣṭhin* in forms such as *daviṣṭha*, the *guṇa* would here also override the *vṛddhi*; for even if the *guṇa* were to occur first, the desired form is established by the subsequent application of *vṛddhi*. Alternatively:

Regarding the elision of the *ṭi* and the *saṃprasāraṇa*, because of the rule "in this [context], the *ṭha*-affix is as if unestablished (*asiddhavat*) with respect to *guṇa*," there is no occurrence of *guṇa* due to the treatment as if it were an *iṣṭhan* suffix. Thus, from the form *śvan*, one derives *śunayati*. By virtue of the treatment as an *iṣṭhan* suffix, the word is treated as a *bha*-stem, and thus the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs; furthermore, by the rule "the monosyllabic root remains in its original form" (*prakṛtyaikāj*), the vowel does not undergo change.

[The rule regarding] the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) [is applied] because [the suffix *ṇic*] is obligatory. The intention is that the elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) is non-obligatory (*anitya*) due to the possibility of its application being superseded by another word-form (*śabdāntaraprāpti*). In the case of *udīcayati*, having separated the prefix (*upasarga*), the *ṇic* suffix is added to the word *ac* itself; thus, the elision of *ṭi* takes place according to the rule *prakṛtyaikāc*.
No; for there is the substitution of *ī* by the rule *uda īt*. And in the case of *anaditām*, there is the elision of the *n* of the *kvip* suffix by the rule *kvip*.
In *udaicicat*, the *luṅ* [aorist] applies; because of the prohibition of the elision of the *ṇi* by the rule *idvirvacane'ci*, there is reduplication of the syllable *ci*.
In *pratīcayati*, there is the elision of *ac* by the rule *acaḥ*, and the lengthening of the preceding vowel by the rule *cau*.

Regarding the form *pratyacicat*: here, when the vowel *a* of the verbal root is elided by the rule *acaḥ*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs for the preceding sound before the augment *āṭ* added before the root *ci*. Nor should it be argued that the augment *āṭ* would apply because the elision is considered "as if not having taken effect" (*asiddhatva*), as is the case with forms like *astām* or *āsann*; for the two operations depend on different bases (*vyāśrayatvāt*). Indeed, the elision is caused by the suffix *ṇi*.
The *luṅ* suffix is marked with the indicator *ṇ*, whereas it is not so in cases such as *āsannita*, which constitutes a discrepancy [between the two].

In the case of *tirāyayati*, because there is no identity of form with a preverb (*upasarga*), there is no separate treatment of *tiras* here; consequently, since the rule *prakṛtyaikāj* does not apply, the *ṭi*-elision occurs. This is what he states with the words "of *añc*."

Regarding the phrase "by the principle of *ciṇ* and *luṅ*": just as in the example *apācitaram*, where after the elision (*luk*) of the *ta* suffix following the *caṇ* substitute, there is no further elision (*luṅ*) of the *tarap* suffix because the first elision is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its intervention—this is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "there is no elision of the *ṭi*": [it refers to the fact that the *ṭi* portion of the suffix is not elided].

The meaning is that there is no elision of the *ik* vowel [of the suffix] in the case of *tiryādi*. "Because it is not an *aglopi*" means that the intention is that even for what is not an *aglopi*, the status of being an *aglopi* is accepted. [This refers to the rule] *devanadyañcam*.

But surely, because of the rule "from a verbal derivative [denoting] an action, the suffixes *ṇic*, *kṛt*, *ta*, *dā*, *ṭac*, and *aṇ* are added," there would result the undesirable form *devān-añcayati* (he causes the gods to bend), just as *balibandhanam ācaṣṭe* results in *baliṃ bandhayati* (he tells of Bali's binding). However, the desired form is *devadrāyayati* (he causes the gods to run). Furthermore:
If the separation of the *kāraka* (participant in an action) were not admitted, even forms such as *adidevadatta* would not be established.

Nor should it be argued that the separation of the *kāraka* and so forth occurs only in narratives well-known from the *Purāṇas*, for this would result in the rule’s non-application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *rājānam āgamayati*. To this, they reply: in whatever narrative...
This [suffix] occurs only there, because it is prescribed by the restrictive rule *kṛ-luk-iṭi*; furthermore,
by the force of the mention of "narratives" (*ākhyāna*), it refers exclusively to matters that have become subjects of common public report.

This is because such examples alone have been cited in the Bhāṣya and other works. However, if there is common usage among great scholars (*mahājana*) in cases such as *devāñcanam ācaṣṭe*, then the form *devānañcati* indeed occurs. Regarding *amumuāyat*: [this is governed by] the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham advirvacane*.

Thus, because the non-establishment [of the condition] is negated, there is doubling of the syllable *mu*. In the case of *abībhavat*, the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the reduplicated syllable occurs by the rule "oḥ puyaṇji" (Pāṇini 7.4.80). Then, the lengthening occurs by the rule "dīrgho laghoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.94). Now, one might object: since the rule for lengthening (*dīrgha*) is subsequent, should it not apply first, and only afterwards the substitution of *i*? It is not so; for the rule "dīrgho... [applies only when the reduplicated syllable is light].

If it is argued that the rule *laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.94) is redundant because it finds its scope in forms such as *ajūhavat*, [the reply is: here they say— since in the rule *vipratiṣedhe param* (Pāṇini 1.4.2),
the word *para* signifies "desired," the substitution occurs before the lengthening in accordance with the requirements of the specific linguistic examples (*lakṣya*).

Furthermore, due to a difference in the scope of application (*lakṣyabheda*), the long vowel may optionally occur for the vowel *i*. Thus, in *abubhravat*: since the labial consonant (*pavarga*) following the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) does not have the vowel *a* (*avarṇa*) after it, whereas the semivowel (*yaṇ*) that has the vowel *a* after it does not follow the reduplication, the substitution of *i* (*itva*) does not apply to the vowel *u* of the reduplication. [Thus one says] *gā-gāvayati*.

*svaśva* means "a beautiful horse" (*śobhanaḥ aśvaḥ svaśvaḥ*), or it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has a beautiful horse. *svāśaśvat* [is formed] because the element identical in form to a prefix is separated [from the root], and thus, by the rule *ajādeḥ*, there is reduplication of the second syllable and the augment *ḍa*. *svayati* [is derived] from the rule *prakṛtyaikāj*.

The meaning is that the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) by the rule *yenanāprāpti* is an exception (*bādhaka*) specifically to the rule *ṭeḥ*, but not to the rule "there is elision of the *ṭi* of indeclinables (*avyaya*) when a *bha*-suffix follows. Regarding the form *asasvaditi*:
by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *oḥ puyaṇjī*, [it is established that] when there is doubling (*dvitva*), the substitute beginning with *a* (*ajādeśa*) [does not take place].
This is stated according to the view that the doubling of the word *svara* occurs either because it is treated as its original form (*sthānivadbhāva*) or because of a prohibition.

However, according to the view that even when accepting the elision of a vowel (*aglopi*), there is no designation of a substitute for a vowel (*ar-ādeśa*) when the substitute consists of both a vowel and a consonant (*aj-jhal-ādeśa*), the doubling applies only to the element accompanied by the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Thus he says: *asisvadat*. [And] *bhāvayati*.

By the rules “*ahorlopo bhū ca bahoḥ*” and “*iṣṭhasya yiṭ ca*,” there is the substitution of *bhū*. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the augment *yiṭ* should also be replaced by *ṇi*, because the locative case in the word *ṇau* (in the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat*) indicates the object of comparison, and it is accepted that the suffix *vat* in the rule *iṣṭhavad* is applied to a word ending in the locative case. Thus...

It is established that when the *niṣṭhā* suffixes (*kta* and *ktavatu*) follow, only that operation which applies to the preceding element is extended [by atideśa], but not the operation belonging to the *niṣṭhā* itself. Thus, in the case of *bahayati*, others [hold] that in the absence of *yiṭ*, there is also the absence of the change to *bhū*, which was taught as being conditioned by that very [suffix].
If it is asked, "In that case, for what purpose has this been presented as the opinion of another school?"—here they say:

[The rule] *prādhānyadiṣṭhavad* is an extension (*atideśa*) of the grammatical operation (*kārya*), but it is not an extension of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) of the treatise (*śāstra*). Thus, since that very extension prescribes the substitution of *bhū* which is seen in the case of the suffix *iṣṭhan*, there is no [need for further discussion] here.
The application of the term *pi* [as a suffix] is taught as a remainder (*śeṣa*) by the *sann*-affix. Thus, the form *bhāvayati* is indeed correct.

As for *srajayati*: by virtue of the treatment as if it were an *iṣṭhan* suffix, there is elision (*luk*) according to the rule *vinmator luk*. [Objection: But surely, since it has been stated that "the suffixes beginning with *ṭha* [and *iṣṭhan*] apply only after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*)," the suffix *iṣṭhan* would be difficult to obtain from the word *sragvin*.

Thus, it should not be said that the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhan*) is improper here; for precisely because of this mention of elision (*luk*), it is accepted that *a*-beginning suffixes occur after words ending in *vini* and after those ending in *matup*.
[The form] *śrīmatīm* [is derived from *śrīmat* with] the elision of *matup*. [The forms] *śrāyayati* and *aśiśrayat* [are derived] when there is reduplication.

When a suffix beginning with *ṇ* follows, there is the substitution of *satya*. By this rule, the reading ‘aśiśrayat’ in the verse from Māgha—“He, wandering through the worlds, by chance took refuge as the abode of Fortune”—is explained;
for, according to the *Manoramā*, the meaning is that he “made [her] possessed of fortune” (*śrīmatīm akarot*).

[This is] established. On this point, some say: "Because there is no occurrence of a verbal activity (*vṛtti*) for those [words] that are dependent [on another], what was stated by Manoratha is incorrect. For no one, when intending to say 'bring that jar which he makes,' uses the expression 'bring that which he makes. Therefore, since it is already established by the rule *tat karoti* alone..."

The previously stated point—that the mention of "muṇḍa" and so forth is for the purpose of introducing the causative suffix (*ṇic*) even from transitive roots—is consistent [only] if the causative suffix were applied elsewhere as well from transitive roots; otherwise, that statement would not be consistent. Nor should it be disputed here that there is no transitivity, as in the verse: "the direction which he made illustrious... (yāṃ diśaṃ śrīmatīmakarot).

This is because it has already been explained by [the author] himself. Nor should it be argued that there is no inconsistency here on the grounds that even in the absence of a compound (*vṛtti*), a connection with the substantive (*viśeṣya*) would still occur for those [words] possessing qualifiers (*saviśeṣaṇa*), since "the quarters" (*diśaḥ*) are the substantives in relation to the sense of "possessing splendor" (*śrīmatīḥ*); for [only] when the substantive is external [to the compound]...

The occurrence of qualifiers [in a compound] is not accepted. For no one admits the formation "rājñaḥ śrīmatam" in the sense of "this belongs to the illustrious king. Furthermore, in the verse of Māgha, the reading "aśiśriyat" alone is seen in many manuscripts, and not...
They say that there is no need for such insistence on justifying the textual tradition with the phrase *tvaśiśrayat*.

Regarding the form *payasayati*: here, when there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *vin* or *mat*, neither the condition of being an *aglopa* (a stem lacking a vowel) nor the application of the *sanvat* rule occurs;
furthermore, even in cases where there is no elision (*anaglope*), the *sanvat* behavior does not apply. This is stated in the sūtra *ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ*.

In this regard, the Bhāṣya stating "he called [him] a king" (arājat) is the authority here. In the luṅ [aorist], it becomes *apipayat*. Likewise, in the case of *asasrajad* from *sragviṇam ākhyat*, there is no *sanvadbhāva*. From *gomantam*, one forms *gavayati*; in the luṅ, it becomes *ajugavat*. Here, because of the elision (*aglopa*), the lengthening prescribed by the rule "lengthening of a short vowel" (*dīrgho laghoḥ*) does not apply. [From *gām*...]
But in the analysis (*vigraha*) "srajam payaḥ," [the following forms] do not occur: *ajūgavat*, *asisrajat*, *payayati*, or *apapayat*.

Because the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its being a "foreign" (*bahiraṅga*) operation, there is no *vṛddhi* substitution here. Furthermore, because the root lacks a penultimate vowel (*aglopi*), the rules for *sanvadbhāva* and lengthening do not apply. This is by way of an exception (*apavāda*) to that [general rule]. By which...

By the principle of "non-attainment" (*aprāptinyāya*), *luk* (elision) is an exception to *ṭilopa*. Thus, in *sthavayati*, there is elision of the semivowel and following sounds (*yaṇādilopa*) as well as *guṇa* by the rule "thūladūraḥ"; nor should it be argued that *vṛddhi* would apply to the *guṇa* by the rule "aco ñṇiti," because once the operation on the *aṅga* has been performed [the rule no longer applies].

Furthermore, because the operation of the [augment] *aṅ* does not apply; or else, because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various cases) in the rule *prātipadikāddhātvarthe*. The *luṅ* [aorist] forms are: *itusthavat*, *davayati*, *yavayati*, and so forth. Here too, as before, there is an absence of *vṛddhi*. The *luṅ* forms are: *idūdavat*, *ayūyavat*, *acīkanat*.

Regarding *nedayati*: [the rule] “*antika-bāḍhyor nedas-ādhau*” applies; there is elision of the *ṭi* suffix. In the *luṅ* [aorist], it becomes *ininedat* and *asasādhat*. Regarding *praśasay*: it becomes *prāśaśasyat*. Regarding “for the sake of separation”: the meaning is that because the original base (*sthānin*) qualified by that [suffix] no longer exists, these two substitutes do not occur. Regarding *jyāpayati*: [this refers to] “of the *vṛddha*...”
The substitution of *jya* occurs; and this is optionally combined with the substitution of *varṣa*, as he says:
"he causes to rain" (*varṣayati*). In the *luṅ* [aorist]: *ijijyapat* (from *jyā*), *avavarṣat* (from *varṣ*);
*apiprapat* (from *prī*), *atisthapat* (from *sthira*). Because they are parts of the substitutes for *sasya*, there is no *ṣatva* [substitution].

Regarding *sphira*, it is derived from the root *apiṣ* with the prefix *ur*. Once the substitution of *vara* has been applied, Mādhava has illustrated that the vowel strengthening (*upadhāvṛddhi*) is optional—either because rules based on a specific technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) are not invariably valid, or due to the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*). He himself states the same: "it causes to choose" (*varayati*) and "it causes to ward off" (*vārayati*).

*avīvarat*. Because it is *aglopi* (having its penultimate vowel elided), [the form] from *baṃhayati* is *ababahat*. From *garayati*, [the form] is *ajīgarat*. From *trāyati*, [the form] is *atitrapat*. From *drāghayati*, [the form] is *adadrāghat*. From *vṛndayati*, [the form] is *avavṛndat*.
Thus ends the section on nominal roots (*nāmadhātu*) in the *Tattvabodhinī*. Now begins the section on causative formations (*ṇyantaprakriyā*).
(351) *tatprayojako hetuśca* | Pāṇini 1.4.55. "The instigator of that [action] is also called the *hetu* (agent/causal agent)."

"And the instigator of that [is also called] the cause (hetu). By the word "that" (tat), the agent (kartṛ) introduced in the preceding sūtra—"the independent one is the agent"—is referred to by the letter *ka*. The "instigator" (prayojaka) of that agent is the prompter; the meaning is:
one who possesses an activity conducive to the activity of that [agent]. The particle *ca* [indicates inclusion].
In order to set aside the application of the single designation [of *kartṛ*], he says: "it has the designation of *hetu* (cause) and the designation of *kartṛ* (agent).

The purpose of the designation *hetu* is seen in rules such as *hīsmyor hetubhaye* ("the suffix *ṇic* is added after the roots *hi* and *smi* when there is fear caused by the cause") and *hiyo hetubhaye ṣuk* ("the augment *ṣuk* is added to the root *hi* when there is fear caused by the cause"), where the instigator (*prayojaka*) is treated as a *hetu*. As for the designation *kartṛ*, however...
By the rule *‘aḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve ca’*, the *lakāra*s (tense markers) and so forth are employed when the instigator (*prayojaka*) is to be expressed.

(352) *Hetumati ca* | 3.1.26 | *hetumati ca*. [The suffixes are applied] when there is an instigator, by means of the relation of being located in [the action], which is defined by the substratumhood residing in itself.

That in which a cause exists is "possessing a cause" (*hetumān*), namely the operation (*vyāpāra*); regarding that which is to be expressed, he says "the causative suffix *ṇic*"—meaning "the operation of the instigator" (*prayojakavyāpāra*). And the instigator is intended here as common to both sentient and insentient beings. Furthermore, in some cases it takes the form of a result (*phala*), as established in examples such as "he causes Devadatta to go" (*devadattaṃ gamayati*).
In cases such as “The king causes [him] to dwell” (*rājā vāsayati*) or “The village causes [him] to dwell” (*grāmo vāsayati*), however, it takes the form of a result.
Regarding “in commanding and so forth”: the instigation of a subordinate, such as a servant, is *preraṇā* (incitement); the meaning is *ājñā* (command).
By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), entreaty, consent, and others are included. Of one who is equal or superior...
The instigation of the officiating priest, the teacher, and so forth, is "requesting" (*adhyeṣaṇa*), which means entreaty.

"Consent" (*anumati*), on the other hand, is the approval of the king and others; since sacrificial and similar rites are not accomplished without it, the king and others are the instigators by mere consent alone.

In the phrase "permission and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes instruction and assistance. For example, a physician and others become instigators merely by giving the instruction, "Drink the decoction. Furthermore, one who restrains a person fleeing while being sought to be killed by someone else is also [an instigator].

The instigator (*prayojaka*) is so called by virtue of being a benefactor (*anugrāhaka*). If it is asked how all these specific distinctions are understood through the suffix *ṇic*, they say in response: the meaning of *ṇic* is the general property of incitement (*pravartanā-sāmānya*) common to all of them, whereas the specific instances are understood from context, purpose, and other factors. But if this is so, [what of] *ṇic*?

If it were argued that the imperative (*loṭ*) and other such suffixes would become synonyms, and consequently, when one ought to say "May you ask now," the causative suffix (*ṇic*) would be used as in "he causes [him] to ask" (*pṛcchayati*), we say: not so. For the *hetu* (mover) is indeed the instigator of the agent; however, the person addressed—such as Devadatta—who is the object of the command, is [the agent].

The person who asks the question is not determined [by the suffix] as being the instigator (*praśnakartṛ*). Furthermore, the distinction between the two is as follows: the activity residing in the instigator (*prayojaka*) which is conditioned by the activity of the one to be instigated (*prayojya*) is the meaning of the causative suffix *ṇic*; whereas the activity of the instigator unconditioned by that [activity of the one to be instigated] is the meaning of the imperative suffix *loṭ*. And it has been said: "But in the case of the command (*praiṣa*) regarding a mere substance..."

"The imperative (loṭ) is prescribed after [roots such as] *pṛccha* (to ask) and others; however, when there is the employment of an agent who possesses an action, that is the domain of the causative (*ṇic*). This is the meaning: the imperative occurs in the sense of commanding (*praiṣa*) someone like Devadatta, whose agency has not yet been determined, as in "Go" (*arcccha*), "Desire to know" (*jñīpsā*), "Eat" (*aṭa*), and so forth.

The instigation (*prayukti*) of that which is the substratum of the activity conditioned by the activity of the one to be prompted (*prayojya*) is the domain of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) when it occurs. Furthermore, the meaning of the imperative mood (*loṭ*) is instigation residing in the prompter (*prayoktṛ*), whereas the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is instigation whose agent is the prompter of the prompter (*prayoktraprayoktṛ*). For in the example "He causes Devadatta to eat," it is the speaker himself who [is the prompter].

The *preraka* (the instigator) is one other than the speaker in cases such as *ācayati*, but it is the speaker himself in cases such as *ācayāmi*; this is the general direction [of the analysis]. (353) *oḥ puyaṇjyapare* | Pāṇini 7.4.80.
*oḥ puyaṇji*: the term *puyaṇji* is the singular locative case of a collective *dvandva* compound.

*Ṭhapare* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. From the rule "atra lopo ’bhyāsasya" (*Pāṇini 7.4.58*), the word *abhyāsasya* ("of the reduplicated syllable") is understood to carry over. [The rule] continues from "hṛñāmī" (*Pāṇini 7.2.31*).

The mention of *it* [refers] from the word "anyataḥ" and also from "sani"; however, "of the aṅga" (*aṅgasya*) is indeed still governing the context. Intending this, he says: "the aṅga which stands before the suffix *san*, etc. What is the purpose of [specifying] "after a labial (*pavarga*), *yaṇ*, or *j*"? [Consider the example: *bubhūṣati*. Why [specify] "labial, *yaṇ*, or *j*" (*pavargayaṇjīti*)? [Consider the example: *ūrṇunaviṣati*. [And consider the examples: *abībhavat*, etc.
‘*hū* in the sense of existence (*satāyām*); *ūṅ* in the sense of purifying (*pavane*); *mṛṅ* in the sense of binding (*bandhane*); *ṭhyu* in the sense of mixing and so forth (*miśraṇādau*);

*ru* in the sense of sound (*śabde*); *ūñ* in the sense of cutting (*chedane*); *u* in the sense of motion (*gatau*). This is a root from the *sūtra*-tradition (*sautra*), mentioned in the rule *ucaṅkramye*. Now, after reduplication (*dvitva*) as *bhū-bhū*, [the following applies]...’

If it is argued that, because the *vṛddhi* and *āv* substitutions have occurred, and then by the rule "kṛtasya ṭhṇau caṅi" (Pāṇini 7.4.1), the short vowel [of the reduplicated syllable] is treated as *sthānivadbhūta*, there is an absence of a light vowel following it; consequently, since the condition for *sanvadbhāva* does not apply, the substitution of *it* for the vowel of the reduplicated syllable in forms such as *abībhavat* would be difficult to obtain—on this point they say: by the very force of the initial formulation [of the rule], there is no *sthānivadbhāva*.

(354) *sravati-śṛṇoti-dravati-pravati-plavati-cyavati-nām vā* || Pāṇini 6.1.78. The rule *sravati-śṛṇoti* [is explained as follows]: the phrase *apare* (followed by a letter other than *p*, *u*, *ṇ*, *j*) is understood here, but not the phrase *puyaṇji* (because the letters of the *p*-class and *j* are impossible in this context). Even though semi-vowels (*yaṇ*) are possible, they are mentioned because they are never absent; thus he says: [The suffix *iṭ* is optionally applied after the roots *sravati*, *śṛṇoti*, *dravati*, *pravati*, *plavati*, and *cyavati* when followed by a suffix beginning with a letter other than *p*, *u*, *ṇ*, or *j*. For example: *susrāva/susruvatuḥ/susruvuḥ*; *śuśrāva/śuśruvatuḥ/śuśruvuḥ*; *dudrāva/dudruvatuḥ/dudruvuḥ*; *paprau/pupravatuḥ/pupruvuḥ*; *puplāva/pupluvatuḥ/pupluvuḥ*; *cucyāva/cucyuvatuḥ/cucyavuḥ*. In the case of *śṛṇoti*, since the root ends in *ṝ*, the substitution of *guṇa* (*ar*) occurs first, resulting in *śṛṇoti*. Then, because the condition for *iṭ* is met, the optional *iṭ* is applied, yielding forms such as *śuśrāva* or *śuśrotha*. In the case of *dravati*, the *guṇa* substitution (*ar*) applies, and the optional *iṭ* is added, resulting in *dudrāva* or *dudrotha*. For *plavati* and *cyavati*, the same process applies. However, for *pravati*, although it is listed among these roots, the optional *iṭ* does not apply because the subsequent rule *na śasadadavādiguṇānām* (Pāṇini 7.2.6) prohibits *iṭ* after roots that undergo *guṇa* substitution, such as *pra* (which becomes *par*). Thus, the form is *paprau* (with *guṇa* substitution of *pra* to *par*). Therefore, the rule is stated: "The suffix *iṭ* is optionally applied after the roots *sravati*, *śṛṇoti*, *dravati*, *pravati*, *plavati*, and *cyavati* when followed by a suffix beginning with a letter other than *p*, *u*, *ṇ*, or *j*. (Note: The mention of *pravati* here is subject to the restriction of Pāṇini 7.2.6, which prevents *iṭ* from being added after roots that undergo *guṇa*. Thus, the final forms are: *susrāva/susruvatuḥ/susruvuḥ*; *śuśrāva/śuśruvatuḥ/śuśruvuḥ*; *dudrāva/dudruvatuḥ/dudruvuḥ*; *paprau/pupravatuḥ/pupruvuḥ*; *puplāva/pupluvatuḥ/pupluvuḥ*; *cucyāva/cucyuvatuḥ/cucyavuḥ*. (Note: The commentary clarifies that the rule *puyaṇji* is not applicable here due to the impossibility of the *p*-class and *j* sounds, and even if *yaṇ* were possible, its inclusion is necessary to ensure the rule's applicability across all relevant cases. They say that this is easily construed with reference to the first *ṇic* alone, meaning "the agent of the one being impelled," which is to say, "the agent who impels. [The rule] "after a root ending in *ṇic*, before another *ṇic*" [is applied as follows]:
the king is amazed (*vismayate*); a human voice causes him to be amazed (*vismāpayate*); by that [voice], the lion...

The meaning is "causing amazement. And thus, since the first *ṇic* suffix denotes causation (*hetu*), the forms *manuṣyavāk* [as the cause] and the subsequent *ātva* and *puk* augmentations are justified by the rule: (371) *krīṅjīnāṃ ṇau* (Pāṇini 6.1.48).
Regarding the roots *krīñ*, *ji*, and *hiṅ*: [the roots] *ukrīñ* (in the sense of "exchanging goods"), *hiṅ* (in the sense of "studying"), and *i* (in the sense of "victory"). [Examples:

*acikrapat* and *adhyajīgapat*. Here, one should not suspect either the application of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* or a prohibition regarding the reduplication of *gāṅ*, which is caused by the suffix *ṇic*.

Since it has been stated that the status of being *sthānivat* (as the original) or the prohibition [of such status] applies only where the first vowel (*avarṇa*) exists in the subsequent portion of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), whereas here, because *gāṅ* precedes,

when there is reduplication according to the rule "the second member beginning with a consonant" (*ajāder dvitīyasya*), the reduplication would belong to the *ṇic* itself; and consequently, the *ṇic* would be conditioned by a following *ṇi*.
