The form [of the root] *vyeñ* in the sense of "to expand" (*vyāyayati*) is identical [to that of *vyai*], because the rule for *yuk* is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *puṅ* augment in the case of "to cover" (*ācchāse*). Nevertheless, there is a distinction in the absence of *ātvam*: from the causative (*ṇijanta*) stem, the forms are *vyāḥ*, *vyau*, and *vyāḥ*; whereas in the alternative case where *ātvam* does not occur, they are *vyaiḥ*, *vyāyau*, and *vyāyaḥ*.

By virtue of the rule-formulating power (*vidhāna-sāmarthya*) of the *Vibhāṣā*, the rule "ṭhādeca upadeśe ’śitī" does not apply even in the alternative (*pakṣe*). Furthermore, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the meaning "to expend" (*vyaya*) is also applicable to the root *vyayi*. (374) *doṣo ṇau* 6.4.90.

The substitution of *doṣ* occurs before the causal suffix *ṇic*. The root *duṣ* meaning "to become corrupted" belongs to the *divādi* class. Why specify "before *ṇic*"? [Because] *doṣaḥ* [is formed otherwise].

(375) *vā citavirāge* 6.4.91. Regarding *cita*: it is derived from the root *cit* (meaning "to perceive") with the suffix *kta*. Thus, one says *dūṣayati* or *doṣayati* [in the sense of "he causes to lose its color"].

It vitiates the mind; it causes one to become disinterested in bathing, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), and so forth. The meaning is that it impels one toward those [actions]. Regarding the word *jṛṇāteḥ*: the intention is that because this root has the augment *apit*, it does not take the designation *mit*. Regarding *ākheṭakam*:

it should be stated that when the suffix *ṇic* is added to the root *rañj* in the sense of "sporting with deer," there is the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*). As for *rajayati*: the deer take pleasure (*rajanti*).

The meaning is that he makes those deer objects of such activities as seizing, killing, and so forth, which are conducive to [those ends]. Regarding the rule "jñapādiciñ," the intention is that because of the designation *mit*, there is shortening [of the vowel]. However, he provides an example to show that the designation *mit* does not apply to roots belonging to the *svādi* group.

Regarding "cāpayati" and so forth: as for "apusphurat," when the doubling (dvitva) is to be applied, because the substitute [for the root vowel] is treated as the original (sthānivadbhāva), or because of the prohibition, the doubling applies to the syllable containing the vowel *u*—namely, *'sphur'*; subsequently, by the rule "isphuror ṇau," the substitution of *ā* may optionally take place.

(376) *ubhau sābhyāsasya* | 8|4|21|. Regarding *ubhau sā*: in the rule *ṭhraṣābhyāṃ ṭo naḥ*, the word *aḥ*—which is in the genitive case with the dual ending—is transformed into a nominative dual form; thus he says, "both *n*s. Now, [an objection]:...

If it is argued that the mention of both (*ubhau*) is redundant because by saying "it shall occur for both" (*ābhyāsye*), it will apply to both anyway, they say here: if one were to accept that only their coexistence (*sāhityamātra*) is intended and not an equal application (*tulyayoga*), then the formation would not be established simultaneously for both; therefore, the mention of both is necessary. Furthermore, even when an equal application is intended...

One should not suspect that the compound *saheti tulyoge* would not apply here; for it has been stated that "the mention of 'tulyoga' (equal connection) is merely illustrative, as in the examples *sakarmakaḥ* and *salomakaḥ*. However, in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, it is said: "If the word *ubhau* were not present [in the rule], then [the substitution of] *ṇ* for the *n* of *aniti* along with its reduplication..."

If it were stated that "it occurs," then by the force of that statement— and provided that the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham advirvacane* ("that which is not established in what precedes a reduplication") is not resorted to— once the doubling has taken place for the form where the *ṇatva* has already been applied, the *ṇatva* would be established by the preceding rule alone (*anantarasyāniter iti*).
Consequently, this present rule for *ṇatva* would apply only for the sake of the *nakāra* that is separated [by the reduplication].
"But by the logic of the case of Takra-Kauṇḍinya, it would not apply to the immediately preceding [element]; therefore, it is stated that 'both' [are meant].

This is the established position. What is the purpose of the phrase "of that which is accompanied by repetition" (sābhyāsasya)? [Consider: *prāṇ namati*. If this [phrase] were absent, the genitive in *ṭhaniteḥ* would denote a general relationship (*saṃbandhasāmānye*).

It might be so; and in that case, even a relationship such as immediate succession (*ānantarya*) would be apprehended. However, when this [relationship of] part and whole (*avayava-avayavibhāva*) exists, it is obtained.
Therefore, the mention of "repetition" (*sābhyāsa*) is purposeful. But if, in accordance with what is desired, [the rule were applied] by [interpreting] *aniteḥ*...

Regarding the sixth case-form *ṣaṣṭhījanam*: here, having first applied the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) and then performed reduplication (*dvitva*), the forms such as *prāṇiṇat* are established; however, this present rule is commenced for the purpose of making known the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the principle "that which is not established [in the formation of a subsequent element] is as if it were non-existent with respect to reduplication" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīyam advirvacane*). By means of that [non-universality],...

In the case of *ūrṇunāva*, because the doubling of the word *nu* occurs precisely before the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, the absence of *ṇatva* in the subsequent portion of the reduplicated stem is established.
(377) Pāṇini 6.1.46: *ṇau gamir abodhane* ("The root *gam* is substituted [for *iṇ*] before an affix marked with *ṇ*, except when it means 'informing'").

Regarding the term *pratyāyayati*: the root *iṇ* preceded by *prati* has the meaning of "cognition. In the aorist (*luṅ*), the form is *pratyāyiyat*. Here, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to *iṇ*, the rule for *vṛddhi* (Pāṇini 7.2.115) applies because it is subsequent, thereby overriding the substitution of *yaṇ* (Pāṇini 6.1.78). Nor can it be argued that doubling occurs first and *vṛddhi* afterwards on the basis of the *jñāpaka* rule *ṭhoḥ puyaṇjī* (Pāṇini 7.4.80); rather, *vṛddhi* takes precedence.

It might be suspected [that this is not the case], because when there is reduplication of the *ṇic* suffix by the rule "the second [element] beginning with a *ṭh*-consonant," the subsequent portion following the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) lacks a vowel (*avarṇa*) as its following element. Thus, the meaning is "or.
The intention is that both of these two explanations are established in the original source (*ākara*).

It should be stated that [the rule applies] to the third [consonant] of the root *īrṣya*. [The question arises: "Of which [consonant]? [The answer is: "Of the letter *ṣ*"; for as for the letter *r*, its doubling is prohibited by the rule *na ndrāḥ*. As for the phrase "but in the second case," this refers to the alternative view that [the rule applies] to the third [consonant] of a monosyllabic root (*ekāc*). The reason it applies in the context of the causative suffix (*sannanta*) is due to the force of the specific statement [in the sūtra]; such is the intention.

Regarding the form *airṣyiyat*: this is an example under the alternative view that [the rule applies] when there is a consonant following the root vowel (*ṛtīyavyañjanasya*). He establishes that the form *airṣiṣyat* is incorrect by means of the phrase beginning with "in the second explanation" (*dvitīyavyākhyāyām*), etc. The phrase "of the second one alone" (*dvitīyasyaiva*) has "that which consists of a single vowel" (*ekāc*) as its understood remainder.

Regarding the phrase "because of non-occurrence": rather, it occurs only with the suffix *san*. For he will cite "īrṣyiyiṣati" as an example immediately following that. Since the rule "artha upayācñāyām" belongs to the section beginning with "ā-garva," it ought to take the ātmanepada; thus [the form] is "arthayante."
Anticipating the objection that the usage found in the *Māghakāvya* and similar works is incorrect, he states the following to justify it:
"Because the causal (*ṇic*) is used when the original sense of the root has ceased" (*nivṛtapreṣaṇāt*). And it has been said:
"The causal suffix (*ṇic*) is prescribed for a root when its primary meaning has ceased. Regarding the phrase "by that," etc., it refers to the intended meaning: "they perform the request."
The meaning is that the application [of the rule] is established. Some, however, explain it as follows:

"prārtha" means "requesting" (from *prārthana*), and they say that those who perform this are "prārthayanti"; but that is incorrect, because when a suffix that triggers the designation of a verbal root (*dhātu-saṃjñā*) is intended to be applied, there must be a separation of the prefixes.
Because the augment *āPuk* would be unavoidable in the case of "artha-veda" due to its being taught [later] as a forthcoming rule;
thus ends the section on the derivation of causative (*ṇic*) forms.
(1370) The suffix *khañ* is used after the word *dhānya* when it denotes a field for growing grain.

[Pāṇini 5.2.1] Regarding *dhānyānām*: from the root *dhivi* in the sense of "to satisfy," the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the agent by the rule *ṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. From this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is the elision of the final vowel and the substitution of *ā* for the vowel *i*.

It is called *dhānya* because it nourishes (*dhinoti*). Furthermore, a mantra is seen stating: "You are to be nourished; nourish the gods. In the expression "*hānyānām*," the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) with respect to the act of being (*bhavana*).

And that [genitive] is itself the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*) by virtue of its very mention. The plural number, however, is for the purpose of excluding the prescription of the word's own form (*svarūpavidhi*).

However, it should be understood that in the extraordinary (alaukika) procedural sentence, this is due to the very power of the injunction itself, following the restatement of the word ending in the genitive case. Here, the verb *bhavati* signifies "origination" (*utpatti*), because of the force of the mention of the "field" (*kṣetra*). For in the Sūtra, there is indeed the inclusion of the verb *bhavati* even when it has the sense of "existing" (*sat*).

The term "field" (kṣetra) is employed so that [the suffix] may not apply [elsewhere]. Otherwise, it would also apply in a case such as *dhānyānāṃ bhavanaṃ kusūlaḥ* ("a granary is the place for grains"). Why "of grains"? [Consider: *tṛṇānāṃ bhavanaṃ kṣetram* ("a field is the place for grasses").
(1371) *vrīhi-śālyor ḍhak* [Pāṇini 5.2.2]. Regarding *vrīhi-śālyoḥ*: here too, by the very fact of its mention, the genitive case is the governing case (*samartha-vibhakti*).
And that [genitive] is, with respect to the act of being (*bhavana*), the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, as explained previously.

(1372) *yava-yavaka-ṣaṣṭikādya-t* 5.2.3. [The suffix] *yat* is applied after *yava*, *yavaka*, *ṣaṣṭika*, and so forth. Here, the genitive case as the governing inflection (*samartha-vibhakti*) is understood by virtue of the requirement of the meaning of the suffix. This rule is stated because it is an optional provision (*vibhāṣā*) where a compulsory rule (*nitya*) would otherwise apply. Examples: *āumīnam*, *bhāhgīnam*.

If it is argued: "Since *umā* and *bhaṅgā* are not included among the grains (*dhānya*), how can the suffix *khañ* be applied here? For in the *Canakānuvāka*, exactly twelve grains are enumerated, and *umā* and *bhaṅgā* are not mentioned," do not say so. [For it is said: "The seventeen [grains] beginning with *aṇu*..."

This is because of the traditional recollection that "grains" (dhānyāni) are so called; and since it is established in the Bhāṣya and other works that grain-status exists for both types of *cama* due to their being listed therein. Nor is there any purpose in enumerating grains within the *camaka-anuvāka*, since even non-grains such as stones and the like are mentioned there.

Since some grains, such as *kodrava* and others, are not mentioned [in the list], the determination of what constitutes a grain (*dhānya*) must come from another source; therefore, it should be understood from the previously cited Smṛti that those two possess the status of being grains (*dhānyatva*).
(1373) *sarvacarmaṇaḥ kṛtaḥ khakhañau* || 5.2.5 || [The suffixes *kha* and *khañ* are applied after the word *sarvacarman* when the sense is "made of all leather"].

[The suffix *khañ* is applied] after the word *sarvacarman*. It was not simply stated as "after [a word ending in] *ha*," because one might otherwise suspect an attraction (anukarṣa) from a previous rule. Here, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*), because it is appropriate for the leather (*carman*) to function as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the sense of the suffix *kṛta*. Thus, *sarvaścarmaṇā* means "made by means of the entire hide."
The sense is that a *taddhita* suffix is not desired in this meaning.

(1374) *Yathāmukhasammukhasya darśanaḥ khaḥ* |5|2|6|. [The suffix] *kha* is applied after *yathāmukha* and *sammukha* when the sense is "that in which something is seen. *Yathāmukha-darśanaḥ* refers to a mirror or the like; [here] *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Since there is a prohibition [of compounding] by the rule "ṭhasādṛśye" (Pāṇini 2.1.7), how can the word *yathā* form a compound when it signifies similarity (*sādṛśya*)? To this, he replies: "By way of an irregularity (*nipātana*). This has been stated following the text of the Vṛtti. However, in the Bhaṭṭikāvya, the word *yathā* is taken to mean "not exceeding the nature of the thing" (*padārthānativṛti*). And so:

Regarding the illusory deer, it was said: "He leaped about, greatly enticing Sītā, appearing right before her eyes" (*yathāmukhīnaḥ sītāyāḥ pupluve bahu lobhayan*). The term *yathāmukham* means "a sight facing [her]. Since the indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) *yathāmukha*—like *inamata-gaṅgā* and other such forms—is a word denoting a substance (*satvavacana*), when it is joined with the power of the object (*karma-śakti*), [the suffix -īna is applied].

The genitive case [ending] is characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix. For that [genitive], there is the substitution of *am* by the rule "āvyayībhāvāt. [The form] is "sarvasya mukhasya" (of the face of all).

It is not stated as "am-mukhasya," because the elision of the final syllable of the word *sama* is prescribed specifically in conjunction with the addition of the suffix. Furthermore, the word *sam-* here does not have the meaning of the word *sama*.

It is observed that in the expression "be facing him" (*abhimukho bhava*), the meaning "facing" (*abhimukha*) is understood; however, in that case, the suffix *kha* is not intended [by the rule]. How then is it that Bhaṭṭi says: "Who could withstand him, who was facing [the enemy] in battle, as he advanced"?
Haradatta [says] that because it stands in front [of the object], by virtue of its capacity, it will [be understood as] "will come to be.

(1375) *tatsarvādeḥ pathyaṅgakarmapatrapātraṃ vyāpnoti* | 5|2|7|. *tatsarvādeḥ*: the word *at* is the case-ending of the second case (*dvitīyā*), which serves as the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*). *Vyāpnoti* means "it pervades."

The meaning [of the suffix] is "condition" (*pratyaya*). The remainder is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*). Since it is impossible for the simple words *pathin* and so forth to be members of the *sarva-ādi* group, the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies even when they are nominal stems (*prātipadika*).
Thus he says: "ending in *pathin* and so forth."
The meaning is: from a nominal stem (prātipadika) ending in *pathin*, *aṅga*, *karman*, *patra*, or *pātra*. Regarding the form *sarvapathīni*:
it is a compound formed by the rule “*ūrvakālaika-*” [Pāṇini 2.1.49]. The suffix *ṭac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule “*ṛkpū-*” [Pāṇini 5.4.74].
Since that [compound] is included by the mention of compounds ending in *pathin*, the suffix *kha* occurs.

(1376) *anupada-sarvānna-āyānayaṃ baddhā-bhakṣayati-neyeṣu* || 5.2.9 || Regarding *anupada-sarvānna-āyānayaṃ*: in the rule for the formation of *baddhābhakṣayati*, there is a *dvandva* compound with an indeclinable (*atiṅanta*) by means of a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). From the words *anupada* and others ending in the second case, [the suffix *ṭhak*] is applied respectively in the senses of "bound" and so forth.

It may be [an indeclinable]. Regarding "anurāyaṃ" and so forth: the meaning is that it is either an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule "yasya cāyāmaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.16), or by the rule "avyayam" (Pāṇini 2.1.6) in the sense of "as it is. Regarding "sarvānnīnaḥ":
the word *sarva* is used here in the sense of "entirety of kind. It refers to whatever foods are obtained, whether hot or cold.
The meaning is that he eats all [the pieces] while they are still fresh (sarasāni). *Aya* means moving clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*).

*Anaya* means moving counter-clockwise (*prasavya*). According to the *Kāśikā*: "That [move] in which the *śāra* pieces moving clockwise and counter-clockwise cannot be occupied by others is called *ayāna*"; one should lead him to that.

Because the root *nī* (to lead) governs two objects (*dvikarmaka*), the second case ending is used for the non-primary object. Regarding the term *āyānayīnaḥ śāraḥ*, the *Kāśikā* states: "The meaning is 'situated on the head of a cart'. (1377) *parovaraparamparaputrapautram anubhavati* | Pāṇini 5.2.10.

Regarding the word *avarasya*: the phrase "of the following" (*ādeḥ*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]. Once the substitution of *o* (*utvam*) has been applied, the *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *a* + *o*] occurs by the rule *ād guṇaḥ*. However, some say that there is another alternative view: that the substitution of *o* (*otvam*) is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity) for the word *para*; therefore, for the *at* (the vowel *a*) following it, the single-substitute *pūrvarūpa* is applied by the rule *eṅaḥ padāntād ati*.

(1378) *avārapārātyantānukāmam gāmī* || 5.2.11 || [The words] *avārapāra*, [and others]. Regarding *gāmī*: by the rule *amer iniḥ, āṅ iṇica* and because of the frequentative expression (*bahulavacanāt*), the suffix *ṇini* occurs even after the root alone. This is according to the rule *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ*.

[The suffix denotes] futurity. The author of the Nyāsa, however, says: "The suffix *ṇini* occurs after [the root] *ava-śya-* in the sense of necessity; that too [denotes] only the future. Regarding the expression *avāra-pāram*:
there is a prohibition of the genitive case by the rule "after [words ending in] *kṛt* and *un*, when [the compound expresses] futurity or a debt. Some, however...
They have explained that in the sūtra *arthakarmaṇī*, the mention of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is for the purpose of prescribing [the case] even in the domain of exceptions;
therefore, the genitive case associated with a *kṛt* suffix does not occur, as in the example *rāmaṃ gantā*.
That is incorrect, because when the prohibition by *ṭhakenoḥ* applies, there is no possibility of the genitive case occurring at all.
"Avārīṇa," and so forth. The intention is that [the suffix *kha*] is desired even after a word that is split or its opposite.
"Atyantam" (excessively) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). "Anukāmam" (according to desire): "kāma" means desire;
"anukāmam" is similar to that, meaning in accordance with desire (*kāmānurūpam*). [This is established by the rule] "avyayaṃ vibhakti... (Pāṇini 2.1.6).
The *avyayībhāva* compound is used in the sense of "according to the object" (*yathārthe*).
(Pāṇini 2.1.6) *samāṃsamāṃ vijāyate* (she gives birth every year).
(Pāṇini 5.2.12) Regarding *samāṃsamām*: the phrase "elision of *ya*" (*yalopa*) means that there is an elision of the letter *ya* in the word *amāyām*.

"It is an irregular form (nipāta) in the first member [of the compound]. The intention is that otherwise, once the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) has been produced, just as the elision of the case-ending (*sup*) occurs in the subsequent member by the rule "after an upasarga, a root, or a nominal stem" (*upa-dhātu-prātipadikayoḥ*), it would likewise occur in the first member. Regarding *samāṃsamīnā*: there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) due to distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
A collection of nominal stems (*subanta*) is the base (*prakṛti*). He explains the word *vijāyate* as "is produced" (*prasūyate*).
The point is that the root *jan*, preceded by the prefix *vi-*, functions in the sense of "the release of the womb.
Since there is no complete pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the entire duration of time in the case of the release of the womb, [the rule] *atyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 3.4.26) does not apply.

With the intention that the second [case-ending] does not occur, he says "in *samām*" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "on the non-occurrence of the suffix *khap*," the meaning is that by means of this *vārttika*, the Vedic usage *samāṃsamām* is justified; for otherwise, the suffix *khap* would have been applied. Thus, [the word] *adyaśvīnā* [is formed].

This is a gender-neutral designation and not a designation in the feminine gender, because it is desired even in cases such as "adyaśvīno gosamūhaḥ" (a herd of cows that will give birth today) and "adyaśvīnaṃ gomaṇḍalam" (a group of cows that will give birth today).
(1380) *Adyaśvīna* [is used] in the sense of "conceived today. 5.2.13.
The intention is that this is a compound used in the sense of "today or tomorrow," due to irregular grammatical formation (*nipātana*).

According to the rule *avāccālambane*, the suffix *ṣa* is prescribed after the root *stambh* when used in the sense of proximity (*āvidūrya*); thus, the word *avaṣṭabdha* refers to being near. For the word *vijāyate* is understood to be present [in the context]. That...
And [the suffix] has the sense of "delivering from the womb. Thus it says: "the meaning is 'one who is about to give birth.
(1381) *Āgavīnaḥ* | 5.2.14 | "In the sense of the agent of the action" (*karmakartari*). This refers to one who goes after having taken the cows in the morning.

"Gopāla" means "in that [place]" (tasmin). Regarding the phrase "until the return of the cow": the word *go* functions by way of indication (*lakṣaṇayā*) to mean "the giving back of the cow"—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the term *āgavīna*:
since it is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) formed according to the rule "āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ," the vowel is shortened by the rule "avo'striyām."
The suffix *kha* has been applied. By the rule *ṭhorguṇaḥ*, [the *u* of *anu-gu* becomes *o*].
(1382) *anugvalaṃgāmī* |5|2|15|. The word *anugu* is understood [from the previous rule]. After the word *anugu*, the suffix *kha* is applied in the sense of "one who goes along with" (*alaṃgāmī*).

It may be [used] as in "behind the cow" (*goḥ paścāt*). This is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "behind. Regarding the word "paryāptim" (sufficiency), it is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). On this point, Haradatta says:
"Because *anugu* is an adverbial modifier, the suffix occurs here after a word ending in the second case. And [this does not apply] to *alaṅgāmī*."

One might argue that because [the word] *upajāta* ends in the suffix *ṇini*, it would take a genitive case governed by its connection with a verbal action (*kṛdyoga*). However, he states that this is not the case, because such a rule does not apply to adverbs, as is observed in examples such as *śobhanaṃ pācakaḥ* ("one who cooks well"). In this regard, some maintain that [the locus of the result] consists in being the substratum of the result produced by the operation (*vyāpāra*) conveyed by the verbal root.
Where that [action] is primary, it is so; but where there is merely the state of being produced by an operation, it is figurative.
Consequently, in the expression "the cooker of rice" (*taṇḍulānāṃ pācakaḥ*), the genitive case characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix occurs in relation to the primary object.
However, in expressions such as "a soft cooker" (*ṛdu pācakaḥ*) or "a good cooker" (*obhanaṃ pācakaḥ*), it does not occur.

They say that his intention is as follows: although there is a conventional usage of the terms "action" (*kriyā*) and "object" (*karman*) with respect to the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*), the result is only figuratively an object, and clay and the like are qualifiers of that [result]. Others, however, [argue] that in that case, by the same logic...

They say that because of the mention of the accusative case for adverbial qualifiers (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), even the [application of] the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [prescribed] in connection with a *kṛt* suffix would not occur; therefore, based on the indication in the rule *adarham*, the sixth case in connection with a *kṛt* suffix is non-obligatory (*anityā*), and thus it is not accepted for adverbial qualifiers—such is the intention of Haradatta, which must be explained in some way. However, in reality:

There is no dispute that this is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "behind" (*paścāt*). Furthermore, the indeclinable *paścāt* is established in the sense of "westward" (*astam*), and although it is common to all three case endings, here, by the force of contextual fitness, it functions in the sense of the locative case. Therefore, of that—
Since it is impossible for [the word] to function as an object (*karman*), it is appropriate to state that the suffix occurs here after a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamā*).
For this very reason, one should understand that there is no possibility of suspecting the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix.
(1383) *abhyamitrāc cha ca* | Pāṇini 5.2.17.

*Abhyamitrāt*. The word *abhyamitra* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) formed according to the rule "the prefixes *ati*, *su*, *ut*, *pra*, *pari*, *upa*, *api*, *ava*, *adhi*, and *ni* [are compounded] with nouns ending in *a* when they denote direction" (Pāṇini 2.1.14), specifically in the sense of facing toward (*ābhimukhya*). Since it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), the second case (*dvitīyā*) is the governing case-ending (*samarthavibhakti*).

(1384) *goṣṭhāt khañ bhūtapūrve* |5|2|18|. The suffix *khañ* is added after *goṣṭha* [to form a word denoting] that which previously existed there. *Goṣṭhaḥ*: "that in which cows stand. The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of a locus according to the rule *hañarthe kavidhānam*. The substitution of *ṣ* for *t* occurs by the rule *ṭhambāmbogobhūmi*. Previously...
*bhūtaḥ* means "having existed previously. The compound is formed according to the rule *upapadāt supā*. (1385) *aśvasyaikāhagamaḥ* |5|2|19|.

[The word] *aśvasya* [is used]; this genitive case indicates the agent, which serves as the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*) by virtue of the very statement [of the rule]. [The term] *ekāhagamaḥ* [means] "one who can be reached in a single day."

The compound is formed according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā*. Now, one might object: here, instead of the suffix *ap* [prescribed by] *rahaṇavṛddhaniścigamaśca*, the suffix *ghañ* would apply by the rule *āyāmānākhyāyāṃ sarvebhyaḥ*;
for there is indeed a designation of measure (*parimāṇākhyā*) here, since a limitation is understood from the expression "it is traversed in one day."
On this point, they say: "It should be understood [as such] precisely because of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
(1386) *śālīna-kaupīne* [are used] in the senses of 'timid' and 'improper act,' respectively.
5.2.20. *śālīna-kaupīne*: these two are irregularly derived (*nipātyete*) by means of the suffix *kha*. These are conventional (*rūḍhi*) words.
The phrase "having somehow become proficient" should not be taken as requiring a strict adherence to the literal meaning of its components.
"Entering the hall" means that, due to a lack of confidence, one is unable to go elsewhere and thus deserves only to enter the hall. "Falling into a well" refers to that which is an improper act.

The meaning is that because it must be concealed, it deserves to be entered into like a well. "Its concealment" means a piece of cloth. Others, however, say: in the word *akārya* (that which should not be done), the root *kṛ* denotes action in general; therefore, by virtue of being a cause for shame and thus unfit to be seen, it refers to the male organ (*puruṣaliṅga*).
‘Aupīna’ refers to that which covers [the body] without touching it.
(1387) *vrātena jīvati* (Pāṇini 5.2.21). This means by means of physical exertion; the sense is by carrying loads and so forth. Although the word *vrāta* in common usage...

It is a word denoting a collection; nevertheless, the sense is that upon careful consideration of the relevant commentaries (*bhāṣya*) and other texts, this very meaning is appropriate here. (1388) *sāptapadīnaṃ sakhyam* | 5|2|22 | [Friendship is established by walking seven steps together.]

*Sāptapadīna* [is derived as follows]: he shows that, by virtue of its fitness, the governing case is the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*)—namely, "by seven steps" (*saptabhiḥ padaiḥ*). Here, *pada* means either conversation or the taking of a step; it is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), with the suffix *-khañ* added in the sense of "that which is obtained."

(1389) *haiyaṅgavīnaṃ saṃjñāyām* |5|2|23|. *Haiyaṅgavīnam*. [This is derived from] *hyogodohasya*. *Go-dohaḥ* means "the milking of a cow"; it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). With that [word], the word *hyas-* forms a compound according to the rule *upapadāt ktaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.72), which is subsumed under *upapada-samāsa*. Then...

The suffix *khañ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *añ*, which is characterized by an *anudātta* accent, when applied to a derivative form. Here, by the word *hyas*, the proximity of time is intended. Regarding the term *navanīta*: although it is stated as *hṛta* ("taken") in the *vṛtti*, Amara likewise says—"That which is *haiyaṅgavīna* is fresh butter (*navanīta*)."

Although it has been stated that "clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is produced from *hyegoha*," this [statement] was made in accordance with the text of Haradatta, who intends by the word *ghṛta* specifically that which is fresh.

(1390) Pāṇini 5.2.24: *tasya pākamūle pīlvādikarṇādibhyaḥ kuṇabjāhacau*. [The suffixes *kuṇap* and *jāhac* are applied after the words *pīlu* etc. and *karṇa* etc., respectively, in the sense of "its cooking" and "its root"].

*Pāka-pākaḥ* means transformation (*pariṇāma*). *Mūlam* means the beginning (*upakrama*). This rule is formulated because the suffixes *aṇ* and others would otherwise apply according to the sense "this belongs to that" (*asyedam*). Since there is no purpose for the letter *j* in *jāhaca*, it does not undergo the substitution of *it*.
[The examples are: *pīlu*, *karkandhu*, *śamī*, *karīra*, *kuvala*, *badara*, [and *aśvattha*].

*Thadirapīlvādiḥ* refers to the *thadirapīlu* group. *Karṇādiḥ* refers to the group beginning with ear (*karṇa*), eye (*akṣi*), nail (*nakha*), mouth (*mukha*), hair (*keśa*), foot (*pāda*), ankle (*gulpha*), eyebrow (*bhrū*), horn (*śṛṅga*), tooth (*danta*), lip (*oṣṭha*), and back (*pṛṣṭha*). The phrase "merely the mention of the root" is used because the intention is that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is declared to be circumflex (*svarita*).
(1391) *pakṣatiḥ* |5|2|25|. The word *pakṣati* [is formed with the suffix *ti*]. It is like *prati*; it means "the root of the wings" (*pakṣamūla*) of birds (*pakṣiṇām*).
(1392) *tena vittaścuñcupcaṇapau* |5|2|26|. [The suffixes] *cuñcup* and *caṇap* are applied after a word ending in the third case (*tena*) when it signifies "renowned for that."

By that [rule], *vitaḥ* is formed; *vitaḥ* means "disappointed. Because of the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*) stating "after a root ending in *vit*, there is the suffix *a* indicating enjoyment," the substitution of *na* for the final letter of the *niṣṭhā* (past participle) suffix—as prescribed by the rule "the final letter of the *niṣṭhā* is replaced by *na* after roots ending in *ad* or *ābhya*"—does not occur. Regarding the expression "indicated as elided" (*luptanirdiṣṭa*): although one could have simply stated "the augment *uṭ* belongs to the suffix," the fact that a separate rule was formulated indicates that the inclusion of the augment *uṭ* is not mandatory (*anitya*).
They state another solution as well:

(1393) *vinañbhyāṃ nānāñau nasaha* 5.2.27. Regarding the mention of *nānāñau*: the *ñ* in *nāñ* is for the purpose of [triggering] *vṛddhi* and for the purpose of the accent (*svara*). The phrase “*na saha*” [is used].
With the intention that this is a qualification of the base (*prakṛti*) and not the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), he says: "the meaning of non-accompaniment," and so forth.

If it were the meaning of the suffix, then according to the principle that "two negations regarding a prefix convey the original sense," the meaning of accompaniment would be understood; thus, instead of "not together" (*a-saha*), it would mean "indeed together" (*na saha api tu saha eva*).

Therefore, it is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*). And this is obtained from the commentary. If this is so, let "together" (*saha*) alone be the meaning of the suffix, since the desired result is established because *vi-* and *nañ* have the sense of negation;
for even in cases such as *vigārdabharathakaḥ*, the word *vi-* is indeed observed to function as a negation.

True. One might understand that the suffix [vini] occurs after the word *vi* when it expresses an action, in the sense of "together with" (*sahārthe*)—that is, "together with what has departed" (*vigatena saha*) or "together with what has been modified" (*vikṛtena saha*). However, the previously stated view alone is correct. This is clear in the commentary of Haradatta. As for the phrase "in its own sense" (*svārthe*), [it means the following].
The meaning is that [the suffix] has not been specified as having a specific sense. (1394) *saṃprodaśca kaṭac* (Pāṇini 5.2.29).
[The rule begins with] *saṃprodaśca*. This suffix is added in its own sense (*svārthe*) after words denoting an instrument (*sādhana*) qualified by an action (*kriyā*).

*Saṅkaṭa* means crowded; that is, the sense of "constricted. *Prakaṭa* means made known; that is, the sense of "manifested. *Utkaṭa* means arisen or prominent. *Vikaṭa* means deformed. These are established words (*rūḍha-śabda*) which are somehow etymologically derived.
An addition [to the rule] is made regarding *rajas* (dust/fiber) after *alābū*, *tila*, *umā*, and *bhaṅgā*. Thus, *alābūkaṭam*.

After these five, when *rajas* is to be expressed, the suffix *kaṭac* occurs. Since *rajas* is a modification (*vikāra*), this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes used for modifications. Thus, *alābūkaṭam*.

In the case of *ṭhorañ* and *mayaḍvaitayoḥ*, *mayaṭ* would have been applicable here. In *tilakaṭam*, *mayaṭ* would have been applicable by the rule *tilayavābhyām* when [the suffix] has the technical designation *ṭha*.
From the word *umā*, because it is *anta-udātta* due to belonging to the *hṛtādi* group, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *anudātādeśca*.

In the case of *ṭhumorṇayoḥ*, the suffix *vuñ* is applicable; and from the word *bhaṅgā*, since it has an initial udātta accent according to the rule "of debts and grains, [the first syllable]," the suffix *mayaṭ* is applicable. Thus, the application of suffixes should be inferred according to what is possible. Haradatta, however, [speaks of] the word *tila*.

Having accepted that [the word *tila*] is oxytone by virtue of belonging to the *ghṛtādi* group, [the author] states that from that [base], either the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule "from what begins with an udātta vowel, *ṭhan*"—provided that *ṭha* is the technical designation—or else *mayaṭ* is obtained by the rule "after *tila* and *yava*. In this regard, the reason for assuming that the word *tila* belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group should be considered. [Also, there is the rule: "And of debts and grains..."

Because, according to the *Phiṭ-sūtra* rule "vdyāṣāḥ," it is only logical that the first syllable be acute; and because in the Veda, in the passage "tilāś ca me," the reading is likewise [with the acute on the first].

Regarding the words beginning with *goṣṭhaja*, they are derived from names of animals in the sense of their place of origin (*sthāna*) and so forth. As for the phrase "beginning with *goṣṭhaja*": [it refers to] the compound *aṅghāte*.
*kaṭa’ji* and so forth are elaborations (*prapañca*) of this very [rule]. Here, in both instances, the word *ādi* (and so forth) denotes a class or type (*prakāra*).

Regarding the phrase “from the names of animals” (*paśunāmabhyaḥ*), the reading *‘aśunāmādibhyaḥ’* is more common in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the example “the place of cows” (*gavāṃ sthānam*), the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of “belonging to this” (*asyedam*) by the rule: “In all cases, when *go* follows, provided it is not preceded by a vowel-initial [word]” (*arvatra gorajādiprasaṅge*).

The suffix *kaṭac* is applied after the word *goṣṭha* when it means "a collection" (*saṅghāta*). Regarding the term "collection": a collection is an aggregate whose constituent parts are not spread out;
however, that whose parts are spread out is an "extension" (*vistāra*). Both *kaṭac* and *paṭac* [function in this way].
There are two exceptions to the collective [suffixes].

*Goyuga* is used when there is duality. Regarding "when there is duality": the meaning is that it is used when the duality of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is to be indicated. *Uṣṭragoyugam* means "a pair of camel and cow. It denotes a pair.
The singular number [in the rule] is used because of the predominance of the aggregate of two parts, as in the case of the word *yugma* and others; the same applies hereafter.

(1395) Pāṇini 5.2.31: *nate nāsikāyāḥ saṃjñāyāṃ ṭīṭañ-nāṭaj-bhraṭacaḥ*. [When a word denoting a name is formed from the root √nam with the prefix ā- in reference to the nose, the suffixes ṭīṭan, nāṭac, and bhraṭac are applied.]
Regarding the word *natam*: the suffix *kta* is used here in the neuter gender with an abstract sense (*bhāve*), thus meaning "bending" (*namanam*). Its meaning is "being low" (*nīcaistvam*).

Regarding *avaṭīṭam*: this is a suffix added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) to the word *ava*, which refers to bending performed by means of the nose. How then is the word *avaṭīṭa* applied to both the nose and a person?

Therefore, he says: "Because of connection with that" (*tadyogāt*). [The suffix] *biḍac* [is added]. The phrase "after the word *nāsikā*, when a name is to be formed" (*nāsikāyāḥ saṃjñāyām*) is understood to carry over. After the word *ni*, when "bent" (*natā*) is to be expressed regarding the nose, the suffixes *biḍac* and *birīsac* occur. Thus, *nibiḍam*. Because of connection with that, the nose is "close-set" (*nibiḍā*).
"Nibirīsā. How then [do we explain] "nibiḍāḥ keśāḥ" (dense hair) and "nibiḍaṃ vastram" (dense cloth)?

It will be due to comparison (*upamāna*). And this is clear in the *Kāśikā*. Some, however, maintain that because of the requirement of the previously stated application, the term "ate nāsikāyāḥ" (from 'ata' after 'nāsikā') does not carry over into this sūtra.
They explain [the sūtra] as follows: "Of the *prakṛti*" means "of the word *ni*. And "the two substitutes" means the two suffixes;

the meaning is that these two substitutes for *ya* and *kha* exist in conjunction with those [suffixes], according to their respective numbers. Furthermore, the suffix *kap* and the substitute *cikna* must be stated. Thus, [the form] *cikinam*.
The substitution of *ci* occurs in conjunction with the suffix *in*. In the word *cipiṭam*, the substitution of *i* occurs in conjunction with the suffix *piṭac*.
Regarding the phrase "of that which is moist" (*klinnasya*): [the suffixes] *cil*, *pil*, and *lac* are applied to it. "Of that which is moist" means *cil* and *pil*.
In this sense, the substitutes *it* and *et* occur; and when the meaning is "his eyes are moist," the suffix *la* and the suffix *ṭha* [are applied].

Furthermore, there is the suffix *cul*. Thus, *cul*—and because of the word *ca* (and), the suffix *la* is also included. Hence, *culla*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is exactly as stated before: "his two eyes are moist" (*klinne asya cakṣuṣī*). How then [is it explained] that "in the sense of one with moist eyes, the forms *culla*, *cilla*, and *pilla* [occur]"? [The answer follows: *yuḥ klinnākṣe cullacillapillāḥ*.

If it is argued that [the forms] *klinne akṣiṇī* and so on are also [governed by this rule], as stated by Amara, they say in response: "One must understand that for words derived from the base *akṣi* when applied to a person (*puruṣa*), there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) extending to its parts. Others, however, say: "In the case of *asya cakṣuṣī*, the word *asya* need not be mentioned; [the forms] *klinne cakṣuṣī* result in *cille* and *pille*."

In the sense of "possessing" (*matvartha*) applied to *puruṣa*, the suffix *ac* is used, because it is prescribed by the rule *vāṅgāddhīnāt* within the *ārṣa* and other groups. (1396) The suffix *tyakan* is added after [words ending in] *upādhi* to denote proximity (*āsanna*) and ascent (*ārūḍha*). Pāṇini 5.2.34.

Regarding the two suffixes [used here]: with the intention that, because this is under the heading of technical names (*saṃjñā*), what is understood here is restricted to specific objects—namely, that which is "near" (*āsanna*) and that which is "ascended upon" (*ārūḍha*)—he says: "of the mountain. "Near" means in the vicinity;
"ascended upon" means a high place. As for the term *upatyakā*, the substitution of *i* [for the final vowel] by the rule *ratyayasthā* does not apply.
It occurs because it has been stated that "there is also a prohibition regarding *yakana*.

(1397) *karmaṇi ghaṭa-aṭhañ* | 5|2|35|. Regarding *karmaṇi ghaṭa*: the suffix *aṭhañ* is applied after the word *karman* ending in the seventh case, in the sense of "striving for" (*ghaṭate*) that object.
It would be *karmaṭha*. [In this case], the substitution of *ika* for *hasya* does not apply;
because when the suffix *aṭhac* is present, the *ṭha* is not a suffix (*apratyaya*), and thus there is an absence of the designation *aṅga*, which is the cause [for that substitution].
(1398) *tad asya saṃjātaṃ tārakādibhya itac* (Pāṇini 5.2.36): "The suffix *itac* is added after words such as *tāraka* in the sense of 'that has come upon him'."

"Tārakitam" (starred): in this manner, examples such as "puṣpitam" (flowered), "phalitam" (fruited), "pulakitam" (bristled), and "romāñcitam" (hair-raised) are to be cited. (1399) *pramāṇe dvayasaj-daghnañ-mātracaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.2.37. [The suffixes] *dvayasaC*, *daghnac*, and *mātrac* are added after a word denoting a measure.

Regarding the suffix *dvayasac*: when a word ending in the first case (*prathamānta*) meaning "measure" (*pramāṇa*)—that is, something existing as a measure—is indicated [by the context], three suffixes (*pratyaya*) may occur to denote the object to be measured (*prameya*). Here, "measure" (*pramāṇa*) refers merely to that which delimits. Among these, *mātrac* is used generally; however, *dvayasac* and *daghnac* occur only in the case of vertical measurement (*ūrdhvamāna*), as in "the first chariot and the second."

Because of the commentary stating "I think [the term] *ūrdhvamāna* [is used] in the sense of 'measured vertically,'" that by which something is measured while standing upright is called *ūrdhvamāna*—such as the *ūrva* and so forth. Therefore, terms such as "a field measuring two *aṇḍajas*" are not employed for horizontal measurements and the like, according to the increasing authority of the sages. For this very reason...

Regarding the statement "‘vikāṇḍā kṣetrabhaktiḥ’" (a field-division consisting of three parts), we have already stated that the rule "vayasac ca luk" mentioned by the Easterners (Prācīnas) should not be respected.

[In the rule] "pramāṇe laḥ" (the suffix *la* occurs when denoting a measure), the term "la" is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for *luk* used by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*). [This applies] in the sense of being a measure (*pramāṇatvena*).
Since these [terms] are well-known, he provides examples where there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix belonging to the subsequent [element]: *śamaḥ*, *diṣṭiḥ*, and *vitastiriḥ*.

The analysis (*vigraha*) is "the measure (*pramāṇa*) of a *śama*," and so forth. In these cases, there is elision of the *mātrac* suffix because it is impossible for the other two; this is because *śama* and the others do not measure upwards.
"Of a *dvigu* [compound], always. Regarding the rule "of a *dvigu*, always":

since a *dvigu* is not a measure (*apramāṇa*) and because there is no application of the rule for elements ending in such a term (*tadantavidhi*), the elision (*luk*) is prescribed here by this sūtra where it was not obtained by the preceding one.
If it is objected that the mention of "always" (*nityam*) is redundant here because optionality (*vikalpa*) has not been under discussion:

Regarding this, they say: Just as the suffix *mātrac*, which will be discussed immediately below in the context of doubt in examples such as *śamamātram*, is not elided—because it falls under the scope of the preceding rule "when [the suffix] *dvayasaC* follows *pramāṇe*" (Pāṇini 5.2.37) rather than the rule "in the case of *pramāṇe*, *laC*" (Pāṇini 5.2.37)—so too, the elision of the suffix after a *dvigu* compound would not occur. And yet, such elision is desired.

*Luk*: There may or may not be two *śama*s; thus it is called "dviśama. Likewise, the mention of the word "nitya" (constant) is for the purpose of including the additional case. Here, some explain that even though it was stated as "luk of a *dvigu*," the repeated mention of *luk* can be interpreted as being for the sake of the constant [application] and for the sake of including the additional case; this is for the sake of variety.
They say that the inclusion of the word "nitya" (constant) [is for this purpose].

When there is doubt regarding number due to the measure or the magnitude, the suffix *mātraC* should be stated; for example, *śamamātram* and so forth. The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: "Is there peace, or is there not? and so on.

(1400) *puruṣahastibhyāmaṇ ca* | 5|2|38 | From *puruṣa* and *hastin*, the suffix *aṇ* [is applied]. By the rule *inaṇyanapatye*, there is the preservation of the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāva*). That which has an elephant as its measure is *hāstina*. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Kāśikā*: "There is always elision (*luk*) of the suffix after a word denoting a 'pair' (*vigoḥ*)."
"Two men [in height] of water," and so forth. And this has been explained by Haradatta:

although this is not a restatement (anuvāda) of the rule "In the case of a measure, *lo* is obligatory after a *dvigu*," because *puruṣa* and *hastin* are not established as measures in the same way that *śama* and other such units are; for this very reason, in cases such as *puruṣadvayasam*, etc. [the suffix *sa* is applied].

The claim that "the suffix *luṅ* does not occur because of the rule *apramāṇe laḥ*" is incorrect, for even so, a previously unestablished (*apūrva*) elision (*luk*) is being prescribed here. However, this is inconsistent; for the unprecedented statement "there is a constant elision (*luk*) of [the suffix] after *vi" has not been uttered by the Three Sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali). In reality, however, the meaning of "is prescribed" (*vidhīyate*) is "is inferred" (*anumīyate*).

The intended meaning is this: while the rules *dvigoḥ* and *addhitalukī* are being carried over, the rule *ūruṣāt pramāṇe 'nyatarasyām* optionally prescribes the suffix *ṅīp*; that very optionality implies the elision (*luk*) [of the feminine suffix].

(1401) *yatadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup* [Pāṇini 5.2.39]. From *yat*, *etat*, and so forth: *yāvān*, etc. After applying the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of the pronoun (*ā sarvanāmnaḥ*), the augment *num* is added by the rule *ugidacām*. Then, the long vowel is applied by *atvasantasya ca*. Finally, the elision of the *hal-ḍy-ādi* suffixes and the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) take place.

While the term *ramāṇe* (in the sense of "measuring") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], the specific mention of *parimāṇa* (measure) is made because of the distinction between *pramāṇa* (dimension/extent) and *parimāṇa* (measure/capacity).
Thus, the Vārttika states: "The mention is stated separately because of the difference in meaning between the two."

"The state [of the vowel] is established for the sake of non-obstruction by the *mātrā* and so forth, in the case of *ḍāp* and *vatu*. This is its meaning: here, in this grammatical treatise, having prescribed the suffix *vatup*, the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) is ordained when that suffix follows. However, the ancient teachers (Pūrvācāryas) prescribed *ḍāvatup*;
it is according to their view that this reference is made as "in the case of *ḍāp* and *vatu*" (*ḍāvatāv iti*). It is thus qualified.
This is the distinction; its state is "distinction" (*vaiśeṣyam*), and [the word *vaiśeṣyam*] means "because of the difference in meaning.

As for the difference in meaning: the sense is that it has already been stated previously that "dimension (*parimāṇa*) applies to all [directions], whereas length (*āyāma*) would be the measure (*pramāṇa*). Now, if there is a difference in meaning between these two, then however much of a path...
The [use of the term] *rajju* and so forth would not be established, for here only length (*āyāma*) is understood.

If you say that it will occur through analogy (*aupamāna*), then let the mention of "measure" (*pramāṇa*) itself be maintained, and let such usages as *yāvān adhvā* (as much distance as... be primary. As for those usages regarding dimension (*parimāṇa*), [they are secondary].
Expressions such as "as much as a heap of grain" and so forth—let these indeed arise from comparison (*upamāna*).

To this, he says: "on account of the suffix -mātra. For the suffix *vatup*, which is prescribed by a specific rule (*yatadetebhyaḥ*), would subvert the suffixes *-mātra* and others, which are prescribed by general rules. Therefore, forms such as *tanmātram* and so on [would not be established].

It might be so. However, the point is that when there is the apprehension of measurement (*parimāṇa*), because the conditions (*upādhi*) are different, there is no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between the suffix *vatup*—which is prescribed for measurement—and suffixes such as *mātraJ* which are also prescribed for measurement. [Objection: Even so, there would still be sublation, because in the rule *“pramāṇe dvayasaJ”* (Pāṇini 5.2.37), the form *prasthamātram* and others are established [by it].

Since the inclusion of the term *pramāṇa* has been explained as being intended merely to signify that which delimits, the suffix *vatup*— being prescribed by the rule "after *yat*, *etad*, etc., comes *vatup*"— remains applicable because it is specifically ordained; therefore, let the sūtra simply read "after *yat*, *etad*, etc., comes *vatup*," and let the mention of *parimāṇa* not be included.

Furthermore, let there be the governing topic of "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*); by this, all such usages as "as long as the rope" (*yāvatī rajjuḥ*) and "as large as the heap of grain" (*yāvān dhānyarāśiḥ*) are established even without resorting to figurative application (*upacāra*). This is another favorable point, and therefore he says: "the state [of being] is established" (*bhāvaḥ siddhaśca*), [referring to] the suffix *ḍāvatu*.
The word ends in the fifth case (pañcamyanta). When there is a difference in meaning, the suffixes *mātra* and so forth are established after words ending in *vat*. For example:

*tat-parimāṇam asya tāvad-dhānyam rāśīkṛtam* ("this heap of grain has that much quantity"); *tāvat-pramāṇam asya kuḍava-ādeḥ āvan-mātram* ("the measure of this [container] such as a *kuḍava* is of such a size"). It means that the value of the grain and so forth when heaped up is of such a kind.

The meaning is "even [in the case] of *kuḍava* and so forth. However, if there were identity of object (*ekaviṣayatva*), then because the qualified object of knowledge would already have been expressed by the suffix *-vatup* itself, suffixes such as *-mātra-ja-* and others could not follow a word ending in *-vatup*. For that which has a certain measure (*pramāṇa*) as its own measure—that too is a measure. That water or other things which have the measure of a knee (*jānu*) as their measure—that too [is a measure].

Because it is possible to say "of the measure of a knee" (*jānupramāṇaka*), in that case the word *tāvat* alone would be employed, and not *tāvanmātra* and so forth. Otherwise, from suffixes such as *mātra*, one would have forms such as: "that is its measure" (*tat-pramāṇam asya* → *tan-mātram*), or "that much is its measure" (*tan-mātram pramāṇam asya* → *tan-mātramātram*).
Because it would lead to an infinite regress of conditions (*pratyayamālāprasaṅga*).
[The rule] *kimidambhyāṃ vo ghaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.40) states: "After *kim* and *idam*, the suffix *vatup* shall occur. Regarding the letter *v* [in *vatup*]:
The intention is that, by the force of the rule for the suffix *gha*, the suffix *vatup* is carried over and is also prescribed here.

Although [the desired form] would be established simply by the rule "of what follows, the first letter" (*ādeḥ parasya*), the statement "of *vah*" (*vaḥ*) is for the purpose of indicating a substitute (*ādeśa*).
Otherwise, *gha* would be understood as a separate suffix (*pratyaya*). As for "in *kiya*"—[it refers to the rule] "for *idam* and *kim*, [there are] *īś* and *kī*" (*idaṃkimorīśkī*).
There is elision by the rule *yasyeti ca*. Regarding the form *iyān*: when the substitute *ī* [for *idam*] is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*, only the suffix remains. And they recite:
"When the subsequent suffix, which is the source of the grammatical system, has arisen, and the manifest world (*prapañca*) has likewise dissolved into its primary state (*prakṛti*), immediately..."

"Who, even if he were a scholar, could measure with his heart that which has arisen as the Word (*pada*)— the pure consciousness (*kevala-pratyaya*)— saying, 'It is this much'? This verse is composed by resorting to the grammatical (*vaiyākaraṇa*) and Upaniṣadic (*aupaniṣada*) systems of analysis.

(1403) *kimaḥ saṅkhyāparimāṇe ḍati ca* |5|2|41|. After the word *kim*, when expressing the measure (*parimāṇa*) of a number—that is, its limitation—the suffix *ḍati* is applied, and [the suffix] *ḍat* also [is applied]. The phrase "in this sense" (*adasīya*) indeed continues to apply. The "measure of a number" is its delimitation; when that is to be effected—

The suffix *ḍati* occurs after the word *kim*, when it is in the first case and denotes a question concerning something that exists within a certain number, provided it stands in a genitive relationship. Why is "number" (*saṅkhyā*) mentioned? To prevent it from applying in cases of censure (*kṣepa*). For example: "What is the number of these ten? [In such cases, the suffix would not apply]. [The suffix applies] to those who do not observe vows, who do not recite mantras, and who subsist merely by their caste—[such people exist] by the thousands.

Since there is no such thing as "assembly-ness" for those who have gathered together, one should understand that here, by way of the suffix *saṅkhyeya*, there is a censure (*kutsā*) regarding the number.
[Pāṇini 5.2.42: *saṅkhyāyā avayave tayap* ("The suffix *tayap* is added after a numeral when denoting a part").

[The suffix] *tayap* occurs after a word denoting a number that expresses a part, provided that the word ending in the first case denotes the whole (*avayavin*) with respect to which the part exists; this is because of the governing rule [Pāṇini 5.4.42], "of this" (*asya*). This is just as in the case of *dvayasa-* and others when they denote measurement (*pramāṇa*).
The meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is the object of cognition (*prameya*), and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is likewise [the same]. (1405) *dvitribhyāṃ tayasyāyaj vā* (Pāṇini 5.2.43).
Regarding the form *trayam*: now, in the usage ‘*trayo ’vayavās tantavo yasya trayaṃ sūtram*’ (“that thread which has three constituent parts”), [how is this explained]?

If it is argued that even though [the three units] exist, the usage "unit-triad" (*unitrayam*) is not tenable because there is no whole (*avayavin*) as a distinct referent for the compound, they reply: In this context, the whole is simply the collection itself. Whether that [collection] is something over and above [its parts] or not is a separate inquiry.

And thus, even on the view that the aggregate (*samudāya*) is something additional [to its parts], because the sages are recognized as constituent elements of that aggregate, the salutation to the "Triad of Sages" certainly possesses the power to destroy obstacles.
(1406) *ubhādudāto nityam* | Pāṇini 5.2.44.
Regarding the rule *ubhādudāto nityam*: here, by the very word *itaḥ*, the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) is already established;

however, the universal acute accent (*sarvodātatva*) is precluded by the statement "a word is unaccented except for one [syllable]. Nor does this apply to the vocative form *he ubhaya*, where the initial acute accent of the vocative (*āmantritādyaudātatva*) would otherwise be precluded.

It should not be suspected that this refers to the *vacana* (the rule for the vocative); for it is easily stated that by the preceding exception (*apavāda*), only the *citsvara* (the accent of a particle) is sublated, and not the *ādyudātta* (initial acute accent) of the vocative and so forth.
Therefore, by the force of the mention of the acute accent (*udātta*), this [rule] applies only to the initial [syllable]. And it is employed accordingly.
"And one hears both. Having intended all of this, he says: "And that" (*sa ca*).
(1407) *tadasminn adhikam iti daśāntāḍ ḍaḥ* |5|2|45|. [The word] *tadasmin* [is used]; the repetition of the word *tat* is for the sake of [the rule] *asya*.

The mention of "that" (*tad*) is intended to exclude the inclusion of anything connected with a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). Since there is no rule for including the end of a compound (*tadantavidhi*) in the prescription of a suffix (*pratyayavidhi*), he says: "from that which ends in *daśan*" (*daśāntāt*). Why is the word "end" (*anta*) mentioned? [Consider the example: "In this hundred, ten are in excess. One should not argue that here the status of "ending in *daśan*" exists by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses the designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).

This is because of the acceptance of the principle *ṭhvyapadeśivadbhāvo ’prātipadikena* (the designation of a whole applies to its parts as well). When the rule for inclusion of the final element (*tadantavidhi*) is established by the maxim *śadanta-pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*, the restriction that the operation applies to what begins with that [initial element] is established by the maxim *yasmāt pratyayavidhis tadādes tadantasya*.

To exclude that [possibility], the term *anta* (end/limit) is included. By this, forms such as *ekatriṃśaṃ śatam* ("one hundred and thirty-one") and *ekacatvāriṃśam* ("one hundred and forty-one") are established. Nor should one fear an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *gośate triṃśadadhikāḥ* ("thirty cows in excess in this hundred of cows"), because [the rule applies] to a numeral (*saṃkhyā*) in the sense of a part (*avayava*).

Because the mention of "number" (saṅkhyā) continues from that [previous rule], the mention of "ending in" (anta) should be applied here immediately after the word "viṃśati," as in "after a word ending in -aḍviṃśati. By this, forms such as *ekaviṃśaṃ śatam* ("one hundred and twenty-one") are established. Otherwise, [the rule] would be "after a word ending in -rahaṇa or -vat."
Because of the prohibition of the rule regarding operations on what follows an element (*tadanta-vidhi-pratiṣedha*), [the suffix] would not occur here.

(1408) *saṅkhyāyā guṇasya nimāne mayaṭ* | 5|2|47|. "Of a number, of a quality" (*guṇasya*). A "quality" (*guṇa*) is a portion (*bhāga*). That by which something is measured or purchased is called *nimāna*.
*Nimāna* means price. It is derived from the root *ni-mā* (Pāṇini 3.3.25, *eṅ praṇidāne*) with the prefix *ni*, in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), using the suffix *lyuṭ*.

Thus he says: "in the sense of the price of a portion. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the genitive": although the word *a* is understood from the rule *adasminn adhike* (Pāṇini 5.2.45), which results in the meaning "that which is more than this" being obtained from a word ending in the nominative case, [the present rule] is intended to express the genitive sense.

Nevertheless, by the "frog-leap" (maṇḍūakapluti) method—since the word *adas* is understood to carry over from the rule "that which has arisen for this" (*adasaḥ saṃjātam*)—the meaning is that the term *aṣṭhalyarthe* ("in the sense of the eighth case") is also obtained. Regarding the example *dvimayam*: because the word *dvi-* is a relative term, it possesses a constant requirement for a correlative.
It should be understood that even though the word "ṭhyavān" exists, the derivation of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) here is not contradictory.
Now, one might object: even so, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *udaśvit* remains difficult to achieve;
for the suffix is prescribed after the element signifying the state of being curdled milk (*udaśvid-bhāga*), and not after the word *udaśvit* itself.
On this point, they say: even when the suffix is prescribed with reference to a part (*bhāga*), it denotes that which possesses the part (*bhāgavat*) due to its own inherent nature of denotation;
thus, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established. This is so because, although one ought to say "in the sense of a small measure" (*ūna-māne*), [the rule applies as stated].
By virtue of being pronounced separately, unity is intended in the rule "the quality [is singular]"; therefore, it does not apply here in the case of:

*yavānāṃ dvau bhāgau nimānam eṣām udaśvitas trayāṇāṃ bhāgānām* ("two parts of barley are the measure for these three parts of buttermilk"). Furthermore, the suffix is desired after a numeral that expresses a larger quantity. Here...

It does not occur [in that way]. In the expression *eko bhāgo nimānam asya* ("one part is its measure"), by the suffix *-īyas-* (as in *hūyasa-*), only the sense of "excess" relative to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is intended, not plurality.
Therefore, it occurs even from the word *dvi-* (two). Regarding the sense of "its filler": "of this" (*asya*).
This is an imitation [of a form] ending in the sixth case (genitive). However, singularity is not intended to be expressed, because it is impossible for one thing to be a "completer" (*pūraṇa*).

A "completer" is that by which something is completed; the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) to the causative root (*ṇyanta*). Regarding the expression "of eleven":

the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is a collection in which the distinction between its parts has become manifest, while the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the individual part. In this context...

Since the rule for the suffix prescribes it after a word expressing a number, the suffix is applied to the completion of that very basis of application (pravṛttinimitta), such as "eleven" and so forth. Just as in rules such as "in the sense of excellence" (atiśāyane) or "in the sense of pervasion" (vyāpye), it is the excellence and so forth of the basis of application itself that is understood— because it is more intimately related (antaraṅgatvāt)— so it is here as well.
The point is that, because of this, there is not even a trace of the suspicion of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of [the expression] "water, etc., which completes eleven jars. Now,

if the suffix denotes the completion (*pūraṇa*) of the occasioning cause (*pravṛttinimitta*), then it would be proper to state the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) here as "the completion of the number eleven."

If this is argued, they say here: just as in the case of the compound *vaiyākaraṇapāśaḥ*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the grammarian is contemptible" (*yāpyo vaiyākaraṇaḥ*), and not "grammar-ness is contemptible" (*yāpyaṃ vaiyākaraṇatvam*), so too should it be understood here.
And thus, when the chapters are understood in reverse order...
When the chapter "vṛddhir ādaij" is counted last, then it indeed becomes the eighth as well. (1409) *nāntād asaṅkhyāder maṭ* 5.2.49.

"Not after a word ending in 'ā' that has an indeclinable as its prior member. Regarding "of *ḍaṭ*": the sense is that since *aṭ* is carried over from the previous rule as a nominative singular, it is here interpreted as a genitive (*āntāt*) by means of a change of case. Although there would be no harm even if *maṭ* were a suffix here, nevertheless, [the same applies] to *tamaṭ* later on.

It must be accepted as an augment (*āgama*) so that it may be unaccented (*anudātta*); for if it were an affix (*pratyaya*), it would be acutely accented (*ādyudātta*) on its first syllable. And it is appropriate to explain the context with uniformity through that [status].
Others, however, say: if it were an affix, the letter *m* together with the vowel *a* should be prescribed; if it were an augment...
"But there is brevity [in saying] 'only the letter *m*'"—this refers to the word *viṃśa*. It means "that which completes twenty.

There is elision [of the final syllable] by the rule *i viṃśaterḍiti*. (Pāṇini 5.2.51) *ṣaṭkatikatipayacaturāṃ thuk*. (The suffix *thuk* is added after the words *ṣaṣ*, *kati*, *katipaya*, and *catur* when followed by the taddhita suffix *thañ*.)

Regarding *ṣaṭkati*: here, because of the mention in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa*), it is clear that *ṣaṣ* and the others are *āgamas* (augmentative elements); thus, for the sake of consistency with that, the suffix *ḍaṭ*—which was previously understood—is transformed into the locative case. This is what [the author] says: "in *ḍaṭ*" (*ḍaṭi*). Why is the augment *thuṭ* not applied to *ḍaṭ* itself? Because of the *ṣakāra* of *ṣaṣ*.

Because of the undesirable consequence of *jaś*-substitution; and because in the fourth case, there would be the undesirable consequence of *visarga* for the letter *r*. Nor should it be argued that, in the rule *āntād*, *mu* alone should be prescribed when *ḍati* follows, for that would result in the non-elimination of the nasal (*n*) in forms such as *pañcamaḥ* and *saptamaḥ*.
The substitution of *catur* for *caturaś*, the elision of the initial syllable, and [the addition of] *thuk*. Regarding "the substitution of *catur* for *caturaś*":

even though the suffixes *cha* and *ya* are specifically prescribed, they do not supersede the suffix *ḍaṭ*, because of the force of the rule prescribing *thuk*. By this, the form *caturtha* is established. Regarding "the elision of the initial syllable": [this applies when the suffix *thañ* follows].

A consonant accompanied by a vowel is expressed by the word *akṣara*; the meaning is "of the initial consonant accompanied by a vowel. Haradatta states that the authority for the explanation "of the consonant beginning with ṭha" is to be understood from the mention of "uryāṇi" in the rule *dvitīyatṛtīyābhyāṃ*.

(1412) *treḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.55):

in the case of *tṛtīya*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *ṛ* sound in place of the *repha* (the letter *r*). However, the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *halaḥ* (6.4.2) does not take place here.
Because the word *aṇaḥ* is understood from the preceding rule *hrasvālope*, the term *reṣṭṛ ca* was not stated here, lest it be understood as a suffix (*pratyaya*).
(1413) *viṃśatyādibhyastamaḍanyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 5.2.56. The suffix *tamaṭ* is optionally added after the words beginning with *viṃśati*.

Regarding the rule *viṃśatyādibhyaḥ*: here, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the words *viṃśati* and so forth that are specifically prescribed (*nipātita*) in the sūtra beginning with *aṅktī* are understood, and not those [words] well-known in common usage (*lokaprasiddha*), because the latter are too remote (*viprakṛṣṭatvāt*).
This is the opinion of the Bhāṣya. However, the author of the Vṛtti maintains that *viṃśati* and the others are indeed ordinary numerical words (*saṅkhyāśabda*).

[The term *gṛhya*] is not intended to include those [suffixes] specified in the sūtras beginning with *paṅkti*, for if it did, the formation of words from bases such as *ekaviṃśati* would not be possible; this is because there is a prohibition against applying a rule to that which ends in a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when that stem itself already possesses a suffix. This being the case, [the rule] “*aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*” [applies], provided it does not begin with a numeral.

It has been stated that a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) is indeed appropriate. Regarding the term "the twenty-first": although, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) is difficult to obtain here, nevertheless, the exclusion of numerals and so forth in the sūtra "aṣṭana ā vibhaktau" indicates that in this section, the extension applies even to those [words] ending in such [numerals].
Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of common usage": if this is the case, then the form *ekānnaviṃśatitama* ("the nineteenth") is also established as the ordinal that completes the number nineteen.
According to the view of the *Vṛtti* that this is "an inclusion of common usage," this would not be established;
for this number occurs prior to the number twenty. And this...

This is clear from the works of Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta. Now, since Kātyāyana— by stating, "Or rather, [the suffix] *ṭhan* need not be commenced, because they are understood as *pratipadika*s (nominal stems), as in the case of *sahasra* and so forth"— has rejected the rule for *paṅkti* and its successors, it follows that *viṃśati* and the others are not included (*anipātita*) in that sūtra.

If it is argued that the view of the Bhāṣya—that [the rules] are "taken up"—is incorrect, they say here: although it was rejected, nevertheless it is necessary for this purpose. For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya stated therein: "One should not be envious where an explanatory derivation (*anugama*) is performed. Therefore, the rejection stated by Kātyāyana—

"It should not be respected. Regarding "the hundredth": although this is established by the subsequent rule *aṣṭādaśace*, nevertheless, he provides an example—*ekaśatatamaḥ* (the one-hundred-and-first)—to suggest that [the suffix] *tamaṭ* is necessary for the sake of expressing numbers and so forth, as in *itthaṃ śatadī*. Regarding "of the month, etc. (*māsādeḥ*).
The sense is that even in the absence of expressing a number. (1414) *ṣaṣṭy-ādeś-cā-saṅkhyādeḥ* | Pāṇini 5.2.58.
Regarding the phrase *ṣaṣṭy-ādeḥ*: since an option (*vikalpa*) was already established by the rule *viṃśaty-ādibhyaḥ*, [this sūtra provides for the compulsory application].

The meaning of "eternal" (nitya) is "without beginning" (amārambha). Regarding the phrase "but of number and so forth": this should be understood as referring to [numbers] prior to one hundred, because it was stated [in the rule] "thus, from one hundred onwards. The suffix *cha* occurs after a word denoting possession (*matvartha*). "In the sense of possession" means: in the domain of the possessive suffix *mat*.

Therefore, in the expression "after *a*," the first case ending (*prathamā*) is the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*), and in "of this, in this," the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is the governing case.
And here, the meaning of the suffix is obtained.
(1415) *adhyāyānuvākayor luk* 5.2.60.
[The mention of] "by virtue of the force of the rule" (*vidhānasāmarthyāt*) [is made] because this sūtra ought to have been formulated right within the section on the *matup* suffix.

Kaiyaṭa states that the prescription of elision (*luk*) for this [suffix] here implies an optional elision elsewhere. [The suffix *vuñ* is applied] after the word *pathin*, when it is in the seventh case-ending (*saptamī-samartha*), in the sense of "skilled in" (*kuśala*). (Pāṇini 5.2.64) *Ākarṣādibhyaḥ kan*: [The suffix *kan* is applied] after [words] beginning with *ākarṣa*.

The suffix *kan* is applied after words such as *ākarṣa*. Since this could have been accomplished by the suffix *vun*, the specific mention of *kan* is for the sake of including stems ending in *i* and *u*. Examples: *śakunikaḥ*, *aśanikaḥ*, *tsarukaḥ*, and *mukhyaḥ* (this is the correct reading). Having explained that "it is called *ākarṣa* because gold and other items are drawn (*ākṛṣyante*) therein" by means of the rule *ghaḥ saṃjñāyām unsi*, those who...
The meaning is that Haradatta has stated: "Those who read [the sūtra] as *ṭhākarṣādibhyaḥ* with the letter *ra*, for them the form *ṭhākarṣa* is derived by means of the suffix *ghañ*.
(1417) *dhanahiraṇyātkāme* |5|2|65|.

Regarding "dhane kāmaḥ": the sense is that the suffix is applied after a word ending in the locative case due to the continued application of the word "atra. From "udarāt": he states [the rule] for the sake of the initial *ūna* and *śarda*.
(1418) Pāṇini 5.2.67: *udarāṭ ṭhag ādyūne*.

"Without the desire to conquer": because the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* for *t* in the suffix *niṣṭhā* is prescribed specifically there [in Pāṇini 8.2.57] by the rule "ivo'vivigīṣāyām". (1419) *sasyena parijātaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.68).

"With *sasyena*": this is the third case (*tṛtīyā*) used in the sense of the agent being also the object (*karmakartṛ*). "Grown all around" (*parijātaḥ*)—he states that it has borne fruit by saying "connected" (*saṃbaddhaḥ*). "For this very reason"—the intention is that it is because of the prohibition [stated in the rule] *ṭhake no’ri*.

(1420) *tantrāt* [the suffix *kan* is added] after the word *tantra* when it means "recently removed" (*acirāpahṛta*). *tantrāt*: Based on the etymological derivation *tanyante tantavo’smin*, *tantra* refers to the shuttle of a weaver. *aciraḥ*: "Not long ago."

In the expression *kālo’pahṛtasya*, the word *acira* [is understood] as "recently taken away"; the compound is formed according to the rule *pūrvakālaika...* (*Pāṇini 2.1.49*). The term *pratyagra* means "new.
(1421) *brāhmaṇakoṣṇike saṃjñāyām* ||5|2|71|| [The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *brāhmaṇa* and *uṣṇa* when they function as proper names.]

In the case of *brāhmaṇakoṣṇika*, the suffix *kan* is prescribed in the sense of the locative case after the word *brāhmaṇa* when it is qualified by the attribute of being a professional warrior (*āyudhīvin*), provided it ends in the nominative case; and after the word *anna* when it is qualified by the attribute of being small (*alpatva*). Thus he says: "āyudha... and so forth.

(1422) *śītoṣṇābhyāṃ kāriṇi* |5|2|72|. From the words *śīta* and *uṣṇa* [the suffix *kha* is added] when [the action] is performed slowly or quickly. *Śītam iva śītam*: "slowly," meaning with a lack of proficiency in performing the task because one is cold. *Uṣṇam iva uṣṇam*: "quickly," meaning swiftly.

The suffix is applied after two words ending in the accusative case that function as adverbs (kriyāviśeṣaṇa). It has been stated, however, that the genitive case—characterized by its connection with a verbal noun (kṛt)—is not applied after an adverb. Furthermore, the suffix does not occur after words used in their primary sense (mukhyārtha), because such usage is not sanctioned by linguistic convention (anabhidhāna).

(1423) *adhika* | Pāṇini 5.2.73. Regarding the word *adhika*: it is derived from the root *ruh* preceded by the prefix *adhi*. By the rule beginning with *atyarthākarmaka*, the suffix *kta* is prescribed after the root *ruh* when used in the sense of the agent or the object. In the first case, by means of the *kta* suffix...

Because the object of the action (*karman*) has not been expressed [by another word], the second case (*dvitīyā*) is employed in connection with the word *adhyārūḍha*. For example, in "the *droṇa* measure is mounted upon the *khārī*," it is like the expression "gone to Rāma. Similarly, when used in conjunction with the word *adhika*, although the second case would also be expected, there is the rule "that from which something is greater" (*yasmād adhikam*) and "that in which something is greater" (*adasminn adhikam*).

In two types of explanations, the fifth and seventh case endings occur: "adhiko droṇaḥ khāryāḥ" and "adhiko droṇaḥ khāryām. However, in the second [explanation], because the object is expressed by the past passive participle (*kta*), the first case ending is used: "adhikā khārī droṇena."
Since the object (*karman*) has already been expressed [by the suffix], the use of the fifth (*pañcamī*) or seventh (*saptamī*) case endings should not be suspected here.
(1424) *anuka-abhika-abhīkaḥ kamitā* | P. 5.2.74.
[The compound] *anuka* is a collective dvandva; its masculine gender is Vedic (*sautra*). Because it is a sūtra, there is a change of gender.

The meaning [of the rule] has been established. Regarding the rule *anvabhibhyāṃ kan* (Pāṇini 5.2.74): the meaning is that the suffix *kan* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) after words expressing an instrument (*sādhana*) qualified by an action (*kriyā*).
(1425) *pārśvenānvicchati* (Pāṇini 5.2.75).
He seeks by the side (*pārśvena*). The suffix *kan* continues from the rule "after *sthā*, *karṣa*, etc., [the suffix] *kan*" (*ṭhākarṣādibhyaḥ kan*).
Regarding the word "crooked" (*anṛju*): because it lies obliquely, the side (*pārśva*) is crooked; by virtue of that similarity, the [two] flanks (*upapau*) are also [so called].
Here, the words *śīta*, *uṣṇa*, *pārśva*, *ayaḥśūla*, *daṇḍa*, and *ajina* are understood only in their secondary (metaphorical) senses.
However, the suffix does not occur in its primary sense because it is not so prescribed.

(1426) *Tāvatithaṃ grahaṇam iti lug vā* |5|2|77|. Regarding the phrase "the taking [of a portion] that many times," there is optionally elision (*luk*). That which completes a certain number is "that-many-th" (*tāvatitham*).
Just as in the rule *tasyāpatyam* (Pāṇini 4.1.92), where there is a general reference to words ending in the genitive case by means of the term *tasya*,
