so too here, in the term *āvatithaḥ*, there is a general reference to words ending in ordinal suffixes (*pūraṇapratyaya*). Furthermore, the suffixes *ṭhak* and *ṭhañ* do not carry over [from the previous rules] even though they are immediately preceding.

Intending to say "because it is not marked with the *svarita* accent," he says: "from *kan*" (*kāṃsyāt*). [He specifies] "of the ordinal suffix" (*pūraṇapratyayasya*); however, it is not the elision (*luk*) of *kan*, because that would result in the redundancy of the mention of the option (*vāgrahaṇa*). For by that [elision], forms such as *pañcamaṃ* and *pañcamakam* would have to be produced; and that—
Because of the authority of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, it is indeed established by option (*vikalpena*) even through the addition of the suffix *kan*.

Therefore, he explains that the elision (*luk*) of the ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*) alone was intended by the author of the Sūtra, stating "dvikam"; however, the author of the Vārttika maintains that there is elision of *kan* alone.

Intending to provide an explanation, he says: "Regarding the question of whether there should be elision (*luk*) based on the rule for the *n*-th occurrence, the statement [of the rule] would be purposeless because of the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*). According to that view, the forms are *dvitīyakaṃ* and *dvitīyam* alone, and not *dvikaṃ*; this is how it should be understood.

Regarding the statement "tāvatithena gṛhṇāti" (he takes by that many), it must be stated [as a rule] and there is always elision (*luk*). Kaiyaṭa says: Since the suffix prescribed in the sense of its own meaning (*svārthe*) after a word ending in a ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*)—which has "taking" as its limiting condition (*upādhi*)—does not apply to one who takes, this [rule] is stated.

(1427) *sa eṣāṃ grāmaṇīḥ* | 5|2|79|. "He is their leader. According to Amarasimha: "The word *grāmaṇī* denotes a barber in the masculine; in the sense of 'best' or 'village headman,' it is used in all three genders. *Karabha* means a young camel.

(1428) *kālaprayojanādroge* [Pāṇini 5.2.81]. Regarding the example *dvitīye ’hanīti*: although the word *dvitīya* is not inherently expressive of time, the point is that, by virtue of the context and so forth, it functions to denote time within the scope of a compound (*vṛtti*). Now, one might object: [...]

If it is asked, "What is the authority for [the rule] that [the suffix *ṭhañ*] does not occur after words like *māsa* when they denote the current time (*sākṣāt-kāla*), but does occur after them when they denote the second [month] and so forth?"— to this they reply: "Because of the attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*) of the technical term (*saṃjñā*) from the subsequent sūtra, or because of the inherent nature of the word (*śabda-svābhāvya*)."
Regarding the phrase "tadbodhyam" (that should be understood):

[the suffix] *ini* is prohibited after the word *vaṭaka*. As for the form *vaṭakebhyaḥ*, this statement is made because the suffix *ka* would otherwise apply. If it is argued that *ka* will not occur here because of the mention of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), what follows from that? Since *ini* would still not be applicable, [the prohibition is stated] for the sake of that.

The statement must indeed be accepted. One should not harbor the hope that the suffix *ini* might somehow be established by the rule “*ata iniṭhanau*,” for there is the explicit statement: “And those two [suffixes] are not prescribed after a locative case.”
(1429) *śrotriyaś chando ’dhīte* |5|2|84|.

[The word] *śrotriyaḥ* [is formed]. He who studies the Veda (*chandas*) becomes a *śrotriya*. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states that the word *śrotriyaḥ* has the sense of the sentence "he studies the Veda."

The position that [the word *chāndasa*] is a single word is based on the sense of the sentence: "it is irregularly formed (*nipātyate*). Furthermore, another position is established: "Alternatively, by Vedic license (*chandasaḥ*), the substitution of *śrotra-* [for *śrauta-*, as in *śrautapatha*] is irregularly formed in this sense, and the suffix *gha* is added.
This has been explained by Kaiyaṭa as referring to the sentence-meaning, which consists of a relationship.

Alternatively, because the nature of an action (kriyā) is non-substantial (asattva-rūpa), whereas the word *śrotriya* denotes a substantial entity (sattva-rūpa), it is by grasping the meaning of the sentence that the one who has studied the Veda (*chando’dhyāyī*), which is the substratum of that [action], is denoted. For the Dharmaśāstra states: "Having studied a single branch [of the Veda], one becomes a *śrotriya*."
Regarding the phrase "due to the recurrence of *veti*": it follows from the rule "the suffix *luk* optionally applies after [a word ending in] *āvatithaṃ grahaṇam*.

(Pāṇini 5.2.85: *śrāddham anena bhuktaṃ iṇ-iṭhan-au*. [The word] *śrāddham*: that in which there is faith (*śraddhā*) is *śrāddham*. [This is derived by] "the suffix *ṇa* is applied after *raja*, *aśraddhā*, and *arcā*. Although...

The ancestral rite (*pitrya-karman*) is expressed by the word *śrāddha*; nevertheless, here it refers to the substance that serves as its means, because the primary *śrāddha* itself cannot be consumed. [In the term] *śrāddhe*, [the suffix] *śrāddhika* is intended to refer to the present day alone; it should not be the case that one who has eaten today would be called *śrāddhika* tomorrow.
(1431) *pūrvādiniḥ* | Pāṇini 5.2.86. The suffix *ini* is added after the word *pūrva*. This suffix is applied to the accusative form *pūrvam*, which functions as an adverb (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
The term denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), namely "by means of this" (*anena*), is understood from the preceding rule. Furthermore, an agent cannot exist without an action.
Since the suffix must be prescribed by supplying some action such as "it arises," he says: "by him this was previously done.
(Pāṇini 5.2.87) *sapūrvācca*.

“Also after [a word] preceded by *sapūrva*. The phrase “by means of this” (*anena*) and the preceding sūtra are carried over (*anuvartate*). The suffix *ini* shall occur in the sense of “by means of this” after the word *pūrva* when it is preceded by something else; thus, the result is that [the suffix applies] after a compound ending in *pūrva*. For example: *kṛtapūrvī* (one who has previously done). [This refers to] the two words *kṛta* and *pūrva*.

The compound is "upsupā. Here, because the governing topic is *prātipadika* (nominal stem), the suffix *ini* is established by the rule "ūrvādiniḥ" itself from the nominal stem ending in the word *pūrva*, namely *kṛtapūrva*. Thus, [the formation of] *kṛtapūrvī* is accomplished.

The rule *apūrvāt ca* indicates the *paribhāṣā*: "There is no application of the suffix *taddhita* to that which ends in a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when that stem itself already possesses [the suffix]. For the sake of establishing the form *ṛtapūrvī*, if one were to accept the rule *apūrvāntāt ca*, then by that very principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as identical with its designation), the form *pūrvī* would also be established.

The rule *ūrvādiniḥ* indicates the existence of the metarule (*paribhāṣā*): "The treatment of a word as if it were its own designator (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) does not apply when [the suffix] follows a non-prātipadika. (1433) *cchandasi paripanthiparipariṇau paryavasthātari* 5.2.89. [In the Vedic language, the suffixes *paripanthin* and *pariparin* are applied after the word *pari* in the sense of 'an adversary' (*paryavasthātṛ*).]
In the Vedic language (*cchandas*), the suffix *ini* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*) to the word *paryavasthātṛ*, which is a synonym for "enemy" (*śatru*);
furthermore, the substitutions *antha* and *ara* are prescribed as substitutes for the word *avasthātṛ*. Examples are:
*ṭhapatyaṃ paripanthinam* and *ā tvā pari pariṇo vidan*; in both cases [the rule applies].

The avagraha occurs before the word *pari*. Regarding the phrase "in the world, however" (*loke tu*), it refers to instances such as *anupasthitaparipanthibhiḥ pārthivaiḥ* ("by kings whose adversaries have not appeared").
(1434) [The suffix] *ṭhan* is applied after *anupad* in the sense of "a seeker. 5.2.90.

*Anupadyanveṣṭā* (one who searches after). The suffix *ini* is applied irregularly (*nipātyate*) to the word *anu*. In the expression *anupadam*, it means "behind the footprint" (*padasya paścāt*). It is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) in the sense of "after. In the phrase *anupadī gavām*, the genitive case is used in relation to the "footprint" (*gopadāt*); that is, the searching after the cows follows immediately from their footprints. Therefore—
Haradatta states that [the suffix] does not occur after words such as *hiraṇya* and others.

(1435) Pāṇini 5.2.91: *sākṣāddraṣṭari saṃjñāyām*. Regarding "in the sense of a direct witness": the suffix *ini* should be applied in the sense of a witness. The word *sākṣāt* is an indeclinable; by means of it—

In this sūtra, there is elision (luk) of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) due to the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "the imitation [of an action] is like the original form" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*). However, in rules such as *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ* and *avācchālambane*, because the extended application of "like the original form" is optional, there is no status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and thus there is no elision of the fifth case-ending.

"Bodhyam" (to be understood). Regarding "sākṣī": there is elision of the suffix *ṭi* by the rule "ṭhavyayānāṃ bhamātre" (elision of the *ṭi* of indeclinables before any nominal suffix beginning with a consonant). Although there are three types of witnesses—the giver, the receiver, and the observer—nevertheless, they say that here, because of the technical designation (*saṃjñā-grahaṇa*), the word "sākṣin" refers specifically to the observer.

(1436) *kṣetriyac* [is used] for that which is to be treated in another’s field. 5.2.92. *kṣetriyac*. The *Manoramā* states: “The suffix *dhac* is applied after the word *akṣetra* ending in the locative case, and the elision (*lopa*) of the word *para* is prescribed as a *nipātana*. Others, however, [interpret it] in the sense of “to be treated in what is not one’s own field” (*akṣetre cikitsyaḥ*).

The form *kṣetrāyaḥ* is derived as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). Some say that a word may be used to express the meaning of a sentence, just as in the case of *śrotriya*. This principle should be inferred in other instances as well. For example, there is the term *kṣetriyo vyādhiḥ* (a hereditary disease). Furthermore, there is *kṣetriyaṃ viṣam* (hereditary poison), which is treated after having been transferred to another body. Moreover—
"Kṣetriya" refers to weeds—those things grown in a field for the sake of grain that must be treated and destroyed. Furthermore, a "kṣetriya" is one who commits adultery;
"another's wife" (paradārāḥ) means another's field (parakṣetra). Therein, he is to be treated—that is, he is to be restrained. All these [meanings] apply here as well.
The suffixes [mentioned] are established in the source-text.
(1437) *Indriya* means "that which has Indra as its mark," "seen by Indra," "created by Indra," "enjoyed by Indra," or "given by Indra.
[Pāṇini 5.2.93]

*Indriya* is derived from the word *indra* with the suffix *ghañ*. It is [so called because it is] seen or known by Indra—in the sequence beginning with "this is my eye," "this is my ear," and so forth; or because it was created by him through the medium of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*); or because it is cherished (*juṣṭa*), meaning gratified or served;
or because it is bestowed (*datta*) according to its proper measure upon the objects of the senses. This is a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*).
It has been explained in some manner.
Now begins the section on the *parasmaipada* (active voice) formations.

Regarding the rule *śeṣātkartari*, since there is a restriction stating that the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) occurs only in cases such as those governed by *anudātetaḥ* and so forth, [the active voice applies otherwise].

In that context, there is the possibility of the *parasmaipada* (active voice). And thus, since the rule "the *parasmaipada* [is used] for the agent" (*kartari parasmaipadam*) restricts it to the *parasmaipada* alone, they say that the mention of the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is for the sake of clear understanding—that this [the *ātmanepada*] will apply only to those [roots] distinct from those [already covered]. [This refers to the rule] *anudāttaṅitaḥ*.

Some maintain that the mention of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is for the sake of clear understanding, because by the restrictive rule "the *ātmanepada* occurs only in these cases," the *parasmaipada* alone will apply there by the rule "after *eṣa*, [the suffixes] occur in the sense of the agent."

(470) *anuparābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ* |1|3|79|. Regarding the phrase "of this [rule] because it sublates": this means "of this [rule], namely *anuparābhyām*. For this very reason, he will state under the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* that this is an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*).

In the view that there is an extension of the rule (*śāstrātideśapakṣa*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is not prescribed by the rule *‘akarmavat karmaṇā’*; rather, the rule *‘hāvakarmaṇoḥ’* which prescribes it is extended. Anticipating the objection that this [extended] rule might be sublated by the subsequent rule *‘ṭhanuparābhyām’* because it occurs earlier, he says:

"Extension from the technical treatise" (*śāstrātideśa*), and so forth. "Because it is marked with the *svarita* accent": the sense is that the purpose of formulating this rule is to provide for the *parasmaipada* even when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent. (471) *paremṛṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.82).

This rule is commenced because [the suffix] would otherwise apply to both [roots] due to their being *svarita*-accented. Regarding the form *parimarṣati*: since the suffix *ṇic* is optional by the rule "optionally from *dhṛṣ* onwards" (*ā dhṛṣād vā*), there is an absence of *ṇic*. (472) Also after the prefix *upa*. 1.3.84.

The word *upāt* is mentioned [in this rule] because it was not stated in the rule "ṭhvyāṅparyupebhyaḥ"; this is so that the term *upa* alone may be carried forward into the subsequent sūtra. (473) Pāṇini 1.3.87: *nigaraṇacalanārthebhyaśca*.
And [the rule applies] after roots meaning "swallowing" and "moving. "Swallowing" means eating.

Although the *ātmanepada* is already established for *pru*, *dru*, and *sru* when they mean "moving," their inclusion in the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*) is for the sake of establishing it even when they do not mean "moving. For this very reason, it is explained there by the words "in the sense of 'he causes to drink'" (*rāpayati*), and so forth.
Śrīharṣa has said: "Then why do you say, 'Why do you wash [only] this face and not the eyes?

If it is argued that the *parasmaipada* ending is appropriate for the root *cam* preceded by the prefix *ā*, they reply here: "Ācāmaya" is a separate word (*pathak-padam*). [The first syllable] *ī* is Lakṣmī; together with her is *se* (the vocative particle), and this is used in addressing her (*tasyāḥ saṃbodhane*).
Regarding "ṭhhe se": some explain it as "O you, wash these two eyes—the *inacakṣuṣī*, that is, the excellent eyes (*śreṣṭhacakṣuṣī*)—what [is the purpose]?
(474) [This refers to the rule: Pāṇini 1.3.88: *aṇāvakarmakāccitavatkartṛkāt*.

Regarding the rule *aṇāvakarmakāt*: when there is a desire to express that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartṛ*), the ātmanepada would otherwise be required; this [rule] is for the sake of the parasmaipada. Why does it say *aṇau*?
So that the restriction—that the parasmaipada follows an intransitive root when it is caused by a *ṇic* suffix—does not apply.

He employs [the horse] as it is being mounted; *ārohayate*. The meaning is that he impels [the horse] which is becoming submissive (*nyagbhavanta*). This is a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for the second *ṇic* affix, following the rule *ṇeraṇau*, based on that which was determined to be the object (*karman*) in the example "he causes to mount" (*ārohayati*). Some, however, [interpret] *aṇau*...

Why? [The rule] should not result in a restriction to the *parasmaipada* (active voice) for roots belonging to the *curādi* class when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*). For example: the roots *puṭṭa* and *pvuṭṭa*, meaning "to become small," form *puṭṭayati* and *cuṭṭayati*, which mean "he becomes small. These two are intransitive (*akarmaka*). Then, with the causative suffix added to express motive (*hetumaṇṇic*), they become *puṭṭayate* and *cuṭṭayate*. Thus.

To offer a counter-example [as some do] contradicts the Bhāṣya and other authorities. For instance, in this context, the word "ṇeḥ" (of the causative suffix) from the rule *budhādi* and others carries over; since only the causative (*hetumaṇṇic*) is possible after roots such as *budh*, this rule applies specifically to that which ends in it. Furthermore, the prohibition regarding "aṇi" (in the case of the primary suffix *aṇ*) also refers back to that very same suffix.

This is logical. Therefore, it is established in the Bhāṣya and other works that the *ātmanepada* suffix indeed occurs after a root belonging to the *curādi* class when followed by the causative *ṇic*. Consequently, the resulting meaning is this: the *ātmanepada* suffix does not occur after a causative *ṇic* if the root preceding that *ṇic* was intransitive (*akarmaka*) and distinct from another causative *ṇic*.

Why say "from an intransitive verb" (*akarmakāt*)? [Consider: *kaṭaṃ yaḥ karoti taṃ prayuṅkte* ("He employs one who makes a mat"), which results in *kaṭaṃ kārayati* ("He causes a mat to be made"). Why say "having an agent like the primary agent" (*citavat-kartṛkāt*)? [Consider: *śuṣyanti vrīhayaḥ tāñchoṣayate* ("The rice grains are drying; he causes them to dry"). (475) Pāda, dami, āṅ-yama, āṅ-ya, sa, pari-muh, ruc, nṛti, vad, and vas [are not included in this rule]. Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.89.

Roots that do not have an object are not necessarily those whose agent is not composed of feet. Although there appears to be a contradiction between the earlier statement that *dam* in the *divādi* group is transitive (*sakarmaka*) and the present statement that it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), they say that here *dam* is intransitive when there is an intention to express the object as the agent (*kartṛtva*). [The example is] *pāyayate*.
Regarding *ācchase*: this is derived from the root *yuk*. Regarding *āyāmayate*:
there is a prohibition of the *mit* designation by the rule *yamo'pariveṣaṇe*. Regarding *vāsayate*: this refers to the root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" (*nivāsa*).

However, there is no prohibition for the root *vas* in the sense of "clothing" (*ācchādane*), because, being transitive (*sakarmaka*), the [application of the *mit* designation] does not apply to it in that sense.

They say that when there is an intention to express the agenthood of the action (*karmakartṛtva*), even though the verb is intransitive (*akarmaka*), it is not included here due to the *lugvikaraṇa* paribhāṣā.
There is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the root *dheṭ*. "Samīcī" is the nominative dual. [The rule applies] optionally (*vā*).

The long vowel of the same class as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is applied by the rule *chandasi*. The sense is that the prohibition applies only to that *parasmaipada* which is obtained through the two rules beginning with *anantarasya*; thus, the *parasmaipada* must indeed occur.
[Thus ends the section on the determination of *pada*s in the *Parasmaipadaprakriyā* of the *Tattvabodhinī*.]
Now begins the section on technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*).
(29) *iko guṇavṛddhī* | 1.1.3 | [The terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* denote the vowels *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ* and their long counterparts.]
The technical term *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* apply to the *ik* vowels. This paribhāṣā operates only in those cases where the actual substituendum (*sthānin*) is not explicitly mentioned,
such as in rules like “*ārdhadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ*” and “*ici vṛddhiḥ*,” but not in rules like “*aco ñṇiti*,” because in the latter case the substituendum is explicitly indicated.

Regarding the phrase "by the words *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*": this is obtained by carrying forward (*anuvartana*) the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* from the two preceding sūtras and applying them through the construction, "those which are *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [as defined] by the rule 'of *uṇ*, *vṛddhi*.

Therefore, in this case, there is no substitution of *a* for the words beginning with *yat* (i.e., *yadādīnām aḥ*), as in *imam*; nor is there the substitution of *āṬ* for *iva*, as in *dyauḥ*. Thus, they are prescribed."

However, where there is a restatement (*anuvāda*), as in rules such as *vṛddhir yasyācām ādiḥ*, the genitive form *ikaḥ* does not apply; the point is that technical rules (*paribhāṣās*) do not apply in the context of a restatement.
The phrase "in a restatement, [the rules] of technical definitions" means "in the case of qualifiers of that which is being restated."

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the result (*phala*) regarding its non-appearance will be clarified under the rule *ṭhudīcām ātaḥ sthāne*. As for [the statement] "ending in the genitive": because the word ending in the genitive in the sūtra is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*), it refers to the actual form of the word; thus, due to its neuter gender, the nominative suffix *su* is elided.

The meaning is that there is no long vowel by the rule *ṭhathvasantasya ca*. Regarding the word *padam*: since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, it is connected in the sequence beginning with "of the stem (*aṅga*) ending in *ṭh* or *ig*.
However, in rules such as "there is guṇa for *idi*" and "there is vṛddhi for *mṛji*," [the connection is different].

Because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible, the *ika* [of the rule] is connected with the *avayava* [of the preceding rule, i.e., the *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* vowels]. (30) And for this reason: 1.2.28.
And for this reason: "short, long," etc. And this is [the meaning of] "a vowel (*ac*) having the duration of *ṭu* is short, long, or protracted."

By carrying forward (*anuvartya*) the terms *hrasva*, *dīrgha*, and *pluta* from the preceding *sūtra* and connecting them with the rule *yo ’j* (Pāṇini 7.3.103) as "the short, long, and protracted [vowel] when *ac* follows," the meaning is obtained. Why [mention] "short" and so forth? [Consider] *iva ut* [from] *dyubhyām*. Regarding the forms *aṣṭau* [from] *aṣṭan* by the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.1.21), and [the form] *aṣṭābhyaḥ* by the rule *aṣṭābhya āṬś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21).

Because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) consisting in the mention of the form *kṛtāt* [in Pāṇini 7.2.101], when the substitution of *ā* by the rule *ṭhaṣṭanaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.95) applies in the domain of *jaś* and *śas*, this [substitution] would not be established if it were not in the place of a vowel (*ac-sthānika*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. [The phrase] "the word ending in the genitive case" (*ṣaṣṭhyantaṃ padam*)—and that, when possible, is connected only through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and not otherwise.

[This occurs] through grammatical coordination (vaiyadhikaraṇya). Therefore, by the rule "hrasvo napuṃsake," the shortening applies only to a nominal stem (prātipadika) ending in /a/. Thus, we have *śrīpam*. But here, *suvāgrabrāhmaṇakulam* [is not shortened]. However, in the rule "amāmaṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ," because grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is impossible, it is connected with "of the vowels (*ac*) of *śam* and so on."

By this, forms such as *āmyati* are established. In the rule *vākyasya ṭeḥ plutaḥ*, although grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, the mention of *ṭi* by its own name (*ṭigrahaṇa*) serves as an indicator of force (*sāmarthya*), leading to the interpretation that the *pluta* vowel is the *ac* (vowel) which is a constituent part of the *ṭi*. Otherwise, [the rule] would have applied to the final letter [by *alo’ntyasya*] or to the *at* [by *ataśca*].

Since the *pluta* vowel of the final syllable in sentences such as "Come, Kṛṣṇa! is already established by the two rules of *paribhāṣā*, what is the purpose of this mention of *ṭi*? By means of it, forms such as "O long-lived Indravarman" are established; this is the general direction [of the argument].

(31) *Ādyantau ṭakitau* | Pāṇini 1.1.46. Those [suffixes] marked with the markers *ṭ* and *k* are respectively placed at the beginning and the end [of the element they are attached to]. *Ṭ*: *bhavitā*—[the suffix *tṛc* is added] by the rule *ārddhadhātukasyeḍ vaḷādeḥ*. *K*: *pāyayati*—[the suffix *nic* is added] by the rule *śācchāsāhvāvyāvepāṃ yuk*. This is according to the maxim of the "prior exception" (*purastādapavādanyāya*).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the status of being a *sthāni* (original element) due to its connection with a specific position. However, by the rule "the suffix [is applied] when *ara* follows," this [present rule] is superseded because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules]. Consequently, forms such as *areṣṭaḥ* and *āpoṣṭā* occur only as the subsequent [forms].

(32) *midaco ’ntyāt paraḥ* | 1|1|47 | The augment *mit* follows after the final vowel among the vowels and consonants (*ac*) [of the stem]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to both the rule of substitution (*sthāneyoga*) and the rule of posteriority (*para*), which states that "an affix (*pratyaya*) follows" and "is subsequent. Examples: *yaśāṃsi*, *vanāni*. [In these cases,] the augment *num* is applied by the rule *apuṃsakasya halacaḥ*.

It obstructs. [The suffix] *śnam* is applied after roots such as *ṛudh*. Now, one might object: "Just like the previous rule, this too should be an exception (*apavāda*) to the application of a substitute by the maxim of 'an exception set before' (*purastādapavāda-nyāya*). This is not so; for, by resorting to a consideration of the general scope of what is to be sublated (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*), everything that would otherwise apply within its own domain is sublated.

This is because it is accepted here [in this system] that [the augment *it*] is present; otherwise, the addition of the marker *m* in the rule for *śnam* would be purposeless. Nor should it be argued that the letter *m* is merely for the sake of pronunciation (*śravaṇārtha*), because of the specific grammatical indication (nirdeśa) in the rule *ṛṇaha i*.
As for the phrase "in the midst of vowels" (*acām madhye*), the intention is that the singular number in the sūtra—*ṭhacaḥ*—is used with reference to the class (*jāti*) of letters.

Why say "in the midst of these vowels"? [Consider the examples: *muñcati* and *lumpati*. According to the interpretation of the ancients—that the *mit* designation applies to a letter following the final vowel—this would not be established. This is because, in the rule *e mucādīnām*, the final vowel is impossible [as there is no vowel at all], and thus the *mit* paribhāṣā [would not apply].

[This would lead] to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the suffix] *niṣṭhā* being applied. Others, however, by rearranging the words to read "after the final consonant of the root (*aco’ntyāt*), the *mit* [augment] should follow," they somehow attempt to justify the earlier explanation as well.
From the preceding sūtra, the word *antaḥ* (end) is understood by virtue of its being designated as *svarita* in that specific portion. Therefore...
He explains: "as an internal part (*antāvayava*). By this, in forms such as *vārīṇi*, the long vowel is established because the stem (*aṅga*) ends in *n*.

If [the suffix] were initial (*parādittva*), that would not be established. However, if it were not a separate element (*abhaktatva*), then in the case of *vahaṃlihaḥ*—where the suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule *vahābhre lihaḥ* and the augment *muṭ* is added by the rule *arurdviṣad...*—[the desired form would fail].

The meaning is that the *anusvāra* would not occur because it is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*). As for what has been stated by some—that if it were not an *abhakta* (non-segmental), the long vowel in "vāriṇī" would not be produced—that is refuted by the very *vārttika* on the rule defining the technical term *aṅga*, which states: "The mention of *ad-ādi* [roots] is for the sake of the *num* augment in the case of *syati*."
This is almost spoiled.
(33) *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā* | 1|1|49|. "The genitive [case ending] is used in connection with 'place' (*sthāna*). The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a connection (*yoga*) by way of place."

The *e*-vowel [in *sthāne*] results from irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Although the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) generally expresses mere relationship, it should be understood in this science as denoting the "place of substitution" (*sthāneyoga*). Is this so without qualification?
No; he says: "when the specific nature of the relationship is not determined. Why the word "not determined"?

In rules such as *ṭhūdupadhāyā gohaḥ* and *āsa id aṅ hṛloḥ*, since it has been determined that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) by virtue of the proximity of the term *upadhā* (penultimate),

let there not be [such an interpretation] in cases like *ohaḥ* and *āsaḥ*. For if, even in those instances, the genitive were understood as denoting the *sthāna* (the position to be replaced), [undesirable results would follow].
The direction is as follows: in the place of *go-hi-āsa* and in the place of the root alone and its *upadhā*, the two vowels *ū* and *it* should occur;
and "place" (*sthāna*) means "occasion" (*prasaṅga*). Nor should one dispute that this word has the sense of "occasion," as in the expression: "In the place of arrows for children."

When it is said, "it should be spread," the understanding arises that *darbha* grasses are intended; likewise, in rules such as *ṭhiko yaṇaci*, when the possibility of pronouncing *ik* arises, the meaning results in the instruction that *yaṇ* should be pronounced instead. (34) *sthāne’ntaratamaḥ* | 1.1.50 | [In the place of an original element, that which is most similar [to the substitute] takes its place.]

"In the proper place" (*sthāne*) means "among those [vowels] which are to be obtained as most similar. For this very reason, in the case of *aṅgodakam*, the vowel *o* is not three-moraic (*trimātra*). Since the word *sthāne* is already being carried over (*anuvartamāna*) from the previous rule, the fact that *sthāne* is mentioned again here indicates that another meaning of the sentence is also intended.
"In a place such as *ālvādi*, that which is the most similar (*antaratama*)— meaning, that which possesses the closest internal correspondence—
is what [should apply] among the things being obtained.
This is what he expresses by saying, "where there are various kinds..."

The meaning is that [the substitution] is fourfold: by way of position (*sthāna*), meaning (*artha*), quality (*guṇa*), and measure (*pramāṇa*). By way of position, for example: *dadhy atra*. Here, the phoneme *y* (in *dadhi-y- atra*) has the same place of articulation (*tālusthāna*) as the phoneme *i* (in *dadhi*), which is the palate. By way of meaning, for example: *vātaṇḍī yuvatiḥ*. From the word *vataṇḍa*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied to form the feminine *vātaṇḍī* according to the rule "from *vataṇḍa* and others" (*vataṇḍācce*) in the sense of a female descendant (*gotrāpatya*).
Regarding the word *yañ*: there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "of *uka* when [the compound] refers to a woman. Due to its inclusion in the *śārṅgarava*-class, the suffix *ṅīn* is applied.
In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *vataṇḍī cāsau yuvatiśca* ("she who is both a Vataṇḍī and a young woman"), the compound is formed according to the rule "with *oṭā*, *yuvatī*, etc.
The masculine term being extended by the rule "*uṃvat* in a *karmadhāraya*" refers to one who denotes the offspring of Vataṇḍa.
The word *vātaṇḍya* becomes *vātaṇḍa* when it denotes his offspring; however, it does not become *vataṇḍādi*.

By way of quality (*guṇataḥ*), for example: *vāgghariḥ*. [In this case], the sound *gha* is exactly like the original *ha*, which is voiced (*ghoṣavat*), sonorous (*nādavat*), and aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*). By way of measure (*pramāṇataḥ*), for example: *amum*, *amū*, *amūn*. This is according to the rule *ṭhadaso’ser* (Pāṇini 8.2.80).

The short vowel *u* replaces a short [vowel], and the long vowel *ū* replaces a long [vowel]. Why is the term "the most" (*tamap*) included? [To ensure that] in the case of *vāgghari*, when the substitution of a homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*) is applied by the rule *hayo ho ’nyatarasyām*, the second [consonant, *gh*, which shares the property of being aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*)] or the third [consonant, *h*, which shares the property of being voiced (*nādavat*)] does not occur.

However, it is so that the fourth [consonant], *gh*, may indeed be a "great-breathed" (*mahāprāṇa*) sound. Regarding the term "more powerful" (*balīya*): the intention is that, in the case of *etā* and *tote*, the vowel *a* is not the closest in terms of phonetic proximity (*āntarya*) when measured by its measure (*pramāṇa*). (35) *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* | 1.1.66 || [When a rule is stated with the word "in that" (*tasmin*), the operation applies to what precedes.]
Regarding the word *tasmin*: this is an imitation (anukaraṇa) of a locative case ending. The sound *i* refers to immediate contiguity (*nairantarya*).

The root *diś* has the sense of "utterance. When it is stated that "in place of *ya*, there is *iṇ*," [the rule] would apply whether there is an intervention or no intervention; however, [by the principle of *pūrvaparayoḥ*] it would apply to both the preceding and the following [sounds], whereas by the principle of *pūrvaparayoḥ pūrvasyaiva*, it applies only to the preceding one. Thus [the purpose of the rule is established].

[The rule] is restricted. The phrase "of that which is not separated" (*avyavahitasya*) is a statement of the resulting meaning. [An example for the question] "Why 'of the preceding' (*pūrvasyaiva*)? is *dadhyudakam*. Here, let it not apply to the vowel *u* [in *dadhi*]. [An example for the question] "Why 'only of that which is not separated' (*avyavahitasyaiva*)? is *agnicid atra somasud atra*. And here, only separation caused by a phoneme (*varṇa*) is prohibited.

But it is not caused by time (kāla). This is because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) consisting of the governing rule for *saṃhitā*. Otherwise, since the non-application of *yaṇ* and other [substitutions] in non-*saṃhitā* would follow simply from the mention of "as specified" (*nirdiṣṭa*), what would be the purpose of that governing rule for *saṃhitā*? Therefore, he explains: "by another phoneme. And thus:
Prescriptions that fall outside the scope of the *saṃhitā* rules can apply even when there is an interruption by time (i.e., a pause).

Therefore, in cases such as *agnāviṣṇū*, even though there is an avagraha (separation), the substitutions such as *ānaṅ*—which are prescribed by rules like "in a *dvandva* [compound] ending in /n/ or /r/" and "in a *devatā-dvandva*"—do occur when followed by a subsequent word (*uttarapada*). This is the general direction of the argument.

(36) *tasmād ity uttarasya* |1|1|67|. Regarding the word *tasmāt*: what is the purpose of the phrase *uttarasya*? It is so that the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*—which prescribes the suppression of accent (*nighāta*)—should apply only to the immediately following [word]. As in *agnim īḷe*. But not here: *īḷe agnim*. [The rule applies] to that which is not separated by an intervening element.

And this is obtained by the continued application of the term *nirdiṣṭa* ("specified"). Therefore, in cases such as *utsaṃsthānam* and *utsaṃstambhanam*, the rule *ṭhudasthe* does not apply to produce a homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*). (37) *alo’ntyasya* | 1.1.52 | [The operation applies] to the final [element] among those [elements] denoted by the term *al*.

"Alo'ntyasya" (P. 1.1.52): The meaning is that whatever is prescribed for that which is indicated by a genitive case denoting "place" (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) should apply in place of the final *al* (vowel or consonant). For example, in the rule "yadādīnām aḥ" (P. 7.2.102), [the substitution of *a* applies] to *saḥ*, *yaḥ*, etc. Why specify "indicated by a genitive case denoting place"? Consider the rule "ṭhārdhadhātukasyaiṭ" (P. 7.2.35); [if it were not so specified, the augment *iṭ* might incorrectly be applied] before the *ṛ*-vowel of the suffix *tṛc*. And this [rule] is [an exception to] "aṣṭhī... (P. 1.1.49).

The word "sthāne" (in place of) is understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over). Why [is the condition] "alaḥ" (of an al [phoneme]) stated? [To ensure that] the substitution of *d* prescribed by the rule "ṭhvasusraṃsu" under the governing heading "adasi" does not apply to the final phoneme of a word, as in examples such as *paramānaḍudbhyām*.

(38) *ṅcci* |1|1|53|. Regarding *ṅcci*: this [term] also [is used]. For example: *avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya*—as in *gavāgram*; *anaṅ sau*—as in *sakhā*. Regarding "of what follows" (*parasya yad*): it is not [the case that] "from this [element], the first letter of what follows [is replaced]" applies here.

This is stated [in the commentary], because the portion "of the initial [consonant]" (*āder*) would result in subverting the universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*). In the final established view (*siddhānta*), however, he will state immediately below that the status of being a universal substitute is the subverter due to its higher priority. "It should be understood as [referring to] the initial" means it should be understood as referring to the initial *al* (vowel). For the term "*al*" is indeed carried over [from the previous rule].

(39) *anekāl-śit sarvasya* | Pāṇini 1.1.55. [The rule states: "That which has more than one *al* [phoneme] or is marked with *ś* replaces the whole. For example: *ṭhasterbhūḥ* [P. 2.4.52], as in *babhūva*. Now, one might object: since it is a well-established principle that "substitutes apply to that which is being indicated," the fact that the substitute has more than one *al* already ensures that it replaces the whole; why then state this explicitly?

So, what is the purpose of this mention of *anekāl*? Nor should it be suspected that, by the rule *alo’ntyasya*, [the substitute] would apply to the final letter, because it is accepted that the word *ca* in the rule *c-ai* serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*).
It is said in reply: in the absence of the mention of *anekāl*, in forms such as *rāmaiḥ*, the substitution of *ais* for *ādeḥ*...

The phrase "of the subsequent" (*parasya*) means that [the substitution] should apply only in place of the letter *bh*, and not in place of the entire word; such is the general principle. An example of a rule containing the term *śit* is: "For *idam*, *iś*" (*idama iś*), and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), rules such as "for *ataḥ*, *ais* after *bhis*" (*ato bhisa ais*) are included. Regarding the phrase "because of its being subsequent" (*paratvāt*): for this very reason, the rule "of the subsequent, starting from the beginning" (*ādeḥ parasya*) applies.

It has been stated that [the word] is separated [from its context]. Now, one might object: since the rule "of that which has more than one letter or is marked with ŚIT, the whole" (*anekāl-śit sarvasya*) precedes [this], should one not instead have read "from this, the first letter of what follows" (*asmād uttarasyādeḥ*)? What is the purpose of formulating this as a separate sūtra?
Nor can it be argued that, in that case, the mention of the term "indicated" (*nirdiṣṭa*) in the rule "when that which is indicated is this" (*asminn iti nirdiṣṭe*) would become redundant.

It should not be said that [the word *nirdiṣṭa*] does not recur here; for since there is no obstacle to reading that rule (*sūtra*) earlier as well, the recurrence of the term *nirdiṣṭa* is established. Do not say so; for in the case of "eight Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇā aṣṭau*), the substitution *auś* would undesirably apply even to the preceding forms of the nominative plural (*jas*) and accusative plural (*śas*) after the word *aṣṭan*.

However, if one accepts the sūtra exactly as it was heard, the portion "of what follows" (utarasya) indeed applies, and thus this fault does not arise. On this point, some state the essential conclusion: for the sake of brevity of syllables, the sūtra should have been formulated as "asmād utarasyādeḥ" (from this, of the following initial [element]) even before the sūtra "anekāl-śit-sarvasya."

Because it is subsequent, it supersedes the portion "of the first" (*ādeḥ*) by means of a universal application (*sarvādeśa*), and because there is no distinction [between the two portions], the portion "of the following" (*utarasya*) is also superseded; thus, under the view that the sentence is processed as a whole (*vākya-saṃskāra-pakṣa*), when *brāhmaṇa* + *as* and *aṣṭan* + *as* have been established,
[the rule] *aṣṭābhya auś* applies in the sense of a directional relation (*dig-yoga*).

By the principle of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*), since [the word] *aṣṭan* is part of the base (*aṅga*), the substitution of *auś* would apply even to the preceding *jaś* and *śas* endings. However, as for the principle of pervasion, even though it is stated that "particles (*nipāta*) are those ending with *rāgvīśvara*," the limit of the rule is established as being up to the sūtra *adhir īśvare* by means of the principle of proximity (*pratyāsattinyāya*).

By the author of the Sūtras himself, who employs the mention of the form *ṭh* (including the *repha*) in the rule *ṭhīśvare tosunkasunau* in order to refute the view that [the suffixes] have a limit (*avadhika*), it is indicated [that the rule applies]. Consequently,
this is for the purpose of not subverting the portion of the rule *ṭh-utarasya*, and for the purpose of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of the specific term (*nirdiṣṭagrahaṇa*).

Furthermore, if the rule *asminniti* were applied after the rule *ṭhāder* [in the formation of the locative singular], then *ṭhāder* would act as a sublater of the universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*). Consequently, in rules such as *ato bhisa ais*, the substitute would apply only to the initial [portion] of the stem; for the rule concerning multiple phonemes (*anekāl*) has already found its scope of application in cases such as *asterbhūḥ*.

Under the alternative arrangement (*yathānyāsa*), however, the portion "of what follows" (*utarasya*) would indeed apply; consequently, *auś* would occur only for the nominative and accusative plural endings (*jaś-śas*) that follow the eight [numerals], but not for those preceding them. Likewise, [the rule] "of the first letter of what follows *asmāt*" would not apply.

This is precisely the intention of the *Manoramā* commentary regarding the passage beginning with "it is not stated in the Sūtra" (*sūtritam*). Others, however, interpret the *Manoramā* as being solely intent on refuting the Sūtra exactly as it is heard. For example: the meaning of "it is not stated in the Sūtra" is not that it was stated in the Sūtra prior to the rule *anekāl śit sarvasya*.

Because this would contradict the subsequent portion of the text which states that the element *ṭha* (in the rule *ṭhādi*) is intended to override all substitutes (*sarvādeśa*), one must instead accept the meaning that it was formulated prior to the sūtra *vaṃ rūpam*. And thus, if it were formulated prior to the sūtra *anekāl-*, [then...]
The intention of the *Manoramā* is that there is indeed no fault. This being the case,

in order to ensure the continuation of the term "nirdiṣṭa" (specified), the rule "asminniti nirdiṣṭe" (when this is specified) should be recited prior to the rule "asmādityukte ādeḥ parasya" (when this is mentioned, [the substitute occurs] in place of the first letter of what follows).

The objection raised—that the suffix *auś* would apply even to the two preceding [sounds] from the word *aṣṭan*—should be resolved as follows: In the rule *“asmādityuttarasyādeḥ parasya”* (Pāṇini 1.1.54), the word *“ādeḥ”* constitutes a separate sentence. Therein, the term *“uttarasya”* is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*. Furthermore, that is a genitive of position (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), as in the rule *“aṣṭhī...”* (Pāṇini 1.4.1).

This is because [the word] *sthāne* is understood [from the previous rule]. And there, the meaning is as follows: "Whatever operation is prescribed by means of a mention in the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*) pertains to what follows"; and "whatever is prescribed in place of what follows (*uttarasya sthāne*) occurs at the beginning [of that following element].
Thus, by resorting to an interpretation through a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), [the rule applies] according to the maxim *anantarasya* ("of the immediate [following]").
Only the portion "of what follows" (*aḥ*) is sublated by the universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*), and not even the subsequent portion "of what precedes" (*ataḥ*);

thus, the aforementioned fault does not exist at all. Furthermore, the explanation through syntactic split (*vākyabheda*) is indicated by the composition of the rule as *utarasyādeḥ* rather than as a compound. Otherwise, [the fault would remain].

One might say that "ṭhutarādeḥ" was not formulated as a sūtra. Furthermore, since the rule "aṣṭana ā vibhaktau" (Pāṇini 7.2.84) involves a directional relation (*digyoga*), the ablative case indicates that it applies equally to both preceding and following elements; thus, even when it is stated that "jaś and śas [are substituted] after the base 'aṣṭan'," those two [suffixes] which serve as the cause for the designation of the base (*aṅgasaṃjñā*)—[namely, the following *jaś* and *śas*]—[would also be included].

Since *jaś* and *śas* alone have rapid presentation (*śīghropasthiti*), the substitution *āṬ* would apply only to the subsequent [sounds] after the word *aṣṭan*, and not to the preceding ones; such is the general direction of the argument.

(40) *svaritenādhikāraḥ* | Pāṇini 1.3.11. The term *svarita* [refers to] the governing rule (*adhikāra*). Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe*). *Adhikāra* means application (*viniyoga*). As for how far the governing rule extends, one must rely solely upon the commentary.

For example: the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for the *aṅga* [section] extends until the completion of the seventh chapter, and not merely until before the rules concerning repetition and modification (*abhyāsa-vikāra*), and so forth. Alternatively, the word "svarita" ends in the locative case;
the meaning is that when a *svarita* accent is perceived, the governing rule ceases. Which one?

The svarita accent is for the purpose of indicating a governing rule (*adhikāra*), and as for what is intended to terminate that [governing force], here indeed only the commentary (*vyākhyāna*) is the refuge. If it is asked: "In that case, since the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) and non-continuation [of a rule] occur simply through the commentary, what is the use of this sūtra?", they say in response: "This sūtra was composed in order to include other meanings."

For instance: *adhi* means "additional" (*adhika*); *adhikāra* is the "additional function. The meaning is that the application of the grammatical rule (*śāstra-pravṛtti*) extends even to secondary (*gauṇa*) elements. Thus, wherever the principle of primary and secondary (*gauṇa-mukhya-nyāya*) is not desired—as in the case of the ablative (*apādāna*) and locative (*adhikaraṇa*)—there the *svarita* accent should be recited. Furthermore, it is an additional function (*adhikaḥ kāraḥ*).
This is the author’s view: that which, being prior, subverts what follows.

Thus, all the subsequent rules regarding prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*)—such as “*nuṭ* [takes precedence] over *uṅ*, *aci-rat*, and *tṛj-vadbhāva*” and so forth—are encompassed; for in those cases, the purpose is already achieved by the mere recitation of the rule with a *svarita* accent.

Regarding the term *paranitya* (eternally subsequent): it is eternal in the sense that it applies even when another rule follows. For example: *tudādibhyaḥ śaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.77], as in *tudati*; and *rudhādibhyaḥ śnam* [Pāṇini 3.1.78], as in *ruṇaddhi*. Because these are eternal (*nitya*), they override the guna substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), which would otherwise apply subsequently. Similarly, in *dhinavāva* and *dhinavāma*, [the subsequent rule] overrides even...

In the case of *dadhnā*, the augment *āṬ* is applied by the rule *āḍ-uta-masya* because it is obligatory (*nitya*), thereby overriding the elision of the vowel *u* prescribed by *upadhāyāśca anyatarasyām mvoḥ*. Furthermore, although the rule *anekāl-śit sarvasya* prescribes a replacement of the entire stem, this is overridden by the rule *iccēti*, which effects a replacement of only the final phoneme. Thus, *dadhnā*.

In the case of *dadhni*, the substitution *anaṅ* applies by the rule *ṭhasthidadhī*. An internal operation (*antaraṅga*) prevails over an obligatory one (*nitya*): as in *grāmaṇinī kule*. Here, the short vowel (*hrasva*) by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake* sets aside the *num* augment which would otherwise apply obligatorily by the rule *iko ’ci* (Pāṇini 7.1.73). For if the *num* were applied first, the word would not end in a vowel (*anajanta*), and thus the shortening would not occur.

An exception (*apavāda*) prevails over that which is internal (*antaraṅga*): for example, in *daityāriḥ* and *rīśaḥ*. Although the internal rule of *guṇa* (by *ādguṇaḥ*) and the subsequent rule of *yaṇ*-sandhi would apply, the long vowel of identical quality (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*) takes precedence because it is an exception. Similarly, in *unnyaḥ*, *sulvau*, and *ulvaḥ*.

In this case, although *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would [otherwise] apply due to their being *antaraṅga*, the rule *eranekāco ’saṃyogapūrvasya* (P. 6.4.82) applies because it is an exception (*apavāda*). Furthermore, by the rule *aco ñṇiti* (P. 7.2.115), *vṛddhi* is applied. Even if an exception is effective elsewhere, when *uvaṅ* and *ci* (the augment *ci*) would otherwise apply due to being *para* and *antaraṅga*, the rule *eranekāco ’saṃyogapūrvasya* applies because it is an exception. By the rule *ṭh-oḥ supi* (P. 6.4.130), *yaṇ* is applied. Even if an exception is effective elsewhere... when *uvaṅ* and *ci* would otherwise apply due to being *para* and *antaraṅga*, the rule *eranekāco ’saṃyogapūrvasya* applies because it is an exception. By the rule *ṭh-oḥ*... [the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs].

Regarding the rule *supi* and the substitution *yaṇ*: even though the augment *āt* would apply elsewhere as an exception (*apavāda*) once its purpose is fulfilled, it is nevertheless superseded by the subsequent rule *ṭh-anekāl-śit* [Pāṇini 1.1.55]. Thus: *jīvatāt*, *bhavatāt*, *ayaje indram*, *grāme iha*, *sarve ittham*. Herein: *ayaja i indram*, *grāma iha*.
Since it is established that "all [rules] are thus," the long vowel by homogeneous quality (*savarṇadīrgha*) is superseded by the internal rule of *guṇa*,
because the former has its application elsewhere, such as in *aiti āriḥ* and *rīśa*, where the bases are not identical.
Regarding the term *asiddham*: by this, in cases such as *acāvedam*, the substitution of *ai* according to the rule *ṭheta ai* does not take place.

Regarding the phrase *akṛtavyūhāḥ*: the meaning is "those for whom the grammatical operation has not been performed. If that were so, the entire treatise would be rendered useless; therefore, he says: "having seen that the cause is on the verge of destruction."
This is a statement of a meaning established in common worldly usage. Alternatively, this is also explained according to the literal meaning of the syllables:

*ūha* means that which is inferred or reasoned—that is, an effect (*kārya*). A "special inference" (*vyūha*) is an effect characterized by being oriented toward destruction. Those by whom no such *vyūha* has been performed are [the *avyūhakṛtaḥ*].

Regarding the rule *akṛtavyūhāḥ*: although another technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is recited as *ṛtam api śāstraṃ nivartayanti* ("even a settled rule may be set aside"), and the result is the same, nevertheless *akṛtavyūhāḥ* alone is more concise, according to the maxim: "It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off."

The meaning is: "they do not apply. For instance, in examples such as *niṣeduṣīm*, although the augment *iṭ* would be applicable to the suffix *kvasu* because it is an internal (*antaranga*) operation, they do not apply it, having considered that the status of being preceded by a consonant (*valāditva*) would be destroyed by the process of *saṃprasāraṇa*. This is the sense.
Thus ends the section on technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) in the *Tattvabodhinī*.

(1470) Pāṇini 5.3.2: *kiṃ-sarvanāma-bahubhyaḥ avyādibhyaḥ* [the suffix *tham* is added after the words *kim*, all pronominals (*sarvanāman*), and the word *bahu*, provided they are not among the group beginning with *ava*].

What is a *sarvanāman*? Why is *kim* mentioned separately [in Pāṇini 1.1.27] when it is already included among the *dvi-ādi* (the group beginning with *dvi*)? The purpose of including the word *kim* within the *dvi-ādi* list is for cases such as *tvaṃ ca kaśca kau*, *ahaṃ ca kaśca kau*, and *bhavāṃśca kaśca kau*, where there is the elision (*śeṣa*) of *kim* according to the rule: “In the co-utterance of words beginning with *yat* with one another... (Pāṇini 1.2.68).
Because it has been stated, "That which remains is the supreme [reality].
(1471) *etado ’n* | 5|3|5|. This reading is established in the Bhāṣya; however, the author of the Vṛtti reads *etado ’ś*.

Having recited [the rule], Śakāra says that [the suffix] serves the purpose of being a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*). He explains: "In *aniti*," when a *prāgdiśīya* suffix follows, there is substitution of the final letter (*antyāt*). This is because [the suffix] consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*). The intention is that there is no purpose for the application of the marker *n* (in *anit*), since the *n* of the suffix itself is intended to serve as an accentual marker (*svarārtha*).

(1472) *ku tihoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.104. In the rule *ku tihoḥ*, the letter *t* at the beginning of *tihaḥ* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). To demonstrate the result of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *vā* ("or"), he asks: "Why? [The answer is: "From what," and "therefore. This is because of the rule *ṛtaddhite*.

Due to its status as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is *luk* elision of the case-ending (*sup*); then, by the rule *tyadādīnām atvaṃ*, [the final vowel becomes *a*]. In one alternative: *yasmāt*, *tasmāt*, *iti*. [In the other alternative: by the rule *idamo ‘ś*, [it becomes *aś*]; in one alternative: *asmāt*, *ataḥ*. By the rule *etado ‘nādeśaḥ*, [there is the substitution of *an*]; in one alternative: *etasmāt*, *amutaḥ*. By the rule *adaso seḥ*, there is the substitution of *mut*; in one alternative: *amuṣmāt*.

Regarding *bahubhyaḥ*: in the alternative case (pakṣe), it is from *bahubhyaḥ*. Regarding *dvābhyām*: although the suffix *tasil* would have applied here because [the word] is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), it does not apply due to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule "not after *dvi* and so forth. Regarding *taseḥ*: this refers to the suffix *tasi* prescribed by the rules "after the fifth case ending in connection with *ati*" and "also after the fifth case ending in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*), except for the roots *hā* and *ruh*."

The meaning is that *tasi* is replaced by *tasil*. Regarding the phrase "and for the sake of the case-ending (*vibhaktyarthe*)": the intention is that otherwise, if *tasi* were applied first because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], then—since it would not belong to the *prāgdiśīya* class—the designation of case-ending (*vibhakti-saṃjñā*) would not apply, and consequently, the substitution of *yat* for the *tad*-class stems (as in *tyadādyatvam*) would be absent, whereby forms such as *yataḥ* and *avagacchati* would not be established. Now, [one might object] regarding *tasi* from *grāmataḥ*...

In such cases, since [the suffix *tas*] has already fulfilled its purpose through [the rule for] *kim* and so forth, the suffix *tasi* does not apply as something that would sublate [the suffix *tas*], because it lacks an unrestricted scope (*niravakāśatva*). Thus, one might argue that the prescription "after *as*, [the suffix *tasi* is used]" is redundant; however, this is not so, because [the suffix *tasi* applies] in the case of "he falls away from the *ut*" (*uto’vahīyate*).

In examples such as ‘uto ’varohati’, the suffix *tasil* has its own scope [of application]. [The suffix *trala*] occurs only after words expressing the meanings of *sarva* and *ubhaya*. In this matter, the very nature of linguistic expression (*abhidhāna-svābhāvya*) is the reason. Therefore, it does not occur here: *pariṣiñcati*.
He sprinkles [it]. *Pari* is used in the sense of "above"; *abhi* is used in the sense of "facing toward. If it is asked:

"In the expression 'he sprinkles around the rice' (*odanaṃ pariṣiñcati*), since *pari* signifies 'on all sides,' how is there the absence of the suffix *tasil*?"—do not say so; for that is established by the continued application of the rule regarding the optionality of the suffix.

(1473) *saptamyāstral* |5|3|10|. Regarding *saptamyāstral*: here, the suffixes *tral* and *tasil* are independent suffixes (*svatantra-pratyaya*), and not substitutes (*ādeśa*) for the locative (*saptamī*) or ablative (*pañcamī*). Consequently, in forms such as *kutra*, *bahutra*, *kutaḥ*, and *bahutaḥ*, the rule *acca gheḥ* [6.1.172] applies.
They say that [the suffix] *herṅ* and so forth do not apply here.
(1474) *kimo’t* | 5|3|12 | Regarding *kimo’t*: the prohibition [stated in] "not before a case-ending (*vibhakti*) when *t*, *s*, or *m* follow" does not apply here.
Because the letter *tha* is used with the long vowel *au* (thamorukāra) for the purpose of protecting the letter *ma* by indicating impermanence (*anityatā*).
Regarding the mention of "or" (*vā*): it would have been more appropriate to state the rule as *ṭh ha ca chandasi*, after having recited the rule *imo’dvā*.

(1475) *kvā* [Pāṇini 5.3.105]: *kutra*. Although the author of the Bhāṣāvṛtti does not accept the suffix *tral* for the word *bāṣā*, it has nevertheless been accepted here because it is observed in extensive usage. And so says Śrīharṣa: "Neither elsewhere nor anywhere else..."
With longing, Amara said: "And [the suffix] *cha* occurs after [a word ending in] *sāhacarya* in certain cases. (Pāṇini 5.2.22).
[The rule is: *vā ha ca chandasi* (5.3.13). Regarding the phrase *vā ha ca chandasi*, this is a re-introduction (*apakarṣaṇa*) of the previously mentioned option (*vā*).
This has been presented for the sake of clarification. "From this" (*ataḥ*) means "from this village.

Because of the inclusion of the term *dṛśi* (to see), [the suffix] occurs only in connection with *bhavadīya*. For example: *tatrabhavantam*, *tato bhavatā*, *tatra bhavatā*, *tato bhavate*, *tatra bhavate*, and so forth. "In the same way" (*evam*) refers to [the subsequent examples] from "then" (*tataḥ*).

The meaning is that [the forms] *dīrghāyuḥ* and *tatra dīrghāyuḥ*, and so forth, are to be inferred [from the rules]. Regarding *sada*: the substitution of *sa-* occurs by the rule *sarvasya so’nyatarasyāṃ dī*. Regarding *kada*: the substitution of *ka-* occurs by the rule *imaḥ kaḥ*. (Pāṇini 5.3.16) *idamo rhil*. (Note: The rule *idamo rhil* is cited as the source for the formation of *kadā* from *idam*.)
Regarding *etarhi*: it is the substitution of *etarhi* for the two [elements] *tad* and *idam*.

(Pāṇini 5.3.16). Regarding *adhunā* (5.3.17): this suffix *adhunā* is acutely accented on the middle syllable due to its being an irregular formation (*nipātana*); and this is the opinion of the Bhāṣya.

The author of the Vṛtti, however, says: "The absence of *idam* [is expressed by] *aś*, and *dhunā* is the suffix. In that regard, Haradatta maintains that the accent of the case-ending is applied by the rule *ṭhūḍidaṃ padāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.171), and that this [accentuation] occurs by the application of the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54).

Therefore, the mention of *dā* is redundant because [the desired form] has already been established; the intention is that the rule should simply be read as *adaśca*. (1479) *anadyatane rhil anyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 5.3.21.

"At this time" is expressed as *etarhi*. [The form] *etad* [is derived] by the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) [Pāṇini 5.3.4], whereby the substitute *etā* occurs in place of the initial [sound] following the *repha* (the letter *r*).

(1480) [The temporal adverbs are: *sadyas*, *parut*, *parāri*, *aiṣamas*, *paredyavi*, *adya*, *pūrvedyus*, *anyedyus*, *anyataredyus*, *itaredyus*, *aparedyus*, *adharedyus*, *ubhayedyus*, and *uttaredyus*.
Regarding Pāṇini 5.3.22, *sadyaḥ* and *parut*: he states that a specific scope is obtained through nipātana (irregular derivation) by saying "on the day" (*ahani*).
This means in the sense of the word *ahan* ending in the locative case.
The substitution of *sa* for *samāna* occurs when followed by *dya* or *ahani*, as in *samāne’hanīti*. Regarding *para udārīca*: *para* is the substitute, and *udārī* are the two suffixes.
(1481) *thāl* is used in the sense of expressing manner (*prakāra*). 5.3.23.
The suffix *thāl* is used in the sense of expressing a "manner" (*prakāra*). A "manner" is a particular that differentiates a general category;

for example, according to Haradatta, the sub-groups such as Māṭhara and Kāṭhaka differentiate the general category of "Brāhmaṇa. Although in the rule *guṇavacanasya raḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.58) similarity is taken as the "manner," here similarity is not intended.

Because it has not been so stated. It should be understood that there is no contradiction between the preceding and the following statements: in the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti* (Pāṇini 2.4.82), it was stated that similarity (*sādṛśya*) is also a meaning of the word *yathā*, whereas here it is stated that for the suffix *thāl* alone, similarity is not the meaning, but rather the "manner" (*prakāra*) itself. Therefore—

"In this manner, so"—it does not occur with a word ending in the nominative case, such as *sa prakāraḥ tathā* ("that manner is so"), because of the very fact that [the formation] is not prescribed [in that way]; this is the underlying intention. Even though the suffix *thāl* is specifically prescribed for words beginning with *kiṃ*, all interrogative pronouns (*sarvanāman*), and polyptote words (*bahuvrīhi*), it is not superseded by the suffix *jātīyar*, because their meanings differ. For *thāl* is used in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*), whereas *jātīyar* is used in the sense of "belonging to the class" (*jāti*).

In that which possesses [the quality], it arises from its own nature (*svabhāvāt*). And having established the suffix *thāl* in this way to denote the mere manner (*prakāramātre*), they employ the suffix *jātīyar* after a word ending in *thāl* to denote that which possesses the manner— such as *tathājātīyaḥ*,
*yathājātīyaḥ*, and *anyathājātīyaḥ*.

This also should be stated as "anena" or "etena. The suffix *thamu* occurs even after a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*), as in "one who has reached this manner" (*itthambhūtaḥ*)—namely, "this" (*imam*) or "that" (*etam*) manner. And here, the evidence is found in Vedic sūtra-usage such as "in the expression of one who has reached such a state" (*akṣaṇetthambhūtākhyāne*). By this...
In what manner has it been explained? It is as follows: in the example *itetau rathau*, there is the substitution of *ita-* for *idam*.
The intention is that by the rule-splitting (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *etadaḥ*, the substitution of *ita-* occurs for *etad* as well.
(1482) *kimaśca* | 5|3|25 | [The suffix *thañ* is applied after *kim* and *etad* in the sense of "therein"].
Furthermore, there is a purpose for this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*): so that in the subsequent sūtra, "hā hetau ca chandasi," only *kim* may be carried over (*anuvṛtti*), and not *idam*.
Thus ends the section on the *prāgdiśīya* suffixes in the *Tattvabodhinī*.

(1235) *tadvahati rathayugaprāsaṅgam* |4|4|76|. [The word] *yugya* means "that which carries the *yuga*"—the meaning being that it carries the *yuga*, which is a part of a chariot. [The word] *prāsaṅga*: [it is derived] from the root *pra-sañj* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), meaning "that which is attached."
(1236) *dhuro yaḍḍhakau* |4|4|77|. After *dhur*, [the suffixes] *ya* and *ḍhak* [are applied]. It would be easier to state it simply as: “after *dhur*, *ḍhak* and *cha*.
(1237) *na bhakurcchurām* |4|4|79|. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is not applied] after words ending in *bhak*, *kur*, and *chur*.
Regarding the rule *na bh- upadhāyāḥ*: the intention is that this is obtained from the preceding sūtra, *upadhāyāṃ ca*.

Why [is it specified] "of the penultimate vowel" (*upadhāyāḥ*)? Consider *pratidīvnaḥ*. Here, although the word ending in *-n* is a *bha*-stem, the prohibition does not apply because the vowel *i* is not penultimate (*anupadhatvāt*).

(1238) *khaḥ sarvadhurāt* | Pāṇini 4.4.78. Regarding the rule *khaḥ sarvadhurāt*: although it should have been stated as *sarvadhurāyāḥ*, the neuter designation is used with respect to the phonetic form of the word, just as in the rule *andhuni bahuvrīhau*. [The example is] *sarvadhuram*.
The compound is *ūrvakālaika*. By the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ—*, the suffix *ap* is added at the end of the compound, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. (1239) *ekadhurālluk ca* | Pāṇini 4.4.79.

"From *ekadhura*, there is elision (*luk*) [of the suffix], and by the word 'and' (*ca*), there is also the suffix *kha*. Thus, it follows that while there is elision of the suffix prescribed in the present context, the suffix *kha* is heard because of its specific rule of application; this is what he states in the words beginning with *ekadhurīṇa*. (1240) From *śakaṭa*, the suffix *aṇ*. [Pāṇini 4.4.80]

[The example is] *śākaṭo gauḥ* ("an ox that draws a cart"). [Objection: But this is already established by the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "this belongs to him" (*asyedam*). For indeed, that which draws a cart belongs to the cart. To this they reply: By the force of the formal introduction [of the rule], there is here an application of the rule to that which ends in [the word mentioned]. Therefore, in the case of *dvaiśakaṭaḥ* ("one who draws two carts"), [the suffix applies].

In the case of the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*, the suffix *cha* does not undergo elision (*luk*) by the rule *vṛddhaluganapatye*; however, in the case of the suffix *aṇ* [introduced] by the rule *asyedam*, there would indeed be elision (*luk*).
(1241) Pāṇini 4.4.81: *halasīrāṭ ṭhak*.

[The suffix] from *halasīra*. Now, an objection might be raised: "In the introductory rule ‘asyedaṃ,’ it was stated that [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after *halasīta*; thus, since forms such as *hālikaḥ* and *sairikaḥ* are already established by that very same secondary (*śaiṣika*) suffix, what is the purpose of this present rule? This is true; however, by the force of its original formulation (*ārambhasāmarthyāt*), the rule for suffixes ending in that [previous element] (*tadantavidhi*) applies here as well.

Thus, it becomes *dvaihalika* and *dvaisīrika*; however, if the secondary suffix (*śaiṣika*) *ṭhak* were applied, there would be elision (*luk*) according to the rule for words derived from place names (*prāgdīvyatīya*). Relying on the etymological derivation "in which the embryo is born" (*jāyate asyāṃ garbhaḥ*), he says:

(1242) *saṃjñāyāṃ janyāḥ* | Pāṇini 4.4.82. [The word] *janī* means "bride. [It is derived as follows: from the roots *jan* and *vadh*, [the suffix] *iṇ* is applied by the rule *ani-ghasi-bhyām iṇ*. There is no *vṛddhi* [substitution] because of the rule *ani-vadhyoś ca*. Then, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṛd-ikārād iti*. After that, the suffix *yat* is applied by this present sūtra.

The term *janya* refers to the bridegroom’s companions (*jāmātuḥ vayasyāḥ*), for it is they who lead the bride to the presence of the groom during the wedding and other ceremonies. Kālidāsa, however, applied the term even to the carriers of the bride’s vehicle— as in the verse, "the maiden spoke to the *janyas* who were departing"— meaning those who carry the bride (*janīm vahanti iti janyāḥ*).

(1243) *vidhyatyadhanuṣā* |4|4|83|. Regarding the term *padyā*: the substitution of *pad* occurs by the rule *adyatyatadarthe*. Why say "not with a bow" (*adhanuṣā*)? [Consider: *coraṃ vidhyati* ("he pierces the thief"). For in the piercing of a thief, the bow is indeed considered an instrument (*karaṇa*). However, when...

When the word *dhanuṣ* is employed [in the sense of "having obtained"], it does not occur precisely because of its being dependent (*sāpekṣatva*). And thus, in the phrase "if the bow is the instrument here," one should understand that the word "is expected" (*saṃbhāvyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder. (1244) *dhanagaṇaṃ labdhvā* | 4|4|84|.

Regarding the term *tṛnnantam*: the sense is that, because the genitive case used in connection with a *kṛt* suffix is prohibited by the rule *a loka-* etc., the usage *hanagaṇam* is free from objection. (1245) *vaśaṃ gataḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.86).

*Vaśaṃgataḥ*. *Vaśanam* is *vaśaḥ*—meaning desire (*icchā*). [The suffix] *ap* is applied by the rule "after the roots *vaś* and *iṣ*, the suffix *ap* is used when not counting" (Pāṇini 3.3.58). (1246) *Mūlam asyābarhi* | Pāṇini 4.4.88. From the word *mūla* ending in the nominative case, which has the qualifier *ābarhi*, [the suffix *cha* is added] in the sense of "this belongs to that."

The suffix *yat* occurs in the sense of the sixth case (genitive). Regarding the word *āvarha*: the root *vṛh* (in the form *ā-vṛh*) means "to uproot" (*udyamana*); it begins with a labial (*oṣṭhya*) and a dental (*adantya*), and not with a letter from the final class (*paravarga*), as seen in usages such as *udvṛha rakṣaḥ sahamūlam indre*. The phrase *mūlyā mudgāḥ* ("mung beans by the root") means they cannot be gathered without uprooting them from the ground.

When [the stalks] are being plucked from the middle, even those remaining in the sheaths would fall at that stage; that is to say, they have reached a state of being perfectly dried. Regarding the suffix *ya*:
by that, the word *dhenuṣyā* has its final syllable accented (*udātta*). The intention is that otherwise, it would be subject to the accent of the *tit* suffix.

(1247) *dhenuṣyā* [is used] in the sense of a name. Regarding the word "in the sense of a name": this is the name for that cow which is given to a creditor for the purpose of milking, in order to repay a debt.
(1248) *Ñya* is added after [the word] *gṛhapati*.

[The form] *gārhapatya* [is derived thus]: the suffix is applied to the word ending in the third case (*gṛhapatinā*), precisely because of the specific mention of *gṛhapatinā*. Due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the condition "when it is a name" (*saṃjñāyām*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to [terms such as] *āhavanīya* and others.

(1249) *nau-vayas-dharma-viṣa-mūla-mūla-sītā-tulābhyaḥ* [the suffix *yat* is applied] after *nau*, *vayas*, *dharma*, *viṣa*, *mūla*, *mūla*, *sītā*, and *tulā*, in the eight senses of "to be crossed," etc., respectively. 4|4|91.
*nau-vayas-dharma-*: After the words *nau* and the others, the suffix *yat* is applied in the eight respective meanings beginning with "to be crossed."

Since it will be stated here that "the third case ending occurs in connection with *tārya* and so forth according to possibility, as well as in connection with the instrumental (*karaṇa*), the agent (*kartṛ*), the cause (*hetu*),

and words having the sense of 'equal' (*tulyārtha*)," it follows by implication that this very [instrumental] is the case-ending expressing capacity (*samarthavibhakti*) in this context. Here, first, there is a *dvandva* compound of the five words ending in *mūla*.

Having formed a compound by means of a *dvandva* with "second" (*dvitīya*) starting from the root [of the suffix], there is a collective *dvandva*. Having formed a *dvandva* of two or three items beginning with "root" (*mūla*), or of the items beginning with "root" alone, there is no *dvandva* among "boat" (*nau*) and the others.

Consequently, because of the absence of homogeneity (*sārūpya*), a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) does not occur. [The example] "to be crossed by boat" (*nāvā tāryam*) is used in the sense of possibility (*śakya*).

By the rule *ṭhṛhalorṇyat*, the third case is used when the suffix denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding the word *vayasya*: Amara states, "A *vayasya* is a friend (*sakhā*) of equal age (*savayas*). However, this does not apply in the case of "an enemy equal in age" (*vayasā tulyaḥ śatruḥ*), because that falls under the heading of technical names (*saṃjñā-adhikāra*). Regarding *viṣeṇa vadhyaḥ*: it means one who deserves death by means of poison.
This is because the suffix *yat* is prescribed after the word *vadha* in the sense of "deserving" (*arha*) by the rule *aṇḍādibhyaḥ*.

Regarding the phrase "to be increased by the principal" (*mūlenābhyam*): "principal" (*mūla*) refers to the capital invested by merchants for the purpose of producing cloth and other goods. From that [capital], the substance consisting of profit (*lābhākhya*) which exceeds one's own [original] amount is directed toward oneself.
That which is made subordinate—that is, made subservient to one's own benefit—is called *ānāmya*.

The root √nam preceded by the prefix *ā* signifies "to overcome. Therefore, although the suffix *yat* would have been expected by the rule *oradupadhāt*, the suffix *ṇyat* is used here due to this very fact of being a conventional irregularity (*nipātana*). Likewise...
And that which is not to be bent down, not to be overcome, must be made subordinate to the Self; and that is precisely the portion called "gain" (lābha).

In common worldly usage, however, the word "price" (mūlya) is well-known to apply to the entire aggregate of goods by which a cloth or the like is sold, and not merely to the portion in excess of the cost-price. And thus...

It should be understood that the word *mūlya*, which is etymologically derived in the sense of "merely obtained," possesses a conventional secondary signification (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) when applied to a compound containing that term. Regarding the word *sītā*: it means the tip of a plough. It is formed from the root *iṇ* with the prefix *sam* and the suffix *kta*;
the meaning is "made level" (*samitam*), that is, made even, free from depressions and elevations.
"Samīkṛtam" (made equal) is the intended meaning. According to the rule "ratha-sītā-halebhyo yad-vidhau," there is an extension of the suffix to the end of the compound.

Thus, *parama-sītyam* (exceedingly even). From the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), a compound is formed meaning "equalized by two furrows" (*dvābhyāṃ sītābhyāṃ samitam*), and from that, the suffix *yat* is applied:
*dvisītyam*. Likewise, "equalized by a balance" (*tulayā saṃmitam*).
"Measured" (saṃmita) means "cut off at the top. This is a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*) because it falls under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*).
For this very reason, the word "equal" (*tulya*) is used in the sense of mere similarity, and no etymological derivation (*āgama-graha*) from the word "scale" (*tulā*) is made.

(1250) *Dharmapathyarthanyāyādanapete* [Pāṇini 4.4.92]. Regarding the term *pathyam*: because this is a section dealing with technical designations (*saṃjñā*), there is a restriction on the meaning; therefore, only that which does not deviate from the path prescribed by the scriptures is called *pathya*. It does not refer to one who does not deviate from a mere road, such as a thief.

(1251) *cchandaso nirmite* |4|4|93|. Regarding the word *cchandasaḥ*: the root *chad*, meaning "to cover," belongs to the *curādi* class; however, because roots have multiple meanings, it also functions in the sense of "desire. From that [root], with the suffix *ghañ*, the word *chandaḥ*—meaning "desire"—is well-established as a synonym.

Thus, in examples such as *avaccchanda-ucchalad-acccha-kaccha*, when the suffix *asun* is applied, that which ends in *s* is the base (*prakṛti*). In this context, because desire (*icchā*) functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act of creation, the suffix is added to a word ending in the third case (the instrumental). This means "that which was made by desire. Even though [this is] in the Veda...

Although the word *chandas* ending in a final *s* occurs in [the list] beginning with *triṣṭubh*, it is not taken here because this is a section dealing with technical names (*saṃjñā*); rather, the intention is that only its synonym "will" (*icchā*) is taken.
(1252) *uraso’ṇ ca* | Pāṇini 4.3.94.

Regarding the word *putra*: because this is a section governed by technical designations (*saṃjñā*), it does not apply here [to the etymological sense]. "That which is produced from the chest is *sukha*. (1253) *Hṛdayasya priyaḥ* |4|4|95|. [The word] *hṛdayasya*. [The word] *priyaḥ* means "that which pleases" (*prīṇati*). The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *igupadhat* (Pāṇini 3.1.135). Because of its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix, the genitive case is used for the object (*karman*).

In the case of non-worldly (*alaukika*) [compounds], however, it occurs by the very force of the statement (*vacanasāmarthya*) even when the *taddhita* suffix is part of the base form (*prakṛtibhāga*). This should be understood similarly in other cases as well.
(Pāṇini 4.4.96): "The suffix *cha* is applied after [the word] *bandhana* when a Ṛṣi is meant."
Regarding "bandhane": it is called *bandhana* because one is bound by it; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). It means a mantra for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
For by it, another's heart is brought under control. This [suffix] does not apply to sages such as Vasiṣṭha, due to the governing rule concerning technical names (*saṃjñā-adhikāra*).

(1255) *mata-jana-hala-kāraka-ja-lpaka-rṣeṣu* || 4.4.97 || The word *mata* [is understood]. "Its instrument" (*tasya karaṇam*)—this is a genitive case used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*).

*Kṛtiḥ* means "instrument" (*karaṇaṃ*), or rather, it is that by which something is performed (*kriyate ’nena*); with this intention, he says: "it is either the action (*bhāvaḥ*) or the means (*sādhanaṃ*)."

The word *jalpa* is a noun derived from the action (*bhāvasādhana*). The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Regarding the word *halasya*: "plowing" is *karṣaḥ*; because of its connection with that [action], the genitive is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).
