Alternatively, when the intention is to express the instrument as the agent (*kartṛtva*), the genitive is used in the sense of the agent. By the rule "*ratha-sītā*" (Pāṇini 5.1.75), there is an extension of the suffix to words ending in those [terms]. Thus: *dvihalyaḥ* (one who plows twice) and *trihalyaḥ* (one who plows thrice).

(1256) *tatra sādhuḥ* | Pāṇini 4.4.98. Regarding the rule *tatra sādhuḥ*: here, "skilled" (*sādhu*) is understood as one who is proficient or fit; that is, a benefactor (*upakartā*). For in that case, by virtue of its higher status, the suffix would have been applied by the rule *asmai hitam*. However, because this is within the governing context of technical designations (*saṃjñā*), it refers to a benefactor.
Others say it is not so apprehended.
(1257) *pratijanādibhyaḥ khañ* 4.4.99.
Regarding *pratijanam*: [the compound] *janaṃ janaṃ prati* means "toward every person," hence *pratijanam*.

The *avyayībhāva* compound occurs in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). Examples include: *pratijana*, *idaṃyuga*, *saṃyuga*, *pāpakula*, *parasyakula*, *amuṣyakula*, *sarvajana*, *viśvajana*, and *pañcajana*.
In the words *parasya* and *amuṣya*, the genitive case ending is not elided (*aluk*) due to this specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*).
(1258) *bhaktāṇ ṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.4.100. Regarding *bhakta*: Amara states, “*bhakta*, *andhas*, and *anna* are synonyms for cooked food (*strī* = feminine). (1259) *guḍādibhyaṣ ṭhañ* | Pāṇini 4.4.103.

The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after [the words] *guḍa* and others. [The list is: *guḍa*, *kulmāṣa*, *saktu*, *apūpa*, *māṣa*, *māṃsa*, *odana*, *ikṣu*, *veṇu*, *saṅgrāma*, *saṅghāta*, *pravāsa*, *nivāsa*, *vṛt*. (1260) The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after *pathin*, *atithi*, *vasati*, and *svapati*. Pāṇini 4.4.104.
Regarding *svāpateyam*: [the word] *vasati* [is derived from the root] *vas* with the suffix *ati*, according to the rule *vaseśca*.
*Svapati* means "one's own master," i.e., the wealthy one; that which is beneficial (*sādhu*) for him is *svāpateyam*. [In the formation of *sabhya*], the suffix *ya* is applied after *sabhā*.

If the suffix were *yat*, there would be an accent on the penultimate syllable (*titsvara*), as in the case of *ukthya* in the expression *ṛturbhavatyukthyaḥ*. Furthermore, it would not have the acute accent on the first syllable by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*.

It is to be suspected [that the latter is correct], because it has been established in the Vedabhāṣya that "at the time of its production, for a word consisting of two syllables, the first syllable of that which ends in 'ya' is udātta. In the alternative view, however, it would be udātta on the first syllable, as in examples such as "amaḥ śaṣpyāya ca phenyāya ca. Thus, since both explanations are necessary, [the former must be accepted].
The essential point is that something should be explained in accordance with the specific context.
(1261) *samānatīrthe vāsī* | 4|4|107|. [The term] *samānatīrthe vāsī* [is formed]; by means of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), the suffix *ṇini* is applied.

Because *graha* and others belong to the class of words formed by adding suffixes to roots (ākṛtigaṇa), [the form] is derived either by this rule (*nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ*) or by the rule *nandigrahī* etc. Regarding *satīrthya*: the substitution of *sa-* for *sa-* occurs by the rule *īrthe ye*. A *tīrtha* is that by which one crosses over; it is formed by the suffix *thak* added to the root *tṛ*. As it is said: "The word *īrtha* [is used] in the sense of scripture, sacrifice, field, means, teacher, and minister; and also in the sense of the womb and a descent into water."
*Viśvaḥ*: Here, however, only that which denotes a teacher (*upādhyāya*) is understood, and not anything else, because this is under the heading of technical designations (*saṃjñā*).
(1262) *samānodare śayitā o codātaḥ* |4|4|108|. "One who has lain" means one who has stayed; the root *śī* is used in the sense of staying. [The example is] *alāśayaḥ*.

The intended meaning is that this is because of the usage [in the Veda] of the form *uśeśayam*. In the compound *samānodara*, a *tatpuruṣa* is formed according to the rule beginning with "ūrvāpara-prathama-"; from that, the suffix *yat* is applied. By way of an exception to the accentuation of the suffix *yat*, the vowel *o* becomes udātta.
(1263) *sodarād yaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.4.109.

The rule *sodarād yaḥ* does not carry forward the phrase *ṭhaścodātaḥ*. The substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs by the rule *vibhāṣedare*. In this context, the word *ye*, which was carried forward from the rule *īd-y-e*, applies.

This is a locative case used in the sense of the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Therefore, from the word *sodara*, the suffix *ya* is applied; this is the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*). The phrase "as before" (*prāgvat*) means that the intended sense is "one who has lain with a common uterine brother" (*samānodare śayitaḥ*). If it is asked, "How then [is the reading] of Murāri: 'Even a brother abandons one going to the place of execution'? [the answer follows].

On this point, they say: "He whose womb (*udara*) is common (*saha*) is *sodara*. The substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs by the rule *ṭhvopasarjanasya*. And because that [substitution] is optional, forms such as *yatra bhrātā sahodaraḥ* are also established.
Thus end the *prāg-dvitīyāḥ* (suffixes introduced before the second book) in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
(1483) Pāṇini 5.3.27: *dik-śabdebhyaḥ saptamī-pañcamī-prathamābhyo dig-deśa-kāleṣvastātiḥ*.
[The suffix] *astāti* is added to words denoting direction (*dik-śabda*) when they signify direction, place, or time, provided they are in the locative, ablative, or nominative case.

Regarding the phrase "in direction, place, and time": here, a correspondence according to the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not intended, because there is no *svarita* accent. (Pāṇini 5.3.27) [The suffix] *astāti* [is added after words ending in *pūrva*].
As in *puraḥ* and *purastāt*. How then [to explain] the verse: "I shall go from there, from here, and from the front (*purataḥ*)"?

"Paścāt" means "behind," according to Bhavabhūti; "yātpuraḥ paruto'grataḥ" according to Amarasimha; and "urato prathame cāgre" according to Viśva. Many scholars maintain that [the usage] such as "samānakālīnam" (contemporary) or "pūrvakālīnam" (prior in time) is merely a scribal error. However, some [hold otherwise].

Since the desired result is achieved by the rule for *tasuc* itself following the roots *akṣi* and *utar*, the explicit utterance of the vowel *a* in the rule *ṭha-tasu* is for the purpose of prescribing it even from other roots. By this, the form *puraḥ* is established.

[The derivation is as follows: from the root *ur* in the sense of "going forward" (*agragamane*), with the suffix *kvip*, we get *pur*. However, the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *hr-sva-voḥ* does not apply here.

It exists because it is a verbal root (*bhūtvāt*). Nor should it be argued that even though the suffix *atasuc* is marked with the *cit* indicator, the pronunciation of the vowel *a* is for the sake of making the first syllable acute (*ādyaudātatva*) in certain cases; rather, they say that it is more logical to assume that its purpose is to provide a rule from another source in accordance with numerous usages.

Because the application of numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyatva*) is not adopted here, forms such as *purastād vasati*, *purastād āgataḥ*, *purastād ramaṇīyam*; *adhastād vasati*, *adhastād āgataḥ*, and so forth, are established.
(1485) *añceḥ luk* | 5|3|30|. [The suffix *tasil* is elided after the root *añc* when followed by the word *puras*.]

"Prācyām prācyā" means "in the eastern direction"—that is, *prāgvasati* (he dwells in the east). Similarly, "come from the eastern direction" is *prāgāgataḥ*, and so forth; these applications should be understood accordingly.

(1486) *enab anyatarasyām adūre ’pañcamyāḥ* | Pāṇini 5.3.35. [The suffix *enap* is optionally used after a word denoting direction when it signifies 'not far', provided that the fifth case-ending is not employed.]

The word ending in the fifth case is used with *vinā*. Not here: *uttarād āgataḥ* (come from the north), *adharād āgataḥ* (come from below), or *uttareṇa* (by means of the north), etc., or *vasati ramaṇīyam* (he dwells pleasantly). In the alternative, it is according to its respective [rule]: *dakṣiṇataḥ*, *uttarataḥ*, *adhaḥ*, *adhastāt*, *uttarāt*, *adharāt*, *dakṣiṇāt*.
(1487) *saṅkhyāyā vidhārthe dhā* || 5.3.42 || [The suffix] *dhā* is added after a numeral in the sense of "manner" (*vidhārtha*). The term *vidhārtha* means the meaning of the word *vidhā*.
Although a lump of boiled rice (*odanapiṇḍa*) is also expressed by the word *vidhā*, it is not intended here. Therefore—

It does not occur in cases such as *ekā govidhā*. For here, although it would have been sufficient to say "after the word *vidhā*," the purpose of including the mention of "meaning" (*artha*) is so that [the suffix] may apply only where the word *vidhā* is most commonly established in its conventional sense. And such a meaning is precisely "manner" (*prakāra*), and that is understood only as pertaining to an action.

Because its inherent nature is that of a designation (*abhidhāna*). Thus he says: "from [a word] occurring in the sense of a mode of action" (*kriyāprakāre vartamānāt*). How then [is it explained] in cases such as ‘*avadhā* is a substance’ (*dravyam*) or ‘a quality is manifold’ (*bahudhā guṇaḥ*)? Regarding this also, Haradatta states that an unexpressed action is understood, namely, “it is taught” (*upadiśyate*).
(1488) *adhikaraṇavicāle* |5|3|43|. [The suffix *ṇic* is applied] also when there is a change of the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). The substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is a substance (*dravya*);
"change" (*vicāla*) means making it otherwise (*anyathākaraṇa*). [The suffix] *ac* is added after the causative (*ṇijanta*) form; and that [suffix] is used here.

He explains that "the production of another number occurs through the proximity of numbers" with the words beginning "of the substance," and so forth. For the production of another number consists in making one many, and making many one. Regarding the first of these:
The example is: *ekaṃ rāśiṃ pañcadhā* (one heap fivefold). This means "make the five heaps. In the second case, however, one should cite:
*anekam ekadhā kuru* (make the many single). Here, the rule is commenced because the manner (*prakāra*) regarding the object of the action is not understood [otherwise].

(1489) *ekāddho dhyamuñ anyatarasyām* |5|3|44|. After the word *eka*, the suffixes *dha* and *dhyamuñ* are optionally [added]. Because the word *dha* is a nominal stem (*śabda-pradhāna*), it does not undergo the grammatical operations characteristic of pronouns (*sarvanāma*). Although this [suffix] is already established here by the very context of the section, the explicit mention of *dha* again is so that it may apply even when prescribed in the sense of "separation" (*vidhā*). [This applies] according to the rule *anantarasya*.

For it is clear from both the *Vṛtti* and the *Padamañjarī* that when there is a displacement of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) by means of logic (*nyāya*), only that which has been specifically prescribed [by that rule] is obtained. By this, the objection that "let *aikadhyam* itself be an independent suffix" is refuted. Regarding *aikadhyam*: it is used in the sense of "separating"—that is, *ekedhyam*.

[The suffix *kha*] is applied [after a word denoting a measure] when it signifies "he eats. However, in the case of shifting the locus (*adhikaraṇavicāla*), it should be understood as in the example: "Make them into a single heap" (*aikadhyam rāśim kuru*). In the same way, this should also be applied subsequently in cases such as "making into two" (*dvaidham*) and so forth. (1490) *edhācca* 5.3.46.

And *edhāc*: after the suffix *dhā*, when it expresses a relationship between two or three [entities], the suffix *edhāc* shall be applied. The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of avoiding a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*). (1491) *pāśap* is used in the sense of something contemptible (*yāpya*). 5.3.47.

In the case of *yāpya*, the suffix *pāśap* [is applied]; it is not prescribed for the word *utsita* itself, because that would lead to an undesired application even after a finite verb (*tiṅanta*). (1492) After a *tīya* ordinal number denoting a part, the suffix *an* is applied [to form a bahuvrīhi]. 5.3.48.

[The suffix] *tīya* is applied after a word denoting a part (*bhāga*) [of a whole] because it signifies a portion (*pūraṇa*). The term "portion" (*pūraṇa*) is used here [in the rule] for the sake of what follows; for a suffix *tīya* does not occur after a word that is not a portion. However, in the case of *mukhatīya*, there is no over-extension because the suffix is meaningless [there]. By the word "fortune" (*bhaga*), the masculine gender is intended. Therefore—
Even when the meaning is the same and the case-ending is intended to be expressed, only the fourth (caturthī) or fifth (pañcamī) case endings occur.
However, if the rule *rāgekādaśabhyaḥ* did not exist, then after the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the forms *caturthā* and *pañcamā* would result [instead of *caturthī* and *pañcamī*].
(1493) *ekādākiniccāsahāye* 5.3.52.

*Ekādhākiniccā*: The suffix *ākinic* shall be applied after the word *eka* when it signifies "without a companion. Regarding the mention of *kunlukau*: there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of either *ākinic* or *kan*, because both are prescribed by this very rule. The inclusion of the term "without a companion" (*asahāya*) is for the purpose of excluding numeral words; otherwise—

Because it is well-known and because of the context of number (*saṃkhyā*), only that [the number one] would be understood. If this were accepted, however, it would not apply in the case of duality or plurality; for [in such cases], one could not say "two solitary ones" or "many solitary ones," since the number one does not exist in two or many. Rather, [what is meant is] being without a companion (*asahāyatva*).

Because there is an absence of mutual assistance (*atirakta-sahāya*) between the two [rules], it applies to both two and many [sounds]. Here, this should be stated as *akiniñeva*; however, the desired result is established by the rule *savarṇadīrgha*. Furthermore, it is established in the commentary of Haradatta that the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule *yasyeti ca* does not occur due to the functional power (*sāmarthya*) of the vocalization of the letter *a*, and so forth.

(1494) *bhūtapūrve caraṭ* | Pāṇini 5.3.53. Regarding the term *bhūtapūrva*: the suffix *caraṭ* should be applied to a word occurring in this sense. It was not stated in the very rule *oṣṭhāt khañ* (Pāṇini 5.2.108), so that the suffix *khañ*, being specifically prescribed there, might not supersede *caraṭ*. [This applies] when they are in proximity.

For in this way, the relationship between the general and the particular becomes clear. Although it would indeed be logical for sublation to apply even to that which is situated at a distance, nevertheless, by accepting the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) here, the intention is that there is no sublation because of the force of the recitation being located far away.

(1495) *ṣaṣṭhyā rūpya ca* | 5|3|54 | [The word] *ṣaṣṭhyā* [is used]; *rūpya* and [the suffix *cha*] also [are applied]. The phrase *bhūtapūrve* ("in the sense of 'formerly been'") is understood to carry over.

Although that [phrase] was previously a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a feminine suffix (*ṅī*) or a long vowel (*āp*), here it is not so; rather, it qualifies the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*).

Because it is a qualifier; because the unrelated cow and so forth, which are implied by that [qualifier], are the primary referents; and because, when both a primary and a subordinate element are present, it is logical that the grammatical operation applies to the primary one. Therefore, he says this: "The suffix -rūpya should be used in the sense of something that previously existed."
(1496) *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau* | Pāṇini 5.3.55.
Regarding *atiśāyane*: [the word] *atiśayana* is derived from the root *śī* preceded by *ati*, with the suffix *lyuṭ*. *Atiśayana* itself is simply *atiśāyana*;

the lengthening of the vowel [in *atiśāyana*] occurs by virtue of this very rule of nipātana (irregular formation), and not because it is a Vedic (*sautra*) term. Consequently, the long vowel is also correct in common usage (*loka*).

There are also irregular formations (*nipātana*) that set aside [general rules]; by this, the short vowel is also correct. Although the root *śvi* alone occurs in the sense of sleeping, nevertheless, preceded by *ati*, it denotes excellence (*prakarṣa*). And here, excellence does not mean abundance, but rather overcoming (*abhibhava*), as in the phrase: "He remained superior due to his great majesty."

Because it is observed in usage. Nor should one object: "Why was it not simply formulated in the sūtra as *atiśaye tamabiṣṭhanau* (‘the suffixes *tamaP* and *iṣṭhan* occur in the sense of excellence’)? For it was stated in that way precisely for the purpose of establishing the technical term *atiśāyana*. Thus, excellence (*atiśaya*) is not the meaning of the suffix; for if it were so, [the following would occur].

The superlative suffix *tama* would result in forms such as *laghutara* and *laghutama*. This is because the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is primary; nor is it the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), for if that were the case, the suffix would apply only to words like *prakṛṣṭa* and *atiśayana*, but not to words like *āḍhya*. Rather, it is a qualifier of the base meaning, while the suffix is merely indicative (*dyotaka*).

This is what he says: "distinguished by excellence," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "this one of these": when, within a collection consisting of two members, the excellence of one is intended to be expressed, then the suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun* will be stated as exceptions [to the general rule]. And thus, by process of elimination, when among many [members] the excellence of a single part...

The sense is that this [suffix] serves to specify its scope (*nirdhāraṇa*). Regarding the term *āḍhatama*: it is the superlative suffix *tamap* added to a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Although the rule *yāpprātipadikāt* continues to apply, nevertheless, it is understood specifically as referring to a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

This must be explained; otherwise, how could the prescription of the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending in rules such as *pūrvāhṇetamām*—by the rule "in the presence of *ha*, *kāla*, and *tana*, there is no elision of the locative ending after a word denoting time" (*hakālataneṣu kālanāmnaḥ*)—be justified? (1497) *tiṅśca* || 5.3.56 || And [the suffixes] following a finite verb (*tiṅ*). 5.3.56.

And regarding the *tiṅ* suffixes: [the suffix] *iṣṭhan* does not occur after them, because of the restrictive rule "the suffixes beginning with *ṭha* occur only after words expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*). With this intention, he says: "there may be *tamap*.
(Pāṇini 1.1.22) *tarap* and *tamap* are designated as *gha*.

The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are designated as *gha*. Although it could have been stated within this very section on comparative suffixes (*ātiśāyanika*)—as in "the *gha* suffix occurs at the beginning" or "the *gha* suffix occurs before *it*"—the fact that the rule is formulated as a heavy sūtra in a separate section indicates that *tarap* is understood to include even the superlative degree (*atyantasvārthika*). By this principle, one understands such forms as *alpāctaram* ("having fewer syllables") and *lopaś ca balavataraḥ* ("elision is more powerful").

Success! For [the rule] *alpāccaiva hyalpāctaram* applies only when both [words] have few syllables. However, in this case, the suffix *-tarap* is not used to express the excellence of one over the other; otherwise, even though forms such as *ivakeśavau* would be established, forms such as *aṅkhadundubhivīṇāḥ* would not.

They say it would be established. (1499) *vyavahitācca* [Pāṇini 5.4.11]: "And even when separated [by intervening elements]. Why is this so? Because if the augment *nuṭ* were omitted from the word *omoru*, then...

In forms such as *pacatitarām*, if the augment *nuṭ* were applied by the rule *hrasvānadyāpaḥ*, the result would have been *pacatitaraṇām*, because the elision of the final vowel (*yasyeti lopa*) is superseded by the subsequent *nuṭ*. However, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), this does not occur because of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*):
"When a term with an indicatory letter (*iranubandhaka*) is mentioned, it does not include a term with a different indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*)," which applies to the prescription of *nuṭ*.
There is no inclusion of this [term]. (1500) *dvivacanavibhajyopapadetarabīyasunau* 5.3.57.

When a word expressing duality (*dvivacana*) or a word used in a distributive sense (*vibhajya*) is the subordinate member (*upapada*), the suffixes *itarac* and *īyasun* are applied. "Duality" (*dvivacana*) refers to the expression of two objects; it is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).

The suffix *lyuṭ* [is applied]. There is a compound with the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). That word by which two meanings are expressed is called "dual. "Vibhājyam" means "to be divided. Since the suffix *ṇyat* would have been applicable by the rule *ṛ-haloḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.124), the suffix *yat* is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to it. However, if *ṇyat* were used, there would be *kutva* (the substitution of *ku* for *j*) by the rule *ajo’r* (Pāṇini 7.3.59).

It should be *vibhājyam*. Haradatta’s statement—that the correctness of the word *vibhājya*, as employed in the *Smṛtis*, is to be questioned—is itself questionable; for the form *vibhājyam* is established by adding the suffix *yat* to the causative (*ṇic*) stem according to the rule "the *ya* of *ṭha* is elided. Nor should one suspect a difference in meaning here.

The point is that the suffix *ṇic* is applied to a verbal root in its primary sense when there is a request (*uvṛta-preṣaṇa*), as established by the rule *ṇeraṇau*. Furthermore, the compound *dvivacanaṃ ca vibhajyaṃ ca* is a *dvandva*;
this forms a *karmadhāraya* with the word *upapadena*. Thus, [the rule applies] when the *upapada* expresses two meanings and is something to be divided.

The literal meaning of the word is "being. However, if one explains it as "when a dual-ending word is the upapada," then expressions such as "the teeth of the lips are smoother" would not be established.
Nor is this established even under the view that "dual number refers to the expression of two things."

If it is argued that because the aggregate (*samāhāra*) is a single entity, whereas the constituent members (*varti-padārtha*) are subordinate, the forms *dvātriṃśaddantāḥ* (thirty-two teeth) and *dvauṣṭhau* (two lips) would not be established— especially since those [members] are plural— then they say in response: the [compound] brings about the number of non-dual unity belonging to the members.
The constituent words [of the compound] are as follows: consequently, through the abandonment of difference, there is non-dual unity;
and through the inclusion of number, the two objects characterized as "teeth" and "lips" are expressed by the word *dantoṣṭha*.
Thus, since there is no dual expression for the two [objects], the phrase "when the dual suffix occurs" refers to this very meaning of the dual suffix.

Regarding the phrase "there is a fault in the alternative view": the details should be understood from the original treatises (*ākaragrantha*). Furthermore, the term *upapada* is literal—it means "a word uttered near [another]"—and not technical;

for that [technical sense] is impossible in the context of the rules for secondary suffixes (*taddhita-vidhi*). And it is employed only in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), not in the derivative formation (*vṛtti*).
However, since the meaning is already established, it is not strictly necessary. This being the case, the mention of the "upapada" (governing word) is for the sake of clarity.

Here, there are two upapadas and two bases (*prakṛti*) consisting of forms ending in *su*-affixes and *tiṅ*-affixes, as well as two suffixes; nevertheless, a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) is not intended.

He illustrates the case where the *upapada* (governing word) is in the dual number with the example "of these two" (*anayoḥ*). Regarding "laghīyas": there is elision by the rule "eḥ"; *num* is added because it ends in an *u*-class vowel; the lengthening occurs by the rule "āntamahataḥ";

and the elisions of the *hal-ḍy-ādi* and the final consonant of the *saṃyoga* apply. He illustrates the case where the *upapada* is separated [from the verb] with the example "from the Easterners" (*prācyebhyaḥ*).

Thus [it is said]: "The fifth case ending [is used] in the sense of division" (*pañcamī vibhakte*). How then is it that one says, "You were clever last year (*arun*), but you are more clever this year (*aiṣamaḥ*)"? On this point, they say: even for a single substratum (*dharmin*), by virtue of the distinction between its attributes (*dharmabheda*) such as existing at that particular time and so forth...

Because of the superimposition of difference, there is a dependence on a counter-correlative; the excellence existing at that time is the basis for the suffix *tap* here. And they designate [the self] thus: "You are indeed another when concealed," and "O Dhanañjaya, you are not that same one."

(1501) *ajādī guṇavacanādeva* | Pāṇini 5.3.58. The suffixes beginning with *ac* and *ādi* are [added] only after words expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*). The particle *eva* is for the purpose of restriction according to the intended meaning; thus, this is a restriction regarding the suffixes. If the particle *eva* were absent, however, it would mean "only suffixes beginning with *ac* and *ādi* are added after words expressing a quality."

Even the restriction of the original form (*prakṛti-niyama*) might be possible; and in that case, forms such as *paṭutara* and *paṭutama* would not be established. (Pāṇini 5.3.59): *tuśchandasī* ("But [the suffix -taraC] occurs in the Vedic language").
The word *tu* [is used] in the Vedic language (*chandas*). This is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the restriction established by the preceding rule;
it is not an original injunction (*apūrvo vidhiḥ*). Therefore, there is no confusion of grammatical conditions (*upādhi-saṅkara*). (1503) *turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu* 6.4.154.

Although the elision of the final [letter] is established by the rule *turiṣṭhemeyassu*, the very fact that this [new rule] is commenced implies that there is the elision of the entire word *tṛ*; thus he says—*kariṣṭhaḥ*. *Dohīyasī* means "she who is the more excellent milker of these two. [The substitution of] *ī* for *has* is established before a *taddhita* suffix ending in *aṅ*.
Because of the rule stating "in the prescription of a suffix," when a taddhita suffix is to be applied, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) must occur first;

thus, once the feminine suffix *ṅīp* has been removed, the suffix is added to the word *dogdhṛ*. Subsequently, when the suffix *tṛc* is removed, the substitution of *dhatva* and *jaśtva* is also removed due to the absence of its cause. This occurs in the non-figurative analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*).

The truth is that their non-application occurs even earlier by means of the *ṭhakṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding the non-modification of a completed formation). However, the *guṇa* substitution does take effect, because the presence of the suffixal characteristic (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) remains certain even when the *tṛc* suffix is elided.
This is supported by the Vedic rule "u" and the rules "uriṣṭhemeyaḥsu."

By the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "ṭhṇāviṣṭhavat," [the suffix] is also used in common worldly usage to denote an agent, as in "kārayati" and so forth; it is introduced here because it will be employed in this context.
(1504) *praśasyasya śraḥ* | Pāṇini 5.3.60. [The substitute *śra* is applied in place of the word *praśasya*.]

The suffix *śra* is substituted for *praśasya*. He says "for *aja* and *adya*" because the phrase *ṭhaj-ādī* (beginning with *ṭha* and *ja*) is understood from the previous rule and is transformed here into the locative case. What is the purpose of [specifying] "for *aja* and *adya*"? [Consider: *praśasyataraḥ* and *praśasyatamaḥ*.
(1505) *prakṛtyaikāc*: A monosyllabic stem remains in its original form (*prakṛti*).

Regarding the word *śreṣṭha*: here, due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), both the elision of *e* by the rule *eti* and the elision of the final syllable by the rule *yasya* do not take place. Regarding *jyādādī*: for the suffix *īyasun* following *jyād*, there should be the substitution of the vowel *ā*.
(1506) *vṛddhasya ca* |5|3|62|. The same substitution applies to the word *vṛddha*.

And regarding the word *vṛddha*, here its own form (*svarūpa*) is to be understood, and not the technical term defined by the rule "that whose vowels beginning with the first are *vṛddhi*" (Pāṇini 1.1.73), because of the [authoritative] commentary. By the rule "for *ṛju* and *sthira*" etc., the substitution of *varṣa* also occurs optionally for this [word *vṛddha*]. Nor should it be suspected that the suffix *iman* has no scope [elsewhere] for that [substitution],

This is because the *manic* affix does not occur after the word *vṛddha*. However, they say that if the rule "for *vṛddha*, [substitute] *varṣī*" were placed right here [in this very section], then the mention of *vṛddha* would not need to be repeated twice, resulting in greater brevity (*lāghava*).

(1507) Pāṇini 6.4.156: *sthūladūrayuvahrasvakṣiprakṣudrāṇāṃ yaṇādiparaṃ pūrvasya ca guṇaḥ*. [In the case of the words] *sthūla*, *dūra*, *yuvan*, *hrasva*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*, when a suffix beginning with a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) follows, the final vowel and the following consonant are replaced by their Guṇa substitute, and the same Guṇa substitution also occurs for the preceding vowel. The inclusion of the word "following" (*para*) [in the rule] is for the sake of ensuring that in forms such as *yaviṣṭha* and *hrasiṣṭha*, the Guṇa substitution applies to the preceding vowel even though it is not immediately followed by the semi-vowel.

"Let it not be so. The mention of "pūrva" (the preceding), however, is for the sake of clarity; for when the subsequent [element] is elided, by virtue of the grammatical capacity (*sāmarthya*), the quality (*guṇa*) is obtained for the preceding [element] alone. Regarding *sthaviṣṭha*:
one should not say that the mention of "guṇa" here is redundant since the form would be established by the rule *ṭhorguṇaḥ* alone.

Because the elision (*lop*) of *para* and so forth is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) by virtue of being *ābhīya* (belonging to a subsequent rule), the *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *o* in *kṣipra* and *kṣudra* would not apply; furthermore, this would result in the incorrect forms *kṣepiṣṭhaḥ* and *kṣodiṣṭhaḥ*. "In the same way" refers to forms such as *preyān*, *stheyān*, *spheyām*, and *varīyān*. [The rule] "there is elision of *ima* and *iyas*" [is applied].
And that [substitution] occurs only by virtue of the rule *ṭhādeḥ parasya* and others.
(1508) *iṣṭhasya yiṭ ca*. [The word] *iṣṭha* [is mentioned]; *yiṭ* also [is added]. The preceding sūtra is carried over in its entirety.
Thus he says: "of *bahu*," and so forth. It should also be understood that there is the substitution of *hū*. Regarding *bhūyiṣṭha*:

here, when the suffix *iṣṭha* has its *āj* portion elided, the syllable *yi* is an augment (*āgama*). Alternatively, the letter *y* is an augment that serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the elision; the vowel *i*, however, is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Both of these two views are established in the Bhāṣya.

(1509) *yuvālpayoḥ kan anyatarasyām* |5|3|64|. In the rule *yuvālpayoḥ*, the term *yuvā* is taken as its own form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*), and not as the descendant of a youth (*yuvāpatya*), because it occurs in conjunction with *alpa* and because of the traditional explanation (*vyākhyāna*). Furthermore, due to the continued application (*anuvartana*) of the condition "beginning with a vowel" (*ajādī*), the suffix *kan* is applied only to those two [words] that begin with a vowel.
With the intention that the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* do not apply to the two [suffixes] *iṣṭhan* and *īyas*, he explains: "of *iṣṭhan* and *īyas*.
(Pāṇini 5.3.65) *vinmator luk*: there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *vin* and *mat*. In the example *srajiṣṭhaḥ*, once the elision of *vin* has been performed...

Because it is a *bhāva* (abstract state), there is no application of the rule regarding the stem-final. By this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), even when not denoting a quality (*aguṇavacana*), the suffixes *vin* and *matup* occur after a word ending in *a*.
(1511) [Pāṇini 5.3.66] *rūpap* is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*).

The suffix *rūpaP* is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). Here, "praise" refers to the completeness (*paripūrṇatā*) of the meaning of the base word (*prakṛtyartha*), and not merely to eulogy (*stu*).
Therefore, it also occurs here: "This man is like a thief (*caurarūpaḥ*)," because he steals even the collyrium from the eyes.
By stealing a hidden object, his thievery is made complete. [Similarly: "like cooking" (*pacatirūpam*).

A verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning. And although action is of a non-substantial nature (*asatvarūpatva*), the singular number (*ekavacana*) applies by default. Therefore, forms such as *pacato rūpam* ("the form of two cooking") and *pacanti rūpam* ("the form of many cooking") occur.
In these cases, only the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used, because other case-endings (*vibhakti*) do not apply; this is the view of many. However, in reality:
In constructions such as *paśya* ("look"), the accusative case is also easily available for the object; its status as a *kḷp* [term] is established by common usage (*lokāt*).
This should also be understood in cases such as *acatikalpa*. (Pāṇini 5.3.68):
"The suffix *bahuc* is optionally used in place of a nominal stem (*sup*), and it is placed before [the word]."

The *vibhāṣā* (optionality) applies to the *sup* (case endings). In the sūtra, the word "upaḥ" is in the genitive case, because it is stated [in Pāṇini 2.3.30] that "the sixth [genitive] is used with words meaning 'direction' (*artha*) and suffixes. [The phrase] "from a *sub*-ending [word]" is correctly in the ablative case; for in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the word "before" (*prāk*), which is a synonym for "purastāt," is used.

Because it is [already] employed. However, it is established in the *Manoramā* that the word "prāk" (before) is drawn back [to the previous rule]. Nor should it be argued that even when joined with the word "prāk," which has the same meaning as the word "purastāt" occurring in the sūtra, the genitive case would apply by the rule "aṣṭhī tasarthaiḥ";
for in the sūtra "anyārād," the term "añc-utarapada" [is specified].

Even though it is a word denoting direction (*dik-śabda*), the separate mention [of *pūrva*] is established as being for the purpose of overriding the rule "by means of a word having the sense of *artha* when preceded by *aṣṭhā*. This is because the example "to the east or west of the village" (*prāk pratyag vā grāmāt*) has been cited. However, in the *Kāśikā*, the word *pūrva* appears before *vṛta*.

The word *prayuktaḥ* is employed [in the rule], and the word *subantāt* is also employed; considering this to be inconsistent, Haradatta has somehow justified it by stating: "This ablative case is used in the sense of *lyablopa* (the elision of a suffix ending in *-lyap*); the meaning is 'having resorted to such a thing as the base (*prakṛti*)'. Regarding the phrase *prāgeva*: the particle *tu* found in the sūtra is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
The sense is that it functions [as such]. And by that, only *bahu* is optionally [substituted], but not *pūrva*.

However, in the absence of the word *tu*, priority (*prāktva*) would be subject to optionality. Consequently, in one alternative case, *bahu* would follow [the stem]. But in the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, this is not the result of the word *tu*.

For instance, in rules such as *udaścitaḥ anyatarasyām*, it is the suffix alone that is subject to optionality because it is the primary element (*pradhāna*), and not its posteriority (*paratva*). This is because it is the suffix itself, qualified by posteriority, that is prescribed; since the qualifier is subordinate (*guṇa*), it follows the principle: "And [words] ending in *uṇ* are for the sake of another."

By logical necessity, here too, by the mention of the term *vibhāṣā*, it will be connected only with the suffix *-bahuc* and not with what precedes; however, the purpose of the particle *tu*, which has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), is something else entirely: namely, that "everything [the rule] shall apply only from this point onward. Consequently, gender and number also [apply] only from this point forward.

Those very [gender and number] which are seen in the state of the base (*prakṛti*) prior to the arising of the suffix remain exactly as they were; furthermore, the application of the plural number occurs only before the base. Therefore, in cases such as *ahuguḍo drākṣā* ("the many jujube fruits are grapes") and *aghurbahutṛṇaṃ naraḥ* ("the man [is] many blades of grass"), the gender remains that of the base alone, and not [that of the compound].

The gender [of the derivative] follows that of the base meaning. Now, if it is argued that this is already established by the rule "secondary derivatives (vārthika) take the gender and number of their base," then what is the purpose of including the word *tu*?
To this they say: this very inclusion serves to indicate that [the rule applies] to those [suffixes] used in the sense of "partial completion" (*īṣadasamāpti*).

"Those suffixes used in their own sense (svārthika) possess both gender and number exactly like the word they signify. By this, forms such as *uḍakalpā drākṣā* ("grapes that are almost like water") and *arkarākalpo guḍaḥ* ("molasses that is almost like gravel") are established. [The rule] *prāgivāt kaḥ* applies;
since *upaḥ* is understood to follow from the previous context, the suffix *ka* does not apply after a verbal form (*tiṅanta*).

(1513) *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.71]. Regarding *avyayasarvanāmnām*: it is understood by means of a "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) from the previous rule; that is the opinion. Furthermore, *yāpprātipadikāt* and *pratyayaḥ* continue to apply as well.

(1514) *kasya ca daḥ* | Pāṇini 5.3.72. Regarding *kasya ca daḥ*: [the rule applies] to an indeclinable ending in *kā*. The mention of "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) and "verbal suffix" (*tiṅ*) is not connected here, because it is impossible for those two to end in *kā*. Nor [does it apply] in cases such as *adhok* or *adhoṅ*.
It must be stated that [the form] is possible, because the substitution of *k* for *ś* is not established as universally valid.

Although a form such as *aśāśak* could theoretically occur through the application of *laṅ* after the *yaṅ*-luṅ (*yaṅluk*) of the root *śak*, nevertheless, because the *yaṅluk* is not universal, no such attested example exists. This applies in Vedic usage (*chāndasi*).

The point is that even when the object of the rule (*lakṣya*) is present in some instances, the rule for *datva* does not apply because of the principle: "In the Vedic language, all rules are optionally prescribed. When a case-ending (*sup*) beginning with *o*, *s*, or *bh* follows, the suffix *aKac* is added before the final vowel of a pronoun.

Regarding the expression "okāra-sakāre": since the term *sup* (nominal suffix) also recurs in the rule for the substitution of *akac*, there arises the possibility of an indefinite application (*avyavasthā*) because one may optionally choose to qualify either the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) or the nominal suffix (*sup*) with *ṭheḥ*. To resolve this, the restriction established by the words of the Bhāṣyakāra is adopted. Furthermore, the limitation expressed in "in the case of *okāra* and *sakāra*" and so forth applies exclusively to the domain of the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.

This is because it has been cited in that very way in the Bhāṣya. However, according to others, *akac* is added specifically to the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, not to the word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). By this, forms such as *sarvakeṇa*, *imakena*, and *bhavakantam* are established. As for *tvayakā* and *mayakā*: [one might object] that if *akac* were added here before the case-suffix (*sup*), then—[the following would apply] regarding the suffix...

If it is argued that even though the two substitutes [ya and a] occur subsequently, the substitution of *y* (as prescribed by the rule *tyo’ci*) would not take place because the condition of being followed by a case-ending (*vibhaktiparatva*) is absent—this is not so. For, relying on the non-universality (*anityatā*) of the maxim regarding the non-application of a grammatical operation when its cause has already been destroyed (*akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā*), the substitution of *y* is ordained precisely before the addition of the suffix *akac*. Thus...
It should be understood that even in the case of *yuvakāmāvakām*, the substitutions *yu* and *āva* occur precisely before the addition of *akac*.

Regarding the rule *śīle ko malopaśca*: "In the sense of habit (*śīla*), the suffix *ka* [is applied]. Here, *śīla* means both natural disposition (*svabhāva*) and a fixed practice (*niyama*). As for the example *tūṣṇīka*, the shortening of the vowel [from *tūṣṇīm* to *tūṣṇī*] occurs by virtue of the rule *eṇaḥ*; however, this is based on the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya, as indicated by the mention of the word *e* in the rule *a-kapī*.

Or they say that it does not occur because of the division of the *yogavibhāga*. Indicating that the second vowel ‘a’ in *akac* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), he provides the example: *pacatakī*, etc.
(1515) *anukampāyām* 5|3|76.
Regarding *anukampā*: Amarasimha states, "Ṛpā, dayā, and anukampā mean compassion.

(1516) *nītau ca tadyauktāt* |5|3|77|. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after a word meaning "compassion" when it is joined with a word signifying policy (*nīti*). Although [in common usage] only a son or similar relative [is the object of compassion],...
The meaning is that although he is directly endowed with compassion, the givers and others are not;

nevertheless, by way of him, the givers and others also possess a connection to compassion. Regarding the word *dhānakāḥ*: the word *dhānā* is feminine; from it, the suffix *ka* is added; then, by the rule *eṇaḥ*, the vowel is shortened.

The suffix *ṭāp* is applied after a word ending in the suffix *kap*. In this case, by the rule "ratyayasthāt," it ought to be changed to *ī*; however, the reading "hānakā" is generally found. Regarding that, Haradatta states that one should observe a transgression of the gender [of the original base]. This is because the form is already established by the rule "armavyatihāre ṇac striyām," and thus the rule "ṇacaḥ striyām añ" [is considered redundant in this context].

Furthermore, by the specific mention of "strī" (female), it is indicated that "secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) sometimes deviate from the gender of their base. Therefore, the intention is that in the word *hānikā*, there is masculine gender.
(Pāṇini 5.3.79) *ghan* and *ilac* [are also added].

"Also *ghan* and *ila*. The *Kāśikā* states that because of the word 'ca' (also), [the suffixes] are used as they are already prescribed. Here, by the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*), *ṭhañ* is prescribed; due to the mention of the option (*vāvacana*), *ka* also [occurs]. However, it must be considered what [suffix] is permitted by the word 'ca', and Haradatta maintains that the purpose of the formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must also be considered."

(1518) *ṭhājādāvūrdhvaṃ dvitīyādacaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.3.83. Regarding *ṭhājādau*: the masculine gender in this *sūtra* compound (*samāhāradvandva*) is a Vedic anomaly (*sauna*). Haradatta maintains that the inclusion of the term *ādi-* ("beginning with") has a questionable purpose, as the desired result is already established by the rule *yasmin vidhis tadādau* ("a grammatical operation applies to that which begins with the element specified").

Regarding the phrase "in this section": the sense is that because both *anukampā* (compassion) and *nīti* (policy) are present in the intellect through proximity (*pratyāsatti*), they are understood. Here, the mention of "ūrdhva" (after) is for the purpose of the elision of all [subsequent parts]; otherwise, by the rule "of what follows, beginning with the first [letter]" (*ādeḥ parasya*), only the first letter would be elided. With this intention, he says: "after the second vowel."

Regarding the word *sarvam*: because the word "elision" (*lopa*) is understood from the rule *ṭhājina-antasya*, he says "it is elided. Now, one might object that the mention of *a* is redundant, since once the substitution of *i* has been made, the result would be established simply by the condition "when followed by an *aj*-beginning [suffix]. To this he replies: "The mention of *a* is for the sake of making the *uk* the second [element]. Thus: *vāyukaḥ*.

When the word *danta* follows the word *vāyu*, the substitution of *ka* [for *ta*] occurs by the rule *ṭhisusuktāntāt kaḥ* precisely at the stage of the *ṭha*-suffix, even while the *valopa* (elision of the *v*) is still in effect. Furthermore, there is another purpose for the separate mention of *ṭha*: namely, when the suffix *ṭhac* is applied in cases such as *citragu*.

Because it ends in a *ṭh*-sound, the substitution of *ka* would apply first; consequently, since the substitution of *ik* would be impossible at that stage, the elision (*lopa*) conditioned by its being the initial sound of a vowel (*aj-ādi*) would not occur.
Therefore, the mention of *ṭh* is for that purpose as well. Thus, when the *ṭh*-stage [of the suffix] remains, there is the elision of the subsequent member (*uttara-pada-lopa*).
It should be understood that because a replacement by *kā* is impossible, the form *itrika* is established through the replacement by *ik*.
He explains [the rule] by breaking down exactly what will be stated later— namely, "after the fourth vowel, when followed by a consonant"— as "after the vowel that follows the fourth [vowel]."

And it should be stated that there is optionally a deletion [of the suffix] when it begins with a consonant other than *a*. "When it begins with a consonant other than *a*" means when it begins with a consonant (*hal*).
[This applies] specifically within this section.

And there is also the deletion of the preceding member. "And there is also the deletion of the preceding member" [occurs] when [the suffix] begins with a vowel other than *a* (i.e., when it begins with a consonant).
And this is to be understood. He explains the statement "the suffix *ta* is desired in that very case when the suffix *ṭha* is present" with the words "even without a suffix.

Regarding the rule "after a vowel ending in *u*, there is *la*, and [the substitution] of *il* for *la*": the meaning of "and [the substitution] of *il* for *la*" is that there is the elision (*lopa*) of *il*. In that context...
The elision of the letter *i* should be understood by the rule "ṭhādeḥ parasya" [Pāṇini 6.4.143].

(1519) *prācām upāder aḍ-aj-bucau ca* [Pāṇini 5.3.80]. For the Easterners, after the root *upa*, the suffixes *aṅ*, *ac*, and *vuñ* are applied; the phrase "after *ahvac* when denoting a human being," etc., is also carried over [from the previous rule]. Thus, *upendradatta*.

Now, one might object: since the single-substitute [ekādeśa] resulting from the formation of the sandhi in the word *ūpendra* is treated as belonging to the preceding part (*pūrvāntatva*), the two suffixes prescribed by the rule *ṭhupādeḥ* might indeed be applied; however, the elision (*lopa*) would apply only to the letter *n* and what follows it. Consequently, the forms *ṭhupaka* and *ṭhupaḍa* would not be possible—what [is the solution]?

In that case, the forms would have to be *tuṣṭhupayaka* and *tuṣṭhupayaḍ*. Similarly, there would be a fault even with respect to the suffixes *ghan*, *ilac*, and *ṭhac*. If it is asked, "Why then was this Vārttika, 'the second [vowel] is a diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*)', not stated right here?", they reply: It was not stated because it can be resolved by another method.

For instance: when *guṇa* is applied [by the rule *ādguṇaḥ*], since it is stated that "the second [vowel] is a *sandhyakṣara*" and so forth, there is also the possibility of the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *a*.

Therefore, by the *akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā*, the suffix would apply precisely before the *guṇa* substitution. Nor can this be prevented by the mention of *samartha* (semantic connection), which refers to a fully established form, as in the case of *sa-utthitiḥ*.
An objection based on a general rule (*paribhāṣā*) need not be feared; for it has been stated in the commentary on the sūtra *rāgdiśo* that "the mention of the word *samartha* [in P.

2.1.1] is removed. Furthermore, even in the view that rejects the mention of *samartha* by the force of the previously mentioned indicator (*jñāpaka*)—namely, the phrase *ṭhakṛtasandheḥ*—one must resort to the interpretation that this indicator has a specific scope (*viśeṣaparatva*).

In cases such as *upendraḥ*, *ṣaḥ*, *upaguḥ*, and *upakartā*, although there is a similarity among the five forms beginning with *upa*— just as in the case of words like *saindhava*— the specific meaning is to be determined by context and other factors.
(1520) [Pāṇini 5.3.81] *kan* is added to the name of a genus (*jāti*).

Regarding names of species (*jātināman*): those words which are well-known as belonging to another species, but are employed as proper names among humans, are the examples here. Regarding the second rule, beginning with "if it is a diphthong" (*dvitīyaṃ sandhyakṣaraṃ cet*), it should be stated that there is elision of the initial [element]. This refers to the phrase "the second," and so forth. [This is governed by] *ṭhecaḥ*.
The term *sandhyakṣara* is the designation used by the Easterners (*prācām*).

It should be stated that for compounds whose prior member consists of a single syllable, there is elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*). For example, *vāgāśīḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "one whose blessing (*āśīḥ*) is in speech (*vāci*). [Another example is] *vācikaḥ*. If, in this case, there were elision of everything after the second vowel, [the form would not be established].
Then, when *vāc + ā* becomes *vāca*, the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*.
Because that [elision] is treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the preceding form is considered a *bha* ending in *ā*.

Consequently, by relying on the internal case-ending, the final *c* is regarded as being at the end of a word (*pada*); thus, the substitution of *k* for *c* (*kutva*) and the substitution of *j* for *k* (*jaśtva*) occur, resulting in *vāgika*.

However, when there is elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*), because [the substitute] is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* due to being an *ajjhal-ādeśa*, the designation *bha*— by the rule "before a *yac*-beginning affix, it is *bha*"— is applied with the same scope [as the designation *pada*].

Consequently, by the principle that "when two designations conflict, the later one prevails," the designation *pada* (by the rule "that which ends in a verbal root or a suffix is a *pada*") is superseded.

The designation *pada* for the word *vādiṣu* is certainly not to be doubted, because the designation *bha*—by the rule *hyaci bham*—is its exception (*apavāda*). How so? Here, too, once the elision of the final member of the compound has occurred, the application of the *jaś*-rule would be difficult to obtain; such is the question.

This is established by the mention of *ṣaṣ* and *ṣaṣṭha* and so forth. Regarding the word *ṣaṣ*: here, only the elision prescribed in the sūtra itself is intended, and not that which is added as a supplementary rule (*aupasaṅkhyānika*). (1521) *Śevala-supari-piśāla-varuṇa-aryaman-ādīnāṃ tṛtīyāt* 5.3.84. [The suffix *cha* is applied after these words when the third case-ending follows.]

Regarding *śevalasupari* and *śevalika*: the suffix *ṭhac* is applied according to the rule *ahvaco manuṣyanāmnaḥ*. However, with the suffixes *ghan* and *ilac*, we have *śevaliyaḥ* and *śevalilaḥ*. As for the elision of the third case-ending that is stated for words beginning with *śevala*, it should be understood as applying to those forms where no sandhi has yet taken place. Thus: *suparyāśīḥ*.

The *Bhāṣya* maintains that the forms are *suparikaḥ*, *supariyaḥ*, and *suparilaḥ*; however, Kaiyaṭa, taking the word *uparikata* as his illustrative example (*pratīka*), explains that "once the operation of *saṃhitā* has been applied and [the semivowel] has been elided, the form would be *aparyika*. The underlying point is this: when the *saṃhitā* operation—the *yaṇ*-substitution—has taken place...

If the elision were applied to the third vowel onwards, then only the portion "īrdata" would be elided; however, the elision of the letter *ā* would occur by the rule "yasyeti ca," and consequently, due to the status of the substitute being like the original (sthānivadbhāva), the substitution of *yaṇ* would not be prevented.
Regarding the term *hrasve*: since designations such as "short" (*hrasva*) or "long" (*dīrgha*) do not apply to substances like oil (*taila*), the example *vṛkṣakaḥ* ("a small tree") has been cited.
Although this form is established by the rule *alpe* alone, nevertheless, in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*)...
They say there is a distinction.
(1523) *Kuṭī-śamī-śuṇḍābhyaḥ raḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.88). Regarding the form *kuṭīra*: "Derivative suffixes (*vārthika*) may deviate from the gender of their base (*prakṛti*). Thus [it is masculine].
The masculine gender here is appropriate.

(1524) *vatsākṣāśvarṣabhebhyaśca tanutve* (Pāṇini 5.3.91). [The suffix *kan* is applied after the words] *vat*, *ukṣan*, *aśva*, and *ṛṣabha* when there is "thinness" (*tanutva*). Thinness means deficiency; and that [deficiency] pertains to the primary cause of application (*pravṛttinimitta*), due to proximity.
In some cases, it refers to other properties concomitant with that [state]. In this context, *vatsa* means one in the first stage of life.
The diminution of the first stage of life is the attainment of another stage of life.
Thus he says: "the second. *Taruna* refers to a bull; the attenuation of youth is...

The attainment of the third stage of life; a horse produced from a mare and a horse is a horse, and "horseness" is its genus (*jāti*). The deficiency of the quality of being produced from a mare and a horse—which is concomitant with that genus—is the state of having a different father. Thus, for example, the mule (*aśvatara*) produced by a donkey and a mare [possesses this deficiency]. A bull is the property of a stallion.

A *voḍhṛ* is one who carries; his *tanutva* (smallness) refers to having little strength in carrying a burden, whereas one who possesses that [strength] is a *ṛṣabhatara*. (1525) *Kiṃ-yat-doḥ* [the suffix] *ḍatarac* is used for the selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) of one out of two.
From *kim* and *yad*: *kataraḥ* Vaiṣṇavaḥ ("Which of the two is a Vaiṣṇava?"). This is a selection based on a quality (*guṇa*).

Regarding the rule for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) by means of the suffixes *kriyā* and *saṃjñā*, forms such as *ataro’dhyāpakaḥ* ("the better teacher") and *ataro devadattaḥ* ("the better Devadatta") should be understood. Now, if the suffix *ḍatarac* occurs when selecting one out of two, then [one might ask] regarding "Devadatta is one of these two" or "one of these two."

This [suffix] would also apply in the case of *ayoranyataraḥ*. Regarding this, they say: by the very nature of its denotation, this suffix occurs only after words expressing that which is being singled out (*nirdhāryamāṇa*); therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) here.
Why [is it said] "of one" (*ekasya*)? So that the genitive in *vayoḥ* does not denote the object (*karman*). For if that were the case—
In such cases as "Which two among this assembly are Devadatta and Yajñadatta?", it would indeed apply [only to pairs].

(1526) *Vā bahūnāṃ jātiparipraśne ḍatamac* (Pāṇini 5.3.93). [The sūtra] states: "vā bahūnām. The term *iyatadaḥ* ("of these") is understood [from the previous rule]. [The compound] consists of *jāti* ("genus" or "kind") and *paripraśna* ("inquiry").

This is a collective dvandva compound. In that context, the term *jātau* (in the sense of a genus) is a qualifier for all [the members of the compound]. However, in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), it would be untenable to extract and establish a connection for the mention of "genus" (*jāti*), which has become a subordinate element.
The inclusion of the term *paripraśna* (interrogation), however, is a qualifier specifically for *kim*. And that is for the purpose of excluding [the sense of] censure (*kṣepa*). In that regard:

The mention of "genus" (*jāti*) is intended as a general rule (*prāyo'bhiprāya*). For it is desired that the suffix *ḍatarac* be used for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) even by means of action (*kriyā*), quality (*guṇa*), and name (*saṃjñā*). Therefore, the mention of "of two" (*dvayoḥ*) in the preceding sūtra is intended as a general rule;
for it is desired that *ḍatarac* be used even when selecting from among many. And so it is said:

The *Vārttika* states: "Since suffixes are prescribed for words beginning with *kim* when they have a dual or plural sense, the [additional] condition (*upādhi*) is purposeless. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa says: "The intention is that [the rules] 'vayas' and 'ātiparipraśne' need not be formulated."

This is what he says: "The source has been rejected. Regarding the word *kaṭha*: one should also cite examples such as, "Who among you is the teacher? Is it Śūra or Devadatta? Regarding *yakaḥ sakaḥ*:
the form *aka* is not mentioned; for even when accompanied by *akac*, this substitution *ka* applies to *imaḥ*.

Because it has been explained thus; [the phrase] "by the Mahāvibhāṣā" means that although the mention of *samartha* and *prathama* has been removed in the rule *rāgidiśaḥ*, the mention of *vā* (optionally) continues to apply—this is the intended meaning. [This refers to] the word *dvayoḥ* in the rule *iyatadaḥ*.
He says "What in this? to refute [the objection].
(1527) *ekācca prācām* |5|3|94|. [The word] *ekāt* [is used]; the mention of *prācām* (of the Easterners) is for the sake of honor. The option (*vikalpa*) indeed continues to apply.

(1528) *kan* [is added] in the sense of "contempt" (*avakṣepaṇa*). [Pāṇini 5.3.95]. *kan* [is added] in the sense of contempt. But when it means "despised," *ka* [is added]. There is a difference in accent. Regarding the phrase *yenetara*:
the word *avakṣepaṇa* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), meaning "that by which something is cast down"—this is the intended meaning.
Thus ends the section on the *prāgivīya* suffixes in the Tattvabodhinī. Now begins the section on *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form).

(73) *plutapragṛhyā aci nityam* | P. 6.1.125. The *pluta* and *pragṛhya* vowels maintain their original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) before a vowel; the *pluta* is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to this maintenance of the original form, because the rule prescribes the maintenance of the original form specifically by referring back to the *pluta*. Why "before a vowel" (*aci*)? Consider: *ānu u jānū*. [This refers to] the *uñ* [vowel].

Even though [the vowel *u*] is a *pragṛhya*, the long vowel by position (*savarṇadīrgha*) occurs here. While the rule for *aci* is still in force, the repeated mention of *aci* indicates that the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) applies only when *aci* is the cause of the substitution.
Consequently, even in these cases, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would indeed occur: *jānu u asya rujati* and *ānū asya rujati*.

In this context, when the optional *v* occurs by the rule *aya uñaḥ*, we have *ānvasya rujati* (he hurts him who follows) and *ehi kṛṣṇa* (come, O Kṛṣṇa). Here, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel occurs by the rule *ūrāddhūte ca*. However, the Easterners (*prācām*) have cited *kṛṣṇā ehi* as an example;
that is incorrect, because of the governing rule *vākyasya ṭeḥ*. This [protraction] is conjoined with a short vowel.

"Let it not be so"—this is the intended meaning. The point is as follows: in cases such as *harī īśau*, the rule *plutapragṛhyā aci nityam* (Pāṇini 1.1.11) finds its scope; however, in a case like *akrī atra*, the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77) applies.
Consequently, in the instance *harī etau*, because the latter rule takes precedence, there would result only the substitution of *yaṇ* (the semivowel *y*) combined with the short vowel (*e*).

But when the word *nitya* (invariable) is employed, by its very force it also sublates what follows [the preceding rule]. Regarding the example *cakrayatra*: here, the elision (*lopa*) of the *ku-* [of *kva*] does not occur because, on the view that the application of a rule depends on the time of its effect (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the substitution of *yaṇ* is considered non-existent (*asiddhatva*) by the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*, and also due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*.

However, the rule "when what precedes is not yet established, [the substitute] does not behave as the original" (*ūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*) does not apply here, because it will be stated later that "this is an exception in the cases of the elision of the first letter of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*), the substitution of *l* for *r* (*latva*), and the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*).
Regarding *pārśvam*: it is a collection (*samūha*) of ribs (*parśu*). The suffix *ṇas* is applied according to the rule "it should be stated that *ṇas* follows *arśas*."
But the *orguṇa* does not apply here, because the designation *pada* (as provided by P. 1.4.14) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the designation *bha*.
(74) *ṛtyakaḥ* | 6|1|128|. [The rule] *ṛtyakaḥ*: as in *brahma-ṛṣiḥ*. Now, one might object: let the rule simply be *ṛtyasya*. [In response: *adhi-*...

In cases such as *ṛcchati*, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is established by the rule *iko’savarṇe* alone; therefore, [the inclusion of *a* in the rule *aṇo’pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*] is unnecessary. This is not so, because the mention of *a* is essential for the sake of preserving the original form in the case of *hotṛ-ṛkāra*. By this, the doubt that there should be only one rule, namely *ako’savarṇe*, is rendered groundless.

Indeed, because the aforementioned defects would not be avoided, and because the prohibition "a samāse" (in the absence of a compound) would apply to the form *saptarṣīṇām*. For the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the Vārttika regarding the prohibition "a samāse" applies specifically to the rule *iko'savarṇe*, and not to the rule *ṛtyakaḥ*. Therefore, he says: "in a compound."
[The word] "this" [is also used]. And in this way, the previously mentioned rule "and for the phonemes ṛ and ḷ" becomes consistent.
(75) *Pratyabhivāde’śūdre* 8.2.83.

Regarding the term *pratyabhivāde*: here, by the word *pratyabhivāda*, a benedictory statement (*āśīrvacana*) is meant. Why [is it said] "not for a Śūdra"? [Consider: "I salute you, O Tuṣajaka! [The response is: "May you be long-lived, O Tuṣajaka! [Or: "May you be long-lived! [In this form,] the *s* of the verb *as* (to be) is replaced by *hi*; and by the rule *hrasvaḥ*, the vowel *e* is substituted.

"From *hu*, *jhal*-ending roots, and *hi*, [the substitute] *dhi* [is applied]. "There is elision of the *al* [portion] of *na* and *as*. Regarding "whether it is a name (*nāman*) or a lineage (*gotra*)," an example for lineage (*gotra*) is to be inferred as follows: "I, Gārgya, salute you; O Gārgya, may you be long-lived!"
(76) *dūrāddhūte ca* |8|2|84|.
Regarding *dūrāddhūte ca*: *hūta* means calling; and since this is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for mere addressing, he says—“when addressing from a distance. Because it is an indicator...
He illustrates the result of the explanation with the verse beginning "saktūn piba" (77): *guroranṛto ’nantyasyāpy ekaikasya prācām* (Pāṇini 8.2.86). [The commentary explains:
*guroranṛtaḥ*; *anantyasyāpi*. Regarding this, they say: if it were for the final heavy syllable...

If it were explained that the word *api* has the sense of "also" (*pluta*), then there would be only an optionality (*paryāyatā*) between the protracted vowels (*pluta*) that occupy the position of a heavy syllable (*guru-sthānika*); and consequently, simultaneous usage with the protracted vowel prescribed by another rule (*lakṣaṇāntara*), namely *ūrāddhūte*, which is enjoined in place of a light vowel (*laghu*), would result.

Therefore, even the word *api* must be explained as being for the purpose of indicating the protracted (*pluta*) vowel of both a heavy (*guru*) and a light (*aguru*) *ṭi*, because "e" is the subject under discussion. As in the example *devadatta*: to achieve the status of a complete sentence (*vākyatva*), the word "ehi" (come) should be understood at its beginning; the same applies hereafter. Every protracted vowel is thus made optional.
Thus [it is said]. By this, the *Bhāgavata* passage, "Vaipāyana, terrified of poison, called out, 'Son!

is explained. The statement of Śrīdharācārya—that "the usage is Vedic (archaic) because the elision (*luta*) is optional"—is to be respected. The detailed discussion, however, is found here [in the commentary].
This should be investigated in the *Manoramā*. (78) *aplutavad upasthite* (Pāṇini 6.1.129).
[The sūtra] states that it performs the substitution of *yaṇ* and so forth. Regarding this, the modern scholars (*navya*) say: "If this were so, then in cases such as *agnī* and *viṣṇū*..."

In this case, having set aside the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) which depends on the *pragṛhya* status, the operation of *yaṇ* and so forth would occur by virtue of this [rule] being subsequent;

consequently, the purpose of employing the term *vat* would be merely for the sake of *yaṇ* and the like. Therefore, the explanation of the ancients alone is correct: "The meaning is that [the *pragṛhya* status] does not effect the *prakṛtibhāva*, which is the effect of protracted vowels (*pluta*)."
[The substitution] is indeed superior. And thus, there is no possibility of the *ig-grahaṇa* (the mention of *ig*) in the rule *iko yaṇ aci* being redundant.

To explain: even in the absence of the mention of *ig* there, since the *yaṇ* is prescribed for those two [vowels] by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the words "short" (*hrasva*) and "long" (*dīrgha*) from the rules *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk* and *īrghāt*, it does not apply to a consonant.
It will occur. However, in the case of *pluta*, it must simply not occur due to its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
This applies to exceptions such as "ṭh-haraya" and so on. But in cases like "upendraḥ" and "kṛṣṇaikatvam," the rules "ādguṇaḥ" and "vṛddhireci" act as sublaters (*bādhaka*).

[The vowels] will be [long]. Just as even when *ig* (the short vowel) is included [in the rule], in cases such as *arīśa*, the substitution of a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*) acts as a sublater;

therefore, there is no purpose in including *ig*. Nevertheless, in cases such as *ṭhehi karabhoru 3 iti*, *utanu 3 iti*, and *cinuhi 3 atre’ti*, [the rule] *ṭhaplutavadupasthite* applies to the *ī* [of *iti*].

Even though the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prohibited by the rule *cākravarmaṇasya*, since no operation such as *yaṇ* substitution is prescribed for these two [sounds], the *yaṇ* substitution would not apply to this protracted vowel (*pluta*).

However, if the terms "short" (*hrasva*) and "long" (*dīrgha*) were not carried over [from the previous rule], the substitution would apply to a consonant. Therefore, the mention of "vowels" (*ig-grahaṇam*) is necessary.

They say that it cannot be suspected [of being] useless. Others, however, state another purpose for the mention of *ik*: so that *yaṇ* may occur only in certain instances, and whatever else might otherwise apply, let that not happen. What else might apply? The *śākala* rule, namely "when *ik* is followed by a non-homogeneous vowel" (*iko'savarṇe*).
And thus, that which was stated as "in a non-compound" and "if [the word] 'iti' [follows]," is subsumed by this [rule]. (79) *īcākravarmaṇasya* 6|1|130.
"cinu hīti. The word "invi" is in the imperative mood (*loḍanta*). "Hī" is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

The protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs by the rule "anantyasyāpi praśnākhyānayoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.97). This is an option (*vibhāṣā*) applicable in both cases; the sense is that it is prescribed because it applies where the previous rule would have applied after the word "iti," and also where it would not have applied elsewhere.

(80) *īdūdeddvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam* | 1.1.11. [The rule] "ending in *ī*, *ū*, or *e*" [is understood]. Here, why is there recourse to the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) by means of the qualifier? It is so that [the designation *pragṛhya*] may apply in cases such as *acete imau*. [Furthermore, it applies] in cases such as *harī* and *viṣṇū*, where [the *pragṛhya* status] pertains to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*).

It should be understood that by relying on the treatment as if they were subsequent [elements] (*parādivadbhāva*), since the vowels *ī*, *ī*, etc., possess the status of dual endings, their status as *pragṛhya* is established even when it is stated that "the forms *īdūt* and *ed* are dual endings. Regarding the term "dual ending" (*dvivacana*):
"In a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñāvidhi*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of that which ends with it."

This is because of the indicator (jñāpaka) in the rule *uptiṅntam*, which includes the mention of the final element (*anta*). By this, forms such as *kumāryagāram* and *vadhvagāram*—meaning "the house of two maidens" or "the house of two brides"—are established.
However, for the ancient grammarians (*prācya*) who explained [the rule] as "that which ends in a dual suffix (*dvivacanānta*) shall be *pragṛhya*," this would not be established.
Regarding the phrase *harī etau*: here, the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) combined with a short vowel does not apply;

this is because it has been stated that in the rule *lutapragṛhyāḥ*, the term *nitya* (invariably) is understood. On this point, the author of the *Vṛtti*, having read [the sūtra] as "the prohibition must be stated for *maṇīva* and so forth," provides the examples *aṇīva* and *rodasīva*.

The form *aṃpatī* has been cited [as an example]. Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that this is not authoritative because it is not mentioned by the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali). This being the case, he justifies the usage in the *Mahābhārata*: “*priyau vatsatarau mamaiva oṣṭrasya lambete aṇī*,” explaining that the particle *iva* is used in the sense of *eva*. He says: “the word *va*,” and so forth. [The word] *vaṃ*...

The *Medinī* states: "One should know that *iva* and *vā* are indeclinables (*avyaya*) in these senses. The *Amara-kośa* says: "*Vā*, *yathā*, *tathā*, *eva*, and *evam* [are used] in the sense of similarity. The intended meaning is that this is also supported by the observation of usage such as "lotuses whose petals were torn by *kādamba* birds" (*kādambakhaṇḍitadalāni vā paṅkajāni*).

(81) *adaso māt* |1|1|12|. Regarding *adaso māt*: the vowel *e* does not carry over here because it is impossible [for it to apply]; with this intention, he says: "when *ī* and *ū* [follow]. Why [is] *adasaḥ* [specified]? [Consider: *śamy atra*, *vāmy atra*.

[Objection: Is not the recurrence of the term *nanu* (the word "not") useless? For in the case of ‘triyau phale vā amū āsāte’ ("these two, whether they be women or fruits, sit here"), the result is already established by the preceding rule (*pūrveṇa*), since even though the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered *asiddha*, the form ends in *e*. To this, he says: "rāmakṛṣṇau. [The result] is not established by the preceding rule when [the referent] is masculine.

The intention is that [the substitution] is due to ending in the vowel *au*. With respect to the rule *adaso mā’d*, both the substitution of *m* and the substitution of *ī* are not considered *asiddha*, because of the force of its specific formulation. In the example *amuke'tra*, however, since the dual feminine form is a *pragṛhya* by the preceding rule, there is simply the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
"In such a case, the letter *e* would also recur. Thus, the meaning is that the mention of *māt* (the genitive singular ending) serves to indicate the intended non-recurrence of the letter *e*.
Regarding *śe*: they say that this is a Vedic form (*chāndasam*), stated for the sake of the purity of the composition. Regarding *asme*:
it means "to us" (*asmabhyam*). By the rule *upāṃ suluk*, there is the substitution of *śe* for the case-ending *bhyas*. [Then] by the rule *eṣe lopaḥ*, [the final *m* is elided].

(83) *nipāta ekājanāṅ* 1.1.14. A particle (*nipāta*) consisting of a single vowel (*ekāc*). Why "particle"? [Consider the example: *aḥ*, derived from the root *at* with the suffix *ḍa*. In the phrase *he a āgaccha* ("O, come here"), let there not be the designation *pragṛhya*. If the mention of "single" (*eka*) were absent, then by the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* ("that by which a rule is prescribed applies to that which ends in it"), [the designation would apply to the entire word].
If the word *tadanta* (ending in that) were not understood from the sūtra, then [the rule] *areda* would apply here; therefore, it is said: *ekaḥ*.

However, *ekāj* is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would remain as it was. Therefore, it is indeed a *karmadhāraya* according to the rule *pūrvakālaika-*. Now, if it is argued that [the rule] *nipāto ’nāṅ* has been stated...

Even though a particle ending in a consonant (*halanta*) would possess the status of a *pragṛhya* by virtue of being a particle, since there is no purpose for it, it would follow that only a particle ending in a vowel (*ajanta*) is applicable;
yet, because of the force of the explicit mention of "vowel" (*aj-grahaṇa*), the *pragṛhya* status is established for only those particles that have the form of a vowel.
What, then, is the purpose of the mention of "single" (*eka*)? Nor [is it for the sake of] forms like *uro asti*, where, if the technical name were applied to a particle ending in a consonant...

It should not be argued that the mention of *eka* (in Pāṇini 1.1.13) is unnecessary because the rule *ato ror aplutād aplute* [Pāṇini 6.1.113]— which prescribes the substitution of *u* for *r*— would not apply here due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), and thus the force of the mention of *ac* (in 1.1.12) would already be exhausted;
for with respect to the designation *pragṛhya*, the substitution of *u* for *r* is considered *asiddha*, and therefore [the word] ends in the letter *r*.

Since the fault does not arise due to the absence of the *pragṛhya* designation, one should not argue that the fault remains as it was— namely, that because the *pragṛhya* designation was applied to the form ending in *s*,

it would also apply to the form ending in *r* by the principle of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), and thus the absence of *utva* (the substitution of *u*) would follow from the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). This is because [the rule for] the *pragṛhya* designation...
Because even with respect to the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form), the substitution of *ru* is considered *asiddha*, the *prakṛtibhāva* does not apply.

Furthermore, for a word ending in *s*, there is no purpose found in the section on established rules (*siddhakāṇḍa*) that would be precluded by the *prakṛtibhāva*. Nor can it be argued that, by the force of the mention of *ac* [in the rule], the *prakṛtibhāva* applies only to words ending in a vowel (*ajanta*).

It should be stated that the mention of the word *eka* (in Pāṇini’s rule) is for the purpose of precluding the doubt that the designation *pragṛhya* might apply to a nipāta consisting of more than one syllable—such as *parā* and so on—and not to a nipāta consisting of a single vowel (*akṣarūpa*).
However, this cannot be the case, because it would render the mention of *anāṅ* (the prohibition of *āṅ*) redundant, as in the example: *vyāharati mṛga*.

Because such statements contradict [the rule], the aforementioned doubt does not arise. Furthermore, even though it is stated that "an *ac* following a particle (*nipāta*) except for *aṅ*," by the force of the prohibition regarding *aṅ*, one must accept that the particle (*nipāta*) functions as a qualifier; consequently, since the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadanta-vidhi*) does not apply, a vowel (*ac*) that is a particle is *pragṛhya*.

Thus, since the status of being *pragṛhya* is established for the particle *a-* alone by virtue of obtaining its specific meaning, there is indeed no purpose for the mention of "one" (*eka*). [Objection:
Even so, the mention of "one" is certainly necessary to exclude the collective whole; otherwise, in the case of *ṭhaiu*, etc., [the rule would apply to the entire group].

If it is argued that in the case of *apehi*, by the principle of "doubling a single vowel" (*ekāj-dvirvacana-nyāya*), the designation (*saṃjñā*) would apply only to the whole and not to its parts, such that the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) would occur only for the final vowel and not for the preceding two— this is not so; for [in the rule] *ṭha-ji*, the singular number is indeed intended to be significant.

Because it is possible to exclude a collection [of sounds], there is no inclusion of the individual parts under the designation "collection," and thus even the maxim regarding the reduplication of a single vowel (*ekāj-dvirvacana*) does not apply. Furthermore, since a designation can be established for a single particle (*nipāta*), a collection of particles is not captured by the term "particle.
