Nor should it be said that when *khyun* is applied, the *mum* augment and the acute accent (*udātta*) would not occur; for this is precluded by the exclusion rule *ṭhanavyayasya*. This is because a form ending in *cvī*, such as one derived from *ūry-ādi*, is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by virtue of being designated as a particle (*nipāta*) according to the rule *ūryādicviḍācaśca*. Furthermore, even when *khyun* is present...
It should be stated that while a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*) is obtained by the rule *upapadam atiṅ* when the suffix *lyuṭ* is absent, it is not so when *lyuṭ* is present;

for even with *lyuṭ*, a *gati*-compound is possible, since that too is a compulsory compound. Nor is there any difference regarding feminine suffixes, because [the feminine form] is derived from *lyuṭ* by the rule *iḍḍhea*, and from *khyun* by the rule located therein (*kṛdikārād aktinaḥ*).

And because [the suffix] *ṅīp* is identical to [the suffix] *khyun* by means of the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*), nor is there any difference in accent; for in the case of *lyuṭ*, there is the accent of the *lit* affix, while in the case of *khyun*, there is the accent of the *nit* affix, and thus there is no difference in the fact that the root *kṛ* is udātta. Nor should it be argued that the mention of "not being a vowel" (*acvau*) is for the sake of subsequent rules, because if it were solely for the sake of subsequent rules, it would have been stated right there.

One might say: "This very point has been stated [in the Bhāṣya] as 'even the suffix *lyuṭ* is not [intended here]'. Regarding the phrase "according to the view of the Bhāṣya," Kaiyaṭa maintains that, by the natural force (*svarasa*) of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika, it is understood that the suffix *lyaṭ* is desired; thus, it is obtained that [the rule] serves solely the purpose of the subsequent [sūtra].
Therefore, Kaiyaṭa concludes that the view of the author of the Vṛtti is incorrect because it contradicts that [evidence].
(650) *kartari bhuvaḥ khiṣṇuc-khukañau* [Pāṇini 3.2.57]. Regarding *kartari bhuvaḥ*: the phrase *acvyanteṣu* ("in the case of those ending in -ac") applies.
The word *acvi* is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*). Otherwise, forms such as *āḍhyībhaviṣṇuḥ* and *āḍhyībhāvukaḥ* would not be possible.

The sense is: "it might be so. The ancient commentators maintain that "the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) is for the purpose of dispelling the misconception that the term 'instrument' (*karaṇa*) is being carried over [from the previous rule], and it is also for the sake of what follows. However, in reality, this is indeed useless;
for since the term is not marked with the *svarita* accent, its non-carrying over is established by itself, and it serves no purpose even in the subsequent rules.

And because it is about to be clarified [later]. The letter *kh* is for the purpose of elision (*mum*). As for the letter *c*, since it is not *svarita*, its non-continuation (*ananuvṛtti*) is established even without it; furthermore, although the augment *iṭ* is applied to ensure the form begins with the vowel *i*, that augment is unaccented (*anudātta*) according to the rule "augments are unaccented. Nor is there...

There would be no inclusion of this [term] in the *svarasūtra* "ṛty-okeṣṇuccārvādayaśca," because the letter *i* (in *iṣṇu*) is *lākṣaṇika* due to the absence of the *anubandha* *c*, and because the form *iṣṇu* does not exist since the substitution for *ṣatva* and *ṇatva* is *asiddha*.

It must be stated [that this is so], because even if the letter *i* were present, by the paribhāṣā "when there is the mention of a term with a specific *anubandha*, that which does not have that same *anubandha* is not included," only the suffix *iṣṇuc* following roots such as *alaṅkṛ* would be grasped, and not this one.
If it is argued that this one is also grasped by virtue of the power of the pronunciation of the letter *i*, then indeed [so be it].

Let there be victory for Khaṣṇu! If one were to argue that once *it* (the suffix) has been established, this [suffix] should also be included by virtue of the power of the indicatory letter *c*, then the question arises: "What is the purpose of the vowel *i*? This point requires reflection. Nor should it be suspected that the vowel *i* might be present for the sake of brevity while the letter *c* itself need not exist.

Since it is universally agreed that "a short vowel consists of one *mātrā* and a consonant consists of half a *mātrā*," the claim made by Haradatta— that this [consonant] is included here by virtue of the force (*sāmarthya*) of the rules for *ṣatva* and *ṇatva*— is merely superficial; for,
rather than stating *ṣṇu*, the mention of *sru* actually results in greater brevity of procedure (*prakriyālāghava*) regarding *ṣatva* and *ṇatva*.
"Because of the unsuitability of the instrument [as the locus], there is no application of the capacity [of the suffix]; this is the general direction. Regarding the term *nivṛtam* (ceased):

if it is objected that since the root *spṛś* is transitive (*sakarmaka*), the suffix should necessarily be prescribed as occurring after the object (*karmaṇi*) by the rule itself, the ancient commentators reply: the word *kartari* (in the sense of the agent) is carried over (*anuvartate*) from the preceding sūtra; and that carry-over applies to the [present] agent.

Since the suffix *kvip* is already established for the agent by the rule *kṛd* alone, [the addition of the word] *kartari* (in the sense of the agent) would otherwise be redundant; therefore, it serves to indicate a plurality of agents (*kartṛpracaya*).

This plurality of agents consists of one agent when a direct object (*karman*) is the subordinate element (*upapada*), and another when an instrument (*karaṇa*) or other such factors are the subordinate elements. Thus, the result is that [the rule applies] "when an *u*-ending word is the subordinate element."

The form *mantraspṛk* and so forth is established even by means of the suffix *kvip*. Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *ku* (the guttural *k*) would not occur in the case of *kvip*, because the possibility of that *ku*-substitution arises precisely from the force of the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that from which the suffix *vin* [is elided]. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Regarding *sadṛk*: [it means] "like him."

People see him; by the etymological derivation that "this one sees like him," the reflexive-passive (*karmakartṛ*) suffix is applied because it accords with the conventional meaning [of the word *paśu*]. (651) [This is governed by] Pāṇini 3.1.61: *satsūdviṣadruhaduhayujavidabhidacchidajinīrājām upasarge 'pi*.
The suffix *kvip* [is applied after roots ending in vowels to form agent nouns].

[The rule] *satsūdviṣa...* [applies to the following roots]: *sad* (to sit), *sū* (to bring forth), *dviṣ* (to hate), *ṣadlṛ* (to perish, etc.). Because of its association with *dviṣ*, the root *sū* taken here is the one belonging to the first class (*bhvādi*), and not the two others, *suvati* and *sūyati*. [The root] *yujir*...

In the case of *yoge*, from the root *yuja* in the sense of concentration (*samādhi*), both [roots] are included. In the case of *vida*, there is inclusion of all three: *vida* in the sense of knowing, *vida* in the sense of discerning (*vicāraṇa*), and *vida* in the sense of existence (*sattā*). However, there is no inclusion of the root *vidlṛ* in the sense of obtaining (*lābha*), because the vowel *a* is intended in the term *videt*. [The word] *dyausat*...

The substitution of *ṣ* in the word *ūrvapadāt* does not occur because of the continued application of the rule *chandasi* (Vedic usage). Thus says Māgha: "by whom [the mind] is placed within the minds of the sky-dwellers. However, regarding the form *āditeyā dviṣadaḥ*, Mādhava and others maintain that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs here because the word belongs to the *suṣāmādi* group. But in the case of *upaniṣad*, [the substitution does not occur].

By the rule *‘adiraprate’*, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs. Regarding the phrase *‘agragrāmābhyām’*: it is stated that the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs even after a word other than a *kṛt*-suffix, as indicated by the grammatical citation *‘a eṣāṃ grāmaṇīḥ’*; thus, they say that *agraṇīḥ* is also established.

[The suffix] *viṭ* occurs after the root *ad-* when not followed by *anna*. This is because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from the preceding rule: "After the roots *ana*, *san*, *khan*, *kram*, and *gam*, the suffix *viṭ* occurs. However, that preceding rule has not been cited here; for in that [rule],...
Because of the continued application of the rule *na chandasi* [from Pāṇini 6.1.126] to the rule *chandasi sahaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.128], [the substitution of *sa* for *sah* does not occur here].
(653) *duhaḥ kaḥ dvyacaś ca* [Pāṇini 3.2.70]: [The word] *kāmadughā* [is formed thus]. The remainder [of the sūtra] is *henuḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "she who milks [fulfills] desire."

(654) *anyebhyo’pi dṛśyante* | 3|2|75|. They are seen after others as well. Here, the suffix *vic* is understood from the rule *vijupacchandasi*; and from the rule *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca*, the suffixes *manin* and so forth are also carried over. Thus he says:
*Maninkvanibityādi* (and so forth).

(655) *Neḍvaśi kṛti* [Pāṇini 7.2.8]: the augment *iṭ* is not applied before a *kṛt* suffix ending in *vaś*. *Suśarma*: derived from *suṣṭhu śṛṇāti*, with the suffix *kvip*. *Prātaritvā*: derived from *prātar eti*, with the suffix *kvanip* after the root *iṇ*.
In some cases, the augment *tuk* is applied by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti*.

By the rule *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt*, there is the substitution of *ā* for the nasal; thus, *avāva* occurs. When followed by the nominative suffix *su*, the long vowel and the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) take place. [The form becomes] *roṭ*.
*reḍiti*: [This is derived from] *ruṣa* and *riṣa*, meaning "to injure. There is guṇa substitution for the penultimate vowel, followed by *jaśtva* and *cartva* changes.

(657) *kvip ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.76): *vāhabhraḍiti*. The analysis of the compound is: "one who falls away (*bhraśyati*) from the horse (*vāhāt*). However, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), it appears as *vahābhraḍiti*.
The reading is *vahaḥ* for *skandhaḥ*; Haradatta states that the final vowel of the preceding member becomes long according to the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*.

The term *antaḥ* (end) continues [from the previous rule]. Here, "end" is understood with reference to the word (*pada*), not with reference to the root *an*, because there is no ambiguity; therefore, he says: "of the end of a word. [In the example] *he prāṇiti*: the root *ana* means "to breathe"; [the suffix] *kvip* is applied; by the rule *anunāsikasya*, there is lengthening [of the vowel]; [and then the elision of the *k*]. *A...* [the rest of the sūtra follows].

In the case of *mitrabuddhyaḥ*, there is a prohibition of the elision of *n*. However, in other instances, the elision of *n* must occur; thus, a form ending in the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) has been cited as an example. Regarding *mitraśīḥ*: even though the *kvip* suffix has been elided, by the rule of "characterization by the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇanyāya*), there exists the status of being followed by a suffix that begins with a consonant (*hal*) and is marked with *k* or *it*; however, this does not apply when the operation depends solely on the phoneme itself (*varṇāśraye*).
The intention is that because it has been stated that the term *pratyayalakṣaṇam* applies only when there is predominance of the suffix (*varṇaprādhānya*).
Regarding *āśāse*: the root *śās* [is used] in the sense of instructing (*anuśiṣṭi*); *āṅ-śās* is used in the sense of desiring and is *ātmanepada*.
Since [the form] is already established by the rule *āsa iḥ* etc., the statement "optionally, the *it* [substitution] occurs for the penultimate vowel" is intended to apply specifically here.

This [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Therefore, according to some, the form *āśāste* is established [by this rule alone]. Others, however, maintain that this is solely for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*) and not for restriction, because there is no prior applicability [of the rule]. Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *it* (short *i*) by the rule "āsa idaṅhaloḥ" is already applicable; [this is not so].

In that context, because of the association with *aṅ*, only the root *ās* (to sit) which is parasmaipada is understood [by the rule]. Although it is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that, due to the separate formulation of the rule "artiśāsti... (Pāṇini 3.1.56), the suffix *aṅ* applies to the root *ṛ* (to go) such that both forms *ārita* and *samāratā* are established in the luṅ tense, nevertheless, [the separate mention] is for the sake of subsequent purposes.

The explicit statement in the *Ākara* (the *Mahābhāṣya*) regarding the continued application of the mention of the *parasmaipada* leads to the conclusion that [the substitution of *śāsa* for *āśās* applies] only to that *śās* which is seen in the *parasmaipada*, followed by an *aṅ* suffix. Thus, they say that in the case of *āśāste*, there is no possibility of the shortening (*itva*) at all. However, in reality, this is because of the rule "In the sense of benediction (*āśis*), the *liṅ* and *loṭ* [are used]."
This is not a new *vārttika*, as it is already established by the very mention [in the rule] "ṣiyāśīḥpraiṣeṣu" and so forth.
The meaning of the statement "the state of being *it* (short *i*) should be expressed for *at*" is that the substitution of *it* is to be explained [there].
This is because of the aforementioned mention in "āśiṣi" and so on; such is the direction. Regarding "sumvau": this refers to [the rule] "ṭhoḥ supi".

(659) *sthaśca ka* (Pāṇini 3.2.77): [The suffix] *ka* is also applied after the root *sthā*. Thus, *śaṃsthā*. When the *kvip* suffix is elided, the substitution of *ī* [for the final vowel] as prescribed by "ahumāsthe" does not occur.

This is because the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) is prohibited by the rule *analvidhau*. Furthermore, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* sūtra is established as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) meaning that it applies only where the unique form of an affix is relied upon.
As for what Kaiyaṭa stated—namely, "the property of *ī*-ness [is present] in *avakārādi* and *ādavi*"—[that is incorrect].

The statement that "the substitution of *ī* does not occur by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule, either because of [Patañjali’s] word or because of the authority of the examples given by the Bhāṣyakāra," is made with reference to the view that the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* sūtra is for the sake of operations concerning vowels (*alvidhi*) when the suffix (*pratyaya*) is predominant, in order to establish forms such as *ṭhatṛṇeḍ*. In that case as well, [the restriction applies] "when [the suffix begins] with *ava* and so forth."

It should be understood that, dissatisfied with the view that [the vowel substitution] occurs by accepting the verbal expression (vacana), as if it were "sudhī," another alternative is accepted. Now, one might object: "In the view where the conclusion is 'this is for the sake of the meaning' (iyamārtham), how could the short *i* (itvam) occur in the previously mentioned word *matraśī*? To this, they say:

"Let there be *śās* + *it*. From that, [the substitute] *aṅ*. This is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). It should be understood that the mention of the term *hal* (consonant) is intended to indicate: "If *it*-ness is to occur before an affix beginning with a vowel (*ajādau*), let it be only after *aṅ*, and not elsewhere"—thus, the mention of *hal* need not be [otherwise] required. Nor does this lead to an error; for even so, since the substitution of *im* is prescribed for *tṛṇah* before a *pit* sārvadhātuka affix beginning with a consonant, forms such as *atṛṇeṭ* and the like [are correctly derived].

It must be stated that since [the desired result] is not established under the view that [the rule applies] only to *niyama*, the alternative view— that it is for the purpose of an *al*-vidhi— must also be accepted; for,

by carrying forward the mention of *hal* from the sūtra "uto vṛddhir luki hali" and applying it to the word *tṛṇahāni* to avoid the undesired outcome, [the condition] "before a vowel" (*aci*) is taken from the sūtra "ābhyastasyāci."
This is explained by following the word "na" (not) [from the previous rule]. This has already been explained in the *Rudhādi* class itself.
It might be argued: "The suffixes *kak* and *kvip* are established by the two rules 'upi sthaḥ' and 'vip ca'.
In the case of *śamī* and so forth, since the suffix *ac* occurs after every verbal root due to the force of the mention of the term 'dhātu' (verbal root), [the form would be incorrect]."

The intention is that just as the suffix *ṭa* [prescribed] after roots such as *kṛ* (to do) subverts [the application of other suffixes], so too would the suffixes *kan* and *kvip* subvert [them]; therefore, the rule “*thaḥ ka ca*” is commenced. Now, one might object: "In that case, why not formulate the rule 'thaḥ ka ca' immediately after 'ami dhātoḥ', with the letter *ca* [in that rule] serving to include the vowel *ac*?"
If it is argued: "Once the *samprasāraṇa* has been combined, there will be a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), resulting in *śaṃsthā*;
thus, because the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*) occupy the same position, the integrity of the textual composition (*saṃdarbhaśuddhi*) is also maintained;
furthermore, no effort need be made to prevent the substitution of *it*, which results in great economy," to this they reply: "Not so. [The text continues with: *aśaṃ...*

In the word *sthā*, the final syllable of the second member would be udātta by the rule "ṭhakchau cāśaktau," because the word *saṃsthā* ends in a vowel (being formed with the suffix *kvip*) and is preceded by a prefix or a kāraka according to the principle "when there is the mention of an *ṛ*-vowel, [the rule applies] even to that which is preceded by a prefix or a kāraka. However, since the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) is formed with a *kvib*-derived form, the original accent of the first member, the negative particle (*nañ*), is established.

(660) *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye* [Pāṇini 3.2.78]. For example, *uṣṇabhojī* ("one who habitually eats hot food"): this means that eating hot food is his habit (*śīla*). Also, *āmantrayitṛ* ("one who addresses"): the root *matri* is used in the sense of "secret conversation" (*guptaparibhāṣaṇe*), belonging to the *cur*-class (*curādi*) with the prefix *āṅ*. Because it is marked with the *idit* designation, the augment *num* is applied; this denotes habitual action (*tācchīlya*).

Because it is intended [to be included], for this very reason, due to the prohibition by the rule *a loke*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of the object is not applied in the word *brāhmaṇān*.
[The phrase] "only when distinct from a prefix" is stated in this sūtra so that only a *sup* (nominal suffix) distinct from a prefix may be obtained,
since the rule *katsūdviṣa-* states "even when there is a prefix."
The sense is that the term *su-* has been mentioned again. [This is] because of the contradiction with the Bhāṣya; for it is stated in the Bhāṣya:

"While *u* is still in force, what is the purpose of mentioning *su-* again? It was intended so that [the rule] would not apply when there is a prefix (*anupasarga*). But this [mention of *su-*, however], is so that it may apply even to a mere *su-* [as in the example] *udāsāriṇyaḥ*."

Regarding the phrase "pratyāsāriṇyaḥ," this is its intended meaning: in the rule *atsūdviṣa*, the term *supi* is carried over from the previous rule *upi sthaḥ*; furthermore, that term refers to something other than a prefix (*upasarga*), because the expression *upasarge’pi* is stated separately. Thus, when it is carried over here, by virtue of the governing topic of meaning (*arthādhikāra*), it refers exclusively to what is other than a prefix.

It might be so. However, in the final analysis, there is no need to include the mention of *sub* here, since the derivation can be maintained by the continued application of the rule *api upasarge*. In any case, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the suffix *ṇini* occurs when a mere *sup*-ending word is the *upapada*, and not only when it is without a prefix (*anupasarga*). And this he employed as follows:

"The rule concerning the remainder of the *liṅga* (gender) is pervasive, provided it is not sublated by specific rules"—this is the general direction. There is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for one who performs an action well (*sādhukārī*). Regarding "one who performs an action well": this is established by a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence).
For in the sūtra *ākveḥ*, one who performs an action well is understood as distinct from "one who has that as a habit" (*tacchīla*), and that...

Even in the absence of the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), the suffix *ṇini* is appropriate when [the word] *brahman* is present, as in "one who speaks of Brahman" (*brahmaṇi vadaḥ*) or "one who speaks regarding Brahman" (*brahmaṇi vada*). However, this [usage] is based solely on a specific scriptural rule (*vācanika*). The phrase "for the sake of [excluding] the sense of habitual action" is clear in the works of Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others. As for that which...

In the Bhaṭṭavārtika, the word *brahmavādin* is explained as referring to one who has that as their habit (*tacchīla*), that as their duty (*taddharma*), or one who performs it well (*tatsādhukārī*). However, since there is no rule under the governing heading *ṭhak-ṭhe* that prescribes the suffix *ṇini* after the root *vad* when combined with *brahman*, how can this [explanation] be consistent?

To this, they reply: This is the intention of Bhaṭṭapāda—the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) by the rule "upon the roots *upa-jan*" (*upyajātau*). Alternatively, by means of an explanatory supplement (*upasaṅkhyāna*) or an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of one who performs an action well (*sādhukārī*).

However, the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*) according to the rule "the suffix *ṇini* [is applied] in the senses of necessity and debt" (*āvaśyakādhamarṇyayorṇini*) pertains to that very quality (*taddharma*).
It concludes that there is no application here of the rule *ṭhā-kveṭa-raḥ*. Now, if it is asked:

"In the phrase *brahmavādino vadanti*, since the word *brahman*—meaning the Veda—is also a term denoting a genus (*jāti*), how can the suffix *ṇini* be justified here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*)? To this, [the author] replies: "In this case..."

The moderns [hold]: “In the rule *ūpyajātau*, only the genus of living beings (*prāṇijāti*) is excluded, because of the co-occurrence with the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), and because this is consistent with the counter-example ‘*brāhmaṇān āmantrayate*’. Thus, [the objection] does not hold.
"There is no inconsistency whatsoever.

(661) *manaḥ* | 3|2|82 | *manaḥ*. Because of the continued application of the term "in various cases" (*bahulagrahaṇa*), only the root *man-* belonging to the *daivādika* class is understood here, and not [the other].

The root *man* belongs to the *tanādi* class, meaning "to awaken" (*avabodhana*). Consequently, in the subsequent sūtra, when the suffix *khaś* is applied, it becomes *śyan* and not the suffix *u*. Thus he says: "of the root *man*" (*manyateḥ*).
(662) *ātmamāne khaś ca* | Pāṇini 3.2.83. [When expressing self-conceit (*ātmamāna*), the suffix *khaś* is also applied after the root *man*.]

Regarding *ātmamāne*: "māna" is the act of measuring (*mananam*); the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). The compound *ātmamāna* is formed with a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), meaning "the measuring of the self. Since the word *ātman* is a synonym for "self" (*sva*) and is present as the meaning of the affix, the agent is its own referent; thus he says: "having itself as the object," and so forth. As for the word *ca* ("and"): [one might ask] "Is this not [already covered] by the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*)?"
If it is asked, "Since the suffix *ṇini* is indeed obtained [by the previous rule], for what purpose is the letter *ca* [used here]?"—on this point they say:

by means of the letter *ca*, the suffix *ṇini* is conjoined (*samuccīyate*) for the sake of delimitation (*avacchedāya*). Consequently, in rules such as "after the root *yaj* in the sense of 'sacrificing' (*araṇe yajaḥ*)," only *ṇini* is carried forward (*anuvartate*), and not *khaś* alone; and thus, in accordance with the stated purpose, [the desired forms are secured].
The rule “ānukṛṣṭaṃ notaratra” (the suffix *kṛt* following *ā-ni* does not apply in subsequent cases) does not operate here. Regarding the example "paṇḍitamātmānam" (he considers himself learned):

it should be understood that even for a single self (*ātman*), there is agency (*kartṛtva*) by its own nature, and objecthood (*karmatva*) by way of being qualified by the state of being learned (*paṇḍitatva*). What is the purpose of [specifying] "in the sense of considering oneself" (*ātmamāne*)? [Consider: "darśanīyamānī devadattaḥ" (Devadatta considers himself handsome).

In the case of *yajñadattasya kālimanyāḥ*, the short vowel [of the first member] occurs because it is an exception (*apavāda*), overriding the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) that would otherwise be required by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*. As for the statement made by the author of the *Prasāda* that the masculine form is here obtained by the rule *yaṅmāninoḥ*, that is merely said in haste, since there is no occurrence of the suffix *mānin*.

Because it is clear. [The word] *divāmanya-* [is formed as follows]: although this [word *divā*] primarily expresses the locative case-role (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), it takes the status of an object (*karmatva*) due to its nature as a compound (*vṛtti-svabhāvāt*).
(Pāṇini 6.3.68) *ica ekāco'mpratyayavacca*: "In place of the single-vowel (*ekāc*) [element] ending in /i/ or /ī/, there is the substitution of /am/, and it is treated like a suffix (*pratyaya*)."

Regarding *ica ekācaḥ*: the term *am* is repeated here; by the first [occurrence], *am* is prescribed, and by the second, the suffix is qualified. Thus it says: "like *svādya*. And so, because of the prohibition "the *tu*, *sa*, and *ma* [at the end] are not [it-saṃjñaka] when followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*)," the *m* does not receive the *it*-designation; for this very reason, it is also *para* (subsequent).

In the rule *ṭhāṬto’mśasoḥ*, it has been stated that because of its association (*sāhacarya*) with *śas*, only the case-ending *am* is understood; therefore, with the intention that the vowel *ā* also occurs after *ot*, he provides the examples:
*gāṃmanyaḥ* and *naraṃmanyaḥ*. The *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *a-u*] is applied by the rule *ṛto’ṅi guṇaḥ*. [The author] says "the author of the Bhāṣya"; this is the intended meaning (*bhāva*).

Just as words such as *praṣṭhā* and others denote a female through connection with a male—as in *praṣṭhī* (the wife of a leader) or *gaṇikā*—so here the word *śrī*, having abandoned its own gender and becoming neuter, denotes a family (*kula*).
In that case, by the rule "the short vowel [is used] in the neuter," the vowel becomes short; however, the augment *mum* does not apply, because it is superseded by the exception *am*.

By the rule *vāmo napuṃsakāt*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *am*. Nor should it be argued that elision would also occur in cases such as *gām anyaḥ* by the rule *upa-dhātu-prātipadikayoḥ*, for they say that this is precluded precisely by the force of the specific injunction (*vidhi*) regarding the suffix *am*. As for the suffix *am* itself...

It is established in the Bhāṣya and other works that, according to the maxim *adhye’pavādāḥ* (subsequent exceptions set aside only those rules which precede them), the rule *upo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* sets aside only the elision (*luk*) prescribed by *svamornapuṃsakāt*, and not the elision prescribed by *vasoḥ samprasāraṇam*.
This might be argued: once the shortening of the neuter vowel has been applied, there is no possibility at all for the occurrence of *mum*.

How else could the statement "there is no sublation here because of the exclusion [apavāda]" be consistent? For in the rule *ṭharurdviṣadajantasya mum* (Pāṇini 6.3.67), since the mention of *anta* signifies proximity (*samīpa*), it is accepted that the short vowel [of the final letter] is for the sake of the *mum* augment under the condition "provided it is not an indeclinable" (*hityanavyayasya*). If that were the case here as well, the *mum* augment would indeed exist.
Regarding the term *prāpti*: (664) *bhūte* 3.2.84.

[The word] *bhūte* [is used]. Since the governing rule *dhātoḥ* (3.1.91) is in force, this [term] qualifies the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). It refers to the sense of "past" (*bhūte arthe*).
The meaning is "from an existing root.

(665) *karaṇe yajaḥ* |3|2|85|. Regarding "in the sense of the instrument": because it is marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*), only the suffix *ṇini* is understood to follow, and not *khaś*; thus he says—*ṇiniḥ*.
It may be thus: "He performed a sacrifice with *soma*," meaning with a particular creeper.

Regarding "Agniṣṭoma": that sacrifice which is completed by the Agniṣṭoma chant is figuratively called "Agniṣṭoma"; the meaning is that he brought about the *apūrva* (unseen potency) by means of it. And it has been said:
In the *Kāśikā*: "The *agniṣṭoma* is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward the fruit.
(666) *Karmaṇi hanaḥ* | 3|2|86|.
Regarding the rule *karmaṇi hanaḥ*, [the example] is *pitṛvyaghātī*. Here, the *Kāśikā* states: "The mention of the word *utsita*..."

It must be stated here so that [the suffix] does not apply in a case such as *coraṃ hatavān* ("he killed the thief"). Although this is not explicitly found in the Bhāṣya, they say that it is obtained through the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvya*).
(667) *brahmabhrūṇavṛtreṣu kvip* 3.2.87. [The suffix *kvip* is applied after a verbal root when *brahman*, *bhrūṇa*, or *vṛtra* are the objects.]

"Fourfold" means this is the intended sense: since they are mentioned in this sūtra, Brahmā and the others are first the subjects (*uddeśya*); immediately after them, because he is the material cause (*prakṛti*), is Hantī; and by elimination, Bhūta follows. However, the *kvip* suffix must be indicated at the very end, because it is that which is to be predicated (*vidheya*). Thus it is.
The analysis of the statement is as follows: "When *brahman* and so forth are the upapadas, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *han* in the sense of the past.

This being the case, by the maxim "where there is a restriction (*ekagraha*), that restriction applies to what immediately follows," the restriction here takes effect on the immediately preceding element.
Consequently, the restriction is understood as "only when *brahman* and so forth [are the upapadas]."

Since it is mentioned immediately after that, the restriction on the root (*prakṛti-niyama*) has the result of excluding other accompanying words (*upapada*). However, in the restrictive rule (*avadhāraṇa*) stating "only *han* is used with *brahmādi* in the sense of the past," although there is no difference in terms of immediate proximity, the restriction on the accompanying word (*upapada-niyama*) applies because of its priority.
It results in the exclusion of other verbal roots [from taking the suffix].

However, in the rule *brahmādiṣu hanter bhūta eva kvip*, although there is no distinction regarding the immediate sequence between the root ending in *kvip* and the words beginning with *brahman*, the restriction on the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*) results in the exclusion of connection with other times, because of its predominance. [In the case of] *brahmādiṣu*...

In the formulation of the rule *hanter bhūte kvi(v)i caiva*, the restriction of time has as its result the exclusion of connection with other suffixes. This is the distinction between the restrictions concerning the base (*prakṛti*), the upapada, the suffix (*pratyaya*), and the time (*kāla*).

Since no specific distinction is being grasped, all four types [of verbal roots] are included here. In that regard, regarding the restriction to the root *han* (to kill) as applied to Brahmins and others, because the term *bhūte* (in the past) is adopted, it occurs not only in the past time but also in the present and future times, even when there is another governing word (*upapada*). For example: *puruṣaṃ hanti* (he kills a man) and *haniṣyati* (he will kill).

Or [he is] "Puruṣahā" (the slayer of Puruṣa). He is "Arihayogavicakṣaṇaḥ" (skilled in the yoga of slaying enemies). The meaning is: he who slays enemies is "Arihā," and he is skilled in that which is both an enemy and yoga, hence "Arihayogavicakṣaṇaḥ. However, the designation "Puruṣahā" (slayer of Puruṣa) refers to the fruit of the regulation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*); there is no application of the term in its literal sense, as Puruṣa has never been slain. [This applies] to Brahmā and the others.

Even though there is a restriction regarding the *upapada* (governing word) by the rule "only after *han*," because the term *bhūta* ("past") is relied upon, the suffix occurs even after other roots in the sense of the present and future tenses—
as in *vṛtraṃ jayati* or *jeṣyati vṛtrajit*. However, the purpose of the restriction regarding the *upapada* is [to exclude the suffix] after *vṛtram*...

There is no usage such as *jitavān vṛtraj*. Even though there is a restriction on the suffix by the rule "only after [the root] *han* when followed by *kvi*", because it is stated that this applies to *brahman* and others, the suffix *kvip* certainly occurs after the root *han* even with other upapadas (governing words) in the present and future tenses. For example: *puruṣaṃ hanati*.

Or [the suffix] *ha* is used after the root *han* (to kill) when preceded by a word signifying an enemy (*ari*), as previously stated. However, the result of this restriction regarding the suffix is that there is no usage such as *brahmahā* (a killer of a Brahmin) with the suffix *ha* in the sense of "one who will kill" (*bhaviṣyati*).

Even though there is a restriction of time [by the rule] *hūte kvipeva* ("after the root *han* with the prefix *abhi*, the suffix *kvip* occurs only in the sense of the past"), because it is specified that this applies to words like *brahman* and others, another suffix may occur even in the past tense when other governing words (*upapada*) are present.

It is indeed so: one who has killed his paternal uncle is called a *pitṛvyaghātī*. Here, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *armaṇi hanaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.88) to denote the past tense (*bhūta*). However, the result of the restriction regarding time is that there is no usage such as *brahmaghātī* for "one who has killed a Brahmin. Furthermore, the suffix is restricted by rule when accompanied by a prefix (*sopapada*), whereas the *niṣṭhā* suffixes [are not].

However, it is indeed the case that [the tradition] says "he killed Vṛtra. But the author of the Bhāṣya relied solely upon the restriction of the base (prakṛti) and the time (kāla). His intention was this: for neither the verbal root (dhātu) nor the time are explicitly mentioned here in the sūtra; rather, they are presented through the weaker means of proof (pramāṇa), namely context (prakaraṇa) and indication (lakṣaṇa).

Therefore, it is logical that the restriction applies only to those two [the verbal root and the suffix], and not to the *upapada* and the suffix, because they are brought forward by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). Thus, Kaiyaṭa concludes that the view of the *vṛtti* must be disregarded, as it contradicts the Bhāṣya supported by such reasoning. As for what is stated here...
Haradatta stated: "Two rules regarding verbal roots (*dhātu*) and suffixes (*upapada*) have been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya.
In this regard, it should be noted that while one ought to say "rules concerning verbal roots and time" (*dhātūkālaviṣaya*), the mention of *upapada* is an error (*prāmādika*).

(668) *sukarmapāpamantrapuṇyeṣu kṛñaḥ* |3|2|89|. Regarding *sukarma*: the sense is that here a restriction to specific verbal roots (*dhātuniyama*) is not intended. Regarding *kvibeva*: this refers to the rule *hūte kvibeve*.
The meaning is: because of the restriction of time, which has as its result the exclusion of connection with other conditions (*pratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "only with *kṛñ*":

the meaning is because of the restriction of the *upapada*, which has as its result the exclusion of connection with other verbal roots (*dhātu*), expressed as "only with *kṛñ*" in the case of [verbs] having an object and so forth. Regarding the phrase "only in the past tense":...

The meaning is that there is a restriction of the suffix [to a specific time] with the result of excluding its connection with other times, as in *‘hūta eva kvib’* (the *kvip* suffix occurs only when [the root] is preceded by *hūta*).
Regarding the phrase *‘svādiṣveva’*: it means *‘kṛñ’ [occurs] only after roots beginning with *su*’.
The meaning is that there is no restriction on the verbal root (*dhātu-niyama*) whose result is the exclusion of connection with other secondary suffixes (*upapada*).
(669) *some suñaḥ* |3|2|90|. Regarding *some suñaḥ*, the commentary (*vṛtti*) states that here too there is a fourfold restriction.

The same applies in the subsequent sūtra as well. In that context, because the suffix *kvip* is restricted to the past tense (*bhūtakāla*), one who has pressed the *soma* is called *somam-sutavān*, which becomes *somasāvaḥ*; and one who has piled the fire-altar is called *agniṃ-citavān*, which becomes *agnicāyaḥ*. In these cases, the suffix *aṇ* does not occur. This is because the root *su* (to press) is restricted to having *soma* alone as its attendant noun (*upapada*), while the root *ci* (to pile) is restricted to having *agni* alone as its attendant noun.

Because [the root] *su* is restricted [in meaning], one forms *surā-sutaḥ* (one who has pressed *surā*) and *iṣṭakā-citaḥ* (one who has piled bricks), but not *surā-sut* or *iṣṭakā-cit*; rather, there occurs only the suffix *-aṇ*, as in *surā-sāvaḥ* and *iṣṭakā-cāyaḥ*. This is because the root *su* is restricted to the sense of pressing *soma*, whereas for *agni*, however—

Because [the suffix] *kvip* is restricted to the sense of "one who performs the action," as in *somakrīḥ* ("one who has purchased Soma") and *agnibhṛt* ("one who has maintained the fire"), the suffix *kvip* does not occur here;

rather, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs, as in *somakrayaḥ* ("the purchase of Soma") and *agnibhāraḥ* ("the maintenance of the fire"). Furthermore, because *kvip* is restricted to the sense of "one who has already performed the action" (*bhūta*), [the suffixes] *śatṛ* and *śānac* do not occur in cases such as *somaṃ sunoti* ("he presses Soma") or *soṣyati* ("he will press").

The suffix *kvip* does not occur in the sense of "he knows. Likewise, in the sense of "he builds" or "he will build" a fire-altar (*agni*), there is an absence of *kvip*; rather, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs. Regarding the rule "after [a root] with an object" (*karmaṇi*), the mention of "contemptible" (*kutsita*) is obtained by the force of the repeated mention of "object" (*karman*), such that it refers to an object which is connected with the action.

The meaning is that it brings contempt for the agent in that context. Since Soma and other such items, when being sold, are prohibited by the scriptures, they bring about contempt. Because of the inclusion of the word "contemptuous" (*kutsita*), [the suffix does not apply] here: "selling grain.
(670) *dṛśeḥ kvanip* | 3|2|94|. The suffix *kvanip* is applied after the root *dṛś* [to form a noun denoting the agent].

The suffix *kvanip* is applied after the root *dṛś*. Although [the formation] is established by the rule "it is seen after others as well," this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*): namely, that just as *manin* and *vanip* are mentioned together [with *kan*], so too *vanip* alone [should apply] and not *manin*, nor *vanip* along with others, nor *aṇ* and the rest. Since the restriction applies only to the suffixes that occur with an upapada (prepositional prefix), the *niṣṭhā* suffixes [are not excluded].

It is indeed so: "having seen the further shore. This being the case, in expressions such as "we ourselves are those whose eyes have seen the universe" (*viśvadṛśvanayanā vayam eva*), there is no fault even if one analyzes the formation with a present participle (*laṭ*)—that is, by taking *kvanip*—as follows: "those who see the universe are 'universe-seers' (*viśvadṛśvāni*); those whose eyes are such [universe-seers] are 'those whose eyes have seen the universe' (*viśvadṛśvanayanāḥ*)."

This is because the authors of the *Vṛtti* and others have explained that this sūtra is intended to exclude other suffixes (*pratyaya*), whereas no learned authorities have stated that it is intended to exclude [the application of the rule] at another time; such is the direction of the argument. (671) *rājani yudhi kṛñaḥ* |3|2|95|.
Regarding the rules *rājani yudhi kṛñaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.95) and *sahe ca* (3.2.96),
it is logical that these two sūtras, like *ṛśeḥ kvani*, are intended as restrictive rules (*niyamārtha*).

In reality, however, because there is no other way to provide a consistent interpretation through the inclusion of the term *dṛśi*, it can also be easily stated that this set of three sūtras is prescriptive (*vidhātrī*). It is established in the *Śabdakaustubha* that the works of the ancient grammarians are indeed indifferent to this point.

(673) *saptamyāṃ janer ḍaḥ* |3|2|97|. [The suffix] *ḍa* is applied after the root *jan* when a word in the locative case is present; as in *mandurāyām*. Amara states: "A stable for horses (*vājiśālā*) is called *mandurā*. (674) *anau karmaṇi* |3|2|100|. [The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *jan*] when the prefix *anu* is present and the word in the accusative case is used.

Regarding the word *pumanuja*: here, the root *jan* (to be born) is transitive (*sakarmaka*), because it functions with respect to birth characterized by compliance (*anurodha*). (Pāṇini 3.2.101) "It is also seen in other [cases]"—it was stated [in the rule] "after *jan*, when the locative case is used," but it is also seen even when the locative case is not used.

Thus he says: "the unborn" (aja), "the twice-born" (dvija). He is "unborn" because he is not born [in the ordinary sense]. He is "twice-born" because he is born twice. This is according to the statement of the learned: "One is born a Śūdra by birth; one is born a twice-born by action. It was stated that [the suffix -a] occurs in the sense of non-birth after a word ending in the fifth case, yet it is seen even in the sense of birth; thus he says "born as a Brāhmaṇa" (brāhmaṇaja).

Regarding the word *api*: although an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) has been made to the section beginning with *ṭhantātyantādhve* stating that "it is also seen elsewhere," this was for the purpose of ensuring its application even in the absence of the past tense (*bhūtakāla*).
In reality, however, [the purpose is served] by the inclusion of the word *api* within the present sūtra itself.

This Vārttika has its purpose already served by the very fact that it is intended to prevent all possible exceptions (*vyabhicāra*). This has been demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya under the rule *ṭhiko guṇavṛddhī*, where, having introduced the suffix *ḍa* after the root *jan*, he states: "This suffix *ḍa* should also be prescribed after the root *am*. And thus, regarding the rule under discussion...

If it is argued that there is a mutual dependence—since the designation "niṣṭhā" is established only when the designation is established, and the rule for *kta* and *ktavatu* suffixes is prescribed only when the designation "niṣṭhā" exists—then they reply: here, a future designation is understood; that is, "that which, once produced, will receive the designation 'niṣṭhā' with respect to what has not yet occurred."

By resorting to the phrase "it occurs" (*bhavati*), it follows by implication that this is a rule for the prescription of the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*; thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply. (Pāṇini 6.4.60) *Niṣṭhāyām aṇyadarthe*.

"Ṇya has the meaning of the abstract state (bhāva) and the object (karman). Although Ṇya occurs after roots such as *dhā* in forms like *dhāyyā* and *ṛc* by virtue of the rule "bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.1.13), nevertheless, because of the statement "of these two alone," it is understood that the meaning directly presented here is only the abstract state and the object; this is the intended sense.

(677) *kṣiyo dīrghāt* |8|2|46|. [The rule applies to] the root *kṣi*. Both *kṣi* in the sense of "perishing" (*kṣaye*) and *kṣi* in the sense of "dwelling and going" (*nivāsagatyoḥ*) are included. An example is *kṣitaḥ kāmaḥ* ("desire has perished"). Because the root has an implied causative meaning (*antarbhāvitaṇyartha*), it becomes transitive, and thus the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object (*karmani*). And this...

This is clear in Mādhava’s commentary on the mantra *ṭhakṣitosanedi ma*. However, in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), examples such as *kṣitam* [meaning] "desired" should be cited. He recalls the rule prohibiting *iṭ*:
*riṣyukaḥ kitī*. [The forms] *kṣutaḥ* and *nutaḥ* [are derived from] *ṭuakṣu* "to sound" and *ṇu* [respectively].

In the context of praise (*stuti*): *vṛtaḥ*. [The roots] *vṛṅ* in the sense of "to choose" (*saṃbhakti*) and *vṛñ* in the sense of "to choose" (*varaṇa*). (678) Pāṇini 8.2.42: *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ pūrvasya ca daḥ*.
Regarding *radābhyām*: here, by the term *radābhyām*, the letter *t* is qualified, not the *niṣṭhā* suffix itself.
In the case of *caritamudita*, [the substitution] does not occur here because the letter *t* has been combined with *iṭ*. This is what he states:
"of the final *t* of the *niṣṭhā* [suffix]. Regarding the phrase "by way of being external" (*bahiraṅgatvena*):
it means that, depending upon the *ñit* secondary suffix (*taddhita*) which stands outside the *t* of the *niṣṭhā*, the vowel at the beginning of the stem (*aṅga*) [is affected].

The intention is that *vṛddhi* is "external" (*bahiraṅga*) because it is being prescribed [later]. Regarding *drāṇa*: the root *drā* means "to go with contempt. Regarding *glānaḥ*, *mlānaḥ*: the roots *glai* and *mlai* mean "the loss of joy.
(Pāṇini 6.1.44: *lvādibhyaḥ*.

Regarding the phrase "of twenty-one": among the *pvādi* group, twenty-two roots are recited; there, excluding *pūñ*, the *lvādi* group is to be understood. In the form *jīnaḥ*, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *halaḥ*.
Because it is established and because it is obligatory (*nitya*), the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) takes place by the rule *rahijyā-vayi-vyadhī-vas-ti-vṛc-chru-dru-sru-jāṃ ca*.
There is no application of the rule *aṃyogāder ātaḥ ra* (Pāṇini 7.2.43).
[The forms] *dugdha*, *dīrgha*, and *gūna* are examples. *Gu* means "to emit" (*parīṣotsarga*).
*Pūñ* means "destruction" (*vināśa*); thus, *vinaṣṭāḥ*. Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, *pūñ* here signifies "purifying" (*pavana*).
Even upon the destruction of this [root], there is the occurrence [of the suffix]. Regarding "sinoteḥ": the root *ṣiñ* means "to bind.

"Grāsakarma" refers to an action in the form of a morsel (*grāsa*); that which has such an action as its object is "grāsakarma," and the suffix follows that *sinoti* which has that as its agent (*kartṛ*).
The meaning is: "May it be completed for us. Regarding the example *sino grāsaḥ* ("the morsel is bitten"):

it should be understood that when a morsel being formed into a ball becomes suitable for binding due to the influence of condiments such as curd and the like, then agency (*kartṛtva*) resides in the object (*karman*) itself. Why [is the word] *grāsa* used? [To exclude cases such as: *rāsa...*

The meaning is: what is the purpose of [the phrase] "of that which has an agent who is also the object" (*karmakartṛkasya*)? [The question] "What is the purpose of 'having an agent who is also the object'? means:
let there simply be [the phrase] "of that which has licking as its object" (*rāsakarmakasya*); what is the purpose of the word "agent" (*kartṛ*)?

However, if one were to say "of that which has licking as its agent" (*rāsakartṛkasya*) while omitting the word "object" (*karman*), then even in the case of "the throat was licked by the cat" (*rāsena kaṇṭhaḥ sitaḥ*), [the rule would undesirably apply].
It should be understood that [the form] *syāt* [is derived thus].

(680) Regarding the rule *oditaśca* (Pāṇini 8.2.45): [the form] *bhugna*. [The root] *bhuja* means "crookedness. Because the substitution of *n* for *t* is considered *asiddha* (not yet established), the *kutva* (substitution of *g*) occurs when a *jhal* consonant follows.

Regarding *ucchūna*: from the root *śvi*, because it belongs to the *yajādi* group, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), followed by the formation of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*), and then the lengthening according to the rule *halaḥ*. Regarding *prahīṇa*: the substitution of *ī* occurs according to the rule *hrī-sthā*. Regarding *sūna*: from the root *ṣūṅ* (to give birth to living beings). Regarding *dūna*: from the root *dūṅ* (to torment). Regarding "in the middle of those ending in *o*" (*odinmadhye*): if [the root] is *ḍīṅ*...

The sense is that if *iṭ* were [inserted] here, the letter *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix could not follow the root; thus, the reading for the purpose of [causing] the substitution of *n* would be rendered useless. Nor should it be suspected that the opposite might be the case—that by virtue of its placement among the *odit* roots, the substitution of *n* would occur even when there is an intervention by *iṭ*.

It is more logical to assume the absence of the augment *iṭ* in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*). Others, however, say that even when the augment *iṭ* is present, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the lengthening of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) is treated as including its preceding element (*pūrvāntatva*), there is no intervention by *iṭ* at all; thus, the desired result is established.

(681) *śyo'sparśe* |8|2|47|. Regarding the form *saṃśyāna*: from the root *śyaiṅ* in the sense of "going," there is the substitution of *ā* by the rule *ādeca upadeśe'śiti*; then, by the rule *saṃyogāderātaḥ*, the *t* of the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is replaced by *n*.

(682) *yasya vibhāṣā* | Pāṇini 7.2.15. Regarding *yasya vibhāṣā*: the genitive *yasya* is used in relation to the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; the meaning is "of that *ārdhadhātuka* suffix which belongs to [the root]. As for *samakna*: this is from the root *añc* in the sense of "manifestation," and not [from *añj*].

The suffix *tvan* [is applied] after the root *īṣ*. Therefore, here there is the elision of *na*. Regarding the form *vṛkṇa*: the root is *ovraścū* in the sense of "cutting. There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *rahijyē*. Because the substitution of *na* for *n* is considered asiddha (not yet established), there is the elision of *s* by the rule *koḥ*, and the substitution of *k* for *c* by the rule *oḥ kuḥ*. Since it has the marker *ū*, it optionally takes the augment *iṭ*; therefore, [the rule] *yasya*... [applies].

In the word *vibhāṣe*, there is the absence of the augment *iṭ* due to the suffix *niṣṭhā*. Because a single portion of a phoneme (*varṇaikadeśa*) is treated as a full phoneme for the purposes of applying the augment *nuṭ*, the rule for substitution (*lādeśa*), and the change of *n* to *ṇ* (*vināma*), the letter *r*—which is a portion of the vowel *ṛ*—serves as the cause;
thus, by the rule *ṭh-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye’pi*, the *n* is changed to *ṇ*. The term *vināma* is the designation used by the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*) for this change of *n* to *ṇ*.

Even according to the literal interpretation of the rule "ṭhṛvarṇānnasya ṇatvam" (the substitution of ṇ for n after a letter of the ṭh-class or a vowel), the inclusion of the word *nṛmanas* in the *kṣubhnādi* list serves to prohibit the substitution of ṇ; however, by taking the vowel *ṛ* as the cause [of the prohibition], the substitution of ṇ still occurs by the rule "aṭ-ku-pvāṅ-num-vyavāye ’pi" (Pāṇini 8.4.2).
This is the general direction.
(683) *prācyabharateṣu* |8|3|75|.
*pariskandaḥ*. This is a nipātana (irregular formation) for the suffix *ac*. Alternatively, according to the Kāśikā, it is a case where the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is elided.

(684) *divo ’vijigīṣām* | 8|2|49|. [The word] *dyaūnaḥ* [is derived as follows]: by the rule *chvoḥ śūḍ*, there is the substitution *ūṭh*. The meaning is "one who has diminished. [The word] *dyaūtam*:
for it is understood that in that [game], dice are thrown with the desire to win; thus, "desire to win" (*vijigīṣā*) is implied.

(685) *nirvāṇo’vāte* | 8|2|50| The word *nirvāṇa* [is formed with a cerebral ṇ] when it does not mean "wind. The root *vā* is used in the senses of "motion" and "smelling. From this root preceded by the prefix *nis*, the substitution of *na* occurs for the final *t* of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), and there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. However, if "wind" (*vāta*) is the agent, this is not the case. Thus, [the form] *nirvāṇa* [is used] when it means "extinguished" by means of wind (*vātena hetunā*).

Regarding the word *dīpa*, they say there is no prohibition [of the suffix *kta*]. Regarding *nirvāta*: the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) by the rule "atyarthākarmaka" (Pāṇini 3.4.76), meaning "one from whom the wind has completely departed. (686) *śuṣaḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.51).

Regarding *śuṣka*: from the root *śuṣ* in the sense of "drying. (687) [Pāṇini 8.2.53] states: *kṣāyo maḥ*. Regarding *kṣāma*: from the root *kṣai* in the sense of "wasting away. There is the substitution of *ā* by the rule *ṭhādecaḥ*.

(688) *prastyo’nyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 8.2.54. Examples: *prastīmaḥ*, *prastītaḥ*. [The root] *styai* (or *ṣṭyai*) means "to sound" or "to collect. When the substitution of *ā* for *ai* has been applied, because the rule *ayogādeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.2) is considered asiddha, the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs first; then, when the single-substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) has been applied...

The long vowel [ā] is substituted by the rule *halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2); subsequently, because the conditions for *yaṇ* and *antatva* (being final) are absent, the substitution of *na* does not occur. However, in the case of *astyāna*, the substitution indeed takes place. (689) *anupasargāt phulla-kṣība-kṛśa-ullāghāḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.55).

Regarding the phrase "in *kṣība* and so forth": [the forms] *kṣība*, *kṛśa*, and *laghu*—derived from the roots *kṣībṛ* (to be intoxicated), *kṛśa* (to become thin), and *lāghṛ* (to be light) with the prefix *ud*—are formed with the suffix *kta*.

Now, one might object: since the forms *phulla* and others are established by adding the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class) to the root *phulla* (to blossom) and the root *ullāgh* (to recover health), and by adding the suffix *ka* (conditioned by the rule for roots with *iṭ* as an indicatory letter) to the other two [roots], what is the purpose [of this rule]?
To the question "By which sūtra?", he says: "But the sūtra...

(690). And [the mention of] *ti* in Pāṇini 7.4.89 is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication) for the purpose of excluding [the application of the rule]. This is because the form *phullavān* [would otherwise be derived by that rule], as would also be the case with the suffix *iṣṭhan*.

It should be understood that this is for the sake of establishing the udātta accent on the first syllable of *dvyajana* (two-syllabled words) beginning with *āditya*, and so forth. Regarding the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for *utphulla* and *saṃphulla*:

although these are established by adding the suffix *pacādyac* to the root *phull*—just as in the case of *praphulla*—nevertheless, [the forms] *utphustaḥ* and *saṃphustaḥ* [would otherwise not be accounted for].
This statement is for the purpose of precluding the application [of the previous rule].
(691) *nudavidondatirāghrāhrībhyo ’nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 8.2.56).
Regarding *nudavidoh*: since the rule *hradābhyām* and *ayogāder ātaḥ* would have applied invariably, this [present rule] allows for an option.

Since [the substitution of] *hrī* does not otherwise apply, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) for both cases. Regarding the word *veti*: thus says the Bhāṣya—"The past participle (*niṣṭhā*) of *vid* is desired as *vidita*; of *vyadh*, as *viddha*; of *viñ*, as *vinna* and *vita*; and of *vit*, as *vitta*; and of *vid*, as *vitata*. Regarding *nunnaḥ* and *nuta*: [this is governed by] the rule "aniditām... (Pāṇini 6.4.24).
Elision of *n* [is taught].

(692) *na dhyākhyāpṛmūrccchimadām* | Pāṇini 8.2.57. Not for *dhyai*, *khyā*, *pṛ*, *mūrch*, or *mad*. *Dhyai* in the sense of thinking; *khyā* in the sense of speaking; *pṛ* in the senses of protecting and filling; *mūrchā*...

In *moha* and *samucchrāya*, [the root is] *mad* in the sense of joy (*harṣe*). Regarding *pūrta*: there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "ṛt-śyukaḥ kitī. It recalls the rule for the elision of the suffix *cha*: "rāllopaḥ. In *mūrta*, there is no *iṭ* by the rule "āditaśca. In *mata*, there is no *iṭ* by the rule "vīdito niṣṭhāyām."

(693) *vito bhogapratyayayoḥ* |8|2|58|. After a root ending in *vit*, the augment *iṭ* must be applied [to the suffix *ktvā*]; however, this does not apply to the root *vid* meaning "to know," nor to *vid* meaning "to exist," nor to *vid* meaning "to investigate," when used in the sense of enjoyment (*bhoga*) or cognition (*pratyaya*).

With the intention that [the object] "comes into being," he says: "of *vindati*. This means of the root *vidlṛ*, which signifies "to obtain. He explains that these two [terms], *bhoga* and *pratyaya*, are derived as nouns denoting the object (*karmasādhana*), by stating: "in the sense of 'that which is enjoyed' (*bhujyate*) is *bhoga*, and 'that which is perceived' (*pratīyate*) is *pratyaya*."

(694) *bhītam* means *śakalam* (a fragment). 8|2|59. Regarding *bhītam śakalam*: the absence of the substitution of *na* for *n*, which would otherwise be required by the rule *ṭhradābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.2.42] when the suffix *kta* follows the root *bhid*, is here prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Amara states: “*hitam* means either a *śakala* or a *khaṇḍa*. Thus, *bhinnam* has a different meaning.
The meaning is "to be torn apart.
(695) *ṛṇam ādhamarṇye* | 8|2|60|. Regarding *ṛṇam ādhamarṇye*: one who has a debt that causes misery is an *adhamarṇa*; the state of being such a person is [the meaning of the term].

The term *ādhamarṇya* (the state of being a debtor) indicates a specific type of legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*). With the intention that the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) is thereby also established, he explains: "the legal proceeding concerning the debtor. Since that proceeding pertains to the relationship between the giver and the receiver, the application [of the term] to the creditor is not contradictory.
In the case of *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication), however, the grammatical authority (*liṅga*) is the rule: "The creditor of Hari" (*hārer uttamarṇaḥ*). (696) *Sphāyaḥ sphī niṣṭhāyām* | 6.1.22.

[The substitute] *sphī* [is applied] for *sphāy*. The root *sphāyī* means "to increase. How then is the form *sphītikāmaḥ* explained? It is derived from *sphīta* [meaning "increased"] with the suffix *ka*. [Thus, it means one who desires what is increased.]

Thus, from the causative (*ṇyanta*) root *ac*, the suffix *i* is applied; there is the elision of the *a* (*allopa*) and the elision of the *ṇi*. (697) Regarding the rule *iṇniṣṭhāyām* [Pāṇini 7.2.47]:

the meaning is that the augment *iṭ* is optional for the root *kuṣ* by the rule *iraḥ kuṣaḥ*. As for the phrase *yasya*: [it refers to the vowel] of which [there is elision]. This is the intended sense.
(698) *uṣavidajāgṛbhyo 'nyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 3.1.38].

Regarding *uṣita*: there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) because it belongs to the *yajādi* group. The substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *āsivasī*. The mention of *vasati* with the suffix *śap* is for the sake of clarity. Since the root *vas* takes the augment *iṭ*, the form must necessarily be *uṣita*.

Regarding the word *kṣudhita*: thus, the usage "this [food] is sufficient for this hungry one" (*asyālam eṣā kṣudhitasya*) is entirely unobjectionable. Therefore, that which is stated in the *Dhātuvṛttis*—namely, that the suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *kṣudh* in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), resulting in the form *kṣudh* because it begins with a vowel other than *a* (according to the rule *ārakāditaḥ*)—is not to be accepted. By the same logic, it will apply to *krudhita* and other such forms as well.
Or it may be interpreted in some other way.

(699) *añceḥ pūjāyām* | Pāṇini 7.2.53. Regarding *añci*: since it is marked with an *u*-diacritic (*udit*), the suffix *ktvā* would optionally apply; however, regarding the *niṣṭhā* suffixes, [the rule applies] to that which...

The statement "vibhāṣā" is made because a prohibition was otherwise applicable. Regarding *añcita*: by the rule "āñceḥ pūjāyām," the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) is prohibited. Regarding *akta*: by the rule "aniditām," there is elision of the nasal. (700) *lubho vimohane* 7.2.54.

The rule *lubho ’īṣatsahe* (Pāṇini 7.2.50) applies when the suffix *ktvā* follows, as there is an option [to substitute *īṣat* for *īṣad*] and a prohibition [of the substitution of *īṣat*] when the *niṣṭhā* suffixes follow; this present rule is stated [as an exception]. (701) *pūṅśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.51).
This is a statement [of a rule] because the prohibition [by Pāṇini 1.2.19], "pūṅśca rṭhśyukaḥ kitī," would otherwise apply.

(702) *pūṅḥ ktvā ca* [Pāṇini 1.2.22]. Regarding *pūṅḥ ktvā ca*: although [the absence of the augment *iṭ*] is already established by [Pāṇini 1.2.18], *a ktvā seṭ*, the explicit mention of *ktvā* here [is for a specific purpose].

To show that [the use of the suffix *ktvā*] is not redundant, he says: "for the sake of the subsequent rule. He adds: "only by *ktvā*, and not by the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes], because it is not carried over [by the particle *ca*]. This is the intended meaning. (Pāṇini 1.2.19) *Niṣṭhā* [is applied] after the roots *śīṅ*, *svidi*, *midi*, *kṣvidi*, and *dhṛṣ*.
Regarding *śeśyita*: the substitution *yaṇ* applies by the rule *eranekācaḥ*.
(704) *ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ kartari ca* |3|4|71|. Regarding *ādikarmaṇi*: it refers to when all the constituent moments (*kṣaṇa*) of an action have occurred at the very beginning.

They say that the statement "because of the absence of the state of having come into being (bhūtatva), the completion [of the action] is not attained" is intended to prescribe the suffix *kta* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) when referring to the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*). Regarding the word "and" (*ca*): the meaning is that otherwise, by the maxim of the curd and Kauṇḍinya (*takrakauṇḍinyanyāya*), it would not apply to the states of being (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*).

(705) *vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.17. Regarding the example *prasvedita*: the prefix *pra-* is for the purpose of indicating the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*). *Sveditam* and so forth refer to the abstract state (*bhāva*). *Bhvādiḥ* refers to this [root] here; it is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as *ñiṣvidā snehanamocanayoḥ* ("to sweat, to release moisture").

Regarding the form *svidyate*: the meaning is that since the root *vid* is listed among the *divādi* roots in the sense of "oozing from the limbs," the form is simply *svidita*, because there is no prohibition against the *kit* suffix. Nor should it be argued that the *svi* belonging to the *adādi* class is also [the one intended], for that would contradict the text of Haradatta; such is the intention.

Regarding this, Haradatta states: "The root *ñikṣvidā* belonging to the *divādi* class, meaning 'to lubricate' and 'to release,' is intended here, and not also the *bhvādi* root *ñikṣvidā* meaning 'indistinct sound,' because of its association with *mid*. This is to be considered; for the root *mid* is also recited among the *bhvādi* roots.

Therefore, because there is no distinction between the two, it is logical that both be included. This is what he says: "The class beginning with *div* and the class beginning with *bhū*. (706) *mṛṣ* [is used] in the sense of endurance (*titikṣā*). 1.2.20.

Regarding the term *avispaṣṭam*: although the root *mṛṣ* has its function restricted solely to the sense of "endurance" (*titikṣā*), the inclusion of the word *titikṣā* in the sūtra itself indicates that roots possess multiple meanings. (707) Pāṇini 1.2.21: *udupadhādbhāvādikarmaṇoranyatarasyām*.
*Rucitam* [is derived from] *ruca*, meaning "to shine. According to the rule *atyarthākarmaka-*, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent.

*Kruṣṭam* [is derived from] *kruśa*, meaning "to call out" and "to weep. By the rule regarding the *vraścādi* group, there is the substitution of *ṣ*, followed by the substitution of *ṣṭu*. This [formation with *kta*] is desired only after roots that take the *śap* conjugational marker (*śabvikaraṇa*). *Gudhitam* [is derived from] *gudha*, meaning "to surround," belonging to the *divādi* class.

(708) *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi* |6|4|52|. [The rule] "vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*)" refers to [the rule] *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti*. *Śūnaḥ*: from the root *śvi* (meaning "to move" or "to increase"). The lengthening is by [the rule] *halaḥ*. The substitution of *na* for the final *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is by [the rule] *oditaśca*.

Regarding the word *gūḍha*: [the suffix] *iṭ* is not applied because of the rule "of that which has an optional [iṭ]. Then there are the changes to *ḍha*, *dha*, *ṣṭu*, the elision of *ḍh*, and the lengthening of the vowel.
Regarding *vataḥ* and *tataḥ*: the elision of *n* occurs by the rule "in the case of roots taught with an anudātta accent. Regarding [the form] with *san* (desiderative):
it is because of the statement, "it should be stated that *iṭ* optionally follows *san* after the roots *ani*, *pat*, and *daridrā*."

Regarding the phrase "of *kṛtī* and so forth": [the inclusion of] *kṛtī* (in cutting), *cṛtī* (in harming and tying), and *nṛtī* (in the movement of limbs) as having the marker *īt* is for the purpose of ensuring that their past passive participles (*niṣṭhā*) do not take the augment *iṭ*; alternatively, it serves to indicate that the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* is not universally obligatory.
The meaning is that it is established [that the word *patita* is used].

(709) *kṣubdha-svānta-dhvānta-lagna-mliṣṭa-viribdha-phāṇṭa-bāḍhāni mantha-manas-tamas-akta-avispaṣṭa-svara-anāyāsa-bhṛśeṣu* | Pāṇini 7.2.18. [The words] *kṣubdha*, *svānta*, *dhvānta*, *lagna*, *mliṣṭa*, *viribdha*, *phāṇṭa*, and *bāḍha* [are used as past passive participles] in the senses of "churning," "mind," "darkness," "clinging," "indistinct," "sound," "effortless," and "intense" respectively.

In *kṣubdha* and *kṣubha*, the substitution of *dh* for *bh* occurs by the rule "haṣastathoḥ. In *svana* and *dhvana*, meaning "sound," there is lengthening by the rule "ṭhanunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ" due to the absence of the augment *iṭ*. In *lage* (to adhere), *mlecccha* (inarticulate sound), and *rebhṛ* (to sound), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule "vraśca," followed by the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*. In *phaṇa*, the meaning is "to move."

The vowel is long; there is the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*. In the case of the root *vah*, with the absence of the augment *iṭ*, there is the substitution of *ṭh* for *th*, the substitution of *dh* for *th*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*, and the elision of *ḍh*. He says "to be accomplished without effort" (*anāyāsasādhya*) because by the word *anāyāsa* (absence of effort), that which is accomplished thereby is indicated.
"Having thrown the entire collection of medicinal herbs into warm water, having immediately pressed [them], and having strained [the liquid], that which is drunk."

They call that *phāṇṭa*. Regarding "in the Vedic commentary": the meaning is that it refers to the explanation of the *Śatapatha-śruti* passage, "Fresh butter belongs to the ancestors; ghee belongs to the gods; *phāṇṭa* belongs to humans.
Regarding "but elsewhere": the meaning is that this applies when [the term] is not used to denote churning and so forth.

(710) *dhṛṣi-śasī vaiyātye* | Pāṇini 7.2.19. [The roots] *dhṛṣi* and *śasi*: *ñi-dhṛṣā* in the sense of boldness; *śasu* in the sense of injury. Although the prohibition of *iṭ* for these two is already established by the two rules "*ṭhāditaśca*" and "*yasya vibhāṣā*," [the present rule specifies that] for these two, [the *iṭ* is prohibited] only when [the meaning is] insolence (*vaiyātya*).
He says "only in the sense of lack of discipline (*avinaya*)," for the purpose of restriction—that it does not apply elsewhere.

One who has gone (*yāta*) to what is contrary (*viruddha*) is *viyāta*, that is, undisciplined (*avinīta*); its state is *vaiyātyam*. Now, since the option "optionally in the sense of a state or an action" (*vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ*) would have applied to the root *dhṛṣ*, [the suffix is used] for the sake of making it obligatory.

To the doubt as to why it does not occur, he says: "It does not exist. The meaning is that it is because it has not been so stated. He provides the authority for this here: "For this very reason. Regarding the phrase "Mādhava, however": the sense is that since the status of being "first" (āditva) is possessed of a result, that which was stated by Haradatta as being questionable is indeed what should be questioned.

(711) *dṛḍhaḥ* [is used] in the sense of *sthūla* (thick/firm) and *balin* (strong). 7|2|20| The word *dṛḍhaḥ* [is derived from the root *dṛh* with the suffix *kta*; it is irregularly formed]. *Bala* means "one who possesses strength"; [the suffix] *ac* is applied according to the rule *ṭharśa-ādibhyo’c*. Thus he says: "one who is strong" (*balavatī*). *Sthūla* means "fleshy"; and although such a person may be physically weak, they are nonetheless "strong" (*balavān*) in the sense of being firm.
The meaning is established as "though thin, he is firm. Regarding the word *tasya*: it means "of the letter *ta*. Regarding the word *hasya*:

if it is argued that since the substitution of *ḍha* by the rule *ṭh-ḍhaḥ* would result in the desired form simply through the elision of *ḍha* before *ḍha* (by the rule *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ*), there is no need to prescribe the substitution of *ḍha* for *ta* nor the elision of *ha*, we say: do not say so. For if that were the case...
Because the elision of *ḍha* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), in the case of *draḍhiṃ*, the substitution of *ra* by the rule *ṭhra ṛto halāderlaghoḥ* would not occur;

in the case of *aridraḍhayya gataḥ*, the substitution of *ay* by the rule *yapi laghupūrvāt* would not occur; and [the form] *pāridṛḍhañī*—meaning the offspring of one who is thoroughly firm (*paridṛḍha*)—would not be formed.

In the case of the word *kanyā*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* applies according to the rule *gurūpottamalakṣaṇaḥ*. Therefore, it is established in the Bhāṣya and other works that the elision of the *hal* (the final consonant) is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity) in order to prevent [the application of] *asiddhatva* (the status of being not yet accomplished). For this very reason, with the intention of regarding the statement of the ancient authors in the rule *hralope*—"what about *dṛḍha*?"—as erroneous, [the form] *tṛḍhaḥ* [is cited].

The word *vṛḍha* has been cited as a counter-example. (712) *paribṛḍhaḥ* [is used] in the sense of "master" (*prabhu*). Regarding the rule 7.2.21, it is stated that this is a formal irregularity (*nipātana*). Furthermore, the purpose for the elision of the *hal* suffixes is also [the formation of] *vraḍhimā*.
The forms beginning with *parivrājaka* up to *siddhidhara* should be understood as before.
(713) *Kaṣaḥ kṛcchragahanayoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.22]. Regarding *kṛcchra* and *gahana*: *kṛcchra* means suffering (*duḥkha*), and by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), its cause is also included.
The root *kaṣ* has the meaning of "to afflict" or "to injure. Thus, *kaṣṭa-mohaḥ* means "delusion that causes suffering," that is to say, a cause of pain.

(714) *Ghuṣir aviśabdane* [Pāṇini 7.2.23]. *Ghuṣir avi*: the root *ghuṣ* in the sense of "not making sound" belongs to the *bhvādi* class; [the form] *ghuṣir aviśabdane* [is used when it does not mean making a sound].
This belongs to the *curādi* group; both [roots] are included generally. Now, one might object:

since the root *dhūṣ* has the meaning "to sound," it must take the causative suffix (*ṇic*) from the *curādi* group. Consequently, because of the intervention of the *ṇic*, there is no *niṣṭhā* (past participle) suffix following *dhūṣ*; so how can there be the contingency of the prohibition of *iṭ*, and furthermore—?

If it is argued that, because there is no prohibition of the suffix *iṇ* in the sense of "speaking" (*viśabdana*), the *guṇa* substitution would apply to the penultimate vowel in the *ṇic*-derivative, and with the subsequent elision of the *ṇic* by the rule "before a suffix marked with *ṭ* or *ṅ* that has an indicatory *iṭ*," the form *hoṣitaṃ vākyam* would also be possible; to this they reply: in that case, the very prohibition regarding the sense of "speaking" (*viśabdana*) serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the [specific] meaning of speaking.
"Regarding the rule *curādi-ṇic-anityaḥ*, the suffix *ṇic* is not always applied; thus there is no fault mentioned above—this is the general direction (*dik*). (715) *abheścāvidūrye* (Pāṇini 5.2.25).
[The word] *abhi*: "far apart" (*vidūra*) means being specifically distant; other than that is "not far" (*avidūra*), the state of which [is denoted by the suffix]."

*Āvidūryam*. The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because the word belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class (Pāṇini 5.1.124). Precisely because of this specific grammatical instruction, the prohibition "not after a tatpuruṣa compound beginning with the negative particle *nañ*" does not apply here. However, the term was not stated simply as "proximity" (*sāmīpya*), for that would have resulted in the failure to include cases of "not too far. Making this point clear, he explains:

"Neither too far nor too near"— thus they say that the ancient commentary on the term *sāmīpya* (proximity) should be understood as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). (716) *ṇeradhyayane vṛttam* | Pāṇini 7.2.26.

Regarding the rule for the root *ṇī*: "it is studied" (*adhīyate*) is called *adhyayana*. By the rule *ṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), and there is the elision (*luk*) of the *ṇi*-augment.

The phrase "it is prescribed" (*nipātyate*) is the remainder [of the explanation]. For if [the *ṇi*] were simply elided (*lope*), then by the principle of "characteristic of an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), a *guṇa* substitution would occur; this is the intended meaning.

(717) *śṛtam* [is used] in the sense of cooking (*pāke*). 6|1|27. *Śṛtam*. Regarding the rule *śrāti-śrapayatyoḥ*: the root *śrā* is listed in the *adādi* class in the sense of cooking; it is also listed in the *curādi* class, and it is listed among the *ghaṭādi* roots for the sake of making it *mit*, as well as under *śrai* in the sense of cooking.
In the *bhū* class (*bhvādi*), that [root] which has already undergone the change to *ātva* is also included here.

They say that by the force of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the paribhāṣā concerning "the distinction between what is taught by a general rule and what is taught by a specific rule" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*) is not resorted to;
thus, the substitution of *śṛ* is irregularly derived. The phrase "the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *yaṅ*" remains in effect from the previous context.

The *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution has not been prescribed [for the root *śri*] so that even for *śrayati*, the form *śritam* alone may occur. Here, the option (*vibhāṣā*) from the rule "optionally when preceded by *abhi* or *ava*" is understood; however, that option is restricted (*vyavasthitā*). Consequently, the substitution of *śṛ* occurs invariably only for *kṣīra* and *havis*, but not at all in other cases.

With the intention that "it comes to be," he says: "the cooking of milk and ghee. Regarding the word "anyat" (other): it refers to vegetables and the like. Regarding the word "śrapitam" (cooked): there is shortening of the vowel for roots ending in a nasal (mit) when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*.
(Pāṇini 7.4.54). (Pāṇini 7.2.27: "The forms *dānta*, *śānta*, *pūrṇa*, *dasta*, *spaṣṭa*, *cchanna*, and *jñapta* are optionally [formed with the suffix *kta* after the respective roots]."

Or: *dam* (to subdue) and *śam* (to pacify) belong to the class beginning with *div* and the class beginning with *cur*; *pū* (to fill) belongs to the class beginning with *div* and the class beginning with *cur*; *das* (to perish); *spaś* (to afflict); *chad* (to cover); and *jñap* is used in the sense of making known (*saṃjñā*), whereas it is stated [elsewhere] to mean "pleasing" (*toṣaṇa*) and "pacifying" (*niśāmana*).

(719) *ruṣyamatvarasaṅghuṣāsvanām* | Pāṇini 7.2.28. Regarding the roots *ruṣ*, *am*, *tvar*, *saṅghuṣ*, and *āsvan*: for the root *ruṣ* (*ruṣa* in the sense of anger), since it optionally takes the augment *iṭ* by the rule *īṣasaha-* (Pāṇini 7.2.48), the prohibition [of *iṭ*] that would otherwise apply permanently by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15) is here overridden, and the optional application of *iṭ* is prescribed. Regarding *am*...

Regarding the roots *gam* and others: they state that the root *am*, meaning "to be ill," belonging to the curādigaṇa (the tenth class), is not included here, because of the governing rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.10). Regarding *ānta*: the lengthening occurs by the rule *anunāsikasya*. Regarding *tūrṇa*: from the root *tvar* (Ñitvarā saṃbhrame), the substitution *ūṭh* occurs by the rule *varatvare*, and there is the nasalization (*ṇatva*) of the final consonant due to being a *niṣṭhā* suffix.

Since the prohibition "ṭhāditaśca" (Pāṇini 1.3.5) would otherwise apply, this [the present rule] provides an option.
