Thus, the result of being "ādi" (having 'ā' as the initial vowel) is merely the Ātmanepada; and that is indeed established even if there were a short indicatory vowel (hrasvānubandha), as in the case of roots like *edh*, with this intention he says: "the result is meager. [The form] *saṃghuṣṭa* [is thus explained].

This option applies when the root *dhūṣ* is preceded by the prefix *sam* and used in the sense of "making a sound," even though the augment *iṭ* would otherwise be required. Furthermore, even when not used in the sense of making a sound, this same option applies to the root *dhūṣ* preceded by *sam*, because it is taught later [in the rules]. Regarding the form *āsvānta*: even when the root *svan* preceded by *āṅ* denotes the mind (*manas*), this same option applies, because it is taught later. Thus, *āsvāntaṃ manaḥ*.
"The mind has been made to resound.

(720) *Hṛṣer lomasu* (Pāṇini 7.2.29). [The rule applies] after the root *hṛṣ*. *Hṛṣu* (meaning "to be false") is *aniṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* suffixes when it ends in an *u*-diṭ vowel; however, *hṛṣ* (meaning "to be pleased") is *seṭ*.
Since there is the inclusion of both [roots], this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases.
(721) *pyāyaḥ pī* 6.1.28. [The form] *pīnam*: because it belongs to the *odit* group, the *niṣṭhā* suffix takes the nasal substitute (*ṇatva*). [The form] *pyāna*: by the rule *vīdito*...

In the absence of the augment *iṭ* by the rule "niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi," there is the elision of *ya*. Regarding the restriction concerning the form with a prefix (*sopasarga*), he states another rule: "not [after] that which has a prefix," and so forth. *Andhuḥ* means a well (*kūpaḥ*). (723) *niṣṭhāyām* 6.4.95.

Regarding *prahlanna*: the root *hlād* means "to rejoice. Because it is marked with the indicatory letter *ī*, there is the absence of the augment *iṭ*. By the rule *hradābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.2.31], the substitution of *n* for *d* occurs. [Regarding the rule] *dyatisyatimāsthāmiti kiti* [Pāṇini 7.4.40]: the roots *do*, *so*, *mā*, and *māṅ*. *Do* means "to cut"; *ṣo* means "to destroy"; *mā* means "to measure"; and *māṅ* means "to measure" (or "to protect").

In *praṇidāne*, [the root] *sthā* means "to stand" or "to remain. The mention of *śtip* is for the purpose of specifying the verbal root; for without *śtip*, the suffix *śyan* is not easily obtained. As for what was stated by Prasādakṛt—"The mention of *tip* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa [reduplication], as in *dādataḥ*..."
[As for the claim that there would be *iṭ* in *sāsāte*: that is not so. For when there is *yaṅluk*, *iṭ* must indeed occur—as in *dāditaḥ* and *sāsitaḥ*.

In those cases, because of the rule "before a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*" (*iṭ kiti*), there is no occasion [for *iṭ*]. Furthermore, it is beyond dispute that the substitute (*ādeśa*) prescribed by the rule "of *dhā*, *da*" (*o dadghoḥ*) replaces the whole [root] because it consists of more than one letter (*anekāl*). And thus...]

They say that since the substitution of *vadh* for the root *han* applies even when it is followed by an elided suffix (*luṅ-anta*), it should likewise apply to the reduplicated form; thus, how could the form *dādataḥ*, which you have cited as an example, possibly occur? [To this, the rule is:
(724) *śācchāser anyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 7.4.41. [This rule provides the option for the substitution of *ghas* for the roots *śā* and *chās*.]
*Śā* [is used] in the sense of sharpening; *śo* in the sense of thinning; *chāe* in the sense of cutting.
(725) *Dadhāter hiḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.42: For the root *dadhāti*, the substitute *hi* is applied. The mention by means of the *śtip* affix is for the purpose of excluding the *ghaṭ* affix.

Because of the continued application of the term *ti*, this [rule] does not apply to the *yaṅluk* (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix). Regarding *dādhitaḥ*, the author of the *Prasāda* has stated: "Since the mention of the form with *śtip* is for the purpose of including the *yaṅluk* formation, the form *dādhītaḥ* is cited as an example for the substitution of *ī* by the rule *hmu-ā-stha-ī-tvam*";
however, that must be rejected just as before.

(726) *do dad ghoḥ* | 7|4|46| The ancient grammarians maintain that here the substitute (*ādeśa*) is one ending in *d* alone, and not one ending in *t*, *d*, or *dh*; for although the *saṃhitā* form would be identical once the *jaś*-substitution has been applied, there is a fault in the process (*prakriyā*). Thus they say:
‘In the case of [the root] *ad*, there is the fault known as lengthening; in the case of *dā*, the fault is the substitution of *niṣṭhāna*;

in the case of *dhā*, there would be the fault known as the substitution of *dha*. Because it is free from these faults, the form ending in *tha* (*thānta*) should be accepted. Following that, he says: “*dathsyāt*” and “*dāta*. [The latter is derived from] *dāp* in the sense of cutting (*lavane*), according to the rule “*ṭhadāb*.”

Due to the prohibition, there is no *ghu*-status. He states that all [forms] ending in *pṣ* are easily established here by saying "or ending in *t*" and so forth. Regarding the "consequence of a long vowel," this refers to [the rule] "of the prefix" (*upasargasya*) in examples such as *vidatam*.
In the case of *astyit*, there are two views: [one is that] the substitute for *iti* ends in the letter *t*.

"Is it 'beginning with the letter *a*'? With the intention that this fault applies to the first alternative (*pakṣa*) but not to the latter, he refutes the stated objection by saying, "in the case of [the suffix] beginning with *t*. Regarding "the state of being *niṣṭhāna*":

[this is established] by the rule "after *ad* and *āp*, *ta* becomes *na*" (*adābhyāṃ ṭam*). Regarding "the condition of *sannipāta*": [it refers to] that which was prescribed having made something beginning with *t* its cause (*nimitta*).

The meaning is that the substitution of *d* for *t* and so forth does not serve as the cause (*nimitta*) for the rule prescribing *n*-hood (*natva*) which would otherwise destroy that *t*. (727) *aca upasargāt taḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.47.
Here, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) is made: the letter *a* after the *t* is for the sake of pronunciation. The term *ṭhacaḥ* recurs;

there, one instance, ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*), qualifies the prefix (*upasarga*), while the other, ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), is explained as "for the sake of obtaining a position" (*sthānalābhāya*) by the words beginning with "ending in *ac*" (*ajantāt*). Alternatively, *ṭhacaḥ* is not repeated.

Let it be that [the substitute] ends in the fifth case (pañcamyanta); however, this substitute consists of two *t* sounds. Because it has more than one *al* (anekāl), it will replace the whole (*sarvasya*) of the original element (*ghoḥ*). For if it consisted of a single *t*, it would override the rule "of the final [element]" (*alo’ntyasya*) and, by the rule "of what follows after [the marker]," it would replace only the initial [element].

It may be so, because of the mention of the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśāt*). If this is the case, then in the subsequent rule *ṭhapaḥ bhi*, since there too there would be only a single *t* (in *ṭha*), it would follow that the entire [stem] is replaced. To this they reply:
because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of "of the vowel at the end of the fifth case" (*pañcamyāntasyācaḥ*), it will be only the *p* following the vowel that is affected.

In that case, when the final [consonant] is elided by the rule *saṃyogāntalopaḥ*, the desired result is established for the preceding [consonant] through the application of *jaśtva*. Regarding the examples beginning with *avadatam* and so forth: the term *ādikarmaṇi* (in the sense of an initial action) is a qualifier specifically for *pradatam*, and not for the others, because it is impossible for them [to denote an initial action]. [The phrase] *dātuṃ prakrāntam ārabdham* means "begun or commenced to give."

The meaning of *pradattam* is as follows: "it is desired" means that this is accepted as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) for the purpose of overriding the substitution of *tā*. Others, however, maintain that by relying on the view that *ava* and the others are mere counterfeits of prepositions (*upasarga-pratirūpaka*), forms such as *avadataṃ* and *vidataṃ* are established; whereas if one relies on their status as actual prepositions, the previously mentioned *avataṃ* [would apply].
Regarding the phrase "vītam" and so forth, they say that this statement is not something new.
[The rule] *da-sti* (Pāṇini 6.3.124) applies. From the rule *ikaḥ kāśe* (6.3.123), the word *ikaḥ* is understood, and from the rule *upasargasya ghañi* (6.3.122)...

Regarding the rule *upasargasya*: the word *dīrgha* (long vowel) is carried over from the rule *hrasve pūrvasya*; and the phrase *uttarapade*, which was carried over from the rule *aluguttarapade*, is qualified by the word *ti*. By the principle *yasmin vidhistadādau*, this refers to a rule that applies to what begins with that [suffix]. Having all of this in mind, he explains as follows:

By the rule beginning with *igantopasargasya* [Pāṇini 6.3.122], etc. Now, one might object that because the substitution of *c* (for *t*) is considered asiddha, the *t* of the substitute *dā* does not exist; therefore, he says: "It is established by virtue of its basis. The sense is that it is like the *r*-substitution in relation to the *u*-substitution prescribed by *ato roḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.113]. Regarding *dhītam*: in the rule *adhāterhiḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.78], the root *dhā* belongs to the *lug-vikaraṇa* class.

The point is that because of the specific mention [of *ghas*] in the rule "ghaṭ pāne" (*DhP* 1.950), the root *bhū* etc. does not become *hi*; nor does *da* [become *hi*], because of the inclusion of *da* in the rule "o daddhoḥ" (*DhP* 7.3.73).
(729) *ado jagdhir lyapi kiti* (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 2.4.36).

The phrase "for the purpose of pronunciation" means that if the suffix were marked with the *it* indicatory letter (*idit*), the augment *num* would occur; this is the intended sense. Regarding "the substitution of *gha*":
this refers to the rule *haṣastathordho'dhaḥ*. Regarding "by the rule *jharo jhari*": the meaning is that by this rule, the optional elision of the consonant *dha* occurs.
Now he elaborates on the meanings of the suffix *kta*: "in the sense of the beginning of an action. This has been explained. [The word] *prakṛtaḥ* [is used].

"Kaṭam" means "he began to make a mat. The suffix "ra" (in *ārebhe*) is for the purpose of indicating the commencement of an action (*ādikarma*). Since the agent has already been expressed by the past passive participle (*kta*), the nominative case is used for the agent. The meaning is "skilled" (*kuśala*).

(730) Pāṇini 3.4.72: [The affix *ktvā* is applied after verbal roots] having the sense of motion, those that are intransitive (*akarmaka*), and after the roots *śliṣ*, *śīṅ*, *sthā*, *ās*, *vas*, *jan*, *ruh*, and *jṛ*.
Regarding *gata*: there is the elision of the *m* by the rule *anudātopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām anunāsikalopo jhali kṅiti*. Regarding *prāpta*: the root *āplṛ* preceded by *pra* means "to pervade.

The sense is that even "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) is intended here by the word "motion" (*gati*) in this sūtra. Regarding *glāna*: the root *glai* means "the loss of joy"; this is intransitive. By the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti*, the vowel substitution (*ātva*) occurs.

The substitution of *n* [for *t*] occurs by the rule *aṃyogāderātaḥ*. Regarding "the remainder": the status of being the object (*karmatva*) is established by the rule *adhiśīṅsthāsāṃ karma*. In *adhiṣṭhita*, the substitution of *i* [for the radical vowel] occurs by the rule *yatisyatī*. In *upoṣita*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *vasatikṣudhoḥ*, and the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *āsivasī*. In *anujīrṇa*, [the root is] *jṛṣ*.

In *vayohāni* ("loss of age"), there is lengthening by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* and *hali ca*; there is no substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. (731) *kto’dhikaraṇe ca dhrauvyagatipratyavasānārthebhyaḥ* |3|4|76|.
Regarding *mukundasya*: that in which one sits is called *āsita*; the meaning is "seating."
That in which one goes is a *yāna*, meaning a path (*mārga*). That in which one enjoys is *bhukta*;
the meaning is "food" (*bhojana*). In all three cases, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the agent according to the rule *adhikaraṇavācinaśca* (Pāṇini 2.3.68).
[The suffix] *kta* follows a root ending in *ñī*. (Pāṇini 3.2.187).

Regarding *kṣviṇṇa*: the augment *iṭ* is not applied by the rule "ṭhāditaśca". Regarding *iddha*: the augment *iṭ* is not applied by the rule "vīdito niṣṭhāyām". There is the elision of *n*. (733) [Pāṇini 3.2.188: *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* ("And after roots having the sense of 'thinking', 'cognizing', or 'honoring'").

Regarding "of kings" (*rājñām*): the genitive case is used by the rule *tasya ca vartamāne*. Regarding "desired" (*iṣṭa*): because [the root] *iṣ* takes the augment *iṭ* optionally by the rule *īṣasaha*, the augment *iṭ* is not applied here by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*. Regarding "practiced" (*śīlita*) and so forth: [the roots are] *śīla* in the sense of concentration (*samādhi*), *rakṣa* in the sense of protection (*pālana*), *kṣamūṣ* in the sense of endurance (*sahana*), *kruśa* in the sense of calling out (*āhvāna*), and *juṣī*.
[The suffix *ṇvul* is applied] after [the roots] *prī* and *sev*.
(734) *suyajor ṅvanip*: 3.2.103. Regarding *suyajoḥ*: [it refers to] *su* and *yaj*. As for *sunoteḥ*: [it refers to] *ṣuñ* (to press). Although here [the root] *su* means "to go,"...
Regarding the rule *prasavevaiśvaryayoḥ*, it is logical that only those [roots] without the *anubandha* should be taken;

nevertheless, the point is that they are not included here either because they are not mentioned [in this context] or because of their association with roots that are *ubhayapadins* (taking both voices).
The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* in the case of the root *su*. As for the letter *p*, however...
The suffix *svar* has the sense of "self" (*ātman*) and "own" (*sva*).

(735) [Vt. 1] From the root *jṛ* ("to grow old"), the suffix *atṛn* is applied [to form the present participle]. Thus, *jaran*. By the rule of *guṇa*, the vowel *ṛ* becomes *ar*; the letter *a* is then substituted for *ṛ*, followed by *r* (as per the rule *rapara*). By the rule *ugidacāṃ sarvanāmasthāne'dhātoḥ*, the augment *num* is added.
Because the elision of a consonant at the end of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the long vowel does not occur.
(736) *Chandasi liṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.105). He states the meaning of the rule *chandasi liṭ* as "in the general sense of the past. Nor [is there an issue] regarding "in the Veda" (*chandasi*).

One might suspect that this is redundant because its purpose is already served by the rule *luṅlaṅliṭaḥ*; however, there is a distinction: for that rule (*luṅlaṅliṭaḥ*) is prescribed under the heading of "connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusaṃbandha*), whereas this [present case] occurs even without such a connection with a verbal root. Regarding this, they have explained: the inclusion of the *kit* marker in *kānac* is for the sake of [the application of] the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām* in forms such as *tistirāṇaḥ*.

This [rule] is commenced when there is a scope for prohibition, in order to prohibit the *guṇa* [vowel strengthening]. However, in the case of *akrāṇa*, the *kit* status is already established by the rule "after a non-conjunct [root], the *liṭ* [affixes] are *kit*" (Pāṇini 1.2.5).
(737) *kvasuśca* || 3.2.107 || And [the affix] *kvasu* [is also *kit* after a root ending in a long vowel]. || 3.2.107 ||

Regarding the phrase "the opinion of the three sages": because the author of the *Sūtra* introduced the topic with "in Vedic [language]" (*chandasi*) and because the subsequent *sūtra* mentions "colloquial language" (*bhāṣā*), and because both the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika* state that for the suffixes *kvasu* and *kānac*,
by the rule "in Vedic [language] both ways," they possess the status of *sārvadhātuka*, and thus [the rule] "a *sārvadhātuka* suffix also [causes the guṇa of the penultimate vowel]" applies.

Having raised the objection that in forms such as *ājīvān* the effects of the *kit* suffix— such as the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*)— are otherwise established, [the author] states that the *kit* designation is made for the purpose of subverting the *guṇa* substitution that would otherwise apply by the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām* in forms such as *titīrvān* and *tistirāṇa*.

This is because it has been established as the settled conclusion (*siddhānta*). Therefore, the notion held by some—that on the strength of the inclusion of the *kit* marker, the suffixes *kvasu* and *kānac* occur even in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*)—is not to be respected;
this is clear from the works of Haradatta, Mādhava, and others. This is the intended meaning [of the phrase] "by poets."
The meaning is: "by way of following what has gone before.
(738) *vasvekājādghasām* | 7|2|67|. Regarding *vasvi*: the mention of *vasvi* is without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*), and thus—

It will be explained [later] with the word *vasoḥ*. Since [the root *vas*] is monosyllabic (*ekāc*) by virtue of its being eternal, once reduplication (*dvitva*) has occurred, it would no longer be monosyllabic; thus, how could the augment *iṭ* apply? To this he says: "of those that are monosyllabic after reduplication has been performed. The meaning is: those which remain as monosyllables even after reduplication has taken place. [The rule continues: "eṅ vaśi... [Pāṇini 6.1.15].

The word "kṛtī" (the root *kṛ*) indicates that this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the augment *iṭ*, which would otherwise apply everywhere by the general rule for roots beginning with *krā* (Pāṇini 7.2.13), thereby overriding the prohibition [of *iṭ*]. Thus he says: "not for others. Regarding the form *ādivān*: from the root *ad* (to eat), after doubling, the application of the rule for the retention of the first part (*halādi-śeṣa*), the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-dīrgha*), and the lengthening of the homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa-dīrgha*) have been performed.

Even though this [root] has undergone reduplication (*dvitva*), it remains *ekāc* (consisting of a single vowel) and thus takes the suffix *iṭ*. For example, *ārivān*: from the root *ṛ* (to go), when the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām* is applied, and after the reduplication and other operations have been performed as before, this too becomes *ekāc*. Similarly, *dadivān*: from the root *ḍudāñ* (to give). When [the operations] have been performed...

In the case of reduplication (*dvitva*), this [root] is not *ekāc* (consisting of a single vowel), and since the elision of the vowel caused by the suffix *iṭ* does not occur when that [reduplication] is absent, the mention of *āt* (the long vowel) is for the sake of [roots] consisting of more than one vowel. For example, in *jakṣivān*:
by the rule *iṭo ’nyatarasyām*, there is the substitution of *ad* for the root-final *ghas*. Once reduplication has been performed, this [reduplicated form] is no longer *ekāc*.

Regarding the inclusion of the term *ghasi*: here they have explained that because it is subsequent [to the rule for doubling], the elision of the penultimate vowel by the rule *hasibhasor halī* would occur before the doubling;
and once that has been performed, because the word would then lack a vowel (*anackatvāt*), the doubling itself would not take place. Nor, when this [doubling] is to be performed...

One might suspect that by the rule "virvacane'ci," there is either the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original) or a prohibition [of reduplication], because there is no vowel (*ac*) that serves as the cause for the doubling. Consequently, this [root] would not become a single-syllable (*ekāj*) after reduplication; therefore, the mention of *ghas* is made, and by the force of its presence, [the desired result follows].

Because it is subsequent, the augment *iṭ* subverts the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*). However, once the augment *iṭ* has been applied, the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule "in *amahan*" (*ama-han-ṇe*), and because that [elision] is not marked with *ñ* or *k*, it is treated as if it were the original position (*sthānivadbhāva*), resulting in reduplication. Alternatively, according to the view that there is a prohibition by the rule "in reduplication, when *ac* follows" (*dvirvacane 'ci*), reduplication occurs even before the elision of the penultimate vowel.

Subsequently, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) by the rule "āsivasighasīnāṃ ca"; then the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule for *ṣatva*, followed by *cartva* (the change of *s* to *ṣ*), resulting in *kṣ*.
Then, by the rule "ṭhabhyāse carce," there is the substitution of the *jaś*-class sound (*jaśtva*) for the *gh* in the reduplicated syllable.
(739) Pāṇini 3.2.108: *bhāṣāyāṃ sadavasaśruvaḥ*.

Regarding the form *niṣeduṣīm*: the root *ṣadlṛ* means "to settle" and so forth. After reduplication by the rule *iṭi dhātoḥ*, the rules *ata ekahalmadhye* and [the following] apply to effect the *etva* (change to *e*) and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*). Then, by the rule *ugitaśca*, the suffix *ṅīp* is added; by *vasoḥ*, there is *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization), and because the suffix begins with a consonant other than *val*, the augment *iṭ* is not applied. By the rule *ādiraprateḥ*, the initial *s* becomes *ṣ*. In the masculine...

[He] has resided [there]. Regarding the form *adhyūṣuṣaḥ*: the root *vas* meaning "to dwell," preceded by the prefix *adhi*, undergoes vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *vacisvapi-*.

Then, doubling, the retention of the first consonant after a double consonant (*halādiśeṣa*), and lengthening of the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) take place. In the genitive singular (*ṅsi*), there is vocalization because the stem is treated as a nominal base (*bha*). However, in the nominative singular, the form is *adhyūṣivān*.

(740) *upeyivān anāśvān anūcānaś ca* |3|2|109|. Regarding *upeyivān*: the augment *iṭ* [which would otherwise be applied] by the rule for roots beginning with *val* is prohibited by the rule *eḍ vaśi kṛti*. It is, however, re-introduced by the rule *vasvekājāddhasām* due to the restriction [imposed by] the rule concerning *ṛkārādi* roots.

By the restrictive rule stating that *iṭ* should be added after roots ending in *ghas*, as well as after monosyllabic roots ending in long *ā* that have undergone reduplication (*dvitva*), and not after others, [the addition of *iṭ*] was prohibited; for once reduplication has occurred, the root is no longer monosyllabic due to its having become polysyllabic (*anekāctvāt*). Nor does the lengthening of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) restore monosyllabism, because of the rule "long vowel for *iṇ*" (*dīrgha iṇaḥ*).

Because the rule "kiti" prescribes lengthening of the reduplicated syllable, one adopts the view that by the force of that very rule, the homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) does not occur; thus, it is precisely this *iṭ* characterized by the condition of being preceded by a consonant (*valādi*) that is reintroduced here, rather than a new *iṭ* being enjoined. Consequently, it does not apply in the domain of *saṃprasāraṇa*. For this very reason, he cites the following example:

Regarding the form *upeyuṣaḥ*: the intention is that if the suffix *ktvā* were present, its substitution by *yaṇ* would result in the form *upeyyuṣaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "not intended [to be expressed]": here, the commentary itself is the sole refuge. Regarding *īyivān*:

when there is reduplication of the root *iṇ*, the substitution of *yaṇ* (by the rule *iṇo yaṇ*) occurs because it belongs to the *āṅga* (suffixal) domain, thereby overriding the rule for *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel coalescence).
For when there is the augment *iṭ* [after the root *vas*], the subsequent suffix begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). Regarding the word *vaceḥ*:

it is derived from the root *vac* in the sense of "speaking" (from *vaca paribhāṣaṇe*), either as the agent of *brū* or of *vac*, but not in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).
And this is obtained through a formal irregularity (*nipātana*).

(741) *vibhāṣā gamahanavidaviśām* |7|2|68|. [The suffix *kvasu* is optionally applied after the roots *gam*, *han*, *vid*, and *viś*. Examples include *jagmivān* and others. In the alternative where the augment *iṭ* is present, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) by the rule *amaṅṇeṭ*.
(742) *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacāvaprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe* |3|2|124|. [The suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* replace the present tense marker *laṭ* when not coreferential with a word ending in the nominative case.]

"Of the *laṭ* [present tense suffix], when there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Although coreferentiality is difficult to find in the case of the *laṭ* because it is never used in isolation from its substitutes, nevertheless,
having observed that coreferentiality in the case of the substitutes *śatṛ* and *śānac*, it is likewise attributed to the original element (*sthānin*) as well.

Regarding "śabādi": the intention is that [the suffix] is a sārvadhātuka because it is marked with Ś. Regarding "pacantam": the augment *num* is applied because the suffix *śatṛ* is marked with ūk. The meaning is: "that which is the substratum of an activity occurring at the present time conducive to softening. (743) *āne muk*. 7.2.82.

The word *ataḥ*, which was carried over from the preceding sūtra as ending in the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*) in the sense of "that which is situated in the place of," is here transformed into the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) by virtue of the locative case (*saptamī*) in the word *āne*. Nor is it the case that the locative-ending word *āne* is transformed into the genitive by virtue of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the word *ataḥ*.

This is to be suspected, because the fifth case [ending] has already fulfilled its purpose in the preceding sūtra, whereas the seventh case [ending] has not yet fulfilled its purpose. This is what he says: "of the *aṅga* ending in *at*.
The explanation given by the Easterners—that it refers to an *aṅga* ending in *at*—is incorrect. As in the example "acamāna."

In such cases, there would be the undesirable consequence that the accent of the suffix *śānac*—prescribed by the rule "that which follows an upadeśa containing *ṭh* is unaccented (*anudātta*)"—would not be established. For, according to the view that "the [suffix] follows a stem ending in *ṭh*," the augment *muk* is part of the stem (*aṅgabhakta*) and thus would not intervene between the stem itself and its own constituent vowel *a*. However, [if it were not part of the stem, it would intervene].
It would indeed create an intervention. However, since it is merely a portion (*bhakta*) of the letter *a*, there is no intervention because it is a constituent part (*avayava*) of it;

thus, there is no fault. Now, one might object: by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating that "in a rule concerning vowels (*svaravidhi*), a consonant (*vyañjana*) is as if non-existent," the *muk* [augment] is as if non-existent.

If it is argued that because there is no intervention, the state of being unaccented (*anudātta*) would indeed occur, [the reply] is as follows: they say that the established doctrine (*ākarārūḍha*) is that "a consonant is as if non-existent only when a vowel-sound (*svara*) is to be obtained for a consonant (*hal*), and not elsewhere. Since there is no obtaining of a vowel-sound for a consonant here, this paribhāṣā is not applicable to the present case. Otherwise...

Even in cases such as *marutvān*, the rule *hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup* would result in the acute accent (*udātta*) on the suffix *matup*; this is the general direction [of the argument]. Regarding the term *liṭ*: although the nominative form is the one under discussion (*prakṛta*), nevertheless, because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the word *dhātoḥ*, the nominative form following the ablative is transformed into a genitive.

This is the intended meaning. Nor should it be suspected that a transformation [of the case ending] might occur here by the same method stated under the rule *vartamāne laṭ*; for the authors of the Bhāṣya have accepted in the commentary on the rule *uṇādayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.1) that the ablative case does not function as a *prakalpaka* (determiner) in the prescription of suffixes.
"Even when there is coreferentiality with a non-nominative [word]"—this is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa). Its meaning is:
"even in the absence of coreferentiality with a word ending in a case other than the nominative. This too is an elliptical expression; its meaning is:
"even in the absence of coreferentiality with a word ending in a case other than the nominative. By this [rule], from *kurvat*, we derive *kaurvataḥ* ("the descendant of one who is acting").

The forms *kurvato bhaktiḥ*, *kurvadbhaktiḥ*, and *kurvāṇabhaktiḥ* are established even when the suffixes (*pratyaya*) and the subsequent members of the compound (*uttarapada*) are present; otherwise,
in cases such as *kurvato’patyam*, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) and the compound (*samāsa*) would not be possible.

(744) *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* |3|2|126|. Regarding *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*: that by which something is characterized is a *lakṣaṇa*, i.e., an indicator. In the example *śayānāḥ*, since the root *śī* is ātmanepada, the suffix *laṭ* following it takes the form *śānac*. Here, lying down (*śayana*) is the *lakṣaṇa*, i.e., the mark.

The definition is stated separately from the cause because the eating has the Yavana as its agent, but neither a fruit nor an instrument. Regarding "arjayan": *arja* belongs to the *curādi* group in the sense of "effort toward acquisition";
thus, the meaning is "dwelling for the purpose of acquiring. Regarding "hari": the vision of Hari [leads] to liberation.
The meaning is "the cause.

(745) *videḥ śatur vasuḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.36. Regarding *videḥ*: although [the form] would have been established by the fact that [the substitute] is *sthānivadbhūta*, the addition of the marker *uk* to *vasu* [in the rule *vasoḥ samprasāraṇam*] is for the sake of... *vasoḥ*.

In the rule *saṃprasāraṇam*, the term *kvasuḥ* is also included for the sake of a general reference; and by virtue of that, the principle "when a suffix with one indicatory letter (*ekānubandha*) is mentioned, it does not include one with two indicatory letters (*dvayanubandhaka*)" does not apply here. (746) *pūṅyajoḥ śānan* 3.2.128.

Regarding *pūṅ* and *yaj*: the *ś* in *śānan* is for the sake of making it a *sārvadhātuka* suffix; the *n* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). This suffix is independent, like *ṇvul* and others, and is not a substitute for *l* (the *l*-suffixes such as *laṭ*), etc., like *śatṛ* and others; for if it were so, one would have to state "optionally" (*veti*) so that forms like *pavate* and *yajate* might also occur with *tiṅ* endings. Nor is this the case.

Alternatively, the derivation may be maintained by the *vāsarūpa* rule; however, it is established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that the *vāsarūpa* rule does not apply to substitutes of *l* (the verbal suffixes). Furthermore, if [the suffix] were a substitute of *l*, then by the rule *aḥ karmaṇi ca*, the suffix *la* prescribed for both the agent and the object would also be employed in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), whereas [this is] not desired.

But [the suffix] occurs only in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). In this way, it should be understood that the *anaś* (present middle participle) and the *śatṛ* (present active participle) possess independence, as indicated by the rule "ṭiṅghāryoḥ. Regarding this, some say: "If the *śānan* were a substitute for *la*, it would result in the low-pitched accent (*anudātta*) of the *lasārvadhātuka*. This is to be considered; for, due to the application of the *nitsvara* (accent on the *ni*t suffix) because it is of higher priority, [the form] *pavamāna* [is established].
Because, in the case of forms such as *ityādi*, the initial syllable is intended to have the acute accent (*udātta*), whereas the suffix *śānan* is intended to be unaccented (*anudātta*).

If it is argued that if these [suffixes] are not accepted as substitutes for *lādeśa*, then in examples such as *omaṃ pavamāna*, the genitive case would apply to the object (*karman*), we say: not so. For in the rule *a loke*, there is the mention of the pratyāhāra *tṛn*.
Because it has been stated thus.
(747) *Tācchīlyavayovacanaśaktiṣu cānaś* (Pāṇini 3.2.129). The inclusion of the term "vacana" (denoting) [in the rule] is for the sake of clarity. Regarding the suffix *cānaś*:

Indicating that the rule applies even after roots that are *parasmaipada* because there is no substitution of *la* and thus no *ātmanepada* status, he provides the example: *nighnānaḥ*. Here, the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *amaṃhanē*.

(748) *iṅghāryoḥ śatrakṛcchriṇi* |3|2|130|. Regarding *iṅ* and *dhāry*: because *iṅ* is marked with the *ātmanepada* sign, the suffix *śatṛ* is not established [for it]; for *dhārayati* as well, it is not established when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent; furthermore, there would be the lack of the *anudātta* accent for the *lasārvadhātuka*.
This is the beginning [of the section]: "He obtains" (prāpnoti).
(749) *suño yajñasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 3.2.132). Regarding *suño yajñasaṃyoge*: the suffix *śatṛ* should be applied to the root *sū* (*sunoti*) when it is connected with a sacrifice.
If it is argued that [the mention of *saṃyoga*] is for the sake of restriction (*vṛtti*), one might object: "In this case, let it simply be 'uño yajñe';
for by explaining it as 'if the meaning of the root *su* pertains to the sacrifice,' it would be possible to exclude examples such as *surāṃ sunoti*. To this, they say: the mention of *saṃyoga*...

This is for the purpose of conveying the sense of the primary agent; therefore, it does not occur elsewhere than in the case of *yaj* and so on. And thus, even by the rule "aṭaḥ śatṛśānacau" (Pāṇini 3.2.124), it does not apply when the agent is non-primary, because of the force of the mention of "consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*)—so says Haradatta. [The suffix] *tya*.

One might raise the objection that while forms ending in the singular number— such as *sunvantam avatu* ("may he protect the one who presses [the Soma]")— can possibly refer to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*),

this is not possible for those ending in the plural number, because in a single sacrifice there is only one sacrificer; however, [the author] counters this by stating that it is indeed possible in the case of a particular type of sacrifice.

He provides an illustration to demonstrate this, beginning with "All are pressing [the Soma]," and so forth. For in a *sattra* sacrifice, there are many sacrificers (*yajamāna*), and they themselves perform the work of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), namely the pressing of the Soma; thus, the meaning is that even a plural form such as "they are pressing" (*sunvantaḥ*) can refer to the sacrificers.

(750) *arhaḥ* [is used] in the sense of praise. 3.2.133. *arhaḥ*. What for the sake of praise? *cauro vadham arhati* ("The thief deserves death"). (751) *ā keṣṭacchīlataddharmatatsādhukāriṣu*. 3.2.134. [The suffix *ṇvul* is applied after a verbal root] up to and including *keṣṭṛ*, in the senses of one who has that as his habit (*tacchīla*), that as his duty (*taddharma*), or one who performs it well (*tatsādhukārī*).

In order to justify the qualification of the three beginning with *śīla*, the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtibhūtadhātvartha*) is indicated by the three demonstrative pronouns (*tad*) that have been mentioned.
The phrase “including *kvip*” refers to what will be stated later: “*hrājabhāsadhurvidyautorjī*. This is the remainder [of the explanation].

In the example *kartā kaṭān*, the genitive case is prohibited by the rule *a lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām*. (752) [The suffix] *iṣṇuc* is applied after the roots *alaṃ-kṛ*, *nir-ā-kṛ*, *pra-jan*, *ut-pad*, *ut-pat*, *un-mad*, *ruc*, *apa-trap*, *vṛt*, *vṛdh*, *sah*, and *car*. Pāṇini 3.2.136.

In the rule *alaṅkṛñ*, only the root *ḍukṛñ* in the sense of "making" (*karaṇa*) is to be understood, and not the root *kṛñ* in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsā*), according to the maxim: "When both [roots] are established or both are unestablished, only the established one is to be taken. The same root *kṛñ* applies even when preceded by the prefixes *nir-* and *ā-*. The root *janī* preceded by *pra-* means "manifestation" (*prādurbhāva*).

In this context, the three roots *ḍupacaṣ* (in the sense of cooking), *patlṛ* (in the sense of going), and *madī* (in the sense of exhilaration) are all recited with the prefix *ud*. Therein, although it would have been sufficient to state simply "after *ud*, [the suffix *iṣṇuc* is added] to *pac*, *pat*, and *mad*," the fact that each is recited individually with the prefix *ud* is for the purpose of excluding other prefixes; consequently, forms such as *samutpatiṣṇu* do not occur.
They say that [the suffix] *bhavati* occurs [after these roots]: *ruc* in the sense of shining; preceded by *apa*, *trapūṣ* in the sense of shame;
*vṛt* in the sense of turning; *vṛdh* in the sense of increasing; *sah* in the sense of enduring; *car* in the sense of moving; and so forth.
As for those included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*): *nirākariṣṇuḥ*, *prajaniṣṇuḥ*, *utpaciṣṇuḥ*, *utpatiṣṇuḥ*.

Regarding the word *unmadiṣṇu*: Bhaṭṭi says, "The two, Kharadūṣaṇa and [Indrajit], who were prone to leaping up (*utpatiṣṇu*) and enduring (*sahiṣṇu*), moved about. Kālidāsa also says, "Leaping up from their halas. Some, however, having read the root *dānta* in place of *pata* in the sūtra, derive the suffix from the root *pad* (meaning "to go").
*unmadiṣṇuḥ*, *rociṣṇuḥ*, *apatrapiṣṇuḥ*, *vartiṣṇuḥ*, *cariṣṇuḥ*.
(753) *ṇeś chandasi* |3|2|137|. [In the example] *pārayiṣṇavaḥ*, the suffix *ay* is applied to the root *ṇī* by the rule *ṭhayāmante*.
(754) *bhuvaśca* |3|2|138|. "Not this" means that the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. (755) *glājisthaśca gsnuḥ* |3|2|139|.
"It is not the case that [the vowel] becomes *ī*. [This refers to] the passage beginning with "humāstha," etc. Regarding the phrase "because it has the marker *g*":

the intention is that in the rule "ṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5), the letter *g* is elided [and read as part of the preceding rule], so that it is explained as "when there is a *g*-marker, a *k*-marker, or a *ṅ*-marker.

Regarding the phrase "due to the elision of the letter *g*": [an objection is raised: "But in this way, since the substitution of *c* for *t* (*cartva*) would be considered *asiddha* (unestablished) when the letter *g* is present..."

If it is argued that there should be the substitution of *ū* [for *i*] by the rule *ṭhhaśic* [Pāṇini 6.4.103], [we reply: True; this is a Vedic (sautra) usage. Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "Because of the *gittva* of *sthā*, there is no *ī* for *stha*; because of the prescription of *īt* for *kṅti*;
the absence of *guṇa* in the three [cases] is to be remembered; and the lack of *iṭ* for *śryuk* when followed by *aniṭ* [roots] ending in *k* or *g*."
Regarding the word *daṃṣṭrāvaḥ*: from the root *daṃś* (to bite), by the rule *vraśca* etc., there is the substitution of *ṣ*; then, by the rule *aḍoḥ kaḥ si*, there is the substitution of *k*;

and by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṣ*. There is no elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule *aniditām*, because the suffix *snau* lacks the *g*-marker (*gitva*), which would otherwise trigger that elision.

(756) *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ* | 3|2|140| [The suffix] *knu* [is applied after the roots] *tras*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣip*. [In the form] *trasnu*, there is no *iṭ* augment by the rule *eḍvaśi*. (757) *śamiṣṭābhyodhinuṇ* | 3|2|141| [The suffix] *dhiṇuṇ* [is applied after the roots] *śam* and *iṣṭa*.

Regarding the rule *śamityaṣṭābhyo ḍaḥ*: the word *iti* has the sense of "and so forth" (*ādyartha*). As for the example *śaminītarā*, the moderns (*navyāḥ*) argue as follows: just as in the case of *vidvattara*, by the rule *tasilādiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.35), there should be the substitution of the masculine form, resulting in *śamitarā*. Nor should it be argued that because there is no purpose for admitting the presence of the *u*-marker (*ugit*), there is only an optional shortening (*hrasva-vikalpa*).

They say that because the inclusion of the marker *u* in the rule for *ūṅ*-stems (*ugit*) has its purpose fulfilled by the optional short vowel, whereas in the alternative case where the short vowel is absent, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would be unavoidable. (758)

The suffix *in* is added after the following roots: *saṃ-pṛc*, *anu-rudh*, *ā-ḍul*, *ā-ḍul*, *pari-sṛ*, *saṃ-sṛj*, *pari-dev*, *saṃ-jvar*, *pari-kṣip*, *pari-raṭ*, *pari-vad*, *pari-dah*, *pari-muh*, *duṣ*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duh*, *yuj*, *ā-krīḍ*, *vi-vic*, *tyaj*, *raj*, *bhaj*, *ati-car*, *apa-car*, *muṣ*, and *abhi-ahan*. (Pāṇini 3.2.142) Regarding *saṃpṛc*: *saṃparkī* ("one who associates"). From the root *pṛc* in the sense of "associating. By the rule *ajaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.50], there is *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *c*). Then, by *guṇa* [Pāṇini 7.3.84], the vowel is strengthened. Regarding *paridevī*: from the root *devṛ* in the sense of "lamenting," belonging to the *bhvādi* class. However, this does not apply to the causative (*ṇyanta*) form of *div* (to play/shine).
The inclusion [of *abhyāghātī*] is because it possesses its own specific characteristic (*lākṣaṇikatva*) and because of its association with roots ending in *-aṇ*. Regarding *abhyāghātī*:
from the root *han* preceded by the prefixes *abhi* and *ā*, the *h* becomes *gh* by the rule for *kutva*; the *n* becomes *t* by the rule *hanasta’ciṇṇaloḥ*;
and the vowel *a* undergoes *vṛddhi* strengthening by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*.

(759) *vau kaṣalasakatthasrambhaḥ* | 3|2|143| [The suffix *yaṅ* is applied after the roots] *kaṣ*, *las*, *katth*, and *srambh* when preceded by the prefix *vi*. *Kaṣ* means "to injure"; *las* means "to adhere" and "to play"; *katth* means "to boast"; *srambh* means "to trust. [The suffix *yaṅ* is also applied] after *laṣ* when preceded by *apa*. *Laṣ* means "to desire."

(760) *pre lapasṛdrumathavadavasaḥ* |3|2|145|. After the prefix *pra*, [the suffix *ini* is applied] to the roots *lap*, *rap*, *lap* (in the sense of distinct speech), *math* (in the sense of churning/agitating), *vad*, and *vas*. Regarding *pramāthī*: the root *math* means to churn or agitate. (761)

The suffix *vuñ* is applied after the verbal roots *nind*, *hiṃs*, *kliś*, *khād*, *vināśa*, *parikṣip*, *pariraṭ*, *parivādi*, and *vyābhāṣ*, as well as after the root *asūy*, when used with an object.
(Pāṇini 3.2.146). Regarding the rule *nindahiṃsa...*: here in this sūtra, the reading is *vināśa*, which is the causative (*ṇyanta*) form of the root *naś* preceded by the prefix *vi*.
This is indeed beyond dispute. *Asūyati* is derived from the root *asūy* with the suffix *yaṅ*;
in the collective dvandva compound of the words beginning with "blame" (*nindā*) and ending with "envy" (*asūyā*), the masculine gender is prescribed by the sūtra.
It might be argued: "The suffix *vuñ* should be applied only to *asūyati*, and not to the others, such as 'blame' and so forth."

Since [the forms] *nindaka*, etc., are established by the suffix *ṇvul* alone, there is indeed no difference between the accent of the *liṭ* suffix and the accent of the *nit* suffix in that case, because in both instances the first syllable is udātta. However, in the case of *asūyaka* with *ṇvul*, the vowel preceding the suffix is udātta by the rule "iti" (Pāṇini 6.1.197), whereas with *vuñ*...

The distinction is that [the suffix] beginning with *ṭh* and *ñ* is always acute (*udātta*), according to the rule "that which begins with *ṭh* or *ñ* is always [acute]. To this, he says: "In the case of *ṇvul*, etc.
[This implies] that *tṛc* and so forth are not [included]. The meaning is that this is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*) concerning *ṇvul* alone, but rather concerns affixes in general.

(762) *devikruśoścopasarge* |3|2|147|. [The word] *devikruśoḥ*: there is the inclusion of both the root *div*, when it ends in the causative suffix (*ṇic*), and the root *div*, when it belongs to the *curādigaṇa* and ends in the suffix *ṇi* (meaning "to cry out").

(763) *calana-śabdārthād akarmakād yauc* |3|2|148| [The suffix] *ya* and *yu* are added after roots meaning motion (*calana*) or sound (*śabdārtha*), provided they are intransitive (*akarmaka*). [Examples: *cala* (to move/tremble), *cupa* (to move slowly), *kapi* (to move); *śabda* (to sound)—belonging to the *cur*-class; *ru* (to sound). "Motion" and so forth [refer to the root meanings]. The substitution of *y* for *u* is by the rule *yuvor anākau*.

(764) *anudātetaśca halādeḥ* |3|2|149|. [The rule states: "And [a root] beginning with a consonant and having an *anudātta* as its *it*. Now, since every such root ending in a consonant necessarily begins with a consonant, one might argue that by the force of the context (*sāmarthya*), the term "beginning with a consonant" (*halādeḥ*) alone would suffice, thereby setting aside the rule of reference to what ends in such a form (*tadantavidhi*). Why, then, is the mention of "beginning with" (*ādi*) necessary?

Regarding this, they say: in the absence of the mention of "ādi" (and so forth), since the *anubandha* (indicatory letter), which has not yet served its purpose regarding bases ending in consonants (*halanta*), serves to specify the entire group [of roots], such is the direction [of the argument].
(765) Pāṇini 3.2.150: *ju-caṅkramya-dandramya-sṛ-gṛdhi-jvala-śuca-laṣa-pata-padaḥ*.

*jucaṅkramya*. *Kram* and *dram* are roots with the *yaṅ* suffix; *kramu* means "to step," while *drama*, *hamma*, and *mīmṛ* mean "to go. Regarding the word "pūrveṇa" (by the former), it refers to the rule *anudātetaśca*. Here, the author of the Vṛtti stated that "the mention of 'adi' (beginning with 'a') is for the sake of [roots] that take an object. However, in the Bhāṣya, it is said that this is not necessary because such forms are simply not used (*anabhidhānāt*).

Since it has been stated that [the suffix] will not occur after a transitive verb, he says—with the intention that this is for the sake of providing an indication—"Let there be no sublation," and so forth. Regarding "mutually": for in the sūtra on *nindā* and the others, it was indicated by the rule of *vāsarūpa* that *tṛc* and other suffixes do not apply to those beginning with *tacchīla*; however, here, in the case of those [suffixes] like *ācchīlika*, [the situation is different].
The sense is that "viveka" (discrimination) means it has been made known that [the two] are not [identical] to one another.
(766) *krudhamaṇḍārthebhyaśca* | Pāṇini 3.2.151.
[Roots meaning] *krudh* (to be angry), *maḍ* (to adorn): *krudh* in the sense of anger; *ruṣ* in the sense of wrath; *maḍi* in the sense of adorning; *bhūṣ* in the sense of decoration.

(767) *na yaḥ* |3|2|152|. Regarding *na yaḥ*: this is not a reference to the root *naya-* as it is listed in the Dhātupāṭha among *aya*, *vaya*, *paya*, *bhaya*, *caya*, *taya*, and *ṇaya* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*), because the suffix *yuc* is already established for it simply by virtue of its being anudātta. Rather, [it refers to a different root].

Thinking that *neti* is a separate word, he says: "from those ending in *yakāra*. Examples are *knūyitā* and *kṣmāyitā*. The root *knūyī* means "to sound" and "to moisten," while *kṣmāyī* means "to shake.
(768) *sūda-dīpa-dīkṣaś-ca* | Pāṇini 3.2.153.

*Sūda-dīpa*: *sūda* means "to flow" (*kṣaraṇe*), *dīpī* means "to shine" (*dīptau*), and *dīkṣa* means "tonsure, sacrifice," etc. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of habitual action" (*tācchīlikeṣu*), the word "mutually" (*parasparam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding the word "generally" (*prāyikam*), it means that the co-occurrence of the two suffixes is not restricted solely to those cases exactly as they are heard in the [Bhāṣya], based on the authority of the Bhāṣya.

It should be noted, however, that the intention of the Bhāṣya is merely to state the general rule (*prāyikatva*). Therefore, in the case of the root *gam*, even though *ukañ* is prescribed by the rule "aṣapatapade," *tṛn* also occurs: *gantā* and *gāmukaḥ*. Likewise, in the case of *ghinuṇ* prescribed by the rule "vau kaṣalase," *yuc* also occurs: *vikatthī*, *vikatthanaḥ*, and so forth.
The sense is that it is accomplished.
(769) *jalpa-bhikṣa-kuṭṭa-luṇṭa-vṛṅaḥ ṣākan* | Pāṇini 3.2.155. [Roots: *jalpa*, *japa*—to speak articulately; *bhikṣa*—to beg, to obtain what was not obtained, or to obtain; *kuṭṭa*...

The roots *ṭu* (in the sense of cutting) and *luṇṭa* (in the sense of stealing) belong to the *caurādika* group. Regarding these, they have explained as follows: for *jalp* (to chatter), since it means "sound," the suffix *ac* applies; for *bhikṣ* (to beg), since it is *anudāteta*, the suffix *yuc* would apply; and for *kuṭṭ* and *luṇṭ*, since they are *ṇi*-roots, the suffix *iṣṇuc* would apply by the rule "after a root ending in ṇi, [the suffix iṣṇuc is used] in the Veda"; however, for *vṛṅ*...

Since the suffixes *kikin* and *kvin* would otherwise apply by the rule "ṭhādṛgamahanajane," this specific rule is prescribed; he says "varākī" to show that the suffix *ṣo* is for the purpose of adding the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*.
(770) *prajoriniḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.156).

The word *prajavī* is derived as follows: the root *u* is a Vedic (sautra) root meaning "to go. (Pāṇini 3.2.157) states: "After the roots *ji*, *dṛkṣi*, *viśrī*, *ṇvam*, *āvyath*, *paribhū*, and *prasū* [the suffix *in* is applied]. The roots are: *ji* in the sense of victory (*jaye*), *ji* in the sense of overcoming (*abhibhave*), *dṛṅ* in the sense of respect (*ādare*), *kṣi* in the sense of destruction (*kṣaye*), and *kṣi*...

The roots *śri* (in the sense of service) preceded by *vi*, and *vyath* (in the senses of fear and trembling) preceded by the negative particle *na*; the suffix is applied after the compound with the root, following the elision of *na* due to irregular formation (*nipātana*). [The root] *am* (in the senses of motion, etc. preceded by *abhi*. [The form] *prasavīti*: from the root *ṣū* (in the sense of impelling).

The suffix *ini* is applied after this [root]. Regarding the roots *ṣūṅ* (in the sense of releasing the embryo of a living being) and *ṣūṅ* (in the sense of the birth of a living being), these two are not included here because they possess an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). It would have been more appropriate to read *prasu* in the very rule for *idṛkṣī* and thereby discard the previous sūtra.
For in that way, one could easily say that there would be no need for a separate case-ending or the particle *ca*.
(772) *spṛhi-gṛhi-pati-dayi-nidrā-tandrā-śraddhābhya āluc* [Pāṇini 3.2.158]. *spṛhi*—*spṛha* in the sense of "desire"; *gṛhū* in the sense of "seizing"; *pata* in the sense of "going.

These three belong to the *curādi* (tenth) class; therefore, the form is established by the substitution of *ay* for the causative suffix *ṇic*. This is the intended meaning. That which precedes it...

Thus it is said. It should be understood that the compound of the word *tat* occurs here due to a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). [The root] *ḍudhāñ* preceded by *śrat* [yields] *śraddhāluḥ*. However, commentators have explained that this is not a form derived from the root *dheṭ*, because that root is never used when preceded by *śrat*. But then, how is it that [the forms] *kṛpāluḥ* and *sparddhāluḥ* are formed?
In the analysis (*vigraha*) of *kṛpāṃ spardhāṃ ca lāti*, the suffix *ku* is applied according to the *mṛgayvādi* group.
(773) *dādheṭsiśadasadoḥ ruḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.159. Regarding *dādheṭ*: only the three roots *ḍudāñ*, *do*, and *ḍeṅ* are included, and not others.
They say [the word] is *dāṇḍāpū*.

(774) *Bhañjabhāsamido ghurac* (Pāṇini 3.2.161): [The derivative] *bhaṅgura* is formed with the suffix *ghurac*. There is *kutva* (the substitution of *g*) by the rule *ajoguṇe*. This occurs because of the inherent nature (*abhidhānasvabhāva*) of the root *bhañj*.
They say [the suffix] applies only when the agent is also the object (*karmakartṛ*). (775) *vidi-bhidi-chidibhyaḥ kurac* (Pāṇini 3.2.162).
Regarding *vidi-bhidi*: only the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing" is taken here, not the one in the sense of "obtaining."
[The word] *cchidura* [is derived] from the commentary. The *vṛtti* states that the suffix is used in the sense of the object as the agent (*karmakartari*).
This is not seen in the *bhāṣya*. And thus Māgha employed it in the sense of the primary agent: "to his beloved... [etc.]
"In the phrase *vapur-guru-matsara-cchidurayā adur-ayācitaṃ aṅganā*, the word division here is *aduḥ*. [Pāṇini 3.2.163 states:
*iṇ-naś-jis-artibhyaḥ kvarap*.

*itvaraḥ*, *itvarī*: from the root *iṇ* [meaning] "to go," there is the suffix *tuK* by the rule "hrasvasya pitī" [Pāṇini 6.1.71]. Because it is marked with *k* (*kit*), there is an absence of guṇa substitution. By the rule "iḍḍhea" etc. [Pāṇini 4.1.45], the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
(777) *jāgurūkaḥ* [is formed by Pāṇini 3.2.165].
*Jāgarūkaḥ*. The word *āguḥ* ends in the fifth case (ablative). He explains it with the words *jāgarter iti*.

The form *jāgarūkaḥ* is established by rule itself and is not a *nipātana* (irregularly formed word), because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the suffix *ūk* would not carry over into the subsequent rule.

(778) *yajajapadaśāṃ yaṅaḥ* |3|2|166|. [The suffix] *uka* is applied after the roots *yaj*, *jap*, and *daś* when they take the intensive (*yaṅ*) affix. [Example: *yāyajūkaḥ*. After the root *yaj*, the *yaṅ* affix is added; then reduplication (*dvitva*) and so forth occur. By the rule *“īrgho’kitaḥ”* (Pāṇini 7.4.63), there is lengthening of the vowel in the reduplicated syllable. When the *a* is elided by the rule *“ato lopaḥ”* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the *y* is elided by the rule *“yasya halaḥ”* (Pāṇini 6.4.49). [Similarly: *jañjapūkaḥ*.

And so forth. The suffix *nuk* is applied by the rule beginning with "apajabhadahadaś-". As for the word *vāvadūka*, it will be discussed under the rule "ṭhulūkādayaśca". Mādhava, however, says: "Because of the very reading of *vāvadūka* in the *kurv-ādi* group, the suffix *ūka* is added to the reduplicated (*yaṅnta*) root *vad*."

(779) *sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.168. Regarding *sanāśaṃsa*: because of the mention of the suffix *an*, there is a reference to that which ends in it (*tadantagrahaṇam*). The roots *ṣaṇu* (in the sense of giving) and *ṣaṇa* (in the sense of sharing/partaking) are not included here; for [otherwise] the word *vijigīṣu* would have to be listed among the *garga*-type words.

From the reading [of the Dhātupāṭha]: the root *śas* in the sense of "desire" (*icchā*) is understood in the word *āśaṃs*, and not *śaṃs* in the sense of "praise" (*stuti*), because it is mentioned together with the prefix *āṅ*. (780) *vindu-ricchuḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.169.
The term *vinduriṣuḥ* [is used]; only the root *vid* in the sense of "knowledge" (*jñāne*) is intended here, not the others.

Similarly, only the root *iṣ* in the sense of "desire" (*icchā*) is intended, and not the roots *iṣ* in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*) or *iṣ* in the sense of "repetition" (*ābhīkṣṇye*), because of the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*) or due to specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*). As for the word *bindu*, however...
That which begins with a labial (*pavargīya*)—from the root *vidi* in the sense of "a part," the suffix *ku* is to be understood by virtue of its inclusion in the *mṛgayvādi* group.
(781) *kyāc chandasi* |3|2|170|. Regarding *kyāc chandasi*: the term *ya* is a general designation for *kyac*, *kyaṣ*, and *kyaṅ*.
The *Kāśikā* states that the suffix *u* occurs after the root *kyant* in the Vedic domain (*chandasi*) when expressing habitual action (*tācchīlya*) and so forth.
Because of the explanation "what is *ky*? and "the suffix *ya*," the *ya*-suffix of the *kaṇḍv-ādi* class is also included.
By this, [forms such as] *uraṇyavo ’ṅgiraso nakṣanta*, *aparyema saparyavaḥ*, and *yamasya yonau* [are accounted for].

The derivation of *śakunam bhuraṇyum* and so forth is established. The roots *turaṇa* (in the sense of haste), *sapara* (in the sense of honoring), and *bhuraṇa* (in the sense of supporting and nourishing) are recited among the *kaṇḍvādi* group. Now, how is it that Bhaṭṭapāda says: "For those who are free from envy accept the words of their friends"?
Haradatta maintains that the word *asūya* should be understood as occurring in [the list] beginning with *mṛgayu*. Regarding *sumnayu*:

from the word *sumna*, when the suffix *kyac* is applied, the suffix *u* is added after that which ends in it. Because of the prohibition "and not in the Veda, except for the word *putra*," neither the substitution of *ī* by "when *yac* follows" nor the lengthening by "in the case of *ṭha*, *kṛt*, and *sarva*" takes place.

(782) *ādṛgamahanajanaḥ kikinau liṭ ca* | Pāṇini 3.2.171. In the rule *ādṛgamahanajanaḥ*, the letter *ṛ* [in the term *ādṛk*] is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukha*), as in the rule *ṛdorap*; it is not the letter *t*. Therefore, because there is no subsequent *t*, the long vowel *ṝ* is also included by the expression *ṛ*. Examples: *taturiḥ*.

The ancient grammarians maintain that the forms *jaguriḥ* are derived from the roots *tṛ* (meaning "to swim" or "to cross") and *gṛ* (meaning "to swallow") by applying the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* according to the rule *bahulam chandasi*. However, in reality, [the word] *āditya* and so forth are qualifiers of the verbal root; the examples are merely illustrative expansions. [The suffixes] *kikinau* [are also used].

Only this much is intended to be expressed: namely, "liṭ. And thus says the Vārttika: "The suffixes *i* and *kan* are general [rules] in the Veda, because they are seen after roots such as *sad*. And it is illustrated in the Bhāṣya with examples such as *sehiḥ*, *nemiḥ*, and so forth. This being the case, even though *āt* is marked with a *t*-sign (to indicate its short *a* length), there is no [need for further restriction].

Intimating that there would be an elision [of the suffix], he says: "from one ending in /a/ or one ending in /ṛ/" (ādantādṛdantāt). In the phrase *babhrir vajram*, the accusative case is used because the genitive is prohibited by the rule *a loka-*. The suffixes beginning with *tiP* do not occur in place of *kviP* and *kvin*, because the extension (*atideśa*) in the rule *iḍvadi-* effects the transfer of grammatical operations while leaving the actual form (*svarūpa*) unaltered.

The presentation of the two Vedic sūtras is for the purpose of distinguishing the scope of the *vārttika* beginning with "dhāñ" and so forth regarding the vernacular language (*bhāṣā*). And although the root *gam* is not seen here in the *vārttika*, it has nevertheless been included because it is observed in the *dhātuvṛtti* and in some manuscripts of the *vṛtti*.
Regarding *jagmir*: there is elision of the penultimate vowel by the rule *amahanajaneḥ*. Regarding *jaghni*: there is the substitution of *ku* (guttural) by the rule *abhyāsācca*.

In the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after the roots *dhā*, *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *gam*, *jan*, and *nam*. Regarding *dadhri*: there is elision of the final *ā* by the rule *āto lopaḥ*.
Regarding *nemir iti*: there is the substitution of *e* for the radical vowel and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-lopa*).

There is an extension of the rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) to include *sāsahi*, *vāvahi*, *cācali*, and *pāpati*. In the case of *sāsahi* and so forth, when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided, there is the elision of the *ya* and the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-dīrgha*), as well as the absence of the *nīg* augment. This is according to the rule *nīg vañcu-*.

The meaning is that there is an absence of the augment *nīk* which would otherwise have been obtained by such rules as those cited. In the word *tṛṣṇak*, there is no *guṇa* substitution because the suffix is marked with the indicatory letter *ṭ*. In the suffix *najin*, the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation.
(Pāṇini 3.2.173: *śavandyorāruḥ* ("after the roots *śu* and *vandi*, the suffix *āru* is added").
"Krukanna-pīti": for this very reason, Amara states, "hīlu-bhīlu-bhīrukāḥ.
(784) [Pāṇini 3.2.175] *stheśabhāsapisakaso varac*: "īśvaraḥ"—here, by the rule *eḍvaśi*, there is the absence of *iṭ*. "peśvaraḥ"—from the roots *pisṛ* and *pesṛ*, meaning "to go."
*kasvara*: *kasa* means "to go.

(785) *bhrājabhāsadhurvidyautorjipṛjugrāvastuvaḥ kvip* [Pāṇini 3.2.177]. Regarding *bhrāj*: since it was stated that [the suffix] *kvip* occurs after roots ending in *ā*, this *kvip* is used here in the sense of "one who habitually does so" (*tacchīla*) and other such meanings. *bhrājṛ* means "to shine."

The roots *bhāsṛ* (to shine), *dhurvī* (to injure), *dyauta* (to shine), *ūrja* (strength and vitalization), *pṛ* (protection and filling), and *ju* (motion)—the latter being a root from the *sūtra*—are preceded by *grāvan*. [The root] *ṣṭuañ* (to praise) is preceded by *vibhrāj*.
In the word *vibhrāṭ*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *vraśca*; then the substitutions of *jaś* and *cart* follow. In the word *dhūḥ*, the elision of *r* occurs by the rule *rāl lopaḥ*.
Thus, there is the elision of *v*. By the rule "rṭhvorupadhāyāḥ," there is lengthening, resulting in *ūrg*. By the rule "oḥ kuḥ," [the *k* is substituted].
Due to the restriction "ātsasya," there is no elision of the final consonant in the cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). [The form] *pūḥ* is derived as follows:
by the rule "udoṣṭhyapūrvasya," there is the substitution of *u*, and by the rule "rṭhvoḥ," there is lengthening.

In the case of the roots *vac*, *pracch*, *yā*, *ata*, *stu*, *kaṭapru*, *ju*, and *śrī*, there is lengthening [of the vowel] and no vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). Thus, from *vac* we have *vāk* (speech) and from *pra-ach* we have *prāṅ* (facing east). Here, there is both lengthening and the absence of vocalization; for vocalization would otherwise have been required by the rules *vacisvapi-* and *rahijyāvayi-*. From *śrī* we have *śrīḥ* (fortune), as in "She who takes refuge in Hari is Śrī. However, according to the Eastern grammarians (*Prācāṃ*)...

The suffix *kvip* is cited here in the sense of the object (*karman*) in the rule "śrayantyetām iti. In that case, there is an obvious contradiction with the sūtra "kartari kṛt" (Pāṇini 3.4.67). As for the principle of "diversity" (*bāhulaka*), it is a resort only when no other way out exists. Regarding the statement "there is reduplication for the roots *dyauti*, *gami*, and *juhoti*," even though reduplication has been applied...
In this context, the designation "abhyāsa" (reduplication) is difficult to obtain, because it applies only to the reduplication of the sixth [syllable] due to proximity;

therefore, having raised the doubt that it does not apply to the eighth [syllable], he says: "because of the mention of *dṛśi*. In the word *didyaud*, there is the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the reduplication according to the rule "of *yu*, *svap*, and *pyai*. In *jagat*, [the substitution of *u* for *m* occurs] according to the rule "of *gam* before *kvip*."

In the rule *malope tuk*, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is conjoined by the word *ca* in the phrase *atra dve ca*; however, this long vowel does not apply to the roots *dyaut* and *gam*. This is because, due to the explicit mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) *acaśca* becomes applicable [restricting the substitution to a single substitute for a single vowel]. With the intention that a long vowel is possible only for the root *hu* when it ends in a vowel (*ajanta*), he says: *juhoterdīrghaśca*.
The term *juhūḥ* [is derived] from the root *hu-* [meaning "to sacrifice"], with lengthening of the vowel;
and by the word "and" (*ca*), doubling is also included. From the root *dhyai-* [meaning "to meditate"], there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*);
thus *dhīḥ*. [That is,] it meditates, hence *dhīḥ*. [This is formed] by the rule "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*).

[The suffix] *dīrgha* [is applied]. Now, one might object: "It is the person (*puruṣa*) who meditates, not the intellect (*dhī*); likewise, it is the person who sacrifices by means of this [intellect]. Since this is universally accepted, how then does the meaning you have stated cohere?
To this, Haradatta says: "When there is an intention to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the instrument (*karaṇa*), the suffix *kvip* occurs."

(786) *bhuvaḥ saṃjñāntarayoḥ* |3|2|179|. [The suffix *kvip* is applied] after the root *bhū* when a name (*saṃjñā*) or another [specific meaning] is intended. [Examples include] *dhanika* and so forth. The sense is that the rule does not apply to one who stands between two villages. And this is obtained by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of the word *dṛśi*. Now, if this is so, regarding the word *pratibhū*:
The term "saṃjñā" (name/designation) is the result [of the derivation]; since the form would be established by the word "aṃjñāyām" alone, what is the purpose of including the intermediate term?

On this point, they say: designations (saṃjñās) persist as long as the substance exists. However, the word "pratibhū" (surety) ceases upon the repayment of the debt even while that person still exists; thus, there is a difference between the two. [The compound] "śambhava" means one who brings about (bhāvayati) happiness (śam).

He says "Śambhu" by way of accepting the intended meaning: "with the [root] contained within. Others hold that he is called Śambhu because "śam bhavati," meaning he becomes the very nature of bliss. Mādhava, however, considers this etymology—derived from the sense of the ablative as in "he arises from this"—to be doubtful, due to the absence of the suffix *ḍu*.

(787) *dhaḥ karmaṇi ṣṭran* |3|2|181|. Regarding *dhaḥ karmaṇi*: the word *karmaṇi* is not a governing term (*upapada*). This is because, immediately following the rule *hvāvāmaśca*, it would have been sufficient to state simply *haḥ ṣṭran*; the fact that *karma* is mentioned separately—either by way of explicit statement or through interpretation—is the intended meaning. Thus he says:

Regarding the rule *karmaṇyarthe*: for this very reason, they explain that *dhātrī* means "she who is held" (*dhīyate*) or "she who is drunk" (*pīyate*), such as a wet-nurse (*stanadāyinī*), and so forth. (788) *dāmnīśasayuyujastutudasisicamihapatadaśanahaḥ karaṇe* [Pāṇini 3.2.182].
*dāmnī* (789). [The rule] *titutratathasisusarakaseṣu ca* (Pāṇini 7.2.9) applies.

Regarding *meḍhram*: by the rule *ṭh-ḍhaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *ṭha*; then there is the substitution of *dha* for *ḍha*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṭhu*, and the elision (*lopa*) of *ḍha*. Regarding *daṃṣṭrā*: although it contains the marker *ṣit*, [the rule still applies].

The suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply here, because it has been stated that *ṭhan* is not always present, as in the rule "*ṣitāṃ ṅīṣ*". Others, however, say that *ṭāp* applies due to its inclusion in the list beginning with *aj*. In the form *naddrī*, there is the substitution of *dh* by the rule "*aho dhaḥ*", and the substitution of *j* (jaśtva) by the rule "*haṣastathordho’dhaḥṭa*". In the sūtra, the word "*aśe*" refers to that which loses its nasal (*nalopin*).
The explanation is indicative: "In some instances, even when *kit* follows, the elision of *na* occurs after the root *daṃś*.

By this, from the root *daṃś* (to bite), with the suffix *lyuṭ*, the form *aśana* (teeth) is established. Nor should it be argued that, due to proximity, the elision of *na* would occur only before the suffix *ṣṭran*; for [the rule applies] to *un...* [etc.]...
Because of the rule "dantadaṃṣṭre" [Pāṇini 3.2.51].
(790) "The suffix *pu* is applied after the root *sū* when 'plow' (*hala*) and 'boar' (*sūkara*) are the objects" [Pāṇini 3.2.183].
"If that is the instrument," and so forth. By this, it is established that 'plow' and 'boar' are both the meanings expressed (*abhidheya*) and the subordinate terms (*upapada*).
[The objection] is rejected; the meaning is "the face," because that is the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in that very context—this is the intention.
(791) *Arti-lū-dhū-sū-khana-saha-cara itraḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.184. Regarding *arti-lū-dhū-sū*: only *dhū* in the sense of "shaking" (*vidhūnane*), belonging to the *kuṭādi* group, is understood here.
Because it lacks a continuous sequence [of phonemes]. For this very reason, in the case of *āṅkuṭ*, since the suffix is marked with Ṅ, there is a prohibition of guṇa, and thus *uvaṅ* is applied.
This is what he states: *dhuvitram*. (792) *puvaḥ saṃjñāyām* | Pāṇini 3.2.155.

*Pūvaḥ*: Both roots *pūṅ* and *pūñ* are included because there is no distinction between them. Since the term "instrument" (*karaṇa*) is understood from the previous rule, he says: "by which [the clarified butter] is poured. (793) *kartari carṣidevatayoḥ* | 3|2|186|.

"It should be [the suffix] *itra* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) and the seer (*ṛṣi*)," meaning "in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*) and the agent (*kartari*). Following the *Kāśikā*, he explains according to the respective order: "in the sense of the seer as the instrument. However, it is understood from the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the rule *kartari kṛt* that there is no such correspondence of order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*).
This concludes the section on primary derivatives (*pūrvakṛdanta*) as established in the *Śabdakaustubha*.
Now begins the section on the *uṇādi* suffixes. (979) Pāṇini 4.2.1: "That by which it is colored, provided it is a dye."
"Rakta" (dyed) [is formed] from a word ending in the third case that is semantically capable, with suffixes applied as prescribed.

[The derivation is: "that by which something is dyed. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, "rāga" means a coloring substance. Here, the meaning of the root *rañj* is the production of a different color in something white.

(980) *lākṣārocanāṭ ṭhañ* || 4.2.2 || [The suffix] *ṭhañ* [is added] after *lākṣā* and *rocanā*. However, the author of the *Vṛtti* has inserted into the sūtra *śakala* and *kardama*, which are found in the *Vārttika*. According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *śakala* refers to bark, a fragment, a colored substance, and a bark garment."
Regarding the addition of *sakala* and *kardama*: the author of the *Vṛtti* says "thus," whereas the intention in the *Bhāṣya* is that this has not been seen as a single unit.
Regarding *nīlyā an*: [the word] *nīlī*; *nīlī* is a specific type of medicinal herb. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*.

(981) *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ* |4|2|3|. [The rule] *nakṣatreṇa*: words denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) receive a suffix when, in the context of a compound (*vṛtti*), they denote the moon as being conjoined with that [mansion]. For example, *puṣyeṇa*, meaning "by [the moon] situated near Puṣya."
The meaning is "by the moon. In this way, common usage such as "the month of Pauṣa" is justified;

for although all days may be in conjunction with the Puṣya asterism, the conjunction with the moon situated near that asterism is not universal. Why [specify] "by an asterism"? [Consider: "a night joined with the moon."
What is time? The moon conjoined with Puṣya.

(982) *lub aviśeṣe* |4|2|4|. The elision (*lub*) applies when there is no specification; because the preceding sūtra is carried over here, it refers to that which is conjoined with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
The meaning understood is that when the time is apprehended as being non-specific, he says "sixty daṇḍas. The point is this:

although by the statement "today is Puṣya" a distinction is implied—namely, that it is not "yesterday" nor "tomorrow"—because the specific sub-divisions of the time consisting of a day and night are not understood, the [suffix] *lu* indeed occurs.

Because a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is resorted to in the rule "in a specific [case]" (*viśeṣe*), the elision (*lub*) does not occur in the case of "a day-and-night consisting of two *auṣas*," even though there is the cognition of a composite time consisting of sixty *daṇḍas*,
since there is also the specific [cognition] of its two constituent parts.

With the intention that [the distinction] is understood, he says: "If it were a specific [distinction], then not so. Regarding the example "Today is Puṣya," one should understand that "He shall invoke the Goddess under Āśleṣā" and "under Śravaṇā" are also examples. (983) *Dvandvāc chaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.2.6.

The suffix *cha* is applied after a copulative compound (*dvandva*). He provides an example for when there is a specific distinction—namely, *tiṣya* and so forth. However, when there is no such distinction, the example to be cited is *adya-rādhānurādhīyam*. Nor should it be argued that, because of the rule "in the case of a specific distinction" (*ubhayaviśeṣe*), the suffix *cha* should undergo elision (*lup*) just as the suffix *ām* does; for this is precluded by the principle of "an intermediate exception" (*madhye’pavāda*).

Because the suffix *aṇ* alone, having been previously established, is the one that undergoes that application. As for what was stated by the author of the Vṛtti—that "the suffix *cha* sets aside [the suffix *aṇ*] due to its posteriority"—that is not correct, because there is no possibility of both [suffixes] being simultaneously applicable. (9.84) *dṛṣṭaṃ sāma* | 4.2.7 | [The word *sāman* is treated as if it were *dṛṣṭa*].

The word *dṛṣṭa* [is used here]. In the sense of "seen by," suffixes such as *aṇ* and others should be applied after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyāntāt*), provided that it is a *sāman* seen by that person. In this sense, it should be stated that the suffix *aṇ* is optionally treated as having an indicatory letter *ṭ* (*ḍit*). Thus, in this sense: [the forms are derived].

The *Ślokavārttika* states: "When [the suffix] *aṇ* is prescribed after the word *sāman* or after a word denoting birth (*jāta*), it optionally becomes *ḍit* or is doubled; for the suffix *tīya*, *edīka*, and *na* do not apply, as they are taught to be like the suffix *aṅka* following a *gotra* name. The grammatical connection is: "In the sense of 'born,' that which is [the suffix] *aṇ* is optionally *ḍit*. One born under the asterism Śatabhiṣaj...

*Śātabhiṣaḥ*, *śātabhiṣajaḥ*. For here, the suffix *aṇ* which would otherwise apply by the rule "rāg-dīvyataḥ" is superseded by *ṭhañ* after a word denoting time; however, that [supersession] is countermanded by the rule "andhivelādi," so this is an example of a double application of *am*. Regarding the phrase "tīyāt": the meaning is that a suffix beginning with *tīya* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*).

*dvaitīyīkaḥ* (the second), *tārtīyīkaḥ* (the third). Regarding the rule *na vidyāyāḥ*: the meaning is that the suffix *īkaṅ* does not occur after a word denoting a branch of knowledge (*vidyā*) ending in *tīya*. For example: *dvitīyā vidyā* (the second science). Regarding the rule *gotrādaṅkavat*:
the suffix which occurs after a patronymic suffix (*gotra-pratyaya*) when used in the sense of a "mark" (*aṅka*) occurs even when it is seen in the sense of a "similarity" (*sāmānya*).
*ĀṬpagava* is derived from *dṛṣṭapagavaka*. Here, the suffix *vuñ* is applied according to the rule *otracaraṇādvuñ* [Pāṇini 4.3.126].
Regarding *vāmadevāḍḍaḷḍḍaḷai* [Pāṇini 4.2.9]:

[The word] *vāmadeva* is mentioned [in the sūtra]; this is for the purpose of excluding other meanings, etc. In the sense of "not that" (*atadarthe*), the rule *hyayatoścātadarthe* [Pāṇini 6.2.156] applies.

The meaning is that when the accent is prescribed for a word with the negative particle *nañ*, there should be no inclusion of the suffixes *ḍa* and *ḍḍa*. By the rule "hyayatośca," the final syllable of a subsequent member ending in *ya* or *ya* following *nañ* would otherwise be prescribed as udātta; this should not apply to the word *avāmadevya*.

However—the established conclusion is that the purpose of applying the marker *ḍ* is so that the accent may belong specifically to the word-form ending in the *avyaya* suffix. Nor should it be suspected that even when the marker *ḍ* is applied, the rule *yayatośca* would not apply because it is marked with *k*; for there is the principle: "When a term with a specific *anubandha* is mentioned, it does not include a term with a different *anubandha*."
This is because of the existence of the two *paribhāṣās*: "When that which possesses a specific *anubandha* is mentioned, that which does not possess it is not [included]" and [the converse].

And these two *paribhāṣās* are indicated right here by the fact that [the suffix] is marked with the *ḍit* designation. Among them, the purpose of the first is as follows: in the rule *pūraṇaguṇa*, when *tavya* is mentioned, *tavyat* is not included.

In the second [sūtra], however, there is the inclusion of *aṅ* and the exclusion of *caṅ*. The remainder is: "for the root *vī*, [the substitution of] *aḥ* occurs when *ah* follows. Thus, *aśvat*; but not when *caṅ* follows, as in *aśiśviyat*. (986) *parivṛto rathaḥ* || 4.2.10 || [The word *parivṛta* is used in the sense of a chariot].

Regarding the term *parivṛta*: the suffixes beginning with *aṇ* (i.e., *aṇ*, *cha*, *ñya*) occur in the sense of "surrounded by," provided that the one surrounded is a chariot (*ratha*). Since the complete covering is accomplished precisely by the cloth, blanket, or other materials used for the purpose of covering the chariot, [these suffixes] do not apply to items such as umbrellas (*chattra*).

With this intention, he says: "surrounded on all sides" (*samantādveṣṭita*). The sense is that the prefix *pari-* occurs in the sense of being on every side (*sarvato-bhāve*). (987) *Kaumārāpūrvavacane* | Pāṇini 4.2.13.

[The word] *kaumārā* [is used]; by "by him" (*tena*), [the previous rule] is excluded. Regarding the statement "never before" (*apūrva*), he says—namely, "in the state of being never-before-married" (*apūrvatve*)—that this is an indication where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary meaning. However, this state of being never-before-married (*apūrvatva*) is intended for the woman alone; as for the man, there is no insistence on whether he has been with a wife never before or not. Thus, [the term] *apūrvapati* means "one whose husband was not previously [married to another]. It is not "previously... [and so forth].
