The term *patiryasyāḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Regarding *kaumāraḥ patiḥ*: the suffix is applied to the word *kumārī* ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) to denote the husband (*upayantṛ*). Thus, *kaumāraḥ*. Here, however, the suffix is applied to the word *kumārī* ending in the first case (*prathamānta*) to express its own meaning (*svārtha*); by the rule *iḍhaḍhāṇñ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. Thus, *kaumārī*.
In this context, the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "herein" (*atra*) applies prior to the sūtra "tatrōddhr̥tā paurṇamāsī" (P.
4.2.20). From words denoting vessels (*pātra*) ending in the locative case, the prescribed suffixes shall be applied in the sense of "drawn out from that.
(988) P. 4.2.14: *tatrōddhr̥tam amatrebhyaḥ* ("Drawn out from that [vessel] when the source is a vessel").

Regarding the word *śārāva*: the author of the Vṛtti explains that it means "the remains of what has been eaten. Its meaning is "what is left over," based on the usage in the Kalpasūtras: "He cuts off [a portion], he does not offer the whole.
Regarding the locative case: the sense is that it functions as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) with respect to the action of placing.

(989) *sthaṇḍilāc chayitari vrate* |4|2|15|. From *sthaṇḍila*, when *vrata*— meaning a restriction prescribed by a scriptural injunction— is to be understood as a whole, a suffix is applied as prescribed after a word ending in the locative case, in the sense of one who lies down (*śayitṛ*).
(990) *saṃskṛtam* [is formed with the suffix *aṇ*] when the meaning is "prepared as food. 4|2|16.
For example, *aṣṭākapālaḥ*. Here, by the rule *vigorluganapatye*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ*.
(991) *śūlokhādyat*. 4|2|17. [The suffix *yat* is applied after *śūla* and *ukhā* to denote what has been prepared therein.]

From *śūla* and *ukhā*. The phrase "food items" (*bhakṣāḥ*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. How then is there the expression "the fire is *ukhya*"? For that [fire] is certainly not food. To this they say: the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the action itself because the word belongs to the *diśādi* group. (992) *dadhnas-ṭhak* [Pāṇini 4.2.18]. [The meaning is: The suffix *ṭhak* is added after the word *dadhi* in the sense of "prepared with. (For example: *dadhika*, "curd-prepared"). The suffix *ṭhak* is added after the word *dadhi* when it signifies something prepared by means of curds. (For example: *dadhika*, "a dish prepared with curds"). The suffix *ṭhak* is added after the word *dadhi* when it denotes an object prepared using curds as an ingredient. (For example: *dadhika*, "a preparation made from curds"). The suffix *ṭhak* is added after the word *dadhi* when it refers to a substance processed with curds. (For example: *dadhika*, "a food item cooked with curds"). The suffix *ṭhak* is added after

*dadhnaṣṭhaṭ* [Pāṇini 4.2.18]. *Dadhni* [is the locative case]. Here, the preparation (*saṃskāra*) is by means of salt and so forth, while the curd (*dadhi*) is merely the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). As for the suffix *ṭhak* which will be taught in the rule *saṃskṛtam* (Pāṇini 4.2.16) under the heading *rāga-vaha-taiḥ*, that should be understood as being introduced after a word ending in the third case. Therefore, [the suffix applies] even to that which is prepared with curd (*dadhnā saṃskṛtam*).
Only *dādhika*.

(993) *isusuktāntāt kaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.51. Regarding *isusuktāntāt*: although it was stated [in the previous rule] that “after *ā*,” it is understood here as “after one ending in *t*” by virtue of being a qualifier of the stem (*aṅga*).

Kaiyaṭa, on the rule *hasyekaḥ*, states that the inclusion of the word *anta-* [in Pāṇini’s rule *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ*] is for the purpose of ensuring that when a suffix is prescribed, the substitution of *ka-* does not occur for the *ṭha-* that follows that which ends in *t*.
He further explains that by the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* alone, the substitution of *ka-* for *ika-* would not take place; therefore, the mention of *anta-* is redundant.
Others say it is *śakyam*. Regarding *udaśvit*: from the root *śvi* with the suffix *kvip*, there is the augment *tuk*;

by the rule "uda for *udaka*," there is the substitution of *uda*; and here, due to a specific irregularity (*nipātana*), there is an absence of vowel-contraction (*saṃprasāraṇa*). (994) [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] in the sense of "that full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) occurs in this [month]. Pāṇini 4.2.21.

The suffix occurs after a word ending in the nominative case (prathamānta) in the sense of "this belongs to it" (*asmin / sā asyāsti*), provided that the meaning of the nominative-ending word is the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). This is because of the word "iti" [in the sūtra]; for that word follows common worldly usage. However, the author of the Vṛtti [explains] this in the sūtra itself.

The word *ajñāyām* has been interpolated [into the text]. Regarding *paurṇamāsī*: Haradatta and others maintain that in the *bahuvrīhi* compound *pūrṇo māso ’syāṃ tithau* ("the full moon is on this lunar day"), the suffix *aṇ* is applied in its own sense (*svārthika*) because it belongs to the *prajñādi* group. However, under the governing rule *adasmin vartate*, there is no *vārttika* stating "the suffix *aṇ* should be prescribed after *ūrṇamāsa*."
"It must be done"—this is his intention.

(995) *sā'sya devatā* |4|2|24|. Regarding *sā'sya*: the word *sā* was previously mentioned in connection with technical names (*saṃjñā*); therefore, it is mentioned again here by using the pronoun *sā*.
They call it a *kṛti* [suffix]. In this very sūtra, by means of a *nipātana*, the suffix *tal* is added to the word *deva* in its own sense (*svārthe*).

Regarding the term *mantrastutyā*: it means "by means of praise through a mantra. By the rule *hetistuśās...* and so forth, the suffix *kyap* is applied, followed by the augment *tuk* and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. As for the statement "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed *āgneya*": here, the Brāhmaṇa is not abandoned with reference to Agni.
The sense is that one should not suspect how this application [of the rule] occurs.

"Because it is subsequent, the initial *vṛddhi* [occurs]"—this solution is necessary for the case of *śrāya*, since the objection can be resolved by that alone; therefore, the capacity of the rule prescribing *it* (the substitution of *it*) has not been relied upon here.
(996) *Apomātrāpānnaptṛbhyāṃ ghaḥ* |4|2|27|. It means "the form *ṛpta*. The meaning is that for the word *apāt*, the form is *ṛpta*.
*Śatarudrāddhaśca*. [The compound] *śataṃ rudrāḥ*. The word *śata* signifies "infinite. *Saumiti*.
There is the elision of *ya* by the rule *ṭh-lopaḥ taddhitasya*.

(997) *rīṅ ṛtaḥ*. By the paribhāṣā "that which pertains to the formation of the stem" (*aṅgavṛtta-paribhāṣā*), the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *ṭh-akṛt-sārvadhātuka-aya-vid-dhiṣu ca* does not apply.

They say that the mention of "long" (dīrgha) is for the sake of [the rule] "yasyeti ca. The intention is that the prescription of *ruṅ* in the case of "itrīyati" has its own scope. As for "uṣasyam," the word *uṣas* is feminine and denotes the goddess who is the daughter of Heaven (*div*).

(998) *dyāvāpṛthivī-śunāsīra-marutvat-agnīṣoma-vāstoṣpati-gṛhamedhāc cha ca* | 4|2|32 | [The suffix] *cha* is added after *dyāvāpṛthivī*, *śunāsīra*, *marutvat*, *agnīṣoma*, *vāstoṣpati*, and *gṛhamedha*; it also serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffixes] *aṇ* and *yañ*. For example, *śunāsīrīyam* is derived from *śunaś ca sūraś ca*.

In the compound *dvandva-devatā-dvandvi*, the suffix *ānaṅ* is applied. Regarding *sunāsīra*, the author of the Vṛtti states that *śunaḥ* refers to Vāyu and *sīraḥ* to Āditya. Haradatta, however, says that others consider the word *sunāsīra* to be a designation for the qualities of Indra; thus, there is a mantra: "We invoke Indra Sunāsīra at this sacrifice."

Indra is called *marutvān* because he possesses the Maruts; [the hymn] belonging to him is *marutvatīyam*, and [the offering] for him is *marutvatyam*. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after *agni*, *soma*, and *varuṇa* [when forming patronymics]. *Vāstoṣpati* means the Lord of the Dwelling (*vāstu*);
it is correct by virtue of this very sūtra being an irregular formation (*nipātana*).
The words *vāstu* and *vāstū* denote the site of a dwelling; they are feminine. *Vāstoṣpatīya* and *vāstoṣpatya* refer to that which pertains to Vāstoṣpati.
*Gṛhamedhīya* and *gṛhamedhya* refer to that which pertains to the *gṛhamedha*. The word *gṛhamedha* ends in the vowel *a*;
thus says Āśvalāyana: "To the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhas."

(999) *kālebhyo bhavavat* |4|2|34|. From words denoting time (*kāla*), those suffixes which will be prescribed in the sense of "originating therefrom" (*bhava*) are extended by this rule to the sense of "whose deity is this" (*asya devatā*). The inclusion of the word *vat* is for the purpose of indicating complete similarity [of application].
Therefore, because it is prescribed by that [rule], it is only that [suffix] which occurs, and not another.
He illustrates this accordingly: *māsikam* and *prāvṛṣeṇyam*. [The former is derived] by the rule *māsād-aṇ-ṭhaṭhau*, and [the latter] by the rule *prāvṛṣa-eṇyaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *mātṛpitṛbhyāṃ pitari ḍāmahac* (Pāṇini 4.2.36), the suffix *ḍāmahac* is applied [to form *pitṛ-ḍāmaha*]. This has been stated in accordance with the *Vṛtti* and other such works. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated that the substitute *ānaṅ* and the suffix *mahac* are both introduced by way of a *nipātana* (irregular derivation); by this means, the *avagraha* (word division) is established.

The forms *averdugdhe*, *soḍhadūṣam*, and *arīsacaḥ* should be stated [with the dental sibilant]. This is because of the rule regarding the reading of the letter *s*. Otherwise, for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*), one would simply read the letter *ṣ*; such is the opinion established in the *Manoramā*. Others, however, maintain that even though the rule *avi-soḍham* prevents the substitution of the cerebral sibilant (*ṣatva*) in those cases, [the dental *s* must still be explicitly mentioned].

In cases such as *ṭhavidūṣam*, the substitution of *ṣ* would indeed occur; for there, since the force of the reading of the letter *s* has been exhausted by the necessity of establishing forms such as *ṭhavidūḥ* from the causative (*ṇyanta*) root with the suffix *kvip*, [the rule does not apply].
Therefore, in the examples cited by the author of the Bhāṣya, such as *avisoḍham* and so forth...
They say that this should be explained as being due to the force of the reading [of the sūtra] with the letter *sakāra*.
(1000) *tasya samūhaḥ* | 4.2.37. Regarding "the collection thereof" (*tasya samūhaḥ*), here [are applicable] *ṭhac*, *iṇ*, *aṇ*, *ṭhak*, *anudātāder añ*, and so forth.
He will explain later that suffixes such as *yañ* are applied word-for-word by rules such as "after *gotra*, *vuñ*" and "after *edārā* and others, also *yañ*.
And thus, [the word] ending in *gotra* is acute on the first syllable like *citavat*.

With the intention that the examples here are devoid of suffixes mentioned by specific rule (*pratipadokta*), he provides the following illustrations: *kākam*, *bākam*, and likewise *vārkam*. The words *kāka*, *baka*, and *vṛka* have their first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*) according to the *Phiṭ-sūtra* "for those preceded by *ku*" (*kupūrvam*). The meaning of the rule is that for words denoting living beings, those sounds preceding the *ka*-class (velar) which constitute the beginning [of the word] shall be acute. This is because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "the beginning [is acute] up to *śakaṭi*. As for the example *śaukam* cited in the *Vṛtti* and *Nyāsa*, that is to be disregarded; Haradatta and others maintain that since the word *śuka* is listed among the *khaṇḍika*-group, the suffix *añ* must apply there.

(1001) *bhikṣādibhyo’ṇ* | Pāṇini 4.2.38. From the group beginning with *bhikṣā*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Thus, *bhaikṣam*. Since it does not end in *cita*, the suffix *ṭhak* would otherwise have been expected. In the case of *gārbhiṇam*, since it begins with an *anudātta* vowel, the suffix *añ* would have been expected; for if that were present, there would be the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyaudātta*) and the elision of the *ṭi* suffix.

[The two suffixes] may [be applied]. Nor should it be argued that, because of the rule "hasyāḍhea" (Pāṇini 6.3.42), which prescribes the transfer of the masculine form, there would be no elision of the *ṭi* (the feminine suffix); for if that were so, the elision of *ṭi* would not occur even in the case of "hāstikam" (a herd of female elephants). Therefore, that [rule] is intended merely to remove the feminine suffix, and not [to apply the masculine form].
It should be understood that this [suffix] serves to indicate the form *rūpa*.

(1002) Regarding the rule *inaṇyanapatye* (Pāṇini 4.1.95): in the case of *yauvanam*, since the word *yuvati* begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*), the suffix *añ* would have applied; therefore, the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed here for its specific purpose.

The reading: the substitution of the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva), the removal of the suffix *tip*, and the preservation of the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule for *ṭhan*. Now, one might object:

since it is accepted in the rule *hasyāḍhea* that "the masculine substitution occurs when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *ṭha* and followed by a vowel is intended," the removal of the suffix *tip* must occur prior to the production of the *taddhita* suffix.

If it is argued that since [the word] *yuvati* is formed with the suffix *kanin* according to the rule "ini-yuvṛṣi," it is already established as having the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyaudātta*), and thus the suffix *aṇ* is indeed valid;

this is true. For this very reason, the inclusion of the word *yuvati* among the *mikṣā*-class (Pāṇ. 4.1.126) was rejected in the Bhāṣya. It is stated there: "In this context, by the force of the inclusion of the word *yuvati*, there is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*)."

The statement of the author of the *Vṛtti* is also refuted for this very reason. Anticipating the objection that, if this were so, usages such as *ārbhiṇam*, *yauvatam*, and *gaṇe* would not be consistent, he says:
"from [the base ending in] the present participle suffix *śatṛ*"—namely, *Pāṇini 7.1.1*: *yuvoranākau*.

In the compound *yuvoḥ*, the masculine gender is used according to the Vedic rule (*sautra*) for a collective dvandva. The vowel *u* is for the sake of pronunciation and does not bear the technical designation *it*. Consequently, in the forms *nandanaḥ*, *kārakaḥ*, *nandanā*, and *kārikā*, the suffixes *num* (prescribed by the rule regarding the *ugit*-class) and *ṅīp* do not occur. [The rule applies] "to the two nasalized [vowels]."
What [is the purpose]? [The word] *ūrṇāyuḥ* [serves as a counter-example].

Regarding the rule "by nature, before a vowel, [the suffix is elided] after *rājanya*, *manuṣya*, and *yuvan*": here, the mention of *rājanya* and *manuṣya* is redundant, because since these are conventional (rūḍhi) words, the elision of *ya* is already established by the rule "and [the suffix is elided] when it denotes a descendant" (*apatya*).
Because of the absence of attainment (*prāpti*). For this very reason, the mention of those two [suffixes] in the rule *otrokṣoṣṭra* is meaningful;

otherwise, they say that since the result would already be established by the mention of *gotra* alone, he would not have mentioned those two. The state of being young is *yovanikā*; the suffix *thañ* is applied because it belongs to the *manojñādi* group.

It should be stated that [the suffix] is also applied after *vṛddha*. Thus, *vārdhakam* [is formed]. If the usage *vārdhakam* exists even when referring to old age (*vṛddhatva*), then [the form] *yauvanikā* is due to its inclusion in the *manojñādi* group; from the *manojñādi* group, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied.
(1004) [Pāṇini 4.2.42: After *brāhmaṇa*, *māṇava*, and *vāja*, [the suffix *yañ* is applied] to denote a school (*adhyāyana*).
O young Brahmin, are these not all three elders? Let the suffix *yañ* be applied to whichever among them is the subject under discussion;

for there is no difference in form whether it is derived from "elder" (*vṛddha*) or from "one who possesses an elder" (*vṛddhādya*), since the resulting form is identical. Nor is there any difference in accent, as it would be udātta in both cases. As for a difference in gender, that is not even worth considering.

If it is argued: "Because [the word *apatya*] is neuter; and because of the inclusion of the term *apatya* in the rule *ṭhyañaśca*; and because the suffix *aṇ* will not be carried over [from the previous rule], since it is not marked with the svarita accent," that is true. However, the mention of *yan* is for the purpose of prescribing it even after bases that do not begin with a *vṛddhi* vowel. Regarding this, the Vārttika states a restatement of an established fact: [The Vārttika: *yan-vidhir apy avṛddhebhyo yathā syāt*. (Sāṅkāśyakaḥ, Kāmpilyakaḥ. [The Vārttika: *vṛddhād api bahvacaḥ*. (It should also apply after a base beginning with a *vṛddhi* vowel that has more than two syllables. An addition [to the rule] regarding "pṛṣṭhāt": namely, the word *pṛṣṭhāt*. *Pṛṣṭham* refers to a specific type of stotra (hymn). *Pṛṣṭhya* refers to a collection (*samūha*) of *pṛṣṭhas*. However, the expression “the *ṣaḍaha* [rite] is *pṛṣṭhya*” should be understood through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
(1005) *grāma-jana-bandhu-bhyas tal* [Pāṇini 4.2.43]. Regarding *grāma*, *jana*, and *bandhu*, the author of the Vārttika has inserted the word *asahāya* into the sūtra as well.
*anudātāder añ* [Pāṇini 4.2.44]: in cases such as *āpūpikam* and *śāṣkulikam*, [the suffix *añ* applies] because it is subsequent [in the order of rules].

With the intention that, according to the rule *ṭhaci hastidhenor ṅaḥ*, only the suffix *ṭac* applies, he cites *kāpotam* as an example in this sūtra. By the Phiṭ-sūtra *aghāvantaḥ*, the words *kapota* and *mayūra* are udātta on the middle syllable. Nor does [the rule] *akunīnāṃ ca laghu...* apply.

It should not be suspected that these two [suffixes] are acute on the first syllable, because it is explained there that "the light syllable preceding the final one is acute. (1006) *Khaṇḍikādibhyaś ca* | Pāṇini 4.2.45.
The rule for *khaṇḍikā* is stated to ensure the initial vowel is udātta and to prevent the application of the suffixes *aṭha* and *aṭhaka*.

(1007) *caraṇebhyo dharmavat* |4|2|46|. From the names of Vedic schools (*caraṇa*): whatever suffix is prescribed after a base in the sense of *dharma*, that same suffix applies to that base [in the sense of *kalpa*].
The meaning "in a collection" may also apply to *prakṛti*. For the suffixes *vuñ* and others will be taught after [the word] *caraṇa*;
therein, however, there is the Vārttika: "after *caraṇa*, [the suffixes are used] in the sense of *dharma* and *āmnāya*.
That too is indicated by this very rule of extended application (*atideśa-sūtra*). Examples include *kāṭhakam* and so forth.

The suffix *vuñ* is applied after [words denoting] lineages (*gotra*) and practices (*caraṇa*). For example, *chāndogyam*: here, the suffix *ñya* is applied by the rule "after *chandoga* and *aukthika*.

Regarding *yaccha*, these two [suffixes] occur according to their respective order. Regarding *ṭhag-aṇau*: the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the word *keśa* because it denotes a non-aggregated [collection].

(1008) *viṣayo deśe* |4|2|52|. Regarding the rule *viṣayo deśe*: he says that the word *asya* ("of this") is understood [from the previous rule], meaning "from a word ending in the genitive case. He explains the meaning of the term *viṣaya* as "that which is completely... [referring to the definition of territory]. From these two groups [beginning with] *bhauriki* and *ābhijit*...
These two suffixes occur respectively [with the words mentioned].

(1009) *Bhaurikyādyaiṣukāryādibhyo vidhalbhaktalau* 4.2.54: [The suffix] *vidhal* is applied after [the group beginning with] *bhauriki*, and *bhaktal* after [the group beginning with] *aiṣukāri*. For example: *bhaurikividha*, and so forth. Their neuter gender is established by common usage (*lokāt*).

(1010) *so'syādir iti chandasaḥ pragātheṣu* || 4.2.55 || The rule *so'syādir iti* [is explained as follows]: Here, "meter" (*chandas*) refers to those such as the *paṅkti*, which are based on the measurement of syllables. From a word denoting such a meter, ending in the nominative case, the suffix *ya* shall be applied in the sense of "that which begins with this," provided that it is a *pragātha*. [Note: The commentary clarifies that the suffix is added to a word in the nominative case expressing a meter, to form a name for a *pragātha* (a specific type of Vedic hymn) that begins with that meter.]

If it has an initial [verse], it is a *pragātha*. It is called a *pragātha* because it is "strung together" (*pragrathyate*). From the root *√granth* in the sense of "composition," the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object according to the rule *ṭhakkartari ca kārake*;
due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the letters *r* and *n* are elided. Others, however, say that it is a *pragātha* because it is "chanted" (*pragīyate*).
From the rule "ai śabde," they say [the suffix] *sthan* is added after the roots *uṣi*, *kuṣi*, and *gāti*. Where two verses are repeated to become three, that is a *pragātha*.
There is an addition for its own sake [to form the word] *traiṣṭubham*. The secondary derivatives (*vārthika*) follow their original base (*prakṛti*).
The sense is that [the suffix] is neuter, according to the maxim: "Words transcend [their original] gender and number.
(1011) *saṃgrāme prayojanayoddhṛbhyaḥ* |4|2|56|. [In the word] *saṃgrāme*, [one might object]: "But surely..."

Since the governing rule [of the previous sūtra] concerns the word *ratha* (chariot), the suffix would apply only to that which is first mentioned as signifying "battle," and not to the "purpose" (*prayojana*) or the "warriors" (*yoddhṛ*). Therefore, he says: *so'syeti* ("that belongs to this"). In this way, by means of the qualifier ending in the nominative case, the purpose and the warriors constitute the base (*prakṛti*). This is indicated by the word *asya* ("of this").
The intention is that it is possible to state that the battle constitutes the meaning of the suffix by means of qualifying the meaning of the suffix [itself].

Consequently, this is the meaning of the rule here: the suffix *aṇ* shall occur in the sense of the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) after words denoting the purpose and after words denoting the warriors, provided they end in the nominative case; and that [genitive] sense is the sense of the genitive case-ending.
Regarding the phrase *saṃgrāmaśced iti*:

[The rule] *tadasyāṃ praharaṃṇam iti krīḍāyāṃ ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.57) states that the suffix *ṇa* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case, provided it has "weapon" (*praharaṇa*) as its qualifying attribute, when the sense of the locative case is intended; that [suffix]...
If [the word] *cet* follows, the suffix *añ* has the sense of "that is the object of sport" (*krīḍā*). What is the instrument (*praharaṇa*)?
A garland (*mālā*) is the ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*) in this [sport]. Why "in sport"? A sword (*khaḍga*) is the weapon (*praharaṇa*) in this army.
(Pāṇini 4.2.58) *Sāsyāṃ kriyā*—the suffix *ñ* [is applied in this sense].

[The rule applies] after *ghañ*. [This is stated] because of the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes]. By this, the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) prescribed for the base (*aṅga*) by the rule "before *ñ* or *ṇ*" is established in the case of *yainaṃpāti*; the intention is that *śyenapāta* is also a word ending in *ghañ*. Why "after *ghañ*"? Consider: *śyenapatanam asyāṃ vartate* ("the falling of a hawk occurs in this"). Why "action" (*kriyā*)? Consider: *prākāro'syām* ("there is a rampart in this").

It occurs. Since "of this" (*asyām*) was already established by the context, the explicit mention of "in this" (*asyām*) is so that there may be the exclusion of [the application of] the rule for "in sport" (*līḍāyām*). For this very reason, he says: (1014) *śyenatilasya pāte ñe* | Pāṇini 6.3.71.
"On this lunar day there is the falling of the staff.

(1015) *tad adhīte tad veda* | Pāṇini 4.2.59. Regarding "he studies that" (*tad adhīte*): a suffix shall be applied after a word ending in the accusative case to denote one who studies or one who knows it.
The mention of "twice" (*dvis*) is for the purpose of prescribing [the suffix] individually with respect to both the one who has studied and the learned man.

Consequently, in subsequent cases, words such as *kratu* and *vasanta*, even when used figuratively for the texts that expound them, still trigger the application of the suffix in reference to the one who has studied them. Otherwise, since the study of those [texts] would be impossible [for the learned man], [the suffix would not apply].
The sense is that the suffix would apply only to words denoting sacrifices.

(1016) *Kratūkthādisūtrāntāṭ ṭhak* [Pāṇini 4.2.60]. [The commentary states: "From words such as *kratu* and *uktha*, etc. This refers to specific sacrifices; the actual word-forms themselves are not intended to be included, for if that were the case...

The word *kratu* would be recited only in the *uktha* and other such [lists], nor among the synonyms for sacrifice (*kratu*), because the word *yajña* is recited in the *uktha*-group; this is the sense. "Also in the sense of the performer" means "even in the sense of the one who performs. "Relating to the *agniṣṭoma*" refers to the word *agniṣṭoma*, which denotes a specific sacrificial form (*saṃsthā*).
"In the sacrifice established therein," meaning in the *nirūḍha* performance; "having that as its characteristic," and so forth—this means the *Prātiśākhya* which explains that [sacrifice].

From the word *uktha*, which primarily denotes the [sacrificial] hymn (*uktha*), the suffixes *ṭhak* and *gaṇa* are not desired. "They are not desired" means [the suffixes *ṭhak* and *gaṇa* are not applied].
The sense is that [the formation] does not occur because it is not so expressed.
It should be stated that [the suffix] does not follow *aṅga*, *kṣatra*, *dharma*, or those preceded by *tri* when ending in *vidha*.

Regarding *trividha*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "he studies three sciences" (*tisro vidyā adhīte*), since it is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), [the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied].
It should simply be ‘rividyaḥ’, because of the application of elision (luk) according to the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*.
[The word] ‘ākhyāyikā’ refers to a composition consisting of prose and verse.
The meaning is "a specific work.

It should be stated that there is elision (*luk*) of the initial portion of words beginning with *sarva* and those beginning with *sa*. Regarding the mention of "beginning with *sarva*" (*sarvādeḥ*): although the rule would have been established by the word "initial" (*ādeḥ*) alone, the inclusion of *sarva* is for the purpose of making known the *paribhāṣā* (metarule) concerning meaningful elements (*arthavat*). [The example is] "with the Vārttika" (*savārtikaḥ*).

The meaning is: "He has studied up to the Vārttikas. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of "limit" (*anta*). The substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs by the rule "In an *avyayībhāva*, except when denoting time. [Regarding the suffixes: *ikan* after a word ending in *pada*, and *ṣikan* after *śata* and *paṣṭi*; and *ṣikan* after *pathin*. As for *ikan*: the word *pada* is the final member (*uttarapada*) [of the compound].
The meaning is that the word *pathin* which follows after the words *śata* and *ṣaṣṭi* [forming a compound] should be designated as having the suffix *thak*. Thus, *śatapathikaḥ*.
However, the author of the Vṛtti, having supplemented the Vārttika with the word "optionally" (*bahulam*), provides the form *ātapathaḥ*.
Thus, although [the suffix] *aṇ* has been cited, it is not seen in the Bhāṣya. He demonstrates the result of its being marked with the indicator *ṣ*—namely, the form *śatapathikī*.
(1017) Pāṇini 4.2.62: *anubrāhmaṇād iniḥ*.

"Regarding the phrase 'to avoid contradiction': this sūtra has indeed been rejected in the Bhāṣya; however, according to that [Bhāṣya] perspective, it should be understood that the suffix *aṇ* will be applied, or else that it does not apply due to non-usage (*anabhidhāna*).
(1018) Pāṇini 4.2.63: *vasantādibhyaṣṭhak*.

Regarding *vasantā*: one may recite the *vasantā* hymns and so forth within the *uktha* and other sections, or one may recite the *uktha* and other sections within the *vasantā* and other sections; thus, either one can be omitted. Regarding *atharvāṇam*:

that which was proclaimed by Atharvan is called "Atharvan" through figurative usage (*upacāra*). Alternatively, under the governing rule “proclaimed by him” (*tena proktam*), [the suffix is applied] after the word *ṛṣi*.
The suffix *lug* (elision) should be stated. Having cited "Vasiṣṭha," "Viśvāmitra," and "Anuvāka" as examples, one may also cite "Atharvaṇa.
This is correct because of the statement in the Bhāṣya: "atharvā," "atharvaṇaḥ.
(Pāṇini 6.4.165): *gāthividathikeśigaṇapaṇinaśca*.

Regarding *gāthividathi*: although [the preservation of the original form] is established by the rule "ṭhinaṇyanapatye" (Pāṇini 6.4.174), this [sūtra] is commenced for the sake of preserving the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) even when the suffix *aṇ* denotes a descendant (*apatya*). Examples: *gāthinaḥ*, *vaidathinaḥ*, *kaiśinaḥ*, *gāṇinaḥ*, *pāṇinaḥ*.

(1020) *ṇyakṣatriyārṣañitoyūni lugaṇiñoḥ* | Pāṇini 2.4.58. [The rule states: "In the case of a patronymic suffix (*yuvan*) derived from a word ending in *ṇya*, *kṣatriya*, or an *ārṣa* name ending in *añ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*. Example: *kauravya*. [This is formed] by the rule *urvādibhyo ṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.91). From that, there is elision of *iñ*.
Thus, *kauravyaḥ putraḥ* ("the son of Kauravya"). [Objection: But surely the word *kauravya* is listed among the *tikādi* group; and thus...

If it is argued that for *Kauravyāyaṇi* the suffix *phañ* should apply and not *iñ*, that is true; however, in that context, what is listed is a form ending in *ṇya*, which is prescribed by the rule “*uru-ādibhyo ṇyaḥ*” for a *kṣatriya* gotra. But in the present case, it must be understood that the form ends in a suffix denoting a *brāhmaṇa* gotra. Thus, [the example] is *Śvāphalka*.

In *ṛṣyaṇdhake*, there is the suffix *aṇ*. From that, there is the elision (*luk*) of *iñ*; thus, *śvāphalkaḥ* is the son. In *vāsiṣṭhaḥ*, there is *ṛṣyaṇ*. From that, there is the elision of *iñ*; thus, *vāsiṣṭhaḥ* is the son. In *taikāyaniḥ*, [the suffix is] *phiñ* according to the rule *ikādibhyaḥ phiñ*. From that, there is the elision of *aṇ*; thus, *taikāyaniḥ* is the son. [The same applies to] *vāmarathā*.

Thus [it is formed]. The suffix *ṇya* is applied because the word belongs to the *kurv-ādi* group. Then, setting aside the suffix *cha* which would apply after a *vṛddha* stem, the secondary suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule “*aṇvādibhyo gotre*” (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.104). Regarding the word “thus”:
the meaning is that it is by the rule cited as “*ṇyakṣatriyārṣe-*” (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.58). [The suffix] is specifically the *ṛṣyaṇ* [suffix]; this applies to the word *pāṇina*.

The intention is that *aṇ* is indeed the general rule (*utsargika*). But is this not in contradiction with the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the sūtra "or, in the case of another sapinda"? Here, the masculine descendants of Atri are "Atris. [The suffix] *ḍhak* applies by the rule "inaśca aniñaḥ. From that which ends in it, for the secondary descendant (*yuvan*), [the suffix] *iñ* applies by the rule "ata iñ. Of that—

They say that because it is stated, "there is elision [of the suffix] when [the patronymic denotes] a non-Kṣatriya," and "there is also elision of the suffix *ḍhaka* when [it denotes] contempt for Atri and Mṛgu," there is elision of *ṣa*. However, if one were to accept only the *aṇ* suffix from the rule "ṛṣya-andhake," then since *ḍhaka* would not be included, there would be no elision of the subsequent *iñ* suffix. But in reality, [this applies to] "the son of Akṣī."

It should be understood that the correctness of this [form] is established by the usage in the Bhāṣya, "pāṇineḥ. Regarding the phrase "and [the suffix] iñ": the intention is that even when there is elision (luk) by the rule "yūni luk," it remains an item ending in iñ by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the technical application of a suffix). As for the phrase "the iñ which [is applied] in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*)," it will be stated therein that "here, *gotra* is technical according to the science [of grammar], not worldly."

The meaning is as follows: regarding the word *svara* [in the rule], if there is no elision (*luk*), the suffix-accent (*pratyayasvara*) would result in an oxytone (*antodātta*) form, and in the feminine, the suffix *ṅīp* would be applied.
However, when elision (*luk*) occurs, the vowel *u* becomes udātta, and the suffix *ṭāp* is established; this is the intended sense. (1021) *sūtrāc chaḥ kopadhāt* 4.2.65.

Regarding the word *aṣṭakam*: by the rule "after a numeral, [the suffix *kan* is added] in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), a collection (*saṅgha*), a sūtra, or a lesson (*adhyayana*)," the suffix *kan* is applied after a numeral that does not end in *ati* or *śat*.
It should be stated that [this applies] when the base is a numeral; thus, it is called *saṅkhyāprakṛtika*. What is meant by "when the base is a numeral"?

[This refers to] a suffix whose base is a numeral, etc. Regarding the term *kālāpaka*: from the word *kalāpin*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "taught by" (*prokta*). By the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for "one who is not a student of sacred knowledge" (*abrahmacārī*), there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). From that [base ending in *aṇ*], the suffix *ayaṇ* is applied in the sense of "its recitation" (*tadadhīte tadveda*). That [suffix *ayaṇ*] is elided by the rule "there is elision (*luk*) after a suffix marked with *ṛ*. [The resulting form is] *kālāpānām āmnāyaḥ*.

Now, [the suffix] *vuñ* is applied after [words ending in] *caraṇa* by the rule *atha ‘otracaraṇādvuñ*. Thereafter, by the rule *adhyetṛveditṛṇo na luk*, there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix. There is a distinction regarding accent (*svara*) and the feminine form. (1022) *cchandobrāhmaṇāni ca tadviṣayāṇi* || 4.2.66 || And the *chandas* (Vedic texts) and *brāhmaṇas* (liturgical treatises) are restricted to that [subject matter]. 4.2.66.

Regarding the term *chandobrāhmaṇāni*: here, the word *proktāt*, which was previously followed by jumping (i.e., from a distance) as a fifth-case form (*proktāt*), is transformed into a plural nominative form (*proktebhyas*) because it must stand in grammatical apposition with *chandobrāhmaṇāni*. Furthermore, the word *prokta* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote a suffix that conveys the sense of "spoken by" (*prokta*).
With this intention, he says: "ending with the suffixes previously mentioned. Regarding the phrase "having that as their object":
by the word "that" (tat), the suffix denoting the student or knower is referred to.
The word "object" (viṣaya), however, here signifies non-difference, and not...
The meaning here, intending that [the word] denotes a place, is that it should not be used without a suffix (*pratyaya*).

The sense is that this rule is for the purpose of restriction, since unrestricted usage would otherwise apply—as in the cases of *pāṇinīyam* and *pāṇinīyāḥ*. Although [the desired result] is established by the mention of *chandas* alone, the mention of *brāhmaṇa* is included...

This is for the purpose of restricting that [suffix] to Brāhmaṇas who were proclaimed from ancient times. Therefore, it is not the case here—namely, that Yājñavalkya and others are "new" (nūtana) in relation to Pāṇini; such is the usage of the authors of the Vṛtti.
The particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*). By this, [the suffix applies to] Kāśyapins, Kausikins, and so forth.
Thus, even in this grammatical rule (*kalpa*), its being the object [of the suffix] is established.

When it is stated, “by the two sages Āśvalāyana and Kauśika,” the suffix *ṇini* is applied, and there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *adhyetraṇ*. Why [is the restriction] “Vedic meters (*chandas*) and Brāhmaṇas” stated? [To exclude: “the Pāṇinian grammar” (*pāṇinīyaṃ vyākaraṇam*).
Thus ends the section on roots meaning "to be attached" (*rakta*) and so forth in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
Now, the *rudh*-class roots. (326) *Rudhādibhyaḥ śnam* | Pāṇini 3.1.78. [The suffix *śnam* is added after the roots beginning with *rudh*.]

The suffix *śnam* is added after roots such as *rudh*. Although it is a suffix (*pratyaya*), because it is marked with the indicator *m*, it is placed after the final vowel of the root. The purpose of its designation as a suffix (*pratyayasaṃjñā*) is that the *ś* becomes subject to the technical term *it*. However, the pronunciation of the *ś* is for the sake of distinguishing it in rules such as "the elision of *a* after *na* and *as*" (*nasorallopaḥ*) and "the elision of *n* after *na*" (*nānnalopaḥ*), and not for the sake of its being designated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

Because there is no result [from applying the rule]. Nor should it be suspected that the result is the prohibition of *guṇa* for a *sārvadhātuka* suffix ending in *ṅ*, because a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *ik* lacks the status of being an *aṅga*. As for *aruṇaḥ*: after the suffix *sip*, the substitution of *ru* optionally applies by the rule *ṭaśca*. The same applies to *abhinaḥ*. [The root] *ucchﬁadṛ*: the letter *u*.

The suffix *ktvā* is for the purpose of making the augment *iṭ* optional. [Examples: *cchﬁatvā*, *ccharditvā*. In the case where *iṭ* is present, because the prohibition of *kit*-status applies by the rule *a ktvā se ṅit* (1.2.18), *guṇa* substitution occurs.
(327) *śnānnalopaḥ* | 6.4.23. [This rule states: There is elision of the *n* of the affix *śnā*.
"There is elision of *n* after [an affix] marked with *ś* or *ñ*. Its primary example is: *anakti*, *bhanakti*.

He states that the term "after *śn*" refers to the inclusion of *śnam* (the affix *śnu*), which has the indicatory letter *a* dropped; thus he says, "of what follows *śnam*. And in this way, in the case of the word *viśnaḥ* derived from the roots *yaj* and *yāc* by adding *ām* with the augment *nuṭ*...

Regarding the word *viśnānām*, they say that because of the application of the two paribhāṣās—the one concerning "that which is taught by its specific definition" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*) and the one concerning "the mention of a suffix" (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*)—there is no possibility of the elision of the *n* at all. In *indhé* and *indhse*, the *n* of the *śnam* suffix undergoes *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa*; however, the elision of the *n* by the rule *aniditām* does not occur.

Because the elision (*allop*) is either considered as not having taken effect (*asiddha*) by the rule "that which is *asiddha* here [is treated as not having occurred]," or because of the status of being *sthānivadbhūta*, [the substitution does not apply]. The root *bhañj* (to break):

the inclusion of the initial vowel *ā* is for the sake of the nasalization (*natva*) in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). *Bhagnaḥ*. The root *bhuj* (in the sense of protecting, etc.): it will be stated that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by the rule "after *bhuj*, except in the sense of protecting. *Bhuṅkte*, *bhuñjāte*, *bhuñjate*.

(328) *tṛṇaha im* | Pāṇini 7.3.92. Regarding *tṛṇaha im*: although it would have been sufficient to state *ṛhū*, the inclusion of the entire *śnam* [the suffix *na* with the augment *ś*] is for the purpose of preventing the replacement of *śnam* by *im*, which is prescribed as a specific rule. Furthermore, this does not apply to the root *tṛh* belonging to the Tudādi class.

One might suspect that [the rule] is intended solely for the purpose of exclusion; however, this is not the case because the subsequent *pit* (sārvadhātuka) beginning with a consonant (*hal*) is separated by the *vikaraṇa*. From the rule "ābhyastasyāci pitī" [6.1.33], the word "pitī" is understood to carry over, and from "uto vṛddhiḥ" [7.2.114], the word "halī" carries over. Thus he says: "when preceded by a consonant (*halādi*)."

Regarding the term *pitī*: according to the conclusion established by the author of the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam," the word *halī* does not carry over [from the previous rule], but rather *pitī* itself does indeed carry over. Consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *ṛṇḍha*. Nor, even if *halī* were to carry over, would there be an over-extension in the case of *tṛṇahāni*.

This must be stated [as a rule], because of the continued application of the prohibition "not before a vowel" (*aci na*). *Undī* means moistening or becoming wet. *Añjū* means manifestation or discernment. *Mrakṣaṇa* means anointing or oiliness. (329) *Añjeḥ sici* [Pāṇini 7.2.71].

The meaning is that after the root *añj*, there is always *iṭ* [augment] in the *sic* [aorist]; thus, the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) does not follow here. Why "in *sic*"? Consider *aṅktā*. From the root *pṛcī*: because it is marked with *īt*, there is no *iṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* (past participle).
In the rule *ṭhapṛkta ekāl...* (*Pāṇini 1.2.41*), the word *apṛkta* is preceded by the negative particle *nañ*.
Thus ends the section on the *rudh*-class roots in the *Tattvabodhinī*.

Regarding *śeṣe* and *lakṣaṇe*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "remaining" (*śeṣa*) and "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), as well as in meanings such as "grasping" (*grahaṇa*), "crushing" (*kṣuṇṇa*), and others not included in subsequent rules.

The meaning is that it is prescriptive. Now, an objection may be raised: first, the *lakṣaṇa* (definition) is redundant, since visual perception and the like are established by the rule "this belongs to that," and grinding-stones and the like are established by the rule "the prepared [grains] are for consumption. Likewise, the *adhikāra* (heading) is also redundant.

To explain: the purpose [of the rule] is either the exclusion of the suffixes beginning with *ṭa* (i.e., *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ṭhañ*, *ṭyaṇ*, *ṭyaP*) ending in *ṭyaL* (*ṭyaP*), which would otherwise apply to the meanings up to the four meanings beginning with "offspring" (*apatya*) under the heading of "eligibility" (*adhikāra*), or the complete inclusion of the meaning "born from" (*jāta*) and so forth. Of these two, exclusion is certainly not the purpose; for [words such as] *ārdraka* and *śāla* are already included [in the list] by virtue of their recitation in the *utkara* group.

This is because of the metarule (*jñāpaka*) stating that "gha" and other suffixes do not apply when [the base] ends in *prācīna*. Otherwise, since the form would already be established by the rule "vṛddhāc chaḥ," the reading of that [specific rule] would result in redundancy. Nor is the completeness of meaning the purpose, because [the forms] are already established prior to the section on "born from" (*jāta*) simply by the force of their placement [in the text].

Because of that gain: if *gha* and the other suffixes were to apply only in the sense of "born" (*jāta*) when [that sense] is proximate, then in the subsequent senses such as "originating therefrom" (*bhava*), where specific limits are desired—as in the case of the rule *rāg-dīvyatoḥ*—only *aṇ* and the like would be prescribed; therefore, immediately after the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "born,"...
If it is argued that this sūtra is redundant because words such as *ṭhrāṣṭrāvārapārāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.96) should also have been recited along with *ṭhrāvṛṣaṣṭhaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.95) and others,

it is replied: this is for the sake of the meaning that will be stated [in the subsequent sūtra], namely, "A secondary (*śaiṣika*) suffix of the same form as a preceding secondary suffix does not apply."

The section on *śeṣa* (the remainder) is necessary for the sake of obtaining the [specific] objects of application. This very section on *śeṣa*, which is composed to indicate the specific operations (*kāryaviśeṣa*) prompted by the *śaiṣika* suffixes, makes known the verse beginning with "from those ending in *aiṣika*, the suffixes expressing possession (*matubarthīya*) [are applied]," and so forth. And this verse is as follows:

This [term *pratyaya*] was read in the Bhāṣya both in the rule for the suffix *matup* and in the rule for the desiderative (*sann*) suffix; however, since it is read here specifically in the context of the desiderative, it will be explained in that very place. Furthermore, this governing heading (*adhikāra*) is necessary to exclude suffixes such as *gha* and others from meanings such as "descendant" (*apatya*) and so forth. Nor can it be argued that this is already established by the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*).

It must be stated that the fault remains as it was, because the indicator (jñāpaka) still depends on a specific condition. Furthermore, there is the possibility of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) such as: "If the suffix *cha* were applied after *ārdraka* and others, it would apply only in the sense of the four *arthas*.
This being the case, in examples such as *cākṣuṣam*, [the suffix is used] to convey a cognition characterized by the mode (*prakāra*) of being grasped by the eye (*gṛhyamāṇatva*), and so forth.

The fact that this [sūtra] also functions as a prescriptive rule (*vidhāyaka*) is easily stated; such is the direction [of the argument]. Regarding the phrase "even from a compound" (*vigrahītād api*) and so forth:
this is merely a statement, because in the sūtra there is a specific pronunciation for the sake of the application of the respective order (*yathāsaṅkhya*).
(1038) *kattryādibhyo ḍhakac* 4.2.95.

"Three things are contemptible. Here, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is also easily explained; in this very case, by virtue of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), the substitution of *kad-* for *ku-* occurs. As for the statement "there is an addition [of the suffix] *tra* when *ad-* is substituted," that should be rejected.

(1039) Pāṇini 4.2.96: *kulakukṣigrīvābhyaḥ śvāsyalaṅkāreṣu*. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after these words to form a *tatpuruṣa* compound denoting a descendant, provided they signify a dog, a mouth, or an ornament respectively.]
*kulyāyā yalopaśca* is a *gaṇa*-sūtra. [The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the word *kulyā*] with the elision of the *ya*. One born in a *kulyā* is *kauleyakaḥ*. [Other examples include:
*katri*, *umbhi*, *kuṇḍina*, *māhiṣmatī*, and so forth.
(1040) *dakṣiṇāpaścātpurasastyak* 4.2.98. [The suffix *tyak* is applied after the words *dakṣiṇā*, *paścāt*, and *puras* to denote direction.]

“Dakṣiṇāpaścāt” [is an indeclinable]. The sense is that it is so because of its association (sāhacarya). And thus, in the case of “ākṣiṇātya,” one should understand that there is no suspicion at all of the application of *puṃvadbhāva* by the rule “arvanāmno vṛtimātre. As for “pāścātya,” how then [is the form] “aścātanaiḥ kaścana” [justified]?
Regarding the phrase "being pushed," it should not be argued that since the word *paścāt* denoting direction or place has its scope [for the suffix *ṭac*],
the suffixes *ṭaḷu* and *ṭaḷul*— which denote time— would supersede it due to their higher status (paratva).
For the supersession of *ṭaḷu* and *ṭaḷul* by the suffix *ḍimac* in the case of *agrādipaścāt* would be unavoidable.
True. The expression "those who weave behind" (*paścāttanvanti paścāttanāḥ*) may be explained in some way [as a compound].
(1041) *Kāpiśyāḥ ṣphak* | 4.2.99. Regarding *kāpiśyāḥ ṣphak*: the suffix *ṣphak* shall be applied after the word *kāpiśī*. Because it is marked with *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added.
He says this: "kāpiśāyanī" (wine from Kāpiśī).
(1042) *raṅkor amanuṣye ’ṇ ca* | Pāṇini 4.2.100: "After *raṅku*, when not referring to a human being, [the suffixes *aṇ* and *cha* are applied]. *Raṅku* is a country; from that [country]...
When [the suffix] *rāga* is used as a verb root (*divyati*), the suffix *aṇ* is first applicable. That being set aside, the suffix *vuñ* is applicable by the rule *avṛddhādapī*.

That too being set aside, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applicable by the rule *ordeśe*. However, that [suffix *ṭhañ*] is set aside by *opadhādaṇ*. Even after that, since the suffix *aṇ* [from the class] *kacchādi* would apply by virtue of its higher status, this [present rule] applies.

The suffixes *ṣpha* and *gaṇa* are prescribed [here]. Since the suffix *aṇ* would already be established by the fact that the word begins with the letter *ka*, Kaiyaṭa states that the inclusion of the word *saṅku* among the *kacchādi* group is for the purpose of prescribing the suffix *vuñ* in the rule "for non-human beings and for things located therein" (*manuṣyat-thayor vuñ*).
For this very reason, he says: "a human being who is *rāṅkava*. In some places, however, it is written as "*rāṅkava*."
This is read [in some manuscripts], but that is a scribal error. It might be argued as follows:

"The mention of *amanuṣya* (non-human) here is redundant, because the suffix *vuñ* by way of an exception (*apavāda*) would subvert both *ṣpha* and *gaṇa*, resulting in the application ending up restricted to *amanuṣya* alone. Furthermore, the mention of *aṇ* is also entirely redundant, since that [suffix] is already established by its inclusion in the *kaccha*-group."

Regarding this, the author of the Kāśikā says: "This is not a simple negation (prasajyapratiṣedha), but rather an exclusion (paryudāsa); therefore, the suffix *ṣpha* is prescribed only for living beings distinct from humans. Consequently, in the case of *rāṅkavaḥ kambalaḥ* ('a woolen blanket'), *ṣpha* does not apply. Furthermore, the mention of *aṇ* [in the rule] is so that the suffix *aṇ* may not be superseded by *ṣpha*, which is specifically prescribed for a particular case."
[The suffix] *kri* is used [in this sense]. However, in the Bhāṣya, both of these [rules] have been rejected by accepting the suffix *ṣphak* even for non-living beings (*aprāṇin*).
(1043) Pāṇini 4.2.101: *dyuprāgapāgudakpratīco yat*.
The meaning is that in the sūtra *dyauprāgapākpratīco yat*, there is a designation by means of the substitution *u* for *v* (as in *iva u*).

*Apācī* refers to the southern direction. It is established that the second letter is the phoneme *pa*, and not the dental-labial [pa], because it is observed as such in passages such as *yad indra prāgapāg udag*.
In the *Manoramā*,

some— relying on the occasional reading of "avācī" with a dental labial (ṭavarga) in the Amarakośa entry "rācyavācīpratīcyāstāḥ"— read "avāc" even in the sūtra and cite "avācyam" as an example; however, in the Veda, it appears as "rāgapāk" by way of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).

Their intention is that the letter *pa* [is substituted] for the letter *va*. Words beginning with *prāk* and ending with *astāt* are indeclinables (*avyaya*), while those different from them are non-indeclinables (*anavyaya*); both types are included here without distinction. How then is the form *“saṃskārāḥ prāktanā iva”* [justified]? To this they say: since the word *prāk* here denotes time, the suffix *yat* [is applied].
Because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], *ṭyaṇ* and *ṭyuṭyul* should be understood as superseding [the previous suffixes].

(1044) *varṇo vuñ* | 4.2.103 | *varṇo vuñ*. [The word] *varṇukaḥ* is formed by adding *vuñ* in the sense of "not far from" (*adūrabhave*), because [the base] belongs to the *suvāstu* group, which takes the suffix *aṇ*.

The suffix *luP* is elided after the word *anu* when the sense is "in the vicinity. This occurs only after *am*, *iha*, *kva*, *tas*, and *atre*. Thus, [we have] *amātya*. Here, the word *amā* signifies "proximity" and belongs to the *svarādi* group; the meaning is "one who exists in the vicinity (*amā*) of [the master]."

(1045) Pāṇini 8.3.101: *hrasvātādau taddhite* | This rule is commenced because the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] would otherwise not apply due to the condition of being at the end of a word (*padānta*). However, the inclusion of the term "beginning" (*ādi*) is redundant, since the desired result is already established by the principle *yasminvidhis tadādāvgrahaṇam*. Why "after a short vowel"? Consider: *gīstarām*.

[The suffix *tara*] is added after [a word ending in] *dhūs*. What is the purpose of that? [In the example] *sarpiḥ sādbhavati*, [the suffix is not applied]. What is the purpose of [the condition regarding] a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)? [In the example] *sarpistarati*, [the suffix is not applied]. It should be stated that there is a prohibition for [a word] ending in the root *iṅ*. [Examples are: *bhindyaustaram* and *dūrādetyaḥ*. [The form] *dūrādetya* means "having come from afar" and so forth.
Regarding *autarāha*: it is called *autarāha*. Here, one should understand that there is an acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

However, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied after the suffix *āhi* by the rule *uttarācca*, and because of the specific enumeration [in Pāṇini 4.1.85] under *ameha*, the suffix *tyap* is absent, then the word *autarāha* has the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) in the feminine.
The addition of *ṅīp* is the specific distinction.
(1046) *Aiṣamo-hyaḥ-śvaso ’nyatarasyām* | 4.2.105.
[The word] "to be mentioned" refers to [the suffixes] *āyañ* and *ciram*, etc., as the remainder [of the rule]. [The word] "will be mentioned" refers to...
In the rule *‘vasaṣṭuṭ ce’ti* (Pāṇini 4.2.104), [the following applies]: *dikpūrvapadād asaṃjñāyāṃ ñaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.107).
Regarding the phrase *dikpūrvapadād asaṃjñāyām*, the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative due to its being a *sautra* (Vedic-style) compound.
With the intention of [explaining] the seventh case, he says: "of that which has become a name" (*saṃjñābhūtāyāḥ*).
Regarding the rule *madrebhyo ’ñ* 4.2.108: because of the mention in the plural, it is the word denoting a country (*janapada*) that is understood, and not [any other].
This is an illustration of the term *bhadraparyāya* (synonym of *madra*). Regarding the rule *diśo’madrāṇām*:

the meaning of the sūtra is that "there is vṛddhi of the initial vowel (*ādi*) of a word denoting a country (*janapada*) which follows a stem signifying a direction and is different from *madra*, when a taddhita suffix beginning with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k* follows. Thus, in the example *paurvamadra*, the word *madra* refers to a specific region within [the larger territory of] Madra.

In the *vṛtti*, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "direction" (*dik*), the compound is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.51] "the meaning of an *adverbial compound* (*avyayībhāva*)," etc.
(1049). [Sūtra 4.2.109: "After a village name located in the north that has more than two syllables and ends in an acute accent.
[Commentary: The mention of "direction" (*udīcya*) is discontinued. Why "after a village name located in the north"? [Example: *mādhuraḥ*. [Why "more than two syllables"]? *bahvacaḥ*.
What [is the example]? *dhvājaḥ*. The word *dhvajī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. Why "ending in an acute accent on the final syllable" (*antodātta*)?

[Consider] *śārkarādhānam*; in the word *śarkarāghāna*, the vowel of the word *dhā* is acute. This is because the accent of the *lit* suffix remains by virtue of the original accent of the second member of the compound being a *kṛt*-derived form. [Another example is] *śaivapuram*.
The suffix *vuñ* does not occur [after a word ending in] *-puravaha*, because the rule *vṛddhāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.114) is excluded there.

(1050) Pāṇini 4.2.110: *prasthotarapadapaladyādikopadhādaṇ*. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied when *prastha* is the final member of a compound, or when the word begins with *palady-*, etc., as the penultimate element. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *añ* prescribed for villages (*grāma*) located in the North. For example: *pāladaḥ* [is derived from] *paladī*.

Some say [the word] ends in *ī*, while others say it ends in *n*. Once the *n* is elided, the *saṃhitā* remains identical due to the substitution of *yaṇ*. Although the word *vāhīka* has *k* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*), it is listed among the *palady-ādi* group specifically to block the application of the suffix *cha*. Otherwise, since *cha* is subsequent, it would indeed apply, superseding the suffix *aṇ*.

The suffix *uṇ* applied after *kopadha* (words ending in a guttural) is [intended] when there is scope for it in the case of non-*vṛddhi* [vowels]. Thus, from *yakṛt-loman*, we derive *yākṛlloma*. However, Haradatta and others maintain that the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) does not apply here, because in this list (*gaṇa*), the elision of *al* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
(1051) *iñaśca* [Pāṇini 4.2.112].

Regarding the statement *sotaṅgameriti*: the suffix *iñ* is applied to *sutaṅgama* and others in the sense of the four types of meanings (*cāturarthika*). Regarding the term *śāstrīya* ("belonging to the technical treatises"):
if it is argued that "since the section on offspring (*apatya*) has concluded, elsewhere the term *gotra* refers to the worldly [lineage]," [the answer follows].
On this point, they say: "In the previous sūtra, by the mention of *gotra*, that which begins with the grandson (*pautra*) is understood as *gotra*;

for there, by restating the *gotra*-suffixes—namely, 'after those ending in suffixes prescribed after Kaṇva and others in the sense of *gotra*, the suffix *aṇ* is ordained'—the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed. And Kaṇva and the others are included within the *garga-ādi* group."
In the rule *argādibhyo yañ*, however, the term *gotre* is understood from the preceding rule *gotre kuñjādibhyaḥ*;

yet, it is not only the technical (śāstrīya) *gotra* that is taken here, because this [section] falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *apatya* (descendant). Indeed, that very same term *gotra* is what continues to apply in the subsequent rule *ṭhiñaśca*.

(1052) *Na vyaCaḥ prācyabharateṣu* 4.2.113. "Not after *vyaCa*" means that this is an exception (*apavāda*), which implies a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). Regarding the non-mention of the Bharatas: by that, the elision of the patronymic suffix (*yuvan-pratyaya*) prescribed by the rule *iñaḥ prācām* does not occur after the [names of] Bharatas.

"ĀṬḍḍālakiḥ is the father, ĀṬḍḍālakāyanaḥ is the son"— thus Kaiyaṭa explains in the *sūtra* "ṭharhādagopucche. [The author] says "jaśtva" (the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stops) with the intention that this suffix is *chādi*, not *śādi*, because the addition of *s* is for the purpose of establishing the designation (*saṃjñā*) of a "word" (*pada*).

(1053) *kāśyādibhyaṣṭhañ-ñiṭhau* |4|2|116|. From the group beginning with *kāśi*: the vowel *i* [in the sūtra] is for the sake of pronunciation. In both cases (*ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*), the letter *ñ* alone is the *anubandha*. The reason for the transposed reading [of *ñiṭha* before *ṭhañ*] is that it serves a specific purpose regarding feminine suffixes; this is the intended meaning. [The word] *āpadādi* [refers to the list beginning with *āpad*].
This is a *gaṇasūtra*.

(1054) *vāhīkagrāmebhyaśca* | Pāṇini 4.2.117. Regarding the phrase *vṛddhādeva*: there is no reversed restriction (*viparītaniyama*) such as "if it is from a *vṛddha* [place-name], then only the suffix *cha* [is applied]".
[This occurs] because there exists no *vṛddha* [word] ending in *u* that does not denote a place in the east.
(1055) *Dhanvayopadhād vuñ* |4|2|121|. Regarding *dhanvayopadhā*: the term *dhanva* is not used here to refer to its own form (*svarūpa*) or its synonyms (*paryāya*).
With the intention that [the word] cannot denote something larger, he says: "a particular desert" (*dhanvaviśeṣa*). Regarding "Airāvata is a desert" (*airāvataṃ dhanva*):

although the gender is stated as masculine by Amara in the rule "marudhanvānau amānau," nevertheless, because the short vowel is read in the *Bhāṣya* in the passage "the desert named Āṣṭaka," the word *dhanva* indeed exists as neuter as well.
The word *bodhya* [is formed] by [Pāṇini 4.2.122]: "Also after [stems ending in] *prastha*, *pura*, *vaha*, and *anta*.
The intention is that [the suffix *yat* is applied] because [the stem] ends in the letter *r*.

(1057) *janapadatadavadhyośca* |4|2|124|. From the *karmadhāraya* compound "janapada-tad-avadhi" (the country and its boundary), only a boundary that is itself a country (*janapada*) is obtained. Now, since [the designation of the suffix] would already be established by the fact that it is a country, is the inclusion of the term "boundary" (*avadhi*) not redundant?

This is because that [suffix] is indispensable for the purpose of ensuring that it is *only* this [word] and no other. For this very reason, the suffix *cha* prescribed by the rule *ṛt-otarapadāt* does not apply after the word *trigarta*, which denotes the boundary of a region;
rather, the suffix *vuñ* applies alone by the subsequent rule: *avṛddhād api bahuvacanaviṣayāt*.

With this intention, he provides an example: *traigartakaḥ*. Regarding the rule *anapadatadavadhyoḥ*, it should be understood that examples for words denoting the limit of a country (*janapadāvadhivācin*) are such as *yāmāyanakaḥ* and so forth. As for *nāgarā brāhmaṇāḥ*, [this refers to] *āhiṣmatī* among the *kattryādi* group.

The intention is that, due to the association with the word *saṃjñā* (name), only the word *nagara* when it functions as a proper name (*saṃjñābhūta*) should take the suffix *ḍhakañ*, resulting in the form *āgāreya*. (1058) *vibhāṣā kuruyugandharābhyām* | Pāṇini 4.2.130.
Explain the *vibhāṣā* (optionality). The word *kuru* is recited among the *kaccha*-group;

by virtue of that, the suffix *aṇ* is established as an option. Therefore, by process of elimination, the mention of *vibhāṣā* is solely for the sake of *yugandhara*. By the rule "also after what is not *vṛddha*," the suffix *vuñ*, which would otherwise apply invariably, is made optional by this [present rule].

However, because of its higher status [in the order of rules], the suffix *vuñ* is indeed obligatory for both [the meanings] "human" (*manuṣya*) and "that which resides therein" (*tastha*). Thus: *kauravakaḥ manuṣyaḥ* ("a human being from Kuru") and *kauravakam asya hasitam* ("his laugh is that of a Kuru"). It is precisely for this purpose that it is recited in the section beginning with *kaccha*. Otherwise, since *vuñ* and *aṇ* would already be established by this very option (*vibhāṣā*), the thought is: what would be the point of that [separate rule]?

(1059) *kacchādibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 4.2.133]. Regarding *saindhava*: the suffix *ṭhañ* would have been applicable by the rule *ordeaśe*. It is established by the suffix *vuñ*, according to the rule *anuṣyatatsthayorvuñ*.
(1060) *gahādibhyaśca* | Pāṇini 4.2.138. From the words beginning with *gaha*, the suffix *cha* is applied when they denote a place.
However, in the case of words such as *pūrvarakṣa* and others, the suffix *cha* is applied by virtue of their inclusion in the list (*pāṭhasāmarthya*), even though they do not denote a place.

*mukhapārśvatasoḥ*—this is a *gaṇasūtra*. The suffix *tasi* is applied by virtue of its inclusion in the *ādyādi* group after these two words ending in the locative case. Regarding *mukhatīyam*: in the sense of "born in the mouth" and so forth, the suffix *cha* is added to the word ending in *tasi*; then, by the rule *ṭhalo’ntyasya*, the *s* of *tasi* is elided.
In the word *yasyeti ca*, there is the elision of the vowel *i*. In *kug-janasya*, this is also a *gaṇasūtra*.

Regarding *svakīyam*: although the word *sva-* ends in the suffix *kan* used in its own sense (*svārthika*), it should be understood—like *pūrvapakṣa* and others—to belong to the class of words beginning with *gaha-*, even though it does not denote a place. For this very reason...

The statement by the author of the Nyāsa, "For there is no rejection of one's own [rule]," in the sūtra *avyayāprākhyānāt*, is consistent [with this view]. However, from the word *aśabda* alone, only the suffix *aṇ* is applied: *sauvam*.
Furthermore, by the rule *dvārādīnāṃ ca*, the substitution *aiC* occurs; and this has been illustrated in the original treatise (*ākara*) under the rule *dvārādīnāṃ ca*.

In the case of the word *vīya*, however, [the suffix] *cha* is applied according to the rule *rākkrītāccchaḥ*. From the word *antara*, by applying *cha* because it belongs to the *gaha*-class, and then forming a compound of the word ending in that [suffix] with the word *na*, and finally adding the suffix *kan* in its own sense (*svārthe*), the form *āntarīyaka* arises;
its meaning is "invariably concomitant" (*avinābhūta*).

(1061) *vṛddhādakekāntakhopadhāt* | Pāṇini 4.2.141. From a *vṛddha* [base] ending in *aka* or *eka*, or having *kha* as its penultimate letter. In the example *brāhmaṇakīya*, the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise be applicable by the rule *opadhādaṇ*. In the example *ayomukhīyam*, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*, which characterize Vāhīka villages, would otherwise be applicable here.

(1062) From words ending in *kanthā*, *palada*, *nagara*, *grāma*, *hrada*, and *tara*, [the suffixes] *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* are applied. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the suffix *vuñ* which would otherwise be obtained by rules such as "from a word having *ṭha* or *ra* as its penultimate letter" (*ṭhropadhetaḥ*) is excluded.

[The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *parvata* to form] *pārvatīya*. However, in the verse "In this place, a terrible battle arose between Raghu and the mountain-dwellers (*pārvatīyaiḥ gaṇaiḥ*)," the suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word ending in *ch*, in the sense of "belonging to the king who is a mountain-dweller" (*parvatīyasya rājña ime*).

(1064) *kṛkaṇaparṇādbhāradvāje* |4|2|145|. The word *kṛkaṇa* and the word *bhāradvāja* here denote a country (*deśavacana*); however, that [country] is not the meaning of the suffix, but rather a qualifier of the base (*prakṛtiviśeṣaṇa*). Thus he says: "the country of Bhāradvāja," and so forth.

(1065) *yuṣmadasmador anyatarasyāṃ khañ ca* [Pāṇini 4.3.1]. Regarding the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*: since these are treated as *vṛddha* by the rule *yadādīni ca*, the suffix *cha* would necessarily apply; this sūtra is stated to prescribe both *khañ* and *aṇ* as well. Thus, in one alternative, *aṇ* applies.

The intention is that this is because of the mention of the word *anyatarasyām* [in the rule]. Thus, some maintain that since these three suffixes are dissimilar in number, there is no correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*). However, in the *Manoramā*, a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) was made in order to prevent correspondence according to order. For it is as follows:

Regarding the rule *yuṣmadasmador anyatarasyām*: after these two [stems], the suffix *cha* may optionally occur. Since the suffix *cha* would have applied invariably by virtue of the rule *yaci bham*, this present rule provides an option. Then follows *hañ ca*.
In the subsequent sūtra as well, a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) should be understood. By means of that, [the suffixes] *khañ* and *aṇ* are applied to the substitutes.
"According to their respective order, not so," and so forth; "of you two," and so forth.

Because the rules for the substitutes *tavaka* and *mamaka* are prescribed for the singular number, a grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) here is not made with a word ending in the singular. (Pāṇini 4.3.2: *tasminnaṇi ca yuṣmākāsmākau*. "In that [context], and when the suffix *aṇ* follows, *yuṣmāka* and *asmāka* [are substituted]."

"And in that [suffix] *aṇ*. By the word "in that," the suffix *khañ* directly prescribed [by the rule] is indicated, and not the one brought forward by anuvṛtti. Furthermore, there is no correspondence of number between the two causes and the two substitutes, because of the force of the separate mention of the case endings in the expression "hañaṇoḥ," which would have been stated simply as "hañaṇoḥ" [if such correspondence were intended].
However, that [distinction] is indeed desired in the case of a substitute (*sthānin*) and its replacement (*ādeśa*).

(1067) *tavakamamakāvekavacane* | 4|3|3|. [The words] *tavaka* and *mamaka* [are substituted for *tvad* and *mad* respectively]. Here, as before, with respect to the two causes (*nimitta*), namely the suffixes *khañ* and *aṇ*, there is a correspondence according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*).
It does not occur [elsewhere], but rather only in the case of the original form (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*); with this intention, he provides the examples: *tāvakīnaḥ* and *māmakīnaḥ*.

Although it would have been sufficient to state simply "after *para*, *avara*, *ara*, *avara*, *adhama*, and *uttama*" [according to Pāṇini 4.3.101], the inclusion of the term *pūrva* [in the rule]...

This is for the purpose of indicating a prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Therefore, even though by the subsequent rule (*uttarasūtra*) the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *yat* would apply when there is a compound of the words "direction" (*dik*), "para," and "avara" with the word "ardha," those suffixes are set aside and only *ya* occurs.

(1068) *dikpūrvapadāṭ ṭhañ ca* |4|3|6|. They say that the mention of "having a word for direction as its prior member" (*dikpūrvapada*) is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule to the word-form itself (*svarūpavidhi*).
(1069) *a sāṃpratike* |4|3|9|.

In the word *sāṃpratike*, the indeclinable *apratī* occurs in the sense of "proper" (*nyāyye*), as seen in such instances as: "The four-night sacrifice is not attained [as it is deficient], and the six-night sacrifice is excessive; this five-night sacrifice is indeed the one that is *saṃprati* (proper). It is neither deficient nor excessive—it is equal (*sama*).

This is the meaning. However, in the sense of "now," the word is well-known, according to Amara’s lexicon: "ṭhetarhi, saṃprati, and idānīm. Thence, by adding the suffix *aṇ* in its own sense (svārthe) because it belongs to the *prajñādi* group, and also the suffix *ṭhak* in its own sense because it belongs to the *vinayādi* group, the two synonyms *sāṃpratam* and *sāṃpratikam* are formed.

"Utkarṣa," etc. The sense is that the word *samprati* is understood here in its proper, primary sense [of "at present"]. (1070) Pā. 4.3.10: *dvīpādanusamudraṃ yañ*. [The rule begins with] *dvīpāt*; *anusamudram* means "along the ocean" (*samudram*), that is, "near the ocean" (*samayā*).

The term *tatsamayā* is an avyayībhāva compound. Since it ends in the locative case, the intention is that it qualifies the specific island by means of the action [of being near] which exists [in the vicinity]; thus he says: "the island which is near the ocean. This [suffix -ka] is an exception (*apavāda*) to both the *kacchādyaṇ* and the *manuṣyavuñ*. Why [is it said] "near the ocean" (*anusamudram*)? [Consider the example: *dvaipam* (belonging to another island), which takes the suffix *kacchādyaṇ*.

A human being from Dvīpa is called *dvaipaka*. [The suffix] *vuñ* is applied by the rule "anuṣyatas-thoḥ. Regarding the form *dvaipyā*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* does not occur by the rule "ṭhyañaś-ca," because it was already stated previously that *ṅīp* applies only to the suffix *yañ* occurring within the governing context of "apatya" (progeny).

(1071) *kālāṭ-ṭhañ* | Pāṇini 4.3.11: *kālāṭ-ṭhañ*. There is no inclusion of the word-form itself [as a source for the suffix]; rather, by the rule *saṃdhivelādi-sūtra*, [the suffix applies] even from non-vṛddha words such as *saṃdhivelā*, *trayodaśī*, *caturdaśī*, and so forth.

Because the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed for the purpose of superseding *ṭhañ*, however, with the intention that all words expressing time are included, he says: "from those expressing time. As for the point established in the *Padamañjarī* and other works—that there is no inclusion of the specific form itself nor its synonyms—that is incorrect; [as seen in] *ālikaḥ*.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of such usages as *saṃbandhaḥ* ("relation") and *ālikī vyāptiḥ* ("illusory pervasion").

Nor should it be argued that the rule *sandhivelādi-sūtra*, which prescribes the suffix *aṇ* after words beginning with *sandhivelā*, serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the fact that [the suffix applies] only to specific [proper names]; for that rule can also serve the purpose of excluding the application of the suffix to the mere phonetic form itself.

Because of its fruitfulness, the maxim of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*) is not resorted to here. Therefore, by association with the *kadamba* flower, the time [of its blooming] is called "the *kadamba*-flower time" (*kadambapuṣpaḥ kālaḥ*);

by association with the awn of rice (*vrīhipalāla*), the time [of its ripening] is called "the rice-awn time" (*vrīhipalālaḥ kālaḥ*). That which occurs therein is "the *kadambapuṣpika*" (pertaining to the *kadamba*-flower time).

"Vrīhipalālikam" is the source [of the term]. For here, regarding the authority [of this usage], they say that by this mention of time (*kāla*), it serves specifically as a qualifier for the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) in the *Sūtra* beginning with "Sandhivela" (Pāṇini 4.2.31). Nor is time the primary meaning of words such as "puṣpa" (flower), because they are derived from the rule "ubaviśeṣe" (Pāṇini 5.2.127); and thus:

It should not be said that the qualification by time is no authority for the stated meaning, because words such as "Puṣya" are used figuratively for a time when the moon is in proximity to Puṣya and so forth; this is also supported by the scriptural rule: "In the case of a specific location."

This is merely an explanation of its secondary application (*gauṇavṛtti*); such is the direction [of the argument]. This being established, the meaning resulting from the root text *ālavācibhyaḥ* is "from those expressing the *āla*.
(Pāṇini 4.3.12: *śrāddhe śaradaḥ*.

"Śrāddha" means a rite for the ancestors (pitrya-karma) performed with devotion (bhakti). It is derived by adding the possessive suffix *aṇ* according to the rule "rañ-śraddhā-arcābhyo ’ṇ," and it does not refer to a person who possesses faith (*śraddhāvān puruṣa*), because such a meaning is not expressed [by the word].
Regarding *śvasastuṭ ca*: because the word *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over, he says "or *ṭhañ* may follow.
By the rule *ṭhaiṣamohyaḥ* etc., *tyap* is also optionally prescribed. When these two [suffixes] are excluded...
The suffixes *ṭha* and *uṭa* are indeed present even in the case of *lāva*.
(1074) And [the suffix *ṭhañ* applies] after words such as *dvāra*:
*śauvastikam*. Now, one might object that because it is *antaraṅga*, the augment *tuṭ* should apply before the suffix *ṭha*.

Because [the word *karma*] lacks the status of being the beginning of an affix (*pratyayādi*), there would be no substitution of *i* for the final vowel in *karma-ṭha*, just as there is not in *ṭhac*. Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *i* occurs first because it is "further" (*para*) in the order of rules; for the augment *tuṭ* applies even before the substitution, due to its being an *antaraṅga* (internal) operation. As for the substitution of *i*, however, it is an *āṅga* (pertaining to the whole stem).

Because it is external (*bahir-aṅga*). If it is argued that when *tuṭ* is applied by splitting the rule (*sūtra-bhaṅga*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *ka* by the rule *ṭhisusuktāntāt*, [the answer is: True. However, in the case of suffixes such as *vuñ*, *chaṇ*, and so on, the *cit* designation is used for the sake of subverting the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*) once the substitution of *ika* has been made. Because the *cit* designation is present, the suffix-accent prevails over the accent of the base. Thus, the objection does not hold.
Thus it is established in the *Manoramā*.

(1075) Pāṇini 4.3.16: *saṃdhivelādyṛtunakṣatrebhyo ’ṇ*. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after [words beginning with] *saṃdhivelā*, as well as words denoting seasons and lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). The explicit mention of *aṇ* is for the purpose of precluding the suffix *cha*; otherwise, [the rule would have been stated simply as] *saṃdhivelādibhyaḥ*...

When it is stated that "the conditions [for the application of suffixes] should be as prescribed," the suffix *cha* would apply after the word *paurṇamāsī* by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*. However, the explicit mention [of this rule] is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *ṭhañ*; this is the intended meaning.

Regarding *taiṣam*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *tiṣya* in the sense of "originating from" (*bhava*) and so forth. But in the sense of "born under" (*jāta*), [the form is *taiṣa*] by the rule *raviṣṭhāphālgunī*.

It would be *luka*. In the rule *ūry-ādi-tya-...*, there is elision of the suffix *ya* because of the statement: "In the case of *iṣya* and *puṣya*, [the suffix is applied] to the names of constellations.
(1076) *prāvṛṣa eṇyaḥ* | 4.3.17 | [The suffix *eṇya* is applied after *prāvṛṣ* to form a word denoting time.]

The suffix *eṇya* is applied after the word *prāvṛṣ*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṛtvaṇ*. [The word] *prāvṛṣ* is derived from the sense "it rains" (*pravarṣati*); the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *ahivṛtī*. That which exists therein is [denoted by this suffix]. As for that which is born [therein], he will state the suffix *ṭhañ*. Although the form would have been established by the rule *raṣābhyām*, they say that the explicit utterance of the letter *ṇ* is for the sake of brevity in the grammatical process (*prakriyālāghava*). Furthermore, [the author] intends to teach the form *prāvṛṣaeṇyam*.

In the word *prāvṛṣeṇya*, the presence of the letter *ṇ* is also for the purpose of its audible pronunciation. From the causative (*ṇijanta*) root, when the suffix *kvip* is applied, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion, the elision of the *ṇi*, and the elision of the *y*.
(Pāṇini 4.3.22: "In all cases [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied, and there is the elision of the *tal*."

"And everywhere. The meaning is that this [word] "hemantāt" is carried over (anuvṛtta) from the rule "hemantācca. Regarding the form *haimanam*: it should be understood that when the word *ta*—qualified by the vowel *a*—is elided, the substitution of the original base (*prakṛtibhāva*) applies by the rule "an," and thus the elision of the *ṭi* portion does not occur by the rule "astaddhite."
