Regarding the form *haimantam*: the elision of the letter *t* does not occur in the suffix *ṛtvaṇ*, because that [elision] is conditioned by the occurrence of the *aṇ* suffix as specifically prescribed by the rule "arvatrāṇ" (*Pāṇini 4.3.16*). This point has been rejected in the *Bhāṣya*.
For instance, there exists the word *heman* as a synonym for *hemanta*, as in the verse: "The winter season approaches."

From such usage as "karṇau" [in the verse], and consequently, from the words *heman* and *hemanta*, the two forms *haimanaṃ* and *haimantam* are established by the suffix *ṛtvaṇ*. However, in the Vedic language (*chandas*), the third form *haimantikaṃ* is also established by the suffix *ṭhañ* according to the rule "ṭh hemantāt ca. Nor is there...

It might be suspected that the suffix *ṭhañ* (forming *haimantika*), being specifically prescribed, would supersede the suffix *aṇ*; however, this is not the case because in Vedic usage (*chandas*), all grammatical rules are optional. Nevertheless, the author of the *Vṛtti*, having drawn down the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) from the rule "after *hemanta*" (*hemantācca*), has accepted the form *haimantika* even in common usage (*loka*).

(1078) *sāyaṃ-ciraṃ-prāhṇe-prage-avyayebhyaṣṭyu-ṭyuL-au tuṭ ca* |4|3|32|. From the indeclinables *sāyam*, *ciram*, etc., the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyuL* are applied, along with the augment *tuṭ*. Now, because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), *tuṭ* is applied first. Just as in the rule *ṛtyu* [Pāṇini 6.1.93] and others, since the word *tyu* is a suffix, that *y* which is the cause for the designation of the stem (*aṅga*)—[the following rules apply].

If [the augment] were prescribed [as *tuṭ*], there would be no occasion for the *anādeśa* (the substitute *s* for *visarga*). Nor should it be argued that "let *tuṭ* alone be applied," because since *tuṭ* is a *pūrvānta* (an element forming part of the preceding item), the *visarga* would not exist [therein], leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the substitution of *satva* (of *s* for *r*) would not occur in *pratatanam*. Therefore, he says: "before *tuṭ*" (*tuṭaḥ prāk*), and so forth.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the rule "hakālataneṣu" is to be understood. Regarding the term *sāyaṃtanam*: the word *sāya*, ending in the vowel *a*, is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the close of day through the suffix *ghañ* added to the root *syati*; however, according to the opinion of the author of the Vārttika, its status as ending in the vowel *m* is prescribed (*nipātita*) by virtue of its association with that specific suffix. But the author of the Bhāṣya [holds a different view].

Relying on the rule *āntāvyaya*, the inclusion of the word *sāyam* [in the sūtra] has been rejected. Nor does it follow that the undesirable form *sāyika* would result from the suffix *ṭhañ* after the word *sāya* by virtue of the rule *kālāt ṭhañ*; for they say this is because that word (*sāya*) does not denote time, or because such a form is not admitted.

The suffix *tanaC* should be stated after the words *cira*, *purā*, and *para*. Thus, [the form] *ciraṃtanam* is derived. The point is that even for the word *cira*, its ending in *m* is prescribed by virtue of its association with this suffix.

Regarding this, they say: since [the word *cira*] is established as an indeclinable simply by being listed at the beginning of the section on indeclinables (*svarādi*), it would have been successful [without this rule] in the sūtra.

The inclusion of the word *cira-* [in the rule] is redundant. Nor should it be argued that the suffix *ṭhañ* would apply to the word *cira-* ending in a short vowel (*a*), because that application is blocked by this very rule. The mention of the ending in long *e* (*edantatva*) is for the sake of forms such as *prāhṇatanam*, meaning "that which has endured until the forenoon," and so on; for in those cases, there is no locative case (*saptamī*). This applies to the sense of "born" (*jātārtha*).
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of past time" (*adhvakālataneṣu*), even *uluka* is established. As for the term *ciratnam*:
because the word *cira* is explicitly included in the sūtra, the suffixes *tṛṇ*, *luṭ*, and *luc* also occur.
Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) of the word *cira* in the sūtra is impossible; [for it is possible] precisely from the indeclinable ending in *m*.

In the rule for *ṭaḷu* and *ṭaḷul*, that [suffix] is possible; [the suffixes] *puratup* and *purvasmin* are used for "in the previous year," *parāri* and *pūrvatare* for "in the year before last"; *agrādi* [is formed with *ṭaḷu*]. The fact that the suffix *ḍimaC* has the marker *ḍi* is for the sake of clarity. (1079) *tatra jātaḥ* 4.3.25: "[The suffixes taught from here on are applied] in the sense of 'born there'."

[The opponent says: "In that case, [the suffix] is formed from the word *jāta*. But surely, since it has been stated that [the rule] *śeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.92) is a governing rule (*lakṣaṇatva*), suffixes such as *aṇ* and others are already established for meanings such as 'born' and so on—just as in the cases of ‘ākṣuṣaṃ rūpam’ (visible form) and ‘śrāvaṇaḥ śabdaḥ’ (audible sound)—and by virtue of the governing context, suffixes such as *gha* and others are also established. Nor can it be argued that [the rule] is for the purpose of restriction, namely, that ‘*aṇ* and others occur only in the meanings beginning with ‘born’.’"

It must be stated that the specification of meanings such as "born" (*jāta*) and so forth is necessary; otherwise, the suffix would also apply in senses such as "he sits here" (*atrāste*) or "he sleeps there" (*tatra śete*), which would result in the incorrect form *ākṣuṣu*. However, in cases such as "he sits at Srughna" (*srudhne āste*) or "he sleeps at Srughna" (*srudhne śete*), the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) does not arise precisely because [the location] is not the primary factor (*anabhidhānāt*).

If it is argued: "In cases such as *bhaviṣyati* (he will be), *aṅgulyā khanati* (he digs with a finger), or *vṛkṣamūlād āgataḥ* (he has come from the foot of a tree), the case endings expressing capacity will be obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*) alone—just as the instrumental case is [implied] in the word *cākṣuṣam* (visible to the eye);
therefore, the specification of the meaning as 'born here' (*atra jātaḥ*) and so forth is redundant," we say: not so.

The mention of *ṛtviṣaṣṭha* and so forth is necessary for the purpose of providing exceptions (*apavāda*). As for those definitions of meaning that are without exceptions, such as *ṛtalabdhakrītakuśalāḥ* and others, they are indeed redundant; such is the general direction [of the argument].
(1080) *saṃjñāyāṃ śarado vuñ* | Pāṇini 4.3.27.

Regarding the word *śarad* [the suffix *vuñ* is applied] when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*). The meaning is: if the name is understood through the whole compound. Why "when it denotes a name"? [Consider: *śāradaṃ sasyam* ("autumnal grain"). This [rule applies] only when there is a name.
The author of the Vṛtti states that some maintain [the application of this rule] up to the word *ṛtalabdha*.
(1081) *Avayavād ṛtoḥ* |7|3|11|.

[This refers to the suffix *ṭhañ*] after a part of a season (*ṛtu*). Examples include *pūrvavārṣika* ("belonging to the first half of the rainy season"), and so forth. [In these cases, the suffix is added] to "the first of the rains" (*varṣāṇām pūrvaḥ*) and "the latter of the winter" (*hemantasyāparaḥ*).

In this analysis (*vigraha*), there is a partial compound (*ekadeśasamāsa*) according to the rule "ūrvāparādharottaram. The word *pūrvāsu* [is formed] as a compound for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Regarding the phrase "in the rule prescribing the augment *vṛddhi* for a season": [it refers to the fact that] the parts [of the season] are included in the rule prescribing the augment *vṛddhi* for a season. Thus ends the section on "in the rule prescribing the augment *vṛddhi* for a season."

When a suffix is prescribed on the condition of being a cause for *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) after a word denoting a season (*ṛtu*), the rule of "extension to that which ends with [the word]" (*tadantavidhi*) must be stated; the meaning is that if this word denoting a season follows its constituent parts [i.e., is a compound]. Regarding the phrase "as in the previous [rule]": this refers to examples such as *pūrvavārṣikaḥ* ("belonging to the earlier rains") and *aparahaimanaḥ* ("belonging to the later winter"). And thus, by the rule *varṣābhyaṣṭhak*, [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied].

By the two rules “*arvāgrāñca talopaśca*” and “[*vibhāṣā*] *pūrvāparātprathamapacimādāña*,” the suffixes *ṭhak* and *aṇ* respectively are applied. What is the purpose of the rule regarding the addition of *vṛddhi*? [Consider] *pūrvaprāvṛṣam*. In the rule “*prāvṛṣa eṇyaḥ*,” because there is no extension of the application (*tadantavidhi*) to that which ends in [the word], here only the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* applies. But in this case—namely, in the example *aurvavarṣika*—it is likewise.

And here—[the meaning is] that only the suffix *ṭhañ* applies by the rule *kālāt ṭhañ*; [this is stated] because there is an absence of being a constituent part (*avayavatva*). Otherwise, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression *pūrvāsu varṣāsu* would not be consistent; such is the intended meaning.
(1082) *susarvārdhāj janapadasya* | Pāṇini 7.3.12.

"From *susarva*, [the suffix *cha* is applied] after a country name or its inhabitants. This means that while that [rule] is still in force, [the suffix is applied] by the rule "even from a non-*vṛddha* [stem], when it refers to the plural.
(1083) *diśo'madrāṇām* | 7.3.13 | [The suffix *cha* is applied after a word denoting a direction, except for those denoting Madra.]

Regarding *diśaḥ pūrvāpara-ādibhyaḥ*: the suffix *añ* [is applied] by the rule *adrebhyaḥ añ*. Thus, we have *pūrvāhṇakaḥ*; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *vibhāṣā pūrvāhṇāparāhṇābhyām*.
(1084) *pūrvāhṇāparāhṇārdrāmūlapradoṣāvaskarādvun* 4.3.28. [The suffix] *vuñ* is applied after the words *pūrvāhṇa*, *aparāhṇa*, *ārdrā*, *mūla*, *pradoṣa*, and *avaskara*.
*Ardrākaḥ* and *mūlakaḥ*: these are exceptions (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 4.3.34]. *Pradoṣakaḥ*:
this is an exception to [the suffix *kan* prescribed by] Pāṇini 4.3.13, *īṣat-pradoṣābhyāṃ ca*.
*Avaskarakaḥ*: this is an exception to the general suffix *aṇ*. As for those [grammarians] who [hold that the suffix applies] "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*), [this is their view].

They maintain that this [rule] continues up to the word *ṛtalabdha*; according to their view, in the case of non-compounds (*asaṃjñā*), the suffixes *aṇ* and others, as well as *gha* and others, should be understood as applicable respectively.
(1085) *amāvāsyāyā vā* |4|3|30|.

Or [the suffix] on *amāvāsyā*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed for the time of conjunction (*saṃdhivelā*). By the rule *amāvasyad anyatarasyām*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied after the root *vas* preceded by *amā*; since the short vowel is optionally substituted for the long vowel (*vṛddhi*), the form *amāvasyā* with a short medial vowel is also included here, because when a base form (*prakṛti*) is mentioned, its derivative (*vikṛti*) is also understood.

Because of its inclusion [in the list]. [The forms] *amāvasyakaḥ* and *āmāvasyaḥ* [are derived from *amāvāsyā*]. However, Haradatta and others maintain that for those who read the word with a short vowel as the penultimate (*hrasvopadha*) in this sūtra and in the *saṃdhivelādi* group, the suffix would not apply to the form with a long vowel as the penultimate (*dīrghopadha*), because the base (*prakṛti*) is not included when there is a mention of a modification (*vikṛti*). But in reality, however...

Others hold that even the reading with a short vowel in the penultimate position (*hrasvopadhā*) can be justified by taking this as an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of what has become the original form of the *vṛddhi* [suffix]. (1086) *aca* 4.3.29.

And [the suffix] *a* [is applied]. The suffix *a* shall be added after the word *amāvāsyā*. This too, as before, should be understood from both [the preceding and following rules]. Thus, *amāvāsyaḥ*. But when the middle vowel is short, it is *amāvasyaḥ*. (1087) *Aṇ-añ-au ca* | Pāṇini 4.3.33.
And [the suffixes] *aṇ* and *añ*. The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of applying them respectively (*yathāsaṅkhyam*).
(1088) Pāṇini 4.3.34: *śraviṣṭhā-phalgunī-anurādhā-svāti-tiṣya-punarvasu-hasta-viśākhā-aṣāḍhā-bahulāl luk*. [The suffix *aṇ* is elided after these nakṣatra names.]

Regarding the word *svāti* in this sūtra, Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others maintain that it ends in a short vowel (*hrasvānta*). Mādhava, however, states in his commentary on the root *sā-ti* (meaning "to go continuously") that it ends in a long vowel (*dīrghānta*). Consequently, in the phrase *svātī tiṣṭhati*, because the form ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is intended, the form *sauvāta*—derived from the stem ending in *aṅīṣ*—is used in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhāva*).
In the opinion of Mādhava, this [suffix] is indeed established even in the sense of a genus (jātārtha). However, in the opinion of Kaiyaṭa and others, it is not correct in the sense of a genus;

for even though the word "ending in ṅīṣ" is mentioned in this rule prescribing elision (luk), the elision of the aṇ suffix occurs after a word ending in ṅīṣ as well, by virtue of the paribhāṣā concerning words qualified by gender (liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā).

(1089) *luk taddhitaluki* | Pāṇini 1.2.49. Regarding the term *upasarjana*: here, "subordinate" (*upasarjana*) is understood as that which is non-principal (*apradhāna*), not the technical grammatical sense [of a word ending in a feminine suffix], because the latter is impossible in this context. Now, one might object: [is this not contradicted by] *ostriyau*?

One might argue: "Let the definition of *upasarjana* found in the Sūtra itself—namely, that which is subordinate (*apradhāna*)—be accepted, and not the technical grammatical rule (*śāstrīya*) 'when [two words] have the same case-ending' (*ekavibhaktau ca*). This is not so; for in the case of *harītakyaḥ phalāni* ("the fruits of the *harītakī*"), there would be the undesirable consequence of shortening the vowel. What is the purpose of the term *upasarjana*? [Consider: *avantī*, *kuntī*, *kurūḥ*.

The suffix *chaṇ* should be prescribed after the words *śraviṣṭhā* and *aṣāḍhā*. [Examples: *śraviṣṭhāsu* (in the Śraviṣṭhās), *śrāviṣṭhaḥ* (born under the Śraviṣṭhās). Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*): by the word "and so forth," [the following are included]: *anūrādhaḥ*, *svātiḥ*, *tiṣyaḥ*, *punarvasuḥ*, *hastaḥ*, *viśākhaḥ*, *aṣāḍhaḥ*, and *bahulaḥ*. The word *bahula*, denoting the Kṛttikās, ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; of that [word, the suffix *chaṇ* is applied].

In the sūtra, there is a brief mention (*hrasvanirdeśa*) by means of a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*). Regarding the phrase "upaśaṅkhyānam" (supplementary statement), the word "uka" is to be understood as the remainder. Regarding "citreti": since the suffix *taddhita* has been elided (*luk*) by the rule "uktaddhite," the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied again. Regarding "ṭānāviti":
due to the force of the specific formulation (*vidhānasāmarthya*), there is no elision (*luk*) of these two [suffixes].
(1090) *sthānāntagośālakharaśālācca* |4|3|35|. In the case of *gośālā* at the end of *sthānānta*, there is shortening due to the neuter gender by the rule *vibhāṣā senā*.
By association with that, the same applies to *kharaśālā*. And thus, in the case of the feminine alternative, there is no elision (*luṅ*).

It should not be suspected [that this is incorrect], for they say that by the paribhāṣā regarding that which is qualified by its gender-mark (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), elision (*luk*) is established there as well. Although the desired form would also be established in the neuter by the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*) even if the forms ending in *ṭāp* were recited, nevertheless, the short vowel is recited for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*). In the case of the neuter gender...
"Shortness" refers to the fact that the word "ūtre" is understood as the remainder [of the rule].
(1091) *Vatsaśālā-abhijit-aśvayuj-chaka-bhiṣaj-to vā* |4|3|36|. From *vatsaśālā*: "born in Vatsaśālā"; it should also be understood as "in Vatsaśālā."
Regarding the phrase "ityādi" (and so forth): by the word "ādi," [the names] Abhijit—namely *ābhijitaḥ*—and Aśvayuk—namely *āśvayujaḥ*—are included.

Regarding the term "pratiprasūtaḥ": the meaning is that the general suffix *aṇ*, which had been set aside by the suffix *ṭhañ* [prescribed] after words denoting time, is once again permitted by the rule "andhivelādi."

(1092) *kṛtalabdhakrītakuśalāḥ* |4|3|28|. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word ending in the seventh case to form a name when it means] "made," "obtained," "bought," or "skilled. [Objection: Since the states of being "made" (*kṛtatva*) and "bought" (*krītatva*) are pervaded by the states of being "produced" (*jātatva*) and "obtained" (*labdhatva*), what is the purpose of including these two [specific terms]? [Response: True. However, even in a cognition where the qualifiers are the states of being "made" and "bought," [the rule applies].

That [suffix] is included for the sake of the secondary derivative (*pratyaya*). For this very reason, even in the case of those [words] that undergo elision (*luk*) when a *jāti* suffix is applied, there is no elision once [the secondary suffix] has been formed.
(1093) *prāyabhavaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.3.39. *Prāya-* refers to the locus of occasional occurrence—this is *prāyabhava*. Therefore, it is not covered by the rule "that which occurs here" (*atra bhavaḥ*).
They say that the meaning [of the rule] has already been understood. However, this was rejected in the Bhāṣya with the statement:
"The mention of *rāya* is useless, because it is already accomplished there by [the mention of] *bhava*.
(1094) *Upajānu-upakarṇa-upanīveṣṭhak* 4.3.40.

*Upajānu*, *trayaḥ*, and *amī*—these three are also avyayībhāva compounds used in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpya*). When these are combined in a collective dvandva compound, the masculine gender is prescribed by the Sūtra. (1095) [Pāṇini 4.3.41] *saṃbhūte*.

In the case of *saṃbhūta*, two things are relied upon here through the use of the suffix *tan* and so forth: the possibility of existence [of one thing] in another, and the non-excess of the contained over the measure of the container. In the example *sraugghna*, it means either "it is possible in Srughna" or "it does not exceed the measure of that [Srughna]."
The meaning is "an army" and so forth.
(1096) *kośāḍḍhañ* [Pāṇini 4.3.42]. From *keśa*: *kauśeya*. This term is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) for a specific type of cloth. In the case of *kośa*...

However, its production (*saṃbhava*) is intended according to the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). In another view, however, within the section on derivatives (*vikāra*), the rule *ośācca* should be recited immediately after *ṭheṇyā ḍhañ*. Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied to *kośa* in the sense of a derivative (*vikāra*); for [otherwise], if it were in the sense of being produced (*saṃbhūta*), the meaning would not be possible."

(1097) *kālāt sādhupuṣpyatpacyamāneṣu* |4|3|43|. From a word denoting time (*kālāt*), [the suffix *ṇa* is applied] when the objects are those that "flower" or "ripen" well (*sādhupuṣpyat-pacyamāneṣu*). The root *uṣ* here belongs to the *divādi* class and ends in the present participle suffix *śatṛ*. Thus he says: "those which flower" (*puṣpyanti*). (1098) *upte ca* |4|3|44|. [The suffix *ṇa* is also applied] after a word denoting time when the object is "sown" (*upte*).

And in the case of *upta*, it is simply *ālā*. The mention of *yogavibhāga* is for the sake of what follows. The sense is that in the sūtra, the past tense (*bhūtakāla*) is not a restrictive factor (*atantram*), as indicated by the fact that [the word] is derived from the root *vap* in the sense of "they are sown" (*upyante*). (1099) [Sūtra 4.3.45: *āśvayujyā vuñ*.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after the word *āśvayujī*. The letter *ñ* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*) and for the sake of vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) in subsequent rules.
Regarding the term *āśvayujyām*: *aśvayuk* is a synonym for the lunar mansion *aśvinī*; the full moon day associated with that is *āśvayujī*, and the meaning is "on that [day]."

(1100) *deyamṛṇe* |4|3|47|. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a word denoting] "that which is to be given" (*deya*) when it refers to a debt (*ṛṇa*). Why say "when it refers to a debt"? [Observe: *māse deyā bhikṣā* ("alms to be given in a month").
(1101) *kalāpyaśvatthayavabusādvun* |4|3|48|. [The suffix *vuñ* is applied after the words] *kalāpī*, *aśvattha*, and *yavabusa*.

Regarding the term *kalāpy-aśvattha*: [the rule] "there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix after *hala*" applies here. Although the use of the masculine gender in this instance is technically improper, they say that the masculine form is employed with the intention that the word *aśvattha* is used figuratively (*aupacārika*) for the fruit.
(1102) *saṃvatsarāgrahāyaṇībhyāṃ ṭhañ ca* |4|3|50|. [The sūtra reads:

*saṃvatsara-ṭhañ ca*. It would be easier to state it simply as *saṃvatsarāgrahāyaṇībhyāṃ vā*. Nor is the mention of *ṭhañ* redundant when one could have said *ṭh vā*, for [the suffix] is required in the list beginning with *sandhivela* (Pāṇini 4.3.16).

Regarding the reading "from *aṃśa*, *vatsara*, *phala*, and *parvan*," it should be stated that the *Kāśikā* and other works explain that when *phala* is intended to be expressed as a debt (*ṛṇa*), the suffix *aṇ* is set aside so that only the suffix *ṭhañ* may apply;
however, by virtue of the etymological definition of the term *taddhita*— namely, "those [suffixes] which are beneficial for that"— the suffix *aṇ* does not apply here.
The moderns [hold] that it can be stated as "it would be so.
(1103) *vyāharati mṛgaḥ* |4|3|51|. Regarding *naiśika*, [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is optionally applied by the rule *iśāpradoṣābhyāṃ ca*.

The phrase *tatra bhavaḥ* [means "that which exists there"]. The word *ālāt* has ceased to apply. Because the word *tatra* is repeated here to exclude the application of the word *atra* when it is connected with time (*kāla*), the word *aḥ* from the preceding sūtra does not apply.

It should not be argued that the inclusion of the word *tatra* (there) is for the sake of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), because the rule could have been easily formulated as *adaso ’tra* (of *adas* here), which would have applied to subsequent cases as well. Furthermore, although the root *bhū* also signifies "origination," it should be understood that in this context it functions only in the sense of "existence" (*satā*), because of the separate mention of "born" (*jāta*) in the phrase *atra jātaḥ*.

(1105) *yat* is [the suffix] after *dig* and so forth. [The list of *digādi* words is: *dig*, *īś*, *varga*, *pūga*, *pakṣa*, *rahas*, *ukhā*, *sākṣin*, *ādi*, *anta*, *mukha*, *jaghana*, *megha*, *yūtha*, *udaka* (provided it is a proper name), *anyāya*, *vaṃśa*.

*Kālya* and so forth refer to the cardinal directions and the like. Here, the mention of *mukha* (front) and *jaghana* (rear) is intended to signify parts of the body that are not limbs (*aśarīrāvayava*).
That which exists at the front (*mukha*) or the rear (*jaghana*) of an army is called *mukhya* (foremost) or *jaghanya* (rearmost).
(1106) *prācāṃ nagarānte* (Pāṇini 7.3.24): [The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in *nagara* when it follows a word denoting a direction, according to the Eastern grammarians.]

"At the end of a city of the easterners. Because of the mention of the locative case (*saptamī*), even the phrase "in the case of *aṅga*" (*aṅge*) which is supplied as a governing rule (*adhikṛta*) is transformed into the locative. Thus he says: "in *aṅga* at the end of a city.
(Pāṇini 4.3.56): *dṛtikukṣikalaśivastyastyaherḍhañ*.

*dṛtikukṣi*: *dṛti* refers to a leather-worker as well as a specific part of the body; *kukṣi* is a word beginning with *dhūma* and others, so when *vuñ* would have been expected by the rule *dhūmādibhyaś ca*, this [sūtra] prescribes *ḍhañ*. *kalaśi* means a churning vessel—as in the verse: "The cowherds churn the heavy *kalaśi* of the ocean."
*Māgha*: Regarding the word *asti*, Amara states: "The word *asti* [is used] in two senses below the navel. That which exists there is called *vāsteya*.

The word *asti* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) that resembles a verbal form (*tiṅanta*). It has both the same meaning as a verbal form and a different meaning. An example of the first is: *astikṣīrā gauḥ* ("a cow that possesses milk"). An example of the second is: *astimān* ("one who possesses existence").

The meaning is "one who possesses wealth. Regarding this, Haradatta maintains that since there is no distinction here, both [types of persons] should be understood as being included. That which originates from a snake (*ahi*) is *āheya*. Amara states: "The word *āheya* applies to three things: poison, bone, and so forth. (Pāṇini 4.3.57) *grīvābhyo ’ṇ ca*.

The suffix *aṇ* is also applied after the word *grīvā*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ya*, which would otherwise apply by the rule "after a word denoting a part of the body. The word *grīvā* refers to a collection of vessels (*dhamanī-saṅghāta*). In that context, the plural number is used in the sūtra with the intention of expressing a collection where the individual parts are prominent. However, when there is an intention to express a collection where the individual parts are concealed, [the singular is used].

However, the suffixes *aṇ* and *ḍhañ* are indeed applied even after a word ending in the singular number; for example, *graiveyam* and so forth. The analysis (*vigraha*) is either "that which exists in the necks" (*grīvāsu bhavam*) or "that which exists in the neck" (*grīvāyām*).
(1109) Pāṇini 4.3.58: *gambhīrāñ ñyaḥ*.

The suffix *ñya* is applied after [the word] *gambhīra*. There is an addition [to the rule] for [words ending in] *pañcajana*: *pāñcajanya*. (1110) Also after an *avyayībhāva* compound: 4.3.59. *avya*... [as in] *parimukham*. If, in this case, exclusion is understood from the word *pari*, [then the suffix applies].

In that case, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound by [Pāṇini 2.1.12] *tad-āṭha-pa-ri-bahi-r-añcaś-caḥ pañcamyām*. However, if it is an *abhividhi* (inclusive) sense, they say that it is an *avyayībhāva* precisely because of this specific nipātana (irregular derivation).
It is desired only after *parimukha* and so forth; thus, "only after *parimukha* and so forth. This...

The meaning is as follows: after the *digādi* group [of words], the *parimukhādi* group—consisting of *parimukha*, *parihanu*, *paryāṣṭha*, *paryulūkhala*, and so on—is recited. Due to its association with that [group], the word *avyayībhāva* in this rule refers specifically to the *parimukhādi* group. This is its [the *parimukhādi*] list.
"Because there is no other purpose [for this rule]. Now, one might object: "In that case, let the rule *arimukhāt* etc.

be formulated specifically; what is the use of this effort? Even if there is a requirement for the term *avyayībhāvāt* later on, it would be more appropriate to formulate it right there. If this is argued:

Haradatta has crossed over this point: when it is stated that [the suffix] *ñya* applies after "parimukha" and so forth, it would follow that *ñya* could also apply after *bahuvrīhi* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds; however, because of the specific mention of *avyayībhāva*, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs after them. It should also be understood that the word *pratiśākha* is included in the *parimukhādi* group.
Likewise, from the root *caṭ* in the sense of "pervasion" (*vyāpti*), the word *prātiśākhya* is formed, meaning "belonging to each branch" (*prati-śākham bhavam*).

Mādhava states that the suffix *ñya* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhavārtha*) according to the rule *avyayībhāvācca*. (Pāṇini 4.3.59). [Then follows: Pāṇini 4.3.60: *antaḥ-pūrvapadāt ṭhañ*.
Regarding *antaḥpūrvam* and *antarveśmam*: the compound-ending suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule *apuṃsakād anyatarasyām*.
For *adhyātmam*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is desired after the class beginning with *adhyātma*; [alternatively], *ṭac* is applied by the rule *ṭhanaś ca*.

(1112) *karṇalalāṭāt kan alaṅkāre* |4|3|65|. After the words *karṇa* and *lalāṭa*, the suffix *kan* is applied [to form a word denoting a person] when the sense is "ornament. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule for the suffix] *yat*. Why say "when it is an ornament"? [Consider: *karṇyam* ("belonging to the ear") and *lalāṭyam* ("belonging to the forehead"). (1113) *tasya vyākhyāta iti ca vyākhyātavyanāmnaḥ* |4|3|66|. [The suffixes prescribed by the previous rules are also applied] after the name of that which is to be explained, in the sense of "one who has explained that."

And regarding the phrase "its commentary" (*tasya vyākhyāna*): that by which something is explained is a "commentary" (*vyākhyāna*). The suffix *luṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). The word *iti* refers to the meaning of the sentence. The particle *ca*, being heard in proximity to it, implies the meaning of the sentence "belonging to this" (*atra bhavaḥ*). [This refers to] the text that is to be commented upon.

The name [of the work] is that which conveys [the subject matter], and this occurs either through primary denotation (*śakti*) or through indication (*lakṣaṇā*); there is no apprehension of it otherwise. Thus, the meaning of the rule is: "Suffixed elements (pratyayas) should occur after a word ending in the locative case when used for the purpose of explaining [a text], and after a word ending in the seventh case when used in the sense of 'being therein' (*bhava*), provided they convey the treatise (*grantha*) to be explained. Of the treatise to be explained...

What [is the purpose] of the name? [For example: Sukosalā is the commentary on Pāṭaliputra; for Pāṭaliputra is explained by her as "being characterized by such an arrangement. However, this is not the name of that which is to be explained, because it is well known that the status of being an object of explanation applies only to texts.
Indeed, the mention of the name [of the specific rule] in the sūtra is made solely for the purpose of including well-known cases.
(1114) *Bahvaco’ntodātāṭ ṭhañ* |4|3|67|. [The word] *bahvacaḥ* [is used]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ*. Why [specify] *bahvacaḥ*? [To exclude: *dvyaṣṭhakam* (from *dvyaśva*).

He will state that this is to be cited as a counter-example for [the rule concerning] monosyllabic suffixes (*ekāc*). It is *sau-pam* (the word *supam* with the suffix *su*). It is *taiṅ-m* (the word *tiṅam* with the suffix *ṭā*). Why "ending in an acute accent" (*antodātāt*)? [Consider] *saṃhitāyāḥ saṃhitam*. This [word *saṃhitam*] is acute on its first syllable by the rule "that which follows *ati* is acute" (*atiranantaraḥ*). The mention of the word "end" (*anta*) is for the sake of clear understanding; for even when it is said "after an acute accent" (*udātāt*), since a letter (*varṇa*) is being referred to, there is the inclusion of what ends in that [acute vowel].
Just as in the rule *ṭhaL anudātāṅitaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.149), [so it is here]:

(1115) *kratuyajñebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.3.68). From words denoting *kratu*s and *yajña*s [the suffix *ṭhaL* is applied]. For example: *agniṣṭomasya vyākhyānaḥ* ("an exposition of the Agniṣṭoma"), used in the sense of the Agniṣṭoma and similar rites.

They say that words such as *agniṣṭoma* occurring in the *mantras*, *brāhmaṇas*, and *kalpas* serve as examples here, because it has been stated that only the names of the texts are to be explained. *Stuti* means *stoma*. [The compound] *agner stomo ’smin* is a *bahuvrīhi*; and "beginning with *ara*"...

And this [term] has its final syllable as the acute (udātta). It is called *peya* because it is drunk (*pīyate*) therein; the suffix *yat* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), according to the rule "after roots ending in ṛ, and for *lyuṭ*, [the suffixes are applied] diversely. *Vāja* is a specific kind of gruel (*yavāgū*);
that which is to be drunk from it is the *vājapeya*. For this [compound], by the rule regarding the original accent of the first member of a *kṛt*-derivative, has the middle syllable as the acute.

Because the word *peya* is acute-accented by the rule "the suffix *yat* [is acute] except in the case of *nau*," [the compound is formed as follows]: it is called *rājasūya* because the king—a Kṣatriya—is consecrated (*sūyate*) therein, or because King Soma is consecrated therein; the suffix *kyap* is applied by the rule "in the sense of *rājasūya* and *sūrya*.
From that very rule, the compound is established by irregular derivation (*nipātana*), or alternatively, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

This [compound] is also oxytone by the natural accent of the final member (*uttarapada-prakṛtisvara*). By the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), the word *sūya* is acute on its first syllable. He gives examples for those who do not accept the *asomaka* [accent]: "pāka" and so forth. The word *pāka* is a synonym for "small. It is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both *pāka* and a sacrifice" (*yajña*). And that...

It is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*). The *navayajña*—the sacrifice with new rice—is the *āgrayaṇa*. [The suffix] *naṅ* is applied by the rule "after the roots *yaj*, *yāc*, *vicch*, etc. The compound is formed by the rule "when a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix denotes the agent or the instrument.

It is accented on the final syllable by the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a *kṛdanta* compound. [The phrase] "for the sake of something not having the final acute" [is used].

The intention is that since this [section] has been commenced for the purpose of the Vājapeya and Rājasūya sacrifices, even though the word "agniṣṭoma" is oxytone (ending in a high-pitched vowel) and thus denotes a sacrifice, it must be treated by this very rule; therefore, "agniṣṭomika" and so forth have been cited as examples.
(1116) *adhyāyeṣv eva ṛṣeḥ* |4|3|69|.
In the case of chapters (*adhyāya*), [the suffix] is used only after the name of a seer (*ṛṣi*). The word "only" (*eva*) is for the sake of clear understanding. [The example is] *vāsiṣṭha*;
here, the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava-artha*).

(1117) *pauroḍāśapuroḍāśāt ṣṭhan* |4|3|70|. From *pauroḍāśa* and *puroḍāśa*, the suffix *ṣṭhan* is applied. Because of the marker *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added. Thus: *pauroḍāśikī* and *puroḍāśikī*. It is called *puroḍāśaḥ* because it is offered (*dāśyate*) before (*puras*). [The root] *dāś* is used here in the sense of giving (*dāne*), with the suffix *ghañ* in the impersonal (*akarmaka*) sense.
By virtue of an irregular grammatical formation (*nipātana*), the letter *d* is replaced by *ḍ*.

(1118) *Chandaso yadaṇau* |4|3|71|. After the word *chandas*, the suffixes *ya* and *aṇ* are applied in the senses of "originating from" (*bhava*) and "explaining" (*vyākhyāna*). Thus, from the word *chandas*, [the forms *chāndasa* and *chāndasika* are derived].

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhak* which has the characteristic of having two vowels (*vdyaj*). "In the Vedic language" (*chandasi*), etc.: it should be understood here that the respective application (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) of *yat* and *aṇ* to these two meanings does not occur because they are not marked with the *svarita* accent. (Pāṇini 4.3.72) *vdyaj-ṛd-brāhmaṇa-ṛk-prathama-adhvara-puraścaraṇa-nāma-ākhyātāt-ṭhak*.

[4.3.72] *vyañ-jṛt*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *aṇ*. For example, *cāturhotṛka*. The name "Four Hotṛs" (*caturhotṛ*) refers to the mantra beginning with "Earth is the Hotṛ, Heaven is the Adhvaryu," and so forth. The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) refers to this.

From the word "ādi" (and so forth), we have *prāthamikaḥ*, *ādhvarikaḥ*, and *pauraścaraṇikaḥ*. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika which states: "The mention of both the compound and the uncompounded forms is for the sake of including both the collective and the individual meanings. In that context, since the suffix would already be established from the word *nāman* itself because it consists of two syllables (*dvyac*), it should be understood that the explicit mention of the uncompounded form (*vigṛhīta*) is for the sake of including verbal roots (*ākhyāta*).

[Nouns are] nominal (nāmika), verbal (ākhyātika), or both nominal and verbal (nāmākhyātika). (1120) Pāṇini 4.3.73: *aṇṛgayanādibhyaḥ*. After the group beginning with *ṛgayana*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the senses of "originating therefrom" (*bhava*) and "explaining it" (*vyākhyāna*). *Ṛgayanādi*: after words such as *ṛgayana*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the meanings of "originating therefrom" and "explaining it."

"Of *ṭhañ* and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), *ṭhak* and *cha* are included. Regarding *ārgayana*: the word *ṭhāyana* is derived in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva-sādhana*). Therefore, in a compound, because of the rule "that which expresses the abstract state or the object [of the action] belonging to *ṭhan* is udātta at the end," it is udātta on the final syllable. Furthermore, through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), that which expresses the abstract state also refers to the treatise (*grantha*) itself. Here...
In the case of *ahvacas*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is obtained by the rule "the word ending in *ahvac* has the acute accent on the final syllable. The same applies to *aupaniṣada*.
From the words *vidyā*, *nyāya*, and *śikṣā*, the suffix *ṭhak* is obtained by the rule "after words ending in *vidyā*, *jṛt*, and *brāhmaṇa* [the suffix is *ṭhak*].
However, from the word *vyākaraṇa*, the suffix *cha* is obtained by the rule "after a word with a *vṛddhi* vowel in the first syllable, the suffix *cha* [is applied]."

(1121) *ṭhagāyasthānebhyaḥ* |4|3|75|. [The suffix] *ṭhak* [is applied after words denoting] *āya* and *sthāna*. *Āya*: that which comes (*eti*) to this [person], or he who comes to this master (*svāmin*); thus, *āya* is the share to be taken by the master.
That in which it arises is the *āyasthāna* (source of income). The use of the plural number [in the sūtra] is for the sake of including both categories.

This [suffix] is intended to exclude the apprehension of the word's own form (*svarūpa*). Because it follows after a word ending in *vṛddhi* in the first syllable, it supersedes [the suffix] *cha*. Examples: *āpaṇikaḥ*, *ākarikaḥ*.
(1122) Pāṇini 4.3.76: *śuṇḍikādibhyo’ṇ*. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after [words beginning with] *śuṇḍika*.

Regarding the phrase "and of Chādi and others": in the case of *kārkaṇa*, the suffix *cha* would have been applicable by the rule "after *ṛkaṇa* and *parṇa*, [the suffix *cha* is used] when [the patronymic is] Bhāradvāja. From the word *tīrtha*, however, the suffix *vuñ* would have been applicable because it belongs to the *dhūma* group.
For the word *ujjāpāna*, the suffix *añ* would have been applicable because it begins with *ut*; such is the meaning.

(1123) *Vun* is added [after a word] denoting a relationship based on learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*). [Pāṇini 4.3.77] The suffix *vuñ* is applied after words that denote relationships established through learning or birth.

This is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*. However, because it is a subsequent rule, it supersedes *cha*. Examples: *ācāryakaḥ* (the state of being a teacher), *mātāmahakaḥ* (the state of being a maternal grandfather).
*mātulakaḥ*.
(1124) *ṛtaṣṭhañ* | Pāṇini 4.3.78. Regarding *ṛtaṣṭhañ*: the phrase "from [words denoting] relations by learning or by birth" (*vidyayonisaṃbandhebhyaḥ*) is understood to carry over.

Thus he says: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *vuñ*. The ancient commentators (*prāñcaḥ*) maintain that since it should have been stated as *uṣkañ*, the inclusion of the long vowel marker (*taparakaraṇa*) and the mention of *ṭhañ* serve no discernible purpose. However, the truth is that the mention of *ṭhañ* is for the sake of deriving the feminine form *autṛkī* (in the sense of "the science [taught] by Autṛ") via the suffix *ṅīp*. Nor is there any need to worry about the rule *iḍḍhea*... [etc.].
It should be stated that the suffix *ṅīp* is established by the inclusion of the word "ka"; otherwise, forms such as *yādṛśī* and *tādṛśī* would not be established.

This is because a term containing a specific *anubandha* does not include one that lacks that *anubandha*, and since the *kañ* prescribed by the rule *tyadādiṣu dṛśaṣṭaḥ* contains two *anubandhas* (*ṭ* and *k*), it would be excluded. Therefore, the mention of the *tapara* (*ṭ*) must be set aside.
"It is well-spoken that it is indeed *ṭhuṣṭha*," they say.

(1125) *Gotrādaṅkavat* | 4.3.80. Regarding *gotrādaṅkavat*: since the section on offspring (*apatya*) has concluded, it has been stated elsewhere that "in this context, *gotra* refers to the worldly [lineage]."

After a word ending in a patronymic suffix (apatyapratyaya), the same suffixes as those prescribed for the sense of "coming from" (ata āgataḥ) may apply, just as in the case of the *aṅka* [chapter] rules. This is an extension (*atideśa*) of everything seen in the *aṅka* section; there is no insistence that it applies only to what is directly prescribed there. Consequently, even the suffix *vuñ*—as in the rule "after *otra* and *caraṇa*, the suffix *vuñ*"—is also included.

It is obtained; for although that suffix is prescribed in a general sense as "this belongs to this" (*asyedam*), it is seen even in the sense of a mark (*aṅka*) in instances other than those ending in *añ*, *yañ*, or *iñ*. Regarding "Veda" and so forth:
since the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed in the sense of a mark by the rule beginning with "*saṅghāṅka-*," here too the suffix *aṇ* follows [a base] ending in *añ*, *yañ*, or *iñ*.

Regarding *āṬpagavakam*: [the suffix] *vuñ* is applied by the rule *otracaraṇād vuñ*. Since it was seen in the sense of "seen in the lap" (*aṅke dṛṣṭaḥ*), here too, *vuñ* is applied after a stem ending in *aṇ*.
(Pāṇini 4.3.81: *hetumanuṣyebhyo ’nyatarasyāṃ rūpyaḥ* ("After words denoting a cause or a person, the suffix *rūpya* is optionally applied").

From *hetu* and *manuṣya*: the mention of *manuṣya* is for the sake of excluding [the word] *ahetu*; the plural number is for the sake of excluding a rule regarding the specific form [of the word]. Regarding "samarūpyam": because of the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) of "vibhāṣā" from "guṇe," the fifth case ending occurs even after a word that does not denote a quality (*aguṇavacana*). As for the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*):...
The indicative mark [is found] in the statement: "The *āhuvaka* [is used] after *prakṛti* when it is not perceived.
(1127) And *mayaṭ* [is added]. 4.3.82. And *mayaṭ*. The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of avoiding a correspondence in order (*yathāsaṅkhya*). *ṭa*.
This is the meaning of the suffix *ṅīp*.
(Pāṇini 4.3.83) *prabhavati* [is used]. In the case of *haimavatī*, it means "she manifests from the Himavat"; that is to say, she is first seen there.

However, the root *prabhavati* in the sense of "originating" is not taken [here], because it is specified as distinct from [the rule] "born here" (*atra jātaḥ*). (1129) *vidūrāñ ñyaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.3.84.

Regarding the word *vaidūrya*: this has the dental *d* in the middle, like the word *śādvala* (a grassy meadow), and not the retroflex *ḍ* in the middle, as in *naḍvala* (a reed-bed). But surely there is an inconsistency here, for it originates from Mount Bālāvāya, whereas it is refined in the city of Vidūra.

True. Therefore, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "If one should say that 'bālavāya' and 'vidūra' are either different roots or entirely different words, then one should treat them like the word 'jilvarī'. The meaning of this is as follows: the word *bālavāya*...

One obtains the condition (*pratyaya*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*); by means of the substitute read in the Sūtra, a corresponding original base (*sthānin*) such as the word *Bālāya* is implied, just as in the case of *laś* and others, by means of the substitutes *viśravaṇa* and *ravaṇa* read therein, a corresponding original base such as the word *Viśvavasu* is implied, as for example: [text fragment].
Just as in cases such as *addan* (instead of *adadan*), the substituend— such as *pāda* or *danta*— is implied in accordance with the substitute form,

so too [here] it means that there exists a distinct base (*prakṛti*) for the word *vidūra*, which denotes not only the city but also the mountain. And thus, under this view, in the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) "it originates from Ālavāya," [the compound is formed].

The sense is that there is no difficulty in the explanation regarding the suffix [being applied] after the word *vidūra*. As for the phrase "not indeed" (*na vai*): the word *vai* expresses dissatisfaction. In that regard, if one were to say that the word *vidūra* is not well-known on that mountain, one would be using the term *jitvarī* (a woman who has lost her husband). For linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) depends upon specific persons.
It is observed that just as merchants themselves use the term *jitvarī* for Vārāṇasī, so too do grammarians use *vidūra* for the mountain [Adri].
(1130) *tad-gacchati pathi-dūtayoḥ* | Pāṇini 4.3.85.
That [suffix] occurs after a word ending in the second case (dvitīyāntāt) in the sense of "goes" (gacchati),

provided that the goer is a path (panthā) or a messenger (dūta). In this regard, as in examples such as *sādhvasiś chhinatti* ("the axe cuts well") or *kāṣṭhāni pacanti* ("the pieces of wood cook"), there is a desire to express the independence (*svātantrya*) of the instrument (*karaṇa*), whereby the path becomes the agent (*kartṛ*).

(1131) *abhiniṣkrāmati dvāram* |4|3|86|. [The suffix *yañ*] is applied after a word ending in the second case [to form a name], when that which one goes out from is a gate (*dvāra*). The meaning is: [the suffix is added to the name of a city] if it denotes the gate through which one departs. For example: *sraughnaṃ kanyakubjadvāram* ("the Kanyakubja gate of Sraughna").
The realized meaning is that [the word *srugghna*] functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the act of exiting toward the front of the ladle (*sruc*).
As before, the instrument possesses the status of the agent (*kartṛtva*).
(Pāṇini 4.3.87): "In the case of a treatise composed with reference to [a person], [the suffix *aṇ* is applied]."

Regarding the phrase "tad ity eva": the accusative case here is used in relation to the word "adhikṛtya" (having taken as the subject). As for the term "śārīrakīya": a contemptible body is a *śarīraka*; that which relates to it is the embodied self (*jīvātman*). A treatise composed by taking that [self] as its subject is called *śārīrakīya*.

The *Śārīrakīya* is the composition of the four-chaptered (*catur-lakṣaṇī*) Sūtras. According to the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*, there is a Vārttika stating *ākhyāyikābhyo bahulam*. This dative case is used in the sense of *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that).
An *ākhyāyikā* is a specific type of literary work consisting of prose. For this very reason, both *ākhyāna* and *ākhyāyikā* are mentioned therein.

In this context, there is a specific mention for the sake of distinction: the meaning is that the suffix which has arisen to denote a narrative (ākhyāyikā) is frequently elided. A narrative composed concerning Vāsavadattā is called *Vāsavadattā*. *Sumanottarā* [is another example]. In some cases, however, it is not so elided—as in *Bhaimarathī*.

Since the meaning is already understood through the metaphorical application of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*), this *vārttika* is not strictly necessary; therefore, it was not stated in the root text (*mūla*).
(1133) Pāṇini 4.3.88: *śiśukrandayamasabhadvandvendrajananādibhyaśchaḥ*.

Regarding *śiśukranda*: here there is a Vārttika—"In a dvandva compound, there is a prohibition [of the neuter gender] for words such as *devāsura*. Examples: *daivāsuraṃ*, *rākṣosuraṃ*. This is due to a nipātana (irregular formation). This is because it was stated under the rule "abhā rāje" that "the word *amanuṣya* is used in its conventional sense (*ruḍhyā*) to denote Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and so forth"; therefore, by that rule [the neuter gender applies].
The sense is that "neuter-ness" is not established.
(1134) *so'sya nivāsaḥ* |4|3|89|.

Regarding *so'sya nivāsaḥ*: after a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntāt*) denoting "that" (*saḥ*), the suffix [cha] is applied in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of "his dwelling" (*nivāsaḥ*). This is as prescribed.

If that which is the meaning of the word ending in the nominative case were the locus (*nivāsa*), then [the example would be] "Srughna is the locus" (*srugghno nivāsaḥ*). This means that Srughna is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) of the act of dwelling. Now, one might object: in the expression *asya* (of him), the genitive case is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) due to its connection with a verbal derivative (*kṛd-yoga*). Consequently, because of the reversal of the relationship between qualifier and qualified, the meaning here would be "the agent who dwells, whose locus is Srughna."
It serves as a *vṛtti* (explanatory gloss). If it is asked, "Since the form *atrabhavaḥ* is already established [by the rule for *taddhita* suffixes], what is the purpose of this?", they reply:
Since dwelling (*vāsa*) is well known to have consciousness alone as its agent, there is a distinction based on the specific mode [of action];
thus, there is no pointlessness. For virtues dwell in love (*preman*).
In passages such as "vastuni," however, it should be understood that this is a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
(1135) *abhijanaśca* | Pāṇini 4.3.90.
The word *abhijana* [is also included]. The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. As it is said: "The *abhijanas* are one's former kinsmen."

The commentary (*vṛtti*) states: the intention is that [the term *bandhu*] is derived from the etymology "those from whom one is born. "Former kinsmen" refers to the father and so forth. The word *bandhu* belongs to the *prajñādi* group [of nominal stems]. From the preceding sūtra, the term *iva-āsaḥ* is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) here.

Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [place], the word *abhijana* ("one's native land") functions through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote what is connected to it. This being the case, he states the resulting conclusion: "In the verse beginning 'yatra pūrvaiḥ'... (Pāṇini 4.3.91):
*āyudhajīvibhyaśchaḥ parvate*. "The suffix *cha* is applied after words denoting those who live by arms, when a mountain is meant."

[The suffix is added] after words meaning "those who live by weapons. This fourth case ending [is used] in the sense of *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that). The meaning is: the suffix should occur to denote those who live by weapons—that is, for the sake of those who live by weapons. The phrase "so'syābhijanaḥ" (that is his ancestral home) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartate*). [The example is: "parvata" (a mountain).
This is a qualifier of the base (prakṛti); he states this with the words "of that which denotes a mountain," and so on. What is the purpose of [specifying] "mountain"? [Consider:

*sāṅkāśyakā āyudhajīvinaḥ* ("the weapon-bearers of Sāṅkāśya"). Here, the suffix *vuñ* is applied by the rule *ṭhyopadhāt*. [Also consider: *śaṇḍika*, *sarvasena*, *śaka*, etc., from which the suffix *ñya* is applied by the rule *śaṇḍikādibhyo ñyaḥ*.

(1137) *sindhu-takṣaśilādibhyaḥ-aṇ-añ-au* |4|3|93|. From *sindhu*, *takṣaśila*, and so forth, the suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* [are applied]. *Sindhu*, *varṇu*, *gandhāra*, *kamboja*, and others are the *sindhvādayaḥ*. These are generally also listed among the *kacchādi* group; since the suffix *aṇ* would have been established from that very group, [the separate mention here serves to restrict the application of *añ* as well].

The suffix *vuñ* is used for the purpose of denoting a person belonging to a particular human class (*manuṣyavuñ*). Examples include *takṣaśila*, *vatsoddharaṇa*, *barbara*, and so forth, which refer to the inhabitants of Takṣaśilā and other such places.
[Pāṇini 4.3.98] states: "The suffix *vun* is added after the words *vāsudeva* and *arjuna*."

The suffix *buṇ* is applied after the words *vāsudeva* and *arjuna*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule that *arjuna* should be placed first according to the two sūtras "that which ends in a vowel beginning with *a* [and is preceded by a consonant] takes the first position" and "the word with fewer syllables takes the first position. The fact that this precedence is not observed serves to indicate the principle: "That which is more venerable (*abhyarhita*) is placed first. Now, one might object: ...
In the sense of "the offspring of Vasudeva," the word *vāsudeva* is derived by applying the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *ṛṣyaṇḍhake*.

Thus, since the subsequent rule *gotrakṣatriyākhyebhyaḥ* would require the suffix *vuñ*, what is the purpose of this [separate] *vuñ*? For there is no difference regarding the *vṛddhi* vowel here, as it is already *vṛddha* (possessing a *vṛddhi* vowel) from the outset. Nor...

It should not be argued that there would be the fault of prohibiting the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) by the rule "of that which has [a cause for] *vṛddhi*" (*vṛddhinimittasya*), because even in the case of the suffix *vuñ*, the prohibition "of a word ending in *k* as an upadhā" (*a kopadhāyāḥ*) is intended to apply. Nor is there any difference in accent, because the accent is identical due to the rule "that which begins with *ñ* or *ṇ* is always acute" (*ñnityādir nityam*). Nor is there [a difference] regarding "that which is most worthy" (*abhyarhitam*)...

If it is argued that the result [of the rule] is simply to make known [the word *pūrva*], and that if this were the case, the author would have used the simpler expression "that which is more venerable" (*abhyarhitam*) alone in the section on prior placement (*pūrvanipāta-prakaraṇa*), the Bhāṣya states here:
"This is a technical name (*saṃjñā*) of the Blessed One. The intention is as follows: "In every respect, he [the Blessed One] is both the whole..."
Because he dwells here, therefore he is celebrated by the wise as Vāsudeva—so says the Smṛti. Here, Vāsudeva is the Supreme Self (paramātman).
Alternatively, by the etymological derivation that "he dwells everywhere" or "everything dwells here," he is *vāsu*; the suffix *uṇ* is applied according to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*).

The analysis of the compound is "he who is both a dweller (vāsa) and a god (deva). Thus, this is neither a designation of a lineage (gotra) nor a designation of a Kṣatriya; therefore, the rule for the elision of the case-ending is indeed appropriate. As for the rule "that which is more venerable comes first," it was merely indicated incidentally; furthermore, that too is not universally obligatory.
It should be noted that this is due to indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as the mantra beginning with *vayuvamaghonām*.
(Pāṇini 4.3.99) states: "The suffix *vuñ* is applied diversely after names of *gotra* and *kṣatriya* lineages.
This supersedes the suffix *cha* prescribed for words with a *vṛddhi* vowel in the first syllable. Thus: *aupagava* (the descendant of Upagu) is his devotion; [the word] is *aupagavakaḥ*.

(1140) *janapadināṃ janapadavat sarvaṃ janapadena samānaśabdānāṃ bahuvacane* ||4|3|100|| [The suffixes] for those denoting inhabitants of a country (*janapadin*) are the same as those for the country itself (*janapada*), in all respects, when they share the same form with the country-name and occur in the plural. [In this context, the suffix] expressing possession (*matvarthīya*) [is applied] in the sense of the relationship between owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*).
"To demonstrate the nature of the base (*prakṛti*) and the affix (*pratyaya*) for those who do not know it.

By this, the meaning of the word *sarva* (all) is demonstrated. Haradatta says that if the mention of *sarva* were absent, then due to its predominance, only the affix would be extended (*atideśa*), and not the base. In this regard—

The author of the Vārttika states the purpose of the word "sarva" (all): "The mention of 'all' is for the sake of including the original base-forms [of the countries], and that is for the sake of Madra and Vṛji. The meaning is this:
even though the original base-forms are extended by implication to the suffixes such as *vuñ* when they are conditioned by *vṛddhi*, [the word "all" is used to ensure their inclusion].

Since an increase (*vṛddhi*) is expected [in the case of *madraka*], but a specific distinction is difficult to find there, one should understand that the distinction between *madra* and *vṛji* lies in the suffix *kan*. That too occurs only when there is not a plurality [of individuals]. "Decrease" (*nirhrāsa*) means reduction or smallness.
For instance: the king of the Madras—by the rule *ṭh-vyañ-magadha* [Pāṇini 4.1.171], the suffix *aṇ* is applied—[we have] *mādraḥ*. From the word *vajri*, however...

From *vṛddha* [names] such as *Kośala*, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied; thus, one who belongs to Vṛji is *Vārjyaḥ*. When there is a reduction of the base (*prakṛtinirhrāsa*)—as in the case of "one whose devotion is to this"—we have *Madrakaḥ* and *Vṛjikaḥ*. According to the rule “*adravṛjyoḥ kan*,” otherwise it would be *Mādrakaḥ* and *Vārjyakaḥ*. As for *Āṅgakaḥ*, it is by the rule “*anapadatadavadhyośca*.”

The suffix *vuñ* is applied even after a word ending in a *ṭh*-vṛddhi vowel. Although the suffix *aṇ* would have been expected after the word *aṅga* when it denotes an owner and ends in the plural, *vuñ* is extended [to this case] as well. For example: *pañcālā brāhmaṇāḥ* ("the Brāhmaṇas of Pañcāla"). Here, the word *pañcāla* is applied to the Brāhmaṇas through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). Why is the plural form specified? [To exclude its application] to the singular and dual.

So that there may be an extended application (*atideśa*) even when there is a difference in the word-form, [the sūtra] says: *āṅgaḥ*, *āṅgau*, or *bhaktiḥ* of it is *āṅgakaḥ*. Here, although the suffix *cha* would have been applicable after a *vṛddha* stem, *vuñ* is used instead.
(1141) *tena proktam* (4.3.101): "That which was proclaimed by him."

"Prokta" means "proclaimed" (spoken with excellence), and it is so called because it was proclaimed, not because it was composed; for that meaning is already covered by the rule "ṛte granthe. "Proclaimed by Pāṇini" means that the grammar—whether composed by himself or by another—has been made manifest through teaching or through the explanation of its meaning.

What is the purpose of [the suffix] *prati*? [As in: *devadattenādhyāpitam* ("taught by Devadatta"). Since this refers only to the teaching of a well-known text, no suffix is applied here by this rule. (1142) *titirivaratantukhaṇḍikokhāc chaṇ* 4.3.102.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning *titirivara*. The meaning is that its application is restricted to that specific domain; thus, there is no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of this [suffix] in the rule *“aunakādibhyaś chandasi”* (Pāṇini 4.3.105), which is why it does not apply in the case of *titirinā proktaḥ ślokaḥ* (“a verse proclaimed by Tittiri”). [The example is] *taittirīyāḥ*.
The suffix *luK* occurs after the affix denoting a student (*adhyetṛ-pratyaya*) following the word *rokta*. The same applies in the subsequent cases as well.

(1143) After the sages Kāśyapa and Kauśika, the suffix *ṇini* is applied [to form patronymics]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *cha*. The letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of causing *vṛddhi* in the subsequent rules. Now, an objection: [is it not so?]

If it is argued that the purpose here is the prohibition of the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule *ṭhvṛddhinimitasya*, the [commentators] say: because a word ending in a *ṇin* suffix refers to one who studies or knows [the Veda], it does not apply to a feminine;
and even if it were to apply, it would be established by the rule *ātesca*, since [the term] is a genus (*jāti*) by virtue of being a Vedic school (*caraṇa*).
What is the purpose of [the word] "from the two sages" (*ṛṣibhyām*)? [Consider: *kāśyapīyam* ("the work of Kāśyapa"), which was proclaimed by Gotrakāśyapa, who is contemporary with us.
(Pāṇini 4.3.104: *kalāpivaiśampāyanāntevāsibhyaśca* ("and from the pupils of Kalāpin and Vaiśampāyana").
The suffix *cha* (forming *kalāpin* and *vaiśampāyana*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*; however, it subverts *aṇ* due to its higher status in the order of rules (*paratva*).
There are four disciples of Kalāpin: Haridru, Chagalin, Tumburu, and Ulapa.
There are nine disciples of Vaiśampāyana: Ālambi, Kaliṅga, Kamala, and Ṛcābha.

Āruṇi, Tāṇḍya, Śyāmāyana, Kaṭha, Kalāpin—these are [the examples]. Hāridraviṇa; likewise Taumburaviṇa, Āulapina; as for Chagalin, he will state the suffix *ḍhinuk*. Ālambina; likewise Kāliṅgin, Kāmalin, Ārcābhin, Āruṇin, and Tāṇḍin.
[The suffix] *śyāmāyani* [is formed by adding *phak*]. He will state the elision (*luk*) after *kaṭha* and the suffix *aṇ* after *kalāpin*.

The words *yājñavalkya* and *āśmarathya* belong to the *kaṇva*-group; therefore, with the intention that the suffix *cha* (which applies after a word ending in *yañ* when the stem is "vṛddha") does not apply after those two, he says: "in the case of *aṇ*, [the rule] 'of the descendant' (*apatyasya*)."
The usage in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts stating that "Yājñavalkya and others are indeed of recent times" has been followed by the author of the Sūtras:
(1145) *kaṭhacarakālluk* | Pāṇini 4.3.107.

The suffix *luk* is elided after the words *kaṭha* and *caraka*. Since the word *kaṭha* denotes a pupil of Vaiśampāyana, it takes the suffix *ṇini*; *caraka* takes the suffix *aṇ*. The elision of these two occurs [only] in the sense of Vedic literature (*chandas*). Thus: *kāṭhāḥ*, *cārakāḥ*, *rślokāḥ*. (1146) After *kalāpin*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. 4.3.108.
The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after *kalāpin*. This is an exception to the suffix *ṇini*, which would otherwise be obtained due to his being a pupil of Vaiśampāyana.

Regarding the rule "there is no substitution of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) when *ṭhin* follows, provided it does not denote a descendant," he says: [this applies] when there is elision of the *ṭi* of that which ends in *n*.

The following should be added to the list [of words taking the suffix *aṇ*]: *sabrahmacārin*, *pīṭhasarpin*, *kalāpin*, *kauthumin*, *taitilin*, *jājali*, *lāṅgali*, *śilālin*, *śikhāṇḍin*, *sūkara*, and *sadmasuparvan*. [This is stated] because of the rule "there is no elision of the *ṭi* of a word ending in *an*" (*nāntasya ṭilopaḥ*). Thus, forms such as *māthurī vṛttiḥ*, *maudāḥ*, *laipaippalādāḥ*, and *śākalāḥ* are established. From the words *muda*, *pippalāda*, and *śākala*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied as an exception to the suffix *ṇini* prescribed by the rule "after these, when they are not proclaimed [by a Vedic seer]" (*urāmaprokteṣu*). After *cchagalin*, the suffix *ḍhinuk* is applied; this is an exception to the suffix *ṇini* which would otherwise apply because he is a pupil of Kalāpin. (1147) Pā. 4.3.110: After *pārāśarya* and *śilālin*, the suffixes [denoting a follower] are applied to form the names of mendicants and actors, respectively, when they refer to their respective Sūtras.

Pārāśarya says that the suffix *ṇini* in *maṇḍūkapluti* is connected here; thus he states, "there should be *ṇini*. Its scope is intended here, and for that purpose, the mention of *chandas* (Vedic meter) must be carried over [from the previous rule]. However, the status of being *chandas* in the two sūtras should be understood in a figurative sense (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*). Thus, [we have] *bhikṣusūtram*.
The form *caturlakṣaṇī* [is derived as follows]. Regarding the term *pārāśariṇaḥ*: *pārāśarya* refers to Vyāsa.
Although he is not a direct descendant (*anantarāpatya*), the suffix *yañ* is applied according to the rule *argādibhyaḥ* because he is treated as a *gotra* (lineage) by metaphorical extension.
By the rule *āpatyasya ca*, there is the elision of the *ya*. As for the suffix *adhyetṛṇ*, it is elided according to the rule *proktāt*.

[The words] *karmanda* and *kṛśāśva*—here too, the application of the meter and so forth is as before. What about the words *bhikṣu* and *naṭa* in the sūtras? [The answer is: *parāśara*, *śailāla*. (1148) *karmandakṛśāśvād iniḥ* | 4|3|111|. [The words] *karmanda* and *kṛśāśva*—here too, the application of the meter and so forth is as before. What about the words *bhikṣu* and *naṭa* in the sūtras? [The answer is: *parāśara*, *śailāla*. (1148) *karmandakṛśāśvād iniḥ* | 4|3|111|. [The words] *karmanda* and *kṛśāśva*—here too, the application of the meter and so forth is as before. What about the words *bhikṣu* and *naṭa* in the sūtras? [The answer is: *parāśara*, *śailāla*. (1148) *karmandakṛśāśvād iniḥ* | 4|3|111|. [The words] *karmanda* and *kṛśāśva*—here too, the application of the meter and so forth is as before. What about the words *bhikṣu* and *naṭa* in the sūtras? [The answer is: *parāśara*, *śailāla*. (1148) *
*kārmandam*, *kārśaśvam*.

(1149) *tenaikadik* | 4|3|112 | *tenaikadik*: After a word ending in the third case, the suffixes *am* and so forth may be applied in the sense of "being in the same direction as that. Example: *ekadik*.
The meaning is that the direction is the same. The repetition of the word "tena" (by that) is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] the rules concerning *chandas* and so forth.

Regarding "saudāmanī": because of the rule "ṭhan," there is no elision of the *ṭi* portion due to the preservation of the base form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Amara states: "Aḍit, saudāminī, and vidyut [are synonyms for lightning]."
(1150) And *tasi* [is used] as well. [This applies] in the previously mentioned scope. (1151) [The suffix *aṇ* is used] for that which is first discovered (*upajñāta*).
*Upajñāte*: known without instruction—this is *upajñātam*.
(1151A) *Kulālādibhyo vuñ* [Pāṇini 4.3.118]: after words beginning with *kulāla*. The group begins with *kulāla*, *varuḍa*, *caṇḍāla*, *niṣāda*, *kumbhakāra*, *śvapāka*, and so forth.

[The suffixes] *kulālādayaḥ* [are taught]. When the suffix *cha* would have been obtained after words such as *kṣudrābhramara* and *pādapa*, the suffix *añ* is prescribed instead of *aṇ*. (1152) *tasyedam* 4.3.120. [This sūtra provides the general rule for the application of these suffixes.]

This [suffix] belongs to that [root]. The five beginning with *aṇ* are general rules (*mahotsarga*), while those beginning with *gha* apply when a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) denotes a related entity (*saṃbandhin*). They do not apply in cases such as "immediately after" (*anantara*) due to lack of usage (*anabhidhāna*); for example, one does not say *devadattasyānantaram*.

However, for the root *vah*, there is also the augment *iṭ* before the suffix *raṇ*. This supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) is for the sake of the augment *iṭ*; however, the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] instead.
The established form alone is restated here. The term “u” is a general reference to both the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc*.

With the intention that since the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth is not yet established (*asiddha*), the augment *iṭ* occurs first in the non-standard analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*) of derivation, and subsequently, due to the absence of its cause, the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth does not take place, he provides the example: *sāṃvahitram*.
*agnid*: [the suffix] *kvip*. This is a specific type of officiant (*ṛtvij*). However, in the phrase "vamagnidṛtāyate," the shortening [of the vowel] is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Regarding *āgnidhram*: the point is that because it is prescribed as a *bha*-stem, the substitution of the voiced unaspirated sound (*jaś*) for the *ha* does not occur. "So'pi" (that too).
The meaning is "from the *āgnīdhra* priest. Now, one might object: "In forms such as *ibāgnidhrātave*, an initial udātta accent is employed;
if it is argued that this [word *āgnīdhra*] is finally accented because of the reading *uraṇ* in the Vārttika, [we reply:
regarding this, they say—the suffix *añ* prescribed by the Vārttika rule *āgnīdhrakasādhāraṇādañi*..."

When the suffix *añ* is used in its own sense (*svārtha*), it should be understood that the first syllable is acute (*udātta*) in that context. Regarding the rule "after *samidh*, [the suffix] *ṣeṇyaṇ* is used in the sense of placing": the word *samidhām* is in the genitive case denoting the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*).

The word *ādhāna* is derived from the root *dhā* with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the instrumental sense (*karaṇe*). Thus, after a word ending in the genitive denoting the object, the suffix *ṣeṇyaṇ* is applied in the sense of the instrument of placing.
It may be so. Regarding the term *sāmidhenyaḥ*: that by which fire is kindled is a *samit* (fuel-stick).

The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) because it belongs to the *saṃpad-ādi* group. The analysis of the compound is *tasyā ādhānam* ("the placing of that"). [The word] *sāmidhenī* [is formed] with the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* due to the presence of the *ṣit* marker; the *y* is elided by the rule *halas taddhitasya*. It is that *ṛc* verse by which the fuel is placed.

That which is used for placing the fuel-sticks is called a *sāmidhenī*; this is the meaning. The verses beginning with “*raṣo vājā abhidyavaḥ*” and ending with “*ājuhotā duvasyata*” are conventionally designated as *sāmidhenīs*.
(1153) [The suffix] *yat* is applied after the word *ratha* etc. (Pāṇini 4.3.121).

This is an exception to [the suffix] *aṇ*. With reference to the Vārttika "after *ratha*, when it means a part of a chariot," he says: "the wheel is *rathya*. Regarding the rule "after *ratha*, *sītā*, and *hala*, when there is the prescription of *yat*," the extension of the rule to include words ending in those stems (*tadanta-vidhi*) is added as a supplement: *paramarathyam*, *uttamarathyam*.

The word *dviratha* means the parts (*aṅga*) of two chariots; here, the suffix *yat* is elided by the rule "the elision of *yat* occurs when it does not denote a descendant" (*vigorluganapatye*). Now, if the suffix *yat* is intended here only in the sense of "a part of a chariot," then how is the form *rathyaḥ* (meaning "one who carries a chariot") derived? If you say it is by the rule "that which carries" (*advahati*), then let this very [suffix] be [the one applied].

If it is argued that, since [the suffix] should be applied as in *rathāṅga* when it carries [something], the mention of *ratha* (chariot) should be omitted from the rule *advahati rathayugaprāsaṅgam*, we say: not so. For in the case of *dvirathyaḥ* ("that which carries two chariots"), there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision (*luk*) of the *prāgdīvyatīya* suffix by the rule *vigorluganapatye*.

Regarding the form *advahati*, because the suffix *yat* does not belong to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group, there is no elision (*luk*); thus, the form *virathya* is established. Now, one might object: since the word *aci* is drawn back (via *ākarṣaṇa*) from the rule *vigorluganapatye*, how can [the elision] apply here after the suffix *yat*?

If it is argued that there is the undesirable consequence of elision (*luk*), the following is said in response: In the rule *tadvahati*, the mention of "chariot" (*ratha*) itself is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that elision occurs even for [stems] beginning with a consonant (*hal*) after the suffix *yat*. Otherwise, the mention of "chariot" in that rule would be entirely purposeless. And thus, in the analysis (*vigraha*) of "the limb of two chariots" (*dvayo rathayoraṅgam*).
The usage *driratha* is correct because it is well-established.

(1154) *patrapūrvādañ* |4|3|122|. [The suffix] *añ* follows a word preceded by *patra*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule regarding *yat*. Regarding *patra*: it is that by which one flies (*patanti anena*).

In the compound *vigrahe*, the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied by the rule beginning with *āmni*. Regarding the phrase *aśvarathasyedam*: the meaning is "a part of that which is an *aśvaratha*," where an *aśvaratha* is a chariot yoked with horses. [The suffix] *aṇ* is the exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix *iñ*]. Regarding *patrādvāhya*: [the term] *patrādvāhya* means "that which is to be carried on a leaf. Here, in the word *pattra*, the meaning is taken; however, the other [term]...
In determining the specific form [of a word], the commentary itself is the sole refuge.

(1155) *Dvandvād vun vairamaithunikayoḥ* | Pāṇini 4.3.125. The suffix *vun* after a *dvandva* compound. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*; however, it subverts *aṇ* because it is taught later in the sequence. For example: *kākolūkikā*.

The meaning is "the enmity between the crow and the owl. According to Amara’s lexicon, under the section on feminine nouns, it states: *vunnantaṃ striyām* (words ending in the suffix *vuñ* are feminine) and *vairamaithunikādibub* (the suffix *buñ* is applied after *vaira*, *maithunika*, etc.). Regarding *kutsakuśikikā*: it means the matrimonial union of Kutsa and Kuśika; that is to say, a relationship in the form of marriage. *Mithunam*... [is the word for] a couple.

Indeed, for a husband and wife (*dampatī*), there is the accomplishment of his ritual actions (*karma-kriyā-niṣpādanam*). The suffix *vuñ* is applied here because the word belongs to the *manojña*-class;

and since this [derivative] ends in *vuñ*, it is feminine by its very nature. On this point, they say: another analysis is also possible—*kutsāś ca kuśikāś ca* (the Kutsas and the Kuśikas), [meaning] "the union (*maithunika*) of those [two groups]," namely the Kutsus and the Kuśikas. Here, both the Kutsus and the Kuśikas...
And thus, one should not insist that the suffix *vuñ* applies only when two [names] are in a copulative compound (*maithunika*).

For in the commentary on the rule *yūni luk*, Kaiyaṭa, having cited examples such as *atribharadvājikā* by way of illustration, explained that the suffix *vuñ* follows from a copulative compound ending in the plural number. [The following rules apply: *saṅghāṅka-pūrvasya*.

There is the objection that [the term] *ghoṣavat* must also be mentioned; for it is said, "there must be a mention of *ghoṣavat*. And thus, since there are three bases (*prakṛti*) and four qualifiers of the meaning of the suffixes (*pratyayārthaviśeṣaṇa*), due to this inequality, the rule of correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*) does not apply.
It occurs [in the form] *gārgya*. By the rule *apatyasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.150), there is the elision of *ya*.

Although it is well known that *aṅka* and *lakṣaṇa* are synonyms—as Amarasimha states: "Ornament (*alaṅkāra*), mark (*aṅka*), sign (*lāñchana*), token (*cihna*), characteristic (*lakṣma*), and mark (*lakṣaṇa*)"—nevertheless, by virtue of their being mentioned separately here, [the distinction is maintained].

He states that the purpose is to specify a particular [type of] relationship: "successive connection" (*paramparā-sambandha*). For example, the relationship belonging to a cow and so forth with its owner is mediated by the cow. "Directly" (*sākṣāt*): for example, the knowledge of the Bidas; or a hamlet (*ghoṣa*) is the abode of Ābhīras. The fact that the suffix is marked with *ṇ* (i.e., *ṇit*) is for the sake of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, and for the sake of prohibiting the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*). [Thus we have] *baudī*.
*Vaidīvidyaḥ* means one whose knowledge is *vaida-vidyā*. The meaning is: one who possesses that knowledge which is unique to the *Bidas*.
(1156) *Chandogaukthikayājñikabahvṛcanaṭāññyaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.3.129. *Chandoga-ukthika-*: the [suffixes] beginning with *saṅgha* have been excluded. From these [words], the suffix *ñya* is applied.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied in the sense of "this belongs to him" (*syātasyedam*) as an exception to [the rule for] words denoting Vedic schools (*caraṇa*).

However, it is an exception to the general suffix *aṇ* in the case of *naṭa*. Because of the statement "in the sense of the Dharma and the Āmnāya," it does not apply here in cases such as *chāndogaṃ kulam* ("a family of the Chandogas").

(1157) *na daṇḍamāṇavāntevāsiṣu* || 4.3.130 || The word *daṇḍa-* [is mentioned]; *tasyedam* ("belonging to this") is understood to follow. "In those [cases], namely among the students" (*teṣu śiṣyeṣu*)—this is the remainder [of the sense], [meaning] when the suffix-meaning is qualified by these. *Dākṣāḥ* ("the descendants of Dakṣa"): [this is formed] with the suffix *aṇ* by the rule *iñaśca*.

(1158) *Raivatikādibhyaś chaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.3.131. The suffix *cha* is applied after [the names] beginning with Raivatika. The word *raivatika* ends in the suffix *ṭhak*, according to the rule *revatyādibhyaṣ ṭhak*.
Thus, *raivatika*, *audameghi*, *vaijavāpi*, and so forth—these are the words beginning with Raivatika.

Since the suffix *vuñ* would have applied previously due to the condition of being a *gotra* name, he says "it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *vuñ*" in order to prescribe the suffix *cha*. Anticipating the objection that the suffix *iñ* might apply instead, he says: (1159) *kaupiñjala-hāstipadād-aṇ* [should be stated]. 4.3.132.

"Because of a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) in this very case": that which has a foot like the foot of an elephant is *hastipādaḥ*. The elision of the suffix *-pād-* does not occur here, because of the rule stating "after *hasti* and others.
Thus he says: "of *hastipāda*" [and] "*hāstipadaḥ*"; from this very irregularity, the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
The word *padbhāva* means "the state of becoming *pad*" (as in *pad-vidha*).

(1160) *Ātharvaṇikasyekalopaśca* | Pāṇini 4.3.133. [The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the word *atharvan* to form *ātharvaṇika*,] and there is the elision of the final *i* of *ātharvaṇika*. [The term] *ātharvaṇika* [is derived as follows]: the Veda proclaimed by Atharvan is called *Atharvā*; this is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the name of the author to the work itself.

One who studies that [text] is called *ātharvaṇika*. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied because it begins with the word *vasantādi*; the absence of *ṭilopa* (elision of the final vowel and following consonant) occurs due to the specific rule (*nipātana*) in the *dāṇḍināyana*-group. Others, however, say: one who studies what was proclaimed by Atharvan is an *ātharvaṇika*.
