Here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "proclaimed by"; thereafter, the rule *chandobrāhmaṇāni* applies.

Since the word *ātharvaṇa* is also recited among "Vasanta" and the others when denoting that subject matter, the suffix *ṭhak* applies to the student; by the force of its specific injunction, the elision (*lu*) does not occur after a word ending in the suffix *prokta*.
Thus, in the *Tattvabodhinī*, the secondary derivative suffixes (*śaiṣika*) are completed.
(802) *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathām ānakṣe* [Pāṇini 5.4.74]. The term *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathām* is in the nominative singular with its case-ending elided; the governing heading *amāsāntāḥ* is also in force.
Therefore, he says: "An affix beginning with *ā* is an integral part (*antāvayava*) at the end of a compound."

Although the word *akṣe* is heard in a general sense, it is connected specifically with *dhur* (the axle) due to semantic propriety (*sāmarthya*), and not with other [words]. With this intention, he explains: "the *dhur* which is on the *akṣa*. However, it is not so for that which ends in *tad*. In the sūtra, the locative case is used because the related member (*saṃbandhin*) is intended to be expressed as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Therefore, that which is related to the *akṣa*...

The meaning is that it does not apply to *dhūstadaṃta*. If this were explained here as "when there is 'na' in the prior member (*pūrvapada*)," then the prohibition would not apply in the case of *ṛḍhadhūrakṣaḥ*. However, if it were explained as "when there is the object of the compound (*samāsārtha*) in the prior member," then it would not apply in the case of *ṛkṣadhūḥ*.

Therefore, for the sake of including both cases, the aforementioned explanation alone is superior. Regarding the term *ardharca*: the compound is formed according to the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*. [In the alternative form] *ardharcaḥ*, the masculine gender is applied according to the rule *ardharcaḥ puṃsi ca*.
Regarding *anṛk* and so forth: because no specific compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) has been prescribed, the suffix *kap* is added by the rule *eṣādvibhāṣā*.
It should also be understood that *ṭha-nṛcakram* and *a-hvacakram* are likewise formed. Regarding *viṣṇupuram*:
although this is established even when the word *pura* is used in a compound, the term *pūḥ* is nevertheless included in the sūtra in order to prevent the undesirable form *viṣṇupūḥ*.

(803) *vdyantarūpasargebhyo’pa īt* |6|3|97|. The meaning is that [the rule applies] to that which has already formed a compound-ending (*samāsānta*), as indicated by the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *yena vidhis tadantasya* with the examples "āpastiṣṭhanti" and "svāpastiṣṭhanti. Examples include *antarīpam* and so forth; [these refer to things] situated within (*antargatāḥ*).

The analysis of the compound is: "those which are adverse (pratikūla) and yet joined (saṅgata) with it. The mention of the prefix (*upasarga*) is intended to indicate [the rule's application] to *pra* and the other prefixes as well. Regarding the form *samāpa*: the intention is that because it is not a prefix (*anupasarga*), the substitution of *ī* does not occur.
However, in the Bhāṣya it is stated: "A prohibition of the substitution of *ī* must be stated for *amāpa*. And that...

It should be understood that [the term] is intended to convey the specific meaning of the form of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), because of the mention of "proximity" (*amīpasamṛddhi*) and because of the example cited in the Bhāṣya, namely "in the vicinity" (*amīpe*). Regarding the word *devayajana*: it refers to the sacrificial site, based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that in which the gods are worshipped" (*ijyante*). Regarding the word *sva*: [it is used here] because of the rule "not after a word of worship" (*a pūjanāt*).

There is an absence of the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). [The rule] "optionally after a word ending in *a*" means: regarding the sūtra *ṭvdyanta*, it should be stated that "the substitution of long *ī* applies when not preceded by an *a*-vowel. This is so that it does not apply here in the case of *rāpam parāpam*.
The meaning is that it is because of the statement in the Bhāṣya, and because of the statement in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *atiśca* (*Pāṇini 6.1.137*), namely "rephaṃ pareṣām.
(804) *ūdanordeśe* (Pāṇini 6.3.98).

Regarding *ūdanoḥ*: the long vowel is for the purpose of indicating a word-break (*avagraha*) in certain recensional branches (*śākhā*). However, the Bahvṛcas do not break the word at *anu* in the phrase *ṭhanūpe gomān gobhiḥ*. As for *anūpa*: it is a region where water has followed into it; thus, *anūpa* means a marshy place. Amarasimha states: "A place abounding in water is called *anūpa*."
(805) *Ac* [is added] after *prati*, *anu*, and *ava* when preceded by *samaloman*.

[The example] *pratisāmam* is either an *avyayībhāva*, a *prādi*-compound (*tatpuruṣa*), or a *bahuvrīhi*. The same should be inferred for *anusāmam* and *avasāmam*. [The example] *kṛṣṇodak* [is formed] by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) with the suffix *ṭhañ*.

The meaning of this is already understood; the subsequent commentary is likewise. The terms beginning with *ṛṣṇabhūma* are *bahuvrīhi* compounds. Regarding *padmanābha*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one who has a lotus (*padma*) at his navel (*nābhi*).
Due to its inclusion in the *gaḍvādigaṇa*, the word ending in the locative case is placed last. Alternatively, it means "one whose navel has the form of a lotus."
Or likewise, *ūrṇanābha* should also be understood in this way; however, in that case, the specific difference is the shortening [of the vowel] by the rule *yāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasor hrasvaḥ*.
(806) [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *akṣi*] except when it refers to the eye. 5.4.76.
"Seeing" (*darśana*) is that by which one sees; it refers to the eye.

With the intention that the non-primary sense is being grasped here through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the word *akṣi* (which denotes that), he says: "from a synonym of 'non-eye'. Regarding *gavākṣa*: "rays" (*gāvaḥ*) are light-beams; the word *akṣi* denotes an aperture. This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

(807) *acatura-vicatura-sucatura-strī-puṃsa-dhenu-anaḍuh-ṛksāma-vāṅmanasa-akṣi-bhruva-dāra-gava-ūrvaṣṭhīva-padaṣṭhīva-ahardiva-rātrindiva-ahaḥsvara-rajani-niḥśreyasa-puruṣāyuṣa-dvyāyuṣa-tryāyuṣa-ṛgyajuṣa-jātokuṣa-mahokṣa-vṛddhokṣa-upaśuna-goṣṭhaśvāḥ* || 5.4.77 || The words beginning with *acatura* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*). The purpose of this irregular formation (*nipātana*) is to restrict the specific type of compound in which they occur.

And there is the elision of the *ṭi* sound and so forth. He states this with the words "the first ones" and "bahuvrīhis. The meaning is that they are exclusively bahuvrīhis. The implication is that by this rule, *tatpuruṣas* such as *acatvāraḥ* and *vicatvāraḥ* remain exactly as they are. In the same way, the restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) should be understood in subsequent cases as well.

The word *tryupābhyām* [is explained as follows]: it is taught that [the suffix *ac*] is applied after the words *tri* and *upa* when they signify "four. Regarding *tricaturaḥ*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "three or four. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule *saṃkhyā-vyaya-āsanna...*. The suffix *ac* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ḍac* prescribed by the rule *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye*. [The example] *akṣibhruvam* [is likewise formed].

Because they are parts of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), there is a singular compound (*ekavadbhāva*): *ūrū cāṣṭhīvantau ca* ("the two thighs and the two knee-joints"). According to Amara: "The word *akthi* is neuter, while *ūru* is masculine"; and also: "*Aṣṭhīvat* preceded by *anu-*, *ūru-*, or *pūrva-* is not feminine. Thus, we have *ūrv-aṣṭhīvam* and *pada-aṣṭhīvam*. Because they are parts of a living being, there is a singular compound. This is a *dvandva* [compound].
"It is elided" means that the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from among dissimilar forms) in the case of "virūpāṇām apū" is set aside; this is the remainder of the sense.

Regarding *sarajasam*: the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs by the rule "avyayībhāve cākāle. As for the usage *sarajaḥ paṅkajam*, the employment of the word *sarajasam* in Māgha’s verse—"sarajasamakarandabharāsu" (*in [the lotuses] laden with pollen and nectar*)—is to be considered problematic.

Such is the intended meaning. Regarding the term *niḥśreyān*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that by which the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) is ascertained (*niścitaṃ*). The example *iḥ śreyaskaḥ* cited by some is incorrect, because the suffix *kap* is prohibited by the rule *īyasaśca*. Regarding *goṣṭhe śvā*: by this, the restriction that [the compound] must be a locative *tatpuruṣa* alone is [refuted].
This has been shown; therefore, in a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound, it is simply *oṣṭhaśva*.
(808) Pāṇini 5.4.78: *brahmahastibhyāṃ varcasaḥ*. [The form] *brahmavarcasam* is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound. Likewise, *hastivarcasam* as well.

And it should be stated [that the suffix *cha* is added] after the words *palya* and *rājñ*. Regarding *palya*: that which deserves meat (*pala*) is a *palya*, meaning one who eats meat; its excrement is *palyavarcas*.
(809) [The suffix *cha* is added] after the word *tamas* when preceded by *ava*, *saṃ*, or *anda*. Pāṇini 5.4.79.

In the compound *avatamasaṃ* and so forth, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the darkness that has descended" (*avahīnaṃ saṃtataṃ ca tamaḥ*). Regarding the word *andhayati*: the root *andh*, meaning "to impair sight," belongs to the *curādi* class. The form *andham* means "intense" (*gāḍham*).
(Pāṇini 5.4.80: *śvas-śvasīyaś-śreyasaḥ*.
Regarding the word *śvas*, those who explain it as being derived from the word *vasu* by adding the suffix *īyasun* according to the rule "from words signifying excellence...
are to be disregarded; this is what the author indicates by stating "the word *vasu*. The sense is that the Vedic usage "He who should desire:
'May I become more prosperous (*vasīyān*')" is also favorable to this interpretation.

Regarding the word *śvas*: although this term generally denotes time, in the present context it refers to a specific meaning due to the inherent nature of its expressive power (*śakti*). He states this very point: "the praise of the meaning of the subsequent member.
This means "the praise that constitutes the meaning of the subsequent member. [The phrase] "the object of a benediction" (*āśīrviṣayam*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
The word *viṣaya* is used here in the masculine gender because it is *ajahalliṅga* (retaining its original gender regardless of the referent).
There is a variant reading in some places: *'utarapadārthapraśaṃsāyā āśīrviṣayatām āha'*.
In either case, the resulting meaning is that this [word] indicates the state of being an object of benediction (*āśīrviṣayatā*).

(811) *anvavataptādrahasaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.4.81. Regarding *anvava*: here, *rahaḥ* signifies "that which is not manifest" (*aprakāśam*). The compound *anvavahīna-rahaḥ* is either a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound) meaning "that which has followed or surpassed secrecy," or a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which secrecy has followed or been surpassed."
*Ptarahasamiti*: the analysis of the compound is "that which is both *āpta* (attained) and *rahas* (secret).

The meaning is "that which cannot be understood by another. Regarding the phrase "prior to this": the intention is based on the statement in the Vārttika, "The term *pūrva* (prior) must be included in the definition of the *bahuvrīhi*."

(812) *kimaḥ kṣepe* [Pāṇini 5.4.70]. Regarding *kimaḥ kṣepe*: the mention of *kṣepa* (reproach/contempt) here could have been omitted, because by the *pratipadokta-paribhāṣā* (the rule concerning specifically prescribed terms), only that compound formed by the rule *iṃ kṣepe* [2.1.64] would be understood. Examples include *kiṃrājaḥ* and so forth. What is there?
In this question, there is either a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) or a descriptive determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*).
(813) *nañastatpuruṣāt* | 5.4.71. [The word] "from a *tatpuruṣa* following *nañ*"—here, "of *añ*" is in the genitive. A *tatpuruṣa* which is related to *nañ*...
Therefore, the meaning is that it consists of the negative particle (*nañ*) as its constituent member.
(814) *patho vibhāṣā* | Pāṇini 5.4.72. [The example is] *apathaṃ vartate* ("he proceeds by a non-path"). This is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of the absence of the object.
Thus end the suffixes applied to the ends of compounds common to all types of compounds.
Thus ends the section on compound-final suffixes in the *Tattvabodhinī*.

(825) *gharūpakalpaceladbruvagotramatahateṣu ṅyo’nekāco hrasvaḥ* |6|3|43| [The suffix] *ṅīp* is applied after a word ending in the feminine suffix *ṅī*, provided it consists of more than one syllable, when followed by the suffixes *gha*, *rūpa*, *kalpa*, *cela*, *bruva*, *gotra*, *mata*, or *hata*; furthermore, the short vowel is substituted for the final long vowel of the stem.
*gha*: The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are designated as *gha*. *rūpa*: The suffix *rūpa* is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). *cela*: The word *cela* means "garment" (*vasana*).

The word *celaḍ* is listed as having a *ṭi*-marker in the *pacādi* group for the purpose of [forming] the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. Regarding the phrase "in the case of suffixes": the intention is that by the mention of *lekha*, it will be made known that under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the final member (*uttarapada*), there is no inclusion of that which ends with the suffix when the suffix itself is being mentioned. In the example *brāhmaṇitarā*, because of the prohibition [by the rule] *jāteśca*, the [application of the suffix] *tasil* etc. does not occur.
The substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs. Regarding *celī*: because the root *celaṭ* is listed in the *pacādi* group, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*.
Regarding *āmalakī*: the words *āmalakī* and *kuvalī* are invariably feminine when referring to a tree.
(Pāṇini 6.3.44): *nadyāḥ śeṣasyānyatarasyām* ("In the case of a river-name, for the remainder [of the compound], optionally").

The remainder [of the rule] has been stated; and since that [remainder] is twofold, he says: "ending in a verbal root" (*aṅyanteti*). This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). With the intention that even the term *bhāṣitpuṃska* is not connected here, he says: "other than feminine" (*strītara*). (Pāṇini 6.3.45) *ugitaśca*.

"Any river that comes after [a stem ending in] *ugit*"—this was stated on the assumption that the technical designation *nadī* applies even to [stems ending in] *ī* and *ū* when they are used alone. "The one who knows more" (*viduṣitarā*)—here, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ugitaśca*, and there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *vasu* [suffix]. "In the Vṛtti and other works"—this refers to the grammatical analysis (*prakriyā*) and its commentaries.
These are included by the word "etcetera" (*cādi*).
(828) *Hṛdayasya hṛd-lekha-yadaṇ-lāseṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.50).

Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of that which ends in the suffix *aṇ*": because of its association with the suffix *aṇ*, the word *lekha* is indicated here specifically as ending in the suffix *aṇ*.
This is the intended meaning. [Objection: But in that case, the mention of the letter *la* would be useless, since the desired result is already established by the mention of the letter *a* alone;

to this he says: "It is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For this very reason, it has been explained that in the rules concerning *gha*, *rūpa*, and *kalpa*, there is no inclusion of those ending in those suffixes (*tadantagrahaṇa*).

(829) *vā śoka-ṣyañ-rogeṣu* |6|3|51|. Regarding *sauhārdyam*: the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class; by the rule *hṛdbhagasindhvante*, there is vṛddhi of both members [of the compound].

(830) *pādasya padājyātigopahateṣu* | Pāṇini 6.3.52. The word *pāda* is replaced by *pada* before the words *āja*, *ati*, *ga*, and *upahata*. Since the subsequent rule contains the mention of *pad*, this substitute *pada* ends in a short vowel *a*; the absence of the case-ending (*vibhakti-luk*) is due to Vedic usage (*sautra*). Thus he says: "the substitute ends in a short *a*. By this, forms such as *padaga* are established.

(831) *padyatyatadarthe* |6|3|53|. [The word] *padyā* is formed with the suffix *yat* by the rule *vidhyatyadhanuṣā*. [The word] *pādyam* is formed with the suffix *yat* by the rule *ādārghābhyāṃ ca*.
In the preceding sūtra, in the list beginning with *ājya*, only the limbs of living beings were intended.

Since the sense of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is possible here as well, the word *pāda* is understood here as denoting that [instrument] alone, not as denoting a measure (*parimāṇa*). Therefore, in the case of "purchased for two feet" (*dvipādyam*, *tripādyam*), the substitution of *pada* [for *pāda*] does not occur by the rule "before *aṇ*, *pāda*, *māṣa*, etc. And this...
This is clear from the works of Vṛtti and Haradatta.

(832) *himakāṣihatiṣu ca* [Pāṇini 6.3.54]. Regarding *patkāṣī*: the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *supyajātau* [Pāṇini 3.2.78]. Regarding *paddhiti*: the suffix *ktin* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).

(833) *ṛcaḥ śe* | 6|3|55|. Regarding *ṛcaḥ śe*: the term ‘e’ is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the suffix *śas*. The sense is that since the word *pāda* does not occur among the *lomādi* group, the suffix *śas* cannot apply in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).

(834) *vā ghoṣamiśraśabdeṣu* ||6|3|56|| Regarding the word *paccchabda*: [the suffix] *śas* is applied by the rule *aṅkhyaikavacanācca vīpsāyām*. (835) *udakasyodaḥ saṃjñāyām* ||6|3|57|| [The substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-* occurs when it forms part of a name.]
"Udamegha": this is a name for a person based on similarity. (836) *peṣa-āvasa-vāhana-dhiṣu ca* |6|3|58|.
"Udapeṣam": [the suffix] *ṇamul* is applied by the rule *nehane piṣaḥ*. "Udadhiḥ": water.
The analysis of the compound is: "that in which something is placed" (*dhīyate asmin*). The suffix *ki* is applied by the rule *karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca*. (Pāṇini 3.3.93).

[The rule] *manthaudanasaktuvinduvajrābhārahāravīvadhagāheṣu ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.60) [applies]. Regarding *udamantha*: *mantha* refers to parched barley flour (*saktu*) prepared with a liquid substance—specifically, with water.
Regarding the analysis of *manthaḥ*, Haradatta maintains that it is a compound formed by the rule *ṛtīya-* through the application of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules).

It should be stated that this [formation] does not apply to indeclinables (*avyaya*) that undergo the substitution of *iy* or *uvaṅ*. For example, in *śuklībhāvaḥ*, the status of being an indeclinable arises from its being an indeclinable particle (*nipāta*) because it ends in the suffix *cv-i* according to the rule *ūry-ādi-cvi-ḍācaś-ca*.

It should be stated as "of *abhru*, *kuaṃsa*, and so forth. Thus, *bhrūkuaṃsa* and so on. Amara states: "A dancer is called *hrakuaṃsa*, *bhukuaṃsa*, and *bhrūkuaṃsa*. And: "*Andrī*, *pramīlā*, *bhrakuṭi*, and *bhrūkuṭi* are feminine [terms for a frown]."
(838) *ekataddhite ca* | Pāṇini 6.3.62. [The word] "eka" [is used] even when a *taddhita* suffix follows. The word "ekasya" is stated with the genitive case elided; thus he says: "of the word *eka*.
The prescription of the short vowel for this [word] is useful only when it ends in *ṭāp*, and not when it is used alone, because of its very nature.

Because of its brevity, he explains it as follows: "come from one," and so forth. (839) *Pāṇini 6.1.13*: "There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *ṣyaṅ* [suffix] before the words *putra* and *pati* in a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Regarding the word *ṣyaṅ*: here, by the term *tatpuruṣa*, both the prior member (*pūrvapada*) and the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) are implied; therein, of the *ṣyaṅ*...

He states "of that which ends in ṣyaṅ" because the preceding member is a qualifier, which implies that [the term] ending in that [suffix] is understood. Regarding the phrase "when putra and pati are the subsequent members": the intention is that if one were to explain it as "ending in putra and pati," there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *ārīṣagandhyāparamaputraḥ*.

(840) *saṃprasāraṇasya* |6|3|139|. The term *saṃprasāraṇasya* [is the heading]. The phrase *uttarapade* is supplied as a governing rule (*adhikāra*). From the rule *hallope*, the word *dīrghaḥ* is understood to follow.
Thus he says: "There shall be lengthening (*dīrghaḥ*) in the subsequent member (*uttarapade*). Here, the lengthening is [governed] by the rule *halaḥ*.
It does not apply, because since the *pratyaya* is elided by *luk*, the designation of the *aṅga* (base) does not occur.
Regarding the form *kaumudagandhyāyāḥ*: [the derivation is as follows: the feminine offspring of *kumudagandhi* is *kaumudagandhyā*.
When the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "asyāpatyam," the substitution *ṣyaṅ* occurs by the rule "ṭhaṇiñoḥ. Then, by the rule "ṣyaṅśca āp," the feminine suffix *āp* is added.

[Objection: But surely, in cases such as *aumudagandhīputraḥ*, there ought to be shortening by the rule *ṭhiko hrasvo’ṅgyo’gālavasya*; the prescription of the long vowel, however, would have its scope in the alternative case. To this, he says: "by means of a restricted option" (*vyavasthitavibhāṣayā*). "Not here" means that there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) in this instance.

Regarding *atikārīṣa*: one who has surpassed Kārīṣagandhyā is *atikārīṣagandhyaḥ*; his son [is *atikārīṣagandhyaputraḥ*]. (841) *iṣṭakeṣīkāmālānāṃ citatūlabhāriṣu* | Pāṇini 6.3.65. [In these cases, the feminine suffix is replaced by the masculine. When *iṣṭakā*, *iṣīkā*, and *mālā* are followed respectively by *cita*, *tūla*, and *bhārin*, [the feminine suffix is elided]. [Examples: *iṣṭakā-citaḥ*, *iṣīkā-tūlam*, *mālā-bhārin*.]
Regarding *iṣṭakacitam*: it is a third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) according to the rule "when [the agent or] the instrument is expressed by a *kṛt* suffix.
Regarding *pakveṣṭakacitam*: the intention is that, because of the governing heading *pada*, the rule for [compounds ending in] a specific element (*tadanta-vidhi*) applies.
Regarding *mālabhārī*: the meaning is "one who bears a garland" (*mālām bibharti*). The suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule "*supyajātau*."
‘Ṭhhāriṣu’ is an alternative reading.
(842) *kāre satyagadasya* |6|3|70|.
Regarding the word *kāre*, [the commentary] says—“*mum* shall occur”—because of the continued application (*anuvartana*) from the rule *arurdviṣad...* up to that point.

*Satyaṅkāraḥ* means the making of an oath. Even in the absence of an oath, by the rule "atyādaśapate," the suffix *ḍāc* is set aside, and only *mum* is applied due to the presence of *pat*. *Agadaṅkāraḥ* means a physician. It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after the root *as* (to be). *Astuṅkāraḥ* means an agreement; that is, saying "astu" (so be it).
An indeclinable (avyaya) that resembles a verb ending (tiṅanta).

[The rule] "dhenorbhavyāyām" [means]: *dhenubhavyā*—the meaning is "a cow that will be. Because of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the rule "havyageye," the suffix *kṛtya* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). And she is both a cow (*dhenu*) and one who is to be (*bhavyā*). If...

This is the analysis of the compound. However, in the Gautama-smṛti, regarding the term *adhenubhavyā*, it should be understood that the augment *mum* is applied due to its being an archaic (ārṣa) usage.
As for *lokampṛṇa*: the root *pṛṇ* has the meaning "to please" (*prīṇana*). Haradatta, however, states that the root *ṛṇati* has the sense of "filling" (*pūraṇa*).
Regarding *anabhyāśam ity anabhyāśasya*: "having approached" (*itvā*) means having gone near (*abhyāśam*).

That which is different from that is *anabhyāśam*. The suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *iṇ* by the rule *heti-tu-śās-vṛ-dṛ-ju-ṣaḥ*. In the examples *bhrāṣṭrāyor indhe* ("he kindles two frying pans") and *bhrāṣṭram indhaḥ* ("one who kindles a frying pan"), there is a compound with an object (*karman*) as a subordinate member (*upapada*).
The same applies to *agnimindh* as well.

Regarding *gile’gileḥ* and *gile’gilasya*: when the word *gila* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the augment *mum* is added for the sake of excluding *agila*. *Timiṅgila* refers to a specific kind of fish.
The suffix *ka* is applied to the root *gṛ* (to swallow) because it belongs to the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*. The substitution of *la* for *ṛ* occurs by the rule *ṭhaci vibhāṣā*.

Regarding the forms *giligila* and *gilagila*: this [sūtra] was commenced based on the analysis *gilagila* as "one who swallows a *gila*" (*ilaṃ gilati iti gilagilaḥ*), specifically "the swallower of whales" (*timīnāṃ gilagilaḥ*).

(843) *rātreḥ kṛti vibhāṣā* | P. 6.3.72. Regarding the rule *rātreḥ kṛti*: although, within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), there is generally no inclusion of a word ending in [the specified element] when the term itself is mentioned as a suffix, nevertheless—since a primary derivative (*kṛt*) cannot occur immediately after the word *rātri*—this [vṛddhi substitution] applies when the subsequent member is a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix.
With the intention that this is a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*), he provides the example: "rātriṃcaraḥ.

Although a suffix such as *ṇvul* is possible after a root ending in *kvip* derived from the sense of habitual practice (*ācāra*), the point is that it is not accepted here because its semantic presence (*upasthiti*) is delayed. [The phrase] "always indeed" (*nityam eva*)...

The intention is that this is by way of a prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Regarding *rātrimmanya*: the suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule *ātmamāne khaśca*; because *khaś* is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*, the suffix *śyan* is applied when it follows.
(844) *sahasya saḥ saṃjñāyām* || 6.3.78 || [In a compound, the word *saha* is replaced by *sa* when a name is being formed.]

Regarding *sahayudhvā*: the suffix *kvanip* is applied by the rule *ahe ca*. Since there is a prohibition [of the feminine suffixes] *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* by the rule *vano na haśaḥ*, they do not occur even in the feminine. Regarding *samuhūrtam*: this is an *avyayībhāva* compound expressing a limit (*anta*).
Since the change to *sa-* is not applicable here—because of the exclusion of time (*kāla*) in the rule *avyayībhāve cā’kāle*—[the form is established as it is].
The inclusion of the word *antagrahaṇa* [is for the sake of excluding the first case].
(845) *dvitīye cānupākhye* | Pāṇini 6.3.80. Regarding *dvitīya*: it is well known in common usage that "that which is subordinate is called *dvitīya*."
That which is not perceptible is *upākhya*; that which is different from that is inferable (*anumeya*). Thus he says: "in the inferable" (*anumeye*).

[In the phrase] *sarākṣasīka*, the suffix *kap* is applied by the rule *adyatanaśca* (Pāṇini 5.2.12). Furthermore, by the rule *samānasya chandasyamūrdhaprabhṛtyudakeṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.84), the substitution of *sa* for *samāna* occurs in Vedic usage when followed by words other than *mūrdhan*, *prabhṛti*, and *udaka*.

The meaning is that the yoga is being analyzed; for this very purpose, even the Vedic rule *amānasyacchandasī* has been cited here. As for the term "bahuvrīhi," by that [rule], the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-*—via the rule *vopasarjanasya*—would otherwise apply.
The state [of being]. (847) *Jyotis*, *janapada*, *rātri*, *nābhi*, *nāman*, *gotra*, *rūpa*, *sthāna*, *varṇa*, *vayas*, *vacana*, and *bandhu*: Pāṇini 6.3.85.
*Sajyotiḥ* means "having the same light" (*samānaṃ jyotir asya*), forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound. In which light...

Impurity that arises under the constellation Āditya and persists until its setting is called *sajyotis* (lasting as long as the light). Here, the compound is not understood as being formed by the rule "the middle term is elided when preceded by *amāna*, *madhya*, and *madhyama-vīra*," because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule "there is a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of words that are not identical in form" (*arūpāṇām ekaśeṣaḥ*). Rather, [it is understood differently].
"Even a *bahuvrīhi* [is possible]," says Haradatta.
(848) *caraṇe brahmacāriṇi* |6|3|86|. Regarding the word *brahmacārī*: the suffix *ṇini* is applied by rule 5.2.101 (*vrate*). Thus, *sabrahmacārī* means "a fellow student" (*samāno brahmacārī*).

And there is the commonality of the *brahmacārin*—due to the commonality of *brahman*. Consequently, the resulting meaning is: "one who observes the vow (*vratacārī*) within the common *brahman*. (849) *tīrthe ye* 6|3|87.

In the word *tīrthe*, the letter *a* is not intended to be significant; however, the qualifier *pratyaye* (in an affix) is obtained through the commentary. Therefore, by the principle that "an operation [applies] to that which begins with [the element specified]," he states: "in an affix beginning with *ya*."

(850) *vibhāṣodare* |6|3|88|. It is intended [to show] that the compound (*samāsa*), which is conditioned solely by the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), is *antaraṅga* (internal); whereas the *yat* suffix is conditioned by the nominal stem (*subanta*) derived from that compound. Therefore, it [the *yat* suffix] does not possess priority (*paratva*).

This was stated with the intention that [the word] is possible. Regarding the term *sodarya*: in the sense of "one who has lain in the same womb" (*amānodare śayitaḥ*), when the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs prior to the suffix, the suffix *ya* is applied by the rule *odarādyaḥ*. However, in the alternative where the substitution of *sa-* does not occur, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *amānodare śayita o codātaḥ*.
‘Amānodaryaḥ’.

(851) *dṛg-dṛśa-vatuṣu* |6|3|89|. [The rule states: “*sadṛk-sadṛśa*” etc. [This is formed] because it is stated that “the suffixes *kvip* and *kan* are added to the root *dṛś* when combined with *amāna* and *anya*.”

Regarding "long" (*dīrgha*): the meaning is that when the substitution of *ā* for *adas* has been made, a long vowel is substituted by way of the rule for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*). This also applies to the preceding and following examples. (852) *bhīroḥ sthānam* (the place of the timid). 8.3.81.
Regarding the phrase "the position of a timid person": even when there is an intervention by the *visarjanīya*, the application of the rule for *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) occurs.
(853) *jyotirāyuṣaḥ stomaḥ* |8|3|83|.
[The example] is *jyotiṣaḥ stomaḥ*. Here, [in the case of] *jyotiḥ stomo’yam*, [the rule does not apply].
It is appropriate to cite the original form.
(854) *eti saṃjñāyām agāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.99).
Regarding *eti saṃjñāyām*: this is a subsidiary rule (*gaṇasūtra*) included within the *suṣāmādi* group.

(855) *nakṣatrādvā* |8|3|100|. Likewise, there is also the rule *akṣatrādvā*. Regarding the form *viṣvaksena*, the point is that because the substitution of *c* for *t* (*cartva*) is considered asiddha (not yet established), there is an intervention by the letter *g*.

(856) *aṣaṣṭhītṛtīyāsthasyānyasya dugāśīrāśāsthāsthitotsukotikārakarāgaccheṣu* || 6.3.99 || The word *aṣaṣṭhī* [in the sūtra] means "not standing in the sixth or third case. *Anyad-āśīḥ* and so forth are *karmadhāraya* compounds.

And this prohibition does not apply when [the word] is in a case-role (*kāraka*). Regarding the statement "this is not a prohibition," they say that although this would have been established by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī-tṛtīyā-sthasya* alone, the repetition of the negative particle (*nañ*) is for the purpose of indicating that the prohibition is not absolute (*anitya*).

And [the suffix] *trau*, and *trau*. This Vārttika is for the sake of excluding words beginning with *an*; it is already established by the very mention [in the rule] "from *atri* and others, the suffix *ḍhakañ*. (857) [The suffix] *kā* is used in the sense of "path" and "eye. 6.3.104.
"Kāpatham" means a contemptible path (*kutsitaḥ panthāḥ*). The suffix *a* is applied at the end of the compound by the rule "ṛkpūrabdhūḥ. Neuter gender is assigned by the rule "athaḥ saṅkhyāvyayādeḥ.
(858) "vibhāṣā puruṣe" [Pāṇini 6.3.106].
Regarding the term *aprāptavibhāṣā*: the intention is that [the condition] *īṣadarthe* does not recur [in the subsequent rules]. (859) *pṛṣodarādīni yathopadiṣṭam* | 6|3|109|.
"Words such as *pṛṣodara* and so forth" means: the word *ādi* here does not denote a fixed limit (*vyavasthā*).

The sense is that [the words] would be rendered meaningless according to how they were taught. Regarding the word "by the learned" (śiṣṭaiḥ): this is to be supplied by ellipsis. In the compound *yathopadiṣṭa*, there is an avyayībhāva with the sense of *yathā* (according to).
The root *diś* denotes the action of uttering. Thus, the meaning is: "those [words] which have been taught by the learned."
This being the case, he states the resulting conclusion: "just as they are uttered, so [they are].
This refers to non-compounded words (*asamāsa-pada*), because of the governing rule concerning the subsequent member of a compound (*uttara-pada-adhikāra*).
For non-compounded words established by the *Nirukta* and other treatises, it is simply "the *uṇādi* suffixes are applied diversely" (*uṇādayo bahulam*).
And because it is established. Although a restriction that [the rule] applies only to the domain of compounds is not tenable—

since the words *haṃsa* and *siṃha* are also cited as examples in the *Kārikā* of the Easterners (*prācām*)— nevertheless, their mention in that *Kārikā* is for the purpose of illustrating an example by supplying the word *yathā*.

They say that the statement of the rule—that [the word *sādhana*] has been formed but not as an example for the sutra under discussion—is indeed correct. Regarding "from the addition of a phoneme" (*varṇāgamāt*): from the root *han*, with the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class), there is the addition of the phoneme *s*.
Regarding "from transposition" (*viparyayāt*): from the root *hiṃs*, with the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class), there is an exchange of positions between the phonemes *ha* and *sa*.
"From words denoting directions, the word *tīra* optionally becomes *tāra*. This is a Vārttika rule.
"The same applies to the rule *uro dāśanāśe*.

In the case of *dur*, there is the substitution of *u* for the final vowel before the words *dāśa*, *nāśa*, *dabhra*, and *dhya*, as well as the retroflexion (*ṣṭutva*) of the initial consonant of the following member. "From the three beginning with *kha*... [refers to the rule *khali*].
The meaning is that *dāśanāśadabhāḥ*—all three—are formed with the suffix *khal* by the rule *iṣadduḥsuṣu*.

Regarding *bṛsī*: “A seat made of grass is called *bṛsī*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class defined by its form). Therefore, [the following applies]: "One may drop the *ṭha* suffix after *avaśyam* when followed by a *kṛtya* suffix; likewise, one may drop it after *tuṃ* and *kāma-manas-*; and [one may optionally drop it] after *sam-*."
The rule "hitatatayormāsasya paci yuḍghañvoḥ" is also included [here].

When a kṛtya suffix occurs as the final member of a compound, one should elide the final *m* of *avaśyam*. For example: *avaśyagantavyaḥ* (that which must necessarily be gone to), *avaśyasevyaḥ* (that which must necessarily be served). Likewise, the *m* of *tumaḥ* is elided when followed by *kāma* or *manas*.

One may elide the final syllable of *māṃsa*. When the suffixes *yu* or *ghañ* follow, if the verbal root *pac* follows immediately after, one may elide the final syllable of *māṃsa*. Examples: *māṃspacanam*, *māṃspākaḥ*.

When the suffixes *kta* or *ktavatu* follow, if the roots *gam* (to go), *man* (to intend), or *sad* (to sit) follow, one may optionally elide the final syllable of the prepositions *sam* and *pra*. Examples: *hitam* (from *sam-hita*), *saṃhitam*; *satatam* (from *pra-tatam*), *saṃtatam*.
When the suffixes *yu* or *ghañ* follow, if the verbal root *pac* follows immediately after, one may elide the final syllable of *māṃsa*. Examples: *māṃspacanam*, *māṃspākaḥ*.
It should be understood here that even the elision of a final consonant in a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) occurs due to the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
(860) *Saṃhitāyām* | 6|3|114|. This [rule] applies when there is *saṃhitā*; therefore, in cases such as *viguṇākarṇaḥ*, the long vowel does not occur in the *avagraha*.

They speculate on the intention of the Sūtra, [concluding] that this is a restrictive rule (adhikāra). Therefore, one should consider such purposes as the fact that in examples like *vidmā hi tvā*, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *vdyaco'tastiṅaḥ* does not occur at the time of the Pada-text recitation, and so forth.

(861) *nahivṛtivṛṣivyadhirucisahitaniṣu kvau* | Pāṇini 6.3.116. Regarding *nahivṛti*: *ṇaha* (to bind), *vṛt* (to turn/act), *vṛṣ* (to sprinkle), *vyadh* (to pierce/strike), *ruc* (to shine/delight), *sah* (to endure), and *an* (to spread).

Regarding the phrase "in those ending in *kvip*": the remainder [of the rule] is "in subsequent words" (*utarapadeṣu*). By this, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *ivaseṣu ruk*. *Upānat*: [derived] from the root *pad* with the prefix *upa*, in the sense of the object (*karma*), by adding *kvip* according to the *saṃpad-ādi* group.
*Nivṛt*: that which turns back (*nivartate*). *Prāvṛṭ*: that which rains forth (*pravarṣati*). [Marmāṇi vidhyati]: that which pierces the vital spots (*marmāṇi*).

*marmāvit*: from the root *vyadh* (to pierce), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *rahijyā*. *nīruk*: from *ni-ṛc*, meaning "one who observes. *ṛtīṣaṭ*: [one] who endures pain (*ṛti*). Haradatta states that the sibilant (*ṣ*) occurs according to the rule *ūrvapadāt*.
Regarding the rule *aheḥ pṛtanatībhyāṃ ca*, the word *aheḥ* [is used].
Others say that it is due to the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) or because the particle *ca* implies an unstated collection (*anuktasamuccaya*).
Still others maintain it is because the *suṣāmādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. [The form] *parītat* is derived from the root *tan* with the prefix *pari*, meaning "he stretches around.
In the rule *amaḥ kvau*, it is stated that "it should be said that [the elision applies] to *am* and so forth," and thus there is the elision of the nasal.

(862) *vanaṃ puragāmiśrakāsidhrakāsārikākoṭarāprebhyaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.4.4. Regarding the statement "of the word *vana*" (*vanaśabdasya*), he explains that *vana* is placed in the nominative case in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhārthe*) by way of transposition (*vyatyayena*). "From these alone" (*ebhya eva*) means that the substitution of *ṇa* occurs only for a following [suffix] when preceded by *puragā* and the others, provided they have a long vowel in their formation (*kṛtidīrgha*). From these... [etc.]

There is no suspicion of a reversed restriction—that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs only for *vana* and not for others—because it is impossible for words such as *puraga* to end in a long vowel when they appear as subsequent members other than *vana*.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of restriction," the intended meaning is as follows: [the rule] "in the case of *puragā* and *miśrakā*"...

From the long-vowel reading (*dīrghanirdeśāt*), it follows that *ṇatva* applies when there is a long vowel in the case of a non-name (*asaṃjñāyām*), whereas in the case of a name (*saṃjñāyām*), it applies when there is a short vowel. Thus, since the *ṇatva* of *vana-* is already established by the rule "after a preceding word ending in [a short vowel], provided it is a name" (*ūrvapadātsaṃjñāyām*), the mention again of the group of five beginning with *puraga-*— which have already undergone lengthening— in this rule for *ṇatva* serves a specific purpose.

"It is for the sake of restriction (niyamārtha) alone" means it is for the sake of an injunction (vidhyartha). The intention is that because [the word *puragā*] is not a proper name (*asaṃjñātvena*), the rule "after a preceding member [ending in a short vowel], if it is a proper name" (*ūrvapadātsaṃjñāyām*) does not apply. Nor is the mention of *puragā* itself for the sake of an injunction, because due to the intervention of the letter *g*, the application of the rule "after a preceding member [ending in a short vowel], if it is a proper name" is absent.
It must be stated that, by accepting the form "ṭhakaḥ" as being in the ablative case, the explanation is given as:

"there is no substitution of *ṇ* for a letter following a preceding word ending in *ā*. However, because the word *puragā* ends in the vowel *ā*, the prohibition "ṭhakaḥ" does not apply. For this very reason, regarding "ṭhakaḥ"...

In the *Ākara* (the original treatise), the example *ṛgayana* alone was cited, and [the rule] was refuted on the basis of the mention [*ṛgayanādibhyaḥ*]. [Examples include] *puragāvaṇam* and so forth;
these are names of specific hells. [The example] *asipatravanam* is [cited] under the rule *ebhyo vanasyaiva*.

The sense is that if the rule were reversed, the substitution of *ṇ* would be unavoidable here. He says "in the nominative" (*prathamā*) because the meaning of the locative case is included within the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
He provides an example of words such as *kiṃśuluka*, namely: *kiṃśulukāgiriḥ*.
The words to be included by the term "etc. (*ādiśabda*) are *ṭhañ*, *janāgiri*, and so forth. Why [is the word] *kiṃśuluka* mentioned? [To show that it is not included:
*kṛṣṇagiriḥ*, *rāmagiriḥ*. (863) *vale* 6.3.118.
Regarding *kṛṣīvala*: the suffix *valac* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*) by the rule *rajaḥ-kṛṣyāsutī-*.

(Pāṇini 5.2.112). Regarding *matau bahvaco ’najirādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.3.119): in the word *amarāvatī*, the *m* of the suffix *matup* is replaced [by *va*] either by the rule *ādupadhāyāś ca* or by the rule *saṃjñāyām*.
Since it is impossible for the suffix *ghañ* alone to function as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), he says: (865) *usargasya ghañyamanuṣye bahulam* [Pāṇini 6.4.93].
Regarding the term "ending in *ghañ*": *niṣāda*. The *pulinda* is a human caste.

A *niṣāda* is so called because "sin (*pāpa*) sinks (*niṣīdati*) in him. The suffix *ghañ* is applied here in the sense of location according to the rule *halaśca*. If it is asked, "How then is the word *pratīhāra* used for a doorkeeper?
they say: *pratīhāra* means a door; the name is applied to the person because of their identity with that [door].

(866) *citeḥ kapi* [Pāṇini 6.3.127]. In the form *ekacitīka*, the suffix *kap* is applied by the rule *eṣād vibhāṣā*. In the Vārttika *aṃṣṭre*, the word is read with a long vowel (*dīrghānta*). However, some, having read it with a short vowel (*hrasvānta*), state that it is *vā daṃṣṭraḥ*.

They say that the lengthening occurs in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, but not in a *tatpuruṣa*. Here, [the word] is "ṣāt. The intention is that the reading with the palatal *ś* in "ārśya" is non-Vedic (*anārṣa*). He provides an example of the substitution of *ṇ* for the *s* of *vana* after words ending in *vanaspati*.

(867) *vibhāṣauṣadhivanaspatibhyaḥ* |8|4|6|. [The example] *śirīṣavanam*. Now, one might object: according to the *Amarakośa*, "A *vanaspati* bears fruit through its flowers; that which does not flower is a *vanaspati*," it follows that for whatever lacks flowers, [the suffix *aṇ* applies].

That which has the manifestation of fruit is a *vanaspati*, such as the *udumbara* tree and others. But the *śirīṣa* is not like that, because it possesses both flowers and fruit; therefore, if one asks how the substitution of *ṇa* [for *na*] occurs here, they say: by the word *vanaspati* here, "tree" in general is indicated. And in this regard, [the rule applies] even when [the suffix] *up* [is present].
The *bhāṣya* on the sūtra "yukta-vat" serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*). For in that context, it is asked: "What is meant by 'denoting individuals'?

It is stated that in the case of "a village not far from *śirīṣa* trees is called *śirīṣāḥ*; their forest is *śirīṣavanaṃ*"—where the substitution of *ṇa* (in place of *na*) ought to be applied—the status of being a "large tree" (*vanaspati*) would also be extended [to the forest]. And that [status] belongs to the *śirīṣa* trees...
It applies only in the case of being a *vanaspati* (tree/plant), and not otherwise; this is the general direction.
[The rule] applies only after two-syllable (*dvyac*) and three-syllable (*tryaj*) bases.

The intention is that this is based on an option that is fixed by specific restriction (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). He states a prohibition regarding what would otherwise apply due to its being an *oṣadhi* (herb/medicinal plant).

A prohibition must be stated for *irikā* and others [regarding the suffix *ith*]. Thus, it is said: "after *irikā* and others, [the suffix *ith* is not applied]. This too is established simply by knowing that this is a rule of restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). Regarding "the Uśīnaras": here, the word *uśīnara* is used figuratively (*bhākta*) for the inhabitants of that region. As for "the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*)," this is by means of the rule: "The suffixes *ṛti*, *alyuṭ*, and others are used diversely (*bahulam*)."
Or rather, since this is an introduction for the purpose of prescribing a substitute, it is an *aprāptavibhāṣā* (an optional rule where [the substitution] was not otherwise required).

(868) *pānaṃ deśe* | 8|4|9|. In the case of *kṣīrapāṇa*, [the analysis is as follows]: *pītiḥ*—*pānam*. The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the neuter gender to denote an abstract state (*bhāva*) by the rule *yuṭ ca*.
That by which one drinks is "pānam" (a drink); [the suffix] *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). "Kṣīrapāṇam" means the drinking of milk.
Regarding the phrase "of mountain-rivers and so forth," the word "or" (*vā*) implies that it should be stated as an option.
They say that this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) applying in both cases: it is already established when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*), and it is not yet established when it is not a proper name.

(869) *prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.11]. In the case of *māṣavāpiṇau*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *ābhīkṣṇye ṇiniḥ*. In the case of *vrīhivāpāṇi*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*.

The substitution of *ṇ* occurs only for that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which constitutes the final member of a compound (*uttarapada*). Regarding the phrase "that which is the final member": the sense is that it is explained in this way in accordance with the desired results. In the example *gargabhaginī*, the word *bhaginī* is the final member, not the word *bhagin*. And in this explanation—
He states the opinion of the ancients—that the inclusion of the term *num* itself is the indicator—by saying "for this very reason.
He then refutes that stated indicator by saying "furthermore.
[In the example] *yuvāderna parikvāni*, the substitution of *ṇ* would have been obligatory by the rule “*umati ca*” (*Pāṇini 8.4.13*).
Although explained previously, it is recalled here in accordance with the context.
Regarding *vṛtrahaṇau*: they are those who have slain Vṛtra; [the suffix] *kvip* is applied by the rule *brahmabhrūṇa-*. Regarding *harimāṇī*:
from the causative of the root *man*, [the suffix] *kvip* is applied by the rule *vīp ca*.

By the rule "atikārakopapadānām" and so forth, the final member of the compound (*uttarapada*) ends in *n* before the addition of case endings (*sub*). Because it ends in *n*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Thus we have *kṣīrapāṇī*.

[The word] *pāṇa* is derived from the root *pā* (to drink) with the suffix *ka* by the rule "āto ’nupasarge kaḥ," when a direct object (*karman*) is the upapada; furthermore, there is the elision of the long *ā* by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca."
The elision (*lopa*) of *ca* is understood here. Regarding the form *ramyaviṇā*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which is both beautiful (*ramya*) and a Viś.

From that [the instrumental case ending], by the rule *āṅe nā ’striyām*. Now, one might object: since the word *viś* possesses the status of a *pada* by relying on the internal case-ending, the prohibition of *ṇatva* by the rule *adavyavāye’pi* would apply. Not so.

Because of the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule by the statement “and when there is a subsequent word (*uttarapada*), [the preceding element is not considered a word] in the application of rules concerning the beginning of a word (*apadādividhi*)”, the word *vi* lacks the status of being a *pada*. However, by the rule “in [the context of] *svādi* [suffixes]”, only the word *ramyavi* has the status of a *pada*, and not the word *vi*; for it is accepted that the status of being a *pada* belongs only to that from which the *svādi* suffixes are prescribed. And thus...

Furthermore, in the word *punarbhūnām*, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] is entirely unimpeded, because the word *bhū* does not possess the status of being a *pada* when followed by the suffix *nām*. (870) *kumati ca* | Pāṇini 8.4.13.

And [the term] *kumati* [is used]. The composition [of the word *kumat*] consists of more than one vowel (*anekāc*) as the final member of the compound. However, the rule was not formulated simply as *au*. For if [the rule were] *yasmin vidhiḥ*, then by the principle of *tadādividhi* (application to that which begins with the element specified), this rule would apply only when the final member of the compound begins with the *ka*-group (i.e., *kavarga*), such as in *harikāmāṇi* and the like, but not in cases such as *vastrayugeṇa*; and thus [it would be incorrect].
He states that a detailed explanation of the exceptions is necessary: "possessing the *ka*-group," etc.

(871). [The rule] *padavyavāye ’pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.38) means "even when there is an intervention by a word. This indicates that even when a word (*pada*) exists between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*), the substitution of *ṇa* (*ṇatva*) occurs.
The meaning is "no. Regarding the expression *māṣakumbhavāpena*: [the derivation is] *māṣakumbhaṃ vapatīti*, with the suffix *aṇ* by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*;

it is a compound with an *upapada*. Regarding *caturaṅgayogena*: this is analyzed in the *Manoramā* as *catvāry aṅgāny asya*, [and then] *tena yogaḥ*. That is incorrect, because when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*)...
Furthermore, because of the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule by the injunction "not when [the word] begins with a case-ending (*apādādi*)", the word *aṅga* does not constitute a *pada*.

Therefore, the analysis must be performed as: "the connection of the members (*aṅgānām*) is *aṅgayoga*; the connection of the four members is *caturṇām-aṅgayoga*. Nor is there any issue with the word *aṅga* even in the analysis "the connection with the four members" (*caturaṅgena yogaḥ*).

One should not suspect that the prohibition regarding the application of suffixal characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa-pratiṣedha*) does not apply because the word *na* is the final member (*uttarapada*) of the compound; for it is indeed the final member of the preceding compound, and the rule "and when there is the status of being a final member" (*uttarapadatve ca*) applies specifically when the status of being a word (*padatva*) must be established for that which constitutes the final constituent of the subsequent compound.

This is because it is accepted that the rule regarding the *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa* (the application of suffixal operations) does not operate when there is a difference from the rules concerning *pada* and so forth.

Furthermore, in cases such as "there is elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapada-lopa*) in words like *ākapārthiva*" and "after *pra* and others, [the suffix] belonging to a verbal root (*dhātujasya*)," the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) refers merely to the final constituent of a compound; therefore, in those instances...

Even if there were no application of the rule regarding the characteristics of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), there would be no harm; however, in this case, the application of the rule regarding the characteristics of suffixes is required in order to obtain the status of being a word (*padatva*). And thus, even in the example *āṣakumbhavāpena*, [the analysis is as follows]:
the sowing (*vāpa*) of a jar (*kumbha*) is "jar-sowing" (*kumbhavāpa*). The word *kumbha* [here] refers to grain measured by a jar.
It is figurative (*bhākta*). The moderns (*navyāḥ*) maintain that it should be analyzed as "the pouring of jars of *āṣā*.

However, some—having construed the meaning of the rule "in the prescription [concerning] word-initials" (*apadādividhau*) as "in the prescription [concerning] word-final *at* letters" (*adāntavidhau*)—argue that since the rule "even when there is an intervening vowel" (*adavyavāye ’pi*) does not concern a word-final element, it does not apply here.

They say that this is a prohibition of the condition (*pratyaya*) as a defining characteristic. Others do not accept that; for if that were the case, one would simply say "in the rule concerning what ends in *at*" (*adanta-vidhau*) for the sake of brevity, rather than saying "in the rule concerning suffixes and word-initials" (*ṭhapadādi-vidhau*). This is the direction of the argument. Furthermore, regarding the statement "when it is the second member of a compound" (*uttarapadatve*), when a rule concerning the end of a word (*padānta-vidhi*) is to be applied...

If one accepts the meaning [of the rule] as a prohibition, there is a contradiction with the *Manoramā* commentary on the sūtra "mo hrasvādaci" regarding the example *pada-m-a-daṇḍinau*. Enough of this.

It should be stated that [the word *daṇḍin-*] is not a *taddhita* derivative; that is, [the condition] "provided it is not a *taddhita*" applies. [The objection is: "If the word *taddhita* is intended as a qualifier of the intervening word..."

The meaning is: "if it does not exist, then there is a prohibition. Regarding the term *ārdragomayeṇa*: here, the word *go* is the first member (*pūrvapada*). One should not suspect the prohibition [of doubling] by the rule *utarapadatve ca*, because the word *gomaya* is the subsequent member (*utarapada*), and the word *go* is included among the words beginning with *va*.
Because it is a word [ending in -a].

(872) *goṣpadaṃ sevitāsevitapramāṇeṣu* | Pāṇini 6.1.145. *goṣpadam*. [The word *goṣpada* is used] in the senses of frequented, not frequented, and measure. In the sense of "not frequented," the word *goṣpada* [is applied].

He provides an example preceded by the negative particle *nañ* because of the impossibility [of the action]: *agoṣpadāni*. They say that even in a place where the movement of cows is absolutely impossible, the mention of *asevita* (unfrequented) is for the sake of the augment *suṭ*.

(873) *āspadaṃ pratiṣṭhāyām* |6|1|1|146|. [The word *āspada* is used] in the sense of "establishment. That is to say, for the purpose of passing time, or for the purpose of prolonging one's life; such is the meaning.
(874) *āścaryam anitye* |6|1|147|. [The word *āścarya* is used] when [the thing denoted] is not permanent.

"Āścarya" (wonder). The augment *suṭ* is applied after the prefix *āṅ* before the root *car*. This is according to the rule: "The augment *suṭ* is applied to *car* after *āṅ* and *ara*, except when referring to the fingers.
(875) "Vapiṣkiraḥ śakunau vā" (6.1.150): [The suffix *kvin* is optionally applied after the root *vap* following *āṅ* when the word refers to a bird.]

*Viṣkiraḥ*: From the root *ṛ* in the sense of "scattering" (*vikṣepe*), the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *ig-upadh-ād-a-k-e* (Pāṇini 3.1.135), and by this [sūtra], the augment *suṭ* is introduced as an irregularity (*nipātyate*). The change to the letter *ṣ* is effected by the rule *ari-ni-vibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.70). Regarding the mention of *vikiro*: in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the text, it says, "The term *viṣkira* refers to a bird, or else *vikiro*."
It should be understood that in the *sūtra*-text, however, there is no mention of the word *vikira*. "Of that too" means "of the word *vikira* as well. (876) *pratiṣkaśaś ca kaśeḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.152.

"From *kaś* alone, *kaśā*" means that the word *kaśā* is derived from the verbal root *kaś* itself. "From another root" refers to the fact that in the expression "ratikaśaḥ," the prefix *prati* belongs to the root *gam*, and not to *kaś*;
this is because of the maxim: "Prepositions (*pra*-etc. are connected only with that [root] with which their own action is joined. This is the intended meaning.

(877) *praskaṇvahariścandrāvṛṣī* 6.1.153. [The commentary states: "Regarding the phrase *amantrārtam*: the point is that in the case of a mantra, the form is already established by the rule *hrasvāccandrottarapade mantre*."

(878) *maskara-maskariṇau veṇu-parivrājakayoḥ* | Pāṇini 5.2.104. They say that although the desired forms could have been established by adding the possessive suffix *in* to the words *maskara* and *maskarin*, the explicit mention of *maskarin* is for the purpose of ensuring that this usage applies only to the mendicant (*parivrājaka*).

(879) *kāstīrā* is [the form] in the city of *ajastunda*. [The word] *kāstīra* [is derived as follows]: by the rule *īṣadarthe*, there is the substitution of *kā-* for *ku-*. (880) *Pāraskara-prabhṛtīni ca saṃjñāyām*: [Words such as] *pāraskara* and others [retain their original forms] when they are proper names (*saṃjñā*).

Regarding *pāraskara*: the analysis is *āraṃ karoti* (“he makes a beginning”). The suffix *ṭa* is applied by the rule *ṛño hetutācchīlye*. Regarding *kiṣkindhā*: the analysis is *kim api dhatte* (“it holds even something”). The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*, and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* follows. By irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is doubling of the syllable *kiṃ*, elision of the *m* of the preceding word, the addition of the augment *suṭ*, and the change of *s* to *ṣ*. [End of] *kiṃ*.

In the opinion of those who analyze [the word] as *kiṃ dadhāti*, the doubling is established by way of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*); elsewhere, however, it is established solely through irregular derivation (*nipātana*). In reality, these are conventional words (*rūḍhi-śabda*) that are somehow derived etymologically;
therefore, one should not insist upon the meaning of the individual components.
The suffix *suṭ* is added to the words *karapatti* when they signify a thief and a deity respectively, provided they follow *tat* and *bṛhat*, and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the final *t*.
Regarding the phrase "to *tat* and *bṛhat*": this is a *gaṇa*-sūtra. Regarding the word "to *tat*": the remainder of the rule is "and the elision of the [final] *t*" (*alopaśca*).

[The rule applies] to *prāya* and *citici*. Regarding *prāya*: this is also a *gaṇa-sūtra*. The *Smṛti* states: "One should know that *prāya* is sin; *citi* is its purification. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
By this, forms such as *paraśśatāni kāryāṇi* ("tasks exceeding a hundred") are established. Here...
The compound is formed either from the analysis of the word as *‘upa-upa’* or from the grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) of *‘añcami’*.
Due to its inclusion in the *rājadantādi* group, the word *śata* is placed last; and due to its inclusion in the *pāraskarādi* group, the augment *suṭ* is applied.
Thus ends the section on rules dependent on compounds in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
Om. Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
The Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakaumudī, adorned with the two commentaries Tatvabodhinī and Bālamanoramā.
The first half of that [work]:
now begins the section on technical terminology (*saṃjñāprakaraṇa*).
The triad of sages.
Having bowed to Viśveśvara together with Ambā and having performed salutation to the Guru, this commentary on the Siddhāntakaumudī, titled Tattvabodhinī, is composed. (1)

Having performed an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) for the removal of obstacles, the author sets forth his intended work by means of the verse beginning with "The Three Sages" (*munitrayam*), binding it [to the text] for the instruction of his disciples. The word *traya* means that which has three parts (*avayava*);
[this is derived] from the rule *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap*. Then, by the rule *vitribhyāṃ tayasya-*, the suffix *ayac* is applied. [The term refers to] the knowers (*mantṛ*).

The sages (*munayaḥ*) are those who have realized the true meaning of the Vedas and the Śāstras. According to the Uṇādi-sūtra "agnerucca," the vowel *a* of the root *man* is changed to *u*, and the suffix *in* is added after *man*. However, the *guṇa* substitution does not occur here, because either the term *kit* is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartana*) from a previous sūtra, or because of the use of the *tapara* marker (*t*). Of them...

The triad of Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali constitutes the "Triad of Sages. Now, one might object: as in the case of the phrase *namaskṛtya vyaṃbhuve*, should not the dative case also apply here by the rule *namaḥ-svasti-* (Pāṇini 2.3.16)?
Not so; for it will be stated later that "the case ending denoting the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) is stronger than the case ending arising from a governing word (*upapada*)."

Because, as in the expression “he pays homage to the gods” (*namaskaroti devān*), the accusative case alone is appropriate. Furthermore, according to the view that "a compound does not retain its own meaning" (*ahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*), the word *namaḥ* here is devoid of meaning; therefore, when used in conjunction with it, the dative case does not occur, because the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the inclusion of "that which possesses meaning" (*arthavat*) applies. [As in: *vayaṃbhuve*.

Regarding the phrase "having paid homage" (*namaskṛtya*), however, if the intended meaning is "in order to propitiate the Self-born One" (*svayaṃbhuvam anukūlayitum*), then the dative case is applied according to the rule beginning with "when a word meaning 'homage' (*namas*) is the accompanying word" (*namo'rthopapadasya-*); this will become clear in the root text itself.
Nor should it be suspected that, in such a case, the word *namaḥ* in the sūtra "amaḥ-svasti-*" is redundant.

In the expression "namo haraye," since the sense of "in order to propitiate Hari" is not intended to be expressed, the genitive case would otherwise apply in the sense of a general relationship; however, because that [dative] is necessary as an exception to that [genitive], it is used.
Regarding the phrase "taduktīḥ": it means the utterances (uktīḥ) of them (teṣām), namely Pāṇini and others.

The meaning is "the Sūtras, Vārtikas, and Bhāṣyas. Even when explaining it as "the utterances of that triad of sages," since neither the Sūtra, the Vārtika, nor the Bhāṣya is spoken of as a collective whole, the expression ultimately results in meaning "the utterances of the individual sages who constitute that collection."

"Having cultivated" (paribhāvya) means "having reflected upon. One should not suspect that, because the root *bhū* preceded by the prefix *pari* has the sense of "disregard," how can it here have the sense of "knowing";
for *pari* is joined with *bhāvī*, which is derived from the causative (*ṇij*) of the *cur*-ādigaṇa root. Some [commentators] here [interpret] it with *bhavati*...

Having undertaken the discussion on *yoga*, they say: In the rule *parau bhuvo ’vajñāne* (Pāṇini 1.3.19), because the term *avajñāna* (disregard) serves as a qualifier for *parau bhuvaḥ*, there is no restriction that the root *bhū* must necessarily mean "contempt" (*tiraskāra*).
This is also evident from the usage of Śrīharṣa in such passages as *anasā paribhāvya kiṃcit*.

For this very reason, there is not even a suspicion of the fault of being "unemployed" (aprayuktatva) here. Others, however, [derive the word from] the root *bhū* preceded by *pari*, ending in the suffix *ghañ*, based on the lexicon which states: "Disregard (*anādara*), humiliation (*paribhava*), subjugation (*parībhāva*), and contempt (*tiraskriyā*)."
They say that there is no suspicion here at all that the perception of contempt arises from anything other than this.
That is weak; for even from the expression "having despised, he despises," the perception of contempt is understood.
Regarding the term *vaiyākaraṇa*: those who study or know grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) are *vaiyākaraṇas*.
It is a moonlight [treatise] upon their established doctrines; that is to say, it is an illuminator.
The word "Kaumudī" is employed because of the similarity in its quality of delighting all people without flaw.
This is said with reference to the *Kaumudī* even though it has not yet been composed, by way of the intellect [anticipating it].

Because it has been brought near, there is the pointing out with the finger: "this. Regarding the word *viracyate*: the word *aye* is to be supplied as the subject. The root *rac* means "to restrain" (*pratiyantra*). *Pratiyantra* means "the imparting of qualities.
From this root preceded by the prefix *vi-*, the present tense suffix is used in the sense of the future to indicate immediate proximity to the present.
(2) aiuṇ — hal.

In *aiuṇ*, the letter *ṇ* is an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) for the purpose of the technical name *aṇ*. Whatever technical name there may be, it must have a specific purpose. In *ṛlṛk*, the letter *k* is for the purpose of the technical names *at* and *kit*. In *eoṅ*, the letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of the technical name *eṅ*. In *aiāṬc*, the letter *c* is for the purpose of the technical names *ac* and *aic*.

Others maintain that there is no euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) in these cases because the *saṃhitā* (continuous flow of phonemes) is not intended for the purpose of making the individual sounds (*varṇa*) unmistakable.
Furthermore, since vowels such as *ca* are listed among the "ādi" group, they receive the designation of "particle" (*nipāta*) by the rule *ādayo 'satve*;
consequently, by the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ*, they are designated as *pragṛhya* (unchangeable), and due to this state of original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), no euphonic combination occurs.

It might be argued as follows: Just as by the instruction of the letter *a* and so forth, the long vowels *ā* and others—which are homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with them—are obtained, and thus the long vowels *ā* and so forth are not taught separately; likewise, since the letters *ṛ* and *ḷ* are also homogeneous, both would be established simply by the instruction of the letter *ṛ*, so what is the purpose of teaching them separately? Nor is it the case that...
Regarding the position that [phonemes] are universals (*jāti*), it must be said that the separate instruction of *a* and *ṛ* is necessary because they belong to different universals;
for by the very fact of their being homogeneous (*sāvarṇya*), the instruction of one universal necessarily entails the acquisition of the other universal as well.

If it is argued that the mention of *aṇ* in the rule *ṭh-aṇ-ud-it savarṇasya* is necessary even on the view that [the term] denotes a genus (*jāti*), in order to establish the technical names for each of the thirty vowels *aṇ* and *ṛ*,
then [the reply is]: here they say that the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between *aṇ* and *ṛ* is non-eternal.

The mention of both [the letters *ṛ* and *ḷ*] is for the purpose of making this known; its result is as follows: one whose topknot (*śikhā*) is arranged is called *klṛptaśikhaḥ*, and when addressing him from a distance, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs in the form *klṛptaśikha*.
However, if the homogeneous relationship (*sāvarṇya*) between *aṅ* and *ṛ-varṇa* were constant, then [the rule] would be *ṭhanṛtaḥ*.

Another solution will also be shown under the rule *ṭhorguṇaḥ*, namely that just as there would be no protracted (*pluta*) vowel for the letter *ṛ* due to its exclusion [from the vowels], the same would apply to the letter *ḷ*. Regarding *hayavaraṭ*:
the letter *ṭ* is an indicatory phoneme (*anubandha*) for the purpose of designating the augment *aṭ*; as for the instruction of the letter *h*, however—

The inclusion of *aṭ* (the augment *a*) and *haś* (consonants other than semivowels and nasals) is for the purpose of including the letter *h*. In *arheṇa*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] by the rule *ṭh-aṅ-v-ayavāye ’pi*. In *devā hasanti*, the *r* of *ro* is replaced by *y* by the rule *ho bha-go-*.
In *devo hasati*, the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule *haśi ca*. [The form is] *lilihiṃdhve*.

*lilihiḍhva*. By the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ*, the substitution of *ḍha* for *dha* is optional. In the term *laṇ*, the letter *ṇ* is an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) for the purpose of designating the technical names *aṇ*, *iṇ*, and *yaṇ*. Now, as for the designation *aṇ*, it is sometimes understood by the preceding *ṇ* and sometimes by the following *ṇ*; however, in the case of *iṇ*, [it is understood by the following one].

[It is] by means of the letter *ṇ* itself. And thus, for the sake of removing doubt, it would have been more appropriate to employ another *anubandha*. True. However, the letter *ṇ* is again used as an *anubandha* in order to make known the *paribhāṣā*: "The specific [meaning] is understood from the commentary; for there is no rule (*lakṣaṇa*) based on doubt."
It is established in its source. *Ñamaṅṇanam*:
here, the letter *m* is for the purpose of designating the technical names *am*, *yam*, *ñam*, *ṅam*, and *sam*. *Jhabhañ*: the letter *ñ* is for the purpose of designating the technical name *yañ*.
*Ghaḍhadhaṣ*: the letter *ṣ*, however, is for the purpose of designating the technical names *jhaṣ*, *bhaṣ*, and *ṣaṣ*. *Jabagaḍadaś*.
The *anubandha* (indicatory letter) *ś* is for the purpose of designating [the letters] as *aś*, *aśv*, *jhaś*, *jaś*, and *baś*.

In the group *khaphacchaṭhathacaṭatav*, the letter *v* is for the purpose of designating [the letters] as *cch* and *v*. In the group *kapay*, the letter *y* is for the purpose of designating [the letters] as *yay*, *may*, *jhay*, *khay*, and *cay*. In the group *śaṣasar*, the letter *r*...
The purpose of the designation *yar*, *jh*, *kh*, *car*, and *śar* is [for the application of grammatical rules]. Regarding *hal*:

the letter *l* is for the purpose of the designations *al*, *ahal*, *val*, *ral*, *jhal*, and *śal*. Furthermore, the instruction of the letter *h* again is for the purpose of including *h* within the categories *val*, *ral*, *jhal*, and *śal*. [Examples: *rudihi*; *svapihi*.

In the case of *snihitvā*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *udādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* because it begins with a consonant (*valādi*). Regarding *adāgdhām*, although the substitution of *gh* (for *dh*) is considered *asiddha*, the *hakāra* is still a *jhal* sound. Consequently, the rule *ktvā seṭ*—which prohibits *kitva*—is set aside, and *kitva* optionally applies by the rule *ṭhralo vyupadhāt*.

In the case of *‘halo jhali’*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *s*. [In *alikṣat*], by the rule *‘alaḥ...’*, there is the substitution of *ksa*. Now, even if the teaching of the letter *ha* were necessary once again, one might argue that it would suffice to read the letter *ha* only after *śar* (i.e., in *śar-ha-jha-lam*), and then apply the rules:
*‘halo’ntyasya’*, *‘halo’nantarāḥ saṃyogaḥ’*, *‘halo jhali’*, and *‘ala...’*.

"Let as many rules as begin with 'igupadhāt' and so forth—which have *l* as an indicatory letter (*lānubandha*)—be made to have *r* as their indicatory letter (*rephānubandha*) by means of the forms 'ṭharaḥ antyasya' and 'ṭharaḥ aṣaḥ anantarāḥ', and let the separate rule 'hal' be abandoned. Do not say so; for if that were the case, [in the word] *harir hasati*, [the substitution would apply incorrectly].

Expressions such as *harir hariḥ* would not be established; for in those cases, there would be the undesirable application (prasaṅga) of rules such as *haravasānayor visarjanīyaḥ* and *vā śari*. Therefore, the rule *hal* is indeed necessary.
And thus, the passage to be cited later—“the final [consonant] in the rule *hal*”—is also consistent with this [interpretation].

It connects [with the following]. "Having as their purpose names that are beginningless" (*anādisaṃjñārthāni*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is: those for which the beginningless names are the purpose (*artha*), that is, the motive (*prayojana*). Alternatively, it is an *asvapada-vigraha* (an analysis where the words are not in apposition): "these [are] from the beginningless names. This is because it will be stated later: "There is an obligatory compound with the word *artha*, and [the resulting compound] takes the gender of the qualified object (*viśeṣya-liṅgatā*)."

"Of these, the final [sounds]" means that among these sūtras, the final sounds beginning with *ṇ* (in *laṇ*) are marked with the technical designation *it*, by virtue of the rule "a sound followed by *ṭh* or *hal* is *it*" which will be stated immediately hereafter. Regarding the phrase "and the vowel *a* in the *laṇ* sūtra":
it is mentioned separately because it is not final. By changing the grammatical number, it is connected with the word "it" (*it*), meaning they receive the designation *it*.

And by this [rule], through the application of *Pāṇini 1.3.2*, "the letter *a* is non-nasal (*anunāsika*) when taught as *ṭu*," and likewise, because the inclusion of *pratyāhāras* will be stated later in the rule "ṇādi with its final *it*," the statement that [these markers] are for the purpose of designating *ṭhaṇ* and so forth is consistent; such is the intended meaning. [The marker] *a*.
The phrase "for the purpose of pronunciation" means that it is not for the sake of a specific function, as the vowel *a* in the *laṇ* sūtra is.

(3) *hal-antyam* [Pāṇini 1.3.3]: "That which occurs at the end, in the final position, is 'final' (*antya*). The suffix *yat* is applied because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. [The rule continues: *upadeśe ’janunāsikaḥ*.

From this [point], the words “in an instruction” (*upadeśe*) and “i” (*it*) are carried over (*anuvartate*). Having raised the objection of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) with respect to the rule *ādirantyena*, he resolves it by means of repetition: “In the rule *hal*, the last [is the name of the preceding group]” (*halantyam*). In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *hali antyam*, there is a locative case (*saptamī*).
The intention is that this is a compound formed either by the rule *sup-supā* through a split in the rules (*yogavibhāga*),
or else it is a genitive tatpuruṣa, since an interpretation is possible according to which the final [consonant] of the rule *hal* would be an *it*.

(4) *Ādirantyena sahetā* (Pāṇini 1.1.71). Why [is it specified] "with the last"? [The author of the *Kāśikā* states: "'Uḍ' is a pratyāhāra [formed] with the final element of the third singular case ending, namely *bhū*. Even though, within the group ending in *ṭ*, the letter *ṭ* is indeed the final one...

Even so, by virtue of the force of the mention of "the last" (*antya*), the pratyāhāra is formed only with that which has the designation *it* (i.e., an *it*-letter) due to its being the final element; for the designation *it* does not apply to the letter *ṭ* in *ṭā* according to the rule "the last [letter] of a *hal* [group] is *it*" (*ṭh-ala-ntyam*).
Nor, in this way, is there a failure to establish the pratyāhāra *ṭhra*.

The intention of the author of the *Kāśikā* is that, by virtue of the commitment to the nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) of the letter *a* in the *laṇ* sūtra, the formation of the pratyāhāra [for vowels] is accomplished even by means of the final *it* [the *ṇ*]. However, the definitive conclusion on this point will be demonstrated here under the sūtra *svaujasamauṭ*.

The detailed discussion, however, should be sought in the *Śabdakaustubha*. Why [is the word] *iti* used? It is so that the pratyāhāra *rap* may be included. For it has been stated in the *Śabdakaustubha* that because of the force of the formal declaration (*pratijñā*) regarding its nasality, it is grasped even by the final letter; and this would not be obtainable in the absence of the word *iti*.
[The sūtra] is established. Here, by means of the first and last members [of a group], the whole—the aggregate—is implied.

Since that [whole] cannot be applied simultaneously to the objects of indication (*lakṣya*), the technical name (*saṃjñā*) descending upon its members comes to rest on those situated in the middle, and not on the first and last, because those two are included within the very form of the name itself.
With the intention of determining that [the word] is for the sake of another, he says: "of those situated in the middle" (*madhyagānām*) and "and of its own" (*svasya ca*).

The sense is that the phrase *svarūpam* (its own form) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). And its own form is understood only of the initial [element], not of the final one, because of the mention of the instrumental case in the subordinate sense in the rule *antyena*.
Because pronouns generally refer to the principal subject. Now, one might object:

if "vaḥ" were to carry over [from the previous rule], then since the expectancy for "aḥ saṃjñī" (the letter *a* is the name) would be satisfied, there would be no further reference to the whole [compound]. And thus, [the rule] "ṭhikoyaṇaci" [would not apply].
In such cases as these, the meaning would be that a *yakāra* should take the place of the vowel *ikāra* when followed by an *akāra*.

This is not so; for if only the initial [letter] were the designated entity (*saṃjñin*), then the very formulation of the technical rule "the first letter [of a group] is designated by the last" (*ṭhādirantyena*) would become purposeless. Furthermore, [this would apply to] *aṇ*, *ak*, *ac*, *aṭ*, *am*, *aś*, and so forth.

Even the separate mention [of the final letter] would be useless, since the designation (saṃjñin) would everywhere belong to the vowel *a* alone; such is the general direction. However, in the Śabdakaustubha, it is established that since the designation of the whole is already accomplished by imitating it through its initial and final parts, this rule is intended to exclude the final letter.

(5) "In the *upadeśa*, the final consonant [is called *it*]. What is meant by "in the *upadeśa*"? The *Kāśikā* gives the examples *agnicit* and *somasut*. If this were not restricted to the *upadeśa*, then the elision (*lopa*) would apply here as well due to the *it*-designation. Nor is the rule for *tuk* redundant, because it serves its purpose in forms such as *āgatya*. Nor is the *pit* designation of the suffix *kvip* redundant.

Haradatta [states] that [the rule] has its purpose fulfilled in cases such as *agnicitau* and so forth. What is the purpose of specifying "the final [consonant]" (*antya*)? It is so that [the designation *itsaṃjñā*] does not apply to the letter *m* in *manin*. For if the *itsaṃjñā* were to apply, [the augment *t*] would follow after the final vowel.
