As in *veśma* and *sadma*, [formed by] the suffix *manin* added after roots ending in *ar*. Why specify "after *ha*" (*hāl*)? [To exclude cases like *pām̐sana*, where the suffix *manin* follows *pām̐s*].

‘*hū* is used in the sense of existence (*satāyām*)’: [the form] will be *bhavitā*. Nor should it be argued that the designation *it* does not apply due to a lack of purpose; for they say that if the designation *it* were applied, the augment *num* would occur by the rule *ṭhiditaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "the first utterance":
the final consonant (*hal*) of that word which becomes the object of the first utterance shall be designated *it*.

The meaning is established. (6) *Upadeśe ’janunāsika it* [Pāṇini 1.3.2]: "In the grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*), a non-consonant (*aj*) that is nasalized (*anunāsika*) is termed *it*. [The sūtra is analyzed as: "In the instruction, a non-consonant...
"Instruction" (*upadeśa*) means the act of teaching; the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). Why specify "in the instruction"?

*abhra* [means] *apaḥ*. Here, the prefix *āṅ* indicates the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*). The vowel *ā* is nasalized by the rule *āṅe’nunāsikaśchandasī*. Although one might argue here that, as in the case of *uñ ai*, the nasalization itself has the force of a rule that precludes the substitution of *it*, this is easily refuted.

Nevertheless, the inclusion of the term *upadeśa* (instruction) right here has been made for the sake of clarity, so that it must necessarily be applied for the sake of subsequent rules. Why is this so? [To ensure] that it does not apply to the *m* of *manin*.
Nor should it be argued that, by the force of the mention of "the final" (*antyam*) in the rule *ṭhhalantyam*, the [ṭit] designation would not apply to a non-final *m*.

Because its purpose is fulfilled by preventing over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) through the suffix *āl* and others; for example, [if the term were not specified], one might ask: "What is the purpose of [specifying] 'anunāsika'? Consider the root *īkṣa* in the sense of "seeing. In the form *īkṣitaḥ*, if the designation *it* were present, the substitution of *iṇ* for *i* (as prescribed by the rule *vādito niṣṭhāyām*) would not occur.
Although it would have been more appropriate to state the technical term *anunāsika* first because it is that which is presupposed here, nevertheless,

since its meaning is already established by resorting to the etymological derivation (*yoga*) "that which follows the nose" (*nāsikām anugata*), the sūtra defining the term *anunāsika* is intended to suggest that it serves little purpose.
This has not been presented here; nor does it follow that, in the rule *ṭhyaro’nunāsike* (Pāṇini 8.4.45),
the meaning would result in "a letter of the *ya-ra* group at the end of a word should become nasalized when followed by a word containing a nasal," because of the *tadrūpa-paribhāṣā*.

Because there is no fault even in the view of the Sūtra school due to the non-assumption of a non-manifested conceptualization (*anupasthitikalpana*), one might object: "Does this not result in a burden of understanding (*pratipattigaurava*) based on the aforementioned explanation? Precisely for this reason, instead of saying "having a purpose" (*saprayojana*), it was stated "having no purpose" (*andhaprayojana*). This refers to the proposition (*pratijñā*).
*Pratijñā* means that which is promised (*pratijñāyate*). The suffix *aṅ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule *ṭhātaścopasarge*.

*Ānunāsikyam* is the state of having a nasal (*anunāsika*). The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied by the rule *uṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ*. The analysis of the compound is: "those for whom there is a promise of nasality. Some, however, [interpret it as] *pratijñānam*.
*Pratijñā* means "a formal assertion"; that which possesses this is *pratijñam*. [The suffix] *ac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*.
They analyze the compound as *pratijñamānunāsikya eṣām* ("the nasalization of these is [subject to] a formal assertion").
Although the reading containing the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) composed by the author of the Sūtras has now been lost, nevertheless...
The sense is that, by the force of the usage of the authors of commentaries (*vṛtikāra*) and others, it is inferred that [the word] existed previously according to its function.
Regarding the term *pāṇinīyāḥ*: that which was spoken by Pāṇini is *pāṇinīyam*. [This is derived] by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114).
Those who study or know that [work] are called *pāṇinīyāḥ*. In the form *adadhīte*, the suffix *aṇ* is elided by the rule “*roktālluk*” (Pāṇini 4.2.61).
Now, one might object that the statement “of *ra* and *la*” (*ralayoḥ*) is incomplete, since the letter *ṭa* is also situated between them. To this, [the author replies:]...

He says: "In the *pratyāhāras*," [referring to] "the nasal" (*anunāsika*) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one should understand [rules such as] "in the presence of *āpāṇaka*, with contemptuous terms" and "after a final *eṅ*, before *at*" and others.
Regarding the term "*pratyāhāra*": it is that wherein the phonemes (*varṇas*) are brought back together, that is, abbreviated.

*Pratyāhāra*: Although the suffix *lyuṭ* would have been expected by the rule *araṇādhikaraṇayośca*, the suffix *ghañ* is used here for the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*) because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. Even though the mere etymological derivation (*yoga*) is over-extended to technical terms such as *akāra* and so forth, the intended meaning is that this is a case of *yogarūḍhi* (a word based on both etymology and conventional usage).
(7) *ūkālo’jjhrasvadīrghaplutaḥ* | P. 1.2.27. Regarding the rule *ūkālo’jjhrasvadīrghaplutaḥ*: the masculine gender in this *sūtra* compound is due to the rule for a collective (*samāhāra*) dvandva.
He explains that the term *ū* is an indication by the conjoining (*praśleṣa*) of the three vowels: *u*, *ū*, and *ū*. Thus: *uśca ūśca ūśca iti vaḥ*.

Regarding "vām": when the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel substitution of homogeneous vowels) has been applied to the three [cases], *yaṇ* is substituted for *vaḥ* when *jas* follows; however, *vām* is substituted when *ām* follows.

The statement "whose time is like your time" (*vāṃ kāla iva kālo yasya*) is an explanation of the resultant meaning (*phalitārtha*). The analytical derivation (*vigraha*), however, should be understood as "whose time is yours" (*vaḥ kālo yasya*). By the word "*ṭhū*," the duration of its own pronunciation is indicated.
It is observed. Why [is this] so? Let it not apply to a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster), as in *pratakṣya* and *prarakṣya*.

Since *ka* and *ṣa* consist of a single *mātrā*, they would be designated as *hrasva* (short); consequently, by the rule "after a short vowel, before a *pit* suffix beginning with a *kṛt* suffix," the augment *tuk* would be inserted.
Regarding *ā ye*: since "nipātas are udātta in their initial syllable," the vowel *ā* is *udātta*.

The word *yad*, however, has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) as *hiṣa*. Consequently, the *jas* suffix following it is unaccented (*anudātta*) because it belongs to the class of *supt* (sup-inflected endings). When the substitution of *yat* for *tyad*-type pronouns occurs, followed by the change to *śī* and the formation of the *ādguṇa* (vowel sandhi), the single substitute vowel (*ekādeśa*) becomes accented according to the rule "the single substitute [of an accented and an unaccented vowel] is accented. Thus, the vowel *e* is accented.

(8) *nīcairanudāttaḥ* |1|2|30|. [The example is] *arvāṅ*. [Derivation: *arvantam añcati iti arvāṅ* ("he goes toward a horse," thus "one who goes toward"). By the rule *ṛtvig-ādi*, the suffix *kvin* is applied to the root *añc-* when a nominal (*sup*) follows as an upapada. From the root *ṛ* ("to go") [in the sense of *arvan*], by the rule *nāmadripadyarti-ādi*, [the suffix *kan* is added].
The word *arvan* is derived from the root *ṛ* with the suffix *vanip*; it is acute on its first syllable by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*).

Because the suffix *vanip* is marked with *p*, it is grave (*anudātta*), and thus the vowel following it is also grave. Furthermore, the letter *a* of the root *añc* is either acute by the accent of the verbal root or by the accent of the *nit* marker. When the compound is formed according to the rule "the subordinate member [is compounded] with a non-finite verb" (*upapadam atiṅ*), the accent of the entire compound is determined by the rule "of a compound" (*samāsasya*).

By the rule "kṛt [suffixes] following a prefix or a secondary word (upapada) [retain their accent]," which serves as an exception to that [previous rule], the vowel *a* of the root *añc* is acute by virtue of the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the *kṛt*-suffix in a compound where the latter member is predominant. Furthermore, when the *n* of the suffix *van* has been elided and a long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) has been substituted, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the *ṭh* (the *ā* of *van*) becomes acute according to the rule "a single substitute for an acute [vowel] is acute. Thus, the vowel *ā* is acute.
According to the rule "the word is unaccented except for one [syllable]," due to the suppression of the remaining syllables (śeṣanighāta), the initial vowel here is unaccented.
This statement was made with the intention of describing what is possible; however, in the Vedabhāṣya, it is established as "arvāṅ = facing towards."
(9) Of that [vowel], at the beginning, there is an acute accent (*udātta*) of half a short [mora] measure. 1|2|32.
"Not the governing factor" (*atantram*) means it is not intended to be expressed. Regarding the phrase "and when followed by an acute or circumflex accent" (*tasya codātasvaritaparatve*):

that which has an acute or circumflex accent as its subsequent element is "followed by an acute or circumflex accent" (*udātasvaritaparam*); the state of being such is "the condition of being followed by an acute or circumflex accent" (*tatvam*).

The meaning is that when this [condition] exists—namely, when an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) syllable follows—the lower half of the preceding circumflex, which is unaccented (*anudātta*), is clearly audible. "Elsewhere" means in the absence of an acute or circumflex following it. "Where? For example: *imo't* and *itsvaritam*.
*va*: It is unaccented because of the governing rule "everything [is unaccented] except at the beginning of a *pāda*. *aśvā*:

In the word *aśva*, the suffix *kvun* is marked with *niṭ*; thus, by the rule "the first syllable is acute," the initial vowel is acute. However, in *saṃhitā*, by the rule "in a single-substitute [resulting from *sandhi*], the acute replaces the acute," the vowel *o* becomes acute when followed by an acute vowel.
Having given an example of a short *svarita*, he states an example of a long *svarita*: "rathānāṃ na yayi. Both words, "ye" and "arāḥ," are accented on the final syllable by the *phiṭ-svara* rule.

However, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is optionally *svarita*, according to the statement: "A *svarita* [is substituted] optionally for [a vowel] at the beginning of a word that is otherwise unaccented (*anudātta*)."

He provides an example for the case where a *svarita* follows: "śatacakram. Regarding the word *ya*: it is acutely accented (*udātta*) at the end by the *phiṭ-svara* rule; then, when the *r*-substitution (*rutva*) and *u*-substitution (*utva*) are applied to the following *s*, and the *guṇa* substitution (*ādguṇa*) is made, the vowel *o* resulting from the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with an acute vowel is itself acute. [The example] is *ahyaḥ*.

Since the vowel *a* ends in a circumflex (*svarita*), the remaining syllables are unaccented (*nighāta*). When the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the vowel *o* is then formed, the vowel *o* becomes circumflex by the rule "or [the substitute] is circumflex when preceded by an unaccented vowel at the beginning of a word. If one asks how this [word *ahya*] has a circumflex at its end, they say: it is derived from the root *ah* (meaning "to pervade") with the suffix *ṇyat* in the passive sense.
‘Its svarita [accent]’: the absence of vṛddhi, however, is due to the fact that a rule conditioned by a technical name (saṃjñāpūrvaka) is not universally obligatory.

As for the prohibition in the rule ‘odātasvarita-’, it applies specifically to what was obtained by the rule ‘udātāt-’ according to the maxim *anantarasya vidhir vā bhavati pratiṣedho vā* (a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding). When the sense is ‘on the day after yesterday’ (*ahyaḥ*), meaning ‘of Vṛtra,’ then [the form is used] optionally in the Veda (*chandasi vā*).

In the word *vacanam*, there is the absence of the *guṇa* [substitution]. By the rule *udātasvaritayoḥ*, it becomes *svarita*. However, the rule *udāttayaṇa* does not apply here because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*). In *agnimīle*, the vowel *ī* is *svarita*, while *le* is *ekaśruti*, which is another term for *pracaya*.
This will become clear in the root text itself within the section on vowels (*svaraprakriyā*). (10) *Mukhanāsikāvacano ’nunāsikaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.1.8.
[The term] *mukhanāsikā* [is a compound]. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound, it is "the mouth and the nose."

Since it is a part of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), if it were treated as a single unit (*ekavadbhāva*), the form would have been *mukhanāsika*; therefore, he says "together with the mouth" (*mukhasahita*). "To be articulated by means of the nose" (*nāsikayoccārya*) is a statement of the resulting meaning.
"Speech" (*vacana*) is that by which something is spoken; the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: "that which has speech consisting of both the mouth and the nose."

(11) *Tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam* [Pāṇini 1.1.9]: "That which has the same place of articulation (*āsya*) and effort (*prayatna*) is homogeneous (*savarṇa*). Regarding *tulyāsya*: he says "the palate and so forth" (*tālvādi*), intending that *āsya* means "that which exists in the mouth" (*āsye bhavam*), according to the rule *arīrāvayavādyat*. Regarding *ābhyantara* ("internal"): this is understood from the force of the prefix *pra-* (in *prayatna*).
The mouth (*āsya*) extends from the lips up to the uvula (*kākalaka*). Why [is it specified as] "having the same mouth" (*tulyāsya*)? [Consider: *tarptā*.
Here, when the letter *p* is followed by the letter *t*, the elision [of the former] by the rule "when *h* is followed by a *jhari*" (*haro jhari*) must not occur.
Why is the mention of "effort" (*prayatna*) included? [Consider: *vākścotati*. Here, there is no elision of the letter *ś*.

Regarding *ñamaṅṇanānām iti* and *nāsikā ca*: by the word *ca* (and), the respective points of articulation such as the palate are included in accordance with their own classes (*varga*). In rules such as *edaitoḥ*, the addition of the marker *t* (as in *etaiḥ*) is for the sake of removing ambiguity, not for the purpose of including sounds of that specific duration; therefore, even the protracted (*pluta*) vowel is included. Regarding *caturdhā* (fourfold):

In the view that [the stops] are produced by expulsion, however, there are five types, because it is accepted that the *ūṣman* sounds involve a slightly opened articulatory effort (*īṣadvivṛta-prayatna*).

"Contacted" (*spṛṣṭa*) and "slightly contacted" (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*): these possess an internal nature because they precede the production of the phoneme (*varṇa*). For instance, the vital air (*prāṇa*), impelled by effort from the region of the navel, moving upward, strikes the articulatory locations (*sthāna*) such as the chest; from that [striking], the phoneme [arises].

This is the production of the sound (*dhvani*) that manifests it. Regarding that production, when the tip, the middle, and the root of the tongue properly touch the respective places of articulation for each phoneme—such as the palate and so forth—that is *spṛṣṭa* (contact); when they touch slightly, that is *īṣatspṛṣṭa* (slight contact).

There is closure (*saṃvṛtatā*) when [the tongue] is merely in proximity [to the palate], and openness (*vivṛtatā*) when it is at a distance. For this very reason, although there is no difference in the palatal nature of *i*, *cu*, *ya*, and *śa*, when the utterance of the *ca*-group is to be performed, there is complete contact (*samyak-sparśa*) with the palate along with the tip of the tongue and other parts; whereas for the letter *ya*, there is slight contact (*īṣat-sparśa*).

One should investigate this matter by following the experience that the letters *śa* and *ka* are situated at a distance from one another, as well as the statements of the authors of the *Śikṣās*. As for *vivāra*, *saṃvāra*, and so forth,
they are external [articulations] because they arise after the production of the phoneme, when the vital air (*prāṇa*)— having struck and turned back at the palate— is withdrawn.

Thus they are described. *Saṃvāra* (closure) arises from the contraction of the glottis, while *vivāra* (opening) arises from the expansion of that very same [glottis]. It should be noted that these two are indeed distinct from the internal [articulatory efforts] consisting of closure (*saṃvṛta*) and opening (*vivṛta*), because they consist respectively in being situated near to or far from those [efforts].

(12) *a a* [Pāṇini 8.4.68]. *a a*. By the rule *upām*, there is elision (*luk*) of the two case-endings. The first [vowel] is open (*vivṛta*), while the second is closed (*saṃvṛta*). Thus he says: "having referred to the open [vowel]" (*vivṛtam anūdya*). This means: "in the place of the open [vowel]."

The state of being open (*vivṛtatva*) indeed exists; therefore, the intention is that by this [rule], the long vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) is established in forms such as *daṇḍāyanam*. (13) *pūrvatrāsiddham* 8.2.1.

"Non-application in the preceding" (pūrvatrāsiddham). If this were an independent injunction, then it would only follow that the three final sections (tripādī) are non-applicable with respect to what precedes them; however, a rule belonging to the three final sections would not be non-applicable with respect to what precedes it as something subsequent. Consequently, in the case of *praśān*, the substitution of *na* by "o no dhātoḥ" [would not be established].
The elision of *n* would be established [by P. 8.2.7], because the rule for the substitution of *n* has its purpose fulfilled in the vocative singular (*saṃbuddhi*).

Likewise, in the case of *anaṅvān*, the elision of *n* would be established by the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), because the rule for the insertion of *num* has its purpose fulfilled in the vocative singular. Thus, in the case of *anaṅvān*.

Because the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is established as valid, there would be an elision of the *n* (nalopa). However, since the rule for the augment *num* has its purpose fulfilled in the vocative singular (*saṃbuddhi*), he says: "This is a heading (*adikāra*). The intention is that if one follows the view that an operation prescribed in the "last three quarters" (*tripādī*) is not established (*kāryāsiddhipakṣa*), then forms such as *amū* and *amūm* would not be established.
How this is not established will be demonstrated by us on the occasion of explaining the word *adaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "of eleven kinds":
although eight [kinds] are mentioned in the Bhāṣya, the acute (*udātta*) and others are not mentioned; nevertheless...
It should be understood that eleven [external efforts] are mentioned following the statement of Kaiyaṭa. Regarding the rule *khayāṃ yamāḥ*:
for the sake of instructing beginners, the external efforts (*bāhyaprayatna*) have been set forth by some through an easy method.

For example: "The *kha* sounds (the velars), along with the sibilants (*śa*), *ṣa*, and *sa*, are characterized by expansion (*vivāra*), breath (*śvāsa*), and lack of voicing (*aghoṣa*); whereas the *ha* sounds (the palatals, etc. are characterized by contraction (*saṃvāra*) and voicing (*nāda*)."

"The voiced consonants (*ghoṣa*), the first, third, and fifth of the classes (*varga*), and the semivowels (*yaṇ*) are weak-breathed (*alpapāṇa*); the second and fourth of the classes, as well as *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*, are strong-breathed (*mahāpāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "accompanied by the emission of breath" (*śvāsānupradāna*), the meaning is that they involve the effort of breath. Regarding the phrase "they open the throat," this refers to their effort of expansion (*vivāra*).
This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "others, however": [they are] *ha*, *śa*, the *yama*s, and the *anusvāra*. Regarding "possessing *nāda*": they are participants in *nāda*;
the meaning is that they do not possess the effort (*prayatna*) [of articulation]. Regarding "odd-numbered":
within the classes (*varga*), the first, third, and fifth letters are the odd-numbered ones. Regarding "those situated in the *yama*s of the classes": [this refers to the aforementioned letters].
The meaning is that they belong to the same class (*vargaga*) and the same sub-class (*yamaga*). Regarding "few" (*alpa*): "few breaths" means having little vitality (*alpaprāṇa*). Amara states:

"In the masculine, *asavaḥ* and *prāṇāḥ* [mean] vitality. Regarding "not useful" (*anupayukta*): the sense is that otherwise, there would be no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between *ka-kha-ga-gha* and so forth. This refers to the examination of "proximity" (*āntaratamya*).

And the examination [of this] will become clear in the root text itself through such statements as: "for the aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*) voiceless (*aghoṣa*) *ṭha*, there is the corresponding *th*; for the voiced (*sahoṣavat*), sonant (*nādavat*), and aspirated *ha*, there is the fourth letter of the class," and so forth.

"Kādayaḥ" (the letters beginning with *ka*) refers to the order as established by common worldly usage. In the fourteen aphorisms (*sūtra*), similarity should be understood in terms of both pronunciation and written form. "Before *ka* and *pa*" is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood as "before *kha* and *pha*. "Semi-visarga" (*ardhavisarga*)...

Similarity [of sound] should be understood in both pronunciation and writing. Regarding the phrase "of the vowels *ṛ* and *ḷ*": the absence of the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention) occurs by the rule "ṛtyakaḥ. As for the analysis (*vigraha*), some say it is: *ā* and *ḷ-varṇa* are *ṛḷ-varṇau*; [the genitive] "of those two" (*tayoḥ*). However, in the *Manoramā*, it is stated: *ā* and *ā* are *ralau*; and those two are the vowels (*tau ca tau varṇau*).
And so on, as established. [The rule] *nājjhalau* [states that] vowels (*ac*) and consonants (*hal*) are not mutually identical. Regarding the phrase "accompanied by the vowel *ā*":
the grammatical indications (*liṅga*) such as the citation in the rule *ālasamayavelāsu* serve as evidence for the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ā*.

Regarding the phrase "the *yaṇ*-substitution and so forth": in the word *śītala*, the long vowel resulting from the *savarṇadīrgha* rule is the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). Here, [there is] the prohibition of *ṭhasi*.

It may also be easily stated that in forms such as *ditya*, the substitution of *ḍha* for *ṭha* (by the rule *ṭh-ṣ-ṭh-o ḍhaḥ*) does not occur. However, it cannot be easily stated that the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* (by the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭu*) also does not occur, because that [substitution] is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the substitution of *ḍha*. This is the general direction [of the argument]. "Otherwise" means: in the event that the rule *ājjhalau* were not formulated. "By the force of the *grahaṇaka-śāstra*" [is the reason].
The intended meaning is this: for if it were admitted that even the letters beginning with *ha* are denotable by the vowel *a*, just like the long vowels and so forth,

then they would possess the status of being vowels (*actva*), because in the case of the *pratyāhāra*s, it is accepted that there is a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) regarding what is denoted and what denotes.

(14) *Aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* |1|1|69|. An *aṇ* which is not being prescribed [as a substitute] indicates its own homogeneous phonemes (*savarṇa*). Therefore, in the case of *itaḥ*, the long *ī*—which would otherwise be three morae (*trimātra*) according to the rule *idama iś*—does not occur. Regarding *udic ca*: here, the term "not being prescribed" (*avidhīyamāna*) does not apply.

Because of the capacity of the *udit* designation [to include its own class]. Therefore, even though it is being prescribed [by the rule], that which is designated as *udit* indeed includes its homogeneous counterparts—as in *kuhoś cuḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.62], as in *jagāda* and *jaghaṭe*. [The inclusion is] by means of the subsequent *ṇakāra*; for a specific understanding arises from the [authoritative] commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
This is because of the use of the *tapara* (long vowel marker) in rules such as *ṭhupasargādṛti* and *ṭhṛta ut*, which serves as an indicator (*liṅga*).

If [the substitution] were to occur by the preceding rule [P. 6.1.89], then the *tapara* designation here would be purposeless; for since the sound *ṛ* is not *aṇ*, it does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). And thus, due to being non-proximate (*aparatva*), there is no long vowel [substitution]: *upa ṛkārīyati*.
The passage to be cited later, beginning with "ityādi," is also consistent [with this view]. The same applies to the vowel *lṛ*.
The phrase "the name of thirty" is to be supplied [to the rule]. This has been stated on the grounds of logical symmetry;
however, in reality, the fact that the vowel *lṛ* includes the vowel *ṛ* is not observed anywhere.

"By the force of the commencement of the sūtra": the sense is that if there were *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity), then because *ai* would be included by *e* and *au* would be included by *o*, the commencement of the sūtra *ṭhAI-auC* would be redundant. "It should not be brought forward": by this, [the forms] *glāvam* and *glāvaḥ* [are accounted for].

That "ṭhāṬtomśasoḥ" does not apply will become clear in the root [text] itself. As for the phrase "even though": the sense is that the rule governing the inclusion [of sounds] (grahaṇaka-śāstra) has not yet been finalized. And this we shall explain under the rule "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ". Regarding the word "ākṣara": [it refers to] of the syllables (akṣarāṇām).
*Samāmnāya* refers to the traditional collection of instructional sūtras. Those occurring therein are called *ākṣarasamāmnāyikāḥ*.
[The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *ahvacontodātāṭṭhañ*. [In the case of *akṣara-samāmnāya*,] the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha* (by the rule *ho ḍhaḥ*) does not take place.
Even though, in the absence of the elision of the vowel *ā* (*praśleṣa*), only the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would apply and not the substitution of *ḍha*.

Since that [condition] is unestablished, it would be more appropriate to say that the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) does not occur here; nevertheless, according to the view that "the technical rules (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) pertain to the time of the *Ārya* (i.e., the time of rule application)," the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* does not apply to an *antaraṅga* operation within the three chapters (*traipādika*). Therefore, in this *antaraṅga* [operation]...

Some maintain that this was stated with the thought that when the substitution of *ḍha* is to be applied, the elision of a word-final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*)— being an external factor— is as if non-existent (*asiddha*). Others, however, hold that the substitution of *ḍha* [is stated] with the intention that the elision can somehow be prevented by the principle that "a rule based on a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not universally obligatory" (*aṃjñāpūrvako vidhir anityaḥ*).
They say, "It is not so," as stated [in the commentary]. The mention of *viśvapābhiḥ* here is illustrative;
the substitution does not occur even in cases such as *viśvapāḥ* and *viśvapābhyām*. The rule *ṭh-ḍhaḥ* is also illustrative;
for instance, in *ṛthagāyuḥ* and similar forms, the letter *gha* does not replace the vowel *ā* according to the rule *hayo haḥ*. This is the general direction.

If, however, in the rule "the spirants are [uttered] with the opening wide [of the articulators]," one carries forward the word "slightly" (īṣat) from the preceding rule "slightly touched" (īṣatspṛṣṭam), and then, having set aside [that word] in the rule "and of the vowels," one establishes the distinction of effort as "the spirants are slightly opened, while the vowels are fully opened."

When it is explained in this way, it is established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that the rule *ājjhalau* can be discarded. Regarding the phrase "those [vowels] are nasalized": the intention is that only those *aṇ* sounds which belong to the traditional list of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) serve as designators (*saṃjñā*) for their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). And thus, the letter *r* and the letter *h* [are also included].

It should be understood that even when situated within a *pratyāhāra*, there is no notion of "destruction" (*kṣaya*), because there is no other [phoneme] of the same class (*savarṇa*) [to replace it]. (15) *taparaḥ tatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70): [A vowel] followed by *t* denotes its own duration.
And that [term] as well as *tāpara*—the sense is that both are intended by the word *tat*. (16) *vṛddhir ādaic* | 1.1.1.
*vṛddhir ādaic*: *ā* and *aic* form a *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction) *dvandva* compound; [this is governed by] *upāṃ sulu*... [etc.]

Or rather, *giti* and *āṭ* [are the two members], with the elision (*luk*) of the *sur* (the case-ending). Alternatively, it is a collective dvandva compound. One should not object that in this case the suffix *ṭac* would apply by the rule "after a dvandva ending in *cu*, *da*, *ṣa*, or *ha*, when it denotes a collective," because the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) is not mandatory. We shall provide the proof for this under the section on compounds.

Alternatively, let *ṭhā* and *iti* be taken as a compound; the word *vṛddhi* may then be construed through *tantra* (simultaneous application) or *āvṛtti* (repetition). Because it is a *bha* by virtue of belonging to the *yasmayādi* group, the substitution of *ku* for *ca* and *u* does not occur. In the case of *ṭhai*, it is indeed two morae (*dvimātra*) because it follows *tā*; therefore, in the expression *ṛṣṇaikatvam*, it is not three morae (*trimātra*).
The rules for *vṛddhi* substitution include "vṛddhir eci" and others.
(17) *adeṅ guṇaḥ* | 1.1.2 | The term *adeṅ* [in this sūtra] includes the *tapara* marker for all purposes. By this, in the case of *aṅgodakam*, [the rule applies].

It does not have three morae (*trimātra*). In the word *‘aratī’*, however, there is only the letter *a* and never the letter *ā*. Nor can the restriction [of the vowel length] be established by proximity based on metrical measurement (*pramāṇa*), because once the substitution of *r* for *l* (*raparatva*) has been applied, one [the *a*] consists of one and a half morae (*adhyardhamātra*) while the other [the *i*] consists of two and a half morae (*ardhatṛtīyamātra*).
The examples of *guṇa* and *pradeśa* are: "ṭhādguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87), "ato guṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.97), and so forth.
(18) "Roots beginning with *bhū* and *vā* are called *dhātu*" (Pāṇini 1.3.1).
Regarding the term "roots beginning with *bhū* and *vā*": *bhū* and *vā* are *bhūvau*; this is a *dvandva* compound.

The term *ādi* (beginning) occurs twice in the compound; it is an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of two words expressing the sense of "arrangement" or "manner. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: *ādiśca ādiśca ādī*; those for whom *bhū* and *vā* are the first (*ādī*). Thus, they are "those beginning with *bhū*" and so forth, being similar to them. And this similarity is by virtue of their denoting action; intending this, he says: "denoting action" (*kriyāvācinaḥ*). "Denoting action" [is repeated].

Why [is the word *bhv-ādayaḥ* used]? So that in examples such as *kim*, *ṭhyāḥ*, and *paśyasi*, there may be no status as a verbal root (*dhātutva*). For if that status were present, the elision of the vowel *ā* would occur by the rule *ato dhātoḥ*. This is established in the *Manoramā*. Why [specify] *bhv-ādayaḥ*? [To exclude] indeclinables (*avyaya*) such as *hiruk* and *ṛthak*, so that [the suffix] *iśya* does not apply to them.

And let there not be [the designation of verbal root] for a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) whose meaning is [already expressed by the suffix]. By the addition of the marker *u* to *stambhū* and others, it is indicated that those listed in the sūtras possess the status of verbal roots (*dhātutva*). The inclusion of *culump* and others is achieved through the *gaṇasūtra*: "This enumeration is illustrative (*adholam*)."
(19) *Prāgrīśvarān nipātāḥ* |1|4|56|.
[The sūtra begins with] "prāgrīśvarāt" (before the word *rīśvara*). Why is the mention of the word qualified by the letter *r* used?

It is so that, by the principle of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*), the rule "*īśvare tosunkasunau*" (Pāṇini 3.4.23) should not be taken as the limit [of the section]. However, if [the limit were determined] merely by proximity (*pratyāsatti*)...

If it is argued that the status of being a limit (*avadhitva*) for the word *adhi* in the rule "adhir īśvare" is thus established, then let it be stated explicitly for the sake of clear understanding: (20) *cādayo’satve* 1.4.57.

The particles beginning with *ca* [are not used when denoting a substance]. Why [specify] "not denoting a substance"? [Consider the example: *paśuḥ*. A substance (*dravya*) is that which is endowed with gender and number.
But here [in the following case], it would indeed be so: *lodhaṃ nayanti paśu manyamānāḥ*. In this instance, *aśu* has the sense of "correctly" (*samyak*).

The word *ca* ("and") is for the purpose of including [the term] *gati* within the designation *upasarga*. Otherwise, according to the rule *ā kaḍārāt*, there would be an optionality. The result of this is seen in forms such as *praṇeyam*.

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] is by the rule *upasargādasamāse’pi*; the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the subsequent member of the compound ending in a *kṛt*-suffix is established by the rule *atikārake*. This is the general direction. Regarding *nis-nir-dus-dur*:
the substitution of *l* for the *r* of *nir* and *dur* occurs by the rule *upasargasyāyatau*, as in *nilayate* and *dulayate*. [The substitution of *l* for the *r* of] *nis*...
And because the substitution of *ru* for *ra* is not established (*asiddha*), there is no substitution of *la*; thus we have *nirayate* and *durayate*.

(22) *na vā* is *vibhāṣā* | 1|1|44 | "Not" (*na*) is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), while "or" (*vā*) is an option (*vikalpa*). Thus he says: "in the case of prohibition and option. This applies in rules such as *vibhāṣāśveḥ* and others.

The two options of prohibition and alternative arise; therein, once the subject has been made uniform by the prohibition, the alternative subsequently operates. In cases such as *śuśāva* and *śiśvāya*, the alternative applies where [the rule] was not otherwise established;
however, in cases such as *śuśuvatuḥ* and *śiśviyatuḥ*, it applies where there is constant application by the rule "vacisvapi... (Pāṇini 6.1.15).

Commentary: Here, this should be understood: the word *sthiti* (position) connects with both [the preceding and following terms] according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). And it effects a reversal of the meanings of the words. Therefore, negation (*niṣedha*) and option (*vikalpa*) are the designatum (*saṃjñin*) of the word *na-vā*; option is the designatum of the word *vibhāṣā*.

And this sūtra is for the purpose of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases; it serves no purpose in an option regarding what has already been established (*prāptavibhāṣā*) or in an option regarding what has not yet been established (*aprāptavibhāṣā*). For in an option regarding what has already been established, since the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) is already proven, the explicit mention of the option (*vibhāṣāśruti*) merely reiterates the positive aspect—as in "it occurs in *akṣa*"—and then [negates it] by saying "it does not occur in *akṣa*."
By restating the negative portion as "it does not occur" and then establishing only the positive portion as "it occurs in the case of *akṣa*," [the rule functions].

However, regarding the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) of the root *śvi* in the rule "vibhāṣā śveḥ," if it were to operate through the mode of affirmation, then the optional substitution of semivowels (*saṃprasāraṇa*) would apply only to those suffixes marked with *p*, but not to those marked with *k*.

Because [the root] belongs to the *yajādi* class, by the rule *vacisvapi-*, the substitution would necessarily occur [before all suffixes]. Now, if its application were by way of prohibition (*pratiṣedhamukhena*), then its application would occur only before *kit* suffixes and not before *pit* suffixes.
Nor can it be argued that it applies in both ways—by way of prescription (*vidhimukhena*) before *pit* suffixes and by way of prohibition before *kit* suffixes.
It cannot be said that "let the application [of the prohibition] occur," because that would entail the fault of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to its dual nature.

However, when the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is applied, following the sequence of the revealed text (*śruti*), the prohibition "e" first applies to the *kit* [suffixes]; thereafter, once a uniform form has been established for all *liṭ* suffixes, whether they are *kit* or *akit*.
The phrase “it occurs in the sense of *akṣa*” functions solely by way of a positive injunction (*vidhimukha*) in its negative form (*akarūpeṇa*). Why is this so?

Because of the statement “*vaṃ rūpam*,” let there not be a technical name (*saṃjñā*) for the word itself, as is the case with the designation *ghu*. For if that were the case, the rule “*vibhāṣā śveḥ*” would mean that the word *navā* is a substitute (*ādeśa*) for the verbal root *śvi*.

When the word *iti* is present, however, it is understood that the meaning (*artha*) is the thing named (*saṃjñin*). For instance, in common usage, a word primarily denotes its meaning; yet in expressions such as “He says ‘au’,” the word comes to refer to its own form (*svarūpa*).
In grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), however, because of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "its own form" (*tasya rūpam*), reference to the word's own form is the general rule (*autsargika*).

However, when used in conjunction with the word *iti*, the distinction is that it refers to the meaning (*arthaparatā*). This alone is what constitutes the so-called "reversal of the word-meaning" (*padārthaviparyāsakatva*) of the word *iti*. In the case of the commentary on rules such as *hr̥kroranyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.4.53), the status of being a technical term (*saṃjñātva*) belongs to the meaning itself, and not to the word *vibhāṣā*.

The removal of the grammatical anomaly (*vairūpyoddhāra*) is the result. For that sūtra (*Pāṇini 1.4.52*) is indeed a *vibhāṣā* (optional rule) in both cases; because the root *harati* preceded by *abhyava-* has the sense of "eating," and because the root *kṛ-* in the sense of "transformation" is intransitive, the status of being the object for the agent in the *aṇi*-state would have been established by the rule *atibuddhi-*, etc., in the *ṇi*-state—[but this is not the case] because of the difference in meaning.

And because that [causative operation] begins even when [the action] has not yet been reached; as illustrated in the Bhāṣya: "When [the action] has already been reached: *abhyavahārayati saindhavān* (he causes the Saindhavas to eat), *abhyavahārayati saindhavaiḥ* (he causes [them] to eat with the Saindhavas);

*vikārayati saindhavān* (he causes the Saindhavas to change), *vikārayati saindhavaiḥ* (he causes [them] to change by means of the Saindhavas). But when [the action] has not yet been reached: *harati* (he carries)."
"Devadatta carries the burden; he causes Devadatta to carry the burden; he causes the burden to be carried by Devadatta.
Devadatta makes a mat; he causes Devadatta to make a mat;
he causes a mat to be made by Devadatta"—this is the general principle.

(23) *Svaṃ svaṃ śabdasyāśabdasaṃjñā* |1|1|68|. A word’s own form [is used] when it is not a technical grammatical term (*saṃjñā*). For example: *agner ḍhak* [Pāṇini 4.2.33] results in *āgneyam*; *āṅe yamahanaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.28] results in *āyacchate* and *āhate*. In these cases, only *agni*, *āṅ*, *yam*, and *han* are the things being designated (*saṃjñin*).

If it is argued: "Since suffixes such as *ḍhak* cannot occur after words like *aṅgāra* which are denotable by terms such as *agni*, they must arise from the word-form itself; and since there is the governing rule (*adhikāra*) beginning with 'from a nominal stem' (*prātipadikāt*), what is the purpose of this sūtra?"—this is true. [However, it is necessary] for the sake of [suffixes occurring] after synonyms of *agni* and so forth, such as *vahni* and the like.

This Sūtra is commenced so that [the word-form] may not [be understood as the meaning]. Now, one might object: even without the mention of *rūpa* (form), the form itself will be understood by the word *sva* (itself), because it does not depend on instruction for its cognition, because it is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), and because its presence is invariably fixed (*niyatopasthitika*). For the meaning (*artha*) requires the apprehension of a relationship for its cognition; it is common (*sādhāraṇa*) since it can be conveyed by synonyms; it is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it is the object of the cognition produced by the knowledge of the word; and it is of non-invariably fixed presence because it is not cognized in the state of imitation (*anukaraṇa*). So what is the use of this mention of *rūpa*? [Response: This is not so. Even though the form is unique, it is still possible for it to be understood as something other than the form itself, such as a quality (*guṇa*), an action (*kriyā*), or a substance (*dravya*). For example, when one says "he eats his own (*svam atti*)," the word *sva* refers to the self (*ātman*), which is a substance; or when one says "he goes to his own (*svam gacchati*)," it refers to the place, which is a substance; or when one says "he makes his own (*svam karoti*)," it refers to the act of making, which is an action. Therefore, the mention of *rūpa* is made to exclude these possibilities. Furthermore, the meaning is not invariably present; for instance, in the case of the expression "the word *go*," the meaning is not understood. Thus, the mention of *rūpa* is necessary. As for the objection regarding the lack of dependence on instruction: although the form is indeed independent of instruction, there is no rule that it must always be understood independently. Since the meaning is dependent on the apprehension of a relationship, it is not invariably present. Consequently, the mention of *rūpa* is indeed required. As for the claim that the meaning is external because it is the object of the cognition produced by the knowledge of the word: this is not a valid reason for exclusion, for the form is also an object of the cognition produced by the knowledge of the word. Moreover, the form is internal because it is directly perceived through the senses, whereas the meaning is external because it is not directly perceived. Therefore, the mention of *rūpa* is necessary. As for the claim that the meaning is of non-invariably fixed presence because it is not cognized in the state of imitation: this is not a sufficient reason, for the form is also not invariably present in cases such as "the word *go*" or "the word *ghaṭa*. Thus, the mention of *rūpa* is established. Finally, the mention of *rūpa* is also necessary to prevent the application of rules such as *svasya ca*, which would otherwise apply to the meaning. It is said: In this treatise, the mention of "its own form" (*svarūpa*) is for the purpose of making it known that meaning (*artha*) is also intended [as a grammatical element] just like its own form. By this, the principle "when there is the mention of something meaningful, that which is meaningless is not included" becomes established.
In that regard, meaning should be understood from the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*), while its own form is understood from the explicit statement "or its own form" (*vā* / *svaṃ rūpam*).

By virtue of the inherent capacity [of the rule], there is the apprehension of a form that possesses meaning; therefore, in the cases of *āśe* and *uśe*, the sound *e* does not receive the designation of *pragṛhya*. However, in the case of *rādūhoḍheaityatra*, by the mention of *ūḍha*, only the word ending in the suffix *kta* is apprehended, and not a portion of a word ending in the suffix *ktavatu*; this is explained in detail elsewhere.

What is the purpose of the condition "not having the technical name *śabda*"? It is so that the suffix *ki* may apply after the roots *dā* and *dhā* when preceded by a prefix (as in Pāṇini 3.3.92), but it should not apply to the root *ghu* when it has the meaning of "sound.
Nor should it be argued that the suffix *ki* would necessarily apply after *dā* and *dhā* simply by virtue of their being assigned the technical name *ghu* in the rule "ā-dhā-ghu" (Pāṇini 1.1.20).
Because the designation [of the term *āta*] is necessary for the rule prescribing the substitution of *ī* for *āta* (Pāṇini 6.4.64),

its capacity [to denote its own form] is exhausted; therefore, in this case, the compound “the designation of the word *ā* (*ā-śabda-saṃjñā*)” is not a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), as that would result in the unintended inclusion of the actual forms of words like *artha* and *araṇa* when they function as designations of meanings (*artha-saṃjñā*).

However, "śabda" refers to the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*). In that context, the term "technical name" (*saṃjñā*) forms a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*), namely "the technical name [occurring] in the science of grammar. Thus he says: "that which is a technical name in the science of grammar. (24) *yena vidhis tadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72).
Regarding the word *vidhi*: in the term *vidhiḥ*, the suffix *ki* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*.

In the word *yena*, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*), and not the agent (*kartṛ*). This is because [the use of the instrumental] supersedes the genitive that would otherwise be required by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix. Nor can it be argued that [the agentive sense is blocked] by the restrictive rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*.
There is no application [of the rule], because since the *karma* (object) has already been stated, there is no possibility for both [the object and the instrument] to be expressed simultaneously.

Thus, in this case, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used solely for the instrument (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, the instrument is dependent, because only that which is presided over by an agent (*kartṛ*) possesses the status of being an instrument.
Consequently, here the third case indicates dependence (*pāratantrya*). Nor is there [such a thing as] "dependence" in cases such as *ṭheraj* and so forth, regarding the vowel *i* and others.

Dependence (*pāratantrya*) belongs to the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth, while independence (*svātantrya*) belongs to [words] such as "axe" (*vāsī*) and so forth, like that of carpenters and the like;
however, this is merely a matter of intention (*vaivakṣika*). Therefore, the qualifier (*viśe�ṣaṇa*) is non-primary (*apradhāna*).
And it follows that this is a designation for another entity; this is what he states: "the qualifier belongs to that which ends in it."

Thus he says: "after [roots ending in] *ktvā* and *san*," and so forth. Why "with *seṭ*"? Example: *bhittvā*.
Having cut [it], he desires to eat.
(387) *āpjñapyṛdhāmīt* (Pāṇini 7.4.55). Regarding *āp*, *jñap*, and *ṛdh*: from the rule *ani mīmā...* onwards, the term *ac* is understood by anuvṛtti; furthermore, *aḥ syārddhadhātuke* applies.

And therefore, [the rule] "sīti ca" (Pāṇini 1.2.19) applies. Thus he says: "ava ītsyādau" (in the case of *ī* when followed by *san* and beginning with *s* or *t*). By specifying that the *ī* belongs to *san*, the result is obtained that it occurs before *s* or *t*. (388) "The elision of the reduplicated syllable" (Pāṇini 7.4.58).

Regarding *īpsati*: by the rule "the second [element] beginning with a vowel," the word *ipsa* undergoes reduplication. Regarding *bibhrajjiṣati*: there are four forms due to the optional addition of the augment *ram* (in the form of *r*), both when the augment *iṭ* is present and when it is absent. Regarding *susvūrṣati*:
when the lengthening occurs by the rule "aj-jhan-gamām saṃyoge," the substitution of *ū* takes place.

(389) *dambha icca* | Pāṇini 7.4.56. Regarding *yiyaviṣati*: because the prohibition of substitution applies when there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*)—as per the rule *na cī*—the doubling occurs first, and then the vowel *u* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) undergoes the change to *i*. Regarding *ūrṇunūṣati*: this occurs in the absence of the augment *iṭ*.

In the expression *ṭhajjhanagamām*, the vowel is long. However, in the alternative view where the augment *iṭ* is applied, there is optionally the substitution of *ṅ* by the rule *vibhāṣorṇoḥ*. And here, it is not the case that [the suffix] *san* is present; rather, the meaning is that it is the word *nu*. Because of its *kit* status, there is no *guṇa* substitution. This means [it applies] in place of *ṇic*.

The suffix *san* should be stated [after a verb] when expressing apprehension (*āśaṅkā*). For example: *svā mumūrṣati* ("the dog is about to die"). The understanding here is that there is an apprehension of death regarding a single dog. Others hold that the meaning is "he becomes the object of an apprehension of death. One should not suspect the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) here on the basis of the rule *ūrvatsanaḥ*, because of the two rules beginning with *ader*.
Because it will be stated later that [the rule] is to be explained by carrying over the word "ano" and splitting the sentence, [we have]:
*sani mīmāghurabhalabhaśakapatapadāmaca iḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.54). In the rule *sani mīmā*, the word *si* is carried over from the previous rule *aḥ si*. This [refers] to that *san*.

Because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the understanding is that [the rule applies] when there is the suffix *san* after a root beginning with *s*. Regarding the phrase "because the form *mī* is not distinguished": one might object that since the form *mī* derived from the root *mī* is based on a secondary derivation (*lākṣaṇika*), its inclusion by the mention of *mī* would not be possible. This is not a fault; for in cases where the verbal form is required as something already established through a secondary derivation (*lakṣaṇā*), [it is indeed included].

Regarding the phrase "akṣaṇapratipadoktayoḥ," Kaiyaṭa has stated in his commentary on the sūtra *ṭhiko jhal* that this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) applies, but not where there is a reliance upon actual usage.
His intention is as follows: in this context, only the form itself is relied upon for usage. [This is because of the rule] *vibhāṣā*.

However, in the rule *diksamāse*, because the word *samāsa* is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to that which is produced by a grammatical rule, the compound specifically prescribed by a rule (*pratipadokta*)— namely, *iṅnāmānyantarāle*— is what is resorted to.

Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the maxim regarding "that which is indicated by a rule versus that which is prescribed by a specific rule" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*), this [maxim] applies in certain instances.
In some places it does not apply; this is the extracted meaning. Regarding *mitsati*:
because the suffix is *kit* by the rule *halantācca*, there is no guṇa substitution for the penultimate vowel. Regarding *śikṣati*:

one might object that, according to the maxim regarding [roots] without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaparibhāṣā*), it would be more appropriate to understand only the root *ak* in the sense of "endurance" (*amarṣaṇe*).

Regarding this, they say: "This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerns the domain of the mention of suffixes (*pratyayagrahaṇa*). For this very reason, the author of the Nyāsa stated that in the rule *'ṛvraścyoḥ'* both *jajṛṣ* and *jṛṣ* are included;
therefore, here too, it is entirely appropriate to include both the *svādi* and *divādi* [roots]."

(391) *muco ’karmakasya guṇo vā* |7|4|57|. Regarding *muc* when it is intransitive: since the absence of *guṇa* would have been established by the rule *halantācca* [Pāṇini 1.2.10] due to its being *kit*, this is a prescriptive rule. Thus we have *vivatsati*. This is by the optional application of the rule *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.92].

The *parasmaipada* [suffixes]. (392) *iṭ sani vā* | Pāṇini 7.2.41: "The augment *iṭ* is optionally applied before the suffix *san*. In forms such as *cikīrṣati*, once the lengthening has been effected by the rule *aj-jhan-gamāṃ sani*, this [augment] does not apply.

[The suffix] *san* occurs; having carried forward the word "upadeśe" from the rule "ṭhekāca upadeśe," it is explained as "after a root ending in ṛ in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*). For this very reason, he gives an example even without [the application of] *iṭ*:
*dudhūrṣati*. [The root is] *hvṛ* in the sense of "crookedness. There is lengthening by the rule "ajjhane."

The substitution of *u* [for the vowel of the root] occurs by the rule *ṭhūlope pūrvasya*; then there is the substitution of *ra* for the following sound; and a long vowel is substituted [for the penultimate short vowel] by the rule *hali ca*.
(393) *smipūṅrāñjvaśāṃ sani* 7.2.74: because of the inclusion of the marker *ṅ* in the term *ūṅ*, only the root *pūñ* [is affected], as in *pupūṣati*. *ṭh*...

Because of the prohibition [of the augment] in the case of the root *san* when followed by a suffix beginning with a *grah*-type consonant (*sani grahe*). Regarding *sisimayiṣate*: since the root *smiṅ* (meaning "to smile slightly") is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment), the introduction of the *iṭ* augment does not apply. Furthermore, because of the restriction "only after roots ending in *t* or *ṇ*," the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur.
Regarding *aririṣati*: since this root is also *aniṭ*, the introduction of the *iṭ* augment does not apply.
Regarding the phrase "of the word *ris*": when the augment *iṭ* has been added to the suffix *san* and the *guṇa* substitution has been applied, the form *aris* remains;

the meaning is that the doubling of the word *ris* occurs by the rule "the second [element] beginning with a vowel" (*aj-āder-dvitīyasya*). Examples include *añjijiṣati* and so forth. The roots *añjū* (in the sense of manifestation, anointing, etc. and *aśū* (in the sense of pervasion) both have the marker *ud*, and thus there is an option regarding the augment *iṭ*.
The root *aś* meaning "to eat" is always *seṭ*. However, the root *aś* belonging to the *kryādi* group is always *seṭ* as well.
Regarding the two sūtras: one is in the second [chapter] and the other is in the sixth. Therein, by the former, the substitute *gāṅ* is applied;
by the latter, *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel-contraction). This refers to the rule: "There is *saṃprasāraṇa* for the root *hve*. And this—
This has been explained under the causative forms (*ṇijanta*), but it is recalled here. *Jijāvayiṣati*: the root *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root mentioned in the rule "ucaṅkramya. *Śuśrūṣate*:
by the rule "ñāśrusmṛdṛśāṃ sanaḥ," the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied.

(394) *stautiṇyoreva ṣaṇy abhyāsāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.61). [The rule] *stautiṇyoreva* implies that the form *riṣādhayiṣā* is correct, whereas *sisādhayiṣā* is not; this is how it should be understood. Regarding the phrase *upasargāt tu iti*: by the maxim of the intermediate exception (*madhye’pavādanyāya*).

The point is that by the rule *tautimyoḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* prescribed by *ṣṭhādeśapratyayayoḥ* alone is sublated, and not that which is ordained by the subsequent rule *thādiṣvabhyāsena ca*. [Examples:
*suṣupsati*; [here,] because the suffix *san* is *kit* by the rule *rudavidamuṣagrahiṣaḥ saṃśca*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening. [Example: *pratīṣiṣati*; here...
The meaning is that when the suffix *san* follows the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going," the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* indeed occurs.
(395) *saḥ svidisvadisahīnāṃ ca* | Pāṇini 8.3.62. [This rule states that the *s* of the root *iṇ* is replaced by *ṣ* before the suffix *san*, as well as before the roots *svid*, *svad*, and *sah*.]

It is not the case that [the rule] "niyamānneha" (restriction does not apply here). Nor should it be argued that if the prohibition here were due solely to the restriction, then the rule "unoteḥ syasanoḥ" (after the root *ūn*, there is optionally *ṣ* before *sy* and *san*) would become devoid of scope;
for that rule is intended to prevent the substitution of *ṣ* in the form "abhisusūḥ," which is derived from the desiderative *abhisusūṣati* when no suffix follows.
Because this is necessary; and this is clear in the *Kāśikā*.

Regarding the term "śaiṣika": some say this is a *Ślokavārttika*, while many hold it to be a *Bhāṣya*. That which exists in the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is "śaiṣika. It is derived with the suffix *ṭhañ* according to the *adhyātmādi* group. It occurs in the sense of the possessive suffix *matup*.
It has the sense of the *matup* suffix. By virtue of belonging to the *gaha*-class and others, the suffix *cha* is applied. "That which possesses the sense of the *matup*" is called *matubarthika*.

The suffix *ṭhan* is added by the rule "after [stems ending in] *at*, the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan*. Thus ends the section on the formation of denominative verbs (*sannanta-prakriyā*) in the *Tattvabodhinī*.

There are five types of *vṛtti*: those consisting of primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), compounds (*samāsa*), the retention of one [of two or more words] (*ekaśeṣa*), and verbal roots with prefixes and suffixes (*sanādyantadhātu*).
He states this incidentally, beginning with "primary derivatives, secondary derivatives," etc. Regarding the phrase "five types of *vṛtti*":
the meaning is that the designation *vṛtti* used by the ancient teachers for these five is adopted here as well.

He states the definition of *parārtha*: "that which has another as its purpose" (*parārtha*). That which is a qualified object—either by being included within the meaning of a suffix (*pratyaya*) or by being included within the meaning of another word (*parapada*)—is *parārtha*.

That by which such an object is expressed is *parārthābhidhāna* (expression for the sake of another). For this very reason, there is no occurrence of *vṛtti* (verbal function) in the case of finite verb endings (*tiṅanta*).

In that case, because the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is not admitted; otherwise, in expressions such as *mṛdu pacati* ("he cooks softly"), the quality of softness would not be construed with the result [of the action], since it is accepted that "there is no occurrence of qualifiers in a compound, nor is there connection with qualifiers for that which has already occurred in a compound. Thus say some regarding the *samartha-sūtra*.

Kaiyaṭa, however, says: "The meaning is that where there is the denotation by another word of that which is the meaning of a subsequent word, that is *vṛtti*. For example, in the case of *rājapuruṣa*, the meaning of 'puruṣa' (person), which was not expressed by the word *rājan* (king) during the stage of the sentence (*vākya*), is denoted [by the compound]. [He adds: "It is without analysis (*avigraha*)."

The meaning is "devoid of worldly form. Regarding the term *asvapada* (non-own-word): the meaning is "not composed of all the words that are being compounded. Regarding the phrase "only in the case of *dvandva* and *bahuvrīhi*": the sense is that since those two are prescribed by means of the mention of "many" (*aneka*) and its subsequent recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), the status of being a multi-word compound is possible only for them.
"Only in certain cases" refers to examples such as *dvayahajāta*. "By name" means by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Regarding *kumbhakāra*: here, the compound with the subordinate member (*upapada-samāsa*) occurs prior to the derivation of the case-ending (*sub*). Regarding *kaṭaprūḥ* and *ajasram*, these are treated under the Vārttika *vibvacipracchi-* and the Sūtra *amikampī-*.
In the word *aṭaprūḥ*, there is a compound with the verbal root due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of the term *ajastram*. [It is used in the sense of] "eat and drink! (*pibatakhādata*).
The compound *ākhyātamākhyātena* is formed because it is included in the list beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka* (Pāṇini 2.1.72).

Thus ends the section on the remainder of all compounds in the *Tattvabodhinī*. (403) *ajādyataṣṭāp* | Pāṇini 4.1.4. [This rule prescribes] the feminine suffix *ṭāp* after nominal stems beginning with *ajā-* and those ending in short *a*.

*ajādyataḥ*: This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose beginning is the word *aja*. It does not mean "that whose beginning is a vowel (*ac*)," because of the specific mention of *ṛc* in the rule *ṛci* (Pāṇini 6.1.173) and by virtue of the force of its inclusion in the list [of *ajādi*]. Furthermore, the term *at* here does not denote the phonetic form itself, as indicated by the evidence in the rule *aṅkhyāyam* (Pāṇini 7.1.2). Thus, it refers to those words beginning with *aja*.

And because of the force of the separate recitation (*pṛthakpāṭha*): although the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "after a *ṅī*, a *yāp*, or a nominal stem" (*yāpprātipadikāt*) applies here, the terms *ṅī* and *yāp* are not connected [to the word *prātipadika*], since it is precisely these two that are to be prescribed in this very rule;
rather, it is the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone [that is the subject]. And that [nominal stem] is qualified by the vowel *a*. And by means of the qualifier...
Because it ends with that [suffix], there is the designation (*lākṣaṇika*); thus he says: "of those beginning with *aja-* and of that which ends in *akāra*.

In the sūtra, the word *ataḥ* is in the genitive case; its meaning is the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*). With the intention that the mention of "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is a reference where the attribute is primary, he says: "that femininity which is to be signified. And this...

This was stated with the intention of the view that "the gender is the meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārtha*). When there arises the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)—"from what does this arise?"—it should be understood that [the suffix] occurs after stems beginning with *a* and ending in *a*, due to proximity (*saṃnidhāna*). This applies in the rule *iko yaṇ aci*.

When there is an expectation as to what follows [the suffix] *aci*, it is like [the rule] *ikaḥ*. The letter *p* in *ṭāp* is for the sake of accent (*svarārtha*), and it is also for the sake of including the general term in rules such as *ṭāṅ-āpaḥ*, *āṅ-cāpiḥ*, and *yāḍ-āpaḥ*. The letter *ṭ* is for the sake of preventing its elision. For if it were stated simply as *āp*, then by the paribhāṣā regarding markers (*anubandha*), [it would refer only to] *ṭāṅ*.

In examples such as *āpaḥ*, this very [suffix] is understood, but there would be no inclusion of the suffix *ḍāp* after *āp*. Now, one might object that since the rule could be established simply by saying "after *at*" (*ataḥ*), the mention of "beginning with *ac*" (*ajādi*) is redundant; nor can it be argued that it is for the purpose of providing a rule where it would otherwise not apply—such as in *ruñcā*, *uṣṇihā*, and *evaviśā*—because they end in consonants (*halanta*). If that were so...

Only the root beginning with *ruñc* is taken here, and not one beginning with *aj*. Therefore, he explains: "The mention of *aj-ādi* [refers to] the *ṅīp* suffix following *ṅīṣ*. Regarding *khaṭvā*: from the root *haṭ* in the sense of "desire," [the suffix] *kvan* is applied according to the rule *ṭhaśū-pruṣi-laṭi-khaṭi-kaṇi-viśibhyaḥ kvan*.
If it is asked, "How then is the grammatical gender established for inanimate words such as *khaṭvā* (bed) and the like?", it is replied:

The gender that consists of specific configurations of body parts such as breasts, which is well-known in common worldly usage, is not relied upon in grammar; for if it were, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the absence of the feminine suffix *n* in words such as *dārāḥ* (wives).

Furthermore, because it would follow that the grammatical operations based on the three genders—as in *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*—would fail to apply as appropriate, the three genders must be merely technical (*pāribhāṣika*). And that [technical gender] is purely positive (*kevalānvayin*). This is the meaning of the verse: "This is the meaning... and "This is the female... [and so forth].

Because words have an unobstructed range of application everywhere in the sense that they denote "this thing exists as an individual," it must be determined through grammatical treatises on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) and other sources which word is capable of denoting one gender, which two, and which three. However, words such as *kumāra* (boy) and *brāhmaṇa* (brahmin) [behave differently].

Words are denotative of the scriptural (śāstrīya) masculinity as qualified by worldly (laukika) masculinity, and of the scriptural femininity as qualified by worldly femininity. Otherwise, how could usages such as *kumārī* and *kumāraḥ* be established? [As stated: "A woman [is denoted] by the two words *ara* and *reṇu*..."

The meaning of "in the sky" (*nabhasi*) is precisely the same as that of "immortal" (*amara*). Now, one might ask: how is the objection raised by the Mīmāṃsakas—that the masculine gender in the word *aśune* is intended to be significant—to be reconciled?
For a technical (paribhāṣika) gender, being non-excluding, renders any such intention irrelevant.
If it is argued that the ordinary (laukika) gender is not understood from the word *paśu*,
they reply: "By the principle of the final topic of the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭhādhyāya*), namely *'chāgo vā mantravarṇāt'*,
a restriction to the masculine gender must be understood for the word *chāga*."

This is because [the word] has the capacity for a technical sense qualified by worldly masculinity. And that consists of three classes; so says one [author]. And it was stated by Hari: "These three classes alone reside in certain things without being contradicted by contradictory classes such as 'cow' or 'human'."

In the Bhāṣya, however, another perspective is stated: "The two genders are to be understood from our own established doctrine as contraction (saṃstyāna) and expansion (prasava). From the root *styai* with the suffix *ḍraṭ*, 'strī' [is derived] for contraction; from the root *sū* with the prefix *sap*, 'pumān' [is derived] for expansion. That which is the interval between these two is the neuter (*napuṃsaka*) in its parts. Thus it is said.

This is its meaning: *saṃstyāna* (contraction) is the female (*strī*), which is the diminution of the qualities (*guṇas*) characterized by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. *Prasava* (procreation) is the augmentation of the qualities; that is the male (*pumān*).
Regarding the root *sū*, the letter *s* (the *sakāra*) is replaced by the letter *p* (the *pakāra*); such is the meaning.

According to Tārānātha, the suffix *ḍumsun* is added after the root *āṬ* (to increase), with the vowel shortened by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). Mādhava, however, states that it is formed from the root *ūṅ* with the suffix *ḍumsun*. When there is an absence of both increase and decrease, that which is intermediate between the two—being dissimilar [to either]—is the neuter. This is according to the rule *amrāṇnapā*.

The sense is that this is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Thus, the neuter gender denotes mere existence as such. For this very reason, words such as *avi* (sheep) function with respect to both the quality (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*), just like words such as *śukla* (white). "According to their own established doctrine" (*svakṛtāntataḥ*) means according to the tenets of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntataḥ*). Amara states: "The words *ṛta* and *anta* both mean the doctrines of Yama."

*Pañcājī*: This is a *dvigu* compound formed by the rule "in the sense of a collective" (*itaretarārthe*) from the five goats (*pañcānām ajānām*). Since the final member of the compound ends in the letter *ṭha*, there is femininity; thus, by the rule "for a *dvigu*," the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Nor should one argue that, because the rule for the application of suffixes excludes the inclusion of the final element (*tadantavidhi*), the suffix *ṭāp* would not apply here and therefore only *ṅīp* could occur.

It must be stated [that this rule applies], because the application of the *ṭāp* suffix is established through the knowledge that the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies to feminine suffixes—by virtue of the mention of "not preceded by *mahat*" (*amahatpūrvagrahaṇa*) and the governing rule concerning "non-subordinate elements" (*anupasarjanādhikāra*). [The phrase] "resting on the collection of the meanings of the compound" [is used]. Now, [one might object]: in the case of a function (*vṛtti*) where the individual meanings are not abandoned (*ajahatsvārthā*),...

If it is argued that the compound (*samāhāra*) also serves the same purpose as [the rule for] *aja* and so forth, this is not so; for even then, that [compound] is extrinsically conditioned (*bahiraṅga*) in its dependence upon the co-occurrence with another word, whereas the application of the suffix *ṭāp* fulfills its function within the intrinsically conditioned (*antaraṅga*) domain. If one asks, "How then [is the form] *paramājā* derived?", [the answer is: it is simply from that which had already been produced previously.

The suffix *ṭāp* occurs there because of the presence of the vowel *śravaṇa*. However, in the case of *ṭhatyajānirajā*, you should understand that the suffix *ṭāp* is applied due to the fact that the stem ends in *tva*. Nor should it be argued that the same should apply here in the rule "añca-ajī" as well; for that [suffix] is superseded by the suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule "vigoḥ. As for *caṭakā*, [the objection] does not hold here.

The suffix *īkāra* [in *mūṣikā*] might be suspected [of being derived from the rule *ratyayasthād iti kāraḥ*], but because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *aṭakāyā airaḥ*, or because of the specific nipātana (irregular formation) in this very context, its exclusion is established. Thus, the modern grammarians (*navyāḥ*) hold that the inclusion of "aṭakā" in the list beginning with *kṣipakā* is not strictly necessary. As for *mūṣikā*: [it is formed by adding the suffix *ṅīṣ*] according to the rule *vṛścikṛṣoḥ*.
Under the governing rule *kikan* (Pāṇini 5.2.34), by the rule *ūṣer dīrghaś ca*, the word *mūṣikā* has the vowel *i* in its middle.

However, as for the word *mūṣaka* mentioned by Mādhava—derived from the root *ūṣ* (meaning "to steal") with a long vowel in the penultimate syllable, followed by the suffix *kvun* in the sense of a name—it is from that [base] that this form [mūṣikā] is derived by adding the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. As for the substitution of *i* [for the final vowel before the suffix], it occurs by the rule *pratyayasthāt...*.

This is the distinction. Some, however, do not apply this word ending in *kvun* to the list beginning with *aja*, because its inclusion in that list is for the purpose of establishing the suffix *ṅīṣ* by virtue of it being a genus (*jāti*), whereas this [word] is a proper name (*saṃjñā*) and thus does not fall under the category of *ajādika*. Likewise...
They say that because it ends in a vowel (*ac*), the suffix *ṭāp* is established from a word ending in *kvun*; however, this is questionable.
For even though it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*) like "vyāghrī" and others, its status as a genus (*jāti*) is not lost.
[The rule] "from *sambhastṛ*, *ajina*, *śaṇa*, and *piṇḍa*, when followed by *phala*" applies; the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "she whose fruits are like a *bhastṛ* (winnowing basket)."

Regarding the phrase *ṅyāpoḥ*: this is established in Mādhava’s commentary on the *Dhātupāṭha* under the rule *halaniṣpatāv iti*. However, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *ākakarṇe*, only the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is seen.
[The rule] *sagada-kāṇḍa-prānta-śataikebhyaḥ puṣpāt* [is explained as follows]: *sadackāṇḍeti*.

Suggesting that the reading ‘atprākkāṇḍe’ is not to be respected, he cites [the example] ‘pratyakpuṣpā’. On this point, the moderns [hold that] the two rules beginning with ‘saṃbhasre’, as well as the rule ‘ūlānnañaḥ’ which is yet to be stated, serve as exceptions to what is obtained by the rule ‘ākakarṇe’.

Although the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp* was recited in the Bhāṣya on that very sūtra, it has been included here by the authors of the treatises because there is no difference in the result; however,
one should not fall into the error of thinking that these are therefore internal gaṇa-sūtras of the "ajādi" group, for there is no evidence for such a status.

However, they say that these are indeed Vārttikas. [The rule] "And a Śūdrā who is not preceded by *mahat* is a caste" means: the word *śūdrā* takes the feminine suffix *ṭāp* if it denotes a caste (*jāti*), but not if it is preceded by *mahat*. The phrase "if it denotes a caste" is connected here as well. Therefore—

The form *mahatī śūdrā* indeed becomes *mahāśūdrā*. Regarding the phrase "in the case of connection with a male" (*puṃyoge tu*): it is not a restriction that "connection with a male" must consist solely of the relationship of husband and wife; rather, the relationship of progenitor and offspring is also included.
Thus says the Smṛti: "From a Kṣatriya [king], however, a Vaiśya and a Śūdra woman give birth to two sons, the Māhiṣya and the Ugra."
Regarding the term *mahīśūdrī*: according to Amarasimha, "The word *ābhīrī* is [also] *mahāśūdrī* in the senses of caste (*jāti*) and connection with a male (*puṃyoga*).

In this context, the rule "not preceded by *mahat*" (*amahatpūrva*) is redundant; for the compound word *mahāśūdra* as a whole denotes the caste of the Ābhīra. Since the constituent part (*avayava*) [of the compound] lacks meaning there, [the prohibition does not apply].

If there is no presence of femininity inherent in the meaning of the word *śūdra*, then the suffix *ṭāp* cannot apply due to the absence of its scope. [Objection: It must be stated that "that" (*tat*) is for the purpose of indicating the rule of application to what ends with that (*tadanta-vidhi*). [Response: No, because the rule of application to what ends with that is already indicated by the governing heading (*adhikāra*) regarding non-subordinate elements (*anupasarjana*). This is the general direction. On this point, the moderns [hold] that the statement beginning with "and a *śūdrā*" (*śūdrā ca*) is the [required] rule.
They say that this is merely a *vārttika* contained within the rule *ṭhājādyataḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.4), and not a *gaṇa-sūtra*.

Regarding *kruñc* and so forth: some maintain that these three are *halanta* (ending in a consonant). However, in the *Bhāṣya*, having cited usages such as *ruñcānālabheta* and *uṣṇihakakubhau*, it is shown that they also end in vowels (*antā*).

[The forms] are accepted [as feminine]. This is because they end in /a/, either by the addition of the suffix *ac* (Pāṇini 3.1.134) or by the suffix *kap* (Pāṇini 7.1.70), as applicable. Regarding the phrase "even in the case of connection with a masculine" (*puṃyoge’pi*): when words such as *jyeṣṭhā* refer to the first-born woman and so forth, the suffix *ṭāp* is established simply by virtue of their ending in /a/. However, when...

If there is an intention to express the feminine gender and so forth for *jyeṣṭhā*, then the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is prescribed by the rule for words denoting a connection with a male (*puṃyoga*)—would be applicable; the word "also" (*api*) is used to indicate that even that [suffix] is superseded by this [present rule].

[The rule applies] after *mūla* and after a negative particle (*nañ*). Why "after a negative particle"? [Consider] *śatamūlī*. [An example of the form] *amūlā*: *amūlā* (is derived from *na* + *mūlā*). Why "after a negative particle"? [Example: *śatamūlī*. [And] *amūlā*.
This is a class of medicinal herbs.
(404) *ugitaśca* | Pāṇini 4.1.6 | By the word *ugit*, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is qualified; by means of this qualifier, the rule of "ending-in" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. And not...

In the formulation of suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*), a prohibition might be suspected; however, by the rule *anupasarjanāt*, it is indicated that for feminine suffixes there is an extension of the application to what ends with that suffix (*tadanta-vidhi*). This is established by the maxim *yena vidhis tadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), with the exception of rules involving suffixes marked with *u*, vowel-specifications, and the mention of phonemes (*ugit-varṇa-grahaṇa-varjam*).

With the intention of stating that it has been so declared, he says: "from that which ends in an *ugic* [suffix]. Here, two types are possible: an *ugic* nominal stem (*pratipadika*) and an *ugic* suffix (*pratyaya*). Regarding the first case, examples such as *atibhavatī* and *atimahatī* (meaning "one who surpasses the 'becoming one'" and "one who surpasses the 'great one'") illustrate that which ends in an *ugic* [stem]. [This applies] to the group beginning with *sarva*.

The designation of the word *bhavat* as having the marker *ugit* is due to its occurrence in the reading *havatu*; however, for the word *mahat*, it is because of its treatment as being like a present participle (*śatṛvadbhāva*). Nor should it be argued that, because of the prohibition "the treatment as if possessing a designation does not apply to a nominal stem (*aprātipadikena*)", the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would not occur after the isolated words *bhavat* and *mahat*.

With the intention that the term *ugit* refers to any word-form whatsoever—whether it be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or not—a prohibition [of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*] does not apply; thus, he provides the example *bhavantī*. He gives a second example of a word ending in an *ugit* sound: *pacantī*.
