From the root *pac*, in the present tense (*laṭ*), with the suffix *śatṛ*, we have *pacat*; then, by the rule *kartari śap*, the suffix *śap* is added. However, if the form *ahavat* found in the *sarvādi* list is derived from the root *hā* with the suffix *ḍavatu* (as in *hāter ḍavatu*), then *ahavatī* would indeed also serve as an example of a second type of word ending in an *ugit* sound. But when the suffix *ṅīp* is applied to *bhavat* ending in *śatṛ*, the augment *num* is obligatory by the rule *apśayanādīnām*.

[The forms] *ukhāsrad* and so forth [are explained as follows]: it falls from the pot (*ukhāyāḥ sraṃsate*), it falls from the leaves (*parṇebhyo dhvaṃsate*). [The roots] *raṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu* mean "to fall. By the rule *vasusraṃsu*, the substitution of *d* for *s* occurs. It should be stated that this applies after a word ending in *van*. [By the rule] *vano ra ca*, the suffix *van* is understood; by the term *van*, a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in that suffix is taken. However, the governing topic [of the rule] refers to a word ending in *van*.

He states that because the base (prātipadika) is qualified, there is an extension of the rule to include what ends with that [base]—namely, "from that which ends in *van* and from that which ends in what ends in *van*. The intention is that both [possibilities] are obtained by carrying forward the word *svam* from the sūtra *yena vidhis tadantasya* and interpreting it as "and of its own [form]. However, if only that which ends in *van* [were intended]...
If it is argued that [the form] is called "ending in *van*" by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*),

then one should not explain [the rule] as "and of *vat*" (*vataś ca*) by carrying over the word "*vat*" from the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya*; nor should one fear the prohibition here— namely, "the principle of behaving like that which possesses a designation does not apply to what is not a nominal stem" (*na vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena*)— for that [prohibition]...

They say that this is because [the word *van*] lacks the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of the general form": the intention is that since the word *vana*—devoid of its indicatory letter (*anubandha*)—is mentioned in the Sūtra, the technical rule concerning indicatory letters (*tadanubandhakaparibhāṣā*) does not apply. [Objection: If there is a mention of *van*, how can one obtain what ends in *van* and what ends in that which ends in *van*?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the case of the mention of a suffix," and so forth. "By that" means by one ending in *vat*. "That which ends in what ends in that" is also obtained; for under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in the feminine," the prohibition—"by a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that contains a mention [of a suffix]"—does not apply.
The intention is that this is established by the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) found in rules such as *ṭhamahatpūrve*. Others, however, say:

although a word ending in *van* is in fact a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), since it has been stated that the element *vana* as it is actually cited in the rule lacks the status of a nominal stem, there is indeed a concern regarding the prohibition [of the elision of the final vowel] based on the principle of "that which is cited [as part of a technical term]."

Regarding *nāsti*: [it is derived from] *sū* with the suffix *kvanip*. Regarding *sutvānam*: the compound is formed according to the rule “*atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe*,” where both [prefixes] take the suffix *kvanip*. Regarding *atidhīvarī*: [it is derived from] the root *dhā* with the suffix *kvanip* according to the rule “*anyebhyo’pi dṛśyate*” (it is seen after others as well). There is the substitution of *i* for *a* by the rule “*humāsthe*” (*humāsthā*); however, in the Bhāṣya, it is stated that [the suffix *kvanip*] is added to the root *dhyai*.

It is established that this is a *saṃprasāraṇa*. Even when the substitution of *r* for the *n* has been made, because that which is modified in one part remains essentially the same (*ananyatva*), the rule "elision of the final letter of *an*" (*allopo’naḥ*) would apply;
however, it does not apply here because of the specific qualification that *an* must end in the letter *n*, as is the case in the rule *vayuvamaghonām*.
It has been explained. Regarding the word *śarvarī*: the suffix *vanip* is applied to the root *śṛ* by the rule *anyebhyo’pi*.

Once the *guṇa* substitution and the replacement of the vowel with *r* (*raparatva*) have occurred, although [the stem] ends in a consonant (*haśantāt*), the prohibition of the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* does not apply here, because the suffix was not prescribed after a stem ending in a *haś* (consonant).

"Or in a *bahuvrīhi*. Regarding "or in a *bahuvrīhi*": it will be explained that this is obtained through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) from the phrase "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*), and not as a new statement. As for *bahudhīvarī*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the city which has many fishermen (*dhīvānaḥ*). In the alternative case:
The form *ḍāv* is derived by the rule *ābhyām*. Thus, in the dual number, there are three forms—*bahudhīvaryau*, *bahudhīvānau*, and *bahudhīve*—which is the intended meaning.
(405) *pādo’nyatarasyām* | 4|1|8|.

Regarding "dvipāt": in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "dvau pādau yasyāḥ," there is the form "adhidhīvarī" [as an example], with the analysis being "the city in which there are many fishermen (*dhīvānaḥ*). In the alternative case, the suffix *ḍāp* is applied by the rule "ābubhābhyām. Thus, it occurs in the dual number.
The meaning is that there are three forms: *bahudhīvarī*, *bahudhīvānau*, and *bahudhīve*.
(406) *ṭābṛci* | Pāṇini 4.1.9: *ṭābṛci*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ṅīp* suffix obtained by the preceding rule. Although this [word]...
Since the *Abhidhānakośa* states, "The word *pada* has the same meaning as *pāda* [foot] in the senses of resolve, protection, place, mark,
and object," the form *ekapade* is established by that very word; nevertheless,
this is for the purpose of avoiding the usage of *dvipād* when *ṛc* (verse) is the intended meaning, as in the form *vipadī*.
This commencement of the Sūtra is necessary because [the rule] is not established.
Furthermore, this description of its non-establishment is useful only in the *kāryakāla* (time-of-operation) view, and not in the *yathoddeśa* (place-of-enunciation) view;

for since a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is made once and for all to serve every purpose, there is no possibility of it being retracted. Nor does [the objection] apply to the case of "na ṣaṭ-catur-bhyaḥ."
It should not be suspected that even though the designation "ending in *añc*" has been applied to the final [form], it is not applied to that which ends in *añc* when the suffix *kṛt* is present;
for they say that what is modified in one part is not different [from the original]. That is incorrect.

For the extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) regarding what is modified in one part applies specifically to the rule "a substitute is like the original (sthānin), except in the case of an operation concerning an *al*."

Since that [substitution] does not even apply in the case of an *al-vidhi* (a rule concerning an *al* sound), it is logical to describe it as "not established" (*asiddha*) even under the *yathoddeśa* view.
"Na ṅīp": the sense is that the word "na" (not) is carried over from the preceding sūtra. (408) *ano bahuvrīheḥ* | 4|1|12|. [The rule states:

"After a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *an*, [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied]. Now, one might object: since it must necessarily be stated for the sake of establishing forms such as *rājayudhvā*, etc., [is this not redundant?]
[Objection: Since the desired form is established by the rule *ṛṣvanas-purudaṃśo-nehas-* alone, what is the purpose of this sūtra? [Response: Not so.

This sūtra must necessarily be commenced for the sake of prescribing the suffix *ṅīp* after a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *ann*, by means of the rule *ābubhābhyām*. And thus, by this [sūtra], when *ṅīp* is applied—

Since that [substitution] is prohibited, even the *repha* (the letter *r*) which would have been obtained by the rule "ṭh-van-oh ra ca" (*Pāṇini 8.2.72*) is likewise difficult to obtain; thus, it follows that the *vārttika* "ṭh-van-oh na haśaḥ" is intended for cases other than *bahuvrīhi*. As in the example *bahuyajvānau*: because of the prohibition "na saṃyogaḥ" (*Pāṇini 6.4.13*), this is not a case of elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*).
Therefore, in this case, the optional rule to be stated later—"after [a stem] ending in a *ṭhan* that undergoes elision of the penultimate vowel" (*upadhālopin*)—does not apply.
(409) *ḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām* | P. 4.1.13:

"The suffix *ḍāp* [is optionally applied] after both. The mention of "both" (*ubhābhyām*) is redundant, since the application follows from the continued reference (*anuvṛtti*) to stems ending in *man* and *an*.

Some say it is for the sake of establishing that result (*tatphalasiddhi*). Others maintain that the mention of *tat* is necessary to indicate the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of both [the preceding and following terms]; otherwise, there might be the suspicion that only the immediately preceding term ending in *annanta* recurs. [Objection: But surely, due to the force of the statement regarding the prohibition and the exception (*apavāda*), there must be an alternation (*paryāya*).

[Objection: Since it is established [by the previous rule], what is the purpose of mentioning "either" (*anyatarasyām*)? [Reply: True. The rule *anyatarasyām* is split; therein, the word *anaḥ* is discontinued. Thus, after a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *an*, the suffix *ḍāp* may optionally occur.
Although this was already established by the previous rule [P. 4.1.12] through *ḍap*, this present formulation is for the sake of [extending the application to] those ending in *ṛn* and so forth.

The suffix *ṅīp* is for the purpose of providing an option; however, the rule "after a word ending in *ṭhan*, provided it undergoes elision of the penultimate vowel" (*upadhālopinaḥ*) is for the purpose of restriction. It means: "that option which applies after *ṭhan* occurs only after a word that undergoes elision of the penultimate vowel. Thus, the three forms *bahudhīvaryau*, *bahudhīvānau*, and *bahudhīvaḥ* are established as stated.

It should be understood that the rule *ahuvrīhau vā* is not an original injunction (*apūrva-vacana*). However, due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*) *upadhālopina eva*, in cases such as *uparvā* and *cāruparvā*, the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur for words that do not have a penultimate vowel elision;
rather, only the suffix *ḍāp* and the prohibition [of *ṅīp*] apply. And this...

A split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, in the case of *adhidhāvarī*, even if the optional *ṅīp* were applied by the rule to be stated later, "after a word ending in *ṭhan* that has a penultimate vowel elision" (*upadhālopina*), one would have to refer back to the *ṅīp* obtained by the rule "after words ending in *ṛn*" (*ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*) and [prescribe] its concomitant application (*tatsaṃniyogena*).

If it is argued that the sūtra *ṭhvanora ceḥ* itself may prescribe both the suffixes *ṅīp* and *raḥ*, we reply: no, because prescribing both would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, even if it were to prescribe both, once *ṅīp* is prohibited by the rule *ano bahuvrīheḥ*, the suffix *raḥ* would also be difficult to obtain.

Because it is taught as a combined injunction (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭatva*). In the *Bhāṣya*, however, it is stated that the rule *upadhālopino vā* should follow immediately after *ṭhan bahuvrīheḥ*, while the rule *ṭhana upadhā* and so forth should remain in its other location, and the mention of *anyatarasyām* in the *ṅap* rule should be omitted.
(410) *ana upadhālopino ’nyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 4.1.28.

The term *ana-upadhā* [is understood here]. From the rule *bahuvrīher ūdhaso ṅīṣ* (P. 4.1.25), the mention of *bahuvrīhi* is carried over (*anuvartate*). From the rule *saṃkhyā-vyayāder ṅīp* (P. 4.1.26), the suffix *ṅīp* is also carried over.

With this intention, he says: "annantādityādi" (beginning with "after that which ends in -an"). It has been stated that this [rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Nor should it be argued that, since the option would already be established by the preceding rule, the mention of *anyatarasyām* here is redundant; for if the mention of *anyatarasyām* were absent, this would be a rule for the sake of obligatoriness (*nityārtha*) rather than an optional one.
Regarding the rule *niyama*: (411) *pratyayasthātkātpūrvasyāta idāpyasupaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.44.
[The phrase] *pratyayasthātkātpūrvasya* [is understood]. The vowel *ā* in *āt* is for the sake of pronunciation; it signifies the consonant alone.
This is what is intended. Otherwise, in examples such as *etikāś caranti*, the substitution of *it* [for the final vowel] would not occur;

for in that case, the letter *k*—as qualified by the letter *a*—would not be situated within a suffix (*pratyayastha*). Nor can it be argued that even with the addition of *akac*, the letter *k* ending in *a* becomes situated within a suffix by virtue of the rule *ato guṇe*.

It should not be argued that [the rule applies] because forms such as *satyetika* are established by the presence of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), for that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of failing to establish forms such as *acakatī*, which will be discussed later. With this intention, he says: "after *ka* and *ā*. For the suffix *kāra* is prescribed when there is a reference to a phoneme (*varṇanirdeśa*). The fact that it is sometimes used after a cluster (samudāya), however, is to be justified by the nature of references such as "the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is at a higher pitch" (*uccaistarāṃ vā vaṣaṭkāraḥ*). Regarding the phrase "when *ā* follows": this is a qualifier of the vowel *ā*. By virtue of its force (*sāmarthya*), the operation occurs even when there is an intervention (*vyavāya*) by *ka* and *ā*, but not in cases such as *putrakābhyām* or *sthakaṭaye*, where there is an intervention by three or four elements.

Therefore, in cases such as *arvikā*, the substitution of *ik* for the initial vowel *ā* does not occur; this is precisely what was stated: "The *ik* [substitute] shall be for *ā*, even when followed by *āp*. However, if the word *āpi* were a qualifier of the letter *k*, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in examples such as *rathakaṭhale*, because even a separated [vowel] would still possess the status of being "followed" (*paratva*). Nor can one find a solution through the *nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the rule regarding specified elements), since it has been accepted that the phrase "in an *anuvāda*" in the rule *anuvāde paribhāṣāṇām* means "in qualifiers of the element being restated" (*anūdyamānaviśeṣaṇeṣu*).

In the rule *āt pūrvasya āt iṭ* (Pāṇini 7.2.85), because the suffix *it* is prescribed after restating the phrase *hiṭataḥ*, the word *ataḥ* functions solely as the subject of that restatement (*anuvādya*), and not as a qualifier of what is being restated. On the other hand, it is clear that *āt* serves as a qualifier of what is being restated; therefore, the *nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the metarule concerning the specific mention of a term) does not apply there. Thus, there is a disparity between the two cases. Furthermore, the principle that the *nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā* does not apply to a qualifier of what is being restated will be made known by the inclusion of the term *sthāne* in the sūtra *udīcām ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.46).

If the rule *ṭhasupaḥ* were an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), then in the example *ahuparivrājakā nagarī* (“the city [named] Ahu-parivrājaka”), the suffix *ṭāp* would indeed occur; for although the final member (*parivrājaka*) ends in a *sup*-suffix, the entire compound does not end in a *sup*-suffix, and thus *ṭāp* would follow after it. Therefore, he states that in this case it is a prohibition by connection (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—namely, "if it is not followed by *āp* or a *sup*-suffix. The meaning is: "provided it is not followed by something ending in a *sup*-suffix. *Sarvikā*: [The suffix] *akac* is applied in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñātārtha*) to the indeclinable *sarva* according to the rule *avyaya-sarvanāmnaḥ*. *Kārikā*: [The suffix] *ṇvul* is applied to the root *kṛ*; due to the *ṇit* marker, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening). *Naukā*: [The suffix] *ṇvul* is applied to the root *nau*. Due to the *ṇit* marker, there is *vṛddhi*.

From the word *auśa*, the suffix *ka* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*), followed by *ṭāp*. Regarding *śakā*: the analysis is "she who is able" (*śaknoti*); the suffix *ac* is added according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*), followed by *ṭāp*. Regarding *bahuparivrājikā*: the suffix *ṇvul* is added to the root *vraj* preceded by *pari*. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that in which there are many wandering mendicants" (*bahavaḥ parivrājakā yasyām*), even though the case-ending (*sup*) of that constituent member has been elided, because the final member (*uttarapada*) is still considered to end in a case-ending (*subanta*) by virtue of the rule on the "characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* follows something that ends in a case-ending; therefore, the substitution of long *ī* (by Pāṇini 6.3.44) does not take place here. Regarding *nandanā*: the suffix *lyu* is added to the root *nand* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*nandigrahī-ty-ādinā lyuḥ*). [The question] "What is the purpose of [specifying] the preceding [word]? [is asked].

This is obtained from the very sense [of the rule]. The question is: once the single-substitute (ekādeśa) for *ṭā* and *ā* has been applied, since there is no short *a*-vowel remaining in the subsequent element, [the rule would not apply]. The other [author] says "of the subsequent," etc., with the intention that by the *nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā*, it would not be obtained as being "preceding the *k*" (*kātpūrvasya*), but rather that it would apply to the *a*-vowel immediately following the *k*, overriding the single-substitute for *ṭā* and *ā*. [The example is] *kaṭūakā*; here, *kaṭu* means "possessing a pungent taste" (*kaṭurasavati*). The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of "known" (*ājñāta*) and so forth.

In reality, however, they say that by simply providing the locative indication "in a suffix" (*pratyayasthe ki*) in the sūtra, the mention of "preceding" (*pūrvasya*) could have been easily dispensed with. Regarding *rākā*: it is derived from the root *rak* by the rule *ṛd-ādhārārci-kalibhyaḥ kaḥ*. Due to the diversity of grammatical operations (*bāhulaka*), the designation *it* does not apply. Because a rule conditioned by a specific technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka-vidhi*) is not universally obligatory, the shortening prescribed by *eṇaḥ* does not take place.

Regarding the supplementary statement for *māmaka* and *naraka*: as for the phrase "of *māmaka* and *naraka*," this statement is made because the letter *k* is not situated in a suffix, and thus [the substitution of *ai* for *ā*] would otherwise not apply. *Mānikā*: "this belongs to me" (*mama iyam*) is *māmikā*.

From the rule *yuṣmadasmador anyatarasyāṃ khañ ca*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; by the rule *avamamamakāvekavacane*, the substitute *mamaka* is used for *asmad*; [the first vowel] undergoes vṛddhi. By the rule *eḍmānake* etc., the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur due to the restriction *saṃjñācchandasor eva*. Regarding *narakā*: from the root *ṇarai śabde* (to sound), [with the suffix *aṅ*], and [the substitution of] *āt* for *ec*.

In the word *upadeśa*, there is the substitution of *it* (short *i*) by [Pāṇini 6.4.92]; by [Pāṇini 3.2.3], *ka* is added after a verbal root ending in *ā* when no prefix (*anupasarga*) precedes; and by [Pāṇini 6.4.64], there is the elision (*lopa*) of the final *ā* before the suffix *iṭ* and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, resulting in the substitution of *it*. Regarding the rule *tyaktyapośca*: the phrase "there is an addition" (*upasaṅkhyānam*) is supplied from the previous context. This is an exception to the optional rule *udīcām ātaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.47]. Thus, we have *dākṣiṇātyikā*; it means "not far from the south" (*dakṣiṇasyām adūre*).

*Dakṣiṇā*: In the analysis (*vigraha*) of "she who does not look back" (*na kṣiṇāti*), the form *dakṣiṇā* arises; by the rule "from *akṣiṇa*, *apaśca*, and *puraḥ*, the suffix *tyat* [is added]," and so forth, there is *vṛddhi* [of the vowel], followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

Then, for the sense of "unknown," the suffix *ka* is added. By the rule "for *eṇ* [there is] shortening," there is shortening, and then *ṭāp*. However, according to the Easterners (*prācām*), from *akṣiṇasyām*...

The analysis "diśi bhavā" has been refuted in the *Manoramā*, because in the rule for the formation of the feminine suffix (tyap), by virtue of its association (*sāhacarya*) with [the word] *dakṣiṇā*, only the word *dakṣiṇā* ending in ā is taken; otherwise, there would result the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) in all compound formations (*vṛtti*) of pronouns. Thus, [the form] is "ihatyikā."
*ṭhavyayātyap’-na sāsayoḥ* | *na yāsayoḥ*. This is a prohibition where [the rule] *ratyayasthā* would otherwise have applied; [it concerns] *yāsa*.

With the intention that this is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *yata* and *tata*, he says: "of *yata* and *tata*. [The forms] *yakā* and *sakā* are derived by adding the suffix *akac* to *yata* and *tata*, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp* after the substitution of *ya* for the initial of *tyad*-class words. He states the result when the actual form is not intended to be expressed: "the letter *ya* and the letter *ta*.
Although it would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as "of *yata* and *tata*," nevertheless...

They say that the rule "a yasayoḥ" was stated for the purpose of making known the non-eternality (anityatva) of the technical designation (paribhāṣā) regarding the combination [of vowels]. However, in reality, even if it were stated as "naṭyatadoḥ," the non-eternality would indeed be established; otherwise—
Since it is difficult for the *a* of these two [suffixes] to be subsequent to *ap*, what is the purpose of this prohibition?
Furthermore, there is a prohibition of *tyakan*. As for the statement "there is a prohibition of *tyakan*":
one might object that, for the sake of brevity in the grammatical process (*prakriyā-lāghava*), one should have stated *yikan*—just as one says *ṛdasti-kan*—instead of *yikann*.

Since the absence of [the suffix] *it* is already established by the force of the rule "yaka-anitya-kāra-nipāta-deśa-sāmarthyāt," what is the purpose of this prohibitive statement? Do not say so; for in cases such as *pañcabhir upatyakābhiḥ krītaḥ* ("bought for five valleys") where the taddhita suffix is elided (*luk*) and the feminine suffix is also elided, the [rule regarding] the letter *a* [would otherwise apply].
Because that [suffix] must be heard [in the final form]. For if it were stated as *yika*, then in the case of *añcopatya*, it would result in *añcopatyika*;
however, what is desired is *añcopatyaka*. Therefore, the statement of the prohibition is indeed necessary.
Furthermore, in the rule *ṛdastikaḥ*, the pronunciation of the vowel *i* is for the purpose of being heard when there is elision (*luk*) of the taddhita suffix, and not otherwise.

This is for the sake of brevity in the derivation (*prakriyālāghava*). Otherwise, in the case of *pañcabhirmṛttikābhiḥ krītaḥ* ("bought for five clods of earth"), after the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *ṭhārhāt*, and its *luk*-elision occurs by the rule *ṭardhapūrve*, the suffix *ṭāp* would also undergo *luk*-elision by the rule *uktaddhitalukī*. Consequently, because the cause [for the following change] would no longer exist, the substitution of *ī* by the rule *pratyayasthāt* would not take place.

It might be argued that in the case of *pañcamṛtika*, the substitution of *ī* by the rule *pratyayasthāt...* is already established even before the elision (*luk*) takes effect, because it is *antaranga*. However, this should not be said, for it is accepted that "an external (*bahiraṅga*) elision (*luk*) subverts even internal (*antaranga*) rules. Precisely for this reason...

In cases such as *anīsraṃsate*, the absence of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is established. Furthermore, in forms such as *pañcakhaṭva*—meaning "purchased for five beds"—there is no single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa*) with the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; otherwise, because the single substitute would behave like the initial element (*ādivadbhāva*), it would be included by the mention of *ṭāp*.

In the rule *uktaddhitalukī*, once the elision (*luk*) of a feminine suffix that is not a *anupasarjana* has been performed, the vowel *a* would not be heard [in the final syllable]. This is clear from both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa. Regarding the word *upatyakā*: it is formed by the rule *upādhibhyāṃ tyakan nāsannāruḍhayoḥ*.

Regarding the term *āśiṣi*: the meaning is that it must be stated that the substitution of *it* (short *i*) does not occur for the suffix *vun* prescribed in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). [Examples: *jīvakā*, *bhavakā*. In the sense of "may he live" (*jīvatu*) and "may he exist" (*bhavatu*), the suffix *vun* is applied by the rule *āśiṣi ca*; when the replacement of *a* has been made for that [suffix], the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added.

[The suffix] *ka* does not [apply] when there is elision of the final member. In the word *devaka*, the suffix *ka* is added in its own sense (*svārthika*) to the word *devadatta*. Since it will be stated later in the section on *prāgivīya* suffixes that "elision may optionally occur before suffixes beginning with *ṭha* or *naC*," there is elision of the portion of the word *datta* following the second vowel. As for the mention of the form *devadatikā*:
This is to indicate the elision of the *dat* suffix and to show that in its absence, there is no prohibition of the *it* augment.
Regarding the rule "and in the case of *kṣipakā* etc.": the word "and" (*ca*) implies the connection of the term "the suffix *e*" (*eḥ*). Examples include *kṣipakā* and so forth.

In *kṣipakā*, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule for roots with an indicatory *iṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.135). Similarly, [the suffix is applied] from the root *dhru* in the sense of steadiness (*sthairye*).

What [is it]? Alternatively, from the root *hru* (meaning "motion" or "stability"), with the suffix *ac* by the rule *pacādyac*; because it belongs to the *kuṭādi* group, there is no *guṇa* substitution due to the presence of the *ṅit* marker, and thus the substitution *uvaṅ* occurs. From the root *aṭ* (meaning "breaking"), with the suffix *ac* by the rule *pacādyac*, and then the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Then the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth.
By the rule *eṇaḥ*, the vowel is shortened; then again, the suffix *ṭāp* is added.
*Tāraka* means a star (*jyotis*). It also means a mark on the body (*tarka*). [The suffix] *ṇvul* is applied to the root *tṛ*, and there is the substitution of *a* for the final vowel.
It refers to a constellation, the pupil of the eye, and light.
It also refers to a specific type of cloak. [This is derived from] the rule: "The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied to the root *varṇ* in the senses of coloring, action, expansion, and expressing a quality."
The suffix *ṇvul* is applied after the root *car* and others. That which is a modification of threads is called *tāntava*; elsewhere, it is called *varṇikā*.
It is a commentary on a specific work and also the composer of a hymn.
Regarding the bird, for the Easterners, it is *vartakā*. As for the term *vartakā*: it is so called because it "turns" (*vartayati*).
This option applies only when the word refers to birds; it should be understood that elsewhere, the substitution of *it* (the long vowel) is obligatory.

[The word] *aṣṭakā* [is used] in the sense of being dedicated to the ancestors as deities (*pitṛdevatya*). Regarding *aṣṭakā*: "ancestors" (*pitaraḥ*) and "deities" (*devatāḥ*) together form "ancestor-deities" (*pitṛdevatāḥ*). An action performed for their sake is "dedicated to the ancestors" (*pitṛdaivatyam*). [The suffix -ya is added] after a word ending in *devatā* in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*).
That on which Brahmins eat is the *aṣṭakā*. [The suffix] *takan* is applied after the words *ṛṣi* and *aśva*;
thus it becomes *aṣṭikā*. "Eight" (*aṣṭa*) is its measure. [The suffix] *kan* is applied after a numeral that does not end in *ati* or *śat*.
The suffix *ka* should be stated after the words *sūtaka*, *putrika*, and *vṛndāraka*. Regarding *sūtaka*:

the suffix *kan* is added to the word *sūta* in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Regarding *vṛndāraka*: the suffix *ārakan* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*) according to the rule "after *vṛnda* and *vṛnda*" [Pāṇini 5.2.121]. Although the word *vṛndāraka* when denoting a deity is masculine, [it is used here in the feminine].

The feminine gender of words denoting "foremost among the beautiful" (*rūpimukhya*) is indeed possible; for this very reason, Amara, beginning with the word *ṛṣūttare*, stated: "*vṛndārakau rūpimukhyau*" ("the two *vṛndāraka*s are the foremost among the beautiful").
(413) *udīcāmatāḥ sthāne yakapūrvāyāḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.46.

"Of the northern grammarians": that which has *yak* as its prior member. Having superimposed the femininity residing in the meaning onto the vowel *ā*, there is the feminine designation "of that which has *ṭhyaK* as its prior member. By this, the feminine suffix is obtained; thus he says:
"of the vowel *ā* which is a feminine suffix. Here, from the rule "a yāsayaḥ," the word "e" [is understood].

The literal meaning is as follows: when the vowel *a*—which stands in place of the feminine suffix *ā* preceded by *yak*—is followed by *ka*, then, according to the opinion of the Northern grammarians (*udīcām*), the substitution of *it* (the short *i*) does not occur. This being the case, he states the resulting conclusion: "it would optionally be so" (*id vā syāt*). The same should be inferred for what follows. [Sixth Case]

Since the meaning [of "in its place"] is already obtained by the word *sthāne* itself, the inclusion of *sthāna* in the sūtra indicates that a *paribhāṣā* does not apply to qualifiers of what is being restated (*anūdyamāna*). Otherwise, in cases such as *aupagavīya*, the suffix *cha* prescribed by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* would apply, but it would not apply in cases such as *ālīya* and *mālīya*. In that regard:

This is because, due to the increase in syllables (*ākāra-vṛddhi*), there is an absence of being in the place of *i*. Likewise, if the paribhāṣā "in the place of *i*" (*ik-paribhāṣā*) were to apply to the rule "guṇa in the place of *at*" (*ato guṇe*), then the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) would occur only in cases such as *edhe*, *pacet*, and *yajet*. [Furthermore,] after the substitution of *e* for the augment *iṭ* in accordance with the rule "of the *ātmanepada* endings, *iṭ* becomes *e*" (*ita ātmanepadānām*).

Because the *guṇa* substitution of the vowel *e* has as its locus (*ik-sthānika*) the same position as the original vowel, [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *havantī* and *pacantī*, since the *guṇa* substitution of the vowel *a* does not have the same locus as the original vowel; this is also to be understood. However, the modern grammarians (navya) hold that, just as the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by the rule *ṛgayanādibhyaḥ* after superseding the suffix *cha* prescribed for words ending in *vṛddhi*.
The word *vyākaraṇa* is recited in the *bhṛguyaṇa* and other groups [of nominal stems] with the sense of "it may be" (*syāt*).
If the *paribhāṣā* were to apply to qualifiers that are being restated (*anūdyamāna*), then that recitation would be purposeless;
for if the vowel *ā* were not the substitute for *i*, the designation *vṛddha* [would not apply].

Because [the suffix] would not apply due to the absence [of that condition], they say that since the intended meaning can be understood from that very reading, the inclusion of the term *sthāne* (in place of) here is for the sake of clarity. Regarding *sāṅkāśyikā*: the city established by Śaṅkāśa is Sāṅkāśya, according to the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*.

[The rule] “*aṅkāśādibhyo ṇyaḥ*” [prescribes the suffix *ṇya* after words such as *sāṅkāśya*]. Then, for the sense of "originating therefrom" (*bhava*), [the rule] “*an-yopadhād vuñ*” [prescribes the suffix *vuñ*]. There is the substitution of *a*. Since that [suffix *vuñ*] would apply to a woman originating from Sāṅkāśya, the vowel *i* would optionally replace even that *a*; therefore, it is stated [in the sūtra] “*ātaḥ*” (after a long *ā*). In this regard:
They say: "Just as this letter *a* does not have the letter *ā* as its locus,

so too it does not have a feminine suffix as its locus"— but this argument is deficient in two limbs (*dvyaṅgavikala*), because although the aggregate "ṭhak" has the suffix *vuñ* (which denotes femininity) as its locus, the letter *a* within it does not.

Therefore, *ātaḥ* is for the sake of clarity alone. Regarding *śubhaṃyā*: the suffix *vic* is applied according to the rule *ṭhanyebhyo ’pi dṛśyate*. The word *śubham* is a particle ending in *m*. However, the suffix *ya* [is applied] invariably after a verbal root or the word *yak*. Thus, *sunayikā* means "she whose guidance is excellent."
*Sunayā*. Then *kaḥ*: by the rule “*eṇaḥ*,” it becomes short (*hrasva*). Thus, she whose cooking is excellent is *supākikā*.
(414) Pāṇini 7.3.47: *bhastraiṣājājñādvāsvā nañpūrvāṇām api*.
"This is a bellows" (*bhastraiṣā*). Regarding the statement "the genitive case ending is elided":
some explain this by dividing the word here as *vāḥ*, asserting that because it is a *sūtra*-form, *jas* is used in place of the genitive case ending.
He says, "therefore, *it* (the vowel) may optionally be *i*," because [the rule] *ratyayasthachādi* follows from the previous context. But [an objection]: is it not...

By the word "api" (also) in the rule *añpūrvāṇām api*, the inclusion of those [stems] consisting of the suffix *añ* alone is intended, and not even those preceded by something other than *nañ*. Consequently, forms such as *irbhastrikā* would not be established; therefore, the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) is necessary.

With this intention, he says: "By the very rule of tadanta," and so forth. The underlying sense is that [the suffix] is a subordinate element (aṅga). And thus, the suspicion that the rule “añpūrvāmām” is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha) is dispelled, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of non-application (avyāpti) in cases such as “irbhastrikā. As for the phrase “of another,” however:

The meaning is that for [a word] that is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*), the desired form is established by the rule *abhāṣitapuṃskācca*. Regarding the phrase "but of these two": however, in the case of *bhastrā*, *ajā*, *jñā*, *svā*, and [words ending in] *ān*, the substitution of short *i* (*itvam*) certainly occurs even when they are preceded by another word; for in those cases, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* follows after the suffix *kap*, and thus it does not follow immediately after a case-ending (*sup*).
The meaning is that the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.1.62], *ṭhasupaḥ*, does not apply here. Regarding the phrase *sapūrvayoḥ*:
it means "of those accompanied by a preceding member," that is to say, "of those having an existing preceding word.
Regarding the phrase *antarvartinīm* and so forth: when the state *a su etad su* has been reached and *akac* is applied, [the rule applies] to the *akac*.

Or rather, once the negative *nañ*-tatpuruṣa compound has been formed, by the maxim "even internal [rules] are superseded," the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and so on occurs even before the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending within the compound; subsequently, when the case-ending (*sup*) is added again to the resulting form,

the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and the subsequent formation of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) take place, after which the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied, and that *āp* follows the case-ending (*sup*).

The meaning is as follows: *aneṣakā*—this is the worldly analysis (*laukikavigraha*) to be understood here: *eṣā* (this) is *eṣakā*; *na eṣakā* is *aneṣakā*; or alternatively, *ajñātā eṣā* is *aneṣā*, and [that] *aneṣā* is *aneṣakā*. In the same way, it should be inferred in what follows as well.
"The word *sva* is a qualifier of *ataḥ*" means that although in Haradatta’s commentary it says "here, in place of *ataḥ*... [the word *sva* qualifies *ataḥ*].

It has been stated that this [the word *sva*] is a qualifier of the word *sva*; nevertheless, the intention is that one should understand that the word *ataḥ* (therefore) is to be supplied immediately after the phrase “of the word *sva*. Regarding the phrase “but in another sense”:
the meaning is “in the case of self, kinsmen, and wealth. Regarding the phrase “always indeed”: [this applies] when the suffix *akac* is added in forms such as *svika*.

Since the short *a* resulting from the substitution [of *ātman*] would be difficult to find here, the present sūtra would not apply; consequently, by the rule "before an affixal *t*," the substitution of *i* (itvam) would necessarily take effect. And thus: "The swan, dwelling within the body and moving about like the mental state of a sage..."

The meaning is that the explanation offered by some— namely, that in the verse of Śrīharṣa, "svikāyām," the substitution of *it* (the shortening of the vowel) is optional according to the rule "hastraiṣa"— is not to be respected. In reality, the usage "svikāyām" in the verse "haṃsaṃ tanau— " is simply ungrammatical.

The modern scholars [hold that] because the word *sva* is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) when it means "one's own," there is the substitution of the augment *syāt*. Having stated the counter-examples, he states the examples—beginning with *nirbhastrikā*: "gone out from a bellows" (*nirbhastrā*). The compound is formed according to the rule: "Words beginning with *nis* [form compounds] with words ending in the fifth case in the sense of 'gone beyond' and so forth."

[The word *upasarjana* undergoes] the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjanahrasva*). Then [the suffix] *ṭāp*. Thereafter, [the suffix] *ka* is added in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth. By the rule *eṇaḥ*, there is shortening. Again, *ṭāp* is added. Regarding the sūtra, the mention of the modified form *ṭheṣe* is intended to be restrictive (*vivakṣitaviṣaya*), and not a mere indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) like [the mention of] *yāsayoḥ*; with this in mind, he says: "because of the mention of the form where *ṣatva* has been applied."

Here, because of the feminine designation "ajājñā," only feminine forms such as *ajā* and so forth are understood; therefore, there is no option [for masculine or neuter] here. For example: *śubhrājikā*, meaning "she whose goat (*aja*) is white (*śubhra*). *Jñaḥ* means "one who knows" (*jānāti*). By the rule *ṭhigupadha*, the suffix *ka* is applied. *Priyajñikā* means "she whose husband (*jña*) is dear (*priya*). [The form] *niḥsvakā* [is explained as follows].

The analysis here is *svasyā niṣkantā* (the exit from her own), and not *svikasyā niṣkāntatā* (the state of having exited from what belongs to herself). For if it were the latter, even in the case of a subordinate element (*upasarjana*), the form would be only one— namely *iḥ svikā*— because the substitution of the vowel *ā* would be difficult to obtain, and thus it would fall outside the scope of the present rule.

(414) *abhāṣitapuṃskācca* | Pāṇini 7.3.48. Regarding *abhāṣita*: the meaning is "from this," that is, from a word that is invariably feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*). He states the result of explaining [the rule] by taking it as a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇatayā*)—namely, the phrase "of the bahuvrīhi. Therefore, the suffix is necessarily applied to that which is prescribed after such a [word].

In the case of *khaṭvā* being expressed as the object of the verb *ā-vid*, in the formation of *ṭhakhaṭve*, because the compound-final suffix *kaP* prescribed by the rule *eṣaḍvi-bhāṣā* is optional, when the suffix is absent,
the shortening of the feminine stem (*upasarjana*) is applied by the rule *ostriyām*.

Furthermore, from the word *akhaṭvā*—which has already been treated as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*)—when the suffix *ṭāp* is applied and then the suffix *kap* is added in the sense of "known" (*jñāta*) and so forth, the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] occurs by the rule *eṣaṇaḥ*. Since this option [of the present rule] does not apply there, the general rule *pratyayasthāt* alone operates.
However, if [the word *akhaṭvīyaka*] were a qualifier of another [word], this option would indeed apply; such is the intended meaning.

The term *ahuvrīheḥ* [in Pāṇini 1.2.48] is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the status of being a secondary member (*upasarjana*); therefore, even in cases such as *atikhaṭvikā*, the shortening is indeed obligatory. As for the statement that it is "only optional": in the case of the bahuvrīhi *atikhadvā*, when the form *a su khaṭvā su* has been established, the suffix *su* is elided by the rule *apo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (6.4.140), and then the shortening of the secondary member (*upasarjana-hrasvatva*) applies.

Having set aside [the application of] *eṣādvibhāṣā*, when the compound-final suffix *kap* is applied by virtue of its higher priority, the shortening of the *upasarjana* does not take effect because the word no longer ends in a feminine suffix; however,
the shortening [prescribed] by *eṇaḥ* applies, as does the optionality of *āp* in the presence of *kap* by the rule *āpo ’nyatarasyām*.
Since there is an optional prohibition, when the short vowel [of the penultimate] occurs optionally, the optionality of the rule "ṭhabhāṣitapuṃskācca" (Pāṇini 7.3.48) applies.

For in that case, the intention is that the feminine suffix *ṭāp* following the word *khaṭvā* is prescribed as being from a stem that does not denote a masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*). In the alternative where the short vowel does not occur—
*tvakhaṭvāka* is another form [of *tvak-khaṭvā-ka*] that is not of that [specific] nature. (415) *anupasarjanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.14).
This is an *adhikāra* (governing rule), because it is intended as having a *svarita* accent; such is the meaning. [The word *anupasarjanāt*] extends throughout [the subsequent rules].
Therefore, the ancients maintain that in the case of *ahalyāyuvā śālā*, the rule *yūnasti* does not apply.
Nor should it be suspected that the suffix *ṅīp*—which is conditioned by a stem ending in *n*—would arise here because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*);
for some argue that by the restrictive rule *alopaḥ supsvare*, the elision of *n* is not considered non-existent with respect to *ṅīp*.

Others, however, argue that because of the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule by the statement "there is a prohibition [of the application of rules] when there is a subsequent word (*utarapada*) and regarding the designation of a word-initial (*apadādi*)," the designation of *pada* does not apply here by relying on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*).
Consequently, since the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not occur, the suffix *ṅīp* should indeed apply. However, [this is not so] because of the rule "ano... [P. 4.1.5].

They say that because of the prohibition [by the rule] "from a *bahuvrīhi*," the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur, and since the suffix *ḍāp* is prescribed in its place, both *ṅīp* and *ḍāp* are absent. "This very one" means that it is precisely the governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding "not being a subordinate member" (*anupasarjana*). (416) [The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after stems ending in] *ḍi*, *ḍha*, *aṇ*, *añ*, *dvayasaC*, *dvan*, *ghaÑ*, *mātraC*, *tayaP*, *ṭhak*, *ṭhaÑ*, *kaÑ*, *karap*.
Pāṇini 4.1.15:

*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. The suffixes beginning with *ṭi*, *ḍha*, and *āṇ* are mentioned; by them, that which ends in those suffixes is understood, and this serves as a qualifier for the base noun (*prātipadika*) which is being carried over from the previous rule.

Although the term *ataḥ* (from "a") continues from the sūtra *ṭhājādyataḥ*, it is a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For this very reason, the rule of application to that which ends in [the stem] (*tadantavidhi*) applies; thus, the explanation "a nominal stem ending in *u*" is indeed consistent. However, in the case of *stanandhayī*,...

He will explain that even though the suffix (*pratyaya*) lacks the *ṭi*-designation, because the *ṭi*-designation of the verbal root (*dhātu*) has not yet served its purpose, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* must indeed apply to the entire complex form.
Others, however, maintain that only the suffixes beginning with *ḍha* are designated as *ṭit*; the rule "that which is *ṭit*" applies to both suffixes and non-suffixes alike.

By this [rule], it should be understood that the base (*prātipadika*) [is meant], as well as any base ending in a *ḍha*-class suffix; this is the meaning. As for the status of being *ṭit* (having a *ṭ* as an indicatory letter), it belongs to the base either inherently in some cases, or it is attributed to it in others, because the property of a part is figuratively applied to the whole. An example of the first type is *kurucarī*.

The example for the second [type] is *nadaḍ*. Because it is listed among the *pacādi* group as ending in the suffix *ṭi*, its status as a *ṭit* (having a *ṭ* as an indicatory letter) is inherent. Regarding the third, they say that it will be exemplified under *kṛdanta* (words ending in *kṛt* suffixes) as in "the word *stanandhayī* is formed because of the *ṭit*-ness of the root *heṭ*" (*heṭaṣṭitvāt stanandhayī*). As for *kurucarī*: it means "one who moves in the Kurus," with the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) serving as the *upapada*.

In the word *‘areṣṭaḥ’*, the suffix *ṭa* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Because it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), the feminine suffix *īp* is not added. In the case of *bahukurucareti*—meaning "she in whom there are many Kurucaras"—it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose primary referent is not the meaning of the final member; thus, because the stem ending in *ṭu* (the suffix *ṭa*) is subordinate, the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply. Regarding the phrase "to be mentioned later" (*vakṣyamāṇeti*), it refers to the root *brūñ* in the *lṛṭ* (future) tense.
From the root *vac*, with the suffix *lṛṭ* (future) in the sense of the present, there is the substitution of *śānac*. According to the rule *ruvo vaciḥ*, there is the replacement of *vac* for *ru*.

From the root *vac* (meaning "to speak"), either in the passive voice or as a future action, the suffix *śānac* is applied. By the rule *syatāsī*, the suffix *sya* is added. Then, the changes of *kutva* and *ṣatva* occur. By the rule *āne muk*, the augment *muk* is added. This is due to its being marked with the indicator *ṭ* and its being an *ugit* stem.

The meaning is "by virtue of the status of being a substitute" (*sthānivadbhāvena*). Nor should it be suspected how the status of being a substitute can apply here on the grounds that it is not a rule concerning an *al* (phoneme), because the prohibition "not in a rule concerning an *al*" (*na alvidhau*) does not apply to operations involving *anubandhas* (indicatory letters), as evidenced by the rule "before *lyap*" (*a lyapi*).
For this very reason, in forms such as *ramayām*, when *ām* is applied by the rule for the feminine suffix *ReĀp* due to its higher priority...

By virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element), the suffix *ām* possesses the marker *ṅ*; thus, the augment *yāṭ*—prescribed by the rule "after [a stem ending in] *ā*, there is *yāṭ* before *āp*"—is established.

[The author of the Vārttika argues that] it does not occur because of a specific *jñāpana* (indicatory implication). Since the markers *ṅ* are obtained for the substitutes of *liṅ* and for the *parasmaipada* endings through *sthānivadbhāva* alone, the fact that the marker *ṅ* is attached to the augment *yāsuṭ* would otherwise be purposeless. Therefore, this very fact serves as the *jñāpana*.
The sense is that [the rule] indicates in a general way that "the operations dependent on the base (*āśraya*) do not apply to substitutes.

This is because, since it will be stated in the *it* group (beginning with *it*) that "an *it* [augment] is not [present] when *ṅ* follows," in the case of *tiP* and other suffixes, the *ṅtva* (the status of having *ṅ* as an indicatory letter) which is derived by extension (*atideśika*) is superseded by the *pitva* (the status of having *p* as an indicatory letter) which is original (*aupadeśika*).

Regarding the objection that the *ṅ* of *yāsuṭ* would be redundant and thus could not serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), he replies to one who raises such a doubt: "By the fact that *śna-* [in *śnā*] is *śit*, etc. [He gives the example] *sauparṇeyī*.
The Śruti states, "And Suparṇī was indeed Aditi. From the word *suparṇī*, in the sense of offspring (*apatya*), [the suffix] *ḍhak* is applied by the rule *amāyā yaḥ*.
Regarding the rule *haścchandasī*, it must be understood that the mention refers only to those two [suffixes] ending in *ḍha*, and not to the suffix *ḍhak*.

This is true; for the suffix *ḍha* after *śilā* occurs only in the neuter by its very nature, as it is impossible for it to occur in the feminine. And the suffix *ḍha* after *sabhā* occurs in the feminine in the Vedic language (*chandas*), as in the word *sabhyī*.

Since no other word without an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is possible to observe in usage, one with an indicatory letter is necessarily accepted by default. Regarding the term *aindrī*: [it means] "Indra is its deity," in which case the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *asya devatā*. Alternatively, the analysis is "this belongs to Indra," in which case the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *asyedam*. In this context...

They explain as follows: even though the rule *kṛdgrahaṇe gatikārakapūrvasya* does not apply here, because the term *prātipadika* qualifies [the word] ending in *aṇ*, that which ends in what ends in *aṇ* is also included;
thus, the suffix *ṅīp* would certainly occur after the word *kumbhakāra*. Or, let us assume that *ṅīp* occurs after the word *kāra* itself; nevertheless...

The form ‘umbhakārī’ is indeed established. It is not the case that the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied solely to the word *kāra*; nevertheless, the form ‘umbhakārī’ is indeed established. Nor should it be argued that if *ṅīp* were not applied to the word *kāra*, then the suffix *ḍhak*—by the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*—could not be added to a derivative ending in that [suffix] to produce the form *kaumbhakāreya*.

This is established because, when a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is not a subordinate element (*anupasarjana*), the restriction regarding the initiality of that [stem] does not apply. Nor should it be suspected that, in the absence of such a restriction, the form *kumbhakāreya* might occasionally arise from the word *kārī* by means of the suffix *ḍhak*; for there is the rule: "A grammatical operation concerning words (*padavidhi*) applies to a complete word-meaning (*samarthapada*)."

Because suffixes such as *aṇ* and *taddhita* do not arise when the [base] is incapable [of taking them], as will be explained later; however, in the *Manoramā*, it is stated that there are multiple sentences in this rule. Among them, because of the interpretation: "The suffix *aṇ* which is not a *anupasarjana*; from that which ends with the vowel *a* belonging to it," the following cases do not occur here: *āpiśalam adhīte* (one who studies the work of Āpiśali) and *āpiśalā brāhmaṇī* (a Brāhmaṇī woman who studies the work of Āpiśali). For in these cases, the sense is that of "proclaimed" (*prokta*).

That which is being heard is the subordinate element (*upasarjana*). However, that which is the primary element (*pradhāna*)—here [referring to the suffix] *taddhita*—is elided by the rule "there is elision (*luk*) after what has been stated. Because the phoneme (*varṇa*) is the predominant factor, there is no application of the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); thus it is established that only the feminine suffix *ṭāp* occurs. But if this is so, then [the form] would be *āpiśalī*.

If it is asked: "Since the mention of *anupasarjana* (non-derivative) is necessary for the sake of establishing the form [of the term], its capacity (*sāmarthya*) is exhausted there; how then can it be the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the rule of extension to that which ends in such a term (*tadantavidhi*)?"—to this they reply: "By the formal declaration (*pratijñā*) of its being *svarita*."
Since this is a governing rule (*adhikāra*), by virtue of its status as such, the mention of "not being a subordinate element" (*anupasarjana*) is redundant;
for there is no difference in accent between the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīn* when applied to a stem ending in *añ*, because the former is already acute on the first syllable. Do not say so.
In the case of *otsī*, meaning "the female descendant of Utsa," [the suffix] *ṅīp*—which is prescribed for stems ending in *añ*—would be superseded [by the present rule].
Because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply by the rule defining *jāti* (P. 4.1.63); since that must necessarily be set aside, this [suffix *ṅīn*] is required.

Nor should one argue that this form is already established by the *ṅīn* suffix under the rule "after *añ* of the *āṅgirasādi* group" (P. 4.1.78), and thus the mention of *añ* here need not be made; for in that rule, the word "after *āt*" (*āteḥ*) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*). Otherwise, [the form] of Śārṅgarava...

In examples such as *strī śārṅgaravī* ("a female Śārṅgarava") and *āutsasya strī āutsī* ("the wife of Āutsa"), even when there is connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), the suffix *ṅīn* would apply by virtue of its higher status rather than *ṅīṣ*; however, it is desired that only *ṅīṣ* applies in the case of connection with a male.
Therefore, since the meaning of "being so" (*bhāva*) and the like is not designated as a genus (*jāti*), [the rule] does not apply to the sense of being so and the like.

The inclusion of the term *añ* here is likewise necessary for the sake of the suffix *ṅīp*; this is the general direction [of the argument]. Regarding forms such as *ūrudvayasī*: she whose measure (*pramāṇa*) is the thighs (*ūru*) is [called] *ūrudvayasī*. This is according to the rule: “*dvayasaC*, *daN*, *ghaÑ*, and *mātrac* [are used] when the measure is expressed. If, in this context, under the rule *a loka-*, the term *dvayasaC* is taken as a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated reference) including *mātrac* by means of the letter *C*, just as *tṛn* was [previously], then...

In that case, it would have been possible here not to include the mention of *daṇḍa*, *māna*, and *paṇya*. [The word] *pañcatayī* means "that which has five parts," according to the rule *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap*.

[The word] *ākṣikī* is formed by the suffix *ṭhak* according to the rule *tena dīvyati*. [The word] *lāvaṇikī* means "that whose merchandise (*paṇya*) is salt (*lavaṇa*)," according to the rule *paṇāṭṭhañ*.

The separate mention of *ṭhak* and *ṭhañ* is for the purpose of excluding *ṭhan*; therefore, it does not apply here: *daṇḍo ’sty asyāḥ sā daṇḍikā* (she who has a staff). Because [the suffix] is *ṭhan* according to the rule *ṭhata iniḥ*, there is no *ṅīp* even when it ends in *ñiṭhan*. *Kāśiṣu bhavā kāśikā* (that which exists in Kāśī); [this is formed by] the rule *āśyādibhyaṣ ṭhañ-ñiṭhau*.

Regarding *yādṛśī*: the suffix *kañ* is applied by the rule *yadādiṣu dṛśaḥ*; the form *yā-* arises from the rule *ṭhā sarvanāmnaḥ*. Regarding *itvārī*: she is one whose nature is to go (*eti tacchīlā*). The suffix *kvarap* is applied by the rule *iṇ-naś-ji-sarti-bhyaḥ kvarap*; the augment *tuk* is added by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk*. The inclusion of either one of the two indicatory letters (*anubandha*) in *kvarap* is for the sake of clarity; [the meaning is conveyed] by just one.

The suffix *varaC* is applied due to the establishment of exclusion (*vyāvṛtisiddhi*). Bhāravi [wrote]: "She for whom the great medicinal herbs of auspiciousness were placed [upon her body], the Sovereign Lady (*īśvarā*). In that context, the suffix *varaC* is applied by the rule *īśāmāse*. However, the form *īśvarī* is derived in three ways: first, one is formed with the suffix *ṅīṣ* under the rule for denoting connection with a male (*puṃyogalakṣaṇe*), which is oxytone; second, while the rule *īccopadhāyāḥ* is being followed...

From the root *sthā*, in the sense of a swift action, with the suffix *varaṭ* (as prescribed in the *uṇādi* list), and because it is marked with the *ṭi*-indicator, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added;

this other [form] has the middle syllable as the udātta accent. From the root *īś*, with either the suffix *kvanip* or *vanip*, and with the addition of *ṅīp* or *brā*, the first syllable is the udātta; the other is different. Regarding the term "tācchīlika": this...
The meaning is as follows: when the suffix *ṇa* prescribed by the rule "śīlādibhyo ṇaḥ" is applied, the operations (*kārya*) belonging to the suffix *aṇ* take place;

this is known from the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) of the rule "ārmastācchīlye. For in that rule, the elision of the suffixal *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) is specifically prescribed (*nipātyate*) in order to override the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-elision) which would otherwise be mandated by the suffix *aṇ* prescribed after words ending in *an*. This would be the case if, however, the suffix were *ṇa*.

If the suffix *aṇ* were not required here, what would be the use of it? It is not applied here because it serves to indicate a derivative in the sense of "having that as its characteristic" (*tācchīlika*). [For example: "In this game, the staff (*daṇḍa*) is the weapon (*praharaṇa*)," thus it is *dāṇḍā*.

[The suffix] *ṇa* is applied by the rule "when the weapon is in this," and the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "after *chatra* and others. Let the sūtra simply be: "After *chatra* and others, *aṇ*."
However, many ask: "What is the point of this erroneous derivation? [The answer is: It means "a thief" (*caurī*). [The suffix] *ī* is added because her habit is stealing (*curā śīlam asyāḥ*).
This is due to the supplementary rule (*upasakhyānam*) regarding the addition of *nañ*, *snañ*, *īk*, *kak*, *khyun*, *taruṇa*, and *taluna*. Regarding *nañ* and *snañ*:
the author of the *Vṛtti*, however, having inserted the mention of *atyakhyun* into the sūtra, states: "after *vara* and *khyun*."

This has been recited, and it will become clear later that this contradicts the Bhāṣya. *Straiṇī* and *pāésnī*: [these are formed] by the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* according to the rule "from *strī* and *pums*. *Śāktīkī*: she whose weapon (*praharaṇa*) is a spear (*śakti*). [The suffix] *ikak* is applied after *śakti* and *yaṣṭi*. *Āḍhaḷṅkaraṇī*: not firm (*anāḍhaḷ*).

In the sense of "she by whom one is made prosperous," the suffix *khyun* is applied after the root *kṛ* by the rule *ṭhāḍhaḷsubhage* etc.; there is the substitution of *yu* for *i* by the rule *yuvor* etc.; and the augment *mum* is added by the rule *arurdviṣad* etc., resulting in *taruṇī*. As for *talunī*:
since *taruṇa* and *talina* end in the suffix *unan*, they have the udātta accent on the first syllable because they are *nit*; this same accent remains when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.
Regarding the statement "but when *ṅīṣ* [is applied], it is oxytone":
(417) *yañaśca* |4|1|16|. The word *yañaḥ* is separated [from the previous rule] for the sake of what follows; [it is mentioned] in the rule *rāṣṭrāṇāṃ ṣpha taddhitaḥ*, where *yañ* [is intended].
So that this [suffix] may follow accordingly:
(418) *halas taddhitasya* |6|4|150|. *halas taddhitasya*: *halaḥ* is in the ablative case. [The rule *yasyeti ca* also applies].

From the Sūtra—*īt* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). From the rule *astāddhite*, *taddhita* is not carried over, because *taddhita* is mentioned again in the subsequent rule *āpatyasya ca*. Therefore, he says: "of a consonant (*hal*) followed by [a suffix]," and so forth. If *taddhite* were carried over here as well, [the rule would apply] even in this case.

It would be *sāṅkāśyakaḥ* or *kāmpilyakaḥ*, [formed] by the rule “*aṅkāśādibhyo ṇyaḥ*” (Pāṇini 4.2.80). Then, by the rule “*hanvayopadhāt*” (Pāṇini 4.2.116), the suffix *vuñ* is applied. The meaning of “of that which has become the *upadhā*” is that the word “*upadhāyāḥ*” from the rule “*ūryatiṣya-”* (Pāṇini 6.4.149) is understood to carry over [to this rule]. Now, one might object: what about the rule “*yasyeti ca*” (Pāṇini 6.4.148)?

When the elision of the vowel *a* (akāra-lopa) has been performed in *yañ*, the letter *y* is indeed followed by the vowel *ī*; so what is the purpose of the continued application of the mention of the "penultimate" (*upadhā*)? Nor can there be the status of being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) for this elision of *a*, because that [status] is prohibited in the case of the elision of *y* (*yalopa*). On this point, they say: in the case of *yalopa*...

Since the elision (*alopa*) [of the *y*] would be considered *asiddha* (non-existent) due to its being *ābhīya* (belonging to the subsequent rule), one must accept that the mention of "the penultimate vowel" (*upadhā*) continues [from the previous rule]. However, others say: by the very force of the commencement of this rule, the elision does not become *asiddha*. Thus, there is no harm here even without the mention of "the penultimate vowel. Consequently, on the grounds stated, the mention of "the penultimate vowel" could also have been omitted from the rule *ūryādiṣye* [Pāṇini 1.4.61]. Regarding *gārgī*: although that which ends in a *gotra*-suffix is a genus (*jāti*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply here by the rule *ātaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.4], because it has a *y* as its penultimate vowel (*yopadha*).

Thus, this word (*anapatyā*) is indeed in the nominative case. Although the *vārttika* "the mention of *apatya* (offspring) must be made" [is required], it nevertheless refers specifically to that which is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *apatya*. And such [a suffix] is only the *yañ* of the *garga*-class and not the *yañ* of the *deva*-class; for the latter is recited even before the *apatya* heading. For this very reason, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, in the rule *yañaś ca*, read the vowel *a* as being joined (*prāśliṣṭa*) in both *añ-kvarapo yañaś ca* and *argādibhyo yañ* as *ayañ*.

And thus, in the rule *ṭhyañañośca* as well, the vowel *a* is elided [in the form *ṭhyaṣkādi-bhyo gotre-ayañañośca*]. This has been stated in accordance with the *Manoramā* commentary. However, the modern grammarians (*navyāḥ*) maintain that the inclusion of the governing heading (*adhikāra-grahaṇam*) here is purposeless, since the form *dvepyā* (meaning "born on an island") is established by the Vārttika exactly as it is heard. Nor should one fear the failure to establish the form *daivyā* (meaning "the female descendant of Deva"), for that is established through the extension (*utkarṣa*) of the rule *ayañaśca* as intended by the author of the Bhāṣya.

For it is not possible to elide the vowel *a* in the rule "ayañ-ñau" (Pāṇini 4.1.96) by means of *praśleṣa* (insertion/elision). Furthermore, if the governing rule (*adhikāra*) were accepted, then in the case of "the female descendant of Abhijit," where the suffix *yañ* is applied to the word ending in *aṇ* by the rule "abhijid-vidabhṛt... (Pāṇini 5.3.118), the form "Ābhijitī" would not be established. They say that even according to the method of the Bhāṣyakāra, the suffix *ṅīp* is possible here by means of the *praśleṣa* of the vowel *a* in the rule "śrumadaṇo’yañaḥ" (Vārtika on Pāṇini 4.1.78). It might be argued: "If the vowel *a* is elided [by *praśleṣa*] and the suffix *yañ* is applied to the *gargādi* group, the form 'Gārgya' would not be established. This is not so; for it is quite clear that [the *praśleṣa* interpretation] contradicts the Bhāṣya, as it serves to reject the Vārtika.

(419) *prācāṃ ṣpha taddhitaḥ* | P. 4.1.17. The suffix *ṣpha* is [added] after [words belonging to] the Easterners; it is a *taddhita*. The mention of "taddhita" is for the purpose of establishing the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) for that which ends in the suffix *ṣpha*. By this, the formation of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* in the word *idgaurī* is established. Now, [an objection]:...
Even without the technical designation *prātipadika*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* will occur by the very force of the inclusion of the marker *ṣ*;

so what is the purpose of this mention of a *taddhita* suffix? Nor should it be argued that its purpose is to effect the elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel in a word ending in *yañ* by means of the rule *yasyeti ca*; for since the desired form is established even through the formation of a long vowel by homogeneity (*savarṇadīrgha*), such elision is not necessary.

In that case, the mention of the *taddhita* suffix is for the purpose of indicating that the suffix *ṣpha* occurs in some instances even after a word ending in *iñ*. By this, what will be stated later—namely, "the addition of *ṭhak* after *āsuri*"—is established.
(420) *ṣaḥ pratyayasya* | 1.3.6 | [The *ṣ* of a suffix is not an *it*.]

Regarding the rule *ṣaḥ pratyayasya* ("The *ṣ* of an affix [is *it*]"): since the word *ṭhādiḥ* ("beginning with *ṭh*") is understood from the previous rule *ṭhādir ñiṭuaḍavaḥ*, he says—intending to clarify—"the beginning of the affix. Why "of the affix"? [Consider] *ṣoḍaśa*. In the rule *ṣaṣa utvam*, this *ṣ* will not receive the designation *it* because it stands in its original form (*upadeśastha*).

The form *mahiṣī* is established simply by [the suffix] *ṭāp*; nor should it be argued that the purpose [of the rule] is for the *ṅīṣ* suffix to have its final syllable udātta in the alternative view, because the *anudātta* [vowel] following *ṭit* would receive the accent of the disappearance of the udātta by the rule "and where there is the disappearance of an udātta,
there is the accent of the disappearance of the udātta" (*anudātasya ca yatro dātalopaḥ*).

[The suffix] *ṅīp* is also [intended to be] acute. Regarding this, they say: in the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanā’bhāve*), there would be the hearing of the letter *ṭ* as well in some cases. And thus, by virtue of being *ṣit*, the formation of *ṭhaviṣī* and so forth would be established through *ṅīṣ*. Therefore, let there be the hearing of the letter *ṣ* alone, and not [the *ṭ*].
The continuation of the term "ādi" (beginning) is for the purpose that there might be the hearing [of the suffix] *taka* as well.

(421) *āyan-ey-īn-īy-iy-aḥ pha-ḍha-kha-cha-gh-āṃ pratyayādīnām* | 7|1|2|. [The substitutes] *āyan*, *ey*, *īn*, *īy*, and *iy* take the place of the initial sounds of suffixes beginning with *pha*, *ḍha*, *kha*, *cha*, and *gha*. In *āyan*, the *n* of *āyanīn* does not become *ṇ*, because of the force of the *ni*-designation (*nit*) applied to the suffix *phin*.
The letter *ḍ* in *phakādiṣu* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). By this, the substitution [of *ḍhak*] for *ḍhrak*, *phiñ*, and so forth, is established.
Why is the word "beginning with" (*ādi*) included? So that it does not apply in cases such as *ūrudangaḥ*. Why is the word "affix" (*pratyaya*) included?
So that it does not apply to the initial sounds of verbal roots (*dhātu*), such as in *phakkati*, *ḍhaukate*, *chādayati*, and *ghūrṇate*.

However, in the case of *ghañ* and other suffixes, because of the rule “*ajoḥ kughiṇṇyatoḥ*” and others, there should be the designation *it*, and thus no substitution occurs. Substitutions such as those in “*amer ḍhaḥ—śaṇḍha*” do not take place here, because of the statement “*tūṇādayo bahulam*”; this is the general direction.
"Successively" means: [the substitution] *pha* [is replaced by] *āyan*, *ḍha* by *ey*, *kha* by *īn*, *ccha* by *īy*, and *gha* by *iy*.

One might raise the objection that since the suffix *ṣpha* is prescribed only for feminine nouns (*striyām*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* should not occur here; anticipating this, he says: "by virtue of the force of the marker *ṣ*" (*ṣitvasāmarthyāt*). It is one and the same.
The sense is that femininity is expressed by both [suffixes].
The mention of "sarvatra" (everywhere) is drawn here from the subsequent sūtra for the purpose of overriding an exception;
thus, in the opinion of the Easterners, it overrides even the *cāp* suffix which is to be mentioned later in the rule "āvaṭaḷacce."

Even from the word *āvaṭaḷ*, only the suffix *ṣpha* occurs; for the rule for the suffix *cāp* has its scope elsewhere according to the opinion of the Northern grammarians. Thus, *āvaṭaḷayanī*. Similarly, even in the domain of *cāp*, only *ṣpha* occurs after words ending in *ṣat* or *yañ* according to the Eastern grammarians, as in *śārkarākṣyāyaṇī*.

(422) *sarvatra* lohitādikatantebhyaḥ |4|1|18|. The word *sarvatra* means "in the opinion of all. He states the resulting conclusion of this: "The suffix *ṣpha* shall always occur. Now, one might object: since the permanence [of the suffix] is already established by the very fact of its being prescribed, the inclusion of the word *sarvatra* is redundant.

Regarding this, they say: there is no pointlessness [of the present rule], because what was employed for the purpose of subverting a sublater in the preceding sūtra is here accepted for the sake of clarity.
Because the term *tyaÑ* is understood to carry over, he says: "from those ending in *tyaÑ*. The *lohitādi* group is a sub-group within the *gargādi* group.

This is the intended meaning. Regarding "Lauhityāyanī," examples such as "Āṃśityāyanī" and "Bābhravyāyaṇī" should also be understood. Now, one might object: since "kata," "kaṇva," and "śakala" are recited in the *gargādi* group, the form "Ākalyāyanī" [should not be derived from it].

It would be established; however, if the word *śaka* were recited even before the word *kata* for the sake of the grammatical operations (*kārya*) such as *lohita*, then the form *ākalyāyanī* would not be established. But if, for the sake of the grammatical operations such as *lohita*, the word *śaka* is recited even before the word *kata*, then...

In the case of the form *śākalāḥ*, meaning "the pupils of Śākalya," the suffix *aṇ*—prescribed by the rule *aṇvādibhyo gotre* (Pāṇini 4.1.103) for the formation of patronymics from the *kaṇva*-class and others—would not be established. It is replied: in the list of words (*gaṇapāṭha*) belonging to the *kaṭakaṇvaśakala* group, the word *śakala* should be read before the word *kaṇva*. This applies also in the rule *katantebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.95).
*Kata* means "end"; *katanta* means "that which has an end. Those whose end is *kata* are *katantāḥ*.

Due to the rule for the class beginning with *śākandhu*, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied. One must accept a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) consisting of both a *bahuvrīhi* and a *tatpuruṣa*: namely, *katantaś ca katantāś ca*. Likewise...

In the rule *aṇvādibhyaḥ* as well, *kaṇvādiḥ* means either "the beginning of Kaṇva" (*kaṇvasyādiḥ*)—a tatpuruṣa compound—or "those for whom Kaṇva is the first" (*kaṇva ādir yeṣām*)—a bahuvrīhi compound; thus, through the retention of only one of these two types of compounds (*ekaśeṣa*), all desired results are achieved. (423) *kauravyamāṇḍūkābhyāṃ ca* | Pāṇini 4.1.19.

Regarding "Kauravyā" [in the verse], although the rule *ṭāṅṅīṣoḥ* applies because it ends in a *y*-vowel (*yopadha*), such that it should be *Kauravyātī*, the reading *Kauravyā* there is merely a scribal error. Alternatively, it was stated thus with the intention of another view, namely that since only a lineage (*gotra*) beginning from a grandson (*pautra*) is technically considered a "jāti" (class/genre), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applicable here.

The object of enlightenment (*bodhya*). Because of its association with *kauravya*, the word *māṇḍūka* here is understood as ending in a patronymic suffix (*apatyapratyaya*), and not as ending in the *aṇ* suffix [meaning] "belonging to this" (*asyedam*). By this, the usage by Bhāravi—“If he, like a frog in a well, is proud of his solitary nature” (*yadyasau kūpamaṇḍūki tavaikāvatikaḥ smayaḥ*)—is established; for in that case, it means "this [nature] of a frog."

With the intention of expressing "wife" (*bhāryā*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form *bhāryā*] according to the rule *asyedam*. (424) [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word denoting] age (*vayas*) in the first [instance]. (Pāṇini 4.1.20). Age (*vayas*) is a state of the body determined by time. That which [is designated as such] without depending on context, purpose, and so forth—

That which conveys age by its mere hearing is called a "term for age" (*vayovācin*), because of its internal connection [to age]. Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *utānaśayā* ("lying on her back") or *lohitapādā* ("red-footed"), because although age may be understood here through context and so forth, it is not conveyed directly by the word itself. For even in the case of *avalā*, [the meaning is understood through other means].

Due to the influence of disease and so forth, she may lie down face-up, and her feet may be reddened by lac-dye. Why [is the word] "prathamā" (first) specified? [To exclude] an old woman. The term "kumārī" (maiden) refers specifically to the first stage of life; it is not applied merely on account of being unmarried, since the word "kumāra" is used for males as well.

The expression ‘an old maiden’ (*vṛddhakumārī*), however, is a figurative usage. It should be stated that [the term *vayas*] refers to what is not the final stage of life. Regarding the statement “not the first stage of life, but rather the second,” this is the introduction of the Vārttika. There are only two stages of life, characterized by growth and decline.
Thus, it should be understood that because youth is also the first [stage], it is established by the very rule [under discussion].

Some say there are four stages of life (*vayas*), as they say: "What will you do in the fourth stage, if you have not studied in the first, nor earned wealth in the second, nor practiced austerity in the third?"

Others say there are three [stages], as they say: "The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the son protects her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence. (425) *dvigoḥ* |3|1|21| [A compound ending in *dvigu* takes the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.]

*Trilokī*: In the compound *trayāṇāṃ lokānāṃ samāhāraḥ* (the collection of the three worlds), the term *dvigu* applies by the rule "in the sense of an aggregate (*addhitārtha*). Femininity is established by the rule "a *dvigu* whose final member ends in the letter *ṭh* [becomes feminine]. *Triphalā*: Here, by the rule "in a *dvigu*," the suffix *ṅīp* would apply, and not the suffix *ṅīṣ* by the rule "after *āḍha*, *karṣa*, etc. In that regard:
Regarding the phrase "āteḥ": it is because [the root] *i* is followed by *anu*. Regarding "tryanīkā": *anīka* means "front" (*agratā*). It is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) of three fronts.
According to the Mīmāṃsakas, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied here because the group beginning with *aj* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. This occurs in the section concerning the *tryanīkā*.

(426) *Aparimāṇa-bista-ācita-kambalyebhyo na taddhita-luki* 4.1.22. [The suffix *ṅīp* does not apply after words denoting measure (*aparimāṇa*), nor after *bista*, *ācita*, or *kambalya*, when a *taddhita* suffix has been elided. For example, *pañcāśvī*. Now, one might object: "In this case, let it be granted that *ṅīp* does not apply by the rule *'vigraḥ'*; however, since the word ends in *ṭhak*, *ṅīp* ought to apply. Nor can it be argued that the prohibition in *'ṭha-parimāṇe'* is without scope."

The *nimitta* (condition) for the five [suffixes] beginning with *añ* is their connection with *dhanapati*. This is because [the suffixes] such as *añ* in *pañcājī* and *pañcoṣṭrī* have scope there; for in those cases, by the rule *adhyardhapūrvād-dvigul-luk ca*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *yat* suffix prescribed by the rule *od-adhyacaḥ saṅkhyāyām*. To this, they say: "The [suffix] is *ṭhak*..."
Because of the explanation that [the suffix] *ṭhak* occurs after a word ending in *a*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Regarding *dvibistā*:
according to Amara, "The words *uvarṇa* and *bista* refer to gold when not used as dice" (*uvarṇabistau hemno’kṣe*). "Ten *bhāras* make one *ācita*.
Regarding *dvikambalyā*: it means "purchased for two *kambalyas*."

*Kambalyam* means one hundred *palas* of wool. [The suffix] *yat* is applied by the rule *ambalācca saṃjñāyām*. From that, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhañ* used in the sense of "bought. Regarding *dvyaḍhakī*: in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "she cooks two *āḍhakas*," the suffixes *kha* and *ṭhan* are applied by the rules *āḍhakācitapātrātkho’nyatarasyām* and *vigoṣṭhṃaśca*.
These two [suffixes] have been prescribed; when they are elided by those two, the suffix *iṣṭhan* applies as before. By the rule "ṭha-dhyardha," there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix].

By this, "dyācita" is also explained. It might be argued: according to the subsequent sūtra "kāṇḍāntāt," that by which something is measured from all sides is a measure (*parimāṇa*), such as an *āḍhaka*, a *kuḍava*, and so forth; however, it is not...
In the *Manoramā*, it is established that [the term refers to] "mere measurement.

Furthermore, since [the prohibition] would already be established by the very fact of being "immeasurable" (*aparimāṇa*), the mention of *bista* and so forth here would be redundant. To this, they say: it is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtham*) stating that "among measurements, the prohibition applies only to *bista* and the rest."
The inclusion of that [term] serves to establish forms such as *vikārṣāpaṇī* and *dvayakṣī*.

(427) Pāṇini 4.1.23: *kāṇḍāntāt kṣetre* ("After a word ending in *kāṇḍa*, [the suffix *ṅīp* is added] when the meaning is 'field'"). [The word] *kāṇḍa* refers to a staff measuring sixteen cubits (*hasta*). Even though it is a qualifier—

The rule regarding [an operation] pertaining to the end of a word (tadanta-vidhi) is established; nevertheless, if the mention of the word "end" (anta) were not present, then because of its being directly heard in the text, the term "khaṭva" would qualify only "kāṇḍa" and not "that which ends in kāṇḍa. Consequently, in the case of "dvikāṇḍī vaḍavā" (a mare bought for two khaṭvas), the prohibition would apply.
