It might be so; however, in this case, the prohibition would not apply—as in "dvikāṇḍā kṣetrabhaktiḥ.
For here, *kāṇḍa* occurs in the sense of measure (*pramāṇa*), whereas in the compound *kāṇḍānta*, it occurs in the sense of a field (*kṣetra*); therefore, the mention of the word *anta* was made.
Here, the words "vigau" and "na taddhitalukī" are understood to carry over.

Thus he says: "In that case, [the suffix] *dvigu* does not take *ṅīp*, etc. Regarding the mention of *mātrac*: the statement of the ancients that there is "elision (*luk*) of *dvayasac*" is not to be respected, because the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that "both *rathama* and *dvitīya* are considered [suffixes] when measuring height. This is the intended meaning. As for the example "a rope of two *kāṇḍas* (*dvikāṇḍī rajjuḥ*"): its measure consists of two *kāṇḍas*.

As before, there is elision of the *taddhita* suffix by the rule "dvigoḥ. [The suffix] *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "dvigoḥ. Now, one might object that here the prohibition by the preceding rule—"not after a word ending in a measure-word"—would apply, because the word *kāṇḍa* refers to length (*āyāma*) and thus does not denote a measure (*aparimāṇa*), since a measure is that by which something is measured on all sides—both in height and in circumference.

For that which is measured is indeed *parimāṇa*—such as an *āḍhaka*, a *kuḍava*, and so forth—but not merely any means of delimitation whatsoever. As they say: "Unmāna is indeed measurement by height;
parimāṇa, however, is from all sides; pramāṇa would be length; while saṅkhyā is external."
Regarding the word "sarvataḥ": for this very reason, it is said that in the case of *vihastā bhītiḥ*, the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur.

To this they reply: this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), so that the prohibition may apply only in the case of *kṣetra*. Thus, in the case of *vikaṇḍī rajjuḥ*, the very occurrence of *ṅīp* is the fruit of the commencement of the sūtra.

(428) *puruṣāt pramāṇe ’nyatarasyām* |4|1|24|. Regarding the word *puruṣa* when it denotes a measure (*pramāṇa*). Since this word ends in *aparimāṇa*, a prohibition [of the feminine suffix] would otherwise apply; therefore, this statement is made for the purpose of providing an option.
Although the word *puruṣa* in common usage denotes a genus (*jāti*), nevertheless, in the expression "two *puruṣas*... [the feminine suffix is optionally applied].

In the sentence "this is its *pramāṇa*," [the word *pramāṇa*] indeed functions as a measure (*pramāṇa*) due to its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *pramāṇa*; however, in the case of the derivative form [such as *dvipuruṣī*], it is solely due to the inherent nature of the word’s expressive power (*śabdaśakti*). Thus, the *Śulvasūtra* states: "A man is five *aratis* long," and "two men high" (*dvipuruṣī*). Here, [it refers to] the object of measurement (*meya*).

The author of the Nyāsa states that there is elision of the dual suffix *sac* according to the rule *lodhvoḥ nityam*. But is not the elision of the *taddhita* suffix impossible here? For since the word *puruṣa* does not denote a measure (*pramāṇa*), the *Ślokavārttika* rule *pramāṇe laḥ* does not apply. Indeed, those [words] which, like *śama*, etc., function as measures...

That [suffix] operates only where it is established [as applicable], and not even upon the word *puruṣa*. Otherwise, there would also be elision (*luk*) in the case of *puruṣadvayasa* (two puruṣas high). Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the suffixes *-dvayasaC* and *-daghnaC* would also not occur after this [word *puruṣa*]; for there is a rule stating: "The two suffixes *-dvayasaC* and *-daghnaC* are desired when measuring height."

Thus, although the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is optional by the rule "uruṣāt pramāṇe," it nevertheless functions here precisely because of its applicability; however, if it is argued that the elision (*luk*) of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is difficult to obtain, they reply: let there be the non-application of the rule "ramāṇe laḥ" here, yet the elision is indeed easily obtained.

For in the rule *uruṣāt pramāṇe*, the phrase *goṣtaddhitalukī* is understood to carry over; by its force, even elision (*luk*) is implied, which makes it easy to explain. What is the purpose of [specifying] "in the sense of measure" (*pramāṇe*)? [Consider:
*dvipuruṣā gauḥ* ("a cow bought for two men"). [In this case, the suffix is not elided] because of the condition "*taddhitalukī*" (only when there is elision of a taddhita suffix).

In the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), as in *pañcapuruṣī*: if it is objected that the word *puruṣa* here does not refer to a person (*puruṣa*) but to a measure (*pramāṇa*), and thus this [compound] is deficient in two respects, they reply: there is no deficiency in the two respects because it is only persons who possess the capacity for measurement (*pramāṇa*) and purpose (*artha*) that are being collected here. And therefore...
If the term *addhitalukī* were not stated, there would be an option regarding the word *pañcapuruṣa*; however, it is desired that by the rule *vigau* [Pāṇini 4.1.8], the suffix *ṅīp* is obligatory.
(429) *ūdhaso’naṅ* [Pāṇini 5.4.131].

Regarding the rule *ūdhaso’naṅ*: although the desired form would be established by the substitution of *an* alone, the inclusion of *anaṅ* is for the sake of the subsequent rule (*hanuṣaśca*). Otherwise, forms such as *ārṅgadhanvā* would not be established;
so they say. In reality, however, it is necessary even for the present case; otherwise—

Others maintain that because [the word *ūdhas*] lacks the characteristic of being a feminine noun (*anolaṅghanikatvena*), the elision [of the final syllable] would not apply. Here, it is stated that the term "in a bahuvrīhi compound" (*bahuvrīhau*) is understood from the rule "in a bahuvrīhi, [the suffix ṅīṣ is added after] *sakthi* and *akṣi*" (*ahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ*); thus he says:
(430) Pāṇini 4.1.25: *bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ*.

Regarding the rule *ūdhontasya bahuvrīheḥ*: although it occurs within the section on compound suffixes (*samāsānta*), the *anaṅ* substitution does not possess the status of a suffix (*pratyaya*); otherwise, the presence of the marker *ṅ* would be rendered purposeless—so say the ancients. In reality, however, even if it were a suffix, its status as a substitute (*ādeśa*) is not contradictory, just like the suffix *ṣyaṅ*; for instance, in the case of *uṇḍodhnī*, once the suffix *ṅīṣ* has been applied...
It should be understood that this is because there is no difference even in the accent. Regarding the word *striyām* (in the feminine):
this is obtained through an *upasaṅkhyāna* (supplementary rule). Regarding the phrase *ḍāmṅīnbiṣedheṣu*:
the optional suffix *ḍāp* applies by the rule *ābubhābhyām*. [The suffix] *ṭhan*.

The suffix *ṅīp* is optionally applied by the rule "upadhālopino’nyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.28). The distinction is that the prohibition of *ṅīp*—which would otherwise have been applicable by the rule "ṛnnebhyo ṅīp" (Pāṇini 4.1.5) through the rule "ṭhano bahuvrīheḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.12)—is established here. As for the statement "ṅīṣ should occur," it is because *ṅīp* alone was not prescribed for the base form due to considerations of accent (*svara*).

Because of the distinction [in the examples]: *kuṇḍodhnī*. She whose udder (*ūdhas*) is like a vessel (*kuṇḍa*) is *kuṇḍodhnī*. Why "from a bahuvrīhi"? [Consider] *prāptodhāḥ*—she who has reached her udder. This is a compound by the rule *prāptāpanne ca*. Regarding *dhainukam*: the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of a collection according to the rule *ṭhaciṭahasti*, and [the final *k* is substituted for the *ṭhak*] by the rule *ṭhisusuktāntāt kaḥ*.
Regarding the statement "because of the supplementary rule [Vārttika] *striyām*": one might object that for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*) in this very context,
the sūtra should be formulated as *bahuvrīher ūdhaso ṅīṣ aci* or *ahanuṣo ṅīṣ*, or alternatively,
by omitting the rule *samāsānteṣu ūdhaso naṅ* and instead stating *ahanuṣo naṅ*.
[Objection: Let it be read [as *kab*]. [Reply: Not so; for in the absence of *kap*, this [suffix] would have scope and would sublate *kap* in that alternative.
In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, because the *anaṅ* is a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), there is no "remainder" (*śeṣa*) here at all, and thus no *kap*.
(431) Pāṇini 4.1.26: *saṅkhyā-avyayāder ṅīp* (the suffix *ṅīp* follows numerals and indeclinables).

Numerals and indeclinables [form a tatpuruṣa compound with a word ending in the sixth case]. By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), this rule applies even when there is an intervention by another word;
for example: *dvividhondhī* ("blindness of two kinds").
(432) [A feminine suffix is added] after a word ending in *dāman* or *hāyana*. 4.1.27.
Since [the application of the rule] is already established by the fact that *dāman* is a qualifier of a *bahuvrīhi*, the inclusion of the word *anta* (end) is for the sake of clear understanding.

Regarding the phrase "beginning with a numeral" (*saṅkhyādeḥ*): although it is mentioned as part of a compound, the intention is that by virtue of its being marked with the *svarita* accent, only one portion [of the compound] is carried over [into the subsequent rule]. [The phrase] "due to the non-carrying over" (*ananuvṛtteḥ*)...
The intention is that [the rule] is not followed by the author of the Bhāṣya. Thus, in the case of *uddāmā*,

since the rule *āmahāyanāntāt ca* does not apply, and the previously mentioned prohibitions of *ḍāp*, *ṅīp*, and *ṅīṣ* would otherwise have occurred, there results a threefold form, just as in the case of *bahurājñī*.
He explains: "The prohibitions regarding the suffixes *ḍā* and *an* also apply.
(433) *Nityaṃ saṃjñācchandasoḥ* | 4|1|29|. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the optional rule "after a stem ending in *ṭhan*, provided it has a penultimate vowel-elision (*upadhālopin*)."

They say that although permanence (*nityatva*) is established by the very force of the rule's introduction (*ārambha-sāmarthya*), the explicit mention of "permanent" (*nitya*) is made to indicate that the option (*vikalpa*) does not carry over into subsequent rules. Regarding the form *śatamūrdhnī*: here, some read *añcadāmni*, but that is incorrect.
Because it is already established by the rule *āmahāyanāntācca* [Pāṇini 5.1.28], [the following is stated]:
*kvalamāmakabhāgadheyapāpāparasamānāryakṛtasumaṅgalabheṣajācca* [Pāṇini 4.1.30].

In the Vedic language (*kevalacchandasi*) alone, [the suffix *matup* is applied] as in: *āmakī tanūḥ*, *itvāvaruṇayorbhāgadheyī*, *tanvaḥ santu pāpīḥ*, *utāparūbhyaḥ*, *amānī va ākūtiḥ*, *āryakṛtī*, *sumaṅgalī*, and *sumaṅgalīriyaṃ vadhūḥ*; however, in these cases, it is by the rule *chandasīvanipau*.

The suffix *ī* should be understood in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). As in: “*ivā rudrasya bheṣajī*” (like Rudra’s healing herb). Elsewhere, as in *kevalā* and so on. Due to the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) regarding *māmaka* and *naraka*, [the feminine form] *māmikā* is formed. From the masculine noun *bhāga*, the suffix *dheya* is added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*). These are denominative suffixes (*vārthika*).

In some cases, gender and number deviate from the base form; thus, there is femininity [in *bhāgadheyā*]. Due to metaphorical treatment as non-different (*abhedopacārāt*), the word *pāpa*, when applied to that which possesses the quality, is dependent on the gender of the substantive (*viśeṣyanighna*);

hence *pāpā*. [The words] *aparā* and *samānā* [are formed similarly]. [The word *kṛtā*] is formed with a *kṛt*-affix before the addition of the case-ending (*sup*), as in "made by an Ārya" (*āryeṇa kṛtā*).

This is a compound. [The suffix] *ṭāp* is applied. In the word *āryakṛtā*, the vowel *e* is substituted by this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*) as an exception to the initial *vṛddhi* [which would otherwise apply] when the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of "this is the physician of. Due to the restrictive rule "only after a name or a Vedic verse," elsewhere it is *bheṣajā*.
(435) *antarvat-pativator nuk* [Pāṇini 4.1.32]. The sense is that the counter-example stated by the Easterners (*prāc*) as "antarvatī" and "pativatī" is incorrect.
The meaning is that in the first case, because there is no co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the suffix *matup* is impossible; whereas in the second case, the suffix *vat* is impossible.
(436) *Vibhāṣā sapūrvasya* | 4.1.34.
"Vibhāṣā sapūrvasya" (Pāṇini 8.3.53). This is an optional rule (*aprāptavibhāṣā*) because it does not concern a connection with a sacrifice (*yajña*).

"Sapūrva" means accompanied by a preceding element; the meaning is: of that aggregate which possesses a prior constituent part. And since that aggregate is not the word *pati*, [the rule applies] by means of the word *pati*.

He states that this is a rule regarding what ends with that [element]—namely, "of that which ends in the word *pati*. Now, one might object: since the suffix *atp* is a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it already implies "that which ends in it," so why is there this mention of "preceded by something" (*sapūrvagrahaṇa*)? On this point, they say: even for the bare word *pati*, by virtue of the principle of "designation as if possessing a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), [the suffix applies].
Because [the word *pati*] ends in the suffix *pat*, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); to prevent this, the term "preceded by" (*sapūrva*) is included.

Here, making it clear that the word "prior" (*pūrva*) refers to a prior constituent part, he provides a counter-example: *gavāṃ patiḥ strī* ("the female lord of cows"). Since the verbal derivative *patiḥ*—derived from the root *pā-* ("to protect")—is a word denoting an action (*kriyāśabda*) and thus possesses all three genders, it is feminine here.

And likewise, it is employed even in the neuter by the Taittirīyas: "May that food, the sovereign lord of sovereignties, protect me. As for the question "How [is it used] when [the words] are separate?", the sense is that the claim made by the Easterners (Prācām) that there is metaphorical usage (upacāra) even when they are compounded is entirely in vain.

(437) *nityaṃ sapatnyādiṣu* | 4|1|35| Regarding the rule "always in the case of *sapatnī* and so forth": since the status of being "always" (*nitya*) is already established by the very force of the rule's commencement, the explicit mention of "always" is for the sake of clarity. It is stated that [the word] is derived as a *nipātana*. In this list (*gaṇa*), the words are: *samāna*, *eka*, *vīra*, *bhrātṛ*, and *putra*.

Only *samāna* and the others are recited; therefore, the intention is that while one ought to say "in the case of *amāna* and so forth," the expression "in the case of *apatni* and so forth" is used for the purpose of establishing the irregular form (*nipātana*) of *sapatnī*. With the view that a *bahuvrīhi* compound is resorted to in the case of *sapatnī* and the others, he says: "she whose husband (*pati*) is the same (*samāna*)."

(438) *pūtakrator ai ca* |4|1|36|. The substitution of the vowel *ai* for *pūtakratu* is indeed a suffix, because of the mention of the term "udātta" (acute accent) in the subsequent rule. [The commentary says: "Not so," for otherwise, in the case of *āghavante*, it would be acutely accented on the middle syllable.

The meaning is that [if one were to argue that] the word *vṛṣākapi* necessitates the occurrence of the acute accent (*udāttatva*) because it is established for the three [words] beginning with *agni* by the rule "in the place [of the substitute], that which is most similar [to the original] (*antaratamaḥ*"), then this would contradict the texts of the Vṛtti and other such works.
(439) *vaṣaṭkārī*, *kapī*, *agni*, *kusita*, and *kusida* have an acute accent on the first syllable. 4|1|37.

Regarding the statement "the vowel *e* is acute": in the rule for the suffix *-u* prescribed after the roots *man*, *ṛṣ*, *snih*, etc., because of the governing heading "the first syllable (*ādi*) is acute (*udātta*) except when there is another [acute accent] (*anyani*)," the word *manu* has an acute accent on its initial syllable.
By this concise statement, he shows that while the term *udātta* (acute) continues to apply,

it connects with the vowel *e* alone due to the continuity of its grammatical relationship, and not with the vowel *ai*. Consequently, what was stated by the ancients— that the vowels *e* and *o* are acute— is [thus clarified].

Regarding the phrase "vṛtipadamañjaryām": *eta*, *śoṇa*, *pṛśni*, and *pṛṣat* are the examples in their respective order. As for the term "acute-accented on the first syllable" (*ādyaudāta*): the meaning is that, according to the rule "a word [consisting of more than one syllable] is unaccented except for one," the word *eta* has its final syllable unaccented due to the "subsequent suppression" (*śeṣanighāta*) of accents. Regarding *tryeṇyā*: here...

The sense is that the word *eta* functions as an upasarjana (subordinate member). The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *ūrvapadātsaṃjñāyām*. Regarding the form *gṛhya*: it is derived from the root *ṛhū* (meaning "to seize") with the suffix *kyap*, according to the rule *ṛdupadhāccākḷpicṛteḥ*.
[The compound means] "she who has these three. Now, one might object: "The words *kṛtra*, *kirmira*, *kalmāṣa*, *śabala*, and *eta*..."

The word *etaśa* is a synonym for *karvura*, meaning "variegated. Thus, some commentators here explain that since there is an absence of variegation in the *śakalī*, there would otherwise be an inconsistency in the meaning;
however, they argue that because the word *etaśa* here refers to the constituent parts (*etā*), there is no such inconsistency in the meaning. Not so.

Nor should it be argued that even so, the use of the neuter gender for the objects of the *guṇas* is inconsistent, because it has been stated that "the *śulka* and others are masculine when they denote a *guṇa*";
for [this is explained] by the interpretation that these [words] refer to the substrata (*adhikaraṇa*) of those respective parts.
Because this word *eta* primarily denotes a quality (*guṇa*) and a gender (*liṅga*), its neuter form is also justified. [The Vārttika] states:

"An addition [to the rule] after *piśaṅga*. Regarding the word *piśaṅga*: since, according to the rule *aghāvante*, the word *piśaṅga* has the udātta accent on the middle syllable, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have applied by the rule *ṭhañ-ya-kau-ṅīṣ*.

The suffix *ṅīp* is added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*). There is a distinction regarding the accent. According to some, in the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffix *knam* is used. Regarding the statement "according to some, *knam*": since the rule *anudātāṭ ṭāp* would require the substitution of *n* for the *t* of *asita* and *palita*, that [substitution] is set aside, and instead, in place of the *t*, [the suffix *knam* is applied].

The meaning is that some teachers desire the substitution of *knam* as well as the suffix *ṅīp* by virtue of its being prescribed in conjunction with that [substitution]. Here, because of the connection with the phrase "some [desire it] in the Veda" (*chandasyeke*), the suffix *nka* certainly occurs in the secular language (*bhāṣā*). This is because the final sense is that while some desire it only in the Veda, others desire it even in the secular language. Otherwise, the mention of the word "some" (*eka*) would be redundant.
The author of the Bhāṣya would not have done so; for no one disputes such Vedic usages as "alinki ridyauvatayaḥ" and others. And thus, the usage "ato gaṇastūrṇamasiknikānām" is not unaccounted for.

Regarding the term *viśuddhavāk* ("pure speech"): it is because the root *aiP* is stated [in the Dhātupāṭha] as "to purify" (*śodhane*). However, the intention is that Amara, due to the common property of purity (*viśuddhatva-sādharmyāt*), has stated: "White (*avadāta*) means bright (*sita*) or fair-skinned (*gaura*). (440) [The suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied after [the word *viśuddha*] when it ends in a different vowel. Pāṇini 4.1.40.

Regarding the rule *laghāvante*: when a heavy syllable (*guru*) followed by many vowels (*bahvaṣaḥ* = *ubahvac*) occurs before a single light vowel (*laghu*) or two light vowels at the end of a word, that heavy syllable shall be acute (*udātta*). [Note: The term *aṣ* is a designation for vowels used by the Eastern grammarians. Examples include *kṛṣṇoti* and so forth. [The form *kṛṣṇa-* is derived] from the root *kṛṣ* with the suffix *na*, according to the rules *ṛṣiccha* and *apeśccha*.
From the root *kṛṣ* with the suffix *ila* added according to the *uṇādi* rules, the words *kṛṣṇa* and *kapila* have their final vowels as udātta.

(Pāṇini 4.1.41) "After [roots ending in] a *ṣit* suffix and after the *gaura*-group, [the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied]. Regarding *nartakī*: it is derived from the root *nṛt* with the suffix *ṣvun* in the sense of an artisan (*ilpin*). The [accent of] *ṣvun*...

The designation *ṣit* (having the marker *ṣ*) qualifies the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in that [root], because it serves no purpose in relation to the root itself. Since the *ṣit* designation of *trapuṣ* has already served its purpose in the rule for the formation of the feminine (*aṅ*), there is no *ṅīṣ* suffix in the form *trapā*. They say that the *ṣit* designation of *mṛj* is not Vedic (non-archaic), because *bhṛj* is read in the *bhidādi* group [of roots]. [This applies] to *mṛj*.
Some say that because [the root] ends in *ṣ*, the reading *mṛj* in the *bhidādi* group is non-Vedic (*anārṣa*). Regarding *gaurī*:

although the word *gaura* denotes color (*varṇa*), it is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*); therefore, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—prescribed by the rule *ṭhanyato ṅīṣ*—does not apply, which is why it is included in this list.
[The word] *anaḍuh* [is included] optionally in the feminine. Thus, one has either *anaṅvāhī* or *anaḍuhī*.

Since it does not end in the vowel *a*, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which would otherwise apply by virtue of its being a genus (*jāti*) or by virtue of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*)—does not occur; therefore, it is recited in this list [of *gaṇa*s]. However, its inclusion together with the suffix [in the form *anaḍuhī*] is for the purpose of allowing the optional addition of the augment *ām* when *ṅīṣ* follows.
*gaura*, *matsya*, *manuṣya*, *śṛṅga*, *gavaya*, *hayamukha* [and *gautama*, *ṭanaṅvāhī*, *anaḍuhī*, *taruṇa*, *taluna*, *śvan*;
and the group beginning with *pippalī*: *pippalī*, *harītakī*, *kośātakī*.]*

"Earth," "grandmother," and so forth. As for the fact that the ancient [commentators] cited *ūnī* as an example under the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*, they say that this was prompted by their failure to observe the word *śvan* in the *gaurādi* list. On this point, some say: because it is invariably feminine (*nityastrītva*).

Since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not apply [to words like *pippalī*] by the rule "after words ending in short *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*, and after those denoting a feminine object," the words *pippalī* and others are listed in the *gaurādi* group [of the *gaura-ādi-gaṇa*].

However, the inclusion of these words in the *ṅīṣ*-ending portion of that list is of doubtful utility. For instance, in a form such as *pippalībhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a *pippalī*"), one might expect the hearing of the suffix *ṅīṣ* (i.e., the form *pippalī-bhārya*) after overriding the rule for masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*). [But this does not occur.]

It must be stated that the meaning of "syāt" (it may be) is "sa" (that), for the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is already established simply by the absence of the quality of having been previously mentioned as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃskatva*). Furthermore, the acceptance of [the word *pippalī*] as belonging to an intermediate sub-class (*avāntaragaṇa*) serves only the purpose of excluding words like *pippalī*. Nor is this the case under the governing rule concerning "jāti" (*jātādhikāra*).

It should not be argued that the statement "there is an addition for *itara*, *revatī*, and *rohiṇī* in the feminine" contradicts the forthcoming text which says "again, *ṅīṣ* [is applied]," because it can also be said that this is due to [the word] being included in the *gaura*-group, which is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). Thus they say.

(442) *sūryatiṣyagastyamatsyānāṃ ya upadhāyāḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.149. Regarding the rule for *sūrya*, *tiṣya*, etc.: although the term *hasya* (of *ha*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], it is not connected here, because any over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is prevented by the very enumeration of the specific scope.

[The rule] "of *matsya* before a feminine suffix (*ṅyām*). That is to say: "of *matsya* before a feminine suffix. This does not apply here: *matsyasyedaṃ mātsyam* ("this belongs to a fish," i.e., *mātsya*).

[The rule] "of *sūrya* and *agastya* before *cha* and a feminine suffix (*ṅyām*). That is to say: "before *cha* and before a feminine suffix. Examples: *sūrīyaḥ*, *sūrī*; *agastīyaḥ*, *agastī*. This does not apply here: *sauryaṃ carum* ("an oblation for Sūrya") and *āgastyam* ("belonging to Agastya").

Regarding the words *tiṣya* and *puṣya*, it should be stated that there is the elision of the suffix *aṇ*. The term "in relation to the stars" (*nakṣatrāṇi*) means: when that suffix *aṇ*—which is prescribed by the rules *akṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ* and *andhivelādyṛtunakṣatrebhyo ’ṇ*—is connected with a star. In that case:

In the case of *tiṣya*, the elision of *y* is prescribed by way of an irregularity (*nipātana*). In the case of *puṣya*, however, [the elision] is prescribed even though it would not otherwise have applied. Thus: *taiṣaḥ* (the time joined with *tiṣya*), and *pauṣaḥ* (the time joined with *puṣya*). Likewise: *taiṣaḥ* (that which occurs in *tiṣya*), and *pauṣaḥ* (that which occurs in *puṣya*). But here it is not so: *taiṣyaḥ* (belonging to *tiṣya*), because [the word] ends in *y*. As for *matsī*: because it has *y* as its penultimate letter (*yopadhatvāt*).
Regarding the form *mātṛṣvasrī*, since it would not have been included by the rule *ātiḥ astrīviṣayāt* (A 4.1.4), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because of its inclusion in the *gaurādi* group.

The statement "in the case of *mātṛ* [the suffix] *ṣic*" is a rule found within the sūtra *pitṛvya-mātula-mātāmaha-*. And that statement must necessarily be stated for the sake of establishing the form *pitāmahī*; thus, it is not a *vārttika*.

[The rule] would be redundant. However, for those who include the word *pitāmaha* in the *gaura*-group [of words], this statement does not accord with their natural interpretation. If you argue that the purpose of the statement is merely to indicate its non-eternality (*anityatva*), then [the same result could have been achieved] by the rule *id-gau-ṇaḥ* itself, which states that [the substitution of *au* for *id*] is non-eternal.

One should simply say "white" (*śveta*); what is the use of this circuitous way? This is the general direction. That by which something is shown is a *daṃṣṭrā* (fang). The suffix *ṣṭran* is applied in the sense of an instrument according to the rule beginning with *āmnīśas-*.

[The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after the following words when they denote respectively: a country (*jānapada*), a water-pot (*kuṇḍa*), a bull (*goṇa*), a shield (*sachalabha*), a vessel (*ājana*), an elephant (*nāga*), black (*kāla*), blue (*nīla*), *kuśa* grass, a lover (*kāmuka*), a braid of hair (*kabara*), a fence (*vṛti*), a vessel (*amatra*), sowing (*āvapana*), artificial (*akṛtrima*), porridge (*āśrāṇā*), thickness (*sthaulya*), color (*varṇa*), clothing (*ācchādana*), an iron product (*ayovikāra*), desire for sexual intercourse (*maithunecchā*), and a style of hair (*keśaveśa*).

[Pāṇini 4.1.42] Regarding *jānapadī*: it means "that which exists in a country" (*janapade bhavā*). Regarding "if it is a fence" (*vṛtiścediti*): a fence (*vṛti*) is that by which one lives; it is a livelihood. Regarding *kuṇḍī*: Amara states, "A water-pot for women is called *kuṇḍī*."
Regarding the word *kuṇḍāni*: this is an action noun (*kriyāśabda*). For this very reason, he says: "the root *kuḍi* means 'to burn' (*dāha*), etc.

However, the word *kuṇḍa* which is a synonym for a jar (*ghaṭaparyāya*) is not an example here, because it is neuter—as in the statement: "a jar, a cooking pot, or a pan is *kuṇḍam*"—and [the present context concerns masculine nouns]. The word is also a synonym for a fire-chamber (*agnyālaya*) and so forth.

The word *kuṇḍa* is fixed in the neuter gender, according to the *Medinīkośa*: "A *kuṇḍa* is a fire-sanctuary, a measure of capacity, or a divine reservoir. Regarding the phrase "if it is a receptacle" (*āvapana*): the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied to the root *vap* preceded by the prefix *āṅ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). That into which grain is sown—that is, deposited—is called an *āvapana*.

That in which a cow goes is [the meaning of] *goṇā*. That which has an accidental name is *akṛtrimā* (unartificial); for example, in the phrase "this is the place (*sthalī*) where you were being searched for," it is *sthalā* (an artificial place).
*Kṛtrimā* means prepared by a person. *Śrāṇā* means cooked.

And in the case of *prāṇin* (living being). Regarding *ayovikāra* (iron product): it is commonly known as *hāla*. Regarding *kuśānya*: the Chāndoga singers use the term *kuśā* for the wooden pegs made of *udumbara* wood used for counting the *stotrīyā* verses; this [term] is indeed well-known in the rule *ataḥ kṛkami...* [Pāṇini 8.3.46]. Regarding *kāmukānya*: [it refers to] a lover.
The meaning is: she whose character (*śīla*) it is to desire wealth and so forth other than sexual intercourse. [The suffix] *ukañ* is applied by the rule "aṣapate" (Pāṇini 3.2.157).
(444) "From *śoṇa*, according to the Easterners" (Pāṇini 4.1.43).

From *śoṇa*: Since the word *śoṇa* denotes color—according to the lexicon (*kośa*) stating "the word *oṇa* means the luster of a red lotus"—it would already be established by the rule *anyato ṅīṣ* (Pāṇini 4.1.40), which prescribes the suffix *ṅīṣ* after words ending in vowels other than those specified in 4.1.39 (such as *taṇa*, etc., which are acute-accented on the first syllable). Nevertheless, this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies only according to the Easterners (*prācām*) and not according to others.

(445) *voto guṇavacanāt* | 4|1|44 | [The suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*). Here, "quality" (*guṇa*) does not mean the phonemes *a* and *eṅ*; this is because of the specific qualification *utaḥ* and because of the inclusion of the term *vacana*. Nor does it mean merely a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

If it is argued that this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as "the mouse is the substance" (*ākhur dravyam*), they reply: "Excluding words for names, classes, and actions, others denote qualities.
The determination [of what constitutes a quality-word] is reached precisely from the essential conclusion of the foundational treatises (*ākaragrantha*) regarding the fourfold application of words.

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is established that: "That which enters into substance (*satva*), departs from it, is seen among various classes (*jāti*), is capable of being added, and is not produced by action—that is a quality (*guṇa*) whose nature is non-substance (*asatvaprakṛti*). Here, *satva* means substance (*dravya*).
The phrase "entering into substance alone" (*satva eva niviśate*) is to be explained as being restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇa*). By this, [the definition] is established.

[The definition] is excluded [from those cases]. For that [existence] resides not only in substance, but in substance, quality, and action as well. [Objection: But since "substanceness" (dravyatva) resides only in substance, there is over-extension (ativyāpti) in that case; therefore, he says: "it departs" (apaiti). The meaning is "it goes away," which implies [the departure] from existence itself.

Just as when yellowness arises in a fruit and so forth, its blueness departs, substance-ness (*dravyatva*) does not depart from the substance (*dravya*). Even so, "cowness" (*gotva*) exists in cows and departs from horses and the like;
since there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case, he says: "it is seen in distinct classes. For cowness—

It is not observed in the various subordinate universals (jāti) within the universal of substantiality (dravyatva), whereas a quality (guṇa) is so observed; just as blueness seen in a mango is also seen in grass and other things. By this first half-verse, there is the exclusion of all [other] universals. If that is so, then action (karma) resides in a substance and then departs from it.

Since it is observed among distinct classes [of objects], there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that regard; therefore, he says: "and it is both produced and unproduced. This means it is both producible and non-producible. Producible—such as the color and other qualities of a jar and so forth, which are born of baking (*pākaja*). Unproduced is that which is not produced. For example: [The text continues: ...the universal (*sāmānya*), the particular (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*). These three are eternal substances. Furthermore, space, time, and self are infinite. Earth, water, fire, air, and mind are atomic. Among these, the four beginning with earth are both eternal and non-eternal. Those consisting of atoms are eternal; those consisting of aggregates are non-eternal. Mind is eternal in its state as an atom, but non-eternal in its state as an aggregate. The remaining nine substances are eternal. Furthermore, substance is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. That which is eternal is the cause but not the effect; that which is non-eternal is both cause and effect. Furthermore, substance is of three kinds: producer, non-producer, and both. Producer—that which produces another substance, such as threads producing cloth. Non-producer—that which does not produce another substance, such as the final conjunction (*antyasaṃyoga*) of the parts of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) with the atoms. Both—that which produces another substance and is itself produced by another, such as a jar. Furthermore, substance is of four kinds: produced, non-produced, both, and neither. Produced—that which is produced from causes, such as a jar. Non-produced—that which is not produced from causes, such as space. Both—that which is produced from causes and is itself produced by another, such as a jar. Neither—that which is neither produced nor productive, such as the universal, the particular, and inherence. Furthermore, substance is of five kinds: visible, invisible, tangible, intangible, and both. Visible—that which possesses color and is perceptible, such as a jar. Invisible—that which lacks color and is imperceptible, such as air. Tangible—that which possesses touch and is perceptible, such as a jar. Intangible—that which lacks touch and is imperceptible, such as air. Both—that which possesses both color and touch and is perceptible, such as a jar. Furthermore, substance is of six kinds: heavy, light, hot, cold, neither-hot-nor-cold, and both. Heavy—that which possesses weight and is perceptible, such as a jar. Light—that which possesses lightness and is perceptible, such as cotton. Hot—that which possesses heat and is perceptible, such as fire. Cold—that which possesses coldness and is perceptible, such as water. Neither-hot-nor-cold—that which lacks both heat and coldness and is imperceptible, such as air. Both—that which possesses both heat and coldness and is perceptible, such as water heated by fire. Furthermore, substance is of seven kinds: possessing smell, lacking smell, possessing taste, lacking taste, possessing color, lacking color, and possessing touch. Possessing smell—that which possesses smell and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking smell—that which lacks smell and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing taste—that which possesses taste and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking taste—that which lacks taste and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing color—that which possesses color and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking color—that which lacks color and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing touch—that which possesses touch and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking touch—that which lacks touch and is imperceptible, such as air. Furthermore, substance is of eight kinds: possessing sound, lacking sound, possessing number, lacking number, possessing dimension, lacking dimension, possessing conjunction, and lacking conjunction. Possessing sound—that which possesses sound and is perceptible, such as a bell. Lacking sound—that which lacks sound and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing number—that which possesses number and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking number—that which lacks number and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing dimension—that which possesses dimension and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking dimension—that which lacks dimension and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing conjunction—that which possesses conjunction and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking conjunction—that which lacks conjunction and is imperceptible, such as air. Furthermore, substance is of nine kinds: possessing disjunction, lacking disjunction, possessing priority, lacking priority, possessing posteriority, lacking posteriority, possessing remoteness, lacking remoteness, and possessing proximity. Possessing disjunction—that which possesses disjunction and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking disjunction—that which lacks disjunction and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing priority—that which possesses priority and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking priority—that which lacks priority and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing posteriority—that which possesses posteriority and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking posteriority—that which lacks posteriority and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing remoteness—that which possesses remoteness and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking remoteness—that which lacks remoteness and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing proximity—that which possesses proximity and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking proximity—that which lacks proximity and is imperceptible, such as air. Furthermore, substance is of ten kinds: possessing fluidity, lacking fluidity, possessing viscidity, lacking viscidity, possessing momentum, lacking momentum, possessing merit, lacking merit, possessing demerit, and lacking demerit. Possessing fluidity—that which possesses fluidity and is perceptible, such as water. Lacking fluidity—that which lacks fluidity and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing viscidity—that which possesses viscidity and is perceptible, such as water. Lacking viscidity—that which lacks viscidity and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing momentum—that which possesses momentum and is perceptible, such as a moving arrow. Lacking momentum—that which lacks momentum and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing merit—that which possesses merit and is imperceptible, such as the body of a virtuous person. Lacking merit—that which lacks merit and is imperceptible, such as the body of a wicked person. Possessing demerit—that which possesses demerit and is imperceptible, such as the body of a sinner. Lacking demerit—that which lacks demerit and is imperceptible, such as the body of a holy man. Furthermore, substance is of eleven kinds: possessing cognition, lacking cognition, possessing pleasure, lacking pleasure, possessing pain, lacking pain, possessing desire, lacking desire, possessing aversion, lacking aversion, and possessing effort. Possessing cognition—that which possesses cognition and is perceptible, such as the human body. Lacking cognition—that which lacks cognition and is imperceptible, such as the body of a stone. Possessing pleasure—that which possesses pleasure and is perceptible, such as the body of a happy person. Lacking pleasure—that which lacks pleasure and is imperceptible, such as the body of a miserable person. Possessing pain—that which possesses pain and is perceptible, such as the body of a suffering person. Lacking pain—that which lacks pain and is imperceptible, such as the body of a healthy person. Possessing desire—that which possesses desire and is perceptible, such as the body of one who longs for wealth. Lacking desire—that which lacks desire and is imperceptible, such as the body of one who has renounced all things. Possessing aversion—that which possesses aversion and is perceptible, such as the body of one who hates an enemy. Lacking aversion—that which lacks aversion and is imperceptible, such as the body of one who is indifferent. Possessing effort—that which possesses effort and is perceptible, such as the body of one who exerts himself. Lacking effort—that which lacks effort and is imperceptible, such as the body of one who is exhausted. Furthermore, substance is of twelve kinds: possessing gravity, lacking gravity, possessing fluidity, lacking fluidity, possessing viscidity, lacking viscidity, possessing momentum, lacking momentum, possessing merit, lacking merit, possessing demerit, and lacking demerit. Possessing gravity—that which possesses gravity and is perceptible, such as a jar. Lacking gravity—that which lacks gravity and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing fluidity—that which possesses fluidity and is perceptible, such as water. Lacking fluidity—that which lacks fluidity and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing viscidity—that which possesses viscidity and is perceptible, such as water. Lacking viscidity—that which lacks viscidity and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing momentum—that which possesses momentum and is perceptible, such as a moving arrow. Lacking momentum—that which lacks momentum and is imperceptible, such as air. Possessing merit—that which possesses merit and is imperceptible, such as the body of a virtuous person. Lacking merit—that which lacks merit and is imper

Space and the like possess magnitude and other qualities. However, since all action is produced and not eternal, it lacks the two-fold nature [of being both eternal and non-eternal] and thus lacks the status of a quality (*guṇatva*). Even so, it follows that substance (*dravya*) would attain the status of a quality; for a composite substance is seen in its parts, such as hands and feet, and it exists in two ways.

[The distinction is] by way of the division between the eternal and the non-eternal; for while the partless—such as the self (*ātman*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*)—is eternal, a substance composed of parts, such as a jar, is non-eternal. Therefore, he says: "the non-substantial primordial matter" (*asattvaprakṛti*). This refers to that which has the nature of a non-substance (*adravyasvabhāva*).
This is the meaning. Regarding the term *pativarā*: the sense is that this is a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) because it expresses the longing for marriage.
(Pāṇini 4.1.45): *bahvādibhyaśca*.

"And after *bahu* and so forth. Although the application [of the suffix] for the word *bahu* is already established by the preceding rule because it denotes a quality (*guṇavācin*), it is mentioned here for the sake of what follows—that is, so that by the subsequent rule "always in the Veda" (*nityaṃ chandasi*), the suffix may always occur after the word *bahu* as well in the Vedic language. In fact, however, the word *bahu* [is included] by the rule "always in the Veda."
And the rule would be rendered useless, because all optional alternatives are already established by Vedic usage.

He states an ancillary rule (*guṇasūtra*): "after a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix containing the vowel *i*. The rule "after *arvanta-* when not followed by *aktin*" is likewise merely an ancillary rule. Due to the nature of the restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it does not apply here: *sugandhiḥ*.

*Priyakatī* means a prostitute. Regarding *ajanani*: the suffix *ani* is applied to the root *jan* by the rule "the suffix *ani* is used after *jan* in the sense of abuse. Here there are other *gaṇa*-sūtras as well: [the word] *śakti* [is formed with the suffix *ktin*] when it denotes a weapon.
*Śaktiḥ śaktī*. What if it does not denote a weapon? *Śaktiḥ* means capability. But if the reading is *śaktiḥ śastrī* (a spear-like weapon), then...
Two words [are taught]: *śastrī* and *śastrī*. From this point on, [the rule applies] to words denoting limbs of living beings: *dhamaniḥ* and *dhamanī*.
After *candrabhāga*, [it is applied] when referring to a river: *candrabhāgī* and *candrabhāgā*. The word *ahan* is read here;
by virtue of that, a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in it should be cited as an example, and there is also the sublation of the governing rule regarding non-initial (*anupasarjana*) elements.

*Dīrghāhṇī* [is formed from] *prāvṛṭ*. In the alternative view (*pakṣe*), there is a prohibition of the suffixes *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn*. [The words] *bahu*, *paddhati*, *yaṣṭi*, *vikaṭa*, *viśāla*, *kalyāṇa*, *purāṇa*, *caṇḍa*, *kṛpāṇa*, *ahan*, and so forth [are examples]. (447) *Puṃyogād ākhyāyām* [Pāṇini 4.1.48]: [The feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a word denoting a male when it is used to denote a female who is his wife.]

Regarding the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām*: here, the word *ṭhpuṃ* is a separate item with its genitive case ending elided, and it recurs [in the subsequent rules]. In the phrase *puṃyogāt*, the ablative case is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*). As for the phrase *ākhyāyām*, the intention is that the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative; thus he says: "that which is the name of a male," and so forth.

The word *umākhya* is a term denoting a male. By the statement "it functions in the feminine due to connection with *uṃ*," a secondary (gauṇī) application is indicated. However, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "this belongs to that" (*asyedam*) based on the primary meaning, then it becomes simply *aupī*. *Yoga* means relationship; and here, that [relationship] is the state of being a husband and wife (*anpatibhāva*).

Thus, there is no insistence on [the meaning] being "only"; rather, the relationship of produced and producer (*janyajanakabhāva*) is also understood, since there is no evidence for restricting [the scope]. By this, the usage of Bhāravi—“*ausalyayā’sāvi sukhena rāmaḥ prāk kekayīto bharatastato’bhūt*”—is consistent. [The term *kekayī* refers to] the daughter of Kekaya.

Regarding Kaikeyī: if the patronymic suffix *añ* were applied to the form *Anapaśabda-kṣatriya*, the resulting name for the offspring would have been *Āikeya*. Furthermore, one should not suspect the elision (*luk*) of the *tadvāja* affix by the rule *ataśca*, because of the prohibition *na prācyabhargādibhyaḥ*. Thus says Kālidāsa: "O Kaikeyī, [your] desires..."

[The rule applies] in the sense of "she has borne [a child]" (*phalitā*). By this, *evakī* is also explained. Why [is it said] "due to connection with a masculine word" (*puṃyogāt*)? [Consider] *devadattā*. For this is a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*) which denotes a female by its own nature, and not because of a connection with a word denoting a male. Why [is it said] "in the case of a name" (*ākhyāyām*)? [Consider] *prasūtā*. For this...

Regarding the word *jātaprasavā*: since that *prasava* (offspring) is caused by union with a male through the medium of conception, there is indeed union with a male here; however, because this [suffix] is not a direct denoter (*vācaka*) of the male, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply.

Regarding the rule *sūryād devatāyām cāp*: this is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṅīṣ*. When [the word] *sūrya* is used in the sense of a deity, the suffix *āp* is applied. "When [the word] *sūrya* is used in the sense of a deity" means: it is an exception to *ṅīṣ*.
Regarding the word *sūrī*: there is the elision of *ya* by the rule *ūryatiṣya-* etc. (Pāṇini 1.4.61). (Pāṇini 4.1.49:
After [the names of] Indra, Varuṇa, Bhava, Śarva, Rudra, Mṛḍa, Himavat, Araṇya, Yava, Yavana, Mātula, and Ācārya, [the suffix] *ānuk* is added [to form a patronymic].

Regarding Pāṇini 6.4.49, *ānuk*: Now, one might object that for the sake of brevity, *anuk* should simply be stated as having a short vowel, so what is the purpose of pronouncing it with a long vowel? To this they reply: if *anuk* were made [with a short vowel], then by the rule *ato guṇe* (P. 6.1.97), the single substitute would be the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). Nor can it be argued that the long vowel will occur by virtue of the power of the explicit utterance of the letter *ā*; for otherwise—

One might argue that one should simply say "let it be so," since [the rule] would have its purpose fulfilled by subverting the rule *ṭhallopo ’naḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.134). However, just as in the case of *atyurnaḥ*, when a substitute (*ādeśa*) is to be applied,
the elision of the *a* (*allopa*) will not occur precisely because of the power of the utterance of the letter *k*, which serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) for the augment (*āgama*).
If it is argued that this is not so, we say no; for in the word *śarva*, the letter *k* has its own purpose.

Indeed, there is no elision there, because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini 6.1.67] stating "not when there is a conjunct consonant" (*na saṃyogāt*). Therefore, since the letters *k* and *a* lack such capacity [to effect elision], the explicit utterance of the long vowel is necessary for the purpose of overriding the rule of *pararūpa* (the single substitution of the subsequent form). Some, however, [hold that] once the augment *nuK* has been applied...

Because it is defined by its specific technical characteristic (*lākṣaṇika*), the rule "the elision of *an*" (*allopo’naḥ*) does not apply; therefore, when the augment *anu* is added, only the long vowel resulting from *savarṇadīrgha* will occur, due to the force of the explicit utterance of the letter *a*. This being the case, the word *ā-anu-g* is analyzed as such, based on the force of the utterance of the long vowel in the term *ānuk*.

In this regard, they say that although [the feminine suffix] *ānuk* is established for Indra and others, by the force of the rule prescribing the augment *āT*, it is inferred that in some cases the suffix is applied even from other sources;
thus, the form *brahmāṇī* (the wife of Brahmā) is established. On this point, the moderns [say]: let it be as stated above.

The long vowel (*dīrgha*) is prescribed elsewhere for the purpose of a specific rule; however, by dividing the word *ṭhā-anu-g* and applying the substitution of *ā* for the *n*, the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha-grahaṇa*) serves its purpose even when *anu* is applied to a base not ending in *ac*, thereby establishing the form *brahmāṇī*. Thus, it is not [the case that the long vowel is redundant].

It must be explained [otherwise], for if both meanings were intended, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Rather, it should be explained as follows: "Indrāṇī" is the feminine of "Indra," derived from the root *ind* with the suffix *kvip* added to the causative form (*ṇyanta*) according to the rule "one who performs that action is called by that name. This derivation is established precisely because of the force of pronouncing the long vowel.
It is more easily stated that the governing rule *ataḥ* and the governing rule concerning non-derivatives (*anupasarjana*) are both set aside;

for rather than accepting the setting aside of both, one may accept the setting aside of only the governing rule *ataḥ*, whereby the substitution of the vowel *ā* and the addition of the suffix *an* occur to establish the forms *brahmaṇaḥ strī* and *brahmaṇī*.

It should be stated that "let it be explained," for the gravity of contradicting both [theories] is more easily tolerated than the contingency of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*). And thus, they say that the passage to be cited later—beginning with "he brings Brahman" and "he lives"—also accords naturally with this view. Regarding the word *himānī*: it is used when there is a connection with greatness.
The feminine suffix is applied to *himā* and *araṇya*.
After *yava*, it is used in the sense of a defect: *duṣṭo yavo yavānī* ("a defective barley"). By this, a different species (*jātyantara*) is denoted;
and this very thing is its defect, because even in the absence of the generic property (*jāti*) of being barley, [it is still called *yavānī*].

"It is the imitation of its form," as in the case of the script [derived] from the Yavanas. Or, it should be stated that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. This is a *vārttika* located within the rule prescribing the suffix *ghañ* (Pāṇini 3.3.18), which begins with "ṭhiṅśca. And he will state there: "In the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*)."
There is an addition [to the rule] regarding the feminine gender, stating that after a word ending in that [term], there is optionally the suffix *ṅīṣ*.
Thus we have *upādhyāyī* and *upādhyāyī*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "one who studies having approached her. Regarding the phrase "in its own sense" (*svārthe*):
if this rule were intended only for the case of union with a male (*puṃyoga*), then even a Śūdra woman would [be called] the wife of a Kṣatriya.
She may be a *kṣatriyāṇī*. The sense is that a *kṣatriya* woman who is the wife of a *brāhmaṇa* would be called a *kṣatriyāṇī*.
Or, by the rule "after *arya* and *kṣatriya*, [the suffix] is optionally used in the same sense," it means she may be a *vaiśyā*. [The word] *aryaḥ* [is used here].

The intention is that [the forms] are established by nipātana (irregular derivation) for the two meanings of "master" and "vaiśya. Here is the summary from Amara: "Aryāṇī and svayamaryā may be used for a Kṣatriya woman; she may also be called kṣatriyāṇī. An upādhyāyī may also be called upādhyāyā, and likewise ācāryā when referring to herself; [her husband is] ācārya, and [his wife] ācāryānī."
"In the masculine it would be *aryī*, and likewise *kṣatriyī*; [and] *upādhyāyā* as well as *upādhyāyī*."—[The question is:

"How so? [The answer is: Because the word *brahman* is not mentioned in the rule (*sūtra*), the suffix *ānuk* is indeed untenable; this is the question. The reply, however, is: "[One who brings a *brahmán*," etc.; [the suffix] *ṭhan* is applied after the causative form (*ṇyantāt*)."]

The intended meaning is that the form *brahmāṇī* is established through the following process: from the root *prāṇ* (meaning "to breathe"), the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of an agent (*karmaṇi*), resulting in *prāṇa*; then, by the rule *ṭhṇer aniṭi*, the suffix *ṇi* is elided; next, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added according to the rule *iḍḍhāṇañ*; and finally, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs in the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*. Thus, the form *brahmāṇī* is derived.

(449) *krītāt karaṇapūrvāt* |1|4|50|. [The word] *krītāt* [is used]. In this section, the words *ataḥ* and *prātipadikāt* are understood; thus he says—“from that which ends in *at*. The remainder [of the rule] is “from a nominal stem” (*prātipadikāt*). [The example is] *vastrakrītī* (“she who has bought [something] with cloth”). [The analysis is: *vastra-*...

When *bhikṣitā* is established, prior to the arising of the suffix *tup*, there is the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* because it ends in the letter *a* following the compound formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe*. Regarding the phrase "not in some cases": due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (diversely) in the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*, the rule *atikārakopapade* which is to be stated later does not apply in certain instances.

The compound is formed with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). In that context, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied first because it is *antaraṅga* (more internal); subsequently, because the final vowel is no longer short *a*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply—this is the intended meaning. Why specify "preceded by an instrument" (*karaṇapūrvāt*)? [To ensure] it does not apply in analyses such as *gavā krītā* ("bought for a cow") or *aśvena krītā* ("bought for a horse"). For the word *pūrva* here denotes a constituent part (*avayava*).

The compound nominal stem (*samāsaprātipadika*) is the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*). That nominal stem in which the instrument (*karaṇa*) precedes is "that which has the instrument as its prior member" (*karaṇapūrva*); the meaning is "from that.
(450) *ktādalpākhyāyām* | Pāṇini 4.1.51. [A feminine suffix is applied after a word ending in the suffix *kta*, provided it does not denote a small quantity.]

Regarding the rule *ktādalpākhyāyām*: here they have explained that "alpākhyāyām" (when denoting a small quantity) is an adjunct (*upādhi*) of the whole compound. In *abhraliptī* ("slightly covered by clouds"), although the first member of the compound is [the word *abhra-*], the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because the entire compound ends in a *kta*-suffix, according to the principle: "When a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned, it includes that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*. Even though the meaning of the prior member...

Although it is the clouds themselves that are understood as being small, nevertheless, since their smallness entails that the smearing by them must also necessarily be small, it is consistent for smallness to be a qualifying attribute of the whole.

(451) *Bahuvrīheś cāntodāttāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.52]. By this, [the term] *bahv-ī-* is formed. The point is as follows: the rules *bahoḥ nañvad uttarapadabhūmni*, *nañ-subhyām*, and *jāti-kāla-sukhādibhyaḥ anācchādanāt ktaḥ akṛta-mita-pratipannāḥ* are indeed prescriptive of the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*). In that context, by stating "preceded by *ati*," there is an exclusion, by implication, of those cases where *bahu* and the others occur as prior members.

It should be stated that [the suffix] follows words preceded by *jāti* (birth), but not those preceded by *sukha* (happiness) and so forth. In the rule "after *sukha* and others when expressing the feeling of the agent" (*sukhādibhyaḥ kartṛvedanāyām*), those words read there—namely *sukha*, *duḥkha*, *kṛcchra*, and so on—are understood here.
Thus, *sukhāyātā*: the analysis of the compound is "she by whom happiness or suffering has come (*āyātam*) or been attained."

Since the option "after a compound whose prior member is a word denoting a limb of one's own body" (*svāṅga-pūrvapada*) will be stated later, the author here provides an example where the prior member is indeed a word denoting a limb of one's own body: *ūrubhinnī*. In the bahuvrīhi compound *bhinnau ūrū yasyāḥ* ("she whose thighs are split"), the word *bhinna* would, by the rule "*iṣṭhan*" (Pāṇini 2.2.36), normally be required to stand first. However, [the subsequent rule prevents this].

The compound is analyzed as a *paranipāta* (reversal of word order) according to the rule: "In the case of words such as *atikāla*, *sukha*, etc., the final member [of the compound] should be expressed [as the first member].
Regarding *bahukṛtā*: it means "she by whom many things have been done.
It is not [a compound] ending in *jāta*. This is stated as "not [a compound] ending in *jāta*."

Just as in the case of "anudātādi" (Pāṇini 6.2.192), although the desired result would be established by the rule "bahuvrīher udātādiḥ" (Pāṇini 6.2.172) alone, the inclusion of the word *anta* is for the purpose of conveying the sense of necessity (*nityatva*). The point is that the rule "vā jāte" (Pāṇini 6.2.173) prescribes an optional acute accent (*udātta*), and not a necessary one.

Regarding the term *pāṇigṛhītī*: it refers to a wife. The meaning is that when a woman is to be designated as one whose hand has been taken in the presence of the fire (*agnisākṣika*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* should be stated after the word *pāṇigṛhīta*. As for the word "another" (*anyā*): it refers to [a woman] who [takes the hand] by way of a marriage-ceremony (*kautuka*) or the like.
She whose hand has been taken by a slave or the like is "pāṇigṛhītā.

(452) *asvāṅgapūrvapadādvā* | Pāṇini 4.1.53. Since [the suffix] was previously established as obligatory (*nityam*) by the preceding rule, this option (*vikalpa*) applies only when the word is preceded by a genus term (*jāti*).
This has been indicated. How then is it that Kaiyaṭa states that in the word *autrahatī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies by the rule *ṭhasvāṅgapūrvapadāt*?
This is because the word *putra* does not denote a genus (*jāti*). Otherwise, in the word *putrādinī*, the suffix *ṇini* would not apply by the rule *apyajātau*. If...

Regarding *ādinī*—derived from the analysis *putrāṇām ādīni* (the distress of sons)—even if it is somehow established as such based on *tvad-anamādaḥ*, there remains a contradiction with the root text that will be cited later: "What is the purpose of [excluding] *āti*? As in *putrāyātaḥ*," which is intended to prescribe an udātta accent on the final syllable by the rule *atikālasukhādibhyaḥ*. Thus, the contradiction is indeed unavoidable.

To this it is replied: another definition has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "The wise know that genus (*jāti*) to be characterized by non-existence [of its own form], manifold in its referents, and simultaneous with the manifestation and destruction of the substance (*satva*) through its qualities. [This means:
"By the manifestation and destruction of the *satva*, that is, the substance..."
That which undergoes manifestation and disappearance; the meaning is that it exists as long as the substance itself does.

It is simultaneously connected with the substance through its qualities. It has many referents; the meaning is that it pervades all individual instances. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa [states] "that is *jāti*," and so forth.

This has already been explained. And thus, since the state of being a son (*putratva*) is characterized by the definition stated—namely, that it persists as long as the substance [the body] exists—the word *putra* denotes a genus (*jāti*).
Therefore, the textual passage stating either *ṭhasvaṅga-* or *ṅīṣ* is not contradicted therein. This is because [genus-words] denote a form (*ākṛti*).

However, if one relies on the primary view beginning with "jāti" (genus), since "sonship" (*putratva*) is not a genus, the question "What is the point of 'jāti'? and the passage "‘putrāyāta’" also become consistent; such is the direction of the argument.
Some moderns, however, [apply] the rule "tādalpākhyāyām" in cases such as *putrahatī* and *putraghnī*.

They say [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* [is applied] in the case of *surāpītī*. That is, "she by whom wine has been drunk" (*pītā surā yayā sā*). By means of the sūtra and vārttika beginning with *atikāle*, the final acute accent (*antodātta*) and the posterior placement (*paranipāta*) of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) are established. In the case of *vastracchannā*, once the accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) has been applied according to the accentuation rule for *bahuvrīhi* compounds, and the rest have been suppressed (*śeṣanighāta*), [the form is derived].
This [term] ends in an anudātta vowel.
(453) *svāṅgāccopasarjanādasaṃyogopadhāt* P. 4.1.54. Regarding *svāṅgāccopa*: here, the word *bahuvrīheḥ* does not carry over.

Some, however, also cite *suśikhā* as a counter-example; but that is questionable, because [the formation] is with a stem ending in *ṭāp*.
The modern grammarians (*navyāḥ*) maintain that because the suffix *ṅīṣ* cannot apply when the compound does not end in a vowel,
and because it cannot be argued that the word ends in a vowel simply by forming a compound with a *kṛt*-derived stem prior to the application of *ṭāp*— for if that were the case,
the meaning "one who has a beautiful crest" (*suśikhā*) would not be obtained. This is so provided that "limb" (*aṅga*) is understood here in its own [primary] sense.

In that case, the term *sumukhā śālā* ("a hall with a beautiful front") would also [incorrectly] apply, because the face (*mukha*) is a part of the hall; and *sukeśī rathyā* ("a street with beautiful hair") would not apply, because hair is not a part of a street.
Therefore, in order to avoid both under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*), he says:

A limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*) is of three kinds: non-liquid, having form, and located on a living being, provided it is not produced by modification. Regarding "having form" (*mūrtimat*): form (*mūrti*) is the dimension of a substance possessing touch. Regarding "living being" (*prāṇin*): breath (*prāṇa*) is the air moving through the mouth and nose. For example, "a beautiful-faced *śālī* plant. The meaning is that arguments such as "or there would be an infinite regress by way of the cause" are based on negligence.
Since a breast located on an image is not seen in a living being, it would not attain the status of a *svāṅga* (limb of one's own body);

therefore, he states the third definition with the words "tena cet" ("if by that..."). [He explains: by which limb a thing in the form of a living being is—as [it was before]— [The rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source text.]

When joined with a limb similar to that [limb], this inanimate object is likewise joined with—or possessed of—that which is like a limb; thus, even in an inanimate thing, it is observed as its own limb.
(Pāṇini 5.4.155): *nāsikodarauṣṭhajaṅghādantakarṇaśṛṅgāṃśca*.

"An exception within [a section] (madhye’pavāda)" means that, according to the maxim "exceptions set aside preceding rules, not subsequent ones," this is the intended sense. Regarding the word *uraḥ* (chest/bosom), Haradatta and others maintain that it is feminine. In that case, once the shortening of the upasarjana has been applied, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would be applicable because the stem ends in the vowel *a*.
Amarasimha, however, states: "The word *aṅka* means the lap or the space between the arms.

Ratnamati, on the other hand, asserts that it is masculine. The author of the *Gaṇaratnamahodadhi* says: "In the *aṇ* [section], the nominal stem *aṅka* alone is recited, and not the form ending in *ṭāp*. Thus...
And because there is no distinction [in the rule], the examples should be understood to apply to all three genders.
Mādhava, however, says regarding the root *ruḍa* "to sink" in the *tudādigaṇa*:
"kroḍaḥ—[formed with] the suffix *dhañ*. *Kroḍā* is the breast of a horse; this word ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*."
By its very nature, [the term] has a specific scope. This is because in the *Kroḍādigaṇa*, only that which ends in *ṭāp* (i.e., the feminine form) is recited.

For the word *kroḍa*, which denotes merely the space between the arms (*bhuja-antaramātra*), the optional suffix *ṅīṣ*—characteristic of words denoting one's own limbs (*svāṅga*)—does indeed occur in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, as in: *kalyāṇakroḍī* or *kalyāṇakroḍā mayūrī*.

"It exists together with hair" (*keśaiḥ saha vartate*). [Pāṇini 4.1.57] states: "The suffix *ka* is applied after a word preceded by *saha*, *nañ*, or *vidyamāna*. Thus, *sakeśā*; and *avidyamānāḥ keśā yasyāḥ sā*—*akeśā*.

(456) *nakhamukhāt saṃjñāyām* |4|1|58|. [The example] is *śūrpaṇakhā*. The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *ūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*. However, when one intends to express merely a descriptive connection—namely, "she whose nails are like winnowing baskets" (*śūrpavat nakhāni yasyāḥ*)—and it is not a proper name (*saṃjñā*), [the rule does not apply].

Therefore, because it is not perceived as such, there is no prohibition of the suffix *ṅīṣ*, nor is there the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*; thus they say that even in the case of *rākṣasī*, by means of *yogavṛtti* (figurative application), the form *arpitanakhī* is obtained. (457) *dikpūrvapadān ṅīp* | Pāṇini 4.1.60.
Regarding the statement "the substitute *ṅīp* for *ṅīṣ*": the word *ṅīṣ* is carried over from the rule *ṭhanyato ṅīṣ*.

The sense is that, by means of the ablative case in *ik-pūrvapādāt*, the nominative case in *ṅīṣ* is understood as being in the genitive. However, if *ṅīp* were an independent suffix, then [the form] would be *arāgulphā*.

The point is that even in the case of *rākroḍa*, [the suffix *ṭhañ*] would undesirably apply; furthermore, there would be heaviness of comprehension (*pratipattigaurava*) because of the continued application of the previously mentioned prohibitions, such as "not after a non-conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogopadhāt*).
[Regarding *prāṅ*: since the first member of the compound is acute by the rule "particles (*nipātāḥ*) are acute on the first syllable," when the preceding word is acute, in a Bahuvrīhi...]

The intention is as follows: since the rule *prakṛtyā pūrvapadam* establishes the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) for the first member of the compound, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would then become udātta by its own suffix-accent (*pratyayasvara*), resulting in the rest of the word being unaccented (*seṣanighāta*). To prevent this, the suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed as being anudātta; thus, the word *prāṅmukhī* has its initial syllable as udātta.

(458) *vāhaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.1.61. *vāhaḥ*: This is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the root *vah* ending in the suffix *ṇvi*. Since the suffix *ṇvi* is prescribed for *vah* only when it has an object as its *upapada* by the rule "vahaśca" (Pāṇini 3.2.64), the occurrence of the simple [root] is impossible.
Intending that the rule for the elision of the final portion applies by implication because [the suffix] does not exist, he says: "after *vāh* ending in *an*" (*vāhantāt*).
"Not *ṅīp*"—the sense is that this is because [the suffix *ṅīp*] is not marked with a svarita accent. Regarding *dityauhī*: when *ṅīṣ* is applied, there is the designation *bha*;

then, by the rules "ūṭh is substituted for *vāh*" and "from a vocalization (*prasāraṇa*), the preceding form [is substituted]," the single substitute is the prior form. This occurs by the rule "before *eti*, *edhati*, and *ūṭh*."
Vṛddhi. (459) *sakhyaśiśvīti bhāṣāyām* |4|1|62|.
Regarding *sakhyāśiśvī*: the suffix *ṅīṣ* is prescribed by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) after the words *sakhi* and *aśiśu*. [The word *aśiśvī*] does not exist...
That which has no child is *aśiśvī*. Why [is it said] "in common usage" (*bhāṣāyām*)? [Consider: "O friend, be one who has walked seven steps.

(460) *Jāter astrīviṣayād ayopadhāt* | 4.1.63 | "Of a genus, not feminine. By the word *jāti*, the word expressing the genus itself is indicated, because a grammatical operation cannot apply to the [abstract] meaning.

However, its own form (svarūpa) is not grasped [as the meaning], because that would lead to the absurdity of rules such as *astrīviṣayāt* being rendered useless; with this intention, he says: "that which expresses a genus (*jāti*).
Genus (*jāti*) is that which is grasped through form (*ākṛti*). In the term *ākṛtigrahaṇā*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).

The neuter gender is used for the general term (*sāmānya*). It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose apprehension is by means of a form" (*ākṛti*); he states this resulting conclusion in the words beginning with "anugatasaṃsthāna" (having a common configuration). [Objection: Since there is an absence of a configuration excluded from [those of] Brāhmaṇas and so forth in a *vṛṣala* (outcaste), there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*).

He states another characteristic—beginning with "and of the genders" (liṅgānāṃ ca), etc. The particle *ca* (and) is to be understood as displaced [in order], following the word *iggrāhya*. In the term *liṅgānām*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*). "Not all genders" means that it does not possess all genders. Regarding the word *sarva*...
Even though it depends on a formal indicator (liṅga), because it possesses the capacity to convey meaning (gamakatva), the suffix *ṇvi* and the compound formation indeed occur;

therefore, one should not suspect a lack of semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) here. Regarding the word *vṛṣalī*: for when the status of being a *vṛṣala* is predicated of a single individual, that [status] applies to her offspring, siblings, and so forth, even without explicit mention.

The intended meaning is "because it is easy to grasp," as in the example "Devadatta. Furthermore, gender does not apply to everything; it is to be determined by being taught once. Now, one might object: if a difference in substance is admitted based on a difference in dimension (*parimāṇa*), there would indeed be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of a single [substance].

[Objection: When the individuality of Devadatta has been stated, it is easily grasped even without stating it in relation to another individual. [Reply: Not so; for authoritative persons do not accept a difference in substance based on a difference in size (parimāṇa).
Or, if such an acceptance were made, [it would follow that] by virtue of their being simultaneous...

Because it is distinguished from other individuals; and thus, at the very time that "Devadatta-ness" is predicated of one individual, another individual Devadatta is unestablished [as a distinct entity], and therefore "Devadatta-ness" is not a universal (*jāti*). However, "Vṛṣalatva" (the state of being a Vṛṣala) and so forth do indeed exist as universals, because it [is perceived] in his father, brothers, and others.
This is the direction [for understanding] because it is easy to grasp. Since it is not encompassed by the two previously stated definitions, he states a third definition:

"The lineage (gotra) together with the branches of study (caraṇa). Regarding the phrase "the lineage together with the branches of study": apart from the context of [patronymic] offspring, "lineage" refers to the worldly [clan]. "Branches of study" refers to those who study the Vedic recensions (śākhā).

He states the result of this as follows: "ending with the suffix denoting offspring" (*apatyapratyayānta*). Regarding this, they have explained: because of the observation of the neuter usage in the phrase "this *nāḍāyana* is a *bahvṛca*," both *gotra* (lineage) and *caraṇa* (Vedic school) possess all genders;
therefore, a separate definition was formulated for them. Consequently, the rule "and [the gender] of [words] denoting gender is not always [present]" (*iṅgānāṃ ca na sarvabhāk*) does not apply here.

It should not be suspected that the meaning has already been conveyed by the second definition. Regarding the form *aupagavī*: this [suffix] *ṅīp* supersedes the *ṅīp* prescribed for stems ending in *aṇ*, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Thus, those who, taking up the word *aupagavī* under the section on secondary derivatives (*apatyādhikāra*), explain it as being formed by *ṅīp* according to the rule *iḍḍhāṇañ* etc., are to be disregarded.

Such is the sense. However, some maintain that because this section deals with offspring (*apatya*), the word "gotra" here refers only to the worldly lineage (*laukika-gotra*) and not to anything else;

thus, only that which ends in a technical *gotra*-suffix (*pāribhāṣita-gotra-pratyaya*) receives the grammatical operations pertaining to a genus (*jāti-kārya*), and not that which ends in a suffix denoting offspring (*apatya-pratyaya*). This is based on the rule: "A *gotra* [is considered] together with the *caraṇas*."

Because the word *vacana* (the Vedic text) occurs prior to the offspring (*apatya*) in the governing context, the statement of the Easterners—that *aupagavī* ending in *ṅīp* is correct when used in the sense of offspring—is indeed right; so they say. Regarding *kaṭhī*: it refers to one who studies what was proclaimed by Kaṭha, or [one who belongs to that school]; [this is derived] by the rule “*aluk ca vaiśampāyanāntevāsibhyaśca*” (Pāṇini 4.3.104).
The suffix *ṇini* is applied because he is a pupil of Vaiśampāyana. Its elision is by the rule “*aṭhacarakāllu*”.

However, the elision of the suffix *adhyetraṇ* is by the rule “*roktāllu*”. Regarding the term *bahvṛcī*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "she by whom many *ṛc*s are to be studied. This is because of the statement: "*anṛca-bahvṛcau* [are used] only when referring to one who studies [the Veda]."

The suffix *ap* is applied as a compound-ending suffix according to the rule *ṭhṛkpūrabdhūḥ*. Although the study [of the Vedas] by women is prohibited, nevertheless, this was the case in ancient times (*purākalpa*). Yama states regarding this: "In ancient times, however, the tying of the girdle (*mauñjībandhana*) for women was desired, as was their instruction in the Vedas."

"Likewise, there is the statement of the Sāvitrī regarding the Vedas. Alternatively: "Let it be that he has not studied [the Veda]; nevertheless, because of his subordination to it, he will receive that designation [of 'Brāhmaṇa'], just as one might apply it to a young boy (māṇavaka) even though he has not yet studied.
This is the case here with the word *brāhmaṇī*. Thus, the intention is that the earlier example of the suffix *ṅīp* was based on a mere oversight."
“Muṇḍā” means one who possesses the quality of being shaven; it refers to the *alākā* (the female ascetic) with a lotus-stalk-like neck.

Regarding “Kṣatriyā”: because the suffix *gha* is prescribed after the root *kṣat* to form the word for offspring (*apatya*), it denotes a lineage (*gotra*); or else, it denotes a caste (*jāti*) according to rules such as “and not all [names] based on gender.”
Regarding the prohibition [of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*] for words ending in *y*, there is no prohibition for *hayā*, *gavayā*, *mukayā*, *manuṣyā*, and *matsyā*.

As for the phrase "the prohibition for words ending in *y*" and so forth, Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that it is understood from this very Vārttika that words such as *go* were inserted into the *gaurādi* group by modern [grammarians].
