An addition [to the rule] is made for the sake of words that do not denote a genus (*jāti*). For example, *sautaṅgamī*. In this case, the suffix *iñ* is applied to *sutaṅgama* and other such words by the rule "ṭhvuñ-ch-aṇ-ādi" in the sense of "originating from" (*nirvṛta*) and so forth; however, this word ending in *iñ* does not denote a genus.
(Pāṇini 4.1.66: *ūṅ utaḥ*).

The marker *ṅ* [in the rule] is for the purpose of specification, according to the principle "the marker *ṅ* serves to specify both the root and the suffix. Otherwise, that prohibition would also apply in cases such as *yagāgvai*. The long vowel pronunciation, however, is for the sake of the word *vaśrū*, since in other instances the form is established even by the substitution of a long vowel for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*). Thus: *kurūḥ*.

By the technical rule regarding gender-distinction (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), the suffixes *svādi* [beginning with *su*] apply. On this point, they explain: "If it were explained that *svādi* applies because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included as part of the preceding element, then in forms such as *āṇḍe* and *uḍaḷe*, the nominative singular suffix *su* would also occur by the general rule 'the singular is the default. To prevent that," [the rule specifies *sup*].
However, if one accepts *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) for the suffix *ṭha*, there is a fault in the present case;

for in the word *vaśrūḥ*, due to the absence of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), the rule concerning the inclusion of the gender-qualified form (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) is necessary. For this very reason, in the word *hrasve*, by treating the single-substitute as ending with the preceding element (*pūrvāntatvena*)...

It has not been explained in the *Manoramā* and other works that [the suffix] *ṅīp* is applied after [the word] *adhvaryu* by virtue of its inclusion [in the *gargādi* group]. Regarding the term *adhvaryu*:
the meaning is either "one who studies the *Adhvaryu* branch" (*adhvaryu-śākhādhyetrī*) or "one born from a lineage of those who study the *Adhvaryu* branch" (*adhvaryu-śākhādhyāyivaṃśodbhavā*).
This is a caste (*jāti*) characterized by its *caraṇa* (Vedic school). In the etymological analysis (*vigraha*), it is "one who goes to the sacrifice" (*adhvaraṃ yāti*).

By the Uṇādi rule *ṛ-gamy-ā-dibhyaḥ kyuṇ*, there is elision of the final vowel of the root *adhvara*, and the suffix *ku* is applied to the root *yā*. There is also an extension of the rule for words such as *rajju* and others derived from roots other than *prāñjāti*. This is because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*). If...
If it is understood from the sūtra as "or" (uta), then the meaning is that there can be no modification (*ūha*) in the case of a bottle-gourd (*alābu*) and so forth.

Regarding the example beginning with *alābu*: neither the nominative nor the accusative form has been cited, because the purpose to be explained later is not possible therein. [This applies] to the rule *noṅdhātvoh*.
The meaning of the sūtra is that when *yaṇ* follows the vowels *ū* and *ūṅ*, the suffixes beginning with *śas* should not be acute-accented.
(464) *paṅgoś ca* | 4|1|68|. [The word] *paṅgoḥ* [is mentioned]. This is for the purpose of excluding the sense of a genus (*ajāti*). For the word *paṅgu* denotes a quality (*guṇavācī*).

There is the elision of the phonemes *u* and *a* in the word *śvaśura*. Regarding the rule "of *śvaśura*": since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would otherwise apply by virtue of its connection with a male [referent], the suffix *ūṅ* is prescribed; and the elision, being prescribed in conjunction with that [suffix], applies—due to proximity—to the final *a*-phoneme alone, and not to the initial one. And this statement [is made] for the sake of [the form] *śvaśrūḥ*.
The mention of *śvaśrū* is intended to state a fact established by the rule itself; therefore, the elision of the first vowel (*ā*) need not be suspected here either.
(465) *ūrūtarapadādaupamye* | Pāṇini 4.1.69.
"From the latter member": it is called *upamā* (simile) because one is compared by means of it; the state of being that is *aupamya* (similarity).

Here, the former member is implied by the latter member. He states the result of this as follows: "the former member expresses the object of comparison. For example: *karabhorūḥ* ("she whose thighs are like those of a young elephant").
"The outer part of the hand from the wrist to the little finger is called *karabha*. She whose thighs are like that is [described as] *karabhoru*.
However, in the expression "the bearer of a water-pot with hands like *karabhas*," the suffix *ūṅ* does not apply;

for although the word *karabha* denotes a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), it lacks the status of being a prior member of a compound (*pūrvapada*). This is because [the rule for *ūṅ*] applies only when [the comparison] is expressed through a compound.

What [is the purpose]? [It is] for the sake of "vṛtoruḥ. While it could have been stated simply as "ṭhūrvantāt," the inclusion of the term "uttarapada" (subsequent member) is for the purpose that it should not apply in the case of "hastitasvāmyūruḥ. For here, the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "she whose thighs are like those of a female elephant" (*hastina iva svāmyūru asyāḥ*). Thus, although it ends in *ūru*, the status of *ūru* being the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is present here.
It does not apply, because the word *vāmyūru* itself serves as the final member (*uttarapada*).

*Saṃhita*. [This refers to a nominal stem] having *saṃhita* and so forth as its prior member and *ūru* as its final member.
Therefore, the suffix *ūṅ* should be applied [to form the feminine]. Regarding the word *śaphau*: although Amara states that it is neuter in the verse "The hoof (*śapha*) is neuter;

the word *khura* is masculine," nevertheless, the masculinity of the word *śapha* is also authoritative, based on the Vedic scripture: "The two hooves (*śaphau*), as it were, are quivering. [And further: "The hoof (*śapha*) is the hoof..."
And from the *Hemacandra-kośa*: "At the base of cows and other [animals], and also of trees.

Regarding the term *vāmorūḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose thighs (*ūrū*) are beautiful (*vāmau*)," with the suffix *itac*. How then is the usage "O lady with beautiful thighs (*īvaroru*), she drinks as it were of the peacock" in the *Kumārasambhava*? For if the suffix *ūṅ* were applied...

It should be *īśvaroḥ*. However, there is no rule here that prescribes the suffix *ūṅ*. On this point, they say: since a rule based on a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), the absence of the *guṇa* substitution in the vocative case allows for the inference of a solution for the established form.

It should be stated that [the suffix *cha*] is applied after both *sahita* and *saha*. [The example is] *hitena saha*. Regarding this, they say: the word *ahita*, derived by the rule “*amo vā hitatatayoḥ*,” is not intended here;
the point is that its formation is already established simply by including *saṃhita* on the basis of partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛta*).

(467) Regarding the rule *saṃjñāyām* 4.1.72: the word *kamaṇḍaluḥ* is a term denoting a genus of four-footed animals; for this very reason, he will cite *āmaṇḍaveyaḥ* as an example under the rule *catuṣpādbhayo ḍhañ* (4.1.135). However, it is not a synonym for a vessel (*pātra*).

This is a counter-example, because that [word] lacks the feminine gender. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the Vedic language" (*ac-chandortham*): the intention is that in the Veda, by the rule *adrukamaṇḍalvoś-chandasī*, the suffix *uṅ* is established for both names (*saṃjñā*) and non-names (*ala-saṃjñā*). Regarding the phrase "the *a*-sound which belongs to *añ*": what is the purpose of qualifying the *a*-sound with *añ*?

*Śūrasenī*: [This is derived from *śūrasena*] by the suffix *añ* according to the rule "after *anapadaśabda*" etc., followed by the elision (*luk*) of *añ* by the rule "also after [stems ending in] *at*"; here, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* applies because it denotes a genus (*jāti*).
(Pāṇini 4.1.73: "After *śārṅgarava* and others, the suffix *añ* takes *ṅīn*."

Regarding *śārṅgaravī*: from the word *śṛṅgaru*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*). There is vṛddhi of the first vowel. By the rule *ṭhorguṇaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs. Then, although the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been applicable by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ-*, it is set aside because the suffix *ṅīn* is prescribed by the subsequent rule *ātaḥ*. Consequently, as a *nit* suffix, it is udātta (accented on its first syllable). If, however, *ṅīṣ* were applied, [the accentuation would be different].
It would be udātta on the final syllable by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). *Baidā* is the feminine descendant of *Bida*.

By the rule "After *bidādi* stems, when not denoting a seer or immediate descent, the suffix *añ* is applied," the suffix *añ* is added. Since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been applicable here by the general rule for feminine gender (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), the suffix *ṅīn* is specifically prescribed. [The examples are: *Śāṅgaravī*, *Kāpaṭavī*, *Brāhmaṇī*, *Gauggulavī*, and *Gautamī*.
And so forth. From the words *śṛṅgāruka*, *paṭu*, *abrahman*, and *guggulu*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *prāgdīvyato’ṇ*.

The word *gautama* ends in the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ*. Since this [word] is also listed in the *gaurādi* group, the suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally occur here; however, according to the view that *ṅīṣ* alone [is applied], [the form is *gautamī*]. But if the term *ātaḥ* (from the rule *ātaḥ*) is not understood as being carried over [into this rule], then...

The point is that in the case of *śārṅgarava-stri* and *bida-stri*, even when there is an intention to express connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), the suffix *ṅīn* alone would apply because it is subsequent [in the order of rules].
The phrase "of *nṛ* and *nara*" refers to a supplementary rule (*gaṇasūtra*) stating "there is vṛddhi for *nṛ* and *nara*. Regarding the expression "of *nṛ* and *nara*": from the word *nṛ*...

Regarding the rule "ṭhṛnnebhyaḥ," when the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, and the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is prescribed by the rule for denoting a genus (*jāti*)—would otherwise apply to the word *nara*, this statement is made for the purpose of prescribing the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening). Now, one might object: "In the word *nara*, wouldn't the *vṛddhi* occur according to the rule 'ṭhalo’ntyasya' (the substitution applies to the final letter)?

To this they reply: "The operation pertaining to the whole stem (*āṅga*) is stronger than that pertaining to a single phoneme (*varṇa*)," and thus the *vṛddhi* of the vowel *ā* occurs [by the rule] "yasyeti ca."
Due to the elision of the *lopa*, there is the lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of even the initial *a* [of the following word]. Alternatively:

*nara* + *aḥ* = *naraḥ*; by the rule of *pararūpa* as in *katanta*, [we have] *nā* and *naraḥ*, i.e., *nṛnara*. Furthermore, of the subsequent [words], only the first *a*-vowel is taken, not the second.

Regarding the phrase "by virtue of proximity" (*parśleṣasāmarthyāt*): it should be understood that because the word *nara-* is included here as having a meaningful sense, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the word *vānara-*. Even though the form *ārī* would be established by the inclusion of either one [of the two terms], both are nevertheless included in order to exclude the undesired forms resulting from the other.

How, then, is the usage ‘kinnarīṇāṃ nārīṇām’ and so forth to be explained? On this point, they say: “A woman who is a man is a *narī*; [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied here by the rule for feminine formation based on connection with a male (*puṃyoga-lakṣaṇa*). In this way, the form *kinnarī* is also established, because it is analyzed as *kiñcit-narī* (a woman who is somewhat a man). However, some [others] say...

Since no specific locus is indicated, the *akṛt-paribhāṣā* applies, and thus by the substitution of *vṛddhi* for the word *nṛ* itself, the form *nārī* arises. However, the inclusion of the word *nara* is solely for the sake of [the formation of] *ṅīp*. In that case, because there is no *vṛddhi* for the suffix *ani*, it must be *narī*; so say some. Others do not tolerate this. If...

If the inclusion of the word *nara* were solely for the sake of the suffix *ṅīn*, then it would have been listed separately in the *śārṅgarava*-class; for its mention in that class-sūtra, which prescribes the *vṛddhi* vowel increment, would otherwise result in redundancy. Furthermore, the word *putra* is read in this class; from it, the feminine form is *putrī* by means of *ṅīn*. Nor is there [any other reason].

It should not be doubted that the word *putra* does not apply to a daughter, for Amarasimha states: "The words *ātmaja*, *tanaya*, *sūnu*, *suta*, and *putra*—all these, when used in the feminine (*strīyām*), are said to mean a daughter (*duhitaram*). Therefore:
"She spreads joy in the heart like a son," and "O daughter of the lord of the earth! (where *putri* is used).

The applications [of the rule] such as *sarvam* and so forth are indeed unimpeded. As for what was stated here by Haradatta—that "the word *putra*, when followed by a *ku*-suffix, does not exist in the feminine"—that should be disregarded, because it contradicts the cited lexicons. [As it says: *ūtikāputri sthavārtikam*.
"It is useless," as established in the *Manoramā*.

(469) *ṅś-cāp* | Pāṇini 4.1.74: *yaṅ-ś-cāp*. Here, the letter *p* is for the purpose of including the general term "feminine suffixes ending in *ṅ*, *ś*, and *c*" [via Pāṇini 1.3.3: *hal-ṅy-āp*]. As for the letter *c*...

Even though its purpose is fulfilled by the non-occurrence of that [substitution], the acute accent on the *cit* syllable (*citsvara*) prevails over the acute accent on the *pit* syllable (*pitsvara*) because it is subsequent [in the order of rules].
Regarding *āmbaṣṭhyā*: she is the female descendant of Āmbaṣṭha. By the rule “*vṛddhetkośalājādāñ ñyaṅ*,” the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied.
Regarding *kārīṣagandhyā*: he whose odor is like that of dried cow-dung (*karīṣa*) is *karīṣagandhi*.
By the rule *ṭhupamānācca*, the substitution of *idant* occurs for *gandhi*. Its feminine descendant is formed with the suffix *aṇ*.

By the rule *ṭhaṇiñoranārṣayoḥ—*, there is the substitution of *ṣyaṅ*. Although this [suffix] is prescribed only for the feminine, nevertheless, by the force of the inclusion of the marker *ṅ*, the suffix *cāp* is added even after that which ends in it. This refers to the suffix *yañ* following a word ending in *ṣ*.
And they say that this [term] is obtained because of the particle *ca* (and) in the rule *ṭhāvaṭaḷacce*, which serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.

Regarding *pautimāṣya*: the word *pūtimāṣa* belongs to the *gargādi* group; the suffix *yañ* after a word ending in *ṣat* need not be specifically stated. These are the secondary derivatives (*taddhita*). The plural number is used for those [suffixes] to be added that have not yet been mentioned.

For the sake of inclusion. However, the formulation of this "great designation" (mahāsaṃjñā) is for the purpose of obtaining an etymological meaning: "those which are beneficial (*hita*) for those operations (*tad-*) are *taddhita*s. By this, they would apply exactly according to their respective operations. Now, one might object:
let this governing rule (*adhikāra*) occur even before the rule for *ṭāp*, so that the mention of *taddhita* in the rule prescribing *ṣpha* [would be unnecessary].
If it is argued that the mention of *īt* (the long vowel *ī*) should not even be included when the rule *yasyeti ca* applies, that is not so;

for otherwise, in forms such as *aṭhavī* and *mṛdvī*, the *guṇa* substitution of the *oḥ* [of *go* and *auto*] would result. However, if one holds that in the rule *yasyeti ca*, the very mention of *īt* indicates that there is no application of *taddhita*-derived operations in the case of the suffix *ṅīṣ*.

If it were accepted, then some say there would be no fault even if the *ṭāp* suffix were included within the *taddhita* section; however, that is questionable. The modern grammarians (*navya*) maintain that this is because [in cases such as] *uru*, the substitution of *guṇa* for *o* would undesirably apply.

(470) *yūnas tiḥ* | 4|1|77| The suffix *ti* is applied after the word *yuvan*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*. Thus, the form is *yuvatiḥ*. Due to the status of being a *pada* by the rule *vā ṣapūrvasya nigama iti vaktavyam*, there is the elision of the *n*. How then [is the following explained]?

The usage is "ṭhyuvatīkarakomalanirmathita" (crushed by the tender hands of young women). Regarding this, some say: according to the rule for the *bahv-ādi* group, "sarvato’ktinnarthāt," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is optional here. Nor can it be argued that the suffix *ṅīṣ* will not occur because femininity has already been expressed by the suffix *tip*.
This is to be suspected, for according to the Bhāṣya, "these [suffixes] occur even when [the word] has been stated.

Nor would it follow that a collection of young women (*yuvatī*) could not be called *yovata* under such circumstances; rather, by the addition of the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "a collection of this" (*asya samūhaḥ*), there would be the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule "before a non-ḍhe taddhita suffix beginning with a vowel," resulting in *yauvana*.

It should be said that [the form] "syāt" is possible because the word *yuvati* is established through the addition of the *kat* suffix—an *auṇādika* suffix added to the root *yu*—by virtue of its frequent occurrence (*bāhulaka*). To avoid this difficulty, he says: "from [the stem ending in] the present participle suffix *śatṛ*" (*śatrantāt*). This is based on the analysis: "she who unites with, i.e., mingles with, her husband."

The suffix *śatṛ* is applied by the rule *aṭaḥ śatṛśānacau*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭhugitaśca*. In this way, the usage *yauvatī* is easily obtained. However, if the suffix *aṇ* were added after a word ending in *tya*, then due to the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), it would simply be *yauvanam*. [Objection: "By the force of its inclusion in the *dhikṣādi* group, there is the masculine form. [Response: This is not so. The inclusion of *dhikṣā* in that list is for the purpose of excluding the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. If the masculine form were intended here as well, then its inclusion in that list would be useless. Therefore, the masculine form does not apply here. Furthermore, if the masculine form were intended, then since the word *yuvan* belongs to the *kanyādi* group, the suffix *aṇ* would be applied by the rule *kanyāyāḥ kanīna ca*, resulting in the form *kaunīnam*; thus, the form *yauvanam* would never be established. Thus ends the section on feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*) in the *Tattvabodhinī*. Now, the section on case-endings (*svādayaḥ*).
*ṣuñ*: *sunvaḥ*. By the rule "the elision of *o* and *ā*," there is the elision of the vowel *u*.

(307) *svādibhyaḥ śnuḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.73]: *sunavāni*. When the augment *āṭ* is applied by the rule "the augment *āṭ* before a suffix beginning with a vowel for a monosyllabic root ending in *ā*," the *yaṇ* substitution occurs by the rule "*huśnuvoḥ*" [Pāṇini 6.4.87].
The *guṇa* [substitution] takes effect because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules].

(308) Regarding *sunoteḥ syasanoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.117]: "of the root *su*, before the affixes *si* and *san*. Because the word "not" (*na*) is understood to carry over from the rule "a rapara" [8.2.1], he says: "the *ṣ* does not [become *ṣ*]."

It may be so. However, in the case of *abhisusūḥ*, when the suffix *san* is added, and subsequently the suffix *kvip* is applied to this *sannanta* (a verbal base ending in *san*), the *lopa* (elision) of the *san* occurs;

then, once *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) has been performed, the lengthening of the vowel takes place. But *susūṣati* is not an example [of this rule], because the absence of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) is already established by the restrictive rule (*niyama*): "The substitution of *ṣ* occurs only after roots ending in *t* or *au* when followed by a suffix beginning with *san*. This is clear in the *Kāśikā*.
*Ciñ*: the act of piling up; a specific kind of arrangement.
(309) *Vibhāṣā ceḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.58: "Optionally after the root *ci*. From the preceding rule (*ajo’ri*), the suffix *kura* is understood to carry over.

From the rule *an-liṭor-jeḥ* and the rule *san-liṭoḥ*, [the suffix] *san* is introduced. An example of *san* is now to be illustrated: *cikīrṣati*. [Next: *ra* (310) *ṛtaś-ca saṃyogādeḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.43.

From the rule "ṭhiṭ sani ve," the phrase "iṭ vā" (the augment iṭ is optional) is understood to carry over. From the rule "iṅsicaḥ" and [the context of] "ātmanepadeṣu," it is understood that this applies to the ātmanepada endings. Therefore, he says: "The augment iṭ may optionally occur before the taṅ endings. Why mention "before taṅ"? [Consider:
*staryāt* and *astārṣīt*.

(311) *babhūthātatanthajagṛbhmavavartheti nigame* | Pāṇini 7.2.64. *babhūtha*, *atatantha*: The absence of the augment *iṭ* is prescribed by irregular rule (*nipātana*) for the roots *bhū* and *tan* when followed by the suffix *thal*. "Thou indeed hast become the first Hotṛ" (*vaṃ hi hotā prathamo babhūtha*). "By which thou hast stretched out the wide mid-region" (*yenāntarikṣamurvā tatantha*). But in the common language (*bhāṣā*), however...

*babhūvitha* and *tenitha*. [In the Vedic example] "I have grasped your right hand, O Indra," in the common language (*bhāṣā*), however, we say *jagṛhima*. Although the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *krādiniyama* is established for the root *vṛ*, the prohibition applies only in the Veda (*nigama*) and not elsewhere. The mention of *vavartha* is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). [As it says: "For you have chosen..."
In the language of the Jyotiṣas, however, [the forms are] *vavaritha* and *vavṛṣe*.
(312) *liṅsicorātmanepadeṣu* |7|2|42|. [The sūtra consists of] *liṅsicoḥ*; from the previous rule, *vṛtaḥ* is understood by anuvṛtti. Why "in the ātmanepada"? [Consider the counter-example: *avārīt*.
*avāriṣṭām*, *avāriṣuḥ*. Because of the prohibition [of vṛddhi] by the rule "ici ca parasmaipadeṣu," the lengthening [of the vowel] does not occur here by the rule "vṛto vā. (Pāṇini 6.1.41).
[The roots] *hinu* and *mīnā* [are treated similarly]. (Pāṇini 8.4.15).
*hinu* becomes *mīnā*. It measures (*pramīṇati*).

(314) *heracaṅ* | 7|3|56|. After the root *hi*, [the substitution of *ghī* occurs] when *acaṅ* follows. *jeghīyate*. Why "when *acaṅ* follows"? [Consider: *ajīhayat*. Here, [it applies] to the causative (*ṇyanta*) form.

Because it belongs to a different verbal root (*dhātvantara*), and because the simple [root] lacks the condition of being followed by an affix caused by repetition (*abhyāsa-nimitta-pratyaya*), there is no possibility of *kutva* at all; thus, the prohibition "not before *acaṅ*" being redundant, it indicates that *kutva* occurs even for [a root] augmented by *ṇi*. By this, [it is established that...]

The forms beginning with *jighāpayiṣati* are established. Regarding *āpnuhi*: because it is preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogapūrva*), the substitution of *lṛṅ* for *hi* does not occur by virtue of Pāṇini 6.4.106, *utaśca pratyayād*.
(315) *rādha* in the sense of "injury" [is treated as such]. 6.4.123.

In the case of the root *rādh* meaning "to injure," although the term *ataḥ* is understood from the previous rule, by virtue of the contextual requirement (*sāmarthya*), only the letter *a* is accepted as the substitute. (316) Also for the root *aś*. 7.4.72.
And regarding the root *aś*: he says "from a long vowel" because the phrase "the augment *nuṭ* after this [root]" is understood from the previous rule.

Why is there a specific mention of the *śnu* conjugational class? So that it does not apply to the root *aś* meaning "eating," which belongs to the *kyādi* group; for example, *āśa*, *āśatuḥ*. Regarding *ñidhṛṣā*: one who is bold or confident with a spear is called *śūladhṛk*.

*Śūladhṛṣau*: The substitution of *ku* occurs even outside the scope of the rule "ṛtvigdadhṛk... because the suffix *kvip* is prescribed there; however, it applies here specifically at the end of a word (*padānta*). *Dambhu*: Deceit (*dambha*) is the performance of actions prescribed for the purpose of deceiving the world. *Tṛpa*: This root is marked with the augment *iṭ*, as indicated by its mention with the suffix *śyan* among the anudātta roots. *Aha*.

Regarding the pervasion [of the rule]: we have already demonstrated in our commentary on the rule *asyādita udātamarddhahrasvam* that the form *ahya* is derived from the root *hṛ* by adding the suffix *ṇyat* according to the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*. Others, however, say that in the verse *atacakraṃ yo hyae vartanīḥ*, the word *ahya* is actually in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). This is because of the rule *herṅtī*.

However, the *guṇa* [substitution] does not apply to the word *ahi* because it belongs to the Vedic language (*chāndasa*). These are the six roots; but according to the view that there is only one root beginning with *aj*, there are five roots.
Thus ends the section on the *svādi* group in the *Tattvabodhinī*.

Now, the *svādi-sandhi* (euphonic combination beginning with *su*). (130) Regarding *su*, *au*, *jas*, *am*, *auṭ*, and so forth—this is the *svādi-sandhi*. By the rule "in the case of *iva* at the end of a word, there is a *visarga*," and by the rule "of that [visarga], when followed by *arcya*... [the following rules apply].

In response to the doubt—how could *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) occur when the suffix *s* is absent in the case of *samabhivyāhāra* (co-utterance)—he says: "by *svaujasamauḍ* etc. Thus, since the original suffix *su* is indeed present here, *rutva* and so forth will certainly occur; however, the *visarga* does not take place in this instance.
Because there is an absence of a pause (*avasāna*).

It should be understood that even before [the application of] the word *arcya*, [the substitution] does not occur due to the anticipation of the destruction of the pause (*bhāvinyavasānabhaṅge*) by the maxim of "not applying a rule once its result has been achieved" (*akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā*), owing to the co-occurrence with the word *arcya*.
(131) *sasajuṣo ruḥ* 8.2.66.

*Sasajuṣo ruḥ*. The term *adas* (from the previous rule) is understood here and qualifies *sasajuḥ*; by virtue of this qualification, the rule applies to that which ends with [the specified element]. Nor should one fear the prohibition—"there is no application of the rule to what ends with [an element] when the nominal stem (*pratipadika*) itself contains the marker *r*"—in the case of the portion of the word *sajūḥ*, because that [prohibition]...

Because it concerns the domain of the application of suffixes (*pratyaya*). A word (*pada*) that ends in *s* or the word *sajuṣ*, for that, *ru* shall be substituted, and that [substitution] occurs in place of the final letter (*al-antyasya*). This being established, he states the resulting conclusion: "of the *s* at the end of a word" (*padāntasya sasya*). "Of the word *sajuṣ*" (*sajuṣ-śabdasya*); the meaning is "of the word ending in that [i.e., *sajuṣ*]. By this, [the forms] *ujuṣau* and *ajuṣa* [are accounted for].

Thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) here either. Nor should it be argued that there is non-application (*avyāpti*) in the case of *ajūḥ*, because of the prohibition: "The treatment as if possessing a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) does not apply to a non-counter-correlative (*aprātipadikena*). For that [prohibition] also pertains specifically to the domain of the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*). Precisely for this reason—

Haradatta stated in his commentary on the sūtra *iva ut* that both of these two paribhāṣās— *ṭhvyapadeśivadbhāvo ’prātipadikena* and *rahaṇavate*— pertain to the domain of rules prescribing suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*). However, in the *Manoramā*, it is established that [the view] belongs to both Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta.
Regarding this, the modern scholars (*navyāḥ*) maintain that Kaiyaṭa’s inclusion [of the word *kaiyaṭena*] is a lapse resulting from oversight, since it was not mentioned by Kaiyaṭa himself.

However, some hold that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is an *utsūtra* (a deviation from the rule) such as *iva u*," and that the collection of rules (*sūtrasamudāya*) constitutes the external referent (*anyapadārtha*). Thus, by the term *iva utsūtra*, [the compound refers to] a *dvandva*...

Since this [sūtra] is also included within the scope of the sūtra beginning with *ce'ti*, and since Kaiyaṭa has stated [this] therein, they justify the *Manoramā* against the aforementioned objection through great effort, as if it were the work of a bad poet.
(132) *ato roraplutādaplute* 6.1.113.

Regarding the concern that, because this [substitution] is not established, even when *utva* has been applied, *yatva* might still occur due to the status of the preceding element as *sthānivadbhāva*, he says: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *yatva*. This is by virtue of the specific force (*sāmarthya*) of the rule for *utva*. Nor can it be argued that one should abandon the rule *ato ror aplutāt* and instead [adopt] *roḥ*...

It should not be argued that, immediately after *supi*, one should simply state *ṭhata ur* for the sake of brevity— what is the point of this laborious recourse to *sāmarthya* (semantic dependency)? For if that were the case, since *ut* would be considered *asiddha*,
the *ādguṇa* rule would fail to apply in instances such as *ivo ’rcya*.

(133) *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* |6|1|102|. Regarding *prathamayoḥ*: here the word *prathamā* is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) for the aggregate of the first and second [cases]; the dual number, however, is in reference to the individual members of that aggregate. From the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, the term *aci* [is understood]. From *akaḥ*... [the term *savarṇaḥ* is understood]. From *dīrghaḥ* [the term *ekaḥ* is understood]. From *pratyayaḥ* [the term *paraḥ* is understood]. From *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* [the term *ādeśaḥ* is understood]. Thus, when a vowel follows an *ak* [vowel], the single substitute for both the preceding and the following is the homogeneous long vowel corresponding to the first [of the two]. [Example: *mālā + ā* = *mālā*. [Example: *agnī + ī* = *agnī*. [Example: *daṇḍān + iha* = *daṇḍān iha*. [Example: *dadhi + atra* = *dadhy atra*. [Example: *madhu + atra* = *madhv atra*. [Example: *dadhi + ā* = *dadhy ā*. [Example: *madhu + ā* = *madhv ā*. [Example: *dadhi + e* = *dadhy e*. [Example: *madhu + e* = *madhv e*. [Example: *dadhi + ai* = *dadhy ai*. [Example: *madhu + ai* = *madhv ai*. [Example: *dadhi + as* = *dadhy as*. [Example: *madhu + as* = *madhv as*. [Example: *dadhi + os* = *dadhy os*. [Example: *madhu + os* = *madhv os*. [Example: *dadhi + am* = *dadhy am*. [Example: *madhu + am* = *madhv am*. [Example: *dadhi + bhis* = *dadhibhis*. [Example: *madhu + bhis* = *madhubhis*. [Example: *dadhi + bhyas* = *dadhibhyas*. [Example: *madhu + bhyas* = *madhubhyas*. [Example: *dadhi + su* = *dadhiṣu*. [Example: *madhu + su* = *madhuṣu*. [Example: *dadhi + na* = *dadhinā*. [Example: *madhu + na* = *madhunā*. [Example: *dadhi + bhyām* = *dadhibhyām*. [Example: *madhu + bhyām* = *madhubhyām*. [Example: *dadhi + bhyas* = *dadhibhyas*. [Example: *madhu + bhyas* = *madhubhyas*. [Example: *dadhi + sya* = *dadhyaḥ*. [Example: *madhu + sya* = *madhvaḥ*. [Example: *dadhi + os* = *dadhyoḥ*. [Example: *madhu + os* = *madhvoḥ*. [Example: *dadhi + ām* = *dadhīnām*. [Example: *madhu + ām* = *madhūnām*. [Example: *dadhi + i* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + i* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + as* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + as* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + au* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + au* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + śas* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + śas* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + bhyām* = *dadhibhyām*. [Example: *madhu + bhyām* = *madhubhyām*. [Example: *dadhi + bhyas* = *dadhibhyas*. [Example: *madhu + bhyas* = *madhubhyas*. [Example: *dadhi + sya* = *dadhyaḥ*. [Example: *madhu + sya* = *madhvaḥ*. [Example: *dadhi + os* = *dadhyoḥ*. [Example: *madhu + os* = *madhvoḥ*. [Example: *dadhi + ām* = *dadhīnām*. [Example: *madhu + ām* = *madhūnām*. [Example: *dadhi + i* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + i* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + as* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + as* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + au* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + au* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + śas* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + śas* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + bhyām* = *dadhibhyām*. [Example: *madhu + bhyām* = *madhubhyām*. [Example: *dadhi + bhyas* = *dadhibhyas*. [Example: *madhu + bhyas* = *madhubhyas*. [Example: *dadhi + sya* = *dadhyaḥ*. [Example: *madhu + sya* = *madhvaḥ*. [Example: *dadhi + os* = *dadhyoḥ*. [Example: *madhu + os* = *madhvoḥ*. [Example: *dadhi + ām* = *dadhīnām*. [Example: *madhu + ām* = *madhūnām*. [Example: *dadhi + i* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + i* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + as* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + as* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + au* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + au* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + śas* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + śas* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + bhyām* = *dadhibhyām*. [Example: *madhu + bhyām* = *madhubhyām*. [Example: *dadhi + bhyas* = *dadhibhyas*. [Example: *madhu + bhyas* = *madhubhyas*. [Example: *dadhi + sya* = *dadhyaḥ*. [Example: *madhu + sya* = *madhvaḥ*. [Example: *dadhi + os* = *dadhyoḥ*. [Example: *madhu + os* = *madhvoḥ*. [Example: *dadhi + ām* = *dadhīnām*. [Example: *madhu + ām* = *madhūnām*. [Example: *dadhi + i* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + i* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + as* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + as* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + au* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + au* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + śas* = *dadhi*. [Example: *madhu + śas* = *madhu*. [Example: *dadhi + bhyām* = *dadhibhyām*. [Example: *madhu + bhyām* = *madhubhyām*. [Example: *dadhi + bhyas* = *dadhibhyas*. [Example: *madhu + bhyas* = *madhubhyas*. [Example: *dadhi + sya* = *dadhyaḥ*. [Example: *madhu + sya* = *madhvaḥ*.

With the intention that the rule "a long vowel replaces [two] homogeneous vowels" (*savarṇe dīrghaḥ*)—from which the words "a long vowel" (*ako dīrghaḥ*) and the sūtra "of the preceding and following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*) are carried over—he explains by saying: "after *ak* [in the first or second case], before a vowel," and so forth. Why "before a vowel"? [Answer: *rāmaḥ*. Why "after *ak*"? [Answer: *gāvau*, *nāvau*. Why "of the first two"? [Answer:]...

In *vṛkṣe* and *plakṣe*. Although this [result] is established by the rule *ādici* alone, nevertheless, just as in *harī*, there would also be a long vowel of the same class as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ*) in *haryoḥ*. To prevent that, it is stated *rathamayoḥ*; such is the direction. Why is the mention of *pūrva-* (preceding) made?

In the case of *ṭhagnī*, let there not be a substitution of the subsequent homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*). Why is the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) included? [It is so that] when the substitute is a three-mora (*trimātra*) original element (*sthānin*), it should not itself become three-mora. This is because of the maxim: "When an exception (*apavāda*) is blocked, the general rule (*utsarga*) remains in force. In this context, the term *hidyo* refers to a river.
The word ‘au’ and so forth is an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

[In the rule] *nādici* 6.1.104, for when the substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) has been prohibited by that [rule], there is again the application of the general rule (*utsarga*) of *vṛddhi*.
"It is established only through actual occurrence (*pravṛtti*), and not otherwise. Now, if the reading were *āntaḥpādam avyapare*,
then in cases such as *ujāte aśvasūnṛte* and *upaprayanto adhvaram*,
the rule *eṅaḥ padāntādati* would indeed be prohibited by that [proposed reading], and if that were prohibited—

Even the general rule (*utsarga*) "ṭh-eco’ḍayavāyāvaḥ" would apply. Not so; for it is accepted that when the sublater (*bādhaka*) is negated, the sublated (*bādhyam*) is also not [applicable] in some cases—thus its establishment [is secured]. (135) *Bho-bhago-agho-apūrvasya yo’śi* | Pāṇini 8.3.17.

Regarding "bho-bhago-": "non-sandhi" means it is established in the *sūtra*. The term "sautra" means that which is performed in a *sūtra*; [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied here according to the rule *ṛt-labdha*.

The meaning is that, because it is *sautra*, the single-substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) for the *o* of the words *bhago* and *agho* and the *a* is not [applied]. However, if [one considers] *bhos*, *bhagos*, and *aghos* as ending in *s* or *r*...

Or, if one were to explain that after applying [the suffix] *anukṛti*, the rule "of the three beginning with *bho*" (*bho-ādīnāṃ trayāṇām*) would apply to the final letter by means of the rule "of the final [letter]" (*alo’ntyasya*), and then the rule "and *ru* for what precedes" (*apūrvasya ruḥ*) would be explained, then it should be understood that the absence of sandhi (*asandhi*) is indeed logical.
Now, an objection might be raised: since the letter *u* in *ru* is an *anubandha*, the substitute for the *visarga* is merely the letter *r*.

And thus, suspecting that the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) would not apply under the rule for the prescription of *ṭha*-suffixes (*ṭhanalvidhau*), he says: "For this is not [the case]. Now, just as in the case of *agṛhīṭ*—where, by virtue of the status of being a *sthānin*, the long vowel [prescribed] by the rule *raho 'liṭi* is considered to have the property of *iṭ*, and thus the rule *iṭ īṭi* applies—so too here.

The intention is that the substitution of *y* for the *r* of the *visarga* should take effect. Although this is indeed an *al-vidhi* (a rule concerning phonemes) based on the interpretation that one carries over *ra* from the rule "ṭhrorī" and explains it as "the *ya*-substitute for that *ra* which is the *repha* [the sound 'r'] of *ru*," nevertheless, the mention of *ru* must be made for the sake of subsequent rules.
The word ‘a’ has been placed right here in order to avoid the inconvenience of its having to recur [from a previous rule]. Regarding the term ‘nipātāḥ’ (particles):
they are to be understood as those specified in the rule *hobhago-* (Pāṇini 8.3.17), because that group is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class).
However, if one follows the *vārttika*: *vibhāṣā bhavadbhagavadaghavatāmoccāvasye*.

If [the rule] were understood as meaning "for these [words], *ru* should be substituted, and in the vocative singular, the vowel *u* may optionally [be elided]," then although forms such as *he hare* would be established for the masculine singular alone,
[forms like] *ho hariharau*, *ho vidvadvṛnda*, and *hogaṅge* would not be obtained.

[Otherwise], the aforementioned [examples] and so forth would not be established. Therefore, the sense is that the *vārttika* "bhavādvibhāṣā" need not necessarily be resorted to. However, in the *Manoramā*, it is stated: "But according to the spirit of the *Bhāṣya*, the *vārttika* 'vibhāṣā' must indeed be commenced. For instance, [in the case of] "he bhavan" (O, sir).

For just as [the form] *itivat* is accepted, so too the usage *ṭhhe bho* is desired; moreover, that [usage] is established by the very commencement of the Vārttika. However, since it is impossible to employ together the particles denoting address mentioned by Amara—namely *yu*, *pāṭ*, *pyāṭ*, *aṅga*, *hai*, *he*, and *bhoḥ*—furthermore, in this case...

Expressions such as *bhavān hariḥ*, *atra bhavān*, and *ato bhavān* are established only when the *vārttika* [Pāṇini 8.1.23] exists, because that rule— stating "they are also seen after other [words]" (*itarābhyo ’pi dṛśyante*)—
intends that the forms *atra* and *ataḥ* ending in all case-terminations are used only in conjunction with words such as *bhavat*. Furthermore, [the following applies]:

When [a word] is addressed (*āmantrita*), the eighth case-suffix (*aṣṭamika*) following it undergoes *nighāta* (elision of accent), and by the rule "that which is addressed is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) with respect to what precedes it," its status as non-existent is established, and so forth; this would not be possible otherwise. Furthermore, for the sake of establishing forms such as "ho hariharau," the particle "ho" [is required].

Even the *nirāta* must necessarily be accepted. However, if the particles *bhaga* and *agha* are also authoritative, then let them remain so; nevertheless, the *vārttika* must indeed be accepted for the purpose already stated—this is the direction of the argument. This might be the case if the particles were not accepted.

If it is argued that in the rule for the suffix *yat*, only those [forms] ending in *-as* should be taken because they are explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*), and not those ending in the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) because they are derived through a grammatical definition (*lākṣaṇika*), this is not so; for in the rule "by means of a *varita* accent there is an *adhikāra*," one may adopt the explanation that *adhikaḥ kāraḥ* is *adhikāraḥ*, and thus follow the requirements of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*).

Because both [types of *bhū*] are included by relying on the fact that the term is marked with the *svarita* accent, and because the maxim regarding "that which is taught by a rule versus that which is taught as a word-form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā*) is not universally obligatory. The evidence for its non-obligatoriness is the inclusion of the term "Great Utterances" (*mahāvyāhṛti*) in the rule *tuṭbhuvaśca mahāvyāhṛteḥ*, and the inclusion of the term "particle" (*nipāta*) in the rule *yāvatpurā*. And it is not the case that...

Even if the inclusion of those [words] possessing technical definitions (*lākṣaṇika*) were accepted, it should be stated that in the case of "this belongs to the All-pervading One" (*vibhoridam*), where *suprabhā* is *gauḥ* (a cow) and he who possesses her is *suprabhaguḥ*,

then "this belongs to *suprabhaguḥ*" (*suprabhagoridaṃ*), and likewise in "this belongs to Raghu" (*raghoridam*), there would result the application of *yatva* (the substitution of *ya*). This is because, by virtue of mutual association (*parasparasāhacaryeṇa*), [the technical meanings of] particles (*nipāta*) [are restricted].

Even if those [terms] mentioned in the *Vārttika* were included, others would not be; however, it should be understood that the co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) of these [three] is for the purpose of indicating the vocative case. If one explains the rule as "for the three beginning with *ho*, there shall be *ya* in place of the final vowel," then by the *paribhāṣā* regarding the inclusion of meaningful elements (*arthavadgrahaṇa*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Not so.

Furthermore, regarding the view that "the function [of a word] does not abandon its own meaning" (*ajahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*), one might suspect that in the expression "this belongs to the All-pervading One" (*vibhor idam*) or "this belongs to the Lord" (*prabhor idam*), the single constituent part *haḥ* (from *vibhoḥ* or *prabhoḥ*) still possesses its own meaning; however, this is not the case under the primary view that "the function abandons its own meaning" (*jahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*).
This is the general direction of the argument.

(136) *vyor laghuprayatnataraḥ śākaṭāyanasya* | 8|3|18|. "Of *v* and *y*, [there is] a lighter effort, according to Śākaṭāyana. The phrase "of *v* and *y*" means "of *v* and *y* preceded by *bhoḥ*, *bhagaḥ*, *aghaḥ*, or *a*. "Ligher effort" (*laghuprayatnataraḥ*) means "lighter pronunciation. And that [substitution] is, by virtue of proximity (*āntaryāt*), *va* for *va* and *ya* for *y*.
Thus he says: "vayau.
(137) *oto gārgyasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.20).
Due to the force of the rule's formulation, [the substitution] does not apply to that which involves even lighter effort.
With this intention, he says: "of one whose effort is not slight" (*alaghupratnayasya*). Regarding "bhoyacyuta":
thus *bhagoyacyuta*, *aghoyacyuta*. An example for the letter *v* is, however, "ṭhasāvādityaḥ.
And this is clear in the *Kāśikā*.

(138) *uñi ca pade* | Pāṇini 8.3.21. Regarding the mention of *pada*, it is said that it is for the sake of what follows. However, in reality, it is not even necessary there, because the matter is resolved simply by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *adasya*. From the rule *uñi ca pade*, [the term] *ade* [is understood].

This is because [the rule] is interpreted as "of a word beginning with *ṭha*," following the principle of *anuvṛtti*; and furthermore, because the ancient interpretation of the rule *ṅmuṇ nityam*—as applied in examples such as *aramadaṇḍinau*—has been refuted in the *Manoramā* on the sūtra *mo hrasvād aci*. Now, [one might object]: "In the case of *hali*..."

In the rule *sarveṣām*, because the term *ad-eh* is understood to carry over [from a previous rule], one obtains the interpretation "in a word beginning with a consonant (*hal-ādi-pade*)"; consequently, in forms such as *vṛkṣavbhyām* and *vṛkṣavbhiḥ*, the elision of the *v* does not occur invariably, but rather its elision is merely optional according to the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya*. Thus it stands.

If it is argued that the purpose of including the mention of *ade* is [to ensure the rule applies here], it is not so; for in the rule *hali sarveṣām*, the word *vaḥ* does not carry over. Furthermore, in forms such as *ābhyām* and *ābhiḥ*, according to your view, the elision would occur only optionally when followed by *bhyām* and other suffixes; however, in that case, [the rule] *hali*...

Because the rule *sarveṣām* does not apply here. Nor can it be argued that such an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) is acceptable, for the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that the mention of the word *pada* in the rule *mo hrasvād aci* is for the purpose of ensuring its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) in the rule *daṇḍinā*. And it should not be said that that very [recurrence] is the sole purpose [of the mention of *pada*].

According to the interpretation that "the augment *ṅmuṭ* is invariably applied to a vowel following a word ending in a *ṅ* which is preceded by a short vowel," there is no possibility of its application in the case of *aṇḍine*.
(139) *Hali sarveṣām* | Pāṇini 8.3.22.

[The word] "of all" [applies] to every [rule]. [The word] "of *yakāra*" [is used]; however, *vakāra* does not follow, because a *vakāra* preceded by *bho*, *bhago*, *agho*, or *a* is impossible. Although a *yakāra* preceded by *a* is possible—as in "vṛkṣav karoti"—nevertheless, the elision (*lopa*) does not apply there.

By carrying forward the term *ṭhaśī* and treating *aś* as a qualifier of the consonant (*hal*), they say that forms such as *vṛkṣavhasati* are incorrect due to a lack of attestation (*anabhidhāna*). However, in the case of *avyam*, there is no status as a word-final element (*padāntatva*).
As for *avyūti*, it has been stated that there is no elision of the *val* sounds because of the elision of the letter *v*. [The example] *devā namyāḥ* [is provided].

Thus [it is said]. Here, the rule *opo vyor vali* does not apply, because with respect to that [rule], the substitution of *y* is considered *asiddha*. Why is it stated as *hali*? [The answer is: the mention of *hali* was made here precisely for the sake of what follows. Consequently, both this [present rule] and the rule *opaḥ śākalyasya* [apply].
The intended meaning is that the distinction between the domains [of application] is established here.
(140) *ro'supi* | P. 8.2.69. Regarding *ro'supi*: if the term *asupi* were a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), then it would refer only to an affix similar to *sup*.

[The rule applies] in cases such as *syādaharyati*, but not even in cases such as *aharbhāti*. Therefore, he explains that it is indeed a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) by stating "but not after a *sup* [ending]. Regarding *aharahar*: the doubling occurs by the rule “*ityavīpsayoḥ*” (Pāṇini 8.1.4). Nor is there any concern here that, because the substitution of *r* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding operation), the *na-lopa* (elision of *n*) would apply first, resulting in the elision of the vowel *a* itself.

It should be stated that "repha" (the substitution of *r*) occurs; for, having restricted the rule "ṭhaha"nn" [Pāṇini 8.2.31] and by means of one [part of it] prescribing the non-elision (*alopa*), the second part prescribes *ru*.
Since this will be explained in the sūtra "ṭhaha"nn," the substitution of *r*, which is an exception to the substitution of *ru*, is thereby established as being in the place of the letter *n*.
Regarding "ahorātra": the compound-ending suffix will be explained by the rule beginning with *ahaḥsarvaikadeśa*.

Its masculine gender is established by the rule *atrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi*. Regarding *ahorathantaram*: *rathantaram* is a *sāman* (chant). This forms either a collective dvandva compound of *ahan* and *rathantaram*, or it consists of two separate words.

Regarding the phrase "of food, etc. (*ahārādīnām*): in both instances, the word "etc. (*ādi*) denotes a class or type. By this, examples such as *varcakṣā rathiraḥ* and *aviḥ kāvyenā svarcanā* are to be understood. (141) *ro ri* | Pāṇini 8.3.14.

Regarding the phrase "an exception to elision" (*visargāpavāda*): the meaning is that the rule *mo rāji-vad-rephasya* prescribes the substitution of *repha* for *m* in order to prevent the application of other modifications. (142) *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.3.111.

*ḍhralope*: The letter *ṭhra* [in the term *ḍhralopa*] is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). *Ḍha* and *ra* are *ḍharau*; that which causes their elision (*lopayati*) is *ḍhralopa*. This is a compound with an upapada [formed] from the causative (*ṇijanta*) root in the sense of the object (*karman*), ending in the suffix *aṇ*. In the forms *tṛḍhaḥ* and *vṛḍhaḥ*, because the root is marked with *ū* (an *ūdita*), it optionally takes the augment *iṭ*; however, by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*).

[The operations of] *ḍhatva*, *dhatva*, *ṣṭutva*, and the elision of *ḍha* [apply]. However, the Easterners have cited *ṛḍha* as a counter-example; that is incorrect, because in that case there is no elision of *ḍha* at all, since it is superseded by *ghatva* in the rule "the roots *ṛḍh* and *sthūlabali*" [take *gh*].
Nor can it be argued that the absence of *iṭ*, the substitution of *ḍha*, and the elision of *na* should be treated as irregularities (*nipātana*).
It should not be argued that the elision of *dh*, *tv*, *ṣṭu*, and *ḍh* will simply take place;
for if that were so, in the form *aridraḍhayya*, the substitution of *ay* for *ṇi*—by the rule *yapi laghupūrvaḥ*—would not occur.
Likewise, in *ārivṛḍhā kanyā*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* (by the rule *ṭitaḥ manuṣyajāteḥ*) would not apply.

It is established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that the suffix *ṣyaṅ* should apply by overriding [the rule] "after a word ending in *ṛ*, the suffixes *ṭhaṇ* and *iñ*," because the elision of *ḍh* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), thereby making the penultimate vowel heavy (*gurūpottama*). Now, one might ask:

how can the substitution of *lyap* occur in the form *paridraḍhayya*, given that when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied to the sense "he causes to become firm" (*paridṛḍham ācaṣṭe*), [the conditions for *lyap* would not be met]?

If it is argued that because the suffix *ktvā* itself is included within the root *pari* when the *ktvā*-suffix is present, there can be no compound, Kaiyaṭa states on this point: "Due to the restrictive rule that the suffix arises only after the root *saṃgrāmayati* when preceded by a prefix and not from any other [root], the word *pari* is separated and the suffix *ṇic* is applied to the word *dṛḍha* alone. [This applies] to the form ending in *ṇic*.

Because it is a verbal root (*dhātu*), when the suffix *ktvā* is applied, there is a compound with that form ending in *ktvā*—which is a *kṛt*-derivative—and thus the substitution of *lyap* is established. [Regarding the rule *raḥ karmakartari*: because of the application of the *iṣṭhavan-bhāva* (the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix *iṣṭha*) to the suffix *ṇa*, the *rabhāva* (the replacement of *ra* by *la*) occurs. Now, one might object:
the mention of "of what precedes" (*pūrvasya*) is redundant, since that [meaning] is obtained simply from the locative indication (*saptamī-nirdeśa*). Therefore...

He says: "The mention of 'pūrva' (the preceding)," and so forth. The meaning is that because the rule *hralope pūrvasya* is situated within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), the lengthening would occur only when followed by *ḍha* or *ra* residing in the subsequent member; it would not, however, apply in cases such as *īḍhaḥ* or *ṭhajarghāḥ*.

Although a long vowel might occur for the letter *ḍha* when it stands at the end of a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) precisely because such a case is impossible, it should be understood that in forms such as *ajarghā*, the long vowel would not apply. In reality, however, since the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) is conventionally restricted to the final constituent of a compound, [the rule] would not apply even in cases such as *punā ramate*; rather, it applies to forms such as *īraktaṃ*.

The truth is that [the rule] would apply only in cases such as *ūrakta*. Regarding *līḍha*: the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *lih* (meaning "to taste"). There is the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha*, the substitution of *dha* for *ḍha*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ḍha*, and the elision of *ḍha*. Here, the substitution of *ṣṭu* is not treated as *asiddha* with respect to the elision of *ḍha*, because of the force of the rule prescribing the elision when *ḍha* follows. For this very reason, [the elision prescribed by] *ho ḍhea lopaḥ*...
Even when situated within a word (*padādhikāra*), the elision of *ḍha* occurs for that which is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*). For example: *ajarghāḥ*.

[Derivation: From the root *ṛdh* in the sense of "desire" (*abhikāṅkṣā*), with the elision of *yaṅ*, there is reduplication and *ruk* of the reduplicated syllable. In the *laṅ* tense, after *sip*, with the elision of *śap*, in the alternative where *īṭ* is absent, there is the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel, followed by *ra*.

In the form *ṭhitaśca*, following the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* [Pāṇini 6.1.68], there is the substitution of the voiced aspirate (*bhaṣbhāva*), followed by the substitution of the voiced unaspirated (*jaśtva*). In the alternative where the substitution of *ru* applies by the rule *aśca* [Pāṇini 8.2.39], we have the form *ṭhajarghar r*. Once the *r* is elided by the rule *ṭh-r-or-ī-* [Pāṇini 6.1.113], the long vowel is substituted by this present rule [Pāṇini 6.3.111]. Here is the easy explanation: "When *ḍh* or *r* is elided, [the long vowel is substituted] for the preceding [vowel]."
The vowel *a* is lengthened [when it follows *ṛ*]. Examples: *līḍhaḥ*, *nīraktaṃ*, *dūraktam*. Why specify "of *a*" (*aṇaḥ*)? [To exclude cases like] *tṛḍhaḥ*, *vṛḍhaḥ*.

The mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*) is for the purpose of lengthening the initial vowel alone, even when there is no subsequent member of a compound (*anuttarapade*). Examples: *ajarghāḥ*, *punā ramate*, *harī ramyaḥ*, *śambhū rājate*.

(143) *vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam* | 1.4.2 | Regarding *vipratiṣedhe*: it is derived from the prefix *vi-prati* combined with the root *sidh*, meaning "to succeed" or "to be auspicious" (*śāstre māṅgalye ca*), or from the root *sidh*, meaning "to go" (*gatyām*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied, and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs according to the rule *upasargāt sunoti*.
And due to the influence of the prefix (*upasarga*), it carries the sense of contradiction. Regarding the word *kāryam*:
by the rule *ṭharhe kṛtyatṛcaśca*, the *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of "what is fit" (*arha*). Therefore, it refers to a contradiction between two things of equal strength.

This [rule] does not apply to those rules that are final, or to rules of unequal strength—namely, general rules (*utsarga*) versus exceptional rules (*apavāda*), obligatory rules (*nitya*) versus non-obligatory rules (*anitya*), and internal rules (*antaraṅga*) versus external rules (*bahiraṅga*). For when exceptional rules and the like are in proximity, general rules and the like are not eligible for operation, because they are sublated by them. Among these, the obligatory rule is sublater due to its necessity; the internal rule is sublater due to its parsimony (*lāghava*); and the exceptional rule is sublater due to the authority of its specific statement. The subject matter of the present sūtra, however, is distinct from these.

For this very reason, it has been stated: "Among rules that are non-optional (*araṇi*), internal (*antaraṅga*), and exceptions (*apavāda*), each subsequent one is stronger. If this were the case even when rules are of unequal strength, then the rule stating that the subsequent one prevails would not be tenable; therefore, he explains: "In the case of conflict between rules of equal strength" (*tulyabalavirodhe*). This sūtra is intended for the purpose of providing a rule regarding the class (*jāti*) as the word-meaning. For in the cases of *vṛkṣeṣu* and *vṛkṣābhyām*, where the rules for *etva* (shortening) and lengthening have already found their scope, there would be a lack of determination (*apratipatti*) in the case of *vṛkṣebhyaḥ* due to the simultaneous application (*yugapatprasaṅga*) of both rules and the absence of a deciding factor (*vinigamakābhāva*).

As it has been said: "Or rather, there is no application [of the subsequent rule], because both possess equal force. Regarding this statement, when the subsequent [operation] has taken place, if the cause for the preceding one also exists, then that too occurs; as in the case of *hindhakī*, where even after *hi* has been substituted for *dhi* due to its priority, *aṭ* is inserted. This is stated as: "It is established by the recognition of recurrence (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*)."

But when the word-meaning is an individual (*vyakti*), since it is impossible for the two rules (*lakṣaṇa*) whose objects are those individuals to find their application elsewhere, they would apply alternatively like [the rules] *tavyat* and *anīyar*. To provide a restriction—that "in the case of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the subsequent rule alone should apply and not the preceding one"—this sūtra exists. Furthermore, from the formulation of this rule, it is inferred that in various instances the preceding rule was not originally intended to be applied. Thus, in the example *uhutāt tvam*, once *tātaṅ* has been substituted [for *hi*] due to its higher status (*paratva*), the substitution of *dhi* [for *hi*] by the rule *hujhalbhyaḥ* does not occur, because of the treatment as if it were the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*).

This is stated: "When two rules apply simultaneously and there is a conflict, that which is sublated remains sublated. Both of these [interpretations] are established in accordance with the observed usage (*lakṣya*). In that regard, under the view that it is a *vidhi* (an original injunction), the reading is "when *utva* or the elision of the *repha* would otherwise apply. Under the view that it is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), the particle *eva* ("only") must be supplied in the commentary (*vṛtti*) as "only this operation should take place," namely, *utvam eva*.

The meaning is that because the two rules—one for *siddha* and one for *asiddha*—possess unequal strength, the rule "in case of conflict, the latter prevails" (*vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam*) does not apply; thus, being without opposition, the substitution of *u* alone takes place. As it has been said: "When a preceding rule is treated as *asiddha*, there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), because of the absence of a subsequent [rule]. By this, the passage to be cited later—"the operation of the case-ending first, and then the substitutions of *u* and *at*"—is explained.

(144) *etattadoḥ sulopo ’kor anañsamāse hali* | 6|1|132 | [The word] *etattadoḥ*: here, the substitution of *tyadādi-ya* and the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) have not been applied, because it is a *sūtra*-formulation (*sautratvāt*).
Or, it may be due to the optional extended application (*vaikalpikātideśa*) based on the rule *‘ra-kṛti-vadanukaraṇāt’*. And thus, the usage *etad-ador* is correct even in a compound (*vṛtti*).
This [rule] was not formulated immediately after *‘hal-ṅy-ābbhyaḥ’* for the sake of brevity.

They say this is because it relies on the section concerning *saṃhitā*. He states that in the sūtra, *u* is a separate word with its sixth case ending elided: "of that *su* which belongs to *eta* and *tad*.
The meaning is: "of that *su* which expresses the number residing in the referents of *eta* and *tad*. [This refers to] *eta-tadoḥ vihitasya*.

In the interpretation [of the rule] as "of *etad* and *tad*," however, there would be no elision of the *su* suffix in examples such as *paramaiṣa dadāti* ("this one gives excellently") and *paramasa dadāti*. Furthermore, the interpretation "after *para*" is not possible, because there is no ablative case form *etattadbhyām*. Nor is it [possible to interpret it as] "an element of *etad* and *tad*."

It is indeed possible [for the suffix *su* to apply], because *su* is a suffix (*pratyaya*). Therefore, the connection based on the meaning alone is adopted. As for the justification (*liṅga*) for adopting that [meaning-based connection], it should be understood as the rule "in a compound not preceded by *na*" (*ṭhanañsamāse*). Why [is it said] "of *etad* and *tad*"? [Consider: *yo dadāti*. Why [is it said] "not after *ak*" (*akoḥ*)? [To exclude cases where the suffixes] *kāc* and *kak* are present.

The question is: "Since it is a different word, the [undesired] consequence does not arise. Regarding the example *eṣakaḥ*: the meaning is that the prohibition *akori* itself indicates the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "that which falls between two [elements] is included by the mention of those two."

(145) *so’ci lope cet pādapūraṇam* | 6|1|134| Regarding *so’ci lope*: it is stated in the *Vṛtti* that the mention of *aci* is for the sake of clarity. The form *as* is an imitation of the nominative singular of the pronoun *tad*.
He states that the genitive case is elided, saying "of this word 'sa'. Regarding the mention of the term *bahulam* (in various cases):
for this very reason, it sometimes occurs even for the purpose of completing a metrical foot (*pādapūraṇa*) without an elision, as in "sāsmā aram.
On this point, they say: those who [wish to justify forms] such as "yo ’ham ājanmaśuddhānām" for the sake of establishing them...

Those who explain the rule with restriction, stating that "the two [augment *ā* and the elision of *s*] are completed only when there is elision of *ā*," face the impossibility of eliding the *s* in examples such as *asmā ara*. For in this case, the analysis is *aḥ-asmai*.
If one attempts to justify that by appealing to the continued application of the term *bahulam* (diversely), then it would apply only to cases such as *o’ham ājanma*.
"Let it be produced in that manner; what is the use of this restriction?
Thus ends the section on the *svādi-sandhi* in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
(1529) *Ive pratikṛtau* 5.3.96.

Regarding the word *aśvaka*: some maintain that the word *aśva* refers only to an actual horse, whereas the suffix *kan* denotes a likeness in the form of a representation; thus, they claim this suffix is not *svārthika* (denotative of its own primary meaning). Others, however, hold that because of the metaphorical attribution of identity based on similarity—just as in the case of "the ox-driver" (*gaurvāhika*)—it is simply the word *aśva* itself [that conveys the meaning].

They say that [the term *pratīka*] refers to a representation (*pratikṛti*), whereas the suffix (*pratyaya*) indicates its very status as a figurative designation. What is meant by "in a representation"? For example: "The *gavaya* is like a cow.
A representation is an object fashioned from grass, leather, wood, or other materials, which is synonymous with an image (*pratimā*).
But the *gavaya* is not like this.
(1530) *Saṃjñāyāṃ ca* |5|3|97|. "If it is a collective whole" means: if the aggregate of base and suffix is a name for something resembling a horse.
(1531) *Lup* [is applied] when it is not a human being. 5.3.98. Examples:

*cañcā*, *vardhrikā*. Because of the retention of the gender of the original form (*yuktavadbhāva*) when the suffix is elided (*lupi*), the feminine gender is maintained. (1532) And [the suffix is elided] when the meaning is "means of livelihood," provided it is not merchandise. 5.3.99.

"Vāsudeva," "Śiva," and so forth—those images which, having been accepted, they wander from house to house begging for alms are referred to in this way. Those very ones are intended by the term *devalakas*, who are [also] considered beggars (*bhikṣus*). However, those [images] which are installed in temples and worshipped [therein are different].

In these cases, there is elision [of the suffix] by the subsequent sūtra. As it has been said: "In the case of images (*arcā*), objects worthy of worship, paintings, and banners, there is elision of the suffix *kan* when used in the sense of 'resembling' (*iva*), as in the case of *devapatha* and others.
Regarding "in images" (*arcāsu*), that is, in statues—of what kind? Those worthy of worship.
In those [deities] who are worshipped in houses or temples, their images are perceived through paintings and banners. An illustration regarding icons (arcā) is Śiva, Viṣṇu;
in paintings (citrakarma)—Arjuna, Duryodhana; and on banners (dhvaja)—the monkey, Garuḍa, and the lion.

Eagles, lions, sea-monsters (*makara*), and so forth appear upon the banners of kings. Regarding the term *hastikān*: it is with reference to such a subject that they recite—“Fie, fie upon that man who sells Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa for the sake of a livelihood! And fie upon him in this verse who does not know the incorrect words (*apaśabda*).”
"Fie, fie upon that scholar of futile intellect! This is the intended meaning:

since it is stated [in the rule] "in the sense of 'for sale' (paṇye)," just as one says "hastikāni" (elephant-children for sale), the actual usages such as "rāmakaṃ," "sītikāṃ," and "lakṣmaṇakam" are indeed grammatically correct.

(1533) *devapathādibhyaśca* |5|3|100|. [The suffix *kan* is applied after] "devapatha" and others. For example: "a likeness like the path of the gods" (*devapatha iva pratikṛtiḥ*) and "a form like the path of the swans" (*haṃsapatha iva prakṛtiḥ*)—such is the analytical explanation (*vigraha*).

(1534) *vaster ḍhañ* || 5.3.101 || [The suffix] *ḍhañ* is applied after the word *vasti*. Regarding *vasti*: Amarasimha states, “*astiḥ* is the two [organs] below the navel. (1535) *dravyaṃ ca bhavye* || 5.3.104 || [The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after *bhavya* to form the word] *dravya*.

The suffix *yat* is applied to the word *dru* in the sense of "fit for" (*bhavye*). The suffix *yat* is introduced after the word *dru* in the sense of "like" (*iva*), and also after a compound whose scope is that [sense of "like"].

By the word "that" (*tat*), the sense of "like," which is the subject under discussion, is indicated; thus he says, "from the scope of the sense of 'like'. [The rule] "thaḥ syāt" should be understood as applying to the sense of "like."

In the case of *ūgāññyaḥ*, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "prāgivāt" [Pāṇini 5.3.70], [the suffix *cha* is applied]. However, in examples such as *śāstrī śyāmā*, there is only one sense of *iva*; and since that sense is included within the compound itself, the suffix *cha* does not occur, because words whose meaning has already been expressed are not employed.

(1536) *samāsācca tadviṣayāt* 5.3.106. [The suffix *cha* occurs] after a compound whose object is that [i.e., the meaning of *iva*]. For example, *kākatālīya*. By this very rule (*prakṛtasūtra*), the compound is formed in the sense of "as it were" (*ivārtha*) as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Or, it is formed by *sup-supā* (P. 2.1.4). In either case, it is devoid of any specific technical designation (*viśeṣasaṃjñā*). And that—

It is precisely the domain of the suffix *cha*. Therefore, the author [of the commentary] states here that there is no independence (*svātantrya*), no connection with another qualifier (*upādhyantara-yoga*), and no etymological analysis (*vigraha*). Here, in examples such as *kākatālīya* and so forth: just as a crow arriving unexpectedly meets the falling of a palm fruit and is killed, in the same way, Devadatta is killed due to the unexpected arrival of a thief.

Thus, for the unborn one who is coming [into existence], death is like a fall into a pit of compassion; this is the meaning realized as "death similar to that. Regarding the phrase "unexpectedly arrived": it means having come about without being thought of;
the sense is that it is accidental.

(1537) Pūgāñ ñyaḥ agrāmaṇīpūrvāt | 5|3|112| The suffix *ñya* is added after a word denoting a *pūga* (a class or multitude), provided it is not preceded by the word *agrāmaṇī*. However, this does not refer to the actual form [of the word *pūga*] itself, because of the specific statement "provided it is not preceded by *agrāmaṇī*. For the word *pūrva* here signifies a constituent part. Why say "not preceded by *agrāmaṇī*"? [To exclude cases such as: *agrāmaṇīpūgaḥ*.
Those for whom Devadatta is the leader are called *devadatākaḥ*. [The suffix] *kan* is applied by the rule “*a eṣāṃ grāmaṇīḥ*”.

Here, the whole compound expresses a *pūga* (a class or guild). Regarding *lauhitadhvajya*: a group whose banner is red is *lohitadhvaja*; that very same thing is *lauhitadhvajya*. [This applies] after the suffixes *vrāta* and *cphañ*.
The distinction of a *vrāta* from a *pūga* lies in its being characterized by physical exertion (*utsedha*). *Utsedha* means bodily toil.
Regarding the form *kauñjāyanya*: the suffix *cphañ* is applied according to the rule “*gotre kuñjādibhyaḥ*” [Pāṇini 4.1.98].
(1538) Pāṇini 5.3.116: *dāmanyāditrāgartaṣaṣṭhāccchaḥ*. [This sūtra prescribes the suffix *cha* after the group beginning with *dāmani*, up to and including *trigarta* as the sixth.]

"From the six [groups] beginning with Dāmanī, with Trigarta as the sixth. This is an ablative case derived from a collective dvandva compound, meaning "from those for whom there are five internal divisions among the weapon-bearers, and the sixth division is the Trigartas.
Who are these whose sixth division is the Trigarta group?
In response to this inquiry, he says: "They say [the group] with Trigarta as the sixth.

Here, the *jānaki* group consists of the Trigarta class. Among those six beginning with Trigarta, the first and fifth—namely the words *kauṇḍoparatha* and *brāhmagupta*—end in the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule for the *śiva* group; the remaining four, however, end in the suffix *iñ*. Some, however...

They read the fifth word, *brahmagupta*, as ending in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*)—namely, *kauṇḍoparathīya*. In the plural, however, one has forms such as *kauṇḍoparathāḥ* and *dāṇḍakayaḥ*.
(Pāṇini 5.3.117: "From the group beginning with *parśu* and from the group beginning with *yaudheya*, the suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* [are applied]."

Regarding the word *pārśava*: the term *arśu* is a name for a country (*janapada*). From that, by the rule *ṭhvañ-magadha-*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to form the patronymic (*apatya*). In the plural, because it is a *tadrāja* (denoting a king), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix. Then, when there is a desire to express a collective group (*saṅgha*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied again by this very rule. Furthermore, because this *aṇ* also belongs to a *tadrāja* in the plural, there is elision of it as well.

He says this: "parśavaḥ" (the ribs). Now, one might object: let the suffix *am* be prescribed by this very rule in its own sense (*svārthe*) from the word *arśu*, which is a name for a region; however, if the suffix *aṇ* were prescribed from the word *parśu*—which denotes offspring—in the sense of a "collection," then it would not be a suffix used in its own sense.
If it is argued that [the formation] would be established [in this way], they say here: the word *parśu* alone denotes a country (*janapada*), but not when it ends in the suffix *aṇ*;

therefore, the suffix *aṇ* is not prescribed for the sake of its own meaning (*svārtha*) for a word denoting a country. Rather, after the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ* by the rules "after *vṛddha*, *vyañ*, and *magadha*" and "of a non-rājan [stem] in the plural," etc., [the form is derived].
The suffix is prescribed in its own sense (*svārthe*) precisely from the word *parśu*, which denotes many offspring; and here, the "own sense" is indeed a collection (*saṅgha*).

Nor should it be doubted that the word *parśu* does not denote a collection, because when it denotes many offspring, its denotation of a collection is necessarily established. Thus, there is no [objection].
"There is no inconsistency whatsoever. Regarding *yaudheya*: he fights (*yudhyate*), thus he is *yudh*.

From the root *yudh*, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule "for roots with *iṅ* as a penultimate vowel" (*igupadhalakṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*). [The word *yudha*] means "the offspring of *yudhā*" (*yudhāyā apatyam*). By the rule "from a base consisting of two syllables" (*dvya-caḥ*), the suffix *ḍhak* is applied.

From that form ending in *ḍhak*, when there is no intention to express a "corporation" (*saṅgha*), the suffix *añ* is applied by this [present rule]. Consequently, *yaudheya* has its acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyaudātta*).
It occurs as follows: furthermore, that which is the mark (*aṅka*) or sign (*lakṣaṇa*) of a Yaudheya is called *yaudheya*.

This is derived from the word ending in *añ* by the rule "aṅkāṅkalakṣaṇe" (Pāṇini 4.3.120). In this same way, regarding all those words such as *śaukreya* and others that end in *ḍhak* and denote the descendants of Yaudheya and so forth, both purposes are required. [The form] *yaudheyāḥ* is derived from the suffix *añ*.

[The suffix] *luk* [is applied]. It has an udātta accent on the final syllable. Nor should one fear a prohibition by the rule "a prācyabharge" etc., because that prohibition applies only to feminine forms.
(1540) After the words *abijit*, *vidabhṛt*, *śālāvat*, *śikhāvat*, *śamīvat*, and *ūrṇāvat*, the suffix *yañ* is applied [to form patronymics].

|5|3|118| Regarding "ābhijitya": from the word *ābhijita*, which ends in the suffix *aṇ*, the suffix *yañ* is applied. Similarly, from *vidabhṛt* and others, after the suffix *aṇ* has been applied, the suffix *yañ* is applied to those forms ending in it—such as *vaidabhṛta*, *śālāvata*, *śaikhāvata*, and so forth.

(1541) After *pāda* and *śata* when they begin with a numeral, the suffix *vun* is added in the sense of distribution (*vīpsā*), and there is elision [of the final phoneme]. [The rule applies] after *pāda* and *śata* when they begin with a numeral. Why "after *pāda* and *śata*"? Consider: *dvau dvau māṣau dadāti* ("He gives two māṣas each").
Why "beginning with a numeral"? Consider: *pādaṃ pādaṃ dadāti* ("He gives a quarter each"). Why "in the sense of distribution"? Consider: [an example where it does not apply].

He provides two words [to form the compound]: *anaimitikatvārtham* (for the sake of the meaning of non-contingency). That which occurs upon a cause (*nimitta*) is *naimitika*. The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule for *adhyātmādi*. Regarding the phrase *taddhitārthe* (in the sense of a secondary derivative), and *samāse* (in a compound):

although there is the repetition (*vīpsā*) of the base element (*prakṛti*) as a qualifier, nevertheless, because it is manifested by the suffix *vun*, it indeed constitutes the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhitārtha*).

The state [of the action] is as follows: "he gives" (*dadāti*). Here, the meaning of the root *dā* is merely the act of surrendering, and not extending as far as the production of ownership in another. For if it were so, it would fall under the scope of the subsequent sūtra.
Some, however, hold that the subsequent sūtra applies only when the root *vyavasṛj* is employed.

They say [the suffix *kha*] expresses the act of engaging (*pravṛti*). Because it is seen elsewhere as well, the intention is that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "he gives two māṣas," because the suffix is not prescribed there.
(Pāṇini 5.4.2) "And after the words *daṇḍa* and *vyavasarga*."

*Daṇḍavyavasarga*: *daṇḍanaṃ daṇḍaḥ* (the act of punishing is "punishment"). Here, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) because the root *daṇḍ* belongs to the *curādi* class. In this example as well, the compound is formed according to the rule "for the sake of a secondary derivative" (*taddhitārtha*). Furthermore, the feminine gender [of the compound] is due to that which is for the sake of the secondary derivative (*taddhitārtha*). Alternatively, the meaning of the primary base itself (*prakṛtyartha*) is what is "for the sake of the secondary derivative," because the suffix *vun* is used in its own inherent sense (*svārthika*). Two feet were punished.

Thus: "by Evadatta, Yajñadatta"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. Since the root *daṇḍ* is used with the non-primary object in the past passive participle (*kta*), the word *yajñadatta* takes the nominative case. However, in the cases of *dvau pādau* and *dvipadikām*, the accusative case is employed.
It has been stated among the roots that take two objects (*dvikarmaka*) that the root *daṇḍ* is for the purpose of seizing. And so:
The modern grammarians (*navyāḥ*) maintain that the referent of the action of grasping by means of two feet—such as Yajñadatta and others—is the meaning [of the word *dvipadika*].

(1543) *sthūlādibhyaḥ prakāravacane kan* (Pāṇini 5.4.3): after words beginning with *sthūla*, the suffix *kan* is applied when expressing a "manner" (*prakāra*). "Manner" (*prakāra*) refers both to a distinction (*bheda*) and to similarity (*sādṛśya*); in both cases, the suffix *kan* is applied as appropriate.

"An exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning [the suffix] *jāti*. By this, it is stated that this [suffix] also applies in the same way as that [suffix], namely to that which possesses a mode (*prakāravat*), and not to the mere mode (*prakāramātra*) itself. [The Vārttika states: "There should be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *cañcat* and *bṛhat*. That is, for *cañcat* and *bṛhat*. These two also [are included].
