The intention is that [the suffixes] should be taught only after [roots meaning] "thick" (*sthūla*) and so forth. Regarding *cañcatka*:
the root *cañcati* has the sense of "moving. Thus, *cañcatka*. Similarly, a specific kind of large object is a *bṛhatka*.
Even though it is not moving or large, a particular gem appears as if moving and as if large due to a specific radiance.
That which is observed is *cañcatkaḥ*, *bṛhatkaḥ*, and *surakaḥ*. [In these cases], the vowel is shortened by the rule *eṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92).

(1544) *anatyantagatau ktāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.4): [The suffix *kan* is added] after a word ending in the *kta* suffix when there is no complete attainment [of the action]. For example, *cchinnakam*; the meaning is "slightly cut. [This occurs] through the action expressed by the base of the *kta* suffix.
The pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) denoted by the suffix *ka* is "complete attainment" (*atyantagati*). That [pervasion] does not exist here.
(1545) *na sāmivacane* | 5.4.5 | Regarding the rule *na sāmivacane*: the term *sāmivacana* is derived through etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) as that which expresses the meaning of *sāmi*.

He says that the mention of the word *vacana* (word) is for the sake of indicating synonyms: "in the sense of a synonym for *sāmi*. Regarding *sāmikṛtam*: it is a compound with *sāmi*. Regarding *ardhakṛtam*: it is either a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) or a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*).
Regarding *prakṛtyaiva*: the meaning is "by the very word expressing *sāmi*. Regarding *jñāpayati*: this is the underlying thought—[namely, that] *na*... [the rule applies].

By the rule *sāmivacane*, there is no prohibition of the suffix *kan* (as prescribed by *ṭhanatyantagatau*), because that suffix cannot apply after words such as *sāmi*, *kṛta*, and so on; for in non-compounds (*asamāsa*) following these, the sense of "not reaching the end" (*anatyantāgati*) is already indicated by the word *sāmi* itself. Furthermore, in compounds, [the suffix *kan*] does not apply because they lack the status of ending in a *kta*-suffix. Nor is it the case that...
One might suspect that the compound possesses the status of ending in a *kta*-suffix by virtue of the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt* suffixes;

however, this is not so, because the word *sāmi* lacks the nature of a *gati* or a *kāraka*. Therefore, it is precisely the *kan* suffix used in its own sense (*svārthika*) that is prohibited. This very statement of prohibition [indicates] that there exists a *kan* suffix in its own sense in certain instances.
It indicates [the following]: (1546) *Aṣaḍakṣāśitaṅgvalaṅkarmālampuruṣādhyuttarapadāt khaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.4.7.
Regarding *aṣaḍakṣīṇa*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which six eyes (*ṣaḍakṣīṇi*) do not exist."

In this context, the word *akṣi* refers to the sense organ of hearing (*śrotrendriya*). By the rule *‘ahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ’*, the suffix *ṣac* is applied; from that form ending in *ṣac*, the suffix *kha* is added by this [present] rule. *Mantra* means *mantraṇam* (the act of deliberating). Regarding the term *āśitaṅgavīna*:
the past participle suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), based on the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) of the rule *‘āṅaḥ śiteḥ kartari’*.

From a causative (*ṇyanta*) root, the suffix *kha* is optionally used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, in both ways, the resulting meaning is "abounding in fodder" (*prabhūtayavasam*). Regarding *alaṅkarmīṇa*: the compound *alaṅkarma* (as in *alaṃpuruṣa*) is formed according to the rule "words such as *arya* [and others] are compounded with a word ending in the fourth case when they mean 'glāna' and so forth. Regarding *alaṃpuruṣīṇa*: it refers to one who is a match for others, such as a rival wrestler (*pratimalla*), and so on. [The suffix *kha* is also applied after] *īśvara*, *adhīna*, and so forth.

Thus [it is said]. It has been stated that the word *adhi* belongs to the *śauṇḍādi* group. "The suffixes beginning with *tama*" refers to those starting with "the suffix *tama* is used in the sense of excellence" (*atiśāyane tamap*). "Before *kan*" refers to before the suffix *kan* prescribed by the rule "the suffix *kan* is used in the sense of contempt. "The suffixes beginning with *ñya*" refers to those starting with "the suffix *ñya* is used after words ending in *ūṅ*, and after words preceded by *agraṇī*. "Before *vuñ*" refers to [the rules] prior to that.

"From that which is prescribed [by the rule] *ādaśataḥ saṅkhyādeḥ*"; "āmādayaḥ" refers to those beginning with *ime ti hyavyayādām*. "Before *mayaṭ*" means prior to the rule *at-prakṛta-vacane mayaṭ*. "Ending in *bṛhatī* and *jāti*"—by the word "*bṛhatī*,"...

The suffix *kan* prescribed by the rule “*ṛhatyā ācchādane*” (Pāṇini 5.1.124) is indicated here. By the word “*ātyanta*,” the suffix *cccha* prescribed by the rule “*ātyantācca*” (Pāṇini 5.2.70) is meant; furthermore, the plural number indicates that [suffixes] such as *āya* are included. For the meaning conveyed by words such as *vaiyākaraṇapāśa* and others is not expressed by the base form alone.
Since they are perceived, it is established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that they too are indeed eternal, like *tamap* and other suffixes.

Although the root form *bṛhatī* alone and the use of the mere generic term *jātyanta* were employed instead of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, this does not constitute a fault, as it was done merely to conform to the archaic style of the sacred texts (*ārṣagrantha*), even though such usage is not strictly expressive.

(1547) *vibhāṣā’ñceradikstriyām* |5|4|8|. The word *añci* optionally [takes the suffix *kha*] when it does not refer to a cardinal direction (*adiś*) and is feminine (*striyām*). Here, the prohibition applies to that which is both a cardinal direction and feminine; however, it does not apply to [the suffix *kha*] in the sense of a direction (*diśi*) or to the feminine gender itself, because of the mention of the singular number in the feminine gender (*strīliṅgaikavacana-nirdeśāt*). For example: *prācīnam*.
When the elision of the letter *a* is performed by the rule "ṭhacaḥ," the long vowel *au* is substituted. This should be inferred in similar cases further on.

Regarding the term *prācīnā brāhmaṇī*: the word *prācīnā* is derived from the sense of "moving forward" (*pra-añcatīti*), and thus this term—whether based on an action or based on place and time—is applied to a Brāhmaṇī woman.

It exists, but there is no prohibition [of the suffix] because it does not mean "in a direction. Regarding *prācīnam*: in the sense of "in the eastern direction," the suffix *it* occurs by the rule *ikśabdebhyaḥ*; then, by *ṭhañcervuṅ*, there is elision (*luk*);
and by *uktaddhitalukī*, there is elision of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.

Because *addhitaḥ* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) according to the rule “*addhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ*,” there is no expression of the feminine gender; however, when the suffix *kha* is applied, it is neuter by its very nature.
(1548) [Pāṇini 5.4.9] *Jātyantāc cha bandhuni*: [The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in *jāti* when *bandhu* follows].
Regarding the term *brāhmaṇajātīya*: like the expression *dvyeka* ("two or one"), the word *brāhmaṇa* here is primarily denotative of an abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*).
It forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the word *jāti*. The meaning is: "an individual body (*piṇḍa*) which is the substratum for the universal (*jāti*) of Brahminhood.
Regarding *brāhmaṇajātī*: it is either a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound, or a *karmadhāraya* compound formed with a word denoting an abstract state.
Regarding the phrase "the manifester of the genus" (*jāter vyañjakam*): it is called *bandhu* because the genus resides within it;

the suffix *u* is added in the sense of a locus according to the rule *ṛ-sṛ-snihi*, etc. Although the word *bandhu* also exists as a conventional synonym for *āpya* (kinsman) in the masculine gender, it is not intended here.
The intention is that [the word] *andhunī* is used in the neuter gender. The explanation of the very term *asthānena* is given as *tulyena*.
(Pāṇini 5.4.10): “When the word *sthāna* ends [a compound], the suffix *cha* is optionally applied if the sense is ‘with its counterpart’ (*sa-sthānena*).”

Regarding the term *pitṛsthānīya*: it is a specific relation of position (*sthāna*) alone; that which is commonly known as a "place" (*pada*). One whose place is like that of a father is *pitṛsthāna*; the meaning is "equal to a father. Regarding *oṣṭhasthānam*: a *sthāna* is a location (*deśa*), in the sense that things "stand" (*tiṣṭhanti*) in it. [The suffix] *-ana* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

This is for the purpose of indicating the intended meaning. Therefore, the suffix *śā* does not occur after a *tatpuruṣa* or *bahuvrīhi* compound whose constituent members have the same place of articulation (*tulyasthāna*).
(Pāṇini 5.4.13) *anugādinaṣṭhak*. [The suffix *ṭhak* is added after the word *anugādin* to form a derivative noun.]

The suffix *anugādin* is intended to illustrate the general form; however, Haradatta states that this specific form is not fit for usage by itself because the suffix *ṭhak* is compulsory [in such cases]. The suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule "after a root ending in *u*, when no genus is denoted. (Pāṇini 5.4.150).
(1551) Pāṇini 5.4.16: *visāriṇo matsye* ("After *visārin*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied when 'fish' is the meaning").

"Visāriṇaḥ": here too, the suffix *ṇini* is applied as in the previous case. Haradatta, however, maintains that the suffix *ṇini* in the rule "supyajātau" occurs only when the verbal root is not preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), provided that a noun (*sub*) is the governing word (*upapada*); it is for this very reason, he says, that *ṇini* is introduced by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in both the preceding rule and this one. That is incorrect, as [the form] "babhūvopajīvinām" [demonstrates].

Since forms such as *anuyāyivargaḥ* ("a group of followers") and "prabhāvo 'nujīvibhir avañcanīyaḥ" ("power that cannot be deceived by subordinates") require the acceptance of the suffix *ṇiC* even when a *sup*-ending word follows an upasarga, one must necessarily resort to the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

Because it would be redundant; since the term *anu* is carried over from the rule "aṇinuṇaḥ," he says: "the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied. Regarding *vaisāriṇa*: there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule "inaṇyanapatye. Regarding the word *saṅkhyāyāḥ*:
if the word *abhyāvṛtti* is understood to mean a second or subsequent occurrence, then [the example] is *ṣaṭkṛtvaḥ*.
It might be argued that there should be five occurrences in the process of manifestation; therefore, he states here the intended meaning: "repetition is birth.
(Pāṇini 5.4.17): *The suffix kṛtvasuc is added to a numeral when counting the repetition of an action.*

Regarding the phrase "many times" (*bhūrivārān*): although the word *bhūri* denotes a worldly number, it is not included here because, in the rule *ahugaṇa*, the inclusion of the word *bahu* serves as a restrictive injunction (*niyamārtha*),
meaning that if the suffix occurs after words denoting indefinite numbers, it occurs only after *bahu*.

The *Manoramā* states that the formulation of the restriction (*niyamaśarīra*) is "only for [stems ending in] *ahan* and *gaṇa*. Others, however, say it is "the formulation of the restriction is 'only for *ahan* and *gaṇa*. Haradatta maintains that because the word *vāra* denotes time as the locus for the arising of an action, the second case ending applies according to the rule "*ālādhvanaḥ*. Now, as for the word *vāra*...

If it is argued: "Since the word *bhūri* also denotes time when it is in grammatical apposition with another term denoting time, it refers to time itself; how then can there be an occasion [for this rule] here?"—to this they reply: "Even though it denotes time, because the repetition of an action (*kriyābhyāvṛtti*) is also understood, there is an occasion. What is the purpose of including the counting of repetitions (*abhyāvṛtigaṇana*)?

In cases such as "five cookings" (*pañcapākāḥ*) or "ten cookings" (*daśapākāḥ*), let there not be [the application of the suffix] when merely counting actions. For what purpose is the mention of "action" (*kriyā*)? Since repetition occurs only of an action—because it has as its object a thing yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and not of substances or qualities, which possess an already established nature (*siddha-svabhāva*)—[is the term necessary?]

If it is argued that because of the verbal expression—namely, in cases such as *punaḥ-punaḥ daṇḍaḥ* (“the stick again and again”) and *punaḥ-punaḥ sthūlaḥ* (“thick again and again”)—it is only the action (*bhavati-kriyā*) being struck that is repeated, and not the substance or the quality, we say:
not so. For the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) is necessary for the sake of what follows.

(1553) *ekasya sakṛcca* |5|4|19|. "Of a single [action], and once. The term "repetition" (*abhyāvṛtti*) does not apply here; for by the word "single," only one instance of an action is denoted, and repetition of that is impossible.

The inclusion of the term *kriyā* (action) here is necessary for the sake of the intended meaning; otherwise, since the word *eka* (one) signifies a number up to ten when applied to a thing numbered (*saṅkhyeya*), the form *eko bhuṅkte* would also occur [in the sense of a single agent]. Thus, the usage *ekaṃ bhuṅkte* would have been applicable here, just as in examples such as *sādhu pacati*.

Kaiyaṭa states that this sūtra is for the purpose of employing the word *sakṛt* [in the sense of "once"]. However, the *Kāśikā* maintains that in the case of *ekaḥ pākaḥ*, [the elision does not occur] because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). Regarding the rule *saṃyogāntasya* [sūtra 8.2.23], he says—[beginning with] *na tu*—"it is incorrect for the older grammarians to state that the *su* [case-ending] is elided by the rule *halṅyādi* [sūtra 6.1.68]. This is because of the rule *pūtisī* [sūtra 8.2.24].
Intending to show that only case endings are understood there by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), he says: "like *sic*.

(Pāṇini 5.4.20) *vibhāṣā baho’rdhā’viprakṛṣṭakāle*. [Example: *bahudhā divasasya bhuṅkte* ("He eats many times during the day"). When the status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*) is intended, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used.
They say that Haradatta’s statement— that the genitive case is applied by the rule *ṛtvo’rthaprayoge kāle’dhikaraṇe*—

is not to be respected, because it contradicts the previously established conclusion that, by the force of this governing heading (*adhikāra*), the eight sūtras have the result of precluding compound formation, and thus the example is with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*).

(1555) *tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ* || 5.4.22 || *tatprakṛta* means "that which is presented as the principal subject. Although the word *prakṛta* is conventionally used for anything merely presented, nevertheless, by virtue of the inclusion of the term *vacana*, this specific [meaning] is intended. Indeed, the inclusion of the term *vacana*...

The purpose [of the rule] is so that there may be expression and communication by means of the suffix *mayaṭ* regarding whatever is the nature of the base (*prakṛta*) in common usage. Regarding "in the first case" (*ādye*): when the base is to be expressed in the nominative case, the suffix is applied.
Because it is a suffix used in its own sense (*svārthika*), the gender and number are those of the base. Thus, even the form *apūpamayaḥ* is established.

In some places it is read thus: "The cake under discussion consists of cakes" (*apūpo ’pūpamayaḥ*). In some cases, derivative suffixes (*svārthika*) deviate from the gender and number of their base (*prakṛti*). On this view, the mention of *tat* (the word "that") would be redundant. On the second view, however, it is necessary—in order to ensure that the suffix is obtained only after a word ending in the nominative case.

Regarding the phrase "in the second [view]": in this alternative, the state of being expressed (*ucyamānatā*) and the state of being the subject under discussion (*prakṛtatā*) are qualifiers of the meaning of the base noun (*prakṛtyartha*). However, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) denoted by the suffix *lyuṭ* is the meaning of the suffix *mayaṭ*. For this very reason, there is agreement with the gender of the substantive (*viśeṣyanighnatā*). Thus he says: "the sacrifice consists of food" (*annamayo yajñaḥ*); here, "food" is that which is under discussion.
The meaning is "in this.
(1556) *samūhavacca bahuṣu* |5|4|22|. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words denoting a multitude when many individuals are meant, just as it is applied to denote a collection. Examples:
*maudakikaṃ*, *śāṣkulikam*. [In these cases, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *ṭhagācitādibhyaḥ*, but here *aṇ* is used instead because the word refers to a multitude.]
(1557) *anantāvasathetihabheṣajāññyaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.4.23. Regarding *āvasatha*: the suffix *athan* is applied by the rule *upasarge vaseḥ*. It is a collection of nipātanas (irregularly formed words).
It denotes the tradition of instruction (*upadeśa-pāramparya*), and by virtue of the specific rule, the suffix is applied directly from that which is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*).
The lexicon states: "Itihāsa is itihya; [the word] itihā is indeclinable. Regarding *bheṣaja*:

from the root *bhiṣaj* (to heal), with the suffix *yag* belonging to the *kaṇḍvādi* class, followed by the suffix *kvip*, we get *bhiṣaj*. This is "of the physicians" (*bhiṣajāṃ idam*), hence *bheṣaja*.
The vowel *e* arises precisely through this irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

(1558) *devatāntāt ātadarthye yat* |5|4|24|. [The suffix] *yat* is applied after a word ending in *devatā* when the sense is "intended for that. For example: *pitṛdevatyam*. [Analysis: *pitaraś ca tā devatāś ca* = *pitṛdevatāḥ* ("the ancestors who are the deities").
The analytical expansion (*vigraha*) is: "this is for the sake of the *pitṛdevatās*."
(1559) [Pāṇini 5.4.25: "And [the suffixes] -pād and -ardha [form a word denoting a portion].
Regarding *ardhya*: Amara states, "In the sense of price and in the rite of worship, it is called *argha*. Regarding "as previously mentioned": this means the suffixes -tṛn, -tṛc, and -naP.

The suffix *añ* is applied [after the word] *āgnīdhra-sādhāraṇa*. Thus, [we derive] *āgnīdhram*. This word *āgnīdhra* has been derived among the secondary (*śaiṣika*) suffixes by the rule "In the sense of a shelter for the *āgnīdhra*, the suffix *raṇ* is added, and it is also *bha*"; it is consequently acute-accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*). From that, the suffix *añ* is applied here in its own sense (*svārthe*). The result is that the initial syllable becomes acute-accented (*ādyudātta*). He also states another result: "in the feminine" (*striyām*).

The term *āgnīdhrī* is the headword (*viśeṣya*). That which has a common support (*samāna-dhāraṇa*) is *sādhāraṇī*. Earth and other such things have an undifferentiated relationship toward many [objects].

Due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, there is the substitution of *sa* for *samāna*. Because this falls under the section on optional rules (*vibhāṣā-prakaraṇa*), the suffix *añ* is absent.
The feminine suffix *ṭāp* [is applied], resulting in *āgnīdhrā śālā* (the Āgnīdhra hall). The ground is common (*sādhāraṇā bhūmiḥ*).

Now, one might object: "In the alternative where the suffix *añ* is absent, by the rule *samānasya sadhāraṇe*, the form would indeed be *sadhāraṇā*, but there would not be the initial *vṛddhi* [as in *sādhāraṇā*].
To this they reply: "Because of the very irregularity (*nipātana*) in the rule *sādhāraṇād añ* [Pāṇini 4.4.113], the substitution of *sadha-* for *samāna-* [is understood to apply here as well]."
Or rather, the desired conclusion is established because of the prescription of the absence [of the feminine suffix].
(1560) *devātala* 5.4.27. *devatā* means "a deity"; it ends in the feminine suffix *tal*.
(1561) *varṇe cānitye* |5|4|31|. Regarding the rule "and when the color is non-eternal": what is meant by "non-eternal"? [Answer: *lohitaṃ rudhiram* (red blood); *lohitā lākṣā* (red lac).
Here, "non-eternality" means being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of a destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) that is co-referential (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*) with itself. Precisely for this reason...

The subsequent rule, *akte*, is purposeful; for in the case of something dyed with lac and the like, because the redness persists as long as its substrate exists, it is eternal, and thus [the application of the previous rule] would not be established. Alternatively, there is a sublation of gender by the word *lohita*. As in: *lohitakaḥ*—that which is red due to anger.

In the case of *paruṣa*, immediately after that very moment, when the anger has subsided, the redness (*lauhitya*) disappears; thus, the color here is impermanent. This is so when one adopts the view that "taddhita suffixes are applied after a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt taddhitāḥ*) and the view that "an exception applies merely by the formulation of the rule for the nominal stem" (*prātipadavidhānamātreṇāpavādatvam*).

In response to the objection that the form *lohitikā* would not be possible if the suffix *kan* were applied before [the rule] "after a vowel ending in *ṭh*, the suffix *kan* is added with an anudātta accent" (Pāṇini 4.1.39), he says: (1562) *rakta* 5.4.32.
"Or there is the sublation of the gender. Here, "red" (*lohita*) is an illustration;

it includes *etikā*, *enikā*, and so forth as well. This is because the view that "taddhita suffixes follow those ending in *u*" is primary, whereas the view that "it provides scope for the suffix *ira* by being an exception" is secondary; therefore, one should rely upon the former.

Since the suffix *kan* is applied immediately after [the rule] "anudātādi" (Pāṇini 3.1.4), and because this *kan*-affix has scope in the masculine gender, it lacks the status of being an "unoccupied" (*niravakāśa*) exception; therefore, this Vārttika need not have been composed. For this very reason, the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* [in the Vārttika] is redundant, and the form is *svāmī*.
And it has been stated in the *Manoramā* and other works that [the word] is "powerful" (*prabala*); this is the general direction.

(1563) *Vinayādibhyaṣṭhak* (Pāṇini 5.4.34). Regarding the term *upāya*: the meaning is that the word *upāya* receives the suffix *ṭhak* and undergoes shortening [of its final vowel]. Here, the word *akasmāt* [is used].

In the reading, it is *dānta* and not *tānta*; therefore, there is no substitution of *kā*. [The rule] "there is elision of the *ṭi* of indeclinables (*avyaya*) before any suffix marked with *b*" applies: *ākasmikam*. (1564) *vācaḥ vyāhṛtārthāyām* 5.4.35.

The word *vāc* has been used [as a feminine]. What [is the purpose] regarding the meaning of the word *vyāhṛtā*? [Example: "Devadatta’s speech is sweet" (*madhurā vāg devadattasya*). (1565) *Aṇ* is added after a word denoting an action connected with that [speech]. Thus, *vācikam*. [As it is said: "Words derived from the sense of speech sometimes transcend their gender."
Neuter gender.

(1566) *prājñādibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 5.4.38]. "One who is wise" (*prājña*) means simply "wise. He is called *prājña* because he knows (*prajānāti*). The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*. From that, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).

*Prājñaḥ* (wise). *Pra-ajñā-iti*: by the rule *iḍḍhea*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. *Prajñānam* is *prajñā*. By the rule *ṭhātaścopasarge*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied, followed by *ṭāp*. She in whom wisdom (*prajñā*) exists is *prājñā*.
[In the masculine form] *prājñaḥ*, the suffix *ṇa* is applied by the rule *rajjāśraddhārcābhyaḥ*.

(1567) *mṛdastikan* | Pāṇini 5.4.39. The suffix *takan* is added after *mṛd*. Although [the form] would have been established by [the rule] *ratyayasthā*, the explicit pronunciation of the vowel *i* is for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*) and so that it may be heard even when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is elided. Example: *pañcabhirmṛtikābhiḥ* ("by five lumps of clay").
A cloth purchased for five earth-clods.

(1568) *sasnau* is used in the sense of praise. 5.4.40. *sasnau*. Here, immediately after the rule "in the sense of praise, the form [is used]," [the following is added]: "after *vṛka* and *jyeṣṭha*..."

In the Vedic language (chandas), it would be more appropriate to say *tiltātilau* and *mṛdaḥ sasnau*, according to the rule *ikaśca*. Nor can it be argued that the suffix *kan* in *sasnau* applies only in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*), for such an argument would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is because one might then assume that the phrase *ikaśca* implies the removal of the condition “in the sense of praise” (*praśaṃsāyām*) from the preceding rule.

It should not be said that there is a lack of evidence; for although one could have simply stated "ṛdaḥ sasnatikanaḥ," the very fact that *tikana* is mentioned separately therein serves as the proof. "Excellent earth" (*praśastā mṛd*)—Amara states: "The words *ṛt*, *mṛtikā*, *praśastā*, *mṛtsā*, *mṛtsnā*, and *bhṛtikā* [are synonyms for excellent earth]. This [suffix] is obligatory (*nitya*).
When only "mṛdi" is stated, because its excellence is not understood, the option (*vibhāṣā*) does not carry over here;
thus, this rule for "sasnuvatuḥ" is indeed obligatory (*nitya*). The sense is that it is even more so because of the inclusion of the word "anyatarasyām" in the subsequent sūtra.

(1569) 5.4.42: *bahvalpārthāc chas kārakād anyatarasyām* | [The suffix] *śas* is optionally [added] after a word denoting "many" (*bahu*) or "few" (*alpa*), provided it functions as a *kāraka*. [Examples: *bahūni* ("many") becomes *bahuśaḥ* ("in many ways/many times"), as in *bahuśo dadāti* ("he gives to many"). It should also be understood that *alpebhyaḥ* ("to few") becomes *alpaśaḥ* ("in few ways/few times"). Why [is it specified] "after a word denoting many or few"? [Counter-example: *gāṃ dadāti* ("he gives a cow").

He gives a horse. [The suffix *śas* is applied] after synonyms and specific terms because of the mention of "meaning" (*artha*). He gives many times; he gives three times. Why say "after a kāraka"? [Consider: the master of many, the master of few. [This rule applies to words expressing] much or little, provided they do not denote auspiciousness or the breaking of a vessel. Regarding the phrase "denoting auspiciousness": [The following examples illustrate the exceptions: *maṅgalaṃ dadāti* (he gives an auspicious object), *abhaṅgaṃ dadāti* (he gives a non-breaking vessel), and *lavaṃ dadāti* (he gives a small fragment).
"He gives abundantly in rites for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), and he gives sparingly in rites that are not desired.
Giving much in rites for prosperity and giving little in rites that are not desired is auspicious (*maṅgala*).
With the intention that giving in the opposite manner does not result in auspiciousness, he says: "not here" (*nehā*).

"In undesirable [circumstances]" refers to gifts given on account of fear and the like. "In those for prosperity" refers to rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) which have prosperity as their purpose. In the original manuscripts, the reading is generally *aṅgalāmaṅgalavacanam*; therein, the inclusion of the term *amaṅgala* (inauspicious) [is intended].

They say [the word] "vṛthā" [is used here]. This statement regarding auspiciousness is general (prāyika), for it is seen elsewhere as well: "With the words *apeta*, *apoḍha*, *mukta*, *patita*, and *apāttra*, [the fifth case is used] only rarely (*alpaśas*). As for the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action), it belongs to the fifth case (*pañcamī*) with respect to the action of compounding (*samāsana*), and the word *alpaśas* functions as its designator (*abhidhāyaka*).
And thus they explain: "A small fifth case [ending] is compounded," with the words "by the Teacher" as the understood supplement. (1570) *saṅkhyaikavacanācca vīpsāyām* |5|4|43|.
"Words denoting measure"—and thus, by the mention of the singular number (*ekavacana*), a single object is expressed.

The point is that, by the sense of "by which," only words denoting measure (*parimāṇa*)—which are restricted to a single meaning in a compound—are understood. Regarding the example *māṣaṃ māṣam*: when it is said "a giver of a *māṣa*," one understands that he is a giver of a mere *māṣa* [of gold or other substances], but there is no understanding that he is a giver of [many] *māṣas*.
This restriction regarding the unity of meaning applies to *vṛta* and so forth; the same applies to *prastha* and others as well. However, words such as *ghaṭa* (pot) are not like this.
For when one says "the giver of pots" (*ghaṭadātā*), the meaning "the giver of [many] pots" is also perceived.
It is for this very reason that he provides a counter-example: *ghaṭaṃ ghaṭam*. Words such as *ghaṭa*...

For genus-words do not denote multiple objects, because the connection with a genus is common to both the one and the many; rather, they take on the number of unity through non-differentiation. And all of this...

This has been stated according to the opinion of Jayāditya. According to the view of Vāmana, however, it occurs even after words denoting genus (*jāti*). Thus, he stated in the rule *aśśaso 'r* (Pāṇini 1.1.14): "Because of the mention of *śas* as accompanied by *jas*, [the substitution] does not occur here: *kuṇḍaśo dadāti*, *vanaśaḥ*."

Regarding the statement "it enters," this is his intention: even if the word *jāti* (genus) has a single meaning through context or other factors when it undergoes *vṛtti*, then the suffix *śas* indeed occurs after it as well. Now, if it is asked: "How can there be the simultaneous use of both the dual (*dvirvacana*) and the suffix *śas* in the expression 'each one individually connected with the ancestors' (*ekaikaśaḥ pitṛsaṃyuktān*)? [The answer follows].

"‘The seers compose [their verses] according to the meters,’ so says Haradatta. For this very reason, it was stated in the *Manoramā* that the passage of the ancients in the rule for *upaḥ*, namely ‘one by one (*ekaikaśaḥ*)’, is erroneous.
In reality, however, *ekaikaśaḥ* is simply *ekaikam* with the suffix *śas* added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), and not [in the sense of distribution]."

Regarding distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), we shall explain under the sūtra *ānyekavacane* (Pāṇini 5.4.43) that the Bhāṣya states: "having given one tawny cow (*kapilā*) one by one (*ekaikaśaḥ*) a thousand times. As for the example "he gives two":
how then [is it explained] in the case of the verse: "Of those who are without vows, without mantras, living merely by their caste, even by the thousands..."?

Regarding the statement, "For those who have assembled, the status of being a *pariṣad* (an assembly) does not exist," if it is argued that there is neither repetition (*vīpsā*) nor the status of being an agent (*kārakatva*) here, they reply: the meaning is that even for those who have assembled in groups of a thousand, the status of being a *pariṣad* does not exist. Thus, there is both agency with respect to the act of assembling and repetition.
"Castyeva" (it is as if cast). By this, the statement "each [word] should receive the designations such as singular and so forth" is explained;

for the meaning of the word *eka* functions as the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to the action of existence (*asti*). Regarding "kṛṣṇataḥ pratīti": since "prati" is designated as a *karmapravacanīya* by the rule "prati is used in the sense of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) or an exchange (*pratidāna*")..."

In the phrase “*ratinidhipratidāne ca yasmāt*,” the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used. There is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) [of the rule] for words beginning with *ādi*. Regarding the mention of "words beginning with *ādi*," the evidence (*liṅga*) for this is the rule: "*yādita udātamarddhahrasvam*" (Pāṇini 6.1.203).

(1571) *apādāne cā’hīyarūhoḥ* |5|4|45|. [The suffix *pañcamī*] is also used after a word denoting the *apādāna* (ablative case) when used with the roots *hī* (to abandon) and *ruh* (to rise), except for the forms *ahīya* and *arūha*. For example: *grāmata āhīyate* ("he departs from the village"). Similarly, one should understand examples such as *adhyayanāt parājayate* ("he fails because of his studies") and *adhyayanataḥ* ("from study"), etc. (1572) *atigrahā’vyathanakṣepeṣvakartari tṛtīyāyāḥ* |5|4|46|. [The suffix *pañcamī* is used] after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) when it signifies "exceeding" (*atigraha*), "not causing pain" (*avyathana*), or "reproach" (*kṣepa*), provided that the word does not denote the agent (*akarta*).

"Is grasped excessively" (*atigṛhyate*) means that it is grasped by people through the transgression of others. He states the result: "it exists without transgressing others. (1573) *rogāccāpanayane* (Pāṇini 5.4.49).

Regarding the term *pravāhikātaḥ*: "Make [him] free from vomiting" (*praccchardikātaḥ kuru*) and so forth are also examples. *Pravāhikā* is dysentery (*viṣūcikā*); *praccchardikā*, however, is the disease of vomiting.
(1574) *Cvi* is added after a word ending in the first case when it is joined with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*, provided that the word is not the agent of the action of becoming (*saṃpadyakartṛ*).
[The rule] "in connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*"—what is meant by "in connection with"? Example: *aśuklaḥ śuklo jāyate* ("that which was not white becomes white").

(1575) *asya cvau* 7.4.32. [The rule] "when the agent is that which becomes" (*sampadyakartari*). The analysis of the compound is: "that which is both *sampadya* (becoming) and the *kartṛ* (agent). [The roots included are: *āghrā*, *ādhmā*, *dheṭ*, and *dṛś*.

The suffix *śa*, prescribed by the rule "śaḥ," also occurs after the root *sampad* due to this very nipātana (irregularity). Haradatta maintains that it is formed with the suffix *śyan* because [the root] belongs to the *divādi* class. Regarding the statement "it should be stated" (*vaktavyam*), the author of the Vṛtti inserted it into the middle of the sūtra "abhūtatadbhāve. [The other view is rejected] because it is erroneous.

It should be stated that the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) does not occur before the suffix *cv-*; this is because it ends in *cv-*. The reason for this is that, being a particle (*nipāta*), it is included under the rule "particles such as *vā* are indeclinables" (*vā-ādi-nipātam avyayam*). (Pāṇini 6.4.152) *kyac-vyoś-ca*.

Regarding the form *gārgībhavati*: here, when the suffix *sup* follows a word ending in *yañ*, and the suffix *cvī* is subsequently applied, the elision of *y* (by the rule *apatyasya ca taddhite ’nāti*) does not take place; this should be understood as being because of the intervention of the vowel *ī*.

(1577) *arurmanaścakṣuścetorahorajasāṃ lopaśca* |5|4|51|. [The forms] *aru*, *manas*, *cakṣus*, *cetas*, *rahas*, and *rajas* [are formed by the elision of the suffix *cvin*]. This is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of *cvin* even though it was already established by the preceding rule; however, the elision (*lopa*) is taught for the sake of its being conditioned by that very [suffix].
(1578) *vibhāṣā sāti kārtsnye* |5|4|52|.

"Vibhāṣā sāti": it is called *vibhāṣā* because it is "optionally stated" (*vibhāṣyate*), that is, it is subject to alternative application. The suffix *a* is added by the rule *urośca halaḥ*, and then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied. However, this [term *vibhāṣā*] is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

Because we see the case-ending in examples such as *vayor vibhāṣayor madhye* ("in the middle of the two optional cases") and *payasas tu vibhāṣayā* ("but optionally from *payas*"). Regarding the word *kṛtsnam*: it means "endowed with all its constituent parts.
(Pāṇini 5.4.53) *abhividhau saṃpadā ca*. (And [the suffix *kvip* is used] after the root *sam-pad* when expressing inclusion).
"The weapon becomes consumed by fire" (*agnisādbhavati śastram*). The singular number is used for the genus; the meaning is "all weapons.
(1580) [The suffix *ṭāc* is applied] diversely after the words *deva*, *manuṣya*, *puruṣa*, *puru*, and *martya*, when they are in the second or seventh case.

"I salute the gods"—*devān vande*, *devatrā vande*; "I delight among the gods"—*deveṣu rame*, *devatrā rame*. This is the final meaning established here. Likewise, "he goes among men"—*manuṣyān gacchati*, *manuṣyatrā*.
He goes; he dwells among men. He goes to men—*purutrā* here means "he goes. He dwells among men—*purutrā* here means "he dwells. The word *uru* is a synonym for "many.
He goes to many, or he dwells among many, [expressed as] *purutrā*. [He goes to] mortals, [or dwells] among mortals.
Or—*martyatrā*.

When *ḍāc* is intended to be applied, the doubling [of the word] occurs diversely (*bahulam*). Regarding the phrase "when *ḍāc* is intended": if it were a locative case (referring to the suffix *ḍāc*), there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). For only when *ḍāc* has been applied and the doubling has occurred does the condition of having two syllables as the minimum constituent part (*dvyajavarārdhatā*) obtain.
And when that [suffix] is present, the sense is "ḍāc. It should be stated that [the suffix] ḍāc is always applied when there is a reduplication (āmreḍita): *kharāṭkharāṭ karoti*.

The doubling of the word and the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occur as previously explained. If, however, the rule "from a stem consisting of two or more syllables" (*dvyañjavarārdhāt*) were not stated, the suffix ḍāc would not apply here.
For here [the word] does not have two syllables (*ardha-vyañjana*), but rather three; that is to say, it is simply *anekāc* (having more than one vowel).
The meaning is that one should remove [the condition] "having at least two morae as its second half" (*dvyañ-javarārdhāt*). As for *paṭiti*:

the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs by the rule "for an unmanifest imitation-sound, when followed by *itaḥ*. But surely, in this case, connection with the verb *karoti* is difficult to obtain because of the word *iti*.
If it is argued that [the term] "anitya" (non-eternal) is redundant because of the intervention [of the suffix], they reply:

by the word *iti*, only the specific manner (*prakāra*) inherent in the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is referred to—namely, "he acts in this very manner. And thus, through its meaning, the word *paṭat* [is connected].
"The yoga [of the suffix] certainly exists.

(1581) *kṛño dvitīyatṛtīyaśambabījātkṛṣau* (Pāṇini 5.4.58). [The word *saha*] is connected with *bījena*. Now, in the plowing of the ground together with the seed (*bījena saha*), there is also [the plowing] of the seeds themselves.

If it is argued that the intended meaning is not established because of the context of plowing (*karṣaṇa*), they say in response: in the domain of verbal function (*vṛtti*), the word "seed" (*bīja*) refers to the act of plowing accompanied by the sowing of seeds. Thus, the meaning is "he performs the act of plowing accompanied by the sowing of seeds."

(1582) *samayācca yāpanāyām* |5|4|60|. [The word] *samā* [is also used]. The meaning is "he passes the time. Taking up the commentary (*vṛtti*) which states: "The arrival of the opportunity for what is to be done is *samaya*; the transgression of that is *yāpanā*," Haradatta [explains it as follows].
He said: "He who says, 'Today is my time for crossing over; tomorrow or the day after is the time for this,' regarding many days, is spoken of in this way.
(1583) *sapatra-niṣpatrāt ativyathane* | 5|4|61| [The suffix *ṇamul* is added after *sapattram* and *niṣpattram* when meaning 'to cause excessive pain'].

Regarding *sapatra-niṣpatrāt*: it is called *pātra* because arrows fall upon the target by means of it; *pātra* refers to the feathers attached to the nock of the arrows. One makes [the target] "with feathers" (*sapatra*) or "without feathers" (*niṣpatra*). The meaning, as far as possible, is that which is accompanied by or devoid of those feathers (*patra*), that is, the leaves.

(1584) *Niṣkulāt* [the suffix *ṇic* is applied] after the word *niṣkula* when the sense is "extracting" (*niṣkoṣaṇa*). *Niṣkoṣaṇam* means the drawing out of internal parts to the exterior. Why "when the sense is extracting"? [Observe: *niṣkulaṃ karoti śatrum* ("he makes the enemy rootless").

After *śūla*, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] when cooking is meant. What is the purpose of saying "when cooking"? [Example: *śūlaṃ karoti kadannam* ("he prepares bad food on a spit"). Here, *śūla* means a stomach ailment. (1586) *satyād aśapathe* |5|4|66|. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *satya*] except when it refers to an oath.
The word *satya* is used in the sense of "truth" and "an oath. It is derived from the root *as* (to be) with the suffix *tyap*, meaning "that which is good (*sādhu*) among the virtuous (*satsu*).

Regarding the rule "the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of 'good in this,'" although *yat* would have been expected here according to the *prāg-dhita* group, the suffix *ya* is used instead due to this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*). This word is udātta-accented on the final syllable;
this is seen, for instance, in the passage "Truth (*satyam*) and Righteousness (*ṛtam*)," where it is stated that "the suffix *ya* is applied after the root *as* in the sense of abundance."

"He makes it true" means: [regarding] the "merchandise"—the collection of goods such as jewels and so forth—"to be purchased" means that he makes it firm through examination and the like with the thought, "This very thing must be accepted," and by the payment of the price for the seal of authenticity (*satyaṅkāra*). "Tathyam" (true) means: it is exactly as it is; [according to Pāṇini 5.4.78: "from *ādṛc* and *dṛgh*... [the suffix *yat* is applied].
And because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned, the suffix *yat* is applied in its own meaning [to form *sva*].
(1587) *madrāt parivāpaṇe* |5|4|67|. Regarding the word *parivāpaṇa*: it is derived from the root *vap*, which signifies the mere activity of an agent, by adding the causal suffix *ṇic*.
Haradatta says that the suffix *lyuṭ* [is used here]. The "activity of the object" (*karmavyāpāraḥ*) is the result (*phalam*), because that [result] resides in the object (*karmaniṣṭhatvāt*).
Thus, they say the meaning is "that which expresses the mere result," as in the word *phalita*.
Regarding the phrase "by the auspicious tonsure," this refers to the *caula*, initiation rites (*dīkṣā*), and so forth.

"And it should be stated [that the suffix applies] after *bhadra*. Regarding the explanation that "after *bhadra*" is a reference to the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*), it should be understood that [the suffix] would also apply after words such as *maṅgala*.
Thus ends the section on secondary nominal derivatives (*taddhita-prakriyā*) in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
Now, the roots beginning with *tan* [are treated]:

(330) *tanādibhyas tathāsoḥ* | Pāṇini 2.4.79. [Examples: *ataniṣṭa*, *atāniṣṭa*. By the rule *asthasthamipām*, there is the substitution of *ta* for the suffixes *tha*, *tha*, and *mi*. From *ataḥ*...

Or, there is *vṛddhi* by the rule "halādeḥ. Regarding *atatat*: by the rule "anādibhyas tathāsoḥ," there is elision of the *sic* suffix and the elision of the nasal. Regarding *ataniṣṭa*: in the alternative where elision does not occur, there is the augment *iṭ*. The root *ṣaṇu* means "to give"; this [root] ends in *n*, and the *ṇ* is merely technical (*lākṣaṇika*). Therefore, in the *yaṅ*-luṅ elision, [the form] is *aṃsanti*.

In examples such as *saṃsantaḥ*, the anusvāra and its corresponding *parasavarṇa* [nasal] occur. The roots *kṣaṇu* (in the sense of harming) and *kṣiṇu* also possess these two [Lakṣa and Kaṇaka] affixes; therefore, in forms such as *caṅkṣanti* and *cekṣeti*, the anusvāra and its corresponding *parasavarṇa* occur.

(331) And regarding [the rule] *ye ca* 6.4.109, which states "there is elision of *sic*": it should not be argued that on this view, by the application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle, there would be *guṇa* substitution in *akṛta*, because that is prohibited by the fact that *sic* is marked with the *k* indicatory letter (*kit*) in the rule *uśca*.

Setting aside the reading found in the *vṛtti*, "aṃparyupebhyaḥ," he says "saṃparibhyām" in accordance with the *bhāṣya* and the *vārttika*. Thus ends the section on the *tanādi* roots. To the question "Why is there no *iṭ*? he replies with "ṛtaśca," etc.
Thus ends the section on the *tanādi* roots in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
(597) "And the *dvigu* [compound]. By the force of the word "and" (*ca*), there is a co-occurrence of two technical designations (*saṃjñā*). And thus, for the *dvigu* and the *tatpuruṣa*...

It should not be suspected that there would be synonymy [between the two designations]. For, by dividing the *yoga*, assigning the designation of *tatpuruṣa* to complete the number [of compounds], and subsequently prescribing the designation of *dvigu*, synonymy is established even without the recitation of the particle *ca*. Nor [does it mean] "that which has two others... [as a bahuvrīhi].

One might suspect an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) here regarding the word *yavanya*; however, this is avoided by following the rule *addhitārthottarapade* and interpreting it as: "In the case of *addhitārtha*, that which was stated there [as being threefold] applies when preceded by a numeral. He states the result of the *dvigu* being a *tatpuruṣa* compound: "the suffix of the compound" (*samāsānta*).

The meaning is "ṭac and ac. Regarding the example with *ac*, it should be understood that in the case of *tatpuruṣataṭsyāṅguleḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.89], when *ac* follows, the form is *dvyaṅgulam*. As for *pañcarājam*: in a *samāhāra-dvigu* compound, the suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule *ājahaḥsakhibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.91]. This [suffix] is indeed an internal constituent (*anta-avayava*) of the compound itself.

Because the final member of the compound does not end in the letter *a*, there is an absence of feminine gender. However, it should be understood that according to the view that "compound-endings are those at the end of the final member for the sake of the compound," even though the final member ends in *a*, the feminine suffix is not applied because it belongs to the *pātra* group. In the *Kāśikā*, however, *pañcarājī* is cited as an example. This...

Haradatta maintains that this is merely a sporadic corruption of the text. On this point, some say that since there is no evidence for classifying [the word *pañca*] as belonging to the *pātrādi* group, the example cited in the *Kāśikā*, namely *pañcarājī*, is also entirely correct.
(598) Pāṇini 2.1.24: A noun in the second case is compounded with *śrita*, *atīta*, *patita*, *gata*, *atyasta*, *prāpta*, and *āpanna*.

The second [case] is that which depends on what has passed; since words such as *śrita* (resorted to) express a specific state of transition (*gati*), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule “*atyarthakarmaka*” (Pāṇini 3.4.72). With the intention that "when a suffix is mentioned, that which ends in it is also included," he says: "ending in the second case."

Regarding the phrase "by those whose base-forms [prakṛti] begin with *śrita*": although it is possible for the status of being a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) to apply to the vocative, nevertheless, since the formation of a compound is desired even in other cases, the meaning is that here the words *śrita* and so forth are understood as being used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for the entire aggregate that contains them. Similarly, [the rules] "after *dṛś*, when expressing censure" and "the suffix *ya* after *arga* and others" [apply].

This should also be inferred for *ñi* and other such suffixes. For it is not possible for *khaṭvā* to end in the accusative case, nor is it possible for *garga* and others to end in the genitive case. It might be argued: if there were a compound of an accusative-ending word with a *subanta* (inflected nominal) whose base is *śrita*, then forms such as *kāṣṭhaśriteya* would not be established.

From the word *śrita* with the suffix *ṭāp*, followed by a case-ending (*sup*), we have *kaṣṭa-śritā*. In the compound *kaṣṭaśritā*, because the word *śritā* itself ends in *ṭāp*, the suffix *ḍhak* would apply according to the rule *strībhyaḥ ḍhak*, resulting in *kāṣṭaśraiteya*. This is because of the rule *atikārakopapadānām*, which prescribes the elision of the case-ending (*sub*) [before the secondary suffix].

If it is argued that when there is a compound with a prior member ending in a kṛt-affix, the desired form is established because the word ending in *śrita* has a feminine suffix ending in *ṭā*, this is not so. For, since the rule regarding the initial element of a compound does not apply when the feminine suffix is primary (*pradhāna*), the form *kāṣṭhaśritā* would be unavoidable. Nor can it be claimed that [the form] could ever arise from the word *śritā* alone.

It should be stated that [the suffix] *ḍhaka* does not apply after [a word ending in] *ad*. For, in the case of a *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) function, the word *śrita* is devoid of meaning, and thus a connection with a descendant (*apatya*) is impossible. Even in the case of an *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning) function, there is no fault; for when both the whole and its parts are present, it is the whole alone [that is understood].

Because it is that which necessitates the grammatical operation; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of forming *saundaradauhitra* from *sundarasya duhituḥ apatyam*. This is the general direction [of the argument]. In the case of *kṛṣṇaṃ śritaḥ*, the genitive case is prohibited by the rule *a loka-*.
In the case of *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ*, the word ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) is placed first according to the rule *rathamanirdiṣṭam*.

Although the word *śrita* is also indicated by the nominative case here, there is no over-extension [of the term *upasarjana*], because it has been stated that "in the rule prescribing a compound, that which is indicated by the nominative is the *upasarjana*.

Now, one might object: if this is so, then for the purpose of assigning the technical designation *upasarjana* to items such as indeclinables (*avyaya*), [the sūtra] *avyayaṃ vibhakti-* etc. must apply...
Since the formulation of the rules for compound formation is necessary, if the rule *upapadamaninā* (P.

2.2.19) were not mandatory, the previously mentioned indicator (*jñāpaka*) would be impossible; thus, in the alternative view where compounds such as *avyayībhāva* and *tatpuruṣa* do not exist, [the rule] *upapadamatiṅ* (P. 2.2.19) [would apply].

If it is argued that by the operation of the rule for compound formation (*samāsa*), analytical sentences (*vigrahavākya*) such as *ṭhapa viṣṇoḥ*, *ṭhapari viṣṇoḥ*, *ṛṣṇaṃ śritaḥ*, and *rājñaḥ puruṣa* would not be established, they reply: the restatement of the rule for compound formation is not solely for the purpose of the technical designation *upasarjana*; for that [designation] can be achieved by another means as well.
This is established as follows: immediately after the rule "prākkaḍārātsamāsaḥ" (P.

2.1.3), having recited "rathamānirdiṣṭamupasarjanam" (P. 1.2.43) and "ekavibhakti cāpūrvanipāte" (P. 1.2.44), [the definition] "prathamānirdiṣṭam" is stated within the governing context of compound formation (samāsādhikāra).

In the commentary, the designation *upasarjana* is indeed established: "If an indeclinable (*avyaya*) containing the suffix *taṭ* [denoting] the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), and so forth, is compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), that compound shall be an *avyayībhāva*;
however, if it ends in the second case (*dvitīyā*), that compound shall be a *tatpuruṣa*."

Thus, since the designations such as *avyayībhāva* and *tatpuruṣa* are established through this very explanation, the separate prescription of the compound (*samāsa*) would be redundant; therefore, that [redundancy] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). But one might object: "This point you have stated would hold true only if rules such as 'an indeclinable [compounds with] case-endings' (*avyayaṃ vibhakti-*) were established as prescriptive of compounds (*samāsa-vidhāyaka*); what is the proof for that very fact?"

If it is argued, "We do not see [this]," some say: since the designation *upasarjana* is already established by the aforementioned method, the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in the rule *prathamānirdiṣṭam* would otherwise be redundant; therefore, it serves to obtain the meaning "that which is designated as the first member in a rule prescribing a compound. By that [mention], for these [words]...

Thus, its status as a rule prescribing compounds is established. Alternatively, the very text of the *Ākara* (the *Mahābhāṣya*) is the authority for the non-obligatory nature of the compound "upapada-supa"; otherwise, in the Vārttika "in the case of an *it* affix and obligatory compounds," the inclusion of the word "iti" would be purposeless, as this [case] would also be established [by the rule].

Otherwise, there would arise an inconsistency with the previously cited passage from the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* beginning with "Is it a horse? Is it not a horse? This is the general direction [of the argument]. Now, one might object:
the meaning of "one who has resorted to Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇa-śritaḥ*) is indeed "the agent of the act of resorting whose object is Kṛṣṇa," and that Kṛṣṇa is what is resorted to (*śrita*).

[Objection: Since [the word] *yena* is easily formed as a *bahuvrīhi* with a past passive participle (*ktānta*) in the objective case, what is the purpose of this specific composition of a compound? [Response: Do not say so; for in a *bahuvrīhi*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the word ending in a past passive participle being placed first, according to the rule "śrita-kṛta... (Pāṇini 2.2.37). Furthermore, [in our analysis] the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) applies by the rule "eṣādvibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 5.4.108).

"...it would follow that *kṛt* [would apply]," such is the direction [of the argument]. Regarding the word *duḥkhātīti*: the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *iṇ* preceded by *ati* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
The remaining examples are also to be inferred. For instance, *kūpapatitaḥ*.
Although [the rule] "after *an*, *pat*, and *daridra*, [the suffix *iṭ* is] optional" makes *iṭ* optional, [the form is established] because of [the rule] "of that which... (*yasya*).

It should be argued that there ought to be a prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule "vibhāṣe'tīṇ" (Pāṇini 7.2.5), yet they say that *iṭ* occurs here due to this very irregularity (*nipātana*). In reality, however, *patitaḥ* is established by resorting to the root 'ata gatau vā' (meaning "to go optionally") listed among the roots ending in short *a* in the *curādi* class; for in the rule "vibhāṣe'tīṇ," the term *ekāc* refers to such a root.
Because this [usage] is universally accepted as a continuous occurrence (anuvṛtti): *grāmagataḥ* ("gone to the village"), *tuhinātyastaḥ* ("passed beyond the frost").
*Atyāsaḥ* means "transgression"; since that too is simply a specific kind of motion (*gativiśeṣa*), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).

Alternatively, one should accept here the *kta* suffix in the sense of the commencement of an action (*ādikarmaṇi*). Examples: *sukhaprāptaḥ* ("attained happiness"), *duḥkhāpannaḥ* ("fallen into suffering").

There is an extension of the rule to include words such as *gamyā* ("to be gone to"). Regarding the phrase "of *gamyā* and so on": words beginning with *gamyā* are to be understood from actual usage. For example, in *grāmagamī* ("one who goes to the village"): the suffix *ini* is added according to the Uṇādi rule *ameḥ iniḥ*.

And that [suffix] occurs in the future tense, according to the rule *haviṣyati gamyādayaḥ*. Because of the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *ṭhakeno'r*, it is used in the sense of the object (accusative).

The second [case ending] is [not applied]. Because of unfitness; the meaning is that since the word *svayam*—which signifies "by oneself" (*ātmanā*)—functions as the agent (*kartṛ*), it is impossible for it to take a second case ending (*dvitīyā*).
(599) *svayaṃ ktena* | 2|1|25|.
Regarding *svāyaṃkṛti*: the intention is that if the compound were not formed, it would have to be *kārti*.
(600) *Khaṭvā* [is used] in the sense of reproach (*kṣepe*). Regarding *khaṭvārūḍha*: Amara states, "An *ālma* is one who acts without reflection. *Vedaṃ vratāni*...

Furthermore, it is indeed prescribed that one who has completed his studies and returned home may ascend a couch; however, he who, even while still in the state of studenthood (*brahmacarya*), ascends a couch, though he be worthy of sleeping on the ground, is a fool (*jālma*). This word is well-established in usage.
Therefore, let him ascend a couch, not a *taṭvā* (a bedstead), for everyone who is intent upon performing what is forbidden is a fool.
He is called "one who has mounted the couch" (*khaṭvārūḍha*). For this very reason, he says: "perpetually" (*nitya*).
(601) *Sāmi* | 2|1|27|. *Sāmi*: this indeclinable is a synonym for the word *ardha* (half).

(602) *kālāḥ* |2|1|28|. The term *kālāḥ* [is used] in the plural to exclude its own grammatical form (*svarūpa*). The meaning of the sūtra is: "Words denoting time (*kāla*), ending in the accusative case, optionally form a compound with a word ending in the suffix *kta*. Now, [one might object]: "The word *kāla*..."

One might argue that it should simply be stated as *atyantasaṃyoge* (in the sense of absolute connection), and that the mention of the word *ktena* (with a past passive participle) should be omitted; thus, there would be no need for the formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). To this, he says: *anatyanta-* (not absolute). In the example *māsapramitaḥ*, the prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of measure (*māne*), and the suffix *kta* denotes the agent (*kartari*) in the sense of an initial action (*ādikarman*). Here, there is no absolute connection between the moon and the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*).

(603) And [the accusative case is used] to express continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). As in the example *muhūrtam* ("for a moment"): the meaning is "extending over a moment. The second case ending is applied by the rule *ālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge*.

(604) *Tṛtīyā tatkṛtārthena guṇavacanena* || 2.1.30 || [The word] *tṛtīyā* [is understood as] "having the suffix elided" (*lupta*), because it is a sūtra-formulation; this is the intended meaning. By the word *tat*, which refers back to that which ends in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*), its meaning (*tadartha*) is indicated. And [the compound denotes] the state of being produced by that meaning.

The qualifier [of the word] denoting a quality is by way of its meaning—that is, by means of the expression of that quality which is produced by the meaning of the third-case ending. He explains this with the words beginning "the meaning of the third-case ending" and so forth. And by the word "meaning" (artha), the sense is that even that [meaning] is an independent cause. Now, [one might object]: "By the meaning... [and so on].

Since a compound is impossible [in this context], the word expressing that [quality] will be understood; what is the purpose of including the term *vacana* here? To this they reply: "One who has spoken of a quality (*guṇam uktavān*) is a 'quality-expresser' (*guṇavacana*). According to the rule *ṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) with reference to the past action. Thus, one who, having spoken of a quality, has also spoken of a substance (*dravya*) is a "quality-expresser" (*guṇavacana*). By that [definition],...

In the expression "pāṭavaṃ ghṛtena" (sharpness by means of clarified butter), no compound occurs with the word [ghṛta] because it denotes merely a quality (*guṇamātra*). Here, "quality" is understood according to the definition: "that which enters into a substance and departs from it," and so forth; it is not the primary cause of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), because that [definition] is impossible in the case of the latter. [The example continues: *śaṅkulayā*...

Regarding the word *khaṇḍa*: here the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). Derived from the root *khaḍi* (meaning "to split") with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), the word *khaṇḍa* first denotes a quality (*guṇa*) that has taken the form of an action;

subsequently, by means of a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the possessive sense (*matvartha*), it comes to denote the substance (*dravya*) possessing that quality, and thus it becomes a "quality-denoting word" (*guṇavacana*).

Regarding the word *dhānyena*: the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). *Artha* means that which is sought—namely, a purpose; [it is derived] from the root *artha-* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). Alternatively, *artha* means seeking or desire; [it is derived] from the root *artha-* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). However, if the word *artha* is taken in its conventional sense (wealth), then in the expression *dhānyena*, the third case is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*). This is established by the rule: "The agent and the instrument [are expressed by the third case] when followed by a primary derivative (*kṛt*)."

Question: The other [author], with the intention that this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction—namely, that [the agent] is only one by whom the action was performed through an instrument—offers a counter-example, saying "by the eye" (akṣṇā). The sense is that blindness is not caused by the eye itself, but rather by karma and so forth. However, the instrumental case here [is used]...
By the rule "ṭyaṅgavikāraḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.36), [the suffix -matup is applied]. Regarding the word *kāṇa*: it is derived from the root *aṇ* in the sense of "closing the eyes," with the suffix *ghañ*.
That this is a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) should be understood for this word as well, just as it is for the word *khaṇḍa* according to the previously stated method.
Why specify "by a word expressing a quality"? [Consider: *gobhir vapāvān* ("fleshy because of cows").

By eating curds and other items related to a cow, Devadatta acquires fatness; thus there is "being produced by that" (*tatkṛtatva*), yet this [word *vapāvat*] is not a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*).

(605) [The suffix *kha* is applied after a word ending in the sixth case when it is construed with] *pūrva*, *sadṛśa*, *sama*, *artha*, *kalaha*, *miṣa*, *nuṣa*, *miśra*, and *ślakṣṇa*. (Pāṇini 2.1.31)

"Similar to the former" (*pūrvasadṛśa*). Here, in connection with *sama* and *sadṛśa*, the third case ending is applied by the rule "with words having the sense of *kalpa*" (*ulyārthaiḥ*). However, in connection with other words, the third case ending is applied either by this very statement or by the rule "in the sense of cause" (*hetau*). In this context, the mention of *sadṛśa* is redundant, because the meaning is already established by means of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Nor [is it redundant] in the case of a tatpuruṣa...

It should be stated that this [sūtra] is for the purpose of preserving the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member in the case of the third case ending used in the sense of equality (as in *tulyārthe tṛtīyā*).

This is established in the *Manoramā*, on the grounds that the desired result is achieved by the rule *adṛśapratirūpayoḥ sādṛśye*. [This is necessary] for the sake of producing a cognition in which the relation of being a cause (*hetutva*) is the mode (*prakāra*) in instances such as *vidyayā sadṛśaḥ* ("equal in learning").

Others maintain that the third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) is also necessary. Still others hold that since it is already established by the preceding rule, the third-case compound is also proven. Regarding the term *ūnārtha* ("having the sense of 'deficient'"):
because the word *artha* was used in the preceding rule to denote the compound itself, its mention here refers to the meaning (*abhidheya*).
The word *ta.* (the affix *tasil*) is connected only with the word *ūna*, and not with *pūrva* and the others; the intention is that this is because *sama* and *sadṛśa* are mentioned separately.
Regarding the addition of *avara*: as for the phrase "of *avara*," the commentators explain here that it is simply [to be understood] as "having the sense of *ūna*."
Because this [meaning] is established, it is indeed easy to abandon. Nor should it be argued that the meaninglessness of the word *avara* is unattested;

for its attestation is found in the Vedic text, "Seventeen at least (*saptadaśāvarāḥ*) should sit for the sacrificial session (*satram*)," and in the rule, "From an imitation of an indistinct sound, provided it consists of two or more syllables and has fewer than half [of those syllables as consonants]."

(606) *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* |2|1|32|. [The sūtra states] *kartṛkaraṇe*. With the intention that this is a locative case derived from a collective dvandva compound, he says: "in the agent (*kartṛ*) and in the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Regarding this, some [maintain]: the dual nominative *kartṛkaraṇe* is qualified by the third case [ending].

They say that because of the inclusion of the term *viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier), there is an application of the rule *tadanta-vidhi* (extension to what ends with that); thus, another interpretation is that a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*)—denoting either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*)—is compounded with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. Regarding the phrase *sarvopādhi*: even that which ends in the third case denoting the agent or the instrument is, in some instances, not compounded due to the mention of the term *bahula* (diversely/variously). In other instances, however...

The meaning is that even a different case-ending may be compounded, precisely because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways). He demonstrates the absence of compounding with the words "dātreṇa lūnavān" and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), examples such as "dātreṇa cchinnavān" and "hastena kurvan" are to be understood. [This applies] even when there is a change of case-ending.

An example of the rule *samasyate* (is compounded) is: *pādahārakaḥ* (a foot-thief) and *galecopakaḥ* (a throat-cutter). The word *hārakaḥ* means "one who takes" (*hriyate*). By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). There is a compound with *pādābhyām*, which ends in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) denoting the point of departure (*apādāna*).

The root *cup* is used in the sense of "slow movement. From this root, with the causative suffix *ṇic* added for the sake of the causal meaning, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the object. Thus, *galecopakaḥ* means "one who cuts [the throat]."

The *lu* elision occurs in *ṭhamūrdhamastaka*. Since agency (*kartṛtva*) and instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) are defined in relation to an action, a compound would only be possible with a *kṛt*-derived form that conveys that action; however, because of the governing rule *upāj...* (Pāṇini 2.2.19), there is no over-extension [of the rule] to include a finite verb (*tiṅanta*). With this intention, he asks: "What is the purpose of [specifying] 'with a *kṛt'-affix'? The other [responds]:...
With the intention that there is no compound of a word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix with a *sup*-ending word derived from a *taddhita* suffix, he provides a counter-example: *kāṣṭhaiḥ*.

(607) *kṛtyair adhikārthavacane* |2|1|33|. Regarding *kṛtyair adhikārtha*: they say that this is merely an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the preceding rule and not intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). The example is *vātacchedyam* ("to be cut by the wind"). Here, the *kṛtya* suffix is applied according to the previous rule.

"Because of its softness, it can even be cut by the wind"—this is praise; or, "because of its weakness, it can even be cut by the wind"—this is censure. Regarding the term *kākapeya*: the suffix *kṛtya* is used in the sense of possibility according to the rule *aki liṅ ca*; thus, because the water is full, it can even be drunk by crows standing on the bank.
Praise, or censure on account of having little water.
(608) *annena vyañjanam* |2|1|34|. [The word] *annena*: "A woman's hissā, bhakta, andha, anna, odana—these are synonyms for food (*anna*)," according to Amara.
In this context, the term *svarūpa* (the word-form itself) is not intended; thus he says: "that which effects refinement," and so forth. (609) *Bhakṣyeṇa miśrīkaraṇam* | 2|1|35|.
[The rule begins with] *bhakṣyeṇa*. *Bhakṣya* means that which is to be consumed as solid, distinct, and substantial food. *Khara* means hard or solid.

"Viśadam" means clearly distinct in its constituent parts; "khādya" means that which is to be chewed and eaten. This is because the usage of the word occurs only in those cases where the suffix *yat* is applied, as well as in the case of the root *bhakṣ* ending in *e*. However, usages such as "abbhakṣa" (living on water) and "guḍadhānāḥ" (sugar-coated grains) are instances of *bhakta* (those who eat). Now, [one might ask: is it not the case that each individual grain...

If it is asked, "How does this example cohere, given that there is an absence of distinct constituent parts?"— do not say so; for since the collection of parched barley constitutes the *dhānās* (parched grains), and since the individual members of a collection possess the status of being parts (*avayava*) with respect to that collection, its validity is established.

(610) *caturthī tadarthārthabalihitasukharakṣitaiḥ* | 2|1|36 | The [compound] beginning with "the fourth case" (*caturthī*) has that as its purpose (*tad-arthārtha*). By the word "that" (*tat*), the fourth case (*caturthī*) under discussion is referred to; because it is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), by virtue of syntactic connection (*sāmarthya*), that which has the fourth case ending is indicated as having that as its purpose.

With this intention, he says: "that which [is used] for the object denoted by a word ending in the dative case. The meaning is that a word ending in the dative case is compounded with a word denoting the wood or other materials used for a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) intended for that which is expressed by the dative.
Regarding the mention of *balirakṣita*, the mention of *hitasukha* is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*), because in connection with that...

The intention [of the author] is that the fourth case (caturthī) occurs even when not expressing "for the sake of that" (atādarthye), because of the possibility of the fourth case being used in the sense of a blessing (āśiṣī). Now, Kaiyaṭa has stated that some say: "A compound does not occur for that which ends in a fourth case prescribed by the rule 'caturthī cāśiṣī', because a blessing is not understood from a compound. Consequently, [the following objection arises]:

If it is argued that even the inclusion of the terms *hita* (beneficial) and *sukha* (pleasurable) in that [Pāṇinian] rule serves merely as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), just like the inclusion of the term *bala* (strength), the modern scholars (*navya*) respond here: "In the examples *brāhmaṇahitam*, *gohitam*, and *gosukham*, a compound is admitted even with words ending in the dative case used in the sense of 'for the sake of' (*atādarthya*). This...

They say that [the use of the fourth case] is indeed correct; for it is possible either by the Vārttika *cātādarthye caturthī* ("the fourth case is also used when there is no sense of 'for that purpose'"), or because the rule *caturthī tadarthe* ("the fourth case in the sense of 'for that purpose'") prescribes a compound with the words *hita* and *sukha*, which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
Thus, the mention of *hita* and *sukha* is not an indicator [of the general principle], and so [the form] *yūpāya* is perfectly valid. Regarding *yūpāya*: [this is explained as follows].

The dative case is used in the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*). This should be inferred accordingly in the subsequent cases as well. Regarding the examples beginning with *aśvaghāsa* ("horse fodder"), this has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya. Now, one might object: "In that case, even in an expression such as *randhanāya sthālī* ('a pot for cooking'), a genitive compound would necessarily occur; therefore, the restriction that [the dative compound] applies only when there is a relationship between a material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛtibhāva*) is useless."

Nor is there any difference in accent; for even in the case of the rule *caturthī tadarthe* ("a word in the dative case [is compounded] when it denotes that for which the other thing exists"), it is intended that the accent of the first member (*pūrvapadakṛtisvara*) applies only when the relationship is one of "original" and "modification" (*prakṛti-vikṛta-bhāva*).

On this point, they say: "Because of the existence of a relationship, and because the aforementioned restriction is rendered effective by the distinction created by the sense of 'being for the sake of that' (*tādarthya*), [there is no fault]."

This is a fault. And the authority for this is this very Bhāṣya itself. Furthermore, usages such as *māṣāṇām aśnīyāt* ("one should eat beans") and *āśarathāya maithilī* ("the daughter of Mithilā [was given] to the son of Śaratha") are likewise to be explained through such a distinction in intended meaning (*vivakṣābheda*).
And thus, in the rule *pūrvasadṛśa-* (Pāṇini 2.1.31), the inclusion of the term *sadṛśa* ("similar") is redundant.
It should be noted that the statement of Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others is based on negligence, because even there, a difference in the resulting verbal cognition (śābdabodha) exists.
It should be stated: "A compound with *artha* is obligatory, and it takes the gender of the qualifier (*viśeṣyaliṅgatā*). [This refers to the rule: "Obligatory with *artha*."

The sense is that otherwise, because the section on *vibhāṣā* (optionality) applies, there would occasionally be the usage “*avijāyārtha*” [instead of *artham*]. And regarding the statement “it takes the gender of the qualified object” (*viśeṣyaliṅgatā*): in the absence of such a rule, since the word *artha* is invariably masculine, it would always take the masculine gender everywhere, according to the principle that “the gender [of a compound] follows that of its final member” (*paravalliṅgam*).
Such is the intended meaning.
(611) *Pañcamī bhayena* |2|1|37|. Regarding *pañcamī bhayena*: the term *bhayena* is taken as a formal expression (*svarūpagrahaṇa*), not as a reference to its meaning.
Because there is an absence of authoritative evidence, and because the *vārttika* begins with the rule "after words meaning 'fear' (*bhaya*) and 'afraid' (*bhīta')",
there is no compound in cases such as *vṛkātrāsaḥ* ("fear of a wolf"). How then are usages such as *bhogoparataḥ* ("ceased from enjoyment") and *rāmanirgataḥ* ("departed from Rāma") formed?

Regarding this, they say: because it was already stated that due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways), even words ending in different case-terminations may be compounded with a *kṛt*-derivative, or else its justification is found in the rule *upa-supe* (Pāṇini 2.1.4). (612) [The word *alpa*] is optionally compounded with *apeta*, *apoḍha*, *mukta*, *patita*, and *apatrasta* [to form a *tatpuruṣa* compound]. (Pāṇini 2.1.38)
The term "fifth case" (*pañcamī*) is understood [from the previous rule], and because of the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), there is an inclusion of that which ends in it.

In the word *alpaśaḥ*, the suffix *śas* is applied by the rule "after a word meaning 'few' or 'little,' when it is a *kāraka*. Although he will later state that "a word meaning 'few' or 'little' expresses both auspicious and inauspicious things," nevertheless, for this very reason [it is used here].

It should be understood that [the form] *chasa* arises through irregular derivation (*nipātana*). However, its status as a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is with respect to the action of compounding;

for the word *alpa*, since it denotes the object of that which ends in the fifth case (*pañcamī*), it possesses the nature of an object (*karman*) in relation to the act of compounding. This is precisely what he states: "the word *alpa* ending in the fifth case."
(613) *stokāntikadūrārthakṛcchrāṇi ktena* (Pāṇini 2.1.39).
[Examples include] *stokānmuktaḥ* ("freed with little effort"), and so forth. In the case of *stokānmuktaḥ*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is applied by the rule *araṇe ca stokālpe*.
However, in cases such as *dūrād āgataḥ* ("come from afar"), the ablative is applied by the rule *dūrāntikārthebhyaḥ*.
(614) [Pāṇini 2.2.8] Regarding the example *rājapuruṣa*: in the ungrammatical analytical statement (*alaukikavigraha*) *rājan as-puruṣa su*,

when the compound is formed and the case-ending (*sup*) is elided, the elision of the *n* does not occur because the status of being a word (*padatva*) is maintained by relying on the internal case-ending.

(615) And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the words *yājaka* and others. 2.2.9: And after *yājaka* and others. *yājaka*, *pūjaka*, *paricāraka*, *pariveṣaka*, *snātaka*, *adhyāpaka*, *utpādaka*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, *bhartṛ*, *rathagaṇaka*, *patigaṇaka*.

Regarding the rule *vṛt*: it should be stated that there is the elision of *tar* when followed by a word expressing a different quality (*guṇāntareṇa*). As for the phrase "when followed by a word expressing a different quality," this Vārttika is recited under the rule *arvaṃ guṇakārtsnye*.
It should be stated that "the sixth case [ending] connected with a *kṛt* suffix is compounded. Regarding the phrase "the sixth case connected with a *kṛt*":

the meaning is "connected with a *kṛt* suffix" by virtue of the rule "the agent and the object [take the sixth case] before a *kṛt* suffix. However, when the prohibitive statement beginning with "in the case of a rule formulated by specific mention (*pratipadavidhāna*)" is commenced, then this [is the case].
An effort must be made to refute that [position]. We shall explain immediately below why that very [position] is not to be undertaken.
