Regarding the term *idhmavraścana*: it is called a *vraścana* because one cuts (*vṛścyate*) with it; thus, it refers to an axe or similar tool. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
There is a compound of this word with *idhmānām*, which ends in a genitive case expressing the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*).

(616) *na nirdhāraṇe* |2|2|10|. In the example "nṛṇām" ("of men"), the genitive case is used according to the rule *yataśca nirdhāraṇam*. Here, the occasion for compounding arises with the word *dvija*; indeed, the genitive depends upon that [word]. The excellence [indicated] is in relation to humans other than the twice-born (*dvija*).

Because they are presented by a common term, it is improper to abandon them and assume something not so presented. Now, how is it that [the word] "Puruṣottama" [is used]? Because [he] is distinguished, and because that which is distinguished is a part, and that which...

The *nirdhāraṇa-hetu* (the cause of selection) is as Kaiyaṭa states regarding the rule *vīpsā-vibhajyo-pa-*: this negation occurs only when these three factors are present. Others, however, maintain that in the case of *puruṣeṣūtamaḥ*, there is a compound formed by the rule *aṃjñāyām* with the locative of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-saptamī*). Nor is it thus...

The inclusion of the word *nirdhāraṇe* (in the sense of "selection") is redundant, because there is a difference in accentuation. For in a locative compound (*saptamīsamāsa*), the original accent of the first member would apply by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārthe*, etc.; whereas in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the final syllable would be acute by the rule *antodāttatvaṃ samāsasya*, which is undesirable—so they say. That [objection] is weak.

Because the compound *ajñāyām* is obligatory (*nitya*), it would follow that an analysis using its own constituent words (*svapadavigraha*) would be untenable; therefore, the modern scholars maintain that the solution stated by Kaiyaṭa alone is correct.
It should be stated that a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhānā*) is not compounded. Regarding the term *pratipadavidhānā*:

it means "prescribed for each individual word" (*padaṃ padaṃ prati vihitā*). The meaning is that every genitive—excluding that prescribed by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (Pāṇini 2.3.50), but including all others such as those prescribed by the rules *ño'vidarthasya* (Pāṇini 2.3.51) and so forth—is a genitive prescribed by a specific rule.

Since the genitive case is prescribed by rules such as *anyo 'vidarthasya* (Pāṇini 2.3.52) precisely upon grasping the distinction between the *dhātu* (verbal root) and the *kāraka* (case-role), that [genitive] possesses the quality of being "prescribed by a specific rule" (*pratipadavidhāna*).
If it is objected that the rule *nirdhāraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.41) is redundant because its purpose is already served by this very [preceding rule], they reply: "And from which... [the following is said].

The sūtra *nirdhāraṇe* does not prescribe the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), but rather the seventh case (*saptamī*) alone. As for the sixth case, it is merely reintroduced (*pratiprasūyate*) so that it may not be sublated by that [seventh case rule]; this is another matter. The same applies to rules such as *avamīśvarādhipatī*. Therefore, [forms such as] *ṛhasvāmī* and *sarveśvaraḥ* are established.

The phrase "‘iṣādādhipati’ ityādi siddham" (the [term] beginning with ‘iṣādādhipati’ is established) is as follows: in reality, however, within the fourteen-sūtra section beginning with “pa’ño’vidarthasya,” one excludes the six-sūtra section beginning with “ivastadarthasya”; thus, in the remaining eight-sūtra section which is without distinction...

The word "eṣa" (this) is understood [from the previous rule]. Thus, just as in cases such as "na māṣāṇām aśnīyāt" (one should not eat beans), where the case ending is already established by the rule "aṣṭhī śeṣe" (the genitive is used for the remaining relations), this section is for the purpose of restriction:
here, only the genitive case is used, and not its elision (*luk*). Consequently, there is no compound at all that would serve as the cause for the elision of the case ending.
This is the established conclusion. Consequently, the statement "in the prescription of the word *rati*" need not be made.

This being the case, the statement "the sixth case [is used] in connection with a verbal root (*ṛd-yogāt*)" should also be omitted. For in the rule "of the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows," the term "with *ṛ*" has been withdrawn. Likewise...
Furthermore, since that [rule] is intended solely for the prescription of a genitive case where it has not otherwise been obtained, there is no possibility of the resulting exclusion of the compound;

for the compound is established by the rule "aṣṭhī" (Pāṇini 2.3.50) itself. Thus, in the example *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee"), although the ghee is in fact the instrument (*karaṇa*), the genitive case is applied by the rule "ña-avidarthasya" (Pāṇini 2.3.51) because one intends to express merely the general relationship (*saṃbandha*). It is thus related to the ghee (*sarpiḥ-saṃbandhi*).
The meaning is "causing to proceed. Regarding the rule *pūraṇaguṇa* [Pāṇini 2.2.11], because the word *artha* is connected with all three [of the preceding categories], he says:

(617) *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārthasadavyayatavyasamānādhikaraṇena* [Pāṇini 2.2.11]. [He explains: "with words having the sense of *pūraṇa* and so forth. On this point, it was stated by the ancients: "The genitive case is not compounded with words having these meanings."
That is deficient. For if that were the case, there would be a grasping only of those [words] ending in *su-hita*, because only those many are compounded with the word *artha*.
Indicating this, he says: "and by *sat* and so forth. Regarding "the sixth": it is the sixth because it completes a group of six; [it is formed] by the rule *asya pūraṇe ḍaṭ*.

Regarding the rule "aṭ-ka-ti-katipaya-caturām thuk," how is it that [the form] "ānyuñchaṣaṣṭhāṅkitasaikatāni" is possible? Some say this is simply an error. However, in the *Manoramā*, it is explained that it should be analyzed as "the sixth among gleanings" (*uñcheṣu ṣaṣṭhaḥ*) or "that which consists of gleanings as its sixth part" (*uñchātmakaṣaṣṭha*).

It is established [that the word *guṇa* here] means "quality. Here, the term *guṇa* is understood as that which is defined by the characteristics such as "it enters into being" (*niviśate*) and "it departs" (*apaiti*), and not as that which is defined by the technical grammatical rules for *aT* and *eṅ*, because the meaning [of the word] is intended. Nor does it mean "number," because of the reference in the Vārttika: "in the case of 'hundred of cows' (*gośata*) and 'hundred of yojanas' (*yojanaśata*). For example, the blackness of a crow.

Regarding the example "brāhmaṇasya śuklā" (the white [cloth] of the Brahmin): the intention is that, by the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the word *guṇa* includes both those denoting a quality alone and those denoting a substance qualified by a quality. Now, one might object:
in the case of "brāhmaṇasya śuklā," there is no possibility of compounding at all, because the word *brāhmaṇa*...
Because of the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) with "teeth" alone, the meaning would be that for a Brāhmaṇa, those which are teeth are white;
therefore, he says "when" (*yadā*). The intention is that the word "white" (*śukla*) itself is what provides the substantive here.

[This is] because, in cases such as "the fragrance of sandalwood" or "the form of a jar," this [rule] would result in a prohibition [of the gender of the qualifier], [but it is not so] by the rule "and by those residing in the same [object]" (*atsthaiś ca*).

By the *vārttika* "A compound should be stated [in cases] involving qualities (*guṇa*)," the formation of a compound is restated. A fragrance perceived as being "gone" (*gandha-gata*) is never co-referential with its possessor (*guṇin*), but rather stands as its own primary subject. This indeed is what is called "abiding therein" (*tātsthya*). Now, [one might object]: "The suffix *iniṣṭha*..."

If it is argued that, because we observe the usage "gandhān" (accusative plural), the word *gandha* is exactly like words such as *śukla* (white) and does not denote a quality residing in something else—[we reply: no. For in the usage "inaṣṭī," the word *andhā* is not a term for a quality; rather, this is because we observe the usage of the word *gandha* in reference to things such as jasmine flowers (*mālatīkusuma*). However...

That [perception] is indeed distinct, being caused by the genus (*jāti*) such as "sandalwood-ness" (*candanatva*). Therefore, in cases such as "the fragrance of sandalwood," its subsistence therein is perfectly established. The same applies to cases such as "the visible form of the cloth. But even so, would there not be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in instances such as "the whiteness of the wall" or "the blueness of the cloth"?

Regarding this, they say: "Since that which is produced from a word denoting a possessor of qualities (guṇin) denotes the quality itself, such as whiteness, there is no fault because the words expressing those [qualities] stand in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the possessor of the quality. And thus, [the distinction between] primary and non-primary [denotation]..."
The meaning is that, while not expressing a substance (*dravya*), it expresses a quality (*guṇa*) residing therein; this is what is meant by "having a quality residing there.

Regarding the phrase "of the fruits" (*phalānām*): the genitive case is used because one intends to express the instrument (*karaṇa*) as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*). Regarding the phrase "there is a difference in accent":
this refers to the fact that [the rule] *atpuruṣe tulyārthe* (Pāṇini 6.2.2) sets aside the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*).

The meaning is as follows: although the rule *hāthā*di-sūtra would result in an udātta accent on the final syllable, that is set aside by the exception *ṛtīyā karmaṇi*, which—given the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*)—intends the initial syllable to be udātta. However, in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), the final syllable would be udātta, and that is not desired. And [the root] *tṛp*...
It is also transitive, as evidenced by the usage of Bhāravi: "He gratified his kinsmen, honored them, and considered them equal.

Therefore, one should not suspect that the suffix *kta* cannot occur in the passive sense after this root. In the example "the twice-born man's doing" (*dvijasya kurvan*) or "the twice-born man's doing" (*kurvāṇa*), this genitive case is not used in relation to objects such as a jar (*ghaṭa*).

Regarding the phrase "vijasya ghaṭṃa kuru" (make a pot for the Brahmin): since a compound would not even be applicable here due to the absence of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*), this prohibition would be redundant; therefore, he explains it as meaning "the servant" (*kiṅkara*). In the case of "brāhmaṇasya kṛtvā," when there is a desire to express the relationship in its general form—namely, the relationship consisting of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*)—[the prohibition applies].
The genitive [case ending] means "that action which belongs to the Brāhmaṇa, immediately after which [the next action occurs].

The point is that this is indeed an indeclinable *kṛt* [suffix], because of the usage of the word *arvāc-paścāt* in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *anekam anyapadārthe*. "And so forth" (*ity-ādi*): likewise, Bhaṭṭi [says]:

He employed [the argument]: "For whose sake do we restrain our enemies? For whose sake, O Kumbhakarṇa, are enjoyments to be accepted without you? Regarding the word *rakṣita*, Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta, however, citing "above the tree" (*vṛkṣasyopari*) as an example under the prohibition concerning indeclinables, maintain that it applies even with an indeclinable that is not a *kṛt* suffix.

The sense is that those two [interpretations] which consider it a prohibition (*niṣedha*) are to be disregarded because they contradict the usage in the previously cited *bhāṣya*; however, [the suffix] *tavyat* certainly does occur, because the *sūtra* mentions the form without an *anubandha*. The compound *svakartavyam* is formed with a genitive of the agent (*kartṛ-ṣaṣṭhī*). "There is a difference in accent" (*svare bhedaḥ*).

The intention is that, by the accent of the base of the preceding member (*kṛd-atarapada-prakṛti-svara*), the accent of the suffix *tit* remains, and thus a circumflex (*svarita*) at the end is desired; however, if there were a compound with *tavya*, the acute accent (*udātta*) would fall on the middle syllable, which is not desired. "He too [is excluded] by this" means that the compound *oṭāyuvatī* is prevented by the sixth-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).
The meaning is that even this genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is prohibited by the rule "ūraṇaguṇe" [Pāṇini 1.1.50].
(618) *ktena ca pūjāyām* |2|2|12|. Regarding the rule *ktena pūjāyām*: in the sūtra, the mention of "veneration" (*pūjā*) is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*).

He says "from the commentary" and provides the rule *mati-buddhi-*. Regarding the word *rājñām* (of kings): the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the agent according to the rule *tasya ca vartamāne*. Regarding the word *bhūte* (in the past): it should not be argued that, by the principle of the curd-and-Kauṇḍinya example, the present time of the *kta* suffix after roots such as *man* and *budh* is sublated by the past time [of the rule *niṣṭhā*]; this is because [the present time] is included from the rule *ekādi-*.

In the context of the rule *ena*, the mention of *upajñāte* indicates that the past tense (*bhūtakāla*) is not superseded; for in the word *upajñāte*, the suffix *kta* denotes the past, not the present. Otherwise, [the rule] *tasya ca vartamāne* would have applied.

Because of the rule prescribing the sixth case (genitive) for the word *upajñāta* when used with that [word], there would be no connection with the third case (*tṛtīyā*). Nor should it be argued that even so, the status of being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*) should apply only to words meaning "knowledge," for, in accordance with the usage “*ūjitoḥ yaḥ surāsuraiḥ*,” the status of being an indicator must indeed be understood as a general one.

Because it is logical [that this prohibition applies only to the agentive genitive]. Others, however, say that this prohibition of compounding applies only to the *kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī* (the genitive denoting a grammatical relation), whereas compounding would certainly still occur with the *śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī* (the genitive of remainder). By this, the usage in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*, "He, honored by Rāma, engaged in a quarrel" (*alahaṃ sa rāmamahitaḥ kṛtavān*), is explained: "He, honored by Rāma, [engaged] in a quarrel..."
The syntactical connection is "he has done" (*kṛtavān*).
(619) *Adhikaraṇavācinā ca* |2|2|13|. Regarding this rule, Haradatta and others maintain that the inclusion of the word *vāci* ("denoting") is for no purpose.

"This belongs to them" (*idameṣām*). The suffix *kta* is applied here by the rule *tasyādhi-karaṇe ca*. By the rule *adhikaraṇavācinaśca*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Although the form would have been established by the rule *adhikaraṇe ca* alone, they say that the inclusion of the word *vāci* ("expressing") in both sūtras is for the sake of clarity. Now, one might object: in the expression *nivṛttaṃ yadvṛttam*, the suffix *kta* does not denote the object (*karman*).

Since the root *vṛ* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), one might ask: "How can there be a compound here with a word ending in the past passive participle suffix *kta* denoting the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)? Do not say so. This *kta* does not denote the locus; rather, according to the rule "atyarthākarmake," it denotes the agent (*kartṛ*). The meaning is: "by whom was it covered?"; that is, "by whom was it brought to completion? (or "accomplished").

(620) *karmaṇi ca* | 2|2|14 | [The word] *karmaṇi* [is used] also. The term *ktena* does not carry over [from the previous rule], because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition in the rule *tena ca pūjāyām* being rendered meaningless. However, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does carry over; but even that—only that which...

A certain genitive case in the sense of the object (*karman*) is not accepted [here]. For if it were accepted, since forms such as *ṛtupāṃ sraṣṭā* would be established by this very rule, the prohibition "after *ṛt* and *kakāra*, the genitive is not used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*)" would become redundant. Furthermore, in cases such as *idhmavraścanaḥ*, a specific statement would have to be made for the sake of establishing the compound. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that there exists a Vārttika stating, “The sixth case [ending] denoting the object of the root √ṛdhi is compounded,” because that has been rejected in the final Siddhānta. Consequently, since particles have multiple meanings, this word *ca* (and) has the sense of *iti*; thus he says, “the sixth case which [denotes] the object. This refers to the singular locative form.
The meaning is: "having uttered a word" [in the context of] that which is prescribed as the genitive case or remains [as such].

This is because it is accepted that restrictive rules (*niyamavidhi*) function in two ways: either in the form of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) or in the form of a prohibition (*niṣedha*). As for the example "the milking of cows" (*gavāṃ dohaḥ*), the mention here of "by one who is not a cowherd" (*agopena*) is intended to illustrate this.

This is for the purpose of demonstrating that both [the agent and the object] are obtained. Now, how is it that [Pāṇini’s work] is called "the instruction of words" (*śabdānuśāsana*)? On this point, they have explained: this genitive case in *śabdānām* is prescribed by the rule "of the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*), and not by the rule "when both are obtained" (*ubhayaprāptau*), because the Teacher is in fact the agent.

Even when the agent (*kartṛ*) is present here, [the rule does not apply] because of the non-employment of the word; for, since the term "in the employment" (*prayoge*) is understood from the rule *ṛtvigarthaprayoge* (Pāṇini 3.2.10), it is accepted that this restriction applies only when the agent and the object (*karman*) are explicitly mentioned.
Indeed, in the example "The milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd is wonderful" (*āścaryo gavāṃ doho ’gopena*), it is the "wonder" (*āścarya*) that is to be expressed, and that...

If the milker is unskilled and the cows are difficult to milk, then [the milk] is obtained only at that time and not otherwise. Therefore, because the agent and the object are specifically mentioned, let there be the application of both [rules]; however, in this case, the statement "this is the instruction regarding words (śabda), and not regarding meanings (artha)" is intended to exclude the meaning.

This statement is intended to exclude a specific agent, and therefore there is no "attainment of both" (ubhayaprāpti). Even if there were some manner of attaining both, it would still cause no harm, because under the rule *ubhayaprāptau*, the alternative view that "the option [applies] without distinction" (*aviśeṣeṇa vibhāṣā*) also exists.

For, on the view that the rule does not apply, the usage "the teacher’s instruction of words" (*ācāryasya śabdānuśāsanam*) is possible. Alternatively, if it is explained that the genitive case is used in the sense of a remainder (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*), then there is no suspicion at all here of a prohibition against compounding.

(621) *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* |2|2|15|. Here, the commentator [Patañjali], indicating that the explanation by the author of the *Vṛtti*—namely, "the genitive case of the agent with *tṛc* and *aka*"—is incorrect, states: "with *tṛc* and *aka* having the agent as their referent."

The inclusion of the term *kartṛ* (agent) is properly understood as a qualifier for *tṛc* and *aka* alone, because those two are explicitly mentioned [in the rule], and not for the genitive case; this is the intended meaning. Although *kartari* is not a qualifier for *tṛc* because there is no deviation [from its application], nevertheless, by virtue of being a qualifier for *aka*, [it serves its purpose].
He states that this is necessary with the words "ikṣubhakṣikā. [The suffix] *ṇvuc* is used here in the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāve*) according to the rule "aryāyārhaṇe.

There is a compound with the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). Now, one might object that the example "vajrasya bhartā" is appropriate, since the word *bhartṛ* belongs to the *yājakādi* group [which governs the genitive].
Anticipating the objection that a compound [of pati and artha] would necessarily follow, he says: "of the word *bhartṛ* [used] in the sense of *pati*.

Although the word *bhartṛ* is not listed among [the group of words] such as *yājaka* when qualified by a specific meaning, nevertheless, because conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is stronger, it is understood there as a synonym for *pati* alone, and not in its etymological (*yaugika*) sense.

[This refers to] the state [of being]. [The phrase] "by the sixth case in the sense of the remainder" is used. However, the author of the Nyāsa says that this [word *tṛn*] ends in *tṛn*, and that the prohibition [in Pāṇini 2.3.69], "not before *loka*," is non-universal (*anitya*), because it is indicated by the fact that when one could have simply said "after *ra* and *ka*" (Pāṇini 8.4.1), the *tṛc* suffix was mentioned with its *anubandha*. Some, however, [cite] "the agent of birth" (*janikartuḥ*).
Some say that because of the rule "at-prayojaka-hetu-śca," this prohibition of compounding is not permanent; however, that is weak,
for the stated rule can be accounted for by means of a genitive compound (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

(622) *kartari ca* |2|2|16|. Here, the rule *tṛc* does not apply. Nor should it be suspected that this is for the sake of subsequent rules; the intention is that Jayāditya has stated that the suffix *tṛc* does not occur after roots meaning "play" (*krīḍā*) or "livelihood" (*jīvikā*).
Vāmana, however, asks: in the rule "ṭhake jīvikārthe" (*Pāṇini 4.4.12*), what is the purpose of including "ṭhake"?
He provides "amaṇīyakate" as a counter-example, thereby indicating that he desires the suffix *tṛc* when the sense is "livelihood.
(623) *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.17).

The suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) by the rule *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ*. Thus, *bhañjanam* (breaking) and *bhañjitā* (one who breaks). In the phrase "of those who have risen" (*utthitānām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The mention of "in the sense of an abstract action" (*bhāve*) is an illustration; for there is no prohibition against the suffix *ṇvul* being applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as well.
With this in mind, it was stated in the *Manoramā* on the rule *ajñāyām* regarding *kṛt*-suffixes that [the word] *uddālakaḥ* [is formed in this manner].
The game in which the flowers of the *uddālaka* tree are broken is called *uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā*.

(624) [Pāṇini 2.2.1: "A word denoting a part [is compounded] with words meaning 'eastern' (*pūrva*), 'western' (*apara*), 'lower' (*adhara*), or 'upper' (*uttara*), when they refer to a single substratum."

The word *ekadeśa* (part) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "that which is prior and posterior. For this very reason, even though it forms a *karmadhāraya* compound, a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is added after it; for the prohibition—"no possessive suffix after a *karmadhāraya*"—does not apply to conventional terms, as in the case of the expression *kṛṣṇasarpa-vān* ("possessing a black snake"). Even though here...

Regarding the phrase "ṭhakago-pūrvādi," the suffix *ṭhañ* would have been applicable; nevertheless, by virtue of this very specific mention, the suffix *ini* is used. This is what he states with the words "by means of the whole" (*avayavinā*). Now, one might object that this sūtra is redundant, since forms such as "ūrvakāya" (the upper body) and others are established simply through a *karmadhāraya* compound.

Just as in the case of the expression *ūrdhvakāya*, because of the maxim that "words functioning for a whole may also apply to its parts," he says: "it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Thus, the intention is that the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.49] is intended to prevent undesirable usages such as *āyapūrva*. *Pūrvam*.

Regarding the word *kāyasya*: although the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would be difficult to justify here— since, by the rule *anyārāditarartedikśabdācūttarapadājāhiyukte* (Pāṇini 2.3.29), the commentary explains that the term *dikśabda* refers to a word seen in the sense of "direction" (*diś*), thereby accepting the fifth case (*pañcamī*) even when joined with a word not currently denoting a direction— nevertheless, [the form is justified] by the rule *asya paramāmreḍitam*.

The sense is that because it has been stated that "the fifth case ending does not occur when used with a word for a direction (*dik-śabda*) denoting a part due to [the presence of] a *liṅga* (indicative mark)," only the sixth case ending occurs. In the phrase "prior to the navel" (*pūrvaṃ nābheḥ*), the meaning is that the portion prior to the navel is a part of the body. In the word "āmer," the fifth case ending is characterized by its connection to a direction (*dig-yoga*). Therefore, in this instance...

The meaning is that for the word *pūrva* (the first part), the navel (*nābhi*) is the limit (*avadhi*), but it is not a part-possessor (*ekadeśin*); therefore, there is no compound with the navel. However, a compound would indeed occur with the body (*kāya*), as in "the upper body from the navel" (*ūrvakāyo nābheḥ*). This is because the word *pūrva* is invariably dependent on something else and is the principal member of the relation. As in the example "the first among the students" (*pūrvaś chātrāṇām*), this [usage] does not occur in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
The genitive [case ending] is used, however, in the sense of a relationship between a whole and its parts.

The plural number is employed because of the intention to express a collection consisting of distinct parts that have become a single entity. Consequently, although the students possess the quality of being partial [to the whole], there is no compound because they lack the qualification of oneness (*ekatva*). This is what is meant by "even all."

The meaning is that it is distinct from "pūrva" and the others. Regarding the phrase "because of the indicator" (jñāpakāt): the intention is that otherwise, the state of being "evening" (sāya) and "forenoon" (pūrva) for the day (ahan) would not be possible. Regarding "madhyāhna": [the suffix] *ṭac* is applied by the rule "rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac"; then, by the rule "ahno'hna," the substitute *ahna* is applied for *ahan*. And this substitution—

It should be understood that the words *madhyāhna* and *sāyāhna* cannot be resolved by a *karmadhāraya* compound—just as in the case of *ūrdhvakāya*—because that [former] is governed by the rule for *ekadeśisamāsa*. Therefore, in this instance, it is indeed appropriate to rely on an *jñāpaka* (indirect indicator). Thus they say; and in this way, forms such as *inamadhyah* and *rātrimadhyah* are not [unaccounted for].
It should not be said that [the rule] would apply; for that which is established by an *jñāpaka* is not universally valid.

(625) *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* | 2|2|2|. When *ardha* denotes a neuter [substance], it is a neuter noun. The word *ardha*, when used to denote a part (*khaṇḍa*), is not invariably neuter, as in *grāmārdhaḥ*.

Regarding the example "nagarārddha": while the word *ardha* denoting an equal portion is invariably neuter, it is that very [neuter] one which is intended here. The intention is that although the neuter gender would already have been obtained by the analysis (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule as “*ardham* [is neuter]"—where the word *ardha* should have been recited in the preceding sūtra alone—the fact that the neuter gender is mentioned again [in this sūtra] serves to specify that particular [neuter] sense.
He explains: "The word *sa* [is used] when [the referent] is eternally neuter. This means that which possesses the gender of a permanent neuter (*nityanapuṃsakaliṅgin*).
"As before" means it is compounded with a whole (*avayavin*) qualified by singularity. Others, however, have explained:
since the neuter gender is already established by the very mention of "half" (*ardham*), [the rule applies].

The mention of the neuter gender is intended to indicate that "in the *sūtras*, the indication of gender is not intended to be significant. Consequently, [the rule] *ena tasyeda* and so forth applies even to all three genders.
In the case of *ardhapippalī*, when the technical designation *upasarjana* is applied by the rule *ekavibhakti cāpūrvanipāte*, [the following occurs].

Fearing that the word "oṣṭrīya" might take a short vowel [by Pāṇini 4.2.90], he provides the resolution: "the statement regarding what does not end in ṣaṣṭhī. The sense is that because the word *pippalī* is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*) in this context, there is no fault. But if this is so...
The compound "pañcakhaṭvī," meaning "a collection of five beds" (pañcānāṃ khaṭvānāṃ samāhāraḥ), would not be established;

for, due to the prohibition of the designation *upasarjana*, the short vowel [ā] in the form "khaṭva" would not apply, and because it would thus lack the final short *a*, the suffix *ṅīp*—prescribed by the rule "vigoḥ"—would not apply. Therefore, he says:

The meaning is that [the rule] "when there is a single case-ending" (ekavibhaktau) refers to words other than those ending in the sixth case (a-ṣaṣṭhy-anta-vacanam). It is specifically concerned with the domain of the *ekadeśi-samāsa* (part-whole compound). The very example cited in the *Bhāṣya*, namely "ardha-khaṭvā," serves as the evidence (*liṅga*) for the restriction of the phrase "other than those ending in the sixth case. Thus is the sense. As for the example "ardha-pippalī": [it is formed by the elision of the case-ending].

The neuter gender [of the compound] is due to the gender of the subsequent member (*paravalliṅgatvāt*). Regarding the example *ardha-pippalīnām*: if a compound were formed, it would necessarily be *ardha-pippalī* alone, because there is identity of the qualified object (*viśeṣyaikyāt*). The point is that even though the gender is extended by the rule *paravalliṅgam*, there is no extension of number (*vacana*).

As for the usage "ardhapippalyaḥ," although it would be incorrect if analyzed as "ardhāni pippalīnām" (halves of peppers), it is indeed correct when there is a collection of parts, because the analysis is "ardhaṃ pippalyāḥ" (half of a pepper) [forming] "ardhapippalī," and then "ardhapippalī ca ardhapippalī ca," and so forth. What is the purpose of the term "ekadeśinā" (with a part-whole relation)?
"Half of Devadatta's goat. Here, Devadatta is the owner (*svāmī*), not the whole (*avayavī*); therefore, there is no compound with him.

This rule was rejected in the *Bhāṣya* on the [sūtra] "the gender is like that of the original" (*aravalliṅgam*). For example: "half-a-pear" (*ardhapippalī*) is established by means of a *karmadhāraya* compound, since words seen to apply to a collection [can also apply to its parts].

This is because of the maxim: "Words also apply to the parts [of what they denote]. Even in cases other than an equal division, this same principle applies to you as well, since we observe such usage as ‘half-eaten,’ ‘half-spoken,’ and ‘half-glanced. Furthermore, in the case of an equal division, one does not employ a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

It cannot be said that this sūtra is intended to set aside [the previous rule], because the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is not desired here. For this very reason, Kālidāsa employed the expression: "by love, she who takes half of Hara’s body.
(626) *Dvitīya-tṛtīya-caturtha-turyāṇy anyatarasyām* | 2|2|3| [The words *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *caturtha*, and *turya* optionally form a compound with a word denoting the whole.]

Regarding the second and third [sūtras]: the author of the Vṛtti stated that this rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), but this is incorrect; suggesting this, he says: "having set aside the prohibition. (627) *prāptāpanne ca dvitīyayā* | 2|2|4|. This is an exception to the prohibition [of compounds] by the previous sūtra. By the force of the word *ca* ("and"), it is understood that there is also an option with regard to the genitive compound. Thus, one may say either *prāpto rājānaṃ* or *prāptarājaḥ*. Similarly, *āpanno rājānam* or *āpannarājaḥ*. The word *dvitīyā* here refers to the case ending (*vibhakti*), not to the specific case itself. Therefore, even when the object is expressed by a noun stem (*prakṛti*) rather than a case ending—for example, in *prāptaguruḥ* ("one who has reached his teacher")—the compound is formed. This is because the term *dvitīyā* is used as a metonym for the meaning of the second case. Alternatively, since the word *dvitīyā* is a relative term (*sāpekṣa-śabda*), it depends on the presence of the first case (*prathamā*) in the same sūtra, and thus refers to the case immediately following it. In the case of *prāpta-jīvikaḥ* ("one who has obtained a livelihood"), the compound is formed with the word *jīvika*, which ends in a *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛd-anta*). Since the word *jīvika* is derived from the root *jīv* with the suffix *ṇvul* (which denotes the agent), it is a word denoting an agent (*kartṛ-vācaka*). Consequently, the word *prāpta*, being in apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it, would normally take the nominative case ending (*prathamā-vibhakti*) according to the rule *kṛd-yogā ca ṣaṣṭhī na samasyate* ("A genitive ending connected with a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix is not compounded"). However, the present sūtra provides an option for this. Furthermore, the word *dvitīyā* here does not denote the specific case ending itself, but rather the meaning of the second case. Therefore, even when the object is expressed by a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix—as in *kṛta-kāraḥ* ("one who has done a deed")—the compound is formed. This is because the word *kṛta* is in apposition with *kāra*, and the latter is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix. In the case of *bhakṣita-pūrva odanaḥ* ("rice previously eaten"), the word *pūrva* is a relative pronoun (*sarvanāman*) and is therefore indeclinable (*avyaya*). Because it is an indeclinable, it cannot form a compound with another indeclinable under the rule *avyayam vibhakti-samīpa...* (P. 2.1.6). However, since *pūrva* here functions as a relative pronoun, it is treated as a non-indeclinable and thus forms a compound with *odana*. In the case of *gata-madhuḥ caitraḥ* ("Caitra whose honey has gone"), the word *madhu* is in apposition with *gata*. Since *madhu* is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, the genitive ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply to it by the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* (P. 2.3.65). However, that genitive ending is not applied here because the word *madhu* is in apposition with *gata*, which is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix. In the case of *ācita-palāśam śastram* ("a weapon with leaves piled up"), the word *palāśa* is in apposition with *ācita*. Since *palāśa* is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, the genitive ending would apply to it. However, that genitive ending is not applied because *palāśa* is in apposition with *ācita*, which is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix. In the case of *upahṛta-paśu rudraḥ* ("Rudra to whom an animal has been offered"), the word *paśu* is in apposition with *upahṛta*. Since *paśu* is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, the genitive ending would apply to it. However, that genitive ending is not applied because *paśu* is in apposition with *upahṛta*, which is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix. In the case of *uddhṛtaudanā sthālī* ("a pot from which rice has been taken out"), the word *udana* is in apposition with *uddhṛta*. Since *odana* is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, the genitive ending would apply to it. However, that genitive ending is not applied because *odana* is in apposition with *uddhṛta*, which is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix. In the case of *paryāhṛta-paśur rudraḥ* ("Rudra to whom an animal has been brought around"), the word *paśu* is in apposition with *paryāhṛta*. Since *paśu* is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, the genitive ending would apply to it. However, that genitive ending is not applied because *paśu* is in apposition with *paryāhṛta*, which is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix. In the case of *vinirhṛtaudanā sthālī* ("a pot from which rice has been removed"), the word *odana* is in apposition with *vinirhṛta*. Since *odana* is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, the genitive ending would apply to it. However, that genitive ending is not applied because *odana* is in apposition with *vinirhṛta*, which is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix. In the case of *sampanna-yavā bhūmiḥ* ("land where barley has ripened"), the word *yava* is in apposition with *sampanna*. Since *yava* is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, the genitive ending would apply to it. However, that genitive ending is not applied because *yava* is in apposition with *sampanna*, which is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix. In the case of *sampanna-yavā bhūmiḥ*, the word *yava* is in apposition with *sampanna*. Since *yava* is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, the genitive ending would apply to it. However, that genitive ending is not applied because *yava* is in apposition with *sampanna*, which is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix. In the case of *sampanna-yavā bhūmiḥ*, the word *yava* is in apposition with *sampanna*. Since *yava* is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, the genitive ending would apply to it. However, that genitive ending is not applied because *yava* is in apposition with *sampanna*, which is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix. In the case of *sampanna-yavā bhūmiḥ*, the word *yava* is in apposition with *sampanna*. Since *yava* is a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, the genitive ending would apply to it. However, that genitive ending is not applied because *yava* is in apposition with *sampanna*, which is a word ending in a *k

In the word *prāptajīvikaḥ*, the shortening of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *ostriyām*. The prohibition of the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅga*) is applied by the upcoming rule *viguprāptāpanna*. Nor should it be suspected that this is redundant because its meaning is already conveyed by a *bahuvrīhi* compound; for there is a difference in accent (*svara*).

In examples such as *prāptasukham*, because the past passive participle (*niṣṭhānta*) would otherwise be placed last according to the rule *atikrāntātikālātītasukhādibhyaḥ*, [the compound is formed] by inferring the elision of the vowel *a* through the inclusion of the particle *ca* in the rule *prāptāpanne ca*; for that *ca* has the sense of a conjunction of the predicate, and thus it indicates that *prāpta* and *āpanna* are compounded.
And it is established in the Bhāṣya that "a" and "atva" would belong to those two.

Regarding this, the ancients maintain that by cutting off the vowel *a* immediately before the *ca*, there is no *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical change) because it is a *sautra* (Vedic/Pāṇinian) usage. To avoid this difficulty, he says: "by the second [word], *a*. [The word] *strī* is obtained; [this refers to] the single substitute (*ekādeśya*).

Because they are grasped as having the sense of "prior limit" (*pūrvānta*), or by virtue of the maxim that "a word qualified by its gender [includes] the same word with a feminine suffix," the compound is also applicable to *prāptā* and *āpannā* when they end in the feminine suffix *ṭā*. (Pāṇini 2.1.49). (628) Kālāḥ parimāṇinā | 2.2.5. [Time-denoting words are compounded with a word denoting the thing measured.]
"Times [are compounded] with that which possesses a measure.
That by which something is measured—that is, delimited—is "measure" (*parimāṇa*), meaning the delimiting factor; that which possesses it is "that which possesses a measure" (*parimāṇin*).
Thus he says: "with that which expresses the object to be delimited. "Times" means words expressing specific divisions of time.

Because of the use of the plural number in the Sūtra and because time in its general form is not a defining characteristic [of an object], [the rule applies]. Regarding the phrase "one month of the born" (*māso jātasya*), this statement is made because a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) would otherwise be expected. Now, one might object: a person who is born has as his defining characteristics things such as having hands or feet, but not time; for that [time]...

If it is argued that [time] is merely a delimiting factor of action (*kriyā*), here they say: although time directly delimits the action, it delimits Devadatta by means of that [action]. For one for whom a month has passed since birth is designated as "born a month ago" (*māsajāta*). In that case—

The month occurring between the time of legal convention (*vyavahārakāla*) and the moment of birth, although itself born through the door of birth, indeed delimits that which has been born. Here, in this analysis (*vigraha*), although it is indicated by the genitive case, the word "of whom" (*yasya*) is stated in order to indicate its predominance in the compound (*vṛtti*). However, in the non-ordinary analytical sentence (*alaukika-prakriyāvākya*), this is not the case.

[This is] the entry [into the topic]. It should be understood that the same applies to the *bahuvrīhi* compound as well. Now, one might object: although the formulation of this sūtra is necessary for the sake of placing the word *māsa* at the beginning in the formation of the compound from the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "the month of Āṣāḍha" (*ātasya māsaḥ*), there is still the cognition having "month" as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

If it is asked, "Since this [meaning] is already appropriate, what is the point of saying 'that which belongs to whom' (*yasya saḥ*)?", they reply: "In accordance with usages such as *māsajāto mṛtaḥ* ('dead after being born for a month'), the analysis (*vigraha*) is accepted as 'that of whom [there is a month]' (*yasya saḥ*). Regarding *māsajāta*: although [the analysis] is *māso jāto yasya* ('of whom a month has been born').

This is also established by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because of the rule stating, "The past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) follows words such as *atikāla*, *sukha*, and so on, when they are to be expressed. Nor is there any difference in accent, since the final acute (*antodātta*) is also established by the rule *vā jāte*. Nevertheless...

This [sūtra] must indeed be commenced for the purpose of providing an exception to the genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa). Furthermore, it must necessarily be commenced for the sake of such forms as *māsajātavān* ("one who has been born for a month"), which would otherwise be impossible.
For the formation of a *dvigu* compound with many [members] by means of a subsequent member that expresses a measure (*parimāṇin*), [this rule is required].

An addition [to the rule] regarding *tatpuruṣa* compounds: "by means of a subsequent member. This means that a three-membered *tatpuruṣa* must be stated for the sake of establishing a *dvigu* compound where the subsequent member is a word denoting measure (*parimāṇin*). This statement is made because [the previous rule] *up-supa* does not apply, since singularity was intended to be expressed there.

From the very commencement of this Vārttika, it is understood that singularity (*ekatva*) is intended in the rule *upapadamanam* (Pāṇini 2.2.19). Regarding the expression *ahnādeśa*: the meaning is that when there is a *tatpuruṣa* compound consisting of three words, and when an intermediate *dvigu* is present by virtue of the rule *addhitārthottarapada-dvigau* (Pāṇini 5.1.28), [the substitution occurs] provided the subsequent word follows. As for "as before": [it refers to the example] *dvyahajāta*.
The meaning here is "in this [context].

(629) *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ* | Pāṇini 2.1.40. [The word] *śauṇḍa* [is used] with a locative case ending; this is known both from the use of the plural number in the rule and from the force of its inclusion in the *gaṇa*-list.

Intending to explain the understanding of the primary sense, he says: "by means of *śauṇḍa* and so forth. In the example *akṣaśauṇḍa*, *śauṇḍa* means "skilled" (*pravīṇa*). Here, the action consisting of attachment is included within the compound, and the semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) is mediated by that [action], as it is in the case of *dadhyodana* (curd-rice), *guḍadhānā* (molasses-grains), and so on.

The capacity [of the compound] is established through such means as pouring over (upasecana) and mixing (miśrīkaraṇa). Therefore, there is no deviation from the rule that "words denoting distance (āraka) are connected only with a verb. Regarding the word *ādhi*, the remainder [of the explanation] is "having the thing contained (ādheya) as the primary meaning. However, when the locus (adhikaraṇa) is the primary meaning, it is necessarily an avyayībhāva compound.

Regarding *adhihari*: as in *kha iti*, the word *ityam* is to be supplied as the remainder [of the example]. This is because it will be stated later that this is due to the force of the inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā* in the rule *vibhāṣāñceḥ*. The word *antaḥ* is recited here, and it primarily denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), meaning "in the middle. When used in conjunction with that, [it refers to] the whole (*avayavin*).

The locative case is used when there is an intention to express the locus (*ādhāra*), as in the example "the branch is on the tree" (*vṛkṣe śākhā*). However, in the expression "he dwells within the forest" (*vane antaḥ vanāntar vasati*), since the word *antaḥ* functions solely as a locus, it necessarily forms an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) according to the rule "when used in the sense of a case-ending" (*vibhaktyarthe*). In the phrase "fire within the reeds" (*anirantaḥ śare*), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs.

Regarding the word *vane*, it means "within the forest" (*antarvaṇam*). Haradatta has stated that because the *tatpuruṣa* compound is optional, there is, in one alternative, an *avyayībhāva* compound; however, this is questionable. For even if the *tatpuruṣa* is optional, the *avyayībhāva* is mandatory [in this case], resulting in *vane antaḥ*.

Because it is impossible for that which has been so stated to have its own members analyzed (svapadavigraha); furthermore, an avyayībhāva compound occurs only when there is a function based solely on the meaning of a case-ending, by virtue of the inclusion of the term "vacana" (number). Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *vṛkṣasyopari* (above the tree). Consequently, [this applies] to that which expresses the middle (*madhya*).

The point is that there is no such contingency at all. [Now follows: 2.1.43: *śauṇḍa*, *dhūrta*, *kitava*, *vyāḍa*, *pravīṇa*, *saṃvīta*, *antar*, *adhi*, *paṭu*, *paṇḍita*, *kuśala*, *capala*, *nipuṇa*—these, when used with words ending in a *kṛtya* suffix, form a compound in the sense of debt (*ṛṇe*).
A compound with [words ending in] *kṛt* suffixes is desired only when they end in *ṛt*. This is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "in small measure" (*alpaśas*).
The plural number, however, is intended to refer to the variety of *prakṛti*s (bases).
He illustrates this accordingly with the example: *māsedeyam*. In the *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is non-elision (*aluk*) by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti*.

It should be given every month. "For the purpose of indicating a fixed rule (*niyoga*)" means that *niyoga* is a determination (*nirdhāraṇa*); the meaning is that it serves to indicate a necessary obligation.
This is a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*); for this very reason, the analysis of its own constituent words (*svapadavigraha*) as "the best among men" (*puruṣottamaḥ*) is inappropriate.
Thus we have stated.
(631) *kṣepe* | 2|1|47|. In the example *avatapte*, [we have] *nakulasthitam*, meaning "standing like a mongoose. This is by the rule: *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā*.

This is a compound. By the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt*-suffixes, the word *nakulasthita* is also considered to end in a *kta* suffix; thus, it forms a compound with a word ending in the locative case. In accordance with the rule *atpuruṣe kṛti*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending.
Here, censure is understood through the perception of instability.

(632) *pātresamitādayaśca* |2|1|48|. The compound *pātresamitādayaḥ* consists of words such as *pātresamitāḥ*. [The form] *samita-* is derived from the root *iṇ* with the prefix *sam* and the suffix *kta*. [The form] *gehenardī* is derived from the root *ard* meaning "to sound" with the suffix *ṇini* according to the rule *ṇinir akṛtpratyayād upyajātau* (Pāṇini 3.2.78). [The term] *ghaṭaka-tayā* means "by way of entering."

"No," [the author replies]. The meaning is that there is only the sentence "those who sit at the same table" (*pātresamitāḥ*), and not another compound formed by [the addition of] suffixes such as *an* or *mahat*. This point is established in the *Śabdakaustubha*.
Others, however, [hold that] it is only the sentence "the weak ones who sit at the same table" (*abalāḥ pātresamitāḥ*), and not—

They say that by the rule "pūrvakālaika... and so forth, another compound is formed: (633) *pūrvakāla-eka-sarva-jarat-purāṇa-nava-kevalāḥ samānādhikaraṇena* || 2.1.49 || [Words denoting prior time, *eka*, *sarva*, *jarat*, *purāṇa*, *nava*, and *kevala* form a compound when joined with a word in grammatical apposition.]

"Pūrvakāla" (prior time) is an indication of the meaning; however, for the other six [categories], there is the apprehension of their own forms. Since "priority" (pūrvatva) is a relative term, the prior time is compounded with the subsequent time. He illustrates this accordingly: *snātānuliptaḥ* (one who has bathed and anointed). Here...

Because they are action-words (*kriyāśabda*), they are synonyms like *pācaka* (cook) and *pāṭhaka* (reader). Regarding "sacrificial experts" (*yājñika*) and so forth: those who study or know the sacrifice (*yajña*) are "sacrificial experts. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "after *ṛtu*, *uktha*, etc. Similarly for "logicians" (*naiyāyika*).
According to the rule "after the root *īryati*, the suffix *atṛn*," the suffix *atṛn* is used in the sense of "being" (*bhūti*). They are both aged (*jarantaḥ*) and logicians (*naiyāyikāḥ*).
And the "ancient Naiyāyikas"—the meaning is "ancient logicians. Those who study or know the Mīmāṃsā are "Mīmāṃsakas," according to the rule *ramādibhyo vun*. "New students" (*navapāṭhakāḥ*):
those who recite are "reciters" (*pāṭhakāḥ*), with the suffix *ṇvul* according to the rule *ṭhṇvultṛcau*. It expresses a number.

The word *nava* is not included here, due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that "the term *saṃjñā* [is applied] when it is counted. Why [specify] "with a word in grammatical apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇena*)? [Consider: "the whiteness of one" (*ekasyāḥ śauklyam*). Furthermore, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) does not occur here either, because of the prohibition [stated in the rule] "in the presence of *uraṇa* and *gum*" (*uraṇapare*).

(634) *dik-saṅkhye saṃjñāyām* |2|1|50|. Regarding *dik-saṅkhye saṃjñāyām*: it is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). The body of the restriction is: "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, only when it is a name (*saṃjñā*) are direction (*dik*) and number (*saṅkhya*) compounded. By this, [compounds such as] *pañcaguḥ* and so forth [are formed].

[The form] is established. How then is Kālidāsa’s usage in the verse “*trilokanāthaḥ pitṛsadmagocaraḥ*” [to be explained], given that the word *triloka* is not a technical name (*saṃjñā*)? Nor can it be a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*), because that would entail the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* by the rule "*dvigoḥ*". Nor should one assume it belongs to the *pātrādi* group [which prevents *ṅīp*], for if...

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the ungrammaticality of such usages as *trilokī gaṇanā parā syāt*. Nor can it be a compound formed by the rule *uttarapade* (Pāṇini 2.2.19), because a three-word *tatpuruṣa* compound of this kind is difficult to justify here.
On this point, they say: the word *loka* here refers to a collection of worlds (*lokasamudāya*). It consists of three parts...

"Loka" refers to the triple world (*triloka*). This is according to the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.60] beginning with *śākapārthiva*, which states that there is elision of the second member of the compound. Regarding the example "five Brahmins" (*pañca brāhmaṇāḥ*): although no difference in form occurs here even when the compound is formed, nevertheless, a difference should be understood in the application of case endings, such as in the form *pañcabhir brāhmaṇaiḥ*. This is for the sake of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*).
The statement is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning. With the intention that even a single locative case (*saptamī*) is differentiated according to the distinction of its objects, he says:

(635) *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca* [Pāṇini 2.1.51]. This means "in the domain of the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)," and so forth. However, if [it were interpreted as] "when the meaning of a secondary derivative is to be expressed" (*taddhitārthe vācye*),...

If it were explained in that way, then in cases such as *aurvaśāla*, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix would not occur, because its meaning is already expressed by the compound itself. The point is that even if one were to assume— on the basis of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *vigorluganapatye*— that a secondary derivative suffix occurs even when its meaning has already been stated, this would result in excessive complexity (*pratipattigaurava*) in understanding the system.

However, the phrase "when a taddhita suffix follows" is not to be explained [in that way], because there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): first there must be a compound when a taddhita suffix follows, and only after the compound has been formed can the taddhita suffix be applied by rules such as *ik-pūrvapadāt*.
And regarding the expression "when the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*) is to be conveyed," by this [rule], in cases such as *pañcagavam*, the meaning is conveyed by the compound itself.

Because the formation of a collective (*samāhāra*) has already been stated, a suffix expressing a collection (*samūha*) does not arise. Otherwise, the suffix *ṭac* would apply here by the rule *or ataddhitalukī*; for the suffix denoting a member of a collection (*samūhika*) would undergo elision (*luk*) by the rule *vigor lug anapatye*. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the rule for the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) in all instances of compound formation involving pronouns (*sarvanāman*): the term "by a pronoun" (*sarvanāmnā*) applies to both the preceding and following examples. Although the desired form could have been established even by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*, it is nevertheless stated here for the sake of [the subsequent rules] such as *uttarapūrva*.

The mention of the term *arvan* is necessary; the intention is that since it is explicitly stated [in the rule], its inclusion here is also logical. Regarding "in both types of derivation" (*vṛtimātre*): Kaiyaṭa explains this as referring to both derivative (taddhita) derivation and compound (samāsa) derivation. Regarding "the vowel *ā* is acute": this would not be the case if there were no intermediate *tatpuruṣa* compound.
The point is that, by the rule regarding the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of a compound, the word *pūrva* would necessarily have its initial syllable acute (*udātta*).

Regarding *ṣāṇmātura*: the substitution of *ud* [for *u*] occurs by the rule “*āturutsaṅkhyāsaṃbhadrapūrvāyāḥ*”. Because it is stated “[in the sense of] not a descendant” (*anapatye*), there is no elision (*luk*) by the rule “*vigoluṅ*” (Pāṇini 4.1.88). Since an option (*vikalpa*) was applicable...

Thus, the word "in the Mahāvibhāṣā" is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the source]. Consequently, the intention is that in the absence of the *ṭac* suffix prescribed for a *tatpuruṣa*, the form *añcagodhana* would also be possible. However, in the *Manoramā*, it is stated: "Since an option [between composition and non-composition] would otherwise arise, this rule—'in the case of *dvandva*s and *tatpuruṣa*s'—is for the purpose of making the compound obligatory. This is the view of the ancients (*prācām*).

This has been stated in accordance with the treatise (*grantha*). In reality, however, when a compound of three words is formed, because the meaning shifts toward the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), there is an absence of mutual relationship; thus, since neither a *dvandva* nor a *tatpuruṣa* would apply, [the rule concerns] a three-word [compound].

When a *bahuvrīhi* compound has been formed, there is invariably a *dvandva* of the two preceding [members]; consequently, by the rule "after a *dvandva* ending in *cu*, *ṣ*, or *ha*," the suffix *ṭac* at the end of the compound is also invariably applied. (Pāṇini 5.4.106). [Furthermore: "After the word *go*, when there is no elision (*luk*) of a *taddhita* suffix. (Pāṇini 5.4.92).
Regarding *gorataddhita*: the phrase *atpuruṣasya* (of the Tatpuruṣa compound) is understood [from the previous rule], as is *ṭac*.

Thus, he says: "after a word ending in *go*, etc. Now, one might object: since a *prātipadika* that possesses a specific suffix does not allow for the extension of a rule (*tadantavidhi*) to what ends with it, the meaning would be that *ṭac* is added to the word *go* which is a constituent part of the Tatpuruṣa compound.

It might be so; however, in that case, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in examples such as *omūtra*. Therefore, he says: "at the end of a compound" (*samāsānta*). This is the intended meaning: because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "the suffixes at the end of a compound" (*samāsāntāḥ*), the suffix *ṭac* must function as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*); furthermore, since the ablative case is heard in the word *goḥ*, [the suffix] must also follow after that. Not [otherwise].

Since this [application] is not possible without the rule regarding that which ends in such [an element], the application of the rule regarding that which ends in such is obtained by implication (*sāmarthyāt*).

Consequently, the genitive form *tatpuruṣasya* is transformed into the ablative form [i.e., *tatpuruṣāt*]. However, this does not mean "when there is elision of a taddhita suffix" (*taddhitaluki*); rather, it means "in the domain of the elision of a taddhita suffix," and not "when the elision of a taddhita suffix has actually occurred."
The compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) apply because they are *antaraṅga* (internal). Why does [the rule] say "except when there is elision of a secondary suffix" (*ataddhitaluki*)? Consider:
*pañcaguḥ* ("bought for five cows"). Here, the secondary suffix *ṭhak* is elided by the rule "*ṭh’ardhapūrve*" (Pāṇini 5.1.28).

(637) *saṅkhyāpūrvo dviguḥ* | 2|1|52|. "A compound preceded by a numeral is called *dvigu*. Regarding the phrase "it is so stated here": the intended meaning is that this technical designation applies only to the scope of the preceding rule, according to the maxim *anantarasyaiva* ("the designation applies only to what is immediately contiguous"). Indeed, it is for this very purpose that two separate rules were formulated.

Otherwise, he would have simply stated: *anyathā ’iksaṃkhyaṃ saṃjñāyāṃ taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāreṣu*. By this [rule], in the case of *aptarṣayaḥ*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member—by virtue of the rule *ṭhigantakālakapāle* and so forth—does not occur; rather, there is only the final acute accent (*samāsāntodātta*) of the compound. And thus:

The examples are: *apta ṛṣayastapase ye niṣeduḥ* ("the seven seers who sat down for austerity") and *aptaṛṣīṇāṃ sukṛtāṃ yatra lokaḥ* ("where the world of the seven well-performing seers is"). Regarding the phrase "it is threefold, preceded by a numeral": it refers to a compound that is preceded by a numeral when it occurs in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), or when a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) is to be expressed. This [is the definition of such a] compound.

This is the meaning. As an example in the sense of a *taddhita* derivative: *pañcakapālaḥ*. By the rule *“aṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ”* [Pāṇini 4.2.16], the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then by the rule *“dvigor lug anapatye”* [Pāṇini 4.1.88], there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. As an example in the case of a subsequent member (*uttarapada*): *pañcanāvapriyaḥ*. By the rule *“āvo dvigoḥ”* [Pāṇini 5.4.99], the compound-final suffix *ṭac* is added. In the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*): *pañcapūlī*.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied [to form *dvigoḥ*]. (638) "A *dvigu* compound is that which has a numeral as its prior member. (Pāṇini 2.1.52).

"A *dvigu* is singular" (Pāṇini 2.1.51). It is called *vacana* because it expresses (*vakti*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*).
‘The neuter is used for the generic. The meaning is that a *dvigu* compound conveys a single meaning.

Since it is not possible for something that is actually multiple in meaning to somehow become a single meaning in reality, he says—“it shall be as one”—to indicate that this is an extended application (*atideśa*) based on the force of the context.

The term “in a collective compound” (*samāhāre*), however, is obtained through an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*). The analysis is as follows: that which is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective is treated as a singular. Why [specify] “in a collective”? So that it does not apply in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). For example: *pañcakapālāḥ*, meaning "prepared in five potsherds," and *pañcagavaḥ*, meaning "bought for five cows."

[The forms] *paṭāḥ* [are explained]. However, in the case of *pañcagave* and *pañcagavāni*, when the singularization (*ekavadbhāva*) of the meaning of the *dvigu* compound has been effected, that collection which constitutes the meaning of the *dvigu* after the formation of the *ekaśeṣa* is not itself the meaning of a *dvigu*; therefore, because it is external (*bahir-aṅga*), this singularization does not apply to it.

This is established in the authoritative source (*ākara*). When, in the rule *addhitārtha* (Pāṇini 2.4.1), the term *samāhāra* is derived as an object (*karman*), then a *dvigu* compound whose primary referent is the collection (*samāhṛta*) would otherwise result in a plural number; it is by this [rule] that the singular status (*ekavadbhāva*) is effected. However, when *samāhāra* is derived as an abstract state (*bhāva*), then...

Since a *dvigu* compound primarily denotes a collection (*samūha*), and since a collection is inherently singular, its singularity is already established; thus, this [rule] serves no purpose. Nor should it be argued that the prescription of singularity is for the sake of establishing neuter gender by means of the rule "a napuṃsakam" (2.4.17), because [that rule applies only] to words denoting a collective whole.

They say that there is no objection to accepting the rule "the neuter gender is used for generalities" (*āmaṇye napuṃsakam*). However, in reality, in the sūtra *adhyardhapūrvadvigor lug* (Pāṇini 5.1.28), the term *samāhāra* refers to the abstract state (*bhāva*) with the suffix *ghañ*, and not to the object (*karman*). This is because, in the case of *pañcagavam*, if one were to accept the meaning "five cows brought together," [it would follow that the neuter form is incorrect].

Because when things are being brought together (*samāhriyamāṇa*), the singular number is untenable due to their plurality. Nor should it be argued that this is not so on account of the rule *vigruhekavacanam* (Pāṇini 2.4.1), for then the form *pañcakhaṭvī* would remain unestablished.
For in that case, five beds are brought together; [the compound refers to] the five beds.

If the analysis were *samāhṛtāsu* (in the collected ones), because there would be an absence of a fixed case-ending due to the possibility of such a compound, the rule *vibhakti-cāpūrvanipāte* would not apply;

consequently, since it would not be a non-subordinate (*anupasarjana*) element, the shortening [of the vowel] prescribed by *oḥ striyām* would not occur. Furthermore, in the alternative view where it ends in *āp*, [the feminine suffix] *ṅīp* would be applied.

In the case of *vigoḥ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—which is conditioned by [the word ending] in a short vowel (*a*)—would not apply. However, if it functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), its status as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) remains entirely unimpeded because it possesses a single case-ending. This is because, with respect to the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), the constituent members necessarily terminate in the genitive case; thus, forms such as *pañcakhaṭvī* are established.
"Without exception"—this is the general direction [of the rule]. "That [word] is neuter"—the meaning of this will become clear in the root text itself.
(639) *kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.43): "Words denoting things censured [are compounded] with words denoting the grounds of censure."

[The words] are contemptible. [In the root] *utsa* [meaning] "to cast down," the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). With the intention that this suffix is prescribed in the sense of the present tense—because in the rule *atibuddhi* the letter *ca* has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*)—he says: "being censured. This means "those which express that [contempt]. In both cases...

The use of the plural number is intended to exclude the possibility that [the term] refers to the actual form [of the word *vaiyākaraṇa*]. Regarding the expression *vaiyākaraṇakhasūci*: from the root *sūc*, by adding the suffix *ṭhac* (which becomes *i*), one obtains *sūci*. One who, having been questioned, forgets the question and points to his own void (*kham*) due to a lack of practice is thus called a *khasūci*; however, this does not mean he actually possesses grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).

Or rather, that study is contemptible because, despite being praiseworthy as an auxiliary limb (*vedāṅga*) of the Veda, it is rendered fruitless due to a lack of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*). Regarding the word *durdurūḍha*:

the root *ul* means "to throw up" (*utkṣepe*), preceded by the prefix *dur*; the suffix *kūṭa* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules, following the rule “*bahulam anyatrāpi*” (the suffix is applied diversely even elsewhere).
The suffix *ṇi* is elided (*luk*). Because of the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) that *ra* and *la* are identical, the *la* is replaced by *ra*.

This sūtra is intended to establish a rule for the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of the specific term. This [suffix] applies only when there is contempt (*kutsā*) regarding the cause of the word's application (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*), due to its proximity [to that cause]. Therefore, it is not used here in the case of "a Naiyāyika of bad conduct."

(640) *pāpāṇakekustitaiḥ* || 2.1.54 || The words *pāpa* and *aṇaka* are both expressive of contempt. As Amarasimha states: "The words *upūya*, *kutsita*, *avadya*, *kheṭa*, *garhya*, and *aṇaka* are synonyms. Consequently, when these two are compounded with another word by the preceding rule (*pūrvāparaprathama...*), they appear as the subsequent members of the compound.

It might be so; therefore, with the intention that this sūtra is for the purpose of establishing a rule regarding the priority of placement (*pūrvanipāta*), he says: "An exception to the preceding sūtra.
(641) *upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ* || 2.1.55 ||

*Upamānāni* (the standards of comparison). That by which something is compared is an *upamāna*. [The term is derived] from the root *māṅ* preceded by the prefix *upa*, with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of instrument (*karaṇe*). It is a *prādi-samāsa* compound. The root *māṅ* preceded by *upa* is conventionally used in the sense of discernment based on similarity. The meaning is: that by which another object is discerned through similarity is an *upamāna*.

As in the case of "the gavaya is like a cow. Here, the cow is the instrument (*karaṇa*), similarity is the cause (*hetu*), and the person is the cognizer (*paricchetā*). For he cognizes the gavaya by means of its similarity to the cow.
Regarding the phrase "by means of words expressing commonality": a common property (*dharma*) is what is meant by "commonality" (*sāmānya*).

The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of the base itself because [the word] begins with *cāturvarṇya* and so forth. The meaning is "by means of words expressing that which is qualified by a property common to both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)," and not merely "by means of words expressing the common property alone.
This is understood from the inclusion of the term "words" (*vacana*). Those which have expressed the commonality are "common-expressing" (*sāmānyavacanāḥ*).

The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) in the past tense (*bhūte*) by virtue of its frequent application (*bāhulakāt*). Those [words] which, having first expressed a universal (*sāmānya*), ultimately terminate in the substance (*dravya*) that possesses it, are described as such.

And that [substance], qualified by the universal, is the object of comparison (*upameya*) itself, as it is implied by the word of comparison (*upamāna-śabda*) because it is a relative term (*saṃbandhi-śabda*).

It is understood that [the term] is technical (*lākṣaṇika*). For this very reason, due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) in cases such as *mṛgacapalā* ("fickle as a deer"), where [the compound] means "fickle like a female deer.
In this context, similarity is understood precisely through the medium of qualities such as blackness and fickleness presented by the second member of the compound.

[The compound is formed] due to proximity (*saṃnidhāna*). If it is asked, "In that case, how can it have comparison (*upamāna*) as its primary meaning?"—understand that it has that as its primary meaning by taking the literal sense (*śakyārtha*) through the principle of what was previously the case (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*). Regarding the rule on "prior placement" (*pūrvanipāta*): otherwise there would be no fixed order;
the intention is that it would be like saying "lame and hunchbacked" (*khañjakubjavat*). Furthermore, in a *tatpuruṣa* [compound...]

This sūtra is also intended to ensure that this very term— as explicitly mentioned in the rule "tulyārthair atulopamābhyāṃ tṛtīyā-saptamy-upamāna-vy-aye" (Pāṇini 2.3.72)— is captured by the inclusion of the word *upamāna*. For this very reason, it is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that [the prohibition] does not apply when the word is compounded as part of the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group.

Furthermore, because it is a relative term, it implies the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). The meaning is: "by means of [words] such as 'tiger,' which function as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). For example, in the phrase "the man is a tiger-like hero" (*puruṣo vyāghra iva śūraḥ*), since the man—even though he is dependent on the hero—is the primary element, a compound would occur here just as it does in "the king's beautiful servant" (*rājapuruṣaḥ sundaraḥ*). To prevent this from happening, [the rule specifies that the word expressing the object of comparison must be placed first].

The intended meaning is that it has been stated [in the *Vārttika*] "when there is no employment of a general term" (*sāmānyāprayoge*). How then is Kaiyaṭa's statement, "Where is the ocean of the *Bhāṣya*, so exceedingly deep? to be explained, given that this [rule] does not apply because of the absence of the employment of a general term? On this point, some say that this is merely an error; for here, similarity by way of depth is not what is intended to be expressed.

However, it is established in the *Manoramā* that because [the compound] possesses qualities such as being extensive (*vitata*) and difficult to fathom (*duravagāha*), there is indeed no application of the rule [prohibiting compounds] for those very qualities;
thus, the compound is unobjectionable.

(643) *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* |2|1|57|. *Viśeṣaṇam*: that by which something is distinguished (*viśiṣyate*) is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here with the intention of expressing the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the agent. Thus he says: "the distinguisher" (*bhedakam*). The meaning is "that which differentiates" (*vyāvartakam*).

Kaiyaṭa maintains that since the qualifier and the qualified stand in a relationship of mutual dependence, the mention of only one implies the other; therefore, the mention of both is for the sake of clarity. And this [is stated] in the passage beginning with "utsitāni..."

The same [objection] applies here in the case of *kutsanaiḥ* as well. Haradatta, however, says: "A compound occurs only where there is mutual deviation (*vyabhicāra*) between the properties of the qualifier and the qualified, which constitute the modes of the cognition produced by the two words being compounded; it does not occur in cases such as *akṣakaḥ sarpaḥ* (a snake that is an artisan), for in that case, the property of being an artisan (*takṣakatva*) does not deviate from the property of being a snake (*sarpatva*). This is mere delusion (*mada*). For it would lead to the inconsistency of such usages as *ailāsādriḥ* (the mountain Ailāsa), *candarādriḥ* (the mountain Candara), *bhāvapadārthaḥ* (the category of being), *tarkavidyā* (the science of logic), *vyākaraṇaśāstram* (the treatise on grammar), and *bhojarājaḥ* (King Bhoja).

If it is objected that, since there is freedom of choice regarding the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), as in the case of "cook" and "reader," the same lack of fixed order might apply to terms like "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*); to this they reply: there is no fixed rule for a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) in relation to a quality-word or an action-word, nor for one quality-word or action-word in relation to another. Therefore, the usage is indeed fixed as "blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*) and "cooking Brahmin" (*pācakabrāhmaṇa*). However, there is no fixed rule for two quality-words, two action-words, or a quality-word and an action-word; thus we have both "lame and hunchbacked" (*khañjakubjaḥ*) and "hunchbacked and lame" (*kubjakhañjaḥ*).

*pācakapāṭhakaḥ* (cook-and-reader), *pāṭhakapācakāḥ* (readers-and-cooks); *khañjapācakaḥ* (lame-cook), *pācakakhañjaḥ* (cook-lame). Here, the basis for the rule is that "the subordinate (*upasarjana*) [is placed first]," which is a technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*). For the subordinate is indeed non-primary (*apradhāna*). And it is perfectly clear that with respect to a substance (*dravya*), both quality (*guṇa*) and action (*kriyā*) are non-primary. (644) *pūrvāparaprathamacaramajaghanyasamānamadhyamavīrāś ca* | 2|1|58| [The words] *apara*, *ardha*, etc., [are also placed first]. This is established in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *aścā* (Pāṇini 2.4.31).

Regarding the phrase "because of the inclusion of the word *bahula*": it should be understood that [the compound] means "one who exerts himself" or "one who displays prowess" among certain preeminent [persons]. (645) *Śreṇyādayaḥ kṛtādibhiḥ* | Pāṇini 2.1.59.

*Śreṇyādayaḥ*. The first word *ādi* (etcetera) denotes a fixed list (*vyavasthā*), while the second denotes a class or type (*prakāra*). This is according to the Bhāṣya: "The *śreṇyādi* group is recited [in the sūtra], whereas the *kṛtādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). The *śreṇyādi* group consists of *śreṇī*, *eka*, *pūga*, *kunda*, *śaśi*, *viśikha*, *nicaya*, *nidhana*, and so forth. The *kṛtādi* group consists of *kṛta*, etc.

*Mita* means "beginning with *bhūta*" or "beginning with *kṛta*. However, when the guilds (*śreṇis*) are already established and have been properly organized, a compound is not desired; with this intention, he says: "those who are not guilds become guilds. Those [who are united] by a single craft or trade...

A group of those who live [by a certain craft] is a *śreṇi* (guild). However, for words ending in the suffix *cv*, there is a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*) by the rule "ugati" (Pāṇini 2.2.17), because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Thus, *śreṇīkṛtam*. But here, the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "vau ca" (Pāṇini 6.3.118). (646) [A word ending in] a *kta* suffix forms a compound with a word not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, provided that the *kta*-word itself is not qualified by *nañ*. (Pāṇini 2.1.60)

The word *viśiṣṭa* (qualified) in the rule is for the purpose of restriction. The meaning of the sūtra is that a compound consisting of [two members] with the addition of *nañ* alone is compounded with a member devoid of *nañ*. Therefore, in this case, it is not [formed]: *siddhaṃ cābhiktaṃ ca*. It should be stated: "even with one qualified by *uḍid*" (*uḍid-adhikena*). Thus: *aśitaṃ cānaśitaṃ ca* = *aśitānaśitam*.
[The forms] *kliṣṭa* and *akliṣṭam* [are derived from the root *kliś*]. According to the rule *kliśaḥ ktvāniṣṭhayoḥ*, there is optionally the augment *iṭ*.

Regarding *kṛtākṛtam*: because one part has been done while another part has not been done, that very thing is called "done-and-not-done. For the sake of establishing compounds such as *śākapārthiva* and others, the elision of the middle word (*uttarapadalopa*) must be added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*).

Regarding the term *śākapārthiva*: *pārthiva* means the lord of the earth (*pṛthivyā īśvaraḥ*), derived by the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule “*asyeśvaraḥ*” (Pāṇini 4.3.129). *Ākapriya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; when this is compounded with the word *pārthiva*, the final member (*priya*) of the preceding compound is elided. The same applies in the case of *avebrāhmaṇa*.
In the aforementioned genitive compound *devasya pūjakaḥ* (*devapūjakaḥ*), it should be understood that there is an elision (*lopa*) of the subsequent member, namely *pūjaka*. (Pāṇini 2.1.61):
*san-mahat-parama-uttama-utkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ* [form a tatpuruṣa compound with words denoting those who are honored].
