This sūtra is intended to establish the rule for the obligatory prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of words such as *sat* (good) when they are compounded with words expressing excellence (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or other [qualifying] words. [The forms] *katara* and *katama* [are used] in an inquiry regarding a genus (*jāti*). Why [is it specified] "in an inquiry regarding a genus"? [Consider: *kataro devadattaḥ* ("Which Devadatta?"). [It is stated in the sūtra: "When there is an inquiry regarding a genus among many, the suffix *ḍatama* [is used]."

Since it is established that this very word *katara* is included by virtue of its association with the word *katama* which has already been explained, the inclusion of the term "inquiry regarding a genus" (*jātiparipraśna*) indicates that the suffix *-tama* is correct even when used in a different sense. And thus it has been illustrated in the ancient commentaries (*vṛtti*).
"Which Devadatta is yours, sirs? Which Devadatta is yours?

(648) *kiṃ kṣepe* | 2|1|64 | "What when used in censure. *kiṃrāja* ("what a king!"). By the rule *imaḥ kṣepe*, the prohibition of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) applies. [This occurs] in censure.

What [is the question]? "Who is the king in Pāṭaliputra? In this same way, examples such as *iṃsakhā yo dahati* ("the one who burns is the friend of the swan") and *iṃgaur yo na vahati* ("the one who does not carry is the bull of the swan") should also be understood.
(649) A *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members have a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is called a *karmadhāraya*. 2.1.42.

*Tatpuruṣa*: a word in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) ending in the suffix *aṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83), meaning "one who cooks in common" (*samānādhikaraṇapācaka*). (650) *Puṃvat karmadhārayajātīyadeśīyeṣu* | Pāṇini 6.3.42. [In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, a feminine word ending in a long vowel is treated like the masculine when followed by a word in apposition, or by the suffixes *jātīya* or *deśīya*.]

"From a word ending in a feminine suffix that has lost its masculine form," and so forth. This will be clarified under the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*. Now, one might object: "Since this is already established for the *karmadhāraya* compound by that very rule, and since it is established for the suffixes *-jātīya-* and *-deśīya-* by the rule *asilādiṣu*, what is the purpose of this [present rule]?"
To this he says: "In the case of *pūraṇī*, *priyā*, and so forth," and likewise "in the case of *mahānavamī*.

[The word] *navamī* means "that which completes nine" (*navānāṃ pūraṇī*). By the rule "the suffix *ḍaṭ* occurs in the sense of completing this [number]," and by the rule "the augment *maṭ* is added after a stem ending in *n*, provided it does not begin with a numeral," [the form is *navama-*]. Because it has the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which is both *mahatī* (great) and *navamī* (the ninth). In the process of applying the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), [the following applies].

The meaning is that when the suffix *kṛt* is applied— as will be explained later— the form becomes large; [this is so] because of the five sūtras beginning with "a kopadhāyāḥ" (*Pāṇini 4.1.45*), "aṃjñāpūraṇyośca" (*4.1.46*), "vṛddhinimittasya ca taddhitasyā’raktavikāre" (*4.1.47*), "vāhṅāccetaḥ" (*4.1.48*), and "jāteśca" (*4.1.49*), which prohibit [the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*].

He gives examples in sequence, beginning with "pācakatrī" (a female cook). He also provides counter-examples for the suffixes denoting genus (*jātīya*) and country (*deśīya*), beginning with "evam. "Pācakajātīyā" means one who possesses the manner of a cook;
[this is derived] by the rule "ṭh prakaravacane jātīyar" (Pāṇini 5.3.69). "Pācakadeśīyā" [is derived] by the rule "īṣadasamāptau" (Pāṇini 5.3.67).

Regarding *deśīyar*: in both cases, the prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) by the rule *a-kopadhāyāḥ* would otherwise apply under the rule *asilādiṣu*. This is because that [prohibition] finds its scope of application in examples such as *paṭujātīyā* and *paṭudeśīyā*. As for the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes *datajātīyā*, *pañcamajātīyā*, and so on.

"Belonging to the Sraugdhnaja class," "belonging to the Sukeśaja class," "belonging to the Brāhmaṇa class. In this way, examples such as "belonging to the Datadeśīya class" and so forth are to be cited. Regarding "possessing the characteristics of both woman and man": the meaning is that a woman who possesses breasts, a beard, and so forth [is meant]. Regarding "udaśvit": for *udaśvit* is curdled milk (*ākr̥ta*), while *mathita* is churned milk; it is half-water and half-milk.
The *Amara-kośa* states that *nirjala* means "without water. Regarding the term *kaṭhadhūrta*: here, the status of being a *Kaṭha* (a follower of the Kaṭha school) is not what is being censured;

therefore, one should not suspect that the rule “*itsitāni kutsanaiḥ*” (words denoting praise are compounded with words denoting censure) has already achieved its purpose [and thus the compound is unnecessary].
This is because that rule applies only when there is censure directed at the very basis for the application of the first term. [The verse continues: “It leads one to the delusion of a night-lily...”
In the expression *dhūrtabako bālamatsyānām*, the term *dhūrtabaka* is indeed ungrammatical (*asādhu*).
[Pāṇini 2.1.66] "And with words expressing praise. The inclusion of the word *vacana* ("words") is for the purpose of including conventional (*rūḍhi*) terms. Therefore, those...

Derivatives such as *praśasta*, *śobhana*, and *ramaṇīya*; those which express specific qualities such as *śuci* (pure) and *mṛdu* (soft); and those which convey praise through figurative application (*gauṇyāvṛtti*)—as in "the boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*)—all these are excluded. [The example] *gavoddha* [is given]; [the suffix] *avaṅ*...

In the word *sphoṭāyanasya*, the substitution of *avaṅ* occurs, followed by the *guṇa* vowel change due to the suffix *ṭha*. According to Amara: “*Atallikā*, *macarcikā*, *prakāṇḍa*, *udgha*, and *tallaja*—these are synonyms for that which is praiseworthy.
Although the possibility of a single compound rule existed in the form “*praśaṃsāvacana-poṭā-yuvati*,” the separate formulation of the rules was made [for specific purposes].
The fruit [of this rule] is to be considered as follows:

(652) *yuvā khalatipalitavalinajaratībhiḥ* |2|1|67|. In the example *yuvakhalatī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṛdikārādaktinaḥ*. [The form *yuvatī* is thus derived. Then, by the rule *uṃvatkarmadhāraye*, [the feminine form is applied to the compound].

There is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) for the word *yuvati*. [Examples are] *jaratī* and *īryatī*; the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṭhugitaśca*. In the same way, one should provide examples such as *yuvapalitaḥ* and *yuvavalinaḥ*. The word *valina* belongs to the *pāmādi* group.

(653) *Kṛtyatulyālyā ajātyā* || 2.1.68 || [The words] called *kṛtya*, *tulya*, and *ālya* [are compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix] when not followed by a generic term (*ajāti*). In examples such as *tulyamahān* (“equal to great”) or *sadṛśamahān* (“similar to great”), the rule *anmahaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.157) takes precedence due to its higher status and thus supersedes this [rule]. However, in the usage found in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*, “*asya satkṛtyaśālinaḥ*,” [the compound is formed].

The compound ‘atāṃ kṛtyaṃ satkṛtyam’ should be understood as a genitive tatpuruṣa compound [meaning "that which is to be done with respect"]. The same applies to examples such as ‘aramapūjyaḥ’ and others.
(654) *varṇo varṇena* | 2|1|69|. [A word denoting color is compounded with another word denoting color.]
The meaning is that a word denoting a color is compounded with another word denoting a color that stands in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

Although this is already established by the rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*, this separate prescription is for the purpose of ordaining the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member according to the rule *varṇo varṇeṣv anete*.

This is for the purpose of ensuring that [the rule] applies only to the prior member of this specific compound as explicitly stated, and not to any other. In the example *kṛṣṇasāraṅga*, the word *sāraṅga* is a synonym for "variegated" (*citra*).
It refers to a substance in which quality is subordinate. The word *kṛṣṇa* is also used figuratively (*bhākta*) to denote something whose parts are black. Thus...

And they say that since the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*) does not apply when there is a secondary (gauṇa) grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), this [rule] must also be commenced for the sake of forming the compound. Now, one might object: "This compound is already established by the very rule 'after *ṛti*'," because the state of being *sāraṅga* is produced by qualities such as blackness (*kṛṣṇa*). Nor is it for the sake of the accent (*svara*).

[Objection: "The distinction [of accent] is established by the rule *atpuruṣe tulyārtha-tṛtīyā* itself, which prescribes the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member. To this they reply: "A compound must necessarily be prescribed by this [present rule] for cases such as *kṛṣṇaśuklaḥ* (black-and-white) and *haritaśuklaḥ* (green-and-white); for in these instances, there is no state of being produced by that [instrumental]."

Although the compound is established here by the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*), nevertheless the desired accent is not established. Nor should it be argued that a compound explicitly prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadokta*) is ineffective because there is nothing to be excluded; for there *is* something to be excluded, such as in the case of "black and white" (*kṛṣṇa-śuklau*).
Regarding the phrase "saṃbhavāt" (because of the possibility):
[the rule] *kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye* (Pāṇini 2.2.38) [is understood as] *kaḍārādayaḥ* (the items beginning with *kaḍāra*), because of the use of the plural number; this is the intended meaning.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the list] includes "Gāḍulaśāṇḍilya," and so forth; this is clear in the Bhāṣya. (656) *kumāraḥ śramaṇādibhiḥ* | 2|1|70|.
This very same [rule applies here]. The letter *e* is for the purpose of clearly indicating the established truth (*siddhatattva*), and not for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

This is because it is possible for the mention of *jaratī* (an old woman) in the sūtra "ṭhyuvā khalati" (*yuvā khalati*) itself to serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For the masculine gender of the word *yuvan* is not compatible with its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *jaratī*.
(657) [Sūtra 2.1.71: "The feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a word denoting a quadruped that ends in *matup*, when it signifies 'pregnant'. (*catuṣpādo gabhiṇyā*)

[The rule applies to] quadrupeds. He says that the word "āti" (cow) is understood here by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūakapluti*) method—namely, [the term] "denoting a genus" (*jātivācin*). What is the purpose of specifying "genus"? [Counter-example: *ālākṣī garbhiṇī* (a pregnant woman with dark eyes).
Why "quadruped"? [Counter-example: *brāhmaṇī garbhiṇī* (a pregnant Brahmin woman). In these counter-examples, the term "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) [is applied].
The compound must indeed be formed; however, there is a distinction regarding the prior placement [of members] in cases such as *garbhiṇī-kālākṣī*.

(658) *Mayūravyaṃsakādayaś ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.72). [The word] *mayūra* [is mentioned]; the particle *ca* here has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). By this, [compounds like] *aramayūravyaṃsakaḥ* and so forth [are included].

No other compound occurs [in this case], such as *dhūrta*. The sense is that since it would have been subject to prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) due to being a quality-word (*guṇavacana*), this specific rule was commenced. Others, however, [cite examples] such as *mayūravyaṃsaka*—meaning "one who deceives like a peacock"—where [the formation is justified] by the rule *upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ*.
This is an exception to the general rule of compound accentuation. Consequently, the final acute accent (*antodātta*) is established here by the rule *amāsasya*;

furthermore, the original accent of the first member of the compound—prescribed by the rule *atpuruṣe tulyārthe* for a preceding word denoting a standard of comparison—is set aside by the specific mention of the term "standard of comparison" (*upamāna*).
They say that this is because [the compound] has fulfilled its purpose in the case of a compound formed according to a specific rule (*pratipadokta*). Regarding *aśrītapivatā*:

here, because the external referent (*anyapadārtha*)—which consists of the action—is predominant, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied due to its feminine gender. The same applies in the following cases as well.
Regarding *rājantaram*: here the word *antara* signifies "different. Regarding *cinmātram*: [the suffix] *ātraṃ*...

According to Amara, *kārtsnya* means "entirety" and *avadhāraṇa* means "restriction. Because of the words *antara* and *mātra*, there is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), and thus in both cases an analysis using separate words (*asvapadavigraha*) is shown. They say that the status of being an obligatory compound is obtained by the particle *ca* which has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). [The examples] begin with "Extract from the storehouse," etc.; [the word] "extract" (*uddhara*).

The analysis [of the compound] is simply "utsṛja" (release). The explanation of "utsṛja" is "dehi" (give). The phrase "from the chest" (koṣṭhāt) is stated to fulfill the requirement for the verb "uddhara" (extract). Regarding "if one is a speaker by way of compounding": one who says "ahi joḍa" repeatedly is called "jahijoḍaḥ. Thus...
"He who says 'leave the pillar' is one who has left the pillar (*jahistamba*).
Regarding the term *nañ*: here, in the rule "elision of *nañ*" (*alopo nañaḥ*), the letter *ñ* serves as a qualifier. And the result of this is...

In the word *naikadā*, there is no elision (*alopa*). Others maintain that the vocalization of the suffix *ñ* (as in *nañ*) is for the purpose of establishing the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable when it is the prior member of a compound, according to the rule *avyaye nañ-kunipātānām*. [The phrase] "it is compounded with a case-inflected word" (*supā saha samasyate*) [is the governing rule].
This compound is one in which the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant. For instance, the state of being superimposed (*āropitatva*) is indicated by the negative particle *nañ*.

Thus, from the word *abrāhmaṇa*, when there is a cognition that "a Brāhmaṇa is superimposed," it results in meaning, by implication, "one who is different from a Brāhmaṇa. Precisely for this reason, because [the negative particle] is not a subordinate element (*anusarjana*), [rules such as] *atasminnasaḥ* apply.
The grammatical operations pertaining to pronouns (*sarvanāma*) are thus established.

Furthermore, the general principle that a *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of its final member as its predominant sense remains uncontradicted under these circumstances. The inclusion of the term "negation" (*anañ*) in the rule *tadetador iti* (Pāṇini 5.3.7) serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this very point, and so forth.
This should be understood according to the *Manoramā*.

(660) *nalopo nañaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.3.73. Regarding *nalopo nañaḥ*: although it could have been stated as *año'śi*, the explicit mention of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is for the sake of including forms with the suffix *sākac* (i.e., those containing the augment *ka*).

They say that by this [rule], forms such as *nañ-akac*, *nañ-ṭhak*, *nañ-brāhmaṇa*, and *nañ-aṭhakan* are established. Regarding the phrase "in a subsequent member" (*uttarapade*): the intention is that this is due to the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "elision of *ṭha* when there is a subsequent member" (*ṭhalug-uttarapade*). Why "in a subsequent member"? [Consider: *ghaṭo nāsti* (there is no jar), *paṭo nāsti* (there is no cloth). But even so, would there not be elision of the *n* in *traiṇārthaḥ* (the meaning of three women)?

If it be argued that this might be so, here they say: by qualifying the negative particle (*nañ*) with the preceding word implied by the subsequent word—on the basis of the explanation "of the negative particle which has become the prior member"—it does not occur. This is because the *nañ*-suffix prescribed by the rule "from *strī* and *pum̐s*" does not constitute a prior member. And for this very reason, in this case...
It cannot be argued that the Paribhāṣā "when both a suffix and a non-suffix are possible, only the suffix is to be understood" does not apply here;

nor can it be said that because of the rule for taking what ends in a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇe tadantagrahaṇam*), a negative particle ending in a suffix can indeed function as a prior member (*pūrvapada*), and thus the Paribhāṣā "between a suffix and a non-suffix" must still apply.

In the sūtra *hṛdayasya hṛllekha*, because of the specific mention of *lekha* (rather than *lekhana*), it is indicated that "when a suffix is mentioned within the governing heading of *uttarapada*, there is no inclusion of that which ends with it. Alternatively,
based on indicators such as *amūrdhamastakāt* and *vibhaktāv aprathamāyām*, [it follows that] there is elision (*alopa*).

In the rule *nañaḥ*, only the indeclinable *nañ* is understood as being referred to, and not the suffix. Therefore, regarding the rule *tasmānnuḍaci* (Pāṇini 6.3.74), just as in the case of *aḥ si dhuṭ*, the locative case (*ac-i*) is interpreted as a genitive (*ac-aḥ*). Thus, [the meaning is: "after that [suffix], *nuṭ* is inserted before a vowel.
*Nuṭ* is applied after that [suffix] when a vowel follows. Just as in the rule *aḥ si dhuṭ*, the locative case is converted into a genitive.

Thus he says: "of *aja* and so forth. The intention is that because the vowel (*ac*) qualifies the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the rule "in which there is an operation" (*yasmin vidhiḥ*) allows for the inclusion of the initial letter of that member. Regarding *anaśva*: since the augment *nuṭ* is added at the beginning [of the suffix], it is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*); therefore, by the rule "after a short vowel, *ṅm* [is replaced] by *ṅmuṇ*" (*ṅmo hrasvāt*), the substitution of *ṅmuṇ* does not occur. Now, [an objection]:...
In the case of *avighnābhyāgamaḥ* (the arrival of non-obstacles) and *avighnāni* (non-obstacles), a *tatpuruṣa* compound would also prevail due to its higher status,
because the *avyayībhāva* has its scope in cases such as *nirmakṣikam* (free from flies). Otherwise, forms such as *anupalabdhiḥ* and *avivādaḥ* would not be possible.
Anticipating the objection that [the desired form] would not be established, he says: "In the absence of the object, by means of an *avyayībhāva* compound with *saha*, etc.

Regarding the term *avighnam*: although a usage such as "*avighnaṃ karma*" (an unimpeded action) is established through a *bahuvrīhi*—meaning "that in which obstacles (*vighna*) do not exist"—nevertheless, in the subsequent...
The meaning is that expressions such as *karmaṇyavighnam astu* would not naturally be established without the *avyayībhāva* compound.
Regarding the rule *naño nalopastiṅkṣepe*: "there is elision of the *n* of *nañ* [when followed] by a *tiṅ*-ending word in the sense of censure. This refers to [a compound] with a *tiṅ*-ending word.

This is a rule provided because [the application of the suffix] would not otherwise occur due to the absence of a compound (*samāsa*). For example, *apacasīti* ("you cook poorly"); the meaning is "you cook in a contemptible manner.

Regarding the phrase "by the word *na*": the intention is that if there were a compound with the negative particle (*nañ*), the form would instead be *anekadha* according to the rule *anekam anyapadārthe*.
(662) *nabhrāṇnapānnavedā nāsatyā*.
The forms *namuci*, *nakula*, *vakra*, *napuṃsaka*, *nakṣatra*, *nakra*, and *nāka* are [irregularly formed] by their very nature (prakṛtyā).

[Pāṇini 6.3.75]. *Nabhrāṭ*. Those who are good (*sādhavaḥ*) in truth (*satsu*) are "truthful" (*satyāḥ*). [This is derived from the rule] "the suffix *yat* is used in the sense of 'good in this'. Those who are not truthful are "untruthful" (*asatyāḥ*). Those who are not untruthful are "Nāsatyas" (*nāsatyāḥ*). Here, the plural number is not intended to be significant; therefore—

The form *āsatyāvaśvinau dasrau* is established. Regarding *namuci*: [the suffix] *in* is added after all verbal roots (*arvadhātubhya in*). Because it is marked with *k* (as in the rule *igupadhātkid*), there is no *guṇa* substitution. It is derived either from the root *kṣar* or *kṣī*; *ṣara* meaning "to move" belongs to the *bhvādi* class, while *ṣi* meaning "to dwell" or "to go" belongs to the *tudādi* class.

(663) *kugati-prādayaḥ* | 2|2|18| The term *kugati* [in this rule] refers to the indeclinable (*avyaya*) word *u*, and not to that which denotes the earth, because of its association with words such as *gati* (motion).

(664) *ūryādicviḍācaśca* | 1.4.61 | *ūryādi*, *cvi*, and *ḍāc*. Because the term "in connection with an action" (*kriyāyoge*) is understood from the preceding rule *upasargāḥ kriyāyoge*, he says: "in connection with an action. [This applies to] *cvi* and *ḍāc*.
The terms *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* are prescribed [in Pāṇini’s rules] as governing the designation of *gati*; by virtue of their association (*sāhacarya*), the same applies to *ūry-ādi* terms.

Therefore, in this case, there is no designation of *gati* in *ūrī paktvā*. However, in the works of Mādhava and others, it is established that—with the exception of the words *āviḥ* and *prāduḥ*—the other members of the *ūry-ādi* group receive the designation of *gati* only when joined with a verbal suffix beginning with *ktvā* (i.e., the absolutive).

He illustrates this in the same way with the example "ūrākṛtya. This has been stated in accordance with the *Manoramā*; however, in reality, since the *Bhāṣya* provides the example "ūrībhūya," he gives only a mere indication (*diṅmātra*) by illustrating it as "ūrīkṛtya" [in order] to introduce the topic. The result of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is compounding (*samāsa*), and the result of that is the suffix *liṭ*.

*Bodhyam* (it should be understood): *ūrī* and *urarī*—these two [express] acceptance. As for the word *āviḥ*, however, because it is listed among the words beginning with *sākṣāt*, there is an option regarding its designation as a *gati* when used in conjunction with the root *kṛ*; but when used in conjunction with the roots *kṛ* or *bhās*, it is always so by this [rule]. How then [is it explained]?
If it is argued that this is like [the usage] in Māgha: "Then, as if the passion of the eye had become indistinguishable from the intoxication of wine," we reply:

even though there is no fault in the present case under the view that the rule *te prāgdhātoḥ* serves to restrict usage, there is not even a trace of a fault under the view that it serves to restrict technical designations (*saṃjñā*).

‘It does not exist,’ ‘it becomes white’: in these cases, the suffix *cvi* is applied after a word ending in *asti* (the verb ‘to be’) when it is used in the sense of ‘becoming something else’ (*saṃpadyakartṛ*). The vowel *i* is substituted for the final *t* by the rule *ṭhasya cvau*. In the case of *paṭapaṭākṛtya*: the word *paṭat* is doubled according to the rule *āci bahulaṃ dve bhavataḥ* (a word is generally reduplicated before a suffix beginning with *āc*). [The suffix *kṛt* is added] according to the rule *avyaktānukaraṇād dvyajavarārddhāt*.

Between the letters *takāra* and *pakāra*, *pakāra* alone is the single substitute (*ekādeśa*). The letter *ca* in the sūtra is for the purpose of ensuring the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the designation of a particle (*nipātasaṃjñā*). Consequently, in the case of *ūrīkṛtam*, when the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) is applied according to the rule "the immediately preceding [element] is [accented]," the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātatva*) occasioned by its status as a particle (*nipāta*) takes effect.

There is an addition [to the rule] regarding the word *kārikā*. [The form] *kārikā* is derived by adding the suffix *ṇvuc* in the sense of an action (*bhāva*) according to the rule "for the sake of effort, worthiness, or honor.

Thus he says: "action" (*kriyā*). The point is that because the word *kārikā* is qualified here by the phrase "in connection with action," the word *kārikā* denoting a verse (*śloka*) is not intended here.
In this context, the meaning of the word *kriyā* is "the maintenance of a limit" (*maryādā-sthiti*); others say it means "effort" (*yatna*).

(665) *Anukaraṇam ca’nitiparam* |1|4|62|. And an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) [is also a particle], except when followed by *iti*, according to the view that restricts the technical designation [of particles] for those [words] preceding a verbal root. Regarding the rule *āṅe prāgdhātoḥ* [1.4.79], in the view that restricts the designation [of particles], [the word *aniti*] is used.

Thinking that [the rule] is useless, he asks: "Why 'not followed by iti'? The other, however, replies with a counter-example, maintaining that on the view that the rule prescribes a restriction regarding usage, the phrase "not followed by iti" is necessary to prevent the designation *gati* from applying to the imitation sound *khāṭ* when followed by the word *iti*.
The sense is this: if the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) were applied [to the sound *ṭh*], this usage would not occur at all; rather, it would have to be "khāṭ kṛtvā" instead of "ṭh iti khāṭ kṛtvā.
Nor should it be argued that "ṭh iti khāṭ kṛtvā" is impossible because the designation of *gati* is prohibited for an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) following the word *iti*.

Regarding the expression *anitipara*, here *itipara* means that which has *iti* as its subsequent member; *anitipara* is thus formed by resorting to a negative *tatpuruṣa* compound within a *bahuvrīhi*.

It might be argued: if the word being imitated (*anukaraṇa*) is followed by the word *iti*, then because there is no connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), it cannot receive the designation of a *gati*.

If it is argued that the form *nāsticīti* (meaning "having made [it] 'not'") is unobjectionable even without the inclusion of the particle *iti*, the following is said in response: the expression *itikṛtvā* functions in the sense of *evaṃkṛtvā* ("having done thus"). Thus, the word *iti* serves as a qualifier of the action.
Thus, because the aggregate formed by that [element] expresses an action, there is indeed a connection with action.
(666) *Antaraparigrahe* |1|4|65|.
One takes possession of what has been struck. The act of going after having struck is twofold: either leaving the struck object behind or taking possession of it.

The first is the primary example (*udāharaṇa*), while the second is the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). The sense is that the phrase "when not preceded by *upa*" (*a-parigrahe*) is a contextual condition (*prayogopādhi*) for the usage, and is not included within the range of the expressed meaning (*vācyakoṭi*). (667) *Kaṇe-manasī* [are used] in the sense of the obstruction of faith (*śraddhāpratīghāta*). 1.4.66.
"Having struck at the grain" (*kaṇehetya*) means that having intensely desired [the drink], one drinks until its cessation;

thus, from the disappearance of faith, its obstruction is understood. The counter-example, however, is "having struck at the grain, he departed. A *kaṇa* is a minute particle of rice; the meaning is "having struck against that."

(668) *puro’vyayam* | 1|4|67| The word *puraskṛtya* [is a karmapravacanīya]. This is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) ending in the suffix *asi*, according to the rule *pūrvādharāvarāṇām*. By the rule *amaspurasoḥ*, the visarga is changed to *s*. However, in the example *amuṃ paraḥ paśyasi*, the augment *tuṭ* is applied.
By supplying the word "sthita" (remained), there is an absence of the suffix *sat* because [the words] are adverbs (*dṛśipratyayatvāt*). Why [is the word] "avyayam" (indeclinable) used? [Example:

*puraṃ purau puraḥ kṛtvā gataḥ* (having placed the city in front, he went). And [the example for *astam*]: *astaṃ ca*. Why [is the word] "avyayam" used? [Counter-example: *astaṃ kṛtvā kāṇḍaṃ gataḥ* (having thrown the arrow, he went). The meaning is "thrown."

(669) *acccha* [is used] in the sense of "going" (*gati*) and "speaking" (*vada*). Regarding *acccham*: the intention is that if it were designated as a *gati*, it would possess the designation of a *nipāta*; consequently, by virtue of being an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there would be elision of the case-ending (*subluk*). [Thus, the form] *adaḥsa-*...
Regarding the word *kṛtya*: this is an example when one reflects upon it by oneself. (670) *ado’nupadeśe* | 1.4.70. In the phrase *adaḥkṛtam*, [the rule] *atiranantaraḥ* applies.

The first syllable has the udātta accent by virtue of the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*). "Counter-example" means such instances as *adaḥ kṛtvā* and *adaḥ kuru*. (671) *tiro’ntarddhau* 1.4.71. [The indeclinable *tiras* is an avyaya when it means disappearance.]

The word *kir* [is used] in the sense of disappearance (*antardhi*). What is meant by "in the sense of disappearance"? For example: *tirobhūtvā sthitaḥ* ("having become hidden, he remained"). The meaning is: "having moved to the side.
(672) *Vibhāṣā kṛñi* | Pāṇini 1.4.72. [The rule states that the particle *tiras* optionally becomes *tiraḥ* before the verb *kṛ* when it means disappearance.]

In the *Vibhāṣā* on the rule for the suffix *kṛñ*, regarding the form *tiraḥ kṛtvā*: in the alternative view where [the word] lacks the status of a *gati*, even the substitution of *s* (as in *tiraskṛtya*) does not occur, because the term *gati* is understood to carry over into that specific rule. Mādhava, however, states that in the sense of "defeat," the form is *tiraskāra*.
Some do not accept the continued application of the term *gati* in the rule for the designation of *satva* because it is seen in usage; thus he says:
(673) *upāje’nvāje* | 1.4.73 | *upāje’nvāje*. These two are indeclinables (*nipāta*) that resemble case endings, [used] in the sense of "strengthening one who is weak."
These two [terms] function in the sense of "possessing capacity. Thus it is said: "durbalasya" (of the weak). The words beginning with *sākṣāt* are:

*sākṣāt*, *mithyā*, *ām*, *addhā*, *lavaṇam*, *uṣṇam*, *śītam*, *udakam*, and *ārdram*. By virtue of their being designated as *gati*s, these five words beginning with *lavaṇa* take the form ending in *m*.
[The word] is treated as an indeclinable: *prāduḥ*, *namaḥ*, *āviḥ*, and so forth; this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).
(674) *sākṣāt-prabhṛtīni ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.74): [the words] beginning with *sākṣāt*. For example, *sākṣātkṛtya*: that which was not directly manifest is made manifest, in such a manner.

The meaning is "having done. However, in the case of words ending in *cv-* (the suffix *-ī-bhāva*), by the rule of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the designation of *gati* is obligatory according to the rule *ṭhūryādicviḍācaśca*. Therefore, in the example *lavaṇīkṛtya*, the status of having a final *m* does not occur; for that [status] is only optional. In this list (*gaṇa*), it is [taught] in conjunction with the designation of *gati*.

This is due to grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). The author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated: "The word *lavaṇa* is optionally substituted for either the word *avaṇa* or the word *lavaṇī*, and there is an option regarding its technical designation (*saṃjñā*). Thus, in both cases, the threefold form is beyond dispute.
(675) *anatyādhāna urasi manasī* |1|4|75|. *Anatyā-*; *uras* and *manas* are indeclinables (*vibhaktipratirūpaka*). (676) *madhye pade nivacane ca* |1|4|76|.

In the case of *madhye* and *pade*, the rule *vibhāṣā ’ṛñi* (Pāṇini 1.4.61) continues to apply, and by the word *ca* ("and"), *atyādhāne* ("placing upon") is also included. In these cases, the substitution of the long vowel *ē* for the final *a* is prescribed without distinction for the specific meanings of "not placing upon" (*anatyādhāna*) and so forth, but not as a necessary concomitant with the technical designation of a *gati*. What is the purpose of excluding "placing upon"? [Consider: *pade kṛtvā śiraḥ* ("having placed the head on the foot").
It is declined [as *nivacanam*]. "Having restrained speech" (*vācaṃ niyamya*)—for *nivacanam* is indeed the absence of speaking.
When there is an absence of meaning, an *avyayībhāva* compound is formed. (Pāṇini 2.4.83). (677) Pāṇini 2.4.77: "The word *haste* is always [used] with *pāṇau* in the sense of marrying."

In the case of *nityaṃ haste*, the final *t* of these two [roots] is optionally changed to *d* when they have the sense of "taking as a wife" (*upayamana*). Thus, *hastekṛtya* means "having married. Why "in the sense of taking as a wife"? [Observe:

*haste kṛtvā kārṣāpaṇaṃ gataḥ* ("Having taken a kārṣāpaṇa coin in his hand, he went away"). However, according to the view that it refers merely to "acceptance," [the form would be used even if one thinks] "it is not enough."

The phrase "the state [of being] for the purpose of giving after having turned back" is to be supplied. Having thus illustrated the *gati*-compounds, he begins to explain the *prādi*-compounds with the words: "the mention of *prādi*."

(678) *jīvikopaniṣadāvaupamye* | 1|4|79|. In the case of *supuruṣa*, because there is an absence of connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), there is an absence of the status of being a *gati*. Since there would otherwise be an unrestricted application of compounding, these rules are recited for the sake of establishing restriction—namely, "the words beginning with *pra*" (*prādayaḥ*). The word *ādi*...
In both cases, the suffix *prakāra* is applied; by this, forms such as *durācāraḥ puruṣaḥ* (a man of bad conduct) and *duṣpuruṣaḥ* (a wicked man) are established.

In the case of *pragata ācāryaḥ* (one who has gone beyond the teacher), he demonstrates by means of this *vṛtti*—which has its meaning already expressed—that it is a *nityasamāsa* (an obligatory compound) through an analysis of its own constituent parts (*svapadavigraha*). Likewise, *pragataḥ pitāmahaḥ* results in *prapitāmahaḥ* (the great-grandfather).
"Grandfather," and so forth.

The rule "atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā" [Pāṇini 2.2.18] states that words beginning with *ati* are compounded with a word in the accusative case when they convey the sense of "having surpassed" (*krānta*) and so on. Regarding the term "atyādayaḥ": by the word "ādi" (and so forth), examples include *abhigataḥ mukham* becoming *abhimukhaḥ* ("facing"), *udgataḥ velām* becoming *udvelaḥ* ("overflowing its banks"), and *pratigataḥ akṣam* becoming *pratyakṣaḥ* ("perceptible"). And so on.
Siddham. Regarding *atimāla*: the short vowel [in *māla*] is by the rule *oḥ striyām*.

The words beginning with *ava* are used with an instrumental case when they have the sense of "surrounded" (*kruṣṭa*) and so forth. Regarding "words beginning with *ava*": because of the word "beginning," we have *pariṇaddhaḥ vīrudhā* → *parivīrut*; *saṃnaddhaḥ varmaṇā* → *saṃvarmeti*.
The words *pari* and others [are used] with the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) in the sense of being exhausted by something, such as study. Regarding "the words *pari* and others":

from the word "and others" (*ādi*), [examples include] *udyuktaḥ saṅgrāmāya* ("he is prepared for battle") and *utsaṅgrāmaḥ* ("he has desisted from battle"). Regarding *adhyayanāya*: the fourth case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*).
The meaning is that he is exhausted by staying at the teacher’s house and so forth for the sake of study.

"Nir- and other prefixes [form compounds] with a word ending in the fifth case when expressing the sense of 'gone beyond' (krānta), etc. Regarding "nir- and others": from the word "ādi" (and others), we have *utkrāntaḥ kulāt* → *utkulaḥ* ("one who has gone out from the family"); *nirgatam aṅgulibhyaḥ* → *niraṅgulam* ("beyond the fingers"). Regarding "prohibition": a prohibition must be stated for the compound that would otherwise be required by the rule "gati-prādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18); and that [prohibition is stated] in the case of *urājā*.

The meaning of "atisakhe" (exceedingly dear friend) is that, because of the application [of the rule] beginning with "bhāṣya," it refers only to *karmapravacanīyas* that are distinct from [the word] *ati*.
This is a prohibition regarding *karmapravacanīyas*. For example: *vṛkṣaṃ prati*. [This is governed by the rule] "akṣaṇettha-bhūte."

If it is argued that there is no compound here because of the force of the rule governing *karmapravacanīya*s, then one should rather cite *api stutastam* as an example. For they say that in cases such as *api stuyād viṣṇum*, the rule *apiḥ padārthasaṃbhāvane* finds its scope, and furthermore, there is a difference in accentuation.
(679) *tatra upapadaṃ saptamīstham* (Pāṇini 3.1.92). Regarding the rule *tatra upapadam*, he explains the phrase *saptamīstham* by means of the words "ending in the seventh [case]," and so forth.
The term "a word denoting that" is understood through the force of the etymological definition (*anvartha-saṃjñā*) of the technical term *upapada*. For this very reason...

Even though *saṃjñā* (name) is feminine, by the inclusion of the term "seventh" (*saptamī*), that which ends in the seventh case is understood. By the force of the separate governing rule (*adhikāra*) "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*), it is obtained that "the governing rule of the root is proximate.
Consequently, the meaning of the rule *li luṅi* is that the affix *cli* occurs after a root when a word ending in *luṅ*—such as *abhūt*—is present as an attendant word (*upapada*).

The inclusion [of the word *tatra*] is not necessary; he explains it as follows: "only when that exists. The meaning is: "only when the *upapada* exists. However, in the absence of the inclusion of *tatra*, as in the case of rules such as *ahaḥ karmaṇi ṣṭran*, even in rules like *karmaṇyaṇ*, the meaning would be that the suffix *aṇ* applies when the object (*karman*) is to be expressed. Furthermore:

Since the mention of the word ending in the seventh case (locative) serves its purpose by providing the designation of "co-occurring word" (*upapada*), it might be thought that the suffix *aṇ* could arise even from a root alone when denoting the agent. However, once the mention of "here" (*atra*) is made, the co-occurring words such as "pot" (*kumba*) are understood to be the cause for the production of the suffix.

There is no suspicion whatsoever of a *kevala* (independent) suffix *aṇ*. This being the case, they say that in rules such as "haḥ karmaṇi," the mention of the meaning (*artha-grahaṇa*) occurs in some instances due to [the requirements of] the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). Others, however, maintain that when the rule "atra upapadam" functions in syntactic unity with rules such as "karmaṇyaṇ," then, upon the application of the technical designation *upapada*, [the desired form is established].

They say that because it would otherwise result in the fault of having no scope [for the rule], the formation of the compound is established there even without the mention of the word *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive).
(680) *upapadam atiṅ* |2|2|19|.

[The word] "with a capable [word]" (*samarthena*) is understood. By this, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *ahāntaṃ kumbhaṃ karoti* ("he makes a pot that has not yet been brought").

The meaning is that although "not ending in a verbal suffix" (*atiṅanta*) is stated, the term "sup" (nominal suffix) continues to apply; thus, it was not explicitly stated as "not ending in a verbal suffix. In the example *kumbham asi*, the suffix *am* is not mentioned because the genitive case is prescribed when used in conjunction with a *kṛt*-suffix. [The question] "Why 'not ending in a verbal suffix'? [is asked] because [the rule] is governed by the heading "sup" (P. 2.4.71), so what is the purpose of this [restriction]?

Question: The other [the opponent], keeping in mind the forthcoming indicator (*jñāpaka*), offers a counter-example: "mā bhavān... The word "ha vā" is inserted in the middle to indicate the absence of a compound.
Regarding the phrase "in the previous rule": by dividing the rule into two parts—"*uprādayaḥ*" and "*atiḥ*"—it is shown that *uprādayaḥ*...

The meaning is that it should be explained as follows: "That which ends in a case-ending (subanta) is compounded with that which ends in a case-ending; however, a motion-word (gati) ending in a case-ending is compounded with that which does not end in a verbal suffix (atiṅ). And so it is said: although, according to the method stated, only the motion-word (gati) and the upapada are obtained, nevertheless, there is a traditional maxim (paribhāṣā) of the ancients concerning all three.

The sense is that here too, [the rule] is made known by way of approval of a partial application (*ekadeśānumati*). As for the factor of the *kāraka*, however, it is established in the *Manoramā* that the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahula*) in the sūtra *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32) is the proof for the stated meaning. Regarding the word "previously" (*prāk*): it refers to the occurrence of case-endings (*sup*) from the final member of a *kṛdanta* compound.
The meaning is that [the compound] must be formed first. However, the mention of the nominative case-ending (*prathamānta*) from the *sub* section continues here;
therefore, in cases such as *ājadarśī*, operations such as the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) in the prior member are successfully accomplished.
Demonstrating the fruit of this paribhāṣā, he provides an example of a *gati*: *vyāghrī*. [It is derived from] *vyājighrati*.

In *vyāghrī*, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ṭhātaścopasarge*. However, it will be stated that the suffix *ṣaṇ* (which would produce *āghrā*) does not apply in the case of a name (*saṃjñā*), because of the specific mention of "with *vyāghra* and others" (*vyāghrādibhiḥ*). There is a compound of the *gati* type between *vyāṅ* and the word *ghra*. If that [compound] were to depend upon the nominality (*subantatā*) of the word *ghra*, then...

For the sake of correct derivation, there must first be dependence on number and so forth, and prior even to that, the connection with gender; thus, by the suffix *ṭāp* conditioned by gender, [the form] should be *ghrā*, not *ghrāṣ*. This is because the word *ghrā* alone does not denote a genus (*jāti*), and therefore it forms a compound with the word *ghrā*.
The point is that because [the word *vi*] does not end in a long vowel (*ā*), the suffix *ṅīṣ*— which is prescribed by the rule for feminine nouns denoting a genus (*jāti*)— would not apply.

Although this [formation] is established even by treating it as a subordinate member (*upapada*), nevertheless, the inclusion of the term "motion" (*gati*) is absolutely necessary so that the word *vi* may subsequently form a compound with *āghra* after [the prefix] *ā* has already been compounded with *ghra*.

It should be understood that although the designation *upapada* is accepted for the root preceded by the prefix *āṅ* due to the rule prescribing the suffix *kap*, it is not accepted for the word *vi*.
He provides an example of a *kāraka*: *aśvakrītī*. [This means] "she who was bought with a horse. [This is derived] by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*.

This is a compound. [In the case of] "rītātkaraṇapūrvāt," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. However, it should be understood that if there were a compound with a word ending in a *su*-case suffix, the suffix would have to be *ṭāp*; thus, because the final vowel would not be short *a*, the *ṅīṣ* prescribed by "rītātkaraṇa—" would not occur. He gives an example of an *upapada* compound: *kaccchapī*. [It is derived as follows: she drinks with her throat (*kaccha*), hence *kaccchapī*.

The suffix *ka* is applied by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) following the word *ūṣi*. Here too, since the compound depends on being a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it would result in the suffix *ṭāp* rather than *ṅīṣ*; this is to be understood as being similar to the case of *vyāghrā*.
However, the statement of the ancients—that "an upapada which is not a finite verb (*atiṅ*) is compounded"—is incorrect, for if that were the case...

Due to the unintended consequence of removing the requirement for the nominative case ending (*prathamānta*), there would be no elision of the *n* in examples such as *rājadarśī* and *carmakāra*, because they would not be at the end of a word (*padānta*). Furthermore, in examples such as *prāṭita*, the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by the rule *ato guṇe* would apply. This might be argued: [if it were] by means of *kaccha* as the instrument...
If it is argued that, by accepting the sense of "one who drinks," since the tortoise (*kacchapa*) functions as a *kāraka*, the form *kacchapī* is established,

and thus this is not a unique example of a secondary member (*upapada*), then in that case, one should cite *hāṣavāpinī* as the example; for when the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule "after a root meaning 'to sow' [the suffix is added] in the sense of an action-class" (*upyajātau*).

In the case of a compound with *māṣa* as the prior member ending in a *kṛt* suffix, the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* at the end of the compound base— provided it follows a cause situated in the prior member— is established by the rule beginning with *arātipadikānte*. However, in the case of a compound with a word ending in a *sup* suffix [as the prior member], [the rule does not apply].

Some maintain that because it is *antaraṅga*, the suffix *ṅīp*—which is characterized by the presence of the letter *n*—is applied first; subsequently, when the word is compounded with *vāpinī*, there would be no substitution of *ṇ* (as in the case of *gargabhaginī*). Others, however, hold that when one intends to express the meaning "she drinks for the sake of the *kaccha*," [the suffix *kvip* is applied].
They say that because *kacccha* is not a causal agent (*akāraka*), the example with the prefix *pūti-* as an upapada is indeed correct.

(681) *amaivāvyayena* | 2|2|20|. [The rule] "only with an indeclinable ending in *am*" is for the purpose of restriction, since it was already established by the preceding rule. [The term] "of equal prescription" (*tulyavidhana*) refers to...
And this is obtainable through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). "That very [word]" means:
that very word which is prescribed as having *am* [as its suffix] when it occurs as an upapada is compounded with the indeclinable, and no other; such is the meaning.
This restrictive particle (*evakāra*) is obtained by the force of the rule (*niyama*), but it is not explicitly present in the sūtra itself. [The example is] *svāduṅkāram*.

The rule *vādumi ṇamul* [Pāṇini 3.4.26] states that the suffix *ṇamul* is used after a verb when followed by the word *vādu*. Why is the mention of the term "indeclinable" (*avyayena*) necessary? Consider the example *kumbhakāraḥ* ("pot-maker").
If the mention of "indeclinable" were absent, only that which is prescribed with the same conditions as *am* (the accusative case-ending) would be compounded with some other capable word.
If that were the case, the compound would occur only in *vāduṅkāraḥ*, but not in *kumbhakāraḥ*.

If it is argued that, for fear of rendering the previous sūtra redundant, this must be a restriction (niyama) specifically concerning indeclinables (*avyaya*), then why could it not be a restriction specifically concerning those ending in *am*? [The rule would be:
"A compound formed with that which ends in *ṭha* occurs only when it is prescribed by the same rule as *am*. In that case, there would be no compound in the example *agrebhojam*, because *agre*...
The intended meaning is that in the case of *bhuktvā kālo bhoktum* ("having eaten, it is time to eat"), the compound must indeed occur. What is that [time]?

It is *kālo bhoktum*, "the time to eat. By the restrictive particle *eva* in the rule *ṭham-e-va*, although compounds are prevented with an upapada that is prescribed by the same rule as *am* or by any other [suffix], [the compound] still occurs with the suffix *tumun*.
Since [the rule] would apply even to that which has an identical prescription, the phrase "that very [suffix]" was stated in order to exclude it.

(682) *Tṛtīyā-prabhṛtīny anyatarasyām* | 2|2|21|. "The suffixes beginning with the third case-ending are optional. This is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both respects; [it applies] only with the accusative (*ama*).

Because this [rule] is commenced for that which is prescribed equally by this and another rule, as well as for that which is not so prescribed. As an example of what is already prescribed (*prāpta*): "In the third case, *upadaṃśa*" (Pāṇini 6.2.39).
*mūlakenopadaṃśam* ("eating with radish"), *mūlakopadaṃśam*. As an example of what is not yet prescribed (*aprāpta*)...
For example: "In the sense of 'not expressing what was intended' (ayathābhipretākhyāna) regarding an indeclinable (avyaya), the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* [are used]," as in *uccaiḥkāram*.

Here, in the case of compounding (*samāsa*), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the *kṛt*-derived word applies—namely, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable by the rule "the first syllable of a word ending in *ṇamul* is optionally acute" (*ādir ṇamuli anyatarasyām*). However, in the case of non-compounding (*asamāsa*), [the accent is different].

They say that *uccaiḥ* has an udātta accent on the final syllable because, under the view that it is a derivative (vyutpatti-pakṣa), the accent of the suffix applies according to the rule *udi ceḍāsiḥ*, whereas under the view that it is not a derivative (avyutpatti-pakṣa), the rule *hiṣaḥ* applies. However, in the *Manoramā*, it is stated that *uccaiḥ* has an udātta accent on the final syllable because it is listed as such among the *svarādi* group.

The word "sthitam" is supplied; he says "by an amanta [word]" because the word "ṭhame" (in the sense of 'enough') is understood from the previous rule. Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *paryāpto bhoktum* ("able to eat"), where the suffix *tumun* is used according to the rule "aryāptivacaneṣu.
Also, by the rule "ktvā ca" (Pāṇini 2.2.22), [the same applies].

And [the word] *ktvā*. The word *ktvā* ends in the third case (*tṛtīyā*). Regarding the elision of *ā* (as in *kṛtvā*), Haradatta maintains that it occurs through a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) from the rule *ātaḥ*, similar to the rule *tvi skandi-syandoḥ*. That is not correct; for the status of ending in the third case is established even by means of the long vowel resulting from *savarṇa-dīrgha* (e.g., *alaṃ kṛtvā*). [The example is] *alaṃ kṛtvā*. [This is governed by the rule] *alaṃ-khalvoḥ*.
Because the rule *pratiṣedhayoḥ* precedes the rule *upadaṃśas tṛtīyāyām*, there is no compound here. [The author] now states the suffixes specific to Tatpuruṣa compounds.

(684) *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṅkhyāvyayādeḥ* |5|4|86|. Regarding the word *tatpuruṣasya*: it sets aside the rule for the final letter (*alontyavidhi*) because, by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), the rules "an affix" (*pratyaya*) and "also [the suffix] ac" (*ac ca*) apply; however, the phrase *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ* refers to the requirement of a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*).

They say that this is a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). Regarding the term *dvy-aṅgulam*: it is a compound formed according to the rule *adhitārthe*. The author of the *Vṛtti* maintains that the suffix *mātrac* is elided by the rule *vigor nityam*; however, in the *Manoramā*, it is established that the suffix *dvayasac* is elided.

The inclusion of the term *ahar* is for the sake of forming a *dvandva* compound; that is, for the purpose of a *dvandva*. The intention is that a genitive *tatpuruṣa* such as "the night of the day" (*aho rātriḥ*) is impossible. Now, one might object that since the word *ahar* can be used figuratively to mean "that which is like a day," or the word *rātri* to mean "that which is like a night," [the compound] could be "day-and-night-like. [To this we reply: it is this...

If it is argued that "rātriśca" (and night) should be understood as a *karmadhāraya* compound, we say no; for when a primary sense is possible, it is improper to resort to a secondary (*gauṇa*) sense. Furthermore, in the rule "hemanta-śiśirāv ahno-rātre ca," we observe the application of a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) in a *dvandva* [compound], which indicates that "ahorātra" is indeed a *dvandva*. Thus, it means "day and night."

In the compound *atirātrapraṇinām*, there is a singular collective formation (*ekavadbhāva*). By virtue of its higher status in the order of rules, the masculine gender prescribed by *rātrāhnāhāḥ* supersedes the neuter gender prescribed by *ana puṃsakam*. By this, the statement of earlier commentators—that the neuter gender results from the singular collective formation—is refuted. [The result is that] "by day and night" (*ahnā rātreṇa*) it would be "a day-and-night" (*ahorātraḥ*).
And because of contradictions with such passages as these: “In the entire night” (*sarvarātra*)—this is a compound formed by the rule *pūrvakālaika-*;

thus, it means “the early part of the night” (*pūrvarātra*). This is a partitive compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*) formed by the rule *pūrvāparādharottaram*. However, when one accepts that the word *rātri* (night) indicates a part [of the night] and adopts a *karmadhāraya* compound, then...

The form *pūrvarātriḥ* occurs, as does *dvirātram*. It will be stated that "a compound preceded by a numeral, ending in *rātra*, is neuter. [Regarding the rule] *ahnaṣṭakhoreva*: although this is already established by the rule *astaddhite*, this is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). The particle *eva* (only) serves to restrict it so that the suffixes *ṭa* and *kha* occur only after *ahan*.

This is for the purpose of dispelling the suspicion that there might be a contrary restriction. The thought is that if one were to dispel that suspicion by applying the rule for *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) in the rule "ātmanau khe," it would result in excessive complexity (*pratipatigaurava*) for the learner. [Question: What is the purpose of the restriction "only when followed by *akha* and *ro*" (*akhoreva*)? [Answer: [Consider] *āhnika*, derived from *ahnā nirvṛttam*. This is within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "after *āl*."

In the word *nirvṛtam*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied [by Pāṇini 4.2.95]. Because there is no elision of the *ṭi* portion, the rule "the elision of *a* after *ṭha*" (*ṭhallopo’naḥ*) does not apply; thus, the vowel *a* is not elided.
(685) [The rule] *ahnakhoreva* [Pāṇini 6.4.145 applies].

Regarding the statement "it is said to be *uttama*": in the rule "in the case of a number denoting a part of a whole" (*arvādekadeśasaṅkhyāta*), there is no substitution of *ahan* for the word *uttama*. [In the example] *dvyahīna*, because the application of the suffix *ṭac* at the end of a compound is not mandatory (*anityatva*), the suffix *ṭac* does not occur; if it were present, however, the substitution of *ahan* would necessarily follow.

And it should not be argued that the suffix *ṭac* does not apply because of the rule for the elision of *ṭi* when followed by *kha*, since that rule has its scope in cases such as *ahīna*. [The reason for this] is its non-eternality (*anityatva*). In this regard, the evidence is the inclusion of the term *ghaṭī* in the rule *aktilāṅgalāṅkuśe*. As for *madrarājñī*: if *ṭac* were applied here...

The point is that, in that case, by applying the rule "asya aḍhea— " [Pāṇini 7.3.109] for the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) and the elision of the *ṭi* suffix, the undesirable form *madrarājī* would result.
(686) *ahno ’hna etebhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.88].

*Ahno’hn etebhyaḥ*. By the word *etad* (these), those [words] situated in the rule "ahar-sarva-ekadeśa—" are referred to. In that rule, however, "ahan" and the others are specifically mentioned, and by the particle *ca*, "saṃkhyā" and "avyaya" are also drawn in. Although there is no distinction in their being present in the intellect, the word *ahan* is not included here.

It is understood [as being included] because of its impossibility; with this intention, he says, "from *sarva* and so on. The phrase "after a compound-ending suffix" (*samāsānte pare*) is obtained from the context. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the substitution of *ahn-* was rejected;

for in the commentary on the rule "the substitution of *ahn-* occurs after these [words], being an exception to the [suffixes] *ac* and *ṭc*," it is stated that "the substitution of *ahn-* occurs only before the suffixes *ṭa* and *kha*."

Since the elision of the *ṭha* suffix would not occur by the rule "niyamāṭṭilopābhāve," and because the form *sarvāhna* and others are established through the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "*ṭhallopo’naḥ*," [the following applies]:
(687) *ahno’dantāt* 8.4.7. [The substitution of *ṣat* occurs for the final phoneme of the word *ahan* when it follows a word ending in *a*.]

Regarding "from *repha*": if, however, by the etymological derivation such as "that which exists in the axle (*lakṣe akṣe bhavaḥ*)," the usage *akṣāhna* also exists, then it should be understood that [the form] *aṣāḍha* also exists, because of the governing rule *aṣābhyām*. Regarding "the elision of *ṭhan*": it is *ṭhaṇo luk*.
The sense is that [the author] considers what was stated by the author of the *Vṛtti* and others to be either correct or incorrect. He states "of the *satra*-days" (*satriyām*) as a digression.

If it is argued that here the feminine gender is difficult to obtain because of the rule "the words *rātra*, *ahna*, and *aha* are masculine," do not say so; for that statement has already been superseded by examples such as *sarvamahaḥ* and *sarvāhna*.

When a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) has been elided, the original gender does not apply; for here, the authority is the extension of gender by the rule *upi yuktavat*. If the rules governing original gender were to apply when suffixes have been elided, those rules would become redundant. For this very reason, in examples such as *lavaṇaḥ sūpaḥ* (salt soup) and *lavaṇā yavāgūḥ* (salt gruel), [the feminine suffix does not appear].

[Otherwise there would be] the fault of neuter gender. Furthermore, since the rule “*viguprāptāpanne*” and so forth prohibits [the word taking] the gender of the subsequent member (*paravalliṅgatva*), the exception to that—namely the rule “*rātrāhnāhāḥ*”—simply does not apply;
thus, this word *dvyahna* follows the gender of the substantive (*viśeṣyanighna*) alone, and is not restricted to the masculine gender. In this way...

And here, even though the *taddhita* suffix expressing the sense of "being there" (*bhava*) has been elided, it is indeed logical that the feminine gender residing in that [base] is also expressed, according to the maxim: "When a suffix is elided, that which remains expresses the meaning of what was elided. This is the general direction. As for the form *ṭāp*: one should not think that *ṅīp* would occur here because of the ending in *ṭhañ*.

This is to be suspected, because the suffix *ṭhañ* has been elided. Nor can there be an application based on the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), because [the rule] depends on a phoneme (*varṇāśrayatvāt*).

For it is explained therein that "the feminine suffix *ṅīp* applies to that which ends in the vowel *a* belonging to the root *hañ*. Precisely for this reason, the authors of the *Vṛtti* and others have stated that even in the alternative where there is a *luk*-elision of the suffix *aṇ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply; for it is said therein: "the vowel *a* belongs to *ṭhañ*."
This is because it has already been explained. Nor should it be argued that even so, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would necessarily apply due to the presence of the suffix *ṭac*;

for since *ṭac* is a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), that which ends in it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) with respect to the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* cites "Āpiśalī" as an example for a Brāhmaṇī who studies what was taught by Āpiśali.

The suffix *ṅīp* cannot even be suspected here because of the prohibition [contained in Pāṇini 4.1.15], "not after a word ending in *ap* when it denotes a measure. Therefore, *ṭāp* alone is appropriate here. He illustrates this accordingly:
(688) "And in the case of *kṣubhna*-type words," [Pāṇini 8.4.39].

Regarding *vdyahna*: in the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra, who—having rejected the substitution of *ahna-* in the rule *ahno’hnah* and having carried forward the suffix *ac* from the rule *ac-praty-anv-ave*—explains that *ac* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ap*, the suffix *ṭāp* here is indeed beyond dispute. How then [is it explained]?

If it is argued that the usage "vdyahnī" occurs in the *Kālanirṇayadīpikā*, on this point they say: in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that lunar day (*tithi*) which has two days," the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is to be understood as being conditioned by the final letter *n*.
As for the explanatory text stating "occurring in two days (*vayorahnorbhava*"), it should be understood as merely expressing the resultant meaning.

Thus, because it is impossible for a *tatpuruṣa* compound—distinct from those beginning with numerals—to function in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*), he says "for the sake of clarity. (Pāṇini 2.4.1–2).
And [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] after *uttama* and *eka*. (Pāṇini 5.4.90).

Regarding "puṇyāham": [the author] will state that the neuter gender applies by the rule "puṇyasudinābhyām. Regarding the phrase "even of the penultimate": just as in the case of "rathamayaḥ," where both the first and second [vowels] are understood due to the dual-number indication, so it is here as well.

By the force of including the word *uttama*, the last two [stages] are understood. Their intention is that in the analysis (*vigraha*) "the two *uttamas* and one," the dual number is used according to Vedic usage (*sautra*).
(690) Pāṇini 5.4.93: *uraso 'grākhyāyām*.

In the sense of "called foremost" (*agrākhyāyām*). This is a locative case used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe saptamī*). "Foremost" (*agram*) means principal (*pradhānam*). The suffix *ṭac* shall be applied to a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in the word *uraḥ*, provided that the word *uraḥ* denotes something foremost. Why say "in the sense of called foremost"? [Consider: *devadattasyoraḥ* (Devadatta’s chest); here it is not called "foremost. *devadatoraḥ*.

(691) *grāmakauṭabhyāṃ ca takṣṇaḥ* ||5.4.95|| [The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *grāma* and *kauṭa* when followed by *takṣan*]. The phrase *ātisaṃjñayoḥ* does not carry over here. Why say *grāme*? [To show that it is not applied in] *rājñaḥ takṣā* = *rājatakṣā*. Regarding *atiśva*: it means one who has surpassed a dog in speed.

(692) *ateḥ śunaḥ* |5|4|96|. After the word *ati*, [the feminine suffix *īk* is added] to *śvan*. For example, *atiśvī*; the meaning is "lowly. (693) *upamānād aprāṇiṣu* |5|4|97|. [The suffix *īk* is added] after a word used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), provided it does not refer to living beings.

"Ākarṣaḥ śveva": this is a compound formed according to the rule "upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ". An *ākarṣa* is a specific kind of wooden tool by which grain situated in a threshing floor (*khalādi*) is drawn out; thus it is so called because it resembles a dog (*śvā*). Why [is the word] "upamāna" (standard of comparison) used [in the rule]?
[Consider: *niḥśvā*, meaning one who has gone out from a dog (*śunaḥ*).

(694) *Uttara-mṛga-pūrvāc ca sakthnam* [Pāṇini 2.4.18]. [The compound] *phalaka-saktham* [is formed by this rule]. From this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), Mādhava maintains that a compound with an object of comparison may occur even when the word expressing the comparison is not a general term (*asāmānya-vacana*).

(695) *nāvo dvigoḥ* | Pāṇini 5.4.99. In the example *dvināvarūpaḥ*, the suffix *rūpya* is applied by the rule *hetumanuṣyebhyaḥ*. In the example *pañcanauḥ*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied in the sense of price (*ārhīya*), and its elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule *adhyardhapūrva-*. [The same applies] to *khāryāḥ*. [The word] *dvigoḥ* [is understood].
The meaning is: [the suffix applies] after a *dvigu* compound ending in the word *khārī*.
(696) From *ardha* as well [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied]. Thus, *ardhakhārī*; its feminine gender is established by the rule “*aravalliṅgam*” (it takes the same gender as its base).

(697) *khāryāḥ prācām* |5|4|101|. [The suffix *ṭac* is added after *khārī* in a *dvigu* compound according to the Eastern grammarians. For example: *arddhakhāram*. Neuter gender is due to common usage, as in the case of *arddhanāvam*. It may optionally take the suffix *ṭac* in a *dvigu* compound. Why "in a *dvigu* compound"? Consider: two *añjalis* = *dvyañjaliḥ*.

(698) *dvitribhyāmañjaleḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.102]. The form *dvyañjalam* is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*). The restriction "provided there is no elision of a *taddhita* suffix" (*ataddhitaluki*) applies here as well; this should be understood from the preceding rule as well. In the example *añjalibhyāṃ krītaḥ*, the word *añjali* [is not used in its primary sense].

It does not mean two hands, because that [measure] cannot constitute a price; rather, what is intended is rice or other grain measured by a handful (*añjali*). Consequently, because it is a measure, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied in the term *ūrdhvāñjali*. However, by the rule "when preceded by *adhyardha*," there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix.

(699) *brahmaṇo jānapadākhyāyām* |5|4|104|. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *brahman* when it denotes a country (*jānapada*). [The term] *jānapadaḥ* means "that which exists in a country. The mention [of the word *jānapada*] is of the nature of a state (*bhāvapradhāna*), as in the rule *vye kayoḥ*; and by proximity, it is understood that this applies when there is a compound (*samāsa*) denoting its name (*ākhyā*).

Thus he says: "In brief, [it refers to] a person from the countryside (jānapada). When there is an expectancy as to whose [it is], "Brāhmaṇa" is understood due to proximity. For example: *surāṣṭrabrahma*. This compound is formed by the rule "aptamī" through a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*). Why say "from the countryside"? [Consider: *devabrahmā* Nārada.
(700) *kumāra* optionally [takes the suffix *ṭac*] when followed by *bhada*. Thus, *kubrahma*. Here, the word *brahman* is a synonym for *brāhmaṇa*.

(701) [The substitution of *at* for the final vowel of the first member occurs] before a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) or before the suffix *jātīya*, provided that the first member is not *mahat*.

Regarding the rule *ānmahataḥ*: the letter *t* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) and not for the purpose of indicating a universal replacement (*sarvādeśārtha*). Thus he says: "The vowel *ā* shall be the final substitute. Here, within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), the "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) is implied. And since that [prior member] is qualified by the word *mahat*, the rule of application to what ends with that term (*tadantavidhi*) is obtained.

Since it has been stated that the prohibition "rahaṇavatā" applies specifically to the domain of suffix rules (*pratyayavidhi*), the usage *atimahābāhuḥ* (one with exceedingly long arms) is valid— just as *mahābāhuḥ* is. However, in the expression *paramamahatparimāṇam*, it means "the dimension of a substance that is supremely great."
The elders maintain that since a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* is accepted [in this case], there is no possibility of the substitution of *ā* (ātvaprasakti) therein.

As for what Vardhamāna stated— that because of the force of the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) regarding the extension of the rule to those ending in those words (*tadantavidhi*) in the context of the governing heading of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapadādhikāra*) in the rule *iṣṭakeṣīkāmālānām*— [the substitution does not apply].

The claim that "there is no *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a rule to that which ends with the specified element), and therefore there is no substitution of *āt* for *paramamahat*" contradicts both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa. For instance, in the Bhāṣya on the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya*,
under the heading of *pada*, it is stated as an intended purpose (*prayojana*) that [the rule applies to] *iṣṭakacitam* and *pakveṣṭakacitam*.

This has been stated, and Kaiyaṭa has explained that by the word *pada*, the final member (*uttarapada*) is understood. This very point is recorded in the *Kāśikā* according to its meaning; however, there is no supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) by Kātyāyana regarding the sūtra *iṣṭakeṣīkā-*. But [one might object]: "In the case of a compound mentioned by its specific form (*pratipadokta*),..."

One might ask: "Since the substitution of *āt* should occur only when that very [word] follows another [word], and not elsewhere, what is the purpose of this mention of 'having the same referent' (*samānādhikaraṇa*)? To this he says: "mahābāhuḥ" (long-armed). The point is that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, and because it is formed by a general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*), it is considered *lākṣaṇika* (derived from a technical rule). [The example for] *aṣṭanaḥ kapāla*...
Thus: when *kapāla* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) or when *havis* (sacrificial oblation) is to be expressed, the substitution of *āt* for *aṣṭan* must be stated; this is the meaning.

In the case of *aṣṭākapāla*, the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed by] "the suffix *aṇ* is applied after words ending in *saṃskṛta* and *bhakṣa*" is elided by [the rule] "there is elision of *aṇ* when the word has a *vigraha* [indicating a derivative], except in the sense of a descendant. As for the explanation given by some that there is elision of *aṇ* by [the rule] "after a word preceded by *adhyardha*," [that is not correct].
[The form] *prāmādika* [is incorrect], because the suffix *aṇ* is not included among those that undergo substitution (*āhīya*).
(702) *trestrayaḥ* | 6.3.48 | Regarding *trestrayaḥ*: because of the reading *trayodaśī* in the list beginning with *saṃdhivelādi*, this substitute [traya] ends in a sibilant (*sānta*).
He says [this] while suggesting: "There would be three," meaning that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of the suffix *su*.
The remainder [of the rule] is "by the rule beginning with *aṅkhyāyāvyaye*" (Pāṇini 2.2.25).

(703) Regarding "one and so forth" (*ekādi*), the analysis is *ad-ug*. However, the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) does not occur due to the force of the phonetic articulation (*uccāraṇasāmarthya*).

It occurs [in the forms] *bhavati* and *dhāsu vā*. Here, only the suffix *dhā*, prescribed by the rule “*aṅkhyāyā vidhārthe*” etc., is intended; this is according to the paribhāṣā “*apratyayaḥ pratyayagrahaṇe*”.
Therefore, it does not apply here: *ṣaḍdhā*, meaning “she places six,” which is formed with the suffix *ka* by the rule “*āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*” and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

The substitution of *u* for the vowel of *ṣaṣ* occurs before the words *dat*, *tṛ*, and *daśat*; furthermore, the substitution of *ṭh* and *ūṭh* for the initial consonants of these [subsequent] words should be stated, and this is optional before *dhā*.

Thus, *ṣoḍan*. [Derivation: "one who has six teeth" (*ṣaḍ dantā asya*) is *ṣoḍan*. By the rule "in the sense of age, the word *danta* [is replaced by *dat*]," there is the substitute *dat*. (704) *tatpuruṣayoḥ* |2|4|26|.

The term *paravalliṅga* [is used here]. In this context, the *dvandva* in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is intended, not the *dvandva* in the sense of collective aggregation (*samāhāra*), because the exception "the neuter" (*a napuṃsakam*) will be stated later. In the sūtra, the expression "*dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ*" is not the locative dual; for if it were so, then in the case of a *dvandva*...
Furthermore, in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, if the gender of the subsequent member were extended to the preceding member—

since the subsequent member, being a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*), implies the preceding member— then in the case of *mayūrī-kukkuṭau*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the elision of the long *ī* in the preceding member. [The result would be] *kukkuṭa-mayūryau*.
However, in cases such as *ardhapippalī*, a feminine suffix would arise in the first member [of the compound].
But with the intention that it is a genitive dual, he says: "of these two.
This means: of the meanings of the *dvandva* and the *tatpuruṣa*. And thus, even in the subsequent usage (*anuprayoga*), that same gender [is maintained].

Success! With the intention that, since the genitive case is admitted for the object of comparison (*upameya*), the suffix *vat* likewise follows only from a word ending in the genitive, he says: "as if [the suffix were added] to the subsequent word. However, in the Bhāṣya, this is rejected by the statement:
"Gender is not to be prescribed, because gender depends on worldly usage."

Regarding this rejection [of gender], by the same logic, the entire teaching on gender (*liṅga*) is rejected; nevertheless, that is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), for otherwise it would follow that grammar itself is useless.
A prohibition must be stated regarding *dvigu*, *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alam-pūrva*, and *gati* compounds.

Regarding the phrase "in *gati* compounds," the mention of *gati* is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the particles beginning with *pra*, since a primary *gati* (as a verbal prefix) is impossible [in this context]. With this intention, he provides the example: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*.

Regarding the term *atantram*: the evidence (*liṅga*) for this is the inclusion of the word "as before" (*pūrvavat*). The sense is that otherwise, since the form would be established by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) alone, what would be the purpose of that [inclusion]? Here, either the gender of the compound's meaning is extended as before, or the gender of the second member's meaning; in both cases, however, [the forms] are *aśvavaḍavau*.
Even when used in conjunction with *śobhanau*, the masculine gender is established. Now, one might object:

even if the referent of the compound is masculine, since the feminine nature residing in its own substratum has not been removed, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of hearing the suffix *ṭāp*. Nor is the extended application (*atideśa*) useless, because it serves to trigger the substitution of *n* for *s* in the case of the *śas* ending during the subsequent usage (*anuprayoga*).

If it is argued that this [feminine suffix] is purposeful because it achieves the status of the masculine gender, they say in response: its disappearance occurs either through the specific irregularity (*nipātana*) in this very rule, or through the irregularity in the rule "aśvavaḍavapūrvāparādharottarāṇām" (Pāṇini 2.4.12), which effects the removal of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

(705) *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi* [Pāṇini 2.4.29]. Regarding the term *ahorātra*: although the Easterners have cited *ahorātram* as an example, it has already been stated previously that this is not correct. On this point, they say: by the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ*, only words beginning with *rātri* [are intended].
Masculinity is prescribed [for the compound]. However, for that which ends in such a suffix, it is established by the rule *aravalliṅgam* alone.
Therefore, because they apply to different domains (*bhinnaviṣayatva*), the principle *vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam* (“when there is a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails”) does not apply.
And thus, since masculinity does not apply by the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ*, in a collective compound (*samāhāra*)...
"It becomes neuter" is said because this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the gender of a compound being that of the final member. That is not correct;

for, according to the reasoning already stated, it would follow that compounds such as *dvyaha* and *tryaha* would also be neuter. Nor is this desired, since [the term] *dvyahastryaha* has been cited by the ancient commentators (*prāc*), which contradicts their own foundational text.
Because it would result in a contradiction, and because it would contradict the lexicon (kośa) which states, “thirty such [units] constitute a day-and-night” (*triṃśadahorātraḥ*), and so forth.

Therefore, the rule for the masculine gender applies only to that which begins and ends with night (*rātri*) and so on, due to the introductory heading “in the case of dvandva and tatpuruṣa compounds”; and thus, since there is no lack of difference in their scope, the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ* [applies].
Masculinity indeed subverts the neuter gender resulting from the collective compound by virtue of its higher priority.

Regarding the rule "A night preceded by a numeral is neuter," the phrase "preceded by a numeral" refers here to the rule on gender instruction which states: "The words *pathin*, *puṇyāha*, and a night preceded by a numeral are neuter."

Root text: In the case of the apprehension of numbers, the maxim regarding artificial (*kṛtrima*) and non-artificial (*akṛtrima*) [terms] does not apply; this is with the intention that the term *aśīti* (eighty) is excluded in the rule *dvy-aṣṭanaḥ saṅkhyāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.47). With this in mind, he provides the example: *dvirātram*.
Regarding the term *gaṇarātram*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "a collection of many nights" (*gaṇānāṃ bahūnāṃ rātrīṇāṃ samāhāraḥ*).
(706) *Apatham* is neuter [when it denotes a distance]. 2.4.30.

*Apatha* is neuter. [The rule] applies only when it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound; however, the mention of *dvandva* does not follow here, because it is inappropriate—this is the sense. In the case of *apanthāḥ*, there is an optional application of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) by the rule *atho vibhāṣā*. This sūtra could have been omitted; for [the form] *athaḥ*...
Because the meaning is already established by the forthcoming *vārttika*, "after a numeral and an indeclinable," he states [the following] as an incidental point: (707) *ardharcāḥ puṃsi ca* 2.4.31.

Regarding the term *ardharca* (half-verse): here, for some words, the grammatical status is determined by a difference in meaning. And that determination is as follows: the word *madhu* is of two genders when denoting liquor, nectar, or honey;
it is masculine when denoting the month of Caitra and others; and it is of two genders when denoting a ghost or a goblin (*piśāca*).
