However, that which expresses an action (*kriyāvacana*) is to be understood as being [governed] by the gender of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), according to the specific case. Between the two rules "ardharcāḥ puṃsi ca" (A 2.4.31) and "a napuṃsakam" (A 2.4.30), the connection of the four-sūtra sequence beginning with "ābādhyākhyāyām" (A 2.4.34) must be considered here. The term *bahuvacanam* means the expression or presentation of many.
With the intention that the extended application (*atideśa*) does not bear fruit here because of the explanation [already given], he says:
(708) *Jātyākhyāyām ekasmin bahuvacanam anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.58). "Even a single object may optionally take the plural. And thus, it is established even by way of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
He provides an illustration while suggesting [the underlying principle]: "Brāhmaṇas are to be honored. What is the purpose of the term *jātyākhyāyām* ("when denoting a genus")?

[Example: Devadatta and Yajñadatta. What is the purpose of the term *ekasmin* ("in the singular")? [Example: rice and barley (*vrīhi-yavau*). [In the rule] *asmado dvayośca*, the phrase *cāt* ("and also") and *ekasmin bahuvacanam anyatarasyām* ("optionally the plural in the singular") are understood to carry over.
This is what he says: "When unity or duality is intended," and so forth.

(709) Regarding the rule *phalgunī-proṣṭhapadānāṃ ca nakṣatre* 1.2.60: [the commentary] states "of *phalgunī* and *proṣṭhapada*" because the word *ca* ("and") draws in the notion of duality; hence he says "in the case of duality."

Regarding the form *phalgunyau māṇavike* ("two girls born under Phalgunī"): from the word *phalgunī*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *akṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*. This suffix is elided (*lup*) by the rule *lub aviśeṣe*. Then, for the sense of "born under" (*jātārtha*), the suffix *ṭān* is applied by the rule *phalgunyaṣāḍhābhyāṃ ṭānau*. Because it has the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. And this [application] is not figurative (*gauṇa*).

Because it is etymologically derived [from the word *nakṣatra*]. Thus, the intention is that by the application of the principle of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*), the inclusion of the asterisms is necessary.
(710) In a copulative compound (*dvandva*) consisting of *tiṣya* and *punarvasū*, the dual number necessarily replaces the plural number.

[1|2|63] *tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ*. [The examples are] *viśākhānurādhāḥ* and *tiṣyapunarvasavaḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) of the former is *viśākhe ca anurādhāśca* ("Viśākhā and Anurādhā"). For *tiṣyapunarvasavaḥ*, it is the same as before by means of the words *tiṣya* and *punarvasu*.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "akṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.3), and its elision (*lup*) occurs by the rule "lubaviśeṣe" (Pāṇini 4.2.4). Thereafter, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "born therefrom" (*jāta*) by the rule "saṃdhivelādi-sūtra" (Pāṇini 4.3.16), but that suffix is elided by the rule "raviṣṭhā-phalgunī-anurādhā-... (Pāṇini 4.3.34). This occurs while the word "nakṣatre" (in the sense of a lunar mansion) is still being carried over [as an adhikāra].

The repetition of the term "nakṣatra" (asterism) is for the purpose that the rule may also apply to synonyms; such is the intention. And thus, forms such as *tiṣyapunarvasū* are also established; this is the direction [of the analysis]. What is the purpose of the plural number? [Answer: This [form] *tiṣyapunarvasu* [is an example]; it is a collective dvandva compound according to the rule "dvandva in the sense of 'artha'."

(711) *sa napuṃsakam* | 2|4|17|. This [compound] is neuter. The maxim *anantarasya* (the rule applies to what is immediately preceding) is not resorted to here; with the intention that otherwise the inclusion of *dvi-gu* would not occur, he says: "the *dvi-gu* and the *dvandva*. In this regard—

They explain: since the object to be referred to (anuvādya) is obtained from the context itself, the inclusion of the word "a" is for the purpose of including even a collective dvandva compound that falls within this context; by this, forms such as "ajñāparibhāṣam" are established. As for "pañcagavam": [it is formed according to Pāṇini 2.4.2].

In the phrase beginning with *addhitārtha*, there is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). In *dantoṣṭham*, there is a *dvandva* compound in the sense of a collective aggregate according to the rule *dvandvaśca prāṇi-* etc.; alternatively, it may end in the feminine suffix *āp*. In *pañcakhaṭvam*, the neuter short vowel [is applied]. [And] *pañcakhaṭvī*.

Since the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasva*) applies when there is feminine gender (*strītva*) due to the word ending in *ā*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *dvigor īp*.

Regarding the rule *ano nalopaś ca vā dviguḥ striyām*: the intention is that the elision of the *n* of *an* would not otherwise apply because of the prohibition of *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa* (the application of rules based on a suffix) by the rule *utarapadatve cāpadādividhau*. Thus, since the condition for the elision of *n* is not met, it is optional.

Here, the word *vā* (or) is connected with the rule *striyām*, and not with the preceding one. Therefore, he states that the elision of *n* is compulsory in cases such as *pañcatakṣam*. Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in *pātra* etc.," the word "femininity" (*strītvam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words). It is desired that the word *ahar* (day) takes the neuter gender when preceded by *puṇya* and *sudin*. Thus, *sudināhaṃ*. Here, the word *sudi* is a synonym for "excellent" (*praśasta*). As it is said: "In auspicious times (*udināsu samāsu*), one should especially investigate this matter."
This is because of the usage beginning with "svayaṃ ca" and so forth.

Regarding the rule "pathaḥ saṅkhyāvyayādeḥ": the meaning is "from that which begins with a numeral or an indeclinable. Thus, in the cases *trapathaṃ* and *vipathaṃ*, the suffix *ap* is applied according to the rule "ṛkpūrabdhūḥ".

Regarding the words *supanthāḥ* and *atipanthāḥ*, there is a prohibition against the application of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsanta*) by the rule *na pūjanāt*. If it is asked, "How then is it that Amara states: 'vyadhva, duradhva, vipatha, tadadhvā, and kāpatha are synonyms'?", many scholars maintain that this is simply an error. However, in the *Manoramā*, it says: "Now... [and so forth].

From the root *gati* (to go), with the addition of the *ac* suffix (*pacādyac*), there exists the word *patha*, derived as "that which goes" or "that which pervades. Accordingly, the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa* states: "The words *vāṭa*, *patha*, and *mārga* are synonyms for road. Therefore, when compounded with that word *patha*, the masculine gender is justified. And it is not thus...

It should not be argued that even if *vipatha* were established, *kāpatha* would not be possible because the substitution of *ka-* is difficult to obtain; for it is established that such a possibility exists by virtue of the rule *ṭhīṣadarthe ca*, since [the sense of] censure is ultimately implied by the meaning. However, some maintain that according to the Vārttika *ṭhpathaḥ saṃkhye*, [the suffix applies] only to that which has already undergone the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*).

They say that because there is no basis for the inclusion [of the word *vipatha*] here—since it does not end in the suffix *ac* added after the root *paci*—the usage *vipathaḥ* and *kāpathaḥ* is indeed difficult to justify.

On this point, Mādhava states: "Because it is an exception to the rule regarding gender following the subsequent member (*paravalliṅga*), this [rule] applies only to *tatpuruṣa* compounds and not elsewhere."

*vipathā nagarī* (the city beyond the path). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. *Atipathā* means "having gone beyond the paths. Here too, [the neuter gender does not apply], because by the rule beginning with *viguprāpta*, the application of the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*) is prohibited. [The word *patha*] is neuter when used in a general sense. Regarding the statement "it is neuter in a general sense": [this refers to the fact that the base form *patha* is neuter when it denotes a thing in general].

This [rule] concerns words whose gender is not fixed. Therefore, in *ādiṃ pacati* and *prātarādiḥ*, the masculine gender alone is used. In *mṛdu pacati*, it ends in the accusative because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
For, with respect to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) inherent in the verbal root, the aspect of the result (*phalāṃśa*) becomes the object (*karman*). And thus:

The accusative case occurs when there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the fruit (*phala*). For this very reason, in examples such as *sakṛllvāv*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs because it is preceded by a *kāraka*. However, where a specific meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), the qualifiers of that [instrument] must necessarily end in the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*).
This is just as in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. This point is made clear in both the Vṛtti and the Padamañjarī on the sūtra *araṇe yajaḥ*.

(712) *tatpuruṣo’nañkarmadhārayaḥ* || 2.4.19 || [A Tatpuruṣa compound that is not preceded by the negative particle *naÑ* and is not a Karmadhāraya is neuter when its final member is a word denoting time.]

The meaning of the sūtra is this: a *tatpuruṣa* compound that is not a negative (*nañ*) compound—that is, distinct from both *nañ*-compounds and *karmadhāraya* compounds—partakes of the grammatical operations to be described hereafter. (713) *upajñopakramaṃ tadādyācikhyāsāyām* | 2|4|21|. [In such a case, the neuter singular ending is used when there is a desire to express that the thing denoted by the compound is the beginning of that which follows.]

*Upajña*: it is called *upajñā* because it is first known (*upajñāyate*). By the rule *ṭhātaścopasarge*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied to form the object [denoting the first knower]. *Upakrama*: it is begun (*upakramyate*), thus *upakrama*. The suffix *ghañ* is applied to denote the object; by the rule *oditopadeśasya*, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi*.
"The first discovery" (*upajñā*) and "the beginning" (*upakrama*) form a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). And that [compound] follows what is being discussed...
This is an adjective of the *tatpuruṣa* compound. By the word "that" (*tat*), the terms "invention" (*upajñā*) and "commencement" (*ādi*) are referred to.

Having intended all of this, he says: "ending with 'invention' (*upajñānta*)," and so forth. The desire to explain is "the wish to tell" (*ācikhyāsā*); here, it is the very intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) that governs the application of a word, and not—

Thus, the actual state of affairs is made known. By this, even such expressions as *saudanyopakramam* ("beginning with kindness") are established. Regarding *pāṇineḥ*: the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Regarding *nandopakramam*:
the analysis (*vigraha*) is *nandasya upakramam*.

(714) *Chāyā* [is used] when there is abundance. 2|4|22. "When there is abundance" means that a Tatpuruṣa compound ending in *chāyā* is formed when it expresses a shadow that exists in abundance. In this case, of what is there abundance?

In response to this inquiry, since shadow is caused by an obscuring substance, it is understood that [the shadow] increases when that [substance] is abundant. With the intention that this obscuring agent is indeed a substance belonging to the preceding category, he says: "when there is an abundance of the preceding substance."

What is the purpose of [the rule regarding] the abundance of the meaning of the first member? *kuḍaḷasya chāyā* = *kuḍaḷchāyā*. It should be understood that this is a case of phonetic fusion (*praśleṣa*).
Some, however, read it as *ikṣucchāyaniṣādinyaḥ*.
(715) *sabhā rājāmanuṣyapūrvā* | 2|4|23|. [The word *sabhā* is feminine when preceded by a word denoting a king or something other than a human.]
Regarding "sabhā-inasabham" and so forth: here the word *ina* is a synonym for "king" (*rājan*) as well as for "lord" (*īśvara*). Now, one might object:
"Since of the rule *vaṃ rūpam*, it is proper to take the word 'king' itself and not its synonym," to which he replies:

It is accepted as belonging to the *paryāya* (synonym) alone; by the word "alone" (*eva*) in the phrase "it is accepted as belonging to the *paryāya*," the exclusion of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) is intended. How then is it [to be explained] in the *Kīcakavadha* passage: "He went to the assembly of the lord of Ṛṣis, not trembling"? On this point, some say: [the compound] is a *bahuvrīhi*, meaning "that assembly in which there is no lord."

They say that since the *karmadhāraya* compound is formed first and then [the suffix is added], the word does not become neuter, because of the rule "not after *nañ* in a *karmadhāraya*" (*ṭhanañkarmadhārayaḥ*). However, Rakṣita says: "Just like 'lord of elephants' (*gajapati*), 'king' (*nṛpati*) is also a specific type of king; therefore, there is no inconsistency here."

(716) *aśālā ca* |2|4|24|. And [the word] *aśālā*. The word *sabhā* denotes both a "hall" (*śālā*) and an "assembly" (*saṅghāta*). In that context, it was stated that when preceded by a word denoting a king or a human being, the word *sabhā* retains its feminine gender if it denotes a hall; however, by this [rule], [it is stated otherwise].
He says "it is prescribed for those denoting a collection" (*saṅghātavācinaḥ*) and explains: "referring to the meaning of a collection" (*saṅghātārtha*).

(Pāṇini 2.4.25) *vibhāṣā senāsurācchāyāśālāniśānām*. Regarding *vibhāṣā senā*: the genitive case is used in the sense of the first member [of a compound], and thus the *tatpuruṣa* is qualified by *senā* and the others.
By means of the qualifier, there is an application of the rule *tadantavidhi* (the inclusion of that which ends with it); thus he says, "ending with this. Regarding the term *śvaniśam*:
it refers to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇacaturdaśī*). On that day, it is said that some dogs fast;
and this is clearly stated in the *Śābarabhāṣya* in the section concerning animals (*tiryagadhikaraṇa*).

The purpose of the governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*) beginning with "atpuruṣa" applies here alone, and not to the group of five rules beginning with "aṃjñāyāṃ kanthośīnareṣu," because neither a non-*tatpuruṣa* nor a *nañ*-compound can possibly occur there; this is established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*). And likewise...

He provides a counter-example: *dṛḍhasena* and so forth. Now, one might object: "In a *bahuvrīhi*, it is indeed logical that the gender of the word should agree with the gender of the final member (*viśeṣya*); so what is the purpose of this mention of the *tatpuruṣa*? Do not say so. For a direct rule (*vacana*) is more powerful than mere logic (*nyāya*). Furthermore, if that [mention of the *tatpuruṣa*] were not present, [the rule would apply] even to a *dvandva*.

Neuter gender would [apply] because this [rule] is an exception to the general rule of following the gender of the subsequent word (paravalliṅga), and because this section is a topical discussion (prakaraṇavāda); such is the direction [of the argument]. Thus ends the Tatpuruṣa compound.

(1187) *prāgvahateṣṭhak* [Pāṇini 4.4.1]: "The suffix *ṭhak* is added before [the rule for] *vaha*. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is made for [words beginning with] *māśabda* etc., in the sense of 'he says that' (*tadāheti*). Regarding 'he says that': this rule for the suffix is applied to sentences; one who prohibits [someone] saying 'let there be no sound' (*mākārīti śabdaḥ*) [is called a *māśabdika*]."

It is called *āśabdika*. Likewise, one who says "sound is eternal" is an *aityaśabdika* or an *āryaśabdika*. Here, a second case ending cannot occur after the word because it is not a nominal stem (*apratipadika*). Therefore, by that word, the mere object (*karmamātra*) is indicated; and that—

They say that it takes the form of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). Regarding the example *aijya syāt*: although the augment *aij* would have been obtained by the rule *ayvābhyām*, its introduction is prohibited by this [present rule], because the negative particle (*nañ*) is understood from the preceding rule *a karmaṇi*.
(1188) And [the augment is not applied] after *svāgata* and so forth: Pāṇini 7.3.7.

Regarding the word *svāpateyam*: [the rule] "after *svapati* when meaning 'dwelling' or 'guest,' the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied" applies. Because the word *sva-* belongs to the *dvārādi* group, the substitution of *aij* (i.e., *ai* for *a*) would otherwise apply. However, the result of its inclusion in the *dvārādi* group is that one should know that in the sense of "belonging to oneself," as in *svasyedam*, the form is *auvam*.

Regarding the rule *āhau prabhūtādibhyaḥ*: the term *āhau* refers to the word *āha*. The phrase "an addition (*upasaṅkhyānam*)" is understood to follow here. In the word *āha*, the portion that constitutes the base (*prakṛtibhāga*) is reproduced as *āhā* by means of an adventitious *iK* vowel [to form *āhi*]. In the example *prābhūtikaḥ*, the suffix is applied to an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) when the speaker is intended.

(1189) *tena dīvyati khanati jayati jitam* || 4.4.2 || [He plays with that, digs with that, wins with that, or has been won by that. Regarding *tena dīvyati*: here, time, person, and number are not intended to be expressed;
thus, from *akṣaiḥ adīvyat*, *deviṣyati*, or *akṣaiḥ dīvyati*, the form *ākṣikaḥ* ("one who plays with dice") is derived.

Thus, one who plays with dice is called *ākṣika*—as in "you will play," "I will play," "they play," "you play," or "we play. However, the agent (*kartṛ*) is indeed intended [to be expressed], because the agent and the object are mentioned separately in the forms "he plays" (*ayati*) and "won" (*jitam*). Therefore, it is said: "played with dice" (*akṣairdyūtaḥ*) and "gambled with dice" (*akṣaiḥ khātaḥ*).

In the sense of "prepared for" (*saṃskṛta*) with respect to an object such as food, [the suffix] does not apply; thus, one does not say *ākṣika* [in the sense of "prepared for dice"]. Regarding *abhri*: Amara states, "The word *abhri* is feminine and denotes a wooden hoe.

Sanskrit: The analysis of the *yoga* (separation of rules) is for the sake of what follows. In the rule *bāhukā*, the letter *ṣ* is *sāṃhitika* (belonging to the phonetic combination), not an *anubandha* (indicatory letter);

therefore, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply. Accordingly, the author will recite at the end of the section the *Ślokavārttika* beginning with "from *ākarṣa*, *parpa*, etc. (*ākarṣātparpādeḥ*) for the purpose of distinguishing those [bases] marked with *ṣ*.
"Nikaṣopala" means a touchstone for the purpose of testing gold. (1191) "Ṣṭhal after *ākṛṣ*" [Pāṇini 4.4.9].
"It is a variant reading"—this is found in the *bhvādi* class within the series beginning with "aṣakhaṣa."

Mādhava has proposed [the reading] "ṭhākarṣāt ṣṭhaḷ iti," but this is inconsistent with the Vārttika "ṭhākarṣāt parpādeḥ. For in that case, if the reading were without the *repha* (r), there would be the undesirable consequence (*asaṅgaprasaṅga*) of [the suffix] *vṛt*.

(1192) *parpādibhyaḥ ṣṭhan* | Pā. 4.4.10. Regarding *parpa*: it is derived from the root *arp* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*). By the rule *halaśca*, the suffix *ghañ* is added to form the noun. Here, there is an internal group-rule (*antargaṇasūtra*) stating *ādaḥ pace*. From the two feet he moves: *padikaḥ*. As for the Vārttika regarding the substitution of *ad*...

The rule "there is an addition [of the suffix] after *carati*" is an elaboration of this very point. [The following are the bases: *prapa*, *aśva*, *aśvattha*, *ratha*, *jāla* (*jala?*), *nyā*, *vyāla*, and *pādaḥ* [replaced by] *pat*.
(1193) After *śvagaṇa*, there is also the suffix *ṭhañ*. Pāṇini 4.4.11.
"And [the suffix] aṭṭhañ after *śvagaṇa*. [The suffix] ṭhak is not applied to words ending in *pāda*. (Pāṇini 5.2.119–120).

Regarding the rule "After *śva* etc., [the suffix] iñ" (Pāṇini 4.1.82), this very [mention of *śvagaṇa*] is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). For the word *śvan* is recited in the *dvārādi* group, but not *śvabhastra*.

The meaning is that the prohibitive rule "vāder iñ" (Pāṇini 4.1.103), being otherwise rendered redundant by examples such as *śvadaṃṣṭra*, serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the application of the rule regarding the inclusion of the initial element (*tadādividhi*) in cases like *dvāra*. The result, however, is that in forms such as *dvārapālasyāyam* = *auddārapālaḥ*, the substitution of *aij* (i.e., *ai* and *au*) takes place.

It should be stated as "when [the suffix] begins with the vowel *i*. This means that in the rule, one should remove the word *iñ* and read it as "when beginning with *i*. Others, however, suggest that instead of *iñ*, one should read *it*. In this way, since the suffix implied by the term *aṅga* (stem) becomes the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
They say that by the rule "that which has an injunction applies to what precedes it," an initial *i* is obtained [for the suffix]. Thus, *śvagaṇikī*:
because the suffix *ṣṭhan* has the marker *ṣ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.
(1195) *padāntasyānyatarasyām* | 7|3|9|.

Regarding *śvāpādasya*: the lengthening [of the vowel] is by the rule "it is seen in other cases as well. As for *dhāvuka*, it is read in the *vetanādi* group as *dhanurdaṇḍa*; that is intended to include both the compound and its constituent parts. Thus, *dhanurdaṇḍikaḥ* and *āṇḍikaḥ* should also be cited as examples.

(1196) *āyudhāc cha ca* | Pāṇini 4.4.14. The suffix *cha* is added after the word *āyudha*. That by which one fights is called *āyudha* (a weapon). The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule “*hañarthe kavidhānam*” (the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of the root *han*).

(1197) *haratyutsaṅgādibhyaḥ* |4|4|15|. From words such as *utsaṅga* and others ending in the third case, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "he takes up" (*upādatte*) or "he carries" (*nayati*). [The words are: *utsaṅga*, *uḍupa*, *utthita*, *piṭaka*, *piṭāka*.

(1198) *bhastrādibhyaḥ ṣṭhan* | Pāṇini 4.4.16. The suffix *ṣṭhan* is added after words beginning with *bhastrā*. *Bhastrā* is a product made of leather. The word *śīrṣabhāra* is included here; the change to *śīrṣa-* occurs by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). These are locative compounds (*saptamī-samāsa*), and the elision of the case-ending does not occur due to the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti*.
In the alternative view, there is *īrṣabhāraḥ*.

(1199) Regarding [Pāṇini 4.4.17] *vibhāṣā vivadhāt*, the Vārttika states: "It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after *vivadha* as well, on the basis of the principle that 'a word remains the same even when a part of it is modified' (*ekadeśavikṛtasya*)."

The sense is that this is intended merely to state a meaning already established by logic. However, the author of the Vṛtti, having inserted the word *vīva* into the sūtra, recited it as: "vibhāṣā vivadha-vīvadhāt.
(1200) *tremamnityam* || 4.4.20 ||
The word *tri* [is used] with the suffix *nityam*. The inclusion of the term *nityam* is to preclude its independent usage.

For this very reason, in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) of common usage, there is the employment of *tiṅnadīnām*, but not of *treḥ*; thus he says: "accomplished by means of a kṛtya. Likewise, in what follows, [one says] "accomplished by means of cooking" (*pākena nirvṛtam*).

The analysis (*vigraha*) should be understood as follows: the word *tri* here is not taken in its sense of a number, because when there is a choice between a suffix and a non-suffix, the suffix alone is selected, and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule "of the three [roots] beginning with *ṭh* and *ṇij*" (*ṭhṇijāṃ trayāṇām*).
Now, one might object: by the inclusion of the word *nitya*, when there is a desire to express the meaning of "being accomplished" (*nirvṛta*), even without the suffix *map*.

If it is argued that even when the application of the suffix *tri-pratyaya* is prohibited, its independent usage remains unavoidable when that suffix is not intended to be expressed, we say: no. By dividing the rule into the two distinct yogas, "iti" and "am," the power of the latter [the second yoga] prevents its independent usage precisely by disregarding any specific meaning.

Regarding *imab*: it should be applied in this manner. The suffix *imab* should be stated as following those words ending in a *bhāva*-suffix (abstract noun suffix). For instance: "after [a word] ending in a *bhāva*-suffix, *imab*" [is added], and then "the *r* is elided" (*reḥ*). Since this is already established by the preceding rule, this present rule is for the purpose of restriction: that *imab* applies only in the domain of [words] ending in three suffixes.
Thus, by this [rule], the application of that which ends in *tripatyaya* is excluded. Then there is *ityam*.

By this, even when the sense of being produced (*nirvṛta*) is not intended to be expressed, the independence of that which ends in *tri* is prevented. And in this way, there is no suspicion at all of the word *tri* being taken as denoting a number.

This is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "after [stems] ending in the affixes *hāv* and *pratyaya*. There is also no difference in accent; for by the *anudātanivṛtti-svara*, the vowel *i* in *ima-p* becomes acute (*udātta*).
(Pāṇini 4.4.21: *apamityayācitābhyāṃ kakkanau*.
Regarding *apamitya*: by the rule *udīcāṃ māṅaḥ*, there is a *gati*-compound with the suffix *ktvā*; *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*.

By the rule *ayater id anyatarasyām*, the vowel *i* is substituted; then, by the rule *hrasvasya*, the augment *tuk* is added. From this form ending in *lyap* and in the third case, the suffix does not occur; rather—
[The suffix] is applied only after a word ending in the nominative case, because of the [grammatical] statement.

(1202) *vyañjanair upasikte* (Pāṇini 4.4.26). Regarding *vyañjanair upa*: that by which the flavor (*rasa*) of rice and other such foods is manifested (*vyajyate*) is called *vyañjana*; [the suffix is applied] after words expressing that.
The suffix *ṭhak* shall be used in the sense of "addiction" (*upasakti*).
(1203) [Pāṇini 4.4.28: After the words *tat-prati-anu*, and after *īpa*, *loman*, and *kūla*, [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied].
Since the root *vṛt* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), how can there be an accusative case ending for it?

In response to the doubt as to how [the word] connects with the phrase "not contrary" (*napratīpam*) and so forth, he says: "because it is an adverbial modifier" (*kriyāviśeṣaṇatvāt*). Regarding "contrary" (*pratīpam*):
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which waters have gone toward" (*pratigatā āpo'smin*). The suffix *-a* is applied at the end of the compound by the rule *ṛkpūr*.
The substitution of *ī* [for *u*] occurs by the rule "after *vi*, *ud*, and prepositions. This is merely for the sake of etymological derivation;
for these are conventional (*rūḍhi*) words whose synonyms are *pratikūla* (adverse) and *anukūla* (favorable). Regarding the form *ānvīpika*:
in the word *anvīpa*, the substitution of *ū* [for *u*] by the rule "of *ūda*, when denoting a region" does not take place, because it is not a region (*adeśa*).

(1204) *parimukhaṃ ca* |4|4|29|. Regarding *parimukham*: since *pari* has the designation of a *karmapravacanīya* by the rule *apa-parī varjane*, the ablative case is used according to the rule *pañcamy apāṅ-paribhiḥ*. [The rule *apa-pari-bahi-rañcavo...* applies.]

The term *pañcamyāḥ* [in Pāṇini 2.1.38] forms an *avyayībhāva* compound. From that, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied. One who serves while avoiding the master’s face is called *pārimukhika*. However, when the word *pari* signifies "on all sides" (*sarvatobhāve*) and forms a *prādi-samāsa*, it refers to wherever the master’s face is directed.
Whoever behaves in such a manner is described thus. In this way, the term *pāripārśvika* (an attendant) should also be understood in two senses.
(1205) *prayacchati garhyam* | Pāṇini 4.4.30.

It provides [the following]: after a word ending in the second case (dvitīyāntāt), the suffix *ṭhak* occurs in the sense of "he gives" (*prayacchati*), provided that which he gives is censurable (*garhya*). In the case of "twofold" (*dviguṇa*), it means for the sake of a twofold amount; the intention is that the designation [of the object] is based on its being for that purpose (*tādarthyāt*). This substance is censurable because it is the object of a gift intended for the purpose of excessive increase (*bahuvṛddhi*).

It should be stated that the substitution of *vṛdhuṣi* for *vṛddhi* occurs [in the sense of one who lives by interest]. Thus, we have *vārddhuṣika*. The analysis of the compound is: *vṛddhi* means "interest";
he gives (*prayacchati*) that, hence the derivation. Now, how is it that Amarasimha says, "One who lives by interest is a *vārdhuṣi*"?
This is because the substitution of *vṛdhuṣi* is accepted as being strictly conditioned by the suffix *-ak*.

On this point, they say: "Poets are unrestrained. Why [is it] considered censurable? [It is so that] in the sense of "the debtor demands interest twice or three times over," forms such as *vaiguṇika* should not occur. (Pāṇini 4.4.31) *kusīdadaśaikādaśāt ṣṭhanṣṭhacau*. [The suffixes] *ṣṭhan* and *ṣṭhac* [are applied after the words *kusīda* and *daśaikādaśa*].

"It is elided. With the intention that for this very reason even the usage of commentators is justified, he provides an example: "ten and eleven" (*daśaikādaśān*). There is a prior placement [of *daśa*] according to the rule "the smaller number [is placed first]. "Only the creditor" (*uttamarṇa eva*)—because he gives ten and receives eleven, it is he alone [who is the creditor].
The meaning is "because it is censurable.
*Uñchati*. *Uñcha* is the gathering of individual grains that have fallen upon the ground.

(1208) *rakṣati* |4|4|33|. [The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the word *samāja* in the sense of "one who protects"]. *Samāja* means that in which people gather (*samajanti asmin*); it is a multitude. (1209) *śabdadarduraṃ karoti* |4|4|34|. [The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the compound *śabdadardura* in the sense of "one who makes a sound like a frog"].

"Produces sound" means that one explains [the word] by means of the division between base and suffix. Due to the inherent nature of verbal expression, this suffix is used specifically for the act of explaining; it is not used here in cases such as "the barbarian or the donkey produces sound. Regarding "dārdurika," the meaning is "potter"; in this context, the term refers to a musical instrument.

The word *darduraśabdaḥ* [is an example]. There is the inclusion of the actual form, its synonyms, and its specific varieties. In the case of *mātsyikaḥ*, because it is included in the list [beginning with] *matsya-ṅyām*, there is no elision of *y* according to the rule *ūry-atiṣya-*.

Regarding the term *hāriṇika*: if it is objected that this is not an example of a synonym (*paryāya*), since *hariṇa* refers to a specific type of deer, and thus no example of a synonym has been shown here—on this point they say: "Among wild quadrupeds, [the word] *hariṇa*..."
The word *mṛga* occurs [in this context]. When the word *mṛga* denotes a deer, then it certainly serves as an example of a synonym for "deer.
(1210) *paripanthaṃ ca tiṣṭhati* | Pāṇini 4.4.36.

And "paripanthaṃ": this *avyayībhāva* compound is either [treated as] *parimukha-* or it is a *tatpuruṣa*. He says "from that which ends in the second case" (*dvitīyāntāt*) because, although the root *sthā-* is intransitive when its object is an action (*kriyā*), "paripantha" is indeed its object. The particle *ca* (and) is displaced in its position.
He says that it combines for the sake of the suffix-meaning: "he stands and he kills.

(1211) *māthottarapadavyadhruvapadaṃ dhāvati* |4|4|37|. Regarding *mātha*: it is called *mātha* because it is churned (*mathyate*) by those who travel; from the root *manth* in the sense of "churning," used in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*).

The suffix *ghañ* [is applied after a verbal root] when the word *pada* follows as the final member (*uttarapada*). That compound in which the word *pada* is the final member is called *padottarapada*. However, it was not stated as "ending in *ad*" (*adanta*), so that [the suffix] would not apply after a word preceded by *bahu-*.
(Pāṇini 4.4.40: *pratikaṇṭhārthalalāmaṃ ca* [is also formed with *ghañ*].

Regarding the term *pratikaṇṭham*: it is an *avyayībhāva* compound meaning "at every throat" (*kaṇṭhaṃ kaṇṭhaṃ prati*), according to the rule “*akṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye*” (Pāṇini 2.1.14). Others say that the *prādisamāsa* (prepositional compound) *pratikaṇṭha*, meaning "that which has reached the throat," is not to be understood here, on account of the [author’s own] commentary.

(1213) *dharmaṃ carati* | Pāṇini 4.4.41. "He practices dharma. Here, the root *car* signifies habitual practice (*āsevanā*), and not mere performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). Therefore, one who has engaged in dharma by chance, even if he is ill-behaved, is not called "righteous" (*dhārmika*). For [the term refers to] habitual practice.
This is a natural inclination. Thus, one who by the force of fate has engaged in unrighteousness is not called "unrighteous" provided he follows the conduct of the virtuous.
(1214) *ṭhañ* is used after *pratipatha*. Pāṇini 4.4.42.

Regarding *pratipatham*: it is an *avyayībhāva* compound used either in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) or in the sense of facing toward (*ābhimukhya*). The suffix *ṭac* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *ṛkpū-*. (Pāṇini 2.4.29).
[The sūtra] *samavāyānsamavaiti* (Pāṇini 4.4.43): [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the word *samavāya* when the sense is "he joins together"].

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words denoting a collection (*samūha*) ending in the second case, in the sense of "he enters into" (*samavaiti*). Here, the meaning of the root *i* preceded by the prefix *sam-ava* is "becoming one part after having entered. In that context, the use of the second case in the form *samavāyāt* is in reference to the entry, which is subordinate to the whole.

In common usage, however, the locative case is generally employed in relation to the object qualified (viśeṣya)— as in the example, "They have assembled at Kurukṣetra. In this context, the rule *ety-edhaty-ūth* does not apply to produce the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*),
because [the word *samaveta*] lacks the initial *ej-* sound.
(1216) Or [the suffixes] ṇya and ṭhak are applied after the word *senā* [in the sense of those who have entered it].

Thus: *sainyāḥ*, *sainikāḥ*. These suffixes (*ṇya* and *ṭhak*) follow a word ending in the second case. As for what is stated in the *Nighaṇṭu*: "Those who have assembled in the army are *sainyāḥ* and *sainikāḥ*."
This should be understood as being intent on stating the resultant meaning [of the rule].
(1217) *saṃjñāyāṃ lalāṭakukkuṭyau paśyati* (Pāṇini 4.4.46).
[The word] *saṃjñāyām* [is an adhikāra]. From the words *lalāṭa* and *kukkuṭī*, the second case ending [is applied]. By means of those two, in the sense of "he looks at," [the suffix ḍaC is added].

The suffix *ṭhak* would apply. "In *saṃjñāprasiddhi*" means in the case of the establishment of correct knowledge; that is to say, regarding an object that has become the domain of such established usage. Regarding the term *lālāṭika*: the meaning is one who stands at a distance and gazes at the forehead (*lalāṭa*) of his master, rather than attending to his duties. [The form is] *lālāṭikaḥ*.
"One who looks ahead only as far as the master's forehead, yet is incapable of performing his duties— he is a 'crow-like' mendicant.
The meaning is that a true renunciant (saṃnyāsī) indeed travels while restraining his vision only as far as the space sufficient for the placement of his feet.
(1218) *tasya dharmyam* |4|4|47|.

Regarding the word *dharmyam*: that which does not deviate from *dharma* is *dharmyam*. [The suffix] *yat* is applied according to the rule: “after *dharma*, *pathin*, *artha*, and *nyāya*, when meaning ‘not deviating from’.”

(1219) *avakrayaḥ* |4|4|50|. *Avakrayaḥ*: [The suffix] *ra* (with the augment *i*) is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) to form *avakraya*, meaning "that by which one hires. (1220) *tad asya paṇyam* |4|4|51|. [The suffix *cha* is applied after a word denoting a commodity to form a derivative meaning] "this is his merchandise."
Regarding *paṇyam*: it is a word ending in *yat* prescribed by the rule "ṭhavad ya-panye" for the sense of an object to be bartered.

(1221) *śalāluno ’nyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 4.4.54]. Regarding *śalāluka*: [the suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule "isusuktāntāt kaḥ. In the alternative case where the suffix *ṭhak* is applied, there is vṛddhi of the first vowel, resulting in *śālālukaḥ*.

Regarding the term *mārdaṅgika*: by the word *mṛdaṅga*, the playing of the drum (*mṛdaṅgavādana*) is indicated. The sense is that it is not used in its primary sense [of the drum itself], because such a usage is not established by linguistic convention (*anabhidhānāt*).
(Pāṇini 4.4.55: *śilpam*.)

*Śilpa* means skill in action; and that [skill] pertains to the playing of the *mṛdaṅga*. The conclusion is that, by virtue of this, the word *mṛdaṅga* has its secondary application (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the playing of the *mṛdaṅga*.
(Pāṇini 4.4.57: *praharaṇam*).

*Praharaṇa* means that by which one strikes; it is a weapon (*āyudha*). Regarding *dhānuṣka*: [the suffix] *ka* is applied after a word ending in *ṭi*, *su*, *uk*, or *t*. By the rule *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*, the *visarga* is changed to *ṣ*. (1224) Pāṇini 4.4.58: *paraśvadhāṭ-ṭhañ*.

The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after *paraśvadha*; the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after *cāṭu*. [In the lexicon: "A *kuṭhāra*, *svadhiti*, *paraśu*, and *paraśvadha* are synonyms for an axe. Regarding the term *paraloka*: this is understood through the inherent power of the word's denotative capacity (*abhidhāna-śakti-svābhāvyāt*). (1225) [The suffix *matup* is applied after words ending in] *asti*, *nāsti*, *diṣṭa*, and *mati*. 4.4.60.

Regarding the term *āstika*: the words *asti* and *nāsti* are indeclinables (*nipāta*). Alternatively, by the force of the statement, the suffix is applied to the verb *asti*, and to the combination of the indeclinable and the verb in *nāsti*. Regarding *diṣṭam*: Amara states, "Thus, *diṣṭa* means destiny or fortune" (*bhāgadheya*). [The text] does not take hold of it.

Māgha uses the term *daiṣṭikatā*. As for the statement of the ancients, "The intellect that follows valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is called *diṣṭā*," it should be disregarded; for if the word *diṣṭa* were feminine and denoted an intellect following valid means of knowledge, it would contradict the aforementioned lexicon. This is the direction of the argument.

(1226) *Cchatrādibhyaḥ ṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.4.62. Regarding the rule *Cchatrādibhyaḥ ṇaḥ*, Kaiyaṭa states in his commentary on the sūtra *Ārmastācchīlye* that it would be more appropriately stated as *Cchatrādibhyaḥ aṇ*. This refers to the suffix *ṇa* [which is actually *aṇ*] when denoting habitual action (*tācchīlya*). [This applies to] the word *karman*.

The intention is that [the suffix] is applied because [the words] belong to the *cchatrādi* group. Regarding "caurī" and so forth: the meaning is that when the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose habit is stealing" (*curā śīlam asyāḥ*) or "one whose habit is austerity" (*tapaḥ śīlam asyāḥ*), the suffix *ṇa* is added; subsequently, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is established after that which ends in *ṇa*.

(1227) *karmādhyayane vṛtam* |4|4|63|. Regarding the rule *karmādhyayane*: the word *adas* is understood from the previous context, and the suffix *ṭhak* is introduced here. Thus he says: "from a word ending in the nominative case," and so forth. *Aikānyikaḥ* means "one [thing] is different."

The compound is formed by taking *vigṛhya* as the object of the *taddhita* suffix; from that, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied. In this manner, examples such as *dvaiyanyikaḥ* and *traiyanyikaḥ* are to be cited. However, in this case, the rule *vṛddhir eci* is set aside, and by the rule *adhvābhyām*, the substitute *aic* is applied. (Pāṇini 4.4.65: *hitaṃ bhakṣāḥ* [“The suffix *cha* is applied after a word denoting a path when the sense is ‘beneficial food’”].

The word *hitaṃ* (beneficial) is [the object]. Although the word *ṭhasya* was the subject under discussion, it is here transformed into the dative case due to its connection with *hita*; or rather, the intention is that the word *adasmai* is drawn back [from its previous position], as expressed in the phrase: "Eating cake is beneficial for him. The point is that the word *apūpa* (cake) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean the eating thereof.
(1229) *śrāṇāmāṃsaudanāṭ ṭiṭhan* | Pāṇini 4.4.67. *Śrāṇā*: "Śrāṇā, *yavāgū*, *uṣṇikā*, *śrāṇā*, *vilepī*, and *taralā* are synonyms for thin gruel," according to Amara.
Regarding *ṭiṭhan*: the letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*); the *ṭ* is for the sake of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of [avoiding] a compound and a split": in the case of *odanika*, this suffix *ṭhañ* was introduced with the *ṭi*-marker specifically to prevent *vṛddhi*. Otherwise, for the sake of brevity, one would simply have prescribed *ṭhañ*. This is the intended meaning. (1230) *tatra niyuktaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.4.69.
Regarding the word *ākarika*: Amara states that "the word *ākara* is used in the feminine sense of 'mine'.

(1231) Pāṇini 4.4.71: *adhyāyinyadeśakālāt*. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after a word denoting a place or time that is unsuitable for study, when [the person] is a student (*adhyāyin*). Why say "after a word denoting a place or time that is unsuitable"? [Consider: *kāśyāmadhīte* ("he studies in Kāśī") and *pūrvāhṇe adhīte* ("he studies in the forenoon").
(1232) *Kaṭhināntaprastārasaṃsthāneṣu vyavaharati* |4|4|72|. Many [commentators] hold that the words *kaṭhinānta*, *prastāra*, and *saṃsthāna* are synonyms for "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*).
*Prastāra* means a sacrifice (*yajña*); [the suffix] *ghañ* is applied by the rule *re sto'yajñe*. Some say *saṃsthāna* means arrangement (*sanniveśa*).

(1233) *nikaṭe vasati* | Pāṇini 4.4.73. [The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the word *nikaṭa* when meaning "he dwells near"]. Thus, one who dwells near a village is called a *naikaṭika* monk. The sense is that an ascetic (*saṃnyāsī*) dwelling near a village enters the village solely for the purpose of begging alms, but does not actually reside there.

(1234) *āvasathāt ṣṭhal* | Pāṇini 4.4.74. From the word *āvasatha*, the suffix *ṣṭhal* is applied. The letter *ḷ* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). That in which people dwell is called an *āvasatha*. The suffix *ap* is applied [to the root *vas*] by the rule "ṭhupasarge vaseḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.61).
[The suffix] is applied after *parpa* and others, after *bhastrā* and others, and after the bases mentioned in the *kusīda* rule.
Regarding the phrase "after the *kusīda* rule," the meaning is: after the two bases included in the rule *kusīdadaśaikādaśāt*.
Here, as in the case of the rule *advyacaṣṭhan*, it is possible that the letter *ṣa* [in these forms] is a *sāṃhitika* (phonetic) insertion.

In counting those very [affixes], there might arise the misconception that the *ṣit*-status of *ṣṭhal* and others is not Vedic; therefore, the author of the Ślokavārttika enumerated all *ṣit* affixes as well. The limit for *ṭhak* is concluded.
Thus ends the section on the suffix *ṭhak* in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
(1323) *pārāyaṇa-turāyaṇa-cāndrāyaṇaṃ vartayati* | Pārāyaṇa: the study of the Veda from beginning to end without interruption.

The *pārāyaṇa* (the completion of study) is accomplished by the student; for if either one is absent, the act of study cannot be brought to completion. Nevertheless, it is established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that the agentive suffix (*pratyaya*) is desired to denote the student alone, and not the teacher. Thus he says: "the student" (*chātra*). As for "the sacrificer" (*yajamāna*): although...

The meaning is that although the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) also carries out the sacrifice by means of preparing the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth, the term ‘*aurāyaṇika*’ is not applied to him there, because it does not denote that role.
*Cāndrāyaṇa* is a specific type of religious vow (*vrata*).

(1324) *saṃśayamāpannaḥ* |5|1|73|. [The word *saṃśayamāpannaḥ* means] "an object that has become the subject of doubt. Thus, in the case of "Is it a post or a person?", the suffix is desired to apply only to the post (*sthāṇu*) and so forth, which have become the objects of doubt, and not to the doubter.

[This is the] state [of being]. If it is asked, "How then is the Amarakośa's definition 'āśaṅkitaḥ saṃśayāpannamānasaḥ' (one who is apprehensive is one whose mind has fallen into doubt) to be understood?"—on this point they say: that object upon which the mind has fallen into doubt is called "one whose mind has fallen into doubt" with respect to that object.
Then it should also be stated: "tato’bhāmanamarhati" and "tato’bhigamanam. In these cases, the suffix is applied after a word ending in the fifth case.
(1325) *pantho ṇa nityam* || 5.1.76 || [The suffix] *ṇa* is always applied [to the word *pathin*].

Regarding *pantha*: for the word *patha*, there is the substitution of *antha* and the suffix *ṇa*. The inclusion of the term "always" (*nitya*) here is intended as a qualification of the meaning of the suffix, and not for the purpose of excluding the formation of a compound; with this intention, he says: "one who goes always. Why [specify] "always"? [Consider] *pathikaḥ* (a traveler). However, in the Bhāṣya, the mention of "always" is...

This has been rejected. For here, the intention of the Bhāṣya is as follows: although the meaning "one who goes on a path" (*panthānaṃ gacchati*) is possible here, nevertheless, the application of the word *pāntha* is not intended in this sense alone, because it is sometimes used even when one is currently going. Nor, even so, is it for the purpose of excluding the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*).

It should not be suspected that the inclusion of the word "nitya" (constant/permanent) is intended; for the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is observed in the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). By the particle *ca* (and), the meaning of the suffix—namely, "goes"—is conjoined.

(1326) And [the suffix *ṭhañ*] is applied after *uttarapatha* when meaning "brought from" (*āhṛta*). [The example is: *auttarapathikaḥ*, meaning "one who goes by way of the northern route. Also, *vāripathikaḥ*: the analysis is either "one who goes by way of water" (*vāripathena gacchati*) or "brought by way of water" (*vāripathenāhṛtam*).
(1327) From a word denoting time [the suffix *aṇ* is applied]. 5.1.78.

Regarding the word *kālāt*: here there is no apprehension of the word-form itself, because in the rule "one who is appointed, hired, past, or future" (*amadhīṣṭo bhṛto bhūto bhāvī*), the second case ending is specified to indicate absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). This is also seen in rules such as "from a word for age" (*vayasas*).
And because [the word] *māsa* and others are qualified by time.
(1328) "Formed from that" (tena nirvṛtam). 5.1.79. "Formed from that": the suffix *ṭhañ* shall be applied after a word denoting time that ends in the third case. "From that" means—

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). However, in the rule *‘ena nirvṛtam’* (Pāṇini 5.2.83), which falls within the scope of the four meanings [of the locative], the distinction is that the third case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). In both instances, the suffix *kta* is applied to the object (*karman*) of the root *vṛt*, which has the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) implied. Regarding the word *āhnika*: it is due to the restrictive rule *‘ahnaṣṭakhoreva’* (Pāṇini 6.4.145), and because of the rule *‘astaddhite’* (Pāṇini 6.4.144).
There is no elision of the *ṭi* [portion].

(1329) *māsādvayasi yatkhañau* | Pāṇini 5.1.81. After the word *māsa*, when expressing age, the suffixes *yat* and *khañ* are applied. The addition of the indicatory letter *ñ* to *khañ* is for the sake of accentuation and for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of the *pūrvapada* form.

*Māsīnābhṛtaḥ* (one who has been hired for a month). Although the four [categories] beginning with *adhīṣṭa* (appointed) are under discussion, by virtue of the sense [of the context], the word *bhūta* (past/perfected) is connected here. For one does not perceive any physical state produced by time when saying "appointed for a month" or "hired for a month," etc.; with this intention, he says: *māsaṃ bhūtaḥ* (one who has existed for a month).
And this is clear from the *Vṛtti* and the *Padamañjarī*. Regarding the word *māsīna*: it means "a child" (*bālaka*).
(1330) *dvigoryap* |5|1|82|. [The suffix] *yap* is applied after a *dvigu* compound. [This applies] to those compounds beginning with a numeral that precede the word *vati*.

Because the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with a specified element) is accepted, *ya* is prescribed by the preceding rule for those cases where *khañ* and [the suffixes beginning with] *a* would otherwise apply; this [suffix *ya*] is *anudātta* due to its being marked with *p*. Consequently, in forms such as *vimāsaḥ*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is maintained by the rule *ṭhidantakāla-* etc. However, if it were stated simply as *hyaḥ*, [the result would be different].

The meaning is that because the suffix [of] *pratyaya* is udātta, *dvimāsaḥ* would be udātta on the final syllable, since the accent taught later is stronger. (1331) *ṣaṇmāsāṇṇyac ca* | Pāṇini 5.1.83.
The word *api* also recurs here; in this matter, the commentary itself is the refuge.
(1332) *samāyāḥ khaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.85]. Regarding *samāyāḥ khaḥ*: Amara states, "The words *hāyana*, *śarat*, and *samā* are not feminine. [The rule applies to] *samām adhīṣṭaḥ* and so forth.
The meaning is that the four topics beginning with *adhīṣṭa* also apply here.
"Or [the suffix] after a *dvigu* compound."

Because it is accepted that "in the case of compounds where a numeral is the prior member, there is a reference to those ending in [the suffix], provided there is no elision (*aluk*)," the [suffix] would have been obligatory by the preceding rule; therefore, this present rule provides an option. Thus, *dvaisamikaḥ* is formed. The point is that when the suffix *kha* is excluded, the suffix *ṭhañ* applies optionally. (1334) *rātryahaḥsaṃvatsarācca* 5.1.87.

Regarding the term *dvaiyahnika*: because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "only after *eḍ* [vowels]," there is no elision of the *ṭi* here. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied by the rules "elision of *ṭha*" and "after *an*," and *aic* is substituted by the rule "after *ay* and *av*. Now, one might object that following the *dvigu* compound by the rule "for the sake of a secondary derivative" (*addhitārthe*), the rule "after *rātri*, *ahan*, and *saṃvatsara*" would indeed supersede this.

Because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the suffix *ṭac* ought to apply; nor should it be argued that the optional application of *ṭac* occurs by virtue of the *mahāvibhāṣā*, because it is included among the items for which the formation is obligatory in the rule "ṛhatījātyantāḥ samāsāntāśca.
Therefore, he says: "of the rule for compound-final suffixes" (*samāsāntavidheḥ*). Even though [the suffix] *ṭac*...
Even if the substitution *āhn-* is applied, the form *avaiyahnikaḥ* is established; nevertheless,
the form *vyahīnaḥ* is not established because, when the suffix *ṭac* is present and the substitution *āhn-* occurs,
that [substitute] would be treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*.

They say that because the compound ending in the word *ahar* (day) is already included by the very mention of "compounds ending in *ahar*" for the application of the suffix *samāsānta*, even if the suffix *kha* were applied according to the rule *ātryaharsaṃvatsarācca*, the undesirable form *vyahnīna* would result.

(1335) *saṅkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasaṅkhyasya ca* |7|3|15|. [The rule] "there is no vṛddhi of the final syllable of the second member" is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). In the word *vivarṣā*, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs by virtue of the rule *vigoluṅca*. This is because the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) [of the present rule] by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *parimāṇa* does not apply here.

Since the prohibition [of the suffix] applies here because [the word] is "not piled with a limited measure" (*aparimāṇa-bista-cita*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule "*dvivarṣe bhṛte ’amadhīṣṭaḥ*" (Pāṇini 5.1.80). Then, by the rule "*varṣālluk ca*" (Pāṇini 5.1.88), there is elision (*luk*). He provides a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) stating "one who has piled" (*acitavān*), because it will be stated later that in the case of the suffix *itavat*, there is obligatory elision (*nityaluka*). Thus, in this context, the meaning of the suffix is "one who has piled."
(1336) *varṣāl luk ca* | Pāṇini 5.1.88. Examples:
*dvivarṣīṇo vyādhiḥ* ("a two-year-old fever") and *dvivārṣiko manuṣyaḥ* ("a two-year-old human"). Regarding this, they say:
because the rule *anitīti* would otherwise necessitate the compulsory elision (*nityaluk*) of the suffix in the case of "human" (*manuṣya*), [the author] says "human" (*manuṣyaḥ*).
Having explained that "an image and the like are similar to humans," the derivation of the term *sthitasya* must be justified.
(1337) [The rule] *citavati nityam* (Pāṇini 5.1.89). *Dāraka* means a young boy. The gloss of *arijayya* is "capable of being attained."

In the rule *‘ṣayyajayyau śakyārthe’*, there is the substitution of *ay* for *ya*. There is an extension [of the application] of the suffix *ṅīp* after words such as *mahānāmnī* when they appear in the genitive case. Thus, in the form *mahānāmnyā nāma*, because it is not a word that has been previously mentioned in the masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*), the transformation into the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur.

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. Regarding [the statement] "Haradatta, however," he considers that this [term] is etymological (*yaugika*), not conventional (*rūḍha*). In the case of *māhānāmikaḥ*, once the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) has been applied, there is the elision of the *ṭi* [portion] by the rule "before a taddhita suffix" (*astaddhite*). [The suffix] *ṇya* is added after *caturmāsa-* in the sense of "born there" (*tatra bhavaḥ*) when [the object] is known (*jñe*). [Regarding the form] *caturmāsāt*: [this is] of the word *māsa*.

The Vārttika is commenced under the heading of "time" because it denotes time; nor should it be suspected that its connection here is difficult to establish due to the absence of a specific denotation of time for the compound, for it is accepted that "in the case of *rājanvat*, [compounds] preceded by a numeral, and those with a numeral as the prior member, there is inclusion of the word ending in that [numeral]. Thus, [the connection] certainly exists.
Regarding the term *saṅgati*:

[it occurs] when there is no designation as *aṇ*. As for the phrase "when there is no designation as *aṇ*": since [the form] is already established by the rule "that which exists here" (*atra bhavaḥ*), the prescription of *aṇ* again is intended to prevent the elision (*luk*) that would otherwise apply by the rule "there is elision of *aṇ* when not denoting a descendant" (*vigor lug-anapatye*).

This [sūtra] has been commenced here for the purpose that [the term] "bhū" [should not apply]. Furthermore, it should be understood that this very vārtika was commenced right here so that the term "cāturmāsāḥ" may be carried over [into the subsequent rule]. Regarding the word *cāturmāsī*: when there is an expectancy as to whose name it is, he says—*āṣāḍhī*.
The meaning is "the full moon day joined with the Āṣāḍhā constellation.

(1338) *tasya ca dakṣiṇā* |5|1|95|. Regarding the rule *tasya ca dakṣiṇā*: the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after words denoting sacrifices (*yajñākhyebhyaḥ*) ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhaḷntebhyaḥ*) in the sense of "its sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇā*).

It might be argued: "Since [the formation of the word] from *dvādaśāha* and other such terms is already established here by the very rule governing time (*kālādhikāra*), the mention of the term ‘name’ (*ākhyā*) is redundant.
Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words: “Because of the mention of ‘name’” (*ākhyāgrahaṇāt*).
And in that context: (Pāṇini 5.1.96) *tatra ca dīyate kārye bhavavat*. (In the sense of ‘given there,’ and in the sense of ‘to be performed,’ the suffixes are applied as in the case of *bhava*.)
And in that regard: after words expressing time, when the meanings "given" or "to be performed" are intended, the suffix *mavāt* (i.e., *ṭhañ*) should occur. As in the example *prāvṛṣeṇyam*.
The sense is that the suffix *eṇya*, prescribed in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava-artha*) by the rule *prāvṛṣ-eṇya*, is here extended [by analogy] as well.

Regarding *śārada*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after words denoting day (*andiva*), time (*kāla*), season (*ṛtu*), and asterism (*nakṣatra*). This marks the final limit of the section governing time (*kālādhikāra*).
(1340) *vyuṣṭādibhyo ’ṇ* 5.1.97: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the group of words beginning with *vyuṣṭa*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words such as *vyuṣṭa*. The word *vyuṣṭa* denotes time and refers to the end of the day.

(1341) [Pāṇini 5.1.99] *sampādini*: "In the sense of one who accomplishes. *Saṃpatti* is the excellence of qualities. The author of the *Vṛtti* states that the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*).

In the same way, one may also cite *vāstrayugikaṃ śarīram* ("a body provided with a pair of garments"), meaning "it necessarily shines by means of a pair of garments. (1342) *tasmai prabhavati santāpādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.101). [This sūtra provides for the suffix *ṭhañ* after words such as *santāpa* when they signify "that which overcomes" or "is capable of enduring" that which is expressed by the base.]
He has power over that; one who is capable or able is said to "have power" (*prabhavati*). (1343) *ṛtoraṇ* | Pāṇini 5.1.105.
Regarding *ārtavam*: it should be understood that the word *puṣpam* ("flower") and so forth is the substantive (*viśeṣya*).

(1344) *kālād yat* | Pāṇini 5.1.107. [The suffix] *yat* is applied after the word *kāla*. Example: *kālyam śītam* ("the morning is cold"). According to Amarasimha: "The dawn, the break of day, and *kalya* [are synonyms]. In that context, one must seek another etymological derivation for the word *kālya* when it refers to the time of morning.

(1345) *prakṛṣṭe ṭhañ* |5|1|108|. Regarding *prakṛṣṭe ṭhañ*: that which is drawn out (*prakṛṣyate*) is *prakṛṣṭaḥ*; here the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). It is stated that time is qualified by that excellence (*prakarṣa*), namely, "long time. The mention of the suffix *ṭhañ* [is for the purpose of introducing the subsequent rule].
This is for the sake of clarity; otherwise, one might suspect that the immediately preceding term [māsa] continues [into this rule].
(1346) *prayojanam* 5|1|109. Examples: *indramahaḥ* ("Indra’s festival"), *mahaḥ*—"festival"; *vaiśākha-manthaḥ* ("the churning-stick of Vaiśākha"); *āṣāḍha-daṇḍaḥ* ("the staff of Āṣāḍha").

The words *vaiśākha* and *āṣāḍha* are used in their conventional sense (*rūḍhi*) to denote the two poles of a churning stick (*manthadaṇḍa*). Haradatta, however, maintains that their etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) may be constructed in any manner whatsoever. Specifically, the particular piece of wood that serves as the support for the churning stick itself is called *mantha*.

(1347) *anupravacanādibhyaś chaḥ* |5|1|111| [The suffix] *cha* is applied after [the group of words] beginning with *anupravacana*. *Anupravacana* is a name for the *brahmaudana* (the rice-offering for the Veda-study).
(1348) *samāpanāt sapūrvapadāt* |5|1|112| [The suffix *cha* is applied] after *samāpana* when it is preceded by another word.
"From a compound with a preceding member" (*sapūrvapadāt*) means "from one that has a preceding member.
(1349) *Aikāgārika-ṭ* in the sense of a thief [is taught]. The suffix *ṭ* is for the sake of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. Thus, *aikāgārikī*. Why is this stated?

Is it not established by the suffix *ṭhañ* itself in the case of *‘yojanam’*? True; however, this rule is necessary for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*) regarding a thief (*caura*). Otherwise, [the suffix] would also apply in a case such as *ekāgāraṃ prayojanaṃ yasya bhikṣoḥ* (“a monk for whom a single house is the purpose”). But even so, wouldn't there be only *ṭhañ* by the rule *ṭhaikāgārāccaure*?

If it is argued that there is no need for the rule of *nipātana* (irregular derivation) stating "what is used for a single purpose" (*aikāgārika*), nor for the suffix *cit-kaṇ*, [the answer is as follows]: On this point they say—the letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of determining the grammatical operation;
namely, that the feminine suffix *ṅīp* alone occurs, and not the accentuation of a *ñit* suffix. As for the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*), it indeed occurs by virtue of the *nipātana*.
(1350) *ākālika-ḍādyantavacane* | Pāṇini 5.1.114. "The substitution of *ākāla-*" means that it is prescribed [as such]. The phrase "of which there is a beginning and an end," etc., follows.
The sense is that, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of the word *asya*, the suffix *ikaṭ* is prescribed in the sense of the genitive case.
"Also after *ākāla* [the suffix] *ṭhañ*. This is a Vārttika. It marks the end of the section for *ṭhañ*.
Thus ends the section on *ṭhañ* in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
The *tud* group consists of those roots ending in a *tiṅ* suffix.
(317) *Śa* is added after the *tud* group [of roots]. (Pāṇini 3.1.77).
Regarding *tudati*: some hold that the suffix *śa* applies because it is obligatory (*nitya*), thereby overriding even the subsequent *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel.

Others say that because of the prohibition regarding *akṛtavyūha*, the *guṇa* substitution does not take effect. Regarding the root *bhrasj* in the sense of "cooking," they state that the meaning of the verbal root here is cooking in the form of roasting, and not the cooking of rice and such, because there is no usage of the root in that latter sense. However, in the reading *hrasjo* found in some texts—
If it were stated as *ṭhoditaśca*, then by the application of the rule for the substitution of the final nasal (*niṣṭhānatva*), forms such as *bhṛṣṭaḥ* and *bhṛṣṭavān* would not be established.
(318) *bhrasjo ropadhayo ram anyatarasyām* |6|4|47|.

[The rule applies] to the root *bhrasj*. The letter *r* in *ropadhayoḥ* is for the sake of pronunciation. Regarding the substitute *ram*, the letter *m* is for the sake of pronunciation; [the *ra*] follows the final vowel.
Fearing that the genitive case-usage in the rule *ropadhayoh* (Pāṇini 7.1.94) would otherwise be redundant if [the substitute] were considered external (*para*), he says:

"It is a removal" (*nivṛtti*). The intended meaning is this: because the designation *mit* is employed in order to obtain a specific locus (*sthānin*), the substitute *ram* does not occur in place of the *r* and the penultimate vowel (*upadha*). For where the locus is not specifically determined by the genitive case...

When something is prescribed after being specifically mentioned, it takes the place of that which was mentioned; for example, in rules such as *ṭhiko yaṇ aci*, the *yaṇ* substitute and so forth take the place of the *ik*. However, in the present case, since *ram* is mentioned by its own form (*tāntrikatvāt*), it does not take the place of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).
This occurs when it functions as a substitute (*ādeśa*) or an augment (*āgama*), just as *śnam* functions as an augment to a suffix (*pratyaya-āgama*).

Thus [they say]. Others, however, considering such an explanation to be improper, maintain that one should carry forward the elision (*lopa*) from the rule *anaḥ ktici* and state that there is an elision of both the *r* and the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of the root *bhrasj*, while *raṃ* is merely an augment (*āgama*). Still others, however, suggest that the rule should simply be *bhrasjo rasaranyatarasyām*; for *rasaḥ*—

The word *ṛ* is the elision (*cheda*). The meaning is that for the cluster consisting of the letters *r*, *a*, and *s*—namely, *ras*—there shall be the substitution of *ṛ*. Consequently, forms such as *bharjakaḥ*, *bharjanam*, and *babharja* are established when the affixes are not *kit* or *ṅit*. However, in the alternative view where the substitution of *ṛ* does not occur, the forms are *bhrajakaḥ* and *bhrajanam*.
Regarding *babhrajje* and so forth: in the case where there is the substitution of *ṛ*, the forms are *bhṛṣṭiḥ*, *bhṛjyāt*, and so on;

in the absence of that [substitution], when *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs, the form remains the same. Thus, in examples such as *barībhṛjyate*, the rule beginning with *anudātopadeśa-* is applied to prevent the removal of the *repha* (*r*) of the *rīk* augment.

The acceptance of the *upadeśa* (original form) must be followed; however, it need not be followed now, for they say there is great economy [of effort] in that one need not formulate a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (priority-exception rule) stating, "the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) takes precedence over the *ram*-augment when a *ṅit* suffix follows. And this is established by the statement: "It is accomplished by the specific mention of *ras*."

This is merely a description of the intention of the Vārttika, and not something new. The word "ṛvacanāt" should be split as either "ṛvaca-nāt" or "ṛ-vacanāt. However, the authors of the Bhāṣya, by stating, "The Sūtra is being split; let it remain exactly as it was composed," have indicated the defectiveness of this interpretation. And that [defect] is in the Manoramā...

This is quite clear. For instance, if the combination of the letters *repha* (*r*), *a*, and *sakāra* (*s*) were to undergo the substitution of *ṛ*, five defects would arise. In forms such as *apilliṭi babharjutaḥ* and *babharjuḥ*, which are desired, the result would instead be *babhṛjatuḥ* and *babhṛjuḥ*. Nor can this be resolved by applying *guṇa* substitution here, because [the rule for] the substitution of *ṛ* applies.

Because the *kit* designation applies to the *liṭ* [affix] following a conjunct beginning with *ṭh* by the rule *kid āśiṣi liṭ*, that [augment *iṭ*] is prohibited. Since there is an option regarding *iṭ* by the rule *an īdanta-*, forms such as *bibharkṣati* are desired, whereas forms such as *bibhṛkṣati* would result. This is because when *ṛ* does not occur, the *kit* designation applies to *san* by the rule *halantācca*. In the *liṅ* and *sic* [affixes], [the form] *bibhṛkṣīṣṭa* [is derived].

The forms *abharṣṭa* and so forth are desired; however, [according to the rule], one would expect *bhṛkṣīṣṭa*, *abhṛṣṭa*, and so on, because [the suffixes] *iṅ* and *sic* are *kit* when used with ātmanepada endings. Furthermore, from the causative (*ṇijanta*) form, *caṅ* is desired as in *ibabharjat*; yet *abībhṛjat* would also result. This is because the rule *ṭhurṛt* serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to *ir-ar-ā-ra*.

When *ṛ* is not substituted [by *ar*], because of the application of the *san*-like behavior (*sanvadbhāva*) by the rule "anvallaghūni," and because of the application of the rule "dīrgho laghoḥ" after the substitution of *it* by the rule "anyataḥ," [the form *ārirātsati* is derived]. Although the form *ababharjat* is indeed established because the rule "ṛtaḥ" is optional, nevertheless, in the alternative case...

It should be understood that *abībhṛjat* would be undesirable [as a form]. If it is argued that such a form is desired because the roots *ṛji* and *bhṛjī* are listed under the *bhvādi* class in the sense of "roasting" (*bharjana*), this is not so.
For such a form is desired specifically in the sense of roasting, and not for cooking in general. Even if one were to admit that both [roots] have the same meaning, [the objection remains].

The four defects mentioned previously are indeed firm; for even they can be easily avoided by means of another grammatical element (*dhātu*). This is because, in the case of *apilliṭ* (the *liṭ* suffix with *ap*), even for the root *bhṛj*, the form *babharjuḥ* and so forth would remain unestablished by that [previous argument] due to the absence of *guṇa* and because it is *ātmanepada* by virtue of being *anudātta*. Likewise...

Since the root *bhṛj* is udātta, the suffixes *san*, *liṅ*, and *sic* that follow it would invariably take the augment *iṭ*; consequently, forms such as *bibharkṣati*, *bharkṣīṣṭa*, and *abharṣṭa* would not be established by that [rule]. By this, the position that “*bhṛj* is the substitute for *hrasji*” is also refuted.

Because it would entail the multitude of faults already mentioned. Furthermore, in this view, there is an additional defect regarding the *yaṅluk* (elision of the *yaṅ* suffix): just as with the substitute *vadh*, when *bhṛjj* is substituted for the reduplicated stem, a second reduplication is difficult to obtain, because of the prohibition "not for that which is not a reduplicated base" (*sthānivattvena anabhyāsasya*) [which applies since the substitute is treated like the original]. Even if [that prohibition] were accepted...

If it were the case that *rug*, *rig*, and *grīk* must necessarily occur after reduplication, then forms such as *bābharjitā* and *bābharjiṣyati*, which are devoid of *rug* and the others, would not be established at all. However, if one wishes to exercise independence out of a preference for brevity (*lāghava*), then one should read the rule as *hrasjerasaḥ*, [thereby establishing] *ras*.
Let the substitution of *ar* be prescribed for the entire cluster; thus, there will be no fault whatsoever. Here is the summary of the argument:
"If *ras*, *ṛt*, *añc*, *apit*, *liṭ*, *san*, *liṅ*, *sic*, and *caṅ* follow, there is a fault in the case of *bhrasj* when followed by *ṇi* and *kṣu*;
likewise, there is a fault in the case of *bhṛj* [in the same environments], and furthermore, there is an additional fault in the *yaṅluk* formation involving the reduplicated stem (*sābhyāsa*)."

For if there were the substitution of *bhṛj* for *han*, as in the case of *vadhi*, then reduplication would not be obtained due to the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) of *vadhi*. Therefore, let it remain as it is in the traditional formulation;
let *rasoḥ* be independent.
By means of the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior contradiction), the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) prevails, overriding the addition of the augment *ram*.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the *pūrvavipratiṣedha*," it is also easy to say that it is because [the *saṃprasāraṇa*] is obligatory (*nitya*). Nor is there a case where the *repha* of the root undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa* first, and subsequently the *repha* of the augmented *ram* does so.
It should not be suspected that the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution is not obligatory simply because another word-form is subsequently obtained;

for, in accordance with the observed linguistic data (*lakṣya*), obligatoriness is sometimes accepted even on the basis of whether an operation applies regardless of whether it has already taken effect or not (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitva*).

(319) *vija iṭ* | 1|2|2|. Regarding the rule *vija iṭ*: it is established in the *Manoramā* that from this point on, by means of a "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) from the previous sūtra *vṛddhir yasya*, the phrase *yasyādiḥ* ("of which [the suffix] begins with") is carried over; thus, a suffix beginning with *iṭ* is obtained.
The modern grammarians, however, maintain that by the term *iṭ* here, the third-person singular ending is not intended;
for if it were so, the augment would apply only in forms such as *vijijiṣīya*, but not in forms such as *udvijita*.
Therefore, the augment *iṭ* is accepted for the sake of achieving the desired result. However, its designation as having the marker *ṅ* is useless.

Since the quality of having that [augment] as its cause is not otherwise obtained, the word *iḍvat* is therefore taken here by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean "that which has *iṭ* as the first element of the suffix. This is a statement of the resultant meaning: "a suffix beginning with *iṭ* is called *ṅt*. Thus, they say that the labor of carrying over the rule *yasyādiḥ* (of that which begins with) for the sake of obtaining the sense "beginning with *iṭ*" is indeed unnecessary.
In this context, both the root *ovij* belonging to the *tudādi* and *rudhādi* groups is intended, and not the root *vijir* meaning "separation" belonging to the *juhotyādi* group,
according to the explanation. As for the reason stated here by Haradatta for not including the *juhotyādi* root— that it is "because it is aniṭ"— that is incorrect.

Because of the possibility of *iṭ* [augment] in the *liṭ* [perfect tense] due to the rule *krādiniyamanena*, one should not argue that the *ṅtva* [the status of being marked by ṅ] of *iṭ* is redundant since its purpose is already served there by its *kitva* [status of being marked by k]. For even if the *liṭ* were *kit*, in the form *vivejitha*, the *ṅtva* would still be absent because of its *pitva* [status of being marked by p]. Regarding *vivraśca*: here the moderns (*navyāḥ*) say—
In rules such as *ṭhvavraśce*, where both semivowels (*yaṇ*) that constitute the reduplicated syllable are subject to the possibility of *saṃprasāraṇa* by the rule *iṭaḷbhyāsasya*,

the sūtra *na saṃprasāraṇe* is accepted to prohibit the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the preceding semivowel. Consequently, by this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is understood that the subsequent [semivowel] undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa* first.

Having accepted the position that "the section on *aṅga* [extends] up to the end of the *pāda*," and having admitted that the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uradatva*) is caused by a suffix implied by the term *aṅga*, one relies on the fact that the semivowel *v* follows a *saṃprasāraṇa* by means of the application of the rule "in place of what precedes a *ṭhac* suffix" (*ṭhacaḥ parasmin*), which effects the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*.

The prohibition of *saṃprasāraṇa* can be established in some way. For if the sūtra were formulated as "there is *saṃprasāraṇa* of *ar*" or "there is *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *yaṇ* that follows *ar*," then the meaning obtained would be that *saṃprasāraṇa* applies only to the subsequent [element] and not to the preceding *yaṇ*; thus, without the aforementioned difficulty, all cases such as *vavrañca* and *yūnaḥ* would be accounted for.

It is established. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the recurrence of the negative particle (*nañ*) would not be obtainable for the purpose of prohibiting *saṃprasāraṇa* in the rules "iṭi vayo yaḥ" and "veñaḥ"; for there is no obstacle to formulating the sūtra as "a liṭi vayo yaḥ," [and the rule] "a saṃprasāraṇe" [would follow].
Furthermore, because two additional *mātrās* would ultimately result from composing the sūtra exactly as it was heard [in the traditional recitation],

and since the desired goal is accomplished by this simpler means, the formulation of the sūtra "na saṃprasāraṇe" indicates that "even in the absence of a difference in the *imita*, when there is a difference in the *sthānin*, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) occurs once again."

And likewise, in cases such as *uddhyupāsya*, after doubling the letter *dh*, there is again doubling of the letter *d* following the *u*; this explanation by the authors of the *Prakriyā* and others is indeed intended by the author of the Sūtras. This is so provided that, even when the substituends (*sthānin*) differ, the cause (*nimitta*) remains the same.

They say: "In some instances, the non-application of an operation is observed; however, since that which is established by an *añjñāpaka* (indicative evidence) does not apply everywhere, let that fault be avoided. [The example] *avraścīt*: because it is marked with *ū*, there is optionally *iṭ*;
by the rule *vadavrajeḥ*, there would be *vṛddhi*, but there is a prohibition of it by the rule *neṭi*. [The example] *abrākṣīt*: by the rule *koḥ*.

There is elision of *sa*. By the rule *ṭhvraśceṭ* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], *ṣa* is substituted. By the rule *aḍhoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.40], *ka* is substituted. Then, there is the substitution of *ṣa* for *sa*. Nor should it be asked how there is elision of the *sa* here, because the root is listed in the Dhātupāṭha with a *sa*. Thus they say: "In verbal roots ending in a consonant (*jhal*), the anusvāra and the *pañcamī* (nasal) are born from the letter *a*; the *sakāra* is born from the letter *sa*."

"Śakāra and the ṛṣāṭṭa-varga are born from the tavarga. [This is] *vyaca*. *Vyājīkaraṇa* means the act of creating a pretext (*cchadmakaraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "by way of exclusion" (*paryudāsena*): the sense is that if it were a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), there would result a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and an ungrammatical compound (*asamarthasamāsa*).

Because it has as its scope only those forms ending in *kṛt* suffixes. By that [rule], the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs in *udvicitā* and *udvicitum*; however, in cases such as *vyacitā* and *vyaciṣyati*, where the scope is a *tiṅ* suffix, it does not occur.
In *vivyāca*, even though the status of being a *kuṭādi* root is established, there is no harm, because of the rule "gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ."

Because it is stated in the Sūtra that "the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ṇit* shall be *ṅit*, [the following applies]: although in the case of the suffix *ṇal* in the perfect tense (*uttama*), if the *ṇit*-designation is absent, then due to the *ṅit*-designation [of the preceding stem], there would be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "ṭhvyi-vyac-", and thus [the form] would not be established; therefore, one must understand that the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "except for *anas-" is necessary. [The roots] *ujjhī*, *uchī*, and *ucchī* [are used in the sense of] gathering.

These two roots have been explained in the *bhvādi* class. Their inclusion here, however, serves the purpose of allowing the optional application of the augment *num* by the rule *ācchīnadyoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.80) in forms such as *uñcchanatī*, *uñcchatī*, *uccchantī*, and *uccchatī*.
The previous placement was for the sake of accent (*svara*). For instance, in forms like *uñcchati* and *uñcchatī* when followed by a *pit* suffix.
