Since the suffixes *śap* and others are *anudātta* (unaccented) because they are *pit*, the word [the verbal base] has its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*) by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). However, in the case of *śnu*, it has its middle syllable accented (*madhyodātta*) by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Now, one might object: since it will be stated later that "the subsequently prescribed accent (*atiśiṣṭasvara*) is stronger, except in the case of *vikaraṇas*," how can this be so here?

It should be stated that the middle syllable is acute (madhyodātta); for in forms such as *kuruta*, although the acute accent of the suffix *tas* and others— which follows the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*)— is stronger than the accent of the suffix itself, the acute accent of the suffix *śas* is nevertheless stronger than the accent of the root because it follows the root.

"Because it is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication). For this very reason, the authors of the *Bhāṣya*, relying on the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "and [the substitution of *ī* for *e*] occurs only after the root *aś* when followed by a vowel," have rejected the mention of the term "having two consonants" (*dvihal*). The sense is that otherwise, that [mention] would not be consistent. In the form *ānarccha*, there is no *ām* because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule "not after *ṛcch*."

The modern grammarians (navyāḥ), however, have explained that because the rule "ṛcchatyṛtām" prescribes *guṇa* when followed by the *liṭ* suffix, the absence of *ām* is established; therefore, it is inferred that the root *ṛcch* exists even in other *gaṇas*. However, in order to prevent *ām* after the *liṭ* suffix for that specific root, [the rule] says "anṛccha."
They say that this is necessary. *micchcha*. *Utkleśa* means intense affliction (*utkaṭaḥ kleśaḥ*). From the root *ṛc* in the sense of praise (*stuti*):
that by which a deity or the like is praised (*ṛcyate*) is an *ṛk*. Here, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*) due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*).
*Lobhitā*, *lobdhā*. [The suffix *iṭ* is optional] according to the rule "after *īṣ*, *sa*, and *ha*" (*īṣasaha*). "Like a child, O wise ones" (*śiśuṃ na viprāḥ*).

The word *iva* is not used in the sense of "like. The term *viprāḥ* refers to the Brahmins; they lick the child with their thoughts (*matibhiḥ*), that is, they harm or diminish it—the meaning being that they belittle it. The root *vṛt* has the senses of harming (*hiṃsā*) and tying (*granthana*). The inclusion of the marker *īt* (in *vṛtī*) is for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *iṭ* by the rule "after a root marked with *ī*, there is no *iṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* suffixes. Even though this...

Although the prohibition of *iṇ* in the *niṣṭhā* suffix is established because [the root] is marked with *veṭ*, nevertheless, the addition of the marker *it* is intended to indicate that the rule "of that which has an optional *iṭ*" (*yasya vibhāṣā*) is not universally valid (*anitya*). By means of this, forms such as *hāvitam ibharājadhiyā* are established; so they say.

In the case of *tṛmph* and others, the augment *num* is to be stated. Regarding *kura* in the sense of "sound," it is said that this applies only to the root *kṛ*, because of its well-known status. For when people say "let him do" (*kuryāt*), what comes to mind for them is only the root *kṛñ*, not [the root *kura*]; such is the intended meaning. *Mura* means "to encircle."

The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ig-upadha-lakṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*. *Mura* refers to a Daitya; Viṣṇu is called *Murāri*. The root *kṣura* means "to scratch"; scratching is cutting. In the phrase “he cuts with a razor” (*eṣāṃ kṣurati*), the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ig-upadha*. *Kṣura* is a weapon. The root *tila* means "to anoint. It forms *tilati*. By the rule *ig-upadha*, the suffix *ka* is applied, resulting in *tila*. [The root] *ila*...

In the sense of "going," from the root *gam* with the suffix *śap*, we have *gacchati*. Regarding the root *likh* in the sense of "arranging letters," the usage *likhitum* and *likhiṣyati* is erroneous. As for the view held by some—that *kuṭādiḥ* means "that which begins with *kuṭa*," and *kuṭādayaḥ* means "those of whom *kuṭa* is the first"—and that *kuṭādiḥ* and *kuṭādayaḥ* [refer to both the singular and plural forms].
Having accepted the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* compound as *kuṭ-ādayaḥ*, [the author] justified forms such as *ikhitum*.

That is incorrect; for in cases such as *ekhitā* and *ekhiṣyati*, there would result the prohibition of *guṇa*. Nor can this be accepted as the intended conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it contradicts the works of the Vṛttikāra, Haradatta, and others.

Furthermore, since the rule could have been formulated simply as "āṅlikhādibhyaḥ," the reading "uṭādibhyaḥ" would result in a violation of its inherent naturalness; moreover, as has already been stated, this would also contradict the Vedic usage in the Sūtra "akuniṣvālekhane. Let this matter rest for now.

The usage *‘ikḥāpayati’* is explained in the *Manoramā* as follows: *āpanam* is *āpaḥ*, meaning attainment; *likhasya āpaḥ* is *likhāpaḥ*, meaning the attainment of writing; that which performs this is [the causative]. *Sphuṭ* means to blossom or expand.
That from which the meaning expands is *sphoṭaḥ*. And that...

It is of many kinds, distinguished by the *padasphoṭa*, *vākyasphoṭa*, and so forth. [In the root list] *kaḍa* (to be pleased) is read among the *kuṭ*-class roots; although it lacks the grammatical operations characteristic of the *kuṭ*-class, it is placed there for the sake of following the roots ending in *ḍ*.
Its repetition here, after having already been listed in the *bhū*-class, is for the purpose of making the optional insertion of *num* possible in the present participle (*śatṛ*).
The previous reading, however, is for the purpose of making the initial syllable udātta in roots such as *kaḍati*, just as it is in *ucchati* and others.
(320) *sphurati-sphulatyornirnivibhyaḥ* |8|3|76|.
Regarding *sphurati* and *sphulati*: since the word "optionally" (*vā*) is understood from the rule *ivādīnām*, he says—[there is] *ṣatva*.
Or it may be [the case that] *pariṇūta* [is formed]. Regarding [the form] *pariṇūta*: there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *ṛt-śyukaḥ kiti*.
(321) *mriyater luṅ-liṅoś ca* (Pāṇini 1.3.61). From the rule *mriyater luṅ-liṅoś ca*, the word *itaḥ* is drawn over (*anukṛṣyate*) by the particle *ca*. Therefore, he says:

"And it is *śit* because it is in its original form. Regarding "taṅ": this means the *ātmanepada*. By this, the form "riyamāṇa" is established. Regarding "for the sake of the accent": in the case of "mā hi mṛta," [the accent is determined] by the rule "āsyanudātenṅdidupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudātam."
When the suffix *ṅti* follows, the *lasārvadhātuka* affix is rendered unaccented (*anudātta*), and consequently the verbal root (*dhātu*) becomes accented (*udātta*).

However, in the absence of *ṅt*, the affix would be accented, and the root would become unaccented. Nor can it be argued that because the elision of *sic* is considered "as if not having taken effect" (*asiddha*), the *lasārvadhātuka* affix does not follow immediately after *ṅt*.
One should not suspect that its *anudātta* status is difficult to justify,
for it can be easily argued that by the force of the *ṅtvi* suffix, the *sij* augment is not considered *asiddha*.
Furthermore, since in the case of *amṛta*, the *āṭ* augment itself possesses the *udātta* accent, the *ṅtvi* of the root *mṛṅ* does not [apply].
The use of the particle *māṅ* in the phrase *ā hi mṛtaḥ* is for the purpose of preventing the substitution of the suffix *aṇ*.

Furthermore, although the rule *iṅṅtiṅḥ* would cause the elision of the accent (*nighāta*) of the finite verb (*tiṅ*), the inclusion of the marker *ṅ* in *māṅ* would otherwise be redundant; thus, the word *hi* is employed. However, when *hi* is used, [the elision of the accent is prevented] by the rule *hi ca*.

It should be understood that the desired accent is established through the prohibition of the *tiṅ* and *anta* elision (*nighāta*). Regarding the root *ri* in the sense of "going," one might raise the objection that the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would apply because it is a subsequent rule; in response to this, he says: "Because it is internal" (*antaraṅgatvāt*).
[Pāṇini 6.1.140: *kiratau lavane*. (6.1.140)

Regarding the roots *kṛ* (to scatter) and *lū* (to cut): from the rule "ṭhupāt pratiyatne" (Pāṇini 6.1.139), the word "upāt" (after the prefix *upa*) is understood to carry over. What is the purpose of specifying "in the sense of cutting"? [Consider the example: *upakirati*.
(323) Also, when *hiṃsā* (injury) is meant, [the augment *ṣat* is applied] after the prefix *prati* as well. 6.1.141.

[The suffix *liṭ* is used] after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *prati* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*), and also [when preceded by *upa*]. As in Māgha’s verse: *ṭhurovidāraṃ praticaskare nakhaiḥ* ("he tore apart the chest with his claws"). This is the *liṭ* [perfect tense] in the sense of the object (*karman*). By the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām*, there is *guṇa* [substitution]. (324) *aci vibhāṣā* 8.2.21. [In this context, the *vibhāṣā* option applies regarding the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* for the semivowel.]

The root *dṛś* (dṛṅ) is used in the sense of respect (*ādara*). Śrīharṣa says: “Furthermore, the wise do not even pay heed (*adriyante*) to nectar. The root *prach* (pracccha) is used in the sense of *jñīpsā*—the desire to know (*jñātum icchā*). Here, the root *jñapi* means "to know" (*jñāne*). According to the rule *ṭhāpjñapyṛdhāmīt*, [the vowel *i* is substituted], and by the rule *atra lopaḥ*, there is the elision of the reduplication. With the suffix *ṇvul*, the form is *pracchakaḥ*. [This is derived] from the word *pṛcchā*.

In the case of *atkaroti*, when the suffix *ṇic* is applied and then *ṇvul*, the form is *pṛcchakaḥ*. However, the word *pṛcchā* should be understood as formed with the suffix *aṅ* after the root *pracch*, due to its inclusion in the *ākṛtigaṇa* beginning with *bhidādi*, which involves vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). Regarding the statement "the roots *kṛ* and others have been explained," these are included in the rule: *hūṣākarmakirādisanām*.

These will be employed in the vārttika concerning the prohibition of *ki* and other affixes that is to be stated hereafter. It should be understood that this [sūtra] is for the purpose of being carried forward (*anuvṛtti*) into the subsequent sūtra, *iraśca pañcabhyaḥ*. Regarding *sasṛjitha*:
by the rule *vibhāṣā sṛjidṛśoḥ*, there is optionally the augment *iṭ* in the *thali* affix.
The augment *num* should be stated as occurring before [the suffix] *masj* (the third person plural ending). The root *vicch* means "to go.
By virtue of its inclusion in the *tudādi* class, the suffix *āya* is applied even after this root, rather than *śap*.
Consequently, there is an optional application of *num* in the forms *vicchāyati* and *vicchāyantī*. Some, however, [hold a different view].

Accepting that the suffix *āya* is optional by virtue of its inclusion in the list of roots beginning with *tud*, they cited forms such as *viccchantī* (from *vicch-*) and *viccchantī* as examples of the optional application of *num*, and further cited forms such as *viccchati*, *viccchataḥ*, and *viccchanti*;
however, in their view, the inclusion [of the root] in the *tudādi* class applies only to the simple [root].

Because its purpose has been fulfilled, the word ends in the suffix *āya*. Therefore, in *vicchāyantī*, the *num* augment is applied by the rule *ap-śyan-or-nityam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.81). Regarding the phrase "of that which is recited": the meaning is "of that which is recited among the parasmaipada verbs in this very list. As for *tarṅtha*: however, its earlier recitation was for the sense of "joining together" (*saṃśleṣaṇe*).
Even when the action is intended for the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*), the meaning of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) applies.
(325) *śe mucādīnām* | Pāṇini 7.1.59. The root *ṣic* means "to sprinkle. Some read it as *sic*, with the vowel *i*. However, that...

It should be disregarded because it lacks a result. Here, by the rule *iṣi-sici-hvaḥ cli-raṅ*, the suffix *aṅ* is prescribed after the root *ci*; this is a rule for what was not previously established (*aprāpta-vidhi*). However, since [the suffix] would already be optionally established by the presence of the indicatory letter *ir*, the prescription is intended to make it obligatory; thus, there is no result [to be gained from the rule]. As for *piṃśatu*, it means "may he illuminate" (*dīpayatu*).
Thus ends the *tudādi* group in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
Now begins the first pāda. (794) *kṛ-vā-pā-ji-mi-svad-i-sādhy-aśū-bhya uṇ* 1.1.138. [The suffix] *uṇ* is added after the roots *kṛ*, *vā*, *pā*, *ji*, *mi*, *svad*, *sādh*, and *aś*.
Now, the *uṇādi* suffixes: *kṛ*, *vā*, *pā*. *Ḍukṛñ* in the sense of making; *vā* in the sense of moving and scenting;

*pā* in the sense of drinking; *pā* in the sense of protecting; *ji* in the sense of overcoming; *ḍumiñ* in the sense of throwing; *svada* in the sense of tasting; *sādha* in the sense of accomplishment;
*aśū* in the sense of pervading. [The word] *viśvakarman* refers to a deity; *kāru* is masculine and means an artisan, while in the three genders it means an agent or a craftsman.

Thus ends the Medinīkośa. Regarding the statement in the Dharaṇikośa, “*āruḥ* [is used] for an artisan (*śilpin*) who is the agent (*kāraka*),” it is with this in mind that he says “*kāruḥ*” and so forth. The distinction is that in the first case there is both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), whereas in the second case there is only etymological derivation. Therefore, in the second...

The connection of the *kāraka*s with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) certainly occurs. Thus says Bhaṭṭi: "Then the monkey-hero Kāru commanded Rāghava that all the monkey armies should arrive quickly. [In the example] "he drinks by means of this... [the instrument is connected to the root].

"Tailādikam" refers to the anus, the region of the rectum; Amara states: "udaṃ tvapānaṃ pāyurnā. In the etymological analysis (vigraha) of "pāti rakṣati" (it protects), it also means a protector. Thus says a mantra:
"huvastasya svatavāṃḥ pāyuragne" ("O Agni, you are his self-strong protector"). [The word] "vatavān" [is used] in the sense of "pāyu" (anus).

The substitution of *ru* [for *ra*] occurs; as Amara states: "Ṭhak, *gadoja*, and *āyuḥ*. Due to its association with masculine nouns, *jāyuḥ* is masculine. As Amara states: "*Āyuḥ*, *pitta*, *kapha*, and *śleṣmā*. According to Ujjvaladatta, a jackal is called *gomāyuḥ* because it emits (*minoti*) or inserts (*prakṣipati*) distorted speech (*vācam*) preceded by the word *go*.

In reality, however, *māyu* is a word meaning "sound," because it has been explained in that very way by the authors of the Vedic commentaries (*vedabhāṣyakāra*) and others in passages such as "the animal made *māyu*" and "one is *omāyu*, one is *ajamāyu*. That which is tasted with pleasure—that is, which is agreeable—is *svādu*; this is a term used in apposition with its substantive.

The same applies to *sādhu*. *Āśu* means "quickly. It is neuter when denoting merely the absence of delay; however, when it refers to a substance qualified by that [quality], it possesses all three genders. Having begun with "now, *śīghram* and *tvaritam*," [the author states]: "In the neuter, *śīghra* and so on occur when there is no [concrete] entity; these [words] take the gender of the object they qualify (*bhedyagāmin*)."

The word *ditya* is masculine when it refers to rice. Because of the rule "the *uṇ* suffixes are applied diversely" (*uṇādayo bahulam*), the suffix *uṇ* occurs after other roots as well. From the root *raha* (to abandon): because he seizes the moon and then abandons or leaves it, he is called *rāhu*. From the root *vas* (to dwell): because everything dwells within him, [he is called *vasu*].
Alternatively, he is *vāsu* because he dwells (*vasati*) everywhere; and since he is both *vāsu* and a god (*deva*), he is *Vāsudeva*.

Regarding the meaning "the offspring of Vasudeva," when the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *ṛṣy-andhaka-vṛṣṇi-kurubhyaś-ca*, the form *Vāsudeva* is derived; this is one further etymological analysis, and so forth.

(795) *cchandasīṇaḥ* |2| [The suffix] *iṇ* [is applied] in the Veda (*cchandas*). The term *uṇ* is understood to follow. [Thus: "He goes (*eti*), he moves (*gacchati*)"—hence *āyuḥ*. "May there not be for us *āyuḥ*" [is another example].
The word *āyuḥ* is listed among the synonyms for "human being" in the Vedic *Nighaṇṭu*. For this very reason...

In Vedic commentaries (*vedabhāṣya*), such as in the mantras "vāmagne prathamamāyumāyave" and "ā nastoke tanaye mā na āyau," this very [grammatical rule] has been explained accordingly. However, modern scholars maintain that the rule "chandasīṇaḥ" applies even to the spoken language (*bhāṣā*) due to the presence of the term "bahulam" (in various cases).
Having accepted this, they explained in the *Amara-kośa* that the word *āyus* ends in the vowel *u*, stating: "The duration of life is called *āyus*.

Now, one might object: since the suffix *us* is prescribed by the rule "after the root *sthā* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), [there is] *us*" (Pāṇini 3.3.90), the word *āyuḥ* ending in *s*—which will be mentioned later—is indeed beyond dispute in both common usage and the Veda; for this very reason, [we find expressions such as] "his matted hair is his life-force" (*jaṭā āyurasya*).
Thus, the usage in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, "having killed Jaṭāyu in battle" (*vigrahe ‘ṛdhnaṃ hatvā jaṭāyuṣam*),

as well as the usage of Śrīharṣa, "if the three worlds were intent on counting, their completion would not occur within one's lifespan" (*yadi trilokī gaṇanāparā syāt tasyāḥ samāptiryadi nāyuṣaḥ syāt*), are both consistent [with this view]. And so, "lifespan" (*āyuḥ*) refers to the duration of life (*jīvitakāla*).

If it is asked, "In this context, let the word *āyus* be explained as ending in *s*; what is the purpose of accepting it as ending in *u*?", they reply: "The word *āyus* ending in *s* is neuter; therefore, it was stated in that way with the intention that its masculine gender does not apply. Others, however, say:

If the rule *chandasi īṇaḥ* does not apply to the vernacular (*bhāṣā*), then the usage by Bhaṭṭi, “*ā vadhīṣṭa jaṭāyuṃ mā*,” and the usage cited by Abhinanda in his description of the Vindhya mountains, “*aṭaĀ vindhyasyādrerabhajata jaṭāyoḥ prathamajaḥ*,” would be untenable.

They say that he should "join" (saṅgaccheta). In reality, however, *jaṭāyuḥ* means "he goes to" or "attains" (*yāti prāpnoti*) matted hair (*jaṭā*); the suffix *ku* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *mṛgayu*. *Āyuḥ* means "he comes" (*āyāti*). Thus, the *Dvirūpakośa* states: "One should know *aṭāyuṣā*, *jaṭāyum*, and likewise *āyum* and *tathāyuṣā*," and [the *Amarakośa* says]: "*vāyunā jagadāyunā*" (by Vāyu, the life-breath of the world).
And the distinction of color is easily established; this is the general direction [of the argument].
(796) From the roots *dṛ*, *san*, *jan*, *car*, and *caṭ*, the suffix *ñuṇ* is applied. [The resulting forms are] *darasani*.
*Dṛ* means "tearing," *ṣaṇu* means "giving," *jana* means "birth," *cara* means "motion," and *caṭa*... [meaning "cutting"].
Regarding *bhedane*: “*dāru* [means] wood; *indhana* and *tvedhas* [are synonyms],” according to Amara. Regarding *cāṭu*:

“*aṭu* and *cāṭu* mean a pleasing word,” according to Haṭṭacandra. “*Āṭu* is a kind word for a man (*nari*),” according to the *Ratnamālā* lexicon. [The term] *nari* means in the masculine (*puṃsi*). [The phrase] “*akara ca bahu cāṭūn*” [is used].
"Like a bold woman," so says Māgha. In the *Māgha*, however, the neuter gender is also shown:
"And she [the dawn] with her unfeigned agitation.
(797) The root √śri takes the affix *ki* when combined with the words *ja* and *ra*. 4/1/140.
Regarding *kiñjara*: the root *śṛ* means "to injure" and *iṇ* means "to go"; the suffix *uṇ* is applied after these two. Regarding *sasya*:
the *Medinīkośa* states, "The word *iṃśāru* refers to the awn of grain (*sasyaśūka*), an arrow-head (*viśikha*), and the *kaṅka* bird. (798) *tro raśca laḥ*. 5.1.122.

*tro raśca laḥ*. [The root] *tṛ* means "to swim" and "to cross. The analysis of the rule is *traḥ raśca*. Some, however, explain it by conjoining *ṛ* and *ṝ* as *ṝ*, forming *trau* through the long vowel of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*), and then stating that for both of those, *ra* becomes *la* after *u* (i.e., *ur*). They further derive this from the root *ṛ* ("to go") with the suffix *ñuṇ*, explaining that *ra* becomes *la*.
They say that *ālu* is a specific type of vessel, such as a jar (*ghaṭī*), and that it means "it flows" (*iyarti*) or "is caused to flow" (*aryate*).
[The lexicon states: "The *arkarī*, the *ālu*, and the *galantikā* [are synonyms].
(799) The suffix *u* occurs after the roots *bhṛ*, *mṛ*, *śī*, *tṛ*, *car*, *tṛ*, *tan*, *dhani*, *mi*, and *masji*. 7.1.58.

The roots *bhṛ*, *mṛ*, and *śī*: *bhṛñ* in the sense of supporting; *mṛṅ* in the sense of relinquishing life; *śīṅ* in the sense of sleeping; *tṛ* in the senses of swimming and crossing over; *car* in the sense of moving; this [root *car*] also in the sense of eating; *tsara* in the sense of moving by stealth; *tanu* in the sense of expansion; *dhana* in the sense of wealth; *ḍumiñ* in the sense of throwing; *ṭuamasjo* in the sense of purification.
*Bharu*: According to the *Medinī*, "The word *haru* denotes gold; it is masculine when meaning a husband.

According to Hemacandra, "*haru* [denotes] a husband and gold. *Śayu*: According to Amara, "The words *śayu* and *vāhasa* both denote a python (*ajagara*). *Taru*: Those who plant [trees] cross over hell by means of this.

Regarding the word *caru*: the ritualists (*yājñika*) say it is boiled rice (*odana*) cooked internally by steam without being drained off. This has been stated likewise in the section concerning the *trivṛt-caru*. However, Kaiyaṭa, on the rule [Pāṇini 5.1.2] *gav-ādibhyo yaḥ*, says: "The word *caru* denotes a cooking pot (*sthālī*); it is applied figuratively (*bhākta*) to the rice because the rice resides within that pot."
The *Medinī* states: “*Anuḥ* [is used] for the body, for skin, and as a feminine noun; it is used in three genders for small, sparse, and thin.
The *Medinī*, under the letter *na*, states: “*Hanuḥ* is masculine for the *priyāla* tree, for a division of the zodiac, and for a bow.
He cites the *Viśvaprakāśa*: “*Dhanuṣā ca*,” etc.; [meaning] together with a bow (*dhanuṣā*), [or] a bow (*dhanuṃ*).
This is the meaning: [the word] "sārdham" (together with) is to be supplied from the verse "yā tanus tanuṣā sārdham.
Dhanvantari says, "Even that which is produced from the lineage of Uddhava will be devoid of merit; what will it accomplish?
Here, as well as in the preceding instance, the word *dhanuḥ* should be understood as ending either in the vowel *u* or in the consonant *s*. And not...

One should not suspect that the word *dhanus* ending in *s* is exclusively neuter; for according to Amara’s statement, “*athāstriyām*, *hanuścāpau*,” it also possesses masculinity. Regarding *kiṃnara*:
Amara states, “*uraṅgavadano mayuḥ*. However, the substitution of *ā* [for *i*] by the rule “*īnātiminoti*” does not apply here.
Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*): the *Viśva* lexicon states, "The word *ayu* is desired [to mean] both a horse-faced [creature] and a peacock.
That which sinks in water is a *madgu*. (800) Also after the root *aṇ*. 8.1.20.

And *aṇ*. From the root *aṇ* (meaning "to sound"), the suffix *up* should be applied; and because of the word "and" (*ca*), [the suffix is also applied] to *kaṭ* (in the sense of "raining" and so forth) and *vaṭ* (in the sense of "encircling"). That which "sounds" (*kaṭati*) the tongue is *kaṭuaḥ*. "The feminine *aṭū* refers to the Kaṭuarohiṇī plant and also to the *latārājikā*; it is neuter in the sense of 'improper action' (*akārya*), and masculine when referring to a mere taste (*rasamātra*)."
According to the *Medinī*: "In the three [genders], likewise in *sugandhi*, in *matsara*, and also in *svara*.

Regarding *vaṭua*: he is called *vaṭua* because he "covers" (*vaṭati*). As the *Saṃsārāvarta* states: "A *vaṭua* is known as the son of a twice-born (*dvijasuta*). The term *naṭavaṭua*, however, is used figuratively (*upacārāt*).
(801) *dhānye ṇit* |9|.

Regarding the phrase "abhivyāptau" (in the sense of pervasion): although the *Nyāsa* commentary states that the rule continues up to the sūtra *halipāṭī*, it is also understood from this that the sense of "maryādīkṛtya" (having delimited) is intended.

Nevertheless, it is more appropriate to say "having pervaded" (abhivyāpya). This is because the word *madhu* is seen to have an acute accent (*udātta*) in such instances as “*ibataṃ saumyaṃ madhu*,” and because Haradatta, in his commentary on the sūtra “*voto guṇavacanāt*,” also explicitly states that it means "having pervaded. This is the intended meaning.
(802) And after the roots *śṛ*, *svṛ*, *snih*, *trap*, *as*, *vas*, *han*, *kḷd*, *bandh*, and *man*.

[Pāṇini 3.1.71] *śṛ*, *svṛ*, *snih*: *śṛ* in the sense of injury; *svṛ* in the sense of sound and affliction; *snih* in the sense of affliction. *trapūṣ* in the sense of shame. *asu* in the sense of throwing. *vas* in the sense of dwelling. *han* in the sense of injury and going. *ṣ* [is the marker].

The root *klid* means "to become moist"; *bandh* means "to bind"; and *man* means "to know. Regarding *śaru*: Hemacandra states that "the word *aruḥ* [is used] for anger, an arrow, and a thunderbolt. Regarding *svaru* as a thunderbolt: Amara states that "the *atakoṭi*, *svaru*, and *śamba* [are synonyms for a thunderbolt]. Regarding *trapu* as lead: for it, upon seeing fire, seems to feel ashamed (*trapate*) or is as if embarrassed.

According to the *Medinī* lexicon, "aṅga-sīsaka-ustrapu" [are synonyms for lead]. They are called *asavaḥ* (vital breaths) because they cast forth (*asyanti*) or project the body; thus, they are the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*). Regarding *hanu*: Vararuci’s lexicon states, "The *hanu* is masculine and is located beyond the cheek.
This word is also feminine; as it is said: "The *hanu* is found in the *haṭṭavilāsinī* plant, at the commencement of a dance, and in a disease."
According to the *Medinīkośa*, [the word *kapola*] refers to a woman or to a part of the two cheeks. The suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyana*).

Thus, *hanumān*. Because of the inclusion of the term "is seen" (*dṛśi*) in the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*, the lengthening of the vowel is optional; hence, *hanūmān*. One who binds with affection is a *bandhu*; from the class beginning with *prajñādi*, the form *bāndhava* is derived.
‘*Andhu* may mean the *bandhūka* flower; *bandhu* refers to a brother or a kinsman,’ according to the Viśva-kośa.
*Manu* is the primordial king, as well as a sacred mantra.
(803) From the root *syand*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the substitution of *dha*. 11.
The root *syandū* means "to flow.
(804) [The rule] *undericcādeḥ* [applies]. From the root *undī*; *undī* means "to moisten."

(805) *īṣeḥ kicca* |13| [The suffix *kvip* is added] after the root *īṣ*, and it is also *kit*. [Root *īṣ*: *īṣa gati-hiṃsā-dāneṣu* (to go, to injure, to give)]. (806) *skandeḥ salopaśca* |14| [The suffix *kvip* is added] after the root *skand*, and there is also the elision (*lopa*) of the *s*.

From the root *skandi* (to move, to dry up). Regarding the word *kandu*: some say it refers to a place of enjoyment (*bhogasthāna*), based on the etymology "that in which people suffer heat. Others, however, say that a *kandu* is a vessel made of iron or other materials, as it "dries up" [the contents] by heating them. For this very reason, it is stated: "In the neuter, *ambarīṣa*, *brāṣṭra*, [and *kandu*]."
According to Amara, *kandu* means "a woman who causes perspiration"; or, because it is construed with the preceding [term] as "or *andu* for a man," the meaning is "a man.
(807) *sṛjeḥ asum ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 15).

From the root *sṛj* (meaning "to emit" or "to create"). In the feminine, the word *rajjūḥ* ("rope") is derived from the sense of "emitting. The augment *s-* becomes *ś-* by the rule of *ścutva*, and then *j-* by the rule of *jaśtva*. The modern grammarians (*navyāḥ*) maintain that it is more appropriately stated as: "from *ṛj*, [the suffix] *ajum* and [the vowel] *e*. The *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *rajju* occurs in the sense of a rope and also in the sense of a quality (*guṇa*)."
(808) And there is a reversal of the beginning and end of the *kṛt* suffix.

Regarding the beginning and end of the *kṛt* suffix: the root *kṛt* means "to cut. [The word] *tarku*: that by which something is cut (*kṛtyate*) is a *tarku*, a specific kind of device for winding thread. The *Hārāvalī* states: "*Tarkuṭī* is a spindle; it is a *tarku*."
(809) Not from *avañci*. [The root] *añc* means "to go. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "In the sense of 'going,' it is used with the suffix *yaṅ*; as a masculine noun, it refers to a deer (*mṛga*).
(810) From the roots *phal*, *pāṭi*, *nam*, *mani*, and *jan*, the suffixes *guk*, *paṭi*, *nāk*, *idha*, and *ta* are respectively applied.

*Phalipāṭi*: [This is the formation of the word *phalipāṭi*. From the roots *phal* (in the sense of "ripening" or "producing fruit") and *paṭ* (in the sense of "going"), with the suffix *ṇya*; from *ṇam* (in the sense of "bending" or "sound"), *man* (in the sense of "knowing"), and *jan* (in the sense of "manifestation"), the suffix *u* is applied, and for these [roots], there is respectively the addition of the guṇa vowel, as well as the substitutions *paṭ*, *nā*, *ki*, *dha*, and *ta*. Here, even though there is only a single genitive case [indicating the relationship between the roots and the suffix].

It is distinguished by the difference in the presence of an augment (*āgama*). For when an augment is added, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes a constituent part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) of the fruit [the word-form];

however, in the four rules prescribing *pāṭhaḷ* and the other substitutes, the genitive case after *pāṭhaḷ* and the others denotes the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Furthermore, that [genitive] is also applied at the end in the rules for the two types of verbal roots (*dhatu*); this is the distinction. Regarding those [roots] which lack an augment...

In the view that these are *ādeśas* (substitutes) accompanied by their original forms (*sāgamaka*), it should be understood that the genitive case is used in the sense of "place" (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *nāku* means 'essence' (*sāra*) when it denotes an object; it refers to a specific river and to Mount Malaya as a feminine noun.
Regarding *nāku* meaning an anthill: "The words *vāmalūra*, *nāku*, and *valmīka* are masculine and neuter."

Thus says Amara. Regarding the word *madhu*: Haṭṭacandra states, “*Madhu* refers to the month Caitra, a Daitya, liquor, and the nectar of flowers. Śāśvata states, “The word *madhu* is a synonym for honey, liquor, and the tax on honey; because it is listed in the *ardharca* group [of nouns], it is used in both masculine and neuter genders. [The root] *bal* means to conceal.

The *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *ṭhvalgu* occurs among the *oṣṭhaḷadi* group; it is masculine when meaning a goat, and is used as a term for 'beautiful'. As for the fact that Ujjvaladatta, having included [the root] in the *oṣṭhaḷadi* group under the rule "alerguk ca," has introduced the root *bal* in the sense of "breathing" (*prāṇana*), [it is as follows].

This [interpretation] should be disregarded because it contradicts the established evidence; for in examples such as *ṭhyaṃ nābhāvadati valgu vo gṛhe*, the reading with the dental *ṣ* is beyond dispute. (811) *śaḥ kitsanvac ca* | 6.1.30. The suffix *śa* is treated like the suffix *kit* and like *san*.

The suffix *kit* follows the root *śo*, meaning "to thin" (*tanūkaraṇe*). From this root, the suffix *up* is applied; by the rule "ādeca upadeśe," there is the substitution of *ā* for the vowel; there is reduplication; by the rule "anyataḥ," the *it* augment is added to the reduplicated syllable; and by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca," the vowel *ā* is elided. Thus, *śiśuḥ*.
(812) *yo dve ca* |21| *yo dve ca*; *yā prāpaṇe*.
(813) *kurbhraśca* |22|

And *kurbhra*. From the root *bhṛ* (to support), with the suffix *kupratyaya* and the doubling of the vowel for the root ending in *ā*, we have *bharati* (he supports), thus *barbhruḥ*. The author states what is found in the *Dharaṇikośa*: "The word *babhru* [is used] for Vaiśvānara, the trident-bearer [Śiva], and Garuḍa; it is masculine when meaning 'large' or 'a mongoose,' and it denotes one who is tawny (*piṅgala*). *Abhru* [is used] for Vaiśvānara, the trident-bearer, and he whose banner is Garuḍa; it is masculine when meaning 'large' or 'a mongoose,' and it denotes one who is tawny.

The *Medinīkośa* states: "It [the suffix] is like that which is to be expressed. Regarding the phrase "and from others as well": some say that although it should have been stated as *hraḥ ku ca*, the suffix was mentioned first because it is a suffix; others say that by the letter *ca* joined with the base *hraḥ*, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of another base.

(814) [The suffix *ku* is added] after the roots *pṛ*, *bhid*, *vyadh*, *gṛdh*, and *dhṛṣ*. Regarding *pṛ-bhid*: *pṛ* means "to protect" and "to fill"; *bhid* means "to split"; *vyadh* means "to strike"; *gṛdh* means "to desire intensely"; and *ñi-dhṛṣā* means "to be bold. [The form] *puru* is derived with the suffix *kupratyaya*.

Following the rule *parataṣṭhudoṣṭhaḷpūrvasya*, the substitution of *u* occurs, with *ra* as the subsequent element (*raparatvam*). The word *uruḥ* means "extensive" (*prājya*) and, like *abhidheya*, it is used in the masculine sense for "the world of the gods," "a specific king," and "pollen.
Some authorities also state that it refers to "serpents" (*rāhavaḥ*) and "bristly hairs" (*hṛṣavaḥ*).

(815) *kṛgrorucca* |24|. From the roots *ḍukṛñ* (in the sense of making) and *gṛ* (in the sense of sound), the suffix *ku* is applied, and the letter *u* is the substitute for the final [vowel] of these two.
[By the rule] *ṭhuraṇ raparaḥ*, the *u* is followed by *r*. [The word] *uruḥ* is masculine in the sense of a king or a devotee, and is used in the plural in the sense of a region (*nīvṛt*).
Thus says the *Medinī* lexicon.
(816) *apaduḥsuṣu sthaḥ* | 25 | [The rule] *apaduḥsu-*; the root *sthā* means "to stop" (*gatinivṛtau*). [This falls under] the group beginning with *suṣāmā*. And this...

This was stated in accordance with [the rules of] *nyāsa* and other works; however, the author of the *Vārttika* has added the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "of *sthā*, *sthi*, and *stṛ*. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *vāma* is masculine when meaning 'not straight' (*apaṣṭhu*) or 'child' (*bāla*), and it is of other genders (neuter and feminine) when meaning 'left' (*vāma*). Here, *vāme* means "in the contrary" (*pratikūle*). Of these...
Rakṣita states that because [the forms] *mṛgayu* and so forth are already established by the rule for the *mṛgayv-ādi* class, this sūtra is not accepted by the author of the Nyāsa.
(817) *arji*, *dṛśi*, *kami*, *yami*, *paśi*, *bādhā*, *mṛji*, *paśi*, *tuki*, *dhuki*, and long *hakāra*.

|27| *arjidṛśi*: for the root *arj* (meaning "to acquire"), there is the substitution of *ṛji*; for *dṛś*, the substitution of *paś*; and for *kam*, the addition of the augment *tu*. *am* (in the sense of) disease or motion, etc.; for this [root], there is the addition of the augment *dhuk*. *paś* (in the sense of) sitting.

This is a verbal root from the *sūtra*. Its vowel is lengthened. For the root *bādhṛ* (in the sense of eating), there is the substitution of *ha*. The meaning is that the suffix *ku* may occur after all six [roots]. Regarding "without distinction": the word *paśu* is listed in the *cādi* group. Dharaṇi states: "The indeclinable *aśu* has the sense of 'seeing'. *Kantuḥ* means *kandarpa* (the god of love). The suffix *ṭhi*.

"Kanturmakarāṅgaḥ"—thus it is stated in the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*. Regarding "pāṃsu": the root *paḍi* (in the form *pasi*) meaning "to destroy" belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in a dental. Regarding "strīpuṃsayoḥ": for it has been stated by Amara, "The two following [words], *bhuja* and *bāhu*, are used in both genders. That is, the two words *bhuja* and *bāhu* are used in both [genders].

The meaning of that [verse] is "in the case of a woman and a man. This word also ends in long ā (ākārānta); for this very reason, Dāmodara states: "Āhaḥ is masculine in the sense of a horse and a forearm. Furthermore, according to the Medinīkośa: "Āhā is feminine in the sense of a forearm; it is masculine in the sense of a measure, a bull, and wind," thus this word also ends in ṭāp (long ā).

(818) *prathi-mradi-bhrasj-ām saṃprasāraṇaṃ sa-lopaś-ca* || 28 || [The roots] *prath*, *mrad*, and *bhrasj* undergo vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the elision of the suffix *sa*. *Prath* means "to become famous"; *mrad* means "to soften"; *bhrasj* means "to cook. From the root *prath*: *prathate* ("he becomes wide/famous") → *pṛthuḥ*.
" *Pṛthuḥ* is used in three genders for 'great'; it refers to the cinnamon tree (*tvakpatrī*) and black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīra*), and as a masculine, it denotes fire (*agni*)."
According to the *Medinī* lexicon, [the word] is used in the sense of "another king. It is called *mṛdu* because it can be softened (*mradituṃ śakyate*) due to its lack of hardness;
it means "tender" or "delicate. According to the *Viśva* lexicon, *hṛgu* refers to Śukra, a precipice, Jamadagni, and the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva).
(819) [The suffix] *valañ* and *bañyaṇ* are applied, with the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). 29.

Regarding the word *laghu*: the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa* states, “*Laghu* is feminine for *pṛkkā*, neuter for ‘swift,’ and also [refers to] black *aguru*. The *Medinī* states, “*Aghu* (variant of *laghu*) is masculine for ‘heavy’ and ‘charming,’ and neuter for ‘insubstantial’; it is feminine for ‘swift,’ black *aguru*, and the medicinal plant named *pṛkkā*.”
The suffix *vā* is applied to the words *mūla*, *laghu*, and *alpa* when they refer to the fingers; or rather, the vowel *o* is substituted for the final vowel. Regarding the term *nṛpabheda*:
by this, the statement of Kālidāsa—"Having considered the meaning of the root *gam* (to go), the knower of meanings made his own son [Dilīpa] 'Raghu' by name"—is explained. Regarding the word *bahu*:
The *Medinī* lexicon states: "They say [the word *ūru*] occurs in numbers such as three and so forth, but when the referent is large, it is used [as a singular].

(820) Regarding the form *ūri*: [it is derived] from the root *ūrṇ* with the elision of the *nu*-suffix. As for *ūru*, Amara says: "The word *akthi* is neuter; *ūru* is masculine. It is that which is covered (*ūrṇūyate*) or concealed.

(823) *āṅparayoḥ khaniśṛbhyāṃ ḍicca* |33|.

Thus, *haridruḥ* means "a tree" (specifically, the *haridrā* tree). Some say it refers to *dāruharidrā* (Indian barberry). *Śatadruḥ* is a specific river.

(825) And in the *Śata* [commentary]: 35. Regarding “tadvān”: by the rule “yaudrubhyāṃ maḥ,” the suffix *ma* is applied.

Regarding the phrase “also from the verbal root”: some say that when the word *nīla* is used as a prefix (*upapada*), the suffix *ṭi* is elided after the root *gam*, the *mum* augment is added to the prefix, and a long vowel is optionally prescribed by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). [The verse continues: “*igu cit...*” (Pāṇini 1.1.3).

The *Medinī* states: "[The suffix] *ku* follows the root *pīl* in the sense of obstructing. It is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words); therefore, from this root *pīl* in the sense of obstructing, the suffix *ku* is applied.

Mādhava, Prasādakāra, and others have likewise followed this. But this is not logical.

This is because the reading with the letter *tha* in such mantras as "vameṣāṃ vithurā śavāṃsi" and "atha viddhā vithureṇācidasrāḥ" is beyond dispute. If this is argued, understand that [the form] *dhuraḥ* is derived from *vi-gata* by means of a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound), because it has been stated exactly so in the *Vṛtti* and *Padamañjarī* on the rule *amāsāntāḥ*. In this case, let it simply be *vyatheḥ kiñci*; by the rule *rahijyā*, the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) would certainly occur, so there is no need for further concern.
It should not be confused; for it has been established that among roots such as *grah* and *jyā*, this [root] is the fourth of its class, not *vyadh*.

55. After the root *kam*. The root *kam* means "to desire. From this, the suffix *ilac* is applied, and *paś* is the substitute for the final portion [of the root]. [As in: *apilā* in the sense of *reṇukā*.

(966) "After the root *rud*, there is the elision of *ṇi*. 1.1.79.

Regarding *rudra*: from the root *rudir* (meaning "to shed tears"), with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *rak* is applied; the *ṇic* is elided by the rule *ṇeraniṭi*. However, if the *ṇic* were simply elided [without the *rak*], the *guṇa* substitution would apply by the rule *ugitaśca*; therefore, it is stated that there is an elision of the *ṇic* [along with the addition of *rak*]. Thus, one who causes to weep (*rodayati*) is called *rudra*. Now, if this is so—

If it is argued that there would be a contradiction here with the Śruti text, “He wept; because he wept, that is the Rudra-nature of Rudra,” they reply as follows: Just as, in accordance with the rule *arti-kṛ-dhṛ-sṛ-jī-vām̐ś-ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.181), the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is accepted in the word *śambhu*—namely, that He brings about (*bhāvayati*) welfare (*śam*)—so too [should it be understood here].

Even in the case of the word *arodīt* ("he wept"), since it is accepted that the causative sense is inherent, the meaning "he caused [them] to weep" is obtained; thus, there is no contradiction with the Vedic text. Nor is it the case that the gods placed desirable wealth in the fire and then requested that wealth from the gods, while Agni merely wept.

It should not be argued that because of the meaning of such Vedic passages as "He wept" (*so ’rodīt*), it is impossible to assume here a causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) [i.e., that Agni caused others to weep], and thus the contradiction with the Śruti is unavoidable; for [the passage means]: the desirable wealth established by the gods was not given to the gods by Agni, and those very gods wept.

They performed [the rite]. However, since it is possible to interpret the meaning as "Agni, not giving that [offering] to him, caused him to weep," or alternatively, let the meaning of the word *rudra* when applied to Agni simply be "he weeps" (*rodati iti rudraḥ*), but nevertheless—

Regarding the term Rudra as it is conventionally designated as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra: the meaning is that even when other suffixes are applied to the root *rud* by means of another Uṇādi-sūtra (*roderṇiḥ*), there is elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇerluk*).
An example in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is: he who nourishes and increases the subjects is Brahmā (*brahmā*). [The word] *śam* means happiness.

“He causes to exist” (bhāvayati) is [the etymology of] Śambhu, and so forth. In Vedic usage, however, the root *vṛdh* means “to increase”: in the passage “may the hymns of praise cause you to increase” (*vardhantu tvā suṣṭutayaḥ*), the meaning is “may they cause you to grow. In the passage “he who generated these” (*ya imā jajāna*), the form is from the root *jan* in the sense of “manifestation” in the perfect tense (*liṭ*); the meaning is “he brought them into existence. Here, when the suffix *ṇal* follows, by the rule “*ata upadhāyāḥ*”... [the vowel is lengthened].

Vṛddhi indeed occurs, because the prohibition [by Pāṇini 1.1.5] "not before ani and vadhi" is accepted as applying specifically to the affixes ciṇ, ñit, ṇit, and kit; nor should it be argued that once the ṇi-affix is elided,
the suffix would be followed by a pratyaya (causing the application of ām by Pāṇini 7.1.32), since [the rule applies] only when not preceded by a mantra.

Because the application of *ām* is excluded by way of *paryudāsa*, the suspicion regarding *ām* is cast far away by the Vārttika “*āsy-anekāca*” (*Pāṇini 6.4.122*), since when the *ṇi*-suffix is elided before the *liṭ* [affix], the condition of having more than one vowel (*anekāctva*) is absent.

Now, one might object: in the case of the *ṇal* [affix], by the rule “*ṇer-aniṭi*” (*Pāṇini 6.4.51*), the *ṇi* is elided before an *ārddhadhātuka* affix beginning with a non-*it* vowel, resulting in *jajāna*.

If it is argued that since *rūpa* is already established, what is the use of this example for elision (*luk*), we say: not so. For when there is elision of the *ṇi*-affix, the rule "the roots *ṇīj*, *ṛṣ*, *sañj*, *suraj*, and those ending in *am* are *mit* in the presence of a *ṇi*" would apply, resulting in a short vowel by the rule "there is shortening of [roots] ending in *i*," because the condition of being followed by a *ṇi*-affix remains possible through the principle of "characterization by the affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇanyāya*). Consequently, [the form] would be *janena*.

It might be so; however, when there is elision (*luk*), the rule regarding the characteristics of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇanyāya*) does not apply, and thus, due to the absence of the status of being a *mit* vowel, the desired form is established. With the intention that, by virtue of the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*), this occurs in some instances even outside of technical names (*asaṃjñā*) and Vedic meters (*chandasi*), he provides the example beginning with "they blow" (*vānti*).
