Furthermore, the *Medinī* also provides the root-usage beginning with "in the sky" (*ūrākāśe*). (1002) [The suffix *ni* is applied] after the root *āp*, and there is a shortening of the vowel. (Pāṇini 3.3.217).
From the root *āp*: *āplṛ* in the sense of pervading; from this root, the suffix *kvip* is applied, and there is lengthening of the vowel of the root.
Due to the treatment as if it were *ślu*, reduplication occurs.
(1003) *parau vrajeḥ ṣaḥ padānte* | 218 || [The substitute *ṣ* is applied in place of *vraj* when preceded by *pari*, at the end of a word.]
The roots *vraj* and *gati* [are used in the sense of] "going.
(1004) *huvaḥ śluvacca* | 219 | *huvaḥ*: the root *hū* [meaning] "giving" and "eating"; from this, the suffix *kvip* is applied, and there is lengthening of the vowel of the root.
The reduplication occurs because of the treatment as *śluv*.
(1005) *sruvaḥ kaḥ* | 220. *sruvaḥ kaḥ*. The root *sru* means "to flow. *Sruva* is a specific type of sacrificial vessel. This is the *sruva*.
[The term *sruva*] is well-known in such instances as "he offers with the *abhijihvṛtī*" and "he performs the *pārvaṇa* oblations with the *sruva*.

(1006) *cik ca* | 221 | *cik ca*. [The word *sruva*] remains [the subject]. The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. [As in] *ka id iti*, by that [rule], *sruk* [is also included].
In examples such as *srucau* and *srucaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution does not occur. (P.
6.4.41) *tanoḥ anaś ca vaḥ*. [The suffix *ṭ* is added after the root *tan* (*tanu* in the sense of "expansion"). *vaḥ* refers to the entire cluster.]
Thus he says: "The substitution of the word *va*. Amara states: "In feminine forms, however, *tvak*, *asṛk*, and *dharā* [are used].
(1008) From the roots *glā* and *nud*, the suffix *ḍau*.
[The roots] *glā* and *nud*: *glai* means 'to lose one's vigor,' and *ṇud* means 'to impel. "The moon is *lauḥ*."
*Kalānidhiḥ* is defined by Amara; and *nauḥ*, *taraṇiḥ*, and *tariḥ* are synonyms for a boat.
Regarding *glaukaroti*: it means he causes that which was not a moon (*aglauḥ*) to become a moon (*glauḥ*). Because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the case-ending (*sup*) is elided.

(1009) *cviravyayam* | 224. The meaning is that [the suffix] *cv* alone constitutes an indeclinable; therefore, words such as *glauḥ*, *nauḥ*, and *gauḥ* do not possess the status of indeclinables. (1010) *rāterḍṬaḥ* | 225. [The suffix] *ḍṬa* [is applied] after the root *rāti*.

From the root *rā*, meaning "to give. Regarding *rā*: by the rule *rāyo hali*, there is the substitution of *ā*. As Medinī states: "The word *rā* is recorded as meaning 'purifier' (*pāvaka*) and 'sharp' (*tīkṣṇa*); *rāḥ* [with visarga] is masculine and means 'gold' (*svarṇa*) and 'wealth' (*vitaya*). And Hemacandra states: "*rāḥ* [with visarga] is used for the sharp, for fire (*dahana*); *rā* [without visarga] is used for gold, for a cloud, and for wealth."
(1011) *gamer ḍoḥ* ||226|| From the root *gam-* [meaning] *gamlṛ gatau* (to go). By the rule *oto ṇit*, we have *gauḥ*.
Keśava states: "The word *go* [denotes] the sun," and so forth. [Also]: *auḥ* [denotes] heaven, a bull, and a ray.

"In *vajra* and *candra*, [the word] *pumān* (masculine) occurs; in *arjunī*, *netra*, *dik*, *bāṇa*, *bhū*, *vāk*, and *vāri*, *gauḥ* is considered [to be feminine]," so says Amara. Regarding "also from the root *dyaut*": the root *dyaut* means "to shine. That in which the gods (*deva*) shine is *dyauḥ* (heaven).
(1012) *ḍūa* is added after the root *bhram*. 227. After *bhram*:

the root *bhramu* means "to wander" (*anavasthāne*), and *gamlṛ* means "to go" (*gamane*). *Agregūḥ* means "a servant. (1013) *ḍosi* is added after the root *dam*. 228. After *dam*: the root *dam* means "to subdue" (*dame*). *Damosiḥ* means "one who subdues."

From the root *dam* (to subdue), with the suffix *ḍa*. Due to the indicatory letter *ḍ*, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion. Regarding the form *doṣ*, its masculine gender is established by the usage of Śrīharṣa: “*oṣaṃ tasya*” (his heat). Its neuter gender is established by the usage in the Mahābhāṣya: “*akuddoṣaṇī*” (the two arms not angry). [And it is also used as feminine: “*ordoṣā ca bhujo bāhuḥ*” (the arm, the forelimb, and the doṣā).
That this [term] is also feminine, as in *dhanañjayakośa*, and so forth, has already been explained in detail previously.
(1014) *paṇerijyādeśca vaḥ* | 229. From *paṇi*: *paṇa* means "to bargain" and "to praise. Amarasimha says: "A merchant (*naigama*), and so forth."
(1015) *vaśeḥ kit* | 230. From the root *vaś*—meaning "to desire"—the suffix *ini* shall be added as *kit*. By the rule *rahijy-*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).

(1016) *bhṛña ūcca* | 231 | From the root *bhṛñ*: from *bhṛñ* in the sense of "supporting," the suffix *ini* shall be added as a *kit*, and the final vowel of the root shall be replaced by *ū*. (1017) *jasisahorurin* | 232 | From the roots *jas* and *sah*, the suffix *urin* is added.

The root *jas* means "to exhaust" (*mokṣaṇe*). The root *ṣah* means "to endure" (*marṣaṇe*). Regarding the mantra "asuraye staryaṃ pipyathurgām," [the word] *jasuraye* means "to one who is exhausted" (*śrāntāya*). In the passage "īcāyamānaṃ jasuriṃ na śyenaṃ," *jasuriṃ* refers to a hungry hawk (*kṣudhitaṃ śyenaṃ*), meaning "like a hawk-bird. [The term] *hutasya vājī*...
Regarding the mantra *sahurir ṛtāvā*, the Vedic commentary (*vedabhāṣya*) states that *sahuriḥ* means "one who is capable of enduring" (*sahanaśīla*).
[Pāṇini 3.2.155] *suyuruvṛño yuc*: after the roots *su*, *yu*, *ru*, and *vṛñ*, the suffix *yuc* is applied.
*Su* is in the sense of extracting (*abhiṣava*), *yu* in the sense of mixing (*miśraṇa*), *ru* in the sense of sound (*śabda*), and *vṛñ* in the sense of choosing (*varaṇa*). [The word *avaniṃ*...]

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "In the sense of a sacrifice (*adhvara*), bathing (*snāna*), and the crushing of Soma. A *Yavana* is a specific type of barbarian (*mleccha*). According to the *Medinī*: "The word *ravaṇa* is used in the senses of sound and tone.
Some say that *ravaṇa* refers to the cuckoo. *Varaṇa* is a species of tree; furthermore, *varaṇā* is the name of a river.
"Varaṇa" refers to the *tiktaśāka* plant; "varaṇa" also means a rampart or a fence—so says the *Viśvakośa*.
"Varuṇa," "varaṇa," "setu," "tiktaśāka," and "kumāraka" [are synonyms]—so says the *Amarakośa*.
(1019) [The suffix] *raś* is applied after the root *aś*, and there is also the substitution of *raś*. 2.34.

From the root *aś* (in the sense of pervading). However, when it refers to the tongue, [it is derived as follows]: *ras* in the sense of tasting belongs to the curādigaṇa; from that, the suffix *lyu* is applied because it belongs to the nandy-ādi group. Alternatively, the suffix *yuc* is applied according to the rule "ṇyāsaśranthaḥ. Thus, *rasanā* means that which tastes or causes tasting. [The lexicon states: "Tasting" (*rasana*) occurs in the senses of tasting and sound, but not in the sense of the tongue.
According to the *Medinīkośa*, "rasanā" is used in the masculine for the neck-tendon (*gāsnā*) and in the feminine for the tongue;

the rule that the form denoting a girdle contains the palatal *ś* while the form denoting the tongue contains the dental *s* has been stated based on the observation of extensive usage. However, in reality, it is the one containing the palatal *ś*.

The word *raśanā* refers both to a girdle and to the tongue; the word *rasanā*, containing the dental *s*, should likewise be understood as having these two meanings. For it is said: "The words *śamba*, *śūkara*, and *pāṃśu* are both palatal and dental, and so too is *raśanā* [used] for the tongue."

In the Viśvakośa, both [meanings] are valid for the tongue: "rasana" is used in the sense of sound (*niḥsvana*), and "rasanā" is used in the sense of a girdle (*kāñcī*) as well as the tongue; thus, according to both the Ajaya and Dharaṇikośas, both are valid for the girdle. And so, regarding the rule *aseraś ca*, [the roots] *aśū* (to pervade) and *aśa* (to eat) [are intended].

Both verbal roots should also be understood here. From the two roots *ras* (in the sense of tasting) and *ras* (in the sense of sound), the suffix *yuc*—which will be mentioned immediately below in the rule "often elsewhere as well"—is applied.
Therefore, they say that the derivation of the component meanings is easily established in all cases.

(1020) *undanalopaśca* |235|. From the root *undī* (meaning "to moisten"), the suffix *yauc* is applied. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *odana* is not feminine; it refers to cooked rice (*bhakta*), while *odinī* is feminine and refers to the plant *balā*."

(1021) *gam-er gaś-ca* |236| [The suffix *kan* is applied] after the root *gam*, and *ga* is substituted for it. The root *gamlṛ* means "to go. Amara states: "The atmosphere is called *abha*, *antarikṣa*, and *gagana*. (1022) *bahulam anyatrāpi* |237| [The suffix *kan* is applied] diversely even in other cases as well.

Frequently [occurring]: *syandū* in the sense of flowing, and *ruc* in the sense of shining. Regarding *syandana*, the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *syandana* refers to the ear, water, the *tiniśa* tree, and a chariot; it is feminine [when referring to] a woman. Regarding *rocana*: "The word *rocana* refers to the red *kahlāra* lotus and a beautiful cowherd woman; as a masculine noun, *rocana* refers to the *kūṭa-śālmali* tree and one who causes to shine."

And regarding the word *triṣu*: the root *cad* means "to delight. According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *candana* refers to sandalwood produced in the Malaya mountains; it may denote a particular species of monkey, while *candanī* refers to a specific river. And according to the *Medinīkośa*: "*Candanī* is a name for a particular river; *candana* is not feminine when referring to sandalwood, but is neuter when referring to the plant *bhadarakālī*."

*Bhadrakālī* is a specific medicinal herb. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *bhadrakālī* refers to the *gandholī* plant and also to the female deity Kātyāyanī. The root *asu* means "to cast" (*kṣepaṇe*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *asana* is neuter in the sense of casting, but masculine when it denotes the *jīvaka* tree. The root *at* means "to go continuously"; with *rāja-* as its prefix, it forms *rājāta*.
"Ājātana occurs in the sense of *kṣīrikā*, *priyāla*, and also *kiṃśuka*," according to the Viśva and Medinī lexicons. Other such [entries] should also be observed.
(1023) The suffix *kyun* is applied after the root *rañj*. 238.

From the root *rañj* (to color/dye): with the suffix *lyuṭ*, it becomes *rañjanam*. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *ṭhrañjanaḥ* means the production of passion; *rañjanam* means red sandalwood. By virtue of the rule for irregularity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *kyun* is also applied to the root *kṛp*; furthermore, there is an absence of the substitution of *l* for *r* as prescribed by the rule "ṛpo ro laḥ". Thus, *kṛpaṇaḥ*.

(1024) *bhūsūdhūbhrasjibhyaśchandasī* || 239 || *bhūsū-*: *bhū* in the sense of existence; *ṣūṅ* in the sense of the birth of living beings; *dhūñ* in the sense of shaking; *bhrasja* in the sense of cooking.
Due to the use of the term "extensively" (*bahula*), these roots are also occasionally used in the common language (*bhāṣā*). [The root *hu*] is also used in the sense of "the world" (*viṣṭapa*).

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "It [the word *bhrāṣṭra*] may mean water, the sky, or a person. According to the *Amara-kośa*: "The words *viṣṭapa*, *bhuvana*, and *jagat* [mean world]. Regarding the form *bhṛjjana*: there is a vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "rahi-jyā," etc.;

the *s* is changed to *d* by the rule for the *jaś*-substitution, and the *d* is changed to *j* by the rule for the *ścutva*-substitution. In the neuter, *ambarīṣa* means a frying pan (*bhrāṣṭra*), but not [in the masculine].
Thus says Amara.
(1025) *kṛ-pṛ-vṛji-mandi-dhāñ-kyuḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.182]. *kṛ-pṛ*: *kṛ* means "to scatter," *pṛ* means "to protect" and so forth, *vṛjī* means "to avoid," *madi*...

In words such as *stuti*, the root is *ḍudhāñ* in the sense of "holding" and "nourishing. According to the *Medinī*: "The word *idhana* occurs in the sense of family and destruction. Hemacandra states: "*Idhana* [occurs] in the senses of family and destruction.
(1026) [The suffix *kvan* is added] after the root *dhṛṣ* with the substitution of *dhiṣ* when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is formed. 241.

From the root *dhṛṣ*—the root *ñidhṛṣ* meaning "boldness"—the suffix *kyu* is applied, and there is the substitution of *dhiṣ* for the verbal root. According to the *Medinī*: "In the sense of teacher, *dhiṣaṇā* [is used]; in the sense of intellect and woman, [it is *dhiṣaṇā*]. And according to the *Amara-kośa*: "The Lord of Speech (*gīṣpati*), the Preceptor (*guru*), is *dhiṣaṇa*."

(1026) *pṛṣad-bṛhan-mahat-jagac-chatṛvac ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.170]. Regarding the phrase "in the present tense" (*vartamāne*) and "like the *śatṛ* suffix" (*śatṛvacceti*): the point is that, according to this rule, the augment *num* is applied by the rule *ugidacām* [Pāṇini 7.1.70], resulting in *mahān*;
and in the feminine, by the rule *ugitaśca* [Pāṇini 4.1.6], the suffix *ṅīp* is added, thereby establishing forms such as *mahatī*. Now, an objection: [is not this already established?]

If it is argued that *pṛṣan*, *mahat*, and so forth should be formed with the suffix *śatṛ* itself— by the rule "after [a root] ending in a vowel other than *a*, there are *śatṛ* and *nāśac*"— and that consequently the rules "in the present tense" and "like *śatṛ*" need not be stated, resulting in great economy (*lāghava*), then they reply: if they were indeed formed with the suffix *śatṛ*, then by the rule "the *śap* augment occurs before the agentive suffix,"...
If the suffix *śap* were present, as in *mahatī* and so on, the augment *num* would apply by the rule *ṭhācchīnadyoḥ*;
however, in cases such as *mahān*, the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix would apply by the rule *āsyanudātenṅdidupadeśāt*. But if it ends in the suffix *ati*, [the following applies].

With the intention that there is no fault mentioned because the suffix *ati* is accepted as being an *ardhadhātuka*, the derivation is accepted as being by means of the irregular form (*nipātana*) ending in the suffix *ati*. [The roots are:
*vṛh* in the sense of increasing, *maha* in the sense of honoring, and *gamlṛ* in the sense of going. The word *pṛṣanti* denotes drops.
The plural form is cited to indicate that the word *pṛṣat* is neuter. According to the *Medinīkośa*:
"The word *ṛṣat* [is used] for a *bhṛga* (a type of insect) as masculine; for a drop (*bindu*) it is not [masculine], nor is *pṛṣata* [masculine] in the two genders;
and for both of these, when joined with the white spot (*śvetabindu*), both are [used] in the three genders. [Also mentioned is] *ṛhatī*.

According to the *Viśva-kośa*: "The word *bṛhatī* refers to the small eggplant (*kṣudravārtākī*), the thorny plant (*kaṇṭakārī*), speech, the great water-holding [cloud], and two types of meters and garments. Because it ends in the suffix *śatṛ*, the augment *num* is applied by the rule *ṭhugidacām*.
*Bṛhat* means vast or extensive. [In another sense,] *bṛhatī* refers to a particular type of lute (*vallakī*) or to a kingdom.
It may be neuter; it is masculine when meaning "the essence" or "the best," according to the *Medinīkośa*.
*Mahatī* refers to the lute of Nārada. As the *Vaijayantī* states: "The *bṛhatī* belongs to Viśvāvasu, the *kalāvatī* to Tumburu, the *mahatī* to Nārada, and the *kacchapī* to Sarasvatī."

"Looking repeatedly at the great [earth]," so says Māgha. Regarding the word *jagat*: it is neuter when meaning "the world" (*viṣṭapa*); it is masculine when meaning "wind"; and it is used in three genders when meaning "that which moves. According to the *Medinī*, *jagatī* refers to the world, the earth, a specific meter, and also to people. Among these, the one denoting wind is masculine.

Due to the designation *śatṛvat* (as if it were a present participle), the suffix *num* is applied by virtue of its being marked with *u*, resulting in forms such as *agan*, *jagantau*, and *jaganta*. However, it should be understood that for the word derived according to the rule "of the roots *yauti*, *gam*, and *juhoti*, there is reduplication" (*yautigamijuhotīnāṃ dve ca*), the *num* suffix is absent, resulting in forms such as *jagat*, *jagatau*, and *jagataḥ*.

(1027) *saṃścatṛ-padehat* || 243 || [The forms] *saṃścatṛ*, *tṛp*, and *dvehat* are derived from the roots *ciñ* (to collect), *tṛpa* (to satisfy), and *hana* (to kill or move). "They are irregularly formed" (*nipātyante*)—the remainder of the rule is that they end in the suffix *atip*. "For the purpose of exclusion"—and thus:

In the word *saṃścat*, there is no possibility of the *num* augment [before the genitive ending] because of the rule *ṭhugidacām*. However, in the word *vehat*, the intention is that the feminine suffix *ṅīp* applies by the rule *ṭhugitaśca*. Regarding the root *sañci*: Subhūticandra, however, states that *saṃścat* is derived from the root *śvayati* preceded by the prefix *sam*. As for *tṛpacchatra*, others say it means "the moon."

*Vehat* means "she destroys the embryo. Regarding *etae ca*: this means that the vowel *i* belonging to the word *vi* becomes *e*. While the term *gauḥ* (cow) is understood as a governing word (*anuvṛtti*), Amara states: "*Vehat* is a cow that destroys the embryo.
(1028) In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffix *asānac* is applied after the roots *śu* and *jṛ*. 2.4.4.

In the Vedic language (*cchandasī*): the roots *śu* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*) and *jṛṣ* in the sense of "loss of vitality" (*vayohānau*). Regarding the word *panthāḥ*: in the two mantras beginning with "rathamanmaha," the word *śavasāna* has been explained as referring to a "goer.
(Pāṇini 3.2.175: *ṛñjivṛdhimandisahibhyaḥ kit*. (The suffix *kvanip* is added after these roots, and it is *kit*.)

From the roots *ṛñj* (in the sense of stretching), *vṛdh* (in the sense of growth), *mad* (in the sense of praise, etc.), and *sah* (in the sense of endurance), the suffix *asan* is added with the *kit* designation. Thus, *ṛñjasānaḥ* means "a cloud. Because *ṛj* is marked with the *it* augment (*idit*), the *num* augment is applied; and precisely because it is marked with *it*, there is no elision of the final nasal (*nalopa*). In this way, these three—*man*, *sad*, and *sah*—are also [treated similarly].

They could have been read in the previous sūtra itself; however, the *kit* designation is useful only for the root *vṛdh*. In the subsequent sūtra as well, the mention of *guṇa* is easily dispensable, since both *artih* and *suṭ* belong to *vṛdh*; yet in the Bhāṣya, only the etymological meaning is accepted.
(1030) *arter guṇaḥ śuṭ ca* | 246 | From the root *ṛ* (to go), there is *guṇa* [substitution] and the augment *suṭ* for the suffix.
However, in the commentary on the mantra *ṭhāsāviṣadarśasānāya*, regarding the word *arśasānāya*, it refers to [the subduing] of enemies.
*Hiṃsitre* has already been explained.
(1031) *samyānac* [is added] after *stu*. 247. *sam*, *ṣṭuñ* [meaning] "to praise. After this root, when *sam* is the prefix, the suffix *ānac* is applied.

(1032) *yudhibudhidṛśaḥ kicca* ||248|| [The suffix] *ānac* is added after the roots *yudh*, *budh*, and *dṛś*, and it is *kit*. *yudh* in the sense of "struggle": *yudhānaḥ* (an enemy). *budh* in the sense of "awakening":
*budhānaḥ* (a teacher). *dṛś* in the sense of "seeing": [the form is *dṛśānaḥ*]. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), *ānac* is also added to *kṛp*: *kṛpāṇaḥ* (a sword).
The sword: "How can one who releases his own treasury at the time of giving to others be counted among the wretched?
(1033) [From the root] *hurch* with the suffix *san*, there is elision of the suffix and elision of the *ch*. 249.

Regarding *hurccheḥ*: from the root *hurcch* in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*), the suffix *sannat* (the desiderative marker *san*) is applied, followed by *ānac*, with the elision of *san* and the elision of the letter *ch*. Regarding the mantra "yuyodhyasmajjuhurāṇamenaḥ," the commentary states: "O [Agni], separate (*yuyodhi*)—that is, keep apart—the crooked (*juhurāṇam*) sin (*enaḥ*), i.e., the evil (*pāpam*)."
(1034) *śvater daś ca* |250|.
From the root *śvit-*—that is, from *śvitā varṇe* (to become white)—the suffix *san* is added, followed by *ānac*. By the rule “*anyaṅeḥ*,” there is reduplication;
the *san* suffix is elided; and the letter *t* is replaced by *d*. Because the term *kit* is understood [from a previous rule], there is no *guṇa* strengthening.
Regarding the term *puṇyakarmā*: Amara states that in the section on adjectives (*viśeṣyanighna*), it is [defined] as "one who is shining and whose action is not black" (*śvit-dāno 'kṛṣṇa-karma*).

The meaning is: one whose action (*karman*) is "not black"—that is, white (*śukla*)—because it is pure due to being free from sin (*niṣpāpa*). However, Kṣīrasvāmin, having forgotten the relevant sūtra, [interprets it as]: "from the root *śvit*, in the sense of whiteness (*śvaitya*), the suffix *kānac* is applied after the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*)."

That [explanation] is incorrect, because the *kānac* suffix is Vedic (*chāndasa*), and because the elision of the *na*-augment is untenable due to the presence of the *idit* marker; such is the direction [of the argument]. (Pāṇini 3.2.135) The suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* are applied after the roots *śaṃs*, *kṣad*, and so forth, when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be expressed, and they do not take the augment *anuṭ*.

"Śaṃstar—" [is derived as follows: from the root *śaṃs* in the sense of "praise," the suffix *tṛn* is applied. Regarding the rule *ṭhaptṛn*, it is stated that the mention of *naptr* and others in the sūtra is for the purpose of restriction: if there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*) for words ending in the *tṛc* suffix derived from the *uṇādi* class, then it occurs only for *naptr* and others. Therefore, he provides an example where there is no lengthening here: *śaṃstarau*.

Regarding the word *śāstṛ*: because it has the suffix *nit*, it is udātta on the first syllable. Thus, there is a mantra: “*rāvagrābha uta śaṃstā suvipraḥ*. From the root *śās* (to instruct), indicated by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), we have *śāstṛ*. He who instructs—that is, disciplines—beings is the Teacher (*śāstṛ*), namely the Buddha. [The forms are: *śāstarau*, *śāstaraḥ*. [And as in the verse: "*āstā samantabhadre nā śāsake*" (O Samantabhadra, you are the Teacher, the instructor).

Furthermore, regarding the term *punaranyavat*: because the root preceded by *pra-* is listed among *naptr* and others, the long vowel is applied by the rule *ṭhaptṛn*. Thus we have *praśāstārau*, *praśāstāraḥ*. [As it is said: "The word *praśāstṛ* denotes a Vaiśya, a priest at a sacrifice, a doorkeeper, a charioteer, a servant, and a son; it may also refer to one who is appointed and to the Creator (Brahmā). It is masculine.

According to the *Medinīkośa*, he says "in the case of a Vaiśya woman. However, Amara says, "and [the son] born of a Śūdra from a Kṣatriya woman. The root *ṇīñ* means "to lead" (*prāpaṇe*) and has the prefix *ut*. *Unnetṛ* is a specific type of officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). "In many other cases as well": in other instances too, the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* occur frequently after verbal roots.
Since the [terms] "thinker," "slayer," and so forth are already established by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the preceding sūtra, this sūtra is for the purpose of elaboration (*prapañca*).

*naptṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, *tṛp*, *tṛ*, *bhrātṛ*, *jāmātṛ*, *mātṛ*, *pitṛ*, *duhitṛ* || 253 || The twelve [words] beginning with *naptṛ* ending in the suffixes *-tṛn* and *-tṛc* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). Regarding *naptṛ*: there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for the negative particle *nañ*; for the root *patlṛ* (meaning "to go"), there is the elision of the vowel *a*; and for the root *ṇīñ* (meaning "to lead"), [there is the elision of the nasal].

The roots *tviṣ* (to shine), *hu* (to give or eat), *pūñ* (to purify), *bhrājṛ* (to shine), *mā* (to measure), *pā* (to protect), and *duh* (to fill) [are used here]. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *vaṣṭā* denotes a male, a divine artisan (*devaśilpin*), a carpenter (*takṣan*), and also a specific Āditya. [The word] *jāyām*.
The root *mā* has the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*) internally implied.
(1037) *suñyaser ṛn* |254|. With *suñ* as an upapada, from the root *asu* (meaning "to throw"), the suffix *ṛn* is applied; there is a *yaṇ* substitution [of *u* for *v*]. *Svasā* means "sister."
The reading *sāvaser* is, however, found in some manuscripts.
(1038) *yeter vṛddhiś ca* | 255 | [The suffix *iñ* is added] after the root *yat*, and there is also vṛddhi [of the first vowel]. [The root is] *yatī* in the sense of "exertion" (*prayatna*).

(1039) *Nañi ca nandeḥ* | 256 | *Nañi ca*. From the root *ṇadi* (meaning "to prosper"), when the negative particle *nañ* is used as an upapada, the suffix *ṛn* is applied. Thus: *na nandati* ("he does not rejoice").
The meaning is: "one who remains satisfied even though service has been performed. [The forms] *uṣā*, *ūṣā*, *nanāndā*, and *nanandā* [are derived similarly].
And [the word] is proclaimed [as such], according to the *Dvirūpakośa*.
(1040) The suffix *ṛ* is applied after the root *div*.

After *div*: the root *div* is used in the sense of playing, desiring victory, and so forth. [The form] *deva* [is derived thus]. While the word *bhrātaraḥ* (brothers) is understood as a carry-over [from the previous rule].
‘*Vāmin* refers to *devṛ* and *devara*,' according to Amara; Śrīharṣa states, ‘[it means] husband, brother-in-law, and Mādhava. (1041) The suffix *ḍi* is applied after the root *nī*. 258.

From the root *nī* (in the sense of "leading," as in *ṇīñ prāpaṇe*), the suffix *ṛ* is applied, and it is marked with the *ḍi*-diacritic. Due to the *ḍi*-diacritic, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*). According to Amarasimha: "The terms *yu*, *pumāṃs*, *pañcajana*, *puruṣa*, *pūruṣa*, and *nara* all denote a man."

(1042) savye sthaś chandasi |259| The root √sthā, meaning "to stop" or "to stand," takes the suffix *ṛ* when the word *savya* is used as an upapada; furthermore, this suffix is marked with the indicatory letter *ḍ*.
In the compound *savyeṣṭhā*, the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is not elided by the rule *atpuruṣe kṛti*.
The addition of *sthā*, *sthās*, *sthūṇām*, and *am* is prescribed. Regarding "prescribed" (*upasaṃkhyānam*), the remainder [of the rule] is "for a vowel" (*atvasya*).
(1043) The suffix *ani* is applied after the roots *ṛ*, *sṛ*, *dhṛ*, *dham*, *śyā*, *vitṛ*, and *pṛ*. 2.4.80.

The roots are: *ṛ* (to go), *sṛ* (to go), *dhṛñ* (to hold), *dhamiḥ* (a Vedic root), *am* (to go), *aś* (to eat), *ava* (to protect, etc.), and *tṛ* (to swim or cross). Regarding *araṇi*, the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *araṇi* denotes a churning-stick (*mantha*), a fire-drill wood (*nirmathyadāru*), and [in two genders] a row (*śreṇi*) or a way (*vartma*). It also states: "*araṇiḥ* [is used] for a row and a way."

Rabhasa [lists it] among words beginning with *dantya* (dentals). The *Medinī* lexicon states: “*Araṇiḥ* is a row, a path, and [the word] is feminine. From the root *śṛ* (meaning ‘to injure’), the suffix *atipratyaya* is applied; thus some say it is *śaraṇi*. Ajaya [states] that it begins with a palatal (*tālavya*): “*Araṇi* is a path and a row. In the mantra “*ṭhimām agne śaraṇim*,” *śaraṇim* means injury (*hiṃsā*).
"Forgive me for the transgression of my vow"—this is the Vedic commentary [on the word *mīmṛṣaḥ*]. *Dharaṇi* means the earth (*bhūmi*).
According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *amanī* refers to a vein (*śirā*) and to a wanton woman (*vilāsinī*).
*Amanī* thus signifies movement (*gati*). A *aśani* is a thunderbolt (*vajra*), so called because by it the kingdom (*rājya*) is consumed (*aśyate*) or enjoyed by Indra.

According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *ṭhaśani* may refer to a woman or a man, and also to the fickle woman or to the sun. *Avani* means the earth; according to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *arani* is masculine when meaning the sun, and feminine when meaning a maiden or a boat.
*Kumārī* is a specific type of creeper; [the *Medinīkośa* states]: "*Araṇī*, *rāmataraṇī*, and *karṇikā*..."
*Cārukesarā*, *sahā*, *kumārī*, and *gandhāḍhyā*—thus it is stated in the *Dhanvantari-nighaṇṭu*.

Regarding the word *rajanī*: from the root *rañj* (to color), the suffix *ani* is applied; the elision of the penultimate *n* occurs by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). By the rule *ṛdikārād iti ṅīṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added, resulting in *rajanī*. [As it is said: "The words *rajanī*, *nīlinī*, *rātri*, *haridrā*, and *ajantu* [denote the night]."
And "kāsu" [is found] in the *Medinī* lexicon.

(1044) *Āṅ-śuṣeḥ sin-aś chandasi* |261|. [The rule states: after the root *śuṣ* (meaning "to dry") with the prefix *āṅ*, when followed by the suffix *sni*, the suffix *ani* occurs in the Vedic language (*chandas*). This applies when *āṅ* is the upapada for this root *śuṣ* (śoṣaṇe) which has taken the desiderative suffix *san*.

(1045) *kṛṣer ādeś ca caḥ* |262|. [The suffix *ini* is added] after the root *kṛṣ*, and the initial [consonant] of that [root] is replaced by *c*. [The root is] *kṛṣ* in the sense of "plowing" or "digging. [The word is] *carṣaṇi*, meaning "people. This is because the word *carṣaṇi* is listed among the names for humans in the Vedic *Nighaṇṭu*: "O you who support the *carṣaṇis* (*omāsaś carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ*)."

This is because the authors of the Vedabhāṣya have explained it in exactly that way in such mantras as these. However, Ujjvaladatta, having read the rule as *ādeśca dhaḥ*, has explained it as *dharṣaṇiḥ* meaning "an unchaste woman.
That is incorrect; for if that were the case, he would have simply formulated the sūtra as *dhṛṣeḥ*.

Because the meaning of the individual phonemes follows from their bold manifestation, and because of the parsimony [of the rule] by omitting the portion "ṭhādeśca dha," they say that the reading in the *Daśapādī-vṛtti*, namely "ādeśca ca," is indeed correct.
(1046) *ader muṭ ca* | 263 | [The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *ad*, and the augment *muṭ* is added. 263.
From the root *ad*—in the sense of eating—the suffix *ani* is applied, and there is the augment *muṭ*.
(1047) And from *vṛt*:

from the root *vṛt* in the sense of moving, the suffix *ani* is also applied; thus we have *vartani*. [This is formed] by the rule "after a word ending in *kṛt*, there is optionally the feminine suffix *ī* when it ends in a vowel."
But with the suffix *ṅīṣ*, it is *vartanī*. Amara says: "The words *araṇī*, *paddhati*, *padyā*, *vartanī*, and *ekapadī* [mean path].
(1048) *kṣipeḥ kicca* | 265 | From the root *kṣip*. *Kṣip* means "to throw" or "to propel. *Kṣipaṇiḥ* is a weapon. As in: "The horse [avoided] the *kṣipaṇi*."
In the Vedic commentary on the mantra *turaṇyati*, however, it is explained as: "following the thrower (*kṣipaṇim*), he hastens (*turaṇyati*) or speeds up (*tvarayati*) in order to go.
(1049) [The suffix] *isi* is applied after the roots *arc*, *śuc*, *hu*, *sṛp*, *chad*, and *ṛd*. 3.2.176.

The roots *arca* (in the sense of worship), *śuc* (in the sense of grief), and *hu* (in the senses of giving and eating); *sṛplṛ* (in the sense of moving); *cchad* (in the sense of covering) with the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*); *ccharda* (in the sense of vomiting). *Arcis* ends in a dental nasal (*t*). There is a mantra: "blazing with *arcis*. [And the phrase: "it whirls as if in sleep, like a path (*ayanam*)."

"Daivamarciḥ" (divine flame) is from Māgha. "Arcis, meaning a flame or light, is neuter"—this is Amara’s definition among words ending in *s* with various meanings. It also ends in *i*. The sense is that the suffix *i* is added after the causative (*ṇijanta*) root *arc*. "Arcis, heti, and śikhā are feminine," according to Amara. "Roci and śoci are both neuter."

And thus: *sarpighṛtam* (clarified butter); *cchadiḥ* (a roof), because it covers (*chādyate*). Regarding this, the *Liṅgānuśāsana-sūtra* states: "The word *cchadiḥ* is exclusively feminine. Consequently, those who claim that *cchadiḥ* is neuter—citing the entry in the *Amara-kośa*, "the roof (*cchadi*) is a layer (*paṭalam*)," based on its association with the word *paṭala*—are to be disregarded. [The root *chard*] means "to vomit" (*cchardyati*).
The analysis of the compound is: "he who has those [namely] vomiting, diarrhea, and colic.
(1050) *Bṛṃher nalopaś ca* |267|.
From the root *bṛṃh*—that is, from *bṛh* in the sense of "growth"—the suffix *isi* is applied. Regarding the rule *kuśaśuṣmaṇoḥ*: *śuṣman* is the name.

Agni is the fire named Śuṣman; having cited "Agni Vaiśvānara Vahni," it is because the Amarakośa states, "Barhis is Śuṣman," and the Medinīkośa states, "Barhis is masculine in the sense of fire, and feminine in the sense of kuśa grass."

(1051) *dyauter isin ādeś ca jaḥ* |268| [The suffix] *isin* is added after the root *dyauti*, and the initial *d* is replaced by *j*. The root *dyaut* means "to shine. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *dyotiḥ* is masculine when it refers to fire or the sun; it is neuter when it refers to sight, a constellation, or light."

(1052) *vasau ruceḥ saṃjñāyām* ||269|| In the sense of "light" (*ruca*), when the word *vasu* is the subordinate term (*upapada*), the suffix *is* is added to form a name (*saṃjñā*). Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), it is also formed from the root alone. As Amarasimha states: "Both *rociḥ* and *śociḥ* are neuter."

(1053) *bhuvaḥ kit* | 270. After the root *bhū*, the suffix *iṣṇu* is applied; it is not *kit*. (1054) *saho dhaśca* | 271. After the root *sah*, the suffix *iṣṇu* is applied, and the letter *h* is replaced by *dh*.
*Saho*: In the sense of enduring (*marṣaṇa*), there is the substitution of *dha* for the final letter of the root *sah*.
(1055) *Pibateṣṭhuk*: After the root *pā*, meaning "to drink" (*pā pāne*), the augment *ṭhuk* is added to the root.

(1056) *janerusiḥ* | 273 | [The suffix] *usi* is added after the root *jan*. The root *jan* means "to appear. (1057) *manerdhaś chandasi* | 274 | [In the Vedic language, the suffix] *dha* is added after the root *man*.
From the root *man*, meaning "to perceive," the suffix *usi* occurs in the Vedic language (*chandas*), and the letter *dh* is substituted for the final letter [of the root].
*Madhu* refers to the purifying substance.
(1058) From the roots *ṛ*, *pṛ*, *vapi*, *yaj*, *tan*, *dhan*, and *tap*, the suffix *ni* is added. 2.4.75.

From the roots *ṛ* (to go), *pṛ* (to protect and to fill), *ḍuvap* (to sow seeds), *yaj* (to worship the gods, etc.), *tanu* (to expand), *dhana* (wealth), and *tap* (to heat), the suffix *usiN* is added and is marked as *niṭ*. Amara states: "The word *vraṇa* is not feminine; *īrma* and *aru* are neuter. [Also, *ranthiḥ* is masculine.]

And [it is said] "parvaparuṣī. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *vapus* is neuter; it means body (*tanu*) as well as excellent form (*śastākṛti*). "Excellent form" (*śastākṛti*) means praised form (*praśastākṛti*). "Yajus" refers to the Yajurveda. "Tanu" means the body (*śarīra*). Subandhu [says]: "O bodiless one, you are extended (*anuṣe*), you are spread out (*tanuṣe*)."
The *Medinī* lexicon states: "They know *dhanu* [as] *yātanu*, *tanuṣā*, and *dhanuṣā*;
it occurs with the suffix *-u* and in the masculine.
(1059) [The suffix] *ṇiC* follows the root *eti*. 276.
From the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going," the suffix *usi* is added. Because it is marked with *ṇ*, the *vṛddhi* substitution is applied, after which the *āy* replacement occurs.
(1060) *cakṣeḥ śicca*: from the root *cakṣiṅ* in the sense of "articulate speech," the suffix *usi* becomes *śit*.

Because of its being *śit*, there is the substitution of *khyāñ* and the elision of *ab*. It is called *cakṣus* because by means of it they see (*cakṣate*) or experience form. (1061) *Muheḥ kicca*: from the root *muh*. *Muh* is used in the sense of bewilderment (*vaicitye*). “*Uhuḥ*, *punaḥ-punaḥ*, *śasvat*, *abhīkṣṇam*, and *asakṛt* are synonyms.”
Thus ends the section on indeclinables according to Amara. Following this, the rule *bahulam anyatrāpi* is omitted as it is self-evident.
(1062) *kṛgṛśṛvṛñcatibhyaḥ ṣvarac* || 280 || From the roots *kṛ* (to scatter), *gṛ* (to swallow), *śṛ* (to injure), *vṛ* (to choose), and *ci* (to gather).

The root *cate* is used in the sense of begging. According to the *Śabdārṇava*: “*Airṛtaḥ*, *karvaraḥ*, and *kravyāt* mean a flesh-eater; *karburaḥ* refers to a *yātu* (demon) or a *rakṣasa* (ogre). According to the *Medinī*: “*Arvarī* means a night or a woman. [Regarding *varvara*]: *Varvaraḥ* is used for a low person, a particular arrangement of hair, or a specific region (*nīvṛdantara*). However, *varvarā* refers to the *phañjikā* plant.

The *Viśvakośa* states: "In the sense of vegetables and flowers. The *Medinīkośa* states: "'Varvara' refers to a low-born person, one with curly hair, or a particular region; it is masculine when referring to the plant *phañjī*, and feminine when referring to specific types of vegetables and flowers.
It also states: "'Atvara' refers to a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or a group (*gaṇa*)."

(1063) *nau sadeḥ* |281|. The root *sadlṛ* means "to perish" and so forth. The suffix *svarac* is applied after this root when preceded by the prefix *ni*. By the rule *adir aprateḥ*, the initial *s* becomes *ṣ*. [The word] *niṣadvaraḥ* refers to the god of love (*smara*) or to the mud (*paṅka*); however, [it also refers to] the night (*niśā*).
"Niṣadvarī" refers to the earth. Thus ends the second section of the Uṇādi-sūtras.
*Chitvara*, *chatvara*, *dhīvara*, *pīvaramīvara*, *cīvara*, *tīvara*, *nīvara*, *gahvara*, *kaṭvara*, and *saṃyadvara*.
(282) Regarding *chitvara*: from these two [roots], namely *chid* in the sense of "cutting into two" (*dvaidhīkaraṇe*) and *chad* in the sense of "covering" (*apavāraṇe*).
According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *chitvara* [is used] in the sense of cutting, a substance, a rogue, and an enemy; it is used in three genders."

The root *ḍudhāñ* means "to hold" and "to nourish," *pā* means "to drink," and *mā* means "to measure. According to some, the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of these three roots is prescribed by rule. Others, however, maintain that from the roots *pīva*, *mīva*, *tīva*, and *nīva*—all meaning "thickness"—the suffix *svarac* is added, and the elision of the semivowel (*v*) is applied according to the rule *opo vyoḥ*. Thus, [the word] *īśvaraḥ* [is derived].

Regarding *kaccchape sthūle*, the *Medinī* lexicon states this. Regarding *mīvara*, some say it is derived from the root *mīñ* (meaning "to injure") with the suffix *svaraj*, in accordance with the sense of "injurer. The *Medinī* states: "The word *īvara* occurs [as a synonym] for the ocean and a hunter. It is also seen in the sense of "a merchant" (*vāṇijaka*) and "a resident" (*vāstava*).
Thus says the *Medinī* lexicon. Some maintain that *upahvara* means "chariot. However, in the mantra "adu prayakṣatam," it refers to the vicinity (*upagantavye samīpadeśe*).
[Pāṇini 3.2.174] states: "The suffix *na* is added after the roots *i*, *siñj*, *dī*, *uṣ*, and *vī*. (1065)

The roots are: *iṇ* (to go), *ṣiñ* (to bind), *ji* (to conquer), *dīṅ* (to perish), *uṣa* (to burn), and *ava* (to protect). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *inaḥ* [is used] for a husband, a king, and the sun. And: "*inaḥ* [is used] for one who deserves, for a Buddha, as a masculine; in three genders, it means a victor. Also: "*īnā* [is used] for a female mouse..."

According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *durgata* means miserable or like another. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *uṣṇa* is masculine when meaning summer; it is of other genders [neuter and feminine] when meaning hot or not cold. The form *varatra* is derived from the root *tṛ* with the suffix *ūṭh*.
*Ūna* means incomplete.
(1066) *Phenamīnau* | 283 | *Phena*: from the root *sphāyī*, meaning "to increase"; its substitute is *phe*. Amara states: “*īndīra*, *abdhikapha*, and *phena* [mean] foam.
*Mīna*: from the root *mīñ*, meaning "to injure. Viśva states: “*īna* [is used] for a zodiac sign and for a fish (*matsya*).”

(1067) *Kṛṣeḥ* varṇe |284| [The suffix] *na* is applied after the root *kṛṣ* when "color" (*varṇa*) is to be expressed. From the root *kṛṣ* in the sense of "plowing" (*vilekhana*), the suffix *na* occurs when "color" is to be denoted. [Examples: *kṛṣṇaḥ* refers to the son of Satyavatī, Keśava, a crow, and Arjuna; [the feminine form] *kṛṣṇā*.

According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *syāt* [is used] for Draupadī, indigo, long pepper, grapes, a woman, and the color dark-green; it is of masculine gender when denoting something else, and neuter for black pepper and iron.
(1068) After the root *bandh*, there are the augment *bradhi* and the substitute *budha*. 2.4.85.

From the root *bandh* (to bind), the suffix *nak* is applied after *bandh* in the sense of binding. Amara states: "The sun is called *hāskara*, *ahaskara*, *bradhna*, *prabhākara*, and *divākara*. Medinī states: "*Udhna* is masculine and denotes both a root and Rudra."

(1069) *dhāpṛvṛsjyatibhyo naḥ* |286| From the roots *dhā*, *pṛ*, *vṛ*, *aj*, and *ati*, the suffix *na* occurs. *Dhā* (√*dhā*) means "to hold" and so forth; *pṛ* (√*pṛ*) means "to protect" and so forth; *vas* (√*vas*) means "to dwell"; *aj* (√*aj*) means "to go"; and *at* (√*at*) means "continuous motion. When the suffix *na* is applied, as in the case of *vasna*, [the following applies].

There would be *saṃprasāraṇa* [vocalization]. However, the point is that in the word *vena*, there should not be *guṇa*. The *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *dhānyāka* is said to mean *hānā*, parched barley, and a newly sprouted plant. The *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *arṇa* means a leaf;
it is not masculine [when used in this sense]. And: "The word *vasna* is masculine in the sense of hire or wages."
And there is also the rule: "it may be neuter. *Vena* means a thief, a plunderer, and a progenitor (*prajāpati*).

(1070) *Lakṣe-raṭ ca*. From the root *lakṣ*, [the suffix *ana* is added] and *raṭ* is substituted. The root *lakṣ* means "to see" and "to mark. Examples include *lakṣaṇa*, etc. The words *lakṣaṇa* and *lakṣmaṇa* [are derived from this].

The term *lakṣaṇa* is neuter when meaning a name or a mark; however, it is masculine when referring to the brother of Rāma. The distinction is that *lakṣmaṇā* refers to the female of the swan (*haṃsa*), whereas *lakṣmaṇa* refers to the female of the crane (*sārasa*). Thus, the rule is: “*Lakṣaṇa* is used for a name and a mark; *saumitri* (the son of Sumitrā) is also called *lakṣaṇa*; [and] *lakṣmaṇa*... [is used for the brother of Rāma].

According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The term *lakṣaṇā* occurs in the sense of a name (*nāman*), a mark (*cihna*), and in some cases, essence (*sāra*). Furthermore, *lakṣaṇā* refers to a specific medicinal herb, a woman possessing excellence (*sāra*), and as a masculine noun, it denotes a brother of Rāma and one who is endowed with fortune (*saśrīka*). However, in another lexicon (*kośa*), it is stated: "*lakṣaṇā* [also] in the sense of essence (*sāra*)."
The reading without the augment *kāra* has been accepted.

in the sense of "not clearly colored," in the sense of "the twilight glow," in the sense of "the charioteer of the Sun," in the sense of "soundless," in the sense of "tawny," in the sense of "a type of leprosy," and as a masculine noun for "one possessing qualities."
In three [senses]: "The word *aruṇā* refers to the *ativiṣā*, the *śyāmā*, the *mañjiṣṭhā*, and the *trivṛt*"—so says the *Medinī*. (1119) And from the roots *aji*, *yami*, and *śīṅ*: 3.2.171.

(1120) From the roots *vṛ*, *tṛ*, *vad*, *han*, *kam*, *kaś*, [the suffix] *sa* [is applied]. (*vṛ* means "to choose"; *tṛ* means "to swim" or "to cross"; *vad* means "to speak clearly"; *han*...).

This has been stated through a careful examination of the Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa, and other works. If it is asked, "How is it then that all the authors of Uṇādi-vṛttis have cited *ṣatva* as an example here?", they reply:
Let it be; by virtue of the authority of the Bhāṣya, even the dental reading *varsam tarsam* is correct. In one view...

However, let there be *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*). Even though the absence of *ṣatva*—which is obtained through the principle of *bāhulaka* (irregularity)—is merely optional, there is no obstacle [to its occurrence]. This is because, after the suffix *ghañ* has been applied to the roots *vṛṣi* and *tṛṣi*, one may either apply the suffix *ac* to the form beginning with the causative (*ṇic*) affix, or apply the suffix *ka* to the causative form according to the rule "the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of an instrument (*hañartha*)."

Because the words *varṣa* (rain) and *tarṣa* (thirst) are difficult to exclude, and because in the commentary on the rule for the suffix *ac*, the word *varṣam* is cited as an example under the heading "the addition of *bhaya* and others in the neuter is for the purpose of excluding forms ending in *kta*," it follows that here both forms are established. Thus, *varṣas* is not feminine, as seen in the *Bhārata* and other texts.

The word *abdah* may mean Jambūdvīpa; according to the *Medinīkośa*, it is used for the rainy season (*prāvṛṭkāla*) in the feminine gender when expressing plurality. It is also said that *arṣaḥ* means greed (*lipsā*) and thirst (*udanyā*). According to the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*, *vatsaḥ* refers to a young calf (*tarṇaka*) or a year (*varṣa*), while in the neuter it denotes the chest. Furthermore, *sadyojātaḥ* means a newborn calf (*tarṇaka*).

The word *ṭhhaṃsaḥ* (or *haṃsaḥ*) occurs in the following senses: it denotes the swan (*mānasa*), a king free from greed, Viṣṇu, the Sun, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), envy (*matsara*), a specific type of yoga, a particular mantra, one of the vital airs (*marut*) within the body, and a specific breed of horse;
thus says the *Medinī*. Furthermore, the word *aṃsaḥ* (or *aṃśaḥ*)—which is not feminine—is used for a luminous substance, bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), a measure, a demon, and a share (*tunā*).

because under the alternative view that "the second letters [of each varga] are substituted," the letter *t* would result in the letter *th*. The word *pakṣa* means a half-month.

"Uttara is recorded as meaning 'excellent' or 'a woman in the form of a man'; it is also considered in some contexts to mean 'the porcupine-fruit', 'a vein', or 'a widow'—so says the Medinī. (1177) [From the roots] *jṛ* and *viś*, [the suffix] *jhac* [is applied]. 406.

From the roots *jṛ* (in the sense of "wasting away") and *viś* (in the sense of "entering"): according to Amara, *veśantaḥ* means a puddle or a small lake. By virtue of the rule regarding diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *jhac* is also applied to the root *arh*; thus, according to the *Vikramādityakośa*, *arhantaḥ* refers to a Kṣapaṇaka or a Jina.

(1178) *ruhinandijīviprāṇibhyaḥ ṣidāśiṣi* |4.3.107| From the roots *ruhi*, *nandi*, *jīvi*, and *prāṇi*, the suffix *jhac* is applied in the sense of benediction (*āśis*), and it is marked with the *ṣit* designation. *ruhi*: *ruha* in the sense of germination from a seed and manifestation; *nandi*: *ṭuanadi* in the sense of prosperity; *jīva*: *jīva* in the sense of sustaining life; *prāṇi*: *an* in the sense of breathing, preceded by the prefix *pra*. From these, *jhac* is applied in the sense of benediction, and it becomes *ṣit*.

Regarding *prāṇanta*: the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] is by the rule "aniteḥ" [Pāṇini 8.4.19]. (1179) *tṛbhūvahivasibhāsisādhigaḍimaṇḍijinandibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 3.2.179]: from the roots *tṛ*, *bhū*, *vah*, *vas*, *bhās*, *sādh*, *gaḍi*, *maṇḍi*, and *jani*. *Tṛ* [means] to cross over or to float; *bhū* [means] existence; *vah* [means] carrying; *vas* [means] dwelling.
The roots *bāsṛ* (in the sense of shining), *sādha* (in the sense of accomplishment), *gaḍa* (in the sense of sprinkling), and *maḍi* (in the sense of ornamentation) are all causative (*ṇyanta*).
*Ji* (in the sense of victory) and *ṭuanadi* (in the sense of prosperity) are also causative. Regarding the form *nandayantaḥ*, Ujjvaladatta himself has followed this [causative] form.

(1180) *hanter muṭ hi ca* |409| [The rule] "of *han*" means: from the root *han*, meaning "to strike" or "to go," the suffix *jhac* shall be applied; there is the augment *muṭ* for that [suffix], and the substitution of *hi* for the verbal root.

(1181) *bhandernalopaśca* |410|. After the root *bhand*—meaning "to be auspicious" or "to be happy"—the suffix *jhac* is applied, and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n* of the root. (1182) *ṛccheraraḥ* |411|. [After the root *ṛcch*, the suffix *ara* is applied.]

From the root *ṛcch* (meaning "to go"). Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), [the following forms arise]: *jarja*, *carca*, and *jharjha*, which denote reviling, injury, and threatening. The *Medinī* lexicon states: "In the sense of a variety of musical instruments or a particular sound. According to Ujjvaladatta, the form *jarjhara* arises from the substitution of *ja* for *jha* by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*).

According to the Medinīkośa: "The word *rasa* is neuter when it means elephant-ornament, as well as cloves (*lavaṅga*), and the two types of *nāgasaṃbhava* powder. And: "The word *hṛṅgārī* may mean a cricket (*jhillikā*), while *kanakālu* is masculine."

(1187) *kañji-mṛjibhyāṃ cit* || 4.117 || From the roots *kañji* and *mṛj*, with the suffix *cit*. The roots *kañji* and *mṛj* mean "to purify. One should not suspect that the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs only after a short vowel ending in *ṛ* or *ikāra*, and not after a long one;

for since the suffix *kāra* is prescribed when referring to a phoneme (*varṇanirdeśe*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* can indeed occur after a long vowel as well by virtue of the rule "after [a stem] ending in *ṛ* or *ikāra*" (*ṛdikārāt*). For this very reason, forms such as *vātapramī*, *śrī*, and *lakṣmī* are easily established as correct in the alternative view where they are treated as feminine stems ending in *ṅī*.

Thus it is protected [by the rule]. And this is clear in the *Durghaṭavṛtti* commentary. Because it has already been explained. Regarding "añjali," the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *añjali* refers to a male [person], a hollowed pair of hands, and also a *kuḍava* measure.

Ujjvaladatta states "ṛbhukṣāṇaḥ. However, in the Daśapādī, having introduced the rule *ṛteḥ bhukṣinak*, the form *ṛbhukṣin* is cited as an example. According to the view that [the word] ends in the suffix *ini*, it is logical for it to have an udātta accent on the final syllable, because the vowel *i* of the suffix *ini* is udātta by the accentuation rule governing suffixes (*pratyayasvara*). The absence of *avagraha* (separation) is due to the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*). However, according to the second view, the absence of *avagraha* is indeed logical; nevertheless, by the accentuation rule governing suffixes, the vowel *u* would be udātta.

Since it would follow that a word ending in the *kṣinaka* suffix should have the middle syllable accented (*madhyodātta*), one must accept by way of the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*) that it has the final syllable accented (*antodātta*). *Parpharīkā*: These words ending in *īkan* are treated as irregular forms (*nipātana*). Regarding the statement "there is a substitution of *parphara*," this is stated according to the system of Ujjvaladatta; however, in reality, what is stated in the *Daśapādī*—namely, that there is reduplication of the root, the change of *u* to *a*, elision of *s*, and the addition of *ruk* to the reduplicated syllable—is alone logical.

Because it is logical that the phrase "ve ruk ca" and so forth should follow in accordance with the subsequent text beginning with "arernu ca," [the word] "kisalaya" is used. Regarding the term "aitośava turpharīparpharīkau": these are the two who tear asunder the enemies of the singers.
The two protectors (*pālaka*) are explained as those who fulfill one's desired objects. Regarding *dardarīka*:

from the root *dṛ* (in the sense of "tearing"), the suffix *īkan* is applied with the substitution of *dardara*. Regarding *jharjharīka*: from the root *jhṛṣ* (in the sense of "decay of age"), the suffix *īkan* is applied with the substitution of *jharjhara*. In reality, however, it is *dardarīka*.

*jharjharīka* and *parpharīka* are to be explained as having reduplication of the root and the augment *tuk* added to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), according to the rule "ruk cābhyāsasya. In the latter part of the word, the vowel *ṛ* undergoes *guṇa* substitution, followed by the replacement of *r* (*raparatva*). Regarding *titiḍīka*:
from the roots *tima*, *ṣṭima*, and *ṣṭīma* in the sense of becoming moist, the letter *m* is replaced by *u*, and the augment *tuk* is added to the reduplicated syllable.
In the *Amarakośa*, however, the term ‘itiḍī’ should be understood as a distinct word [from ‘ciñcā’].
Accordingly, Vācaspati states: “*itiḍī*, *amlīkā*, *ciñcā*, *titiḍīkā*, and *kapipriyā*.
Candra states: “*amlīkā*, *amlīkā*, *ciñcā*, *titiḍīkā*, and *titiḍā*. [The term] *amlīkā*...

*cukrakrikā*, *cukrā*, *sāmlā*, *śukrā*, *śuklikā*, *amlīkā*, *ciñcakā*, *ciñcā*, *titiḍīkā*, and *sutintadā*—thus it is stated in the *Dhanvantari-nighaṇṭu*. Regarding [the derivation] from the root *car-*: from the root *car-* meaning "to move" or "to eat," the suffix *īkan* is applied, with reduplication of the root and the addition of the augment *num* to the reduplicated syllable.

‘*Hramara*, *cañcarīka*; *rolamba*, *madhusūdana*; *indindira*, *puṣpakiṭa*, *madhudra*, *madhukeśaṭa*—thus [it is stated] in the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*. Regarding *marmarīka* and so forth: from the roots *mṛṅ* (to perish) and *ḍukṛñ* (to make), the suffix *īkan* is applied, the root is doubled, and the reduplication [is treated according to the rules].’

Regarding *ruṇḍarīka*: according to Amara, *ruṇḍarīkā* means a water-pot (*argharī*). In the sense of a meritorious action (*puṇya-karmaṇi*), the suffix *ṇa* becomes *ḍa*, and there is the augment *ruṭ* for the suffix. According to the Medinī lexicon: "The word *uṇḍarīka* refers to a white lotus, a white umbrella, and a medicine;
it denotes a tiger, a fire, a cardinal direction, an elephant, and also a type of silk-worm."

(1228) *iṣeḥ kikidhrasvaśca* |461| From the root *iṣ* [in the sense of] "to go," the suffix *īkan* is applied, and there is shortening [of the vowel]. Because it is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* substitution.
Although the absence of *guṇa* is already established by the very fact that the shortening is prescribed, [the mention of shortening] is for the sake of subsequent rules.
They call him a gambler (*kitava*). According to the *Dvirūpakośa*: "It may be *ṭhiṣīkā* or *īṣikā*; [the words] *anāyuja* and *javanāyuja*. (1229) And from the root *ṛji*. 462.
From the root *ṛji*: *ṛji* means "to go.
(1230) *sarter num ca* |463|. From the root *sṛ*, meaning "to go," the suffix *īkan* is added, and it is marked as *kit*; furthermore, there is the augment *num* for the root.
‘Lālā is saliva that trickles from the mouth,’ according to Amara [1231].

*Mṛḍaḥ* [yields] *kīkaca* and *kaṅkaṇa*. 464. *Mṛḍaḥ* [yields] *kīkaca*. From the root *mṛḍa* in the sense of “to delight” (*sukhane*). There is a reading in the *Ujjvaladatta* and other lexicons: *mṛḍaḥ kīkan*.

This is incorrect; for the word *mṛḍīka* has its final syllable accented by the *cit-svara* (the accent assigned to a suffix marked with *c*), as is observed in such instances as *ṛḍīke asya sumatau syāma*. (Pāṇini 6.2.173) Furthermore, [the group] beginning with *alīka* [is also included]. (Pāṇini 6.2.174)

"Alīka means forehead, and it also means one who is fond of falsehood," according to Hemacandra. Thus, it is employed by the learned: "In this world, to whom would the locks of hair of the long-lashed women—not to mention their glances—cause agitation, as would wicked men? For the base are always..."
"Those who possess playful deceit and do not abandon crookedness over time.

Here, *alīkalamnāḥ* may be understood as "those clinging to the forehead" (*bhālalamnāḥ*), or "those clinging to what is unpleasant" (*apriye lamnāḥ*), according to the context. As it is said: "The word *vyalīka* is used for the unpleasant, the improper, embarrassment, and pain; [the word] *nā* [is used] for a city-dweller."

*Medinī*: "In the sense of covering (*saṃvaraṇa*), [the word] *valmīka* occurs at the edge of a layer (*paṭala-prānta*) in an anthill (*vāmalūra*)," according to Amara. From the root *val*, with the augment *muk*, comes *valmīka*; "and *vāmalūra*, *cañcū*, and *valmīka* are masculine and neuter," according to Amara. From the root *vah*, there is the substitution of *vadh*. [The word] *vāhīka*.

*gorasvaśca*, *suprapūra*, *avādiṇa*, and *tuṭ*; *supratīka*. From the root *śam*, [we derive] the seer *śamīka*. With the intention that other such forms are also to be inferred, he says "and so forth. (Pāṇini 3.2.466): *śṛpṛbhyāṃ kicca*.

From the roots *śṛ* (in the sense of "injuring") and *pṛ* (in the sense of "protecting" and so forth), the suffix *īṣan* is added with the *kit* designation. By the rule "ṛta iddhātoḥ," the vowel *ṛ* is changed to *i*, and by the rule "uraṇ raparaḥ," the *r* is substituted as the subsequent element. Thus, *śirīṣaḥ* denotes a particular kind of tree.
By the rule "udoṣṭhyapūrvasya," the vowel *u* is substituted; *urīṣam* means excrement, feces, or dung (not feminine).
"Viṣṭi and aviṣṭi are feminine," according to Amara.
(1234) *Arjer ṛja ca* |467|. From the root *arj*—*arja* meaning "to acquire"—the suffix *īṣan* is added, and it is *kit*.
And there is the substitution of *ṛj* for the verbal root. He cites the statement of Amara: "it is called *ṛjīṣa*. Furthermore, it is that from which the juice has been extracted;

even the residue of the *soma* creeper is *ṛjīṣa*. This is clear from the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on such mantras as "the *ṛjīṣin* [Soma] and the *vṛṣaṇas* [bulls] attend for glory" and "may the true Maghavan, the *ṛjīṣin*, protect us."

(1235) Ambarīṣaḥ | 469 | Regarding this [word], the meaning is that the suffix *īṣan* takes the augment *aruḍ*. He cites the statement of Vopālita: "Ambarīṣam. Amarasimha states: "Ambarīṣam is neuter; it is also called bhrāṣṭra, but not [in the masculine]. [And: "Ambarīṣa [is used] in battle..."

According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *bhrāṣṭra* denotes a eunuch, a particular king, a specific division of hell, a young horse, the sun, the *āmrātaka* tree, and a follower. (1236) [The suffix] *īran* is added after the verbal roots √kṛ, √śṛ, √pṛ, √kaṭ, √paṭ, and √śauṭ. 470.

The roots *kṛ* (to scatter), *śṛ* (to injure), *pṛ* (to protect and to fill), *kaṭe* (in the sense of raining and covering), *iṭ*, *kiṭ*, and *kaṭī* (in the sense of going); in the *cur*-class (*curādi*), *paṭ* and *puṭ* in the list of verbal roots have the meaning of speaking; and *śauṭṛ* (in the sense of pride). [The word] *karīra* is masculine and neuter in the sense of a bamboo shoot.
According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *pumān* [is used] for two things: a tree and fire; *karīrā* is used for a type of grass and the root of an elephant's tusk.
It is called *śarīram* because it perishes (*śīryate*). According to Amara: "*Arīram*, *vardhma*, and *vigraha* [are synonyms for body].
Due to its inclusion in the *ardharca*-group of words, *śarīra* is also masculine. Thus, it is *parīram*.

The etymological analysis (*vigraha*) is "that by which something is filled. Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), from the root *hiṇḍ* meaning "to move" or "to disregard," one who moves here and there is called *hiṇḍīra*. Amara states: "Foam is *hiṇḍīra*, the froth of the ocean. The *Dvirūpakośa* also says: "*iṇḍira* and also *hiṇḍīra*."
Words such as *kirmīra*, *jambīra*, and *tūṇīra* should also be understood through the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*).
According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *irmīra* [is used] for an orange (*nāgaraṅga*), for something variegated (*karbura*), and for a particular type of Rākṣasa.
And: "*Jambīra* may refer to the *psthapuṣpa* flower or to the *dantaśaṭha* tree."

(1237) *vaśeḥ kit* |471| From the root *vaś* [meaning] "to desire," the suffix *īran* is added with the marker *k*. Because of the *k*-marker, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and so forth. Thus, *uśīra*, which is the root of the *vīraṇa* grass; *uśīra* is also used. It is said: "The word *uśīra* is masculine and neuter when it means 'root'; it is also *abhaya* and *nalada*."
"Sevya" [is derived from] the root *kaś*, according to Amara.
(1238) *Kaśer muṭ ca* | 4.2.472. From the root *kaś*; *kaśa* is a Vedic (sautra) root; from this, the suffix *īran* is applied, and there is the augment *muṭ*.
*Kāśmīraḥ* [is derived] by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. (1239) *Kṛña īran*.
4.2.38. From the root *kṛñ*—specifically *ḍukṛñ* in the sense of "making"—the suffix *īran* is applied; there is the substitution of *au* for the final vowel of the root, followed by the letter *r*.

(1240) *ghaseḥ kicca* || 474 || From the root *ghas* (*ghaslṛ* in the sense of eating), the suffix *īran* shall be added as a *kit*. By the rule *amahaneti*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), followed by the substitution of *k* and *ṣ*. According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *sīra* refers to both milk and water."
(1241) *gabhīra* and *gambhīra*. [Pāṇini 6.4.155] From the root *gamlṛ* in the sense of "going," the suffix *īran* is applied, with *bha* as the substitute for the final letter;
optionally, the augment *num* is also prescribed by nipātana. Amara states: "The words *nimna*, *gabhīra*, and *gambhīra* mean 'deep'."

(1242) *viṣā* and *vihā*. 476. From the roots *viṣ* in the sense of "ending" (*antakarman*) and *hā* (*ohāk*) in the sense of "abandoning" (*tyāga*), the suffix *na* is prescribed as a substitute after these two when preceded by the prefix *vi-*.
*pacaḥ*. From the root *ḍupacaṣ* (to cook), the suffix *elimaC* shall be applied. This [suffix] occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
However, among the *kṛtya* suffixes, *kelimaR* is also prescribed as an addition.

(1244) *śīṅ* [takes] *dhuk*, *lak*, *va*, *lañ*, and *alanaḥ*. 478. *śīṅ*: *śīṅ* means "to sleep. That by which one sleeps is *śīdhu*, a specific kind of liquor. Amarasimha states: "The fermented liquor *āsava* made from *airā* is called *śīdhu*. Because it is included in the *ardharca* group, it is also neuter.

“*Dāru*, *jīvātu*, *sthāṇu*, and *śīdhu* [are used] for the neuter and masculine genders,” according to the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*. “*Īlam* [is used] in the sense of nature (*svabhāva*) and good conduct (*sadvṛtta*),” according to the *Medinī*. “*Ala* and *nīlī* are *śevāla* and *śaivala*,” according to *Amara*. “*Śaivala* may refer to the wood of the lotus (*padmakāṣṭha*), but [it is also used] for *śaivāla* (aquatic moss).”
The *Medinī* states that "pumān" means "this man. He cites the statement from the *Śabdārṇava*: "śaivālaṃ śevalam. (1245) *Mṛkaṇibhyām ūka-ukaṇau*.
[The rule] *mṛkaṇi*: *mṛṅ* (to die, to abandon life) and *kaṇa* (meaning sound). *Ūka* and *ukaṇ* are the suffixes *ūka* and *ukaṇ*.
These two suffixes occur in their respective order. The root *val* means "to cover" (*saṃvaraṇe*).
(1246) Regarding *ulūka* and others: Pāṇini 4.1.56 states *ulūkādayaś ca*.
According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *ulūka* is masculine; it denotes a crow, Indra, and a warrior of the Bharatas."

The suffix *ūka* is added after the root *vad* when it is in its *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive) form. According to Amara: "One who is skilled in speech is called *vācoyuktipaṭu*, *vāgmī*, or *vāvadūka*; the last term refers to one who speaks excessively. Regarding the word *bhallūka*: the suffix *ūka* is added to the root *bhalla*, meaning "to speak" (*paribhāṣaṇe*).

(1247) *śamer buk ca* | 481 | From the root *śam*: from *śama* (to pacify), the suffix *ūka* is applied, and there is also the augment *buk* [inserted before the suffix]. According to the *Medinī*, "a *śambūka* is at the end of an elephant's frontal globe (*kumbha*), in a *ghoṇṭā* tree, and in a Śūdra ascetic."

Due to the rule of frequent occurrence (*bāhulaka*), the form with a short vowel in the middle also exists. The *Dvirūpakośa* states: "They call it *ambūka*, *jambuka*, and also *śambuka*, *śambuka*. Forms such as *jambūka* and *bandhūka* should also be understood in this same way. [The lexicon] says: "*Jambūka* refers to a jackal, a base person, and also the lord of the western quarter."
The *Medinīkośa* and *Viśvaprakāśa* state: "The word *bandhūka* may refer to the *bandhujīva* flower; *bandhūka* also refers to the *pītasāraka*.
(1248) [The suffix] *ūkaṇ* is added after the roots *śali* and *maṇḍi*. 482.

*Śalimaṇḍi*: *śali* means "to go" (*gatau*), and *maḍi* means "adornment" (*bhūṣā*) and "joy" (*harṣa*). Starting with the entry, "The *augandhika* is the *kahlāra*," and continuing with "the root (*kanda*) of these is the *ālūka*," so says Amarasimha. And the root—the bulbous root—is that of these [plants] beginning with *saugandhika* and ending with *kumuda* and *kairava*.
The meaning is "lotus root" (*śālūka*). It adorns the rainy season, thus it is *maṇḍūka*, the frog.
(1249) *niyo miḥ* | 483 | *niyo miḥ*. From the root *ṇīñ* in the sense of "to lead. That which leads the wheel is *nemi*, a part of the wheel.
According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *emirnā* [is used] for a well made of *tiniśa* wood, a small water-pot, and the end of a wheel;

[it is used] for a woman. Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), it may also occur elsewhere. The root *yā* means "to go" or "to reach. According to the *Rabhasa* lexicon, beginning with the labio-dental sounds: "*Yāmiḥ* [is used] for a sister and a woman of one's own family. Also: "*Āmiḥ* [is used] for a sister and a woman of one's own family."

The *ajayakośa* begins with the third letter of the *ca*-group. According to the *dvirūpeṣu*, the *viśva* lexicon states: "The word *aja* is also said by Jābhi to refer to one's own sister and a woman of the same lineage. (1250) [The rule] *arterucca* [is stated]. 484.

The word *ūrmi* is derived from the root *ṛ* (meaning "to go") with the suffix *mi*; there is also a substitution of the vowel *u* for the root vowel. It would have been more appropriate to state it as *uca*, because when the substitute *ra* is applied, a long vowel could occur by the rule *halica*.
The term *ūrmi* may denote a male or female, as well as light, speed, a break, or a fold-line in clothing.
According to the *Medinī* lexicon, [the suffix *min* is applied] after the roots *vid*, *pad*, and *piḍ*.
(1251) "After *bhū* with the *kit* suffix": 4.85. After the root *bhū*, the suffix *min* shall be *kit*. Since beings (*bhūtāni*) exist (*bhavanti*) in it, it is called *bhūmiḥ* (earth).
The *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *ūmi* may denote the earth (*vasundharā*) as well as a mere place or a woman.
The *Amara-kośa* states: "*Ūr*, *bhūmi*, *acalā*, and *anantā* [are synonyms for the earth]," and so forth.
(1252) [The suffix] *ra* is added after the root *aś* (to pervade). 486.

From the root *aś* [is derived *raśmi*]. From the root *aśū* in the sense of pervading (*vyāptau*), the suffix *ni* is applied, and there is the substitution of *ra* for the root-initial *a*. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *raśmi* is masculine; it occurs in the sense of a ray of light, as well as in the senses of a wing and a rein. (1253) From the roots *vīj*, *yaj*, and *jvar*, the suffix *ni* is applied. [Pāṇini 3.3.88]

Regarding *vījyā*: the root *vī* means "to go," *jyā* means "loss of vitality" (aging), and *jvara* means "disease. He cites the statement of Amara: "It shall be *veṇiḥ*" and so forth. By the rule *ṛdikārāt*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *veṇī* [is used] for a braid of hair; for the interval between rivers, etc.; and for a Devatāḍa tree. Also: "*Veṇī* is harsh and heavy."

"Devatāḍa means a cloud," according to Amara; "yāni [means] loss and a flowing river," according to Viśva. In the word *varatrā*, the penultimate vowel and the letter *v* undergo *ūṭh*. *Jūrṇiḥ* is a female disease.
(1254) [The suffix *ni* is added after the roots] *sṛ* and *vṛṣi*, with the *k* marker. 489.

From the roots *sṛ* (to go) and *vṛṣ* (to sprinkle), the suffix *niḥ* is applied as a *kit*. Amara states: "The word *sṛṇi*, meaning a goad (*aṅkuśa*), is not feminine; it is feminine. Another lexicon states: "*Sṛṇi* is masculine when it means a goad. For this very reason [the poet says]: "Disregarding the sharp-pointed goad that was immersed in the fire for protection..."

Thus, in the *Māgha*, there is the usage of the masculine gender. Regarding this, the *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *vṛṣṇi* refers to a descendant of Yadu and a ram; *vṛṣṇi* [also means] a heretic and a ram. In the Vedic scripture, "In the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice dedicated to Indra, [one offers] a *vṛṣṇi*," the meaning is "a ram."

(1255) *agnilopaśca* |490| [from] the root *aṅg*. The root *ag* has the meaning "to go. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *agni* may refer to Vaiśvānara (fire), and is masculine in the sense of a leopard and the medicinal plant called *citraka*."
(1256) The suffix *ni* is added after the roots *vah*, *śri*, *śru*, *yu*, *dru*, *glā*, *hā*,
and *tvar*. *vah* (to carry), *śriñ* (to serve), *śru* (to hear), *yu* (to mix), *dru* (to run),
*glai* and *mlai* (loss of joy), *ohāk* (to abandon), and *ñitvarā* (to hasten)— after these, the suffix *ni* is applied.

*Pratya* would be [the suffix] *niṭ*. According to the *Medinīkośa*: “*Vaiśvānara* occurs in the sense of fire (*vahni*) and is masculine in the sense of the medicinal plant called *citraka*. *Śreṇi* means a row or a line. As the *Medinīkośa* states: “*Iḥ* (the suffix *i*) signifies a ladder (*adhirohiṇī*);
*śreṇi* is feminine and masculine; it refers to a row, a similar group, or a guild of artisans (*śilpisamūha*).”

*Śroṇiḥ* refers to the region of the hips. Amara states: "The words *aṭiḥ*, *śroṇiḥ*, and *kukud* denote the hips. *Yoniḥ* means the female organ. Medinī states: "The word *yoniḥ* may refer to a woman, a man, a source, or the abode of Smara (the god of love). *Droṇiḥ* refers to a trough for watering. By the rule "from roots ending in *ṛ* or *ṛt*," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied to form *droṇī*.

According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *droṇa* refers to a measure of capacity (*āḍhaka*) when not feminine; it is masculine when referring to the fourfold measure beginning with the *āḍhaka*; it is masculine for the Lord of the Earth (the King) and the black crow; and it is feminine for a type of inhabited region (*nīvṛt*). *Glāni* means exhaustion, weakness, loss, decrease, and decay. *Tūrṇi* means a measure.

(1257) *ghṛṇi*, *pṛśni*, *pārṣṇi*, *cūrṇi*, *bhūrṇi* || 492 || The suffix *ni* is applied with the absence of *guṇa* [vowel strengthening] as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) to the roots: *ghṛ* (to sprinkle), *spaś* (to touch), *pṛṣu* (to sprinkle), *car* (to move), and *ḍubhṛñ* (to support or nourish). Thus, we derive *ghṛṇi*, *pṛśni*, *pārṣṇi*, *cūrṇi*, and *bhūrṇi*.
"Furthermore, *ghṛṇiḥ* [means] 'in the waves of the flame of rays'—so says Hemacandra.

*Ṛśniḥ* [means] 'one with a small body'—so says Amara. *Āṣṇiḥ* would be [used for] an intoxicated woman; it is used for both [genders] in the sense of the rear of an army, and also for the ankle-joint and the lower lip"—so says Medinī. [The word] *bhūrṇiḥ*..."
In the commentary on the mantra "akvā na bhūrṇiḥ," however, it is explained that *bhūrṇi* means "a supporter" (*dhāraka*) or "a nourisher" (*poṣaka*).
[Pāṇini 3.2.174] states: "The suffix *vin* is applied after the roots *vṛt* and *vṛdh*. (1258)

The roots *vṛ* (in the sense of choosing), *dṛ* (in the sense of choosing), and *dṛ* (in the sense of respect/respectful regard): for these, when feminine, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṛdikārād iti*. Thus, *darvī* (a ladle).
(1259) [Vārttika: The suffix *kvin* is added after the roots *dṛ*, *śṛ*, *stṛ*, and *jṛ*. 6.4.94.

Regarding the roots *jṛ* and *śṛ*: *jṛ* means "decay of age," *śṛ* means "injury," *stṝ* (with nasal) means "covering," and *jāgṛ* means "cessation of sleep. Because the suffix *kvip* is marked with *k*, the rule "ṛta id dhātoḥ" applies, resulting in the substitution of *i* for the *ṛ*, followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*; thus we obtain *jīviri* and so forth.
(1260) *divo dve dīrghaścābhyāsasya* ||495|| [The root] *div*: from *div*, meaning "to play" and so forth, the suffix *kvin* is applied. Due to the *kit* designation, there is an absence of *guṇa*.
According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *īdivi* is used in the sense of gambling and eating. [Regarding] "those who possess *īdivi*..."
Regarding the term *dhiṣaṇā*, the *Medinī* states: "The word *dhiṣaṇā* is feminine and means earth. *Dhiṣaṇa* refers to Bṛhaspati.
According to the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*: "Īḍivida has twelve hands; he is the eye, the preceptor of the gods, and the Guru.
And according to the *Hārāvalī*: "Īḍivida has twelve rays; he is Jīva (the planet Jupiter) and the son of Prākphalgunī."

Regarding the statement in the *Amarakośa*, "ṭhodanaḥ, astrī, sadīdiviḥ," the interpretation here as "sadīdiviḥ" [meaning] "together with dīdivi" is the correct one. In this context, because of the qualifying term "sa" (it), the interpretation held by some that "dīdivi" is masculine should not be accepted. Thus [is defined] Indra, the Sutraman. Rudra states: "The word *karman* is considered to be used in the masculine and neuter genders when it signifies an action or that which is pervaded. Medini states: "*Karman* is used in the sense of action and a board."

“ipṛtāṃ no bharīmabhiḥ” (RV 1.140.6) and “vātasya sarge abhavat sarīmaṇi” (RV 1.143.7).

This is because it is consistent with such mantras as “*tarṇaṃ barhiḥ suṣṭarīmā juṣāṇā*,” “*yasmāmatirbhā adidyautatsavīmani hiraṇyapāṇiḥ*,” and others, as well as with their commentaries; furthermore,
since the aforementioned usages are not observed in the spoken language, it is logical that they follow the requirements of Vedic meter (*chandas*).

For this very reason, he will employ the term *sarvatra* ("everywhere") in the sūtra *ṭhveñaḥ sarvatra*. (1350) *janimṛṅbhyām imanin* [Pāṇini 5.1.123]. [The roots] *jani* (from *jan*, "to be born") and *mṛṅ* (from *mṛ*, "to die"). *jana* means "birth," and *mṛṅ* means "the relinquishing of life."
(1351) *veñaḥ* everywhere. 589. *veñ*: the root *veñ* means "to weave" (*tantu-santāne*).
(1352) *nāman*, *sīman*, *vyoman*, *roman*, *loman*, *pāpman*, *dhyāman*.
"They are treated as irregular forms (*nipātyante*)"—the remainder [of the rule] being "those ending in *ani* or *an*. For the root *mrā* in the sense of repetition:
there is either elision of *m* or the substitution of *nā*. *Nāman* means a name or designation. For the root *ṣiñ* in the sense of binding: "*īmasīme* are both feminine dual endings."

Thus says Amara: from the roots *vyeñ* (to cover) and *ru* (to sound). *Roma* refers to the hair on the body. From *lūñ* (to cut), *loma* has the same meaning. It is called *sāman* because it pacifies (*syati*) or causes suffering (*duḥkhayati*) due to its difficulty to master.
