And: (1355) *sikan* is added after the roots *han* and *maś*.
593. *han*: *hana* [is used] in the senses of injury and motion; *maśa* in the senses of sound and anger. [The word derived is] *akṣikā*, meaning a female bee.
"Syāt" [is used] in the *Hārāvalī*.
(1356) *Koraran* |594|. *Ku* in the sense of sound. *Kavaraḥ*—fire; because of the identity of *ba* and *va*, it is also *kabarī*.
Regarding the arrangement of hair: by [the rule] "āna-pada," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied; elsewhere it is *kabarā*.
(1357) *gira-uḍac*: from *giraḥ*. The root *gṛ* means "swallowing. Some, however, omit this sūtra and derive it from *garutā ḍayate*.

They laboriously derive the word *garuḍa* by adding the suffix *ḍa* to the root *ḍīṅ* after prefixing *vi*, and then deleting the letter *t* of *garta* on the basis of its belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* class.
(1358) [The word *indukamī* is derived] from the root *ind* with the suffix *kami* and the elision of *n*. 596.

Regarding *indeḥ*: the root *idi* signifies supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*). However, Ujjvaladatta read [the suffix] as *kam-in*, which is to be considered doubtful; for in examples such as "this vessel is Indra’s drink" (*idam tyat pātram indrapānam*) and "this honey is for you, O gentle one" (*idam te somyam madhu*), there is an absence of the *nit-svara* (the acute accent on the first syllable caused by a *nit* suffix). In the *Daśapādī*, however, it is stated: "from *iṇ*, the suffix *damak*."
This has been stated in the Sūtra. The word *idam* is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) that refers to what is proximate.
[The suffix] *ḍimi* is added after the root *kāyati*.
[The rule states: "After *kāyati*. [The roots] *kai* and *gai* mean "to sound. Due to the absence of any purpose [for it], the letter *m* does not receive the designation *it*.

In the form *siddhe*, the letter *ḍi* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), while the letter *ḍa* is for the purpose of causing the elision of the *ṭi*-portion (*ṭilopa*). In the *Daśapādī*, however, the rule is formulated as *ḍimi* ending in *m*. The word *kim* is an interrogative pronoun (*sarvanāman*). (1360) Sūtra 598: *sarvadhātubhyaḥ ṣṭran*. "The suffix *ṣṭran* is added after all verbal roots."

[The suffix] *ṭran* [is applied] after all roots. However, in the *Daśapādī*, with the intention that it would apply to all roots by implication, only "after *ṭru*" was indicated. For this very reason, they say that [the mention of other roots] has been added as a supplement. [Examples: *vasa* (to dwell), *asu* (to throw), *śasu* (to injure), *chada* (to cover)—this is causative (*ṇyanta*). [The word] *astraṃ*.

According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *praharaṇa* [is used] for a bow (*cāpa*) and a sword (*karavāla*), and it is neuter. The root *patlṛ* means "to go. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *patra* refers to a vehicle, a leaf, a wing, an arrow, and a bird. The root *pā* means "to drink. From this comes *pātra*. Because it is marked with the *ṣit* designation, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *ātra* (i.e., *pātra*) is used in three genders; it is neuter when referring to a vessel such as a *sruva* ladle."

*Rājamantriṇi*: According to the *Medinī* lexicon, this means "suitable between two banks. *Daṃśa*: [The root] *daṃś* means "to bite. By the rule beginning with *vraścādi*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs, followed by the substitution of *ṣṭu*. Because the addition of the suffix *ṅīṣ* for roots marked with *ṣ* is not mandatory, the suffix *ṭāp* is used instead, resulting in *daṃṣṭrā*. (1361) *bhrasjigaminamihaniviśyaśāṃ vṛddhiśca* |599| [The rule states that there is Vṛddhi substitution for the vowels of the roots *bhrasj*, *gam*, *nam*, *han*, *viś*, *yā*, and *śā* when the suffix *kta* follows.]

From the roots *bhrasj* (in the sense of cooking), *gamlṛ* (in the sense of going), *ṇam* (in the senses of bowing and sound), *han* (in the senses of killing and going), *viś* (in the sense of entering), and *aśū* (in the sense of pervading), the suffix *ṣṭran* shall be applied, and there shall be *vṛddhi* for these [roots]. Thus, *bhrāṣṭra*. Here, the first letter of the conjunct is elided by the rule "elision of the first member of a conjunct" (*saṃyogādilopaḥ*). Then, by the rule "*ṭhvraśce*" (*Pāṇini 8.2.36*), the *j* is changed to *ṣ*, and by the rule "*ṣṭuan*" (*Pāṇini 8.4.41*), the *r* is changed to *ṣ*.
According to Amara, *ambarīṣa* means "frying pan" (*bhrāṣṭra*). *Viṣṭapa* is derived from *viṣṭam*.
(1362) *Diver dyauś ca* |600|. From the root *div*: from *divu*, meaning "to play," the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied; there is the substitution of *dyau* and the increase of the vowel (*vṛddhi*).
From the root [dhātu].
(1363) *uṣi-khani-bhyāṃ kit* (601): From the roots *uṣ* (in the sense of burning) and *khan* (in the sense of digging), the suffix *ṣṭran* shall be added as *kit*. *Uṣṭraḥ* (a camel).
*Kramelaka* [means camel]. Amara states: "The words *kramelaka*, *maya*, and *mahāṅga* denote a camel.
(1364) [Sūtra 602: "After the roots *siv* and *muc*, there is the substitution of *ū* for the final vowel of the root.
*Siv* (in the form *ṣivu*) means "to sew" (*tantusantāne*), and *muc* (in the form *muclṛ*) means "to release" (*mokṣaṇe*). From these two...

The suffix *ṣṭran* shall be applied, and there shall be the substitution of *ū* for the final letter (*ṭi*). This sūtra is intended to establish the forms [of *sūtra* and *mūtra*] by means of the suffix *erac*, since they cannot be derived from the roots *sūtri* and *mūtri* when followed by the causative marker *ṇic*. Nor can their formation be achieved by the suffix *dhañ*, because the rule *ṭerañ* (Pāṇini 3.3.56) supersedes *dhañ*. Furthermore, *sūtra* refers to a book of instructions.
"Regarding the distinction between *sūtra* [thread] and *tantu* [cord]," according to the *Viśva* lexicon.

(1365) [The suffix] *ktra* is added after the roots *ami*, *ci*, *midi*, and *śas*. [The meanings are: *ami*—to go, sound, or share; *ci*—to accumulate; *ñimidā*—to be oily or moist; *śasu*—to praise.
In the sense of "violence. Regarding the word *āntra*: the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *anunāsikasya*.

Kālidāsa says: "The girdle of entrails belonging to Roṇi and Lambi. Amara says: "The words *ākhyā*, *carya*, and *citram* [are used]. [And: "*Citram* is not used for two things; it refers to a friend or the sun."
According to the *Medinī* lexicon: “*puṃs* [is masculine]”; and “*astra* is neuter in the sense of metal or a missile, but feminine in the sense of a dagger.

By virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), these words are oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable). Examples include: “*una āntrāṇi pece*,” “*itram devānām*,” “*itram nayanam*,” and “*astrasya śastram asi*,” etc.

In this sense, there is another etymological derivation for the word *putra*: by applying the suffix *ka* according to the rule *ataḥ anupasarge kaḥ*.

In the word *opo vyauḥ*, there is elision of the *y*. Because it has the marker *ṭi*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Amara states: “*trī*, *yoṣit*, *abalā*, *yoṣā*, *nārī*, *sīmāntinī*, and *vadhū* [mean woman].
(1368) The suffix *tra* is added after the roots *gṛdh*, *vīpac*, *vac*, *yam*, *sad*, and *kṣad*. Pāṇini 4.1.70.

The roots *gṛdhṛ* (in the sense of an indistinct sound), *dhṛñ* (in the sense of holding), *vī* (in the sense of motion, procreation, etc.), *ḍupacaṣ* (in the sense of cooking), *vaca* (in the sense of speaking), *yama* (in the sense of ceasing), *ṣadlṛ* (in the sense of falling apart, going, etc.), and *kṣada* (a root found in the Sūtras). The *brāhmaṇa* belongs to the caste immediately following [the *kṣatriya*].
(1369) From the roots *hve*, *yā*, *mā*, *śru*, and *bhas*, the suffix *sran* is applied.
[The roots are: *hve* in the sense of giving and eating; *yā* in the sense of reaching; *mā* in the sense of measuring; *śru* in the sense of hearing; *bhas*...

[Bhartsana] means threatening and [dīpti] means brilliance. *Hotra* means an oblation (*āhuti*). Regarding the word *hotrā*, Haradatta and others state in the rule "ṭhhotrābhyaśchaḥ" that it is feminine even when referring to officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *yātrā* may mean torment (*yātanā*), and in the feminine gender, it denotes going (*gamana*) and a festival (*utsava*). [Ātrā] refers to an ear-ornament.

"Vita" means pride or an ornament; "akṣara" refers to a minute part or a syllable; and "klība" signifies entirety or determination. According to Amara, "arṇa," "śabda," and "graha" denote the ear, as do the feminine words "śruti," "śravaṇa," and "śrava. Furthermore, "hasrā" refers to a leather pouch.
(1370) And after the root *gam*, [the suffix *a* is added].
608. From the root *gam*—that is, from this root *gamlṛ* meaning "to go"—and from roots ending in long *ā*, [the suffix *a* is applied]. [Examples include:
*ātra* (in the body), *maṅga* (in the body), *iṣṭaka* (brick), *levara* (body); and in the classification beginning with *stamberama* (elephant), *agrajaṅgha* (long-shanked), and so forth.
"Samīrita" is [defined] as "proclaimed" in the Viśva [kośa].
(1371) *Dādibhyaś chandasi* |609|. From roots beginning with *dā*: from *dāp* (to cut) and others, the suffix *ran* is applied. Thus, *dātram*.

An instrument for cutting grain and the like. *Pā* means "to drink. According to Amarasimha, *pātra* refers to a vessel or a worthy recipient. *Kṣi* means "to dwell" and "to go. The forms *kṣitra* and so forth are to be applied accordingly.
(1372) The suffix *ṇitran* is added after roots beginning with *bhū* and after the root *gṛ*.

The roots beginning with *bhū*: *bhū* in the sense of existence (*satāyām*). *Bhāvitra* refers to the three worlds (*trailokyam*). *Vad* in the sense of distinct speech (*vyaktāyāṃ vāci*), with the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*):
*vāditra* refers to musical instruments such as drums (*tūryādi*). *Gṛ* in the sense of swallowing (*nigaraṇe*). (1373) [Pāṇini 4.4.52:
After the root *car*, the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied when the meaning is "excepting" (*vṛte*).

From the root *car* (in the sense of "to move"), the suffix *itran* is applied when the word *vṛtta* is to be expressed as the object. As Amara states: "The word *vṛtta* refers to both verse and conduct (*cāritra*). Now, one might object: "If it is said that *caritra* is formed by the suffix *itran*, and since *cāritra* is established by adding the *aṇ* suffix from the *prajñādi* group, what is the purpose of this [present rule]? This is not so; for there is a difference in the accent (*svara*).

(1374) *aśitrādibhya itrautrau* |612|: From roots such as *aśū* "to pervade" and others, the suffix *itra* is applied; from roots such as *traiṅ* "to protect" and others, the suffix *utra* is also applied. Thus, *vahitram* [is formed]: from *vaha* "to carry. *Dharitrī*: from *dhṛñ* "to hold," [the feminine form is derived] because it belongs to the *gaurādi* group.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* [is applied].
(1375) *amerdviṣati cit* | Pāṇini 4.1.3: After the root *am* (in the sense of "to go"), the suffix *itrac* occurs, and it is *cit*. However, the suffix *utrac* does not follow here.
Because it is not *svarita*-accented. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of "not a friend" (*na mitram*), the term *amitram* is neuter.
(1376) *āḥ samiṇ-kaṣibhyām*: *āḥ* [is added] after *sam* and *iṇ*. *iṇ* means "to go. From this root, with the suffix *ā*, there is *guṇa* substitution, and subsequently the replacement by *ay*.
Regarding *keṣara*: the root *kaṣ* (as in *kaṣa khaṣa*) belongs to the *daṇḍaka* group. The words *samayā* and *nikaṣā* signify proximity.

From the root *duṣ*, by virtue of its inclusion in the *bahulaka* category, we derive *doṣā*. From the root *div*, with the suffix *ā*, by *bahulaka* alone, there is an absence of *guṇa*, resulting in *divā*. From the root *svad*, with the suffix *ā*, by *bahulaka* alone... [the same applies].
And there is the substitution of *dhān* for the root *dhā*. [The example is] *svadhā*, etc.
(1377) *citeḥ kaṇaḥ kaśca*: after the root *cit*, the suffix *kaṇ* is applied, and *ka* is the substitute for the final letter.
[That is,] from the root *cit* (*citī* "to perceive"), the suffix *kaṇ* occurs, and *ka* is the substitute for the final letter.
Amarasiṃha says: "cikkaṇam" [is the word for smooth].

(1378) *Sūceḥ sman* | 616 | From the root *sūc*, meaning "to indicate" or "malice," belonging to the curādi class, the suffix *sman* is applied; there is elision of the *ṇi* augment, followed by the changes to *kutva* and *ṣatva*. Thus, "sūkṣmam."
According to the *Medinīkośa*, [the word *kaṇṭaka*] occurs in the sense of a thorn (*adhyātma*), a man (*pums*), an atom (*aṇu*), and in three genders as something small (*alpaka*).

(1379) [The suffix] *ḍumsun* is added after the root *pāti*. Regarding *pāti*: from the root *ā* in the sense of "to protect," the suffix *ḍumsun* is applied; because it is marked with *ḍi*, there is elision of the *ā*.
According to Ujjvaladatta, the letter *ṭh* is for the purpose of pronunciation;

however, in reality, it is for the sake of the grammatical operations (*kārya*) triggered by the marker *uṅ*, as in the form *supuṃsī*. By the rule *ugitaśca*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. The letter *n* is for the sake of accent (*svara*). This is stated by both Nyāsa and Rakṣita regarding the rule *puṃso'suṅ ṅiti*.

Furthermore, it is stated [in the grammatical tradition] that *ḍumsun* follows the root *mṛkṣ* with a short vowel; others, however, say it follows the root *pū*. In the Bhāṣya, however, it is said that the word *pumān* is derived from the root *sū* with the suffix *sap*. The truth is this: "The means for attaining the goal are not fixed."

(1380) *kiṣya* is added after *ruc* and *bhuj*. *ruc* [means] to shine and to find pleasure; *bhuj* [means] to protect and so forth. According to the *Medinī*: "The word *hujiṣya* refers to one who is independent, a jeweler (*hastasūtraka*), and a slave (*dāsa*); in the feminine, it refers to a female slave (*dāsī*) and a courtesan (*gaṇikā*)."

(1381) *vasestiḥ* |619| From the root *vas*: *vasa* in the sense of dwelling (*nivāse*), and *vasa* in the sense of covering (*ācchādane*). Regarding *śāsa*: *śāsu* in the sense of instruction (*anuśiṣṭau*).

*Asyati* means "he throws. The root *asu* is used in the sense of "throwing. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *astiḥ* [is derived from this root] with the suffix *ṭhak*; it refers to the pot-born [Agastya], and is also a masculine term for the two types of *vaṅgasena* trees. (1382) [The suffix] *sa* occurs after the root *vas*. 6.2.0.

(1383) *vau taseḥ* |6|2|1| After the root *tasu* meaning "to perish," when preceded by *vi*, the suffix *ti* occurs when *ava* is the preceding word. [This refers to the form] *avaṭaṅguṣṭhe sakaniṣṭhe*.
"Vitasti is twelve aṅgulas," according to Amara; "Vitasti may be used for both male and female [nouns]," according to the Amaramālā.
(1384) [The suffix] *ni* is added after the roots *pad* and *prathi*. 6.2.2.

(1487) *līrīṅerhrasvaḥ puṭ ca ta rau śleṣaṇakutsanayoḥ* || 733 || Regarding *līrīṅoḥ*: *līṅ* means "to adhere" (*śleṣaṇe*), and *rīṅ* means "to flow" (*śravaṇe*). "Respectively" (*kramāt*) means that when "adhering" is to be expressed, the suffix *ta* is applied; when "contempt" (*kutsita*) is to be expressed, the suffix *ra* is applied. [The word] *iptam* is used for poisoned food and for what has been eaten.
"Vilepita means 'to be expressed' (*vācya*)," according to the *Viśva* lexicon.

(1488) *Kliśer īccopadhāyāḥ kan lopaśca lo nām ca* |7|3|4|. [The rule] *kliśeḥ*: the root *kliśū* means 'to afflict'. [The suffix] *kan* is added, there is elision (*lopa*) of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), and the augment *nām* is inserted; "of the suffix" (*pratyayasya*) is the understood remainder.

Regarding the word *cintya*: the sense is that the absence of *guṇa* (vṛddhi) is established by the very force (*sāmarthya*) of the rule prescribing *ī*. According to the *Medinīkośa*: “*Īna* denotes a ploughman, a mean person, one who strikes secretly, or [the god] Yama; it is used as a masculine.”

(1489) *aśnoteḥ āśukarmaṇi varaṭ ca* |735|. From the root *aś*, meaning "to pervade" (*aśū vyāptau*), the suffix *varaṭ* shall be applied when the sense of "quick action" is to be expressed. [The form] *īśvarī* [is derived thus].
When that which possesses quick action—such as the act of granting boons—is to be expressed, it means "one who gives quickly. [The form] *īśvara* [is likewise derived].

In the feminine, however, because of the *ṭit* designation, there is the suffix *ṅīp*. In *īśvarī*, the accent falls on the middle syllable due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). But in the case of *īśvarī* derived from the root *īś* with the suffix *vanip*—where the rule "*vano ra ca*" applies to form the feminine in *ṅīp* and *ra*—the accent falls on the first syllable due to the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). In the case of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* used to denote a woman connected to a male (*puṃyoga*), the accent falls on the final syllable. [Furthermore, in *aiśvara*] the suffix *varac* is applied according to the rule "*theśabhāsapisakasaḥ*."

The distinction is that the suffix *ṭāp* is applied after a word ending in *īśvara*. Regarding the term *īśvara*: "The word *īśvara* is used in the sense of the god of love (Manmatha), Śambhu, Nārada, and a master (svāmin); it is declinable [as both masculine and feminine]. *Īśvarī* refers to Umā; and *īśvarā* [is also used]," according to the Medinīkośa. The analysis is: *īśvarā—umāyām* (the word *īśvarā* means Umā). "The word *īśvara* is used for Śaṅkara, a sovereign, and for his wife, *īśvarī* and *īśvarā*," [according to other lexicons].
*Bopālita* [comments]: Bhāravi [states], "The great auspicious herb was placed upon the Lord’s [forehead].

However, there is another rule (*sūtra*) for ten syllables: *hante ran ghaśca*. From the root *han*, meaning 'to kill' or 'to go,' the suffix *ran* is applied, and *gha* is the substitute for the final letter. Thus, *hanyate*.

A *ghara* is that which is gone to by guests; it is a house (*gṛha*). (1490) *Cateruran* | 7.3.6 | From the root *cat*, meaning "to beg," the suffix *uran* is applied. The letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation.
The suffix *ām* is applied [to the word *catvār*] by the rule "‘aturanaḍuhorāmudātaḥ’" [Pāṇini 7.1.98], resulting in *catvāraḥ*.
(1491) Regarding the rule "prā’tateraran": after the root *at*, preceded by *pra*, the suffix *aran* is applied; the vowel *a* follows the letter *r*.
The purpose is for pronunciation. It is an indeclinable because it is listed among the *svarādi* group. *Prātar*.
(1492) *amestuṭ ca* |7|3|8|. [The rule] *ameḥ*: from the root *am*, meaning "to go," "sound," or "share," the suffix *aran* is applied, and there is also the augment *tuṭ* after this [root].
The word *antaḥ* is also an indeclinable, like the word *prātaḥ*.

(1493) [Pāṇini 6.3.92: "In the case of the root *dah*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*go*), and *d* is replaced by *n*. Regarding *dah*: the root *dah* means "to reduce to ashes. [The word *aga* is used] for a tree, a mountain, the sun, and fire.
Thus [ends] the *Medinī*.
(1494) *Siceḥ saṃjñāyāṃ hanumau kaśca* |7|4|0|. From the root *sic*, meaning "to sprinkle. Regarding "the substitution of *h*": this means the final letter of the root. *Iṃhaḥ*...

"Siṃhī occurs in the sense of a lioness (*kaṇṭhīrava*), in the seventh lunar mansion (*rāśi*), in the sense of being situated to the north, and in the sense of a mother of Rāhu, the wife of Vāsaka, among small and large [plants]," says the Viśva-kośa.
(1494) [The suffix] *ci* is applied after the root *ghrā* preceded by *vi-* and *ā-* to denote a genus (*jāti*). 7.3.74.1.

From the root *ghrā* (meaning "to smell"), when the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of a genus (*jāti*), there is the elision of the long *ā* due to its *kit* status. Thus, *vyāghra* is formed. It is used for the tiger (*śārdūla*) in the masculine;
for the *rakta-uraṇṇaka* and the *karañja* tree; for one who is preeminent among men and others; and for the *kaṇṭakārī* plant in the feminine.
Thus says the Medinī.

(1495) *hanter ac ghura ca* | 7.42 | From the root *han*: the suffix *ac* shall be applied after *han*, and there shall be the substitution of *ghura* for the root. As in: "The *hora* [is] in the formidable Hari."
*Viśvaḥ*. (1496) *Kṣamer upadhālopaś ca* |743|. From the root *kṣam-*; *kṣamūṣ* means "to endure. According to Amara: "The earth is called *kṣmā*, *avanī*, *medinī*, and *mahī*."
(1497) The suffix *ḍri* is added after the root *tṛ*.
|744| After the root *tṛ*, meaning "to cross" or "to swim," the suffix *ḍri* occurs. Because it is marked with the indicatory letter *ḍ*, there is elision of the *ṛ* vowel (*ṭilopa*).

(1498) *graher aniḥ* | 745 | From the root *grah*. [The root] *grah* means "to seize" (*upādāna*). Regarding the suffix *ṅīṣ*: it is by virtue of the rule "after a root ending in *ṛ* or a vowel" (*ṛdikārāt*). Amara states: "*rahaṇī* is *ruk*, [a type of] dysentery" (*pravāhikā*).
(1499) *prathama-c* | 746 | From the root *prath*.

The root *prath* means "to become manifest. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *prathama* occurs at the beginning [of a series] and also denotes 'the foremost,' functioning like an adjective (*vācyavat*). Because of the rule "optionally [treated as] a pronoun" (*vaikalpika-sarvanāmatvāt*) for the form *prathama-c*, there is optionally the substitution of *jas* [for the nominative plural].
The substitution of *śī* [for *asi*]. In the first [case], the nominative endings (*prathamā*) are used.

(1500) *careśca*. Also after the root *car* [the suffix *am* is applied]. From the root *car*, meaning "to move" or "to eat," the suffix *am* is added. In the last [case], the accusative endings (*caramā*) are used.
The analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) has an intended purpose. It would have been sufficient to simply say "after *rathi* and *carin*" (*rathicaribhyām*).
(1501) *maṅgeralac* [Pāṇini 3.2.163]. After *maṅgi*: in the list beginning with *ukha* and *ukhī*, the root *māṅg* meaning "to go" is recited. "Auspicious..."

*Maṅgalaṃ śubham* (Auspiciousness is welfare). *Maṅgala* is a type of planet. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *maṅgala* [denotes] white dūrvā grass and Umā in the feminine; it denotes Mars in the masculine; and it is neuter in the sense of auspiciousness, all objects, and protection. By adding the suffix *ṣyañ* to express the abstract state (*bhāva*), we have *māṅgalyam*. In this context...

Regarding the word *sādhu*: according to the *Medinīkośa*, "The term *aṅguli* refers to the *syonāka*, *āyāmāṇā*, *aśvattha*, *bilva*, and *masūraka*; it is feminine when referring to the *śamyā*, the *adhaḥpuṣpī*, *misi*, *śuklavacā*, *rocanā*, and *dadhi*; it is a neuter noun [meaning 'finger'], and in the masculine it means 'one who acts auspiciously' (*śivakara*). This concludes the fifth section among the *Uṇādi* suffixes.
The *pāda* [section]: There are three hundred and twenty-five (*325*) *uṇādi* suffixes; their detailed analysis has been performed here by Jñānendra Svāmin. ||1||
However, it is clear that the author of the *Prākṛtaprakāśa* has presented only a few of the *uṇādi* suffixes, and not all of them;
furthermore, even those presented were not treated as a single continuous section, but rather in scattered fragments.
Among those very [fragments], certain errors have been pointed out in the *Manoramā*.

We shall point out some instances of negligence. In the second *pāda*, under the section on the suffix *ṇvi*—having introduced the rules "ṇvi after roots ending in *ha* or *ja*" (*hajo ṇviḥ*), "in the Vedic language, after *sah*" (*chandasi sahaḥ*), and "after *vah*" (*vahaśca*)—the rule "the substitution of *ṣ* occurs for the final *j* of *vraj* before *ṇvi* when at the end of a word" (*arau vrajeḥ ṣaḥ padānte*) is cited.
By that very rule, the *ṣ* is substituted [to form *parivrāj*]; thus, the form *parivrāṭ* is indeed the reading of the ancient grammarians.

In his commentary on that [work], the author’s grandson stated, “This is recited in the *Auṇādika-sūtra* beginning with *aṅca-pādya*”; however, both of these statements are due to negligence, because the rule for the suffix *kvip* and the lengthening of the vowel is introduced with the words “*vib-bavaci*,” and the rule is subsequently read as “*arau vraje*. Regarding this point:

Because the *Pañcapādī* and the *Daśapādī* form a single coherent whole (*ekavākyatva*). Furthermore, as for the statement that even the reading of the ancient [commentators] has been employed, it lacks authority because the phrase "some say" (*kecid iti*) is used regarding a meaning that is not universally accepted and is not established in the Sūtra itself. Moreover, as for...

The reading “*han-ṛti-cakṣiṅ-vapi-tapi-jani-yaji-ruḥ*” is cited [in some texts], but that too is unauthoritative. For instance, the universally accepted reading is: “*anu-r-iḥ*, *ṛt-pṛ-vapi-yaji-tani-dhani-tapi-bhyaḥ niṭ*; *ṭher-ṇiṭ ca*; *akṣeḥ śiṭ ca*. [And it continues: “*apūṃṣi tasmai*... [and so forth].
It is also consistent with the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātta*) found in mantras such as *vapuṣo vapuṣṭaram*.
The Vedic commentary (*vedabhāṣya*) stands exactly thus. These and other such errors occur in the second quarter (*pāda*).
In the third quarter as well—[there is the rule]: "From the roots *stan*, *dūṣi*, *puṣ*, *gidi*, *mad*, *hṛd*, and others, [the suffix] *itnu* follows *ṇi*."

This was read by Prācya; however, neither *dūṣi* nor *hṛdī* are found in the works of any of the commentators (*vṛttikṛt*) on that point. Furthermore, the usage *dūṣayitnuḥ* and *hṛdayinnuḥ* is not seen in the original source (*ākara*), for the reading in the Pañcapādī is: "from the roots *tan*, *hṛṣ*, *puṣ*, *mud*, *gad*, and *mad*."

The fact that the word *huṣigandhimaṇḍijaninamibhyaḥ* is read as an addition in the Daśapādī [Dhātupāṭha] is a separate matter. Furthermore, although the Easterners (Prācya), having read the rule *rudakṣispṛhiddṛgṛhijṛbhya āyyaḥ*, have stated the forms *darāyya* and *jarāyya*, that too is incorrect.

Because the inclusion of the root *dṛṅ* (or *dṛg*) is not recorded in the original grammatical sources. Furthermore, although the ancient commentators, having stated the rules "from *ṛ*, *viś*, and others, *jhac*" and "from *aṇḍi*, *maṇḍi*, *jan*, and *nandi*, *ac*," cited *gaṇḍayataḥ* and *janayantaḥ* as examples, and having taken the word *gaṇḍayantaḥ* as a heading, explained it as a name for a cloud; [this is incorrect].
The commentators have explained that *gaḍi* means "in one part of the face," but all of that is merely due to negligence.

For instance, having listed *gaḍi* without the nasal *anusvāra* (*niranuṣaṅga*) in the *Uṇādi* [sūtras], it is explained as *gaḍa secane* ("to sprinkle"); and this is likewise found in all works such as the *Vṛtti*, the *Nyāsa*, and the *Haradatta* commentary on the rule *ṭhayāmante*.

It is stated thus in the works of Mādhava, and it is likewise in the work of Mādhava; and this is appropriate, because for the purpose of explaining [the word] as "cloud" (megha), the root meaning of "to sprinkle" (√sic) alone is suitable. Furthermore, the reading of the root √jan is unauthentic; having read the root √ji, [it says] "O son of Pākaśāsana, who art full of [victory]."

Because [the forms] are all [already] explained, and because the object of the definition (*lakṣya*) "janayantaḥ" has not been shown by anyone, and because they are unestablished, "caṭ" and so forth are errors in the third quarter. Now, regarding the fourth: as for that which was stated—"The suffix *kvin* is applied after the roots *ṛ*, *gṛ*, *stṛ*, and *jāgṛ*; [thus] *kīrviḥ*, *gīrviḥ*."

The statement made by the ancients that [the root] is *stīr* is also due solely to a scribal error. Furthermore, the explanation offered by those commenting on the ancient text—namely, "kṛ vikṣepe," "gṛ nigaraṇe," and "stṝñ ācchādane"—is itself corrupt because of an impurity in its source. For the correct reading is indeed: "ṛśṛstṛjāgṛbhyaḥ kvin."

This is the consensus of the authors of the *Uṇādi-vṛtti*, such as Mādhava and others; for in their treatises it is established that *jīrvih* means "an animal," *śīrvih* means "cruel," and *stīrvih* means "an officiating priest (*adhvaryu*)". Indeed, it is only when the root *stṛ* ends in a long vowel that the substitution of *i* (as prescribed by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ*) is obtained, and not otherwise.
Even though it ends in a short vowel, it is proper to accept [the forms] exactly according to their order; this is the direction [of the argument].
As for what was stated by the ancients—namely, "niḥ is added after glā, jyā, hā, and tvar"—that too is without authority.
For in the authoritative source (the *Mahābhāṣya*), having read "niḥ is added after vī, jyā, and jvar," [the author] places it immediately after two sūtras.
Regarding the statement "from *vah*, *śrī*, etc.," namely the rule "niḥ after *lā*, *hā*, *tvar*, and *ari*," that too is not the original source (*anākara*).

For in the original sources (*ākara*), having read "niḥ after *vī*, *yaj*, *jvar*, etc.," the rule "niḥ after *lā*, *hā*, *tvar*, and *ari*" is formulated in the sūtra "from *vah*, *śrī*, etc. immediately following those two rules.

Furthermore, because we observe the acute accent (*udātta*) in forms such as *‘ūrṇīrathaḥ sadānavaḥ’* and others; nor should it be argued that this is merely a Vārttika situated under the governing rule *‘striyāṃ ktin’* (Pāṇini 3.3.94) which was cited by the ancients,
and not actually part of the *uṇādi* sūtras— because even so, the inclusion of the root *tvarati* would be inappropriate, for it [is not listed there].

This is the direction [indicated] in the Vārttika. Similarly, the citation from the ancients, “*aṃstyāne styāyaterḍraṭ*,” is also without authority (*anākara*), because the original source (*ākara*) for the sūtra is found in both the *Pañcapādī* and the *Daśapādī* as simply “*styāyaterḍraṭ strī*” [meaning:
the suffix *ḍraṭ* occurs after the root *styai-* in the sense of a female fetus].

The reading "sūteḥ sapprasave pumān" is found in the *Bhāṣya* as a verse (śloka-pāṭha); it was indeed cited by Mādhava, yet such a form is not seen in the reading of the *Sūtra* itself. In this way, the errors of those who have commented upon that work are also to be inferred; for example, the phrase "āṇinyādimunī" [is another such instance].

The commentators have stated, "By the rule *agneruccopadhāyāḥ*," for there is no such rule in either the *Pañcapādī* or the *Daśapādī*; rather, since *it* is being carried over [from the previous rule], the rule is formulated simply as *agneruca*. This is the direction [of the argument]. Thus end the errors of the ancients in the fourth quarter. Thus end the *uṇādi* suffixes.
Thus ends the section on the *uṇādi* suffixes in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
Now, the section on secondary suffixes (*kṛt*).

(1502) *uṇādayo bahulam* 3.3.1: "The *uṇ*-class [suffixes] are applied diversely. From the rule *vartamāne laṭ* ("*laṭ* is used for the present time"), the mention of "present" (*vartamāna*) is carried over; [and from the rule] *uvaḥ*...
The mention of *saṃjñā* (name) from the previous rule [Pāṇini 3.3.109] also carries over here. Thus he says: "These...
For in this sūtra, the words *dhātoḥ* (from a root), *pratyayaḥ* (suffix), and *ṛt* as well as *ṅit* carry over; therefore, by [the rule] *ṛvāpājimī* etc., [the suffix *kvip* is applied].

The designation *pratyaya* (suffix) and the designation *kṛt* are established even for those [suffixes] such as the *uṇādi*s that are not included within the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*. Accordingly, all *uṇādi* suffixes occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*) in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*), according to the rule *kartari kṛt*. Furthermore, for a word ending in an *uṇādi* suffix, [the designation *prātipadika* is established] by the rule *ṛtaddhite*.

When the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is established, everything desired—such as the derivation of *khādi* and so forth—is accomplished. The inclusion of the term "variously" (*bahulam*) is for the purpose of completing those *uṇādi* suffixes that are incomplete. He states its result: "some [suffixes] are applied even though not prescribed. The suffix *ulac* is prescribed after the root *hṛṣ*, but that...
The form *śaṅkulā* also occurs, as seen in actual usage.

Furthermore, the suffixes *phiḍa* and *phiḍḍa* are not prescribed anywhere; these two, namely *ṛphiḍa* and *ṛphiḍḍa*, are derived from the root *ṛ*, and their status as *kit* (having a *k* as an indicatory letter) is to be inferred. Likewise, in the case of the word *ṣaṇḍha*:

"Non-existence of sentient beings," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in notions" (*saṃjñāsu*): they say it refers specifically to beginningless notions, and not to all notions whatsoever. Having observed the suffix *ulac* in the rule *hṛṣerulac*, the base *śaṅki-* is inferred; by that, the form *śaṅkula-* is established. [This applies] to roots such as *ṛ* (to go), and so on.

The suffixes *phiḍa*, *phiḍḍa*, and so forth are understood. Regarding the rule "one should know [the suffix] from the grammatical effect" (*kāryāt vidyāt*): in cases such as *ṛphiḍa*, one should recognize the *anubandha* (indicatory letter), such as the letter *k*, by virtue of the necessity for grammatical effects like the prohibition of *guṇa*.
In the word *anūbandham*, there is lengthening according to the rule *upasargasya ghañi*. This is the treatise regarding the *uṇādi* suffixes.
The meaning is "that which is to be instructed.
(1503) *bhūte ’pi dṛśyante* | 3|3|2|. They are seen [to be used] even for the past. But if this is so, what is the purpose of the mention of the present tense (*vartamāna*) and [the rule] "uṇādayaḥ"?

If it is argued that the word *bahulam* need not be carried over here, and that both this rule and the subsequent sūtra may be discarded because the suffixes are obtained without distinction across all three times, they reply: "They occur generally in the present, but in the past and future only occasionally."
To demonstrate this distinction:

(1504) *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ* |3|3|3|. Regarding the future tense, there are words such as *gamyādayaḥ*. For example: "He will go" is expressed as *gamī grāmam* ("one who will go to the village"). Similarly, "He will come" is expressed as *āgamiṣyatīti*.

The suffix *ini* is applied after the root *gam* [to form *āgāmī*]. However, because the prefix *āṅ* is followed by a *ṇit* suffix, there is vocalic strengthening (*upadhāvṛddhi*) according to the rule *āṅi ṇit*. (1505) *bhīmādayo’pādāne* 3.4.74.

*Bhīmaḥ* | *Bhīṣmaḥ*: [The suffix] *ṣuk* is optional by virtue of the rule *hiyo hetubhaye ṣug*, which prescribes the suffix *map* in connection with it. *Praskandanaḥ*: "One from whom one might leap away"; [the suffix] *lyuṭ* in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*).

*Prarakṣaḥ*: "One from whom one protects"; [the suffix] *ac* according to the rule *pacādyac*. *Mūrkhaḥ*: "One from whom one becomes bewildered"; [from the root] *muh*. [The suffix] *kha* according to the rule *uheḥ*.
"He faints; he stumbles because of this, thus it is *khalati*, meaning 'one whose head is hairless'—as was stated previously.

(Pāṇini 3.4.75) "Other than those two, [the suffixes] beginning with *uṇ* [apply]. Regarding the phrase "other than those two": if the word "from these two" (*ābhyām*) were not stated, then [the suffixes] would apply only to the immediately preceding ablative (*apādāna*).
The sense is that the meaning would be "other than the point of departure (apādāna) from which there is grasping. Regarding the phrase *tato’sau*:

the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) after the root *tan*. The nasal is elided by the rule *anudātopadeśa...*. The form *asau* [is derived] from the root *tan* with the suffix *tu*, in the sense of "he becomes extended" (*vistṛto bhavati*) from that. Regarding the word *vṛtam*.

That path which is accomplished by going and so forth is "vartma. [The suffix] *manin* is applied in the sense of the object of the root *vṛt*. According to Amara: "The words *sthāna*, *vartman*, *mārga*, and *adhvan* [are synonyms for 'path']" (1507).
[The rule] *tumun-ṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.10) [applies here].

The suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* [are used after a verbal root]. That whose purpose (*prayojana*) is an action (*kriyā*) is "for the sake of an action" (*kriyārthā*); [the suffixes are used] in such a case. Here, this should be understood: although there is no distinction between *tumun* and *ṇvul* as both are *kṛt* suffixes, by the rule "after roots ending in *avyaya*, *tumun* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*)," *tumun* occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), whereas *ṇvul* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Thus, [it is said] "in an action" (*kriyāyām*).

Regarding the mention [of the word] in the locative case (*saptamīnirdeśāt*), for words such as *yāti* which express that [action], the status of being an *upapada* is established by the rule "that which stands in the locative is an *upapada*" (*atropapadaṃ saptamīstham*). For example: *kṛṣṇaṃ draṣṭum*. The meaning is: "the act of going is the instigator of that future act of seeing which has Kṛṣṇa as its object. Similarly: *kṛṣṇaṃ darśakaḥ*.

The meaning is: "the act of going has as its agent one who will see a black deed, and its purpose is seeing. [Question: Why is there a restriction to an action (*kriyā*)? [Answer: "His matted locks (*jaṭāḥ*) are for the purpose of begging (*bhikṣiṣye*). Here, the matted locks are for the sake of begging;
however, they are a substance (*dravya*), not an action. As for the usage "matted locks for the purpose of begging" (*bhikṣituṃ jaṭāḥ*), [it is explained as follows].

The [sūtra] is to be justified by supplying the word "dhārayati" (he holds). What is the purpose of the phrase "kriyārthāyām" (when it has the sense of another action)? Consider: "hāvataste patiṣyati daṇḍaḥ" (As you run, the staff will fall upon you). Here, although there is the action of "running," this action does not have the falling of the staff as its purpose.
Rather, running is the cause of the staff's falling, not its intended object; such is the general direction.

(1508) *samānakartṛkeṣu tumun* |3|3|158|. Regarding the rule *samānakartṛkeṣu*: [it applies] when the actions do not have another action as their purpose (*akriyārtha*). In the expression *bhoktum icchati* ("he desires to eat"), what is understood is a desire directed toward the act of eating, not a desire for the sake of eating. Therefore...

The sense is that there is no application [of the rule] to the preceding case. He states that the word *samāna* found in the sūtra expresses oneness—namely, "in cases where there is a single agent"—by saying:

"in cases where there is one agent. Why [is the word] *eka* used? [Consider: *putrasya paṭhanam icchati*. Here, in the word *putrasya*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes the agent; the meaning is "reading having the son as its agent" (*putra-kartṛkaṃ paṭhanam*). In this sūtra...
In the absence of the condition "having different agents" (*amānakartṛka*), the usage would be *utkaḥ paṭhitum icchati* ("he wishes to read with eagerness").

The *Kāśikā* states: *devadattaṃ bhuñjānam icchati* ("he wishes Devadatta to be eating"). Even in the absence of such usage, however, in cases like *icchan kartuṃ gacchati* ("wishing to do, he goes"), [the suffix] is applied by the rule *tumun-ṇvulau* (Pāṇini 3.3.10).

This is to be considered. For it is impossible for the infinitive suffix *tumun* to apply in the sense of "he does" (*karoti*), because that suffix denotes an action (*bhāvārthaka*). Furthermore, in this context, the agent is understood through the present indicative suffix (*laṭ*). To say that the usage "desiring to do what?
(*kaṃ cicchaṅkarta*) is not desired is an empty statement, since the usage "desiring to do" (*kartum icchan*) [is indeed accepted].

Because it is universally accepted; and because the sequence of words is dependent upon one's own will, as in "bring the vessel" (*āhara pātram*) and "bring the vessel" (*pātram āhara*). The detailed discussion on this point should be sought in the *Manoramā* and other such works. Regarding the word *vaṣṭi*:
the root *vaś* means "to desire" (*kānti*), and since desire is a wish, the root *vaś* also has the meaning of "to wish."

(1509) *śak-dhṛṣa-jñā-glā-ghaṭa-rabha-labha-krama-saha-arha-asti-artheṣu* || 3.4.65 || *śak-dhṛṣa-*: This rule is also commenced for the purpose of [excluding] those cases where the upapada does not denote an action (*akriyārthopapada*). For in the example "he is able to eat" (*bhoktum śaknoti*) or "he knows how to eat" (*jānāti*), the meaning of the root *bhuj* (to eat) is connected as the object (*viṣaya*), and skill (*naipuṇya*) [is also implied].
It is understood [as follows]: in the expression "he is weary to eat" (*glāyati bhoktum*), an incapacity regarding the act of eating is understood.
In "it is fitting to eat" (*ghaṭate bhoktum*), however, there is the fitness [expressed as] "he is worthy to eat.
In "he begins to eat" (*ārabhate bhoktum*), there is the initial stage of the act of eating, namely, that he commences or exerts himself toward it.
In the case of *abhate*, there is no denial (*apratyākhyāna*); however, in expressions such as *asti bhoktum*, there is merely the sense of possibility (*saṃbhava-mātra*).
(Pāṇini 3.3.66) [The suffix *tumun* is used] after verbs expressing sufficiency (*paryāpti*) when they have the sense of being capable (*alam*).
"Paryāpto bhoktum" means "capable of eating"; that is, having the ability to eat.
(1511) *Kāla-samaya-velāsu tumun* (Pāṇini 3.3.167).
[The author] states its purpose by saying "upalakṣaṇārtham" (for the sake of indication), and provides the result of that with the example "anehā."
The *Amara-kośa* states: "‘Ālodiṣṭa’ means ‘even after a long time. Therefore, it is said here: "not in this case. The meaning is that [the suffix] does not occur in a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Regarding "yāgāya": the meaning is "in order to sacrifice" (*yaṣṭum*). The dative case is used according to the rule:
"After a word expressing an action denoting the sense of the suffix *uṇ*, [the dative is used]."
(1512) *aṇ* is used for the object (*karman*) as well [Pāṇini 3.3.12].

The meaning is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇvul*. Since the suffix *tumun* is prescribed for the sense of "being" (*bhāva*) by the rule "*avyayakṛto bhāve*," there is no possibility at all of its application here.

(1513) *padarujaviśaspṛśo ghañ* | Pāṇini 3.3.16. Regarding *padaruj-*: "That by which one goes" (*padyate’sau*). Here, it should be understood that there is an intention to express the instrument (*karaṇa*) as the agent (*kartṛ*). The resulting meaning is: "that by which one goes."

(1514) *sṛ* [is used] when the agent is firm (*sthira*). Regarding *sṛ sthire*: the mention of *sati* includes both roots beginning with *bhū* and those beginning with *hu*. By specifying "when the agent is firm," he indicates that the term *sthira* qualifies the agent—the meaning of the suffix—and is not an *upapada* (an accompanying word). Thus he says: "when the agent is firm."

Regarding the term *kartarī*: the inclusion of the word *sāra* in the list beginning with *ardharca* (Pāṇini 2.4.31) is the authority here. Regarding *vyādhi* and so forth: this statement is for the sake of [denoting] non-stable objects. By that, in the case of *visāro matsyaḥ* ("the fish that glides about"), the meaning "it moves in various ways" (*vividhaṃ sarati*) becomes consistent. In *atīsāra*, there is lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *upasargasya ghañi*.

"Sāra" means strength (*bala*). Here too, the root *sṛ* has an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*), because it conforms to the meaning "it causes to move" (*sārayati*) or "it impels" (*ceṣṭayati*). For only one who possesses strength moves. The phrase "having reached the state of accomplishment" (*siddhāvasthāpanna*) implies that, whereas in cases such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), the meaning of the verbal root is in a state of being accomplished (*sādhyāvasthāpanna*).
(1515) Regarding *raphurati* and *sphulati* with the suffix *ghañ*:
[the form] *ācameti*. The intention is that in the rule *odātaḥ*, it was stated "except for *ācam*" (*anācame*).
In that very same rule, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* follows from the *vārttika*: "not for *ācam*, *kam*, *vam*, and *mī*. (*anācamikamivamīnām*)

He says "no"—that [the word] *kāma* means *vāma*. It is un-Pāṇinian because, since the root *śram* is taught with an udātta accent, the suffix *ghañ* would result in a lack of *vṛddhi*; therefore, if one were to assume *vṛddhi* based on the causative (*ṇic*) as in examples such as "make those who are weary rest" (*viśrāmaya*), then the suffix *ac* would be applied to that causative form.
When that [suffix] is applied, the form is established. Nor should one fear a prohibition of *vṛddhi* even when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is present;

for in the rule "odāte," the term "ṛtī" is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*), and thus there is no prohibition regarding the causative suffix. Furthermore, one should not fear that the shortening rule "itāṃ hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.92) would apply here, since the word "vā" (or) is carried over [from the preceding rule].

The absence of the short vowel [in *niṣedhati*] is established by resorting to the *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (optional rule with fixed application). However, the intention is that if one assumes the presence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the meaning would differ. In reality, however, there is no fault if one intends the rule "the suffix *ṇiC* is added to a root denoting the act of sending forth or commanding" in its primary sense.

This is how it should be understood. And thus, poetic usages such as "The sick man, the long-traveler, he who eats another's food, he who sleeps in another's house—what he lives is his death, and what he dies is his rest," are indeed correct; this is how it should be known.

(1516) *avodaidhaudmapraśrathahimaśrathāḥ* | 6|4|29| *Avoda*: [The form] *avoda*. [It is derived from] the root *undī* (meaning "to moisten") preceded by the prefix *ava*; when the suffix *ghañ* is applied, the elision of the nasal (*n*) is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). *Edha*: [The form] *edha*. When the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *indh* (meaning "to kindle"), the elision of the nasal (*n*) and the substitution of *guṇa* are prescribed as irregularities. *Audma*: [The form] *audma*. [It is derived from] the root *ud* (meaning "to rise") preceded by the prefix *ā*; when the suffix *man* is applied, the substitution of *guṇa* is prescribed as an irregularity. *Praśratha*: [The form] *praśratha*. [It is derived from] the root *śranth* (meaning "to loosen") preceded by the prefix *pra*; when the suffix *ghañ* is applied, the substitution of *guṇa* is prescribed as an irregularity. *Himaśratha*: [The form] *himaśratha*. [It is derived from] the root *śranth* preceded by the prefix *hima*; when the suffix *ghañ* is applied, the substitution of *guṇa* is prescribed as an irregularity. [End of section] *a*.
It should be understood that this is a formal exception (*nipātana*) for *guṇa*, since it would otherwise not apply due to the prohibition [stated] as "dhātulope" (Pāṇini 1.1.4).
Regarding *odman*: from the root *und*, the *man* suffix is added according to the *uṇādi* rules; here too, the elision of *n* and the *guṇa* substitution are treated as formal exceptions.
Regarding *śranthi*: [the form] is treated as a formal exception when the prefix *pra-* or *hima-* precedes the root and the *ghañ* suffix is applied.
Thus it should be understood.

(1517) *Ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.27). Regarding [the statement] "it is mostly so" (*prāyikam*): if one were not entirely to abandon the apprehension of the technical name (*saṃjñā*), then in the case of *ṛtaḥ kaṭara*, there would be *āraḥ*.
The intention is that [the word] "kaṭa" should be [formed]. However, in the Bhāṣya, this is rejected on the grounds of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*).

(1518) *Parimāṇākhyāyāṃ sarvebhyaḥ* |3|3|20|. Regarding the phrase "in the expression of measure": "from all"—that is, from all verbal roots (*dhātu*). "Measure" (*parimāṇa*) means delimitation (*pariccheda*).

*Ākhyāna* means *ākhyā*, which is to say *ukti* (utterance). The meaning is: "when there is an utterance of a delimitation. If it is asked, "Of what, then, is there delimitation? it is said: "of the meaning of the suffix. The mention of *ākhyā* is for the purpose of excluding conventional usage (*rūḍhi*); therefore, by the inclusion of "measure" (*parimāṇa*), "number" (*saṅkhyā*) is understood here. From all [these]...
What [is the reason]? Otherwise, by the principle of "prior exception" (*pūrvāpavāda*), the suffix *ghañ* would subvert only *ācam*, but not *apa*.
[As in] *taṇḍulanicāyaḥ*. [The word] *nicāyaḥ* means that which is piled up or heaped together;
here, by the singularity of the heap, the delimitation of the individual components is understood by implication. [This is derived] with the suffix *ac* by the rule *ṭe-raḥ*.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied because it is obtained [by the rule]. That rice and the like which is *niṣpūyate*—meaning it is cleansed by the removal of the husk and so forth—is called *niṣpāva*.
Although the suffix *ap* (as in *ṛdor ap*) would also have been applicable, *ghañ* is used here. The word *śūrpeṇa* is in the instrumental case;
its composition with the word ending in the instrumental is formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*. In this context:

The measurement of rice and the like is also delimited by the winnowing-basket (*śūrpa*); however, the duality of the winnowing-basket is merely implied (*ārthika*), not expressed by the word (*śābda*). On the other hand, the duality residing in the *niṣpāva* (a specific measure) is indeed expressed by the word. Although here the suffix *ghañ* is obtained by the rule “*irabhyoḥ pūlvoḥ*,” nevertheless, by the force of the inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*), it is also [obtained] by this [rule].

The term *bhāva* means "it ought to be. He provides the primary example for [the suffix] *apratyaya*: "two *kārau*. The root √*kṛ* means "to scatter"; *ghañ* is added in the sense of the object (*karman*). A heap of grain and so forth scattered by a winnowing basket or similar tool is a *kāra*. In this case, the exception (*apavāda*) pertains solely to the base (*prakṛti*), and not to the meaning (*artha*).

Because it is understood in that very way through the mention of the ablative case in the word *sarvebhyaḥ*, this *ghañ* suffix, which depends on the verbal root (*prakṛti*), does not become an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ktin* suffix. Thus, *ekā tilocchritiḥ* ("a single heap of sesame").

Here, *ktin* is applied after the root *śri* preceded by the prefix *ud*, in the sense of the object (*karman*) or the abstract state (*bhāva*). It means "that which has been raised up" or "made into a heap."

This is the meaning. To indicate this, it was stated that [the suffixes] *ṭha* and *ap* are exceptions (*apavāda*). Since those two also depend on the base (*prakṛti*), it is appropriate that the exception (*apavādya*) and the counter-exception (*apavāda*) share the same scope.

As for *ktin* in the feminine, however, it depends on the meaning (*artha*); such is the direction of the argument. Regarding *dāra* and *jāra*: [they are used] when not denoting the agent (*akartari kārake*).

Because of this governing context (*adhikāra*) and because [the suffix] *ghañ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ṛdorap*, this statement is intended to provide for *ghañ* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). The phrase "and the elision of *ṇi*" (*ṇiluk ca*) implies that *ghañ* is also included by the word "and" (*ca*). For if there were an elision [of the *ṇi*], the *vṛddhi* substitution dependent on *ghañ* would not occur, because the elision of *ṇi* would create an intervention (*vyavadhāna*) by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*. Nor is [the *vṛddhi*] caused solely by the *ṇi*.
One should say, "let there be *vṛddhi*," because in the word *jāra*, the shortening [of the vowel] would otherwise occur by the rule *itāṃ hrasvaḥ*;

however, due to the designation *mit* for the root *jṛ* in the form *anījṛ* when followed by *ṇi*, [the *vṛddhi* is not applied]. But when there is elision (*luk*), since that [elision] lacks a subsequent cause, the prohibition applies by the rule *vilugupadhā* regarding what is elided in a *kvip* suffix.

The sense is that by this [rule], the form *jāraḥ* is established due to the absence of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). By this, the statement of certain scholars— that since those who split are *dārāḥ* (wives) and that which causes one to age is *jāraḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* may simply be applied to the roots ending in the causative marker *ṇic* (*dṛ-ṇic* and *jṝ-ṇic*) to denote the instrument, so what is the need for this specific rule?— is refuted.
Because the general rule (*utsarga*) *ghañ* is difficult to apply in a domain where the exception (*apavāda*) *ṭhañ* applies;

furthermore, since the rule of non-identity of suffixes (*asarūpa-vidhi*) is not accepted after the section on feminine derivation (*stryadhikāra*), the suffix *ac*— which is itself an exception to the rule "in the sense of agent and locus" (*karaṇādhikaraṇayoḥ*)— is also difficult to obtain here due to its being superseded by *lyuṭ*, and this is another matter.
Regarding *upetya*: it means "having approached," that is, having gone near the teacher (*guru*). Regarding the term *apādāne* ("in the sense of the ablative"):
by the principle of the prior exception (*purastādapavādanyāya*), since *iṅśca* is an exception specifically to the rule for the feminine gender (*acaḥ*), [the suffix *lyap* applies here].

Since the suffix *ktin* would otherwise apply, this [sūtra] is commenced to block that. Because of the statement, “The enumeration of *hañ* is for the scope of *ap*,” *ghañ* would not occur in the feminine; therefore, the mention of the feminine (*striyām*) is made. Regarding "upādhyāyī":
these two forms occur when one is personally teaching her [the Veda]. But in the case of a connection with a male (i.e., a husband), only the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies.

And it has been stated that "following" (*anugā*) is optional. [The form] *karaṇe ktaḥ* means [the suffix] *kta* is applied after the root *vṛñ* (to choose). Regarding *nīśāra*, there is lengthening of the vowel by the rule *upasargasya ghañi*. But how is the usage *radakṣiṇaprasavyagāmināṃ śārāṇām* possible? [It is explained by the rule] *vāyuvarṇe*.

If it is argued that this is because of the enumeration of meanings [in the Dhātupāṭha], they say in response: "Precisely for this reason, based on the usage in the Vārttika, the suffix ghañ is applied to the root *śru* even when used with the word *akṣa*.
(Pāṇini 3.3.22): *upasarge ruvaḥ*.
Regarding "rava": the suffix *ap* is applied by the rule *ṭhAñdor ap*. (1521) Regarding *śriṇībhuvo’nupasarge* [Pāṇini 3.3.24]:
"the policy (*naya*) of a king" is derived from the root *ṇīñ* (meaning "to lead") with the suffix *yat*, as prescribed by *aco yat* [Pāṇini 3.1.97].

(1522) *yajñe sami stuvaḥ* |3|3|31|. In the sense of "sacrifice" (*yajña*), after the prefix *sam*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *stu*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *lyuṭ* used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). (1523) *cchandonāmni ca* |3|3|34|. And [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] when the word is the name of a Vedic meter (*cchandas*).

The word *cchandaḥ* [is mentioned] because it is not covered by the preceding rule due to its being the object of the domain of sound (*śabda-viṣayatva*); however, some do not carry forward the word *vā* here, following the usage in examples such as *ara-stārapaṅkti*. (Pāṇini 3.3.35) *udi grahaḥ*.

Now begins the section on the suffix *ghañ*. The suffix *ghañ* occurs after verbal roots in the sense of a state (*bhāva*) and so forth. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ap* which would otherwise apply by the rule "raha-vṛ-dṛ... (Pāṇini 3.3.58).

(1525) Pāṇini 3.3.37: After the roots *nī* and *iṇ*, when preceded by *pari* and *ni* respectively, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the senses of "not losing" (*abhreṣa*) and "not deviating from the proper course" (*ābhreṣa*).
*Parinyoḥ*: Gambling with dice and the like is *dyūta*. Acting according to what has occurred is *abhreṣa*. (1526) *Parāvanupātyaya iṇaḥ* |3|3|38|.
Regarding *parāvanu*, they have explained here: "The double mention of *pari* is redundant; it should have been stated only once."

It is possible; for instance: "arau niyo dyaūte," "iṇo’nupātyaye," and "āvabhreṣe. Here, the intention is that the desired forms are established because "iṇaḥ" is understood to carry over [from the previous rule] in the case of "iṇo’nupātyaye," whereas in the case of "parā” [in "parāvabhreṣe"], "iṇaḥ" carries over [from the preceding rule]. Now, one might object:

In the previous sūtra, *anupātyaya* was explained as having the sense of "synonym" (*paryāya*); thus, although the desired result would have been established by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of that term alone, the explicit mention of *paryāya* here serves to set aside that [previous] rule so that this specific *ghañ* suffix occurs.

(1527) *nivāsacitiśarīropasamādhāneṣvādeśca kaḥ* |3|3|41|. Regarding the word *ākāya*: it is called *ākāya* because bricks (*iṣṭakā*) are piled up (*ācīyante*) in it; the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*).
One should pile (*cinvīta*), that is, one should produce by means of piling, the fire-altar (*agni*), specifically a particular location for the fire.
The meaning of the Śruti [is as follows]:

(1528) *saṅghe cānautarādharye* | [Pāṇini 2.4.2] "And in a collection (*saṅgha*), provided there is no relation of superior and inferior. Regarding the term *anautarādharya*: "superior" (*uttara*) and "inferior" (*adhara*) are *uttarādhara*; the state of these is *autarādharya*. [The negative prefix *na* applied here indicates the absence of that state.]

Regarding the priority and posteriority (*autarādharya*): "In the case of *sūkara*" (pig)—this is a counter-example; for when pigs lie down for the sake of suckling in a state of priority and posteriority, then this [rule] applies.
But when they remain separately, like mendicants (*bhikṣu*), then here too the suffix *ghañ* is used.

(1529) *karmavyatihāre ṇac striyām* |3|3|43|. In the sense of reciprocal action, the suffix *ṇac* is applied. Reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*) is the mutual exchange of actions; that is to say, performing an action for one another. The meaning is: [the suffix is applied] after a verbal root used in that sense. [This applies] in the abstract sense (*bhāve*).

Regarding the suffix *ṇa*: they say that it does not occur when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed [as the object of the action], because such a case is not expressed [by the rule]. As for what was stated by the ancients—that it occurs "after *hāvā* and so on"—that should be disregarded, because it contradicts the original sources (*ākaravirodhāt*). (1530) *ṇacaḥ striyāmañ* | Pāṇini 5.4.14.

*ṇac* [is applied] in the feminine. By this rule, it is indicated that the letter *ca* in the term *ṇac* is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*). Why "in the feminine"? [Observe: *vyatipākaḥ vartate*. (1531) *na karmavyatihāre* 7.3.6. [The suffix *ṇac* is not applied when there is a mutual exchange of action.]
"Not so," [he says]. By the prohibition of what would have been obtained through the rule "a yvābhyām," there is only the initial vṛddhi.

The point is that although the suffix *ṇac* is not a taddhita, the suffix *añ* is a taddhita. According to the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt* suffixes, since the verbal root with its prefix ends in *ṇac*, the suffix *añ* is applied after it.
With the intention that the augment *vṛddhi* applies to a prefix when preceded by such [roots], he provides the example: *vayāvakrośī*.

[The roots] *kruś* mean "to call out," and *has* means "to laugh. This might be argued: since this rule for *man* should be prescribed in the very section beginning with "striyāṃ ktin" (A 3.3.94), the word "striyām" (in the feminine) need not be stated here, which would result in greater brevity (*lāghava*).

If you say this is not so, it would follow that the prohibition of the *vā-sarūpa* rule (Pāṇini 3.1.94) would apply under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "in the feminine" (3.3.94). However, the form *vyāvakruṣṭiḥ* is desired. Furthermore, even the suffix *ktin* is sometimes desired in the domain of exceptions when referring to the feminine—e.g., *vyāvacorī*. Here, the suffix *yuc* (from Pāṇini 3.3.107: *ṇy-āsa-śrantho yuc*) would otherwise have applied. [In the case of] *vyātyakṣī*, here...

By the rule "urośca halaḥ," the suffix *a* would be applicable; however, in certain instances, only the suffix *a* is desired, and not *ṇac*. Thus, forms such as *vyatīkṣā* and *vyatīhā* result. Although this restriction is difficult to justify through formal logic (*nyāya*), it must be accepted on the basis of the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*).

(1532) *abhividhau bhāve inuṇ* || Pāṇini 3.3.44. Regarding "in the sense of *abhividhi*": what is the purpose of specifying "*abhividhi*" [in this rule]? [Consider the example: *saṃrāvaḥ*. By the principle of *vāsarūpa*, the suffixes *ghañ* and *kta* do not occur here, because of the repeated mention of the word "bhāva" [in the rule]. Nor is it for the sake of excluding other *kārakas* besides the agent (*kartṛ*).

It should be stated that there is no apprehension of the abstract state (*bhāva*), because—as in the previous sūtra—the suffix *inuṇ* does not apply due to the very nature of the verbal root's capacity (*śakti-svābhāvyāt*). However, co-occurrence with the suffix *lyuṭ* is desired, as in "saṃravaṇam" (the act of sounding together). And that [suffix] is obtained through the principle of "diversity" (*bāhulaka*), according to the authoritative source (*ākara*).
(1533) *aṇ-inuṇ-aḥ* |5|4|15|. Regarding *aṇ-inuṇ-aḥ*: it is implied that the *ṇānubandha* in *anuṇ* is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*).
As for *sāṃrāviṇam*: it means "sound on all sides. The prefix *sam-* indicates pervasion (*abhividhi*).

The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *parvavatsagatikādaṇ*. Because *aṇ* is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), there is vṛddhi of the first vowel. (1534) *ākrośe’vanyor grahaḥ* |3|3|45|. Regarding the word *ākrośe*: although [the suffix *ghañ*] would have applied by the rule *grahavṛdṛ*, this sūtra is commenced [to specify its application]. *Avagrahaḥ* means "of a word"; the meaning is a particular kind of division. *Nigrahaḥ* means restraint or suppression.

(1535) *pre lipsāyām* |3|3|46|. [The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *grah*] when preceded by *pra*, provided that the sense is "desire to obtain" (*lipsā*). When *nau* is an upapada, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *vṛñ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) and so forth. For example: *nīvārā kanyā*. (A girl who is "chosen by a boat.")

By the rule *‘raha-vṛdṛ’* etc., the suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). Now, one might object: since the object is qualified by femininity, the suffix *ktin* ought to apply because it is subsequent [to *ap*], according to the statement: *“In the case of feminine [objects], the suffixes *ṭha*, *ac*, and *ap* are superseded by *strī*, *khal*, and *ana* respectively.”* To this, he says:

It should be understood as masculine.
(1537) *raśmau ca* |3|3|53|. Also when it means a rein. A rope for the purpose of restraining horses yoked to a chariot and so forth is called *raśmi*.

In this [section] concerning the meanings to be expressed, when *pra* is the upapada, the suffix *ghañ* may optionally occur after the root *grah* in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and so forth.

*ud-grahaḥ*, *muṣṭi-grahaḥ*, *ava-grahaḥ* (in the sense of not crying out), *pari-grahaḥ* (in the sense of desire), and *anu-grahaḥ*.

In the *Yajñe* [section], regarding the prohibition of the suffix *varṣa*, there is the option (*vibhāṣā*) stated as *are vaṇijām* and so forth; immediately after the rule *arau bhuvo ’vajñāne*, the rule *āṅ rupluvoḥ* should have been placed, but it was not done in that way.

(1538) *vṛṇoter ācchādane* |3|3|54|. From the root *vṛ* [in the sense of covering]. [The example is] *prāvāraḥ* ("an outer garment"). [In this case], by the rule "the long vowel is substituted for the first syllable of a prefix before the suffix *ghañ*, provided it does not refer to a human being," there is a lengthening of the prefix. The meaning is "praised. (1539) *parau bhuvo’vajñāne* [Pāṇini 3.3.55]. [The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *bhū* when preceded by *pari* in the sense of contempt. *Paribhāvaḥ*. Amarasimha states: "Disregard, humiliation, *paribhava*, *parībhāva*, and insult (*tiraskriyā*)."
For since *kt* and *lyuṭ* would apply by virtue of their higher status, this [rule] results in a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
And thus, the maxim of "optionality due to dissimilarity" (*vā’sarūpa*) does not operate here, because it is not an exception (*anapavāda*). (1540) *erac* 3.3.56.

Regarding the word *varṣam*: since there is the usage in the Bhāṣya, "the bull (*vṛṣabhaḥ*) because of raining (*varṣaṇāt*"), the suffix *lyuṭ* is also applicable; thus, *varṣaṇam*. (1541) *ṛdorap* 3.3.57.
*Ṛdorap*: [The suffix] *ap* is applied after verbal roots ending in short *ṛ* or *u*. In the compound *añca-ucca*, there is neuter gender by Vedic usage (*sautra-puṃstva*).

The [suffix] in *ṭhaÑ-doḥ* does not have a *takāra*; rather, it has a *dakāra*. Because of the rule "after *iṇ* and *rabhi*, [the suffix] *ap* replaces *pūlvaḥ*" as an exception (*apavāda*) prescribing *ghan*, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the suffix *ap*] is applied even after roots with long vowels; thus he gives the example: *lavaḥ*.

Regarding *pava*: it is an exception (*apavāda*) to both the *ghañ* and *ac* suffixes. The distinction is that in the case of *iścaya*, there is the application of *ac*, whereas elsewhere there is *ghañ*. However, for the sense of "taking with the hand," *ghañ* is cited after the root *ci* preceded by *pra*.
(1542) Pāṇini 3.3.58: *grahavṛdṛniścigamaśca*.

Regarding the rule *vaśiraṇyor iti*: this is a statement made because the suffix *ghañ* would otherwise have applied. *Vaśa* means "the act of ruling" (*vaśanam*). *Raṇaḥ* means "battle," as in that wherein they "sound" (*raṇanti*) or make noise. (1543) *Ghañapoś ca* | Pāṇini 2.4.38.
*Vighasa* is that which is specifically chewed or eaten; it refers to the food remaining after the *vaiśvadeva* offering.
*Ghāsa* is the fodder for quadrupeds. Amarasimha states: "Tender grass is called *ghāsa*.
(Pāṇini 3.3.61: *vyadhajaporanupasarge*).

*Upajāpa* means the divulging of secret counsel (*mantrabheda*). Regarding the term *svāna*, Amarasimha states: "The words *abda*, *nināda*, *ninada*, *dhvani*, *dvan*, *rava*, *svana*, and *kvaṇa* [denote sound].
(1545) Furthermore, by Pāṇini 3.3.65, *kvaṇa* is used in the sense of the lute (*vīṇā*) as well.
*Kvaṇa*, *ikvāṇa*, *nikvaṇa*, *kvāṇa*, *kvaṇa*, and *kvaṇana*—these terms denote the sounding of a lute (*vīṇā*). With prefixes, such as *pra-kvāṇa* and *pra-kvaṇa* are also used. Thus says Amara.
(1546) [The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *mad* when no prefix is present. Pāṇini 3.3.67.
*Mada*: When a *sup*-ending word is present as an upapada and there is no prefix (*anupasarga*), the suffix *ap* is invariably used for the formation of abstract nouns (*bhāva*) and the like.

(1547) *Pramada-sammadau harṣe* (Pāṇini 3.3.68): *pramada* and *saṃmada* [are formed with *ap*] when meaning "joy. However, it is not stated that [the suffix *ap* is used] after *pra* and *sam* when meaning "joy" [in general], as in *prasaṃmadaḥ* and *saṃpramadaḥ*.
"Let there be no joy.

(1548) *prajane sarteḥ* |3|3|71|. Regarding *prajane sarteḥ*: *prajana* means procreation (*prajanana*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), according to the rule *ani-vadhyoḥ*.

The prohibition of reduplication [is stated]. Due to the force of the prefix *pra*, there is here a different meaning from that of the root *jan* (to be born), just as in the case of *pratiṣṭhate*, where it means "manifestation. This is what he says: "the mention of 'first' and 'womb'. This was stated in accordance with the *Kāśikā*; however, there is no insistence on whether it be the first or the second [occurrence].
Others say it means "conception" (*garbhagrahaṇa*).
(1549) *hanaśca vadhaḥ* | 3|3|76|.
Regarding *hanaśca vadhaḥ*: it is stated that [the word] is oxytone (*antodātta*). In the sūtra, the word *vadha* is pronounced as being oxytone.
Thus ends the section on bhāva [derivatives].
(1550) *agāraikadeśe praghaṇaḥ praghāṇaśca* |3|3|79|. Regarding *agāraika*: “*praghāṇa-praghaṇa* refers to the *alinda*, the porch outside the door,” according to Amara.

(1551) *saṅghoddhau gaṇapraśaṃsayoḥ* |3|3|86|. Regarding *saṅgha* and *uddha*: "The words *atallikā*, *macarcikā*, *prakāṇḍa*, *udgha*, and *tallaja* are synonyms for that which is praiseworthy (*praśasta*)," according to Amara.

(1552) *ḍvitaḥ kriḥ* | Pāṇini 3.3.88. Regarding *ḍvitaḥ*: this [refers to the suffix *kri*]. For this very reason, one analyzes [the compound] as *pākena nirvṛtam* ("accomplished by cooking"), and not as *pakvena* ("by the cooked").

As for what was stated by the ancients—that it occurs "in the sense of 'calling' (*hāva*) and 'taking' (*ādāna*)"—the intention is that this is not so. [The suffix *kri* denotes] the object (*karman*).

This has been explained among the *taddhita* suffixes. Regarding the mention of "always" (*nitya*), there the rule is divided as "always" (*nityam*); by the force of that [separation], the scope of the suffix *maP* is determined regardless of any specific meaning.
However, if it were a single unified rule, [the suffix would apply] only when [the word] is derived (*nirvṛta*).

The sense is that, due to this governing rule (*adhikāra*), if the meaning of "accomplished" (*nirvṛta*) were not intended to be expressed, independence (*svātantrya*) would result; consequently, the usage *pakri* would occur even without the suffix *map*. Regarding *uptrimam*:

because the root *vapi* belongs to the class beginning with *yaj*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) before a *kit* suffix. The meaning is "that which has been accomplished by sowing" (*vāpena nirvṛtam*).

(1553) *yaj-yāc-yata-viccha-praccha-rakṣaḥ naṅ* 3.3.90. The roots *yaj*, *yāc*, *yat*, *vicch*, *pracch*, and *rakṣ* take the suffix *naṅ*. The phrase "in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or a factor other than the agent (*akartari kārake*)" is understood to carry over from the previous rule. For this very reason, in the passage "By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice" (*yajñena yajñam ayajanta devāḥ*), commentators explain that *yajña* is derived from the root *yaj* with the suffix *naṅ*, meaning "that which is sacrificed to" (*ijyate*). [It is called *viśna*.]
By the rule *‘chavoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca’*, *ś* is substituted for *ch*.
(1554) *Upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* |3|3|92|.

When a prefix (*upasarga*) is present, the suffix *ki* is added after a root ending in *ghu*. Mādhava states that by virtue of its frequent occurrence (*bāhulaka*), it is also used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). For this very reason, [the form] *upa-u-*...

They explain that an *upādhi* is so called because it places its own property (*svadharma*) in proximity; the elision of the long vowel *ā* occurs because of the suffix *kit*. Regarding the word *antardhi*:

its status as a prefix (*upasarga*) is established by the Vārttika rule, "The word *antar* [is a prefix] in the application of suffixes beginning with *aṅ* and *kit*. [The term *upādhi* is derived from] "that by which something is placed near" (*upādhīyate’neneti*); by this, the root *upa-u* [in the sense of] "nearby" is indicated.

The term *upādhi* means "that which bestows its own nature" (*svadharmam ādadhāti*). It has been implied that the statement in the works of Mādhava and others—that the suffix *ki* occurs in the sense of the agent by virtue of the rule *bāhulakāt*—is not to be respected. Furthermore, in the case of the expression *vidhātā viśvasṛḍvidhiḥ*, let there not be the suffix *ki* in the sense of the agent; rather, [the root is] *vidha* in the sense of "arranging" (*vidhāne*).
Thus, the form is established by [Pāṇini 3.1.135] *ig-upadhāt kit*, which prescribes the *kit* suffix.
(1555) *striyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94): "The suffix *ktin* is used in the feminine. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ghañ*. As for those who, while explaining the *prakriyā* text...
They say: "In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated that 'the suffix -ka- [is used] when there is an additional meaning,' and thus the suffix -ghañ is also cited.

This is due to haste; for one should understand that in that instance, the meaning is not a state (*bhāva*) qualified by femininity, but rather one qualified by masculinity. As for the suffixes -ac and -ap, their scope is, for example, *cayaḥ*.

Lava: Regarding the absence of the suffix *ktin*—[examples are] *kṛtiḥ* and *hṛtiḥ*. However, in the case of the roots *ci* and *stu*, when both [suffixes, *ktin* and *a*] are applicable for feminine nouns, the meaning is that *ktin* prevails due to its higher priority. [This is an error; the intention is that since the rule "for the root *phi*, there is *sphī* in the *niṣṭhā*" prescribes the change to *sphī* specifically in the *niṣṭhā* suffix, [the form *citā* would be expected instead].]
Regarding *śruyajīti*: because [the suffix] *lyuṭ* would otherwise apply by the rule "after [roots ending in] *araṇ* and *adhikaraṇa*," this statement is made.

*Śrutiḥ* means the ear (*śrotra*). Regarding *yajeḥ*: from the root *yaji*, with the suffix *ktin*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "of *vac*, *svap*, etc.," and the change to *ṣ* by the rule "of *vraśc*, *bhrasj*, etc.," resulting in the form *iṣṭiḥ*. It is that by which one sacrifices (*ijyate*).

[The suffix] *ghañ* is applied: thus, that by which one desires is called *iṣṭi*; that by which one praises is called *stuti*. In these cases, there is no substitution of *n* for *t*. However, in words such as *kīrṇi*, the substitution of *n* occurs by the rule *ṛdābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.2.42]; whereas in words such as *lūni*, it occurs by the rule *lvādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.44]. This is the distinction. [The word] *hlāda*.

The meaning is: "in the case of [the rule] *ṭhhlādo niṣṭhāyām*. Regarding *cūrti*: by the rule *i ca*, there is the substitution of *u* for *car* and *phal*; then, by the rule *ṛtvor upadhāyā dīrghaḥ*, there is lengthening of the vowel. Regarding *cāyateḥ*: the root *cāyṛ* means "to honor" and "to observe. Regarding *ktinn api*: because of the prohibition [by the rule] *na striyām*, it does not occur in the feminine.
This was stated because the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) is not set aside [by the subsequent rule].
[Pāṇini 3.3.95] states: "After the roots *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, and *pac*, the suffix *aṅ* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṅ*. According to the principle of the priority of exceptions (*purastādapavādanyāya*), this applies to the roots *sthā* and the others [before the application of Pāṇini 3.3.106, which prescribes the suffix *a* after roots ending in long *ā* when preceded by a prefix].

Thus, the meaning is that while the suffix *aṅ*—which would otherwise be obtained by the rule "from *idam*, *bhid*, and so forth"—is set aside, it is not so for the suffixes *ṇvul* and *iñ*. However, *ṇvul* and *iñ* do indeed occur because they are subsequent [rules]. This is evident from the usage of the Bhāṣyakāra: "āṃ tvaṃ sthāyikāṃ, kāṃ tvaṃ sthāyim. As for the form *prasthatiḥ*: [it is derived with the suffix *ktin*].
In *yatiṣyati* and *māsthā*, the substitution of *ī* for *ā* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.66]. In *saṅgītiḥ*, the substitution of *ī* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.65], starting with the rule *humāsthe*.

(1557) *Ūti-yūti-jūti-sāti-heti-kīrtayaś ca*: [The feminine suffix *ktin* is applied after the roots *av*, *yu*, *ju*, *so*, *han*, and *kṛ*, and the resulting forms are *ūti*, *yūti*, *jūti*, *sāti*, *heti*, and *kīrti* respectively.]

“*udāta* (acute)” means that it follows from the rule *antre vṛṣeṣe*. Thus, since the acute accent on the initial syllable would otherwise apply to a word ending in *ktin*, the resulting meaning is that words such as *ūti*, *yūti*, and so forth, are acute-accented on the final syllable. “The absence of *it*” means the absence of the *it* augment that would have applied by the rule *yatisyatī*.

This is the meaning. Regarding the word *hanter*: it should be understood that there is an *it* (vocalization) of the *n* in the root *han*, whereas for the root *hinoti* (from *hi*), there is *guṇa*. Regarding *kīrti*: although the suffix *yuc* would have applied by the rule "after roots ending in *ṇi*, *ās*, and *śranth*" (*ṇyāsaśranthe*), the suffix *ktin* is irregularly prescribed (*nipātita*), as well as its acute accent (*udāttatva*). Example: *āṃ sute kīrtim*.

(1558) *vraja-yajoḥ bhāve kyap* ||3.3.98|| [The suffix] *kyap* is applied after the roots *vraj* and *yaj* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). The condition "having an udātta vowel" applies here as well. However, the inclusion of the marker *p* is for the sake of the subsequent rule. (1559) *saṃjñāyāṃ samaja-niṣada-nipata-mana-vida-ṣuñ-śīṅ-bhṛñ-iṇaḥ* ||3.3.99|| [The suffix *kyap* is applied] after the roots *samaja*, *niṣad*, *nipat*, *man*, *vid*, *ṣuñ*, *śīṅ*, *bhṛñ*, and *iṇ* when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be formed.

"By the side of the neck" (galapārśve): the sense is that by this [mark], she is known to be angry. "Bed" (śayyā) is so called because one lies upon it. "Maintenance" (bharaṇa) refers to service (bhṛtyā), that is, a livelihood. According to the *Hārāvalī*: "The term 'umārabhṛtyā' denotes the nursing of a pregnant woman."

"‘[The word] is governed by [the rule for] *umāra*, *mṛtyu*, and *akuśala*,' says the *Raghu* [commentary]. Why [is the condition] ‘in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*)’ stated? [Consider: *matiḥ*, *bhṛtiḥ*, *āsutiḥ*. And thus it has been employed [in the sūtras]: ‘after [roots] meaning intellect (*mati*), understanding (*buddhi*), and honor (*pūjā*), [the suffix] *ka* is added'; ‘in the sense of wages (*bhṛti*) after the root *bhṛ*; ‘[the suffix] *ktin* after *raj*, *kṛṣ*, and *āsū*,’ and so forth. By this..."
By the very application of the sūtra "atibuddhi" and others, the correctness of words such as *mati* and *bhṛti* is established;
thus, the argument of Durghaṭavṛtti and others is refuted.
(1560) Pāṇini 3.3.100: "And [the suffix] *śa* after the root *kṛ*."

Regarding the term *kriyā*: when it refers to the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), then the suffix *yak* is applied by the rule *ārdhadhātuke yak*. By the rule *ṭhriḥ śayagliṅkṣu*, there is the substitution of *ṛiṅ*.
