In other cases, however, even in the absence of *yak*, once the substitution of *ṛiṅ* has been made before the suffix *śe*, the form is identical as *iyaṅ* due to the presence of *si*.

(1561) *icchā* |3|3|101|. The term *icchā* [is derived] from the root *iṣ* in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*). The meaning is that it is not used even for a non-agentive *kāraka*. For this very reason, it was previously stated that in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), [the form] *iṣṭiḥ* is used, as in "that by which one desires" (*iṣyate'nayā*). Regarding the removal of the letter *y*: [this occurs because the suffix] begins with a consonant (*halādiḥ*).
But there is no remainder [of the definition], because the designation *abhyāsa* (reduplication) is accepted only when there is a sixth [element] or when there are two verbal roots;
and here, neither of those two conditions exists—this is the intended meaning. Regarding *aṭāṭya*:
when the suffix *ap* is added to the root *aṭ* after it has undergone *yaṅ*-intensive reduplication, then, upon the elision of the *a* by the rule *ato lopaḥ*, the rule *yasya halaḥ* applies.

When *y* is elided, the forms *aṭāṭa* and *aṭeti* are to be understood; for when there is reduplication and the application of *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, the rule *dīrgho’kitaḥ* causes the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable. Regarding *jāgarti*: after the suffix *śa*, *yak* is added by the rule *ārdhadhātuke yak*; then, by the rule *āto ṅkiti ca*, *guṇa* substitution occurs.

(1562) *gurośca halaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.3.103. Regarding *gurośca*: by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *dhātoḥ* (from the previous rule) and its application as a qualifier for *hal*, the rule *halantaḥ* (ending in a consonant) is obtained through the principle of *tadantavidhi* (specification of that which ends in). And this [consonant]...
The term "guru" is possible [as a bahuvrīhi compound]. For "guru" refers to a vowel (*aj*), and thus it indicates the sense of possession (*matvartha*).

This is what he says: "of that which possesses a guru [vowel]" (*gurumataḥ*). Now, one might object: let the opposite be the case, namely, "a *hal* [consonant] ending in a *gu* [long vowel]," since there exist such verbal roots as *ḍukrīñ* and others; but this is not so.

Because of the rule "in the sense of wishing for that which has not yet occurred" (*eṣṭāyām anadhvani*) and the indication "as if it were already past in the sense of wishing" (*āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca*), no contrary doubt arises.
[Pāṇini 3.3.104: *ṣidbhidādibhyo ’ṅ*.

[The root] *ṣidbhidā* [is used]. How then is it that Māgha says "ukhābjagandhalabdheḥ" and Amara says "rekṣopalabdhiḥ"? Since [the root] is marked with *ṣit*, the suffix *aṅ* should apply, and thus "ibhe" alone would have been appropriate.
True. [However, there is the rule: "But those [roots] which are meaningless [are treated as such] when not perceived according to each individual letter."

The suffix *ktin* should also be understood [as applicable] due to its usage in the Bhāṣya or by virtue of the rule of "occurrence in abundance" (*bāhulaka*). The detailed explanation here should be sought in the *Manoramā*. Regarding *bhidā* and so forth: such forms ending in long *ā* are listed in the Gaṇapāṭha as complete words; among them, those which constitute the verbal roots, such as *bhid*, *chid*, and others, are included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).

These have been specified in the Sūtra. However, the specific reading in the *Gaṇapāṭha* is for the purpose of including certain meanings well-known in common usage that do not otherwise fall under the scope of technical grammatical operations (*alākṣaṇika-kārya*). Regarding *bhitti*: it is called *bhitti* because it is split (*bhidyate*), as in a wall (*kuḍya*). Regarding *ccheda*: this refers specifically to the act of splitting into two; however, elsewhere—

*Chiti* means a hole (*chidra*). *Mṛja* [is derived from] *bhṛjū*, which means purification; it is listed in the *Bhidādi* group because it does not end in *ṣ*. (1564) *Cintipūjikathikumbicarcaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.105).
In *cintipūji*, the *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been mentioned; by this, *tulā* is formed from the root *tolayati*.
Haradatta [comments]: For this very reason, the author of the *Naiṣadha* says, "When he ascended the elephant with Dantavakra.

[The phrase] "an exception to *yuC*" means it is an exception to what will be stated in the rule *ṇyāsaśranthe* [Pāṇini 3.3.107]. (1565) *ṇyāsaśrantho yuc* | 3.3.107 | [The suffix] *yuc* [is applied after roots ending in] *ṇi*, *ās*, and *śranth*.

Regarding *āsana*: the analysis of the compound is "that in which one sits" (*āsyate asyām*). By the rule *ṛ-halor ṇyat*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, resulting in *āsya*. One should not suspect that the irregular formation rule (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply in the case of feminine suffixes; for although the exception (*apavāda*), namely *yuc*, occurs in the section on feminine suffixes, the general rule (*utsarga*), namely *ṇyat*, does not. [This applies to] the roots *ghaṭṭi* and *vandī*.
The root *vid* is taken here in the sense of "acquisition"; however, when it has the sense of "knowledge," the form is *saṃvit*. Regarding the root *iṣ*:

the suffix *yuc* is applied when it does not mean "desire"; but when it means "desire," as in the case of the root *iṣ*, the form is simply *icchā*. (Pāṇini 3.3.108) The suffix *ṇvul* is frequently applied after a verbal root to denote a disease.

The suffix *ṇvul* is frequently applied to verbal roots to form names of diseases; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to suffixes such as *ktin*. For example: *pracchardikā* (vomiting), from the root *charda* meaning "to vomit. *Pravāhikā* (diarrhea):
it is called *pravāhikā* because it causes one to flow out repeatedly (*pravāhayati*), that is, it causes frequent discharge; it refers to the *grahaṇī* (the digestive tract).

Regarding *vicarcikā*: the root *carc* means "to study. The understanding of it as a disease arises from the prefix and the suffix. Amara states: "Āma, pāmā, and vicarcikā [are types of skin diseases]. Regarding *śirorti*: it is pain in the head. The root *ard* means "to injure. By the rule *itutre*, there is no *iṭ* augment. This is a designation of the meaning of the verbal root; that is, a designation of the action.

This is the meaning. *āsikā* and *śāyikā* mean "sitting" and "lying down," respectively. [The suffixes] *ik* and *tip* are used for the indication of verbal roots—that is, for their citation-form (*anukaraṇa*). Because the word *bahulam* ("in various ways") is understood from the previous rule, [the suffixes] are not applied in some cases, as in *upti*, *jik*, *it*, and *kid* with the suffix *san*, or *hu* with the augment *vuk* in the *luṅ* and *liṭ* tenses. [An example is] *pacati*.

Based on such indications as *ṭhupasargātsunoti suvatisyati-hyāyateḥ saṃprasāraṇam ca*, the suffixes *śap* and others are applied even when a *sārvadhātuka* [suffix] follows that does not denote an agent (*akartṛvācin*). Likewise,
the suffix *yak* is sometimes applied even when a *sārvadhātuka* denotes the action itself (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), as in the rule *vibhāṣā līyateḥ*.
For instance, it has been stated there: "The mention [of the root] is in the form *īḷiṅ* with *ya*, but not in the case of *śyan*.
As for what the ancients said—"By the force of the *śit* suffix in *tiP*, *śap* and the others [are excluded]"—that is not correct;
because in forms such as *pibati* and *glāyati*, the substitutes *piba-* and so on would apply, and the substitution of *āt* (for *a*) would be precluded.

Because the purpose of the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.69] has already been fulfilled. "From a phoneme" (varṇāt) means "from an imitation of a phoneme," and not "from a phoneme being uttered. For if that were the case, the rule would apply only in instances such as *satyakāraḥ*, but not in cases such as *kakāraḥ*, because here a composite (*saṅghāta*) is being uttered. However, the object of imitation (*anukārya*) here is...

It is merely the phoneme; it also arises from a cluster beginning with the letter *a*, as indicated by the sūtra: "The *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is at a higher pitch. Furthermore, all instances of the suffix *-kāra* are rejected based on the usage in the Bhāṣya and because of the frequent use of the term *bahulam*. In this context, regarding the suffix *-kāra*:

Although [the suffix] is not prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), it receives the designation *kṛt* because it occurs after the initial vowel of a verbal root; therefore, by virtue of ending in a *kṛt* suffix, it acquires the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Due to the absence of any purpose, the letter *k* does not receive the designation *it*.
Because it lacks the status of an *ārddhadhātuka*, the augment *iṭ* does not apply. However, in rules such as "ṭhasya cvau" (Pāṇini 7.4.32), etc.,...

The absence of the *kāra* suffix occurs precisely due to the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*). [In the case of *rapha*,] *pha* is substituted for *ra*; by the rule of "optionality when forms are dissimilar" (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*), *kāra* may also be used. Therefore, such usage as "O Pārvatī, for me who hears names beginning with the letter *ṛ*" is indeed grammatically correct. Regarding the elision of the vowel *a*: this is because [the following element] is neither a *taddhita* suffix nor a *bha* stem.

The sense is that there is no application of the elision (*lopa*) for the word *yasya*. Here, the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), which is obtained because it ends in a *kṛt* suffix, should be understood as before. In the rule *asau matvarthe*, the suffix *cha* does not apply due to the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*).
However, in the rule *aiṣakānmatubarthīyāt*, the suffix *cha* is indeed applied after the word *matubartha* precisely because of *bāhulaka*.

Others, however, say that this is not a *kṛt*-derived form; rather, having analyzed it as *bhava* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), they claim it is a *taddhita*-derived form ending in the suffix *cha* because it belongs to the *gaha*-class. [The suffix] *iṇac*: this is an exception to the *ṇvul* suffix which would otherwise apply when indicating the meaning of a verbal root. The same applies to *ājiri*. Regarding *ājiri*, by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), there is the substitution of *vī* for the root *aj*.
Not so;

[the suffix is used] when it is a name (*saṃjñā*). 3.3.109. Regarding "when it is a name": this rule is commenced to provide for the sense of the locative case (*adhikaraṇa*) by means of the suffix *ṇvul*. For example: *uddālakaḥ* (the *uddālaka* tree), *śleṣmātakaḥ* (the *śleṣmātaka* tree).

That action in which its flowers are broken is called *bhañjikā*; "breaking" (*bhañjana*) is the same as *bhañjikā*, formed with the suffix *ṇvul* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). Others say it means "the breaking of *uddālaka* flowers.
In the sūtra, although the word *ākhyāna* should have been placed first because it has fewer syllables, [the order] was changed for the sake of the explanation (*vyākhyāna*).

He explains by following the sequence of meanings obtained through the preceding questions: "In [the senses of] questioning, narration, and so forth" (1568). [The suffix] *ṇvuc* [is applied] in the senses of turn (*paryāya*), honoring (*arhaṇa*), and origin (*utpatti*). (Pāṇini 3.3.111).

Regarding the word *paripāṭī*: [it is derived from] the root *paṭ* in the sense of "going," preceded by *pari*. The suffix *iṇ* is applied according to the rule *ṭhiṇajādibhyaḥ*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *ṛdikārāt*.
(Pāṇini 3.3.112) *Ākrośe nañyaniḥ*: [The suffix *yani* is applied after the prefix *nañ* when expressing an abuse.]

Regarding *ākrośe*: *ākrośaḥ* means a curse (*śāpaḥ*). The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) in the neuter gender. Now, one might object: since it is established by the rule "the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal*-affixes denote both the abstract state and the object" (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*)—applying universally across all three genders—that the *kta* suffix is already established for the neuter abstract state, what is the purpose of this [separate rule]?

If it is argued that this is due to a different rule (*punarvidhāna*), they say here: with reference to the word "having called" (*hūte*), the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) for the *kta* suffix prescribed by the rule *iṣṭhā* is [restricted] by the rule *ayoreva*;
however, by this [present] rule, the *kta* suffix is prescribed in the neuter gender for the abstract state in general time (*kālasāmānya*). And thus...

Because [the suffix] *ghañ* is a sublater (*bādhaka*) of *ap* due to its higher status within its own domain, it follows by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that these [suffixes] have the masculine as their scope. Furthermore, since the rule "and after intransitive roots" (*hāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*) is not present here, this [suffix] occurs even after transitive roots, just like *ghañ* and the others. Thus...

This is seen in such passages as *tiriścīnam anūrusāratheḥ*. Thus, there is no doubt in this matter. [Objection: But in that case, when used in conjunction with a *kṛt* suffix, the accusative would be required for the object, because the genitive—which is prescribed by the rule governing connection with a *kṛt*—is prohibited by the rule *a loke*. And so, [one would have to say] *haṭhaṃ kṛtam*.

[Otherwise,] such constructions as *vṛkṣaṃ bhinnaṃ* ("the tree [is] split") would result [as improper]. However, in the case of *anūrusārathi* ("one whose charioteer is not Urvaśī"), it might be argued that a third-case ending for the agent (*kartari tṛtīyā*) does not apply; for even though the use of the sixth case is prohibited when a specific *kāraka* relation is intended, a sixth case can still occur by intending it as a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*). But this is not so, because [the prohibition applies specifically] to the use of the sixth case in connection with a *kta*-suffix used in the neuter sense of an abstract action (*napuṃsake bhāve*).

If it is argued that this Vārttika was rejected in the original treatise (*ākara*) by relying on the intention to express [the object] as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*), because the second case ending does not apply to the object (*karman*) due to its being specifically enumerated [in the rules], then, by virtue of that authority, let it be accepted that the intention is generally to express it as a remainder;
thus, this Vārttika was rejected in the original treatise. If [you say] so, then...

Let it be that, by virtue of its authority, there is generally only the intention to express subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*). And thus, [the objection] such as "the act has been performed" (*kṛtaṃ haṭham*) does not apply at all. In some cases, however, even the accusative case is seen, as in:
"He traversed a region difficult with many forts" (*hrāntaṃ deśamanekadurgaviṣamam*); this is the general direction.

(1570) *karmaṇi ca yena saṃsparśāt kartuḥ śarīrasukham* | 3|3|116| [The rule] *karmaṇi ca*: the word "kartuḥ" (*of the agent*) is in the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), according to the restriction [Pāṇini 2.3.66]: *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*. The word *yena* is in the instrumental case. Thus he says: "by which, when touched, there is bodily pleasure for the agent."

"The suffix *lyuṭ* should occur"—this should be understood as referring to the neuter gender in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). For this very reason, he says "by the preceding [rule]"; the meaning is: by the rule "and *yuṭ*" (*yuṭ ca*). "Not here" means that even though the teacher is the agent of the act of bathing, he is not the agent of the causative act of bathing (*snāpana*), but rather the student is. Why is the mention of "the body" (*śarīra*) made?
The embrace of one's son is happiness; here there is mental pleasure. (1571) *karaṇādhikaraṇayośca* |3|3|117|.

[The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied] in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). By the principle of "that which is not otherwise obtained" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), [the suffix applies specifically to these two].

This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ghañ*; it supersedes the feminine suffixes *a*, *jap*, and others because it is of higher priority. For it has been said: "The feminine suffixes *strī*, *khal*, and *na* [supersede] *ṭha* and *ac*; *khal* and *na* [supersede] the feminine suffix *strī* by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
Regarding *idhma*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that by which fuel-sticks (*idhmāni*) are cut" and "that in which a cow is milked."

(1572) *chāder ghe ’dvyupasargasya* | Pāṇini 6.4.96. [The long vowel is substituted for the final of *chādi* before a word ending in *gha*, provided it is not preceded by two prefixes. Thus: *ākurvanti* ("they perform here"). Because they come (*etya*) and carry out their business (*kurvanti*) in this place, it is called an *ākara*, meaning a source or place of origin. (1573) *ave tṛsror ghañ* | Pāṇini 3.3.120. [The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the roots *tṛ* and *sṛ* when preceded by the prefix *ava*.]

When *ava* is the preceding word (*upapada*), the suffix *ghañ* shall be applied after the roots *tṛ* and *stṛ* in the masculine, when denoting an instrument (*karaṇa*) or a location (*adhikaraṇa*), provided it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). This is an exception to [the application of] *ap*.
(1574) *adhyāya*, *nyāya*, *udyāva*, and *saṃhāra* [are also formed with *ghañ*]. 3.3.122.

Regarding "avahāra" and so forth: the author of the Vṛtti, however, having inserted the words *ādhāra* and *āvāya* into the sūtra, included the word *avahāra* by means of the particle *ca*; that is clearly incoherent. (1575) *udaṅko ’nudake* || 3.3.123 ||

Since the form *udaṅka* is already established by the rule *halaśca*, this [sūtra] is for the purpose of prohibiting *udaka*. In the case of *udakodañcana*, although the suffix *gha* would have been expected by the rule *usi saṃjñāyām*, the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed instead. If it is argued that since *ghañ* is prohibited in the sense of *udaka*, only *gha* should apply and not *lyuṭ*, this is not so.

By the force of the prohibition, *ha* also does not apply; for here there is no difference in form whether [the suffix] *gha* or *ghañ* is used, nor is there a difference in accent: if *gha* were present, the final syllable would be udātta by the rule for the original accent of the second member of a kṛt-derivative compound, whereas with *ghañ*, it would be so by the rule for *thā-thādi* compounds.
"Likewise.

(1576) *jālam ānāyaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.3.124. *Jāla* is derived from the root *jāl* (meaning "to weave" or "to spread") with the suffix *ṇa*, according to the rule *jvalitikasantebhyo ṇaḥ*. Thus, it means a net.
*Ānāya* is derived from the root *ā-nī* (meaning "to bring") with the same suffix *ṇa*; it means a snare or net. Both refer to a net.
The word *jālamāśa* is established [by this rule]. Therefore, one should not be mistaken into thinking that the word *jāla* itself is being introduced here as an irregular form (*nipātana*).

(1577) *khano gha ca* | Pāṇini 3.3.125. Regarding the statement "the suffix *gha* is added after the root *khan*": the addition of the marker *g* is for the purpose of [triggering] the substitution of *ku* by the rule *ajó ’ghnyāyām* in forms such as *ākhana*.

The intended meaning is that there is no possibility [of such an objection]. Regarding *bhaga* and *pada*: if it is asked what the purpose of the suffix *gha* is in the word *pada*, they say here: if *gha* were used according to the rules "in the sense of locus" (*araṇādhikaraṇayoḥ*) or "in the case of a name" (*uṃsi saṃjñāyām*), then the neuter form *ada* would not occur.
If it is established by this [rule], then there is the attainment of the desired result. "These" means the six beginning with *ākhan* (digging), etc.

(Pāṇini 3.3.126): *īṣad-duḥ-su-ṣu kṛcchrā-kṛcchrārtheṣu khal*. [The suffix *khal* is used after a verbal root when the prefixes *īṣat*, *duḥ*, or *su* signify difficulty (*kṛcchra*) or ease (*akṛcchra*).]

In the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu*, although the terms are stated in a general sense, the specific distribution of their domains is obtained by the force of their inherent compatibility. Here, *dur* has the meaning of "difficulty" (*kṛcchra*), while the other two have the meaning of "non-difficulty.
He demonstrates this with the words "in difficulty, difficult to perform," and so forth, ending with "it occurs."

In the phrase *a loke*, because the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is prohibited, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the agent (*kartṛ*). Why [is it said] "in *kaccha*, etc."? [Answer: *īṣatkāryam* (an easy task). The meaning is "a very small task. Regarding *khal*: the letter *l* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*), while the inclusion of the *kh* is for the purpose of elision (*mum*) in what follows. In *nimimīti*: [this refers to the rule] "of the roots *īṅ*, *āp*, *mī*, *min*, and *dīṅ*..."

Furthermore, although the rule "vibhāṣā līyateḥ" would have applied [to allow the suffix *yat*], it is here prohibited. [The examples] such as *nimaya* and so forth are formed with the suffix *erac*. Since the form would have been established by the rule "upasargāt khal-ghañoh" alone, he states that this [present rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), saying: "only after a prefix."
(1579) *na sudurbhyāṃ kevalābhyām* |7|1|68|. When *su* and *ati* [are used],— as in the case of *uḥ pūjāyām* and *ati atikramaṇe ca*— these two possess the status of *karmapravacanīya*.
(1580) *kartṛkarmaṇośca bhṛkṛñoḥ* |3|3|127|.

[The word] *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* [is part of the rule]. The particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of conjunction (*saṃniyoga*). When there is simultaneous usage of both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), as well as words such as *īṣat* and so forth, only then does the suffix [occur], as follows.
It might be argued: "Let it be that the agent and the object are indeed the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), and not the *upapada* (governing word). This should not be said;

for if only words such as *īṣat* were considered *upapadas*, then the fact that the suffix *khal* is marked with the letter *k* would be rendered purposeless. That marker *k* is intended for the purpose of the *mum* augment; and the *mum* augment is prescribed only for non-indeclinables (*anavyaya*).

Therefore, in the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*, [the words] are indeed only *upapadas*. This is what he states: "and in the case of *īṣat* and so forth. There are two [words], *kartṛ* and *karman*, and two [roots], *bhū* and *kṛ*; a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*) between them was obtained and accepted by the author of the Kāśikā, as well as by Haradatta, the author of the Padamañjarī, and others.

The same has been stated by the ancient [commentator] and approved by his commentators; all of that should not be respected, as it contradicts the Bhāṣya on the *yathāsaṅkhya* sūtra. Indicating this, he says:
"the correspondence of order (*yathāsaṅkhya*) is not intended. Now, an objection: "Is there not a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority between two subordinate words (*upapada*)?"

It is not established; for the separation of the parts [of the prefix] from the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) is desired only in the case of the roots *bhū* and *kṛ*, but not in the case of words such as *īṣat*. If it is asked, "In that case, how is the desired restriction established here?", they reply:
the desired restriction is established by the continued application of the term *bahulam* (diversely) and by the example from the Bhāṣya: *durāḍhaḷmbhavaḥ*.
"It is accomplished. Having this in mind, he says: "And when the agent and the object [are both expressed].

He gives an example for the agent (*kartṛ*) of the root *bhū*: "by one who is not wealthy, by one who becomes wealthy. But for the object (*karman*), the analysis is: "the non-wealthy person is made wealthy" (*anāḍhya āḍhyo bhūyate*).
Its meaning is "he is caused to become" (*bhāvyate*). The same applies hereafter as well.

Two analyses are to be inferred: [the first is] "it is done by itself, without being prompted," and [the second is] "one who was not prompted becomes prompted; it is made to become prompted. (1581) *āto yuc* | Pāṇini 3.3.128.
Regarding the phrase "ityādi" (and so forth): by the word "ādi," [the following are included]: *durdarśanaḥ*, *durdharṣaṇaḥ*, *durmarṣaṇaḥ*.
(1582) *kticktau ca saṃjñāyām* |3|3|174|. The suffixes *ktic* and *kta*. The *ca* in *ktic-ca* is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] as "not *ktic*" (*na ktic*). "Not *ktvā*" (*na ktvā*).

The point is that if [the suffix] *kta* were mentioned [without the marker *i*], there would be the inclusion of *ktin* as well; however, Haradatta maintains that the exclusion of *ktin* is established by the paribhāṣā regarding [suffixes] with a single *anubandha*. As for what they say—that the letter *c* in the rule *titutratatha...* is for the sake of including the general term—otherwise...

Because it has only one indicatory letter (*ekānubandha*), only this [suffix] would be grasped and not the *ktin* suffix; however, due to that haste, since the form qualified by an indicatory letter is not explicitly mentioned in the rule "itutre" (*Pāṇini 7.2.37*), the paribhāṣā concerning that which has only one indicatory letter [does not apply].

Because the very possibility of such an expression does not exist. By this, the doubt that "in the rule *itutre*, only that [root] with a single *anubandha* is understood and not this *ktic*, and consequently the form *rodati* would not occur," is also refuted. As for the word *bhūti*: although here, by virtue of [the subsequent rule being] more powerful...
Although the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "ṛt-śyukaḥ kiti" alone is more logical, nevertheless,
because it is necessary for the purpose of prohibiting *iṭ* after [roots ending in] *vant* and *tanti*, and because there is no difference in the resulting form,
the rule "it-tu-re" has been cited.

(1583) *na ktici dīrghaśca* |6|4|39|. [The commentary] says "dīrghānunāsika" etc., because both the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ* and the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) by the rule *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ*, as well as the elision of the nasal by the rule *anudāttopadeśe* etc., would otherwise apply.

The words to be explained are *yantir* and so forth. [The roots are: *yama* in the sense of "to cease," *rama* in the sense of "to sport," *vanu* in the sense of "to beg," and *tanu* in the sense of "to expand.

(1584) *alaṃkhalvoḥ pratiṣedhayoḥ prācāṃ ktvā* |3|4|18|. [This sūtra prescribes the suffix *ktvā* after these roots when preceded by *alam* or *khalu*, which express prohibition, according to the Eastern grammarians.]

Regarding the rule *alaṃkhalvoḥ*: [the word] "for the sake of honor" (*pūjārtham*)—if it is argued that it should instead mean "for the sake of optionality" (*vikalpārtham*), so that the two forms *alaṃ ruditvā* and *alaṃ rodanena* may be established, do not say so; for this is already established by the principle of *vāsarūpa*. Nor does the rule *talyuṭtumunkhalartheṣu* apply here.
Or, it might be argued that the rule *vāsarūpa* applies here because of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the *vāsarūpa* principle holds for *lyuṭ*;

however, the distilled meaning of that principle is: "Derivatives such as *talyaḍ* and others, being exceptions (*apavāda*), invariably supersede that which they are meant to set aside. But in this case, there is a discrepancy, because *ktvā* is an exception to *lyuṭ*. Now, [one might object]: [The objection continues: "But..."

If it is argued that by the rule *raiṣādiṣu kṛtyāśca* (P. 3.4.18), it is indicated that after the section on feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*), the requirement of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa*) does not necessarily apply, what follows from that? There is no obstacle to accepting that [indication] in accordance with the desired result, based on the principle that "what is established by an indicatory mark (*jñāpaka*) does not apply everywhere. Enough!
"Having given"—the resulting meaning is that it should not be given to an unworthy recipient.

(1585) *udīcāṃ māṅe vyatīhāre* |3|4|19|. "Of the Northerners"; *vyatīhāra* means exchange or reciprocal action. This form *māṅ* is derived from the root *meṅ* after it has undergone the change to *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for *e*).

The mention [of *anunāsika*] makes known the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "the state of not ending in a nasal is determined by the presence of the *anubandha*"; by this, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *daiP* from the designation *ghu*—via the rule *adāP*—is established. (1586) *mayater id anyatarasyām* | 6.4.70 | [The *ik* substitute is optionally applied for the root *mā*].
Regarding *apamitya*: by the rule to be stated later, “*amāse ’nañpūrve*,” there is the substitution of *lyap* for *ktvā*, and the elision (*tuk*) of the final vowel.
The meaning is: having borrowed, he returns it.
(1587) *parāvarayoge ca* | 3|4|20|. And [the suffix *lyap* is used] when there is a connection with what is prior (*para*) or subsequent (*avara*).
"Without reaching the higher and lower": for those situated in the southern region, this means the Vindhya mountain without having reached the Gaṅgā;

that is to say, the Vindhya situated in a location characterized by its separation from the Gaṅgā. Here, it is understood that the Gaṅgā is beyond (parā) the Vindhya. "Having transcended": this [expression] also applies specifically to those situated in the southern region.

The application [of this principle] is as follows: for here, it is understood that "the Vindhya is to the east of the Gaṅgā. In this context of the three sūtras, although the suffix *ktvā* denotes merely the abstract action (*bhāva*), the relations between the qualifier and the qualified differ;
thus, there is no pointlessness [in the rule]. This is the direction [of the argument].

(1588) *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle* 3.4.21. Regarding *samānakartṛka*: although this occurs within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of verbal roots (*dhātu*), the intention is that "having the same agent" can only apply to two actions; therefore, he says "of the two meanings of the verbal roots. The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), while the locative case (*saptamī*) is used for the rule itself.

The meaning is: "from that verbal root-meaning which possesses a prior time between the two verbal root-meanings. Thus, it follows that the locative case used for selection (*nirdhāraṇa-vibhakti*) itself indicates that *pūrvakāla* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. As for the statement "there should be *ktvā*," that [suffix] occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*).

Because of the statement "that which is made [by] an indeclinable" (*ṭhavyayakṛta*), here even the state (*bhāva*) is not in a perfected condition as it is in the case of *ghañ* and other suffixes, but rather in a beginning stage. And that is obtained by the verbal root itself. Furthermore, the action, which constitutes the meaning of the root in the case of the *kvā* suffix, serves as a qualifier with respect to another action, because of the rule regarding the connection of roots (*dhātusaṃbandha*). And here, the relation is one of conjunction (*saṃsarga*).

There is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the relation of prior and posterior time. In this context, suffixes such as *ktvā*, *ṇamul*, and others serve to indicate the specific relation of connection (*saṃsarga*). Here, coreferentiality is established by the portion of the rule stating "of two [actions] having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkayoḥ*).
This is because it results in that state [of being the agent] by virtue of being the substratum for the act of giving and taking; this is the general direction [of the argument].

Regarding the term "duality" (*dvitva*): [an objection is raised]—"If it is said, 'Bring these Brahmins from the front,' the middle one is not brought; likewise here too, when there is a co-utterance of many actions, [the suffix should apply] to that which expresses the middle action."

If it is argued that the *ktvā* suffix would not be applicable here, they reply: even in this case, the action expressed by the verb (*ākhyāta*) is the primary element; all actions presented by forms ending in *ktvā* are qualifiers of that [primary] action, and there is no mutual relationship between those [subordinate] actions themselves, according to the maxim: "And because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another."
Therefore, expressions such as "having bathed, having drunk, having eaten, he goes" are used without restriction.
Since an option would have been obtained by the rule *varatisūti* etc.,
he states *svaratyādeḥ* in order to establish its obligatory application.

(1589) *ktvi skandi-sandoḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.31. Regarding the suffix *ktvā* after the roots *skandi* and *sandi*: *skandir* means "to move" and "to dry up. According to the Vārttikakāra, the letter *i* alone is designated as *it*; therefore, the prohibition in the rule *aniditām* does not apply here.
The term *skandigrahaṇam* means "it does not proceed. Regarding *skantvā*: by the rule *ekācaḥ*, the augment *iṭ* is not applied.
(Pāṇini 1.2.7) *mṛḍamṛdagudhakuṣakliśavadavasaḥ ktvā*.

[Roots] *mṛḍ*, *mṛd*, *gudh*, *kuṣ*, *kliś*, *vad*, and *vas* [take the suffix *ktvā*]. *mṛḍ* means "to soothe," *mṛd* means "to crush," *gudh* means "to envelop," and *gudh* [also] means "to be angry."
And: *kuṣa* in the sense of extracting; *kliś* in the sense of harming (belonging to the *divādi* class); *kliśū* in the sense of afflicting (belonging to the *rkyādi* class);
*vad* in the sense of distinct speech; *vas* in the sense of dwelling. Regarding "kiṭ":

the meaning is that the term *kit* is understood from the rule "the *liṭ* [affixes] following a root ending in a conjunct consonant are *kit*. Regarding *uditvā*: [this is derived from the root *ud*].

The semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs because [the root] belongs to the *yajādi* class. In the form *uṣitvā*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *vasatikṣudhoḥ*; the semivowel substitution occurs because it belongs to the *yajādi* class; and the sibilant *ṣ* is applied by the rule *āsivasī*. In the form *gṛhītvā*, the semivowel substitution occurs by the rule *rahijyā*; and the lengthening of the *iṭ* augment occurs by the rule *raho liṭi*.

(1591) *nopadhātthaphāntādvā* | 1|2|23 | The term *th* refers to that which has *th* as its final element; the inclusion of the word *anta* (final) is for the sake of clarity. Even if it were stated simply as *thaph*, since the suffix *ktavatu* is prescribed only after a verbal root (*dhātu*), the rule "ending in *th* or *ph*" is understood through the principle of *tadantavidhi* (specification by what ends in that), by virtue of the proximity of the qualified term (*viśeṣya*).

From the root *lābha*; having boiled (*kothitvā*); having boasted (*rephitvā*). [The roots] *kuth* is used in the sense of becoming putrid, and *ripha* in the senses of boasting, fighting, censuring, harming, and giving. Here, the optional rule [*ṭhralo vyupadhāt*] does not apply, due to the force of the inclusion of the term "not" (*na*) in the mention of the penultimate vowel (*nopadha*).

(1592) *vañci-luñcy-ṛtaś-ca* |1|2|24|. [The suffix *ktvā* takes the substitute *iṭ* after these: *vañcitvā*—from the root *vañc*, meaning "to deceive"; *lucitvā*—from the root *luñc*, meaning "to remove"; *ṛtitvā*—the root *ṛti* is a Vedic (sautra) root meaning "to give" or "to feel compassion," which [takes *iṭ*] in the domain of *ardhadhātuka* affixes.
Since the suffix *īyaṅ* is optional for the root *tṛ*, its absence is optionally provided by this [rule].
(1593) *tṛṣimṛṣikṛśeḥ kāśyapasya* |1|2|25|. *tṛṣi-mṛṣi-*. [The roots] *ñitṛṣā* (in the sense of thirst), *mṛṣa* (in the sense of endurance), and *kṛśa* (in the sense of making thin).
Because the word "or" (*vā*) is carried over from the previous rule [Pāṇini 6.1.137] *upadhāyāśca*, the mention of Kāśyapa is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*).

Regarding *añceḥ*: since the option provided by [Pāṇini 1.2.12] *udito vā* would otherwise apply, this rule is commenced. In *añcitvā*, because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini 1.2.18] *na ktvā seṭ*, the suffix is not *kit*; therefore, due to the absence of *kit*-status, there is no elision of the *n* [in *añc*]. Thus, here [the form is derived as] *āñceḥ*.
They say that the statement by Prasādakāra—that there is no elision of the *n* in the word *pūjāyām*—is useless.
(1594) *jṛ-vraścyoḥ ktvi* |7|2|55|.
Regarding *jṛ-vraścyoḥ*: from the root *jṛ*, because of the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule *ṛt-śyukaḥ kitī*, [the form *jīrṇa* arises].

Since the root *vraśc* is marked with the indicatory letter *u*, the option [of the augment *iṭ*] would apply; this statement [of the rule] is made to provide for the alternative. Thus we have *jarītvā*.

By the rule *vṛto vā*, there is optionally a lengthening of the *iṭ* augment. Thus we have *vraścitvā*. Here, because the prohibition of *kit*-status by the rule *na ktvā seṭ* applies, there is no vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *rahijyā*.
(1595) *udito vā* |7|2|56| [The suffix *ktvā*] optionally takes the augment *iṭ* after a root marked with *u* as an *it*. In the case where *iṭ* is absent, *ūṭh* is substituted by *cha-voḥ* |6|4|19|.
(1596) *kramaśca ktvi* |6|4|18| [The substitution of *ūṭh* for the final vowel of *kram* also occurs before the suffix *ktvā*].
Regarding the phrase "in the presence of a *jhal* letter": the meaning is that this must be stated in the rule *āntanaśām*.
(1597) *Jāntanaśāṃ vibhāṣā* 3.4.32. [Examples: *khātvā*, *khanitvā*. The suffix *iṭ* is optionally applied by the rule *udito vā*.

(1598) And after the root *aś* (to eat), when followed by the suffix *ktvā*. [Pāṇini 7.1.43] Thus, *jagdhvā* [is formed]. There is optional elision of the *dh* sound according to the rule *haro jhari*.
(1599) In a compound that does not have *nañ* as its first member, *lyap* is substituted for *ktvā*. [Pāṇini 7.1.37]

"In a compound (*samāsa*) that is not *nañ*": this means a compound whose first member (*pūrvapada*) is something other than *nañ*, that is to say, an indeclinable (*avyaya*). He explains this as "that which has an indeclinable as its prior member. Regarding the word *prakṛtyā*:

the prefix *pra-* indicates the excellence inherent in the meaning of the suffix *-ktvā*; furthermore, by the rule "prepositions and *prādi* words [are compounded with their objects]," it is a *gati*.

That which ends in *ktvā* is always compounded [with a word ending in a case-suffix]. The term "paryudāsa" (exclusion) is used here; for if one were to rely on *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), then the suffix *lyap* would indeed occur in this instance—this is the intended meaning. (1600) *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.86. [The substitution of *ṣ* and the application of *tuka* are treated as not having taken effect.]

Regarding the rule *ṣatvatukoḥ*: he provides an incidental example concerning the domain of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*), namely *ko’sicat*. When *kaḥ* and *asicat* are in juxtaposition, the single substitute *e* is applied by the rule *eṅḥ padāntādati*, which effects a *pūrvarūpa* (prior-form) sandhi. By the rule *antādivacca*, this substitute is treated as if it were the end of the preceding word (*anta-vat*) and the beginning of the following word (*ādi-vat*). Consequently, by the rule *ātpadādyoḥ*... [the *ṣatva* substitution applies].

In the absence of a prohibition, the substitution of *ṣ* would have applied because of the position following *iṇ*; however, since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), there is an intervention by the vowel *a*, and thus, due to the lack of the condition of being followed by *iṇ*, it does not occur. He illustrates the operation regarding *lyap* under discussion with the examples "adhītya" and "vidhāya"; [in the latter], the *hi* of the root *dadhāti* is replaced by *na*.
(1601) Or [the substitution of *ya* for *ktvā*] occurs when the suffix *lyap* follows. For example:

*pradāya*—here, the rule "odaddhoḥ" does not apply. *Prakhanya*—here, the substitution of *ā* by the rule "anasanakhanām" does not occur. *Prasthāya*—here, the substitution of *ī* by the rule "yatisyatītī" does not occur. *Prakramya*—here, the rule "ramaśca ktvi" applies.

[The substitution of] *ū* for *dīrgha* does not occur [in *pradīvyati*]. [In the case of] *āpṛcchya* and *pradīvyeti*, by the rule "of *ch* and *v*" (*chvoḥ*), *śū* and *ṭh* [are substituted]. However, the example for the absence of *iṭ* should be understood as being in forms such as *prakhanya pradīvyeti*. (1602) *na lyapi* 6.4.69. [The substitution of *ū* for *dīrgha* does not occur before the suffix *lyap*.]

Regarding the rule *na lyapi*: if it is asked how the usage by Śrīharṣa, “*ipīya yasya*,” is justified, they say here that there is no fault because it is derived from the root *pīṅ* (to drink) belonging to the Divādi class; thus, the suffix *lyap* does not trigger the prohibition. Furthermore, in the examples *praśāya* and *pracchāya*, there is also the absence of the *it*-augment which would otherwise be required by the rule *ācchāderanyatarasyām*.
*bodhyaḥ* | (1603) *lyapi laghupūrvāt* | 6|4|56 | Regarding *laghupūrvāt*: that from which a light vowel (*laghu*) precedes [the final consonant].

The meaning is "after a light vowel preceded by a preceding letter. Regarding the word *vigaṇayya*: one might object that here, because of the substitution of *al* (the elision of *ṇi*) for *ṇi*, and because of the status of being a *sthānivat* (as if it were the original) with respect to what precedes it, there is no state of being "after a light vowel preceded by a preceding letter. No.
Because of the force of the initial undertaking [of the rule], and because [the suffix] *mit* has already fulfilled its purpose in cases such as *anugamayya*, it is here stated:

"In the case of a rule concerning what precedes, the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) is non-eternal," as indicated by the evidence in the rule *iṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi*. Thus, since the status of being like the original does not apply here, the substitution of *ay* for *ṇi* indeed occurs.

The fact that the rule *iṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.52) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of its non-eternality has already been demonstrated by us in the very rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), and thus it is not demonstrated here. Regarding *praṇamayya*:
because it ends in *am*, the *mit* designation applies, and by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92), the vowel is shortened. Regarding *prabebhidayya*: [the same applies].
From the causative form *bebhidy-ya* (the *yaṅ*-intensive of *bhid*), after the elision of *ya*, there is the elision of *y* by the rule "yasya halaḥ.
Now, one might object:

since the elision of the short vowel (*hrasva-lopa*), the elision of *ya* (*ya-lopa*), and the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) are all *ābhīya* (belonging to the same stage of derivation), they are considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*). Consequently, [the preceding vowel] would not be followed by a light syllable (*laghu-pūrva*).

If it is asked: "Since *ṇi* does not exist here, how can there be the substitution of *ṇi* for *ra* [in *ṇirayati*], or how could it occur in cases such as *gaṇayati*?"—do not say so. For in the rule *asiddhavadatrābhāt*, it has been explained that "when an operation is to be performed upon that which depends on something other than itself, that [operation] shall be treated as if it were non-existent. Therefore, no such doubt arises here.

[The substitution] does not occur, because *hiṇ* is applied to short vowels (*hrasva*) and so forth, whereas the substitution of *ay* for *ṇi* occurs when *lyap* follows; thus, there is a difference in their respective bases (*vyāśrayatvāt*). (1604) *vibhāṣā''paḥ* | 6.4.57.

Regarding the word *āpnoteḥ*: although there exists the form *āpi*—derived from the root *iṅ* after the causative suffix (*ṇic*), where the vowel substitution *rīṅ* is applied by the rule *rīṅjīnāṃ ṇau*, followed by the augment *puK* by the rule *artihrī* etc.—nevertheless, that [form] is not intended here because it is *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a secondary grammatical operation); this is the underlying sense. [The word] *prāpya* [is used]; by this...

The usage by Śrī Harṣa—"Having incurred the whirlpool of the sky due to the sins of killing a yogi’s wife, he is surely cast down"—is explained [by taking *avāpya* as *avapya*]. This is because the meaning of "causing to descend" (*avapayya*) is possible for the word *avāpya*.
By this, those who experience difficulty by claiming that a causative sense is implied (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) therein are refuted.

Since the substitutes for the *lyap* suffix are marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*), the rule "vacisvapi... would require the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization of the semivowel); in order to prohibit this, he says: "And [the substitution does not occur] when *lyap* follows" (1605).
And [the substitution does not occur] after *jyā*. 6.1.42.
And [in the case of] *jya*, there would be no *saṃprasāraṇa*. The same should be explained for *vya* as well.
(1606) *vibhāṣā pareḥ* | 6.1.44. How so? Because the suffix *ktvā*, which is the original element (*sthānin*) for the substitute *lyap*, would be difficult to obtain in its application.

This is because [the rule] specifies "prior time" (*pūrvakāla*). That condition does not exist here; for he first sleeps and afterwards opens his mouth, and at the very moment he laughs, he simultaneously closes his eyes. Thus, since the suffix *ktvā* is difficult to obtain in such cases, there is no possibility for the suffix *lyap* to apply—this is the question.

He explains this with the words beginning "vyādāna" (opening). By this, such statements as "the Lord exists pervading everything" and "he remains having known [everything]" are explained. However, in passages such as "having seen the peak of Mount Rīśaila, there is no rebirth," the phrase "of one who stands" (*sthitasya*) and so forth is used for the sake of establishing grammatical coreferentiality (*samānakartṛkatā*).
The [suffixes] should be supplied as appropriate.
(1607) *Ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca* | 3|4|22|.

Regarding the rule "In the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), there is also *ṇamul*": [one might ask], "But surely, by the principle of 'non-identity of form' (*asarūpa-nyāya*), the suffix *ktvā* [should also apply]?"

If it is argued that the mention of the term ‘a’ here is redundant because [the future tense] will [already] occur, this is not so. For if the aforementioned reasoning were accepted, then the *laṭ* (present tense) and other suffixes would also apply here. Nor is this a desired consequence, as it would lead to the contingency of the mention of the word ‘optionally’ (*vibhāṣā*) in the sūtra to be stated later, namely, “*vibhāṣāgre*. For in that [sūtra]:
The suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are optionally prescribed by means of the mention of *vibhāṣā* for the purpose of allowing their co-occurrence with *laṭ* and other suffixes.

Even though *laṭ* and the rest would be established by the rule of "dissimilarity" (*asarūpa-nyāya*) alone, nevertheless, the rule of dissimilarity does not apply in cases where the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed together with *ṇamul*.

The inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā* is for the purpose of making this known; its result is the non-application of the *laṭ* and other suffixes in the rule "ṭhābhīkṣṇe ṇamul ca. Consequently, since the *ktvā* suffix is obtained by the particle *ca* itself, there is no redundancy whatsoever. Furthermore, if one were to accept the *ktvā* and *laṭ* etc. even without [the principle of] "optionality when forms are dissimilar" (*vā'sarūpa*), [it would lead to undesirable consequences].
Furthermore, if [the rule] "yadi anākāṅkṣe" were applied, then just like the suffix *ktvā*, the *laṭ* and other verbal endings would also not be established.
Consequently, the example "yadayaṃ bhuṅkte tataḥ paṭhati" (when he eats, then he studies) would not be possible.
However, in the final view (*siddhānta*), because of the specific rules "ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca" (the suffix *ṇamul* is used after a verb when frequency is indicated)...

Since the prohibition applies only to the *ktvā* and *ṇamul* suffixes, the *laṭ* and other suffixes prescribed in general do indeed occur; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever—this is the direction of the argument. Regarding the phrase "in the preceding scope": the meaning is "when two actions have the same agent, [the suffix is used] for the action occurring at the earlier time. As for "pāyaṃpāyam," [it is derived from the root *pā* with the suffix *ṇamul*,] where *yuk* is added by the rule *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ*, and the lengthening is optional (*vā dīrghaḥ*).

The meaning is that when the suffix *ṇamul* follows a root ending in *ṇic*, and the shortening (*hrasva*) of the vowels *mit* has been applied, there is optionally a lengthening (*dīrgha*). The phrase "even of that which ends in *ṇic*" implies that the view presented by the ancients—that there is optional *vṛddhi* for roots ending in *ṇic*, as well as for *jāgarti* after *ciṇ* and *ṇamul*—is un-Pāṇinian; this is the intended sense.

(1608) *na yadyanākāṅkṣe* || 3.4.23 || *na yadi*: [The compound] *anākāṅkṣa* is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) with a word ending in the suffix *ac* (Pāṇini 3.1.134). He demonstrates this by saying: "if it does not require [another verb]. Regarding this, they say: "In the case of *ced*, [the rule applies] when [the action] occurs at a prior time (*pūrvakāla*)."
Because of the explanation that "one does not obtain that [which one has already reached]," the suffix *ktvā* also does not occur.
(1609) *vibhāṣāgreprathamapūrveṣu* |3|4|24|.
[The rule] *vibhāṣāgre*: although the word *agra* also signifies a particular location, [it is here taken as a temporal term].

Because of usages such as *‘agrato bhunakti’* (he eats before others), even so, in this context [of the rule], only that which denotes a specific time is understood, due to its association with the word *prathama*. In examples such as *‘prathamaṃ bhunakti’* (he eats first), only time is indeed perceived. The form *‘agre’* is an elliptical citation of the locative case (*saptamyanta*).

Because the rule "an imitation [is expressed] by means of the word-form itself" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*) is optional, the case-ending is not applied, as in the example *asyavāmīyam*. Regarding *agre bhojam* and *agre bhojam*:
according to the restriction "only with an indeclinable (*avyaya*) [is there composition]," this is a separate construction (*vyasta*), and not a compound formed with an upapada.

If it is objected that since priority in time is expressed by the words *agra*, *prathama*, and *pūrva*, how can the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* be used here, they reply as follows: for the meaning of the sentence is "having eaten before other eaters, he departs. In that context, by means of the words *agra* and so forth, [priority] is expressed in relation to the other eaters.

If it is argued that priority is expressed here as well—since [the agent] goes before other enjoyers—then there is no doubt at all that priority relative to the act of going is what is indicated by the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul*. Thus, the rule is indeed eternal; for in the case of "he eats first" (*agre bhuṅkte*), the suffix *laṭ* and so forth [are used].
The sense is that it is employed [as a suffix].
(1610) *svādumi ṇamul* |3|4|26|. Regarding *svādumi*: the term *svādumi* is taken as a reference to the meaning; this has been explained. He states accordingly:
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of 'tasting'": as for the form *māntavam*, one might object: let the rule simply be *vādau* (Pāṇini 3.4.25);

there is no need for the suffix *ṇamul* here. Let *khamuñ* be understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over from the previous rule). Then, by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya mum* (Pāṇini 6.3.67), the augment *mum* will occur. In this way, the ending in *m* would be established even without a specific nipātana (irregular formation).

If you argue that there is no difference between the heavy and the light forms, it is not so. For the suffix *mum* would apply to a word ending in *cv-*; this is because of the rule stating "not for an indeclinable" (*anavyayasya*).

Consequently, in the case of *svāduṅkāram*, the rule *vau ca* would require lengthening of the vowel, and in cases such as *ampannaṅkāraḥ*, the rule *ṭhasya cvau* would require the substitution of *it*. Furthermore:

Regarding the feminine form, since the rule *ṭhvoto guṇavacanāt* would require the suffix *ṅīṣ*, resulting in *svādvī-kāram*, the form *svādu* is here established as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Consequently, because it does not end in a vowel (*anajanta*), neither the substitution of *it* nor the lengthening occurs, nor is there the suffix *ṅīṣ*. This irregularity applies specifically to the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) alone; therefore—

The form *svāduṅkṛtvā* is also established. It might be argued: "To avoid the aforementioned fault, let the sūtra be accepted as *svādu-mī* alone; let the suffix *ṇamul* be abandoned, for even when the suffix *khamuñ* is applied to the root *kṛ*, forms such as *svāduṅkāram* are likewise established. But this is not so.

Likewise, since *kham* would follow by virtue of its presence in the subsequent sūtras, there would be the addition of the augment *mum* to the preceding word in cases such as *kanyā-darśanam* and *brāhmaṇa-vedam*; this is the general direction of the argument.

(1611) *anyathā-evaṃ-katham-ittham-su siddhā-prayogaś-cet* || 3|4|27 || [The suffix *kṛtvasuc*] is not applied after [words ending in] *anyathā*, *evam*, *katham*, or *ittham* if [the sense is already] established; this is because it would be redundant (*vyarthatvāt*), meaning because it would serve no purpose. He demonstrates this by saying: "the meaning is 'he eats in this manner' (*itthaṃ bhuṅkte*). Although there is a distinction in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) here, this is the resulting meaning (*phalitārtha*).

By the phrase "being intent on speaking" (*kathanaparatayā*), it is stated that the form ending in the suffix *ṇamul*—namely, *kāram*—is fruitless, because it serves no significant purpose. The detailed discussion should be sought in the *Manoramā* and other such works.
Regarding the expression "having turned his head otherwise" (*śiro'nyatheti*): here, having turned his head otherwise, he eats rice and so forth.

The employment of the verb *karoti* is necessary for the sake of conveying this meaning. In its absence, however, only the manner pertaining to the act of eating would be understood, and not the alteration of the head; therefore, since there is a requirement for the employment of *karoti*, the sense is that the form ending in *ṇamul* is not used here.
(1612) When *yathātatha* is used in response to an expression of envy, [the suffix *ṇamul* is applied]. 3.4.28.

Regarding the phrase *yathākāram*: if one asks while being unworthy to ask, then this is the answer. Here too, by the rule of *asarūpa* (irregular formation), the suffix *ktvā* should be understood as an alternative option.
(Pāṇini 3.4.29): "The suffix *ktvā* is used after the roots *dṛś* and *vid* when they take an object, provided that the action is performed in its entirety."

Regarding "kanyādarśam": here, since the meaning of the sentence applies to all the girls who have become objects of sight, their totality is understood. Regarding "sarvā" (all): the meaning is "all those who have become objects of sight"; this is intended to express an excellence. Regarding "brāhmaṇavedam": [vida...]
Having considered the meanings of the verbal roots— *vid* in the sense of "knowledge," *vidlṛ* in the sense of "attainment," and *vida* in the sense of "investigation"—
he explains [the term] with "he knows," and so forth. The intention is that the root *vid* in the sense of "existence" (*satā*) is not to be understood here, as it possesses multiple meanings.

(1614) *yāvati vindajīvoḥ* |3|4|30|. *yāvati* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the root *vid*, in the sense of "obtaining" (*lābha*). For in forms such as *vindati*, there is the augment *num* by the rule *e mucādīnām*. Thus: *yāvallabhate*.
By this [sūtra], he indicates incompleteness; for if completeness were intended, it would already be established by the rule *karmaṇi dṛśividoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.29).
(1615) *carmodarayoḥ pūreḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.31).

Regarding *carmodara* and *karmaṇīti*: thus, the reference is to the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of the root *pūr*, and not to the simple root indicated by the vowel *i* according to the rule *ṭhikśtipau*. The intention is that [the simple root] is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Examples such as *carmapūram* mean "having filled the skin" or "having filled the belly."

The meaning is: "the act of eating characterized by the filling of the stomach. Here, the term "prior in time" (*pūrvakāla*) is not connected [to the compound], because it is impossible and because it is not perceived. In other cases as well, it should be understood accordingly. The meaning is: "the act of eating characterized by the filling of the stomach. Here, "prior in time" is not...

It is connected [with the preceding rule] because of the impossibility [of its application otherwise] and because it is not perceived [as a separate rule]. In this way, it should be understood elsewhere as well, according to the possibility of the case.
Regarding *cele*: they say that the meaning is taken by virtue of the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). That is, "in the sense of clothes" (*celārtheṣu*).

"Like wet clothes," and so forth. The meaning is that just as clothes make a sound when it rains, so too [does the earth] when it has rained. Others, however, considering the root-meaning of the *mamul*-suffix in *knopayati*—derived from *knūyī* (to moisten) and *klidū* (to become wet)—explain it as being like the falling of rain.
They explained that it had rained as soon as the clothes became wet.
(1617) Pāṇini 3.4.34: *nimūla-samūlayoḥ kaṣaḥ*. Regarding *nimūlam*: that whose root is certainly [extracted] is *nimūlam*; together with the root is *samūlam*.
The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is that "the eradication [of the enemy] is an eradication that is not distinct from being root-and-all-and-rootless. Regarding the word "by that" (*tena*):

here this should be understood—generality is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), while particularity is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). This is because it is the common experience of all people that in expressions such as "a mango tree," the mango is the qualifier and the tree is the substantive.

Therefore, in this context, [the term] *nimūlakarṣaṇa* (uprooting) and so forth are the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), while *karṣaṇa* (drawing/pulling) alone is the qualified (*viśeṣya*). (1618) *piṣaḥ* [is used] in the sense of making unctuous (*snehana*). 3.4.38. Regarding *snehane*: the inclusion of the word *snehana* was not made in the very rule *uṣkacūrṇe*; for in that [rule],...

From the sūtra *armaṇi dṛśividoḥ*, the term *karmaṇi* (in the objective case) is understood to carry over; however, here from the preceding sūtra, the term *karaṇe* (in the instrumental case) must be carried over. (1619) *haste vartigrahoḥ* | 3|4|39|.
In the word *haste*, the term *hasta* is used to signify the meaning [of the word]; thus he says: "in the sense of *hasta*.
(1620) *saṃjñāyām* | 2|4|42|. Regarding *saṃjñāyām*: this rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding the case of a locative (*adhikaraṇa*).

(1621) *Kaṣādiṣu yathāvidhyanuprayogaḥ* || 3.4.46 || "In the same manner" means that examples such as *mūlakāṣam kaṣati* ("he scrapes up the roots") have been cited. (1622) *Upadaṃśas tṛtīyāyām* || 3.4.47 ||

Regarding the expression *mūlakopadaṃśam*: this is the meaning—[the sentence] "he eats with radish" (*mūlakena bhuṅkte*). Having done what? Having eaten as a side-dish (*upadasya*). What is eaten as a side-dish? By implication, it is connected with "radish" (*mūlakam*). "By this much alone" means:
even in the absence of a verbal connection, by means of a mere semantic connection. "By the force of the statement" means...

For if the suffix were to occur only when there is a verbal syntactic connection (śābdānvaya) as in the case of a word ending in the third case, then [the author] would have simply said "ṭhupadaṃśaḥ karaṇe," just like [the rule] "araṇe hanaḥ. Consequently, the intention is that the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) for another action is intended for the word *mūlakena*. And this...

This has been stated according to the *Manoramā* treatise. On this point, some say: "In that case, let the rule simply be *'upadaṃśaḥ karmaṇi'*; or rather, let it be just *'upadaṃśaḥ'*. By carrying forward the word *'karmaṇi'* from the rule *'upamāne karmaṇi'*, [the meaning would be] when *'upadaṃśa'* has a verbal root having an object as its *upapada*."
Let it be explained that the suffix *ṇamul* is applied to the root *daś* preceded by the prefix *upa*; what is the use of this forced interpretation?

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would necessarily be a compound when a word in the accusative case (*karman*) is the *upapada*, for the same fault applies even if [the rule] were stated as "when the instrumental case (*karaṇa*) is the *upapada*. Furthermore, regarding the sūtra "ṛtīyā-prabhṛtīni... [it is not the case...].

It should not be argued that there is no fault at all in stating "beginning with *araṇa*," because the doubt is removed by accepting the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) which states, "Specific understanding [of the rule's application] comes from the commentary; for a rule is not [invalidated] on account of doubt. This is because the option (*vikalpa*) begins from the rule "hanaḥ ra" when applied to *araṇa*.

Even though it is stated in the sūtra *ṛtīyāprabhṛtīni* that [the rule applies] "starting from *armaṇi-prabhṛtīni*," there is no fault; for there is doubt as to whether the option begins with *armaṇyākrośe kṛñaḥ khamuñ* or with *armaṇo dṛśividoh*.

Since this can be avoided by the technical rule (paribhāṣā) "the specific [meaning] is understood from the explanation," they say that the *Manoramā*— which suggests one should simply state "upadaṃśaḥ karaṇe" (the root daṃś with upa- is used in the sense of the instrument)— is to be reconsidered. In fact, however, when it is stated that "karmani-prabhṛtīni anyatarasyām" (the group beginning with karman is optionally [used]),...

If one accepts the view that the sūtra is simply "upa-daṃśaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.4.40), with the word "karmaṇi" (in the sense of the object) being carried over from the preceding rule "ṭhupamāne karmaṇi ca," then the application of the verb in its original form (*yathāvidhyanuprayoga*) after roots such as *kaṣ* would also be optional. Resorting to the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūakapluti*) method of interpretation, however, is a desperate measure (*agatikagati*). [The alternative reading is] "upa-daṃśaḥ karmaṇi."

Even in the view that accepts the rule as a *sūtra*, the form *ūlakopadaṃśam* [is established]; however, according to the statement in the *Manoramā*—"the words beginning with *araṇa* [form a compound with a word ending in the third case]"—in the alternative where a compound is not formed, the form *ūlakenopadaṃśam* is indeed established, because the instrumental case (*karaṇatṛtīyā*) applies. This is the general direction.

(1623) And [the same applies] to verbs meaning "to injure" when they have the same object [as the main verb]. 3.4.48. *Kālayati*—the root *kal* in the sense of "to scatter" belongs to the *curādi* group; it means "he impels. *Daṇḍatāḍam*—the root *taḍ* in the sense of "striking" also belongs to the *curādi* group.

(1624) *saptamyāṃ copapīḍarudhakarṣaḥ* |3|4|49|. Regarding the phrase *saptamyāṃ co*: [the rule states] "after [roots] preceded by *upa*. The intention is that in the sūtra, a collective dvandva compound is formed from *pīḍa*, etc., and then there is a compound with elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*), namely *upapūrva-pīḍarudhakarṣa*.

Here, the masculine gender [of the root] is according to the Sūtra, and it should be understood that the nominative case is used in the sense of the ablative. The mention of *karṣati* with the suffix *śap* is due to the pronunciation of the root *kṛṣ* (meaning "to plow") together with its *guṇa* strengthening; the result of this is the exclusion of roots belonging to the *tudādi* class. Although that [root *kṛṣ*] is also recited in the *tudādi* class as meaning "plowing," nevertheless...

That [suffix] is employed only when there is scratching directed toward a field, as seen in the expression "he ploughs with five ploughs. Thus, after the root *kṛṣ* meaning "to scratch," only the suffix *ktvā* occurs—as in *kṣetre upakṛṣya* ("having scratched upon the field") or *halenopakṛṣya* ("having scratched with a plough")—and not the suffix *ṇamul* in this context; so it is established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*).

(1625) *samāsatau* |3|4|50|. Regarding *samāsatau*: in the expression *keśagrāham*, whether the seizing by the hair actually occurs or not, this [term] is intended solely to indicate close proximity (*sannikarṣa*).
(1626) And [the suffix *kan* is used] after a word denoting a measure.

3.4.51. Regarding the expression *dvyaṅgulotkarṣam*: the combination of two fingers (*aṅguli*) is *dvyaṅgulam*. This is according to the rule: “In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the final vowel of] *aṅguli* is replaced by *a* when preceded by a numeral or an indeclinable. (*atpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*)
[This concerns] the suffix added at the end of a compound. "Having raised [it] by two finger-breadths" means having measured it. A very small fragment is a *khaṇḍikā*.

It is stated in the *Manoramā* that a short fragment is a *khaṇḍikā*. Although the word *hrasva* is generally used for sentient beings as a synonym for "dwarf," [it is also used] in the sense of "small" or "short."
Although this is so because of the natural force of the separate sūtra, they say that it occurs even in some insentient things, on account of the mention of "short," "long," and so forth.
[And] in the case of the second [case-ending], Pāṇini 3.4.53.

[The rule applies] in the second [case], specifically "when there is a desire for haste" (*parīpsā*). How then is it that [the rule] "a word is unaccented except for one syllable" (*anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam*) applies, since haste is not perceived here? To this they say: in this *paribhāṣā*, haste is indeed intended. Therefore, the meaning is: wherever an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) [accent] occurs...

In that case, it is prescribed that at the very same time [the first syllable is uttered], the remainder—excluding that single syllable—should be made unaccented (anudātta), and one must not delay. "Grasping the staff," and so forth: indeed, they hasten for battle in such a way that they run even while seizing whatever is at hand, such as a staff, and do not wait for their weapons.
The sense is that they are waiting.
(1628) *apaguro ṇamuli* [Pāṇini 3.4.49]: regarding *asyāpagoram*, the meaning is "having raised the sword."

(1629) *viśi-pati-padi-skandām vyāpyamānā-’sevyamānayoḥ* || 3.4.56 || The purpose [of this rule] is for the sake of the designation *upapada*. Since the word *dvitīyāyām* is understood to follow in the sūtra *viśi-pati*, the meaning is that the designation *upapada* applies to that which ends in those [roots].
(1630) After the root *kṛ*, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are used when an indeclinable (*avyaya*) expresses something contrary to what was intended.

[Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.59] The term "indeclinable" (*avyaye*) and "contrary to what was intended" (*ayathā*) mean: that which is not as intended is "contrary to what was intended" (*ayathābhipreta*); the expression of such is "expressing contrary to what was intended.
To speak loudly of what is pleasing and to speak softly of what is displeasing constitutes "expressing contrary to what was intended."

This means "in the case of describing the opposite of that. If one asks, "Why was it not simply stated as 'in the case of describing what is unpleasant'? they reply here: even speaking pleasantly in a low voice is indeed "describing what is pleasant," and not "describing what is unpleasant," as in the expression, "Having made [him] do it in a low voice, he speaks what is pleasant."

Otherwise, there would be no such usage [of the suffix -am]. Likewise, since speaking unpleasantly in a low voice is also "speaking what is unpleasant," there would also be the usage "speak what is unpleasant by doing so in a low voice" (*nīcaiḥ kṛtvā nīcaiḥ kāram apriyaṃ brūta*). Therefore, it was stated [in the rule] "when speaking what is unintended."

(1631) *tiryak* [is used] before *apavarga*. (Pāṇini 3.4.60). *Tiryakkṛtvā*: having made [something] crooked; that is to say, having moved from the front to the side because of being non-straight, one has gone.
(1632) Before a word ending in the suffix *tas*, when it denotes a part of one's own body (*svāṅga*), [the indeclinable particle *sam* is used] with the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*. (Pāṇini 3.4.61).

Regarding *svāṅge*: some say that when a word ending in *tas* is the affix (*pratyaya*), and a word denoting a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*) is the attendant word (*upapada*). Others say that by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning the mention of an affix, [it means] when a limb of one's own body ends in an affix ending in *tas*. It is a *karmadhāraya* compound: "that which is both *tas* and an affix. Thus, it refers to a limb of one's own body occurring before an affix ending in *tas*.

Regarding this, the ancients maintain that "in that" (*tasmin*) refers to the *upapada*. Although in that context a mere *svāṅga* (body-part) is not the *upapada*, it should nevertheless be understood that the phrase "in that" refers to the entire aggregate of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).
Examples are *mukhataḥkāram* and *mukhatobhūya*. [This applies] to the *ktvā* and *ṇamul* suffixes, and to the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*, respectively.
The intended meaning is "it will be led away. In the word *mukhataḥ*, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*) according to the rule for the group beginning with *ādi*.
Why is there a mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*)? [Consider: *mukhe tasyati* → *mukhataḥ*. Here, the root *tasu* (meaning "to perish") takes the suffix *kvip*;
because it is a verbal root (*dhātu*), the lengthening rule "of that which ends in *ṭha* or *as*" does not apply here. Thus, one says: *mukhataḥ kṛtvā gataḥ* ("having acted from the mouth, he went").

This is established in the *Kāśikā* and other works. However, in reality, since the desired result is achieved simply by excluding [vṛddhi] when there is a suffix that does not have the sense of a suffix (*apratyaya*), the mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is easily dispensable.
(1633) *nādhārthapratyaye cvyarthe* 3.4.62. [The vṛddhi substitute is not applied] before a suffix having the sense of *nañ*, nor before a suffix having the sense of *cvī*.
The suffixes *na* and *anā*, prescribed by the rule "ṭvinañbhyām" [Pāṇini 5.2.27], do not have the sense of *dhā*.

The suffixes beginning with *dhamuñ* [Pāṇini 5.3.44] have the sense of *dvitva* (twoness) and *tritva* (threeness). With the intention that the suffix *dhā*—prescribed by the rule "aṅkhyāyā vidhārthe dhe" [Pāṇini 5.3.42]—possesses the sense of *dhā*, he provides the example: "having become single-fold" (*ekadhābhūya*), and so forth. Thus...
One should cite examples such as *dvaidhaṃ kṛtya*, *dvaidhaṃ bhūya*, and *dvaidhaṃbhāvam*. Now, [one might object:
"The suffixes *añ* and *dhā* are distinct suffixes, whereas *dhamuñ* and others are prescribed by the rule *ṭhakād dho dhyamuñ anyatarasyām*"; to this, he says: "ha".

He raises an objection: "What is the purpose of the mention of *pratyaya* (suffix)?"—even though, by following this [rule], the suffixes such as *dhamuñ* and others become *dhā*-suffixes through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original element), despite their being treated as substitutes (*ādeśa*).
He does so because, although the mention of *dhā* would include *dhamuñ* and the rest according to the method already stated, [the mention of *pratyaya* is necessary for a further reason].

The inclusion of the word "artha" (meaning) here is redundant because [the suffix] occurs [by rule]. Nevertheless, the inclusion of "artha" is for the purpose of including those forms ending in the suffix *ḍa*, according to the rule: "after a root ending in *am* or *u*, the suffix *ḍa* is seen in the sense of 'becoming' (*bhāve*). Its result, however, is the usage of such forms as *dvaidhīkṛtya*.
(1634) *tūṣṇīm* [is used] with *bhū*. 3|4|63. Regarding *tūṣṇīm*: the mention of *tūṣṇīm* is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *kṛñ*.
(1635) *anvac* [is used] in the sense of conformity. 3|4|64.

Regarding *anvacyā*: here, after the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *ṭhacaḥ*, it would have been more appropriate to specify the form as *anūcī*—with the lengthening of the preceding *aṇ* vowel by the rule *vau*—just as it was done for *pratīcī* in the sūtra *prāg-apāg-udak-pratīcaḥ*. The same applies to the sūtra *iryacy apavarge*.

If it is argued that it is more appropriate to designate it as *iraścī*, some here say: "An action prescribed by the Śāstra is effective only when it possesses a purpose (*artha*), and that purpose is understood precisely as it is well-known in the world.
Regarding those whose word-meanings are clearly manifested, who are independent, and renowned in the world—the meaning of the Śāstra applies to them."

[This is] because of the maxim: "That which is prescribed [for a specific case] should not apply when that case is being imitated. Therefore, since [the rule] will not apply in the case of imitation, the form *anvacī* is indeed correct.

This, however, is to be reconsidered. For if that were so, then in rules such as "after *si*, following a long vowel," *iyaṅ* and the like would not occur; furthermore, even the form *ratīcaḥ* would not be established.

In reality, however, because the rule "an imitation is like the original" (*anukaraṇam prakṛtivat*) is optional, there is no fault in the mention of *anvacī* and so forth; and its optionality is established by the application of the substitution of *tyad*-class elements in the rule "from *yad*, *etad*, etc. (*yatadetebhyaḥ*), as well as by the observation of the absence of *ekaśeṣa*.
That it is "determined" has already been explained at length. Regarding the phrase "in front," and so forth:

this is stated to suggest that since the word *anvak* rests solely in the sense of "favorability," there is no restriction regarding its denoting a specific location. Its meaning is "having come behind."
Here, by the word *anvak*, it is not touched upon whether [the person] is favorable (*anukūla*) or unfavorable (*ananukūla*),
because that term culminates merely in a specific location. Even if favorability is obtained in some instance through another means of knowledge, the word *anvak* does not convey that.
One should understand that because there is an absence of activity (*vyāpāra*), the suffix *ṇamul* does not apply; rather, only *ktvā* occurs—this is the established rule.
Thus ends the section on subsequent *kṛt* suffixes.
Thus [ends the chapter].

In the *Tattvabodhinī*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntakaumudī* composed by Jñānendra Sarasvatī, the servant of the feet of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Vāmanendra Svāmī, the section on primary suffixes (*kṛdanta*) is completed. This *Tattvabodhinī* is now finished.

(1161) *tasya vikāraḥ* || 4.3.134 || "His modification. From a word ending in the genitive case, the suffixes *aṇ* and others shall be applied in the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*). [This refers to] that which is connected with the *gha*-class suffixes.

The phrase "of this" (*asya*) was stated again in order to exclude that [previous] mention; however, *aṇ* and the others are not excluded, because they have a specific limit [defined by the rule] "from *rājan*, the sense of 'playing' (*dīvyati')" and "from *rājan*, the sense of 'becoming' (*bhavana*"), and thus are not governed by this [current] context. Here, [the suffix] *añ* is applied after words beginning with *rañji* and *rajata*.

Considering that exceptions will be stated by such rules as "ṭhoran", "ṭhanudātādeśca", "mayaḍvaitayoḥ", "ityaṃ vṛddhaśarādibhyaḥ", and "iṣṭācce"t, one should take as examples [words] that are non-living, have an udātta accent on the first syllable, are not vṛddha, and for which no suffix has been specifically prescribed in each individual case.

He illustrates this with the word *āśma* and so forth. The words *aśman* and *bhasman* end in the suffix *manin*. According to the rule *ṛdastikan*, all three [words] have their first syllable accented acute (*udātta*) due to the *nistvara* accent.
Since the preceding term *tasya* has been withdrawn, the suffixes mentioned in the governing context (*adhikāra*) do not apply.
The suffix *ṭhak* does not apply here; [the examples are] *hālaḥ* and *sairaḥ*.

(1162) Pāṇini 4.3.135: "And [the suffixes taught for products] also [denote] a part, when derived from words meaning living beings, medicinal herbs, or trees. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), the suffixes to be mentioned [hereafter] apply to these three categories—living beings, etc.—in two senses.
The result is that [the suffix] *vikāra* (denoting a modification) applies only to others. Regarding the example *māyūra*:

[it is formed] by the rule *rāṇirajatādibhyaḥ*, which prescribes the suffix *añ*. Since the suffix *añ* is already established for words beginning with an *anudātta* (unaccented) vowel, this [rule] is necessary for the sake of [words] beginning with an *udātta* (accented) vowel, and to prevent the application of *mayat* to *vṛddha* (vṛddhi-incremented) words; furthermore, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], it applies even to those beginning with an *anudātta* vowel.

It proceeds. He provides examples from medicinal plants: *maurvam*. The word *mūrvā* has its first syllable acute according to the rule “of debts and grains that have two vowels” (*ṛṇadhānyānāṃ ca dvyaṣām*). The word *pippala*, however, has its first syllable acute by the rule “that which ends in a long vowel” (*aghāvante*).

(1163) *bilvādibhyo’ṇ* |4|3|136|. The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after [the group of words] beginning with *bilva*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *añ*, *mayaṭ*, and others. The group beginning with *bilva* consists of: *bilva*, *vrīhi*, *kāṇḍa*, *mudga*, *masūra*, *godhūma*, *ikṣu*, *karpāsī*, *veṇu*, and so forth.
(1164) *trapu-jatunoḥ ṣuk* [Pāṇini 4.3.138]. Regarding *trapu-jatunoḥ*: because the word *aṇ* is understood from the rule *ilvādibhyo ’ṇ*, he says—“*aṇ* shall apply.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *torañ*. Since it does not begin with a living being (*aprāṇyādi*), it does not apply to a part.
