With the intention that "it becomes [so]," he says: "in the case of a modification" (*vikāre*). Regarding *trāpuṣam*: it is a modification of tin (*trapu*).
Similarly, a modification of lac (*jatu*) is *jātuṣam*.
(Pāṇini 4.3.139): *orañ*.
The word *orañ* is an example here other than those beginning with an *anudātta* vowel; for instance, *daivadāravam*.
The words *devadāru* and *bhadradāru* have their initial syllable accented (*udātta*) by the rule “*itardvarthānām*” and so forth.
(Pāṇini 4.3.140): *anudātādeśca*.

Regarding *dādhitya*: [it is derived] from the sense "that which stands in curds" (*dadhi tiṣṭhati*). By the rule *upa-sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.4), the suffix *ka* is applied. This is a compound with an upapada.
Due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the letter *s* is replaced by *t*.
The final syllable is udātta by the rule regarding the natural accent of the first member in a *kṛd-uttarapada* compound. The same should be understood for *kapittha* as well.
(1167) *Palāśādibhyo vā* |4|3|141|. From *palāśa* and the others, there is an option. This is an option applying in both cases (*ubhayatra-vibhāṣā*).
Since [the suffix] would necessarily apply to *palāśa*, *khadira*, *śiṃśapā*, and *syandana* because they begin with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*), [the rule provides an alternative].
Because the words *karīra*, *śirīṣa*, *vikaṅkata*, *pūlāsa*, *yavāsa*, and *śabda* are prescribed where they were not previously established.
Regarding the word *pālāśam*: the word *palāśa* is oxytone (accented on the final syllable) due to its inclusion in the *ghṛtādi* group.
The word *khadira* is derived from the root *khaḍ* with the suffix *kirac*, as prescribed in rules such as "in the sense of *ṭhajira* and *śiśira*," etc.

The word *śiṃśapā* has its middle syllable accented (*madhyodātta*) by the rule “*āntānāṃ gurvādīnām*” (Pāṇini 6.2.192), which applies while the rule “*atha dvitīyam prāg īṣāt*” (Pāṇini 6.2.144) is in force. [The word *kampyate*] is derived from the root *kapi* meaning “to move slightly,” with the suffix *yuc* according to the rule “*anudātetashca halādeḥ*” (Pāṇini 3.3.148). Regarding *kārīra*: it is formed from the root *kirati* with the suffix *īran*, [the accent being determined] by the *nit* designation.

This word *karīra* has its initial syllable accented acute (ādyaudāta), according to the rules “*ṛtṛbhyām īṣan*” and “*ṛpṛbhyāṃ kicca*. Similarly, the word *śirīṣa* also has its initial syllable accented acute as before. The words *vikaṅkata*, *pūlāsa*, and *yavāsa* have their initial syllables accented acute according to the rule “*rāmādīnāṃ ca*.”

(1168) *śamyāḥ ṣlañ* | 4|3|142|. Because it is marked with *ṣ*, there is *ṅīṣ*; because it is marked with *ṭ*, there is *ṅīṣ*; however, Mādhava says that because it is marked with *ṭ*, there is *ṅīp*. (1169) *mayaḍvaitayorbhāṣāyāmabhakṣyācchādānayoḥ* | 4|3|143|. In the common language (*bhāṣā*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is optionally used for these two [suffixes], except when they denote food or clothing.

[The rule] *mayaḍvaitayoḥ* [applies]. Why [is it said] "in the spoken language (*bhāṣāyām*)"? Because the author of the Vṛtti says: "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is made of *khadira* wood. If it is argued that this is already established because the suffix *mayaṭ* is optional, they say here: in the Veda, the suffix *mayaṭ* following a word with many vowels (*bahvac*) has exclusively a different meaning [from the base word].

This [mention of "in speech"] is solely for the purpose of apprehending the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Although this [rule] is already covered by the rule *vyacaś chandasi* if that sūtra is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) in the sense that "the substitution occurs only after *vyac*," nevertheless, the mention of "speech" (*bhāṣā*) was made to remove the suspicion of a contrary restriction, namely, that "it occurs only in the Veda after *vyac*."

Since the terms *vikāra* (modification) and *avayava* (part) are already obtained from the governing context (*adhikāra*), the explicit mention of "of these two" (*etayoḥ*) is for the purpose that the rule should also apply in the domain of those suffixes which convey specific meanings, such as *añ* prescribed after words like *rāji*, *rajata*, and so forth. For example: *kapotamayam* (made of pigeon[-bone]) and *lohamayam* (made of iron). In this case [the suffix is applied].

The term "vikāra" (modification) and "avayava" (part) are each connected with the phrase "ṭha [is used] after words meaning 'what is not edible' and 'covering'" due to the indication of a compound; therefore, there is no correspondence according to the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṅkhyam*). Regarding the form *āśmana*: by the rule stating, "Even without a suffix, the elision of either the first or the second member of a compound may be stated," the word *aśmabheda* [is formed].

When the suffix *bha* (indicating a distinction) is elided, "āśman" remains as a word ending in *n*. Similarly, the son named Aśmaka was begotten by Vasiṣṭha upon Madayantī, the wife of King Kalmaṣapāda;
in that case, because the suffix *ka* (which indicates a proper name) is absent, the name is simply "Aśman."

In its parts, it is called *āśmana*, and even in its modification (*vikāra*), it remains simply *āśmana*. Nor should it be argued that there would be a loss of the *ṭi* suffix (the *a* in *aśman*) by the rule "after *aśman* in the sense of a modification" (*aśmano vikāre*); for, due to its greater conventional usage, it is more appropriate to understand the word *pāṣāṇa* as the one intended there. In reality, however:

In the case of the general intention to express "this belongs to that," even the word *aśman*, which denotes a stone, will take the form *āśmana*— just as in the cases of *paiṣṭī surā* ("liquor made from flour") and *maudgaḥ sūpaḥ* ("soup made of mung beans")— as well as *kārpāsa* ("cotton"). This is because the word *mudga*...

[The word *ghṛta*] is oxytone because it belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group. From the root *kṛ*, by the rule *kṛñaḥ pāsaḥ*, the suffix *pāsa* is applied; with the resulting *guṇa* and the substitution of *ra* for the semivowel, the word *karpaśī* is formed, ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule for genus (*jāti*). From those two [words], the suffix *añ* prescribed by the rule *anudātādeśca* is set aside, and instead, the suffix *aṇ* is applied due to their inclusion in the *bilvādi* group.

(1170) *Nityaṃ vṛddha-śarādibhyaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.3.144. Regarding *nityaṃ vṛddha*: here, the commentary (*vṛtti*) states that the phrase “in common usage (*bhāṣāyām*), except for food and clothing (*abhakṣyācchādanayoḥ*)” is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). Now, [one might object]: if this is so, then in the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa*, Śaṅkarācārya [wrote] “another...”.
In the Śruti text, "The Self consists of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), it is stated that the suffix *mayaṭ* denotes a modification (*vikāra*).

How, then, is this consistent? If it is argued that it would be more appropriate to say that *mayaṭ* here denotes abundance (*prācurye mayaṭ*), the following is said in response: even if *mayaṭ* denotes abundance, there remains the presence of suffering (*duḥkha*), which is contrary to the meaning of the base word (*prakṛtyartha*).

Their intention is that, because it is obtained through partial recurrence (*leśato’nuvṛtti-lābhāt*), the meaning of "modification" (*vikāra*) is established in the present context. Alternatively, in the rule *ityaṃ vṛddha* (Pāṇini 4.3.140), the mention of "colloquial speech" (*bhāṣā*) does not recur;
even if it were to recur, one may assume that *mayaṭ* is used invariably in colloquial speech, while elsewhere it is only occasional.

It is easily established. Alternatively, while the rule *hetumanuṣyebhyaḥ* is still in effect, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied in the sense of "obtained from" (*āgata*) by the sūtra *ayaṭ ca*. The mention of "modification" (*vikāra*) is merely an explanation of the implied meaning. Therefore, the statement of Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda is indeed faultless. Regarding the term *śaramayam*: *śara*, *darbha*, and *mṛtkaṭī* [are the materials].

*tṛṇa*, *soma*, and *balvaja* belong to the *śara* group [of words]. Regarding the rule *ekāco nityam*: the mention of *nityam* (always) in the rule *nityaṃ vṛddhe* is for the purpose of prescribing [the suffix] in some other instances as well by means of a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*); such is the intended meaning by which this result is obtained.

They say that since the [suffix] is already established by the fact of having a single vowel (*ekāctva*), the inclusion of the word *mṛd* among the items beginning with *śat* is for the sake of clarity.

(1171) *gośca purīṣe* | 4.3.145. "And after *go*, [the suffix *yañ* is applied] in the sense of 'its dung. Dung is neither a modification (*vikāra*) nor a constituent part (*avayava*); nevertheless, it is expressed as 'this belongs to that' (*asyeda*)."

This suffix is used in the sense of "belonging to" (matvarthe). However, the suffix *yat* will be taught for the words *go* and *payas* in the senses of "modification" (*vikāra*) and "part" (*avayava*). Why [is it not taught] for *purīṣa*? [Because the suffix would not apply there; e.g.,] *gavyam payaḥ* ("cow's milk").
(1172) [The suffix *yat* is applied] after the words *tila* and *yava*. Pāṇini 4.3.149.

Regarding the word *yāvaka*: from the word *yava*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of a product (*vikāra*); then, from that form ending in *aṇ*, the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārtha*) by the rule *yāvādibhyaḥ*. (Pāṇini 5.4.29).
[Also: *tālādibhyo’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.152).

Regarding the rule *tālādibhyo’ṇ*: it says "after [words ending in] *añ* and *mayaṭ*. From the words *tāla* and *śyāmāka*, *mayaṭ* would have been expected because they contain the *vṛddhi* vowel. *Bārhiṇam* means "a product of peacocks" (*barhiṇ*).
By the rule *rāṇirajatādibhyo’ñ*, the suffix *añ* is applied; subsequently, by the rule *ñitaśca tatpratyayāt*, *añ* would again have been expected.

From the remaining [roots], however, the suffix *añ* would apply because they begin with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*). For instance, from the roots *viś* and *dṛś*, with the word *indra* as an upapada, the suffix *ka* applies according to the rule for the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*. By the rule *anyeṣām api*, the lengthening of the vowel occurs. Thus we have *indraviśaḥ* and *indrādṛśaḥ*. From the root *ap* in the sense of "consoling," the suffix *ac* is applied after the prefix *apa*; thus we have the word *āpapīyūkṣā*.

The word *aghāvanta-* is middle-accented (*madhyodātta*). In the case of *hiṣaḥ*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied from the root *hiṣ* even before the accentuation takes effect, because it belongs to the *ādi-kārāḥ* group. The word *indrāyudha-* is end-accented (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*). The mention of the suffix *aṇ* is for the purpose of preventing the sublation [of the intended accent] by other rules; thus, when a suffix is prescribed according to the rule, the suffix characterized by *vṛddhi* applies after the word *bārhi-*.

They say that the suffix *mayaṭ* should apply here, because the statement [of the rule] finds its purpose by overriding the suffix *añ* through the rule "and after a word ending in *ṭh* or *ñi*, [the suffix *mayaṭ* is used]. The phrase "tālāddhanuṣi" is a *gaṇasūtra*. Regarding the word *hāṭaka*:
here, the suffix *mayaṭ* conditioned by the [word being] *vṛddha* would otherwise have applied.
Regarding *tapanīya* and so forth—the suffix *añ* would have been applicable by the rule "anudātādeśca" (Pāṇini 4.3.140). (1174) *prāṇirajatādibhyo’ñ* (Pāṇini 4.3.154):
[The word] *prāṇi*. Since the suffix *añ* is already established for words beginning with an anudātta vowel, this is an example of the remaining cases.

Thus he says: "śaukaṃ bākam" (made of parrot-feathers, made of crane-feathers). The words *śuka* and *baka* have the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable according to the rule "of Pāṇini’s followers, those beginning with a guttural [have the acute on the first syllable]. Regarding "rājatam" (made of silver): *rajata*, *sīsa*, *udumbara*, *kaṇṭakāra*, and so forth, are the words beginning with *rajata*. Among these, the repetition of those beginning with an anudātta [is for the sake of a specific grammatical application].
The suffix *mayaṭ* is for the purpose of setting aside [the application of] *mayaṭ*. Otherwise, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], *mayaṭ* would indeed apply.
(1175) *Ñitaśca tatpratyayāt* |4|3|155|. From *śāmīla*, the suffix *imi*. The word *śāmīla* ends in *ṣlañ*, as per the rule *amyāḥ ṣlañ*. From *dadhittha*...
The suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *ṭhānudātādeśca*. Thus, from *dāḍhitti*, we have *dāḍhittha*; and from *bilva*, we have *bailvama* (meaning "made of *bilva* wood").
The word *bilva* ends in the suffix *aṇ*.
(1176) *krītavat parimāṇāt* | 4.3.156 | [The suffixes prescribed after words denoting measure are applied] as [they are applied] after words [denoting price] in the sense of having purchased.

Regarding *naiṣkikam*: [the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *tena krītam*. Thus, *śatyaḥ* and *śatikaḥ*; [the suffixes] *ṭhan* and *ṭhañ* are applied by the rule *ataśca ṭhanyatau*. (Pāṇini 5.1.20).
[The suffix *kan* is applied] optionally after *ūru* and *ūrṇā*. (Pāṇini 5.1.158).

Regarding the term *aṇañau*: the word *umā* is udātta on its first syllable according to the rule “*ṛṇadhānyānāṃ ca*” and so forth; however, the word *ūrṇā* is udātta on its final syllable by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). This is the intended meaning. (1178) *eṇyā ḍhañ* | Pāṇini 4.3.159.

The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after *eṇī*; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *añ* prescribed for living beings. Because of the mention of the feminine gender, he says: "of the male *eṇa*. (Pāṇini 4.3.160) *gopayasoryat*:

[the suffix] *yat* is applied after *go* and *payas*. Although *yat* is prescribed everywhere in place of [the suffixes] that would otherwise apply to *go* when followed by vowels other than *a*, etc., nevertheless—
In the alternative view that "it is not a dvita," this rule for *yat* is stated again in order to set aside the *mayaṭ* suffix that would otherwise apply.
This [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to both *torañaḥ* and *ekāco nityam*, as well as to *mayaṭ*.

Regarding the word *dravya*: it is derived from the root *dru* (to run/flow) with the suffix *yat* according to the rule *aco yat*, based on the etymology "it is that which is run to (*drūyate*) or resorted to (*āśrīyate*) by qualities (*guṇaiḥ*). This is distinct from the word *dravya* as it is employed in rules such as *orguṇaḥ*, *vānto yi pratyaye*, and *dravyaguṇakarmasu*.

(1181) *māne vayaḥ* |4|3|162|. The suffix *vaya* is applied [after the word *dru*] when a measure (*māna*) is denoted. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning *yat*. Thus, *druvayam* means "a measure such as a *prastha* that is a modification (*vikāra*) of wood (*dru*)."

(1182) *phale luk* |4|3|163|. Regarding the rule *phale luk*: [it applies] under the heading *vikārāvayava-* (P. 4.3.134). The fruit of a tree that has borne fruit is both a part (*avayava*) and a modification (*vikāra*). Therefore, the suffix is applied optionally to either sense. In the word *āmalakam*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *mayaṭ*.

There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṅīṣ* by the rule "when there is elision of an *addhita* suffix" (*uktaddhitaluki*). Nor should one suspect here that the elision [of the final vowel] would apply by the rule "and that which is designated as *yasya*" (*yasyeti ca*), because it is accepted that "what is elided by *uk* is not subject to *sthānivadbhāva*.
For this very reason, in the case of *pañcapaṭuḥ*—meaning "bought for five clever women"—the rule "in the case of *adhyardha* and those preceded by a numeral" (*adhyardhapūrve*) applies.

When the suffix *ṭhañ* has been elided by *luk*, because the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is also elided by *luk*, it lacks the status of being "as if present" (*sthānivat*); consequently, the *yaṇ* substitution for the vowel *u* does not take place.
(Pāṇini 4.3.164): *plakṣādibhyo ’ṇ*.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [the group of words] beginning with *plakṣa*; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *añ*. From the words *śigru* and *karkandhū*, the suffix *arañ* (which is the same as *aṇ*) applies by the rule "after *śigru* and *karkandhū*, the suffix *arañ*. From other [words in the list], however, the suffix *añ* would otherwise apply because they begin with an unaccented vowel (*anudātādi*). [The list is: *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, *iṅgudī*, *śigru*, *karkandhū*, *bṛhatī*. Among these, the word *plakṣa*...
The word *hiṣa* is udātta on the final syllable. The word *nyagrodha* is udātta on the middle syllable by the rule *aghāvante*.

The word *aśvattha*, however, is udātta on the final syllable because it belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group. The words *iṅgudī* and *bṛhatī* end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the *gaurādi* class. [The compound] *āśvatthavaiṇavaplākṣanaiyagrodhaiṅgudam*...
*phale* [is used], according to Amara;

(1184) *nyagrodhasya ca kevalasya* 7.3.5. [The rule states: *nyagrodhasya ca*. Why [does it say] *kevalasya* ("of the solitary")? [Consider: *nyagrodhamūle bhavā* ("born at the root of a *nyagrodha* tree").

*nyāgrodhamūlāḥ*—rice plants. In the view that *nyagrodha* is derived from the etymology "that which grows downwards" (*nyak rohati*), [the rule] is for the purpose of restriction; however, in the view that it is not so derived, it is for the purpose of an injunction. (1185) *jambvā vā* | 4.3.165.

Regarding the word *jambu*: it takes the neuter short vowel [by Pāṇini 4.3.163]. As it is said: "O farmer! *jambū* is feminine; *jambu* and *jāmbava* are [neuter]. There is an addition to the rule regarding words that wither upon the ripening of their fruit (*phalapākaśuṣām upasaṅkhyānam*). Regarding the term "ripening of fruit" (*phalapāka*): [it refers to those] which wither through the ripening of their fruit.

*phalapākaśuṣaḥ* (fruits that wither upon ripening), *vrīhayaḥ* (rice grains), and *mudgaḥ* (mung beans). [In these cases,] there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ* derived from *bilva* and others. Regarding flowers and roots, [the suffix is applied] diversely (*bahulam*). In *mallikā*, there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix *añ* characterized by being anudātta;
furthermore, according to the *phiṭ-sūtra* "ādīnāṃ ca," the second syllable in the word *mallikā* is udātta.

The words *jātī* and *vidārī* end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. In the case of *pāṭalāni*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied because they belong to the *bilvādi* group. The word *sālva* is udātta on the final syllable by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
(Pāṇini 4.3.167: *harītakyādibhyaśca*) [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the group beginning with *harītakī*].

And [the suffix is elided] after *harītakī* and so forth. Here, after words such as *drākṣā*, there is the elision (*lup*) of the suffix *mayaṭ* which would otherwise apply by the rule "after [words] with a high-pitched vowel (*vṛddha*), [there is] *mayaṭ*"; after those beginning with an anudātta vowel, the suffix *añ*; and after the others, the suffix *aṇ*. As for the statement "only the gender [is transferred]," the number (gender) indeed follows the qualified object itself, because it has been stated that "in the case of *harītakī* and so forth, the individual entity (*vyakti*) [is the basis]."
The state [of being]. (1187) *kaṃsīya-paraśavyayoḥ yañañau luk ca* |4|3|168|.
Regarding *kaṃsīyam*: under the governing rule *krītāt chaḥ* ("the suffix *cha* after words ending in *krīta*"), the suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule *asmai hitam* ("suitable for this").
And as an exception (*apavāda*) to that *cha* suffix, [the rule] "from *paraśu* and others, *yat*" applies: *paraśavyaṃ dāru* ("wood for an axe").

Since the word *paraśavya* begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātādi*), the suffix *añ* would have been established [by P. 4.3.134]; therefore, this statement is made so that *yat* may take its place in conjunction with it. Nor does the elision of *ya* by the rule "of that which belongs to *iti*" (P. 6.4.148) apply here, because of the rule "of a taddhita suffix beginning with a consonant" (P. 6.4.150).
One should not be deluded into thinking that the desired form is established by the elision of *ya*, because the word *īt* continues [from the previous rule].

Thus ends the section on derivatives expressing modification (*vikāra*) and those beginning with *prādīvyatīya* in the *Tattvabodhinī*. Now follows the euphonic combination of the visarga (*visargasandhi*).
(120) The visarga is replaced by *s*.
As in "viṣṇuḥ trātā" (Viṣṇu is the protector). When the suffix *su* is added to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) according to the rule "from a nominal stem [comes] *su*, *au*, *jas*, etc.," then...
When *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) has been applied by the rule "ahar-avasānayoḥ" and the *visarga* has been produced, [the rule] "visarjanīyasya saḥ" applies to change it to *s*.

Furthermore, one should not suspect the occurrence of *rutva* for this [final *s*], because the status of the *visarjanīya* as being *sat* (i.e., the presence of the *s*) is considered *asiddha* with respect to *rutva*.

(121) *śarpare visarjanīyaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.35. Regarding *śarpare visarjanīyaḥ*: *śarpare* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The term *khari*, which is being carried over [from the previous rule], is the word for the other member (*anyapadārtha*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *s* (*satva*) and so forth. However, if [the word] were *arpare*...

If it were not stated [as "not so"], then even though the original *satva* (the substitution of *s*) has been prohibited, the substitutions of *k* and *p* for *kup* would still occur in cases such as *vāsaḥ kṣaumam* and *adbhiḥ psātam*.
With the intention that the mention of *visarjanīya* serves only to block the mere modification [of the *s*], he says: "no."
"But it is something else. He clarifies this very point with the words "here" (*iha*).

(122) *so’padādau* | 8|3|38|. [The rule] *so’padādau*. [The commentary says: "In the two words *apadādyoḥ*, there is a singular number used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*) in the sūtra. However, if..."

In the rule *ṭhvisarjanīyasya saḥ*, the term *khaḥ* (the letter *kh*) is carried over by *maṇḍūkapluti* from the rule *arpare visarjanīyaḥ*; if that *khaḥ* were also carried over here and specified as "when followed by *r*" (*rapare*), such that the rule would read *apadādau raḥ*, then [the form] would be correct according to the literal text. However...
The sense is that there would be the labor of repeating [the rule] like the leap of a frog. Others, however, say:

it is possible to carry on even without the "frog-leap"; for in the rule *vā śari*, by taking *khar* as the qualifier of *śari* and explaining it as *akārānta-rūpe khari*, [the application of] *upvoḥ*...

And because there is no harm in explaining the sūtra as *upvoḥ kharī* [Pāṇini 8.4.64]. Regarding *payaspāśam*: [the suffix] *pāśap* is applied in the sense of "somewhat" (*īṣad*), *kalpap* in the sense of "incompleteness" (*īṣadasamāpti*), *ka* in the senses of "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and "excessive" (*utsita*), and *kāmyac* by the rule *āmyacce*. [This occurs] in the context of the suffixes *pāśa*, *kalpa*, *ka*, and *kāmya*.
Commentary: This is an illustration of possibility, not an exhaustive enumeration, because nothing else is possible.

Regarding the term *prātaḥkalpam*: although the word *prātaḥ* primarily denotes the locative capacity (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), in this context within a compound (*vṛtti*), it refers to that which possesses the capacity (*śaktimat*), meaning "the day that has become morning" (*oṣābhūtam ahaḥ*) or "that which has become daylight."
It is like the word *rātriḥ*. [One might argue:

"In the case of *gīḥ kāmyati*, even though there is a negation of *satva* (the substitution of *s*), would not *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) apply here by the rule *ṭhiṇaḥ ṣaḥ*? This should not be said; for even in that rule, the phrase *āmye roreva* is understood to carry over. However, if [one were to apply] *ṭhiṇaḥ ṣaḥ*...
In this very context, it is read as follows: "If, then, even when there is a prohibition of *ṣatva* alone, *satva* would still occur by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 8.3.70].
*Inaḥ ṣaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.39] is an exception (*apavāda*) to *so’padādau* [8.3.38]. (124) *Namaspurasorgatyoḥ* [8.3.40]:
as in *puraḥ praveṣṭavyāḥ*. [The root] *ṛ* [is used] in the sense of protecting and filling; [the form is derived] by [the rule] *bhrājabhās...* etc. [Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.177].
The suffix *kvip* [is applied]. The nominative plural (*jas*) follows that which ends in it. To make clear that they end in the nominative plural (*jas*), the example "ūḥ purā" was introduced.
(125) Pāṇini 8.3.41: *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya*.
[The rule] *idudupadhasya* [applies]. Why [specify] *idut*? [Consider: *gīḥ karoti*, *pūḥ karoti*.

Here, the connection is one of different grammatical loci (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*): "of that aggregate which has *i* or *u* as its penultimate [element], the *visarga* which is a constituent part thereof [is replaced]. However, in the case of the rule *apratyayasya*, it refers to "the *visarga* which is [the substitute for] the suffix *ap*."

Thus it is connected [to the preceding]. For when grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, it is improper to assume a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Nor should it be said that the status of the *visarga* as a suffix (*pratyaya*) is unestablished, because in examples such as "agniḥ karoti" (the fire acts), [it is indeed established].

This is because that [substitution] is established through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original). Nor should it be suspected that the *tripādī* (the final three chapters of Pāṇini’s grammar) is *asiddha* (non-existent/ineffective) with respect to an *atideśa* (extended application), for this is already established by the very prohibition in the rule *ṭhapratyayasya*. For this very reason, the substitution of *visarga* for *ru* in forms such as *agniḥ* is accomplished; otherwise, it would not occur because the *ru* would not be at the end of a word (*apadānta*).

The rule for *visarga* (the rule *unaḥ*, etc.), however, has its application in cases such as *unā*. Furthermore, an indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends upon a specific context; therefore, the rule *ṭhasya eṣ icaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* does not apply to forms like *trāpādyām*.
Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that "in the case of what is not established [by a subsequent rule], there is no *sthānivadbhāva*" is based on the reasoning stated above.
However, it is established in the *Manoramā* that [the rule] is based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*).

On this point, they say: in the rule "of the suffix *ṭha*" (*ṭhapratyayasya*), the meaning established by the letter *ā* is precisely that the *visarjanīya* which belongs to the suffix *ṭha* does not [become *ś*]; thus, [the phrase] "the *visarjanīya* which is the suffix *ṭha*" [is understood].

Co-referential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not tenable; for even though the optional substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "ṭhisusoḥ sāmarthye" applies in the case of *arpis karoti*, there would result the obligatory substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "idudupadhasya ca" in the sentence *iṣṭatu sarpiḥ pibatu tvam udakam*.

Nor should it be argued that even in the opinion of Akalaṅka, since the suffixes beginning with *uṇ* are accepted as being based on non-etymological derivation (*avyutpatti*), the desired conclusion is already established; for if one relies on etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), the defect remains as it was. This is evident from the example "he prepares ghee" (*arpiṣkaroti*) given under the rule *ṭhisusoḥ*.

This is because it can be inferred that the author of the Vārttika accepts only the position of *vyutpatti* (derivation); otherwise, since the optional application of *ṣatva* would already be established by the rule *ṭhidudupadhasya* itself through the distinction between the *vyutpatti* and *avyutpatti* positions, the citation of that example [in the Vārttika] would result in being irrelevant. Furthermore:

In cases such as *iṣṭatu sarpiḥ*, since the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ṭhidudupadhasya* is desired, there would be a contradiction with one's own fundamental text, which states: "The word *sarpiṣkuṇḍikā* is included among the *kaska*-type words for the sake of [the substitution of] *ṣ*, even when it is not a compound and even in the absence of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). Regarding this:

Some say that although it would have been sufficient to state "of a *visarga* not preceded by *ṛ* or *u*" (*ṛt-udbhdyām-apratyayasya*), the inclusion of the term "having *ṛ* or *u* as its penultimate" (*ṛt-ud-upadhasya*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs only for a *visarga* that has *ṛ* or *u* as its penultimate,
so that it does not apply in cases such as "avibhiḥ kṛtam," which is the *visarga* of the case-ending *bhis*. For...

[The opponent argues: "In cases such as *ṛāmaiḥ*, there is no constant state of having *it* or *ut* as a penultimate vowel (*idudupadhātva*), because that [state] is absent there. This is not correct;

for if that were so, the general rule (*āharaṇa*) would become inconsistent due to the prohibition in the case of *agniḥ karoti*. Furthermore, in cases such as *eva*, there is the state of having the vowel *a* as a penultimate (*akāropadhatva*), and in cases such as *riyacatvā*, there is the state of having the vowel *ā* as a penultimate (*ākāropadhatvena*).
This argument— that [the rule] would fail to apply in cases such as *atuṣkapāla* due to the non-occurrence of *ṣatva*— is trivial. Others, however,

maintain that if one provides an explanation such as "the *visarjanīya* which belongs to a suffix marked with Ṭ does not [become ṣ]," then since *ṣatva* would not apply in the aforementioned examples anyway, the requirement of the word *upadhā* (penultimate) could be easily dispensed with.

It might be argued as follows: It was stated that the very mention of the suffix *ṭha* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, with respect to the rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ*, the Tripādī is established [as having authority].
However, this would not be established for those who accept the connection [of the words] through grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). On this point, they say: "Not *mu*..."

In the rule *ne’* (Pāṇini 6.1.65), the word *e* is separated as a distinct *yoga*, and it is explained that "with respect to the sūtra *sthānivat* (1.1.56), the *tripādī* is not *asiddha*. Furthermore,
indications such as *pratyayaḥ* (3.1.1) and *paraśca* (3.1.2) are favorable to this interpretation.

Because the purpose of the *yogavibhāga* (the splitting of a rule) is to establish what is desired, [the visarga] remains indeed *asiddha* with respect to the rule "ṭhacaḥ parasmin—" (Pāṇini 1.1.57). Consequently, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "when what precedes is *asiddha*, there is no *sthānivadbhāva*" (Pāṇini 1.1.58) is grounded in reason; thus, everything is consistent. [This applies to] the visarga which is not a suffix (*apratyaya*).

Thus, regarding the position of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he states— "of that which is caused by a rule for a single substitute"— anticipating the objection that in forms such as *kṛpe* from *kartuḥ*, there would be the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ṭhidudupadhasya*. For in the case of *kartuḥ*, the rule for a single substitute, *ṛta ut*, is the indirect cause (*paramparayā prayojaka*) for the visarga.

In the original treatise (*ākara*), however, the prevalent reading is *ṭhakādeśanimittād iti*. Therein, "ekādeśa" refers to the grammatical rule for single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa-śāstra*); the meaning is "from that [word] whose vowel *u* is caused by such a rule.
Now, one might object: if this is so, then the view of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the rule *ṭhapratyayasya* is also sanctioned by the original treatise.

If they say here: "The view that 'conjunction is a single entity'—though accepted in the foundational treatises—is as devoid of purpose as this [other] view; rather, the view of non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is absolutely necessary. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*apatti*) of the failure of such expressions as 'Let him eat ghee; you drink water.'"

Regarding the statement "because of the recitation of the word *bhrātuṣputra*": one should not argue that since the rule for single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is "asiddha" (non-existent) by the rule *atvatukorasiddhaḥ*, the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) does not apply, and therefore the recitation of that [word] in the list is merely for the purpose of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) and not for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpaka*). For [the rule *atvatukorasiddhaḥ* applies only] when *atva* or *tuka* is to be applied to the end of a word and the beginning of a word.

This is because of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that "only a portion of *sat* itself is unestablished" (*asiddha*). Otherwise, even in the case of *akaḥ ṣu*, the substitution of *ṣ* would not occur. In the derivation of *śakahvāḥ*—meaning "those who call the Śakas"—after the substitution of *ā* by the rule "ādeca upadeśe," the elision of the suffix (*kvip*), and the occurrence of *saṃprasāraṇa*, [the form *śakahvāḥ* is derived] by the rule "aṃprasāraṇācca."

And when there is a single-substitute [resulting from] the preceding form, the lengthening [prescribed] by the rule *ṭhalaḥ* occurs; for indeed, in examples such as *o'sicat* and *o'sica*, the substitute occurs at the junction of the end of one word and the beginning of another. Consequently, the prohibition of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) is established in those cases, but not in the case of *akaḥ ṣu*. And thus, it is also the case in *hrātuṣputra*.

It has been stated that the rule for single-substitute (ekādeśa) taught in *ādaṛtukoḥ* is not *asiddha*; thus, the [implication of the] indicator (*jñāpaka*) remains perfectly sound. [Objection: On account of the aforementioned indicator, would there not likewise be an absence of *ṣatva* in *akṛṣvi*, just as in *āduḥ kṛpe*? [Reply: Not so; for the indicator applies only to things of a similar class.
And what is of the same class [as *ku*]? That which is [the word] *kupvoḥ*; such is the direction [of the argument]. (126) *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur* [are used] in the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas*).
8.3.22. Regarding *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur*: here, from the two words *dvi* and *tri* ending in *su*...

By virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), the word *catur* shall also be understood as having the suffix *su* (i.e., *catuḥ*). However, the inclusion of the term *kṛtvo'rtha* (meaning "expressing frequency") serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that association does not always determine the application [of a rule]. Consequently, in the rule *īd-īd-vevīṭām*, even though there is association with verbal roots (*dhātu*), the augment (*āgama*) *iṭ* is included.

Regarding the term *catuṣkapāla*: it means "prepared in four potsherds" (*caturṣu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ*). Here, the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed by the rule] *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* is elided by the rule *vigor lug anapatye*. In this regard, the *Manoramā* states that the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] is obligatory by the rule *ṭhidudupadhasya*. And thus, [the form] *vitaṃ*...

The usage "tritam" in the author's own root-text (svamūlagrantha) in the verse beginning with "catuḥpañcāśat" would be questionable, because even there, as in the case of "catuṣkapāla," the substitution of *ṣ* would necessarily apply. Therefore, in order to prevent that *ṣ*-substitution here, [the rule] "of the suffix" (*pratyayasya*) must be interpreted as "of the *visarjanīya* which belongs to the suffix."

The very meaning [of the rule] must be accepted as follows: they say that in the case of *atuṣkapāla*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs because the group beginning with *kaska-* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. (127) *isusoḥ sāmarthye* | Pāṇini 8.3.44.
"Even in the absence of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*)" means, for example, in such cases as "iṣṭatu sarpiṣkuṇḍikām ānaya" ("Bring the vessel of clarified butter").

(128) *Nityaṃ samāse ’nutarapadasthasya* | Pāṇini 4.3.45. [In a compound, the suffix *ṣyañ* is always applied to the word ending in *sarpiṣ*, provided it does not stand at the end of a subsequent member.]
Regarding the phrase "in the case of expectancy" (*vyapekṣāyām*): the meaning is "in this [example], *idaṃ sarpiṣkuṇḍikāyāḥ*.

It should be understood that here the word *sarpiḥ* is an uncompounded term. For if it were a compound, the rule would already be established by the statement "in such a compound," and thus this [present rule] is intended to indicate the absence of compounding.

The word *sapir* has been stated as a qualifier, and [the word] *nityārthaḥ* [is also used]. This is the intended meaning: in the case of a non-compound (*asamāsa*), since there is no mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) and [the rule] would otherwise never apply (*atyantāprāpti*), the reading is for the sake of making the substitution of *ṣ* obligatory (*nityatayā*).
However, in the case of a non-compound where there is mutual expectancy, since the rule "ṭhisusoḥ" applies optionally, the reading is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nityārtha*).

(129) *ataḥ kṛkami-kaṃsa-kumbha-pātra-kuśā-karṇīṣv-anavyayasya* |8|3|36|. [The rule] "combined with *ayas*" [is applied]; however, it does not mean "a modification (*vikāra*) of iron," because [if it were so], the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not apply due to the prohibition in the rule *āna-pade*. [The example] *ayaskarṇī* means "one whose ears are like iron. [The feminine suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *āsikodara*.

*adhaḥśirasi*: regarding these two, it should be understood that in the *sūtra*, the nominative case is used in place of the genitive. *adhaspadam*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "below the foot" (*padasyādhaḥ*). The compound is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. *śiraspadam*: this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Thus ends the section on the euphonic combination of the visarga (*visargasandhi*) in the *Tattvabodhinī*. Now begins the section on the formation of the *yaṅ* (intensive) stem:

"The suffix *yaṅ* is added to a root that consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*), begins with a consonant (*halādi*), and denotes the frequent repetition (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) of an action" (Pāṇini 3.1.22).

Since it has been stated that [the suffix yaṅ] occurs after a root (*dhātu*) when there is an intensification of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), one might ask why the rule specifies "after a root" (*dhātoḥ*) since it would follow from the context that it applies to a root and not to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
[The sūtra] asks: "Why [say] 'after a root' (*dhātoḥ*)?

(396) *guṇo yaṅ-lukoḥ* | 7|4|82|. [This sūtra provides the answer: "There is guṇa substitution for the vowel of a monosyllabic root before the suffix yaṅ and before luk-elision. [This implies that the restriction to roots is necessary because the operation of guṇa is prescribed specifically for the root-vowel.]

Regarding the phrase "bruvo vaciḥ" and so forth: the meaning is that the purpose [of the rule] is the derivation of forms such as *vācyate* (it is spoken) and *ākhyāyate* (it is told). Furthermore, in the absence of the mention of the word "dhātu" (root), the suffix would also apply to the indeclinable *dhik*, because it expresses an action and consists of a single vowel; therefore, the mention of "dhātu" is also for the sake of excluding that.

They say that the mention of the term *dhātu* (root) is necessary. Regarding the rule *yasya halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.49), it is stated that there is a reference to a "cluster" (*saṅghāta*). By this, [the rule applies] in cases such as *īrṣyitā* and *aharyīt*.

The elision of *y* does not [apply here]. Because the mention of a "cluster" (*saṅghāta*) brings to mind the paribhāṣā "the mention of a meaningful unit," there is no over-extension [of the rule] to cases such as *putrakāmyā*. However, in the case of a mention of a single phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), since the aforementioned paribhāṣā is not brought to bear, the elision of *y* would indeed occur here; this is the intended meaning. Why [is it specified] "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*)?
*lolūyitā*, *popūyitā*.

(398) *dīrgho’kitaḥ* | [Pāṇini 7.4.83] "The long vowel [is substituted for the reduplicated syllable] when it is not followed by *kit*. Why say "not followed by *kit*" (*akitaḥ*)? Consider: *yaṃyamyate*, *raṃramyate*. Now, [an objection is raised:]...
By means of the "long" (dīrgha) [rule] which has been brought forward,
the term "of the reduplication" (abhyāsasya), which is carried over from the rule "there is elision of the reduplication" (ṭha-lopo'bhyāsasya), would be qualified.
Consequently, because the meaning would be that "a long vowel occurs for a reduplication ending in a vowel," [the long vowel] would apply only in cases such as *pāpacyate*.

The long vowel [substitution] would not apply in cases such as *jaṅghanīti*, because once the *nuṭ* augment has been applied there by virtue of its higher priority, the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) no longer ends in a vowel (*ajanta*); thus, the possibility of the long vowel even arising does not exist. So what is the purpose of this rule *akitaḥ*? Nor can it be argued that the long vowel applies to the vowel that is a constituent part of the reduplicated syllable.
If one were to accept a construction based on different grammatical substrata (*vaiyadhikaraṇya-anvaya*), it would have to be argued that the mention of *akit* is purposeful;

however, when a construction based on identical substrata (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, a construction based on different substrata is improper. Furthermore, by the maxim of "that which applies where another does not" (*yena nāprāpti-nyāya*), the rule for *kit* is accepted as an exception (*apavāda*) to the lengthening [of the vowel]. Therefore, [the term used is] *akitaḥ*.

If it is argued that this is futile, they say here: in the case of *ḍoḍhāṬkyate*, since the rule "the short vowel of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsahrasva*) is superseded by the subsequent rule "a long vowel for a root not ending in /i/" (*dīrgho’kitaḥ*), the form would result in *ḍoḍhāṬkyate*. Therefore, among the modifications of the reduplicated syllable, the rules prescribing the general operation (*utsarga-vidhi*) do not supersede those that are exceptions (*bādhaka*).

The mention of *akitaḥ* must be made for the sake of providing this indication (*jñāpana*). Thus, in order to justify the aforementioned indication, one must resort to the grammarians' position that "the vowel of the reduplicated syllable" [is meant] in the rule *dīrgho’kitaḥ*; consequently, in forms such as *yaṃyamyate*, the *nuṭ* augment occurs even before the lengthening takes place.

Even if [the suffix] *k* were applied, the form would still be long; therefore, the restriction "provided there is no *kit*" (*akitaḥ*) is necessary—this is the general direction. Regarding the example *aṭāṭyata*: here, the doubling (*dvitvam*) applies to the word *ṭaḷ*.
(Pāṇini 7.4.30: *yaṅ ci*).
Furthermore, what [is the point]? Here, everything including “*uṇo ṛtisaṃyogādyoḥ*” is understood to follow.

[The rule] “of the *repha* followed by *yakāra*” means that if the example in the Bhāṣya were an indicator (*jñāpaka*) based on a general consideration, then forms such as *āryam ākhyat* and *āraryat* would be established.

(400) *nityaṃ kauṭilye gatau* | 3|1|23|. Regarding the word *nityam* [in the rule], he states that the word *nityam* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇārthaka*), namely: "only in the case of crookedness" (*kauṭilya eva*). Although the desired result is established by the *takrakauṇḍinyanyāya* (the maxim of the curd for Kauṇḍinya), the inclusion of the word *nitya* serves to indicate that...

This is for the purpose of making known that the rule of *nyāya* (logical consistency) is not absolute. Consequently, since the suffix *kta* is not barred by the rule "after words meaning 'excessive' (*ati*), 'intelligence' (*buddhi*), or 'worship' (*pūjā*)," the *kta* suffix is established after words meaning worship in the sense of the past tense. Therefore, the genitive case prescribed by the rule "and [the genitive] for that [participle] in the sense of the present" does not apply; thus, one says "he who has been worshipped" (*pūjitaḥ*).

In the expression "surāsuraiḥ," the instrumental case is indeed correct. Regarding the phrase "and so forth": *jaṃjabhyate*, *daṃdahyate*, *daṃdaśyate*, *baṃbhajyate*. The root *as* ending in a dental [s], which is Vedic (sautra) and means "to go," is mentioned by Mādhava in the commentary on the rule *spaśa bādhanasparśanayoḥ*. [Examples include: *paṃpasyate*. However, in the *Kāśikā*:

In some cases, a palatal [consonant] is seen at the end; for example, *jañjabhīti*. Likewise, forms such as *dandahīti* and others should be cited as examples of the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*). (401) *gro yaṅi* (Pāṇini 8.2.20).
Furthermore, from the rule *‘ṛpo ro liḥ’*, the phrase *ro la* (repha becomes la) continues [into this context].
Thus he says: "the substitution of *la* for *repha*. Regarding *cekrīyate*: because the rule for *rīṅ* is subsequent, *rīṅ* is applied first, and then reduplication.
In *saṃceskrīyate*, after *rīṅ* and reduplication, the augment *suṭ* is added. Nor is there—

It should not be argued that in this state, because *suṭ* follows after a double consonant (*dvitva*), the *guṇa* substitution would occur before the application of *rīṅ* due to the word beginning with a conjunct (*saṃyoga*);
for by the introduction of the rule "even when there is intervention by *aṭ* or reduplication" (*aḍabhyāsavyavāye’pi*), *suṭ* applies only when *aṭ* and the reduplication have already been performed.

This is because of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that [the operation] occurs prior to that. By this, the resolution offered by some—namely, "there is no guna due to the status of being preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*), because the augment *uṭ* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*)"—is refuted.
For when *suṭ* is applied after the reduplication, it belongs to the entire stem (*aṅga*) including the reduplication.

Because there is no occurrence of the state of beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) or ending in the vowel *ṛ*, there is an absence of the application of the augment *guṇa*. Now, [one might object]:

in order to reject the Vārttika "even when there is intervention by the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the augment *suṭ* comes before the *k*," the author of the Bhāṣya accepted the position that "the root is first joined with the prefix (*upasarga*)," and thus... *saṃ*... [is formed].
In such cases, because *suṭ* is internal (*antaraṅga*), it is accepted that the doubling applies to the form including *suṭ* itself;

thus, the form *saṃceṣkriyate* would not be established. For if *suṭ* were applied there first, the rule *ṭhyaṅ ca* would apply by virtue of its being subsequent (*paratva*) and would override the rules for *rī*, *ṝ*, and *ā*, resulting in the undesirable form *saṃcāskaryate*.

If, however, it is argued that the desired form is established by adopting the view that "the root is first joined with its suffixal element (sādhana) and only afterwards with the prefix (upasarga)," and thus applying the substitution *rīṅ* and reduplication before adding *suṭ*, then:

If it is argued that the rule "even when there is intervention by *aṭ* or the reduplication (*abhyāsa*)" must necessarily be accepted, they say in response: even without the Vārttika beginning with "in the case of *aṭ* and the reduplication," etc., [the desired result is achieved].

The author of the Bhāṣya adopted the position that "the root is joined with the prefix before [the suffix]" in order to establish forms such as *saṃcaskāra* and *saṃcaskaratuḥ*. For the establishment of forms such as *saṃcaskāra* and *saṃcaskaratuḥ*, however, the derivation of *samaceskriyata* and so forth is achieved [by the alternative view].
"Or rather, it is simply the *vārttika* itself.

(402) *sico yaṅ* | Pāṇini 8.3.112: "The *yaṅ* [augment] after *sic*. [Regarding the rule] "the *ṣatva* of the *sakāra* of the reduplicated syllable [occurs] after a prefix in the case of *sunoti*," that which follows from it is...

This is a prohibition [of the substitution of *ṣ*] which would otherwise have applied by the rule "and in the case of *sthā* etc., through repetition" (*thādiṣvabhyāsena ca*). Why [is it specified] "in the *yaṅ* [intensive]"? [Consider:
*abhiṣiṣikṣati*.
(403) *na kavater yaṅi* 7.4.63. [The substitution of *ṣ* does not occur for the root *kavate* in the *yaṅ*.]

There is no *yaṅ* [intensive suffix] after the root *kavati*. Although one could simply say "after *kuḥ*," the mention of *kavati*—indicated by the presence of the *śap* [present indicative marker]—shows that only the root *kūṅ* "to sound" belonging to the *bhvādi* class is intended, and not the root *ku* "to sound" belonging to the *adādi* class, nor the root *kūṅ* "to sound" belonging to the *tudādi* class; with this intention, he says:

Regarding the phrase "but in the case of *kauti* and *kuva*": if it is argued that even when "o" is stated [in the rule], there is no possibility for *kūṅ* because it ends in a long vowel, and furthermore, by the paribhāṣā concerning roots with elided suffixes (*lugvikaraṇa*), there is no possibility for *kauti* either—on this point they say: "But when 'o' is stated..."

Since the paribhāṣā "ninubandhakaparibhāṣā" (the rule that a term with a single indicatory letter [n] does not include its homophonous counterpart with multiple indicatory letters) is also active here, both [the root *kṛ* and the suffix *kvip*] would be included.

Therefore, the mention of *śap* must be made in order to exclude *kvip*. And once that is done, the intended purpose is that it also excludes *kvip*. In this context, it would be more appropriately stated simply as "uṅ."

(404) Regarding the rule *nīg vañcu-sraṃsu-dhvaṃsu-bhraṃsu-ka-sapa-tapa-da-skandām* (Pāṇini 7.4.84), etc.: *danīdhvanyate*, *banībhrasyate*, *canīkasyate*, *panīpatyate*, *panīpadyate*, *canīskadyate*. Also, *vanīvañci* and *sanīsraṃsi*.
Examples such as *danīdhvaṃsīti* and so forth should be cited for the elision of *yaṅ*.
Regarding the root *han*, when *yaṅ* is applied in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*), the substitution of *ghnī* should be stated. As for the statement "the substitution of *ghnī*":
even though the substitution of *ghnī* has been made, the form *jeghnīyate* is established by the rule *abhyāsācca* (Pāṇini 7.3.55) which prescribes the substitution of *k* [for *h*]. Nevertheless...

The *Manoramā* states that the term *ahnī* was mentioned for the sake of brevity in the grammatical process (*prakriyālāghava*). Others, however, hold the view that just as the vowel *i* in the rules *erhiḥ* and *erniḥ* prevents the substitution of *u* (by the rule *ṭheruḥ*) due to the force of its pronunciation, so too, if the substitution of *hnī* were made, the substitution of *k* (by the rule *ṭhabhyāsācca*) would not occur.

They say that the substitution of *ghnī* has been effected. Regarding this, some maintain that by the very substitution of *dhi* for the direction [of the root], the doubling is not barred, because of the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñānāt*). However, in reality, the doubling applies to the second syllable of the stem ending in *yaṅ*, starting from the initial vowel; as for the substitution of *ghnī*, [it occurs]...
The duality [of the suffix] due to the distinction of objects in the case of *prakṛti* alone is indeed unimpeded. (405) *rīgṛdupadhasya ca* | Pāṇini 7.4.10.
[The rule] *rīgṛdupadhasya ca*. What is the purpose of the term *ṛt*? [Consider: *cekīrtyate*. In the alternative view where the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is absent—
The suffix *yaṅ* is applied because [the root] consists of a single vowel.

(406) *svapisyamivyeñāṃ yaṅi* (Pāṇini 6.1.19): [Substitution of *ī* for the penultimate vowel] occurs in the case of *svapi*, *syami*, and *vyeñ* when *yaṅ* follows. Why is *yaṅ* mentioned? [To exclude cases like] *svapnak* and *sesimyate*. [The root] *yamu* means "to sound."

Since *danti* does not end in a vowel (*ajanta*) and thus lacks the status of being an *aṣopadeśa*, [the substitution of *kī*] is not for the sake of the *yaṅ-luk* (elision of *yaṅ*). For this very reason, the prohibition "when there is elision (*luṅmat*)" also does not apply; therefore, even in the case of *yaṅ-luk*, *cāya* would indeed become *kī*. Thus: *cekītaḥ*.
(407) *ī ghrā-dhmoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.31. *ī ghrā-dhmoḥ*. The long vowel (*dīrgha*) is pronounced as before.

[The inclusion of the long vowel is easily explained as being for the sake of the rule *tuṭ ṭhasya cvau* and others; thus we have *śāśayyate*. [Note: The commentary suggests that the mention of the long vowel in this sūtra is intended to facilitate the application of the rule *tuṭ ṭhasya cvau* (Pāṇini 7.4.32), which prescribes the augment *tuṭ* after the root-final consonant when the suffix *cvi* follows. This allows for forms such as *śāśayyate* to be derived correctly.]
"Because it is subsequent and because it is *antaraṅga*, the substitution of *ayaṅ* occurs first, and then reduplication.
Thus ends the section on the *yaṅ*-intensive formations in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
Now begins the section on the *yaṅluk* (elision of *yaṅ*) formations.

(408) *yaṅo ’ci ca* | 2|4|74| In the rule *yaṅo ’ci ca*, because of its association with *yaṅ* (the intensive suffix), the term *aci* refers to a suffix (*pratyaya*), not to the technical abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*) *ac*.
From the preceding rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣe-* [2.4.58], the elision (*luk*) is carried over here. Thus it is said: "There is elision when an *ac*-suffix follows."
It may be so. He says that by the word "ca" (and), the term "bahulam" (frequently) is drawn over from the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (in Vedic usage, frequently);

thus, "there may be elision (luk) frequently. Some, however, draw over the term "chandasi" (in Vedic usage); according to their view as well, [elision occurs] occasionally in the colloquial language (bhāṣā).

The elision (*yaṅluk*) indeed occurs; for although the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule "hūsuvoḥ" would have already established it, the form *bobhūtu* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this is so, due to its being a Vedic archaism (*nipātana*). This will become clear in the root text itself.
This [elision] is not conditioned by anything else (*anaimitika*), whereas the elision of *yaṅ* prescribed when the suffix *ac* follows is indeed conditioned by that [suffix].
Thus, in forms such as *lolūya* and *popuva*, the prohibition [of doubling] by the rule *na dhātulope* (P.
1.1.4) is established. [The phrase] "because it is a *yaṅ*-intensive" refers to the genitive case in *any-yaṅoḥ*, and not the locative;

otherwise, since the *yaṅ* would be elided by *luk*, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the treatment of an element as if present despite its elision) would not apply, and consequently, the doubling would not occur.

[This is] the state of affairs. Nor should it be argued that even the locative interpretation (*saptamī-pakṣa*) is faultless because, since the prohibition "a lumate" applies only to operations prescribed under the heading of *aṅga* (the stem), reduplication would indeed occur here; for in the rule "a lumate," the heading of *aṅga* is not taken into account, but rather...

This is because of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that everything prescribed for what precedes an affix—whether it pertains to the base (*aṅga*) or not—occurs when that affix follows. Otherwise, in examples such as *rājapuruṣa*, the elision of *n* would not take place;

for according to the method you have stated, if the operation were triggered by the technical designation "affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the status of being a "base" (*bha*) would sublate the status of being a "word" (*pada*). Even though...

Although the doubling (*dvitva*) prescribed by the rule *ṭhaki ca* is prohibited by rules such as *ati pāśap-*, it nevertheless occurs; for this is because the rules prescribing reduplication operations— such as *uṇo yaṅ-lukoḥ* and *rug-rikau ca luki*— indicate that there is no prohibition of doubling.

Regarding the phrase "pratyayāpratyaya": the designation *ṅt* is seen in suffixes (*pratyaya*), as in the rule "ṛter īyaṅ" and others; it is also seen in non-suffixes (*apratyaya*), as in "citraṅ" and others. Thus, the meaning is that when there is *luk*-elision of the *yaṅ* suffix, one should not suspect the occurrence of the *ātmanepada* ending—which is an operation dependent on the *ṅt*-designation of the *yaṅ*—by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the rule that an elided suffix still exerts its influence). This is the point. *Ti*.

The rebuttal that "this is because of the mention of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*)" has not been stated here, because roots such as *bhū* and others are not mentioned with an indicatory letter in the same way that *śīṅ* and others are. Furthermore, since the *ṅ* of *yaṅ* is an indicatory letter of the suffix (*pratyaya-anubandha*), it is not an indicatory letter of the entire complex; thus, even a form ending in *yaṅ* [is not excluded].

It should be understood that a verbal root (dhātu) is not specified when it is mentioned by means of its suffixal connection (*anubandha*). In the case of *sudṛṣat*, the word *dṛṣat* ending in the nominative plural (*jas*) occurs within a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "in which there are beautiful stones. [The rule] "there is no long vowel" applies because the suffix *ṭha* exists both as a suffix and as a non-suffix.
The meaning is that because the suffix does not rely on its own unique form (*asādhāraṇarūpa*), there is no absence of continuity (*asantatva*) with the moment of the suffix.

"Even from those" means even from those [roots] which are marked as *anudāteta* (unaccented) and which have the marker *ṅ*, even without the application of the rule for suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). "Because of the reading in the *adādi* [class]" refers to the rule: "After [roots] beginning with *ad*, there is the elision of *śap*."
By this [rule], the meaning is that there is elision (*luk*) of *śap* following a stem ending in *yaṅ-luk*.
From the rule *yaṅo vā*, [the phrase] *piti sārvadhātuke* is supplied from the rule *ābhyastasyācī*, and *uta*...
From the rule *vṛddhiḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.1], the term *hali* is understood to carry over; and from the rule *ruva īṭ* [Pāṇini 7.3.94], the term *īṭ* is understood to carry over.

This is what he states with the words "from that which ends in *yaṅ*" (*yaṅntāt*) and so forth. Even when there is elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ* suffix, it is considered here to end in *yaṅ* by virtue of the technical designation of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). By this, it is shown that a sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with a consonant (*halādi-pit*) cannot occur after a form ending in *yaṅ*.

The interpretation that the word *yaṅ* indicates the *yaṅ-luk* (elided *yaṅ*) form is refuted, because according to the reasoning already stated, its status as a *yaṅ*-stem remains intact. Furthermore, since a suffix beginning with *val* cannot follow a *yaṅ*-stem, even if the *yaṅ-luk* form were indicated by the word *yaṅ*, the doubling [of the root] would still apply to the *yaṅ*-stem itself by the rule *any-ṅeḥ*.
Because the purpose [of the rule] has already been fulfilled, there is an absence of the seed for the application of the *yaṅluk* suffix;

thus, it follows that there would be an absence of reduplication (*dvitva*) when *yaṅluk* occurs. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Regarding the phrase "due to a Vedic irregularity" (*chandasi nipātanāt*):
since the prohibition of *guṇa* is already established, this irregularity [indicates] that the prohibition of *guṇa* applies only in the Veda.
The meaning is that [the rule] "nānyatra" (not elsewhere) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Regarding the form *bobhūtu*:

since the whole (*samudāya*) is something distinct [from the individual parts], the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule "hūsuvoḥ" does not apply; thus, there might be the suspicion that this *nipātana* (irregular formation) is not for the purpose of restriction. To this, he says: "No."
If [it is argued that] there is a double application [of the rule], then it follows that when a root is mentioned, the form ending in *yaṅluk* is also included;

this is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*) and is not a new statement (*apūrva vacana*). Thus, [we have] *bobhuvatī* (from *bhū*), according to the rule *adabhyastāt*; and *bobhūvīt*. Some [hold that] here, in the rule *huvo vuk*, [the suffix *vuk* is applied].

From the rule *ṭhoḥ supi*, the word *or* is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*). Thus, since the meaning is that *vuk* applies to the root *bhū* when it ends in an *u*-vowel, once *guṇa* has been applied, there is no occasion for *vuk*; therefore, *vuk* is non-obligatory (*anitya*).
Furthermore, it is superseded by the subsequent *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Consequently, they state that the form is *ābobhavīt*.
That is questionable, because it contradicts the passage in the Bhāṣya which states, "The substitution of *vuk* is eternal (*nitya*) because [the rule] is permanent.

Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya—who, relying on the eternality of *vuk*, rejected the sūtra "and after *ḍhidhi* and *bhavati*"—certainly accepted the continuation of the word "of *u*" (*or*). [This is clear from the mention of] "of *ā*" (*ātaḥ*).
Anticipating the objection that this might be a restrictive rule (*niyama*) concerning the nature of *jus*, he says: "based on the reduplicated base" (*abhyastāśraya*). The meaning is this:

by the rule "ijabhyaste," *jus* is obtained based on its following the suffix *sic*; this restriction applies only to that *jus*, and not to a *jus* based on a reduplicated base. [This is understood from] the rule "usi ca."

Anticipating this objection regarding the *guṇa* vowel, he says: "Because it is eternal (*nityatva*), [the substitution is] *bug*. Regarding the form *abobhūvi*: one should not argue that here, because it is subsequent, the substitution of *at* by the rule *adabhyastāt* would apply;
for that rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *at* substitution based on the *abhyasta* (repeated) stem. Regarding *pāspardhīti*: the root *spardh* means "to compete" (*saṃgharṣe*).

In the form *īrgho’kitaḥ*, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). By the rule *ṭhyaṅe ve*, there is an optional insertion of *īṭ*. In the absence of *īṭ*, there is either the substitution of *dh* by the rule *haṣastathoḥ*, or the elision of *dh* by the rule *haro jhari savarṇe*. In the *liṭ* (perfect tense): *pāspardhācakāra*. In the *luṭ* (periphrastic future): *pāspardhitā*. In the *lṛṭ* (simple future): [pāspardhiṣyati].

He will vie: *pāspardhiṣyati*. In the *loṭ* (imperative) mood: *pāspardhītu*, *pāsparddhu*, *pāspardhāt*, *pāspardhām*, *pāspardhatu*, *pāsparddhīti*. When *hi* is substituted [for *hi*], there is optionally the elision of *dh*. In the *laṅ* (imperfect) mood, in the alternative where the augment *iṭ* is applied: *apāspardhīt*. In the alternative where *ru* is applied: *apāspardhīt*. But in the other alternative, however: *apāspat*.

**Aorist (luṅ):** *apāspardhīt*, *apāspardhiṣṭām*, *apāspardhiṣuḥ*. [Note: By the rule *ṭhiṭisico’pṛkte*, the augment *īṭ* is necessarily applied. By the rule *ṭhiṭa īṭi*, there is the elision of the *s* of the suffix. **Conditional (lṛṅ):** *apāspardhiṣyat*. **Desiderative (liṅ):** *pāspardhyāt*, *pāspardhyātām*, *pāspardhyāstām*. **Imperfect (laṅ):** *apāspardhat*, *apāspardhatām*, *apāspardhan*. **Imperative (loṭ):** *pāspardhatu*, *pāspardhatām*, *pāspardhantu*. **Present (laṭ):** *pāspardhati*, *pāspardhataḥ*, *pāspardhanti*. **Root Aorist (luṅ):** *apāspardhīt*, *apāspardhiṣṭām*, *apāspardhiṣuḥ*. **Conditional (lṛṅ):** *apāspardhiṣyat*.

*Jāgāddhi*: from the root *gādhṛ*, meaning "to stand firm" and so on. In the alternative where the augment *īṭ* is applied, it is *jāgādhīti*. In *jāghātsi*, the substitution of *bhaṣ* occurs by the rule "ekācaḥ". Then, the change of *dha* to *t* occurs by the rule for *cartva*. *ajāgādhuḥ*. In the *luṅ* [aorist]: *ijāgādhīt*, *ajāgādhiṣṭām*. The roots *nāth* and *nādhṛ* mean "to beg" and so forth. [In the present tense: *nāthati*. *Acogūrdīt*; in the alternative case, *acokūri*. This means that in the alternative where there is *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) after the vowel *a*, [the form is as stated].

In the case of a root ending in a nasal, the augment *nu* is applied according to the rule "after *ugata*. Thus, from *jaṅghanti*, we have *jaṅgmati*. In the case of the root *han*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) according to the rule "in *ahan*" (Pāṇini 6.4.98). Thus, *ajaṅghan*. However, in the alternative where the augment *īṭ* is present, it is *ajaṅgamīt*. [The forms are: *ajaṅgatām*, *ajaṅgmuḥ*; *ajaṅgamīḥ*, *ajaṅgatam*, *ajaṅgata*.
*ajaṅgamam*, *ajaṅganva*, *ajaṅgama*. Regarding the phrase "with reference to the general rule" (*sāmānyāpekṣā*), the intention is as follows:
because of the mention of "a single vowel" (*ekāj*) in the rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.1), reduplication would not apply anywhere in the case of the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*).
Consequently, the strengthening (*guṇa*) prescribed for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) by the rule *uṇo yaṅlukoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.83) [would also not apply].

Since [the rule] would find no application without reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the statement "by *tip* and *śap*" indicates that none of the prohibitions apply in certain instances of *yaṅ*-elision (*yaṅluk*). Thus, it is employed as in the example:
"ājā vṛtraṃ jaṅghanat" (He struck Vṛtra down repeatedly), and so forth. However, reduplication does not occur; thus, [the form] is *vadhyāt*.

Regarding the form *avadhīt*, the meaning is that once the reduplication has been performed, the substitution of *vadh* for *han*—by the rules “*ṭhhano vadha liṅ*” and “*uṅ ci*” [i.e., *liṭi ca*]—prevents further reduplication. He states the reason for this:
"by virtue of being *sthānivadbhāva*. Regarding the phrase "preceded by *āṅ*": when a verbal root (*prakṛti*) is mentioned, it includes its *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive) form as well.

The meaning is "because of being grasped. Regarding the form *cañcūrti*: the root *car* is used in the senses of "going" and "eating. By the rule *araphalośca*, the augment *nuK* is added to the reduplicated syllable. By the rule *ṭhutaparasyātaḥ*, the vowel *u* is substituted for the *a*. By the rule *hali ca*, the vowel is lengthened.
However, in the case of *acañcūḥ*, because it concerns the end of a word (*padānta*), the lengthening occurs by the rule *ṛtvoḥ upadhāyāḥ*.
Regarding *caṅkhanīti*: the root *khanu* means "to dig. Regarding *caṅkhāta*:
some maintain that whatever grammatical operation is performed by the mention of a verbal root applies also to the *yaṅluk* (elision of *yaṅ*).
Thus, when there is no lengthening of the vowel due to the rule *an-asane* (Pāṇini 6.4.39), the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.15) does not apply for lengthening either.

It occurs. For, because of the requirement of *kvip*, only a *kṛt*-derivative beginning with a *jhal* consonant is understood there, and not the form ending in *caṅ*—as they claim by accepting [the presence of] a *tiṅ* suffix. That is incorrect; for there is no evidence that the rule applies to a *kṛt* derivative when *yaṅ*-elision (*yaṅluk*) occurs due to the mention of "root" (*dhātu*). Even if such evidence existed, [one might argue] "the *āt* vowel substitution is optional."

And since it is designated as such by the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), who can prevent that form? As for what was said regarding the rule *anunāsikasya*, namely that because of association with *kvip*, even a [suffix] beginning with *jhal* is understood to be only a *kṛt* suffix—that too has already been addressed. For if *kvip* were indeed only a *kṛt* suffix, then the mention of "association" would be appropriate.

It would apply; however, there indeed exists a *kvip* suffix used for the sense of "conducting" (*ācāra*) even after a *kṛt*-derived stem. For this very reason, Mādhava and others have stated that in forms such as *rājānati* and *carmāṇati*, the lengthening is caused by the *kvip* suffix.
As for *caṅkhāhi*: because *hi* is treated as having the marker *ṅ*, it undergoes the substitution of *ā* by the rule *inasana*.

Regarding *acaṅkhānīt*: the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) occurs either by the rule "after [a prefix ending in] a consonant, [the initial vowel of] a root beginning with a consonant" (*ato halādeḥ*). As for *jāheti* and so forth: the forms of the roots *hāṅ* (to go) and *hāk* (to abandon) are identical, because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) conditioned by the marker *ṅ* does not apply when there is *yaṅ*-elision (*yaṅluk*). This is because of the rule "for *hrī*, *mī*, and *hāṅ*, [the penultimate vowel becomes short]" (*hrī-mī-nā-v-ām it*), which applies the shortening of the vowel of *hāṅ*.

Furthermore, because the lengthening of the abhyāsa (repeated syllable) is specifically prescribed for *ślu* and *ni* substitutes; and one should not suspect that the lengthening of the abhyāsa of the root *hā* is impossible due to the prohibition "not when followed by a *kit*"— for in the rule "not when followed by a *kit*," the meaning is "that abhyāsa which does not have a *kit* suffix."

A *bahuvrīhi* compound is adopted; therefore, because the rule "the application of doubling is sixth" (*viḥ prayogo dvirvacanaṃ ṣāṣṭham*) is accepted, even though the root has the *kit* designation, there is no fault—even if the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) were also *kit*—because, as in the case of forms such as *vanīvañcīt*, the *kit* designation does not apply [to the reduplication]. Furthermore, in the absence of doubling...

Even though a single element may possess meaning, it is universally agreed that when there is a pair, the collection as a whole alone possesses the meaning. Likewise, let the status of being a *kit* (a marker with specific grammatical effects) belong to the collection as a whole and not to each individual constituent; thus, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the application of the long vowel [substitution]. [The example] *jāhīyāt* [is formed from the root *hā* with the suffix *liṅ*]; [the rule applies] because of the suffix *ī*.

The substitution of *ī* [for *au*] occurs by the rule *halyaghoḥ*. Regarding the statement "it is elided by *luk*": this is because the rule for *luk*-elision is stronger than all other rules. Furthermore, the meaning is that by the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*, one should not even suspect that the *utva* [substitution] could occur prior to the *luk*-elision. The phrase "the *utva* does not occur" is a statement of the resultant meaning.
The meaning is that the *saṃprasāraṇa* which would otherwise be prescribed by rules such as "vapiṣyati" and so forth does not take place here.
In the form *asāsvāpīt*, the optional *vṛddhi* is applied by the rule "ato halādeḥ". (410) *rugrikau ca* | Pāṇini 7.4.91.
And *rugrikau*. By the word *ca* ("and"), *rīk* is drawn forward from the rule "rīgṛdupadhasya" [Pāṇini 7.4.90]. In *ruk*, the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation.
(411) *ṛtaśca* [Pāṇini 7.4.92].

And [the word] *ṛtaḥ*. The member (*aṅga*) following *ṛta* is specified; the meaning is: "of that which is the reduplication of a member ending in *ṛ*. *varvṛtāt*, *varvṛtām*, *varvṛtatu*, *varvṛddhi*. Regarding the mention of *aṅ*: it is by the rule “*uṣādidyautādī*” [Pāṇini 6.1.195]. Regarding *carkarīti*: from the root *ḍukṛñ* (to make). As for "but in the case of *ri* and *rī*": the meaning is that thus the form *ariyarti* is identical for both.

But for the middle and highest persons, it is *ararṣi*.

*ariyarṣi*, *ararīṣi*, *ariyarīṣi*; *arṛthaḥ*, *ariyṛthaḥ*; *ararmi*, *ariyarmi*; *ararīmi*, *ariyamariṣmi*; *arṛvaḥ*, *ariyṛvaḥ*; *ariyṛmaḥ*. In the *liṭ* [perfect tense]—*ararāṃcakāra*. But for *rig* and *rīk*—*ariyarāṃcakāra*. In the *luṭ* [periphrastic future]—*ariyṛtām*.
Present tense (*laṭ*): *āratu*, *ariṛtu*, *arṛhi*, *ariyṛhi*, *ararāṇi*, *ariyarāṇi*, *ararāva*, *ariyarāva*.
