*arṛyātām*, *ariyṛyātām*; *arṛyuḥ*. Regarding "in the *liṅ*": this means in the benedictive mood (*āśīrliṅ*).
Regarding *ariyṛti*: when *rig* and *rīk* become *ariyṛ*, the substitution *iriṅ* applies.

Because *riṅ* is considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*), it is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purpose of the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), and this is also due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to the rule *acaḥ parasmin*. Furthermore, one should not suspect the prohibition [of *sthānivadbhāva*] by the rule *na padānte*.

Because it has been stated that in the cases of vowel-lengthening (*svaradīrgha*) and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), only a substitute (*ādeśa*) consisting of an elision (*lopa*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*.

Nor should one suspect that the *iyaṅ* replacement does not occur due to the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*, because since the *riṅ* substitute is *sthānivadbhūta*, there is no destruction of the cause [for the application of the rule], and thus the aforementioned *paribhāṣā* does not apply. For this very reason, the form *ariṇāti* also occurs.

Siddham. In that case as well, because the *sthānivadbhāva* [of the semi-vowel] prevents the destruction of the cause [of the grammatical operation], the aforementioned paribhāṣā does not apply. For this very reason, forms such as *ariti* are also established. In that instance too, by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the *yaṇ*.

Because there is no disappearance of the *nimitta* (the cause for grammatical operation), the aforementioned technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) does not apply, and thus *iyaṅ* is established. However, in some original manuscripts, with the intention that *iyaṅ* does not apply because *rīṅ* is applied first—due to its being subsequent (*para*) and obligatory (*nitya*)—it is stated: "aririyāt" and "arīriyāt."

This is how it is read, though only superficially; for otherwise, since the form *ariti* would be unestablished, there would arise a contradiction between the preceding and following passages. [Examples of the *luṅ* (aorist): *ārārīt*, *āiriyārīt*.
[Example of the *lṛṅ* (conditional): *āririṣyat*. [Regarding *jargṛhīti*: There is a prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule "ābhyastasyācī" (Pāṇini 1.1.3).
In the middle and highest [voices], however: *jargṛhīṣi* 3; *jargharṣi* 3; *jgṛḍhaḥ* 3;
*jargṛhīmi* 3; *jargarhmi* 3; *jargṛhvaḥ* 3; *jargṛhmaḥ* 3; *jargṛhatu* 3; *jargṛhāṃcakāra* 3; *jargarhitā*; *jarigarhitā*; *jarīgarhitā*.
Here, because of the mention of the suffix *an*, the optional *iṭ* prescribed by the rule *ūdit* is not to be applied.

Thus: *jargṛhītu*, *jargṛḍhām*, *jargṛhatu*, *jargṛḍhi*, *jargṛhāṇi* (in the first person singular), and *ajargṛhīt* (in the imperfect). In the absence of *iṭ*, the substitution of *bhaṣ* occurs by the rule *ṭhEkācaḥ*. Thus: *ajargharṭ*. Although here...

Although the substitution of *bhaṣ* is difficult to obtain here because of the prohibition "where there is the mention of a single vowel (*ekāj*)," nevertheless, the substitution of *bhaṣ* does apply in this case; for by the rule "after *uṇ*, in the elision of *yaṅ*" (*uṇo yaṅlukaḥ*), it is indicated that the prohibition [of *bhaṣ*] found in rules such as "after *tiP*, *śap*, etc. (*tipā śapādi-niṣedha*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
Thus they say: *ajargṛḍhām* (3), *ajargṛhuḥ* (3), *ajargharṭaḥ* (3), *ajargharḍ* (3), *ajargṛḍham* (3), *ajargṛḍha* (3), *ajargṛham* (3), *ajargṛhva* (3); *jargṛhyāt* (3);
*ajargarhīt* (3), *ajargarhiṣṭām* (3), *ajargarhiṣyat* (3); [the derivative] *jāgrahītī* from the root *grah*.

In the case of *upādāne*, because the suffix *yaṅ* has been elided by *luk*, the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) prescribed by the rule *ra-hi-jy-āp-ya-va-śām* does not apply here; this is the intended meaning. Regarding *jargṛḍha*: [the rules] *uraṅ* and *dīrgho ’kitaḥ* apply.
In that context, since the term *ekācaḥ* (of a monosyllabic root) is understood as continuing from the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya*, it refers to the rule *ekāco dve*.
The meaning is that this has been stated by Haradatta. As for "Mādhava, however":

the sense is as follows—by examining the Vārttika, its Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, and other works on the rule *raho liṭi* (Pāṇini 6.1.31), which states "and [the substitution occurs] when there is the elision of *yaṅ*," [it is established] in cases such as *jarīgṛhītā*.
Regarding the long vowel [substitution] for that *iṭ* augment which follows the roots *grah*, *yaṅ-anta*, *tṛc*, or *tās*, two justifications are obtained in the absence of its lengthening:

some hold that there is the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) even for what precedes a rule; others hold that the long vowel applies to that *iṭ* which follows *grah* when it is not followed by *vi*. Of these, the first position is according to the method of the authors of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika.

For by those two [grammarians], relying on the principle "when that which is not established previously [is to be applied], it does not behave as a substitute" (*asiddhe na sthānivat*), the mention of "long vowels and so forth" (*dīrghādi*) was rejected; because, in their view, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) could easily be asserted regarding this long vowel—distinct from the long vowels belonging to the *traipādika* section—that is to be applied. The second [view], however, follows the method of the Sūtra itself; by that [method]...
However, since it is impossible to state that the status of being *sthānivat* applies to the general rule regarding lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*),
there is no obstacle whatsoever to the application of lengthening in the case of *yaṅluk*,
because *yaṅluk* is not conditioned by anything else (*anaimitikatvāt*) and because it is a substitute for both vowels and consonants (*ajjhalādeśatvāt*).

Because the status of being "as if that" (*stānivadbhāva*) is impossible; for according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "the second usage [of a root] is reduplication, and it belongs to the sixth [case]," there is no loss of the fact that [the suffix] is prescribed after *grah* following a base ending in *yaṅ*-elision (*yaṅluk*), since it is prescribed after *grah*.
[The claim that this is] contrary to the *Bhāṣya* and other works—the word "and others" (*ādi*) including Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta—is incorrect.

Furthermore, the contradictions in this matter have been established in the *Manoramā*. To illustrate: regarding the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya*, Kaiyaṭa, citing the Bhāṣya passage *raheraṅgāt*, states:
"For in the case of the root *ṛc*, it is *arīgṛh* that is the *aṅga*, and not *grah* itself; for [the designation of the root] is due to the power of the qualification."

Regarding the phrase "resorting to the form as it was heard": although this was stated there with reference to the *yaṅ*-intensive (*yaṅnta*), nevertheless, due to the equality of the underlying logic, it is understood that there is no lengthening even in the *yaṅluk* (elision of *yaṅ*) forms.
Haradatta also supports this view by continuing the application of the rule for "a single vowel" (*ekāj*). For, under this alternative, [the desired result] does not follow.

In the case of the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*), there is the possibility of the lengthening [of the vowel]. And thus, according to the principle that "there is the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* even for an operation prescribed on the basis of what precedes," if one were to rely on the form exactly as heard— namely, that the augment *iṭ* prescribed after the root *grah* is [replaced by] *raḥ*— then in forms such as *gṛhīta*, the lengthening of the *iṭ* would not occur.
It must be stated that at the time the technical designation *aṅga* (stem) is applied, the form exists exactly as it is heard [in the root].

However, this is not the case in examples such as *rāhita*. As for the solution provided by the rule *ekācaḥ*, it applies only to cases distinct from the causative (*ṇic*), because when the *ṇic* suffix is elided by the rule *iṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi*, [the stem remains as it was].

In forms such as *grāhitam*, since the status of having a single vowel (*ekāctva*) is not lost, it is thus stated: "The occurrence of the long vowel [substitution] for the root *grah* is established in two ways, three ways, and four ways—from the form ending in *yaṅ*-luṅ, from the form ending in *ṇic*, and from the form ending in *yaṅ*. The meaning of this is as follows: when the long vowel substitution is applicable from the form ending in *yaṅ*-luṅ...

There are two solutions: [the first] is the explanation that [the rule applies] "from *grah*" as a root-form, with the continuation of the term "having a single vowel" (*ekācaḥ*); [the second] consists of three solutions: the absence of the actual form of *grah* when it is causative (*ṇijanta*), the qualification of what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*), and the status of being like the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Furthermore, there is a fourfold resolution [of this objection]: the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "ekācaḥ," the three previously mentioned resolutions, and [the following]. Regarding *ajarghā*: the root *gṛdh* is used in the sense of longing (*abhikāṅkṣā*).
Here, even for a *repha* that is not at the end of a word, the elision (*lopa*) by the rule "ro rī" indeed occurs; in that case—

Because of the continuation of the word *pada* by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūakapluti*), [we have] *pāpraṣṭi*. [The root] *prach* is used in the sense of desiring to know. By the rule *vraśca*, the letter *ṣ* is substituted. [The forms are:
*pāpracchitā*, *pāpracchiṣyati*, *prāpaṣṭua*, *pāpraṣṭāt*, *pāpraṣṭām*, *pāpraccchatu*, *pāpraḍḍhi*, *pāpracchāni*, *apāpracchīt*, *apāpraṭ*.

*apāpraṣṭām*, *apāpracchuḥ*, *apāpraṣṭhīḥ*, *apāpraṭ*, *apāpraṣṭām*, *apāpraṣṭa*, *apāpracccham*, *apāpracchava*, *apāpraśma*. It is indicated in the Bhāṣya: in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *chāeḥ śūḍ*, regarding the mention of *kṅt*, it says "the substitution of *ṣ* for *ch* must be stated."

The point is that if this [substitution] were not applied, then once *śatva* (the substitution of *ś* for *ch*) had been performed, the substitution of *ṣ* would occur simply because the sound is now *śānta* (ending in *ś*).

Thus, in order to establish forms such as *praṣṭā* and *praṣṭum*, it would not be necessary to include the mention of *ch* in the rule *vraśca-ādi-sūtra*. By speaking in this manner, the author of the Bhāṣya [indicates that the inclusion of *ch* is unnecessary] even for those [roots] where *ūṭh* is about to occur.

It has already been stated that there is no *yaṅluk* [elision of the *yaṅ* suffix]. Otherwise, in forms such as *dedeti* and *dedeṣi* from the root *div* when *yaṅluk* occurs, there would be a great discrepancy between the presence and absence of the augment *īṭ*. In that case, if the reference to *kṅt* were not carried over, the augment *ūṭh* would apply, resulting in *dedyoti*.

Because specific forms such as *dedyoṣi* and so forth are obtained [from this root], the restriction "only this much" (*aitāvāneva*) would be contradicted. Regarding *srivimavyoḥ*: *srivu* means "to move" and "to dry up"; *mava* means "to bind. Regarding *jāhāmīti*: in the case where the augment *īṭ* is applied, it is *jāhayīmi*; in the imperative (*loṭ*), it is *jāhayītu* and *jāhuta*.
jāhatāt | jāhatām | jāhayatu | jāhahi | jāhatāt | jāhayāni | jāhayāva | jāhayāma | In the *laṅ* [aorist]: *ijāhayīt*, *ajāhat*, *ajāhatām*, *ajāhayuḥ*,
*ajāhayīḥ*, *ajāhaḥ*, *ajāhatam*, *ajāhata*, *ajāhayam*, *ajāhāva*.
*ajāhāma*, *ajāhayyāt*. There is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "ṭhhmyantakṣaṇe. [The forms are] *ajāhayīt*, *ajāhayiṣṭām*, *ajāhayiṣyat*. Regarding the roots *jvar*, *tvar*, etc.:
(412) *jvaratvarasrivyavimavām upadhāyāś ca* P. 6.4.20. [In these roots, there is the substitution of *u* for the penultimate vowel and for the vowel following the *ṣu* augment.]

Regarding the root *jvar* in the sense of fever, and *ñitvarā* in the sense of agitation: here, in this commentary, he states that the mention of "after a consonant (*hal-ādau*), before *k* or *ṅ*, and *t* (*kṅtī*)" applies only in those two specific instances—namely, *drabhaya* and *sakṛt*—by saying, "the term *kṅtī* does not carry over [from the previous rule]. Regarding the form *avatu*: after the roots *vṛ* and *tvṛ*, when the *ūṭh* augment is applied to the penultimate *v* and *t*, and the *guṇa* substitution has been made...
The meaning is that when the *man* suffix is elided by *ṭilopa*, the form *com* is established. Examples from the *jvarādi* group are as follows:
with *kvip*, *jūḥ*; *jurau*; *juraḥ*. But before *jhal*-beginning suffixes: *jūrtiḥ*; *jūrṇaḥ*; *jūrṇavān*. From *tvara*: *tūḥ*; *turau*; *turaḥ*; *tūrtiḥ*; *tūrṇaḥ*; *tūrṇavān*. From *sriv*: *srūḥ*.

*sruv-au*, *sruv-aḥ*; *srū-tiḥ*; *avi-ūḥ*, *uv-au*, *uvaḥ*; *ū-tiḥ*; *mava-ūḥ*, *mu-v-au*, *mū-taḥ*, *mū-tiḥ*; *mā moṣi* etc. It should be understood that in the case of the augment *īṭ*, there are forms such as *māmavīṣi*, *māmavīmi*, *māmavītu*, *amāmavīt*, and *amāmavīt*.

*rāllopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.21): "The elision of *r* [occurs] after [the suffix] *ap*. The phrase *chavoḥ śūḍit* is continued from [the previous rule], as is *chavoḥ*. What are the examples for *kvip*?—*tūḥ*, *turau*, *turaḥ*. *dhurvī*—*dhūḥ*, *dhurau*, *dhuraḥ*. *murcchā*—*mūḥ*, *murau*, *muraḥ*.

(413) *na dhātulopa ārddhadhātuke* | 1|1|4| "Na dhātulopaḥ": he explains by way of implication (*lakṣaṇayā*) that there is no elision of a verbal root (*dhātu*) when an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix follows—namely, "when a portion of the root [is elided]. Although [the rule] *uriṇo lopaśca* [applies] to the *uṇādi* suffixes...

Although the elision of the verbal root (*dhātulopa*) is well-known in the case of the suffix *rak*, it is nevertheless not well-known as being purposeful here, because since the root *iṇ* has already been elided, there is no possibility of *guṇa* substitution. Furthermore, the status of being a verbal root does not exist in connection with the suffix. In this context, "in which there is an elision of the root" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; the qualified term (*viśeṣya*) [is understood].
With the intention that [the suffix] is an *ardhadhātuka*, he says: "when there is a cause for elision. He means that the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions do not take place.

Although, in the rule *ṅiti ca*, it was explained that "the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutions] characterized by *ṅ* do not occur"—so that in the word *aiṅgavāyana* there would be no prohibition of *guṇa*—nevertheless, here...
It was not stated that "in the absence of a defining characteristic" because there is no purpose [for such a rule]. Why is "dhātu" (root) mentioned? Consider *lūñ*—the form *lavitā*;

and *pūñ*—the form *pavitā*. If it is argued that this [example] is deficient in two parts because the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix does not serve as the cause for the elision of the *anubandha* here, they reply: when the term "dhātu" is included...

By understanding this as a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that in which there is the elision (*lopa*) of a verbal root"—the sense is obtained that [the term *ārddhadhātuka*] refers to what is caused by such elision.

However, in the absence of that [interpretation], since the meaning would be "when an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix follows," a fault would certainly arise in forms such as *lavitā*. But when *lopa* is understood as "that which causes elision" (from *lopayati*), then [the term applies] to that which is the cause of elision.

If it is explained that "in the domain of *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* do not apply to *ik*-sounds," then the mention of the term *dhātu* (root) is for the sake of clear understanding. However, according to the view of Kaiyaṭa and others—that a root is that which has its *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) discarded—the inclusion of the term *dhātu* in the rule *dhātulopa* is unnecessary, provided one does not rely on a *bahuvrīhi* compound; rather, it would suffice to refer to the elision of a portion (*avayava*) of a root.

From the root *satyārddhaśabda*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied by the rule *ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.22]; then there is the elision (*luk*) of that *yaṅ*. Since the form ending in *yaṅ* is a verbal root (*dhātu*), and since *yaṅ* is a constituent part of that root and has been elided, the prohibition [of the *guṇa* substitute] would apply here as well; therefore, this is stated so that such a prohibition does not occur.
Now, one might object: "In this case, because the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*) is not occasioned by any external cause (*anaimitikatvāt*), the initial vowel..."

If it is argued that because the condition of "being followed by a cause for elision" (*lopanimittaparatva*) is absent, the rule is deficient in two of its constituent parts (*dvyaṅgavikala*), the following is said in response:
When the term *ārddhadhātuka* is present, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is obtained through the acquisition of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*);
however, in its absence, when there is elision of a member [of the compound], the meaning is that *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions do not occur, as in the case of *roravīti*.

"There would indeed be a fault. However, some explain that *dhātulopaḥ* means "the elision of a verbal root" (*dhātuṃ lopayatīti*). Just as in the rule *hrasvālope*, they maintain that by accepting the analysis *armany-a-ṇ*, one need not resort to a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound; rather, they state that when the elision of a portion of a verbal root is the cause, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions do not occur. [This applies to] *ika*.

What [is the example]? *rāgaḥ*. In *abhāji*, because of the rule "after the root *kaṭh* (rañj), when *ghañ* follows, there is elision of *n* in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) or instrument (*karaṇa*)," the elision of *n* is applied and then *vṛddhi* occurs. However, in *abhāji*, the *vṛddhi* occurs due to the rule "there is elision of *n* after the root *hañj* (rañj) when *ciṇ* follows. Thus, the prohibition does not apply here. This is the illustration of the sūtra.

One should understand *loluvaḥ*, *popuvaḥ*, *marīmṛjaḥ*, and so forth. In that regard, from the words *lolūya* and *popūya*, when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*) by the rule "ṭhyaṅe’ci ca," the potential occurrence of *guṇa* substitution—which would otherwise apply by depending on the *ac* suffix (the *pacādyac* suffix)—is prohibited. However, in the case of *marīmṛja*, [the prohibition applies] as follows:

[The rule for] *vṛddhi*. Now, an objection: when the suffix *ac* is applied after roots such as *lolūya*, by the rule "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*), there is elision of the letter *a*; then, by the rule "elision of *yaṅ* before a vowel" (*yaṅo’ci ca*), there is elision of *yaṅ*.

Because that elision of *a* is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), [the penultimate vowel] would be subject to *vṛddhi* by the rule "before an *ārdhadhātuka* or *sārvadhātuka* suffix" (*ārdhadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*).

[If this were so,] the *guṇa* [substitution] and the *vṛddhi* [substitution] prescribed by the rule "ṛjervṛddhir eci" would not occur; so what is the purpose of this prohibitory rule? Nor can it be argued that even in cases such as *olūva*, once the *uvaṅ* substitution has taken place, the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) would apply, and thus this prohibition is necessary to prevent that—because the *uvaṅ* is [already] substituted for the original vowel (*ādeśāt*).

It should not be argued that, when the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) is to be applied, there is an absence of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element) because [the *uvaṅ*] is not prior to the vowel; for the *uvaṅ* is indeed observed to be prior to the vowel by way of its substituend (*sthānin*). Even though it is observed by way of the substituend, the principle that "it becomes like the original" is stated in the rule *a padānte*.

This is made known by the inclusion of the term *savarṇa*. For in the example *śiṇḍhi*, the *anusvāra* is not seen as preceding the vowel that constitutes the *sthānin*; rather, it exists by way of the *sthānin*. And thus, when the *parasavarṇa* of the *anusvāra* is to be applied, there is a prohibition of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision (*lopa*) of *śnam* in that context.

Since the inclusion of the term *savarṇa* (homogeneous) has been made, the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is established here. However, in the case of *nonau*, since the *yaṅ* suffix is elided—specifically that which is characterized by the vowel *a*—by virtue of the rule regarding "diversity" (*bahulagrahaṇa*) even prior to the arising of the *liṭ* suffix, the status of the substitute does not apply;
thus, there is no possibility of fearing the absence of *vṛddhi*. This is why [the rule] states: "provided there is no elision of a verbal root element" (*na dhātulope*).
If it is argued that there is no purpose for this sūtra, that is true; therefore, it has been rejected in the Bhāṣya—this is the summary. Regarding *totortī*:
although here the elision of *v* is established by the rule *opo vyoḥ*, nevertheless, in forms such as *otūrta* and so on, [the sūtra is necessary].

The elision of *ṭh* in *valopārtaṃ* was introduced by the rule "ṭhral-lopaḥ. Otherwise, in that case, the elision [of *v*] by the rule "oṣo vyaḥ" would be superseded, and *ūṭh* would apply to *va* by the rule "chvoḥ śūḍ. [Examples such as] *tortha*, *ortha*, etc., follow. The roots *thurvī*, *durvī*, and *dhurvī* mean "to injure. [The root] *murchā* [means "to faint"].
In the case of *mohasamucchrāya* (the act of fainting or rising from delusion): *momūrcchīṣi*, *momorṣi*, *momūrthaḥ*, *momūrtha*, *momūrcchīmi*, *momormi*, *momūrcchvaḥ*, *momūrmaḥ*;
[the perfect tense forms] *momūrcchāñcakāra*; [the periphrastic future] *momūrcchitā*; [the imperative] *momūrcchītu*, *momortu*.
*momūrtāt*, *momūrhi*, *amomūrcchīt*, *amomoḥ*, *amomūrcchata*, *momūrcchayāt*, *amomūrccchiṣṭām*, *amamomūrccchiṣyat*.
Thus ends the section on the formation of the *yaṅ-luk* (intensive without suffix) in the *Tattvabodhinī*.
